<meta>This page serves as the opening preface to Cristoforo Landino’s influential 1481 commentary on Dante Alighieri’s Divine Comedy. The previous page ended with shorthand notes and diagram references for the transition into the higher spheres of Paradise. Here, Landino begins his formal dedication and defense of the poet, establishing Dante’s work as a pinnacle of both knowledge and the Florentine language.</meta>

<meta>p mark at top right margin</meta>

# THE COMMENTARY OF CRISTOFORO LANDINO
# ON THE COMEDY OF DANTE ALIGHIERI THE POET

ALTHOUGH TO NO class of learned writers, most illustrious lords, is the human race not owed immortal thanks—considering especially that every vigilant study and every laborious lucubration <note>original: "lucubratione"; meaning intensive study or writing performed late at night by candlelight.</note> they have undertaken is to benefit themselves and their contemporaries, and to bring no small utility to all men who will follow—nonetheless, since there is an almost infinite abundance of those who have left memory of themselves in either the Greek or Latin tongues, it is fitting to compare and equal them to the Poet. He, certainly through the depth and variety of his doctrine <note>In this context, "doctrine" refers to the breadth of academic and spiritual knowledge.</note> and the sublimity of his style, can not only show us great things pertaining to our life and moral salvation, but by covering them under a marvelous veil <note>A reference to "allegory," where literal stories hide deeper spiritual truths.</note>, he adorns them so that, beyond an incomparable utility, such varied doctrine brings incredible delight to the soul and pleasure to the senses which a well-educated ear takes from such a poem. But of the praises of the poetic faculty we shall speak shortly. Meanwhile, having been persuaded since my early adolescence by very clear arguments, and being further moved by the authority of many most learned men who in various nations and languages have always preferred poets to other writers, I have consumed no small part of my age in the knowledge of them. Now, because I had recently interpreted and returned to Latin letters the allegorical sense of the Virgilian *Aeneid*, I judged it would not be useless to my fellow citizens, nor unpleasant, if with as much study and industry as I could muster, I similarly investigated the arcane and hidden—but altogether most divine—senses of the *Comedy* of the Florentine poet Dante Alighieri. And as I had expressed the Latin poet in the Latin tongue, so I would interpret the Tuscan poet in the Tuscan tongue.

This is an undertaking, without doubt, which because of the greatness and multiplicity of the matters, and especially because of its novelty, could bring the highest honor to any of the most learned men. But for me, who am adorned with neither doctrine nor eloquence, it has been most laborious and perhaps tainted by temerity <note>excessive boldness or rashness</note>. But the burning love for this species of Muses has made the weight less heavy, and as the trite proverb of the wise says: "Nothing is difficult to the mind." But perhaps there will be some who judge our counsel to have been either vain—if I do not lead what I proposed from the beginning to its proper end—or superfluous, given that many have commented on this poem. These others, by having been either contemporaries or close to the poet's time, seem to have been better able to understand his mind; and by having made a profession of theology, they might more easily interpret the profound senses hidden within him, which he treated divinely from the intimate secrets of that science, not without the astonishment of those who read. 

Two of his sons commented on our poet: Francesco and Piero. Benvenuto da Imola commented on him, and he did so in Latin. Iacopo of Bologna <note>referring to Iacopo della Lana</note> commented on him in his native tongue. Riccardo, the Carmelite friar and theologian, commented on him. Andrea—I believe a Neapolitan—commented on him, as did Guiniforte, a jurist from Bergamo. Our Boccaccio began to comment on him, but did not bring the work further than halfway through the first cantica <note>the *Inferno*</note>. All of whom I commend because they have said many things worthy of their doctrine and not useless to the listener. Finally, Francesco da Buti commented on him in the Pisan tongue. He, after Boccaccio, strove more than the others to open the allegorical sense, but not in all its parts. But it seemed to me necessary to repeat the mind and purpose of Dante from a higher principle, and with a steady gaze investigate in him a more recondite <note>hidden or obscure</note> doctrine, which when I revolve it in my mind, a sudden, horrendous wonder is born in me, and I become almost like a bat in such great light. And as those who live near the cataracts of the Nile become deaf from the excessive sound, so in me all sharpness and judgment of the intellect is lost, overcome by the material and the intention. To which I am not only unequal, but even after a long interval, I find myself barely fertile. 

Yet, with divine favor helping my fervent will, I have discovered in some part some of the barely searchable footprints of so divine a poet—following him first through the descending slopes into the deep abyss <note>the *Inferno*</note>, and then, drawn by his aid up to the arduous ridge of Purgatory, I have conducted myself along a difficult path, and finally, elevated by his wings, I have seen the end of so long a pilgrimage. In this, I will leave the judgment of how much profit and utility I have achieved to those more learned than I. This alone I affirm: I have liberated our citizen from the barbarism of many foreign idioms in which he had been corrupted by commentators. And at present, so pure and simple, it seemed my duty to present him to you, our most illustrious lords, so that through the hands of that magistrate which is supreme in the Florentine Republic, he might be restored to his homeland after a long exile; and recognized as neither Romagnol, nor Lombard, nor of the idioms of those who have commented on him, but purely Florentine. Of how much this language surpasses all other Italian tongues, let it be manifest testimony that no one in whom genius or doctrine appears ever wrote verses or prose without striving to use the Florentine idiom—but we shall speak more of the language in its place. You, therefore, our most illustrious lords, recognizing in this our volume the divinity of Dante’s genius—which anyone who reviews a numerous series and continuous succession of centuries and an ancient and very clear memory of all nations could count among the very few—recognizing also a stupendous heap of doctrine, so varied, so recondite, and so hidden that he who has known most has barely known a mediocre part, will congratulate your homeland to which the supreme God has granted such a gift. And you will frequently read your poet—the first splendor of our name, of eloquence, and of doctrine, and an excellent and rare example—because by imitating him, you will gain eloquence and dignity in speech, prudence and probity in life and customs, and doctrine and humanity in the mind.

# APOLOGY IN WHICH DANTE AND FLORENCE ARE DEFENDED FROM FALSE CALUMNIATORS

The order of things required that the life and customs of the poet be continued and joined to the proem <note>preface</note>. But a false opinion, long ingrained in the minds of many, constrains me to defer the life for a brief space and confute this error first, so that at one and the same time both my homeland and the poet may be liberated from a grave calumny by which both are undeservedly offended. Many read in various places of this Comedy very sharp invectives against the Florentines who ruled in those times, and very bitter reproaches for their various and most wicked vices. This not only seems to be a disgrace to the city, but also seems not to be without blame for the poet, as it obscures the adorned fame of his homeland, which he, as a dutiful or rather pious son, should praise. 

We, therefore, will first demonstrate that it is false that Dante vilifies his homeland. Then, by running through some examples of the things administered, we will prove that not only does our Republic not deserve blame, but on the contrary, it is necessary that by all those who are void of envy and do not lack judgment, it be placed most honorably among the first Republics. But let this be the starting principle: our poet was of such a generous soul that he would have been indignant to openly call himself a Florentine if he had judged it to be an infamous homeland. But he, in many places of the work, seems to glory in being Florentine. Therefore, he judges Florence a most noble city. But it is not necessary to search for conjectures of his opinion and of what...

<summary>In this preface, Cristoforo Landino dedicates his commentary to the Florentine Signoria, arguing that Dante is the supreme poet whose work contains profound allegorical truths. He seeks to "restore" Dante to Florence by stripping away foreign linguistic influences from previous commentaries and begins a defense against the claim that Dante’s criticisms of the city were unpatriotic.</summary>
<keywords>Cristoforo Landino, Dante Alighieri, Divine Comedy, Florence, Florentine idiom, allegory, Apologia, literary defense, Renaissance humanism, commentary traditions</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Cristoforo Landino’s defense of Dante Alighieri. On the previous page, he established Dante’s authority as a poet. Here, he specifically addresses the relationship between Dante and his home city of Florence, defending the poet against accusations that he hated his fatherland and transitioning into a broader praise of Florentine civic and intellectual life.</meta>

<page-num>9</page-num>
<sig>& H i</sig>

In many places he gives such praise. For in *Hell*, through the mouth of the magnanimous Farinata, he calls it noble; in *Paradise*, he desires greatly to return to it, calling it the "beautiful fold" <note>original: "bello ovile"; a reference to Dante's hope to return to Florence to receive the poetic laurel</note>. But a fold is a receptacle for the benign. Thus he praises the city; and he praises the people contained within it for both beauty and virtue, and in the canto where he says: *Florence within the old circle* <note>original: "Fiorenza dentro dalla cerchia antica"; referring to the ancient city walls</note>, from which she still takes the third and ninth hours, she remained in peace, "sober and modest" <note>original: "sobria & pudica"</note>. There is no greater praise for a republic than to live in peace. This cannot happen without supreme prudence and justice. And that she lived with these two virtues, which make for perfect temperance.

But let us read, I pray, this whole canto, and we shall understand how wonderfully the good poet excels in these verses: *To such a restful state. To so beautiful a life of citizens. To so faithful a citizenry.* <note>Landino is paraphrasing Dante’s *Paradiso* XV</note>. And in the sixteenth [canto] he writes: *With these people, and with others with them, I saw Florence in such great repose that she had no cause for tears. With these people I saw your people glorious and just, so much so that the lily was never placed backward on the staff... nor made crimson.* <note>A reference to the Florentine coat of arms, the lily, before it was changed by civil strife</note>.

What madness then can be given—or rather, what praise can be taken away from that people—who are just? For such a thing cannot exist without supreme continence; and let them be glorious, since glory cannot be born except from many, excellent, and long-lasting virtues. I leave behind many other places in which, with every kind of magnificent praise, he extols so great a city. 

But someone will perhaps say they have read places in which he vituperates <note>to criticize harshly</note> the Florentines. To which I respond: he does not vituperate the Florentines. He, as we have shown elsewhere, calls them sober and tranquil, he calls them glorious and just; for it would be a great levity in such a poet to write repugnant things and ones contrary to themselves. But he vituperates those Florentines who, through ambition and faction, had become unjust, rapacious, cruel, and greedy. In the same way, Sallust <note>Roman historian</note> vituperates Rome by vituperating the ambition and luxury of his times, and the perfidy of Catiline, or Lentulus, or the other conspirators. Or noting with supreme infamy Albius, Calpurnius, Scaurus, or many others. But by praising the ancient Roman discipline, he shows how much these men had degenerated from their progenitors. 

Dante, then, vituperates those wicked governors—or rather, robbers—of his people. And those who, in the place of true shepherds of the "beautiful fold," are in fact young men he affirms to be wolves. This we must concede to him, both because he narrates true things, and also because if he hurls a tragic invective against the worst citizens—or rather, impious tyrants—these are like a new Archilochus's <note>An ancient Greek poet famous for his stinging, satirical verses</note> iambic verses made in the form of pestiferous arrows. Nonetheless, in many places, he honorifically exalts many others worthy of true praise and adorns them with perpetual fame. Add also that, having been justly made an exile and rebel by them from his homeland, he deserves excuse if he somewhat exceeds the limit through just indignation. 

And this is enough in defense of the poet. Now, in praise of our republic, I will dare to affirm among the first things that she has never degenerated in form from her authors; that she has always shown herself to be a true colony of Roman citizens. For immediately around her beginnings—though these, as happens in all things, may have been meager—nonetheless she laid great foundations of justice and magnanimity. And afterwards, in following times, administered with the best institutions and laws, she first claimed her liberty. Later, loved for her supreme justice and held in great frankness of spirit in avenging injuries, she added many peoples to her empire without wrongdoing. 

But so that the many and most egregious virtues of our people may appear more clearly, let us remember that, by the judgment of philosophers, there are only two generations of life among those living according to reason. One is of those who, raising themselves in contemplation, are all given to the investigation of the most excellent disciplines and doctrines; and this is called the **contemplative life**, signified in the Mosaic doctrine by Rachel, and in the New Testament by Mary. The other is of men who, knowing themselves to have been produced not solely to benefit themselves but others as well, insofar as they extend their own strength, have taken up the care and government of the public. Loving the social and civil life, they live in company; which life is expressed by the Hebrews through the mystery of Leah <note>original: "Lya"</note> and by the first Christians through the active care of Martha <note>original: "Marcha"</note>. 

Who, then, will be so unjust a judge and estimator who, reviewing our ancient annals, would not confess that there have been innumerable excellent men in the Florentine people in both one and the other life? But because always, in every nation and in every century, there have been more civil men than contemplative ones, look back, I pray you, from the first cradles and from the origin of our city, and we shall see in every age how great has been the abundance of those who, through supreme prudence and sharpness of wit, have known how—and with greatness of soul and true liberty, have been able—and with ardent charity, have wanted—to well counsel and administer the republic. 

And because it is a Sallustian sentiment (but born from the intimate sanctuaries of Platonic discipline) that in civil administration it is necessary first to consult well, and after wise counsel, to execute what has already been determined with mature speed. I could speak of the obscurity of our annals; which, because they were written by men more truthful than eloquent, gain faith for their simplicity from those who read them. But by few are they read because of their rough style. Nonetheless, I could bring to light from their obscurity many who, in arduous and ambiguous cases, have imitated the prudence of Numa Pompilius, and of Fabius Maximus, and of the two Catos, of Sertorius, and many others. If these men had not been celebrated by writers, they would be submerged in the same darkness as our own. And certainly, I approve the opinion of those who judge that the Athenians did great things; but the abundance and eloquence of their writers are the reason why they appear much greater. Thus, I do not doubt to affirm that in our people, the style of those who wrote has been more lacking than the matter of those who acted. 

But let our oration return to where it began. Our ancestors did not lack prudence; but so that strength may also be known alongside prudence: what time was there ever in which they did not show invincible spirits and supreme confidence in adverse things? The city of Lacedaemon <note>Sparta</note> was universally held to be of frank spirit, as was Carthage; but we see both were surpassed by the Romans. And among the Romans, Julius Caesar had a spirit equal to such great felicity. The two Scipios were frank men, who, manfully opposing Hannibal in Spain, fell. From the same family were two Africani, and in the Aemilian house two Pauli. Without any fear, Marcellus ran to every great undertaking, as did that Gracchus who, with a slave army, conquered the invincible Hannibal. But the Florentine people have always had not just one Farinata, but many at different times. 

Nor does it seem to me necessary to investigate particular examples in this, for I intend to show that my entire republic at all times has had an invincible soul. And in every calamity, she has always risen more manfully and more boldly. Florentine liberty was miserably oppressed by Walter <note>Gualtieri di Brienne, the "Duke of Athens," who briefly seized power in Florence in 1342-43</note>, who with false titles wished to be named the Athenian Duke. To him, after many civil discords, the people granted a yearly dictatorship, as to a man esteemed by all to be a true friend; and certainly, that shifty and subtle prince showed no small signs of treachery and injustice. Thus, it was easy to persuade the credulous people that finally, through his authority, he had to settle every civil sedition and bring about true tranquility and firm peace. 

But, O true God, how many are the hiding places in human breasts! How hidden are the counsels! With how many simulations are good men deceived by fox-like minds! The wicked Walter, then, with the appearance of a clement shepherd, took the legitimate magistracy committed to his seat, but inside he was a most rapacious wolf. Every power given to him he converted into tyrannical cruelty; and with the favor of his own princes and of the army granted to him, he offended the people with those very arms they had granted him for their defense. And with supreme perfidy, he occupied the tyranny. 

But celestial help is not lacking to those who do not fail themselves, and in generous souls, a righteous purpose overcomes every difficulty. The grief for lost liberty appeared universal in all, and not light. But since there was no one ready to make himself duke and guide to all in such a small space of time, various men were chosen by various groups, and at the same time, many conspiracies—none of which knew anything of the others—armed themselves against the tyrant. Armed with impetus, they revealed themselves in such a way that, having killed not a few of his men, he was forced to seek his safety by fleeing. In this magnanimous recovery of liberty, I do not know which is more worthy of admiration: the greatness of soul in daring to assault one who was protected by a great abundance of arms and men, or the faith and silence in which all the conspirators constantly persevered. 

But hear this other thing. In the age of our fathers, through a wicked deed or the imprudence of the hired leaders of our armies, the rout of Zagonara <note>A battle in 1424 where Florence was defeated by the Milanese</note> was most unhappy, and no less calamitous to us than the slaughter at Cannae was to the Latins. The men-at-arms were lost. The horses were lost. The baggage was lost. And that which exceeded every loss: the captains were lost, who had been hired shortly before with innumerable money. Whereupon the enemy...

### CIVIL LAW.

It is strange to now put an end to doctrines. But I fear that the jurists would not accuse me of injustice. <meta>This page continues the introductory discourse by Cristoforo Landino on the merits of Dante Alighieri, transitioning from a defense of poetry in general to a specific celebration of Dante as a master of all sciences, culminating in a celebratory oration by the philosopher Marsilio Ficino.</meta>

...the hatred of Juno <note>original: "dio di lunoē," likely a transcription of "l'odio di Giunone"</note>. He does not recount the wounds of Mars, in which things we see Homer and Virgil toiled so much. But with the help of the immortal God, who with the depth of mind embraces the heaven, embraces the earth, and embraces the Tartarean <note>The underworld or hell in classical mythology</note> realm; and having already expressed from the center the eternal pains of the wicked to frighten men from sins, ascending through Purgatory with eagle-like wings, he flies to the supreme seats. These things, although they hide a supreme science beneath various veils, nevertheless in no place depart from true theology. And what theologian, with more order or with more manifest demonstrations, has been able to express to us mortals that which the mortal spirits contemplate up there in the most lucid fountain of nature? What physicist ever wrote with clearer reasons of all natural motions, whether according to place, or according to form, whether imperfect or perfect, whether animate or inanimate? What course of a star, what conjunction, what revolution of the sky was omitted by him? What transformation of one element into another? What alteration in the air—of hail, rain, winds, lightning, or other similar things? What composition of minerals created beneath the earth have the physicists demonstrated that this poet has not at least touched upon? The soul has four powers <note>The four faculties of the soul in Aristotelian/Scholastic philosophy: vegetative, sensitive, appetitive, and intellectual</note>, it has various offices and various properties, but of all these we have true knowledge through Dante. And who does not know with what true knowledge and grace he describes now the universal site of the earth, now some particular region within it? But what shall I say of that philosophy which Socrates first recalled from heaven to earth, and with the greatest utility to men introduced into republics, into private houses, and finally within the human breast? In what philosopher are there more apt and manifest arguments which lead us to the supreme good and true happiness, or rules and precepts which belong to good and blessed living? With what ardor, with what sharpness does he thunder against and vilify injustice, perfidy, incontinence, cruelty, pusillanimity, insolence, and all other vices! With how much praise and how many rewards does he invite us to virtue and persuade us to observe justice, to use temperance, to have a frank and constant mind, and for one's country, for parents, and for friends, not to refuse any small thing; to have religion toward God, supreme piety toward one's elders, and ardent charity toward all? For which thing it is truly concluded that his entire poem contains nothing other than the praise of virtue; and as the Greeks say of Homer, it can be affirmed that he is like the ocean. For just as all rivers are born from the ocean and return to the ocean, so all the sciences are drawn from him and redound in him. Add to this the knowledge of histories, and what a diligent investigator of antiquity he has been—not only of our own affairs, but also of the Greek, the Hebrew, and of all other nations. If he treated these things without any ornament of eloquence, we should nevertheless speak of them diligently for the great utility acquired from the knowledge of them. Now, there being such an incredible abundance of speech, adorned with such admirable gravity of sentiments, illustrated with such grace of style, and distinguished with such a variety of lights and colors: who will not add, if necessary, even nighttime vigils, seeing that in such reading the highest utility is joined with the highest delight? We, therefore, invoking divine help, shall set ourselves to plow so vast a sea, and we shall use, as far as our strengths suffice, the office of a faithful interpreter. Nor shall we only open the natural <note>The literal or "historical" sense</note> sense, but also the allegorical, tropological <note>The moral sense, teaching how to act</note>, and anagogical <note>The spiritual sense, relating to eternal glory</note>. These three senses, because they have much agreement among them, we shall call all "allegorical." May it please Him from whom every good proceeds to lift us as much as our Marsilio Ficino <note>Ficino (1433–1499) was a central figure of the Italian Renaissance and leader of the Platonic Academy in Florence</note> demonstrates in one of his letters, whose example—so that it may be a perpetual testimony of our mutual and immortal benevolence—we shall transcribe here below.

## OF MARSILIO FICINO THE FLORENTINE

->Florence, long sad but at last happy, congratulates her Dante Alighieri, now returning after two centuries, restored to his homeland and finally crowned.<-

You once prophesied, my Dante, while placed in exile, that there would be a time when piety, overcoming impiety, would happily restore you to your fatherland and crown you with the festive Apollinean wreath in the high temple of John the Baptist. Not in vain did your parents teach you this augury; for recently your father Apollo, having pitied my long weeping and your long exile, commanded Mercury to glide entirely into the pious mind of the divine seer Cristoforo Landino. And having put on the face of Landino, first with his nurturing wand he awakened you from sleep; then, lifted up by the rowing of wings, he brought you into the Florentine walls; and finally, he bound your temples with the Phoebian laurel. Today at last, the command of Phoebus <note>Apollo</note>, the pious work of Mercury and Landino, and the prophecy of Dante have been divinely fulfilled. You have come at last, O Dante, to the vow of Florence, with Minerva showing the way and Mercury as the guide. The illustrious band of all poets accompanies you. Finally, as you entered, the Graces happily received you. The Muses and the nymphs gave you embraces and kisses. You have come at last, and your hard journey has been overcome by piety, just as your parent expected. It is granted to see your face, my son, and to hear and return familiar voices. So indeed I was led in my mind, and I thought it would be, and my care did not deceive me. O, more beautiful and more blessed I receive you now, sweet son, than when you were wretched. That former mortal face of yours has changed into one immortal and divine. Florence is changed as night into day; all the sorrow of your Florentines is changed into joy. Rejoice all and exult, most happy citizens, for whom now wonderfully, instead of one sun, a twin sun arises—not with twin flames, but with twin rays. Today, the very heavens congratulate your happiness with uncorrupted grace. Look up, O citizens, look up at the sky for a moment. Behold now, behold, while our Dante here is crowned, the house of almighty Olympus is opened; the flames of the Empyrean heaven, seen by no others, shine clearly for us today, congratulating the crowned Dante. Therefore, how great, how new, how sweet do you think this sound is that now fills your ears? Truly it is the sound of the prophets and the nine Muses, heard in no other ages. Today it openly applauds the coronation of Dante. Hear the sweet songs of the Dominations from the globe of Phoebus. Hear again the wondrous hymns of the Archangels singing from the globe of Mercury himself: "Glory in the highest to supreme Apollo, glory to the Muses, glory to the Graces; peace, joy, happiness to the Florentines now rejoicing in the twin sun."

Florence, for a long time grieving but finally happy, greatly congratulates her poet Dante, resuscitated after two centuries and restored to his fatherland, and already gloriously crowned. O my Dante, in the time when you were placed in iniquitous exile, you predicted in your sacred poem that when piety should conquer cruelty—which kept you outside your fold—then you would return to your fatherland much more adorned than before, and in the high temple of the Baptist you would worthily take the poetic crown. This foresight of yours was not in vain, but because you predicted it from the highest paradise, you predicted it with truth. Since your father Apollo, moved to mercy by your long exile and my weeping, committed to Mercury in these times to fly quickly into the pious mind of the divine poet Cristoforo Landino, and transformed into the image of his face, to use the miraculous wand to restore you to life, and wings also to carry you back to your fatherland, and beyond this, the Apollinean leaves to crown you. Finally, on this day, the mandate of the supreme Phoebus is seen fulfilled; the pious work of Mercury transformed into man; your prophecy, O my divine Dante. The long desire of Florence: today piety, overcoming cruelty, has at last returned you to me, my most desired son. The goddess Minerva showed the way; Mercury has conducted him together with the most illustrious company of all the poets. Upon entering within these walls, the Graces joyfully placed their hands on you; the gracious nymphs also kissed your brow. O most chosen and most happy day, in which at present I receive my second sun, by whose splendor the night becomes day for me! O how much more beautiful and more blessed, my poet, you return to me by the grace of piety than when you departed by the fault of cruelty! You departed from me with a human face; you return truly with a divine face. Wherefore my ancient sorrow is already converted into supreme joy. Therefore, make feast and exult in joy, happy Florentine citizens! For you, in place of one sun, two suns already rise in duplicated rays, and not flames. Now, do you not see that today the heavens make feast for your happiness? Lift up your eyes, citizens, lift them high! Behold, while our Dante is crowned, the Empyrean heaven opens above us, and to show joy at such a coronation, it shows to our eyes its admirable splendor, never before seen in other times. Beyond this, do you not hear this suave sound, so sweet, so great, which likewise delights and fills our ears? This, without doubt, is the harmony of the nine spheres and Muses, never before heard, which makes feast for the crowned Dante. Hear also, hear the sweet songs and hymns of the Dominations and the Archangels, who from the sphere of the Sun and Mercury diffuse such a song toward us: "Glory in the highest to supreme Phoebus, glory to the Muses forever, and to the Graces. Finally, Peace, Joy, Happiness to the Florentines, already wonderfully adorned with two suns."

### SITE, FORM, AND MEASURE OF HELL AND STATURE OF THE GIGANTS AND OF LUCIFER

<summary>This page concludes Landino's argument for Dante's mastery over all fields of knowledge—from physics to theology—and presents a highly rhetorical, Neo-Platonic oration by Marsilio Ficino celebrating Dante's symbolic "return" and coronation in Florence.</summary>
<keywords>Dante Alighieri, Cristoforo Landino, Marsilio Ficino, Humanism, Florence, Apollo, Mercury, four senses of scripture, allegory, poetry, Renaissance philosophy</keywords>

--- Page 21 ---
<meta>This page continues the introductory section of Cristoforo Landino’s 1481 commentary on Dante Alighieri’s *Divine Comedy*. Having established Dante’s mastery of the sciences, Landino now turns to the specific architectural and mathematical genius of Dante’s vision of Hell, citing the calculations of the Florentine architect and mathematician Antonio di Tuccio Manetti.</meta>

...in every thing he is marvelous. Nevertheless, I cannot without supreme wonder consider his invention, devised by no other. Homer situated Hell; Euripides situated it on high. So did the Greeks. Furthermore, Virgil, Ovid, and Claudian, and others among the Latins. But what figure do they give it? What site do they provide by which, as if in a known thing and painted by an **Apelles** <note>A renowned painter of Ancient Greece, used here as a metaphor for perfect artistic representation</note>, they might guide the listener? For through his high fantasy, illustrated by a most subtle mind and by **mathematical discipline** <note>The study of geometry and proportions used to map the physical structure of the afterlife</note>, he presents it in such a way that it can be understood through determinate measurements. Having largely understood this through **Antonio di Tuccio Manetti** <note>A Florentine architect and mathematician (1423–1497) famous for his calculations of the dimensions of Dante’s Hell</note>—who, through long investigation, has (if I err not) precisely understood the general and particular layout of this poet's entire Hell—I judged it a most grateful thing to demonstrate how clearly this can be seen before we come to interpret the text.

Regarding this: many excellent mathematicians, but especially Dante in his *Convivio* <note>The Banquet, one of Dante's prose works</note>, place the earth as a sphere...

...45 and 5/11. Now, imagining that he has descended into Hell, it is certainly likely that, imitating Virgil, he places the same entrance; and this is near **Lake Avernus**, not far from Naples. Entering from here, and placing the void of Hell entirely as he does, one can understand that the center of this circle is on a line beneath **Jerusalem**, because in the final canto of the *Inferno* he says: *And if thou art now come beneath the hemisphere which is opposite to that which the great dry land covers, and beneath whose summit was consumed the Man who was born and lived without sin.* <note>Original: "Et se hor sobto lhemisperio giunto / Che e oppofito a quel che la gran secca Couerchia / & sobto el cui colmo consumpto / Fu lhuom che nacque & uixe sanza pecca." This refers to Christ being crucified in Jerusalem, which Dante places directly above the center of Hell.</note> The man who was born and lived without sin is Christ, who was consumed and died at Jerusalem. Therefore, because from Avernus (where the circumference is) to Jerusalem (where he places the center) is measured at **1,750 miles**, which is the **radius** <term>mezo diametro (half-diameter)</term>, his circumference will be **11,000 miles**. Dante enters through the aforementioned gate on the night between the 5th and 6th of April in the year of salvation 1300, at the meridian of Naples. He places the moon on its sixteenth day and in Libra; and on the previous night, in which he was lost in the woods, it had been the full moon. Hence, in the twenty-first canto: *And already yesterday evening the moon was round.* The sun was in Aries. Because of this, he writes in the first canto: *The sun was mounting up with those stars*—that is, with the stars of Aries—as you will understand in the commentary written upon that place. In his journey, which is always to the left, he always descends from circle to circle. This he demonstrates in many places, but especially where he says in the fourteenth: *And he to me: thou knowest that the place is round; and although thou hast come much, always descending to the left down to the bottom.* <note>Original: "Et egli ad me tu sai chelluogho e tōdo: Et tutto che tu sia uenuto molto Pure a sinistra giu calādo al fondo."</note> He descends, therefore, from cliff to cliff until **Geryon** <note>The monster representing Fraud who carries Dante and Virgil down into the lower circles</note>. But the distance and the circle are not always the same thing. Thus, the first distance is immediately upon entering the gate, where the wretched are who were never alive; but this is not named a "circle" by him. It is the first place and the first species of vice.

**H**ere also is the river **Acheron**. After this is the second station, but the **first circle**, and this is **Limbo**. Here are the moral people who lived without the Christian faith, and the innocent children who died without baptism. We shall therefore call this second distance the first circle, the second place; and here is the second species of souls, who are the moral pagans, and the third, who are the innocent children. The third distance is the **second circle**, the third place, and the fourth species of souls, which are the **Lustful**. The fourth distance is the **third circle**, the fourth place, and the fifth species of souls, which are the **Gluttonous** punished in the rain; hence he says, *I am in the third circle, of the rain.* The fifth distance is the **fourth circle**, and the fifth place of those who spend without measure; and here is the sixth species, who are the **Prodigal**, and the seventh, who are the **Avaricious**; and he says: *Thus we descended into the fourth ditch.* The sixth distance is the **fifth circle**, the sixth place, and the eighth species, who are the **Wrathful**, and the ninth, the **Sullen**. The seventh distance is the **sixth circle**, the Sepulchers, the seventh place, and the tenth species, the **Heresiarchs**. Within this same distance is the **seventh circle**, the eighth place, the first ring, and the eleventh species of sinners, who are the **Violent against their neighbors**. Item, within the ninth place is the second ring where the **Violent against themselves** are punished, being the twelfth species. Item, the tenth place and third ring: the thirteenth species of sinners, who are the **Violent against God, Nature, and Art**. These last three species are all on one level in the seventh circle, and it is the first "small circle" named by him. But each species has its own ring, of which there are three. Therefore, the seventh circle is the first small circle and contains three rings. Thus, until Geryon, we find seven distances, seven circles, ten places, and thirteen species of damned—excluding those behind the banner [the neutrals], the moral pagans, and the children in Limbo. The Lustful are moved by the wind; the Gluttonous in the rain; the Prodigal and Avaricious turn weights; the Wrathful and Sullen are in the Stygian marsh; the Heresiarchs are in the sepulchers; and the three species of the Violent: here is blood, here are thorns, here the parched sand. And that there are no more than seven circles is proven by these verses in the 17th canto: *Thus again by the extreme edge of that seventh circle, all alone, I went where the sad people sat.* Thus, there are seven descents.

Now it follows that in the third ring of the burning sand, he sees the small stream and describes the statue of the island of **Crete**. This denotes that in that place they were on a perpendicular line beneath Crete where he describes the statue, and they had not yet circled the entire circle. But to understand how much more they had to turn, we shall make on a **nautical chart** a straight line from Rome to Damietta in Egypt, and we shall find that it crosses through the island of Crete; in this way, we shall understand where Dante was beneath the earth. Then, crossing a straight line from **Cuma** (where he imagines the gate of Hell to be) to Jerusalem, and measuring with compasses up to a thousand miles, we will understand that little remains to finish the whole circle. Therefore, it is to be estimated that he had finished it all in that place where he mounts upon the shoulders of Geryon. And being very close to the number of a thousand miles, it is estimated that he has circled Hell with this thousand-fold number. Of what we have said regarding the statue, the words he says to **Ser Brunetto** are testimony: *Up there above in the serene life, I lost myself in a valley before my age was full. Only yesterday morning I turned my back on it.* He will have gone, therefore, to Geryon one thousand miles, measuring them upon the surface of the earth, and one thousand miles toward the center of the earth. Therefore, he has descended one thousand miles of the radius perpendicularly; and subtracting these from the radius of the earth, there remain **2,245 and 5/11 miles** perpendicularly to go until the center. Similarly, we shall make the measurement of the width of the top of Geryon’s pit, which is **1,346 miles**. The greatest width of Hell, measuring it on the surface of the earth, is **3,500 miles**—that is, from Cuma to Jerusalem—and as much more beyond that, Jerusalem being in the middle, as is shown in the last canto of the *Inferno* where it says: *And if thou art now come beneath the hemisphere which is opposite to that which the great dry land covers, and beneath whose summit was consumed the Man who was born and lived without sin.* In which verses he describes Jerusalem, as we shall say in its proper place. Therefore, the circumference of this greatest width on the surface of the earth is **11,000 miles**. It is likely that, having descended one thousand miles through ten places, he shows in seven circles that he went through the tenth part of each of those. Now, because from Geryon downward the manner of traveling toward the center changes—having already shown how wide the mouth of Geryon’s ravine is—it is manifest that the diameter is **1,346 miles**.

Dante descends upon the shoulders of Geryon downward in a perpendicular line until a width of diameter of **35 miles**. And here is joined the field of **Malebolge**. It remains to see the diameter of each ditch <term>bolga</term>, with which one can determine the circumference, in which the largest of those measures thirty-five miles. And the rule he gives us is the ditch of the penultimate one, where he says the valley is **twenty-two miles**...

But seeking the proportion, that which encloses should always be twice as much, as twenty-two is to eleven. Because the third would have forty-four, and proceeding thus, the tenth would be five thousand miles, according to thirty-two <note>The translator notes a likely calculation of diameter/circumference ratios used by the commentator</note> and the greater width of one thousand five hundred miles. So you see that toward the center there would be more width than on the surface. This is also consistent with the description of the heights that he provides above and their supports. But we shall say that it is always eleven miles more than the enclosed space: and thus all the ditches <term>bolge</term> <note>Malebolge, meaning "Evil Pouches" or "Ditches," is the eighth circle of Hell, consisting of ten concentric trenches</note> will equally have a distance of eleven miles, just as when many moats surround a castle with equal distances, where each moat is one and three-quarter miles wide with a diameter of thirty-five miles. And this is also easily understood in his narration where he does not show the ultimate distance, which is only half a mile in width, while the others are all one mile and three-quarters. And this corresponds with the greater width of Hell, which we set at three thousand five hundred and ten. Therefore, the first ditch is thirty miles <margin>First part</margin> of the Malebolge, and has a diameter of thirty-five miles and a circumference of one hundred and ten. Therefore the first ditch is thirty-one miles, which contains the panderers <note>ruffiani</note> and seducers. The second contains the adulators and flatterers and has a diameter of thirty-one and a half miles. The third, of the simoniacs, is twenty-eight. The fourth, of the diviners, is twenty-four and a half miles. The fifth, of the barrators <note>corrupt politicians</note>, is twenty-one miles. The sixth, of the hypocrites, is seventeen and a half miles. The seventh, of the thieves, is fourteen miles. The eighth, of the fraudulent counselors, is ten and a half miles. The ninth, of the sowers of discord <note>scismatici</note>, is seven miles. Therefore, the circumference of such a diameter will be twenty-two miles. Wherefore Virgil says:
> Consider if you can count them / for twenty-two miles the valley winds. <note>original: "Pensa se tu annumerar gli puoi / Che miglia ventidue la valle volge" – Inferno XXIX, 9</note>

The tenth and last of the Malebolge, where the falsifiers and alchemists are, has a diameter of three and a half. Wherefore he says, although it turns eleven miles, it is no less than half a mile across. And certainly, taking from its diameter two half-miles, which they occupy in the circle, there remains a void diameter of two and a half miles; and this last one has from one top of the bank to the other a distance of half a mile. Now the circles of Malebolge could, on a flat plane, enclose one another successively with equal space between each; and being thus, the ten valleys would be one and three-quarter miles wide from the top of one bank to the other. But the place is not on a plane, but on a slope descending toward the center. Wherefore he says in Canto XXIV:
> Because all of Malebolge slopes / toward the entrance of the lowest pit / the site of each valley carries / that one bank rises and the other descends. <note>original: "Ma perché Malebolge inver la porta / Del bassissimo pozzo tutte prende / Lo sito di ciascuna valle porta / Che l’una costa surge e l’altra scende" – Inferno XXIV, 37-40</note>

And elsewhere he shows the bottom and the steepness of these valleys, saying:
> Here he gently set down his burden / gently along the jagged and steep rock / which would be a difficult pass even for goats. <note>original: "Quivi soavemente spose el carcho / Soave per lo scoglio sconcio et erto / Che sarebbe alle capre duro varco" – Inferno XXXI, 140-142</note>

Therefore it is necessary that the valleys be wider, though only slightly when measured on a plane. Thus it seems to me that the half part of the half-diameter of the widest part of such a site—which comes to be the half of seventeen and a half miles—is the figure of the slope of this site; that is, the end of the Pit of Geryon is eight and three-quarter miles higher than the bank of the Pit of the Giants. From the end of the Pit of Geryon, which is the beginning of Malebolge as I have said, until the center of the earth is thirty-two and a half miles; and subtracting that which Malebolge slopes, which seems to me eight and three-quarter miles, there remain twenty-three and three-quarter miles. And this shall be sufficient to have said of the site of Hell. But likewise, to understand the immense stature of the giants, we will investigate in the verses of the poet several measurements written by him; and first we will note in Canto XXXI what he writes of Nimrod <note>Nebroth</note>:
> His face appeared to me as long and large / As the pine cone of Saint Peter’s in Rome / and in its proportion were all his other bones. <note>original: "La faccia sua mi parea lunga & grossa / Come la pina di san Piero a Roma / & a sua proportiõ tutte laltre ossa" – Inferno XXXI, 58-60. The "pine cone" refers to a famous 13-foot-tall Roman bronze sculpture</note>

According to these verses, the height of the head of this giant will be five and two-fifths Florentine cubits <term>braccia fiorentine</term> <note>A "braccio" was a standard unit of measurement in Florence, roughly 58 centimeters or 23 inches</note>; for we know that such is the size of the aforementioned bronze pine cone in Rome. Learned painters in symmetry say that a well-proportioned man is as long as eight of his heads; therefore, this giant would be forty-three cubits or more. This then will be the height of the giants according to the poet's position. It follows that by certain principles set down by him, we may likewise measure the greatness of Lucifer. But first we will note that after the circles and smaller circles and rounds of which we have spoken until now, there remain four spheres of bloody and frozen water, which have as their center the universal center; and in the one furthest from the center is founded the Pit of the Giants; and this is called Caina. Within this is enclosed the second, called Antenora. And in this the third, named Ptolomea; and by Ptolomea is enclosed the one called Giudecca, the smallest of all; of which we will narrate particularly in their place.
<margin>This contains within itself the universal center: and in the center.</margin>
This contains within itself the universal center; and in the center is Lucifer, who, placed in the ice, emerges from the middle of his chest upward. And of Lucifer, the poet writes:
> And I am more comparable to a giant / than giants are to his arms. <note>original: "Et più con un gygante io mi convegno / Che giganti non fan cholle sue braccia" – Inferno XXXIV, 30-31</note>

Dante says, therefore, that his body has more proportion to giants than the bodies of giants have to the arm of Lucifer. And because Dante was of medium stature, estimated at two cubits and seven-eighths, and we concluded above that giants, according to the measure of the face equal to the pine cone of Saint Peter, are forty-three cubits high. Therefore, Dante would fit fifteen times into a giant. Consequently, a giant would fit fifteen times into an arm of Lucifer. It follows that the arm of Lucifer is six hundred and forty-five Florentine cubits. And because we see a well-proportioned man to be the measure of three cubits, and the arm of such a man to be one and one-sixth cubits long, it follows according to such proportion that if the arm of Lucifer is six hundred and forty-five cubits, his body is not far from two thousand cubits. In fact, according to the measurement, it would be exactly one thousand nine hundred and eighty cubits. But because he showed that giants are barely comparable to his arm, we can set it at that number. The same is true if we look at the measure in palms, for every three palms is one cubit, and the measure of the wings, which are about two Florentine cubits. And this is as to the body. But the sphere of Giudecca, in which is the universal center, and from which Lucifer emerges from the middle up, seems to me to have a diameter of half the said two thousand cubits, which is one thousand cubits. Because from the middle of the chest to the top of the head is the measure of two heads; and just as much—that is, the measure of two other heads—should emerge from the top of the legs, since he has the middle of his body at the universal center, which is likewise the center of this sphere, as denoted in these verses:
> When we were at the point where the thigh / turns exactly upon the thick of the haunch / the Guide with labor and with anguish / turned his head to where he had his shanks / and grappled to the hair like a man who climbs / so that I thought we were returning to Hell again. <note>original: "Quando noi fumo là dove la coscia / Si volge apuncto in sul dosso dellanche / El duca cõ fatica & con angoscia / Volse la testa ovegli hauea le zanche..." – Inferno XXXIV, 76-81</note>

Thus, there would remain in the sphere the measure of four heads, which are half of the total of Lucifer. Therefore, the diameter of Giudecca will be one thousand cubits. And Ptolomea, which is contiguous to this, will be, I believe, the size of the whole body of Lucifer, which is two thousand cubits. And then Antenora, which encloses this, three thousand cubits; and Caina, which is the largest, will be four thousand cubits. And if you ask what conjecture leads me to this opinion, I answer because in the circles of the rounds and in the ditches of Malebolge, this same rule is seen. Nor have I anything else that can contribute to the location of Hell and the stature of the giants and of Lucifer. Therefore, we will remain in this opinion until another of greater judgment comes and shows us better the description of Dante, which we follow in this. His exit from Hell is quite clear because of a long small stream that ends in the tomb of Lucifer, and on the surface of the earth in the other hemisphere, and on the island where the mountain of Purgatory is, where he writes thus:
> There is a place down there as far from Beelzebub / as the tomb extends, which is known / not by sight but by the sound of a rivulet / that descends here through the hollow of a rock / which it has worn with its winding course / and it slopes a little. My Guide and I entered by that hidden way / to return to the bright world / and without caring for any rest / he climbed up first and I second / until I saw the beautiful things / that the heaven carries, through a round opening / and from there we came out to see the stars again. <note>original: "luogo è laggiù da Belzabù remoto..." – Inferno XXXIV, 127-139</note>
And that the exit facing this is Cato, he demonstrates in the first canto of Purgatory with these words:
> Who are you, who against the blind stream / have fled the eternal prison? <note>original: "Chi sete voi che contro al cieco fiume / Fuggito hauete la prigione etherna" – Purgatorio I, 40-41</note>
he said, moving those venerable plumes. The End.

->CANTO FIRST.<-

a ii

# CANTO ONE OF THE FIRST CANTICLE, OR RATHER COMEDY, OF THE DIVINE FLORENTINE POET DANTE ALIGHIERI: CHAPTER ONE.

<image-desc>A large, ornate historiated initial 'N' begins the poem. The letter is decorated with white-vine (bianchi girari) scrollwork on a field of red and blue, framed in gold. Within the negative spaces of the initial and its square border, the words of the first line are printed in block capitals: "NEL MEZO DEL CAMIN DI NOSTRA VITA".</image-desc>

MIDWAY UPON THE JOURNEY OF OUR LIFE
I found myself within a dark forest
for the direct path had been lost
And ah, how hard a thing it is to tell
what this forest was, wild, rough, and harsh
which in thought renews the fear
So bitter it was that death is little more
but to treat of the good that I found there
I will tell of the other things I perceived
I cannot well repeat how I entered there
so full of sleep was I at that moment
that I abandoned the true way
But after I had reached the foot of a hill
there where that valley ended
which had pierced my heart with fear
I looked on high and saw its shoulders
clothed already in the rays of the planet <note>The "planet" refers to the Sun, which in medieval astronomy was considered a planet that moved around the Earth.</note>
that leads others straight by every path
Then the fear was somewhat quieted
which in the lake of my heart had endured
the night that I passed with such pity

<column-break/>

**W**e have narrated not only the life and the title of the book, and what a poet is, but also how ancient and venerable, how noble and varied, and how useful and pleasant such learning is. How effective it is at moving human minds, and how much it delights every noble spirit. Nor did we judge it right to remain silent about how excellent the genius of our poet was in such divine discipline. In this, if I have been briefer than perhaps was appropriate, let the reader consider that the numerous and almost infinite abundance of things which must be treated forces me—not wishing the volume to grow excessively—to compress and entwine rather than explain and extend many matters, especially those which, even if I were silent, would not leave the exposition of the text obscure. We shall come, therefore, to that exposition.

But because I estimate that there is no reader of such low wit or little judgment who, having understood the depth and variety of the learning and the excellence and divinity of the genius of our Tuscan and Florentine poet, is not persuaded that this beginning of the first canto must, in its sublimity and grandeur, be equal to the stupendous learning of the things that follow: therefore, with all industry, I will investigate what <term>allegorical sense</term> <note>The deeper symbolic or spiritual meaning behind the literal words.</note> this "midway of the journey" brings with it, and what "forest" might be. Regarding this, I see that there has been no small difference among the interpreters and expositors of this canticle.

For some say that the "midway of human life" is sleep. They are moved, I believe, by the opinion of Aristotle <note>original: "Aristotile"</note> where he says in his *Ethics* that there is no difference between the happy and the wretched in the half of life, because the nights, which are half of the time, induce sleep, and from that it follows that we can feel neither good nor evil. Therefore, these people want the poet to put "midway of life" for the night, and night for sleep, to note that this poem is nothing other than a vision that appeared to him while sleeping, through which he had knowledge of the things described by him in these three comedies. They say, then, that he imitates John the Evangelist, who, sleeping upon the breast of Christ the Redeemer, had a vision of celestial things; or indeed, he sets the scene at night to demonstrate that he began his poem at night, when the soul, gathering itself into itself and absolving and freeing itself from every care, understands better.

But although such an opinion might suit the poet, nevertheless the words do not demonstrate it except with such obscure ambiguity that it does not seem worthy of the elegance of such a poet. First, because it does not follow that although in the revolutions of time the nights occupy as much space as the days, for this reason by saying "I wrote at the midpoint of my age," it should be understood "I wrote in the night." This is because sleep and nights occur in the beginning and the end of human age just as in the middle. Therefore, by the same logic, one could make such an interpretation for the day as for the night.

Others say that he wished by "midway of the journey" to mean that he gave a beginning to his poem in the middle of his age. But there is not one single opinion regarding the limit of our age, because different writers feel differently. Aristotle, in his *Politics* <note>original: "de republica"</note>, seems to approve the opinion of certain poets who divided age by the <term>septenary number</term> <note>Groups of seven years.</note>: attributing the first seven to infancy, the second to childhood, the third—reaching twenty-one—to adolescence. Then they place two septenaries for youth, reaching thirty-five; and Aristotle wants this same point to be the perfect age to celebrate marriages. After youth follows the <term>virile age</term> <note>Maturity or adulthood.</note>, which through two septenaries reaches the forty-ninth year; at which time, because men are of perfect counsel and have not yet diminished their bodily strength, that great philosopher judges that man is very fit for the government of the Republic. And finally, he places the rest of age in three septenaries. And he wants the limit to be seventy years, as if prophetic of his own death, which was in the seventieth year of his life. And he was moved to this especially because the septenary number is made not only of seven, but is also multiplied by ten, a perfect number. This same opinion is held by the Psalmist, saying:

->Our years shall be considered as a spider’s web: the days of our years in themselves are seventy years. But if among the strong they are eighty years: and more of them is labor and sorrow.<-
<note>original Latin: "Anni nostri sicut aranea meditabunt: dies annorũ nostrorũ in ipsis septuaginta anni. Si autem in potentatibus octuaginta anni: & amplius eorũ labor & dolor." This is a reference to Psalm 90:10.</note>

Pythagoras of Samos placed the end of age at the eightieth year of life, and similarly at that time he died; Solon of Athens also set eighty years. The astrologers, who refer everything to the course of the stars, grant us ninety-five. These wish that the Moon contributes four; Mercury, ten; Venus, eight; the Sun, nineteen; Mars, fifteen; Jupiter, twelve. Then, in the rest of the "decrepit" age, Saturn rules; and in this there is coldness, toil, anguish, and heaviness of body and mind. Therefore, there are few who reach it. There were some who, as Servius refers in the fourth book of the *Aeneid*, said there were three types of limits to our life: of nature, of fate, and of chance. They want nature to extend until the fourth course of Saturn; which, because he makes his revolution in thirty years...

<meta>This page continues the commentary by Cristoforo Landino on the first Canto of Dante's Inferno, transitioning from the introductory biography of the poet to a philosophical and allegorical explanation of the poem's opening lines.</meta>

->**INFERNO.**<-

...will reach one hundred and twenty years: fate completes three cycles of Saturn <note>In traditional astrology, Saturn takes roughly 30 years to complete one orbit; three cycles equal 90 years, considered a natural limit of life.</note>. Because of this, death comes in the ninetieth year. But if the favor of some fortunate star breaks the malignancy of Saturn, a man can reach the fourth cycle mentioned above. Wherefore Josephus, in his *Antiquities of the Jews*, writes that God, after Noah’s flood, shortened the years of human life—which before the flood had in some cases passed nine hundred—and established that the final limit should be one hundred and twenty. For this reason, certain interpreters of the poet Statius believe that when he writes of King Adrastus, "There King Adrastus, verging on old age, held his people in a peaceful middle boundary of life," <note>original Latin: "Rex ibi tranquille medio de limite iuitae. In senium uergens populos Adrastus habebat."</note> he intends it to mean he was in his sixtieth year, which is the middle of one hundred and twenty. Nevertheless, because the common opinion of men follows Aristotle and David <note>Referring to Psalm 90:10, "The days of our years are threescore years and ten."</note>, they understand the middle of life to be thirty-five years. Although such an exposition is not entirely discordant with the truth, it seems that for so high a poem, another principle is required.

To better express this, we will briefly repeat some things from further back, which will open the author's mind to us in such a way that it will be easy to interpret this beginning. It is likely, then, that Dante proposed for himself the same goal that Homer among the Greeks and Virgil among the Latins had proposed. Just as those poets—one through Ulysses, the other through Aeneas—demonstrate how one arrives at the knowledge of vices and, having known them, purges oneself of them to finally reach the contemplation of divine things; so Dante, under this fiction of a pilgrimage he feigns to have made with Virgil, demonstrates that same journey in his own person.

Man is composed of soul and body. The soul is divine, simple, immortal, and incorruptible. Because it is produced by God in His image and likeness, it is divine and full of light, and is capable through contemplation of reaching the knowledge of divine things and enjoying God. In this consists our highest good, as we shall treat more fully in another place. The body, on the contrary, being composed of the matter of the four elements, is by its nature corruptible, dark, and full of shadows. The soul, therefore, submerged in this dark prison, loses almost all its celestial vigor; and through the shadows of the body, it remains almost deprived of every light of reason. One could say it is buried beneath the corporeal mass.

Wherefore the divine Plato wisely posits two types of death. One he calls "animal death," a thing known to all, which occurs when the soul separates from the body. The other is the "death of the soul," and this occurs when the soul—submerged, as we have said, by the weight and darkness of the body—loses so much vigor that it can use none of its excellent powers. Because of this, we see that man lives solely according to the senses, not only in the first infant and childhood years, but in a large part of adolescence and youth. And because he knows nothing else, he does not believe himself to be anything else, and considers nothing good except those things that delight the corporeal senses, nor anything evil except that which grieves them. Like a drunkard oppressed by deep sleep, he neither knows himself, nor understands for what end he was produced, nor knows his own ignorance or misery until he reaches a mature age. Then, partly through the experience of many things and partly through acquired learning and precepts from the wise who have gone before, reason begins to awaken. Finally, he recognizes that he is in a **DARK FOREST**—that is, that his soul is oppressed by ignorance and vice through the contagion of the body.

This, then, is the meaning of the text: **I FOUND MYSELF WITHIN A DARK FOREST.** This signifies: "I realized my soul was submerged in the body, through the contagion and shadows of which I had lost the direct and true way." **MIDWAY UPON THE JOURNEY OF OUR LIFE:** that is, in the middle of the course of human life, at which time discretion begins to awaken in man, which until that point had been almost extinguished. Once awake, he notices his error and takes the path of salvation—unless he allows himself to be so overcome by sensuality that he does not proceed forward, but rather returns backward into the darkness of the forest. From this misery, David prays to the Lord to guard him, saying: "O Lord, do not call me back in the middle of my days." It is not necessary to interpret "middle" as the exact point that is equidistant from its extremes—as one might say nine is the middle of seventeen because it has eight on each side. The "middle" should not be interpreted so strictly, because even among philosophers, the "middle" is often said to be that which is distant from the extremes, even if it is not equally distant.

**OF THE JOURNEY.** This is excellently put, for our life is not set in eternity where everything is stable and in eternal rest, but in time, which is nothing other than a continuous flux and course. Furthermore, as the Apostle says, we are not here in our fatherland, nor do we have a permanent city. Rather, this life is a pilgrimage which, if we proceed by a certain path, leads us to the celestial Jerusalem, the fatherland where we are holy citizens and members of God’s household. Nor should we overlook in the explanation of this passage that he said "I found myself" and not "I entered." For the soul enters the body as soon as it is created, but it does not notice its own ignorance except in the "middle of the journey," as we have said.

Nor is it without cause that he placed the forest in the body, and consequently in vice; for both Plato and many other philosophers call corporeal matter <term>hyle</term> in Greek, which in Latin is translated as <term>selva</term> <note>meaning "forest" or "wood"</note>. Just as the soul has every excellence and happiness through its indivisible, incorporeal, and incorruptible nature, so on the contrary it has every calamity and every vice through the "forest"—that is, through the body which is corruptible. Wherefore Plato rightly calls God the cause and fountain of all goods, and conversely calls the forest—that is, our earthly prison—the cause of all evils. Thus Boethius wisely writes: "Happy is he who could break the heavy bonds of earth." <note>original Latin: "Felix qui potuit grauis terre rumpere uicula."</note> And certainly, blessed is he who can break the ties of the heavy earth, loosen the soul from the contagion of the body and sensuality, and lift himself to celestial things.

For this reason, the Greeks call the body <term>demas</term> because <term>dein</term> means "to bind," and the body, as stated, is the bond of the soul. Certainly, just as a fly attracted by the sweetness of honey plunges in so far that it drowns, so the soul, ensnared and entangled by earthly sweetnesses, from the beginning submerges and plunges so deep into their pleasantness that, having become entirely drunk, it wakes with difficulty; nor can it taste the nourishment of true joy, which is the contemplation of celestial things. Thence it arises that although our soul is produced for this contemplation, nevertheless the forest makes it lose the way, because the contagion of the body takes away its knowledge. If the soul possessed this knowledge, it would understand how much our nature exceeds that of other animals. For those animals feel nothing except the pleasures of the body, and toward those they direct themselves with every impulse. But the human mind is nourished by learning and is always investigating through thought, or is truly engaged in some action.

He posits the "forest," therefore, for the contagion of the body and for shadows and ignorance, imitating his master Virgil, who said: "Forests hold all the middle parts." <note>original Latin: "tenent media omnia sylvae."</note> **STRAYED:** and not "lost," because someone who has already wandered into vices, whenever they return to virtue, had not "lost" but "strayed" from the path. **AND AH, HOW HARD A THING IT IS TO TELL.** Here is a rhetorical ornament called an exclamation. It is used when we want to demonstrate the greatness of a thing, or when we want to express a just indignation against something that seems highly blameworthy, as when one says: "Ah, Constantine, of how much evil were you the mother!" And therefore he used this word, "ah," which the Latins call an <term>interjection</term>. Thus, "ah how hard a thing"—that is, how difficult it was to tell—that is, to narrate—what quality this **WILD FOREST** had. That is, this forest was derelict, abandoned, and remote from all cultivation and human habitation. For vice is entirely remote from human nature, since with effective demonstrations, both Platonic and Aristotelian philosophers prove that to live according to nature is to live according to virtue. Therefore it is "wild," as if to say it is bestial and not human; for he who is infected by vices, although he retains the human likeness, has nevertheless in his habits become a most cruel beast against God, against himself, and against his neighbor. **HARSH:** certainly the forest of vices is harsh, for just as nothing is sweeter than having a pure conscience—which keeps the soul tranquil, joyful, and without any fear—so the...
