<meta>This page continues Cristoforo Landino’s commentary on the opening of Dante’s Inferno. Having discussed the timing of Dante's vision (the "midway point" of life), Landino now moves into a deep philosophical and allegorical analysis of the dark forest, the nature of vice, and the soul’s struggle toward virtue and reason.</meta>

->**.INFERNO.**<-

<margin>19</margin>
<note>The handwritten "19" in the margin likely refers to a later archival page numbering.</note>

*a iii*

Vice continually goads us with constant fears—either of the future eternal punishments ordained for the soul of the sinner, or of the present punishments with which civil and moral laws threaten us. The flaming caverns of Etna or **Mongibello** <note>Mongibello is the local Sicilian name for Mount Etna, derived from the Arabic 'Jabal' and Latin 'Mons', both meaning mountain.</note> do not heave or boil as much as the conscience of the sinner. **HARD**: because the habit already contracted in vice is difficult and almost impregnable. **WHICH IN MY HEART RENEWS THE FEAR**: And certainly, just as we remember laudable deeds with a certain pleasure and supreme satisfaction of conscience, so on the contrary, when we have reduced ourselves from vice to virtue, we remember our past and vicious life with horror and supreme repentance. For this reason, **Plato** warned his friends to remember that bodily pleasures were momentary and brief, and left nothing behind them but regret. **IT IS SO BITTER that death is little more**. **BUT TO TREAT OF THE GOOD THAT I FOUND THERE, I will tell of the other things I perceived**. There is death, as we said a little before, of the animal, and there is death of the soul. And death of the soul is also understood in two ways: either according to the **Platonists**, when the soul, entering the body, is submerged and suffocated by it and loses almost all its vigor; or when the soul separates from the body and remains dead in sin. It is this latter type he intends at present, because it is the most horrendous, seeing as it has no redemption and such death is eternal and perceptible to the senses. Therefore, the soul is dead not because it does not remain immortal and endure forever, but because it is placed in supreme misery for eternity. Thus, we will say that the forest is bitter because such is the vicious life of a man still living in the body. But because he has redemption and can convert to God and perform good, it follows that the death mentioned just above is "more bitter" because it is beyond all hope. **BUT TO TREAT OF THE GOOD THAT I FOUND THERE**. And certainly, it is no small good to recognize the darkness of the forest—that is, the vice which deprives the soul of all light. For once known, it becomes so abominable that we flee and purge ourselves of it with all industry. Thus, we find this good in the forest. For this reason, **Horace** wisely said: *Virtue is to flee vice, and the first wisdom is to have been free of folly.* <note>original Latin: "Virtus est vitium fugere: et sapientia prima stultitia caruisse"</note> Some say that the poet wants to demonstrate that even in Hell good is found, because there is justice there, which is the highest of the moral virtues. Although this is true, nevertheless the first interpretation fits the text better. **I CANNOT WELL REPEAT HOW I ENTERED IT, so full was I of sleep**: This declares what we said above regarding the forest and the entry of the soul into the body, and then of all that time when reason is dormant and nothing but the senses can act within us. A man, therefore, cannot say how or in what manner he enters the forest—that is, how the soul enters the body where it contracts many vices—because at that point he is **full of sleep**; that is, he becomes so intoxicated by the <term>corporeal mass</term> <note>The physical weight and sensory distractions of the human body that "drown out" the soul's divine reason.</note> that reason falls asleep within him and does not wake until the "midway point of the journey." And so it follows: **SO FULL WAS I OF SLEEP at that point**: That is, the soul was so lulled by the drunkenness of the senses that reason, thus asleep, left the straight way—that is, the path of the virtues, which cannot be seen by one who walks in darkness. And moral virtue, as every philosopher confesses, is a "middle" established between two extremes. As an example, there is a virtue regarding the distribution and spending of our money, which observes a moderate middle ground between the "too little" and the "too much," and it is called **liberality**. This has two extremes: the defect called **avarice**, because it falls short and does not reach the middle; and the excess called **prodigality**, which is not restrained within the boundaries of the middle but exceeds and passes them. Therefore, just as if you draw a line through the middle of a wide and spacious field, it must be straight, and all others bending to any side will be crooked, even if they were innumerable; so too virtue alone is "straight" because it always proceeds at an equal distance from the extremes. And all vices are "crooked" because they twist toward one extreme or another. Similarly, just as in that field it is impossible to find the middle line in the dark and continue in it without twisting, so without the light of reason it is impossible in human life to find the middle ground of virtue and persevere in it without straying into some extreme where the vices are. For this reason, walking in the dark, one does not find the middle line, which is only one—or if it is found by chance, it is not maintained. But of the others, which are many, it is easy to find them without any light, and easy also to decline from one into another, always erring. Therefore, the Greek poet **Hesiod** wisely said that vice could be taken all at once <note>referring to the ease and broadness of the path to vice</note>, but God did not want one to come to virtue without sweat. And **Arcesilaus**, the Academic philosopher, said that the way leading to hell is easy because one goes there with eyes closed—that is, without the light of reason—because every sin proceeds from ignorance, which is nothing other than the privation of reason. For this reason, **David**, speaking of the works and actions of the sinner, said: *Let their ways be dark.* <note>original Latin: "Fiant viae illorum tenebrae" (Psalm 35:6)</note> And certainly, the ways of the sinner are darkness, because in them he does not discern the truth. I believe I have shown quite aptly why the poet calls the way of virtue "straight" and why sleep makes one lose it. Therefore, let us proceed. **BUT AFTER I HAD REACHED THE FOOT OF A HILL, there where that valley ended**: Let us first understand according to the historical sense that, walking through the forested valley, he encountered a mountain in such a way that it was necessary either to twist the path, wishing to avoid the climb of the hill, or to ascend the hill, desiring the path to be straight. One does not come to the virtues except by the ascent of the mountain. For this reason, **Basil** said: *Rough at first and nearly impassable, and full of continuous sweat and labor is the way that leads to virtue. Wherefore it is not for just anyone to undertake it because of that steepness, nor for the one undertaking it to easily ascend to its summit.* <note>original Latin: "Aspera principio et paene invia et sudoris continui et laborum plena est via quae ad virtutem ducit..." quoting Basil of Caesarea's "Address to Young Men on Greek Literature."</note> The mountain, then, is **contemplation**, and at the summit is the **sun**—that is, wisdom. And just as **Virgil** places the golden bough, which is wisdom, on the heights of a tree surrounded by valleys; so Dante places the sun at the summit of the mountain. Virgil places the doves, representing contemplation, as guides for **Aeneas** to the golden bough because they fly high, and elsewhere says: *Therefore search on high with your eyes.* <note>original Latin: "Ergo alte vestiga oculis" (Aeneid VI)</note> Thus, by the tree and the doves and by this verse, he demonstrates the height that Dante demonstrates by the mountain. While he looked into the valley, he saw nothing but darkness, because in earthly things one does not see the sun—that is, wisdom. But it is seen on the mountain—that is, in the elevation of the soul to divine things. Whence David: *I lifted up my eyes to the mountains.* <note>original Latin: "Levavi oculos meos in montes" (Psalm 121:1)</note> Under this figure, we will understand the same thing that **Pythagoras**, the Samian philosopher, expressed through the letter **Y**, which he discovered. This letter has a single line at the beginning until it reaches the point of the fork. There it divides into two, and one goes straight up on the right, the other twists to the left. This represents all of human life: for there is almost a single life for all men until the years of discretion, because nothing done in the first age is imputed to either perfect virtue or complete vice, where ignorance is excusable without true choice. Therefore, here the poet by the way of the forest meant the first part of the aforementioned letter. Then at the end of the valley, he found that the way which had been one until then divided into two: one followed straight up the steepness of the hill, the other twisted to the left at the foot of its base. Having reached this crossroads, just as until now he had gone in darkness, so then he began to see the light of the sun, which was already striking the shoulders of the mountain, and having seen it, he straightened himself toward it. For when we reach the years of discretion, the light of reason begins to shine in us, showing us the mountain already resplendent and inviting us to climb it. This signifies that reason directs us to contemplation and the knowledge of divine things, in which our supreme good consists. God created in His image and likeness not our body, but our soul. Therefore, there is innate in the soul a supreme and <term>seraphic</term> <note>Referring to the Seraphim, the highest order of angels, associated with burning love and light.</note> love to join ourselves with Him. And through such love, reason is awakened—which until this time had been drunk and sleepy—and having fallen in love, it deserves to be illustrated by <term>cherubic</term> <note>Referring to the Cherubim, the order of angels associated with divine wisdom and knowledge.</note> light, with which it sees and knows God as much as its nature is capable. He placed the mountain for...

<summary>Landino provides an allegorical commentary on Dante's "dark forest," equating it with vice and the "sleep" of reason. He explores the concept of virtue as a middle path and the hill as the beginning of spiritual contemplation and divine wisdom.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Cristoforo Landino’s commentary on Canto I of Dante’s Inferno. Landino is currently explaining the allegorical significance of the mountain (Contemplation) and the sun (Reason), as well as the physiological and moral state of the narrator as he attempts to escape the "dark forest" of vice.</meta>

# INFERNO

...this contemplation. Two things are noted about the Mountain: it is elevated and closer to heaven. This admonishes us that all our inquiry and research should be concerning high and celestial things, and not the lowest and earthly ones. Likewise, it is steep because one does not arrive at such contemplation without difficulty. Nor has this poet alone used the mountain to represent such contemplation; many writers of sacred letters also place it in a similar figure, especially the poetic prophet David in the psalm where he says: <note>original Latin: "Quis ascendet in monte domini aut quis stabit in loco sancto eius."</note> "Who shall ascend the mountain of the Lord, or truly, who shall stand in his holy place?" He asks nothing else but who shall arrive at this knowledge. He ascended the mountain with the aid of the sun, which showed it to him; for without the sun—that is, without **Reason**, which is the true guide of human virtue and the queen of our aid—one cannot perceive the path that leads us to contemplation. This sun is that which conducts us to salvation through every path, which is to say, every way. For none of our actions can be perfect if reason does not show it to us and judge it to be so. Nor can a person in any way operate in the **active life** or investigate in the **contemplative life** in a form that achieves the proper end, except through reason. We shall treat this more distinctly when the occasion arises. Nor is it a new thing for him to place the sun for reason, as it is also found among sacred writers: <note>original Latin: "ne occidat sol super iracundiam vestram."</note> "let not the sun go down upon your wrath."

**THEN** the fear was somewhat quieted: excellently put, because when reason begins to shine within us to show us the mountain—that is, the road that goes to the end of salvation—fear does not cease entirely. For although we have seen the way, we are not yet upon it. Nonetheless, the mind is somewhat appeased, and fear diminishes, because hope of being able to arrive at the end is born in us, seeing now the true way.

**WHICH IN THE LAKE** of my heart had endured: The human heart has three ventricles. In the middle one, nourishment reaches its perfection. And of the two extremes, one is the receptacle of the blood, which it draws from the liver; the other is the receptacle of the spirit, drawn from the lungs. In the heart is the principle of life. And because the spirit—which, like a craftsman, forms the limbs—would perish as soon as it is created if it did not have a certain seat in which it could receive the increase of its essence and generation, the heart is created in the body of the animal before any other member as the seat of the spirit. All principal heat and virtue come from the heart; hence, according to the quality and quantity of the heart, greatness of soul is born, and likewise timidity. We have disputed this more prolixly in our second dialogue *On the Soul*, written in the Latin language. And for this reason, the poet said "in the lake of the heart." Note that this fear lasted a great while, from the time he noticed he was off the true path until the sun gave him hope of being able to return to it.

**THE NIGHT:** That is, all the past age which, deprived of the light of reason and obscured by ignorance, is deservedly called "night."

**ANGUISH [PIETA]:** Lamentation. It is first to be noted that in the Florentine language, one finds *pietà* with a grave accent on the last syllable, meaning "compassion" <note>In modern Italian, *pietà* means pity or mercy.</note>; as below, "Here pity lives when it is well dead." <note>A reference to Inferno XX, 28, where Dante plays on the double meaning of *pietà* as pity and piety.</note> Likewise, *pieta* with an acute accent on the penultimate syllable means "lamentation" apt to move one to compassion, and it is in this sense the poet uses it here. Nor is it without reason that he says **THE NIGHT** I passed with such anguish: because he wants to demonstrate that when he realized he had lost the way, he grieved for it. And by this, we understand that although he was in vice, he had not yet made a firm habit of it; therefore, he could more easily extricate himself from it. He was, then, not **intemperate**, but **incontinent**. 

So that this may be more clearly understood, let us say there is a virtue called **temperance**; in which one who has formed a habit is restrained and abstains from every pleasure and vicious, dishonest lust, such that no difficulty hinders him, nor is abstaining troublesome to him. Likewise, one who has formed a habit in the vice of **intemperance** gives himself entirely to a lascivious and voluptuous life, and to every lust without any hindrance of shame or remorse of conscience. And for this, we say that the former is true virtue and the latter, intemperance, is true vice, because in each there is a "habit," without which there can be neither virtue nor vice. But before a man contracts such habits of temperance or intemperance, we have two dispositions through which we slip into the habit. One leads us to virtue and is called **continence**. For the continent person wants to abstain from a lascivious life, but he does not restrain himself without great effort because he has not yet formed the habit of temperance. But persevering in this continence through long practice, he forms a habit and thereafter restrains himself without difficulty; he is no longer "continent," but "temperate." The other leads us to vice. For the **incontinent** person also would prefer not to fall into vice and fights against lust just as the continent person fought; but he does not conquer it as the continent person does, but lets himself be conquered. And after many times, he forms a habit in lust and no longer fights, but willingly follows it and becomes intemperate. 

Therefore, following the fiction of Virgil, **Dido** in the beginning when she saw Aeneas was temperate, and willingly and without effort abstained from all lasciviousness. Hence he says: <note>original Latin: "Tum breviter Dido vultu demissa profatur"</note> "Then briefly Dido, with eyes downcast, speaks." Afterward, after the banquet, beginning now to incline toward love, from temperate she became continent; for as the flames grew, she inclined toward love, but even though it was difficult for her, she nonetheless abstained from lustful acts. Therefore she was no longer temperate, but had become continent, and fought with vice but still conquered it. Wherefore she says: <note>original Latin: "Si mihi non animo fixum immotumque sederet / Ne cui me vinclo vellem sociare iugali / Huic uni forsan potui succumbere culpae"</note> "If it were not fixed and unmovable in my mind / that I would not wish to join myself to any in the bond of marriage / perhaps I could have succumbed to this one fault." And a little further down: <note>original Latin: "Agnosco veteris vestigia flammae"</note> "I recognize the traces of the old flame." She is, then, buffeted by love, but still conquers it. Wherefore she concludes that she would rather be struck by Jove's lightning than violate her chastity. But not much later, she becomes incontinent. For as love continued to torment her, she finally let herself be conquered, though unwillingly, especially by the persuasions of her sister. Nor did she stop falling to the bottom until she became intemperate, because having now formed a habit in lasciviousness, she willingly gave herself to it. This the poet shows by saying: <note>original Latin: "Nec iam furtivum Dido meditatur amorem"</note> "No longer does Dido contemplate a secret love." You see, then, what things are Temperance, Continence, Incontinence, and Intemperance. Therefore, returning to the subject, **Dante** was not intemperate because he had not made a habit of vice, but incontinent because although he fought with vice, he nonetheless allowed himself to be conquered.

And as he who, with panting breath,
having escaped from the deep sea to the shore,
turns to the dangerous water and gazes;
So my mind, which was still fleeing,
turned back to look again upon the pass
that never yet left any person alive.
After I had rested my weary body a little,
I took up my way again across the deserted slope,
so that the firm foot was always the lower one.

<column-break/>

**AN** excellent comparison and true similitude: that having exited the forest, he looked back at the forest, considering the danger into which he had run, no differently than a man does who, having been shipwrecked and finally brought to shore, looks back at the sea and considers the grave danger he escaped. And truly, the soul is in no less vexation and agitation when, having lost every rudder and sail of reason, it is transported by the impetuous waves of the sea—that is, by furious perturbations and passions that proceed from appetite and sensuality. These cause it to break upon the rocks of vice, from which one can bring oneself to shore only with the greatest difficulty. And certainly, while our soul, having lost its reason, is transported by disordered appetite—whether by vain joy, or grave sorrow, or too much fear, or immeasurable greed—it is like a ship in a heavy storm. This I demonstrated quite clearly in my *Camaldolese Disputations* in the allegory of the Virgilian storm.

<meta>This page continues Cristoforo Landino’s commentary on Canto I of Dante’s Inferno. Landino previously discussed the sun as a symbol of Divine Reason and the mountain as the height of the contemplative life. Here, he begins to interpret the physical and moral state of the traveler as he encounters the first of the three symbolic beasts.</meta>

# CANTO FIRST

...where Juno, with the help of Aeolus, forces the Trojans to be submerged. This signifies that the greed of ambition persuades the lower reason to turn Aeneas away from Italy—that is, from the contemplative life—and drive him toward Carthage—that is, the active life. BREATH [<term>Lena</term>: <note>Landino explains this as the physical capacity to breathe or the internal stamina required for effort.</note>]: In our language, this means what the Latins call respiration—that is, a quiet and tranquil breathing which, while in a person, is maintained without difficulty and joyfully within their strength. But too much labor of the body or too much perturbation of the mind often causes such breath to labor. Therefore, if someone endures long in any exercise without becoming exhausted, we say that person has "breath" or stamina. PERILOUS: that is, dangerous. And WATCHING: that is, as he watches, he reflects upon the past danger. WHICH STILL FLED: that is, he was still in fear. For just as one who has a strong and joined spirit in horrific situations is said to have "present spirit," so conversely we say that the spirit "flees" from those who fear out of horror of those things. And he demonstrates here what happens: for even if the danger that made you fear ceases, nevertheless the fear does not cease so suddenly. But how shall we interpret when he says that the pass from which he emerged never left a living person? Since he himself did not perish there? We shall say, then, that he uses that rhetorical figure which the Greeks call <term>hyperbole</term> <note>original Greek: "ὑπερβολή"</note> and the Latins "Exaggeration" [<term>Superlatio</term>]. This is where, to demonstrate the greatness of a thing, one goes beyond the truth. It is understood as: IT NEVER LEFT A PERSON ALIVE because, although some might pass through safely, they are so few that one can say "none" in comparison to the infinite number who perish there. And certainly, those who escape from the darkness of ignorance in a way that they arrive at the light of true knowledge are very rare. Some understand that no one was ever so adorned with virtue that they did not sin while in this life; hence: "the just man sins seven times a day" <note>original Latin: "septies i die peccat iustus"</note>; and whoever is found in sin is dead. Therefore, THAT PASS NEVER LEFT A PERSON ALIVE, meaning it would eventually kill anyone; or rather, it NEVER LEFT A PERSON ALIVE because the way of sin kills whoever walks upon it. Whence: "the soul that sins shall itself die" <note>original Latin: "aia quæ peccauerit ipsa morietur"</note>. Some want "living person" to be the agent and say that no living person ever left that pass; because as we have said, no one comes into life who is not from the beginning oppressed by ignorance, from which sin is born. AFTER I HAD RESTED MY WEARY BODY: He prudently makes mention of the body. For notwithstanding that climbing the mountain—that is, the contemplative life—is that wherein our supreme good consists, and for this reason man must attend to purging the soul of vices so that it becomes capable of holy doctrines (since the spirit of wisdom does not enter a malevolent soul), nonetheless the body is not to be deprived of necessary things. It is an excellent precept of the Apostle who says: "Chastise the body and bring it into servitude" <note>original Latin: "Castiga el corpo & reducilo in seruitu"</note>; for one must not nourish it with such delights that the appetite rebels against reason. But he does not command that it be abandoned entirely, for it must not be deprived of necessary things, because if it is infirm or too weakened, it impedes the soul and does not let it operate according to virtue. Thus, the poet prudently shows that the body should not be kept in too much ease, but rested when it is weary, and rested only a little—that is, as much as necessity requires. ALONG THE deserted slope: That is, abandoned, because "desert" in Latin means abandoned. And from this we call deserted places uninhabited. And certainly it is true that the path which leads man to knowledge is abandoned, because very few are those who give themselves to contemplation. Whence Petrarch said: "Poor and naked you go, Philosophy / says the crowd, intent on base gain / Few companions will you have on your path." And when he says that the firm foot was always the lower one, he demonstrates the manner of walking uphill. For in such a journey, the foot that moves rises, and the one that is firm remains lower. And allegorically he shows that our thought must proceed in order, and not raise one foot if the other is not first firm. This signifies that we should not proceed forward in contemplating higher things if we are not first well-confirmed in the knowledge of lower ones. We can also say that the foot signifies love and the appetite for things. For just as the body is carried by the feet, so the soul is carried by the appetite. Whence he said in the eighteenth chapter of *Purgatorio* that if love is offered to us from without, and the soul does not walk with another foot, whether it goes straight or crooked is not its merit. Therefore, the lower foot signifies the love of inferior things, and this was "firm" because it still had more power in him than the higher foot—that is, the love of celestial things—because he was not yet purged of vices.

It is a custom born of deep doctrine that our poet, not without reason, proposes Virgil as his guide and leader. For he goes about imitating him in every part, though so subtly that few perceive it. Virgil, through Aeneas, wishes to demonstrate how man can arrive at the supreme good; and he posits three principal inconveniences which impede us from attaining our end. The first of these is **Lust** [Luxury], understanding by lust every lasciviousness and every unrestrained voluptuousness and pleasure of the senses, which reigns in us when our soul is not held under the rein of temperance. And this he figured through Troy, which would not let Aeneas leave in any way if Venus, standing for divine love, had not inspired him to depart, as I demonstrated in our 

> And behold, almost at the start of the ascent,
> a leopard, light and very swift,
> which was covered with a spotted hide;
> and she did not depart from before my face,
> rather she so impeded my journey
> that I turned back many times to return.

<column-break/>

allegories. The second is **Avarice**, which he expresses through Thrace and the Strophades islands and through many other things. The third is **Ambition** and immoderate greed for the honors of magistracies and empires, which vice he especially demonstrates through the immortal enmities of Juno against the Trojans. Therefore, the man who by his nature loves virtue and hates vice, and desires his supreme good and flees misery, would always proceed by the straight way if three things did not impede him. These are pleasure, utility, and honor; and to pursue these, we often twist away from the straight road. This same thing, then, Dante signifies at present by the three beasts: the leopard is pleasure, the wolf is utility [greed], and the lion is 

<column-break/>

honor. He had already emerged from the forest and, having seen the summit of the hill illuminated by the sun, was preparing to reach it by climbing the ascent; which we have explained allegorically above. And so it happens that when a man arrives at the years of discretion, reason being excited in him, he prepares himself to desire the supreme good. But this good will is impeded by the aforementioned vices. And first by voluptuousness [pleasure]: for in the years of childhood and youth, the pleasures of man are most ardent, and it is difficult to put a rein on them in the heat of the blood. Whence infinite is the crowd of the intemperate or the incontinent; for rare are those at that age who, affected by the flatteries of a lascivious and voluptuous life, do not abandon the climb of the mountain. This the poet signifies to us by the leopard [<term>lonza</term>], which was the first beast that tried to impede his ascent. Many doubt what animal the *lonza* is. And certainly, we find three species of beasts that have skin marked with various spots: the "wolf-stag" [<term>ceruero</term>] called by the Greeks *lynx* <note>original Greek: "λύγξ"</note>; the pard; and the panther. Some, therefore, want the *lonza* to mean the lynx; and because Virgil suggests that Venus, appearing in the hunt of the sisters, shows them to be dressed in the skin of such an animal. And because this beast is very forgetful; and there is no vice that leads us into greater oblivion of excellent things than corporeal pleasure. If the *lonza* is a pard, the significance will be the same. Because this animal has the same skin and is very much inflamed with lust. Wherefore not only with its own species, but also, as Pliny posits, it mingles with the lion; moreover, it does not want to be seen when it feeds, and in feeding it sucks the blood. This is characteristic of lust, because more than anything else it empties us of blood. Whence Virgil: "For she gradually saps the strength, and burns by looking at the woman" <note>original Latin: "Carpit. n. uires paulatim: uritq; uidēdo femina"</note>. And Juvenal: "Let him indeed receive the reward of blood; and so he grows pale..." <note>original Latin: "Accipiat sane mercedē sāguis: & sic pal..."</note>

<sig>a iiii</sig>

<vocab>Dante Alighieri, Inferno, Canto Primo, Leopard (Lonza), Wolf (Lupa), Lion (Leone), Virgil, Aeneas, Allegory, Cristoforo Landino, Petrarch, Pliny, Juvenal</vocab>

<summary>Landino interprets Dante's encounter with the leopard (Lonza) as an allegory for the vice of Lust, which prevents the youthful soul from ascending toward reason and contemplation. He explains the physical and psychological struggle of the narrator, using classical references to Virgil, Pliny, and Juvenal to define the nature of the three symbolic beasts.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante's Inferno, Canto I. Having discussed the three beasts in general, Cristoforo Landino now focuses on the "lonza" (leopard) as an allegory for lust, before transitioning into a detailed astrological and chronological explanation of the poem's start date.</meta>

<note>original: "ut nudis pressit q calcibus anguē"</note> as one who has stepped on a snake with bare heels. I believe this moved Homer to depict Paris—a man of lustful nature—dressed in the skin of a leopard. The authority of Giovanni Boccaccio also carries weight here: he writes that the Florentine children, seeing the leopard, would shout "look at the *lonza*!" We can also very appropriately understand this as the panther: many do not distinguish it from the leopard except for having a whiter color. Some hold that the panther is the female among leopards. Pliny asserts that its skin is so beautiful and graceful that every wild beast desires it; but they fear the ferocity shown in its head. Therefore, the panther, by hiding its head and showing its back, attracts various beasts with the beauty of its skin, and then with a sudden rush, it captures and devours them. This is very similar to the vice <note>lust</note> in which beauty flatters and draws us in, then devours us because it consumes our time, money, reputation, body, and soul. He <note>Dante</note> places this same beast for the same vice of lust in the sixteenth chapter <note>Inferno XVI, 106-108</note>: "I had a cord wound around me, and with it I once thought to capture the *lonza* with the painted skin." And he spoke most excellently: **And behold, almost**: because this word "Behold"—which the Latins call *ecce*—is never used by poets except when they show something unforeseen and unexpected happening. And thus, pleasure is such a friend to the sensory appetite that it occupies a man before he even notices. **The lonza was light and swift**, because there is great mobility in the life of pleasure. Thus the ancient poets depict Love as winged. Regarding which Propertius said: <note>original: "Non frustra ventosas addidit alas: Fecit & humano corde volare deum. Scilicet alterna quoniam iactamur in unda: Nostraque non ullis permanet aura locis."</note> "Not in vain did he <note>the painter</note> give Love windy wings: and he made the god fly into the human heart. Naturally, since we are tossed on alternating waves: and our breeze stays in no single place." And certainly, one can be captured by love in a single moment. It is indeed difficult not only to say, but even to think how great is the lightness and instability of a lover. **By the spotted skin**, that is, distinguished by various colors, he shows that lascivious love consists in the skin—that is, in the surface of the body. Nothing else is sought but extrinsic beauty, and the variety of its colors and scents to satisfy sight, hearing, and smell. But even more, it seeks things that delight taste and touch, which two senses are more corporeal and seek more shameful and vicious pleasures. **AND IT DID NOT move from before my face**, because the form of the beloved thing always stays fixed in the mind. Virgil demonstrates this in Dido, who says she saw and heard Aeneas even though he was absent. This greatly impedes the path, because there is nothing that so withdraws us from contemplation as lascivious love; in a way that often twists even other geniuses and marvelous men from the true path. And who was more elevated in the knowledge of divinity than King David and his son Solomon? And nevertheless, both were so troubled by love that King David—although he had so many wives and concubines—nonetheless, captured by the beauty of Bathsheba, did not hesitate to send Uriah her husband into battle in such a way that he was killed. Thus, so great a King and so great a prophet, of whom God said <note>original: "Inueni hominem secundum cor meum"</note> "I have found a man after my own heart," for the sake of enjoying a common woman, endured having the governor and leader of his army killed, not without the greatest public harm; and he stained himself with three most grave crimes: murder, treason, and adultery. I could recount many philosophers; but let the prince of the Peripatetics, Aristotle, be enough, who, overcome by love, performed for his concubine Herpyllis <note>The text says "Hermia," likely a confusion with her father or patron Hermias</note> those same sacrifices that the Athenian people performed only for the Eleusinian Ceres, a most celebrated goddess among them.

### It was the time of the beginning of the morning
### and the sun was mounting up with those stars
### that were with him when divine love
### first moved those beautiful things
### so that they were cause for me to have good hope
### of that beast with the gaily-painted skin
### the hour of the day and the sweet season

<margin>The poet uses a *chronographia* here, that is, a description of time. Note, then, that he began the ascent at the start of the day, which hour we call morning (*mattino*), for the Latins call it *mane*. Nor is it without reason that he takes this hour, for it is called *mane*, a word which in the Sabine language means "good." And certainly the hour is not only good, but optimal, in which we begin to set ourselves on the path of salvation. Furthermore, it shows that good works should be started early. This is a just complaint in Petrarch: <note>original: "Ma la colpa è pur mia: che più per tempo / Dovea aprir gli occhi e riguardare al fine: / Ch'a dire il vero omai troppo m'attempo."</note> "But the fault is mine: for earlier I should have opened my eyes and looked to the end: for to tell the truth, I am getting too old now." It can also be added that wanting to show that the poet had</note>

in a vision the things he writes, he set the time at dawn: because in that hour visions and dreams are true, as he directly demonstrates elsewhere, saying: "But if near morning the truth is dreamed." In which place we shall strive to prove this same thing with physical reasons. Furthermore, it is an excellent principle to take the path of contemplation at the time when the sun begins to appear—that is, when reason awakens in us, without whose light one cannot proceed in any knowledge. Thus David says: <note>original: "Mane astabo tibi & uidebo: quoniam deus nolens iniquitatem es"</note> "In the morning I will stand before you and see: for you are a God who does not desire iniquity"; he judges, therefore, that the morning is the appropriate time to know that He is God who does not want iniquity. **The Sun was mounting up.** After the description of the hour of the day, he also describes the season of the year; and he posits that the sun was in Aries, that is, in the Ram; by which sign he denotes the Spring. There are four seasons of the year: Spring, which begins when the sun enters Aries; Summer when it enters Cancer; and similarly, entering Libra begins Autumn, and Capricorn Winter. The beginning of the struggle was thus in the morning, and at the entry of the sun into Aries. By this, according to many, he wants to show that this excellent purpose of climbing the mountain came to him on Good Friday, which was on the 25th day of March, on which day even in the time of Christ the sun was already in Aries through the correction of the year made by Caesar the dictator. But in the present year 1481, the sun enters Aries in March in such a way that on the 11th at midday it will be at the 34th minute of the first degree of Aries. And certainly the Author of human salvation willed to suffer in that season of the year in which the world was created by Him: since when that first day began, which can deservedly be called the birthday of the world, the sign of the Ram was in the middle of the sky. And because the middle of the sky is as it were the summit and head of the whole heaven, therefore the mathematicians place Aries as the first of the signs of the zodiac; because in its beginning of light, it being in the most exalted part, it can appropriately be called the head of the world. But since we have made mention of the birth of the universe, I will briefly set forth the position of all the heavens. In the eighth heaven, where the other fixed stars are, is a circle called the Zodiac, which surrounds the whole heaven, named from the Greek word *zoon* meaning "animal," because it is divided into twelve signs figured in the form of animals. These are Aries, Taurus, Gemini, Cancer, Leo, Virgo, Libra, Scorpio, Sagittarius, Capricorn, Aquarius, and Pisces. Under this eighth sphere are seven other spheres, and in each of them is a planet. Of these, the highest is Saturn. Then in order are Jupiter, Mars, the Sun, Venus, Mercury, and the Moon. This is the lowest of all and closest to the Earth. They say, then, that in such a beginning, the Ram being as we have said in the middle of the sky, the Sun appeared in Aries, and the Moon in Cancer; Mercury in Virgo, and Venus in Libra; and similarly Mars was in Scorpio, Jupiter in Sagittarius, and Saturn in Capricorn. For which reason whichever of the seven aforementioned signs are called the domiciles and houses of that planet which they then received. Of the twelve, five remain; and if we remove from these the Sun and the Moon, which planets have no other domicile than those already mentioned, they are distributed to the other five: in a way that Aquarius belongs to Saturn, Pisces to Jupiter, Scorpio to Mars, Taurus to Venus, and Gemini to Mercury. These, then, have two domiciles, and the Sun and the Moon only one: the Sun has Leo, the Moon has Cancer. I have spoken briefly of these seven planets and the twelve signs of the zodiac not only for the understanding of the present text, but because such knowledge will be useful for the interpretation of many other places. See, then, that the poet shows he moved himself along the path of salvation and made himself ready for contemplation in that season.

He then moves into a detailed astronomical and astrological explanation of why Dante sets the start of his journey at dawn during the spring equinox.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the opening of Canto I. Landino is explaining the significance of the "sweet season" (spring) and the constellation of Aries, transitioning from the first beast (the leopard/lust) to the second (the lion/pride).</meta>

of the year, which was the beginning of the world and in which He who created us free, and who later redeemed us after we had fallen into servitude, created us. **WITH those stars**: understand this to be Aries <note>the Ram</note>, which has eighteen stars. Aries means "ram." And the poets say that this ram, which was turned into this sign, was the one that possessed the golden fleece and traveled across the sea with Phrixus and Helle—though Helle fell into the middle of the sea, Neptune preserved her and from her fathered Paeon. This ram was the son of Neptune and Theophane. Because Neptune, loving this young girl, transformed himself into a ram in order to have her, and transformed her into a sheep; because both were in the form of a ram and a sheep, their offspring was a ram. The poets say the gods transformed this ram into this sign of the zodiac. Nigidius writes that this is the ram that appeared to Bacchus <note>original: "Eaccho," likely a transcription error for "Baccho"</note> when he was leading his army through the sandy Libyan desert where there is no water; it showed him a spring, which is the only one in that region. For this favor, Bacchus transformed it into this sign, and where the spring was, he established a temple to Jove, his father, which is nine days' journey from Alexandria in Egypt. This sign has one star in its head, three in its nostrils, two in the neck, one in each of the front feet, four on the back, one in the tail, three in the belly, and one in each of the hind feet. 

But leaving aside the fables, this sign is named "the Ram" by mathematicians to express the nature of the sun. Just as it is the nature of the ram to lie on its left side in winter and on its right side in summer, so the sun in winter goes to the left hemisphere and in summer to the right. We conclude for all these reasons that, beyond the hour of the day, the season of the year also gave him hope, as it was the season in which God created man and, having created him, subjected every other mortal creature to him, as the prophet testifies: *You have subjected all things under his feet: sheep and oxen, and also the beasts of the field* <note>original Latin: "Omnia subiecisti sub pedibus eius oves & boves universa insup & pecora campi" (Psalm 8:6-7)</note>. It is as if he said: if this is the season in which God was so liberal and gracious toward man—first creating him and giving him dominion over so many things, and then, after he had died spiritually through his own fault, recreating him anew—I can easily hope for the grace to ascend the mountain. Nor would his hope have been in vain had it not been hindered by the three beasts. For without doubt, a man can hope, through divine grace, to reach true knowledge, provided he is not impeded by vices. 

But let him whose soul is stained by the foulness of vice not hope for it, because as Wisdom says: *The spirit of wisdom will not enter into a malevolent soul* <note>original Latin: "In animam maliuolam non introibit spiritus sapientie" (Wisdom 1:4)</note>. And David, as said above, asks: *Who shall ascend the mountain of the Lord? Or who shall stand in His holy place?* <note>original Latin: "Quis ascēdet in mōtem domini. Aut quis stabit in loco sancto eius"</note>—which is nothing other than rising to the knowledge of divine things. He answers: *He who is innocent of hands and pure of heart* <note>original Latin: "Innocens manibus & mūdo corde"</note>. By "innocent of hands," he means one who does not sin in vicious deeds; "pure of heart" is he who does not sin in thought. For this reason Plato, who placed the supreme good of man in the contemplation of divine things (which are known through the intellectual virtues), nevertheless wants us to begin first with the moral virtues, so that we may first purge ourselves of vices with them; for as he himself says: *It is a sin for the impure to touch the pure* <note>original Latin: "Purū ipuro attigere nefas ē"</note>. And certainly it is a nefarious and wicked thing that one who is impure and vicious should attempt to grasp divine things, which are most pure. Nor does the immense Majesty wish for *that which is holy to be given to dogs*.

**MOVED First** those beautiful things: He created the heavens and the other creatures; and not without reason did he say "Moved," because every natural body has its own motion, and God alone is immobile yet moves everything. Whence Boethius: *Remaining stable, You grant all things motion* <note>original Latin: "Stabiliſq; manēs das cūcta moueri"</note>.

**SO THAT The hour of the time and the sweet season** gave me hope of being able to have the skin of the gaudy beast <note>original: "gaetta," referring to the leopard's spotted coat</note>: that is, to be able to kill it and carry off its skin as a sign of victory. **THE HOUR of the time**: because it was morning; and he who begins his journey early in the day can reach his desired end before night. This hour is praised by the prophet, saying: *In the morning hours I will meditate on You, because You have been my helper* <note>original Latin: "In matutinis meditabor i te qa fuisti aiutor meus"</note>. And Horace: *Father of the morning, or Janus, you listen with favor*. And because this is the best hour, the Latins call it *mane* <note>morning</note>, which in the Lanuvian language means "good." And the sweet season of spring, in which the world had its beginning and in which man was redeemed. A man can therefore hope for every happiness in that season. 

Some raise a doubt, saying that the sweet season of spring should have given him fear rather than hope of defeating such an animal, considering that in such a time every animal is naturally incited to lust. But this is not against the poet's words, but in his favor. The meaning is this: if in that time, when man is more stimulated than usual by the lust of the senses, I could begin the ascent—that is, overcome the difficulty found in the contemplative life—it was to be hoped that in any other season I could ascend much more easily. 

**BUT DANTE** in this place, as a poet of most excellent genius and artifice, wished to secretly imitate Virgil. So that this may appear more clearly: Aeneas, at the time he was striving with all his strength to defend Troy, was persuaded by Venus to leave such an undertaking because the gods wanted that city to perish and him to sail to Italy. The allegory of this—as I demonstrated in the fourth book of my *Camaldolese Disputations* written in the Latin language—is that Aeneas in his youth loved Troy greatly (that is, the voluptuous life) and was ready to put himself in any danger for its defense, until Venus (that is, the love of heavenly things) showed him that the gods, and especially Pallas, were the ones destroying Troy; she persuaded him to go to Italy, which Virgil uses to represent the speculative <note>contemplative</note> life. Thus Virgil shows in that place that Aeneas would never have abandoned Troy (the voluptuous life, in which tender and youthful age places the supreme good) nor would have gone to Italy if Venus had not led him. Here he places Venus for the love of heavenly things; and certainly the way of virtue is so arduous and difficult that if the love of it did not pull a man, no one would endure such labors. For this reason, it is quite manifest to whoever diligently investigates the sense of this passage that, just as Virgil shows Aeneas would have perished in Troy (the voluptuous life) if Venus (the love of heavenly things) had not persuaded him to depart, so Dante would not have hoped to defeat the leopard if he had not been aided by the sweet season of Venus (that is, of heavenly love), for as the Florentine proverb says: *Love carries every heavy burden.*

> but not so that fear did not seize me
> at the sight that appeared to me of a lion
> This one seemed to be coming against me
> with its head high and with ravenous hunger
> so that it seemed the air trembled at it

**T**his lion is configured as the second vice, which we can call pride or, by a more common term, ambition. For just as in youthful years pleasures and delights bind and ensnare our souls so that they abandon virtue, so later in mature age there awakes in us an immeasurable appetite for honors, magistracies, empires, and lordships. These things, although they may seem to come from an excellent and generous soul, nevertheless involve many vices in their acquisition. And there are far more who strive to reach such heights through fraud, betrayal, and corruption than through true virtue.

---

It would be very long to narrate the slaughters and homicides committed to acquire lordships, and the wars by which not one or two cities, but vast and most powerful kingdoms have been overturned. Son has killed father, and brother has killed brother; not only a single Eteocles <note>original: "Teocle"</note> and Polynices, or Atreus and Thyestes, but they have been infinite. And what else has taken from republics not only their empire but their leisure, peace, and finally their liberty, if not the parties and factions born among citizens, each wanting to be first in honors and more powerful than the laws? Although I could easily prove this with domestic examples, I wish rather to refer to external ones and call to memory Marius, Sulla, Cinna, Octavius, Caesar, Pompey, and infinite others. But let us suppose that some seek dignities through virtue and justice and administer them with all honesty, desiring with their toil and sweat to benefit the republic and its citizens, and to suppress civil discords and nourish concord with a paternal rather than a tyrannical government; nevertheless...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante’s "Inferno," following the discussion of the Leopard (representing lust) and the Lion (representing pride). Landino here explores the spiritual and psychological symbolism of these beasts before introducing the third and most dangerous: the She-wolf (avarice).</meta>

<header>INFERNO.</header>

...less occupied in worldly and transitory things, they leave behind the investigation of celestial and divine things: in which consists all our happiness. For truly, as in all other things, so in this, Truth itself said: <note>original: "Martha Martha sollicita es: & turbaris erga plurima. Maria autē optimā ptẽ elegit que nõ auferetur abea"</note> "Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things. But Mary has chosen the best part, which shall not be taken from her." This means that Martha was occupied in constant thoughts and cares, and not without great perturbation, in various worldly affairs; while Mary had chosen the best part, which cannot be taken from her. And in the Old Testament, they present Leah as bleary-eyed <note>meaning perhaps short-sighted or focused on the immediate</note> but fruitful in conceiving and giving birth; and Rachel her sister with bright and healthy eyes, but sterile. Most wisely, therefore, Dante expresses this same idea through the Lion, which Virgil used to represent Juno—who was always the greatest enemy to the Trojans and to Aeneas as he wished to come to Italy. It is read that the lion does not attack those who throw themselves to the ground and yield, but those who stand against it. Thus, the ambitious man seeks to be superior; he accepts those who yield and contends with those who do not. As Plautus said: <note>original: "Supbus minores despicit maioribus inuidet"</note> "The proud man despises his inferiors and envies his superiors." And Boethius: <note>original: "Ire intempa tis fremit ut leonis animū geftare credatur"</note> "He rages with intemperate anger, so that he is believed to carry the soul of a lion." **THIS** appeared to be coming against me: Not without reason did he say this of the lion, which he had not said of the leopard, because it is an easy thing for an elevated mind moved toward contemplation to recognize that a life of pleasure is not the "sweet dream." But dignity and honors have in them such force and such an appearance of honesty that they deceive excellent souls. Therefore, he could easily cast away pleasure from himself, but not ambition; and so he feigns that the lion came to meet him. All these things denote the elation and haughtiness found in the ambitious man. Whence he shows that it comes with its head high, because ambition is never without pride. **AND** with a ravenous hunger: because such greed is an insatiable and rabid appetite. Hence Caesar used to frequently recite the verse of Euripides, the tragic poet: <note>original: "Se la ragione & la giustitia fi debba uiolare e da uiolarla p fignoreggiare"</note> "If reason and justice must be violated, they are to be violated for the sake of ruling." Nor without reason does he add **SO THAT** it seemed the air trembled at it: because those who reach a high rank greatly desire to be feared, and especially by the "air"—that is, by superiors and great men. This is denoted by the air, which is the superior element.

> And a she-wolf, who with all cravings
> seemed laden in her meagerness,
> and had already made many people live in sorrow;
> She brought such heaviness upon me,
> with the fear that came from her sight,
> that I lost the hope of the height.

<column-break/>

By the she-wolf, he means Avarice. Those who describe the nature of the wolf report that no animal is more greedy or voracious; nor does it only harm the flocks, because the injury reaches not only the devoured beast but the man who is the master of that beast. Nor does it only take prey by attacking openly, but also by lying in wait: either on dark nights or on foggy days, with ambushes and snares it stealthily carries away the animal. And if it is not discovered by shepherds or dogs, it does not stop until it has killed the whole flock, believing it can never be filled. Thus the avaricious man, now with

<column-break/>

fraud and deceit, now with open robbery, takes that which brings detriment to others. Yet he can never accumulate so much that his desire is satisfied. But like the dropsical man <note>one suffering from "hydrops" or edema, traditionally thought to have an unquenchable thirst</note>, drinking does not extinguish the thirst but increases it; thus avarice grows in a man as much as his treasures grow. Hence Horace in his Odes: <note>original: "Crescit indulgēs sibi dirus hydrops: Nec fitim pellit nisi causa morbi fugerit prius & aquosus albo corpore langor"</note> "The dire dropsy grows by indulging itself; nor is the thirst driven out unless the cause of the disease has first fled, and the watery languor from the pale body." And Virgil: <note>original: "Quid nõ mortalia pectora cogis auri facra fames"</note> "To what do you not drive mortal hearts, O accursed hunger for gold?" Seneca: <note>original: "Auaro deest tā quod habet quā quod nõ habet"</note> "To the miser, that which he has is as much missing as that which he has not." And the wolf is consecrated to Mars, the god of war, because wars are not started except to usurp what belongs to others. Therefore, the wolf is deservedly placed for avarice. And this same reason is why prostitutes, who sell their chastity and reputation for money, are called "she-wolves" <note>original: "lupe"</note> in Latin, and the places where they publicly reside are called "lupanars" <note>brothels</note>. Therefore, just as the age of youth is hindered by pleasures, and manhood by ambition and the desire for honors, so is old age by avarice—certainly the worst vice of all. But of this we shall treat more extensively where the avaricious are punished. And the sentiment of Sallust is true: that avarice makes both the soul and the body become effeminate. **THIS** She-wolf seemed—that is, showed herself—to be laden with all cravings: that is, with all greeds and desires, because to crave means to desire very affectionately. **IN** her meagerness: He portrays the wolf as thin, because the thinner an animal is, the more famished it is. Every other vice is sooner satisfied and filled than avarice, which is compared to the dropsical man, as I said. And the miser is always thin because he dares neither to eat nor drink as much as necessity requires, so as not to diminish his riches. **AND MANY** people she had already made live in sorrow <note>original: "grame"</note>: That is, grieving and discontented, for this is what this word means in the Lombard language. And certainly, avarice saddens the miser and those who are despoiled by the miser. The miser is always in toil, both to earn and to guard what is earned; and by accumulating, he never enjoys what he has acquired. He is like Tantalus, placed in the underworld by the poets, oppressed by hunger and thirst: he is in the clearest water up to his lower lip, and various fruits and berries hang above him down to his lip; but when he bends to drink, the water recedes; when he rises to eat, the fruits pull away. This happens to the miser: for though he may be in abundance of every good, nonetheless avarice ensures that he relieves neither his hunger nor his thirst. The same is denoted by the fable of Midas: the poets intended nothing else by feigning that when this king touched any food or drink it immediately became gold, except that through avarice he wanted to make money out of that which should have sustained his life. And he adds that the fear which came from her sight—that is, from her appearance—weighed him down so that he lost the hope of reaching the mountain. And certainly, the greed for earthly goods so encumbers the soul and so presses upon it that it cannot be elevated to any high contemplation. Nor is there any vice more an enemy to virtue than avarice, as we shall demonstrate in its proper place.

> And as one who is glad in gaining,
> and the time arrives that makes him lose,
> who in all his thoughts weeps and is saddened;
> Such did that restless beast make me,
> who, coming against me little by little,
> was pushing me back to where the sun is silent.

<column-break/>

This is an excellent comparison, through which he shows that just as the more a man is greedy for gain, the greater is the pain when it happens that he loses; so it was more distressing to him to be pushed back down, the greater his will had been to climb. The restless beast came toward him—that is, avarice, in which there is never any rest. Instead, there is toil in gaining, and toil in preserving what is gained. And it brings with it an inextinguishable thirst and a blind greed, which grows the more it acquires; it never lets a man rest. **AND** it came little by little: because at the beginning we propose to ourselves a temperate desire, and it will seem to you that you ought to be

<column-break/>

content with a thousand; and then, having earned those, the wish and desire to double them grows; then to triple them. And thus, adding sum upon sum, one proceeds to infinity. And through this care for momentary and transitory things, the burdened soul loses the lightness needed to climb; and by that beast, it is pushed back to where there is no sun—that is, where only appetite and sensuality reign, full of ignorance and darkness, and where the sun of reason does not shine.

<summary>Landino explains the symbolism of the Lion (Pride) and the She-wolf (Avarice) in Dante's Inferno, arguing that while pride deceives even noble minds, avarice is an insatiable "restless" vice that prevents spiritual progress. He uses classical references to Horace, Virgil, and the myths of Tantalus and Midas to illustrate the self-defeating nature of greed.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the first Canto of the Inferno. The previous section established the three beasts blocking Dante's path: the Leopard (lust), the Lion (pride), and finally the She-wolf (avarice). Here, Landino introduces Virgil, the guide who represents human reason, and begins to explain the deep allegorical meaning of their encounter.</meta>

# CANTO FIRST
a i

> While I was rushing down to the lower place,
> before my eyes one offered himself to me,
> who through long silence seemed faint:
> When I saw him in the great desert,
> "Have mercy on me," I cried to him,
> "whatever you may be, whether shade or certain man."

---

> He answered me: "Not a man; a man I once was,
> and my parents were Lombards,
> and Mantuans by homeland, both of them.
> I was born under Julius, though it was late,
> and I lived in Rome under the good Augustus,
> in the time of the false and lying gods."

<column-break/>

This is a marvelous invention, wonderfully adorned with profound doctrine and supreme eloquence, and wisely distinguished and divided. In it, the poet demonstrates how the human mind, having reached the years of discretion, becomes aware of the forest in which it finds itself and of its own ignorance. Having seen the sun of reason at the summit of the mountain, it sets out to climb toward contemplation to know those things which can make it blessed. Then, we are taught that although our will may be burning for such an enterprise and our spirit may be ready, nevertheless, the infirmity of the flesh hinders the ascent—now through the voloptuousness and pleasures of the flesh, now through the glory and pomp of the world, and now through avarice. These are such obstacles that, by ourselves, if some help is not given to us, we cannot reach the desired end.

Nor should anyone be moved by the fact that although there are so many and such varied vices which are obstacles to virtuous living, the poet presents only three. For these three contain all the others, since one who is not corrupted by pleasures (the leopard), or by the greed for possession (the she-wolf), or by the desire for honors, status, and power (the lion), can be conquered by no vice. This, then, is what has been treated up to this point.

In what follows, he places the help received. He adds that while he was falling back down, unable to resist the she-wolf, Virgil appeared to him in the desert, to whom he recommended himself and from whom he obtained help. It was said above that our blessedness is located at the height of the mountain—that is, in the contemplation of divine things. Nevertheless, the human mind cannot make itself fit and suitable for such an ascent if it does not first purge itself of every vice, as we have shown above. Nor can one purge oneself of vices if one does not first know them. From this it follows that Dante could not reach heaven—that is, the knowledge of celestial things—if he did not first go through Hell and Purgatory; that is, if he did not first know the vices, and then, having known them, purge himself of them.

And because our frailty makes it impossible, or very difficult, to make this journey without a leader and guide, the poet shows that he has taken Virgil. First, because in truth he very subtly imitated him in this work of his. Next, he allegorically takes Virgil to represent moral philosophy and all the doctrine of the gentiles <note>The "gentiles" here refers to the pre-Christian Greek and Roman philosophers.</note>. And because such doctrine is sufficient to achieve the first two parts—that is, knowing vice and purging oneself through Purgatory—but it is not sufficient to give us true knowledge of divine things, which can be drawn from no other source than that of the sacred theology of the Christians. Therefore, he establishes that Virgil guides him only through Hell and Purgatory, because for Paradise, as we shall see in its place, he will need a more learned guide.

But so that in the progress of the poem this name does not lead us into any error or difficulty in understanding the allegorical sense, let it be known from this beginning that Virgil will be used not in a single sense but in various ways. Sometimes he will mean nothing other than the poet himself. Sometimes he will signify human reason simply, and Dante will be sensuality. At other times, we shall interpret him as the intellect illustrated by various and many doctrines. Other times, we shall express through him the "superior reason," and then Dante will signify not sensuality alone, but also the "inferior reason."

Returning then to the text, it follows: *WHILE I was rushing down to the lower place*: That is, while the she-wolf was keeping me from climbing to contemplation and making me fall back into the low desires of earthly things, so that I despaired of being able to conquer such a cruel beast by myself, Virgil appeared before me. And in this part, he demonstrates what usually happens to circumspect men: who, seeing that they cannot reach where they desire by themselves, investigate who might be a more useful guide. Thus, Dante, searching in his mind, was offered Virgil, who *through long silence seemed faint*.

Because Virgil signifies doctrine and the rational part of man, he is not undeservedly called faint through long silence; for a long time, sensuality rules in man before reason does. Sensuality governs and commands the man, and with its beastly government rules him, while reason, as if asleep, remains silent. It does not wake or speak until one is at the "midpoint of the journey." And even then, it speaks faintly because, although reason begins to be excited, it is still submerged in sensuality and cannot speak clearly from the start. Therefore, in the first years, reason is entirely silent. Then it begins to speak, but speaks faintly because it is still confused and does not discern well. Finally, it speaks clearly.

We can also say that Virgil seemed faint through long silence because until Dante’s time, the Latin language had been poorly understood for many centuries and was almost in silence, and especially Virgil. Dante was the first who investigated the high meanings of Virgil. Because it would be too long to recount them all here, I expressed and declared them as much as my talent allowed in the third and fourth books of our *Camaldolese Disputations* <note>original: "disputationi chamaldulesi"</note>, which volume our disciple Andrea Cambini translated into the Florentine language.

*WHEN I saw him in the great desert*: He sees Virgil in the desert, but does not yet know who he is. That is, he sees reason beginning to appear, though faintly, in the uncultivated forest of the infinite movements of sensuality. But he does not recognize it. Yet, because he already understands his misery, he asks for help. There is a time when we are in ignorance and do not realize it; then comes a time when we begin to realize it but not very clearly because reason is still confused. Yet we still seek a remedy, because reason pushes us, once our evil is known, to ask for help against it.

*HAVE MERCY on me, I cried to him*: Because when sensuality sees itself perishing, it asks for help from reason. *I cried* because, being near the she-wolf and seeing himself in manifest danger, he wanted to show that he needed immediate and undelayed help. And by this he admonishes us that when we perceive ourselves being persecuted by vices, we should not delay in asking for help; because by delaying, such a habit can be formed that we later become too late.

The rest of the following verses are simple history and do not require allegory. He asks if he is a shade or a certain man because in desert places, shades or phantoms often appear. And allegorically, in the desert—that is, in the sensory part of the soul—there often appear not "men" (true reasons) but "shades" (vain and false reasons), which show to be good that which is not. But he who goes wandering through the forest—that is, he who is still involved in vices—asks help from the shade as if from a certain man; that is, he allows himself to be persuaded by false reason just as by true reason, whereby he remains deceived.

**V**irgil responds, therefore, that he is not a man, but was. For neither the soul alone nor the body alone is called "man," but these two joined together according to the Aristotelians. Whence man is defined as a "mortal rational animal." "Animal" signifies an animated body. Therefore, it is not an animal where there is not soul and body together. Nor is man mortal except from the part of the body, because the soul is immortal. Nevertheless, the Platonists, when they say "man," intend only the soul, and they want the body to be as if it were a vessel...

He explores the philosophical definitions of man according to Aristotle and Plato, and interprets Virgil's "hoarseness" as both the dormancy of reason in youth and the historical neglect of Latin literature.</summary>

# CANTO FIRST

> "I was a poet, and I sang of that just
> son of Anchises who came from Troy,
> after proud Ilion was consumed by fire.
> But you, why do you return to such misery?
> Why do you not climb the delightful mountain,
> which is the beginning and cause of all joy?"

<column-break/>

where the soul is contained. But we shall discuss this more extensively in a more convenient place. Furthermore, we can say that there is an allegory here as well: Virgil says, "I was a man and at present I am not," as if to say, "In the time of the pagans I was a man," <note>original: "homo"</note> meaning I possessed doctrine that then seemed sufficient for man. But now, in the time of Christians, "I am not a man," meaning the doctrine of the pagans is not enough for the fulfillment of man.

**PARENTS:** <note>original: "EPArenti"</note> That is, the father and the mother, because in the Latin language this word *parens* signifies both. **LOMBARDS:** Because Mantua, his homeland, is in Lombardy. "Both of them" <note>original: "Ambo dui"</note> is a Lombard expression meaning the two of them; he adapted the vocabulary to the person, who was Lombard.

Publius Virgilius Maro was born on the 15th of October in the year that Pompey the Great and Marcus Crassus were consuls, in the year of the world 5131, and in the second year of the 177th Olympiad, and 68 years before the birth of Christ. There are thus 1,522 years <note>Landino is likely referencing a specific chronological system or a later edition's printing date here</note> in this year of salvation 1480. He was born in the territory of Mantua in a village called Andes. His father was named Maro and his mother Maia. The mother dreamed the night before the birth that she gave birth to a laurel branch, and once planted, it grew in a short time and, having become large, produced various pomes and fruits. He studied at Cremona and Milan; he took the <term>toga virilis</term> <note>the "toga of manhood" worn by Roman boys to mark their transition to adulthood</note> on the same day that the poet Lucretius died. He also studied at Naples and became most excellent in medicine and all mathematics. Later, having come to Rome, he became a very close friend to Maecenas, and through his intercession, he entered the friendship of Caesar Augustus. He held such authority with Augustus that he obtained the restitution of possessions for all Mantuans, which the Emperor had previously taken and divided among his soldiers. It would be very tedious to recount the various doctrines and the supreme eloquence of this poet: "The pen cannot keep pace with the will," nor does the place require it, and the matter is manifest to every learned person. But I conclude for many most manifest reasons that he does not yield to Homer, who was the first poet among the Greeks.

**I WAS BORN UNDER JULIUS:** We will speak of Julius Caesar and Augustus below. He calls Augustus "good" because in truth, among the twelve Caesars, he ruled more justly than many others. **THE FALSE AND LYING GODS:** These are the idols which in those times were adored by the Romans. **THE JUST SON OF ANCHISES:** He means Aeneas, who was of royal stock in this manner: Dardanus, first king of Troy, fathered Erichthonius; from Erichthonius was born Tros; from Tros was born Ilus, successor to the kingdom, and from Ilus, Laomedon; from Laomedon, Priam. Furthermore, from the said Tros was also born Assaracus, and from Assaracus, Capys, and from him Anchises, father of Aeneas. The poet thus calls Aeneas "just" because Virgil always presents him as such in his book titled the *Aeneid*, where he describes the virtues of Aeneas: <note>original Latin: "Rex erat Eneas nobis quo iuſtior alter / Nec pietate fuit nec bello maior & armis"</note> "Aeneas was our king, than whom no other was more just in piety, nor greater in war and arms."

**PROUD** <note>original: "SVpbō"</note> in this place signifies "noble," and in bringing Virgil to speak, Dante adapts Virgil's own words, for Virgil says: "And proud Ilion fell." <note>original Latin: "ceciditque ſuperbum Ilion"</note> And understand that Ilion is the city of the Trojans, so named after King Ilus mentioned just above. And thus the whole region and the country of the Trojans is called Troy after the aforementioned Tros, just as one might say "Tuscany," while the city itself is Ilion, just as one might say "Florence." **CONSUMED:** <note>original: "Cō buſto"</note> burned, because *comburere* in Latin means to burn.

**BUT YOU:** "Why do you return to such misery?" As great as the misery of the darkness of the forest, and of ignorance, and of the vices from which you had emerged shortly before. He introduces Virgil, that is, the rational part of the soul and the doctrine which reproves <term>sensuality</term> <note>the lower, physical appetites</note> when it allows itself to be conquered by vices and falls from its good purpose. And in this part, the poet demonstrates the progress of man who, although he begins to see his errors, is nonetheless not "temperate" at the beginning. This is because the temperate man has already despised worldly pleasures and has conquered them in such a way that they no longer struggle against him. Dante is not yet temperate but is <term>continent</term> <note>In Aristotelian ethics, a 'continent' person does the right thing but must struggle against their desires to do so</note>. For the continent man fights against vice and conquers it, but abstains with difficulty, and often wavers so that if the appetite were not continually restrained by reason, the wolf and the other beasts would push us back into the forest.

**WHY:** "Why do you not climb the delightful mountain?" Understand "delightful" to the soul, which feeds and nourishes itself on contemplation, and rests in it and delights in it. **WHICH IS THE BEGINNING AND CAUSE** of all joy, that is, of all good. Only God is the total and supreme good, and good in such a way that no other thing is good except insofar as it participates in the divine goodness. Therefore, the mountain clothed in sun—that is, the contemplation of the soul illuminated by the sun of the intellect—is the beginning and cause by which we know God; and knowing Him, we love Him; and loving Him, we enjoy Him; wherein consists all joy, that is, our entire and perfect good and happiness.

<column-break/>

> "Then are you that Virgil and that fountain
> which pours forth so wide a river of speech?"
> I answered him with a shameful brow.
> "O honor and light of the other poets,
> may the long study and great love avail me
> that has made me search your volume.
> You are my master and my author;
> you are the only one from whom I took
> the beautiful style that has done me honor.
> See the beast for which I turned back;
> help me against her, famous sage,
> for she makes my veins and pulses tremble."

<column-break/>

Dante responds to the words of Virgil, who, when asked who he was, had not pronounced his own name but had revealed himself through <term>circumlocution</term> <note>talking around a subject rather than naming it directly</note>. Stupefied, then, that Virgil had appeared to him in such a place, Dante says: **THEN ARE YOU THAT VIRGIL.** And he deservedly calls him a "fountain," because just as the fountain is the origin of the river, so this poet was the origin from which perfect and polished Latin poetry was born. The first poet in the Latin language was Livius Andronicus, and after him many others, and among the first were Ennius, Plautus, Terence, and Lucretius. But before Virgil, the Latins did not have perfect poetry. He equates eloquence to a "river" because the Greek and Latin writers do so. Thus, there had previously been some fountain from which a river was born, but not so wide nor so abundant. And certainly Virgil—that is, the rational part in man—is the fountain and principle from which every river of doctrine and wisdom and the true knowledge of divine things is born in us.

**WITH A SHAMEFUL BROW:** This arose from the reverence he felt for him. Shame is the fear of erring. And this especially assails us when we are in the presence of someone we esteem greatly. For then we desire that not only our deeds and words, but even our gestures be approved. He could also be ashamed for not having recognized him at the first meeting—and this pertains to the literal sense. But allegorically, Dante—that is, sensuality—is ashamed for not having previously recognized Reason. This is an excellent sign, for he who feels shame for a fault gives a demonstration of the intent to correct himself. He calls him "honor of the other poets" because he holds the primacy among the others, and from him proceeds the splendor of the glory which poetry possesses. Or truly we say that he is the honor and light of the others because by imitating him they acquire honor and the splendor of fame and from his doctrine...
