<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante’s first encounter with Virgil. Having established Virgil’s identity, Landino now moves into an allegorical and rhetorical analysis of Dante’s plea for help, explaining why Virgil represents the power of human reason and how the structure of Dante’s speech follows classical rules of persuasion.</meta>

# CANTO FIRST

are illuminated. But allegorically, Virgil is the "honor and light" of other poets because all the other powers of the soul and especially
the internal senses—although they may be excellent at comprehending (like the common sense), or composing and dividing (like the imagination),
or judging what thing is to be sought and what is to be fled (like the <term>cogitative power<note>In medieval psychology, the "virtus cogitativa" was the faculty that compared individual sensory perceptions.</note></term>), and finally retaining what has been judged (like the
memory), or moving the soul to pursue what is judged (like the appetite)—nonetheless, if such senses are not il-
luminated by reason, they cannot move from the particular to the universal, nor distinguish particulars any differently than brute animals do.
Therefore, Virgil is the honor and light of poets because reason illuminates the senses and makes them more excellent in man than
in the brutes. But because this speech which Dante makes to Virgil is very ornate and suited to the person, the place, the
time, and the matter, it will be a useful and pleasant thing for the listener to briefly demonstrate its artistry. And first, there being three gen-
era of causes—demonstrative, deliberative, and judicial—this one is in the deliberative genre. Its goal is either to persuade that a thing is
useful and honorable, or to dissuade from it as useless and dishonorable. The poet wants to persuade Virgil to defend him from the she-
wolf. And he makes a beginning which has the force of a proem. Every writer strives in the proem to make the listener either attentive, or docile, or
benevolent. We will not speak at present of attention and docility, because in such a large multitude of things it is necessary to over-
look many if we do not want the volume to grow to infinity. We acquire, therefore, the benevolence of the listener in many
ways, but especially when we praise him for some excellent virtue, and by that demonstrate that we esteem him greatly. And in this part, we
will always praise that virtue which is useful for us that he show in our petition. Just as, <note>original: "verbi gratia"</note> it is useful to Cicero if he
wants to win the case that Caesar show mercy toward Quintus Ligarius, whom he desired to be pardoned: Therefore, he praises the gen-
tleness and mercy of Caesar above every other virtue. Thus Dante, having need of the doctrine and eloquence
of Virgil, praises him for that. **O HONOR AND LIGHT OF THE OTHER POETS.** He has until now captured benevolence from Virgil by prais-
ing him. But because in the deliberative genre where we ask for something it is necessary to show that thing to be easy, use-
ful, and honorable—and if possible, necessary—it should be understood that his petition contains the request that he defend him from the wolf. This
contains nothing else but that Virgil provide him with so much light from his doctrine that he might not be conquered by avarice. He shows this to be
easy for Virgil. For if his doctrine has brought honor and light to other poets, it can do the same for him. After
this, his petition was just, saying: **MAY THE LONG STUDY AND THE GREAT LOVE AVAIL ME.** For justice supremely requires that
we favor and help those who are students of our work and call upon us with such intensity. And finally, having captured benevolence and
demonstrated the ease and honor of the matter, he comes to the petition. And let this suffice to show the artistry of the oration. **MAY IT AVAIL
ME, THE LONG STUDY:** at once he captures benevolence as he has already done and shows the petition to be honorable as we have said.
But he also teaches the method to anyone who wants to become learned. For it is not only necessary to study, but to study for a long
time. Because great and many things cannot be understood in a few months or years, but require a long and lasting span of time.
Whence Hippocrates laments in the beginning of his aphorisms that "art is long and life is short," <note>original: "larte e lungua & lauita e brieue"</note> and "experiment is deceptive." And
Theophrastus, the disciple of Aristotle, grieved that nature had granted a long span of life to crows, but to man—
who through his intellect could learn many things—a brief life was attributed. And Petrarch said: "But time is brief and our
will is long." We see, therefore, that study is necessary for anyone who wants to know. And understand that study is nothing other than a fer-
vent and constant application of the mind to the thing we desire to know. Therefore, to study is to keep the mind always occupied
and intent on that thing we seek to know. And because this cannot be done without great labor and sweat and wakefulness, where
it is necessary to leave behind many delights and pleasures, and also many utilities, men would not support these hardships if they
were not inflamed by a most ardent love for the doctrine they seek; because the proverb is true that "love carries the
bundle." Wherefore, Dante, understanding all these things, did not only say "May study avail me," but added "The long." And because the
hardships of long study are not supported unless there is a love that is not mediocre, he added **THE GREAT LOVE THAT HAS MADE ME SEARCH
THROUGH YOUR VOLUME;** because only love made him constant and patient in enduring hunger, thirst, sleep, heat, and cold, and leaving be-
hind many pleasures. These things he would not have supported without love. **YOUR VOLUME:** Although Virgil wrote many other works in his
adolescence, nonetheless there are three principal ones: the *Bucolics*, the *Georgics*, and the *Aeneid*. From the first two he
drew some things; but the *Aeneid* he imitated in everything. **SEE THE BEAST FOR WHICH I TURNED BACK:** These words can move
 the listener to great com-
passion. "See the beast," as if to say, "You yourself can consider its ferocity, and you see that since it is present, it is inevitable that I
perish if your help is not ready." Therefore it is an honorable request. **DEFEND ME FROM HER, FAMOUS AND WISE SAGE:** He makes him benevolent
by calling him famous and wise. And in part he shows that he can easily provide the doctrine, being famous and wise. And in
this way he makes his petition easy. **FOR SHE MAKES MY VEINS AND PULSES TREMBLE.** Veins are those where the blood is. But some
have much blood and less spirit. Others have less blood and more spirit; and these in Latin are called arteries or <term>pulsating
veins</term>, and we call them "pulses" because <note>original: "pulsant .i. battono"</note> they pulse, that is, they beat. And every time we have fear, the pulses tremble, that is, they beat
more often. Therefore, "she makes my veins and pulses tremble," that is, the pulsating veins; meaning, she makes me terrified.

It is an easy thing to obtain just things from the just. Moved, there-
fore, by just prayers, Virgil determines to help him and dem-
onstrates that it is impossible that he can flee the forest by the way of the wolf, be-
cause we cannot escape from the ignorance and blindness of worldly things
by the path of avarice. We want to go from the forest (that is, from igno-
rance) to the mountain (that is, to contemplation) by the way of the wolf (that is, of avar-
ice); but this is impossible because it blocks the way and keeps us in the
desire for riches, so much so that it kills us before we can ar-
rive at the goal. And it is true of anyone who is held by the wolf. This is nothing else but
to form a habit of avarice. This habit kills the vice, it kills the soul,
and extinguishes in it the light of reason. And if someone should say, "I
know that avarice prevents the going, nonetheless the miser can
give himself so much to seeking treasures that he becomes very rich; and just as a
hungry man, once he is filled with food, is free from hunger, so this
man, having become rich, will no longer be a miser. But free from avarice, he will be able to climb the mountain." To which Virgil responds that the nature of
avarice is never to be satisfied. But it is so wicked and cruel that it never fills the greedy (that is, the desiring and covetous) will. But after
the meal (that is, after riches are acquired) it has more hunger and thirst for treasure than before. Therefore, a miser should never hope to extinguish
or satisfy his will and, once satisfied, give himself to the contemplative life, because it never satisfies; but the more he acquires, the more he desires. Whence
he never has time left to give himself to contemplation. And what is even worse, from avarice proceed many other vices; they entirely
remove him from every virtue through which he could give himself to the knowledge of celestial things; whence follows:

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante’s Canto I. Having previously discussed Virgil as the embodiment of Human Reason, Landino now turns to the prophecy of the "Veltro" (the Greyhound) and the nature of the She-wolf, which represents the vice of Avarice.</meta>

# INFERNO.

Some explain it this way: **MANY are the animals to whom she weds herself:** that is, many are the men to whom this "translation" <note>In this context, Landino uses "translation" to mean the metaphorical application of the animal's nature to a human</note>—that is, avarice—is wedded. That is to say, it joins with them inseparably, just as a wife cannot be separated from her husband by the bond of marriage. And certainly, when we have formed a habit of avarice, it is almost impossible to separate oneself from it. And he excellently said "animals," as if they were men in whom reason is buried; for it is by reason alone that we are men and different from the brutes. And he does not call them "men," to demonstrate that in infinite numbers of people, reason does not reign. One can also give another interpretation to this text: since he has already shown avarice under the name of the wolf—a wild animal—he wishes to stay within the metaphor and uses "animals" to represent the vices. And

### Many are the animals to whom she weds herself,
### and there will be even more, until the Greyhound
### comes, who will make her die in pain.
### He shall not feed on land nor pewter,
### but on wisdom, love, and virtue;
### and his nation shall be between felt and felt.
### He shall be the salvation of that humble Italy
### for which the virgin Camilla died,
### and Euryalus, Turnus, and Nisus of their wounds.
### He shall hunt her through every city
### until he has put her back into Hell,
### from whence envy first let her loose.

<column-break/>

having already shown that avarice is not only a great vice, but also of a quality that always grows and never diminishes, he now adds that besides this, it accompanies many other vices. For avarice induces falsehood, fraud, perjury, theft, robbery, killings, assassinations, and other innumerable pests to human life. These vices proceed from avarice, and every day more will proceed from it until someone comes who will destroy it. And to stay within the metaphor he has made from the vice to the beast, he calls the one who will kill it a "Greyhound." This is because wild beasts are killed by hunting with dogs, and we call "Greyhounds" <term>veltri<note>A swift breed of hunting dog, often used as a symbol for a future political or spiritual savior in Dante's time.</note></term> those who with speed overcome the beasts in the race and, having reached them, catch and kill them. Therefore, it is manifest that he puts the Greyhound for the one who will kill avarice. But who this person may be is very ambiguous. Nevertheless, a great part of the commentators understand it to be Christ when He shall come to judge. And they want the sense to be this: "Many are the animals," that is, bestial men, to whom avarice "weds itself," that is, joins inseparably. And they will always multiply until the day of the Last Judgment, when Christ shall come to judge the living and the dead, and then avarice shall cease. And "neither land nor pewter"—that is, neither earthly fruits nor any kind of metal—"shall feed him":

<column-break/>

shall feed him: that is, avarice shall not reign, which consists either in wanting to possess many estates or in accumulating treasures which are gold and silver and other metals. And because "pewter" is not a simple metal but a compound of several, he used this kind of metal to stand for all the others. **BUT WISDOM, love, and virtue.** The food Christ will offer us will not be temporal goods, but wisdom, love, and virtue. For since man has fallen into vice through ignorance and disobedience (which proceeds from not loving one's superior), Christ, to restore him to his original dignity, will offer him wisdom against ignorance, love against contempt and disobedience, and moral virtue against vices. We can also set "love, wisdom, and virtue" as three principal things through which we can attain beatitude. For no one will acquire this beatitude if he does not first know where it consists—which wisdom gives us. Nor is it enough to know it if we do not love and desire to have it—and for this, love is necessary. Nor, once it is known and loved, can we possess it if we are not purged of all vices—which we do through moral virtue. **AND HIS nation:** They do not understand the birth of Christ when He, incarnate, came from the womb of the Virgin Mary, but they interpret it as the appearance He will make when He comes to judge the world; for everything that appears anew can be said to be "born." **SHALL BE between felt and felt:** that is, between heaven and heaven <note>Landino is interpreting "felt" (feltro) as the substance of the celestial spheres</note>, because He will appear in the air. This is because felt is composed of hairs compressed together and not woven with thread like cloth; and hairs are less corporeal than threads, and the heavens are less corporeal than the elements. Many, therefore, as we have said, want the poet to put the Greyhound for Christ coming to judge the world at its consummation, which he deservedly estimated should not be far off, because he wrote his work in the sixth age of the world, which the sacred writers say is its senescence and old age. I believe that the poet, as an excellent mathematician, had seen through astrology that in the future there were to be certain revolutions of the heavens through the benevolence of which avarice would altogether cease. These will certainly be Golden Ages in which this will occur, provided it comes soon. The Greyhound will therefore be such an influence that shall be born "between heaven and heaven," or rather, that prince who shall be produced by such an influence. Whence he will say later on, "I see it clearly and therefore I tell it." And certainly in the year 1484, on the twenty-fifth day of November at 13 hours and 41 minutes of that day, there will be the conjunction of Saturn and Jupiter in Scorpio in the ascendant of the fifth degree of Libra, which demonstrates a change of religion. And because Jupiter prevails over Saturn, it signifies that such a change will be for the better. Therefore, as there can be no religion more true than ours, I have firm hope that the Christian republic will be reduced to an excellent life and government. In such a form that we could truly say: **Now the Virgin returns, the Saturnian kingdoms return** <note>original: "Iá redit & uirgo redeūt saturnia regna"; a quote from Virgil's Fourth Eclogue predicting a new Golden Age.</note>. Nor does a third opinion of learned men displease me, who say that Dante, being a great lover of the teaching of Virgil, wished in this place to be ambiguous and obscure in imitation of that passage of the *Bucolics* where he says: **Now the Virgin returns, the Saturnian kingdoms return, a new progeny is sent down from high heaven** <note>original: "Iam redit & uirgo redeunt saturnia regna lá noua progenies celo demittit' alto"</note>. Which verses have such obscurity and are so ambiguous that some interpret them as the coming of Christ according to the verses of the Sibyl; others understand Octavian; others the son of Pollio; and others still other things. Therefore, let the reader take from these expositions the one he judges best fits the text. Or if he finds a more convenient one, let him set these aside and with his own industry illuminate those who walk through the darkness. **OF THAT humble Italy he shall be the salvation:** By Italy, understand every country where one lives under the Christian religion. And he used Italy for the whole as the most principal part, and for many other very well-known reasons, and especially because the Apostolic See and the head of the Christians is at Rome in Italy. He said "humble" perhaps in imitation of Virgil, in whom he had read: **And we see humble Italy** <note>original: "Humilē que uidemus Italjá"</note>. Or rather he said "humble" not because it was humble then, but because it will be humble and devout when avarice ceases. But so that we may understand the force of this word "humble," <term>humus</term> in Latin means earth. Whence "humble," which means not high nor elevated, but low and depressed, and almost touching the earth, which among the four elements is the lowest. And then by "translation" <note>metaphor</note> we call a man "humble" who lowers himself and makes himself more inferior and of less esteem than his genius, or merits, or state, or condition requires. And this sometimes proceeds from pusillanimity and cowardice of spirit, which causes us to fail in magnanimous enterprises and not take that daring and frankness that befits an excellent spirit. And this is a vice condemned by all true doctrine. And in this sense the ancient Latins used it, saying "humble" meaning vile and cowardly, and it means "humble" that is, low and ignoble of lineage. Whence Petrarch says: "And many others who were of humble nation." Therefore he calls it a "humble nation," meaning ignoble. Sometimes humility is taken by theologians not for cowardice of spirit, which is a vice, but for a virtue which they want to be a kind of innocence. Justice has several parts within itself, among which is innocence. And innocence is justice through which you do not inflict injury, nor violence, nor villainy upon anyone. The

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante's Inferno, Canto I. After discussing the "Veltro" (the Greyhound) as a savior, Landino provides a historical and mythological breakdown of the figures Dante mentions—Camilla, Euryalus, Turnus, and Nisus—linking their deaths to the birth of the Roman Empire. He then shifts into a deep philosophical and Platonic analysis of the human soul, specifically the conflict between Reason and Appetite.</meta>

# CANTO FIRST

Innocence has in itself two properties: humility and gentleness. And humility is that by which, not out of baseness but out of humanity, we submit ourselves of our own will and depart from and withdraw from our glory and excellence. **FOR WHOM the virgin Camilla died:** He says this as if referring to the part of Italy where Rome is, which, through the greed of the popes, is more oppressed by this vice <note>Landino refers to Avarice</note> than other parts. Because the death of these four names mentioned in the text results from the struggle to obtain the Latin empire, which is the origin and principle of the Roman Empire. Therefore, that Italy for which Euryalus and Nisus died to obtain, and for which Camilla and Turnus died to defend. Euryalus and Nisus were distinguished young men in the army of Aeneas, of whom Virgil makes mention in the fifth book when he describes the games; and later in the ninth, sent by Ascanius to meet Aeneas, they encountered the men-at-arms that King Latinus was sending to Turnus. By these, Euryalus was killed first, and then Nisus, who avenged him as a most dear friend and, fighting bravely, was finally killed. Camilla was the daughter of Metabus, King of the Volsci, where Priverno is located (a city called Piperno in our times). They say that Metabus, driven from his kingdom and fleeing enemies who pursued him, arrived with Camilla in his arms (whom he was still nursing) at the river Amasenus; despairing of being able to cross with her, he wrapped her in cork bark, tied her to the spear he had in his hand, and threw it to the other bank; the spear fixed itself in the ground and preserved Camilla so she did not perish. Later, staying hidden in the forests, he nourished her with the milk of wild beasts. And because in throwing her he had vowed her to Diana, he wished that as she grew, according to the custom of Diana, she should exercise herself in hunting and use the bow and the spear. Wherefore she became so vigorous that, having returned to her kingdom after the death of her father and there being war between the Latins and Trojans, she came to the aid of the Latins; and in fighting, she took the lives of many. But finally, she was killed by Arruns the Trojan, who placed himself in ambush to treacherously shoot her with an arrow. Turnus, son of Daunus (wherefore Puglia is sometimes called Daunia by poets), was King of the Rutulians; and before Aeneas came to Italy, he had been betrothed to Lavinia, daughter of King Latinus. Later, because Latinus, encouraged by oracles and various prodigies, gave her to Aeneas who had already arrived in Italy, Turnus, enraged and with the help of his mother-in-law Amata, turned Latinus against him and moved him to make war on Aeneas. In this war, Turnus was the captain of the Latins; and with his courage and sword, he did marvelous things and killed Pallas, son of Evander and a soldier of Aeneas. But in the end, Aeneas killed him. Wherefore Petrarch elegantly said: *I saw him who wept for Antandros; the death of Creusa took away his love from him who took his son from Evander.* <note>original: "Vidi colui che pianſe Antandro... ad Euandro." This refers to Aeneas, who lost his wife Creusa but killed Turnus, the one who killed Evander's son, Pallas.</note> Evander was King of Pallanteum, which city was where Rome later stood. Giovanni Boccaccio reports in the *Book of Genealogies* that in the time of Emperor Henry III, the body of Pallas was disinterred not far from Rome; it was still intact and so large that, standing upright, it surpassed the Roman walls. **HE shall hunt her through every town:** He says this meaning that just as in vicious ages justice was driven from the earth and returned to heaven from whence it had descended, so in this happy time, avarice, driven from the earth, shall be sent back to Hell, to which the envy that the Devil bears toward man had led it. Although man exists in his free will and in his hand is placed both death and life, nonetheless the Devil—who was envious of human happiness, seeing that man was to succeed to his place in the glory of heaven from which he had been cast out—tempted the first man so much that he made him a transgressor of the commandments of God, from which proceeded avarice and all other sins. Because it is true that envy moved avarice from Hell. We can also say that avarice proceeds from Hell because riches—from the greed for which avarice proceeds—are in Hell, that is, in the lowest part of the world, which is the earth, because they consist either in possessions of the earth or in metals and stones that are beneath the earth. Wherefore the ancients held that Pluto, god of Hell, was also the god of riches; and the rich man in Latin is called *dives* from this name *Dis*, which signifies Pluto. Avarice came, then, from Hell, that is, from the greed for lowly things; and he <note>the Greyhound</note> will drive it back into Hell because avarice is extinguished when we despise riches and leave them in the depths as a lowly thing. And we can also say that the greed for riches is born of envy: for man would be content with little if he did not see others having more than he. But seeing high palaces, jewels, fabrics, horses, and other similar things, he is moved by envy to seek the same for himself. Wherefore Jerome rightly said: *The eyes are those through which we cannot bear poverty.* <note>original: "Oculi fũt p quos paupertaté ferre nõ poſſumus"</note> Envy is nothing other than sadness and pain of the soul which we take from the prosperous things of others, even though they do not harm us.

> Wherefore, for your own good, I think and discern
> That you should follow me, and I will be your guide,
> And I will lead you from here through an eternal place
> Where you shall hear the desperate shrieks
> Of those ancient spirits in sorrow,
> Where each cries out for the second death;
> And then you shall see those who are content
> Within the fire, because they hope to come,
> Whenever it may be, to the blessed people.
> To whom, if you then wish to ascend,
> There shall be a soul worthier than I for that;
> With her I will leave you at my departure;
> For that Emperor who reigns above,
> Because I was rebellious to His law,
> Wills not that through me one comes into His city.
> In every part He empowers, and there He reigns;
> There is His city and His high throne:
> Oh, happy is he whom He chooses to be there!

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial O featuring a seated figure in a circular frame within a square border.</image-desc>
A most excellent conclusion to the proposal. Because if it was necessary for Dante to exit the forest, and if the way he had already set upon was forbidden to him by the beast, and if by himself he knew no other path, it was necessary that he have a leader and guide to conduct him to safety. This, Virgil promises him; and the poet proceeds with an excellent allegory. In order that this may be better understood, we must remember that in man there is Reason (or Mind) and Appetite. The former, like a queen, ought to hold dominion over all of life and rule and command; and the latter, like a servant, is bound to obey the precepts of Reason. Appetite is of two species: one is placed in Reason and always obeys it, and is called the Will; the other is in the Senses, and is a friend to them, being contumacious, rebellious, and disobedient to Reason. This, among modern philosophers and theologians, has no other name than Appetite. But the ancient Latins called it *libido*, that is, unbridled concupiscence, alienated and rebellious from all reason. Similarly, Reason is divided into two parts: one is called Superior and operates concerning universals—as, for example, if it is the proper office of the king to tame the proud and those who are not patient toward reason, and to defend the innocent from a tyrannical life. The other is called Inferior, which operates concerning particulars—for example, if it is a duty of the Florentine Republic to provide aid in these times to Pope Sixtus against the Turk. The Superior part is in the contemplative life, and the Inferior in the active life. I leave aside many subdivisions of the mind and the appetite. But I will not omit that only the appetite is that which moves the soul either to desire what appears good to it, or to flee what is or appears evil. Because the divine Plato, wishing to express the essence and powers of our soul, said:

it is like a chariot whose yoke is winged and is pulled by two horses: one white, beautiful, and well-made, and one black, ugly, and ill-made; and upon the chariot, he places the charioteer, that is, the ruler of the horses. The chariot, then, is the essence of the soul; the horses that pull it are the appetite; by the white, he means the rational appetite, and by the black, the irrational.

<meta>This page continues the philosophical commentary on Canto I of the Inferno. Having previously discussed the historical figures who died for Italy, Landino now shifts to a deeply Platonic and Aristotelian analysis of the human soul, specifically focusing on the conflict between Reason and Appetite, and the distinction between the Active and Contemplative lives.</meta>

# INFERNO.

This was not unknown to the divine genius of **Petrarch**, who, wishing to show that in himself appetite was disobedient to reason, describes it in the likeness of a black horse <note>A reference to the Chariot Allegory in Plato's *Phaedrus*, where the soul is a charioteer with two horses: one noble (will) and one rebellious (appetite).</note>, saying:
> So strayed my mad desire <note>Original: "Si trafeurato el folle mio desio." Landino is quoting Petrarch's Sonnet 6.</note>
> In following her who is turned in flight,
> And from the snares of love, graceful and free,
> She flies before my slow running;
> For the more I strive to follow her,
> Through the safe path the less she guides me.
> Nor does it avail me to spur it or turn it,
> For love by its nature makes it restive.
> But then as it gathers the bit by force to itself,
> I remain in lordship of it,
> Which against my will carries me to death.

The Platonic poet thus demonstrates that the black horse carries us to death because irrational appetite leads us to vice, which is the death of the soul. The chariot, therefore, is our soul. The horses are the appetite. And the charioteer, or rather the orator, is the mind and reason which rules and governs the soul. The reader should therefore commit this division to memory, not only for the explanation of this text, but because it will be necessary many times in the course of this work.

But to return to our purpose: **Dante**, who desires to leave the forest and climb the mountain but cannot because he is hindered by the beasts already mentioned, signifies the rational appetite obedient to the "lower reason," that is, to the **active life**. This life by itself cannot come to bliss, which consists in the doctrine and knowledge of celestial things, because the active life contains within it "beasts"—that is, various disturbances of the soul. As long as a man is disquieted by these, he cannot have a soul as tranquil as is necessary for one who wishes to be fit and suitable for **contemplation**.

He who is the Truth itself <note>Jesus Christ</note> expressed this marvelously in the Gospel of Matthew <note>Landino mistakenly attributes this to Matthew; the story of Mary and Martha is found in Luke 10:38–42.</note>. Setting **Mary** for the contemplative life and **Martha** for the active life, He says Martha is full of cares and labors and takes on disturbances in many things, while Mary has chosen the "best part," which never abandons the soul. This is because the active life and civil operations (signified by Martha) last only as long as we live in this present mortal life. But the contemplation of divine things is never taken from us and follows us into the other life, which is eternal.

**Dante** desires but cannot climb the mountain. Wherefore **Virgil**, who signifies "superior reason" and science and the contemplative life, looking upon Dante’s good will, is moved to compassion. Sent by the Graces (of whom we shall speak below), he promises his help. But it should be noted that Virgil signifies only the "doctrine of the gentiles" <note>Ancient Greco-Roman philosophy and wisdom.</note> through which we can know vices and, having known them, purge ourselves of them. But this is not enough without Christian **theology** to give us that knowledge of celestial things in which our bliss consists. For this reason, Virgil offers to guide him through Hell and Purgatory—that is, to show him the nature of vice and how he may be purged of it—but he will not be able to lead him to Paradise. Let this be said briefly for the exposition of this passage; now returning to the text, it follows: **WHEREFORE I for your better think and discern.**

"Wherefore," that is, "for which reason," is the conclusion of all the words already spoken. **Think** and **discern** are different acts. For we "think" when, seeking the best in a thing, we go about examining and weighing all the parts to understand which of them all is the one to be most valued. Afterwards, having examined them all, we "discern," which is to choose the best, and that we elect. Here it should be noted that every choice a man takes must be prudently considered.

**Prudence**, according to **Plato** and **Aristotle**, is a certain reason with which we rightly administer all things in the active and civil life. To this, Aristotle, in the sixth book of the *Ethics*, attributes good consultation, skill <note>Original: *solertia*.</note>, sagacity, and judgment <note>Original: *sententia*.</note>. As the same Aristotle sets down in his book on the Republic <note>The *Politics*.</note>, there are two things in which every commendation of right action and government consists: first, that the end we propose for ourselves be true and right; second, that we find the things which lead us to the proposed end.

Therefore, for Prudence (whose end is to arrange all human operations rightly and with the best method and order), several things are necessary: first, all the virtues that lead us to the end and those that operate around the end. And first is **consultation**. This is nothing other than a diligent inquiry into those things that lead us to the end. Counsel has three offices: first, it investigates if any way is found that leads us to the end. Second, if several ways are found, which they are. And having found one or more, in the third place it seeks in what way we can use them. All this is within deliberation and consultation.

After this follows **judgment**. Its office, once we have found the aforementioned paths, is to dispute and weigh which of them is most suitable, or most honest, or most useful. Once judgment is given, **election** follows, which is nothing other than taking that which we have already judged to be better. The philosophers define "election" as a consulted appetite and desire for those things that guide us to the end. Counsel is right and directed by good consultation and skill. "Consulting well" is nothing other than leading conveniently to a good end through honest ways and means. And **skill** <note>Original: *solertia*.</note> is a prompt and wakeful investigation of the paths and means already mentioned. Judgment becomes perfect through **sagacity**, which is right and most prompt judgment, and also through **sentence** <note>Original: *sententia*.</note>, which they define as the judgment of goodness and equity.

Wishing, therefore, to persuade Dante to follow him, Virgil wanted to show that he had taken such a course with perfect prudence. When he said **I THINK**, he placed counsel investigated with good consultation and skill. And when he said **I DISCERN**, he placed judgment aided by sagacity and election. For this reason, Dante must consent to the path taken with all the parts of prudence.

But let him who reads understand that our order and purpose is this: every time that, through the interpretation of the text, it happens that we must explain some point of philosophy or another science, I will strive to show it in its entirety with brevity. This is so that if it is touched upon again in some part by the poet, the reader can return to the same place where the whole is explained. In this way, the reader will have everything collected together, and we will not have to repeat the same thing many times.

Up to here, we have seen that if Dante—that is, the lower reason with rational appetite—wishes to arrive at knowledge, he must follow Virgil—that is, superior reason and speculative science. Virgil promises to lead him out of this "low place" of sensory and material things, guiding him first through the knowledge of vices. And he calls it an **eternal place**, either because Hell (that is, the pains of the damned) shall have no end—wherefore it says below, "Before me were no things created but eternal, and I eternal last"—or because science is not of particulars, which are corruptible, but of universals, which are eternal and incorruptible.

**DESPERATE way:** Because they are without hope. This desperation increases the pain of the damned just as the hope of one day being free lessens the pain for those in Purgatory. And therefore he says of these that they are **content in the fire**, because they hope to come to bliss after their purgation, whether it be long or short.

And he says that the damned cry out, that is, shouting they ask for the **second death**. Here some believe the "second death" will be the second damnation at the final judgment given by Christ on the Day of Judgment; when the souls are reunited with their bodies, both together will be damned. They say the damned do this moved by envy, meaning that they will then have more companions. But it pleases me more that by the "first death" we understand the separation of the soul from the body, and by the "second death" we understand that they desire that even the soul, already separated, might become mortal and be annihilated. For the pain is so great that they would rather be nothing than be in such labors.

**TO WHOM then you will wish to ascend:** To those blessed people, that is, to Paradise. **A SOUL shall be more worthy of this than I:** And here he means **Beatrice**, whom he sets for Christian theology, which alone can lead to Paradise. And not I, Virgil, who (because I was rebellious to the law of that Emperor who reigns above, that is, the Supreme God) cannot enter. For the Gospel law says:
> Unless one is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven. <note>Original Latin: *Nisi quis renatus fuerit ex aqua & spiritu sancto nō intrabit in regnū celorum*. John 3:5.</note>
Virgil, that is, the poet himself...

<summary>Landino provides a philosophical commentary on Dante's soul, using Plato's chariot allegory and the biblical figures of Martha and Mary to distinguish between the active and contemplative lives. He explains that Virgil (Human Reason) can lead Dante through vice and purgation, but Beatrice (Theology) is required for Paradise.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Cristoforo Landino’s commentary on Canto I of the Inferno. Following the previous discussion on the nature of the soul and the struggle between reason and appetite, Landino here explains why Virgil—representing human reason or pagan philosophy—is unable to lead Dante directly to Paradise, and interprets Dante’s plea for guidance through the lens of theological and moral philosophy.</meta>

# FIRST

<b>b</b>

<margin>
...he who
...you possessed
...narrating
...that Virgil in
...also for
...Wherefore Persius
</margin>

And Virgil, representing also the knowledge of the gentiles <note>Pagan Greeks and Romans.</note>, was rebellious because such knowledge does not lead to paradise—that is, to the knowledge of divine things. **IN ALL** parts <unclear>it is subject to God</unclear>. Wherefore the Apostle says: *At the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of things in heaven, and things in earth* <note>original: "In nomine iesu omne genus flectatur celestium terre"; Philippians 2:10.</note>. His royal throne is in heaven, in the manner that we shall demonstrate in the first canto of *Paradiso*. Wherefore it is said: *The heaven of heavens is the Lord's* <note>original: "celum celi domino"; Psalm 115:16.</note>. Likewise: *He that dwelleth in the heavens shall laugh at them* <note>original: "qui habitat i celis irridebit eos"; Psalm 2:4.</note>. And the same sentiment is found in the eleventh [canto] of this text, but expressed with greater love. Likewise in the first [canto] of *Paradiso*: *In that heaven which receives most of its light*. **O HAPPY** he whom he chooses there. Wherefore Christ, speaking of the highest good, said: *You who have followed me... shall receive a hundredfold, and shall inherit everlasting life* <note>original: "Vos qui secuti estis me cetuplum accipietis & uita eterna"; Matthew 19:29.</note>. Here the poet uses a rhetorical device which is called exclamation, which poets and orators use when they wish to move the listener either to indignation, or to compassion, or to wonder. In this place, Virgil uses exclamation not only to demonstrate the marvel of such great bliss, but also out of compassion for himself, being deprived of it. And certainly, it is a heavy punishment for the damned to recognize the good of which they are deprived. Wherefore Persius, the satirist poet, desires no other punishment for the vicious than that they should know how much good consists in virtue, so that they may grieve more bitterly for having abandoned it. He asks of God, therefore, that he punish them: *Let them see virtue, and pine away for having left it* <note>original: "Virtutem ut uideant intabescantque relicta"; Persius, Satire III.</note>.

---

And I to him: "Poet, I beseech you,
by that God whom you did not know,
so that I may flee this evil and worse,
that you lead me where you just said,
so that I may see the gate of Saint Peter,
and those whom you make out to be so sorrowful."
Then he moved on, and I kept behind him.

<column-break/>

**D**ante responds and prays that he might do what he has said. This denotes when the appetite and the lower reason begin to be illuminated by the higher reason; the soul turns entirely toward it and desires to achieve what is shown. Morally, it admonishes that when true doctrine is offered to a less learned person, he should show every sign of desiring it and, above all, pray for it. He prays to Virgil, therefore, saying: "by that God whom you did not know"—that is, by the true God whom you did not know in life. Virgil knew God as a gentile philosopher, as the Prime Mover and the First Cause. But he did not know distinctly the Trinity, the Incarnation of the Word, the redemption of human generation, and the other things without the 

---

knowledge and faith of which, according to the Christian religion, no one can go to bliss. And he did not say "you do not know," but said "you did not know," for you did not know in life, but at present you do know. It is a matter of great doubt whether the soul, which while joined to the body had no knowledge of God, can have it later once it is separated and damned. Nevertheless, the theologians conclude that the soul separated from the body has such sharpness of sight that it knows not by conjectures (which can be false), but by demonstrative reasons, that the light and beauty of God are infinite. This knowledge causes them the gravest pain, seeing themselves deprived of it. But they do not know Him "distinctly" <note>In this context, to know "distinctly" means to know God through the Beatific Vision, which brings joy.</note>, because from such knowledge they would take the highest joy and participate in the Highest Good. 

For example: if a youth had not been in Florence at the time of the annual celebration and pageantry performed for the Baptist <note>St. John the Baptist, the patron saint of Florence.</note>, and someone narrated to him that it was so beautiful that the youth, most greedy for such spectacles, believed it entirely and without doubt, there is no question that he would feel no small displeasure seeing himself deprived of it. This is because he sees the beauty in a confused way, which does nothing but kindle his desire to understand it distinctly and in its proper order. 

**SO THAT I MAY FLEE THIS EVIL:** that is, the evil of ignorance and vice. **AND WORSE:** that is, the damnation which follows from not knowing how much evil there is in vice. He who does not know how pestiferous vice is does not flee it, from which follows grave detriment; and from this is born another more grave, because by not fleeing it, he makes it a habit which kills the soul. **SO THAT I MAY SEE THE GATE OF SAINT PETER.** By this, understand the entrance to Purgatory. For Peter—that is, the Supreme Pontiff and all the priests who have his authority—by absolving the soul from guilt, makes it able to go to be purged; and if it were not absolved, it would be damned to Hell. It does not seem to me that one should understand this as the gate of Paradise, because Virgil has already shown above that he is not sufficient to lead him there. **THEN HE MOVED ON:** Dante, who is the rational appetite and the lower reason, prays to the higher reason to guide him to contemplation; and then reason, excited by the appetite, turns to contemplation, and Dante—that is, the appetite itself—follows behind him because he has become obedient to him.

<summary>Landino explains Virgil's status as a 'rebellious' soul due to his paganism and interprets Dante's request for guidance as the alignment of human appetite with higher reason. He clarifies that the 'Gate of St. Peter' refers to Purgatory, emphasizing the necessity of ecclesiastical absolution for the soul's journey.</summary>
<keywords>Virgil as Reason, rational appetite, lower vs higher reason, knowledge of God, pagan philosophy, Purgatory, St. Peter's Gate, Persius, Petrarch, Landino commentary</keywords>

<sig>b ii</sig>

->SECOND CANTO OF THE FIRST CANTICLE<-

**L**o, the day <unclear>was departing</unclear> and the darkened air
took <unclear>the animals</unclear> that are on earth
away from <unclear>their</unclear> labors; and I, alone,

Was preparing myself to endure the war
both of the journey and of the pity:
which the mind that does not err shall retrace.

O Muses, O high genius, now aid me;
O mind that wrote down what I saw,
here shall your nobility be revealed;

<column-break/>

**W**e can say that the preceding chapter was almost a <term>proposition</term> <note>an introductory summary of themes</note> of the entire work, through which the author not only demonstrates in brief words what he has to say throughout the whole work, but also the reason why he maintains such an order. The appetite <note>the human desire or will</note> was awakened, seeking its own good, and, illuminated by reason, it flees the forest and climbs the mountain where it sees the sun. But because of the beasts, it was forbidden from ascending. This signifies that once it is known—though not very distinctly—that the <term>supreme good</term> <note>God</note> consists in enjoying God, the soul seeks knowledge of Him in the "civil life" where <term>inferior reason</term> <note>practical human logic</note> reigns. This reason is often deceived by the senses. And where the civil virtues are not perfect, the disturbances of the soul—which seek pleasure, honor, and utility—can do much; these do not follow true joy, nor true utility (which can never be hoped for apart from what is honest), nor true honor. For honor follows virtue like a shadow follows the body; it is a reward worthy of virtue and should not, nor cannot, be given except to the good. But in place of these three, men follow the pleasure of the body, the possession of fleeting and earthly goods (which is avarice), and finally the vain glory of the world, which is ambition. No one can reach

<note>The following section contains a printer's duplication of several lines from the previous paragraph, a common error in early hand-pressed books.</note>

the true and sincere praise which is itself the reward of virtue and should not, nor cannot, be given except to the good. But in place of these three they follow the pleasure of the body... so that the human mind, with only inferior reason and in the civil life where the disturbances that father all vices are powerful, cannot come to the sun. But yet, being desirous of it, the soul deserves to be succored by Virgil—that is, by <term>superior reason</term> <note>divinely inspired logic or philosophy</note> and by doctrine. This shows him that if he wishes to go to Paradise—that is, to happiness—it is necessary first to pass through Hell and Purgatory; that is, to descend into the knowledge of vices and, having known them, to purge oneself of them. Once the mind remains purged of these, it can then easily come to the knowledge of divine things, where beatitude consists. And Virgil rightly promises to lead Dante safely through Hell and Purgatory, but confesses he cannot lead him to Paradise because, as we have said, <term>philosophical science</term> can give us the knowledge of vices and instruct us in how to purge them, but it cannot lead us to Paradise—that is, to the knowledge of divine things. For this is the proper science of the Sacred Theology of Christians. Therefore, one can truly say that the first canto stood in place of a "proposition." In this second chapter, he places the <term>invocation</term> <note>a prayer to the Muses or God for inspiration</note>, which we showed above to be the second principal part of the whole work. And afterward, he moves a doubt to Virgil, distrusting that he is sufficient to make such a journey, since he is neither Aeneas nor the Apostle Paul. After which doubt, Virgil comforts him to follow, and gives him firm hope by demonstrating to him that he does not come by his own strength alone (which perhaps would not be sufficient), but that one has come from Heaven who demands it. He begins then: "THE DAY was departing," and he performs a <term>chronography</term> <note>a description of time</note>. He shows the author had descended into Hell in the nighttime. This he feigns truly because one goes into Hell by night—that is, through the darkness of ignorance—because every sin comes from ignorance when disordered appetite extinguishes the light of reason in us. For this reason, some ancient philosophers said that it was easy to go to Hell because one went there with eyes closed; and Virgil said: <note>original: "Ibant obscuri sola sub nocte per umbras"</note> "They went along, shrouded in darkness, under the lonely night, through the shadows." Or truly, by the night, he wishes to show the nighttime vigils which are necessary for anyone who wishes to make progress in the contemplation of great things; and the mind is much more sharpened in nightly studies because it is free from all the noise and tumult of the day. He shows, therefore, that at that hour in which the night comes and spreads darkness through all our hemisphere, all animals give themselves to sleep and rest, while he alone prepared himself to "sustain the war." This passage is drawn from the fourth book of Virgil <note>The Aeneid</note> where he depicts Dido staying awake through grief and taking her rest in that hour when all animals repose. "AND THE darkened AIR." The air is a <term>diaphanous</term> body <note>transparent</note>, but by its nature dark if it is not illuminated by the sun or other light. Therefore, when the sun descends to the other hemisphere, the shadow of the earth spreads through ours and makes night. For night is nothing other than the shadow of the earth. "TOOK the animals that are on earth from their labors": Because the night, being useless for performing any work due to its darkness, invites animals to sleep, which is a great recreation for the body. Allegorically, he shows that he alone—that is, the man given to <term>speculation</term> <note>contemplation or deep study</note>, who is "alone" because it is necessary that he live in solitude and separated from every crowd and frequency and tumult that impedes thought—consumes the night in speculating, while other men and animals who seek the comforts of the body consume it in sleeping. Therefore, "I alone," meaning I placed in solitude. Or truly "I alone" demonstrating that the contemplative are alone and very few; whence Petrarch says: <note>original: "povera & nuda vai philosophia"</note> "Philosophy, you go poor and naked," and "the crowd, intent on base gain... few companions will you have on your path." And certainly, because man, considering this composite of soul and body, always seeks company, one does not find anyone living solitary except either he who through a melancholic humor has corrupted his imagination and become almost a beast, or he who through highness of genius, hoping for human things, transcends with speculation toward divine things. Whence Aristotle rightly says in the *Politics*: "he who leaves the sociable and civil life has become either a beast or more than a man." "PREPARED to sustain the war, both of the journey and of the pity." The literal sense is that walking through dark places was laborious, and the pains of the damned moved him to pity. But allegorically, he shows that one cannot go into Hell—that is, have true knowledge of vices—without war and combat; because in this, the soul often combats with itself, since the sensory part tires in contemplation and flees such labor, while the mind and the intellect seek to understand, because "the spirit is willing and the flesh is weak." Furthermore, it is a "war" because appetite judges the same thing differently than reason. For example: in defrauding one's family of their due food, the appetite of the miser falsely judges that this is a virtue called parsimony, and reason truly judges that it should be called avarice. He was therefore prepared to sustain this war; likewise the "war of pity." For we cannot know vices without also knowing that they proceed from the infirmity and imbecility of human nature, which proceeds from the bodily mass that weighs down the soul. And this rightfully moves to compassion anyone who enters into such speculation. Whence: <note>original: "Vidit deus figmentum nostrum & misertus est nostri"</note> "God saw our frame and had mercy on us." And for this same reason, Heraclitus the Ephesian, seeing continuously the infinite errors in human life, wept perpetually, moved by compassion for its misery. "WHICH" (that is, the wretched path and the pity) "my mind shall redraw," as if describing it and committing it to letters. For it was not the hand of the poet (which is an instrument) but the mind (in which he has such knowledge) that wrote. "SHALL REDRAW, the mind that does not err": He captures attention and goodwill here. For we become well-disposed and listen attentively to that writer who promises us to write true things without error. And most excellently he said, "The mind that does not [err]..."

The commentary by Landino explains the allegorical significance of the night as the darkness of ignorance and the necessity of "superior reason" (Virgil) to overcome vice.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the opening of Canto II, focusing on the philosophical definitions of the soul and the invocation of the Muses and Genius.</meta>

# INFERNO

<margin>
In the particulars where true knowledge is not permitted and the incorruptible heals the body and the mind. Furthermore...
</margin>

...errs. Because the lower reason, which administers the practical and civil life through prudence, can err; but the mind—that is, the intellect and the higher reason—cannot err because it exercises itself in universals. But so that we may better understand what the "mind" is, I say that although our soul is one and indivisible, it nonetheless has various and diverse names according to its various powers and virtues. Insofar as it gives life to the body, it is called the soul. Insofar as it feels, it is called Sense. Insofar as it possesses wisdom, it is called the spirit. Insofar as it understands, it is called the intellect. When it discerns, it is called reason. When it remembers, it is called memory. That rational and intellectual light with which we perform discourse and understanding is called the "mind" by philosophers. This mind is formed in the image and likeness of God, by whom it is shaped without the mediation of any other nature. It is called "mind" <note>Italian: *mente*</note> because it is the most eminent or excellent part of the spirit. In short, the mind is the eye of our soul. The gaze of this mind is reason, and its seeing is the intellect. It is therefore necessary for every rational soul to have this eye healthy and to look with it in order to see. This eye is healthy when it is purged and removed from all desire for mortal things. It looks when it fixes its eyes upon the light of God. And finally, it sees when, in that contemplation, it knows how much joy, how much gladness, how much serenity, and how much delight there is. To repeat: health makes this eye serene, the gaze makes it direct, and seeing makes it blessed. 

The mind, therefore—this light of the spirit—will "retrace" <note>original: *ritrarra*</note>, that is, it will express and demonstrate where the eye was fixed and what it saw and knew. He most excellently used the word "retrace," meaning to demonstrate openly. For we say one "retraces" or "portrays" when a painter or sculptor resembles something in its own likeness in such a way that it is recognized in the work as if it were the thing itself. In this way, we say that Apelles <note>the most famous painter of ancient Greece</note> portrayed Alexander the Great, and Giotto portrayed Dante, because he formed him in such a way that whoever saw the painting saw Dante. Thus, the poet's mind will paint with words what he achieved in contemplation. 

**O MUSES**: Hesiod writes in his *Theogony* that the Muses are the daughters of Jove and Mnemosyne (that is, Memory). He adds that Jove joined with her on Mount Pierius for nine nights, from which the nine Muses were born. Their names are: Clio, Euterpe, Thalia, Melpomene, Terpsichore, Erato, Polyhymnia, Urania, and Calliope, who is the most excellent above all others. Macrobius <note>a 5th-century Roman philosopher</note> holds that there are nine to demonstrate through the first eight the song of the eight celestial spheres, and through the ninth, the harmony and consonance that arises from them. This was perhaps the reason Hesiod said Calliope, the ninth, is the most beautiful. Anaximander of Lampsacus and Xenophanes of Heracleopolis demonstrate that the nine Muses signify nine things which generate the voice: first, four teeth struck by the tongue (without which a hiss is born rather than a voice); then the two lips; the tongue; the hollow of the palate; and the arteries that produce the breath from the lungs. Finally, because Apollo is placed with the Muses, they add the lungs for Apollo. 

**Clio** signifies fame, because the Muses acquire fame for those who exercise them and those praised by poets. **Euterpe** signifies delight, which is great for those who write verses and those who hear them. **Thalia** is named because in Greek *Thallin* means "to turn green" or "to bloom" <note>original: *riuirdiure*</note>; thus we say a "thallus," and the memory of poets always blooms anew. **Melpomene** means song, because song is proper to poets. **Terpsichore** means joy, which poets give in the highest degree. **Erato** means love, without which one cannot endure the great labor of writing a poem. **Polyhymnia** means memory of many things, without which there can be no perfect poetry. **Urania** means celestial, because as we said above, poetry is a celestial thing. **Calliope** means "good song," because no music delights as much as a well-composed poem. 

**O HIGH GENIUS** <note>original: *alto ingegno*</note> **now aid me**: The Latins call "genius" that force of the spirit by which we are capable of learning. This has two parts: one is that sharpness with which we each tend to investigate and learn, which the ancient Latins call "docility" and modern philosophers call "apprehension." The second is that virtue by which we retain what we have already understood, and this is called memory. Therefore, "O high genius" means "O power of the spirit fit to achieve the knowledge of great things." For this reason, Augustine said that genius is that power of the spirit with which the spirit sharpens and exercises itself to know what it did not yet know. Thus it is defined: "That genius is the extension of the intellect to the knowledge of the unknown" <note>original: *Quod ingenium sit extentio intellectus ad incognitorum cognitionem*</note>. Therefore, the genius investigates, and the reason judges the things investigated by the genius, and the memory stores them once judged. 

**O MIND THAT WROTE DOWN**: We showed above what power in the soul is called the mind. But often writers use "mind" to mean "memory," as Virgil does: "The judgment of Paris remains stored deep in her mind" <note>original: *Manet alta mente repostum iudicium paridis*</note>. And so here the poet turns to his memory, saying, "O memory, which wrote down," meaning "you who made a record and retained within yourself all that I saw." For writing is that which makes us remember, and thus we may say, "write this in your memory." **HERE SHALL YOUR NOBILITY BE REVEALED**: He says this as if to say that if he can remember all of his contemplation, his memory will certainly be noble.

---

<columns>2</columns>

I began: "Poet, who guides me,
look at my virtue, if it be powerful,
before you trust me to the deep pass.

You say that the father of Silvius <note>Aeneas</note>,
while still corruptible, went to the
immortal world and was there in his senses.

But if the adversary of all evil <note>God</note>
was courteous, thinking of the high effect
that should come from him, and who and what he was,

It does not seem unworthy to a man of intellect
that he was chosen in the empyrean heaven
as the father of noble Rome and her empire.

Which Rome and which empire, to tell the truth,
were established for the holy place
where the successor of the greatest Peter sits.

For this journey, for which you give him glory,"

<column-break/>

Here the author moves a doubt to Virgil, his guide, and demonstrates that his spirit is not sufficient for such an arduous path—that is, such a difficult undertaking. Morally, he admonishes that no one should undertake an enterprise beyond their strength. Hence Horace: "You who write, choose a subject equal to your strength, and turn it over long in your mind, what your shoulders can bear and what they refuse" <note>original: *sumite materiam uestris qui scribitis equam uiribus. & uersate diu quid ferre recusent quid ualeant humeri*</note>. And he adds that although Aeneas and Paul went, he knows himself not to be equal to such men, and should not expect that what succeeded for them will succeed for him. We have shown above that making this journey is nothing other than going toward the knowledge of things. One goes there either to stay in that contemplation and live the contemplative life, or to speculate, and by speculating, to investigate what the virtues are by which the active life is governed. For example: if man is a civil animal, and what a "city" is, and into how many parts it is divided; if the moral virtues are necessary to civil life; and if in general there are more than three—Justice, Fortitude, and Temperance—and into how many species these three are divided. And because Prudence, one of the intellectual virtues, is added as a guide to the moral virtues. And many other similar things. Therefore, he very wisely shows that two have made this path: Aeneas and Paul, placing the first for the active life and the second for the contemplative life. Because Aeneas was a builder of cities and a just administrator of the republic, and Paul went so high with his vision...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante's Inferno, Canto II. The previous page discussed the nature of the "mind" as the highest part of the soul; here, the commentator transitions into the specific examples of Aeneas and St. Paul as predecessors to Dante’s journey.</meta>

# CANTO TWO

...heard things that were the cause
of his victory and of the papal mantle.
**Afterward, the vessel of election went there** <note>St. Paul is the "vessel of election" (Latin: *vas electionis*), chosen by God to spread the Gospel.</note>
**to bring comfort to that faith**
**which is the beginning of the way of salvation.**
**But I, why should I go there? Or who allows it?**
**I am not Aeneas, I am not Paul;**
**neither I nor anyone else believes me worthy of it.**
**Because if I surrender myself to coming,**
**I fear the journey may be folly.**
**You are wise and understand me better than I speak.**

<column-break/>

contemplation <note>The text begins mid-word with "-culatione," likely *speculatione* (contemplation or study).</note> that he was caught up even to the third heaven and saw those things which it is not permitted for man to speak of. Dante thus demonstrates his terror at such a great undertaking, for which he judges his own strength insufficient. And in truth, the human mind can by itself understand things lower than itself, but not those superior to it. He then shows that if Aeneas and Paul went there, it was granted to them by special grace from God. It was granted to Aeneas because from his successors the Roman Empire was to be established, and Rome finally was to be the head of the Christian republic and the seat of the Apostolic Church. It was granted to Paul so that he might illuminate the Christian faith.

Dante says then to Virgil—that is, the lower reason speaking to the higher—"before we begin the journey, you who understand more, consider if my virtue (that is, human virtue) is powerful enough by itself before you trust me to the 'high pass'" (meaning the great undertaking). He rightly said "pass" <note>Italian: *passo*</note> because one who walks takes steps; and here he describes his contemplation in the form of a pilgrimage and a journey. He says "HIGH" <note>Italian: *alto*</note> or rather "deep," just as we say the "high sea" for the deep sea, referring here to the descent into Hell. Or, better yet, he says "high" because nothing is a higher thing than such an investigation which reaches even to the Divine Essence.

THE PARENT OF SILVIUS: that is, the father, as the Latins say. This was Aeneas, whose genealogy is this: Dardanus, son of Jove and of the daughter of Atlas named Electra, came to Troy, which according to Eusebius <note>A 4th-century Christian historian.</note> was in the thirty-fifth year of Moses and the year of the world 3737. He fathered Erichthonius, who was his successor in the kingdom and reigned forty-seven years. He left as son and successor Tros, from whom that region, previously called Dardania, was renamed Troy. Ganymede was born to Tros, and from Ganymede came Ilus, from whom the city of Troy took the name Ilium. Ilus fathered Laomedon, father of Priam. There was also a son of Tros and brother of Ganymede named Assaracus, who fathered Capys, and Capys fathered Anchises, and Anchises fathered Aeneas. While still in Troy, he fathered Ascanius by his wife Creusa, daughter of King Priam. Afterward in Italy, Aeneas having acquired the empire of Latinus, he left Ascanius as his successor. But there is doubt whether it was the one he fathered in Troy by Creusa or the one he fathered in Italy by Lavinia. This man founded Alba and left Silvius as successor, from whom was born Aeneas Silvius, after whom all subsequent kings were called "Silvii."

And these were, in order: Latinus, Alba, Atys, Capys, Capetus, and Tiberinus (from whom the river Tiber, formerly called Albula, took its name). Tiberinus was succeeded by Agrippa, from whom was born Romulus Silvius, and from him Aventinus (who gave his name to the Aventine, one of the seven hills of Rome). After him reigned Proca, and from Proca was born Numitor, and from Numitor came Romulus, the founder of the Roman people. Therefore, the "parent of Silvius" (Aeneas), according to Virgil, went to the underworld. Virgil uses Aeneas to represent the man who desires to reach the Supreme Good. And since happiness is placed in the contemplation of divine things, he has him come to Italy, using Italy to represent the contemplative life. Once arrived in Italy, he follows the Sibyl and descends into the subterranean and infernal places. There he finds Tartarus—the place where the souls of wicked sinners are punished with eternal sufferings—and other places where lesser sinners stay until they are purged. Finally, he reaches the Elysian Fields, where the souls of the blessed reside.

Through all of this, he demonstrates allegorically that once Aeneas reached Italy (contemplation), he first investigated the nature of vices, then purged himself of them, and once purged, could contemplate the things in which blessedness consists—as I have written more extensively in our allegories. Therefore, both of these poets <note>Dante and Virgil.</note>, though their readings are different, nevertheless move toward the same end.

STILL CORRUPTIBLE: meaning still alive and joined to the body, which is corruptible; because it is composed of the four elements, once abandoned by the soul, it corrupts and, dissolving, returns to those four elements. Allegorically, he says "corruptible" because he places him in the active life, which is corruptible. TO THE IMMORTAL WORLD he went: because Hell, as we shall say below, is eternal. Allegorically, we understand that he went to the contemplation of the sciences, which are eternal because they deal with universals. AND IT WAS SENSIBLY: because he went while still in life and with the body, from which the senses proceed. In truth, even though we are burdened by the weight and heaviness of the body, we can still go to "Hell"—that is, to the contemplation of the things we have already discussed.

THE ADVERSARY OF EVERY EVIL is God, who is the Supreme Good; and no one can be contrary to all evil except He who is all and Supreme Good. God is so much the supreme and unique good that no other thing is good except by participation in Divine goodness. HE WAS COURTEOUS: He was liberal and gracious to Aeneas by letting him descend to Hell. THINKING OF THE HIGH EFFECT THAT WOULD COME FROM HIM: because from him came the founders of the Roman Empire, within which the Papacy and the Empire of Christians were later established. Therefore, it was a just cause to move God to grant this special grace to Aeneas, since such an end was to come from it. Thus it did not seem "unworthy" (meaning an inconvenient thing), but will seem a worthy and just thing to every man who judges with intellect and reason, considering the effect and the end.

And through these words, he secretly demonstrates what I interpreted above: that allegorically, Aeneas stands for the active life. And if it seems absurd to anyone that our poet, imitating Virgil, places Aeneas for the active life when Virgil placed him for the contemplative, I reply that the name does not give weight to the things <note>The label is less important than the concept.</note>. This could easily be demonstrated; nevertheless, we can also say that he places Aeneas for contemplation as written poetically and according to the doctrine of the pagans, and Paul for that which is according to our theology. Thus, Dante will be the third to descend to this contemplation, composed of both the aforementioned. For he writes in a poetic style and adds Christian theology to it. Thus it is a "third thing" beyond the two already mentioned. And it is perfect, mixing the sweetness and ornament of poetic eloquence with the gravity of divine science.

According to Cassiodorus <note>A 6th-century statesman and scholar.</note>, this was the characteristic of the first divine writers, when he said: <note>original: "Omnis splendor eloquentiae omnis modus poeticae elocutionis a divinis scriptoribus sumpsit exordium"</note> "All splendor of eloquence, every mode of poetic expression, took its beginning from divine writers." Certainly, the first divine writers taught through figures and metaphors, which is the proper tool of the poet. Plato, the most eloquent of all philosophers, observes this same method. Let no one believe that God forbids the doctrine of the ancients. He intended nothing else when, in a figure, He commanded His people to "spoil the Egyptians" of the vessels of gold and silver borrowed from them, and to carry them away as they fled. This means nothing other than that we should take from the pagans their gold of wisdom and their silver of eloquence. We must therefore "flee Egypt" (that is, depart from the religion of the pagans) and return to the "Promised Land" (that is, to Christian doctrine); but we should carry away their gold and silver to adorn the sacred letters. Thus did Paul, who in his epistles took many things from the poets; thus did Augustine, Jerome, Ambrose, Lactantius, Leo, and the other early Doctors. Would to God we had not degenerated from them, we others who have followed...
