<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante's Inferno, Canto II, following the explanation of Aeneas’s descent. The previous page established that Aeneas was chosen by God to found Rome, which would eventually become the seat of the Papacy. Here, the commentator Cristoforo Landino expands on the theological and cosmological significance of Rome and St. Paul’s journey, while analyzing Dante’s humble hesitation.</meta>

# INFERNO

...to grieve much that so much excellent and admirable doctrine should be written with such barbarism <note>The commentator refers to the "barbarous" or unrefined state of the Italian language before Dante elevated it</note>; and that so beautiful, shapely, and robust a body should be wrapped in such vile garments. Therefore, our poet deserves divine and immortal praise, for by embracing all of Christian theology, he illustrates and illuminates it with every poetic ornament. **THAT SHOULD ISSUE** <note>original: "CHVSCIR"</note> from him: that is, of whom he was to be the cause. Some explain "That should issue from him" because from him [Aeneas] was born Iulus Ascanius, from whom the Julian family had its origin. From this family was born Julius Caesar, the first emperor. But it is better to take the universal meaning rather than the particular. **WHO** denotes the substance; **WHICH** <note>original: "quale"</note> denotes the quality and the power. For when we say "who is he?", the answer is "Paul," because we desire to know his essence, such as whether he is a man, or a father, a citizen, or a foreigner. But when we say "of what kind" <note>original: "quale"</note>, we want to understand his quality. To which the answer is "he is learned." Therefore, this essence was to issue from him—that is, the Empire and the Papacy—and this is the "who." Which Empire and Papacy were to be very useful and salvific to the Christian republic; and this is the "of what kind." **THAT**: that is, which Aeneas was elected and predestined by God to be the father and first author. **OF THE nourishing Rome.** "Almo" <note>original: "almo"</note> in the Latin language signifies a thing that gives nourishment, increase, and maintenance, because "alere" <note>Latin: "to nourish"</note> signifies to nourish. Hence Virgil said "Alma Venus" <note>Latin: "Nourishing Venus"</note> because through her all species of living creatures are maintained and increased. Similarly, he says "Alma luce" <note>Latin: "nourishing light"</note> because light proceeds from the sun, which generates and nourishes all things. Thus he said "nourishing Rome" because she created and nourished such an Empire and Priesthood.

**IN THE empyrean heaven**: there are seven primary circles, each of which contains only one planet. These are, starting from the lowest: the Moon, Mercury, Venus, the Sun, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn. After these is the eighth heaven, which is adorned and filled with a vast number of stars, although astrologers have no knowledge of more than one thousand and twenty-two <note>Landino cites the traditional Ptolemaic star count</note>. From these, seventy-two signs <note>constellations</note> are formed, and it is called the firmament. The ninth is called the Crystalline because it is entirely transparent. And the tenth is the habitation of God and is called the Empyrean because it is all light, and light is proper to fire; thus it is called "empyrean," as if "on fire," because "pyr" <note>Greek: "fire"</note> in Greek signifies fire. He was chosen in the Empyrean heaven—that is, by God, whose providence governs all. This God dwells in the Empyrean heaven, uncircumscribed. **WHICH** Rome and which Empire the true God ordained to arise so that it would be an honored seat for the Apostolic Church, where the shepherd of the Christian flock was to reside, the successor of the first vicar of God, the Apostle Peter, whom he calls "greater": because every pontiff, in respect to the dignity he holds, can be called "Peter." And Saint Augustine, in the book *The City of God*, says Rome was created like another Babylon, and daughter of the first Babylon, through which it pleased God to conquer the whole world and reduce it to a single republic with the same laws. But returning to Peter: both for his sanctity and for having been the first, and for the doctrine received from the Holy Spirit, and especially because he founded our republic with his blood, Dante deservedly calls it a "holy place," because this seat was constituted in supreme holiness and most holily ruled by the first pontiffs. And if their successors later became degenerate <note>original: "generato," likely meaning "degenerate" or "strayed" in this context</note>, it is not because the place is not holy by its nature. **WHERE HE SITS.** <note>original: "V SIEDE"</note> That is, where he sits. For our ancestors said "U" in the place where we say "dove" <note>Modern Italian: "where"</note>, as the Sienese still say in these times. Thus Petrarch wrote: "Where [U] are the charms, where [U] are the honors."

And through this "going," **WHEREFORE**—that is, through which—you give him boast, that is, praise to Aeneas by Anchises his father, who showed him all that was to be, meaning the things that were the cause of his victory against Turnus; and from that victory was born the Empire of Rome and from that the Papacy. **Afterward, the vessel of election went there**: that is, Paul the Apostle, whom Jerome, in the preface to Genesis, writes that God chose as a chosen vessel <note>Latin: "vas electionis"</note> and a storehouse of the holy scriptures. It seems an absurd thing that Dante says Paul went to Hell, since one reads that he was "caught up" not to Hell but to the third heaven. To this one responds that in that rapture he had knowledge of Hell, Purgatory, and Paradise. He was a "vessel," that is, a receptacle of "election," meaning of the will of God. For he, above all others, understood the true sense of evangelical doctrine. **TO bring comfort.** For there can be no greater comfort to one who has no direct knowledge of a thing but believes it, than the authority and testimony of a man of great reputation. Thus, Paul testifying to part of the things he saw when he was caught up even to the third heaven greatly comforted and corroborated our faith. **THAT**: which is the beginning of our salvation. He said "beginning" because no one can be saved without faith; but it is not everything. For faith without works is dead. I would define at present what faith is, but because it will be necessary to define both this and the other two theological virtues in a more convenient place, we will defer the definition until that time.

**BUT I, why should I come?** If I am not powerful enough to support such difficulty. **Or who allows it?** As if to say: why should I deserve this special grace of being fit for such contemplation, not being equal to these others? Thus Horace said: "Is it true that whatever Maecenas does, you should also do, being so different and striving as a lesser man?" <note>Latin: "An quodcunque facit maecenas te quoque verum est / Tanto dissimilem & tanto certare minorem"</note> Likewise: "It does not happen to every man to go to Corinth." <note>Latin: "non cuius homini contingit adire chorinthum." A proverb meaning not everyone can achieve difficult things.</note> **I AM NOT Aeneas, I am not Paul**: the vigor that was in these two is not in me. That fruit cannot come from my coming. Nor yet, according to my judgment and that of others, am I worthy of such grace. And certainly, in this, the poet, beyond his doctrine, was also admirable in the ornament of his words. Because, having to mention Aeneas and Paul twice, he used an artful variety to avoid causing distaste to the ears of the listener. Thus, in the first instance, he did not use their proper names but used a rhetorical color called circumlocution <note>term: "circuitione" - speaking around a name using a description</note>, which is when what can be said with a proper name is said with many words. As when we want to say "Hercules," we say "the invincible grandson of Alcaeus." And for this reason, he said "the parent of Silvius" <note>Aeneas</note> and "the vessel of election" <note>Paul</note>, which brings ornament with it. Now, in this second place, putting the proper names, he says, "I am not Aeneas, I am not Paul." These two names bring with them gravity and authority. **Because if I surrender myself to coming.** He rightly concludes that not cowardice of soul, but reasonable fear moves him to doubt that his coming might be "folly," that is, foolish. And certainly, it would be a foolish thing to undertake what was not meant to succeed: for it is the judgment of all wise men that it is better not to begin than to have to abandon the undertaking later.

**YOU ARE WISE and understand me better than I speak.** According to the Greek Hesiod, there are three generations of men. Of these, the best are those who, through their own wisdom, know what is good and the direct path, and follow it; and these are very rare. The second generation is of those who, knowing they cannot act by themselves, willingly follow the advice of those who know and obey them. These, although they are not perfect, nonetheless deserve no small commendation, because it is no small sense to know one's own deficiency and seek a remedy for it. For "Virtue is to flee vice, and the first wisdom is to have been free from folly." <note>Latin: "Virtus est vitium fugere & sapientia prima stultitia caruisse."</note> The third generation is of those who neither know by themselves nor want the advice of others. And these are not useful in any part. Therefore, the poet places himself in the second generation. And in this place, he does several things. For first, he demonstrates morally that in great undertakings we must ask advice from the wiser. He also demonstrates the manner of asking for advice. For when we wish to be advised in something, we must first examine it ourselves with all diligence, and we will propose all the doubts that occur to us together with the matter in which we seek advice. And finally, through allegory, he demonstrates that the lower reason in universal things must submit itself to the higher. And it follows:

# CANTO SECOND

...so that from the beginning all is taken away.
Such I became on that dark slope,
so that by thinking I consumed the enterprise
which was at the beginning so swift.

<margin>Bewildered by the greatness of the undertaking, he proposes his doubts to his higher reason and almost repents, beginning to un-will what he first willed; and through this new thought—which was to consider on one hand his insufficiency and on the other the difficulty of the task—he changes his purpose and almost decides not to begin, not hoping to be able to finish. This happens to him while he is still on the "dark slope," that is, in ignorance. And he consumes and annihilates the enterprise which he had begun so suddenly. And certainly, once reason has judged something to be good, the appetite immediately desires it. But afterward, the aforementioned difficulties arise, which make him change his purpose. Therefore, Virgil responds to him thus:</margin>

"If I have well understood your word,"
replied the shadow of that magnanimous one,
"your soul is offended by cowardice,
which many times encumbers a man
so that it turns him back from an honored enterprise,
just as false seeing makes a beast shy away when it sees a shadow.
From this fear, so that you may dissolve yourself,
I will tell you why I came and what I heard
at the first point when I felt grief for you.
I was among those who are suspended,
and a lady called to me, so blessed and beautiful
that I requested her to command me.
Her eyes shone brighter than the star,
and she began to speak to me, sweet and low,
with an angelic voice in her own tongue."

<column-break/>

the will to investigate it. Afterward, made cowardly by the greatness and difficulty of the thing and by the fatigue of the mind, he becomes dismayed and would withdraw from the enterprise if higher reason did not help him. This appears in the forest—that is, in blindness—to the lower reason, which by itself was directing him toward the good path, but hindered by vices, it turns back. Whereupon the higher reason comforts it to hold a different journey than that in which the beasts are found, whom the soul desires to obey, but...

<image-desc>Large ornamental drop-cap H</image-desc> We have shown above that Dante represents himself as <term>sensuality and lower reason</term> <note>the part of the human mind dealing with practical, everyday matters and physical desires</note> and practice, which consists of particulars and can be deceived. And Virgil stands for the <term>higher reason</term> <note>intellectual and philosophical reasoning</note> illuminated by doctrine—not sacred doctrine, but that of the Gentiles—which is fit to speculate on vices and virtues and to show that vices lead to misery and virtues to the highest good. It can teach in what way we may flee vices and acquire virtues, but it cannot give true knowledge of divine things, which Christian philosophers have had, not through human possibility but through divine revelation and the light of the Holy Spirit. 

Having understood this, it is easy to understand that since the lower reason (which knows only through the senses and particulars) is made cowardly, it despairs of being able to reach universal truths. The higher reason comforts it and demonstrates that if such contemplation is above human strength, it will be made powerful by divine help, as were Aeneas and Paul. Virgil, then—that is, higher reason—comforting the lower reason and sensuality, shows that he can lead the soul to salvation, if not with its own strength, at least with the help of divine grace, without which so arduous an enterprise would be in vain. And then he shows, according to true and Christian doctrine, what the way is by which we can arrive at so exalted a place. 

To understand this better, it is necessary to repeat from a bit further back, because the poet feigns that a celestial lady (whom he does not name <note>referring to the Virgin Mary, though she is unnamed in the text</note>) moved Lucia to help Dante. And Lucia moved Beatrice to descend into Limbo to Virgil and persuade him to become a guide to Dante. Indeed, true theologians affirm that although there is <term>free will</term> <note>libero arbitrio</note> in man to act well or poorly, nonetheless no one can purge himself of vices and act according to virtue without divine grace. Wherefore Solomon says: "Trust in the Lord with all your heart" <note>original: "Esto confides in domino i toto corde tuo"</note>. "In your own wisdom do not be exalted" <note>original: "In tua aute sapientia ne exalteris"</note>. "In all your ways acknowledge him, that he may make your paths straight" <note>original: "In omnibus uis tuis cognosce eum ut rectas faciat uias tuas"</note>. 

Therefore, as Jerome says in the third book against the Pelagians: "We must not trust in our own wisdom nor in any other virtue of ours, but only in the help of God who directs our steps." And for this it is written: "Make my way straight in your sight" <note>original: "Recta faci cospectu tuo uiam mea"</note>. And Solomon: "Commit your works to the Lord, and your thoughts will be established" <note>original: "Deuolue super dominu opera tua & firmabuntur cogitationes tue"</note>. And Paul the Apostle: "Such trust we have through Christ toward God; not that we are sufficient to think anything of ourselves, as of ourselves, but our sufficiency is from God" <note>original: "Fidutiam aute tale habemus p christu ad deu non quod sufficientes simus cogitare aliquid ex nobis quasi ex nobis Sed sufficientia nostra ex deo est"</note>. And elsewhere: "He who glories, let him glory in the Lord; for it is not he who commends himself that is approved, but he whom God commends" <note>original: "Qui gloriatur i domino glorietur no eni qui se ipsum comedat ille probatus est sed que deus comedat"</note>. 

Nor should anyone conclude that because we cannot act by ourselves, there is no free will in us. Because there is certainly free will, and as Thomas Aquinas affirms, man is master of every operation of his, both of willing and not willing, through the deliberation of reason within him, which can turn to this side or that. But although he is master of deliberating or not deliberating thus or so, nonetheless it is necessary that this be through a preceding deliberation. And so that one does not proceed to infinity, it is necessary finally to come to this: that our free will must be moved by some external principle that is above the human mind, and this is God. Wherefore Aristotle in the book *On Good Fortune* affirms that the mind of man does not have dominion over its works in a way that it would not be necessary for it to be moved by God. 

And the Master of Sentences <note>Peter Lombard</note> writes that the "prevenient grace" of God prepares our will—not that it creates a will, because that was there before grace came, but that it makes it good and right. Therefore it does not follow that there is no free will. And such grace was not only infused in man from the beginning in general, but is also ready to help us in singular and particular operations. Wherefore David sings: "Unless the Lord builds the house, they labor in vain who build it. And unless the Lord guards the city, he watches in vain who guards it" <note>original: "Nisi dominus hedificauerit domu inuanu laborauerut qui hedificat ea Et nisi dominus custodierit ciuitate frustra uigilat qui custodit ea"</note>. 

Wanting to demonstrate this, Dante feigns that Virgil—that is, reason and our intellect by itself—cannot judge us unless he is sent by Beatrice—that is, unless he is instructed in sacred letters, because the author always takes Beatrice for Christian theology with grace acting through the virtues. Nor is this grace simple and one, but triple. But so that we may better understand that without these three graces we cannot be blessed, I demonstrate with manifest theological reasons that to achieve celestial beatitude, it is necessary that we become contemplative of spiritual, incorporeal, and divine things. Nor can one climb to so high a place except by the steps of the virtues. Nor can there be virtue in us if there is no reason, because every virtue proceeds from right reason. 

Therefore, it is necessary that the man wishing to become blessed have reason, and from that, virtue is born, which by purging us of vices makes us fit for contemplation. And from this, our poet forms his three canticles. For with reason, he discourses through the knowledge of vices, which is the *Inferno*. With the virtues acquired through reason, he purges himself of them, which is the *Purgatorio*. And once purged, he can climb to the contemplation of divine things and become blessed, which is the *Paradiso*. But because none of these three things can be perfect without divine help, three graces come to us from God. The first illuminates the reason and makes it capable of forming virtue, which is nothing other than directing the will...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the second canto of the Inferno. It provides a theological and philosophical breakdown of the three "heavenly ladies" (Mary, Lucia, and Beatrice) and then moves into a detailed definition of the virtue of Magnanimity, applied to Virgil’s character and his literary works.</meta>

# INFERNO

...added to what she finds in our **free will** <note>original: "libero arbitrio"</note> to rightly desire the good. This is called **prevenient grace** <note>original: "pueniente"; the grace that comes before human action to stir the soul</note>, and it is represented by the poet as the "first lady" <note>This refers to the Virgin Mary, though the commentator notes she is unnamed here because the will is unknown before it acts</note>. It disposes us toward willing. The second is **illuminating grace**, through which the good will enlightens and helps us to know what we ought to do. Because it offers us the light of knowledge, he deservedly calls it **Lucia** from the word for "light." On this subject, Augustine says: the first grace makes us willing; the second ensures that such a will is not in vain, meaning that we are able to act. The Church asks for these two graces every day in her prayers, saying: *We beseech you, O Lord, that you precede our actions with your inspiration and then follow them with your help.* <note>original: "Preghiami signore che tu preuẽga le noſtre opationi cõ la tua iſpiratione: & dipoi leſeguiti col tuo adiuto."</note> The third is **perfecting grace** or "true consummation," which fulfills our entire desire because it helps us to contemplate and know the Highest Good. This he calls **Beatrice**, whom we said above represents **Theology**, which gives us the knowledge of divine things. Certainly, she is Beatrice because she makes us blessed <note>The name Beatrice is derived from the Latin *beatus*, meaning blessed</note> by making God known to us. For by knowing the spirit and loving Him, we enjoy Him. 

It does not seem right to omit what the poets say concerning the **Graces**, for anyone with wit can easily see how they align with what we have gathered from the true theologians above. **Hesiod** <note>An early Greek poet</note> writes in his *Theogony* <note>A poem regarding the origins of the gods</note> that the Graces are three, and thus he does not disagree on the number. They are the daughters of **Jove**. This signifies nothing other than that every grace proceeds from God alone. Thus, Paul says: *By the grace of God I am what I am.* <note>original: "gratia dei id sum quod sum"</note> And the Apostle James says: *Every best gift and every perfect gift is from above, descending from the Father of lights.* <note>original: "Omne datũ optimũ. & omne donũ perfectũ deſurſum eſt deſcendẽs a patre luminũ."</note> Jove fathered them with **Eurymone**. In Greek, Eurymone signifies "wide pasture," because there is no more abundant pasture for the soul than divine grace. This is why David says in the Psalm: *The Lord, merciful and compassionate, has made a memorial of his wonders; he has given food to those who fear him.* <note>original: "Memoriã fecit mirabiliũ ſuoꝝ miſericors & miſerator dominus eſcã dedit timẽtibus ſe"</note> 

Their names are **Aglaia**, **Euphrosyne**, and **Thalia**. *Aglaos* in Greek means "splendid," and certainly only divine grace makes our soul splendid because it illuminates it. *Euphrosyne* means "joy" because it alone makes us joyful. *Thalia* means "flourishing" and "greening," because grace makes every virtue flourish and turn green again within us. They add that the latter two look back toward the first, because from her splendor depends and proceeds the fact that the human soul is joyful and flourishing. 

A man will not hesitate, then, to set out on the path of contemplation, having already disposed his senses to obey reason, and having as his guide the **intellect**, which is not only enlightened by all human doctrines but also ennobled by the three divine graces. If I have been too long or too wordy on these points, let it be blamed on the difficulty of the subject and the utility of knowing it. For once this passage is well understood, many other things will become known to us through it. Now, coming to the text:

**THE SHADOW:** that is, the soul. For the ancient Latins often used this name for the soul. **OF THE magnanimous one:** **Magnanimity** is a type of **fortitude**. But to better open up this virtue and all its parts, we shall say that fortitude is excellence, height, and greatness of soul, which desires great and high things and despises the vile and low. With certain reason, it applies itself to every heavy labor and danger to achieve honorable utility. This has seven species within it: **Constancy**, **Confidence**, **Magnanimity**, **Perseverance**, **Patience**, **Magnificence**, and **Security**. 

**Constancy** is that which shapes, grounds, and confirms the soul in honest works, so that it allows it to depart from them in no way. **Confidence** is when the soul has a firm purpose in great and honest things with firm hope of achieving them. **Magnanimity** is that frankness of soul that pushes us toward distinguished and great things with an affection for honesty and utility; its companions are two: **Dignity** and **Liberality**. Dignity gives us honest authority and reputation for which we are honored and revered. Liberality is that which, with benevolence and modesty, distributes reasonably according to rank. **Perseverance** is when we persist with firm stability in an undertaking that was well-considered from the start. **Patience** is when, for an honest cause and utility, we endure difficult and laborious things for a long time and without perturbation of soul. **Magnificence** is height of soul in doing great things from which honor and fame ought to result. Its companions are: **Glory**, **Amplitudine** <note>Abundance/Greatness</note>, **Study**, and **Exercise**. Glory is fame with praise. Amplitudine is an abundance of offices, honors, and riches. Study is the vehement application of the soul with desire and will to do something. Exercise is the movement of the will which moderately pushes us to act. The last part of fortitude is **Security**, which ensures the soul has no remorse of conscience in worthy undertakings. 

These are the species of fortitude, among which we have shown that Magnanimity is that which, through the expectation of honesty and utility, spurs the soul to do great deeds. And thus **Virgil** is magnanimous, if we consider the person of the poet, because in his works he undertook to write of great things. For seeing that the first life of men in the earliest centuries was **pastoral**, because they lived among herds and flocks of animals; and the second was in **cultivating the earth** and living off its fruits; and the third was **civil**, in which, dwelling together, they built cities and established republics, laws, and magistrates to govern them. Virgil wished to describe and embrace all these lives in his poems: in the *Bucolics* the first, in the *Georgics* the second, and in the *Aeneid* the third he wrote and demonstrated. 

And if we look at the present story, he was magnanimous in comforting Dante toward such great things. And if we go to the allegory: the "higher reason" is certainly magnanimous because it does not lower or debase itself in particulars where there can be no true science. Instead, it dares to rise to universals and to the contemplation of divine things. And certainly, although many epithets could be given to Virgil, nevertheless in this place it is necessary that he who comforts one who has become base be magnanimous.

> **YOUR SOUL** O Dante, **is offended by cowardice** <note>original: "uilta"</note>, a vice contrary to magnanimity.

This cowardice often encumbers—that is, fills and occupies—a man in a way that turns him back from an undertaking already made, which was excellent and worthy of honor. And it happens to him as to a horse or similar animal which, fearing something that is not to be feared, shies away <note>original: "aombra," to take fright at a shadow</note> because of **false seeing**, that is, because it seems to see what is not there. As also happens to a man, especially at night, seeing a tree it seems to him he sees an armed man, and it seems to him that he moves and comes toward him. All of which is false and lying sight. 

**But so that you may dissolve yourself:** That is, untie and free yourself from this fear. **I will tell you why I came, and what I understood at the first point when I grieved for you.** So that you may understand that I am moved by divine will. And he who follows divine help can conquer every difficulty and danger. And to persuade him better, he continues:

> **I WAS among those who are suspended:**

That is, those who are not damned to the punishments nor saved for glory, as I will show below when we treat of **Limbo** <note>The border of Hell for the virtuous unbaptized</note>. But allegorically, understand that Virgil—that is, higher reason—is "suspended," meaning he stays in doubt within a man when he is not yet directed toward one end or another. But when prevenient grace begins to move him toward the right end, he no longer stays in doubt.

> **AND A LADY called me, blessed and beautiful.**

This is **Beatrice**, who makes us blessed, and calls and excites our mind and conducts it to beatitude. And "beautiful," because nothing is more beautiful than beatitude.

> **SO THAT I requested her to command me:**

Because it happens that when the human mind begins to be illuminated by this grace, it immediately disposes itself to obey her precepts.

> **HER EYES shone brighter than the star.**

This is an excellent comparison. For the star shines, but not so perfectly that it shows things as the sun does. Then Beatrice: **And she began to speak to me, sweet and low.** He describes the manner of a modest and bashful woman, whose words ought to be sweet and without any pride, and "low" or "plain," as if to say rested and modest. Furthermore, it is the voice of **Theology**, full of sweetness and delight, because there is nothing that makes our mind more tranquil.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante’s Inferno, Canto II. Having previously discussed the three types of Grace, the commentator now examines the nature of Theology as a stabilizing force for the soul before transitioning into Beatrice’s famous speech to Virgil.</meta>

### CANTO SECOND

...and more than any other part of its life, theology, which, by purging us of vices, makes our conscience tranquil and without any disturbance, removing every sting of fear regarding punishment or death. **PLAIN:** <note>original: "PIANA"</note> meaning low, because in life it always possesses gentleness, humility, and charity; these virtues are entirely contrary to the haughtiness of pride. Or we might say **plain** means "open," because while there are various types of theology among the pagans <note>original: "gentili"</note>, none demonstrate openly who God is and what the true path to our happiness is like Christian theology does. **WITH an angelic voice in her own speech:** Because God inspires sacred theology and its high and profound meanings through the medium of angels, as we will demonstrate at length in both Purgatory and Paradise. **IN HER own speech:** Which is divine, and is the persuasive mode of speaking toward all virtues.

->O courteous Mantuan soul,<-
->whose fame still endures in the world,<-
->and shall endure as long as the world lasts;<-
->My friend, and not the friend of fortune,<-
->on the deserted slope is so hindered<-
->on his path that he has turned back for fear;<-
->And I fear he may already be so far astray<-
->that I have risen too late to his aid,<-
->from what I have heard of him in heaven.<-
->Now move, and with your ornate speech<-
->and with whatever is necessary for his escape,<-
->help him, so that I may be consoled.<-
->I am Beatrice who makes you go;<-
->I come from a place where I desire to return;<-
->love moved me, which makes me speak.<-
->When I am before my Lord,<-
->I will often offer praise of you to Him.<-
->She was silent then, and I began:<-

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Large decorative woodcut initial 'Q' set in a square frame, containing a circular motif with an interior figure.</image-desc>

This is the oration that Beatrice makes to Virgil to persuade him to move immediately to Dante’s aid. And if we wish to understand the oratory and poetic art within it, we would say it belongs to the **deliberative genre** <note>a style of speech intended to persuade someone to take a specific action</note>. First, at the beginning, she gains his goodwill <note>original: "capta beniuolẽtia"</note> through the person of Virgil, praising him for his liberality and observing the precepts of the orators. For we must always praise the virtue we wish someone to use toward us in the person from whom we desire to obtain something. Therefore, Beatrice, needing Virgil to be liberal <note>in the sense of generous or "courteous"</note> in offering help to Dante, said **Courteous soul**, meaning liberal. 

She then follows with praise, demonstrating the longevity of his fame, which has not only lasted so many centuries but will still endure as long as the world remains distant—that is, as long as it stretches on. After the introduction <note>original: "lexordio"</note>, she places the narration in which she demonstrates that she asks for something just, because it is just to ask for the escape of one who is a true friend, and who falls into ruin not out of malice but out of fragility. And so that the rescue might be quick, she demonstrates that since he is already turned toward ruin, help will be of no use unless it is swift. She also demonstrates that it will be easy for him through his eloquence and learning. And so that he understands she deserves to be heard, she says she is Beatrice, that she comes from heaven, and is moved by love. Finally, she promises him a reward. Let this suffice to demonstrate the artifice of this oration. 

Now follows the exposition of the text. **O COURTEOUS soul:** Truly "soul" because he was without a body. **COURTEOUS:** This he had understood because he had offered himself to her when he said, "So that I requested the command." <note>Referring to Virgil's earlier willingness to guide Dante</note>. And certainly Virgil—that is, the **intellect**—is not a body but is incorporeal, and his help had to be in things not corporeal but spiritual. The intellect is "courteous" because it is that which gives us every excellent teaching. She adds then that Virgil's fame is to endure as long as the world, because the fame of human learning is not meant to be eternal like the knowledge of celestial things.

**MY FRIEND, and not of fortune:** <note>original: "L AMICO mio & nō della uẽtura"</note> He is a true friend who loves the friend and not his prosperity. For there are many who, like swallows, come in the summer and flee in the winter. Likewise, while the summer of prosperity lasts for a friend, they are always around him. But when winter comes—that is, some adversity—they immediately leave him, just as Polymnestor left Priam. Therefore Beatrice rightly says that Dante is her friend and not a friend of her prosperity, because many love Beatrice (meaning the doctrine of divine things) not for herself nor to possess her, but to acquire worldly fame, reputation, riches, and dignity. These things are the goods of fortune. Therefore, they do not love her, but her good fortune. 

Many become great theologians not to amend their errors with that doctrine which demonstrates the Highest Good and directs us toward it, but to achieve honors and dignity, and to become bishops, archbishops, and cardinals. Hence these cannot be called virtuous, because they do not seek virtue for the sake of wanting it or living according to it, but to become either famous, powerful, or rich. Wherefore Juvenal said: *For who embraces virtue itself if you take away the rewards?* <note>original: "Quis n. uirtutẽ amplectitur ipsam premia si tollas?"</note>. 

Concluding according to the distinction of the holy doctors: some desire to know only for the sake of knowing, and this is **curiosity**. Some to be known—that is, to be famous and reputed—and this is **vanity**. Others to gain profit, and this is **avarice**. Some to edify themselves and also others, and this is **true charity**. These are the friends of Beatrice and not of the fortune and prosperity that proceeds from her. Of the first three, Solomon writes in Wisdom: *Vain are all men in whom there is no knowledge of God.* <note>original: "Vanis sunt oēs homines in quibus nō est sciẽtia dei."</note> And in Ecclesiastes: *In much knowledge is much sorrow.* <note>original: "In multa sciẽtia est multa indignatio."</note> Of the last ones he similarly speaks in Wisdom, saying: *He gave him the knowledge of the holy ones and honored him in his labors.* <note>original: "Dedit illi sciẽtiã sanctōrū: & honestauit illū in laboribus."</note> 

Therefore Beatrice demonstrates that Dante is among those who love and seek doctrine according to these last ones. Or we can say "my friend and not of fortune" because Dante was a friend of divine doctrine, but fortune was always adverse to him as we see in his life. This most often happens to the learned. Wherefore Aristotle in the *Book of Good Fortune* says: *Where there is much virtue, there is little fortune.* Nevertheless, the first interpretation fits better in this place. 

**IS HINDERED** by the beasts already mentioned on the **SLOPE** of virtues. **DESERTED:** abandoned because few, as we have said, follow them. **THAT he has turned back for fear:** He deserves to be helped because he did not turn from the true path out of malice, but out of fear—that is, out of fragility—for which a man who errs is worthy of greater compassion. **AND I FEAR that he may already be so far astray that I have risen too late to his aid:** Understand that in the Tuscan tongue, a thing is called "astray" <note>original: "smarrita"</note> which, although it is not found, must nevertheless be found eventually. And "lost" is that which is neither found nor will be found. 

Furthermore, whoever turns back from the true road that leads to salvation goes by the way of vices, which lead to perdition. Our sinning is in three degrees. First, the wicked thought is born, and the directing of oneself toward vice. Secondly, staying fixed in the captive thought and frequently performing vicious operations. In the third degree, through frequent operations, one becomes so established in sin that the frequent acts have created a **habit** <note>a permanent disposition of the soul</note>. Wherefore the prophet in the first Psalm says: *Blessed is the man who does not go into the counsel of the ungodly, and does not stand in the way of sinners, and does not sit in the seat of pestilence.* <note>original: "Beatus uir qui nō abiit in cōsiliū impiorū: et in uia peccatōrū non stetit in cathedra pestilentię non sedit"</note> Which is to say: Blessed is the man who does not go into the counsel of the impious (meaning he does not take captive counsel in his actions). Then: *And in the way of sinners he did not stand*, which signifies the acts and operations. And: *In the seat of pestilence he did not sit*, meaning he did not make a habit of vice. And thus, first is the vicious purpose; then the act and operation; and ultimately...

### INFERNO

habit. In the first two states, the man is not lost because he can return to the true path. But he is **astray** because he cannot find himself again before he returns. In the third state, he is lost because, as Aristotle says: <note>original: "Chi ha facto habito del uitio e impoſſibile o molto difficile che ſe ne rimanga."</note> *Whoever has made a habit of vice, it is impossible or very difficult for them to leave it.* And for this reason, Beatrice says: *and I fear he may already be so far astray:* that is, that he has not already performed such frequent acts of vice that he is close to the habit. If that were so, help would come too late. **By WHAT I have heard of him in heaven.** Those who are blessed by the vision of God see all things in God as if in a mirror. Thus, Beatrice affirms having heard these things about Dante in heaven. **NOW move, and with your ornate speech.** Two things are necessary in an eloquent person: *Copia* <note>An abundance of content</note> and ornament of words, combined with gravity of thought. Therefore, she placed both by saying "with the ornate speech": that is, with eloquence, and "with whatever is necessary": that is, with those arguments and reasons that are needed. And if we consider Virgil, she spoke optimally by saying "With your ornate speech": because he is a poet full of eloquence and learning. And referring allegorically to "higher reason": which must persuade with certainty, eloquence is necessary along with wisdom. It is not without reason that Marcus Tullius <note>Cicero</note> laments those who have divided these two joined things: some have given themselves only to eloquence, which without wisdom and learning is a furious and harmful thing to men; and some only to wisdom, which by itself can help little, being unable to persuade others of what it understands. This was also the judgment of the most excellent in our religion, who were learned and eloquent among both the Greeks and the Latins. And Augustine, in his book *On Christian Religion*, demonstrates how useful eloquence is. **HELP him so that I may be consoled.** It will not be a small help, but it will be enough for his salvation if he is helped in such a way that she who loves him remains consoled. **I AM Beatrice who makes you go.** Beatrice was a Florentine lady loved by our poet, as we narrated above in the account of his life. But in this place, he uses Beatrice to represent Theology, as we have already said. **I COME from the place where I desire to return / Love moved me, which makes me speak.** Most excellently, holy Theology descends from heaven and returns to heaven, because it is the science of divine things, and a celestial instinct is what moves us to seek it, and with that, it finally leads us back to heaven. **Love moved me, which makes me speak.** Only love moves God to infuse such knowledge in us, and only love excites us to want to learn it, as we will treat more extensively in *Purgatory* and *Paradise* when we discuss the angelic hierarchies, especially the Seraphim <note>The highest order of angels, characterized by their burning love for God.</note>. **WHEN I am before my Lord:** that is, before God. **I WILL often praise you to Him:** that is, many times to Him. If we understand this to be Virgil's soul placed in Limbo, Beatrice could promise him no other reward. For the soul has no need for the goods of the body or of fortune. She should not, therefore, promise him health, beauty, or strength, nor treasures or power. And of the goods proper to the soul—the greatest of which is beatitude <note>Supreme blessedness or heavenly happiness</note>—she could not give them to him, he being already condemned to Limbo. She promises, therefore, only what she can do: to praise him before God. This should be pleasing to any soul in whatever state it may be. And Beatrice can deservedly praise Virgil: that is, Christian theology can praise the doctrines of the pagans <note>original: "gentili"</note>. For despite theology dealing with things revealed by the Holy Spirit or acquired by theologians through God's help—such as the Trinity and the distinction of three persons in one essence, the incarnation of the Word, the redemption of man, and many other things—nonetheless, the doctrine of the ancients has given them great help in many places. Hence, they are often cited not only by other doctors but even by Paul the Apostle. For he did not flee from familiarity with Seneca and approved of his doctrine in many places. And writing to the Athenians about God—that "in God we live, in God we move, and in God we are"—he adds, "as some of your own philosophers have said." And if we allegorically understand Virgil as the "higher mind" which is excited by theology and by cooperating grace, it is a great reward for it that God understands that the mind does not resist such instinct and such a calling, because for this, it deserves that God should make it blessed.

<column-break/>

Virgil refers to Dante the words which he spoke in reply to Beatrice. **O WOMAN of virtue.** Every science contains some virtue within itself. But Theology embraces them all. For in the precepts by which it gives us the rule of living according to God, it places Prudence, Justice, Fortitude, and Temperance, with all the species of each; and these are the moral virtues. It also places Faith, Hope, and Charity, which are the proper virtues of theology. And similarly, in speculative matters, it does not omit any intellectual virtue, which are: Intelligence concerning principles; Science concerning conclusions; and Wisdom, which embraces within itself intelligence and science and makes a third thing above those two. Therefore, she can truly be called "woman of virtue," *through whom*—that is, by means of whom—**THE HUMAN species.** That is, the human race. **EXCEEDS:** Conquers and surpasses. **EVERY content:** of that heaven which has the smallest circles. This is the heaven of the

Moon: which, being the last and closest to the Earth (which acts as the center of the heavens), must necessarily be the smallest. **Every content:** that is, every creature that is contained from the heaven of the Moon downwards. For from the Moon downwards, there is no creature capable of the knowledge of God, in which beatitude consists. And man attains such knowledge through theology. Therefore, theology is the reason why man surpasses every other creature that is under the Moon. And he correctly said that man conquers all creatures from the heaven of the Moon downwards. For if the opinion of the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle</note> is true—that every sphere has its own angel that turns it—man does not conquer the creatures that are from the heaven of the Moon upwards. For the angels have greater knowledge of divine things than we do. **SO MUCH does your command please me:** it is so grateful and pleasing to me what you command me, that if I were to obey you in that very instant you command me, I would judge that it were late. Therefore, **you need no longer**—*huopo* <note>original: "huopo"</note> in the ancient Florentine tongue means "need" or "necessity." Likewise in the first canto of *Paradise*: "But now with both I must [me huopo] enter the remaining arena." And it is derived from the Latin noun *opus*. **open:** show and manifest **YOUR Desire:** your will. And in this tercet, it is shown allegorically that the "higher reason" in man, excited by Beatrice (which signifies the love of theology moved by preventing and cooperating grace), immediately disposes itself to obey. **BUT TELL ME the reason why you do not fear.** He raises a doubt by which, according to the literal sense, he asks how a blessed spirit would want to come from heaven (where her beatitude is) into Limbo (where there is a privation of beatitude). And according to the allegory, it is asked how God deigns that a sinner—whom the She-Wolf has already turned to flight—be illuminated and excited by the love of theology and by the aforementioned grace, without deserving it. But whenever man recognizes his error and with his free will deliberates to leave it, divine grace succors his good will.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante’s Inferno, Canto II. ### CANTO TWO

**The descent** here below into this **center**: that is, to the hell at the center of the earth, which, as we said above, is the center of the universe. **FROM THE AMPLE place**: that is, the wide and spacious heavens. This is because the highest heaven, being furthest from the center, must necessarily exceed all the lower circles in its circumference. **WHERE you burn to return**: You desire it. For every great longing and wish is an "ardor" of the soul. Thus Virgil said <note>original: "Ardet abire fuga"</note> *He burns to depart in flight*, meaning he vehemently desires it. And there follows the response of Beatrice.

**Since you wish to know so far within,**
**I shall tell you briefly,** she replied to me,
**why I do not fear to come within this place.**
**One should fear only those things**
**that have the power to do another harm;**
**of the others, no, for they are not fearful.**
**I am made such by God, by His mercy,**
**that your misery does not touch me,**
**nor does the flame of this burning assail me.**

**A gentle Lady is in heaven who laments**
**this impediment for which I send you,**
**so that harsh judgment is broken up there.**
**She called upon Lucia in her request**
**and said: "Now your faithful one has need**
**of you, and I commend him to you."**
**Lucia, the enemy of every cruel thing,**
**arose and came to the place where I was,**
**sitting with the ancient Rachel.**
**She said: "Beatrice, true praise of God,**
**why do you not help him who loved you so much**
**that for you he left the common crowd?**
**Do you not hear the pity of his weeping?**
**Do you not see the death that combats him**
**upon the river over which the sea has no boast?"**
**Never were people in the world so swift**
**to seek their profit or flee their harm**
**as I was, after such words were spoken,**
**coming down here from my blessed seat.**

<column-break/>

Virgil induces this doubt in Beatrice: because although the answer is known to theologians, the <term>science of the Gentiles</term><note>The philosophy of non-Christians or those relying purely on human reason</note> does not know it in all its parts. **SINCE you wish to know so far within**: that is, things not manifest to everyone but hidden, and for which human science is not sufficient without divine revelation or inspiration. **I SHALL TELL YOU briefly**: Because she was urging him to go to Dante’s rescue, she ought not to delay him with a long sermon. She says then: I do not fear to descend here, because we ought not to fear anything except those things that can harm us. And this is an excellent sentiment and one to be noted: for great ignorance blinds men, from which it often proceeds that, thinking something is not evil when it is, we do not fear it; and we behave so incautiously that we prepare no remedy for what could often be repaired. And so, conversely, by not diligently considering the nature of things, we fear what is not to be feared. Because of this, we live in constant anxiety and distress, and often flee from the toil and laborious study of honest things. This is known to Virgil, but what follows was not perfectly known to him. And therefore she adds: **I AM made such by God, by His mercy.** She gives the reason why the descent cannot harm her, neither in Limbo nor in Hell. And if we take Beatrice to be a blessed spirit, it is a true sentiment that every soul placed in beatitude is so confirmed in grace and made in an <term>impassible form</term><note>Incapable of suffering or being affected by external pain</note> that neither compassion, nor hatred, nor any other passion can disturb it. In these passions consists human misery. Therefore, she is made so by God by His mercy, that is, by His grace. And note that he says "by God." For no one is worthy of celestial beatitude by their own merits; nonetheless, without some merit, one does not acquire it. For God wants us to work as much as our fragility allows, and then where our merits do not reach, He supplies with His mercy. For this reason, Augustine said <note>original: "Qui fecit te sine te non saluabit te sine te."</note> *He who created you without you will not save you without you.* **SUCH that your misery does not touch me**: that is, it does not affect me. For *tango* in Latin means "I touch." **NOR does the flame of this burning place assail me**: By this "place" she means Limbo along with the rest of Hell. Therefore, I can go through Limbo, and your misery—that is, the misery of you who are deprived of beatitude—does not move me to compassion. For one who is blessed has their mind so conformed to the will of God that nothing pleases them except what pleases God. Hence, they cannot have compassion for the misery in which God wills the sinner to remain. Nor can the flame which torments the damned harm me. And if we take Beatrice to represent the love of <term>Theology</term><note>The study of divine things</note> sent by divine grace, as we have said, this divine science is not defiled or stained by vices, even though it must treat them. Nor does the flame of this place's burning assail her: because he who is a friend of Beatrice and not of Fortune—that is, one who seeks the science of theology not for worldly pomp nor for the greed of acquiring treasure, but to edify and correct himself and others—is not assailed by the fires of insatiable desires for earthly things. Nor does such a person consider it a misery for a man to be in poverty, or sickness, or exile, or many other calamities, provided he is not in sin. For he knows through this doctrine that nothing can be evil to a man except fault and sin.

We have shown above that as soon as human reason, with its free will, turns to seek the way out of the forest of ignorance (from which all vices proceed), God is moved to compassion for our imbecility. Because He sees that our power fails our will, He inspires the graces of which we spoke above. And first, a grace which, because it comes through simple divine liberality, is called **prevenient** <note>Grace that comes before human action to prompt the will</note>. Hence the prophet Jeremiah says: <note>original: "Cōuertemee & cōuertar qa deus meus"</note> *Turn me, and I shall be turned, for you are my God.* And it is called <term>grace freely given</term> <note>original: "gratia gratis data"</note>. This directs the will of man toward a good purpose through free will. And after this comes the second, called **illuminating grace**, by which our good will (born of reason and free will and confirmed by the first grace) is illuminated and made capable of learning the truth and showing him the way, which is to know God and oneself through the medium of true theology. Whoever directs themselves there acquires this. Of this, the Psalmist says: <note>original: "Notas mihi fecisti uias tuas"</note> *You have made your ways known to me*; and elsewhere, *For you will not leave my soul in hell*; and elsewhere, *For you have delivered my soul from death, and my feet from falling, that I may please God in the light of the living.* The third grace is called **cooperating**: that is, working together, because it operates together with man. It is also called **consummating** or **perfecting**, because it leads to the required end. Dante, then, places this **Gentle Lady** as the first, and **Lucia** as the second, and **Beatrice** as Theology together with the third grace. Although we have set out these graces distinctly above, nonetheless, because it is not easy for every man to understand, it was not a burden to repeat them briefly. **GENTLE Lady**: *Gentile* in Tuscan means "noble," derived from the Latin, because *gens* stands for the family; thus, "gentle" is like saying a man of family. But because the Hebrews call "Gentiles" all those who were not...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante’s Inferno, Canto II. The previous page discussed the conversation between Virgil and Beatrice in Limbo. We now move to the explanation of the "Gentle Lady" (the Virgin Mary) and the chain of grace that leads to Dante's rescue.</meta>

<margin>
trusting in your noble speech, which honors you and those who have heard it
<note>original: "fidandomi del tuo parlare honesto / chonora te & quei chudito lhanno"</note>
</margin>

...not of the people of God: therefore Christians call all pagans "gentiles." Thus this name "gentile" has various meanings. For theologians, following the custom of the Hebrews, call pagans "gentiles." And the Latins call "gentiles" those who are of the same race—that is, the same family—whom we call kinsmen. And the Tuscans say "gentile" to mean noble. It is in this sense that the poet places it in this passage. **GENTLE lady.** He deservedly calls "prevenient grace" <note>Prevenient grace is a theological term for the grace that comes before any human action to incline the soul toward God.</note> "gentile," meaning noble. For true nobility brings with it a greatness of soul; hence we say: "A great soul, a generous soul," meaning noble. And just as one who has a small soul is always a miser—which is seen in women and the elderly—so, conversely, one who has a great soul is liberal <note>generous</note>. Therefore, if one who is noble is magnanimous, and one who is magnanimous is liberal, this lady is certainly liberal, since prevenient grace, without any merit on our part, inclines itself to our aid through its own inherent liberality. 

But if true nobility consists in virtue alone, then he will be most noble who possesses the most excellent virtue within himself. And this lady had within herself perfect charity, which is a virtue more excellent than the others. As the Apostle says to the Corinthians: "If I should have all faith, so that I could move mountains, but have not charity, I am nothing." <note>original: "Si habuero omnem fidem ita ut montes transferam Caritatem autem non habuero nihil sum." From 1 Corinthians 13:2.</note> Therefore she was truly noble. Or indeed, because many believe that nobility consists in the antiquity of one's bloodline, this shall be a "gentle lady" because none of these graces is more ancient in man, as it is the first to arrive. Nor did the poet wish to give her a specific name as he did for the second and the third, because she is less understood and more unknown than the other two.

**IN heaven:** Because God is within it. **WHO laments:** That is, she is moved to compassion. And truly God, having compassion for our fragility, sends us this grace. Hence it is written: "God saw our frame and had mercy on us." <note>original: "Vidit deus sigmentu nostru & misertus est nostri." A paraphrase of Psalm 103:14: "For he knoweth our frame."</note> And if someone should ask how God can have compassion, since in God there can be no passion or disturbance, the answer is that in truth there can be no passion in Him; but we attribute it to Him through a certain likeness, for reasons which we shall demonstrate in their proper place. **OF THIS impediment** which the She-wolf gives to Dante. **WHERE:** to which I, Beatrice. **I SEND you:** I send you, Virgil. **SO THAT:** this lamentation. **BREAKS:** that is, shatters. **UP THERE:** that is, in heaven. **HARSH judgment:** that is, the severe judgment. Divine justice wills that since man has the reason to know good from evil and free will to be able to choose, he should be punished for leaving the true path. And this is the "harsh judgment"—that is, severe and inflexible. And nonetheless, divine mercy breaks such severity of judgment. 

**THIS:** prevenient grace. **CALLED upon Lucia:** that is, "illuminating grace," which gives us such light that we can perceive and discern the path that leads us to salvation; and therefore he calls her Lucia <note>Lucia derives from the Latin "lux," meaning light.</note>. **IN HER request:** in her asking. And she said: **LUCIA**, your faithful one has need of you: that is, Dante, who, having chosen the path of virtue, or being established in that will by prevenient grace, has need of someone to illuminate him regarding what he must do. And he calls him the "faithful one" of Lucia because he who has a firm will to follow the truth has undoubting faith that this light will illuminate his intellect. 

**AND I commend him to you:** And I, the gentle lady, commend him to you, Lucia. And certainly prevenient grace, which directs our will to want the good, commends us to Lucia—that is, to "cooperating grace." For by the gift of the first grace (which is that our will be upright and good), the second descends into us, which brings that will to action. The author has set down the words that the gentle lady used toward Lucia in favor of Dante, which are appropriate to the person and full of artfulness. For prevenient grace incites illuminating grace. And she shows that her petition and request is easy, useful, and honest. It is easy because she asks of her that which is her own proper office; therefore she can do it without difficulty. It is honest because all justice and equity requires that we succor the salvation of those who are faithful to us. Nor is it without utility to preserve one's friends.

**LUCIA, enemy of every cruel thing.** Virgil shows that Lucia, persuaded by the words spoken to her, did not consume the time (which was short) in a long response—which is the habit of a flatterer rather than a true friend—but immediately moved to provide help, which was to send Beatrice. For if the supreme good is to know God, and such knowledge is given to us by theology, she alone can lead us to salvation. **LUCIA, enemy of every cruel thing:** He called the first grace noble for the reasons stated above. Now he calls the second the enemy of every cruel thing. For if it is the highest piety to succor and help so that a good will may be put into action, certainly this second grace, because it does this, is supremely pious. And because everything is an enemy to its opposite, and cruelty is the opposite of piety, it follows that Lucia, being supremely pious, is the enemy of every cruelty. Nor should it be doubted that she is supremely pious, since she shows the way to those who have lost it.

**She moved and came to the place where I, Beatrice, was.** Lucia comes not to Virgil, nor to Dante, but to Beatrice, to denote the true order. For the first grace that directs the will goes to Lucia—that is, it moves the second grace, which allows the well-directed will to act. And Lucia moves Beatrice, who is the "perfecting grace," signifying contemplation—that is, the knowledge of celestial things which makes us blessed. And Beatrice "sits" for Virgil in Limbo—that is, she comes to our intellect which is enclosed within the darkness of the bodily senses and illuminates it. And Virgil becomes the leader and guide to Dante because inferior reason and sensuality become obedient, guiding him to the knowledge of vice, then to its purgation, and after purgation to contemplation.

**WHO SAT with the ancient Rachel:** We read in Genesis that Isaac, son of Abraham, told his son Jacob not to take a wife from the generation of Canaan, but to go to Mesopotamia of Syria to Laban, son of Bethuel and brother of Rebecca, the wife of Abraham and his grandmother. Jacob obeyed his father and went, and on the journey, he had in sleep the vision of the ladder that reached from earth to heaven, and the angels were descending and ascending by it. God was leaning against the ladder, from whom he received the great promise that his seed would be spread throughout the whole earth—to the east, west, south, and north—and that He would be his guardian on every journey. After such a vision, Jacob continued his way and came to Laban, by whom he was kindly received.

Laban had two daughters, the elder of whom was Leah, who was bleary-eyed <note>original: "cipsa" / "lippa" - meaning having dim or watery eyes</note> and not beautiful; the younger was Rachel, who was very beautiful. Jacob, being in love with her, made a pact with Laban that if he gave him Rachel as his wife, he would serve him for seven years. When that time was fulfilled, Laban celebrated the wedding, but not without deception, for he arranged that at night Leah was put with Jacob in place of Rachel. The following day Jacob realized the trick played on him, but his love for Rachel was so great that he endured serving another seven years for Laban to have her.

This history has a great mystery within it. In short, learned interpreters of the Holy Scriptures take Leah for the "active life," which is bleary-eyed because it does not see nor is it capable of divine things. And they take Rachel for the "contemplative life," which is very beautiful; and thus nothing in human generation is more beautiful than speculation. Therefore, in the Old Testament, these two kinds of life are prefigured by these two sisters: that is, by Rachel the contemplative and spiritual, and by Leah the active and bodily. Just as in the New Testament, Mary is taken for the contemplative and Martha for the active. And he correctly called her "ancient" because contemplation is in the angel, who existed before man; but the active life was not before man. Therefore, it precedes not only in dignity but also in age.

**SAT** Beatrice correctly "sat" with Rachel because the proper subject of theology is knowledge and contemplation, and in that, she stops and places her seat. It does not follow from this that she does not sometimes follow Leah—that is, the active life. For this science <note>referring to Theology as the "queen of sciences"</note> also treats of the moral life and civil government, but she does not "sit" there because it is not her own proper place.

**AND SAID: Beatrice, true praise of God.** Many philosophers and pagan theologians have striven to investigate the excellence of the divine nature. But none has been able to find the truth of it as the theology of the Christians has. Therefore, only Beatrice is true...

It uses the biblical figures of Leah and Rachel to explain the distinction between the active and contemplative lives.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary by Cristoforo Landino on Canto II of Dante’s Inferno. The previous page established that "Prevenient Grace" (symbolized by the Virgin Mary) moved "Illuminating Grace" (Lucia) to call upon "Theology" (Beatrice), who in turn sent "Reason" (Virgil) to rescue Dante. We now examine Beatrice’s motivation and the symbolic meaning of Dante's struggle against the "beast" of greed.</meta>

### CANTO TWO

**praise of God.** <note>original: "loda didio"</note> That is, our theology alone praises God with true praises. **WHY:** <note>original: "CHE"</note> that is, why do you not help. **HIM:** <note>original: "QUEL"</note> that is, he **WHO loved you so much.** He demonstrates through these words that she asks for just things, because justice requires that we favor those who love us. And Beatrice rightfully ought to show the true way to Dante, since he had been a devoted student and had, because of her, "left the vulgar herd"—that is, the crowd of the common people where ignorance reigns and all learning is banished. Therefore, he loved Beatrice supremely; for if he had not loved her, he would not have endured the labors and vigils he bore to acquire her. Nor can any learning be achieved without great labor and long study. Hence Horace says: *He who strives to reach the desired goal in the race has endured and done much as a boy: he has sweated and shivered, and abstained from love and wine.* <note>original Latin: "Qui studet optatā curfu cōtingere metam Multa tulit fecitq; puer sudauit & alsit abstinuit Venere & Baccho."</note> Beatrice, then, ought to want to help him. And similarly, she did not lack the power, because the paths that lead to salvation are known to Theology. Hence the Psalmist says: *You have made known to me your ways.* <note>original Latin: "Notas mihi fecisti uias tuas."</note> And those paths which liberate one from Hell. Hence he says elsewhere: *Because you will not leave my soul in hell.* <note>original Latin: "Quoniā nō relinques animam meā in inferno."</note> **DO YOU NOT hear:** as if to say, you must surely hear. **THE PIETY of his weeping:** and certainly he who supplicates with so much weeping deserves to be heard. Within "the piety of his weeping" are two things: the tears and the humble request for help. Without these, no one established in the misery of sins can obtain help from God. For first, it is necessary that one repents of past errors—which is denoted by the tears. Then, humbling himself, he must confess that he cannot, by himself, be liberated from sin without divine help. **DO YOU NOT SEE the death that battles him:** because he was being battled by the beasts, which is to say, by vices, which are the death of the soul. **UPON the flood:** <note>The OCR reads "fiamma" (flame), but Landino's commentary clarifies he is discussing the "fiumana" (flood/river) from the poem.</note> we should understand that Dante had been thrown back by the she-wolf down to the river which ran at the foot of the hill. And in this place, he takes the "flood" to mean the appetite and concupiscence <term>concupiscence: strong desire or lust for worldly things</term> for earthly things. And for this the Psalmist says: *The sorrows of death surrounded me, and the torrents of iniquity surrounded me.* <note>original Latin: "Circū dederunt me dolores mortis Et torrentes iniquitatis circū dederūt me."</note> And certainly, the sea struck by winds does not rise in such a turbulent tempest as do the tempestuous disturbances and various passions which continually surge in a mind full of worldly desires. Hence we see that Moses was able to divide the sea with his rod and make the path dry in the midst of the waters. The rod is the fortitude and continence with which the virtuous man can separate the passions from himself in such a way that, without hindrance, he can pass through the middle of them. Therefore, he says most excellently that such a flood of tempest surpasses the sea. **WHEREFROM:** <note>original: "ONDE"</note> that is, from which flood **the sea has no boast:** that is, the sea cannot boast or call itself the victor. Afterward, he adds that having heard the words of Lucia, Beatrice was faster to come to the rescue than anyone is to flee their own harm or pursue their own gain, to show that when illuminating grace comes into a man, he can swiftly acquire learning. And note that Beatrice did not come to act as a guide to Dante herself, but sent Virgil. This allegorically signifies that it is necessary for a man, before he ascends to heaven—that is, to the contemplation of divine things—to know vice and, having known it, purge himself of it. For this, Beatrice (Christian theology) was not necessary; rather, Virgil (the superior reason of man combined with the moral philosophy of the gentiles <note>Landino uses "gentiles" to refer to non-Christian classical philosophers like Virgil or Aristotle.</note>) was enough. But it is indeed necessary that Virgil, who is our intellect, be moved by Beatrice as the ultimate goal, because we do not purge ourselves of vices except for the purpose of achieving the knowledge of God. **I CAME down here from my blessed seat:** Theology, as we have said, has its seat in the contemplation of divine things, in which our happiness consists; therefore he said "blessed seat." But when it comes to the knowledge of vices, it descends from heaven into hell and employs the means of Virgil—that is, it takes the precepts given by the moral philosophy of the ancients and trusts in the "honest speech" of Virgil, meaning in moral doctrine. This doctrine leads to virtue and an honest life. And as Virgil led Aeneas to happiness, as we have demonstrated in our *Camaldolese Disputations*, <note>Landino’s own philosophical work, *Disputationes Camaldulenses*, written around 1472.</note> he acquires honor for himself and praise for the one he guides.

> After she had reasoned thus with me,
> she turned her piteous eyes, weeping,
> which made me hasten more to come.
> And I came to you just as she willed;
> I drew you away from that beast
> which took from you the short way up the beautiful mountain.
> What is it then? Why, why do you hold back?
> Why is such cowardice lodged in your heart?
> Why do you not have courage and frankness,
> since three such blessed ladies
> care for you in the court of heaven,
> and my speech promises you such good?

and he spurs him to follow her. Or we shall say: **WHICH made me hasten more to come.** Because the compassion shown by "cooperating grace" makes the "superior reason" hurry more. **AND I CAME to you just as she willed.** We saw above how much Virgil persuaded Dante that he should follow him. But afterward, realizing that he [Dante] was rendered useless [by fear], Virgil showed that not only he—that is, superior reason and moral virtue—but also the aforementioned graces together with Theology will be his guide. Hence he concludes that he must cast down all cowardice and take up the enterprise with a frank heart. **AND I CAME to you:** that is, to your aid. **JUST AS she:** that is, Beatrice **willed.** As if to say that whatever has moved superior reason to Dante proceeds from the divine will. A man must not, therefore, doubt to follow Virgil—that is, superior reason—in any arduous and difficult enterprise when it is inspired by divine grace. **FROM that beast I drew you away:** that is, from the she-wolf, which signifies the greed for earthly things. For superior reason, illuminated by the graces, ensures that the man who wishes to acquire true knowledge removes himself from vices. **WHICH took from you the short way up the beautiful mountain.** It would be a short path if, as soon as we recognize where happiness consists, we could achieve it. But because, as the prophet says: *No one can ascend the mountain of the Lord except he who is innocent, both in deeds and in thoughts,* <note>original Latin: "Nessuno puo salire al monte del fignore se nō chi e innocēte: et nelle operatiōi: et nelle cogitatiiōi." paraphrasing Psalm 24:3-4.</note> it is therefore necessary to take the long circuit through Hell and through Purgatory—that is, to know sins well and purge oneself of them. **What is it then? Why, why do you hold back?** This is the conclusion of this entire speech which Virgil has used toward Dante. Its beginning was: "If I have rightly understood your words." In which, having demonstrated the allegorical sense as much as was possible,

<column-break/>

Dante has, up to this point, recounted the words which Beatrice used to Virgil to persuade him to aid Dante; now he shows that, beyond words, she wept to move him further to help. And by this, he wishes to demonstrate the compassion that God has for the sinner; for God does not want the death of the sinner, but that he be converted and live. Beatrice’s eyes were "shining." This demonstrates the splendor of theological doctrine and its great visual power; for she truly has the eyes of an eagle, with which she can look at the sun and not be blinded—that is, she has the power to look upon the splendor of divine truth and endure it. They were, furthermore, "tearful." This denotes compassion. For truly, Sacred Scripture is very discrete and full of compassion toward the sinner. Hence it is said: *Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart.* <note>original Latin: "discite a me: quia mitis sum et humilis corde" (Matthew 11:29).</note> And elsewhere: *For my yoke is easy and my burden is light.* <note>original Latin: "Iugum enim meū suaue est et onus meum leue" (Matthew 11:30).</note> Nor does it ever command anyone to do something that is above their strength. Nor does He who redeemed us say: "Take up my cross and follow me," but He says: "Let each one take up *his* cross and follow me." This means nothing other than that it is enough for each person to do as much as they can. **WHICH made me hasten more to come.** By this, we shall understand that the clemency of Theology hastens a man along.

<summary>This page explains the allegorical necessity of Dante's journey through Hell, arguing that while Reason (Virgil) guides the purging of vice, it must be motivated by Theology (Beatrice) and Divine Grace. Landino justifies Dante's worthiness of rescue through his scholarly devotion and characterizes the "short path" to the mountain as impossible without first understanding and cleansing one's sins.</summary>
