<meta>This page continues Cristoforo Landino’s commentary on Canto II of the Inferno. Having explained the chain of divine grace from the Virgin Mary to Beatrice, the text now focuses on Virgil’s successful persuasion of Dante and the famous "simile of the flowers."</meta>

# INFERNO

We shall demonstrate our weak intellect, but with brevity, regarding something pertaining to the oratorical art. First, we note that this speech is of the deliberative genre—which is when we wish to either persuade or dissuade someone from something. We persuade when we demonstrate that what we want done is honorable, useful, delightful, and easy to do. Virgil, then, wished to persuade Dante to follow him through Hell, Purgatory, and Paradise. Dante did not lack the will to go, but he lacked the spirit, as he did not feel himself sufficient for such an undertaking. Therefore, it was not necessary to show him that this was honorable and useful, for he knew that for himself; rather, it was fitting to demonstrate to him that the undertaking was easy. This was because, despite his own strength not being enough for such labor, he was aided by the strength of others. He posits that a gentle lady <note>The Virgin Mary, representing Prevenient Grace.</note>, wishing to help, moved Lucia to do the same, and Lucia moved Beatrice, and Beatrice moved Virgil; he shows that each of these has sufficient power to help him. Dante, therefore, having a good will of his own for such an undertaking, and having understood that he could do through the means of others what he could not easily do by himself, is persuaded to follow Virgil. **SO WHAT IS IT:** <note>original: "DUNQUE CHE"</note> what is it that makes you so cowardly? Why do you stop—that is, why do you withdraw from the undertaking? And this is the conclusion. **WHY does so much [cowardice] lodge in your heart?** And certainly, many times when a man takes counsel with his sensuality <note>In Renaissance philosophy, "sensuality" refers to the lower animal instincts or physical senses.</note> and with his inferior reason rather than the superior, he makes himself cowardly. **SINCE three such blessed ladies:** He shows how great the help is, coming not from one, but from three—and three such as these, meaning of such quality, and "blessed," as if to say loved and sent by God. **CARE for you in the court of heaven:** that is, they are your advocates and intermediaries in the court of heaven, as if to say in that place where they can acquire for you supreme beatitude. **MY speaking:** that is, the words of me, Virgil; this signifies the discourse made by "superior reason," which is not deceived by false arguments and does not deceive others, because it knows the truth, its discourse being through universals—of which there is true science—and having known the truth, it demonstrates it to others.

> As little flowers, by the nocturnal frost
> bent down and closed, once the sun whitens them
> all straighten up, open upon their stem,
> Such I became with my exhausted virtue,
> and such good daring ran to my heart
> that I began like a person set free:
> "O compassionate was she who succored me,
> and you, courteous, who obeyed so swiftly
> the true words that she offered you!
> You have with desire so disposed my heart
> toward the coming, by your words,
> that I have returned to my first purpose.
> Now go, for a single will is in us both:
> you guide, you lord, and you master."
> Thus I spoke to him; and after he moved,
> I entered upon the deep and wild path.

<column-break/>

Virgil had finished his speech. After which, wishing to show that the poet had been entirely persuaded—and being strengthened such that from such cowardice he had returned to the best hope—he demonstrates this through a comparison. He says that just as the flowers which the cold of the night had made pale and closed—that is, made languid and withered—open and straighten themselves and renew their color when the sun comes, so Dante, who through the cold of the night (that is, through timidity, because timidity always arises from a lack of heat), I say through the cold of the night (meaning that such timidity arises from nocturnal shadows, which is ignorance), was strengthened by the coming of the sun (that is, by the light of reason illuminated by the aforementioned graces). **THEY STRAIGHTEN all open upon their stem:** that is, upon their stalk. *Stile* in Greek <note>original: "Stile in greco"</note> signifies "column"; hence we call "style" and "stem" [stelo] anything upright and fit to support. **AND SUCH good daring ran to my heart:** that is, I took up daring again, which is born in the heart; hence we use the term "to encourage" [rincorare] for "to strengthen." **THAT I began like a person set free:** that is, free from all fear. **O COMPASSIONATE was she who succored me.** And certainly it arises from divine compassion that our soul is illuminated by such grace. **AND YOU, VIRGIL, courteous.** "Courteous" is one who is liberal and kind in helping those in need. Therefore, it is the office of Virgil—that is, of superior reason when it is illuminated and moved by the three ladies—to be courteous and prompt in succoring the inferior reason and the sensuality, teaching it to obey its precepts. **TO THE true words she offered you.** Because Beatrice—that is, Theology—who wants Virgil to help Dante, always uses true words and reasons. **YOU HAVE with desire disposed my heart.** He shows how effective Virgil's persuasion was, since he not only persuaded him, but persuaded him with "desire." That is, he so inflamed him that he not only wants to obey him, but regrets not having obeyed him sooner. For desire is a pain of the soul for the thing we do not have and would wish to have. **NOW GO, for a single will is in us both.** To wish to keep well to the path that leads us to happiness, it is necessary that one and the same will belongs to Virgil and to Dante—that is, to the Reason that guides and the Sensuality that obeys. This means nothing else but that the appetite obeys reason. **You guide, you lord, and you master.** We said a little earlier that it is necessary for man's salvation that the appetite obeys reason. For this reason, it happens that sometimes the appetite follows reason, judging it to be wiser, and then reason is its "guide." Sometimes the appetite is so rebellious that it is necessary for reason to constrain it to obedience, as a lord constrains a servant; then reason is "lord." Sometimes it happens that the appetite follows reason as one illuminated and taught by it; then it obeys as if to a "master." **AND AFTER he moved.** That is, after Reason moved. Because the appetite must not move if Reason does not move first. **I entered upon the deep path:** that is, profound, as we say "deep sea" [alto mare] and "deep river"; because the first path was through Hell, which is the knowledge of vices, which are the lowest things because they always consist of earthly things. **AND WILD:** because, as we said in the beginning, sins are born from the "forest" [selva]—that is, from matter, which is the body.

<summary>This page analyzes Virgil's successful use of rhetoric to restore Dante's courage, culminating in the famous flower simile and the alignment of Dante's will with Virgil's guidance. Landino explains these movements as the harmony of divine grace, superior reason, and the human appetite.</summary>

<header>INFERNO</header>

--- Page 55 ---
<meta>This page continues the transition from the introductory cantos to the start of the journey through the gate of Hell. The commentary by Cristoforo Landino continues to provide theological and philosophical context for Dante's allegorical journey.</meta>

<page-type>text</page-type>
<columns>2</columns>
<header>CANTO THREE</header>

->### CANTO THREE OF THE FIRST CANTICLE<-

Through me you go into the city of woe;
through me you go into eternal pain;
through me you go among the lost people.
Justice moved my high maker;
<margin><gloss>made me</gloss></margin> divine power made me,
the highest wisdom, and the primal love.
Before me there were no created things,
except eternal ones, and I endure eternally.
Abandon all hope, you who enter.
These words of dark color
I saw written above a gate;
therefore I said: "Master, their meaning is hard for me."

<column-break/>

**S**ome people believe that the first two chapters were intended as a prologue, and that this third one is the beginning of the narrative. But if we consider the material diligently, it can easily be proven that the narrative begins in the first chapter, at the verse: *I cannot well say how I entered.* <note>original: "Io nō ui so ben dire chom io uētrai."</note> This is because Dante narrates his pilgrimage as having found himself in the woods, having lost the way, and having arrived at the foot of the mountain. And then, having turned toward the sun along the steep path that would have led him to salvation if the three beasts had not pushed him back down. Finally, reduced almost to the bottom, he received the help of Virgil and the three ladies. Through Virgil’s words, he was persuaded to leave the short path up the mountain and follow him through Hell and Purgatory—a path which, without sinister mishap, can lead him to Heaven. This signifies what we have already demonstrated above. And if anyone should say that in both of these cantos he writes many things to capture goodwill, attention, and docility <note>Landino uses the classical rhetorical terms "benevolentia, attentio, and docilitas," which were goals for the introduction of a speech.</note>, it is not forbidden to do this in any part of the poem. Indeed, it is especially required of the writer to capture these whenever he finds an opportunity.

Now, because we are already at the point where the poet descends into Hell, I judge it useful to explain what Hell is, and in how many ways one is said to "descend into Hell." Hell <term>Inferno; from the Latin "infra," meaning "below"</term> is the lowest and deepest part of the world. Not only is Hell established by the people of God, but also by many poets, especially Homer, Virgil, Ovid, Statius, and Claudian. It is described even more excellently by the prince of philosophers, Plato, in the *Crito* <note>Landino likely means the *Phaedo* or the *Republic*, as the *Crito* does not discuss the afterlife in this detail.</note>, in which he introduces Socrates disputing the immortality of the soul. He demonstrates that human souls after death are judged according to their faults and tormented in Hell until they are purged, if the sins were not very grave. But those who have committed enormous crimes and are "unpurgable" are, according to him, sent to a deeper place called Tartarus, and there they are afflicted eternally with the heaviest punishments. This opinion is very similar to the Christian faith and encompasses both Hell and Purgatory. 

The majority of writers seem to agree that such a place is at the center of the earth or near it; and especially Christians believe this because there "outer darkness" exists—that is, distant from the light—and there is "weeping and gnashing of teeth." The Prophet writes: "The Lord has delivered my soul from the lowest hell." <note>original Latin: "Eripuit dñs aiam meā de inferno inferiori."</note> And Truth itself <note>A common reference to Christ in medieval/Renaissance texts.</note> said that the Son of Man had to be in the heart of the earth for three days and three nights. Because the center is in the middle of the globe of the earth, just as the heart is in the middle of the body. 

And because many say this cannot be—since in the solidity of the earth there cannot be a cavernous and empty place—it is shown that just as celestial spirits (and even impure ones) can easily penetrate every hard and solid thing, so souls can penetrate everywhere unless God forbids it. Nevertheless, anyone who diligently reads the *Morals* of Gregory <note>Pope Gregory the Great’s *Moralia in Job*.</note> will see that Hell extends from the beginning of our misty air down to the center. The misty air begins five miles above the earth, because in this space there are many vapors rising from the earth that create clouds, winds, rains, snow, hail, and similar things, as Aristotle treats in his *Meteorology* <note>original: "meteora," which Landino notes many call "metaura" through ignorance of the Greek language.</note>. 

And rightly, considering the height of the heavens, this air can be called "Hell," that is, a "low place." Thus, when the apostate angels rebelled against God and were cast down from their celestial seats into this misty air, the Apostle Peter said they were in Hell. I leave behind the division made by the Platonists in distinguishing the infernal places from the superior ones. Nor do I narrate what the ancients meant in the fable of the division between the three brothers: what it signifies that Heaven fell to Jove, the Sea to Neptune, and Hell to Pluto—things that are undoubtedly useful to know, but not very pertinent to our purpose. 

I do not want to omit, however, that Richard of Middleton <note>original: "Riccardo de media uilla," a 13th-century Franciscan theologian.</note> maintains that Hell proper is that part around the center; the part above that is Limbo; and above Limbo he places Purgatory. Then, above Purgatory, up to the surface of the earth, he places the "Bosom of Abraham." But we will speak of these at the beginning of the second canticle. 

Now, having spoken of Hell, it remains to understand what it means to "descend into Hell" and in how many ways one can be said to go there. Taking our starting point from here, we will say that the **first descent**, according to the Platonists, is when the soul comes into the body. But we will say nothing of this at present because it could not be explained without many words, and it is not very necessary for the present work; nor can it be in all parts harmonious with the Christian religion. 

The **second descent** we call when our soul falls into vice by sinning, because it distances itself from celestial sublimity and buries itself in earthly desires. And if it does not amend itself, it always collapses into a lower place, so we can say that soul is in Hell. To understand this better, it should be noted that man was placed by his Creator at the boundary between rational and irrational creatures. Above him, he has rational creatures, such as the angels. Starting from the first Seraphim and descending through the three hierarchies and nine orders, man follows after the last angels; and after him, there is no other rational creature. Instead, the irrational creatures and brute animals follow. It remains, then, that man is placed at the boundary of rational and irrational creatures. But because God created him immediately in His image and likeness, and left him with free will to do good and evil, it happens that by his virtue and the favor of divine grace, he can elevate himself high above the human condition and ascend to the heavens. Likewise, when through his errors he is destitute of divine grace, he declines downward, falls from the human condition, and becomes a beast. Just as through virtue we raise ourselves to heaven, surpassing the human state, so through vice we collapse into Hell. And this is the second descent into Hell. 

The **third** is when, after death, the sinful soul is damned to inhabit such a place, and is relegated there as if in a perpetual prison. 

The **fourth** follows, and just as the two above are pernicious to our salvation, so this one is salutary. For we say one "descends into Hell" when we enter into the contemplation of vices to know them; and having known them, we seek to abstain from them and purge ourselves, making ourselves fit to rise to contemplation. In this way, Virgil depicts Aeneas as having descended into Hell. And in this same way, at present, Dante follows Virgil and goes to Hell, as we have already demonstrated several times. Nevertheless, in describing Hell, he follows what Christians posit regarding the eternal punishments for the damned. In this way, he treats both the "essential" Hell and the "moral" Hell simultaneously. 

The **fifth descent** is posited by some through the magic arts, which will be discussed below. According to Dante's description, the beginning of Hell is at the surface of the earth and descends to the center. Thus, the further one descends, the more it narrows...

# INFERNO

to the place: and the pains may be greater. Nor do I wish to omit the marvelous genius and invention of Dante in every part: who, with an unusual form, imagines that Hell and Purgatory are made of the same matter, <note>Landino refers to the Aristotelian idea that when Lucifer fell, he displaced earth to create the void of Hell, and that displaced earth formed the mountain of Purgatory.</note> though he changes the site of Purgatory and introduces a new region for it. Nevertheless, he says nothing against the <margin>rio and/</margin> truth. And he satisfies two not insignificant doubts, as we shall demonstrate shortly below. He intends, therefore, that Hell was not created from the beginning, but was made at the same time that it was decided that sin should be punished in Hell. And since the earth is a solid thing, and for this reason not easy to receive so large a <margin>rio.</margin> capacity for Hell, he imagines that when Lucifer fell from the heavens and plunged to the center, he pushed as much earth from our hemisphere as remained as a void. And that earth, thus pushed, rose in the other hemisphere and made the mountain of Purgatory. This fiction of his makes it plausible that under the earth there is a vacuum in Hell. And because, according to the philosophers, the other hemisphere is as habitable as ours, it would seem that nature had made it in vain if there were no one to inhabit it. It remains, through Dante’s fiction, that it is not habitable in vain, since the souls of Purgatory inhabit it. And we shall not be constrained, according to the philosophers, to confess that there are men there as there are here, inhabiting the souls. For if there were human inhabitants, an impropriety would arise: because they would not have been able to receive the evangelical doctrine as we have. Or they would have to fall into the error of origin, which said that Christ was crucified another time in that hemisphere to redeem them as he had redeemed us. But of the site and space of Hell described by this poet, I hope we shall speak more distinctly when we arrive at the bottom, and with more demonstration than perhaps anyone else has written—especially with the help of our Antonio Manetti, <note>Antonio Manetti (1423–1497) was a Florentine mathematician and architect famous for his "Calculations" on the site, shape, and size of Dante’s Hell.</note> who with his mathematical genius has investigated things that are very plausible and almost demonstrative. But returning to where we left off: it should be considered that sometimes he treats vices in the way they are in souls separated from the body and damned in Hell; at other times, in the way they are in a man still living and in the body. **THROUGH ME one goes.** <note>original: "PER ME si va."</note> The poet imagines here that this is the gate of Hell, and above the gate these words are written, which the gate speaks: and it says, "through me, the gate, one goes into the city of woe"—that is, I am the entrance through which one goes into Hell, which he calls the "city of woe" because in it nothing is found but sorrow. For if we understand Hell as the place where, according to our true religion, the souls of the damned are tormented, what greater pain can there be than to find oneself in constant and greatest supplications without hope of any end? And if we understand it morally according to the ancients—that descending into Hell is to contaminate and stain one’s soul with vices and wickedness, which by its nature is pure and simple and without stain—what greater torture can there be than the constant torment of conscience? Which day and night goads us: and the fear of civil penalties, and of infamy, and of the wrath of God? And note that the poet adorns this beginning with two rhetorical colors, using repetition and exposition. They call it repetition every time several clauses begin with the same expression or word, as here in three verses there are three clauses. And understand that a clause is a part of speech which, as a part, is complete: as saying, "Through me you go into the city of woe." We see that this is a complete part of speech. There are, therefore, in three verses three clauses, and each begins with this phrase "through me." This, then, is repetition. Exposition is when in several clauses, although the words are different, the meaning is nonetheless almost the same: as here, where although the words are different—"Through me you go into the city of woe," and others "through me you go into eternal pain," and others "through me you go among the lost people"—nonetheless, it is almost the same sentiment. Furthermore, he makes an "augmentation": because he places these three verses in a form where what follows always adds something more. For the first has "pain," the second has "eternal pain," the third has "perdition," which makes the pain greatest. It is, therefore, pain, and eternal pain, and the greatest pain. Nor could the poet use more horrendous words to frighten men from vices. And he made no mention that the gate opened. Therefore, it follows that it stands always open. This denotes that at any time and any age, and in every state, man can fall into vice. But to return from those to virtue is difficult. <note>original: "Facilis descensus averni."</note>

> The descent to Avernus is easy: 
> night and day the door of dark Dis stands open; 
> but to recall one's step and escape to the upper air, 
> this is the task, this is the labor. <note>Quoting Virgil’s *Aeneid*, Book VI, lines 126–129.</note>

IN THE CITY. He used this name "city" as he uses the place: for he calls every great congregation of men a city, in whatever way they live. But the learned call only a multitude of men congregated to live well and rightly in concord a "city." Whence Cicero demonstrates that Rome was not a city in the time when captives ruled and the good were in exile. But to Aurelius Augustine, <note>Saint Augustine of Hippo.</note> it seems that every class and congregation should be called a city: and therefore he posits two. One according to the flesh; the other according to the spirit. That according to the flesh is the city of the wicked, and he calls it Babylon, which signifies "confusion," because in vices there is always confusion; and it began with Cain, who out of envy killed his brother Abel. Whence he committed the first homicide and was a fratricide. The other city, which is according to the spirit, is that of the good, and it began with Abel and is called Jerusalem. That of Babylon plunges its inhabitants into Hell and makes them citizens of it. In this way, it can be called a city. That of Jerusalem makes them ascend to heaven where the celestial Jerusalem is, inhabited by the blessed, whom the apostle calls citizens of the saints and members of the household of God. <note>original: "ciues sanctorũ & domeštici dei." Landino references Ephesians 2:19.</note> And as these are two different cities, so from them are born two species of different loves. For the celestial one loves God so much that it esteems itself as nothing. The earthly one loves itself so much that it does not esteem God. And this is the city that the poet presently says is "woeful." JUSTICE moved my high maker: No one, therefore, can complain about Hell, since it is founded upon justice. And certainly it was a just thing that God ordained suitable punishments for sins. For as Aurelius Augustine says, the order of justice shines more in Hell than in heaven. Because no one is in Hell who does not deserve it, and no one is in Paradise who deserves it entirely. <note>Landino alludes to the concept of Grace being necessary for Heaven, while Justice is sufficient for Hell.</note> MY high maker: There can be no "high maker" if it is not God. Therefore, it must be eternal and irrevocable. Let no one lament, it having been made justly and by him who is omnipotent; he uses a rhetorical color called "interpretation." This is when we have placed a term and then interpret what it signifies. He said "my high maker," that is, God. And as a Christian, he demonstrates this God to be unique in essence. For he said "my high maker," and not "my high makers." He is, therefore, one God in essence. Then he demonstrates that in this essence there are three persons: Father for power, Son for wisdom, Holy Spirit for love. God as Father creates; as Son, he orders and distributes; as Holy Spirit, he preserves. But concerning the Trinity, it will happen that we speak more extensively in another place. But here he has made mention of it to demonstrate that it is not to be doubted that Hell is eternal, since it is made by him who through supreme power was able, through supreme wisdom knew how, and through love willed to make it so. DIVINE power: therefore irrefragable. SUPREME wisdom: therefore infallible. Primal LOVE: therein is stable will. BEFORE me were no things created, except eternal ones: Eternal creatures were the primary matter, the heavens, and the angels. It is, therefore, the best argumentation to prove that Hell is eternal. For if those who were to be in pain are eternal, it is necessary that the place of the pain be eternal. It is plausible that the angels were created before Hell. For the fault must come before the punishment for the fault. Therefore, when God created heaven and earth, he established in the center of that earth the place where the angels rebellious against God would have eternal pains. Nor should it seem absurd that man is punished eternally, although he sins temporally: because sin formally is against God, who is eternal. This is what Gregory <note>Pope Gregory the Great.</note> says: and Augustine adds that it pertains to divine justice that he should never lack torment who never willed <insert>to turn away from sin.</insert>

<header>CANTO THREE</header>

never be free of sin. **ABANDON all hope, you who enter.** This is understood to refer to the souls who, after being separated from the body, remain damned. It can similarly be understood to refer to those who go to "hell" in this life: that is, those who enter into vices and turn them into a habit. For it is either entirely impossible or extremely difficult for someone who has made a habit of vice to be able to free themselves from it. And if someone were to say that if it is true that one who has formed a habit cannot abstain from the vice even if they wish to, then it should not be imputed to them as a vice—since neither virtue nor vice is counted as such unless it is voluntary, and this would be involuntary—I respond according to Aristotle in the *Ethics* <note>original: "secondo Aristotele nelletica"</note> that even if it is not within a man's power to withdraw from vice after the habit is formed, it is nonetheless a voluntary sin. This is because the beginning of the vicious acts was voluntary and he could have withdrawn then. It is like shooting an arrow to kill a man: although once it has left the bow one might wish it not to strike, nevertheless, if it strikes and kills, we say it was voluntary because in the beginning it was in his power to shoot or not to shoot the arrow. **OF A DARK color:** A fitting color for Hell, which, being underground, must be dark. Hell is dark because where the rays of the sun do not reach, there must be shadows. The sun signifies knowledge and truth; while these are within a man, the darkness of ignorance—from which every vice proceeds—is not there. There is, therefore, obscurity and darkness in Hell to denote that every vice is born when the light of reason is extinguished in the soul, whereby it remains in darkness; and he who walks in darkness stumbles. Thus, the Lord’s precept is a healthy one: that we should walk while we have the light. Truly, the words written above Hell were of a dark color to denote that, just as in the dark it is difficult to discern things, so it has been difficult to understand Hell. For even Origen <note>Alexandrian theologian (c. 184–253 AD) whose views on the non-eternity of Hell were later deemed heretical.</note>—a man of such learning and such excellent life—and several others erred greatly in believing that Hell was not eternal, but that after a long time every soul would be saved. **THEIR SENSE to me was harsh.** That is, the meaning of these words is painful and bitter to me. And deservedly it must have seemed "hard" to him to have to enter a place from which he had no hope of exiting. Certainly, the "lower reason" <term>lower reason: the part of the mind dealing with earthly desires and sensory input</term> together with "sensuality" judges it very hard and difficult to descend into the meditation on vices without remaining caught by their charms and flatteries, like a bird in lime or a fish on a hook. He was, therefore, doubting this, and was assailed by cowardice. Recognizing this, Virgil responds:

**And he to me, as a discerning person:**
->**"here one must leave behind all suspicion:"**<-
->**"all cowardice must here be dead:"**<-
**"We have come to the place where I told you"**
->**"that you shall see the sorrowful people"**<-
->**"who have lost the good of the intellect:"**<-
**And after he placed his hand in mine**
->**with a joyful face, from which I took comfort,**<-
->**he led me into the secret things:**<-

<column-break/>

As we have said, the fact that Dante is terrified by the words written at the top of a gate signifies nothing other than this: the "lower reason," though persuaded by the "higher reason" <term>higher reason: the part of the soul directed toward divine truth and morality</term>, judges that if one wishes to arrive at happiness, it is first necessary to descend into Hell—that is, into the contemplation of vices—and, having known them, to purge oneself of them. But then, reading these words—that is, considering that whoever makes a habit of vice cannot escape it—he becomes terrified. He fears that by rethinking pleasurable and joyful things according to the senses, he might find the serpent hidden among the grass and flowers. But the higher reason admonishes him to take a frank and strong spirit, and in no way to become base; and it offers him its hand, which is to say, its help. Virgil does for Dante now exactly what the Sibyl did for Aeneas when she admonished him to take the path with a frank spirit and keep his sword out of its sheath. This signifies that in such meditation one must have a strong and

<column-break/>

unconquered soul, armed against vices so as not to be overcome by them. **AND HE to me as a discerning person:** that is, provident and circumspect and quick to understand. Certainly, higher reason is that through whose circumspection and foresight we prevent the ruin into which the appetite and lower reason would fall if it did not intervene. **HERE ONE must leave behind all suspicion:** Suspicion arises from a lack of knowledge. Because Dante—that is, the lower reason—doubts whether one can pass through the knowledge of vices without being defiled by them, he fears that by entering he might form such a habit that he cannot leave. But higher reason understands that vices contrary to moral virtues are not committed by knowing them, but by acting according to them. **ALL cowardice:** which is born from suspicion. He admonishes him, therefore, to arm himself with frankness of soul. Similarly, the Sibyl exhorts Aeneas: <note>original: "Tuq; iua de uiam uaginaq; eripe ferrum. Nunc animis opus est Eneas/ nunc pectore firmo."</note> "Go on your way and unsheathe your sword from its scabbard. Now there is need for courage, Aeneas, now for a firm heart." **WHO HAVE lost the good of the intellect.** That is, they have lost God, who is the ultimate bliss and truth. As Aristotle affirms in the third book of *On the Soul* <note>original: "dellaia" (De Anima)</note>: <term>The good of the intellect</term> <note>original: "Bonū intellectus"</note> is the ultimate bliss. For this reason, Thomas Aquinas demonstrates in his book *Against the Gentiles*: <note>original: "Oportet ultimū finē uniuersi esse bonum intellectus. Hoc autem est ueritas Oportet igitur ueritatem esse ultimum uniuersi totius finem."</note> "The ultimate end of the universe must be the good of the intellect. This, however, is truth. It is necessary, therefore, that truth be the ultimate end of the entire universe." Regarding this, Augustine said that the wicked, if they could, would rather be in Hell and see God than be outside of it and not see Him. **AND AFTER he placed his hand in mine:** Dante cannot enter without the help of higher reason and moral doctrine. For this reason, Virgil offers him his hand; that is, he assists him with his power. For "hand" is often used to mean "power." **WITH A joyful face.** Because the intellect, having true knowledge, is secure and shows itself joyful to the sensuality. **INTO THE secret things:** If we understand this as the actual Hell, we call them "secret things" because they are not known to any living person except by revelation. If we understand it as the contemplation of vices, they are "secret things" because they are not known except to those who possess learning and contemplation.

**There sighs, sobs, and loud wails**
->**resounded through the starless air,**<-
->**so that at first I wept thereat:**<-
**Diverse tongues, horrible speech,**
->**words of pain, accents of anger,**<-
->**voices loud and hoarse, and the sound of hands with them,**<-
**Made a tumult, which swirled**
->**forever in that air tinted without time,**<-
->**like sand when the whirlwind blows.**<-

<column-break/>

The poet is already inside the gate of Hell. And because in such meditation we must receive the actions and operations of man—for in those consist the moral virtues if the rule of reason corrects them, and conversely the vices if they are not corrected—those whose operations were either nothing or so useless that they remain in obscurity occur to our minds first. As Sallust writes: <note>original: "Horū uita morsq; iuxta est: quoniā de utraq; siletur."</note> "The life and death of these are much the same, since silence is kept regarding both." He expresses, therefore, the vice of cowardice and pusillanimity, which hinders the man who is produced by God either to work in the active life or to meditate in the contemplative life; instead, he grows lazy for lack of any generosity of soul, abandoning every honorable and excellent enterprise. And although we are born, as Plato writes, to be useful to ourselves and to others, nevertheless this man...

# INFERNO

**And I, whose head was girt with error** <note>original: "derrore" — some editions of Dante read "d'orrore" (with horror)</note>
**said: Master, what is it that I hear?** <note>The original OCR reads "chiodo" (nail), but this is a transcription error for "ch'i' odo" (that I hear).</note>
**And what people are these who seem so overcome by grief?**

[He] is of no use to himself or to others. And he lives in such <term>pigritia: laziness or spiritual sloth</term> that he becomes loathsome to himself. And just as those who give themselves to some honest exercise grieve when they lack the time for it, so these people, by contrast, lament that time hangs heavy upon them. Francesco Petrarch expresses this most wisely in these verses: "O wretched is he who counts the days, and a thousand years seem like one to him, for he lives in vain, and never faces himself on this earth." <note>Petrarch, *Canzoniere* 362</note> It is no wonder, then, if finally realizing they have lost the time which they could have spent most usefully, they feel supreme repentance and remain in weeping and mourning. For as Persius writes: "Then yesterday’s 'tomorrow' has passed, and they have already late lamented the life they left behind." <note>Persius, *Satires* V.68-69; the Latin text discusses how procrastination leads to a wasted life.</note> Wanting to show this repentance, Dante describes what those in great pain do. For sighs come from anxiety and anguish of heart. **WEEPING:** these are tearful voices. **WAILS:** querulous and complaining voices. **RESOUNDED:** they echoed. **WITHOUT STARS:** Because beneath the earth stars are not seen. Furthermore, these most base people are "without stars," meaning without any splendor of glory. And allegorically, where there are vices, there are no stars: that is, there is no light, but everything is darkness. He imitates Virgil where he says: "They went dark through the shadows under the lonely night, through the vacant halls and empty realms of Dis." <note>Virgil, *Aeneid* VI.268-269</note> **WHEREFORE I** at the beginning **WEPT FOR IT:** It is a human thing to have compassion for the afflicted and to grieve for those in the darkness of sin. **DIVERSE LANGUAGES:** to show that they were gathered here from every region. And allegorically, the "tongues" of sinners are diverse. For just as in virtue there is a perpetual consonance and harmony, so by contrast in vice there is discordance and contrariety. Whence Aristotle in the *Ethics*: "With the truth, all things harmonize; but the truth quickly clashes with what is false." <note>Aristotle, *Nicomachean Ethics* I.8</note> **HORRIBLE SPEECH:** as if horrendous reasonings. This is born from supreme desperation. **WORDS OF GRIEF:** that is, such as pain produces. **ACCENTS OF ANGER:** We call "accent" the proper pronunciation of the voice, and there are acute, grave, and circumflex accents. And we see that those in joy and pleasure pronounce the same words with different accents than those in anger or other disturbance. Whence it often happens that hearing some people speak, although we do not discern their words nor understand what they say, we nevertheless perceive by the accents whether they are angry or happy. And certainly, what greater pain can there be for one who has lived without any virtue than to know at the end how much good he has left behind? For this reason, Persius prays to God not to punish wicked tyrants with any other penalty than to show them how excellent a thing virtue is, so that they may grieve and gnaw at themselves with rage for not having followed and practiced it—which torment exceeds and surpasses all others. **LOUD VOICES:** that is, shouts. **AND FAINT:** The second is born from the first, for he who continues to shout becomes hoarse. **AND SOUND OF HANDS:** because through pain one often strikes the hands together, or truly strikes the breast and face with them. For this reason, the Latins specifically use the word *plangere* <note>to beat the breast in mourning</note>. Therefore, they are "of hands," meaning the noise born from striking the hands. **WITH THEM:** that is, with those loud and faint voices. All these things mixed together generated in the air a **TUMULT:** that is, a confused and disturbed voice and sound. **WHICH** always whirls in that air: Sound and voice are born from the percussion of air, and the struck air bounces back and spreads in a circle <note>original: "sinigro" — likely a transcription error for "in giro"</note>, as we see happening in water when a stone is thrown into it and makes a circle which successively widens. **TINTED WITHOUT TIME:** The air that belongs to us who dwell upon the earth is "tinted," that is, dark, not always but at times—namely, when the sun has departed from our hemisphere. But when it returns, the air becomes bright. But here, because the sun can never reach it, it is always tinted. And it is a fitting thing that he who always lived in obscurity, and never performed an act that gave him the light of fame, should remain forever in darkness. **LIKE THE SAND WHEN THE WHIRLWIND:** That is, at the revolution of the wind. **BREATHES:** that is, it whirls by the spirit of the wind. It is an excellent comparison. For just as sand is sterile and has infinite grains, so these people are without any fruit and are infinite in number; and every wind turns them. *Turbo* <note>Latin for whirlwind or a spinning top</note> in the Latin language signifies an instrument that whirls; whence a "top" and a "whirligig" are called *turbo*. Likewise, they call *turbo* a wind that does not go straight but whirls in one place. Whence sand and dust moved by the wind likewise whirl. Therefore, that confused sound composed of diverse voices will whirl through the air just as sand does when the wind turns it. But a *turbo* is properly when the wind comes out of vapors so dense they have become clouds, as if it were coming out of a cave, and it sends to the ground whatever it finds while whirling. **AND I, WHO HAD MY HEAD GIRT WITH ERROR:** That is, with ignorance. Other texts have "horror," and then we would say "I had my head girt with horror," meaning with dread for the tumult I heard. The author places in this spot a space that goes in a circle between the aforementioned gate and the river of which we will speak shortly below. And from the river to the center, he makes nine circles, which descend in steps so that the inner one is always smaller. In this first space, he places those who lived in lazy idleness and without acting for good or evil. For this reason Virgil [wrote]: "Before the vestibule itself and in the first jaws of Hell, Grief and avenging Cares have set their couches." <note>Virgil, *Aeneid* VI.273-274</note> Nor was it appropriate to put them in any of the nine circles, because they cannot be assigned under any distinct sin. These lazy and cowardly <note>original: "pusillanimi"</note> souls can be called "cold." For Greek and Latin poets, just as they call "burning" those who are vehement, diligent, and solicitous in action—whence Virgil: "The Tyrians stood burning [with zeal]" <note>Virgil, *Aeneid* I.423</note>—so by contrast they call the lazy "cold." From this, Terence said: "Truly, the man is cold here." <note>Terence, *The Eunuch*</note> Furthermore, they are cold because they are without love, which alone makes men burning for action. Whence the poets call love a "flame." "From this comes the soft flame in the marrow," <note>Virgil, *Aeneid* IV.66</note> and "Unhappy Dido burns [with love]." <note>Virgil, *Aeneid* IV.68</note> Love is, therefore, the principle of action. Whence the first order of the first hierarchy of angels is the Seraphim, which name signifies "ardor" and "love." But of these things we will speak more extensively and starting from a higher point in the places that more require it. It suffices for the present that love is the principle of our operations. But because, as Plato writes in the *Symposium*, there are two species of love, there are therefore two Venuses: one celestial and the other terrestrial. The celestial draws us to the love of celestial things, from which virtues, actions, and contemplations according to them are born in our souls. The terrestrial inflames us with the love of earthly and fleeting things, from which all vices and ignorance of God and ourselves are born in us. Therefore, repeating what was said, we will say there are three generations of men: First, those not in love, who operate neither good nor evil. Second, those in love with earthly things, who operate evil. And third, those inflamed with celestial things, who operate good and according to virtue. Of these three, the first two are vicious, because it is not only a vice to operate evil, but it is also a vice—though a lesser one—not to operate according to virtue. For we were produced in life as rational animals, and God has left us, as Solomon says, in the hand of our own counsel—that is, of free will—so that with it we might acquire eternal happiness, either in the social and civil life according to Martha, or in the contemplative life according to Mary <note>The biblical sisters Martha and Mary are traditional symbols of the active and contemplative lives</note>. Certainly, we commit a great sin by not using the instrument of reason with which eternal life is fashioned. It is not enough, therefore, to abstain from evil if one does not do good. Whence the Truth says in the Gospel: "He who is not with me is against me. And he who does not gather and collect with me, scatters and spreads." <note>Matthew 12:30</note> Recognizing this, our divine poet places these first ones—who were cold and without love—in the first place of Hell. After whom, through the rest of Hell, he distributes according to those who have been...

He uses classical references to Virgil, Aristotle, and Plato to argue that a life without the "flame" of love or the use of reason is itself a form of sin.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Cristoforo Landino’s commentary on Canto III of Dante's Inferno. ### CANTO ONE <note>Though the header says Canto One, this refers to the start of the first book (Inferno). The text specifically addresses Canto III.</note>
**e iii** <note>This is a signature mark used by early printers to track the order of the pages during binding.</note>

...[you were] kindled with love: not true, not pure, not divine, but false, filthy, and defiled in worldly things. And they always burned in intemperate lechery, in insatiable avarice, and in proud and Luciferian ambition—from which three cupidities <term>cupidities: excessive or illicit desires</term> all other vices are born. And from these come fitting punishments. Just as they lived a life of complaining and grief in the world, so they still live across the veil. For as John says in the Apocalypse: *For their works follow them* <note>original: "Opera . n . eorũ sequũt illos" (Revelation 14:13)</note>. And the life of these people can be called death, and their fate and condition is most base. These people always live in sighs through the anguish and sadness of the heart, and in the other tribulations caused by their impatience. Similarly, through the diversity of languages, he demonstrates the various changes of their purposes. Of such men one can say the verse of Horace: *We, a worthless people, born only to consume the fruits of the earth* <note>original: "Nos uiles populus fruges consumere nati" (Horace, *Epistles* I.2.27)</note>. Truly, there are diverse languages because they gather here from every part of the world. Thus Virgil writes: *Hither the whole crowd, poured forth, was rushing to the banks—mothers and men* <note>original: "Huc omnis turba ad ripas effusa ruebat Matres atq; uiri" (Virgil, *Aeneid* VI.305-306)</note>.

> And he to me: "This wretched mode
> is held by the weary souls of those
> who lived without fame and without praise.
> They are mixed with that base choir
> of angels who were not rebels,
> nor were faithful to God, but were for themselves.
> The heavens drive them out to not be less beautiful,
> nor does deep Hell receive them,
> for the wicked would have some glory from them."

[They] did not exercise themselves in even mediocre things. Nor is "praising" anything other than proving that what is being spoken of was done correctly. But we will speak of fame more extensively elsewhere. Of these people it is written: *Let them be blotted out from the book of the living, and not be written with the righteous* <note>original: "Deleátur de libro uiuétiũ: & cũ iustis nõ scribant" (Psalm 69:28)</note>. **THE HEAVENS DRIVE THEM OUT** to not be less beautiful. And deservedly so, for it is not fitting that Heaven, where the fountain of divine light is, should be inhabited by anything other than bright and perfect things, without any blemish. And just as a place takes no small ornament from the excellence of its inhabitants, so conversely it becomes ignoble if it is inhabited by defiled people. **NOR DOES DEEP HELL RECEIVE THEM:** If sins are not equal—as theologians and also philosophers hold (except for the Stoics)—then the punishments and tortures should not be equal. Therefore, if they do not stay in Heaven because they have erred, they do not stay in the depths where the most heavy tortures are, because they have not erred so much. **FOR THE WICKED WOULD HAVE SOME GLORY FROM THEM.** The great sinners could boast that, having sinned more gravely than these, they were nonetheless not in greater punishment <note>i.e., the truly wicked would feel superior if the "indifferent" were punished alongside them in the deep pits of Hell.</note>.

> And I: "Master, what is so heavy
> for them that makes them lament so loudly?"
> He answered: "I will tell you very briefly.
> These have no hope of death,
> and their blind life is so low
> that they are envious of every other lot.
> The world allows no report of them to exist;
> mercy and justice disdain them;
> let us not speak of them, but look and pass on."

...[mercy] disdains them, because they are not saved. Likewise, justice disdains them, because they are not inside Hell with the other damned. But allegorically, no compassion is had for men established in such baseness, because everyone judges that every calamity deservedly befalls them. And similarly, every generous soul is ashamed to take revenge on such vile cowards. For which reason Virgil concludes that they are not worthy of accurate mention, but should only be touched upon in passing.

> And I, looking, saw a banner
> that whirling ran so fast
> that it seemed to me unworthy of any rest;
> And behind it came so long a train
> of people that I would never have believed
> that death had undone so many.
> After I had recognized some among them,
> I saw and knew the shadow of him
> who through cowardice made the great refusal.
> Immediately I understood and was certain
> that this was the sect of the base,
> displeasing to God and his enemies:

<column-break/>

**B**y the words said just before, I think it is manifest enough what the life of these people was, and what their sin. Thus, at present, he sets down the punishments they endure for it. And first he shows that such men lived without fame or praise. He says this not to show that man must seek fame—for we must exercise virtue to become perfect through it, and not to acquire fame as the vainglorious do. Therefore, he uses the rhetorical device called <term>denominatiõe: metonymy or denomination</term>, because he places "fame" (which follows virtue like the shadow follows the body) for virtue itself, which precedes fame. **THEY LIVED** without fame and without praise. Not without cause; for fame being a name widely known and spread through many places, it cannot be born except from excellent things. But praise can also exist for mediocre things. Therefore, they are not only without fame, because they did not do excellent things, but they are without praise, because they did not even...

**V**irgil uses brief words because these people are of such a quality that they hardly deserve to be remembered. **THESE HAVE NO HOPE OF DEATH:** Immortality is common to all human souls, because their substance is incorruptible. But the damned are said to be "dead" because of the deprivation—not of being, but of *blessed* being. Hence Augustine says that in Hell there is "death without death." But in this place, he means allegorically those who live in such baseness and <term>pusillanimity: small-mindedness or cowardice</term> that they not only despair of other refuges in their misery, but see themselves as not being heard by death, which they often call upon. Hence it follows that their blind life is in such a low state that they bear envy even toward the wretched and those who have died miserably. And although every man naturally seeks fame, these people do not know what fame or honor is. **MERCY AND JUSTICE** disdain them. If you understand this as the essential Hell: Mercy...

**H**e imagines that all this crowd, without any rest, circles around this perimeter of Hell. And truly, such men, not knowing how to propose any certain end for themselves—because they cannot imagine anything so low that the life of the soul does not frighten them—always wander in their minds. For they desire many things and grow weary of them all, and they rush from one to another without any weight of judgment. And they all follow one banner; for just as among men of judgment and soul there is a great difference in the goal they set for themselves—some giving themselves to the government of the republic, some to principalities and kingdoms, some to religion, some to doctrine—because in many ways one can acquire glorious and honest fame and true happiness. Hence it is written in the Gospel: *In my Father's house are many mansions* <note>original: "i domo patris mei mãsiões mltẽ fũt" (John 14:2)</note>. So, on the contrary, in these people there is no difference. And therefore they all follow one banner, upon which he places no image, because nothing can be discerned in such an obscure life. Furthermore, he shows it to be an infinite crowd. For there are many more who live to eat than those who eat to live. And it is a marvel that although in all men there is...

Landino explains that these souls are rejected by both Heaven and Hell because they lived without taking a stand, and he interprets their eternal aimless running behind a banner as a reflection of their lack of purpose in life.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Cristoforo Landino’s commentary on Canto III of Dante’s *Inferno*. In the previous section, the commentator described the sounds of the "Vestibule of Hell." Here, he explains the physical punishment of those who were neutral in life and begins a deep philosophical and allegorical exploration of the infernal rivers.</meta>

# INFERNO.

> *These wretches, who never were alive,*
> *were naked and greatly stimulated*
> *by horseflies and wasps that were there.*
> *They streaked their faces with blood,*
> *which, mixed with tears at their feet,*
> *was gathered by loathsome worms.*

<br/>

> *After I set myself to looking further,*
> *I saw people on the bank of a great river;*
> *wherefore I said: "Master, now grant me*
> *that I may know who they are and what custom*
> *makes them seem so ready to pass over,*
> *as I discern by the dim light."*
> *And he to me: "The things will be known to you*
> *when we stay our steps*
> *upon the sad shore of Acheron."*
> *Then with eyes shameful and cast down,*
> *fearing my speaking might be a burden to him,*
> *I refrained from speaking until the river.*

<column-break/>

the rational soul. Nevertheless, so rare are those who, among such infinite and innumerable throngs of mortals, leave the herd and rise to any excellence. We can also say that in this place they are in a state of constant running and without rest: because it is a fitting punishment to punish the lazy and sleepy with the opposite thing: such as running and constant motion. **WHEN I HAD RECOGNIZED SOME**, I saw and knew the shadow of him **WHO MADE THROUGH COWARDICE THE GREAT REFUSAL**. Not without reason does the poet mention only one: because such men are unknown, unless they are someone whom fortune has pulled to a high rank, and they, through a lack of spirit, have thrown themselves to the ground. Thus their cowardice <term>viltà: a lack of moral courage or baseness</term> is known by the greatness of the thing in which they exercised that cowardice.

But who this might be who made the "great refusal" is a matter of doubt. For many understand it to be Pietro da Morrone, who, having been created Pope Celestine, refused the papacy. Thus he called it the "great refusal," because among Christians there is no greater dignity. It cannot be denied that this man was of a most holy life. He lived for a long time as a hermit; then, due to his holiness, after the death of Nicholas Orsini IV, he was made Pope Celestine V. And because he had been forced to leave his solitary life, and felt himself more suited to that than to governing—and everyone should proceed according to the vocation to which they were called—and partly through the fraud of others (as we shall say when treating of Boniface VIII) [he resigned]. Some say this man did not renounce the pontificate through cowardice, but through excellence of spirit: because it is a greater spirit to despise great dignities than to seek them; and Mary is of more excellence than Martha <note>In Christian tradition, Mary represents the contemplative life and Martha the active life; the contemplative is traditionally held as the higher path.</note>. And they conclude that he did not renounce through cowardice, but through magnanimity. This is demonstrated by his end: for afterward, he was canonized by Pope Clement and placed in the catalog of saints.

Others add that the author instead meant Esau, the son of Rebecca and Isaac; who, as Jerome <note>St. Jerome, the 4th-century scholar and Bible translator.</note> excellently said, was no less "hairy and shaggy" <note>original: "hyrauto & piloso"</note> in mind than in body; who from good grain degenerated into weeds; who for a vile meal of lentils renounced to his brother Isaac <note>Landino likely means Jacob, who bought the birthright from Esau.</note> the place of the firstborn, from which was to proceed by succession the lineage from which Christ our salvation was to be born. I estimate that the poet, for several reasons, placed this example without a name. First, to avoid marking such a holy man with infamy; for although he maintained a holy life, it was nonetheless Dante's opinion that he proved cowardly in governing. Or perhaps because he did not wish to single out one more than another, leaving it to the judgment of the listeners to decide which one best fits this place. Or perhaps because, speaking of men without fame, it seemed appropriate that no name be given.

**THE SECT OF CAPTIVES**: "Captive" <note>original: "Captiuo"</note> in the Latin language signifies a man taken in war and led into servitude. And certainly, in the battle that the flesh wages against the spirit, the souls of these people are conquered by sensuality and become its servants; in such a way that they please neither God nor his enemies (that is, neither the good nor the wicked) because they do not warm to either side, but remain trembling in every operation. And elegantly he said they **NEVER WERE ALIVE**. For there are three generations of life: Vegetative, Sensitive, and Rational. And no thing can truly be said to live if it does not live according to its own proper life. But the vegetative life is not proper to man; for it is common not only to brute animals but to trees and herbs, which take nourishment, grow, and generate their own kind. This is proper to the vegetative life. Nor yet is the sensitive life proper to us, because it is common to us and other animals, which taste, touch, and use the other senses. But only the rational life belongs to man, because no other animal participates in it. This is divided into two parts: that is, in civil operations and actions—and this is called the "active life," expressed in the Holy Scriptures by Leah and Martha—and in the investigation and contemplation of truth—called "contemplative," noted under the name of Rachel and Mary. Therefore, these people having lived neither according to the one nor the other, it can truly be said that they never were alive. These same people are not assaulted by lions or bears, nor by other terrible beasts, but by horseflies or wasps: that is, their minds have never been pierced by noble and high thoughts, but by vile and ignoble ones. And their blood is collected by loathsome worms, which are born of earthly corruption; he uses "blood" for "life" because the life of the animal consists chiefly in the blood. Therefore, most vile thoughts and a sluggish idleness rather than anything else pierce and stimulate their lives; and the worms—that is, the lowest desires for earthly things—consume such a life.

**THESE HAVING PASSED**, he saw further ahead the banks of Acheron, the infernal river, and many souls waiting for Charon to pass them across in his ship. The author imagines that the river Acheron circles and encloses within itself the first circle of Hell, and consequently all the others. For one embraces the other, and the lower one is always of a smaller circumference. But since the river Acheron is mentioned here, it will perhaps be not useless to the reader if we relate in order, but with as much brevity as possible, what the ancients—poets and philosophers—understood allegorically by the infernal rivers. And first, taking our beginning from the prince of philosophers, Plato. He holds this—which opinion Origen largely follows—that our souls were all created together by God. But afterward, at various times, weighed down by the desire for earthly things, they fall to earth and enter bodies. And they understand "Hell" to be nothing other than the body, into which the soul enters; it happens that, submerged in this matter, as if intoxicated by it, it forgets all the things of which it had knowledge in heaven. And they call this matter a "river," which they divide into four rivers.

The first they call **Lethe**, which in Greek signifies "oblivion" <note>Greek: *λήθη*</note>; because the soul, submerged in the body, falls into the aforementioned oblivion. From Lethe is born **Acheron**, which name signifies "deprivation of joy" <note>A common medieval etymology: *a-cheron*, "without joy."</note>; for the soul loses through oblivion all that joy which it took when, pure and without the contagion of the body, it stood fixed in contemplating God. From Acheron is born the marsh of **Styx**, which signifies "sadness" <note>Greek: *στύξ*</note>; for he who is deprived of joy must necessarily live in sadness. And from Styx is born **Cocytus**, which in Greek signifies "wailing and mourning" <note>Greek: *κωκυτός*</note>. And because from long-lasting mourning men are inflamed into insanity and burning fury, they imagine that from Cocytus is born **Phlegethon**, so called because *Phlegethon* signifies "burning" <note>Greek: *φλεγέθων*</note>. These things are shown at length by Plato in the *Phaedo* <note>The transcription says "Phedro" (Phaedrus), but the description of the rivers is famously in the *Phaedo*.</note>. But we who firmly believe that human souls are not created before they are in...

<meta>This page continues Cristoforo Landino’s Neoplatonic and allegorical commentary on Dante's *Inferno*, Canto III. Having previously discussed the "neutrals" in the vestibule of Hell, Landino now moves toward the first infernal river, Acheron, providing an etymological and philosophical breakdown of the geography of the underworld.</meta>

# CANTO THREE

...or of sensuality makes it fall into sin where it drinks from **Lethe**, <note>In classical mythology, Lethe is the river of forgetfulness.</note> that is, it forgets its creator; and from Lethe proceed the other rivers as we have said above. But to speak more clearly, by Lethe we understand the submersion of reason into sensuality: because then is born the oblivion of all virtues. From Lethe is born **Acheron**, which represents the deliberation to sin. For this reason, Seneca said it runs swiftly and not without noise: because our intellect, in which there is some remorse of conscience and possesses within itself <term>synderesis: the innate spark of moral conscience that distinguishes good from evil</term> <note>original: "synderisi"</note>, cannot deliberate upon sin without the noise of a protesting conscience. And for this reason, this deliberation is a transition of the will, which carries the soul toward sinning; therefore, they imagine that **Charon** is here, who in his boat transports the souls. After this transition into sin, there follows sadness and grief. Because just as a pure conscience always keeps the soul joyful, so one who is aware of his own crimes and feels himself stained within is always in perpetual anxiety; nor does he ever rejoice or have peace within himself. For as Plato says, carnal delights pass in a brief time, leaving nothing behind but repentance. Nor can he ever rest whose conscience is always a witness to the sin committed. And as Juvenal says, *To carry [one's own guilt] in the breast night and day* <note>original: "Noctes atque dies gestare in pectore te"</note>. Likewise, the Pythian prophetess responded to a certain Spartan. And most excellently Cicero said, *There is no greater theater than one's conscience* <note>original: "Nullum est maius theatrum conscientia"</note>. Therefore, from Acheron is born the **Stygian** marsh, which signifies sadness; from which, because greater mourning and weeping proceed, they say that the river **Cocytus** emerges from it, which in Greek signifies "wailing." And he who for a long time consists in tears dries out the body and is inflamed with fury. Deservedly, the river which flows out of Cocytus is called **Phlegethon**, as if "burning," because *phlegethōn* signifies to burn. You have in brief what the infernal rivers signify. This should be committed to memory, because it will be necessary for you for the exposition of many other places in this poem. Now returning to the text, Dante asks what **custom** <note>original: "costume"</note> makes the souls so ready and eager to want to pass over. And he wisely said "custom." Because every operation of ours is moved either by nature or by custom—that is, by habit. Nature is the best guide to those who follow it. And he who lives according to sincere and uncorrupted nature always arrives at a good end, because it persuades us and draws us toward the true good. But captive custom often corrupts it. Whence men, following habit, leave virtue and give themselves to vice. And Petrarch expressed this, saying: *Our nature conquered by custom* <note>original: "Nostra natura vinta dal costume"</note>. Therefore, Dante, wishing to express that this appetite of the souls to pass Acheron was not natural, but moved by depraved habit, said "custom." Nor did he speak without great learning when he said:

### MAKES THEM SEEM so ready to pass over:
Using this verb **to seem** <note>original: "parere"</note>. For there being fixed and innate in man a firm appetite to always follow the good and flee the evil, we must understand according to the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle's philosophy.</note> that there are two kinds of good: namely, the **existent good** and the **apparent good**. The existent good is the true good; he who follows it becomes blessed, because he recognizes virtue and understands God to be the true good. The apparent good is when our soul, blinded by sensuality, follows pleasures and worldly delights, which are not existing goods but "seem" like goods to the senses. Therefore, the soul corrupted by sensuality is ready to pass Acheron—that is, to go toward sin as if toward a thing which is not good, but "seems" good to it. And it is as Petrarch says: *Greedy for such a thing, which is sweet to the sense but deadly to salvation.*

### DIM light:
That is, clouded and obscure. **Dim** <note>original: "fiocho"</note> is properly that which the Latins call "hoarse" <note>original: "rauco"</note>. But just as by metaphor from light to the voice we say "a clear voice"—meaning well-expressed and without offense—even though "clear" properly belongs to light; so although "fiocho" refers to a voice that is not clear, by the same metaphor we say "dim light," meaning not clear. But it is to be noted that the poet makes this entrance to Hell obscure, but not entirely deprived of light, to denote that when man passes into sin, he has begun to lose the light of reason; but he is not yet entirely in the dark, because in the beginning he has not yet made it a habit. And there remains to him some amount of the light of reason, by which our soul feels remorse, as I explained more extensively in Virgil on that verse: *Just as by an uncertain moon under a malicious light is the journey in the woods when Jupiter has hidden the sky in shadow* <note>original: "Quale per incertam lunam sub luce maligna Est iter in siluis ubi celum condidit umbra Iuppiter"</note>. And from this it arises that at the beginning we make some resistance to temptation, although in the end we let ourselves be conquered and we grieve for our error. But once the habit is formed, because we remain entirely in the shadows, there is no more remorse of conscience and we sin willingly.

### AND HE TO ME: "The things will be known to you."
An excellent precept where he demonstrates that one ought not to ask about things before arriving at their place. As if to say that every investigation should be done in its own time and place, observing the manner and the order—which order the appetite would not observe, desiring to know everything at once if reason did not admonish it.

### UPON THE SAD shore:
He interprets the name of Acheron by saying "sad shore," because Acheron signifies sadness.

### AND I, with eyes shameful and cast down.
He demonstrates what the disciple ought to be toward the teacher: for he must not only believe him, but also carry such reverence toward him that he is ashamed of every ill-considered question he asks. And in the same way, the appetite should behave toward reason. For every time it moves without reason, having been admonished by it, it should grieve and show signs of repentance.

---

And behold toward us coming by boat
an old man, white with ancient hair,
crying: "Woe to you, wicked souls!
Do not ever hope to see the heavens:
I come to lead you to the other shore
into eternal darkness, into heat and ice.
And you who are there, a living soul,
depart from these who are dead."
But when he saw that I did not depart,
He said: "By other ways, by other ports
you shall come to the shore, not here to pass;
a lighter vessel must carry you."
The Leader to him: "Charon, do not vex yourself:
it is willed thus where there is power to do
that which is willed; and ask no more."
Then were quieted the woolly cheeks

<column-break/>

He demonstrates that arriving at the river they saw Charon the ferryman, who, having already unloaded the boat on the other bank, was returning to fill it with those who were waiting. He describes, therefore, Charon and the boat guided by him through the river Acheron, where many identify Charon as **Death**, which, separating the soul of the sinner from the body, conducts it to Hell. Some want Acheron to be **disordered appetite**. But it seems to me better to give it the same sense that we gave in our dialogues written on Virgil: we shall say, therefore, that if Acheron is understood as the movement the soul makes to pass into sin, **Charon** is **Free Will**, the **boat** is the **will**, and the **oar** is **choice** <note>original: "electiōe"</note>. And therefore I conclude that where there is no free will, there can be no choice, nor can the will be used. And that which is not voluntary and by choice is imputed as neither vice nor virtue. For this reason, violence and non-negligent ignorance excuse the sin. Therefore one does not go to Hell unless the boat—that is, the will—carries them there, directed by Charon—that is, by free will. Charon is named from *charis*, which in Greek signifies **grace** <note>original: "gratia"</note>; because nothing is more free than grace, since it is done without obligation. Furthermore, they say he is the son of Death—that is, of blindness and ignorance. For if there were in us an open and lucid cognition of the true and the good, not obscured by any darkness of ignorance, our will by itself would go toward the good without the need for choice.

<summary>This page provides an allegorical interpretation of the infernal rivers and the figure of Charon, framing them as psychological states of the soul descending into sin. <meta>This page continues Cristoforo Landino’s allegorical commentary on Canto III of Dante’s Inferno. Landino is currently interpreting the character of Charon and the crossing of the river Acheron as metaphors for the soul's descent into sinful habits and the role of free will.</meta>

<header>INFERNO</header>

to the ferryman of the livid marsh
who had circles of flames around his eyes.

...decreases **free will** <note>original: "libero arbitrio"</note> in us. This figure shouts to the souls who are ready and willing to pass, telling them never to hope to see heaven; for nothing can convince the soul that it deserves Hell except for free will. If this were not within us, we could commit neither vice nor virtue. **I COME** <note>original: "IO VENGO"</note> to lead you to the other shore: because they are not content for Charon to pass them, but once reached the other bank, they remain there for eternity. Therefore, the first bank is the inclination of **depraved counsel** in which the soul, corrupted by the flattery of sensuality, allows itself to go. This sensuality makes the soul delight in worldly things, which are a pestiferous poison to it. Having arrived, then, at this counsel—which is a "bank," meaning a firm thing, because such a judgment remains firm in the soul: namely, that it is good to proceed with such an action. Afterward comes the river, which is the motion and the acts that lead one to the **habit** <term>habit: in Aristotelian philosophy, a settled disposition or character trait (habitus) acquired through repeated action</term>. And after the river is the other bank, where the eternal habitation of sinners begins, which is nothing other than the habit. These three things—inclination (or depraved counsel), acts, and habit—the Poet expresses through divine verses in the first Psalm. For when it says, *Blessed is the man who does not walk in the counsel of the wicked* <note>original: "Beatus uir qui nō habit i cōfilio impioꝝ"</note>, it demonstrates the depraved counsel. Adding: *And has not stood in the way of sinners* <note>original: "Et in uia peccatoꝝ nō ftetit"</note>, it denotes the acts, which are the way that leads to the habit. And finally: *And has not sat in the seat of pestilence* <note>original: "Et in cathedra peftilētię nō fedit"</note>, it places the habit, which is the seat in which the vicious man dies. Next, he calls Dante a **living soul**, not only because he was still alive, but because he was not dead in sin and was not going to Hell like the others—that is, he was not falling into vices. Rather, he went to contemplate and know the vices; and therefore, he did not have to go by the river, which deprives one of joy, nor by the boat that carries sinners, but by a lighter vessel. For whoever descends into vice goes by the boat weighed down by the concupiscence of vices; but whoever goes to speculate is carried by a pure and light will. **MY GUIDE**, Charon, do not vex yourself. Virgil could have assigned many reasons to Charon, and Charon could have responded to them; but at once, cutting off all questioning, he says that Dante, still alive, goes to Hell guided by divine grace. And by this, he demonstrates what all theologians—and especially Jerome—affirm: that any man can go into sin by himself through his own free will. But to acquire virtue and live without sin, man cannot do so by his free will alone without divine grace. This is why Virgil has Aeneas pass in the same boat as the other souls: because the pagan philosophers believed that free will was sufficient for salvation just as it was for damnation. But Dante, as a Christian, does not depart from the Christian opinion. Nor without cause did he say "do not vex yourself." In this, he imitates Virgil, who shows that Charon is angered against Aeneas and the Sibyl. Virgil induces Charon to refuse to carry Aeneas, saying: *It is forbidden to carry living bodies in the Stygian boat* <note>original: "Corpora uiua nefas ftygia uectare carina"</note>. This signifies that free will, insofar as it is free will, does not want to yield to reason, because it wants to debate before it comes to action. But Aeneas—that is, virtue—has already made the choice and does not wish to remain longer in deliberation and consultation; rather, he wishes to pull free will toward doing what he has already chosen. Hence, although the will is always free in potential, it is nonetheless no longer free in act to do or not do. For, pulled by reason, it must do what reason dictates. Therefore, from the beginning, when Charon saw Aeneas coming armed, he feared his weapons, because force should not be used against free will. But after the Sibyl—that is, the superior reason of the virtuous man—tells him that neither force nor fraud shall be done to him, and shows him the **golden bough**, that is, the light of wisdom, he immediately yields. For this same reason, our poet has Charon refuse to pass him. But Virgil does not appease him as the Sibyl did by showing the golden bough—that is, human wisdom—because, as we have already said, human wisdom is not enough for the salvation of man; instead, he shows that God wills it so. This is nothing other than saying he comes accompanied by divine grace. **IT IS WILLED THUS** where what is willed can be done, and ask no more. He says two things: first, that Charon must yield to Dante because God wills it, who alone can do whatever He wills. Thus, he comes with divine grace, which directs free will toward the good. The second is that he warns Charon not to seek why God wills it so, because it is the height of temerity to search into the secrets of the divinity, and why one follows such grace rather than another; for His judgments are incomprehensible, as David says. And elsewhere he writes: *Your judgments are a great deep* <note>original: "Iudicia tua abiffus multa"</note>. And Solomon in the Proverbs: *As it is not good for one who eats much honey, so he who is a searcher of majesty shall be overwhelmed by glory* <note>original: "Sicut qui multū mel comedit nō ei bonum:Sic qui fcrutator eft maieftatis opprimetur a gloria"</note>.

### But those souls, who were weary and naked,
### changed color and gnashed their teeth,
### as soon as they heard those cruel words.
### They blasphemed God and their parents,
### the human race, the place, the time, and the seed
### of their sowing and of their birth.
### Then they all drew back together,
### weeping loudly, to the evil shore
### that awaits every man who fears not God.
### Charon the demon, with eyes of burning coal,
### beckoning to them, gathers them all;
### he beats with his oar whoever lingers.

...they turn pale; and they lose the heat which is in the blood, and remaining cold, they tremble. Therefore, by this, he denotes the fear that was born from the threats made by Charon. And certainly, the sinner never considers his own perdition except when he sees himself in Hell—and this is as far as the dead are concerned. But as for the living, the sinner then realizes his damages when he sees that his free will leads him to the habit of vices. **THEY BLASPHEMED** God and their parents. By these words, the poet denotes a sum of despair and fury by which the damned would rather lose their existence and be annihilated than stay in perpetual pain, so that he agrees with...
