...of free will. Nor without reason do they feign that Charon is old: because nothing is more ancient in the soul than free will. Here Virgil adds that although he is old, nonetheless old age in him is green and robust: *Now he is elderly, but the old age of a god is fresh and green* <note>original: "Iam ſenior fed cruda deo uiridifq; fenectus"</note>. This demonstrates that never, by any length of time, is it...

**T**HEY WERE **WEARY** from pain and **NAKED**: that is, stripped of their bodies. Or truly, naked of divine grace, and thus of every defense. And certainly, the soul damned to Hell, because it has formed a habit in vice, is weary and deprived of all vigor with which it might rise up against vice. And it is naked, that is, without weapons with which it can defend itself; for the weapons of the soul against vices are the liveliness of the light of reason, which is entirely extinguished. Hence, the soul remains in darkness. Nor can it discern the true good unless divine grace illuminates it anew. Regarding this, the prophet prays, saying: *To enlighten those who sit in the shadow of death* <note>original: "Illumiare iis q in umbra mortis fedet"</note>. **THEY CHANGED** color and gnashed their teeth. He gives to the soul, which is incorporeal, that which belongs to the body; and he places the signs which, in the human body, demonstrate great fear. For when great consternation is born in the mind, nature—fearing it cannot save the whole city, that is, the whole body—strives at least to save the fortress with which it might afterward regain the whole city. And this is the heart, which is the fortress and principal seat of life. Therefore, it recalls the blood to the heart, in which life chiefly consists. Hence, the external parts, deprived of blood, lose their color and...

<meta>This page continues the commentary by Cristoforo Landino on Canto III of Dante’s Inferno. The previous page discussed the arrival at the banks of the Acheron and the nature of the souls gathered there. This section focuses on Charon’s role, the famous simile of the falling leaves, and the physical transition Dante undergoes at the end of the canto.</meta>

<header>### CANTO THREE</header>

The words of Christ against Judas: *It would have been better for this man if he had never been born* <note>original: "Meglio farebbe a questo huomo che mai nō fussi nato"; referencing Matthew 26:24</note>. These words and blasphemies signify that they would rather not have been born, or that God and every creature should come to the same damnation. **CHARON** the demon with **eyes of burning coal**. Taken from Virgil, who posits that his eyes are flames. This is because free will has one flame, which is the light of the intellect, which shows it the good; and another, which is the heat of concupiscence <term>concupiscence: strong sensual longing or desire, often viewed in theology as a leaning toward sin</term> placed in the senses; and this invites it to worldly delights. The demon Charon says that the free will which transports the soul to Hell is not the free will guided by the grace of God, but that which is seduced and deceived by diabolical temptation. **STRIKES** with his oar whoever **lingers** <note>original: "fadagia," a variation of "s'adagia," meaning to settle or slow down</note>, that is, whoever becomes slow and tardy. But if the souls are prompt to cross as was said above, why does he say here that some linger—that is, are tardy and slow? I answer that although sensuality makes the sinner prone to vice, it nonetheless happens that in the beginning, before a habit has been formed, reason and conscience oppose sensuality and delay the sinning. But Charon—that is, the free will that has already been persuaded by sensuality—pushes them, striking them with the oar: that is, with the choice <note>original: "electiōe"</note> which has already made a habit of sinning. Nor is the oar with which Charon moves the boat to be understood as anything other than the choice to follow what the appetite has judged to be good.

> As in autumn the leaves lift off
> one after the other, until the branch
> sees all its spoils upon the ground;
> Similarly, the evil seed of Adam
> cast themselves from that shore one by one,
> at signals, as the falcon to its recall:
> Thus they go over the dusky wave,
> and before they have descended on the other side,
> a new troop gathers again on this side.

A most fitting comparison. For just as leaves, having lost their natural moisture through the summer heat, fall dry to the earth; so our souls, having dried out the moisture of reason that nourished them through the heat of concupiscence, fall into earthly desires. And it is a passage taken from the sixth book of Virgil: *As many as the leaves that fall in the forests at the first frost of autumn, or as many as the birds that flock to the land from the deep sea* <note>original: "Quā multa in siluis autūni frigore prio Lapsa cadunt folia aut ad terrā gurgite ab alto quā multē glomeratf aues"; referencing Aeneid VI, 309-311</note>. And thus they cast themselves into the river to the demon Charon—that is, without any considered reason they go to a depraved free will: as a bird flies to the fowler when he shows it food, whereby they do not realize they lose their liberty and become slaves. The fowler shows the food to the bird, and the bird, seized by greed for such food, flies to him, not realizing it loses its freedom. So the sinner, when sensuality through free will shows him worldly delights, immediately casts himself toward them. **THE EVIL seed of Adam.** Both the good and the wicked proceed from Adam; but the good are saved, and the wicked are lost in their iniquity. Therefore, he did not say "the seed" absolutely, but "the evil seed." Or, we may say that the body has its origin from Adam, and the soul from God. And because the body is a great cause of the soul's contagion, he therefore said "the evil seed of Adam." And he wisely said **they cast themselves**. For "to cast oneself" signifies going inconsiderately and without reason. And thus does the sinner. Certainly, he who lives according to virtue goes considerately and with determined steps. But he who walks the path of vice casts himself without consideration, now into one extreme, now into another.

> "My son," (said the courteous master),
> "those who die in the wrath of God
> all gather here from every country:
> And they are prompt to cross the river,
> for divine justice spurs them on,
> so that fear is turned into desire.
> No good soul ever passes this way;
> and therefore, if Charon complains of you,
> you can well know now what his speech signifies."

**Son**: Because the disciple should hold the teacher in both reverence and love, the place of "son" is given to the preceptor. And thus the preceptor should be courteous and liberal with doctrine toward the disciple—not like many who, either through greed or envy, do not teach as much as they could. Furthermore, for the reasons stated above regarding the father and the lord, the poet signifies here that in such contemplation, sensuality must be so obedient to the intellect that the intellect can instruct it with fatherly mercy, and not with that hardness and rigidity that a master uses toward a slave. **DIE in the wrath of God.** Everyone who falls into sin dies, and dies in the wrath of God, and arrives at the river in the manner we have already described. **AND divine justice spurs them.** Because by beginning to make a habit, they begin to take pleasure in what ought to displease them. This is permitted by divine justice because they have made themselves unworthy of every grace of God, with which they could have defended themselves from vice. Therefore, **the fear**—that is, the dread—which they ought to have of vice, and which they had before they formed the habit, **TURNS into desire**: that is, into a longing, because they crave what they ought to flee. And if we wish to understand this passage more clearly, it is necessary to remember the difference we showed above between the *incontinent* and the *intemperate* <note>Landino draws here on Aristotelian ethics: the incontinent person knows they do wrong but lacks the will to stop; the intemperate person has made a habit of vice and no longer feels it is wrong</note>. **HERE no good soul ever passes.** We showed above that he who falls into vice and allows himself to be overcome by it descends into Hell, as do all sinners. He also descends who enters to contemplate vices in order to know them and guard against them, as Homer feigns of Ulysses, Virgil of Aeneas, and Dante of himself. But the first group enters in the way we interpreted allegorically above regarding Charon and the Acheron, because the ship—that is, their depraved will guided by free will—conducts them. The second group is conducted by a will carried by the angel—that is, by the grace of God—which directs the free will to want and choose the true good.

> When this was finished, the dark countryside
> trembled so strongly that, from the terror,
> my mind is still bathed in sweat.
> The tearful earth gave forth a wind
> that flashed a vermilion light,
> which overcame every sense in me,
> And I fell like a man whom sleep seizes.

Various commentators explain this text in various ways. But in my judgment, it demonstrates nothing else than that he who descends into Hell in order to return—that is, enters into the speculation of vices to guard against them—must do so through an abstraction of the mind, and the senses must remain asleep so that they become accustomed to obeying reason without any resistance. For whoever considers the bodily delights found in vices, and does not yet have their sensuality subjected to reason, often finds the serpent hidden among the flowers. Hence Petrarch: *This earthly life is almost a meadow / Where the serpent lies among flowers and grass / And if any part of it pleases the eyes / It is to leave the soul more ensnared* <note>original: "questa uitta terréa e quasi un prato / Chel serpēte fra fiori elherbe iace / Et falchuna sua uista gliocchi piace / E/ p lasciar piu lanimo iuuisca"</note>. One remains trapped and taken by carnal delights and poisoned by the serpentine bite of sin. Therefore, it is necessary that Dante—that is, the...

<meta>This page continues Cristoforo Landino’s Neoplatonic commentary on Dante’s Inferno. Having discussed the crossing of the Acheron and the figure of Charon, Landino now interprets the moment Dante falls into a deep sleep and the earthquake that concludes Canto III. He frames this as a necessary transition where the "sensuality" (the physical senses) is hushed so that "reason" can proceed into the intellectual realm of the underworld.</meta>

-># INFERNO<-

sensuality must be carried into Hell while asleep so that it does not rise up against reason. And it is carried by the angel—that is, by divine grace. Dante thus reaches the crossing of the Acheron, which is the entrance to speculation <term>speculation: here meaning philosophical or spiritual contemplation, from the Latin 'speculari' to watch or observe</term>. And although he had previously given himself entirely to Virgil, demonstrating that they shared a single will, he nonetheless begins to waver, reconsidering how arduous and difficult this undertaking is. It does not seem to him a weight for his own shoulders; and in truth, human powers alone, without divine help, could not pass into Hell and return. He sins, therefore, not through malice—which does not deserve mercy—but through timidity and weakness, for which God often has great compassion; because: **God saw our frame and had mercy on us** <note>original: "Vidit deus figm̄ntū nostrum & misertus ē nostri"; a reference to Psalm 103:14</note>. Especially for one who implores and asks for His help with tears. Therefore, He sends the angel to put him to sleep and, while asleep, carry him across.

What else does this denote if not that divine grace makes up for our fragility, and separates and abstracts the mind and the intellect from the senses, so that it can rise to speculate upon the great things for which it was born? And it puts sensuality to sleep so that it does not hiss at or disturb reason. Nor is "to philosophize" anything else—as **Plato** says, and the Platonic **Cicero**—than to call the mind away from the senses, and to ensure that the soul, while it is in the body, stays as separated from it as possible, and learns to die <note>original: "impari a morire"; a famous Platonic concept from the Phaedo where philosophy is a 'practice for death' or detachment from the physical</note>—that is, to live separated from the body. Having understood this, we will adapt the words of the text to the aforementioned meaning.

And first the poet says: **FINISHED this, the dark plain trembled so strongly**. That is, after the words spoken by Virgil, which showed great difficulty in crossing the **dark plain**—which is Dante’s sensuality. It is a "plain" (that is, an open and spacious place) because the desires of the senses are many and extend widely in every direction. And it is "dark" because sensuality is oppressed by much darkness of ignorance. **IT TREMBLED** because of the great bewilderment and fear of not being able to proceed. And he grieved at having to abandon the undertaking, which happened because of his distress. We have shown, if I err not, that Dante’s sin proceeds not from a malice of "not wanting," but from a desperation of "not being able."

From this it arose that **THE TEARFUL EARTH gave forth wind**. That is, the tears of the earth—meaning of our sensuality—**gave forth wind**—that is, they created movement, which moved God to mercy. **WHICH**—that is, which wind—**FLASHED a vermillion light**. That is, it produced a fiery light with the speed of a lightning bolt. This light is divine grace, which God—having seen the good will of those who wish to lead themselves to salvation but waver out of timidity—sends suddenly to strengthen and direct that will. And this grace is "light" because it illuminates the mind and shows it the true way; and it is "vermillion" (that is, fiery) because, in addition to showing the way—which is a **Cherubic** work <note>Landino references the hierarchy of angels; Cherubim represent divine wisdom/intellect</note>—it kindles and inflames the soul with **Seraphic** love <note>Seraphim represent divine love/fire</note>. This is necessary in the speculation of great things, because since these cannot be done without laborious difficulty, if a man did not fall in love with them, he would not endure such toil.

Whence Virgil, wishing to guide **Aeneas** to contemplation, has him follow **Venus**—that is, the love of divine things. This light overcomes every feeling in Dante—that is, it lulls and puts sensuality to sleep for the reason mentioned just above. And this passage has a similarity to the one in Virgil where he depicts **Anchises**, after Troy has burned, not wanting to leave or live any longer. And we demonstrated there that Anchises is sensuality, which refuses to leave corporeal pleasures. But Aeneas—that is, higher reason—carries him out on his shoulders, because the intellect raises up the appetite and does not let it touch the ground—that is, think of earthly things. Instead, he guides him to Italy—that is, to contemplation. Nonetheless, before he reaches Italy, he buries him, and then finds him again in the underworld. So here, Dante falls asleep and then wakes up having crossed the river.

<summary>Landino provides a Neoplatonic interpretation of Dante's fainting spell at the end of Canto III, explaining it as divine grace putting the physical senses to sleep so the intellect can perceive spiritual truths. He compares this transition to the philosophical "learning to die" found in Plato and the journey of Aeneas in Virgil’s Aeneid.</summary>

<meta>Continuing from Canto III, where Dante had fainted at the banks of the Acheron after the earthquake. This page opens Canto IV, where the poet awakens on the other side of the river to find himself at the edge of Limbo.</meta>

<header>CANTO FOURTH</header>

# CANTO FOURTH OF THE FIRST CANTICLE.

A heavy thunder broke the deep sleep in my head,
so that I shook myself
like a person who is awakened by force:
And I moved my rested eye around,
having stood straight up: and I looked fixedly
to know the place where I was:
Truthfully, I found myself on the brink
of the sorrowful valley of the abyss,
which gathers the thunder of infinite woes:
Dark and deep and cloudy,
so much so that by straining my sight to the bottom
I could not discern anything there.

"Now let us descend down here into the blind world,"
began the poet, quite pale,
"I will be the first and you shall be the second."
And I, who had noticed his color,
said: "How shall I come if you are afraid?
For you are usually the comfort to my doubting."

<column-break/>

The poet treats the first circle of hell: in which he places those who, although they are not to be punished for great sins: nevertheless, because they did not have baptism, they do not deserve heaven. <note>This region is known as Limbo, where Virgil and other virtuous non-Christians reside.</note> Man cannot pass to the contemplation of vices if the <term>sensuality</term> <note>In Renaissance philosophy, "sensuality" refers to the lower, animal instincts of the soul that react to physical stimuli.</note> that resists reason is not first put to sleep. Now, having arrived at this contemplation, the sensuality is awakened by the thunder: and it turns its rested eyes around. This signifies that in the beginning, when man decides to leave the active life and go toward the contemplative life, sensuality would not remain obedient to reason. For this reason, it is necessary for it to fall asleep: and once asleep, it is carried there. But once we have arrived at the contemplative state, the thunder wakes it: that is, reason thundering over it and severely rebuking it for its laziness makes it vigilant: and attentive to obeying reason in great matters; therefore, it can turn its "rested eye," meaning it can use its senses in a quiet state, no longer inflamed and infuriated by the desire for earthly things. 

It is a known thing in philosophy that only the intellect speculates and contemplates: because it alone can have knowledge of universal truths. But because it is necessary for the beginning to be born from particulars, and these are found in the senses: therefore the intellect seeks to make sensuality subject to itself. This sensuality, at the beginning, is stirred and moved on one side by the lures and flatteries of momentary and temporal things. And on the other side, being repressed by reason, it becomes entirely base: because it is not yet perfectly obedient to reason. Therefore, it is necessary to put it to sleep, as has been said. But after we have already entered into contemplation without the resistance of the senses—which were put to sleep then—because they are now entirely obedient, reason excites and wakes them: and joins them to itself: because man has now reached such perfection that he discerns with the mind and discerns with the body: because our corruptible and bodily senses are converted into reason: and reason into intellect: and intellect into intelligence: and intelligence into God. 

Nor should it be wondered at if the soul, made in the likeness of all wisdom, has within itself the likeness of all things. Whence also by Aristotle it is called the "likeness of all things": because it has within itself powers with which it investigates every thing: and is like every thing, even though it is one. It is like the earth through sense. To water through imagination. To air through reason. To the firmament through the intellect. To the heaven of heavens through the intelligence. He writes, therefore: **A HEAVY thunder** broke the deep sleep in my head: that is, the same grace of God: which first had put sensuality to sleep: so that it would not impede reason in passing to contemplation, now wakes it: so that it may be joined with it. And he said "it broke" to denote that he did not let it wake on its own and finish its sleep. This signifies that sensuality would never wake from its laziness if it were not awakened by divine grace: and he said "deep sleep": that is, profound sleep: because the sleep and laziness of sensuality is very deep. 
> For the spirit is willing but the flesh is weak. <note>original: "Quia spiritus próptus est caro uero infirma." (Matthew 26:41)</note>
**IN THE head**: he said this because sleep proceeds from vapors: which, rising from nourishment, go to the brain: and there, cooled by the coldness of the brain, and by this condensed, they close the path to the heat and to the spirit: which in the brain gives perfection to the senses. **SO THAT I shook myself.** It is not without a great movement when a man is awakened by force. But there is also no small movement in the soul when sensuality is seized by reason. **AND I MOVED my rested eye around.** Just as the body has eyes with which it looks and sees: so the soul has power with which it investigates and discerns. The mind, therefore, is the eye of the soul: and reason is its looking: and the intellect is its seeing and discerning. Therefore, the soul turns its rested eye when it discourses with tranquil reason: and reason is tranquil when the senses and appetite are obedient to it and follow it everywhere. **STANDING straight up**: to show that sensuality rose from low and earthly things to follow the intellect. **AND FIXEDLY I looked**: it is necessary, if we wish to contemplate rightly, that the mind, tranquil and empty of every disturbance and passion, moves around: that is, turns to all parts: and with the gaze of reason stays firm and fixed: because it is not enough for one who wants to find the truth to discourse through all things: unless he turns there with every sharpness of wit and "settles" it: that is, holds it firm: and does not depart from there: so that from the eye and from its looking may be born seeing—that is, understanding—and knowing the place where we find ourselves. 

**TRUTH/ that on the brink I found myself.** This is the effect of the turning of the eye and the fixed looking: because from this is born seeing: that is, not a doubtful opinion but indubitable and true science: and therefore he says **True it is/** because contemplation in universal things finds the truth: which is the ultimate end in the intellectual virtues: just as the good is the end in the moral virtues. **ON THE brink of the abyss:** That is, at the beginning of the depth of hell. And certainly nothing is deeper, nor further from celestial things, than vice. **WHICH:** that is, which valley. **GATHERS THE THUNDER of infinite woes:** It gathers within itself the sound of infinite woes. When a valley surrounded by very high mountains is filled with men: who variously cry out: and use various complaints and shrieks, it would make, through the mixture of so many voices and the echoing of the valley, a confused sound gathered in the air of all those voices: because the concavity of the place does not let them out. But they circle around and multiply through the percussion: and together they gather: and make almost a thunder. And this is felt especially by one who is above, as Dante was. But allegorically he means that in the contemplation of vices one recognizes that from so many and so many diverse ones—and contrary among themselves, but all harmful—there results an extreme misery. 

**IT WAS DARK:** Because he who, by contemplating, wants to know the nature of vice, finds everything dark: that is, he understands that every vice consists in ignorance: which is born from having lost the light of the intellect. **SO MUCH THAT BY straining my sight to the bottom I could not discern anything there.** He who contemplates vice, which is in the darkness of ignorance, cannot see anything there. For vice is not a thing in itself: but is only a privation <note>In scholastic philosophy, "evil" or "vice" was defined not as a positive substance, but as the absence or "privation" of good/light.</note>. This is, therefore, the reason why hell is dark: and why nothing can be discerned there. Which Virgil also expressed in these verses:
> They went dark through the shadows under the lonely night, through the empty houses of Dis and the vacant kingdoms. <note>original: "Ibant obscuri sola sub nocte per umbras / Perque domos ditis uacuas & inania regna." (Aeneid VI.268-269)</note>

Dante finds himself on the other side of the river Acheron: nor does he know how he passed over. But then, as he turns his rested eye around, Virgil appears to lead him into hell: and says: **NOW let us descend down here into the blind world:** That is, into the contemplation of vices. In which there is nothing other than blindness and the privation of the light of reason. And for this the Psalmist supplicates for these, saying:
> To give light to those who sit in darkness and in the shadow of death. <note>original: "Illuminare iis qui in tenebris: et umbra mortis sedent." (Luke 1:79/Benedictus)</note>
Virgil was pale and death-like: which signifies a striking of the soul, as much by compassion as by fear. But...

<meta>This page continues the opening of Canto IV. In the previous page, Dante had just awakened on the edge of the abyss and noted Virgil's sudden paleness. Here, Virgil clarifies that his expression is one of compassion for those in Limbo, not fear of the descent. The commentary explains the transition from the vestibule of the Neutrals across the Acheron into the first circle of Hell.</meta>

<header>INFERNO</header>

And he to me: "The anguish of the people
who are down here paints upon my face
that pity which you mistake for fear:
Let us go, for the long way urges us on."
Thus he set out, and thus he made me enter
the first circle that girdles the abyss.

There, as far as one could tell by listening,
there were no laments, but only sighs
that made the eternal air tremble:
This came from the grief without torments
felt by the crowds, which were very large,
of infants, and of women, and of men.
The good master said to me: "You do not ask
what spirits are these that you see?
Now I want you to know, before you go further,
That they did not sin; and if they have merit,
it is not enough, because they did not have baptism,
which is part of the faith that you believe.
And if they lived before Christianity,
they did not duly worship God:
and of such as these, I am one myself.
For such defects, and not for any other crime,
we are lost, and only so far afflicted
that without hope we live in desire."

<column-break/>

Dante turned this conjecture and sign toward fear. This signifies <margin>signifies</margin> that often our intellect turns toward a good thing, but the <margin>sensuality</margin> interprets it in a worse way until the intellect <margin>satisfies</margin> it. And for this reason, Virgil responds that the color changed in his <margin>face</margin> comes from pity, which Dante feels as fear; that is, he interprets it as <margin>fear</margin> and estimates it to be fear. **I SHALL BE** the first, and you shall be the second <margin>second</margin>. This is rightly so, because when Dante—that is, <margin>And</margin> sensuality and lower reason—goes toward contemplation, he must follow Virgil—that is, higher reason—as a true <margin>guide</margin>, because the appetite predominates in <margin>contemplation</margin> and draws the senses behind it. But for one who goes to hell never to <margin>return</margin>, <margin>return</margin> <margin>that</margin> <margin>is</margin>

that is, one who falls into vice, then Dante draws Virgil with him, and Virgil does not guide Dante, because the appetite predominates over reason. **AND HE** said to me the anguish of the people. This shows that although the Stoics <note>A school of ancient Greek philosophy that taught the suppression of emotions.</note> do not wish for the wise man to fall into any passion or perturbation of the soul, nonetheless, according to the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle's philosophy.</note> and Christian theologians, it is a human thing to have compassion for the misery of men. And for this reason, he imagines that Virgil, entering hell, shows different temperaments. And although both knew following Heraclitus of Ephesus <note>A Greek philosopher known for his melancholy view of humanity.</note>. For two philosophers were of different temperaments. And although both knew the foolishness of men to be infinite, and almost all their actions to proceed from ignorance rather than from prudence. Nonetheless, one, who was Heraclitus of Ephesus, wept whenever he saw such foolishness in anyone. But the other, who was Democritus of Abdera <note>A Greek philosopher known for laughing at the follies of mankind.</note>, on the contrary, laughed, mocking the vanity of men. Therefore, it is concluded that it is not contrary to the constancy of the philosopher, when contemplating the misery in which those in hell find themselves—that is, those oppressed by vice—to have compassion for them, without exceeding the limit, because it is a human thing. And as the Terentian Chremes says: <note>original: "Homo sum Nihil humani a me alienum puto"</note> "I am a man; I consider nothing human alien to me." **LET US GO** for the long way urges us on. If you consider the site of hell, it is a long way, because it is from the surface of the earth to the center. But allegorically, the knowledge of vices is long and difficult, because they are of many kinds, and often some are so similar to virtues that it is difficult to discern one from the other. **THUS** he set me. When Dante—that is, sensuality—is put into hell by Virgil—that is, by reason—then he recognizes how detestable vice is and guards himself from it. But when he enters by himself, he allows himself to be baited by it, and remains like a fish on a hook.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'D' containing a figure, beginning the word 'Dalla'.</image-desc>From the gate to the river Acheron, the poet showed there to be a place in which—because it was not entirely in hell, nor entirely outside of hell—those were placed who could be called neither entirely good nor entirely wicked. This was like a precinct and vestibule of the whole place. Now, after the river Acheron, he describes the beginning of hell and places the first circle, which, because it girdles all the others, is called **Limbo** <note>From the Latin 'limbus', meaning edge or hem.</note> by a certain similarity, since properly 'limbo' in Latin signifies a fringe which surrounds the whole garment. And in this, he intends that as it is higher than the others and further from the deep, so the lighter sins are punished there. He places there first those who, not having had baptism in Christianity, died in original sin, which deprives them of the eternal vision and glory of God. Likewise, those who, having been before Christ, did not duly worship God, because they did not believe in the Trinity of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, nor in Christ to come. These, because they lived according to the civil virtues, did not deserve tortures. But for the reason stated, they do not deserve glory. But because in this place the poet shows the souls of children, whom baptism has not washed of original sin—which is a debt of punishment contracted from the fault of the first father—I think it will be pleasing to the ears of the reader to hear briefly what justice allows that innocent children, who could not sin by free will or choice, should be deprived of the divine vision in which our beatitude consists. Since it is written: <note>original: "Quod filius nō portabit iniquitaté patris"</note> "The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father," and elsewhere: <note>original: "Aia que peccauerit ipsa moriet'"</note> "The soul that sins, it shall die." But first it must be understood that original sin is the lack of **original justice**, which was

our debt to have. Man was made upright by God. But he, by departing from his creator, made himself weak and infirm, and subjected himself to infinite ways of sinning. Adam was thus created with such uprightness that in him the lower things were subject to the higher: the fleshly form was subject to the soul so that nothing could happen to it that would cause it to rise against the soul. And similarly, the appetite was subject to reason. This was divine justice, because justice requires that the lower always be under the higher; and it was called "original" because Adam [received it] from his divine justice, because justice requires that the lower always be under the higher... <note>The text repeats a phrase here, likely a printer's error.</note> descendants, because they were to be as members of Adam. But since Adam rebelled against his superior, God required the order of justice: that the lower things should rebel against him. And thus the flesh rebelled against the soul, and because of this, contrary dispositions fell into it. Whence that which could have not died through sin, now dies by necessity. And similarly, the appetite rebelled against reason; because he who by his uprightness could have not died and not sinned, falls into the necessity of dying and sinning. But not to be prolix, we will say as **Giles** <note>Likely referring to Aegidius Romanus, a medieval theologian.</note> writes: that God having made man perfect and absolute with original justice, then by his spontaneous liberality and by a free gift granted him, beyond his nature, that as long as he stayed without sin he could enjoy the divine presence. Because of which, Adam could have, if he had preserved himself in a state of innocence, left us such a gift by law of inheritance. But not having preserved it, he lost it before we were born, and having lost it, he cannot leave it to us. This will be better understood by this example: A man-at-arms, for having reinforced the battle and been the cause of victory, received from the king as a reward for his virtues a city. Afterwards, becoming a traitor, for the treason committed, the king took back from him the city already given. The children of the knight should have had this as his heirs if he had remained in the faith. Now, what injury does the king do them if they do not have that which...

The commentary provides a philosophical and theological justification for the existence of Limbo, explaining original sin through an analogy of a forfeited inheritance.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the transition into the first circle of Hell, Limbo. The previous page concluded with Virgil explaining that his paleness was not from fear, but from the pity he felt for the souls residing here. This page contains the actual poetic text of Canto IV and an extensive commentary explaining why these virtuous souls—including infants and those who lived before Christ—are denied the presence of God.</meta>

# CANTO FOUR

<column-break/>

->**CANTO FOUR**<-

Great grief seized my heart when I heard this,
because I knew people of great worth
who were suspended in that Limbo:
"Tell me, my master, tell me, my lord,"
I began, wishing to be certain
of that faith which conquers every error: <note>Dante is asking about the Harrowing of Hell—the belief that Christ descended into Limbo to rescue the righteous souls of the Old Testament.</note>
"Did anyone ever leave here, either by his own merit
or through another's, to then be blessed?"
And he, who understood my veiled speech, <note>Dante speaks "veiled" because he is hesitant to name Christ directly in Hell.</note>

Answered: "I was new to this state,
when I saw a mighty one come here, <note>Virgil died in 19 BCE; Christ's descent occurred roughly 50 years later, making Virgil "new" to the afterlife at the time.</note>
crowned with a sign of victory:
He drew out the shade of our first parent, <note>Adam</note>
of Abel his son, and that of Noah;
of Moses the lawgiver, and the obedient one."

<sig>js</sig>

<column-break/>

Was it never theirs nor part of their inheritance? For this reason, since the vision of God is not according to our human nature, no injustice is done if it is not given to us: just as if someone, by the grace of God, had wings and could fly—which would be above human nature—and then his children were to grieve at not having wings like their father. Our soul has no faculty, once it has exited the bodily prison, to enjoy the divine sight unless it is cleansed and pure: because it is not permitted for the impure to touch the pure. But if the pure is so, it is because of perfect and absolute grace. Therefore, the small child could not see God. Nevertheless, the child is not deprived of any hope, because such a gift had been given to Adam beyond his nature, not by any merit of the receiver, but by the liberality of the giver. He lost it by wishing to please his wife rather than obey God. But of what can the little child complain if he is not given what is above his nature? From which it follows that there is no <term>punishment of the senses</term><note>Physical torment or pain.</note>, but only the <term>punishment of loss</term><note>The pain of being deprived of the sight of God.</note>. Therefore, the punishment for all of these is the deprivation of glory, and of the hope of ever having glory. Therefore, in that place, as far as one could imagine by listening, there was no weeping, which proceeds from the pain of punishments. He says "by listening" because this species of damnation is entirely a matter of faith. **BUT ONLY SIGHS**: That is, nothing but sighs; this is a way of speaking that is more Lombard than Florentine, for they say "this is not but good," meaning "this is only good." **THERE WAS NO** weeping but only sighs: That is, that place had no other weeping except sighs. For true weeping is where there are tears and sad voices, and it signifies pain and punishment of the sense; but the sigh signifies punishment of loss and the desire for an absent thing. Thus Juvenal says: <note>original: "Suspirat longo non visam tempore matrem"</note> "He sighs for his mother, not seen for a long time." And the sigh is an anguish of the spirit. And he said "the air," that is, the eternal atmosphere: because Hell, as was said above, lasts eternally. And it demonstrates the greatness of the sighs, since they were so great that they moved the air. **THIS CAME FROM GRIEF WITHOUT TORMENTS**: It was grief of the mind, but not <term>martyrdom</term><note>Meaning physical torture.</note>, which is punishment of the senses. **OF INFANTS**: Infancy is the first age of man, which lasts until seven years. And they are called in this age <term>infantes</term><note>From the Latin "non fantes," meaning "not speaking."</note> because either they do not speak or they do not yet have ready speech. **THE GOOD MASTER**: A teacher is good who not only teaches when asked, but also invites the disciple to ask. **LET US GO**: <note>original: "Andi"</note> A Roman word and not Florentine; because in our language we do not use the singular of the present tense of this verb; for they do not say *Ando*, *Andi*, *Anda*; but instead use *Vo*, *Vai*, *Va*. And the poet imagines in this place that Dante does not ask about the damnation of these people, but Virgil says it without being asked: because in truth, original sin, which damns them, is not known to us by natural science (which has its beginning from the intelligence found in the senses and lower reason) but through theology. And because the senses do not inspire any inquiry into this, no doubt arises about which one might ask. **IT IS NOT ENOUGH BECAUSE THEY HAD NO BAPTISM**: He places two kinds of men who are not saved, even though they lived morally: those who, after Christ, have not had baptism. For <note>original: "Quicunque crediderit & baptizatus fuerit hic saluus erit"</note> "Whoever believes and is baptized shall be saved." And those who lived before the coming of Christ, when baptism was not necessary. **THEY DID NOT ADORE** God as was due: That is, they did not believe in the Trinity—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—nor in the Christ who was to come. And among these, he places himself. **FOR SUCH DEFECTS**: That is, for this failing of not having true faith. **AND NOT FOR ANY OTHER CRIME**: That is, not for crimes committed; we have punishment not of the senses, but of the mind: because we live in "desire," that is, in longing for the glory of heaven. **WITHOUT HOPE**: That is, without hope of ever having it. Whoever is in glory and enjoys God is in the highest good. Whoever is without glory either has the hope of going there eventually, like those in Purgatory, or they are without hope. And these are of two kinds: for some are placed in eternal sensible punishments, like those in all the other circles of Hell; or they are without punishments of the sense, like these. These have no torments of the senses, but of the soul. And their punishment is desire. Nor is there any other desire but the craving to have present that thing which is absent, which absence continually torments the soul.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial D inside a square frame with floral motifs.</image-desc>
**Two** things are treated in these verses. In the first, he shows having great compassion for the men who, having lived morally and being full of many virtues, and having (either through science or military discipline) done many benefits for the human race or at least for their homeland, are nonetheless damned for not having had the Christian or Hebrew faith. In the second place, he wants Virgil to be his witness and make him nearly certain of what he held by faith: that is, that Christ with his precious blood redeemed those who, although they had held the right religion, had died in original sin. **TELL ME, MY MASTER, tell me, my lord**: In the first chapter, we showed why he calls Virgil master, lord, and father. It is not necessary to repeat it now. **FOR WISHING to be certain**: Although every believer believes what the Holy Church commands, nevertheless every great mind, being able, willingly seeks the science and certification of what it believes. **OF THAT FAITH which conquers every error**: He said this to demonstrate that although he had no [direct] knowledge, he nonetheless holds the Christian faith to be most true and without error. **BY HIS OWN MERIT or through another's**: Although no one can by themselves leave sin unless aided by divine grace, it is nonetheless necessary that we work toward the good as much as our frailty allows. Thus Augustine said: <note>original: "Qui fecit te sine te non saluabit te sine te"</note> "He who created you without you will not save you without you." Therefore, he wants to show here that those of Limbo left not only through the merits of the passion of Christ (without which no one is perfect enough to be saved) but also through their own merits, because both are necessary. **MY VEILED speech**: Because he expressed what he clearly wanted to say [indirectly].

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial I inside a square frame with floral motifs.</image-desc>
**Virgil understood** that Dante desired to be certain of what he believed: that is, if Christ drew the souls of the ancient patriarchs from Limbo as the Holy Church posits. And therefore he responds: **I WAS NEW to this state**: because I had come here only a short time before. For...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Canto IV of the Inferno, specifically focusing on the "Harrowing of Hell." Following the previous discussion on why virtuous pagans are in Limbo, Landino now provides a historical and theological breakdown of the biblical figures Christ rescued during his descent into the underworld.</meta>

# INFERNO

Virgil died in the twenty-sixth year of the reign of Octavian Augustus, who reigned for 56 years. And Christ died in the eighteenth year of the reign of Tiberius, Augustus's successor. Therefore, Virgil had arrived in Limbo forty-eight years before Christ drew out the souls of the ancient fathers. **A MIGHTY ONE**: that is, Christ. And note that since Virgil was not a Christian, it did not seem right to Dante that Virgil should name Christ. Because he was not instructed in Christian doctrine, he did not know Christ as Christ, nor as the cause of the liberation of those souls, because he did not know by what means he could do this. But he called him "mighty" because of the effect he saw. Nor does this disagree with the saying of the prophet: <note>original: "At tollite portas principes uestras: & eleuamini porte eternales: & introibit rex glorie. Quis e iste rex glorie? Deus fortis & potes deus potes in prelio."</note> "Lift up your heads, O gates; and be lifted up, O eternal doors, and the King of Glory shall enter. Who is this King of Glory? The Lord, strong and mighty, the Lord mighty in battle."

Abraham the patriarch, and David the king;
Israel with his father and with his children,
and with Rachel, for whom he did so much;
And many others, and he made them blessed.
And I want you to know that before these,
human spirits were not saved.
They did not stop walking because he spoke,
but they passed through the forest all the while—
the forest, I say, of crowded spirits.

<column-break/>

**WITH A SIGN of victory.** If he had been mighty in war, he deserved to have the sign of that victory, of which none was greater: because by dying he conquered our death, and by rising he restored life to us—which the sin of Adam had taken from us—and he triumphed over the devil, the prince of this world. **DREW FROM HERE**. i.e., he pulled out from here **THE SHADE**. i.e., the soul. **OF THE FIRST** parent. That is, the father: and this was Adam, the "protoplast," meaning the first creation of God, from whom all men are born. **OF Abel** his son.

<column-break/>

"Adam" in the Hebrew language signifies, according to the interpretations of the Bible, "bearing witness" or "testimony." Abel was the second son of Adam and Eve, a just and very religious man. He was a shepherd; and because God had commanded him and Cain, his brother and Adam's firstborn, to make a sacrifice, Abel always sacrificed the best animals of his herds and flocks with a ready will. And for this, he deserved that God should prosper him. Cain was a greedy man and showed little reverence to God; because he was devoted to agriculture, he sacrificed the most barren ears of his grain. And finally, moved by envy, he killed Abel. Abel was mourned by his parents for one hundred years in a valley, which for this reason is named the "Valley of Tears." "Abel" in Hebrew signifies "gain," "fear," "vanity," and "miserable." Noah was the beginning of the second age, which lasted until Abraham; from Adam until him lasted the first age. This man alone among all the men of that century was found just. And God, angered by the universal wickedness of all men and wishing to kill and extinguish them with a flood of water, commanded him—when he was already eight hundred years old—to make the ark, as the Bible states. It took one hundred years to build, and he entered it with his three sons, Shem, Ham, and Japheth, with their wives, and two animals, male and female, of every species. After the flood, Noah and Shem lived in Asia, Ham in Africa, and Japheth in Europe.

<margin>**Moses, lawgiver and obedient**</margin>
Moses, the lawgiver and obedient one. From Abraham until Moses lasted the third age. He was born of a father and mother of the tribe of Levi in Egypt; and at that time, the King of Egypt had all the males born of the Hebrew people thrown into the river. Therefore, his mother, seeing his excellent appearance, kept him hidden for three months. Then, no longer able to conceal him, she placed him in a vessel made of reeds, smeared with bitumen and pitch, and left him on the riverbank. He fell into the hands of Pharaoh's daughter and, through the work of the boy's sister, she had him raised by his own mother and adopted him. And because she had found him near the water, she called him Moses. Later, when Moses reached adulthood and saw in what affliction the Hebrew people were, having almost become slaves to the Egyptians, one day in the sight of a Hebrew, he killed an Egyptian and hid him in the sand. Then, hearing that the homicide was discovered, he fled in fear from the presence of Pharaoh, who was searching for him, and went to the region of Midian to a priest. By chance, finding his seven daughters from whom other shepherds had taken the water they had drawn to water their flock, he defended them and helped them water the flock. For this, he received one of them, named Zipporah, as his wife. And while pasturing the herds of his father-in-law, he arrived at Mount Horeb, where God appeared to him in the form of a flame. He was instructed by God as to what path he should take to liberate the people of Israel from the hands of Pharaoh. It would be very tedious to relate his innumerable and distinguished virtues, for which he deserved to see God face to face, not only at Horeb but also at Sinai. He was a man most admirable in doctrine, military discipline, and holiness of life. Finally, he died on Mount Nebo after God had shown him the Promised Land. He lived one hundred and twenty years. He lived during the times when Cecrops reigned in Athens. **LAW-GIVER** and obedient: Law-giver because God gave the laws to the Hebrew people through his hands. **OBEDIENT**: because he observed the divine precepts so strictly that no danger or toil ever turned him from them. Let no one complain if I run through these histories very briefly, because one cannot otherwise fit many things into a small space.

<margin>**ABRAHAM**</margin>
**ABRAHAM the patriarch**: That is, the first of the fathers. This was the first faithful elder to whom God revealed the Trinity. From the year of the flood until Abraham was born was one thousand and seventy-two years. His origin was from Shem, son of Noah. From Shem was born Arpachshad; from him Cainan; and from Cainan, Shelah; from Shelah, Eber; from Eber, Peleg; from Peleg, Reu; from Reu, Serug; from Serug, Nahor; from Nahor, Terah; from Terah, Abraham was born. He was born in the land of Chaldea during the time when Ninus, son of Belus, reigned. By God's command, he came to live in Canaan, and God promised him that He would give that region to his seed—from the river of Egypt to the Euphrates—and that his seed would multiply so much that whoever could count the dust of the earth could count them. He lived then in the valley of Mamre. In the tenth year after his arrival in Canaan, Sarai, seeing herself sterile, encouraged Abraham to have seed by her handmaid, Hagar. Hagar, seeing herself pregnant, began to grow proud against Sarai, and being afflicted by her, she fled. But by the words of the angel, she returned and bore Ishmael to Abraham. Later, when he was already one hundred years old, God told him that he would have a son by Sarai, who was ninety years old. And He commanded him to circumcise all males, and that he should no longer be called Abram, but Abraham; and similarly his wife Sarah, and not Sarai. Abraham laughed to himself, thinking he would generate a child at one hundred years. But later, he called the son of Sarah Isaac. Abraham circumcised himself and his son Ishmael when he was ninety-nine years old and the son was thirteen; and so he did to all his others. Then, when Isaac was born, he circumcised him on the eighth day. This is the one whom he was content to sacrifice to obey God. For this, he deserved that God should bless his seed. After the death of Sarah, he had another wife, Keturah, and by her, he fathered more sons. He lived one hundred and seventy-five years. "Abraham" signifies "exalted father," but "Abraham" means "father seeing the people" or "father of a multitude." "Isaac" means "laughter." "Ishmael" means "man heard by God," for truly he receives the hearing of God. "Sarah" signifies "princess," or "coal," or "veil," or "distress." "Sarai" means "my princess" or "my coal."

<margin>**DAVID**</margin>
**DAVID** signifies "strong of hand" or "desirable of face." He was the second king of the people of God. He reigned 40 years. He was a prophet and a poet, as appears in his Psalms. He reigned in the time when the Athenians, after Codrus died, no longer wanted to be under a king. This was in the fifth age, which lasted until Christ. I will not dwell on his history because it would be too long. But God showed what kind of man he was by saying he had found a man after his own heart.

<margin>**ISRAEL**</margin>
**ISRAEL** with his father and with his children. Israel was Jacob, so called because...

# CANTO FOUR

->who, going into Mesopotamia, saw a ladder that reached from earth to heaven, with angels ascending and descending upon it, and God leaning against it. Because "Israel" signifies "man who sees God" or "vision of God." Therefore, he drew out Jacob with his father Isaac, the son of Abraham, who lived one hundred and sixty years and died during the reign of Xerxes, the first king of the Assyrians. AND WITH his offspring, that is, his children, who were twelve; and from these descended the twelve tribes of Israel. From Leah, he had Reuben, Simeon, Levi, and Judah. And from Rachel's handmaid, he fathered Dan and Naphtali. And from Zilpah, Leah’s handmaid, he fathered Gad and Asher. Afterward, Leah conceived by him a fifth son, who was Issachar, and a sixth, Zebulun. And from Rachel, he had Joseph and Benjamin. AND RAchel for whom he did so much. Laban was the brother of Rebekah, Jacob's mother, and lived in Mesopotamia. Jacob went to him, and having been received as a kinsman, he promised to serve him for seven years by guarding his flocks if he would give him his younger daughter Rachel as his wife, who was very beautiful. But when the time was finished, Laban deceived him; on the first night of the wedding, he gave him his elder daughter Leah, who was not as beautiful as Rachel and was bleary-eyed <note>original: "cispa"; likely referring to the biblical description of Leah having "weak eyes."</note>. Afterward, when the deception was discovered in the morning, Jacob agreed to serve another seven years so that Laban would give him Rachel. And therefore the poet said "FOR WHOM," that is, for which Rachel, "HE DID SO much"—meaning he toiled so much, serving for fourteen years to have her. THEY DID NOT STOP walking: why does he say this? Because he places two types of souls in this Limbo. One consists of those who departed the body in early infancy without baptism; the other consists of those who, although they were illustrious for many virtues, are nonetheless condemned for not having had baptism. The first, having done nothing worthy, he wants to be like a forest. A forest is an uncultivated place, shady and without sun; it has dense trees without any fruit and is inhabited by wild beasts rather than men. So these souls are not cultivated by any <term>doctrine</term> <note>Meaning formal teaching or intellectual enlightenment.</note> because in life they did not have the time to comprehend it. For this reason, they remain shadowy and obscure, since no doctrine shines within them, nor the sun of any truth. The forest being very dense and thick with trees denotes the infinite crowd of such souls.<-

ma nō si chio non discernessi in parte
chorreuol gente possedea quellocho:
O tu chonori ogni sciẽtia & arte
questi chi son channo cotanthoranza
che dal modo deglialtri gli diparte

And he strives to imitate Virgil in these lines. But as much as our religion allows: **OUR WAY WAS NOT yet long.** That is, they had not moved very far "this side of the summit," meaning from the top where one descends into the first circle. Some texts have "somno" (sleep), and then we would say "on this side of the sleep," meaning from the place where he was placed while sleeping, which was the bank of the Acheron. **A HEMISPHERE** of darkness it conquered. A round body, like a ball, is called a sphere; hence, "hemisphere" means half a sphere. And by this, he denotes that the fire illuminated from the middle of the sphere upward. **FROM AFAR WE WERE** still a little way. **BUT NOT** so far that I could not discern in part that honorable people possessed that place. Although it is a distant thing to know doctrines and discern them, nonetheless Dante—representing the "lower reason"—even if he does not fully discern them, can still perceive that literate men are worthy of honor, especially when he sees them honored by others. **O YOU WHO HONOR** every science and art. Certainly, every doctrine is honored by its own nature. But when it is adorned with poetic eloquence, it is much more honored. It is therefore the proper praise of such a poet and poems, which are most full of every kind of doctrine. And it can truly be said of him that just as gold adorns the gem set within it, so he makes more illustrious every science of which he treats. Allegorically, there is no doubt that the human intellect, when filled with great and varied doctrine, is not only honored by it, but that same doctrine in his mouth and in his writings becomes more worthy of admiration. **THESE** who are they who have such "onranza"—that is, "honoranze" (honors); he used <term>syncope</term> <note>A poetic device where a syllable is removed from the middle of a word to fit the meter.</note> for the sake of the verse. Dante recognized the honor in them, but he did not know the science from which such honor came. Therefore, he asks Virgil; because, as I have said, the intellect alone is what can give true judgment of it.

Et quegli ad me lornata nominanza
che di lor suona su nella tua uitta
gratia acquista nel ciel che si giauanza
In tanto uoce fu per me udita:
honorate laltissimo poeta
lombra sua torna chera dipartita
Poiche la uoce fu restata & queta
uidi quattro grãdi ombre a noi uenire
fembianza haueuon ne trista ne lieta
Lo buon maestro comincio a dire.
mira cholui cō quella spada in mano
che uien dinanzi a tre si chome sire

<column-break/>

WE HAVE seen that this first circle contains two generations: that is, little children who were not baptized, and also those who lived before baptism and through doctrine, or through feats of arms and other civil virtues, acquired great fame in the world. But he places the first group in the first part of the circle in the form of a forest. The second group he places separately in the second part, in a luminous and elevated place. He speaks of the first group according to Christian opinion. Of the second, he writes as a poet, but not without reason. For it is reasonable that, although their many great virtues were not enough to save them because they did not have baptism nor worshiped God properly, they should nonetheless have some advantage and prerogative over those who lived wickedly. Especially since Truth says that no good should go unrewarded. And for this reason, he attributes to them a pleasant and joyful place, almost describing the <term>Elysian Fields</term> <note>In Greek mythology, the dwelling place of the virtuous after death.</note>.

It seems a just thing that, having raised themselves from the earth with singular virtues in this life, in the next life—even if they are not saved—they should at least have a place with some honor and dignity. **GRACE ACQUIRES** in heaven. Virtue is pleasing to God even in those who did not worship him properly. Hence, as Augustine says, the Gentiles received many benefits from God as a reward for their virtues. For that virtuous life moves God to want them to be in a better state. He then feigns having heard a voice that encouraged those spirits to honor Virgil, who a short while before had departed to aid Dante. And he shows that four poets went to meet him, similar to the honors men give one another in this life. And he shows the appearance of these poets to have been neither sad nor joyful; truly because their state was not mournful since they were not in sensory pain, nor joyful because they were not in glory. Or truly because the demeanor of the wise man always remains in a suitable <term>mean</term> <note>The "golden mean" or middle ground between extremes.</note>; he is neither easily gladdened nor basely saddened. He places Homer with a sword in his hand because he was the first poet among the Greeks of whom it can truly be said that he wrote of battles.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Canto IV of Dante’s Inferno. The previous page ended mid-word, discussing the biblical patriarchs. # INFERNO

### That one is Homer, the sovereign poet;
### the next is Horace the satirist who comes;
### Ovid is the third; and the last is Lucan.
### Because each of them agrees with me
### in the name that the single voice sounded,
### they do me honor, and in that they do well.
### Thus I saw assemble the beautiful school
### of those lords of the loftiest song
### who fly above the others like an eagle.

<br/>

### After they had reasoned together a while,
### they turned to me with a welcoming sign,
### and my master smiled at that.
### And they did me even greater honor still,
### for they made me of their company,
### so that I was sixth among so much wisdom.
### Thus we went on until the light,
### speaking things of which silence is beautiful,
### just as speaking there was appropriate.
### We came to the foot of a noble castle,
### seven times encircled by high walls,
### defended around by a lovely stream.

<column-break/>

Wherefore Horace <note>In his *Ars Poetica*</note> showed in what meter **the deeds of kings and leaders and sad wars** <note>original: "res gestas regumque ducumq;: & tristia bella. Qua scribi possent numero mōstrauit"</note> could be written. Homer’s father was Marone and his mother Ornithone. Others affirm that a daughter of Melampus named Critheis gave birth to Homer and did not know who the father was; she gave birth to him in Smyrna near the river Meles, and for this reason he was called Melesigenes. She raised him in extreme poverty. Later, because of his admirable intellect, he was adopted by a teacher of grammar. Having become an adult and learned, he went traveling through the greater part of the cities of Greece, and finally in Colophon he became blind; and for this reason he was called Homer, because the Colophonians call the blind *homeroi*. He returned then to Smyrna and there practiced the poetic art. In this he was so excellent that until now no one has surpassed him, nor has he been equaled by anyone except Virgil. He was forced by poverty to go about singing his verses for a price. And in the region of Phocis, he made a pact with a certain Thestorides that if he provided him with food and clothing, he would attribute to him all the verses he made. But after some time, Thestorides went away to the island of Chios, and there he recited Homer’s verses as his own. Finally, wanting to go from Samos to Athens, he was proposed an enigma—that is, an obscure saying—which he, being unable to solve, died of grief. The enigma was that some men of Arcadia <note>Other versions say fishermen from Ios</note> asked Homer, "What have we taken?" They replied: **"Those that we have caught, we leave behind; and those that we have not caught, we carry with us."** <note>original: "Quegli che noi habbiamo preso noi lasciamo & portiancene quegli che non habbiamo preso"</note> Homer understood this to mean fish, and therefore could not solve it; but they meant the lice they had upon them. But in truth, this seems an unsuitable death for such a great man; therefore I rather agree with Herodotus, who writes that he died overcome by extreme old age. Nor is it very clear what his homeland was. Some say Smyrna, others Colophon, others Chios, others Athens. Similarly, there is controversy among writers as to when he was born: Herodotus says one hundred and forty years after the destruction of Troy; Eratosthenes says one hundred; Philochorus one hundred and eighty; Apollodorus the Athenian two hundred and forty. HORACE Flaccus, a satirist and lyric poet, was born in Venusia on the eighth day of December in the third year of the hundred and seventy-eighth Olympiad. His father was a herald and a freedman—that is, born of a man who had once been a slave. In satire, he was cleaner and purer than Lucilius; very bold in his reproofs, and in lyric verses almost alone among the Latins. OVID was born in Sulmona in the third year of the hundred and eighty-sixth Olympiad; a man so open to every kind of poem and of such genius that if he had not shirked the labor of "polishing" <note>original: "elimare"; the process of refining and editing poetry</note>, he would have been inferior to no one. He died on the island of Pontus, where he had been exiled by Octavian. MARCUS Annaeus Lucan was the nephew of Seneca the philosopher, born to Marcus Annaeus Mela, his son. He was from Cordoba, a city in Spain. He was similar to his grandfather in life and habits, and such a lover of liberty that he became one of Piso’s conspirators against Nero. For this, condemned to death, he had his veins cut and died on the last day of April in the twenty-seventh year of his life, in the third year of the two hundred and tenth Olympiad, and in the sixty-seventh year of Christ. He wrote the *Saturnalia*, ten books of *Silvae*, *Medea*, *Orpheus*, and the *Pharsalia*, where the civil wars between Caesar and Pompey are found. The order in which the author places these three Latin poets—giving the first place to Horace, the second to Ovid, and the third to Lucan—can be argued for and against, and judgments vary. Nor does it please me that some place these four poets as symbols for the four moral virtues. EACH AGREES WITH ME IN THE NAME: That is, each is a poet. THEY DO ME HONOR AND IN THAT THEY DO WELL: This denotes that those who share the same doctrine or art should always honor and favor one another, although envy most often produces the opposite effect. SCHOOL <term>scola: from the Greek for "leisure" (otium)</term> signifies leisure and refers to the discussions where men, in leisure and having set aside all other business, exercise their intellect in some liberal doctrine; it is also used for the place where this is practiced. LOFTIEST CANTO: He calls poetry this, which in the best and most ornate song of verses embraces all doctrines, and especially theology. For the first poets were theologians, as appears not only in Orpheus, Musaeus, and Linus, but in David and Job and many others, as we shall write more extensively in the preface of this book. WHO ABOVE THE OTHERS LIKE AN EAGLE FLIES: The eagle has such strength that it gazes at the rays of the sun and is not dazzled; so the poetic fury transcends infinitely toward the divine, as Plato demonstrates when he writes of the four species of divine furies.

The greeting that the poets give to Dante and making him the sixth among them signifies nothing other than that he became a poet by being drawn by the beauty and the doctrine of their works, and by having imitated them. Nor is it without reason that they spoke **things of which silence is beautiful** <note>original: "chose chel tacere e bello"</note>, just as it was beautiful to speak of them in that place. For it was reasonable that there should be reasoning among them of things belonging to their doctrine, which was fitting there, but would not be fitting in the present work. Where it is to be noted that it is not enough to reason about beautiful things, but they must also be suited to the time, the place, and the matter being treated. Furthermore, he shows that they dwelt in a high castle because they are placed in high fame and renown, which is impregnable because nothing harms true fame. Therefore, as high walls defend the castle, so the doctrine and the eloquence of poets preserve immortal fame. Whence Ovid said of himself: **"And now I have finished a work which neither the wrath of Jove, nor fire, nor sword, nor devouring age shall be able to destroy."** <note>original: "Iamque opus exegi quod nec iouis ira nec ignis. Nec poterit ferrum nec edax abolere uetustas." from *Metamorphoses*</note> And a little below: **"Above the high stars I shall be carried, everlasting, and my name shall be indelible."** <note>original: "Super alta perennis astra ferar nomen que erit idelebile nostrū."</note> And certainly, as the shadow follows the body, so fame follows virtue. Whence Horace says: **"He shall live on through a long age, known for his fatherly spirit toward his brothers; surviving fame shall carry him on a wing that fears no melting."** <note>original: "Viuet extento procul eius euo Notus in fratres animi paterni. illum aget penna metuente solui fama superstes." from *Odes* 2.2</note> By the walls that defend the castle, understand the virtues and the doctrines, which are those that defend fame. These are seven: Three moral—Justice, Fortitude, and Temperance—which purge the soul of every perturbation and make it fit to receive the doctrines. One active: which is Prudence, which directs and regulates action...

<meta>This page continues Cristoforo Landino’s commentary on Canto IV of the Inferno. Having introduced the "beautiful school" of ancient poets on the previous page, Landino now analyzes the symbolism of the "noble castle" and its surroundings, specifically the number seven and the nature of the "little stream" the poets cross.</meta>

# CANTO FOUR

...of the moral virtues. There are three speculative ones: Intelligence, Science, and Wisdom. Furthermore, he sets the number at seven for the perfection of virtue. For according to the philosophers, this is a perfect number. But it would be too lengthy to recount all the arguments with which the Pythagoreans <note>Followers of Pythagoras, who believed numbers were the fundamental reality of the universe.</note> and the Platonists prove this. Afterward, they use nature as a witness; nature, being most wise, uses the number seven in many things because it is perfect. With this number, they describe the generation of the World Soul. There are seven wandering stars, which in the Greek tongue they call *planets*, though we say "pianeti." The moon moves according to the number seven, for in four times seven (which is twenty-eight days) and eight hours, it returns to the same place in the sky from which it departed from the sun. In the seventh month, the birth in a woman’s womb is mature. Similarly, human life is divided into septenaries <note>periods of seven years</note> as I demonstrated in the first canto. I leave behind infinite other things worthy of being heard, but they are too long for such a large collection. Some say he set seven walls for the seven liberal arts <note>Grammar, Logic, Rhetoric, Arithmetic, Geometry, Music, and Astronomy—the core curriculum of medieval education.</note>, from which all true fame proceeds. For the little stream, some suggest the abundance of earthly things, without which it is difficult to acquire learning. But I believe it is a more scholarly interpretation and fits better to equate the little stream with that species of river which the Latins call a *torrent*. Regarding this, Petrarch said: *In this alpine and rapid torrent.* A torrent is therefore a small river that descends from the mountains and flows into larger rivers; it is called a "torrent" because in the summer it *torret*—that is, it dries up. But because of the rains, it grows and runs with great force. Thus the Latins use this abundance and force to describe a forceful style and the abundance of eloquence as a "torrent." From this, Juvenal says: *A speech more prompt and more torrential than his own* <note>original: "Sermo promptu & ipseo torrentior"</note>. Therefore, our poet, not wishing to say "ditch" (which is what it is called in the Florentine language), said "fiumicello" (little stream). Furthermore, in Latin, when they wish to show a great abundance of speaking, they often say "a river of speech" <note>original: "fiume dicendi"</note>. Therefore, we shall take it to mean the fluency and eloquence of writers, who truly defend fame. For the illustrious deeds of excellent men would fall into oblivion if the eloquence of writers did not make them eternal, as Sallust demonstrates regarding the Athenians. And Petrarch said: *My Pandolfo, these works are fragile / and go a long way; but it is our style / which makes men immortal through fame.* And that he uses the river for eloquence is denoted by Petrarch saying: *That it is pointed out as a miraculous thing / that a river is born from Helicon* <note>Mount Helicon was the home of the Muses; the "river" is the source of poetic inspiration.</note>. We could also take the river for the movement of the soul toward learning, which would be nothing other than the appetite for it.

->**This we passed as if it were dry land;**<-
->**through seven gates I entered with these sages;**<-
->**we came into a meadow of fresh green.**<-
->**People were there with eyes slow and grave,**<-
->**of great authority in their appearance;**<-
->**they spoke rarely, with sweet voices.**<-
->**We withdrew thus to one of the sides,**<-
->**into an open place, luminous and high,**<-
->**so that they all could be seen.**<-
->**There, directly upon the green enamel,**<-
->**the great spirits were shown to me,**<-
->**so that I exalt myself within for having seen them.**<-

<column-break/>

<margin>¶</margin> **THIS we passed as if it were dry land.** That is, without getting wet; and it almost demonstrates that although he equates eloquence to the river, it is nonetheless stable and durable. Truly, if you take the river for the appetite for learning, it shows that it is firm and constant. **THROUGH SEVEN gates:** because there were seven walls; and it is best that they entered through the gates, because in every virtue and every doctrine, one must enter through the gate—that is, through its principles and with a certain order. For there are many who reverse the order in learning and wish to learn the final things before the first. Hence the proverb was born that *he who wants to learn well should enter through the gate.* This signifies that we must begin from the beginning and not from the end. **WE CAME into a meadow of fresh green.** He says they were in a meadow because such a place is delightful for its various flowers and herbs. And we say that stable fame is always green. In this, he also imitates Virgil, who says: *They came to the happy places and the pleasant green spaces* <note>original: "Deuenere locos letos: & amena uireta"</note>. And a little further on: *Some exercise their limbs in the grassy wrestling grounds* <note>original: "Pars in gramineis exercet membra palestris"</note>. The meadow stays always green, and without being cultivated, it produces its fruit; thus the word for meadow (*prato*) is almost like "prepared" (*parato*). For the fields of grain and the vineyards are not "prepared" to produce

<meta>The catchword "re lutilita" at the bottom of the column matches the start of the next section, "re lutilita," confirming the physical sequence of the pages.</meta>

the utility expected from them without some cultivation; but the meadow alone produces by itself. Thus fame, which is born of true virtue, always stays green and by itself produces praise. Afterward, he shows that he noticed from their manners and gestures that they were people of authority. This denotes that it rarely happens that gestures and outward appearance do not show the quality of a man; and especially the eyes are like windows through which we see the soul placed inside the body. **SLOW and grave:** He did not show them to be slow because their intellect was slow—which the Greek calls <term>brady</term> <note>original: "brady"</note> and the Latin *bardo* (that is, dull-witted)—but they were slow, meaning weighed and considered. For just as a foolish levity and frequent changeability without reason is easily recognized in the eyes, so conversely maturity and gravity appear there. Therefore, they were not slow as some dull-witted, stupid, and dreaming people are, but as we see in grave, considered, and thoughtful men. Their eyes were slow and grave because in investigation it is not necessary for the eye—that is, the intellect—to run and judge before it knows. Rather, it is necessary that with the passing of time it considers minutely and without levity, and with gravity examines every part, both for and against, if it wishes to find the truth. **AUTHORITY:** We call that by which reputation and esteem increase in a man, which is the reason that we often believe them even if no reason is shown to us. **APPEARANCE** (*sembianti*): almost like gestures and "action," to speak more expressly of their demonstration. And it is a French word, for they say *assembler* for "to resemble," and it comes from the word *exemplo* (example). Thus we say someone shows goodness in their appearance. **THEY SPOKE RARELY:** This signifies maturity and wisdom. For as it is written: *In much speaking, sin is not lacking* <note>original: "In multiloquio non deest peccatum"</note>. **WITH SWEET voices.** This signifies humanity and affability; and he included this so that it would not be thought that their rare speaking proceeded from pride or austerity. Therefore, in speaking rarely, he shows gravity and modesty; and through the sweet voices, he denotes humanity and cheerfulness. And certainly, it is perfect praise in a man when we see in him the highest gravity joined with the highest cheerfulness. **WE WITHDREW thus to one of the sides:** For so does he who wishes to see better. And he imitates Virgil, who said: *He takes a mound from where he can see everyone in a long row facing him and learn their faces as they come* <note>original: "Et tumulu capit unde omnis longo ordine possit Aduersos legere: & uenientum discere uultus"</note>. And it secretly signifies that he who wishes to know and speculate withdraws to one of the sides—that is, into solitude—because the crowd and the frequent company are enemies of speculation <note>In the Renaissance sense, "speculation" means deep philosophical or theoretical contemplation.</note>. And afterward he adds: **IN AN OPEN place, luminous and high.** For just as one who wishes to see with bodily eyes seeks an open place—that is, one not occupied by trees, or movements, or obstacles that take away the view—and one that is luminous—that is, in pure daylight without fog—and one that is high, so that he stands above the thing he wishes to see (like Zacchaeus who climbed the sycamore tree). So in speculation, it is necessary to remove and consume all obstacles and doubts that take away the sight of truth. Furthermore, we shall see luminous, perspicuous, and clear discourses; and we shall stand in a high place, such as is First Philosophy <note>Another name for Metaphysics, the study of the fundamental nature of reality.</note>, which is the source from which every truth derives. **EXALT MYSELF...**

<summary>Landino provides an allegorical commentary on the "noble castle" of Limbo, interpreting the stream as eloquence and the seven walls as the liberal arts. He explains the dignified behavior of the ancient "great spirits" as a model for philosophical contemplation and intellectual gravity.</summary>
