<meta>This page continues Cristoforo Landino’s commentary on Canto IV of Dante's Inferno. On the previous page, Landino discussed the symbolic meaning of the "noble castle" and the "seven walls" representing the liberal arts or moral virtues. Here, he begins identifying the souls of the virtuous pagans dwelling within, starting with the heroes and rulers of the active life.</meta>

# INFERNO

<meta>Catchword: super/ (proud/haughty)</meta>

Because contemplating the outstanding deeds of the magnanimous causes the observer's soul to rise and desire to imitate such greatness of spirit.

**I saw Electra with many companions**
**among whom I knew Hector and Aeneas**
**Caesar armed with hawk-like eyes**
**I saw Camilla and Penthesilea**
**on the other side I saw King Latinus**
**who sat with Lavinia his daughter.**
**I saw that Brutus who drove out Tarquin**
**Lucretia, Marcia, Julia, and Cornelia**
**and alone, apart, I saw Saladin.**

<column-break/>

In this speculation, he first places the men who were excellent in the active and civil life. Afterward, he places those who were outstanding in the contemplative life—not because he prefers the active life over the contemplative, but because in considering the nature of man as a human being, action occurs before contemplation (which consists of universals). ELECTRA was the daughter of Atlas. Atlas had seven daughters: Electra, Maia, Taygete, Asterope, Alcyone, Celaeno, and Merope <note>These are the Pleiades of Greek mythology.</note>. Electra was the wife of Corythus, a king in Italy, after whom his principal city was named Corythus. I believe this is the city not many today call Corneto <note>Modern Tarquinia.</note>. Electra, therefore, not by her husband but by Jove, fathered Dardanus. Dardanus, after the death of Corythus, coming into conflict with his brother lasius (his mother's son and the son of Corythus), decided to leave him alone in the kingdom and sailed with part of the people to Samothrace, and afterward to Phrygia, where Troy was later built; and from him the Trojans had their origin.

---

This was in the thirty-fifth year of Moses, and in the year of the world 3,737. With many companions: as if to say the people who followed Dardanus, or rather the many kings who were excellent in Dardanus's lineage. But because these were less famous, he shows he did not fully know them as he did Hector and Aeneas, because these two were most excellent. Hector was the son of Priam, and of such virtue that he alone was nearly the reason Troy defended itself for ten years. According to Homer and other writers who follow Homer, he was killed by Achilles. But Dio Chrysostom <note>original: "Dione chrisostomo"</note>, a supreme philosopher and diligent investigator of antiquity, demonstrates—both through the histories of the Egyptians and by many signs—that it was not Achilles who killed Hector, but Hector who killed Achilles; and that Troy was not destroyed by the Greeks, but rather the Greeks were broken and largely consumed by the Trojans. Regarding Aeneas, we spoke above. He not undeservedly places Caesar among the Trojans because he was of the Julian family, who descended from Iulus Ascanius, the son of Aeneas. He mentions the Trojans and the Romans descended from them because the Roman Empire was founded by such a successor, which the poet exalts in many places. Gaius Julius Caesar was the one who waged civil wars against his son-in-law, Pompey the Great. At last, he obtained victory and became perpetual dictator. He was a man, without fail, so admirable for his innumerable virtues that if he had not obscured them with ambition and the lust for lordship among noble mortals, he could have held the first rank. Nor could any be placed before him in military discipline. In ten years, he subjugated innumerable and most warlike peoples of all France, Germany, and England. He conquered Spain, Africa, and a great part of the Eastern regions. In fifty judged battles, he was superior, and in his skirmishes, one million and one hundred ninety-two thousand men were killed. And beyond his expertise in deeds of arms, he was a man of much and varied learning, and the first who, through astronomical reasoning among the Latins, reduced the year without error to the number of days it currently has. He was adorned with such eloquence that, although he had quickly noted down the wars he fought in his *Commentaries* to leave a memory for those who wished to write history, they are nonetheless so polished and eloquent that no one ever hoped, even with careful and vast leisure, to write a history that equaled them. He was of such swift wit and of such counsel and memory that at one and the same time he read, dictated, and gave audience. He dictated four letters at once, even if they were of great importance; and if not attending to other things, he dictated seven. He was adorned with all civil customs, but most especially one recognized in him the most excellent humanity and affability. No one was ever more liberal toward friends; no one more merciful in forgiving every injury. For these things, many are of the opinion that if he had not been killed so soon, he would have returned liberty to the Republic. Finally, excellent men and lovers of the Republic conspired against Caesar as against a tyrant, and he was killed in the Senate. The leaders of the conspiracy were Brutus and Cassius. WITH HAWK-LIKE EYES <note>original: "CON gliocchi griffani"</note>: that is, bright and sparkling, which signifies a sharp and vehement intellect. He attributes such eyes to Julius Caesar, just as Virgil gives them to Caesar Augustus where he said, "From whose happy temples double flames pour forth" <note>original: "Geminas cui tempora flammas leta uomunt"</note>. He said "griffani" because hawks molted in the forest have such eyes. Bird-catchers call hawks "nestlings," "branchers," and "haggards" <note>original: "Nidiaci raminghi & griphani"</note>. Nestlings are taken in the nest. Branchers are those that have newly left the nest and do not yet fly much but rest much on the branches of trees. Haggards are those that, having passed a year, have molted in the wild. He said "armed" as a sign of military virtue, and "with hawk-like eyes" as a sign of the vivacity of his wit and learning. CAMILLA: We spoke of her above. AND PENTHESILEA: Near the Thermodon river, there was a generation of women who lived with such industry and boldness of soul and body in military discipline that they held the empire of many regions. They reduced their men under their power, and from childhood, they weakened their legs and arms so they remained without strength. Because of this, the men performed effeminate duties and the women performed masculine ones. To better use the bow, they burned off the right breast of the small girls so it would not grow; hence they were called Amazons, which in Greek signifies "without a breast" <term>Amazon: derived from 'a-' (without) and 'mazos' (breast)</term>. They founded a most noble city at the mouth of the Thermodon, and in time extended their empire to the Tanais and on the other side as far as Syria. But finally conquered by Hercules, they were nearly brought to ultimate extermination. He took Hippolyta their queen and gave her as a wife to Theseus, King of Athens. But after a few years, Penthesilea, having wandered because she had killed her sister, came to the aid of the Trojans, and in that war performed miraculous deeds; but finally, she was killed by Achilles. LATINUS: Saturn, the most ancient king of Candia (once called Crete), having been driven out by his sons, came to Italy. Janus, who then reigned in the parts where Rome would later be, shared the kingdom with him. From Saturn was born Picus, and from Picus, Faunus, and from Faunus, Latinus, who reigned when Aeneas came to Italy. Moved by his father's oracles and various omens, he betrothed his daughter Lavinia to Aeneas, whom he had first promised to Turnus, King of the Rutulians. This was the cause of the wars between Aeneas and Turnus. He said "SAT" <note>original: "SEDEA"</note> to show that his fame arises more from the maturity of his counsel than from the ferocity of arms, as seen in Virgil. I SAW THAT Brutus who drove out Tarquin: The first Tarquin was the fifth king of the Romans, the son of Demaratus of Corinth. He was born in the city of Tarquinia in Italy, from which he took his name. Afterward, persuaded by his wife Tanaquil—a woman very skilled in omens by which she predicted future things—he came to Rome. He was in such authority under Ancus, King of the Romans, that upon his death, the king left him as guardian of his children. But through ambition, Tarquin used such art that he was made king. His son then succeeded not him, but his son-in-law Servius Tullius; and because of his arrogant and cruel life, he was called Tarquin the Proud <note>original: "tarquino super/"</note>...

<meta>This page continues Landino’s commentary on the inhabitants of Limbo in Canto IV. Having introduced the Roman heroes on the previous page, he now provides the historical background for Lucretia, the establishment of the Roman Republic, several noble Roman matrons, and the Sultan Saladin, before moving to the philosophers led by Aristotle.</meta>

### CANTO FOUR

In the times when this king <note>Tarquin the Proud, the seventh and final King of Rome.</note> was laying siege to Ardea, a city of the Rutuli, an argument arose between Sextus Tarquinius, the king's son, and Collatinus over who had the most virtuous wife. Finally, it was judged that Lucretia, the wife of Collatinus, was the unique example of chastity among Roman women. This was so bothersome to Sextus that he secretly left the camp and came by night to Lucretia; he was generously received by her as a kinsman. Later, wishing to take her chastity, he threatened her: if she did not consent, he would kill her and one of his servants, and then claim he had found her committing adultery with the man. Lucretia consented with her body, but not with her soul, to flee everlasting infamy. But the next day she summoned her father, Spurius Lucretius, and her husband. The latter brought Publius Valerius with him, and the former brought Lucius Junius Brutus. Lucretia told them the whole story; and although she was comforted by them—and they showed her that where the will had not consented, there could be no sin—nevertheless, with a knife she had hidden beneath her garment for this purpose, she killed herself, saying first that she did not want any Roman woman to take a bad example from her. Lucius Junius was, as we said, present at this death. Until that time, to escape the cruelty of Tarquin (who killed or exiled anyone showing any prudence), he had feigned being a fool and lived almost like a brute animal; for this reason, he was called Lucius Junius Brutus <note>Latin: *brutus*, meaning dull or stupid.</note>. Showing the knife bloody from the death of Lucretia, he summoned the Roman people and with a long speech demonstrated the cruelty and pride of Tarquin. He persuaded them to send the sons into exile and deprive them of the kingdom. In this way, the monarchy ended in Rome, which had lasted two hundred and forty-four years. This Brutus was the son of Tarquin's sister, and a man so in love with liberty that, having been made consul, he put his own sons to death because they, along with their cousins the Aquilii, had conspired to restore the kingdom to the Tarquins. From him derives the House of Brutus, from which came that other Brutus who, to free his country from the tyrant, killed Caesar. The first killed the last king; the second killed the first tyrant. We have, with the greatest brevity, run through the history of Tarquin, Brutus, and Lucretia. Now we shall speak of Marcia and Cornelia. Marcia is noble both for her chastity and the excellence of her husband; she was the wife of Cato of Utica, and bore him two children. Later, it appearing to Cato that these were enough for him, and seeing that his close friend Hortensius was without children, he divorced her and married her to Hortensius, while he himself lived a celibate and chaste life. Nevertheless, once Hortensius died, moved by compassion for her, he took her back. Julia was the daughter of Caesar and wife of Pompey; she loved her husband so much that when his robe was brought to her house stained with blood (which had come from his nose), and remembering the civil discords, she felt such grief fearing he had been killed that she fainted. She miscarried her child and died shortly after, not without universal mourning; for she was of such virtue that it was the constant opinion that had she lived, she would have been such a bond between Pompey and Caesar that the civil wars would not have followed. "Corniglia," that is Cornelia, was the daughter of Scipio Africanus the Elder and the wife of Gracchus; she was a woman of prudence and a manly spirit. For this reason, she was so loved by her husband that, when two serpents appeared and the diviners said it was necessary for one to be killed—and if the male were killed, Gracchus would die, and if the female were killed, Cornelia would die—Gracchus insisted the male be killed, judging that her life was more useful to his family than his own. She was most eloquent, and she raised Tiberius Gracchus and Gaius Gracchus, her sons, who surpassed all the orators of that age. When she was sometimes asked by other women to show them her jewels, she showed them her sons, adorned with every good character and eloquence, and said these were her jewels. After she became a widow, she was sought in marriage by many princes and kings, but she always observed a most chaste widowhood. Saladin was the Sultan of Babylon <note>In the Middle Ages, "Babylon" was a common name for Cairo.</note>. He acquired the empire with fraud and wickedness by killing the Caliph, his lord; this was in the year of Christ 1163. Later, in 1187, he dealt a great defeat to the Christians and took Jerusalem, which the Christians had held with great glory for eighty-eight years after Godfrey <note>Godfrey of Bouillon.</note>. Finally, after long conflict and the slaughter of Christians, he died in Damascus in the year 1194, a man excellent in military discipline. Not without reason did the poet say **AND ALONE** in part **I saw Saladin**, to denote that few of that nation have been excellent. In the times of Saladin, there was a passage of Christians to recover Jerusalem, which Saladin had occupied. For this reason, he took counsel to note and spy on all the states and forces of the Christians. With two of his closest friends and three servants, disguised in the habit of a merchant, he passed into Armenia, and then into Greece, and afterward into Sicily, considering everything with diligence. From Sicily, he passed to Naples, and from Naples to Rome. Having understood the government of the Church, he passed through Tuscany and Lombardy and crossed the Alps. He traversed Gaul, traversed Spain, and Germany; and finally, like a new Ulysses made prudent by having seen many lands and various customs of men, he returned by sea to Alexandria.

When I raised my brows a little higher,
I saw the Master of those who know
seated among the philosophical family.
All look to him, all do him honor:
there I saw Socrates and Plato,
who stand closer to him than the others;
Democritus, who attributes the world to chance,
Diogenes, Anaxagoras, and Thales,
Empedocles, Heraclitus, and Zeno;
And I saw the good collector of qualities,
I mean Dioscorides; and I saw Orpheus,
Tully, and Linus, and Seneca the moralist;
Euclid the geometer, and Ptolemy,
Hippocrates, Avicenna, and Galen,
Averroes, who made the great commentary.

<column-break/>

The poet had already recounted some of those who acquired fame in the civil and active life. Now he places those who are situated in a more exalted rank because they are ennobled in the intellectual virtues and in the contemplative life, which is undoubtedly preferred over the active life. This is signified when he says **WHEN I raised my brows a little higher**, because to know who is in a higher place, it is necessary to raise the eyes higher. Among these, he gives the first place to Aristotle, a man undoubtedly of marvelous genius and profound doctrine, and one who holds the palm for having placed all of philosophy in perfect order, and for having treated all its parts with the best distinction. For this reason, the poet places him before Plato, moved not only by this but perhaps also by his profession, because he was a Peripatetic. I would not dare to give my judgment here between two such great men; nor could I if I wished, prohibited by the weakness of my intellect and the lack of learning within me. But I see that among the Greeks, Aristotle is held in the highest admiration in physical doctrines, and Plato is judged superior in metaphysical and divine matters. Hence, they call Aristotle "daemonic" and Plato "divine." And certainly all the ancient Latins who did not surpass the eloquence of the doctrine hold that the prince of philosophers is Plato; nor is there small hatred for those things Aristotle incurred for having condemned him in many places. Seeing that even...

<meta>This page continues the catalog of famous figures in Limbo from Canto IV. After discussing Roman heroes and the Sultan Saladin, Landino now moves to the "family of philosophers," focusing on the lives and teachings of Aristotle, Socrates, Plato, Democritus, Diogenes, and Anaxagoras.</meta>

-># INFERNO<-

A good portion of the commentators on Aristotle defend Plato where Aristotle condemns him. Cicero calls him the "Homer of philosophers." And Augustine said he had chosen the Platonists because they understood divinity better; elsewhere he writes, "Let Aristotle be silent, who compared to Plato is always a child." And our Petrarch places him first, saying: *I turned to my right and saw Plato, who in that troop went closest to the goal reached by those to whom it is given by heaven. Then came Aristotle, full of high genius.* <note>Quoting Petrarch’s *Triumph of Fame*, where Plato is ranked above Aristotle, contrary to the medieval scholastic preference for Aristotle.</note> 

Aristotle, then, was from the city of Stagira, and the son of Nicomachus, who descended from Nicomachus, son of Machaon, and grandson of Asclepius <note>The legendary Greek god of medicine</note>. Apollodorus writes that he was born in the first year of the ninety-ninth Olympiad <note>Approximately 384 BCE</note>; at the age of seventeen, he began to hear Plato, and was his student for twenty years. He stayed with Philip, King of Macedonia, who gave him his son Alexander <note>Alexander the Great</note> to educate for fifteen years. He persuaded Philip to rebuild Stagira, his homeland. He taught philosophy and rhetoric together. He used to dispute while walking through the school; hence his followers were called **Peripatetics**, because *peripatein* in Greek means "to walk." He was accused because he offered the same sacrifices to his concubine, whom he loved dearly, that the Athenians offered to Ceres, a great goddess among them. For this reason, he fled to Chalcis and died there in the same year that Demosthenes died in Calabria.

**Socrates** the Athenian, son of Sophroniscus the sculptor, was an assistant to Eupolis in writing tragedies. He heard Anaxagoras, and after he was condemned, Socrates moved to Archelaus. He was a sculptor and made the *Graces* which were placed in the citadel of Athens. He was vehement and sharp in the oratorical art, but the Thirty Tyrants forbade him from teaching it. They write that he was the first—though his disciple Aeschines opened and expanded the fields and oratorical ornaments. For this, he was rebuked by Aristophanes the comic poet as a man who could, by the force of eloquence, make an unjust cause appear just. He was the first discoverer of the precepts of **moral philosophy**, because the others before him had focused only on **physics** (that is, natural philosophy). He did not merely debate it but lived according to it, filled and adorned with all virtues; a despiser of all pleasure, he cheerfully endured poverty and sustained his life with the craft learned from his father, until Crito, through his liberality, helped him and made him leave the craft. He then became his disciple and taught in the workshops of craftsmen without any pomp, but with great utility. He proved with the testimony of Homer that moral philosophy is more useful to men than natural philosophy. Finally, because he was judged by the Oracle of Apollo to be the wisest of all men, he attracted so much envy that Anytus provoked the poet Aristophanes against him and moved Meletus to accuse him of not worshipping the gods of his country, inducing new gods, and corrupting the youth. Finally condemned to death, he drank the poison given to him, for in this way the Athenians killed those condemned to death.

**Plato**, the prince of philosophers, was an Athenian and the son of Ariston <note>The OCR reads 'aristotē', likely a scribal or transcription error for Ariston</note>, and through his mother’s blood descended from Solon. His proper name was Aristocles, but they called him **Plato** either because of his excellent physical build, or because of his wide range of speech; others say because of his wide and spacious forehead, since *platos* in Greek means "wide." He was a student of painting and poetry. Socrates dreamed that a small swan grew in his lap, and once grown, it flew and sang wonderfully; then the following day, when Plato's father gave him to him as a disciple, Socrates said, "This is the swan." No oratorical genius can conquer such vast material, nor can one traverse the sea of such great wisdom and his immortal and varied virtues in a brief time. Three times he went to Sicily to bring it to liberty. And he so offended Dionysius, the tyrant there, that the tyrant sold him to Pollis the Spartan. Later, he was ransomed in Aegina by Anniceris of Cyrene and sent back to Athens. Because of his great desire to acquire every doctrine, he searched a great part of the earth. For twenty years he heard Socrates; at twenty-seven, he went to Megara to Euclid the mathematician. Then to Cyrene to join Theodorus. He came to Italy to join Philolaus and Eurytus, the Pythagoreans. He sailed with Euripides to Egypt to see the priests in whom there was supreme doctrine. To Babylonia to the Chaldeans; he wanted to go to Persia to the Magi but was hindered by the Asian war. Thus he accumulated so much knowledge that after him it was not necessary for any Greek to seek other studies than those of Greece. He died in the first year of the 108th Olympiad while sitting at a table at a wedding feast, in the eighty-first year of his age.

**DEMOCRITUS** who attributes the world to **chance**. Democritus was from the city called Abdera, a man entirely given to the investigation of the secrets of nature. He heard the priests in Egypt and the Magi in Persia. Some say he also went to India to see the gymnosophists. In these travels, he spent his entire patrimony, which was one hundred talents; therefore, it was necessary for his brother to support him. But later he was in such authority that his republic honored him with great wealth and made statues of him. He lived always in deep meditation and did not converse with others. He laughed at everything he saw people doing, despising human works as being full of vanity and foolishness. Because of this, his citizens, thinking he had lost his mind, called Hippocrates, the most divine physician, to cure him. Hippocrates came and realized that he seemed foolish not out of stupidity, but out of supreme wisdom. He wrote many things, but because he was obscure in speech, he is called by the Greeks *skoteinos*, that is, "shadowy." His opinion was that there is an infinite space, entirely empty, in which infinite **atoms** (that is, bodies so small they cannot be divided) fly about. These, by touching and sticking together by chance, create innumerable worlds within this infinite vacuum. Therefore, fortune and chance—and not divine craftsmanship—make them. This is why the Poet says that he "attributes the world to chance," meaning he believes the world was generated by chance.

**Diogenes**, son of Icesius, was from the city of Sinope. His father was a money-changer and falsified coins. Some say he also falsified them. But later, changing his life, he became a **Cynic** philosopher. These held the same opinion as the Stoics: that nothing was good except virtue, and nothing was evil except vice. But they dressed in sackcloth and did not refuse any menial labor. They lived an austere and hard life. They rebuked everyone bitingly; hence they were called Cynics, which means "dog-like" in the Greek language. Diogenes then came to Athens and gave himself to the discipline of Antisthenes, the leader of the Cynics. His dwelling was an overturned earthen vessel <note>The famous barrel or tub of Diogenes.</note>. He begged for food and did not receive more than he needed for that day. He was a man most patient with every hardship. He slept wrapped in his cloak. He ate little besides bread and herbs. And when Aristippus said to him, "If you knew how to flatter King Dionysius, you would not live in such penury," he replied, "And if you knew how to live in such penury, you would not have to be a flatterer to Dionysius." He was in such reputation that Alexander the Great went to visit him and found him under his vessel facing the sun. Alexander offered him many things, to which Diogenes replied he wanted nothing else except that he not take away the sun. Alexander recognized such greatness of soul and understood that Diogenes was richer than him, because in the philosopher there was no greed, as he lived most content with little. Alexander felt in himself such ambition and desire to dominate that, hearing from Democritus that there were many worlds, he wept in despair of being able to conquer them all. For this reason, he used to say that if he were not Alexander, he would want to be no one other than Diogenes.

**Anaxagoras** was from the city of Clazomenae; he studied philosophy in Athens under Callias, whose disciple he was for thirty years. He said that the moon contained within itself great lands, mountains, and valleys. Asked why he was born, he replied: "To contemplate the sky, the sun, and the moon." He said that the poetry of Homer was entirely composed of virtue and justice. He was a natural philosopher; and the beginning of his work is: "In the beginning all things were confused and mixed together. Then the **Divine Mind** ordered and composed them." He said that the Mind was the principle of motion...

After discussing the giants of Greek thought like Socrates and Plato on the previous page, he now provides biographical and doctrinal sketches of the Pre-Socratics, the Stoics, and the great scientists and orators of antiquity.</meta>

<header>CANTO FOUR</header>

## AND THALES.
Thales was born in Phoenicia to the noble lineage of King Agenor; he came to Miletus, an island <note>Miletus was actually a city on the coast of Asia Minor, though Landino identifies it as an island here.</note>, and was made a citizen there. He was one of the Seven Sages of Greece, and the first to be called a "sage." Callimachus writes that he discovered the Little Bear <note>Ursa Minor</note>, by which the Phoenicians navigate. He was the first in Greece to dispute concerning physics. He held that even inanimate things possessed a soul, drawing this conclusion from the magnet and from amber, because the former pulls iron and the latter pulls straw. Wishing to demonstrate how easy it would be for him to become wealthy, and knowing through astrology that there would be an abundance of olives that year, he bought them all up before the season and earned a great sum of money. He posited that water is the beginning of all things, and that the world is a living being full of spirits. He thanked Fortune for three things: that he was a human and not a beast; a man and not a woman; and a Greek and not a barbarian—though others attribute this saying to Socrates. He said that God was the most ancient of all things, most beautiful, unbegotten, and the maker of all. Empedocles was from Sicily, from the city of Agrigento. He posited six principles for all things: namely, the four elements, plus Love and Strife. According to Aristotle in *The Sophist*, he was the first inventor of the art of oratory; and in the *Book of Poets*, Aristotle calls him "Homeric" <note>original: "homerico"</note> because he was an outstanding poet. Satyrus writes that he was an excellent physician and an excellent orator, and the teacher of Gorgias of Leontini. Gorgias claims to have been present when Empedocles practiced the magical arts, giving potions to drive away diseases and old age <note>original: "senectu"</note>, and making prosperous winds come while ceasing adverse ones. Heraclides writes that he brought a dead woman back to life. He wrote five thousand verses on physics and purifications, and six hundred on medicine.

**HERACLITUS:** Heraclitus was from Ephesus, a city in Asia. Through constant and most ardent study without a teacher, he became singular in his brilliance. And just as Democritus continually laughed at the foolishness of men, Heraclitus, by contrast, wept, moved to compassion by human misery. Seeing the wicked customs of his fellow citizens, he lived in the mountains in solitude. Zeno of Citium established the sect of the Stoics. While sailing with Phoenician purple dye toward Greece, he was shipwrecked and lost his merchandise. Disconsolate, he came to Athens and, turning to philosophy, listened to Crates the Cynic philosopher. He became so learned that he was held in the highest veneration, so much so that the Athenians entrusted him with the keys to the city gates. He was also honored by public decree with a golden crown and a bronze statue, and given a burial in the Ceramicus. And Antigonus, King of Macedonia, always listened to him when he came to Athens. His opinion was that nothing is good except virtue, and nothing is evil except vice. The philosophers of his sect were first called "Zenonians" after his name. Later, because he disputed in the porch <note>The *Stoa Poikile* or Painted Porch</note> of Pisianax, and "porch" in Greek is called *stoi*, they were named Stoics after that porch. Dioscorides was an excellent physician and investigator of the qualities and virtues of herbs, trees, and stones.

**ORPHEUS** was from Thrace. Because he was a most excellent musician and poet, they say he was the son of Apollo and Calliope. Diodorus Siculus writes that Bacchus would have perished due to the snares set for him in Thrace by Lycurgus, had not Charops, a man of that region, warned him beforehand. For this reason, Bacchus gave him the kingdom of Thrace and taught him how to perform his sacrifices. From Charops was born Oeagrus, and from him Orpheus. Orpheus, adorned with great prudence and learning, refined and greatly embellished the sacrifices taught by Bacchus. Because he wished that on the days these sacrifices were performed men should sleep apart from their wives, the women conspired against him and killed him. Other writers say that he went to Egypt and learned the doctrine of the priests, and upon returning, introduced the sacrifices of the Egyptian Bacchus to Greece. They say that with the sound of his lyre he gathered wild beasts to him, moved mountains, and stopped rivers. This is nothing other than saying that with his eloquence he drew savage men toward a civilized life, moved dull and crude men toward virtue, and quieted the impulse of the furious.

**TULLIO.** <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero</note> It would perhaps be better to say nothing of such a man than to say too little. And certainly, this is not the place to be able—I do not say to adorn—but even briefly to narrate his many great and divine virtues. For if we consider his governance in the Republic, it seems that nothing of his time could be left over for study and doctrine. If, on the other hand, we note the things he wrote, we would judge that he never departed from his studies. Nevertheless, he served both the active and the contemplative life perfectly. In the conspiracy of Catiline, he alone preserved liberty, at a time when Roman liberty was abandoned by all the nobles had he not come to its aid. For this reason, he deserved to be called "Father of the Fatherland" <note>original: "padre della patria"</note> by public decree of the Senate and the Roman people. And Pompey the Great, returning in triumph, said that he owed every obligation to Cicero, because if Cicero had not preserved the fatherland, Pompey would have had no place in which to triumph. He was, therefore, the Father of the Fatherland, and no less the father of Latin eloquence, which he brought to such sublimity that since then no one has been able—I do not say to raise it further—but even to maintain it where he placed it. **LINUS** was a Theban, and because of his supreme eloquence, some poets say he was the son of Mercury and Urania, others of Apollo. He was the first among the Greeks to find melody and proportion in music, and he was excellent in the poetic art. He adapted the letters that Cadmus brought from Phoenicia into the Greek language. He had many disciples, but the most excellent were Hercules, Thamyris, and Orpheus. He wrote of the deeds of the first Dionysus. They say that because Hercules was of a dull wit in learning to play the lyre, and was often beaten by his master with the very lyre he was learning on, Hercules killed him.

**SENECA.** Lucius Annaeus Seneca was a Spaniard born in Cordoba, and later made a Roman citizen. From him was born the Seneca currently being discussed, a man admirable in doctrine, especially Stoicism. He was no less laudable for his natural wisdom and sanctity of life, for which virtues he was given as a tutor to the Emperor Nero. In the beginning, he was highly honored by him. But later, as Nero's cruel tyranny displeased him more each day, and as he often tried to block Nero's rages, he fell under suspicion. Furthermore, he was often bitten by detractors in Nero’s presence, accused of being a man who sought to increase his vast wealth (greater than that of a private citizen) and to win the favor of the citizens, almost wishing to contend with Nero in the magnificence of his villas and the beauty of his gardens. Seneca, therefore, wished to free himself from such envy under an honorable pretext, and offered to return all these things to Nero, demonstrating that due to his old age he was no longer fit for the governance of so many things. But Nero, then pretending to love him, would not accept them. Later, no longer able to hide his hatred, Nero determined that he should die. But granting him the choice of whatever death he wished, Seneca had his veins cut in a bath of warm water. He was a very close friend of the Apostle Paul, as shown by several letters sent from one to the other. This persuaded Jerome that he might be among the blessed <note>original: "beati"</note>. But Dante, as no baptism of his appears, nor finding him in the catalog of saints, places him in Limbo.

**EUCLID** was from the city of Megara, a most studious reader of the books of Parmenides. He became an excellent physicist and mathematician. For this reason, after the death of Socrates, Plato and his other disciples fled from Athens to Euclid in Megara for fear of the Thirty Tyrants. He believed the "Good" to be a single thing, calling it at times God, at times Mind, and at times Prudence.

**PTOLEMY** was from Egypt, though not of the royal line of the Alexandrian Ptolemies descended from Lagus, a soldier of Alexander. He was from the city of Pelusium and lived in the times of the Emperor Trajan. He wrote on the geography of the earth and many things in astrology <note>In the Renaissance, "astrologia" often referred to both astronomy and astrology.</note>.

**HIPPOCRATES** was born on the island of Cos. He was so excellent in medicine that he was reputed a god in that field. He lived in the times of Artaxerxes, King of Persia.

**AVICENNA** was a rival of Averroes and the son of a Spanish king <note>A common medieval misconception regarding the Persian philosopher Ibn Sina.</note>. He organized the works of Galen. He lived in the times of Antoninus Pius.

**AVERROES** was a supreme physician and philosopher, and a rival of Avicenna, from the same homeland. He is the foremost among those who have commented on Aristotle.

<summary>This page provides a series of biographical sketches of ancient figures in Limbo, ranging from the earliest Greek philosophers and poets like Thales and Orpheus to the great Roman orator Cicero and the medieval Islamic commentators Avicenna and Averroes. Landino emphasizes their contributions to science, ethics, and the civilizing power of eloquence.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes the commentary on Canto IV of Dante's Inferno. Having finished listing the great souls of antiquity residing in the noble castle of Limbo, Landino now explains the transition as Dante and Virgil leave the "company of six" poets to descend further into the active punishments of Hell.</meta>

<header>INFERNO</header>

I cannot portray them all in full
because the long theme so drives me on
that many times the word falls short of the fact.
The company of six is divided in two;
by another way the wise guide leads me
out of the quiet air into the air that trembles,
and I come into a place where there is nothing that shines.

<column-break/>

He makes an excuse regarding the theme: that is, the subject matter proposed is so long that he cannot dwell distinctly and particularly on all its parts. And in this, he advises any writer who has to treat many things in one volume not to extend themselves so much on each one that it becomes too long; as, for example, **Petrarch** <note>Francesco Petrarca (1304–1374), whose work *I Trionfi* (The Triumphs) serves as Landino's point of comparison for structural length.</note> treats only one species of men in each triumph; and for this reason, he can be prolix in narrating many of them. BUT Dante, not treating in this hell only the famous, but the lustful, gluttonous, envious, avaricious, and proud, and many other vicious ones, must not name many in each of these species because he would proceed to infinity. Rather, it is necessary that *the word*—that is, the narration—*falls short of the fact*: that is, let it not be as numerous as there are men who have acted; and through their own deeds, they are in that place where their life puts them. **THE COMPANY OF SIX** is divided in two. Because Homer and the other three remained behind. And he describes how, just as in the castle the air was tranquil and bright, so outside the castle where the damned were tormented, it trembled and was dark. **BY ANOTHER WAY.** Because just as one proceeds to the contemplation of famous men by the way of virtue, so to the contemplation of the vicious, one goes by recognizing vices. Therefore, by *another way* the wise guide—that is, our intellect enlightened by science—leads us; with one reasoning he shows us the virtuous man, and with another the vicious. **OUT OF THE QUIET AIR.** Those in the castle were not blessed, because they did not enjoy God; nevertheless, they were in "quiet air": that is, immobile and quiet, because their moral virtue was sufficient to keep them in tranquility. But outside the castle, the air was trembling, because in vicious men the soul is always in varied motion and full of perturbations. It is no less moved and seething, agitated by diverse passions, than the sea struck by various winds. **WHERE THERE IS NOTHING THAT SHINES.** That is, in which place there is nothing that glows or gives light. And certainly in the soul infected by vices; because as the prophet says: "They lie in the shadow of death" <note>original: *In umbra mortis iacent*, a reference to Psalm 107:10 or Luke 1:79.</note>. Furthermore, the poet wishes to conform to the **Gospel**, which shows that in hell there is "outer darkness" and "gnashing of teeth"—that is, trembling and cold.

<summary>Dante explains that he must move quickly through his narrative due to the vast number of souls in Hell, contrasting his broad scope with Petrarch's more focused "Triumphs." Landino interprets the transition from the "quiet air" of Limbo to the "trembling air" of the lower circles as a move from the stability of moral virtue to the chaotic, storm-tossed nature of a soul governed by vice.</summary>

<keywords>Dante, Inferno, Cristoforo Landino, Petrarch, Homer, Limbo, virtue vs. vice, shadow of death, allegory of intellect</keywords>

->CANTO FIVE<-
39

### CANTO FIVE OF THE FIRST CANTICLE OF DANTE.

Thus I descended from the primary circle
down into the second, which encompasses less space
and so much more pain that it pricks into wailing.
There Minos stands horribly and snarls;
he examines the faults at the entrance,
judges and sends according to how he girds himself.
I say that when the ill-born soul
comes before him, it confesses everything;
and that connoisseur of sins
sees which place in Hell is for it;
he girds himself with his tail as many times
as the degrees he wants it to be cast down.
Always before him many stand;
they go in turn, each to the judgment,
they speak and hear and then are whirled down.

<column-break/>

<insert>d</insert> We said above that because the poet has distinguished Hell into circles, it is necessary according to the physical dimensions: because it departs from the circumference and little by little approaches the depths which is the center, that the lower circle must always be smaller than the upper one. And because the place, the more it approaches the depths and the further it departs from heaven, is more suited to punishment, therefore the order of this descent makes the beginning start from the less grave sins, and then continues descending always to the more grave. And this is true regarding the site of the world and the essential Hell. And regarding the moral sense, it is the same order. For only the offense is that which deprives us of God and of our happiness. Therefore, the less grave the sin, the less far the human is from God; and the more grave it is, the closer one is to the depths. For which reason it is appropriate that since the spirits in the first circle were for debt <note>referring to those in Limbo who lacked baptism</note>, in this second circle the least grave sin should be punished: and this is **lust** <term>luxuria: the sin of excessive sexual desire</term>. It is manifest why he said: **WHICH ENCOMPASSES LESS** space: that is, it surrounds. **AND SO MUCH** more pain that pricks into wailing: because besides the pain of the mind, which those of the first circle also feel, they feel that of the breath <note>or 'the wind'</note> which makes them wail: that is, lament. **THERE MINOS STANDS**. There were in Greece three kings: Minos, Aeacus, and Rhadamanthus, sons of Jove. Because they were very just princes, the poets imagine that after their deaths they were made judges of Hell, who had to examine the souls and then punish them according to what their crimes deserved. But regarding Rhadamanthus and Aeacus, we will speak in another place. Minos was the son of Jove and Europa; he reigned on the island of Crete, today called Candia. And according to Diodorus Siculus, he built many cities there. But the most noble were three: Knossos, placed toward Asia; Phaistos, placed in the southern part; and Cydonia, located to the west. He gave laws to the Cretans, which, so that they would have greater authority, he feigned to have received from Jove. And he often entered a certain cave and showed himself to have colloquy with him. Strabo says that in this he imitated a certain Rhadamanthus—not his brother, but another who lived many centuries before. He was the first, according to Pliny, who fought naval battles and acquired many islands and maritime lands. And many peoples were obedient to him, moved more by his justice than by force. Dante, therefore, imitates the ancient poets, and especially Virgil, who writes: <note>original Latin: "Quesitor minos urnā mouet ille silentū Cōciliūq; uocat uitas: & crimina discit"</note> "The investigator Minos moves the urn of the silent; he calls a council of lives and learns of their crimes." Nor is Minos anything other than the judgment of the **conscience**, of which we will speak a little below. This figure is described by Virgil in human form; but Dante configures him as a beast, giving him the tail and the snarl which is proper to a dog. But it is not without reason, because he intends Minos to be the conscience of the damned man—that is, one who has already made a habit of vice—because these are bitten by conscience, which is no longer "human" because such remorse does not turn them back from doing evil. For they have extinguished in themselves the light of reason, by which we are human; instead, it only goads them and makes them become furious. Hence one can say that the conscience in the damned, and in those who have made a habit of vice, is a most cruel beast. Furthermore, he posits that with his tail he denotes the place where the sinner must be put. The tail is the last part of the body of the beast. Therefore, by this, he signifies that such men never feel the remorse of conscience except at the end, and when they have committed the sin. And certainly that alone is that judge which no one can flee. Hence Juvenal: <note>original Latin: "Prima hec est ultio quod se iudice nemo nocens absoluit improba quāquam Gratia fallacis pretoris uicerit urnam."</note> "The first punishment is that no guilty person is acquitted with himself as judge, even if the wicked favor of a deceitful magistrate wins the trial." **THERE MINOS STANDS**. Not without merit does he say "stands there," because the conscience is always in our soul, nor does it ever depart; but continually this judge makes his residence in us. Nor is it to be wondered at that if Minos is the remorse of conscience, and every sin brings such remorse, why the poet did not place Minos in the first circle where there is some species of sin. Because in that circle are the "un-baptized" <note>OCR 'cutiffimi' likely intended for 'decidutissimi' or similar context of the unbaptized</note>, who are punished not for having acted, but for not having acted; and for this they could not have remorse, not knowing how much evil it was not to do good. Or there are the Gentiles, who lived with such virtues that no conscience bit them, and of baptism they had no knowledge. **HORRIBLY** he snarls: There is nothing that snarls and barks and threatens more horribly than the conscience, which day and night goads the one who has committed the crime. The conscience does three things: First, it acts as the punishment itself, as the worm that gnaws at us. Second, it always stands against us as a witness that reproves us. And therefore Juvenal says: <note>original Latin: "Nocte dieque suum gestare in pectore testem Spartano cuidam respondit pythia uates"</note> "The Pythian prophetess replied to a certain Spartan that he carries his witness in his breast night and day." In the third place, it judges the punishment that the sin deserves. Hence, as I said a little above: "The first punishment is that no guilty person is acquitted with himself as judge." And for this, perhaps, the poets placed three judges in Hell: Minos, Aeacus, and Rhadamanthus. **EXAMINES** the faults: Always the conscience re-thinks the committed failure within itself and judges the penalty. **JUDGES AND SENDS**. He posits three things that the conscience does. First, it examines; then it judges; then it sends to execution whatever is judged. **ACCORDING** to how he girds <term>avinghia: from the Latin 'vincire', to bind</term>: That is, he embraces; it is an ancient Florentine word and comes from the Latin word *vincire*, which means to bind, because he who embraces, binds. Hence our peasants still say "a girding" <note>una vinghiata</note>, meaning an armful. **I SAY** THAT when the soul is ill-born: That is, when it is defiled in sin. Which makes it miserable, just as Christ said of Judas: <note>original Latin: "Melius fuisset hoi isti si nūquā natus fuisset"</note> "It would have been better for that man if he had never been born." Do not understand "ill-born" to mean that at its birth it had such an influence from the stars that it was a necessity to sin; because this would take away **free will**, and it is false not only according to our theologians but also according to the philosophers, who hold that the stars can incline, but not necessitate. Because the soul, created immediately by God without the mediation of secondary causes (which are the heavens), is not subjected to the heavens like the body, which through the senses can give some inclination to the soul, but not so much that it does not remain free and in its own power to work well or ill. For which reason the learned astrologer said that the wise man rules the stars. Therefore "ill-born" means born for its own ill, since it has been so foolish that from being free it made itself a servant of sin. **ENTIRELY** it confesses. Because nothing can be hidden from our conscience. **AND THAT** Connoisseur...

<meta>catchword: AND THAT Connoisseur</meta>

<summary>This page presents the opening of Dante's Inferno Canto V, introducing the judge Minos and the moral geography of the second circle. The commentary by Landino interprets Minos not just as a mythological figure, but as an allegory for the human conscience and the psychological weight of sin.</summary>

<meta>The previous page concluded with the descent into the second circle of Hell, where the transition from the relatively painless Limbo to the true torments of the damned begins. This page introduces Minos, the infernal judge, and explores the philosophical nature of fate and providence.</meta>

<header>INFERNO</header>

...king of sins. And certainly no one knows sins better than the conscience: for this reason, Cicero said: "No theater is greater than that of the conscience" <note>original: "Nullum maius theatrum conscientia"</note>. ALWAYS before him many stand; THEY GO in turn. This passage is taken from Virgil: "Minos, the presiding judge, shakes the urn; he calls a council of the silent ones and learns their lives and crimes" <note>original: "Quesitor minos urnam mouet ille silentum conciliumque uocat uitasque et crimina discit"</note>. Virgil says, therefore, that because there is an infinite crowd of souls there, their names are all written down and placed in a vessel, and they are drawn by lot. And whoever is drawn is examined. THEY GO in turn: that is, they go according to the turn that touches them. For "turn" [uicenda] means the turn that comes by lot; and it is derived from the Latin word meaning a "turn" or "change" <note>original: "uice"</note>. THEY SPEAK AND HEAR and are whirled down. In a very brief space of time, and almost at once, they speak their sins and hear Minos, who pronounces the penalty; and they are whirled down because the devils turn them over to the torment. And this is certain. For at the same point, your conscience reminds you of the sin, your reason condemns you, and anxiety afflicts you.

---

**O you who come to the house of pain,**
**Minos cried out to me when he saw me,**
**leaving the act of such a great office:**
**"Look how you enter & in whom you trust;**
**let not the breadth of the entrance deceive you."**
**And my leader to him: "Why do you cry out?**
**Do not hinder his fated journey;**
**it is willed thus where there is power**
**to do what is willed, and ask no more."**

<column-break/>

It is not inappropriate that Minos should want to frighten Dante: because often sensuality (which is aware of its own fragility) discourages itself from entering Hell—that is, into the contemplation of vices—fearing it might remain captured by their pleasures. But superior reason opposes such a conscience and shows that divine grace will lead him safely. Conscience is nothing other than the knowledge a person has of themselves, of their merits, and of their own strengths within themselves. Therefore, this knowledge that sensuality has of its own fragility, and the small power it has to defend itself from carnal pleasures, cries out to him and says: **O YOU who come to the house of pain.** That is, to the painful dwelling: meaning the contemplation of vices. **LOOK how you enter** into such speculation. **AND IN WHOM you trust:** As if to say, you trust in your own strengths, but they will not be sufficient to sustain you. **LET NOT THE BREADTH deceive you:** that is, the

---

width of the entrance: As if to say, the entrance is wide, but the exit is narrow; for anyone can enter into vices, but not leave them. A person can enter into vices by themselves through their own free will, but cannot leave them without divine grace. And as I said, sensuality being frightened by the recognition of its fragility, Virgil—that is, superior reason, which knows that divine grace does not abandon those who help themselves and set out on a good journey—restrains such a conscience and says: **DO NOT HINDER his fated journey.** That is, do not oppose his good purpose, which proceeds from fate—that is, from a disposition ordered by divine providence. And because Providence can do whatever it wills, it is the height of human folly to wish to oppose it or wish to know the reason why it wills so: for "incomprehensible are your judgments, O Lord" <note>original: "incomprehensibilia sunt iudicia tua domine"</note>. Fate is defined differently by various philosophers. I cannot discuss them all at length in such a crowd of things. But because Christians follow Plato more than the others in divine matters—since, as Augustine says, he approached the truth more closely in these things—we will say what fate is according to Plato. But first, understand that the opinions of the philosophers were varied regarding whether God cares for and provides for things or not. Leucippus, Democritus, Protagoras, Theodore, Aristippus, and Epicurus want everything to be by chance without any governance. Some believe God governs everything from the moon's heaven upward, and does not care for inferior things. Some say he cares even for inferior things, but only the great ones. Plato, prince of all philosophers, wants divine providence to extend to all things, even the smallest, and govern them all; with which sentiment Empedocles, Hippocrates, Heraclitus, Pythagoras, and the Stoics agree. Aristotle writes in a way that some interpret as him positing divine providence, and others the opposite. Plato therefore wants the wisdom of God, knowing its own essence and power, and through that, every thing that depends on it, the will immediately loves and desires the order of things which wisdom has judged to be best; and he describes it in himself and constitutes it in a form that cannot be otherwise. Therefore, this constitution, order, and law of things which must necessarily be, and yet do not hinder free will, is called Providence. This same order, considered in the things themselves, is called Fate. And he says Fate is divine law, through which the inevitable thoughts and beginnings of God are fulfilled. For this reason, Augustine does not contend with or oppose those who call the connection and continuous order of all causes "Fate," by which that which is done is done. But he himself does not want to call it Fate, because this name is drawn into different meanings by the ancients and could deceive men. Therefore, Dante said "his fated journey," <term>i.</term> <note>that is</note> his journey which proceeds from the order placed by God in the causes of things; and so it follows: **IT IS WILLED thus where there is power to do what is willed.** These verses are explained as they were explained above.

---

**Now the dolorous notes begin**
**to make themselves heard; now I have come**
**to where much wailing strikes me:**
**I came to a place mute of all light,**
**which bellows like the sea in a storm**
**if it is buffeted by conflicting winds.**
**The infernal hurricane, which never rests,**
**drives the spirits with its rapine;**
**whirling and striking, it molests them.**
**When they arrive before the ruin,**
**there are the shrieks, with wailing and lament;**
**there they blaspheme the divine virtue.**

<column-break/>

We have already shown that throughout this work it is necessary for the text to denote two things: namely, the pains sustained by the damned in the essential Hell, and an allegorical sense, which demonstrates the perturbations induced by the vice being discussed. Therefore, here, dealing with carnal love—which sin is universally called "lust"—and because our author is both a poet and a Christian theologian, I will strive to satisfy both doctrines. And first, understanding the Hell of the damned: **NOW BEGIN the dolorous notes:** that is, shrieks and wailing, because the sensory pains begin. And he places these in a dark place because, having sinned greatly with their eyes (which are the guides in love) and having taken delight in bodily beauties (which all consist in seeing), it is no small penalty that they are deprived of the use of that sense with which they sinned. Furthermore, because it is the custom of lovers to delight in various sounds and songs and harmonies, it is appropriate that this sense be punished...

<summary>This page describes Dante's encounter with the judge Minos, providing a detailed philosophical discussion on the nature of Fate and Divine Providence through the lens of Plato and Augustine. It also begins the description of the Second Circle, where the lustful are punished in a dark, storm-tossed landscape.</summary>

--- Page 83 ---
<meta>This page continues the commentary on the second circle of Hell, where Minos has just judged the souls and the poet now encounters the specific punishment of the lustful. The previous page ended with Minos's warning to Dante about the dangers of the descent.</meta>

<page-num>40</page-num>
<header>CANTO FIVE</header>

> I understood that to such a torment
> were damned the carnal sinners
> who subject reason to desire:
> And as the starlings carry their wings
> in the cold season in a wide and full flock,
> so that breath carries the evil spirits;
> From here, from there, from up, from down it leads them;
> no hope ever comforts them:
> not of rest, but of lesser pain.

<br/>

> And as the cranes go singing their lays,
> making a long line of themselves in the air,
> so I saw coming, uttering wails,
> Shadows carried by the said strife.
> Therefore I said: "Master, who are those
> people whom the black air so punishes?"

<column-break/>

They hear bellowing and other troubling voices. Likewise, because lust induces blindness of mind and lack of consideration, through it the mind loses the light of superior reason. It can no longer contemplate any excellent thing. And similarly, it loses the light of interior reason, because the soul occupied in unchaste love loses all its honor and utility in civic and active life. Therefore, the poet places them in darkness. These two types of blindness—one of superior reason and the other of inferior—were excellently expressed by Virgil: the first in Aeneas, who for Dido's sake abandoned Italy (that is, the investigation and contemplation of celestial things); the second in Dido, who, hindered by love, neglected everything else. Whence: "The towers begun do not rise" <note>original: "non coeptae insurgunt turres"</note>. 

Furthermore, lust induces inconstancy. This is why Love is depicted with wings. On this point, Propertius, assigning the reason why he is winged, said: "Of course, since we are tossed on alternating waves, and our breeze remains in no place" <note>original: "Scilicet alternis quoniam iactamur in undis / Nostraque non ullis permanet aura locis"</note>. Thus the poet said: **THE INFERNAL HURRICANE** which never rests. Likewise, in love, counsels are headlong—that is, inconsiderate and without reason. And for this, he places the "ruin" <note>The "ruin" refers to a physical collapse of rock in Dante's Hell, but Landino treats it as a metaphor for the lover's downfall.</note>. And whoever wishes to understand precisely the inconstancy of lovers and the ruin of their counsels from one extreme to another, let them read the *Triumph of Love* written by Francesco Petrarch; it is a very useful thing to consider well for those seeking to free themselves from such cruel servitude. 

**NOW the doleful notes begin:** He places great weeping and laments here because, of all human disturbances, there is none that makes men more complaining, more tearful, and with greater mourning than love. **OF ALL LIGHT mute:** that is, deprived of it; and he used a term for hearing in place of a term for seeing <note>Dante uses "mute" (a sound term) to describe a lack of light.</note>. The disturbances of the soul are four in genus, but many more in species, as we shall demonstrate elsewhere. All these things extinguish in us the light of reason. But above all others, Love makes a man entirely blind. Whence the poets depict him as blind. Likewise as a child, to show that he lacks all judgment. On this Propertius says: "Whoever he was who painted Love as a boy, do you not think he had wondrous hands? He first saw that lovers live without sense, and that great goods perish through light cares" <note>original: "Quicunque ille fuit puerum qui pinxit amorem / Non ne putas miras hunc habuisse manus? / Is primum uidit sine sensu uiuere amantes / Et leuibus curis magna perire bona."</note>. 

And he well makes the comparison to the sea, which—as we showed in Virgil's *Aeneid*—is excellently used to represent appetite and sensuality. For just as the sea is peaceful by itself, but when moved by winds (and especially if they are contrary) it rises in a great storm, so our appetite, quiet by itself, is disturbed by various passions. These are often contrary in the mind, as shown by Terence's character Pamphilus, who is pushed on one side by love and compassion for Glycerium, and on the other is pulled back by paternal reverence. These contrary winds make the sea "bellow"—that is, they move the lover's sensuality to bellows and to wails. 

**THE INFERNAL HURRICANE.** A true *bufera* [hurricane or squall] is what they call it in the mountains when the falling snow is swirled around and agitated with ruin by various winds. He imagines, then, that those spirits were in the same way whirled and transported through the air, which signifies nothing other than the continuous instability, inconstancy, and sudden change in lovers. For as Terence says, all these things are in love. Therefore, this constant inconstancy and furious change ravishes the soul, turning it from purpose to purpose and striking it—that is, troubling and afflicting it with heavy pains. And when they reach the "ruin"—that is, when they fall from the beloved object and are deprived of it—there are the shrieks, the weeping, the laments, and they blaspheme the divine power. This signifies extreme fury, such as is common in lovers, and demonstrates the perversion in such love. For they prefer such love to the love of God and of their father. 

**WHO SUBJECT REASON TO DESIRE:** That is, to appetite and the inclination of the soul, and of appetite for voluptuousness and sensory delight. Whence *atalentare* means to consent. 

**AND AS the starlings carry their wings:** An excellent comparison of birds to souls because of their lightness. And because starlings fly quickly and in a great throng, it expresses the multitude and speed of the spirits. **FROM HERE, From there, from up, from down it leads them:** The lover never stays in one state; but now rises in the grace of the beloved, and now falls into ruin through enmities and dissensions. 

**NO HOPE ever comforts them, Not of rest, but of lesser pain.** Regarding the essential Hell, this is true of every damned soul for whatever sin. And therefore the author placed it here in the first place of the punishments, so that it might be understood for all the others. But regarding the allegorical sense, it is specific to the lustful, because such a disturbance is insatiable. The more it is exercised, the more the appetite is kindled. Nor do the poets mean anything else by Tityus, the son of Earth, who wished to do violence to Latona, the mother of Phoebus, except lust which is born of the desire for earthly things; although the vulture gnaws his liver, just as much is continually reborn as that great bird devours. Furthermore, the lover is never without pain. For if he is deprived of the beloved, he wastes away with the desire to have her. If he possesses her, he is always in jealousy and in suspicion of losing her.

Just as through the comparison of starlings he expressed the multitude and speed of the spirits, so through the cranes he signifies their laments. And he rightly said, **they go singing their lays:** that is, laments. For almost all the verses and all the songs of lovers contain complaints and regrets and things that move one to commiseration. Whence the Greeks call such verses *Elegi* [Elegies], because *eleos* in Greek means mercy and compassion <note>original: "elos" [error for eleos]</note>. 

**MAKING a long line of themselves in the air.** He does not say that the spirits were flying making a long line of themselves, because above he showed they flew in a throng like starlings. But he says they flew singing their "lays" like cranes do when, flying, they form a long line. 

**WHO ARE those people?** He does not ask about all the people in that circle, because he already knows what kind of sinners are tormented there. But specifically he asks about those who are near him. And because they are names from ancient history, he asks about them. And throughout the poem, he almost always observes this method: he has Virgil speak of ancient histories, while modern ones—those which occurred after Virgil—he has others tell.

<summary>In this passage, Landino provides an allegorical and philosophical commentary on the punishment of the lustful in Dante's Inferno, comparing their erratic movement to starlings and cranes and citing classical authorities like Virgil, Propertius, and Terence to explain the psychological nature of desire.</summary>

# INFERNO

<margin>
The first of those about whom news
</margin>
"The first of those about whom you wish
to have news," he said to me then,
"was empress over many tongues:
She was so broken by the vice of lust
that she made pleasure lawful in her law,
to remove the blame into which she had fallen:
She is Semiramis, of whom it is read
that she succeeded Ninus and was his spouse:
she held the land that the Sultan now rules.
The other is she who killed herself for love:
and broke faith with the ashes of Sychaeus.
Next is Cleopatra, the lustful.
I saw Helen, for whom so much evil
time turned; and I saw the great Achilles,
who fought with love at the end.
I saw Paris, Tristan; and more than a thousand
shades he showed me and pointed out with his finger,
whom love had parted from our life."

<column-break/>

Semiramis was the wife of Ninus, king of the Assyrians. Diodorus Siculus <note>A Greek historian of the 1st century BC.</note> writes fabulous things about her origins. For he writes that she was born in a forest near a lake in the city of Ascalon. Her mother was a goddess <note>original: "p īdia" likely referring to Derceto or Atargatis</note> who was worshipped there, and her father was a young man who sacrificed to her. He says that once born, she was hidden in a cave and there nourished by doves with milk, which they took from shepherds while they were milking. Finally, she was found and given to Simma, the king’s chief shepherd. She was then named Semiramis because she had been nourished by doves, for in the Syrian language, *Semiramis* means "dove." As she grew, she became of such marvelous beauty that Menon, the king's first counselor, married her. In this woman, prudence was no less than beauty. Thus, her husband did nothing without her advice. At this time, Ninus, king of the Assyrians, was with his army against the Bactrians and was besieging Bactra, the capital of that region. Seeing that the siege would be long, Menon sent for Semiramis, without whom he lived only in sorrow. The woman came, and by diligently observing the site of the land, she finally took the city's fortress by a difficult and unguarded path, because that part seemed impregnable. Thus the Bactrians were forced to surrender. This gave the woman great fame. And the king, moved as much by her beauty as by her virtues, asked her from her husband, promising him his daughter Sosane in exchange. When he refused, the king threatened to blind him. Menon, out of grief, hanged himself. In this way, Semiramis became the wife of Ninus, and bore him Ninyas. When Ninus died, he left her the kingdom. Wishing to perform outstanding deeds, she built Babylon upon the Euphrates. Its walls stretched for as many stadia <note>A stadium was an ancient unit of length, roughly 600 feet.</note> as there are days in the year, and a stadium was a fraction of a mile. Therefore, 365 stadia are forty-six miles. The walls were made of brick. They had 250 towers. In the raw bricks were pressed various shapes of wild beasts, each in its own color, so that the entire circuit depicted a hunt; and in place of mortar, she used bitumen from the asphalt marshes. I leave behind many stupendous things about this work, because to describe them would require a whole volume. She conquered the Medes, where she left admirable works—gardens, aqueducts, and roads. She conquered the Persians, where she leveled many mountains and raised many mountains on the plains for the tombs of her friends. She conquered the Indians, against whom she led three million men on foot, fifty thousand on horse, and one hundred thousand chariots. She was very lustful, but she did not want a permanent husband. She chose from among the youngest and most handsome men, and afterwards sent them to a place from which they were never seen again. This is what Diodorus writes. Justin <note>A Roman historian.</note> says that she was finally killed by her son because she wanted to have relations with him. Some say she took him as a husband, and to cover her infamy, she established by law that it should be lawful for everyone to do the same. **THE OTHER IS** she who killed herself for love <note>original: "sancise amorosa"</note>, that is, died for love. Dido follows. She was the daughter of Belus, king of Phoenicia, and wife of Sychaeus. Because Sychaeus had much treasure, he was killed by Pygmalion, Dido’s brother, who hoped to possess his riches. But Dido fled with the treasure to Africa, where she built Carthage and lived in great chastity, never breaking her faith to her dead husband. Finally, seeing herself being forced by Iarbas, king of Mauritania, who wanted to marry her, she killed herself with her own hands to avoid breaking her faith to Sychaeus. But Virgil, to ornament his poem, feigns that Aeneas arrived at the Carthaginian shores due to a storm; and while visiting her, she fell in love with him. Fleeing the rain during a hunt into a cave where they sought shelter, she knew him. Afterward, when Aeneas left for Italy, Dido, overcome by excessive love, killed herself. Therefore, Dante, in following Virgil in other matters, follows him also in this history. **CLEOPATRA** was the daughter of Ptolemy "the Flute-player" <note>original: "pythone," likely a corruption of "Auletes"</note>, king of Egypt, and the sister and wife of Ptolemy Dionysius, who killed Pompey. Civil strife arose between them; and in the conquest that Caesar made of Alexandria, she—with both her beauty and her ornate speech and sweet manners, which were wonderfully present in her—allured Caesar into her love, and bore him Caesarion. After the death of Caesar, with the same arts, she so drew Mark Antony to herself that he loved her ardently, and for her sake, he rejected Octavia, the sister of Octavian. They lived in Alexandria in many delights and great luxury. Finally, once Antony was defeated by Octavian, they fled to Egypt. Antony, seeing he could not otherwise escape Octavian, killed himself. Cleopatra, taken alive and fearing she would be led in a triumph, killed herself with poison. She was a woman of great spirit and very prudent, but no less lustful; and, as Plutarch writes, she was more effective through a certain charm, her gestures, and her alluring ways than through her beauty. **HELEN** was the daughter of Leda, wife of Tyndareus, king of Lacedaemonia. The poets say that Jove, in love with her, transformed himself into a swan (a certain very white bird), and thus by lying with her, two eggs were born; from one was born Pollux and Helen. When she reached mature age, she married Menelaus. In those same times, Paris, son of King Priam, was reputed to be a just judge. Therefore, three goddesses—Juno, Minerva, and Venus—contending over which of them surpassed the others in beauty, submitted the dispute to him. Paris accepted the arbitration, but judged not without corruption. For he favored Venus because she promised to let him have Helen, the most beautiful of all women. Under this hope, he sailed to Greece and abducted Helen. Although some say he did not abduct her, but she followed him of her own will and came to Troy. This injury moved the Greeks to lead an army to Troy, and after ten years they conquered the city, burned it, and sacked it; and Menelaus recovered Helen. Although Herodotus writes that Helen never went to Troy, but that Paris by chance landed in Egypt, and there she was taken from him by a king named Proteus and kept until Menelaus went for her after the Trojan destruction. Dio Chrysostom perverts this whole history. But one cannot, in such a multitude of things, treat each one fully. **FOR WHOM so much evil time turned.** Greece was flourishing, and the riches of the Trojans were incredible before Helen was abducted. But because of her, all of Greece then armed itself to recover her, and all of Asia to defend Troy. From this followed the slaughter of infinite men. Most excellent princes perished. There arose fires, looting, robberies, and the destruction of many cities. Hence Petrarch wrote: "And the world was turned upside down by it." <note>original: "Et furne el mondo sotto sopra uolto"</note> **ACHILLES** The origin of this man is from Jove...
