# CANTO FIVE

For Aeacus was born of Jupiter and Aegina; and from Aeacus came Peleus; and Peleus, by the sea-goddess Thetis, fathered Achilles. His mother dipped him entirely into the Stygian marsh <note>The River Styx in the underworld</note> except for the heel by which she held him. Thus, they say he could not be wounded except in the heel. He was raised on Mount Pelion by the centaur Chiron; in that time, he never ate cooked food. For this reason, he was named Achilles: because in Greek, *A* signifies "without" and *chilos* means "cooked food" <note>original: "A. significa senza: & chilos cibo cocto." This is a medieval etymology; modern scholars usually link the name to "grief" or "lips."</note>. From Chiron, he learned astrology, music, and medicine. Later, as Thetis did not want him to be led to the Trojan War, she brought him while asleep to the island of Skyros to King Lycomedes. There, he stayed with the king's daughters in women's clothing, so that he was not recognized as a male. And yet, in that time, he fathered Pyrrhus by Deidameia, the daughter of Lycomedes. Finally, being discovered through the cunning of Ulysses, he was forced to go to Troy, where according to Homer, he showed incredible strength. The Trojans never won while Achilles was in battle. But while he was angry with Agamemnon because he had taken Briseis from him, he refused to fight; Patroclus, dressed in Achilles's armor, went against Hector and was killed by him. Then Thetis had Vulcan forge new armor for him, with which he killed Hector and avenged Patroclus. Although Dion Chrysostom <note>A Greek orator and philosopher</note> tells the opposite and proves that Hector killed him. But following Homer, Achilles killed Hector and Troilus. Later, having fallen in love with Polyxena, daughter of Priam, he went to a meeting with her mother Hecuba in the temple of Apollo Thymbraeus to obtain her hand; while kneeling to honor Apollo, he was wounded in the heel by an arrow from Paris, who was lying in wait to do this. Thus he died, which is why the poet said: WHO fought with love at the end.

**TRISTAN** was the nephew of Mark, King of Cornwall, and he fell in love with Queen Iseult, the wife of King Mark. The King found him in the bedchamber and, with Tristan's own lance—which he had left outside the door—he struck him, thrusting the lance through a hole in the door. Tristan died from this wound shortly after. He was the foremost of the knights called "errant," whose feats are more fabulous than true. On this, Francesco Petrarch said: "Behold those who fill the pages with dreams: Lancelot and Tristan and the other wanderers."

After I had heard my teacher name
the ladies and the knights of olden times,
pity overcame me, and I was as if lost.

And I began: "Poet, I would willingly
speak to those two who go together
and seem to be so light upon the wind."

And he to me: "You shall see when they are
closer to us; and then you shall entreat them
by the love that leads them, and they will come."

As soon as the wind bent them toward us,
I moved my voice: "O weary souls,
come speak to us, if another does not forbid it."

As doves, called by desire,
with wings raised and steady, to the sweet nest
come through the air, carried by their will;

So they emerged from the troop where Dido is,
coming to us through the malignant air,
so strong was the affectionate cry.

"O gracious and kind living being,
who goes visiting through the dark air
us who stained the world with blood,

If the King of the Universe were our friend,
we would pray to him for your peace,
since you have pity on our perverse evil.

Of what it pleases you to hear and speak—"

<column-break/>

This demonstrates that Dante—that is, the <term>sensuality</term> <note>Referring to the lower faculties of the soul, susceptible to emotion</note>—takes compassion on the pains of the lovers and is almost lost, because he deviates from <term>reason</term>, which does not want us to have compassion for those who are rightfully tormented. For pity and mercy are commended when we feel compassion for one who is undeservedly placed in misery; but toward one who deserves punishment, we ought to have no compassion at all.

<margin>ae. ne.</margin> Hence, he says elsewhere: "Here pity lives when it is well dead; who is more wicked than he who feels passion at God's judgment?" <note>original Latin/Italian: "Qui regna la pieta quãdo e ben morta: chi e piu scellerato di colui: chal giudicio di dio passion porta." A reference to Inferno XX, 28.</note> Nevertheless, considering the quality of the vice of lascivious love—which does not proceed, like many other sins, from cruelty or any inhumanity (which is entirely against human nature), but rather from gentleness of spirit and humanity, however poorly regulated it may be—and considering how difficult it is to resist it, since even the wisest have been caught by its hook, it is no wonder if our sensuality takes pity on it. Petrarch confirms this same thing in his first sonnet when he says: "Where there is someone who knows love through experience, I hope to find pity, not just forgiveness."

He asks Virgil for advice on whether it seems right to speak with these spirits. This allegorically signifies that before we speak or serve in a matter that might bring infamy to anyone, we should seek the counsel of reason. WHO GO TOGETHER: because those who sin together are punished together. Furthermore, they share in the same infamy. AND SEEM TO BE SO LIGHT UPON THE WIND: Lightness is shown by speed. They were faster because they were pulled more by the wind—meaning they had greater pain, which they deserved for being related <note>Francesca was the sister-in-law of Paolo</note> and of high status, because these circumstances weigh more heavily on the sin. And morally, those who are relatives and in high status are more defamed. Thus Juvenal says: *Every vice carries a deeper brand of shame in proportion to the high rank of the one who commits it.* <note>original Latin: "Omne ai uitiũ tãto cõspectius i se crimẽ habet quãto maior qui peccat habetur."</note>

He made a comparison to doves not only because they are fast in flight, but also because the dove is a bird suited to lovers. The dove is a very lustful animal and affectionate in love. For this reason, the ancients dedicated doves to Venus, just as the eagle was dedicated to Jupiter, the raven to Phoebus, the crow to Minerva, the woodpecker to Mars, the peacock to Juno, and finally others to other birds. SO THEY EMERGED FROM THE TROOP WHERE DIDO IS: That is, where Dido was, of whom we spoke above.

It might perhaps seem to someone that these spirits should not speak unless they were first asked; and also, having to speak, the man should have spoken rather than the woman. To the first, one responds that since Dante had requested they speak, it was easy to know that he wanted nothing else but to know something of their life and their habits. Furthermore, lovers take great pleasure in happiness and great consolation in adversity by relating what happened to them in love. Especially to one who shows compassion for them, as Dante had shown by those words: "O weary souls, come speak to us if another does not forbid it." And for this reason, she often narrates...

<header>INFERNO</header>

we shall hear: & speak to you
while the wind, as it does, stays silent.
The land where I was born sits
on the shore where the Po descends
to find peace with its followers.
Love, which quickly kindles in the gentle heart,
seized this man for the fair person
that was taken from me: and the manner still offends me.
Love, which pardons no loved one from loving in return,
seized me with a pleasure in him so strong,
that, as you see, it does not yet abandon me.
Love led us to one death;
Caina awaits him who quenched our life.
These words were offered to us by them.

<column-break/>

Furthermore, to those who do not ask him. In the second part, there is no doubt that the female is more perturbed in love and more complaining: and she laments that the female is less considered in speech: and more loquacious. O GRACIOUS AND BENIGN ANIMAL: He said "animal" <note>original: "animale"</note> because he saw him with both body and soul. For an animal is an animated body. GRACIOUS AND BENIGN: He said this because he understood it from his words when he said: "O weary souls, come speak to us if another does not deny it." WE STAINED the world blood-red: Because we were killed, and we shed our blood upon the earth. WE SHALL HEAR & speak to you: That is, to us. The author usually adapts some words of the homeland of whoever he induces to speak. This is why he said *uui* <note>original: "uui," a dialectal form of "voi" (you)</note> not only to make the rhyme, but because this Francesca was from Romagna. WHILE THE wind, as it does, stays silent: This seems contrary to what he said of the "infernal hurricane that never rests." But understand that it was paused for the benefit of Dante regarding these two. And allegorically he means this: that although love is in continuous motion, nevertheless, to one who considers it from outside of love in others, it has no fury, just like avarice, which is considered by one who investigates the nature of vices without any greed. Then he describes the site of Ravenna, her homeland, which is near the mouth of the Po on the sea. The Po runs with its followers: that is, the rivers that enter it until the sea: and here, like other rivers, it ceases its course. But of the Po we shall speak in a more convenient place. FRANCESCA was the daughter of Guido da Polenta, lord of Ravenna, a woman of great beauty and excellent manners; and the wife of Gianciotto <note>The text uses "Lanciotto," a variant of Giovanni "Gianciotto" Malatesta</note>, son of Malatesta, lord of Rimini, a warlike man of great spirit, but ugly of body and lame. He had a brother named Paolo, beautiful of body and of sweet manners and customs, and more suited to leisure than to arms, and almost a Paris in comparison to Hector <note>Paris was the lover who sparked the Trojan War; Hector was the great warrior</note>. And by interacting familiarly with Francesca as a sister-in-law, the long practice gave birth to lascivious love between them. And finally, reading one day the book of the Round Table <note>The Arthurian legends of Lancelot and Guinevere</note>, the captive example incited them to the captive act. And following this purpose for some time, Gianciotto noticed it and lay in wait for them; and catching them in the act, with one same blade and blow, he transfixed both of them. They say that her mother wanted to give her to Paolo, and Gianciotto went to Ravenna to marry her on his behalf; but seeing her so beautiful and being enamored, he asked for her for himself; and because he was a powerful and terrible man, she was given to him more for fear than for love. LOVE WHICH quickly kindles in the gentle heart: It is a true sentiment that the generous and elegant soul—that is, one sharp in choosing—easily loves beautiful things. For love is nothing other than the desire for beauty. We call a soul "gentle" <term>gentile: noble or refined in spirit, not necessarily of noble birth</term> when it is humane, affable, clement, benign, gracious, eager to please, and alienated from the opposite; it delights in beautiful and well-composed things. And it holds in horror all cruelty and ferocity, all of which things show that it is disposed by nature to love. Or rather, to have a universal love for all. Therefore, it will be easy to love one person in particular. Many things worthy of being understood remain for me regarding love; but because they are divine and proper to true love, they do not fit in this place where we treat of lascivious love, which so degenerates and strays from true love that it becomes its contrary. Therefore, I defer them to another time when we shall treat of that. LOVE WHICH quickly kindles in the gentle heart: Here is a rhetorical color called "Sententia," which is speech drawn from our life, through which what is done is demonstrated, or what reasonably ought to be done. And although it is placed in a particular thing, it can nonetheless be transferred to the general, as when Petrarch says: "He knows little who so much faith so quickly forgets" <note>original: "Mal sa chi tanta fe si tosto oblia"</note> and "A beautiful death honors the whole life" and "The pain is no less because others feel it first," and similar. Furthermore, in these three stanzas <note>tercetos</note> there is another rhetorical color called "repetition," which is when the same word is repeated several times at the beginning of clauses: as is here "Love which... Love which... Love... Love led us..."; likewise Petrarch in the song "If I ever said." THE MANNER Still offends me: that is, the manner of this love which was disordered: because the sin committed offends me at present with the punishment: and morally every crime committed afterwards always offends the delinquent by the remorse of conscience. And certainly the rational soul cannot be without love: but "the manner" <note>moderation or proper order</note> is necessary. It does not offend her that he loved her, but that he loved her in a disordered way. CAINA AWAITS: that is, it expects him who killed us. And Caina is a place which he will mention below where traitors and homicides are punished, named after Cain, who was the first murderer, as will be more fully treated there.

---

Since I heard those offended souls,
I bowed my face, and held it so low,
until the poet said to me: "What are you thinking?"
When I replied, I began: "O alas,
how many sweet sighs, how much desire
led these ones to the woeful pass!"
Then I turned back to them and spoke,
and I began: "Francesca, your martyrdoms
make me weep, sad and pious.
But tell me: in the time of the sweet sighs,
by what and how did love grant
that you should know your dubious desires?"

<column-break/>

AFTER the sensuality expressed by Dante moves to compassion: and the bowing of the face to the earth signifies that it has more care for the corporeal pleasures of which these souls are deprived than for true and immortal pleasure. But the superior reason excites him and makes him look up. HOW MANY sweet sighs. Certainly, corporeal pleasure is very sweet to the senses: but if followed, it has within it a hidden poison which leads us to extreme ruin. Whence the excellent Tuscan lyric <note>Petrarch</note> said: "I know how the snake lies hidden among the flowers" <note>original: "So chome sta tra fiori ascoso langue"</note>. Therefore, we must do with pleasure what the old Trojans said of Helen: "Certainly this woman is beautiful, but yet let her rather go away than that Troy should perish." Pleasure is a very sweet thing and very delightful to the senses: but let it leave rather than the soul perish: because it leads us to the "woeful pass," which is not only the essential Hell, but also the moral one, because no perturbation torments the soul more than this. THAT YOU SHOULD KNOW your dubious desires: that is, you came to the point that one manifested their desires to the other. For the lover does not dare to discover himself to the beloved while the desires are dubious—that is, unknown. But once he understands that she wants the same, then he takes heart to reveal himself.

# CANTO FIRST.
e

When the soul leaves the body pure and without any contagion from any sin, it remains simple in its own nature: it thinks of nothing other than its own happiness, which is to enjoy God; and because it is not weighed down by any earthly mass, it flies easily and with supreme desire. But that soul which departs filthy and defiled by sins, in which it placed all its happiness, desires nothing else but to practice those same sins. Wherefore the Apocalypse most excellently said: *For their works follow them* <note>original: "Opera enim illǫ sequuntur illos"</note>. And Virgil: *What pleasure in chariots and arms they had when living, what care to pasture their sleek horses, the same follows them when they are laid in the earth* <note>original: "Quę gratia currũ Armorumq; fuit uiuis quę cura nitentes Pascere equos eadem sequitur tellure repostos"</note>; and to think of past pleasures in a time when they can no longer practice them is their great passion and no small tormen-

-t. This, therefore, he demonstrates as a general maxim, saying: that no sorrow is greater than to remember the happy time in misery. And he adds: AND THIS your teacher knows. Because Virgil, in the sixth book, signifies this same sentiment in the verses already mentioned. Others say: THIS YOUR teacher knows, because he is currently damned in Limbo and deprived of the glory which he once held near Octavian <note>The Emperor Augustus</note>. But the first interpretation fits better. Then he continues: for even though it is painful to remember the happy time in misery, nonetheless it is no small consolation to relate it to one who shows compassion for it. These first stanzas serve as a preface to her speech. In the first, she captures attention through the gravity of the rhetorical device called "sententia" <note>A pithy moral saying or maxim</note>, and also gains goodwill through commiseration. In the second, she makes him attentive. Then in the third, the narration begins, which she makes brief—because she puts nothing superfluous in it—and lucid and open—because she observes the order and uses clear words. It is also plausible, because she shows all the means were present that could lead to such an end. First, the reading of amorous things and a similar case, which could even make those love who were not in love. And everyone understands that an example easily moves one to do the same, especially when there is the authority of esteemed persons, such as Lancelot and Guinevere. Next, because they were alone. And finally, without suspicion. These conveniences could make one sin who had not previously been inclined to it; for as the proverb says: *At an open chest, even a just man sins* <note>original: "A archa aperta giusto ui pecca"</note>. Let this be a demonstration of the art. But morally, it shows that idleness, lewd readings, the example of those who have done what we wish to do—especially if they are men of authority—and finally the convenience of place and time easily induce men to lewd and forbidden love. WE WERE READING one day for delight. To read for delight signifies being in idleness <note>original: "otio" - leisure or idleness, often seen as the root of vice in medieval thought</note>. For he who is occupied does not seek amusement, but seeks to expedite his affairs. Therefore, they were in idleness. And idleness, together with lewd amusement, generates carnal love. Whence Petrarch says: *It is born of idleness and human lewdness*; and Ovid: *If you take away idleness, Cupid's bows perish* <note>original: "Otia si tollas periere cupidinis arcus"</note>; and Te-

---

-rence's Menedemus shows to his son that idleness is what makes men fall into lewdness, just as, conversely, fatigue and occupations preserve chastity. Divine Juvenal says: *Their humble fortune used to keep the Latin women chaste, nor did it allow their small homes to be touched by vice: labor, short sleep, hands worn and hardened by the Tuscan fleece, and Hannibal close to the city* <note>original: "Preftabat castas humilis fortuna latinas..." from Satire VI</note>. OF LANCELOT how love constrained him. In Dante's time, a book called *The Round Table* was held in high esteem, in which it is written that Lancelot was in love with Guinevere, the wife of King Arthur <note>The text says "King Marco," a likely slip or variation referring to the Prose Lancelot or Tristan legends</note>. And Galeotto <note>Galahaut</note> was the intermediary so they could come together. Therefore, this book and he who wrote it was a Galeotto—that is, he was an intermediary for us, as Galeotto was for Lancelot and Guinevere. The book was thus an intermediary for us because under the guise of reading the book, we could treat of other things; and he who wrote it was also an intermediary because his lewd verses moved us to love. SEVERAL TIMES that reading drove our eyes together and drained the color from our faces. That reading pushed our eyes together because, while reading the deeds of others which we ourselves desired, we looked at one another before we dared to begin. AND DRAINED the color from our faces: that is, it made us pale, which color is proper to lovers. Whence Ovid: *Let every lover be pale; this is the color suited to a lover* <note>original: "Palleat ois amãs color est hic aptus amanti"</note>. It drained the color from our faces because of the sudden and great labor the soul was feeling. BUT JUST one point was it that overcame us. For when we reached that passage in our reading where it was pleasing to Guinevere to be kissed, both he and I agreed to do the same. And he follows: THESE: that is, this same sin. KISSED MY mouth all trembling. He expresses by this trembling the great commotion which is in the lover. GALEOTTO was the book: that is, the book was the intermediary as has already been said. THAT DAY we read no further in it: As if to say, we were occupied with other things; and with very modest words, she hints at that which cannot be said openly without blushing, like Terence: *What then? What then, you fool?* <note>original: "Quid tum? Quid tum fatue."</note>. WHILE THE one spirit: that is, Francesca. the other: that is, Paolo. WEPT: to show that he was in no less pain. SO THAT OUT OF PITY, and so forth. Here, through his compassion, he demonstrates that same thing which we said above regarding sensuality.

### CANTO SIX OF THE FIRST CANTICLE BY DANTE.

Upon the return of the mind, which closed
before the pity of those two kinsfolk <note>referring to Francesca and Paolo from the previous canto</note>,
which had utterly confused me with sadness,
New torments and new tormented ones
I see around me, however I move,
and however I turn, and however I gaze.
I am in the third circle of the rain,
eternal, cursed, cold, and heavy;
its rule and quality are never new.
Large hail, dark-tinted water, and snow
pour down through the gloomy air;
the earth stinks that receives this.

Cerberus, a cruel and strange beast,
barks like a dog with three throats
over the people who are submerged here.
His eyes are red, his beard greasy and black,
his belly wide, and his hands clawed;
he scratches the spirits, flays, and quarters them.
The rain makes them howl like dogs;
they use one side to shield the other,
the wretched heathens often turn themselves over.

<column-break/>

After the sin of lust, he appropriately places that which the Greeks call *gastrimargia* <term>gastrimargia: from the Greek, meaning "stomach-madness" or excessive gluttony</term>, and by the Latins is called gluttony. To better define this sin and the one discussed above: nature, wishing for animals to last for their prescribed time and for the species to be immortal through succession, first placed pleasure in eating and drinking. It is impossible for a living body composed of these four qualities—hot, dry, moist, and cold—to survive if the heat constantly consumes the moist and dry parts; the animal would perish in a very short time if matter were not gradually supplied to replace that which has perished. Therefore, when the "dry" is diminished in an animal, a desire and appetite called hunger is born, through which we crave food; once cooked and digested, it converts into the substance of the body and restores the missing parts. And when the "moist" is diminished, thirst is born, which craves drink to supply the consumed moisture. Since eating and drinking are necessary, nature placed pleasure in food and drink, so that the animal, moved by such pleasure, might be more prone to maintain its life.

Therefore, he who takes food and drink for such refreshment and restoration at proper intervals of time, and in such quantity that it is not too much, and in such quality that it is not harmful, and has respect only for necessity, does not sin—even though such food or drink gives him pleasure. But he who has no respect for necessity, but seeks only pleasure, and to achieve it either exceeds moderation or is more occupied than required in seeking sweet and exquisite flavors, this man sins and is called a glutton. Similarly, the species would not last, because every animal meets death if, while alive, they do not generate someone to succeed them. Nature, fearing that negligence or the labor of nourishing and raising children might hinder such generation, placed pleasure in intercourse. Therefore, he who uses this not to seek pleasure but to generate children, and uses it how, when, and with whom is appropriate, does not sin; he who does otherwise, sins.

The gluttons are therefore punished in this third circle. The poet shows that, upon returning to himself, he found himself among them. Regarding the essential Hell <note>the physical punishments of the underworld</note>, he sets an appropriate penalty, because every sin should be punished by its opposite. Therefore, where pleasure had been found in the finest wines, the sweetest foods, and exquisite dishes, the penalty is cold and heavy rain, and "tinted" <note>dark or foul</note> water in place of wines, and in place of foods, there is hail and snow.

As for the moral meaning, everyone understands that excess food and drunkenness cause various humors and catarrhs <note>excessive fluids or mucus, thought in medieval medicine to cause disease</note> to descend from the head, which induce apoplexy, tremors, coldness of the nerves, and stupor of the soul. This is denoted by the "gloomy air," because they induce darkness and oblivion in the soul; these humors, having fallen into the stomach, rot there not without a "fomenter" <note>something that aggravates or heats the condition</note>. All this generates pain in the head, stomach, sides, and gout, which make men howl like dogs. It is a true sentiment and a common proverb: that the gullet kills many more than the sword. It is a "rule and quality" because similar effects always arise. Therefore, "it is never new," that is, it is not unusual, because that rule and quality are always the same.

**Cerberus the beast.** The Greek poet Hesiod writes that Cerberus was the dog of Pluto with three heads, son of Typhon the giant and Echidna the serpent. He also wishes that from the same parents were born Orthrus, the dog of Geryon, and the Chimera, which had three heads: one of a lion, one of a dragon, and one of a goat. We demonstrated in the allegories of Virgil that Cerberus is placed to represent the necessity of the body, which is food and sleep, without which an animal cannot live. Therefore, Dante has most excellently placed him in this location, because gluttony consists of food and drink when we exceed in them as has been said.

**Cerberus, a cruel and strange beast.** This serves the fiction; he is "cruel" because of the pain he inflicts. "Strange" <note>original: *diversa*</note> from other beasts, or "strange/diverse" because he has diverse mouths. "Cruel" because gluttony consumes everything. Whence Juvenal <note>Roman satirist</note> says: "For what is the end for you, as your purse fails and your gullet grows? ...your father’s bronze and his possessions being swallowed into a belly that devours interest, heavy silver, flocks, and fields." <note>original Latin: *Quis enim te deficiente crumena et crescente gula manet exitus? ... paterno Atque rebus mersis in ventrem fenoris atque argenti gravis et pecorum agrorumque capacem.*</note> "Strange/Diverse," because he is not content with a simple food but seeks a variety of them from the earth, the sea, and the air.

**Barks.** To "latrate" <note>original: *latrare*</note> in the Latin tongue means to bark.

**His eyes are red.** As for the fiction, he gives him red eyes to show the beast's anger, because every angry person has red eyes. As for the allegory, it shows that such an effect is produced by superfluous food, and especially wine.

**His beard greasy.** This is characteristic of gluttons. By the "greasy beard," he signifies the greed of those who stuff themselves too much while devouring, because not only the mouth but the whole face becomes oily.

**The belly wide.** To demonstrate the engorging of food. Whence the Prophet says: "Whose god is their belly." <note>original Latin: *Quorum deus venter est.* (Philippians 3:19)</note>

**His hands clawed.** This denotes rapacity and greed for food, because he snatches what he devours.

**Scratches, flays, and quarters.** He places before the eyes the voracity of gluttons, and on the other hand, shows the torments men suffer for the vice of the throat, through which they fall into various diseases where it is necessary to cut, to apply fire, and in many ways tear the body. And he adds that they "howl," to demonstrate various pains. Whence it happens that stomachs, sides, gout, and fevers give great pain. But they have a proverb: "One morsel and two woes."

**They use one side to shield the other.** That is, defense. It shows that from the throat is born the illness which induces turning now on this side and now on that.

**Wretched heathens.** "Profane" <note>original: *profani*</note> in the Latin tongue means "far from the temple" <note>original Latin: *procul a fano*</note>, that is, far from the temple and from religious things. Whence they call "profane" those who are wicked and contrary to all religion.

<header>INFERNO</header>

When Cerberus, the great worm, noticed us,
he opened his mouths and showed us his fangs;
he had no limb that he kept still;
My leader <note>Virgil</note> stretched out his palms,
took the earth, and with full fists
threw it into the ravenous gullets.
As a dog that, barking, yearns for food,
and grows quiet once he bites his meal,
for he only strives and fights to devour it,
So did those filthy faces
of the demon Cerberus, who thunders
at the souls so that they would wish to be deaf.

He took as much earth as he could in abundance. Because he stretched his palms over the ground and then gathered them, clenching the earth in his fists: where he denotes by "vile foods" <note>the earth represents the low quality of food sought by gluttons</note> and by "both fists" the abundance of those foods, because the body must be fed abundantly, but with low-quality foods. And certainly, nature—if not depraved by habit—is content with little. Whence Lucan says: "Learn by how little life may be sustained, and how much nature requires" <note>original: "Discite quam paruo liceat producere uitam: Et quantum natura petat"</note>. And elsewhere: "River and grain are enough for the people" <note>original: "Satis est populis fluviuſque cereſque"</note>. THREW IT into the ravenous gullets. And this denotes that food should not be offered to the body except when it is famished. And not without reason did he throw it not into the mouth—where the sweetness of food is tasted by the palate—but into the pipes of the throat. Once the food and drink have reached that place, they no longer provide any sweetness. This denotes that he who eats out of necessity, and not out of gluttony, is not occupied in tasting and savoring, but it is enough for him that the stomach receives the necessary food. AS IS THE dog. He compares Cerberus to a dog who, barking from hunger, grows quiet once he has taken food. And certainly our appetite, when the body has received what it needs, is easily quieted, and in a temperate man, it asks for no more. WHO THUNDERS: the word *intronare* comes from *tronitruo*, that is, from thunder. Every time a voice is so loud that, besides being heard, it also offends the sense of hearing like a thunderclap. Because our senses have a certain proportion to sensible things, and if they exceed such proportion, the sense fails and cannot perform its office. Therefore, a voice that is too small is not heard, and if it is too loud, it corrupts the sense. Thus they say that those who live where the Nile falls <note>referring to the Great Cataracts of the Nile</note> become deaf from the immeasurable noise of that river. These souls, then, have this punishment besides the others: that Cerberus continually thunders at them. And in life it also happens that gluttons are "thundered at" and excited by this vice; and the more they fill themselves, the more they crave. And allegorically you will understand that whoever wishes to go toward contemplation, as Dante does, is "thundered at" by Cerberus—that is, he is terrified by the thought of necessary physical things—unless he quiets that appetite as we have described.

We passed over the shadows that the heavy
rain subdues, and placed our soles
upon their emptiness, which appears as a person.
They all lay on the ground,
except for one who sat up quickly
when he saw us pass before him.
"O you who are led through this Hell,"
he said to me, "recognize me if you can;
you were made before I was unmade."
And I to him: "The anguish you have
perhaps pulls you out of my mind,
so it does not seem I ever saw you.
But tell me who you are, placed in such a mournful
spot and having such a punishment,
that if any is greater, none is more displeasing."

...in the belly, and became much more like a sheep than a man. Whence Virgil and Dante—that is, reason and the appetite obedient to reason—tread upon such vile men who, by their outward form, seem like men. But they are not, because they retain nothing of man except the physical image and effigy. And reason and virtue, which alone make us men, are not in them. Thus in their habits they are beasts, because they are obedient to the belly. Which, as Sallust says, is the property of beasts. And certainly one can be called "vain" and "utterly empty" if nothing remains to him but that which is common to the brute animals. Then the words of Ciacco <note>a Florentine character known for gluttony</note> serve the history, because in truth he died during the time Dante was alive, and they had known each other in life. Therefore, "you were made"—that is, created and born—before I was "unmade"—that is, dead. And it is reasonable regarding the essential Hell that such martyrdom clothes the sinner in forms and appearances so changed that it is not easy to recognize him; and regarding the moral sense, Dante—that is, reason...

<column-break/>

The necessity of the body presents no small impediment to the man who directs himself toward the contemplative life and the investigation of divine things. For without sustenance and without food, life cannot be maintained. And then it happens that, within this natural necessity, depraved and corrupt habit craves many more delicacies and varieties of food than nature requires, which is content with little. Whence Cicero: "Nature is content with few and very small things" <note>original: "Paucis minimiſque natura contenta eſt"</note>. Therefore, it is a great impediment to the man who wants to pursue contemplation to have to think about the things needed for sustenance, as that is necessary for life. But the wise man realizes that such necessity can be satisfied with things of little cost. Returning then to the text: he calls Cerberus a "great worm" because a worm is born of putrefaction and feeds on the earth; and by Cerberus is understood the appetite, which we have already said is for earthly things. HE OPENED his mouths: which are three, as we have shown, and he demonstrates hunger; and by depicting him in the form of a dog, he does not depart from the canine nature, which moves all its limbs when it craves food or is angry. MY LEADER: That is, the rational part, to quiet the natural appetite...

The journey continues after he has finished. And although he has to deal with souls—which, because they are incorporeal, cannot be perceived by sight, hearing, touch, or any other bodily sense—it is nevertheless necessary to depict them in a way that they can be seen and heard. This is easily granted to the poet. And many also maintain that they can take on an aerial body which, although it yields to touch—like a cloud, for example—can still be seen and can form a voice that is heard. Whence he says they were treading on shadows, which regarding touch were a "vain" or empty thing. But regarding sight, they appeared as people. Virgil depicts this same thing when he says: "Three times I tried there to put my arms around his neck; three times the image, grasped in vain, escaped my hands" <note>original: "Ter conatus ibi collo dare bracchia circū Ter fruſtra conprenſa manus effugit imago"</note>. PERSONS: that is, men, as we say in our language, although in Latin it has a different meaning. WHICH SUBDUES <note>original: "adona"</note>: which gathers and congregates. And he depicts this because a great rain commonly makes many people gather together, because they can better defend themselves one by another. He places the gluttons lying on the ground because no vice makes a man more vile or more inclined toward earthly things. The lustful man loves another person, even if he loves the viler part of them. The envious man is moved by greater things. The greedy man seeks riches, which are instruments for many things. All sin and have their minds occupied by vile things. But the object of the glutton is the vilest of all, because his supreme good is...

It also introduces the gluttonous souls who lie in the mud, specifically the character Ciacco, and discusses the philosophical distinction between human reason and animalistic indulgence.</summary>

inferior: and the appetite was obeyed before Ciacco died: <note>The commentator argues that gluttony is a sin of youth/appetite that should be overcome by reason as one matures.</note> that is, before the sin of gluttony perished. But in the process of time, Ciacco dies and Dante remains alive. Because in a man’s first youth, in which appetite has more power than reason, this sin lives. But after reason is strengthened and the appetite remains subject to it, the vice of gluttony decays in the man and the man remains alive and it passes so much into oblivion that he does not recognize it unless, in his journey, it meets him: that is, if in contemplating vices it does not occur to the mind. And certainly this sin draws the human soul so far out of its nature that it no longer has the likeness of a rational thing, but seems entirely a sheep. **FROM ONE** who rose up quickly to sit. Because it suddenly came to Dante's mind as he was speculating on this vice: and he did not rise except to sit: because although a vile thing occurs to our imagination, it does not rise up much. He chose Ciacco rather than another noble and rich man: because the vice of gluttony is more condemned in the poor and commoner than in the rich and powerful. Hence Juvenal says: "If Atticus dines excellently, he is considered refined; if Rutilus does so, he is considered insane." <note>original: "atticus eximie si cenat lautus habetur Si rutilus demens." Juvenal argues that the same behavior is judged differently based on one's social status; a poor man (Rutilus) spending on luxury is seen as mad.</note> **THAT IF ANOTHER IS** Greater, none is so displeasing. There is no doubt that pride and avarice are greater vices and consequently deserve greater punishment. Nevertheless, this one is more displeasing: because in those others there is some excuse and some part of a manly soul. But the glutton lies in the mud like a pig, and the soul in that body does nothing worthy of a man. And it can be said that to such men the soul is given in place of salt: <note>A common medieval trope suggesting the soul in a glutton serves only to keep the meat of the body from rotting, like salt preserves meat.</note> because it does nothing else except maintain the body so that it does not putrefy and corrupt.

> And he to me: your city which is full
> of envy so that already the sack overflows
> held me with it in the serene life:
> You citizens called me Ciacco:
> for the damaging fault of gluttony
> as you see: I am broken by the rain.

He induces Ciacco to revile envy, which in those times reigned in our republic. Because he tacitly wanted to report that his exile did not proceed from his own failings, but from the envy of his adversaries. **THAT ALREADY** The sack overflows. In the serene life. He imitates Virgil, who induces those who are in hell to always praise life, as here: "Those who, deprived of sweet life and snatched from the breast, the dark day took away and plunged into bitter death." <note>original: "Quos dulcis uite exortes & ab ubere raptos Abstulit atra dies funerique immerſit acerbo" from Aeneid VI.428-429.</note> And certainly, just as human life in comparison to celestial spirits can be called miserable, so comparing it to hellish places it will be reputed happy. Or truly he said **IN THE** serene life because in his times the state in Florence was quite tranquil, which at present was most disturbed. **YOU CALLED ME** Ciacco. Ciacco in the Florentine language signifies "hog": <note>A derogatory nickname for a pig.</note> and because this animal is born only to fatten and fill its belly, it happened that this man was so named by his citizens. They say he was a man quite eloquent and full of urbanity, jokes, and witticisms, and of the sweetest conversation, and not unwise, and in other things worthy of being loved. But he was such a slave to gluttony that in a short time, having consumed his substance, like an actor or parasite, he frequented the houses of the powerful: and with his witticisms and jokes, he "hunted for good morsels." <note><term>uccellaua a buon bocconi</term>: literally "hawked for good mouthfuls," meaning he used his wit to get invited to fine dinners.</note> Giovanni Boccaccio makes mention of him on the ninth day and in the novella of Lauretta: and shows how deftly and with ingenuity he took revenge on Biondello. <note>Refers to Decameron IX.8, where Ciacco tricks a man named Biondello into a social embarrassment.</note> **AND I, A WRETCHED SOUL** am not alone. Every glutton is commonly ashamed of such a vice. But he excuses himself by alleging he has many companions in it.

> I began: Ciacco, your distress
> weighs on me so that it invites me to weep:
> but tell me if you know what they will come to,
> the citizens of the divided city,
> if any there is just: and tell me the reason
> why such discord has assailed it:
> And he to me: after long contention
> they will come to blood: and the woodland party
> will chase the other out with much offense.
> Then afterwards it is necessary that this one falls
> within three suns: and that the other rises
> with the force of one who currently tacks.
> It will hold its forehead high for a long time,
> keeping the other under heavy weights,
> however much it may weep or be ashamed:
> Two are just, and they are not heard there;
> pride and envy and avarice are
> the three sparks that have set hearts ablaze.

To many, it seems an absurd thing that the poet induces a man of such low status to speak of great things and gives him the divination of future things. But whoever considers the genius of this man will see that, as Boccaccio also shows, he was a man of no small prudence, which at first was natural in him. Later it increased greatly through long practice and through assiduous habit and familiarity that he had with all the citizens of Florence, both of one party and the other, such that he knew the ambition, the desire, and the passions of each, by which with the sharpness of his mind he could easily conjecture the future. Dante therefore asks him not as a parasite and glutton, but as one who is shrewd and learned in customs through long experience: and of the wills and the honors and the wits of the governors of the republic, which things were causes that could easily produce the effects that he predicts. **I BEGAN** Ciacco, your distress. An excellent beginning to the speech by which Ciacco is made benevolent, showing him compassion for his pain. And this inclines him to answer willingly. Then he briefly poses his question, which contains three parts: First, that he tell him the future. Second, who in Florence is just. Third, the cause of the civil discord. **DIVIDED CITY** Citizenship divided into Whites and Blacks. <note>The warring factions of the Guelph party in Florence.</note> Nor does it please me that in this place he understands "divided" as those who were of the Romans and of the Fiesolans: because the first meaning is more to the point. **IF YOU KNOW.** Because he doubts if the damned have knowledge of the future. But of this he will speak more fully in the tenth canto. **AND HE TO ME.** Ciacco responds in order, and first to the first part. For the declaration of these words, it is to be noted that the Florentine republic, being in the year 1300

above a thousand in the highest reputation and opulence, and in serene tranquility: as has happened to many other cities, it occurred that too much prosperity gave birth to the gravest discord. The nearest seed of which, like many others, came from Pistoia. Because the Cancellieri family, then most powerful in that city, was divided by internal discord into two parts: one called the Blacks, the other the Whites: and having occupied all that city and the places near it, it penetrated as far as Florence. In those times, the Donati and the Cerchi were families and quite close neighbors, and of almost equal power. The Cerchi were powerful in riches; although they were new in the city because shortly before they had come from Acone, a place in Val di Sieve, they became arrogant and won great favor from the common people. The Donati, as much as they were surpassed in riches, so much they excelled in antiquity of blood: and were much esteemed for the virtue of Messer Corso, head of that house, and whose name was celebrated throughout all Italy. But they were almost suspected by the common people, as if they were directing their minds [to tyranny]...

<meta>This page transitions from the general discussion of the vice of gluttony to a detailed historical and political commentary on the civil strife in Florence between the White and Black factions. It continues the explanation of Ciacco’s prophecy regarding the city's future and the exile of the "White" party, including Dante himself.</meta>

# INFERNO

...to a life more tyrannical than civil. This meant that the Cerchi, being more popular, were better loved by the people. Therefore, the leader of the **Whites** was Messer Vieri de' Cerchi, and the leader of the **Blacks** was Messer Corso Donati. And as a grave calamity prepared to befall the city because of this division, Pope Boniface VIII attempted to persuade Messer Vieri to reconcile with Messer Corso. But Vieri—whether because the adverse fates of our Republic so willed it, or because agitation had more power over the knight than reason—did not comply. Instead, he said he did not wish to make peace because he was not at war. Not long after, as contentions arose between some members of one side and the other, at a dance, the nose of Ricoverino de' Cerchi was cut off. Then, seeing himself in grave danger, Messer Corso attempted to have Pope Boniface send someone from the House of France to Florence who would take the government of the Republic away from the Cerchi and the popular men. This incited such indignation that Corso, with many of his supporters, was sent into exile. But fortune did not strip Corso of his prudence; instead, always helping himself boldly together with Geri degli Spini, they persuaded Boniface to call into Italy **Charles Lackland**, <note>Charles of Valois, known as "Sans Terre" or "Lackland" because he was a king's son with no kingdom of his own.</note> brother of Philip the Fair, King of France—the same man who not long after would cause Boniface to die. And he let Charles Lackland pass. This man came under the guise of settling the civil discords and then proceeding against the Sicilians in aid of Charles II. Having thus given a kind response to the Florentine ambassadors, and showing that he came to pacify that republic, he was most honorably received into the city. Having sworn an oath that he would preserve its tranquility, he was granted supreme authority to settle every controversy. But being greedy and already corrupted by the money of Messer Musatto the Frenchman, a Florentine knight <note>Musatto was a wealthy Florentine merchant and financier active in France.</note> who had brought him to Italy at his own expense, and valuing them more than his word, he abandoned the common cause. Wholly turned toward favoring Messer Corso, he brought him back into the city with many of his friends. Thus the Whites were oppressed with great calamity. And although Cardinal Matteo d'Acquasparta came to Florence and reconciled both parties together, nonetheless the Blacks, who were more powerful, would not suffer the Whites to have any portion in the government of the city. The Cardinal departed in anger, and therefore such peace lasted little. Because Simone, son of Messer Corso, killed Messer Niccolò de' Cerchi, although he had first been wounded by him. And finally, some excellent men of the White party, being summoned to judgment and fearing to appear, fled, some to Pisa and some to Arezzo, where they joined the Ghibelline Florentines who were then rebels. In this number was our poet, as we showed in his biography. And Charles confiscated their goods. I have discussed these few things out of many, not to narrate a history, but to open the meaning of the text. Therefore he says: **AFTER LONG STRUGGLE**, that is, long contention. **THEY WILL COME TO BLOOD**, that is, to killing, as I have said. **AND THE WILD PARTY**, that is, the White party, of which the Cerchi were the leaders—men new to the city who had come a short time before from Acone and from the woods of Val di Sieve. Hence in the sixteenth canto of *Paradiso* he says: "The Cerchi would be in the parish of Acone." <note>original: "Sarieno ecerchi nel piuier dacone."</note> **THAT**, this group, that is, the Whites. **WITHIN THREE SUNS**, within three solar years. And although others say "Three suns, that is, three days," <note>original: "Tres soles .i. tres dies."</note> nonetheless the poet said "three suns" for three solar years. For the ancients posited three species of years. The **Lunar**, which is from one conjunction of the moon with the sun until the next; this space is some hours less than thirty days, because it stays in each sign two days, six hours, and two-thirds of an hour, returning in twenty-seven days and eight hours to where it started. But because the sun has moved more than seventeen degrees of a sign in that time, it consumes the rest until it reaches it again and joins with it. The second year is the **Solar**, that is, when the sun has made its revolution through all twelve signs of the zodiac, which is three hundred sixty-five days, six hours, and the hundredth part of an hour. And it is this the poet intends; and commonly when "year" is said, this is understood, because the solar course creates all the seasons. The third year is called by astrologers the **Great Year**, which is when, all courses being finished, the sun with all the other planets recommence their courses from the same sign. Though opinions vary on this span of time, they commonly say it is thirty-six thousand years. **WITH THE FORCE OF SUCH A ONE** who coasts. To "coast" <term>piaggiare</term> is to stay in the middle, as we say of one who goes along the shore [piaggia], almost between sea and land. Or rather, he has not yet given his sails to the wind but stays on the shore and has not moved. He intends this for Charles Lackland, as we have said. **HIGH LAND**, the forehead; he will live in a great state. **FOR A LONG TIME**, specifically until the violent death of Messer Corso, which will be told in the twenty-fourth canto of *Purgatorio*. **DO NOT BE ASHAMED**, that is, do not have shame or spite. **TWO ARE JUST**. Brother Guido del Carmine said in the commentary he made on twenty-seven chapters of this book that these two were Dante and Messer Guido Cavalcanti. Some understand that the "two just" are Divine and Human law, and these are not "heeded" there, as if to say that divine and human laws are well-ordered in Florence but are not understood because they are not observed. **AND THEY ARE NOT HEEDED THERE**, because no faith is given to their counsel. **PRIDE, ENVY, AND AVARICE**. It did not seem likely that without very great causes a most flourishing state like that of our Republic in those times—strengthened by the immense riches that were in the city, both public and private, and by no small reputation and authority which it held throughout Italy—should fall into such calamity. Therefore he posits the causes that must be present, from which supreme discord then proceeds; as Sallust writes: "Through harmony small things grow; through discord even the greatest things fall apart." <note>original: "Concordia parue res crescunt Discordia etiam maximę dilabuntur." A famous maxim from Sallust's *Jugurthine War*.</note> He says the causes of the future discord are three vices: Pride, Envy, and Avarice. **NOR** is there any vice that more excites discord among people than these three. Discord is born when equality is removed, which happens when citizens wish to overreach. This is born either from wanting more honor than is their due—which is **Pride** and ambition; or from wanting to become unjustly rich and selling magistrates and judgments, and for this they snatch from the public and the private—which is nothing other than **Avarice**; or from grieving at another's good which does not harm them—whence **Envy** is born. Therefore one concludes that whenever citizens in their republic do not crave more honor, convenience, or utility than honesty allows, and will not have envy for those who are deservedly honored, they will always live in supreme concord. Nor can any external power harm a united city. But of pride, avarice, and envy we will speak in their proper places. **THESE ARE** the three sparks. For just as the spark is the seed of every great fire, so these vices are the seed of discord. **HEARTS ENKINDLED**, because every craving is a burning of the soul.

> Here he put an end to the tearful sound;
> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;and I to him: "I still want you to teach me,
> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;and make me a gift of more speaking.
> Farinata and Tegghiaio, who were so worthy,
> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Jacopo Rusticucci, Arrigo, and Mosca,
> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;and the others who set their minds to doing good..."

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Ornamental drop cap 'D' depicting a figure or floral motifs</image-desc>
**H**e had already put an end to his sound, that is, to his sermon. **TEARFUL**, that is, worthy of tears and compassion, announcing such calamities to the fatherland. But Dante, having understood the general state of the Republic, desired to understand particularly about those citizens who had been of great spirit and prudence in civil government. But as happens to the majority in the lives of mortals, where great virtues were accompanied by great vices, so in these men the clear light was obscured by dark shadows, which made the poet hesitant...

->VI<-
# CANTO VI

“Tell me where they are and let me know them,
for a great desire constrains me to know
if heaven sweetens them or hell poisons them.”
And he: “They are among the blackest souls;
different crimes weigh them down to the bottom;
if you descend so far, you will see them.
But when you have returned to the world,
I pray you bring me to the minds of others;
I say no more to you and answer no more.”
He then twisted his straight eyes into a squint;
he looked at me a little and then bowed his head,
falling with it alongside the other blind ones.

<column-break/>

which might have had more power: their virtue in elevating them to heaven or their vice in depressing them to hell. Morally, one might doubt—having examined every work of their lives—which was greater: the merit or the demerit, the praise or the blame. For example, if we wished to judge **Caesar**, we would examine in him, on one hand, supreme clemency, supreme liberality, no mediocre learning, admirable eloquence, an unconquered spirit, and most excellent military discipline. On the other hand, the ambition through which he did violence to his fatherland and constrained it to bear the yoke. In such an examination, we would remain doubtful as to which is greater in this man: the virtue or the vice; the praise or the blame. And this seems to me the true meaning of the text. I do not approve of the opinion of those who claim the poet speaks ironically, intending that in them were supreme vices without any virtue. This can be confirmed not only by the words of the present verses, but also by what he will say below. For he will make mention of **Messer Farinata degli Uberti** in the tenth chapter <note>Inferno, Canto X</note>; and of **Messer Tegghiaio Aldobrandi** and **Messer Iacopo Rusticucci** in the sixteenth. **ARRIGO** was a noble knight of the ancient and honored Fifanti family. Of **Mosca dei Lamberti**, he will make mention

<column-break/>

in the twenty-eighth chapter. And then we shall narrate more extensively of their lives and characters. **WHO WERE SO WORTHY**: As if he almost grieves that, having been so celebrated for their great virtues, nevertheless the vices they had on the other hand caused doubt. **THAT WELL-DOING MIGHT TURN THEIR WITS**: As if to say that they turned the sharpness of their natural intellect to laudable works. He shows a desire to know their end because, naturally, every good person desires that men adorned with virtue should reach a happy port, even if they recognize vices in them. **IF HEAVEN SWEETENS THEM**: Because beatitude gives sweetness and delight, and Hell contains in itself supreme misery which is such a poison to the soul that, although it is immortal, one may say it kills like a toxin by depriving it of the sight of God, who is life. We say **Toșco** in Florentine <note>original: "Toſco"</note> from what the Latins call *toxicum*, and they take it for every poison; but *toxicum* properly is that which is made from the yew tree, which we call **nasso**. Ciacco responds that these are below among the "blackest souls," that is, damned in a darker place; and it is an imitation of **Virgil**, who, wishing to say that Daphnis was a celestial soul, said: *Candidus insuetum miratur limen olympi* <note>Latin: "Bright [Daphnis] marvels at the unfamiliar threshold of Olympus."</note>. If, therefore, those of heaven are white, those of hell are black. Furthermore, "white" is used for pure and immaculate, and "black" for the opposite. Hence **Juvenal**: *Qui nigra in candida vertunt* <note>Latin: "Those who turn black into white."</note>; and **Horace**: *Hic niger est hunc tu romane caveto* <note>Latin: "This man is black; you, O Roman, beware of him."</note>. **TO THE SWEET WORLD**: that is, to the place where men dwell, which he calls "sweet" because in it he could fulfill his carnal desires, which a soul polluted by vice pulls along with it. Or perhaps he says "sweet" in comparison to hell, where whoever is there would willingly return to the labors he endured in life. Hence Virgil: *Quam vellent et here in alto nunc et pauperiem et duros perferre labores* <note>Latin: "How they would wish now to endure both poverty and hard labors in the upper air."</note>. **And I pray you**: that you keep him in memory, to show that even those who are in the lowest state and damned for abominable vices desire fame. Furthermore, Ciacco was in a place where he could ask for nothing else. **STRAIGHT EYES INTO A SQUINT**: "Squint" (*bieco*) by corruption derives from "oblique," which means something placed crosswise. His looking in this manner demonstrates nothing else but that with pain he thought at the same time of both past pleasures and present pains; and then, moved by despair, he threw himself down to lie.

<column-break/>

The leader said to me: “He wakes no more
on this side of the sound of the angelic trumpet,
when the enemy power shall come.
For each shall see again his dismal tomb,
shall take back his flesh and his form,
and shall hear that which echoes in eternity.”
Thus we passed through the filthy mixture
of the shades and the rain with slow steps,
touching a little upon the future life.
I said to him: “Master, these torments,
will they increase after the great sentence,
or be lesser, or will they be just as burning?”

<column-break/>

He wishes to show that the damned souls must stay in that same state in which they are placed until the Last Judgment, unless by divine will it is disposed otherwise. **HE WAKES NO MORE**: As if to say he will not rise again. **ON THIS SIDE of the sound of the angelic trumpet**: that is, before the Judgment, to which all souls shall be summoned by the angelic trumpet. **THEIR ENEMY POWER**: The Son of God, who has supreme power and is an enemy to sinners; and at that time, because they must take back their bodies, they will go to the **tomb** (*tomba*), that is, the burial place, so called from the Greek name. For the Greeks call the burial place *Tymbe*, and the Latin changes *y* into *u* to make *tumba*, and the Tuscan changes *u* into *o* to make *tomba*. **DISMAL**: mournful, because they will not take back their bodies without supreme sadness, as the bodies must be tormented together with the soul. **HIS FLESH**: that is, his own flesh, and that which they had before death. But because this point matters much to our salvation, it does not seem right to me to omit it. But
I shall speak of it with that brevity required of one who has infinitely many other things to narrate. Therefore, the resurrection of bodies is not only affirmed by Christian theology, but also that generation of philosophers in Persia who are named **Magi**, according to **Laertius**, hold that men must be resurrected and be immortal. Furthermore, as **Saint Augustine** shows in his twenty-second book of *The City of God*, **Plato** said certain things and **Porphyry** others; which, if they could have communicated them together, they could have been Christians. Plato writes that the souls, even of the wise, cannot be eternal without a body. And for this reason, he estimates that after a long time they return to the body. Porphyry wrote that souls having left the body most pure and returned to their origin will never return to the evils of the world. Therefore, if both had said both things, they would not disagree from the Christian, because they would say that souls must be blessed with bodies. And Porphyry would say with Plato: "souls will return to bodies." And Plato with Porphyry: "souls will not return to the evils of the world." Thus the Christian

<column-break/>

faith believes that all men in the Great Judgment must be resurrected, each taking back his own body. Therefore, **Hymenaeus** and **Philetus** are reproved, who understand the resurrection not as corporal but spiritual—when the soul rises from sin. But **Paul** to the Corinthians shows that it must be corporal, saying: *Oportet corruptibile hoc induere incorruptionem et mortale hoc induere immortalitatem* <note>Latin: "It is necessary for this corruptible [body] to put on incorruption and this mortal to put on immortality."</note>. But this "corruptible" and "mortal" is the body. Therefore, it shall be resurrected and shall be that same body that we leave at death, and no other. Hence **Job** the Idumean said: *videbo deum salvatorem meum in carne mea* <note>Latin: "I shall see God my savior in my flesh."</note>, that is, in the flesh that I had before death: *Ipse et non alius* <note>Latin: "Himself and not another."</note>, that is, not with another body than that which I had before. Nevertheless in some...

<meta>This page continues the theological commentary by Cristoforo Landino on Dante’s Inferno, specifically concluding the discussion of the resurrection of the body before returning to the narrative of Canto VI where Dante and Virgil encounter Pluto.</meta>

**INFERNO**

...the sinner rises otherwise than the blessed. In some other respects, the resurrection will be equal. Since it is necessary that for the damned the bodies be proportioned to the soul—and the souls of the damned, though their nature is good because it is created by God, nevertheless have their wills disordered—their bodies will rise again. Inasmuch as the nature of the soul is good, they will rise whole and in a perfect age without any defect that they might previously have had from nature or illness. Hence Paul says to the Corinthians: **The dead shall rise incorruptible** <note>original Latin: "Mortui resurgent incorrupti"</note>. But insofar as the will is rebellious against God and adverse to Him, their bodies will not be made spiritual as if subject to the spirit. Nor will they be agile, dexterous, or balanced so as to serve the soul without difficulty. Instead, they will be heavy and unbearable to the soul, and capable of suffering <term>passible: able to feel physical pain or sensation</term>, although they are incorruptible, just as their souls suffer torment from being deprived of the divine light. They will be dark and gloomy just as their souls are deprived of the divine light. Paul denotes this when he says to the Corinthians: **We shall all indeed rise, but we shall not all be changed** <note>original Latin: "Quod omnes resurgemus sed non omnes immutabimur"</note>. 

And because it seems impossible for a body to be capable of suffering without being corruptible, this question is excellently solved by **Thomas Aquinas** <note>Landino refers to him as "the Aquinate," the influential 13th-century theologian</note> in the book *Against the Gentiles*—a matter worthy of being heard. But I cannot place so many things in such a narrow and cramped space. However, just as the bodies of the glorified will be elevated above the celestial bodies, so those of the damned will rightfully be thrust down and pushed into the lowest depths. Hence it says in the Psalm: **Let death come upon them, and let them go down alive into hell** <note>original Latin: "Veniat mors super eos: & descendant in infernum uiuentes"</note>. And in the Apocalypse it is written: **The devil who deceived them was cast into the lake of fire and sulfur, and the beast, where also the false prophet shall be tortured day and night forever and ever** <note>original Latin: "Quod diabolus qui seducebat eos missus est istagnu ignis: & sulfuris: & bestie: ubi & Pseudo prophete cruciabutur die ac notte In secula seculorum"</note>. 

So much for the bodies of the damned. Let us see what those of the glorified will be like. We shall see these entirely subject to the soul; through the clarity of the soul, which is elevated to the divine vision, the body will also acquire light, for it will be filled with the radiance of life. Thus Paul to the Corinthians: **It is sown in ignobility, it rises in glory** <note>original Latin: "Seminatur corpus i ignobilitate surget i gloria"</note>; because our body is now opaque, then it will be clear. Matthew demonstrates this—or rather the Truth itself through Matthew—saying: **The righteous shall shine like the sun in the kingdom of my Father** <note>original Latin: "Fulgebunt iusti sicut sol i regno patris mei"</note>. 

Furthermore, these bodies will be agile, dexterous, and light. Hence Paul says: **It is sown in weakness, it rises in power** <note>original Latin: "Seminatur corpus i infirmitate surget i uirtute"</note>. At present, the body cannot satisfy the speed and lightness of the soul, but it will be able to then. Concerning this, Wisdom says in the third chapter regarding the just: **They shall run to and fro like sparks through a reed grove** <note>original Latin: "Quod tanquam scitille i aru dieto discurret"</note>. No deformity shall be in these bodies, and they will experience delight in the senses according to things that do not conflict with the state of incorruption. And as the blessed soul will participate supremely in divine goodness as much as its nature allows, so the body of such a soul will participate as much as possible in its properties: in the clarity of the senses, in the ordering of bodily appetites, and in every perfection of nature. This moved the aforementioned Apostle in the same place to say: **It is sown a natural body, it rises a spiritual body** <note>original Latin: "Seminatur corpus animale surget corpus spirituale"</note>—not because it is then a spirit, but because it will be subject to the spirit. Therefore, just as the glory to which the human soul is elevated exceeds the natural power of the celestial spirits, so the glory of the resurrected bodies exceeds the natural perfection of the celestial bodies. Thus they will be more lucid, more capable of feeling, more dexterous, apt, and agile than those. 

But it is common doctrine that they may appear as we read of the angels and of Christ. They will rise as male and female with their own sexes, not because they are to use them, but so that the body may be perfect. They will rise at the age of Christ <note>thirty-three years old</note>, because it is perfect, whereas other ages are either immature or too advanced. 

**THAT WHICH RESOUNDS IN ETERNITY** means hearing the Judge whose words will echo this word "forever," because He will say: "Depart, you cursed, into eternal fire." 

**THROUGH A FOUL MIXTURE** Because it was a hideous thing to see those souls turned over in that filthy water like pigs in the mire. By this, he wishes to express how foul a thing it is to consider the human soul—born for the contemplation and knowledge of great things—allowing itself to be so conquered by gluttony that it wallows like a brute pig in the pleasure of corruptible and putrid bodily foods, when its proper food is knowledge and doctrine. For just as the body, composed of the four elements, is nourished by foods made of a similar composition, so the incorporeal soul is nourished by incorporeal things. 

**WITH MEDITATIVE STEPS** <note>original Italian: "apassi letitiche," likely a corruption of "lentitiche" or "lentitidie"</note> denotes contemplation, because one who is deep in thought walks slowly and often stops. This expresses what Virgil writes in the *Aeneid* regarding Achates: **To whom the faithful Achates goes as a companion, and with equal cares plants his footsteps** <note>original Latin: "Cui fidus Achates It comes: & paribus curis uestigia figit"</note>. 

**TOUCHING A LITTLE UPON THE FUTURE LIFE** reasoning, albeit with brevity of words, about the life that will be after the last judgment. The discussion was that Dante asks if the pains of the damned are to be greater, or lesser, or stayed after the judgment.

> And he to me: "Return to your science,
> which wills that as a thing is more perfect,
> the more it feels the good, and so the pain.
> Although this accursed people
> never attain true perfection,
> they expect to be more so after than before."
> We circled round along that road,
> speaking much more than I repeat;
> we came to the point where the descent begins;
> there we found Pluto, the great enemy.

<column-break/>

Having understood the question, he responds: if you understand philosophy well—which he professes to know—you will recognize that every thing feels both good and evil more when it is in its perfection than when it is imperfect. For example, the sense of sight recognizes colors better when that sense is perfect than when it has some defect. Therefore, since man is composed of soul and body, he will then be naturally perfect when the body is reunited with the soul. He speaks, then, of this natural perfection in which even the damned will be after the judgment, and not of another perfection which is not natural to man but is granted by divine clemency—not to all, but only to the saved. The saved receive four gifts from their glorification: **Agility, Subtlety, Clarity, and Impassibility** <note>the traditional "four dowries" of the resurrected body</note>, which we spoke of above. 

Then he adds: **ALTHOUGH THIS ACCURSED PEOPLE NEVER ATTAIN TRUE PERFECTION.** Because as I have said, this supernatural perfection belongs only to the saved. The text is ordered thus: **ALTHOUGH**, that is, "even if." **THIS ACCURSED PEOPLE**, meaning the damned. **NEVER ATTAIN TRUE PERFECTION**, meaning that supernatural perfection containing the four aforementioned gifts. Nevertheless, they **EXPECT TO BE MORE PERFECT AFTER**, that is, after the judgment, because at least they will have that natural perfection. **THAN BEFORE**, that is, before the judgment, when they have neither the natural nor the supernatural perfection. 

Afterward, he concludes the chapter, showing that having departed from Ciacco, they followed the road which was circular and round. They circled the entire place where the gluttonous were punished. Morally, this signifies that in this vice they diligently contemplated the whole matter from every side. 

**WE CAME TO THE POINT WHERE THE DESCENT BEGINS**, that is, where one goes down. For he imagines that one always descends from the wider circle into the narrower one. In truth, the more grave the vice is, the further down it descends, and the further it moves from heaven. 

**THERE**, that is, at the beginning of the next circle. **WE FOUND PLUTO, THE GREAT ENEMY**, about whom we shall speak in the following chapter.

<summary>This page concludes a theological discourse on the nature of the resurrected body for the damned and the blessed, then explains Dante's transition from the circle of Gluttony toward the next circle guarded by Pluto.</summary>

<keywords>Resurrection, Last Judgment, Paul the Apostle, Thomas Aquinas, Gluttony, Pluto, perfection of the body, four gifts of the blessed, Canto VI commentary</keywords>

--- Page 95 ---
You will understand philosophy, profession. You will know every thing: what feels good, what feels bad, when there is perfection, when imperfect. As, for example, if I live, one knows better, and those who, when their sense is perfect, have no defect. Therefore, man, composed of soul and body, will then be naturally perfect when the soul is rejoined. Therefore, it speaks of this natural perfection, which even the damned will have after judgment, and of another perfection, which, though natural to man, is granted by divine clemency to the saved. And these, in glorification, have four gifts: Agility, Subtlety, Clarity, Impassibility, of which we have spoken above. It adds: ALL damned people never reach true perfection. Because this supernatural perfection is said to be only for the saved. The text states: ALL the damned go into natural [perfection] and [do not have] the four said gifts. Nevertheless, it awaits to be perfect at judgment. At least it will have natural [perfection]. Before judgment, it is not in the natural, nor in the supernatural. Then, the chapter concludes, demonstrating the groups, each one followed the road, which was circular, round. They circled all that, the punished and the daring ones. Which signifies, morally, that the restless living diligently contemplated the whole and every part. WE CAME to the point where it slopes down, descends. Because it is always imagined that the wide circle descends narrowly. Truly, the living descends so much like a stone, far from heaven. THERE
