<page-num>SEVENTH</page-num>
<header>CANTO SEVENTH</header>

## SEVENTH CANTO OF THE FIRST CANTICLE BY DANTE

"Pape Satan, pape Satan aleppe!"
began Pluto with a clucking voice;
and that gentle sage who knew all...
<note>Original: "Pape satan pape satan aleppe / comincio Pluto con la uoce chioccia: / et quel sauio gentil che tutto seppe." This famous opening line is intentionally obscure, representing the nonsensical or demonic language of the underworld's guardians.</note>

<column-break/>

In this seventh chapter, the author describes the fourth circle; and this he divides into two parts. In the first, he places the punishments of the avaricious and the prodigal; and in the second, those of the wrathful and the slothful. At the entrance of the circle, he imagines Pluto the demon as a guardian and lord of this circle. To better interpret this fiction, we should recall how the ancient poets said Pluto was the son of Saturn and Rhea and the king of hell. There were four sons of Saturn who represent the four elements: Jove (Jupiter) is fire, Juno is air, and Pluto is earth. By Saturn, they mean Time; and they imagine that he ate all his other children except these four, because time consumes everything except the elements. Therefore, since Pluto represents the element of earth, they also consider him the god of riches:

---

because whatever men seek in terms of riches is either under the earth—as we see in every kind of metal and every quarry of precious stones—or truly they are born from the earth, such as grain, fruits, and animals. For the same reason, they make him the god of hell, because the earth is the lowest part of the world; and Pluto—that is, riches—always draws the human soul to vile and base things. And they want him to have in hell his city called Dis <note>original: "Ditte"</note>, into which according to Virgil no just man can enter, for he who is greedy for riches cannot be just. Nor is it unknown to me that Pluto is also understood in many other meanings, and especially as the power that the sun infuses into the earth, by which it not only brings forth all herbs and trees, but also that same power creates gold, silver, and all other metals and jewels in the earth. Therefore, for this reason too, he is the god of riches. Fittingly, then, our poet places him at the spot where the avaricious are punished. For avarice is nothing other than an immoderate desire to possess. Not without cause did he call him, at the end of the previous canto, the "great enemy" <note>original: "gran nimico"</note>. Because without fail, he too much infests and molests the human race.

Avarice stirs up and moves discord between relatives of blood, friendship, and country. Avarice produces injustice, from which tumults, seditions, and civil wars are excited. Avarice is the cause of foreign wars. Avarice fills the sea with pirates and corsairs, and the roads with robbers. Avarice produces in the city thefts, homicides, poisons, and perjuries—which are common and corrupt everything. Finally, it makes the father of the family a cruel enemy to his wife, children, and himself; for fear of consuming what he has gathered, he defrauds himself and his whole family of necessary things. From it flee the laws and magistrates, and modesty and chastity. Therefore Pluto is a "great enemy." And certainly, there would be great tranquility among men, and they would live in perpetual peace, if everyone were content with their own and with what natural need requires. The realm of Pluto—that is, wealth—is acquired with great difficulty <note>The text notes that seeking wealth leads to hardship and vice</note>. Therefore, since Pluto signifies riches, the poet deservedly places him as the lord of the place where the avaricious and the prodigal are punished, which two vices have no other subject than riches. Pluto is the devil of that place; that is, those who are punished here have sinned regarding riches. One by holding them too much, the other by scattering them too much.

In order that this may be better understood, let us remember that all moral virtues consist not only in right knowing, but more in right acting. For he is not just who simply knows what justice is, but he who uses justice in the administration of things. Furthermore, every virtue is a certain "middle ground" <term>mediocrita</term> <note>The Aristotelian concept of the "Golden Mean," where virtue is the balance between two opposing vices.</note> placed between two extremes, of which one is "too little" and the other "too much." And just as that middle ground is virtue, so the extremes are vice. Therefore, in the distribution of our riches and faculties, there is a middle path, which follows the rule of giving as much as is appropriate, to whom it is appropriate, and for the right reason; and this action is virtue and is called liberality. One of the extremes of this middle, which leans toward the "less" and does not reach the middle ground—and thus has a defect—is not giving as much as is appropriate nor to whom it is appropriate; and this vice is avarice, which a little further down we will divide into two parts. The other extreme is excess, because it passes the middle ground and gives more than is appropriate, neither considering if the recipient deserves it nor if the reason is just; and such a vice is called prodigality. Therefore, although avarice and prodigality are opposites, nonetheless, because they deal with the same subject, they deserve to be punished in the same place. And what is said of the extremes of avarice, understand similarly for prodigality.

Now returning to the text, Dante suggests that Pluto is both marvelling and grieving that he [Dante] descends to his kingdom. In two ways one descends into these vices: either by sinning in them, which happens when sensuality rebels against reason—and in this way all the avaricious and prodigal descend here, and Pluto rejoices at their coming. Or when sensuality, accompanied by reason and obedient to it, descends into the consideration of such vices not to be defiled by them but to be purged of them, as Dante imagines for himself. And at such a coming Pluto grieves, for he desires not the salvation but the damnation of souls. And therefore, seeing him come, and doubting that he could prohibit him with his own strength, he calls Satan to his aid, saying: **PAPE SATAN, PAPE**. "Pape" is an interjection of wonder <note>Latin: *interiectio admirantis*</note>; that is, it is a voice that shows amazement. From this, the Supreme Pontiff is called "Papa" [Pope] as something most marvelous among Christians. Therefore, to say *Pape Satan* is like saying "O Satan!" and to demonstrate greater wonder, he doubles it, saying twice "Pape Satan, Pape Satan," "O Satan, O Satan!" And then to show his grief, he says **ALEPPE**. For in Hebrew they call *Aleph* what the Greeks call *Alpha* and the Latins "A." And because he who grieves uses this interjection "Ah!"—as seen later [in Canto XIX]: "Ah, Constantine, of how much ill was mother, not your conversion, but that dowry..." <note>original: "ah Constantino di quanto mal fu matre / Non la tua cōuersione : ma quella dote"</note>. Therefore, in place of the Latin name which is "A," he took the Hebrew *Aleph*, and to make the rhyme, he changed the "h" to "p" and added an "e," and said *Aleppe*.

Thus, interpreting the whole verse, we will say: "O Satan, O Satan, Ah!" By these interjections and voices, it is shown that he suddenly fell into the greatest wonder and greatest fear. We have explained the cause of the fear. The wonder, as far as the story goes, arose because a living man was coming to the place of the dead. As for the moral meaning, it is a marvelous thing that any man should descend into the contemplation of these temporal goods and so submit his appetite to reason that he esteems them only as vile, transitory, and momentary things. *Satan* in Hebrew signifies "contrary," "adversary," "prevaricator," and "transgressor." And many say this is the name of the prince of devils, whom he calls to his aid, distrusting his own strength. And certainly, Pluto—that is, riches—could not draw man to such enormous wickedness without a great diabolical stimulus. **WITH THE VOICE:** clucking <note>original: "chioccia"</note>, i.e., with a hoarse voice, which signifies sudden fear; because a sudden shock to the soul diminishes the voice or loses it entirely; as Virgil, wishing to show sudden fear in the souls of the Greeks, said: "Some raised a tiny voice; the started cry mocks their gaping mouths." <note>Latin: "pars tollere uocem / Exiguam inceptus clamor frustatur hiantes" from *Aeneid* VI, 492-493.</note> And **THAT SAGE** gentle who...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the opening of Canto VII of Dante's Inferno. The commentator is expanding on the description of Virgil as the "gentle sage who knew all," transitioning into Virgil’s rebuke of Pluto and the descent into the fourth circle.</meta>

<page-num>LXXI</page-num>
<header>INFERNO</header>

...knew everything. This is great praise for Virgil, and well-deserved: for whoever reads his poem attentively sees it to be so full <note>original: "refertissimo"</note> of such diverse things that they easily understand him to have been universal in all the disciplines of the ancients. As I strove to demonstrate at length in my preface at the beginning of my lectures on the *Aeneid*. And if one were to say that it is false that any man, however learned, can know everything, I respond that the poet here uses a rhetorical device called **hyperbole**—that is, an overstatement of the truth used not only by writers but also in daily speech, as when we say, "I haven't seen you in a thousand years." Therefore, he "knew everything," meaning he knew a great deal, and as much as almost any man can know.

But if Virgil is viewed allegorically as the intellect filled with wisdom and accompanied by divine grace, it can truly be said that he "knew everything." **GENTLE**: Noble and generous, as if to say he not only understood through wisdom but was also able to express what he understood through eloquence. For many have been most learned, yet because they lacked the eloquence to express what they understood, they remained obscure and ignoble, and achieved no fame. Or truly, he said **GENTLE SAGE**: that is, wise in the doctrines of the gentiles <note>The "gentiles" refers to the pre-Christian Greeks and Romans.</note>, which we showed above to be sufficient for understanding Hell and Purgatory; and in that sense, we say he knew everything in those doctrines. For speech must be interpreted according to the subject matter; if we are speaking of astrology and say someone "knows everything," it is understood to be within that specific science.

---

->To comfort me / he said: do not let your<-
->fear harm you: for whatever power he has<-
->he shall not take from you the descent of this rock.<-

->Then he turned back to those swollen lips:<-
->and said, "Silence, accursed wolf!<-
->Consume yourself within by your own rage."<-
->"Not without cause is this journey to the depths:<-
->it is willed on high, there where Michael<-
->took vengeance for the proud assault."<-
->As sails, swollen by the wind,<-
->fall entangled when the mast snaps,<-
->so fell that cruel beast to the earth.<-

->Thus we descended into the fourth ditch,<-
->taking in more of the sorrowful slope<-
->which sacks up all the evil of the universe.<-
->Ah, justice of God! Who stuffs together<-
->so many new labors and pains as I saw?<-

<column-break/>

He admonishes Dante not to fear Pluto, because such fear would be harmful. Those who fear Pluto are those who lack the spirit to despise earthly goods; they are so faint-hearted that they do not trust they can live without them. This degrades them so much that they do not dare to descend with a frank soul into such meditation. But the superior reason, instructed by philosophy, comforts the **sensuality** <note>In medieval psychology, "sensuality" refers to the lower, physical, and emotional part of the soul, while "reason" is the higher part.</note>, demonstrating that Pluto has no power to forbid such a descent. Truly, the appetite for riches is never so great that one who resolves to conquer it with reason cannot do so. **TO COMFORT ME**: sensuality has need of the comfort of reason and doctrine. **DO NOT LET YOUR FEAR HARM YOU**: As if to say, "Do not fear, because fear itself would harm you." **THIS ROCK**: that is, this slope.

Once Dante is comforted, he uses an almost stinging invective against Pluto—that is, against the rich and the avaricious man—because he imagines him with **swollen lips**. By this, he wishes to express elation and pride in appearance and words. This is characteristic of the rich; as Aristotle demonstrates in his *Rhetoric*, they are so arrogant that they believe everyone should be inferior and obedient to them. Hence, when the wife of Hiero of Syracuse was asked which was more worthy, wisdom or riches, she replied that she often saw the wise frequenting the houses of the rich, but never the rich frequenting those of the wise. This was an entirely foolish answer, proceeding from a soul made proud by wealth. If the rich knew their need for the wise—to become good and virtuous through their counsel—as well as the wise know their need for the rich to provide for the body's necessities, we would constantly see the houses of the wise full of the wealthy. **SILENCE, ACCURSED WOLF**: The author recalls that in the beginning <note>Referencing the Three Beasts in Canto I.</note>, he used the She-Wolf to represent Avarice. Therefore, he most aptly calls the avaricious man a "wolf," as an insatiable beast. **ACCURSED**: No one can praise avarice, because it harms both oneself and one's neighbor. From it proceed infinite evils, for it is a greed insatiable beyond all others. Thus the miser is accursed and hated by friends and relatives as much as by enemies. **CONSUME YOURSELF WITHIN BY YOUR OWN RAGE**: He says this to demonstrate the constant worry in the mind of the miser, thinking of how to accumulate; this worry and thought continually consumes him. Boethius also demonstrates this:
> <note>original: "Sed senior ignibus ethne Feruens amor ardet habendi."</note> "But older than the fires of Etna burns the fervent love of possessing."
And Jeremiah:
> <note>original: "Sunt in populo meo impii insidiantes quasi aucupes"</note> "There are among my people wicked men who lie in wait like bird-catchers."
And Horace:
> <note>original: "Impiger extremos currit mercator ad indos per mare pauperiem fugiens / per saxa per ignes."</note> "The tireless merchant runs to the farthest Indies, fleeing poverty through the sea, through rocks, through fires."
**NOT WITHOUT CAUSE IS THIS JOURNEY TO THE DEPTHS**: As if to say, our descent into hell is not fortuitous, by chance, or without counsel—which would make it easier to forbid. Rather, it is by Divine Will, which no power can resist. And certainly, **IT IS WILLED ON HIGH**: that is, in heaven. I ask why God wills it: because he wants everyone, by acting well, to purge themselves of every vice, and for this he gave us reason, which comforts us in this. This is why it is the will of God. He said "It is willed on high" to demonstrate **predestination**, which he placed above through so many graces. **THERE WHERE MICHAEL**: As if to say, where you wicked angels were cast out for your pride. He places the Archangel Michael for all the others who fought and cast out those who were adversaries to God. We shall treat this more extensively elsewhere. **ASSAULT** <note>original: "strupo"</note>: This term signifies any violent coupling, especially of a virgin. But here he uses it for the proud violence of Lucifer, who wished to violate the incorruptible divine light; he used *strupo* in place of *stupro* <note>The commentator notes a metathesis or poetic variation of the word for "violation/rape."</note> for the sake of the rhyme. **AS SAILS, SWOLLEN BY THE WIND, FALL TO THE EARTH**: An excellent comparison, through which he demonstrates the nature of the wrathful and proud man, who swells up marvelously. But once overcome, he is immediately debased, and all his pride falls. Just as sails swell from the wind while the mast supports them, but fall when the mast breaks, so the elated and proud man swells while pride supports him, but is humbled when it is quelled. **CRUEL BEAST**: Avarice is a beast because it is alien to all humanity, harming both itself and its neighbor; it is truly cruel for the same reason.

**THUS WE DESCENDED**: that is, having first comforted the lower reason and sensuality to endure every difficulty and labor and to take great heart, and having repressed appetite. For one cannot otherwise descend into the contemplation of vices without remaining entangled in them. **INTO THE FOURTH DITCH** <note>original: "lacca"</note>: that is, slope; it is a name derived from *labor, laberis*, which in Latin means "to slip," because one slips in very steep places. **TAKING IN MORE OF THE SORROWFUL...**

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante's Inferno, specifically Canto VII. Having previously discussed Virgil’s wisdom, the text now moves into the description of the Fourth Circle, where the Avaricious and the Prodigal are punished. The commentator, likely Cristoforo Landino, provides a deep linguistic and philosophical analysis of Dante’s verses.</meta>

### CANTO SEVEN

...and why our guilt so tears us apart.
As the wave does there above Charybdis,
which breaks against that which it meets,
so it is necessary for the people here to dance.
Here I saw more people than elsewhere, a vast crowd;
and from one side and the other, with great howling,
rolling weights by force of chest:
They struck against each other; and then right there
each turned back, rolling his weight,
shouting: "Why do you hold?" and "Why do you toss?"
Thus they ran through the dark circle
from every side to the opposite point,
shouting again their shameful meter;
Then each turned back when he had reached
through his half-circle to the other joust;
and my heart was nearly pierced with grief.

<column-break/>

...sloping rim <note>original: "lacca"</note>. Take more of it: because the descent is steeper there. **WHICH**: that is, the rim which enfolds and takes into itself the evil of the universe: that is, all the sinners. Meaning the rim that contains within it all the circles of Hell. Or truly we shall say: **WHICH**: that is, the fourth rim <note>original: "lacca"</note>—the fourth circle—**ENFOLDS** <note>original: "insaccha," literally "pouches" or "sacks"</note> all the evils of the universe. This is because from avarice—which is punished in this circle—proceed all wicked acts and all the evils that befall men. Concerning this, Seneca most excellently said: "Remove these names *Mine* and *Thine*, and every discord that arises among men will be removed." Then, contemplating the infinite and most grave punishments by which the miser is struck, with both wonder and compassion, he follows by saying: **OH JUSTICE** of God: because truly no vice deserves to be punished more according to divine justice than this one, which harms both oneself and one's neighbor, and is the source and root of all other vices. Avarice, according to Cicero, is the immoderate desire to possess. And Augustine, writing on the literal interpretation of Genesis, writes: that it is not only the immoderate desire to have riches and other things subject to fortune, but also to have dignity and knowledge. But this is avarice taken in a very broad sense. There are two types of avarice. Properly speaking, a miser is one who does not give where and how much he ought, and one who takes from where he ought not. From these acts, creditors are defrauded; deposits are denied through perjury, false witnesses, and adulterated goods. From here come usury, theft, robbery, ransoms, barratry <note>The buying or selling of ecclesiastical or state offices</note>, and assassinations. From here come simonies and the incorrect distribution of sacred things. **WHO STOWS** <note>original: "chi stipa"</note>: *Stipare* in Latin means

---

to stow: that is, to fill by trampling down. Thus we say a galley is at the "stowage" <note>original: "stiua"</note> when wool and similar things are trampled down. Therefore, he who "stows" is he who accumulates and gathers together. It is as if he says: "You, Justice, gather so many punishments." And the text is ordered: **OH JUSTICE** of God, who stows—that is, who accumulates so many "new troubles"—that is, so many labors and pains not seen elsewhere, such as are here, and so many penalties. And certainly every vice gives trouble to man, but none as much as avarice, as we have already shown above.

**AND WHY** our guilt "tears us apart" <note>original: "fine scipa"</note>: that is, it distracts or torments us. It comes from the Latin word *scerpo*, which means to distract, lacerate, and tear. And the meaning is: why our guilt lacerates us—that is, why our sin torments us. **AS THE WAVE DOES THERE ABOVE CHARYBDIS**. In the strait that divides Sicily from Italy, called the Faro, there are two rocks: one on the side of Italy called Scylla, of which we shall speak another time; the other on the side of Sicily called Charybdis. The poets pretend this was a most rapacious woman; because she stole cattle from Hercules, she was struck by Jove’s lightning and converted into this monster. There, due to the narrowness of the place, the sea boils and runs from north to south and south to north, where the waves constantly break against each other; being now swallowed and now spat out by the caverns beneath the rocks, they pull ships into such perils. Therefore, the author says that just as those two waves, meeting, strike one another, so two ranks—that of the avaricious and that of the prodigal—part from the same place in the circle. But turning their backs to one another, one went to the right and the other to the left, so that, without leaving the circle, they met in the middle and struck each other. It should be noted that the poet used the comparison of Charybdis not only to show this encounter but also because it fits well: for poets use Charybdis to represent avarice, as we demonstrated at length in our allegories of Virgil. Just as Charybdis pulls the waves to herself and absorbs and swallows everything, so avarice wants to seize and swallow everything. **SO IT IS NECESSARY THAT HERE THE PEOPLE DANCE** <note>original: "riddi"</note>: that is, dance and go in the manner of a dance around the circle. He speaks with a certain derision, for in dancing there is joy, but here there is sadness. *Ridda* in our language means a ball or dance. From this noun, the poet formed a verb that is not in common use, and in the present subjunctive he said *riddi*, meaning "should dance." And certainly, the poet’s genius was admirable in the invention of these punishments. He expressed that two extremes—Avarice and Prodigality—come even to the middle to meet one another, but they do not stop there. This is because the middle point between these two extremes is **Generosity** <note>original: "liberalita"</note>. They depart through the circle from a point where Generosity is, because everyone leaves it, and they come to the other opposite point where the excesses are. But one goes to the right and the other to the left, because the prodigal departs from the middle by giving more than generosity requires and goes to the extreme of excess. The miser departs by not giving as much as is appropriate and goes to the other extreme, which is deficiency. Therefore, the middle is that in which virtue alone consists. As Horace says:
> There is a measure in things; there are, in short, fixed limits, beyond and short of which virtue cannot consist. <note>original: "Est modus in rebus sunt certi denique fines: Quos ultra citraque nequit consistere uirtus."</note>

From this middle, the miser and the prodigal depart and go to different extremes by different paths. The poet imagines that these people push stones of heavy weight with their chests. In the chest is the heart, and in the heart are the cares and thoughts which, in the miser, are continuously great. His heart is never quiet; he is continuously turning some ponderous stone—that is, turning some laborious thought in his mind. As Horace says:
> You see with what labor of mind and head you avoid what you believe to be the greatest evils: a small income and a shameful rejection. <note>original: "Vides que maxima credis esse mala exiguum censum turpemque repulsam Quanto deuites animi capitisque labore."</note>

And avarice always goads, and as Persius writes, it says:
> "Arise!" says Avarice. "Come, arise!" You refuse? It persists: "Arise!" <note>original: "Surge inquit auaritia Eia surge Negas Instat Surge."</note>

Therefore, **BY FORCE OF CHEST** <note>original: "di poppa"</note>: that is, of the breast where the breasts <note>original: "poppe"</note> are, in which chest is the heart, and in the heart the cares and anxieties. **HERE I SAW MORE PEOPLE THAN ELSEWHERE**: Because there is no vice that occupies more men than avarice. **AND FROM ONE SIDE AND THE OTHER**: That is, from two extremes. On this side the misers, on that side the prodigals, as was said above. **HOWLING** <note>original: "urlli"</note>: shrieks; a name derived from the Latin *ululatus*. Because "howling" belongs to wolves, it is well-suited to the misers, whom he equates to wolves. **SHOUTING "Why do you hold?"**: These are the words of the prodigal who reproaches the miser for retaining what he should give to others. **"AND WHY DO YOU TOSS?"**: *Buriare* in the Aretine tongue means to throw. These are the words of the miser who reproaches the prodigal for throwing away what he should keep. And many ask the reason why Dante, above where he punishes lust and gluttony, does not place the contrary vices to these, as he does here where he punishes avarice and places prodigality as its contrary. To this I respond: that although every vice has its contrary, nevertheless, in the two already mentioned, they do not appear. For despite the fact that lust is...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante's Inferno, Canto VII. It provides an interpretation of the physical punishment of the Avaricious and the Prodigal—who clash weights against one another—and transitions into Dante’s inquiry regarding the identity of the tonsured souls among them.</meta>

<page-type>text</page-type>
<columns>2</columns>
<header>INFERNO</header>

...excess in coitus: Nevertheless, the defect—that is, not taking as much pleasure as is required—is found in no one, or in very few, and without much harm. And we shall say the same of gluttony. The poet says: that having reached the point and struck one another, they turned back to repeat the same course anew. And having returned to the point from which they first departed—which is opposite to where they clashed again—they began the joust once more. This signifies that the miser never ceases to strike the prodigal—that is, to snatch and to hold—nor does the prodigal cease to strike the miser—that is, to squander. But note: rarely is there prodigality without avarice. In order to be able to give much, they take and snatch from others, as Cicero writes of Caesar, who despoiled many of Pompey’s followers to give to his own. And they always shout their shameful **meter**—that is, verse: the one "why do you hold?" and the other "why do you toss?" **AND I, WHO HAD** my heart nearly pierced—that is, I who was much afflicted by compassion for such great pains.

I said: "My master, now show me
what people these are, and if all were clerics,
these tonsured ones on our left."
And he to me: "All these were squint-eyed
of mind in their first life,
so that with measure they made no spending.
Quite clearly their voices bark it out
when they come to the two points of the circle
where contrary guilt separates them.
These were clerics, who have no hairy
covering on the head, and popes, and cardinals,
in whom avarice practices its excess."
And I: "Master, among such as these
I should surely recognize some
who were filthy with these evils."

<column-break/>

<image-desc>A hand-colored blue paragraph mark (pilcrow) precedes the start of the commentary text.</image-desc> Deservedly, Dante always raises doubts and asks questions; and Virgil, answering him, resolves them. This is because to the lower reason, when it investigates, everything appears doubtful; but the higher reason, with its doctrine, finds the truth and resolves the doubts. He asks if all the "tonsured ones"—that is, those he saw with the tonsure—were **clerics**, that is, priests. **ON OUR left**: by the left, he demonstrates greater wickedness in avarice. For just as "right" is used for the happy and good, so "left" is used for the contrary. Clerics in our language are what the Latins call *clerici*. It is not, however, a Latin word but a Greek one, because in Greek *cleros* signifies "lot" or "share." Whence *clericus* signifies one elected by God by lot. And although God calls us all, nevertheless He allots and elects priests as kings to rule the laity—that is, the non-priests—with good customs and doctrine. Thus they wear the circle of hair on their heads, shaving the rest in the likeness of a crown. Therefore, vice is much more ignominious in the priest than in the layman, because he who rules should be an example of all sanctity to those who are to be ruled. And by sinning, the opposite occurs. Thus Juvenal says: "Every vice of the soul is so much more conspicuous in itself as the one who sins is held to be greater" <note>original: "Omne animi uitium tato conspectius in se crimen habet: quanto maior qui peccat habetur"</note>, as we have said above. The priest is therefore of worse example, because vice is more noted in him and appears more clearly. Thus the poet deservedly reproves them more than the others. **AND HE**: that is, Virgil, **TO ME** "understand," he said, "**ALL** were squint-eyed." Dante asked if all those he saw with the tonsure were priests; and Virgil responds that they were all **squint-eyed**: wishing first to demonstrate their vice rather than the state they held in life. They were, therefore, squint-eyed—understand this as the eyes of the mind and intellect—because not looking straight, they did not know how to discern the truth and see the **measure**—which contains virtue. Instead, looking askance, they took to the extremes. **IN THE first life**: that is, while they live in this world. **THAT NO**: that is, they did not do here. **ANY spending**: that is, any distribution of their substances with measure, in which consists the middle ground and the virtue called liberality. But they sinned either in the "too much," whereby they became prodigal, or in the "too little," and were misers. And this their voice clearly demonstrates when they come to the two points of the circle where they meet, and where they say: "Why do you hold?" and "Why do you toss?" And he says **barks** to liken them to dogs, because with words they bite one another. Truly he says "barks" as if to say "in vain," because any reproof given there is worth nothing, there being no place for penitence in Hell. And similarly, in the "moral hell" <note>The psychological state of being trapped in sin while alive.</note> there is no redemption for a habit already contracted in vice. **WHERE CONTRARY guilt**: that is, prodigality and avarice, which are contrary vices. **SEPARATES THEM**: that is, divides them, because each of the parties turns back through his half-circle until the other point. Then he responds to Dante’s question and affirms that all those whom he sees with the tonsure were clerics. And for two reasons he vilifies the priests in this place: first, because they are more involved in these two vices than all other men. And without even needing examples from past centuries, one may look to the complaints of our Petrarch regarding "avaricious Babylon" and so on, and elsewhere: "May fire from heaven rain upon your tresses." Who has not seen in our times men, or rather monsters of men, without letters, without morals, not sufficient to be entrusted with the care of a lowly country chapel, who because fortune has elevated them to great dignity, have used therein every extreme avarice to accumulate infinite treasure through **simony** <term>simony: the buying or selling of ecclesiastical privileges or offices</term> and various kinds of robbery; and then extreme prodigality in consuming them in every shameful luxury, in such a manner that Sardanapalus and Heliogabalus <note>Ancient rulers notorious for decadence and excess.</note> could be considered most continent in comparison to them. This, notwithstanding that it is very painful to any well-disposed mind wherever the Christian name exists, nevertheless hurts more for certain prelates most adorned with every kind of doctrine, and who are a most lucid mirror to all others in life, and most prudent in every action and most wise in speculation, than for others. Because there being so much infamy in their order, it seems impossible that in some part it does not overflow onto them, though undeservedly. For which reason, as much as a most just indignation drives me against those most luxurious misers, so much does compassion move me toward these most innocent ones. But the reverence I bear to such a college makes me keep silent about that which is known to the whole world. This, then, is the first reason that moved Dante to vilify the priests. The second is that the vice is more blameworthy in them than in the layman. Since the apostolic—that is, priestly—church is founded upon chastity and poverty. Whence Petrarch says: "You were not then nurtured on feathers in the shade, but naked to the wind and barefoot among the thorns. Now you live so that you become a stench to God." Furthermore, they are those who have the government of the Christian republic. Whence they are called *clerici*: that is, elect, and as if chosen, and great men, because *cleros* signifies lot. And us they call *laici* <note>laity</note>, that is, plebeians, because *laos* signifies people. They ought, therefore, being the administrators, to give the best example of themselves. Especially since they mean to signify something else by having shaved their hair: namely, that they have cut away every superfluity and sliced off every greed. And the circle that is above the shaved hair demonstrates a crown, to denote that they are our kings, and it is their office to rule us and direct us along the good path. The third reason is because there is no cause that should make them greedy to accumulate treasure, having neither wives nor children to support. **IN WHOM**: that is, in whom. **AVARICE practices its excess**: As if

# CANTO SEVENTH

...though all avarice exceeds the limit, whether by pulling to oneself or by not giving: nevertheless, it practices its excess in prelates <note>High-ranking clergy such as bishops or abbots.</note>; that is, they have as much excess as can exist within it. **AND I, MASTER.** Dante marvels that among so many prelates he does not recognize any. To which Virgil responds:

> **And he to me: "You gather vain thoughts:**
> **the undiscerning life that made them foul**
> **now makes them dark to every recognition.**
> **In eternity they shall come to the two collisions:**
> **these shall rise from the sepulcher**
> **with closed fists, and these with shorn hair:**
> **Ill-giving and ill-keeping the beautiful world**
> **has taken from them, and placed them in this scuffle:**
> **what it is like, I do not embellish words to say.**
> **Now you can see, son, the short puff**
> **of the goods committed to Fortune:**
> **for which the human race scuffles.**
> **For all the gold that is beneath the moon,**
> **or that ever was, of these weary souls**
> **could not make a single one rest."**

<column-break/>

True answer. **THAT THE UNDISCERNING life:** that is, the form and manner of their living, which was undiscerning—meaning it lacked any noble or recognizable character. **MADE THEM FOUL:** that is, infamous; **AND NOW makes them dark:** that is, obscure and without fame. Allegorically, this demonstrates the stupidity of the miser, who is useful neither to himself nor to others; for this reason, he can never achieve lasting fame. It is certainly a great misery to toil in accumulating treasure with which one neither provides for one’s own needs nor acquires any honor. They live unknown, without friends, without the intimacy of anyone, and are hardly known by their neighbors. We can also call it an "undiscerning life" because the life of the miser is so different from the priestly profession that one cannot recognize them as priests. Their office <note>The duty or "officium" of a cleric.</note> is to distribute the fruits and revenues for the repair of the temple and to assist, according to the degrees of charity, those who are in poverty, keeping for themselves only what is necessary for a sober life according to their status. When priests do this, their life makes us recognize them for what they are; but when they live as described above, such a life offers no sign that they are priests. **IN ETERNITY they shall come to the two collisions:** because, as each group runs half-way around the circle and strikes the other before turning back, they collide at two opposite points of the circle. **THESE.** That is, the misers. **SHALL RISE from the sepulcher with closed fists.** This symbolizes avarice. **AND THESE.** The prodigals.

---

**WITH SHORN hair:** which signifies squandering or dissipation. **ILL-GIVING.** That is, prodigality, which gives without regard to whom, how much, why, or when. **AND ILL-keeping.** Avarice, which holds more than it should. Since "well-giving" is liberality and "well-keeping" is parsimony—both of which are virtues. Therefore, these two vices have taken the "beautiful world" from them. It is as if he said they have lost the happy life; for men would certainly live in the highest happiness if avarice and prodigality did not deprive them of all peace and tranquility. For both the prodigal and the miser are always anxious and greedy to snatch—the latter to keep, the former to waste on others. Alternatively, "beautiful world" refers to heaven and eternal life, which contains supreme beauty and delight. Some interpret "Ill-giving and ill-keeping the beautiful world" to mean worldly goods, which are beautiful by their nature. **HAS TAKEN from them.** That is, it has taken these people away from their true selves. For avarice and prodigality rob a man of his own soul. Therefore, it has taken them from themselves and placed them in this scuffle. Just as a sold slave is no longer his own but belongs to the master who bought him, so when a man is made a servant of greed, he is no longer free, but is placed by greed into this conflict. **IN THIS SCUFFLE.** Referring to these two collisions. Or understand "this scuffle" as the dissensions and discords that first arise within the soul of the miser, who is torn by two different wills: one which encourages him toward quiet, rest, and the enjoyment of his gains, and the other which pushes him into dangers and toils to acquire even more. Persius clearly expressed this internal battle <note>The commentator refers to the Roman satirist Persius, Satires 5.154–156.</note>. For after showing that avarice pushes a man to every danger and toil for gain, while luxury draws him toward leisure and quiet, he concludes: <note>original: "En quid agis? duplici in diversum scinderis hamo: Hunccine an hunc sequeris? subeas alternus oportet Ancipiti obsequio dominos alternus oberres."</note> "Behold, what are you doing? You are split by a double hook pulling in different directions: will you follow this one or that one? You must needs serve both by turns, and wander to and fro in wavering obedience to your masters." We can also interpret "this scuffle" as the dissensions and contentions that arise among men because of avarice and robbery, which is a most obvious truth. **WHAT IT IS LIKE:** whether good or bad. **I DO NOT EMBELLISH words:** I do not use decorative language. It is as if he said: I do not seek an oratorical style to vituperate this scuffle with ornate words, because the matter is so manifest in itself that it needs no adornment. **NOW YOU CAN see, son, the short puff.** Here, Virgil rightly admonishes Dante lovingly like a father; that is, the higher reason admonishes the lower reason and the senses not to place hope in the goods of Fortune. One should not be greedy for them, as they are neither lasting nor stable; rather, placed in the rashness of Fortune, they briefly shift from place to place. Furthermore, it should be noted that in the two circles already passed, Virgil did not admonish Dante as he does here. This is because it is more difficult for a person dedicated to the pursuit of great things to abstain from avarice than from the pleasures of touch or taste (lust and gluttony). **THE SHORT PUFF.** The brief vanity. Benvenuto <note>Benvenuto da Imola (c. 1330–1388), an early Dante commentator.</note> says this, and Francesco da Buti <note>Another 14th-century commentator.</note> explains "puff" [buffa] as derision. But "buffa" specifically means a gust of wind. Hence we say "to puff" [buffettare] of one who blows air from the mouth, or "to huff" [sbuffare] when one threatens with windy and inflated words. From this we get "to muddle" or "scuffle" [rabbuffare], meaning to disturb and move things out of their proper order. We call it a "rebuke" [rabbuffo] when we disturb someone’s mind with words. From this follows: "the human race scuffles" [si rabbuffa], meaning it is disturbed and leaves the true order of things because it takes sovereignty away from reason and gives it to the senses. Therefore, he used "wind" to signify vanity and something unstable. **OF THE GOODS that are committed to Fortune.** It is the height of stupidity to place your happiness in something that is not in your power but at the whim of Fortune, who, making a game of men, often takes wealth from those who deserve it and gives it to those who do not. **FOR WHICH the human race scuffles.** He speaks with indignation: that the human race—the only animal on earth made a participant in reason—lets itself be so carried away by greed for these goods that it falls into such great contentions. **SCUFFLES.** As we said, "puff" [buffa] is wind, from which comes "to scuffle" [rabbuffare]. **FOR ALL THE GOLD THAT IS BENEATH THE MOON.** Here finally human stupidity and vanity are revealed. Since we ought to toil for those things that can make us blessed, he shows that the goods of Fortune are so far from this goal that even if one person possessed all the gold in the world, it would not provide even one hour of rest—let alone happiness. Or, if we reason according to the nature of Hell: no damned soul can be saved by all the treasures of the...

# INFERNO.

world. Or according to the moral sense: one who does not know that the greed of the miser is never extinguished by accumulating. But as Horace says: *The dire dropsy grows by indulging itself, nor does it banish its thirst unless the cause of the disease has first fled the watery languor of the pale body.* <note>original: "Crescit indulgens sibi dirus hydrops Nec sitim pelit nisi causa morbi fugerit prius aquosus albo corpore langor." This quote from Horace's Odes (II, 2) compares greed to "dropsy" (edema), a medical condition where drinking water actually increases the patient's thirst.</note> Therefore, just as in the dropsical person <note>original: "rituopico," a likely typo for "idropico" (one suffering from dropsy).</note> thirst is not quenched by drinking if the cause from which the disease proceeds does not first cease; so too greed does not cease in the miser by the piling up of gold if the mind does not find rest. Hence Cicero said: *It is the mind of the man, and not his coffer, that should be called rich.* <note>original: "Animus hominis: & non arca diues appellandus est." From Cicero's Paradoxa Stoicorum.</note> Nor is he rich who possesses much, but he who is content with what he has. Therefore, Alexander [the Great] was not rich, for whom one world was not enough; but Diogenes was rich, who lived content in the highest simplicity.

**"My Master," I said, "now tell me also**
**about this Fortune you touched upon,**
**who is she, who holds the world's goods so tightly in her claws?"**
**And he to me: "O foolish creatures,**
**how great is the ignorance that harms you!**
**Now I wish you to take in my judgment:**
**He whose wisdom transcends all**
**made the heavens and gave them those who guide them,**
**so that every part shines to every other part,**
**distributing the light equally;**
**similarly, for worldly splendors,**
**He ordained a general minister and guide**
**to shift, in due time, the vain goods**
**from people to people, and from one blood to another,**
**beyond the defense of human wisdom.**
**For this reason, one nation rules and another languishes,**
**following her judgment,**
**which is hidden like a snake in the grass.** <note>original: "chome in herba langue." Usually "angue" (snake). The text evokes Virgil's own phrase from the Eclogues, "latet anguis in herba."</note>
**Your wisdom has no contest against her:**
**she foresees, judges, and pursues**
**her reign, as the other gods do theirs.**
**Her permutations have no truce;**
**necessity makes her swift,**
**so often does one come who claims her turn.**
**This is she who is so much put upon the cross**
**even by those who ought to give her praise,**
**wrongly giving her blame and ill report.**
**But she is blessed and does not hear it;**
**happy with the other primal creatures,**
**she turns her sphere and, blessed, enjoys her state."**

<column-break/>

Since Virgil made mention of the "goods of Fortune," it was fitting in this place—where we treat of avarice and prodigality, the subjects of which are the goods of fortune—to briefly define what that thing is. In order for this to be better known, I judge it useful to relate (but with brevity) what Fortune is, circumscribing it in a way that our <term>Free Will</term> <note>The human capacity to choose between different possible courses of action unimpeded.</note> is not diminished by it. And first, we must understand that according to the Peripatetic philosophers <note>The followers of Aristotle.</note> there are three generations of goods: those of the soul, the body, and fortune. The goods of the soul are those that benefit the soul and preserve it pure in its nature; and these are the virtues, either intellectual—such as Intelligence, Science, Wisdom, Prudence, and Art—or moral, such as Justice, Fortitude, and Temperance, which we have to treat in various places. The goods of the body are those that benefit the body, such as health, beauty, strength, dexterity, speed, and the like; just as, conversely, the evils are disease, ugliness, weakness, slowness, and the like. The goods of fortune are riches, dignity, magistracies, empires, fame, and glory; just as the contraries are poverty, infamy, low esteem, and the like. These goods are called "of fortune" because they are largely subject to her.

But it is a long and laborious thing to dispute fully about Fortune and Chance, because they can hardly be explained without the knowledge of Providence and Fate. Therefore, with brevity, we will demonstrate as much as is necessary to express the mind of the poet. And <term>Divine Providence</term>, according to Boethius, is a supreme reason in God which orders and disposes all things. <term>Fate</term> is a certain disposition in changeable things, through which Providence connects and composes each thing in a certain order. And those things which Providence embraces within the Divine mind, Fate disposes in a form so that they proceed by order from time to time. Therefore, Providence is a certain form of future things through order in various ages, which is immobile and simple. Fate is a certain mobile connection and temporal order of things that the Divine simplicity disposed to be. It follows that whatever is under Fate is also under Providence. Perhaps there is no other difference between these two, except that Providence is when we consider it in the Divine mind, and Fate when we consider it in the temporal order of things. Neither Providence nor Fate obstructs or hinders our Free Will, as the Aquinian theologian <note>Saint Thomas Aquinas.</note> subtly demonstrates in the book *Against the Gentiles*. 

Theologians say Fortune is like a certain lady who turns and changes human affairs extravagantly, and dispenses them with an end different from the intended purpose, neither thought of nor expected. Hence Boethius calls her a *blind power* <note>original: "cecu numen" (caecum numen).</note>. And she inclines herself equally 

---

to the wicked as to the good without any selection. And if you investigate what the difference is between Fate and Fortune, the learned respond that Fortune exists only in those things which appear fortuitous and come by chance, where no manifest causes appear that ought to produce such an effect. Fate has its causes immobile and imposed by God or by the stars upon things. 

But returning to Fortune, they say it exists only in the soul and where there is reason, which directs every operation of its own to a certain purpose. Therefore, no inanimate thing, nor brute animal, nor little children can have Fortune. Because they do not operate according to a purpose, nothing can happen to them outside of their intention and purpose, which is the proper characteristic of Fortune; rather, they have "Chance." Hence we say that the horse returns home "by chance." It seems to me, if I am not mistaken, that I have in brief words distinguished Providence, Fate, Fortune, and Chance. 

But I believe the poet in this place wishes to indistincly blend Fate and Fortune. Because in both there are the causes from which the effects proceed, but in Fortune they are unknown to us. Therefore, the ignorant man who, while plowing, finds a treasure will say it is "good fortune." But the astrologer, who through the man's nativity knows the cause that makes him find it, will affirm that it is "Fate." Virgil expressed this same sentiment by saying *Omnipotent Fortune and ineluctable Fate.* <note>original: "Fortuna omnipotens: & ineluctable fatum." A quote from the Aeneid (VIII, 334).</note> We will conclude, then, that Fortune is nothing other than the various influx of the heavens hidden from us, which—according to the conjunctions, oppositions, trines, quadratures, and sextiles, and other various aspects of the planets in various houses of the Zodiac—governs all things that are beneath the sphere of the moon, as things inferior to them; except for the souls of men. For our soul cannot be dominated by the stars. Therefore, I confess that the superior powers are created by God with this privilege: that they always have dominion over the inferior; but the rational soul, although placed in the body it inhabits an inferior place, nevertheless because it is created by...

It argues that while Fortune governs material goods and "lower" things, the rational human soul remains free from stellar influence.</summary>

--- Page 103 ---
<meta>This page continues the commentary by Cristoforo Landino on Canto VII of Dante's Inferno. The previous page ended with Virgil beginning his explanation of Fortune to Dante, refuting the idea that human greed or celestial influence can override the soul's fundamental freedom.</meta>

God, without the mediation of the heavens or the stars, is not inferior to them, but superior. Hence, not only our sacred writings—in which there can be no error because they are derived from the fountain of truth—but also all philosophers worthy of any esteem, and all mathematicians who subject the government of earthly things to the will of the heavens, affirm that the soul is free and possesses its own judgment. For this reason, the divine Plato demonstrates with most true arguments that no good can benefit the soul and no evil can harm it that is not within our own power to either possess or be deprived of; because virtue alone is good, and vice alone is evil. Neither can the former be taken away from us, nor the latter be given to us by the influence of the heavens. For as Ptolemy says: the wise man rules over the stars <note>original: "el sauio signoreggia alle stelle." This famous medieval maxim, *Sapiens dominabitur astris*, suggests that while the physical body might be influenced by astrology, the rational mind remains free.</note>. Nor can it be done by the violence of man or any other animal. See, therefore, that if physical goods are in the hands of the heavens and of other men, those of the soul are in our liberty; and only these can truly be called ours. This was truly understood by the Platonic Cicero, whose sentiment in his *Paradoxes* is that nothing can be called "mine" or "yours" or another’s if it can be robbed or stolen or lost in any way. 

The city of Priene had fallen into the hands of enemies under the condition that its citizens were allowed to leave with as much property as they could carry. Bias, one of the seven sages of Greece and a citizen of that land, was walking away empty-handed; when asked why he carried nothing, he replied that he was indeed carrying everything that was his. A true saying, and fitting for such a wise man, for he knew that by carrying the virtues of his soul, he was carrying all his possessions. Perhaps I have strayed too far from the topic, but I have recounted all this so that we may understand: although what we have discussed is "Fortune," and within her recklessness and fury are placed all fleeting and transitory goods, the soul nevertheless remains free. Without her help, and in spite of her, the soul can become happy—not only in the next life, but in this one. 

But returning to the text. Dante says: "Tell me, Virgil, what is this Fortune, who holds **THE GOODS OF THE** world **IN HER CLAWS**"—that is, in her power. Temporal goods, according to that saying: *My kingdom is not of this world* <note>original: "Regnum meum non est de hoc mundo," quoting John 18:36.</note>. **AND HE:** that is, Virgil. "Listen to me," he says. **O FOOLISH CREATURES:** that is, stupid ones. We call food "weak" [*fiocca*] when it is without salt. And because we often take "salt" to mean prudence, we call the imprudent person "weak" [*fiocco*] <note>Landino is playing on the Italian word *fiocca* (feeble/faint) and the Latin *sal* (salt), which metaphorically represents wit or wisdom.</note>. **HOW GREAT** is that ignorance which harms your intellects? And he rightly said "harms," because just as the intellect becomes perfect through science and knowledge, it conversely becomes imperfect and harmed by ignorance. This causes us to believe that Fortune has as much power over the soul as over the body, and that she is a master rather than a servant. **MY** judgment "into your mouth" [*imbocche*]: that is, receive and take what is said; a metaphor taken from a dog when it catches a wild beast in its mouth. **HIS KNOWLEDGE** transcends all: that is, God, whose wisdom advances and surpasses all others and infuses itself into everything. **HE MADE THE** heavens: whence the Psalmist says: *By the word of the Lord the heavens were made, and all their host by the breath of his mouth* <note>original: "Verbo dei celi firmati sunt & spiritu oris eius omnis uirtus eorū," from Psalm 33:6.</note>. And similarly, He created all other things, but mentions the heavens here because he must demonstrate that every fortune arises from their motion. 

**AND GAVE TO THEM ONE WHO** guides: Because according to Aristotle, He gave to each heaven an "Intelligence" to move it—a sentiment the author [Dante] also follows in a song that begins: *You who by understanding move the third heaven.* **SO THAT** every part of their power **TO EVERY** worldly **PART** fit to receive it **SHINES**, and in shining, infuses. But concerning brilliance and light, we shall speak more conveniently in *Paradiso*: how it exists in God, in the angel, in reason, in the spirit, and in the body. And if you first delight to understand it all, read in the second book of the *Epistles* of our Marsilio Ficino <note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499) was the leader of the Florentine Platonic Academy and Landino's close associate.</note>, the most learned of all the Platonists of our age, and you will be satisfied. **DISTRIBUTING** equally: Because God, the giver, infuses equally into all creatures; but they receive more or less according to their capacity. 

**SIMILARLY** to worldly splendors: that is, to riches, dignities, and honors. **HE ORDAINED** a general minister: Because Divine Providence—which has disposed these worldly goods temporally by means of Fate and Fortune—administers everything. In this, the movements of the heavens and angelic power serve her. Therefore, these will be the "general ministers," because these movements create Fortune. **WHO WOULD CHANGE** in due time the **VAIN** goods: that is, the aforementioned worldly splendors which are not true goods. For that is a true good which makes its possessor good, and this is virtue alone. But worldly goods induce infinite evils. They are, therefore, vain and apparent, and not true and existing goods. Fortune changes them according to her judgment. Whence it is written in the first book of Kings: *The Lord makes poor and makes rich; he brings low and he exalts. The pillars of the earth are his, and he has set the world upon them* <note>original: "Dominus pauperem facit Ditat. humiliat: & sublimat. Ipsius sunt cardines terrę: & posuit super eos orbem," from 1 Samuel 2:7-8.</note>—that is, the wheel of Fortune. 

And Boethius, speaking in the person of Fortune, says: *Riches, honors, and other such things are within my right. Slaves recognize their mistress; this is my power. We play this continuous game. We turn the wheel in a revolving orb; we delight to change the lowest things with the highest, and the highest with the lowest* <note>original: "Opes honores ceteraque talium sunt mei iuris Dominam famulę cognoscunt hec mea uis est Hunc continuū ludum ludimus. Rotam uolubili orbe uersamus infima summis Summaque infimis mutare gaudemus." From Boethius's Consolation of Philosophy, Book II.</note>. Thus Fortune speaks and demonstrates that empires, riches, and powers are in her jurisdiction; and like servants, they recognize her as mistress. She enjoys the continuous raising and lowering. And Ovid says: *With uncertain steps, fickle Fortune wanders, and she stays in no place firm and steady* <note>original: "Passibus ambiguis fortuna uolubilis errat: Et mãet in nullo firma tenaxque loco." From Ovid's Tristia.</note>. **FROM NATION** to nation: as we see empires being transferred from people to people with constant mutation. The Assyrians were the first, of whom we read that they reigned in the Eastern parts through the virtue of Ninus and Semiramis. But from them, the empire transferred to the Medes, and from the Medes to the Persians, of whom the first was Cyrus. 

It cannot be recounted without a long narrative how, with constant volatility, empires have continually changed among the Medes, the Egyptians, and the Scythians—so much so that at one time, having defeated the male sex, women reigned, as we read of the Amazons. The Greeks reigned. The Africans reigned. The Romans reigned. Nor is it only shifted from nation to nation, but in the same region from city to city, and in the same city from family to family. **BEYOND THE** defense of human wisdom: because truly human wisdom can maintain the goods of the soul (which are the virtues) against Fortune, and with those, acquire a blessed and eternal life. But it cannot, without her favor, maintain states and other vain goods. Thus Cato and Cicero and other excellent citizens could maintain their virtues, but they could not, with all their great prudence, defend their own and the public liberty. 

Therefore Seneca rightly said: *Every kingdom is under a greater kingdom. Let no one trust too much in prosperity. Clotho mixes these things with those and forbids Fortune to stand still; she rotates every fate. God turns our affairs, stirred by a swift whirlwind* <note>original: "Omne sub regno grauiore regnum. Nemo confidat nimium secundis: Miscet hec illis prohibetque Clotho Stare fortunā rotat omne fatū Res deus nostras celeri citatas turbine uersat." From Seneca's tragedy Thyestes.</note>. And Boethius: *What else does the cry of tragedies bewail but Fortune turning happy things with an indiscriminate blow?* <note>original: "Quid tragediarum clamor aliud deflet nisi fortunam indifereto ictu felicia uertētem?" From Boethius's Consolation of Philosophy, Book II, prose 2.</note> The tragic poet laments, therefore, that Fortune disturbs happy things without choice. **FOR WHICH ONE** nation rules and the other languishes. Caesar, raised up by the favor of Fortune, obtained the empire. Pompey, made an enemy by her, lost it. **LANGUISHES:** that is, falls into languor—meaning sorrow and pain—fleeing defeated into foreign kingdoms. **FOLLOWING** her judgment: because no one can appeal against the judgment given by Fortune. It is necessary to comply with it, which is hidden from us like a **SNAKE:** that is, a serpent, which hidden in the grass deceives our sight by the similarity of color, so that it is not seen by the one who treads on it. Similarly, Fortune hides a pestilential poison amidst happiness and vain hopes that kills us. **YOUR KNOWLEDGE** has no contest against her: almost the same sentiment as the verse that spoke against the defense of human wisdom. **HAS NO** contest: that is, it cannot resist, even if it foresees her blows. And certainly, there have been many who, either through prophecy or some other kind of divination, have foreseen their calamity. Nevertheless, they could not resist. Astyages, King of the Medes, saw in a dream that from the genital parts of his daughter grew a vine whose branches overshadowed all of Asia. And the diviners interpreted that from her...

<meta>This page continues the commentary by Cristoforo Landino on Canto VII of Dante's Inferno. The previous page discussed the philosophical nature of Fortune and human free will. # INFERNO: COMMENTARY:

A child was to be born who was destined to seize the kingdom. Therefore, although Astyages took many precautions against this—first marrying his daughter in Persia to a most base man, and then commanding that the child, once born, be left in the forest to the wild beasts—nevertheless, Fortune willed that the boy, who was Cyrus, should escape every danger. Once grown, he took the empire from Astyages and transferred it to the Persians. <note>Astyages was the last king of the Medes; his grandson Cyrus the Great eventually overthrew him, fulfilling a prophecy Astyages had tried to thwart.</note> I could refer to infinite examples in confirmation of this sentiment, but the greatness of this volume does not allow me to dwell too long on such a manifest matter. 

**PROVIDES,** judges, and pursues: This demonstrates that since Fortune is an influence proceeding from the movements of the heavens, and since the motion of the heavens is guided by the Intelligences placed by God as their motors, everything born from it proceeds from reason and not from chance, as it seems to us. Therefore, the primary Reason first provides—as if consulting on what is to be done—and after consultation, it judges. Then it pursues—that is, it puts into execution what it has judged to be good. By saying "provides," the poet hints at Divine Providence, from which all influences proceed. 

**THE OTHER** gods. The other Intelligences. He calls Fortune a goddess, and likewise all the motors of the heavens according to the poets, who called all the stars "gods." Because they are in continuous movement and are bodies, the Greeks called God *theos* from the verb *thein*, which means "to run." <note>original: "theos da qsto uerbo thein." This is a traditional but folk etymology relating the Greek word for God to the word for running/moving.</note> But even the Sacred Scriptures call men "gods." Whence: "You are gods and sons of the most high, all of you." <note>original Latin: "dii & filii excelsi omnes" from Psalm 82:6.</note> Therefore, in that same way, he calls the motors of the spheres "gods." 

**THEIR** permutations have no truce: that is, the permutations of earthly goods, which proceed from celestial influences, have no truce—meaning rest. This is a metaphor drawn from soldiers who rest and do not fight during a truce. 

**NECESSITY** makes her swift. Certainly, if Fortune is this mutation of temporal goods, and such mutation is born from the constant and swift movement of the heavens, it is necessary that such mutation be swift. Fate, or rather Fortune, turns with a certain necessity just as the sun and the other planets turn in their courses. Nor is free will taken from us by this, because we are free not to trouble ourselves with earthly goods, which are entirely subject to Fortune. But if we do trouble ourselves with them, it is inevitable that we submit ourselves to Fortune regarding them. Therefore, such necessity exists in those things that, being subject to Fortune, of necessity change according to her will—and not in us, who can choose to labor or not labor for them. Certainly, if we draw near to God in a way that we entirely despise earthly things, we become entirely free from Fortune. If we give ourselves to divine things and yet still desire temporal goods, we will not be entirely free. But if, leaving divine things, we give ourselves entirely to earthly ones, we are entirely servants of Fortune, not by necessity, but by our own will. A man who is out of the sea can choose to enter or not enter the sea; but once he has entered, it is necessary to obey the winds and the waves. Thus we can choose not to seek the goods of Fortune; but if we seek them, we ourselves submit to that necessity from which we were previously free. See, therefore, that the necessity the poet posits is not against free will. Whence Boethius also posits it, saying:

> He who departs further from the primary mind is entangled in the greater bonds of fate. But something is freer from fate the closer it seeks the pivot of things. But if it cleaves to the firmness of the supernal mind, lacking motion, it also transcends the necessity of fate. <note>original Latin: "Qui longius a prima mente discedit/maioribus fati nexibus implicatur. At tanto aliquid fato liberius est: quanto rerum cardinem uicinius petit .Sed si superne mentis haeserit firmitati motu carens fati quoque supergredit necessitatē." From Boethius, *The Consolation of Philosophy*.</note>

Now returning to the text, it says that the permutations of Fortune never have a truce, because they happen continuously. And this is because someone often comes who "follows in turn"—that is, whose turn it is, and who succeeds to your happiness while you fall from it. Whence Claudian:

> While Croesus holds the top of the wheel, Codrus holds the bottom. Julius [Caesar] ascends, the great [Pompey] descends to the depths; Sulla lies down, Marius rises: but with the axis turned, Sulla rises, Marius falls. <note>original Latin: "Sūma rote dū cresus habet tenet infima Codrus. Iulius afcēdit dēscēdit magnus ad ima: sylla iacet surgit marius: Sed cardine uerso Surgit Sylla cadit Marius." These verses describe the shifting fates of famous historical figures.</note>

**THIS IS** she who is so much "put on the cross"—that is, so much tormented with blasphemies, complaints, and laments. 

**EVEN BY** those who ought to give her praise. If we understand this to mean those who are fortunate and happy, it is a true sentiment. For men are so ungrateful that if, after a long period of happiness, a brief unhappiness occurs, they complain greatly about the small evil and give her no thanks for the long-lasting good. If we understand it to mean those who have not received benefit from Fortune, it is likewise an excellent sentiment; for I complain about not having wealth or power, when I should instead praise my lot, considering that it is a more tranquil life to live in leisure than in tumult, and it is sweeter to be governed than to govern. Furthermore, no one can complain if Fortune either takes back what she had given or never gives it at all. Since these are her goods, she can both take them back and not give them without any injustice, as Boethius proves at length in the book *On Consolation*. 

**BUT SHE IS BLESSED** and does not hear this. Because such influence does not lose its vigor due to our complaints or insults; and "she does not hear," meaning she does not care because it does not harm her. And the poet subtly wishes to touch upon the truth: that such influence is an inanimate thing, although the author poetically calls her a goddess. 

**WITH THE OTHER** first creatures: that is, with the heavens, which must exist before the influence proceeding from them; they are therefore first, if not in time, at least in origin. 

**TURNS HER SPHERE:** that is, she turns these worldly goods as if they were in a sphere. Or rather, she "turns her sphere" because Fortune is the influence that proceeds from the revolution of the heavens. And indeed, she turns this wheel: for wealth creates pride; pride, impatience; impatience, war; war, poverty; poverty, humility; humility, patience; patience, peace; and peace, wealth. 

**AND BLESSED, she enjoys herself:** because she cannot be hindered or offended by our complaints.

---

->Now let us descend to greater sorrow<-
->already every star falls that was rising<-
->when I set out; staying too long is forbidden<-

Having described the punishments of those who poorly administered money, either through avarice or prodigality, it seems to the author time to descend into the fifth circle where Wrath and Sloth are punished. 

**NOW LET US DESCEND:** as if to say, we have stayed long enough. And as it was often more than half the time, they had to hurry. Here Virgil admonishes Dante to hurry, showing that the night—in which alone they could be in Hell—was already more than half gone. Therefore, with so much of the journey remaining, he wanted to imply that Dante was later in departing than was fitting. This allegorically demonstrates how difficult it is for the senses to leave behind riches and the goods of Fortune; those who care for and prize these things too much can never rise to true contemplation. Whence Truth said in the Gospel: "No one can serve two masters, God and Mammon"—that is, God and money. For he who is greedy for treasures, which are earthly things, cannot elevate his mind to divine things. Regarding the difficulty placed upon the rich man entering heaven: I believe that by "rich" is meant not one who possesses, but one who is greedy for riches and a lover of them. Riches do not harm the one who does not seek them nor prizes them more than they are worth, nor makes himself a slave to them. Rather, they are an excellent instrument for many virtues. Therefore, the vice does not consist in the riches themselves, but in the excessive greed for them and in their captive use. 

**TO GREATER SORROW [pity]:** to greater punishment; for the greater the punishment, the greater the compassion. 

**ALREADY EVERY** star falls that was rising when I set out: By this description of the time, he shows that midnight has passed. For if those stars that—at their departure, which was at the beginning of the night, as he showed by saying "The day was going"—were rising from our horizon, had already passed the quarter of the sky (which is the middle of our hemisphere and the highest part over our heads) and were beginning to descend toward the west, then midnight had passed. And this is a passage drawn from Virgil where he says, "Night..."
