### CANTO TEN. <note>Though the header says "Canto Ten," the text and commentary clearly refer to Canto Seven of the *Inferno*.</note>

"Aeneas rushes on; we pass the hours in weeping." <note>original: "ruit Aeneas nos flendo ducimus horas." This is a paraphrase of Virgil's *Aeneid* VI.539, where the Sibyl warns Aeneas that time is passing as they journey through the underworld.</note> STAYING TOO LONG is forbidden: because, as we demonstrated above, it was not permitted to stay in Hell for more than one night. This is a poetic device because we must not remain in the night and darkness of vices any longer than is necessary to contemplate their ruin once.

---

**We crossed the circle to the other bank**
**above a spring that boils and pours over**
**through a ditch that derives from it.**
**The water was far darker than purple-black,**
**and we, in the company of the murky waves,**
**entered down by a strange path.**
**Into the marsh that bears the name Styx**
**this dismal stream goes when it has descended**
**to the foot of the gray, wicked slopes.**

<column-break/>

He describes the place and the site of this fifth circle and their descent, saying: WE CROSSED the circle. Crossing [original: *ricidere*] means to divide. But here he says "we crossed" as if to say we went through the middle of the circle and came to the opposite bank. ABOVE A spring that boils and pours over. He shows that at the summit of the valleys a spring arose, which, as it surged, was boiling—that is, it sent out a bubble of water. And from this overflow the river was born, which ran through the valley to its lowest point. There, finding no easy exit, it created a marsh. BOILS: to denote that anger is nothing other than the boiling of the blood. AND POURS OVER: because this boiling inside the chest pours out, appearing in the face and creating a stream that runs. This signifies the fury of the choleric person, which lasts a short time and is not a great vice. Hence Horace says: "Anger is a brief madness." <note>original: "Ira furor brevis est." From Horace, *Epistles* 1.2.62.</note> But it is a supreme vice when it stagnates and becomes a marsh—that is, when it endures, from which hatred is born. It is not without reason that anger is not punished in the spring or the river, but only in the marsh. For the boiling of the spring, which is the first movement of the blood, and the river, which is that precipitous and sudden fury arising from it, deserve pardon, because first movements are not within our power. But the marsh—that is, the perseverance and dwelling in anger from which it becomes hatred—is the vice that deserves punishment. THE WATER was dark—that is, obscure and much more so than "perse" <note>A dark purple-black color.</note>. This denotes the obscurity and blindness of the mind in the angry person, because every light of reason is extinguished in him. AND WE in the company of the murky waves—that is, not bright—IN COMPANY walking along the river. WE ENTERED down, going down the slope, they were accompanied by the river. BY A STRANGE PATH: meaning difficult, as this word signifies in the Florentine dialect; and it rightly shows that the path leading to anger is difficult. For no one falls into this vice except through things which seem harsh and difficult to them. One does not get angry at pleasant things but rejoices in them. This stream, which is born from the aforementioned spring and is "dismal"—that is, deprived of all joy—having descended the aforementioned slopes (which he describes as GRAY or murky), forms a marsh called Styx. But because the description of the Styx and the other infernal rivers contributes much to the allegorical sense which we strive to give this poem, we will refer to it below where the poet writes of it more extensively.

---

**And I, who stood intent on looking,**
**saw muddy people in that swamp,**
**all naked and with a look of fury.**
**These were striking each other, not just with hands,**
**but with the head, the chest, and the feet,**
**mangling each other with their teeth, piece by piece.**

<column-break/>

He attributes a fitting place to anger. Since anger is nothing other than the setting of the blood on fire around the heart to take revenge, it is fitting that such an impulse proceeds from the sorrow and sadness taken from the injury received. And we have shown the Styx marsh to signify sadness and sorrow. And anger, according to Aristotle, is the appetite for giving pain to one's adversary because of an apparent slight, where the person judges this to be just. Thus Augustine said: that to no angry person does it seem that his anger is unjust. But because anger is permitted when it does not pass its due limits, and is forbidden when those limits are crossed, I will repeat with some brevity something of the nature

---

of our souls, so that once the origin and the end of anger are understood, we may know how great a vice it is. Therefore, although our soul is simple, incorporeal, and indivisible, nonetheless, because it has various powers and various forces, we say it is divided into such powers and forces. One we call the vegetative, another the sensitive, and another the rational. And the sensitive power has its senses, partly external and partly internal. From the senses proceeds judgment. For the eye, seeing that this object is yellow, and the common sense judging it to be sweet, makes the thinking power conclude that it is good. Therefore, the senses determine what thing is good and what is contrary. After the senses, there is another power in the soul which, having understood the judgment of the senses, rises up either to desire what has been judged to be good, or to flee what is judged to be evil. This power is called "appetite." That which desires is "concupiscible." That which flees is "irascible." And just as through the concupiscible power we desire what the sense judges to be good, so through the irascible power we rise up against that which is evil, or which stands in the way of our good. For just as nature has given fire not only lightness, which leads it to its good (the higher place), but also heat, with which it burns and consumes every obstacle that would prevent it from rising; so to the animal she has rightly given the concupiscible and the irascible. And of this it is written: "Be angry and sin not." <note>original: "Irascimini & nolite peccare." From Psalm 4:5 or Ephesians 4:26.</note> But when it boils in us without reason, the capital vice of anger is born, which they define as the boiling of blood around the heart to avenge oneself, as I have already said. This, in the beginning, is called "excandescence," and by the Greeks *thymos* <note>original: "thymos" (θύμος).</note>. If it perseveres for a while, it is called "wrath," and in Greek *menis* <note>original: "menis" (μῆνις).</note>. But if it perseveres and remains a long time and grows old in the soul, it becomes "hatred," which the Greeks call *koton* <note>original: "coton" (κότον).</note>. And the seat of anger is in the heart, just as concupiscence is in the liver. The poet has signified these three things: the first by the boiling spring, the second by the river, and the third by the marsh. This wrath must therefore be compressed, because as Horace says: "He who does not moderate his anger will wish undone what grief and mind have prompted. Also: Anger is a short madness; rule your mind, which, unless it obeys, commands; restrain it with bridles, restrain it with chains." <note>original: "Qui non moderabitur ire Infectum esse uolet dolor quod suaserit & mens. Item ira furor breuis est animum rege qui nisi paret imperat: hunc frenis hunc tu compesce cathenis." From Horace, *Epistles* 1.2.60-63.</note> He who does not restrain his anger plunges himself entirely into the...

# CANTO VII

...of black humor makes the man black. Just as cheerfulness brightens the face of man and makes it shining, so sloth <note>original: *accidia*, a state of spiritual apathy or "sluggishness" considered a capital sin</note> clouds it and makes it dark. **NOW WE** are saddened in the black beauty: that is, now we are in the habit of sloth: and you can interpret this in that same sense that we interpreted as being fixed in the depths. **THIS HYMN**: hymn signifies a verse composed in praise of God or some blessed one: because *hymne* <note>original Greek: *hymnos*</note> in Greek signifies to praise, especially during sacrifices, and they are most especially sung with joy. But here the opposite is true, because with sadness they pronounce not the praise of a celestial spirit, but the infamy of infernal spirits. However, there is no error on the poet’s part. For he speaks through irony, that is, he uses words in the opposite sense. This gives the speech a sense of gravity and wit, as seen in Virgil: *Meanwhile, his excellent wife* <note>original Latin: *Egregia interea coniunx*, from the Aeneid; Virgil uses "excellent" ironically to describe the treacherous Helen of Troy</note>. He will use this same irony further below when he says, "Rejoice, Florence, since you are so great." **THEY GURGLE** in the throat. This expresses the voice of one who wants to speak but has the pipe of the throat full. For they do not speak, but gurgle. **THROAT** <note>original: *strozza*</note> is the channel that goes from the lungs to the mouth, through which the breath comes: which, struck against the palate, the tongue, and the teeth, is shaped into a distinct and articulate voice. Thus it is called "throttling" <note>original: *strozzare*</note> when you squeeze the throat in such a way that the breath cannot pass and the animal suffocates. **WHICH THEY CANNOT SAY** with a whole word because, the breath not having free exit, it cannot form distinct and complete words.

<columns>2</columns>

> Thus we circled the filthy pit
> in a great arc between the dry bank and the marsh
> with eyes turned toward those who swallow the mud
> We came to the foot of a tower at last

<column-break/>

Between the marsh, as we have seen in the circle, and the edges of the circle, there remained some space on dry ground. And through this space Virgil circled with Dante until they reached the tower. **FROM THE** filthy pit. That marsh was filthy: that is, sullied: because it was muddy. **PIT** <note>original: *pozza*</note>: properly signifies a small gathering of water. But here he takes it to mean the great marsh of Styx. For this reason, he uses a figure of speech very common among

<columns>1</columns>

Greek and Latin poets called <term>tapinosis<note>original Greek: *thapinosis*, a rhetorical device where a writer uses a humble or "low" word to describe something much larger or more significant, often to show contempt or to emphasize a grim reality</note></term>, which is a kind of "lowering." This occurs when a great thing is belittled by describing it with a term for something small, as in Virgil when he says *in the vast whirlpool* <note>original Latin: *in gurgite vasto*</note>: where he uses *gurges* (a pool or pit) to describe the sea. **GREAT ARC**: One who goes all the way around a circle makes a round; but one who goes around only a part of it makes an arc. **BETWEEN THE** dry bank: that is, the bank of the marsh not touched by water. **AND THE MIDDLE** <note>original: *mezo*</note> that is, that part which was soaked by water. In the Florentine dialect, *mezi* refers to apples when they are so ripe that they begin to dissolve into rot: which the Latins call *mellow fruits* <note>original Latin: *poma mitia*</note>. Therefore, from this Latin word *mitia* comes the word *mezo*. And since an overripe apple is soft, we apply the word *mezo* to anything soft or mushy. Thus, "between the dry bank and the *mezo*" means the soft, soggy part of the marsh. **SWALLOWS** <note>original: *ingoza*</note> or gulps down: because *gozo* signifies the throat <note>original: *gorgozule*</note>. Whence *sgozzare* <note>to slit the throat</note> means to cut the throat.

<header>CANTO EIGHT</header>
<sig>s 3</sig>

### THE EIGHTH CANTO OF THE FIRST CANTICLE BY DANTE.

> I say, continuing, that long before
> we reached the foot of the high tower,
> our eyes went upward to its summit
> because of two small flames we saw placed there;
> and another from afar gave a signal,
> so distant that the eye could hardly catch it.

The author begins by narrating that before they had arrived, they saw the signal made upon the summit. But Giovanni Boccaccio—a man worthy of faith both for his learning and character, and for having lived close to Dante’s own time—relates having heard from Andrea, son of Leone Poggi and a nephew of Dante, a specific story. He says that after Dante, along with Messer Vieri de' Cerchi, was exiled from his homeland, his wife Gemma, before the mob could rush her house, moved her most precious belongings to a safe place, including Dante’s writings. 

Then, five years or more later, wishing to recover some of her husband's possessions in the name of her dowry, she sent Andrea with a lawyer to the place where the writings were kept to retrieve certain documents necessary for the case. Among the papers, the lawyer found a small notebook in Dante's own hand containing these first seven chapters. Delighted by them, he took them to Dino di Messer Lambertuccio Frescobaldi, a man of letters experienced in Tuscan verse. Dino, reading such a noble beginning with no small amazement and seized by a great desire for the work to be finished, sent the notebook to the Marquis Moroello Malaspina in Lunigiana. 

He begged him through letters to see to it that Dante, who was with him at that time, should complete the work. This was most pleasing to Dante; for he, believing these chapters had perished along with many other things plundered by the people, had abandoned his purpose. But having them restored to him then, and being persuaded by the Marquis, he decided to continue. And taking up the material again, he gave this beginning to the eighth canto: **I SAY, continuing** the work already begun before my exile. 

Boccaccio said he heard this from Andrea. Furthermore, he adds having heard from Ser Dino Perini—who had been very intimate with Dante—that *he* was the lawyer sent by the wife, and that he, not Andrea, had brought the notebook to Dino. Finally, Boccaccio expresses doubt as to whether this is true, because in the fifth chapter <note>Canto VI</note> Dante has Ciacco speak of things that happened three years after Dante’s exile. Dante could not have guessed these things. Nor does Boccaccio like the response that the author could have added Ciacco’s words later, because since Dino had many copies made, Boccaccio claims he never saw nor heard of anyone who had seen a copy where Ciacco’s words were absent. But this matters little either way, as it does not change the meaning of the text. 

Returning to the text, we shall explain: **I SAY, continuing** in the narration already started. **THAT BEFORE** we were at the foot of the tower (to which he showed above that he had arrived). **OUR EYES went**: meaning they looked intently. **TO THE SUMMIT**: at the top. **BY TWO small flames which he saw placed there**: the meaning is that the space from this tower to the city of Dis <note>original: "Dite"</note>, where there is another tower, is occupied by a marsh. Therefore, it is necessary to cross by boat. He feigns that the guards placed at this tower signify the arrival to those at the other tower by a fire signal; they make as many flames as there are souls arriving. And so they placed two flames for Virgil and Dante, and the tower of the city responds to the signal to show it has understood, and immediately sends the boat to pick up those who have arrived. **SO DISTANT THAT THE EYE COULD HARDLY CATCH IT**: that is, perceive it. By this, he demonstrates the great expanse of the marsh that was between one tower and the other. 

Here we can apply the allegorical sense, understanding by the towers and the flames placed on the summit the transcendence of wrath <term>iracundia: the state of being prone to sudden, violent anger</term>; and by the three flames, the three species of anger of which we spoke above. But as for the literal sense, this is in imitation of what men do in dangerous times, when one town signals to another by day with smoke and by night, as it was then, with fire.

> And I turned to the sea of all wisdom
> and said, "What does this say? And what does
> that other fire respond? And who are they who made it?"
> And he to me: "Across the filthy waves
> you can already discern what is expected,
> if the smoke of the marsh does not hide it from you."
> No cord ever shot an arrow from itself
> that ran through the air so swiftly
> as I saw a tiny boat
> come through the water toward us just then,
> under the guidance of a single pilot,
> who shouted: "Now you are arrived, wicked soul!"

...can discern the truth. Then he demonstrates the speed of the boat through the simile of a bolt leaving a crossbow. Thus, a crossbow **CORD NEVER shot an arrow from itself** (which arrow is **SWIFT**: meaning direct and straight) that ran through the air; he says "swift" because a crooked or too thick arrow is not as fast as a straight and clean one. **AS I SAW a tiny boat.** By the boat, he represents the movement of the irascible appetite; and he shows it to be under the governance of only one person, to demonstrate that this is the irascible appetite when it is disobedient to reason; and therefore, it is a vice. For that which is obedient to reason was...

<column-break/>

Although the canto changes, it nevertheless still perseveres in the fifth circle, where the wrathful and the slothful are punished. It shows how, by the signal made from the tower, Phlegyas <note>The mythological king who set fire to Apollo's temple, here serving as the ferryman of the wrathful</note> came and embarked them; and while sailing, they found Filippo Argenti in the marsh; and finally, they arrived at the city of Dis. **I SAY, Continuing** can be understood simply: that the author, wishing to link the beginning of this chapter with the end of the previous one, uses these words: "I say, continuing in my narration." And note that although he said above that he had arrived at the tower, he turns back somewhat in his speaking.

**OF ALL wisdom** <note>original: "DI TVTTO fenno"</note>: This demonstrates the same phrase used elsewhere: "And that gentle sage who knew everything." Therefore, interpret it in the same way. **WHAT DOES THIS say**: that is, what the fire of this tower signifies. **AND THAT other**: that is, the signal in the other tower that responds. And if you consider this tercet <note>a three-line stanza</note> with diligence, you will judge it worthy to be numbered among the most elegant for its marvelous brevity, with which it expresses many things with the highest clarity and no small ornament. 

And Virgil responds to Dante: "You can already discern **ACROSS the filthy waves** <note>original: "fucidonde"</note> (that is, obscure and black) what is expected." For Virgil already saw the boat moving. **IF THE SMOKE of the marsh does not hide it from you.** He shows that marshy and swampy places are always filled with thick vapors and a sort of mist, which impede the sight. But allegorically, Virgil—that is, superior reason illustrated by learning—immediately perceives the truth. But he fears that Dante—that is, lower reason—might be hindered by the "smoke." For in this lower reason, anger is born; because it is a boiling of the blood, it raises certain thick vapors to the brain, which impede the senses so that they cannot...

Having discussed the historical preservation of the first seven cantos, Landino now shifts to the literal and allegorical analysis of Phlegyas, the crossing of the Styx, and the theological categorization of the sins punished here.</meta>

<header>INFERNO:</header>

not a vice. Therefore, he is not at the helm of this ship. And he said *Galeotto* <note>Galeotto: Landino is discussing the term for "helmsman" or "pilot."</note> with one "T" and not with two, although it should be written with two: but this is permitted to the poet so that the rhyme corresponds with *uoto* [vain] and *aloto* [distant]. HE CRIED OUT: which is characteristic of the wrathful man. WICKED SOUL: he spoke of one and not of two: either because he only saw one soul stripped of its body, or because he used the singular for the plural. Or perhaps the poet wished to express the vice of the wrathful man: who, in his frenzy, often neither sees nor hears enough.

"Phlegyas, Phlegyas, you shout in vain,"
my lord replied on this occasion,
"you shall not have us longer than the crossing of the mire."
As one who listens to some great deceit
done to him, and then laments it:
such did Phlegyas become in his gathered rage.

My leader descended into the boat:
and then he made me enter after him:
and only when he was inside did it seem laden.
As soon as the leader and I were in the vessel,
the ancient prow went its way, cutting
through the water more than it usually does with others.

<column-break/>

<insert>c</insert> Just as the poet above placed Pluto for the vice of avarice, adapting his fiction to what the ancients wrote about Pluto, so at present he places Phlegyas for the vice of anger and pride, not departing from what was written of such a man by the gentiles <note>Gentiles: A term for the ancient Greeks and Romans or non-Christian authors.</note>. They say, therefore, that Phlegyas was the son of Mars, and had two children: a male named Ixion, and a female named Coronis. She was violated by Apollo, and from this union was born Aesculapius, a man so excellent in medicine that he was called the god of that art. But Phlegyas conceived such anger against Apollo for having violated his daughter that he set fire to and burned his temple. This occurred in the year 3,752 after the creation of the world. And the poets feign that Apollo, with his arrows, drove him into hell and gave him such a punishment: that he should have a great stone over his head, which would keep him in constant fear of it falling upon him. And of this Virgil said: *A massive rock he rolls for others, and they hang bound to the spokes of wheels; the unhappy Theseus sits and will sit forever, and Phlegyas, most wretched, warns all and testifies with a great voice through the shadows.* <note>original: "Saxum ingens uoluit a liis radiisq/ue rotar/ū districti pendēt: sedet eternumque sedebit infelix Theseus Phlegiasque miserrimus omnes Admonet & magna testatur uoce per umbras." — Aeneid VI. 616–620.</note> Therefore, seeing that this man had been so conquered by anger that he became impious and sacrilegious toward the gods, the poet places him in this location for anger. Not only for anger, but also for pride: because in this part where the marsh is enclosed between the two towers, pride is also punished. And by the towers one can denote their haughtiness, and by the flames the ardor of overbearing behavior, and by the ship the impiety of pride, which swiftly wishes to trample everyone, just as the ship stands above the waters. And he places a single helmsman, because the proud man always wishes to be alone and without equal. Nor does the proud man deserve any other punishment than that, in wishing to stand above all, he finds himself beneath the slime and the mud. Whence Jeremiah says: *The proud one shall fall, and there shall be none to raise him up; and the crown of the proud shall be trampled.* <note>original: "Cadet superbus & nō erit qui resuscitet eū: & conculcabitur corona superbi." — Jeremiah 50:32 and Isaiah 28:3.</note> And Job: *If his pride should mount up to heaven, and his head touch the clouds, like a dunghill in the end he shall perish.* <note>original: "Si ascenderit in celū superbia & caput eius nubes tetigerit quasi sterquilinium in fine perdetur." — Job 20:6-7.</note> And David: *I will blot them out like the dust of the earth. Like the mud of the streets, I will crush them.* <note>original: "Delebo eos ut puluerem terra. Quasi lutum platearū cōminuam eos" — Psalm 18:42.</note> And for the same reason Virgil demonstrates that it is the proper duty of one who justly administers the republic: *To spare the submissive and to war down the proud.* <note>original: "Parcere subiectis & debellare superbos." — Aeneid VI. 853.</note> Nor was it without careful judgment that the poet placed Anger, Sloth, Pride, and Envy in similar punishment, because there is a great connection between these vices. This is more clearly shown by following Augustine: that just as virtue is "ordered love," so conversely, vice is "disordered love." And this disordered love exists in three ways. The first is when it is too great for small goods: that is, temporal ones. And from this are born Lust, Gluttony, and Avarice. The second way is when love is too small for great goods: that is, the goods of grace. From this proceeds Sloth, which, because it participates in sadness along with the wrathful man, deserves to be punished with him in the Stygian marsh. In the third way, love is disordered when it is a love of evil. And this is recognized in pride, envy, and anger. For the proud man loves the harm of others for his own good. He loves the harm of his neighbor for his own exaltation. In the envious and wrathful man, there is only the love of another’s harm. But envy has its origin in its own malice, that is, from pride, because the envious man wants his neighbor's harm so that the neighbor does not become his equal. Anger is born from the love of the neighbor's harm for the desire of vengeance. Therefore, these four vices are similar. For this reason, they are deservedly punished together. And certainly, as soon as pride is born in us, envy is also awakened, because by desiring vain reputation and power, we begin to feel envy toward others so that they do not equal us. And because of this, we lose gentleness, and in its place succeeds anger, which makes us sad and leads us into sloth. For which reason, without error, we can conclude that these four vices are punished in this swamp. And the two towers serve both the rising and elevation of anger, and the haughtiness of pride, which is twofold: for we are proud of intrinsic goods, attributing everything to our wisdom and our learning, as well as of extrinsic ones, becoming elated by riches, power, dignity, and honors. We have said this in another place, but I repeat it here: the poet holds one order in the Inferno and another in Purgatory regarding the vices. This he does not only to vary the narration—so that the reader does not grow weary by hearing the same thing many times in the same way—but also because in the contemplation of vices we must consider the "affects" of the soul, which are more than just the vices themselves. And in purgation, it is sufficient to know those vices that proceed from the affects.

<insert>d</insert> We said that the wrathful are punished in this marsh. According to the "essential" Hell, this means that the souls who, passing from this life, remained damned by such a vice are punished here. But allegorically we will say that those who have made a habit of this vice, and are therefore damned in it, are submerged in the Styx: that is, in perpetual sadness. But those who descend into this place not to be defiled by the vice, but to know and contemplate it, do not fall into the marsh. Instead, they are carried across the surface without getting wet, so that, remaining dry—that is, pure from sin—they see those who are submerged. MY LEADER descended into the boat: Virgil enters the boat first. For in the contemplation through which we find the truth, "Superior Reason" <note>Superior Reason: A technical term in Scholastic philosophy for the part of the intellect directed toward divine or eternal truths.</note>, as a true guide, goes first; and Dante, who signifies "Sensuality" <note>Sensuality: Here meaning the physical/emotional part of the human being that is subject to Reason.</note> obedient to Reason, follows him. And Virgil makes him stay near him: that is, he does not let him depart from his obedience. AND ONLY WHEN he was inside did it seem laden. Regarding the fiction, it is a fitting thing that Dante, having a body, should weigh down the boat much more than Virgil. And allegorically, Superior Reason is so light and so far from vice that in contemplation it always stays afloat and does not sink. But Sensuality, although it is disposed to follow Reason, nevertheless, due to its fragility, cannot help but sink somewhat. Virgil expressed this same sentiment when he said: *And it took in much water in the leaky marsh.* <note>original: "Et multā accepit rimosa palude." — Aeneid VI. 414.</note> And as soon as they were in the vessel—that is, in the ship that carried them—this...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Canto VIII. Having just described Phlegyas and the crossing of the Styx, the text now moves to the encounter with the wrathful soul of Filippo Argenti and Virgil’s subsequent praise of Dante’s righteous indignation.</meta>

<header>CANTO EIGHT</header>

While we were crossing the dead slough,
one full of mud rose up before me
and said, "Who are you who come before your time?"
And I to him, "If I come, I do not stay;
but who are you, who have become so foul?"
He answered, "You see that I am one who weeps."
And I to him, "With weeping and with mourning,
accursed spirit, may you remain;
for I know you, though you are all filthy."
Then he stretched out both hands to the boat;
whereat the wary master pushed him back,
saying, "Away there with the other dogs!"

<br/>

He then threw his arms around my neck,
kissed my face, and said, "Disdainful soul,
blessed is she who bore you in her womb!
This man was an arrogant person in the world;
no goodness is there to adorn his memory;
thus is his shadow here in such a fury.
How many now hold themselves up there as great kings
who here shall wallow like swine in the mire,
leaving behind horrible contempt for themselves."

<column-break/>

"Placed" signifies the will to contemplate. THE ANCIENT PROW WENT ITS WAY: Prow signifies the front of the ship, which is the part that is pointed forward and divides the waters. Hence, it is used here to represent the sharpness of the intellect in the contemplative life, with which we can open up obscure things. IN THE WATER understand more with me. THAN IT USUALLY DOES with others. Here, apply the same allegory as above. AND ONLY when I was inside did it seem laden. ANCIENT: because such a passage existed when Hell—of which he said earlier, "before me no things were created except eternal ones"—was made. Or, having explained the prow as the sharpness of the intellect in contemplation, we can say "Ancient" because speculation in the first man existed before action.

While we were crossing the dead slough. He uses a word improperly <note>The commentator notes that Dante uses "gora" (conduit) for a rhyme, even though a conduit usually flows and he calls it "dead" or still.</note> for the sake of the rhyme. For in the Florentine dialect, we call a *gora* a canal of running water, like those that turn a mill. But he qualifies it with the opposite adjective, calling it "dead." For just as we call "living water" that which flows, so "dead water" is that which does not flow. BEFORE ME rose one full of mud. We said above: because anger and pride are stuck in the mud. And Dante asks who he is, and the spirit says he comes BEFORE THE HOUR: that is, before his time. This is because souls do not go to Hell before they depart from the body. And allegorically, one is not counted among the wrathful who has not first made it a habit. And Dante not only had not made it a habit, but had descended to contemplate it so as not to perform any such act. But the damned spirit did not understand that those who direct themselves toward the good descend into Hell not to soil themselves with vices, but to know them so they can guard against them. AND I TO HIM: he creates a certain contention between Dante and the spirit to denote the nature of the wrathful man in the spirit, and to signify that Dante—that is, <term>sensuality</term> <note>In medieval philosophy, "sensuality" refers to the part of the soul that perceives and feels, which must be guided by Reason.</note>—while contemplating vices, often pursues them with just disdain. Yet, because the contagion of the physical body makes it prone to fall, it would eventually be defeated; this is clearly shown when the poet feigns that the spirit, after such contention, stretched out his hands to embrace him and pull him into the mire. This signifies that sensuality was being attacked by the vice. But Virgil—that is, higher Reason—defended him by pushing the spirit back into the mire. For when Reason sees sensuality being attacked by sin and yet resisting, it then awakens itself and awakens the sensuality; by showing the destruction that the sin brings with it, Reason drives it entirely away from the appetite. But I return to the text: AND I TO HIM WITH weeping and with mourning, accursed spirit, may you remain, for I know you. He asked at first who he was, and then he knew him without the spirit telling him. This denotes that he who goes about speculating often does not understand at first and asks a teacher about that which, in time and without others' help, he comes to know. Furthermore, he wants to show that the disturbance of anger is so vehement that it transforms a man's appearance so much that at first he is not recognized, they become so foul. Hence, Plato commanded that the angry man should look at himself in a mirror. Therefore he adds: THOUGH you are all filthy. Similarly, pride transforms a man and strips him of all humanity—which belongs to man alone—and clothes him in cruelty, a vice entirely contrary to man and proper to wild beasts. Therefore, he who contemplates such a vice recognizes no human likeness there. BECAUSE THE Master: he calls him Master because higher Reason is that which instructs sensuality with its precepts. WITH THE OTHER dogs: because the angry man is much like a dog.

This shows that Virgil, having pushed the spirit back into the water, turned to Dante and embraced his neck and kissed his face. This signifies that when Reason has defended sensuality—which was already helping itself—it then embraces it and almost entirely surrounds it to make it better armed against vices; and it kisses his face: that is, it applauds and almost coaxes it toward doing good. AND HE SAID, Disdainful soul. Understand this as "just disdain." He wants to show that just as that anger which is a vice was shown in the spirit, so in Dante is shown that irascible part which moves with just disdain against vices, which the Greeks call <term>Nemesis</term> <note>original: "Nemesin"</note>. In the Florentine language, this properly signifies reasonable and just indignation; and just as pride is a vice, so disdain is a virtue. This was excellently expressed by Petrarch: "And in a lady in love I still find pleasure / that she appears haughty and disdainful / not proud and reluctant" <note>original: "Et in donna amorosa anchor maggrada / Chen uista uada altiera et disdegnosa / Non superba & ritrosa."</note>. BLESSED IS SHE who bore you: that is, blessed be your mother, who when she was pregnant with you wore a belt over her womb where you were. Literarily wanting to show the congratulation Virgil offered to Dante, he used the words common in the custom of praising a tree when it produces good fruit. Nor should Dante be blamed for praising himself here, because he does not praise himself. Rather, under his own name, he praises sensuality when it takes up just disdain against vice. And allegorically we can understand that Reason always commends the appetite when it is obedient to it; and it shows his mother, which is Reason itself, to be blessed. For such an appetite is created by reasonable judgment and not by the senses. THIS MAN WAS AN arrogant person in the world. Pride signifies arrogance: that is, he who attributes so much to himself that he cannot suffer anyone to oppose him or contradict any of his opinions, or touch him in any way. And nevertheless, he is worth little. Therefore, it is fitting that no fame remains of such men except for their bizarre behavior, because they had no goodness or virtue in them for which they could be named. There can be no greater punishment for the arrogant than to acquire infamy instead of fame. And princes and lords are greatly stained by this vice; being swollen by their good fortune, they lead themselves to believe they are wiser than others. And certainly...

<summary>This page covers Dante's encounter with the wrathful Filippo Argenti in the Styx. Landino explains the allegory of "just disdain" (Nemesis) versus sinful anger, interpreting Virgil as the Higher Reason that protects and rewards the soul for rejecting vice.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante’s Inferno, Canto VIII. It discusses the moral fall of the proud and moves into the specific encounter with the Florentine knight Filippo Argenti, followed by the approach to the City of Dis.</meta>

<header>INFERNO.</header>

It is a difficult thing not to become proud in times of prosperity, and not to be deceived about oneself—especially <note>original: "maxime"</note> because there are very few who dare to show a ruler their errors. Instead, they always have an infinite crowd around them of flatterers and "yes-men," who are ready to praise even those things worthy of the highest blame. Thus, while they are in a good state, everyone praises them; but afterward, everyone blames them. When they realize this, they gnaw at themselves and fly into a rage. And for this reason, the poet rightfully says: HOW MANY hold themselves up there—that is, in life and in prosperity—as GREAT KINGS, great princes. It is as if he says they consider themselves worthy of that status, and so everyone proclaims them. They hold themselves as kings, but they are not. For he is truly a king who rightly rules himself and others. Therefore, Alexander the Great <note>original: "Alexandro magno"</note> was not a king when he was conquered by anger or by wine; nor was anyone else who did not judge rightly or contain themselves within the bounds of temperance. For this reason, the Stoics <term>Stoics: an ancient Greek school of philosophy that taught that virtue and wisdom are the only true paths to freedom</term> rightly conclude that only the wise man is a king, because no one unless he is wise can rightly rule himself and others. WHO HERE IN HELL: that is, either after death or when they have fallen from such a high rank. WILL STAND LIKE pigs in the mire. They will be depressed, despised, and cast into infamy, because men will then dare to speak the truth about them. Thus, in place of the good fame they craved, they leave behind ignominy.

### And I: "Master, I would be very eager
### to see him dunked into this swill
### before we leave the lake."
### And he to me: "Before the shore
### lets itself be seen, you shall be satisfied;
### it is fitting that you enjoy such a desire."
### A little after this, I saw that soul
### so mangled by the muddy people
### that I still praise and thank God for it.
### All cried out: "At Filippo Argenti!"
### and the bizarre Florentine spirit
### turned his teeth upon himself.
### There we left him, so that I tell no more of him;
### but a wail struck my ears,
### so that I leaned forward with eyes wide open.

The poet proceeds most wisely. For since Dante is in a state where his appetite is obedient to reason, and because of this he has been moved to righteous indignation, he desires that the "bizarre" one be punished. And Virgil—who represents reason, which ensures that every sin is followed by its punishment—promises him that he will see him mangled. Furthermore, Dante includes this to show that the arrogant are hateful to every man, and that everyone desires to see them punished. And he wants him dunked IN THE SWILL <note>original: "nella broda"</note>. In Florentine, we say *brodo* and *broda*. *Brodo* <term>broth</term> is that in which food is cooked and eaten. But *broda* <term>swill or dishwater</term> is the wash-water of filthy vessels and any murky water. Here he uses it to mean infamy and ignominy. AND HE TO me: "Before the shore lets itself be seen"—that is, before you can see the bank of the marsh toward which we are sailing. YOU SHALL BE SATISFIED: that is, you will see him so mangled that it will be enough for you. AND IT IS FITTING that you enjoy such a desire, because he enjoys what he desires who obtains it. A LITTLE AFTER THIS: shortly after Virgil's words, I saw this man being mangled by the muddy people—that is, by those who were stained by the same vice. This denotes that one proud person punishes another. Nor did Dante feel compassion for these, because no reasonable man regrets the punishment of such people. There are some vices for which, although a man is reasonably punished, they nevertheless move our senses to compassion. Thus, he showed above—both in the punishment of Francesca and others like her—that he felt no small compassion. And so, conversely, there are other vices that move us to indignation and not compassion, such as this one, and all those involving contempt or cruelty. For in the punishment of these, we raise our hands to heaven. ALL cried out: that is, shouting they said, "AT FILIPPO"—that is, "get Filippo." According to what Boccaccio <note>Giovanni Boccaccio, the famous author and early commentator on Dante</note> says he heard from Coppo di Borghese Domenichi, this man was a knight of the noble Cavicciuli family, who are a branch of the Adimari. He was so rich that he used to have his horse shod with silver <note>Italian: *argento*, hence his nickname "Argenti"</note>. He was a man of great stature, well-muscled, of dark complexion, and of marvelous strength. But he was so conquered by anger that at every little offense, he would flare up beyond all measure. THE FLORENTINE spirit, bizarre: excessively wrathful, which is what "bizarro" means in our language. We do not call anyone "bizarro" unless they flare up often, suddenly, and for every small offense. UPON HIMSELF he turned with his teeth: that is, seeing himself attacked and being unable to defend himself, he bit himself out of rage. By these words, the author shows the beastly nature of the wrathful. It also denotes that he who flares up in anger harms himself more than others. THERE we left him, so that I tell no more: we leave him here because the wrathful man remains in this state, and his end is to turn his anger upon himself in one of two ways: either when he cannot avenge the injury, or when he repents the error committed, like Alexander the Great who many times wanted to kill himself when, after his anger had passed, he recognized how much he had erred. SO THAT I TELL no more: that is, one cannot describe a more extreme fury of the wrathful than this—that he turns his rage upon himself. And when we have told this of the wrathful, we can say no more; or he said "I tell no more" to show that such men are not worthy of being spoken of. BUT A WAIL STRUCK my ears: that is, I heard a sorrowful voice. We hear when a voice reaches the ear and strikes it. SO THAT I leaned forward with eyes wide open: that is, having heard the voice, I immediately opened my eyes wide with attention on every side. FORWARD: looking ahead of me; for when we hear a voice, we are accustomed to look diligently to see if we can perceive where it comes from.

### The good master said: "Now, my son,
### the city named Dis draws near,
### with its burdened citizens and great throng."
### And I: "Master, I already discern
### its mosques clearly there in the valley,
### vermillion, as if they had come out
### of fire." And he said to me: "The eternal fire
### that burns within them makes them look red,
### as you see in this low hell."

Sailing along, they were already so near the city located in the middle of the marsh that the largest and tallest buildings were beginning to be discerned. Here it is to be understood that the poet in this imitates Virgil as much as our religion allows. For Virgil describes hell and in the first circles places the lesser sins, those which were mixed with some image of virtue. Afterward, he describes Tartarus surrounded by the Phlegethon, a fiery river. He places gates with columns of adamant. He places a tower of iron. He places the infernal fury Tisiphone to guard the gate. Similarly, Dante in the upper circles has placed the lighter sins, which, because they proceed from incontinence, are worthy of some commiseration. And as for the moral sense, although it is difficult to change any habit...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante’s Inferno, Canto VIII. It explores the transition from the sins of upper Hell (incontinence) to the more severe sins found within the City of Dis (violence and fraud). The translator notes that the text focuses on the psychological and philosophical nature of "habitual" sin.</meta>

# CANTO VIII

Nonetheless, it is more difficult to change one's course regarding those sins which proceed either from violence or from fraud. Furthermore, the sinners already discussed are not entirely stripped of some shadow and image of humanity. But those who are punished in the City of Dis have their origin in supreme cruelty and inhumanity. And the further our soul is distanced and removed from humanity by such wicked crimes, the more difficult it is to return to it. This is why, although the first gate—which embraces and includes within itself all the descended vices—says *abandon all hope, you who enter* <note>Dante’s famous inscription at the gate of Hell: "Lasciate ogne speranza, voi ch'intrate."</note>, showing that there is no redemption for those who have turned vice into a settled habit, this is nonetheless found much more so in the more serious sins. For this reason, the poet imagines this city to be impregnable. THE CITY WHICH IS NAMED DIS APPROACHES. The author names this city after its lord. For the poets say that Pluto, whom the Latins call Dis, is the lord of the underworld. WITH GRIEVOUS [CITIZENS]: that is, full of gravity and distress. WITH THE GREAT THRONG. This denotes that those who go there by sinning are infinite in number. AND I, MASTER, ALREADY DISCERN ITS MOSQUES therein. He means to say: "I see the largest buildings within it," which he calls "mosques" <term>Meşhite: Landino uses the term for mosques to describe the demonic architecture, reflecting a 15th-century view of non-Christian temples as sites of "false" worship</term>. In the Turkish language, this signifies their temples where they worship Muhammad. These have high towers where a man climbs to call the people with loud voices, as they do not have bells to gather them. And he deservedly calls the place where sinners are tormented "mosques," because here one can say is the temple where sacrifice is made to the devil. VERMILION: As if glowing red; for he imagines these buildings to be made of fire, and made red-hot by the constant flames. In this, he imitates Virgil <note>original: "Que rapidus flamis ambit torrentibus amnis tartareus Phlegeton"</note>: *Which the Tartarean Phlegethon, a river, surrounds with rapid, burning flames.* Also <note>original: "Stat ferrea turris ad auras"</note>: *An iron tower stands up toward the air.* And certainly, much greater and more furious fires burn in the souls of such sinners, and there is more hardness in their hearts than in those who are outside of Dis.

> We finally arrived inside the deep ditches
> that moat that desolate land;
> the walls seemed to me to be of iron.
> Not without first making a great circuit
> did we come to a place where the boatman loudly
> shouted to us: "Out with you, here is the entrance."

<column-break/>

WE FINALLY: that is, at last. As if to say: "Although the voyage was long, we nonetheless arrived." INSIDE THE DEEP DITCHES. This shows that the land was impregnable. For it first had very deep ditches which MOATED it: that is, surrounded it—this is a Latin-derived word. THAT DESOLATE LAND: that is, the place where the damned have no consolation. Then it had walls of iron, as we said above. He who descends into the ditches moves away not only from heaven but from the surface of the earth. Likewise, the soul that has made a total habit of wicked vices always sinks deeper and is submerged in earthly things, distancing itself from heavenly ones. This makes the city of Dis very impregnable, because it does not let the man escape from sin. And just as a blind man without a guide easily falls into a ditch, so the man who has lost the light of reason falls into the ditch of vices with his blind appetite. NOT WITHOUT first making a great circuit: If we wish to apply this to one who enters this city through contemplation, we would say "not without a great circuit"—that is, not without a long discourse of reason and a circuit of speculation does one come to the knowledge of these vices. If applied to those who enter to remain in eternal torment, this too is "not without a great circuit," because such a habit of vice is not formed—from which one cannot escape—unless we have first circled around it many times with many operations and actions; for *habit is formed from repeated actions* <note>original: "Habitus fit ex frequentatis actibus"</note>. And so that this boatman and this gate do not seem superfluous (having placed another gate above where it is written "Through me one goes," etc., and another boatman at the Acheron), we must understand that up to this point he has described the first precinct, and almost the suburbs of the city, in which he placed those who sin through incontinence. Now he sets the second precinct where the sins committed through violence are punished. And further inside, another boatman and another precinct where those who have committed fraud are tormented. And although many interpret the rivers as the passage into some form of knowledge, it pleases us to interpret them as the appetite which leads the ship of will and choice into sin. And above we have shown what reason moves us to give such an allegory.

<column-break/>

> I saw more than a thousand upon the gates
> rained down from heaven, who spitefully
> said: "Who is this man who, without death,
> goes through the kingdom of the dead people?"
> My wise master made a sign
> of wanting to speak to them secretly.
> Then they shut in their great disdain a little
> and said: "Come you alone, and let him go
> who so boldly entered through this kingdom.
> Let him return alone on his mad path;
> let him try if he knows it, for you shall remain here,
> you who have escorted him through such a dark country."
> Think, reader, if I lost heart
> at the sound of those cursed words,
> for I did not believe I would ever return.

<column-break/>

I SAW More than a thousand: He uses a specific number for an indeterminate one. As Persius says <note>original: "Mille hominum species"</note>: *A thousand species of men.* Therefore, I saw many. RAINED DOWN FROM HEAVEN: Demons, who, following the side of Lucifer, rain down from heaven as we said above. SPITEFULLY: Wrathfully. WHO IS THIS MAN who without death goes through the kingdom of the dead people? Those in Hell are "dead" because there is no redemption, and those in the flesh are "living" because there is redemption. Allegorically, he is dead who has made a habit of vice, because he cannot detach himself from it. And he is living who has not made a habit, nor is entangled in it, but wishes to enter into vice through contemplation, which subsequently causes him to guard himself against it. Therefore the demon, who desires damnation, just as he willingly appears to those who remain there, so conversely he does not want to open to the living. That is, he does not want those who have not made a habit of it to have the knowledge by which they can guard themselves, and so they strive to take it from him. Virgil—that is, the rational part, without which Dante could neither enter the city nor return back. For if sensuality and the lower reason were abandoned by the higher reason in the knowledge of vices, they would allow themselves to be baited and captured by them. They would make a habit of it and could not leave Hell, nor enter into the contemplation of vices. Not without cause did he say "more than a thousand," because the temptations that lure us to vices are innumerable. MY WISE master made a sign of wanting to speak to them secretly. Virgil wants to speak to the demons in secret from Dante; that is, the higher reason by itself, which has knowledge of universals, wants to placate the guardians of that city so they might open the gates, because every speculative science deals with universals and not with particulars, which [do] not...

<meta>The catchword at the bottom "ra" likely leads into "ragione" (reason) or "rappresentano" (represent) on the following page.</meta>

<summary>Dante and Virgil reach the iron-walled City of Dis, representing the transition from sins of passion to habitual, malicious sins. Landino explains the allegorical necessity of reason (Virgil) to navigate these deeper vices without becoming trapped by habit.</summary>
<keywords>City of Dis, Pluto, mosques, habit of sin, Phlegethon, demons, reason vs. sensuality, Cristoforo Landino, allegory of Hell</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the philosophical commentary on Dante’s Inferno, Canto VIII. It explores the psychological struggle when the "superior reason" (represented by Virgil) and the "inferior reason" or "senses" (represented by Dante) encounter the City of Dis. It focuses on the demons' attempt to separate the two, and Virgil's role in comforting Dante’s "fainting spirit."</meta>

# INFERNO

...Dante acts: that is, the senses and the inferior reason. There can be no temptation that overcomes the soul in which ignorance does not fall. Therefore, to overcome temptation, the superior reason, instructed by judgment, is necessary; this judgment was not in the senses. **THEN THEY STIFLED a little their great disdain**: That is, they hid their design and showed themselves somewhat pacified. **And they said, come you alone and let that one go**. As if to say that only the superior reason is admitted into speculation <note>Landino interprets the scene as an allegory for intellectual contemplation, where the higher mind "enters" the problem while the lower senses must wait outside.</note>, nor can the gate be barred to it because it knows the first principles. And let Dante go, representing the inferior reason mentioned just above. **WHO SO BOLDLY ENTERED through this kingdom**. And certainly it is not without temerity that the inferior reason sets itself to contemplate, because it is not suited for universal contemplations, but for particular actions. Nevertheless, the demon could not reasonably reprove Dante for temerity, because he did not set himself alone to contemplate, but followed the superior reason. But the demon often tempts the inferior reason in the human soul to make it cowardly so that it does not set itself to knowledge. And certainly, if it were not accompanied by the superior reason, it would grow weary and fall into despair. **LET HIM RETURN ALONE by his foolish road**: That is, let him return alone in his folly. This is a poetic way of attributing to a thing what belongs to the man. Thus Virgil wrote: *Savage [Fury] sitting upon arms* <note>original: "Seva sedens super arma." A reference to the Aeneid, describing the personification of Rage bound and defeated.</note>. Truly he said "foolish road," because the road that leads to vice is full of foolishness, seeing as sin is born from ignorance. And he says "let him return alone" as if to say it will be impossible for him. For without superior reason, the sensuality would not emerge or untangle itself from vices. Hence, Dante demonstrates this by saying he never believed he would return from there—that is, emerge from Hell (vices) and return to life. **LET HIM TRY if he knows how**: This is our way of speaking: "let him try if he knows how," as if to say he will not know and will not be able. **FOR YOU SHALL REMAIN HERE**: because in truth our intellect, signified by Virgil, always turns around speculatable things, and it is that which provides light through the darkness—that is, it demonstrates obscure things to the inferior part.

---

O my dear leader, who more than seven
times has restored my confidence and drawn
me from other perils that stood against me,
do not leave me, I said, so suddenly;
and if passing further is denied us,
let us retrace our steps together quickly.

<column-break/>

Excellent. He says: **O MY DEAR LEADER**: Because reason is naturally the guide of the sensitive part. But in a man who follows appetite and not reason, such a guide is not dear to him. Yet it is very dear to one who submits his appetite to it; and the appetite follows it not by force, like a bad slave follows a master, but willingly, like a good son follows a father. **WHO MORE than seven times**: That is, many times; he uses a specific number to represent many, as we showed above. And he names the number seven not without cause, because as we mentioned before, it is a perfect number. From this, Pallas <note>The Greek goddess Athena, representing wisdom.</note> is named. Let us understand, therefore, by **seven times**, which is a perfect number, the perfection of the thing: because in truth the sense perishes when it is rebellious to reason. But when it follows it, it is perfectly drawn by it from every danger. **YOU HAVE restored my confidence and drawn me from danger**: He mentions two things which can exist one without the other. For we can be in some danger and, by not knowing it, we do not fear it. In that case, we are "secure"—that is, without fear—and nonetheless we are in danger. Therefore he shows that Virgil not only gave him confidence but also drew him out of danger. This occurred when you lifted me from before the three beasts, and when you calmed the wrath of Charon, of Minos, of Cerberus, and of the others who opposed our path. **DO NOT leave me suddenly**. And certainly the appetite in the human soul is destroyed "suddenly" if reason abandons it, because finally it perishes. **AND if passing further is denied us**. Nothing else feeds the human mind but the knowledge of things; and because one must go to that knowledge cleansed of every stain, as we showed above, we must begin from the knowledge of vices. Having made some progress in this, if we cannot proceed further—that is, to know them all—we must turn back: that is, exit from those which we have recognized. And he shows that we have to observe three things to turn back. First, to return by the same tracks. This signifies that just as we descended into vice only by way of knowing it (and not by staining ourselves with it), once known, we must repent by the same path. The second is to return together, because every time the appetite separates from reason, it perishes. The third is that we must return quickly. For having recognized the malignancy of vice, we must immediately depart from it. We can also give it another meaning, by which Dante shows that the inferior reason, when it finds some difficulty in virtuous operation, willingly withdraws from its purpose—as Virgil said: *And in the middle of the work, he left the plows fixed* <note>original: "Atque opere in medio defixa aratra reliquit." A quote from Virgil's Georgics, used here to describe the loss of resolve.</note>—if the intellect does not restrain and comfort it.

---

And that lord who had led me there
said to me: "Fear not, for our passage
no one can take from us; by such a One it is given.
But wait for me here, and comfort and feed
your weary spirit with good hope,
for I will not leave you in the low world."

<column-break/>

Reason comforts the weary sensuality, which has already fallen into despair. Therefore, in this part, he rightly calls him "lord." We have shown that reason is a guide to the appetite when the appetite follows it. But because here Dante—that is, sensuality—wished to return without waiting for the deliberation of reason, reason like a lord constrains him to proceed. **AND THAT lord who had led me there**. As if to say: having conducted me safely this far, I should hope he would do the same for the rest of the journey. **FEAR NOT**: and he gives the reason: because no one can take this passage from us. **BY SUCH A ONE**: that is, by one so powerful. **IT IS GIVEN**: Because it was granted to them by God to go through all of Hell. Nor can any diabolical temptation harm one who is accompanied by divine grace. **BUT WAIT FOR ME HERE**: wait for me here. And certainly, when the intellect arrives at some difficulty in contemplating, the appetite must stop and wait until the intellect overcomes that difficulty and understands what it seeks to understand. **And comfort and feed your weary spirit**. The sensitive and appetitive part <term>appetitive part: the faculty of the soul responsible for desires and emotions, which must be governed by the intellect</term>, and even the active part, cannot rise to where the intellectual part ascends. Rather, it needs some rest and to be comforted by the intellect. **WITH good hope**: Not every hope is good, but that which the undisturbed soul takes in honest and possible things. **FOR I WILL NOT leave you in the low world**: And certainly sensuality would remain in the "low way." For it is always prone to earthly things if the intellect does not lift our soul to divine ones. Take this hope, then, and trust in it.

<summary>This page contains Cristoforo Landino's commentary on the psychological and philosophical journey of Dante at the gates of the City of Dis, emphasizing the necessity of the "superior reason" (intellect) to guide the "inferior reason" (senses) away from vice. It interprets Virgil's comfort as the intellect providing "good hope" to the human appetite to prevent it from falling into despair or remaining trapped in earthly desires.</summary>
<keywords>inferior reason, superior reason, sensuality, appetite, Virgil, City of Dis, seven times, Pallas, allegory, divine grace, repentance, intellectual contemplation</keywords>

--- Page 115 ---
<meta>This page continues the commentary on Canto VIII of the Inferno, specifically focusing on the moment Virgil leaves Dante to negotiate with the demons at the gates of the City of Dis. It explores the allegorical separation of the "intellect" from the "senses."</meta>

# CANTO EIGHT.

->It shows that after these words were spoken, he departed, going toward the demons, and left him.<-

**AND THERE he abandons me, the sweet father:** He leaves Dante here because <term>sensuality</term> <note>In Landino’s commentary, "sensuality" refers to the lower, physical part of the human soul that reacts to the world through the senses rather than logic.</note> could not reach that height. But he does not abandon him to desert him, but to clear the way through which he may later guide him. **SAID THE sweet father:** To denote that he did not leave him out of hatred or cruelty, but out of paternal love; just as a father often leaves his small children—who cannot follow him—to provide for their needs and return with things prepared, so Virgil left Dante with the intention of returning for him when he has provided what is needed. **AND I REMAIN in doubt:** That is, in uncertainty whether he will return or not. This is better declared by saying: **FOR "NO" AND "YES" contend within my head:** In the head, where the vir-

So he goes; and there he abandons me,
the sweet father; and I remain in doubt;
for "no" and "yes" contend within my head.
I could not hear what was then offered to them;
but he did not stay there long with them,
for each rushed back inside to prove it.
Those adversaries of ours closed the gates
in the breast of my lord, who remained outside,
and he turned back to me with slow steps.
His eyes to the earth; and his brows were shorn
of all boldness; and he said in his sighs:
"Who has denied me the houses of sorrow?"

<column-break/>

-tue of <term>judgment</term> <note>original: "estimativa"</note> is born, from which judgment arises. **Contend** <note>original: "tenciona"</note> means to fight, and it is an ancient Florentine word that we rarely use in our times. But so that the allegory may proceed: Virgil guides Dante, and as long as the way is not denied to him—that is, superior reason—he guides sensuality while he can show it the truth. But when something arrives that reason does not understand, it is necessary for the appetite to stop until the intellect acquires knowledge of that which it does not yet possess. And having acquired it, he returns to Dante and moves him to follow the path; that is, he moves the appetite to follow in contemplation. But the appetite, abandoned by reason and not wanting to rashly take a side without her counsel, stops and remains in doubt whether Virgil will return or not—that is, whether the intellect will be able to arrive at such knowledge or not. **I COULD NOT hear what was then offered:** Sensuality cannot hear what the intellect says, because speculation belongs only to the intellect. **BUT HE DID NOT stay there long:** That is, not much. **Long** <note>original: "guari"</note> is an ancient Florentine word and signifies "much," and is not in use in our times. The meaning is that Virgil, not being able to make the gates open in a short time, returned to Dante. For when the intellect cannot understand something by itself, it quickly realizes that it cannot understand, and returns to sensuality.

---

**THEY CLOSED THE gates, those adversaries of ours:** This verse is pronounced with sorrow and complaint, because it seemed an unworthy thing that the gate should be closed to such a man. And certainly we are amazed when we see a man of great learning reach doubts which he does not know how to solve. **IN THE BREAST of my lord, who remained outside:** This denotes that thought is in the heart, and the heart is in the breast. Therefore, our adversaries—that is, diabolical fraud—prohibit the thought of the learned man from entering inside the gate; that is, he cannot enter into knowledge through the true way. **AND HE TURNED to me with slow steps:** The intellect returns to sensuality when it cannot proceed in knowledge, so that if it cannot guide it further forward, at least it keeps it firm where it is, until with the help of others it can bring it inside the gates. **WITH SLOW STEPS:** As every deep thinker does, because he goes along thinking and often stops. He who thinks engages in a discourse of the mind, and in that discourse he often stops where he finds an ambiguous place. And by stopping the soul, he makes the body stop, or go as slowly as the discourse goes. This was expressed by Virgil: <note>original: "Cui fidus achates It comes & paribus curis vestigia figit"</note> *With whom faithful Achates goes as a companion and fixes his steps with equal cares.* **EYES TO the earth:** And this is also the habit of a man who thinks—to fix his eyes on the ground. The eye, when it turns to various things, distracts the mind from its discourse; and it seems that it pushes the intellect wherever it looks. Therefore, to steady the soul, we also steady the eyes, and especially on the ground where there can occur no variety or motion that might distract it. **And HIS BROWS were shorn:** As if empty of all boldness; and certainly in the eyes one recognizes who has boldness—that is, who confides in himself—or who has lost it. **AND HE SAID IN HIS SIGHS, who has denied me the houses of sorrow:** Virgil was not speaking, but he came along thinking, and in his sighs it seemed he said that. **WHO HAS denied:** As if he says: "He who can do nothing against the will of Him who sends me." And truly, although it always pains us to be defeated, nonetheless it is much more troublesome to be defeated by those who are inferior to us.

---

And to me he said: "You, though I am angry,
do not be dismayed, for I shall win the trial,
no matter who circles within to defend.
This arrogance of theirs is not new to me;
for they used it already at a less secret gate,
which still stands without its bolts.
Above it you saw the dead writing,
and already from this side of it descends the slope,
passing through the circles without a guide,
such that by him the land shall be opened to us."

<column-break/>

Virgil does not want Dante to be dismayed because he himself is indignant. For although the intellect cannot understand by itself, it nonetheless hopes to be able to do so with divine favor. And therefore: **DO NOT be dismayed, for I shall win the trial:** if not with my own strength, then with divine help. **NO MATTER who circles within:** that is, whoever it may be who goes around inside to make a defense so that we might not enter. And he said "circles" <note>original: "saggiri"</note> truly to show the habit of those who stand in defense of a land, who go around the walls to provide for every part. Or truly he said "circles"—that is, he toils in vain. For the Florentine says "he goes around" <note>original: "lui si va aggirando"</note> when he makes no progress in his labor. And to show that it is not to be wondered at that they are so bold that they set themselves to defend what they cannot defend, he says it is their ancient habit to do this. Therefore: **IT IS NOT NEW:** that is, unusual, **THIS ARROGANCE of theirs:** that is, presumption and impudent audacity. Hence he says "The arrogant race," meaning bold and reckless.

---

**FOR THEY USED IT ALREADY at a less secret gate:** He means by this the first gate of Hell. Between that gate and this one in the sixth circle are the punished who proceed from incontinence, which is more easily understood; therefore Virgil—that is, human intellect—was able to guide Dante by himself. And for this reason it is "less secret," meaning less obscure. And he refers to when the demons tried to resist when Christ despoiled Limbo. Wherefore the Psalmist said: <note>original: "Tollite portas principes vestras & introibit rex glorię"</note> *Lift up your gates, O you princes, and the King of Glory shall enter.* This signifies that all laws and sentences given against the disobedience of the first man were broken. **WHICH STILL stands without its bolts:** because from the Passion of Christ until now, it can no longer hold the souls of the baptized just. **ABOVE IT you saw the dead writing:** This responds to the verse: *These words of a dark color I saw written above a gate.* **AND ALREADY from this side of it descends the slope:** He says that already the angel sent by God to open the gate has entered the first gate and descends the slope. Every steep place has an ascent and a descent; but it is called an "ascent" <note>original: "erta"</note> to one who climbs it, and a "slope" <note>original: "china"</note> to one who descends it. Therefore he used "ascent" for "slope" since the angel was descending, just as Virgil uses the end for the beginning: <note>original: "Oceani finem iuxta: solemque cadentem"</note> *Near the end of the Ocean and the setting sun.* Or truly he said "ascent" in regard to himself, who—

# INFERNO.

...[holding] them, being already below, the path became steep for him again. **PASSING through the circles without an escort:** because divine power has no need for an escort. <note>The commentator explains that the Heavenly Messenger, as an agent of God, requires no guide or protection to navigate the depths of Hell, unlike Virgil and Dante.</note> **SO THAT THROUGH HIM:** that is, by his means, the gate of the land may be opened to us: that is, the gate of the city. <note>The "land" or "city" refers to Dis, the lower part of Hell where more grievous sins are punished.</note> And we shall explain this allegory better in the following chapter.

<header>CANTO NINE</header>

## CANTO NINE OF THE FIRST CANTICLE BY DANTE.

That color which cowardice painted on my face
seeing my leader turning back
more quickly repressed his own new color

Attentive he stopped like a man who listens
for the eye could not lead him far
through the black air and through the thick fog
Yet it will be necessary for us to win the battle
he began, if not... such a one offered herself to us
O how long it seems to me until another arrives here.

I saw well how he covered over
the beginning with what came after
for the words were different from the first:
But nonetheless his speech gave me fear:
because I drew from the broken word
perhaps a worse meaning than it held:

<column-break/>

IN this ninth chapter, he describes the counsel of Virgil regarding the entry into the city and the infernal monsters that are there: and by whose help they entered: and finally, he demonstrates with what punishments the heretics are tormented. The subject matter is almost new: and where there are horrible sins: which do not deserve any compassion: because they do not arise from the stimulus of the flesh: like disordered love: or gluttony, or anger. But from the wicked malice of a perverse soul: And although in all vices frequent acts create a habit. Nonetheless, in the past ones there is more incontinency than intemperance. <note>In Aristotelian ethics, "incontinency" is a failure of the will, while "intemperance" is a deliberate choice of vice.</note> But in these, one sees a most perverse obstinacy. And because for whoever makes a habit of these it is almost impossible that they can withdraw themselves: therefore he puts them inside the city surrounded by walls of iron. To denote that it is impregnable: as we said above: But to return to the text, the meaning of the first tercet is that Dante being frightened: and for this reason turning pale because of the change he had seen in the face of Virgil: And Virgil, noticing this, repressed his indignation and his perturbation: and cleared his face: and brought it back to its natural color: so that Dante too might set aside his fear. And certainly, every time that the rational part in man takes fright at not being able to achieve something, the sensuality <note>The "sensuality" refers to the lower, physical emotions and instincts.</note> is much afraid. And it latently admonishes that whoever is placed in government and the ruling of others must often in dangers show himself to be of good spirit: so that those who are under his government do not take fright. Which Virgil attributes to Aeneas when he says: **He feigns hope on his face, while pressing deep grief in his heart.** <note>original: "Spem uultu simulat premit altum corde dolorem" from Virgil's Aeneid, Book I, line 209.</note>
And the text is ordered. *That color which cowardice* that is, fear, *painted* out, understand on the face. Because paleness in the face is nothing other than a lack of blood: which through fear flees to the heart: and leaves the veins of the face empty. *SEEING My leader turning back.* As if he said without victory and driven away: because we say an army is "turned back" when, overcome by enemies, it turns its back. *MORE QUICKLY INSIDE his new color he repressed.* The pale color was new in Dante, because fear had made him become pale. Similarly, the flushed color was new in Virgil: because indignation had flushed his face. Because anger being the boiling of blood around the heart, as it boils it runs through all the veins: But it appears more in the face: because there are many subcutaneous veins: that is, in the skin so that they manifest themselves entirely. But Virgil seeing the fear of Dante arise from the change of his face, feigns to immediately repress such color within. Therefore; that color which was in me through fear born of cowardice repressed more quickly his new one: that is, Virgil’s. Because Virgil removed from his face the new color, i.e., the natural color. <note>Landino clarifies that Virgil is controlling his expression to hide his own frustration and reassure Dante.</note> But that which had newly appeared through indignation, seeing that Dante feared because of it: And this he said to denote that the wise man can anticipate in driving from himself the perturbations of the soul.

*ATTENTIVE He stopped.* It happens that when in a dark place we wait for someone: because the eye is of no use there, not being able to discern, we use hearing: so that by the noise or some other sound we perceive when he comes. Virgil did the same: But allegorically it is understood that when the intellect by itself cannot see the truth, occupied by the darkness of ignorance, it attentively awaits inspiration and divine help. *LIKE A MAN who listens* since the anger ceases: *FOR THE EYE could not lead him far.* He gives the reason: why he used the sense of hearing: because sight did not serve him from afar. *THROUGH THE BLACK AIR.* The more difficult the thing is, the more there is black air: that is, the greater is the obscurity of ignorance. Wherefore the psalm asks in this for divine favor saying: **To give light to those who sit in the shadow of death.** <note>original: "Illuminare iis qui in umbra mortis fedent" from the Song of Zechariah, Luke 1:79.</note>
*YET FOR US It will be necessary to win the battle.* This ignites the human intellect: when it reaches the contemplation of such high things: that it cannot understand them by itself. But when it then takes hope: that by divine help it still will. And in comfort of himself and of the lower reason he says *YET*: Almost finally *FOR US IT WILL BE NECESSARY to win the battle*: the contest of entering the gate. Which is to enter into knowledge. *HE BEGAN:* He began. *IF NOT:* And "if not" you might add "we could win the battle by ourselves, we will be helped." *SUCH A ONE offered.* i.e., such a one offered himself to us; like a man deep in thought he speaks with broken words: and does not finish the prayer. Which makes Dante doubt: But this we will explain a little below. *O HOW long it seems to me:* O how it delays in my opinion. *UNTIL ANOTHER arrives here:* that is, the angel that I expect. Because as Seneca says, to one who is in a hurry, every great speed seems a delay. Allegorically the intellect awaits the help of God and divine grace: and especially the "prevenient" <note>Prevenient grace is a theological concept referring to grace that precedes human decision, preparing the soul for salvation.</note> grace: which does not wait to be requested: But often runs ahead of the good will: Because as soon as our free will disposes itself to choose the good, the prevenient grace directs it along the good way.

Virgil *covered over* the beginning of his speech: in which he did not give certain hope, with the other speech that followed when he said *If not such a one offered herself:* which words were broken. Because it is necessary to supply: "such a one offered herself who will make us win," such a one, that is, one so powerful, and he means of God, "offered himself to us": And these were words different from the first: because those showed that he could win: These, that he had need of the help of others. But nonetheless, being different they are not opposite or contrary. But in short, they show more difficulty than he believed from the start: And it denotes that the intellect sometimes believes with continued discourse to achieve the knowledge of the thing: that it investigates. Then it realizes that it has need of greater light.
