<header>INFERNO.</header>

> Into this bottom of the sorrowful shell
> does anyone from the first grade ever descend
> who for punishment has only their hope cut off?
> I made this question, and he: “Rarely,”
> he replied to me, “does it happen
> that any of us makes the journey on which I go.
>
> It is true that once before I was down here,
> conjured by that cruel Erichtho
> who called shadows back to their bodies.
> My flesh had but recently been stripped of me
> when she made me enter inside that wall
> to draw out a spirit from the circle of Judas.
>
> That is the lowest place and the darkest,
> the furthest from the heaven that revolves all things;
> I know the path well; therefore, rest assured.”

<column-break/>

**D**ante strongly doubted his ability to enter the city; and having entered, he doubted whether Virgil knew how to guide him through the lower circles as he had guided him through the upper ones. And therefore he asks if anyone from the first circle <note>Limbo</note>, in which Virgil resided, had ever descended to the bottom. In this, he denotes that the lower reason—because it does not discern universal truths—doubts that even the higher reason knows how to discern them. And Virgil, sensing his fear, affirms that he has descended there to give him comfort. 

In this passage, our poet differs from Virgil <note>The author of the Aeneid</note>. For Virgil feigns that the Sibyl did not wish to lead Aeneas inside this city, but instead narrates to him the punishments found within. Dante, however, feigns that Virgil did lead him inside. Nevertheless, they are similar in this: both show that the guide had been there before (Virgil for Dante, and the Sibyl for Aeneas), so that Aeneas would trust what she narrated, and Dante would trust Virgil to remove the fear we showed above. Some argue that Dante writes this story of Virgil’s previous descent as a fiction to show that wise men often feign something not to deceive, but to introduce a concept. 

Furthermore, as we have said, he imitates Virgil in some way. If one asks why Dante, wishing to imitate Virgil, here seems to contradict him, I reply that it is not as contradictory as it seems. Virgil says, when showing that the Sibyl does not want to lead Aeneas into this city: <note>original: "Nulli fas casto sceleratum insistere limen"</note> “It is lawful for no holy person to tread upon the threshold of the wicked.” He means nothing else by this than that it is not permitted for any good person to remain there—that is, no one can be good who stays there and makes a habit of vice. But it seemed better to the Sibyl to narrate the vices to him and keep him outside—that is, to give him knowledge of them without him making a habit of them. Dante feigns that although Virgil leads him there, he nonetheless does not stay; which signifies the same thing: namely, entering into the knowledge of vice, but not making a habit of it. And this is more in accordance with the Christian religion, which believes that everyone enters this city—that is, everyone sins in some way. Whence David said: <note>original: "Omnis homo mendax"</note> “Every man is a liar”; and elsewhere: <note>original: "Septies in die cadit iustus"</note> “Seven times a day the just man falls.” But it is no small thing not to make a habit of it.

**IN THIS BOTTOM OF THE SORROWFUL SHELL:** In this low part of Hell, which he has described in the form of a vessel, which begins at the top with a wider circle and narrows as it goes lower. **FROM THE FIRST GRADE:** From the first circle where Limbo is, and where he placed the souls of virtuous men who were without faith. For these, as a penalty—that is, in place of punishment—they have **CIONCHA:** that is, their hope is cut off or severed, as he said above: “without hope we live in desire.” <term>Cioncho</term> is a Lombard word and signifies "cut off" and "diminished," and so he uses it here; but in Florentine, <term>cionchare</term> means to drink immoderately. 

**I MADE** this question: that is, this demand. For *querere* in Latin signifies both to seek and to ask. **AND HE:** And that Virgil replied saying **RARELY:** It happens rarely. **THAT ANY OF US:** that is, of us. **MAKES** the path by which I go. He says that although it happens rarely, it does sometimes happen. And allegorically he shows that few are those who descend into the meditation of vices to purge themselves of them. 

**IT IS TRUE THAT ONCE BEFORE:** He shows he was there shortly after his death, conjured by Erichtho. She was, according to Lucan, a sorceress in Thessaly who, at the request of Pompey the Great, drew a soul from Hell back into its body and made it say what the end of the civil war between Caesar and Pompey would be. Dante thus feigns that Virgil feigns this about himself for his comfort. Beyond this, it fits an ancient opinion that Zoroaster, the inventor of this art <note>magic</note>, practiced it to have knowledge of the immortality of the soul and its nature and power. We will speak of the magic arts below when that sin is treated. 

But as for the present text, it is to be doubted how Dante posits that Virgil’s soul was conjured and compelled, since our religion forbids it; for theologians do not believe that the magic art has this power. Therefore, Aurelius Augustine writes that the pythoness <note>the Witch of Endor</note> described in the first book of Kings, who spoke in the person of the prophet Samuel, was not Samuel, but a demon who feigned being Samuel. But one might reply that these are not the words of Dante or his opinion, but those of Virgil, who speaks according to the opinion of the pagan poets, as we see in Homer and Lucan and others. Furthermore, Dante notes in this place the fourth descent into Hell posited by the ancients. For as we said above, one descends into Hell in the first way when the soul, departing the body in mortal sin, goes into eternal damnation. In the second way, when still in the body, one descends into the habit of vice. In the third, when we descend into the contemplation of vices to purge ourselves of them. And according to these first three ways, he always writes throughout this first canticle. And he touches on the fourth in this place: not because he approves of it, but so that he does not omit any. 

**MY FLESH HAD BUT RECENTLY BEEN STRIPPED:** the flesh was naked—that is, deprived of me, Virgil. And he says "of me" excellently, because although man consists of soul and body, nonetheless, because man is defined by reason and intellect, the soul is truly what the man is, and the body is like a garment to the soul. 

**INSIDE THAT** wall: which you see is made of iron, to draw out a soul that was in the lowest circle, in which Judas is punished, and from him it is called **GIUDECCA**. **THAT IS THE** lowest place. If Hell descends to the center of the earth, and this circle is the lowest, it follows that it is in the center. And because every center is the part furthest from the circumference, it is furthest from the heavens **THAT REVOLVE ALL THINGS:** which, revolving, contain everything within themselves. **I KNOW THE PATH WELL:** He perceived that Dante feared he did not know the way because he had not been there; and therefore he concludes that he knows it. And perhaps Dante feigns that Virgil feigned being there to show that morally, wise men often say what is not true—not to deceive, but to comfort and encourage those who have taken some fright to persevere in good works.

<column-break/>

> This marsh which breathes out the great stench
> surrounds all around the sorrowful city
> where we cannot enter now without anger.

<column-break/>

**H**e shows that this Stygian marsh which breathes—that is, which exhales the great stench—does so because vapors and mists of foul odor rise from it. This is natural for any swamp. But also allegorically, from the sadness of the heart, many stenches arise: that is, many...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Canto IX of the Inferno. The previous page discussed Virgil's reassurance to Dante regarding their descent into the lower circles of Hell. This page begins with the appearance of the three Furies atop the tower of the City of Dis and explains the psychological and moral symbolism behind them.</meta>

# CANTO NINE.

And he said more: but I do not have it in mind
because my eye had entirely drawn me
toward the high tower with the glowing summit:
Where in an instant there suddenly stood upright
three infernal furies stained with blood
who had the limbs and behavior of women
And were girt with the greenest hydras:
they had small serpents and horned vipers for hair:
with which their fierce temples were bound.

---

And he, who well knew the wretched handmaidens
of the queen of eternal wailing,
said to me, "Look at the fierce Erinyes:
This is Megaera on the left side:
the one who wails on the right is Alecto:
Tisiphone is in the middle": and then he was silent.

<column-break/>

vices: GIRDING THE CITY OF DIS AROUND. SORROWFUL: because of the various and unbearable torments that are there. And certainly, vices do not leave behind anything other than repentance and sorrow. Hence Petrarch says excellently: *Repentance and sorrow behind the shoulders* <note>original: "Penitentia & dolor doppo le spalle"</note>. WE WILL NOT BE ABLE: where we will not be able TO ENTER without anger: because the adversaries oppose us. Nor should anyone marvel that he displays anger in the place where anger is punished. For here the poet wishes to demonstrate that there can be anger which is not only not a vice, but is a virtue: because it is just indignation that makes the soul courageous for every honorable undertaking. For as we have said, there is not only that part in our soul that desires the good—that is, the concupiscible <note>The "concupiscible" power is the faculty of the soul that seeks basic desires and pleasures.</note>—but also that which removes the obstacles that impede the good, and it is called the irascible <note>The "irascible" power is the faculty that deals with anger, courage, and overcoming difficulty.</note>. AND HE SAID MORE but I do not have it in mind: this shows that he was so suddenly drawn by the wonder of what he saw that, due to the sudden disturbance of his mind, he forgot many things that Virgil had said. And certainly, when a sudden movement arises in the soul, it is so disturbed that it forgets the precepts given to it by reason. This fiction of oblivion serves two things: first, that which we have said. Second, it happened that Virgil had to instruct him on many things which, if he had narrated them, would have made the sermon too long. Therefore, although he does not narrate them, he nevertheless hints to the listener what he ought to imagine. BECAUSE THE EYE had entirely drawn me toward the high tower: I say that forgetfulness of many things Virgil had told me came upon me because the eye—that is, my vision—HAD drawn me entirely: that is, it had snatched my whole soul. It is one thing to be guided, another to be drawn. For we go guided by our own will, but we go drawn by force. Therefore, reason guides us because, by persuading us and showing us that such a path is good, it makes us follow it voluntarily. But when a sudden perturbation of anger, or hatred, or love, or fear arises in us, even though we judge that what such passion shows us is not good, we are nonetheless drawn by it by force. What then does Dante—or let us say the sensory appetite—say? Certainly nothing else but that the sight of the furies drew him. This denotes that they led him by force, as if he were incontinent <note>Incontinence refers to the inability to restrain one's passions despite knowing what is right.</note>. But mention was made of the incontinent and the intemperate above in the first canto, and similarly of the temperate and the continent; therefore, you shall draw from there what serves this place. Now returning to the text, the poet wishes to denote in this fiction that reason admonished sensuality, but perturbation drew it in the opposite direction. HAD DRAWN ME ENTIRELY: drawn entirely, because a great perturbation occupies the whole mind so that reason is not heard. TOWARD THE TOWER: toward the tower of which we spoke above. GLOWING: On fire: because there is a great flame in fury and great heat. WHERE IN AN INSTANT there suddenly stood upright Three furies: who were in the dress and act of women. The furies, according to the poets, were the daughters of Acheron and of Night. Acheron signifies the deprivation of joy, and from the deprivation of joy arises fury; and night is dark, and from blindness and darkness of mind proceeds fury. Their names are Alecto, Tisiphone, and Megaera. Alecto signifies "without rest" <note>original: "sanza quiete"</note>, and restlessness is the beginning of fury. Tisiphone in the Greek language sounds like "avenger of slaughter" <note>Greek: *tisis* (vengeance) and *phonos* (slaughter)</note>, and this is the remorse of conscience of which we spoke above. Megaera takes her meaning from "hatred," from which one reaches extreme fury. They take the furies for the disordered appetite, which like a fury sets the human mind on fire, blinds it, and makes it fall headlong without counsel or virtue. For love, anger, hatred, ambition, and all other unbridled desires are nothing other than fury, which like an unbridled horse carries a man away over ditches and cliffs until it breaks his neck. Thus, headlong fury without reason carries away the soul. Hence, not without reason did he say: "Where in an instant there suddenly stood upright." For just as reason leads the soul with discourse, maturity, and counsel, so on the contrary, the infuriated appetite draws it suddenly without any counsel. THREE FURIES: as we have said, Alecto, Tisiphone, and Megaera. INFERNAL: the furies inhabit hell because they are always in vices. Or he said "infernal" because there is also found divine fury, of which we shall speak in a more convenient place—a thing described by Plato and excellently interpreted by our Platonist, Marsilio Ficino <note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499) was a famous philosopher and head of the Platonic Academy in Florence.</note>. STAINED WITH BLOOD: because from the furies are born discords, and from those, wars and killings. WHO HAD female limbs and behavior: They had the body and appearance of women. This is feigned because a woman is much more easily set on fire in fury than a male. Hence, even Virgil, when he wanted Alecto to cause the stag of Tyrrheus—the shepherd of the Latins—to be killed in Ascanius's hunt, caused the fury to be in the female dogs and not in the male dogs. The reason is that, there being less soul <note>meaning "strength of spirit" or "rational control"</note> in the female, she can less resist passions and perturbations. AND WITH greenest Hydras they were girt: He shows that in place of belts they had various species of snakes: because there is no more pestiferous poison to our souls and to the lives of mortals than fury. The Hydra is a serpent that inhabits the water, so called in Greek because *hydor* means water <note>original: "hydor significa acqua"</note>. And the poets say that in the Lernean swamp of Thessaly there was a hydra serpent, daughter of Echidna and Typhon, which Juno nourished against Hercules. And it was such an untamable monster that if one head were cut off, seven grew back. But Hercules, not being able to kill it with iron, was instructed by Minerva to burn it. Cerastes are serpents in Libya that have horns, so called because *ceras* means horn <note>original: "ceras significa corno"</note>. The furies appeared on the summit of the tower because fury cannot remain hidden, nor is it ever without pride and supreme burning.

---

And he: that is, Virgil, who WELL KNEW THE WRETCHED ONES: the furies, who truly are wretched, that is, miserable; because if tranquility of mind brings supreme joy, fury brings the opposite; and if wisdom is the supreme good, insanity is the supreme misery. Nor is it without reason that Virgil knows them and Dante does not: because the intellect is that which knows fury and the cause from which it proceeds, and not the senses, which—occupied by such insanity—lose all light and do not know the fury in which they find themselves. OF THE QUEEN of eternal wailing: of Proserpina, queen of hell. LOOK, HE SAID TO ME: It is not enough that the intellect knows what a pestilence these furies are, but it is necessary that it makes the appetite aware of them so that it may flee them. ERINYES: the Greeks call the furies Erinyes because *eris* means contention <note>original: "eris significa contentione"</note>. THIS IS Megaera on the left side: because hatred is worse than restlessness; but worst of all is the torment given by Tisiphone, and therefore he places her in the middle.

# INFERNO;

> With their nails they each tore at their breasts,
> they beat themselves with their palms and cried so loud
> that I pressed close to the poet out of fear.
> "Let Medusa come, and we will turn him to stone,"
> they all cried out, looking downward;
> "we ill-avenged the assault of Theseus."

<image-desc>Decorative initial 'D' inside a circular frame.</image-desc>
**He demonstrates** by the scratching of the chest and the beating of palms the rage of the furious; and he says that because of their loud cries he drew close to Virgil to be able to defend himself with his help. And certainly, against the onslaught of fury—which is born from some inner disturbance—lower reason <note>In medieval psychology, "lower reason" deals with earthly matters, while "higher reason" contemplates divine truths.</note> could not defend itself without the help of the higher. LET Medusa come, and we will turn him to stone. From Phorcys, a sea god, and Ceto, daughter of the sea and the earth, three daughters were born according to Hesiod: Stheno, Euryale, and Medusa. These were commonly called the Gorgons; the first two were immortal and Medusa was mortal. They had only one eye among all three of them, and

they used it in turn, now this one, now that one. Neptune burned with love for Medusa, and he joined with her in the temple of Pallas; for which incontinence Pallas conceived such hatred toward Medusa—she being the goddess of chastity and wisdom—that as vengeance, she converted Medusa’s hair (which, being very beautiful, had greatly moved Neptune to love) into little snakes. And she granted that whoever looked upon her would turn to stone. By these, the poets mean earthly and momentary goods: which, if desired for one's own necessity or to practice honorable liberality, are virtues—and this is shown by the two immortal sisters. But if they are desired to fulfill a disordered appetite, it is a supreme vice—and this one is mortal. And Neptune loves her, which signifies the sea, and is put for the appetite <note>Renaissance thinkers often compared the "appetite" or physical desires to the turbulent sea.</note>, because the appetite, disobedient to reason, prefers fleeting and mortal things to celestial ones. And he especially loves the hair—that is, the superfluous—and joins with her in the temple of Minerva, who is the goddess of chastity and wisdom, because either one acquires goods through prudence, or under the guise of some sanctity, deceit and fraud are committed to acquire them. And Minerva changes her beautiful hair into little snakes because wisdom finally uncovers such fraud and reveals its poison. Medusa turns men into stones because the excessive and disordered greed for false goods makes them seem so beautiful that we become stunned [stupefied] by them. And to every other thing we are blind and deaf, and almost without sensation. They say Medusa was killed by Perseus with the sword of Mercury and with the shield of Minerva, which, because it was crystal-clear, allowed him to see Medusa through it and not be seen by her. Perseus is put for the wise man, who with the sword of Mercury—that is, eloquent doctrine—kills Medusa: because he knows, and knows how to show others, that riches, lordships, dignities, powers, and similar things (which the ignorant common folk and all fools estimate to be good) are fleeting; they soon fail and always generate scandal, perturbations, and misery in human life. And when he kills her, he hides behind the shield of Minerva, because he opposes reason and wisdom between himself and these false goods, which defends him in such a way that they cannot harm him or draw him to love them. Medusa, therefore, stands well in the city where such atrocious wickednesses are punished; because if it were not for the immense greed for worldly goods, men would have their minds so raised that they would come into true knowledge of God; and desiring Him, they would not become impious against God, and would not commit any of those enormous errors that are punished inside the city of Dis. For this reason, the demons call Medusa against us. For diabolical temptation cannot overcome us except by inciting us so much to the greed for temporal goods that we become senseless to every virtuous operation. **WE ILL-AVENGED:** that is, we did not avenge. *Veggiare* signifies "to avenge" in the ancient Florentine language, and derives from *vendicare* by syncopation <note>The shortening of a word by dropping sounds from the middle.</note> and by the mutation of the 'd' into 'g'. **THE ASSAULT OF THESEUS:** that is, if they had avenged the injury received from Theseus, this man [Dante] at present would not have dared to come, also alive, into our kingdom. And allegorically, understand that as in evil, so too in good, example can do much. Therefore, if the furies, who desire evil, had punished Theseus for coming alive—that is, coming to purge himself of vices—Dante would not have followed him. Theseus was the son of Aegeus, king of Athens; and many tamed monsters are narrated of him, similar to those of Hercules. The Athenians and Megarians had killed, out of envy, Androgeus, son of Minos of Crete; and Minos conquered them, and in vengeance for his son imposed a harsh law: that each year seven Athenian youths, chosen by lot, should go to Crete to be devoured by the Minotaur. In the fourth year, the lot fell to Theseus; but with the help of Ariadne, daughter of Minos, he killed the Minotaur and returned free to Athens. He was a man of great counsel, and of no less spirit. He was the first, according to Pliny, who found confederations and leagues. The poets feign that together with Pirithous he went to the underworld to kidnap Proserpina. On this fable, Coluccio Salutati <note>A significant Florentine humanist and chancellor (1331–1406).</note>, a most learned Florentine and teacher of Leonardo Aretino [Bruni], wrote a most subtle allegory. For, since the poets feign that Hercules, Aeneas, Theseus, Pirithous, Amphiaraus, and Orpheus descended to the underworld, he demonstrates that in these are expressed various kinds of desirable things. So that this may be better understood, let us repeat that human life is either active or contemplative. Contemplation is directed toward the true; the active toward the good. Not that truth and goodness are not the same thing: because that which is good is true, and that which is true is good. But the true is insofar as it is knowable, and the good is insofar as it is desirable. Therefore, the contemplative tends toward the true; the active toward the good. But the good is of three kinds: that is, honest, useful, and pleasurable. The honest is the true good; hence the Stoics placed the supreme good in virtue. The pleasurable is that which the Epicureans affirmed to be the supreme good. The useful is the opinion of the common people. Understanding this, our Coluccio wants the speculative good and the knowledge of the truth to be expressed in Homer by Hercules and in Virgil by Aeneas; and similarly the honest good, provided that the doctrine is determined. But when it is uncertain, as among the Academics <note>Followers of the later Platonic Academy who practiced skepticism.</note>, such a descent is figured by Amphiaraus. The pleasurable is figured by Orpheus. The useful by Theseus and Pirithous. And in this, he takes Theseus for the soul and Pirithous for the body; and as these were the greatest of friends, so the soul and the body are joined with the greatest friendship. And he demonstrates reason through Theseus, and sensuality through Pirithous—certain things worthy of his doctrine and his intellect. But because they are prolix and not very relevant to this place, I omit them. Let it be enough that the demons complain of not having punished Theseus while he burned alive—that is, descending to the underworld while speculating—by whose example Dante has taken the same daring. For if they did not restrain him who descended to the underworld for the knowledge of the "useful" (a completely common thing, and in which he does not demonstrate any divinity of reason), they give boldness to Dante, that they will not be able to restrain him as he descends there for the knowledge of the "true" and of "honest" celestial things, which are always accompanied by divine favor.

> "Turn yourself around and keep your eyes closed,
> for if the Gorgon shows herself and you should see her,
> there would be no returning back up."

<image-desc>Decorative initial 'O' inside a circular frame.</image-desc>
**Optimally** reason admonishes sense that it should not look upon such a monster, so that it might not be converted into stone by it, as we allegorically explained. But because sensuality, even though admonished, would not be sufficient by itself for defense if the higher reason did not corroborate and strengthen it...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante's *Inferno*, Canto IX. The text on the left contains the concluding lines of the poetic scene where Virgil protects Dante from the sight of Medusa, followed by the famous address to the reader regarding the "hidden doctrine." The right column provides a dense theological and philosophical commentary, explaining the transition from sins of "incontinence" (dealt with in upper Hell) to the more severe sins of "malice" found within the City of Dis. The commentary specifically mentions the need for "sanctifying grace" to overcome these deeper vices.</meta>

### CANTO NINE.
-> g ii <-

Thus spoke the master, and he himself
turned me around; and he did not rely on my hands alone,
but covered my eyes with his own as well.

O you who have sound intellects,
behold the doctrine that is hidden
under the veil of these strange verses.

And already there came across the turbid waves
a crash of a sound full of terror,
from which both shores trembled;
it was not otherwise than a wind,
impetuous because of opposing heats,
which strikes the forest without any restraint,
it shatters the branches, beats them down, and carries them away;
dusty and proud, it moves forward,
making wild beasts and shepherds flee.

He released my eyes and said: "Now direct the nerve
of your sight over that ancient foam,
there where that smoke is most bitter."

<column-break/>

[The autho]r feigns <note>The text begins with "ro finge," the end of "L’autore finge" (The author feigns), continuing from the previous page.</note> that Virgil admonishes him to cover his eyes with his own hands; and not content with this, he covers them with his own. By "hands" we understand "actions." Therefore, if the demons were to show Medusa to Dante—that is, if they were to tempt his sensuality by placing before him the delights of earthly goods—he, conquered by them, would never return upward, because he would make a habit of them. For this reason, it is necessary that first the sensuality and the lower reason be covered by one's own hands—that is, that one uses every good action possible to them—and submits to the higher reason. Then, the higher reason covers him with its own hands—that is, it defends him with the virtues it possesses within itself.

Because in this entire *Comedy* of the *Inferno*, there is no chapter that has a deeper allegory than this one, the poet captures the attention of his listeners and admonishes them to note the allegory within it: **O YOU WHO HAVE SOUND INTELLECTS**—that is, the wise. For he who is not of great intellect would look in vain. **BEHOLD**: diligently consider. **THE DOCTRINE** that is hidden under the veil: under the fiction. **OF THESE STRANGE VERSES**: that is, diverse verses, in which the words sound like one thing, but the meaning hidden within is another. For he wishes to show that, just as reason resists on its own (with grace freely given <note>original: "gratia gratis data"</note>) against the vices proceeding from lack of restraint and intemperance—where Virgil sufficed against Charon, Minos, Cerberus, Pluto, Phlegyas, and Filippo Argenti—so now, to enter into the contemplation of the more grave vices proceeding from malice and bestiality <term>bestialità: a state where human reason is entirely lost to animalistic cruelty</term>, reason with "grace freely given" is not enough. Special grace from God is needed, called by theologians "grace making one pleasing" <note>original: "gratia gratum faciens"; this refers to sanctifying grace that transforms the soul.</note>. And the entry is much more difficult because not just one demon, but many are on guard. This signifies that such sins have many different species and roots, and a thousand ways and arts of harming. Therefore, Virgil cannot appease these demons; rather, they have closed the gate in his face. The Furies are the roots of pride and envy, and they have serpents in place of hair, which denotes malice, fraud, and deceit. Thus, Virgil writes in the *Aeneid*: "A thousand arts of harming" <note>original: "Mille nocendi artes"</note>. This hinders Dante. Theologically, this signifies that the demon does not want a living man—that is, one proceeding with reason—to enter into the knowledge of sin, because the demon knows that by knowing it, the man would guard against it. But he wants the dead man—that is, he in whom sensuality is superior to reason. Such a man is "dead" because there are no longer human actions in him, but entirely bestial ones. Dante draws close to Virgil out of suspicion of the Furies. For when the appetite submits to reason, it can never be assaulted by the Furies, which are born from the most ardent and unrestrained desire for illicit things. And these Furies, seeing they could not harm him, called Medusa—that is, they abandoned him to the alluring delights of worldly things, by which, if we allow ourselves to be captured (as we said above), we "turn to stone." Many hold that Medusa signifies "oblivion" and "ignorance," and this makes a man become a stone—that is, hardened and obstinate. And against this, reason turns the sensuality away from the sin and makes him put his hands to his face—that is, return from vice to good actions. And reason also places its own hands there, which are the intellectual contemplations. And this was a sufficient remedy so that vice would not offend Dante; but it was not enough for the knowledge of it, and therefore he waits for the angel to grant him entry.

Dante was now armed against the harm of the Furies and the Gorgons. Now it remains for them to enter the city with the help of the angel. He describes, therefore, his arrival. He describes how Virgil taught Dante to revere him. He describes how he opened the gate with his wand, rebuked the demons for their arrogance, and then returned; and how Virgil and Dante entered and what they saw. **AND ALREADY THERE CAME** across the turbid waves: This shows the coming of the angel, whom we interpreted above as the grace of God. He came over the waves of the Styx <note>The marshy river of the fifth circle of Hell.</note> to denote that the light received from God in this part was for the knowledge of infernal things. **A CRASH** of a sound: That is, such a sound as is common in a crash; and we specifically call a "crash" a great sound proceeding from the ruin and breaking of things, because "to crash" means to break. **FULL OF TERROR**: This accords with the theologians, who say that every vision proceeding from God terrifies at the beginning and reassures at the end. We can also understand that when, through the coming of divine grace, we enter into the knowledge of the greatest vices and realize what a cruel plague and grave danger they are to our soul, from such knowledge a terror and consternation of the mind is born—not a small one, but one full of horror. **FROM WHICH BOTH SHORES TREMBLED**: That is, both banks of the swamp. Limolese <note>Likely referring to the early commentator Graziolo Bambaglioli.</note> interprets that the one who comes to open the gate is Mercury, the god of eloquence, and he cleverly fits the text to this allegory. But whoever diligently considers Dante’s purpose easily knows that it can be nothing other than divine grace acting upon a well-disposed will. **NOT OTHERWISE** than a wind: He perfectly likens the angel, who is incorporeal, to the wind, which is such a thin body that it remains invisible. Furthermore, this shows with what speed divine grace descends to a well-disposed will. **WHICH STRIKES**: Which hits or wounds. **IMPETUOUS** because of opposing heats: which takes its impetus from the heats diverse from it—that is, opposed to it. Winds are generated by hot and dry vapors raised from the earth up to the region where clouds exist; and there, struck by the superior heats, they are pushed sideways and strike the air, and the struck part strikes the next, and that the next, hand to hand; because wind is nothing other than struck air. And the more the heats are opposed, the more impetuous the wind is. There are also certain more impetuous types that can almost be called lightning-bolts, such as the storm-blast, the cloud-wind, the typhoon, the whirlwind, and the fire-wind <note>original: "procella, ecnephia, thyphone, turbine, prester"</note>. The nature and distinction of these I leave behind, as it is a long explanation.

He has described the impetus of the angel’s coming. Now he posits that Virgil—who had previously closed Dante's eyes so he would not see Medusa—now conversely opens them so that he may see the angel. For it is the office of our intellect to rule...

The commentary explains the allegorical necessity of Virgil covering Dante's eyes to prevent him from becoming "hardened" by the sight of Medusa, representing the temptation of earthly delights and ignorance.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante’s Inferno, Canto IX. The previous page ended with the Heavenly Messenger approaching across the Styx and Virgil instructing Dante to look toward the "ancient foam." This page explains the allegory of the Messenger’s arrival, the nature of the damned souls’ flight, and the philosophical meaning of the Messenger’s physical gestures.</meta>

<page-type>text</page-type>

<header>INFERNO</header>

### As frogs before their enemy
### the snake, vanish through the water all of them
### until each settles on the ground:
### I saw more than a thousand ruined souls
### flee thus before one who at a pace
### crossed the Styx with dry feet.

<column-break/>

[This sight] <note>Continuing from the previous page's discussion on the "nerve of sight."</note> informs the appetite <note>The "appetite" here refers to the soul's desires or inclinations.</note> that has closed its eyes to every disturbance, and thus opened them to every divine inspiration. Sensuality is very far from divinity; but the intellect stands in the middle, and in many things, by itself, it governs the senses. And in those matters where it is not sufficient by itself to govern them, it at least prepares the soul to receive that which will govern it through divine grace. **HE RELEASED MY EYES**, removing his hands and mine for the reason already stated above. **AND HE SAID: "DIRECT the nerve of the face"**; he almost awakens the visual power, using "nerve" to represent that power. This is because bodily forces consist of nerves. Or rather, he said "nerve" because in the crossing of the optic nerves—which come from the brain to the eyes—

<column-break/>

consists the visual power. **ACROSS That ancient foam**: If he moved the waters, it was necessary that foam be born from them. And he called it "ancient," not because the foam itself was old (having been born from a new movement), but "ancient" meaning from the "ancient swamp" <note>Referring to the Styx.</note>. Some say "ancient foam" means "white foam," because all foam is white; just as the Latins say *canas pruinas* <note>original: "canas pruinas," meaning hoary or white frosts.</note>, meaning white frosts, because the hair of an old man is white. Thus Dante said "ancient foam" as if to say hoary or white foam. But it fits well to say that the Styx is an ancient swamp because sadness is ancient in the human generation, since the first man, Adam, as soon as he had fallen into sin, fell into gloom and sorrow. The angel did not come flying over the swamp, but he came *through* the swamp, although he walked across it without wetting his feet. This denotes that such grace was an aid to the recognition of vices and not of virtues. **WHERE THAT SMOKE IS MOST BITTER**: most vehement and most dark. For such grace does not come through luminous places—because the intellect sees those by itself—but through the dark ones, which the intellect cannot see without grace. Or rather, he has it come through a dark place because such grace comes hiddenly, nor is it recognized by the path it takes. **AS THE FROGS**. An excellent comparison from frogs, swamp animals, to the souls placed in the mire. And it is a fitting thing to say that the damned souls flee from the grace of God; because all those who have made a habit of vice and take pleasure in it become most unfit to receive divine grace; for **Into a malevolent soul the spirit of wisdom shall not enter** <note>original Latin: "In animam maliuolam non introibit spiritus sapientię." From the Book of Wisdom 1:4.</note>. Therefore, making oneself unable to receive the grace of God is the same as fleeing it. Furthermore, just as the saved are confirmed in an excellent will, so the damned can no longer be anything but obstinate in sinning. **SNAKE** <note>original: "Biscia."</note>: A serpent; and it is a figure called onomatopoeia—that is, a fictional name—because *biscia* is a name created to mimic the noise the serpent makes when it goes whipping and sliding with velocity. **THEY VANISH** <note>original: "SI DILEGVANO."</note>: To vanish means to disappear, a word taken from the Latin *Deliquesco* <note>original: "Deliquesco," meaning to melt or dissolve.</note>, which means to melt away; because one who vanishes exits the eye's sight suddenly, like snow when it melts. **SETTLES** <note>original: "SABBICA" or "S'ABBICA."</note>: Heaps up. A *bica* is a heap in the likeness of what the Latins call a *meta* <note>original: "meta," a conical heap or boundary stone.</note>, which is a round form that gradually points upward; and in this form the farmer heaps the sheaves of grain. Thus *abbicare* means to accumulate. **RUINED** <note>original: "DISTRVCTE."</note>: Damned. For the soul deprived of its "good" can be called destroyed. **FLEE BEFORE one who at a pace**: to the place where the passage was. **WITH Dry feet**: because the grace of God, and the one who contemplates through it, cannot be wetted in the swamp of sadness and hatred—that is, he is not stained by the vices which he contemplates. And he orders the text thus: "I saw more than a thousand souls flee before one who at a pace crossed the Styx with dry feet, just as frogs vanish through the water before their enemy the snake until they all heap themselves on the ground."

---

### From his face he moved that thick air,
### waving his left hand before him often:
### and only from that anguish did he seem weary:
### Well I perceived that he was sent from heaven:
### and I turned to the master: and he made a sign
### that I should stay still: and bow down then:
### Ah, how full of disdain he seemed to me!
### He reached the gate: and with a little wand
### he opened it, for it had no resistance.

<column-break/>

He continues by describing what the angel did; and he shows that he used his left hand to drive away the thick air—that is, the fog. This signifies that divine grace performs two works in the human intellect. First, it removes every fog of ignorance from the face—and understand this as from the eyes of the mind—preparing us for virtues by purging us of vices. This is the first virtue and the first act of wisdom; as Horace rightly said: **Virtue is to flee vice, and the first wisdom is to have been free from folly** <note>original Latin: "Virtus est uitium fugere & sapientia prima stultitia caruisse." From Horace, Epistles 1.1.41.</note>. Then, having removed the fog—that is, the vice and the ignorance—and having thus become pure (as you will see more easily in Purgatory), it leads us into the knowledge of God and the truth. Whence Wisdom in the Evangelist says: **Blessed are the pure in heart: for they shall see God** <note>original Latin: "Beati mondo corde: quia ipsi deum uidebunt." Matthew 5:8.</note>. Those are blessed, therefore, who have a pure heart, because they will see God; that is, they will be able to rise to the contemplation of divine things. But because this first work is the greater difficulty—namely, removing ignorance and purifying the mind—rather than the subsequent induction of knowledge, he said: **WAVING THE LEFT hand before him often**: because one must perform very frequent virtuous acts before the habit of virtue follows. And he adds: **THAT ONLY FROM THAT Anguish did he seem weary**: because all our difficulty and exhaustion and tedium is in purging ourselves of vices and removing ignorance. For once we have already made a habit of virtue, nothing, however difficult it may be, exhausts us or seems laborious. Because he who has made a habit of virtue takes pleasure and delight in exercising it; and the greater the difficulty, the more he enjoys it. As I demonstrated more clearly in our discussions on the fourth book of Virgil: **But the boy Ascanius in the midst of the valleys rejoices in his spirited horse, and now in the race he passes these, now those, and prays with vows that among the sluggish herds a foaming boar be given to him, or a tawny lion descend from the mountain** <note>original Latin: "At puer Ascanius mediis in uallibus acri gaudet equo iamque hos cursu iam preterit illos Spumantemque dari pecora inter inertia uotis optat aprum aut fuluum descendere monte leonem." From Virgil's Aeneid IV, 156-159.</note>. And we will demonstrate it more clearly when it happens to be explained that the moral virtues are of four kinds. Therefore, he seemed weary only from having to remove the fog from before his face—that is, removing the ignorance of the soul. And he says that he did this with the left hand, as if to say with the less noble hand; because of the two acts, that one was still the less noble. For having two works to do—first removing ignorance, then with the wand opening the gate that leads into knowledge—he had to reserve the right hand for this second work as the more noble one. Furthermore, removing ignorance is removing vices, which are symbolized by the left; and opening the gate is inducing knowledge of the virtues, symbolized by the right hand. **WELL I PERCEIVED THAT he was sent from heaven**. I perceived that he was sent by God. This denotes that even the lower reason perceives when the mind is illuminated by divine splendor; but before it comes, the lower reason does not foresee it as the higher reason does. And therefore he stated above that Virgil was waiting for him. But it will perhaps seem to many that since the poet showed from the beginning that...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante’s Inferno, Canto IX. The previous page discussed the arrival of the Heavenly Messenger across the Styx and the physiological nature of sight. Here, the commentator explains the Messenger’s disdainful attitude and the symbolism of his wand, followed by the Messenger’s rebuke of the rebellious demons at the gates of the City of Dis.</meta>

# CANTO NINE.

All this pilgrimage of his is guided by divine grace, which, being triple, is signified by three women. It might seem superfluous that it is placed later under various veils in many places. And he repeats this in this canticle as in the others. To which I respond that although the beginning and the entire progress are aided by divine grace, nonetheless, in many difficulties and in grave and varied cases that occur, it is appropriate that divine help appears more expressly. For this reason, like an excellent theologian, he places them in every major difficulty; and like an excellent poet, he always varies the invention and the fiction. This is the highest praise for the "priests of the Muses" <note>A classical reference to poets.</note>; and in such virtue, I see no poet who precedes ours. And if I were not Florentine, I would dare to say that in this, no one equals or matches him. But I return to the text. **AND I TURNED TO THE MASTER:** because the lower reason needs to be instructed by the superior. **AND HE MADE A SIGN:** As if to say he made no great fuss. This denotes that Dante—or let us say, the lower reason and sensuality—was so obedient to the superior that every minimal sign was enough. And he signaled to me **THAT I SHOULD STAND QUIET.** For it is not for the lower reason to ask or make any dispute concerning knowledge and science, which reside in universals, while lower reason is only in particulars. But Virgil does not speak either, because where knowledge comes through revealing grace, the intellect does not labor much. . . **AND I BOWED DOWN THEN:** that is, at present and without delay; he who bows shows reverence, and bowing signifies yielding to a superior and being prompt to submit and obey. This is what the lower reason should do, and thus the superior shows him. **AH, HOW** he seemed to me full of disdain. The Angel remembers the ancient battle that took place between the good and the evil in heaven, and the pride of Lucifer and his followers, and their obstinacy. This moves him to most just disdain. And allegorically, divine grace, which succors our intellect, must act with force against ignorance, which is that which closes the door; and it should have disdain that man, born for the contemplation of divine things, is forbidden by ignorance from being able to reach them. And he does not say "he was full," but "he seemed"—not to Virgil, but to sensuality—because no alteration can exist in divine actions. But it seems so to sensuality, which believes that the perturbations found in itself are also in God, and that He does not punish without anger or forgive without mercy. Therefore, as the poet and sacred theologians will say elsewhere, they attribute passions to God which are not in Him, because otherwise our senses could not comprehend His works. **HE CAME TO THE GATE AND** opened it with a small wand. There were those who said the poet wanted to show by this wand how easy it was for him to open it. But if I do not err, it is to be understood in this place that the poet, having proposed to imitate Virgil and the other ancient poets where Christian theology does not forbid it, feigns here the Angel sent by God (which is consistent with our religion). But to adorn the place with poetic fiction, he gives him the wand of Mercury. In this way, he does not simply place Mercury there—as it seemed to the man from Imola <note>Referring to the commentator Benvenuto da Imola.</note>—because that would seem like idolatry; nor does he depart entirely from poetic fiction, giving him the wand as to Mercury. But here the wand signifies the power which is in the grace of God to rule and teach the human mind. Such grace carries the wand, that is, the scepter, to denote that no one can resist its empire, and that every diabolical force and fraud yields. And that wand opens the door for us to the knowledge of inward things.

**"O** outcasts from heaven, despised folk,"
he began upon the horrible threshold,
"whence does this insolence harbor in you?
Why do you kick against that will
whose end can never be cut short,
and which has many times increased your pain?
**Y**our Cerberus, if you remember well,
still bears his chin and throat peeled for it."
Then he turned back along the filthy path,
and spoke no word to us, but seemed like a man
whom another care constrains and bites
than that of him who is before him;
and we moved our feet toward the land,
secure after those holy words.

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Decorative red initial 'P' at the start of the commentary.</image-desc>

Having opened the gate, the Angel gives appropriate words, and they correspond to the disdain he showed. **O OUTCASTS** from heaven. This is an invective, and it is in the demonstrative genre where he highly vituperates the operations of the demons from beginning to end. And he begins with an exclamation in which there is great gravity and vehemence in rebuking. He shows that for having wanted to oppose the divine will, Lucifer and the others were not only cast out from the sublime heaven, but also ruined in the lowest part. Not only did they lose their preeminence and highest honor, but they remain in extreme reproach and vilification, because where they were once the first creatures, they have become the last. And therefore he said: **DESPISED FOLK:** that is, despised by God and by all His other rational creatures. **UPON THE HORRIBLE THRESHOLD.** He shows by this that the Angel did not enter inside, and in some part this conforms to the saying of the Sibyl in the sixth book of Virgil: <margin>It is not permitted for any pure soul to step upon the wicked threshold. <note>Original Latin: "Nulli fas casto sceleratum insistere limen."</note></margin> **WHENCE DOES THIS** "whence," that is, from what reason. **THIS** that. **INSOLENCE** pride. He speaks as if to say "from none." For it is the height of folly to be proud for one who does not excel others for any reason. And you have fallen from such height into the deepest bottom, both as to location and as to condition and dignity. Therefore, it is bad for anyone to be proud, but worse for you. **WHY DO YOU KICK AGAINST** that will: He demonstrates their folly,

<column-break/>

first in attempting things clearly impossible. For it is known to all that no one can obstruct the divine will. Secondly, in attempting harmful things. And finally, he shows that these two things are proven by example, inducing the case of Cerberus. **WHY do you kick:** why do you oppose yourselves; and it is a metaphor from a horse or similar animal which, not wanting to obey the one who guides it, kicks out. **AGAINST THAT** will: to which the end can never be cut short, that is, which cannot be prevented from arriving at its proposed end. **AND WHICH MANY TIMES** has increased your pain, because every time you have opposed it, either in heaven or in hell, you have been defeated and punished. **WHAT DOES IT PROFIT TO KICK AGAINST THE FATES?** We spoke above of fate. And according to what we demonstrated there, we will say "in the fates," that is, in divine providence, whose order can neither be changed nor moved. Therefore, what does it profit to butt against—that is, to repugn—that which divine providence has ordained? **YOUR CERBERUS.** Certainly Cerberus is of the infernal regions, because indigence and the need for things belonging to the health of the body—for which he is figured along with other diabolical temptations—hinder us from the contemplation of truth. But because against this the unique remedy is to provide for necessary things and cast away the superfluous, therefore Virgil feeds him with a bit of mash <note>A mixture of honey and meal used by the Sibyl in the Aeneid.</note>, and Dante feeds him with dust. But Hercules, whose descent into hell we narrated shortly above, dragged him out of hell with chains. This denotes that heroic virtue—which the poets feign in Hercules—not only knows how to keep the body content with necessary things, but entirely reduces it into its power and...

<meta>This page concludes the commentary on the arrival of the Heavenly Messenger in Canto IX and transitions into the description of the Sixth Circle of Hell. The previous page detailed the Messenger’s approach and his opening words to the rebellious demons at the gate of Dis. Here, the commentator explains the theological and allegorical significance of the Messenger's brief, stern departure, followed by Dante and Virgil's entry into the city where they encounter the tombs of the heretics.</meta>

# INFERNO;

...makes himself a servant. To which Paul said: "I discipline my body and bring it into subjection." <note>Original Latin: *Castigo corpus: & in servitutem redigo* (1 Corinthians 9:27).</note> But I wrote more extensively about Cerberus in the sixth canto. **NOR DID HIS GULLET YET HAVE FUR:** because having been dragged by Hercules by the chains he had on his three necks, reason dictates that the chain had stripped the hair from his throat and chin. Nor was a longer speech or one of a different quality appropriate for the angel; therefore, he was brief and vehement in rebuking them. He was brief so that it would not seem that he valued them more than they deserved. He was bitter in his speech because their pride required it. **THEN HE TURNED BACK:** having said these words, he returned the way he came. **BY THE FILTHY ROAD:** that is, the foul way by which he had arrived. **AND HE SAID NO WORD TO US** but he bore the appearance and look of a man who is pressed and bitten by a greater care than that which is before him. Through these verses, he denotes that the duty of one who is sent by his superior is to perform what is commanded with as much brevity as possible, and then return by the direct path without undertaking other cares. Allegorically, it demonstrates that divine grace does not stop with just one person but always extends to others. **AND WE MOVED OUR FEET:** With the gate of knowledge opened to the speculative intellect by divine grace, and grace guiding it, the lower intellect enters into speculation because it becomes secure and remains full of hope, comforted by divine aid.

->and I see on every hand a great countryside<-

->and from them such hard laments issued forth<-

->more than you believe, the tombs are burdened.<-
->Here, like is buried with like,<-
->and the monuments are more and less hot."<-
->And then, after he had turned to the right hand,<-
->We passed between the torments and the high ramparts.<-

<column-break/>

<image-desc>decorative initial 'd' in a circular frame</image-desc>

We said above that outside the City of Dis, the author placed sins that proceed from <term>incontinence: the inability to restrain one's desires or impulses</term>, where sensuality allows itself to be ensnared by the pleasures of the body. Because these do not proceed from malice or from a savage soul, but from the fragility of the senses, they deserve much less punishment. Now, inside Dis, where more grievous punishments are prepared, he places the sins which proceed from an irrational and disordered elevation of the soul, through which one truly fails to recognize God as superior. Nor does such a person deign to submit to human and divine laws, or to just principles, or to those who surpass them in integrity and wisdom. Generally, this can be called Pride (*superbia*), from which all sins proceed. For, according to Augustine, every sin is a departure from God and a refusal to submit to Him. Therefore, he positions the two towers, which signify Boasting and Arrogance; and the Furies, which signify most vehement impulses and burning desires; and Medusa, who signifies the pleasure taken in them. From this, an indelible habit is born, and almost the same thing is denoted by the walls of iron. In this city, he places the sixth, seventh, eighth, and ninth circles, of which we will speak particularly in the proper place. Pride, therefore, is an immoderate desire to surpass and stand above others. But so that the sin may be better distinguished, we will say that this desire to excel is either natural or non-natural. If natural, it is either spiritual or personal. If spiritual, it is not a sin but a just desire; nor does he deserve rebuke who desires to be more just or stronger than others, or to surpass all in science and wisdom. Likewise, it will not be a vice if it is personal, because a man can justly wish to be superior to all brute animals, for the dignity of the human species deserves it; and God, in the precepts given to the first man, said: "Rule over the fish of the sea." <note>Original Latin: *Dominamini piscibus maris* (Genesis 1:28).</note> But if it is non-natural, it is a sin; and we say it is non-natural when we seek to stand above other men, because nature produced us to live in consort and company, from which republics are born. Such company cannot last where there is not a universal equality. Nor did God command that we should lord over other men. Therefore, such a desire to be superior to other men will be vicious, desiring such excellence for oneself and for our own respect. But desiring it to help other men, to maintain justice, and to preserve equality among subjects—from which tranquility is born—and not to use it for oneself in any way, will not be a sin, but a merit. Nor should it be overlooked that pride is either interior or exterior. Interior pride is either in the affect or in the intellect. In the intellect, it manifests in four ways: First, when a man presumes to have from himself whatever good he possesses. Second, when he believes it is from God but by his own merits. Third, when

---

he judges that to be a virtue which is not. Fourth, when, despising others, he desires to appear as that which he is not. In the affect, it is sometimes presumption and sometimes ambition. Presumption is when we presume that which we ought not, either before the time or beyond our own strength. Ambition consists either in lordship, or in mastery, or in simple excess in any of the graces given by grace, such as riches and the like. Exterior pride is considered either from the cause that produces it or from the thing in which it consists. In the first way, we consider if it is born from the goods of nature, or the goods of fortune, or of grace. Natural goods are either of the body or of the soul. In the body, they are strength, beauty, dexterity, speed, size, and the like. In the soul, they are sharpness of wit, quickness, good memory, the power to sustain spiritual exercise, and natural aptitude. The goods of fortune are those which are outside of us and can be taken from us, such as riches, dignity, dominion, glory, and fame. If we consider the subject, we will see if it is in a private or public man, or in a priest or a layman, and the like. Companions of pride are curiosity, levity, arrogant joy, defense of sin, feigned humility, and license in sinning. The daughters of pride are irreverence, heresy, disobedience, vainglory, hypocrisy, boasting, pertinacity, discord, and envy. To all these vices, which proceed from savagery and a malignant mind, he places the punishments in these four...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante's *Inferno*, Canto IX. Following the angel’s departure, Dante and Virgil enter the city of Dis. The commentator explains the transition from the upper circles to the lower ones, providing historical and theological context for the landscape of tombs they encounter and a comprehensive list of Christian heresies.</meta>

# CANTO NINE

...circles placed inside the walls of Dis: and they are appropriate to the vice. They are in the lower circles. Note that even in human life, those who elevate themselves too much are depressed and lowered, at least by the vileness of sin. And they are in a heavy and annoying stench, because the proud person generates nausea, disgust, and stench to all men and to himself: because, desiring always a higher rank, it seems that the place where he currently is reeks to him. **WE ENTERED WITHIN WITHOUT WAR:** <note>Canto IX, 106</note> without resistance, having the divine light so illuminated the intellect that every difficulty and obscurity ceased. **AND I,** Dante—that is, the appetite, which is what moves the soul to investigation, as we said above—and therefore he says that he had a desire to look at the condition: that is, the state and fortune of that place. **I SEND MY EYE AROUND.** I turned with my eyes. **AND I SEE A GREAT PLAIN:** a great flatland. And by the great space of the place, he demonstrates a great multitude of sinners. **ARLES** is a city in Provence placed at the mouth of the Rhone, not more than three leagues distant from Avignon. It is called *Arelate* in Latin. <note>original: "Arelate"</note> Regarding the abundance of tombs that are around it, they recount this story: Charlemagne fought in this place with a great number of pagans and reported a most bloody victory, for many Christians died there. And Charlemagne, desiring to recognize the bodies of his own from those of the enemies to bury them the following morning, found a great abundance of sepulchers, and all the Christians had their names written on their foreheads. For this reason, they were buried in such tombs. But it is more likely to be believed that ancient custom created such sepulchers. **POLA** is a city at the tip of Istria near the gulf in the Adriatic sea called Quarnaro. This gulf is about forty miles wide and is very dangerous because of the South wind, which in that region is similarly called the Quarnaro. **WHICH ENCLOSES ITALY:** because here Italy ends, and the shores of the Quarnaro are the boundaries of Italy. I find no history that narrates the origin of such sepulchers. I believe that through long custom they have multiplied. **THAT IRON ASKS FOR NO MORE** in any art. The sepulchers were so heated that no craftsman heats iron more when he wants to manufacture something from it and harden it into a new form. Because in this place heresy is punished. We shall note that "heresy" is a Greek word and means "choice." <note>The commentator notes the Greek etymology *hairesis* (choice/selection), original: "electione"</note> For the heretic departs from the common opinion or faith and chooses for himself what he wishes to believe. We shall say, then, that heresy is the selection of one's own opinion against the determination of the Apostolic Church. And briefly, we shall say that a heretic is anyone who holds an opinion different from the true religion. This cannot be without extreme arrogance, because he attributes too much to his own wisdom who deviates from the common opinion of many most learned men. It is, therefore, one of the daughters of Pride. There are some who, regarding this sin, interpret the Furies by placing Alecto for evil thought, Tisiphone for the evil publication of such thought, and Megaera for evil action; and Medusa when he openly approves his own falsehood. But such an allegory does not seem to me preferable to the one I set down above. Nevertheless, let each person approve the one they judge fits better. **HERESIARCHS,** that is, the princes of heresies, were many. But taking the beginning from where Gratian <note>referring to the legal scholar Gratian and his *Decretum*</note> takes it, we shall say the first was **Simon Magus**, whom Peter cursed in the Acts of the Apostles because he tried to buy the grace of the Holy Spirit with money. From him are named the **Simoniacs**, those who sell or buy sacred things. Their heresy is that the creature was not made by God, but by a certain supernal power. **Menandrians** take their name from Menander the Magician, a disciple of Simon; they say the world was not made by God but by angels. **Basilidians**, from Basilides, who did not want Jesus Christ to have suffered. **Nicolaites**, from Nicholas the Deacon (who was established by the Apostle Peter along with Stephen), who left his wife to her own judgment to join with whomever she pleased; and he instituted the change of marriage. **Gnostics** wish to be called so for their "excellence of knowledge." <note>From the Greek *gnosis*</note> These people say the soul is of the nature of God, and that God is both good and evil. **Carpocratians**, from Carpocrates, who said Christ was only a man and born of a male and a female. **Cerinthians**, from Cerinthus; these observe circumcision and say that a thousand years after the resurrection they will live in the pleasure of the flesh. Hence in Greek they are called **Chiliasts** <note>original: "ciliaste"</note> and in Latin **Macilists**. **Nazarenes** confess Christ and nonetheless live according to the law of the Old Testament. **Ophites**, named from the serpent, which in Greek is called *ophis* <note>original: "ophis"</note>; they adore the serpent and say that he brought the knowledge of virtue. **Valentinians** believe that Christ took nothing of a body from Mary, but entered into her as if through a channel or a small pipe. **Apellites**, from Apelles, held that an angel was the God of the Law of Israel, and affirms him to be made of fire; he said Christ was not God in truth but had appeared as a man in a fantasy. **Archontics** want the universe created by God to be the work of archangels. **Adamites**, imitating Adam, pray naked and stay together naked, both males and females. **Cainites** adore Cain. **Sethians** say Seth, son of Adam, was Christ. **Melchizedekians** say Melchizedek the priest was not a man but a power of God. **Artotyrites** are named from *artos*, that is, bread, and *tyros*, that is, cheese <note>original: "artos .i. pane & tyros .i. formaggio"</note>, because they offer bread and cheese in their sacrifices, affirming that the first men celebrated sacrifice with the fruits of the earth and the livestock. **Aquarians** put only water in the chalice of the sacrifice. **Severians**, named from Severus, do not drink wine, nor believe the Old Testament or the resurrection. **Alogi**, that is, "without the Word," because in Greek *a* signifies "without" and *logos* "word," <note>original: "a significa ſanza & logos uerbo"</note> because they do not believe God is the Word and do not believe the Apocalypse. **Paulicians**, from Paul [of Samosata], who did not say Christ had been eternal, but had his beginning from Mary. **Manichaeans**, from Manes the Persian, who established two natures and two substances, one good and one evil, and that our soul derives from God as if from a certain fountain; they do not accept the Old Testament and accept the New only in part. **Anthropomorphites** believe that God has the form of a man, and from this they have taken their name, because *anthropos* signifies "man" and *morphe* "form." <note>original: "antropos ſignifica huomo: & morphi forma"</note> **Heraclians**, from Heraclius, receive no one but monks; they damn marriages and do not believe that infants possess the kingdom of heaven. **Photinians**, from Photinus, a bishop in Galatia: they said Christ was born of Mary and Joseph by carnal union. **Aetians** say the Son is unlike the Father and the Spirit unlike the Son. **Origenists**, from Origen, say that the Son cannot see the Father nor the Holy Spirit the Son; they affirm also that souls sinned in the beginning of the world and, according to their diversity, they have taken different bodies from heaven down to the earth, and for this reason they say the world was made. **Noetians** do not place three persons in God but only one, and say Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are names of office and not distinction of persons. Hence they are called **Patripassians**, because they maintain that the Father also suffered. **Sabellians** are named from Sabellius, a disciple of Noetus, and are in the same error. **Arius**, bishop of Alexandria, distinguished the essence of the Son from the Father against the word of the Lord, who said: "I and the Father are one." <note>Original Latin: *Ego & pater unum ſumus* (John 10:30)</note> **Macedonius**, a bishop, did not want the Holy Spirit to be God. **Apollinarists**, from Apollinaris, who says that Christ took a human body but not a soul. **Priscillianists** <note>The text here attributes some views of Priscillian to a general "Princiani" or "Prisciani"</note> say the substance of human flesh was made by the devil. **Donatus** came from Numidia and subverted all of Africa, saying that the Son is less than the Father and the Holy Spirit less than the Son. **Bonosus**, a bishop, and from him the **Bonosians**, say that Christ was not the proper Son of God but an adopted one. **Circumcellions** kill themselves with their own hands to die as martyrs. **Priscillianists** in Spain made a sect mixed with the errors of the Gnostics and Priscillianists. **Paterniani** say the lower parts of the body are made by the devil. **Arabics** were heretics in Arabia who affirmed the soul dies with the body and on the day of judgment both are resurrected. **Tertullian**, a Carthaginian priest, says the soul is immortal but corporeal, and that sinful souls after death turn into...

g iiii
Dante Alighieri, Inferno, Canto IX, Arles, Pola, heresy, Simon Magus, Gnosticism, Manichaeism, Arius, Sabellius
