<meta>This page continues the catalog of heretics encountered in the sixth circle of Hell. The previous page ended with a description of the cemetery-like landscape of Arles; this page provides a detailed theological breakdown of various historical heresies (Pelagianism, Nestorianism, etc.) and focuses specifically on the "Paterene" sect, before returning to the literal commentary on Dante's dialogue with Virgil regarding the "Heresiarchs" and the nature of their punishment in burning tombs.</meta>

<header>INFERNO.</header>

demons. The **Nyctages** <note>original: "Nicetagee"; a sect that argued against night vigils</note> are said to act against God by consuming the night in vigils, since God made the night for rest. **Pelagius**, the monk, places free will before divine grace, affirming that the will alone is sufficient to follow the commandments of God. **Nestorius**, Bishop of Constantinople, affirms that Mary was not the mother of God, but only of the man [Jesus]. For this reason, he makes one person of the flesh and another of the deity; and he posits Christ as separated: that one is the son of God and another is the son of man. **Eutyches**, an abbot of Constantinople, denies that Christ, after his human assumption, consists of two natures; rather, he maintains that only the divine nature remains in him. The **Acephalites** <note>original: "Acephalite"; from the Greek 'a' (without) and 'cephale' (head)</note>—meaning "without a head"—are so called because no single head or inventor of this sect can be found. They deny that there are properties of two substances in Christ, but want there to be only one nature in his person. This same error was held by **Theodosius** and **Gaianus**, who were ordained bishops by the perverse people of Alexandria on the same day. They therefore make of two natures only one in Christ, like Eutyches and Dioscorus; but the **Theodosians** claim it is corruptible, while the **Gaianites** claim it is incorruptible. From the Theodosians proceed the **Agnoetae** <note>original: "agnoite"; from the Greek for 'ignorance'</note>, so called from their ignorance: because they affirm that the divinity of Christ was ignorant of what was written regarding the day and final hour; nor do they remember that in the person of Christ, Isaiah says: *The day of judgment is in my heart.* <note>original: "Dies iudicii in corde meo."</note> The **Tritheists** <note>original: "Tritonite"</note> said that there are not three persons in one God, but rather three gods, contrary to what is written: *Hear, O Israel, the Lord your God is one.* <note>original: "Audi israel Dñs deus tuus unus est."</note> There are also some who do not want Christ to have been born of the Father from eternity, but with a beginning in time. Some do not believe that the descent of Christ into Hell liberated mankind; some believe that our souls after death are converted into demons, and even into every kind of animal. Some posit innumerable worlds, following the opinion of **Democritus**; some posit that water is co-eternal with God, like **Thales of Miletus**. Some go barefoot; some do not eat with other men. There remain many other sects; if I were to narrate them all, I might sooner be damned for curiosity than praised for diligence. 

But most well-known is the opinion of the **Fraticelli** <note>original: "fraticegli"; a radical offshoot of the Franciscans</note>, very close to our own age and perhaps not yet extinguished. Most malignant are the **Paterenes**, who, besides many other errors they hold in common with the **Manichaeans**, say our souls are malignant spirits infused into bodies by the devil. They say that the soul and the body of Christ and of Mary were created in heaven as incorruptible, and that they never ate or drank corporal food. They say that baptism is not necessary; that the Eucharist is not the body of Christ, but simple bread and wine in memory of the true body. Furthermore, they say that marriage is not a sacrament, nor is anyone who is in that state in a state of salvation. They do not want anyone to confess their sins specifically, but only to confess that they are a sinner, and that it is enough for the Paterene to place his hand on their head, which they call "consolation." They say our bodies are not to be resurrected. They do not use the sign of the cross, but say it is idolatry to venerate it. They do not want anyone to defend themselves in such a way that the attacker might be harmed. They affirm it is a mortal sin to kill any animal except for fish, fleas, and lice. Likewise, they forbid swearing for any reason. They deny it is a sin to practice usury if it is done without fraud. They say that in Tuscany, the true church is the Florentine one, which extends from Pisa to Arezzo, Montepulciano, and Grosseto. 

These heresies, although they are discrepant among themselves, nevertheless all conspire against the apostolic faith. All are condemned by the apostles and other holy men and councils. And in short, whoever understands the Holy Scripture otherwise than the sense of the Holy Spirit requires—from whom the Scripture proceeds—even if he does not depart from the Church, he can nevertheless be called a heretic. And all heretics must be excommunicated according to that saying: *A brother who is rebuked by the church and does not obey, let him be to you as a heathen and a tax collector.* <note>original: "Frater q corripitur ab ecclesia & nō obedit sit tibi sicut ethnicus & publicanus."</note> By "sepulchers," understand the soul of the heretic to be buried in obstinacy without redemption. For just as the virtue of faith gives birth to grace in us, which leads us faithfully to salvation, so incredulity extinguishes every divine light in the heart. Thus we remain in the hardest obstinacy; and for this reason, he places the tombs of stone. Nor without cause does he place heresy after pride; for Solomon says: *The beginning of all sin is pride.* <note>original: "Initiū omnis peccati est supbia."</note> The expositor says: from that, heresy is born. And Jeremiah: *Your arrogance and the pride of your heart have deceived you.* <note>original: "Arrogãtia tua & superbia cordis tui decepit te."</note> Because in truth, heresy does not spring from ignorance, but from pride, the man wanting to acquire authority and grace by being the inventor of a new thing. They stay in the sepulchers for the reason already mentioned, or because heretics keep their beliefs hidden, and hold their congregations and synagogues in dark and hidden places. From this, Job says: *By design they departed from God and did not wish to understand His ways.* <note>original: "De industria recesserunt a deo & uias eius intelligere noluerunt."</note> What the Psalmist says also applies to this figure of the tombs: *In it He prepared the instruments of death and made His arrows burning.* <note>original: "In eo parauit uasa mortis & sagittas suas ardētes effecit."</note> Where the Church says the "vessels of death" are the heretics who bury their own souls. And elsewhere: *Shall anyone declare your mercy in the grave?* <note>original: "Nunquid narrabit aliquis in sepulcro misericordiã tuā."</note> And elsewhere: *Their throat is an open sepulcher.* <note>original: "Sepulchrū patēs est guttur eorū."</note> For just as a great stench comes out of an open tomb, so from the mouths of these people come fetid opinions, because they are hardened in their views. The fire denotes the immeasurable love they have had for themselves and their own opinion; or alternatively, a continuous excuse and fluctuation that exists in the heretic, and an ignited fury; for although he is hardened in his opinion, nevertheless, seeing himself disagreeing with the opinion of an innumerable multitude of men—who through holiness could have divine revelation of the truth, and through much and varied doctrine are of great authority—they can never find rest. 

**Dante** therefore asks who are those buried in the **"arks"** <note>term: ark (archa); here used as a synonym for a sarcophagus or tomb</note>—that is, the sepulchers—which he understands to be there because he hears their sighs, which spring from the greatest anguish of soul. And certainly, he who does not agree with the common opinion, going about searching with his mind for what seems more true to his foolish intellect, is always in anxiety and anguish. 

**"AND HE TO ME"**—understand, he said. **"HERE THESE TOMBS ARE THE HERESIARCHS"**—that is, the princes of the heretical sects, of which we have briefly narrated above. **"AND THEY ARE VERY LADEN"**—that is, full—**"THE TOMBS"**—the sepulchers—**"MORE THAN YOU BELIEVE."** This is to note that there are more heretics among men than others believe. Therefore, in order not to always say the same word (which generates boredom in the reader), he uses this variation, which brings with it ornament and pleasantness, saying now "sepulcher," now "ark," now "tomb," now "vault." <note>original: "sepolchro hora archa hor tomba hor auello"</note> **"LIKE"**: Here, like is buried with like; as if to say Manichaeans with a Manichaean, and Priscillianists with Priscillian, and so with the others. 

**"AND THEN TO MY RIGHT HE TURNED"**: Here he posits that Virgil turned to the right hand; and then he shows that a little after some travel, he turned to the left. This denotes that the journey was taken to the right because they went to have knowledge of sin, and not to be polluted by it, but to be purged of it; which action is virtuous. Then he turned to the left to denote that although the operation is virtuous, nevertheless the matter and the subject is vice. Thus, he wisely takes the leftward path from the right hand. 

**"MARTYRS"**: *Martyres* in the Greek language are "witnesses." But because those who chose to suffer pain and death rather than deny the Christian religion were the best witnesses that it was true, they have been called martyrs: that is, witnesses of our true faith. This is the proper meaning of the word. But because they made such testimony with grave torments and bitter deaths, for this reason we often take "martyrdom" to mean pain and torment; and so it is here. Thus Petrarch said: *Brief help for such long martyrdoms.* 

**"AND THE OTHER RAMPARTS"** <note>original: "spaldi"</note>: This word is not very common nor known to many. Wherefore some say **spaldi** means the walls. Others say that *spaldo* in the Romagnol language signifies what we call the "space" or floor, and the Latins call *pavimentum*.

<meta>This page continues the transition from the city of Dis into the sixth circle of Hell, following the encounter with the Medusa and the opening of the gates by the heavenly messenger mentioned in the previous canto.</meta>

# INFERNO: TENTH CANTO OF THE FIRST CANTICLE BY DANTE.

<column-break/>

<margin>h</margin> **Now** he goes along a secret path
Between the wall of the city and the torments,
My master, and I behind his shoulders:
**"O supreme virtue,"** who through the impious circles
Turn me as it pleases you, I began,
"Speak to me and satisfy my desires.
**The people** who lie within the tombs,
Could they be seen? For already raised up
Are all the lids, and no one stands guard."

**And he to me:** "All shall be closed up
When they return here from Josaphat 
<note>The Valley of Josaphat, where tradition holds the Last Judgment will occur.</note>
With the bodies they have left up above.
**Their cemetery** on this side is held
By Epicurus 
<note>A Greek philosopher whose followers were (incorrectly) thought by medieval Christians to believe the soul dies with the body.</note>
with all his followers,
Who make the soul die with the body.
**Therefore**, regarding the question you ask me,
Inside here you shall soon be satisfied,
And also regarding the wish you keep silent from me."
**And I:** "Good Guide, I do not keep hidden
My heart from you, except to speak little,
And you have disposed me to this not just now."

<column-break/>

**This** tenth canto contains far less difficulty than the ninth, because there are few places that require any allegory other than what has already been stated, and a great part of it is spent on history. It deals with the heretics and prepares for the ascent into the seventh circle. He finds Farinata degli Uberti and Cavalcante de’ Cavalcanti, Florentine knights; and from Farinata, he hears of future events and learns the reason why those placed in Hell can foresee the future. **NOW HE GOES**: He had shown that Virgil led him among the torments; now, continuing, he states that the path along which Virgil led Dante was between the wall of the city **AND THE TORMENTS**: that is, the tombs where the tormented were. This denotes that these tombs were near the walls, which signifies the hardness and obstinacy of the heretics. We can also understand that just as one who is near the walls of a city is almost outside of it, so the heretic, although he may be a Christian,

**is nonetheless**, by his depraved religion, almost outside the Christian name. It similarly denotes that such men hold their gatherings in separate and remote places. **PATH** [calle] signifies a road that is not public but narrow, and made by the callous feet of beasts. This denotes that the path which guides one safely through heresies is a very narrow way; and certainly, it is difficult to find the truth among so many falsehoods. The text is ordered thus: My master now goes along a secret path (that is, a way), which you understand was between the wall of the city and the torments. **AND I BEHIND HIS SHOULDERS**: because sensuality, if it does not wish to err, must always follow its master Virgil (that is, the powers of the intellect), and then follows: **O SUPREME VIRTUE**. O Virgil, you who are of supreme virtue. **WHO TURN ME**: who turns me as you please. **THROUGH THE IMPIOUS CIRCLES**: That is, through impious circles where the impious and pitiless sinners are. For there can be no greater impiety than to hold a poor opinion of God. Some texts say **WIDE** [ampli]: meaning broad, to denote the abundance of sinners. **SPEAK TO ME AND** satisfy me: that is, speak to me in a way that satisfies my desires and my will. This is the order of the text. But remember that, as has been said at other times, the epithets the author gives to Virgil are always suited to the place where he puts them. Therefore, he calls him "supreme virtue" here because Virgil (that is, the intellect) has five virtues: Intelligence concerning first principles; Science 
<note>original: "Scientia"</note> 
concerning things that follow from principles; Wisdom 
<note>original: "Sapientia"</note> 
which, while embracing the two already mentioned, is nonetheless neither of them, but a third virtue beyond the two; Prudence, which is the right guide in particular actions and civil life; and Art, which is a known thing. Of these five, the most excellent is Wisdom, because it is the knowledge not only of human things, but of divine ones. Therefore, he could not lead him through heretical falsehoods except with Wisdom, which has true knowledge of divinity as far as the capacity of the human mind allows. And not without reason did he say: "Turn me as it pleases you." For although in all forms of knowledge it is necessary that the lower reason and the senses allow themselves to be turned and guided by the intellect, it is especially necessary in this. And he makes an excellent introduction to this brief speech; for first he gains goodwill by calling him "supreme virtue," and through those same words he shows that what he asks is easy for him, since he possesses supreme virtue. He can, therefore, do it. Then he shows that he should do it, because equity requires that we satisfy the will of one who gives himself entirely to our judgment. **THE PEOPLE**. He has shown up to here both that Virgil can and that he should answer him. He now poses the question for which he wants an answer: which is whether one can see those who lie in the tombs. He easily believes this to be possible, both because the tombs are open and because no guard is seen there who forbids looking at them. The reason why they are open we shall state shortly below. **THERE IS NO GUARD**: because the Holy Church does not keep heretical opinions hidden and does not forbid them from being read and understood; but with effective arguments, she confutes them. And then she wishes that their foolishness and the wisdom of the sacred theologians be known to everyone, so that having understood that what they say is false, and having rejected it with true reasons, they may be mocked and scorned rather than imitated and prized. And certainly, just as a pit in the road should not be hidden but manifested, so that no one falls into it through imprudence, so false opinions should come to light along with their true refutations, so that no one falls into similar error through ignorance.

<margin>o</margin> **This is the excellent** speech of a good teacher, who often not only answers what the disciple asks, but also adds of his own accord all the other things which he signifies are useful for him to know. Dante asked if the people in the tombs could be seen, since they were open; and Virgil not only answers that they can be seen, but even says they will be closed after the universal and final judgment, which will be at the end of the world, when all of human kind, having resumed their own bodies, will gather in the valley called Josaphat near Jerusalem, where Jesus Christ will descend to judge the good to eternal glory and the wicked to eternal pains. **JOSAPHAT** signifies "He judges" or "Judgment of the Lord." At that time, then, these summoned souls will return for their own bodies, and after the judgment, they will return with them to these tombs, and then they will be closed. They stay open now because the bodies are not there, and this is the essential reason regarding Hell. But as for the allegorical sense, we can understand that as long as human generation lasts, they remain open to receive the heretics who arise from time to time. It is as if to say that there are and always will be heretics. But when the world ends, they will cease, because human generation will fail. **TRULY**, we shall understand with more subtlety that beneath the universal judgment he points to the particular one, and wishes to mean that the heretic, as soon as he is...

<meta>The catchword at the bottom "mo cõ piu" (more with more) indicates the continuation of the philosophical discussion on the next page regarding the "particular judgment" of the individual soul.</meta>

<meta>This page continues Landino’s commentary on Canto 10 of the Inferno, specifically focusing on the theological and philosophical implications of the Epicurean heresy—the belief that the soul dies with the body—and detailing Landino's own scholarly efforts to harmonize ancient philosophy with Christian doctrine.</meta>

# TENTH CANTO

...has buried reason in such error. But the tomb is not locked until his particular judgment, because one can still return to the true faith. Therefore, the tombs stay open because divine grace can pull them out of the shadows and lead them to the light before the judgment—that is, before death. For this reason, heretics should not be killed, but rather imprisoned, admonished, and returned to the fold as much as possible. **For he who wanders should not be killed but returned to the fold.** <note>Original Latin: "Quis enim errabunda occidi non debet Sed ad caulam reduci." Landino argues for the conversion of heretics rather than their execution.</note> This is also demonstrated in the Book of Kings, when Absalom, the son of David, went in unto his father’s concubines. In this context, the concubines are understood to represent the heretics.

->THEIR CEMETERY<-

He ordains that all the followers of the philosopher Epicurus, together with him, have their cemetery in this part of Hell. And he correctly used the word **cemetery**, as there are tombs here. For a cemetery is where Christians bury the bodies of dead men; it is a Greek word <note>Original: "uocabolo greco"</note> and it means "a place of lying," because here lie the dead bodies, derived from *cime* <note>Original: "cime cioè giacio," referring to the Greek *koimao*, meaning to sleep or lie down.</note>.

->WHO MAKE THE SOUL DIE WITH THE BODY.<-

A most wicked opinion and a total ruin for the future life; but no one of a sane mind believes this. But they, as the Psalmist says: **They have placed their hope in a lie, and they have hoped for a deceptive work.** <note>Original Latin: "Posuerunt mendacium spem suam: & mendactum operi sperauerunt."</note> And Solomon: **They have wandered from the paths of their own cultivation and they gather fruitless things in their hands.** <note>Original Latin: "semitas proprie culture errauerunt et colliguat in manibus infructuosa."</note>

Epicurus the philosopher said that the soul dies together with the body. Various are the opinions of the soul according to different philosophers; many believed it to be a body, many to be a corporeal thing, and it would be a long story to narrate them all. But I, in the first of the three books I wrote in the Latin language regarding the soul, set down the opinion of each one and then refuted it, demonstrating that the soul is neither a body nor a corporeal thing, but incorporeal. I then set down Aristotle’s definition; and because that definition is common to all life and not specific to the human soul, I drew from the Platonic doctrine. In that doctrine, such a great philosopher investigates first why the soul exists. Then, what it is. Whether it existed before the body or after the body. Whether it can be divided into several parts. Whether in one and the same man there are several souls—that is, whether the vegetative soul is one, the motive another, the sensitive another, and the rational another. Or rather, whether it is a single soul that embraces all these four powers within itself. And finally, I set down its definition: that it is a rational, incorporeal substance that moves itself.

After such a definition, I proved why it is a substance and not an accident, and why it is incorporeal and not corporeal. And I explained what Plato means when he says that the soul moves itself, and what active and passive motion are, and how wrongly this definition is attacked by the Peripatetics <note>The followers of Aristotle.</note>. I also said that souls were not all created together as Plato writes, nor do they enter bodies because they are weighed down by the desire for earthly things, as the same Plato suggests. Nor do they do so because they wish to flee the harsh commands of the gods and the constant revolutions they must perform to turn the heavens, as Heraclitus writes. Nor is it to suffer punishment and torment in the bodies for the sins they committed in heaven, as Empedocles and also Origen believe.

I added that souls are created from time to time, and at the same moment they are created, they are placed in the body. They are created by God, but not of his substance, as the Stoics and later many Spanish heretics affirmed (who followed Manichaeus and Priscillian). Nor are they created from his breath, as Viceto Victore <note>Likely referring to Victorinus.</note> would have it. But they are created out of nothing: rational and immortal, and with free will, through which it follows that life and death are in our hands—that is, the power to save or damn ourselves.

Then, in the second book, I treated the vegetative power: how it nourishes the body, how it grows it, and with what seed it generates more. I treated the motive power; I treated the external and internal senses. I treated the appetite and the disturbances that arise from it. I treated all the intellectual and moral virtues. I did not only describe all these parts and powers, but I also demonstrated all the instruments of the body which the soul uses in them.

In the third book, I added the rational power, and I distinctly narrated the possible and agent intellect <note>Aristotelian terms for the capacity to receive knowledge and the power to process it into abstract thought.</note>, and what lower reason and higher reason are, and what the intellect and intelligence are. And I refuted the opinion of Averroes <note>An Islamic philosopher who argued there was only one collective human intellect.</note> and many others, demonstrating that there are as many souls as there are men, and that it is false that there is only one universal intellect. And in the last part, I placed many arguments to prove the immortality of the soul. Therefore, through all these things, we understand that the soul was never before the body. We understand its essence, its parts, and its powers. We understand what it performs in the body, with what instruments, and how it remains after it has left the body.

I did not cite my own books because I am so arrogant as to prefer myself to others, but because in them are collected many things which are not found elsewhere together; for I joined the Platonic with the Aristotelian and Stoic disciplines, and I subjected those to the Christian truth. In narrating this, I pulled them from the thorny arguments of dialectic and made them clear and open with an oratorical style, so that not only men practiced in philosophy, but even citizens—provided they have some knowledge of letters—can easily understand them. And let this be enough regarding the soul.

I return to Epicurus. He was an Athenian, the son of Neocles. He said that our soul is a body composed of such thin parts that it penetrates throughout the entire body. The matter that makes this soul are atoms—that is, bodies so minute that they are indivisible. He claimed these atoms are very round. And because every body is composed, and every composite dissolves, and consequently perishes, it follows that since the soul is a body, it must perish. Therefore, he claims the soul is mortal. This same philosopher placed our happiness in the pleasure <note>Original: "uolupta"</note> and gratification of the body, and unhappiness in the pain of the body. This sentiment is more suited to a beast than a man, for we are not born to fill our bellies or satisfy lust, but to contemplate divine things. Nonetheless, he lived better than he spoke; for he lived with supreme temperance, both in food and in venereal matters. He endured pain with great courage. He was most observant of faith. He was most faithful in friendships, for which reason he had many friends. He was very liberal and merciful. For this, he is much praised in many places by Seneca, a most grave philosopher.

But returning to the text: our poet, seeing that there are so many heresies that he could not treat them all, set down this one, which is more pernicious to the human generation than any other. For whoever considers the soul mortal removes every foundation for just civil living and true religion.

->WHO MAKE THE SOUL MORTAL WITH THE BODY.<-

They do not "make" it so in reality, for it is not in their power to make it dead or alive; but they "make" it so, meaning they judge it to be so.

->THEREFORE TO THE QUESTION YOU ASK ME, IF THEY CAN BE SEEN. WITHIN HERE<-

In this nearby space.

->YOU SHALL SOON BE SATISFIED<-

Because you will see the souls come out of the tomb.

->AND ALSO THE WISH THAT YOU KEEP SILENT FROM ME.<-

He had asked if the souls could be seen, but his intention was specifically to see Farinata and Cavalcante, whom he believed were there, knowing they were stained with such a vice.

->O GOOD GUIDE, I DO NOT KEEP<-

Hidden from you my heart: that is, I did not stay silent to hide my heart from you—meaning my desire.

->BUT TO BE BRIEF.<-

Because he who asks in general terms is briefer than he who searches for particulars. And he adds that he wishes to be brief because Virgil, not only now but many times, has admonished him to this. And Dante subtly demonstrates the difference between the superior and inferior intellect. For the superior turns toward universals and not particulars; for example <note>Original: "uerbi gratia"</note>, it does not search to see if the homicide committed specifically by Milo against Clodius, or the robbery committed by Verres in Sicily, is evil. Rather, it searches universally if homicide and robbery are evil. But the inferior intellect considers the particular, as we see in civil life. But Dante, wishing to arrive at the true science of things, which is found in universals, leaves his own manner and takes up that of Virgil, following the universals; for Virgil, wishing to unite him to knowledge, always admonishes him to this. And yet he does not hide his heart from him. For the superior intellect knows this universal: that the inferior intellect seeks particulars.

Landino highlights his own scholarly work in synthesizing Platonic and Aristotelian thought with Christian theology.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Canto X of the Inferno. The previous page established the theological setting of the heretics' tombs and the nature of the Epicurean error—denying the immortality of the soul. Here, Dante encounters the soul of the great Ghibelline leader, Farinata degli Uberti.</meta>

# INFERNO.

> "O Tuscan, who through the city of fire
> alive you go thus speaking honestly,
> may it please you to stay in this place.
> Your speech makes you manifest
> as a native of that noble fatherland
> to which perhaps I was too troublesome."
> Suddenly this sound came out
> from one of the tombs; therefore I drew closer,
> fearing a little more, to my leader.

---

> And he said to me: "Turn around! What are you doing?
> See Farinata there who has risen:
> from the waist up you shall see him all."
> I had already fixed my face in his;
> and he rose with his chest and with his forehead
> as if he held all Hell in great disdain.
> And the spirited, prompt hands of the leader
> pushed me toward him among the sepulchers,
> saying: "Let your words be discreet."

<column-break/>

The poet presents the words of the spirit, who was Farinata degli Uberti; these words are appropriate for a magnanimous and prudent man of composed manners, as he was. **O TUSCAN** or "O you from Tuscany": as if to say, "O Florentine," since that city is the head of Tuscany. **THROUGH THE CITY of fire**: through the City of Dis, which is filled with fire. **ALIVE YOU GO**: and not dead in your vices as we are. **SPEAKING honestly**: because Farinata had heard how Dante responded to Virgil. **STAY**: stop. **YOUR SPEECH**: this shows that Farinata recognized him by his accent. **OF THAT Noble fatherland**: your homeland and mine. He uttered these words not without sorrow. For every fault committed leaves behind a sense of repentance that continually goads the conscience. Therefore, by calling it "that noble fatherland," he shows he regrets having offended it; for by saying "noble," it is as if to say it was "unworthy of being harassed." And so he adds: **TO WHICH perhaps I was too troublesome.** But he said "perhaps" so as not to deprive himself entirely of an excuse—as if to say: "If I was impious toward her, my adversaries gave me the cause." **SUDDENLY This sound came out**: the poet speaks and describes where these words came from. Because they caused him some fright, being a sudden and unexpected thing, they made him draw closer to Virgil. By this, the poet denotes that whenever the "sensuality" (or the lower reason) takes on some perturbation, it ought to join itself with the "higher reason" <note>In medieval psychology, "lower reason" deals with worldly senses and fears, while "higher reason" or the intellect judges truth and divine law.</note>. For in the higher reason there is perfect judgment; it knows whether that which causes fear should be fled or not. And if it is not to be feared, it comforts the appetite to go forward. And so follows the text.

It was no wonder that Farinata’s words perturbed the "sensuality." For no one can respond to heresy unless they are aided by the intellect. But to one who draws near to it, the intellect gives courage to respond. **TURN AROUND, what are you doing?** As if to say, "Why do you delay?" This denotes that one must rise up against heresy quickly and with audacity before any false opinion grows old in the mind. **LET YOUR words be discreet**: that is, prompt and well-considered, so that the adversary may have no opening to seize upon. **SEE FARINATA**: a Florentine knight of the noble Uberti family. He was the leader of the Ghibellines in Florence. By his counsel, the Ghibellines were victorious in the most unhappy conflict of Montaperti in the Val d'Arbia <note>The Battle of Montaperti (1260) was a bloody defeat for the Guelfs of Florence.</note>. Following this, the Guelfs fled; abandoning Florence, they traveled through a large part of Italy with a most flourishing army, and in Bologna, Parma, and Modena, they restored the Guelf faction. Finally, armed in aid of the Pope against Manfred, they were the most powerful cause of the defeat

<column-break/>

of Manfred <note>Manfred was the King of Sicily and a patron of the Ghibellines; his defeat at Benevento in 1266 marked the end of Ghibelline dominance.</note>. Farinata was without doubt a man of great spirit and no less counsel; but he held a wicked and false opinion regarding the human soul, believing that it perished along with the body. Therefore, he judged it good in this brief life to take every bodily pleasure. Thus, in his victuals and food, he surpassed all modesty. Dante noted this in the sixth canto when he asked Ciacco if Farinata was with him. **I HAD already fixed my face in his**: in my sight, that is, my eyes. **FIXED in his**: because I was staring at him fixedly to recognize him. **AND HE ROSE with his chest and with his forehead**: Heresy can consist of three parts: feeling it within oneself, speaking of it with others, and making an open profession of it. Therefore, Dante, wishing to show him as a heretic in every part, first gave him the speech; now he shows him rising with his chest, where thought resides, and with his forehead, which signifies open and manifest profession. This is why, according to the laudable institution of Christians (whose religion consists chiefly in the Gospel), when they hear the Gospel, they sign their forehead, their mouth, and their chest. This demonstrates that they believe with the heart, speak with the tongue, and make profession with an open forehead. Furthermore, the poet wishes to show the habit of a haughty man, as Farinata was; for such men, out of elation, walk almost leaning back, showing off their chest and forehead. Hence Juvenal says: **"Reflecting much of the supine Maecenas."** <note>Original Latin: "Multum referens de Mecenate supino." Juvenal uses "supine" to describe the lazy or arrogant posture of the wealthy Maecenas.</note> **AS IF he had Hell in great disdain.** It is the nature of the small-minded to be afflicted and dismayed in torments; but he who is of a great mind retains a certain pride and haughtiness, and it seems he would rather despise the torment than grieve over it. And the poet said *dispicto* instead of *dispecto* [disdain], changing the "e" to "i" to make the rhyme. **AND THE SPIRITED hands of the leader prompt.** It was necessary that the lower reason be corroborated by the excellence and frankness of the higher. And so the poet feigns that the "spirited hands" of the leader pushed him; they were not only spirited, but also prompt—that is, cautious and swift. He commanded that his words be "discreet": that is, clear and open. Because anyone who wishes to be free of heresy must write and speak without any ambiguity, and should not proceed unless sent by the intellect. For it is foolishness for one who does not have an intellect illuminated by true Christian doctrine to dispute, especially in public, with heretics and infidels; for being defeated by the sharpness of one who affirms a falsehood, he makes those who listen waver. Hence it is prohibited for anyone who is not a declared Master of Sacred Theology to dispute in public.

<column-break/>

> When I was at the foot of his tomb,
> he looked at me a bit and then, almost disdainful,
> he asked me: "Who were your ancestors?"
> I, who was desirous to obey,
> did not hide it from him, but revealed it all;
> at which he raised his eyebrows a little bit.
> Then he said: "Fiercely were they adverse..."

<column-break/>

In the first tercet, the poet describes the gestures and words of Farinata, through which his haughty nature is demonstrated; for with a certain pride, he asked who Dante's "greater ones"—that is, his ancestors—had been. **I, WHO WAS Desirous to obey**: refer this to Virgil, who had told him, "Let your words be discreet." **AT WHICH HE RAISED His eyebrows a little bit.** This is the gesture of a man who hears something he does not like. And then he said: "These ancestors of yours were fiercely different and adversaries to me, and to my ancestors, and to my party." For they were Guelfs and his were Ghibellines. **SO THAT TWICE I scattered them.** Because twice the Guelfs were driven out. **BUT YOU...**

Landino uses the interaction to allegorize the relationship between the senses and the intellect when confronting the "city of fire" and the sin of heresy.</summary>

# CANTO TEN

...to me and to my ancestors and to my faction
so that for two times I scattered them.
"If they were chased away, they returned from every side,"
I replied to him, "the one and the other time;
but yours did not learn that art well."

True religion has often been driven out of many places by heretical depravity. Finally, it always returned to its state. But on the contrary, no sect of heretics has ever been extinguished that was afterwards revived.

Then there rose to sight, uncovered,
a shade alongside this one, up to the chin;
I believe it was raised on its knees.
He looked around me as if he had a desire
to see if someone else was with me;
and after his suspicion was entirely quenched,
Weeping he said: "If through this blind
prison you go through height of genius,
my son, where is he? and why is he not with you?"
And I to him: "I come not of myself.
He who waits there leads me through here,
whom perhaps your Guido held in disdain."
His words and the manner of the punishment
had already told me the name of this man;
therefore the response was so full.
Suddenly upright he said: "How?
did you say 'he had'? Does he not live still?
Does the sweet light not strike his eyes?"
When he noticed some delay
that I made before the response,
he fell back supine: and appeared no more outside.

<column-break/>

**YOURS DID NOT** learn well that art of returning: because having been driven out once, they never returned afterward, nor does any hope remain for them to return. And it can be said that under these names—Guelphs and Ghibellines—one may allegorically understand Catholic and Heretic. For in truth, the Guelphs were always proponents and defenders of the Apostolic See <note>the Papacy</note>, and for this reason he places them as Catholics; and the Ghibellines as heretics, since they rebelled against the Church. And it is true that if they were chased away, they always returned. Because notwithstanding that—

After Farinata he places Cavalcante de' Cavalcanti, a Florentine born of the ancient and most splendid family of the Cavalcanti, who in his time was enumerated among the Guelph princes of our republic for his virtue and prudence. But he only incurred infamy for holding the Epicurean opinion <note>the denial of the soul's immortality</note>. But because he spoke of it with more modesty and more covertly than Farinata, the poet does not make him rise as far out of the tomb as him. The Cavalcanti family is very ancient in our city, and ennobled by not a few excellent men produced by it, as can easily be seen in the Florentine chronicles. But to return to where we left off: from Cavalcante was born Guido, excellent not only in civil life, but also practiced in every kind of speculation <note>theoretical philosophy</note>, but especially a most acute dialectician and an outstanding philosopher, and not little practiced in Tuscan verses, which even today live full of gravity and doctrine. But because he gave himself entirely to philosophy, he did not care much to read the Latin poets, nor to investigate their art and ornaments; he lacked that style and grace which is proper to the poet. Nevertheless, except for Dante, he far surpassed all others who wrote in rhyme until his age. I have seen a moral poem by Guido whose beginning is "A lady entreats me" <note>original: "Donna mi priegha"</note>, "because I wish to speak / Of an accident that is often fierce / And is so haughty that it is called love." In this moral poem, which consists of five stanzas, he treats of love not according to the divine like Solomon <note>referring to the Song of Songs</note>, nor according to the pagan poets like Ovid, but according to the philosophers. He demonstrates love to be an accident <term>accident: a philosophical term for a quality or state that exists only within a substance, like heat in water, rather than being a thing itself</term> and not a substance, just as appetite is in the soul, and as all passions are. He demonstrates that it is a fierce and great accident and that it has its being in the memory, because the impression of the image of the beloved thing is in the memory, as light proceeding from a luminous body is retained in a transparent <note>diaphanous</note> body. He also demonstrates how love is created, and many other things with so much doctrine that Giles of Rome <note>original: "Egidio Romano"</note>, a most noble physicist and metaphysician, and Dino del Garbo, an excellent Florentine

---

doctor, commented on it. He wishes, therefore, to signify all these things: and so he says: **THEN THERE ROSE** to sight, uncovered. At the open mouth of the tomb. **A SHADE**: and a certain one. **I BELIEVE IT WAS** raised on its knees: because if he had stood up, he would have shown not only the chin but the chest like Farinata. **DESIRE**: will. Where "to please" means to consent: which is to make another's will one's own. **THAT THE SUSPICION** was entirely quenched. We say "to know," "to believe," and "to suspect." He who knows has true knowledge of the thing. Believing is when we are not certain, but we have such firm faith that it is so that we do not doubt it. Suspecting is believing but with doubt. He said: "if you go through this hell by **height of genius**: why is my son not with you?" as if to say: he who, like you, is of high genius and great doctrine. And note that these words "if through this blind prison you go through height of genius" serve both the fiction and the allegory. For according to the literal sense we will say "by height of genius" as if to say "if by some admirable art you can go alive and without pain through hell." But according to the allegory, understand: "If through height of genius and great doctrine you go through the contemplation of vices, my son is such that he should be able to do this same thing." **AND I TO HIM**: I come not of myself: As if to say, my genius would not have given me such an invention. **BUT LEADS ME** he who waits: that is, he expects the doctrine and the poetic invention of Virgil, whom I have imitated. **LEADS ME**: guides me to create such fiction, because it is not much different from his own. **WHOM PERHAPS YOUR GUIDO held in disdain**: As if to say, because your Guido, having given himself entirely to philosophy, did not deign to favor the poets; his philosophy was not enough to make a similar poem, which he could have done if he had deigned to read Virgil and imitate him. **HIS WORDS**: He shows that through his words, which denoted Guido rather than anyone else—both because he was very learned and because he was his closest friend—and the punishment, which was for heretics, was due to Master Cavalcante. **SUDDENLY** upright. He shows that because Dante said "he had" as one is accustomed to say of those in the past, and did not say "he has" (which is said of the living), it gave terror and fear to Cavalcante that Guido was not dead. **DOES NOT STRIKE**: The sweet light does not strike his eyes. This occurs to the living, because the rays of the sun are those that illuminate the air, a transparent body, without which two things (or things similar to these) the sight cannot use its power. **WHEN HE NOTICED** some delay. The first conjecture he took from that word "had" made him doubt. Now the second induced in him a firm opinion that he was dead. And certainly when we ask a friend about the life or health of one of ours, and he does not answer quickly, immediately fear is born in us that he is not as we desire. And it demonstrates in the words of Cavalcante how great a father's love is toward his son, since he loves him so much even in Hell. It is asked according to philosophers whether the love of one's own remains in the soul separated from the body. **FELL BACK SUPINE**. It gives to the soul the state that usually happens to a man when, due to a great passion of mind, he falls into a faint and becomes weak.

The first two tercets present little difficulty and merely demonstrate the nature of a man with a **great and unconquerable spirit**: one who makes no gesture or act that does not signify his being undefeated. Then, the poet matches the words to the gestures. For to one of such a spirit, neither torment nor death is as painful as having to yield to an enemy. Similarly, one can note the **obstinacy of the damned**: even after death, they do not set aside the passions and disturbances they held in life. **BUT NOT FIFTY TIMES shall be rekindled the face of the lady who rules here.** This refers to Proserpina, who is the same as the Moon. the underworld. Smitten by the beauty of the girl, he kidnapped her and made her his wife. Such an injury greatly grieved Ceres, and she would by no means remain patient while her daughter stayed with the abductor, until Jove settled the dispute. He was the brother of Pluto and the father of Proserpina; chosen as arbiter by the parties, he judged that she should stay six months with Pluto in the underworld and six with her mother. She has power in heaven, where she is called the **Moon**. She has it on earth, where she is called **Diana**. She has it in hell, and they call her **Proserpina**. And because of this triple power, Virgil said: *Triple Hecate, the three faces of the virgin Diana* <note>original: "Tergemina hecaten tria uirginis ora Diane"</note>. And because for six months of the year she waxes and for six she wanes, the poets imagined that she spent those six months in the underworld and six above. They imagine the Moon to be the goddess of the underworld because she operates most greatly upon inferior bodies; her power is supreme regarding the formation and growth of terrestrial bodies. The poets imagine many other things about Proserpina through which they wish to express the nature of the Moon, but they are not relevant to the present purpose. Therefore, I return to the poet, who says that the face of the lady who rules in hell—that is, the Moon, who is Proserpina—shall not be "rekindled" fifty times; that is, fifty months shall not pass. Since the Moon is a body that is dark in itself but receives its light from the sun, it is said to be "rekindled" by him. Thus, he means that fifty months will not pass before Dante himself is exiled. This, according to <term>Giovanni Boccaccio</term><note>The famous 14th-century author of the *Decameron* and a noted commentator on Dante.</note>, happened before two years or a little more had passed. **AND SO MAY YOU ONE DAY... in the sweet world:** It is "sweet" in comparison to those who are in hell. Thus Virgil says: *Whom, deprived of sweet life and torn from the breast, a black day carried off* <note>original: "Quos dulcis uite exortes & ab ubere raptos Abstulit atra dies"</note>. **RETURN:** that is, go back. And the phrasing here is not a simple conditional—as in "tell me if you ever return"—but rather a prayerful wish, as when we say: "Tell me the truth, so may God help you." It is as if he says: "I pray God helps you if you tell me the truth." **IN EACH OF ITS LAWS:** because in truth they never used such cruelty against any Ghibelline family as they did against the Uberti. It is recorded that no penalty was ever remitted nor any benefit granted to the Ghibellines from which the Uberti and Lamberti were not excluded, because of the cruelty of the <term>rout of Montaperto</term><note>A bloody battle in 1260 between the Guelphs and Ghibellines.</note>. This was in the year 1258. In this year, as the pride of the Uberti sought to subjugate the people, the city rose in revolt, and in the tumult, Stiatuccio Uberti was killed and Ubertuccio was beheaded. Sir Farinata, with many noble Ghibellines, fled to Siena.

Farinata had asked for what reason the Florentine people were so cruel toward him and all the Uberti. Dante replied that the slaughter and the cruel killing which, through Farinata's cunning and plotting, was inflicted on the Guelphs in the rout of Montaperto, where the Arbia river ran red with blood. **CAUSE SUCH PRAYERS TO BE MADE:** It makes the people desire and pray to the magistrates that such laws be made. **IN OUR TEMPLE:** This is a metaphor. Since he had spoken of "prayers," he used "temple" to mean the court and public place where the affairs of the Republic are handled. And this is because, as I said above, Sir Farinata was in exile; and being a man of great spirit and no less prudence, desiring not only to return but to bring back those of his faction, he went to Siena—a refuge in those times for the Ghibelline party and very hostile to the Florentine Guelphs.

---

And there, through secret intermediaries, he plotted with the Ghibellines remaining in Florence for what followed. Then he sent certain Friars Minor on behalf of those who ruled in Siena to the <term>Anziani</term><note>The "Elders" or high-ranking magistrates of Florence.</note> of Florence, saying that if they approached Siena with the army, they would give them a gate. Therefore, the Florentine people determined to undertake such an enterprise, although some wise citizens forbade it. Under the pretext of wanting to supply Montalcino, our ally, they came as far as Montaperto in the Val d'Arbia. There, against all their expectations, the Sienese came out to meet them with German men-at-arms, whom Manfredi had sent through Farinata's efforts. And at the start of the battle, many in the Florentine army who favored the Ghibellines fled to the enemy's side. It took great courage for our men to resist such force and so many frauds, and they sustained the battle for a long time. Finally, Sir Bocca degli Abati, with supreme perfidy, approached Sir Iacopo del Vacca of the ancient Pazzi family, who was carrying the standard, and cut off his hand. Thus, the standard fell to the ground. Four thousand Florentines were killed in this rout, which took place on Saturday, the fourth of September, in the year of our salvation 1260. **AFTER HE HAD SHAKEN HIS HEAD, SIGHING:** This gesture depicts the various disturbances in his soul: partly indignation at the injury received, partly remorse for having acted against his homeland. And therefore, excusing himself, he says: **IN THIS I WAS NOT ALONE:** because many other rebels were with me. **NOR CERTAINLY WITHOUT CAUSE with the others would I have moved.** In short, he shows that coming against his homeland was a common act shared with many, but defending it, he was alone. Thus follows: **BUT I WAS ALONE THERE, WHERE IT WAS AGREED / BY EVERYONE ELSE TO WIPE OUT FLORENCE / TO DEFEND HER WITH AN OPEN FACE.** This refers to the fact that after the return of the Ghibellines to Florence, the ambassadors and principal men of all the Ghibelline lands of Tuscany gathered to provide for the conservation of the common state of that faction. Among many other things, it was advised that the final extermination of the Guelphs was to destroy Florence, the primary head of that party, and reduce the city to small villages, so that the Guelphs already sent into exile would lose

lost every hope of returning there. At that council, since they were the sole salvation of that party—not only the others, but even the Florentine Ghibellines agreed—that day would have brought a horrific slaughter to our homeland if it had not been for Messer Farinata, who alone opposed it. As is shown in the history by Leonardo Bruni <note>original: "Lionardo aretino"; Bruni was a famous humanist historian and Chancellor of Florence</note> in a speech he had Farinata deliver at the Empoli congregation: where he not only contradicted them with words, but like a new Scipio at Cannae, with a naked sword he threatened anyone who persisted in such an opinion. Hence, in the elegies entitled *Xandra* written in my youth, I wrote this epigram about him:

> I confess we overcame the Guelph ranks under my leadership:
> The Arbia flowed with water red with blood.
> But so that you, Florence, might keep your ancient seat,
> Farinata’s great mind alone granted it to you.

Farinata therefore opposed them all, demonstrating that if he was an enemy to the Guelphs, he was not an enemy to his homeland: for the love of his country carried more weight with him than the enmities of his adversaries. Therefore, through him alone was Florence defended so that she did not perish.

<column-break/>

Farinata had demonstrated that not only should he not be in a worse grade than the other exiles, but in a better one. For at the Arbia he had done no worse than the others, and at Empoli he had done better. And perhaps he would have added other things, if Dante, eager to hear for what reason the damned foresee the future and not the present, had not cut off his words and added: "MAY YOUR SEED EVER FIND REST," I prayed to him; and it is arranged thus: I spoke to him saying, "O, solve for me that knot <note>a metaphor for a difficult doubt or problem</note> which has here entangled my judgment, if ever your descendants may find rest," that is, your descendants who are currently living and those who are to come. And this word "if" is deprecatory <note>an expression of a wish or prayer</note>, as we said above, and not conditional. He takes the "knot" to mean the doubt. Because having heard Ciacco earlier, and now Farinata, predict painful things, and on the other hand seeing that Cavalcante did not know of present things, it seemed incredible to him that, not knowing the present, they should know the future. WE SEE like "THOSE WHO HAVE BAD LIGHT." There are two types of imperfect vision. For some have clear vision, but not much, and these see better up close. Some have much vision, but it is obscured; hence they see better from afar, because as the visual rays go out in the process, they become clearer and made bright and fit for seeing. But the first, because they have visual spirits that are too bright, if they proceed too far through the illuminated transparent medium, they are overwhelmed by the light, and therefore they do not see. Therefore Farinata says: "We are similar to those who have bad light," that is, they have obscured visual spirits which do not see unless they proceed a long distance through the luminous air, which clears them and makes them fit to see. But certainly it seems incredible that these souls, seeing future things, do not also see present ones. Wherefore some understand that he, by memory of past things, makes a conjecture of the future; as, for example, Farinata, remembering the nature and customs of his citizens and the civil discords, foresees what must follow from them, and sees it from afar. But because he does not know exactly when it will be, it could already be present and he does not know it. And in this way they save Dante’s judgment: that the damned soul sees the future and not the present. But Thomas Aquinas says that the soul stripped of the body no longer has the knowledge of the senses, which concerns particulars; therefore it no longer knows this or that thing unless it learns it from another soul that arrives anew or from some spirit. But it knows according to the nature of the intellect, which concerns universals, and in this way it knows future things as universals, and cannot turn itself to the imagination <note>the faculty of processing sensory images</note> as when it is in the body. But the saved soul understands things past, present, and future according to Thomas and Gregory, because it sees them in God, in whom nothing is hidden. WHEN THEY APPROACH OR ARE—when they draw near or are present—ALL IS VAIN our intellect: that is, we understand nothing and know nothing of your human state, nor of anything that is done among men. Whence Augustine: "It must be confessed that the dead do not know what is being done here while it is being done, but later they hear from those who go from here to them by dying; they can also hear something from angels." <note>original Latin: "Fatendum est nescire mortuos quid agatur dum agitur ised postea uero audire ab iis qui hinc ad eos moriendo pergunt: Possunt etiam ab angelis audire aliquid."</note> UNLESS ANOTHER BRINGS IT TO US: unless another soul or a malignant spirit reports it to us. THEREFORE YOU CAN UNDERSTAND that our consciousness will be entirely dead: that is, we will know nothing from that point when the door of the future shall be closed. This will be after the Day of Judgment: because the tombs <note>arche; the sarcophagi in this circle of Hell</note> will be locked, and even more so because, there being no more men to be born, there will be no more future events.

Once the poet understood the reason why the damned saw the future and not the present, he grieved for not having responded to Cavalcante. For it often happens that a mind occupied with a greater care leaves aside another thing, which it then regrets after such occupation has passed. Therefore, now grieving for the fault committed in not having responded to one who had been his friend, he responds now, and prays Farinata to tell "that fallen one," that is, Cavalcante, THAT HIS BORN ONE—his son—is still joined with the living, he is still in life. AND IF I WAS a little while ago MUTE TO THE RESPONSE, it was not because I did not want to answer him. But because my mind was occupied in thinking about the doubt which Dante had with Farinata and Cavalcante, i.e., he had descended into particular things. Now Virgil, that is, the higher mind, recalls him from these particulars to lead him back to the universals of which there is true science. But before he departs, he learns that here is the second Frederick, who was the son of Emperor Henry VI and grandson of Frederick Barbarossa; Henry took as his wife Constance, daughter of the good King William of Sicily, formerly a nun; but the Pope gave her a dispensation, and she received as a dowry the Kingdom of Sicily, which was occupied by Tancred, born of the house of King Roger; and he left it to William his son. This man, then, was conquered by Henry. Wherefore the entire kingdom then remained to Frederick...

<header>INFERNO.</header>

Henry, his son, and of Constance: of whom we are presently treating. Since he remained an orphan as a child, he was raised with diligence under the guardianship of the Supreme Pontiff <note>Innocent III</note>. Having reached manhood, he took possession of the kingdom, and not long after was crowned King of the Romans by Pope Honorius in the year of our salvation 1220. After this coronation he lived thirty-three years and fell into discord with the Church because, when he wished to review the accounts of the administration of the kingdom, the prelates did not want to show them. Afterwards, reconciled in agreement, he prepared an army against the Sultan, as was required by the conditions of peace; and this was in 1236. And while he was already overseas with the army, the Pope, by letters, advised the Sultan on how he might manage to defeat and kill him; and in the meantime, he caused Sicily and Apulia to rebel against him. To sow discord among Christians, the Sultan sent these letters to Frederick. From this, peace was born between them, even though Frederick could have recovered the entire Holy Land. He therefore returned to Italy and reacquired the kingdom; and in contempt of the Pope, he sent for many Saracens from Tunisia and allowed them to inhabit Lucera, today called Nocera <note>Lucera dei Pagani</note>, which is in the plains of Apulia. He moved war against the Pope and used much cruelty against the prelates; finally, he greatly afflicted the Roman Court and much weakened the Guelfs of Tuscany, the supporters of the Church. He sent one of his sons, born of a princess of Antioch, against the Florentines with fifteen hundred cavalry; for this reason, he called him Frederick of Antioch. The princess of Antioch did not wish to join with Frederick, hearing that he already had a wife. Wherefore, he caused two ships to arrive with black sails, carrying ambassadors who falsely said that his wife was dead; and with this fraud, he deceived the princess. Finally, he died in Apulia. Because he had heard from astrologers that "Florence" would be fatal to him and that he was destined to die there, he never wished to pass through our territories <note>the territory of Florence in Tuscany</note>. And finally, he fell ill in Apulia and was brought to a town in Apulia called Firenzuola <note>Little Florence</note>. For which reason, having then understood the name, he judged himself a dead man; and so he died excommunicated. And some say that Manfred, his natural son and Prince of Taranto, smothered him with a pillow to seize his treasures. He was a man of military character and great spirit, much feared by both Christians and Saracens. Had he not been provoked by the fraud of the Pontiff, perhaps he would not have been so cruel toward the Church, which treated him in a way that he can deservedly be placed among the heretics.

**THE CARDINAL:** All writers agree, especially those close to Dante’s time, that he means Cardinal Ottaviano degli Ubaldini. He was certainly a man of great governance and invincible spirit, but in his life and habits, he was more like a tyrant than a priest. He was so favorable to the Ghibellines that he did not care if he acted against the Pontifical authority to help them. When he was not aided by them in certain needs, he said that "if a soul exists, I have lost it for the Ghibellines," which words showed him to be an Epicurean <note>A follower of Epicurus, believing the soul dies with the body</note>. His prudence and authority were so great that he disposed of the Roman Court in his own way; and once he held it in the mountains of Mugello in the lands of the Ubaldini, and against the will of the Pontiff, he always favored the Ghibellines. His favor created the first Archbishop of the Visconti of Milan and led them to the dominion of that city. He was called nothing other than "The Cardinal"; and every time one said "the Cardinal says" or "does," it was understood to be him.

**F**arinata finished his words and returned below; and Dante turned back to Virgil, reflecting on those words that Farinata had spoken regarding his exile, which seemed hostile and harsh to him. And Virgil asked him why he was so lost in thought; and Dante replied that it was because of the adverse fortune which Farinata had predicted for him. Virgil gave him excellent advice: which is that he should preserve in his memory what he has heard, and then seek to understand from Beatrice the entire course of his life. This denotes that when evil is announced to us, we should not choose to afflict ourselves with excessive fear, nor judge with our physical senses <term>sensualita (physical perception)</term> how unhappy and miserable that thing might be. For the judgment of the senses is poor, because it insists that all adversities affecting the body or fortune must be great and intolerable, and that because of them, men become miserable. This is entirely false. Therefore, reserve this judgment for Beatrice, and she will show you that only he is in misery who is divided and separated from God by the vice he has committed, even if he were in every abundance of wealth and status; and on the contrary, he is most happy who is joined with God through virtue. This sentiment is not only Stoic but Christian: that nothing is an evil except for vice, which alone takes away the blessed life. And because vice cannot be given to us except by ourselves, John Chrysostom wrote his *Paradoxes* <note>original: "paradoxa"</note>, through which he proves that "no one can be harmed except by himself." Because only vice and sin can harm, and vice and sin do not come except

from our own will and choice; nor can any power force us to this if we do not wish it. **AND NOW** attend and here I point my finger. He points his finger to make him attentive and to demonstrate with that gesture that what he had to say was a notable thing. For we point the finger when, speaking of any matter, we wish to testify that it is true and of some importance. Or rather, he wished to show that it was not enough to attend to the precepts of Beatrice, but it was necessary to put them into practice; and by the finger and by the hands, action is signified. Wherefore the Psalmist said: *And I lifted up my hands to your commandments, which I loved* <note>original: "Et leuaui manus meas ad mãdata tua que dilexi"</note>; which means nothing other than lifting the hand to God’s commandments to put them into work. **WHEN** you shall be before the sweet ray. For sacred theology contains within itself the truth, with which it illuminates the minds of all; and its eye sees every thing, because it sees the truth. Therefore, in Hell, one learns of the loss one suffers of temporal things. But the remedy against the pain that these bring with them is not shown to us except by Beatrice; and she teaches us the journey of our life: and what is the highest good, and which are the vain goods. **TO THE LEFT** hand, to depart from the wall and enter through the middle. Which he clarifies by saying **WE LEFT** the wall and went toward the center **BY A PATH** <note>original: "per un sentiere"</note>; *sentier* is a French word; which **STRIKES** <note>original: "fiede"</note>, that is, it heads straight toward a valley where one descends into the seventh circle. **WHICH EVEN** up there: which valley stank so strongly that even to the end of that path it **MADE** its **STENCH** <term>lezo (a heavy, natural odor)</term> spurt out, as if reverberating. Strictly speaking, *lezo* is a powerful odor that is unpleasant, which does not arise from a corrupt body like the fetor and stink thrown off by a rotten or decaying thing; but it is natural to such a thing, and proceeds from the sweat and evaporation that a body gives off, even if it is not corrupted. Wherefore a billy-goat and a living goat do not "stink" in the sense of decay, but they have a *lezo*. But they "stink" <note>original: "pute"</note> when, being dead, they already decay. Nor is *lezo* found only in the sense of smell, but also in taste. Wherefore we say buffalo meat has a *lezo*, and certain herbs when tasted we say taste of *lezo*. And it is specifically in taste or smell that which Pliny in his...

<sig>h</sig>

...natural history <note>A reference to Pliny the Elder’s *Naturalis Historia*, a standard classical reference for the medieval world</note> and other Latin writers call *virus* <note>original: "uirus"; in this context, it refers to a poisonous or foul-smelling secretion rather than a modern biological virus</note>. Although this same word sometimes signifies poison, [the poet] more properly said *lezo* <note>original: "lezo"; an archaic Italian word for a nauseating, stagnant stench</note>: because such a foul odor is innate to this place, as we will show more clearly a little further ahead.

--- Page 136 ---
<meta>This page marks the beginning of Canto XI. Following the encounter with the heretics in Canto X, Dante and Virgil pause at the edge of the transition to the lower circles. This page provides the structural "blueprint" for the rest of the Inferno, categorizing sins of Malice into Violence and Fraud.</meta>

# CANTO XI OF THE FIRST CANTICLE BY DANTE

<margin>i</margin>
Upon the furthest edge of a high bank
formed by great broken rocks in a circle,
we came above a more cruel crowded pit.
And here, because of the horrible excess
of the stench which the deep abyss throws out,
we drew back behind the lid
Of a great tomb, where I saw an inscription
which said: "I guard Pope Anastasius,
whom Photinus drew from the straight path."

<margin>1</margin>
"Our descent must be slow," [said the Master],
"so that the sense of smell first becomes used
to the foul breath, and then it will not matter."
Thus the Master; and I: "Find some compensation,"
I said to him, "so that the time does not pass
in waste." And he: "See, I am thinking of that.
My son, within these stones,"
he then began to say, "are three small circles,
descending step by step like those you leave.
All are filled with cursed spirits;
but so that the sight alone may later suffice you,
understand how and why they are constrained.

Of every malice that gains hatred in heaven,
injury is the end; and every such end,
either by force or by fraud, afflicts others."

<column-break/>

In this eleventh canto, he describes the descent into the seventh circle. But so that we have full knowledge of what follows, the author places the punishments of the violent and the fraudulent in the seventh, eighth, and ninth circles. And because both of these sins proceed from malice, there is no doubt that their end is injury. Injury is done either by violence or by fraud. Injury by violence is done to: one’s neighbor, oneself, or God. To one's neighbor, injury is done to their person—such as beating, wounding, or killing them—or to their things—such as inflicting fires, thefts, and robberies. To oneself, injury is similarly done by killing oneself or squandering one's own goods. In the third place, injury is done to God by blaspheming Him, or denying Him, or acting against His offspring: that is, against Nature. For this reason, this seventh circle is divided into three small circles or rounds. In the first and uppermost, those who used violence against their neighbor are punished. In the second, those against themselves. Then we follow with the eighth and ninth circles, where fraud is punished. This is committed either against those who do not trust—and these are punished in the eighth circle—or against those who do trust, for whom the ninth is established, because it is more grave. This is because it breaks two degrees of love: the natural and universal, and the accidental and particular. **UPON THE FURTHEST EDGE of a high bank.** This shows into what a precipice such sinners fall: because they ruin themselves from the excellence of man to the depths of beasts. No animal is higher than man, because no animal is rational except man; but if that reason is converted to vice, no animal is more pernicious. **GREAT STONES** because the ground could not support them. And by the hardness of the stones, understand the firm and immutable habit of these vices, and the great weight of these sinners: that is, how much they are burdened by conscience. With **GREATER** crowded pit <note>original: "stipa"</note>: that is, a hedge that surrounds the sinners worthy of a more enclosed prison. Or *Stipa*, meaning a crowd; because *stipare* in Latin means to surround and to pack tightly, and we say *stiva* as a great filling-up of cruelty, as we will understand better below. He places the stench in this place to represent the abomination belonging to these sins, and the supreme infamy into which such sinners fall. For if, as Augustine says, <note>original: "Fama bona est odor bonus"; "A good reputation is a good scent,"</note> it follows that infamy is a heavy stench. **I SAW AN inscription which said I guard Pope Anastasius.** Photinus, a cleric of Thessaly, along with Acacius, were heretics and held that the Holy Spirit did not proceed from the Father, and that the Father was greater than the Son. They persuaded Pope Anastasius to this heresy. He was a Roman, and reigned in the time of Emperor Theodoric; making an open profession of such heresy and being reproved by many prelates, he reached such obstinacy that he wished to uphold it in public consistory. But it happened that while debating, he was forced by the necessity of the belly to go and put down his weight, where all his entrails suddenly spilled out, and thus he perished. And not without reason does the poet place the inscription on this tomb: for it denotes that the heresy of a Supreme Pontiff must be known to all; because the more excellent the one who sins, the more the sin is known. Whence Juvenal, as has been said many times: <note>original: "Omne animi uitium tanto conspectius in se crimen habet quanto maior qui peccat habetur"; "Every vice of the soul carries a more conspicuous crime within itself, the greater the status of the sinner."</note>

They had to descend into the seventh circle, but because the stench was unbearable, Virgil warns Dante that they should wait a while until they are accustomed. For every hard thing is better endured after a man has become used to it than at the beginning. Thus Dido in Virgil says: <note>original: "Tempus inane peto requie spatium que furori Dum mea me uita doceat fortuna dolere"; "I seek a void of time, a rest and space for my madness, until my fortune teaches me, defeated, how to grieve."</note> And allegorically we understand that we must not descend to the meditation of such vices with a sudden impulse of the soul, but maturely and with reason, because otherwise we could be seized by them. **THUS THE MASTER** It is the best prudence of men that when they cannot do something without an interval of time, they spend such an interval usefully on another thing. **FIND** some compensation so that the time does not pass in waste. Find something else for us to do that compensates for the time we lose in this. **SEE, I AM THINKING of that** he was thinking, therefore, before he descended—that is, before he came into such an inquiry—to set out the division and almost the definition of all these vices; because as Cicero says:
> <note>original: "Omnis que a ratione suscipitur de aliqua re institutio debet a diffinitione proficisci : & intelligatur id de quo disputetur"; "Every rational inquiry into any subject must begin with a definition, so that the subject of the discussion may be clearly understood."</note>

**MY SON within these stones.** A most excellent order, because Dante—that is, the lower reason—together with the appetite compliant and obedient to it, had to descend into the contemplation of these horrible sins. Therefore, the higher reason, as the best guide, wants him first to get used to enduring the stench and to understand what they are, and then he will lead him among them; because it is first necessary that we become accustomed to being able to endure the disturbances of the soul that proceed from them. And most excellently we know what they are, and how harmful they are to us; and then finally we put ourselves among them because, having become cautious and constant, they will not offend us. The text itself is clear.

Let whoever reads this canto consider it diligently and with the highest attention, because it is the proposition of all the rest of this canticle. Most excellently, therefore, he shows that injury is the end of all malice, which acquires hatred in heaven: that is, it is hated by God. And not without reason...

<summary>Dante and Virgil pause by the tomb of Pope Anastasius to acclimate to the stench of the lower circles, while Virgil explains the moral structure of Hell, categorizing sins of Violence and Fraud. The commentary provides theological and classical justifications for these divisions, citing Augustine, Juvenal, and Cicero.</summary>
