<meta>Continuity Note: This page continues the structural breakdown of Hell in Canto XI. Dante and Virgil are still atop the rocky embankment overlooking the lower circles. Landino's commentary here transitions from the general definition of "injury" to the specific classification of the seventh circle (Violence) and the reasons why Fraud (the eighth and ninth circles) is considered a more grievous sin against God.</meta>

### CANTO TWELFTH <note>Though the header reads 'Duodecimo' (Twelfth), the text continues the verses and commentary of Canto Eleven. Early printed editions sometimes featured running headers that anticipated the next chapter.</note>
<sig>h ii</sig>

But because fraud is a man’s own unique evil,
it more displeases God; and therefore, further down
the fraudulent are placed, and greater grief assails them.
The first circle is entirely for the violent;
but because force is done to three persons,
it is divided and constructed into three rings.
Against God, against oneself, and against one’s neighbor,
force can be applied—I mean to them and to their things—
as you shall hear with clear reasoning:
Death by force and painful wounds
are inflicted on one’s neighbor; and on his possessions:
ruin, arson, and harmful extortions.
Hence, murderers and each who strikes maliciously,
despoilers and plunderers—the first ring torments them all
in various groups.

It is a sin to use reason badly, for by reason we are in a certain way similar to God; whereas by force we are similar to the beasts. And certainly, when a thing is more noble, it is a greater sin to use it poorly. And therefore they are placed further down, so they might be further from the Supreme Good, from which greater pain arises. Since God is our supreme good, the more we are removed from Him, the more miserable we are. **THE FIRST CIRCLE IS ENTIRELY FOR THE VIOLENT.** The violent—that is, those who have committed injury with force—are punished in the first circle: that is, the seventh, which is the first of the three that remain. And this is divided into three rings where three kinds of violent people are punished, as he clearly demonstrates, and as we have distinctly declared just above. **TO GOD, TO ONESELF, TO ONE'S NEIGHBOR.** These are the three persons to whom force can be done. And to each of these three, it can be done in two ways: either to themselves or to their things. And note that when he proposes these three persons, he follows the natural order. For in each case, in the first degree one must place first God, then oneself, and in the last, one's neighbor. But when he then distinguishes these sins, he leaves this order and follows the order of the three rings of the seventh circle. Because in the first ring stay the less grave sinners, he speaks first of those who have used violence against their neighbor, who have a less grave sin, and he lists many kinds of injuries done to a neighbor. To the person: death and beatings. To goods: ruins, arson, and extortions <note>Italian: *tollette*; refers to illegal taxes, theft, or forced payments</note>, that is, robberies. **IN VARIOUS GROUPS:** As if to say, murderers in one, despoilers in another, and so the others in the rest, although they are all in the first ring.

A man may have a violent hand against himself
and against his own goods; and therefore in the second
ring it is necessary that he repent without benefit:
Whoever deprives himself of your world,
gambles away and squanders his faculty,
and weeps there where he ought to be joyful.

Violence may be done against the Deity
by denying and blaspheming Him in the heart,
and by despising Nature and her goodness.
And therefore the smallest ring seals with its mark
Sodom and Cahors,
and him who speaks, despising God in his heart.

...place. Therefore **SODOM AND CAHORS** seals with its mark. As if to say, it brands such sinners by placing its seal upon them. Sodom and Gomorrah were two cities in Syrian Palestine which, because of the wicked vice against nature, God affirmed to Abraham after his circumcision that he would destroy. And he sent two angels into Sodom in the form of boys, who stayed in the house of Lot, an innocent man, having been invited by him. And before they went to sleep, the crowd of Sodomites came to attack the house and seize the angels and violate them. Lot prayed that they would cease such fury and offered them his two beautiful daughters, who were still virgins. But they, persevering in their evil purpose, were struck by the angels and immediately went blind. Lot and his wife and two daughters were led by the angels to safety so they might be saved. And God rained fire and sulfur upon Sodom and Gomorrah, and burned the city and the surrounding region with all the inhabitants and animals and plants. In the Hebrew language, **Sodom** signifies "Yellow," "sterile," and "blindness," or "silent pasture." **Gomorrah** signifies "blindness," "sedition," and "fearful people." Solinus <note>Gaius Julius Solinus, a 3rd-century Latin grammarian and compiler</note> writes that in this region the earth, which is black and almost like ash, shows the past conflagration; and

<column-break/>

added these words: Because there are some malices and cunning which are not hated by God, because they do not do injury. He says then: that injury is the end of the malices displeasing to God, or because such malices are committed to do injury. And understand that injury is every work that man does against reason and justice. Therefore Cicero rightly said that those are injuries which either with vileness offend the ears, or with beatings the body, or with some calumny and reproach stain one's reputation. **AND EVERY SUCH END:** Every end so made, that is, every injurious end. **EITHER WITH FORCE OR WITH FRAUD** constrains another. That is, offends either by force or by fraud, as we have shown above. **BUT BECAUSE FRAUD IS MAN’S OWN EVIL.** Although man has physical strength, nevertheless these forces cannot be called man's own, because they are not only common to him and other animals, but even in those he is surpassed by many. But reason is that which is proper to man, for by that we are named, and by that—and not by force—we are different from the brutes. Therefore, if reason is the proper good given by God to man, fraud—which is the abuse of reason—will be man's own evil, because it is not common to us and the brutes. Furthermore, he who deceives offends the one who in some way trusted him or was not on his guard, and thus he breaks faith. But he who uses force often uses it against one who defends himself. **IT MORE DISPLEASES GOD.** Because it is more grave...

The second kind is of those who use force on themselves by killing themselves, or on their goods by dissipating them. **OF YOUR WORLD** that is, of this life. **REPENT WITHOUT BENEFIT:** <note>Italian: *sanza pro*; literally "without profit"</note> Because repenting in Hell is of no use. And morally, although one who has formed a habit repents, it is difficult to change. It is not to be understood that he repents with true penitence, for as we have shown elsewhere, just as the saved are confirmed in grace and in optimal will, so the damned are in perpetual obstination. But he says "he repents" because he grieves that he originally formed such a habit in vice.

This is the third kind, of those who do violence to God. Here you must understand: that God cannot be harmed. But they do violence as far as they are able by blaspheming and denying Him. Nor without cause does he say **HE SPEAKS IN HIS HEART**, for someone might deny God with words out of fear of death or torment, but not with his heart. Or they do violence to His things: that is, to Nature, which is the daughter of God, such as the Sodomites who commit sin against nature. Or to Art, which is the daughter of Nature and grandchild of God, as are the usurers <note>Cahors was a city in France famous in the Middle Ages for its moneylenders and usurers</note>. And in what way these act against Art will be shown in its place.

<summary>This page outlines the tripartite division of the Circle of Violence (Circle 7), distinguishing between violence against neighbors, self, and God/Nature/Art. It also provides Landino's philosophical defense of why fraud is a greater sin than violence, citing reason as man's unique, God-given attribute.</summary>
<keywords>Fraud vs. Violence, Circle of Violence, Sodom and Gomorrah, Cahors, Usury, Scholastic Philosophy, Cristoforo Landino, Cicero, Reason and Faith</keywords>

--- Page 138 ---
<meta>Continuity Note: This page continues the structural breakdown of Hell in Canto XI. Dante and Virgil are still atop the rocky embankment overlooking the lower circles. Landino's commentary here transitions from the general definition of "injury" to the specific classification of the seventh circle (Violence) and the reasons why Fraud (the eighth and ninth circles) is considered a more grievous sin against God.</meta>

# INFERNO.

[The author] adds that such fruits are produced there which appear ripe on the outside, but inside are soot; and when pressed even slightly, they dissolve into ash. This is certainly a divine miracle, so that for all ages there remains an eternal testimony of divine judgment and severe punishment for a vice so beastly—indeed, more than beastly, because no animal except man commits it. <note>The commentator is referring to the legend of the "Apples of Sodom" as a metaphor for the sin of sodomy.</note> Cahors is a city in Provence <note>Cahors is historically in the Quercy region, but was often associated with Provence in older texts.</note> which for many centuries has been a haunt of usurers.

**Fraud, by which every conscience is bitten,**
**a man can use against one who trusts him,**
**and against one who harbors no confidence.**
**This latter way seems to destroy**
**only the bond of love that nature makes;**
**wherefore in the second circle are nested**
**Hypocrisy, flattery, and those who practice sorcery,**
**falsity, theft, and simony,** <term>Simony: The sin of buying or selling sacred church offices or spiritual things.</term>
**panderers, barrators, and similar filth.** <term>Barrators: Officials who take bribes or trade public office for personal gain.</term>

THIS SECOND WAY: that is, committing fraud against those who do not trust you. Although it is not as atrocious as the first—which breaks two bonds, namely the natural one and that of particular friendship—it is nonetheless grave because it breaks the bond of nature, which binds all men to help one another and not to harm each other, and to have confidence in one another. And for this reason, such sinners are punished in the eighth circle, which he calls the "second" because it is the second of these final three.

**By the other way, that love is forgotten**
**which nature makes, and that which is added later,**
**from which special faith is created;**
**hence in the smallest circle, where the point**
**of the universe sits, upon which Dis resides,**
**whoever betrays is eternally consumed.**

<margin>special traitors.</margin> The fraudulent are in the eighth circle, which is divided into ten *bolge* <note>original: "bolgie", meaning pouches or ditches</note> because there are ten types of them. The traitors are in the ninth. And because betrayal is committed in four ways, this circle is divided into four parts. Thus, Hell is divided into nine circles: five of which are outside the City of Dis. The sixth is inside, but close to the walls, where the heretics are punished. The seventh contains the violent and is divided into three rings. The eighth holds the fraudulent in ten ditches. The ninth encloses the traitors within itself.

**And I: "Master, quite clearly proceeds**
**your reasoning, and quite well distinguishes**
**this abyss and the people who possess it;**
**But tell me: those of the fat marsh**
**whom the wind drives, and whom the rain beats,**
**and who encounter each other with such harsh tongues,**
**Why are they not punished within the ruddy city,**
**if God holds them in His anger?**
**And if He does not, why are they in such a state?"**

<margin>concerning the slothful.</margin> WHOM THE WIND DRIVES: that is, those driven by the wind, meaning the lustful placed in the second circle. AND WHOM THE RAIN BEATS: who are the gluttons placed in the third circle. AND WHO ENCOUNTER EACH OTHER with such harsh tongues: he means the prodigal and the avaricious, who are placed in the fourth circle and rebuke one another, shouting "Why do you hold?" and "Why do you squander?" WHY WITHIN the ruddy city: why are they not punished inside the city of Dis, which he calls "Ruddy," <note>original: "Roggia", meaning red-hot or glowing</note> meaning red from the fire; it is a French-derived word. Some say "roggia" means "rozza," signifying harsh. Dante asks this question to have the opportunity to show the reason why some are punished outside the city and others inside. This question is not particularly sharp or prudent, as it does not follow that because the vices are not equal, the punishments should be the same. Nor does the Christian faith hold that all vices are equal, as the Stoics claimed; rather, they are greater or lesser both by their nature and by the circumstances, as will appear shortly. It is therefore a most evident thing. But sensuality, because it lacks reason, doubts even manifest things. And therefore Virgil responds.

**And he to me: "Why does your wit**
**wander so far from what it usually does?**
**Or where else is your mind looking?"**

<column-break/>

He had distinguished violence; now he divides fraud into two species. One is against those who trust you, considering you a friend, which we will discuss shortly. The other is against those who do not trust you, and under this latter he places hypocrites, flatterers, and those who "bewitch" <note>original: "affactura", from *affatturare*, to cast spells or enchantments</note>, meaning those who practice sorcery. Falsifiers of any kind. Theft. Simony. Panderers and barrators—all of whom we will clearly explain below. THE FRAUD by which every conscience of the one who commits it is bitten: That is, the fraud which is a sin. For there are some frauds that do not gnaw at the conscience because they are not sins, such as if you were captured by infidels and deceived them in order to escape. A MAN CAN USE against one who trusts: that is, against a friend who trusts you. AND AGAINST ONE WHO does not harbor confidence: such as those who are neither your friends nor your enemies; although they have no specific trust in you, they nonetheless do not expect that you wish to deceive them.

He sets down the second species of fraud, where two bonds are broken. To better understand this, nature made man a sociable animal, and as equals, we are linked by a universal bond of nature to love one another. And this is called "universal love," through which I love all men, and to this, universal faith is pledged. Then there is another species of love, which is called "additional" because it is added upon the natural one; this is toward relatives and friends, and it can be called "special love" because it creates "special faith." Therefore, both he who breaks universal faith and he who breaks particular faith commits fraud. But those who break the universal bond are called "fraudulent"...

Having heard Dante's distinction of the entire site of Hell, he moves a doubt to Virgil by asking a question: it seems to him that if the vices punished in the five circles placed outside the city displease God, they ought to be punished inside the city; and if they do not displease Him, they ought not to be punished in any place at all. AND I SAID: "O Master, your reasoning proceeds clearly enough in dividing THIS ABYSS": that is, the depth and voracity. For Hell is nothing other than a voracity from the surface of the earth down to the center. "Abyss" <note>original: "Baratro", from the Greek *barathron*</note> is a dark and deep place; it is a Greek word. AND THE PEOPLE who possess it: that is, the sinners who inhabit it. BUT TELL ME: Those of the fat marsh: that is, of the Stygian marsh which has greasy and swampy waters, meaning those of the fifth circle where the wrathful are punished and...

Wishing to resolve the doubt raised by Dante, Virgil tacitly rebukes his reasoning, which was: if those punished outside the city have not sinned, why are they punished? If they have sinned, why are they not punished inside like the others?

<summary>This page outlines the classification of Fraud and Treachery, distinguishing between sins that break natural human bonds and those that break specific bonds of trust. It also features Dante questioning Virgil on the geographical and moral logic of why certain sins (like lust and gluttony) are punished outside the walls of the City of Dis.</summary>
<keywords>Fraud, Treachery, City of Dis, Cahors, Usury, Simony, Barratry, Universal Love, Special Love, Circles of Hell, Styx, Virgil's reasoning</keywords>

->**CANTO ELEVENTH**<-
**68**
h iii

**Do you not remember those words**
**with which your Ethics treats**
**the three dispositions that heaven does not want:**
**Incontinence, malice, and mad**
**bestiality; and how incontinence**
**offends God less and receives less blame?**
**If you regard this sentence well**
**and call to mind who those are**
**who endure penance outside [the walls of Dis],**
**you will see well why they are separated**
**from these wicked ones, and why less angered**
**divine justice hammers them.**

Virgil begins to speak this sentence: why do you wander from the straight path from which you do not usually stray when judging vices and moral virtues? But Dante attributes this to himself not to praise himself, but to show that Dante—that is, lower reason, which exercises itself in particular matters—is not usually mistaken in moral virtues. **OR WHERE ELSE DOES YOUR MIND GAZE?** We err in two ways: either when our genius is not sufficient to find the truth, or when, even if it is sufficient, it does not understand because it is occupied with many other things. **DO YOU NOT REMEMBER:** Do you not recall. **OF THOSE words:** which. **TREATS:** that is, perfectly treats. **YOUR ETHICS:** the book of Ethics: that is, the book of moral philosophy by Aristotle. And he does not say "your" as if it were written by you, but because you are very familiar with it and understand it well. **THE THREE DISPOSITIONS: Which heaven does not want:** because they are vicious, and heaven—that is, the divine majesty—does not want vicious things. So that we may better understand, we should recall that Aristotle, in the seventh book of his *Ethics*, posits three types of dispositions that must be avoided in life and conduct. There he says that a good choice cannot exist without true reason and a right appetite. Therefore, when one of these is lacking, such a choice must be avoided. Thus, if the perversion proceeds from the appetite and yet reason remains straight, **incontinence** is born. This happens when reason judges rightly, but the disturbed appetite pulls in the opposite direction; like Medea in Ovid, who judged rightly that it was a supreme wickedness to betray her father and abandon her homeland, but the appetite to be with Jason pulled her against reason. Whence she says: <note>original: "Video meliora proboque: Deteriora sequor."</note> "I see the better things and approve them; I follow the worse." But if at any time the corrupt and perverse appetite rises so much against reason that it becomes the total master of it, and reason itself is corrupted, then reason follows the appetite, judging what is proposed by it to be good, and makes a captive choice. Thus it is called bad judgment, and such a disposition is **malice**. Therefore, in the first [incontinence], only the appetite sinned, but reason judged rightly, though it was pulled by force by the fury of the appetite. In the second [malice], both sin, and they agree that what is evil is good. Like Dido, when the poet says of her: <note>original: "Nec iam furtivum Dido meditatur amorem: Coniugium vocat."</note> "No longer does Dido contemplate a secret love: she calls it marriage." But sometimes the perversion of the appetite and of reason is such that they not only agree to sin, but as if forgetting what it means to be human, they surpass every limit of the human species and take on the habits and nature of a wild beast; and such a disposition is **bestiality**. Against these three vicious dispositions are excellent remedies. For to incontinence, **continence** is opposed; to malice, **moral virtue**; and to bestiality, **heroic virtue**—that is, more than human virtue. For "heroes" according to the ancients are more than men and less than gods, like Hercules and Theseus and the like. But so that we understand how a man acquires heroic virtue, it should not be unknown to us that the human soul is in the middle between angels and brute animals. Insofar as it has the intellect in common with the former, and the senses with the latter. Therefore, just as the sensitive part is sometimes depraved in man until he becomes similar to the beasts—and this is called bestiality, exceeding human malice—so, conversely, the intellectual part is sometimes strengthened and made so perfect that it rises above the common mode of human perfection and almost to the likeness of angels. And this the ancients called **heroic virtue**, through which they believed men were converted into gods, like Hercules and the like. And just as this virtue is rarely found in men, so bestiality, which is its opposite, is found rarely. It is born either from bestial customs and habits—because they live without any law or teaching, like the **Anthropophagi** <term>Anthropophagi: A Greek term for cannibals (eaters of human flesh).</term>, the Laestrygonians, and the Cyclops, and some who eat human flesh. Aristotle mentions wild men who lived in forests not far from the Black Sea who eat human flesh. And Jerome, writing against Jovinian, says there were some barbarians who ate the buttocks of children and the breasts of women. We conclude, therefore, that incontinence is bad, malice is worse, and bestiality is worst. Therefore, the first is punished outside [Dis], and the last two are punished inside.

**you content me so when you solve [my doubt],**
**that doubting pleases me no less than knowing.**

which division is not sufficient, but should be thus: either they have sinned or not. If they have not sinned, they deserve no punishment, neither outside nor inside. And if they have sinned: either they have sinned gravely, like those who are inside Dis, and then they would deserve to be punished inside; or they have sinned, but not so gravely, and then they deserve to be punished for the sin committed, but not with as much pain as those in Dis. Therefore, they must be outside of Dis. This is a sufficient division, which if Dante—that is, lower reason combined with sensuality—had seen, he would not have fallen into this doubt. Therefore, Virgil, responding to him, openly reproves him for having fallen into such error, and says: **WHY DOES YOUR GENIUS RAVE SO MUCH?** <note>Landino plays on the word "delira" (raves/wanders). "Sun" is often taken to mean **wisdom**. ### INFERNO;

From the divine intellect and from its art;
and if you well note your *Physics* <note>referring to Aristotle's *Physics*</note>
you will find, not after many pages,
That your art follows nature, as much as it can,
as the pupil follows the master,
so that your art is almost God’s grandchild;
From these two, if you bring to mind
*Genesis*, from the beginning it is fitting
for man to take his life and advance the people.
But because the usurer <term>usurer: one who lends money at interest</term> takes another way,
he despises nature in itself and in its follower <note>human industry/art</note>,
since he places his hope in something else.

---

But follow me now, for it pleases me to go;
for the Fish <note>the constellation Pisces</note> quiver on the horizon,
and the Wain <note>the Big Dipper</note> lies entirely over Caurus <note>the Northwest wind</note>,
and the descent of the ridge is further on.

<column-break/>

**HIS ART:** that is, his operation and his will: because as God understands, so he wills: and as he wills, so he operates. **YOUR PHYSICS:** that is, the *Physics* in which you delight. **NOT AFTER MANY PAGES:** Because it is not far from the beginning of the book. **THAT OUR ART FOLLOWS THAT AS MUCH AS IT CAN:** *Art imitates nature as much as it is able* <note>original Latin: "Ars imitatur naturam quoad potest"</note> just as **THE PUPIL:** that is, the disciple follows the master. **ALMOST A GRANDCHILD:** by a certain similarity: because if nature proceeds from God as its principle, it is like a daughter; and if our art then proceeds from nature, being the daughter of nature, it is the grandchild of God: because God has implanted art into the minds of men by means of nature. Aristotle says: *God is an eternal and best living being, from whom heaven and nature depend* <note>original: "idio e animal sempiterno & optimo"</note>; which nature is imitated by our art as much as possible. Therefore, since art depends on nature, it is like its daughter, and consequently the grandchild of God. Thus, he who offends nature offends God immediately; and he who offends art offends God through the offense to nature. But the usurer offends nature: because it is not natural for money to give birth to money without its own corruption <note>the Aristotelian idea that for something new to be generated, something else must be consumed or transformed</note>. Nature wills that the corruption of one thing be the generation of another. Likewise, he offends God: because he does not exercise art according to what God commanded the first man when he said: *by the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread* <note>Genesis 3:19</note>. Likewise, it is not "artful" for money to give birth to money, as the usurer wants, who places "use" in a thing where use cannot be given. For if I lend you a garment or a horse, these things are consumed by use; but money is not. And other arts and trades are subject to the accidents of fortune, but not the usurer. **IF YOU BRING TO MIND GENESIS:** that is, the sentence written in *Genesis*, where it treats the creation of the world and the first man and the order of life, which began where it is written: *It was necessary from the beginning of the age for the human race to take up life and for one to surpass another through nature and arts* <note>original Latin: "Oportuit ab initio seculi humanum genus sumere uitam: & excedere unum alium per naturam & artes"</note>. **IN THE BEGINNING:** that is, as appears in its beginning. **IT IS FITTING FOR THE PEOPLE TO TAKE THEIR LIFE:** that is, the manner and order of living. **AND TO ADVANCE** one another in wealth and temporal goods: and this is lawful either through one's industry and exercise, or with possessions, or with livestock, which things naturally yield fruit. **AND BECAUSE THE USURER TAKES ANOTHER WAY:** different from that of nature (not keeping money in livestock) and that of art (because he does not work or exercise). **HE DESPISES IN ITSELF:** that is, as much as is in him, **NATURE AND ITS FOLLOWER:** which is art. He acts against nature because inanimate things cannot multiply like living ones. Usury is prohibited in the Old Testament. Where in *Leviticus* it says: *You shall not give your money to your brother for usury, nor shall you exact an overabundance of crops* <note>original Latin: "Pecuniam tuam non dabis fratri tuo ad uſuram & frugum ſuperabundantia non exiges," Leviticus 25:37</note>. And the Psalmist says: *Who shall dwell in your tabernacle? He who has not given his money for usury* <note>original Latin: "Quis habitabit in tabernaculo tuo? Qui pecuniam non dederit ad uſuram," Psalm 15:1-5</note>. And in the New Testament, Luke writes in the sixth chapter: *Lend, not despairing of anything* <note>original Latin: "Date mutuum nec in deſperantes," Luke 6:35</note>.

---

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'C' at the start of the second commentary block, featuring detailed foliage and vine motifs.</image-desc>
Just as Virgil had been the reason for staying still, so now he is the reason for following on. And certainly, every power of the soul ought to submit to the intellect and follow according to its judgment. Virgil says, therefore: "it pleases me to follow on the journey, because the Fish are already at our horizon." This shows that day is already approaching. We showed above that Dante feigns having had this vision on Good Friday before daybreak; and therefore he said the sun was in Aries, because from the month of March until the eleventh of April it is in that sign. And he intends to have spent that whole day struggling with the beasts and reasoning with Virgil. Then he shows that on Friday night he descended into Hell, when he said "the day was departing and the air was growing brown." Now he adds that a great part of that night had already passed in this search of Hell, and it was almost two hours before day. For the sun rose in our hemisphere with Aries, and the Fish <note>Pisces</note> precede Aries. And each of these rises with sixteen degrees: that is, with one hour and a fifteenth of an hour. It follows that two hours of the night remained, during which they had to search all of Hell. And therefore he admonishes Dante that time is not to be lost. And it is a place similar to that in Virgil: *By this exchange of speech, rosy Aurora in her four-horse chariot had already crossed the midpoint of the sky in her ethereal course; and perhaps they would have drawn out all the allotted time in such things, but his companion the Sibyl briefly spoke and warned: Aeneas, night is coming on, while we spend the hours in weeping* <note>original Latin quote from Virgil's *Aeneid*, Book VI</note>. **THAT THE FISH QUIVER:** He had respect for the nature of the fish, which quivers—that is, it moves through the water with great ease. And in short, they were already beginning to rise at our horizon. **OVER THE HORIZON:** Over the circle that divides one hemisphere from the other, which is called the horizon: that is, the finisher and terminator, which terminates our sight; because of the whole sky, which is round and spherical, we see only half. Therefore, that last part which we see all around the sky where our sight ends—because the earth prevents us from seeing further down—is called the horizon. And because the sky makes an entire revolution in twenty-four hours, it is always necessary that some sign of the zodiac rises at our horizon. The Fish were rising then, which as I said take an hour and a fifteenth part of an hour to be entirely out of the horizon; and after those, Aries rose with the sun, the birth of which makes the day. Therefore, there remained as much of the night as the duration for the whole sign of Pisces to come out, and also all those degrees of Aries that were before the degree where the sun was found. Pisces is the last sign of the zodiac and is the house of Jupiter and of this triplicity; but in *Purgatorio* we will speak of this more accurately. **THE WAIN LIES ENTIRELY OVER CAURUS:** This is the second sign the poet uses to show that day is approaching. For if the Fish were rising then, it was necessary that Leo, the sign opposite to them, was going down. So that you may understand this better: the Wain consists of seven stars which turn around the North Star <note>original: "tramontana"</note>. And the first four are two by two and make the wain; and three then come in a line, although the last one turns somewhat and makes the pole [the handle]; this last one is always straight toward Leo. Therefore, when Leo is about to set, the pole is straight to the west, and the four that make the wain are already turned between the west and the north, from where the wind Caurus blows. Therefore he said rightly: "and the Wain lies entirely over Caurus."

It also uses astronomical observations of Pisces and the Big Dipper to establish that it is roughly two hours before dawn on Holy Saturday.</summary>

### CANTO XII OF THE FIRST CANTICLE BY DANTE.

The place where we came to climb down the bank
was rugged, and because of what was there,
it was such that every eye would recoil from it.
Just like that landslide that struck the flank
of the Adige on this side of Trento,
either by earthquake or for lack of support:
For from the top of the mountain where it moved
to the plain, the rock is so shattered
that it would provide a path for one who was up there;
Such was the descent of that ravine,
and on the edge of the broken pit
the infamy of Crete lay outstretched:
Who was conceived in the false cow;
and when he saw us, he bit himself,
like one whom rage breaks from within.

My sage cried toward him: "Perhaps 
you believe the Duke of Athens is here,
who in the world above brought you death?
Get away, beast, for this man does not come
schooled by your sister,"

<column-break/>

<margin>c</margin> In this twelfth canto the poet describes the descent from the sixth circle into the seventh; and he divides it as we have said above, and then the punishments of those who are violent: first against their neighbor; then against themselves; and lastly against God. He places the monstrous Centaurs as guards of the place, and especially the Minotaur of Crete. He shows that this descent was a precipice of broken and ruined boulders, and harsh; just like the landslide of Mount Barco between <note>likely Rovereto</note> and Trento. And on the edge of the ruin where the descent begins, the Minotaur was stretched out. Mount Barco, having had its roots heavily eroded by the river—either because of this or due to earthquakes—collapsed in large part into the Adige river in such a way that it moved aside for a good distance. And through this ruin the "roccia"—that is, the <term>rock</term> <note>original: "rocca. i. emassi" - meaning the masses of stone</note> and the bank of the mountain—is so shattered from the summit to the plain that it would provide some path, though it would not be very easy. **TO ONE WHO WAS UP THERE**: that is, to whoever was at the top. **SUCH** from that "burrato" <note>ravine</note> from that ruin: the Florentines call a deep ditch, almost an abyss, a *burrato*. **AND ON** the point, on the summit. **OF THE BROKEN** pit: that is, the descent, named from the verb *labor* <note>Latin: to slip or fall</note>. **WAS OUTSTRETCHED**: as if he were lying down. **THE INFAMY OF CRETE**: that is, the Minotaur; who, being born on the island of Crete (today called Candia), was the disgrace of said island, being not a man but a monstrous thing. **WHICH INFAMY**: that is, the monster. **WAS CONCEIVED**: that is, the Minotaur was conceived. **IN THE FALSE COW**. In order that this may be more aptly understood, we will briefly narrate the fable. Because Venus, in the adultery she committed with Mars, was discovered by the Sun and accused to her husband Vulcan, she became such an enemy to the Sun that, unable to take revenge on him, she took revenge on his daughters. Therefore, Pasiphae being the wife of Minos, King of Crete, and daughter of the Sun, she was so inordinately incited to lust by Venus that she was led to love a bull from her husband’s herds. Some say that Minos, desiring in the sacrifice he wished to make to Jove his father to have an animal worthy of such a god, Jove sent him a very beautiful and shapely bull. But Minos, moved by avarice and a desire for such a beautiful animal, sent it to his herds and sacrificed a less beautiful bull to Jove. Wherefore Jove, enraged, induced Pasiphae to love that one. But whichever bull it was, they add that Pasiphae asked Daedalus to show her how she could join with the bull; and Daedalus made a wooden image of a cow, and enclosed her within it; and thus she joined with the bull, which believed her to be a cow. From this union was born the Minotaur, a horrendous monster, who was half man and half bull. And Minos, to hide the disgrace, enclosed him in the labyrinth, and there he devoured living men. A little before those times, Androgeos, the son of Minos, had been killed by the Athenians out of the envy they bore him, because he defeated everyone in the games of the gymnasium. Minos, taking revenge and having conquered them, imposed a law on them: that every year they must send to Crete fourteen of their children, seven males and seven females. These were drawn by lot; and after some years the lot fell upon Theseus, son of Aegeus, King of Athens. He went there: but before he entered the labyrinth, because of his beauty, he attracted the love of Adriana—or rather Ariadne—daughter of Minos; she promised that she would be his wife, and she prepared to free him from such a cruel death. She gave him, therefore, a ball of thread, balls of pitch, and an iron-tipped mace. Theseus tied the end of the thread to the door, and took the rest with him so that by following it he would know how to return outside. And when the Minotaur opened its mouth to devour him, he threw the balls of pitch, which plastered its mouth so that it could not open it. And then with the mace he struck its head and killed it. You have the fable; now hear the allegory. Some writers of no mediocre learning propose that by Pasiphae—a very beautiful woman and daughter of the Sun—is meant the human soul created by God, the highest Sun; and being made beautiful for its innocence, it becomes the wife of Minos, the inventor of laws, because it joins itself to Reason, which with its laws directs it onto the right path. To her, Venus is an enemy—that is, concupiscence—which always opposes Reason. And if the appetite approaches concupiscence, the soul separates from its husband Minos (that is, from Reason) and, pulled by the flattery of the flesh, loves the bull: that is, the delights of the world, which at first glance seem beautiful. But then, by using them poorly, we come to be joined with bestiality. And Pasiphae, enclosed in a wooden cow, uses the bull because with the artifice of our intellect we use natural things not according to the law of nature. From this is born the Minotaur, which has members partly of man and partly of bull. This is the vice of bestiality of which we spoke above. For those who are defiled by this vice appear human in aspect, but in their habits they are beasts. The Minotaur is put in the labyrinth. This denotes that the human breast is entangled in various frauds. But Theseus, warned by Ariadne—that is, the learned man warned by Reason—kills the Minotaur: that is, the vice. By such an allegory you will easily understand that with excellent reason Dante placed such a monster in the place where the cruel and savage sins are punished. **AND WHEN HE SAW US he bit himself: Like one whom rage breaks from within.** This shows that bestial violence born of pride is always accompanied by anger: because at the same time it is painful not to obtain what one desires, and one gnaws with rage. On the other hand, one grieves that when fear is removed, no one honors them.

<margin>d</margin> This shows how Virgil admonishes the Minotaur, who should not fear being killed by Dante because he is not Theseus, who killed him in Crete. Here it is shown allegorically that the Minotaur could be killed up here in the world, but it cannot be killed in Hell: because, speaking Christianly, he who is in life can be brought to repentance. And thus he kills the vice of bestiality. But he who is in Hell has no room for repentance. And morally in life—that is, while there is not yet an obstinate habit of vice—we can...

<header>INFERNO.</header>

...but he goes to see your punishments.
As is that bull that breaks loose
which has already received the mortal blow
and knows not how to go, but leaps here and there,
I saw the Minotaur do the same;
and he <note>Virgil</note>, being alert, cried: "Run to the pass!
While he is in a fury, it is good that you descend."

So we took our way down through the discharge
of those stones that often moved
beneath my feet because of the new weight <note>the weight of a living body</note>.
I was already thinking, and he said: "What are you thinking
perhaps about this ruin which is guarded

But certainly a little before, if I discern well,

"But fix your eyes on the valley, for it approaches,
the river of blood, in which boils
anyone who by violence harms others."
O blind greed, o foolish wrath,
that so spurs us in this short life
and then in the eternal one so evilly drenches us!
I saw a wide ditch, bent in an arc,
like one that embraces the whole plain

<column-break/>

...to kill him: but in Hell: that is, since we are reduced to a most obstinate habit, we cannot kill him. **CRIED**: To demonstrate that higher reason must rise up vividly and with vehemence. Which he expresses through cries, and not coldly. **THE DUKE OF ATHENS**: Theseus, Duke of Athens, who as we have said is understood as the wise man: who is "Duke of Athens." For just as Athens was a city in Greece, the domicile and receptacle of all doctrines—without which a man cannot be wise—he gave him death in the world as we have said. This he could do through the teachings of Ariadne, that is, of virtue, which is in such a way the sister of bestiality: because both are conceived by the soul: which, when it joins with Minos—that is, with reason—gives birth to virtue; when with the bull—that is, with concupiscence—it gives birth to the Minotaur, i.e., vice. **BUT HE GOES To see your punishments**: He does not kill the sin: but contemplates your punishments: that is, the nature of sin and the evil that comes from it, so that knowing it, one may beware of it. **AS IS THAT BULL**: It is an excellent comparison, and very fitting to compare the Minotaur to the bull: and also through that motion, it expresses the fury of this monster: and denotes that the intellect rising against obstinate bestiality convicts it by reason. But that monster, due to its obstinacy, rages rather than yielding. **AND HE, BEING ALERT**: An excellent precept from the intellect to the lower reason: that when the obstinate one rises in fury, one should yield to him, and go through the entrance he abandons: that is, through the reason which puts us into this contemplation.

He was descending now through the discharge: that is, through the ruin which had discharged many stones from the mountain: and many were left half-torn in such a way that when Dante placed his feet there, they moved because of the **NEW**: that is, unusual load: since no one descended there except souls without bodies, except for Dante. Therefore Dante went sometimes stumbling, the stones moving beneath him. Which signifies that while the <term>sensuality</term> <note>original: "rēfualita", likely referring to the lower sensory appetites</note> with the lower reason descends into the contemplation of vices, it cannot be that sometimes it does not go stumbling: because the pleasures that vices bring with them flatter it. For the habit of heroic virtue is not yet made: or as we wish to say according to Plato, the habit of the virtues of the soul already purged. But it suffices that it does not fall—that is, does not ruin—into vice. Nor without cause does he show that this ruin leads to where fierce violence is punished. Because the soul cannot descend into such cruelty and violence if the mind does not first fall from the excellence of its nature and harden itself to cruelty: because naturally we are born to love and help, and not to hate and harm. Therefore the poet expressed both these things through the ruin and through the stones, which are a very hard thing. **I WAS ALREADY THINKING**: understand: about the ruin. Because lower reason always thinks of particular things: and the higher reason perceived this: and therefore solved the doubt of his thinking. **IN THIS RUIN WHICH IS Guarded by that bestial wrath**: For the step through which we enter into violence is pride accompanied by wrath, through which we forget humanity and become beasts through cruelty. **WHICH I JUST NOW QUENCHED**: because the intellect extinguishes wrath with reason. **NOW I WANT YOU TO KNOW**: He feigns that this, along with many others, ruined at the sixth hour of Holy Friday when the earthquake occurred at the death of Christ: and allegorically he hints that through the death of Christ every violence of the devil against us was broken. **HE WHO [took] the great prey**: i.e., Christ who despoiled the Limbo of the Holy Fathers; they before were in the prey **OF DIS**: that is, of Pluto, i.e., of Lucifer. **OF THE CIRCLE** of Limbo: which is the first and highest circle. **SO THAT I THOUGHT the universe felt love, by which there are those who believe**: That is, there are some who believe that several times the world has returned to chaos. He places the sentence of Empedocles <note>Greek philosopher who taught that Love and Discord govern the universe</note> who posited six principles: that is, four elements and Love and Discord: and said that when the elements and motions of the sky were in concord, everything returned to chaos: and when concord ceased and discord came, the world returned to its pristine form. **AND AT THAT POINT** of the sixth hour **THIS ANCIENT rock** / this ancient bank. **HERE AND ELSEWHERE** as will be said below.

He shows first that the punishment of these sinners was that they were boiled in blood. Then he is indignant against the unrestrained desires: which push men with such fury to want to possess in this brief time of life that for which they will then be damned eternally: and finally he shows the punishers of this to be the Centaurs. **BUT FIX your eyes to the valley**: that is, below. **FOR IT APPROACHES**: that is, because it gets closer. **O BLIND Greed**: He said "blind" meaning without reason. **O FOOLISH WRATH**: We said above that the force of the irascible appetite is to take away all obstacles that do not let us achieve what we desire. Therefore such an appetite is foolish and stupid, which all day long pushes furious souls, greedy for tyranny, to a thousand small deaths and infinite labors: even though it is much sweeter...

centaurs were running, armed with arrows,

<column-break/>

...water, bread, glass, and wood are found when their sap groans. <note>The commentator appears to be finishing a thought regarding the nature of substances that "weep" or bleed when burned or broken, likely referencing the upcoming Forest of Suicides.</note> And it is a fitting punishment for cruel men and tyrants that they should be punished in the boiling blood. Because for he who delighted in blood, divine justice promises that he shall be punished in blood: as happened to Cyrus, King of the Persians. After the gravest defeat he gave to the Scythians, and after a most cruel slaughter of them, he was finally defeated by Tomyris, their queen, whose son he had killed along with others. He was killed together with two hundred thousand Persians. And Tomyris, to demonstrate her thirst for human blood, took his head and placed it in a leather skin full of blood, saying: "You thirsted for blood, and I satisfy you with tepid blood." Furthermore, the violent boil in the blood because they are incited by anger, which is a boiling of the blood. And morally, he who has delighted in homicide later takes such repentance for it that day and night he is tormented by the memory of it. Violence is force used for the harm and evil of others, and it is born from cupidity, which has its origin in pride.

**IN AN ARC**: <note>original: "IN ARCHOTORTA"</note> Because it went in a circuit, according to the site that he <note>Dante</note> establishes. **AT THE FOOT** of the bank: Among the roots of the mountain. **ARMED CENTAURS** ran in a trail: That is, all in a line, as if following the track of one another. "Track" <note>original: "traccia"</note> signifies a vestige or a footprint. Whence "to track" is to follow the footsteps.

Poets say the Centaurs were monstrous men in Thessaly who were half-horse and half-man, the sons of Ixion. This Ixion was the son of Phlegyas of Thessaly, and he was the first among the Greeks who attempted to occupy a tyranny by force. For this reason, the poets feign that he wished to join himself with Juno, the wife of Jove. And Jove, mocking him, made an image of mist similar to Juno. Ixion joined with her, thinking she was the true Juno, and from such a union the Centaurs were born. By Ixion, we understand all men greedy for kingdoms or power, who attempt to acquire principalities or lordships beyond their strength. And because Juno is the goddess of realms, they feign that he wished to join with her. But she mocks him and deceives him by showing him such an image as we have described; for there is no one who can join with Juno as he desires—that is, to acquire as much lordship as he proposes in his mind, which, in the tyrannical life, is insatiable. Because once he has acquired what he first desired, and in which he believed he would find rest, there is born in him a desire for something greater. And he never arrives at that quiet life which he proposes to himself, which he would quickly reach if he put a brake on his cupidity and stayed content with his present state, as the wise Cineas aptly demonstrated to the infuriated Pyrrhus. This makes men always thirsty to increase their empire, where such insanity is manifested that Alexander the Great, hearing that the Epicurean philosophers affirmed there was not just one world but many, wept in despair that he could not conquer them all, not having yet conquered this one. Therefore, the thoughts of Alexander were monstrous, because without doubt they were above all human strength and were against all humanity; for, unprovoked by any injury, he wished to make slaves of those who by nature were free as he was.

Whence it follows clearly that the Centaurs—that is, unbridled and cruel desires—are the children of Ixion, that is, of the tyrant. And he generates them from the mist—that is, from the false concept that he makes in his mind. For just as mist from a distance seems a great thing, but then, drawing near, it is found to be nothing, so such thoughts at the beginning give great hope of success, but later they vanish and return to nothing. Furthermore, just as the body of the Centaur has its first members human and its last members those of a beast, so tyrannical desires have at the beginning some part of reason; but later, the further they pull forward in their progress, the more they become bestial.

Furthermore, they say that Jove cast him into Hell, and there made him be bound to wheels that always turn and are full of serpents. Which signifies that the mind of the tyrant is always turned by anxious thoughts and continually bitten by poisonous reflections. And certainly nothing is found more brutal, and more contrary to human nature, than the life and customs of those who, either in their republics or in their principalities, wish to be more powerful than the laws and to overbear those whom God and nature made their equals. Nor were the founders and governors of republics found for the purpose of lording over others or cruelly tormenting them and depriving them of dignity, property, and finally life. Nor to convert every convenience and utility to themselves, and to leave others with the inconveniences and damages. But they were instituted so that the multitude might have a guide and government toward an honest life. And so that with their prudence and justice, they might be an example of every virtue, and by means of holy laws, they might rule their citizens in peace and concord. They should institute the people to exercise themselves in every laudable art; to perform their due duty toward their citizens; to offend no one; to help everyone; to love, according to their degrees, their relatives and friends. To be of such fervent charity toward the fatherland that they are always prepared for it, if necessary, to give their life. And finally, so that they might toil so that others might rest; they should watch so that others might sleep securely; they should put themselves in danger so that others might live safe.

And for all these things, they should expect no other reward than honor, which is the unique reward of virtue. These are called *Basylee* <note>original Greek: "Basileus"</note> by the Greeks because they are a firm base upon which the entire public weight rests. The Latins call them *Reges* <note>Kings</note> because they rule and sustain others with their industry and do not let them slip into any iniquity. Christians call them *Pastores* <note>Shepherds</note> because, like good shepherds, they do not seek their own convenience, but that of the flock committed to them; so good princes seek the salvation of those who are committed to their government. And they remember the words of Truth: that the good shepherd gives his life for his sheep. This is, therefore, the office and the duty of one who governs and rules. And he who does the contrary of this is not a king nor a governor, but a tyrant. He is not a shepherd but a wolf. He does not guard the sheep but kills them. He does not toil for those who are subject to him but wishes to live off their toil, to triumph over their spoils, to behave toward them like a devil, and to be adored as a god. He wants his lust to be like a divine precept, his avarice to be a just law, and cruelty to befit him. They enjoy the torments of the just. They rejoice in shedding the blood of the innocent.

For which reason, not only are they not kings, but they are not men; but stripped of all humanity and clothed in every brutality, they are the supreme destruction of men. Nero and Mezentius retained the human form; Sulla and Marius retained it; but they totally put aside the human soul and became tigers and bears. These sin so excessively that they not only harm other men, as we have said, but as much as is in them, they harm God; because they trample the laws, which are the daughters of God; they destroy men, who are the creatures of God. They harm themselves, because from the highest and celestial rank where man is placed, similar to an angel or rather to God, they ruin into the profound precipice and abyss of the beasts. And often, wishing to shed the blood of others, they shed their own. Whence Juvenal says: *To the son-in-law of Ceres, few kings descend without slaughter and wounds, and few tyrants by a dry death.* <note>Juvenal, Satires 10.112-113. "The son-in-law of Ceres" is Pluto, ruler of the Underworld. A "dry death" refers to a natural death without the shedding of blood.</note> Of these the Psalm says...

# CANTO TWELVE

...mixed. <note>original: "Non perdam cū impiis uitam meā: Et cum uiris sanguinum animam meā In quorum manibus iniquitates sūt & dexte ra eorum repleta est muneribus"</note> "I will not lose my life with the ungodly, nor my soul with men of blood, in whose hands are iniquities, and whose right hand is full of bribes." <note>This is a quotation from Psalm 26:9-10.</note> And the prophet Habakkuk <note>original: "Ipse diabolus de regibus triumphabit: & tyranni ridiculi eius erunt"</note> says: "The devil himself shall triumph over kings, and tyrants shall be his laughingstocks." And certainly, tyrants lose their lives—not only the eternal one but also this transitory one. For, being feared by everyone, it is necessary that they also fear everyone. Therefore, they always live in the utmost anxiety and fear, as Cicero clearly demonstrates in the fifth book of the *Tusculan Disputations* with the example of Dionysius, the tyrant of Syracuse. He was not only forced to guard himself against friends and family and deprive himself of every pleasant custom, but he trusted neither his wives nor his daughters. And the better men are, the more the tyrants fear them. For as Sallust says: <note>original: "semper illis aliena uirtus formidolosa est"</note> "to them, the virtue of others is always a source of dread." But perhaps the just indignation I hold toward that detestable generation of men has carried me too far from my purpose. In conclusion, there is no greater pain for ambitious men than to "generate centaurs"—that is, for their enterprises to fail—and therefore the poet places centaurs in this location. Now, returning to the text, it follows: **SEEING US** descend—that is, go down to the plain where the ditch of blood was—each of those centaurs stopped. And three departed from the troop, coming toward us with bows and arrows ready to strike us. Dante wanted to descend to the plain—that is, to the contemplation of this vice. But as we have said in several places, the centaurs (representing vice) confront concupiscence <note>The physical desire or drive toward worldly things.</note>, and with their arrows (their stings/impulses), they would overcome it if Virgil (representing the intellect) did not tame them. Nessus was with these three. The centaurs wanted Virgil and Dante to say from a distance what martyrdom they were coming to—as if to say that he who looks at vice from a distance does not know its intrinsic nature, and therefore hopes for pleasure and happiness. Thus, if he did not watch himself, displeasure and misery would be born within him. **MY MASTER** said we will give the answer to Chiron. Chiron the centaur was not the son of Ixion and the cloud like the other centaurs, but of Saturn. Saturn, having fallen in love with a nymph named Philyra, joined with her; but his wife coming upon them, so as not to be caught in manifest adultery, he transformed himself into a horse. Therefore, from such a union, Philyra gave birth to Chiron, half-man and half-horse. He was learned in music, and in this, he was the master of Achilles; likewise in that branch of medicine called <term>surgery</term> <note>original: "chyrurgia," from the Greek for "hand-work."</note>, which he taught to Aesculapius. He was called half-horse because he was a warlike man, as the horse is an animal suited for war. Thus Achilles, a warlike man, is called his disciple. Therefore, by him, we shall understand that soul which, although it may be brutal in its ambition and lust for lordship, is nonetheless not without some doctrine and reason, and possesses some justice and civil custom. And so Virgil does not wish to answer Nessus, in whom there is nothing but fury, but says he will respond to Chiron. This signifies that the speculative intellect does not wish to proceed with hasty, impetuous, and furious counsel, as was Nessus when—without considering how much injury he did to Hercules, a man capable of taking violent revenge—he kidnapped Deianira. Rather, the intellect wishes to proceed with reason and equity, as was found in Chiron. And he will reproach Nessus, showing that his fury and his fixed and unconsidered will finally had to harm him, because he was killed by the arrows of Hercules. And certainly, all the unconsidered enterprises of furious tyrants are killed by Hercules—that is, they are overcome by prudent and strong men, as we understand by "Hercules."

Then he shows that Chiron, like a philosopher, recognized that Dante was alive—that is, with his body. For philosophers demonstrate that everything that moves by touching must be a body. And therefore he added: **THE FEET OF THE DEAD ARE NOT ACCUSTOMED TO DO SO.** Because the soul, remaining incorporeal, has no touch. Then he says that Virgil was already at the breast of Chiron to show how quickly the intellect anticipates the fury of vice.

and takes away every impulse, striking it down with reason. **AT THE CHEST**: Where two natures are joined. Centaurs are formed with such a figure that the horse-like limbs are below, and the human ones are above from the chest up. Thus, sin is the joining of the horse and the man. And because thoughts and reflections reside in the chest, it shows that Virgil approached that spot: that is, reason struck the thought, which was part beast and part human. And he says to Chiron **HE IS WELL AND ALIVE**: which shows that he has not descended into Hell to make a habit of sin, for such people are not truly "alive." Rather, he descends into Hell—that is, into the contemplation of sin—to guard himself against it. For this reason, it is necessary that Virgil—that is, the intellect—shows him the dark valley, which represents the sins. **NECESSITY LEADS HIM AND NOT DELIGHT**: because the knowledge of vices brings no pleasure to the soul, but it is necessary so that one can guard against the unknown enemy. In contrast, the knowledge of virtue brings with it the greatest delight. **ONE WHO LEFT FROM SINGING ALLELUIA**: This shows that Beatrice (of whom it was spoken in the first canto) moved Virgil to guide Dante. She came to him from Heaven, where "Alleluia" is sung—that is, where there is all joy. For this word in Hebrew signifies "praise God" and "joy." <note>original: "alleluia" — derived from the Hebrew *Hallelujah* (Praise Yah/God).</note> **WHO ENTRUSTED ME WITH THIS NEW OFFICE**: Because, in terms of the poetic fiction, it is a new thing for a living man to be led through Hell. Allegorically, it shows that there are few who come to such deep contemplation. **HE IS NO THIEF**: This shows he does not come to be punished, for he is no thief—that is, a violent man. For a "thief" <note>original: "ladrone"</note> is one who steals by force, and a "fura" <note>original: "furo"</note> is one who takes by deception. **NOR AM I A FUGITIVE SOUL**: that is, a thief. He says this in imitation of Virgil, who depicts the Sibyl excusing Aeneas to Charon, showing that he does not come to kidnap anyone from Hell, neither Cerberus nor Proserpina, nor any other. Whence he said: <note>original: "Nullae hie insidie tales absiste moueri: Nec uim tela ferunt licet ingens ianitor antri eternum latrans exangues terreat umbras Casta licet patrui feruet Proserpina limen." — Aeneid, Book VI. Translation: "No such treachery is here; cease to be moved. Nor do our weapons bring violence; let the huge gatekeeper of the cave [Cerberus] bark forever to terrify the bloodless shades; let chaste Proserpina keep to her uncle's threshold."</note> Therefore, just as the Sibyl shows there is neither fraud nor violence in Aeneas, so Virgil shows there is neither violence in Dante (as with thieves) nor fraud in himself (as with the fugitive thief).

**BUT BY THAT POWER**: He conjures him by the divine power to which even the infernal beings must yield. **GIVE US ONE OF YOURS** centaurs. **TO WHOM WE MAY BE NEAR**: that is, who may accept us, which is to say, who may hold us dear and provide good company. Or truly, "to whom we may be near" <note>original: "approuo"</note> could mean "by experience": that is, through the guide by whom we are led and find ourselves tested. **AND WHO MAY CARRY THIS MAN UPON HIS BACK. FOR HE IS NO SPIRIT WHO CAN GO THROUGH THE AIR**: This meaning is clear regarding the fiction. But regarding the allegory, it shows that Virgil, who is without a body, has no need to be carried across the ditch because he can go through the air. This denotes that the intellect has knowledge of "universals," <note>In medieval philosophy, "universals" are general concepts that exist beyond specific physical objects.</note> which are not confined to any matter, time, or place. But the lower reason considers "particulars," which are included in matter. Therefore, Virgil will pass through any place. But Dante will be carried by Nessus, because the senses do not recognize vice in a universal sense, nor can they consider "tyranny" abstracted from any subject; rather, they consider it in the particular, such as in Phalaris, in Nero, and the like.

This text is clear in itself except for the historical references. **Alexander the Great**, King of the Macedonians, deserves without any doubt to be numbered among the tyrants, because in truth, without being provoked by any injury, he occupied the tyranny not only of Greece but of a large part of Asia. For which reason Petrarch truly said: <note>original: "Alexandro chal mondo brigha die" — Alexander, who gave the world trouble.</note> He practiced many cruelties, and many signs clearly show that he consented to the death of his father, who was killed by Pausanias. He was of such insanity that he wished to be called and esteemed the son of God and not a man; and having conquered the Persians, he wished to be worshipped as a god according to the barbaric custom, to the great indignation of his own people. And Callisthenes, an excellent philosopher and his fellow student under Aristotle, who tried to draw him back from such insanity, he caused to die most cruelly. In anger and drunkenness, he killed Clitus, a man so much his friend that afterward, repenting, Alexander wished to kill himself. Nor could one narrate, without a historical volume, I do not say his treatment of particular friends—such as Clitus, who was among the first because he modestly admonished him not to set himself above his father Philip—but the peoples and nations which, without having received any injury, he sent to ultimate extermination. And he attacked kings by whom he had never been provoked. Whence Lucan rightly called him the "robber and plunderer of the universe" <note>original: "predone & raptore delluniuerso"</note> and wished that his bones, in vengeance for such ferocity, were scattered throughout the whole world. And certainly, if we diligently consider his life and customs, we will say that there were few virtues in him which he did not use badly. I grant that he was most excellent in military deeds. But who does not know that war, by its nature, is entirely opposite to the bond of charity which naturally embraces the whole human generation? But it is approved by God and by wise men only for the defense of oneself, one's people, and one's country; to tame monsters; to lead back peo...

# CANTO TWELVE.

...ferocious people to a tranquil peace. But Alexander <note>Alexander the Great, often cited by medieval commentators as a archetype of the "violent" conqueror.</note> turned it to the ruin of all: by imposing a yoke upon those who lived in liberty. To take away peace and leisure from those who, without injuring others, enjoyed their own goods; and it seemed to him that he was worthy that all men should serve him, while he himself was a slave to wine and anger. Nor was he ashamed to make himself the son of Jove <note>Jupiter/Zeus</note> and to wish to be adored as a god. Dionysius <note>Dionysius I, the tyrant of Syracuse (c. 432–367 BCE).</note> was a Syracusan of noble stock. His mother, while pregnant with him, dreamed that she gave birth to a little satyr. And the interpreters of dreams predicted that he would be most powerful. And Hymera, a noble woman in Syracuse, dreamed of being led into heaven: and that she saw under the feet of Jove a man with red hair and freckles, bound with a thousand chains; and her guide told her that this man was to be the slaughter and destruction of Sicily. Later, in the course of time, after Dionysius had occupied the lordship, as soon as the woman saw him, she cried out that he was the man she had seen in her dream in chains; these words were the reason that Dionysius had her killed.

He became the lord of Sicily after the Carthaginian armies, which were very powerful on that island, were consumed by pestilence and left the island free. Having become king, he crossed into Italy against the Greek cities, and first conquered Locri. Then he besieged Crotone. But when new Carthaginian armies arrived in Sicily, he was forced to abandon the enterprise and return to the island. He was very cruel, and the city of Syracuse, which at that time was most splendid, he oppressed in heavy servitude because by nature he was wicked and unjust. He seized the tyranny in the twenty-fifth year of his life and held it for thirty-eight years, but with the utmost misery. Although he was a noble and learned man, and a poet of some account, and therefore desired the familiarity and conversation of many men, it was nonetheless necessary for him to guard himself against everyone. For as Sallust <note>original: "Salustio"; Gaius Sallustius Crispus, Roman historian.</note> says, "Tyrants always fear the good more than the wicked, because the good are greater lovers of liberty."

He lived, therefore, with slaves and barbarians. And out of the desire to rule, he had enclosed himself in a narrow prison; and how great his misery was, he himself demonstrated to Damocles, who, greatly praising his happy life, Dionysius said: "I want you to taste it." And immediately he had a most noble banquet prepared. He commanded Damocles to sit in a place where, having companions on every side, he could not leave at his own will; and above his head, he had a very sharp sword tied to the ceiling by a single horsehair, which seemed as if it might fall on his head at any moment. The table was adorned with vessels of gold and silver. It was filled with many varied and most sweet foods. There were young and expert servants. But such was the fear that the sword would fall on his head that he took no pleasure in the things already mentioned. Thus, he demonstrated that the life of a tyrant was similar: in which the continuous fear of being either killed or driven out makes it impossible to take any pleasure in one's power or in external pomps.

He had two wives; he never entered the chamber of either without first sending someone to investigate diligently that they had not hidden any weapon. And because he did not trust the barber, he had himself shaved by his daughters; and when they were of adult age, he took the razor away from them and had his beard singed with glowing walnut shells. He was very impious toward the gods. He plundered the temple of Proserpina; and then, having a good voyage, he added mocking words to the sacrilege, saying: "See how much fair weather the gods give to those who rob them." King Hiero had adorned the statue of Jove with a cloth of gold. Dionysius took it and gave him one of wool, asserting that gold was useless for every season, because in winter it was too cold and in summer too heavy. The ancients made statues of Apollo depicting him as a youth, and those of Aesculapius his son as elderly and with a long beard. Therefore, he removed the beard, which was made of gold, from Aesculapius, asserting that it was not a fitting thing that the son should be bearded while the father was beardless.

**AND AZZOLINO.** This man was called Azzolino <note>Ezzelino III da Romano (1194–1259), a notoriously cruel Ghibelline leader in Northern Italy.</note> from Romano, a castle of Treviso. Although Mussato of Padua, in a tragedy of his—in which he feigns that he was the son of the devil—calls him Ecerino; and Giovanni Villani in his chronicle states that he was of noble stock. He was a most powerful tyrant in the March of Treviso in the times of Frederick II. Furthermore, he ruled Padua, Vicenza, Verona, and Brescia; and through his brutal cruelty, he killed countless men and sent others into exile. And after the rebellion of the Paduans, in the field <term>prato</term> of Padua, he enclosed twelve thousand men inside a palisade and had them all burned. And regarding this cruelty, it is told that having grown suspicious of one of his chancellors named Ser Aldobrandino, and therefore determining to put him to death, he asked if he knew who were those enclosed in the palisade. And the chancellor responding that he had noted them all in a notebook, Azzolino said he had determined to present their souls to the devil for the many benefits received from him. Therefore, he wanted the chancellor to go to hell with the notebook along with them, and specifically to present them on his behalf; and so, together with the others, he had him burned. This man moved his army against the Milanese, and having reached the Adda and finding the bridge occupied by the Marquis Pelavicino, his adversary, he set out to ford it. Reaching the bank at a disadvantage, he was broken by the Marquis, wounded, taken prisoner, and led to Cassano, a nearby castle, where, not wanting to eat or tend his wounds, he died of hunger and grief in the year of our salvation 1260. He reigned in Verona for thirty-four years, as we shall say more extensively in the ninth Canto of the *Paradiso*.

**AND OBIZZO DA ESTE.** This man was of the family of the Marquises of Ferrara. Having been made Marquis of the March of Ancona by the Apostolic See, he gathered a great treasure through plunder and cruelty. Finally, one night he was smothered with a pillow by his son, whom Dante calls "stepson" <note>Dante uses "figliastro" (stepson) to imply that his unnatural cruelty made him no true son.</note> because it did not seem credible that he was his true son, having used such cruelty upon him. I leave the history of these men of Este, for it is sufficiently celebrated by our commentator from Imola <note>Benvenuto da Imola, an early and influential commentator on Dante.</note>.

**THEN I turned to the poet.** It seemed to Dante that Virgil ought to be the guide and not the centaur. And therefore he turned to him; and Virgil, understanding his desire, said that he wanted the centaur to be the first in that place. And this is feigned allegorically because Dante—that is, appetite subjected to reason—in every contemplation and cognition, desires no judgment other than that of Virgil, which is to say, the intellect. But since the intellect has knowledge of universals, Virgil can judge what violence and cruelty are, and what punishment they merit. But for particulars—such as saying that Dionysius and Azzolino are cruel—the senses and the lower reason judge better, especially in a man who has practiced cruelty, as the centaurs have. Therefore Virgil did not say, "Let this man be your first" absolutely; but he said, "Let this man be your first *now*"—that is, in these particulars. And he [Virgil] wishes to be the second in this place, because our soul, having already recognized the actions of Marius and Sulla to be cruel, abstracts cruelty from these particulars and considers not them, but in a universal way what cruelty is; and in this form, Virgil becomes the second guide. The poet is therefore of marvelous genius, noting under such a fiction the difference between the intellect and the lower reason.

> After the centaur moved further on,
> over a people who, up to the throat,
> seemed to emerge from that boiling stream,
> he showed us a shade alone on one side,
> saying: "He, in the bosom of God, pierced..."

<column-break/>

**B**ullicame <note>The *Bullicame* is a famous hot spring near Viterbo; here used as a generic term for the boiling river of blood (Phlegethon).</note>: They call every water that rises from the veins with the boiling of heat a "bullicame." Hence the bath of Viterbo is called Bullicame for this reason. **HE SHOWED US A SHADE**: A soul which he says is alone in that place because there was no one else who had committed such an atrocity. And he means Count Guy de Montfort <note>Guy de Montfort (1244–1291), who murdered Prince Henry of Almain in a church at Viterbo in 1271.</note>. To express this with brevity: there was a King of England, Henry III, who, because he was a squanderer and a prodigal...
