<header>INFERNO.</header>

...the heart that on the Thames is still honored. <note>Dante refers to the heart of Henry of Almain. The commentator interprets "si cola" as "is honored," though it literally means "is strained" or "drips."</note>
Then I saw people who, out of the river,
held their heads and even their whole chests;
and of these, I recognized many.
Thus, lower and lower it became,
that blood, so that it cooked only the feet;
and here was our passage across the ditch.

"Just as you see on this side
the boiling stream <term>bullicame: a boiling spring or stream of hot water</term> that always diminishes,"
said the Centaur, "I want you to believe:
That on this other side, it presses more and more
its bottom, until it rejoins the place
where tyranny is fated to groan.
Divine justice pricks from this side
that Attila who was a scourge on earth;
and Pyrrhus, and Sextus; and eternally milks
The tears that with the boiling it unlocks
from Rinier da Cornetto and Rinier Pazzo,
who made such war upon the highways."
Then he turned back and recrossed the ford.

<column-break/>

...in consuming the things of a foreign kingdom, he alienated the barons, such that with their favor the King of France sent Simon, an excellent man suited to rule. This man imprisoned King Henry <note>Henry III of England</note> and Richard his brother, and all the sons except Edward <note>The future King Edward I</note>, who escaped by the speed of his horse. But Simon did not know how to use his good fortune; he became so arrogant that all the barons rebelled. Therefore, Edward took the opportunity to recover the realm; he defeated and captured Simon and killed him, tearing him into pieces; and he had his shameful member <note>his genitals</note> put into his mouth. And thus he liberated his father, his uncle, and his brothers. 

Later times followed in which Guy, son of Simon, having become great through the friendship of Charles, Duke of Anjou and brother of King Louis of France, avenged his father with extreme wickedness in this manner. Charles came to Italy, called by the Pope against Manfred; and having defeated Manfred and acquired the Kingdom of Puglia, he appointed Guy—whose work had been most useful in all the wars—as Vicar of Tuscany. He held this vicariate from the Church, and previously Pope Gregory X had released him from the prisons where he had been placed as an excommunicant after he had come to obey. 

A little later, while King Charles was returning from Tunis together with King Philip of France and Henry of England <note>Henry of Almain</note>—nephew of King Henry who was captured by Simon, and son of his brother Richard who had been elected Emperor after the deposition of Frederick II—they came to Viterbo. There, the Pope having died, the cardinals were in discord over creating a new pontiff. Here Guy, wishing to avenge his father who was justly killed by Edward, assaulted Henry in the Church of San Silvestro while the priest was showing the body of Christ <note>during the elevation of the Host at Mass</note>. He killed him and, dragging him out of the church by his hair, fled into the Maremma to the lands of the Red Count, his father-in-law. This was not without infamy for King Charles, who, if he was not complicit as many suspected, should have punished him. 

The body of Henry was carried to London and buried in the chapel of the other kings. Above the tomb was placed a golden statue which holds a golden cup in its right hand, and within it his embalmed heart; and above the heart a knife as testimony of the murder. In the left hand, it holds a brief <note>a written inscription</note> whose words are: "I give the heart pierced by the knife to my relative," meaning to Edward. And from this it arises that Edward was never again a friend to Charles or the House of France. It was therefore a great excess: first, because vengeance for his father's death was not called for, as he was killed justly; second, because of the place, being in a church and when the body of Christ was shown, and in the Roman court, and upon the person of a king's son. For this reason, Dante places him alone, because he committed a singular excess.

**HE MADE IT IN GOD'S BOSOM**: in the church, which is the bosom of God. **THE HEART THAT ON THE THAMES IS STILL HONORED**: that is, it is honored because to worship [original: *colere*] in the Latin language means to honor. **ON THE THAMES**: that is, London, through which the river Thames passes. **THEN I SAW PEOPLE**: This shows that as the ditch proceeds further, it has less depth. Therefore, the lower the souls were, the more they were out of the blood. He says he recognized many, which shows that sensuality, combined with lower reason, can by itself recognize such vices in individuals, especially having heard of them before others. And that the blood is less deep and some sinners are further out than others shows that he who has sinned less is in less punishment, contrary to the Stoics, who maintain that all crimes are equal. Dante crossed the ditch where the blood became shallow, which means nothing other than that he who contemplates vice and is guided by Virgil passes through it without taking any stain.

It is a fitting thing that as the ditch on one side grades down and decreases, so on the other side it deepens, so that according to the greater and lesser sins there are greater and lesser punishments. And therefore the centaur adds that divine justice pricks and pierces here—that is, where the blood is deepest. **THAT ATTILA WHO WAS A SCOURGE ON EARTH**: Attila, King of the Huns, as Paul the Deacon writes, in the year 442, being lord of Dacia, Hungary, Macedonia, Mysia, Achaia, and Thrace. A man most greedy for empire and thirsty for human blood, and cruel above all others, he turned his fury toward Italy with innumerable troops. With all force and industry, he besieged Aquileia, which was so manfully defended by its citizens that not without the gravest hardships and after three years did he finally win it; and cruelly with sword and fire, he brought it to final ruin. Then he destroyed Concordia, Altino, and Padua, and sacked Vicenza, Verona, Brescia, Bergamo, Milan, and Pavia, not without the greatest slaughter, and many other lands in Lombardy and Romagna. Finally arriving where the Mincio flows into the Po, while he deliberated whether he should go to Rome, Pope Leo arrived; and not without a divine miracle, he obtained from such a cruel tyrant that he should leave Italy and return to Hungary. To which he did return, having first taken as his wife Honoria, sister of the Emperor Valentinian. In Hungary, at a banquet, he died from an abundance of blood that issued from his nose: a man greedy for blood drowned in blood. Nor should another miracle be omitted, which gave him the cognomen by which he was called Attila, the Scourge of God. Attila had arrived at Modena with his hostile army, and Geminiano, Bishop of that city and a man of holy life, trusting in divine aid, went out to meet him. When asked who he was, he replied: "I am Attila, the Scourge of God." To which Geminiano replied: "And I am Geminiano, the servant of God." After these words, he opened the gates to him, and Attila, moved by divine terror, passed through the middle of the city without harming anyone.

**PYRRHUS**: This was Pyrrhus, son of Achilles, who was called Pyrrhus from the color of his hair, which was red and fiery, because fire [original: *pyr*] in Greek means fire. Likewise, he was called Neoptolemus, as if "new soldier," because after his father's death, while still a youth, he was led into the army at Troy. This man killed with his own hand Polites, son of Priam, and sacrificed Polyxena, Priam's daughter, at his father's tomb. He killed the aged Priam near the altar where he had fled. He spared neither old age nor youth, nor the female sex, nor religion. He led Hector's wife, Andromache, into servitude. Later, taken by love for Hermione, the daughter of Menelaus whom he took from Orestes, he gave Andromache to Helenus, son...

...of Priam with part of the kingdom: because Helenus with his prophecy <note>Helenus was a son of Priam gifted with prophecy; he advised Aeneas and others on how to avoid the dangers of the sea.</note> saved him from the perils of the sea. But finally, Orestes, having returned from the Tauric region, killed him in the temple of Apollo. There are some who believe Dante does not name this man, but rather Pyrrhus of the Epirotes <note>Pyrrhus of Epirus (318–272 BCE), the famous Greek king who fought the Romans</note>, born of his line, a singular and most excellent leader in military discipline but most ambitious; and he, to rule, provoked many nations from which he had received no injury. He came to Italy, and under the pretext of helping the Tarentines, sought to subjugate the Romans. He spent four years in great campaigning <note>original: "glaſſatico," likely a corruption of a term for military campaigning or glory</note>. He then passed into Sicily and, having made himself lord of it, many times fought successfully against the Carthaginians. But in a short time he lost the island. And because, having returned to Epirus <note>The text says "egypto" (Egypt), but historically and contextually it refers to Epirus</note>, he moved war against Antigonus, King of Macedonia, and drove him most unjustly from the kingdom. Not content with this, he pursued him to Argos where he had fled. Having entered the city by force, he was killed with a roof tile thrown at him by an old woman from a window. Some understand Sextus to mean Sextus Pompey, son of Pompey the Great; who after the death of his father and brother occupied Sicily and in those seas became almost a pirate. But all this was to return to his homeland occupied by Augustus, therefore I do not see why he deserves to be placed among tyrants. Therefore, I believe we can more correctly understand Sextus Tarquinius, son of Tarquin the Proud, the last king of the Romans; who, pretending to have been beaten and driven out by his father, went to Gabii—a city not far from Rome—to try to take it through treachery, since his father had not been able to conquer it with arms. And his fraudulent plan succeeded: for the Gabines, believing what he feigned to be true, received him: and in a short time, as a man experienced in military discipline, they committed to him the government of the city and the army. Whereupon he gave it to his father. <margin>Master Rinier da Corneto</margin> Rinier da Corneto: Master Rinier da Corneto, who in his time kept almost the entire coastline <term>maremma: the marshy coastal lands of Tuscany and Lazio</term> of Rome in terror and as prey through the most cruel robberies on the Roman road. <margin>Rinier Pazzo</margin> Rinier Pazzo: Master Rinier de' Pazzi of Valdarno; these words denote a man of the same habits who practiced banditry and robbed the roads. Then he turned back: Nessus, recrossing the same ford.

### CANTO XIII OF THE FIRST CANTICLE BY DANTE.

Nessus had not yet reached the other side
when we set ourselves through a wood
that was marked by no path.
No green leaves, but of a dusky color;
no straight branches, but gnarled and twisted;
no fruit there, but thorns with poison.
Those savage beasts that hold in hatred
the cultivated lands between Cecina and Corneto
do not have thickets so harsh or dense.
Here the foul Harpies make their nests,
who drove the Trojans from the Strophades
with a dismal announcement of future harm.
They have wide wings, human necks and faces,
feet with claws, and a great feathered belly;
they make lamentations upon the strange trees.

<column-break/>

Where here begins the second ring: in which those who have used violence against themselves and their own things are punished. He describes a most dense forest without any path. A forest, I say, not of trees, but of thorny thickets. **Nessus had not yet reached the other side**: This shows their speed in walking. For before Nessus had crossed back over the ditch, they had already entered a wood, that is, a forest—a Tuscan word derived from the Greek. For we call a forest a "bosco" because animals graze there, and in Greek "to graze" is called *boskein*. **By no path**: by no way. **Dusky**: black. **Thorns with poison**: thorns and briers pricking with poison, because the punctures from these were as if they were poisoned. **Do not have so [harsh]**: The Cecina is a river that enters the sea not far from Vada where the Maremma of Pisa ends; and from this place as far as Corneto—which is a castle in the Patrimony <note>The "Patrimony of St. Peter" was a historical territory of the Papal States.</note>—there are many thickets of thorns so dense that they are inhabited only by wild beasts.

Some texts have not "Cecina" but "Cecila," which is a land named Centumcellae <note>Modern-day Civitavecchia.</note> by the ancients; and indeed, between this and Corneto, they say these dense thickets exist, which he uses here for comparison. And this seems more appropriate because between the Cecina river and Corneto there is a great distance. It is a fitting thing that he places the souls of those who have killed themselves to be transformed into thickets. For there being in us three powers of the soul: the first is called **rational**, by which we are different from all other animals and similar to the angels and made in the image of God; and with which we contemplate, investigate, acquire sciences and arts, and have prudence in administering ourselves, the family, and the republic. The second is called **sensitive**, by which we have external and internal senses and the appetite either to follow what we judge useful or to flee the contrary; and this is common to us and all other animals. The third is named **vegetative**, which nourishes and grows the body and generates another like itself; and this is common not only to animals but also to plants. It seems fitting that he who kills himself has first lost the rational part which—not only according to theological precepts, but also according to Platonic philosophy—forbids us from driving out the soul from the body which God has given it in custody; rather, we should return it when it is asked for by Him who created it. Then he also loses the sensitive part, by which not only man but every worm flees death. Therefore, nothing remaining to him but the vegetative part—which is in plants as it is in us—it is a just thing that he be transformed into a plant. And he makes it a non-fruit-bearing plant because such a death produces no fruit, neither of fame—like those who for the safety of the fatherland have gone to a voluntary death, like the Decii <note>A famous Roman family whose members sacrificed themselves in battle for the state.</note> and many others—nor of salvation, like the innumerable host of martyrs who, by voluntarily supporting a most cruel death, have acquired eternal life. Nor does it have straight branches or beautiful leaves: that is, it is not delightful or pleasant, nor of a straight and sincere mind, nor of any good demonstration. But it is black, which signifies gloom and sorrow; and full of twists: that is, of many thoughts and works [of darkness]; and of thorns: that is, of the sharpest stings and remorses of conscience which lead to such despair. And certainly, it is a marvelous fiction in this place: because not only with this does he excellently express the properties of this vice, but he also does not depart from the sacred writers. Hence Solomon in Ecclesiastes <note>Landino attributes this to Ecclesiastes, but it is actually from the Book of Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) 6:2-3.</note>:

> Do not exalt yourself in the thoughts of your soul like a bull, lest your strength be dashed to pieces through folly, and you be left like a dry tree in the desert. <note>original: "Ne extollas te in cogitatione animae tuae sicut taurus: Ne forte elidatur virtus tua per stultitiam: & relinquas it velut lignum aridum in heremo."</note>

Therefore he remains like a dry tree in the desert. Nor is it a marvel, because he who falls into despair remains without divine grace. And as Matthew says in the twenty-first [chapter]: **A man without grace is like a withered fig tree** <note>original: "Figura hominis absque gratia est sicut ficus arrida." Refers to Jesus cursing the fig tree.</note>. And Bernard: **A man without grace, despairing, is like a wild tree bearing fruits upon which the infernal pigs feed** <note>original: "Homo sine gratia desperans velut arbor silvestris ferens fructus quibus porci infernales pascuntur."</note>. And certainly, the devil, who is the infernal pig, feeds upon the effects of the despairing man. And if we look closely at all the fictions the poet makes of the punishments and torments of the damned, we will realize that it never happens that they do not, in some way, spring from sacred Christian doctrine. It is certainly a wonderful thing that from the sentences of others he makes his own fiction, and is at once an excellent poet and an excellent Christian. But to return to the first point, he also makes these thickets dense and thorny because such places are refuges and dens for wild beasts, and no mind can be more beast-like than that which is an enemy to itself. He makes the wood pathless: for the despair which induces a man to kill himself arises because he sees no way or path that can lead him where he desires. Furthermore, because by such sins the way of salvation is taken away, and it becomes a sin against the Holy Spirit. I know that in this place philosophers and theologians raise a doubt whether a man can have hatred for himself, since the Creator has ingrained in not only man but all created things a singular love regarding their own conservation. And Paul to the Ephesians says: **No one ever hated his own flesh** <note>original: "nemo unquam carnem suam odio habuit." Ephesians 5:29.</note>. How then does any man conceive such hatred against himself that he kills himself? Especially because, as Thomas Aquinas says, man naturally always desires the good, and to love is to desire good for the thing loved, and to hate is to desire evil for the thing hated. To which it is answered that he who kills himself does not do it because he wishes to harm himself, but he believes he is helping himself and chooses that [death] in place of a good.

The Harpies, according to Hesiod in his *Theogony*, were daughters of Thaumas and Electra, daughter of Oceanus; and he names two: Aello and Ocypete. Other poets, and especially the Latins, say they are the daughters of Neptune and the Earth and want there to be three, adding Celeno. These Harpies are placed for **Avarice**, which induces men to robbery. Whence they are called Harpies because *harpazein* in the Greek language means to snatch. And they are daughters of Thaumas: that is, of "wonder" [admiratione], because the wonder we have for riches and the opinion of thinking they are very good leads us to robbery. And others say they are daughters of Neptune—that is, the sea—and the Earth, because by sea and by land robberies are committed. SOME interpret that three things are in avarice. First, to desire the things of others. Second, to snatch them. Third, hid-

<summary>This page introduces Dante's Wood of the Suicides in Canto XIII, with Cristoforo Landino's commentary explaining the philosophical and theological reasons why those who commit violence against themselves are transformed into gnarled, fruitless trees.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the Harpies and begins the exploration of the Wood of the Suicides in Canto XIII of Dante’s Inferno. The previous page introduced the physical description of the Harpies; this page explains their allegorical meaning before moving into the narrative where Dante breaks a branch from a speaking tree.</meta>

# CANTO TWELVE
<i>i</i>

interpret them similarly, saying that **Aello** is named as if from the Greek *allon* <note>original: "elin allon"</note>: that is, to choose and desire the things of others. **Ocypete** comes from *ocys* meaning "swift" and *petin* meaning "to fly": because they fly swiftly toward those things. **Celaeno** in Greek signifies "black": and by black they understand obscurity and darkness, as if to hide the things they have seized. **WHO DROVE FROM THE STROPHADES and the Trojans**. In the dialogues we are writing concerning the allegorical sense of Virgil, we demonstrate what this means. Virgil describes them in this form:
*No monster more dismal than these, nor any more cruel pestilence and wrath of the gods ever rose from the Stygian waves. They have the faces of birds with the countenances of virgins; most foul is the discharge from their bellies, they have clawed hands, and their faces are always pale with hunger.* <note>original Latin: "Tristius haud illis monstrum : nec seuior ulla Pestis & ira deum stygiis se se extulit undis: Virginei uolucrum uultus foedissi/ ma uentris Proluuies uneque manus & pallida semper Ora fame." from Aeneid III.</note>

He calls them monsters because robbery is entirely against human nature; and he writes that they come from hell because it is not a human thing, but diabolical. And because robberies arise from wealth, we showed above how they belong to Pluto. They are depicted with a virgin's face because the miser, at first meeting, shows the greatest modesty: he does not spend his own money out of parsimony and temperance, and always preaches this. The rest of the body is a bird of prey with terrible claws, to demonstrate the rapacity of the miser. They have large wings, which signifies that the greed of the miser extends far and flies to every thing. The great belly and the greed for devouring denote an insatiable appetite. And they defile the tables with their dung because the miser is filthy in everything. **THEY MAKE LAMENTATIONS upon the strange trees**. This denotes that the miser always complains as if he were dying of hunger. And if anyone should ask why the poet has placed the Harpies in this place to signify the robbery of the miser, I respond that no one can commit a more injurious robbery than to rob oneself of one's own life.

---

"The good master, before you enter further,
know that you are in the second ring,"
he began to say to me, "and you will be there
until you reach the horrible burning sand;
therefore look well, and you shall see
things that would take away belief from my speech."
I heard wailings being drawn from every side,
and saw no person who might make them;
whereat I stayed, all bewildered.
I believe he believed that I believed
that so many voices came from among those stumps
from people who were hidden from us.
Therefore the master said: "If you break
some little twig from one of these plants,
the thoughts you have will all be cut short."
Then I stretched my hand a little forward
and plucked a branchlet from a great thornbush;
and its trunk cried out: "Why do you tear me?"
After it had become dark with blood,
it began to cry again: "Why do you mangle me?
Have you no spirit of pity whatever?
Men we were, and now are turned to brush;
truly your hand ought to be more merciful
even if we had been the souls of serpents."
As a green log that is burning
at one of its ends, and from the other groans
and hisses because of the air escaping,
so from that broken splinter came forth
words and blood together; whereat I let the tip
fall, and stood like a man who fears.
"If he had been able to believe it before,"
responded my sage, "O wounded soul,
what he has seen only through my rhyme,
he would not have stretched his hand against you;
but the incredible thing made me
induce him to a deed that weighs on myself.
But tell him who you were, so that in turn..."

<column-break/>

**T**hese five tercets are quite easy in themselves. Virgil admonishes him: that as far as the wood extends is the second ring, until the boiling sand where he will enter the third. And because he is to see incredible things here, he does not predict them to him, admonishing us that when a thing is incredible, it is better not to speak of it, but to wait until it manifests itself. He then shows that those thickets into which the souls are converted were lamenting. But he, seeing no one, did not think the voices came from them. Understanding this, Virgil, to clarify it for him, told him to break a branch. He shows that Virgil manifests this to him not only because the intellect is what creates such fictions, but also because Virgil in his third book <note>referring to Book III of the Aeneid</note> feigns something not very dissimilar to this: when Aeneas, snapping a shoot growing on the tomb of Polydorus, saw blood come out and heard a human voice.

**W**e have already said why the author wants these souls to be converted into thickets. Now he makes them thorny because, like briars, they are intractable and harmful to whoever touches them; so these people have been harmful to themselves. Nor do they deserve any other body, those who have stripped themselves of the human body. **AS A LOG** <note>original: "STIZO"</note>. We call a piece of scorched wood a "stizo" or "stizone," and it is an excellent comparison: for just as this, when it burns at one end, hisses and blows at the other end. Thus, through that broken end came forth wind which then made words. **BY WIND that goes away**. He shows the cause. Every time moisture in a narrow place is oppressed by heat, because it cannot escape all at once, it converts into spirit and wind, which exits with the force of that narrowness. As we see in the **bombard** <note>an early type of cannon</note>: where the nitre, a very humid thing driven by heat—which it makes with the sulfur and is maintained in the powder—generates such a fury of wind that it pushes every great weight and hurls it from afar. **WHEREAT I LET THE tip fall and stood like a man who fears**. This happens to one who unexpectedly hears or sees a miraculous thing. For he stops, and his mind remains so occupied in that wonder that the forces abandon the body. And if he has anything in his hand, it falls; and he takes horror from such a thing, especially if it proceeds from something he himself has done, as here, where by having broken the branch, that break sent out words and blood.

**V**irgil responds: **O WOUNDED SOUL**: That is, offended. If you had been able to believe it only by my rhyme—that is, by my words—meaning what he has now seen, he would not have stretched his hand out to you. **BUT THE incredible thing made me induce him** to break this branch. **WHICH WEIGHS ON MYSELF**: that is, it is troublesome to me that he has offended you. **BUT TELL HIM WHO YOU were** in the world, so that instead of any **blemish** <note>original: "menda"</note>—that is, in exchange for some restoration for the damage he has done you—he may **REFRESH** your fame in the world: that is, renew your fame. As if to say: if he has offended you by breaking you, in place of this damage he will restore you by refreshing your fame in the world. **WHERE HE IS ALLOWED**: that is, where it is permitted and he can return. It is the office of the intellect, whenever the senses err, to placate the offended party. Therefore he first excuses himself, Virgil saying that this...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante’s Inferno, Canto XIII. Having encountered the Harpies in the previous section, Dante now speaks to one of the trees in the Wood of the Suicides. This page contains the famous speech of Pier della Vigna and the beginning of Cristoforo Landino’s extensive historical and etymological commentary on his life and death.</meta>

INFERNO;

<margin>...refresh your fame from any stain in the world above, where he is permitted to return.</margin>

<gloss>For this vice, he gives him fame above many other virtues, as you will see.</gloss>

# The trunk replied: "You so entice me with your sweet speech
# that I cannot remain silent; and may it not burden you
# if I am lured a little into conversation.
# I am he who held both the keys
# of Frederick’s heart, and I turned them,
# locking and unlocking so softly,
# that I excluded almost everyone from his secrets.
# I bore such faith to that glorious office
# that I lost both sleep and life <note>original: "le vene e' polsi" - literally "veins and pulses."</note> for it.
# The harlot <note>meaning Envy</note> who never from the house
# of Caesar turned her whorish eyes—
# the common death and vice of courts—
# inflamed all minds against me;
# and those inflamed so inflamed Augustus <note>The Emperor Frederick II</note>
# that my joyous honors turned to dismal mourning.
# My soul, in its disdainful mood,
# thinking to escape disdain by dying,
# made me, who was just, unjust against myself.
# By the new roots of this tree,
# I swear to you that I never broke faith
# with my lord, who was so worthy of honor.
# And if either of you returns to the world,
# comfort my memory, which still lies prostrate
# from the blow that envy dealt it."

<column-break/>

This is one of the things that lower reason would not have believed without experience. Afterwards, Dante promises to compensate the injury in the only way he could: by giving him fame. And certainly it is so. For even if Dante breaks a branch—that is, defames him below—he shows here that the highest prudence and the highest faith were within him.

<image-desc>Decorative initial N, featuring a figure or foliate pattern within a square frame.</image-desc>

Dante could not have used a more fitting speech toward one who had died with a false reputation among men than to promise to refresh his fame. Hence the soul responds that it is "enticed" <note>original: "adescata"</note> by his words. For there can be no greater bait for one who has been wrongly defamed than the hope that his reputation will be restored. Nor is there any soul so base that it is not greedy for glory and fame. Therefore, everyone strives to flee the infamy given to them, especially if it is undeserved. **ENTICE** <note>original: "ADESCHI"</note> is a metaphor from bird-catchers who put out bait <note>original: "esca"</note> for birds to accustom them to the place where they can later be caught. **LURE** <note>original: "Minueschi" or "m'inveschi"</note> comes from the same metaphor. For when we hold someone with pleasing words, we are like the bird-catcher who holds birds with birdlime <note>original: "visco" or "pania"</note>. **I AM HE**. This man was called Messer Piero delle Vigne <note>Pier della Vigna (c. 1190–1249), a diplomat and poet</note>, who was from Capua. Though of very humble and low condition, he possessed a noble mind and quick wit. Having devoted himself to study, he became an excellent jurist and as eloquent as those times allowed, so much so that his letters were held in great reputation. Because of these virtues, he was appointed chancellor and secretary by Frederick <note>Emperor Frederick II</note>. In a short time, through his industry, he reached such a level that he alone could do everything with the Emperor. Because of this, he incurred such envy from many barons of that court that some, astutely using forged and counterfeit letters and suborned and false witnesses, were able to persuade the Emperor that Messer Piero had secret dealings with Pope Innocent <note>Pope Innocent IV</note>, who was then the Emperor's enemy, and that he had revealed secrets of great importance. Frederick, being too credulous, had him blinded <note>original: "abbacinare" - a process of blinding with a red-hot metal basin</note>, so that he remained sightless and deprived of his dignity. After this, Messer Piero went to live in Pisa. There—either because the Pisans did not treat him as he felt he deserved, or because his unhappiness tormented him more each day—he fell into total desperation. One day he asked his guide where in Pisa they were, and hearing they were near the church of San Paolo on the banks of the Arno, he had his face turned toward the wall of the church. Then, moving with as much force as he could, with his head forward like a

---

ram going to butt, he struck the wall with a blow; and thus, his brain being shattered, he died instantly. Others say that after the Emperor had him blinded—who at that time was in San Miniato al Tedesco—he had him placed on a horse and led to Pisa. There, stationed before the church of Saint Andrew, Piero asked where he was, and hearing it, such was his indignation at having been falsely accused and condemned that he struck his head against the wall until he died. Some say he died while imprisoned. Others say that while he was in his palace in Capua and the Emperor was passing by, he threw himself from the windows. They add that before the palace in Naples stood a statue of the Emperor and one of Messer Piero; at the Emperor's feet were men asking for justice, and a scroll on the Emperor's statue said: "Go to Piero delle Vigne," who had all authority from him in everything. This was shown to prove how great the authority of this secretary was. **WHO HELD BOTH THE KEYS**: of yes and no, of denying and granting; because Frederick neither denied nor granted anything without his counsel. **THAT FROM HIS SECRETS Almost everyone I excluded**: because he trusted almost no one but me. **I BORE FAITH TO THE GLORIOUS office**. It was a great glory to be his chancellor, and I exercised that office faithfully. **VEINS AND PULSES**: that is, life, which consists of the blood in the veins and the vital spirits, whose movement is called the pulse; for *pulsare* in Latin means "to beat." **THE HARLOT**: He uses the harlot as a metaphor for Envy, which is a common vice. For just as a harlot approaches a man not out of true love, but out of greed to have what is his, so Envy looks at another's good to steal from it and diminish it. **FROM THE HOUSE OF CAESAR**: From the court of the Emperor. For every emperor is called "Caesar" because the first to establish such a seat in Rome was Gaius Julius Caesar. **WHORISH EYES**: that is, like a prostitute’s, greedy to usurp the goods of others. "Harlot" <note>original: "Meretrice"</note> in Latin signifies a woman who sells her modesty for gain. Therefore, even if a woman is unchaste or an adulteress, she is not a "harlot" unless she does it for profit; and she is called *meretrice* because *merere* in Latin means to earn a base profit. Thus, he correctly called Envy a harlot; because just as a harlot grows rich by impoverishing others, so Envy desires to do. **INFLAMED AGAINST ME**: that is, she kindled with spite and envy the minds of all the barons who were annoyed that I was so honored. **AND THE inflamed minds of the barons INFLAMED AUGUSTUS**: that is, with false testimony they incited the Emperor, who is called "Augustus" for this reason: after Octavian, born of his sister and made his adopted son by his will, succeeded Julius Caesar in the empire, the entire Roman city desired to honor him. Because the city was divided into three orders—Senatorial, Equestrian, and Plebeian—each gave him a name as an ornament. Therefore there were three: Caesar, Quirinus, and Augustus. The name "Caesar" made him like his father. "Quirinus" made him like Romulus, the first founder of Rome, who was called Quirinus, meaning "Lord," because *kyrios* in Greek signifies "Lord" <note>original: "ciranos in greco"</note>. Or it was because of the spear he used in battle, which the Sabines, neighbors to the Romans, called *Quiris*. "Augustus" signifies...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante’s Inferno, Canto XIII, specifically focusing on the life and character of Pier delle Vigne and the nature of the punishment for those who have committed violence against themselves. The header "Canto Twelve" appears to be an error in the original printing, as the content describes the Wood of the Suicides found in the Thirteenth Canto.</meta>

->CANTO TWELVE<-

...a place venerable and consecrated with an omen. Therefore, Augustus is as if sacrosanct. From this, it follows that all his successors in the Empire until these times are called Caesars and Augusti: just as all the kings of Alba from Silvius, the first king, were named Silvii; and all the kings of Egypt from Ptolemy, the first king, were named Ptolemies. Therefore, the name of this emperor was Frederick II: but Caesar and Augustus is a name for all emperors. **THAT Joyous honors** turned into sad mourning: because he was imprisoned and afterwards blinded. **UNJUST I made me against me just.** I was just because I had not erred against Frederick: but I became unjust against myself by taking my life undeservedly. **TO MY Lord who was so worthy of honor.** It seems that the author contradicts himself by calling Frederick worthy of honor, whom he previously placed as a heretic and enemy to the Apostolic See. But I respond that it is not the poet speaking now, but Messer Piero, who, wanting to persuade that he did not betray him, calls him worthy of honor; so that by this it might be plausible that he would not have betrayed one so worthy. Alternatively, let us say that although he had the vice already mentioned above, he was nonetheless excellent in many other things: and especially in military discipline and in lordship. For he was much feared by Christians and Saracens alike. He was Emperor of the Romans, King of the Germans <note>original: "Alamanni"</note>, Duke of the Swabians <note>original: "Suevi"</note>, King of Apulia <note>original: "Puglia"</note>, and held a great part of Syria. He had noble sons, namely Henry the Lame—who was of high intellect—the beautiful Conradin, and the most liberal Manfred. He built many castles. He was of medium stature, of a cheerful appearance, quite prudent and literate, universal in every thing, and skilled in many mechanical arts. He possessed the Latin, German, French, Greek, and Turkish languages. Brave in arms, though prone to lust.

I waited a little; and then, since he was silent,
the poet said to me: "Do not lose the hour,
but speak and ask him if more pleases you."
Wherefore I to him: "Ask him yourself again
of what you believe will satisfy me;
for I could not, such pity aches my heart."
Therefore he began again: "So may the man
freely do for you what your speech prays,
imprisoned spirit, may it please you still
To tell us how the soul becomes bound
in these knots; and tell us, if you can,
if any ever from such limbs unfolds."

Then the trunk blew strongly, and then
that wind was converted into such a voice:
"Briefly shall you be answered.
When the ferocious soul departs
from the body from which it has torn itself,
Minos sends it to the seventh abyss:
It falls into the wood, and no part is chosen for it,
but there where fortune flings it,
there it germinates like a grain of spelt <note>A hardy type of hulled wheat</note>:
It rises as a shoot <note>original: "vermena"</note> and as a wild plant.
The Harpies, then feeding upon its leaves,
cause pain, and to the pain, a window.
Like the others, we shall come for our remains,
but not so that any may clothe themselves in them,
for it is not just to have what a man takes from himself.
Here shall we drag them, and through the mournful
wood shall our bodies be hung,
each on the thorn of its troublesome shade."

We were still attentive to the trunk,
believing that it wished to say more,
when we were surprised by a noise.

<column-break/>

<margin>i</margin> He shows that as Piero falls silent, Virgil encourages Dante to ask him if he wants to know more. And Dante responds: "You ask of those things that you believe will satisfy me." And this is the right order in the human soul: whose appetite is already made obedient to reason. For Dante—that is, the appetite—does not move to ask if Virgil—that is, the intellect—does not admonish him to ask. And even then, he does not ask himself, because the appetite and the lower reason do not know how to choose what is good to know if the intellect does not show it to them. And therefore he requests Virgil to ask for him the things that he judges will satisfy him. And Dante says he cannot ask himself because of the compassion he feels for that spirit. But allegorically, he demonstrates that the various perturbations which are in the appetite and the lower reason do not allow one to ask and contemplate noble things. Then Virgil asks for what reason the soul is enclosed in that wood, and if it ever escapes.

<margin>d</margin> Virgil had asked two things. First, in what way the soul is bound in those thorns. Second, if it is ever released. The spirit responds to the first: that when the "ferocious soul"—that is, cruel and savage toward itself—departs from the body from which it violently uproots itself, it falls into this seventh circle. **IT FALLS** like a heavy thing due to the weight of sin, and like a thing precipitated by fury. **AND NO PART IS CHOSEN** for it. Because in those who kill themselves out of desperation, it does not seem there is a degree where one deserves more punishment than another. **WHERE FORTUNE** flings it: and allegorically it demonstrates that the desperate person strikes where fortune pushes him without any consideration. And where it falls in the wood, there it stops and begins to put down roots as a seed sown in the earth does. **GRAIN OF SPELT**: He used the species for the genus, saying "grain"—that is, a grain of spelt—for every seed. **IT RISES AS A SHOOT**: He describes the natural succession and growth of the plant. For first the seed sprouts, then a tender shoot <term>vermena: a thin, flexible branch or sprout</term> rises, and finally, growing, it becomes a tree. **AS A WILD PLANT**: because it is not fitting that a savage soul be converted into a fruitful and domestic plant. **THE HARPIES** then feeding on its leaves: they denote the constant memory of the robbery committed against one's own life and one's own body. These feed on the leaves: that is, such recollection gnaws at the mind. **THEY CAUSE PAIN**: because by tearing the leaves, they induce pain. **AND TO THE PAIN THEY MAKE A WINDOW**: because through such a rupture, the spirit sends out its voice. **LIKE THE OTHERS WE SHALL COME**: he shows that in the resurrection of bodies, these souls will return for their bodies like the others. But they will not "clothe" themselves in them, because having thrown them away as a vile thing, it is not just that they should have them back. It is as if to say: it is not just to have back that which a man has taken from himself.

<margin>h</margin> He has placed up to this point those who have used violence against their own persons. Now he places the punishments of those who have used violence against their own property and have beastly consumed it. He describes them as naked because they are stripped of their substance, and scratched because everyone reviles and tears at them.

<sig>i i</sig>
<meta>Handwritten 46 at bottom left margin.</meta>

<meta>This page continues the exploration of the Seventh Circle of Hell, transitioning from the souls of the suicides (who are turned into trees) to the squanderers, who are pursued by hounds through the same forest. It continues the commentary likely by Cristoforo Landino on Dante’s Inferno, Canto XIII.</meta>

->INFERNO:<-

Just as one who hears the boar
and the chase approaching his post,
hearing the beasts and the branches crashing.
And behold, two from the left side,
naked and scratched, fleeing so fiercely
that they broke every barrier of the forest.
The one in front cried out: "Hurry, come death!"
And the other, who seemed to think he was too slow,
cried: "Lano, your legs were not so nimble
at the jousts of the Toppo!"
And then, perhaps because his breath failed him,
he made a huddle of himself and a bush.
Behind them, the forest was full
of black hounds, eager and running
like greyhounds that have slipped their chains.
On him who was hidden, they set their teeth,
and they tore him apart piece by piece,
then carried off those suffering limbs.

Then my guide took me by the hand,
and led me to the bush that was weeping
through its bleeding fractures in vain.
"O Jacopo da Santo Andrea," it said,
"what has it profited you to make a screen of me?
What fault have I in your wicked life?"
When the master had stopped above it,
he said: "Who were you, who through so many wounds
blow out a mournful speech with blood?"

And he to us: "O souls who have arrived
to see the shameful slaughter
that has thus separated my leaves from me:
gather them at the foot of the dismal shrub.
I was of the city that for the Baptist
changed its first patron; for which reason
he will always make it sorrowful with his art;
and were it not that at the passage of the Arno
some sight of him still remains,
those citizens who later rebuilt it
upon the ashes that remained from Attila
would have had the work done in vain.
I made a gibbet <note>A gallows or place of execution.</note> for myself of my own house."

<column-break/>

...their fame and their ugly life. They flee: because those who are placed in such misery, being ashamed, flee through the forest: that is, through dark and solitary places away from the sight of men. **THEY BREAK THE BRANCHES** of the spirits: because as an excuse for themselves, they defame those who have killed themselves, saying "he did even worse than I." Or truly, they break the barriers <note>original: "roste"</note>: that is, having consumed their own goods, they take from the goods of others. He places, then, two fleeing: and the one in front said "Come, death." This was Lano of Siena <note>original: "Lano Sanese"</note> who consumed all his wealth. Being in the Sienese army sent against the Aretines in favor of the Florentines, and later returning, they were ambushed at Pieve al Toppo in the territory of Arezzo and defeated. There Lano, although he could have retreated to safety, nonetheless, like one in despair, threw himself among the enemies; he preferred to die rather than live in such poverty. This is what Jacopo of Padua <note>original: "iacopo padoano"</note> now reproaches him for, saying "your legs were not so nimble to flee the jousts of the Toppo": that is, the clashing of spears in the battle which took place at Pieve al Toppo between the Sienese and the Aretines. And having said these words, his breath failing him—that is, his power in running—he finished the loop and made a "huddle" <note>original: "groppo," a knot or tangle</note> in a shrub where there was a soul. **BEHIND THEM THE FOREST WAS FULL OF BLACK HOUNDS eager and running.** He imagines these souls being persecuted by hounds: and by the hounds he intends the remorses of conscience for having thrown away one's wealth, as well as hunger, thirst, and the lack of clothing and other necessities. Also the infamy and the scorns they see and hear made of themselves. These things are all terrible bites to the soul of man. They are black, meaning full of filth and sorrow, and eager to bite. **AND RUNNING:** because these anxieties follow a man with the greatest speed wherever he goes; nor can he hide in any place where he is not found and torn by them.

**My guide:** and rightly so, because the intellect is our guide which leads the appetite safely. **TOOK ME BY THE HAND:** as one does who wants to guide someone so they do not wander from the path or fall. Thus the higher intellect guards the senses so that while it follows in contemplation, it does not wander or fall into the sin being contemplated. **AND LED ME TO THE bush that was weeping:** because it had been broken and torn by the fury of the hounds that had mangled Lano. **O JACOPO DA SANTO ANDREA:** This was a noble Paduan man from the chapel of Saint Andrew. He was very rich, but most beastly consumed his substances. Among his other follies, while going by boat to Venice with other noble youths and seeing that each of them practiced playing music or singing so as not to appear idle, he threw his coins one by one into the river. Another time, when many youths were coming to his villa and seeing them from afar, to do them honor, he set fire to all the huts and houses of his farmers. **WHAT HAS IT PROFITED YOU to make a screen of me?** That is, a shelter. As if to say: "You hid in my bush to protect yourself with it from the hounds, and it profited you nothing." "Screen" <note>original: "schermo"</note> means a shelter, from which we say "to fence" <note>original: "schermire"</note>, which is nothing other than sheltering from blows. And Petrarch says: "I find no other screen to save me from the manifest notice of the people." **THROUGH SO MANY WOUNDS:** Through so many punctures and bites received from the hounds when they tore Jacopo apart while he was hidden in you. **BLOWING OUT A Mournful speech:** that is, speaking.

The spirit responds: first praying that they gather the leaves. The poet demonstrates that this spirit requests his leaves be gathered for no other reason than to show how innate the desire is in every creature to preserve its being, even if it is in the depths of misery. Through this supreme desire, he silently hints at how great the repentance is for having taken his first life, since in the second—though most unhappy—he desires to maintain himself. This concludes that he would willingly return to the first life. And this is the sentiment of Virgil where he says: <note>original: "Proxima deinde tenent mesti loca..."</note> "Next, those sad ones occupy the nearby places who, though innocent, brought death upon themselves with their own hands and, hating the light, threw away their souls. How they would now wish to endure poverty and hard labors in the upper air! Fate stands in the way." <note>Aeneid VI, 434-437</note>. The spirit, then, answers this first. Afterward, he relates that he is Florentine, not naming the name of Florence, but using a circumlocution saying: "I was of the city which changed its first patron." In the time of the Gentiles, this was Mars; later it was the Baptist, that is, Saint John the Baptist. Since Florence was built by Roman citizens...

### CANTO TWELFTH. <note>original: "CANTO DVODECIMO." Although the header says Twelfth, the text continues the commentary on Canto XIII, specifically the transition from the god Mars to John the Baptist as the patron of Florence.</note>

...building of Mars: who was the principal god of the Romans: and they built a temple to him which still stands today <note>The author is referring to the Florence Baptistery, which medieval Florentines believed was originally a Roman temple to Mars.</note>: and in it was his equestrian statue, honored with solemn sacrifices until the evangelical truth was spread in Florence. Afterward, once this city became Christian, they dedicated the temple of Mars to the highest God under the title of Saint John the Baptist. And they chose him as patron in place of Mars. **WHEREFORE FOR THIS CAUSE:** that is, for this reason, that the temple dedicated to him was rededicated to the Baptist. **HE WILL ALWAYS MAKE IT SORROWFUL.** That is, the land will be in sadness and tribulation. **WITH HIS ART:** with wars, which are the art of Mars. For they will always be in wars, either civil or external. Giovanni Villani <note>A famous 14th-century Florentine chronicler.</note>, a diligent writer of the Florentine chronicle, relates that when the temple of Mars was dedicated to Saint John the Baptist, they removed the statue of Mars, which was equestrian—that is, on horseback—made of gray stone <note>original: "macigno," a common Tuscan sandstone.</note> and by a skilled sculptor. And because there were certain ancient prophecies in which it was read that this statue had been made under such a constellation that if it were held in an unworthy place, or if any violence were done to it, great harm would follow for the city. They placed it upon a tower near the Arno: and there it stayed until Florence was destroyed by Attila <note>The text follows a common medieval error, confusing Attila the Hun with Totila the Ostrogoth, who laid siege to Florence in 542 AD.</note>. Attila, King of the Goths, having destroyed many cities in Lombardy and Romagna, passed into Tuscany and besieged Florence. Not being able to take it by force, he turned his mind to deceit. And with many false persuasions, he induced the citizens to receive him inside the city. And it was put to a vote. He, under the guise of honor, had the principal citizens summoned to him: and while they passed from one chamber to another, he had them killed and thrown into a conduit that passed under the capitol, fed by the Arno. The people realized the slaughter when they saw the water of the conduit turn bloody. Whereupon the people rioted, and Attila sent his soldiers through the land, ordering that all males and females, small and large, be killed. None escaped except those who fled. And among the others, Maurice, the Bishop of Florence, a man of most holy life, was killed. After such a slaughter, he destroyed the city with iron and fire: and at that time, the statue of Mars fell into the Arno. And he says this happened in the year of our Lord 450, on the twenty-eighth day of June, five hundred and twenty years after its building. Those who escaped the slaughter and their descendants often wished to rebuild the city; but being forbidden by the Fiesolans <note>The people of nearby Fiesole, ancient rivals of Florence.</note> and by certain nobles around them, they ceased until the time of Charlemagne. Charles, Emperor of the Romans, and the Roman people, moved by the prayers of the Florentines, provided help to rebuild it: and many noblemen came from Rome to inhabit it together with those who remained. It was rebuilt in the years of Christ 802, at the beginning of April; others say on the 30th of March. Then the statue of Mars was found in the Arno, though broken: and because of that same opinion they had of it, they placed it on a pillar at the Ponte Vecchio. And there it stayed until the year of Christ 1333, in which year such a flood came that the Arno carried away the Ponte Vecchio and the other two bridges below it: and in this way, the statue was completely ruined. Therefore, in this place, Dante places the opinion that our ancestors had of this statue, which many say is a heretical opinion. But these are not his words, nor his opinion, but that of the spirit who speaks: whom he induces to say this to manifest a common opinion of many. I believe also, always saving a truer judgment, that it is not against our religion that, according to astrology, a statue might be fashioned with such a constellation that it has some influence and power within it. Wherefore Paolo the Florentine <note>Paolo dal Pozzo Toscanelli (1397–1482), a famous mathematician and astronomer.</note>, a most excellent mathematician in his time, placed the statue of the lion <note>The "Marzocco," the lion symbol of Florence.</note> upon the railing that encircles the Florentine palace, whose head looks toward Milan; many believe this was of no small help against the power of the Visconti <note>The ruling family of Milan, who were major enemies of the Florentine Republic.</note>, who were formidable to our republic in those times. It is also read that Zoroaster the Persian fashioned in Thebes of the Hundred Gates, a city of Egypt, the statue of Memnon with the lyre, which sang. As for the ruin and destruction of Florence, I do not dare to speak against the opinion of so great a poet. But I do not know how Attila could have done this: since Paul the Deacon <note>An 8th-century historian of the Lombards.</note> and others who wrote the history of Attila affirm that he never came into Tuscany nor ever crossed the Apennines. Furthermore, Alcuin <note>original: "Alchindo." Likely referring to Alcuin of York, the scholar at Charlemagne's court.</note>, who diligently wrote the deeds of Charlemagne, makes no mention that he restored Florence; he only relates that he spent two Easters in Florence. **AND WERE IT NOT THAT AT THE PASSAGE OF THE ARNO:** He concludes, as it were, that if the said statue had not been honorably replaced on the pillar of the Ponte Vecchio, this rebuilding would have been in vain, because the city would have perished once more. **SOME SIGHT:** Because it was not whole but broken, and what remained was eroded by the injury of time and antiquity. **I MADE A GIBBET.** This spirit concludes that he hanged himself in his own house. *Jubetto* <note>original: "Iubetto," from the French "gibet" (gallows).</note> in the city of Paris is the place where the gallows are, and where those condemned to such punishment are hanged. Therefore, he made a gallows of his houses: that is, he made them a place for hanging. He does not expressly state who this man was. But some want it to mean Messer Rocco de’ Mozzi, who, having consumed his many and various riches, hanged himself to flee the hardships of poverty. Others understand it as Messer Lotto degli Agli, who, out of repentance for having given a false sentence, hanged himself with his own golden belt. Messer Giovanni Boccaccio says that in those times many Florentines hanged themselves: and for this reason, Dante leaves it ambiguous who this man was.

<header>CANTO XIV.</header>

# CANTO XIV OF THE FIRST CANTICLE BY DANTE.

Since the love of my native place
constrained me, I gathered the scattered leaves
and gave them back to him who was already faint.
Thence we came to the boundary where
the second ring is divided from the third, and where
the horrible art of justice is seen.

To properly manifest these new things,
I say that we arrived at a moor
which removes every plant from its bed.
The sorrowful wood garlands it
around, just as the dismal moat <note>The "dismal moat" refers to the Phlegethon, the river of blood.</note> girds the wood:
here we stayed our steps right at the edge.
The space was a dry and thick sand,
made in no other fashion than that
which was once trodden by the feet of Cato. <note>original: "Caton" — referring to Cato the Younger, who led a famous march through the Libyan desert in 47 BCE.</note>

O vengeance of God, how much you should
be feared by everyone who reads
that which was made manifest to my eyes!
I saw many herds of naked souls
who all wept most miserably;
and different laws seemed imposed upon them.
Some people lay supine upon the ground;
some sat all hunched up;
and others moved continually.
Those who went around were the most numerous,
and those were fewer who lay down in the torment,
but they had their tongues more loosened by the pain.
Over all the great sand, with a slow falling,
dilated flakes of fire rained down,
like snow in the Alps when there is no wind.

As Alexander <note>Referring to a legendary account of Alexander the Great in India, popularized in the Middle Ages via a spurious letter to Aristotle.</note> in those hot regions
of India saw over his host
solid flames falling even to the ground:
Wherefore he provided for trampling the soil
with his ranks, because the vapor

<column-break/>

IN this fourteenth canto, the poet treats the punishments of those who have used violence against God. He demonstrates that, constrained by the love of his native place—that is, his homeland, because he was Florentine—he gathered the scattered leaves <note>The "leaves" are the broken branches of the suicide-trees.</note> torn by the black hounds, as the spirit had begged him, and returned them to him; he who, through many laments, was already faint. And in passing, he shows how tight the bond ought to be among those who are children of the same homeland. And it is a most excellent fiction by Dante: for if he speaks of **Messer Rocco de' Mozzi** <note>The identity of the unnamed suicide at the end of Canto XIII.</note>, because he had used violence against his own person, Dante appropriately placed him first; and because he also deserved ill for his handling of property, he had him torn by the hounds. And then they came to the boundaries that divide this second ring from the third, where those who have been impious toward God are punished.

WISHING to manifest the third ring, I say that we arrived at a moor: that is, a sandy plain; for so "moor" <note>original: "landa"</note> and "lowland" <note>original: "lama"</note> signify. It removes every plant from itself, because neither grass nor tree grows there. **THE SORROWFUL WOOD** which garlands: that is, encircles and surrounds it. **AS THE DISMAL MOAT**: that is, the river of Phlegethon surrounds that same wood, of which we shall speak below. **THE SPACE WAS A SAND**: he says that the space of this plain was of such sand as that of the deserts of sandy Libya, which **Marcus Cato**, after the defeat at Thessaly and after the death of Pompey in Egypt, led the relics of the Pompeian armies through to join them in Africa with Juba, King of the Numidians, who followed the Pompeian party. Deservedly he places this location as sandy and without any plants: for just as the sand produces no fruit

and is always sterile, so the sin which is against God and against nature—besides that it kills the soul—is also without any fruit or utility to the body. Fire rains there from heaven because no sin, of any kind, makes the flaming wrath of God descend from heaven more. Furthermore, God, the most high, is offended; therefore the highest element <note>In the medieval worldview, fire was the "highest" of the four elements.</note> is the punishment. Furthermore, there can be no greater burning of most proud punishment than to use it against God; nor more burning lust than to use it against nature; nor more ignited greed of avarice than to use it against art. <note>This refers to the three types of "violent against God": blasphemers (direct), sodomites (nature), and usurers (art/industry).</note> And it is also fitting that He punishes them with fire, for we see that God prepared such a punishment for Sodom and Gomorrah. And this sand is surrounded by the wood, the receptacle of wild beasts, because such vice has no species of humanity in it, but is entirely bestial. And just as the wood is dark, so the minds of these people are entirely deprived of the light of reason. In this place they stayed their steps **at the edge** <note>original: "aranda" — meaning "skirting" or "bordering."</note>, that is, grazing it. This signifies that they did not set foot at all into the burning sand: but they approached as much as they could to denote that to speculate upon this vice we must examine it closely, but in no way must we put our feet—that is, our thoughts—into it. For it is a horrendous and most abominable thing not only to commit such a sin, but to even think of it.

**O VENGEANCE of God.** We say Justice is a virtue which, with constant and perpetual will, attributes to each his own right as is fitting to him. And this is divided into Religion, Innocence, Peace, Concord, Piety, Integrity, and Vengeance. And vengeance <note>original: "vendicatione o uero uendecta"</note>, when it is a species of justice, is defined as being justice which, with measure and reason, punishes him who has committed an injury or defends him who is injured. Therefore, he did not say "vengeance" for a certain satiation of anger as many do—who avenge themselves for injuries not to observe justice, but to satiate their anger and hatred—but he said, "O vengeance," that is, "O Justice," which avenges injuries with reason and punishes him who has done them. This belongs chiefly to God. Therefore, this vengeance ought to be feared by everyone who reads of the punishments with which God avenges injuries. Then he shows that the souls placed in this ring were under different laws and conditions. For those who had used violence toward God and deserved greater supplication lay supine. And those who had used it against nature and art, such as the usurers, sat hunched up to touch as little as possible of the sand. And nonetheless, they had more pain than those who were walking. And those who had used it against nature were walking; these are the sodomites. Not undeservedly does he place these violent ones to be punished by fire for the reasons already stated above.

INDIA begins from the Middle Regions, a most healthy region; and twice a year it has summer, and it produces two harvests of grain. Megasthenes and Dionysius write that it once had five thousand cities and nine thousand peoples. And it is so fertile that no part of the people of India ever departed to dwell elsewhere. It was judged to be the third part of the world.

...tightened around itself while it was alone <note>The fire falling on the sands.</note>:
Thus descended the eternal heat,
whence the sand caught fire like tinder
under the flint, to double the pain.
Without rest ever was the dance <note>original: "tresca" — a lively folk dance. The author uses it ironically to describe the souls' frantic movements to avoid the fire.</note>
of the wretched hands, now here, now there,
shaking off the fresh burning.

<column-break/>

Bacchus was the first who triumphed over India. Afterward, Alexander the Great. And the greatest rivers of that land are the Ganges (otherwise called the Gihon) and the Indus (otherwise called the Pishon). And from this river, India is named. The poet says, then, that such flakes of fire fell upon these sinners as Alexander saw fall in India upon his army.
This miraculous thing is not written of by Quintus Curtius, who diligently narrates his history; nor by Justin, who sets it down concisely; nor by Plutarch in his *Life*. But they say that Alexander writes this to Aristotle <note>A reference to the "Letter of Alexander to Aristotle," a popular medieval fictional account of wonders in the East.</note>. And Albertus Magnus, in his *Meteorology*, says that that region is under the sign of Cancer, where the sun’s heat burns up the watery vapor and draws up the thick earthy vapor, which is then driven

<column-break/>

out by the coldness of the earth, and it ignites, falling in the form of snow down to the ground. And the remedy that Alexander used was excellent, in that he had the ground much trampled to extinguish the vapor already ignited before one flake could join with another. **UPON HIS HOST:** his army. **BECAUSE:** He provided to kick and trample. **THE GROUND:** the earth, which in Latin is called *solum*. **WHILE IT WAS ALONE:** Not joined to anything else that could ignite it. **WITHOUT REST:** Ever was the dance. *Tresca* signifies a dance which has within it a fast movement. Whence here he says "the dance of the hands": the fast movement of the hands to shield themselves from the flames.

---

I began: "Master, you who overcome
all things except the harsh demons
who came out against us at the entry of the gate <note>Referring to the gates of the City of Dis in Canto VIII.</note>:
Who is that great one who seems not to care
for the fire and lies scornful and twisted,
so that the rain seems not to ripen him?"
And that same one, who had perceived
that I was asking my leader about him,
cried: "What I was alive, such am I dead.
Though Jove wear out his smith <note>Vulcan, the blacksmith of the gods.</note>, from whom
he took in anger the sharp thunderbolt
wherewith on my last day I was smitten;
and though he wear out the others, one by one,
at Mongibello <note>A local name for Mount Etna in Sicily, where Vulcan's forge was said to be located.</note> in the black forge,
crying, 'Good Vulcan, help, help!'
just as he did at the battle of Phlegra <note>The site of the battle between the Olympian gods and the Giants.</note>,
and though he hurl at me with all his might,
he could not have a happy vengeance."

<column-break/>

He begins to treat the punishments of those violent against God. And he feigns that the first he saw of these such people was Capaneus, of whom we will speak a little below. **YOU WHO OVERCOME ALL THINGS:** Except the harsh demons. Above, when we treated the entry into the city of Dis, we explained allegorically why Virgil had overcome every other thing they had found in Hell, except the demons placed to guard the gate of Dis, whom he could not harm. Therefore, I will not repeat what has already been said once. **WHO IS THAT:** Great one who seems not to care for the fire. This demonstrates excellently the nature of the impious man: for no pride can be equal to that of him who denies the Divine Essence, and thinks that the world is governed rather by chance than by Divine Providence. And for any adversity or calamity that comes upon him, he does not change his purpose; and he does not believe that such unhappiness is sent by Divine Justice as the earned punishment for his impious wickedness. Instead, he stands obstinate, and grows in pride and in anger, both in his deeds and in his words. **AND SEEMS NOT TO CARE FOR THE FIRE:** Because through pride he wishes to show that he does not let himself be overcome. **AND LIES:** Not humble and with repentance for the error committed, **BUT SCORNFUL AND TWISTED:** Which signifies the obstinacy of the soul and its perversity, its crooked mind, and depraved opinion. **SO THAT THE RAIN:** Seems not to ripen him. We call "unripe" the soul of him who still stands defiant and resistant against that which he ought to be obedient to. And by the same logic, we say a man is "mature" or "ripe" who finally, after many scourges, recognizes himself, and yields, and humbles himself. And this is a metaphor drawn

<column-break/>

from apples: which while they are unripe are stubborn and adverse to the taste, and when ripe are the contrary. **AND THAT SAME ONE:** Dante (that is, the lower reason) asks Virgil (who is the higher reason): "Who is that great one?"—that is, "What is the nature of this impiety?" But before Virgil answers him, Capaneus—that is, such a vice—manifests itself. And truly no vice is greater than this; yet also none manifests itself more than this. Nor is Virgil needed—that is, any recondite doctrine or sharpness of intellect—to recognize it. **CRIED: 'WHAT'** I was alive, such am I dead. He "cried," which is a sign of pride; and he cried to denote that they demonstrate themselves and publicly boast of such bestiality. This proceeds from supreme foolishness. Whence the Prophet says: *The fool said in his heart, "There is no God."* <note>original Latin: "Dixit insipiens in corde suo non est deus" — Psalm 14:1 / 53:1.</note> **WHAT I WAS** alive, such am I dead: that is, that even now as one damned, I do not repent, which could not be a greater pain for him. For it is an insupportable torment to one who denies and despises the power of another, nevertheless to see himself continually and most bitterly afflicted by that very power. **OR RATHER:** What I was alive—that is, the same pride and impiety which I had when alive, placed in supreme happiness—such am I dead—that is, afflicted by supreme misery. **THOUGH JOVE WEAR OUT:** By the words the author makes Capaneus say, he demonstrates and perfectly expresses the nature of this Luciferian pride. For such men, even when placed in extreme misery which should tame them, always grow prouder; like this man who, struck by Jove’s lightning into the bottom of Hell, is so obstinate that he says that if Jove wore out all his smiths in making bolts, and spent them all on him, he would not humble himself. **THOUGH JOVE WEAR OUT** his smith: understand Vulcan, whom the poets feign makes the bolts for Jove. The ancients posit Jove, Minerva, Vulcan, and Vesta to express the various natures of fire. For we consider fire in its superior element, which is harmless, and for this they call it Jove—because he "helps" [*gioua*]—because it is an active and generative element. And its highest and most subtle part they call Minerva, who is pure in herself and simple and without any mixture. And for this they say that Jove generated Minerva from his head without joining with a female—that is, without the mixture of matter. We consider furthermore fire in this middle region when it ignites the vapors raised from the earth, from which ignition thunderbolts and arrows are generated; and this they call Vulcan. Wherefore the poets feign that he is Jove's smith and makes the bolts for him when he wishes to strike something. They feign him the son of Jove and Juno: of Jove because he proceeds from the superior element called Jove; of Juno because he is conceived in the air, which is Juno, since it is in the air that the terrestrial vapors ignite. They also take Vulcan for this fire that men use, which burns as much as the matter on which it feeds allows. See...
