<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante’s Inferno, Canto XIV. While the previous page discussed the historical and miraculous accounts of fire falling from the sky (such as in the legends of Alexander the Great), this page transitions into a mythological and scientific explanation of fire, lightning, and the forge of Vulcan.</meta>

<header>CANTO XIV.</header>

...therefore, what they understand by Minerva, what by Jove, and what by Vulcan. There remains the spear, which they claim is the fire enclosed within the earth, as we see when it is drawn from stones and wood and other terrestrial things. They attribute three smiths to Vulcan: Brontes, Steropes, and Pyragmon. The first two names denote the effects of the lightning bolt: for Brontes signifies "thunder," which is born from the fracturing and violent breaking of the cloud in which the vapor is ignited. Steropes signifies "lightning flash," which is nothing other than the flashing of the fire that appears from the broken cloud. The third, which is Pyragmon, expresses the tools of the smith. For *pyr* is fire and *agmon* is anvil <note>original: "pyr e’ el fuoco: & agmon l’ancudine"</note>. These are the names Virgil provides: "Both Brontes and Steropes, and Pyragmon with naked limbs" <note>original: *Bronteque Steropeque & nudus membra Pyragmon* from Virgil’s *Aeneid*</note>. But Hesiod, in his *Theogony*, does not include Pyragmon; in his place, he puts Arges <note>The text uses "Harpes" but refers to the Greek *Arges*, meaning "bright" or "shining."</note> to denote the violence of the bolt, which makes a "rapine" or "seizure" of everything; it is named from *harpasin*, which means to snatch or seize. These are said to be the children of Heaven and Earth because the bolt is born, as we have said, from fire (a celestial thing) and from elevated vapors (a terrestrial thing). They are called <term>Cyclopes</term> in the Greek language because, according to the poets, they had a single eye in their forehead. Some also claim that Vulcan is served by those whom the Greeks call <term>Telchines</term>. The fables say these were children of the sea, and they were the first inhabitants of the island of Rhodes. They were inventors of many arts; they sculpted statues for the gods; furthermore, they could induce winds, rain, hail, and snow wherever they wished, and change the forms of things as magicians do. Let this be sufficient regarding the smiths of Jove.

Now, because mention is made of the celestial bolt, which the Latins call *Fulmen* and *fulgure*, I believe it will not be unpleasant for the reader to review, albeit briefly, its nature. The matter, then, from which it is made is a vapor that is very dry and hot, which easily catches fire and ignites. And the place in which this vapor stays, as if in its own vessel, is a vapor that is watery, concave, and cloudy. These two vapors are drawn up together by the powerful heat of the sun. But the first, due to its dryness, gathers together and constricts itself. The second, due to its humidity, spreads around the first, and clothes and covers it from every side. Thus, the dry vapor flees the moist one as its opposite, and retreats from every side toward the center. But this surrounding vapor also contracts and gathers toward it because of the coldness of the region, and it beats against it greatly. That which is so struck rubs one part against the other, especially on the exterior, and by such motion, it ignites. Thus, the fire, driven by its opposite, unites and increases its strength and breaks the watery cloud; in such a rupture, the lightning flash and the thunder are revealed, and those two occur at the same time. But the flash is seen first because the sense of sight is faster than that of hearing. This is why, if a tree is being cut far away, we see the axe strike first, and then we hear the blow. I will not dwell on demonstrating how three types of thunder are generated from such a rupture, nor why sometimes the sound is heard without the flash—knowledge certainly worthy of study. But in such a vast and varied abundance of things, one cannot insist too long on particulars.

However, I do not judge that I should omit the diversity of the cloud that contains the thunder, nor the diversity of the colors of the fire within it, nor the diversity of how the bolt falls. The cloud is sometimes black in its own coldness, which condenses it in a way that the ray does not penetrate it; and not penetrating it, it cannot whiten it. Because this cloud strongly condenses the vapor within itself and ignites it, it gives a greater thunder. Sometimes the black is seen to turn reddish, which shows that in the thick cloud, the vapor is already ignited; this gives a stronger blow than the black. But the worst is the one that mixes green and black with some redness; for it shows by its blackness that it has much vapor, by the green that it has much water, and by the red that it has much fire. From this cloud, because the heat fights strongly with the cold and the dry with the moist, there fall bolts of great stones <note>Referencing hailstones or "thunderstones" believed to fall during storms.</note>, and it casts down every great building and burns animals. The white cloud is little to be feared because it contains little of either material; thus, its flame is extinguished before it ignites the thing it touches, unless the material is very flammable, like dry wood.

Furthermore, we must diligently observe the colors of the lightning flash, which are essentially three: clear red, a somewhat ignited white, and a red like the color of wine. The first is generated from vapor that is not very dry, and the moisture gives it the red color, like the flame in green wood. In this, because the moisture binds the matter together, it does not spread and thus ignites more easily. The white flame is of dry vapor, like the flame in dry wood; for this reason, it does not spread and only ignites very flammable things. The wine-red color, because it is of very dense and terrestrial vapor, ignites.

The bolt falls in four ways. The first is when the red ignited vapor falls from a green and deep cloud; this generates stone, because the vaporous mixture of terrestrial vapor ignites, and touching the green cloud (which is already converting into water), it hardens like flour that becomes dough with water. Because the great burning does not allow it to be extinguished by the moisture of the cloud, it hardens through the vehemence of the heat and becomes like a fired brick. And because heat flees moisture, the lower part of such a stone is pointed, because it begins to distill the vapor there. The second way is when the vapor is less condensed in a less watery cloud; then it is not held together but nonetheless comes out ignited with force, and breaks by its impulse, and ignites again through inflammation, but it breaks nothing but wood. The third way is of clear red vapor and does not make stone, but it does not separate the flame from the vapor. This does not break anything except small and very dense bodies, for if they were of great size, they would resist. This kills men, and the smell of burning is felt in them, yet no wound is seen; because of its subtlety, it penetrates without breaking. And if it finds gold or silver in a purse, it melts it and does not break the purse; for the leather, being porous, gives it passage. Sometimes the same vapor, when it is thinner and comes from a more watery cloud, penetrates without dividing or manifestly igniting; it greatly harms grapes, especially those well-covered by vine leaves. Such vaporization not only harms by falling directly, but its ray offends whoever it touches; thus it happens that those who look at it often have their faces swell or are blinded. The fourth way is when white vapor comes from a dry, unconstrained flame; for this reason, it does not spread through the air but comes out with great force because the cloud is very deep and very watery. This breaks things and, in breaking, is extinguished; it leaves the things it touches white, and no sign of combustion appears. When it has great force, it kills; and sometimes by its scattering, and because the vapor is not continuous, it strikes one person and does not touch another standing nearby, but then hits another who is further away. And sometimes it reflects off one and does not harm him, yet goes to another and harms him. Sometimes it is so weak that it burns the clothing and in that loses its strength, not harming the man. The fifth way <note>The author adds a fifth, despite mentioning four initially.</note> is when the same vapor comes out of the cloud so weakened that it harms nothing, because as soon as it touches the air, it is extinguished; and in one moment, the fire and the violence cease. We have spoken of the smiths and the bolt; it follows:

**AND IF HE** tires the others, shift by shift: <note>Refers to Jove calling upon Vulcan and his smiths.</note> That is, exchanging them group by group. For when many are at the same exercise and do not all work at once but in turns, they are said to be working in shifts (*mute*).

**IN MONGIBELLO.** This is a mountain in Sicily called Etna by the ancients, and Mongibello by the moderns. Because it is cavernous and contains much sulfur, it often burns or casts out smoke; for this reason, the poets claim that here is the forge in which Vulcan fashions the lightning bolts for Jove. And it adds that if Jove, in anger, urged Vulcan to fashion the bolts with that haste with which he urged him when...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante’s Inferno, Canto XIV. Following the discussion of the elemental nature of fire and lightning associated with the forge of Vulcan, the text now transitions to the mythological figure of Capaneus and the giants who challenged the heavens, as well as the beginning of the journey toward the infernal river of blood.</meta>

<header>INFERNO.</header>

...fought with the giants in the battle of Phlegra <note>A mythical plain where the battle between the Olympian gods and the Giants took place.</note> where he had need of many lightning bolts to kill them all. Nevertheless, he would not see a happy vengeance: because he could not make me repent or yield. And the giants, according to the poets, were sons of the Earth; but they were of such pride because they were of immeasurable stature that they had the audacity to want to drive Jove <note>Jupiter/Zeus</note> from heaven. Therefore, they took three mountains of Thessaly—Pelion, Ossa, and Olympus—and placed them one upon the other to climb into heaven. But Jove killed them with his lightning bolts. And he [Dante] prudently makes mention of the giants in the place where the most prideful impiety is punished: because by the giants they mean nothing other than those men who, intoxicated by the great power they have in earthly things and not remembering human fragility, rise up like a new Lucifer against God; and they wish to have power over human nature and to think nothing of God. Whence Cicero in his *Cato the Elder* <note>original: *Cato Maiore* or *De Senectute*</note> said: "To wage war against the gods in the manner of the giants is nothing other than to rebel against nature" <note>original: *Nihil aliud e' more gigãtiũ aduersus deos bellũ gerere quã naturę repugnare*</note>. And Macrobius said: "What else do we believe the giants were if not a certain impious race that denied the gods?" <note>original: *Quid aliud credimus gigãtes fuisse nisi quãdã impiã gẽtẽ deos negatẽ*</note>. They are therefore born of the earth because they think of nothing other than earthly things. And in their most vain thoughts, they wish to have more power than God. Wherefore they place mountains upon mountains; that is, they accumulate swollen and proud thoughts and enterprises. But the celestial bolt, which is the divine wrath, casts them to the ground. But returning to the fable: this battle was in Thessaly; and according to some poets, in that stretch of countryside where Pozzuoli and Cuma are, which is called Phlegra according to Strabo. Nevertheless, Pliny in his geography places Phlegra not far from the mountains mentioned above, which seems more likely.

Then my leader spoke with such force
that I had never heard him so loud:
"O Capaneus, in that your pride 
is not extinguished, you are more punished;
no other pain except your own rage
would be a complete sorrow for your fury."
Then he turned to me with a better expression <note>original: *labbia*, literally "lips" or "face," implying a gentler manner.</note>
saying: "That was one of the seven kings
who besieged Thebes; he had, and seems to have,
God in disdain, and seems to prize Him little;
but as I said to him, his own insults
are quite fitting ornaments for his breast."

<column-break/>

**Heard** Virgil speak to the proud Capaneus **SPOKE WITH FORCE:** that is, with bitterness and with vehemence; and with great shouts he rebuked him in a way that Dante affirms he had not yet heard him speak so sharply. This signifies that the intellect is not more disturbed by any other vice than by this impiety. **IN THAT** your pride is not extinguished, you are more punished. It is a very true sentiment that no punishment is greater for the proud than the rage and anger they feel at being defeated and depressed; which increases all the more the more they are trampled. **AND NO OTHER** pain: that is, fury and pain that anyone might use against you. **WOULD NOT BE** complete sorrow: that is, sufficient and enough punishment. **THEN HE TURNED** to me with a better expression: with better lips: that is, with better words, which are formed in the mouth by the tongue, the teeth, and the lips. And this is the way of the wise: for he rebukes vice with grave bitterness, but in admonishing and teaching a man eager to know, he uses humane and loving words. **SAYING THAT** he was one of the seven kings who besieged: that is, who laid siege to Thebes. Laius, king of the Thebans, had a son named Oedipus, who according to the oracles was to kill his father; wherefore he gave him to servants to be killed. They, out of pity, granted him his life; and having pierced his feet with a willow-binding <note>original: *uincolo*</note>

---

they left him in the woods. Found by shepherds, he was given to Polybus, king of Corinth, and by him was raised as his own. Later, having reached a perfect age, he heard from the oracle of Apollo that in Phocis of Boeotia he would find his true father. He went therefore to Phocis and killed his father, not knowing him. There was at that time in Thebes a monster called the Sphinx, who proposed enigmas—that is, obscure sayings—with this condition: that whoever could not solve them should be killed; and whoever solved them should have as his wife Jocasta, queen of Thebes, then a widow by the death of Laius. And Oedipus solved the enigma, which was this: "What animal is it that first goes on four feet, then on two, and finally on three?" And Oedipus said this was man, who as an infant goes on all fours; then he goes on two feet; and finally in old age he goes on three feet because he supports himself with a staff. Therefore, having known how to solve the enigma, he deserved to be given the queen, who was Jocasta, as his wife; and he took her, not knowing she was his mother. By her he had two sons, Eteocles and Polynices. Finally, recognizing his father and his mother and the wickedness he had committed, he blinded himself and lived in darkness. After his death, discord arose between the sons because each wanted to rule. Finally, they agreed to rule in turns, each for his own year; and it falling to Eteocles first, Polynices, leaving his homeland to his brother for that year, arrived in Argos. From Adrastus, king of Argos, he was given the king's daughter as his wife. When the year ended, and Eteocles was unwilling to observe the pact, Adrastus, together with six other kings, went to attack Thebes. The kings were Adrastus, Polynices, Tydeus, Hippomedon, Amphiaraus, Parthenopaeus, and Capaneus. This last one was a scorner of all religion; he asserted that there was no God and that fear was what had induced men to believe there was a God. He trusted greatly in his own strength, for he was very large and robust; and in the battle fought at Thebes, he moved the walls by force; and shouting, he boasted that he would conquer the city in despite of the gods, and he provoked the Theban gods Hercules and Bacchus to battle. Then, being ashamed to have to fight with lesser gods, he invited Jove to battle. And Jove struck him with lightning and killed him.

---

"Now come behind me and watch that you do not yet
set your feet on the scorched sand;
but always keep your feet close to the wood."
In silence we came to where there gushes
out of the wood a little stream,
the redness of which still makes my hair stand on end.
Like the stream that comes out of the Bullicame <note>A hot sulfur spring near Viterbo, notorious in Dante's time.</note>
which the sinful women then divide among themselves;
so that stream flowed down across the bank.
Its bottom and both its slopes
were made of stone, as were the margins on the side;
whereby I perceived that the crossing was there.

<column-break/>

**NOW** they are near the end of the boiling sands: because they were approaching the place where a little stream comes out of the wood, from which all the infernal rivers are born. And for this reason, Virgil admonishes Dante that until they reach that river, he should not yet set his feet in the sand. And he shows that for all the space that remained, they went in silence, which signifies the contemplation of the matter. Virgil wants Dante to follow him, because in contemplation, sensuality and the lower reason must follow the higher reason. This higher reason admonishes him not to set his feet in the sand: that is, that his appetite should not enter into such concupiscence of such pride. But he should keep them in the wood, which is a solitary place and suitable for contemplation. Therefore, in the investigation of vices, the lower reason must follow the higher and not enter with appetite into the burning and concupiscence of those vices, but contemplate their wicked and harmful nature. **WHERE IT GUSHES:** that is, where it comes out. **A LITTLE** stream: which crossed that circle. **THE REDNESS OF WHICH** makes my hair stand on end: that is, gives me horror, because "capriccio" [shiver/horror] specifically signifies the head...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Canto XIV of Dante’s Inferno. Having previously described the violent punishments of the burning sands and the blasphemous giant Capaneus, the text now focuses on the red, boiling river that crosses the desert and introduces the allegorical figure of the "Old Man of Crete," who represents the history of human decline and the source of Hell's rivers.</meta>

<page-type>text</page-type>
<columns>2</columns>
<header>CANTO XIV.</header>
<page-num>79</page-num>

**Bristles:** This is when the hair stands up on the head. This happens due to cold, and such cold often comes from fear. He says that every time he remembers the boiling of this river, he is struck with horror. **JUST AS the Bullicame.** <note>The Bullicame is a famous natural hot spring near Viterbo, Italy, known for its sulfurous steam and boiling water.</note> He shows by comparison that this water was as boiling as that which comes out of the Bullicame of Viterbo: which then, after some distance, reaches the brothel, that is, the place where the harlots stay; and having already become lukewarm, it is divided among their dwellings, and they wash themselves with it. And it is a fitting comparison considering how it passes: because just as the water that comes out of the Bullicame runs through the dwellings of the harlots, so the water that comes out of Phlegethon <note>The river of fire or boiling blood in the Inferno.</note> runs through the sand where the sinful souls of the sodomites are punished. **SUCH THROUGH the sand.** It went down from the third circle, and stones made the bottom and the slopes, that is, the banks; and he clarifies better by saying the margins, that is, the edges. **WERE MADE of stone:** It does not entirely depart from the nature of water, because in some places water generates stone from itself, as we see happen at the river Elsa. <note>The Elsa river in Tuscany is known for its high mineral content, which can petrify objects.</note> **BECAUSE I perceived that the path was there.** Because it was easy to pass upon those stones; and allegorically understand that since we have withdrawn our desires from the aforementioned fires with solitude and patience, we come to a firmness and hardness so as not to slip back into vice. Nor without reason does he add that the water hardened into stone. Because through contemplating vice while following Virgil—that is, the intellect and moral doctrine—our burning greed is restrained, and it hardens like a stone and moves no more. It serves, then, the allegory: And as we said above, it does not depart entirely from the nature of water. And certainly, if we consider it with diligence, the poet has not written anything more notable up to this point: for in all the other circles he has described only the vice that is punished in that place, and with what kind of penalty it is punished. But here, returning to the beginning of the origin of the human generation, he shows what its progress has been and from whence every sin is born in us. But perhaps someone will wonder why he did not make such a description at the beginning of his work, or at the entrance to Hell. Since both the nature of things and true art require that before the writer commits to letters what he has proposed in his mind, he should always divide his entire invention into its principal parts, and then describe each with a certain and distinct order. For this reason, it seems to many that if the poet wished to express the different states of the human species and show the origin of vice within it—wishing to prove how vice guides us to Hell, wishing to distinguish the site of Hell and the rivers that run there—it would have been more convenient to place the fiction of this statue at the beginning: because although under an allegorical veil, it contains the division of the whole work. But the resolution of such a doubt will occur to our minds without much difficulty if it is known to us: that one thing is appropriate for the beginning of Hell, describing the site found by those who descend there; and another for the beginning of sin, speculating on where it draws its origin. Therefore, the poet, describing the site of Hell, showed it immediately from its beginning. Then, wishing to place the beginning not of the site and place of Hell, but the beginning—that is, of the vice—that shuts the human species in Hell, he judged it appropriate to defer the statue to the place where the proud against God are punished: because from here proceeds the origin of our sin; because nothing else drew the first man from the state of innocence and contaminated him with sin but pride, which led him to transgress the divine precept.

*Among all else that I have shown to you*
*since we entered through the gate*
*whose threshold is denied to no one,*
*Nothing was discerned by your eyes*
*as notable as the present stream,*
*which quenches all the flames above it.*
*These were the words of my leader;*
*wherefore I prayed that he grant me the food*
*for which he had granted me the desire.*
*In the middle of the sea lies a wasted land,*
*I said to him then, which is called Crete,*
*under whose king the world was once chaste.*
*A mountain is there, which once was glad*
*with waters and with leaves, and was called Ida;*
*now it is deserted like a forbidden thing.*
*Rhea chose it once for a trusted cradle*
*of her son; and to hide him better,*
*when he cried out, she had clamor made there.*
*Within the mountain stands a great old man,*
*who keeps his back turned toward Damietta*
*and looks at Rome as if it were his mirror.*
*His head is formed of fine gold,*
*and pure silver are the arms and the breast;*
*then he is of brass down to the fork.*
*From there downward he is all chosen iron,*
*save that the right foot is baked clay;*
*and he stands on that one more than the other.*
*Every part except the gold is broken*

<column-break/>

Virgil captures the greatest attention in this place by showing Dante that from the beginning of Hell until now, he had not seen a more notable thing. **WHOSE threshold is denied to no one.** Because, as Virgil says, the gate of Pluto <note>In this context, Pluto refers to the ruler of the underworld (Dis/Hades).</note> stands open day and night, whence it is easy to descend into Hell: because falling into vice is easy for everyone. **WHICH QUENCHES all the flames above it. These words.** Dante, moved by Virgil's words and becoming very eager and desirous to know—because this was the most notable thing—prays that he give him the food for which he has given him the craving, that is, the desire. Which means nothing other than that he should give him the knowledge and meaning of this marvelous thing for which he has made him desirous. And not without merit does he call such knowledge food and sustenance: for just as the body is nourished by the four elements of which it is composed, so the soul is nourished by the truth, which is the doctrine and the knowledge of things human and divine.

In these tercets written above, the author discerns with his own fiction the origin of the infernal rivers: and he imagines that in Mount Ida of Crete there is a cracked statue which drips tears; and these form a stream which, piercing the mountain, descends to Hell. **IN THE MIDDLE OF THE SEA:** that is, in the Mediterranean Sea, and in that which the Greeks call the Aegean Sea, and today by us is named the Archipelago. **LIES:** is placed. **A WASTED LAND called Crete.** He said "wasted" because for a long time now it has lacked many cities: for in ancient times they said it was Hecatopolis <note>original: "Ecatopolon"</note>, that is, of a hundred cities. But after it lost its sovereignty, it was wasted almost entirely. **CRETE** was in the earliest times called Ida; then it took its name from Crete, the daughter of one of the Curetes and wife of Hammon; and today it is called Candia. This has the Aegean Sea to the north and the African Sea to the south, which reaches the Egyptian Sea; and it is, in its length, one thousand three hundred stadia <note>A stadium was an ancient unit of length, roughly 185 meters.</note>; and eight stadia make a mile. The width is proportional to the length. Whence its circuit, according to Sosicrates, is five thousand stadia; according to Artemidorus, four thousand one hundred. Others describe it as larger. The highest mountain of this island is Ida, surrounded by three cities in the shape of a garland, and it is located almost in the middle of the island. Its circuit is six hundred stadia. This island was excellently governed by the laws of Rhadamanthus and Minos; and by their laws, being reduced to a civil and human way of living, it was adorned with a hundred lands; and for this, Homer calls it Hecatopolis <note>original: "hecatompoli"</note>. **UNDER THE KING the world was once chaste.** Under Saturn, who was king of Olympus and of Crete. **WAS ONCE the world...**

<summary>This page analyzes the transition to the myth of the "Old Man of Crete" (Veglio di Creta), explaining how human sin and historical decay serve as the source of Hell's rivers. It provides geographical and mythological context for Crete as the cradle of civilization and the starting point of humanity's moral decline.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante's Inferno, Canto XIV. It focuses on the origin of the infernal rivers (Acheron, Styx, Phlegethon, and Cocytus) through the allegory of the "Old Man of Crete," a monumental statue representing the history of human civilization and its moral decline.</meta>

<page-type>text</page-type>
<columns>2</columns>
<header>INFERNO.</header>

> ...from a crack that drips with tears:
> which, gathered, pierce this cavern.
> Their course rushes down into this valley:
> they form Acheron, Styx, and Phlegethon;
> then they go down through this narrow channel:
> until they reach where one can descend no more:
> they form Cocytus: and what that pool is like
> you shall see, therefore it is not told here.

<column-break/>

...chaste: because the poets imagine it so. The father of Saturn was Caelus <note>The Roman god of the Sky.</note> and the mother was Vesta, who signifies Earth. But those who write sacred history say he was a most powerful king; and that he gave the name of his father to the sky, and that of his mother to the earth, whereas previously they were called by other names. This name "Saturn" is sometimes understood as a man who, according to history, held his kingdom in great tranquility without homicides, without thefts, without adulteries, or other wickednesses. And for this reason, the poets imagine that in his time there was an "Age of Gold": because just as gold is pure and never rusts, so that age was pure from every vice. Sometimes we take Saturn to be the first of the seven planets, whose nature we will treat at length in the *Paradiso*. Sometimes Saturn signifies Time. Whence in Greek he is called *Cronos*, a name which, when the breathing mark is removed, derives from *chronos* <note>original: "chronos"</note> which means Time. This is why they created the fables that he devoured all his children except Jove, Juno, Neptune, and Pluto: because time consumes all things that are born. And "all things that arise must fall, and all things done grow old" <note>original: "Et omnia orta occidunt, et acta senescunt." A quote from the Roman historian Sallust.</note> except for the four elements; which, although they undergo constant mutation from one into another—because the subtler parts of a coarser element change into the nearby one. Thus, earth is converted into water, and water into air, and air into fire; and likewise, conversely, the coarser parts of the subtler elements are returned to the coarser forms, so that fire becomes air, and air water, and water earth. Nevertheless, nothing of the four elements perishes; rather, one changes into the other, and every thing generated and composed from them returns to its beginning when it perishes. Nor is a body ever consumed after death in such a way that it becomes nothing; but as it was composed of four elements, so in resolving it returns to them. Therefore, time devours everything except Jove (who is fire), Juno (who is air), Neptune (water), and Pluto (earth). And let this suffice for Saturn.

But add further, for a clearer understanding of this statue, that the excellent poets have divided the ages according to the nature of different metals. And the first, they say, was of gold in the time of Saturn: and by gold, they mean virtue and innocence. The second of silver, in which men began to degenerate from virtue just as silver does from gold. There follows the third of bronze, and the fourth of iron. **A MOUNTAIN** is there that once was joyful. Ida is a mountain in Crete; from whose name there is another mountain in Troy, which was called Ida by Teucer, who went from Crete to live in Troy. But this one in Crete was named thus after the nymph Ida. This mountain was once cultivated, and its forests and springs were maintained; now it is stripped of everything **LIKE A THING** conquered: that is, old. **RHEA CHOSE** it once as a faithful cradle. Rhea, the wife of Saturn, having given birth to Jove, did not give him to Saturn, who wanted to devour him as he had devoured the other children. Instead, she gave him a stone in his place, and hid Jove on Mount Ida; and because he was nurtured there, the poet calls it the cradle of Jove. *Cuna* means cradle, and it is a common word in the Latin language, but derived from the Greek because *kumi* means to lie down; and this is made so that little children may lie there. Therefore, he calls Ida the cradle of Jove because he lay and was nurtured there. **AND TO CONCEAL HIM** better when he cried, she had him make shouts: that is, noise and clamor so that the crying would not be heard. <note>This refers to the Curetes, mythical warriors who clashed their shields to drown out the infant god's cries.</note>

The poet wishes to describe the different states of the human species, and to show that all of them except the first were vicious; and that from those vices proceed all our misery and damnation, which is our Hell. And such a lesson, as a poet, he hides under a veiled and allegorical sense, imagining that on Mount Ida in Crete there is a statue composed of various metals, and from that statue the infernal rivers are born. And certainly, the genius of Dante was marvelous: because at once, imitating the statue that appeared in a vision to King Nebuchadnezzar, and the fiction created by excellent poets describing various ages under the figure of various metals, he introduces a third sense which fits his purpose. He places, therefore, a large statue of an old man on Mount Ida. And this statue turns its back to Damietta, which is a noble city in Egypt located on the Nile, and turns its face toward Rome. By this, he means Time, which began with the world and will end with the world. Time is nothing other than motion, which is the measure of the motion of the heavens and the stars. Therefore, before the creation of the world, there was no time, but only eternity, into which time then came. He imagines this statue as old and large because, among the things that have had a beginning and will have an end, almost nothing is older than time; and time is a great thing among mortal matters. But he does not simply place such a statue for time, because together with that, he intends to express the human generation, which is placed in this flux and course of time, and its different states. For which reason, this old man will be Time; he will be the human species. He will be, through the metals of which he is composed, the different states of it.

And he places such a statue in Crete for two respects: the first was because Crete is the seat of Saturn, who among the ancient poets (as we said in his fable) signifies Time. The second respect is that, understanding it as the human generation which inhabits this globe of the earth divided into three parts—Asia, Africa, and Europe—it is a fitting thing to have placed it in the center, and in that place which borders all three of these parts; and this is shown to be Crete. Furthermore, having to describe the different states of the human generation, although its beginning was in the first man placed in the paradise of delights <note>The Garden of Eden.</note>, and his first state of innocence was nowhere else but there, Dante nevertheless wished to hide this Christian truth under a poetic veil. He said the statue was in Crete because, according to the poets, the Golden Ages of Saturn were there, and the great observance of laws, which expresses innocence. Not without reason does he place it on a mountain, because a mountain signifies a heap of earth, to denote that he does not place it for particular men, but for their heap—that is, for the whole mass and the human species. To which also corresponds the name of this mountain, called Ida, because *idos* <note>original: "idos"</note> in Greek signifies "species" or "form" <note>The Greek word *eidos* (εἶδος).</note> and not a particular individual.

And that it turns its shoulders to Damietta and its face to Rome has a double allegorical sense. First, we can understand that it denotes the course of empires, which had its beginning in the eastern parts—not starting with the Assyrians, but with the Egyptians, who had Osiris and Bacchus and Hercules much earlier than Ninus, king of the Assyrians. Therefore, he placed Damietta, a very ancient city of Egypt; and from this beginning, passing through the Assyrians, Persians, Medes, and many other nations, it finally rested with the Romans. And therefore it turns its back to Egypt, as to an empire already passed, and its face to Rome, as to a present empire. For things passed are behind us, and those we see are present to us. The second sense is that by this he denotes that all things go toward death, and as soon as they are produced... [the statue is made of] four metals and one foot of clay. This is not unlike the statue of Nebuchadnezzar. King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon saw in a dream a very large statue, which watched him with a terrible aspect. Its head was of fine gold; its chest and arms of silver; the rest down to the legs of bronze; the legs were of iron; and the feet were partly iron and partly baked clay. And the statue stood in the sight of the king until a stone, cut from a mountain without hands, struck its feet and crushed them; and the baked clay, the iron, the bronze, the silver, and the gold were broken and crushed together, and all was...

<meta>catchword: por (all was carried away...)</meta>

<summary>This page explains the allegory of the "Old Man of Crete" (Vegghio di Creta), identifying it as a symbol of human history, time, and moral decline from the Golden Age to the present. The text draws parallels between Greek mythology (Saturn/Rhea) and the Biblical vision of Nebuchadnezzar to explain the source of Hell's rivers.</summary>
<keywords>Saturn, Chronos, Four Elements, Ages of Man, Mount Ida, Crete, Damietta, Rome, Nebuchadnezzar's Statue, Allegory of Time, Human Decline</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the "Old Man of Crete" from Canto XIV of Dante’s *Inferno*. Having described the statue’s physical appearance, the commentator now interprets its materials as a timeline of human history and the moral origin of Hell’s rivers.</meta>

<page-type>text</page-type>
<columns>2</columns>
<header>CANTO XIV.</header>

...carried away by the wind; and they found no place. And the stone that struck the statue became a great mountain. This statue signified the mutation of kingdoms: And the head of gold demonstrates the empire of King Nebuchadnezzar, which occupied almost all the eastern parts and was most rich. Two arms and a chest denote the empire of the Persians and the Medes: because at one time Cyrus reigned over the Persians and Darius over the Medes; in whose times the doctrines signified by silver were held in high prize, for silver is splendid and sonorous. The copper denotes the kingdom of the Macedonians and the Greeks: because in those times eloquence flourished, signified by copper, a very resonant metal. The iron demonstrated the empire of the Romans: who, by military virtue, occupied all the other empires. The earth <note>terracotta or clay</note> mixed with iron in the feet of the statue noted the civil discord in the Roman Republic: for just as baked earth never bonds well with iron, so in civil discord there is never a true conjunction between citizens. The stone cut from the mountain without hands is Christ born of Mary: who by excellence is equaled to the mountain; "without hands" means without human operation. This Christ changes all empires: But I will proceed no further in this interpretation, because it is not of the present work. Therefore I return to our poet: who with supreme genius, joining the making of this image with the ages distinguished by poets through various metals, forms a third allegory, reducing the fiction to a true and Christian sense. 

And he says that only the head of this statue was of gold, meaning by the head the beginning of human generation and the first parents who, for some space of time while they stayed in the garden of delights <note>Eden</note>, lived in a state of true innocence. Nor was any other time afterward ever truly innocent. Therefore only the head was of gold. Then, by the chest and by the arms of silver, he places the second age: which the poets say was under Jove <note>Jupiter</note>; and he understands this as that which succeeded Adam: which, although it was not entirely innocent, began to become clear and shining like silver through the multiplication of generation. Then follows the rest down to the fork all of copper: and this is the third age: which, through copper (a metal more sonorous than any other), signifies the fame acquired by finding various opinions and arts. The thighs and legs of iron, a hard and warlike thing, demonstrate the fourth age: in which, as avarice and ambition multiplied, various wars were born to usurp the riches and empires of others: as notably began with Ninus among the Assyrians; then his successors, Medes, Persians, Greeks, Macedonians, Carthaginians, and Romans. Then he adds that the right foot of the statue is of baked earth. This signifies the fragility of human things, and how weak is the foundation of empires and other goods subject to fortune and death. He said the "right foot": because the forces of empires, which are denoted by the right foot, consist entirely of earthly things, and are void of every virtue, both moral and intellectual. And there are few princes who approve the sentiment of Plato: who affirms that republics cannot be blessed unless they are administered by wise men; but all their trust is in the forces of the body and in riches, which are earthly things. 

The statue was broken in every part except for the gold. The break signifies vice: which has broken integrity and innocence; and thus has stained all the ages except for the state of innocence, which was without vice. And from this break were born the tears: which make the infernal rivers: that is, the human miseries which generate the pains that afflict us. For just as virtue makes man blessed and happy and joyful and glad; so vice makes us miserable and sad and full of mourning. And these tears pierce the cave that separates these parts where men live from hell. And certainly it is true that from our vices is born that sorrow which opens the way leading us to unhappiness. The poet, therefore, wanted to place the origin of the infernal rivers in that place where there is tyrannical pride, from which all other vices are born, which lead us to hell. These tears make the four rivers. First is Acheron: which signifies deprivation of joy <note>original: "Acheronte"</note>; because sin generates in us repentance and deprives us of gladness. From Acheron is born Styx: that is, sadness: because after the deprivation of joy comes sadness. And then follows Phlegethon, that is, heat: because he who is established in sorrow always feels in his mind a fire that boils through various cares. Whence Virgil: *And he fluctuates with a diverse tide of angers* <note>original: "Varioque irarum fluctuat aestu"</note>. And from Phlegethon the water descends to the bottom of hell and forms the pool of Cocytus. For from the deprivation of joy, and from sorrow, and from the burning of cares, is generated Cocytus: that is, lamentation: which signifies, as it were, a confirmed grief. And therefore he wishes it to pool in the final part of hell: because perpetual mourning places us in the depth of the abyss and holds us there in eternal misery.

<column-break/>

> "And I to him: 'If the present streamlet
> so derives from our world,
> why does it appear only at this rim?'
> And he to me: 'You know the place is round;
> and though you have come far,
> always descending to the left toward the bottom:
> You have not yet turned through the whole circle;
> therefore if something new appears to us,
> it should not bring wonder to your face.'
> And I then: 'Master, where are found
> Phlegethon and Lethe? For of one you are silent,
> and the other you say is formed of this rain.'
> 'In all your questions you certainly please me,'
> he replied, 'but the boiling of the red water
> should well have solved the one you ask.
> Lethe you shall see, but not in this pit;
> there where souls go to wash themselves
> when their repented guilt is removed.'
> Then he said: 'Now it is time to depart
> from the wood; see that you come behind me;
> the margins provide a path, for they are not scorched,
> and above them every vapor is extinguished.'"

<column-break/>

The meaning in brief is this: that Dante marvels that if this "streamlet"—that is, the little river, which he calls thus because *rigo* <term>rigo: to moisten or water</term> in Latin means to soak—derives from our world: why, having already descended so far, has he not seen it elsewhere than at this "rim": that is, at this extremity. *Viuagno* <term>viuagno: the selvage or hem of a cloth</term> signifies the edge of a cloth. And Virgil answers him: "You know the place is round," being divided by circles. And you, descending, have always come toward the left hand: therefore there can be something on the right hand that you have not yet seen. But how he has not yet turned through the whole circle was shown at the beginning of the work under the universal picture of the site of this hell.

---

Because Virgil made no mention above of either Phlegethon or Lethe: therefore Dante asks where these rivers are. And Virgil answers him that although he had not given a name above to the river that was boiling, nonetheless he could, by such boiling, understand that it was Phlegethon: because *phlego* <note>original: "phlego"</note> in Greek signifies to burn and to kindle. And he says Lethe is not in this pit: that is, in this depth of hell. But it is after Purgatory: for there he places two rivers on the left, Lethe, and on the right, Eunoe: of which we shall speak in the second canticle <note>The *Purgatorio*</note>.

<meta>This page continues the journey into the Seventh Circle of Hell, specifically focusing on the third ring where the "Violent against Nature" are punished. The previous page ended with fragmentary definitions of words like "pain," "fire," and "soul." <header>CANTO XV.</header>

# CANTO XV OF THE FIRST CANTICLE OF DANTE.

<columns>2</columns>

Now one of the hard margins carries us away,
and the steam of the stream casts shade above,
so that it saves the water and the dikes from the fire.
As the Flemings between Wissant and Bruges,
fearing the flood that rushes toward them,
make the bulwark so that the sea may be repelled;
And as the Paduans along the Brenta,
to defend their villas and their castles,
before Carinthia <note>Original: "chiarentana"; referring to the mountains in the Eastern Alps where the snows melt to feed the Brenta river.</note> feels the heat:
In such a likeness were these [dikes] made,
although not so high nor so thick,
regardless of who the master was that made them.

<column-break/>

In this fifteenth canto, together with the sixteenth, the poet deals with those violent against nature <note>A reference to "sodomy" in the medieval classification of sins.</note>. In the beginning he describes what his path was and the souls he found, and first he mentions Sir Brunetto Latini. They were walking, therefore, upon one of the two margins: that is, the two banks of the river. They are called HARD because they were made of stone. And he shows that the heat of that stream was so great that such smoke rose from it that it "shadowed" <note>Original: "aduggiaua"; to cast a stifling or darkening shade.</note>—that is, it darkened the air above. And it was so thick that it extinguished the flames that rained down; this is a natural phenomenon, that smoke should extinguish flame. For if one places a candle above smoke, it goes out; this occurs because smoke drives away the air, without which a flame cannot live, for it lacks its exhalation. Therefore they could pass safely, as no flames rained upon the dikes. Thus it is true according to physical reason that smoke extinguishes flames. But it also serves the allegory, where we must remember that always—both in this poet and in Virgil—we have used "water" to represent appetite <note>The commentator explains "appetite" here as human desire or sensory impulse.</note>. Therefore, using the river to represent the appetite—not of the sinner, but of the observer of the evil nature of sin—is a fitting thing:

<columns>1</columns>

that from such water a vapor should rise to extinguish the flames. For just as in physical waters a cold and humid vapor rises, which generates clouds that shade us against the heat of the sun and create rain that puts out fire, so too from the appetite of the observer of vice (because he follows reason) there arises an obstacle against the fires of concupiscence. Thus the river (the appetite) and the hard dikes (the firm purpose of the mind) are not harmed by such flames. AS THE FLEMINGS between Wissant and Bruges: these are two cities in Flanders located on the shores of the Ocean sea, which lies between England and Flanders. In those places, the ocean moves from east to west twice in twenty-four hours and returns just as many times; in its movement, it leaves its place and enters into the land. Albertus Magnus <note>A famous 13th-century philosopher and scientist.</note> states in his book *On the Causes of the Properties of the Elements* that although all planets produce effects in lower bodies, the sun and moon are the most powerful, both because of the quantity of light and because of the moon's proximity to the earth. Hence, it rules the moisture of lower bodies, and through the shared nature of earth and water, it moves all things in which earth and water predominate. And the sun, because it is the source of life-giving heat, makes humors boil up, for humor naturally evaporates toward the rising heat. Hence the Egyptians say the sun drew up moisture as food for the stars. Nevertheless, the seas have different motions. Some do not move, like the Pisan and Genoese seas. Some grow from the new moon until the full moon and decrease until the next new moon. Some, in the space of twenty-four hours, rise twice and fall twice, such as the Persian Gulf, the Indian Sea, and all the islands between them; and the sea between Constantinople and Venice; and that between England and Flanders and Germany, although they differ greatly in being more or less intense. There are four points in the sky: one is the eastern horizon when a star is born and rises in our hemisphere. The second is when it has climbed to the middle of the sky at the zenith of our heads, called the "angle of the mid-heaven." The third is when it arrives at the western horizon and descends into the other hemisphere. The fourth is when it is opposite our zenith, the angle of the middle of the earth and the night. Thus, when the moon arrives in the east, the sea rises; when it is in the middle of the sky, it decreases and recedes; when it is in the west, it grows and rises again; when it reaches the angle of the middle of the earth, it decreases. Thus, the Flemings have made dikes to hold back the flood <note>Original: "fiotto"; a term used by sailors for the tide or surge.</note> so that it does not spread further. And Albertus Magnus says that over a long period of time, such dikes have caused the sea to move away from Bruges. THE BULWARK: The defense. AND AS the Paduans along the Brenta: the Brenta is a river in Padua which originates in the Carinthia <note>Original: "chiaretana"</note> mountains in the Alps, which divide Italy from Germany. These are cold and snowy places where the snow does not melt until the heat arrives, and then the Brenta grows marvelously. When it reaches the plains, it would flood many villages if there were no dikes. This they do BEFORE Carinthia feels the heat: that is, before the snows of Carinthia melt from the warmth.

<columns>2</columns>

Already we were so far from the wood
that I would not have seen where it was,
even if I had turned myself backward:
When we encountered a troop of souls
who were coming along the dike, and each
looked at us as one is wont at evening
To look at another under a new moon;
and toward us they sharpened their brows
as an old tailor does at the needle's eye.
Thus eyed by such a family,
I was recognized by one who took me
by the hem and cried, "What a marvel!"

<column-break/>

We were already so far from the wood (of which we spoke in Canto XIII) that even if I had turned back, I would not have seen it. This denotes that the nature of the vice discussed here is different from that punished in the wood, and requires a different consideration. WHEN WE ENCOUNTERED A TROOP OF SOULS: this encounter denotes the contemplation of this vice. The "troop" <note>Original: "fchiera"</note> denotes the great number of those who are stained by such beastly wickedness. Each of these souls looked at us as one looks at another when it has already become night and the moon is new, because at that time the evening is not entirely without light, but there is so little light that one cannot discern another unless looking with great diligence. This imitates Virgil where he says: "Like a journey in the woods under the flickering moon's unkind light, when Jove has buried the sky in shadow, and black night has stolen the color from things" <note>Original Latin: "Quale per incertam lunam sub luce maligna Est iter in siluis: ubi celum condidit umbra Iuppiter : & rebus nox abstulit atra colorem." From Aeneid, Book VI.</note>. Always, the obscurity and the lack of light in Hell denotes the ignorance and blindness of the mind from which every vice proceeds. THEY SHARPENED THEIR BROWS: Whoever...

<meta>The text cuts off here with the catchword "Chi" (Whoever), which will begin the next page's explanation of the souls' intense scrutiny of Dante.</meta>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the Seventh Circle of Hell. Having established the setting of the scorched dikes along the Phlegethon, the narrative now introduces the encounter between Dante and his former mentor, Brunetto Latini.</meta>

->**INFERNO**<-

> And I, when he stretched his arm toward me,
> fixed my eyes upon his scorched appearance,
> so that his burnt face did not prevent
> my intellect from recognizing him;
> and bending my face down to his,
> I replied: "Are you here, Ser Brunetto?"
> And he: "My son, let it not displease you
> if Brunetto Latini turns back with you a little
> and lets the file of souls go on."

Ser Brunetto was greatly disfigured: and nonetheless Dante recognized him. He wishes to denote nothing else by this except that men adorned with some excellent virtue—as this man was, even though he had some vice in him—nevertheless, their fame remains and makes them known. For he is not as Juvenal says: "A monster redeemed from his vices by no virtue." <note>original Latin: "Monstrum nulla virtute redemptum a vitiis."</note> Ser Brunetto Latini was a Florentine and a very universal man in many liberal arts, especially in physics and metaphysics. He wrote a book called the *Tesoretto* <note>The "Little Treasure," an allegorical poem in Italian.</note>. In the art of the notary, he surpassed all others; and in that profession, having been accused of falsity, he chose to be condemned rather than confess to an error. Out of such disdain, he went to live in Paris, and there he wrote another book in the French language which he called the *Tresor* <note>The "Treasure," an encyclopedic work.</note>. But because he was stained with the vice that is punished here <note>The sin of sodomy.</note>, the poet feigns finding him in this place. They say he was an excellent mathematician <note>In the medieval context, this included astronomy and astrology.</note>; and having seen the hour of Dante's birth, he predicted how he would arrive at the highest degree of learning.

> I said to him: "I pray you as much as I can,
> and if you wish that I sit with you,
> I will do it, if it pleases him with whom I go."
> "O son," he said, "whoever of this flock
> stops for a moment, then lies for a hundred years
> without fanning himself when the fire strikes him.
> Therefore go on; I will come at your hems,
> and then I will rejoin my troop,
> which goes weeping for its eternal losses."
> I did not dare descend from the path
> to walk level with him, but I kept my head bowed,
> like a man who walks reverently.
> And he began: "What fortune or destiny
> leads you down here before your final day,
> and who is he who shows you the way?"
> "Up there above, in the serene life,"
> I replied to him, "I lost myself in a valley,
> before my age was full.
> Just yesterday morning I turned my back on it;
> this one appeared to me as I was returning to it,
> and he leads me back home along this path."

<column-break/>

...old: and when one wishes to look at a minute thing because their sight is weak, they sharpen their brows. The visual spirits failing—hindered either by thickness or some other cause when they cannot see well—force us to sharpen our brows: because thus we restrict the visual power into a smaller space, which, being thus united, has more strength. And as Aristotle says in the *Problems* <note>original: "problemati"; referring to the Aristotelian "Physica" or "Problemata."</note>, crossbowmen do the same when they take aim. **ARE YOU HERE** Ser Brunetto: The poet does not ask what he sees, but rather he marvels that he is there. And certainly it seems no small marvel that a man adorned with such virtue and learning should let himself slip into such a stain. Furthermore, he shows that it was with difficulty that he could recognize these souls, being so badly burned by the fire. This denotes allegorically that the heat of beastly cupidity so spoils the form of the face that the man is no longer recognized; that is, it removes every image of a human and makes them similar to beasts.

He prays Ser Brunetto to stop, and Brunetto gives the reason why he cannot sit. **O SON**: so he calls him because he was his disciple. **WHOEVER** Of this flock stops. This is an invention taken from Virgil and translated into another sense; Virgil says that the bodies of those who are not buried wait a hundred years before Charon carries them across the river. But the poet feigns that whoever stops in this circle must then lie for a hundred years. This can be understood as moving from a lesser sin into a greater one; for since those here are the violent against nature, disobeying divine law, by stopping when they are commanded to move, they become violent against God. And thus it is fitting that they lie still like those others <note>Those who are violent against God, the blasphemers, are punished by lying still on the sand.</note>. And allegorically we understand that whoever stops—that is, becomes more firmly habituated in sin—has no defense against such burning cupidity. **WHAT FORTUNE** or destiny: we have spoken of fortune and destiny (or fate) above. It seems he wishes to say: what happy celestial influence or what divine providence. Since Ser Brunetto was an astrologer and a theologian, he mentions both. For celestial influence does not contradict divine providence, as we shall demonstrate in the *Paradiso*. In short, he asks two things: how he arrived in that place, and who did it. And Dante responds as follows: **IN THE SERENE LIFE**: that is, in this present life, which, in comparison to the celestial life, is miserable and calamitous, but in comparison to the infernal life—where there is never rest from pain nor place for penitence—is happy and blessed. **I LOST MYSELF** in that valley. Of this valley and the lost path and the help of Virgil, we spoke at length in the first canto. **BEFORE MY AGE WAS FULL**: that is, perfect. The ages of human life, as we have already said, are divided by the number seven: in the first seven years, infancy ends. In the second, which reaches fourteen, childhood <note>original: "pueritia"</note> ends. The third age, which is adolescence, goes until twenty-one. The fourth, which is youth, contains two septenaries and goes to thirty-five. Two more septenaries, which reach forty-nine, make the fifth age, which is the virile age. Aristotle holds that this age is fit for the government of the republic because it is strong in spirit and body, and is mature and full and perfect. Therefore, the poet was lost before he reached this age; it is the age that has reached perfection, which the first four—infancy, childhood, adolescence, and youth—had not yet reached. In that age, life stays still and does not suffer diminution, as do the other two that follow: namely, old age, which with two septenaries reaches sixty-three and begins to diminish vigor somewhat. And from that time on is the decrepit age, in which there is a great and manifest diminution of strength. **JUST YESTERDAY MORNING** I turned my back on it. By this he shows it was night in Hell, because the day was consumed in defending himself from the beasts and in the arrival of Virgil; and "yesterday morning" was the morning of Good Friday. **I TURNED MY BACK** on it: when he wished to climb the mountain already illuminated by the sun. But hindered by the three beasts, he would have returned into the valley if Virgil had not come to his aid. But we have shown this more extensively at the beginning of the description of the entire infernal site. And he rightly led Ser Brunetto to ask such a question so that, through the response, he might better explain in this place what the first canto had left obscure. **THIS ONE APPEARED TO ME**. This is the answer to the second question. "This one appeared" while pointing to Virgil. **RETURNING** I into that: when, pushed back down by the three beasts, I was returning to the valley from which I had emerged. **AND LEADS ME BACK** home: that is, to the house. Our house and fatherland is Heaven; because in this world we have no permanent city, but we are on a pilgrimage and a continuous journey. And by taking the good way, we return to our house where we were [created]...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante's *Inferno*, Canto XV. The previous page concluded with Virgil being described as the "illuminated intellect" who guides the soul. This page transitions into the specific prophecy given by Brunetto Latini to Dante regarding his future exile and the corrupt nature of the Florentine people.</meta>

# CANTO XV.

"And he to me: 'If you follow your star,
you cannot fail to reach the glorious port,
if I observed rightly in the lovely life;
And had I not died so prematurely,
seeing heaven so gracious to you,
I would have given comfort to your work.
But that ungrateful and malignant people
who descended from Fiesole of old,
and still holds to the mountain and the rock,
Will become your enemy for your good deeds;
and it is right, for among the sour sorbs
it is unfitting for the sweet fig to bear fruit.
Old fame in the world calls them blind,
a people greedy, envious, and proud;
from their customs see that you cleanse yourself.
Your fortune reserves such honor for you
that one side and the other will have hunger
for you; but let the grass be far from the goat.
Let the Fiesolan beasts make fodder
of their own seed, and let them not spoil the plant,
if any still rises in their dung,
In which the holy seed is revived
of those Romans who remained there when
the nest of such malice was made.'"

<column-break/>

...created. And by taking the evil path, we ruin ourselves down into the depths of hell. The true way to return to heaven is the contemplation of vices to flee them, and of virtues to follow them. Therefore, he rightly said that through this path—that is, through this way of contemplation—Virgil, which is to say the intellect illuminated by true doctrine, leads him back to the home and eternal fatherland.

This is the second principal part of this canto, in which Ser Brunetto responds to Dante. First, he praises him and predicts what is to come for him. Afterward, he uses satire against the Florentine people, and finally, he names those who are with him in this circle.

**IF YOU FOLLOW YOUR STAR.** As an astrologer, he shows that the stars promise him good fortune if he follows them. In this, he observes excellent moderation: for he wishes to suggest that influence comes from the heavens—which inclines us—but not from necessity. He informs us that it is in our power to follow or not follow; in this way, he reserves power for the stars without taking away <term>Free Will</term> <note>The theological concept that humans choose their actions rather than being strictly predestined.</note>.

**YOU CANNOT FAIL TO REACH THE GLORIOUS PORT.** Glory is clear and illustrious fame accompanied by praise. Just as sailors, if they follow the star well, are guided safely to port, so you, if you follow this happy influence, will arrive at the port of honor. For you receive such doctrine and eloquence from the heavens that if you labor in writing, you will acquire immortal fame.

**IF I OBSERVED RIGHTLY** in the lovely life. It is difficult in Hell to have knowledge of our future things except through conjecture, astrology, or revelations. But the blessed see the future because they look into that mirror where everything is present. Whence Saint Gregory says: "What is there he does not see, who sees Him who sees all things?" <note>original Latin: "Quid est quod non uideat qui uidet uidentem omnia"</note>. Therefore, he shows that while he lived, he knew of Dante's future glory through his knowledge of astrology. He adds that if he did not speak of it then and did not comfort him in continuing the work, it was because death occupied him.

**BUT THAT** ungrateful people. Our poet is to be excused if, in shaming his homeland, he exceeds the bounds of that modesty which ought to be in a philosopher and theologian. He forgets the reverence and piety which every citizen ought to have for his republic, because having been—with great injustice—deprived of honors, dignity, patrimony, and homeland, and finally relegated to a harsh exile, he could not restrain himself against such a fresh injury. Truly, it would have been more the duty of his wisdom to speak more modestly. There were long controversies between the Fiesolans and Florentines, not without damage to both peoples. Finally, the Florentines conquered Fiesole and destroyed it, uniting their republic with the Fiesolans. It was destroyed in the time of the first Emperor Henry <note>Henry I, though Landino may be conflating historical events regarding the early medieval conflicts.</note>.

**WHO DESCENDED** from Fiesole of old. Because the Sullan soldiers, who were sent to the new colony, inhabited Fiesole. Hating the harshness of that mountain, they descended to the nearby plain and built Florence. For this reason, he said "of old," meaning from the beginning—as if to say, at the first building of the city.

**AND STILL HOLDS** to the mountain and the rock. <term>Macigno</term> <note>A specific type of grey sandstone common in the hills around Florence.</note> is a species of stone which is quarried from the mountain of Fiesole for all the buildings of Florence. Therefore, they "hold to the mountain," meaning they are wild, and "to the rock," meaning they are hard and harsh like that stone. Some say that by "the rock" he means envy, because sandstone is livid and dry.

**WILL BECOME YOUR ENEMY** for your good deeds. This proves the hardness of the people. For just as one is soft and flexible who takes compassion even on those who do not deserve it, conversely, he is hard and inhuman who persecutes those who deserve reward. **WILL BECOME YOUR ENEMY.** The cause increases the perceived hardness. For if one is hard who becomes an enemy after being injured, he is even harder who has not been injured, but rather benefited.

**AMONG THE** sour sorbs. "Lazo" in the Florentine tongue signifies a flavor that is both harsh and very restrictive, such as is found especially in the fruit of the <term>sorb</term> <note>The service-apple, known for being extremely tart until overripe.</note>. Physicians call this "pontic." Therefore, by metaphor, he calls the cruelty of the people "sorb" and the innocence and humanity of the poet the "fig." According to Galen, flavors come from heat, cold, or a mixture of the two. From heat, which is of a thinner substance—like pepper—comes a sharp flavor. From that which has a thicker substance, bitterness is born. But if it is in the middle between these two extremes, it produces "false" flavor. In a cold thing of thin substance, it is vinegary. From thick substance comes the "pontic" flavor. From the medium comes the "styptic" flavor—dry and restrictive. But in a temperate thing, if it is thin, it makes an oily flavor; if thick, sweet; if medium, insipid and dull. This is what Galen writes, with whom Avicenna agrees on the first eight flavors. But regarding the ninth—the insipid—he says it is not a flavor. Averroes maintains that just as white and black proceed sometimes from heat and sometimes from cold, so the bitter and the sweet are easily found in both these contraries. For we see some apples: though they are warm, they are nonetheless bitter when tart and sweet when ripe. And some are cold by nature, and nonetheless sweet when ripe. "But it is not for us to settle such great disputes among them" <note>original Latin: "Non nostrum inter hos tantas componere lites," a quote from Virgil's third Eclogue.</note>. Therefore, I return to the text that follows.

**OLD FAME** in the world calls them blind. Why the Florentines are called blind, I find nothing authentic in any scripture. Nor is it fitting, because this people is sharp and ingenious. Unless it is this story, which Boccaccio also records: The Pisans once went with such a large fleet to the conquest of the island of Majorca (once called Baleares) that their city remained almost without guards. Because they were very friendly with the Florentines in those times, they requested that someone be sent to guard Pisa until they returned, for they feared the impetus of the Lucchese, who were preparing an army against them. It seemed an ignominious thing to leave the prize. Therefore, our people guarded it with faith and diligence. The Pisans returned victorious and brought back rich prey from the conquered island, including two noble spoils: the doors of a very ornate temple and two columns of porphyry. Wishing to give one of these two things to the Florentines as a gift, and estimating that they would choose the columns, moved by envy, they tarnished them with fire and broke them, and after...

# INFERNO

...they dressed them in rose-colored cloth: The Florentines, not suspecting such fraud, took them; they did not notice the defect until they had already been brought to Florence and uncovered. Therefore, the Florentines were called "blind" for such inadvertence; and the Pisans, for having deceived their equal friends who had guarded their city with such faith, were called "traitors." <note>This refers to a medieval legend where the Pisans gave the Florentines two porphyry columns that had been dulled by fire, covering them in red cloth to hide the damage.</note> **YOUR FORTUNE:** your happiness. **SO MUCH HONOR:** Such fame for your learning **THAT EITHER** side: both the Whites and Blacks of Florence <note>The rival political factions whose conflict led to Dante's exile.</note>. As if to say: although you have been exiled by the factions, nonetheless both sides will desire you. **BUT FAR** from the goat be the grass. As if to say that your wicked citizens will not enjoy your teaching. **LET THE** Fiesolan beasts make fodder of their own seed. This refers to what he said above: that he descended from Fiesole of old. And he truly calls the ungrateful citizens "beasts"; and "to make fodder" means to take the grain and make a bed of it for the beasts. Since "fodder" in Latin <note>original: "strame"</note> signifies something beaten down and spread on the ground. And through this metaphor, he wants to show that the Florentine people of his seed—that is, those who descend from them (since a son is the seed of the father)—**MAKE FODDER:** that is, they despise him and hold him as a vile thing, like straw thrown under beasts. **AND DO NOT** spoil the plant if any still rises in their dung: This is another metaphor, but it reduces to the same meaning; and he calls the vicious people "dung." And because even from them someone distinguished and virtuous is born, he calls him a "plant" rising from such dung. And he shows that such a plant is not spoiled by the people because his virtues are not honored. **IN WHICH RUINS** the holy seed of those Romans. As if to say the Florentine people were born of Roman men, virtuous and just; but such a seed has degenerated, just as when grain is sown in the Alps and degenerates into rye. **WAS MADE** the nest: that is, Florence, which he calls the nest of every vice.

"If all my prayer were fulfilled,"
I answered him, "you would not yet be
placed in banishment from human nature;
For in my mind is fixed, and now pierces me,
the dear and good paternal image
of you, when in the world from hour to hour
You taught me how man makes himself eternal;
and how much I cherish it while I live
it is fitting that it be discerned in my life.
What you narrate of my course, I write down,
and keep it to be glossed with another text
by a lady who will know how, if I reach her.
This much I wish to be made manifest to you:
so long as my conscience does not chide me,
I am ready for Fortune as she wills.
Such a pledge <note>original: "arra"</note> is not new to my ears;
therefore let Fortune turn her wheel
as she pleases, and the peasant his hoe."

My master then upon his right
cheek turned back and looked at me;
then he said: "He listens well who notes it."

Nor nonetheless talking did I go

<column-break/>

**D**ante responds that if everything he asked for were granted, he would not be "placed in banishment from human nature"—that is, he would still be alive. For man is a conjunction of soul and body. **PATERNAL IMAGE:** It brings passion to my mind, your death, when I remember that you loved me with paternal affection and showed me the way and the method by which man "makes himself eternal"—that is, makes himself eternal and immortal through fame. And **HOW MUCH** I cherish it while I live will be "discerned"—that is, it will be distinguished and known in my tongue. As if to say: I will always name you with honor. Afterward, he adds that he writes down—as if committing to memory—what he has heard from him; but he keeps it to be "glossed"—that is, to be interpreted and declared by Beatrice together with "another text"—that is, with what Farinata told him <note>Farinata degli Uberti, who previously prophesied Dante's exile in Canto X.</note>. Whose words were these: *“But the flame of the lady who reigns here shall not be rekindled fifty times before you shall know how much that art weighs.”* In short, he concludes that he saves the words of Ser Brunetto and those of Messer Farinata to have them explained by Beatrice; and he does this by the precepts of Virgil, who told him: *“Let your mind preserve what you have heard against yourself,”* that wise one commanded me; *“and now attend here,”* and he pointed his finger. *“When you are before the sweet ray of her whose beautiful eye sees everything, from her you shall know the journey of your life.”* This is in the tenth canto. And by this, we understand that the intellect of the learned warns that although astrologers or other diviners predict something for us, nonetheless we should believe only as much as theology (represented by Beatrice) dictates to us. **IF I REACH HER.** He spoke with a condition so as not to appear arrogant, because it is a great thing to be able to reach Beatrice. Nor are our strengths sufficient without divine grace.

Afterward, he responds that he is ready to yield to Fortune insofar as his conscience does not chide him. **CONSCIENCE** is the knowledge of oneself, and it can be for good or for evil. But when it is for good, it makes the mind contented and quiet. Hence the Apostle [Paul says]: "Our joy is our conscience" <note>original: "Gaudium nostrum est conscientia nostra"</note>. And certainly, nothing else can be our joy but our conscience. And when it is for evil, it disturbs and afflicts us. Hence Juvenal: "Night and day he carries his witness in his breast," as the ancient Pythia responded to a certain Spartan <note>original: "Nocte dieque suum gestare in pectore testem..."</note>. He concludes, therefore, that he is ready to support every adverse fortune and yield to it in all things, except in those in which his conscience would remorse him because they were not honest. **NOT NEW** to my eyes is such a pledge <note>original: "arra"</note>. This demonstrates what all noble philosophers concede: that the premeditation of adverse events prepares us to bear them more easily when they come. Hence Petrarch: "A wound foreseen hurts much less." A "pledge" <note>original: "arra"</note> is a demonstration of a sale. And "the wheel as she pleases": as if to say, whether she puts me at the bottom or the top, I will always be a rigid guardian of virtue. Nor can happy fortune make me elated or proud, nor adverse fortune make me so vile that I depart from the true rule of living. And certainly, the wise man goes "By the weapons of righteousness on the right and on the left" <note>original: "Per arma iustitię a dextris & a sinistris"</note>. **THE PEASANT HIS HOE.** As if to say: let every thing do its office, and I will persevere in mine.

**V**irgil turned to the right: that is, the intellect, which always goes to the right, turned to Dante (the lower reason) and said: **HE LISTENS WELL:** As if to say, he makes good use of it who notes it. And by this, he means that the best sentiments in speech should be put into practice when the need arises. And one should not do like many who are philosophers in words but not in deeds. Because moral philosophy consists in action and not in doctrine.

moral philosophy consists in action and not in doctrine.
