# CANTO XV.

...with Sir Brunetto and I ask who are
your companions and the most noted and most high:
And he to me: "To know of some is good;
of the others it is laudable for us to be silent,
for the time would be too short for such speech."
In summary, know that all were clerics
and great men of letters and of great fame,
soiled in the world by the same sin.
Priscian goes with that wretched crowd,
and Francesco d'Accorso you can also see there;
and if you had a craving for such scurf,
you could have seen the one who by the Servant of Servants <note>A traditional title for the Pope, here referring to Boniface VIII or Nicholas III.</note>
was transferred from the Arno to the Bacchiglione, <note>From the bishopric of Florence to that of Vicenza.</note>
where he left his ill-stretched nerves. <note>A reference to his death or his physical state due to his vices.</note>
I would say more, but my speech and my stay
cannot be longer: for I see
new smoke rising there from the sand.
People are coming with whom I must not be;
let my *Treasure* be recommended to you,
in which I still live: and I ask for no more.

Then he turned back and seemed like those
who run for the green mantle at Verona
across the fields: and he seemed like one of those
who wins, and not like the one who loses.

<column-break/>

...being stained by such a vice. Nevertheless, they were of such learning that they deserve fame. And first he says that all were clerics: meaning almost the majority of them. And there are also men of letters. He places these two classes of men together because, since they live with great reputation and cannot easily mix with women, they fall into such vice more than others. Then he names Priscian. He was from Caesarea in Cappadocia, a man highly practiced in philosophy, and he came to Rome. At the request of Julian the Apostate—being an apostate himself—he wrote most elegantly fifteen books of grammar. The first thirteen are called *Priscianus Major*, where he treats all parts of speech. The last two are *Priscianus Minor*, treating construction. It is not found in any reading that Priscian was actually stained by such a vice; but I believe that just as the poet placed Cato in Purgatory for the sake of liberty, so in this place he placed Priscian to represent every grammarian. Because such men are commonly stained by having a wealth of youths around them, he places him here. Francesco was a most notable legal scholar, the son of that Accorso of Florence who wrote the glosses to the laws which are written together with the text. **BY THE SERVANT OF SERVANTS:** By the Pope, a title found by Pope Gregory I out of humility. **WAS TRANSFERRED FROM THE ARNO to the Bacchiglione:** Messer Andrea de' Mozzi was the Bishop of Florence; because he had very little prudence and was entirely "without salt" <note>An idiom meaning lacking in wisdom or wit.</note> and a dishonest sodomite, Messer Tommaso Cavalcanti, his brother, took care to distance him from himself. He was transferred by Pope Nicholas Orsini <note>Pope Nicholas III.</note> to the bishopric of Vicenza. Therefore, because the Arno river passes through the middle of Florence and the Bacchiglione runs along the walls of Vicenza, he uses the rivers to represent the cities. This man, dying in Vicenza, left his body there. **THE ILL-STRETCHED:** that is, extended nerves; because he was almost contracted by gout. Or truly he means something obscene and bestial, and calls it "ill" because he exercised it against nature. **People with whom I must not be:** Here he denotes that although throughout this circle those who sinned against nature are punished, nevertheless there are various species of such sin—male with male, or female with female—which Saint Paul demonstrates in his Letter to the Romans <note>original: "Paolo ad Romanos"</note>. Therefore he says that those he now sees are not of his flock. **LET MY TREASURE BE RECOMMENDED:** We said above that Sir Brunetto wrote two works. The first in the Florentine language and in verse, in which he treats the customs of men, the accidents and mutations of fortune, and the human state; he titled it the *Tesoretto* (Little Treasure). The other is larger and he calls it the *Treasure* (*Li Livres dou Trésor*); it is written in the French language and in prose, divided into three books. The first is almost a chronicle of the times and of things done in the Old and New Testaments, the kingdoms of the gentiles, the prophets, the apostles, the adoption of the Church, and the Roman Empire translated from the Greeks to the French and Germans. It also treats the elements, the site of regions, and animals. In the second he treats moral philosophy. In the third, rhetorical precepts, and he writes of the administration of the city. He calls the first "common currency," the second "precious stones," and the third "purest gold." According to some others, the work called *The Keys to the Treasure* is also his. **IN WHICH I LIVE:** A damned man should not ask for anything pertaining to the body, because being deprived of corporal life, such things are of no use to him. Nor anything pertaining to the soul, because for the damned there is no redemption. It remained, therefore, that he should seek for his fame to endure. This could happen if his book did not perish, and for this reason he recommends it to Dante. For when the learned praise a book, they give it a reputation; and books with a reputation are copied by many, and in this way, they live.

### CANTO XVI OF THE FIRST CANTICLE OF DANTE.

<margin>g.</margin> I was already in a place where the boom was heard
of the water falling into the next circle,
similar to the hum that beehives make: <note>The original "larme" is interpreted by the commentator as "arnie" (beehives).</note>
When three shades departed together,
running from a troop that was passing
under the rain of the harsh torture.
They came toward us, and each one cried out:
"Stop, you who by your dress seem
to be someone from our wicked land."

Ah me, what wounds I saw on their limbs,
recent and old, branded by the flames!
It still grieves me just to remember it.
At their cries, my teacher turned
his face toward me and said: "Wait now;
to these, one should be courteous.
And if it were not for the fire that shoots
the nature of the place, I would say
that haste would better suit you than them."

And they began, as we stopped,
the old cry <note>original: "ei", an exclamation of grief or "alas"</note>; and when they reached us,
they all three formed a wheel.
Just as champions are wont to do, naked and oiled,
watching for their grip and their advantage,
before they are struck and poked between them;
Thus rotating, each one directed his face 
toward me, so that the neck made 
a continuous journey contrary to the feet.

Who, like the gladiators in the theater, moved about: Thus these three circled around Dante. THE CHAMPIONS. This word in the Tuscan language means great and strong: But perhaps it is better in this place to understand it as referring to the <term>palestra: a school for wrestling and athletics</term>, that is, the game of the arms. The ancients performed many games in theaters: among which was the game of the arms called *palestra*, in which strong and trained men stripped themselves and strove to make such a grip on one another that they could throw him to the ground. These stood naked so as not to be held by clothes: and they oiled themselves so that when they were caught by the adversary, they could escape his hands like slippery eels. Hence Virgil <note>original: "Exercent patrias oleo nitete palestras."</note> <insert>They practice their ancestral wrestling matches, shining with oil.</insert> These went around the theater one after another, thinking of how they could embrace the adversary to their advantage: and having embraced, they then struggled and pushed and struck each other to the ground; and this is what is signified by saying "struck and poked." THUS ROTATING. In a similar way, circling around, these three souls went forward with steps, and always turned their necks backward toward Dante. Thus the neck made a journey contrary to that of the feet. And it is a fitting thing that in a man who proceeds in such a vice, the foot which moves for greed goes forward and pulls toward lust; and the neck twists the head backward where reason is, because reason flees such wickedness. Some want to express by this circling the nature of the vice that is punished here. Because just as a circle has no natural beginning or end, so this vice has no natural beginning or end.

"And if the misery of this soft place
renders us and our prayers despicable,"
began one, "despite our grim and flayed appearance,
let our fame bend your soul
to tell us who you are, who with living feet
tread so securely through Hell.
This one whose footprints you see me tread,
even though he goes naked and skinless..."

<column-break/>

Although the canto has changed, the poet nevertheless still treats the same material that he treated in the previous 15th canto. He describes how, near the end of this circle, he meets a troop of the violent against nature, who were military men. He had thus arrived at the edge of the circle where the water fell into the next ring, and it made such a noise as a hum—that is, the confused noise made by the hives, which are the vessels where the bees or drones are. When three shades departed: that is, three souls. FROM A TROOP: i.e., from a multitude. But strictly the Latin <term>turma: a squadron of cavalry</term>; and so, making mention of men excellent in deeds of arms, he said *Turma*. But in our language, it is taken for any multitude. UNDER THE RAIN of fire.

He continues describing the punishments and adds that he was encouraged by Virgil to wait for them. This means that even reason wills that we have compassion for men damned by some vice, and we must honor them if on the other side some outstanding virtue shines in them. AND IF IT WERE NOT for the fire that shoots the nature of the place: that is, if it were not for the fire, which the nature of the place shoots, I would judge that haste would better suit you than them. As if to say, except that the burning and frenzied greed of these men could harm you by conversing with them too familiarly, I would say that you should rather seek to know them for their virtues than they you. And certainly we must be eager to know men in whom some virtue shines. But we must not throw ourselves into the flames in which they burn: that is, imitate their burning lust.

These, having reached us—we who stopped to wait for them—say "alas" <note>original: "ei"</note>: which voice signifies grief: and he says THE OLD CRY: because they were in the habit of lamenting thus. And then because Dante was still and they could not stop—as was shown above regarding Ser Brunetto—they circled around. Because of this, they were always moving, and yet they did not move away. In this way, they simultaneously observed the law of moving and yet could talk with Dante. JUST AS CHAMPIONS ARE WONT. He makes a comparison of these to gladiators. Gladiators were, among the ancients, men sacrificed to the people; they fought in the theater in various ways and with various weapons. In which battle the victor killed the vanquished if the surrounding people did not save him. Thus...

He presents the oration of Jacopo Rusticucci, a Florentine knight, which is full of artifice and is in the deliberative genre, and captures goodwill and attention from their persons by showing that although the place where they are is currently miserable and unhappy, and their appearance defiled by the burning shows them as vile and unworthy of being heard, nevertheless the good fame acquired in the world should move him. SOFT PLACE [loco sollo] means elevated and not condensed or hardened. Hence we say of armor that it is "soft" [solla] when in that part the iron is not well condensed; and this place was soft because it was sandy, and sand does not harden but stays loose. BROLLO <note>usually "bare" or "naked"</note> strictly means weighed. Whence we say...

<header>INFERNO.</header>

He was of a higher rank than you believe.
He was the grandson of the good Gualdrada;
Guido Guerra was his name: and in his life
he achieved much with wisdom and with the sword.
The other who treads the ground behind me
is Tegghiaio Aldobrandi, whose voice
should have been welcome in the world.
And I, who am placed on the cross with them,
was Iacopo Rusticucci; and certainly,
my fierce wife galls me more than anything else.

The father <note>Bellincion Berti</note> heard the girl's words; and pricked by honest shame, she stood up and said: "My father, do not be so liberal in promising me, because no one shall ever kiss me who is not my legitimate husband." The Emperor <note>Otto IV</note> was stunned by the chaste and prudent response of the girl. And immediately he called one of his barons named Guido, and at that moment had him marry her; and as a dowry, he gave him the Casentino and part of Romagna and made him a count. From him originated the family of the Counts Guidi. From Guido and Gualdrada were born two sons, Guiglielmo and Ruggeri. From Guiglielmo came Guido Novello, who followed the Ghibelline party. From Ruggeri came Guido Guerra, of whom mention is presently made. He was most excellent in the military arts, and of great prudence and counsel. Thus, in the battle fought at Benevento between Charles and Manfred, he was considered the principal cause of Charles's victory, because he was there as captain of four hundred Florentine Guelf knights and exiles. These men, after such a defeat, returned to Florence, and with the help of Charles, drove out the Ghibellines. **Tegghiaio Aldobrandi** was highly esteemed among the Adimari family, both at home and in the armies, for many marvelous deeds and counsels. He advised against the enterprise against the Sienese, showing that victory could not be had. But his counsel was not accepted. From this followed the most unhappy defeat at the Arbia, or rather at Montaperti, and from that, the exile of the Guelfs from Florence. **IACOPO RUSTICUCCI** was a Florentine knight, not from a very famous family, but abundant in wealth and of great spirit, and full of liberality. But he had a wife of such perverse customs that it was finally necessary for him to separate from her; and such a life was the cause that, remaining without a wife, he fell into the abominable vice for which he is punished in this place.

<meta>catchword: place and is punished.</meta>

If I had been shielded from the fire,
I would have thrown myself down there with them;
and I believe the teacher <note>original: "doctor", referring to Virgil</note> would have allowed it.
But because I would have been burnt and cooked,
fear overcame my good will,
which made me greedy to embrace them.

Then I began: "Not contempt, but sorrow
for your condition fixed itself within me
so deeply that it will be slow to leave.
As soon as my lord spoke to me
words through which I thought
that such people as you are were coming.
I am of your land, and always
your deeds and honored names
I have recalled and heard with affection.
I leave the gall, and go for the sweet fruits
promised to me by my truthful leader;
but first, I must descend to the center."

"So may your soul long lead
your limbs," he then replied,
"and so may your fame shine after you:
Tell us if courtesy and valor dwell
within our city as they used to,
or if they have been cast out entirely?
For Guglielmo Borsieri, who grieves..."

<column-break/>

...is a wretched man and stripped of every good. **QUESTI** (These). **LORME DI CVI** (Whose tracks): whose vestiges and footprints you see <term>tread: meaning to walk upon</term>, because following him, he placed his foot where the other had left his shape. **TVTTOCHE VADA NUDO** (Though he goes naked) and hairless: that is, although he goes naked because the flames have removed his hair and skin. **FV DI MAGIOR GRADO** (He was of higher rank): that is, of greater dignity and fortune and reputation. **DELLA BVONA** (Of the good): that is, chaste and wise Gualdrada. He was the son of Count Guido, son of Gualdrada. This girl was most beautiful and the daughter of Messer Bellincion Berti of the Ravignani, a very ancient Florentine family and one of the branches of the Adimari. And while the Emperor Otto IV was in Florence, at the gathering of women celebrated for the feast of the Baptist, he was amazed by the girl's beauty and asked who she was. Messer Bellincion was near the Emperor, and before the others, he replied that she was the daughter of a man who would allow him...

¶ There is nothing else to note here except that he wishes to show that close familiarity with men adorned with many virtues should be sought, even if there is some great vice in them. And if we can be "covered from the fire"—that is, defend ourselves from vicious desires—we should have conversation with them to imitate them in their virtues; and the teacher <note>Reason/Virgil</note> would allow it. But fearing the fire—that is, the contagion of vice—we shall abstain from it.

He responds that their miserable state did not cause contempt in his heart, but sorrow and compassion. **DI VOSTRA terra** (Of your land): I am of your homeland. **ET SEMPRE ritraſſi** (And always recalled): As if to say, I wrote and committed to the memory of others. Or "recalled" as in imitated: as we say a painter "recalls" Dante, meaning with the picture he imitates the image of Dante. **ET ASCOLTAI** (And I heard) from those who spoke of you. And by this, he shows he has always held them in the highest veneration. Hence it follows that he cannot hold them in contempt now. **LASCIO LO fele & uo per dolci pomi** (I leave the gall and go for the sweet fruits): He manifests in one verse the entire journey of one who goes toward beatitude. For he goes through Hell—that is, through the consideration of vices, which are gall <note>original: "fiele", meaning bile or bitterness</note>—to leave it behind. And he wishes, through purgation, to arrive at Paradise, where the sweet apple and fruit of the virtues is, which is happiness. **PROMESSI A ME** (Promised to me) by my truthful leader: Virgil, that is, the Intellect. When we choose him as our leader and follow him, he promises us happiness, and he does not lie to us, but gives it to us because he is truthful and not a liar. **MA PRIA** (But before) I go to such fruits, I must return: As if he must go down to the center, which place, being the lowest in the world, contains the bottom of Hell—that is, he must go with knowledge to the very depths of all vices.

¶ This shade prays to Dante; and to bend him to his will, he wishes him two things which the damned judge to be greatest: the first is a long life, the second is perpetual fame after life. Therefore, **SE LANIMA conduca** (If the soul leads): and as if maintains and preserves for a long time **LE TVE MEMBRA** (your limbs): your body, which, while the soul is included within it, is preserved whole and uncorrupted. Afterwards, once the soul has departed, it immediately dissolves and corrupts. In short: if you live long...

...with us and goes yonder with his companions;
he torments us greatly with his words.
**"New people and sudden gains**
**have generated pride and excess**
**in you, Florence, so that you already weep."**
**Thus I cried out with my face raised high;**
**those three, who understood this as the answer,**
**looked at one another as truth is looked upon.**

**"If at other times it costs you so little,"**
**they all replied, "to satisfy others,**
**happy are you to speak thus at your will.**
**Therefore, if you escape these dark places**
**and return to see again the beautiful stars,**
**when it shall please you to say 'I was there,'**
**see that you speak of us to the people."**
**Then they broke their circle; and in fleeing**
**their nimble legs seemed like wings.**
**An "Amen" could not have been said**
**as quickly as they vanished;**
**wherefore it pleased the Master to depart.**

**I followed him, and we had gone but a little way**
**when the sound of the water was so near**
**that for speaking we would hardly have been heard.**
**Like that river that follows its own path,**
**first from Mount Veso <note>original: "monte ueso," modern Monviso</note> toward the east,**
**from the left slope of the Apennines—**
**which is called the 'Quiet Water' <note>original: "acqua cheta"</note> further up,**
**before it spills down into its lower bed,**
**and at Forlì it is vacant of that name—**
**it bellows there above San Benedetto**
**of the Alp, falling in a single leap**
**where it should have been received by a thousand;**
**thus down from a steep, jagged bank**
**we found that blood-stained water <note>original: "acqua tincta," referring to the Phlegethon</note> resounding,**
**so that in a short time it would have offended the ear.**

<column-break/>

...kept alive: or rather leads as if he held them in high regard. AND IF YOUR fame shines—resplendent—AFTER YOU: after your life. SAID: Iacopo [Rusticucci] dwells and inhabits our city. COURTESY AND VALOR: liberality and strength, or rather magnanimity; these two virtues in the republic maintain harmony and increase the empire. For the first generates harmony and acquires friends; the second makes men fit for every great undertaking. **GUGLIELMO Borsiere.** Some say "Borsiere" <note>Pursemaker</note> because originally he made purses. Others claim Borsiere to be a noble family name. In any case, he was a knight of the court and had dealings with all the lords of Italy, a well-mannered man of noble behavior. It was his duty, and that of similar knights, to negotiate peace among great and noble men, to intervene in arranging marriages, and sometimes to refresh the minds of listeners with witty and pleasant stories. They say that while in Genoa, he was asked by Messer Ermino Grimaldi—a man both very rich and very miserly—what he could have painted in the hall of a newly built house that was unknown and never seen before. He replied: "Messer, I will teach you something of which you have never had knowledge: paint **Liberality** there." This word so moved the miserly soul of Messer Ermino that he changed his nature and became quite liberal. The poet feigns, then, that this man, having recently died, has brought fresh news of Florence. WHO GRIEVES with us: that is, he bears the same sorrow and pain that we bear because he is damned for the same vice. AND GOES WITH his companions: He is in that troop from which we have just now departed. It angers or torments us—that is, it gives us great pain—THE New people. Here Dante responds, saying "The new people," meaning the rustic folk who have recently come to inhabit Florence. AND SUDDEN gains: As if to say, made through illicit contracts and extreme avarice. PRIDE and excess: commonly the latter is born from the former. For when new men become rich and acquire status, they become proud and full of excess, because they are so arrogant that they want more than what belongs to them. Pride <note>original: "orgoglio"</note> in the Florentine tongue signifies arrogant haughtiness. Thus Petrarch says: *Wherefore I grieve much / when an excessive pride / in a beautiful woman hides many virtues.* THUS I cried out with my face raised high: Which demonstrates indignation. AND THESE THREE LOOKED at one another as truth is looked upon: When those who hear something look at each other’s faces, it seems they approve that what they hear is true.

The meaning is that those three responded to Dante that if at other times it was so easy to respond to whoever asked him, certainly he is happy since he speaks at his will: that is, since he can speak at his will, with such ornament and brevity. Then, having gained such goodwill by having praised him so, they pray that when he returns to the world, he brings them to the memory of men. We can also interpret the aforementioned tercet to mean Dante is happy if it costs him so little to satisfy others and if he speaks at his will. WHEN it shall please you to say "I was there": That is, when you have escaped such dangerous places and returned to a place of safety, it will please you to narrate past things. For as Cicero says: To remember past danger once we are returned to safety gives us delight and pleasure. I SAW THE WHEEL BREAK: The circle they had made around us. AND THEIR NIMBLE LEGS: that is, swift. SEEMED LIKE WINGS: that is, they resembled wings because they were as fast in running as wings are in flying.

It had already pleased Virgil to depart from those souls, because reason remains in such virtues only as long as is sufficient for the knowledge of them; then it departs, and appetite and sense follow it. And they arrived at the end of this circle, where there is the bank that descends into the eighth circle, through which the Phlegethon falls, making such a noise to anyone nearby that they could not hear one another. And he adds that the fall of this river was like that of the Montone <note>river near Forlì</note>, which separates Provence from Italy. From this starts the Apennines, though some say the Apennines begin at Monaco on the Genoese Riviera and go along toward Pietrapana, leaving to the left Monferrato, Turin, and Vercelli, and to the right Lunigiana and part of the Riviera; it twists somewhat and leaves to the left Piacenza, Parma, Reggio, Modena; and to the right Luni, Lucca, Pistoia. Then proceeding, it leaves to the left Bologna, Romagna, and the March; and to the right Florence, Arezzo, Perugia, and the Patrimony <note>lands of the Church</note> as far as Rome. Then continuing, it leaves to the left Abruzzi, Terra di Bari, Puglia, and Terra d'Otranto; and to the right Campania, Terra di Lavoro, Salerno, and part of Calabria; and to the left the other part of Calabria as far as the Faro of Messina; and it used to continue even into Sicily. For opposite...

<header>INFERNO.</header>

at its end in Italy and Mount Pelorus in Sicily: which corresponds to it in a shape that looks like a coast torn away from the Apennines. And where the Apennines in Italy are cut off by the strait and end there is Reggio: which name in Greek demonstrates the "breaking" of this mountain by the sea that divided it. For in that language *Rhegmin* <note>original: "Rhegmin," likely referring to the Greek verb 'rhegnymi' (ῥήγνυμι)</note> signifies to break and shatter. For this reason, one reads in Persius: "Thus we have drawn the coast from the long Apennine" <note>original: "Sic costam longo subduximus apennino"</note>. And many writers believe that Sicily was once joined with Italy, and then was separated either by the force of the continuous waves or by earthquakes. And Virgil says: "These places, they say, were once shattered by force and vast ruin—such is the power of time's long passage to change things—they leapt apart, though before both lands were one; the sea came in the middle with its waves and cut the Italian side from the Sicilian" <note>original: "Hec loca ui quondā & uaſta conuulſa ruina Tantū æui longiqua ualet mutare uetuſtas Diſſiluiſſe ferunt cū protinus utraque tellus Vna foret uenit medio ui pontus & undis Hespiū siculo latus abscidit." Aeneid III, 414-419.</note>. And because we have made mention above of the right and the left, understand the **right part** as that which is to the south, and the **left** as that which is northern. Because as we turn toward the head of the world, which is the East, the northern site remains on our left, and the meridian <note>the South</note> on our right. All those rivers, then, which are born from the left side of the Apennines before this one, enter into the Po—whose origin is in the roots of Mount Viso—and do not go into the sea by their own course. But this one does the opposite. Because it does not enter the Po but goes by its own course. And the text orders it thus: **"Like that river that follows its own path first"**; that is, the first one that has its own path. **"FROM MOUNT VISO toward the east"**: Do not understand that it is born on Mount Viso, which is more than two hundred miles distant from the mountain above Forlì where this river is born. But he said "from Mount Viso," meaning from the side of Mount Viso. It is called **"Quiet Water"** <note>original: "acqua cheta"</note> before it descends the mountain; and it **"diverts itself"**, that is, it descends through the valley. **"DOWN INTO ITS LOW BED"**, that is, into the plain of Romagna. **"AND AT FORLÌ"**, it is vacant of that name because it is no longer called "Quiet Water" but "Montone," and it enters the sea near Ravenna. **"IT BELLOWS THERE ABOVE SAN BENEDETTO"**: Because here it begins to fall. **"AT A LEAP"**: This is an abbey above that part of the Apennines that divides the Mugello from Romagna. Therefore this mountain takes its name from the abbey. **"WHERE IT SHOULD HAVE BEEN RECEIVED BY A THOUSAND"**: Giovanni Boccaccio writes that he heard from the abbot of this San Benedetto that the counts who were lords of that country once discussed building a castle near this waterfall and bringing many nearby villages there. But the death of the one who desired it more than the others interrupted the plan. Therefore Dante says, "Where it should have been received," meaning a receptacle and room and habitation for a thousand, that is, for many. **"THUS"**: He returns to the subject and says that thus that water of Phlegethon bellowed through that valley. **"STEEP"**: that is, headlong and very sharp. **"IN SUCH A WAY THAT IN A SHORT TIME"**: that is, in a brief time. **"IT WOULD HAVE OFFENDED THE EAR"**: that is, the sense of hearing, which is offended by an excess of sound and voice. So that you may better understand this: although our soul is incorporeal, nonetheless it exercises the power of the senses with corporeal instruments. Therefore it is necessary that just as the corporeal instrument is finite and limited, so the sense is finite and limited. Thus, every sensible excess must offend the sense because it exceeds its proportion. For this reason they say that those who live where the Nile falls <note>referring to the Nile cataracts</note> become deaf from such a great and continuous noise.

-> I had a cord girt around me, <-
-> and with it I thought at one time <-
-> to catch the leopard with the painted skin. <-
-> After I had loosed it all from me, <-
-> just as the leader had commanded me, <-
-> I reached it to him, knotted and coiled. <-
-> Wherefore he turned toward the right side, <-
-> and somewhat far from the edge <-
-> he threw it down into that deep ravine. <-
-> "It must be that something new will respond," <-
-> I said to myself, "to the new signal <-
-> which the master follows so with his eye." <-
-> Ah, how cautious men should be <-
-> near those who do not see merely the surface, <-
-> but look with their wisdom into the thoughts! <-
-> And he said to me: "Soon will come from above <-
-> what I await; and what your thought dreams of <-
-> must soon be discovered to your sight." <-

<column-break/>

This place contains within it a rather obscure fiction. The poet posits that by the command of Virgil, he unloosed a cord that he had girded, and reached it coiled up to Virgil. Wherefore some say that Dante in his youth took the habit of Saint Francis, and later, having departed, he left it. And for this reason, they posit the cord with which he was girded stands for **hypocrisy**. This I do not believe, nor does it seem likely to me. But it is a manifest thing that in what follows, the poet treats ten species of **fraud**. Therefore it is a fitting thing that Virgil, wishing to show Dante what fraud is, asks him to ungird the cord he had worn. This denotes that if a man wishes to rightly know fraud—which is a thing more implicit and obscure than any other vice—he cannot see the universal with his intellect if the sense does not represent some particular instance to him. For example, I would not know what "friendship" is in general if I did not first understand a particular friendship, such as the one between me and you, which makes it so that there is one same will between us in all things. This particular instance, carried from the sense to the intellect, causes the intellect to abstract such a particular friendship into consideration and reduce it to the general. And it understands friendship in itself, no longer understanding only that which is between Scipio and Laelius <note>Scipione and Lelio; famous Roman archetypes of friendship from Cicero's "De Amicitia"</note>, but another. But in general, it is nothing other than a consensus of wanting and not wanting among several men. Thus, in this place, Virgil and Dante are a single man (as we have already shown many times); when he wishes to understand frauds, the intellect must ask the sense for the cord it has girded. And by the cord is understood his particular fraud, which is born from the sense aided by the lower reason. He ungirds it, which signifies wanting to leave it, and reaches it to the intellect, because he seeks with it to know its malignancy. But he reaches it "knotted," that is, tied and wound up, because fraud is always full of knots and entanglements. Or rather, we shall say that the sense and the lower reason reach the coiled cord because they are not sufficient by themselves to explain the nature of such a vice. But the intellect can explain it, and therefore he reaches it to him. And he rightly uses the cord to represent fraud. The cord is made of hemp, a thing suitable for entangling and impeding. And the same nature is in fraud. Furthermore, it is twisted and composed of many threads. And similarly, fraud twists and composes together many malices, and nothing in it is simple and open. Nor is there that difference in the Tuscan language between *fune* <note>rope</note> and *corda* <note>cord</note> that exists in Latin. For the Latins call *fune* that which is made of hemp or other similar material suitable for binding. *Chorda* is a Greek name and signifies the guts with which one plays viols, harps, lutes, and similar instruments, and in that same significance the Latins use it. But we take *fune* and *corda* as almost the same thing. Thus he said "cord," meaning rope. Nor does the poet stray from the Psalmist, who, putting the rope for fraud, said: "The cords of sinners have wrapped around me" <note>original: "Funes peccatorū circumplexi sunt me" - Psalm 119:61</note>; and Isaiah: "Woe to you who draw iniquity with the little cord of vanity" <note>original: "Ve qui tranſitis iniquitatem in funiculum uanitatis" - Isaiah 5:18</note>. **"AND WITH IT I thought at one time to catch the leopard"**: Having shown that the poet had ungirded his own fraud, he presently adds two things. First, that such fraud had not been about very grave expectations, such as using fraud...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante's Inferno, specifically focusing on the transition to the circle of fraud and the summoning of the monster Geryon.</meta>

<header>INFERNO</header>

In avarice or in proud ambition. But only in lust having used it to catch the leopard: <note>The "leopard" (lonza) is one of the three beasts Dante encounters in Canto I, often interpreted as a symbol of lust.</note> that is, in amorous and lascivious things: because the leopard represents lust. Whence it follows that as much as the sin of lust is less grave than the others: so much less detestable is such fraud. The second is that even in lust he had rarely thought of it. Whence he says "sometimes" therefore he had not made a habit of it. Wherefore it was easy to ungird himself from it, that is, to lay it aside. **WHENCE HE TURNED** toward the right side. Reason always turns toward the right side: that is, toward upright and virtuous thoughts: and he threw the cord far from the edge almost into the middle. **INTO THAT DEEP** that is, profound. **GORGE** ditch. We call a "borrato" that small river which, being in a deep and narrow valley, has high banks on every side. He threw it into the middle to find the center of that abyss: from which center all lines originate. **AND YET IT MUST BE** that novelty responds. Dante, as a prudent man, estimated within himself that Virgil does nothing without the highest consideration. Therefore from every one of his actions an excellent and new thing should be expected: And he admonishes us that we should always place faith in those who are wiser. For as Cicero writes in the second book of *On Duties* <note>original: "De Officiis"</note>: *We have faith in those whom we judge to know more than ourselves: and whom we believe can foresee future things.* **THAT THE MASTER** follows it with his eye. It is an excellent conjecture that Virgil did not throw the cord by chance: but with consideration: because he follows it with his eye: that is, because he pursues it with his gaze. Therefore he stands attentive to wait for the end of such a matter. **AH HOW CAUTIOUS**. It is an excellent precept that when we are near wise and learned men: and those whom we judge to do nothing by chance or without exquisite reason, we must with the highest attention observe and note not only their deeds and words: but every minimal gesture and sign: because such men do not only see what is "above," that is, what is present: but with the eyes of the mind they look at the effect that must follow. **HE SAID TO ME**. In one and the same time Virgil thought of what was to follow from the thrown cord: and comforted Dante that soon that which he expects would manifest itself: and that which Dante was dreaming of. And certainly the intellect of the cause foresees the effect as a certain thing and expects it: But the sense and the inferior reason do not see it because they rather know the cause through the effect than the effect through the cause. Whence before the effect follows, although one has seen the cause, one does not foresee it. But one goes imagining diverse things similar to one who dreams: and rarely guesses correctly.

---

<margin>
Firstly and with great artifice, having to tell an incredible thing, he demonstrates that he intends that one should not narrate incredible things even if they are true unless necessity constrains us: because they bring us shame wrongly: because by telling the truth we are held to be liars. And because few things are more opposite and contrary to the nature of man than a lie: Since nature has given us speech: which is not given to any other animal so that we may express and manifest outwardly what we have conceived in the mind: and we use it for the contrary: therefore man should not only not tell a lie: But also not say what seems a lie if necessity does not constrain him. Therefore Dante, to gain faith for that which by its nature seems incredible, shows he knows what we have said: But that he is constrained by necessity to say it: because without it in this place the matter would remain imperfect: He says it then: and to give it faith he affirms it with an oath by those things that are dearest to him: and he swears in this sentiment: So may the notes be full of long grace: that is, the words of this comedy which I write, as I saw this beast coming. This is an effective oath. Because there is nothing that the writer so much desires / as that the written work should have grace. And especially
</margin>

> **S**o to that truth which has the face of a lie
> a man should close his lips as far as he can
> because without fault it brings shame
> But here I cannot be silent & by the notes
> of this comedy reader I swear to you
> so may they not be void of long grace.
> That I saw through that thick & dark air
> come swimming a figure upwards
> marvelous to every steadfast heart
> Just as he returns who goes down
> sometimes to loosen the anchor that catches
> on a reef or other thing hidden in the sea:
> Who stretches upward & draws in his feet.

---

Dante desires it not for vainglory. But because writing things necessary for the salvation of man / he desires to be read so that his laborious vigils may produce the best fruit for many. **THAT I SAW THROUGH THAT THICK & DARK AIR COME SWIMMING A FIGURE UPWARDS.** Many have been deceived believing because he says "I saw swimming" that place to be filled with water: And they do not realize that he imitates Virgil: who makes a reciprocal translation from the sea to the air: Whence he said *The sail-flying sea* <note>original: "Mare velivolum"</note> i.e. through which one flies with sails: And "to fly" / is only in the air: & likewise from the air to the sea. Whence in Mercury he said *The oarage of wings* <note>original: "Remigio alarum"</note> although oars are only of the sea. Similarly Dante said "come swimming" although the swimmer is properly in the water: And certainly it is a marvelous fiction & entirely of the divinity of such great genius. He wants to describe fraud: & says I saw a figure: But I did not yet see what figure it was: which denotes that fraud is seen: & at first is not recognized. The Trojans saw Sinon: & heard his words: But they did not know to what end he had come. <note>Sinon was the Greek spy who convinced the Trojans to bring the Wooden Horse into their city.</note> Furthermore he saw it through the thick & dark air: which not only denotes that in hell, that is, in the habit of vices, there is obscurity, i.e. ignorance: But he wants to demonstrate that fraud is always shadowed & darkened in a way that it cannot be discerned. It came swimming through the air to signify that it does not stand in a solid & firm place, that is, in the truth: But it swims: because the fraudulent man always varies & changes things: & when you believe he is in one place he is / in another. It came upwards: because fraud from a hidden place eventually comes into the light: And it is / marvelous to every steadfast heart: Because no one is of such invincible spirit that he does not fear fraud: since force, which is brought against us openly, gives some space to provide for defense. Whence the magnanimous man takes confidence: But fraud strikes us before we can foresee it. Wherefore the generous man cannot exercise or demonstrate any of his strength to resist those: & for this reason he greatly fears such assaults. Understand then why Dante saw it through the dark & thick air: why it came swimming: why it came from below to above: why it was fearful even to steadfast men. And finally he demonstrates that coming up it acted like one who has gone to the bottom of the water to loosen an anchor attached either to a reef or to another thing covered by the water: who returning upwards stretches the first parts: that is, the neck & the arms: & the last which are the legs he draws in: that is, he crouches: And truly the fraudulent man always stretches the first parts because he begins from some true thing: & that he wants to be manifest. Then in the end he adds the false: & this he crouches & wraps up so that it stays hidden: & is not understood.

<meta>This page continues from the previous discussion regarding the descent into the lower circles of Hell. Here, Dante and Virgil encounter Geryon, the symbolic representation of Fraud, who will carry them down the Great Barrier.</meta>

<page-num>87</page-num>
<header>CANTO XVII.</header>

### CANTO XVII OF THE FIRST CANTICLE BY DANTE.

“Behold the beast with the pointed tail,
who passes mountains and breaks through walls and weapons;
behold the one who makes the whole world stink.”
Thus did my leader begin to speak to me,
and he signaled to it that it should come to the shore,
near the end of the marble path we had walked.
And that filthy image of fraud
approached and brought its head and its torso to land,
but did not pull its tail onto the bank.
Its face was the face of a just man,
so benign was the appearance of its skin,
and of a serpent was all the rest of its trunk.
Two paws it had, hairy up to the armpits;
the back, the chest, and both its sides
were painted with knots and little circles.
With more colors, interwoven and superimposed,
never did Tartars or Turks make cloth,
nor were such webs ever laid out by Arachne.

<column-break/>

In this seventeenth canto, the author presents the form of Geryon <note>In classical mythology, Geryon was a giant; Dante transforms him into a hybrid monster representing Fraud.</note>, whom he intends to be a figure of **Fraud**, because he must deal with the fraudulent. First, he shows that it has a tail so sharp that with it, it can cross mountains and break through walls and weapons. Certainly, fraud does not show its harm except in the "tail"—that is, in the end. This is because the fraudulent person hides and conceals their thoughts and counsel, and under the cover of some good, they deceive you. The end of fraud is always harmful. You cannot perceive the trickery except at the conclusion. Hence the proverb was born: "In the tail lies the poison" <note>original: "nella coda sta el ueleno" / Latin: *In cauda venenum*</note>. And fraud is so powerful that it "passes mountains," meaning it overcomes every great power. **AND BREAKS walls and weapons**, which denotes that no repair or defense is effective against it. **THIS IS the one who makes the whole world stink.** The world has a "good odor" and is uncorrupted when men observe faith and love the truth. Of such people the Psalmist says: "He that hath clean hands and a pure heart; who hath not taken his soul in vain, nor sworn deceitfully to his neighbor" <note>original: "Innocens manibus et mundo corde qui nō accepit in uanum animam suā: Neq; iurauit in dolo proximi sui"</note>. Conversely, the world is corrupted and stinks through perfidy and fraud.

**AND HE SIGNALED TO IT** to come to the shore. The beast was in the air because fraud has no stability; it cannot be grasped or held, but slips away like air. But Virgil calls it to the margin, which is made of marble—a hard substance. This is because the intellect considers and contemplates fraud by founding itself on true and stable reasons, and thus makes it come onto the stone. But the beast puts only its head and torso there, and not the tail, because, as we have said, the beginnings of the fraudulent are based on the truth. To use a familiar example, Sinon <note>The Greek spy who convinced the Trojans to bring the Wooden Horse into their city.</note>, in order to deceive the Trojans, begins his story with true things, demonstrating the trickery of Ulysses in the death of Palamedes. Then, under this truth, he hides his lie by feigning the hatred Ulysses bore him, and many other things. Therefore, the first parts of fraud are on the "rock"—that is, on something solid and true—while the tail remains in the air, a mobile thing.

**ITS FACE WAS the face of a just man.** This monster had the face of a man, the rest of the body of a serpent, and the tail of a scorpion. Some say this signifies three types of fraud. One in words, denoted by the human face, because only man uses speech. The second in things—that is, in crafts and merchandise—denoted by the serpent, which is a cunning animal of various colors, just as such frauds are varied and diverse. The third is in the deed, such as thieves and assassins, who, like the scorpion, give poisoned stings. But I judge the truer <term>allegory</term> <note>A story or image that reveals a hidden moral or political meaning.</note> to be that every fraud is composed of these three forms. If one considers it correctly, fraud has a "face"—its first appearance—of a just man, because the fraudulent person initially shows humanity, benevolence, and every appearance of justice. As Sallust says: "One thing he has ready on his tongue, and another closed in his breast" <note>A reference to the Roman historian Sallust's description of Catiline's conspirators.</note>. From such people David prays to the Lord to defend him, saying: "Deliver my soul, O Lord, from lying lips, and from a deceitful tongue" <note>original: "Libera animā meā a labiis iniquis & a lingua doloſa"</note>.

**SO BENIGN was the appearance of its skin.** This denotes that such benevolence is not inside (in deeds) but only in the skin (in appearance). Hence Persius says: "I know you inside and out" <note>original: "Ego te intus & in cute noui"</note>. **AND OF A serpent was all the rest of the trunk.** The serpent is a cunning and prudent animal. Cunning and cleverness can be a virtue when, without fraud or harm to our neighbor, we strive to defend ourselves from the malice of others and rightly administer our affairs. It can be a vice when we use such cleverness in fraud. Therefore, the serpent is sometimes used in a good sense, as when the Truth says in the Gospel: "Be wise as serpents and simple as doves" <note>original: "Estote prudentes sicut serpētes & ſimplices ſicut columbe"</note>. Other times it is used in a bad sense, as in the first part of Genesis where the diabolical temptation of the first man is written in the figure of a serpent, which had a human face to denote what we have said.

I cannot consider without the highest amazement the greatness of the genius of this poet, who in one and the same place mixes classical things with Christian things, adds of his own, and makes such a blend of diverse things that it optimally expresses his intention; while maintaining great gravity, he adds wonderful delight. Thus, the fraudulent person has a beginning full of humanity and goodness in appearance to entice the souls of men and remove any thought of being deceived; then their process is serpentine, cunning, and varied, until they arrive at the completion of the fraud, which is the tail of a scorpion because it harms most greatly.

**TWO PAWS.** By this we understand two types of cunning: fraud in action and deceit in words. **HAIRY**, as if covered and hidden, because the counsel of the fraudulent is always covered and hidden; and it is also full of cruelty. **UP TO THE ARMPITS**, meaning up to the shoulders, which he calls armpits from the Latin word *axilla*. **THE BACK, the chest, and both sides.** In short, the rest of the body was covered in serpent skin, which is full of knots and circles. Allegorically, this signifies the simulations that are always implicit, involved, and colored. The methods of fraud are varied and intertwined so that one enters the other, and they are circular so that they return to where they began. **WITH MORE colors.** Whoever has seen such fabrics understands the comparison is excellent.

**NOR WERE SUCH webs ever laid out by Arachne.** The fables say that in Lydia there was a woman named Arachne, born in a small village and of lowly lineage. But she was so skilled in the art of embroidery and in every artifice of the needle and loom that by a long interval she surpassed all others. This made her so arrogant that, not content with surpassing mortals, she wished to compete with the gods and contend with Pallas <note>The goddess Athena, often associated with wisdom and weaving.</note>, the goddess of wisdom. But Pallas defeated her, broke and cut her web, and converted her into a spider. This animal still does not cease making artificial webs. By this fable, it is shown that Arachne—that is, human fraud—overcomes all others except Pallas, who is the goddess of wisdom. For divine wisdom knows the fraud of man, and God is the "searcher of hearts" <note>original: "scrutator cordium"</note>. Therefore, let no Arachne believe she can defeat Pallas, for she will defeat her and break every web; that is, God will know our fraud and break all our designs.

Landino provides a moral commentary, blending biblical references with classical myths like Arachne to illustrate that Divine Wisdom ultimately exposes human trickery.</summary>

# INFERNO.

Thus stood that beast, part in the air and part on the ground, just as barges <note>original: "eburchi"</note> sit, or as beavers <note>original: "ebeueri"</note> do. This animal is called *fiber* <note>original: "fibro"</note> by the Greeks. And Pliny says that by natural instinct, knowing that the hunter seeks it for its testicles <note>original: "granelli"</note>—which are medicinal, especially for paralysis and the "falling sickness" <term>falling sickness: epilepsy</term>—it castrates itself with its teeth. For this reason, Isidore writes that the Latins call it *castor* because it castrates itself. It has a terrible bite: it cuts trees with its teeth no differently than a man does with iron. And if it bites a man, it does not let go until it feels it has crushed the bone of the limb it bites. It is similar to the otter, and like the otter, it inhabits both land and water. But it has back feet like a goose, with which <column-break/> it is very adept at swimming. Its tail is wide and scaly like a fish, and it always keeps it in the water, and this part alone is considered precious food; the other limbs are of an abominable stench. It builds ingenious houses on the rivers with multiple levels, so that even as the water rises and falls, it can keep its tail in the river and the rest of its body dry. It feeds on fish and tree bark. Those who are stronger make slaves of the weaker ones, making them go upside down through the river, and between their back legs and belly, they load them with wood for the construction of their houses, pulling them by the tail to the chosen spot. Albertus Magnus writes that it is false that they castrate themselves, because they have their testicles attached to the spine or the backbone in a way that they cannot be removed without death. Dioscorides affirms the same. Useful hats are made from their skin. **Among the gluttonous Germans** <note>original: "lurchi"</note>: that is, among those who are greedy and eat great meals; and he says this because the Danube, where beavers are found, runs through those

<gloss>d</gloss> Virgil shows that it was necessary to go right up to the beast, because to have a full knowledge of the fraudulent, it was necessary to come to the consideration of cunning. **IT IS NECESSARY TO TURN our path.** He says this because until now they had turned to the left hand, except for a few times to cross over as they do now. And we have already shown above why he feigns this. **THEREFORE we descended to the right side**: to note that the consideration of cunning was for the purpose of guarding oneself against it, and not for using it. **AND TEN STEPS we took upon the edge**: Understand this as the edge of the seventh circle. By "ten steps," understand ten types of cunning which he will treat successively in the eighth circle. Afterward, Virgil sends Dante to know the people who are there, and he remains to speak with the beast. This signifies that for the knowledge of particular things, inferior reason is sufficient; but to consider the whole nature of cunning in general, one needs Virgil: that is, superior reason and the intellect, which persuades the beast to place them on its strong shoulders and carry them into the eighth circle. For our intellect cannot go to the knowledge of the punishments in that circle unless it knows cunning and its types, and knows how to distinguish the places according to those types. **PEOPLE sitting nearby**: One and the same punishment—that is, the fire falling from the heavens—punishes both the sodomites and the usurers, because each of these does violence to na-

ture. But the sodomites walk and the usurers sit to demonstrate that usury is a greater sin, because it does violence not only to nature but also to art <term>art: in this context, human industry or labor</term>. **HERE THE MASTER**: We have already explained this place above. **THEIR CONDITION**: their behavior, their actions, and movements; because *menare* <note>to lead or conduct</note> means to move, whence we say "he moves [mena] his head." **LET YOUR talk there be brief.** Since we have recognized the nature of usury, we must immediately depart from such consideration. **WHILE you return I will speak**: It has already been stated that only superior reason understands the universal.

### So again, along the furthest head
### of that seventh circle, all alone
### I went to where the sorrowful people sat.
### Through their eyes, their grief was bursting forth;
### here and there they helped themselves with their hands,
### now against the vapors, now against the hot soil.
### Not otherwise do dogs in summer,
### now with their snout, now with their paw, when they are bitten
### by fleas, or flies, or gadflies.

<gloss>d</gloss> He shows how he went alone to the usurers. And he shows how they sit and do not walk, and we have said the reason above. He makes a comparison that just as dogs continuously defend themselves from the bites of insects that bother them, so these people defend themselves with their hands, now from the flames that rain down, now from the "hot sun," that is, from the hot earth. And because we have arrived at such a sin, we will speak briefly of usury. Usury is the sale of the use of things that have no use, or of those that are only consumed by use. And it is to be noted that certain things have use, and certain do not. Those things have use that are useful to human life either by necessity or for well-being, such as bread, wine, and clothing. Those things have no use <note>meaning no "fruit" or natural increase</note> without which we can live comfortably, such as gems; and they have no multiplication, because gold does not make gold, nor do gems make gems.

Furthermore <note>original: "Preterea"</note>, of things in use, some are consumed by use alone, such as bread and wine. Others are consumed over time, such as houses, clothing, and the like. Therefore, he who takes a price for lent money sins, because money has no use <note>In medieval theology, money was "barren" and should not "breed" interest; its only use was in being spent.</note>. Similarly, he who takes a price for lent bread or wine commits usury, because it is consumed in its use. But lending a house, which is consumed by time and use, does not constitute usury when taking a price, for it worsens with use and must be repaired from time to time. We spoke of usury in the eleventh chapter.

**H**e shows that these souls were so scorched by the fire that they could not be recognized. This means allegorically that the vice of usury makes men infamous and deprives them of every good name and reputation; and among noble spirits and prudent men, they are held in no esteem, and such men do not deign to know them. Indeed, although ambition is a great vice, it nevertheless possesses some nobility of spirit. Lust has some species of benevolence. But avarice is a sordid, vile, and ignoble thing. For this reason, he feigns that he recognized them by the pouches they had at their necks. This shows that such men are not known for any virtue of their own, but only for the heap of money illicitly gathered. ...to have a good, that is, a just and discreet lord, and hearing himself threatened by him, he takes heart: because he knows that he would not command him to do things that he could not do, or that would not be useful to him. **I TURNED TO SAY.** So I wanted to say: that is, "I know you embrace me." <image-desc>Decorative initial Q containing a profile of a man's face.</image-desc>
**AS HE HIMSELF** This demonstrates that reason, by itself, comes to the aid of the senses. **WITH HIS ARMS** clasped me and sustained me. This is to say that the strength of reason aids the fragility of the senses. **And he said Geryon.** The poet’s ingenuity has been marvelous: with great art, he conveniently adapts all the monsters described by the ancient poets to his own purpose, in such a way that, without departing from the Christian religion, he adorns his poem with them. Thus, he found Geryon in the Virgilian underworld placed among the monsters where it says: "Gorgons and Harpies and the form of the three-bodied shade." <note>original: "Gorgones Arpieque: & forma tricorporis umbre." From Aeneid VI, 289.</note> And because beyond the fable one reads in history that this man was astute <note>Astute is used here in the sense of being deceitful or fraudulent.</note>, he placed him in this location so that, as in the other circles, there would be a monster suitable to express the vice punished here. They say Geryon was King of Spain and had three bodies. This is a fiction because he was king of three islands, namely the two Balearics, which are Majorca and Minorca, and Ebusus <note>Modern-day Ibiza.</note>; and that Hercules, fighting him three times, killed a body each time. This denotes that the virtuous man can extinguish those three species of fraud demonstrated above. **MOVE NOW.** Let the circles be wide and the descent slow. When we want to descend or climb a slope with greater ease, we are accustomed not to go straight, but to make wide circuits so that we descend little by little, especially when we have a heavily burdened beast. Therefore, the poet says: "Since you are burdened with Dante, who having a body weighs more than the souls without bodies, do not descend steeply; but go circling." And allegorically, he shows that to lead the senses to the recognition of fraud, it is necessary to proceed with a slower pace: because man does not understand without discourse and does not have that speed in comprehending that an incorporeal spirit has. **AS THE LITTLE BOAT.** An excellent comparison and so clear that it needs no other explanation. **AT PLAY.** We say a vessel is "at play" when it is in a place

---

so open that it can turn wherever it wishes; and similarly, we say this of a ship when it is out of port and a narrow place and can turn expeditiously. **WHERE THE CHEST WAS:** that is, at the banks of the seventh circle. **TURNED ITS TAIL.** It went backward until that point and then turned. **AND THAT** quickly: that is, promptly, and moved it through the air as an eel does through the water. **GREATER FEAR I DO NOT** believe there was. The meaning is: I do not believe that Phaethon had greater fear when, terrified, he let go of the horses' reins. Nor Icarus when he felt himself deprived of his feathers. So that this may be better understood, we will briefly narrate both fables. Phaethon was the son of the Sun and Clymene. At the same time, there was Epaphus, son of Jove, who, proud of such a father, despised Phaethon and denied he was born of Phoebus <note>The Sun god.</note>. Phaethon complained to his mother; instructed by her, he went to the house of Phoebus and asked him for an unnamed favor. Phoebus swore that he would grant whatever he asked. Then the rash youth asked that for one day he be allowed to drive his chariot. Phoebus regretted having sworn and tried to dissuade him; but finally, as the boy stood by his rash proposal, he granted him the solar chariot, which the poets imagine to be guided by four horses. These are: Pyroeis, Eous, Aethon, and Phlegon. Phaethon was already in the middle of the sky when the horses, not fearing such a weak guide, left the fourth heaven in which the sun revolves and descended not only below the third heaven of Venus and the second of Mercury, but below the moon which is in the first. The earth felt the too-close proximity of the sun, and everything burned. Therefore, moved to compassion, Jove struck Phaethon with celestial lightning and cast him into the Po river; and here he died, not without an example for all men, which warns them not to undertake enterprises beyond their own strength. Icarus was the son of Daedalus, of whom it would be too long to narrate every story; but being unable to escape otherwise from Crete, because he was of the highest industry and art in many things, he fabricated wings for himself and his son, warning the latter neither to fly too high nor too low; because in the upper parts, the heat would melt the wax that held the feathers, and in the lower parts, the humidity would weigh them down too much. They both flew safely until the son followed behind the father; but after some distance, Icarus, from too much desire to fly high, became disobedient to the salutary precepts of his father. He rose like an eagle so high that the wax that held the feathers liquefied, and he remained without wings and fell into that sea which was then named Icarian after his name. Such fear, then, did Dante have, seeing himself carried down through the air by Geryon, as Phaethon and Icarus had when they plummeted to the earth. By these two, the poets mean all those who, moved by too much presumption of themselves and by temerity, dare to undertake enterprises above their strength and faculties. Whence it happens that they cannot bring such an enterprise to the proper end and fall along the way under the burden. Thus, the senses, raised by the contemplation of craftiness, were terrified of being able to achieve such knowledge. Because seeing nothing but air signifies the contemplation of craftiness in general, not circumscribed by place or time, which is entirely incorporeal—that is, stripped not only of matter but even of the accidents of matter.

...except that on my face from below a wind blows.

making beneath us a horrible roar;

And I saw then—what I did not see before—
the descent and the circling, by the great evils

As the falcon that has been long on the wing,
who, without seeing lure or bird,
makes the falconer say: "Alas, you stoop!" <note>The falconer cries out because the bird is descending without having caught its prey.</note>
Descends weary, from where he moved swiftly,
through a hundred circles, and settles far
from his master, disdainful and sullen;
So Geryon set us at the bottom,
at the very foot of the jagged rock,
and, having unburdened our persons,
He vanished like the notch from the bowstring.

<column-break/>

...man does not descend without the circuit of the discourse of reasoning: and not with that speed as the separate substances <note>A scholastic term for angels or spirits who move instantly, whereas human reason must move step-by-step.</note>.
**BUT I DID NOT PERCEIVE:** He did not notice that he was descending, except that in the descent he felt wind on his face, as one would feel who was descending by a rope. And allegorically it shows that fraud leads in such a way that man does not notice it. **I ALREADY FELT Upon the right hand the whirlpool.** Thus the beast has gone to the left: and in passing had left the whirlpool—that is, the river—on the right hand. **MAKING BENEATH Us a horrible roar:** that is, the sound born from the fall of the water. Because of which I stretch—that is, outward—my head with my eyes downward: with eyes cast down. **THEN I WAS more fearful** than before: **OF THE PRECIPICE** at the fall of the water: because I recognized how great the drop was. **AND I SAW THEN WHAT I did not see before.** One who is either in water or in air in such a way that they do not see land on any side does not perceive that the thing carrying them is moving. But when they begin to see the land, then they perceive the motion. And if you are at sea, you see by looking at an island whether the ship goes straight or if it turns. And allegorically it shows that when we approach the fires and laments—that is, the harm to which fraud leads us—then we perceive the circling and the descent of the beast: that is, we recognize the circuits and the turnings of fraud.

Through this comparison he shows that Geryon, who had gone for a while wheeling and sustaining himself on his wings, had descended little; then he stooped like a falcon which, after it has been for a time in the air and sees no bird to strike, stoops without being enticed either with a bird or with the lure. **DESCENDS WEARY:** that is, tired. **FROM WHERE IT Moves swiftly:** that is, from that place from which it had departed. **SWIFTLY:** that is, dexterous and fast. **THROUGH A HUNDRED Circles:** that is, through many circles: and it settles far from the falconer, angry and sullen. And this allegorically is true of the fraudulent person, who

---

holds the matter suspended for a time in a way that you do not understand what he is leading you to with his turnings; and having led you to the bottom, he vanishes from before you and leaves you at the bottom. **HE VANISHED:** he disappeared with that speed with which the notch of the arrow <note>original: "choccha"; the nock of the arrow where it meets the string.</note> leaves the string. Because even though you perceive the fraud, he has vanished before you can take revenge. Theseus led Ariadne to the island of Naxos. Nor did the girl perceive the betrayal except when she understood that the said Theseus had already vanished: and had left her without a ship with which she could follow him.

<header>CANTO XVIII.</header>
<sig>i iii</sig>

->CANTO XVIII. OF THE FIRST CANTICLE BY DANTE.<-

**T**here is a place in Hell called Malebolge <note>original: *male bolge*. *Bolgia* can mean a pouch, a pocket, or a dark ditch; *Malebolge* translates to "Evil Pouches."</note>, 
all of stone and of an iron color, 
just like the circle that revolves around it. 
Right in the center of this malignant field 
yawns a pit, quite wide and deep, 
of which its place will tell the structure <note>original: *lordigno*, meaning the design or mechanical arrangement of the place.</note>. 
The circle that remains is therefore round 
between the pit and the foot of the high, hard bank, 
and its bottom is divided into ten sections.

Just as where, for the guarding of the walls, 
many and many ditches encircle the castles 
to make the place where they are secure, 
such an image these formed here; 
and as from the thresholds of such fortresses 
there are small bridges to the outer bank, 
so from the base of the rock moved crags 
that crossed the embankments and ditches 
down to the pit which cuts them off and collects them.

In this place, shaken from the back 
of Geryon, we found ourselves; the poet 
kept to the left, and I moved behind him. 
To the right hand, I saw new misery, 
new torments, and new scourgers, 
with which the first ditch was filled. 
At the bottom were naked sinners; 
from the middle toward us, they came facing us; 
from the middle beyond, they went with us, but with larger strides. 
Just as the Romans, because of the great army <note>original: *lexercito molto*, here referring to the massive crowd of pilgrims.</note> 
in the year of the Jubilee, have taken measures 
to allow the people to pass over the bridge: 
so that on one side all have their faces 
toward the castle and go toward Saint Peter’s; 
on the other side, they go toward the mountain.

<column-break/>

**I**n this eighteenth canto, the author begins to treat the eighth circle where fraud is punished against those who do not have a special bond of trust <note>Dante distinguishes between simple fraud and treachery (fraud against those with a bond of trust).</note>. For in the preceding canto, he described craftiness in general in the figure of Geryon, by whom they were transported from the circle of the violent to that of the fraudulent. And there Geryon set them down, which denotes that after the contemplation of fraud in general, they began to consider its species and particulars. And because there are ten species of fraud, this circle is similarly divided into ten ditches. But in the present canto, he treats only the first and begins the second. He first describes the site of this eighth circle and says THE PLACE OF HELL CALLED, that is, named, MALEBOLGE. *Bolgia* signifies a repository, a bosom, a gulf, and a receptacle. Therefore, it is a fitting name to be called: the evil repository and receptacle of the place of fraud. And it is very fitting that the fraudulent should be punished in valleys and enclosed places, because fraud always remains enclosed and never comes into an open place, but seeks hiding places and shadows. ALL OF STONE: because the fraudulent person has a hard heart and is void of all charity. AND OF AN IRON COLOR: the color of iron. Because not only is he void of charity, but he is armed with cruelty. It can also be shown through this that fraud is covered with double hardness. For the violent person only sins by acting against his neighbor, but the fraudulent person, in addition to this, adds deceit to the harm. IN THE RIGHT CENTER. "Center" is taken in two ways: improperly, when we call "center" anything that is between two extremes; and properly, when we call "center" that part which is equally distant from every extreme. Thus he said "in the right center," that is, in the true center, and deep, because fraud harms more than <unclear>other sins</unclear>. YAWNS A PIT. It is a concave and deep, hollow place—that is, empty. And this is the ninth circle, which because of its narrowness and depth in comparison to the others, seems like a pit. QUITE WIDE: to denote that although he called it a pit, it is nonetheless wide, because it punishes within itself three species of traitors. AND DEEP: because it goes down to the center of the earth. AND THE STRUCTURE: that is, the artificial site of this place. He will say it in its own place, when he treats the ninth circle. THE CIRCLE: this demonstrates the eighth circle, which remains girded on the inner side by the ninth, and on the outer by the bank that divides it from the seventh. And this is divided into ten ditches. You will understand this site precisely in the topography <note>original: *topographia*</note> which we placed at the beginning of the book.

**J**ust as many ditches are made around a fortress, and nonetheless from the gate of such a fortress out beyond all the ditches there were bridges, so all these ditches which were around the ninth circle were crossed by crags, which served as bridges. These ditches denote the depth of fraud; and it is a fitting thing that just as fraud always remains in the depths and never shows itself in an open place, so the fraudulent are punished in a deep place. And the crag that crosses the ditches and makes a bridge by which Virgil and Dante pass signifies the process of speculation <note>In this context, *speculation* refers to intellectual observation or philosophical study.</note>, which is on solid and firm ground because it is founded upon the truth. And this crag, which is one and continues from the base of the bank where Geryon had lowered them down to the pit, cutting across—that is, traversing—all the ditches and is not interrupted in any place, demonstrates that the same will of contemplation carries us in a continuous discourse through the knowledge of all things.

**G**eryon, shaking his back, unloaded us in the place mentioned above. This denotes that after the consideration of fraud in general, they began to consider the particulars, as we said a little while ago. And the poet kept to the left for the reason we have already cited above, and Dante kept behind him. TO THE RIGHT HAND. Because, circling the place from the left hand, the place where the sinners were remained to their right. NEW TORMENTS: because he had not yet found souls who were being scourged, nor scourging demons for said souls. At the bottom were naked sinners who were being beaten. And he shows that this ditch was divided into two parts. For from the side toward Dante, the sinners were coming toward them; the others who were in the other part were going that way like us, but with larger strides than ours. Therefore, this ditch was divided like the bridge at Sant'Angelo <note>The Ponte Sant'Angelo in Rome.</note> in the year of the Jubilee, which, divided lengthwise, on one side receives those who go toward the Castel Sant'Angelo and toward Saint Peter's, and on the other side those who come from Saint Peter's. THE YEAR OF THE JUBILEE. Jubilee in the Hebrew language signifies a year of remission and liberation <note>original: *rimessione & liberatione*</note>. For the Hebrews, having finished...

From this side and that across the dark rock

longitudinally; and one part served those who were going to Saint Peter's: and the other for those who were returning. Thus, then, is this path of the evil ditches <note>original: *male bolge*</note> divided: and along one part go those who have corrupted women with words or with money to provide them to others <note>The panderers or procurers.</note>: and along the other go those who in the same way have corrupted them to have them for themselves <note>The seducers.</note>: These people, then, did not allow the women to live in their peace: so they have demons behind them who beat and drive them with whips. For just as they did not allow women to live in their peace, but with the whips of either flattery or rewards drove them to their will: so now the demons drive them: And we can rightly understand the demons as the remorses of conscience: which always distress those who are stained by such a vice. **FROM THIS SIDE AND THAT:** That is, both where those who go are, and where those who come are. **UPON THE DARK ROCK:** Black and hideous. I saw demons who, running behind them, beat them cruelly in a way that made them run swiftly: And always at the first lash they leaped away. **LIFT THEIR SHANKS:** Their legs. Here it should be noted that he shows the penalty of seducers: and seduction is to induce someone by deceit to do what they should not: And although seduction may be of many kinds: nevertheless, here he treats the seduction that induces the vice of the flesh. And this is committed in two ways: either they seduce a woman so that she consents to another: or to himself. And because the vice of lust is the least grave sin among mortal sins: therefore he places seduction in this vice as less grave than in the others.
