HERE he introduces having found Master Venedico de’ Caccianemici of Bologna. And not without reason does he suggest that this man feigns to hide himself. For such a vice is so abominable not only among the good: but even among the wicked, that no one is so impudent or brazen that he is not ashamed to be noted for such infamy. There are many vices which, although they should be fled from: nevertheless have in them some shadow of manliness. But this is noted as the vilest even among the vilest: Master Venedico de’ Caccianemici of Bologna was the go-between so that the Marquis Obizzo d’Este, Lord of Ferrara, had his sister: who was called Ghisola the Fair. **AND NOT THE ONLY** Bolognese weeping here. He denotes that many Bolognese are filthy with such vice, saying that so many tongues are not **TAUGHT**—that is, prepared—**TO SAY SIPA.** Between the Savena and the Reno: As if to say there are not so many tongues in Bologna where one says *sipa* instead of *sì* [yes]: which Bologna is in the middle of two rivers: one of which is called Savena, about two miles from Bologna toward Romagna on the eastern side. The other is the Reno, of which Pliny makes mention when narrating of the reeds fit for making bow arrows; he writes that no reed is more suited for arrows than that which grows in the Reno of Bologna: because it has much pith and swift weight: this is on the western side of Bologna toward Lombardia. **AND IF OF THIS** you want faith or testimony, recall to mind our greedy hearts. He demonstrates that avarice and the greed for money lead men to such vile and abominable vice. Therefore, the sentiment of the Satirist is most welcome to the avaricious: <note>Juvenal, Satires XIV, 207</note> *No one asks where you get it from, but it is necessary to have it.* <note>original Latin: *Vnde hēas quē rit nemo: sed oportet habere.*</note> **HERE THERE ARE NO** women for coin: that is, for money that is counted. And he says this because he who wants to corrupt a woman has no greater means than money. It is well known that avarice is born from vileness and timidity of soul. Therefore, the elderly and women, because they are of little spirit—the former by the accident of age, the latter by nature—are always avaricious. And of this I could refer to infinite examples: for many have been found similar to Eriphyle: who, corrupted by gifts, betrayed her husband Amphiaraus, who was hiding so as not to be forced to go to the Theban war, in which according to his auguries he was to be killed.

WHERE A CRAG: An arch of a bridge of those that were mentioned above. **FROM THE BANK.** Which he showed encircled the seventh circle and the first ditch of the eighth. **QUITE EASILY.** As for the literal sense, it shows the path was not fatiguing: and allegorically it signifies that having had knowledge of fraud in general, it was an easy thing to recognize this specific kind.

...and turning to the right upon its spur,

which was a spur of rock that came out of a bank. He could not otherwise see the other crowd of souls who, coming with them, turned their backs to them. **FROM THOSE** eternal circles: that is, we moved away from the outermost circle which encompasses all the others, as was shown above. Thus, up to this point, Dante had not yet entered the first bridge. Rather, he was still on the edge or bank which encloses all the ditches within itself; and going to the left he encountered Venedico <note>original: "Venetico," referring to Venedico Caccianemico of Bologna.</note>: having left whom, he now arrives at the first entrance of the first bridge, or rather the first arch of the bridge.

When we were at the place where it hollows
beneath to give passage to the lashed,
the leader said: "Wait, and let the sight 
of these other ill-born spirits stay with you, 
whose faces you have not yet seen, 
because they have been walking with us."
From the old bridge they watched the file 
that came toward us from the other side, 
and which the lash likewise drives away.

The good master, without my asking, 
said to me: "Look at that great soul who comes, 
and for all his pain seems to shed no tears. 
What a royal aspect he still retains! 
That is Jason, who by heart and by wit 
deprived the Colchians of the ram. 
He passed by the island of Lemnos, 
after the bold and pitiless women 
had given all their males to death. 
There, with tokens and with polished words, 
he deceived the young Hypsipyle,

He left her there, pregnant and alone; 
such guilt condemns him to such torment, 
and revenge is also taken for Medea. 
With him go those who deceive in such a way; 
and let this suffice to know of the first valley 
and of those whom it grips in its teeth."

<column-break/>

species: **TO THE RIGHT**: <note>original: "AMANDEXTRA"</note> According to the literal sense, it was necessary to keep to the right hand. **UPRIGHT**: wishing to climb the bridge; and allegorically, one who seeks the knowledge of things always goes to the right hand. **UPON ITS SPUR**: Upon the ridge of such a rock which is hollowed out beneath, as we see in all arches of bridges. And through that vacuum the souls passed; who, because they had not yet been seen face to face, Virgil made me stop and look from the edge of the bridge from which they were entering, so that I could see their faces. **WHERE THE BRIDGE HOLLOWS BENEATH**: that is, it is empty. **TO GIVE PASSAGE TO THE LASHED**. Because they passed under the bridge through the empty space of the first arch. **WAIT**: Be attentive and turned toward them in such a way that the sight which comes from these may **STAY** <note>original: "SEGGIA," literally 'sit' or 'rest'</note> in you. **ILL-BORN**: that is, born to this misery. **STAY** fixed in you: Because being turned toward them, their sight will come to meet you. **FROM THE OLD BRIDGE THEY WATCHED THE FILE**: as if to say the multitude. **WHICH CAME TOWARD US**: until now this multitude had not come toward Dante, but along with Dante. But now, because Dante had crossed their path by climbing onto the bridge under which they passed—and looking from the side where they entered, and not where they exited—he can truly say they came toward us. **FROM THE OTHER SIDE**. **AND WHICH THE LASH LIKEWISE DRIVES**: because just like the others mentioned above, they were beaten by demons. Since it was the same sin, it was deservedly punished with the same penalty.

The meaning is: when we were in the middle of the first circle which is hollowed out beneath, as we see in all arches of bridges. And through that vacuum the souls passed; who, because they had not yet been seen face to face, Virgil made me stop and look from the edge of the bridge from which they were entering, so that I could see their faces.

In this second species of seduction are those who have, with flatteries, drawn women to their will. He gives Jason as an example and many stories intertwined together, which we will not narrate fully at present, because the place does not allow for such length. Nor will we leave them behind entirely, so that the reader does not remain completely untaught regarding them. There were in Thessaly two brothers: Pelias, King of that region, and Aeson. From Aeson was born Jason, who because he was both very beautiful of body and robust, and of great and excellent spirit, desired to do something worthy of memory. Toward this his uncle also incited him, not so much to favor his glory as because he feared—having no male children—that Jason and his father might plot fraud to take the kingdom from him; and he hoped that if Jason crossed the sea for arduous things full of danger, he might easily perish. For this reason, he encouraged him to undertake the task of taking the golden fleece of the ram of Phrixus, which was in Colchis, a city of the Pontus. But so that we may briefly mention the golden fleece:

From Athamas and Nephele <note>original: "Neiphila"</note> were born Phrixus and Helle, who were afterwards driven away by their father due to the falsity of their stepmother Ino. Juno commanded them to mount their ram, which the father had given them, and with it cross the sea. But in this transit Helle, a fearful girl, fell into the sea; and from her that sea is afterwards called the Hellespont. Phrixus arrived in Colchis where Aeëtes <note>original: "Eta"</note> reigned, and consecrated the skin of the ram to Mars. This is what Jason wanted. And for this, he built on Mount Pelion the ship which was called *Argo* after the craftsman who composed it, or else from its velocity, because *argos* in Greek signifies swift. With him went the leaders of Greece, among whom were Hercules, Telamon, Orpheus, Castor, and Pollux. And first they arrived in Lemnos, which island was without males. For when they had gone against the Thracians, they first made sacrifice to all the gods except Venus. Venus wished to avenge herself, and for this she ignited those women with such fury that by common counsel they first killed those males who had remained on the island. Afterwards, when the others returned with victory, they waited for night and when they were asleep, each woman killed her man except Hypsipyle <note>original: "Iſypile: o adir meglio Hiſypile"</note>; who, moved to compassion for her father Thoas the king, secretly sent him out of the island, pretending with honorable funeral rites that she had already killed him. In Lemnos they stayed one year, mingling with the women. And Jason, in order to have Hypsipyle who was then queen, promised to take her as his wife and return there; and he left her pregnant with two sons, Thoas and Euneo. Nor did he ever return to her afterwards. He reached Colchis, but could not have the golden fleece unless he first killed the great serpent that guarded it, and tamed two fierce bulls which had feet of bronze and breathed flames through their nostrils; and with those it was then necessary to sow the teeth of the already dead serpent. From such seed were born armed men whom it was necessary for him to kill. Human strength could not suffice for such a horrendous war. He used cunning, therefore, and with his flatteries drew Medea, the daughter of the king, into his love, and promised to make her his wife. She, who was a very great sorceress, and love for Jason being more powerful in her breast than the bond and obligation...

# INFERNO

With her father’s herbs and incantations, she made Jason the victor; and having stolen the Fleece, she fled with him. But Jason, having arrived at Corinth, showed little gratitude for the benefit—indeed, he was most ungrateful—and repudiated Medea. He took as his wife the daughter of Creon, King of Corinth, called Glauce according to Lactantius, or Creusa according to Seneca. This ingratitude forced Medea to serve Jason his two children as food <note>In most versions of the myth, Medea kills the children to spite Jason, rather than feeding them to him, though the commentator here suggests a more cannibalistic revenge similar to the myth of Atreus.</note>, whom he had fathered with her. Furthermore, having sent poisoned gifts to Creusa, she burned both her and her palace. The corruption of these two women, therefore, is why Jason is punished in this ditch. **BY HEART AND BY WIT:** by greatness of soul and by prudence. He could not have accomplished such an exceptional feat otherwise, had he not possessed great courage in such grave dangers and great prudence in conducting them. For as Sallust says: "There is need of deliberation first, and when you have deliberated, of timely action." <note>original Latin: "Prius consulto: & ubi consulueris mature facto opus est."</note> Therefore, in great matters, prudence is necessary, which first shows you whether a thing should be done or not; and if it is to be done, by what path and in what manner. Then, one must have strength and courage, so that the difficulty and danger do not make one cowardly. Because it is not likely that Jason could have done such great things without these two virtues, the poet attributes them to him. Furthermore, Diodorus Siculus writes the same of him; many of his excellent deeds have been committed to writing, for which divine honors were attributed to him and temples built—which I believe Alexander the Great, moved by envy, caused to be thrown to the ground. **THEN HE PASSED BY THE ISLAND OF LEMNOS.** Lemnos is the island upon which Vulcan fell when his mother Juno, thinking him ugly, threw him from heaven. **OF THE FIRST VALLEY:** of the first ditch, in which the deceivers of women are tormented—those who draw them to do their will, whether for themselves or for others.

Already we were where the narrow path
crosses with the second bank
and makes of that a shoulder for another arch.
From there we heard people who whine
in the next ditch, who snort with their snouts,
and beat themselves with their own palms.
The banks were encrusted with a mold
from the breath below that sticks to them,
which fought with the eyes and with the nose.
The bottom is so deep that the eye
cannot see it without climbing to the back
of the arch, where the rock hangs over most.
There we came, and from there down in the ditch
I saw people plunged in a filth
that seemed moved from human privies.

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Decorative floriated initial 'D' within a square frame.</image-desc>
He describes the second ditch, and shows that they had already passed the first; they arrived at the last "thigh" or slope of the first arch, which is founded upon the bank that divides the first ditch from the second. From that same bank begins the second arch, which goes over the second ditch. **THE NARROW PATH:** the narrow way, that is, the space of the bridge. **CROSSES:** it joins in a cross because these arches do not go along the direction of the valleys, but across them, forming the shape of a cross. **AND MAKES OF THAT BANK A SHOULDER FOR ANOTHER CIRCLE:** that is, for the second one. Having described the path that led them over the second ditch, he describes what kind of punishment is contained within it. He shows that this ditch is full of human excrement, and that souls are plunged into it. They "whine" <note>original: "nicchiano"</note> in this form, which is to say they lament; specifically, *nicchiare* signifies lamenting with a low and complaining voice. **SNORT:** they blow; *sbuffare* is to blow in such a way that the breath comes out with force and a sudden jerk. Therefore, when an angry person grieves and at the same time reviles and threatens with arrogant words, we say he "snorts." **THE BANKS WERE ENCRUSTED WITH A MOLD.** This happens in damp and enclosed places where the vapors rising from such humidity, unable to exhale, remain stuck to the walls and create mold. So in this place, the breath—that is, the exhalation rising from the bottom—rose up so thick that it stuck to the banks and made such a crust <note>original: "gromma"</note> that it fought with the nose and eyes; that is, it offended the nose with its foul odor and the eyes with its ugliness. <meta>catchword: eyes with</meta>

---

it could not be well seen unless one climbed onto the back of the rock, which was like the arch of a bridge. From there, one could look straight down. In this vile and sordid place, the flatterers are punished, who in the Florentine tongue are called *moinieri* <note>Wheedlers or those who use "moine" (fawning gestures/caresses).</note>. Flattery is nothing other than speech containing false praise for the sake of pleasing and acquiring the favor of the one being praised. This vice proceeds only from a vile and servile soul, in which there is no vestige of liberty. Truly, they can be called the dregs of humanity, because in them nothing remains but corruption. Just as in the body of an animal the dregs are nothing but the corrupted part—which nature, in the first digestion made by the stomach, separates from the uncorrupted nourishment and sends down to the lower belly—so from the uncorrupted truth, which nourishes the soul and maintains moral life, the flatterer is separated like a thing corrupted and harmful to human life. Justly, then, it can be said that the flatterer is submerged in dregs, swallowing and vomiting them. Because the flatterer is full of lies, he is nothing but corruption; he feeds on nothing else, nor does he feed others anything else. This person demonstrates friendship and benevolence, yet is the worst enemy. No more pernicious thing can be found by anyone in a position of dignity or lordship than flattery, which, to please them, persuades them that what is evil is good and just. From this proceed many errors that are often the cause of the ruin of princes and great men. Because they believe the false praise, they not only fail to correct themselves of evil, but come to believe things about themselves that are not true. Of this, Juvenal said: "There is nothing a person cannot believe about themselves when their power is praised as equal to the gods." <note>original Latin: "Nihil est quod credere de se non possit cum laudatur diis equa potestas."</note> And rightly Diogenes the Cynic, when asked which beast bites most fiercely, replied: "Among wild animals, the slanderer; and among domestic ones, the flatterer," because with his false praise he leads you to ruin. He added that words composed not to reveal the truth but to please are a honeyed halter. And Plato shows that while an arch friend <note>meaning a true or primary friend</note> aims for health, the flatterer is like a cook compared to a doctor. For the doctor, in giving food, does not seek to please the palate, but to provide health. But the cook intends only to please the taste, and does not care if it is healthy or harmful. So the true friend only has respect for telling the truth to his friend to preserve him in virtue and lead him to it. But the flatterer does not care if others err; it is enough for him to say something that pleases in order to gain his own advantage. Therefore, Cicero in his book *On Duties* warns us: "And even in the most prosperous circumstances, we must especially use the counsel of friends, and give them even greater authority than before. Finally, in these times we must beware lest we open our ears to flatterers, or allow ourselves to be flattered, in which it is easy to be deceived. For we think ourselves such that we are justly praised, from which innumerable sins are born when men, inflated by opinions, are shamefully mocked and fall into the greatest errors." <note>original Latin: "Atque etiam in secundissimis rebus..." from Cicero's De Officiis.</note> We can also say that the poet places them in such punishment to punish the superfluous delicacies, excessive luxuries, and splendid foods which they sought with their flattery and fawning when they were alive; for a vice is most excellently punished by its opposite. <meta>catchword: for</meta>

# CANTO XVIII

And while I searched down there with my eyes,
I saw one with a head so fouled with excrement
that it was not clear if he were layman or cleric.
He cried out to me: “Why are you so greedy
to look at me more than the other filthy ones?”
And I to him: “Because if I remember well,
I have seen you before with dry hair;
and you are Alessio Interminelli of Lucca:
that is why I eye you more than all the rest.”
And he then, beating his pate, [said]:
“Down here the flatteries have submerged me,
with which I never let my tongue go dry.” <note>A metaphor for the constant "licking" or fawning characteristic of a flatterer.</note>

After this, my Leader said to me: “See that you push
your gaze a little further forward,
so that your eyes may fully reach the face
of that filthy, disheveled wench
who scratches herself with dung-filled nails,
and now crouches, now stands upon her feet:
Thais, the harlot, who replied
to her lover when he said: ‘Do I have great
thanks from you?’ <note>original Latin: "apud te"</note>—‘Nay, marvelous!’
And with this let our sight be satisfied.”

<column-break/>

He places in this spot Master Alessio Interminelli, a Lucchese knight and a very great flatterer. **LAYMAN OR CLERIC.** These two words are Greek. Here it is to be noted that Christians are divided into two types: namely, priests and scholars. The priests are the Apostolic Church: and they are the part chosen to rule the secular world: and to instruct them with excellent precepts and an honest life. For which reason they are called clerics: that is, the chosen <note>The commentator derives "cleric" from the Greek *kleros*, meaning "lot" or "portion," signifying those chosen for God's service</note>. But through a corruption of speech, we say clerics. The seculars are the Catholic—that is, the universal—church: and in the spiritual life, they must obey the priests. Therefore, they are called laymen, which is to say "of the people" or plebeian. This concludes that doctrine should reside in the priests: for which reason it is a great infamy for those who are entirely unlearned.

Thais is the harlot of Terence <note>A character from the Roman playwright Terence’s comedy *Eunuchus*</note>: To whom Thraso, a military man, gave a handmaid or, if you prefer, a little slave girl. He then asked Gnatho—through whom he had sent the handmaid—if the gift had been pleasing to Thais, and if she had returned great thanks to him. Gnatho, to flatter him, replied: "Not just great, but marvelous." Therefore, the flatterer was Gnatho; but the poet places Thais here because it was by her will that he used such flattery, and because every harlot—since they do not love the man but his money—is always full of pretenses and flatteries. And because there are two generations of flatterers: some of some name and dignity, although they stain it with such a vile vice; and some who are entirely low, intent on the lowest gain. Therefore, he placed Alessio for the first type and Thais for the second. **DISHEVELED WENCH.** The punishment for the lustful person who adorned their hair in life is that it should now be disheveled. And the punishment for the stubborn pride toward their lovers is that she should be a wench and a slave to torment. And the nails filthy with dregs punish the excessive perfumes she sought in life. And that she now crouches and now stands has its allegory. But it is better to leave wrapped in its own obscurity that which cannot be decently explained. <note>The commentator chooses to avoid describing the more graphic or "obscene" physicalities of the scene for the sake of propriety.</note>

The commentator explains the etymology of clerical and lay terms and justifies the inclusion of these specific figures.</summary>

P. In this place, Messer Alessio Interminei, a knight, was a very great flatterer. LAIC or CLERIC. These two words are Greek. Where it is to be noted that Christians are divided into two types: namely, priests and seculars. And priests are the apostolic church: and they are the elected part to govern the seculars. And to instruct them with excellent precepts and an honest life. Which are of the clerics, that is, the elect: But by corruption we say 'clerics'. ## CANTO XIX OF THE FIRST CANTICLE BY DANTE.

O Simon Magus, o wretched followers,
you who the things of God, which by rights of goodness
ought to be the brides: and you, rapacious,
For gold and for silver you adulterate;
now it is fitting that the trumpet sound for you,
since in the third <term>bolgia<note>A 'bolgia' is a ditch or pouch in the eighth circle of Dante's Hell, where specific types of fraud are punished.</note></term> you stay.
Already we had to the next tomb
mounted upon the rock, at that part
which hangs exactly over the middle of the ditch.

---

O supreme wisdom, how great is the art
that you show in heaven, on earth, and in the evil world,
and how justly your power distributes!
I saw along the sides and across the bottom
the livid stone full of holes,
all of one width, and each one was round:
They seemed to me neither less ample nor larger

<column-break/>

This nineteenth canto: in which it is shown that in the third bolgia the <term>simoniacs<note>Those who buy or sell sacred things, named after Simon Magus.</note></term> are punished: and simony is the sale or purchase of sacred and spiritual things for money or for things equivalent to money. Therefore, whoever sells or buys the sacraments of the church: or any spiritual dignity: or benefice: or other similar things: of which the true price is not gold nor silver, but holiness of life and of character: and virtue: and doctrine, is a simoniac. This name comes from Simon Magus: who was the first to attempt this wickedness in the New Testament. So that this may be more clearly understood, it is written in the Acts of the Apostles: that after the death of the <term>protomartyr<note>The 'first martyr', referring to Saint Stephen.</note></term> Stephen, Philip preached the <note>original: "verbum dei"</note> word of God in Samaria: and converted many through the incredible miracles he performed. There was at the same time in that city Simon, [called] Philip and Magus: who, through the things he did with his magical arts, was held in the highest authority and reputation. This man, together with the others, believed in Philip and was baptized. But as yet the Holy Spirit had not come upon the baptized of Samaria: But when Peter and John later arrived, they prayed for the baptized: and after the prayer they laid their hands upon them: and they received the Holy Spirit. Because it seemed a great thing to Simon that the Holy Spirit should come through the laying on of hands: he offered money to the apostles, so that they might give him such power: that by laying his hand upon a baptized person, the Holy Spirit would come to them. To whom Peter replied: May your money perish with you. And certainly because you thought that the gift of God could be had for money, you have no part nor lot in this matter: And your heart is not right in the sight of God. Keep your money: and pray to God if it is possible that this thought may depart from your heart: because I see you are in the gall of bitterness: and in the bond of iniquity. From this Simon, therefore, those who trade sacred things for a price are called simoniacs in the New Testament: just as in the Old Testament they were named after Gehazi, the servant of Elisha the prophet. When Elisha the prophet cured Naaman, the prince of the army of the King of Syria, of leprosy by the power of God, he would not receive any reward from him: although he had brought many treasures. But Gehazi, Elisha's servant, once Naaman had departed, ran after him and caught up to him: and pretended that two of the sons of the prophets had come to him from Mount Ephraim: and asked for them a talent of silver: and two changes of clothing. Naaman gave him the clothes and two talents. Elisha knew the fraud and avarice of the servant: and predicted to him that the leprosy of Naaman would cling to him: and remain in his generation: and immediately he became white with leprosy. These people, therefore, act against the Gospel of Matthew: which in the tenth chapter writes <note>original: "Quod gratis donante deo accipiunt gratis dent"</note> "That which they receive freely from God's gift, let them give freely." Christ therefore commands through Matthew that spiritual things, which they receive without price from God, they should similarly give to those who deserve them without price. O SIMON, the first author and prince in the Christian church of such wickedness: and you are the first in this bolgia to receive appropriate punishment. MAGUS: that is, an enchanter. 'Magus' in the Persian language means wise man. For this reason, those who among the Greeks were called philosophers, the Persians call Magi. And of this species of philosophers were those three who came to adore Jesus with offerings of gold, incense, and myrrh. But because Zoroaster, one of these Magi, was the first who found such art: therefore it is called the magic art: and those who practice it are called Magi. O WRETCHED followers. O all others equal in having followed the footsteps of this man, you find yourselves in extreme misery. WHO: who are equal. ADULTERATE: you corrupt. THE THINGS of God: the things dedicated to God as we said a little before. WHICH: that is, those which ought to be the brides of goodness: that is, of virtue and of doctrine: and of honest life: and character. An adulterer is he who corrupts and joins himself with her who has a husband. A husband is he who joins himself with her who by legitimate marriage is made his. And because spiritual dignities and benefices should deservedly be conferred upon good and learned priests, we, by a certain similarity, call such things the brides of such men: and those men the legitimate husbands of them. And conversely, all those who acquire them not through any virtue, but through a price—just as the adulterer joins with the adulteress through corruption—are deservedly called adulterers. Wherefore the <term>Aquinate<note>Saint Thomas Aquinas, the famous theologian from Aquino.</note></term> Thomas writes that the simoniac causes the church, which is the bride of Christ, to become pregnant by others than the groom: and simony causes her, though she ought to be impregnated by the Holy Spirit, to be impregnated by the evil spirit. For he knows that God nourishes the adulterous children and disinherits the legitimate ones: because the corruptors possess the benefices they buy with money: and the good and learned, to whom the dignities should be given, remain without any benefice. NOW IT IS FITTING THAT FOR YOU the trumpet sound: that is, it is necessary that I manifest and publish [your sins] in my verses: and this is a metaphor from town criers: who, when they have to publish something with the sound of the trumpet, invite those nearby to listen. ALREADY WE HAD MOUNTED to the next tomb. We said that 'tomb' means burial place. Therefore here he deservedly calls this deep place a burial, where the souls, because they are damned to eternal death, can be said to be buried. FROM THE ROCK: which acted as a bridge. WHICH HANGS EXACTLY OVER the middle of the ditch: that is, it corresponds in a line over the middle of the ditch. 'To plummet' [piombare] is what masons say when they use a plumb line to straighten a stone or the corner of a wall, so that it rises in a straight line.

With this excellent exclamation, he shows that the supreme God, through his infinite wisdom, has known how: and through supreme power, that is, strength, has been able to create the world: which he administers with admirable justice, distributing with perfect proportion to every creature what is due to them: either of reward or of punishment. Therefore, he beatifies the angels. On earth, he gives space and convenience to act in a way that we merit heaven. AND IN THE evil world: that is, in hell, he punishes sinners with more or less heavy penalties according to the crime. I SAW ALONG THE sides: that is, along the banks of the bolgia. AND ALONG THE BOTTOM: that is, down...

> like those that are in my beautiful San Giovanni <note>The Baptistery of San Giovanni in Florence, where Dante was baptized.</note>
> made as places for the baptizers.

that which is born underground: perverts the office of man by contemplating earthly things instead of celestial ones. Therefore, it is a just thing that his face is stuck in the earth. **IN TRAMBE** <note>original: "INTRAMBE"</note>: that is, between one and the other. <term>As if between both<note>original Latin: "quasi intra ambas"</note></term>. **THEY QUIVERED**: they moved with speed. **THE JOINTS**: the articulations. This shows that since they could not move their legs because they were enclosed in the pit, they moved their feet at the joint which connects them to the legs. This literally demonstrates great pain, because we see that those who feel great pain distort their feet. But allegorically, by the feet we understand the desire for earthly things: and by the fast movement of the feet, we understand much greed: and by the fire, the ardor of such greed. **AS IS THE CUSTOM**. An excellent comparison by which he shows that just as the flame follows the oil on the surface: so these souls have followed external fat: that is, worldly goods: and not the internal: that is, celestial goods. **RITORTE**: twisted twigs used for tying bundles. **STRAMBE**: that is, ropes made of <term>alpha grass<note>original: "stramba"; a type of tough grass used for cordage</note></term>: which the Latins call <term>spartum<note>Latin for esparto grass.</note></term>.

> "Who is that one, Master, who torments himself,
> quivering more than his other companions,"
> I said, "and whom a redder flame sucks?"
> And he to me: "If you want me to carry you
> down there along that bank which is more sloped,
> from him you shall learn of himself and of his wrongs."
> And I: "Whatever pleases you is good to me;
> you are my lord, and you know that I do not depart
> from your will, and you know what is left unsaid."
> Then we came upon the fourth bank;
> we turned and descended on the left hand
> down into the bottom, full of holes and narrow.
> The good Master, not yet from his hip
> did he set me down, until he brought me to the cleft
> of the one who was lamenting with his shanks.

Where the author demonstrates that the lower reason and the senses are entirely submitted to the higher reason: which, when it occurs, means there is never discord in the soul: but it always has right and true judgment. So that this may be better understood, let us consider two people: in one, the sensuality is entirely in accord with reason; in the other, it is in discord. We will see that in the latter there will be two different judgments: for reason will judge that divine things should be valued more than money, but sensuality will judge that money should be preferred to divine things. In the former, sensuality is so obedient to reason that it always approves its judgment. Therefore, only that thing is beautiful and good to Dante—that is, to sensuality—which pleases Virgil—that is, to the intellect. **YOU LORD**. Because higher reason ought to command and sensuality obey: and it never departs from its will when it is well-disposed. Furthermore, because reason had knowledge when sensuality was joined with it, it understands not only what is said: but also what is thought, even if it is kept silent. **IS SO GOOD**: that is, lovable and desirable: because <term>love, according to Plato, is nothing other than the desire for beautiful things<note>A reference to the Platonic theory of Eros found in the *Symposium*.</note></term>. **YOU ARE my lord and you know that I do not depart from your will.** He declares the same thing more clearly. **AND YOU KNOW what is left unsaid.** Because reason can comprehend the thoughts of the soul, which he also signified above when he said: *Ah, how cautious men ought to be against those who do not see only the surface, but look into the thought with their wisdom.* **UPON THE FOURTH BANK**: which is between the third and fourth <term>bolgia</term>. And the master did not set him down until he arrived at the pit: because science does not leave us until we arrive at the particulars. **SHANK** <note>original: "zancha"</note> signifies leg.

<column-break/>

in the depths. **THE STONE**: That rock full of round holes, no wider than necessary to receive a single man. And to express himself better, he adds that they were in the likeness of those four equal pits in the temple of John the Baptist <note>The Florence Baptistery.</note> which are around the font placed in the middle of the temple, made so that the priests who baptize may stand in them, so they are closer to the water. **ONE OF WHICH**. It happened that while several children were in the temple of San Giovanni and playing, as is their custom, one fell into one of the double pits; and since he could not be gotten out in any other way, Dante struck it; and with his own hand he broke the pit and saved the child. **AND LET THIS be a seal to undeceive everyone.** He says this so that no one believes he wished to violate sacred things, or that out of impiety he had broken that pit, but rather to save the child. **FROM THE mouth of said pits: OF EACH ONE**: that is, each pit. **PROTRUDED**: the feet and the legs extended out. **UP TO THE CALF**: up to the flesh where the leg begins to thicken. And certainly he assigns a very fitting punishment for this vice. For whereas man was created to contemplate God and celestial things, and for this reason was produced with his face raised to heaven, which the beasts bow toward the earth—the simoniac, who out of greed sells divine things to have gold and silver, which are born under the earth, perverts the office of man.

Dante asks who is the one who torments himself more than the others: and Virgil says he does not know, but promises to carry him to him. This signifies, as we have said many times, that science does not give knowledge of particulars: but it leads you right to them. Just as, <term>for example<note>original Latin: "verbi gratia"</note></term>, science does not show that Boniface is a simoniac. But by demonstrating this universal truth—that whoever sells sacred and divine things for money is a simoniac—it conducts the senses and the lower reason to recognize that Boniface, who sells sacred and divine things for money, is a simoniac. Therefore, Virgil carries Dante to the bottom where he was: that is, the intellect carries the lower reason into the knowledge of that vice in general, in which Dante then sees Boniface: that is, he knows the particulars. **QUIVERING more than his other companions**: that is, the others who are placed in the same sort of punishment. **REDDER FLAME**: The redder the flame, the greater the vitality and force it demonstrates. **SUCKS**: correctly said, because heat draws moisture to itself; therefore it sucks it. **WHICH MORE pleases**: which is deeper. **OF HIMSELF and of his wrongs**: that is, of his errors and vices: because just as every virtue has rectitude, so every vice is "wrong" or "twisted." **IS SO GOOD to me**: that is, it seems so beautiful to me As much as it pleases you. The meaning is that a thing seems beautiful to me in proportion to how much it pleases you: as if to say that according to whether it pleases you more or less, it seems more or less beautiful to me—that is, desirable.

<summary>Dante describes the physical punishment of the simoniacs, buried head-first in holes with their feet on fire, and explains his past action of breaking a baptismal font to save a child. The commentary interprets Virgil as Higher Reason leading Dante (Lower Reason) to recognize specific sinners like Pope Boniface VIII.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Canto XIX of the Inferno, where Dante encounters the Simoniacs. The previous page described the physical setting of the third bolgia (ditch), and this page identifies the specific souls punished there—notably Pope Nicholas III—and provides a scathing historical critique of the papacy, including the "prophecy" of Boniface VIII’s damnation.</meta>

# CANTO XIX

-> "O you, whoever you are, who keep your upper part down,
sad soul, planted like a stake,"
I began to say, "if you can, speak a word."
I stood like the friar who confesses
the treacherous assassin who, once he is fixed,
calls him back so that his death is delayed.
And he cried out: "Are you already standing there,
are you already sated with that wealth
for which you did not fear to take by deceit
the beautiful lady, and then make a mockery of her?" <-

**PLANTED**: <note>original: "commesso"</note> that is, fixed in the earth as one drives a stake. **I STOOD**: **Assassin**: an assassin is one who kills a man for money. It comes from this Latin verb *assideo* <note>original Latin: "assideo", meaning to sit beside</note> which means to stop near something. This is because such people lie in wait near the place where they estimate the person they want to kill must pass. The punishment for assassins is that they are to be "planted" <note>original: "propaginati", a legal punishment where the condemned was buried alive head-first</note>. Therefore, it happens that the assassin, once his head is fixed in the pit, often calls back the friar to listen to some remaining sin because he does not die immediately. Thus, the confessor must bend his ear to the ground if he wishes to hear the voice coming from beneath the earth. And so Dante had to do, wanting to hear that soul. And certainly, whoever wishes to consider the nature of the simoniac <note>someone who buys or sells sacred church offices</note> must fix his eyes and ears to the ground: that is, direct his thoughts toward earthly things. **AND HE CRIED OUT**. The poet’s marvelous genius is shown here; wishing to damn Pope Boniface for simony, and not being able to find him in Hell because he was still alive at the time of the vision, he has this soul predict his arrival. This shows that the soul's opinion was mistaken in thinking Boniface had died some years earlier than expected. Dante does this because he wants the shade to believe he is speaking to the one he expects, having been deceived by Dante's voice. **ARE YOU SO SOON SATED WITH THAT WEALTH**. Through these words, he damns the folly of men: those who labor so hard to acquire treasures, only for death to sate them in a short time. Pope Nicholas of the Orsini family <note>Nicholas III, reigned 1277–1280</note> lived as Pope for three years, eight months, and twenty days. This man, in order to leave his relatives wealthy, was a great simoniac. In life, he understood through prophetic revelation that Boniface was to be a great simoniac and remain in the papacy for eight years and nine months. After Nicholas came Martin <note>Martin IV</note>, a man who would have been of laudable life were it not for his gluttony. After Martin succeeded Pope Celestine <note>Celestine V</note>, of whom we spoke above in the third canto; and after Celestine, Boniface. **THE WRITING HAS LIED TO ME BY SEVERAL YEARS**. If you are already there, the prophecy is not verified: because eight years and nine months are still missing two years and nine months. For this is the time Boniface lived after the day Dante feigns to have descended into Hell, which was in the year of salvation 1300, and Boniface died later in 1303. **TO TAKE THE BEAUTIFUL LADY BY DECEIT**: Because with fraud he occupied the papacy of the Christian Church, which he calls a "beautiful lady." So that this may be properly understood, I say that in the year of Christ 1294, the cardinals were in Puglia, much pressured by the Pugliese because through their discord they had been without a Pope for more than two years. Therefore, after much debate, they elected Brother Peter of Sulmona, a man of holy and very austere life, who lived in penance on Morrone, a mountain not far from Sulmona. He was Celestine V. In the month of September, he created twelve cardinals, four of them from across the mountains, to please Charles II. Afterward, he went with the court to Naples, seeking to renounce the papacy because he was a very simple man and little suited to governing. There was in the College of Cardinals Sir Benedetto of Anagni <note>the future Boniface VIII</note>, a very effective man of great prudence and cunning, extremely greedy for power and of great spirit. He, knowing the will of the cardinals and of Charles—who both greatly desired to change the Pope—persuaded Celestine to make a decree by which it was lawful for any Pope to renounce the papacy. Once this was done, Celestine, during the celebration of Saint Lucia and in the presence of the cardinals, renounced the papacy. With great joy, he returned to his cloister to perform his accustomed penance, after having sat in the papacy for five months and eight days. Then, through the favor of Charles—to whom he had promised to use all the forces of the Church to recover Sicily for him—the aforementioned Sir Benedetto was elected High Pontiff and became Boniface VIII. He, seeing that by law Celestine’s renunciation might not be valid and that every good Christian considered him the true Pope, took him from the mountain at San Angelo in Puglia, where he had retired to holy solitude, and imprisoned him in the fortress of Fumone. There, in a short time, he died and was buried in a small church of the friars of his order, placed more than ten cubits deep so that he could not be found. Boniface was more greedy for power than is becoming for a priest, and with his prudence, he increased the state of the Church. He was very greedy for money without any conscience, and had a proverb that for the exaltation of the Church, anything was lawful. **YOU DID NOT FEAR TO TAKE BY DECEIT** because he fraudulently persuaded Celestine to renounce. **THE BEAUTIFUL LADY**: that is, the Roman Church, which he calls a lady because she is the bride of Christ and of his vicars. **AND THEN MAKE A MOCKERY OF HER**: because he did not hold her as a husband, but as an adulterer with his simonies, selling her.

-> I became like those who stand
for not understanding what is answered to them,
as if mocked, and they do not know how to answer.
Then Virgil said: "Tell him quickly..." <-

<column-break/>

**B**ecause a man's recognition consists in his face, Dante could not recognize this man, who did not show his face, but his feet, as he held his lower part up. **THE UPPER PART**: <note>original: "EL DI su"</note> that is, the part that is beaten from above. And certainly, those men who stand with their heads fixed—that is, all their thoughts and speculations, which they ought to raise to heaven, they submerge in the earth through avarice (that is, in the greed for earthly things)—hide their faces from us in a way that we cannot know them. This means nothing other than that they transform their character so much that they seem more like cruel beasts than men. Nor can one know they are men because they do not live according to reason, which alone makes us men, but according to appetite, which is common to us and all beasts. Nature, therefore, gave us—alone among all animals—a face raised to heaven, to show that our thoughts ought to be of celestial things. And to the brutes, she gave a face bent toward the earth because, being without reason, they can look at nothing but earthly things. For this reason, anyone who leaves the thought of high things and looks only at the low turns his head upside down. Ovid clearly demonstrates all this in these verses: <note>original Latin from Ovid's Metamorphoses, Book I</note> <term>While other animals look down at the earth, He gave to man a face held high, and commanded him to look at the sky and raise his upright countenance to the stars.</term> <meta>Catchword: "CHome pal" (like a stake)</meta>

**I**t happens to everyone who asks a question: if the answer given is such that he does not understand it, he remains in shame and ambiguity. **THEN Virgil**: it was necessary with "superior reason"—which, when we do not find the truth regarding particulars, returns to universals. And therefore he feigns that Virgil teaches him such an answer because it is a universal thing: that when one person mistakes you for another, someone else shows you that he is the... <meta>Catchword: "lon" (likely "lontano" or part of a name)</meta>

The commentary provides an extensive historical account of the transition of the papacy from Celestine V to Boniface VIII, emphasizing the themes of greed and the subversion of spiritual office for earthly gain.</summary>

# INFERNO

"I am not he, I am not he whom you believe,"
and I replied as was commanded me.
At this the spirit twisted both his feet;
then, sighing with a voice of weeping,
he said to me: "Then what do you ask of me?
If it matters so much to you to know who I am
that you have for this reason run down the bank,
know that I was vested with the great mantle <note>The "great mantle" refers to the papal robes, symbolizing the office of the Pope.</note>.
And truly I was a son of the she-bear <note>original: "figliuol dellorsa"; a reference to the Orsini family (from "orsa," bear), one of the most powerful noble houses in Rome.</note>,
so greedy to advance the 'little bears' <note>his nephews/kin</note>
that I put my wealth up there, and here I put myself in a purse <note>A pun on the "bolgia" or pouch of hell and the money-purses used in simony.</note>.
Below my head are the others dragged down,
who preceded me in committing simony <term>simony: the sin of buying or selling sacred church offices or spiritual preferences</term>,
flattened through the fissures of the rock.
Down there I shall also fall when
he comes whom I believed you were
just then when I made my sudden question.
But the time is already longer that my feet have cooked
and that I have been thus upside down
than he shall stay planted with red feet;
for after him shall come a lawless shepherd <note>A reference to Pope Clement V, who moved the papacy to Avignon.</note>
of even uglier deeds, from the west,
such that he must cover both him and me.
He shall be a new Jason, of whom one reads
in the Book of Maccabees; and as to that one
his king was soft, so to this one shall be he who rules France."

I do not know if I was here too foolish,
that I replied to him in this same meter:

<column-break/>

...far from the truth. **IF IT MATTERS SO MUCH TO YOU TO KNOW WHO I AM.** He replied, therefore,
that he had been the Supreme Pontiff. **AND TRULY I WAS A SON OF THE SHE-BEAR.** That is, I was of the House of Orsini. But I can deservedly call myself a bear: because just as that animal is insatiable in its food, and especially because it provides for its young, so I was insatiable for money to advance my "little bears" <note>The "orfatti" or cubs, referring to his nephews</note> to glorious deeds: so that I (that is, while in the world) put my wealth into a purse because I accumulated money. **AND HERE** in Hell I put myself in a purse—calling the hole in which he was "the purse." **BELOW MY HEAD ARE THE OTHERS**: that is, the simoniac popes who were my equals. **PRECEDED**: they went before me and were my predecessors. **DRAGGED**: pulled to the bottom through this fissure in the entrance of which I am placed. **DOWN THERE I SHALL FALL**: I will drop to the bottom. **ALSO**: similarly to them; and I will leave this entrance vacant for Boniface, whom I believed you were. But he will stay for less time than I have been thus planted; because after him, from the western parts, will come a shepherd of even uglier and more foul deeds than his, so that my shameful misery and that of Boniface will be covered by his own. These words were spoken by Giovanni Gaetano of the Orsini family. Who, in 1277 <note>The text says 1276, but Nicholas III was elected in late 1277.</note>, was created Pope Nicholas III. This man, before he reached the pontificate, led a laudable life. But afterward, his spirit growing through the heat of comforts, he attended to extolling his kin; and he skillfully permitted them to use every kind of simony. He made them very rich and lords of many lands; he created seven Roman cardinals nearly all related to him. And among these was Jacopo Colonna to reconcile that family to himself, so that they would not league with his enemies, the Annibaldeschi—not without the astonishment and offense of many, because the Colonna family had been condemned and deprived of every ecclesiastical dignity by Alexander III, because their origin being from Germany, they had favored Frederick I against the Church. He built grand palaces near Saint Peter’s; he occupied Bologna and the entire countryside of Romagna, which the Emperor Rudolph had pledged because he did not cross into Italy. This was considered an unjust thing, as it was manifest to all that it was not lack of will, but great impediments that prevented Rudolph from crossing. He then appointed Bertoldo Orsini, his nephew, as Count of Romagna, and sent Latino Brancaleoni, the son of one of his sisters and already a cardinal, as legate to Bologna. **FROM THE WEST A LAWLESS SON.** After Boniface came Benedict XI, a man excellent in both letters and character; he died, as many believe, in the ninth month and was buried in Perugia. After him, the cardinals remained in contention for eight months because they were divided into two parties: one headed by Matteo Orsini and Francesco Gaetano, nephew of Boniface; the other by Napoleone Orsini dal Monte and Niccolò da Prato, who before the cardinalate had been in the Order of Preachers <note>The Dominicans</note>, a man much esteemed for both doctrine and prudence. This man joined cunning to force, and in secret persuaded Francesco Gaetano to consent to Raymond de Got, Archbishop of Bordeaux, who was a Gascon and an enemy of the King of France. And then he wrote immediately to the King, who was Philip the Fair in Paris, that if he desired to recover his status with the Church and raise up the Colonnesi, his friends, he should reconcile with Raymond, who had already been elected Pope as his enemy. The King wrote immediately to Raymond that he should come to meet him for most important matters, and Raymond, riding with speed, was with him on the sixth day. They swore faith to one another upon the altar. The King first reconciled him with Charles of Valois, called "Charles Lackland," his brother. Then he said it was in his power to make him Pope, and that he would do so if Raymond promised him certain things. Raymond, most greedy for such dignity, threw himself at the King's feet and thanked him greatly for returning good for evil, promising to be always ready for his every demand. The King asked first that he re-communicate <note>lift the excommunication of</note> him and his followers for the excesses committed against Boniface. Second, that he grant him the tithes of his kingdom for five years to cover the expenses made in the Flemish war. Third, that he extinguish and annul the memory of Boniface. Fourth, that he restore to the cardinalate Jacopo and Pietro Colonna, who had been deprived by Boniface. Fifth, that he abolish the Order of the Templars. The sixth grace he reserved in his heart. Raymond consented and, like a wicked simoniac, bought the papacy with this price. The King wrote back to the Cardinal of Prato to ensure those of his party consented to Raymond, Francesco Gaetano, and his followers. By this fraud, Raymond was created and called Clement V, on the fifth day of June 1305, the Church having been vacant for six months and ten days. And then on the eleventh day of November, he was crowned at Lyon on the Rhône, and he observed the promises to the King of France. Furthermore, he made twelve cardinals, some Gascon, some French, but all men of the King. **NEW JASON.** This man was a Hebrew, brother of Onias, High Priest of Syria, who held Jerusalem <note>original: "hierosolima"</note>; and he promised to give three hundred and sixty talents of silver, and eighty from other revenues, and besides these, another hundred and fifty talents if the King would grant him the principate. Having obtained it, he abandoned the ancient sacrifices and the Mosaic laws, and instituted the cult of the Gentiles, and wrestling pits, and gymnasiums where he made the youth exercise lasciviously. And in the brothels he kept boys. And finally, he had led all the priests to the games of the Gentiles and to every generation of luxury. Nor were they ashamed to send to Tyre for the quinquennial games 300 drachmas to make a sacrifice to Hercules. But after three years he lost the principate, deceived by Menelaus just as he had deceived his brother, and went into exile among the Ammonites. Clement will thus be a "New Jason," because he will acquire the pontificate through simony, just as Jason acquired the High Priesthood.

It seems doubtful whether an inferior should rebuke a superior. And for this reason, the poet takes his excuse, so that without arrogance he may, with utmost liberty, rebuke the extreme...

<meta>This page continues Dante’s dialogue with Pope Nicholas III in the third ditch of the eighth circle. After the Pope finishes his prophecy regarding his successors, Dante launches into a stinging rebuke of the papacy's corruption, which the accompanying commentary explains in historical and theological detail.</meta>

# CANTO XIX.

"Tell me now, how much treasure did
our Lord require from Saint Peter
before he put the keys into his keeping?
Surely he asked for nothing but 'Follow me.' <note>original: "uienne retro"; a reference to the Gospel of Matthew where Jesus calls Peter.</note>
Nor did Peter or the others take from Matthias
gold or silver when he was chosen by lot
for the place that the guilty soul <note>Judas Iscariot</note> had lost.
Therefore stay there, for you are rightly punished;
and guard well the ill-gotten money
which made you so bold against Charles. <note>Charles of Anjou, King of Naples and Sicily.</note>
And were it not that I am still forbidden
by the reverence for those supreme keys
which you held in the joyful life,
I would use words even more grave;
for your avarice brings grief to the world,
trampling the good and elevating the wicked.

The Evangelist <note>John the Apostle</note> was aware of you shepherds
when she who sits upon the waters
was seen by him fornicating with kings;
she who was born with the seven heads,
and from the ten horns had her strength,
as long as virtue pleased her husband. <note>Dante uses the imagery of the Whore of Babylon from Revelation to describe the corrupt Church.</note>
You have made a god of gold and silver;
and what else is there between you and the idolaters,
except that they worship one, and you worship a hundred?
Ah, Constantine, of how much evil was the mother,
not your conversion, but that dowry <note>The "Donation of Constantine," a forged document used to justify the Pope's temporal power and wealth.</note>
which the first wealthy Father <note>Pope Sylvester I</note> received from you!"
And while I sang these notes to him,
whether anger or conscience gnawed at him,
he kicked out fiercely with both his feet.

<column-break/>

avarice and the wicked <term>simony: the sin of buying or selling sacred church offices or spiritual preferences</term> of the unjust shepherds who adulterate the bride of Christ <note>The Church is traditionally viewed as the "Bride of Christ."</note>. **NOW TELL ME** how much treasure our Lord wanted. Here he shows that Christ did not sell his office to Peter for gold or silver, nor did he ask anything of him except that he follow him. For the Gospel of Matthew says that Christ, having given the keys to Peter, said only "Follow me and come after me," which signifies following his doctrine and observing his precepts. **NEITHER PETER NOR the others**: someone might say Christ did not ask gold of Peter, but human fragility and need cannot be equaled to divinity. And for this, he adds that not even the Apostles sold the place of the apostolate to Matthias, which the wicked soul of Judas lost. For when the eleven Apostles wished to elect one in place of Judas, they took Joseph called Barnabas and Matthias; and after casting lots, it fell to Matthias. And one can rightly compare the simoniac to Judas: because Judas sold Christ, and the simoniac sells the grace of the Holy Spirit. **THEREFORE STAY THERE**, you, Nicholas: as if to say, you are not worthy that anyone should have compassion for your just punishments. **AND GUARD WELL the ill-gotten money**. This is a bitter mockery, which is deservedly suited to such a wicked simoniac. For comforting him to look after the treasure unjustly acquired—which he cannot do, because here one leaves every earthly good, and there it cannot be used—is nothing other than reproaching him for his folly, in that he wished to prefer transitory things to eternal ones. And this is a rhetorical device called **concession** <note>Granting a point ironically to mock an opponent.</note>. As when Virgil says: "Go then to Italy with the winds, seek your kingdom through the waves" <note>original Latin: "Isequere italiā uentis pete regna p undas"; from the Aeneid, Dido’s bitter farewell to Aeneas.</note>. **WHICH MADE YOU bold against Charles**. Nicholas took such courage from his riches that he requested of Charles I, who was of the royal blood of France, that he give one of his nieces to his own nephew. But Charles replied that although he had "red feet" <note>A reference to the red boots of the French nobility.</note> he was not worthy to make a marriage alliance with the blood of France. These words created such indignation in the heart of Nicholas that he took the vicariate of Tuscany away from Charles, and in time consented to the rebellion of Sicily <note>The Sicilian Vespers of 1282.</note>, for which he received a great sum of money through the hands of Messer Giovanni da Procida, the leader and author of the rebellion. And in this way Charles lost Sicily, which he had held from the Church, and acquired not without much blood. **AND IF IT WERE NOT**. He shows that the reverence for the papacy which he held does not let him use more bitter words; and he uses a rhetorical device called **occupation** <note>also known as praeteritio: mentioning something by saying you won't mention it.</note>. For he shows he does not wish to say what he is actually saying.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'U' showing a robed figure, possibly the Evangelist John, holding a book and gesturing towards the heavens.</image-desc>

The poet wishes in this place to interpret a text from the Apocalypse, that is, from the Revelation of John the Evangelist, showing that everything said there was directed against simony and the other vices of the shepherds. John writes thus in his Apocalypse:

"One of the seven angels who had the seven bowls came and spoke with me, saying: 'Come, I will show you the damnation of the great harlot who sits upon many waters, with whom the kings of the earth have committed fornication, and those who dwell on the earth have been made drunk with the wine of her prostitution.' And he took me away into the desert in spirit: and I saw a woman sitting upon a beast full of names of blasphemy, having seven heads and ten horns. And the woman was arrayed in purple and gilded with gold, and precious stones, and pearls, having a golden cup in her hand full of the abomination and filthiness of her fornication. And on her forehead was written: 'Babylon the great, mother of the fornications of the earth.'" <note>This is a translation of the Latin text from Revelation 17:1-5 provided in the original.</note>

Therefore, this harlot adorned with gold and gems, who sits upon the water on a beast which has seven heads and ten horns, is a figure of the cardinal Church corrupted by simony and luxury. This woman sits upon the waters, that is, upon the peoples, because scripture often uses water to represent people. While she pleased her spouse, Christ, she was well placed upon the beast, red with the blood of martyrs, and with seven heads which are the seven sacraments: Baptism, Confirmation, Eucharist, Penance, Ordination, Marriage, and Extreme Unction. Or else the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit: the gift of Piety against envy; of Fear against pride; of Knowledge against sloth; of Fortitude against anger; of Counsel against avarice; of Understanding against luxury; of Wisdom against gluttony. Or else the seven virtues: the four moral ones—Prudence, Justice, Fortitude, and Temperance—and the three theological ones—Faith, Hope, and Charity. She had strength from the ten horns, meaning she was demonstrated and figured by the ten commandments given to Moses while **VIRTUE pleased her husband**. This signifies while virtue pleased the Pope, who is the husband of the Church. For while the Popes lived virtuously and without avarice and luxury, it was verified that this woman sat upon the beast of the ten horns. But afterward, she began to "play the harlot" with kings, that is, to become a prostitute for temporal kings, because for money she sold her dignity and benefits and her liberty, just as the harlot for money sells her body and her chastity. **YOU HAVE MADE a god of gold and silver**: because, setting aside all religion and fear of God, you consider money to be God. **AND WHAT ELSE**. There is no difference between you and those who worship idols, except that they worship one idol and you worship a hundred; and he uses "a hundred," a finite number, for the infinite, because the money you worship is infinite. Of these the prophet Hosea says: "They have reigned, but not by me; they have been princes, and I knew them not." <note>Hosea 8:4.</note>

<summary>Dante delivers a fierce denunciation of Pope Nicholas III and the sin of simony, equating the corrupt Church with the Whore of Babylon from the Book of Revelation. The commentary provides historical context on the political feuds between the Pope and Charles of Anjou and interprets the biblical symbolism used in the poem.</summary>
<keywords>Simony, Pope Nicholas III, Revelation, Whore of Babylon, Charles of Anjou, Donation of Constantine, Seven Sacraments, Seven Virtues, Biblical Commentary, Sicilian Vespers, Avarice</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Cristoforo Landino’s commentary on Canto XIX of the Inferno. It concludes the rebuke of Pope Nicholas III and describes Virgil’s approval of Dante’s harsh words. The text focuses on the "Donation of Constantine" and the transition from the third to the fourth ditch of the eighth circle.</meta>

->### INFERNO.<-

"Of their silver and gold they made idols for themselves, that they might be cut off." <note>original Latin: "Aurum suum & argentum suum fecerunt sibi idola ne interiret" from Hosea 8:4.</note> And the Psalmist says: "The idols of the nations are silver and gold." <note>original Latin: "Simulacra gentium argentum & aurum" from Psalm 115:4.</note>

**AH CONSTANTINE.** The poet implies that while the Church was poor and had no property of its own, it lived always in the highest sanctity. But once it began to possess worldly goods, wealth introduced every kind of vice. It is for this reason that Petrarch, with righteous indignation, rises up against the apostolic Church, saying: *You were not nurtured on feathers in the shade, but naked to the wind and barefoot among the thorns; now you live so that the stench reaches God.* <note>Landino quotes Petrarch’s Sonnet 138, which criticizes the corruption of the Papal court in Avignon.</note> Therefore, because Constantine—having been converted by Pope Sylvester and made a Christian—was the first to endow the Church, the poet laments not his conversion, but the "dowry" <note>The "Donation of Constantine," a document later proven to be a forgery, which claimed the Emperor gave the Pope temporal power over Rome and the West.</note> he gave to the Pope, the father of Christians. He was the first to become wealthy, whereas the others had lived in extreme poverty. The poet follows the most common and universal opinion regarding Pope Sylvester and the Emperor Constantine. However, because there are various opinions concerning his conversion and the endowment of the Church, and each has very serious authors, I do not wish to be so arrogant as to interpose my own judgment. For this reason, we shall leave the dispute undecided and leave the final judgment to more learned men.

**WHILE I SANG SUCH NOTES TO HIM:** that is, I spoke such words to him openly. He says "notes" to maintain the metaphor of singing, for one who sings uses notes. **EITHER ANGER,** to which Dante’s harsh words incited him, **OR CONSCIENCE** regarding his <term>simony</term> <note>Simony is the sin of buying or selling sacred things or ecclesiastical offices.</note>—whichever of these two things it was—**HE KICKED HARD:** that is, he writhed. **WITH BOTH HIS SOLES:** <note>original: "piote," a term for the soles of the feet.</note> "Springare" means to move the legs forcefully as if to strike. Thus we say a horse "springs" when it kicks.

<column-break/>

I truly believe it pleased my Guide,
  as he always listened with such a satisfied expression
  to the sound of the true words I spoke.
Therefore, he took me in both his arms,
  and once he had me completely against his chest,
  he climbed back up the path where he had descended.
Nor did he tire of holding me so close,
  until he carried me to the top of the bridge
  that crosses from the fourth to the fifth bank.
There he gently set down his burden—
  gentle because of the rugged and steep ridge,
  which would be a difficult path even for goats.
From there, another valley was revealed to me.

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'A' featuring a seated figure and floral vine work.</image-desc>

Dante perceived that Virgil was pleased by the reprimand given to the Pope, because **WITH ATTENTIVE LIPS,** that is, he listened with attentive lips, which signifies hearing in silence. This demonstrates that it is always very pleasing to the intellect when, in human actions and the active life, <term>prudence</term> <note>represented here by Virgil</note> reproves and condemns wicked vices with great freedom. And the fact that he carries Dante back up the mountain shows that once the "lower reason" has understood a specific point, the intellect leads it back to "universal truths" by a steep path—that is, through difficult speculation. By carrying him and pressing him to his chest (where thought resides), it denotes that the contemplation of universal truths is what gives us true knowledge. Not without reason does he make a comparison to **GOATS.** For this animal, while grazing, always climbs upward and does not descend. Hence, the sign of the winter tropic is called **CAPRICORN,** because the sun begins to ascend there. Similarly, whoever proceeds in contemplation must always ascend to more excellent things and never descend.

<meta>This page continues the transition from the nineteenth canto (dealing with simonists) to the twentieth canto of the Inferno, where Dante describes the punishment of those who attempted to see into the future.</meta>

<header>INFERNO.</header>

### CANTO XX OF THE FIRST CANTICLE BY DANTE.

Of new punishment I must make verses
and give material to the twentieth canto
of the first song concerning those who are submerged.
I was already fully prepared
to look into the uncovered depths
which were bathed in anguished weeping.

And I saw people through the round valley
coming silent and weeping at the same pace
as processions <note>The original refers to "letanie," the solemn litanies or religious processions common in the medieval world.</note> make in this world.
As my gaze descended lower upon them,
it appeared marvelously to be twisted,
each one between the chin and the start of the torso,
For the face was turned toward the loins;
and it was necessary for them to come backward,
because seeing forward was taken from them.
Perhaps by the force of paralysis <note>original: "parlaſia"</note>
someone was once so completely twisted;
but I did not see it, nor do I believe it to be so.

So may God let you, reader, gather fruit
from your reading, now think for yourself:
how I could keep my face dry

<column-break/>

The poet continues in the first description of the trenches <note>The "bolge" or ditches of the eighth circle of Hell.</note> and states that in the fourth trench, the diviners of whatever kind are punished. And certainly, it was a very ancient opinion confirmed by the consensus of all nations: that among men there is a certain presumption and science of future things, which the Latins call *divination* <note>original: "diuinatione"</note> and the Greeks call *Mantice* <note>original: "Mantice," referring to mantic arts or prophecy.</note>. This is either natural or artificial. Natural divination involves divine frenzy and dreams. Since many were moved by divine frenzy, such as the oracles among the pagans and the prophets among the Hebrews, they predicted future things. Dreams are of three kinds: Sometimes one dreams what is to happen, but it requires interpretation—like the man who dreamed of pressing grapes into a cup, and Joseph interpreted that he would become the king’s cupbearer <note>A reference to the story of Joseph in Genesis.</note> and serve him at the table. Sometimes one dreams of seeing the thing in the same way it will be, and this is called a *vision* <note>original: "uiſione"</note>. Sometimes someone appears in the dream to tell you things clearly as they will be, and this they call an *oracle* <note>original: "oracolo"</note>. But often these are combined, as in Virgil’s Aeneas, who saw Hector in a very sad and mournful form and heard the words in which he comforted him to flee. Artificial divination includes Haruspicy, Augury, Astrology, and Sortilege. Haruspicy <term>Haruspicy: the ancient practice of divining the future by inspecting the entrails of sacrificed animals</term> involves the divination taken from the shape, location, and color of the internal organs of the animal they sacrificed; as on the morning of the day Caesar was killed, the heart of the ox he sacrificed was not seen. Augury <term>Augury: interpreting the will of the gods through the behavior of birds</term> is the divination made either from the eating habits or the chirping of birds. For augurs would sometimes offer food to chickens kept in cages for this purpose, and depending on how they ate, they interpreted the outcome of an event. Sometimes they watched the flight and song of birds in the air, and judged according to their species. For there is one augury from the crow, another from the magpie, another from the woodpecker, and others from different birds; and it matters if they sing or fly in one way or another, or if they come from the right or from the left. Nor are birds alone used; other animals also give good and bad auguries, such as wolves, foxes, dogs, and snakes. Nor are the "monsters" and omens <note>original: "portenti"</note> which occur against nature very different from these. Hence, in the army of Xerxes, because a mare gave birth to a hare, the augurs announced the timid flight of that army. Astrology predicts future things according to the various courses of the stars, in which there are conjunctions, oppositions, sextiles, trines, quadratures, and other aspects. And they claim Geomancy <term>Geomancy: divination by interpreting markings on the ground or patterns formed by tossed handfuls of soil, rocks, or sand</term> is a species of this, which we will discuss in Purgatory. And *Sortes* [lots] were found according to the ancients in the city of Praeneste, today called Palestrina. There is also Pyromancy <term>Pyromancy: divination by fire</term>, Necromancy <term>Necromancy: communicating with the souls of the dead</term>, Hydromancy <term>Hydromancy: divination by water</term>, and Chiromancy <term>Chiromancy: palm reading</term> which considers the lines of the hand. All these things would require a long discourse if we wished to explain them in order. But time is not enough for one who proposes such a long and diverse subject. **OF NEW PUNISHMENT.** As if unusual and unheard of and greater than the others; he makes the listener attentive by promising unusual and significant things. **AND GIVE MATERIAL** to the twentieth canto: that is, to the twentieth chapter. **OF THE FIRST SONG:** that is, of the first canticle. There are three canticles: Inferno, Purgatory, and Paradise. The Inferno contains 34 cantos, and the other two each contain 33 cantos. Thus, in total, there are one hundred cantos divided into three canticles. **CONCERNING THOSE WHO ARE SUBMERGED:** that is, those whom I plunged into the center of the earth. He does not submerge the song, but describes the submerged Hell within it. Some texts say: "Of the first songs and of the submerged," meaning the damned who are submerged in the center of the earth. And it follows that he was already disposed to see the uncovered depths of the earth: that is, what he could see from the bridge where he was. **WHICH WAS BATHED IN WEEPING:** by those who are being punished.

1. The punishment of these people is set as this: that they have their faces turned backward. And to see where they are going, they must walk backward. This is a very appropriate punishment, where the contrary is punished by its contrary. He who wanted to see too far ahead <note>to see the future</note> may now only see behind. And he who was so bold as to want to see the future—which God has denied to man as something not useful to him—is thus restrained. It is not likely that if God could give us true knowledge of future things and if they were useful to us, He would have withheld them; for God wills every good, being supreme goodness. **PERHAPS BY FORCE OF PARALYSIS.** *Paralysis* in Greek is a disease which, because it loosens the connections of the nerves, induces trembling of the limbs or twists them; in our language, it is called "palsy" <note>original: "parletico"</note>. He concludes that although this disease twists the limbs, nonetheless it never twisted anyone into this form. One might see a neck twisted by paralysis so that the person looks sideways, but no one is seen so twisted that they look backward. This is an excellent comparison. For just as the paralytic always trembles, so these people who seek future things

always tremble: that is, they live in fear and anxiety about whether what they predicted will happen or not. They are always wavering and doubting, considering their points and moments, signs, bird songs, changes in the air, from which side it thunders or lightnings, marks on the ground, the movement of fire; and finally, a sneeze often makes them change their purpose.

**SO MAY GOD LET YOU GATHER FRUIT** from the reading, meaning he who learns by reading. Therefore, the fruit of this reading is to recognize the folly of those who want to foresee the future. And not without reason does Dante show great compassion. For since knowledge is the supreme perfection of our soul, it seems that...

The commentary provides an extensive encyclopedia of ancient and medieval divination methods, from astrology to animal entrails.</summary>
