<meta>This page continues the commentary on the twentieth canto of the Inferno, where Dante and Virgil observe the Fourth Trench of the eighth circle, containing the sorcerers, diviners, and false prophets who are punished by having their heads twisted backward.</meta>

<header>INFERNO CANTO XX.</header>

When I saw our human form from nearby
so twisted that the weeping from the eyes
bathed the buttocks at the cleft,
I certainly wept, leaning against one of the crags
of the hard rock, so that my guide
said to me: "Are you still among the other fools?
Here piety <note>The Italian word "pietà" means both "pity" and "piety." Virgil is using a wordplay: true piety toward God's judgment requires the death of pity for the damned.</note> lives when it is well dead;
who is more criminal than he
who feels passion for God's judgment?"

He wept, and Virgil rebukes him, which signifies that the sensory part [of the soul] induces passion for every punishment, even if it is justly given; but reason prohibits a man from being moved to pity by punishments justly inflicted by God. And then he says "Here," meaning in Hell, where the one who has erred is punished. "Piety lives when it is well dead," as if to say, this place is piety without having pity. But it should be noted here that "piety" <note>original: "pieta"</note> among the Latins is a virtue through which one bears due affection for one's country and those joined to us by blood, and from this are born compassion and congratulation. Compassion is sorrow for the neighbor’s ill, and congratulation is joy for the neighbor’s good. Therefore, in this place, he uses "piety" for "compassion." Furthermore, it seems to be the conclusion of the wise that in no way should we have compassion for the punishments of the sinner, but rather for his misery, grieving that he has fallen into such error. However, although Dante—who signifies sensuality—has felt compassion for the sinner in many places, he has nonetheless not been rebuked by Virgil as he is here. This shows us that for those who have sinned through fragility, there is some excuse; but the error of these people [the diviners], even in life, has always been mocked.

"Lift your head, lift it, and see him for whom
the earth opened before the eyes of the Thebans,
so that they all shouted: 'Where are you rushing,
Amphiaraus? Why do you leave the war?'
And he did not stop falling headlong
down to Minos, who seizes everyone.
Look how he has made a breast of his shoulders:
because he wanted to see too far ahead,
he now looks behind and walks a backward path."

I saw Tiresias, who changed his appearance
when he became a woman from a male,
transforming all his members;
and afterward, he had to strike again
the two entwined serpents with his rod
before he could regain his masculine plumage.

<column-break/>

...compassion for him who, by laboring to know, becomes more ignorant. And some say that he shows so much compassion toward these people because he recognizes himself to have been in such error; but I do not believe this, because Dante was a true mathematician, a science which no wise man ever despised.

**W**HEN our image from up close I saw so twisted: that is, Dante perceived the human image, and then the image of these people was distorted when he was near them. This is to signify that one does not recognize this vice unless it is well considered. For at first glance, wanting to pursue this science <note>referring to divination</note> seems like a virtue and not a vice. But we understand that foreseeing the future is not of human nature, but belongs to God. Whence he says: *Tell me the prior things and the newest things, and I will say that you are gods* <note>original Latin: "Praeiora & nouissima nunciate mihi & dicā quod dii estis," from Isaiah 41:23</note>. And Lucan: *The mortal race is knowledgeable of the fates of the gods* <note>original Latin: "Sortifque deorū gnarū mortale genus"</note>; and in the Book of Kings: *For man sees only those things that appear, but God looks upon the heart* <note>original Latin: "Non. n. uidet homo nifi ea que apparent. Deus autem intuetur cor," from 1 Samuel 16:7</note>. Dante.

**L**ift your head. Because weeping, Dante stood with his head bowed. "And see him for whom the earth opened." Before the eyes of the Thebans: that is, in the sight of the Thebans, and before their seeing eyes. This was Amphiaraus, who had his origin from Jove. For from Aeolus, son of Jove, was born Erithius; and from Erithius, Amythaon, who fathered Bias; and from Bias, Antiphates; and from Antiphates was born Oicles, father of Amphiaraus. This man was most skilled in auguries <note>original: "augurii," the practice of divining the future from the flight or song of birds.</note>. In his time, Adrastus, king of the Argives, was preparing a great army to restore Polynices, his son-in-law, to the Theban kingdom. For this reason, he went up to the mountain with Melampus and learned through auguries that he was to perish in that war. Therefore, striving to flee the danger, he hid himself so that he would not be forced to go; but Argia, wife of Polynices, promised Eriphyle, wife of Amphiaraus, a noble necklace adorned with most precious stones, which Vulcan had made, if she would reveal him. The greedy and vain wife revealed him. Thus, forced to go to the war, in the first battle, being armed in his chariot, he was swallowed by the earth with the chariot and the horses. Whence Dante feigns that he fell headlong into Hell. This man was held in such reverence that the ancients built him a temple and established sacrifices for him. "WHERE ARE YOU RUSHING..." Where are you falling? "And why do you leave the war?"—hostile words full of derision and scorn.

**T**iresias, according to the fables, was a Theban; and making his journey one day through a forest, he encountered two serpents entwined together, which, upon being struck with his rod, caused him suddenly to change from male to female, and in that sex he remained for seven years. Then, in the seventh year, returning to the same forest in the same place, he found the same serpents; and thinking they had the power to change sex again, he struck them with the rod and returned from female to male. They also say that there being a dispute between Jove and Juno as to which was the greater pleasure in intercourse, that of the male or the female, and not agreeing, they submitted to the judgment of Tiresias, who had experienced both. He pronounced that in females there was greater fury and lust. Nor did he give such a sentence without natural reasons. For granted that the male is hotter than the female—because his complexion is more sanguine while that of the female is phlegmatic—nevertheless, in the male there is only one pleasure in the casting of the seed. But in the woman it is double: both in the casting of her own and in the receiving of that of the male into the womb, which, being by nature quite cold, once warmed by this seed, takes great pleasure in it. And the heat lasts a long time because the thicker the matter that is heated and the colder it was, the more it maintains the heat, as we see in iron and other similar things. Furthermore, in the female, the instrument is always ready; the opposite is true in the man. Pronouncing therefore such a sentence, Tiresias...

<summary>Dante observes the agonizing physical distortion of the diviners and is rebuked by Virgil for his misplaced pity. The commentary provides mythological and "scientific" backgrounds for Amphiaraus and Tiresias, explaining their presence in this circle of Hell.</summary>

<columns>2</columns>

Juno was so offended that out of anger she took away the light of his eyes <note>Referring to Tiresias, who was blinded by Juno for siding with Jupiter in an argument about whether men or women enjoy pleasure more.</note>: and Jove, in compensation and restoration for this loss, gave him the light of the mind. Thus he made him a diviner and gave him knowledge of future things. Therefore, when the Cadmeans <note>The descendants of Cadmus, the founders of Thebes.</note>, lords of Thebes, were in danger because they were besieged by Alcmaeon, Tiresias predicted to them that their escape lay in fleeing and abandoning the city. Consequently, they withdrew to Tilphossa, a region of Boeotia. There, when Tiresias died, he was buried most honorably by the Cadmeans. Thebes was taken and sacked, and Daphne, daughter of Tiresias, was sent to Delphi to the temple of Apollo and dedicated to him. There she became excellent in the art of divination and composed many oracles in verse, many of which Homer placed in his poem; and she was called a Sibyl, because in that language <term>Sibyllen</term> <note>original: "sybillen"</note> signifies giving the oracle with a living voice. Homer also feigns that in the underworld Tiresias predicted many things to Ulysses. **Changing all the limbs.** Because not only is the sex different in a woman, but also all the limbs have a different quality in a female. **And first and then** understand that first it was necessary for him to strike the serpents to change from male to female, and afterward to strike them again to return from female to male. **The masculine plumage.** He uses "plumage" <note>original: "penne"</note> to mean hair. It is as if he says the beard and other hair which the male has and the woman does not.

---

**Aruns is the one who has his belly as a back,**
**who in the mountains of Luni, where hoes**
**the Carrarese who dwells below,**
**had a cave among the white marbles**
**for his dwelling, from which to watch the stars,**
**and the sea did not cut off his view.**

**And she who covers her breasts,**
**which you do not see, with her loosened tresses,**
**and has all her hairy skin on the other side,**
**was Manto, who searched through many lands,**
**then settled there where I was born;**
**concerning which it pleases me that you listen a little.**
**After her father had departed from life,**
**and the city of Bacchus became enslaved,**
**she wandered for a long time through the world.**

...of the wives of the kings already dead, whose bodies Creon forbade to be buried; Theseus, king of Athens, came with an army against Creon and took the city from him and made it tributary. Thebes having been reduced to servitude, Manto searched many countries and finally came to Italy, where by Tiberinus—the god of the Tiber—she gave birth to Ocnus, whom Virgil in the tenth book <note>Aeneid X, 198-200</note> writes built Mantua.
> He too, Ocnus, summons a troop from his native shores,
> son of prophetic Manto and the Tuscan river,
> who gave you walls and his mother’s name, O Mantua. <note>original: "Ille etiā patriis agmen ciet Ochnus ab oris / Fatidice mātus & tuſci filius amnis / Qui muros matris que dedit tibi Mātua nomē."</note>
This Ocnus, because he was very strong in body and soul, was also called Bianor, because <term>bia</term> in Greek signifies bodily strength, and <term>aner</term> signifies what the Latins call <term>virum</term> [man]. Thus Bianor is interpreted as "manly strength." His tomb was famous near Mantua. Whence in the *Bucolics* <note>Eclogue IX, 60</note>, the same Virgil writes: "For the tomb of Bianor begins to appear." <note>original: "Nanque sepulcrū incipit apparere Bianoris."</note> Ocnus therefore built Mantua and gave it the name of Manto, his mother. Although Dante varies the history somewhat, you will read it in the following verses.

**Above in beautiful Italy lies a lake**
**at the foot of the Alps that shut in Germany,**
**above Tyrol, which is named Benaco.**
**By a thousand springs and more, I believe, it is bathed**
**between Garda and Val Camonica and the Apennines**
**with the water that stagnates in said lake.**
**There is a place in the middle where the bishop of Trent**
**and those of Brescia and Verona...**

<column-break/>

**ARUNS IS THE ONE.** Lucan places this man as a Tuscan augur in the city of Lucca. He was called to Rome by the Senate, which was eager to know what end the war between Caesar and Pompey would have. There, having sacrificed a bull and attributing part of the entrails to Pompey and part to Caesar, he recognized in them that Caesar was destined to win. **Aruns is the one who has his belly as a back** <note>original: "el uentre flagatterga"</note>: that is, for whom the belly, which should be the front part, **is made a back** <note>original: "se glatterga"</note>: that is, it becomes the rear part. For <term>tergum</term> in Latin signifies the back and the loins, which are the rear parts of a man, just as the chest and the belly are the front part. But because this man had his face turned around, it happened that the belly was in the place of the back. **WHO IN THE mountains of Luni:** He states that this augur inhabited the mountains of Luni, below which is Carrara; and therefore says **Where the Carrarese hoes** <note>original: "ronca"</note>: that is, cultivates the land. And he used one species and part of agriculture for all agriculture. For <term>runcare</term> in Latin signifies to uproot and pull out weeds and briars and harmful things. Luni was once a noble city, but today it is extinct; the nearby region is called Lunigiana. **AMONG White marbles.** It is as if he says: he lived in the quarries of white marble which are in the district of Carrara. Whence his view was not **CUT OFF** <note>original: "tronca"</note>: that is, lopped or sliced, from seeing the stars and the sea.

<insert>G</insert> <image-desc>Decorative initial G with a face in profile looking left.</image-desc> Great abundance and eloquence are found in our poet, who, having already shown in three persons that the face was turned toward the shoulders, does not state the same meaning with the same words, but with different ones. For first he says, "When I saw our form from nearby so twisted that the weeping from the eyes bathed the buttocks at the cleft." And afterward he said, "Aruns is the one who has his belly as a back." And at present he says, "And she who covers her breasts." Thus there are three different ways of speaking, and nevertheless all signify that these people have their faces turned over their shoulders. **AND HAS ON THE OTHER SIDE:** that is, behind. **ALL HER HAIRY SKIN.** Because the pubic area <note>original: "pettignone"</note> in which the hair is found, and which is naturally in front, in these people is behind because they have the face turned around. And the hair [of the head] which, hanging down, usually covers the loins, in this person covers the belly. Manto, according to Diodorus Siculus, was the daughter of Melampus. This man, being a great diviner and having freed the Argive women from the furies—whom Bacchus had made mad—deserved that Anaxagoras, son of Megapenthes king of Argos, should give him two parts of the kingdom and his daughter for a wife, who was named Iphianira; and by her he fathered Manto. This is what Diodorus writes. But others say she was the daughter of Tiresias, and they say that after the death of her father, the city of Bacchus—that is, Thebes, where Bacchus the inventor of wine was born—became enslaved. For after the battle of the Seven Kings, Eteocles and Polynices the Theban kings being dead, Creon, a most cruel man, occupied the tyranny in Thebes. But shortly afterward...

<column-break/>

Virgil, being induced to state the origin of Mantua, his homeland, it was appropriate that such a poet should narrate concerning his homeland not without the highest eloquence and various ornaments of speech. Therefore, this <term>chorographia</term>—that is, the description of the Mincio river and the region—demonstrates Virgilian eloquence and the site where Mantua is. **Up above** in the world: which is a place above those who are in Hell. **BEAUTIFUL ITALY:** for so he shows it in his *Georgics*, in which he treats its praises. **AT THE FOOT OF THE Alps that shut in Germany.** These are the mountains which divide Italy from Germany <note>original: "magna"</note>. **TYROL** <note>original: "Tiralli"</note>: This is a county at the entrance of Germany whose counts are called Tyrolese. **WHICH lake...**

could mark it as his own, if he took that path:
There sits Peschiera, a beautiful and strong fortress
to face the Brescians and the Bergamasques,
where the shoreline descends the furthest:
It must be that there falls away
whatever cannot stay in the lap of Benaco;
and it becomes a river down through green pastures.
As soon as the water begins to run,

all the way to Governo where it falls into the Po.
It has not run far before it finds a hollow,
through which it spreads into a marsh;
and in the summer, it is sometimes sickly.

Passing through there, the cruel virgin
saw land in the middle of the swamp,
without cultivation and bare of inhabitants.
There, to flee all human company,
she stopped with her servants to practice her arts;
and there she lived, and there she left her empty body.
The men who were scattered around later
gathered at that place, which was strong
because of the swamp it had on all sides.
They built the city over those dead bones;
and for her who first chose the place,
they named it Mantua without any other omen.
Already its people within were more crowded,
before the madness of Casalodi
received deceit from Pinamonte.
Therefore, I charge you, if you ever hear
of my city having a different origin,
let no lie defraud the truth.

And I: "Master, your reasonings
are so certain to me and so take my faith,
that others would be like spent coals to me.
But tell me of the people who precede us,
if you see any among them worthy of note."

<column-break/>

**IT IS NAMED BENACO.** This is its ancient name. Whence Virgil: *rising with waves and a roar, Benacus, like the sea.* <note>original: "fluctibus & fremitu assurgens Benace marino"</note> But today it is called Lake Garda, because Garda is a town situated on the shore of this lake. Benaco, therefore, is located between narrow mountain valleys, such that the force of the winds generated by such narrowness stirs up fluctuations and storms in this lake similar to those of the sea. Furthermore, they say that its bottom holds golden sand, upon which the carp feed—most delicious fish, which many say are not found in any other water. **BY A THOUSAND AND MORE.** Infinite streams and springs and rivers fall from the nearby mountains into Benaco. Garda is on the shore of the lake toward Verona. Valmoniaca <note>referring to Val Camonica</note> is a valley in the territory of Brescia. The Apennines are a most celebrated mountain range, which begins at the promontory of Monaco—formerly called Meneto—facing the Ligurian Sea. It divides all of Italy along its length; on the right, it has the Tyrrhenian Sea, called the "Lower" sea, and on the left the Adriatic, called the "Upper" sea; and it passes all the way into Sicily, as we have said elsewhere. **A PLACE IS** In the middle, there where the pastor of Trent <note>the Bishop of Trent</note>. He shows that this lake is in the middle of Trent, Brescia, and Verona, such that the dioceses—that is, the bishoprics—of these cities reach the middle of the lake and border each other there. Thus, the pastor—that is, the bishop—of each of these three cities could mark, that is, give his blessing there as if in his own diocese. This is because, by Canon Law, no bishop can give a blessing except in his own diocese. **COULD MARK IT** If he took that path: that is, going through that place. **PESCHIERA** is a strong castle located at the end of the lake, and it is in the diocese of Verona. **EQUIPMENT** <note>original: "arnese"</note> signifies an instrument, or household goods, or decoration. **TO FACE** to encounter, resist, and withstand. **WHERE THE HOLLOW:** <note>original: "lama"</note> properly, a "lama" is a concave and humid place. For this reason, near rivers, we call certain grassy places covered by trees "lame." But here he calls the lake a "lama." **DESCENDS THE FURTHEST:** is lower. Whence the water exits from here, and beginning to run out of the lake, it changes its name and is called the Mincio. **ITS HEAD:** <note>original: "mette co"</note> reaches its head, because "co" in the Lombard language means "head" <note>the source or beginning of the river</note>. The Mincio is born from Benaco and comes all the way to Mantua where it again stagnates around the city, generating heavy and unhealthy air. **GOVERNOLO** is a castle located where the Mincio stagnates and forms a swamp, which in the summer, because it almost dries up, creates bad and diseased air. **AND IN THE SUMMER** it is sometimes sickly: We call "gramo" <note>sickly/wretched</note> one who is greedy and desirous; and because he who desires lacks what he wants, we also call "gramo" one who is needy; and because he who is in need is in misery, we call "gramo" one who is miserable and unhappy.

<image-desc>Decorative historiated initial 'D' showing a scholar seated at a desk with an open book, representing the commentator Cristoforo Landino or the poet.</image-desc>
He shows how Manto, after searching through many countries, stopped in the place surrounded by this swamp as a solitary thing, suitable for her incantations, by which she fled human company; and for this reason, he calls her "cruel." He further shows that after the death of Manto, the surrounding inhabitants built the city where Manto had lived and was later buried; and from her name, they called it Mantua. **SHE LEFT HER EMPTY BODY:** that is, void; because the dead body remains void of the soul. **WITHOUT OTHER OMEN** <note>original: "sanza altra sorte"</note> i.e., without seeking lots or auguries to name the city. For the ancients, once a city was built, they named it after some augury, as Alba was named from the "alba"—that is, the white sow—found there. **ALREADY WERE THE PEOPLE.** He touches on a history that is not very ancient. They say, therefore, that Casalodi was a castle in the territory of Brescia, and it had counts called the Counts of Casalodi, who occupied Mantua and became its lords and tyrants. There were at that same time in Mantua many families of gentlemen, of whom those lords were not a little suspicious, and they greatly feared their power. Among these, Pinamonte de' Buonacolsi, a man of great spirit and no little prudence, took the wise counsel to seize the lordship from Casalodi. Therefore, seeing that the people were very hostile toward the gentlemen, and estimating that once these were driven out it would be easy for him to obtain the prize, he simulated great affection toward the lord, who was Count Alberto da Casalodi. He persuaded him to banish all the nobles to the countryside for a time, demonstrating that this would be so pleasing to the people that, for such a benefit, they would become favorable to him. Alberto believed the fraudulent counsel. Thus, Pinamonte, seeing the city empty of gentlemen, made himself head of the people, and with their favor, having driven out the Casalodi, he became the lord.

<image-desc>Red rubricated initial 'C'.</image-desc>
A fitting response from a disciple toward his teacher. For the first quality a disciple should have is to lend undoubting faith to his doctrine. And therefore he says, "your reasonings take my faith": that is, they acquire my faith and make it so that my faith is entirely in him. "So," that is, in such a way. **THAT OTHERS:** that is, other reasonings. **ARE SPENT COALS TO ME.** i.e., they give me no light or knowledge. "But tell me of the others, if any there are worthy of..."

on which alone my mind resides:
Then he said to me: "The one who from the cheek
stretches his beard over his brown shoulders,
was there when Greece was so empty of males
that they barely remained for the cradles,
an augur; and he gave the signal with Calchas
in Aulis to cut the first rope.
Eurypylus was his name: and thus sings
my high tragedy in some place;
you know it well, for you know the whole work.

&nbsp;

That other who is so thin in the flanks
was Michael Scot, who truly
knew the game of magical deceptions.
See Guido Bonatti, see Asdente,
who now wishes he had attended to his leather
and his twine, but he repents in vain.
See the wretched women who left the needle,
the shuttle and the spindle, and made themselves diviners;
they performed sorceries with herbs and with images.

&nbsp;

But come now, for he who holds the confines
of both hemispheres and touches the wave
below Seville—Cain and the thorns—
And already last night the moon was round;
you should well remember, for she did you no harm
at any time through the deep forest."
Thus he spoke to me, and meanwhile we walked on.

<column-break/>

¶ **NOTE** <note>original: "nota"</note> that is, worthy of making note and mention: because my mind and will **RESIDES**, that is, it stops only for this. **THE ONE WHO FROM THE CHEEK STRETCHES HIS BEARD OVER HIS SHOULDERS.** Dante had already shown the same meaning in three ways. Now he shows it in a fourth. For the beard cannot fall from the cheeks onto the shoulders unless the face is turned backward. **IT WAS WHEN Greece was empty of males:** that is, in the times when Agamemnon, King of the Greeks, went against the Trojans, and led such a multitude in his armies that he left behind almost no one but children; and this is a hyperbole. **AUGUR** he was an augur and his name was Eurypylus: who, together with the other augur named Calchas, when all the ships were full of Greeks in the port of Aulis, told them the hour and the prosperous moment to leave the port. And therefore he says: **TO CUT the first rope:** that is, the rope of the first ship, which is to say the flagship. Because ships in port stay at anchor, and when they are in a hurry to leave, they do not wait to pull up the anchor, but cut the rope that is tied to it. Whence Virgil says: <note>original: "Tortosque incidere funes"</note> *And to cut the twisted ropes.* Aulis is a port in Boeotia, not far from Tanagra, where Agamemnon gathered a thousand ships to go to the siege of Troy. Eurypylus was the one who Sinon says the Greeks sent to the oracle of Apollo to learn how they could appease the gods so they would grant a favorable voyage to return to Greece. Whence Virgil says: <note>original: "Suspensi Eurypilum scitatum oracula Phebi mittimus isque aditis hec tristia dicta reportat"</note> *In suspense, we send Eurypylus to consult the oracles of Phoebus [Apollo], and from the shrine he brings back these grim words.* **AND THUS IT Sings, my high tragedy, in some place:** Called a tragedy both for the excellence of the style, which belongs to tragedies—for which reason in the *Eclogues* <note>original: "buccolica"</note> he says: <note>original: "Sola Sophocleo tua carmina digna coturno"</note> *Your songs alone are worthy of Sophocles' buskin [the high style of tragedy]*—and for the subject matter, which is indeed tragic.

&nbsp;

<insert>¶ Some want this Michael to have been Spanish, whose custom in those times was to wear very affected clothing and to gird themselves tightly. Whence they want him to say: *He who is so thin in the flanks.* Others say he was from the island of Scotland, and therefore he calls him Michael Scot. But all conclude that he was an excellent astrologer and a great magician. And often he would host banquets without any preparation of food, and then at the hour of eating he would compel spirits to bring it from various places; and he would say: "This comes from the kitchen of the King of France," and "This from that of the King of England." He was the astrologer of Frederick II <note>Holy Roman Emperor, known for his scientific interests and patronage of scholars.</note>, and wrote a book for him which Benvenuto <note>Benvenuto da Imola, an early commentator on Dante.</note> claims to have read, and in it he says he had knowledge of many signs of nature. He predicted to Frederick that he would die in Florence; but the ambiguity of the name deceived him. For he did not die in our city, but in Apulia in a castle called Firenzuola. He saw that his own death would come from a small stone of a certain weight, and so it happened. For being in church with his head uncovered to honor the body of Christ, the bell rope caused a small stone to fall on his head; weighing it, he knew it was the weight he had foreseen and judged himself dead; and so he died. **GUIDO BONATTI** was from Forlì; and how excellent an astrologer he was is shown by a book of astrology which he composed, and today is much esteemed by astrologers. He was accepted by Count Guido da Montefeltro, who was lord of Forlì; and they say he never moved against enemies, nor went into battle, except at the hour given to him by this man, and that he always returned victorious. Furthermore, when Guido Bonatti went with him into battle against the French, he predicted that he would be wounded in the thigh; and so it was, and he immediately treated himself with egg whites and tow <note>coarse flax used for bandages</note> which he had carried for this purpose. Nevertheless, he was once outdone by a lowly peasant, who affirmed that it would rain on a day when Guido said it was impossible to rain; and asked how he knew this, he replied: from his donkey, which, when pulled from the stable, had shaken its ears a great deal. **ASDENTE** was from Parma and a shoemaker, a man without letters; and nonetheless he gave himself to the art of divining, and in that—either by the kindness of the heavens which inclined him to this, or by some other means—he was excellent and predicted many things. And especially that Frederick had to attempt to build the city called Victoria near Parma and would be defeated. **BUT TOO LATE HE REPENTS:** for in Hell there is no redemption <note>original: "in inferno nulla est redemptio"</note>. **SEE THE WRETCHED WOMEN:** After specific cases, he comes to the general, and shows many women to have been malicious and enchantresses, who, leaving sewing, weaving, and spinning—feminine arts—gave themselves to sorceries using various herbs and images of wax and earth.</insert>

&nbsp;

<insert>¶ He admonishes Dante that it is now time to depart because the day approaches; and he uses "Chronographia," that is, a description of time. He says then: **COME NOW:** because already the moon, which is in opposition to the sun, touches the western horizon; that is, it is already setting and going below. The sky is round and therefore is called a sphere. But because half is above us and the other half is below, this sphere is divided into two parts; and they are called hemispheres, that is, half-rounds. And let us imagine a line which girds all the sky on every side around and divides the upper hemisphere from the lower; and it is called the horizon, that is, the boundary and almost the divider. Therefore, when a star rises from the hemisphere below to ours and reaches the horizon, which is the confine between one and the other, then it begins to be seen by us. Likewise, on the opposite side, when it has descended through all our hemisphere and already touches the western horizon, then it sets and is no longer seen. Furthermore, it is to be noted that when the moon is round [full], then it is in opposition to the sun. And therefore when the sun rises on the eastern horizon, the moon sets on the horizon...</insert>

<summary>In this passage, Virgil identifies several famous diviners and magicians in the fourth trench of the eighth circle, including Eurypylus, Michael Scot, and Guido Bonatti. The commentary provides rich anecdotal history for these figures and concludes with an astronomical explanation of the time.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Cristoforo Landino’s commentary on Canto XX of the Inferno. The previous page ended mid-sentence discussing the geographical location of the sunset; this page concludes that thought and proceeds to explain the astronomical and allegorical significance of the moon’s position as Virgil and Dante prepare to leave the fourth bolgia.</meta>

<page-num>91</page-num>
<header>INFERNO</header>

...western. Therefore, by the poet saying that the round moon touches the boundary of both hemispheres—that is, the western horizon which is below **Seville**—it demonstrates that day was approaching, because the sun was beginning to reach the eastern horizon. And this is stated perfectly according to <term>physics</term> <note>Here referring to natural science and astronomy.</note>. But when he says "touches the wave," he speaks according to the opinion of the common people. For when a star goes beneath the other hemisphere, because the sea lies between us and it, it appears to fall into the sea. But since the heavens have a spherical nature, and the elements likewise, and it being the nature of heavy things to descend from every side toward the center, it is necessary that in whatever part the moon finds itself, it is always equally distant from the water with an equal interval. And in this, he imitates the Latin poets, who, not out of ignorance but to imitate the folk tales of the common people, often describe the sun or another planet as either plunging into the sea when it sets or emerging from it when it rises.

**CAIN AND THE THORNS**: That is, the moon, in which the common people—seeing a certain shadow—believe there is a Cain who carries a bundle of thorns on his shoulder <note>This refers to the medieval Italian folk belief regarding the "Man in the Moon."</note>. But what this shadow truly is will be demonstrated in the third <term>cantica</term> <note>The *Paradiso*, specifically Canto II.</note> and in the description of the Heaven of the Moon. **Cain** was the firstborn of Adam and was a farmer, just as his brother Abel was a shepherd. He was the first murderer. For, seeing that the sacrifice Abel made to God from the firstborn of his flock was more pleasing than the one he made from the first fruits of his grain, moved by envy, he killed him. And **Cain** in the Hebrew language signifies "possession" or "lamentation" <note>original: "poſſeſſione ouero lamentatione"</note>.

**BELOW SEVILLE.** This is a noble city in the western part of Spain. From it is named the strait <note>The Strait of Gibraltar.</note> that emerges from the Ocean sea and divides Spain from Africa.

**AND ALREADY LAST NIGHT**: When you found yourself lost in the forest; and then it helped you somewhat that the moon shone through the darkness of the night and the forest. Night signifies blindness and ignorance, in which we go wandering in the forest of vices. Nor can we see the sun—that is, the light of true reason. Nevertheless, Dante not yet having formed a fixed <term>habit</term> <note>A philosophical term for a settled disposition or character trait.</note> in vice—although he did not see the sun which might show him the true path—the light of the moon (which is nothing other than the reflection of solar rays) nonetheless showed it to him in some part. But so that I may better express my concept: I say that he who is in vice but has not yet made it a habit, although he does not possess the sun (true reason), nonetheless clothes himself in the reflection of it in the moon—which represents earthly things. For knowing the truth of earthly things is a good beginning for wanting to flee them and seek the divine.

<meta>This page begins the commentary and text for Canto XXI of the Inferno. It follows the transition from the fourth to the fifth ditch (bolgia) of the eighth circle, Malebolge.</meta>

# INFERNO CANTO XXI OF THE FIRST CANTICLE BY DANTE.

The twenty-first canto follows, in which he places the fifth <term>bolgia</term><note>A 'bolgia' is a ditch or trench; Dante uses this term for the ten circular trenches that make up the eighth circle of Hell.</note>: and in it, he describes the punishment for the sin of <term>barratry</term><note>In the Middle Ages, barratry referred to the selling of public offices, or political corruption and graft—the secular equivalent of simony.</note>. He shows, therefore, that in this ditch there is a lake of pitch which continually boils. In this, the barrators are plunged. The punishment is certainly fitting for the sin. First, it should be noted that barratry is the selling or buying of that which

> Thus from bridge to bridge, speaking of other things
> which my comedy cares not to sing,
> we came and held the summit when
> we stayed to see the other fissure
> of Malebolge and the other vain laments;
> and I saw it miraculously dark.
> As in the arsenal of the Venetians
> the sticky pitch boils in winter
> to caulk their unsound ships
> that they cannot sail; and in its place
> one builds his ship anew, and another plugs
> the ribs of that which has made many voyages.
> One hammers at the prow and another at the stern;
> others make oars, and some twist ropes;
> one patches the foresail and another the mainsail.
> So, not by fire but by divine art,
> a thick pitch boiled down there
> which overspread the bank on every side.

ought to be done by one's own office without a price; thus justice is sold as well as injustice. Because that which we ought to do for free and without price, we do for a price. And if someone deserves to obtain something because they ask for it justly, nonetheless we do not grant it to them unless they buy it back. And likewise, we absolve those who deserve to be punished. Therefore, they boil in the pitch. Just as pitch is black and dark, so is the reputation of these people blackened and infamous. Hence Solomon says: <note>original Latin: "qui tetigit picem coinquinabitur ab ea"</note> *He who touches pitch shall be defiled by it*. Likewise, as pitch is tenacious and viscous, so he who is infected with barratry—which is born of greed—cannot be detached from it. Likewise, as pitch is dark and nothing can be seen within it, so the barrator is covered and hidden, and this vice is committed secretly. **THUS from bridge to bridge**: that is, from the bridge of the fourth ditch to that of the fifth. **OTHER speaking which my comedy cares not to sing**: As if to say, we discussed many other things pertaining to divine matters which I have not written in this book. And certainly, besides the principal types that have some shadow of knowledge, many are so old-womanish and childish—which silly women believe can predict the future—that they are so ridiculous a learned man is ashamed to write them. **HELD the summit**: that is, the top of the bridge which is the middle point from where one could best see the whole valley of the fifth ditch. **STAYED to see the other fissure**: that is, the other valley which was like a crack between those rocks. **VAIN laments** because they bear no fruit and are of no use. **AND I saw it**: that is, I saw that which was: **MIRABILment** [miraculously] **dark**: that is, much darker than the others for the reason given above. Because both the judge or others who sell, and similarly the one who buys, hide themselves as much as

<column-break/>

can be hidden, and there is no thing that is done more secretly: because infamy results for both parties. And it is certainly a thing altogether adverse to humanity: because from this is born the overthrow of kingdoms and republics. From it, discord is born in public and in private. Wherefore, with the greatest detestation of such a horrendous vice, Virgil cries out: 
<note>original Latin: "Vendidit hic auro patriam dominúmque poteté imposuit pretioque leges fixit atque refixit." From Aeneid VI. Translation: "This man sold his country for gold and imposed a powerful master; for a price he made and unmade laws."</note> 
**As in the arsenal**: no differently did that pitch boil there than it boils in the arsenal of Venice when they wish to tar the ships with it. **In winter**: When one does not sail, so that they may be repaired for the summer when one does sail. **AND one builds his ship anew in its place**: that is, in that exchange. **AND others twist ropes**: that is, make ropes which are made by winding and twisting hemp. **AND one patches the foresail and another the mainsail**: there are three sails on ships, the largest is the mainsail <note>original: "artimone"</note>, the smallest is the foresail <note>original: "terzeruolo"</note>, and one in the middle of the two which is called the 'meza' [middle sail]. **SO not by fire but by divine art**: that is, by divine order. **WHICH overspread the bank on every side**: The literal meaning is clear. But allegorically, to 'overspread the bank' signifies that both he who sells justice and judgments and he who buys are 'overspread'—that is, trapped by greed. Thus the courts of republics and princes, and especially the Roman court, are an arsenal where in the winter—that is, in the fluctuations and tumults of men—the pitch boils; that is, greed, which ensnares and ignites minds to the desire for possession. Because of this, he who has in his power magistrates, preeminences, judgments, and sentences does not contribute or judge without a foul price. Whence it happens that the good are depressed and the wicked exalted.

> I saw it clearly, but saw nothing in it
> except the bubbles which the boiling raised,
> and the swelling and settling of it all compressed.
> While I was gazing down there fixedly,
> my leader, saying "Look, look!"
> drew me to himself from the place where I stood.
> Then I turned like a man who is slow
> to see what he must flee from,
> and whom a sudden fear unnerves,
> so that for all his looking he does not delay his departure;
> and I saw behind us a black devil
> come running up over the crag.

**I SAW it clearly**: because pitch is thick, one does not see the thing plunged into it as one does in water. **BUT saw nothing in it**: that is, nothing but the bubbles; and this is a manner of speaking more Lombard than Tuscan. For we say "I saw nothing in it but bubbles," and the Lombard says "**But that the bubbles**" <note>original Italian: "Ma che le bolle"</note>. And he calls bubbles that swelling which water makes when it boils. **AND swelling all**: when water boils, because it is thinner, it does not swell equally throughout. But pitch, because it is a denser thing, swells all over: and then it all falls back, which he calls **settling compressed**. This vice is visible because it swells everything and generates indignation in everyone, but one does not see who boils inside for the reason already stated. **WHILE I [was gazing] down there**: that is, while I was occupied looking down from the bridge, a devil came running to throw someone from the banks where I was standing to watch; and he would have struck me if Virgil had not pulled me to him, as often happens when one would be trampled by a running horse if another who sees it first did not pull him away. And this allegorically signifies: that in contemplating a vice, one's sensuality would be struck and pushed into that vice by that impetus which arises from the pleasure of that [vice].

<summary>Dante and Virgil arrive at the fifth ditch of Malebolge, where barrators are punished in boiling pitch. The commentary compares the scene to the Venetian Arsenal and explains the allegorical nature of the sin of political corruption.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the fifth ditch of the eighth circle, transitioning from the general description of the boiling pitch to the arrival of a demon carrying a soul from Lucca. Note: Although the header says Canto XX, the text and commentary correspond to Canto XXI of the Inferno.</meta>

<page-num>XX</page-num>
<header>CANTO XX</header>

### Ah, how fierce he was in his aspect!
### And how bitter he seemed to me in his act,
### with wings outspread and light upon his feet!
### His shoulder, which was sharp and high,
### bore a sinner by both haunches,
### and he held the sinew of the feet gripped tight.

<note>original: "hic niger est hunc tu romane caueto"</note> <note>This Latin phrase, "This man is black [wicked]; you, O Roman, beware of him," is from the Roman poet Horace. The commentator uses it to link the "blackness" of the demon to moral wickedness.</note> He describes this devil as being fierce and bitter: because nothing is more cruel and more bitter than temptation. For when an unrestrained desire arises in our soul, its appearance terrifies us so that we do not dare to resist. Furthermore, he depicts him as very swift both in running and flying because nothing is swifter than the cupidity <term>cupidita</term><note>A term for intense desire or greed, often used in a theological sense to describe the root of many sins.</note> that is born from temptation; for in that state, there is no mature consideration, nor long consultation, nor well-examined counsel by which we might discern what should or should not be done. Instead, we act with thoughtless and reckless speed, in which there can be no true understanding.

He demonstrates the haste of the demon: who did not wish to wait to plunge that soul but called his companions, who are called by the general name <term>Malebranche</term><note>Literally "Evil Claws," the name given to the group of demons guarding this ditch.</note>, which is a fitting name for barrators because they have lion-like claws to snatch money. Indeed, they are the primary magistrates of Lucca, just as the Priors are in Florence. And he notes in this place that in Lucca they sell

### From our bridge he said: "O Malebranche,
### here is one of the elders of Saint Zita!
### Put him under, while I return for more
### to that city which is well provided with them;
### everyone there is a barrator, except Bonturo;
### there, for money, 'No' is turned into 'Yes'."
### He threw him down, and along the hard rock
### he turned back; and never was a mastiff loosed
### with such haste to pursue a thief.

Therefore, the words sound as if everyone in Lucca were a barrator except Bonturo Dati. But he means <note>ironically</note> that Bonturo is a greater barrator than the others. And it follows that there, FOR money, "Yes" is made of "No": that is, they ensure that even if one is not worthy of honors and magistracies, nevertheless for money they grant them as if he were worthy. HE THREW HIM DOWN. This shows with what speed he threw down that soul and returned to Lucca: and he uses an apt and very appropriate comparison. Princes and great masters are accustomed to keep mastiffs suited to biting those who come and are not familiar with the house, and they keep them tied up. Because when they are loosed, they are even more eager to run. Therefore, a mastiff loosed by its master does not run so hard after one who was fleeing.

### That one plunged in, and came back up face-first;
### but the demons, who were covered by the bridge,
### shouted: "The Holy Face has no place here!
### Here one swims differently than in the Serchio!
### Therefore, if you do not want our scratches,
### do not stay above the pitch."
### Then they struck him with more than a hundred hooks,
### saying: "Covered you must dance here,
### so that, if you can, you may snatch in secret."
### Not otherwise do cooks make their scullions
### plunge the meat into the middle of the cauldron
### with hooks, so that it does not float.
### The good master, so that it may not appear
### that you are here, said to me: "Crouch down here
### behind a rock that may offer some screen;
### and for any offense that may be done to me,
### do not fear, for I have these things known,
### and another time I was in such a fray."
### Then he passed beyond the head of the bridge;
### and as he reached the sixth bank,
### it was necessary for him to have a steady countenance.

<column-break/>

vice, which occupies a man before he notices it, if provident and cautious reason does not pull sensuality toward itself and defend it. THEN I MOVED. He narrates what commonly happens: that when we are frightened by a sudden fear, in our haste to flee, we do not look at what scares us, but seeking to escape, the fear takes away our strength. SEE THE DEVIL: He places the devil for temptation. He describes him as black either because temptation is harmful—and in Latin, "black" is used for "harmful"—or because temptation is born of ignorance. For whoever has perfect knowledge of a thing cannot be deceived in it. Or "black," meaning vicious. Whence here <note>reference to Horace's "niger" above</note>

magistracies and dignities are sold. Wherefore here were honored not those who had the most virtue, but those who could spend the most. OF SAINT ZITA: From the city named after the saint for whom they have great devotion. This was a woman of holy habits, and in life and death she performed miracles. <note>Francesco da Buti was a famous 14th-century commentator on Dante.</note> Francesco da Buti believes that this man, whom the poet does not name, was Martino Bottaio, who died while serving as an Elder. In those times, there were faction leaders in Lucca who guided half the people, and Bonturo Dati, who had the following of the other half. Whence, being an ambassador to Pope Boniface, and Boniface in the course of speaking, taking him by the arm as one does who wants to show another that he is too malicious, shaking him, said smilingly: "Ambassador, you shake half of Lucca for me." EXCEPT BONTURO: Here is a rhetorical device called irony, when by saying one thing we mean the opposite. Like when he says "Rejoice, O Florence, since you are so great."

He narrates what happened to the plunged soul who, returning to the surface as those who go to the bottom do, the demons who were under the bridge, mocking him, said: "Your Holy Face <note>The 'Volto Santo' is a famous wooden crucifix in Lucca, still venerated today.</note> has no place here," meaning it will not be granted to him to stay out of the pitch. And at the same time, it alludes to the Lucchesi who hold the Holy Face in veneration and, invoking it often, trust in its help; the demons say that the Holy Face in which you trust has no place here. And in these words, the poet signifies that in Hell no saint or prayer can help. HERE ONE SWIMS DIFFERENTLY THAN IN THE SERCHIO. You Lucchesi are accustomed to swim for pleasure in the Serchio, a river near Lucca, which the Latins called <note>original: "Auseris"</note> Auseris. Regarding the Holy Face, Benvenuto da Imola <note>Another prominent early Dante commentator.</note> reports having read that Nicodemus, a disciple of Christ, had the face of Christ painted from life, which upon dying he left to Isachar; and he, out of fear of the Jews, kept it hidden; and by succession, it remained with his descendants. And finally, it was in Jerusalem in the hands of a very Christian man named Saletio. In those times, a holy bishop named Gualfredo went to the Sepulcher and, through a revelation had in a dream, understood where this Holy Face was; and with much skill and prayers, he obtained it from Saletio and carried it to the city of Joppa. And there, by divine grace, a very ornate ship appeared which, without the help of sails or oars, conducted itself into the port of Luni. By which miracle, the Lucchesi being amazed, they wanted to board the ship, but could never touch it until the bishop went...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the fifth ditch of the eighth circle. While the header reads "Canto XX," the text actually covers Canto XXI of the Inferno, specifically the confrontation between Virgil and the demons (the Malebranche) led by Malacoda. The previous page discussed the arrival of a corrupt official (barrator) from Lucca; this page explains the allegory of Virgil (Reason) protecting Dante (Sensuality) from the "hooks" of temptation.</meta>

<header>CANTO XX.</header>

Then he passed beyond the bridge's head,
and as he reached upon the sixth bank,
it was necessary for him to have a steady brow.

With that fury and with that storm
that dogs rush out upon the poor man
who suddenly begs or stops:
Those [demons] came out from under the little bridge:
and turned all their hooks against him:
but he cried out: "Let none of you be wicked!
Before your hook catches me,
let one of you step forward to hear me,
and then take counsel on hooking me."
They all cried out: "Go, Malacoda!"
Wherefore one moved—and the others stood still—
and came to him saying: "What does this profit him?"

"Do you believe, Malacoda, to see me here,
having come," my master said,
"already secure from all your defenses,
Without divine will and a favorable fate.
Let us go, for it is willed in heaven
that I show another this wild path."
Then his pride was so fallen
that he let the hook drop at his feet:
and said to the others: "Now, let him not be struck!"

<column-break/>

...man of Lucca named Giovanni: who with great veneration carried this image <note>The "Volto Santo" or Holy Face of Lucca, a famous wooden crucifix.</note> to Lucca; and they honorably placed it in the church of San Martino: where, according to what the people of Lucca say, it has performed many miracles. **SO THAT IF YOU CAN** grab him covertly: that is, snatch and hook him: to denote that the <term>barrator</term><note>A "barrator" (barattiero) was someone who accepted bribes or engaged in political corruption, the secular equivalent of simony.</note> snatches the money of others in secret. Then the poet feigns that Virgil hid him and went to scout if he could obtain passage. This demonstrates that one must contemplate this vice with great caution. For it often happens that while one seeks to know a vice in order to flee it, the sweetness of the money entices one in such a way that they fall into it. Therefore, it was not good for Virgil to lead Dante with him to these devils: that is, the appetite should not go together with reason. For it would have been overcome by the devils and by temptation. But Virgil, that is, higher reason, hid Dante—meaning the sensory part—and revealed himself. And when he had bargained with the demons and brought them to his will, then he called Dante to him: because reason first considers and knows the ugliness and damnation that is in sin, and judges that it must be fled; and then it reveals this to the sensuality which, even after the judgment given by reason (although it consents to it), nevertheless, through its fragility, fears that the temptations which have yielded to reason might yet overcome it. **THE GOOD MASTER:** no one is a better master than reason, which does not go to battle if it does not first subdue the appetite in such a way that it does not appear to be there. And he wishes for him to hide behind a rock, which is a hard thing; and certainly by no other thing is it easy for temptation to conquer the appetite, except because the appetite is very effeminate and soft. Therefore, it is necessary that for its shield, that is for its defense, it should take on hardness. **THAT YOU MAY HAVE SOME** shield: that is, that you may have some defense. **AND FOR ANY** offense that may be done to me, do not you come. An offense is done to higher reason when it cannot so quickly understand the truth. But in this case, he does not want the appetite to help him in any way, because it would have the opposite effect. **FOR I HAVE** the things known, because another time I was in such a battle: that is, in such a struggle. Nor only one other time: but often and in various things the intellect [struggles] with demons, that is, with temptations. Then, having arrived at the end of the bridge where the devils were, it was necessary that he have a steady brow: that is, that he show boldness of spirit: for in the brow is shown the quality of the soul, whether it is constant or fearful.

<image-desc>Ornamental blue letter G with red flourishes.</image-desc> Having reached the demons, Virgil saw them all come toward him with that fury with which dogs rush out against a poor man who stops at a door or asks for alms. And in truth, as soon as our intellect turns to the cognition of vice, various temptations assault it. And because it would be confused if it wished to consider them all together, it rebuffs all the others and stops with <term>Malacoda</term><note>Literally "Evil Tail." The commentator interprets the name as "bad end" (cattivo fine).</note>: which can be interpreted as "evil end." Therefore, when we turn to want to know if a thing is good or bad, although the natural order of cognition is from cause to effect, nevertheless, human ingenuity begins from the end—that is, from the effect—and returns to the cause. This, then, is the reason why it is enough for the poet to convince Malacoda: that is, to know the effect of the vice. Furthermore, it agrees with the description made of <term>Geryon</term><note>The monster of fraud from earlier in the Inferno, who had a scorpion-like tail.</note>, who was said to have the tail of a scorpion, which is most wicked. Therefore, Virgil first deals with Malacoda. Because human ingenuity, wishing to consider the vice of barratry, begins to know it from the evil end that it produces; and when this one is moved, the others stand still. For once the end is known, the other things are easily known through it.

<image-desc>Ornamental red letter S with blue flourishes.</image-desc> It is the opinion of sacred theologians that although there is free will in us, and that God has placed life and death in our hands, nevertheless, without the favor of God we cannot disentangle ourselves from sin. This we have already demonstrated above. Therefore, what Virgil says to Malacoda is the reasoning that the intellect makes within itself against temptation. And having already overcome temptation in the other vices with divine favor, he hopes still to be able to do the same in this one. Therefore, since we have known the thing to be evil by its end, the lure of sin can still have power in us to pull us toward following it. For this reason, Malacoda would not cease to annoy us. But when the divine will is in our favor, then we can conquer every temptation. For this reason, Virgil most excellently says: **DO YOU BELIEVE** Malacoda, to see me come here. As if to say: do you believe that I could have proceeded so far through Hell, conquering step by step every sin...

---

...sin **SECURE FROM** all your defenses: that is, defense and repairs. As if to say: you have so many repairs to defend yourselves so that we do not conquer your temptations, that I would not have been able to come securely this far. **WITHOUT DIVINE WILL:** that is, without divine favor. **AND FAVORABLE FATE:** that is, prosperous predestination. And in this sense he has placed fate, about which we spoke more extensively [before]. **LET US GO, FOR IN HEAVEN IT IS** willed: Which is like saying: it is necessary to let me go since in heaven it is so willed. That is, since this is the will of God, which cannot be resisted. **THAT I:** Virgil, that is, higher reason and intellect. **SHOW ANOTHER** understand: to the lower reason and to the sensuality. **THIS WILD PATH.** that is, the way of vices which are born from matter, which is the body; which matter the philosophers call <term>hyle</term><note>From the Greek "hylē" (ὕλη), meaning wood, forest, or matter. Landino uses this to explain why Dante describes the path of vice as a "wild wood."</note>, that is, wood/forest, as we disputed at length in the beginning of this comedy. Or rather, he calls the path of vices "wild" because living according to vice is not according to the reason by which we are men. But it is...

<summary>This page covers Virgil's confrontation with Malacoda and the Malebranche demons, allegorizing the triumph of Reason (Virgil) over the temptations of corruption (Barratry) through divine grace. Landino explains the symbolism of the "wild path" as a metaphor for material existence and vice, using the Greek concept of hyle.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the scene in the fifth ditch of the eighth circle of Hell. Virgil has successfully negotiated with the leader of the demons, Malacoda. Now, he calls Dante out from his hiding place among the crags of the bridge. The text explores the historical reference to the surrender of the fortress of Caprona and provides the famous chronological calculation that dates Dante's journey to the year 1300.</meta>

<header>INFERNO.</header>

My leader said to me: "O you who crouch
among the crags of the bridge, all on all fours,
<note>The original "quattro quattro" literally means "four by four," but the commentary clarifies it refers to "quattarsi"—crouching low or hiding on all fours to avoid being seen.</note>
you may now return to me in safety."
Wherefore I moved and came to him quickly,
and the demons all pressed forward
so that I feared they would not keep their word:
Just as I once saw the infantry fear,
who marched out of Caprona under treaty,
<note>Caprona was a Pisan fortress that surrendered to the Lucchese and Florentine Guelphs in 1289. Dante, as a young soldier, was likely present and witnessed the fear of the surrendering troops as they walked through the enemy lines.</note>
seeing themselves among so many enemies.
I drew close with my whole body
beside my leader, and I did not turn my eyes
from their faces, which were not good.
And they lowered their hooks, "Do you want me to touch him?"
one said to the other, "on his backside?"
And they answered: "Yes, see that you nick him."
But that demon who was holding speech
with my leader turned around very quickly
and said: "Stay, stay, Scarmiglione!"

Then he said to us: "To go further by this
cliff will not be possible, for the sixth arch
lies all shattered at the bottom.
And if going forward still pleases you,
make your way up along this ridge;
nearby is another cliff that provides a path.
Yesterday, five hours later than this hour,
one thousand two hundred and sixty-six
years were completed since the road here was broken.
<note>This is Malacoda’s famous chronological marker. He refers to the earthquake at the death of Christ, which happened 1266 years prior. By adding the 34 years of Christ's life, Dante establishes the date of his vision as 1300.</note>
I am sending some of my men over there
to see if anyone is airing themselves out;
<note>original: "fciorina" — literally "to shake out laundry," used here to describe the sinners surfacing from the boiling pitch.</note>
go with them, for they will not be wicked."

<column-break/>

...according to the irrational appetite which is proper to the beasts who inhabit the forest. **THEN HIS PRIDE WAS SO FALLEN.** That is, his audacity and his arrogance. Because the diabolical temptation loses all audacity against divine fury. **THAT HE LET THE HOOK DROP AT HIS FEET.** Which signifies that he laid down every intent to harm. **AND SAID TO THE OTHERS:** demons. **NOW, LET HIM NOT BE STRUCK.** Because once the temptation—which consists of the end goal of the thing—is conquered, the others are easily overcome.

After Virgil came to an agreement with the demons, and had convinced them, he called Dante to him. And so it happens that after the intellect has achieved true knowledge and has convinced the demons—that is, condemned the vice and overcome the temptation as a wicked thing—then it calls to itself the hidden appetite: that is, it excites it to flee the thing already judged by itself as evil. And the appetite, which is obedient to reason, moves immediately. But it happens that before it joins with reason, the demons frighten it. Because the temptations of the flesh and its softness dismay us, showing us how difficult and laborious is the path of virtue. **ALL ON ALL FOURS:** that is, hidden. We properly say someone is "crouching" (*quattarsi*) when they bend and lower themselves so as not to be seen. **RETURN TO ME SAFELY.** Because every time the intellect has recognized the truth of a thing and judged whether it is good or evil, the appetite can safely follow it. Nevertheless, before we make a habit of virtue, the demons often frighten us, as was said. **JUST AS I ONCE SAW.** Caprona was once a castle of the Pisans on the banks of the Arno; it was taken from the Pisans by the Lucchese, who, allied with the other <term>Guelphs</term><note>The Guelphs were a political faction in medieval Italy that supported the Pope, while their rivals, the Ghibellines, supported the Holy Roman Emperor.</note> of Tuscany, made war against Pisa, the head of the <term>Ghibellines</term>. Later, being besieged by a large army of Pisans, the Lucchese soldiers who were guarding it, lacking water, gave themselves up with their lives spared. And having come out into the field, they were all tied to one rope by Count Guido, so that they would not separate, for if separated they would have been killed by the peasants; and having been led to the borders of Lucca, they were released. Nevertheless, because while they were passing through the enemy camp everyone shouted, "Hang them! Hang them!", they were greatly afraid. **I DREW CLOSE** with my whole body beside my leader: as does one who, fearing, places trust in another; for he draws near to him and watches the thing he fears. **AND THEY LOWERED THEIR HOOKS.** Those demons lowered their hooks as one does who wants to snag someone. And one said, "Do you want me to grab him with the hook on his backside?" and others replied yes. **BUT THAT DEMON WHO WAS HOLDING SPEECH:** that is, the conversation, turned very quickly to the one who wanted to strike—who was called Scarmiglione—and commanded that he stop. And this is true: because every time the intellect has recognized the malice of the goal, it easily despises all other temptations, and this knowledge refutes them.

The "tail" <note>The "tail" refers to the end of Malacoda's speech, or a "sting in the tail"—the lie.</note> does not depart from the nature of the fraudulent: which is to start from the truth to gain the trust of the listener, and then mix the false with the truth to deceive. It was, therefore, according to Dante's fiction, true that the bridge of the sixth ditch was broken and fallen to the bottom. But it was not true that in this ditch any whole ridge remained that provided a path. Because the poet feigns that at the passion of Christ all the arches of this ditch, where <term>hypocrisy</term> is punished, were broken—meaning by this that at that time the synagogue of the Jews was disintegrated, along with the fraud of the hypocrisy of the priests. Therefore, all the arches of the sixth ditch were broken. But the "tail" confesses what it cannot deny, but lies about the others. Wherefore the author warns us that we must not believe the devil, even though we perceive that he tells the truth in some part; for he never says it except to mix in falsehood. Furthermore, he expresses here the fallacy of the <term>barrator</term>, who, to entice you to give him a price, shows you ways to lead his cause which do not exist in the natural order of things. <note>original: "in rerum natura"</note> **YESTERDAY, FIVE HOURS LATER THAN THIS HOUR.** Dante wants to demonstrate that he found himself in Hell in 1300, calculating the years from the incarnation of Christ. If, therefore, the day of Holy Saturday made 1266, it remains that it was in 1300. Because we must add 33 years that Christ had lived, and one year more because he had been nine months in his mother's womb. Therefore, adding 34 years to 1266, it will be 1300. Dante lived 56 years in his life and died in 1321, as appears in Ravenna at his tomb. And taking 21 from 56, 35 remain. And that many years he happened to have in 1300 when he feigns having had this vision. And therefore he said, "In the middle of the journey of our life," because the middle of seventy, which is the common life for man, is thirty-five. Although in that place, allegorically, they gave it a very convenient sense, if I am not much mistaken. And because he says "yesterday, five hours later than this hour," he shows that just as at the sixth hour of Good Friday the monuments were opened and the veil of the temple was divided, so these circles were broken. And because when he spoke with Malacoda it was the first hour of Holy Saturday, therefore, meaning the sixth hour of Friday, he said: "Yesterday five hours later than this hour"—that is, this first hour of Holy Saturday. And he adds that he sends [demons] out to spy if any sinner "airs himself out"—that is, comes out of the pitch. And these he says will not be "wicked"—that is, they will be useful to show them the way.

The commentary explains the historical siege of Caprona and provides the complex chronological calculations used to date Dante's journey to the year 1300.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the narrative of Inferno Canto XXI, despite the header mistakenly reading "PURGATORIO." The translation maintains the flow from the previous page, where Malacoda, the leader of the Malebranche demons, has just guaranteed Virgil and Dante safe passage over a broken bridge that doesn't actually exist.</meta>

-># PURGATORIO CANTO<-
<note>While the header says Purgatorio, the text is actually from Inferno, Canto XXI.</note>

"Step forward, Alchino and Calcabrina,"
he began to say, "and you, Cagnazzo;
and Barbariccia, lead the ten.
Let Libicocco come forward, and Draghignazzo,
tusked Ciriatto and Graffiacane,
and Farfarello and mad Rubicante.
Search around the boiling pitch;
let these poets be safe until the next ridge
which crosses entirely over the dens."

<column-break/>

These are the names of the ten demons whom Malacoda sends as an escort; I believe that through these, the poet intends to express various passions, actions, and effects of the <term>barrators</term> <note>Corrupt politicians or officials who trafficked in public offices for money.</note>. **ALCHINO** represents the inclination toward such vice, <note>original: "Quia alios inclinat" — because he inclines others.</note>. After the inclination follows the corruption of the soul when it has already made a purpose to follow the sin, called **Calcaborina**: that is, "trampling the frost." In the sacred letters, frost signifies divine grace. The third is the malediction into which the sinner falls after having driven away divine grace, and he is called **Cagnazzo**, like a "captive dog" or a biting one. The fourth is the cunning that hides this vice for the time being, called **Barbariccia**: that is, "curly beard," because according to <term>physiognomy</term> <note>The historical practice of judging character from facial features.</note>, a frizzy or curled beard demonstrates fraudulence. The fifth is the burning desire to bring the act of barratry to perfection once the reward has been received, and he is called **Libicocco**: representing "burning lust," that is, unbridled and burning desire. The sixth is the infection of the vice which, like a per-

<column-break/>

<note>The following lines of commentary span the width of the page under the first verse block</note>

-nicious venom, defiles and stains others; he is called **Draghignazzo**, named after the "venom of the dragon." The seventh is the offense done to one's neighbor, whom the barrator mangles and tears just as a boar tears with its tusk; and therefore he calls him **Ciriatto the tusked**, because *cyro* <note>original: "cyro" — derived from the Greek "choiros" for pig.</note> means pig, not only in our rustic tongue but also in the Greek language. The eighth denotes the oppression of one barrator by another when the more powerful one tears at the less powerful; this one is **Graffiacane** because he "scratches the dog"—scratching the one who bites others. **Farfarello** is the ninth, through whom he demonstrates the irascible one and the hunter. **Rubicante** is "red-hot," as if inflamed, furious, and audacious.

---

"O my master, what is this that I see?"
I said, "pray, let us go alone without escort
if you know the way, for I do not ask it for myself.
If you are as wary as you usually are,
do you not see that they gnash their teeth
and with their brows they threaten us with grief?"
And he to me: "I do not want you to be afraid;
let them gnash as they please,
for they do this for the boiling sufferers."
By the left bank they turned;
but first each had pressed his tongue
between his teeth toward their leader as a signal;
and he had made a trumpet of his backside.

<column-break/>

It is the nature of the tempting demon to always end by frightening the senses, just as, conversely, the angel always ends by bringing comfort. Thus, Dante is frightened by the gestures of the demons because they gnash their teeth like dogs eager to bite and threaten by moving their brows. But his "superior reason" <note>Referring to Virgil, who represents human reason.</note> comforts him so that he does not fear, asserting that such gestures are made for the damned. This signifies that they cannot harm anyone except the vicious. **BUT FIRST**: each had his tongue pressed. This passage seems to many to lack dignity or propriety, but certainly, the poet wished to show how much the barrators, once they have cheated someone, mock and deride them. Pressing the tongue between the teeth signifies making such a noise with the mouth as the wind makes when it exits from the posterior parts. This is what shameful buffoons do when they mock someone.

<summary>This page lists and allegorically interprets the ten demons (the Malebranche) assigned to escort Dante and Virgil through the circle of the barrators. It concludes with the demons' vulgar signal to their leader, Malacoda, symbolizing the mockery inherent in corruption.</summary>
<keywords>Malebranche, Alichino, Barbariccia, barratry, corruption, allegory, Virgil, Dante's fear, demons, mockery</keywords>
