<meta>This page continues the commentary on Canto XXII of the Inferno, following the introduction of the ten demons (Malacoda's squad) listed at the end of the previous page. The text transitions from the general description of the Fifth Bolgia (the grafters/barrators) to the specific military-like movements of the demons and the sinners' behavior in the pitch.</meta>

->CANTO XXII.<-

### CANTO XXII OF THE FIRST CANTICLE BY DANTE.

The same ditch is still being discussed, and the same sin is being punished. However, in the previous chapter, he placed those barrators <note>corrupt officials who trade public office for money</note> who sold their republic. In this twenty-second canto, he places those who, having been placed in high favor by some lord, have sold that favor. Continuing, therefore, he describes the form of the punishment for those submerged in the pitch. Then he makes special mention of one soul, and in the third part, he induces this soul to reveal others. In the final part, he recounts the cunning that this spirit used to deceive all the demons. **I SAW.** He shows that he has seen a field of men-at-arms depart, which requires the utmost prudence and caution; for it contributes greatly to safety and victory to properly position and move the camps—a virtue said to have been supreme in Pyrrhus, King of the Epiriotes. **AND START A SKIRMISH:** that is, a battle. A "skirmish" (*stormo*) is properly a multitude of fighting men-at-arms, perhaps derived from the Latin word *turma* <note>original: "turma," meaning a troop or squadron</note>. Or truly it is an onomatopoeia, that is, a name taken from the noise and din heard in combat. **AND GIVE THEIR** Muster, and sometimes depart for their escape. The meaning is: I have seen the signal given to soldiers, either when they move camp, or when they fight, or when they perform a muster, or when they flee. But never with such a sound. **SCOUTS I saw.** Here, according to some, he touches upon the expulsion of the Ghibellines from Florence, who then took Arezzo. But it is difficult, amidst the many and frequent changes of those times in the city of Arezzo—by which it was almost desolated—to understand which specific event he describes here. **RAIDING PARTIES** (*gualdane*) was the specific name the ancients gave to the cavalry raids that one city made upon the territory of another to cause destruction and carry off booty. And these are all warlike things and are done in times of war between one enemy and another. But **tournaments and jousts** are military exercises performed for festivals and games, and to give delight to the people. A tournament is when squads go against one another and represent a kind of battle. A joust is when one goes against another body-to-body and represents individual combat. **With signals from castles** which are made by day with smoke and by night with fire. But I never saw anyone move **WITH SUCH A STRANGE REED-PIPE:** that is, a sound, using the specific instrument to represent the whole category of signals. **NOR SHIP AT** a sign from land or castles. Sailors, when they can see land—that is, some promontory—navigate according to that; and when they cannot see land, they follow the North Star.

**I have seen horsemen moving camp,**
**and starting a skirmish, and making their muster,**
**and sometimes retreating for their own safety;**
**I have seen scouts across your land,**
**O Aretines, and I have seen raiding parties go out,**
**the clashing of tournaments and the running of jousts;**
**Sometimes with trumpets, and sometimes with bells,**
**with drums and with signals from castles,**
**and with things of our own and those from abroad;**
**But never with such a strange reed-pipe**
**did I see horsemen or infantry set forth,**
**nor a ship by a sign of land or of a star.**

<column-break/>

**We went along with the ten demons—**
**ah, savage company! But in church**
**with saints, and in the tavern with gluttons.**
**Yet my attention was fixed on the pitch,**
**to see every condition of that ditch**
**and of the people who were burning within it.**
**Like dolphins when they give a sign**
**to sailors with the arch of their backs,**
**so that they may prepare to save their vessel,**
**So, at times, to alleviate the pain,**
**one of the sinners would show his back,**
**and hide it again in less time than lightning.**

In passing, the poet shows that although we should always flee the fellowship and company of the wicked, nonetheless, sometimes either the place, the time, or some other cause leads us to go out with them. Therefore, "in the tavern with gluttons" should be understood as not being there for gluttony—for it is never permitted to associate with the vicious to commit a vice—but to take necessary food; and so it is here. Since Dante was in Hell and had need of a guide, it was necessary for him to follow the demons. And allegorically, wishing to know the malice and malignity of such a vice, it was necessary for them to have knowledge of things so closely. <note>Landino explains that one must sometimes observe evil to understand it.</note> **YET MY ATTENTION was fixed on the pitch.** Dante had his "intesa"—that is, his attention—on the pitch to see some of the submerged sinners, because the lower reason seeks the knowledge of particulars and not of universals. **LIKE DOLPHINS.** Just as sometimes dolphins in the sea come so far to the surface that they show their backs—which is a sign that a storm is soon to arise, whereby sailors, seeing such a sign, immediately prepare for escape—so those sinners, to alleviate their pain, sometimes pulled their backs out of the pitch. But for fear of the demons' hooks, they put them back under in less time than a flash of lightning. The dolphin, above all other fish, delights in the sight of man and loves him greatly. This is known, as writers show in many cases, but most clearly in the case of **Arion**. Arion of Methymna, a city in Lesbos, was a most skilled musician, and for this art, he was very well-received by Periander, King of Corinth. But, eager to see the world and spread his fame (not without profit), he sailed to Sicily and thence to Italy, where by his craft he accumulated great wealth. But after some time, desiring to return to Periander, he boarded a ship of certain Corinthians. These men, moved by greed and devoid of all humanity, agreed to throw Arion into the sea and take his money. Understanding this, the musician first turned to prayers and tried to recover his life from them. Then, seeing that he prayed in vain, he asked for a space of time before they threw him in, so that he might sing with his kithara, dressed and adorned in the most precious robes and jewels he had. It was granted to him; and he, upon the prow, sang; and after the song, he threw himself into the sea. And immediately, received by a dolphin, he was carried in safety as far as the island of Taenarum. From there he went to Corinth, and Periander summoned those who had wanted to drown him in the sea; they, stunned by the unexpected presence of Arion, could not deny it. And Herodotus affirms that in Taenarum, where the dolphin landed him, there was a bronze statue of him sitting upon the dolphin. Pliny also writes that a dolphin in the Gulf of Baiae became so tamed by a boy—who gave him bread every day—that finally, every hour the boy called him, he came and carried him across the narrow gulf from Baiae to Pozzuoli. And after some years, when the boy died, the dolphin stayed on the shore to wait for him, not without signs of sorrow; and finally, when the boy did not appear, he died of grief. It would be very tedious to report many other similar things written by Theophrastus, Aristotle, and other writers.

# INFERNO.

The dolphin is of such speed that it surpasses not only other fish in swimming, but even birds and arrows. No fish could escape it were it not that the dolphin cannot catch prey unless it is on its back. This is because its mouth is located far from its snout, almost in the middle of its belly. And because it breathes like the whale and the sea-calf <note>original: "uecchio marino," likely referring to a monk seal</note>, it must return to the surface with incredible speed from the depths where it follows its prey. It gives birth to live young and not eggs, and nourishes them with milk. It carries its small ones on its back and accompanies and guides the young. They live thirty years. Their voice is similar to a human lament. They love humans greatly and take much delight in music. If one dies, the others carry it out of the water. I have written these few things out of many, invited more by the noble nature of the animal than because I judged it necessary in this place. Now I return to the text.

<column-break/>

In this passage, no other allegory is required: but to decorate the scene, he describes only the place of punishment and employs the simile of the frogs. **I SAW AND ALSO:** that is, still. **THE HEART:** where the seat of thought is located. That is, I saw then and even now, as it passes through my mind. **SHUDDERS AT IT:** that is, it gives me dread. *Capriccio* <note>shiver or whim</note> in the Florentine dialect signifies what the Latins call *horror*, which is when the hairs stand on end; and this happens through cold, or because in fear the body becomes cold. Since the blood, in which heat consists, runs to the heart and abandons the other members, a "shiver" (*capriccio*) is born; and it is called *capriccio* as if it were *capo arriccio* <note>literally "curled head"</note>, because the hairs on the head stand up. And we say *arricciare* <note>to curl or bristle</note> from that animal which we call *riccio* <note>hedgehog</note>, that is, "spiny," because when it fears, it closes itself up, and in closing, it straightens its spines. **ONE WAITING.** I saw that of all those who held their snouts out of the pitch, only one did not flee at the coming of the demons; and all the others fled, as sometimes happens when someone comes to the ditch where there are frogs. **LEAPS AWAY:** that is, flees. Because Graffiacane with his hook: that is, just as a fisherman draws an otter from the water having caught it with a hook or other device. An otter is an animal not much smaller than a fox, but long and with black fur, and it has a pointed snout; it feeds on those fish which it sees in the nets, and it willingly gnaws and tears the nets.

So that the reader does not wonder how he knows the names of all ten demons, he shows that he noted them when they were chosen, and later when they called one another. **MY GUIDE DREW CLOSE TO HIS SIDE.** Because the narration of the souls whom the author finds in Hell would bring boredom and distaste if he always maintained the same manner. Therefore, he marvelously varies and shows different ways, as anyone who reads diligently can note. **I WAS IN THE KINGDOM OF NAVARRE.** This man was Giampolo (or Ciampolo), son of a noble lady. But his father, having consumed his patrimony, left him poor. Therefore, his mother placed him with a baron of King Thibault of Navarre. And his industry was such that in the process of time he became so accepted by Thibault—a most just king—that he committed every great matter to him. But he did not know how to restrain his greed; and because, as Terence says, "We are all made worse by license" <note>original: "Omnes sumus deteriores licentia"</note>, he became a supreme barrator. **CIRRIATO FROM WHOSE MOUTH CAME FORTH.** These verses are clear enough. And I judge this place to be more an ornament of the poem than for allegory. Nevertheless, it expresses well enough the nature of these demons in their acts according to the interpretation already stated above. **THE GUIDE THEN,** "Now tell of the other wicked ones." Virgil asked the Navarrese if any Italian is among these barrators. And he replies that a little while before he had departed from one of whom he will speak below. Then he writes that Libicocco tore an arm from him with a hook and carried off a "lacerto," that is, a muscle. By the "arm" is understood the power of the work. And it was already said above that by Libicocco is understood the preoccupation with the work. This is when the judge, corrupted by money, is hindered from doing justice. Dragnignazzo signifies the entanglement and tightening of affection. For every man by his nature is inclined to do justice, but barratry often binds such affection. This demon wanted to strike at his legs, because feet and legs signify human affections. And this signifies that it often happens that in the judge there is a good affection toward doing justice, and it is not extinguished in him; but avarice makes him err, and it is almost against his will. **WHEN THEY WERE A LITTLE PACIFIED.** For the clarification of this text, we shall note that the island of Sardinia is by...

Cagnazzo at such a word raised his snout,
shaking his head, and said: "Listen to the malice

<column-break/>

● ...called *Sandaleoti*: because it has the shape of a footwear called by us a slipper. It is eight miles from Corsica. This island, being in the possession of the African Saracens, was acquired in the year 1116 by the Pisans; and in the same year it was lost, recovered by Musetto, King of Africa. And the following year, the Pisans, allied with the Genoese, acquired it again, having made a pact between them that all the plunder should belong to the Genoese and the lordship should remain with the Pisans. They divided the island into four parts, and these they called the four *Judicates* <note>judicial districts</note>: because over each they placed a Judge who ruled it as the lord of that place. The first Judicate was called Logodoro, that is, "place of gold" <note>Italian: "luogo d’oro"</note>, because it was the richest part of the island. Others called it the Judicate of the Towers. The second, Cagliari, from Cagliari, a noble and ancient city. The third, Gallura, because from the beginning it was given to certain Pisan counts who bore the rooster <note>Italian: "gallo"</note> as their insignia. The fourth, Arborea. The Lord of the Judicate of Gallura was once Nino, a citizen driven out of Pisa, as we shall more aptly describe in the eighth chapter of the *Purgatorio*. And Friar Gomita was his enemy, a very astute man and a supreme barrator, who had so occupied the mind of his lord that the latter would not lend faith to anyone who warned him of his vices. Nevertheless, in the end, because he released certain enemies of Nino who had fallen into his hands for money, he was hanged by him. He calls him therefore "Friar Gomita of Gallura" and a "vessel," as if he were a receptacle of every fraud. OF EVERY KIND of fraud. WHO HELD THE ENEMIES OF HIS LORD <note>original: "domno," from the Latin "dominus"</note>, that is, of his master. For in Sardinia, the lord is called "domno." AND LET THEM GO SMOOTHLY: that is, in peace. FREQUENTS WITH HIM LORD MICHEL ZANCHE. Frederick II had a natural son named Enzo, to whom he gave the Judicate of Logodoro. This man finally died in Bologna in prison. Whereupon Michel Zanche, his seneschal, through his frauds and barratry, induced Enzo's mother, who remained the Lady of the Judicate, to take him as her husband. And in this way, having become lord, he allied himself with Messer Branca Doria, giving him his daughter as a wife—or according to others, taking Doria’s sister for himself.

---

WHO GNASHES. To gnash means to twist the face in such a way that the mouth opens and shows the teeth. This signifies either grieving within oneself or being angry toward others, or sometimes laughing. BUT I FEAR THAT HE. I fear that he. TO SCRATCH MY ITCH. A Florentine proverb: for when we want to signify beating someone, we say "I will scratch his itch." THE GREAT PROVOST, Barbariccia. In short, although he is a decurion—that is, a captain of ten—he calls him "provost" because he was set over the others. He turned to Farfarello. WHO WAS ROLLING HIS EYES. We say a person is "rolling their eyes" <note>original: "stralunare gli occhi"</note> when they turn them with a fierce look upon someone and, keeping them very wide, fix them and hold them still. This signifies wrath and threats. WICKED BIRD: because all the demons are imagined as winged. In short, he says that Farfarello would have struck him if their captain had not forbidden it. And it follows that the Navarrese, although frightened, promises to make Lombard and Tuscan spirits come out of the pitch if the demons pull back. And therefore he says, let the "Evil Claws" of the demons stand back a little <note>original: "in cesso," meaning at a distance</note>, and I, whistling, will make them come out; for thus we are accustomed to call one another. Nor is it without reason that the poet feigns this: because those who commit such wicked deeds know more by signs than by open speech. Furthermore, he feigns that some demons touch him and others do not touch him because not all parts of this vice fall upon every barrator.

---

It is the nature of the dog to discover who is hiding by barking. Therefore, he deservedly discovers the malice of this man with his words; for he, under the guise of wanting to call others, said that the demons should move away so that they could escape their hands and dive back in. And allegorically it shows that by speaking together, the corruptor and the corrupted often discover their vices. RAISED HIS SNOUT. We say "mouth" for a man, and "beak" for birds, and "snout" <note>original: "muso"</note> for other animals. Therefore, having figured him above as a dog...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante's Inferno, Canto XXII. We are in the fifth ditch of the eighth circle, where barrators (corrupt politicians) are punished in boiling pitch. The Navarrese prisoner, Ciampolo, is attempting to trick his demon captors into letting him go by promising to lure more of his companions to the surface.</meta>

-># INFERNO:<-

"I am too malicious," he replied,
"when I seek to increase my own sorrow."
Alichino could not hold back, and in opposition
to the others, said to him: "If you drop down,
I will not follow you at a gallop,
but I will beat my wings above the pitch;
let us leave the ridge and let the bank be a shield
to see if you alone are worth more than us."

<note>Landino interprets Alichino's name and actions as representing a "sudden inclination of the will."</note> As stated above, this signifies a sudden inclination of the will. Therefore, he performs his role here by swaying the will of his companions with his speech. **AND IN OPPOSITION.** Almost as if standing across and facing them. **I WILL NOT FOLLOW YOU at a gallop.** That is, running. "Galloping" <note>original: "gualoppare"</note> is midway between a trot and a run. **BUT I WILL BEAT my wings above the pitch:** meaning I will fly to catch you again. **LET THE ridge BE LEFT:** as if to say, let us throw ourselves down from the hill. **AND LET THE bank BE A SHIELD.** As a shelter and defense. **TO SEE IF YOU ALONE ARE WORTH MORE THAN US.** And you shall see who is more powerful, you or us.

O you who read, you shall hear a new sport:
everyone turned their eyes to the other side,
he first who was most resistant to doing so.
The Navarrese chose his time well;
he planted his feet on the ground, and in a moment
he leaped and freed himself from their purpose.
At this, each one was stung with guilt,
but he most of all who was the cause of the failure;
therefore he moved and cried out: "You are caught!"
But it availed little, for wings could not outpace
fear; the one went under,
and the other, flying, turned his breast upward.
Not otherwise does the duck suddenly
dive down when the falcon approaches,
and the falcon returns up, angry and defeated.
Enraged, Calcabrina, mocking the joke,
flew after him, eager
that the sinner should escape so he could have a scuffle.
And as soon as the barrator <term>barattiere: one who profits from the misuse of public office</term> had disappeared,
he turned his claws upon his companion,
and was locked with him above the ditch.
But the other was indeed a fierce hawk
at clawing him well, and both
fell into the middle of the boiling pond.
The heat was an immediate mediator <note>original: "schermidor," literally fencer or protector, but here meaning it separated them</note>;
but nevertheless, there was no way of rising,
so "limed" <note>sticky like birdlime</note> were their wings.
Barbariccia, grieving with the others,
made four of them fly from the other side
with all their hooks; and very quickly,
on this side and that, they descended to their posts;
they reached their hooks toward those who were caught,
who were already "cooked" inside their crusts;
and we left them thus embroiled.

The heat of the pitch which they felt acted as an immediate "fencer" <note>original: "schermidore"</note> because it caused each of them to immediately attend to defending themselves from it. But it helped little, because their wings were already so covered in pitch that they could not withdraw. **BARBARICCIA** With...

<column-break/>

...shrewdly said "snout." He raised his snout; for this is what one does when moving and becoming attentive to what he hears. **SHAKING HIS Head:** This is the act of one who perceives the malice of others and wants to demonstrate that he is not being deceived; and therefore he says: "Hear the malice he has thought of to throw himself down." **WHENCE HE Who Had snares:** that is, malice in abundance. This demonstrates the nature of the fraudulent man, who, seeing that others have noticed his malice, contrives to cover it with other words; and he says that if he is malicious, it is in procuring greater sorrow for his companions. As if to say: "I seek to make them come out so that they may be mangled," because he knows that demons take pleasure in this. And it is irony; as if to say: "If I were malicious, I would not do this." **ALCHINO** <note>Alichino</note> did not refrain from speaking: for him, as was said...

[The commentator addresses] the attentive listener, promising that he will hear a **SPORT** <note>original: "ludo"</note>: that is, a mockery and **NEW** derision: that is, unusual; because he will hear that the demons, who are more malicious, were deceived by the spirit who ought to have been less malicious. **EACH ONE** of the demons turned their eyes the other way, ceasing to watch the spirit. **AND HE WHO FIRST was most resistant to doing so:** that is, Cagnazzo, who showed that he could not be deceived. **THE NAVARRESE.** Ciampolo of Navarre. **CHOSE Well his time:** that is, he aptly seized the occasion and the convenience of the moment; specifically, when he saw the eyes of the demons turned elsewhere, he threw himself into the pitch. Wherefore he planted the soles of his feet on the ground to make a swifter step and in a moment leaped. **AND Freed himself from their purpose:** that is, from their intent, which was to mangle him. **AT WHICH EACH ONE of the demons was stung with guilt:** that is, in himself he judged himself guilty for having been negligent in guarding him. **BUT HE MOST OF ALL, Alchino**, more than the others: because by his speech he gave security to the others. Wherefore Ciampolo had space to flee. Therefore he was the first to fly after him, but it did him no good: for his wings, that is, his flying, could not outpace—that is, overcome—**FEAR.** Specifically, the fear of the spirit. In essence, the fear the spirit had of the demons made him swifter than Alichino’s wings. For as Virgil says: "Fear added wings to his feet" <note>original: "Pedibus timor addidit alas"; from the Aeneid VIII, 224</note>; and the Florentine proverb says: "Need makes the old woman trot." **THAT ONE.** That is, Ciampolo, went under and dived into the pitch. **AND THAT ONE, Alchino, TURNED his breast flying upward:** that is, he flew up; and it happened as when the falcon follows the duck, which, because it dives into the water before he reaches it, leaves the falcon angry and "broken"—that is, exhausted—at the point where he was stooping to have it, finally unable to reach it. And here the poet denotes how great the cunning of the barrator is; who, although he often gives cause for suspicion of committing such fraud, is nevertheless so dexterous in "diving into the pitch"—that is, he covers it so dexterously—that he is not caught. **ENRAGED CALCABRINA At the joke.** When Calcabrina (which signifies "deliberation") joins with Alichino (which is the "inclination of the will"), it is inevitable that they fall into the pitch: that is, into the fraud of barratry. He was therefore "eager"—that is, enamored, greedy, and desirous—that the spirit should escape so as to have cause to scuffle with Alichino. And for this reason, as soon as Ciampolo had dived, he seized him: that is, he took him with his claws while both were on the wing above the great ditch. And Alichino seized him, for he is a **fierce hawk** <note>original: "sparueri griffagno"</note>: that is, valiant and bold. They call hawks "nestlings" <term>nidiace</term> when they are taken small in the nest and cannot yet fly; "branchers" <term>ramingo</term> when they begin to fly and stay on branches; and "haggards" <term>grifagno</term> after they have molted in the wild. And these last, although they are tamed with more difficulty, are nonetheless more spirited in hunting. **AND BOTH fell.** And this denotes that when someone rich and ready to buy favors arrives at court, he often finds multiple barrators, and each would like to draw him to himself; and finally they contend over him and fall into the pitch, for they are discovered and disgraced. **THE HEAT was an immediate mediator:** that is, the heat...

<summary>Ciampolo the Navarrese successfully tricks the demons into looking away, allowing him to leap back into the boiling pitch. The ensuing chaos leads to a mid-air brawl between the demons Alichino and Calcabrina, who both fall into the sticky pitch and must be rescued by their companions.</summary>

# INFERNO.
## CANTO XXIII OF THE FIRST CANTICLE BY DANTE.

He uses the song together with the punishment. Because in this sixth *bolgia* <note>The "bolge" are the ten circular trenches of the eighth circle of Hell, where different types of fraud are punished.</note> he deals with hypocrisy and its torment and suffering. But at the beginning, he describes their progress toward this trench, the persecution they faced from the demons, and how Dante was saved by Virgil. **SILENT:** Which signifies that each was reflecting on his own sorrow. **ALONE:** Each by himself, which signifies the same thing; for when we wish to think diligently about something, we separate ourselves from others. Hence, the character Simon in Terence's play said: *Venit Meditatus aliunde ex solo loco* <note>original Latin: "He comes having meditated elsewhere from a solitary place."</note>, that is, without the company of others. **ONE BEFORE:** That is, Virgil. **THE OTHER AFTER:** That is, Dante. And by this, he wishes to show that in the

<column-break/>

Silent, alone, and without company
we went, one before and the other after,
as Minor Friars <note>The "Frati Minori" are the Franciscans, known for their humble way of walking in procession.</note> walk along the way.
My thought was turned toward Aesop’s fable
by the present brawl,
where he spoke of the frog and the mouse;
For "now" and "at this moment" are not more alike <note>Dante uses the words "mo" and "issa," both meaning "now" in different Italian dialects.</note>
than the one is to the other, if one couples
the beginning and the end with a fixed mind.
And as one thought bursts forth from another,
so from that one another was born,
which made my first fear double.
I thought thus: "These ones, because of us,
are mocked, and with such damage and insult,
that I believe they must be greatly annoyed."
If anger is grafted onto ill-will,
they will come after us more cruelly
than a hound after the hare it snaps at.

---

Already I felt all my hair stand on end
from fear, and I stood looking back intently,
when I said: "Master, if you do not hide
yourself and me quickly, I am terrified
of the Malebranche; <note>The "Malebranche" (Evil Claws) are the demons guarding the trench of the barrators.</note> we have them already behind us;
I imagine them so vividly that I already feel them."

<column-break/>

contemplation of difficult things, the higher reason that deals with particulars cannot be equal to the superior reason, which has knowledge of universals. Therefore, the former goes ahead as a more worthy thing, and the latter follows it. **AS MINOR FRIARS GO ALONG THE WAY.** A fitting comparison both for the manner of walking and for the silence. For the observant friars on a journey go one after the other in silence and deep thought. They were, therefore, alone in body, but the mind was accompanied by contemplation and investigation, which proceed better then and more easily find the truth, of which the soul can have no better company. It happens, therefore, in the learned man, that the more the body is unaccompanied, the more the soul is accompanied. This is why Scipio Africanus used to say that he was never less alone than when he was alone, nor ever less idle than when he was idle. And Leonardo Aretino <note>Leonardo Bruni (c. 1370–1444), a famous humanist scholar and chancellor of Florence.</note>, a man of most ornate eloquence and genius and well-lettered, when a citizen of ours—an unrefined man without learning—wished to accompany him, saying "I do not want you to go so alone," replied: "I would be alone if I were with you." And Seneca in an epistle affirms that the wise man is never alone. **TURNED WAS TOWARD AESOP'S FABLE.** Aesop the Phrygian was a Greek poet and wrote *apologi*, <term>apologi: moral fables that contain hidden precepts for living well.</term> One of these fables is that while a mouse was going through a field, he came upon a ditch full of water; not daring to cross, a frog offered to carry him across, tying the mouse to himself with the intent of pulling him under the water and drowning him. But to the mouse, he pretended to tie him so that he would not fall. At that time, a kite, seeing the mouse and wanting to feed on it, swooped down and snatched it; in carrying it away, it also carried away the frog because it was tied to the mouse. And so it happened that the fraud the frog had devised to harm the mouse turned into its own death. Dante, therefore, remembered this because it was a similar case. For just as the frog, thinking to trick the mouse, was caught, so it happened to the two mentioned above <note>Alichino and Calcabrina, the two demons who fell into the pitch while fighting.</note>. And it demonstrates subtly that similar things often happen among barrators: that while one seeks to trick another, a third comes and tricks both the tricker and the tricked. **IN THE PRESENT BRAWL:** That is, in the present scuffle between Alichino and Calcabrina. And it follows that there is no greater similarity between **MO AND ISSA.** For both these words in different parts of Lombardy signify what we call "now" and "just now." This similarity exists between Aesop's fable and the scuffle of these demons, comparing the beginning—that is, the cause that moved the frog and the cause that moved the demon, which in each was to deceive—**AND THE END:** That is, the effect that followed, which was that each remained deceived. **WITH A FIXED MIND:** That is, firm. **AND AS ONE THOUGHT BURSTS FROM THE OTHER:** That is, is born; this is a metaphor from many flowers, which are not born unless the bud in which they are enclosed bursts open. **SO FROM THAT ONE ANOTHER WAS BORN:** From thinking about their scuffle. **ANOTHER:** Which was that they might want to take revenge on us and therefore pursue us. **WHICH MY FIRST FEAR:** Which was when he saw they had to go in their company. Hence he said: "O my master, what is this I see? I pray that we go alone without escort." Therefore, this thought doubled my fear. And then he says that thinking to himself, he said: "Since these ones, on our account, have received damage and mockery, they must certainly have conceived anger toward us. And if that particular anger toward us **IS GRAFTED:** That is, links and joins itself with their ill-will." For by their nature, they willingly harm every man, nor can they wish for good, being obstinate in evil. **THEY WILL COME AFTER US MORE CRUELY THAN HOUNDS.** For if the hound chases the hare, not for a particular injury received from it, but out of natural and universal hatred, how much more cruel will these ones be, having both particular and universal hatred? "Hare" in Latin is called *lepus*, as if it were *leuipes* <note>A folk etymology: "levipes" means light-footed.</note>, because it runs swiftly. Archelaus wrote that each has both sexes in itself and that they conceive by themselves. And certainly no other animal except the badger <note>Landino likely means the hare here, following ancient biological myths.</note> conceives upon a conception; for at one and the same time, it suckles a young one already born, and in the womb it already has one covered in fur and perfect, and one not yet covered, and one not yet entirely formed. Some believe that in the Alps there is a species of hare that stays under the snow in winter and feeds on it.

---

Universal speaking says that imagination brings about the event. This is the opinion of all the greatest philosophers and especially of Aristotle, especially when the soul has a fixed imagination. Therefore, by such imagination, the poet was oppressed by great fear, so that his hair stood on end. For such imagination creates fear, and because fear constricts the heart, the blood runs entirely to its aid, because in the heart is the fountain of life. Because of this, the exterior limbs remain cold, and the cold shrinks the bodies, and those...

# CANTO XXIV

<column-break/>

> **And he: "If I were leaded glass,**
> **I would not draw your outward image into me**
> **as quickly as I receive that which is within.**
> **Just now your thoughts came among mine**
> **with similar action and similar face,**
> **so that from both I made a single counsel."**

<column-break/>

[Fear and cold] tightened, they create a rigor which raises the hairs found therein. From this, the "capriccio" <note>A "capriccio" here refers to a shudder or a sudden shivering of the skin caused by fear.</note> is born. WHEN I SAID: Master, if you do not hide: that is, conceal. YOU AND ME. It is not without reason that Dante shows himself to be the one who goes about conjecturing that the demons—both because they are harmful by nature and because of their particular anger—must be striving to harm them. And that Virgil responds to him: and that Dante’s imagination came into his as clearly as a corporeal image comes into a mirror. For the lower reason is that which discourses upon particulars. And the higher reason comes from these particulars to universals. Because by turning itself to the images

---

of particular things which it finds in the senses, it reduces those to universals. Man has within himself five internal senses: <term>common sense</term> <note>The faculty that unifies data from the five external senses into a single perception.</note>, <term>imaginative</term>, <term>estimative</term>, <term>phantasy</term>, and <term>memory</term>. The common sense is that to which the external senses refer what they comprehend; and insofar as it is a sense, it receives the images of things without their matter—but only while the matter is present. For instance, I see you, and my common sense receives the image of your body without the body itself, but only while the body is present. And as common sense, it gives perfection to the sensory operation. The external senses do not do this. For the eye sees and the ear hears, but the eye does not realize it sees, nor the ear that it hears. Only the common sense is that by which we understand what we see and hear. And the same occurs with smell, taste, and touch. Furthermore, even when things are present to the external senses, none receives any sensation other than its own. Sight receives nothing but colors; hearing nothing but sounds. But the common sense, from the image of one sense, understands that which belongs to another sense. For if the visual power represents the yellow color of honey, the common sense, by itself and without the taste, conceives that it is sweet. But let it suffice to have said these few things about the common sense. Following this comes the <term>imaginative faculty</term>, which not only receives the image of the present thing, but retains and preserves it after the thing has departed. You saw <note>original: "Marsilio"</note> Marsilio <note>Likely Marsilio Ficino, a contemporary philosopher and friend of the commentator.</note> yesterday in the temple; today you do not see him. Nevertheless, his image, because it is reserved in this second sense in the same form in which you saw him, retains in you not only his face and features and color, but his gestures and expression. And both of these senses are in the front part and in the first ventricle of the brain. After this is the second ventricle, and at the beginning of this is the third sense, called <term>estimative</term> in other animals, but in man, <term>cogitative</term>. At the end is the fourth, called <term>phantasy</term>. In the third and last ventricle is the <term>memory</term>. The estimative faculty has this power: turning toward the imaginative, and finding therein the stored images of things now absent, it draws from them something even more incorporeal than the images themselves, which philosophers call "intention." For example <note>original Latin: "verbi gratia"</note>, the image of Marsilio is stored in my imaginative faculty; in which, although he is absent, I see his person: of what stature, what features, what color. In it, I see how he walks, with what gestures he speaks, and similar things. Thus, turning to this image, the estimative faculty draws the "intention," which is whether he is a friend or an enemy; whether he is a citizen or a foreigner; whether he is learned or unlearned. And having drawn this intention, it immediately judges whether one should speak to him or not; whether to love him or not love him, and similar things, which, as I said, are more incorporeal than the image. In the fourth place is <term>phantasy</term>, whose faculty is to divide and compose all the images it finds in the imaginative sense and the intentions it finds in the cogitative. Therefore, my phantasy can take the image of Mount Morello and that of gold, and make a golden Mount Morello; it can take the horns of a deer and a horse and form an image of a horse with deer's horns. It can make a city that runs or a river that stands still. But because these judgments made by the estimative and phantasy would perish as soon as they were made, they would not remain in our mind. Thus, although today I have judged that Antonio Canigiani and Giovanni Cavalcanti are most singular friends and deserve to be loved, it would nevertheless be necessary to do so again every hour if there were no memory to preserve for us what was already done. Repeating, then, what pertains to the present passage: Dante saw the ten demons. This was the office of the eye and the common sense. And he not only saw them present, but their images remained fixed in the imaginative faculty, whose office is to preserve them even in the absence of the thing. Therefore, his cogitative faculty, turning to the imaginative, found these images there no differently than if he saw them in a mirror, and from the images, it drew the intentions. For just as a dog, seeing its master, draws from that image the intention, which is another, more incorporeal image—and this is benevolence—and seeing a wolf, draws from its image the intention of enmity, and judges that it should welcome the one and bite the other; so Dante’s cogitative faculty drew from the images of the demons the intentions, which were cruelty, perfidy, malevolence, and the like. Therefore, he judged it useful to flee them. And the imagination was so powerful that it seemed to him he felt them coming. This judgment is proper to the senses, and because of this, it is not only in man but also in other animals; but it is always in particular things, because the sense cannot comprehend universals. Thus Dante—that is, the sensitive part—makes this particular judgment: that at this time and in this place, these demons must be fled. Toward this judgment Virgil turns—that is, the intellect—and approves it because it is true. But he leads it from the particular to the universal, and judges that not only at this time and in this place should these demons be fled, but at all times and in all places, all similar demons must be fled. Therefore, it is most true that reason, pouring itself over the sense, receives the judgment given by it no differently than a mirror receives the image of the body to which it is turned. And if such a judgment is well-given, it immediately approves it. You, then, noting with diligence what we have said about the judgment of sense and reason, will easily understand the text to which I return. WE HAVE THEM Already behind us. Not that he saw them, but the imagination was so powerful that it seemed to him he saw them and felt them. Thus he says: I IMAGINE THEM SO: that is, so strongly: THAT ALREADY I FEEL THEM. And this we explained a little above. AND HE: understand Virgil, replied. IF I WERE LEADED glass: that is, if I were a mirror. Which is glass covered on the back side with a thin plate of lead, which is attached to the glass with certain liquids and juices of herbs that few know how to make. It happens, then, that when a body is placed before the glass, because the glass is "diaphanous"—that is, transparent—it receives within itself the image of such a body. But it does not retain it or multiply it within itself, because it passes through it. But finding on the other side of the glass the lead, which is an opaque and shadowy body, it cannot pass through it; and therefore it remains in the glass and multiplies its rays there and becomes visible. And in this place, Dante has used "periphrasis"—that is, circumlocution—because he said in many words what he could have said in one: he could have said "mirror," and he said "leaded glass," which is almost the definition of a mirror. THE IMAGE FROM Outside: that is, the corporeal image, I would not draw to myself sooner than I. RECEIVE <note>original: "impetro"</note>: that is, fixedly contain. THE IMAGE within: that is, that which you imagine and think. JUST NOW: just recently. YOUR thoughts CAME among mine. Because the sense and the reason think...

...to that same one. WITH SIMILAR ACTION: that is, fearing as you do. AND HE DOES SIMILARLY <note>original Latin: "ET SIMIL faciat"</note>: that is, with a similar appearance: because that same thing represents itself to me as it does to you. But I, taking your particular judgment, make it universal. And I judge that such things must always be fled. Reason does not only judge what the sense perceives, but transcends it with its power: and does what the sense could not do: because through the discourse of reason it consults and investigates if there is any way to flee: and if there are several ways, which is the safest: and all the other things which we treated extensively when we set down the parts of <term>prudence</term> <note>One of the four cardinal virtues, involving the ability to govern oneself by the use of reason.</note>. This discourse is the duty of prudence: and it is proper to reason and not to sense. Because Dante having led himself to speak as much as the sense can, he then leads Virgil to investigate what is proper to reason. Whence follows:

**If it be that the right bank lies so**
**that we can descend into the other trench**
**we shall flee the imagined chase**
**He had not finished giving such counsel**
**when I saw them coming with wings outspread**
**not very far off, wishing to seize us**
**My leader suddenly took me**
**like a mother who is awakened by the noise**
**and sees the leaping flames near her**
**Who takes her son and flees, and does not stop**
**having more care for him than for herself**
**so much that she wears only a shirt:**
**And down from the ridge of the hard bank**
**supine he gave himself to the sloping rock**
**Which closes one side of the next trench:**

**Water never ran so fast through a sluice**
**to turn the wheel of a land-mill**
**when it approaches nearest to the paddles**
**As did my master down that border**
**carrying me away upon his breast**
**As his son, not as a companion**
**Hardly were his feet joined to the bed**
**of the bottom below, when they reached the hill**
**above us: but there was no suspicion:**
**For the high Providence that willed to**
**place them as ministers of the fifth pit**
**takes from all the power to depart from there.**

**Down there we found a painted people**
**who went around with very slow steps**
**weeping and in appearance tired and defeated.**

<column-break/>

Virgil sets forth his counsel, which was to descend from the right bank into the other <term>bolgia</term> <note>A "bolgia" is a ditch or trench in the eighth circle of Hell.</note>. HE HAD NOT FINISHED. Virgil had hardly spoken these words when the demons arrived. And it demonstrates the love and speed he used toward Dante through a very appropriate comparison: and says that like a mother in whom there is supreme love, when waking she sees the house burning: she leaves every other care and takes her son to save him, having more care for him than for herself: so much so that she wears only a shirt: and does not care to flee naked for her safety. Thus Virgil placed Dante upon his breast and, feet forward, almost supine, let himself slide down to the bottom of the sixth trench. TO THE SLOPING rock: that is, to the steep cliff. WHICH closes: that is, shuts off the sixth trench from one of its sides. But so as not to leave behind the allegory of this place: Dante and Virgil depart from the <term>barrators</term> <note>Corrupt politicians who traded public office for money; the inhabitants of the fifth trench.</note>: that is, from the contemplation of this vice. And Dante fears that the demons might harm them: that is, he fears the appetite: that the knowledge of such vice might tempt him. And Virgil discourses in the same consideration: and concludes that it would be useful to descend into the other valley: that is, into the consideration of another vice: but the demons arriving: that is, the temptation stimulating the appetite faster than reason—Virgil—estimated, he suddenly took Dante and placed him on his breast: and slid feet-first down all that bank to the bottom of the other trench. Note that the departure from a vice already known must be quick and fast. And certainly, man slides to the bottom supine: because even if he descends to the knowledge of another vice, and the feet—that is, greed—carry us into that, nevertheless, in going supine the face looks upward: so that the knowledge of the vice is for the purpose of rising from it and not for remaining submerged in it. And he joins Dante to his breast, which is the seat of cognition. Note that the appetite must approach that which reason thinks and considers: which with maternal love, seeing him in danger, leaves every other care and only attends to saving him. Nor can the demons placed in the trench of the barrators follow Dante into the other trench: because the temptations of the vice from which he has already departed cannot stimulate him in the consideration of another vice. And it excellently shows that reason loves the appetite with maternal love, to demonstrate an extreme affection, which is even greater in the mother than in the father. Because as <term>Aristotle</term> <note>Referring to the *Nicomachean Ethics*, where Aristotle argues mothers love their children more because of the certainty of parentage and the greater effort of childbirth.</note> writes, the mother loves the child more than the father does: because she is more certain that it is hers than the father is, and because she endured more labor. For before the birth it weighs upon her, in birth it hurts her, and after birth she remains anxious and hardworking.

This shows the descent of Virgil to have been faster than the course of water through a very steep sluice of a land-mill. For the water that turns a French mill has a smaller fall: because such a mill has large wheels on the side. But the land-mill has small ones underneath. Whence it is necessary that the water come with impetus. And allegorically it demonstrates an incredible velocity that is in the discourse of the human mind, and the celerity that reason must use in the aid of sensuality. THE PADDLES: in the wheel, they are those which the water strikes. APPROACHES: as if it lands and descends. ALONG THAT border. "Viuagno" <note>Original: *vivagno*</note> properly is the edge of a cloth, but here he used "border" for that strip which he took in the descent. AS A son and not as a companion. It shows the affection of reason toward the appetite to be paternal: because notwithstanding that sensuality often rises up against reason, nevertheless, reason always directs it, corrects it, and lifts it up as much as it can.

IN this trench the author found the hypocrites, the sixth species of fraud. A hypocrite is said to be one who, being wicked, nevertheless in his habit and in his acts and in his words strives to counterfeit the good and to appear what he is not. This vice the Christians set down to be of three species. The first is when someone feigns in the sight of men to be full of religion, and in truth fears God not at all. The second, when one does some good...

### CANTO XXIII.

**They had cloaks with hoods low**
**before their eyes, made to the same cut**
**as those made for the monks in Cologne.**
**On the outside they are gilded so that they dazzle:**
**but inside all lead, and so heavy**
**that Frederick used to make them of straw.**
**O eternally wearying mantle!**
**we turned again still to the left hand**
**along with them, intent on the sad weeping.**
**But because of the weight, that weary people**
**came so slowly that we were new**
**in company at every movement of the hip.**

<note>original: "crita" — likely a truncated reference to "hypocrita" (hypocrite)</note> And by the wool, which is white, they mean the outward demonstration of a good that is not there. Wherefore, seeing a priest strike himself out of a semblance of zeal, Paul said: "May God strike you, you whitewashed wall" <note>original Latin: "Percutiat te deus paries dealbata" from Acts 23:3. Paul uses this metaphor to describe someone who looks holy on the outside but is corrupt within.</note>. And certainly they are like a wall which is whitewashed on the outside but black within. Nor is there any vice that more harms the human race. Since with appearances they persuade others that they are such that everything can be believed of them, so that under such faith they can better deceive. These, as Plautus writes, show you bread in one hand to entice you, and in the other they hold a hidden stone to strike you when you do not expect it. It is no wonder, then, if Juvenal <note>original: "laquinate" — referring to Juvenal, who was from Aquino.</note> thunders against them with such force and vehemence in his satire, the beginning of which is: "I feel like fleeing from here beyond the Sarmatians and the icy ocean whenever those who pretend to be like Curius and live like Bacchanalians dare to speak of morals" <note>original Latin: "Vltra sauromatas fugere hinc libet & glacialē oceanū quoties aliud de moribus audent Qui curios sımulāt & bacchanalia uıuunt" — Juvenal, Satire II.</note>. And a little further down: "There is no trust in the face; for what street does not abound in gloomy obscenities? You rebuke foul things when you are a well-known ditch among Socratic sodomites" <note>original Latin: "Frōtis nulla fides: quis. n. nō uicus abundat Trıstibus obſcęnis: caſtigas turpia cū ſis inter ſocraticos notıſſima foſſa cinędos"</note>. And certainly he who confesses his error when sinning and does not deceive you is worthy of excuse. Whence the same poet says: "Therefore Peribonius is truer and more honest; I attribute his vice to the fates, for he confesses it in his face and walk. For these, madness itself gives pardon. But those are worse who attack such things with the words of Hercules" <note>original Latin: "Verius ergo Et magis ingenue peribonus Hunc ego ſatis imputo qui uultu morbiū inceſſeque fatetur His furor ipſe dat ueniā Sed peiores qui talia uerbis Herculis inuadunt."</note>. Concerning these, Cicero most wisely concludes in his book *On Duties*, affirming that the worst generation of men is that of those who, when they wish to deceive, strive to be held as good men. This is, therefore, the nature of the hypocrite. But returning to the text: the poet feigns that these were "painted," that is, polished. For just as a woman who is naturally ugly appears beautiful by applying white or red color, so these men, ugly through some vice, by mimicking themselves in outward acts appear beautiful in the soul, that is, virtuous. Or truly he says they are painted because just as a painting is an ornament only on the surface, so these have virtuous customs on the surface. **SO SLOWLY** With slow steps. This expresses the nature of the hypocrite, who in all gestures wants to demonstrate gravity, restraint, and severity. Whence the same satirist says: "Speech is rare for them and they have a great desire for silence" <note>original Latin: "Rarus ſermo illis & magna libido tacedi."</note>. And elsewhere: "Shaggy limbs indeed and stiff bristles on the arms promise a fierce soul" <note>original Latin: "Hiſpida mēbra quidē & durę p brachia ſetę promittunt atrocem aium."</note>. They show gravity, therefore, in slow steps. These same men, in order to better deceive their neighbor with false tears, show commiseration and compassion toward him; and they show themselves to be tired and worn out so that they appear removed from all idleness and pleasure, and full of labor and distress, performing heavy penance. Which is strictly forbidden by the Author of our salvation, saying: "Do not be like the hypocrites, gloomy, who disfigure their faces so that they may appear to men to be fasting" <note>original Latin: "Nolite facere ſicuti hypocritę triſtes qui extennāt facies ſuas ut appareāt homini bus ieiunantes" from Matthew 6:16.</note>. **THEY HAD CLOAKS.** Commonly those who wish to seem holy use cheap and poorly made garments, as we see the cloaks of monks; and they pull the hoods down over their eyes.

<column-break/>

...not moved by the love of that good, but to appear good. The third type is when one shows himself not to be good so that others believe he is even better and not a hypocrite. Hypocrisy is, therefore, a clever and astute cloaking of a hidden vice. These are truly "painted"—that is, superficially adorned—because a painting adorns only the surface and shows one thing to be what it is not. Whence Virgil: "And he feeds his soul on the empty painting" <note>original Latin: "Atque animū pictura paſcit inani" from the Aeneid.</note>. This name "hypocrite" is Greek. For *Hypocrino* means to mimic or counterfeit. Whence actors are called <term>hypocrites</term> <note>From the Greek *hypokritēs*, meaning an actor or stage player.</note> among the Greeks. For just as in festivals and plays the actors with masks and various clothes counterfeit themselves and appear to be what they are not, so these men counterfeit themselves to appear good. Of these, the Evangelist Matthew—rather, our Savior through the mouth of the Evangelist—says: "Beware of false prophets who come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly are ravening wolves" <note>original Latin: "Attendite a falſis prophetis q ueniunt in ueſti mētis ouiū Intrinſecus uero ſunt lupi rapaces."</note>. This vice is detested in Deuteronomy, where it is written: "Do not wear a garment woven of linen and wool together" <note>original Latin: "Ne induatis ueſtē que ex lino & lana cōtexta eſt" from Deuteronomy 22:11.</note>. It forbids, therefore, that they wear a garment woven of linen and wool; and by linen is signified proud, secret, and hidden thoughts. Which is proper to the hypocrite <margin>May God strike you, whitewashed wall.</margin> ...beating himself out of a semblance of zeal, he said: "May God strike you, whitewashed wall." And certainly they are like a wall which on the outside is... **MADE TO THAT cut:** that is, to that form which exists in Cologne, a city of Germany <note>original: "magna" refers to Magna Germania.</note> where the monks wear very large and poorly made cloaks in a form that is more like a sack than a garment. Francesco da Buti <note>A 14th-century commentator on Dante.</note> relates in this place (I do not know if it is history or fable) and tells that there was once an abbot so insolent and ambitious that he pretended to obtain from the Pope that his monks could wear scarlet cloaks, and belts and spurs of gold, and gilded silver stirrups for their horses. This petition moved the Pope to just indignation, and he commanded that for the future they should use black cloaks, very poorly made, and belts and stirrups of wood. Cologne is in Lower Germany on the Rhine, so called because it was a colony of the Romans. It was built by Agrippa, the son-in-law of Augustus; for this reason it is called *Colonia Agrippina*. **ON THE OUTSIDE THEY ARE GILDED SO THAT THEY DAZZLE, but inside all lead.** By the gold, understand virtue; by the lead, vice. Therefore the cloaks are so well gilded on the outside that they dazzle with their splendor. This denotes that the outward acts demonstrate every virtue. And they dazzle well because he who is dazzled seems to see what he does not see; so these men show themselves to us to be what they are not. The lead inside signifies the sordid and vicious life. For lead cannot maintain any splendor, but always produces rust that stains it, because it is of an earthy and watery nature, and of the nature of <term>Saturn</term> <note>In traditional astrology and alchemy, Saturn is associated with lead, heaviness, and melancholy.</note>. And therefore it remains dull and dark. The same happens to the vicious soul defiled by the desire for earthly and low things, and like unstable water. Gold is of the nature of fire, which illuminates and purges and refines, and proceeds from the Sun, which produces life and every perfect thing. We conclude, therefore, by the lead the vice which in these sinners makes the soul sordid and obscure; and by the gold the inward splendor of simulated and entirely lied-about virtue, the significance of which deceives us and does not make them better. **TO THE SAD weeping.** He said "sad" because the nature of the hypocrite is always to show sadness. Whence the Gospel, speaking of these, said: "When you fast, do not be like the hypocrites, gloomy" <note>original Latin: "Cum ieiunatis nolite fieri ſicut hypocritę triſtes."</note>. And certainly we see many truly religious people who, although they are diligent in vigils, fasts, and meditations, nevertheless always appear cheerful and with a happy face. Regarding this, I can testify of Bernardino <note>St. Bernardino of Siena (1380–1444), a famous Franciscan preacher.</note>, a friar of the Order of Minors, who was worthily recorded in the catalog of saints; he was never seen with a troubled face. Conversely, I know some who in life and customs are a foul sewer of enormous vices, and yet always in the sight of others have a tearful and sad face to hide their dishonest pleasures, which they practice in secret like new Sardanapaluses <note>Sardanapalus was a legendary Assyrian king known for extreme luxury and decadence.</note>. **THAT FREDERICK.** Frederick II, of whom we spoke above in many places. He was naturally cruel. This he demonstrates in the perpetual imprisonment of his firstborn son, and in the blinding of Pier delle Vigne. This man, when he wished to punish those who had acted against the crown, would have a very thick leaden garment made for them, and put them in a vessel over a fire until that lead melted, and thus he would make them die. Therefore he says that the cloaks of these sinners were so heavy that, in comparison to these, those of Frederick seemed to be...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante’s Inferno, Canto XXIII, where the poets observe the hypocrites trudging under the weight of gilded leaden cloaks. The text explains the symbolic weight of hypocrisy and introduces the historical figures of the Jovial Friars.</meta>

# INFERNO:

...were of straw. **OR ETERNALLY.** With wonder, he demonstrates how exhausting it was to carry such a weight, and that such punishment is eternal—if we understand it as the essential and eternal Hell. If we understand it morally, it is also true: because a hypocrite is always in constant anguish to hide his vices, and this is a most heavy burden to them. And it follows that they walked with them: but the sinners, because of the weight, went so slowly that at every step the poets left them behind and reached those who were ahead. Thus, at every movement Dante made, they had new company. And here he clearly expresses what has already been said of their betrayal; and it also signifies that there are many ways of being a hypocrite. Therefore, at every step—that is, at every thought in their consideration—they find new ways and new forms of being hypocrites.

Wherefore to my leader: "See if you find
someone who by deed or name is known,
and move your eyes around as you go."
And one who understood the Tuscan word
shouted behind us: "Stay your feet,
you who run so through the dark air!
Perhaps you will have from me what you ask."
Whereat the leader turned and said, "Wait,
and then proceed according to his pace."

I stopped, and saw two showing great haste
in the expression of their faces to be with me,
but the load and the narrow way delayed them.
When they had arrived, with a slanted eye
they stared at me without saying a word;
then they turned to each other and said:
"This one seems alive by the movement of his throat;
and if they are dead, by what privilege
do they go uncovered by the heavy cloak?"
Then he said to me: "O Tuscan, who to the college
of the wretched hypocrites has come,
do not disdain to tell us who you are."
And I then: "I was born and grew up
above the river Arno in the great city,
and I am with the body I have always had.
But who are you, from whom there distills
such great grief as I see down your cheeks?
And what punishment is this that glitters so?"
And one replied: "The orange cloaks
are of lead so thick, that the weights
make their scales creak so."
"I was Catalano, and this is Loderingo,
named and taken by your land together,
as a single man is usually chosen
to preserve its peace; and we were such
that it still appears around the Guardingo."

<column-break/>

It was the office of the Intellect <note>Represented by Virgil</note> to investigate hypocrisy; which, in investigating it in general, causes a particular instance to be recalled to memory. And because the knowledge of particulars is suspect to the lower reason, Virgil therefore admonishes Dante to hold his step until the one shouting behind catches up to them, and then to walk together with him. This denotes that this vice involves so much simulation and dissimulation that such men are not known except by those who have long familiarity with them. **WHO BY DEED OR NAME** may be known. He said this because men are easily known either by name or by some deed they have done. **TUSCAN:** that is, Tuscan language, because Dante spoke in the Tuscan tongue. **DARK:** that is, black.

They showed haste in the expression of the face. This refers to the demonstration of the countenance. For it often happens that the soul, through the face, demonstrates what it feels within; but they did not show haste in walking, because they could not quicken their pace. And allegorically it means that the hypocrite often has a desire in his soul to hasten and bring something to a conclusion; but in order not to discover his malice, he uses a long time to do what he could have done briefly. **BY THE MOVEMENT** of the throat: that is, in breathing. **CLOAK** <note>original: "stola"</note>. They call that mantle by this name. For in Latin, a *stola* is a garment reaching down to the feet. **AND I THEN: I WAS BORN AND GREW UP.** Here he uses circumlocution, for he could have said in one word: "Born in Florence," which is situated upon the Arno. And it is a "great villa"—that is, a city, speaking in a phrase where the city is called a villa. **AND I AM WITH THE** body I have always had: in contrast to the aerial body which the soul takes after death, with which it presents itself and speaks and shares, according as he places it in the second canticle <note>Purgatorio</note>. **DISTILLS** the grief down the cheeks: that is, the tears, which proceed from grief. **THE CLOAKS** Orange <note>original: "rancie"</note>: that is, orange-colored; and it is a metaphor from flavors that are in the taste, applied to weight which is felt by touch. Therefore, this weight was as troublesome to bear as a "rancid" flavor—that is, the flavor of stale things—is to the taste. **THAT THE WEIGHTS:** of the cloaks. **MAKE** them creak: because of their heaviness. For just as when something ponderous is pulled up or placed in a balance it makes the bones and joints of the one carrying it creak. And he called the legs "scales," which, to better support it, go balancing and counter-balancing the weight a man carries to level it and make it more bearable. **JOVIAL FRIARS** <term>Frati Gaudenti: A military-religious order (Knights of Saint Mary) founded to keep peace, but often accused of corruption.</term> They were Bolognese. In the times of Pope Urban IV, there were some noble men of no mediocre status and wealth, especially in Bologna and Modena, who, in order to live in leisure and be exempt from public charges and burdens, gathered together. By common counsel they sent to the Supreme Pontiff and obtained the right to constitute a new religion in which they could live in leisure and contemplation. Urban established the order whose title was "Friars of Saint Mary," and the habit was honorable, but very different from that of the Preaching Friars <note>The Dominicans</note>; and they wore a white shield with a red cross. No one could be of this order unless he were a knight, but they could not wear gold spurs or have gilded bridles. They stayed in their own houses with their wives and children, and made profession to be ready to fight against infidels and those who violated justice. And although they were named "Friars of Our Lady," nevertheless, because of their splendid and copious life, they were called by the common people "Jovial Friars," especially because they were immune from every public tribute and burden. It happened, therefore, that after the death of Manfred, they began to take ease in our republic <note>Florence</note>... [the text continues to describe the Guelph and Ghibelline conflicts].

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante’s Inferno, Canto XXIII. Having met the hypocrites in their leaden cloaks, Dante now speaks with two "Jovial Friars" from Bologna who served as governors of Florence, and he discovers the punishment of Caiaphas, the high priest who presided over the trial of Jesus.</meta>

# CANTO XXIII.
### 108

->to settle the popular unrest, they elected as governors <note>The term "Podestà" refers to the high-ranking magistrate or governor of a city-state.</note> not one, but two: one of whom was a Guelf and the other a Ghibelline <note>The Guelfs and Ghibellines were the two main rival political factions in medieval Italy, supporting the Pope and the Holy Roman Emperor respectively.</note>. They were to have supreme authority and the power to return the people to whatever state seemed most peaceful and tranquil to them. They thus elected two "Jovial Friars" <note>The "Frati Gaudenti" or "Jovial Friars" was a nickname for the Ordo Militiae Mariae Gloriosae, a religious military order intended to maintain peace, though they were often accused of corruption.</note> from Bologna: Catalano de’ Catalani, as a Guelf, and Loderingo degli Andalò (others say de’ Lambertucci), as a Ghibelline. These men appeared to be full of justice and severity. They lived in the public palace near Saint Apollinare and, from both political parties, they elected thirty-six men whose counsel they used to limit superfluous spending and reform all parts of the republic. Later, seeing that the Guelfs were superior following the death of Manfredi and the victory of Charles of Anjou—as Virgil says: "Following the affairs of Agamemnon and the victorious arms" <note>original: "Res Agamemnonias uictriciaque arma secuti"</note>—and being further corrupted by money, they determined to favor only the Guelfs under the guise of the universal good. This so weakened Guido Novello, the vicar in Florence for Manfredi, that although he had five hundred German knights and many infantrymen called from the surrounding cities, he nevertheless fled to Prato on Saint Martin's Day in the year of our salvation 1266. Then, in the following year, because of the arrival of Guy de Montfort sent by King Charles, the Ghibellines fled the city of their own free will and never returned thereafter. **THE GUARDINGO.** This was the street where the houses of the Uberti, noble Ghibellines, once stood; they were burned down, and the Palace of the Priors <note>Now known as the Palazzo Vecchio.</note> was built there with the square that surrounds it. **FROM YOUR LAND**, meaning from Florence. **TAKEN**, that is, both elected as governor, where usually only one man is solitary—that is, alone. It is as if he says: "The two of us were elected to a position of power that is usually held by one alone." And in fact, Florence was not peaceful, as was said above. **AND WE WERE SUCH** that it is still visible around the Guardingo. For we favored the Guelfs so much that the Ghibellines were oppressed, as shown by the ruin of the houses of the Uberti, the heads of the Ghibelline party.<-

->I began: "O Friars, your evils..."
but I said no more, for to my eyes there ran
one crucified on the ground with three stakes.
When he saw me, he distorted himself all over,
blowing into his beard with sighs;
and Friar Catalano, who noticed this,
said to me: "That transfixed one you gaze upon
counseled the Pharisees that it was expedient
to put one man to martyrdom for the people.
Crosswise and naked he lies in the path,
as you see, and it is necessary that he feel
how each one weighs who passes by.
And in such a way his father-in-law is stretched
in this ditch, and the others of the council,
which was a seed of evil for the Jews."<-

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Ornate decorative initial 'Q' featuring a human figure within floral motifs.</image-desc>

Here is a rhetorical device called "aposiopesis" <note>original: "precissione." A rhetorical break where a speaker stops mid-sentence due to strong emotion.</note>. This occurs when we begin to speak of a thing and leave the speech cut off, interrupted by some passion or disturbance; as Virgil says: "Whom I... But it is better to calm the restless waves." <note>original: "Quos ego. Sed motos prestat componere fluctus." This refers to Neptune's famous unfinished threat in the Aeneid.</note> Therefore, here the poet wanted to show that he had compassion for the pains of these people. But then, moved by the sight of the crucified soul, he left the speech unfinished as a man seized by a greater concern. **ONE CRUCIFIED on the ground with three stakes.** Because just as Christ was crucified with three nails—since each hand was pierced separately and the feet were pierced together—so this man, who had given the counsel that Christ should be killed, deserved a similar punishment. But Christ was suspended on high because his death called sinners to heaven. This man was on the ground because his malicious and hypocritical sentence was the cause of his eternal death and that of many others. This was **Caiaphas**; whose name signifies "sagacious" or "investigator." Also "one vomiting from the mouth," or "the vomit of the mouth." **WHEN HE SAW ME, he distorted himself all over, blowing into his beard.** These are signs of his grief that Dante should see him. He grieved because the hypocrite suffers when he sees his hypocrisy and fraud discovered. He grieved also seeing that the death of Christ, which he had counseled, gave salvation to Christians but brought eternal death to him. **COUNSELED the Pharisees:** Because, bearing envy toward Christ for his miracles and his preaching, and fearing that the people following Christ would abandon the priests, they nonetheless did not dare to speak openly against him. But as a false hypocrite, he demonstrated, out of the zeal and affection he claimed to bear for the people, that he sought the death of Christ; and he said it was useful for one man to die for the people so that all the people would not perish. And therefore the author says: *He counseled the Pharisees that it was expedient to put one man to martyrdom for the people.* **Pharisees** in the Hebrew language signifies "divided," or "dividing," or "violent," or "squanderers." But because he mentions the Pharisees here, we shall remember what Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus, a 1st-century Romano-Jewish historian.</note> writes in his *Antiquities of the Jews* and in *The Jewish War*: among the Jews, there were three sects of philosophers established from the beginning: **Essenes**, **Sadducees**, and **Pharisees**. The **Pharisees** lived soberly and without any luxury, and in every thing they followed the judgment of reason. In no way did they resist those whom they had to obey; they greatly honored the elderly. They believe that everything is ruled by fate, and yet they do not take away man's free will. They believe there will be a divine judgment, and each will be judged according to their merits. They posit that souls are immortal and that they will have suitable dwellings in hell <note>The author uses "inferno" here to refer to the general afterlife or Hades.</note> according to their virtue and vice. Some will remain in perpetual prisons; some will have the power to return to life. For this reason, they maintain that we must build temples and offer prayers. Because of this, they were in the highest veneration among the people and had a great following. The **Sadducees** posit that the soul is mortal along with the body; they have no other observance but the Law. They consider it the highest glory to contradict the teachers of their philosophy. But few possess their doctrine. The third, whom they call **Essenes**, refer everything to divine power. They posit that the soul is immortal. They hold that one should fight until death for the defense of justice. They do not perform any sacrifice together with the common people, because they consider that in purity and holiness they are very different from them. For this reason, they sacrifice separately from the multitude. Their customs and habits are full of virtue. With the greatest diligence, they attend to agriculture. And it is a wondrous thing among them, which is found neither among the Greeks nor any other nation: that they all live in common. Nor is there any among them who has private property. It cannot be said that one is richer or poorer than another. None has a wife. They are unwilling to keep servants, because a wife is a cause of discord, and keeping servants seems an iniquitous thing. Instead, they help each other in all duties and needs. They have those who diligently keep account of all income, and also those who distribute and divide to each person a sufficiency of the fruits of the earth. They elect as priests those whom they repute to be better than the others. These live on simple food and without variety in their meals. They have clothing that is not sumptuous, but clean and neat. To these three sects, Judas added a fourth: who in other things are similar to the Pharisees, but in defense of liberty they are entirely immovable and invincible. They wish for no other lord than God; and they endure every grave punishment and death, and the loss of children, relatives, and friends, so as not to be forced to accept another lord. This was Judas of Gamala; and when the people had agreed to submit and consent to the Roman census, he, together with—
