<meta>This page continues the commentary on the hypocrites in Dante’s Inferno, Canto XXIII. After discussing the Jovial Friars, the text now focuses on the unique punishment of Caiaphas and the realization that the demon Malacoda had deceived Virgil regarding the state of the bridges over the ditches.</meta>

# INFERNO.

Zadok <note>A leader mentioned by Josephus who, along with Judas the Galilean, opposed the Roman census, viewing it as a form of slavery.</note> stirred the people from such a purpose, affirming that such a census was manifest servitude. He incited the people to endure every danger to defend their liberty, affirming that God does not help those who do not have such a purpose. **CROSSED** and naked upon the path. This demonstrates his punishment, which is very fitting. Since he was the highest of the hypocrites, it was not enough that he should bear the weight of his own cloak; rather, he had to feel the weight of all those who passed over him. And in the same torment was placed his father-in-law, who was Annas, and all the other priests who were present at the council in which it was concluded that Christ should die. This council **WAS THE BAD** seed for the Jews, because it produced the destruction of Jerusalem and the dispersion of that entire nation. Furthermore, the poet feigns that he lay across the path, which is a public and manifest place. This signifies that the greater the vice that hypocrisy hides, the more it eventually manifests itself. His being naked signifies the same thing.

---

<columns>2</columns>

> Then I saw Virgil marveling
> over him who was stretched out on a cross
> so vilely in his eternal exile;
> Then he directed to the brothers these words:
> "Do not be displeased, if it is permitted, to tell us
> if on the right hand there lies any opening
> by which we both may be able to depart
> without constraining the black angels
> to come to this depth to take us away."

<column-break/>

Virgil marvels: that is, the doctrine of the Gentiles <note>Virgil represents human reason and the wisdom of the ancient, non-Christian world.</note> marvels at the punishment of those who betrayed Christ. This denotes that through human science we cannot attain the things said of the incarnate God. Nor can it be proved through such science that Christ is true God and true man. **THEN HE DIRECTED.** He asks the brothers Catalano and Loderingo to reveal to them if that ditch has any opening—that is, any exit—on the right hand. Because they had turned to the left when they entered, they had to turn to the right to exit. **IF IT IS PERMITTED:** that is, if it is allowed to you; for the damned souls have no free will to know or to say everything. **WITHOUT CONSTRAINING THE BLACK ANGELS.** That is, the demons. And in this he demonstrates that everything is subject to the power of God.

<columns>1</columns>

---

<columns>2</columns>

> He answered then: "Nearer than you think
> a rock approaches, which from the great circle
> moves and crosses all the valleyed seats,
> except that over this one it is broken and does not cover it;
> you can climb up by the ruin
> which lies against the side and heaps up at the bottom."
> The Leader stood a while with head bowed low,
> then said: "Poorly did he account the matter,
> he who hooks the sinners over there."

<column-break/>

Catalano replied: closer than you, Virgil, believe, a rock approaches which moves from the circle that girds all ten ditches <note>The Malebolge, or "Evil-Pockets," which make up the eighth circle of Hell.</note> and cuts through the middle of them all, forming a bridge over them—except that over this one it is broken. Because, as was said, it broke on the day of Christ's Passion <note>Refers to the earthquake that occurred at the moment of Christ's death, which Dante imagines caused collapses throughout Hell.</note>. But nonetheless, you will be able to exit from here by climbing up the ruins located there; for that path is not entirely steep or sheer, but it "lies against the side"—that is, in collapsing, it left a slope suitable for climbing—and "heaps up at the bottom"—that is, it did not collapse all the way to the floor. **THE LEADER STOOD** a while with his head bowed, as one does when thinking. Then he said that he who hooks the sinners—that is, Malacoda, who torments sinners with hooks as was shown above—"accounted our need poorly." For he said there was another bridge that made a path, and this was false. But it is the custom of the devil to lie. For when he tempts the sinner

<columns>1</columns>

to sin, because he cannot entirely take away the sinner's intellect such that he does not recognize in some part that it is evil, he strives to show that there is an excuse and a remedy. And therefore he said above: "There is a bridge that makes a path." For when he encourages the sinner toward hypocrisy, and the sinner resists because he knows it is a sin, the devil puts before him some excuse and shows that with time he will be able to find a way out of it.

---

<columns>2</columns>

> The friar: "I once heard it said in Bologna
> of the devil’s many vices; among which I heard
> that he is a liar and the father of lies."
> After this the Leader with great strides went on,
> disturbed by anger somewhat in his look;
> wherefore I from those burdened ones departed,
> following the prints of his dear feet.

<column-break/>

He shows that Friar Catalano had heard it said in Bologna—that is, in that city where the study of all the good arts flourishes, and especially theology—that the devil is a liar and the father of lies <note>original: "Diabolus mendax est & pater mendacii"</note>. And certainly the name signifies it, because "devil" in Greek <note>original: "diabolos"</note> signifies "calumniator"; and calumny is nothing other than false infamy and deception. For if you speak evil of another to me falsely, you seek to deceive me, so that I might have a false opinion of one who is innocent. Wherefore calumny was excellently depicted by Apelles of Ephesus, a most noble painter, in this

<columns>1</columns>

form: At the right hand sits a man with ears like those of an ass, in the manner of Midas; and he stretches out his hand to Calumny, who comes toward him. Around this man stand two women, one called Ignorance and the other Suspicion. Opposite them is Calumny, whose form is beautiful but full of rage and disdain; in her left hand she holds a small torch, and with her right she drags behind her a youth who raises his hands to heaven and invokes God as witness to his innocence. Before her goes Envy with a sharp but pale eye, like one who has been oppressed by a long illness. Around Calumny are two who adorn and guide her; these are Treachery—that is, ambushes—and Fraud. But behind her follows Repentance, dressed in black and torn clothes, full of weeping and confused by shame; and she looks back at Truth, who comes to succor the youth wrongly slandered. This is, then, the description of Calumny, which I have set down in brief words because, as I said, "devil" in Greek signifies "calumniator"—that is, one who accuses with lies. And it arises from this verb *diaballein*, which signifies "to slander." **AFTER THIS** the leader went on with great strides. And certainly our intellect immediately departs from falsehood when it recognizes it, because it is desirous of the truth. And when a man realizes he has been deceived by the devil and by sensuality, he is indignant and becomes angry with himself. But it is an anger that does not sin; rather, it excites our mind against sin and makes it eager to flee from it. Therefore he said: "disturbed somewhat by anger." And he added "in his look" to signify that such fire is more in his outward actions than in his soul. **WHEREFORE I** from the burdened ones—that is, from those hypocrites who were burdened by the leaden cloaks—**DEPARTED.** For once we have recognized a vice, we must depart from it and follow the prints and vestiges of the dear feet of Virgil—that is, of the intellect. For once the vice is recognized, the higher reason judges that we must flee it. Reason thus departs from fraudulent hypocrites, and Dante—who is sensuality obedient to reason—follows her.

<header>INFERNO CANTO XXIV. OF THE FIRST CANTICLE BY DANTE.</header>

I n that part of the youthful year
when the sun tempers his locks beneath Aquarius
and already the nights move toward half the day <note>original: "amezo di" — Dante refers to the time nearing the spring equinox when night and day approach equal length.</note>
when the hoarfrost mimics upon the earth
the image of her white sister <note>The "white sister" is snow.</note>
but little it lasts, for its sting is soon tempered
The little peasant who lacks provisions
rises and looks and sees the countryside
all turned white, whereat he smites his thigh
Returns indoors and here and there complains
like a wretch who knows not what to do
then laughs and regains his hope
Seeing the world has changed its face
in a short hour; and he takes his crook
and drives the little sheep out to pasture

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Large decorative woodcut initial 'C' depicting a figure in a landscape.</image-desc>
This twenty-fourth chapter continues from the preceding one. It shows that in this seventh ditch <note>term: "bolgia" - the deep, concentric trenches where different types of fraud are punished</note> the thieves are punished. Because at the end of the previous chapter the poet was somewhat dismayed seeing Virgil troubled, he shows at the beginning of the canto how in a brief time he regained comfort. He expresses all of this through a comparison: just as it happens that a shepherd, seeing the hoarfrost in the morning, fears he cannot lead the sheep to pasture and grieves over it, but shortly after, once the frost is destroyed by the sun, he takes heart again and leads the flock to graze—so Dante, after the dismay received from Virgil’s troubled look, was comforted by the same poet. **IN THAT** part of the youthful year: He uses chronography, which is the description of time. And because he mentions the "year," we will step back a little to show how varied the types of years have been in different nations and different centuries. "Year" <note>original: "Anno"</note> is a Latin name called *annus* as if it were *annulus* (a ring), because just as a ring is round and returns into itself, so the year goes circularly; starting from one sign of the zodiac and passing through all others, it returns to that same one. For it is the sun that creates it, which, starting from one sign, runs through all, and when it has returned to the same place from which it departed, the year is finished. Some say that "year" is named from a Greek verb *Ananeuite* <note>original: "ananeoute" - to renew</note> which means to renew, because when the year is finished, it renews itself. And although the true year is a completed course of the sun through all twelve signs of the zodiac—which space is three hundred sixty-five days and a quarter part, namely six hours and a hundredth part of a day—nevertheless, various nations among the ancients took the year differently. Among those of Arcadia, the year was three months. The Acarnanians had a year of six months. And all the rest of Greece had a year of 354 days. Romulus <note>The mythical founder of Rome.</note> decreed that the Romans should have a year of ten months, beginning in March. This first month they named after Mars, the father of Romulus. The second after Venus, the mother of Aeneas, from whom the Romans descended; thus they said *Aphrodite* <note>original: "haphrodile"</note> for April, because in the Greek language Venus is called Aphrodite. And because the city was divided into elders and youths <note>original: "maggiori & minorit"</note>, May was named for the elders (*majores*) and June for the youths (*juniores*). Then the following months were named by number: and so the fifth was called *Quintilis*, the sixth *Sextilis*, the seventh September, and similarly from the eighth October, from the ninth November, and from the tenth December. In these ten months, there were six months of thirty days and four of thirty-one.

---

Therefore they made a total of 304 days. I will not be occupied at present with demonstrating the intercalary days <note>Leap days added to align the calendar with the solar year.</note>. We shall only say that in the following times, Gaius Julius Caesar the Dictator—of no less genius in learning than in military discipline—corrected every error and ordered the year to be 365 days and a quarter of a day and a hundredth. He willed that every fourth year should be 366 days, to account for the four quarters that in four years make one whole, as we have served extensively in our letter to Francesco Baldovini regarding intercalation and the bissextile <note>term: "bixesto" - the leap day added to February in the Julian calendar.</note>. And in this he imitates the Egyptians, who through mathematical doctrine knew that the solar year is finished when the sun has made its circle through all twelve signs, which it does in the number already written. Therefore Caesar added to the year of Romulus: January and February. He ordered that the beginning of the year should be January, and for this reason he named it after Janus, whom the pagans believed to be the god of every beginning. And February he named from *februa*, which means purification, because in this month they performed sacrifices to purify the souls of the dead. For this reason, the Roman Church, following this order, places January as the beginning and head of the year. This moved the poet to say: **IN THAT Part** of the youthful year, to denote January being the first age of the year, in which, because it is the beginning, the year is still youthful. This is according to the custom of the Romans and the Church. But according to the astrologers, youth is not in the month of January; rather, it is the old age of the year. Since the true beginning of the year is the first entry of the sun into Aries, as is shown in the first canto of this canticle, it follows that January would be near the end. Astronomers therefore divide the year into four parts: the first is Spring, which begins from the entry of the sun into Aries. This is the childhood and adolescence of the year. For just as in this age a man grows and keeps his limbs tender and abounds in heat and moisture—which is the nature of blood, and is like Air, which element is hot and moist—so Spring gives this complexion to the earth, by which all plants germinate and grow and keep themselves tender. The second is Summer, of the nature of Fire, hot and dry, similar to our youth. For when a man has finished his time of growth, he is called a youth, and has already hardened his limbs, being hot and dry, and becomes strong and robust; so Summer is hot and dry, and makes the plants hard and robust and strong. Summer begins as soon as the sun reaches the first degree of Cancer. Then while it passes through Cancer, Leo, and Virgo, the time of Summer always lasts. But when it touches Libra, Autumn begins, which is moist and cold and therefore similar to Water, and gives maturity to the fruits. For this reason it is similar to the "virile age" <note>Adulthood/middle age.</note>, which, leaving behind games and pastimes, becomes of mature counsel and seeks fruitful and honorable things. Winter is cold and [dry] <note>Landino likely meant cold and dry, though he writes "freddo & freddo" (cold and cold).</note> of a melancholic complexion, similar to the Earth, and it is the old age of the year, beginning at the first degree of Capricorn. From all these things, it follows that when Dante calls January the youth of the year, he speaks not according to the astrologers, but according to the custom of the Romans. **BENEATH AQUARIUS** tempers. Aquarius is the domicile of Saturn; and the sun runs through it in this year 1481 from the 10th day of January until the 9th day of February. It is a fixed and masculine sign. By day Saturn rules it, by night Mercury, and Jupiter participates with these. It is of the triplicity of Air; its first face is of Venus, the second of Mercury, the third of the Moon. This sign contains eighteen stars. It rules over the legs of man down to the joint of the foot. It makes a man boastful of a beautiful and colored face, but with one leg longer than the other, and it is the house of friendship. The fables say that Aquarius is Ganymede, snatched up by Jove. It is called Aquarius because it induces rain, and according to Albertus Magnus, it is the cause of a universal deluge when the conjunction of seven planets begins in this sign...

the part which they call Hydra <note>original: "hydra" — a constellation</note> and passes into Pisces. Nor will I say at present why the year has its beginning from the entry of the sun into Aries rather than from the entry of any other sign, because in the first canto of this canticle <note>The *Inferno*</note> we provided the reason. I will only add that there are three types of years. This one which is solar. The second is lunar, which is the space from one conjunction of the moon with the sun until the next. The third year is called the "great year," which according to the opinion of most contains thirty-six thousand solar years. **TEMPERA HIS LOCKS** <note>original: "TEMPERA ECRINI" — referring to the sun warming its rays</note> that is, he tempers his burning rays, because the sun does not heat much while in this sign. **AND ALREADY THE NIGHTS TO THE MIDDLE AND THE DAYS DEPART** <note>original: "ET GIA LE Nocte amezo & edi ſen uanno"</note> that is, the nights and the days are already going to the middle, which signifies that already the nights and the days are divided by half. Not because it is yet the equinox, but the day has already grown so much and the night diminished that although they are not at the middle, they are beginning to go there. He did not say therefore "they already are," but "they already go." Some read "and already the nights to midday depart," that is, already the day has begun to grow and the nights to fail, because until the sun has gone to Capricorn the nights have grown and the days failed. And then, having departed from the winter tropic, it comes degree by degree toward the equinoctial, and the nights begin to diminish until it arrives at the equinoctial where the night is equalized with the day, and they occupy only the middle. And this is in the first degree of Aries. And then the nights follow in their diminution until the summer solstice which is in Cancer, so that the days come to be greatest and the nights smallest. **THE HOARFROST.** The sun while it is above the earth draws humors to itself, and those which it does not consume fall back down immediately when it goes below. But in the summer such humor is called dew, because in Latin it is called *ros*; and in the winter we call it hoarfrost <note>original: "brinata"</note> because the Latins call it *pruina* from "burning through" <note>original: "a perueredo" — Landino derives this from the Latin *perurere*, meaning to burn or shrivel with cold</note>, because with its cold it burns the tender plants. Aristotle defines it thus: that hoarfrost is dew congealed in the middle region of the air by the frigidity of the place and the time when there is no part of heat. By the cold, therefore, that humor which was first dew hardens and becomes white, because the cold gathers and restricts it. **THE IMAGE:** that is, the form of her sister, the snow, which he calls the sister of the hoarfrost because of the similarity that is in them. Therefore in these times the hoarfrost is so great that it resembles the snow. **BUT LITTLE IT LASTS:** because when the sun warms it, it is suddenly destroyed. **AND ITS pain it tempers:** that is, by dissolving itself it diminishes the cold, which when it is excessive because of the great frost is a pain to every thing that has a vegetative soul <note>Plants and living things</note>. Some read "pen" <note>original: "penna"</note> and they want the meaning to be that the frost tempers the pen: that is, it lasts as little as the tempering of a pen lasts for a writer. But to me it seems more likely that the text says "pain" <note>original: "pena"</note> and not "pen," because such a translation is too harsh. **THE LITTLE PEASANT to whom provisions fail** because he is poor, or rather he lacks "provisions," that is, the straw to feed the sheep. **LIKE A WRETCH** <note>original: "Tapino"</note> miserable and placed in a low state, because *tapeinos* in Greek signifies dejected and low. **THEN HE LAUGHS and hope regains** because he had lost it. **SEEING** the world has changed, that is, changed its face because it is no longer white from the frost which is already dissolved.

In this same way was I dismayed, and just as quickly the plaster reached the ill, that is, the remedy to my dismay. **FOR AS.** This shows the reason why he quickly recovered his spirit, because when we were reached the ruined bridge which, as we said, had fallen over the sixth <term>bolgia</term> <note>The deep trenches of the eighth circle of Hell</note>, my leader turned to me with that look, that is, with that aspect which he showed me when he first appeared to me at the foot of the mountain from where the three beasts chased me, as we saw in the first canto. **HE OPENED HIS ARMS after some counsel.** The arms are placed by the Holy Scripture to represent help, and reason always helps the senses. Therefore he shows that the intellect and the superior reason succored the inferior, which by itself was not enough. And he succored after some chosen counsel. This denotes that the human intellect does not come into true consideration without discourse. And for this reason, before Dante embraces <note>The commentator refers to Dante as the "lower reason"</note>—which is when he brings the lower reason back to himself—it is necessary that through such discourse he comes into knowledge of the truth, and this is to consider the ruin.

The author describes what the office of the intellect and of the wise man is: who always, before he makes any enterprise, discourses with the mind. And thus he lifts Dante, who is the lower reason and the sensuality. **TOWARD THE SUMMIT:** that is, toward the top, which is speculation and contemplation. **OF A GREAT ROCK:** that is, of a piece of stone from the ruin. **WATCHED another crag.** As if another great rock. And thus it happens because the intellect not only considers the present, but also looks to the future, and provides for and commands the lower reason—which performs in particulars what must be done—and admonishes it not to set about doing anything that is above its strength. And therefore while Virgil pulls the sensuality to difficult things, before he is at the first considered place, he admonishes him that he should then grab onto another higher one; but before he trusts it, he wants him to test if the crag can support him. The intellect excites the lower reason and the sensuality to great things, and wants them to exit the ditch where the sinners are punished, and rise up to the speculation of the truth with its help. But because not every man has such a gift from nature that his wit serves him for great things, therefore every man should have enough intellect to examine his own possibility, and not take on doing a thing that is above it. And therefore he says "test first." **IT WAS NO way for one clothed in a leaden cape.** He has placed in this depth the hypocrites with capes of lead. He says, therefore, that such a steep way was not for men who had such heavy garments; and allegorically he shows that he who is burdened by the habit of sin cannot exit from it, since those who have not made a habit of it only free themselves with difficulty. **FOR WE hardly, he being light:** that is, Virgil himself who is light. **AND I PUSHED.** He says that Virgil was light because the intellect illustrated by science is light to fly like an eagle to sublime and celestial things; and I pushed, because sensuality and the lower reason, although by its nature—

The commentary by Cristoforo Landino interprets Dante’s physical struggle to climb the steep rock as an allegory for the arduous nature of attaining moral and intellectual virtue.</meta>

<header>INFERNO.</header>

And if it were not that on that precinct
the slope was more twisted than on the other,
I know not of him, but I would have been quite overcome.
But because Malebolge <note>The eighth circle of Hell, meaning "Evil-Ditches"</note> toward the gate
of the lowest pit all slopes down,
the site of each valley carries this:
That one side rises and the other descends;
we finally arrived at the point
where the last stone breaks away.
The breath was so milked from my lungs <note>original: "La lena m era del polmon si muncta"</note>
when I was up, that I could go no further;
rather, I sat down at the first arrival.

"Now it behooves that you thus shake off sloth,"
said the master, "for sitting on down feathers,
one does not come to fame, nor under blankets;
Without which, he who consumes his life
leaves such a vestige of himself on earth
as smoke in the air, and foam in the water.
And therefore rise up; conquer the panting
with the soul that wins every battle,
if it does not collapse with its heavy body.
A longer ladder it behooves you to climb;
it is not enough to have departed from these;
if you understand me, now act so that it profits you."

<column-break/>

[natu]re <note>The text begins mid-word, likely completing "natura."</note> will be heavy. Nevertheless, when it obeys the intellect, it is pushed by it. **THEY COULD mount up from crag to crag:** that is, from shard to shard. And here he shows that Virgil and he did not fly upward: but with difficulty they went up, climbing from one shard to another. Which allegorically can be referred to moral and intellectual virtue. Since, if moral virtue is that which distances us from the bottom of vices and pulls us to the summit of the mountain, no one ever made a habit of virtue except bit by bit and with intervals of time: and if we refer it to intellectual virtue, we have already said that the human soul does not know without discourse <note>In the sense of logical progression or reasoning.</note>. Therefore, it goes from shard to shard.

The poet shows in this part that if the side of this precinct of the sixth ditch had not been more twisted—and because of this, less steep and a lesser struggle—he would have remained overcome by the difficulty of the climb: **I KNOW NOT of him, but I would have been quite overcome.** This allegorically signifies that sensuality, at the very least, if not reason, would have been overcome by such great difficulty. And he rightly said: **I KNOW NOT of him.** Because, on one hand, considering the excellence of reason, which is fit to conquer every resistance, and on the other, seeing the great difficulty, he remained in doubt as to which would have been overcome. But he did not doubt himself: that is, his sensuality: because its fragility cannot resist. **BUT BECAUSE Malebolge toward the gate Of the lowest pit all slopes.** He assigns the reason why this slope was lower than the one above. Because the site of the eighth circle, which above he called Malebolge, slopes entirely toward the ninth; which, because it is the innermost and lowest circle of the others, we call the "pit": because it must be deep, being at the center, and narrow, being the innermost. And it is true that the site of each valley **CARRIES:** that is, brings with it

this: **That one side rises and the other descends.** Because these ten ditches step down in a form where the second is lower than the first, and higher than the third; the third is higher than the fourth, and lower than the second. And so from step to step. Therefore, this sixth ditch had a shorter slope than the fifth. **THE LAST Stone breaks away:** That is, departing from the other bridge, it falls. **THE BREATH WAS milked from my lungs.** The lung embraces the heart where the fountain of natural heat is; and because of excessive heat, it is in need of continuous refreshing. The lung, as if failing, draws the exterior air and refreshes it with that. And this is our bellows <note>original: "altare," though likely a typo for "mantaco" or similar, given the context of bellows ("mantachare") later.</note>. But because the heat of the heart increases the more it moves and tires the body, it is necessary that the pumping of the lung be more frequent and greater, and draw more air to itself. Wherefore it happens that it is much refreshed by it: in such a way that the man reaches such a state of panting that, if he is not succored with fresh and humid air, he would fail in life, because the lung could no longer breathe. And without such respiration, the heart would perish. Therefore he says well: **THE BREATH:** that is, the power. **WAS SO MILKED:** So emptied out. Because just as the teat is emptied by milking, so the lung is by ventilating. **THAT I BUT SAT.** that is, I placed myself to sit: and I rested at the first arrival. And indeed, sensuality tires itself much in exiting from sin, in such a way that it remains so breathless near the end that it goes no further. But reason, which knows that it is not enough for a man to abstain from one vice if beyond that he does not follow through into the knowledge of another to similarly abstain from it—and then, having abstained from all, if he does not rise to the virtues, he has tired himself in vain. For as Horace says: Although **Virtue is to flee vice** <note>original: "Virtus est uitium fugere"</note>, it is nonetheless necessary that, having conquered the difficulty which is leaving sin, one also conquers that which is in rising to the virtues. Therefore Virgil, that is the intellect, comforts and pushes the sensuality to such labor. And therefore follows:

See what reason the intellect assigns to sensuality to push it toward arduous things, in which consist moral and intellectual virtue. **NOW It behooves that you thus.** i.e., As you know at present. **SHAKE OFF SLOTH.** *Poltro* signifies "bed" <note>An archaic term related to laziness or a pallet.</note>. Whence we call lazy and sleepy men *poltroni*: and *spoltrie* signifies to exit the bed: that is, to wake up, and leave sleep and idleness, and give oneself to the virtues, the path of which is fatiguing and steep. And he places "lying on down" and "staying under blankets" (which is the cover of the bed) for the somnolent, lazy, idle, delicate, and voluptuous life, which is the enemy of every virtue and the mother of every vice. Whence Petrarch says: **Gluttony, sleep, and the slothful feathers / Have banished every virtue from the world.** <note>original: "La gola el sonno & lotiose piume Hanno del mondo ogni uirtu sbandita." — Petrarch, *Canzoniere* VII.</note> The master said then—that is, the intellect, which is the true master of the soul—that he who lives in an idle and delicate life does not acquire fame. Where it seems that in admonishing Dante, Virgil should have said "virtue" rather than "fame." Because man ought to direct all his actions to virtue, and should rather want virtue with infamy than fame with vice. Of this sentiment all the Holy Scriptures are full, and every grave philosopher affirms that virtues should be sought for themselves and not to acquire fame. But because fame follows virtue as the shadow follows the body, fame should not be fled if it comes behind virtue, provided that virtue is not sought just to have fame. To this we will answer that it was not without cause that he said "fame." Because in this place, Virgil, who is a learned and wise man, admonishes Dante, who is taken for him in whom appetite and sense can still do more than true reason. Therefore, having to comfort such a man toward virtue, which is full of difficulty and labor, the wise exhorter must allure him with fame, which is desired by every man. And just as the wise doctor, seeing the child refuses the healthy medicine frightened by its bitterness, mixes in honey, so that that sweetness pulls him to drink even the bitter thing; so the wise preceptor, seeing that the appetite is more greedy for...

<summary>In this passage, Virgil urges a physically exhausted Dante to overcome his fatigue, using the promise of fame as a "honeyed" incentive to pursue the difficult path of virtue. The commentary by Landino explains the geography of Malebolge and provides an allegorical interpretation of the climb as the transition from avoiding vice to actively practicing moral and intellectual virtue.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante’s Inferno, Canto XXIV. In the previous section, Virgil exhorted Dante to shake off sloth and pursue fame, as a life without fame leaves no more trace than smoke in air or foam on water. Landino is now expanding on the philosophical definition of fame and the necessity of transitioning from vice to virtue through active effort.</meta>

<header>CANTO XXIV.</header>

fame rather than of virtue. Wherefore the satirist Juvenal said: <note>original: "Quis enim uirtutem amplectitur ipſam premia ſi tollas?"</note> "For who embraces virtue itself if you take away the rewards?" He proposes fame because, through its sweetness, you might more easily accept the bitterness found at the beginning of the path to virtue. One could also say that the poet used a poetic figure, putting that which follows for that which precedes: and he said "fame," meaning "virtue," which gives birth to fame. Fame is a "middle name," meaning one that extends to both evil and good. And we say a man has "fame" when his deeds are made public and spoken of everywhere; if these deeds are vicious, they lead to "ill fame" (infamy). This is why the description of Fame placed by Virgil in the fourth book <note>referring to the *Aeneid*</note> denotes bad fame—that is, the infamy incurred by Aeneas for having abandoned the right course of virtue and giving himself over to a voluptuous and base life, as I described at length in the fourth book of our *Camaldolese Disputations* where I declared the allegories of Virgil. But if the deeds are virtuous, good fame follows. And it is called "fame" because *fari* in Latin signifies "to speak"; and fame, as stated, is the "frequent speaking" of someone. And from fame—that is, from the frequent speaking of one’s deeds—is born the "name," because such a man is named everywhere; and from the name, he acquires "glory." And glory is a certain splendor resulting from good fame and a good name. **WITHOUT WHICH HE WHO CONSUMES HIS LIFE.** He who lives without fame leaves no other vestige—that is, no other sign that he ever existed—than smoke leaves in the air or foam in the water, which, as we see, soon perish and leave no sign after them. "Vestige" <term>vestigio: a footprint or track</term> is properly the form left by a foot on the ground, which we call a track or a trail. Whence we say "to track" and "to trail" and "to investigate" when we follow the tracks of someone to find them. By extension, we say "to investigate" meaning to search with diligence. And we call "vestige" any sign which, remaining, demonstrates that a thing once existed. This is why we say the ruins of a collapsed house are the "vestiges" of a house. **AND THEREFORE RISE UP:** that is, rise from sitting, which signifies rising from vices and from base and earthly things. **CONQUER THE PANTING.** <term>ambaſcia: breathlessness or intense physical distress</term> "Ambascia" is an excess of breath which greatly troubles those who climb steep places. Thus, just as the body, in going uphill, is troubled by breathlessness, so too is our sensuality named by that difficulty when it sets out upon the steep path of virtue. But it is necessary to stir up fortitude and the endurance of the soul, and with these, conquer every difficulty. And certainly, while the spirit is willing but the flesh—that is, sensuality—is infirm or weak in resisting, it is necessary that the intellect stir within us fortitude, endurance, patience, and perseverance, which, by overcoming every difficulty, push the sensuality upward. **IF WITH ITS HEAVY BODY IT DOES NOT COLLAPSE.** We properly say a thing "collapses" <note>original: "accaſciarſi"</note> when, being unable to support itself due to its heaviness, it lets itself fall to the ground. Thus, sensuality and appetite, being oppressed by the weight of the body, collapse. But the soul, which by its nature is inclined to choose, easily rises to the knowledge of divine things if it does not allow itself to be weighed down by the contagions of the body. **A LONGER LADDER IT BEHOOVES YOU TO CLIMB:** than the one you have already climbed. **IT IS NOT ENOUGH TO HAVE DEPARTED FROM THESE.** Allegorically, understand that it is not enough to depart from vice if one does not also ascend to virtue. **IF YOU UNDERSTAND, ACT SO THAT IT PROFITS YOU.** Note that it is not enough for a man to understand what must be done if he does not do it. Nor is he just, or temperate, or strong, who merely knows what justice, temperance, or fortitude are; but rather he who lives according to such virtues and puts them into practice. Whence Aristotle says: <note>original: "Virtutis .n. laus omnis in actione conſiſtit."</note> "For all the praise of virtue consists in action." And understand this especially regarding the moral virtues. Because in the intellect, a man can be virtuous through knowledge alone even if he does not put it into practice. Thus we call one a "good physician" when he perfectly understands natural reasons even if he does not apply them to anything; and similarly an "arithmetician" although he performs no calculation; and a "geometer" although he measures nothing, is called one who knows well how to count and understands every measure and proportion.

## I rose then, showing myself provided
## with better breath than I felt myself to have,
## and said, "Go on, for I am strong and daring."
## Up over the ridge we took our way,
## which was craggy, narrow, and difficult,
## and much steeper than the one before.
## I went along speaking, so as not to seem feeble,
## whereat a voice came out from the other ditch,
## unsuited for forming articulate words.
## I know not what it said, even though I was already
## atop the back of the arch that crosses there;
## but he who spoke seemed moved to anger.

<column-break/>

[The poet intends] to describe the nature of one who is obedient to a teacher, who, although he does not feel strong enough for the labor imposed upon him, nonetheless shows himself to feel so, and says he is. "I ROSE": because Virgil had said, "And therefore rise up." "AND I SAID, GO ON": as if to say, "I will follow you." "I AM" made strong by the hope of the reward you proposed to me; because, as Tully <note>Cicero</note> says: <note>original: "Honos alit artes omneſque accendimur ad ſtudia gloria."</note> "Honor nourishes the arts, and we are all kindled to studies by glory." "UP OVER THE RIDGE we took our way, which was craggy": which hurts the feet, which desire to find a delicate and level path. "NARROW": A steep path is more difficult when it is narrow, because you cannot go zig-zagging as you can on a wide one. "AND DIFFICULT": It follows that being steep, craggy, and narrow, it was difficult. "MUCH MORE than the one before": The further they go toward the bottom, the more grave the vice they find; and the graver it is, the more difficulty it gives to those who wish to know it in order to flee from it. Some say the poet wants to show the difficulty he had in finding the invention to poetically express this vice. "I WENT ALONG SPEAKING, so as not to seem feeble": because the lower reason, already disposed to obey, moves further ahead of the intellect than

---

it is able, to demonstrate with what good will it obeys. **WHEREAT A VOICE CAME OUT from the other ditch:** and this was "unsuited"—that is, not convenient or apt for forming words, because it was confused and poorly distinct, as happens to those who are inflamed with anger. And this was the reason that he—although he was upon the back of the arch, which was directly above the one speaking—did not understand; it was not due to the distance of the place, but from the confusion of the voice, which is greatest in an angry man.

---

## I was leaning down, but my living eyes
## could not reach the bottom because of the dark;
## wherefore I said, "Master, see that you arrive
## at the next belt, and let us descend the wall;
## for as I hear from here and do not understand,
## so I look down and discern nothing."

<column-break/>

The meaning is that although he held his eyes—that is, the physical eyes such as we use in life—nonetheless, due to the darkness of the place, he could not discern the figures from the bridge, even though he could see [something]; just as he heard the voice but did not discern the words. And here it denotes that the soul, shut up in the body, cannot see or hear except for bodily things. Furthermore, the senses and the lower reason cannot know and distinguish except for things very low and in particulars. Therefore, he prays to the higher reason <note>Virgil</note> to lead him, because that reason possesses the knowledge of all things.

<summary>In this passage, Landino interprets Dante’s arduous climb into the seventh ditch of Hell as an allegory for the difficult transition from vice to virtue, emphasizing that true virtue requires action and the pursuit of honorable fame. The physical darkness and indistinct voices of the ditch represent the limitations of human senses and lower reason when confronted with grave sins.</summary>
<keywords>fame, virtue, allegory, Aristotle, Juvenal, sensuality, intellect, moral philosophy, Virgil, Malebolge</keywords>

# INFERNO.

> I give no other answer to you, he said,
> except the doing: for the honest request
> should be followed with the work, in silence.

<note>original: "Altra riſpoſta diſſe non ti rendo / ſe non el fare: che la domanda honeſta / ſi de ſeguir con lopera tacendo."</note>

...one may have a veiled knowledge of particulars: nonetheless, one cannot distinctly comprehend them. Furthermore, he wishes to draw closer to see particularly, implying that although the science our souls acquire is of universals, it must nonetheless be born in us from particulars, as we have demonstrated elsewhere. **I GIVE NO OTHER ANSWER.** The wise poet excellently demonstrates in passing that when a man in whom the intellect reigns knows the request made of him to be honest, he does not occupy time with a long answer: but in silence, he fulfills what has been asked of him.

> We descended the bridge from the head
> where it joins with the eighth bank,
> and then the ditch was manifest to me:
> And I saw within it a terrible throng
> of serpents of such diverse kinds
> that the memory still curdles my blood.
> Let Libya boast no more of her sands,
> though she produces *chelidri*, *iaculi*, and *phareae*,
> and *chencri* with *amphisbaena*;
> Neither so many nor such cruel pestilences
> did she ever show with all Ethiopia,
> nor with that which lies above the Red Sea:
> Among this cruel and most dismal abundance
> ran naked and terrified people,
> without hope of a hole or helitrope.
> They had their hands tied behind with serpents,
> which thrust their tail and head through the loins,
> and were knotted in front.

<note>original: "Noi diſcendemo el ponte dalla teſta..." onwards. This passage lists various types of snakes found in the 7th ditch, comparing them to those of North Africa and the Middle East.</note>

Cato <note>Marcus Porcius Cato the Younger</note> passed through there to join the Pompeian armies which were in Africa with Juba and Scipio. The nature of the place produces these serpents: but the fables say that when Perseus passed through this region with the head of Medusa, such serpents were generated from the drops of blood which fell from it. These are of various species and generations: among which are **chelidri**, called almost like *cherhydri* <note>original: "cherhydri"</note> because they live equally on land and in water; for *chersos* in Greek signifies "land" and *hydor* means "water." Furthermore, **iaculi** are so named because in the form of a dart they launch themselves from trees and pierce limbs; and the Latins call a dart *iaculum*. **Phareae** are serpents which walk on their tails and are otherwise elevated from the ground. **Cencri** are serpents which are dotted with points similar to grains of millet; so called because *cencron* <note>original: "cencron" (kengchron)</note> in Greek signifies millet: they travel straight and do not twist like other serpents. **Amphisbaena** have two heads: one where it naturally should be, the other in the tail. Albertus Magnus <note>13th-century philosopher and scientist</note> denies they have two heads, but writes that they appear so because of the great mobility of the ribs from every part. It is in the first order, whose venom kills in three hours. **NEITHER SO MANY Pestilences**: nor animals so pestilential. **ETHIOPIA.** *Etho* <note>original: "Etho"</note> in Greek signifies "I burn." Hence Ethiopia is named for the immeasurable heat of the sun, which has the power to produce black men in that region. Ethiopia is full of immeasurable serpents, which lie in wait and attack elephants; they put their heads into the nostrils where the elephant cannot reach with its trunk <note>literally: "hand"</note> and suck the blood. Many serpents are found in that part of Ethiopia where the people called Asachei live. There they are found twenty cubits long. It is said that on those shores four or five intertwine together and travel by sea like ships, carrying their heads high in the manner of sails. In India they are as large as Megasthenes <note>ancient Greek historian</note> writes, swallowing entire deer and bulls. Pliny and many other historians affirm that Marcus Atilius Regulus, consul of the Romans in the first war against the Carthaginians, killed a serpent one hundred and twenty feet long in Africa near the river Bagrada using catapults and similar instruments. And in Italy there is a species of serpent called **boia**; and in the time of Emperor Claudius, one was found in Rome on the Vatican Hill which had an entire small child in its body. **THE RED SEA** begins in Egypt and reaches Palestine. Through this sea Moses passed with the people liberated from the hands of Pharaoh. It is called red not because its water is red, but because the earth beneath it is red and shows the water to be red. Others say it is named the Erythraean from King Erythras; but because *Erithro* in Greek signifies "red," they therefore called it red. **AMONG THIS Cruel and most dismal abundance.** Among this abundance of cruel serpents full of sadness and continuous mourning ran naked people full of terror which they took from the serpents; and they did not hope to find a <term>pertuſo</term> <note>a hole or hiding spot</note> to hide from the serpents. **NOR HELITROPE:** that is, nor any thing which would make them invisible so that the serpents could not see them, as the <term>helitropia</term> <note>heliotrope</note> does. Solinus writes in his book *On the Wonders of the World* <note>original: "de mirabilibus mũdi"</note> that the heliotrope is a stone found in Cyprus, but more noble ones are in Ethiopia and Africa; it is of a green color but clouded and distinct with purple spots. But placed in a copper cauldron, it causes the rays of the sun striking it to reflect as bloody. There is also a herb likewise called Heliotrope because it always turns toward the sun: and *helios* in Greek signifies "sun" and *trepo* signifies "I turn." The <term>magi</term> <note>magicians or wise men</note> write therefore that by anointing such a stone with the juice of such a herb, and consecrating it with lawful prayers, the man who wears it becomes invisible. Therefore these sinners do not hope...

<column-break/>

**FROM THE OTHER CIRCLE:** that is, from the other bank that surrounds this valley. **I SEE** And I discern nothing clearly: because the inferior reason is like one who sees something in a place where there is little light. Such a person, although they see some shadow, nonetheless cannot distinguish and figure it: so it is with the inferior reason. Although it...

**S**he continues by describing the eighth ditch <note>bolgia</note>. And in that, she describes the punishment of thieves; and sets down the pains with which they are tormented. And we shall treat these shortly below. But first, returning to the text, he demonstrates that wishing to descend into the seventh ditch, they passed the bridge which is above it; and from that head of the bridge which joins the eighth bank, they descended into the seventh ditch. He descended, therefore, the bank—not on this side, but on that—which was born not from that rock which divides the sixth from the seventh, but the seventh from the eighth. **AND I SAW WITHIN** a terrible throng: that is, a frightening congregation. *Stipare* in Latin signifies "to pack" or "to stow." Hence he said "throng" <note>stipa</note> as if it were "stowed" <note>stiva</note>: that is, a narrow and packed congregation. **OF SERPENTS OF such diverse kinds:** that is, of such diverse movement, as if to say of such diverse species. **THAT THE MEMORY:** that is, the remembering of it. **STILL CURDLES** <note>original: "SCIPA"</note> that is, scatters the blood: and he said "scipa," that is, scatters, from this verb *scerpo, scerpis*. And the meaning is: that even now when I remember it, such fear comes over me that the blood vanishes through the veins and I remain pale. **LET LIBYA BOAST NO MORE.** One of the three parts of the world is named Africa by us, as if *a-neu phrycas* <note>original Greek: "α-νευ φρίκης"</note> meaning "without cold," because it is a hot region being placed in the south. Others wrote that Africa took its name from Aphros, son of Hercules. This is called Libya by the Greeks, and took such a name from Libya, daughter of Epaphus and mother of Busiris. In Libya is a part named "sandy Libya." This is arid and dry, deprived of rivers, springs, and wells, and where rain never falls. Its land is all sand and sterile, bare of grass and trees. It is filled with various species of serpents, of which Lucan writes when he shows that...

<meta>This page continues Cristoforo Landino’s commentary on the seventh ditch (bolgia) of the eighth circle of Hell, where the thieves are punished. # CANTO XXIII.
<note>The header indicates Canto XXIII, but the text on this page consists of the verses and commentary for Canto XXIV of Dante's Inferno, beginning with the description of the thieves and the transformation of Vanni Fucci.</note>

...to be able to find the heliotrope <note>A legendary gemstone, also known as bloodstone, believed in the Middle Ages to grant invisibility to the wearer.</note> through which they could become invisible. **WITH SERPENTS** Their hands were tied behind. Why does the author place the punishment for theft in this ditch? We shall note that there are two ways one takes what belongs to another: either openly and with violence, as bandits, assassins, and highwaymen do—taking and stripping not by theft but by robbery, and often killing to plunder—or truly by theft and in secret, with fraud and deception. The former were called *robbers* <note>original Latin: "latrones"</note> by the Latins. The latter are called *thieves* <note>original Latin: "fures"</note> from the word *theft* <note>original Latin: "furtum"</note>, which in Latin signifies black and dark; because he who wishes to commit a theft seeks night, shadows, and darkness. Therefore, since this seventh ditch is one of those where fraud and not violence is punished, it seems that one should deal here with thieves and not robbers. Nevertheless, because even those who commit robberies with violence first use fraud—using it more than force, as we see in the bandit who hides in ambush before assaulting the traveler and uses many other frauds—theft and robbery are punished together. They stand, therefore, among the serpents, which are animals full of craftiness and cunning, to demonstrate that fraud and deceit are those vices with which they stain the soul and with which they afflict and perturb the conscience, by which they are always bitten by remorse after the error is committed. They pass, then, with the head and the tail through the loins to the chest where the heart is, the seat of thought: because such fraud, with the head—that is, from the beginning before the sin is committed—gives great anxiety to the mind, thinking not only of the sin one prepares to commit but much more of the danger of infamy and the harm that may result. And then with the tail—that is, after the end—rethinking what has been done and waiting every hour for such wickedness to be discovered, whence infamy and punishment result for him. This is the head. This is the tail of the serpent: which, passing through the loins to the chest, pierces the heart and knots itself in front; because such thought and such sting of conscience do not pass away, but remain tied in the mind and always stay there. Nor can they hide or flee such a sting of conscience, nor find any remedy for it; for as Juvenal says: "This is the first punishment: that with himself as judge, no guilty man is acquitted." <note>original Latin: "Prima hęc eſt ultio quod ſe iudice nemo nocēs abſoluitur."</note> Therefore, no one who has committed any wickedness is acquitted by himself, because his conscience always judges that he deserves punishment for the sin committed and, as a witness to such wickedness, stings him night and day. Wherefore the same poet said: "To carry his own witness in his breast night and day, the Pythian prophetess answered a certain Spartan." <note>original Latin: "Nocte dieque ſuū geſtare in pectore teſtem Spartano cuidam reſpondit pythia uates."</note> They bind the hands behind because fraud induces perverse and depraved actions. The hand signifies the work, and just as the front parts show right and laudable operations, so the posterior parts denote the contrary. **THEY RUN** Naked and terrified. Running demonstrates the discourse of the mind in investigating frauds. They are naked because most of the time poverty drives them—understanding poverty as the greed for possession, because everyone who does not have as much as they desire is poor. And terrified because while they think of doing evil, the fear of being punished terrifies them. The serpent is cunning, and so is the thief. The serpent, sliding, enters through every hole. The thief thins himself to enter everywhere. The serpent is hated by everyone; the thief the same. The serpent hidden in the grass strikes. The thief harms in secret.

---

And behold, at one who was near our bank,
a serpent sprang up that pierced him
where the neck joins the shoulders.
Neither "o" nor "i" was ever written so quickly
as he caught fire and burned all to ashes;
it was necessary that, falling, he became so.
And after he was so destroyed on the ground,
the dust gathered itself together
and immediately returned to that same form.

---

So by the great sages it is confessed
that the phoenix dies and then is reborn
when the five-hundredth year approaches.
In its life it feeds on neither herb nor grain,
but only on tears of incense and amomum,
and nard and myrrh are its final swaddling bands.
And as one who falls and knows not how,
pulled to the ground by the force of a demon
or other blockage <term>opilation: a medical term for an obstruction or seizure</term> that binds a man,
when he rises and looks around,
all bewildered by the great anguish
he has suffered, and looking, sighs:
Such was the sinner after he had risen.

<column-break/>

They do not give the opinion of those who wish the poet to place three types of thieves. The first is of those who have not yet made a habit of it, but finding the occasion for stealing, they do not abstain; because, as the proverb says, "at an open chest, the righteous man sins." The second is of those who have already made a habit and always strive to steal, but nonetheless use such discretion that they do not steal everything, nor in every place, nor from every person. The third is of those who have no regard for place, time, or person. Therefore, here he treats the first species, showing that although one has not made a habit of stealing, yet happening upon the chance to take something conveniently, the appetite is suddenly kindled; and he burns in such greed, and burning becomes ash, to show that such heat makes him no longer a man, having lost his reason and being so blinded by such desire that he feels or hears nothing else. But after he has fulfilled his desire, reason returns, and he becomes a man again and judges that he has erred. But hindered either by shame or greed, he does not return the stolen goods. Therefore the serpent, which is the desire to commit fraud, pierces him and in a moment burns him and turns him to ash—that is, it transforms him from a man into a senseless thing—and then having fallen into sin, he collects himself and returns to being a man. He has expressed, therefore, the first species of thieves.

---

No differently does he affirm that this man is reborn from his ashes than the phoenix does. This bird, they say, is in Arabia, as large as an eagle; its neck is the color of gold, the rest of the feathers are purple, except that the tail is azure, but marked with feathers the color of a rose. They write that it lives five hundred and sixty years. Manilius the senator was the first of the Romans who wrote of the phoenix, and said that no one ever saw it feed, but that in Arabia it is consecrated to the sun. When it is old, it makes a nest of twigs from the cassia tree and of incense, and fills it with fragrances, and in that it dies. From its marrow a worm is born, which then becomes a phoenix, and immediately celebrates the funeral rites for its already dead mother. And it carries the whole nest near to Panchaia <note>A legendary divine island in the Indian Ocean, associated with the sun.</note>, a region of Arabia, to the city of the sun, and places it upon the altar. Its death is the revolution of the Great Year, when the qualities of the times and the stars return to their beginning. And this begins around the noon of that day when the sun enters Aries. Cornelius Valerianus writes that the phoenix once flew in Egypt and was brought to Rome at the time when Claudius was emperor and censor, and placed in the... <note>The text likely refers to the "comitium" or public assembly area.</note>

Landino distinguishes between different types of thieves and provides a classical description of the Phoenix bird according to ancient authorities like Manilius.</summary>

--- Page 228 ---
<meta>This page continues Landino’s commentary on Canto XXIV of the Inferno. Having described the serpents that torment the thieves, the text now focuses on a specific sinner (Vanni Fucci) who, after being bitten by a serpent, dissolves into ashes and is reborn like the Phoenix. Landino provides a detailed natural history of the Phoenix and an allegorical analysis of human reason versus bestial instinct.</meta>

INFERNO:

## O power of God, how severe it is,
## that crashes down such blows for vengeance.

...one thousand eight hundred years from the founding of Rome <note>Landino is discussing various historical accounts of the Phoenix's lifespan.</note>: But no one doubts that this is false. Others write that when the Phoenix approaches death, it turns toward the rays of the sun, and these, reflecting off its splendid feathers, create fire. From this, it burns together with its nest; it is reborn first as a worm, and after three days its wings grow. **IT FEEDS ON NEITHER GRASS NOR GRAIN**, as other birds feed. But it feeds only on **TEARS**: that is, gums or the resin of incense and of amomum <note>Amomum is an ancient aromatic spice plant, often identified with cardamom or ginger species</note>, which distills from its trunk like tears, and then solidifies as we see in the juniper and many other trees. Incense in Latin is called *thus* <note>original: "thus"</note>. Amomum, cinnamomum, and cinnamon are the same thing: it grows in Ethiopia in sterile places. It is a small tree that grows no higher than two cubits <note>A cubit is an ancient unit of length based on the forearm, roughly 18 inches</note>; they do not harvest it without the permission of Jove <note>The Roman name for Jupiter</note>. And they obtain this with forty-four entrails of oxen, goats, and rams. When they have harvested it, they give half to the sun, and suddenly it catches fire and burns by itself. Vespasian <note>Roman Emperor, 69–79 AD</note> was the first who dedicated a crown of this wood adorned with gold in the Capitol and in the Temple of Peace. **AND NARD AND MYRRH** are the final swaddling clothes: that is, it makes its final nest of nard and myrrh in which it burns. Nard grows in India and produces spikes, which is why it is called *spigo* <note>Spikenard</note>. It also grows in Syria; it grows in Gaul, and this is better known to us—it even grows and seeds itself in Florence. It also grows in Crete. Myrrh is a tree that grows in Arabia in the same forests as incense. Others maintain that it grows in more regions of Arabia, whereas incense grows in no more than one called Sheba <note>Sabaea</note>. And this is a thorny tree and grows up to six cubits. The leaves are like olive leaves but wrinkled and sharp. Others describe it as similar to the juniper and of that flavor. **AND AS IS HE**. A perfect comparison by which he demonstrates that after this man returned from ash to his first form, he became stunned, bewildered, and dazed, as happens to one who falls by the **POWER OF A DEMON** or by some **OBSTRUCTION** <note>original: "opilatione," a medical term for a blockage of the bodily humors</note> and, having been unconscious, comes back to himself. But in that beginning, he is astonished and almost senseless. **BY POWER OF A DEMON**: that is, by incantation, as we read of Simon Magus <note>A biblical figure who attempted to buy spiritual power; in medieval lore, he was a powerful sorcerer</note>, who through magic arts made men faint in such a way that they appeared truly dead, and then, making them recover, he led the common people to believe he had the power to raise the dead. **OR BY ANOTHER OBSTRUCTION** that binds a man, such as the **COMITIAL DISEASE** <note>original: "morbo comitiale," an ancient term for epilepsy, so named because if a person had a seizure during the Roman *comitia* (assemblies), the meeting was suspended</note> or the falling sickness. Allegorically, this means that just as one who faints—whether by diabolical incantation or by infirmity—remains stunned and marvels when he returns to himself because he does not remember how the event occurred, so when the sinner has fallen into theft, either by diabolical temptation or by the inherent weakness of his sensuality, he later marvels within himself how he allowed himself to be overcome by such a sin. **O POWER OF GOD**. With this exclamation, he admonishes the sinner that although God is full of mercy toward the living, nonetheless after death He uses nothing but severity, which is justice without any mercy. O how severe is the power of God. **WHICH CRASHES DOWN**: that is, it strikes with vehemence and great impetus such blows, meaning pains and punishments. Hence we say a "crash of water" when the rain falls with great force. **FOR VENGEANCE**: that is, for punishment; because vengeance is sometimes taken for judicial punishment and as a form of justice.

## The guide then asked him who he was,
## to which he replied: "I rained down from Tuscany
## a short time ago into this fierce gorge.
## A bestial life pleased me, and not a human one,
## like the mule I was. I am Vanni Fucci;
## Pistoia was a worthy den for me."
## And I to the guide: "Tell him not to slip away,
## and ask what fault pushed him down here,
## for I saw him once as a man of blood and rages."

**I RAINED DOWN**: that is, I fell down here among the damned, as it is said of the demons who rain down from heaven. **INTO THIS GORGE**: that is, into this hell which swallows and devours souls. Or rather, he called this narrow valley a "gorge" because the Latins call such places *fauces* <note>Latin for "throat" or "narrow passage"</note>, meaning a throat. **A BESTIAL LIFE PLEASED ME, and not a human one.** Although there are many kinds of living—for some give themselves to pleasure, wallowing in the mud like pigs; some to sleep and idleness; some to cruelty and robbery—nevertheless, none of these can be called a human life, because they are not according to the nature of man, but of beasts, which by their nature follow only appetite. But since man is different from other animals solely by reason, only that which is according to reason—in which the other animals do not participate—can be called a human life. But it must be considered 

that in us there is a double reason. One is called by philosophers **SUPERIOR REASON**, which turns and exercises itself concerning the knowledge of the truth, and such is found in universals, where Intelligence, Science, and Wisdom consist. The other is **INFERIOR REASON**, and this has knowledge of particulars and uses Prudence, which is the true rule in human operations, and directs it toward right living by means of justice, fortitude, and temperance. Therefore, from the superior reason is born the **CONTEMPLATIVE LIFE**, in which we seek true knowledge of human and divine things. From the inferior is born the **ACTIVE LIFE**, in which, with the moral virtues, we direct ourselves, our families, and our republic toward right living: ourselves with ethics, the family with economics, and the republic with politics. For this reason, as I more clearly demonstrated in the first book of the *Camaldolese Disputations* <note>Landino's own philosophical work, *Disputationes Camaldulenses* (1472), a key text of the Italian Renaissance</note>, only these two kinds of life are proper to man: the contemplative, represented by Rachel in the Old Testament and by Mary in the New Testament; and the active, represented by Leah and by Martha, because they are conducted with reason. And every other kind of life where everything depends on unbridled appetite—as appears in all the vices—is not human, because it is without reason. Rather, it is bestial, because appetite alone rules the beasts. Therefore, this man having given himself to homicides, robberies, extortions, thefts, and larceny, he did not follow the reason proper to man, but the appetite according to which beasts live; he led a bestial life. **LIKE THE MULE THAT I WAS**. It is no wonder that I lived like a beast, being a mule and not a man. He alludes to this name "mule," which is a beast, because we commonly call bastards "mules," and he was a bastard. **PISTOIA WAS A WORTHY DEN FOR ME.** As if to say that just as he was bestial, so Pistoia was a worthy habitation for him, because that city was a receptacle for bestial men; and therefore he calls it a "den," because a den signifies a cave in the woods where wild beasts dwell. **TELL HIM NOT TO SLIP AWAY**: that is, do not let him flee. **FOR I SAW HIM AS A MAN OF BLOOD.** A cruel man and a shedder of human blood. **AND OF RAGES**: that is, wrathful. Dante marvels that such a man—violent, tyrannical, and a murderer—is not placed in the higher circles <note>Specifically the Seventh Circle, where the violent are punished in the river of blood</note> where such people are punished. Vanni was the son of Messer Fucci de’ Lazzari from Pistoia, a noble family, but he was a bastard; he was of cruel, tyrannical, and bestial character. It happened that many Pistoians were dining together one evening in a temple; after dinner, with lutes and other instruments, they went singing through the land. Finally, they arrived at the house of Ser Vanni della Nona, a very excellent notary of good character who was in their company. The others stopped to celebrate because he had a good and very beautiful wife. Vanni, with two companions, being always stimulated by diabolical thoughts, went toward the Bishop's...

<summary>Landino explains the myth of the Phoenix as a metaphor for Vanni Fucci’s transformation and delves into a philosophical defense of the "human life" (reason) versus the "bestial life" (appetite). He identifies the sinner Vanni Fucci, a bastard from Pistoia, whose violent and thievish nature makes him a "mule" in both name and character.</summary>

<page-num>113</page-num>
<header>XXIV INFERNO <note>The original header mistakenly reads "VXX PURGATORIO," but the text clearly belongs to Inferno Canto XXIV.</note></header>

...to which the house of Ser Vanni <note>Vanni della Monna, a notary</note> was nearby. Here some say they found the door of the church and the sacristy of **Saint James** open by the negligence of the priests, who on that night of **Carnival** had gone out for their pleasures, as is customary. Others say that they opened it with tools and lockpicks. Finally, they took from the sacristy all the silver and the jewels of the altar of Saint James, which were of great value, and they returned to their companions. Although the companions strongly reproached the deed, they nonetheless agreed to hide the items in the house of Ser Vanni, both because it was the closest place and because they believed that, due to the man's good reputation, such a house would never be searched. In the morning, the canons discovered the theft and gave notice to the **Podestà** <note>The chief magistrate of the city</note>. He, investigating diligently, examined and tortured everyone known to be of ill repute. Thus it happened that many, although they were innocent of this deed, nevertheless confessed to other crimes they had committed due to the pain of the torture, and were justly condemned to death. At last, Rampino, the son of Messer Francesco, a noble citizen, was taken; and although he did not confess to the theft—because in truth he was innocent—the Podestà was so incensed against him, due to his poor reputation, that he resolved to condemn him. He had already assigned a certain term by which the stolen goods had to be produced. Because Rampino was in utter despair, he had arranged with relatives and friends that on the night preceding the final day of the term, they would rush to the palace of the Podestà with fire and take the young man by force. But **Vanni Fucci**, who had retreated to Monte Carelli in the Florentine countryside, loving Rampino dearly, advised Messer Francesco to have Ser Vanni arrested. This man was taken one morning during Lent while he was in the church of the Friars Minor <note>The Franciscans</note> to hear the divine sermon. He was led away, not without the indignation of the people, because he was considered a man of excellent character. He confessed to having the entire theft in his possession, and said that he had often tried to take it out of the city, but every time he approached the gate, he seemed to see the **Cavalier** <note>Saint James, often depicted as a knight</note> coming to search for him. For this, he was hanged and Rampino was freed.

---

The sinner, who did not pretend not to hear,
but directed his mind and face toward me,
And was painted with a look of sad shame.
Then he said: "It hurts me more that you have caught me
in the misery where you see me,
than when I was taken from the other life.
I cannot deny that which you ask:
I am put down so far because I was
a thief in the sacristy of the beautiful ornaments,
And falsely it was once attributed to another.
But so that you do not enjoy such a sight,
if ever you are out of these dark places,
Open your ears to my announcement and hear:
**Pistoia** first is thinned of the **Blacks**;
then **Florence** renews people and ways.
**Mars** draws a vapor from **Valdimagra**
which is wrapped in turbid clouds,
and with a tempest, impetuous and bitter,
It shall be fought over the **Piceno field**,
where it will suddenly break the mist
so that every **White** shall be struck by it.
And I have said this so that it may cause you grief."

<column-break/>

Dante shows that Vanni felt shame when he saw him, and affirmed that death was not more painful to him than being caught in such a place. This denotes that thieves feel such great pain from the infamy of being exposed that they would rather die. Then he narrates the theft committed; and like an unfriendly man, thinking that Dante takes pleasure in seeing him in such misery, he predicts what must happen to the **Whites** in order to corrupt Dante's pleasure with some pain. *Open your ears to my announcement and hear:* For the understanding of this text, you should note that in the year 1300, Pistoia was in great prosperity. In that city, the **Cancellieri** family had great power, having more than a hundred men of military rank; therefore it was in great reputation and esteem, not only in its own homeland but in all of Italy. By a wicked accident (of which we shall speak below in Chapter 32), this family divided into two parties with deadly hatred: one called the **Whites** and the other the **Blacks**. From this, division arose in all the rest of the city, and shortly thereafter our own republic <note>Florence</note> became infected with the same disease, as we narrate more extensively in the sixth canto. In the following year, in the month of May, the Whites of Pistoia, with the help of the Whites of Florence, drove out the Blacks of Pistoia.
   Then the Blacks formed an army and gave its command to the **Marquis Marcello Malaspina** <note>Historical sources usually identify him as Moroello Malaspina</note>, whose marches are in **Valdimagra** (today called Lunigiana, from Luni, a very ancient city). And in the **Campo Piceno**, which is not far from Pistoia, they broke the Whites. And so he says: *Mars draws a vapor from Val di Magra*, because Mars is the signifier of war. *Draws vapors*, that is, causes: which stir up war, just as terrestrial vapors drawn upward generate smoke, winds, and sudden rains, to which the impetuous movements of wars are similar. *It shall break the mist*: that is, it will make a cruel battle that will strike like a lightning bolt; that is, it will act with great force, like lightning (the celestial arrow) which is born from the refraction of clouds, as we have shown elsewhere.
