<meta>Continuity with previous page: The translation continues the narrative of Dante's Inferno, transitioning from the punishment of the thieves to the specific encounter with Vanni Fucci and the centaur Cacus in Canto XXV.</meta>

# INFERNO CANTO XXV OF THE FIRST CANTICLE BY DANTE.

At the end of his words, the thief
raised his hands with both "figs"
crying: "Take that, God, for I square them at you!"
<note>The "figs" is a vulgar, obscene gesture made by thrusting the thumb between the index and middle fingers. To "square" them is a gesture of extreme defiance and insult toward the divine.</note>
From then on the serpents were my friends,
because one coiled itself then around his neck
as if to say, "I do not want you to say more."
And another around his arms and bound him again,
clinching itself so firmly in front
that he could not even give a nudge.
Ah Pistoia, Pistoia, why do you not decree
to turn yourself to ash so you last no longer,
since you surpass your own seed in evil-doing?
<note>Pistoia was the hometown of Vanni Fucci; Dante implies the city's wickedness has surpassed even that of its infamous founders.</note>
Through all the dark circles of Hell
I saw no spirit so proud against God,
not even he who fell from the walls at Thebes.
<note>This refers to Capaneus, a king who defied Jupiter during the siege of Thebes and was struck down by a thunderbolt.</note>

And he fled so that he spoke no further word;
and I saw a centaur full of rage
come crying: "Where, where is the bitter one?"
Maremma, I do not believe, has as many
snakes as he had upon his haunch
until where our human face begins.
<note>Maremma is a coastal marshland in Tuscany once famous for being infested with malaria and snakes.</note>
Over the shoulders, behind the neck,
with open wings, there lay a dragon
which sets on fire whoever it encounters.

Now sacrilege. Vanni took sacred things from a holy place. Cacus took the things of God: Hercules being one of the gods of the gentiles. Cacus, of whom Virgil says: *Cacus, the horror and infamy of the woods of the Aventine* <note>original: "Cacuſ auetine sceluſ atque infame siluæ"</note>, was the son, according to the fables, of Vulcan, the god of fire. Because he was an infamous thief and robber, he laid waste to all neighboring lands with fires and blazes. Thus, they imagine that fire and smoke issued from his mouth. He lived on the Aventine, one of the seven hills of Rome, and in it had a terrible cave, the entrance of which he closed with a very heavy rock, and there he brought all his prey. Finally, when Hercules was returning from Spain and leading the herds of cattle he had taken from Geryon, the king of Spain, Cacus, greedy for new prey, stole four of them and pulled them by their tails into the cave, so that by the direction of the hoofprints it would appear they had not gone into the cave but had come out of it. Hercules searched for them a long time, and finally, not finding them, was already leaving when he heard their lowing and realized where they were. He ran to the cave. Cacus defended himself by sending out smoke and flame, but the strength of Hercules was greater; he lifted the rock that covered the cave, jumped inside, and with his club killed Cacus and took away the cattle. Maremma: any maritime place where the winter is less cold and the grass lives for the sustenance of flocks and herds, we call "maremma," as if "maritima" <term>maritima: coastal or relating to the sea</term>. And this especially occurs in Tuscany, because such coastal lands are turned toward the midday sun; and in the Maremma of Pisa there is such an abundance of snakes that some places are uninhabitable because of them. "Upon his haunch": because the centaur from the belly up has human limbs; he calls the belly the "face" <note>labbia</note> because in it is the dregs and the foulness which in Latin is called *labes* <term>labes: a stain, blemish, or ruin</term>. The snakes denote the frauds which he places on the centaur's haunch, which is the beast-like part of him, to show that the frauds were savage and cruel. "Over the shoulders, behind the neck, with open wings, there lay a dragon": he places a dragon in the same spot, positioned in the rear parts, to show that he uses cunning in vicious works. A man does not notice the cunning used against him except from behind—that is, after the deed is done. "With open wings": which demonstrates the vehemence and speed in doing evil. "Which sets on fire whoever it encounters": that is, whomever he runs into. For every man who encounters fraud perishes by its fire.

My master said: "That is Cacus,
who beneath the rock of Mount Aventine
many times made a lake of blood.
He does not go with his brothers on one path
because of the theft he fraudulently committed
of the great herd that he had nearby."

<column-break/>

The text continues by describing the nature of Vanni, showing how much pride and impiety he used toward God, since out of contempt he showed Him the "figs." But immediately after the sin, the due punishment followed: for a serpent coiled around his neck as if it wanted to squeeze his throat so he could not speak, and another bound his hands behind him and then clinched itself in front so that he could not move. Allegorically, this shows that it is no small torment for the wicked person who delights in sinning in words and deeds to have the power of speaking and acting taken away. For speaking, it ties his throat; for acting, his hands. "Ah Pistoia": he uses an exclamation that moves indignation against Pistoia. Furthermore, he uses repetition, doubling the name, which makes the speech more effective and grave. "Why do you not decree": that is, why do you not deliberate. "To turn yourself to ash": to burn and become cinder. "Since you surpass your own seed": that is, those who founded you, who were the seed from which you were born. And here many explain that the first founders were the soldiers remaining after the defeat and death of Catiline, who, as Sallust writes, were full of wickedness and impious toward their homeland. But this cannot proceed, because it clearly appears that Pistoia existed before the conspiracy of Catiline. Therefore we will simply say: "Your seed," meaning your ancestors. And he concludes that he has not seen in all the circles of Hell a soul more proud toward God, not even "he who fell at Thebes from the walls": meaning Capaneus, who was mentioned above.

Above, in the chapter where the tyrannical and violent men are punished, the poet placed the centaurs, and of those we spoke sufficiently. Now he places Cacus here, who—although he is not the son of Ixion and the cloud as the centaurs are imagined to be—nonetheless he depicts him as half-man and half-horse, and calls him a centaur because his habits were savage and bestial. But he does not put him among the violent, but among the fraudulent, because in his thefts and robberies he mixed fraud with violence, and fraud is a graver sin than violence. It shows that he is not only punished in this place but also punishes the others. Vanni Fucci is accompanied with him because they were similar in committing not only thefts, but also sacrilege.

It is fitting that Virgil tells him the history of Cacus, because he includes it in his *Aeneid*. "Who beneath the rock of Mount Aventine": in the cave which was under a cliff on Mount Aventine. This is one of the seven hills of Rome near the Tiber, named "Aventine" from Aventinus, king of the Aborigines, who was drowned here in the Tiber and buried on this mountain. Others want it that the Sabines, to whom Romulus granted that they might inhabit this mountain, called it Aventine after a Mount Aventine which they had in their own lands. Others say it is named Aventine from the "brought" <note>the text cuts off here</note>...

### CANTO XXV

Wherefore his wicked deeds ceased
under the mace of Hercules, who perhaps
gave him a hundred blows, and he did not feel the ten.
<note>Dante refers to the myth where Hercules killed Cacus with his club. The "hundred and ten" implies Hercules struck him so many times and so hard that Cacus died instantly after the first few, feeling nothing of the rest.</note>

While he was speaking, he dashed away,
and three spirits came beneath us,
of whom neither I nor my leader took notice,
Until I cried out: "Who are you?"
Whereat our story was interrupted,
and we attended only to them.
I did not know them; but it happened,
as it often follows by some chance,
that one was obliged to name the other,
Saying: "Where has Cianfa stayed behind?"
Whereupon I, to keep my leader attentive,
placed my finger up from chin to nose.
<note>A gesture calling for silence and close observation.</note>

If you are now, reader, slow to believe
what I shall say, it will be no wonder;
for I, who saw it, barely admit it to myself.
As I kept my eyebrows raised toward them,
behold, a serpent with six feet launches itself
in front of one, and clings entirely to him.
With its middle feet it gripped his belly,
and with the forward ones it took his arms;
then it bit him through both cheeks.
The hind feet it spread down to the thighs,
and thrust its tail between the two,
and stretched it up behind along the loins.
Never was ivy so rooted
to a tree as the horrible beast
entwined its own limbs with those of the other.
Then they stuck together as if they had been
made of hot wax, and mixed their color;
neither one nor the other seemed what he was before.

<column-break/>

That is, from the coming of men <note>Original: "aduenimento deglhuomini"</note>, because at that time the Temple of Diana stood there—where Saint Sabina is today—which was common to all Latin peoples. Alternatively, because this hill was once surrounded by the river and one traveled there by boat. Regarding the "lake" he made many times: he killed the men who passed there and flooded the place with their blood. He does not go with his brothers <note>The other Centaurs in the Circle of Violence.</note> not because he was not the son of Ixion like them, but because of the similarity of members and vices. And he does not go by the same path because they are punished as violent, while he is fraudulent, for he stole the cattle of Hercules with fraud. Hercules, although he gave him a hundred blows with his mace, nonetheless he did not feel ten of them, because the first blows were so heavy that he died.

**While Virgil spoke**, Cacus dashed away and passed by. And three spirits, whose names follow below, came beneath them because they were walking through the ditch <term>bolgia: the specialized ditches of the Eighth Circle of Hell</term> and the poets were above on its bank. Neither Virgil nor Dante had yet noticed them, which signifies that neither ancient history (which Virgil would know) nor modern history (which Dante might have read) makes mention of these specific men. But Dante had heard them named, and therefore adds that he did not know them personally. But it happens by chance that one named the other. In this poet, the variety of narration is a marvelous thing for those who pay close attention; he always varies with great artistry and always changes the form of storytelling with new invention. This variety refreshes the reader's mind and removes the boredom and weariness that arises from similarity. No one can listen attentively to many things if they are all told in the same way. Furthermore, because his narrations are based more on the persons than on the things, he always attributes to each character a speech suited to their nature and habits; such artistry is easy for the learned to recognize and difficult for the unlearned. **Where has Cianfa stayed?** This man was of the Donati family, according to many writers. No one else records what theft he committed, but here the poet subtly shows that it often happens by chance that, without realizing it, one thief reveals another. **So that my leader might stay attentive:** there is a philosophical reason why Dante notices them before Virgil. Universal science <note>Represented by Virgil/Reason.</note> does not enter the intellect unless Dante, representing the senses and lower reason, first recognizes the particular. Many will perhaps wonder why I repeat the same thing so often regarding the difference between higher and lower reason. But let necessity be my excuse, which constrains me to repeat it as many times as it occurs, for without this one cannot give the allegorical sense to the text. **I put my finger from chin to nose:** this is a gesture by which we show we want silence. Between the chin and the nose is the mouth, which, when pressed closed, makes silence. Whence Juvenal says: "Restrain your lip with a finger" <note>Original Latin: "Digito compeſce labellum."</note>.

**His intention**, whether through fiction or allegory, is not only to delight but to lead the listener's soul into the greatest wonder. At the beginning, he makes the reader attentive by showing he has new and unusual things to say, which he who saw them can hardly believe. And therefore he says: **If you are now, reader, slow to believe.** He says then that a serpent with six feet launched itself at one of the three spirits and joined its head and face with that of the spirit. It joined its front feet and legs with the spirit's arms and hands, and with its middle legs it embraced the chest and belly; the hind ones it extended so far that they joined with the spirit's legs. Regarding the "essential Hell," this denotes that after death such a soul is joined with the demon that tormented it. Allegorically, it shows that when a man has made a habit of fraud, he is joined with it in such a way that human intelligence no longer appears in him, but a serpentine nature, into which he converts all his sharpness to harm with venom. Yet he is not entirely serpentine, for he still retains some part of human reason. This is the second species of those who, although they have formed a habit in such a vice, nonetheless have some restraint against stealing everything from everyone. Thus, from the serpent and the man, a certain thing is made that is neither serpent nor man. **As I kept my eyebrows raised:** this signifies that by contemplating the nature of theft with diligence, one recognizes this transformation. **With its middle feet it gripped his belly:** the serpent clings...

The accompanying commentary by Landino explains the allegorical nature of fraud and the poetic techniques Dante uses to maintain reader interest.</summary>

<meta>Continuity with the previous page: The poet Dante has been describing the horrific transformation of the thief Agnel Brunelleschi, who has been seized by a six-legged serpent. The two bodies are beginning to fuse into a single, monstrous form.</meta>

# CANTO XXV.
<note>This signature mark "o iiii" indicates the fourth leaf of the "o" gathering in the printed book.</note>

### As there proceeds before the heat
### up through the papyrus a brown color
### which is not yet black, and the white dies.

Therein lies the end and the effect, which possesses the cunning and venom of a serpent aided by the depraved reason of man. **IVY** was never so rooted to a tree. The nature of ivy is to cling to trees and walls: it goes along tangling itself, putting out certain barbs and roots everywhere with which it attaches itself. Whence in Latin it is called *hedera* from *herendo* because *hereat*: that is, it adheres. <note>original: "hedera ab herendo quia hereat"</note> **LIKE TENDRILS** That is, it attaches itself as the vine attaches with its tendrils. **THEN THEY STUCK TOGETHER.** As the most acute writer demonstrates, there are three stages in this transformation: first, that being separate, the spirit and the serpent bound themselves tightly; and through all the limbs like ivy which, beginning from the lower part of the stalk, goes attaching itself up to the top. Nevertheless, though they were thus attached, they were not yet incorporated. Then follows the second stage in which they began to flesh together as if two candles of hot wax were stuck together. The third stage is in which they mixed as if two vessels, one of gold and the other of silver, were melted and mixed together: and from two metals a third body was made, which had the color of neither gold nor silver. And this he demonstrates by the comparison of the wick of a candle: which, first white, becomes black when burned. But first, before it is burned, it takes on a brown color between white and black. Whence he says **AS THERE PROCEEDS** before the heat a brown color. Brown is a color which is not fully black, but leans toward black. This the Latins call *fuscus*. **UP THROUGH THE** papyrus. That is, through the wick which is made of cotton. Although papyrus is a species of reed in Egypt, from whose pith the ancients made many things which we now make of cotton. <note>The commentator explains Dante's famous simile of a burning piece of paper or a candle wick, where the "brown" color precedes the actual charring.</note>

### The others looked on, and each
### cried: "Oh me, Agnel, how you change!
### See that you are now neither two nor one."
### Already the two heads had become one,
### when there appeared to us two figures mixed
### in one face, where both were lost.
### Two arms were made of four strips;
### the ribs with the legs, the belly, and the chest
### became members that were never seen before.
### Every former aspect was canceled;
### the perverse image seemed both
### of one and of none; and such it went away with slow step.
### As the lizard, under the great scourge
### of the dog days, changing hedges,
### appears like lightning if it crosses the path.
### So it appeared, coming toward the bellies
### of the other two, a small, enflamed serpent,
### livid and black as a peppercorn.
### And that part through which we first take
### our nourishment, it pierced in one of them;
### then it fell down stretched out before him.
### The pierced one gazed at it but said nothing;
### rather, with feet fixed, he yawned,
### just as if sleep or fever had assailed him.
### He looked at the serpent, and it at him;
### one through the wound and the other through the mouth
### smoked violently, and the smoke met.

<column-break/>

the head with the head: because the senses of the man become the senses of the serpent. Similarly, the joining of the torso where the heart is signifies thoughts and meditations; and by the joining of the arms and hands he intends works; and by that of the legs and feet, the affections and desires. **AND THRUST HIS** tail between both. This—

You could read how many transformations any poet, Greek or Latin, once made; but if I err not, you will find none that equals this in invention. In which the reader may so delight, marvel, and be stupified by its novelty and well-hidden allegory. But let us follow the text. With admiration the companions said: **OH AGNEL** <note>Agnello Brunelleschi, a Florentine nobleman and thief.</note> how you change; how you can convert into a species that is neither you nor the serpent. And he rightly says that there were two figures mixed in one face, and in that face they were lost: because there was no longer the figure of either serpent or man. **WERE MADE** two arms from four strips. Because to the two arms were attached two legs. **EVERY FORMER ASPECT** was canceled: that is, annulled. Both that of the serpent and that of the spirit. And the perverse image—that is, changed into its opposite—appeared neither as one nor two. This allegory we have opened above, and the passage seems to me incomparable.

The author begins here to treat of the third species of theft, in which are those who not only have made it a habit, but furthermore in stealing have no regard for man, nor thing, nor place. He feigns, therefore, that while they were occupied in watching three spirits, a little serpent came with such velocity as a lizard crosses the path in the great heat. And it bit the navel of Master Buoso. <note>Buoso degli Abati, another Florentine thief.</note> And finally the bite became a serpent, and the biting serpent resumed the human form which it had lost; because previously it was the soul of Master Francesco Cavalcante, as will appear below. **AS THE** lizard. The comparison is well-known: but some wish that by the various spots the lizard has, one should understand the various cunnings and frauds used by the thief. **UNDER THE GREAT SCOURGE.** We call a scourge a *scutica* or *scuriata* <note>Latin terms for a whip or lash.</note> with which we strike either man or animal. Whence we say "to scourge" is to strike with the lash. And by metaphor we call the "scourge of the sun" those most burning days when they lash us with more heat. Therefore, "under the great scourge," under the great heat of the dog days. <term>Dog days (caniculari)</term>: days of intense summer heat associated with the rising of the Dog Star. Among the Greeks, the Dog Star is called **Syrio** for its splendor, because it is a star of the first magnitude and shines greatly. Others want *Syrio* to come from *syrin*, which means to draw and extend: because this image extends over a long interval and occupies with its greatness almost the space of three signs. Furthermore, it is situated in the middle center of the heaven. When the sun rises to it, such heat is born that human bodies are inflamed. In a way that, as Homer writes, various diseases and fevers molest them, unless they are relieved by the benevolence of another star. It is born, according to Albumasar <note>A famous 9th-century Persian astronomer.</note> in the 29th degree of Cancer; and from this they are called the dog days, in which Hippocrates and other noble physicians prohibit phlebotomy <note>bloodletting</note> and all purgative medicine. The Greek poets feign that this is the dog which was given along with a serpent to the guard of Europa, daughter of Agenor, King of Phoenicia, and beloved by Jove. Later, Cephalus the Athenian took it to the hunt of Thebes against the fox that was wasting that countryside. And because it was ordained by the fates that neither the dog nor the fox could be killed, Jove transformed the fox into stone and the dog into this image. Some say that Icarius the Athenian was the inventor of wine in that region; and the shepherds who first drank of it, having become drunk, believed they had been poisoned and killed him. Erigone, his daughter, searching for her father's body, was led by her dog named Maera to the place where—

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante's Inferno, Canto XXV. The previous page discussed the physical melding of Agnel Brunelleschi with a six-legged serpent. This page begins by concluding a mythological and astronomical explanation regarding the constellation of the Little Dog (Canicula) before moving into the specific transformations of the Florentine thieves Francesco Cavalcanti and Buoso Donati, and comparing Dante's poetic skill to that of Lucan and Ovid.</meta>

# XXV INFERNO

...lay dead. For this reason, Bacchus prayed to Jove that the girl should be converted into the sign of the Virgin, and the hound into this "Canicula" <note>The dog-star, Procyon</note>. And the image of the Canicula has these stars: One in the head called Isis; one in the tongue, more splendid than all others and of the first magnitude, and this is properly called Canicula. Two in the neck. In each shoulder, one obscure star; in the breast, two obscure ones. In the left front foot, three. In the right, one bright one. At the end of the back, three. In the belly, two. In the left thigh, one. In the hind left foot, one. At the tip of the tail, one. There are, therefore, twenty. We said a little above that the Canicula, in the time of Albumasar <note>A famous Persian astronomer, 787–886 AD</note>, rose in the 29th degree of Cancer. But at present, it rises in the 22nd degree of Leo.

**LIGHTNING** It seems, because of its great speed, like a flash of lightning. **IF IT CROSSES THE PATH.** Because once it has left the hedge and entered the path, it does not feel safe until it enters the other hedge. **TOWARD THE BELLY.** Toward the bellies and the guts. *Epa* in Tuscan signifies that part which is from the stomach to the pubic bone. **A** little serpent, kindled. This is shown to be Master Francesco Cavalcanti, who for the sin of theft had become a serpent; and now he bites the navel of Master Buoso, transforming him into a serpent while he himself returns to being a man. And by this, it is shown that one thief makes another a thief, either by example or by persuasion. And afterwards, it often happens that the serpent who has bitten the man—that is, the thief who has induced someone who was not a thief to steal—recognizes the ugliness of this vice in the one who, by his bad example, has become a thief; and having recognized it, he removes himself from the vice. And just as Buoso from a man became a serpent (that is, through the example of others he became a thief), so did Francesco return to manhood. And this is most clearly expressed by narrating that the smoke of one met the smoke of the other: because he recognized the ruinous nature of such vice in others, he became a man again. **HE GAZED AT IT BUT SAID NOTHING.** Because by staring at the operations of the thief, things take the form of stealing so that the mind is entirely alienated and falls to the ground: that is, into the greed for earthly things. **KINDLED.** By this is shown the flame of greed, without which no one would be a thief. **LIVID** that is, harmful: because the thief harms his neighbor greatly by taking what is his; or rather, "livid" meaning envious. Because out of envy that others might be richer than we are, we set ourselves to stealing. And certainly, we would endure poverty in peace if we did not see the riches of others. Whence Jerome writes that *Oculi sunt per quos paupertatem ferre non possumus* <note>original Latin: "The eyes are the means through which we cannot endure poverty."</note>. **AND BLACK.** As if to say poisonous and harmful. Whence Horace: *Hic niger est hunc tu romane caueto* <note>original Latin from Satires 1.4.85: "This man is black [wicked]; you, Roman, beware of him."</note>. **AND THAT** part where. Through which our food—that is, nourishment—is first taken. This signifies the navel, through which the child in the mother's body receives nourishment before taking it by mouth. He feigns that it bit the navel where the first nourishment comes from, perhaps to denote that those who are so given to theft are those who from the beginning of their creation have received such influence from the stars. Or truly, he bit the navel, that is, he awakened concupiscence: because the navel is used to represent that. **THE ONE PIERCED** gazed, but said nothing. Because he was so occupied by the kindled serpent—that is, by the greed for stealing—that it gave him the bite of the serpent: that is, of the thief. **THAT** he said nothing: as if to say he could not argue against such great greed. **RATHER WITH STEADY FEET.** The feet are put for the affection and for the greed which carries the soul to its operations, just as the feet carry the body. And certainly, no power moves the soul to act except the appetite. For this reason, Homer feigns that Achilles could not be wounded except in the soles of his feet. **HE YAWNED** as if sleep or fever had attacked him. To yawn in Latin is called *oscitare*: that is, to open the mouth. The yawn is born from thick and cold vapors generated by the stomach from leisure and laziness, which rise and mount to the mouth by way of the food passage and spread through the jaws. Wherefore nature, eager to push them out, breathes with the mouth appropriately open. **HE** the serpent. The thief considers the fraud to seize it, and the fraud looks back at the thief because it persuades him. **ONE THROUGH** the wound of the navel and the other through the mouth smoked. Because he who persuades the theft smokes through the mouth because he uses words; and he to whom it is persuaded smokes through the navel because his greed is kindled. **THE SMOKE** met: because the words reached the greed, and the greed was set ablaze by the words.

---

<columns>2</columns>

Let Lucan now be silent where he tells
of the wretched Sabellus and Nasidius,
and wait to hear what now is released.
Let Ovid be silent of Cadmus and Arethusa,
for if he converts the one into a serpent
and the other into a fountain in his poetry, I envy him not.
For two natures front to front
he never transmuted so that both forms
were ready to exchange their matter.

<column-break/>

**The poet demonstrates** here that neither Lucan nor Ovid, in inventing fables as poets do, have imagined such a marvelous transformation as I saw in this ditch. For they describe one thing being transformed into another. But I saw two, where one was transformed into the other. Therefore, **LET LUCAN BE SILENT**: because the transfiguration seen by me surpasses that which he describes of Sabellus and Nasidius. Lucan writes that Sabellus, a soldier of Cato in the sandy Libya, was stung by a serpent called a *seps*; and such a sting in a short time consumed the whole body, breaking the skin and the flesh, and finally, like a most burning flame, reduced him to a little ash. And after this, the same poet describes the opposite effect of another venom which a serpent called a *prester* used to sting Nasidius, a soldier of the same army; and such a bite so bloated his body that his breastplate burst; and he grew so large that 

<column-break/>

no limb or joint could be discerned. Nor did any wild beast or bird taste of such a body without dying. Some say that the *prester* is a species of asp, and it always goes with its mouth open and smoking; it causes the body it stings to swell, as was said, and after the great swelling, it putrefies. Let Lucan, therefore, be silent in his transformations, because they are not as wonderful as these, which have such power in two that one is transformed into the other. And similarly, let Ovid equal or match all his *Metamorphoses*—that is, transformations—of Cadmus and Arethusa to those which I saw. Agenor was king of Phoenicia. His daughter, called Europa, was abducted by Jove, who was transfigured into a bull. For this reason, he commanded Cadmus, his son, to search for her and never return without her. Cadmus, after a long search, despairing of finding her, decided to settle in Boeotia, a region of Greece; and there he killed a serpent consecrated to Mars, and with the advice of Pallas, he sowed its teeth; and from such seed were born armed men, who, immediately entering into battle among themselves, killed each other, except for a few who helped him build Thebes. It would be tedious to narrate the many misfortunes of Cadmus and his family; but finally, afflicted by them, perhaps thinking that changing his country would change his fortune, he departed in his old age with his wife and came to Illyria, today called Capo d'Istria. And there, repeating one day with his wife the various cases of fortune, they were converted into serpents. This the poets figure to demonstrate that men who are of long life and have experienced various and diverse cases of fortune become, through experience, very prudent, and transform themselves into serpents, because the serpent is a most prudent animal. And Ovid adds that such serpents harmed no one, and even gladly saw men. Which can signify nothing else than that in them was that prudence, which is the virtue that regulates us to live civilly and seek concord and...

The commentary also argues that Dante's poetic description of these transformations surpasses the classical accounts found in Lucan and Ovid.</summary>

# CANTO XXV.

...tranquility and to benefit ourselves and others and to harm no one. And it was not a certain malice and evil cunning which leads men to deceive other men: because the sacred scriptures, wishing to comfort us not toward vicious wickedness, but toward virtuous prudence, say: *Be prudent as serpents and simple as doves.* <note>Original Latin: "Estote prudentes sicut serpentes & simplices sicut columbę." Matthew 10:16.</note> It is as if to say: use serpentine prudence, but be so simple, without cover or deceit—just as doves harm no one, so you should not harm anyone. But be beneficial like Cadmus, who performed many favors for men; that is to say, he was a builder of cities, and to the Greeks (as Pliny reports), he brought sixteen <note>Original: "fedeci," likely "sedici"</note> letters of the alphabet from Phoenicia to Greece. Aristotle says eighteen, to which Palamedes later added four during the Trojan War. He was the first in Greece to find gold and the method of smelting it. Arethusa was a nymph companion of Diana; returning from the hunt to refresh herself, she bathed naked in the river Alpheus, which flows through Arcadia. Whereupon Alpheus, the god of that river, immediately seized by love for the nymph, wished to defile her. Arethusa, being virginal and chaste, fled from him, and in running, through much sweat, she was transformed into a fountain. Diana, moved by mercy, opened the earth for her. Thus, that water flowed under the earth and under the sea and arrived in Sicily without mixing with the salt water. Yet Alpheus did not cease his pursuit; but transformed into a river, he ran after her all the way to Sicily. Poets invent this because, in truth, the river Alpheus (according to most distinguished writers) dives underground in Arcadia and re-emerges in Sicily at the fountain called Arethusa. If HE—that is, Cadmus—was converted into a serpent, AND SHE—that is, Arethusa [into a fountain]—I DO NOT ENVY HIM. <note>Dante is comparing his poetic skill to Ovid, who wrote of these single transformations in the *Metamorphoses*.</note> It is as if to say: I do not consider those transformations greater than the one I saw; rather, they are lesser. And therefore he says "I do not envy him," meaning "I do not bear him envy," because we bear envy toward things greater than ours, and not toward lesser ones. And he assigns the reason why their transformations were lesser: because never can two things together be transformed one into the other, as I saw Buoso into a serpent and the serpent converted into Buoso.

---

Together they rested in such a way
> that the serpent split its tail into a fork,
> and the wounded man drew his tracks together.
The legs with the thighs joined themselves
> so that in a short time the joint
> showed no sign that could be seen.
The split tail took on the shape
> that was being lost by the other, and its skin
> became soft, while the other's became hard;
I saw the arms enter through the armpits,
> and the two feet of the beast, which were short,
> lengthen by as much as those arms shortened.
Then the hind feet, twisted together,
> became the members that a man conceals,
> and the wretch from his own had produced two legs.
While the smoke veils both of them,
> it generates new color and hair on one side,
> and on the other, it strips the hair away.

<column-break/>

It does not seem to me that any other allegory is sought in these verses. But one must admire the genius of the poet, who, to make the transformation believable, describes the form and the manner with great industry. He says that the tail of the serpent divided into two parts and became two human legs, and the legs of Buoso joined together and became a serpent's tail. And thus the man's skin became the hard hide of a serpent, and the serpent's hide became tender human skin. And similarly, the arms of Buoso retracted into the armpits—that is, into the shoulders—and became short like the paws of a serpent; and the front paws lengthened and became the arms of a man; and the hind ones wound together and became THE MEMBERS that a man conceals and hides—that is, the male member. AND THE WRETCHED Buoso HAD short <note>The commentator glosses this as "distesi" or extended</note> two feet from his male member. WHILE THE smoke veils—that is, covers and hides—BOTH OF THEM, i.e., the serpent and Buoso, IT GENERATES hair upon one part. Arrange it thus: the smoke generates its hair. Understand this to be on the pubic area <note>Original: "pectignone"</note> for one part, specifically for the serpent, which, becoming a man, had to be hairy in those parts. And on the other side, which was Buoso's, IT STRIPS THE HAIR: that is, removes the hair, because he was to become a serpent, which has no hair.

---

One rose up and the other fell down,
> yet without turning away their wicked eyes,
> under which each was changing his face.
The one who was standing drew [his snout] toward the temples,
> and from the excess material that came there,
> ears emerged from the smooth cheeks;
That part which did not run back and was retained,
> of that surplus, made a nose for the face,
> and thickened the lips as much as was fitting.
The one who was lying down thrusts his snout forward,
> and pulls his ears back into his head,
> as a snail does with its horns.
And the tongue, which he had whole and ready
> before for speaking, splits; and the forked one
> in the other closes up; and the smoke stops.

<column-break/>

Up to this point, he has transformed the parts from the shoulders down, in such a way that Buoso has become a serpent and Francesco has become a man. Now he continues in transforming from there upward. And therefore he says: ONE ROSE UP: and this was Francesco, who, having made human legs from the serpentine tail, stood on his feet. AND THE OTHER fell down. And Buoso, because his legs had become a serpent's tail and he could no longer stand upright like a man, fell. THE ONE WHO was standing: that is, Francesco, who was already standing, began to change the serpent's snout into human form. And the method was this: as we know, the snout of a serpent is not as wide or thick as a man's face, but is long and thin. Therefore, it was necessary that as he pulled the snout back, he shortened it to the measure of a man's face; and in shortening, there was surplus material to make the ears, the nose, and the thick lips, which are things found in a man and not in a serpent. And therefore he writes that he DREW TOWARD the temples: he pulled back toward the temples. AND FROM the excess material that came there: and from that matter which, by pulling it back, had come toward the temples, EARS EMERGED: the ears were made, which protrude from the cheeks, which in the serpent were smooth <note>Original: "scempie"</note> because it does not have ears protruding outward like a man. THAT WHICH did not run back: all that matter of the snout which was not pulled back...

The author explains the anatomical process of the metamorphosis, including the redistribution of "matter" to form human features from serpentine ones.</summary>

# INFERNO.
### l

...into the temples. But the face held back before him, and the nose and lips grew large, just as we see in a man. **HE WHO** lay there. Buoso, having already become a serpent from the shoulders down, begins to change in the face; and as Francesco, shortening his snout, took on the face of a man, so Buoso, lengthening his face, took on the snout of a serpent. **AND THE EARS** he pulls back through the head: as if they return backward, and he stretches them out, just as the snail pulls back its horns. The Latins call those that carry their house *cocleas*, and those that have no house *limaces*. In the Florentine tongue, the former are called *chiocciole* <note>Snails with shells.</note> and the latter *lumache* <note>Slugs or snails without shells.</note>. But the poet, to make the rhyme, said *limaccia* from the Latin word *limace*. **AND THE TONGUE** that Buoso had was **UNIFIED**, that is, whole, **AND READY**: and prompt. **IT SPLITS**: It divides like that of the serpent. They say the serpent’s tongue is two-forked or three-forked because it appears so due to the great speed with which such an animal moves its tongue. Hence Virgil wrote: *And he flickers with three-forked tongues in his mouth.* <note>Original Latin: "Et linguis micat ore trisulcis." Virgil, Georgics 3.439.</note> **AND THE FORKED ONE**: and that which was forked and divided into two parts. **IN THE OTHER**: meaning in Francesco, who had the serpent's tongue. This one, which was forked, now closes up and reunites like the tongue of a man. **THE SMOKE STOPS**: This denotes the end of the transformation. For the spirit of the one had gone entirely into the body of the other. And certainly, when a thief is completely stained by such a vice through the persuasion of another thief—and then, with the one who has committed the theft, the one who was not a thief before recognizes in others the infamy of such a vice which he did not previously recognize in himself, and amends himself—one becomes a man from a serpent, and the other becomes a serpent from a man.

->The soul that had become a beast<-
->flies hissing through the valley,<-
->and the other, speaking, spits behind him.<-
->Then he turned his new shoulders toward him<-
->and said to the other: "I want Buoso to run<-
->as I have done, crawling through this valley."<-
->Thus I saw the seventh ballast<-
->change and transmute; and here let the novelty<-
->excuse me if my pen goes astray:<-
->And though my eyes were somewhat<-
->confused and my mind dismayed,<-
->they could not flee so hidden<-
->that I did not clearly recognize Puccio the Cripple:<-
->and he was the only one of the three companions<-
->who had come first and was not changed:<-
->the other was he whom you, Gaville, mourn.<-

<column-break/>

Here he places what followed from such a transformation: and he narrates that Buoso, having become a serpent, hissed—which means to whistle as serpents do. And he said "soul" (*anima*) because such a transformation was in the soul and not in the body. And Francesco, returned to being a man, spoke and spat, which men do, and no other animal. **THEN HE turned his new shoulders to him.** New: because he had newly retaken them. **HE TURNED** his shoulders: He abandoned him and returned to Puccio and said: **I WANT** Buoso, who has become a serpent, **TO RUN**—not on feet like men, **BUT CRAWLING**: like four-footed beasts. **AS I HAVE DONE**: while I was a serpent. Many, because of this mutual and reciprocal transformation, wish to interpret that Messer Francesco and Messer Buoso had been partners in theft, and had committed thefts in turn. **THUS I SAW the seventh ballast**: that is, the seventh <term>bolgia</term> <note>One of the ten circular ditches in the Eighth Circle of Hell, where different types of fraud are punished.</note>. Ballast (*zavorra*) is sand and gravel placed in the bilge of ships so that they do not tip due to light weight. Therefore, the poet prudently equates this ditch to sterile ground and a dark and fetid place like the bilge where the ballast sits. **CHANGE AND TRANSMUTE**: as has been shown above. **AND HERE Let the novelty excuse me.** Certainly, he who has to narrate new and unheard-of things deserves excuse: if the style and the manner of speaking **SHOULD BUNGLE** (*abborra*): that is, if it arranges poorly what you describe; for *abborracciare* in the Florentine tongue signifies to arrange poorly and incorrectly. Then he adds that although his eyes were confused by

the novelty of the things, and his mind was **DISMAYED**: that is, drawn out of its being and almost lost. Nonetheless, he recognized Puccio **THE CRIPPLE** (*sciancato*); and earlier, by hearing them named, he had recognized Agnolo and Buoso. And these were the three he saw at first. Afterward, through description, he declares that the one who had returned to a man from a serpent was Messer Francesco "Guercio" de' Cavalcanti, who was killed by the men of Gaville. This is a village located in the Upper Valdarno, or in Chianti, fertile with the best wines. **YOU MOURN**: because in vengeance for Cavalcanti, many villagers of Gaville were killed. <note>Francesco "Guercio" Cavalcanti was murdered in the town of Gaville; his family took a bloody revenge on the townspeople, hence why Gaville "mourns."</note>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante’s Inferno, specifically the opening of Canto XXVI. The previous pages covered the punishment of the thieves in the seventh ditch; here, the author transitions to the eighth ditch and Dante’s famous invective against his home city, Florence.</meta>

<page-num>XXVI</page-num>
<header>CANTO XXVI</header>

## CANTO XXVI OF THE FIRST CANTICLE BY DANTE

<margin>i</margin>
In this 26th canto, Dante shows how he arrived in the eighth <term>buglia<note>Dante’s word for the "ditches" or "pouches" of the eighth circle of Hell, usually rendered as *bolgia*.</note></term>, in which he posits that fraudulent counselors are punished within burning flames. Here, he also hears from Ulysses regarding his end. But at the beginning, with the gravest indignation, he reproaches his fatherland for the wicked sin of theft; he especially grieves that she is so shameless as to not be embarrassed by it, but rather thinks herself great. Several rhetorical <term>colors<note>Rhetorical devices or "colors of rhetoric" used to embellish speech.</note></term> are used here. First is <term>apostrophe<note>original: "apostrophe"</note></term>, or exclamation, which occurs when we direct our speech to a person or an absent thing as if it were present, just as we see the poet turn his speech toward Florence. This is done for many reasons, but especially out of indignation, grave complaint, and reprimand. Then there is another device called <term>irony<note>original: "ironia"</note></term>, which occurs when words have a meaning contrary to what we intend. Therefore, he says "Rejoice" and in-

Rejoice, Florence, since you are so great
that over sea and land you beat your wings
and through all of Hell your name is spread.
Among the thieves I found five such men,
your citizens, from which comes shame to me,
and you do not rise to great honor by them.
But if the truth is dreamed near morning,
you shall feel, within a little time from now,
what Prato, not to mention others, craves for you.
And if it had already happened, it would not be too soon;
would that it were so, since it must be,
for it will weigh on me more the more I age.

<column-break/>

-tends that she should be supremely saddened. "Since you are so great that over sea and land you beat your wings": that is, your fame is spread by sea and by land. He said "beat your wings," meaning you fly, or perhaps because fame is depicted with wings. As Virgil said: <note>original: "Nocte volat" — "She flies by night."</note> "And through all of Hell your name is spread": as if to say your fame is spread everywhere. But it was named much more for vices than for virtues. "Among the thieves": every learned writer must, after irony, place words that manifest what the irony made doubtful. Therefore, by saying he has found five noble citizens, he shows that when he said "Rejoice," he meant she should be grieved. The five are: Gianfa Donati, Agnello Brunelleschi, Buoso degli Abati, Puccio Sciancato, and Francesco Guercio. "Such men": such noble people, which is a greater disgrace; for the greater the authority of the person, the more ugly every vice is in them. Just as the more beautiful a garment is, the more the stain is out of place on it. "But if the truth is dreamed near morning": he shows that he has foreseen through a dream the calamities and civil dissensions between the <term>Whites and Blacks<note>The rival political factions in Florence: the White Guelphs (Dante's party) and the Black Guelphs.</note></term> that were to afflict Florence; these had indeed occurred before the poet wrote this work. But he feigns having written it before. Therefore he said: "if my dream made near morning is true, which ought to be true." There are five species of dreaming: three true and two false. The true ones are called <term>enypnion<note>original: "enipnium" — a dream reflecting current states of the body or mind.</note></term>, <term>vision<note>original: "visionem"</note></term>, and <term>oracle<note>original: "oraculũ"</note></term>. 

A <term>Dream<note>original: "Somnium"</note></term> is when we dream the truth but it is obscure and cannot be understood without interpreters, like when the man who was in prison with Joseph dreamed he was pressing the grapes of three branches into the cup of Pharaoh; and Joseph predicted to him how in three days he would be liberated and would then become the king's <term>pincerna<note>A cup-bearer or butler.</note></term>, that is, his servant of the cup. And Polycrates, King of Samos, dreamed that Jove washed him and Phoebus, god of the sun, anointed him; and shortly after, the prefect of Xerxes had him crucified, and he remained on the cross until Jove—that is, the air—rained upon him, and Phoebus—the sun—liquefied and melted the fat of his body, whereby he became anointed. An <term>Oracle</term> is when, while sleeping, it seems that someone speaks to us, and what they say turns out to be true. A <term>Vision</term> is when, while sleeping, we seem to see something that is then exactly as we saw it. Two false species of dreaming are <term>insomnium<note>A disturbed dream caused by physical or mental distress.</note></term> and <term>phantasm<note>An apparition seen in the transition between waking and sleep.</note></term>. <term>Insomnium</term> is when we dream false things, and it proceeds either from too much food taken, which, by raising fumes to the head, makes it seem we are flying or rising, or by sending down catarrh, it seems we are falling. Sometimes it comes from too little food, whereby we seem to have hunger; sometimes from corrupt humors, whereby bile makes us see fire and similar things; phlegm, water; blood, cheerful things; and melancholy, true and terrifying things. It can also arise from the cares and thoughts of the soul, whereby we often dream that what we were thinking about has been given to us or taken away. But when we have the mind free from every thought, and the body not burdened by food nor humors, it happens that our soul, through sleep, almost loosens itself from the body and returns to its nature, which is divine, and can foresee future things. And this happens especially around daybreak, because having finished digesting our food, we remain more clear and the body burdens us less; and for this reason the poet says, "But if the truth is dreamed near morning." Similarly, Ovid: <note>original: "Namque sub aurora iam dormitante lucina Somnia quo cerni tempora vera solent." — "For near dawn, when the morning light is already sleepy, is the time when true dreams are usually seen."</note> Nor should it be omitted that sometimes dreams come through diabolical illusion. Hence Job in chapter seven: <note>original: "Terrebis me per somnia" — "You terrify me through dreams."</note> And Gregory: <note>original: "Ideo sanctos quo vigilando tentare non valet gravius per somnia dormiendo tentat." — "Therefore, those holy ones whom he cannot tempt while they are awake, he tempts more severely through dreams while they sleep."</note> For which reason the supreme teacher, Christ, commanded his disciples to watch, so that they might not enter into temptation. "You shall feel within a little time from now of that": that is, of those things. "Which Prato craves for you": that is, desires for you. "Not to mention others": this is a larger and more distant land; as if to say, not just distant cities, but even a nearby castle. Many believe he says "Prato" in respect to Niccolò, Cardinal of Prato, who was very hostile to our republic. And certainly, a small event of the poet's happened: for while games were being held with great display at the <term>Carraia Bridge<note>Ponte alla Carraia in Florence.</note></term>, which at that time was made of wood, the crowd of people was so great that the bridge collapsed, and many perished and more remained crippled. For this reason, it filled the city with sudden mourning, not only for those who had lost their own in that event, but also for those who believed they had lost them. This display represented Hell, with fire and the demons who tormented damned souls therein with various punishments. Such an event was an omen both of the civil war that was born in the same year between the Whites and Blacks, and of the fire that consumed over two thousand two hundred houses and many precious things; the fire began from the fire worked by the Neri of the Abati and the prior of San Pietro Scheraggio, who set fire to the houses of their kinsmen. "And if it had already happened, it would not be too soon." The author shows himself desirous of this evil, not out of the ruin of his fatherland, which was very dear to him, but for the punishment of the wicked citizens who administered it iniquitously; and therefore he desires it to be soon, so that those who have erred may be punished. And similarly he shows that the more it ages—that is, the more it delays and lingers—the more it is troublesome to him. Because he desires that such fortune punish the wicked leaders and free the unhappy people.

<page-num>LXX</page-num>
<header>INFERNO CANTO</header>

> We departed, and up the stairs
> which the rocky spurs had made for our descent before,
> my master climbed again and drew me up;
> and following the solitary way,
> among the jagged shards and rocks of the cliff,
> the foot without the hand did not make its way.

That is, the solitary path. This signifies that the path by which we contemplate the ugliness of vice is solitary, because few walk upon it; as Petrarch says: "Poor and naked you go, Philosophy, says the crowd intent on base gain; few companions will you have on your path." <note>Petrarch, *Canzoniere* 7: "Povera e nuda vai, Filosofia... Pochi compagni avrai per la tua via."</note> *Among the jagged shards and rocks of the cliff*: he calls "cliff" that stone that forms a bridge over the <term>bolge<note>The "ditches" or "pockets" of the eighth circle of Hell.</note></term>. *Shards* are fissures made along the length of the cliff, and *rocks* are breaks made across it. *The foot without the hand did not make its way*: There was such difficulty in the ascent that one could not climb unless they supported themselves with their hands; and by this, he denotes the difficulty of escaping from sin. Because the feet, which signify the "affection" <note>In medieval psychology, "affection" refers to the soul's inclinations or desires.</note>, do not depart from the sin in which we have formed a habit and in which we take pleasure, unless the hands—which are our operations and actions—pull us up, meaning virtuous actions and operations which pull us out of the habit of vice and place us in the habit of virtue.

These two <term>tercets<note>Stanzas of three lines.</note></term> have the force of a preface to the narrative concerning the vice of fraud, which is treated in the eighth ditch. And by admonishing himself about what he thinks he must guard against, he makes the listener attentive and captures goodwill by condemning the vice. And so that his meaning may be more clearly understood, we will speak here of the punishment of those who used the height and subtlety of the intellect granted to us by God for good, but instead used it for deception.

> Then I grieved, and now I grieve again
> when I direct my mind to what I saw,
> and I rein in my genius more than I am wont,
> lest it run where virtue does not guide it;
> so that, if a good star or something better
> has given me the good, I do not begrudge it to myself.

The pain of grieving occurred then, but one must persevere in that purpose and grieve continually. And this will easily be done by "directing the mind": that is, continually considering what we have seen happens to those who are fraudulent. *And I rein in my genius more than I am wont*: he describes the fruit that is born from this continuous and assiduous meditation. And this is: seeing the evil that arises from such vice, we restrain our genius and our sharpness, so that it does not run unless virtue guides it. Because if we use it for good, it will be prudence; if for evil, it will be fraud. *So that, if a good star or something better has given me the good, I do not begrudge it to myself*: This is the reason why he wants his genius not to run without the guidance of virtue. Because if I have received this good of having an excellent genius—either from a star or from "something better," that is, from God—I do not want to "envy" it to myself; that is, I do not want to take it away from myself, for by taking away the good, it would seem that I bore envy toward myself. And note why the poet says of this gift of sharp genius that either a "star" or "something better" gave it to him. Because the human soul—not only according to theologians but also according to many philosophers, and especially the Platonists—is created immediately by God. Thus you have received an immense dowry from the highest God in your creation, especially because He created it in His image. Thus it is capable of reason and intellect, and therefore it receives its virtues and powers from God. And as for itself, it is not subject to celestial influences but is superior to them. But because while it is in the body, the soul cannot exercise its forces and powers without bodily instruments, and these are subject to the stars; and because the stars induce in some bodies excellent and optimally disposed instruments, and in others coarse, inept, and ill-disposed ones, it happens that although souls are created equal, nevertheless some men—having through a benign celestial influence fit organs and instruments—are ingenious and subtle. Others, having them through an unhappy influence, are conversely coarse and slow. Hence it can be said that sharpness or slowness of intellect reaches us from the stars; not because they can do anything to the soul itself, but in respect to its instruments. Therefore he said "a good star" in respect to the instruments of the body, and "something better" in respect to the soul being created immediately by God.

<column-break/>

This demonstrates the difficulty of returning, which denotes that falling into the valley of vices is easy, but departing from it is difficult. As Virgil says: <term>The descent to Hell is easy. But to retrace one's steps and escape to the upper air: this is the task, this is the labor.</term> <note>original: "Facilis descensus auerni. Sed reuocare gradum superasque euadere ad auras. Hoc opus hic labor e." — Virgil, *Aeneid* VI.126-129.</note> And he writes *up the stairs*, which when they had descended them had made them *borni*: that is, dazzled and of poor sight. For *bornio* in the Bolognese dialect signifies this. *My master climbed again*: Because the intellect is that which, having recognized the ugliness of vice, returns to virtue. *And drew me*: the intellect by itself returns to virtue, but sensuality would not return if it were not pulled back by the intellect. *The solitary path*: to warn the neighbor or to admonish the listener that whoever has from nature a subtle genius, fit to achieve knowledge in all practical and active things, ought to use that for the utility and honor of himself and his neighbor. And in this way, he will be called "prudent." For prudence is nothing other than a right discourse of the mind in governing and handling the things that consist in civil life, of which we spoke. *Then I grieved* when I knew that those were punished here who had used the subtlety of genius not in prudence but in fraud and cunning to the harm of their neighbor. *And now I grieve again*: He demonstrates what is required to wish to strip oneself entirely of the habit of vice; because it is not enough to have moved oneself from the

> As many as the peasant who rests on the hill
> in the season when he who brightens the world
> keeps his face least hidden from us,
> when the fly gives way to the mosquito,
> sees fireflies down through the valley,
> perhaps there where he harvests and plows:
> With as many flames all was shining,
> the eighth ditch, as I perceived
> as soon as I was where the bottom appeared.

Having now arrived upon the cliff from where the eighth ditch could be seen, by an excellent comparison he saw as many flames in that ditch as the peasant, resting on the hill of the valley when the day's labor has ceased in the evening, is accustomed to seeing fireflies. With so many flames all the eighth ditch shone. *As many as the peasant*: understand "as many fireflies." *The peasant*: the rustic who *rests on the hill*, because having ceased his fatigue of the day, he rests in the evening on the hill. *In the season when he who brightens the world keeps his face least hidden from us*: There is here a rhetorical figure called <term>circumlocution<note>original: "circulo cutione"</note></term>. He could have simply said "in the time of summer," but to adorn the poem he used more words, saying *In the season when he who brightens the world*, which means the time of the sun. For the sun is that which brightens, that is, makes the world clear and luminous. He says then, when the peasant rests in the time when the sun keeps its face least hidden from us and for the shortest space. And this is summer, because its face is hidden at night, and in that season the nights are brief.

to stay. And then he follows and describes the night with the same color of circumlocution, and says: *As the fly yields to the gnat.* As the night comes. For the fly, which comes out during the day, retires when the night arrives. And it *yields*: that is, it gives place to the gnat, which, staying hidden during the day, comes out at night. *He sees fireflies down through the valley*, that is, down through the valley, perhaps there where he harvests and plows, that is, in his fields and vineyards. *With so many flames the eighth ditch was all resplendent*: he arranges it thus: the eighth ditch shone with as many flames as there are fireflies down in the valley where one harvests and plows. *The peasant sees them while he rests on the hill* in the time when *he who illuminates the world* <note>The Sun.</note> *keeps his face least hidden from us* <note>During the summer solstice.</note>; and he sees them in the evening *when the fly yields to the gnat*. And I noticed this when I had arrived upon the bridge from which I saw the bottom of the ditch. *Fireflies*: these are "shining ones," an animal known to all; the Greeks name them <term>lampyride<note>From the Greek *lampyris*, referring to a glow-worm or firefly.</note></term> from *lampas*, which means light. The poet feigns, not without the greatest prudence, that the fraudulent are punished in fire. And if we understand the fire that will be in the essential Hell, it is a fitting punishment that he who has through fraud set others aflame should himself burn in like manner. But allegorically we will say that such fraud is fire because it has the power to ignite dissension, discord, and wars. And for this the Psalmist says: <term>The sons of men, whose teeth are weapons and arrows, and their tongue a sharp sword with coals that lay waste.<note>original: "Filii hominū dentes eorū arma & sagitte potetes & acute cum carbonibus desolatoriis." A combination of Psalm 57:4 and Psalm 120:4.</note></term> Furthermore, it is fire because it is born of a sharp wit. And sharp wit is born from the heat of the blood; whereas, conversely, cold blood produces slowness of wit. Wishing to express this, Virgil said: <term>Cold blood had gathered around the heart.<note>original: "Frigidus extiterit circū precordia sanguis." From Virgil's *Georgics*, II, 484.</note></term> The flame is seen and not the sinner: because the speech of the fraudulent person is manifest, but his fraud is hidden and concealed. Dante did not see the ditch of the thieves [clearly] because that place was dark, for in it every action and speech is concealed. He sees the ditch of the fraudulent because the words are manifest, but the counsel is hidden. And this generation is the worst. The sinners stay separated, each in his own flame, because he who wishes to deceive does not communicate his counsel to others, unless they were of the same will; and for this reason he places Ulysses and Diomedes together.

> And as he who avenged himself with the bears
> saw the chariot of Elijah at its departure
> when the horses rose erect toward heaven,
> 
> Who could not follow it so with his eyes
> as to see anything but the flame alone,
> like a little cloud ascending upward;
> 
> So each one moves through the throat
> of the ditch, for none shows its theft,
> and every flame steals away a sinner.

<column-break/>

As demonstrated above: the whole valley of the eighth ditch was full of flames. Now he shows that each of such flames
**H**eld a sinner hidden within itself, so wrapped in it that he could not be seen. And all these flames rose up through the throat of the valley, keeping the sinner hidden within. Just as perhaps the chariot of Elijah, when wrapped in fire, it ascended to heaven. And Elisha, turned upward, saw the chariot rising, but did not see Elijah in it, because the flame covered him. *And as he who avenged himself*: that is, he who was the avenger. *With the bears*: this was Elisha. But for the declaration of this text, we recall in the Fourth Book of Kings <note>Known as 2 Kings in modern Bibles.</note> of the Hebrews, which is part of the Old Testament and contained in the Bible. One reads that Elijah was a supreme and true prophet in the time when Joram reigned. And after many miracles, God wished to take him up to heaven. Therefore, from Jericho he came to the Jordan River with Elisha. And he took off his garment and with it touched the river, and immediately the waters divided and left a dry path by which the prophets might pass. Then, continuing on their way,

suddenly there descended from heaven a chariot of fire guided by horses of fire, in which Elijah ascended, and was snatched on high. Elisha, having gathered the garment that had fallen during the ascent, returned to the Jordan and with it divided the water, and returned to Jericho. And while going from there to Bethel, some children came to meet him, and mocking him, they said, "Come up, bald head!" almost as a reproach that he claimed Elijah had been so snatched away. Elisha cursed them in the name of God, and suddenly two bears came out of the woods and mauled forty-two of those children. You see, therefore, why by saying *he who avenged himself with the bears*, he means Elisha, who saw the chariot of Elijah snatched to heaven. *By horses erect*: that is, standing up and raised. But although he followed it with his eyes, he could not discern anything but the flame, which mounted upward like a cloud from the earth mounts into the air. And he arranges the text thus: each flame moves through the throat of the ditch in the same manner as the chariot of Elijah, which Elisha saw when the horses rose erect to heaven; and Elisha could not follow the chariot except in such a way that he saw nothing but the flame alone. *And every flame steals away*: a sinner; that is, it hides a sinner within itself and does not show the "theft" <note>Here, "theft" refers to the sinner being stolen from sight by the flame.</note>. In this eighth ditch are punished those who, under the appearance of giving faithful and prudent counsel to their neighbor, give him harmful counsel through fraud. This counsel can be given not only by speaking or writing, but also with gestures and signs. Sinon deceived the Trojans with words. They are followers of such counsel: Simulation, Dissimulation, Lying, Falsehood, and the like; and it brings forth harm to one's neighbor in his person or his property. It is therefore a fitting punishment that such a sinner stays enclosed in the flame, as we have shown above. The flame—that is, his words—is seen. The sinner—that is, the fraud that is in the words—is not seen.

> I stood upon the bridge, having risen to see,
> so that if I had not taken hold of a rock,
> I would have fallen down without being pushed.
> 
> The Leader, who saw me so attentive,
> said: "Within the fires are the spirits;
> each swathes himself in that which burns him."

<column-break/>

**H**e shows that because of the novelty of the thing, he came into such wonder and with such stupor gazed at the flames that if he had not embraced a rock, he would have fallen. *Surto*: that is, suspended. And it is a word derived from this Latin participle *subrectus*, and by syncope *surcto*, just as from *erectus* comes *erto*. *Without being pushed*: knocked or shoved. *The Leader who saw me*: Sensuality, being untaught, did not understand what that flame was, and therefore he was amazed. But Virgil, who is superior Reason, shows him the truth, and says that inside those flames are spirits who swathe and wrap themselves in the flame by which they are burned.

> "My Master," I replied, "by hearing you
> I am more certain; but already it seemed to me
> that it was so, and already I wished to tell you..."

<column-break/>

**H**e shows that the flame nearest to them, and which came toward them, had two points, to demonstrate (as we shall say shortly) that in that flame were two spirits. *Which seems to rise from the pyre*: that is, from the fire. The Greeks and Latins did not bury...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the 26th Canto of Dante's Inferno. The previous page introduced the landscape of the eighth bolgia, where the fraudulent counselors are encased in tongues of fire. Here, the text focuses on the specific figure of the "double flame" containing Ulysses and Diomede, providing a deep dive into classical mythology and the allegorical meaning of their punishment.</meta>

<page-num>114</page-num>
<header>CANTO XXVI.</header>

"Who is in that fire that comes so divided
at the top, that it seems to rise from the pyre
where Eteocles with his brother was placed?" <note>Eteocles and Polynices, sons of Oedipus, who killed each other in a duel for the throne of Thebes; legend says even their funeral flames split apart in mutual hatred.</note>

He answered me: "Within there are martyred
Ulysses and Diomede; and thus together
to the vengeance they go as to the wrath.
And within their flame they groan for
the trick of the horse that made the gate
whence issued the gentle seed of the Romans. <note>The Trojan Horse, which led to the fall of Troy and the flight of Aeneas, the legendary founder of the Roman lineage.</note>
Within it they weep for the craft through which the dead
Deidamia still grieves for Achilles;
and for the Palladium punishment is borne there." <note>The Palladium was a sacred statue of Athena/Minerva stolen from Troy by Ulysses and Diomede.</note>

"If they can, within those sparks,
speak," I said, "Master, much I pray you,
and pray again that the prayer be worth a thousand:
That you do not deny me the waiting
until the horned flame comes here;
see how with desire toward it I bend."
And he to me: "Your prayer is worthy
of much praise, wherefore I accept it;
but see that your tongue restrain itself;"

<column-break/>

...whole bodies, but they burned them: and they gathered the ashes and put them into the sepulcher. And that little hut, or rather mound of wood, in which they burned them, the Greeks called <term>pyra<note>From the Greek *pyr*, meaning fire.</note></term> because *pyr* means fire: and the Latins called it <term>rogus<note>A funeral pyre.</note></term>. Therefore he says that this flame did not rise with one point like the others, but with two, as it rose from the pyre in which Eteocles and Polynices were burned. These were the sons of Oedipus, King of Thebes. And they agreed between them to reign alternately, each for one year. The first year fell to Eteocles: but he, unwilling to yield to his brother Polynices when the year was finished, Polynices—with the help of his father-in-law Adrastus, King of Argos, and his brother-in-law Tydeus—led an army of seven kings to Thebes. He fought with his brother with such fury that they killed each other. Creon, who succeeded Eteocles in the kingdom of Thebes, forbade them burial. But Argia, wife of Polynices, left Argos, and Antigone, sister of them both, left Thebes; and having met on the field, they took the body of Polynices and carried it to the fire where they found Eteocles already burned. As soon as they placed him near his brother, the wood trembled and rejected Polynices. Wherefore the flames of the two bodies fled from each other as if, though dead, they still retained their ancient hatred. Hence Statius says: <note>original Latin: "Ecce iterum fratres primos ut contigit arctus Ignis edax tremuere rogi : & nouus aduena busto Pellitur exundant diuerso uertice flammę."</note> "Behold again the brothers: as the devouring fire touched the first limbs, the pyres trembled, and the new arrival is driven from the tomb; the flames overflow from a divided peak." And Lucan: <note>original Latin: "Scribitur in partes geminoque cacumine surgit Thebanos imitata rogos."</note> "It is split into parts and rises with a double summit, imitating the Theban pyres."

Ulysses, son of Laertes and King of Ithaca, was the most prudent above every Greek: and by his effort Achilles was found. By his effort the Greeks obtained the arrows of Philoctetes, which was a supreme benefit to the Greeks because, according to the fates, Troy could not be taken without these arrows, nor without one of the lineage of Aeacus, of whom Achilles was the grandson. By his effort the tomb of Laomedon was destroyed and Rhesus was killed. The Palladium was stolen: and in the clothes of a beggar he entered Troy unknown, and spied on all that was done in Troy, though Helen recognized him. Because of this, Homer demonstrates that Ulysses' cunning was worth more in capturing Troy than Achilles' strength. For this reason, Homer frequently calls him in his *Iliad* <term>Ptolyporton<note>From the Greek *ptoliport hos*, meaning "sacker of cities."</note></term>: that is, the conqueror of cities; and to Achilles he attributes such a name in no place. After the capture of Troy, Homer feigns that he wandered for ten years through many seas: and arrived at the Cicones, the Lotus-eaters, Polyphemus, and Aeolus, King of the Winds, who gave him skins full of his winds. He was already approaching his homeland, but his companions, thinking there was gold in the skins given by Aeolus, opened them; wherefore the winds, rushing out with force, stirred up such a tempest at sea that Ulysses wandered again and arrived at the island of Circe, who changed men into various forms. She had already changed some of his companions, but he received from Mercury such a potion or drink that he could go safely to Circe, and from her obtained that his companions should become men again. He fathered by Circe a son named Telegonus. Then in one night he sailed into the Ocean sea: and having made certain sacrifices, he descended into Hell. From there he returned to Circe. Then he sailed to the Sirens. He passed through the middle of Charybdis and Scylla. And because he had plundered the cattle of the Sun, he was shipwrecked at sea; and with the mast of the ship he came to the nymph Calypso on the island of Ogygia. After seven years, departing from her, he was again shipwrecked at sea: but with the help of the sea-nymph Leucothea, in three days he arrived at Alcinous, King of the Phaeacians, and by Minerva was led to Arete, wife of Alcinous, from whom he had many gifts; and having fallen asleep, he was put on a ship and finally brought back to his homeland. But all this is Homer's fiction: by which he demonstrates nothing else than how man, passing through many vices and then purging himself, arrives at the Supreme Good. In this, Virgil imitated him in the first six books of the *Aeneid*: and Dante in these three canticles followed Virgil. And in this place he puts him with Diomede, tormented for those frauds they committed together: first, that Thetis having hidden Achilles on the island of Scyros with the daughters of King Lycomedes in female clothes so that he was not known, and the Greeks seeking him to lead him to the capture of Troy, Ulysses and Diomede by their cunning recognized him and led him to Troy, where he was killed by Paris. Then with great cunning they entered Troy by night and took from the temple of Minerva the statue of this goddess, which was called the Palladium, without which the Greeks could not take Troy. And finally, they arranged the horse full of armed men with such fraud that the Trojans put it inside the city; and so that it could enter, they broke a gate and the tomb of Laomedon which was above that gate. Therefore the poet says: **THE JOINING OF THE HORSE**, because with that they joined—that is, deceived—the Trojans who broke the gate. From which Aeneas then departed, from whom the Romans had their origin. And they still weep for Ulysses and Diomede, for the art and the deceit they used in finding Achilles, for whom Deidamia his wife grieves, though she is dead. Deidamia was one of the daughters of Lycomedes, whom Achilles knew when he was hidden among them, and by her he fathered Pyrrhus. And similarly they are punished for the Palladium which they stole.

Dante shows himself very desirous of speaking with Ulysses and Diomede, if they, enclosed in the sparks—that is, in the flames—can speak. This denotes that the lower reason is always greedy and eager to know every detail. **AND HE TO ME: YOUR PRAYER IS WORTHY.** The higher reason approves the desire of the lower. But he does not want Dante to be the one who asks. And it is not without reason: because having to deal with this vice which arises from sharpness of wit and from intellect, it is necessary that the higher reason be the one that examines it. Therefore he admonishes him to restrain his tongue—that is, keep silence—and adds: **LET ME SPEAK.** Because **I HAVE CONCEIVED**: that is, understood and comprehended: **THAT WHICH**...
