<meta>This page continues the commentary on the 26th Canto of Dante's Inferno. The previous page discussed the arrival of the "double flame" containing the spirits of Ulysses and Diomede. This page transitions from Virgil's instruction to Dante into the famous monologue of Ulysses (Odysseus), followed by Cristoforo Landino’s detailed humanistic commentary on the text's linguistic and allegorical layers.</meta>

<header>INFERNO.</header>

"Let me speak, for I have conceived
what you wish; for they might be shy
of your speech, since they were Greeks." <note>Virgil suggests that because Ulysses and Diomede were ancient Greeks, they might respond better to a fellow poet of high antiquity rather than a medieval Italian.</note>
After the flame had come there,
where it seemed to my leader time and place,
in this form I heard him speak:

"O you who are two within one fire,
if I merited from you while I lived,
if I merited from you much or little,
when in the world I wrote the high verses,
do not move; but let one of you say
where, being lost, he went to die."

The greater horn of the ancient flame
began to shake itself, murmuring,
just like a flame that the wind exhausts.
Then, moving its tip here and there,
as if it were the tongue that spoke,
it cast forth a voice and said: "When
I departed from Circe, who withheld
me more than a year there near Gaeta,
before Aeneas had so named it, <note>Gaeta is a city in central Italy; according to legend, Aeneas named it after his nurse, Caieta.</note>
neither sweetness for a son, nor the piety
for an old father, nor the rightful love
which should have made Penelope glad, <note>Ulysses refers to his son Telemachus, his father Laertes, and his wife Penelope, all of whom he abandoned to pursue further travels.</note>
could conquer within me the ardor
I had to become experienced in the world,
and of human vices and of valor;
but I put myself upon the deep open sea,
only with one ship and with that small
company by which I was not deserted.
One shore and the other I saw as far as Spain,
as far as Morocco and the island of the Sardinians,
and the others that the sea bathes round about.
I and my companions were old and slow
when we came to that narrow strait
where Hercules set his markers: <note>The Strait of Gibraltar, considered the edge of the known world in antiquity.</note>
so that man should not set himself further;
on the right hand I left Seville;
on the other, Ceuta had already left me."

<column-break/>

**YOU WISH** to understand from them. Therefore, he could ask them.
**THEY WOULD BE SHY because they were Greeks, perhaps, of your speech.** The literal meaning is that things written in Greek seem to tolerate the Latin language more readily than the Tuscan <note>Tuscan refers to the Italian vernacular Dante used; Landino suggests the ancient Greeks would find Latin more dignified.</note> language. But allegorically, it is what we said above.

After he had warned Dante to be silent, Virgil began to speak: and he prays them by the fame which he gave them in life and of them in his *Aeneid*: that Ulysses relate to him where he was lost: that is, as for himself, dead. **WENT**—went to die: because, as you will see shortly below, Dante does not describe that after many errors he returned home: but that he perished in the ocean. And not without reason did he say: **WHEN I WROTE THE HIGH VERSES**; because Virgil, besides many small works which he composed in his early youth, wrote three volumes: the *Bucolics*, the *Georgics*, and the *Aeneid*. Of these, the first is in the low style. The second in the mediocre. The third in the high and sublime style. Therefore, by saying "the high verses," he meant the *Aeneid*.

Because he has already imagined that in one same flame are Ulysses and Diomede: and for this reason it has two points, or let us say two horns. He shows at present that the larger horn contained Ulysses: and that one began to speak. And he makes the horn of Ulysses larger because in him there was greater cunning and more fraud. Therefore: **THE GREATER HORN** where the spirit of Ulysses was. **FROM THE ANCIENT FLAME**. He said "ancient" because of the long time it had been in Hell until the time of Dante. **TO SHAKE ITSELF, MURMURING**: An excellent poet who, imagining an impossible thing—that a flame should speak—strives as much as he can not to depart entirely from the nature of a flame; which is that although it does not speak, it nonetheless murmurs; and such murmuring is born when a certain wind coming out of the burning matter strikes it. **TO SHAKE ITSELF**. To move with murmuring. **LIKE THAT WHICH**: which. **THE WIND EXHAUSTS**: that is, beats and moves. **THEN THE TIP**: the summit. He strives, as much as the nature of the thing allows, to make his narration plausible. **CAST FORTH** a voice. As if to say, he did not speak entirely like a man: but he cast or pushed out the voice without much order. **AND SAID**. And then follows the narration of Ulysses and begins: **WHEN I DEPARTED from Circe** as we said above. Circe, according to some, was the daughter of the Sun and of Colchis; she came to Italy and lived on the island named after her, Circeea <note>Now Mount Circeo.</note>, which island in the course of time became mainland. The poets say that by magic art she converted men into various beasts: and that she converted the companions of Ulysses. But afterwards Ulysses, with the help of Mercury, frightened her and she restored his companions to their original form. By Circe, they understand bodily pleasures and worldly delights, which, by taking away every virtue from man, make him a beast. But Ulysses, with the help of Mercury, obtained from Circe that she return them to being men: That is, the wise man, by means of his wisdom and eloquence—which belongs to Mercury—can persuade the voluptuous and lascivious man to leave vice and return to virtue. **WHO WITHDREW ME**. Almost with flatteries in a bad way, so that a year passed before I noticed my delay. And to better understand the force of the word, and from that the sense of the text: *Subtrahere* in Latin signifies to pull to oneself stealthily and hiddenly. <note>original: "Subtrahere in latino ſignifica furtiuaméte & di naſcoſo tirare ad ſe"</note> Whence we say to "withdraw" (subtract) someone when, in a cunning way that they do not notice, we lead them to say what they would not say. Therefore here the poet says: "Withdrew me," as if she stole me from myself. **THERE NEAR GAETA**. The place where Circe lived was Caieta, today Gaeta, a maritime and very noble land. And according to Virgil, it took this name from Caieta, the nurse of Aeneas. Others say she was the nurse of Creusa, his wife. Others of Ascanius, his son. Others say that because by chance Aeneas's ships burned in that place, the city took its name from that fire: because *chein* in Greek signifies to burn. <note>note: Landino refers to the Greek "kaiein" (καίειν).</note> **BEFORE Aeneas so named it.** The meaning is that Ulysses was with Circe on the island of Circeii near Gaeta. But he was there before Gaeta had been given this name. For according to Virgil, Ulysses, departing from Troy, navigated these seas before Aeneas. This is mostly imagined because of Aeneas's arrival at the rocks of Polyphemus, for there he finds Polyphemus already blinded by Ulysses. **NEITHER SWEETNESS of a son nor piety.** Wishing to make it plausible that Ulysses endured so many toils and put himself in such dangers to have knowledge of various things, it is necessary to show that there was in him an immeasurable love for understanding and knowing: because only love is that which knows how to endure every labor and inconvenience. Nor is it against reason: but it is entirely natural that a man of excellent genius loves the knowledge of things more than anything else.

<meta>This page continues the humanistic commentary by Cristoforo Landino on Canto 26 of Dante's Inferno. Having introduced the figure of Ulysses (Odysseus), Landino now provides a philosophical and geographical analysis of Ulysses’ famous speech, explaining why the drive for knowledge outweighs even the most sacred family bonds.</meta>

<header>INFERNO</header>
<sig>P</sig>

Because nature compels not only man, the rational animal, but also the brutes; and not only the brutes, but even animate things, to love and desire their own perfection above all other things; and the perfection of the human soul is knowledge. Therefore, the love of knowledge in an excellent mind is greater than any other love. And this he demonstrates by comparing those loves which in men overcome all others, which are three: for the son, for the father, and for the wife. And not without great learning does he distinguish these three species of love with three different epithets, calling the love for the son "sweet," for the father "more," and in marriage "joyful." For the father sees himself in the son, and in him sees himself extended into perpetuity, which is most sweet to him. From this, Virgil said: "All the care of the dear parent rests in Ascanius." <note>original: "omniū in Ascanio cari stat cura parentis" from Virgil's Aeneid, Book I.</note> The love of the son for the father he calls "more" because, as we demonstrated above, "piety" <note>Landino uses the Latin sense of *pietas*, meaning duty toward family and gods.</note> is a species of justice through which we love our country, our father, our mother, and others joined by blood. **CONCERNING** the word "old," it seems well-added to "father." For despite it being a duty of piety not to abandon one's father, nonetheless, when they are still in their green and robust age, it seems a lesser cruelty to abandon them than when they are oppressed by extreme old age; for then, languid and without strength, they require from the son that which they cannot do for themselves. Therefore, we should take an example from the storks, who, in that same nest where they were nourished and raised by their parents, later nourish those old ones. And finally, he calls the love toward the wife "joyful," because the conversation of a wife who is chaste and obedient is the highest joy and pleasantness. And we are constrained by the debt of nature and by divine and human precepts to love a wife in whom such character exists. And because Penelope is described by writers as most chaste and most obedient, he therefore mentioned the "rightful love" which should have made Penelope joyful—for she would have been joyful if she had had her husband with her. Therefore, the poet demonstrates that all these three loves, which are very great, can be overcome by the love of knowledge. Penelope was the daughter of Icarius <note>original: "caro"</note>. Others say she was a most chaste woman from Caryotus, who, when Ulysses did not return from Troy after the war and it was believed he was dead, was urged by her father to take a new husband, and many sought her. But she, wishing to persevere in her good purpose, feigned wanting first to finish the web she was weaving; and so that it would not be finished, she unwove at night as much as she wove during the day. Therefore, "these three loves could not conquer the ardor I had to become expert"—that is, learned through experience of the world, and of human vices and of valor (meaning virtue). Here he expressed what Horace says when interpreting Homer: "Who saw the customs and cities of many men." <note>original: "Qui mores hominū multorū uidit & urbes" from Horace's Ars Poetica.</note> And certainly, a man cannot be prudent if he has not had experience of many and varied things, and if he does not know the nature and customs of different men and nations. And he spoke of "human vices" because, since it is given to man by nature to desire the good and flee the evil, as soon as we have known the nature of vices and how harmful they are to the human species, an ardent desire will be kindled in us to flee them and purge ourselves of them. And having reached this stage, we shall acquire the highest good. "But I put myself upon the deep open sea": he means the Ionian Sea, which is wide and spacious. **ONLY** with one ship: we can here refer to that same allegorical sense that we placed above regarding Charon's boat. And "with that small company": Homer presents Ulysses navigating as the human soul which sets itself to investigate the highest good, and finally brings it back to Ithaca and to his homeland—that is, to happiness—because Homer thought that the highest good could be in this life. But Dante feigns that it could not be found in his navigation, because no port (the highest good) is found in mortal things or in the doctrine of the gentiles. Therefore, the ship perishes before it arrives at Purgatory. Thus, he leads a "small company." For the soul having four powers in general, which are divided into many species—namely, Vegetative, Sensitive, Motive (from place to place), and Rational—only the rational parts, with some of the sensitive parts obedient to the rational, are those that follow it. Therefore, they are few. But these few never abandon it. Whence he said: "by which I was not deserted," meaning I was not abandoned. "One shore and the other I saw as far as Spain": He navigated through our Mediterranean Sea to the West, where it is to be noted that "day" can easily represent human life, and the western part represents the end of human life. Therefore, Ulysses navigated to the West: that is, he investigated what our end might be. And he searched "one shore and the other" because he wished to have knowledge of virtue and vice. He who navigates to the West leaves the North on the right hand and the South on the left. The North is a harsh and austere place because of the cold, but sublime and high; it can be interpreted as Virtue, whose path is difficult and arduous but leads upward, that is, to heaven. The South <note>literally "midday"</note> is pleasant and sunny and full of delight, but low and bottomless. This denotes Vice, which brings earthly pleasures and various delights but finally leads to the bottom of Hell. And deservedly, Ulysses had this shore on the left side, which signifies Vice, and the other on the right, by which we understand Virtue. But it is necessary that he who is kindled by the love of knowledge and of investigating the end, in order to have true knowledge of the end, must see "one shore and the other": vice to flee it, and virtue to follow it. And let this suffice for the allegorical sense. Spain: this region is called Iberia by the Greeks and Hispania by the Latins. Among the ancients, it was divided into two parts, one called "Ulterior" (Farther) and the other "Citerior" (Nearer). In these centuries, it is divided into several kingdoms. As far as Morocco: this region is in Barbary and is called Maurusia by the Greeks and Mauritania by the Latins; later, through corruption of the word, it became Morocco. The island of the Sardinians, Sardinia, was called "Sandaleon" by the Greeks because it is in the shape of a human foot, and a "sandal" <note>original: "sandalio"</note> is a type of footwear; it is distant from Corsica by eight thousand paces. "I and my companions were old and slow": Old, because they had been at the siege of Troy for ten years and had spent another ten years navigating. Slow, on account of being old. "When we came to that narrow pass where Hercules set his markers": He describes the strait through which the Ocean enters the land and divides Spain in Europe from Africa, and creates all our Mediterranean seas. Where Hercules set his markers: where he placed the columns to demonstrate that one should not navigate further. And he placed in that strait two columns, one on the side of Africa (that is, Barbary), called Abila, and on the side of Spain, Calpe; these are called the Pillars of Hercules, though in truth they are two natural mountains. "On the right hand I left Seville": this is a noble city in Spain, fifty miles from the sea. "Ceuta" <note>OCR: "Setta"</note> is a city in Barbary on the opposite shore; and because it is not as far toward the Ocean as Seville, he said: "Ceuta had left me."

> "O brothers," I said, "who through a hundred thousand
> perils have reached the West,
> to this so brief vigil
> of our senses that remains,
> do not choose to deny the experience,
> following the sun, of the world without people."

<column-break/>

<image-desc>large decorative initial S in red ink</image-desc>

**U**lysses continues in his narration and delivers a short speech, which he used with his companions to comfort them in enduring hardships and troubles, and not to be dismayed by perils. This is in the deliberative genre; he proposes the honest and honorable parts, demonstrating that man was not produced by God in His likeness to live in idleness and give himself to Bacchus, Ceres, and Venus <note>Metaphors for wine, food, and lust.</note>, nor to live according to sensuality, which desires nothing other than momentary and corruptible earthly things. But rather to excel in virtue and to investigate the truth. Therefore, they must follow Ulysses, who comforts them toward that for which they were produced. And it is the exordium of...

<meta>This page continues Cristoforo Landino’s commentary on Canto 26 of Dante’s Inferno. Having previously discussed the tension between family duty and the thirst for knowledge, we now reach the climax of Ulysses’ speech to his men and the description of their final, fatal voyage beyond the known world.</meta>

# CANTO XXVI

Consider your sowing:
you were not made to live like brutes,
but to follow virtue and knowledge.
I made my companions so keen
with this brief speech for the road
that I could hardly have held them back.
And having turned our stern toward the morning,
of our oars we made wings for the mad flight,
always gaining ground on the left side.
Already the night saw all the stars
of the other pole, and our own so low
that it did not rise from the ocean floor.
Five times rekindled and as many quenched
was the light beneath the moon
since we had entered the deep passage,
when there appeared to us a mountain, brown
in the distance, and it seemed to me so high
as I had never seen any before.
We rejoiced, but soon it turned to grief,
for from the new land a whirlwind rose
and struck the first corner of the ship.
Three times it made her whirl with all the waters;
at the fourth, it lifted the stern aloft
and the prow went down, as pleased another,
until the sea was closed over us.

<column-break/>

This speech is similar to that which Aeneas uses for his companions after the storm received at sea: <note>original: "O socii neque enim ignari sumus ante malorum / O passi graviora dabit deus his quoque finem" from Virgil's Aeneid, Book I. Translated: "O companions, for we are not ignorant of previous evils; O you who have suffered worse, God will also give an end to these."</note> He says then: "O brothers, who have reached the West," <note>original: "al occidente"</note> that is, the Western Ocean, through a hundred thousand perils—as if to say, since you have escaped so many infinite dangers until now, you ought to have hope for the future. And this is the opening of the speech. Then he declares what he wants them to do and says: "Do not choose to deny experience to this so small vigil of our senses," meaning to this brief space of life. For life is a "vigil" and an awakening of the senses, which fall asleep in death. "What remains": that which is left to us. And in short, the meaning is: let us choose to consume this little bit of life that remains to us in the knowledge of great things. And this is to "go behind the sun" toward the "world without people," which is nothing other than saying to go from this hemisphere into the other. For once we reach the West and keep following the sun, we follow that which no longer belongs to our hemisphere, but to the other, which he calls the "world without people" because it is not inhabited. But we shall investigate this place more diligently in the first canto of *Purgatorio*.

"Consider your sowing": <note>original: "femenza" (seed/origin/lineage)</note> that is, your origin. And you will understand that you are made in the image of God by the reason given to you by Him. And because the nourishment of the intellect and its happiness is knowledge, you must not follow the life of brutes, which consists only in the pleasures that satisfy the appetite. Rather, follow moral virtue, in which the active life consists, and "recognition" <note>likely referring to the discovery of truth</note> in which the speculative life is founded.

"My companions": having made the speech, he shows that his companions became so eager for the navigation that he would have had difficulty holding them back. And through this, he demonstrates allegorically that when the internal senses and the appetite are illustrated by the light of the intellect, they are so entirely persuaded that they never abandon the intellect, but are obedient to it like excellent children to a wise father.

"And turned our stern to the morning": he who sails to the West has his prow turned toward it and his stern to the morning—that is, to the East. "Of oars we made wings": because oars are to a ship as wings are to a bird. Whence Virgil said: "by the oarage of wings he crosses over," <note>original: "Remigio alarum transfertendo"</note> and elsewhere, "crossing through the sea," transferring the act of flying to rowing. "For the mad flight": he continues the metaphor, for having called the oars "wings," he calls the voyage "flight." "Mad": foolish, because it is the height of folly to undertake an enterprise beyond one’s possibilities. Nor does this contradict the allegorical sense given above where we identified Ulysses as the man who seeks wisdom. For he does not condemn Ulysses’ purpose of wanting to reach the blessed life, but shows the "flight"—that is, the life—to be "mad," meaning foolish.

"Always gaining on the left side": although they sailed toward the West, they nevertheless leaned toward the left side, which was toward the South for them. For this reason, they were already so far under the Antarctic pole that the pole which is depressed and low for us was elevated over their heads, such that at night they saw the stars of that pole which we cannot see. And our Arctic pole, which for us is always elevated—that is, over our heads—was for them depressed and so low that its stars, which for us always appear and never set, did not appear and did not rise for them. 

The heavens have two points upon which they turn, and these are called "poles." One of these is always seen by us because it is so far above our heads; even though the sky turns, we never lose the stars that are very close to it. And this is called the "Arctic" pole by the Greeks because, according to the fables, Jupiter transformed Callisto into these nearby stars—she was his beloved whom Juno had previously transformed into a bear. <term>Arctos</term> in Greek means "bear." The Latins name it the <term>Septentrio</term> [the North]. This image of the Bear is otherwise called Helice; it has twenty-four stars, among which are the North Star, the "Horn," and the "Wagon" [the Big Dipper]. The fables say that Juno, noticing that this Callisto, a nymph of Arcadia, had been known by Jupiter her husband, changed her into a bear out of jealousy. And Jupiter, as compensation for such damage, converted her into the aforementioned sign. And Juno obtained from Tethys, the sea goddess, that she would never let her bathe in the sea as the other stars do. The poets feign this because other stars, when they are in the West and set, appear to dip into the sea; but this does not appear to happen to the Bear because it never sets. And similarly the other called the Lesser Bear, and also "Cynosura," by which the Phoenicians navigated just as we navigate by the Greater Bear.

"Five times rekindled and as many quenched": in the *Paradiso* we shall demonstrate the reason why the moon every month is rekindled by growing and then, waning, is extinguished. 

"When there appeared to us a mountain, brown in the distance": after sailing for some months, they discovered a mountain. "Brown in the distance" because it was still so distant and far away that it appeared brown and dark. Many believe this is the mountain of Purgatory and the Terrestrial Paradise, which they say is beneath the equatorial region and so high that it reaches even to the heaven of the moon. Wherefore he adds: "and so high as I had never seen any before." We shall speak of this at the beginning of *Purgatorio*.

"We rejoiced": as sailors rejoice when, after long navigation, they see land where they hope they can rest. "And soon it turned to grief": for from where we hoped for salvation, from there came the wind that submerged us. And certainly, he who makes a great enterprise beyond his strength fails just when he hopes to be at the point of perfection. "From the new land": new to us, because we had never seen it before. "A whirlwind rose": that is, a great revolution of wind. Above we have shown what a "whirlwind" <note>Latin: "turbo"</note> is. "And struck the first corner of the ship": it struck the prow, which is the first part of the ship. "Three times it made her whirl with all the waters": for the waters whirled and made an eddy, and as the waters whirled, the ship whirled. And at the fourth time, it lifted the stern up and the prow went down, "as pleased another"—that is, God, or fortune, or fate. "Until the sea was closed over us," and we remained under the water.

Landino provides an extensive commentary on the geographical, mythological, and philosophical implications of this overreach.</summary>

<meta>This page transitions from the end of Ulysses’s speech in Canto XXVI to the introduction of Guido da Montefeltro in Canto XXVII. The commentary continues to explain the nature of fraudulent counsel and the transition between these two figures of Italian history and myth.</meta>

# CANTO XXVII OF THE FIRST CANTICLE OF DANTE

<margin>f</margin> **V** Though the poet is constrained by the number of verses to change cantos, he nevertheless continues with the same subject of fraudulent counselors. And just as in the previous canto he brought Ulysses to speak, so in this one speaks Count Guido da Montefeltro. He therefore connects this canto with the previous one, saying that after the flame containing Ulysses and Diomede had finished its speech, it straightened its tip—which it had bent toward Dante—and, having grown quiet, departed with Virgil’s permission. At the same time, another flame came toward Dante; because a confused sound came out of it, they turned their eyes toward its tip. Like the Sicilian bull: this is an excellent comparison, by which he demonstrates that just as the bull made of brass—with a man placed inside so that when he cried out, a sound came from the animal’s mouth that seemed like its lowing and not a human voice—so this spirit, speaking within the flame, sent out through the tip

<margin>g</margin> **N**ow the flame was already erect and quiet,
having no more to say, and it departed from us
with the permission of the sweet poet,
When another, which came behind it,
made us turn our eyes toward its tip
because of a confused sound that came out of it.
As the Sicilian bull, which bellowed first
with the bellowing of him—and that was right—
who had tempered it with his file,
Bellowed with the voice of the afflicted one,
so that, although it was made of copper,
it still seemed pierced by pain;
So, for lack of a way or an opening
from the beginning within the fire, into its own language
the dismal words were converted.

But after they had found their way up
through the point, giving it that vibration
which the tongue had given in their passage,
We heard it say: "O you to whom I direct
my voice, and who were just now speaking Lombard,
saying, 'Now go, I do not provoke you further,'
Though I have arrived perhaps somewhat late,
let it not irk you to stay and speak with me;
see, it does not irk me, and I burn!
If you have but now into this blind world
fallen from that sweet Latin land
from which I bring all my guilt,
Tell me if the Romagnols have peace or war;
for I was of the mountains there, between Urbino
and the ridge from which the Tiber is unlocked."

<column-break/>

of the flame a confused sound. But so that you may understand the history: Phalaris was king of Agrigento, a city in Sicily, who out of extreme cruelty offered a prize to anyone who would find a new torture or torment against men. At the same time there was Perillus, an Athenian craftsman of great genius. He fashioned a bull of bronze from very thin plates, into which he wanted those who were to be killed to be placed, and a fire built around it. Thus, when from excessive heat the man placed inside cried out, he would emit a voice that seemed like the horrific lowing of a bull. Phalaris gave him a worthy reward for such a work, for he commanded that he should be the first to experience such a punishment. And certainly it is a just thing that the inventor of cruelty should perish by his own device. Ovid expressed this perfectly: <note>original: "Non est lex aequior ulla Quam necis artificem fraude perire sua."</note> "There is no law more just than that the architect of death should perish by his own artifice." Propertius mentions Perillus: <note>original: "Et gemere in tauro saeve perille tuo."</note> "And to groan in your own bull, cruel Perillus." And Juvenal: <note>original: "Phalaris licet imperet: ut sis falsus Et admoto dictet periuria tauro Summum crede nephas animam preferre pudori."</note> "Though Phalaris should command you to be false and dictate perjuries with the bull brought near, believe it the highest sin to prefer life to honor." Therefore he said most excellently: "The Sicilian bull." The bull fabricated in Sicily by Perillus, which bellowed first with the weeping of him who had tempered it with his file—and this was Perillus, as we have said. It bellowed with his voice because it was inanimate, but with the voice of the afflicted—that is, with the voice of him who was tormented inside.

**A**nd that was right: and this was a right and just thing, because the cruelty of such an inventor deserved such a punishment. So that, although this bull was made of copper, it nevertheless seemed to low as a living bull does when it is pierced by pain. So, because that soul was enclosed in the flame, having "no way or opening"—meaning no aperture—from the beginning of the fire, they were converted into "dismal words"—that is, unhappy and miserable ones.

<margin>p</margin> **H**e describes how Count Guido, having noticed by the words spoken to Ulysses that the poets were Italians, asks them about the state of Romagna, being eager to hear news of his homeland. He says that after the words—which at first were a confused sound because they found no exit from the flame—made their way up through the tip of the flame, it gave such a vibration—that is, such a motion—as the tongue had given in their passage. "Vibrating" <note>original: "Guizzare"</note> means to move quickly. We heard—Virgil and I—"O you," Virgil, to whom I direct my voice, who were speaking just now "Lombard." This refers to Virgil’s homeland <note>Virgil was from Mantua, in Lombardy</note>, saying "**ISSA**": that is, "now." "I do not provoke you further" <note>original: "Ten va piu non t'adizzo"</note>: "adizzo" means to provoke or irritate. "Somewhat late": the Count considers himself to have arrived late—that is, after the centuries in which Homer and Virgil flourished. It is as if he says: "If I had lived in your times, you would have written of me as you wrote of Ulysses." Alexander the Great also lamented this when, arriving at the tomb of Achilles, he said: "O happy youth, who found such a herald for your praises!" and without doubt it is the happiness of an eminent man to find a most eloquent writer of his praises. "If you": he organizes the text: if you have only now fallen "into this blind world." He calls the essential Hell a "blind world" because it is in the darkness of the center, and morally because every vice is blind, for it comes from ignorance, which is blindness of the mind. "From that sweet Latin land": from Italy. "From which I bring all my guilt": because in it I committed the error for which I am punished, as will be shown below. "Tell me if the Romagnols": he has used a fitting introduction <note>term: exordium</note> in this petition of his. First, he makes him attentive, praying that it not be burdensome to stop, since Virgil is outside the flames, while it is not burdensome to him who burns. Then he shows it is easy to ask him for something so easy for him, since he comes newly from Italy. And finally, he makes an honest petition, because it is an honest thing to ask about the state of Romagna, being a Romagnol himself. "For I was of the mountains there, toward Urbino": understand this as Montefeltro. For these mountains where the Tiber is born divide Romagna from Tuscany.

# CANTO XXVII.

Just as ancient histories most often have Virgil speak, so in modern ones he is the questioner or narrator. **YOUR ROMAGNA.** First, he demonstrates in general that the minds of the people of Romagna—and especially the tyrants of that region—are always intent on war, although at present none is openly manifest. Then he comes to particulars. Ravenna is a very ancient city in Romagna, of which in those times Guido Novello da Polenta was lord, a circumspect and eloquent man who held our poet in the highest veneration during his life and honored him magnificently in death. Nor did he forget Dante's children after his death, but maintained them in the goods given to their father. And there his succession has remained; and today it is in—

I was still looking down, attentive and bent,
when my leader touched me on my side,
saying: "You speak; this one is an Italian <note>original: "latino"; in this context, it refers to someone from the Italian peninsula.</note>."
And I already had my response ready;
without delay I began to speak:
"O soul who are hidden down there,
your Romagna is not, and never was,
without war in the hearts of its tyrants;
but I left none openly manifest there now.
Ravenna stands as it has stood for many years:
the eagle of Polenta broods there,
so that it covers Cervia with its wings.
The land that already underwent the long struggle
and made a bloody heap of the Frenchmen
finds itself under the green claws.
The old mastiff and the new from Verrucchio,
who made such bad government of Romagna,
there where they are accustomed to use their teeth as an awl,
The city of the Lamone and of the Santerno
is led by the small lion of the white nest,
who changes sides from summer to winter.
And that city whose flank the Savio bathes,
just as it sits between the plain and the mountain,
so it lives between tyranny and a free state."

<column-break/>

Ravenna. Dante's son, descended from Dante, was a very literate and eloquent man and worthy of such blood; he is one who should deservedly be recalled to his ancient fatherland and our republic. The body of the poet lies honorably in Ravenna. It is the judgment of every wise and literate man that the Florentine people ought to bring him back to his fatherland and honor him with a sepulcher worthy of such a poet. Now he shows Ravenna to be "brooded over" by the eagle, which signifies that it is clemently ruled and governed by the lords of Polenta, as a mother does her small children. Their coat of arms is an eagle, half white on a blue field and the other half red on a gold field. And because these same men were also lords of Cervia, a land placed on the shore of the Adriatic sea fifteen miles from Ravenna, he shows that this eagle extends its wings so far that it covers that land with its pinions. *Vanni* <term>vanni: a poetic term for wings or primary feathers</term> are the feathers of the wing after the first ones, which are called "knives." Polenta is a small castle near Bertinoro, which was the origin of this lineage. **THE LAND That already underwent the long struggle.** He means Forlì, which the Romans called *Forum Livii* <note>original: "forum liuii"</note>, situated almost in the middle of Romagna. Of this city, this Guido was once lord, and here he had victory over the French. In 1282, Martin III <note>Historically Martin IV</note>, the Supreme Pontiff, who was by birth from the kingdom of France, sent as Count of Romagna John of Appia, a man most expert among all the French in deeds of arms, who favored the Guelph party at the time when the aforementioned Guido, head of the Ghibelline party, held Forlì. He came, then, and at his first arrival took Faenza, and from there made war on Forlì. But Guido, considering John's strength and his robust army of Frenchmen, resorted to his usual cunning; by a treaty, he later induced John to come to Forlì with the whole army on the first day of May before dawn. Believing he would be received as a friend, John entered with a chosen part of his people through a gate that Guido had caused to be opened, and left the others crowded under the shade of an oak tree. The French then entered, and because they are by nature greedy, they immediately gave themselves to plunder. As John entered, Guido secretly exited through the other gate and in a short time broke those who had remained at the oak tree.

---

And afterward, having returned to Forlì, he turned to the slaughter of the enemies already scattered through the houses to plunder. Thus, there were few who were able to remount their horses and flee the land; the others were killed in great number. This was the beginning of a greater war, because the following year Martin sent a new army to John, and with that, he finally took Forlì and drove out Guido. **THE LAND THAT already underwent the long struggle:** because for a long time it resisted the Pope. **AND OF THE FRENCHMEN A bloody heap.** That is, a mountain and pile. *Mucchio* in the Florentine dialect signifies what in Latin is *cumulus* <note>original: "cumulus"</note>, which is a mound made of things gathered together. **UNDER THE GREEN CLAWS it finds itself.** It is under the Ordelaffi family, whose arms are a green lion from the middle up on a gold field, and from the middle down with three green stripes and three gold. At this time, Sinibaldo Ordelaffi was lord. **THE OLD MASTIFF.** The poet uses an artful and very playful variety in this description, setting down now the coat of arms and now the nicknames of the lords. For the declaration of this text, it is unknown to no one that a mastiff signifies a large and biting dog. Therefore, by an appropriate similarity, he calls the tyrant a mastiff, who most cruelly mangles and devours his subjects. And here he means two Malatestas, father and son, violent and cruel men who held Rimini. These lords had their origin from a Malatesta who was from Penne de' Billi, a castle located in the county of Montefeltro; who, for his many prowess in military discipline, deserved that the people of Rimini should make him their citizen and honor him with fine houses and other rewards. From him was born another Malatesta, a man of great spirit and warlike, who broke Count Guido at Monteloro—though he was afterward broken by him at the bridge of San Procolo—and he had such authority and following that he made himself lord of Rimini. This man fathered Gianciotto <note>original: "Gianni scianchato", meaning John the Lame</note> and Paolo, of whom we spoke above when we made mention of Francesca and Pandolfo. Also Malatestino, who was blind in one eye and a man of great cunning, and succeeded his father. And from Malatestino was born Ferrantino, who succeeded his father together with Pandolfo his uncle; and these were lords of a great part of the March of Ancona. Therefore, here he means the "old mastiff" for the first Malatesta lord, and the "new" for Malatestino. **FROM VERRUCCHIO.** This is a castle which the people of Rimini gave to the first Malatesta. Hence, although their origin was from Penne de' Billi, they were nevertheless named from here. **MONTAGNA** was a noble knight of the Parcitati family of Rimini, head of the Ghibelline party, whom Malatesta, with other Ghibellines, caused to be captured and gave into the guard of Malatestino; and later, when asked many times if he was guarding him well, he had him put to death. **THEY USE THEIR TEETH AS AN AWL.** Having called them mastiffs, he continues the metaphor. Because the mastiff harms with its teeth, he says they make a *succhio*—that is, a small suck or a drill—with their teeth, because they pierce their subjects. **THE CITY OF THE LAMONE AND OF THE SANTERNO.** He means Faenza, by which runs the river Lamone, and Imola, where the Santerno runs. This was called *Forum Cornelii* <note>original: "forum cornelii"</note>.

<header>INFERNO</header>

Afterward, because he was fervent in the faith, from this word *imolare*—which means to sacrifice—it was called Imola. And it refers to Maghinardo; and the history is this: Maghinardo Pagano was from a castle in the mountains above Imola. He, no less through luck than through virtue, became lord of Forlì, of Faenza, and of Imola, although he did not possess them all at once. For in the year 1290, and on the twelfth of November, Stefano da Ghinazzano, a Roman and Count of Romagna, was captured in Ravenna by those of the Polenta family. This gave Maghinardo the opportunity to make himself lord of Faenza, and the Bolognese to take Imola. Afterward, the Pope sent Bandino, Bishop of Arezzo, from the family of the Counts Guidi of Romena, who brought the lands of Romagna back to obedience to the Apostolic See <note>The "Apostolic See" refers to the central administration of the Catholic Church and the Pope's authority.</note>. But afterward, in the following year, and on the twenty-third of December, he took Forlì by stealth at night, and in it Count Aghinolfo da Romena, brother of the aforementioned bishop; and near Forlì he besieged Cesena where the Count of Romagna was. And in the year 1296, having made a league with Azzo III d'Este against the Bolognese who had taken Forlì from him, he took Imola from them, not without damage and ignominy to them. For he fought with them—who were about four thousand—and captured and killed many of them. **THE LITTLE LION** of the white nest: Maghinardo Pagano da Susinana, whose coat of arms was a blue lion. Some say it was crimson on a white field. **WHO CHANGES** sides from summer to winter: This man, as we said above, was from the house of the Pagani in Romagna, who were Ghibellines <note>The Ghibellines supported the Holy Roman Emperor, while the Guelfs supported the Pope.</note>. Nevertheless, because he was left as a youth under the guardianship of the Florentines after the death of his father Pagano, and was always defended and maintained by them, as a most grateful man he was always in their favor in every enterprise. Thus in the winter—that is, in Romagna, which is to the north of us and a cold region—he was a Ghibelline. And in the summer—that is, in Tuscany, which is to the south of Romagna and a warm region—he was a Guelf. Some explain this passage simply, saying that he changed sides often, so that if in summer he was for one, in winter he was for another. **AND THAT CITY TO WHICH THE SAVIO**: He means Cesena, past which runs the river called the *Sapis* by the Romans, and called the Savio by us. In those times, among so many tyrants in Romagna, only Cesena governed itself in liberty. Although at times the principal citizens there practiced some tyranny.

---

"Now, I pray you, tell us who you are;
do not be more stubborn than others have been,
so that your name may hold its front in the world."
After the fire had roared for a while,
it moved its sharp point in its own way
this way and that; and then it gave forth this breath:
"If I believed my response were being made
to a person who would ever return to the world,
this flame would stand without more flickering;
but since never from this depth
has anyone returned alive, if what I hear is true,
without fear of infamy I answer you.

I was a man of arms, and then a cord-wearer,
believing that, so girded, I could make amends;
and certainly my belief would have come true,
if it were not for the Great Priest—may evil take him!—
who put me back into my former sins;
and how and why, I want you to understand from me.
While I was the form of bones and flesh
that my mother gave me, my works
were not leonine, but those of a fox.
The stratagems and the hidden ways,
I knew them all, and I so managed their art
that the sound of it went out to the ends of the earth.
When I saw myself reaching that part
of my age where everyone should
lower the sails and gather in the ropes,
that which had pleased me before then grieved me,
and repentant and confessed I yielded myself;
ah, wretched me, and it would have been enough!"

<column-break/>

Our poet, having been generous to this soul, now requests that he tell his name, adding: **SO THAT YOUR NAME** may hold its front in the world: that is, remain in fame. For just as we say someone "has no front" <note>An idiom meaning someone lacks shame or a sense of honor.</note> when they have no respect for honor, we can say the opposite: that he who is honored "has a front." To which the soul responds that if he believed he were answering someone who was to return to the world, he would not say a word. And this is because, having left a good reputation of himself by having become a friar, he would not want his damnation to be known. But he is content to reveal himself, hoping that Dante will not return to the world, having heard that whoever enters Hell cannot leave it. And the poet writes this to demonstrate how great the desire for fame is among all men, in whatever state they find themselves.

¶ This is the response that Count Guido makes, through which he shows that his occupation was in deeds of arms; and then toward the end of his life he became a "cord-wearer." This signifies a friar of Saint Francis, because they gird themselves with a cord, believing that in this way they can make amends—that is, atone for their sins. And he reveals his thoughts to him: **IF THE GREAT PRIEST**: that is, the Pope, had not persuaded him to return to his first sins and first errors: to the frauds and fraudulent counsels in which he had been practiced in his past life. **AND HOW AND WHY** <note>original: "ET CHOME ET QUARE"</note>: and in what manner and for what reason **I WANT YOU TO UNDERSTAND ME. WHILE I WAS THE FORM OF BONES AND FLESH**: that is, while I was alive and was soul and body together. For here he takes "form" for the soul, and "flesh and bones" for the body. And certainly the form is what gives being to a thing. As for example <note>original: "Verbi gratia"</note>, we see a bronze statue of Mercury. In that, therefore, it is not the bronze—which is the matter—that makes it Mercury, but the form which is in the matter. Likewise, man is not man for having a body composed of the four elements of which the bodies of all other animals are composed, but for having a rational soul without which we would not be men. Therefore, understand the text this way: "While I was the form of bones and flesh," i.e., of the body, which has bones and meat—that is, while this soul was joined with the body. **WHICH MY MOTHER GAVE ME**: which bones and flesh my mother gave me. For in generation, the paternal seed is nothing other than "spirits" which are the craftsmen that form the body. But the mother gives her blood, from which—as from matter—the paternal seed forms the human body. Whence she is called *mater* <note>Mother.</note> because she provides the *materia* <note>matter; this is a traditional medieval etymological explanation.</note>. **MY WORKS WERE NOT LEONINE**: I did not use force openly and without snares or fraud as the lion does; but they were fox-like works. For

---

my wars and my deeds were covered, insidious, and full of cunning and fraud. Wherefore Cicero in the book *On Duties* says: "Since injury is done in two ways, namely by force or by fraud, fraud seems characteristic of the little fox and force of the lion. Both are most alien to man, but fraud is worthy of greater hatred. Of all injustice, none is more capital than that of those who, even when they are most deceptive, act so that they appear to be good men." <note>original Latin: "Cum autem duobus modis .i. ui aut fraude fiat iniuria Fraus quasi uulpeculę Vis leonis uidetur Vtrumque homini alienissimum. Sed fraus odio digna maiori. Totius autem iniustitię nulla capitalior quam eorum: qui tum: cum maxime fallunt id agunt ut boni uiri videri velint."</note>

<header>INFERNO</header>

...is seen <note>original: "deatur," likely part of "videatur," meaning "it seems"</note>. And certainly, the injury done with fraud is much greater than that done with force. And without doubt, human life would be in much greater tranquility if—just as on the island of Crete <note>referred to here as "Candia"</note> according to Pliny there are no foxes—there were likewise no fox-like minds among men.

**And the arguments and the hidden ways.** This demonstrates what "fox-like work" is, which has two parts: first, sharpening the wit to find the fraud (which he calls "arguments"), and then finding hidden ways and paths that lead us to fraud before being discovered. **I knew them all.** This denotes that no species of fraud was unknown to him, and he proves this by the effects. For he used so many and of such variety that he was known throughout as a supreme master of fraud by a very widespread reputation. And because of this, he says: **I conducted and guided their art so.** That is, the sound that fame derives from it. **To the end of the earth:** even to the furthest parts of the world. And this was my life until old age.

**But when I saw myself arrived at that part of my age** where, in that old age, **everyone should lower the sails and gather the ropes.** Human life is similar to navigation; for in life, fortune varies—at times giving us serene happiness and at times cloudy adversity—just as the winds make the sea now serene and tranquil, now turbulent and tempestuous. Our living is a navigation through this sea, and old age is like a port of this life. And therefore he says: **When I saw myself arrived at that part of my age.** He means: when he had reached old age. **Every man should lower the sails and gather the ropes.** This is a metaphor; for just as sailors reaching port put an end to their navigation and disarm by lowering the sails and gathering the ropes, so men reaching old age should leave behind all worldly operations and bring them to an end.

And so did Guido, who converted from sin to spiritual works. In this place, he touches upon three things necessary for one who wishes to be reconciled with God. The first is **contrition**, which means we recognize the sin and it displeases us. Hence he says: **What had pleased me before then grieved me.** The second is **penitence**, which means we repent for the error committed and grieve for it with the intent of not erring in the future, and of satisfying what we are bound to satisfy. Hence he says: **And repented.** The third is **confession**, which means that having recognized the sin, the man humbles himself and is ashamed. Hence follows: **And confessed, I surrendered myself.** This is because the sinner seeks peace with God, against whom sin had made him a rebel. This is the absolution of the priest, which is like a form imprinted upon our soul. Since the soul is like the matter that must receive such an impression, it is necessary that the matter—that is, the soul—prepares itself to receive that form. It cannot be prepared without the three aforementioned things. For if we offend God first by thinking, then by speaking, and finally by acting evilly, it is proper that contrition satisfies the evil thought, confession the evil speech, and penitence the evil action. Furthermore, because in sin there concur deliberation, delight, and perseverance, contrition restores the evil deliberation; repentance (because it carries pain within) restores the delight; and confession interrupts the perseverance. **Ah, wretched me, it would have helped.** He grieves that having made a good beginning with which he could have been saved, the Pope drew him away and removed him from it.

> The evil prince of the new Pharisees
> having war near the Lateran
> and not with Saracens nor with Jews,
> For every enemy of his was Christian,
> and none had been to conquer Acre,
> nor a merchant in the Sultan’s land.
> Neither the supreme office nor sacred orders
> did he respect in himself, nor in me that cord
> which used to make its wearers thinner.
> But as Constantine sought out Sylvester
> within Soracte to cure his leprosy,
> so this man sought me out as a master
> To cure the fever of his pride;
> he asked me for counsel, and I stayed silent
> because his words seemed drunken.
> And then he said to me: "Let your heart not doubt;
> from this moment I absolve you, and you teach me how
> to throw Palestrina <note>referred to as "Preneſtrina"</note> to the ground.
> I can lock and unlock Heaven,
> as you know, for the keys are two,
> which my predecessor did not hold dear."

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Large decorative initial G containing foliage and floral motifs, spanning several lines of text.</image-desc>
**Guido** had been led to the port of salvation. But the Pope induced him to return to the ancient sin of giving fraudulent counsel. Guido did not want to give it at first because he feared the sin, but he was deceived by the Pope, who absolved him of that which he could not absolve, as we will say shortly below.

**The prince of the new Pharisees:** the Pope is the prince of the prelates, whom by metaphor he calls Pharisees, who in the ancient law were held in great esteem within the priestly order. But we spoke of the Pharisees a little while ago.

**Having war near the Lateran.** The history is this: In 1287 <note>historically 1297</note>, Pope Boniface, having conceived an implacable hatred against the Colonna family—whose houses are near Saint John Lateran—because two cardinals of that family, Lord Giacomo and Lord Pietro, had been opposed to his election, and afterward Sciarra della Colonna had stolen certain sums from his treasures, he deprived this family of all honors and benefits. He commanded the two aforementioned cardinals to lay down their hats and cardinal robes. And because they did not obey, he deprived the entire family of every honor and dignity, destroyed their houses in Rome, took their castles—giving part to the Orsini and destroying part—and finally besieged Nepi, which surrendered under certain pacts. Afterward, being unable to take Palestrina <note>referred to as "Preneſte"</note>, an impregnable city, he sent for this Count Guido, now a Friar Minor. Being unable to prevail upon him to become his captain in this war, he asked him for counsel. He received the advice to "promise much and deliver little." Therefore, Boniface, pretending to be moved to mercy, or through common friends, suggested that they humble themselves. The cardinals, with their relatives, came in black and dejected robes and threw themselves at his feet, confessing themselves sinners and asking for mercy. The Pope promised them the restitution of everything if they gave him Palestrina. Once he had it, he destroyed it to its foundations and had it rebuilt at the foot of the mountain on the plain, calling it the "City of the Pope." This so terrified the two aforementioned cardinals that they remained in hiding from then on, until finally Boniface, by those same arts with which he had deceived others, was made to die miserably by Sciarra.

**HAVING war near the Lateran.** He had war with the Colonna family, who lived in Rome near Saint John Lateran. **AND not with Saracens nor with Jews.** Therefore it was an illicit war. He lists the circumstances that aggravate the sin; it is alien to the pontifical gentleness to make war, but more alien to make war on Christians, and most alien on those who are his neighbors.

**And none had been to conquer Acre.** This removes every excuse, because not only was he making war against those who were Christians, but against those who, being Christians, had never acted against the religion. For they had never denied God like those who went with the Sultan of Babylon to conquer Acre. Nor had they been merchants who had carried merchandise prohibited by the Church to the infidels. And so that we may better understand the history, we will remember that the Christians having lost Antioch and Tripoli and every other land in Syria except for Acre—which was where Joppa was anciently—they retreated to this...

<header>CANTO</header>

...all the forces of the Christians were positioned against the infidels. Because it is on the shore of our sea, near Jerusalem—seventy miles—and in the middle of Syria, and almost in the center of the world. It was a port open to both Eastern and Western merchants. For this reason, it was a sanctuary for every nation and every language. Here was the home of the King of Jerusalem and Cyprus, and the Prince of Antioch. Here was the congregation of the Hospital of Saint John <note>The Knights Hospitaller</note>. Here resided the Pope's legate and the lieutenants of the King of France and the King of England. There were so many others in that city that there were seventeen courts, each with "jurisdiction of blood" <note>the legal power to pass death sentences</note>. This generated great confusion in the administration of the land.

Because of this, it happened in the year 1291, while there was a truce between them and the Sultan <note>original: "soldano"</note>, that the truce was broken by the Christians. This was because the aforementioned princes had about fourteen thousand soldiers who, being poorly paid, were driven by hunger to rob and kill the Saracens who came into Acre under the faith of the truce. The Sultan, moved by such injury, sent ambassadors to demand the stolen goods and the thieves; and not obtaining them, he came with an army so large that the camps spanned twelve miles. Our men initially resisted manfully with the vigilance and great counsel of the Grand Master of the Temple; but he, being wounded in the arm by a poisoned arrow and dying within a few days, there was no one left who could lead such a crowd gathered from various nations and languages. They no longer observed orders; they did not obey; and many, abandoning the land out of fear, fled to the sea. This gave victory to the Sultan. He then took the land, sacked it, and more than sixty thousand—between males and females—were killed.

Therefore, none of the enemies of Boniface <note>Pope Boniface VIII</note> had acted against the religion. Neither the supreme office nor the holy orders did he respect in himself. Nor did he consider that he, being the Supreme Pontiff and priest, should not ask anyone for fraud. Nor did he respect the <term>capestro</term> <note>the hemp rope or cord worn as a belt by Franciscan friars</note>, where the cord takes the place of a belt. It used to be that those girt with it were leaner <note>a reference to the fasting and asceticism of the early Franciscans</note>; here, by transition, he censures the Friars Minor who did not observe the abstinence they used to observe, for which they were once thin. 

But he says that just as the Emperor Constantine, being a leper, sought out Pope Sylvester—who lived on Mount Soracte—to heal him of his leprosy, so with that same desire Boniface sought me as a master to heal his "proud fever." He calls it a fever by metaphor, referring to his burning pride and his wrath to take revenge against the Colonna family <note>original: "colonnesi"</note>. For just as a fever is burning and induces thirst, so his wrath burned with a great thirst for vengeance.

**Constantine:** he reigned for thirty years and ten months, and at the end of his life was baptized by Eusebius, Bishop of Nicomedia; but he held the Arian heresy. Being infected with leprosy, he heard from his doctors that his only health lay in bathing in the pure blood of small children. Constantine, although he greatly desired to be freed from such a disease, nevertheless would in no way be so impious that so many children should die for him. Therefore, it pleased the Father of all mercy and the Supreme God that the following night, in a vision, the princes of the apostles, Peter and Paul, appeared to him. By them, he was admonished to seek out Pope Sylvester, who, because of the persecution carried out against Christians and to perform harsh penance, was living in the caves of Soracte. **Soracte** was called "Syracte" among the ancients, a very rugged mountain in the region of the Hirpini, or rather the Falisci.

**He asked me for counsel and I was silent.** Not out of pride or for lack of supreme reverence for the Pontiff, but because his words seemed drunken to me; that is, his words seemed without reason, as those who are drunk most often speak. And it is to be noted here: although it is a divine precept that we must obey superiors, nevertheless, such a precept is to be obeyed in just things. And then he said to me: **"Let your heart not suspect"**; fearing that I might hesitate because of the sin, he promises to absolve him and demonstrates that he has the authority. **"That your predecessor did not hold dear."** This was Pope Celestine <note>Celestine V</note>, who, as we have shown above, renounced the papacy.

> Then his heavy arguments pressed me
> until silence seemed to me the worse choice,
> and I said: "Father, since you wash me
> of that sin into which I must now fall,
> a long promise with a short keeping
> will make you triumph on the high seat."
> 
> "Francis came for me as soon as I was dead,
> but one of the black cherubim
> said to him: 'Do not take him; do not do me wrong.
> He must come down here among my wretches
> because he gave the fraudulent counsel,
> since which time I have been at his hair;
> 
> for he who does not repent cannot be absolved,
> nor can one repent and will [the sin] at once,
> because the contradiction does not allow it.'"
> Oh, miserable me! How I shook myself
> when he seized me, saying to me: "Perhaps
> you did not think I was a logician!"
> 
> He carried me to Minos, and that one twisted
> his tail eight times around his hard back,
> and then out of great rage bit it,
> saying: "This is one for the thieving fire."
> Therefore, where you see, I am lost,
> and thus clothed, walking, I grieve.
> 
> When he had thus completed his speech,
> the flame, sorrowing, departed,
> twisting and tossing its sharp horn.
> We passed onward, I and my guide,
> along the ridge up to the next arch
> that covers the ditch where the fee is paid
> by those who, by dividing, acquire a burden.

<column-break/>

The arguments the Pope used prevailed upon me, and for this reason **silence was the worse choice for me**; that is, it seemed the worst path. Because it seemed to me that by not obeying, it might appear that I doubted his authority and power, whereby he might proceed against me as a heretic. Therefore I said: that promising much and delivering little would make him triumph—that is, acquire victory.

He feigns quite appropriately that, having been a leader of the Order of Saint Francis, the saint should have taken up his patronage. And if we wish to speak allegorically, we will say that the conscience of one who, at the request of a prelate, has committed fraud, remains ambiguous after death (i.e., after the sin is committed). For on one side, Francis (i.e., the very religious order at whose request he acted) persuades him that it was not an error. On the other side, the devil (who is the sin itself) condemns it. Hence, **black cherubim**: i.e., a devil; and therefore black, who before the fall was of the order of Cherubim, of which we shall speak more fully in *Paradiso*.

**For he who does not repent cannot be absolved:** the reason the devil assigns to Saint Francis is that the Count <note>Guido</note> cannot be saved unless he is absolved. Nor can one be absolved who does not repent of the sin committed. Nor can one at the same time want to commit the sin and repent of it, because wanting and not wanting are contraries. **Oh, miserable me!** Then he spoke of the great perturbation that had come upon him. **He carried me to Minos, and that one twisted...** regarding Minos, enough was said above in Canto V, both in recounting the histories and fables and in demonstrating the allegorical sense. **And then out of great rage bit it:** this is the end of those who are condemned by their own conscience, who out of desperation become furious even against themselves. **This is one of the...** namely, of those condemned to enter the flame, which covers and steals away the soul so that it cannot be seen within. And therefore he said above: **And every flame steals away a sinner**, and thus I am clothed in this flame. **I grieve** <note>original: "miracuro"</note>: i.e., I lament and bear hatred toward myself. For "rancor" is hidden hatred.

**Up to the next arch:** up to the bridge of the ninth ditch <note>bolgia</note>. **Where the fee is paid:** i.e., the tax and tribute; as if to say: the punishment of those who, by "unseaming" with false slanders, dividing and separating those who were joined and friends. **Acquire a burden:** they acquire sin, which is a load and weight upon the soul.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante's Inferno, transitioning from the eighth circle's fraudulent counselors to the ninth ditch (bolgia) where sowers of discord are punished. ### CANTO XXVIII OF THE FIRST DIVISION OF DANTE

In the two preceding cantos, our author treated the fraudulent counselors punished in the eighth <term>bolgia<note>A 'bolgia' is a 'ditch' or 'pouch' in the eighth circle of Hell, where different types of fraud are punished.</note></term>. Now he places the sowers of scandals, schisms, and heresies. Because they, through their fraud, destroyed and separated those who previously lived joined in concord, they are justly placed here to have their own members separated, divided, and mangled, more or less according to whether they sowed greater or lesser discords. In this place, the saying of the Psalmist fits: *The sons of men, their teeth are weapons and arrows: and their tongues are a sharp sword.* <note>original: "Filij hominum dentes eorum arma & sagitte: Lingue eorum gladius acutus."</note>

Who could ever: as the best of poets, having to treat great and tragic things, he uses such an opening to make the listener attentive, demonstrating that for the greatness of these things, one cannot find suitable words. Similarly Virgil says: *Not if I had a hundred tongues and a hundred mouths, or a voice of iron, could I grasp all the forms of their crimes, or run through all the names of their punishments.* <note>original: "Non mihi si lingue centum sint oraque centum. Ferrea uox omnes scelerum comprendere formas. Omnia penarum percurrere nomina possem."</note> He imitates Virgil, then; and Virgil imitated Homer. Therefore, "who could ever": it is as if he says, "no one."

> Who could ever, even with words set free,
> tell fully of the blood and the wounds
> that I now saw, though he told it many times?
> Every tongue would certainly fall short
> because of our speech and our minds,
> which have little capacity to comprehend so much.

*To tell of the blood and the wounds:* The quantity of blood and the cruelty of the wounds. *Fully:* sufficiently. *Even with words set free:* <note>Dante uses the phrase "parole sciolte," referring to prose, which is "untied" or "free" from the constraints of poetic meter and rhyme.</note> in prose speech; for he who writes in verse uses words bound together with a certain measure, but he who writes in prose uses words free and released from every measure and rhyme. The meaning is this: No one could sufficiently describe the horrible slaughter even if they wrote in prose, where it is easier to express what we wish than in verse. Alternatively, *to tell it many times:* this text can be arranged in two ways. Either: "who could tell of the wounds which I saw with the intent of telling them many times?" Or we shall say: "Who could ever tell fully even if, though not just once, he told it many times?" *Every tongue would certainly fall short:* in the telling. And he gives the reason. *Because of our speech:* which is insufficient. *And because of the mind:* which is insufficient. *Which have:* that is, which speech and mind possess. *Little capacity:* <note>Dante uses "piccolo seno," literally "small breast" or "small fold," meaning a small receptacle or limited capacity.</note> they are hardly capable. *To comprehend so much:* that is, to understand so great a thing.

<margin>1</margin>
> If all the people were assembled again
> who once lay upon the fortunate land
> of Puglia, grieving for their own blood,
> Through the Trojans, or through the long war
> that made such a high heap of rings,
> as Livy writes, who does not err;
> With those who felt the pain of blows
> for opposing Robert Guiscard;
> and the others whose bones are still gathered
> At Ceprano, where every Apulian
> was a liar; and there by Tagliacozzo,
> where the old Alardo won without weapons;
> And if one showed his limb pierced and another his lopped off,
> it would be nothing to equal
> the foul fashion of the ninth ditch.

The meaning is that the wounds given in all the battles fought at different times in the countries he names would be nothing in comparison to the wounds of those who were in this new ditch. And therefore he says: *If all were assembled:* that is, if all the people were gathered together who were once grieving for their blood spilled upon the fortunate land of Puglia. He calls Puglia "fortunate" because Fortune demonstrated much variety there. And he lists five wars:

The first was between Aeneas and Turnus, which Virgil writes most elegantly in his last six books, demonstrating terrible slaughter and killing. *Or through the long war that made such a high heap of rings:* he means the conflict at Cannae in Puglia and the great defeat that Hannibal, captain of the Carthaginians, gave to the Romans because of the rashness of Marcus Varro the consul. Against the advice of Lucius Paullus, his colleague, Varro chose to join the battle when he could have avoided it and gradually worn down the armies of Hannibal, who could not replace his soldiers every day. He entered battle at that hour of the day when the sun struck the eyes of the Roman soldiers. Similarly, the wind harmed them greatly, carrying dust from dry places against their faces. On that day eighty senators were killed, two quaestors, twenty-one military tribunes, and several men who had been consuls, praetors, or ediles. Forty thousand infantry were killed and two thousand seven hundred knights. Out of so many bodies, Hannibal had a bridge made with which his army crossed. The Roman forces were so weakened that if Hannibal had known how to use such prosperous fortune and had come to Rome immediately before their terrified spirits recovered or provided some defense, he would have taken Rome. But his delay took away his victory. Wherefore Maharbal the Carthaginian cried out in indignation: "You know how to win, Hannibal, but you do not know how to use the victory." <note>original: "tu sai uincere hanibale ma nō sai usar la uictoria."</note> Regarding this, Petrarch wisely said: "Hannibal won, but he did not know how to use his victorious luck well afterward."

*With those who felt the pain of blows:* there was an ancient Duke of Normandy named Richard, and he had two sons: Richard, who succeeded his father, and Robert Guiscard. In the year of salvation 1070, Robert came to Puglia. The Duke of Puglia at that time gave him great help in the wars against the Prince of Salerno, and finally, having no male children, made Robert his son-in-law and successor to the duchy. Thus, Guiscard, through military virtue, conquered Puglia, Calabria, and the whole realm of Sicily, which Alexius, Emperor of the Greeks, had occupied; and later he was in favor of Pope Gregory VII against Henry III. His successors reigned until the time of Henry, father of Frederick II.

*And the others whose bones are still gathered:* he refers to the war and the defeat that Charles I [of Anjou] gave to Manfred, not without the prompt help of the Florentine Guelfs, as was said elsewhere.

*And there by Tagliacozzo:* this is the other battle that the aforementioned Charles fought against Conradin, nephew of Manfred, on the plain of San Valentino near Tagliacozzo. *Alardo:* this was a Frenchman, Alard de Valéry, who in those times was returning from the Holy Land, a baron of no small authority and already old. Seeing the small forces of Charles against Conradin, he advised him to trust more in counsel than in arms. This advice had such authority with Charles that he committed the care of everything to him; and through his prudence, though almost defeated in the battle, he recovered the victory most fully. But the battle was not without great killing on every side, in the year of salvation 1268, on the twenty-fourth day of August. And Charles afterward, in memory of the event and for the salvation of the souls of the slain, built an excellent abbey called "Victory" <note>The Abbey of Santa Maria della Vittoria.</note>.
