<page-num>125</page-num>

# CANTO XXVIII.

He establishes a fitting punishment, because he who divided others—whether between man and man, or between God and man—now justly appears open and divided himself. These are the ones who sowed scandal, discord, and schism. Allegorically, this happens to such men because their minds are always distracted and divided. He imagines that the heretics are split down the middle even to the head, because they divided the Church of God, which should be one body of which Christ is the head. He first presents one person split open from the crotch to the chin, comparing him to a barrel that has lost its middle-piece—called a *mezule*—or its side-piece, which some call a *lulla* and others a *rulla*.

> No cask ever, for the loss of its middle-piece
> or side-piece, was ever so split open
> as I saw one, broken from the chin to the place one farts.
> Between his legs hung his intestines;
> the vitals appeared, and the wretched sack
> that turns into excrement what is swallowed.
> While I stood there, fixed on seeing him,
> he looked at me and with his hands tore open his chest,
> saying: "Now see how I mangle myself!
> See how Muhammad is torn apart!
> Before me, Ali goes along weeping,
> his face split from the chin to the forelock.
> And all the others whom you see here
> were sowers of scandal and of schism
> while they lived, and therefore are they so split."

Therefore, whoever committed heresy in the faith is divided from the chin downward, because he divided the body of the Church of which Christ is the head. Those who committed scandal between princes, who are the heads of the people, have their wounds in the head. Those who divided relatives have their hands cut off; and those who divided son from father have their heads cut off and carry them in their hands.

But because the history of Muhammad is not to be entirely passed over, we shall note how in the year of our salvation 610, during the papacy of Boniface III and the reign of the Emperor Honorius <note>The author likely means Heraclius; Honorius reigned much earlier. This reflects historical inaccuracies common in Renaissance commentaries.</note>, there was in Arabia a Muhammad, a magician of great cunning and greedy for not human but divine honor. In his youth, he saw various lands and nations; in Jerusalem, he learned the Mosaic law, and elsewhere the Christian law. Thus instructed, and using magic arts to perform "miracles," he persuaded the unlearned multitude of Arabia that he was a messiah come from heaven. He gave new laws, mixing in many voluptuous things, by which he easily drew the crowd to his devotion. With this favor, he acquired lordship, especially by feigning a most holy life and character. With great cunning, he had trained a white dove to feed from his ears, into which he secretly placed millet or similar bait; thus, when he was preaching to the people, he would let the dove fly, and it would immediately come to his ear. He claimed it was the Holy Spirit showing him what was good to do.

To such cunning was added another most ruinous plague. A monk named Sergius, falling into the <term>Nestorian heresy<note>A 5th-century belief that Christ existed as two separate persons, one divine and one human, rather than one person with two natures.</note></term>, was expelled by other monks. He traveled to Arabia and joined Muhammad. Because he was very learned and full of trickery, he provided many shrewd counsels. Muhammad kept him hidden, claiming he was the Angel Gabriel who instructed him in all things useful to the soul. Some say Sergius was sent from Rome to preach to the Arabs and turn them to our religion, having been promised that if he behaved valiantly, he would receive the [cardinal's] hat. Later, when the promise was not kept, he returned to Arabia and "sang the palinode"—that is, he preached the opposite of what he had preached before. He was of such great help to Muhammad that he was reputed a true messiah not only in Arabia but throughout Egypt. He established that his people should be called Sarains or Saracens, from Sarah, the legitimate wife of Abraham, as if they were the legitimate successors of the divine line. He was of such talent that he even used his ailments to his purpose; being frequently oppressed by the "falling sickness" <note>An archaic term for epilepsy.</note>, every time he came to himself, he feigned that the Angel Gabriel had appeared to him, and that he fell because he could not support such splendor. He was left fatherless from childhood and poor, raised by his uncle. He died in July in the year of our salvation 621 (others say 632), after which the Caliph obtained his principality. The Caliph was succeeded by Achaly, and after he was driven from the principality, Ali reigned. But because Ali was very superstitious, the Egyptians created a new prince, the Caliph, against him.

**THAT TURNS INTO EXCREMENT.** Although this description is foul, the poet used it not merely to show a natural thing, but to signify allegorically that whatever enters the mouth of the schismatic becomes dung—that is, whatever doctrine he learns becomes corruption for other men. Certainly, he was a great corruption among men, which is not only not extinguished, but God, the just judge, allows such a religion to expand its borders to avenge and punish His enemies with His enemies. Wherefore, in this year, to the supreme infamy of the Christian name and no small ruin for wretched Italy, he [the Turk] has taken Otranto (anciently called Hydruntum) in Calabria. I do not know what will follow, but the sins of the princes of this age—almost all of whom are infected—and the Italian discords bring us more fear than hope. *May God have mercy on us and let his face shine upon us.* <note>original: "Misereatur nostri deus et illuminet uultum suum super nos." (Psalm 67:1)</note>

**ALI:** Several believe he was the uncle of Muhammad and a helper in all his enterprises.

> A devil is back there who splits us
> so cruelly with the edge of his sword,
> resetting each of this ream [of souls]...

<column-break/>

And he says **CASK**: that is, a barrel, which in Latin is called *veges*. **IS NOT SO SPLIT**: is not so pierced and opened. "Thus for losing the middle-piece or side-piece as I saw one broken from the chin to the place one farts": that is, to the end of the torso where the outlet for the sutures of the belly is, and from where foul wind exits, which some call *trulla* <note>original: "trulla"</note> when it comes out with sound and noise, though not learnedly. **INTESTINES**: that is, the guts. **SWALLOWED** means gulped down. **WHILE I STOOD FIXED**: I was entirely stuck, that is, I stood completely intent. **I MANGLE MYSELF**: I tear and open myself.

We have said above that the author here places the punishments for the ninth species of fraud, which is called scandal or schism; these sins are types of envy. For it is the opposite of the love contained within charity, and envy is contrary to charity. These sowers of scandal and schism commit fraud to the harm of their neighbor under the appearance of good. But there are differences between **Infidelity**, **Schism**, and **Heresy**. Infidelity is opposite to faith; it is not believing what the faith believes in every part and thing. Heresy is to depart from the faith in some part or to make some change in it. Schism is to depart entirely from the faith and from its union. Because this is greater than the first two, the poet imagines it is punished in this lower part. Schism, then, is the division and severance of the unity of faith and charity. But also, the division within cities between one party of citizens and another, and also between man and man, is comprised under this sin.

<insert>d</insert> It shows that those damned to such punishment go continually around that ditch, and a devil, every time they return to him, renews their wounds with his sword. This signifies that the schismatic always revolves in the same error, and a devil...

When they had completed the circuit of the sorrowful road:
because the wounds are closed up
before any of them returns before the devil again.
"But you, who are you who linger on the crag,
perhaps to delay going to the punishment
that was judged upon your own accusations?"
"Neither has death reached him yet, nor does guilt lead him,"
replied my master to torment him,
"but to give him full experience,
it falls to me, who am dead, to lead him
through the Inferno down here from circle to circle;
and this is as true as that I speak to you."
More than a hundred there were who, when they heard him,
stopped in the ditch to look at me,
forgetting their torment in their wonder.
"Now tell Fra Dolcino, then, to arm himself—
you who perhaps will see the sun shortly—
unless he wishes to follow me here soon,
with such provisions that a stress of snow
does not bring victory to the Novarese,
which otherwise would not be easy to attain."
After he had lifted one foot to depart,
Muhammad said these words to me;
then he stretched it out on the ground to leave.

Another, who had his throat pierced through
and his nose cut off right up to the eyebrows,
and who had only a single ear,
having stayed to look on in wonder
with the others, before the others opened his windpipe,
which was crimson on the outside in every part,
and said: "You, whom guilt does not condemn,
and whom I saw above on Latin land,
unless too much resemblance deceives me:
Remember Pier da Medicina,
should you ever return to see the sweet plain
that slopes from Vercelli down to Mercabò.
And make known to the two best men of Fano,
to Messer Guido and also to Angiolello,
that if our foresight here is not in vain,
they shall be cast out from their vessel
and weighted down near Cattolica
through the treachery of a fell tyrant.
Between the islands of Cyprus and Majorca,
Neptune never saw so great a crime—
not from pirates, nor from Argive folk.
That traitor who sees with only one eye,
and holds the land that someone here with me
would wish he had never fasted from seeing..."

<column-break/>

That is, his diabolical persistence keeps him continually divided. **NEITHER HAS DEATH REACHED HIM YET.** He reveals to Dolcino that he should provide himself with victuals before the snows come: because then he could not carry them, being on such a rugged mountain. **THAT HE DOES NOT SEEK VICTORY:** that is, that he does not let himself be conquered by the Novarese citizens. <note>Fra Dolcino led a radical movement called the Apostolic Brethren; they were eventually besieged by a crusade called by the Pope.</note> Fra Dolcino was in the time of Boniface VIII, from Novara in Lombardy; and in Vercelli a priest named Augustus raised him, from whom after some time, having been caught in a theft, he fled to Trento. In the mountains near this city, being eloquent and of great intellect, under the habit of a friar, he persuaded those crude and unlearned people to join a new sect, affirming himself to be a true apostle sent by God. He wanted everything to be held in common out of charity, especially women, except for mothers and daughters. Hearing this, the Bishop of Trento had them driven out. Dolcino, seeing the multitude that followed him grow every day, believed he would be invincible if he retreated into the mountains of Brescia, Bergamo, and Como, and did not descend to the plain, those places being well-fortified by nature and by snows. But finally driven from there, he retreated to a most rugged mountain between Novara and Vercelli, where he had with him more than three thousand men capable of bearing arms, both because they could fulfill his every desire and because he delighted every man with his eloquence. But because God did not wish such grave wickedness to go unpunished, he was finally besieged by an army gathered of Lombards, Savoyards, Provencals, and Frenchmen. Finally, through hunger, his followers surrendered, and he was captured and led to Novara. There, although urged by many, he never wished to return to the true law. For this, he was tortured with hot pincers throughout the city and cruelly killed—a man who, without fail, had he not fallen into such error, would have been worthy of immortal fame, because in the midst of such torments he never changed his expression nor ever lamented, but continually comforted his followers to persevere in his precepts. Nor was Margaret of Trento, his wife, of lesser fortitude of spirit; she, both beautiful and very rich, though she could have found noble husbands, preferred the same tortures rather than renounce the schism. The siege lasted one year and the schism two.

<image-desc>Ornamental drop cap 'D' containing a landscape scene with rolling hills and a winding river.</image-desc>
**IT SHOWS** that Pier da Medicina, having remained with the others as if stupefied to see Dante—who was in that place—not only spoke to him but gave him a message. This man was from Medicina, located in the territory of Bologna. Because of the many scandals and discords he sowed among the gentlemen of the Bolognese countryside and the citizens of Bologna, and furthermore between the Bolognese and the tyrants of Romagna, he deserved to be punished here. He had his throat cut because he had erred with words, which are formed in the throat; and also his nose cut off, a great ornament of the head, because he divided the countryside (the ornament of the city, which is the head); and he had an ear cut off for having divided the great citizens, who are the senses of the head. He admonishes the living to beware of scandals, not because those in Hell do not want everyone else to come there, but because having been the source of so many evils, he feared that the more evil followed, the more his own punishment would increase. He describes the plain of Lombardy as far as Romagna. **MERCABÒ** is on the Po at the edge of Romagna on the shore toward Venice, built by the Venetians, then taken by Roberto da Polenta; it was destroyed when the Venetians were defeated at Ferrara in 1308. Thus he places the entire plain of Lombardy and Romagna beginning from Vercelli and coming as far as Mercabò. **TO THE TWO BEST** from Fano: Malatestino, Lord of Rimini, under the guise of a banquet, arranged at Cattolica for two principal citizens of Fano to come and dine with him, pretending he wished to discuss great matters with them. As they came by sea, by his order they were drowned by Messer Guido del Cassero and Angiolello da Cagnano. **OUT OF THEIR VESSEL.** He says this because their souls will be driven out of the body, which is like the vessel of the soul. **MAZERARE:** <term>mazerare</term> <note>original: "macerare"</note> means to tie a man in a sack with a stone attached and throw him into the sea. **BY A FELL TYRANT.** This was Messer Malatestino, of whom we spoke above. **BETWEEN THE ISLAND OF CYPRUS AND MAJORCA.** He demonstrates that in all the Mediterranean Sea there was never a more cruel thing done. For he places Cyprus as the most eastern island and very distant from Ma...

Majorca which is to the west. Cyprus was once joined to Syria as Sicily was to Italy: and as Euboea was to Boeotia. And this island is placed to the east in the Pamphylian Gulf, and from the west it is opposite Sicily and Syria, a very effeminate island in which there was an ancient law that commands that every woman once in her life must go to the temple of Venus: nor does she leave before she knows a stranger. Majorca are two islands near the coasts of Spain called *Gymnasiae* by the Greeks: because the inhabitants of those islands in summer stay almost naked, and *gymnos* in Greek means naked. And the Latins call them the Balearics: because they skillfully use slings. The larger of these is called Majorca and it is near Spain as far as one can sail in a day. Therefore, Cyprus being very far to the east and Majorca to the west: by saying "between the island of Cyprus and Majorca," Dante wants to encompass the entire sea from the East to the West. Neptune: who being the god of the sea, should reasonably have seen everything that was ever done in the sea. And in the genealogy of the pagan gods, Saturn was the lord of the heaven, of the earth, and of the sea. And from him remained four children: three males—Jupiter, Neptune, and Pluto—and one female called Juno. To Jupiter fell by lot in the division the heaven. And Juno, whom he took for his wife, had the air for her dowry. Neptune was content with the sea, and Pluto with the underworld. The allegory of the fable is that the universe was created by God and placed in time. And Saturn means nothing other than time. Whence in Greek he is called <note>original: "chronos"</note> *Chronos* from *chronos*: that is, time. And they say that he devoured all the children who were born to him except for four, whose allegory we demonstrated above. And in the verse, "Neptunno" is spelled with a single 'n' and not "Neptunno" with two 'ns' <note>The translator is noting a poetic spelling choice</note> out of respect for the rhymes that follow. Not of pirates: of sea corsairs. Not of Argolic people: Greek people: because the Greeks are called Argolics from Argos, the principal city of Greece, who were for a long time almost masters of the seas. Or rather, he said "Argolic people" to mean people who sailed: and he calls the sailors "Argolic" from *Argo*, the first ship, about which we will speak elsewhere. That traitor: that is, Malatestino. Who sees only with one: that is, he sees with one eye, because he was blind in the other. And holds the land: understand Rimini. That such a one is here with me who would wish he were fasting from seeing it: and understand Curio. This man was a Roman orator, very eloquent, of whom Cicero writes. He was restless and factious and much favored Caesar’s party in the civil war against Pompey. And as Caesar was bringing his army from Gaul to Rome, he stopped at Rimini because according to the laws he could not cross the Rubicon river with the army. Curio came from Rome, who at that time was a tribune of the plebs. And he so moved Caesar with his eloquence that where he was still doubtful whether to cross or not, he decided to cross. Fittingly, therefore, Curio being a great cause of the civil dissensions, especially through his eloquence, the poet places him without a tongue. Therefore, he would wish he had never seen Rimini: because in that place he committed the scandal for which he is damned here. He will make them come to talk with him: and then he will kill them. And for this reason, they will not need to make vows or prayers to the wind of Focara. Focara is a place in the sea between Pesaro and La Cattolica, so dangerous because of the storm of winds that all the sailors who pass there make vows and prayers to God for their escape. But since these men will be dead, they will no longer have to sail through this place to return home.

Dante asks who is he of the bitter sight: that is, who is that one to whom it seems bitter to have seen Rimini, because he had said that he would wish he were fasting from seeing it. And Pier then with his hand opened Curio's mouth, who was his companion in that place, and shows that his tongue had been cut out. This penalty was fitting for him: because having deservedly sinned with the tongue, he ought to be punished in it. This man: Curio, chased from Rome by the Pompeians. Submerged: removed and took away the doubt of Caesar. For when Caesar had reached the end of his province, although the desire for mastery pushed him to cross the Rubicon river and to make war on the Pompeians, nonetheless reverence for the laws held him back. But Curio inflamed him to cross, affirming that "he who is prepared always suffered harm from waiting." This verse is taken from Lucan, where he induces Curio to persuade Caesar to undertake the enterprise against Pompey, especially since he was equipped and prepared with both armies and everything else necessary for war. Whence he says: <term>Delay not: it has always harmed those prepared to wait <note>original: "Tolle mora: semper nocuit differre paratis"</note></term>. Therefore Curio affirmed to Caesar that he who is equipped—that is, prepared—always suffered harm from waiting: that is, from lingering. Which means it is always harmful to those who are prepared to defer and delay. Oh, how dismayed Curio seemed to me: a most fitting punishment, that he who had sinned with eloquence and with audacity should be punished with their opposites, which are silence and dismay.

In those same times, Mosca dei Lamberti <note>original: "Mosca de glubertin"</note>: a noble and famous family, almost the principal one in the Ghibelline sect. This man, more reckless than wise, was present at the consultation held by the Uberti, Lamberti, Amidei, and others of the Ghibelline faction against Messer Buondelmonte: who a little before had refused the bride given to him from the Amidei and had married one of the Donati. And being prudently advised by some elders that they should proceed with maturity and consider the end, he on the contrary advised that it should happen suddenly, saying: <term>"A deed done has a head" <note>original: "cosa facta capo ha"</note></term>. And after he consulted with men like himself, it happened. From which infinite discords were born, and the exile now of the Ghibellines, now of the Guelphs. Lifting the stumps: that is, raising the arms without hands: because the end of the arm deprived of the hand is called a "stump" <note>original: "moncherino"</note>. And by raising his arms, the blood that came out of the stumps fouled his face. WHO said, alas: "A deed done..."

<page-num>XXVIII</page-num>
<header>CANTO</header>

...has done as we explained above. This was a "bad seed" <note>original: "mal seme"</note> because from this counsel infinite discords and wars proceeded, not only among our citizens, but also throughout all of Tuscany. And I, Dante, added to his words: **"And death to your kin"** <note>original: "Et morte di tua stiatta"</note>; as if to say, "you glory in the fact that your words were a bad seed for the Tuscan people, and I add that they were also the destruction of your own lineage and progeny." And Dante’s words added **"sorrow to the sorrow"** <note>original: "duolo al duolo"</note> of his punishment, in such a way that, confused and grieving, he went away like a wretched and vicious man, a fool lacking in prudence. This is said because, in truth, Mosca’s counsel was that of the worst kind of citizen, a man who had completely abandoned himself to malice and was void of all prudence.

### But I remained to watch the throng
### and saw a thing that I would be afraid
### to tell alone without more proof,
### Were it not that conscience reassures me,
### the good companion who emboldens a man
### under the breastplate of feeling itself pure.
### I saw certainly, and I still seem to see,
### a trunk without a head walking just as
### the others of that wretched flock were walking;
### And it held the severed head by the hair,
### hanging from its hand in the manner of a lantern,
### and that head looked at us and said, "Woe is me!"
### Of itself it made a lamp unto itself,
### and they were two in one and one in two;
### how that can be, He knows who governs above.

<column-break/>

Curio had his tongue cut out, because with it he had sown discord. Mosca had his hands cut off, because his counsel had been to use hands and force. And for the same reason, the poet depicts Bertran <note>Bertran de Born, the troubadour and lord of Hautefort</note> having his head separated from the rest of his body. This punishment is imagined to be prepared for those who sow discord among blood relatives, because they have divided those who should have been joined like members in one body. Morally, we can understand that such men have divided the head from the trunk because they have one thing on their tongue and another in their heart.

**"The throng"** <note>original: "Lo stuolo"</note>: the multitude. Properly, a *stuolo* is a troop armed for battle. **"And I saw a thing that I would be afraid to tell"** without a witness: for he who narrates incredible things and does not wish to be considered a liar seeks witnesses. Here, as an excellent <note>original: "optio," likely meaning "ottimo" or "chosen"</note> poet, he shows that he knows it is difficult to persuade others of what he narrates, so that he is not held to be foolish or improvident; by demonstrating he knows this, he gains authority and belief. Thus Ovid says: "Who would believe this, unless antiquity stands as a witness?" <note>original Latin: "Scit quis hoc credat nisi sit pro teste uetustas"</note>.

**"Were it not that conscience reassures me"**: a man would fear saying things that would make him seem a liar because they appear impossible. But being true, the conscience—which is pure—gives daring, because conscience is a good guide to making the soul bold and frank. And just as a man-at-arms protected by a **"breastplate"** <note>original: "osbergo"</note> or cuirass does not fear putting himself among the swords of enemies, so when a man feels pure and knows he speaks the truth, he takes confidence in speaking, even if the matter seems impossible. Certainly, conscience gives great frankness not only in speech but in every human action.

**"I saw certainly"**: Two things cause lies to be told. First, when for some reason of our own will we say what we know to be false. Second, when although we do not wish to tell a lie, we nevertheless tell it, believing it to be true either through error, simplicity, or bad information. Therefore, the poet has shown above that he does not sin through malice in telling a falsehood. Now he shows that he does not lie through ignorance either, since he narrates what he saw where he could have been deceived. But what he saw, he saw so clearly that it still **"seems he sees it."**

**"And I still seem to see"**: He shows he has what he then saw so fixed in his memory that he still seems to see it. In passing, this shows that memory retains well those things that caused wonder or fear, or other great disturbance, because such things make a deeper impression.

**"A trunk"** <note>original: "Vn busto"</note>: in Latin *bustum* signifies the place where human bodies were burned to then place the ashes in a small tomb; it can also mean the tomb itself. Nevertheless, in our language, we call the **"bust"** the whole human body except for the head.

**"Held the severed head by the hair"**: held it by the locks. **"Hanging"** <note>original: "Pesol"</note>: i.e., suspended and dangling, as in Latin they say *pensilis*. **"In the manner"** <note>original: "A guisa"</note>: in the likeness and form **"of a lantern"**: thus he carried his head before him to see with its eyes, just as we carry a lantern when we want to see in the darkness. And that head looked at us and said, **"Woe is me!"**

**"Of itself it made a lamp unto itself"** with its eyes: although separated from the trunk, it provided light for its path and for its trunk. **"And they were two in one"**: because the head was separated from the trunk. **"And one in two"**: because one and the same soul was in the trunk and in the head.

**"How that can be, He knows who governs above"**: That one and the same soul is in the head and the trunk joined together is natural and easily understood. But that it should be in one and the other when separated is impossible according to the nature of the animal. Because although the soul in the body is "all in the whole and all in every part," nevertheless, the origin and source of the spirits—which are the vehicle <term>vehicle: the medium through which the soul's powers are transmitted</term> that carries the powers of the soul—is in the heart, and the place where from the aforesaid spirits sense and motion are generated (or at least given perfection) and from whence the motive and sensitive nerves originate, is the head. Therefore, since neither the heart by itself nor the head can give perfection to sense or motion, the animal can in no way live when the head is separated from the rest of the body except by supernatural power. Therefore, He who governs up there, who is the supreme and only God, knows how this can be. But man, who cannot know the soul and the body except according to their nature, does not understand how this can happen contrary to its nature.

<header>PURGATORY</header> <note>Though the header says Purgatory, the text clearly describes the eighth circle of Hell (Inferno).</note>

### When it was directly at the foot of the bridge,
### it raised its arm high, along with the head,
### to bring its words closer to us,
### Which were: "Now see the troublesome penalty,
### you who go breathing, seeing the dead;
### see if any is as heavy as this one.
### And so that you may carry news of me,
### know that I am Bertran de Born, he
### who gave the young king <note>The original Italian "regi ouanni" (King John) refers to Henry the Young King, son of Henry II of England, though the commentator confuses him with King John Lackland.</note> wicked encouragement.
### I made the father and the son rebels to each other;
### Ahithophel did no more to Absalom
### and to David with his malicious goading.
### Because I parted persons so joined,
### I carry my weary brain divided, alas,
### from its beginning, which is in this trunk.
### Thus is the <term>contrapasso</term> <note>The law of retaliation, where the punishment fits the crime.</note> observed in me."

<column-break/>

When the spirit reached the place where Dante stood, it brought its head close to Dante so that he could better understand its speech. Then he said he was Bertran de Born. This was Bertran de Born of England—though others say of Gascony—entrusted with the care of John, whose nickname was John <note>historically Henry the Young King</note>, son of Henry, King of England. He was raised in the court of the King of France, and it happened one day that the King denied a favor requested of him; the young man who had asked it left confused with shame. Because of this, the King turned to those around him, asking which was more troublesome: to ask for a favor or to deny one. John responded that to a generous soul, it was more troublesome to deny. The King judged this sentiment so wise that he surmised John would turn out to be most wise and of great spirit. And indeed, in his adult years, he became so liberal that his father could not sustain such heavy expenses. Perhaps the youth would have regulated himself if Bertran had not encouraged him to prodigality. Finally, the father was forced to wage war against him, and in battle the son was mortally wounded. Asking the company of the Bardi <note>A famous Florentine banking family.</note> of Florence for one hundred thousand florins, he made a will; in it was a legacy in which he left his soul to the devil if his father did not satisfy the Bardi. **"You who go breathing"**: that is, you who are alive. To **"breathe"** means to draw breath, for no one can live who does not breathe. Therefore, it means "you who come living among the dead." **"Ahithophel did no more to Absalom"**: In the second book of Kings <note>Known today as 2 Samuel.</note> it is written that Amnon, the firstborn of David,

---

fell in love with Tamar, his sister. On the advice of a trusted friend, he prayed David to send Tamar to him to prepare food. Tamar went, and Amnon took her by force, though the girl always resisted him; and then, because it seemed to him she had been harsh toward him, he drove her away. To avenge this wickedness, her brother Absalom initially kept the matter silent on advice. After two years, Absalom invited his father David and all his brothers to a banquet at one of his villas; at the end of the banquet, he had Amnon killed and fled to Syria. But after three years, Joab, the prince of David's military, reconciled him to his father, and he returned to Jerusalem—though for two years David would not allow him into his sight. In the third year, he pardoned him absolutely and spoke with him. But Absalom, through various arts, won over many tribes and made them enemies of his father, and they called him king. He drew to himself Ahithophel, David's counselor, into his conspiracy. David ordered that another of his counselors, named Hushai, should pretend to rebel and join Absalom just as Ahithophel had; he arranged it so that Ahithophel’s counsel was no longer accepted by Absalom. Because of this, Ahithophel hanged himself. Absalom, believing the fraudulent advice of Hushai, was finally defeated in Ephraim. Then, in his flight, passing suddenly <unclear>u</unclear> <note>likely "under" or "through"</note> an oak tree, he remained hanging from the branches by his hair, and was killed by Joab, one of David’s captains. **"Because I parted persons so joined"**: I divided father and son. My brain is divided from its "beginning," the heart, which is the beginning of the spirits. **"Which is in this trunk"**: in this torso, because the heart is in the middle. **"Thus is the contrapasso observed in me"**: In civil law, the **"penalty of retaliation"** <term>Lex Talionis</term> <note>The law of "an eye for an eye."</note> is ordained; which is that whoever has committed an injury shall be punished in that very same way. For example: whoever cuts the hand of a living person, the law is that his hand shall be similarly cut. In Latin this punishment is called **"suffering in return"** <note>original: "contra passu"</note>, because he has suffered the opposite of what he inflicted on others. Therefore, the poet says the **"contrapasso"**, that is, suffering the opposite of what I have done, is observed in me. Since I divided the son from the father, who are one body—for **"father and son are considered the same person"** <note>original: "pater & filius censentur per eadem"</note>—therefore my body, in return for this, is divided.

<summary>Bertran de Born explains his punishment of decapitation as the "contrapasso" for sowing discord between King Henry II and his son, drawing a parallel to the biblical rebellion of Absalom against David.</summary>

<header>CANTO</header>
<page-num>XXIX</page-num>

extracted from him. And at the end of the banquet, he had Amon killed and fled to Syria. But after three years, Joab, prince of David's militia, called him back: although for two years David did not want him to come into his presence. In the third year, he absolutely forgave him and spoke to him. But Absalom, with various arts, reconciled many tribes to himself and made them enemies of his father, and Ahithophel, David's counselor, was in his conspiracy. David ordered that another of his counselors, named Hushai, should act deceptively. Passing quickly where the oak remained, he was hung by his hair from the branches. And by Joab, one of the causes, persons so joined: father and son divided. My brain is divided from its source, the heart, which is the source of the spirits. Which is in this trunk: that is, separated because the heart is in the chest. Thus the contrapasso is observed in me: and in civil law the penalty of talion is ordained: which is: that he who has done injury should be punished in that same way. As for example: He who cuts off a hand from someone: there is such a law that his hand should similarly be cut off: and in this way, the one thus punished receives the ultimate contrapasso: because he has suffered in return what he had inflicted on others. Therefore, the poet said: the contrapasso, that is, to suffer in return for what I have done, is observed in me. Because I, having divided the son from the father, who are one body: because father & son are united by the same things. And therefore my body, in return for this, is divided.

# CANTO XXIX. CANTO XXIX OF DANTE'S FIRST CANTICLE

The many people and the diverse wounds
had so intoxicated my eyes
that they were eager to stay and weep.
But Virgil said to me: "What are you still gazing at?
Why does your sight still support itself
down there among the sad and mutilated shadows?
You have not done so at the other pits;
consider, if you think to count them,
that the valley circles for twenty-two miles.
And already the moon is beneath our feet;
the time now granted to us is short,
and there is more to see than what you believe."

->Dante is admonished by Virgil.<-

**THE MANY PEOPLE.** Not only were there many people, but they also had wounds that were not similar, but **DIVERSE WOUNDS**. **HAD** The lights: that is, the eyes. **SO INTOXICATED.** When the eye of our mind is sober—that is, not occupied by any passion—it sees the truth. But when it is intoxicated by the contagion of the body, it willingly follows its appetite. But Virgil, who represents higher reason, says, "What are you still gazing at?" because **YOUR SIGHT STILL SUPPORTS ITSELF.** It leans and fixes itself. **CONSIDER IF YOU THINK TO COUNT THEM** That the valley circles twenty-two miles. Allegorically, higher reason admonishes the lower reason not to waste time wanting to have knowledge of particulars, because they are innumerable. To demonstrate this, he affirms that the circuit and circumference of that pit <note>original: "bolgia"</note> is twenty-two miles <note>The text says "twenty-two" here, though earlier it mentions "twenty-four"; this reflects historical debates on the geography of Dante's Hell</note> and is full of shadows. Therefore, it is easily concluded that it is impossible to count them. He said the circuit was twenty-two miles to show that they are already near the center of the earth, because nothing remained except the tenth pit and the ninth circle—which in itself contains four circles, and in the fourth is the center. But before we entered this work, we demonstrated this circuit of 22 miles in our description of the site of Hell. **AND ALREADY THE MOON is beneath our feet.** The time granted was one natural day. Therefore, he reached the center after the night and half the day had passed. The other half of the day became night for him once he passed the center, in such a way that he arrived at Cato <note>at the Mountain of Purgatory</note> in the morning. Therefore, the first night was whole, and the following day was from midday into the night. And when the second night returned to our hemisphere, he was already moving from the center toward the surface of the other hemisphere, finding the dawn there when it became night here. This shows, therefore, that when they were in this pit, the day was approaching our hemisphere. And because the moon was in opposition to the sun, it was already beginning to be in the other hemisphere, which is "under the feet" of those in ours. Having passed the middle of Lucifer's body, he began to ascend. Therefore, having traveled through the night and part of the day of our hemisphere, and beginning to ascend to the other when it was day for us, he found a new night with which he rose from the center to the surface, and reached the dawn. **AND THERE IS MORE TO SEE.** Because there remained the tenth pit and the ninth circle, which embraced four others.

"If you had," I replied then,
"attended to the reason why I looked,
perhaps you would have allowed me to stay longer."
Meanwhile the leader went on, and I went
behind him, already giving my answer
and adding: "Within that hollow
Where I held my eyes so fixedly,
I believe a spirit of my own blood weeps
for the guilt that costs so much down there."
Then the master said: "Let not your thought
break itself upon him from now on;
attend to other things, and let him remain there.
For I saw him at the foot of the little bridge
point at you and threaten fiercely with his finger,
and I heard him called Geri del Bello.
You were then so completely occupied
with him who once held Hautefort
that you did not look that way until he was gone."

<column-break/>

We have finally arrived at the tenth pit <note>original: "bolgia"</note>, in which the falsifiers are punished. **Falsity** is the tenth species of fraud. There cannot be falsity unless one thing is shown for another to the harm of one's neighbor. Generally, it is to deny the truth or to feign that what is false is true. There are two species: in words, which is called a **lie**, and in deeds, which is properly called **falsity**. Although one can falsify writings and other things, here he places the falsifiers of metals, who are **alchemists**, and the falsifiers of money <note>counterfeiters</note>. This is done either by falsifying the alloy or falsifying the stamp. He places at the beginning how he, out of wonder and compassion, willingly stopped to weep. But Virgil admonishes him that he must distribute the time given to him for such a journey in a way that he can complete it, since there still remain many and more horrific things to see. Certainly, higher reason, when it has seen things in general, wants to pass to other knowledge, because science is not of particulars. Beyond this, it considers the nature of things without any passion. But lower reason and sensuality revolve around particulars, and in those, it does not remain without passion—whether of love, hate, envy, or compassion. Therefore it is necessary that they have similar but **DIVERSE WOUNDS**.

Dante replied: "If you knew the reason why I was looking, you would have permitted—that is, forgiven—my staying." **MEANWHILE:** In this interval, Virgil walked, and Dante, following him as he walked, similarly followed him in the answer already begun, adding: "I believe a spirit of my blood and my generation weeps in that hollow where I held my eyes so fixedly"—this is a metaphor for one who takes aim at a target. And Virgil replied, "Let not your thought break"—do not break or interrupt the thoughts you have of other things to think about him; attend to other things and let him remain. And he adds that he saw this spirit and heard him called **Geri del Bello**. This man was Geri del Bello, brother of Messer Cione del Bello degli Alighieri, a kinsman of Dante. He was very schismatic and for such a vice was killed by one of the Sacchetti family. No vengeance was taken for him until thirty years later, when a son of Messer Cione killed one of the Sacchetti at the door of his house. This is a legitimate excuse for the poet to be able to name other vicious people, since he does not spare his own relatives. Many say that Dante feigns not to have seen this spirit in Hell to denote that he never saw him alive there, and that Virgil comforting him not to care for him signifies that the intellect comforts us that, although someone may be joined to us by blood, we nevertheless ought not to have compassion for the evil that he reasonably <note>justly</note> suffers. **YOU WERE THEN So completely occupied** with him who held Hautefort. Above that Bertran <note>Bertran de Born</note> already mentioned, who held in his guard **Hautefort**, a fortress in England <note>actually in Aquitaine, though the commentator notes English control</note>, which he held for John <note>John Lackland</note>.

<sig>q</sig>

<summary>Dante is rebuked by Virgil for lingering in the ninth pit to grieve for his kinsman, Geri del Bello, before they proceed to the tenth pit where falsifiers and alchemists are punished. The commentary explains the nature of falsification as a form of fraud and justifies why Dante shouldn't feel pity for his kin's just punishment.</summary>

The author provides the reason why he thought the spirit had fled, which was mentioned above. **BUT THE FACT** Much more pious. As if to say, his indignation made me more pious toward my kinsmen and made me eager to avenge him. **UNTIL THE PLACE** first. Walking and talking together through this pit until that rock from where the other pit begins to be seen.

<column-break/>

one could see all the way to the bottom if there were not so little light. **ON THE LAST** cloister: In the last enclosure. **SO THAT ITS LAY BROTHERS.** It stands in the translation: and having called that great valley a "cloister" <note>original: "chiostro"</note> because the sinners are locked in there just as in the cloisters of monasteries monks and **lay brothers** <note>original: "conversi," a pun on those "turned" by sin and those who serve in a monastery</note> are locked in, he calls those people the "converts" of such cloisters. **LAMENTS** Diverse: because they were varied and came from different parts. **PIERCED ME:** They stung my heart with pity: and these laments shot "arrows" at me, which had the "iron" <note>the arrowhead</note> made of tears. The iron is what makes the arrow penetrate; therefore, the tears were the iron because they moved me more to compassion. This moved me to such passion that to avoid hearing them I plugged my ears. Allegorically it shows that just as Ulysses plugged his ears to the songs of the Sirens—that is, he did not want to hear a voluptuous thing—so I did not want to be overcome by any compassion for those who deserve every heavy punishment. **WHAT PAIN WOULD BE** Such pain is understood among those sinners as is seen in August among the sick if all those from **Valdichiana**, **Maremma**, and **Sardinia** were in one ditch. Where it is to be noted that he says "in August" <note>the text mentions July to September</note> because in that month there are many and difficult diseases. Wherefore Juvenal said: *And poets reciting in the month of August* <note>original Latin: "Et augusto recitantes mense poetas"</note>. Because the corruption of the air and water in hot seasons and by the southern winds generates many diseases; and especially in thick, stagnant air. And for this reason, he names Valdichiana and Maremma and Sardinia. **Valdichiana** is between Arezzo, Cortona, Chiusi, and Montepulciano, where there is the Chiana river, called *stagnant Clanis* <note>original Latin: "Clanis stagna"</note> by the Latins. And it makes the air thick, especially when the mud that remains dry boils in the summer; from which various diseases are born. **Sardinia**, which due to excessive heat has pestilental air, especially in the places closest to the shore.

It shows that when they had passed the bridge and were on the bank beyond, he began to see better the spirits of that pit, who were punished in the depths by justice, which he rightly calls the justice of the "high Lord," God. **I DO NOT BELIEVE.** He uses an excellent simile saying that there was nothing more sad or more horrid than to see the disease in the island of **Aegina** <note>original: "Egina"</note>, by which every animal died and it remained void of inhabitants. Wherefore men were then born from ants. Such it was to see the sick spirits of that pit. **Asopus** <note>original: "Asopo," a river god</note> had two daughters, Aegina and Thebe. Jupiter fell in love with Aegina and knew her in the form of fire; and by her, he fathered **Aeacus** <note>original: "Eaco"</note>, father of Peleus, who fathered **Achilles**, the strongest of all the Greeks according to Homer; and according to this fable, the great-grandson or we might say the great-great-grandson of Jupiter. From this Aegina, the island was named Aegina, which was previously called Enopia. Aeacus reigned in Aegina, and in his time there was such a great and grave pestilence that the island remained desolate. Therefore Aeacus prayed to his father Jupiter that he either give him death or restore to him the lost people. And afterward, walking through the island, he saw an infinite number of ants climbing up and down an oak tree, and he desired his people to be like that. Jupiter fulfilled the son's desire and converted the ants into men. The fables feign this because, the inhabitants of the island being lacking, Aeacus filled it with rustic people and new cultivators of the land who were similar to ants: because they were blackened by the constant stay in the sun; they were robust and capable of much labor and exercise. They were frugal and with industry they put away and preserved the grain. All of which is seen in the ant. These people were called **Myrmidons** <note>original: "myrmidoni"</note>, because *myrmex* <note>original: "myrmix"</note> in Greek signifies "ant." These, besides his other people, Achilles, grandson of Aeacus, led into the armies of the Greeks against the Trojans.

He continues narrating and describes how the sick spirits lay in "heaps" <note>original: "abbichati," like shocks of grain</note>; that is, accumulated one on top of the other; and some went on all fours. And we have shown above that in this pit and the other, the falsification of metals and money is punished. Now we will show that the penalties which are placed by the poet are very appropriate to such a sin. These then are ten: first, they weep and lament. Which denotes their infirmity. Prete...

<header>CANTO XXIX.</header>

who could not lift their bodies,
I saw two sitting, leaning against each other,
as one pan is leaned against another to warm,
spotted from head to foot with bloody scabs.

And I never saw a currycomb <note>original: "stregghia," a metal comb used for grooming horses</note> handled
by a stableboy for whom his master waits,
nor by one who stays awake unwillingly:

As each one frequently drove the bite
of his nails upon himself for the great rage
of the itching, which has no other relief.

Thus the nails pulled down the scabs,
just as a knife scrapes the scales of a bream <note>original: "scardova," a freshwater fish</note>,
or of another fish that has even larger ones.

...that he might succeed. The itching represents the great cares and anxieties involved in hiding falsehoods, and in searching for new ways, new proofs, and new arts. The trembling signifies the fear of being discovered and caught. They bite one another, which denotes the envy that exists among them. They lie down, therefore, because their subject is the accumulation of money—a vile thing, as we have shown many times. They go on all fours like brute animals. **WHO COULD NOT LIFT THEIR BODIES**: men given to avarice cannot detach themselves from the earth. **I SAW TWO**: whom he will name below. **SITTING Leaning against each other**: because they could not stand by themselves. These men scratched themselves and moved their nails over the scabs and mange more quickly than a pressured stableboy handles a currycomb. **BY HIS MASTER**: By his master; and even more quickly than the currycomb is handled by one who, being sleepy and desiring to sleep, hurries to finish the grooming; and by this is denoted the assiduous care and constant anxiety that is always present in these alchemists. **OF THE ITCHING Which has no other relief** Except to scratch oneself in that manner. **THUS THE NAILS PULLED Down the scabs**. The crust of that leprosy: just as the knife pulls down the scales or flakes of the bream. This is a fish with many scales.

"O you who with your fingers unmail <note>original: "dismagle," a metaphor for pulling off scabs as if they were links in chainmail</note> yourself,"
my leader began to one of them,
"and who sometimes make pincers of them,

Tell me if any Latin <note>original: "latino," meaning an Italian</note> is among those
who are here inside, so may your nails last you
eternally for this labor."

"We are Latins whom you see so wasted
here, both of us," replied one weeping;
"but who are you who asked about us?"

The leader said: "I am one who descends
with this living man down from ledge to ledge,
and I intend to show Hell to him."

Then the common support was broken;
and trembling, each turned toward me,
along with others who heard it by rebound <note>indirectly, like a ball bouncing</note>.

The good master drew all close to me,
saying: "Tell them then whatever you wish."
And I began, since he willed it:

"So may your memory not fly away
from human minds in the first world,
but may it live on after many suns,

Tell me who you are and of what people;
let your foul and tedious punishment
not frighten you from revealing yourselves to me."

"I was of Arezzo, and Alberto of Siena,"
he replied, "had me put to the fire."

<column-break/>

...it rarely happens that either a counterfeiter or an alchemist is not discovered and does not pay the penalty for the sin, from which grief is born. Secondly, they were lying down to demonstrate their vileness. Usually, such men possess great genius; thus, lying down shows that they have applied that genius—which they could have used for noble things—to vile things and the accumulation of earthly goods. Thirdly, they are naked, which shows that such men are poor, as is seen every day through experience. Fourthly, they stink, to denote their abomination and that they are shunned by every man. They are lepers, which signifies their corruption without generation <note>meaning they create nothing new or living</note>. Alchemists corrupt many things to make something better out of them, but they do not succeed. Therefore, just as leprosy is a corruption from which nothing is generated, so this art corrupts metals and other things and does not produce what it desires. They are full of sores, and this signifies the infamy that follows them. They are dropsical <note>suffering from edema/swelling</note>, by which disease avarice is denoted, as we showed above. And as such a disease makes a man sluggish—wherefore Virgil describes it as sloth, saying: *He did not allow his realms to grow numb with heavy sloth* <note>original Latin: "Nec torpere gravi passus sua regna veterno" — from Virgil's Georgics</note>—and the sluggish stay quite still in one place, so the alchemist never departs from his purpose, even though...

Having seen the spirits, Virgil asked them who they were and, turning to one of the two: **O YOU Who unmail yourself**: that is, by scratching you skin yourself and remove the crust, like one who unmails a piece of armor <note>original: "paziera," a breastplate or piece of mail</note>. And sometimes you make pincers of your fingers because with them you stick to the scabs as pincers stick to a nail. And then, praying him to say if any there are Latin, he entreats him by those things he must value highly: because, deprived of every other hope, there only remains to him the ability to keep his nails with which he mitigates the itching. The spirit responds and says that he and his companion were Latins, and in turn asks Virgil who he is. And Virgil replied that he was one who leads his living companion through Hell, descending from ledge to ledge. In this place, there is no allegory that cannot easily be drawn from what has already been said. These words caused such wonder in the two spirits—who were leaning one against the other—that they broke away from that leaning, which was their common reinforcement and support; because by leaning together, one sustained the other. Here is denoted the misery of alchemists who, seeing that none of their experiments succeed, often seek help from those who perhaps know much less than they do. **And trembling out of amazement. With others who heard it by rebound.** This is a metaphor from those who play ball: who do not hit it when it is sent, but hit it after it bounces. Thus, they heard the voice that did not come directly to them. And that Virgil had Dante ask the questions denotes that the higher intellect finds the universals, and then leaves the particulars to be found by the lower reason, as we demonstrated more clearly above.

This man was Master Griffolino of Arezzo, who was a great alchemist. And one day, to please a certain Alberto of Siena, the son of the Bishop of Siena—who was a foolish man and very credulous—he said that he knew through magic how to make a man fly. And for a long time, he kept Alberto in suspense with words, pretending to teach him such an art, and in the process, he extracted money from him. Hearing of this, the Bishop condemned him as a necromancer and had him burned. Therefore, he says in his excuse that he is in Hell not as a magician, because he never practiced that art, but as an alchemist. **PUT TO THE FIRE**: that is, to burn. **BUT THAT**: for which I died; that is, the magical art here in Hell. **SPEAKING IN JEST**:

<meta>This page continues the narrative of Canto XXIX, focusing on the second half of the circle of falsifiers. It transitions from the story of Griffolino of Arezzo, who was burned for "falsely" promising to teach the Bishop of Siena's son how to fly, to a broader critique of Sienese vanity and the introduction of the alchemist Capocchio.</meta>

<header>INFERNO</header>

**“But that for which I died does not bring me here.**
**True it is that I said to him, speaking in jest,**
**‘I would know how to raise myself through the air in flight’;**
**and he, who had much desire and little sense,**
**wanted me to show him the art; and only**
**because I did not make him a Daedalus <note>In Greek myth, Daedalus was the master craftsman who built wings of wax and feathers to fly.</note>, he had me**
**burned by one who held him as a son.**
**But to the last of the ten pits,**
**for the alchemy I practiced in the world,**
**Minos <note>The judge of the underworld in Dante's Hell.</note> condemned me, who is not allowed to err.”**

That is, speaking jokingly. **AND HE** <note>Referring to Alberto of Siena.</note> **WHO HAD DESIRE**: that is, vain longing and little sense, had me burned only because I did not make him a Daedalus: that is, I did not make him fly, as the poets imagine of Daedalus, a fable told elsewhere. **BY ONE WHO HELD HIM AS A SON**: To the Bishop, who considered him his son. He almost says that, not being born of legitimate marriage, it could easily be that he was not the Bishop’s son; for a woman who joins with one who is not her husband rarely stays faithful to him, and if she gives birth, she most often gives the child to the wealthiest man so that the son might have a better father. But Minos condemned me to the last pit as an alchemist and falsifier of metals. **WHO IS NOT ALLOWED**: It is not permitted for him to err, because conscience never lies to a man. And we established above that Minos represents conscience. 

And although the poet rightfully condemns alchemy—which is an operation of art upon metals in imitation of nature—nevertheless it should be noted that not every kind of alchemy is entirely illicit. For there are two species: one true and the other "sophistic" <note>In this context, "sophistic" means fraudulent or counterfeit.</note>. The true is licit, the sophistic is illicit. And it is reasonable that the true may be used, because it brings metal to perfection. So that this may be better understood, know—according to Aristotle in *On Minerals* <note>original: "de mineralibus"</note>—that all metals are the same thing in terms of their matter and substantial form. For all are generated from mercury <note>original: "argento uiuo," literally "living silver."</note> and sulfur, and are a composite of those. But they are different in their accidental form. This happens because nature intends from the beginning to produce metal to perfection; and if it produces it, it generates gold. If it fails in this perfection, it is outside nature’s intention, and then, according to how much it fails, less precious metals are formed. Such imperfection proceeds from the matter not being fit to receive the operation of nature. For if the matter is well-disposed—that is, the mercury is purified and the sulfur is red and clean—then it can receive the operation of nature to perfection and produce the perfect metal, which is gold. But when the mercury is putrid and the sulfur is white or corrupt red, it makes a baser metal according to the degree of corruption. Therefore, true alchemy, with its art and calcination and distillation and juices of herbs with fire, can purify the mercury and sulfur, and do by art what nature does inside the earth. Thus, it is clear that he who performs this art well can bring metal to its perfection. And such art is licit. But sophistic alchemy induces falsehood and makes that which is not silver or gold appear to be so. This is revealed by the test of fire. For this reason it is forbidden, because it deceives man to his gravest harm, taking for gold that which is not.

---

**And I said to the Poet: “Now, was there ever**
**a people as vain as the Sienese?**
**Certainly not even the French by a long shot.”**
**Whereupon the other leper who heard me**
**replied to my words: “Except for Stricca,**
**who knew how to make moderate expenditures;**
**And Niccolò, who first discovered the rich custom**
**of the clove <note>Cloves were an incredibly expensive luxury spice in the 13th century.</note>**
**in the garden where such seed takes root;**
**And except for the brigade in which Caccia d’Asciano**
**squandered the vineyard and the great thicket,**
**and the Dazed One <note>original: "labbagliato," likely referring to Abbagliato, a member of the Spendthrift Brigade.</note> offered his wisdom.”**

Finding the occasion, the poet vituperates the vanity and pride of the Sienese, saying: **Now, was there ever a people more vain?**—meaning boastful—than the Sienese, though the French are very boastful. And Capocchio, who was near Griffolino, confirming Dante's sentiment, names some Sienese who he says should be exempted from such vanity; but he speaks with irony, as if to say these are the most boastful of all. **EXCEPT FOR STRICCA who knew how to make moderate expenditures**: This he also says through irony, wishing to show that out of pride and vanity he was so prodigal that he consumed all his substance. Here it should be noted that in Siena many rich young men formed a company for dinners and banquets, and out of pride they made many luxurious and superfluous expenditures both in feasting and in riding and in dressing their servants in livery; and there was one who even shod his horses with silver. This was called the "Spendthrift Brigade" <note>original: "brigata ghodereccia."</note>. They put two hundred thousand florins into a common fund among them, and in twenty months they consumed all their wealth. Among these, Stricca was more prodigal than the others. **AND NICCOLÒ**: This man was of the Salimbeni of Siena, who continually studied with every wit to find new and sumptuous foods. Hence many say that he invented *blancmange* and Ubaldine fritters. And they had a cook who wrote a book of the foods they invented. And this Niccolò found the way to put cloves and other spices into pheasants and similar roasts. This custom was called the "rich custom." Some say they even roasted the meat over coals made of burning cloves. **IN THE GARDEN WHERE SUCH SEED TAKES ROOT**: By a metaphor he calls Siena a garden, because just as in a garden the seeds thrown there quickly sprout and multiply, so in that city every such custom quickly multiplies. **CACCIA OF SIENA** had beautiful and large vineyards at Asciano, a castle in Sienese territory, and he consumed them in gluttony. **AND THE GREAT THICKET** <note>original: "la gran fronda."</note>: Many woods, or he means his purse. **OFFERED HIS WISDOM**: He made it manifest and spoke ironically, as if to say he demonstrated his vanity.

---

**“But so that you know who thus seconds you**
**against the Sienese, sharpen your eye toward me,**
**so that my face may answer you well;**
**and you will see that I am the shade of Capocchio,**
**who falsified metals with alchemy;**
**and you must remember, if I eye you rightly,**
**how I was a good ape of nature.”**

Capocchio had pointed out many other Sienese, and now he wishes to speak of himself. This man was Sienese, and they say that together with Dante he studied natural philosophy and became very learned. Through this, he labored much wanting to find true alchemy; and not being able to find it, he finally gave himself to the "sophistic" kind and subtly falsified metals. Some say that on Good Friday, while abstracted in meditation, he drew the entire progress of Christ’s passion upon his fingernails; and Dante, arriving, wiped it away with his tongue. This was annoying to Dante, because it seemed to him a more marvelous work than that of the man who wrote the *Iliad* of Homer so subtly that he fit it into a walnut shell. He says, therefore, so that you know I am the one who "seconds" you—that is, follows you in speaking against the Sienese: **SHARPEN YOUR EYES**, look at me closely, as if to say "you will recognize me, having known me in life." **WHO FALSIFIED metals with alchemy**: I did not use natural alchemy, which does not falsify metals but works by correcting and purifying the matter so that a less precious metal becomes gold; rather, I used the sophistic kind. This does not make gold, but counterfeits and falsifies it in such a form that what is not, appears to be; and for this, he was a **GOOD APE OF NATURE**: i.e., he knew well how to counterfeit natural things, just as alchemy mimics the operations of nature through human effort.

<summary>Dante encounters the shade of Capocchio, who mocks the legendary extravagance of the Sienese "Spendthrift Brigade" and explains his damnation for practicing fraudulent alchemy as an "ape of nature."</summary>
<keywords>Capocchio, Alchemy, Siena, Spendthrift Brigade, Aristotle, Falsifiers, Griffolino d'Arezzo, Vanity, Natural Philosophy</keywords>

<header>INFERNO:</header>

but that for which I died does not bring me here.
It is true that I said to him, speaking in jest,
"I would know how to lift myself through the air in flight."
And he, who had curiosity and little sense,
wanted me to show him the art; and only
because I did not make a Daedalus, he made
him who held him as a son burn me.
But in the last bolgia of the ten,
Minos condemns me for the alchemy I practiced in the world,
to whom it is not permitted to err.

metals in imitation of nature: Nevertheless, it is to be noted that not all alchemy
is of the same kind, one true and the other sophisticated: The true is licit: the sophisticated is illicit: And it is
because it produces metal in perfection. So that this may be better understood,
it is to be known that all metals, by matter and by substantial form, are one and the same
[composed of] mercury and sulfur: and are a composite of those. But they are different in form
[because] nature intends from the beginning to produce metal to perfection: and if it produces [something]
generated outside of its intention: and then, according to what lacks, more or less precious
is the matter that is not [perfect].

# CANTO:
## CANTO XXX OF THE FIRST CANTICLE BY DANTE.

->At the time when Juno was enraged:<-
->On account of Semele against the Theban blood,<-
->as she demonstrated on one and then another occasion,<-
->Athamas became so insane<-
->that seeing his wife with two sons<-
->walking burdened on either hand,<-
->He cried: "Let us spread the nets so that I may catch<-
->the lioness and the lion-cubs at the pass,"<-
->and then he extended his pitiless claws,<-
->Taking the one who was named Learchus,<-
->and whirled him and dashed him against a rock;<-
->and she drowned herself with the other burden.<-
->And when Fortune cast down<-
->the highness of the Trojans who dared everything,<-
->until the king was destroyed together with his kingdom,<-
->Hecuba, sad, wretched, and captive,<-
->after she saw Polyxena dead,<-
->and [found] her Polydorus on the shore<-
->Of the sea, the sorrowful woman recognized him;<-
->out of her senses, she barked like a dog,<-
->so much did grief twist her mind.<-

<column-break/>

The thirtieth canto joins with the twenty-ninth: because just as in that one the poet treated falsifiers, so he treats them here: but because the species of falsity changes, he also changes the punishments. In the past ones, we saw leprosy and lethargy. The present ones are divided into three species. The first are those who falsified their own person <note>These are impersonators who pretend to be someone else to commit fraud.</note>: and these go about rabidly biting one another. The second are those who falsified money. The third have falsified speech <note>These are liars or perjurers, such as Sinon of Troy.</note>. This is demonstrated in two very ancient spirits. At the beginning, therefore, wishing to demonstrate the rage of the spirits by which they bite and strike one another, he says by way of comparison that neither was Athamas so rabid toward his son whom he struck against the rock, nor was Hecuba when, out of grief against her enemies, she became a dog. **AT THE TIME THAT JUNO.** Cadmus, of whom we have spoken sufficiently above, had four daughters by his wife Harmonia: Semele, Agave, Autonoe, and Ino. Semele conceived Bacchus by Jove. This was so bothersome to Juno that she became an enemy to the entire Theban generation, and many times took revenge against many of them. For she incited these four sisters to such fury that, while they were making a sacrifice to Bacchus in the woods, seeing Pentheus, son of Agave, it seemed to them he was a wild boar and they killed him. Afterward, Ino already having two sons by her husband Athamas, she drove Athamas to such fury that when Ino came with the children, it seemed to him she was a lioness with two cubs. Therefore he took the one named Learchus and dashed him against a rock. Whereupon Ino, terrified, ran to the sea, carrying the other with her whose name was Melicertes, and threw herself into the sea with him. And they were made sea gods; the Greeks called her Leucothea and the Latins Matuta, and him Palaemon, and the Latins Portunus. Athamas therefore did not show as much fury against his children as these spirits showed among themselves. **AND WHEN FORTUNE CAST DOWN the state of the Trojans.** We have already shown many times what region Troy is, and that the city in it is Ilium. Nor have we passed over the history of the unhappy Priam. It remains, therefore, that to that we add the misery of Hecuba, who 

<margin>The catchword "nella" indicates the start of the next page.</margin>

---

in the Greek siege saw a great part of her children killed. She saw her old husband cruelly dead. She saw the city destroyed by iron and fire. And after so many calamities, reduced to servitude along with Polyxena, she saw her dearest daughter die at the tomb of the most cruel Achilles. And then, being dragged to Thrace, the ghost of her son appeared to her; whom she thought still lived and was safe with a good part of his father's treasures with Polymestor. This caused her long-lasting sadness and heaviest mourning to turn into extreme rage, and incited by such fury, with every kind of vileness she cursed all the Greeks and bit them with the harshest words. Therefore the poets feigned that she was converted into a rabid dog. **SHE RECOGNIZED:** because at first she did not know the wicked event, which happened in this way. Priam had already sensed the preparation of the Greeks against him, and as a man of provident mind, he wished that for anything that might happen, someone of his lineage would remain, and not without treasures. Therefore he sent his son Polydorus to Polymestor, King of Thrace, with great treasure, trusting that this king, being always a friend, would preserve the son and the money. "But cursed is the man who trusts in man" <note>original: "Sed maledictus homo qui confidit in homine"</note>. For as Plautus writes, "man is a wolf to man and not a man" <note>original: "lupus est homo homini & nō homo"</note>. And every feigned friendship, because it is not true, lasts as long as it is useful. Therefore Polymestor, seeing Priam and his kingdom fallen, remembered neither his given faith nor his friendship; but turned to the Greeks where fortune had already turned, and killed Polydorus, and unjustly kept the treasures. When therefore Hecuba, led into servitude by the Greeks, arrived at the shores of Thrace, the ghost of Polydorus (as Euripides writes) came out from the underworld and revealed his death and the wickedness of Polymestor. From which followed what we said a little before. **THE HIGHNESS.** He almost imitates Virgil in his second book: "After the affairs of Asia and Priam's kingdom were overturned" <note>original: "Postquam res asie priamique enertere regnum"</note>. **WHO DARED EVERYTHING.** This was manifested through Paris, who, trusting in the greatness of his kingdom, dared to seize Helen, the wife of so great a king, in the middle of Greece, [a land] most powerful in men-at-arms and wisdom. Until the king was destroyed: that is, deprived of life together with the kingdom: because the kingdom also perished according to Homer and many Greek writers, because no one of the lineage of Priam remained who was not either dead or led away prisoner. Although Dio Chrysostom proves both by Egyptian histories and by many plausible conjectures that Homer lied about this destruction, and that Achilles did not kill Hector, but Hector killed Achilles; and the Greeks did not take Troy, but were driven away by the Trojans. This is made plausible by the little reputation with which, as Homer himself demonstrates, they departed from Troy, given that many of the leaders remained dead, few returned to Greece, and those were killed by their own, like Agamemnon by Clytemnestra his wife and Pyrrhus by Orestes; and many went into voluntary exile, like Diomedes and Ulysses. **HECUBA TRISTA** <gloss>melancholy</gloss> **MISERA** <gloss>unhappy</gloss>, because from a queen she had become a slave. **CAPTIVA** <gloss>prisoner</gloss>. **POLYXENA DEAD.** Achilles, being in love with her, promised great things if Hecuba would give her to him for a wife; and Paris, under the pretense of giving her to him, called him to a meeting in the temple of Apollo Thymbraeus near the walls of Troy. Achilles went, and while he was kneeling adoring Apollo, he was treacherously shot in the soles of his feet, in which alone he could be wounded, and [Paris] killed him. For which reason afterward Pyrrhus, son of Achilles, in revenge for his father, killed Polyxena at his tomb. The text orders it: After Hecuba saw Polyxena dead, and after that same sorrowful Hecuba recognized her son Polydorus on the shore of the sea on the beach where she found him buried, she was out of her senses, that is, she had lost her mind. **BARKED:** *Latro* in Latin means to bark; and this happened to her because great pain made her mind **TWISTED**, that is, her soul infuriated; because every time any passion disturbs the soul so that it loses reason—which is straight and directs us to right actions—we can say that our mind is twisted.

<summary>This page introduces the transition to the final group of falsifiers in the eighth circle, using the mythological rages of Athamas and Hecuba to illustrate the insanity of those who falsified their identities. Landino provides an extensive classical commentary on the fall of Troy and the tragic fate of Priam's family.</summary>
<keywords>Canto XXX, Inferno, falsifiers, impersonators, Athamas, Hecuba, Troy, Polydorus, Polyxena, Juno, Landino commentary, classical mythology</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the tenth bolgia of the eighth circle. While the previous page discussed the falsifiers of metals (alchemists), this page moves to those who falsified their own persons (impersonators) and those who falsified money.
