# CANTO XXXIII.
<sig>q iiii</sig>

I demonstrated above the fury of the Theban Athamas and of the Trojan Hecuba: Now, bringing the comparison to the point, he concludes that neither in Theban nor Trojan fury was there ever seen such cruelty as the fury he saw in two spirits. Although these are falsifiers, they did not falsify metals, but rather falsified themselves in others, or others in themselves; for this reason, he makes them suffer different punishments. He introduces them as furious, naked, and pale, running and biting. They are furious because falsifying metals is more a sickness of the mind, but doing what we have said <note>referring to impersonation</note> is extreme madness. They are naked as a punishment of "lex talionis" <note>the law of retaliation, where the punishment fits the crime</note> because through their deception they stripped others of their property or their honor. Allegorically, it is because in the end these deceptions are revealed, and they remain naked.

**But neither Theban nor Trojan furies**
**were ever seen in anyone so cruel,**
**not in goading beasts, much less human limbs,**
**As I saw two shadows, pale and naked,**
**who ran biting in the same manner**
**as a pig when it is let out of the sty.**
**One reached Capocchio, and at the joint**
**of his neck fixed its teeth, so that pulling him,**
**it made him scrape his belly on the hard floor.**

It made him strike the hard floor of the trench. It is as if he says he stretched him out on the ground: because he who casts others down with infamy, others cast him down. Nor can anyone who gives such bites to others stand for long without falling to the bottom and into a low state.

**And the Aretine who remained trembling**
**said to me: "That goblin is Gianni Schicchi,**
**and he goes rabid, mangling others so."**
**"Oh," I said to him, "so may the other not fix**
**its teeth in you, let it not be a burden**
**to tell us who it is before it breaks away from here."**
**And he to me: "That is the ancient soul**
**of wicked Myrrha, who became**
**a friend to her father beyond rightful love.**
**She came to sin with her father in this way,**
**falsifying herself in another's form,**
**just as the other who goes there endured,**
**To gain the lady of the herd,**
**to falsify himself as Buoso Donati,**
**making a will and giving the will its form."**

...nor how much the love of the free <note>likely a reference to her father, Cinyras</note> gave her to hang herself. The nurse noticed this resolve and prevented her death. After many pleas, having understood what cause induced her to kill herself, she sought to remove such an impious love from her heart. But being unable to persuade her, from a good counselor she became a most wicked servant. She went to Cinyras and said she had the opportunity to bring a most beautiful girl to his bed. Cinyras consented and for many nights she slept with her daughter, believing he was sleeping with someone else. Finally, desiring to know the girl, contrary to the given promise, he brought a light into the room and recognized his daughter, and wanted to kill her. But the wicked Myrrha, helped by the shadows of the night, fled and, wandering through many lands, arrived in Arabia. There she was transformed into the tree named after her, Myrrh. When the ninth month came, she gave birth to Adonis, son and grandson of his father, and brother and son of his mother.

**And after the two rabid ones had passed**
**upon whom I had kept my eye fixed,**
**I turned to look at the others, ill-born.**
**I saw one shaped like a lute,**
**provided that he had had his groin**
**cut off from the side where a man is forked.**
**The heavy dropsy, which so unpairs**
**the limbs with the humor that it ill converts,**
**so that the face does not match the belly,**
**made him hold his lips open.**

<column-break/>

They are pale because such people put themselves in great danger, which cannot happen without constant fear. They bite while running. By the running is denoted their restlessness and their various cares, which distract the soul in different directions. Whence Virgil:
> *And now he divides his swift mind hither and thither,*
> *and hurries it into various parts and turns it through everything.*
<note>original Latin: "Atque animū celerem nunc huc nunc diuidit illuc / In partesque rapit uarias per que omnia uersat"</note>
They bite because they gnaw at the goods of others by changing or spending false metals for true money and pure merchandise. **LIKE A PIG When it is let out of the sty.** The nature of the pig is very cruel, and when irritated, it pardons no one. **ONE Reached Capocchio.** Capocchio in life was a mocker and a censurer beyond measure. These people commonly find someone who bites them. For this reason, the poet feigns that he was bitten and taken by the neck, because those who wrongly rebuke others do not know how to respond when they are themselves rebuked. Therefore they are taken by the neck because he who squeezes the neck and the throat makes one silent. **ON THE HARD FLOOR.** He stretched him on the ground: because he who casts others down with infamy, others cast him down. Nor can anyone who gives such bites to others stand for long without falling to the bottom and into a low state.

Having burned Capocchio <note>referring to Capocchio's death by fire in history</note>, Griffolino the Aretine, who was in his company, trembled with fear that the same would be done to him. And he told Dante that the one who had bitten Capocchio was Gianni Schicchi. Then, asked by Dante, who was eager to know who the one running with Gianni was, he said it was Myrrha. Gianni Schicchi de' Cavalcanti was a very <term>eutrapelic</term> man <note>from the Greek 'eutrapelos,' meaning witty, versatile, or quick-witted</note> and apt at counterfeiting whatever he wished. He was a great friend of Simone Donati. Thus, when Messer Buoso Donati died—a very rich man—without making a will, and having closer relatives than Simone who would succeed him <term>ab intestato</term> <note>Latin legal term meaning 'without a will'</note>, Simone, in order to become the heir, hid Messer Buoso's body and had Gianni enter the bed. Counterfeiting Messer Buoso, he made a will and left Simone as the heir. Simone gave him a mare of great value, which was in the herd and was called "the lady of the herd," as he had promised him. Myrrha was the daughter of Cinyras, king of Paphos, a very lustful island. For this reason, she was consecrated to Venus; whence Horace:
> *O Venus, queen of Cnidos and of Paphos, spurn your beloved Cyprus;*
> *and transfer yourself into the beautiful temple of Cinyras, who calls to you with much incense.*
<note>original Latin: "Uenus regina gnidi paphique ſperne dilecta cypron: / Et uocatem thure te multa Cynarę decorem trãffer in ędé." Translator's note: The name "Cynarę" in the text is likely a corruption of "Glycerae" in the original Horace ode.</note>
Myrrha in her tender age loved her father so ardently that, long-combatted now by the love that inflamed her, now by the shame that withdrew her from such wickedness, she miserably wavered like a ship tossed by contrary winds. Finally, to flee the many pains that love gave her, she decided to hang herself.

Turning his eyes from the one over whom the two rabid ones had passed, the poet turned elsewhere and saw one who, because he was <term>hydropic</term> <note>suffering from dropsy or edema, an accumulation of fluid in the body</note> or you might say <term>ritrupico</term>, his belly was so swollen that if his legs (where a man is forked) were cut off from the groin down, leaving the belly with the head, he would have looked like a lute. This is because this disease, which arises when the humor which should be converted into true nourishment is instead converted into water and wind, swells the body in a way that "unpairs"—that is, makes unequal—the limbs, so that they have no proportion. Like this man, whose belly exceeded the proportion of his head and neck, so that he looked like a lute, which has a large belly and a thin neck and head. This disease brought him a very great thirst, and because of it, he kept his lips open as a <term>hectic</term> <note>one suffering from a wasting fever or consumption</note> person does.

<summary>This page describes the punishment of the impersonators (Gianni Schicchi and Myrrha), who run rabidly biting others, and introduces Master Adam, whose punishment for counterfeiting money is a bloating dropsy and eternal thirst.</summary>
<keywords>Gianni Schicchi, Myrrha, Buoso Donati, Master Adam, dropsy, impersonation, Canto XXX, Capocchio, Cinyras</keywords>

--- Page 266 ---
<meta>This page continues the exploration of the tenth bolgia (ditch) of the eighth circle of Hell. Having previously discussed the alchemists (falsifiers of metals), the text now focuses on Maestro Adamo, a counterfeiter of currency, and explores the physical torment of dropsy as a metaphor for his greed.</meta>

->### INFERNO:<-

...as the hectic feverish man does, who because of thirst
turns one lip toward the chin and the other upward.
"O you who are without any punishment,
and I know not why, in this wretched world,"
he said to us, "look and pay attention
to the misery of Master Adam;
when alive, I had enough of what I wanted,
and now, alas, I crave a drop of water.
The little streams that from the green hills
of Casentino descend down into the Arno,
making their channels cool and moist,
are always before me, and not in vain,
for their image dries me out far more
than the malady that withers my face.
The rigid justice that scourges me
takes occasion from the place where I sinned
to send my sighs even faster into flight.
There is Romena, where I falsified
the alloy sealed with the Baptist,
for which I left my body burned above.
But if I could see here the wretched soul
of Guido, or Alexander, or their brother,
I would not trade the sight for Fonte Branda."

"One is already inside, if the enraged
shades who circle around speak the truth;
but what does it avail me, with my limbs bound?
If I were still so light that
in a hundred years I could move one inch,
I would have already set out on the path,
seeking him among this hideous folk,
even though the circuit is eleven miles,
and not less than half a mile across.
Because of them, I am among such a family,
who induced me to strike the florins
that had three carats of dross."
And I said to him: "Who are the two wretches
who smoke like wet hands in winter,
lying close to your right boundaries?"
"I found them here, and they haven't turned since..."

<column-break/>

...the one who has the hectic fever <note>A "hectic fever" (original: *febbre ethica*) was a term used for a persistent, wasting fever, often associated with consumption or tuberculosis.</note>: and because of thirst turns one lip up and the other down. Dropsy <note>original: *Hydropeſis*</note> is named from *hydor*, which in Greek signifies water: because in this disease water multiplies between the skin and the flesh.

The author has described the form and the manner of Adam. Now he sets down his words, as he said: "O you, Virgil and Dante, who are without punishment in this wretched, miserable, and unhappy world" (for "wretchedness" <note>original: *grameza*</note> in the Lombard dialect signifies a miserable and heavy longing for that which one cannot have), "look at me and pay attention to my misery." Adam was from Brescia and was a moneyer <note>A person licensed to strike coins.</note>; and in that art, he was an excellent master. Out of great avarice and greed for money, he made an agreement with the Counts of Romena, and there he secretly falsified the Florentine florin, which on one side has the image of John the Baptist, protector of our republic, and on the other, the lily. **I HAD ENOUGH WHEN ALIVE.** To his greater pain, he who finds himself in calamity and penury of things was once rich; because one who is not used to poverty endures it with greater difficulty. **AND NOW**, alas, I crave: I greatly desire a drop of water. He could not demonstrate greater misery than having a vast desire for that which cannot be had; and the pain increases when one sees oneself deprived of a thing of which no one is so poor that they do not have plenty, such as water, and he cannot have even a single drop. **THE LITTLE STREAMS.** The pain increases greatly when, in our desire, the image of the thing desired is always represented before our eyes. Thus, the rigid and inflexible divine justice that scourges and goads him draws the cause of his punishment from the place where he committed the sin. Since he sinned in Casentino, the image of the little streams—that is, the brooks and rivulets which descend from the mountain ridges into the Casentino—is always turning in his mind; and that image gives me much more thirst than the sickness I have. **THERE IS ROMENA.** Where I falsified: because, as we said above, he made an agreement with those Counts. **THE ALLOY** of the Baptist: The Florentine florin, which has the Baptist for its stamp and imprint. **FOR WHICH I.** For which thing I left my body burned. For he was burned opposite Romena on the road that comes from the village to the hill, where even today a pile of stones is seen; and the locals who are there now affirm that their ancestors had heard from their own ancestors that it was so. **BUT IF I SAW** the wretched soul. He desires that these Counts of Romena, who persuaded him to commit such falsity, be in the same punishment, not out of love for justice, but out of hatred and envy. For the damned soul is never purged of its vices, and all the perturbations of the soul remain with it; therefore, it would wish to drag every other soul into its torment, and is always malicious. But the soul that is absolved of guilt, though it may not be free from punishment (as we see those in Purgatory to be), does not desire nor would it wish that any other suffer torture. Rather, it rejoices in the good of others. This is proper to our nature if it is not corrupted by a habit already formed in vice, as are the spirits punished in Hell. **AND OF THEIR BROTHER.** That is, Aghinolfo, the third brother of Guido and Alexander. **FOR FONTE BRANDA** I would not trade the sight. Although I have inextinguishable thirst and am entirely deprived of all water, nevertheless, if it were granted to me which I would rather have of the two—to see these Counts in these pains, or to have Fonte Branda—I would rather see their punishment than have water as clear as that in Fonte Branda. This fountain is in Siena, very abundant and limpid.

He demonstrates how much heavier the vengeance is that one sees than that which one hears of. One of those Counts was already there. This was a consolation to him; but two things diminished it: first, that he did not see him but only heard of him; second, that he heard it from the enraged spirits, in whom full faith was not to be placed. Even though the circuit is eleven miles, as we demonstrated in the layout of Hell. **WHICH HAD THREE** carats of dross <note>original: *mondigla*</note>. The purity and fineness of gold is divided into 24 carats; and that which is fine in perfection is 24 carats. Then, when something else is mixed in, it is of so much less. Therefore, they struck gold which should have been 24 carats, and it was 21. **AS WET HANDS** in winter: Every breath and vapor that comes out of every living animal carries with it some vital heat. But because in summer it finds the air warm, it immediately mixes and dissipates due to the similarity and is not seen; but in cold weather, because it shrinks together while fleeing its opposite, it happens that it maintains itself and condenses more, and therefore it is seen. **I FOUND THEM HERE:** because many hundreds of years they had been dead before him. **THE FALSE WOMAN** who accused Joseph. From Jacob, the son of Isaac, twelve sons were born. From whom later descended the twelve tribes of the Jewish people. But of all of them, Joseph was very dear to Jacob, both because he was of great intellect and because he was born in his old age. But from the great love the father bore him, there followed envy among the brothers...

### CANTO XXX.

*he replied, "when I rained down into this ditch,*
*and I do not believe they have moved in eternity:*
*the one is the false woman who accused Joseph,*
*the other is the false Sinon, the Greek from Troy;*
*because of acute fever, they cast off such a great stench."*

---

that Potiphar’s wife was so vehemently inflamed by the beauty of the youth <note>Joseph, son of Jacob, from the Book of Genesis</note>: that first through flattery, and then by force, she wished to draw him to her perverse will. But Joseph fled, leaving his cloak behind as she held him—certainly an excellent thing. He merited no less praise than Hippolytus, and ran into the same danger, because her love turned into cruel hatred. For as <term>Seneca</term> <note>Lucius Annaeus Seneca, Roman Stoic philosopher</note> says: *A woman either loves or hates* <note>original: "Aut amat femina aut odit"</note>. Certainly, without any middle ground, she goes from one extreme to another. And <term>Virgil</term> <note>Publius Vergilius Maro, the Roman poet who serves as Dante's guide</note> wisely wrote: *A woman is always a fickle and changeable thing* <note>original: "Variu & mutabile femp femina"</note>. Thus, the wicked woman accused the innocent man: and where she had been the one to solicit the youth, she claimed he had made demands of her. For this, Joseph was imprisoned. But after two years, Pharaoh dreamed that he saw seven fat cows being devoured by seven lean ones, and seven full ears of grain likewise consumed by seven empty ones. None of his wise men knew how to interpret this dream. Joseph interpreted it, showing that this signified that the first seven years would be fertile, but the following seven would be very sterile. This persuaded the King that a divine spirit was within Joseph; he freed him and made him prefect of the entire kingdom. It would be a long story to narrate with what diligence and prudence he administered everything. He reserved the grain from the fertile years to withstand the sterility. He provided for his father and brothers, bringing them to Egypt where he petitioned the king to settle them in an excellent region. But it suffices here to understand that the wicked wife of the Eunuch <note>Potiphar is described as a eunuch or officer of Pharaoh</note> was punished for the false accusation she made.

THE OTHER IS Sinon. The Greeks had been at the head of Troy for ten years; despairing of their strength, they decided to attempt cunning and deceit. They built a very large horse of wood, but empty, and inside they shut many of the leaders of the army. Then Sinon came to the Trojans as a deserter and feigned having received many injuries from the Greeks, and finally claimed they wanted to sacrifice him to the gods, and for this reason, he had fled. Because of this, he was accepted as a friend by Priam <note>The King of Troy</note> and asked what hope the Greeks lived by. Then the fraudulent and most cunning Sinon feigned that they had built that horse and consecrated it to Minerva <note>Athena</note>, making it so high so that the Trojans could not bring it whole into Troy. For they wanted it so that if the Trojans destroyed it, Troy would be taken; but if it were led inside the city whole, then the Greeks would be defeated by the Trojans. These words were the reason the Trojans cut a gate and brought the horse inside. Consequently, the following night, the armed men came out of the horse, set fire to the land, and opened the gates to the army. In this way, Sinon deceived the Trojans, and thus Troy was taken. He was the son of Autolycus, the son of Mercury, who was a very great thief; and from him was born the first Sinon, likewise a very great thief. He sired Sisyphus and Autolyca, who was the mother of Ulysses; and from Sisyphus was born the Sinon mentioned by the poet here. And as you see, he was the cousin of Ulysses.

It is a likely thing that he who has made a habit of sin is always accompanied by it, and never leaves it, neither here nor there. Because as it is written in the Apocalypse: *For their works follow them* <note>original: "Opera enim illorum sequuntur illos"</note>. Therefore, "one of them," meaning Sinon. WHO TOOK OFFENSE: to whom it was annoying. AT BEING NAMED: nominated. SO OBSCURELY: with such infamy. Since he named him for the betrayal he committed; because good fame generates splendor, and infamy generates obscurity. STRUCK HIM IN THE <term>EPA CROIA</term> <note>Dante's term for the hardened, distended belly caused by dropsy</note>: the belly: CROIA: hardened. He imagines these two enemies at odds with each other to demonstrate that among the vicious there is always envy, just as among the virtuous there is always concord. WHEN YOU WERE GOING TO THE FIRE: where you were burned. The nature of the vicious is always to reproach one another for their vices. TRUE WITNESS: When asked by Priam for the truth, you spoke falsely. I AM HERE FOR ONE FAULT: for a single fraud that I committed at Troy. YOU ARE HERE FOR MORE THAN ANY OTHER DEMON: because you have falsified metals infinite times. REMEMBER THE PERJURY: Here he increases the vice, showing that it is known throughout the whole world. And the other reproaches him for the disease <note>Dropsy, which involves extreme thirst and swelling</note> which gives him thirst and swells his body so much that it forms a hedge before his eyes so that he cannot see further. <term>RASIEPA</term>: It interposes itself in front. THEN THE MINTER: Adam said, your mouth gapes. That is, it opens wide to speak ill. And "if I have thirst, the humor RE-STUFFS ME" <note>original: "MI RINSARCIA"</note>: As if to say, if I have thirst, the fluid of this dropsy fills me up. YOU HAVE THE BURNING AND THE HEAD THAT ACHES: because these two things are produced by the <term>hectic fever</term> <note>A persistent, wasting fever associated here with Sinon</note>. AND TO LICK THE MIRROR OF NARCISSUS: And if you were to drink from a fountain, like the one in which Narcissus saw his reflection, as is shown more extensively elsewhere.

# INFERNO.

I was completely fixed on listening to them
when the master said to me: “Just keep looking,
for it is nearly the case that I quarrel with you.”
When I heard him speak to me with anger,
I turned toward him with such shame
that it still circles through my memory.
And like one who dreams of his own harm,
who dreaming desires to dream,
so that he longs for what is as if it were not,
Such I became, unable to speak,
for I desired to excuse myself, and I did excuse
myself nonetheless, and did not believe I was doing so.
“A greater fault is washed away by less shame,”
said the master, “than yours has been;
therefore, unburden yourself of all sadness.
And reckon that I am always at your side
if it happens again that fortune catches you
where there are people in a similar dispute;
For wanting to hear such a thing is a base desire.”

<column-break/>

The author had given himself over to listening to these people. Wherefore Virgil reproves him, saying: "Keep on looking," for it often seems that we grant what we deny; as when one says, "go ahead and do evil and you will be loved" <note>This is an example of ironic speech, where Virgil’s "Go ahead, keep looking" is actually a sharp rebuke</note>. FOR IT IS LITTLE / that little is missing / that I do not quarrel with you: <note>original: "madisso"</note> I do not stir myself to wrath. *Aissare* and *aizare* mean to irritate. Then Dante was so ashamed that even now such shame revolves through his memory: that is, he still remembers it. In this, as in many things, it signifies the difference between the <term>appetite</term> <note>The base desires or sensory impulses</note> and the <term>inferior reason</term> <note>The part of the mind dealing with immediate, worldly matters</note>, which allows itself to be overcome by the appetite, and the <term>superior reason</term> <note>The higher intellect focused on divine or universal truths</note>. The <term>intellect</term>, therefore, which always seeks universal truths, does not want to occupy its time with particulars. Furthermore, the rational part does not want sensuality to occupy the time in such base things that should be spent on excellent matters. A GREATER FAULT IS WASHED by less shame. Although the appetite and the inferior reason are divided from the intellect and err, nonetheless, when the intellect turns back upon them and reveals their sin and error—which they, blinded by their disturbance, did not see—they perceive that they have erred and feel shame, and every error is easily washed away. For whoever is ashamed of an act repents of it, and in repenting, leaves it behind and returns to the obedience of the intellect. Therefore, such shame is enough for the intellect; because when it sees the appetite being obedient to it, it always stays by its side, admonishing and ruling it. And the appetite, looking toward the intellect, takes care not to fall into similar error again when it happens to find itself by chance where there are similar people—that is, when it happens to fall into such a thought—because when the appetite desires to think on such things, it is a very base desire.

<summary>Virgil reprimands Dante for his voyeuristic interest in the base argument between the falsifiers. Dante's intense shame leads to Virgil's forgiveness, which the commentary explains as the triumph of higher reason over base sensory appetites.</summary>
<keywords>Virgil, Dante Alighieri, shame, intellect, appetite, reason, repentance, Canto XXX, Inferno, moral philosophy</keywords>

# INFERNO. CANTO XXXI. OF THE FIRST CANTICLE BY DANTE

Thus I hear that the spear of Achilles

first of a sad and then of a good gift. <note>Dante compares Virgil's rebuke and subsequent comfort to the legendary spear of Achilles (inherited from his father Peleus), which could both wound and heal.</note>

<column-break/>

<margin>h</margin> The poet has treated the preceding circle, divided into ten ditches <note>original: "bolge." The 10 circular trenches of the 8th circle of Hell.</note>: because in those are punished ten types of fraud which break only the bond of nature. He had therefore already searched the tenth ditch of the eighth circle and arrived at the end of it. Now he describes the descent into the ninth circle, where the bond of nature and of faith is broken. But first he narrates what he found on the bank through which he descended. And because he showed above how much shame confused him by the rebuke of Virgil, he now shows through an excellent comparison that that same tongue of Virgil which had bitten him with the rebuke later medicated such a bite; and then how much comfort he received from him through the words which he added after the rebuke. Here it is to be noted that the anger of a wise man is very useful to one who errs; as Seneca says: "The anger of an upright man is most welcome." <note>original: "Gratissima est probi hominis iracundia."</note> Now, therefore, such a tongue was similar to the spear of Achilles. Telephus, king of Mysia and an ally of the Trojans, wishing to drive the Greeks from his kingdom, was wounded by Achilles. And finding no other remedy to heal the wound, he received word from the oracle that it would heal if Achilles, with the same spear, were to strike him again in the same place; and so it happened. The poets feign this because Achilles had learned from Chiron that part of medicine which they call <term>surgery</term> <note>original: "cherusica," from the Greek for "hand-work."</note>. And afterward he found by himself that it was an excellent remedy for healing wounds if they were treated with the rust from the point of the spear, whether it was of iron or copper. And certainly Pliny reports that in this case Achilles was painted scraping such rust with a knife.

<margin>n</margin> WE TURNED OUR BACKS. We turned our shoulders to the ditch of the tenth pouch. UP ALONG THE BANK THAT GIRDS IT. That surrounds it: which was the boundary between the eighth and the ninth circle. CROSSING OVER: Already they had circled around to see the damned souls; now they crossed through it to leave. WITHOUT ANY SPEECH. He shows that they were taken away from the contemplation of this sin because they had already known it. IT WAS LESS THAN NIGHT AND LESS THAN DAY. It was not entirely darkness, but little light. And for this reason HIS SIGHT sent little forward: as if to say, I saw little further than where I was. BUT I HEARD A HORN SOUND. I did not see much, but I heard; because where light was lacking for seeing, sound abounded for hearing. And this was so great that a thunderclap would have seemed faint in comparison to it. And this sound, following its path against itself—that is, proceeding forward—DIRECTED. It was the cause of my directing my eyes to one place from which the sound came. It is to be considered why in this place one did not see but heard. The giants are placed in this location for their pride, which makes men so reckless that they wish to exceed natural forces and to have more power than nature allows them; but we will speak of these a little further down. He places them in darkness because pride is born from the ignorance of not knowing oneself. But it is heard because the things done by the proud are such that many speak of them. AFTER THE PAINFUL: It is Roncesvalles <note>original: "Runcisualle"</note> in the Pyrenees mountains which divide Gaul from Spain. Here, by the treachery of Ganelon of Maganza <note>original: "Gano da pontieri."</note>, the paladins were broken by Marsilius, king of Spain. And Orlando sounded his horn so strongly after the flight of his men that he gathered a hundred; and with those he made an assault and killed Marsilius. But of Orlando, we shall speak in the 18th Canto of the Paradiso.

<margin>s</margin> He follows in his speaking, saying: "I held my head turned there but a little," that is, after the sound made me turn toward it, I went a little while looking toward it. THAT IT SEEMED TO ME TO SEE. But they were not. MANY HIGH TOWERS. And believing they were truly towers, though he did not ask which city that was. And here, if we wish to consider it allegorically, the poet denotes how much the lower reason, joined with the sense, errs when it wishes to investigate things from too far away. And if we look simply at the senses of the body, it means to denote that the visual power cannot fulfill its office if it does not correspond to its virtue: the distance of the place, the size of the object (that is, of what it has to see), and the clarity of the light. Whence it happens that one eye requires one distance and another eye another, because they are of different strengths; and thus the same eye sees differently in greater or lesser light.

<margin>c</margin> That Virgil takes Dante by the hand and kindly shows him that those which seemed to him to be towers are not towers but gi... <note>The text cuts off mid-word "giganti" (giants).</note>

so that the fact may seem less strange to you,

<column-break/>

giants. This signifies nothing other than when lower reason submits itself to the intellect, which kindly reveals one’s errors. **THEN TENDERLY he took me by the hand.** Understand that his "hand" signifies help: for our senses cannot properly foresee pride if the intellect does not point it out. **AND SAID BEFORE we go further forward, so that the fact may seem less strange to you.** All things that are foreseen cause less distress than when they happen unexpectedly. Hence, Petrarch says: *A wound seen in advance hurts much less.* <note>original: "Piaga atiueduta assai men duole." From Petrarch’s *Trionfi*.</note> **They are not towers: but giants.** Lower reason recognized those to be giants and not towers; that is, it realized this was not simple haughtiness, but Pride. This is in imitation of Virgil (though very subtle) where Venus shows Aeneas that he cannot see how the gods are destroying Troy, but she will remove the mist that takes away his sight, and then he will be able to see them. And certainly, among the ancients, giants are placed as symbols of pride. According to the fables, giants were sons of the Earth who, trusting in their own strength, wanted to take heaven from Jove <note>Jove or Jupiter, the king of the gods.</note>. To do this, they took three mountains in Thessaly—Olympus, Pelion, and Ossa—and placing one atop the other, they wanted to climb up to heaven. Jove struck them with lightning and caused the mountains to collapse, and cast the giants into Hell. They are called sons of the Earth because all pride is for the acquisition not of divine knowledge, but of riches, dignity, honor, and power—earthly things. These are the "steps" because they want to rise higher than they deserve. They fight with the gods: for as Cicero says, giants fighting the gods is nothing other than resisting nature and wanting to conquer it. For this, they "pile mountain upon mountain"—that is, they make a great display and a great effort—but God scatters and dissipates them. Thus the Psalmist says: *And a giant shall not be saved by the greatness of his strength.* <note>original: "Et gigas no saluabit propter multitudine uirtutis sue." From Psalm 33:16.</note> **WHO ARE IN the pit**, in the ninth circle; which, because it is narrower and lower than the others, he calls a "pit." **FROM THE NAVEL downward, every one of them:** because they were out of the ice from the navel up. **JUST AS When.** It happens that when the fog, which has been very thick, begins to let one discern what is there (though it appeared to be something else), and then it dissipates—that is, it scatters—the gaze and the sight little by little recognize what they did not recognize before, because the terrestrial vapor which thickens and condenses the air (turning into mist) **CONCEALS IT**: hides it. Thus it happened to Dante: the closer he approached, the more the mist thinned and the better he saw. Thus error fled little by little, because he saw they were not towers; and fear grew, because he began to perceive they were giants, and such a sight made him afraid. Dante did not fear at first when he believed they were towers, but he was in error. Now, seeing they were giants, he began to fear: because he knows that such height of spirit is Pride, which is to be feared; for no vice is more ruinous to the human race. Nor should anyone marvel why pride is placed here when dealing with fraud: for this species of treachery being discussed has its beginning and origin in pride. The Bible mentions giants in Genesis: *And there were giants in those days.* <note>original: "Et gigantes erant in diebus illis." From Genesis 6:4.</note> And the Book of Kings mentions the giant Goliath. The giants were from the waist up outside the pit, and the rest inside: because no one was ever so proud that he could elevate himself entirely; but although his beginnings are high and elevated, God nevertheless strikes him down so that in the end he remains in the depths. And he binds their arms: because he takes away their power. **FOR AS UPON its circular wall.** Just as around the bank of the ninth circle the giants were seen like towers, just as on the circular walls of Monteriggioni (a castle of the Sienese) the towers rise up all around. This is a castle between Staggia and Siena.

**A**pproaching, he began to discern the face, the belly, and a large part of the chest: because the arms they had tied in front occupied part of it. Hence he says: **AND BOTH ARMS down along his sides.** **NATURE CERTAINLY.** An excellent digression in which he commends Nature for having ceased to produce more giants. Because men of such strength were great "executioners for Mars"—that is, victors in every battle—and through their immeasurable strength they tyrannized all others. Therefore, Nature is to be commended for no longer producing such men because they have too much strength. And if one should say that she still generates elephants (which exceed other land animals in size) and whales (which are larger than other fish), he responds that although such animals have great strength, men are nevertheless superior in wit and industry, with which they not only resist them but conquer them. But in the giants, because they were...

The commentary explains the giants as symbols of Pride (Superbia) and discusses why Nature was wise to stop creating beings with both human intelligence and such overwhelming physical power.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the nature of giants, following the discussion of how Nature was wise to stop creating such beings. It specifically concludes the thought that when intelligence is paired with malice and power, it becomes an unstoppable force.</meta>

# INFERNO.

...adds to ill will and to power,
no remedy can the people make against it.

In these men, intelligence was joined with strength. **AND WHEN THE** argument of the mind—that is, intelligence—does not turn toward virtue, but instead takes up an evil will toward others and possesses great power, it cannot be resisted. This is because it acts through intelligence, has the ability through strength, and desires because it is malignant. But brute animals, even though they may desire and have power, nevertheless do not act in this way. Nor is it a fabled thing that there were giants. For Hebrew, Greek, and Roman histories write of them: such as Nimrod, Hercules, and Antaeus. There were some in Sicily; there were some in England. And Augustine of Hippo <note>original: "Aurelio Auguftino"</note> affirms having seen on the shore of Africa near Utica a molar tooth so large that a hundred of our teeth could be made from it. Furthermore, he writes that shortly before the arrival of the Goths in Italy, there was a woman of giant-like appearance in Rome, to whom all the people flocked to see. **FOR WHERE THE** argument of the mind adds to ill will and to power: All brute animals of great strength have ill will when they are incited by anger, fear, hunger, jealousy, or the safety of their young to go against man. But although they desire and have power, they nevertheless do not act [effectively] because they lack rational intelligence and industry. Thus, man has some defense. But because in the giant the "argument of the mind"—that is, industry and intelligence—adds to his ill will and his great power, no defense can be made against him; for he wills, he can, and he acts.

His face seemed to me as long and as wide
as the pine cone of Saint Peter's in Rome,
and his other bones were in proportion to it;
So that the bank, which served as an apron

**RAPHEL Bai ameth zabi almi.** These words signify nothing; and even if they did signify something, no complete meaning could be drawn from them. But the poet induces Nimrod <note>original: "Nembroth"</note> to speak thus to signify the confusion of languages that originated from him.

My leader turned toward him: "Stupid soul,
keep to your horn, and vent yourself with that
when anger or another passion touches you;
Search your neck, and you will find the strap
that holds it tied, O confused soul,
and see it where it crosses your great chest."
Then he said to me: "He accuses himself;
this is Nimrod, through whose evil thought
one language alone is no longer used in the world.
Let us leave him be and not speak in vain;
for every language is the same to him
as his is to others, which is known to no one."

<column-break/>

**IT SHOWS** by comparison that this man's face was as large as a bronze pine cone. They say this pine cone was once atop the dome of the "Holy Mary the Round," called the Pantheon; but having been thrown down by a lightning bolt in my time, it was on the steps outside the Church of Saint Peter in the Vatican. <note>This ancient bronze pine cone, the "Pigna," now stands in a courtyard of the Vatican Museums.</note> But this is discussed in the topography of the Inferno. **AND IN HIS** proportion were the other bones: because the other limbs corresponded to the size of the face. **SO THAT THE BANK** which was an apron: The bank covered him from the navel down, where the limbs are that are not shown without shame. Thus, he calls the bank an "apron" <note>original: "perizoma," a Greek-derived word for a loincloth or covering.</note> because it covered the giants from the navel down. **IT SHOWED SO MUCH** from the navel up that three Frieslanders would have uncomfortably boasted of reaching his hair. *Perizoma* is a garment that covers the limbs which are not named or shown without shame. Frieslanders are tall men, such as those in the Frisian part of Germany. <note>The text mistakenly mentions "Phrygia," likely a confusion between Frisians and Phrygians.</note> **FOR I** saw thirty great spans starting from the place where the cloak is buckled—which is at the end of the throat—down to the navel that was visible.

**STUPID SOUL:** without salt: <note>A metaphor for lacking wisdom or "salty" wit.</note> that is, without any prudence. For who can be more foolish than he who wishes to oppose God? **KEEP TO** your horn: As if to say, do not use words since no one understands them; and use the horn, a sound suited to your ferocity and bestiality. **When anger** or another passion touches you. To brute animals, nature has not given articulated speech, because through that, the concepts of the mind are expressed, which proceed from reason. And because brutes do not have reason, but only the appetite from which passions are born—such as love, anger, fear, and the like—it was enough for them to have a confused and inarticulate voice with which they can express such passions. Therefore, since Nimrod did not use reason but only appetite, he is not worthy of using distinct words, but rather the voice of the horn with which dogs are called to the hunt. He [Dante] imagines that he has tied to his neck with a strap—which is a leather thong—this horn which hangs upon his chest. By the horn, he signifies his pride which binds his neck, because such sin makes him a servant to punishment; and it hangs upon his chest because pride was born from

---

evil thought, which is in the heart. **AND SEE IT.** See that same horn which "togas" you: it covers your great chest. It was therefore a great horn, since it covered so great a chest; and by this, it denotes his great pride. *Toga* is a Roman garment, whence he can "togare," that is, clothe himself. **HE ACCUSES HIMSELF.** Because by speaking in a language known to no one, he demonstrates his own confusion. Therefore, the words spoken by him cannot be interpreted. **LET US LEAVE** him be and not speak in vain, let us not speak in a vacuum. For he would not understand us; and every language is the same to him as his is to others. Nimrod would not understand Virgil because the irrational appetite, guided only by perturbations and the passions of the soul—such as sorrow, fear, anger, and the like—does not understand Dante (the lower reason) nor Virgil (the superior reason). **THIS** is Nimrod. Nimrod was the son of Ham, and Ham was the son of Noah. This man truly can be said to have been among men what Lucifer had been among the angels. And because he was in abundance of all things, and bold and most robust, he persuaded others that their happiness did not come to them from God but from their own virtue. He encouraged his relatives to seize tyranny, hoping to draw men away from the fear of God and place all hope in himself. And so that God could not punish them with a flood, as He had done in the time of Noah, his grandfather, he resolved to build a tower so high that the flood could not reach it. He built it, therefore, of bricks instead of stones, and of bitumen instead of lime. And each day he had twenty thousand men at such work, and all were in total agreement in such iniquity. But God, "who has put down the mighty from their seats and exalted the humble," <note>original Latin: "que depofuit potētes de fede & exaltauit hūiles," quoting the Magnificat.</note> did not wish to extinguish the human race again as He had done by the flood. Instead, He determined to disunite and confound them. Therefore, He threw the tower to the ground; and where before they used one and the same language, He generated confusion through the diversity of languages He gave them. For this reason, the tower was called Babylon, because *Babel* [means confusion].

# INFERNO.

<margin>the tower of babel</margin>
Regarding languages, the author <note>original: "lepno", likely a misprint for "Stephano" (Byzantinus) or "Beroso"</note> affirms that with our most high tower, they believed they could climb to heaven. But the gods, with winds, destroyed the tower and divided the language, giving to each his own. Thus, such a city was called Babylon. ¶ **THROUGH WHOSE** ill-will: through whose wicked desire to rebel against God. ¶ **NO MORE THAN ONE LANGUAGE** is used in the world: as was shown above.

<margin>Ephialtes and Otus, sons of Neptune.</margin>
<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of the giant Ephialtes, depicted from the waist up. His torso and arms are bound by thick, heavy chains that wrap multiple times around his body and neck. He has a muscular build and a thick beard.</image-desc>

They continued the journey to the left, and within the distance of a crossbow shot, they found Ephialtes, more fierce and larger than Nimrod. I do not know who the master was to gird and bind him: but with a chain he had bound the left arm in front and the right behind. And this chain cinched him five times from the neck down to where he began to be covered. This proud Ephialtes wished to be tried: that is, to experience his power against Jove <note>Jupiter, king of the gods</note>; and he made great trials in the war that the giants waged against Jove. Ephialtes and Otus were the sons of Neptune and Iphimedeia, wife of Aloeus, one of the Titans. They grew nine inches every month, and according to Homer they were...

<margin>Allegorical significance</margin>
...by the arrows of Phoebus <note>Apollo</note> while they were still beardless. Allegorically, this demonstrates Pride. And they are sons of Neptune because grave movements and grave storms stir up the proud, just as Neptune—that is, the sea—stirs them. They conquer Mars <note>the god of war</note> because they become victors in battles. But Juno, who is the goddess of kingdoms, has Mars taken from them by means of Mercury. This signifies that the just administration of the kingdom, with the help of prudence and wisdom, resists tyrants, and often takes from them the victory they had already gained.

<margin>Briareus the giant, his origin and deeds.</margin>
<margin>Homer the poet</margin>
<margin>Conspiracy of many gods against Jove:</margin>
<image-desc>A woodcut illustration showing the upper body of a massive giant, Antaeus, emerging from the ground or a cave. He is looking to the right and appears more mobile than the previous giant, as his arms are not shown bound.</image-desc>

To vary the narration of these giants, so that the same form would not generate boredom, he [Dante] asks about Briareus. Virgil replies to him that Briareus is much further on; and because he is bound in the same manner as Ephialtes, it is not worth the effort to see him, being made in the same way, except that he is more ferocious in the face. But he says that he will see Antaeus, who speaks and is unbound. And by him, they will be placed in the bottom of all guilt—that is, of Hell, where there is every evil. Briareus and Cottus were once sons of Heaven and Earth. And they had a hundred hands and fifty heads. They were the strongest and most beautiful above all others. Here the poet follows the opinion of other poets who place Briareus in Hell as an enemy of Jove. But Homer places him as a friend and tells the fable, the sum of which is this: Juno, Neptune, and Pallas conspired together with Nereus, the sea god, to forge a chain with which they would pull Jove out of heaven. Thetis, the sea goddess, revealed this conspiracy to Jove. And Jove called Briareus to his aid, who so terrified them that they abandoned the enterprise. And he [Dante] agrees with the Scripture by placing them in bonds, because the Psalmist writes: <quote>To bind their kings in fetters and their nobles in iron manacles.</quote> <note>original: "Ad alligandos reges eorum in compedibus & nobiles eorū in manicis ferreis"</note> And similarly we shall speak of the pit, because the same Psalmist says: <quote>But you, O God, shall lead them down into the pit of destruction.</quote> <note>original: "Tu uero deus deduces eos in puteu interitus"</note> And elsewhere: <quote>Let not the storm of water submerge me, neither let the deep swallow me up, and let not the mouth of the pit close over me.</quote> <note>original: "Non me demergat tempestas aquae. Neque abforbeat me profundum. Neq urgeat super me os putei."</note> ¶ **NEVER WAS AN EARTHQUAKE**: He shows by comparison with an earthquake how strongly Ephialtes shook himself. Certainly, no thing causes a greater movement among men and induces greater fear than pride. This gave so much fear to the poet that he fears death more than ever; and there was no need or necessity to make him die more than a *docta*—that is, a brief space. For whoever allows himself to be conquered by this vice dies in his sins. *Docta* in the Florentine language signifies a brief space of time. In essence: in any brief time that I stayed with such fear, I would have died. But the shackles and bonds that I saw, which were not broken by his shaking, took away my fear. Then they went to Antaeus, who was five ells tall without his head above the cave. An "ell" <note>alla</note> is the name of an English measure of two Florentine "braccia" <note>A 'braccio' is a traditional unit of length, roughly an arm's length</note>.

For Publius Cornelius Scipio Africanus the Elder, having been made consul against Hannibal, judged that the Carthaginians could be better defeated in Africa than in Italy. Therefore, he passed from Pisa to Sicily, and from Sicily to Carthage, and set up camp in the place that was first called the Kingdom of Antaeus; and afterward it was called the *Castra Cornelia* after that same Cornelius Scipio. ¶ **FORTUNATE VALLEY** to the Cornelian people, because Cornelius Scipio Africanus the Elder reduced Carthage to servitude; and afterward he conquered and destroyed Lesser Africa. ¶ **AND THAT IF YOU HAD BEEN** at the high war: he calls it "high" because it was against the gods. <meta>Continuity note: This page continues from the previous discussion regarding the descent into the final pit of Hell, specifically the transition into Canto XXXII where Dante encounters the frozen lake of Cocytus and the giants.</meta>

-># INFERNO<-
->## CANTO XXXII OF DANTE’S FIRST CANTICLE.<-

<margin>f</margin>
**If I had the rhymes harsh and clucking,**
**as would befit the dismal hole**
**on which all the other rocks weigh down,**
**I would press out the juice of my concept**
**more fully; but since I do not have them,**
**I bring myself to speak not without fear;**
**For it is no undertaking to take in jest**
**to describe the bottom of the whole universe,**
**nor for a tongue that calls "mamma" and "daddy."**

Because the weight of the vice makes these things difficult and almost unspeakable, the poet makes an excuse and demonstrates that he is insufficient for such great matter; these words make the listener attentive. Then he invokes the help of the Muses so that what he cannot do by himself, he may do with their help. **IF I HAD the rhymes**: the verses which are in rhyme. **HARSH and clucking**: The true praise of the poet is that the verse should be accommodated to the subject matter; for it is not only his task to narrate, but he must almost paint the thing with words in a form that makes it appear to the eyes of the mind just like those things seen with physical eyes. Hence many have defined poetry as a "silent picture that speaks." <note>This is a reference to the Horace’s *ut pictura poesis* and the saying attributed to Simonides of Ceos.</note> This is seen most clearly in Virgil. Therefore, since he has to treat the horrid, terrible, and harsh things in this last circle, he knows it requires "harsh and clucking" rhymes—that is, hoarse sounds through which sorrow and sadness are shown—as is befitting the **dismal hole**. This last circle is a hole in the center of the earth. **ON WHICH all the other rocks weigh down**: that is, they lean and press, all the other stones of the valley and the circles already mentioned above; because all the weights of every round body press toward the center as the lowest place. Or, if we take "rocks" to mean filth—and more specifically, the filth of vice—we might say that all vices weigh down upon this circle, which represents pride. <note>Landino suggests a moral allegory: Pride is the foundation of all sin.</note> Because pride is the root of all. **I WOULD press out the juice of my concept**: before anyone writes, they always think of what they want to write, and after they have made their invention, they begin to write it down. Thus the mind conceives within itself, just as, for example, a herb has conceived its juice within itself. Then, just as it is necessary to press the herb to make the juice come out, so when we manifest with words what we have already conceived in the mind, it is like pressing the juice of what we have conceived. The meaning is: if I had verses suitable to the matter, I would express my concept more fully. But because I do not have them, I do not bring myself to speak without fear. And the reason he does not speak without fear is that wanting to treat such matter is no undertaking to take in jest—that is, as a joke or a game—to want to write about the **bottom** (meaning obscurely) of **the whole universe** to all men. And then because the Florentine language in which he writes is understood with difficulty outside of Italy where one says "daddy" or "mamma," <note>original: "babbo o mamma"</note> he adds "nor for a tongue that calls mamma or daddy," meaning the Italian language. For in all of Italy there is only one language, but it is divided into many properties because each region has its own. And these properties in Greek are called **idioms** <term>idiomati: dialects or regional varieties</term>. The Latins have no idiom because the Latin language, being from Latium (a small stretch), does not vary in anything; but Greek, because it extends through many regions, has many properties or idioms: Attic, Aeolic, Doric, Ionic, and the like.

**But may those ladies help my verse**
**who helped Amphion to close up Thebes,**
**so that the telling be not different from the fact.**
**O above all ill-born rabble**
**who stay in the place whereof to speak is hard,**
**it would have been better if you had been sheep or goats here.**

**As we were down in the dark pit,**
**under the giant's feet, much lower,**
**and I was still looking at the high wall,**
**I heard someone say: "Watch how you pass;**
**go so that you do not tread with your soles**
**on the heads of the weary, wretched brothers."**
**Wherefore I turned and saw before me**
**and under my feet, a lake that through frost**
**had the semblance of glass and not of water.**

<margin>g</margin>
Having reached the pit, they found themselves lower than the feet of the giant. And Dante, because he was intent on looking up at the height of the wall that encircled this ninth circle, did not see that he was in a frozen lake. But in passing, he heard one who said: "Watch that you do not tread, that you do not trample the heads of the wretched brothers." That is, of these who are your brothers in terms of generation, and are wretched because of the pain they suffer in this ice. Now, to understand the poet’s fiction precisely, this ninth circle is divided into four...

<column-break/>

...narrated of the proud. Now, because from pride—beyond all other infinite vices—proceeds betrayal, he explains the punishment of traitors in this canto. These are divided into four parts, and the first is for those who have used betrayal against their kin; these he places in the ice because they are entirely deprived of any heat of charity. And since this virtue (charity), being most acceptable to God, is placed nearest to Him in the highest heaven in the order of the Seraphim, so this vice must be in the most remote and lowest place, being its opposite. Charity is in the highest height and the greatest heat; therefore, betrayal will be its opposite in the deepest depth and the greatest frost. **Where there is weeping and gnashing of teeth** <note>original: "Vbi est fletus & stridor dentium"</note>; the gnashing of teeth denotes the cold, and Cocytus denotes the weeping, because **Cocyzin** in Greek signifies **to weep** <term>Cocytus: the frozen river of Hell, derived from the Greek "kokytos" (wailing)</term>. Therefore, the author begins the narration of the things he finds in the ninth circle.

Since he has shown the greatness of the matter through its power, he now gives hope that although he is not sufficient in himself for such a great thing, he will still be able to do it with the help of the Muses whom he invokes. Regarding the Muses and the reason why poets invoke them, we wrote above in the second canto. **But those ladies**, namely the Muses, who helped **Amphion** to close up **Thebes**—to make the walls of Thebes—shall be those who help my verse so that my words correspond to the fact and express it fully. Antiope conceived three sons by Jove according to Homer: Amphion, Zethus, and Calais. Amphion, with his sweet music, drew the stones to himself and made them assemble in such a way that they formed the walls of Thebes. This signifies nothing other than that he, with his prudence and most sweet eloquence, was able to lead the men of that region—who lived scattered through the fields and woods—to live civilly in one and the same city. **O ABOVE all**: after the invocation, so that the narration may have suitable gravity, he begins with an exclamation, which always gives gravity to speech, saying: **O RABBLE**, O vile people. For there can be no gentility or nobility in the vicious, because **virtue is the one and only nobility**, as Juvenal says <note>original: "Nobilitas una atque unica uurtus"</note>. **O ill-born rabble**: unhappily created above all other men, even above those who are in the other circles, which stay in the place whereof—that is, of which—it is **hard** (meaning difficult) for me to speak. **WOULD THAT YOU HAD BEEN sheep or goats** <note>original: "zebe"</note>: sheep or goats or other brute animals, so that your life would have been mortal, for you would not have suffered these eternal pains. He calls the goats "zebe" because our shepherds call them thus.

<summary>This page contains the opening of Canto XXXII, where Dante and Virgil arrive at the frozen lake of Cocytus at the bottom of Hell. The commentary explains the poet's struggle to find language "harsh" enough for the gravity of betrayal and identifies the frozen state as the complete absence of divine love (charity).</summary>

# CANTO XXXII.
rii
<meta>image quality: good; catchwords: none; handwritten "137" at bottom left</meta>

**Wherefore I turned me, and I saw before me,**
**And underfoot, a lake that through the frost**
**The semblance had of glass, and not of water.**

If we subtly speculate upon these types of betrayals, we will see that they contain not only pride but also envy, which he has not specifically treated because it is such that it pours itself into various vices. And because this envy comes from pride, the first proud and envious one was Lucifer. And because the fraud committed against one who trusts is called betrayal and comes from pride and envy, it is punished here. If it is among those joined by blood, it is punished in the first circle, which is called Caina, after Cain, who out of envy killed his brother Abel; this is against natural faith. If it is against one’s country, where there is a bond of birth, it is worse because it is against many; this is punished in the second circle and is called Antenora. Or truly, if one breaks the faith given to a friend, this happens in two ways: either against one whom we have seduced into giving us benefits, and then it is the third degree, which is worse than the second because the faith was not only given but earned; this is punished in the third, called Ptolomea, after Ptolemy, who invited priests and killed them at the banquet. Or it is committed against a benefactor friend, which degree is worse than the others, and this is the fourth degree. This fourth degree is worse because it is ingratitude, and it is called Giudecca after Judas Iscariot, who betrayed the humanity of Christ. In the center of this pit, as in the place furthest from heaven, Lucifer is punished, because his crime is above all others.

**The Danube in Austria never made**
**For its course so thick a veil in winter,**
**Nor the Tanais <note>original: "Tanai"; the Don River in Russia</note> there under the cold sky,**
**As was there here; for if Mount Tabernic**
**Had fallen upon it, or Pietra Apuana <note>original: "pietra pana"; a peak in the Apuan Alps</note>,**
**It would not even at the edge have given a creak.**
**And as the frog sits croaking**
**With its muzzle out of the water, when the peasant girl**
**Often dreams of gleaning,**
**Livid, as far as where the color of shame appears,**
**Were the sorrowful shades within the ice,**
**Setting their teeth to the note of the stork.**

The shades were out of the water just as the peasant woman stands at the time of harvest. **OFTEN**: many times; she dreams of gleaning and gathering the fallen ears of grain; he says "dream" because a person often dreams of doing what they have in mind to do. **LIVID**: this demonstrates great coldness and similarly assigns a color appropriate to envy; hence the Latins call envy *livor*. <note>original: "liuore"</note> **AS FAR AS WHERE Shame appears**: up to the face, which makes a demonstration when one is ashamed. In the same ice, he places the traitors of relatives, friends, and country. But those who are lower are always in greater cold because they are closer to the center; it is reasonable that he who has committed the greater betrayal should be further from the fire of charity. It is a greater betrayal when one breaks the path to the country, because it is done against many rather than against parents; and greater still against friends, and most of all against God. **Setting their teeth to the note**: in the song of the stork, because trembling, they chattered their teeth, making that noise that the stork makes when it strikes its lower beak against the upper one. By this chattering of teeth, great cold is demonstrated, and that which the Gospel calls the "gnashing of teeth." <note>original: "stridor dentium"</note>

**Each one held his face turned downward;**
**By the mouth the cold, and by the eyes the sad heart,**
**Among them procures testimony.**
**When I had looked around me for a while,**
**I turned to my feet and saw two so pressed together,**
**That they had the hair of their heads intermingled.**
**"Tell me, you who so press your chests together,"**
**I said, "who are you?" and they bent their necks;**
**And after they had lifted their faces toward me,**
**Their eyes, which before were only wet within,**
**Gushed through the lids, and the frost bound**
**The tears between them, and locked them up again.**
**No clamp ever bound wood to wood**
**So strongly; wherefore they, like two he-goats,**
**Butted together, such anger overcame them.**

<column-break/>

He informs us that the first circle is the widest and embraces the second, and the second the third, and the third the fourth; in this way, the one further in always has a smaller circuit and descends further toward the center, though there is no distinction in depth shown yet. The first, which is closest to the wall and is widest, is called Caina; the reason for this will be known below. The second is Antenora. The third is Ptolomea. The fourth is Giudecca. And we shall see that it contains not only pride but also envy.

<image-desc>Decorative initial C with floral and scroll patterns</image-desc>
**T**he ice was so thick that the Danube in Austria, nor the Tanais, freezes so strongly. Austria <note>original: "osterichi"</note> is the coldest part of Germany <note>original: "magna"; referring to Alemagna</note> and in Latin is called Austria, through which passes the Danube, the largest river in all Europe. It rises in the mountains of Germany and passes through Hungary and enters the Euxine <note>term: Euxine; the Black Sea</note> Sea with such impetus that for more than sixty miles into the sea it maintains fresh water. In winter it freezes so strongly that entire armies pass over it with horses and carts; it is commonly called the Danube. The Tanais rises to the north in the Riphean mountains where there are immeasurable colds; it divides Asia from Europe and enters the Euxine Sea near the city of Theodosia. The ice was so thick that if these very high mountains, Tabernic and Pietra Apuana, had fallen upon it, not only would the ice not have broken, but it would not even have moved slightly at the edge where it makes a "creak" sound when it moves. Tabernic is a very high mountain in Slavonia. Pietra Apuana <note>original: "Pietra pana"</note> is in Tuscany in the Garfagnana above Lucca; by the Latins it is called *Petra Apuana*. And in truth, there is a very great coldness in the heart of the proud and the traitor, as we said above. They stood with their heads...

<image-desc>Decorative initial O with floral and scroll patterns</image-desc>
**E**ach one held his face turned downward. It is the nature of the traitor never to look anyone in the face. Furthermore, they are ashamed by necessity because they remember having always acted against human nature. And certainly, traitors always turn their faces downward and consider nothing other than earthly and low things. **WHEN** I had looked around me for a while: The first four tercets are well known. But that the tears froze in a way that locked their eyes denotes that the envious person, although he sees misery, nevertheless the cold—that is, the lack of charity—does not let him see or be moved to compassion. **AND ONE: NOT** responding, those two, another shade replied. **ONLY WITH THE FACE** downward, as we said above. **THE VALLEY OF BISENZIO**: Bisenzio is a river between Florence and Prato, and it enters the Arno six miles from Florence. **ALL** of Caina: we said that he names this first circle from Cain, who was the son of Adam, the first man, and was a farmer. And he had Abel his brother, a shepherd. Abel sacrificed the firstlings of his flock, and such firstlings were accepted by God. Cain offered the firstlings of the fruits of the earth, and they were not accepted by God. Wherefore Cain, moved to envy, said to his brother "let us go outside"; and when they had come to the countryside, Cain killed his brother. And God said, "Cain, where is your brother?"

# INFERNO:

And one who had lost both his ears
from the freezing cold, with his face turned down,
said: "Why do you mirror yourself so much in us?

If you wish to know who these two are,
the valley from which the Bisenzio flows
belonged to their father Alberto and to them.

They came from one body; and throughout all Caina
you could search and not find a shade
more worthy of being fixed in this jelly;

Not even he whose chest and shadow were pierced
with a single blow by the hand of Arthur;
not Focaccia; not this one who blocks

My view with his head so I can see no further,
who was named Sassol Mascheroni;
if you are Tuscan, you well know who he was.

<term>Io.</term> <note>This "Io" marks a commentary section explaining the historical context.</note> From this patricide followed such scandal that all of Tuscany was troubled by it for many years: because from here derived the factions of the Whites and Blacks that first divided Pistoia and then Florence. **NOT THIS ONE who blocks my head:** and stands before my eyes so that I cannot see further there. This was Sassol Mascheroni of Florence, who similarly murdered his own uncle.

And so that you do not put me to further speech,
know that I was Camicion de’ Pazzi;
and I await Carlino to exonerate me."

Afterward I saw a thousand faces made dog-like
by the cold, which gives me a shudder
and always will when I think of frozen ponds.

<note>original: "Inganno efuci ghibellini..."</note> Through deceit, the Ghibellines and the White faction surrendered the castle. **I SAW a thousand faces:** a great many faces. **Dog-like:** shriveled and purple from the cold like dogs. **Gives me a shudder:** a feeling of horror and shivering.

And while we were going toward the center
to which every weight is drawn,
and I was trembling in the eternal chill,

Whether it was will, or destiny, or fortune,
I do not know; but walking among the heads,
I struck my foot hard against the face of one.

Crying out, he scolded me: "Why do you trample me?
Unless you come to increase the vengeance
of Montaperti, why do you molest me?"

And I: "My Master, now wait for me here,
so that I may clear a doubt concerning this soul;
then you may hurry me as much as you wish."

The Leader stopped, and I said to that one
who was still bitterly blaspheming:
"Who are you, who thus insults others?"

"Nay, who are you, who goes through Antenora,
striking the cheeks of others," he replied,
"so hard that, were you alive, it would be too much?"

"I am alive," was my response, "and it could be dear
to you, if you ask for fame,
that I put your name among my other notes."

<column-break/>

To which Cain replied: "I do not know. Am I my brother’s keeper?" And God said: "His blood cries out to me; the earth shall swallow you and shall not yield its fruit to you, and you shall be cursed upon the earth." <note>This refers to the biblical Cain, for whom the first ring of the frozen lake, Caina, is named.</note> **NOT HE WHOSE chest and shadow were broken:** that is, the chest and the back. Because the shadow of the chest goes to the back. This was Mordred, son of King Arthur, King of Britain and head of the Round Table. Mordred rebelled against his father and lay in wait to kill him. But Arthur, discovering the ambush, pierced him with a lance through the chest, and the spear passed through his back <note>Legend says the wound was so great that a ray of light passed through it, "breaking" his shadow.</note>. **Focaccia** was of the Cancellieri family of Pistoia; he treacherously killed his uncle. In the year 1300 there were three brothers in this family who were knights. Focaccia, a most audacious young man of the worst character, was the son of one of these. It happened that while playing in the snow, Focaccia’s father struck a nephew of his because he had too harshly insulted another child with the snow. He did this as the head of the family, being his uncle. But the boy, more reckless and malicious than his age required, hid his pain and after a short time pretended to want to whisper in his uncle’s ear; the uncle leaned down, and the boy struck him with a dagger. The father was grieved by it, and left the boy to the uncle so he might punish him in his own way. But the uncle, thinking no more was needed than what a child required, instead of a beating, kissed his face and sent him back to his father. But the wicked Focaccia, his son, cut off the hand of this boy; then he ran to the house of the father—who was his own uncle—and killed him.

**And so that you do not put me to further speech:** to ask me who I am. This **Camicion** was Messer Alberto Camicion de’ Pazzi of Valdarno, who treacherously killed Messer Ubertino, his relative. **Carlino** was also of the Pazzi of Valdarno; and while the Florentines were besieging Pistoia, he occupied a castle called Castel di Piano in Valdarno on behalf of the Ghibellines. For this reason, the Florentines were forced to leave the siege of Pistoia and come to Valdarno. They camped at this castle for twenty-eight days; finally, Messer Carlino, corrupted by money, surrendered the castle.

The poet enters the second circle called **Antenora**, after Antenor, who according to many betrayed Troy; here the narrative continues until the middle of the following canto. **THEY WENT toward the center:** toward the center which is the middle of every spherical body; therefore, when they were going down. **WALKING among the heads I struck one:** but I do not know if it was will, or fate, or destiny, or fortune. **WILL** proceeds from free choice. **DESTINY:** fate born from the universal alignment of stars. **FORTUNE** proceeds from a particular alignment. This striking of the foot signifies that it came into his mind, while treating this sin, to deal with this man—whether his will led him by choice, or fate, or fortune. **OF MONTE APERTI**, about which we will speak below <note>Referring to the Battle of Montaperti (1260), a bloody defeat for the Florentine Guelphs.</note>.

**Wait:** that Virgil should wait for him because inferior reason is that which, as we have said, descends into particulars. He feigns that this soul did not wish to be known because betrayal is such an abominable vice that no one is so wicked as not to be ashamed of it; furthermore, there is no sin committed with more secrecy. And for this reason, you see that he does not accept Dante’s offer to name him. **THROUGH ANTENORA:** through this second circle named after Antenor, who betrayed Troy, his homeland. **THEN I took him by the scruff:** by the hair at the back of the neck, and he feigns striking him in that member because memory resides there; and he forced him to bring back to memory who he was. **You may strip me of hair:** that is, pull out my hair. And the rest of the text is clear.
