# CANTO XXXII
r iii

And he said to me: "I desire the opposite;
get away from here and give me no more annoyance,
for you poorly know how to flatter in this icy slope."
Then I took him by the scruff of the neck
and said: "It will be necessary that you name yourself,
or that not a single hair remains up here on you."
Then he said to me: "Even if you strip me of my hair,
I will not tell you who I am, nor show you,
even if you fall upon my head a thousand times."
I already had his hair wrapped in my hand,
and had pulled out more than one tuft,
while he barked with his eyes kept down,
When another cried out: "What is the matter, Bocca?
Is it not enough for you to chatter with your jaws,
without barking? What devil is touching you?"
"Now," I said, "I do not want you to speak,
wicked traitor; for to your shame
I will carry true news of you."
"Go away," he replied, "and tell what you will;
but do not be silent, if you get out of here,
about him who just now had his tongue so ready.
He weeps here for the silver of the French;
'I saw,' you can say, 'him of Duera,
there where the sinners are kept cool.'
If you should be asked who else was there,
you have at your side him of Beccheria,
whose gorge Florence sawed through.
Gianni de' Soldanier, I believe, is
further on with Ganelon and Tebaldello,
who opened Faenza while it slept."

---

We had already departed from him,
when I saw two frozen in one hole,
so that one head served as a hat to the other.
And as bread is devoured out of hunger,
so the upper one set his teeth into the other
there where the brain joins with the nape.
Not otherwise did Tydeus gnaw
the temples of Menalippus out of disdain,
than he did to the skull and the other parts.
"O you who show by such a bestial sign
hatred over him whom you are eating,
tell me the 'why'," I said, "on this condition:
That if you have a reason to complain of him,
knowing who you are and what his sin was,
I may yet repay you in the world above,
if this <note>The "tongue" or "voice" of the poet.</note> with which I speak does not dry up."

<column-break/>

It does not benefit the traitor to want to cover and keep his wicked deeds hidden because there is always someone who reveals them: and this the poet signifies through the one who named **Bocca**, who did not want to reveal himself. **CHATTER with your jaws:** to strike the teeth together because of the cold. **If you do not bark:** *latrare* <note>original: "latrare"</note> is a Latin term meaning to bark, and it is a sound specific to dogs.

**GO AWAY, he replied:** when the wicked have been discovered and can no longer hide themselves, it is their custom to turn to naming others who have committed similar errors; to excuse themselves, they accuse others. **Messer Bocca degli Abati** of Florence, of whom it was spoken above. <note>Bocca was a notorious traitor who, during the Battle of Montaperti in 1260, cut off the hand of the Florentine standard-bearer, causing panic and the defeat of the Guelphs.</note> **ET PIANGE:** "And he weeps," referring to this one whom you see thus. **WEEPS for the silver of the French:** this was Messer Buoso of the Duera family from Cremona; he was a Ghibelline and was ready with others to block the passage of Guy de Montfort, who was leading the army of Charles I of France into the Kingdom of Naples to fight Manfred. But, corrupted by money, he betrayed his allies and acted in such a way that the French were able to pass. **Of BECCHERIA:** This was the Abbot of Vallombrosa, from the Beccheria family of Parma. Having been sent to Florence by the Church, he plotted treachery to take the state from the Guelphs and give it to the Ghibellines. When the Guelphs discovered this, they cut off his head during a popular riot in the Piazza di San Apollinare, for which the city was excommunicated.

**IANNI SOLDANIERI.** In the time when the "Jovial Friars" were the governors (*podestà*) in Florence, as we said above: the Ghibellines tried to use armed force to overthrow the Guelph leaders of the people. Therefore, the people gathered under arms at the Church of Santa Trinita. Messer Giovanni Soldanieri—who was a Ghibelline from a noble and ancient family—betrayed his own side to become powerful, making himself the head of the people who finally won and chased the Ghibellines out. **GANELLONE:** <note>Also known as Ganelon from the "Song of Roland".</note> After Charlemagne recovered Spain and returned it to the orthodox Christian faith, he sent Ganelon as an ambassador to the remaining Saracen kings to demand they be baptized and pay tribute. But the Saracens corrupted Ganelon with a great sum of money to betray the Christians. Ganelon advised the Saracens to secretly occupy the Pyrenean mountains and wait in ambush for Roland and Oliver, whom Charles had kept in the rearguard. The paladins arrived with twenty thousand armed men; although they fought manfully and won the first encounter, they were eventually exhausted and killed by a fresh force of 30,000 Saracens. We spoke of Roland's death earlier.

He had moved away only a little when he saw two souls so close together that one head was a "hat" to the other because it touched it; and the **upper one**—the one on top—gnawed with his teeth the back of the neck of the other where the brain joins the skull. **NOT OTHERWISE did Tydeus gnaw.** We explained the history of Eteocles and Polynices earlier: Tydeus, son of King Oeneus of Calydon, arrived in Argos at the same time as Polynices. Although they were initially enemies, they were reconciled by King Adrastus and became faithful friends and brothers-in-law. Later, in the battles for Thebes, they fought together: Tydeus on the side of Polynices and Menalippus the Theban on the side of Eteocles. Menalippus mortally wounded Tydeus, but Tydeus managed to kill him. Before dying, Tydeus asked for the head of Menalippus and, in a fit of rage, gnawed upon it.

### CANTO XXXIII. CANTO 33 OF THE FIRST CANTICLE BY DANTE.

He lifted his mouth from the savage meal,
that sinner, wiping it on the hair
of the head he had wasted from behind.
Then he began: "You wish that I renew
a desperate grief that presses on my heart
even at the thought, before I speak of it.
But if my words are to be the seed
that bears the fruit of infamy for the traitor I gnaw,
you shall see me speak and weep at the same time.
I know not who you are, nor by what means
you have come down here, but a Florentine
you truly seem to be when I hear you.
You must know I was Count Ugolino,
and this is Archbishop Ruggieri;
now I will tell you why I am such a neighbor.
That by the effect of his evil thoughts,
trusting in him, I was taken
and then killed, there is no need to say;
But what you cannot have heard—
that is, how cruel my death was—
you shall hear, and know if he has offended me."

<note>The text here transitions into a prose explanation of the historical events in Pisa.</note>

...who incited the people against him: and he in person <insert>was taken</insert> along with his children and imprisoned in the tower which is in the square of the Elders: And they threw the keys of the prison into the Arno so that no one could open it: And the prisoners were denied food. Thus, that tower from that time on was called the Tower of Hunger. The poet, therefore, in the person of the Count, narrates how they all died of hunger: and the circumstances which in truth neither the poet nor anyone else could know: But because it was manifest that they had died of hunger, he feigns the circumstances and makes the thing plausible: and induces the Count to say: PERO <note>original: "Pero" - Therefore</note> what you cannot have heard.

A narrow slit within the cage <term>muda; a place where hawks are kept while shedding feathers</term>
which for me bears the title of hunger,
and in which others must yet be shut,
Had shown me through its opening
several moons already, when I had the evil dream
that rent for me the veil of the future.
This man appeared to me as master and lord,
hunting the wolf and the wolf-cubs toward the mountain
because the Pisans cannot see Lucca.
With lean, eager, and trained hounds,
Gualandi with Sismondi and with Lanfranchi
he had placed at the front.
In a short course, they seemed weary to me,
the father and the sons, and with sharp fangs
it seemed to me I saw their flanks ripped open.

<margin>439</margin>
When I was awake before the dawn,
I heard my sons, who were with me,
weeping in their sleep and asking for bread.
Cruel indeed you are, if you do not grieve already,
thinking what my heart foretold;
and if you weep not, at what do you ever weep?

<column-break/>

**O**ptimally linked is this 33rd canto to the one above because it continues the narrative already begun: And it induces one of the two already found to respond. Therefore, the narrative of this second circle <note>Antenora</note> follows: And then it will enter the third. And this beginning is most suited to capture attention, both by the cruel act of Count Ugolino and by his words which promise rare and justified things. HE LIFTED THEREFORE: that is, the Count raised his mouth FROM THE savage meal: from the head upon which he ferociously fed: and he wiped that mouth on the hair of that head: which, while gnawing, he had already wasted at the nape of the neck. And prepared to narrate, he shows how much it must pain him if his words are to bring infamy to the Archbishop: whom he was gnawing. Then he reveals himself to be Count Ugolino: and the one he gnaws is Archbishop Ruggieri: And he shows he does not wish to narrate how, by trusting him, he was betrayed by him: and by such betrayal captured and killed: because that history was very well known. But he wishes to narrate the cruel fortune of his death, which he considers less known. He remains silent, therefore, about that which in the telling would bring him infamy. And he narrates what shall be to the perpetual ignominy of his enemy. This Count Ugolino was of the Gherardesca counts: and was so great a captain that he governed Pisa: And in those times the Pisans lost the greater part of the countryside which was taken from them by the Florentines: and other <term>Guelphs; a political faction supporting the Pope</term> of Tuscany; it was the opinion that he, although a <term>Ghibelline; a political faction supporting the Holy Roman Emperor</term>, reached an understanding with the Guelphs and wished to weaken the forces of the Pisans to make himself lord. At that time, the Archbishop of Pisa was Messer Ruggieri Ubaldini: and it happened that a nephew of his was killed by a relative of the Count over jealousy for a woman whom each of them loved, which injury the Archbishop thought to avenge upon the Count. He increased, therefore, that suspicion: and incited many enemies against him: and especially three principal families, the Gualandi, Sismondi, and Lanfranchi, informing the people against him.

**B**REVE <note>original: "Breve pertuso" - Narrow slit</note> within the *muda*: they call *muda* the place where they shut up birds of prey so that they may *mudino*, that is, change their feathers. But here, by an appropriate metaphor, he calls this prison a *muda* WHICH for me has the title of hunger: because by my death it is called the Tower of Hunger. IN which it is fitting that yet others be shut: he imagines this because of the frequent changes of government that city underwent. HAD shown me through its opening: through its hole and small window. He shows that he was still awake when the dawn came in such a way that the window already gave light: then he fell asleep and dreamed. And as we said above, the dream near daybreak is true, WHICH from the future rent, or broke, THE VEIL of the darkness: because through this dream I understood what was to be. The dream was that it seemed to him a prelate was shown to him who was hunting: and led with him the three families mentioned. AND HOUNDS lean and ready: by the prelate is shown the Archbishop: and by the hounds the people. They hunted a wolf with its cubs: which was the Count with his sons. These were running toward the Pisan mountain <note>Mount San Giuliano</note> which is between Pisa and Lucca: and takes away the view so that from Pisa one cannot see Lucca: And this signifies that the Count, being in doubt, had planned to retreat to Lucca where the Guelphs ruled. But in a short time they were exhausted. Which denotes that they could not reach Lucca. Wherefore the hounds reached him because the people captured him.

**Q**uando <note>original: "Quando fu desto" - When I was awake</note> before the morrow, before the morning and the clear day, I heard my sons weep in their sleep: because they dreamed as I had dreamed of their misery and the coming hunger, and therefore they asked for bread. And it happens many times that those same constellations that bring misery also bring dreams of it.

# INFERNO

They were already awake, and the hour approached
when our food was usually brought to us,
and because of his dream, each one was afraid.
And I heard the door below being locked
of that horrible tower; then I looked
into the faces of my sons without saying a word.

I did not weep, I turned so to stone within;
they were weeping, and my little Anselm
said: "Father, you look so; what is wrong?"
Still I did not shed a tear, nor did I answer
all that day nor the night that followed,
until another sun came forth upon the world.
As soon as a small ray of light had made its way
into that doleful prison, and I discerned
in their four faces the aspect of my own,
I bit both my hands out of grief;
and they, thinking that I did it out of a desire
to eat, suddenly stood up
And said: "Father, it will be much less pain for us
if you eat of us; you clothed us in
this miserable flesh, and so you should strip it off."
I calmed myself then, so as not to make them sadder;
that day and the next we all remained silent.
Ah, hard earth, why did you not open up?
When we had come to the fourth day,
Gaddo threw himself outstretched at my feet,
saying: "My father, why do you not help me?"
There he died; and just as you see me,
I saw the three fall one by one
between the fifth day and the sixth; then I began,
Already blind, to grope over each of them;
and for two days I called them after they were dead.
Then, fasting had more power than grief.

likewise dreams that manifest it: And this is what he says a little below: *and because of his dream, each one was afraid.*

---

<margin>i</margin> **I did not weep**: because I turned to stone: that is, I hardened inside. That great grief prevents tears is manifest. **THEY WERE WEEPING**: Here the author provides every detail that can move one to mercy and compassion: first, from the omen of his dream and that of his children. So says Virgil: <note>original: "In somnis ecce ante oculos mestissimus Hector Visus adesse mihi."</note> "Behold, in sleep before my eyes, most sorrowful Hector seemed to appear to me." Then from his children: because it is the greatest pain for a father to see his children in extreme misery and not be able to help them. **WHEN WE HAD COME TO THE FOURTH DAY**. The poet shows that they all lived without food until the fourth day: and on the fourth day Gaddo, the youngest, died, overcome by hunger. Then between the fifth and the sixth, the three remaining children died: and he, already blind, survived for two days—that is, the whole of the sixth and seventh. Then he adds that *fasting had more power than grief.* Regarding this, our Martino Novarese—may God increase his wisdom and diminish his arrogance—interprets it to mean that fasting had more power than grief—that is, that the desire to eat overcame his piety and paternal love and forced him to feed on the flesh of his children. I shall leave to the judgment of the reader how absurd this opinion is. And I shall strive to reveal two remarkable points not recognized by him, with which the author, as both poet and <term>physician|A student of natural philosophy and medicine</term>, most highly adorned this speech. And first we shall treat "physically" of the endurance of fasting. It is not unknown to anyone that through the constant depletion of the natural <term>humors|The bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—thought to control health and temperament</term> in a living body, it is necessary that when hunger (which is nothing other than a craving and desire for dryness) and thirst (for moisture) are felt, the animal must continually generate new <term>chyle|A milky fluid produced during digestion</term> with new food and new drink to restore what is missing. And if one does not take nourishment, in a short time he perishes. But because such depletion of the nutritive humor that kills a man does not happen equally in everyone, it happens that some endure starvation and fasting more and others less without ruinous harm. And when physicians seek the causes of this variety, they attribute them chiefly to four things: **Age**, **Complexions**, the **Substance of the humors**, and the **Pores**. Therefore, someone who is either in a tender age and not yet consolidated and firm, or in a declining age, endures it less than a man in his prime. Thus children and the elderly require more frequent nourishment than a man in his perfect age. In the second place, we shall note the **complexions**, in which the less the humor is dissolvable, the less hunger can be endured. Thus the <term>choleric|Associated with yellow bile; quick-tempered and dry</term> person perishes in a very short time. The <term>melancholic|Associated with black bile; somber and dry</term> endures a little more. The <term>sanguine|Associated with blood; lively and moist</term> somewhat more. And the **tempered complexion** is sustained longer than the sanguine. And finally, the <term>phlegmatic|Associated with phlegm; calm and moist</term> lasts longer than the four already mentioned because he abounds in humor; and because it is very viscous, it does not dissolve easily; and when it does dissolve, it is easily converted into blood fit to sustain life. For this reason, we see many phlegmatic animals, such as snakes, <unclear>tapsi</unclear>, dormice, and the like, go into dens in the winter and live without food: because the phlegm that abounds in the stomach is slowly converted into blood and nourishes them. Furthermore, one notes the essence of the humor in any complexion. The thinner it is, the more quickly it dissolves and the less it endures hunger. And conversely, the thicker it is, the more it has the opposite effect. One also notes **porosity**. For the more porous body is emptied more quickly. Thus it feels hunger sooner. And in the less porous, understand the opposite. Now, if I am not mistaken, I have with great brevity pointed out rather than narrated the natural causes of the endurance of fasting. But external accidents also contribute not a little, such as air, whether thick or thin, or hot or cold; or food, whether more or less dissolvable, and other similar things. But especially the various accidents of the soul. For just as joy, by relaxing and expanding the soul, also expands the humors and makes them more dissolvable—whereby hunger is less endured—so grief, by constricting them, makes them less dissolvable. For this reason, the greater the grief, the more a man endures fasting and the longer he lives without food. All of these things, known to the poet, distinguished the length of the fast according to age and according to grief. And because the children were in the growth of their age, he leads them to die first: and among them he places first the one youngest in age; and then the others according to whether they were more or less advanced in years. And he places himself last, both because he was in his prime of age and because he was oppressed by greater grief. He induces the first to die on the fourth day; the others from hour to hour until the sixth. He wept for them for two days afterward—that is, the sixth and the seventh. And on the seventh, although grief, by condensing and constricting the humors, prohibited their dissolution—which prolonged his life—nevertheless, the length of the fast had more power than the prohibition of dissolution proceeding from grief. Nor without natural reason did he take the limits of the fourth and seventh day, because in human life these days are <term>critical|Days on which a disease was expected to reach a turning point</term> because of the movement nature makes in them. This proceeds from the lunar course: for the moon in its first quarter has movement toward its sextile, and in the seventh toward its quadrature; these movements have great power over human life. Nor is it incredible regarding the seventh day. For Ficino, a physician and surgeon of no small renown and father of our Marsilio Ficino, affirms...

# CANTO XXXIII.

...been in the hospital of Santa Maria Nuova, who said he had seen in that place Lionardo of Pistoia, a very religious man of such great restraint that, by gradually increasing his fasting over time, he brought himself to eat only once a week. I believe we have spoken sufficiently of fasting. But it does not seem right to me to overlook the ornaments and oratorical power with which the Count, the author, has composed this speech; for it can move even the hardest heart to compassion. But so that the artistry may be better understood, let it be known that rhetoricians call "pathetic oratory" <note>original: "oratioē pathetica"; from the Greek "pathos" meaning emotion or suffering</note> that which moves the souls of the listeners either to anger and hatred, or to mercy and compassion; because *pathos* in Greek signifies passion and disturbance. Such a movement is stirred by various means. First, a great commiseration is stirred by the manner and the place. Thus, here he shows that such a death occurred in a dark tower, just as Virgil says: *And to scatter the youth across the wide fields* <note>Latin: "Et latos iuvenē spargere per agros"</note> and elsewhere, *He dragged him trembling to the very altars.* <note>Latin: "Altaria ad ipsa tremētē traxit"</note> Compassion is stirred by the manner. For it is hard to kill a man, but much more to kill him with hunger than with the sword. For this reason, Cicero laments the one who had been killed by the smoke of green wood. And Virgil: *He even joined dead bodies to living ones.* <note>Latin: "Mortua qn et iūgebat corpora uiuis"</note> Therefore, he moves the listener not just because he died, but because he died in prison and died of hunger. Furthermore, he presents the dream; just as Virgil: *Lo, in my sleep, most sorrowful Hector seemed to appear before my eyes and to shed many tears.* <note>Latin: "In somnis ecce āte oculos mestissimus Hector Visus adesse mihi largoscp effudere fletus"</note> Likewise: *But the very image of her unburied husband came in her sleep, lifting his pale face in a wondrous way.* <note>Latin: "Ipsa sed in somnis inhumati uenit imago Coniugis ora modis attollens pallida miris"</note> Nor is a calamity already anticipated told without compassion. Whence, most excellently, each one doubted because of his dream. Nor did Virgil overlook this: *I was not unaware how much new glory in arms [could do].* <note>Latin: "Haud ignarus eram quātu noua gloria in armis"</note> It also greatly disturbs to lose hope; and for this reason, it is a tearful thing when he says, "AND I heard the door below of the horrible tower being locked." Whence Sinon in Virgil says: *Nor do I have any hope now of seeing my ancient fatherland, nor my sweet children.* <note>Latin: "Nec mihi iā patriam antiquam spes ulla uidendi: Nec dulces natos"</note> Therefore, if we grieve for one who weeps, how much will we grieve for one who, through grief, cannot weep? The weeping of the children was a great sorrow to the father. It was a great sorrow to the children that the father could not weep. The length of time in which they were afflicted by hunger also moves us. Virgil often employs this device: *Whence they say he [wept] for seven whole months in a row* <note>Latin: "Vnde Septem illū totos perhibēt ex ordine mēses"</note> and in the story of Palinurus: *Scarcely on the fourth day did I look out at Italy from the top of a wave.* <note>Latin: "Vix lumine quarto prospexi Italiā fumma sublimis ab ūda"</note> Weakness also moves us. Whence he said: "And I, already blind, began to grope over each of them." Just as Virgil says of Mezentius: *He raises himself on his sick thigh.* <note>Latin: "Attollit in egrum se feinur"</note> Youthful age also moves us, as in Virgil: *Unhappy boy, and an unequal match for Achilles.* <note>Latin: "Infelix puer atcp impar congressus achilli"</note> Likewise, the sight of it: *As when youths are placed upon the funeral pyres before the eyes of their parents.* <note>Latin: "Vt impositi que rogis iuuenes ante ora parentum"</note> And because it gives greater pain to see a calamity than to hear of it, he said: "AND AS you see me, I saw the three fall." So Virgil: *And the most miserable things which I myself saw.* <note>Latin: "Queque ipse miserrima uidi"</note> I could show many other passages in this speech most apt for moving compassion. But with these, we might investigate the supreme artistry of the poet both here and in many other parts of the work.

When he had said this, with eyes askew,
he took up again that wretched skull with his teeth,
which were strong as a dog’s upon the bone.
Ah, Pisa, shame of the people
of the beautiful country where "sì" is heard,
since your neighbors are slow to punish you,
let Capraia and Gorgona move
and make a hedge for the Arno at its mouth,
so that it may drown every person within you!
For if Count Ugolino was rumored
to have betrayed you in your castles,
you should not have put his sons to such a cross.
Their youthful age made them innocent—
a New Thebes!—Uguccione and Brigata,
and the other two named in the song above.

<column-break/>

As soon as the Count had finished his story, he returned to biting the skull of his enemy. The poet feigns this because one who is injured, and the injury stays before the eyes of the one who injured him, is stimulated day and night and his conscience is bitten. AH PISA, shame of the people of the beautiful country where "sì" sounds: that is, the shame of the beautiful country of Italy in which "sì" is used for "yes." For just as the Frenchman says *oy* <note>modern French: "oui"</note>, and the German *io* <note>modern German: "ja"</note>, and the Greek *ne*—and certainly it is a shame to the Italians for not having punished such cruelty, a vice that is very abominable in the Italian nation, which more than others has always been humane and merciful. SINCE your neighbors are slow to punish you, let Capraia and Gorgona move. These are two small islands located in the sea not far from the mouth of the Arno. He wants these to block the Arno so that, unable to flow into the sea, it swells back into Pisa (through which it passes) and floods it. Count Ugolino, to establish his power, married two daughters, one to Count Guido di Battifolle and the other to Albrandino, Count of Santa Fiore. To Guido he gave Ripafratta as a dowry, and to Aldobrandino, Suvereto. FOR IF Count Ugolino was rumored: that is, he had a reputation. He speaks very artfully, first saying that it was a great cruelty to kill the Count without being certain of his betrayal; but let us concede that one should believe THE RUMOR <note>original: "ALLA VOCE"</note>, that is, the reputation, and for this reason he should be punished. Nevertheless, you should not have punished the children, especially with such a cross: that is, with such a heavy

martyrdom. And he gives the reason: because their "new" and tender age made them innocent, for they were still young children who neither thought of matters of state by themselves, nor were they summoned by their father to any of his councils. NEW THEBES. A city as cruel as Thebes was, in which the first founders, brothers born from the sown teeth of a serpent, killed each other; and the mother and aunts killed Pentheus. Athamas killed his son Learchus; Oedipus lived with his mother; Eteocles and Polynices, brothers, killed each other out of a lust for power. Then he shows that the age of the children was still "new" by naming Uguccione and Brigata, who were the two eldest; and the other two whom THE SONG ABOVE names <note>referring to the previous verses</note>. These were Gaddo and Anselmuccio. And he arranges the text thus: O New Thebes, the youthful age of Uguccione and Brigata and the other two whom the song names above made them innocent.

<margin>140</margin>
We passed further on, where the frost
roughly swaddles another people,
not turned downward, but all reversed.
The very weeping does not let them weep,
and the grief that finds a barrier upon the eyes
turns inward to increase the agony.

<column-break/>

This is the third ring, and it is called Ptolomea. Here the souls are held in the ice upside down; and the first tears that come out, because they cannot find release, freeze in the hollow of the eyes and form something like a crystal visor. Then those tears that follow, finding the exit closed, return inside and make the agony grow. And he devises this because here are punished those who, under the guise of benevolence and love, have betrayed. They have, therefore, shown a sign of charity so that the person they intended to betray would be less on guard...

# INFERNO.

For the first tears form a knot,
and like a crystal visor,
they fill the whole cavity beneath the brow.

And although, as if from a callus,
because of the cold, every sensation
had ceased to hold its place in my face:
It already seemed to me that I felt some wind,
wherefore I: "My Master, who moves this?
Is not every vapor extinguished down here?"
And he to me: "You will soon be where
your eye shall give you the answer,
seeing the cause that rains down the blast."

And one of the wretched of the cold crust
cried out to us: "O souls so cruel
that the last station has been given to you,
Lift from my face the hard veils,
so that I may vent the grief that impregnates my heart,
but only for a moment before the weeping freezes again."
Wherefore I to him: "If you wish me to help you,
tell me who you are; and if I do not release you,
may I be forced to go to the bottom of the ice."
He answered then: "I am Friar Alberigo;
I am he of the fruits of the evil garden,
who here receive a date for a fig." <note>This is a proverbial expression meaning he is being paid back with interest, or that his punishment is even greater than his crime.</note>

"O," I said to him, "are you already dead?"
And he to me: "How my body stays
in the world above, I have no knowledge.
Such a privilege has this Ptolomea,
that often the soul falls here
before Atropos <note>The Fate who cuts the thread of life.</note> grants it death.
And so that you may more willingly scrape
the glassy tears from my face,
know that as soon as the soul betrays,
As I did, its body is taken from it
by a demon, who thereafter governs it
until its full time has turned."

<column-break/>

**...betrayal:** And this is expressed by lying supine, which is to look upward toward heaven. But they are positioned in such a way that the tears cannot exit: because such charity is false. Therefore, the weeping does not allow them to weep, and the anguish increases: because that false charity increases the betrayal, wherefore it deserves greater punishment. **VISORS:** almost like eyeglasses. **THE WHOLE cavity:** all the concavity that is beneath the brow, in which the eyes are located.

<term>And</term> it happened that although every sensation had thus ceased—that is, removed its "stay" or dwelling from my face as if from a callus—meaning that my face had no more feeling in it than a callus has, which, because it is dead flesh, does not feel. And this happened to me because of the cold. In essence: although my face was so numbed by the cold that it felt neither cold nor heat any differently than a callus does, nevertheless it seemed to me that I felt some wind, at which I marveled. For wind is born from warm and dry vapors raised by certain stars, and especially by the sun; the power of which does not seem able to penetrate down into the center to resolve vapors into wind. **AND HE TO me: You will soon be where:** because the causes of many things cannot be seen with the eyes, nor felt with any consensus, it is necessary that they be demonstrated with natural reason. But where the sense perceives it for itself, reason is not needed. Therefore, the sense will demonstrate from whence this wind is caused. And it is a most subtle fiction: that just as in the highest heaven the Holy Spirit is born from divine power and wisdom, which inflames one toward charity—and for this reason is likened to fire and the southern wind—so from Lucifer proceeds the most frigid wind of pride, which kills every heat of charity, and hardens and freezes all human hearts.

<term>While</term> passing among the frozen ones, Friar Alberigo prays that Dante lift the ice from his eyes. And Dante promises to do so with a curse upon himself regarding what he intended to do anyway—and this was to go to the very bottom of Hell. **O SOULS Cruel:** since you do not help my pain. **SO MUCH that the last station is given to you.** He believed that Dante and Virgil were also damned for betrayal, and being newly arrived, were not yet placed where they were to stay. Wherefore he says **SO MUCH:** until such time as the last station—the final place where you must always stay—is given. **Lift the veil** that veils my eyes so that with tears I may vent the grief, which, not being vented, impregnates the heart. It shows that although they are damned, and those who have made a habit of betrayal sometimes wish to open the eyes of charity, the ice of pride and of God does not allow it. **I AM Friar Alberigo.** This man was of the Manfredi, lords of Faenza. And in his later years he became a "Jovial Friar" <note>A member of the *Ordo Militiae Mariae Gloriosae*, often criticized for corruption.</note>; wherefore he was called Friar Alberigo. And he was so cruel that, being in discord with his relatives and desiring to remove them from the earth, he feigned a wish to be reconciled with them. And after the peace was made, he invited them to a magnificent banquet; and at the end of the banquet, he commanded that the fruits be brought, which was the signal given to those who were to kill them. Therefore, they immediately leaped inside and killed all those whom Alberigo wished to die. Wherefore even in our days, proverbially, when we want to show someone has been struck, we say that they have had "Friar Alberigo’s fruit." Therefore he said "of the fruits of the evil garden," because it was a captive garden that gave such fruits. **WHO HERE receive a date for a fig:** for as much as the date is more excellent than the fig, so much greater is the punishment he receives here than that which he gave to his relatives when he killed them.

<term>To the</term> privilege. He spoke with irony. For beyond other evils, the traitor has this: that his soul comes to eternal pains before the time of his death arrives. And he feigns that a demon enters the body of the traitor and governs it until the appointed death. And by this he wishes to signify that the obstinacy of the traitor is so great that he never repents. This is also shown by the Evangelist regarding Judas, saying that after the betrayal the devil entered the body of Judas; and he, despairing, said: "My sin is greater than that I might deserve mercy." <note>original: "Maius est peccatum meū quā ut ueniam merear"</note> Therefore, notwithstanding that he lives many years after the act of betrayal, we can say that the soul is damned, because it is obstinate in sin; and a devil—that is, such obstinacy—governs the body, in a way that it seems to be a living man, but as for his character, he is a devil. **PTOLOMEA.** Just as the circle above was called Antenora after Antenor, so this is Ptolomea after Ptolemy. So that this may be better understood, we will repeat briefly from the Book of Maccabees how the Maccabees, after the times of Alexander the Great...

# CANTO XXXIII

How its body is taken from it
by a demon who thereafter governs it
until its full time has fully turned.
She <note>Referring to the soul.</note> falls headlong into such a cistern;
and perhaps the body still appears above,
belonging to the shade who winters here behind me.
You must know, if you have only just come down:
he is Sir Branca Doria, and many years
have passed since he was thus shut in."

"I believe," I said to him, "that you deceive me;
for Branca Doria has not died at all,
and he eats, and drinks, and sleeps, and wears clothes."
"In the ditch above," he said, "of the Malebranche <note>Literally "Evil Claws," the demons of the eighth circle who guard the barrators.</note>,
there where the tenacious pitch boils,
Michel Zanche had not yet arrived
When this man left a devil in his stead
within his body; and so did a kinsman of his
who committed the treachery along with him.
But reach out your hand here at last;
open my eyes." And I did not open them for him;
and to be churlish to him was a courtesy.

Ah, Genoese! Men estranged
from every good custom and full of every flaw,
why are you not scattered from the world?
For with the worst spirit of Romagna <note>Friar Alberigo, who is from the Romagna region.</note>
I found one of you who, for his deeds,
already bathes his soul in Cocytus,
and in body seems still alive above.

<column-break/>

Just as the upper circle was called Antenora after Antenor, so this one is called Ptolomea after Ptolemy. In order that this may be better understood, we shall briefly repeat from the Book of the Maccabees: how the Maccabees reigned in Israel after the time of Alexander the Great. There were three brothers adorned with most excellent virtues: Judas Maccabeus, Jonathan, and Simon. Successively, they were high priests and most valiant in deeds of arms. Especially Simon, who with the greatest justice and strength defended the liberty of the Hebrew people against many kings and renewed the alliance with the Romans. This man had a son-in-law, Ptolemy son of Abubus, who was entirely unlike his good father-in-law, being wicked and impious toward the one who had so honored him. Having been appointed governor in Jericho by Simon, and trusting in his great treasures, he dared to attempt with ultimate wickedness to seize the principality and the high priesthood from his father-in-law. Simon came to Jericho 

with two sons, and Ptolemy received them most magnificently with a splendid banquet; at the end of it, he had the old man and his sons and all the others who had come with him murdered. <term>ATROPOS</term>. The poets propose three Fates, which they call <term>Parcae</term>. Through them, they demonstrate the beginning, the progress, and the end of human life. Thus, the first, signifying our birth, is called Clotho, who holds the spindle with the thread. The second is called Lachesis, because *lanchanō* <note>original: "lanchano"</note> in Greek means to allot or distribute; for to every man who is born, she gives his lot—that is, the portion of life that falls to him. AND THEREFORE they imagine that she spins the thread held by Clotho, because she produces the course of life. The third denotes the end of the course, which is death; wherefore they imagine that she breaks and snaps the threads of Lachesis and call her Atropos; because *a* in Greek means "not" and *trepin* <note>original: "trepin"</note> means "to turn," because death does not turn nor bend for anyone’s pleading and spares no one. Rather, she is immobile and inflexible. The ancient Latin poets called these three Parcae: Nona, Decima, and Morta. THE TIME has fully turned: He rightly said "turned," because time is nothing other than the measure of motion, and it is born from the revolution and circuit of the planets, and especially the sun, which in the revolution it makes through the twelve signs creates the year. And perhaps the body of the shade which "winters me"—that is, remains in the cold here behind me—still stays above: As if to say, he keeps himself alive through a demon who governs him. And you should know it, if you come down to Hell "just now"—that is, just recently. HE IS SIR Branca Doria. This Sir Branca was a Genoese of the Doria house, the son-in-law of Sir Zanche, lord of Logudoro in Sardinia, who was mentioned above in the ditch of the pitch. To gain his lordship, he invited his father-in-law to dinner and had him murdered. Therefore Dante imagines that immediately after the treachery, his soul was dragged to Hell and a devil entered his body; for indeed, when Dante wrote this, Sir Branca was still alive. And he said "Ser" <note>Sir</note> and not "Messere" <note>Lord</note> in derision, because the Genoese call every gentleman "Messere." Or truly, he induces this Romagnuolo to speak thus because it is their nature not to honor anyone with words.

In these verses, not much exposition is required. For Dante does not believe that Branca Doria is dead, having seen his body performing all the functions of the living; and the spirit answers him what was already said above, and shows that his kinsman, who committed the murder and treachery alongside him, Michel Zanche, is also with him in this way. BUT EXTEND your hand at last: This shows that when the spirit asked him for his promise, Dante did not observe it for him. By this, he wishes to suggest that we should not keep any promise that goes against justice. And here, the ultimate injustice was to impede divine justice. Furthermore, it is not wrong to draw out the truth from someone by using cunning, especially while observing one's oath. For Dante said to him, "if I do not release you, may I be forced to go to the bottom," and so he shall go <note>Dante's oath was a clever trick: since he was already going to the very bottom of Hell as a traveler, he wasn't technically lying, even though he had no intention of helping the sinner.</note>. And he concludes that in such men, it is the highest courtesy to be churlish.

A worthy and well-placed exclamation against the Genoese people for many reasons, which I do not set down at present to avoid using invectives against my custom, but they are known to all. MEN Estranged from every custom: because you are alien and contrary to every good custom. And full of every flaw: just as a man is not completely good if he merely avoids vice but does not practice virtue, so one cannot be called an absolute captive to sin if he is merely alien to virtue but does not practice vice. And therefore, wishing to show the Genoese to be completely captive to sin, he said "full of every flaw." WHY ARE YOU Not: He marvels at how divine justice suffers them and does not extinguish them. But as Valerius writes: "For with a slow step the divine wrath proceeds, and it compensates for the slowness of the punishment with its severity." <note>original: "Lento enim gradu divina procedit ira tarditatemque supplicii gravitate compensat."</note> FOR WITH THE worst spirit of Romagna: This is a great intensification in this comparison. In order that this may be better understood, it is a universal reputation that the Romagnuoli are of the worst customs. Whence the 

---

Tuscan proverb: "Red Lombard, black Romagnuolo, of every hair." <note>A proverb suggesting that while certain types of people are bad, a Romagnuolo is bad in every possible way.</note> Therefore, if a Genoese is worse than a Romagnuolo, one cannot climb any higher in vice.

## CANTO 34 OF THE FIRST CANTICLE BY DANTE.

"The banners of the King of Hell come forth <note>original: "Vexilla regis prodeunt inferni." This is a parody of a Latin hymn used in the liturgy for the Passion of Christ.</note>
toward us; therefore, look ahead,"
my master said, "if you can discern him."
As when a thick fog breathes,
or when our hemisphere grows dark,
a mill that the wind turns appears from afar,
such a structure I then seemed to see;
then because of the wind I shrank back
behind my leader, for there was no other shelter:

<note>This passage explains that the intellect and doctrine did not provide a defense against such a bitter vice. There are three winds from three wings: Ingratitude, Cruelty, and Hatred. Against these vices, there is no other escape than to have Reason as your shield and protection, which opposes those three with three virtues: Gratitude, Pity, and Charity.</note>

I was already—and with fear I put it into verse—
where the shadows were all covered,
and shone through like straw in glass.
Some are lying down, others stand upright,
this one with the head, and that one with the soles,
another like a bow, turning the face to the feet.

<note>In the ice of cruelty and ingratitude. "I was already, and with fear I put it into verse": He says this as if he trembles even while writing it, capturing the reader's attention by showing the magnitude of the thing, which causes horror just to consider it.</note>

When we had moved so far forward
that it pleased my master to show me
the creature who once had the fair semblance,
he stepped away from before me and made me stop.
"Behold Dis," <note>Dis is another name for Lucifer or Satan, derived from Roman mythology.</note> he said, "and behold the place
where you must arm yourself with fortitude."
How frozen and faint I then became,
do not ask, reader, for I do not write it,
because all speech would be insufficient.
I did not die, and I did not remain alive;
think now for yourself, if you have a grain of wit,
what I became, deprived of both.
The emperor of the sorrowful kingdom
from the mid-chest stood out of the ice;
and I am more comparable to a giant
than giants are to his arms:
see now how great that whole must be
which conforms to such a part.
If he was as beautiful as he is now ugly,
and lifted his brows against his Maker,
well must all grief proceed from him.

<column-break/>

We have arrived—which will be for our salvation—at the depths of Hell and the fourth ring of the ninth circle; which is named <term>Judecca</term> after Judas Iscariot, the first and greatest of all traitors. Virgil speaks to Dante, saying *Vexilla regis inferni prodeunt* (the banners of the infernal king appear and are already seen). Therefore, look ahead if you can discern him; he calls the wings of Lucifer "banners." Then, by comparison, he describes his appearance. Pluto <note>The commentator here uses "Pluto" interchangeably with Lucifer.</note> appeared as a windmill turned by the wind appears when seen in a thick fog, or when night falls in our hemisphere. He saw Lucifer in the darkness because diabolical temptation does not appear except in hidden ways. **THEN BECAUSE OF THE WIND:** To flee the three winds that proceed from the three wings of Lucifer, having no other shelter, he pulled back behind Virgil. And certainly Dante, who represents sensuality, would freeze in the wind stirred by Pluto if Virgil,

who is the intellect and doctrine, did not provide a shield against such a bitter vice.

He describes four types of punishment: one for those who lie flat and face down; and these are the traitors who have betrayed their equals. The second for those who stand with their feet up and head down; and these have betrayed their superiors, such as lords, masters, and those of any higher rank. The third for those who, contrary to these, stand with their feet down and their head up, which denotes that they have betrayed their inferiors. The fourth for those who equally betray superiors and inferiors; and these are shaped like a bow with their head and feet down. And all lie supine because they have used treachery brazenly and without shame. Thus they stand.

When we were so far forward that it pleased Virgil to show me Lucifer—who, before he sinned, was very beautiful—he stepped out from in front of me, whereas before I had stayed behind him to escape the wind. **DIS:** He calls the prince of darkness Dis. We discussed this name when we identified Pluto. **BEHOLD THE PLACE** where it is necessary to arm yourself with fortitude: because there is no place so horrifying to sensuality and to lower reason as this one. It is difficult for sensuality to resist any vice because, through the contagion of the body and through temptation, it is easily inclined toward it. But there is no vice that one can conquer with greater difficulty than **PRIDE** (*superbia*). For there is born in man a certain haughtiness which wishes to obey no one and seeks to be superior to every man. If this is done according to virtue, it is fortitude; if without reason, it is pride, a vice entirely intolerable, from which infinite vices proceed. And therefore he says, do not ask how I became frozen and faint, because such haughtiness deprives us of all fire of charity; hence we remain cold and, through the cold, faint. Lucifer emerged from the middle of his chest upward. And he says "I compare you" <note>original: "ti conuengo"</note>—I promise you—that what was seen was more than a giant; and he gives the reason, saying that giants do not "make," meaning they do not match or equal the arms of Lucifer. Therefore, consider how great the rest must be to be proportioned to what is seen. But of his greatness, we spoke in the topography of Hell. **IF HE WAS SO BEAUTIFUL:** He states with a condition what our religion affirms absolutely. Because he lifted his brows—that is, he rose up in pride against his Maker—divine justice requires that as much as he was higher than the others, so much should he be put lower; and as much as he was beautiful, so much should he be ugly. But since the poet mentions Lucifer now, we will say with extreme brevity a few things about the nature of demons. And first, let it not be unknown to us that in the beginning, the production and creation of the

---

good angels and those who rain from heaven into Hell was the same. For as **Albertus** <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a prominent medieval philosopher and theologian.</note> writes in his *Compendium of Theology*, God made all angels good, though not supreme. But placed between the Supreme Good and mutable good, in such a way that by turning themselves to love God—who is the Good above them—they could rise to a state of grace. But by turning themselves to mutable good—which is a good inferior to them—for this they had to fall into the evil of guilt and punishment.

<meta>This page transitions from the general description of the frozen center of Hell to a detailed theological and physical analysis of Lucifer himself. It continues the commentary on Canto 34, moving from the movement toward the center to the specific attributes of the fallen angel.</meta>

...which is not the ignominy of sin without the ornament of justice. The ruin of the devil was twofold: because he fell both from his dignity and from the place in which he was created. He fell from dignity because he fell from the strength of his nature. He fell from the flexibility of free will toward the changeable good. From light into darkness; from knowledge into ignorance; from innocence into guilt; from happiness into pain; from love into hatred. Because after his fall, he became impotent and obstinate in evil, blinded to the truth, disordered in good, weakened in virtue, and excluded from divine contemplation. Furthermore, his impious will turned to hatred of man and to envy. For this reason, with every effort, he strives to subvert humanity, even with various temptations. And as for his local ruin, he fell from heaven where he was created into Hell, or into the gloomy air which is in the middle, between the part near the earth and the upper part near the sphere of fire. Nor did God wish for the demons to be in the upper part, so that they might not enjoy much light; nor even in the lower part, so that they would not be too close to harm us. Some say that the demons fell from heaven on the second day. But the approved opinion is that of those who write that they fell immediately after their creation. It is believed that a tenth choir of angels fell—not because there were ten choirs, but so many fell from each choir that they could constitute a whole choir. There are nine choirs of angels, and each choir has its legions, and each legion has six thousand six hundred sixty-six angels. And there are as many legions in each choir as there are angels in each legion. I could cite many reasons from Augustine and Damascene <note>referring to St. Augustine and St. John of Damascus, prominent Church Fathers</note> and other doctors by which they prove the sin of the devil to be unpardonable. But returning to those matters, we shall say that demons are impure spirits, enemies of the human race, possessing a rational mind. They are subtle in every iniquity, eager to do harm, puffed up with pride, and always intent on fraud. They distort the senses, corrupt the affections, disturb the waking, and disquiet the sleeping with dreams. They induce diseases and stir up tempests. They transform themselves into good angels. They always carry their own hell with them. They do not usurp divine power. Through them, the magic arts are performed. They lay snares for the good. They possess a triple sharpness of mind: they have natural brilliance through evening cognition <note>original: "vespertina cognitione," a scholastic term for knowledge of created things</note>; they have the experience of long time; and they have revelations from the superior spirits. By the first way, they understand present natural things; by the second, future things; and by the third, the secrets of the will. He is named Devil, which in Greek means "calumniator." He is named Belial, that is, "without a yoke" or "without a master," because he always rebels against Him. He is named Demon from his knowledge, because in Greek it means "to know." He is named Beelzebub, that is, "man of flies," which refers to sinful souls who abandon Christ, the true spouse. Also, Satan, that is, "adversary." Also, Behemoth, that is, "beast." Also, Leviathan, that is, the "addition" of those who pile sin upon sin. Lucifer was of the first order of the supreme hierarchy, and in that held the highest rank. To him, as to a prince, many from all the choirs attached themselves, whom he pulled with him into ruin. This one was blinded by the consideration of his own beauty. He tempted the first man, that is, Adam, and defeated him. He tempted the second, that is, Christ, and was defeated. The sin of Lucifer was that he loved his own private good; and he was presumptuous of the height received from God as if he held his excellence from himself and not from another. He desires to be like God, not to imitate Him, but to have power; he wished to have subjects and not be subject to any other. And it is fitting that, the demon being an incorporeal and rational substance, his punishment is intellectual. And his torment proceeds especially from his location. For just as an aquatic animal stays upon the land and out of the water not without pain, and a terrestrial animal in the water, so the nature of the demon, created in heaven—his natural place—cannot inhabit the center of the earth, the opposite and contrary to heaven, without the greatest pain. The devils are obstinate in evil because, the angel having been created with free will, justice requires that just as God confirmed the good angel in grace who chose the good, so He confirmed the wicked one in his evil purpose who by his free will chose the evil. Therefore, he remains obstinate in it.

> O how great a marvel it seemed to me
> when I saw three faces on his head!
> One in front, and that one was crimson;
> Of the other two, which were joined to this one
> above the middle of each shoulder,
> and they joined at the top of the crest:
> The right one seemed between white and yellow;
> the left one to look at was such as

> Beneath each one came forth two great wings,
> as was fitting for such a bird;

<column-break/>

The conclusion made by all theologians is that every vice proceeds from Lucifer. Therefore, the author depicts him with a crest; and such a crest signifies Pride and its daughter, Envy. The three faces are the other three spiritual sins: Wrath, Avarice, and Sloth. The red face denotes Wrath, which is the inflammation of the blood; wherefore he deservedly makes it red. The face between white and yellow is sallow, and it denotes Avarice, because the miser so diminishes his food that he is always thin and pale; and he is always in great fear of losing his acquired riches, from which he likewise becomes pale. The third is black, by which Sloth <note>original: "accidia"</note> is best understood, which proceeds from the melancholic humor, which is black; it never rejoices, nor does it ever clear the face, and it always remains dark. Each face has two eyes, and these are two disordered perspectives. In Wrath, the right eye is too much regard for one's own good, and the left is too much regard for fleeing evil. In Avarice, one is too much for conserving your own, and the other too much for seeking that of others. Similarly, Sloth regards fleeing labor and taking rest. The two wings are two incitements and liftings. For Wrath has agitation and fury, from which proceeds the wind of Cruelty. Avarice has rapacity and tenacity, and from this is the wind of Ingratitude. Sloth has sadness and negligence, and from here is the wind of Hatred. These three winds—Cruelty, Ingratitude, and Hatred—freeze Cocytus and extinguish Charity, Pity, and Knowledge. The size of the wings signifies the excessive stirrings of the soul. Each face has its mouth because each of these vices devours and torments those who fall into it. The tears on the chin signify repentance at the end and after the deed is done.

# CANTO XXXIII

<note>original: "cifero"</note> Lucifer is like one of the birds that fly at night; and night represents ignorance. This denotes that our ignorance is what gives way to diabolical temptations. And for this reason, we are admonished that we should walk while we have the light, so that the darkness does not catch us. **WITH SIX** eyes he wept: because all those six excessive elevations <note>This likely refers to the six stages of pride or fallen nature discussed in medieval theology.</note> repent after the sin has been committed. **DOWN THREE** chins the tears dripped. By the chin, which is the last part of the face, you should understand that repentance which occurs only at the end and after the sin has been committed. **AND BLOODY** foam: Because as he crushes the sinners, it is natural that the blood drips. And allegorically we shall say that from pride proceed the most cruel killings.

From every mouth he shattered with his teeth
a sinner in the manner of a hemp-brake
so that he made three of them feel such pain
To the one in front, the biting was nothing
compared to the clawing, for at times his back
remained completely stripped of skin
"That soul up there who has the greatest punishment,"
said the Master, "is Judas Iscariot,
who has his head inside and kicks his legs outside.
Of the other two who have their heads down,
the one hanging from the dark face is Brutus—
see how he writhes and says not a word;
And the other is Cassius, who looks so sturdy;
but night is rising again, and now
it is time to depart, for we have seen everything."

<column-break/>

**H**e shattered with his teeth from every mouth a sinner **In the manner:** in the form **Of a hemp-brake.** <term>Maciulla</term> <note>A hemp-brake (maciulla) is a wooden tool used to crush the stalks of flax or hemp to separate the fibers from the hard outer husk.</note> is what they call an instrument with which they break [the stalks] so that the husk and the exterior part (which alone they spin to use for cloth) may be separated from the hard wood. **JUDAS** Iscariot: who for thirty coins betrayed Christ to the Jews. Most ungratefully, therefore, he deceived his best and most generous master, though he had been raised to such a high degree as a disciple. He deceived the Creator of all creatures and led Him to the ignominious death of the cross—the very One who desired to raise him to the highest heaven and establish him in eternal glory. He killed the One who had come to resurrect him and the others dead in sin. The most cruel servant killed his Lord, in whom there was such mercy that He would have forgiven him even then if he had turned to penance. Therefore, no greater cruelty can be imagined in a creature, nor greater clemency in the Creator. Of these two—the unheard-of wickedness and the ineffable clemency—I shall not speak at present because I could not express in words as much as I conceive in my mind. But it is a most just judgment that Lucifer, most ungrateful for such privilege received from God and worthy of the place and the punishment in which the poet places him for his greater torment, should torture those who deserved no lesser executioner, nor a lesser henchman. Thus, the greatest of the chosen sinners punishes the greatest of the sinners of the earth. And the highest God, through His

---

enemies, takes just vengeance upon His enemies. **BRUTUS:** It was a fitting thing that, just as Lucifer tortured Judas, the traitor of the divine Emperor, so too should he punish those who had betrayed the human emperor and monarch. And because by the common consent of the Christian name it is established that the Roman Emperor is the head of the temporal administration of the entire Christian republic, just as the Pope is in the spiritual administration, [Dante] places Caesar first. He does so not for the sake of Caesar himself—who, not being just, could not be a just emperor—but for the sake of the Empire. And Brutus and Cassius, who kill him, are not placed there for Brutus and Cassius the men, but for those who kill the true monarch. Just as in Purgatory he places Cato—who according to our faith can in no way be saved—not for the soul of Cato, but for the Liberty of which he was the fiercest defender. And certainly, it would have been unheard-of cruelty and entirely alien to the doctrine and equity of such a great poet to place in eternal, heavy punishment those who, out of most ardent charity, gave themselves to death to free their homeland from the yoke of servitude. If they had been Christians, they would have acquired a most honorable seat in the highest heaven. I do not deny that Caesar was adorned with many varied and excellent virtues; but as soon as such savage impiety was born in him that, in the hope of seizing tyranny, he crossed the Rubicon river, he turned from an excellent man into a most cruel beast. And with this single wickedness, he submerged and extinguished all the benefits for which Rome confessed herself his debtor. Therefore, Brutus and Cassius do not kill that Caesar who, with most laborious labor of ten years and with horrific difficulties and gravest dangers, acquired for the Roman people all of Gaul, all of Germany, and Britain (which we call England). They do not kill that Caesar who in ten years and in various battles killed with his victorious armies one million one hundred ninety-two thousand men who were enemies to the Roman name. They do not kill that Caesar in whom there was supreme liberality, unheard-of clemency, most ornate eloquence, and much varied learning. But they kill the one who, most ungratefully, turned the forces he had received from his homeland against that very homeland. The one who most wickedly took away the liberty of the one he was supposed to defend. And certainly, what can be a greater virtue than to avenge the wrongs of the homeland? For her sake, every good citizen is bound not to spare his property, nor his children, nor his own life. O excellent men, entirely worthy of having Rome as a homeland, and of whom an eternal memory will always remain! Let all the laws of any well-constituted republic be read, and we will find that no greater reward is offered to anyone than to him who kills the tyrant. But someone might say that I am acting against my purpose by reproaching the poet in this place. I do not reproach him in any way; but I have wished to demonstrate his intended meaning, so that no one, through a false opinion, should think that he truly wants to damn Brutus. It is not difficult to believe that, just as Trajan’s justice moved Gregory to such compassion that with prayers already foreseen by God he brought him from damnation to supreme happiness, so someone else accepted by God may have done the same for Brutus. **BUT NIGHT IS RISING AGAIN:** One night and part of the following day were consumed in searching through Hell. And deservedly so: because the night, which signifies ignorance, leads to vice; but he who must exit stays there during the day, because with the light of reason and doctrine it is necessary to know the nature of vice—which, once known, causes us to flee from it. In the beginning of the book he said, "The day was departing." And in the twentieth canto he shows that the day was being born; and at present, that part of that day has passed. And this place has a similarity to the verses of Virgil:
> Night rushes on, Aeneas, while we spend the hours in weeping.
<note>original: "Nox ruit Eneas nos flendo ducimus horas." — Aeneid VI, 539</note>
Thinking carefully about this journey feigned by the poet, I believe they had already consumed the entire night in Hell, in the beginning of which they made their entry, and part of the following day, for the reason I demonstrated a little above. And having already arrived at Lucifer, who is in the very center, Virgil admonishes Dante that it is good to exit from Hell—which is nothing other than passing the center. Once that center is passed, immediately that space of the day that remained to them in Hell (which is in our hemisphere) became night in that other hemisphere; and through that...

# INFERNO

They went from the center up to the surface where they found Cato <note>Cato the Younger, the guardian of the shores of Purgatory.</note>. And then, as night was falling there, the day began on the other side. Therefore, from the beginning of Hell until the beginning of the plain of Purgatory, they consumed one natural day of twenty-four hours. But because the day that came after the night was as long then as the time they found themselves on this side of the center—and as much night as they consumed from the center until they reached Cato—they spent one night, half a day, and half a night. Although elsewhere we have suggested two continuous nights without the interposition of day.

As it pleased him, I clasped my arms around his neck,
and he took advantage of the time and place;
and when the wings were opened wide enough,
He laid hold of the shaggy flanks;
from tuft to tuft he then descended
between the thick hair and the frozen crusts.
When we had reached the point where the thigh
turns exactly upon the thick of the haunch,
the leader, with great labor and anxiety,
Turned his head to where he had his legs <note>original: "zanche"</note>,
and grappled onto the hair like a man who climbs,
so that I thought I was returning back to Hell.
"Hold on tight, for by such stairs as these,"
said the master, panting like a weary man,
"must we depart from so much evil."
Then he emerged through the opening of a rock
and placed me on its edge to sit;
then he directed his cautious step toward me.

I raised my eyes and thought I would see
Lucifer as I had left him,
and instead I saw him holding his legs upward;
And if I then became perplexed,
let the common folk <note>original: "gente grossa"</note> imagine it, who do not see
what that point was that I had passed.
"Rise up," said the master, "on your feet;
the way is long and the road is difficult,
and already the sun returns to mid-third." <note>term: "mid-third" (meza terza) — roughly 7:30 AM, halfway between sunrise and the "third hour" of 9:00 AM.</note>

...which he cannot walk unless he first purges himself of the vices he has recognized. The intellect shows him this and further admonishes him that the way is long and difficult. Because to make a habit of the moral virtues once one has left the habit of vice is very difficult. **AND NOW** the sun. Here it denotes that if it was night in the other hemisphere, it means the sun had gone below. Therefore, it had risen in this other one and was returning to mid-third. Thus, they spent all the rest of this day—which was night on the other side—until they reached Cato. Nor is it without reason that they made that journey in the night. Because, notwithstanding that we have already exited from vice, nonetheless until we arrive at the purgatorial virtues, we are always in the darkness of ignorance.

It was no palace hallway,
there where we were, but a natural hollow <note>original: "burella"</note>
which had a bad floor and a lack of light.
"Before I tear myself away from the abyss,"
I said, my master, when I had stood up,
"to draw me out of error, speak to me a little:
Where is the ice? And how is he fixed
so upside down? And how in so little time
has the sun made its transit from evening to morning?"

<column-break/>

Virgil wanted Dante to cling to his neck and clasp him, that is, encircle him with his arms; and then he waited until Lucifer had his wings raised and then descended down the flanks, clinging to his tufts of hair. And he did this, feet first, until the beginning of Lucifer’s thigh. And having reached here, he turned himself around, putting his head where he had his feet, to demonstrate that here he had to climb; because he was passing the center and had passed into the other hemisphere where it was necessary to climb by clinging to the hair of Lucifer's flanks and legs. He posits that Lucifer, whose stature we have described, is in the lowest part of the world, which is the center of the earth. But because the center is an indivisible point and cannot contain such a large body, it happens that he has his middle at the center. And from the middle to the head, he remains in our hemisphere. Therefore, it was necessary for the poets, who were descending from the surface of the earth in our hemisphere, to descend along Lucifer's body until the middle, which was at the center. And then, having passed the center and wanting to mount into the other hemisphere, they climbed along the rest of the body until the feet. **WATCH OUT.** It is necessary that the appetite and the lower reason cling to the higher. **PANTING.** This shows that even the higher reason labors; and it is difficult to exit from Hell and from ignorance. **HE EXITS** by Lucifer's hair. Because the consideration of the deformity of Lucifer, and of the beauty in which he existed before, pulls our soul out of Hell. **HAVING EXITED** outside: according to the history, we understand that when Lucifer was cast out of heaven and condemned to the center of the earth, it was necessary for him to pierce the rock that hindered him until his middle passed the center. And allegorically, whoever is in Hell, which is the damnation of vices, has formed a habit of vice. This can be compared to a rock. **HE PLACED ME** to sit: before the soul entirely leaves Hell, it is necessary for reason to set down—that is, to steady—the sensuality outside, and then proceed toward it.
Having exited from the point that is from the circumference, one no longer flows downward but begins to climb to the other hemisphere. Therefore, Lucifer held his navel at the center; and from the navel upward, he stood upright in the hemisphere where Hell was; and from the navel downward, he stood upright in the other hemisphere. Thus, anyone who does not know the nature of the center and passed through it, departing from Lucifer's head, would wonder why his legs were turned upward. And therefore, the common folk can consider how much he marvels. **RISE UP** on your feet. Since Dante—that is, sensuality and appetite—has exited from the depth of Hell, which is the habit of vice, it is necessary that he sit and steady himself for a while, and no longer feel desire until reason shows him that he should rise, that is, turn himself to desire better things. And this is the knowledge of divine things...

Palace hallway <note>original: "caminata di palagio"</note>. Hallways in Lombardy are called *caminate*. Therefore, it was not a palace hall, because palace halls are usually level and bright, and that path was dark and uneven. It was dark because at the beginning, the way of virtue is unknown to one who has been in vice in the past, and it is very difficult. But a natural hollow: *burella* signifies a narrow and dark place; hence in Florence, a narrow street not far from the Praetor's palace is called *Burella*. **IT HAD** a bad floor: because it was uneven and steep and rugged. **WHERE** is the ice: Dante seemed to have returned to our hemisphere from which he had descended, rather than having climbed to the other. And this error made him wonder how, having been in the evening a short while before, he now found himself in the morning; and having seen Lucifer with his head up, he now saw him with his legs up.

<summary>Dante and Virgil pass through the center of the Earth, experiencing a shift in gravity and time as they move from the northern to the southern hemisphere. The commentary explains the physical transition alongside the allegorical journey from vice toward virtue.</summary>
<keywords>Lucifer, center of gravity, hemispheres, mid-third, spiritual ascent, burella, reason and appetite</keywords>
