<meta>This page concludes the final canto of the Inferno. Following the previous page where Dante and Virgil began their climb down Lucifer’s body, they have now passed the center of the universe and are ascending toward the surface of the southern hemisphere.</meta>

# CANTO XXXIII.
<page-num>XXXIII.</page-num>
<sig>aa</sig>

And he said to me: “You imagine you are still
on the other side of the center, where I took hold
of the hair of the evil worm that bores through the world:
You were on that side for as long as I descended;
when I turned myself, you passed the point
to which weights are drawn from every side.
And now you have arrived beneath the hemisphere
opposite to that which the great dry land
covers, and beneath whose peak was consumed
The man who was born and lived without sin <note>Refers to Jesus Christ.</note>;
you have your feet upon a little sphere
that forms the other face of the Judecca <note>The final zone of the ninth circle of Hell.</note>.
Here it is morning when it is evening there;
and he who made a ladder for us with his hair
is still fixed just as he was before.
On this side he fell down from heaven;
and the earth, which before stood out on this side,
for fear of him made a veil of the sea,
And came to our hemisphere; and perhaps
to flee from him, that land which appears on this side
left this place empty and rushed upward.”
There is a place down there as far removed from Beelzebub
as the tomb <note>Hell is described here as the eternal tomb of the damned.</note> extends,
which is known not by sight but by the sound
Of a little stream that descends there
through the hollow of a rock that it has worn away
with its winding course that slopes but little.
My leader and I, by that hidden path,
entered to return to the bright world;
and without caring to have any rest,
We climbed up, he first and I second,
so far that I saw the beautiful things
that heaven carries, through a round opening,
And then we emerged to see the stars again.

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Decorative historiated drop cap initial 'T' containing a figure in robes seated at a desk, representing the commentator or author.</image-desc>**You** imagine you are still on that side. He calls "that side" our hemisphere: because he feigns, as you have seen, to be in that which is opposite to us. **OF THE WORM** that bores through the world, as we said above: You were on that side while I descended as far as the thighs. But when I turned here and placed my head where I had my feet, I passed the center or point which—because in a spherical body it is equally distant from every surface—comes to be at the lowest part. And because the nature of heavy things is to go downward, weights are drawn to that point, and heavy things from every part of the circumference come there.
**AND IF** now you have arrived beneath the hemisphere. You are not in the hemisphere that covers the earth inhabited by men. **WHERE WAS BORN** the man without sin, and lived without sin: and he means Christ, who was consumed (that is, died) to recover us. And he silently signifies that he was crucified in our hemisphere and in Jerusalem, and not in the other hemisphere as Origen heretically writes. And he denotes Jerusalem as being almost the center of the earth. **YOU HAVE** your feet upon a little sphere. He means that the place where Dante was was a circle around the center as far from that hemisphere as the one that forms the Judecca in our hemisphere. **Here it is morning** when it is evening there: You must not, therefore, marvel if at present you see the sun in the east, whereas a little before you saw it in the west: because, having passed the center, you are in the opposite hemisphere. For when the sun goes beneath us, it begins to rise in the other hemisphere.
**FIXED** in the ice, or if you will, in the rock, as he was before; his state has not changed. But you have changed your place, and having passed the center, you are above. **A PLACE** is down there. He shows that from the center where Beelzebub <note>original: "Belzabu"</note> (that is, Lucifer) is, to the surface of the other hemisphere, is as much space as the tomb extends (that is, as much as Hell extends, which is the eternal burial place of the damned). Therefore, because Hell is from the surface of our earth to the center, it follows that the same space exists from the center where Beelzebub is to the surface of the other hemisphere where Cato <note>Cato the Younger, the guardian of Purgatory.</note> is. But this place is not known by sight because it is dark, but by sound: because by the echo of the river that falls there, one imagines the distance. **Of a little stream**. This is the one that he feigned in the 14th Canto <note>The source text says xiii (13), but the origin of the rivers is discussed in Canto XIV.</note> comes into the world and goes into Hell. And from this are born Acheron, Styx, and Phlegethon; and then it descends into the center of the earth and enters the bottom of the pit in this place that the author feigns here, and it makes Cocytus, which freezes because of Lucifer’s wings. This little stream comes up from the world and from the other infernal rivers that it creates and spreads into the pit. Through the hole of a rock that is worn away. By the course that there: that is, it winds around that rock because it descends by turning through the circles of Hell; and sometimes crossing over as was shown above. But here it turned around the pit somewhat and sloped little, because it fell from a small height.
**HIDDEN PATH**: dark because of the shadows. **They returned to the bright world** without caring to rest. He says this because, having recognized our vices, we must go without intermission to the purgatorial virtues. **To see the stars again**. To see the sky again: because he who leaves Hell (that is, from vices) returns to see the stars (that is, he leaves the bestial life and returns to the human life), which is produced to contemplate celestial things. Now, by the grace of God, the author returns from Hell, and here he describes the place from which he exited and the manner of exiting.
**PLACE** is down there: beyond the center. **REMOVED** from Beelzebub: distant from Lucifer. **AS MUCH** as the tomb extends. He calls "tomb" the vacuum he has placed around Lucifer: that is, the ninth circle already called by him a "pit," which goes to the bottom, the bank of which he made of giants, and inside he put the traitors. Now he shows this pit to be round. And as much in that hemisphere to which they had to ascend as in ours, where they had descended as far as Lucifer. They went, therefore, through this tomb to the surface and there they emerged through a round hole onto an island surrounded by the ocean; and in it, he places an extremely high mountain, in which Purgatory is found step by step; and at the summit is the Paradise of Delights <note>The Earthly Paradise or Eden.</note>.

<meta>Continuing from the end of the Inferno (Canticle I), where the narrator and Virgil have just emerged from the center of the earth to see the stars again. This page begins Cristoforo Landino’s famous 1481 commentary on the second part of the Divine Comedy, the Purgatorio.</meta>

<header>PURGATORY.</header>

# PROLOGUE BY CRISTOFORO LANDINO, FLORENTINE, IN THE COMMENTARY ON THE DIVINE POET DANTE ALIGHIERI REGARDING THE PURGATORY, THE SECOND CANTICLE.

<image-desc>A large ornamental drop cap 'D' begins the main text. The letter itself is white and set against a square block decorated with complex interlacing strapwork and floral motifs in red, orange, and yellow ink.</image-desc>

IT DELIGHTS ME, AND DELIGHTS ME EXCEEDINGLY, Most Serene Highness, to have partly emerged from the outer darkness of the work where we witnessed inconsolable weeping. There, through the cold of the northern wind stirred by the eternal motion of the seat of Beelzebub <note>Beelzebub is another name for Lucifer or the Devil, placed at the frozen center of Dante's Hell.</note>, we heard the gnashing of teeth. I hope this has frightened our minds with such terror that we shall never return there. May it please you thus, Almighty Jupiter, ruler of the high Olympus <note>original: "Iuppiter omnipotes summi regnator olympi." Landino, a Renaissance humanist, often uses classical names like "Jupiter" to refer to the Christian God.</note>: you who are Three and One, with your supreme power, infinite wisdom, and unspeakable love, lend your light to those who walk through the darkness, so they may be led to where every servant becomes free. And after gaining that freedom, having been recalled from a most happy exile by the right of return <note>original: "iure post liminii," a legal term for regaining one's status upon returning from captivity or exile.</note> and restored to his most sweet fatherland, which is Jerusalem, the city above. There we are neither pilgrims nor foreigners, but citizens of the saints and members of the household, family, and noble courtiers of the King, whom all kings serve, and by serving, they reign. His kingdom, just as it was without beginning, so shall it be without end. There we shall rest in the life that is without death; where for all ages of ages we shall be fed on ambrosia and nectar, which is the unique bread and unique wine of all the angelic hierarchies. Grant, I pray you, O supreme Giver of goods, grant to the human generation—which you made in your image and likeness, not for its pain but so there might be those who succeed to the seats which the angels, first most beautiful and then black, lost through their most foolish pride. Grant, I pray you, to all men, and particularly to the Florentine people, grace so that they may say: The Lord looked down from heaven upon the earth <note>original: "Dominus de celo in terram aspexit."</note>. From the depths we cry to you, O Lord; Lord, hear our voice. Let your ears be attentive to the voice of our supplication <note>original: "De profundis ad te clamamus domine... Fiant aures tue intendentes..." Landino is quoting Psalm 130.</note>. Reach out to us a staff to sustain our weak and wavering steps so that we do not fall down. Remember what David, stirred by your divine fury, sings in the psalm: The dead shall not praise you, Lord, nor all those who go down into hell. But we who live bless you <note>original: "Non mortui laudabunt te domine... Sed nos qui uiuimus benedicimus tibi." From Psalm 115.</note>. It is not the damned, Lord, who truly can be called dead; nor those who, through such damnation, fall into hell, who will praise you. But we who live—either through true life, being confirmed in the habit of virtue, or at least we live because we still have free will to take the path to the right hand—we bless you. Give light to those who walk through the shadow of death, and direct our feet in the way of peace. And succor me with your help in this interpretation in such a way that my labor is not in vain, but brings praise to your name and some utility to the reader. I am poor and needy <note>original: "Paup & egenus sum ego."</note>, but you, Giver of all goods: Have mercy on me, O God, and bless me <note>original: "Miserere mei deus & benedic mihi."</note> in this second canticle.

And because we must treat of Purgatory, we shall say, according to the truest opinion of the theologians, that there are three things we must consider in this place. First, if there is a Purgatory after this life. Second, who those are who go to Purgatory. Third, if there is any certain place in which souls are purged. To the first, I say that the Holy Scripture and many authorities of the saints and various revelations establish Purgatory. And the Holy Church affirms it; especially Christ says through Matthew: Whoever speaks a word against the Holy Spirit, it will not be forgiven him, neither in this age nor in the one to come <note>original: "Qui dixerit uerbum contra spiritum sanctum non remittetur ei neque in hoc seculo neque i futuro." Matthew 12:32.</note>. Thus Christ demonstrates that in the other life some sins are purged and forgiven. And Gregory <note>Saint Gregory the Great.</note> demonstrates that in the other life there are certain faults which fire purges. Nor do only Christians establish Purgatory. But also Plato, who wills that the soul separated from the body, if it is defiled and stained with most grave and nefarious wickednesses, remains in eternal punishments. But if the sins are less grave, it is purged and then returns to other bodies. And Virgil in the sixth book <note>The Aeneid.</note> says the same thing: Until a long day, when the cycle of time is complete, has removed the ingrained stain and left pure the ethereal sense and the fire of simple air <note>original: "Donec longa dies perfetto temporis orbe Concretam exemit labem: purumque reliquit Aethereum sensum: atque aure simplicis ignem." Aeneid VI, 745-747.</note>. And let this suffice to demonstrate that Purgatory exists.

But wishing to understand, according to the Christian religion, where it is located: it is the opinion of Richard of Middleton <note>Richard of Middleton (Riccardo de Media Villa) was a 13th-century Franciscan theologian.</note> that there are four places beneath the earth. In the lowest part, which is the center of the earth, is where the damned stay in perpetual pain for actual sin. And above this part are those damned for original sin. The first of these two, which is lower and near the center, is the true Hell. The second is Limbo. There follows the third place, located above Limbo, called Purgatory, where souls are purged by common law; although some are purged elsewhere for some special reason, which is either to reveal something to the living or to obtain help from them. Then, in the higher part near the surface, which is the fourth from the center and the first from the circumference, at present there are no souls; but before our redemption accomplished by the passion and death of Christ, the souls of the Holy Fathers used to dwell there after they had completed their purgation in Purgatory. And also those who had emerged from their own bodies without a stain that needed purging. And this place was named Abraham's Bosom <note>original: "feno dabraham." Landino uses "feno" (hay/fold) for "seno" (bosom), referring to the resting place of the righteous before Christ.</note>, because he was the first who separated himself from the infidels and took the distinctive sign of faith. Therefore, the place that was made for the rest of the soul through faith formed in charity was called Abraham's Bosom for the reason already stated.

Nonetheless, Hugh of Saint Victor <note>Hugo de Sancto Victore, a 12th-century mystic and philosopher.</note> wills that no common place be assigned to such souls that have to be purged, it appearing more probable to him that each one is purged in the place where it committed the crime. But the Doctors do not approve of such an opinion except in special cases by divine dispensation, and not by common law for all. To Purgatory go those who have remained in venial sins. Second are those who did not perform penance before death, as happens to one who dies without confession and yet is entirely repentant and contrite. Third are those who did not fulfill the penance imposed on them by the priest. The penance given to us by the priest is either greater, lesser, or equal [to the sin]. If it is greater, what the man has done extra in life redounds to him and returns to his glory. If it is equal, that alone suffices for full satisfaction. If it is lesser, that which is lacking is fulfilled in Purgatory by divine justice. See, then, what the Christians say in summary about Purgatory.

But Dante, a man of admirable genius and admirable invention, found a new site which is in no way substantially against Christian opinion. And it serves several things, as we have shown in the third canto of the Inferno. He posits, therefore, that the earth which Lucifer and his followers pushed out from our hemisphere rises in the other hemisphere and made a very high mountain reaching up to the element of fire. And in that is located Purgatory, divided into different terraces <note>term: "gironi." In the Divine Comedy, these are the circular ledges or terraces of the Mountain of Purgatory where specific sins are purged.</note>. In the first ones, various types of negligence are purged. Then, in those that follow, each one purges his own sin; but the more serious crimes are always purged lower down. This mountain, then, remains to be climbed—a climb, without doubt, harsh and hard and full of labor and sweat. But let us set ourselves on the path and with a bold spirit. Let us not despair of being able to reach the summit, because where our own strengths fail, divine grace will copiously supply the rest. And He who sustained us in descending to the depths so that we did not perish will now take us up until we find the yoke <note>The mountain ridge or summit.</note>.

<summary>In this prologue to the Purgatorio, Cristoforo Landino celebrates the transition from the horrors of Hell to the hope of Purgatory. He provides a theological and philosophical defense for the existence and location of Purgatory, contrasting traditional scholastic views with Dante's unique poetic invention of the mountain.</summary>

<drop-cap>I</drop-cap>T DELIGHTS ME AND GREATLY DELIGHTS ME to have completed that part of the work concerning the outer darkness, where we have seen inconsolable weeping. And by the cold of the northern wind, stirred by the eternal motion of Beelzebub's wings, we have heard the gnashing of teeth: which I hope will have so terrified our minds that we will no longer return there. May it thus please you, Jupiter omnipotent, supreme ruler of Olympus. And who, three and one, with your supreme power, infinite wisdom, and ineffable love, will lend your light to him who walks through the darkness, so that he may be led where every devout servant is set free. And after having obtained freedom, recalled from the most difficult exile, now by postliminium, and restored to his
</p>

--- Page 299 ---
<meta>The previous page concluded the general prologue to the Purgatorio, transitioning from the darkness of Hell to the hope of the second kingdom. This page begins the actual text of Canto I with the famous metaphor of the "little ship of the intellect" and provides Cristoforo Landino’s opening commentary on the rhetorical structure and metaphors used by Dante.</meta>

<header>FIRST CANTO.</header>

# PURGATORY: THE SECOND CANTICLE OF THE DIVINE POET DANTE ALIGHIERI:

<image-desc>A large, ornate, illuminated initial 'P' begins the text. The letter is red with white filigree and is set within a square gold-leaf frame decorated with black and red floral motifs. To the right of the initial, the opening line of the poem is printed in exceptionally large, bold capital letters arranged vertically in short clusters.</image-desc>

# **T**O RUN O VER BET TER WA TERS NOW LIFTS THE SAILS

now the little ship of my intellect,
which leaves behind it a sea so cruel;
And I will sing of that second kingdom
where the human spirit purges itself
and becomes worthy to ascend to heaven.

Well-instructed and learned in the poetic art is our author. This second canticle of his—in imitation of Virgil, Statius, <note>The original text says "distintio," likely a printer's error for "Stazio" (Statius) or a reference to the "distinction" of parts, but in the context of "heroic poets," Landino usually cites Statius.</note> and other Latin heroic poets—he divides into three parts: the <term>proposition</term> <note>the statement of the subject</note>, the <term>invocation</term> <note>calling upon the Muses</note>, and the <term>narration</term> <note>the story itself</note>. However, the first two, which are the proposition and invocation, serve as the prologue. And because it is the specific office of a prologue to make the listener fit and suitable to hear, we will easily achieve this if we make them well-disposed, attentive, and docile <note>In the classical sense of "ready to be taught."</note>. He gains **goodwill** from the subject matter, promising that he will sing of Purgatory, a thing most excellent for human souls because it is the only means by which they can arrive at divine cognition, in which the highest good consists. He also gains goodwill from **his own person**, showing that he labors to write what is not only useful but necessary for the moral generation. Furthermore, he makes the listener **attentive** by the greatness of the subject matter: for we listen with the utmost attention to things that are either great or unusual, and especially if they pertain to the universe, to us individually, or to our kin and friends. Nor does he move attention in a mediocre way by his style of speaking. For by using <term>translation</term> <note>metaphor; carrying a word from its literal to a figurative meaning</note> and not literal terms, he increases the dignity and authority of the subject, as we see in Virgil and in many other poets, both Greek and Latin. Nor is it only poets, but also orators who adorn their style with this "color," the power of which we will demonstrate shortly. Finally, he makes the listener **docile**—that is, ready to understand what must be treated. This happens whenever we propose and explain in brief words what will be treated later in the entire work, as he does here by promising to treat Purgatory. But understand, reader, that although these are distinct things—

goodwill, attention, and docility—nevertheless, one helps to achieve the other. For he who becomes well-disposed becomes attentive. And he who stands attentive to hear the beginning easily becomes docile. And often in a single word, the writer acquires goodwill, attention, and docility, as in this verse: *AND I WILL SING of that second kingdom WHERE the human spirit purges itself.* For such a proposition, because it is useful, creates goodwill. Because it is a great thing, it creates attention. Because it explains what he wishes to narrate, it creates docility. **TO RUN OVER BETTER WATER** is the sentiment that his intellect rises to speak of better material than that which he has spoken of until now. But he pronounces such a sentiment not with literal words, but through metaphor. And so that we may better demonstrate this rhetorical ornament, let us say that all the words we use are either literal or metaphorical. Literal words are those found by use or reason to express the subject matter of such words, as when he says: *In the time when Juno was enraged.* <note>A reference to Inferno, Canto XXX.</note> For "time," "was," "Juno," and "enraged" are literal words for those things the poet wished to express. But these literal terms are sometimes in common use and worn and customary for everyone, such as when we say: "I greatly rejoice in your honor," and "often I praise your many and varied virtues." Sometimes they are so ancient that they remain almost outside of all custom, such as *guari* <note>much/long</note> and *fouente* <note>often</note>, both of which are Florentine but are no longer in use. Thus our Giovanni Boccaccio said *non guari di lontano* <note>original: "uon guari di lontauo"</note>, i.e., "not very far away." This was in custom then, but today it is not. Sometimes words are new and manufactured by the author himself, as when Dante says: *sio mintuassi chome tu tinmii* <note>translated as: "If I could 'in-thee' myself as thou 'in-me'est' thyself" (Paradiso IX).</note> For before Dante, no one in the Florentine language said *intuare* or *inmiare*. **Metaphorical** <note>original: "Translate"</note> words are when we transfer words from their literal meaning to another meaning not unlike the literal one, as the poet says here: *The little ship of my intellect.* For just as a ship carries a man across the sea to the desired port, so the will carries the intellect and our mind to the knowledge of the thing we desire to know. Nor does the said writer ever use a metaphor without persevering in that metaphor through the whole sentence. Thus, having said "little ship" in this place, he said "water" because we use the ship in water; he said "sails" because without sails the ship does not go. Quintilian proposes this color, which we call <term>translation</term> and the Greeks call <term>Metaphor</term> <note>original: "Methaphora"</note>, above all other ornaments; which metaphor is so granted to us by nature that often unlearned men use it without realizing it. We use it either for brevity—as when we say "In the flood of the Goths which submerged Italy"—or to avoid dishonest words, or to increase or diminish, or to adorn. But returning to the text, we will say: *The little ship of my intellect now raises [sails] to run*, that is, to navigate, *better water*. He puts "little ship" for the "will," as we said in the past canticle, which is that which transports the soul. And in the allegorical explanation, we treated distinctly of the will and of many other powers and forces and virtues of human spirits. **BETTER WATER.** Better subject matter. For reducing it to allegory, Hell is "good" matter—that is, the speculation on vices—because the speculation of them induces hatred against them and a will to flee them. But Purgatory is "better" because, having known them, we begin to purge ourselves of them. But I will set myself to narrate this more openly in a more accommodated time; and certainly one cannot nor should one crowd many things into one same place, for then neither order nor distinction appears. **THE SAILS.** And of these we similarly treated when the matter required giving some allegory to the navigation in the explanation. **SEA SO CRUEL.** Although the consideration of vice, as we have said, is good, nevertheless vice is the cruelest thing there is because it kills the soul, which no other thing can kill. Nor did he say "sea" unlearnedly, because as we said in the Virgilian allegories, every appetite is like the sea, and none is more cruel, nor tossed by more contrary winds, than that which leads to vice. For not only is he who goes to Hell—that is, into the habit of vices—submerged by the turbulent storm in such a sea, but even he who goes to contemplate the nature of vice, often fought by the allurements of various pleasures, hardly escapes the dangerous rocks and hidden shoals of such a sea. **AND I WILL SING:** makes the listener docile—

<meta>The previous page introduced the opening lines of Purgatorio and Landino’s division of the prologue into the proposition and the invocation. This page continues Landino’s commentary on the "second kingdom" and the nature of the human spirit, followed by a detailed classification of the four types of Platonic virtues. It then moves into the formal invocation of the Muses, specifically Calliope, and the mythological context of the Pierides.</meta>

<header>PURGATORY</header>

describing with brevity that which he is to treat throughout the entire work: SECOND KINGDOM: because in the first state, the goal is to recognize vice; in the second, to purge oneself of it. WHERE THE HUMAN spirit purges itself. He spoke excellently when he said "human": because above man there is no spirit that needs purging. This is because the angels who did not sin are confirmed in grace, and remaining pure, there is no need for them to be purged. And below man, there is no animal that possesses an immortal soul. Therefore, when the sensitive soul dies along with the body, nothing remains that can be purged. AND TO ASCEND TO HEAVEN becomes worthy. For indeed, the soul can finally ascend to the contemplation and knowledge of divine things only when it is purged of vices. Whence: **Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.** <note>original: "beati mundo corde quoniam ipsi deum uidebunt"</note> But because there is no stain that can make the soul foul and ugly except for vice, and nothing removes vice except virtue, it is not only useful but necessary to understand better—and with brevity—how the moral virtues are divided according to the Platonists into four species: Civil, Purgatorial, of the Soul Already Purged, and Exemplary.

**Civil virtues** belong to man because he is an animal born not to be solitary, but to live in congregation and company. From this, cities are born, and he uses these virtues to administer the republic. With **Prudence**, he investigates what is useful; with **Justice**, by distributing honors and burdens equally, he preserves union and concord. With **Fortitude**, he makes a soul bold and unconquered to endure every labor and danger to defend the fatherland. And with **Temperance**, he desires nothing of which he must later repent; in nothing does he exceed the limit or the law. But these virtues are not perfect in the civil and active life: because men who converse in that life alone do not possess true wisdom. 

After the civil virtues follow the **Purgatorial** ones: these do not occur in civil life, but belong to the few men who are capable of divine things. Such virtues expedite and free the soul of him who is disposed to purge himself from the contagion of the body and give himself entirely to divine things and flee human ones. He should not labor with Martha, but give himself entirely to Mary—that is, leave behind the active life entirely and follow the speculative <note>In medieval and Renaissance thought, Martha represented the "active life" of work, while Mary represented the "contemplative life" of prayer and study.</note>.

Beyond these Purgatorial virtues are those of the **Soul Already Purged**: which has remained without any stain. In this state, the office of Prudence is not merely to prefer divine things over human ones (as the Purgatorial virtues do), but to choose only the divine as if nothing else existed, and to look at those alone. The office of Temperance is not to restrain desires, but to forget them entirely. The office of Fortitude is not to drive away fear of horrific things, but to not even know what fear is. And finally, they use Justice to join themselves with the Divine Mind in such a way that they never depart from it.

The fourth types are **Exemplary virtues**, which belong to God alone. For since the Platonists place the Ideas <note>original: "dee," referring to the Platonic Forms or Ideas</note> of all things in the Divine Mind, much more so will the Idea of Virtue be there. Therefore, there, Prudence is nothing other than the Divine Mind itself. Temperance is that Mind turning toward itself with perpetual intention. Fortitude is that it is always the same and never changes. Justice is that, with eternal law, it never removes itself nor bends from the eternal continuation of its work. These are the four generations of moral virtues: although they are all against the passions and perturbations of the soul, they are nonetheless different in themselves. For the first do not entirely remove passions, but mitigate them; the second remove them; the third forget them; and in the fourth, it is a wicked thing even to name them. I have therefore treated this at length so that the reader, when these topics occur in many other places, may return here.

---

> But here let dead poetry rise again,
> O holy Muses, since I am yours;
> and here let Calliope rise up somewhat,
> accompanying my song with that sound
> from which the wretched magpies felt
> such a blow that they despaired of pardon.

---

After the proposition follows the **invocation**. And he ordains: **O holy Muses, RISE AGAIN here**: be resuscitated in this place. **DEAD POETRY**: as if to say, "I pray you, holy Muses, that you inspire in me the poetic faculty, which for a long time now has been dead." For many centuries before Dante, Italy had been prey to various generations of barbarians, and so afflicted and oppressed by many wars and tumults that every liberal art had lain dormant. He was among the first who tried to draw this faculty of poetry out of the darkness. And how much profit he made, we endeavor to express in his *Life*; and his present poem clearly manifests it. This is therefore the reason that led him to say, "But here let dead poetry rise again." Or truly, he wants dead poetry to rise again as if to imply: "up until now we have treated Hell, where everything is dead; but hereafter we shall treat Purgatory, through which the soul resuscitates." And certainly, the soul dead through vice rises again through purgation.

**O HOLY MUSES**: we spoke sufficiently of the Muses in the second canto of the *Inferno*. Therefore it would be superfluous to replicate at present what we have already written. **SINCE I am yours**: because I am a poet, and poets are dedicated to the Muses as their priests. Whence Virgil: **"But as for me, first and above all, may the sweet Muses please me, whose sacred symbols I bear."** <note>original: "Me uero in primis placeant ante omnia musae: quarum sacra fero." From Virgil's *Georgics* II, 475.</note> And he makes his petition honest by saying that honesty requires the Muses to favor one who is theirs. 

**AND HERE let Calliope rise up somewhat**: let her lift herself up a little, as if to say that since this is higher material, a higher style is appropriate. And certainly, for whoever pays attentive ears, it is easy to recognize that the style he uses in the *Inferno* is almost the lowest. For one beginning is **"In the middle of the journey of our life"**, while another is **"to run over better waters he lifts the sails."** And he said "somewhat" because he will lift himself even higher in the canticle of *Paradise*. And he specifically invokes Calliope among the Muses because she is the most excellent among them, and her name signifies "good voice." And he who invokes her invokes all the others. Whence Virgil said: **"O Calliope, I pray you, breathe upon the singer."** <note>original: "Vos o calliope precor aspirate canenti." From Virgil's *Aeneid* IX, 525.</note> 

**FOLLOWING my song**: because he does not begin his work with Purgatory but follows after Hell. Therefore, let Calliope rise up as if before the style and make it more sonorous, following my work. **WITH THAT sound**: with that voice from which—**THE WRETCHED MAGPIES**: that is, the wretched daughters of Pierus, were converted into magpies. And this is the "blow" which they felt from the voice of Calliope. These were the nine daughters of Pierus of the city of Pella, women certainly learned in many arts. But they were so proud of them that they thought nothing of the Muses and presumed to precede them in everything, especially in song. Nor were they content until they went to Parnassus to find them, near the Pegasean spring, and there with rude words provoked them to sing. The commission was given to Calliope, who defeated them by a long margin and converted them into magpies. This is a talkative bird and easily learns human speech. *Pica* in Latin means the jay and also the magpie. But Pliny, in his book of *Natural History*, calls this **the tailed magpie** <note>original: "pica caudata"</note> because it has a long tail. The meaning is therefore: "Let Calliope rise here, following my song with such a voice as that with which she defeated the magpies," which must have been sonorous and excellent, otherwise she would not have won. And by this he shows his petition to be easy: by the magpies who provoke the Muses, we shall understand every rash person who presumes to be able to defeat or be equal to the Muses—that is, to the divine doctrines.

-># CANTO ONE<-

After the proposition and invocation are already completed and finished by the poet, the narration begins. He wishes his beginning to be a description of the time and the quality of the time in which he emerged from Hell into the other hemisphere opposite to ours, where the mountain of Purgatory is located. The meaning is that when he emerged into that hemisphere, the sun had not yet risen, but it was not far from its birth. This is because Venus was already appearing in the east; and because she was in Pisces, and the sun in Aries—neighboring signs with a short interval—she rose just before the sun. Furthermore, he shows that at that time the air was most pure, and full of serenity and tranquility. Therefore, the color of the air, which was like that of an oriental sapphire, restored—

**Sweet color of oriental sapphire**
**that gathered in the serene aspect**
**of the pure air as far as the first circle**
**To my eyes began again the delight**
**as soon as I emerged out of the dead air**
**which had saddened my eyes and breast.**
**The beautiful planet that to love comforts**
**made all the east to laugh,**
**veiling the Fishes that were in her escort.**

—for Dante had such delight before he entered Hell, while standing in the serene air. Then, entering the infernal darkness, he lost it. Now, having emerged from it, it returns to him again. And although he appears to speak of the delight of the physical eyes, nonetheless allegorically he means the spiritual ones. The eyes take delight in bright and beautiful things; and the beauty of a thing is its good proportion with suitable color. Therefore, just as the physical eyes take delight in physical beauty and sensible light, so the eyes of the mind greatly delight in their own light, which is reason, and in their own beauty, which is virtue. Whence Plato writes that if we could see with the eyes of the mind the beauty of virtue as we see the beauty of the body with physical eyes, the love that would inflame us for it would be incredible and most ardent. THE EYES: that is, the visual sense; and THE BREAST: the mind. THE BEAUTIFUL PLANET that to love comforts: The star of Venus. He says, then, that it was the morning time and not long before daybreak. Because the sun was in Aries, which sign begins to rise after Pisces has completely emerged from the east. Because a good part of the sign of Pisces had already risen, Venus was visible, being in that sign. And we showed in the first canto of the first canticle <note>Inferno</note> that in this he imitates Virgil. And just as that poet establishes that Aeneas had Venus—not the earthly but the celestial—as his guide and leader, so in that place and in this one, Dante shows that the celestial Venus leads him. Therefore, return to that place and you will fully understand the allegory that is appropriate here. Furthermore, know that Pisces is the house of Jupiter, which planet induces chastity, justice, and religion. Therefore, Venus in this sign will be celestial and not earthly. Furthermore, she will be powerful in inflaming us toward divine things, because she is exalted in that sign. And according to Isidore, it is called the sign of Pisces <note>the Fishes</note> because when the sun comes to such a sign, through the dissolution that its heat causes in moisture, the fish scatter their seed and engender. Macrobius, who wants the names of all signs to be traced back to the nature of the sun, writes that they are called Fishes to denote that not only the terrestrial and aerial animals, but also all those that inhabit the water [are influenced by the sun]. The poets, according to Nigidius, say that in the Euphrates, a river of Assyria, a very large egg was found, which two fish pushed to the shore. And doves brooded upon it, and the goddess of Assyria was born from it, whom they call Venus; she is very religious toward the gods and toward men she is supremely merciful and dutiful. She was the inventor of many arts and other things useful to human life. Hearing this from Mercury, Jupiter allowed her to ask for whatever grace she wished. The goddess asked that he make the two fish immortal, which had preserved her generation. Jupiter translated them into this last sign of the Zodiac. But one of the fish is northern and the other southern, and they have their tails turned one against the other. And between them is a bond that holds them together as far as the feet of Andromeda. The northern fish has twelve stars; the southern one fifteen. The bond has twelve stars. So in all there are thirty-nine. Because of this benefit, the Syrians do not eat fish, and they adore doves as goddesses. Therefore, even according to this fable, Venus will be well-placed in Pisces. VEILED: Covered. Because whoever looks upward from the earth first finds with their eyes Venus in the third heaven, rather than Pisces in the eighth. Whence it follows that with her body she takes away some part of Pisces from view. Or truly he said "Veiled" to denote that the splendor of this star is so great that it obfuscates and makes those stars around it disappear.

**I turned myself to the right hand and fixed my mind**
**on the other pole: and I saw four stars**
**never seen except by the first people:**
**The heaven seemed to rejoice in their flames:**
**O northern widowed site**
**since you are deprived of seeing those.**

<column-break/>

—delight to my eyes. SWEET COLOR: gentle and delightful color. And although sweetness is properly a matter of taste, nonetheless every other thing that delights any other sense is called sweet. Whence Petrarch: "And how she sweetly speaks and sweetly laughs." <note>original: "Et come dolce parla & dolce ride."</note> And Horace: "I will love Lalage, sweetly laughing, sweetly speaking." <note>original: "dulce ridentem lalagen amabo dulce loquentem."</note> ORIENTAL SAPPHIRE: Pliny shows that there are Sapphires of purple color and of blue color; of which the poet makes mention in this place, and says that the blue ones are called "male" Sapphires. WHICH GATHERED in the serene aspect: Because if the air were not serene it would not be blue. And the poet takes great pains to show that the air in that place was pure and transparent, contrary to the cloudy air of Hell. For just as vice generates obscurity, so the purgation of vice induces serenity. OF THE PURE AIR as far as the first circle: as far as the first sphere, which is the heaven of the moon, from which downward mutable things begin. Therefore, the serene color of the air restored delight to my eyes.

Because in the layout of the world the east is the forward part, it happens that whoever turns toward it has the north to their left and the south to their right. And because just as the arctic pole is in the north and is seen by us, so the antarctic pole is in the south and is seen by those of the other hemisphere, where the poet feigns Purgatory to be. Therefore, wanting to turn from the east to the south, where the antarctic pole is, he turned to the right hand. TO THE OTHER pole: not to ours, but to the one opposite ours. AND I SAW four stars never seen except by the first people: "Pole" in Greek signifies the highest part of the heaven, upon which the heaven turns. As if, for example, you took a material sphere and stuck a rod through the middle, which from one surface of the sphere, arriving at the center in a straight line, passes to the other surface; those two parts that are near to both holes where the rod is placed are called poles, because the sphere turns upon them. And "poli" in Greek signifies "to turn." And in Latin they are called *vertices*, because *uerto* in Latin is what I call "to turn" in Tuscan. Whence Virgil, speaking of the arctic pole, said: "This pole [vertex] is always high above us, but that one the black Styx and the deep shades see beneath their feet." <note>original: "Hic uertex nobis ſemper ſublimis at illum: ſub pedibus ſtyx atra uidet maneſque profu..." from Virgil's *Georgics*.</note>

<meta>This page continues Landino’s commentary on Canto I of the Purgatorio. The previous page described the atmospheric beauty of the island of Purgatory and the rising of Venus. Here, the author interprets the "four stars" seen by Dante as symbols of the Cardinal Virtues and introduces the guardian of the mountain, Cato of Utica, explaining his presence as an allegory for moral and spiritual liberty.</meta>

-># PURGATORIO<-

**NEVER SEEN EXCEPT** by the first people: If these stars are in the Antarctic pole <note>The southern celestial pole.</note> they cannot be seen except by those who are in the other hemisphere. We do not inhabit that hemisphere, but according to the poet's fiction, our first parents <note>Adam and Eve.</note> dwelt there while they were still without sin, because here he places the "earthly paradise of delights." From this it follows that, aside from the first parents, these stars have not been seen by any man. Thus he excludes the error of Origen <note>original: "D'origine"; referring to the early Christian theologian Origen, who speculated on the existence of the Antipodes.</note>, who claims that the other hemisphere is inhabited just as this one is; for if it were so, it would have been necessary for Christ to have been crucified there as well for their redemption. These four stars he seems to set down as the four <term>Cardinal Virtues</term> <note>Prudence, Justice, Fortitude, and Temperance.</note>, which do not exist in men, or at least not perfectly, unless they are in a state of grace. And therefore they were never seen except by our first parents when they were in a state of grace. To better understand this, we should recall the division of Plato which we set down above: that these four stars, so splendid, are the four moral virtues of the third kind, where they are called the "virtues of the soul already purified." And if one should ask why he mentions them here in Purgatory, where the "purgatorial virtues" (which we enumerated in the second kind) are more appropriate, I respond that on this very mountain is the paradise of delights where our first parents stood in a state of grace. Therefore, ascending this mountain with the purgatorial virtues, we arrive at the summit where the paradise of delights is, above which appear these stars—that is, the virtues of the soul already purified. **HEAVEN SEEMED TO REJOICE** in their flames: in their splendor, because truly the heavens and the higher things rejoice in perfect virtues. **O WIDOWED NORTHERN** region: with an exclamation he turns to our northern pole, which, although it is adorned with many stars, nevertheless their light is so inferior to the light of these four that it can be said to be "widowed" and deprived of light. Widowed are the souls deprived of Truth and Goodness, to which they are wedded. And in truth, the men of our pole—that is, the vicious—are not men when compared to the virtuous. It is not without reason that he places the vicious in the North, a cold place, and the virtuous in the South, a warm region. For every virtue has its movement of charity and love for the truth and the good, and charity is a flame; just as vice is born from a lack of love and the fire of it. For this reason the Latins use "cold" <note>Latin: "frigidus"</note> for something harmful and vicious. Whence Virgil says: *Where the cold star of Saturn withdraws itself* <note>original: "Frigida saturni quo sese stella receptet" from the Georgics.</note>. And Juvenal: *The listener blushes, whose mind is cold* <note>original: "Rubet auditōr cui frigida mens est" from the Satires.</note>.

---

> As I from their gaze was departed
> turning a little toward the other pole
> from where the Wain had already vanished,
> I saw near me an old man, alone,
> worthy of such great reverence in his look:
> that no son owes more to a father:
> His beard was long and mixed with white hair,
> similar to the hair on his head,
> of which a double tress fell to his breast:
> The rays of the four holy lights
> so adorned his face with light,
> that I saw him as if the sun were before me.

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Ornamental historiated initial 'S' at the beginning of the commentary text, depicting a figure seated in a landscape with hills and a blue sky.</image-desc>
IT follows that after he had seen the four stars in the Antarctic pole, he turned toward the Arctic and did not see the "Wain" <note>The Big Dipper or Ursa Major.</note> where the Bears are, to denote that just as in this hemisphere we cannot see the stars near the Antarctic pole, so in the other hemisphere one cannot see the stars that form the Bears, which in the north are called the "Wain" <note>original: "elcarro"</note> and the "Horn." **I SAW NEAR ME** an old man, alone: from the preceding words it appears that although this old man was beside him and consequently in the Antarctic hemisphere, he nevertheless stood facing the Arctic. This is meant to be <term>Cato of Utica</term> <note>Marcus Porcius Cato (95–46 BCE), a Roman statesman who committed suicide rather than live under Caesar’s tyranny. Dante makes him the guardian of Purgatory.</note>. And because it might seem to many that the poet deviates from the Christian religion by placing a pagan man, who died without baptism, in a place of salvation, I respond that he does not place Cato here for the soul of Cato (which we are constrained to believe is among the damned). Rather, he places him for **Liberty**, taking this name because this man, more than any other, was a lover of liberty. And as we shall see below, he preferred it to his life. Nor is anything more appropriate to this place than liberty. For after Hell—that is, the knowledge of vices—because we recognize that we have become servants to them, and that they are cruel

---

tyrants, nothing else pushes us to want to purge ourselves and to endure every labor to become clean except the love of liberty; because once purged, we become good and healthy. And whoever is good and wise is always free. Therefore, he lives in the highest tranquility. He serves no worldly thing, because he esteems nothing. He fears no adversity, because he knows that neither death, nor illness, nor poverty, nor exile, nor any other calamity or blow of fortune can harm him—only vice, of which he feels clean. Only by following the virtues does he serve God, whose service not only makes us free but makes us reign. Recognizing this, the <term>Stoic philosophers</term> in their paradoxes wrote: *All the wise (that is, the good) are free, and all fools (that is, the vicious) are servants* <note>original: "Omnes sapientes liberos esse: & omnes stultos seruos."</note>. But returning to the text, he places him facing the north—that is, facing vices—because this supreme love of liberty rises in us as soon as we have known the misery that is in the servitude of vice. He does not wish to demonstrate here the "first liberty" that was in the soul before the transgression of our first parents and before sin (for he would have placed that in the South, which denotes virtue), but that liberty which we regain when we disentangle ourselves from vices, of which we were previously servants. He feigns that he is an old man because nothing is more ancient in the soul than liberty, since at one time it was created and placed in its <term>free will</term>. Whence it is wisely written: *He left her in the hand of her own counsel* <note>original: "Reliquit eam in manu consilii sui" from the Book of Sirach.</note>. He is therefore old. Thus he describes him with a beard and with long hair, not all white but mixed, because he had in mind what Virgil feigns of Charon: *He is now an old man, but his old age is fresh and green for a god* <note>original: "am senior sed cruda deo uiridisque senectus" from Aeneid VI.</note>. Just as Virgil introduces Charon as an old man—but an old man who is robust and of youthful strength—so through this description Dante wishes to demonstrate the same in Cato. For although liberty is old in the soul, it has not for this reason diminished its strength. He adds: **WORTHY OF SUCH GREAT REVERENCE** in his look that no son owes more to a father. And certainly, liberty is that which makes our soul worthy of every veneration. Consider a man who is a servant to vices: make him a servant to lust, make him a servant to avarice, and you will see him do and say things for which he will be a laughingstock and a mockery to all men. Hercules was so highly regarded, yet through unrestrained lust he became the servant of a lowly girl <note>Omphale.</note>, or rather of lust itself. Alexander the Great wanted to conquer the world and make himself lord of innumerable peoples and nations, yet by not resisting anger he became its servant. And he achieved much more infamy from such vice than true glory from so many victories. Therefore the paradox of the Stoics is most true, as I said a little before: *All wise men are free, and all fools are servants.* See then that because we are servants of vices, we become ridiculous and infamous, and we make a mockery of ourselves. Put on the other side one who is free from all greed, who is not subject to lust, nor to avarice, nor to ambition, but in whom reason reigns, free from every human passion. Certainly, we would see such gravity, such modesty, such prudence in him that we would not only render him supreme reverence, but if it were lawful, we would worship him as a god. Therefore, our poet most rightly states that this old man is worthy of as much reverence as a son should bear for a father. Nor could a poet choose a more fitting—

<meta>This page continues Cristoforo Landino’s commentary on Canto I of the Purgatorio. On the previous page, Landino began explaining the symbolic nature of the four stars (the Cardinal Virtues). Here, he transitions to the introduction of Cato of Utica, the guardian of Purgatory, and interprets the initial encounter between the travelers and this venerable figure.</meta>

# CANTO FIRST

no comparison. For after God, we should hold no one in greater reverence than a father. But the text states: nor greater reverence to any father. We shall not, therefore, say "any son to a father," but "son to any father." And with supreme reason he said "any father" and not simply "father": because there are certain fathers who, beyond having generated the son, have done him no other benefit. Rather, on the contrary, they have harmed him: directing him along the bad path, and encouraging him toward a life of delight and pleasure, toward avarice and unrestrained greed for money, or toward ambition. There are others who with every industry strive so that from a tender age their children may take on good habits and learn good doctrines <note>Landino is distinguishing between biological fatherhood and moral/spiritual mentorship.</note>. Therefore, there is no doubt that a different reverence is owed to these than to those, though all may be fathers. **THE RAYS OF THE FOUR HOLY LIGHTS.** It is entirely fitting that the rays of the four stars—which we have interpreted as the four virtues—so illuminated the face of the old man <note>Cato of Utica.</note> that he appeared as if illuminated by the sun. For just as the free will of the soul is clouded by shadows and lost through vice, which draws us into servitude, so from these virtues it receives light and through them it is maintained.

> "Who are you that against the blind stream
> have fled the eternal prison?"
> he said, moving those honest plumes <note>original: "piume"; referring here to Cato's beard.</note>:
> "Who has guided you? And who serves as your lantern,
> coming forth out of the deep night
> that always makes the infernal valley black?
> Are the laws of the abyss thus broken,
> or is some new counsel changed in heaven,
> that you, though damned, come to my grottoes?"

<column-break/>

In the fourth canto of the first canticle <note>Inferno.</note>, mention was made of the river that descends from our hemisphere into Hell. And in the final canto, he describes how it enters the center of the earth from the other hemisphere and wears away a rock where the center of the universe is, and wearing through it, it passes and creates Cocytus. And against this stream, as shown in the last canto, Dante came when he exited Hell. **BLIND STREAM.** Because it runs through dark places, as he has shown. And allegorically this river is understood as vice, which runs to the center of Hell and conducts whoever navigates it; it is dark because every vice is born of ignorance and the blindness of reason. Therefore, whoever goes to Hell follows the stream. But whoever exits it and goes to purge himself comes against the stream, because he opposes vices. **YOU HAVE FLED THE ETERNAL PRISON.** Theologically, the eternal prison of the damned is Hell, because they never leave for any time. And morally, if Hell is the habit of vice which holds our soul in eternal servitude, it is also an eternal prison. For the majority of those who have made a habit of vice remain eternally prisoners of it. And very few are those who can exit it. **PLUMES:** he used this for the beard, which a speaker moves by moving the jaws. **WHO HAS GUIDED YOU AND WHO SERVES AS YOUR LANTERN.** Two things are necessary to exit the habit of vice: illuminating grace, which shines and acts as a lantern; and cooperating grace, which acts as a guide to those who wish to act according to virtue. He who serves as your lantern to exit out of the deep night: that is, from the depth of the long-standing habit of vice. **ARE THE LAWS OF THE ABYSS THUS BROKEN OR IS SOME NEW COUNSEL CHANGED IN HEAVEN.** As if to say: if divine justice has established an eternal prison for the damned, and you have come out of it, it must be that you have come out by force or that God has changed His purpose. But the first is not to be believed, because no force prevails against God. Nor yet the second, because divine wisdom is immutable. **THE LAWS OF THE ABYSS** as if to say the laws ordained by God. For the "abyss": that is, for the depth and lower part of the world, which is called "abyss," which in the Greek tongue signifies "depth." **OR IS HEAVEN CHANGED:** as if to say, where there is no change, but everything is stable.

---

> My leader then took hold of me,
> and with words, and with hands, and with signs,
> made my legs and my brow reverent.
> Then he answered him: "By myself I did not come;
> a Lady descended from heaven, by whose prayers
> I aided this man with my company."

<column-break/>

A fitting thing: that Virgil should admonish Dante—that is, that Reason should admonish Sensuality—to revere Cato. For the appetite will not show reverence for the liberation of the soul, but will always be prone to vices. **MY LEADER THEN TOOK HOLD OF ME.** Because one cannot love liberty if Reason does not bring the appetite and sensuality into its power and make them bend and revere liberty. And with words persuading him; and with hands handling him; and with signs demonstrating to him. Sensuality is admonished with words, that is, with manifest doctrine; with hands, that is, with excellent works which are an example to us to follow virtue; and with signs, which are more obscure meanings. **MADE MY LEGS REVERENT** by making me kneel. **AND MY BROW:** by bowing the head. And rightly so: because the knees are attributed to mercy. Hence, when we wish to move someone to mercy, we are accustomed to kneel and likewise embrace the knees of the one we wish to placate. **AND THE FOREHEAD:** where the brows are, and it is attributed to shame. Sensuality, therefore, feels shame. This is a sign that it repents of its error and desires to amend itself and asks for mercy, without which—as we have shown elsewhere—man cannot save himself. **THEN HE ANSWERED.** Cato had asked who was the guide and what was the light that had drawn them from Hell. And he had wondered whether the laws were broken or the will of God changed. Therefore Virgil responds first: that he has been a guide to Dante, having been prayed to by Beatrice. And we showed in the second canto of the Inferno how Reason, illustrated by natural and philosophical doctrine (which is Virgil), became a guide to Dante to show him the vices through the prayers of Beatrice, who is cooperating grace sent by Light <note>God.</note>, and by another whom he does not name <note>The Virgin Mary and Saint Lucia.</note>, who are prevenient and illuminating grace. And he has satisfied the questions, which were **WHO GUIDED YOU** and **WHO SERVED AS YOUR LANTERN.** Then he continues.

---

<margin>148</margin>
> "But since it is your will that more be unfolded
> of our condition, how it truly is,
> it cannot be my will that you be denied.
> This man never saw the final evening."

<column-break/>

Virgil had already satisfied the first two questions of Cato and shown him what guide and what light had conducted them. Now he responds to the third: demonstrating that because they had exited from Hell, the laws were not broken. For none...

<summary>Cato of Utica challenges Dante and Virgil as they emerge from Hell, questioning how they escaped the "eternal prison." Virgil intervenes, compelling Dante to show physical signs of reverence (kneeling) and explaining that they are traveling under the divine authority of Beatrice.</summary>

I have shown him all the wicked people,

Therefore, he had not descended into Hell as one damned, because such souls are not guided by Virgil, that is, by Reason, but by
irrational and beastly appetite. But he had descended to have true knowledge of vices, so that having known how harmful they are, he
would develop the desire to free himself from them. **THIS MAN NEVER SAW** the final evening: i.e., death, which is the final night and
darkness of man. This signifies he has not died yet; that is, he has not made a habit of vice. And therefore, with my guidance, he was able to escape
it. **BUT THROUGH HIS** folly: through his foolishness and ignorance. Because through a lack of reason we fall into vice,
he was so near to it that very little time was "to turn": that is, was yet to come; and he said "turn" because the revolution of the planets,
and especially of the sun, creates time. Wherefore Petrarch, wishing to describe the sun, said: *When the planet that distinguishes the hours*, that is,
when the sun, which by its revolution distinguishes the hours and every space of time; and he imitates Virgil, who said: <note>original: "Voluentibus annis"</note> *With the passing years*.
There remained, then, little time to be able to help him. This denotes that if he had persevered longer in vices, he would have made such a habit that
he could not afterwards escape. But Beatrice sent him Virgil, that is, Divine Grace, and that of the intellect, Reason, which made him
know vice. And he says well: "And there was no other way than this through Hell." Because when vice has seized us, it makes itself so
flattering with delights that it shows us—if Reason did not show us their ugliness and pain, which is to lead us through Hell—we
would never desire to free ourselves from them. Therefore, Reason could not lead him to salvation if it did not make the way through Hell. And for this
reason, he says he has shown him all the wicked people: that is, all the generations of vices. And now I intend to show him Purgatory. For
from knowing the malignancy of vices arises the desire for purging oneself. **UNDER YOUR** authority. Although everything is under
divine power, nevertheless it can be said that Purgatory is under the authority of Cato, i.e., of Liberty; because no one can
enter Purgatory unless they repent of their errors. And no one repents of being a slave to vices unless they become eager and desirous
for liberty. **HOW I HAVE LED HIM** would be long to repeat: how many things Reason shows

power. Since, as we have said, without divine help the human soul is not freed from sin, and is not led to see

free will to be sufficient for our salvation.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante's Purgatorio, Canto I. On the previous page, Virgil began his plea to Cato, the guardian of Purgatory, asking for passage for Dante by invoking the name of Cato's wife, Marcia. This page explains the allegory of Marcia and Cato as symbols of the active and contemplative lives, and describes the ritual Dante must undergo before ascending the mountain.</meta>

<page-num>149</page-num>

### CANTO ONE

The poet presents Cato as a symbol of liberty: likewise, he presents Marcia as a symbol of the <term>civil life</term> <note>The "civil life" or "active life" refers to a life of social and political engagement, as opposed to a life of solitary prayer or study.</note> and the administration of the republic. This is similar to what we demonstrate in our Latin allegories on Virgil: that Dido is presented for this same purpose. Therefore, Marcia—that is, the civil life—always wants Cato for a husband, because she always desires to be joined with liberty. And while Cato was among civil men—that is, while liberty is exercised and labors in the active and civil life—he loves Marcia and does everything for her. But when <term>free will</term> passes to the contemplation of heavenly things, it does not move except at the request of those things. But returning to where we left the text, it says: **O HOLY FATHER**. Here he almost imitates Sallust, who demonstrates that no holy person ever hesitated to die for liberty. **INCLINE** to us **FOR HER LOVE**, and let us go **THROUGH YOUR SEVEN kingdoms**.

This refers to Purgatory, where the seven mortal sins are punished, about which we will say more below. And it is not without reason that Virgil is made to pray through Marcia and not through Beatrice. This is because Virgil, with his own doctrine, cannot elevate the mind enough to perfectly know Beatrice—that is, the liberty that exists in a perfectly purged soul, according to our theology. But he knows her in the civil life. Hence, Cato cautiously reproves him and demonstrates our theology of the purged, saying: "But if a lady from heaven moves and rules you," as you will see a little further down.

**"Marcia was so pleasing to my eyes,"**
**"while I was over there," he said then,**
**"that whatever graces she wanted from me, I performed."**
**"Now that she dwells beyond the evil river,"**
**"she can no longer move me, by that law"**
**"which was made when I came forth from there."**
**"But if a lady of heaven moves and rules you,"**
**"as you say, there is no need for flattery:"**
**"let it be enough that you ask me for her sake."**
**"Go then, and see that you gird this man"**
**"with a smooth rush, and that you wash his face"**
**"so that all filth is there extinguished."**
**"For it would not be becoming for an eye overcome"**
**"by any cloud to go before the first"**
**"minister who is of those of paradise."**

<column-break/>

While I was with Marcia—that is, in the civil life—she pleased me, and I did everything for her liberty. But since I have passed the **evil river** <note>The "evil river" represents the turbulent active life where many vices are found.</note> and am here—that is, in the <term>contemplative life</term>, which is deprived of every vice—Marcia does not move me, nor can she move me. **By that law which was made when I came forth**: this is divine law instituted by God according to the nature of things: that the love of civil liberty should last only as long as that civil life lasts. But once the contemplative life arrives, the law of that life must be observed, because the contemplative life is eternal. Hence, in the Gospel: <note>original: "Maria autem optimam partem elegit: que nō auferetur ab ea."</note> "Mary has chosen the best part, which shall not be taken away from her." <note>This biblical reference (Luke 10:42) compares Martha (the active life) with Mary (the contemplative life).</note> And therefore he adds: **BUT IF A LADY of heaven moves or rules you**—as if to say, I am no longer bound to Marcia, but to a celestial lady; if she guides you, **AS YOU SAY, there is no need for flattery**. He uses the word "flattery" excellently. For men are induced to do our will either by reasons we allege or by flattery. Reason aims at truth and help. Flattery works through pleasure which it shows you, and with fraud it persuades you that something is good which is not. Therefore, to pray for the love of Marcia is flattery, because the active life labors in earthly goods, which find us and make us love them with their flattery, showing in life and appearance that which they are not. But Cato, who has passed the evil river—that is, appetite—has abandoned the active life. The care for earthly goods does not move him through pleasures and

---

their flattery. But having passed to the contemplation of heavenly things through the love of them—where there is no flattery, but sincere truth—he can be easily persuaded. And being persuaded, he shows Virgil that he must gird Dante with a **smooth rush** in which there is no knot, and wash his face. It is the nature of the rush to be born in low places, not to grow very high, and to have no knots. Hence the proverb: <note>original: "nodum in scirpo quaeris"</note> "you are looking for a knot in a rush." We say this when someone wants to find something in a thing that is not there. We say that whoever wants to purge themselves must be humble and lower themselves—that is, be continent—and not let themselves fall into concupiscence, like the rush, which by its own nature contains itself and never bends and has no knot—that is, it is not tied to any earthly desire—nor does it have leaves. This signifies that one should not seek worldly honors or worldly things, except as much as is required for the necessity of food and clothing, which requires few things. Therefore, Cicero says: <note>original: "Paucis minimis que natura contenta est."</note> "Nature is content with a few small things." Many want this "girding" to happen twice: one belt being strength against carnal appetites, and the other being patience in penance. And because Saint John distinguishes sins into three types—the pride of life, the concupiscence of the flesh, and the concupiscence of the eyes—against two of these are humility and continence (found in the rush), and against the third, one washes the eyes with the dew fallen from heaven and not dried by the heat of the sun. This is the illuminating grace, not dried by the splendor of worldly goods. And he adds that it is not becoming to go with eyes **overcome**—that is, blinking and almost dazzled—which signifies the intellect clouded by ignorance and by the desire for mortal things. **Overcome** <note>original: "sopprifo"</note> in our language means "condensed." Hence we say "compressed milk" when, with certain flowers of a herb called rennet, it becomes dense. Therefore, the eye sees through its clarity, which when it becomes too condensed, diminishes sight. **TO THE FIRST MINISTER**: who is the angel, whom he will describe a little further on.

<margin>149</margin>
**"This little island, around its very base,"**
**"down there where the wave beats against it,"**
**"bears rushes upon the soft mud."**
**"No other plant that puts forth leaves"**
**"or grows hard could have life there,"**
**"because it would not yield to the blows."**
**"Then, let your return not be this way;"**
**"the sun, which is now rising, will show you"**
**"how to take the mountain by an easier ascent."**

<column-break/>

He imagines an island in the ocean in the other hemisphere, placed directly opposite Jerusalem. And he rightly wants Purgatory to be an island: because whoever sets out to purge themselves of vices is beaten by various waves of many perturbations and desires, which would seek to remove the soul from its good purpose. But just as the island, although surrounded by the sea, nevertheless resists all the blows of the waves, so whoever has come into the purgatorial virtues cannot be conquered by any perturbation so that they are moved from their true purpose. These shores, which are beaten by the waves, produce nothing but rushes. By the **rushes** we understand tolerance and patience, which must exist in those who wish to free themselves from vices, because they are continually beaten by most ardent desires that would lead them back to pleasure, or to avarice, or to ambition.

<summary>Cato explains that while he once loved his wife Marcia, he is now bound by a divine law that separates the souls of the saved from the concerns of the active, earthly life. He instructs Virgil to perform a ritual of purification on Dante using a smooth rush and heavenly dew, symbolizing humility and the rejection of worldly knots.</summary>
<keywords>Cato, Marcia, active life, contemplative life, allegory of the rush, humility, purification, Purgatory as island, divine law, illuminating grace</keywords>
