<meta>This page continues Cristoforo Landino’s influential 1481 commentary on Dante’s *Divine Comedy*. Having concluded the encounter with Cato of Utica, the guardian of Purgatory’s shores, the text now focuses on the ritual of purification. Virgil must wash the stains of Hell from Dante’s face using the morning dew and gird him with a smooth reed, symbolizing humility.</meta>

<page-type>text</page-type>
<columns>2</columns>
<header>PURGATORIO</header>

Thus he vanished; and I rose up
without speaking, and drew myself back 
to my leader, and fixed my eyes on him.

**He began: "Son, follow my steps;**
**let us turn back, for this plain slopes down**
**to its lower limits."**
**The dawn was overcoming the morning hour**
**which fled before it, so that from afar**
**I recognized the trembling of the sea.**
**We went across the lonely plain**
**like a man returning to a lost path,**
**who until he finds it seems to travel in vain.**

...would be. And certainly: he who does not bend in adversity, and does not bow his shoulders, is conquered by it. Nor is it necessary that they "carry fraud"—that is, have a desire for vain and fleeting things, like leaves, which appear beautiful but last little and produce no fruit. **THEN LET IT NOT BE** your return this way. Because one who goes to purgation must not turn back, but proceed forward. Whence also John said: "They went and did not return" <note>original: "Ibant & non reuiertebantur." Likely a reference to the movements of the living creatures in the vision of Ezekiel 1:12, symbolizing steadfast progress.</note>. **THE SUN WILL SHOW YOU** that it rises now. He feigned in the other canticle <note>Inferno</note> that his entry into Hell was at the beginning of the night, because falling into vice comes from ignorance and blindness of mind. In this one, he shows that the ascent to Purgatory was at the birth of the sun. Because leaving vice to return to virtue proceeds from the rising within us of the light of reason. And therefore he said: "the sun shows you that it rises." Because the light of reason, which in the past was submerged, can be taken up again, and it shows us the way of purging ourselves. **TAKE THE MOUNTAIN** at its gentlest ascent. Difficult and steep is the way that leads to virtue; hence he admonishes here that we must always take the path that has less harshness, provided it leads us where we must go. He wants us to climb. But because until we are well-confirmed in a good purpose, we must begin with the easiest things, so that they do not lead us into desperation. And afterward, already accustomed to such difficulty, the labor will seem less hard to us. **THUS HE VANISHED**: as if wanting to denote that it was not the essence of Cato, but an image placed to signify liberty. **AND I ROSE UP without speaking.** In this consultation, reason alone must be employed. And the appetite must listen with reverence, and then give itself entirely to reason, and look to it, so that it does nothing else except what reason commands or signals.

...which has already diminished the darkness. But not as much as the dawn, because this makes the air white, and is so called because *albus* in Latin means white. **IT FLED BEFORE.** Just as the dark night flees the morning, so the morning flees the dawn. There was, therefore, so much light that I discerned the "trembling"—that is, the light rippling of the sea. There was already so much light that although I did not discern everything, I nonetheless discerned this. Which denotes that although I did not yet have so much light of intellect that I could fully speculate, nonetheless I knew it was necessary to be purged, because I had entered into the purgatorial virtues. And I saw the "trembling of the sea"—that is, I already recognized not only the great movements of the appetite (which even the defeated recognize as vices), but the minimal ones, which the <term>civil life</term> <note>The active life of a citizen, which seeks earthly excellence but lacks the refined spiritual perception of the "purgatorial virtues."</note> does not judge as defeated because it does not have perfect virtues. **WE WENT through the lonely plain.** Infinite is the crowd of those who go to Hell—that is, fall into vices. But very few are those who leave to go and purge themselves. Whence Virgil: "The descent to the underworld is easy; but to retrace one's steps and escape to the upper air, this is the task, this is the toil" <note>original: "Facilis descensus auerni. Sed reuocare gradum fuperafque euadere ad auras Hoc opus hic labor est." From Aeneid VI.126-129.</note>. Therefore this plain is lonely and solitary, because few arrive there. **LIKE A MAN WHO RETURNS.** A very appropriate comparison. For a man who has come out of Hell and set out on a path that is not the true one to go to Purgatory, regrets having to turn back, and it seems to him he goes in vain until he returns to the true way, as does one who loses the path on a journey. But as Petrarch says, it is wisdom for one who has lost the way to turn back.

**When we were where the dew**
**fights with the sun, and being in a part**
**where there is shade, it evaporates little,**
**both hands upon the grass spread**
**gently my master placed.**
**And I, who was aware of his art,**
**offered toward him my tearful cheeks;**
**there he made entirely clear**
**the color that Hell had hidden from me.**

And then the dew took away that color and filth which occupied the eyes outwardly, so that they could not see Hell. For although Virgil, who is the superior reason, showed the sensuality the ugliness and vileness of vice and the detriment it brings to the soul, nonetheless, because the soul was occupied by the desire for earthly things, it understood it, but not perfectly.

<column-break/>

Especially when, in order to give ourselves to this contemplative life, the comforts of the body, or possessions, or honors fail us; where we must endure many hardships and many anxieties, and believe in the blows of fortune, bending and not breaking. And he says well: that no other plant produces reeds, because no one reigns there except the one who has this patience. For the plant that is not flexible breaks.

Virgil calls Dante "son" and "well-deserving"; because he willingly and with love obeyed Virgil, not as a lord, but as a father. And already several times we have shown that this signifies the appetite being made obedient to reason. **Follow my steps**: because without reason, the senses would again become entangled in vices. **LET US TURN back**: we cannot enter into Purgatory if we do not turn back to recognize the vices that are in us. And therefore he wants him to go down—that is, to the recognition of vice—before he begins to climb. Others take this descending for humility, which is necessary for those who desire to be purged; which interpretation does not displease me. **THE DAWN WAS OVERCOMING the morning hour.** Dawn is that time in which, although the body of the sun has not yet appeared, it is nonetheless so close to our hemisphere that it already illuminates the east and overcomes the morning time...

**When we were where the dew fights**: that is, battles with the sun, which wants to evaporate it with heat, thinning and drying it. But because it is "in a part"—that is, in a place where there is <term>dorezza</term> <note>Landino explains "dorezza" as being derived from "orezza" or "rezzo," meaning shade or a cool breeze.</note>—that is, where there is shade—it defends itself, thins little, and does not dissolve. Virgil bathed his hands in it to wash Dante's face. Why he takes the dew, and why the sun, we said a little above. Therefore reason, with its "hands"—that is, with good works—takes the dew; it receives the <term>illuminating grace</term>. And rightly with good works, because God does not give it to us if we do not help ourselves on our part. Whence Augustine says: "He who created you without you will not save you without you" <note>original: "Qui fecit te sine te non faluabit te sine te." A famous quote from St. Augustine's Sermon 169.</note>. God has compassion for those who help themselves, and sends them such grace. **AND I WHO was aware.** Reason wants to lift up the sensuality to remove the filth that darkens its eyes. And the sensuality itself, having already been made obedient to reason, does not flee but rather stands ready.

<summary>This page covers the transition from the encounter with Cato to the purification ritual on the shore of Purgatory. Landino explains the allegorical significance of the dawn as the light of reason and the morning dew as a symbol of God's illuminating grace, which requires human cooperation through good works to be effective.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Cristoforo Landino’s commentary on the first Canto of *Purgatorio*. The previous page discussed the transition from the darkness of Hell to the dawn of Purgatory, emphasizing that the journey of purgation is a forward movement of the soul toward reason and light. Here, Landino explains the symbolism of the "desert shore" and the ritual of the reed.</meta>

<page-type>text</page-type>
<columns>2</columns>
<header>CANTO ONE</header>

Where he says: **THAT COLOR**, that grime which Hell had hidden. Not entirely hidden, but "almost" hidden, because poets sometimes omit this distinction of "almost," which is nevertheless understood. Thus Virgil says: "The Gauls were present among the houses and were holding the citadel" <note>original: "Galli per domos aderat arcemque tenebāt." A reference to the Aeneid, 8.657.</note>, meaning they were *almost* holding it. And certainly, since his sensuality was not yet purged, he had not yet fully recognized the ugliness and the filth of vice, which Hell—that is, ignorance—had hidden from him.

We then came upon the desert shore,
  that never saw navigate its waters
  any man who later had experience of returning;
There he girded me as it pleased the other,
  o wonder! that just as he chose
  the humble plant, such was it reborn
Suddenly, there where he plucked it.

<column-break/>

Having washed his face, we came to the shore, which never saw any man navigate its sea and then return back. This is obvious regarding the dead: no one goes to Purgatory who then returns back. Rather, they proceed forward, ascending to heaven. But it is also true for the living. For whoever passes from vice to purgation does not then turn back, but goes from the purgative virtues to those of the soul already purged. He says then: "we arrived at the desert shore"—abandoned and solitary, as was said above regarding the path. Which shore never saw a man navigate its waters who was afterwards "experienced"—that is, had tried and attempted to turn back. And poetically he gives sense to the senseless thing, as Virgil does: "And now they were climbing the hill which hangs over the city in its great mass" <note>original: "Iamque ascēdebāt collem qui plurimis urbi Imminet." Aeneid, 1.420.</note>. **THERE HE GIRDED ME** as it pleased him. Because it is within the judgment and choice of reason to impose how much and what kind of humility, patience, and penance it wishes. Other texts have "the other" <note>original: "altrui"</note>, and then you understand that it was thus commanded. But that another reed should suddenly be reborn where the first was plucked is an imitation of Virgil, who shows that as soon as Aeneas plucked the golden bough in the forest, another grew in its place. Whence he says: "When the first is torn away, a second of gold is not lacking, and a branch of similar metal puts forth leaves" <note>original: "Primoque auulso non deficit alter aureus & simili frondescit uirga metallo." Aeneid, 6.143.</note>. Therefore, as we demonstrated in that place in our Virgilian allegories: the virtues, which are the goods of the soul, do not diminish by being taken. Rather, they grow, because they multiply among more people. So our poet understands here. Let there be a thousand who clothe themselves in humility; humility will not be lacking for another thousand who wish to clothe themselves in it. Indeed, these latter will clothe themselves more easily by the example of the first. But you will find the opposite in physical goods; for the more they are taken from the pile, the more it diminishes.

<summary>Landino explains the ritual of the reed, symbolizing humility, and the "desert shore" of Purgatory from which no one returns to vice. He uses Virgil’s Aeneid to illustrate how spiritual virtues, unlike material goods, are not depleted when shared but rather increase through example.</summary>

<header>CANTO SECOND SECOND</header>

# CANTO SECOND, OF THE SECOND CANTICLE BY DANTE.

The sun had already reached the horizon
whose meridian circle covers
Jerusalem with its highest point;
And night, which circles opposite to him,
was coming out of the Ganges with the Scales <note>original: "bilancie" (the constellation Libra)</note>,
which fall from her hand when she exceeds [the day];
So that the white and vermillion cheeks
of the beautiful Aurora, where I was,
due to too much age were becoming orange <note>original: "rancie" (rust-colored or orange, indicating the fading of the early dawn colors)</note>;

<margin>151</margin>
We were yet along the edge of the sea,
like people who think upon their journey,
who go with their heart while the body stays behind;
And behold, as when near the morning,
through the thick vapors Mars reddens
down in the west over the ocean floor;

<column-break/>

Truly, the divine genius of our poet—aided by divine grace—rightly establishes three stages of time after he emerged from Hell: the morning, in which the splendor of Venus overcame the darkness; then the dawn; and at present, the rising of the sun. But we shall speak of these below. To better understand, I say that before arriving at the gate of Purgatory, one climbs a certain space of ground where those who were negligent in coming to penance remain for a time. There, while waiting, they purge such negligence; once purged, they enter Purgatory proper to purge the sins they committed. Because he divides such <term>negligence</term> <note>the failure to repent promptly during life</note> into six parts, he similarly divides this place into six parts, so that every kind of negligence has its own proper place.

The first place is the shore up to the mountain. In this part, the negligence of those occupied by vain and worldly delights who delayed their penance is punished. Then follows the second place, which is the first ledge. On this are the negligent who delayed penance because they were under the contumacy of <term>excommunication</term> <note>expulsion from the communion of the church</note>. He writes of these in the third canto. In the fourth canto, he places the second ledge and third place, where he puts those naturally negligent in all their actions. In the fifth canto is the third ledge and fourth place; in it are the negligent who delayed penance due to the preoccupations of war. In the sixth canto, he places the fifth place and fourth ledge, and in that, those who delayed penance due to the preoccupations of their studies. In the following sections, he places the sixth place, for those who delayed due to the preoccupations of lordship or government.

All these souls must wait to enter Purgatory as long as they delayed turning to penance in the world, except for the excommunicated, who must wait thirty years for every year [of their delay]. Furthermore, any of these negligent ones may go as far as the gate of Purgatory, but then they must return to their place until the time is fulfilled. But we shall see all these things more extensively in the process of the work. For in this second canto, he treats only the first type of negligent souls.

But first, he describes the time, showing that the sun was already rising in that hemisphere, and in ours, the night was beginning. **THE SUN HAD ALREADY reached the horizon.** The sun had descended to the circle which divides our hemisphere from the other, which in Greek is called <term>horizon</term> <note>from "orizin," meaning to limit or terminate</note>. It is a fitting name because, as I have said, this is the limit between our hemisphere and the other. Thus, having arrived there, it leaves this one and enters the other, creating sunset for us and sunrise for the other. It follows that for us, it becomes night, and for the others, day. 

Furthermore, you must understand that just as the horizon is the circle that divides one hemisphere from the other, so there is another circle that divides each hemisphere into two equal parts, which the sun reaches at midday. This is because it is as distant from the east as it is from the west. Therefore, it is called the <term>meridian circle</term>. So, the sun was at the horizon that is western to us and eastern to the other hemisphere. But the meridian of this horizon in our hemisphere **COVERS**: that is, it stands over Jerusalem with its highest point—that is, when it is at its greatest height. From this, it follows that Jerusalem is in the center of the world.

**JERUSALEM.** <note>Landino cites the etymology of the city</note> Isidore writes that Shem, the son of Noah, built this city in Syria after the flood and called it Salem. Later, inhabited by the Jebusites, it changed its name and was called Jebus by them. Later they composed the two names, calling it Jebusalem. At another time, Solomon named it <term>Hierosolyma</term> <note>Jerusalem</note>, and the Romans called it Solyma. Hence Juvenal: <note>original: "Solimarúque facerdos"</note> "The priest of Solyma." Finally, the Emperor Aelius Hadrian decreed that it should be called Aelia after himself.

**AND NIGHT, which circles opposite to him**, was seeking the sky. **WAS COMING OUT OF THE GANGES**: just as the Ebro, the river of Spain, is called the western mouth because it runs to the west, so the Ganges, a river in India, is called the eastern mouth because it runs to the east. The Ganges is a river in India named after Ganges, a very ancient King of India. Its origin is not well known. Many say it is born in the high mountains of Scythia and falls with a great noise to the plain into a lake. From there it exits and runs placid and quiet. They say large and navigable rivers enter it. Where it has the least width, it is eight miles wide; where it has the most, one hundred. In no place is it less than twenty feet deep. Many believe it is the river that the Sacred Scriptures call <term>Pishon</term> <note>one of the four rivers of Eden</note>, which means "abundance" or "inundation."

**WAS COMING OUT with the Scales.** He showed above that the sun was in Aries. Because that is where the equinox occurs, and the sun stays as long in our hemisphere as in the one below, it follows that when the sun is at sunset, the <term>Libra</term> <note>the Scales</note>—which is the sign opposite to Aries—rises in the east. And therefore he said "with the Scales," that is, with Libra. **WHICH FALL from her hand when she exceeds.** When the night grows longer [than the day], the science is this: there being two equinoxes in which the night is equal to the day, when the sun is in the first point of Aries, it is the spring equinox. But when it leaves the first degree, the day begins to grow. Hence Petrarch: <note>original: "Era nella stagione che lequinoctio el di fa uincitore"</note> "It was in the season when the equinox makes the day the victor." The opposite effect occurs at the autumn equinox, when the sun is in the first point of Libra.

**SO THAT THE WHITE AND vermillion cheeks.** The poets imagine that Aurora <note>the goddess of Dawn</note> is a very beautiful goddess who stays in the east, because this time of day appears in the east shortly before the sun. Wanting to show that the sun was rising, he says that the cheeks—that is, the "white and vermillion" cheeks of Aurora—those two colors which, as we have said, appear in the air before the sun is fully revealed, had become orange, aged, and old; that is, they had vanished.

We were still on the shore and were like one who thinks to find the way and the road, and not yet knowing it, does not move his body, but the spirit has already set out. And while in such thought, Dante saw a light on the sea quite far from him, which was of that fiery color that Mars usually has when it happens to be almost opposite the sun, so that as dawn arrives, it is near setting. At that time, this planet being red by nature, it happens that in the thick vapors exhaling from the sea and already reddening from the...

As such appeared to me—and may I see it again!—
a light coming over the sea so swiftly
that no flight could equal its motion.
From which, once I had withdrawn
my eye for a moment to question my leader <note>Dante’s guide, the Roman poet Virgil</note>,
I saw it again, brighter and larger.
Then on each side of it appeared to me
an unknown whiteness, and from beneath it,
little by little, another emerged.

My master still did not say a word
until the first whiteness appeared as wings;
then, when he clearly recognized the pilot <note>original: "galeotto"</note>,
he cried: "Bend, bend your knees!
Behold the Angel of God! Fold your hands!
From now on you shall see such officials <note>heavenly ministers or messengers</note>.
See how he scorns human means,
so that he wants no oar, nor any sail
other than his wings, between shores so distant.
See how he holds them pointed toward heaven,
fanning the air with eternal feathers,
which do not change like mortal hair."

Then, as he came closer and closer toward us,
the bird of God appeared more brilliant,
so that the eye up close could not endure it.
But I lowered my gaze, and he came to the shore
with a vessel so swift and light
that the water swallowed none of it.
At the stern stood the celestial pilot,
who seemed "blessed" by his very description <note>original: "per scripto," meaning his holiness was written upon him or ordained</note>;
and more than a hundred spirits sat within.
->When Israel went out of Egypt<-
<note>original: "In exitu Israel de Egypto" (Psalm 114). This psalm celebrates the liberation of the soul from the "Egypt" of sin.</note>
they all sang together with one voice,
with as much of that psalm as is written afterward.
Then he made the sign of the holy cross over them,
whereupon they all threw themselves upon the shore,
and he departed as quickly as he had come.

<column-break/>

the dawn: it appears redder and larger. And the poet arranges it thus: **WE WERE** along the seashore, etc. And behold, a light appeared to me such—that is, of such color—as Mars reddens, not only by its own nature but also through the thick vapors **NEARBY**: at the time near the morning of the dawn. We shall speak of Mars in the *Paradiso* when we come to its sphere. But following the text, the light came so fast that when I turned my eyes to Virgil, it had already approached in a form that appeared brighter and larger. **THEN ON EACH SIDE** shows what happens in vision: one does not see from a distance except confusedly and without distinction. Approaching then, he began to discern the white wings. But first he discerned the color rather than the wings, and therefore he said "a whiteness" and "he did not know what." **AND FROM BENEATH** little by little another emerged: first he saw the whiteness of the wings because they were higher up; then, approaching closer, he began to see the white robe. Because, as I have said, such is the nature of the senses.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'P' at the beginning of the paragraph.</image-desc>**P**atiently Virgil waited, if at first he did not recognize that the one approaching was the Angel. And by this we interpret that the learned man should not affirm to others that he knows a thing unless he first understands it clearly. Or truly, it signifies that no knowledge of universals comes to the human intellect except through the phantasms <note>mental images or sensory impressions</note> of particulars. **SEE HOW HE SCORNS** human means. Because he who is in the "purgatorial virtues" begins to leave behind every human contagion and directs himself to rise from the earth. But because he places a ship here, and a pilot is necessary—just as at the beginning of the *Inferno* he showed who the pilot was who led souls to eternal damnation—so now he places one who leads to Purgatory, where there is firm hope of ascending to heaven after purgation. There he placed Charon, the boat, and the oar. And Acheron: where we said Acheron signifies the motion that makes the soul pass into sin, which motion, because it is full of perturbation, is best likened to turbulent and black water. Here he places the sea, which is not in a tempest, but has small waves and is pure water, to demonstrate the motion of the soul toward purgation, which is without any perturbation. Charon signifies free will there; because it is not illuminated by any divine grace, he describes him in the form of a foul demon. Here, the Angel of God is placed for free will, because our soul in this place uses free will for virtue and not for vice. And because it is guided by divine grace and illuminated by it, he makes him bright and fiery to denote the light of grace and the ardor of the desire to be purged. The boat is taken for the will, which carries free will, both there and here. But in Hell the boat is leaky and weak, and can take on water; whence: *And the leaky marsh-craft took in much [water]* <note>original Latin: "Et multam accepit rimosa paludem" (Virgil, Aeneid VI.414)</note>. This signifies that there the will allows itself to be filled by perturbations. But in Purgatory it is good and receives no water. In Hell, the pilot guides it with an oar. In Purgatory, he pushes it with the sail, which he makes of his wings. The oar and the sail signify choice <note>original: "electione"</note>. But the oar, because it always touches the water, signifies the choice of earthly things; the sails rise above the ship and are airy, which are given to those who inhabit the air, and are wings directed to heaven. This signifies the choice of celestial things. There are some who wish this to be the good Angel who is given as a guardian to the soul.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'S' at the beginning of the paragraph.</image-desc>**S**ome people, by this "swift vessel"—that is, a light little boat—understand the absolution performed by the priest, which has the power to lead the soul to Purgatory. And let the Angel with the two wings be "cooperating" and "perfecting" grace. And that the water swallowed nothing of the ship signifies that the grace of the Holy Spirit—which is acquired in absolution—makes us so light upon the sea of the bitterness of death that we are not submerged in it. This allegory I highly approve of, and it is very fitting. But returning to our allegory, we will say that just as Charon's boat was very pitched and took in much water—whence Virgil said: *And the leaky marsh-craft took in much [water]*—which signifies that the will of vice is always in worldly things, so the Angel's little boat comes lightly over the water because it rises to celestial things and does not dip into the worldly. **BECAUSE THE EYE COULD NOT ENDURE IT**: because Dante had newly entered the purgatorial virtues and was not yet so purged that he could suffer such light; because, as we said before, the impure cannot touch the pure. **HE SEEMED BLESSED BY DESCRIPTION**: he appeared "written," that is, confirmed as blessed. Which is not false, because whoever goes to Purgatory is already confirmed in grace. **WHEN ISRAEL WENT OUT OF EGYPT**: This psalm was written in the presence of the Hebrew people when they left Egypt and the servitude of Pharaoh, and were led by Moses through the desert to go into the land of promise. THEN HE MADE the sign to them of the holy cross: By this sign, which is characteristic of our religion, the poet denotes that such souls held the Christian faith; without it, no merit or virtue of theirs could make them worthy of Purgatory.

The crowd that remained there seemed wild
of that place, looking all around
like one who tastes new things.
On all sides the day was shot through
by the sun, which with its sure arrows
had chased Capricorn from the mid-sky:
When the new people raised their faces
toward us, saying to us: "If you know,
show us the way to go to the mountain."
And Virgil replied: "You perhaps believe
that we are spirits of this place;

We came just a little while before you
by another path, which was so rough and hard
that climbing now will seem like play to us."

The souls who had noticed me,
by my breathing, that I was still alive,
marveling, turned pale:
And as toward a messenger who bears an olive branch
the people pull to hear the news
and no one shows themselves shy of crowding:
So upon my face those
fortunate souls fixed themselves, every one,
almost forgetting to go and make themselves beautiful.

I saw one of them draw forward
to embrace me with such great affection
that it moved me to do the same.

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Large decorative woodcut initial L with floral and architectural motifs.</image-desc>
The crowd of those spirits remaining there seemed wild to the place because they stood as "savage" <note>original: "salvatica," meaning unaccustomed to their surroundings</note>: like those who are new and are not yet sure of themselves. And by this he shows that although we have voluntarily departed from sin and come to purgation, nonetheless at the start such a life frightens us somewhat because we are not accustomed to it. They willingly ask who is used to it and what manner must be held. But Virgil and Dante do not yet have such knowledge because they too are new, so they cannot yet show the way. TO ALL PARTS. The sun was "shooting" the day—that is, it spread its rays, which are the day. For day is nothing else but the light of the sun. Therefore he shows that the sun was already raised so high above our horizon that it spread its rays everywhere. He wishes to show that since the sun was in the first degree of Aries, not only was it above the horizon, but all of Aries had already emerged. Because whenever the first degree of Aries arrives at our eastern horizon, the sixth sign from it must fall into the western horizon. It follows that the third sign from it, which is Capricorn, touches the mid-heaven with its first degree. Therefore, when all of Aries is above the horizon, all of Capricorn will have passed the mid-heaven. For this reason, if the sun (in the first degree of Aries) chased all of Capricorn from the middle of the sky, it means one full sign was already above the earth. We spoke of Capricorn in the *Inferno* <note>Dante’s first book of the Divine Comedy</note> and showed that the sun in that sign creates the winter solstice. WITH THE SURE ARROWS: "true" and "certain," because the rays of the sun never change their order in how they strike. BY ANOTHER PATH. He says that having come through Hell, where they knew the hard servitude of vice and the damnation that proceeds from it, the "climbing"—that is, the purging of oneself—although it is harsh, will seem like a game and a light thing by comparison.

<image-desc>Large decorative woodcut initial A with a figure and floral patterns.</image-desc>
They noticed that Dante was alive because he "sighed"—that is, he drew breath. Drawing breath is proper to a living animal, for neither the body without the soul nor the soul without the body breathes. Breathing is necessary for two things. First, because the heart is the seat of life; if the heart perishes, life perishes. Not being able to endure the heat within it unless it is continually refreshed, nature placed the lungs around the heart in the form of bellows, which continually draw in air to cool it. The second reason is so that the air drawn from the lungs to the heart may nourish and restore the vital spirit <note>term: vital spirit (spirito vitale). In medieval medicine, this was a subtle substance that carried life and heat throughout the body.</note> in the heart, as Albertus Magnus <note>A famous 13th-century scholar and theologian</note> shows in his book *On Animals*. AS TO A MESSENGER. This is a fitting comparison by which he shows that the spirits crowded around Dante just as people run and gather around someone who brings news, especially if he carries an olive branch. This denotes bringing news of either peace or victory. The olive is a tree dedicated to Minerva, goddess of wisdom. The fables say that there was a contest between this goddess and Neptune as to who should name the city that was later called Athens. Jove commanded that each should strike the earth—Minerva with her spear and Neptune with his trident—and the winner would be the one whose strike produced the better thing. Neptune struck and a horse was born; Minerva struck and an olive tree was born. Because the horse is a creature of war and the olive a plant of peace, victory was judged to Minerva. Thus, because her name in Greek is Athena, the city was called Athens. And because it is a tree of peace, all those who went to ask for peace carried the olive. Theophrastus <note>A Greek philosopher and student of Aristotle</note> affirms that it did not grow further than forty miles from the sea. And Fenestella, a notable writer, writes that in the times of Tarquin the Elder <note>original: "Tarquinio Prisco," the legendary fifth King of Rome</note> this tree was not yet in Italy, Africa, or Spain. In Athens, all victors were crowned with olive. It was reasonable for the spirits to marvel that a living man was there, because in a living man there is still appetite and sensuality, which are difficult to subject to reason to make them obey and be purged. ALMOST FORGETTING: forgetting. TO MAKE THEMSELVES BEAUTIFUL: that is, to be purged. Here he notes how great their wonder was, since for the sake of seeing him they deferred their purgation. This also notes the negligence of delaying purgation, for which they are punished, as you will see shortly.

<image-desc>Large decorative woodcut initial D with a profile of a figure.</image-desc>
He shows here that the souls are incorporeal; they are seen only because they have taken on an aerial body, which, though it appears like mist or a cloud, cannot be touched. Whence Christ said in the Gospel: "For a spirit has not flesh and bones" <note>original: "Quoniam spiritus carnem & ossa non habet" (Luke 24:39)</note>. Therefore he says: "O empty shadows, except in appearance," and adds that three times he tried to embrace the shade, and each time his hands returned to his own chest, finding nothing in his arms. This is an imitation of Virgil <note>Referring to the *Aeneid*, where Aeneas tries to embrace ghosts</note>. Three times...

O empty shades, except in appearance!
Three times I joined my hands behind it,
and as many times I returned with them to my breast.
I believe I was painted with wonder,
for the shade smiled and drew back,
and I, following it, pushed myself further forward.
Softly it told me to rest;
then I knew who it was, and I begged

therefore I stop; but you, why do you travel?"

"My Casella, to return another time
to where I am, I make this journey,"
I said, "but how has so much time been taken from you?"
And he to me: "No outrage has been done to me,
if he <note>The celestial pilot/angel</note> who takes up whom and when he pleases
has denied me this passage several times;
For his will is made of a just will.
Truly, for three months now he has taken
anyone who wished to enter in total peace.
Wherefore I, who had then turned to the seashore
where the water of the Tiber becomes salt,
was kindly gathered up by him.
To that river-mouth where he has spread his wings,
because there are always gathered those
who do not descend toward the Acheron." <note>Acheron is the river of the underworld for the damned; those destined for Purgatory gather at the Tiber.</note>

<column-break/>

[Three times he attempted] there to throw his arms around the neck. Three times the image, grasped in vain, escaped his hands, like the light winds and most similar to a fleeting dream. <note>original Latin: "tus ibi collo dare bracchia circum. Ter frustra comprensa manus effugit imago. par leuibus uentis uolucri que simillima somno." A quotation from Virgil’s Aeneid describing Aeneas trying to embrace his father's ghost.</note>
**WITH WONDER** I believe I was painted: because I was greatly marveled. I believe that on my face appeared that color which usually appears when one remains stupefied by a thing. Whence it is common to say: "I became a thousand colors." **FOR THE SHADE** smiled: because it noticed the deception <note>the misunderstanding</note> that I had fallen into, believing that the shade had a palpable body. **SMILED.** It rose modestly. And note that the soul could have embraced him, and therefore it moved as a friend. But then, seeing Dante's error, it withdrew so that he would not try the impossible further. And having withdrawn, seeing that he was following it, it told him to "rest"—that is, that he should not try to embrace it again. But it spoke "softly" so he would understand it was speaking out of affection and not out of anger. There are some who say Dante contradicts himself in this place, since in the *Inferno* he makes the soul palpable, where he says: "Then I took him by the scalp... and I said it would be better if you name yourself, or that no hair remains on your head." <note>referring to Dante's interaction with the traitor Bocca degli Abati in Inferno XXXII</note> To which some respond that in Hell it is necessary for the soul to be palpable so it may be fit to receive corporal punishment. But this does not solve the question. Therefore, we shall rather say: that in Hell, he poetically attributed to the soul that which it naturally does not have, and here he physically reveals the truth, so that this place does not deceive anyone.

**THIS** Casella was our fellow citizen <note>a Florentine</note>, a man of an easy nature and cheerful customs. He was an excellent musician in his time. Our poet, tired from long study, would refresh his weary spirits with Casella's singing, imitating the Pythagoreans, Socrates, and many other philosophers who, for the reason already mentioned, delighted in music. Dante demonstrates, then, that he goes to Purgatory to return there another time; by which words he wants the listener to understand that this fiction of having gone to Hell and Purgatory denotes the consideration of vice and then the will to purge oneself of it. This causes us, after death, to truly go to Purgatory and not to Hell. Then he turns to Casella, and because he knew he had died many years before, he asks him: "Why so much time?"—that is, why has so much time been taken from him, marvelling that from his death until now he had not been transported to Purgatory sooner. And Casella responds that no outrage (that is, injury) has been done to him, although he (the angel who carries them in the boat, passing to Purgatory at every hour, when and to whom it pleases him) had denied him this passage several times. And he gives the reason why no injury was done: because the will of the angel is just, since it is born from the most just will of God. We shall understand this allegorically of the living, who, falling into vices, become dead. And being dead, they are then, by the clemency of God, illuminated by His grace so that they are brought back

---

to purge themselves of such vices. But not all who have fallen into vice are illuminated at the same time; some early and some late. Nor can one who receives such grace late complain for this reason. Nor can the cause that moves God be known, for "Thy judgments, O Lord, are incomprehensible." <note>original Latin: "icōprensibilia sūt iudicia tua domine"</note> Wherefore no one should wish to search them out with curiosity, because "The searcher of majesty shall be overwhelmed by God," <note>original Latin: "Scrutator maiestatis deiiciet a deo," a paraphrase of Proverbs 25:27 warning against prying into divine mysteries</note> as we said in another place. But returning to the fiction: he writes that the souls who are to come to Purgatory are taken from the mouth of the Tiber by the angel. By this, he means that whoever goes to Purgatory must depart from Rome—that is, come from the obedience of the Church. But from there, some are taken sooner and some later, as it pleases God, except in the year of the Jubilee, in which every soul is taken at their own request. And therefore he says "for three months now he has taken in total peace"—that is, without any contradiction—whoever has wished to enter. And he says "for three months now" because he fakes that this descent of his was in the year 1300 in March, and the Jubilee had begun in December for the Nativity of Christ. Thus, at the mouth of the Tiber, where the angel has his wings spread, of which he makes a sail—that is, he enters the sea and it becomes salt—Casella was gathered by him at that mouth of the Tiber, where the angel has his wings spread, as was said above. And he directs himself here because from here he takes with his boat all the souls who have to go to Purgatory and do not descend toward the Acheron, from whence one goes to Hell. Furthermore, it is manifest that he wished, without departing from his purpose, to imitate Virgil, who feigns that Charon does not pass the souls of those whose bodies are not buried until after a hundred years.

---

And I: "If a new law does not take from you
memory or the use of the amorous song
that was wont to quiet all my desires,
may it please you to comfort my soul
somewhat with it, which, coming here
with its body, is so very exhausted."

<column-break/>

**IF A NEW** law, which is imposed from eternity by God in these places. Therefore it is not new in regard to the law itself, but new to Casella, who was newly subjected to this law. In summary, he prays to Casella that if the law of that place does not take from him the memory of singing (in a way that he has forgotten it) or take away its use (that is, the power to use it), he should sing; so that, just as in life he used to content him, so now in his death he may comfort him and give refreshment to his soul, which is exhausted from having come with the body by such a difficult way. And he, to please Dante, sang a song <note>a "canzone" or lyric poem</note> made by the poet, the beginning of which is: "Love that discourses in my mind." <note>original: "Amor che nellamēte mira," actually "Amor che ne la mente mi ragiona" from Dante's Convivio</note>

<summary>Dante encounters the soul of his friend Casella, a musician, who explains how souls are gathered at the Tiber's mouth to be ferried to Purgatory. Casella then prepares to sing for Dante to ease the exhaustion of his journey.</summary>

->### PURGATORY<-

**“Love, who in my mind discourses with me,”**
he then began so sweetly
that the sweetness still sounds within me.
My master and I, and those people
who were with him, seemed as content
as if no other thing touched their minds.

The mind desires things made of that same substance; thus our soul supremely yearns for harmony. This moved **Aristoxenus** <note>A Greek philosopher and pupil of Aristotle who argued the soul was a form of musical harmony</note> to say that our soul was harmony itself. And certainly, it is a natural state: as **Boethius** <note>An influential early medieval philosopher</note> demonstrates in the preface to his *Music*, it delights every age. It is so powerful that it changes every man. **Empedocles** <note>A Greek pre-Socratic philosopher</note> mitigated and quenched the anger of a young man who wanted to kill his father’s accuser with his music. **Pythagoras** <note>The famous mathematician and philosopher</note> restrained a man who wanted to burn down a house where his mistress was with his rival and competitor. **Aristotle** says in his *Problems* that both the sorrowful and the joyful use music—one to diminish pain, the other to increase happiness. There are two species of song: one is "grave" (serious), which the Spartans and Romans used, and in which **Plato** wishes the youth to be exercised. **Athanasius** <note>St. Athanasius of Alexandria</note> forbade music in church to avoid all lewdness. **Ambrose** <note>St. Ambrose, who introduced antiphonal chanting</note> commanded its use to excite our minds toward religion. **Augustine** disputes for and against it. Now the author, following the opinion of Ambrose, denotes through our **Casella** that he who must endure the difficulty and fatigue of climbing the mountain—that is, to purify himself—should hear that music which invites one to goodness, virtue, and religion. Nor is it without great prudence that Dante induces Casella to sing this specific song out of the many he composed: "Love, who in my mind discourses with me." For, as he himself interprets in his *Symposium* or rather the *Convivio* <note>Dante's philosophical treatise, the "Banquet"</note>, he demonstrates in this song that his love is not for a mortal thing, but for **Philosophy and Theology**. Thus he said that "Love discourses with him"—that is, speaks with reasoning and the discourse of reason. And it speaks "in the mind"—that is, in the intellect. Therefore, it is the love of intellectual and celestial things.

<column-break/>

...courses: <note>Continuing the sentence from the previous column: "...dis-courses"</note> which song delighted both Dante and Virgil and the souls who came with Casella so much that it seemed they had no other care in their minds. This is very fitting, because just as the entrance to Hell was full of laments and woes, by contrast, the beginning of Purgatory should have sweet songs. For there one goes to manifest damnation, but here to certain salvation. It shows that the souls, Dante, and Virgil listened to the song with great attention, for there is no one whom music does not delight. Because our souls are created most perfectly, they cannot exist without supreme proportion, which is nothing other than harmony. For just as the body is composed of... <note>The commentary logic here explains that the soul naturally responds to music because both are built on mathematical proportions.</note>

We all stood fixed and attentive
to his notes; and behold the noble old man <note>Cato of Utica, the guardian of Purgatory</note>
crying out: "What is this, lingering spirits?
What negligence, what staying is this?
Run to the mountain to strip off the slough <note>The outer "skin" of sin or worldly attachment</note>
that does not let God be manifest to you."
As when, gathering grain or tares,
the pigeons assembled at their pasture,
quiet, without showing their usual pride,
if something happens that gives them fear,
suddenly they let the bait be,
because they are assailed by a greater care;
so I saw that fresh company
leave the singing and go toward the slope,
like a man who goes, but knows not where he may come out;
nor was our departure any less swift.

...because lustful love does not "discourse"—that is, it does not use reason—as we demonstrated in the first *cantica* <note>Inferno</note>; instead, it excites and moves sensuality, not in the mind but in the appetite. We conclude, then, that the poet signifies that since we must endure the grueling difficulty of the climb, we must restore and seek the mind through music, than which nothing is more a friend to the soul. But it must be with that music which contains within itself celestial and divine love, and not an earthly love submerged in sensuality.

<insert>d</insert> It demonstrates that it often happens that even though we are disposed to purge ourselves of vices, nevertheless sometimes a delight in earthly and fleeting things entices us, and makes us leave behind things of importance to linger in those. But after some time, **Cato**—that is, the love of liberty—reproves us and urges us to our purification. **WE STOOD FIXED**: as if to say, we were not only stopped, but stopped with the intent to stay. **WHAT NEGLIGENCE IS THIS**: It is bad to use negligence in all things we must do, but much worse to use it in seeking liberty. **RUN TO THE MOUNTAIN**: to purge yourselves of that stain which takes away your sight, so that you do not see God.

->CANTO THREE<-
bb iii
<meta>catchword: not in Virgil:</meta>

## THIRD CANTO OF THE SECOND CANTICLE OF DANTE:

Although the sudden flight
scattered them across the countryside,
turned toward the mountain where reason goads us,
I drew closer to my faithful companion:
and how would I have run without him?
Who would have pulled me up the mountain?
He seemed to me self-reproached;
O dignified and clear conscience,
how bitter a bite a small fault is to you!

When his feet left behind the haste
that mars the dignity of every act,
my mind, which was first restrained,
expanded its intent as if eager:
and I set my face against the slope
which rises highest toward heaven from the waters.
The sun, which behind was flaming red,
was broken before me in the shape
that had in me the support of its rays.
I turned to the side with fear
of being abandoned, when I saw
the earth dark only before me.

<margin>154</margin>

<column-break/>

In this third chapter he places the souls who have been negligent and have deferred their penitence and conversion, remaining stubborn against the sentence of the Shepherd <note>The "Shepherd" refers to the Pope or the Church authorities who issued the excommunication</note>, living as excommunicates. And through pride they were not reconciled. And because this negligence coming from pride is more grave than the others, it is therefore punished in a lower place. Following the narration, then, he shows that although the other souls, due to the severe rebuke of Cato, had set off in a scattered run, he nevertheless did not leave; rather, he drew close to Virgil as a faithful companion. 

For when the desire for liberty spurs a man to leave every delight that might feed the senses in order to purge himself of vices, the senses and the <term>lower reason</term> <note>The part of the human mind concerned with worldly affairs and sensory input</note> should want to hasten to such work. But nonetheless, one should not move without Virgil: that is, without <term>higher reason</term> <note>The part of the mind capable of contemplating divine truths and moral principles</note> being illuminated, as we have said; because without that, one would err and often, due to the difficulty, would abandon the enterprise. For higher reason is that which pulls the lower after it toward arduous and laborious things. Whence he said: "Who would have pulled me up the mountain?" as if to say "no one," because reason alone pulls one toward the purgatorial virtues. 

HE SEEMED TO ME self-reproached. It is a fitting thing that when higher reason, adorned with true doctrine, sometimes allows itself to grow slightly old <note>Landino uses "grow old" here to mean "become stagnant" or "lose focus"</note> by some pleasure—though for a brief time and in a pleasure not foul or ugly, such as this listening [to the song]—it should sting us; because in such a man of perfect conscience, every minimal error seems grave to him. Whence he said: "He seemed to me self-reproached." O DIGNIFIED conscience. This is an exclamation moved by wonder. For in truth a dignified and clear conscience is an admirable thing, both for its excellence and because they are rarely found. 

I am not displeased by what is said by many: that the free will in man is the queen of all, and the intellect and reason are her two assessors and counselors; and discretion and conscience are two officials; and the flesh and the spirit are two messengers. The former [flesh] is flattering and a liar; the latter [spirit] is harsh and severe. And therefore when the flesh brings forward vicious and worldly things, and the lord <note>The "lord" here refers to the Will</note> contradicts them and accords with discretion, conscience, reason, and intellect—then this is <term>conscience</term> <note>Landino plays on the Latin etymology: "con-scientia," or "knowledge held together"</note>. But when the lord believes the flesh, the spirit is saddened and the conscience cries out; then it is "against conscience." But sometimes, aided by the world and the demon, the flesh imprisons the spirit, the conscience, the reason, and the intellect, and puts in their place as its vicar "obstinacy," which plugs the ears of the lord so that he does not hear the cries of conscience. Whence he said: "O dignified conscience," full of dignity and clear, because every small fault reproaches it greatly.

It shows that Virgil, together with the others, began to run. But it lasted little, because to hasten in taking any side and not to do things with maturity and consultation, but to precipitate oneself after appetite—even if the thing in itself is honest—is not good. But we must always use maturity, which is the <term>mean</term> <note>The "Golden Mean" or middle ground between extremes</note> between practicing negligence or slowness and being over-hasty. Whence it happens that sometimes our intellect and reason, moved by excellent purpose, use too much haste at the beginning, in a way that does not observe gravity and propriety; but quickly it realizes this and tempers itself, so as not to "mar"—that is, not to disturb the order which requires honesty and appropriateness. This, the Latins call <note>original: "decorum"</note> propriety, and the Greeks call <note>original: "prepon"</note> the fitting. 

And when Virgil—that is, higher reason—leaves such haste, Dante, who is lower reason, likewise leaves it; and his intention, which was constrained in 그 celerity, expands. AND I SET my face against the slope. He did not restrain the haste because he had changed his purpose, but to do that same thing with more order and appropriateness. Therefore he did not turn his back to the mountain of Purgatory, as one does who wants to distance himself from it, but gave it his face because he was going toward it. WHICH TOWARD the heaven highest "un-lakes" itself <note>original: "sidislaga"</note>: that is, it dilates or expands. For we say "to lake" <note>original: "allagare"</note> when water, by stagnating, spreads out. 

THE SUN WHICH BEHIND. Dante, in walking, turned his back to the sun; therefore he saw his shadow before him. And not seeing Virgil’s shadow, he feared that Virgil had abandoned him. "The sun which behind was flaming was broken before me": it made a shadow in front of me, which shadow exists because the sun, finding a support—that is, opposition and an obstacle—IN ME (that is, in my body), is broken and does not penetrate. ONLY BEFORE me the earth dark: shadowed. When we begin to climb toward purgation, the sun—that is, illuminating grace—accompanies us. But its rays penetrate Virgil in such a way that he leaves no shadow of himself. But they do not penetrate Dante, because he has a dense body with which he holds back the rays and does not let them penetrate. Whence it happens that his shadow is seen in front. Virgil is higher reason, which is entirely penetrable by the light; indeed, it is almost the light itself. Therefore, from that, no obscurity or ignorance proceeds. But Dante (that is, sensuality) has a dense body and is not penetrable by rays. Whence it makes a shadow, signifying ignorance. Reason is entirely illuminated and has light in itself, like the sun. Sense and appetite are like the moon, which has no light of its own; and that which comes from the sun illustrates the surface but does not penetrate. Therefore, on that side where the sun does not strike it, it remains dark. Thus appetite and sensuality have no light except what they receive from reason, and that does not penetrate them. Therefore it remains shadowy on the other side. This is, then, the reason why Dante sees the shadow (that is, ignorance) in himself and not in Virgil.

<summary>Dante and Virgil begin their ascent of Purgatory; Dante panics when he sees only his own shadow, leading to a philosophical explanation of how higher reason (Virgil) is transparent to divine grace while human sensuality (Dante) remains opaque.</summary>

<header>PURGATORIO</header>

Virgil noticed that Dante suspected he had been abandoned by him; therefore, turning completely toward him, he said: "Why do you distrust? Do you not believe I am with you, and that I guide you?" And then he adds: "If you do not see my shadow as you do your own, know that this happens because I do not have my body with me as you have yours. For that body, at my death, I left in the other hemisphere, where it is already evening—that is, evening—because in this place it is morning. NAPLES HAS IT and from Brindisi it was taken," because the poet died in Calabria. But the body was later transferred to Naples, where his epitaph is:
> <note>original: "Mantua me genuit: calabri rapuere. Tenet nūc parthenope cecini paſcua rura duces."</note> Mantua bore me; Calabria took me. Now Naples holds me. I sang of pastures, fields, and leaders.
And this much for the history. But allegorically, the soul that has laid down the body...

El mio conforto perche pur diffidi
adir micomincio tutto riuolto:
non credi tu me teco/& chio te guidi?
Veſpero e/gia cola doue ſepolto
locorpo dentro alquale io facea ombra:
napoli lha & da branditio e tolto:
Hora ſennanzi ame nulla ſadombra/
non timarauigliar piu che decieli/
che luno allaltro raggio non ingombra:
Aſſofferir tormenti & caldi & gieli
ſimili corpi la uirtu diſpone:
che chome fa non uuole chauoi ſi uueli

...reveal. And therefore he said: *si veli*, that is, be revealed. And this passage is much debated by theologians. For all natural reasons seem to conclude that since the soul is incorporeal, it cannot be afflicted by corporeal fire. For this reason, Thomas Aquinas <note>St. Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the influential Dominican friar and philosopher whose theology underpins much of Dante's work.</note> maintains that they suffer by means of the body; because despite the fact that they remain stripped of their own bodies, nonetheless God can bind them to some body by way of form, just as He bound them to their own bodies to give them life. Or truly, without this, He can bind them as necromancers, by the power of demons, bind spirits to some image.

Matte chi ſpera che uoſtra ragione
poſſa traſcender lainfinita uia
che tiene una ſubſtantia in tre perſone.
State contenti humana gente alquia
che ſe potuto haueſſe ueder tutto.
meſtier non era partorir Maria.
Et diſiar uedeſti ſanza fructo:
tai/che ſarebbe ellor diſio quetato
chethernalmente e dato lor per lucto.
Io dico dariſtotile/& di plato/
& dimoltaltri: & qui chino la fronte
& piu non dixe & rimaſe turbato

...that is, to have knowledge of all divine things. IT WAS NOT NECESSARY for Mary to give birth. For it would not have been necessary for God to become incarnate if man had not sinned; nor would he have sinned if he could have known everything. AND YOU SAW DESIRE without fruit: He proves by the example of the ancient philosophers that the human intellect cannot have perfect knowledge of divine things; since Aristotle and Plato, men of the highest genius, although they were supremely satisfied in investigating and supremely desired—that is, longed—to find the truth, nevertheless we see that their desiring could not acquire such knowledge. Therefore it was without fruit, and they labored in vain. The text is organized thus: You saw desiring without fruit such men—that is, such men as were Aristotle and Plato—and their desire would have been quieted—that is, they would have contented their desire for knowing—had they been able to investigate the truth. But not having been able, such desire is given to them for eternal mourning—that is, for eternal pain. For the pain of such men placed in Limbo, according to Dante, is not being able to have knowledge of that which they sought. And here he bowed his brow: which signifies shame and confusion, and shows himself defeated. AND HE SAID NO MORE: because human reason can say little else of divine things than what has been said. AND HE REMAINED troubled, considering himself deprived of the Supreme Good.

Noi diuenimo intanto apie del monte
quiui trouamo la roccia ſi erta:
chendarno ui ſarrien le gambe prompte
Tra lerice & turbia lapiu deſerta:
la piu romita uia e una ſcala:

<column-break/>

...vices, which proceed from the contagion of the flesh, do not cast a shadow, because only light remains. And being completely illuminated, no ignorance remains in it. NOW BEFORE ME nothing is shadowed. If the sun, which striking my shoulders, does not cast a shadow in front of me as it does for you, do not marvel; because I do not have a dense body like yours, but a rare one like the celestial bodies. Therefore, do not marvel at these things more than at the heavens. For although those of the planets are seven, and the eighth is where the fixed stars are, and one includes the other, nonetheless because they are of a rare and transparent body—<term>diaphanous</term> and clear—they give passage to their rays so that they penetrate to the earth and to our eyes, so that we see as far as the fixed stars. And this is because one does not block the ray of the other. TO SUFFER torments, and heat and frost. He solves a question which might arise here. For it seems very doubtful: if souls are stripped of bodies—which, being composed of four contrary elements, can suffer pain—how can these souls suffer? To which he responds: that the divine power, which every nature serves, wills that they suffer. And He does not want it to be known to us how they can suffer.

Therefore, he is a fool who hopes that our reason—that is, the human intellect, which is finite—can traverse, can by the discourse of its reason arrive at the end of the path: God. And he rightly said "path," for it is that discourse of reason that leads us to the conclusion. WHICH HOLDS ONE substance in three persons. This signifies the Trinity, of which we will narrate some small part in the place that requires it more. And certainly he is a fool who believes he has knowledge of divine things. Wherefore Saint Paul says excellently in the Epistle to the Romans:
> <note>original: "O altitudo diuitiarum ſapietię & ſcietię dei: quā incōprēſibilia iudicia eius: & inueſtigabiles uię eius."</note> O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past finding out!
Therefore, let no one seek how the soul, which is incorporeal and a simple form, can suffer. For a simple form should be incapable of suffering. And let us remember:
> <note>original: "Nolite ſapere pluſquā oporteat ſapere."</note> Do not seek to know more than it is appropriate to know.
BE CONTENT, human race, with the "because." <note>The commentator explains the scholastic distinction between *quia* (the fact) and *propter quid* (the reason why).</note> Aristotle says: In Latin there are two terms, *quare* and *quia*. *Quare* is the "why" that asks; *quia* is that which responds. Therefore, let us imitate the disciples of Pythagoras, to whom they showed such reverence that it sufficed that in teaching, they believed "this is so because it is so." THAT IF IT HAD BEEN POSSIBLE to see all...

While Virgil was reasoning as has been said, they arrived at the mountain of Purgatory, which was very high, and at that gate where they had come, it was so steep and upright that for anyone who had a body and had to go on legs, it would have been in vain to be prompt and ready to climb. Because it was impossible. And it was a comparison: that even on the Riviera of Genoa—which from the east and toward the Gulf of La Spezia has for its final limit the castle of the Genoese, Lerici, and from...

<vocab>Purgatorio: The second kingdom of the afterlife in Dante's poem. Virgil: The Roman poet serving as Dante's guide. Danthe: The protagonist and author. Naples: The city where Virgil's tomb is located. Aristotle and Plato: Ancient Greek philosophers placed in Limbo. Maria: The Virgin Mary. Pythagoras: Ancient Greek philosopher known for the "ipse dixit" (he said it himself) authority. Thomas Aquinas: Medieval theologian who explained the state of souls after death. Saint Paul: Apostle whose writings caution against human intellectual pride. Limbo: The circle of Hell for virtuous pagans. Trinity: The Christian doctrine of one God in three persons.</vocab>

<header>### CANTO THREE</header>

...towards that one, easy and open:
**N**ow who knows on which hand the slope declines,
said my master, halting his step,
so that he who goes without wings may climb?
And while, holding his face down,
he examined the path in his mind,
and I was looking up around the rock,
From the left hand appeared to me a group
of souls who moved their feet towards us,
and yet they did not seem to, they came so slowly:

<note>The commentator explains that Dante has his body with him and cannot "fly" like a soul without a body. Allegorically, this means Dante, not yet being purified, cannot detach himself from earthly things to rise to the divine. Virgil’s downward gaze represents the "posture of one occupied in research and profound cognition," citing Virgil’s own poetic description of deep thought.</note> <note>original: "Et paribus auris ueſtigia figit" – Landino likely references Virgil's Aeneid, though the Latin here is slightly corrupted from "paribusque haeret vestigia figit," meaning "he stayed his steps with equal pace."</note> Dante, representing sensuality, does not exhaust his mind but instead looks with his bodily senses at the difficulty of the climb. FROM THE LEFT hand. Therefore, on the right hand is the path leading to purgatory. These are those of whom we spoke above: and he feigns that they go slowly, just as in life they were slow to abandon their defiance of the Holy Church and return to penance.

Raise, I said, Master, your eyes:
behold over here those who will give us counsel,
if you cannot have it from yourself.
He looked then, and with a free look
replied: let us go there, for they come slowly;
and you, confirm your hope, sweet son.
That people was still far off—
I mean after our thousand steps—
as far as a good thrower could cast by hand,

<note>As an excellent "physician" of the soul, the poet knew that particulars are found in the senses, and from these, the intellect gathers them and reduces them to universals according to the Peripatetic philosophers (followers of Aristotle). Hence the Aristotelian phrase: "It is necessary for the one who understands to use the imagination."</note> <note>original: "Oportet intelligentem fantaſticari."</note>

When they all pressed together against the hard rocks
of the other bank, and stood firm and close
like those who stop to look while in doubt.
"O you who ended well, O spirits already elect,"
Virgil began, "by that peace
which I believe is awaited by you all,
Tell us where the mountain slopes,
so that it may be possible to go upward;
for lost time displeases most those who know most."

As the little sheep come out from the fold
by ones, by twos, by threes; and the others stand
timidly, casting eyes and muzzle to the ground;
And what the first one does, the others do,
huddling against her if she stops,
simple and quiet, and they know not why;
So I saw the head [of that group] move forward.

<column-break/>

...the western part has at its furthest end toward Provence very steep mountains, uninhabitable due to their harshness. Nevertheless, the most deserted and remote of those is like a [easy] staircase compared to this slope of Purgatory. Therefore, the intellect was intent on finding which way was easiest, given that the path of purgation is so steep and difficult. Certainly, it is the office of wisdom for whoever enters into these second types of virtue to begin from the easiest path before they become a habit. But little by little, the closer we approach the habit, the easier they become at every hour, as we shall show in the process. But when we have already made a habit of them, they are not only not difficult and laborious, but they are even easy and pleasurable. "Now who knows," as if to say "not I," on which hand the slope declines, either from the right or from the left. HALTING HIS STEP, as one does who is in doubt. SO THAT HE MAY CLIMB WHO GOES WITHOUT WINGS: that is, Dante, who has his body with him and does not fly like a soul without a body.

**D**ante admonishes Virgil to ask counsel from those who are coming because such knowledge, which is "at the beginning"—that is, coming from the effects to the cause—has its origin in the senses and in lower reason. And therefore it is easier for man, although that which comes from principles—that is, proceeding from the cause to the effects—is more in accord with nature. Hence Aristotle said: "Plato rightly doubted [the way] from principles to principles." <note>original: "Recte dubitauit Plaito a principiis ad principia."</note> Virgil thinks, and not finding the way in universals, he encounters a "particular," which is found in the senses. HE LOOKED THEN AND WITH A FREE LOOK: when our soul has had knowledge of the particular by abstraction, it comes to the universal. This abstraction the intellect performs through what it finds in the sense and in reason. Therefore Virgil rejoices in these "particulars" (the souls) and goes toward them. And this is what led Dante to feign that he, in this place, showed them to Virgil: because as an excellent natural philosopher, he knew that particulars are in the senses, and from those, the intellect takes them and reduces them to universals according to the Peripatetics. Whence Aristotle: "The one who understands must use the imagination." <note>A fundamental Aristotelian concept that the human mind requires mental images (phantasms) to process abstract thought.</note>

**H**e gains their goodwill by saying, "O spirits who ended well": that is, those of you who finished your life well, with the grace of God. O ALREADY ELECT. For notwithstanding that those in Purgatory are still in their punishments, they are nonetheless already chosen for beatitude. Allegorically, we understand that whoever sets himself on the path of purgation—because he returns through it to virtue—can already be called "elect." Having gained goodwill, he now makes the request. TELL US WHERE THE MOUNTAIN SLOPES: that is, where it is less steep; and in this way, he makes the request honorable, because it is an honorable thing to ask for help in a good purpose. FOR LOST TIME DISPLEASES MOST THOSE WHO KNOW MOST: And this further ignited the honorableness [of the request]; for it is a laudable thing to consume time in virtuous things and not in idleness. And he said this especially to these souls who were supremely repentant and were much displeased to have consumed great time in the laziest idleness.

**H**e likens these souls to sheep for their meekness and for their simplicity, and because in this they changed the habits of sheep. THEY EXIT THE FOLD: from the enclosures where the shepherds shut them at night. BY ONE, BY TWO, BY THREE: They are by nature fearful. Pliny writes that in great thunders, if a sheep finds itself in the pasture alone and far from the others and is pregnant, it often miscarries out of fear. <note>A reference to Pliny the Elder's *Natural History*, common in medieval/Renaissance science.</note> For the same reason, they willingly follow whoever leads them; therefore there are few who begin, but many who follow, and that timid nature makes them lower their head and eye and do what the first one does. SO I SAW: that is, in this manner.

<header>### CANTO THREE</header>

...of that fortunate flock then,
modest in face and honest in gait.
As those in front saw broken
the light on the ground from my right side,
so that the shadow fell from me to the grotto,
they stayed and drew back somewhat,
and all the others who came after,
not knowing why, did the same.
<column-break/>
**THE HEAD:** the first and the guide. **MOVED THEN:** <gloss>meaning at that moment when Virgil spoke to them.</gloss> **FORTUNATE FLOCK:** happy. *Mandra* [flock] is a Greek word and signifies a cave, or a place where sheep gather in the shade <note>original: "Mandra e uocabolo greco." Landino notes the Greek etymology of the word "mandra" (μανδρα), which can mean an enclosed space or fold.</note>. But "mandra" is taken here to mean the herd. And from this we call a governor of the flock an "archimandrite." Therefore, having compared them to sheep, he stays with the metaphor by saying "flock." **MODEST in face:** with a modest appearance. This is appropriate for one who is preparing for purgation. **SAW BROKEN the light:** They saw my shadow which broke the light of the sun. And by this they knew that I had a body, as was said above. **THEY STAYED:** They stopped. Those first ones out of wonder, which they felt at finding a soul in that place who was in his own flesh; and those who came after, although they had not yet seen the shadow, stopped upon seeing the first ones stopped. And certainly the soul stripped of the body can marvel that a soul which is still within such a dark prison can disentangle itself in form from the contagion from which it wishes to be purged.

---

"Without your question I confess to you:
that this is a human body that you see,
by which the light of the sun on the ground is split.
Do not marvel, but believe
that not without virtue that comes from heaven
does he seek to overcome this wall."
Thus the master: and those worthy people
said: "Turn then, and enter before us,"
making a sign with the back of their hands.
<column-break/>
**VIRGIL:** that is, reason illuminated by much doctrine, as we showed in the first canticle <note>referring to the *Inferno*</note>, admonishes the souls that although the body has fallen, nevertheless, whoever is accompanied by celestial virtue—that is, by the cooperating and perfecting grace of God—can win the battle and "overcome the wall," which means climbing the cliff that leads into Purgatory. **THUS THE MASTER:** So Virgil spoke; and those souls, immediately acquiescing to reason, showed the way. **AND WITH THE BACK of the hand they made a sign:** That is, they beckoned. **TURN:** They advise them to turn toward the east and to the right hand. This denotes every virtue. They entered before them because those [souls] were to remain outside of Purgatory <note>Landino refers to the "Late Repentant" who must wait in Ante-Purgatory.</note>.

---

And one of them began: "Whoever
you are, speaking thus, turn your face:
consider if you ever saw me back there."
I turned toward him and looked at him fixedly:
he was blond and beautiful and of noble aspect,
but a blow had divided one of his eyebrows.
When I had humbly denied
ever having seen him, he said: "Now see,"
and showed me a wound at the top of his chest.
Then smiling he said: "I am Manfred,
grandson of the Empress Constance;
wherefore I pray you that when you return,
go to my beautiful daughter, mother
of the honors of Sicily and Aragon,
and tell her the truth, if something else is said."
<column-break/>
The author wishes to demonstrate how great divine mercy is, and that no one is so great a sinner that, even at the extreme point of his life, he cannot be saved. And therefore he places Manfred in this spot. Manfred, although he had been a most cruel enemy to the Holy Church and to his own people (as we showed in the 28th Canto of the first canticle), and finally died excommunicated, was nonetheless able to save himself by surrendering himself in guilt. I will not dwell on his history, because we narrated it at length above. I will only add this: that Manfred was a very prudent man and ruled his empire well. He was beautiful of body, and in his manners pleasant and cheerful. He delighted in all music—in songs, sounds, and dances. But he was very ambitious and luxurious, of an Epicurean life, and without religion. There was in Puglia the ancient city of Siponto, but because of the unhealthy air, he moved it two miles further onto the coast and named it Manfredonia after himself. Dante feigns that he sees him as blond and showing his wounds because he had read this of him and heard it by fame. But in life he could not have seen him, for Manfred was defeated and killed on the last day of February in the year of our salvation 1265. And he was buried at Benevento in a royal sepulcher. What the poet writes of Manfred’s wounds is entirely poetic. For according to theologians, and especially Thomas Aquinas, all bodies—both of the damned and the saved—will rise without any defect that might have come to them, whether by nature's fault or by any case or accident. Therefore, if there will be no defect in the body, much less will there be in the soul. **EVER SAW ME?** <note>original: "MI VEDESTI unque?"</note> "Never," because in Latin they say *unquam*. **WHEN I HAD humbly denied:** With humanity I confessed not having seen him ever. **SMILING:** Showing himself friendly and benevolent. **GRANDSON Of Constance:** She was the daughter of Tancred, King of Sicily, and wife of Henry VI the Emperor, father of Frederick II, who was the father of this Manfred. Thus, he was the grandson of Constance. And he named himself after her because through her the kingdom of Sicily came to the Emperor Henry. **TO MY DAUGHTER:** Who was similarly called Constance; and she was the "genitress," that is, the mother of Don Frederick, King of Sicily, and of Don James, King of Aragon. **IF SOMETHING ELSE is said:** Because it was common rumor that, having died excommunicated, he was damned.

---

After I had my body broken
by two mortal points, I surrendered myself
weeping to Him who willingly pardons.
Horrible were my sins,
but the infinite Goodness has such great arms...
<column-break/>
It demonstrates how great is divine mercy, which even if one is a very great sinner and delays to the extreme point to convert (like this man who delayed until after his mortal wounds), nonetheless, whoever surrenders to God weeping with contrition for his sins can be saved. For we receive the soul from God pure and immaculate, and we must maintain it in such a state until death, and thus return it to Him. And if we have...

<summary>In this passage, Dante encounters the soul of Manfred, the former King of Sicily, who reveals that despite his excommunication and "horrible sins," he was saved through a last-moment act of repentance. The commentary by Landino emphasizes the boundlessness of divine mercy and provides historical and theological context regarding the nature of spiritual bodies.</summary>
