which takes what turns toward it.

### If the Pastor of Cosenza, who to the hunt
### of me was sent by Clement then,
### had in God well-read this page,
### the bones of my body would still be
### at the head of the bridge near Benevento,
### under the guard of the heavy rock-pile.
### Now the rain bathes them and the wind moves them
### outside the Kingdom, almost along the Verde,
### where he transported them with extinguished lights.

<column-break/>

...we have stained: confession and contrition wash it. **WHO WILLINGLY** forgives. Wherefore it is said: *The earth is full of the mercy of God* <note>original: "Misericordia dei piena est terra"</note>. **HORRIBLE** were my sins: God does not forgive one who does not confess as a sinner and does not repent of having sinned. And therefore the author shows that this man was both. He confessed, because he says: *Horrible were my sins.* He repented, because he says: *I surrendered myself weeping.* **HOW INFINITE GOODNESS** has such wide arms. The arms of God are mercy toward those who convert, and justice which rewards every merit. **IF THE PASTOR of Cosenza.** The Cardinal of Cosenza was the legate of Pope Clement IV in the army of Charles [of Anjou] when King Manfred was killed. And after the victory, he had his body dragged from the great tomb which was **AT THE HEAD:** that is, at the start of the bridge of Benevento, as if he were an excommunicated man. Therefore, if this Pastor of Cosenza **HAD READ in God,** that is, in Holy Scripture, **THIS page:** that is, that passage where 

this sentence is treated—that until the final moment of life, divine mercy awaits us—he would have been able to consider that I could be saved, and he would not have dragged me from underneath **THE HEAVY rock-pile.** At the head of the bridge at Benevento, there was a high tower to guard the passage, and there a small church where Manfred was buried. He calls the tower a *mora* <note>In Italian, "mora" can mean a delay, a rock-pile (cairn), or a Moor. Landino explores different etymologies here.</note> because it causes a delay [dimoranza] for those who would wish to pass by force; or perhaps he said *mora* to serve the rhyme in place of *mola* [a mass]. For others say that Charles, the victor in this battle, not wishing to bury him in a sacred place due to his excommunication, had him placed in a pit at the head of the bridge, and then had each of the soldiers throw a stone upon him. For this reason, a very great mass remained upon him. Both *moles* and every heavy weight; but especially the great sepulchers made by the ancients were called *moles*. Thus, Castel Sant'Angelo in Rome, because it was the tomb of the Emperor Hadrian, is called the *Mausoleum of Hadrian* <note>original: "Moles Adriani"</note>. **NOW the rain bathes them** and the wind moves them: because they are disinterred and in the open. **OUTSIDE THE Kingdom.** Some say the legate had sworn to chase him out of the kingdom; and not having been able to chase him out alive, he chased the body "almost along the Verde." Verde is a river that flows into the Tronto, not far from Ascoli. **WITH EXTINGUISHED LIGHT:** without the honor of candles. And he said "with extinguished light" to denote that the Cardinal held him as excommunicated; for when someone is excommunicated, the priest throws down the light in a way that it is extinguished.

---

<columns>2</columns>

### Through their malediction one does not so lose,
### that the eternal love cannot return,
### while hope still has a flower of green.
### True it is, that he who dies in contumacy
### of Holy Church, even if at the end he repents,
### must stay outside this bank
### for thirty times as long as he has been
### in his presumption, if such a decree
### does not become shorter through good prayers.
### See now if you can make me happy,
### by revealing to my good Constance
### how you have seen me, and also this prohibition:
### For here, through those back there, much is gained.

<column-break/>

**THROUGH THEIR malediction:** through excommunication. **THEIR** refers to the prelates. **ONE DOES NOT SO LOSE:** one is not lost in such a final way. **THE ETERNAL love.** The grace of the eternal God; [it is not possible] that this eternal love cannot return, even though the excommunication had cast him out. **WHILE hope has a flower of green:** While we are in life and can return to penance, it "has a flower of green," that is, it has hope. Whoever is excommunicated by the "greater excommunication" is cast out from the fellowship of Christians. He does not participate in the orations or prayers made by the Church. And he is outside the grace of God, and dying in such rebellion, he is damned to Hell. But returning to obedience before he dies, and being restored to the communion of Catholics, he returns to the grace of God. And if, by the prevention of death, he lacks the time to reconcile himself with the Church, and nonetheless repents of his error and dies with true repentance and contrition, the infinite divine clemency remits the fault, and he goes to Purgatory and is saved. But Dante feigns here that before he can enter Purgatory, he must go wandering around it for every time that he lived in contumacy multiplied by **THIRTY**, so that he may first purge his negligence, as we have said above. But it is difficult for such contrition to be known to the Pastor. And therefore he says:

...dies in **contumacy** of Holy Church: understand this in terms of the outward demonstration. For he who dies in contumacy regarding the inward act—that is, he does not repent nor humble himself—is damned. **FOR EVERY time thirty that he has been:** that he lived **IN HIS presumption.** I believe he uses "thirty" for every number, wishing to show that he who dies excommunicated, although he returns to penance, is nevertheless very remote from God; and because he deferred penance for a long time and received grace late, his sins multiplied. Thus, he is purged late. **IF SUCH a decree does not become shorter through good prayers.** It is the right faith to believe that alms, sacrifice, and prayers can induce God to shorten the pains of those who are in Purgatory. Wherefore the Apostle Paul proves this through the Maccabees, who sent money to the Temple to be offered for the souls of the dead. These prelates of ours must therefore endure it in peace if in some place our poet has reproved and vilified their captive customs, because here he says that which works greatly in their favor; and he shows that he had no hatred against priests, but against the wicked life of captive priests. **SEE NOW:** prayers are of value to us who are in Purgatory; he says this as if to say, following the sentence set down above, that you understand how you can make me happy. By revealing to **Constance**, my daughter, that I am in a place where she can help me with prayers. **AS YOU HAVE seen me.** As you have seen me, and also by revealing **HOW I STAND under prohibition:** that is, forbidden and prohibited from entering Purgatory. And if anyone should ask what joy it gives you that Dante reveals this: because she will pray for me, and her prayers will make me shorten the time; for here in this place where we purge our negligence, **THROUGH THOSE back there**—through those who are still in life—**much is gained.** Much is acquired.

<header>CANTO FOUR</header>

### FOURTH CANTO OF THE SECOND CANTICLE OF DANTE.

When through delights or through pains
Which any of our faculties grasp
The soul gathers itself entirely to it
It seems it no longer attends to any other power
And this is against that error which believes
That one soul acts upon another within us:
And therefore when one hears or sees a thing
That keeps the soul strongly turned toward it
Time passes: and the man does not perceive it
For one power is that which listens
And another is that which holds the soul whole
The latter is as if bound, and the former is free
Of this I had true experience:
Hearing that spirit and marveling:
For though the sun had risen fifty degrees
And I had not noticed when
We came to where those souls gather:
They cried to us: "Here is what you ask for."

<column-break/>

The same subject continues: and he climbs the first ledge: still the place of the excommunicated. Then in the second he finds those who purge the negligence caused by sloth <note>original: "accidia," one of the seven deadly sins involving spiritual apathy</note>. But as for these six tercets: he shows that he had heard Manfred with such attention that the sun had passed a quarter of the day, and he had not noticed. Regarding this matter, so that no one marvels: he shows that when our ego <note>original: "io"</note> is oppressed by some vehement perturbation: entirely taken in that form: so that no other faculty <term>uirtu|The Italian 'virtù' here refers to a 'faculty' or 'power' of the soul, following Aristotelian psychology</term> operates. **WHEN THROUGH** delight or through pains: He posits two of the four perturbations: delights—that is, joy, which comes from a present good; and pain—through sickness and sorrow, which comes from a present evil. **WHICH ANY** faculty of ours: any power of our soul might grasp: as for example <note>original: "uerbri gratia"</note>: the sensory faculties of sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch. Therefore, the eye sees something that delights it greatly: the whole soul gathers itself so much to that visual power, not providing its strength to any other power, so that it seems it no longer attends: not only to any other sensory power, but not even to the powers of memory: such as the apprehensive, imaginative, and retentive [faculties]. These powers are all types of the powers of the soul: which are the vegetative, the sensitive, and the rational: and each has its specific types: which the poet calls "faculties" <note>original: "uirtu"</note>. The whole soul turns so much to a single faculty because of a powerful object of that [faculty], that it abandons the others. **AND THIS** is against that error which believes: against that false opinion of those philosophers who say **THAT ONE SOUL** acts upon another within us: that is, that we do not have a single soul, but

---

four. That there are three types of soul is manifest. First is the **vegetative soul**: which alone, without any other soul, is in plants: such as herbs and trees: through which they grow, nourish themselves, and produce another like themselves. Second is the **sensitive soul**: and this is in brute animals. It contains the external senses: such as sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch. And the internal senses: common sense, imagination, cogitation, fantasy, and memory. The third is the **rational soul** in man alone. There are not three souls in man, but one with three powers. For if there were three souls, at every instant and point in time, each soul would operate its own power. And this is false: as we see here in Dante: who was so occupied in hearing that no other power operated. But if the vegetative and the rational had been distinct souls, the sensitive could well occupy all its powers, but not the powers of the others. In man, the vegetative is that which gives life to the body, and grows it, and nourishes it: and it begins as soon as the seed is transformed <note>original: "corropto," used here in the biological sense of one form changing into another</note> in the mother's womb. Second is the sensitive. This extends, moves, and feels. Then when the fetus still in the mother's womb has all its members and organs, or rather completed instruments: God creates the human soul from nothing within the body: which takes and unites the vegetative and the sensitive with itself: and gives them that perfection which they would not have on their own. And this union is such that it is the cause of all operation, and is never dissolved: but when it separates from the body, the soul takes these powers with it, although they no longer have any ability for physical action. Furthermore, the soul created by God is adorned with three virtues, which it exercises more when separated from the body than when it is in the body. These are **memory, intellect, and will**. There are not, therefore, three souls, nor four in man: but only the rational human soul: which finding in the fetus the vegetative power (which we have in common with plants) and the sensitive power (which is common to us with brute animals): does not add itself as a third. But it unites those two with itself: and thus they are together one soul, and not three. Because as he said a little above: if they were three distinct souls, it would not follow that when one was entirely occupied in one of its powers, the other two souls would not also be occupied. **AND THEREFORE** when one hears or sees a thing. When sight or hearing is much occupied, in such a way that the whole soul turns to it: **time passes**: Because that power that would perceive this remains dormant. This often happens: for when we hear something that delights us for four hours, they seem like one. **FOR ANOTHER POWER**: He assigns the reason why one does not notice: because it is not one and the same power that sees or hears and that which can notice that time is passing; and because that which sees a delightful thing draws the whole soul to itself, the soul is not free or available for other things. It happens that the power which should recognize that time passes remains abandoned by the soul and cannot operate. **OF THIS I HAD** true experience: I knew this by experience. Because hearing and marveling at that spirit: that is, while I was hearing. But this was not enough to make the soul turn entirely to that: because we often hear something and nonetheless in the meantime we know and notice many other things. And therefore he adds: "and marveling": because wonder <note>original: "admiratione"</note> is what draws the whole soul to itself. **FOR FULL fifty degrees** the sun had climbed: through such wonder I did not notice the journey made, nor that time had passed. For each of the two hemispheres is divided by mathematicians into one hundred and eighty degrees. Therefore, five degrees more than a quarter of the day had passed, because a quarter of one hundred and eighty is forty-five. **WHEN WE CAME** where. To that place in which. **THOSE SOULS** gather. All together. **THEY CRIED** "Here." Showing us the pass. "Is what you ask for." It is the place for climbing to purgatory, which you ask about. These negligent ones show the way to Virgil and Dante. This signifies that often the error of others makes us cautious: and we see that the voluptuous life of others makes us continent: because such a vice displeases us in those people.

It is no wonder if the way that leads to purgatory is narrow and steep. For this way consists of the purgative virtues of which we spoke above: which, until we have formed the habit of them, are full of toil and sweat. Whence Hesiod <note>Ancient Greek poet</note> affirms...

<header>PURGATORIO</header>

That there was no place from which to climb,
my leader; and I followed alone,
as the crowd departed from us.
One goes to San Leo and descends to Noli,
one climbs Bismantua and to the peak
with one's feet; but here it behooves that a man fly;
I say with nimble wings and with the feathers
of great desire, behind that guide
who gave me hope and made a light for me.

No, "cacume" <note>original: "cacume," from the Latin *cacumen*, meaning peak or summit</note> is a very steep mountain in the countryside. Some say "in cacume" means on the summit of the mountain of San Leo. In all these places, although they are very steep and rugged, one can nevertheless go on foot. But the ascent of this mountain is almost like a wall, in a form that requires wings. He mentions the places stated above for the height of earthly things, such as riches, power, and lordship, or for the lowliness of the voluptuous life, such as Noli. To which feet—that is, human appetite—can arrive. But to the purgatorial virtues, which have no defensive flatteries, it is necessary to fly with the wings of great desire. Because he who does not leave behind his feet, which signify sensory love, and does not take up wings—that is, the love of incorporeal things—cannot climb there. It is not unknown to me that some understand "wings" as hope and faith. This is not absurd in this place. And Plato writes that the soul, having come into this low world, cannot return to heaven without two wings, of which one is religion and the other is justice. By "religion" he understands all intellectual virtues, and by "justice" all moral ones. **BEHIND THAT GUIDE.** Behind Virgil, my conductor, who gave me hope of being able to climb. Because superior reason, adorned with true doctrine, gives hope that a man may ascend. And it shows the way; wherefore it says: **AND MADE A LIGHT.**

---

We climbed through the broken rock,
and on every side the edge squeezed us,
and the ground below required both feet and hands.
After we were on the topmost edge
of the high bank, on the open slope,
"My Master," I said, "what way shall we take?"
And he to me: "Let no step of yours fall;
ever up the mountain gain ground behind me,
until some wise guide appears to us."
The summit was so high it defeated my sight,
and the slope was much steeper
than a line from the center of a quadrant to the midpoint.
I was weary when I began:
"O sweet father, turn and behold
how I remain alone, if you do not stay."
"My son," he said, "pull yourself up to here,"
pointing out a ledge a little further up,
which circles the entire hill on that side.

to do to things dejected, low, and earthly. **EVER UP THE MOUNTAIN.** Gain ground up the mountain behind me. Follow reason, always ascending toward the virtues, until **SOME GUIDE APPEARS.** Because when a man sets out on the journey to climb to the purgatorial virtues, following reason, after some progress, God has mercy on his good purpose; and that which our fragility cannot do, He supplies with illuminating, cooperating, and perfecting grace, which are "wise guides." Of these we spoke in the first canticle. **THE SUMMIT.** The top of the mountain. **WAS SO HIGH THAT:** in a way that it defeated the sight of my eyes. And indeed, these purgatorial virtues are so exalted and arduous that the eyes of Dante, in the knowledge of sensuality and inferior reason, do not reach them. And to demonstrate this difficulty of climbing, he adds that the slope was "prouder" or steeper than the "alistra"—that is, the line that goes from the center of the quadrant through the middle of it to the circumference. <term>quadrant|An early astronomical instrument used to measure angles up to 90 degrees, often used as a sundial</term> among the ancient Greeks was called a <term>Gnomon</term>. Nor was there a horologe <note>original: "horiuolo," a device for telling time</note> of any sort in Rome before this one. And according to <term>Varro</term> and <term>Pliny</term>, <term>M. Valerius Messalla</term> was the first who brought a quadrant from Catania, a city in Sicily, which he had conquered during his consulship in the year 377 after the founding of Rome. And although it was not very accurate, nor did its lines correspond well to the hours, they used it for ninety-nine years. Until <term>Quintus Marcius Philippo</term>, who was censor with <term>L. Paulus</term>, placed another more orderly one near it. This was very pleasing to the people. But because the quadrant is useless when the sun is covered, <term>Scipio Nasica</term> invented a horologe not of dust <note>original: "poluere," referring to an hourglass</note>, like ours, but of water, which, dripping very minutely, distinguished the hours. And this was five hundred...

<column-break/>

...that the gods have placed sweat before virtue. <note>This refers to a famous passage by the Greek poet Hesiod: "Before virtue the immortal gods have placed sweat."</note> **GREATER OPENING.** First he shows the narrowness of the way, and says that a man of the villa—that is, a peasant—at the time **WHEN THE GRAPE** darkens, begins to turn black because it is ripening. **WITH A BUNDLE OF THORNS:** he repairs with thorns **A GREATER** opening, a larger gap, **WITH A SMALL FORK.** With as many thorns as fit on a small pitchfork. **WHICH WAS NOT** a local path, i.e., the narrow way. *Calles* in Latin properly signifies narrow paths made by the callous feet of animals; hence we say "calle" <note>path</note>. **ONE GOES TO SAN LEO.** This land is on the summit of Montefeltro; to which, whoever wishes to go finds a difficult steep. **NOLI:** is a land on the Genoese Riviera, located in a valley where one descends with great difficulty. **BISMANTUA:** is a mountain in the territory of Reggio, very difficult to climb. **CACUME.** Although *cacumen* in Latin means any summit, nonetheless "Cacume" is a very steep mountain in the countryside <note>referring to Monte Cacume in the Lepini Mountains of Lazio</note>.

<image-desc>A large decorative historiated initial 'I' used for the start of the commentary on the second poetic section. Inside the upper circular loop of the initial is a small circled letter 'd'. The body of the initial is ornate with architectural and floral motifs.</image-desc>
It demonstrates that the way was made by the force of a chisel, breaking the rock to show that without force and industry we cannot overcome the difficulty of this ascent, which for the reason stated above is more laborious and troublesome than the rest. Wherefore the Apostle said: *Long habit of sinning makes the way of virtue unpleasant and harsh for us.* <note>original Latin: "Insuauem & aspera facit nobis uiam uirtutis longa cosuetudo peccadi."</note> And <term>Tullio</term> <note>Cicero</note>: *The best form of living is to be chosen, which habit will then make pleasant.* <note>original Latin: "Optima forma uiuendi eligenda e quam iocundam reddet cõsuetudo."</note> **AND ON EVERY SIDE** the edge squeezed us. The way was very narrow because virtues consist in the middle, which, in respect to the extremes, is very narrow. And it is like a line that goes from one part to the other through the center. And every time one leaves this line, one falls into one of the extremes: either in excess or in defect. And he adds that the ground below was so steep that it required feet and hands—that is, it was necessary to go on all fours. Allegorically, this signifies that one needs "feet"—that is, appetite—and "hands"—that is, action and operation. Because it is not enough to have a supreme appetite for climbing, that is, for purging oneself, if such desire is not put into action. Because as <term>Aristotle</term> says in the *Ethics*: moral virtue consists in operation. And in a Christian sense we can say that affection is not enough if satisfaction is not added. **ON THE TOPMOST EDGE.** They had climbed to the highest extremity of the ledge, between which and the next ledge was the open slope. For while they were climbing the ledge, they went through that narrow, dark, and deep way and could not see. But having reached the edge, they saw the clear slope. **WHAT WAY SHALL WE TAKE?** It is an excellent thing that although the appetite is kindled for the purgation of the soul, nonetheless one must do everything with the counsel of superior reason. And he responds to him: **LET NO STEP OF YOURS FALL.** Do not go downhill—that is, never turn back; and do not stop...

<header>PURGATORIO</header>
<meta>Handwritten "158" in the bottom left corner.</meta>

Sixty-six years after Rome was built, I find that neither the Romans nor other people in those times had bells or clocks <note>original: "oriuoli"</note> or anything else. I have mentioned this briefly regarding the quadrant <note>an astronomical instrument used to measure angles and time</note> that shows the hours. But so that one may better understand the sense of Dante—which is not that the path was as straight as a wall, because it would have been impossible for him to climb it, but that it was only slightly less sloped—we will say that he describes it in the manner of an astronomer's quadrant. Astronomers have three principal instruments: the Material Sphere <note>also known as an armillary sphere</note>, which shows the entire sky and its circles; second is the round astrolabe, but flattened in the shape of a platter, in which the entire position of the sky is shown; the third is a quadrant, which is the fourth part of an astrolabe. Therefore, if you divide a platter from the center by straight lines to the circumference into four equal parts, one of those makes the quadrant. And if you take this quadrant and draw a line through the middle from the center to the circumference, and then lay the quadrant down on one of its two sides, you will see that the line made will not be entirely straight. Nonetheless, it will lack very little of it. He concludes, then, that the climb was very steep, but not shaped exactly like a wall. **I was weary.** Sensuality <note>the physical senses and lower instincts</note> and lower reason are always exhausted by the difficulty of virtuous works. And therefore, he asks for comfort. Because the intellect often goes forward and leaves sensuality behind, which would remain there if the intellect did not turn back and comfort it. And note that Dante calls him "father" and Virgil calls him "son," because he wishes to show that sensuality is already so in accord with reason that it obeys—not like a slave to a master who obeys by force, nor like a disciple to a teacher who wants to understand the reason before obeying openly, but like a son to a father, who wants his own will to be the same as his father's. When this state exists in any man, he will not doubt that he can arrive at purgation. Dante signified these three types of obedience in the first canticle <note>Inferno</note> when he said: *You father, You teacher, You lord.* And we explained them there. **Pull yourself up to here:** strive to lead yourself to this point. Because afterward the way will be less steep; and in arduous things, the beginning is always more than half of the whole. **Pointing it out to me:** showing me with his finger the ledge <note>original: "cinghio"</note> that encircled the hill on the side where Dante was, as we shall see below, because on the other side of the hill there were ravines.

> So his words spurred me on
> that I forced myself, crawling after him,
> until the ledge was beneath my feet.
> There we both sat down,
> turned toward the east from where we had climbed,
> for looking back is wont to help a man.
> I first directed my eyes to the low shores;
> then I raised them to the sun, and marveled
> that we were struck by it from the left.

> The poet well perceived that I stood
> all amazed at the chariot of light,
> where it entered between us and the North wind. <note>original: "aquilone"</note>
> Whereupon he said to me: "If Castor and Pollux
> were in the company of that mirror
> which carries its light up and down,
> you would see the ruddy Zodiac <note>original: "zodiaco rubecchio"</note>
> rotating even closer to the Bears,
> unless it strayed from its ancient path.
> How that can be, if you wish to be able to conceive it,
> collected within yourself, imagine Zion
> standing with this mountain upon the earth
> so that both have a single horizon
> and different hemispheres; therefore the road
> that Phaethon, to his harm, knew not how to drive,
> you will see how it must needs go
> on one side of this mountain, when it goes
> on the other side of that, if your intellect observes clearly."

<column-break/>

Higher reason with its comforts ensures that lower reason achieves the nearly impossible. And it is not without cause that Virgil does not want him to rest until he is upon the ledge. For the slope is a slippery and treacherous place, and he who rests there can slip and fall down; but he who climbs to the ledge, because it is not without some level ground, can sit without fear of slipping. Therefore, in very arduous matters, it is necessary for a man to rest, because otherwise he becomes so exhausted that he could not reach the end; but he should not rest until he is in a place where he will not fall back. **They sat down turned toward where they had come from:** because he who has labored turns back so that he may be comforted by the view. And allegorically: he who turns his mind back to consider the climb he has made—that is, the difficulty already passed—is comforted and emboldened to endure what remains. **Turned to the east from where they had climbed:** because from there they had begun the ascent. **I first directed my eyes to the low shores, then I raised them:** he who has already set out on the path of virtue takes great comfort in considering the lowliness of earthly things from which he has departed, and then the height of divine things to which he has proposed to climb. **And I marveled:** because in this hemisphere <note>the Northern Hemisphere</note>, one who stands facing east is struck by the sun from the right shoulder, because the midday is there; but in that place, it struck us from the left. And in this you will note that it is a very great ornament to the poet when, beyond the proper subject of his poem, he illuminates, distinguishes, and flourishes it with many other things, such as here, deviating somewhat from the main topic to touch upon certain points of astronomy.

Virgil noticed that I stood eager and full of wonder, seeing the **chariot of light**—that is, the sun—being between the North <note>original: "septentrione"</note> and us. I was wondering at having it from the North, since in this hemisphere it is toward midday <note>the South</note>. The poet wishes here to show that the other hemisphere—where he feigns to have been—is the opposite of this one. Therefore, just as the sun always moves toward the midday for us and casts shadows toward the North, so for those people there, the sun moves toward our North. And Virgil and Dante happen to be beside the equator; our Arctic is on this side. Dante would not have marveled at having the sun from the North if he had considered that he was in the other hemisphere, beyond the torrid zone toward the Antarctic. Whereupon Virgil responds that he would see the sun even closer to the North—as it was in Aries—if it had been with **Castor and Pollux** (that is, in Gemini). Where it is to be understood that, starting the Zodiac from...

<meta>This page continues the astronomical and allegorical explanation of the Mountain of Purgatory. Having established the steepness of the climb, the text now addresses the orientation of the sun in the Southern Hemisphere, contrasting it with the familiar sky of the Northern Hemisphere (Jerusalem).</meta>

<page-num>IIII</page-num>
<header>CANTO</header>

from Aries. We see that this sign is next to the equator: and it begins there: after which comes Taurus toward the north <note>original: "septentrione"</note>. And after Taurus are the Gemini. And these are very close to the north: and here the summer tropic <note>the Tropic of Cancer</note> ends. Afterward is Cancer, which begins on the other side of the north. And after it is Leo, which declines toward the equator. And after that is Virgo: which ends at the equator. After these is Libra: which begins below the equator just as Aries does above. The other signs follow, moving away from the equator and approaching the antarctic pole <note>the South Pole</note> until Sagittarius, where the winter tropic <note>the Tropic of Capricorn</note> ends. And here begins Capricorn, then Aquarius, then Pisces: which end at the equator where Aries begins. Virgil therefore says: that if the sun were in Gemini, Dante would see it even closer to the north: because that sign is further north. He places Castor and Pollux for the Gemini: following the poetic fables as a poet, which narrate that Castor and Pollux were born of Jupiter, who had turned into a swan, and Leda, wife of Tyndareus. Others say that Leda gave birth to two eggs by Jupiter turned swan: and from one was born Pollux and Helen, the wife of Menelaus who was kidnapped by Paris; and these two were immortal. From the other came Castor and Clytemnestra. Others say there was only one egg: and from it were born Castor, Pollux, and Helen. Others say that Castor was mortal and not born of Jupiter, but of Tyndareus. Pollux and Castor, returning with the Argonauts <note>the heroes who sailed with Jason to find the Golden Fleece</note>, kidnapped the daughters of Leucippus who were betrothed to Lynceus and Idas. Wherefore Lynceus killed Castor, and Pollux killed Lynceus to avenge his brother. And Idas would have killed Pollux if Jupiter had not come to his aid. Jupiter then took them up into heaven and placed them in the third sign of the zodiac called Gemini <note>the Twins</note>, because it is made of these two brothers who were twins, born of one birth. And Pollux, being immortal, shared his immortality with Castor. The poets feign this because when one of them descends to the opposite hemisphere, the other rises to ours. Others say they earned heaven because they purged the Greek sea of pirates. Others because during the voyage of the Argonauts they saved the ship *Argo* from many storms; for which reason they were afterward invoked in heaven by sailors as salutary and propitious stars. And when they appeared in the form of lights <note>referring to St. Elmo’s fire</note>, the storm would cease: as Pliny describes, and Horace in his Odes: "As soon as their clear star has shone upon the sailors, the winds die down, the clouds flee, and the threatening wave settles back on the sea because they willed it so." <note>original: "Quorum simul alba nautis stella refulfit. Concidunt uenti leuif afflat aura. Et minax quia sic uoluere ponto unda recumbit."</note> This is similar to what is said in our times regarding Saint Elmo. The first, that is Pollux, has nine stars: of which one in the head and two in the shoulders are very bright. Castor has ten stars. There are nineteen in total. If they were in the company of that mirror of the sun. Which: that which goes up and down: in the hemisphere above and in that below, because it illuminates both. Thus Virgil: "And when the rising Sun has breathed upon us with his first panting horses, there the red Evening Star lights its late lamps." <note>original: "Nosque ubi primis equis oriens afflauit hanelis. illic sera rubens accendit lumina uesper."</note> Others say "up and down" because from its light it gives to Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn—planets placed above it—and similarly to Venus, Mercury, and the Moon, which are lower than itself. You would see the zodiac reddish: you would see that part of the zodiac where Gemini is reddish, which would glow red because of the sun, if it were within it, as it is in Aries. Rotating even closer to the bears <note>the constellations Ursa Major and Minor, indicating the North</note>: because that sign, as we have said, is the closest to the north. If it did not leave the old path: if it did not take a course other than its own. But if you wish to be able to understand why the sun is to the north in this place: Gathered within: that is, gather your mind within yourself and think of nothing else. And imagine: which is the mountain of Jerusalem. With this mountain: of Purgatory. To stand as an island of earth: understand this as being opposite: because Zion <note>Jerusalem</note> is in our hemisphere, and that mountain is in the other, opposite to one another. And he explains it saying: So that both have a single horizon: that is, the lunar circle that divides one hemisphere from the other: but different hemispheres, as has been said. Therefore, just as in our hemisphere the habitable quarter is toward our arctic pole: so the island of Purgatory is in the other hemisphere toward the antarctic pole. They say that Jerusalem is at the very center of the earth in our hemisphere: just as Dante feigns that the mountain of Purgatory is in that other hemisphere. This is the road: the path of the sun which never leaves the zodiac. That Phaethon did not know how to drive to his misfortune: that which, to his own harm, Phaethon did not know how to keep with his chariot. To his misfortune <note>original: "MAL non seppe"</note>: with his own harm: with his own ruin he did not know. Phaethon was the son of the Sun, and he asked his father to promise him with an oath to grant him whatever favor he might ask. The Sun promised. Phaethon asked to be allowed to drive his horses through the sky for a single day. The father granted it so as not to be a perjurer. But first, with many reasons, he tried to discourage the rash youth from the undertaking because he would not be able to control the ferocity of his horses. But Phaethon did not know how to control the horses, which, leaving the sun's path, came so low that they burned the earth. Wherefore Jupiter was forced to strike Phaethon with his celestial bolt; because of which, dead, he fell into the Po river. And for this reason Petrarch said: "I hear of Phaethon who fell into the Po and died." You will see. You will understand by these reasons how it is necessary for the sun to pass by this man from the antarctic pole on one side: that is, from the left. When to that man: of our arctic pole it passes from our arctic pole on the other side: that is, from the right. If your intellect attends <note>original: "bada"</note>: that is, pays attention; *badare* in our language is what in Latin they call *vacare* <note>to be free for, or to devote oneself to</note>.

"Certainly," I said, "master, never for a moment
did I see so clearly as I now discern
where my intellect seemed most lacking:
That the middle circle of the high motion,
which is called the Equator in a certain art,
and which always remains between the sun and winter,
By the logic that starts from here,
moves toward the north, while the Hebrews
see it toward the hot region.
But if it please you, I would gladly know
how far we have to go, for the hill rises
higher than my eyes can climb."

<column-break/>

**D**ante demonstrates that he has understood, to denote that sensuality—although by its nature it is not rational—can nonetheless be made a participant in reason. And as a disciple, he narrates to Virgil what he understands, so that he, as the master, may correct him where he is lacking. The middle circle: mathematicians place five parallel circles—that is, equidistant circles—between one pole and the other. The first is near the arctic pole and is called the arctic parallel. And Virgil calls this the cold zone, beneath which one cannot live because of the extreme cold. And after that, at an equidistant space, is another circle called the summer tropic. For the sun rises as far as that in the north. And when it leaves Gemini, it creates the summer solstice, and then it is the longest day of the entire year. And all the space that is between the said circle and the other of the pole is called the temperate zone: and beneath that, one can dwell. Afterward is the third circle called the equinoctial, or the equator: because when the sun is here, the days are equal with the nights. And this is at the beginning of Aries when the sun approaches us: because until that time, the nights were longer. And at the beginning of Libra, when the sun moves away from us: where the days which were equal or greater become equal with the nights. For from the beginning of Aries until the end of Gemini, the day always increases. Afterward, from the beginning of Cancer until the beginning of Libra, it decreases in such a way that it arrives there because such a sign touches the equatorial circle. On the other side opposite to Aries, it is fixed so that the day equals the night. From...

<meta>This page continues the astronomical and allegorical explanation of the Mountain of Purgatory. Having established the steepness of the climb, the text now addresses the orientation of the sun in the Southern Hemisphere, contrasting it with the familiar sky of the Northern Hemisphere (Jerusalem).</meta>

<page-num>159</page-num>
# CANTO FOUR

then it continues to decrease through the southern signs: which are from Aries to Libra, through Scorpio and Sagittarius: and at the end of Sagittarius, it makes the longest night of the year. Then, at the beginning of Capricorn, it reaches the tropic and the winter solstice, and the sun begins to rise toward the north <note>original: "septentrione"</note> and the days begin to grow: in such a way that at the beginning of Aries, they have returned to being equal to the nights.

### THE MIDDLE CIRCLE
This is the equinoctial circle: which is called the "equator" because when the sun is at that degree—either in Aries or Libra—which touches this circle, the day and the night are equal.

### IN SOME ART
Such as astrology: **OF THE CELESTIAL MOTION**. The equatorial circle is in the middle, equidistant from the two poles, the Arctic and Antarctic: which mathematicians say are fixed and immobile. In these, the **Primum Mobile** <term>the outermost moving sphere in the ancient geocentric model</term> moves from Aries toward the West, pulling behind it the eighth sphere <note>the sphere of the fixed stars</note> in which the zodiac and the other fixed stars and all seven planets are located. Thus, in twenty-four hours, all these heavens make one full revolution. Nevertheless, the eighth sphere turns with a contrary motion of one degree every hundred years. Similarly, all the planets turn with a contrary movement. This revolution occurs upon two mobile poles, which emerge from the two immobile ones mentioned above. And because the space from one pole to the other is 180 degrees, the equator is ninety degrees distant from each pole. Therefore, the equator is the "middle circle" because it is in the middle of the poles and divides the zodiac into two halves.

### AND WHICH ALWAYS REMAINS
between the sun and winter. Because if the sun is on this side—that is, in the northern signs—we have summer; and in the other hemisphere, which is beyond the equator, it is winter: and likewise for the opposite. Therefore, this circle always remains between the sun (which creates summer) and winter.

### FOR THE REASON
that it departs from here. The reason is that the sun departs from here—that is, from this hemisphere, which is under the southern signs: which are Libra, Scorpio, Sagittarius, Capricorn, Aquarius, and Pisces. And it goes toward the north, because then it was in Aries, which touches the equator from the upper side toward the north.

### AS MUCH AS THE HEBREWS
that is, just as much as the Hebrews. These people are as close to the equator in our hemisphere as Dante was in the other hemisphere. The meaning is: that the sun is as far from the Mountain of Purgatory in that hemisphere, moving toward the north, as it is from Jerusalem, moving toward the southern signs. And therefore he says, "toward the hot part." Nor does it seem to me that any other history is touched upon here.

### BUT IF IT PLEASES YOU
The poet remembers the truest sentiment: "The spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak" <note>original: "Spiritus promptus est caro uero infirma"</note>. Therefore, although Dante—that is, sensuality—may be obedient to reason, nevertheless virtuous works seem difficult to him at the beginning. Thus, it is no wonder if his eyes do not reach the summit of this mountain: because one who is still at the beginning of the purgatorial virtues cannot understand the progress until the end.

->And he to me: "This mountain is such,<-
->that it is always heavy at the start below,<-
->and the higher one goes, the less it hurts.<-
->Therefore, when it shall seem sweet to you,<-
->so much so that going up is as light for you<-
->as going down a river in a boat,<-
->then you will be at the end of this path;<-
->there, look to rest your weariness.<-
->I answer no more, and this I know for certain."<-

---

At the sound of it, each of us turned,
and we saw to the left a great rock <note>original: "petrone"</note>,
of which neither he nor I had taken notice before.
We drew near it; and there were people
who stayed in the shade behind the stone,
as a man settles himself to stay through negligence.

<column-break/>

Often in the same man, a dispute arises between appetite and intellect. Therefore, where the true habit of virtue is not yet established, the performance of those virtues is difficult for the senses. But when reason is questioned by the senses as to when the climb will end, it does not set a determined space; for if one always had to perform virtuous works, the senses would be dismayed. Instead, it shows what is true and can greatly comfort the senses, saying: "Climb frankly." For the nature of this steepness is such that the more one climbs, the easier it becomes. Certainly, this is because frequent and repeated actions little by little induce a **habit** <term>habitu: a settled disposition of the soul</term>; once acquired, the actions that previously seemed difficult become easy. It happens that the closer we get to the habit through practice, the less heavy it is for us. Therefore, when this climb seems sweet to you—meaning that the ascent will be as easy as it is to sail down a river—then you will be at the end of the climb, that is, at the perfection of actions, which is the "habit." For this reason: **THERE, LOOK TO REST YOUR WEARINESS**. It is as if he says: "Postpone all your rest until that place, and in the meantime do not stop on the way," because virtuous actions would not lead you to the habit if you did not continue them.

### I ANSWER NO MORE
because this is sufficient. Hold it for true, because a little above, as we mentioned concerning Aristotle, he says so. For all philosophers give it as a certain thing, and experience agrees with their authority: that the sign of having formed a habit is to take delight in the actions. But most especially, he places the habit of "purgatorial virtues" here, because they are much more perfect than civil virtues. This will be easy for you to understand if you return to the place where I have spoken of them at length.

### AND AS HE HAD spoken his word
**A VOICE NEARBY SOUNDED: "PERHAPS..."** Who this was, you will understand shortly below. And he says "sounded" as if to show that he spoke clearly and with a certain efficacy. Because he spoke from his soul. And since he had always fled from fatigue, this climb seemed much more difficult to him than it does to one who is used to some virtuous exercise.

Virgil and I turned toward where the voice came from. And we saw those souls on the left side, to denote the evil and slow leisure of negligence. And not without reason does he say that they had not yet noticed them. Because the life of the negligent is similar to death. He performs no action by which he might become known, either for good or for evil. Therefore, they were passing without taking notice of them, had one of those souls not said: **"THAT YOU WILL HAVE NEED TO SIT BEFORE THAT"**, meaning discomfort. These words were meant to discourage Dante. This signifies that whatever notice we have of such men is that, either by example or by words, they discourage us from virtuous undertakings. But being these souls in Purgatory, it is not to be understood that he used such words to harm Dante. Rather, he could not contain himself: having such horror for the most laborious slope, he spoke his opinion more out of compassion than out of envy. The rock that took the heat from them—that is, the light of the sun—is the stupor and the heaviness of laziness, which takes away the heat of the sun (the love of virtue) and the light (the light of reason).

# PURGATORIO

And one of them who seemed to me weary
was sitting and hugging his knees,
holding his face down low between them.

"O my sweet lord," I said, "look
at that one who shows himself more negligent
than if laziness were his own sister."

Then he turned to us and paid attention,
moving his face just over his thigh,
and said, "Now you go up, since you are so strong!"

I knew then who he was; and that distress
which was still quickening my breath a little
did not prevent me from going to him; and then,

When I had reached him, he barely raised his head,
saying, "Have you seen well how the sun
drives his chariot from the left shoulder?"

His lazy actions and his short words
moved my lips a little to a smile;
then I began: "Belacqua, I do not grieve

For you anymore; but tell me, why
are you sitting here? Are you waiting for an escort,
or has your old habit taken hold of you again?"

And he: "O brother, what is the use of going up?
For the bird of God <note>This refers to the Angel who guards the gate of Purgatory.</note> who sits at the gate
would not let me go to the penance.

First it is necessary that the heavens circle me
outside of it for as long as they did in life,
because I delayed my good sighs until the end,

Unless a prayer helps me first,
one that rises from a heart living in grace;
what good is the other, which is not heard in heaven?"

And already the poet was climbing ahead of me
and saying, "Come now; see that the sun has touched
the meridian, and from the shore,

Night already covers Morocco with its foot."

<column-break/>

The author could not better express a negligent person than by placing him sitting on the ground with his legs gathered together: he indicates that by wanting to look upward, he directs his gaze over his thighs. And even though it is uncomfortable to sit in that way, nevertheless laziness holds him there. Wherefore Solomon says: *The lazy man hides his hands under his armpits, and it exhausts him even to bring them to his mouth.* <note>original: "Abscondit piger manus suas sub ascellas suas: & laborat si eas ad os cõuertit." — Proverbs 26:15</note>

Furthermore, these words **NOW YOU GO UP** since you are so strong, demonstrate that same character. Because the negligent man feels disdain that another is diligent, and mocks him with ironic words. He does something similar a little further down when he says that he "barely raised his head" and mocks Dante for wanting to know why the sun cast a shadow to the left; for the lazy always mock those who are diligent in investigating anything worthy. **THAT DISTRESS WHICH WAS QUICKENING MY BREATH**: which hurried my panting or rather my breath. For whoever goes uphill finds their breath comes in abundance, and it gives them trouble. Because the exertion and the weight of carrying the body upward excites heat; and the more the heart heats up, the more air and breath are needed for the lungs to draw to the heart to cool it; thus, so much breathing causes distress. **A LITTLE TO A SMILE**: because a modest man does not use too much laughter. **I DO NOT GRIEVE FOR YOU**: because I see you in a safe place. He gains favor <note>original: "Capta... beniuolentia"</note> from the person himself, showing that it would have been painful to have found him in a worse state. And having made him well-disposed, he rebukes him to rouse him from such great laziness. **ARE YOU WAITING**: Do you expect? **BELACQUA**: He calls him by his proper name. This denotes love and benevolence when we speak to an equal or an inferior. Wherefore Virgil’s Juno, speaking to Aeolus, names him saying: *Aeolus, for to you the father of gods and king of men [has given the power...]* <note>original: "Eole namque tibi diuum pater atque hominum rex" — Aeneid 1.65</note>

**O BROTHER**: O brother. **WHAT IS THE USE**: What does it profit **OF GOING UP**. As if to say "nothing." And the reason is that the bird of God—that is, the angel—who sits at the gate of Purgatory (of whom we will speak below) would not let me enter. Because it is necessary that the heavens circle me for as much time outside that gate of Purgatory as passed during my life. And this is according to the literary device <note>original: "fiction"</note> established above: because I delayed my "good sighs" until the end of my life—sighs which proceed from true contrition and repentance for errors committed, and from a supreme desire to return to the right path. They are therefore "good" because they profit and make good those who use them. And note the author’s opinion: which is that the prayers of those who are in mortal sin do not profit those in Purgatory.

Reason <note>represented by Virgil</note> did not wish to delay any longer in laziness, and therefore he admonished Dante to rise. See that the meridian—that is, the equatorial circle—is touched by the sun. Therefore, if the sun had reached this circle, it signifies it was midday; and already Night covers with its foot from the shore of Morocco—that is, coming from the sea near Morocco—that is, Mauritania, which is a region of Africa located in the West. The meaning is this: that since it was already midday in the hemisphere where Dante was, from the shore of Morocco (which is West to us, but was then East to them), Night rises. And by this he inserts that neither the day nor the night is equal in all parts of the hemisphere: because it is midday in the East before it is midday in the West.

<summary>Dante encounters his friend Belacqua, who represents the "Negligent" souls forced to wait outside the gate of Purgatory for delaying their repentance. The commentary explains the physical and moral traits of laziness and provides an astronomical update, noting it is midday at the mountain and nightfall in the West (Morocco).</summary>

### CANTO FIFTH OF THE SECOND CANTICLE BY DANTE.

I had already from those shades departed,
& was following the footsteps of my leader,
when one behind me, pointing his finger,
Loudly cried: "Look, it seems no light shines
from the left of the one below:
& he seems to conduct himself like a living man:"
I turned my eyes at the sound of these words:
& I saw them watching with wonder:
at me alone, me alone, & the light that was broken.

"Why does your mind so entangle itself,"
said the master, "that you slacken your pace?
What does it matter to you what is whispered here?
Follow behind me & let the people talk;
stand like a firm tower that never shakes
its summit, no matter how the winds blow:
For always the man in whom thought sprouts
upon thought, distances himself from his goal,
because the force of one softens <note>The original term "insolla" refers to making something weak or flaccid.</note> the other."
What could I say in return, except "I am coming"?
I said it, somewhat sprinkled with that color
which makes a man sometimes worthy of pardon.

Meanwhile, across the mountain slope,
a people came a little way ahead of us:
singing the *Miserere* <note>original: "miserere" — Psalm 51: "Have mercy on me, O God."</note> verse by verse.
When they perceived that I gave no place
for the passage of the rays through my body,
they changed their song into a long & hoarse "Oh!"
And two of them, in the form of messengers,
ran toward us & asked us:
"Make us wise to your condition."

And my master: "You may go your way,
& report back to those who sent you,
that the body of this man is true flesh.
If they stopped because they saw his shadow,
as I suppose, they have their answer;
let them do him honor, for it may be dear to them."
Ignited vapors <note>A poetic reference to shooting stars or meteors.</note> I never saw so quickly
at midnight cleave the serene sky,

<column-break/>

IN this fifth canto he places those: who, driven by military discipline, deferred their repentance until death. And these he finds on the third ledge. He had therefore departed from those whom he placed above: when he was pointed out by another: because they perceived: that he was there with his body: because he cast a shadow: & the sun did not penetrate him: as it does incorporeal souls: but remained "broken." By many in this Ante-Purgatory it is noted as a marvel that Dante is there with his body. This demonstrates the great [sluggishness] of these lazy ones. Who, if they had been in exercise [of virtue], would have turned their thoughts elsewhere.

REASON reproves the sensuality which is eager to stop among the negligent. And [notes] that he pays too much attention to what is "whispered" among them, i.e., spoken with murmuring: & he [Virgil] encourages him to follow him, that is, to follow Reason. And just as the tower does not move: nor bend for the blowing of winds, so he who wishes to climb to the purgatorial virtues: must remain firm in his good and established purpose. Nor for any vanity: that he hears from those who through negligence do not climb: should he abandon the enterprise. The tower does not move its summit, i.e., he who has made a firm purpose to climb: does not change his mind: for the "blowing of winds," i.e., for the vain reasons of others: FOR ALWAYS THE MAN IN WHOM THOUGHT SPROUTS. After a good and established purpose, a man should not go wavering with his mind: with various thoughts: & cogitations. Because being a vagabond in the diversity of thoughts, he distances himself from the "mark": which is the end at which he had purposed to arrive: & begins to be ambiguous & perplexed. Because the succeeding thought "softens" <term>insolla: renders vain and annihilates the first</term>. And just as if a crossbowman distances himself from the target: more than he should: the shot he takes "softens," i.e., vanishes: because his crossbow does not carry that far: so it happens to this man. We properly say "soft" [*solla*] of iron: when in any part it is not well condensed: & solid: but leaves a void inside itself. SPROUTS [*rampolla*]: is a metaphor from trees: in which new branches are always put forth. Wherefore a sprout [*rampollo*] signifies a new branch: born upon the old. WHAT COULD I SAY. When sensuality & appetite are made obedient to reason: & reason then shows it the truth: & invites it to that: what can it respond except "I follow you." And this Dante shows he has done. But his face was covered with a vermilion color: which signifies being ashamed. And he adds: that being ashamed makes a man worthy of pardon. And he said "sometimes": because shame does not always merit pardon: but only when it is the cause: either that we do not begin to err: or if we have already begun, it takes us away from it. Whence Aristotle says: that shame is good in children: but not in the old. Because in children there is hope: that they will refrain from it. In the old it is not [good]: because they have made a habit of it.

MEANWHILE: in the midst of Virgil reproving me. ACROSS THE SLOPE: which we were climbing now: being on the other ledge. ACROSS: they came from across: because they were circling the mountain: & we were climbing straight up. AHEAD of us: because they arrived at the straight path: that we were making: but somewhat above us. WHEN they perceived. A marvelous imagination: that he says this same sentiment in so many various ways: THEY CHANGED their song: because of the stupor: that they had upon seeing a living body: they left off singing the *Miserere mei* <note>original: "Miserere mei" — Have mercy on me.</note>. And like one who marvels, they said "Oh!" with a long pronunciation: & a hoarse voice. Because he who is oppressed by any sudden perturbation: makes the voice hoarse. And two, like messengers sent by the others, asked us saying: MAKE US WISE. Make us instructed & learned. OF YOUR condition. Of your state.

THEY MARVELED that one with a body could climb the mountain. Which signifies nothing else: than that it seems impossible: that a man still in life can reach the purgatorial virtues. And certainly it is a marvelous thing: that the soul oppressed by the contagion of the body: submerged in pleasures: & corporeal desires: can be liberated from them. Whence in Wisdom <note>Referring to the Book of Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) 31:8-10.</note> it is said not without wonder: "Blessed is the man who is found without blemish: & who has not gone after gold. Nor hoped in the treasures of money. Who is this? & we will praise him. For he has done wonderful things in his life: Who has been tested in it: & made perfect." <note>original: "Beatus uir qui inuentus eſt ſine macula: & qui poſt aurum non abiit. Nec ſperauit in pecunię theſauris. Quis eſt hic? & laudabimus eum. Fecit enim mirabilia in uita ſua: Qui probatus eſt in illo: & perfectus eſt."</note> But Virgil, i.e., the intellect, knows: that although this excellence is in few: nonetheless it exists: Wherefore he adds: "Let them do him honor."

because in truth the man who reaches this degree deserves immortal praise. Aristotle writes in his *Meteorology*: <note>Aristotle’s "Meteorologica" was the standard medieval textbook for understanding weather and atmospheric phenomena.</note> that terrestrial vapors drawn up by the sun: sometimes are so thick & corpulent: that they do not pass the middle region of the air. But they are frozen by the cold, or truly they dissolve & fall down. But those that are thinner rise higher. And of these, the less viscous are resolved into wind by the heat. And the more viscous, being unable to resolve, rise so high that, near the sphere of fire, they ignite; & if they are of small quantity, they quickly resolve: & thus ignited they fall in the form of a star. Hence Ovid says: **"Which, if it did not fall, could have been seen to fall."** <note>original: "Que si non cecidit potuit cecidisse uideri." — Ovid, Metamorphoses II, describing the fall of Phaethon.</note> And of these the

AUGUST CLOUDS. When the sun is in Leo & especially when it is near the dog star: <note>The "Canicula" or Sirius, the Dog Star, associated with the hottest "dog days" of summer.</note> it happens that the clouds, pushed by the heat, descend swiftly. Because heat enclosed with humidity always generates wind: & the wind pushes the clouds.

"O soul that goes to be happy
with those limbs with which you were born,"
they came crying, "quiet your step a little.
Look if you ever saw any of us,
so that you may carry news of him over there.
Ah, why do you go? Ah, why do you not stop?
We were all once killed by force,
& were sinners until the final hour;
then a light from heaven made us aware,
so that repenting & forgiving, we departed
life at peace with God,
who pains us with the desire to see Him."
And I: "Though I gaze at your faces,
I recognize no one; but if it pleases you,
well-born spirits, I will do anything I can.
You speak, & I will do it for that peace
which, following the footsteps of such a guide,
makes me seek it from world to world."

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'V' containing a seated figure in a classical or pastoral landscape.</image-desc>AND THE LIGHT from heaven. The illuminating grace of the Holy Spirit. REPENTING: & forgiving: one cannot end their life in a way that their guilt is remitted if they do not repent of the errors committed. And if one does not forgive; hence in the prayer instituted by God: **"Forgive us our debts as we also forgive our debtors."** <note>original: "Dimitte nobis debita nostra sicut & nos dimittimus debitoribus nostris." — The Lord's Prayer.</note> WHO WITH THE DESIRE: Of the desire for God, he said "pains us," <note>original: "naccora" — derived from 'cuore' (heart), meaning to pierce or grieve the heart.</note> it inflames us & constricts our heart. Nor should it be said that it does not seem just that one who has sinned all their life can be saved at the end by repenting at the last. Because just as the body, while health remains in the heart, can be restored to optimal wellness even if the rest is sick, so the soul, sick with sin, is restored to health when <term>prevenient grace</term> <note>A theological term for grace that "comes before" human action, pre-disposing the soul toward God.</note> remains in it, which induces & disposes; after which disposition there supervenes the illuminating, cooperating, & perfecting grace. I remember having spoken of divine grace in the second canto of the first canticle <note>Inferno, Canto II.</note> as much as that place required, where it treated the virtues inferior to the purgatorial ones. Now, because the purgatorial virtues are more excellent, I will add some things about divine grace to those we wrote above, many of which are useful to know. And first, that man cannot without divine help & grace attain blessedness. Because it is manifest that man, according to the suitableness of his nature, arrives at participating in the highest good—which is God—more highly than inferior creatures. And because he has intellect, he can understand through his operation that truth which is not perceived with the senses. As, for example, the truth that honey is sweet is understood with the sense of taste, which is common to us and other animals. But that God is our highest good, we do not understand with the senses, but with the intellect, in which no animal other than man participates. Never-
<meta>catchword: theless</meta>

<column-break/>

theless, the human intellect is not sufficient by itself to reach its highest good, which is placed in a certain knowledge of truth that exceeds our natural faculty. If, therefore, man is ordered toward that end which transcends his strengths, it is necessary that he be aided by divine grace. Nor for this should anyone say that by the help of divine grace, man is forced to act according to virtue. Though Christ says in the Gospel: **"No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him."** <note>original: "Nemo potest uenire ad me: nisi pater qui misit me traxerit eum." — John 6:44.</note> And Paul to the Corinthians: **"The love of Christ urges you."** <note>original: "Caritas Cristi urget uos." — 2 Corinthians 5:14.</note> Because divine grace provides for all things according to the proper mode of each, as the Aquinate <note>Thomas Aquinas (c. 1225–1274), the preeminent scholastic theologian.</note> clearly demonstrates in "Against the Gentiles." But it is proper to every rational creature that it operates voluntarily, & be the master of its operations. Therefore, one operates according to virtue by the help of divine grace, which corroborates the will but does not constrain it; because man cannot come to his ultimate happiness without virtue, that being the prize of the virtues; & forced operations are not of virtue, since virtue is not without choice, nor choice without will. Hence we do not say brute animals are happy, except by metaphor & similitude, because they do not operate according to virtue. This is demonstrated in the 30th chapter of Deuteronomy where it says: **"Consider that today the Lord has set before you life & good; & on the contrary death & evil: that you may walk in his ways."** <note>original: "Confidera quod hodie proposuerit dominus in conspectu tuo uitam & bonum... " — Deuteronomy 30:15-16.</note> And in Ecclesiasticus: **"Before man is life & death, good & evil. What pleases him will be given to him."** <note>original: "Ante hominem est uita: & mors bonum: & malum. Quod placuerit ei dabit illi." — Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) 15:17.</note> Nor do I wish to allow in this place that anyone by their own merits can attain divine help. Although this is proved with many arguments, this one will suffice: every prize & price that is given & conferred ought to have proportion to the merit, so that in retribution just equity is observed, & the prize is not greater than the merit. But the effect of divine help, without any proportion, exceeds & transcends our operations, which we do according to our own faculty. Therefore, through his own operations, man does not merit divine grace. Which is why Paul said to Titus: **"Not by works of righteousness which we have done. But according to his mercy he saved us."** <note>original: "Non ex operibus iustitie que fecimus nos. Sed secundum suam misericordiam saluos nos fecit." — Titus 3:5.</note> Nor let there be anyone who, because of the words of the prophet saying: **"Turn to me, & I will turn to you,"** <note>original: "Conuertimini: & conuerrar ad uos" — Zechariah 1:3.</note> believes that our operations precede divine grace. Rather, our conversion, with which we turn to God, subsequently helps that grace. From this is manifest the error of the Pelagians, <note>Followers of Pelagius, who argued that humans could take the first steps toward salvation without divine grace.</note> who wanted us to receive such help for our merits, & that the beginning of our justification be in us, & then the perfection come from God. It is, therefore, not a prize for our merits, but grace. Hence Paul to the Romans: **"If it is grace, then it is no longer of works. Otherwise grace is no longer grace."** <note>original: "Si gratia est: iam non ex operibus. Alioquin iam gratia non est gratia." — Romans 11:6.</note> Nor is it difficult to understand that through <term>grace making one pleasing</term>, <note>original: "gratum faciens" — A technical term in Scholastic theology for grace that justifies the soul before God.</note> man achieves that he loves God: because grace itself is in us an effect of love.

<header>CANTO FIVE</header>

...makes us love God. And certainly the first intention of one who loves is that he himself be loved by the one he loves. And the beloved cannot help but love in return. Therefore, by the same [grace], we are loved by God. Wherefore Paul says to the Romans: "The charity of God is poured forth in our hearts by the Holy Spirit, who is given to us." <note>original: "Caritas dei diffusa est in cordibus nostris per spiritum sanctum: qui datus est nobis." — Romans 5:5.</note> And in John: "He who loves me shall be loved by my Father, and I will love him, and will manifest myself to him." <note>original: "Qui diligit me diligetur a patre meo. Et ego diligam eum: Et manifestabo ei me ipsum." — John 14:21.</note> The divine doctors demonstrate that divine grace creates faith in us; it creates the hope of pure beatitude. It demonstrates that man, without divine grace, cannot persevere in good. Nor can he, without it, be freed from sin, nor flee from it. But let us return to the text. **BY THAT PEACE** as if to say, by the true peace: which is not that of the world, but that which our Redeemer left to us as a final testament when ascending back to where he had descended. In this way, one can also say that peace is the highest good. Wherefore the Psalm sings: "Praise the Lord, O Jerusalem; praise thy God, O Zion. For he hath strengthened the bars of thy gates; he hath blessed thy children within thee. He maketh peace in thy borders." <note>original: "Lauda hierusalem dominum: lauda deum tuum syon. Quoniā cōfortauit seras portarum tuarum: benedixit filios tuos in te. Qui posuit fines tuos pacem." — Psalm 147:12-14.</note> Thus the Psalm says that its end—that is, its highest good—is peace. And a little below it defines the peace of the celestial city as a most ordered and most concordant society and company in the enjoyment of God. **WHO FOLLOWED AT THE FEET OF SUCH A GUIDE.** For as we have shown, if the appetite does not follow reason, it will never acquire peace. But by following it, reason will hold it from world to world, leading it first through Hell—that is, through the knowledge of the vile ugliness and detriment of vices, which leads us to hate and flee them. And consequently, we desire to be liberated from them. From Hell we pass into Purgatory—that is, we come to the knowledge of those things that may purge us. And being purged, we ascend to Heaven.

---

And one began: "Each of us trusts
In your good office without your swearing it,
Provided that 'I cannot' does not cut off 'I will.'
Wherefore I, who speak alone before the others,
Pray you, if ever you see that country
That lies between Romagna and the land of Charles,

That you be courteous to me with your prayers
In Fano, so that they may rightly pray for me,
That I may purge my grave offenses.
From there I came; but the deep gashes
From which the blood flowed in which I had my seat,
Were dealt to me in the lap of the Antenori,

There where I believed I would be most secure.
He of Este had it done, who held me in wrath
Far more than justice would allow.
But had I fled toward La Mira
When I was overtaken at Oriaco,
I would still be yonder where men breathe.

Instead, I ran to the marsh, and the reeds and mire
Entangled me so that I fell; and there I saw
A lake of blood from my own veins form on the ground."

<margin>162</margin>
Then another spoke: "So may that desire
Be fulfilled that draws you to the high mountain,
With gracious pity help my own.
I was of Montefeltro, I am Bonconte;
Giovanna and the others have no care for me,
Wherefore I walk among these with lowered brow."

And I to him: "What force or what chance
Led you so far astray from Campaldino,
That your burial place was never known?"

<column-break/>

**W**ITHOUT YOUR SWEARING IT: Without you having to say "by that peace." And it is ordered thus: EACH ONE trusts in your benefit; PROVIDED THAT "I cannot"—that is, the lack of power—does not cut off, sever, or impede "I will"—the will. **BETWEEN ROMAGNA AND** the land of Charles: that is, Puglia, of which King Charles <note>Charles I of Anjou.</note> was ruler, formerly Count of Provence without land, and then King of Puglia. And he refers here to the March of Ancona.

**A** long history is recited by the commentator from Imola <note>Benvenuto da Imola, a 14th-century commentator on Dante.</note> regarding the war between Azzo III, Marquis of Este, and the people of Bologna and Parma; which, because it does not seem necessary to this place, I omit. Let it suffice only that in those times, Azzo, striving to gain many friends in Bologna and eager to make himself its lord, caused such suspicion among those people that many of his friends were exiled and some killed. At this time, Messer Jacopo del Cassero, a citizen of Fano, became the Podestà <term>Podestà</term> <note>A high-ranking city official or chief magistrate in medieval Italian communes.</note> of Bologna; he, with crude and shameful words, insulted the reputation of the Marquis. Among other things, he said the Marquis had slept with his stepmother and that he was descended from a washerwoman. This was so offensive to the Marquis that from that time forward he had him tracked by secret assassins. Finally, while Jacopo was going to be Podestà of Milan, he sailed from Fano to Venice, and from there toward Padua. In the territory of Padua, in the marshes which are near Oriaco Mountain, he was killed by the aforementioned assassins. **FROM THERE**—that is, from Fano—was I. **BUT THE DEEP GASHES**: The deep and mortal wounds. **FROM WHICH THE BLOOD FLOWED IN WHICH I HAD MY SEAT**: He speaks according to those philosophers who say that the blood is the seat of the soul. <note>An ancient physiological belief, often attributed to Empedocles or mentioned in Aristotelian contexts.</note> **IN THE LAP OF THE ANTENORI**: That is, in the territory of the Paduans, who descended from the Trojan Antenor. After the destruction of Troy, he sailed to Italy and founded Padua, which he called *Patavium* according to Servius, from *petesthe*, meaning "to fly," because he took an omen from the flight of birds; or truly *amate*, because with an arrow he struck a bird. <note>original: "quia telo petiuit auem." — "because he sought the bird with a weapon."</note> **HE OF ESTE**: Because the Marquises of Ferrara are of the House of Este. And Este is a castle twenty-five miles distant from Padua, from which these Marquises originated. **WHO HELD ME IN WRATH**: Who bore me more hatred than justice—**THE RIGHT**—allowed; for equity and justice did not permit it. For just as an unjust thing is called "crooked," so a just thing is called "straight" or "right." **TOWARD LA MIRA**: La Mira is a castle in the Paduan territory. **WHERE MEN BREATHE**: Where people dwell, where they live—that is, among the living. **ENTANGLED ME**: They enveloped and impeded me.

**B**onconte was the son of Messer Guido, Count of Montefeltro, whom we treated in the 27th Canto of the *Inferno*. This man, fighting against the Guelphs in the rout of Casentino, <note>The Battle of Campaldino in 1289.</note> was killed there, and his body was never found. Therefore the poet feigns that which he describes here. **WHAT FORCE OR WHAT CHANCE**: For either his own strength or good fortune should have pulled him from the hands of the enemies. **CAMPALDINO** is a plain in Casentino at the foot of the mountain of Poppi toward the village of La Collina. There the Guelphs, in a pitched battle, defeated the Ghibellines. William, Bishop of Arezzo and captain of the Ghibellines, sent Bonconte to scout and spy on the camps of the Guelphs and how they were governed and ordered. Bonconte, finding everything in excellent order, advised...

# PURGATORIO

...to the bishop: that he should not start a fight. But the bishop, more rash than skilled, wished to fight. And he was killed. Buonconte was killed likewise, along with about two thousand Aretines. Our people <note>The Florentines</note> had this victory, mostly through the industry and boldness of Corso Donati, as appears in the Florentine annals.
