<column-break/>

THE ARCHIANO is a river which is born on this slope of the Apennines which is above the Hermitage of Camaldoli; it descends into the Casentino and enters the Arno between Poppi and Bibbiena. He arrived, therefore, fleeing by the Aretine road and along the Arno, as far as where the Archiano, entering the Arno, loses its name. And therefore he says: **WHERE THE NAME**—that is, its name—**becomes vain**. **THERE I ended**: I died. **IN THE NAME OF Mary**: Rendering myself guilty <note>Seeking penance</note> and invoking Mary for my help. **REMAINED my flesh**: my body alone without the soul. Our body is much inferior to the soul, because the soul is simple <note>In the philosophical sense of being indivisible and non-material</note> and the body is composite. The former is incorruptible; the latter, corruptible. The former is of eternal life; the latter has no life unless it receives it from the soul. Therefore, in the separation, it appears that the soul does not remain alone, because it remains alive and with all its powers. But the body remains deprived of life, motion, senses, and all its virtues—therefore, it is alone. **THE ANGEL of heaven took me**: because of my conversion and contrition. And he from Hell, because of my past errors, lamented that the "eternal part of me" was taken from him—that is, my soul, which is eternal and immortal. **BUT I WILL MAKE of the other**: of the mortal and corruptible part. **A DIFFERENT governance**: because you lead the soul to salvation, and I will destroy the body. And it follows in what manner: by moving a sudden rain, he buried him in the silt and sand of the Arno.

THERE FOLLOWS the Aristotelian doctrine on the generation of rain. For this philosopher writes in his *Meteorology* <note>original: "meteora"</note> that humid vapors from the earth, elevated by the sun, rise to the second region of the air; and there, struck by the cold, they resolve into water. The Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle</note> divide the air into three parts: of which the upper, being bordering on fire, is always hot. The lower is similarly hot, because the rays of the sun, striking the surface of the earth, warm it with their reflection. For this reason, only the middle part remains cold, as it is neither near the fire nor reached by the aforementioned reflection, up to this place which many hold to be sixty stadia—that is, five miles above the earth. The sun draws humid vapors from the earth and the sea, which, being condensed there by the cold, are converted into clouds and distilled into rain. **JOINED TO That ill will**: the angels were created with free will. And being able through that to turn their will in whichever direction they pleased, the angels who became black <note>Demons</note>, elevated by pride, turned it to evil, just as those obedient to God turned it to good. Therefore, being damned, their evil will remains immutable, as the Aquinate <note>Thomas Aquinas</note> demonstrates with many reasons in the book he wrote *Against the Gentiles* <note>original: "contra gentiles"</note>. And that demons have power [over the elements] appears both through Saint Augustine and through Albertus Magnus in a small book of his titled *On the Power of Demons* <note>original: "de potētia demonū"</note>. **MOVED THE SMOKE and wind**: He calls the vapor "smoke," which, drawn up by the sun, resolves into the humid and cold part as water, and into the hot and dry part as wind. From this, sudden and impetuous rains are born. **THE RAIN fell AND to the gullies came: of it whatever the earth did not endure**: The rain falls and the earth, sucking it up, suffers and endures what water it can. The rest runs to the gullies, and from the gullies to the rivers, and from the rivers to the sea. Therefore, the gullies swelled the Archiano; and the Archiano, becoming raging and impetuous, found the body of this man at its mouth—that is, where it enters the Arno—and pushed it into the Arno, and the Arno rolled it for some distance. But in rolling it, it broke his arms, which he, dying and asking mercy for his sins, had made into a cross. And finally, it covered and girded him with its prey—that is, it submerged him and covered him with the silt <note>original: "bellecta"</note> it had taken from the fields.

**THE THIRD spirit**: For the first was Messer Jacopo del Cassero from Fano. The second was Buonconte. And Pia was the third spirit. She was Sienese and the wife of Messer Nello della Pietra of Siena. Who, being a governor in Maremma, found her (as it is believed) in a fault, and killed her so secretly that it was not known then. **SIENA made me**: because I was born in Siena. **AND MAREMMA unmade me**: because I was killed there. And because the manner was secret, she says: "he knows it, who previously wedded me and gave me the ring"—that is, it was my husband. The Sienese [records] write that this Pia was of the Tolomei, a noble family of Siena. And Messer Nello being very powerful in the Maremma, he often lived there; and one day, while the lady was at the window, he commanded one of his servants to throw her down. The reason that led him to this was not well known.

<header>CANTO SIX</header>

### CANTO VI OF THE SECOND CANTICLE BY DANTE.

When the game of <term>zara</term><note>A popular medieval gambling game played with three dice; the name likely comes from the Arabic "zahr," meaning "dice."</note> breaks up,
the one who loses remains there, grieving,
repeating the throws and sadly learns his lesson;
With the winner, all the people go along:
one walks ahead, another catches him from behind,
and another at his side brings himself to mind.
He does not stop, listening to this one and that;
those to whom he stretches his hand press him no more,
and so he defends himself from the crowd.
Such was I in that dense throng,
turning my face toward them here and there,
and promising, I freed myself from them.
Here was the Aretine who at the fierce arms
of Ghino di Tacco met his death,
and the other who drowned while giving chase.
Here prayed with hands outstretched
Federigo Novello, and the one from Pisa
who made the good Marzucco appear so strong.
I saw Count Orso, and the soul divided
from its body through spite and envy,
and not, as he said, for any fault committed—
I mean Pierre de la Brosse; and let the Lady
of Brabant take heed while she is still here,
lest she end up in a much worse flock.

<column-break/>

In this canto, the poet continues his description of those who delayed their conversion and penance until their violent death. And thereafter, he begins to treat those who, because of family cares or some particular learning, similarly delayed their penance. In the first verses, he wishes to show that many were gathering around him; and he, turning now to this one and now to that, and promising as much as they asked, rid himself of them. He uses the comparison of the man who departs as the winner from a game.

**HERE WAS THE ARETINE:** **Sir Benincasa of Arezzo**, a man most learned in <term>civil law</term><note>original: "iure ciuili"</note>, was the deputy of the <term>Podestà</term><note>A high-ranking city official or chief magistrate in medieval Italian cities.</note> of Siena. He condemned to death Turino da Turrita, a castle in Sienese territory, who was the brother of Ghino di Tacco, along with Tacco his uncle, because they, together with Ghino, had stolen a castle from the Sienese Republic called Radicofani and practiced banditry in the Maremma. Nevertheless, it was Ghino's custom, even though he raided the roads, not to wish for any of his captives to be killed. After this time, Sir Benincasa went to serve in the papacy of Boniface as a judge of the Roman tribunal; others say an auditor of the <term>Rota</term><note>The highest appellate tribunal of the Roman Catholic Church.</note>. Hearing this, Ghino was of such bold spirit that he went to Rome and entered the house and the hall where Sir Benincasa sat on the bench; and in the sight of many, he killed him and escaped to safety with the head, which he had cut off. They say Ghino was large of stature, muscular and very robust, and very liberal; he practiced banditry not out of greed, but to be able to practice generosity. He always wanted those who fell into his hands to set their own ransom, and afterward, he would return a good part of it to them. And if he found scholarly men, he gave them money and encouraged them in their studies. Boniface, recognizing that he plundered only for the sake of generosity, called him to Rome and made him a Knight of the Order of St. John<note>original: "caualier friere"</note>, so that he could live honorably. Yet finally, he was captured at Asinalunga. This Ghino is the one about whom Giovanni Boccaccio tells a story, where he recounts how he cured the stomach of the overly fastidious Abbot of Cluny. **AND THE OTHER** refers to the Aretine. This was Ciacco of the Tarlati of Arezzo, who drowned while fleeing in the rout of Montaperti. But I believe more those who say otherwise. In Arezzo, the Tarlati, lords of Pietramala, were very powerful citizens; the Bostoli were also a most noble family. Tarlato fathered Angelo and Cione. From Angelo was born Guido, Bishop of Arezzo, who ennobled his homeland with walls, streets, castles, and many other things. Cione, the Bishop's uncle, was a very robust man of great spirit. In those times, there was war between the Tarlati and the Bostoli. But the Bostoli, having been driven out of Arezzo, had occupied the castle of Rondine, not far from Arezzo. It happened then that in a skirmish pursuing the Bostoli, Cione was carried by his horse into the Arno river near Rondine and drowned in it. Federigo was the son of Count Guido, who were of those of Battifolle, and he was killed by one of the Bostoli called Fornaiuolo. **THE ONE FROM PISA.** Sir Marzucco of the Scornigiani of Pisa was a knight and a doctor; riding one day from Suvereto to Scarlino, a snake of stupendous size crossed his path. He was so terrified that he vowed to become a Friar Minor if he should escape. After becoming a friar, his son Farinata was killed. In this calamity, he showed such constancy that, together with the other friars, he celebrated the funeral rites and accompanied him to the grave. Afterward, appearing before his kinsmen with a long and most fitting speech, he persuaded them to peace. And he himself kissed the hand of the murderer who had killed his son. He was like another Anaxagoras, who, hearing of the death of his son, was not at all disturbed but said to the messenger: "You tell me nothing new, for I knew I had fathered a mortal." And Cato in a similar case said: "My son has satisfied nature, because he was mortal." But not to leave behind the case of the serpent: they say it fed on piglets, to the great horror of the locals. As a last resort, they gathered all the sows of the surrounding area in the place where the serpent lived. Sows are very fierce animals against those who offend them; and gathered together in great concord and packed closely, they made a simultaneous assault on the enemy. By these, then, the serpent was torn apart and killed. **I SAW COUNT ORSO.** Some believe he was of the Alberti of Val di Sieve, killed by his kinsmen. This family has been ennobled in our republic by many virtues and by supreme humanity and generosity. And especially by the splendor of two most excellent men: first, Sir Alberto, who for a long time served with supreme integrity and prudence in the government of lands subject to the Church, deserving that Pope Eugenius IV, with the great favor of the entire college, should make him a cardinal. The second is Leon Battista, the delight of our city, a most eloquent man in both the Latin and Tuscan languages, born to investigate the secrets of nature and filled with every kind of science. If I were to enter into his praises now, time would fail me before the subject matter. He was most acute in every branch of philosophy and a supreme mathematician. His book on architecture surpasses all writers of our century. However, some—which I am more inclined to believe—say he was the son of Count Napoleone of Acerbaia, and was killed by Count Alberto of Mangona, his uncle. **Pierre de la Brosse** was the secretary and counselor to Philip the Bold, King of France. Because he had great influence with the King, he was, through the envy of the barons...
<meta>The text cuts off mid-sentence with the catchword "dabarom," referring to the "barons" (baroni) who conspired against Pierre de la Brosse.</meta>

<header>PURGATORY</header>

...put in such hatred at court by the king's wife that she accused him to her husband, claiming he had attempted to corrupt her chastity. Therefore, the too-credulous King had him killed. But the same did not follow in all cases. The Emperor Otto, who faced a similar accusation—because the truth was of great value—later learned the truth and had his false accuser of a wife burned. Therefore, let the Lady of Brabant <note>Marie of Brabant, Queen of France, accused Pierre de la Brosse of treason/molestation; he was executed in 1278.</note> take heed, and let her perform penance for this false accusation while she is still alive, so that after death she does not remain among the damned.

### As soon as I was free from all
those shades who prayed only that others might pray,
so that their purification might become holy,

### I began: "It seems that you deny me,
O my light, expressly in a certain text,
that a decree of heaven can be bent by prayer;
And yet these people pray for just this.
Would their hope then be vain,
or is your meaning not clearly manifest to me?"
And he to me: "My writing is plain,
and the hope of these souls does not fail,
if one looks well with a sound mind.
For the peak of judgment does not stoop
because the fire of love fulfills in one instant
that which he who dwells here must satisfy.
And there where I fixed that point,
the fault was not mended by prayer,
because the prayer was disjoined from God.
Truly, regarding such a deep suspicion,
do not stop until she tells you,
she who makes a light between the truth and the intellect.
I do not know if you understand; I mean Beatrice;
you will see her above on the summit
of this mountain, smiling and happy."

---

And I: "Lord, let us go with greater haste,
for I am not as tired as before;
see now that the hill no longer casts a shadow."
"We will go forward with this day,"
he replied, "as much as we now can;
but the reality is of a different form than you suppose.
Before you reach the top, you will see him
return who is already covered by the hillside..."

<column-break/>

Dante raises a question to Virgil, saying: "These souls have hope that prayers made to God for them will shorten the term of their punishment. And yet you, in one of your texts, show that God is not bent by prayers." Specifically, in the sixth book [of the *Aeneid*], when Palinurus prays that Aeneas might carry him across the Acheron, the Sibyl responds: *Cease to hope that the decrees of the gods can be bent by prayer.* <note>original: "Define fata deum flecti sperare precando"</note> Dante concludes that since he does not doubt that Virgil is right, he is left wondering if these souls have a vain hope.

Virgil responds that his "writing"—that is, the text quoted above—is "plain," meaning clear and open. Therefore, Dante understands correctly. On the other hand, the hope of these souls does not "fail," meaning it does not deceive them. Because prayers do move God. And yet, one side does not contradict the other. For whoever looks with a sound mind knows that God is immutable; and nevertheless, through prayer, He shortens the punishment of the souls who must be purged. God's justice is not lacking even if the time of punishment is shortened. Thus he says: **FOR THE PEAK OF JUDGMENT**, meaning the height of judgment, **DOES NOT STOOP**; it does not diminish. **BECAUSE THE FIRE** of love—because the heat of charity which is in the heart of the one who prays for the dead—fulfills in one instant **THAT WHICH MUST BE SATISFIED** by **HE WHO DWELLS HERE**; he who stays above here.

Or we might say that God from eternity knows who sins, and how much that sin deserves to be punished, and also how much the charity of an intercessor can decrease that time. Therefore, He judges the soul to stay in Purgatory not as long as the sin deserves, but as long as remains after the prayers of others have diminished it, as the Sacred Scripture says: *Charity covers a multitude of sins.* <note>original: "Caritas operit multitudinem peccatorum"</note> And this is according to the <term>Master of Sentences</term> <note>Peter Lombard, a 12th-century theologian whose textbook was the standard for medieval theology.</note>: because of the good works that the soul in Purgatory performed in life, they have merited that such prayers should avail them.

But as for those who are still in this life, it is clear that one who is repentant for sin can recommend themselves to God with such fervor, and pray with such heat for the remission of sins, that they satisfy in one instant, through an excessive degree of love, what they otherwise would not satisfy in many years. **AND THERE WHERE I FIXED THAT POINT**. He shows that Virgil was in Hell when he said that prayers cannot change God's mind, because those in Hell are already separated from every mercy of God by the sentence given. **AND THERE WHERE I** fixed that point—that is, in Hell—where the Sibyl affirmatively tells Palinurus that he must stay a hundred years as he has been judged. **THE FAULT IS NOT MENDED**; it is not purged by prayer, because God does not hear prayers made for the damned. And therefore he says that in Hell, prayer was "disjoined from God."

**TRULY**. This is excellent advice, useful to every Christian: that in such doubts one should seek no other determination than that of Sacred Theology, lest one fall into many heresies. **SHE WHO TELLS YOU**. Just as visible things are the object of the eye but cannot be understood without light, so the truth is the object of the intellect and is understood through the medium of natural light. But this is not sufficient for the knowledge of every truth. For the knowledge of divine things, which transcend our natural light, the light of illuminating grace is necessary, which is signified by Beatrice. And we see her at the summit of the mountain because she surpasses all earthly things. **UPON THE SUMMIT**: on the peak of this mountain where Purgatory ends, where the author imagines the <term>Earthly Paradise</term> <note>The Garden of Eden, located by Dante at the top of the Mountain of Purgatory.</note> to be. He wishes for Beatrice to be in such a paradise, "smiling and happy," because our first father [Adam] received such grace in this place, and while he stayed there, he was smiling and happy. And certainly, among us mortals, whoever is made worthy of such grace continuously feeds upon the sweetest nectar and ambrosia in the contemplation of divine things.

---

This shows that once he understood Beatrice was at the summit, Dante felt such a desire to see her that love made him both more vigorous and more light-footed. And certainly, every time we are certain where the end we aim for lies, and we realize we are on the way, a marvelous desire to hasten our pace arises in us, and every labor becomes lighter. And therefore he says: **FOR I AM NOT AS TIRED** as before. **WE WILL GO FORWARD WITH THIS DAY**. Virgil responds: we will move upward as long as the day lasts, because one cannot climb at night. This is because vices cannot be purged in the darkness of ignorance, but only with the light of reason. Hence the divine precept: *Walk while you have the light, lest darkness overtake you.* <note>original: "Ambulate dum lucem habetis: ne tenebre uos comprehendant"</note> And he shows that a single day will not bring him to Beatrice. This signifies that without a length of time, one does not form the habit of virtue...

<summary>Dante questions Virgil on whether prayer can change divine decrees, leading to a theological explanation of how charity satisfies divine justice and the introduction of Beatrice as the symbol of illuminating grace.</summary>

<header>CANTO SIX</header>

...so that you do not block its rays:
But see there a soul who, placed
all alone, looks toward us;
he will show us the quickest way.

from the side of the mountain: it will rise again from the east. In this poetic invention, the author shows that although one travels through Purgatory with the light <note>The sun represents the light of God or human reason in Dante's allegory.</note> and lamp of reason, nevertheless, because those in this state are not yet in the perfection of virtue, the darkness of sensuality can sometimes hide the light of reason from us. At such times, we cannot proceed along the path of salvation. But because reason finally overcomes the senses, the sun returns. We shall say, therefore, that those in Hell never see the sun but always walk in darkness. But those in Paradise are never overtaken by darkness; instead, standing before the mirror of eternal light, they continually see all things within it. One who is in Purgatory is sometimes with the sun and sometimes with darkness. But he cannot ascend except when he is with the sun, which represents reason—as we showed a little earlier.

**BUT SEE THERE:** Here it signifies that he has come to the fifth category of those who were negligent in their penance due to family preoccupations or certain studies. He places that soul alone because the management of a family and the study of specific doctrines are more private matters than public ones.

We came to him—O Lombard soul,
how you stood proud and disdainful,
and in the movement of your eyes, dignified and slow!
He said nothing to us,
but allowed us to pass, only watching
in the manner of a lion when it couches.
Yet Virgil drew near to him, praying
that he might show us the best ascent;
but he did not answer his question,
But asked us of our country and our life.
And the sweet leader began:
"Mantua..." and the shade, all rapt in itself,
Rose toward him from the place where it stood,
saying: "Mantuan, I am Sordello
of your own land!"—and they embraced each other.

This man <note>Sordello da Goito (c. 1200–1269), a famous troubadour from the same region as Virgil.</note> had not been a student of philosophical and theological matters, but only of histories and geography <gloss>that is, of the form and location of regions</gloss> and their cities; he had written nothing else. For this reason, he could not dispute with those learned in other doctrines. **AND THE SWEET LEADER BEGAN** to answer, wanting to say: "Mantua was my homeland." But Sordello, as soon as he heard "Mantua," interrupted his speech: because he was so devoted to his homeland and loved every citizen of it so much, he immediately revealed himself and embraced him with the highest affection. Sordello was a Mantuan and a very studious man, an investigator of whoever had been excellent in doctrine, talent, or counsel at any time. He wrote a volume which he titled *The Treasure of Treasures* concerning such things.

Ah, enslaved Italy, hostel of grief,
ship without a pilot in a great storm,
no mistress of provinces, but a brothel!
That noble soul was so ready,
only for the sweet sound of his native land,
to welcome his fellow citizen here;
And now within you, your living inhabitants
never stand without war, and they gnaw at one another—
even those enclosed by the same wall and moat.
Search, wretched one, around your shores,
your coastlines, and then look into your heart,
to see if any part of you enjoys peace.

<column-break/>

...obligatory. **BADLY DONE.** But this ascent is of another form and manner, and of another reason—as if to say, it is much more difficult. **THAT YOU DO NOT DELAY.** <gloss>that is, that you do not establish in your mind</gloss> because a long and very steep journey remains for us. He demonstrates here that in beginning difficult tasks, we are often deceived. For it seems to us immediately at the start that we have acquired much more than we actually have; and he adds that before you are there, the sun—which is now setting in the west—is taken from us.

Many read: "we came to her" and then understand that Virgil said, "O Lombard soul." And if anyone objects, asking how Virgil knew he was a Lombard, I answer: that the clothing, and a certain quality and air, and almost the specific property of each region—which the Latins call *captus* <note>original: "captus" — a Latin term for 'appearance' or 'disposition.'</note> and is better understood than expressed—made him recognize it. But it seems to me that Dante, in narrating, says: **WE CAME** to him; and afterward uses this exclamation in praise of Sordello while writing, when he already knew it had been Sordello. **PROUD AND DISDAINFUL:** in our language, we call a man "proud and disdainful" who, through excellence of soul, does not look upon or give thought to base things, nor deems them worthy. Thus it demonstrates a refined generosity of spirit without vice. For when one despises others not through greatness of soul but through too much arrogance, he is called not proud, but haughty. And likewise, one who through that same arrogance does not yield to anything is called stubborn. Hence Petrarch used such words in their proper meaning when he said: "Proud and disdainful, not haughty or stubborn." **HE SAID NOTHING TO US, BUT ALLOWED US TO PASS.** He let us go on, only watching us as a lion does when it lies down. He most excellently compares Sordello’s nobility to that beast, which is by nature very noble. That Sordello did not respond to Virgil, who was asking about the way to ascend, but instead asked him about their homeland and country, is said to denote that this man...

The supreme love that Sordello showed to Virgil because they were compatriots gave Dante the occasion to make an invective against all the cities of Italy, in which, because of the opposing parties of the Guelphs and Ghibellines <note>The warring political factions of 13th and 14th-century Italy.</note> who were then fellow citizens, all civic charity was extinguished, and they persecuted one another with deadly enmity. **ENSLAVED.** As if to say: while there was union and virtue in you, you were the empress of other regions. Now, through your discords and vices, you are a slave. But why does he say "slave"? We shall say that one finds "master" and "servant" according to nature, and according to custom and law. But Nature, that excellent mother, makes servant and master according to merit. For just as in a man, reason is naturally the master, and to it belongs the kingdom, and it ought to be obeyed—because through prudence it understands what is to be done, and with justice does it rightly—and the appetite is the servant, and ought to obey reason, because by nature it is of robust impulse and vehement to follow what is useful and flee the opposite. So it is in the company of men: those who, either by natural counsel or by long experience, or by acquired...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante's "Purgatorio," specifically the famous political lament in Canto VI. The text shifts from the encounter with Sordello to a direct indictment of the political state of Italy, focusing on the absence of a strong Emperor to guide the nation.</meta>

<page-type>text</page-type>
<columns>2</columns>
<header>PURGATORY</header>

What good was it that Justinian refitted the bridle
if the saddle is empty?
Without it, the shame would be less.
Ah, people who ought to be devout,
and let Caesar sit in the saddle,
if you well understand what God notes for you!

Look how this beast has become savage,
for not being corrected by the spurs,
since you put your hand to the bridle.
O German Albert, who abandons
her who is untamable and wild,
and who should have straddled her saddle-bows:
May a just judgment fall from the stars
upon your blood, and let it be new and clear,
so that your successor may have fear of it!
For you and your father, held back
by greed for those distant lands, have suffered
the garden of the empire to be laid waste.

<column-break/>

teachings precede others in prudence and goodness: they are naturally free and they ought to command. And others in whom bodily strength abounds, but who lack industry and sense, are servants and ought to obey their superiors. See, therefore, that [the status of] free man and servant is by nature. But also, a certain consensus of men and many civil laws establish this, although differently, for free men and servants. Free men are of three kinds: *Ingenui* <note>meaning "free-born"</note>, *Liberti* <note>meaning "freedmen"</note>, and *Libertini* <note>meaning "children of freedmen"</note>. *Ingenui* are those who are born free, of a father and mother who were always free. By *Liberti*, understand those who at one time were servants, and afterwards, for having served faithfully, were made free. And of these, the ancients chose

not those who, through faith and prudence, were fit for domestic government; they treated them almost like sons and committed to them all family care. *Libertini* were those who, although born free, nevertheless had parents who had been servants. Although at some times, as Suetonius shows in the *Life of Claudius*, the term "libertini" is used with the same meaning [as freedmen]. This much regarding free men. Servants are those who, captured by enemies, lose their liberty and remain in the power of those who possess them. There are also servants by civil law: those who are born of female servants, and the master of the female servant could sell them. Later, in canon law, it is prohibited to sell or hold in servitude anyone born of a Christian. There was also a law among the ancients by which a magistrate could adjudge a debtor as a servant to his creditor. And these were called *addicti* <note>original Latin: "addicti," meaning "assigned" or "bound"</note>. **INN OF GRIEF.** A dwelling of pain. Because its inhabitants, due to factions, are in constant wars, from which spring infinite calamities and tribulations, which bring constant grief with them. **SHIP WITHOUT A PILOT** in a great storm. The government of the republic is likened by all writers to sailing. Because in a ship, it is necessary to have someone to hold the rudder and direct it on a good path. Thus, every civil government must have a governor. And just as the sea, by the force of contrary winds, rises in a great storm, so in cities, through various perturbations of the citizens, many discords, dissensions, furies, and tumults arise. Therefore, Dante, judging that the Emperor ought to be the head of Italy, and seeing that he was not there—like a ship in a storm without a pilot—it must perish. Thus a city in discord, if it has no excellent guide, goes to ruin. **NOT LADY OF PROVINCES.** Not the mistress of other regions, as she used to be. **BUT A BROTHEL**, but a prostitute; he uses the place to represent those who inhabit it. He says metaphorically that Italy is no longer a "lady" <note>meaning a noble or chaste mistress of a house</note>, who is chaste, uncorrupted, and modest, worthy of reverence, who does not bend from the right path for any reason and governs her family most honestly and with good prudence and equity. Therefore, she is not a "lady"—that is, a just governess—**BUT IS A HARLOT.** This name in Latin does not signify every unchaste and lustful woman, but only she who for a price offers her body, who for money sells her honor and chastity. Therefore, Italy is a harlot, because the spiritual and temporal governments within her do not proceed with justice and restraint. Instead, through the price of barratry <note>the sale of public offices</note> and simony <note>the sale of church offices</note>, black is made into white. Thus, Italy is a harlot, because for money she sells honor, honesty, and justice. **THAT SOUL.** These two stanzas are clear. To the shame of those living today, they show what a sweet reception Sordello gave just upon hearing the name of his homeland. **SEARCH, O ITALY,** your coastlines. **ALONG THE SHORES,** around the extremities. For Italy is in the middle of two seas: she has the Tyrrhenian to the south and the Adriatic to the north. It is as if he says: consider all your borders and then observe if there is any part embraced by these boundaries that enjoys peace. **WHAT GOOD WAS IT** that Justinian refitted the bridle? Justinian freed Italy from the Goths and reformed her with excellent laws, as we shall say in the 6th Canto of *Paradiso*. **IF THE SADDLE IS EMPTY.** He continues the metaphor: for it is not enough to bridle the horse if no one mounts to guide it. Thus, it is not enough for Italy to have the laws of Justinian if the Emperor is not allowed to govern the cities of Italy. In this, he wants to rebuke the Guelfs <note>the political faction supporting the Pope</note>. They can most excellently excuse themselves, for they did not rise against the Empire, but to defend the liberty of their homeland, which the Ghibellines <note>the faction supporting the Emperor</note>, with the favor of the Emperors, wanted to occupy with tyrannical pride. And to defend the sacred majesty of the Apostolic See, they opposed their unjust arms. **WITHOUT IT, THE SHAME WOULD BE LESS.** For it would be a lesser infamy for Italy to have no laws than to have them and not live according to them. And he adds that the Italian people ought not to take jurisdiction away from Caesar. For God commands it in the Gospel: when he said, "Render unto Caesar what is Caesar's, and unto God what is God's" <note>original: "Reddite que sunt Cesaris cesari: & que sunt dei deo"</note>. He showed that in temporal things He wants us to obey temporal lords, and in spiritual things, spiritual lords. And the same thing is denoted by the figure when, at His last supper, the apostles said, "Behold, here are two swords" <note>original: "Ecce duo gladii"</note>, He replied that they were enough.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'O' depicting a crowned figure, likely an emperor or king, seated on a throne.</image-desc>
**O** SON OF ALBERT the Emperor, who has abandoned Italy, which he calls the garden of the empire, as the most beautiful region. Wherefore she remained without a legitimate lord and has become fell <note>savage or cruel</note> and stubborn, like a horse that is not ridden; he continues the metaphor already begun above. This Albert was the Duke of Austria, the firstborn son of Rudolph Caesar. And in the year of our salvation 1298, after Adolf (who had already been elected) died in battle, he succeeded to the kingdom. And the following year, through his ambassadors, he signaled to Pope Boniface [VIII] that he wished, according to custom, to come to Rome for the crown of the Empire. To these, the Pope replied that Albert was not legitimately elected. Nor did he deem him worthy of the empire, as he had unjustly waged war against the King, his lord, and killed him through fraud. In this response, Albert was armed in the royal seat, with the crown on his head. And after the words of the delegates, indignant, he put his hand to the sword with which he was girded and said: "Why can I not defend the empire, being Caesar?" Nevertheless, there being later a war between him and Philip [the Fair], King of France, Boniface made a confederation with him. And he called him

<margin>
I in Italy the year that I was taken in Anagni, his homeland.
</margin>
to Italy the year that I was taken in Anagni, his homeland. **YOU PUT YOUR HAND TO THE REINS,** to the bridle. *Predella* is that...

# CANTO FIVE <note>Though the header says "Canto Five," the verses and commentary actually correspond to Canto VI of the *Purgatorio*.</note>

<columns>
2

the part of the bridle that is held in the hand. **LET IT FALL.** Therefore, let a just judgment come from heaven, and let it be **new**, that is, unusual, and **open and manifest**, so that it may cause greater terror. This intervenes—or rather, it had already happened—though the author, following his custom of setting the poem in the past, places it as a future event. For in the year 1308, on the first day of May, **Albert**, after crossing the river and stepping off the boat, was killed by his nephew, whose inheritance of the Duchy of Austria he had unjustly occupied. **WHICH YOU HAVE ENDURED.** That is, why have you and your father endured being **distanced by greed**, meaning the greed to stay in your own country? From this follows the discord of Italy. To which they say that **Henry** <note>Henry VII of Luxembourg</note>, his successor, wished to bring a remedy by coming to Rome. But death intervened. Therefore he turned:

Come see the Montagues and Capulets,
the Monaldi and Filippeschi, O man without care:
those already grieving, and these in dread!
Come, cruel one, come and see the oppression
of your noblemen, and tend to their wounds;
and you shall see Santa Fiora, how secure she is!
Come see your Rome, who weeps,
widowed and alone, and day and night she calls:
"My Caesar, why do you not accompany me?"
Come see the people, how much they love one another!
And if no pity for us moves you,
come to be ashamed of your own reputation.

<column-break/>

These were two families in Verona who drove out Azzo II, Marquis of Ferrara and governor of Verona. But he, with the favor of the Counts of San Bonifacio, won and returned to Verona. The **Monaldi** and **Filippeschi** were two opposing families in Orvieto. **THE OPPRESSION** of your noblemen: the oppression that the lords of Italy inflict upon their subjects. **AND TEND TO THEIR WOUNDS.** Correct their failings and vices. **AND YOU SHALL SEE SANTA FIORA.** These are the Counts of Santa Fiora. They are located in the Maremma, between the territories of Pisa and Siena. **HOW SECURE SHE IS.** How she is governed—or truly, "how secure" she is, spoken ironically to say that the country is broken and full of robbers and thieves. **WIDOWED AND ALONE.** Because the Emperor is the King of the Romans, when Rome is deprived of the Emperor, she remains widowed and alone. And finally, come to see how much the people "love" each other, and you will see hatred and enmity instead of love. And if you have no pity for Italy, come to be ashamed of your infamy. Certainly every prince ought to be ashamed who does not rule with supreme justice and most humane clemency those who are under his protection. For as **Plato** writes, and as all philosophers affirm and the theologians command: Kings and all other princes were not raised to such dignity for their own profit or leisure, but for the **peace** of all the peoples subject to them. They toil so that the people may rest. They stay awake so that the people may sleep. They do not flee dangers so that the people may live securely. No other reward is proposed to them but honor. Therefore, they must not usurp what belongs to others, but preserve it, and always think of the best things. Hence **Isaiah** says: *The prince devises things worthy of a prince.* <note>original: "Princeps que sunt digna principe cogitat."</note> For this reason, they were called **kings** (*reges*) from **ruling** (*regendo*). For ruling is nothing other than sustaining the people so that they do not fall, and directing them to a tranquil life in which each person keeps what is his and abstains from what belongs to others. And the Greeks call them **Basilees** <note>original: "Basilees," from the Greek "Basileus"</note> because they are the **foundation of the people** <note>original: "basis iau," a medieval etymology linking "basis" (foundation) and "laos" (people).</note>. For they ought to be those upon whom the quiet of all is founded and established. And **Homer** and all the other poets call them **shepherds of the people** <note>original: "pimenas laon," from the Greek "poimenas laon."</note>, because they ought not to strip them, but to guide them firmly—not like a tyrant, but like a good shepherd who feeds and nourishes. But it often happens because of the sins of the people that God permits not a King, but **tyrants** to govern them. For this reason, **Augustine** said in *The City of God* <note>original: "in ciuitate dei"</note> that God allows the hypocrite to reign because of the sins of the nations. And certainly no one is a greater hypocrite than he who, under the appearance of a king, becomes a tyrant, who is a wolf instead of a shepherd. No government is better than a single prince, who is called a **monarch**, about whom Dante disputes most acutely in his *Monarchia*. The opposite of this is the tyrant. Of him, **Solomon** says: *Keep far from a man who has the power to kill.* <note>original: "Longe esto ab homine habente potestatem occidendi"</note> And **Virgil**: *Alas, flee these cruel lands, flee the greedy shore.* <note>original: "Heu fuge crudelis terras: fuge littus auarum"</note> And Solomon in the Proverbs: *A roaring lion and a hungry bear: a wicked prince over a poor people.* <note>original: "leo rugiens & ursus efuriens: princeps impius super populum pauperem"</note> And **Cicero** writes that the prince of the city should be content with glory. And **Aristotle**: *A prince for whom the reward of honor and glory is not enough becomes a tyrant.* <note>original: "Princeps cui non satis est premium honoris & glorie tyrannus efficitur"</note>

<margin>†</margin> And if it is lawful for me, O highest Jove,
Who was on earth for our sake crucified,
Are your just eyes turned elsewhere?
Or is it a preparation that, in the abyss
Of your counsel, you make for some good,
Entirely severed from our perception?
For the cities of Italy are all full
Of tyrants, and every peasant who comes
To play the partisan becomes a Marcellus. <note>Dante likely refers to the Roman consul Marcellus, an opponent of Caesar, symbolizing factionalism.</note>

<column-break/>

Men who are inflamed by some disturbance are accustomed at times not to grieve, but to marvel that God allows such great injustices. Then, finally, one who has true religion and true prudence corrects himself and concludes that every evil that God permits is for some good end. **IF IT IS LAWFUL FOR ME.** It is as if he says: I ask you, highest God, if it is lawful for me to ask you if you have turned your just eyes elsewhere—as if to say, if you have withdrawn your love from Italy. **HIGHEST JOVE.** Among the pagans, Jove signifies various things, as we said above. But here it signifies the highest God. Since God cannot have a proper name, as no word can be found that can entirely express the divinity, it is not inappropriate to call Him Jove, which name signifies "help" or "benefit." For from Him comes all help, benefit, and salvation. **OR IS IT A PREPARATION.** It would be an impious thing to believe that God would abandon—I do not say Italy—but even the smallest of creatures. For the belief of the **Epicureans** is false, who say that God does not care for human affairs. Therefore, leaving aside the doubt, which would be impious if stated affirmatively, he comes to that which can be said religiously: Since God is supreme goodness, He never permits any evil except to the end that it be a **preparation** for some greater good. Thus, for the sins of the people, He permits civil discords, robberies, wars, famine, and plague. Part of this is to punish sins, and part is to punish and amend men and lead them back to just living. But our finite sight cannot understand the infinite depth of divine judgment. Hence he said: "or is it a preparation for some future good," which You make in the **abyss**, that is, in the depth of Your counsel, of Your providence, with which You govern the whole, which is **entirely severed**, meaning divided, from our perception. For as I said, our intellect cannot reach such...

</columns>

# PURGATORIO

depth. **AND BECOMES A MARCELLUS.** This shows that every commoner, every man—even those of low condition—when they come to any aforementioned position, wants to become a "new Marcellus" in that city. In this passage, however Francesco da Buti <note>A famous 14th-century commentator on Dante.</note> may speak, it is necessary to understand that the Marcellus family in Rome was ennobled by many excellent men. But the most excellent was Marcus Marcellus, who in Lombardy on the banks of the Po near Casteggio killed Viridomarus, prince of the Gauls. He was the third after Romulus and Cossus to carry the *spolia opima* <term>spolia opima: the "rich spoils" taken by a Roman general who had killed the enemy commander in single combat</term> into the temple of Jupiter Feretrius. Regarding this, Petrarch wrote: "He was on the banks of the Po near Casteggio / He killed with his own hand the great rebel." This same man conquered Syracuse, a most noble city. And having brought the whole island under the power of the Roman people, he returned to Italy and in several battles drove back Hannibal. But it seems more likely that the poet refers to the Marcus Marcellus who was consul at the beginning of the civil war between Pompey and Caesar. With all his industry, he opposed Caesar in defense of the Senate and of Pompey. But after the victory, Caesar mercifully pardoned him, as appears in an oration by Cicero <note>Pro Marcello</note>, in which Cicero, in his own name and that of the Senate, gives thanks to Caesar for having restored him to his homeland. The poet, therefore, wants to show that every lowly man who acquires status wants to oppose the Emperor, just as Marcellus opposed Caesar. And he secretly condemns such people.

->My Florence, you may well be content<-
->with this digression, which does not touch you,<-
->thanks to your people, who so argue.<-
->Many have justice in their hearts, but the arrow is slow to fly,<-
->lest it come to the bow without counsel;<-
->but your people have it at the tip of their tongues.<-
->Many refuse the common burden;<-
->but your people respond solicitously,<-
->without being called, and cry: "I’ll shoulder it!"<-
->Now make yourself glad, for you have good reason:<-
->you who are rich, you with peace, you with wisdom!<-
->If I speak the truth, the result does not hide it.<-
->Athens and Lacedaemon, who made<-
->the ancient laws and were so civilized,<-
->made only a small hint toward living well<-
->compared to you, who make such subtle<-
->provisions that by mid-November<-
->what you spun in October does not reach.<-
->How many times, in the time you remember,<-
->laws, money, offices, and customs<-
->have you changed, and renewed your members?<-
->And if you remember well and see the light,<-
->you will see yourself like that sick woman<-
->who cannot find rest upon the feathers,<-
->but fends off her pain by tossing and turning.<-

<column-break/>

Writers use a **digression** when they depart from their main subject for some purpose, just as the poet here has departed from his subject to rebuke the civil discords of Italy, and especially of our Republic. For this reason, he speaks with **irony**—that is, with the opposite meaning—saying that Florence can be "content" because what he said in that digression does not touch her; it is as if he were saying that it touches her more than any other city. **THANKS TO YOUR PEOPLE**: This too you should read as irony, because he condemns the people who do not "argue" (strive) to rise up against the tyranny of the powerful. **MANY HAVE JUSTICE IN THEIR HEART**: lest they "come to the bow"—that is, to action—without counsel, or rather without being able to put it into practice. The meaning is that many would wish to live justly, but they do not want to reveal themselves unless they first see that they can achieve some fruit, so that they do not harm themselves while trying to help others; and therefore the arrow "is slow to fly." Thus Sallust says: "To strive in vain, and to seek nothing but hatred by one's fatigue, is the height of madness." <note>original: "Frustra autem niti: nec aliud se fatigādo nisi odium querere extremę demetię e."</note> **BUT YOUR PEOPLE HAVE IT AT THE TIP OF THEIR TONGUES**: as if to say their will always comes before they consider or see how they might bring that will to perfection. **MANY REFUSE THE COMMON BURDEN.** Many refuse the government of the Republic. But the Florentine people are so prompt that every day one sees new changes. Hence he says with irony: "You who are rich, you with peace, you with wisdom." **ATHENS** was ennobled first by the laws of Draco, then by the laws of Solon. Solon’s laws were admirable, among which are these: Whoever does not nourish his father and mother shall be treated as infamous. He who lives in idleness may be accused by anyone. The children of those who die in battle shall be nourished by the public. He who puts out an eye shall have both of his own removed. **LACEDAEMON** <note>Sparta</note>, through the laws imposed by Lycurgus, was reduced to such severity of life and customs that, with their incredible justice and unyielding strength, they were able to obtain leadership over all of Greece and part of Asia. **LIKE THAT SICK WOMAN.** The nature of the sick person is to be eager to change position often to find rest; and if they could leave the illness in the place they depart from, it would help them. But because they carry it with them, they must suffer wherever they move. So too the people: if they could leave behind injustice by changing their government, they would live in peace. But because injustice persists in whatever magistrates they create, it happens that such a change does not help them.

# SEVENTH CANTO OF THE SECOND CANTICLE OF DANTE
<meta>catchword: therefore</meta>

After the honest and joyful greetings
were repeated three and four times,
Sordello drew back and said: "Who are you?"
"Before the souls worthy of ascending to God
were turned toward this mountain,
my bones were buried by Octavian.
I am Virgil, and for no other crime
did I lose heaven than for not having faith."
Thus my leader replied then.
As one who suddenly sees something
before him, whereat he marvels,
who believes and does not, saying: "It is, it is not,"
such he seemed, and then he lowered his brow,
and humbly returned toward him
and embraced him where the lesser takes hold. <note>original: "enel minor ſappigla" — This refers to the custom of an inferior embracing a superior around the knees or lower body as a sign of deep respect.</note>

<column-break/>

TRULY the poet set Sordello as an example of a good citizen: who, being always affectionate toward his fellow citizens, loves and honors them wherever he finds them. And to show how great his affection was, he posits that upon hearing that the other was Mantuan, without seeking further, he embraced him with every feeling of charity. Now following this, he shows that such greetings were not made once, but three and four times. And he calls them honest and joyful to show that there was gravity in them, along with pleasant joy. This canto places those who, due to the occupation of kingdoms or other lordships, and through governments and magistracies, have deferred their penance until the end. I AM VIRGIL: of whom there is nothing to narrate at present because in Canto I of the Inferno, we set down his life. But we can in short agree with the opinion of Macrobius <note>A 5th-century Roman writer and philosopher whose commentary on Cicero was highly influential in the Middle Ages.</note> who affirms that no praise can increase his glory, and no detraction or blame can diminish it. THREE AND FOUR TIMES. He imitates Virgil, who said: "O thrice and four times blessed" <note>original: "o ter quater que aeati" [o ter quaterque beati]</note>. And as Macrobius shows, in these two numbers is the height of perfection. LOWERED HIS BROW: first as a citizen he performed the aforementioned greetings. Now as to a citizen well-deserving of his homeland, and for his learning and eloquence worthy of every veneration, he shows him the highest reverence. And he embraces him beneath the arms to

---

->show himself inferior. Lowering the brow demonstrates reverence and at the same time compassion: that such a great man should be deprived of beatitude, which is the divine vision.<-

<column-break/>

"O glory of the Latins," he said, "through whom
our language showed all it could do,
O eternal pride of the place where I was born,
what merit or what grace shows you to me?
If I am worthy of hearing your words,
tell me if you come from Hell, and from which cloister."
"Through all the circles of the grieving kingdom,"
he replied, "I have come here;
a virtue from heaven moved me, and with it I come.
Not for doing, but for not doing, I lost
the sight of the high Sun which you desire
and which was known too late by me.
There is a place down there not sad with torments,
but only with darkness, where the lamentations
sound not as wails but as sighs.
There I stay with the innocent little ones,
bitten by the teeth of death before
they were exempt from human fault.
There I stay with those who did not clothe themselves
in the three holy virtues, and without vice
knew the others and followed them all.
But if you know and can give us some sign
so that we may come more quickly
to where Purgatory has its true beginning."
He replied: "No certain place is set for us;
it is permitted for me to go up and around;
as far as I can, I join myself to you as a guide.
But see already how the day declines,
and one cannot go up by night;
therefore it is well to think of a fine resting place."

<column-break/>

GREAT praise: but in no part too much for such a poet. Rather, as I said a little before with the authority of Macrobius, it is not equal, but much inferior to his eloquence and learning. O ETERNAL PRIDE: that is, through whom Mantua—where I was born—is and will always be in pride and honor because of you. And he shows he honors him not so much for his learning as for the fame he has given his homeland. WHAT MERIT: what have I done that I should deserve to see you? As if to say, nothing. Therefore, if it is not my merit, WHAT GRACE: as if to say, from where do I have such grace from the Giver of Graces? NOT FOR DOING: not for committing errors and sins from which the civil virtues can purge us. BUT FOR NOT DOING: for not believing and not observing the things commanded by the Christian religion. WHICH WAS LATE: because when he knew it, he was already in a place where penance or amendment is of no use.

IN the canto of the Inferno, he described this place in detail, in which he placed the children who died without baptism, who, if they had received it, would have been exempt and free FROM THE HUMAN FAULT: that is, from original sin. And this is according to what the Church posits. WITH THOSE WHO [the] three holy [virtues]. He shows that besides the little children, he stays with those Gentiles who through learning and civility were adorned with the moral virtues, which are <term>Prudence</term>, <term>Justice</term>, <term>Fortitude</term>, and <term>Temperance</term>. Of which we spoke above. But for not being instructed in Christian doctrine, they did not clothe themselves in the three holy virtues: <term>Faith</term>, <term>Hope</term>, and <term>Charity</term>, of which we will speak in the third canticle [Paradiso]. HAS TRUE BEGINNING: the real start. Because they were not yet where the souls are purged of their vices, but where, because of the negligence they committed, they have to wait, as was said above. And this whole place up to the gate of Purgatory is called by many the <term>antipurgatory</term>.

AS Virgil shows in the sixth book [of the Aeneid], those in the Elysian Fields have no fixed place: <note>original: "Vt nulli certa domus lucis habitamus opacis" — Since for none of us is there a fixed home, we dwell in shady groves.</note> So Dante, although for another reason, induces Sordello to say that same thing. For the negligent person cannot have a fixed place in penance, because he has not established any certain order within himself. Furthermore, he shows that when night comes, one cannot ascend. By "the day," one can understand <term>illuminating grace</term>, which illuminates the human intellect just as the sun illuminates the sense of sight. Without which light, one cannot come to liberation from vices.

# CANTO SEVENTH

"There are souls off to the right nearby;
if you permit me, I will lead you to them now,
and they will be known to you with no small delight."
To which it was replied: "Could he who wished
to climb at night be hindered
by another, or would he just be unable?"

...comes the desire to resolve it. And from the same teaching, one understands how to be free of it: nevertheless, history is not useless: for the specific details and experience we gain from histories are of no small benefit. From these comes prudence, which persuades us to rise toward other doctrines. Therefore Sordello—representing <term>action|In this allegorical interpretation, Sordello represents the 'active life' or the study of human history, which prepares the soul for higher spiritual truths but cannot reach them alone.</term>—cannot do this alone. But he can discern that the souls who are on the right—that is, those who have taken a virtuous path, even if not a theological one—can provide delight until day arrives. And certainly, I confess that such studies cannot guide us upward. Nevertheless, until the sun is born, they exercise the mind in a useful way and lift us from lazy and sleepy idleness.

The good Sordello rubbed his finger on the ground,
saying: "Look, you would not cross even this line
after the sun has departed.
Not because anything else would offer hindrance,
except the darkness of night poured all around;
that, by the lack of power, entangles the will.
One could well return downward with it
and wander the slope, strolling about,
as long as the horizon keeps the day closed."

Then my lord, as if in wonder,
said: "Lead us then where you say
that one can have delight while staying."
We had moved a little distance from there
when I noticed the mountain was hollowed out,
in the way that valleys hollow them here.
"There," said that shade, "we shall go,
where the slope makes a lap for itself,
and there we shall await the new day."

Between the steep and the flat was a winding path
which led us to the side of the hollow,
at the point where the edge dies away by more than half.
Gold and fine silver, scarlet and white lead, <note>original: "cocco & biaccha" — These refer to expensive pigments: 'cocco' is a deep red dye, and 'biacca' is lead white.</note>
shining and serene Indian wood, <note>original: "indico legno" — Likely referring to ebony or indigo, prized for their deep, lustrous colors.</note>
fresh emerald at the moment it is broken—
each would be surpassed in color by the grass
and by the flowers placed within that fold,
as the lesser is always bested by the greater.
Nature had not only painted there,
but from the sweetness of a thousand odors
she made there an unknown, indistinct fragrance.
"Hail, Holy Queen" <note>original: "Salue regina" — A traditional evening hymn to the Virgin Mary, here sung by the souls in the valley.</note> upon the green and among the flowers
I saw souls sitting and singing,
who, because of the valley, were not visible from outside.

...because the red in it is much illuminated by the white, and the white receives a pleasing color from the red. Nonetheless, the solidity of sulfur contributes more to the generation of gold than does the airy, watery quality of <term>quicksilver|mercury</term>. And for this reason it is more...

<column-break/>

They also identify the sun with the rational part of man: which, as long as it does not lose its light, can proceed forward in purifying itself. But I believe it is not unsuitable to set the sun for both together: that is, for reason illuminated by divine grace. Therefore, while this prevails in us, we proceed. And let us remember the precept: *Walk while you have the light.* <note>original: "Ambulate dum lucem habetis" — A quote from the Gospel of John 12:35, reinforcing the theme that spiritual progress requires the light of God's grace.</note> **THERE ARE SOULS TO THE RIGHT:** Sordello was not fit to lead them upward. For Sordello’s teaching was history. And that which leads to purification is philosophy and theology, through which reason has knowledge of the foulness of vice; and by coming to hate it through that knowledge, one understands how to be free of it. Nevertheless, history is not useless: for the specific details and experience we gain from histories are of no small benefit. From these comes prudence: which persuades us to rise toward other doctrines. Therefore Sordello—that is, action—cannot do it by himself. But he can discern that the souls who are on the right—that is, those who have taken a virtuous path, even if not a theological one—could delight them until the day comes. And certainly I confess: that such studies cannot guide us upward. Nevertheless, until the sun is born, they exercise the mind in something not useless. And it lifts us from lazy and sleepy idleness.

He declares more clearly what was said above, showing that a single line could not be climbed without the sun. It is as if he says: we can make no progress, even the smallest, without the light of the intellect and reason. **ONE COULD WELL RETURN** with her. Although the appetite alone is what moves the soul to every action, nonetheless it never leads us upward—that is, to contemplation—if it is not illuminated by reason. But it can certainly lead us downward and wandering around the mountain—that is, to vicious actions. No crossbowman can hit the target if he is not an excellent craftsman in that art, but elsewhere any ignorant person can hit, even with eyes closed.

This place serves more for the fiction that Dante creates for this ascent than for the allegory. Because Virgil—that is, superior reason, illuminated by all divine graces and human doctrine—should not have wondered that one could not climb without the day, for he should have understood this by himself. Unless one wants to take Virgil here only as lower, unrefined reason, and without any science. Sordello leads him to the shade, that is, to the knowledge of history: which, while the day waits—that is, until the time comes when we can give ourselves to contemplation—gives us honest delight, free from every vice. In which, if we cannot acquire great doctrine in contemplation, yet the soul feeds on those things which, as I said just before, offer some help. **WHERE THE SLOPE MAKES A LAP FOR ITSELF:** a ravine, or ditch, or valley in the mountain can be said to be its "lap."

He uses chorography—that is, he describes the region where they went—and first the path that led them. He says therefore that the path was narrow, and the word is derived from *semita* [path]; it was "winding" (*ghembo*), as paths on mountains must be, which twist here and there to avoid the more difficult passes, between steep and flat, because they were neither entirely climbing nor entirely on the level. **WHICH** path led **US TO THE SIDE.** On the extremity: where the descent begins into the hollow of the **HOLLOW** (*lacca*): of the ditch. The "side" is therefore the edge of the valley, and the *lacca* is the descent that begins from the side and drops toward the bottom. **MORE THAN HALF** the edge dies away: it passes the midpoint of its concavity. We say the "hem" (*lembo*) is the extreme part of a garment, which often forms a lap; and for this reason the poet uses this word for the concavity of the valley. **GOLD AND SILVER.** He shows that place to be clothed with such green grass and such a variety of flowers and such vivid and bright colors that the color of gold and silver and the stones he mentions here would be lost and remain defeated. All this denotes the variety and the delight and the utility that we seek in the active life, which especially desires gold. This is the most precious of all metals. And of the most beautiful and good color. It is created in the earth from subtle and broken sulfur, and from subtle and white quicksilver. Whence its color is most pleasing...

<meta>This page continues the transition from the discussion of the physical properties of the "Valley of the Princes" to the specific historical figures Dante encounters there. <header>PURGATORY</header>

...gold: heavier than silver: And because of such density, it does not diminish when melting: and it is very healthy for the human body. And taken with food, it comforts all the limbs: not because it nourishes them, but because it gnaws away and purges every superfluity in them. For this reason, it preserves one from leprosy. If you mix its filings with borage juice and the bone of a stag’s heart, it is very effective against heart disease. No metal extends further, nor withstands the hammer better than gold. Silver is created from quicksilver <note>mercury</note> and white sulfur; but it participates more in the airy and watery quality of quicksilver than in the solidity of sulfur. For this reason, it weighs less than gold. Not only these two aforementioned metals, but all others have their origin in quicksilver. Therefore, some say it is a simple element. Cochineal, according to Dioscorides <note>A Greek physician and botanist of the 1st century AD</note>, is a branchy herb, and on its stalks, it has berries similar to lentils. White lead in Latin is called *Cerusa*: stones of perfect vinegar, placed in a covered vessel. Indigo is a blue color. Shimmering wood, like ebony, which is a very shiny black. Others read "Indian wood" because there are marvelous trees in India. And then they say "bright serene," denoting the purity of the air. The emerald has a more pleasant appearance than any other gem, and it greatly comforts the sight. The Emperor Nero used to watch the battles of the gladiators through an emerald, because it is a most lucid mirror and makes the images of things that appear in it from afar seem large. Pliny states there are twelve species of emeralds. Of no precious gem are larger pieces found. And Theophrastus, a disciple of Aristotle, writes of having read in the commentaries of the Egyptians that the King of Egypt sent as a gift to the King of Babylon an emerald four cubits long and three high. And Apion Plistonico states that in the labyrinth of Egypt, there is a colossus of Serapis made of a single emerald nine cubits high. All these things placed inside that grass—that is, the valley, which is the grass of the mountain—would be surpassed in color by the flowers and the herbs. **NOT ONLY.** Not only were the colors marvelous, but the scents were also most sweet; from all of them mixed together resulted a most sweet composition, unknown and indistinct, because one could not recognize any certain thing in that composition. In this place, Francesco da Buti <note>A prominent 14th-century commentator on Dante</note> understands allegorically that Dante signifies by those seven things the seven virtues: four moral and three theological, in which the lords could be excellent if they were not all hindered by sloth. But my opinion is that it rather demonstrates the state and condition of temporal lordship. And first, he posits that the path leading to this place is between steep and flat. Because lordships and states are acquired sometimes with virtue and sometimes with vice. And similarly, it is curved for the same reason. He places them in the valley, whose whole is almost submerged under the earth because it has slopes on every side that block the view. And certainly, whoever hungers for lordship hungers for earthly things, the greed for which quickly takes away the prospect and sight of celestial and divine things. And for this reason Leah—who in the Old Testament denotes the active life—is described as bleary-eyed and rheumy <note>original: "lippa & cispa"</note>. Nor can the active mind, because it is distracted by various and diverse cares, gather itself in contemplation of great things. Wherefore also of Martha, who in the New Testament signifies the same thing, True Wisdom <note>Christ</note> said: *Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things* <note>original Latin: "Martha Martha sollicita es: & uerfaris circa plurima"</note>. I will not dwell on this, because we treated it fully in the first canticle. It is therefore enclosed in the valley: that is, hidden and wrapped in earthly things. Nor is it without cause that such a valley is clothed in the greenest herbs and flowers most beautiful to the sight and sweetest to the smell. Because honors, dignities, states, and lordships are like herbs and flowers: just as they delight the sense of smell but quickly wither and dry up, so such a state brings great delight to men. In them, sensuality can do more than reason, but it quickly passes. Wherefore Petrarch says: *A beautiful mortal thing passes and does not endure.* **HAIL, HOLY QUEEN.** Since he has denoted what the state of lordship is like, he posits that these souls were singing "Hail, Holy Queen" <note>original: "Salve Regina"</note>, a most excellent prayer ordained in praise of the Queen of Heaven and Virgin Mother; intending by this prayer the conversion that temporal lords make from earthly cares to true religion.

<column-break/>

Sordello advises that it will be better to see the souls in the valley from an elevated place than to go among them. So that they may more conveniently see a multitude from a separate and high place than by mixing with them. And he imitates Virgil where he says: *And he takes a mound from where he can read all their faces in long order and speak of their strong expressions.* <note>Original Latin from the Aeneid: "Et tumulum capit unde omnes longo ordine possit Aduersos legere & uebementi dicere uultus."</note> He sets the time at the last hour of the day because such souls deferred their conversion until the night of death.

**RUDOLPH the Emperor:** This man was German and acquired the Duchy of Swabia and conceded it to Albert, his son. And having been made Emperor, he reigned twenty years. He killed the King of Bohemia in battle, who did not deign to obey him. This was in the year of salvation 1277. But afterward, he reconciled with the son and chose him as a son-in-law and restored to him the kingdom of Bohemia. He was a just and religious man and very powerful in military matters. And if he had come to Italy, he would have reduced it all to his empire. Therefore, the poet accuses him of negligence, because Pope Gregory X had chosen him so that he might succor Italy and then go to the conquest of the Holy Land. But he, greedy for lordship across the mountains, did not wish to pass. But he conceded Bologna and Romagna to Pope Nicholas of the Orsini. This is what the poet means by saying: *and he does not move his mouth to the others' songs.* **THE OTHER:** This was his son-in-law, son of the King of Bohemia, to whom he restored the realm. **AND THAT SMALL-NOSED ONE.** He means Philip the Bold <note>Philip III of France, nicknamed "le Hardi" or "the Bold," but here referred to by his nose</note>, son of the good Louis, King of France, who for his holiness was placed in the catalog of saints. This Philip had for a wife the sister of Don Peter, King of Aragon; and having heard of the rebellion of Sicily, which Don Peter had taken from Charles I, his uncle, he moved war against Don Peter with twenty thousand cavalry and eighty thousand French, Provençal, and German infantry of the crusade, with Charles his son and with a Cardinal legate of the Pope, and with a fleet of one hundred and twenty ships. And he joined with Don James, the King's brother and his enemy, because he had taken from him the island of Majorca. He came into Catalonia and by siege took Girona. And in a battle, he was wounded.

is a most true sentence interposed by our poet, and adorned with a metaphor <term>translation<gloss>metaphor or transposition of meaning</gloss></term>, placing the father for the tree and the children for the branches. He says, therefore, that human probity—that is, the virtue which is in man—RARELY: he does not deny that it happens sometimes, but says it is rare that it rises through the branches, that is, through the children, who have their origin from the father, like branches from a tree. This is because if souls are all created by God with their free will, the son cannot have a dependency on the father, because the father is not the generator of the soul where the virtues reside, but of the body, which is often similar to the father's body. We could refer to many, both those noted in history and those we have seen in our own times, who, born of excellent fathers, have been of the worst character. Nonetheless, because the soul exercises many powers with the instruments of the body, and the body gives many inclinations to the soul—and we see that the instruments of the senses, if they are well-disposed, make those sharp, and if poorly, make them dull—[if the disposition] of the heart makes a man timid or bold, it follows that the son may have similar habits and intellect. Not because free will [is constrained], and this is willed by Him who grants it <note>God</note>. And this God permits, who grants it. For the [soul does not come] from maternal blood like the body, but as soon as [the child is] in the womb, [He creates] the soul and infuses it into the already living body. and it immediately unites [to itself the powers]. <header>CANTO EIGHT.</header>

### EIGHTH CANTO OF THE SECOND CANTICLE OF DANTE.

He describes the evening very poetically. And he includes no small allegory in this comparison. The meaning is true: the evening was already coming, which brings desire to sailors who, having left the port in the morning where they have left behind relatives and friends, find that when evening comes, the memory of them causes them to be overcome by a passion of the soul which the Latins call "desire." And the same thing happens to one who begins a journey.

It was already the hour that turns back the desire
of sailors and softens their hearts
on the day they have said goodbye to sweet friends;
And which stings the new pilgrim with love
if he hears the bell from afar
that seems to mourn the day that is dying;
When I began to render useless
my hearing, and to admire one of the souls
who had risen and requested to be heard with a hand.
She joined and lifted both her palms,
fixing her eyes toward the East,
as if she were saying to God: "I care for nothing else."
*Before the light* <note>original: "Te lucis ante"</note> so devoutly
issued from her mouth with such sweet notes
that it made me step outside of my own mind.
And the others then, sweetly and devoutly,
followed her through the entire hymn,
keeping their eyes upon the supernal wheels:

ra. <note>likely a fragment of "Evening"</note> FIXING her eyes: that is, looking intently toward the East. Because our religion has the custom of turning toward the East when praying. Hence, ancient churches have always had their altars facing that way. AS IF SHE WERE SAYING TO GOD: she looked so intently and devoutly that she seemed to say, "I care for nothing else" <note>original: "ALTRO NON calme"</note>, meaning nothing else matters to me. And she began to sing the hymn that is sung at Compline <note>The final church service of the day</note>, the beginning of which is: *Before the end of the light, Creator of all things* <note>original: "Te lucis ante terminum rerum creator"</note>. She sang so sweetly that her sweetness drew all my senses to it, so that I did not remember myself. And in passing, he shows that in praying we must lift the eyes of the mind to heaven and have the mind entirely turned to God, in such a way that we remember nothing else.

Sharpen your eyes well, reader, to the truth,
for the veil is now so thin
that surely passing through it is easy.
I saw that noble army

Green as leaves just newly born
