in the Christian church, it is sung at the beginning of the night. And the Lord is prayed to guard us from every nocturnal phantom and from every harmful thing, and to remove from us every temptation. These souls, then, having finished the hymn, watched the sky in silence, waiting for help. PALE: because of the fear of the serpent; and HUMBLE: so that the prayer would be more acceptable to God. But so that we may understand the allegory of this text: there is no doubt that as the light departs for the coming night—that is, as we lose our reason and divine grace through ignorance and sin—we are tempted by the devil and the flesh. Therefore, the grace of God is necessary for us, without which our own strengths would not be enough to defend us. And for this reason, the souls ask for it in that verse of the hymn. This grace is signified by the angels. And because temptation comes in two ways: either by negligence, leaving behind meritorious acts and works, or by suggestion, which is when the devil tempts us by suggesting and supplying things that lead us to [sinful] living.

<column-break/>

*It was already the hour that turns back the desire:* that is, it was the hour of evening, which turns back the desire—that is, the longing—to think of those whom they left in the morning <note>original: "lo dì"</note> while saying goodbye. AND WHICH: that is, the hour which stings the "new pilgrim," meaning the one who has newly taken up the journey. WITH LOVE: for those he has left behind. IF FROM AFAR HE HEARS the bell <note>original: "squilla"</note>: the church bell, which seems with its sound to mourn the day that is departing as the night comes. Allegorically, he places this here for those who are in the "purgatory virtues," because the soul is not yet fully purified; if night catches it—that is, if it falls into some disturbance where it loses the light of the mind—the past pleasures to which it had said goodbye return to its memory. SWEET: For whoever departs from vices to go to Purgatory, although they have made a purpose to strip themselves of them, yet because they do not yet have the habit of true virtue, they force their appetite with reason rather than persuading it; because sensuality is still entangled in the pleasures and delights of vice and detaches itself unwillingly. Virgil expresses this when he says: *With tears I leave the shores and harbor of my homeland* <note>original: "Litora cum patriae lachrymis portumque relinquo"</note>. And certainly, we should imitate those old Trojans of whom Homer writes: seeing Helen coming, they greatly praised her beauty and took supreme pleasure in it. But finally, they concluded it was much better that Helen should go away, for it was not worth keeping her if it meant Troy would be lost. So the wise man, although stimulated by the pleasure of the senses, prefers that "Helen"—that is, those pleasures—depart from him because they are pernicious and lead to vice, rather than wishing for "Troy"—that is, their soul—to perish. WHEN I: I began to render hearing useless, because the souls who before were singing to the Queen were now silent. And I began to admire—that is, to see. RISEN <note>original: "SURTA"</note>: raised to her feet, from the Latin verb *surgo*. WHO REQUESTED TO BE HEARD: she asked to be listened to, as if to say she requested silence, not with words but with her hand—that is, with gestures she made with her hand. AND LIFTED: that is, she raised both her palms toward heaven, as one does who prays.

He admonishes the reader to sharpen their wit to understand the allegorical sense of this fiction; and he demonstrates that the veil of this allegory is not obscure. Rather, it is so transparent that it will be easily seen. Then he presents the fiction, saying that having sung the hymn, that "army"—that is, that multitude—[remained silent]. But note that "army" signifies a multitude of men who fight, or who are prepared to fight if necessary. Therefore, this word fits well in this place, because those who exercise themselves in the purgatory virtues always stand ready to fight against temptations and those vices. SILENT. He shows the prayer of these spirits; and he said "silent" because God understands the heart and does not desire prayer from the mouth, although sometimes affection sends words out. Whence the Psalmist: *With my voice I have prayed to the Lord* <note>original: "Voce mea ad dominum deprecatus sum"</note>. And elsewhere: *My heart was glad and my tongue rejoiced* <note>original: "Laetatum est cor meum & exultavit lingua mea"</note>. Let us say then that God does not desire words. For this reason, Damascene says that prayer is when our intellect directs itself to God. And for this, Augustine: *What profit is the noise of the lips if the heart is hardened?* <note>original: "Quid prodest strepitus labiorum si induratum est cor?"</note> And Solomon: *The prayer of him who humbles himself will pierce the clouds* <note>original: "oratio humiliantis se penetrabit nubes"</note>. This hymn is well suited, because in the

### PURGATORIO

Therefore, he places two angels, that is, the double grace of God, which defends us from two temptations. One is placed on the right side of the valley to guard us from negligence. The other is on the left, and this is against suggestion <note>In medieval theology, "suggestion" is the first stage of temptation</note>. The two swords are justice, which are blunted because such justice is mixed with mercy. He places two swords because Paul also said, "the armor of righteousness on the right hand and on the left" <note>original Latin: "l'arma iustitię a dextris & a sinistris," referencing 2 Corinthians 6:7</note>. The fire denotes charity. Therefore, the immeasurable love of God sends the angel, that is, the defense; and He sends him to us with justice, so that he may make us worthy through prevenient grace <note>The grace that precedes human action to incline the soul toward God</note>, which leads to asking for illuminating, cooperating, and preserving grace. Whence the psalmist: "May God be merciful to us and let his face shine upon us, and have mercy on us" <note>original Latin: "Misereatur nostri deus & illuminet uultum suu super nos: & misereatur nostri," from Psalm 67</note>. Thus, prevenient grace makes us turn to God to ask for mercy and light, so that we may perform meritorious works. But because our own just works are not enough, it is necessary for God’s mercy to supplement them. The angels have wings and green garments because the grace of God always keeps itself green within us and never withers, provided we desire it. The clothing defends us from heat and frost; the wings lift us above the earth and raise us to heaven. And we can take the two wings to represent justice and religion, as you will find according to Plato in the prologue of the third canticle <note>referring to the Paradiso</note>.

They stand above because grace comes from heaven, and they place the souls in the middle because grace is needed on the right and on the left, that is, in prosperity and in adversity. The blond hair signifies incorruption. And the splendor was so great that my eye could not endure it without being dazzled. For the sense, because it has a bodily instrument, cannot support so much light. **FROM MARY'S LAP.** That is, from our Redeemer, who was born from the lap of Mary. He uses the container for the thing contained <note>a literary device called metonymy</note>. The serpent is the diabolical temptation which assaults us with every cunning to deceive us. **BUT I WHO DID NOT KNOW BY WHAT PATH** because the devil is very astute and has many ways by which he tempts us; it is difficult to understand from where he will come. Therefore we must draw close to Virgil, that is, to reason illuminated by true doctrine, because that makes us cautious so that we may foresee from where we must provide defense. **FROZEN WITH FEAR:** because of the fear of the serpent. **TO THE TRUSTED SHOULDERS:** the shoulders are the limb best suited to support every weight we carry. And especially all of a man's armor: the helmet and the gorget rest on the shoulders; the breastplate hangs from the shoulders; the hand and arm have their strength from the shoulders. Therefore he used the shoulders to represent the strength that is in superior reason, suited to defend us from every diabolical fraud.

Sordello, having been invited to enter among the shades so that he might speak with them, descended three steps and was below. This signifies, according to some, that in descending—not ascending—to penitence, one requires contrition of heart, confession of mouth, and satisfaction in work <note>The three traditional parts of the Sacrament of Penance</note>. But to me it seems that in the contemplation of the civil life it is not necessary to have the three speculative virtues: Intelligence, Science, and Wisdom. Rather, prudence is enough, and for this reason he subtly—as with all other things—used these words: that he descended by three degrees. **AND I WAS BELOW:** to denote how much the civil life is inferior to the contemplative life. **THE AIR WAS DARKENING:** <note>original: "laer serenaua"</note> although when the sun is out, the air is clear. Nevertheless, we say the sky is "serene" when the sun is below the earth. **JUDGE NINO.** This man was of the house of the Visconti of Pisa, a man full of nobility and very robust of body; the nephew of Lord Ubaldo de' Visconti of Pisa, who with only two companions, Scarpetta degli Ubaldini and the Marquis of Montferrat, challenged one hundred Germans chosen by the Emperor (who was then in Pisa) and defeated them. But returning to Nino: he was the judge of the judicial district of Gallura in Sardinia. And he had for his wife Beatrice, marchioness of Este, who after his death remarried Galeazzo de' Visconti of Milan. But she first had a daughter by Nino named Giovanna, who was the wife of Lord Riccardo da Cammino of Treviso. Nino asks how long it has been since Dante came across the distant waters, believing that he had come across the ocean, led by the angel, according to Dante's fiction. And Dante replies that he did not come by the ocean sea, but through the sad places of Hell. And "I am in my first life," because I come with my body.

Sordello and Nino fell into extreme amazement, hearing from Virgil that I was alive. And Nino turned to Currado Malaspina, who was near him, so that he might see what God had willed through grace. For it was by special grace that, contrary to the human condition, Dante, still clothed in a mortal body, could make such a pilgrimage. Then Nino turned back to Dante and said: "I pray you, by that singular degree, that is, the singular privilege, that you owe—that is, for which you are a debtor—to God, who hides and oc..."

<column-break/>

**H**ides His first "why": that is, His first cause which has no ford. This first cause God keeps so hidden within Himself that it has no "ford," meaning that men cannot reach it. This is a metaphor taken from a river, which we say has no ford when it is so deep that we cannot cross it. **Tell my Giovanna that she should call for me**: that is, by calling, she should intercede for me there where the innocent are answered—meaning where the prayers of the righteous are heard. This occurs in the Christian Purgatory. Whence the Creator said: "My house shall be called a house of prayer" <note>original Latin: "Domus mea domus orationis uocabitur," from Matthew 21:13</note>. And because it seemed surprising that since his wife Beatrice was still alive, he would rather have this said to Giovanna his daughter than to her, he says that he does not believe her mother—that is, Beatrice—loves him anymore. This is because, having left the veils and the state of widowhood, she remarried Messer Galeazzo, as I said above; and he announces to her that a time will yet come when she will long for that state of widowhood which she has now abandoned, because of the way she will be treated by her second husband. **Through her**: by her example, one understands easily how little the fire of love lasts in a woman. For woman is very fickle and changeable. Whence Virgil: "A woman is always a fickle and changeable thing" <note>original Latin: "Variū & mutabile semp̄ femina," from the Aeneid</note>. And because she is faint-hearted, she rarely raises herself to great enterprises. Instead, she follows the senses more than reason; therefore, she continually seeks bodily pleasures. For this reason, she loves a man fervently while she takes pleasure from him, which consists chiefly in sight and touch. And when the pleasure fails, the love is extinguished. **The viper**: the new husband, who is of the Visconti of Milan, whose insignia is a viper, will not make for her such a beautiful tomb as the cock would have made—that is, I, the judge of the jurisdiction of Gallura, whose arms are a cock. **Of the stamp**: of righteous zeal. The form of love was imprinted on his face and almost sculpted there, which made his color burn.

**I** was continuously watching the sky. This signifies that the sensuality, now most obedient to reason, had turned all its appetite toward heavenly things. **Ever there where the stars are slowest**: that is, at the highest part of the sky, which they call the pole, as we showed above. **Where the stars are slowest**: If we had a wheel full of stars that was turning, there is no doubt that the stars placed further toward the circumference and the edge of the wheel make a wider circle than those that are closer to the axle—or let us say the handle of the wheel, which is the center—and nonetheless, they finish their revolution in the same amount of time. For this reason, those closer to the circumference turn out to be faster, and those closer to the axle are slower. Therefore, if we imagine a rod that starts from the summit of the heaven and goes through the middle of the world’s machinery to the opposite summit, and the heaven moves around the ends of this rod, the stars that are closer to these poles are slower because they make a shorter circuit in the sky; just as those in the dawn would be closer to the rod, that is, the axle. Dante was therefore looking at the highest part of the sky, that is, the Antarctic pole. And he learned from Virgil that the four stars which were in that part of the sky in the morning had already gone below; and in that same place, three had risen which were so spendid that they illuminated the entire hemisphere of Purgatory. This is a plausible fiction according to the nature of the heavens; but allegorically, according to many, by the first four stars he means the four **moral virtues** <note>Justice, Prudence, Temperance, and Fortitude</note>, and by these three he means the three **theological virtues** <note>Faith, Hope, and Charity</note>. And he feigns that the four were in the middle of the sky in the morning because in the first age and before the coming of Christ, civil men governed themselves according to them. But afterward, after the coming of Christ, the theological virtues were understood, which set all the pole here on fire—that is, the other hemisphere where Dante was and where he imagines Purgatory to be. For no one seeks to purge themselves unless they have most ardent charity, firm hope, and indubitable faith. Therefore, he saw the four in the morning because the moral virtues were in the first age. These he sees in the evening because they were not known except in this last age, when Christ showed them. Nor would it perhaps be foreign to take the four as stated, and the three for the **intellectual virtues**. For just as those make the active life, so these make the contemplative life, which is not born in a man in his early years but toward old age. Whence they write that Jacob went out into the fields toward evening, denoting by that the contemplative life.

**T**he snake came from the lower part of the valley. For valleys in the mountains are descents and have slopes on every side except from below. He rightly places the serpent to represent **temptation**, because the serpent is cunning and likewise is a very terrestrial animal. And thus temptation is full of malice and fraud.

# CANTO EIGHT

> ...licking like a beast that smooths itself.
> **I** did not see them, and therefore I cannot say
> how the celestial falconers moved,
> but I clearly saw both one and the other moved.
> Feeling the air cleft by their green wings,
> the serpent fled, and the angels turned back,
> flying up to their posts in equal measure.

...know that the snake, meaning <note>original: ".i." used for "id est"</note> diabolical temptation, often comes under the guise of virtue. And certainly, that temptation which is not shadowed by some honesty has little power. Or truly, they take the grass and flowers to mean worldly lusts and pleasures, against which men resist with difficulty. For some are irritated by bodily lusts. Some are drawn by money. Many by ambition. Petrarch meant nearly the same when he said: *And how the snake lies hidden among the flowers* <note>original: "Et chome sta fra fiori ascoso l'angue"</note>. THE EVIL streak: the evil snake, which goes streaking through the grass. TURNING its head back from time to time. It often turned like a cat or a dog, or another beast that smooths <note>original: "filisci"</note>, meaning that it licks its back, preening with its tongue; this demonstrates that temptation always adorns itself and shows itself to be pleasing and delicate so that we might accept it. I DID NOT SEE IT: by this he denotes that man does not feel when the grace of God comes into him, but he saw them moved afterward because he knows grace later by its effects. CELESTIAL FALCONERS: the angels being winged and going to strike the serpent, he not undeservedly compares them to goshawks <note>Dante uses "astori," a type of hawk used in falconry, to describe the swift, predatory grace of the angels</note>. The serpent fled, feeling the air struck by the green wings of the angels, and it fled deservedly. For when divine grace comes into us, every temptation is frightened and flees.

> **T**he shade that had drawn near the judge
> when he called out during that entire assault,
> was not for a moment released from watching me.
> "**S**o may the lamp that leads you on high
> find in your own will as much wax
> as is needed to reach the highest enamel <note>The "enamel" refers to the flowery meadow of the Earthly Paradise at the summit of Purgatory</note>,
> **H**e began, "if you have true news
> of Val di Magra or its neighboring parts,
> tell it to me, for I was once great there.
> **I** was called Currado Malaspina;
> I am not the ancient one, but descended from him;
> to my own I bore the love that is here refined."

> "**O**h," I said to him, "through your lands
> I have never been; but where does one dwell
> in all of Europe where they are not known?
> **T**he fame that honors your house
> proclaims the lords and proclaims the countryside,
> so that he who has never been there knows of it.
> **A**nd I swear to you, as I hope to go on high,
> that your honored race does not strip itself
> of the glory of the purse and of the sword.
> **C**ustom and nature so privilege it
> that, even if the wicked head twists the world,
> it alone goes straight and despises the evil path."

> **A**nd he: "Now go, for the sun shall not return to rest
> seven times in the bed that the Ram <note>The zodiac sign of Aries</note>
> covers and straddles with all four feet,
> **B**efore this courteous opinion
> shall be nailed into the middle of your head
> with better nails than the speech of others,
> **I**f the course of judgment is not halted."

<column-break/>

And it always invites us to earthly and transitory things. And for this same reason, he feigns that the serpent comes from the bottom part of the valley and the angels come from above, because preparing, illuminating, and cooperating grace are divine and celestial things, while the serpent is earthly. PERHAPS THE SAME THAT GAVE EVE THE bitter food. Many ask why he said "perhaps." But one may answer that it is hardly credible that any temptation could be similar to that which was made to the first humans, when the tempter persuaded them that they would be like gods if they tasted of that fruit. AMONG THE GRASS AND FLOWERS. In my judgment, one can take the grass and flowers for different things: that is, beautiful and virtuous operations, or desires under the appearance of virtue. And certainly, that temptation which is not shadowed by some honesty has little power. Or truly, they take the grass and flowers for worldly lusts and pleasures, against which men resist with difficulty. For some are irritated by bodily lusts. Some are drawn by money. Many by ambition. Petrarch meant nearly the same when he said: *And how the snake lies hidden among the flowers*. THE EVIL streak: the evil snake, which goes streaking through the grass. TURNING its head back from time to time. It often turned like a cat or a dog, or another beast that smooths, meaning that it licks its back, preening with its tongue; this demonstrates that temptation always adorns itself and shows itself to be pleasing and delicate so that we might accept it. I DID NOT SEE IT: by this he denotes that man does not feel when the grace of God comes into him, but he saw them moved afterward because he knows grace later by its effects. CELESTIAL FALCONERS: the angels being winged and going to strike the serpent, he not undeservedly compares them to goshawks. The serpent fled, feeling the air struck by the green wings of the angels, and it fled deservedly. For when divine grace comes into us, every temptation is frightened and flees.

**G**ives a fright, the coming of the serpent; Currado in such a way that he never turned his eyes from Dante. And by this, he demonstrates that he who is accustomed to resisting temptations for a long time does not care for them. IF THE lamp that leads you on high. If grace, that is, the enlightened intellect which guides you while contemplating even unto the first enamel: should find in your judgment, that is, in your will and choice, that you have done so much by going about speculating—so much wax, so much matter to lead you even to the first enamel, meaning the first cause, which, while remaining motionless, moves all things. And he calls the first heaven "enamel." Or perhaps better, up to the summit of this mountain, where the paradise of delights is, adorned with grass and flowers, which are like enamels. And he used a similar word in the first canticle <note>Inferno, Canto IV</note> when he mentioned the meadow of excellent men, which was almost like the Elysian fields. VAL DI MAGRA. Magra is a river which divides Tuscany from Liguria, and today that country is called Lunigiana, from Luni, a very ancient city. The Malaspinas rule there, of whom this Currado was one.

**H**e demonstrates that he had never been in Lunigiana, where the Marquises Malaspina are. But he says that the excellent fame of that family is such that it resounds through all of Europe and proclaims—that is, makes much known—the lords and the countryside, meaning the land. Whence it arises that even those who were never there know it. And I, Dante, swear to you, as I go above—meaning, so may I reach the summit of this mountain—that your people do not adorn themselves with the "purse," meaning avarice and the greed for riches, nor the "sword," meaning violence, robbery, and tyranny. Custom and nature: He demonstrates that in them is true virtue. Of which nature gives us certain seeds, which, if they are then well cultivated with good and assiduous habit, produce perfect virtue through right operation. Therefore, nature gives the best beginnings of true virtue to your family, and thereafter assiduous habit makes it perfect.

**T**he sun shall not return seven times to its bed in the Ram, meaning the sign of Aries, into which it returns every year. Therefore, he said seven years shall not pass. WITH all four feet it covers and straddles, because it is so figured. THAT this courteous opinion—that this opinion which you have of the Malaspina family, and he calls such an opinion "courteous," meaning liberal, because Dante had copiously praised this family. SHALL BE nailed in the middle of your head: as if to say, it will be confirmed in your brain. And he said very well "in the middle of the head," because the <term>cogitative faculty</term> <note>In medieval physiology, the brain was divided into "cells"; the middle cell housed the power of thought and judgment</note> has its seat distinct from the imaginative and the memory, located in the middle of the head. WITH greater nails than the speech of others: the sentence is, you have this as an opinion because you have heard it so; but the time will come when you shall know it for yourself. For having been sent into exile, Dante was most liberally received by the Marquis Marcello Malaspina, of whom we already spoke in the eighth canto of the first canticle.

<summary>Dante encounters Currado Malaspina, who prophesies that within seven years Dante will experience the legendary hospitality of the Malaspina family firsthand. The commentary explains the symbolism of the serpent of temptation and the virtues of the Malaspina lineage.</summary>
<keywords>Currado Malaspina, Lunigiana, Val di Magra, serpent of temptation, celestial falconers, divine grace, cogitative faculty, seven years prophecy</keywords>

<page-num>IX</page-num>
-># CANTO NINE<-

# CANTO NINE OF THE SECOND CANTICLE BY DANTE.

<margin>n</margin> In the present canto, after the description of the time, he relates how, having fallen asleep upon the grass, he seemed in a vision to be snatched up by an eagle to the base of Purgatory. Then, having awakened, he learned from Virgil that he had indeed been carried there. Whereupon he moved to enter Purgatory. And he describes the gate and the entrance. **The Concubine of ancient Tithonus.** The ancient historians say that from Laomedon, King of Troy, were born Priam and Tithonus. Priam remained in the kingdom. Tithonus, with a powerful army, passed into the eastern regions: and there acquired a most flourishing empire. Wherefore they say,

**The concubine of ancient Tithonus**
**already grew white on the eastern ledge**
**away from the arms of her sweet friend;**
**With gems her forehead was shining,**
**set in the figure of the cold animal**
**that with its tail strikes at people;**
**And Night had already made two of the steps with which she climbs**
**in the place where we were,**
**and day was already bending down its wings;**
**When I, who had with me that of Adam,**
**conquered by sleep, leaned upon the grass**
**there where all five of us were sitting.**

**At the hour when she begins her sad lays,**
**the little swallow near the morning,**
<note>The swallow's song is traditionally associated with the morning and the tragic myth of Philomela and Procne.</note>
**perhaps in memory of her first woes;**
**And when our pilgrim mind,**
**more from the flesh and less by thought possessed,**
**in its visions is almost divine;**
**In a dream there appeared to me, suspended,**
**an eagle in the sky with golden feathers,**
**with wings open and intended to descend.**
**And it seemed to me to be there where were**

<column-break/>

the fables that the Dawn <note>original: "Aurora"</note> was his wife: and she loved him greatly. This signifies: that the nations from which the dawn comes were subject to him: and he was loved by those people. By Dawn he fathered Memnon: who in the Trojan war came to the aid of Priam, his uncle. And he was killed by Achilles. And while, according to ancient custom, they were burning him, through the prayers of Dawn, his mother, he was changed into a bird. And many other birds came out of that fire: which were called Memnonii <note>original: "Memnonii"</note> according to Solinus. And his tomb is near Troy, and they say that continually from Ethiopia great flocks of birds fly there. Tithonus lived until extreme old age. Wherefore Propertius says: <note>original: "Cum sene non puduit talem dormire puellam. Et cane totierum oscula fere tume." translated: "She was not ashamed to sleep with an old man, such a girl, and so often to bear the kisses of a white-haired man."</note> and they say he easily turned into a grasshopper. They feign this because the old are very talkative. **The concubine of Tithonus**, that is, the dawn, whom they feign comes out of Tithonus's bed in the morning. Wherefore Virgil says: <note>original: "Titoni croceum linquens aurora cubile." translated: "Aurora, leaving the saffron bed of Tithonus."</note> **With gems her forehead was shining.** This shows that this dawn was rising in that hemisphere together with the Scorpion. This is the eighth sign of the zodiac: and is called Scorpio: although many maintain that the configuration of this animal occupies the space of two signs: and with its claws makes the sign of Libra and with the rest that of Scorpio. The fables say that because Orion the hunter had sworn not to leave any wild beast alive on earth, the Earth itself created this scorpion to kill Orion. And later he obtained from Jove that he be transferred into the zodiac. Nigidius writes that the earth did not produce it, but Diana formed it on Mount Cilippo on the island of Chios so that it would kill Orion: who, out of supreme insolence, preferred himself to her in hunting. It is configured with nineteen stars and is the domicile of Mars. And this is a new fiction: because the other poets never place the dawn except for that brightness that appears in the east before the sun. This cannot be the case here. Since the sun was in Aries, it was necessary for the dawn to rise either with that same sign or with the end of Pisces. But by placing it in Scorpio, he shows that he takes such a dawn at present for that brightness that comes before the moon; which, because it had already departed from the opposition it had made in Libra while the sun was in Aries, had already entered Scorpio. So that this may be clearly understood, we will remember that as the poet shows in the *Inferno*, the night he found himself lost in the woods, the moon was in opposition. Then the following day he spent part in fighting the beasts and part in the discourse he had with Virgil. On the second night, he descended through all of hell and passed through the center to the other hemisphere. And at the beginning of the second day, according to the precept of Cato, he girded himself with the reed: and all that light he spent in climbing the ledges of Purgatory. Now he has come to the third night, which he will spend in this valley. And on the morning of the third day, while sleeping, he will be carried by Lucia to the gate of Purgatory. But the night he spent partly reaching the center and partly from the center to the surface of Purgatory was double. For leaving at the end of the night our hemisphere where the day was already coming, it follows that in the other hemisphere he found a new night. **Of the cold animal:** this seems contrary to Virgil, who said: <note>original: "la bracchia contrahit ardens scorpius." translated: "the burning scorpion contracts its arms."</note> But Virgil had respect for the nature of Mars: the lord of this sign: which is a burning planet. And Dante to the proper nature of the sign: cold, fixed, and nocturnal. **That with its tail strikes at people.** And rightly so: because the astrologers call this sign the house of death and of fear and of toil and of loss and of contention. And just as the scorpion is an animal that stings with its tail, so the sun when it is in that sign is a cause of harm and stinging in the human body: because beginning to decline, it warms the air less. For which reason the air, distempered by the cold, soon offends and stings bodies: as Isidore writes. **And the night had made two of the steps with which she climbs.** By the steps of the night, he means the hours. Therefore, it was already two hours into the night. **In the place where we were:** which was the hemisphere over there. **Day was already bending down its wings:** meaning from that same hemisphere. **Of that of Adam:** I had a body: and as to the body we are all descended from Adam, but the soul is entirely from God.

The author, while sleeping, had already passed so much of the night that day was approaching and the dawn was beginning: at which time the swallow, when it is the season of spring, begins to sing; when there appeared to him in a vision to be on Mount Ida, which is near Troy: where the poets feign that Jove, in the form of an eagle, snatched up Ganymede. And in the sky there appeared to him to see an eagle with golden feathers, ready to swoop down to take prey. Whereupon he said to himself, perhaps the custom of this eagle is to sit in this forest: and it does not disdain to carry prey to heaven except from here. **At the hour when she begins her sad lays:** the little swallow in the time of morning: when the swallow begins. **Her lays:** her laments: and here he touches upon the fable: which is this. Pandion, King of Athens, had two daughters: one named Procne and the other Philomela. They lived in those same times. Tereus, King of Thrace: who, allied with Pandion, was courageously of no small help to him in war.

<summary>Dante describes falling asleep in the Valley of the Princes as the third night begins, introducing the myth of Tithonus and the astrological position of Scorpio. He then experiences a prophetic dream of a golden eagle, paralleling the myth of Ganymede and the tragic story of the swallow.</summary>
<keywords>Canto IX, Tithonus, Aurora, Scorpio, Ganymede, Philomela, Pandion, Dante's Dream, Astrology, Purgatory, Virgil</keywords>

<meta>Continuity: Following the previous page, Dante has fallen asleep in the Valley of the Princes. He begins to dream of a golden eagle, a vision that marks his transition toward the gate of Purgatory.</meta>

abandoned his own, by Ganymede,
when he was snatched to the high consistory:
<note>original: "sommo consistoro" – the divine assembly or council of the gods.</note>
To myself I thought: perhaps this one stays
here only by habit; and perhaps from other places
it disdains to carry one up on its feet:

<margin>149</margin>
She wove the whole story <note>The story of Philomela, who was raped by her brother-in-law Tereus and had her tongue cut out; she communicated the crime by weaving it into a tapestry.</note> and sent it to her sister. Procne, moved not so much by pity for Philomela as by a doubled hatred toward the adulterous husband who broke faith with two sisters, pretended she wished to celebrate the sacrifices of Bacchus, which were performed at night in the woods. She went where her sister was and secretly brought her into the palace. She killed Itys, the son she had by Tereus, cooked him, and served him as a meal to his father. After he had finished eating, she placed before him the head and feet of his eaten son. I will not recount how much cruelty the infuriated father prepared for the woman who had made him a sepulcher for his own flesh. But out of the compassion the gods felt, they transformed them all: Tereus became a hoopoe, a foul bird but with beautiful feathers and a crown, so that it seems he retains his former royal attire. Itys became a pheasant; Philomela a nightingale, who lives in the woods and whose tongue is not seen when she sings. Procne became a swallow, and remains red on her breast from the blood of her son with which she was stained. **AND THAT OUR PILGRIM MIND FURTHER FROM THE FLESH.** This refers to the time when the soul is more of a pilgrim—that is, further from the body—as if to say it is more untangled and free from the contagion of the body. Above, in the first canticle <note>Inferno</note>, we demonstrated through philosophical reasons why dreams at this hour are more true than at others. **IN A DREAM IT SEEMED TO ME.** The vision he creates is this: he seems to see an eagle with golden feathers suspended in the sky with open wings, which seemed to be continually wanting to swoop down. Allegorically, according to Francesco da Buti <note>A famous 14th-century commentator on Dante.</note> and several others, the eagle represents Divine Charity. Since God is charity, the eagle standing ready with open wings to swoop signifies that Divine Charity is always ready to snatch human souls toward God; and the golden feathers show the rays of charity, shining and pure like gold. Then the author adds that it seemed to him he was on Mount Ida, where Jove, in the form of an eagle, snatched Ganymede. The aforementioned Francesco understands this to mean that holy men who do penance in the forests are more easily snatched by divine charity; and by this, the author means he was prepared to purge himself like such men. I do not reject this interpretation in any way, for it is pious and suited to the Christian religion. Nevertheless, when I consider the depth of the poet’s genius, I judge that he wishes to show that while sleeping, there came to him that species of dream which the Latins call *somnium* <note>original: "somnium" – a dream that predicts true things but obscurely under a veil.</note>, which predicts true things but obscurely and under a veil, in a form that cannot be understood without an interpreter. Therefore Dante, who is the sensitive soul, dreams. And then the higher reason interprets the dream for him. For this reason, we will say that Dante falls asleep in the valley, weary from the steep journey—that is, having begun to climb toward contemplation. And becoming weary in this, human weakness (represented by Sordello, i.e., civil doctrines) is lifted from the climb and led to the civil life, where he falls asleep—that is, becomes sluggish. And God, seeing his good will, has compassion for his fragility and sends him illuminating grace, which in this dream is figured as the eagle, which snatches him to the fire, the heat of which wakes him. We understand nothing else in this fiction except that illuminating grace leads him to Seraphic love <note>The highest order of angels, associated with fire and love.</note>, from which, being set aflame, he acquires Cherubic intelligence <note>The second order of angels, associated with knowledge and judgment.</note>. And observe how covertly he imitates Virgil. It does not seem absurd to me to express this here. Both of these poets wished to show that men who give themselves to contemplation—whether weary from labor, or terrified, or dismayed by difficulty—change their purpose and return to the civil life. And perhaps they would stay there if they were not excited and lifted by divine help. Virgil signifies this in Aeneas, who, afflicted by the storm stirred by Juno and Aeolus, abandons the undertaking of going to Italy (which, as I showed in our allegories, always represents the contemplative life). He decides to go to Carthage—that is, to the active life. And there, having become the husband of Dido, he would have rested, if Jove had not sent Mercury to excite him and warn him not to abandon the first undertaking—that is, if God had not shown him through true doctrine how much Mary is to be preferred to Martha <note>A reference to the biblical sisters representing the contemplative and active lives.</note>. Similarly, at present, our poet shows that the ascent to the purgatorial virtues is so arduous that, weary, he rests and falls asleep in the valley, which we take for the civil life. But divine grace excites him and snatches him away, as you will see below. **IT SEEMED TO ME I WAS WHERE.** It seemed to Dante he was in the forest of Ida in Troy where, while Ganymede was hunting, he was snatched by Jove in the form of an eagle. And it is excellently placed in the forest—that is, in a solitary place—to denote the contemplative life, which is solitary, and which he desired, even though the hard labor of climbing had made him fall asleep. The eagle perfectly signifies illuminating grace because, just as such grace is full of light, so the eagle more than any other bird is always of the light, for it can endure the rays of the sun and mirror itself in them. No other animal can do this. Furthermore, there is no bird that rises higher or lifts itself further from the earth. And similarly, grace lifts our intellect. **ABANDONED HIS OWN, BY GANYMEDE.** And he said well that Ganymede abandoned them, and was not abandoned. For he who goes to the solitary life leaves those who remain in the active life. **WHEN HE WAS SNATCHED:** snatched to the high consistory: to the council of those who gather in heaven. **TO MYSELF I THOUGHT:** it seeming to me that I was in the place where Ganymede was snatched, I thought to myself: perhaps this eagle does not strike—that is, does not wound, as if it does not take prey—except from this place. And certainly, the mind cannot be raised to such contemplation, nor is it snatched by divine grace, unless it is in the forest of Ida—that is, in a solitary life, separated from all noise, tumult, and desire for low and earthly things. Let Ganymede be the human mind, which Jove—that is, the supreme God—loves. Let his companions be the other powers of the soul, such as the vegetative and sensitive. Jove intends that the mind be in the forest—that is, removed from mortal things—and with the aforementioned eagle, he lifts it to heaven. Whereupon the mind abandons its companions—that is, the vegetative and sensitive—and is abstracted and, as Plato says, removed from the body and having come into oblivion of corporeal things, it is entirely placed in the contemplation of the secrets of heaven. And the name of the forest also serves this allegory, because *idin* in Greek means to see and know. <note>The author refers to the Greek *idein* (ἰδεῖν), meaning 'to see'.</note>

Then it seemed to me that, having wheeled a little more,
terrible as a lightning bolt it descended,
and snatched me up as far as the fire:

<column-break/>

As soon as a man is carried away to the contemplation of the purgatorial virtues: so much does the eagle and he catch fire, that is, so much does grace catch fire in him, and he in the love of divine things: that the fire wakes him from sleep, that is, it awakens him from all laziness. NOT OTHERWISE DID ACHILLES STARTLE.
We told of Achilles in the first canticle <note>original: "prima cantica" – the Inferno.</note>. But as to this text: we will remember that Thetis his mother, fearing that he would be forced to go to the Trojan War, decided to hide him. Therefore she made him fall asleep: and thus asleep she took him from Chiron, his master: and carried him to the island of Scyros to King Lycomedes: who, in female habit and dress, kept him with his daughters: nor was he known as a man: in which time he impregnated Deidamia, one of the King's daughters. And from this was born Pyrrhus: who after his death went to Troy in his place.

He calls Virgil "his only comfort": because the rational part, illustrated by various sciences, is the only one with which we can ascend to purgation and to such speculation. Therefore Sordello—who denotes history—did not follow Dante in this ascent; nor Judge Nino—who is the knowledge of laws; nor Marquis Currado—who is conveniently taken for military discipline. But they remained in the valley: because these disciplines belong to the civil and active life. But Virgil, that is, our intellect adorned with doctrine, is the one who follows Lucia, that is, divine grace, to the purgatorial virtues.
THE SUN WAS HIGH more than two hours: because the whole of Aries, with which the sun rises, was outside the horizon. Therefore Dante could have ascended: because it was already two hours into the day. MY FACE WAS turned to the sea: This shows that by him looking at the sea, and not the mountain, he could not notice that he had ascended. By the sea we understand the appetite. DO NOT HOLD BACK but release. This signifies: do not fear, but hope. Just as our soul contracts and tightens through sorrow or fear, so through joy or hope it spreads and dilates. Lucia, who is illuminating grace, as we showed in the first canticle, snatched him to Purgatory. This signifies: she illuminated him with those things that were necessary for his salvation. And Lucia came in the dawn that precedes the day: because such grace thus brings the divine light into the mind, just as the dawn brings the daylight. And when she came, Dante's soul was sleeping: because before her arrival the soul grows lazy in the pleasures of mortal things. UPON THE FLOWERS: in the delight of earthly things, with which the valley below is adorned: with which the civil life is decorated. LET ME take this man: as if she admonishes Sordello, and Judge Nino, and Marquis Currado, that is, the occupations that are in the active life: that they should yield and allow such grace to lead the mind. SHE TOOK YOU: illuminating grace snatched away the sensuality, and the intellect followed the tracks of such grace; and this shows [the way]. This verse has no allegory: but serves the fiction made of the sleep.

He admonishes the intellect and the sensuality: that it should not fear, being illuminated by divine grace. And as soon as he sees it free from fear, and empty of every care, and full of hope: he leads it where illuminating grace showed him the entrance of Purgatory: and the sensuality follows him. MY READER, you see well: He excuses himself so that no one wonders if he, more than usual, adorns his poem with various fictions in this place: demonstrating that the height of the subject matter requires it.

From a distance it seemed to him to see a narrow crack. But approaching, he saw that it was a gate: because when at first, not yet released from the love of earthly things, we begin to consider the purgatorial virtues: the way seems very difficult and very narrow. But when afterwards we approach it, that is, we turn our mind more to it, and consider it better: we see that it is a gate, and not a crack: because it is an easy and wide way. To this gate one ascends with three steps... <note>The text ends here mid-sentence, preparing to describe the symbolic colors and materials of the three steps of Penance.</note>

And a gatekeeper who as yet spoke no word,

I saw him seated upon the highest step,
Such in his face that I did not endure it.

<note>This passage describes the Angel at the gate of Purgatory, acting as a confessor-priest.</note>

To be good in the true priest. **THE NAKED SWORD:** signifies just actions, and shows that the rays from the face of the priest struck the sword, and the sword reflected them into the faces of Virgil and Dante. Because the doctrine and good character of the priest shine in his just actions, and those reflect the rays onto the sinners. And they are an excellent example. Wherefore our sensuality cannot gaze upon such a reflection.

"Tell me from there, what do you want?"
He began to say; "Where is the escort?
Beware that coming up does not harm you."

"She told us: 'Go there, there is the gate.'"
"And may she advance your steps toward good,"
The courteous gatekeeper began again,
"Come forward then to our steps."
There we came, and the first step
Was white marble and so polished and clear
That I mirrored myself in it exactly as I appear.
The second was tinted darker than perse,
<note>Perse is a medieval color term for a very dark purple or blackish-blue.</note>
Of a rough and scorched stone,
Cracked through its length and across.
The third, which massed itself above,
Seemed to me porphyry so flaming,
As blood that spurts out from a vein.
Upon this he held both his feet,
The Lamb of God sitting upon the threshold,
Which seemed to me a stone of diamond.

<note>The three steps represent the three parts of the Sacrament of Penance: Confession, Contrition, and Satisfaction.</note>

Rare: for whatever way one exits the sin already committed. The third step was of porphyry. This stone is very hard and red in color. In this, therefore, he expresses **satisfaction**, which must be entire, and that nothing be diminished, just as porphyry does not diminish; and it must be with the fervor of charity. These three steps lead us to purgatory and to the washing away of all our filth. For just as we sin in three ways—with the heart, with the tongue, and with action—so by these same ways we must amend ourselves with contrition of heart, confession of the tongue, and satisfaction of action. The gatekeeper plants his feet upon the last step to show that confession is not enough if we stop there and do not proceed further. Nor is contrition enough, but we must not cease until we reach satisfaction. The threshold of this gate upon which the priest sits is of diamond. This stone cannot be broken or conquered. And so the priest must be whole and severe and not be corrupted. They also say that whoever carries a diamond upon them drives away fear; so whoever approaches confession does not fear demonic assaults. Furthermore, they write that the diamond, placed near a loadstone, does not let it draw iron to itself. Similarly, confession, while it is near the human soul, prevents any hardness or obstinacy from drawing it.

Through the three steps with good will
My leader drew me, saying: "Ask
Humbly that he may undo the lock."
Devoutly I threw myself at his holy feet;
I asked for mercy and that he might open to me.

<column-break/>

The steps are of different colors. And he sits upon the sovereign, that is, the highest step. This is the priest who puts us into purgatory. Therefore, he describes what the priest should be like. This man I call a gatekeeper, because to him are left the keys of the kingdom of heaven. <note>original: "Et quodcunque ligauerit in terris: erit ligatum & in celis Et quodcunque soluerit in terris: erit solutum & in celis"</note> "And whatsoever thou shalt bind on earth shall be bound in heaven; and whatsoever thou shalt loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven." This man remains in silence if another does not approach him. For the priest should not absolve those who do not ask for absolution. He sits because he must always wait for the sinner. **SUCH IN HIS FACE THAT I DID NOT ENDURE IT:** Shows that he was so radiant that Dante could not look at him. And in this, it denotes the rays of doctrine and character that should be

A man must speak it before he approaches the priest; that is, he must deliberate and will it before he goes to confession. Nor should he go without an escort, which is illuminating grace, from which we have the best inspiration, without which confession harms more than it helps. Therefore Virgil responds that they have the escort with them because a little while before Lucia had shown him the way. Seeing this, the gatekeeper replied: "And may she," that is, Lucia herself who acted as your escort, "advance your steps toward good," that is, increase your steps in goodness; because in truth no good gain can be made in confession if Lucia, illuminating us, does not inspire us. **COME THEN:** The priest must examine whoever comes to confession to see if they come by inspiration. And having recognized the good inspiration, he receives them courteously and with the utmost humanity.

One ascends to purgation by three steps. Wherefore the Psalmist says: <note>original: "Deus per gradus eius cognoſcetur."</note> "God shall be known through his steps." And Job: <note>original: "per singulos gradus meos pronuntiabo eum"</note> "At every one of my steps I will proclaim him." The first of these is of white marble, and so burnished that one can see oneself mirrored. This signifies **confession**, which must be simple, pure, and open, and not with fraud, but of a simple heart. Hence the Psalmist sings: <note>original: "Confitebor tibi domine in toto corde meo."</note> "I will confess to thee, O Lord, with my whole heart." The second is of black stone, rough, scorched, and cracked in every direction. This signifies **contrition**, and repentance, and sorrow. Wherefore the prophet Joel says: <note>original: "Scindite corda ueſtra. & non ueſtimenta."</note> "Rend your hearts, and not your garments." And it is contrition: the recognition of the sin committed with sorrow and repentance for having committed it, and the resolve not to fall back into it. And in truth, such contrition must be of a stony hardness, that is, to have an immutable purpose. It must be black—that is, full of sorrow and affliction—and rough from the torment that the soul takes from it. Similarly, scorched by the flames that burn in the conscience. And cracked in every direction, which signifies how much the mind must be torn.

Virgil drew him up with good will, that is, reason pulled up the sensuality which, already inspired by divine grace, followed willingly. And Virgil admonishes him that he should humbly ask the gatekeeper to open for him. For after the ascent of the three steps—that is, after confession, contrition, and the intent to satisfy—we must humbly ask for absolution. **I ASKED FOR MERCY.** A man cannot, through any action he performs, merit the remission of guilt, for if he merited it, he could demand justice. But because he does not merit it, he asks for mercy. PRI

# CANTO IX

<page-num>IX</page-num>

It denotes that the good and prudent confessor shows that every sinner sometimes sins in all seven mortal sins, <note>The "seven P's" carved on Dante's forehead represent the seven capital sins: Pride, Envy, Wrath, Sloth, Avarice, Gluttony, and Lust.</note> and he wrote them with the point of the sword <margin>1.</margin> with the reason of justice. Because the prudent priest, when he sees the sinner disposed to purge himself of sins, must show him that he is tainted by all of them; and therefore he writes them on his forehead and tells him that when he is inside—meaning in the place fit for purification—he should remove them all, that is, be purged of all of them.

But first upon my breast three times I struck,
Seven P's upon my forehead he inscribed
With the sword’s point, and: "See that you wash
These wounds when you are inside," he said.
Ashes or earth that is dug up dry
Of one color was his vestment,
And from beneath it he drew two keys;
One was of gold and the other of silver.
First with the white and then with the yellow
He worked the gate so that I was content.
"Whenever one of these keys fails,
So that it does not turn rightly in the lock,"
He said to us, "this passage does not open.
One is more precious, but the other requires much
Art and intellect before it unlocks,
Because it is the one that unties the knot.
From Peter I hold them, and he told me: 'Err
Rather in opening than in keeping it locked,'
Provided that the people fall at my feet."

Just as gold surpasses every metal, and always remains incorrupt and without rust, and does not become soiled even if submerged in mud, similarly this authority given to the priest is never corrupted; and though he may be a sinner, nevertheless it does not contaminate nor stain such authority. Silver is bright and shining and of a clear sound. Thus the Gospel doctrine shines through its truth and probity, and makes itself heard everywhere. Whence it is written: "Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world." <note>Original Latin: "In omnē terram exiuit sonus eoru. Et in fines orbis terre uerba eorū." (Psalm 19:4 / Romans 10:18).</note> **FIRST** with the white. Hearing the confession, there must be doctrine so that, having been absolved, all sins are recognized together with the sinner; and because many are various and manifold and entangled together, he must distinguish them and declare them to the sinner and show which is more or less grave. This he cannot do except with the knowledge of the Gospel doctrine, which is signified by the silver key. And after having performed such an examination and admonished the sinner, he must absolve him with the authority granted to him from Peter—that is, by the Apostolic See—which is signified by the golden key. Therefore, the poet’s judgment is true: that he first opens with the white—that is, with the silver one—and then with the yellow, which is gold. Because first, doctrine and prudence are necessary to know the sins and their quality and to distinguish them, and to show to the one who confesses what they entail, and afterward to absolve him. **HE MADE** the gate creak, I was content: because it opened as I desired; and he said not without prudence "so that I was content," because he wants to demonstrate how content the sinner remains, and how light and unburdened of every remorse of conscience. **WHENEVER** one. Whoever hears the confession of a sinner and lacks either the authority to absolve or the knowledge to recognize the sins, such absolution is invalid. And therefore he said: "this passage does not open," <note>Original: "Non sapre questa calla."</note> that is, this narrow entrance; and it is narrow for the reasons we have stated above. **MORE** precious is one: who doubts that the gold one is more dear and more precious than the silver one? Since man can receive no greater gift than this authority, because it is divine and not human. Nor by his own nature does man have the power to forgive injuries done to God or to one's neighbor, but it is a supernatural privilege given to the creature by the most clement liberality toward the sinner. **BUT** the other requires much art and intellect. The authority to absolve can exist, as we often see, in a man without doctrine, art (that is, prudence), and without intellect. But to know how to recognize sins and give true judgment upon them requires prudence and intellect. Therefore, the silver key has need of art and intellect, because in truth this is the one that "unties the knot," that is, distinguishes and clarifies. <note>The commentator notes a distinction between "art" and "prudence" in Latin terminology but explains they are used here synonymously for knowledge/science.</note> **FROM** Peter I hold them: This shows that no priest can have authority to absolve unless according to the form of the apostolic canons. **AND HE TOLD ME** that I should err rather in opening than in keeping it locked. This denotes here that God always mixes mercy with justice; and therefore He wills that the priest should rather err in absolving than in not absolving. Because: "God does not desire the death of the sinner, but that he be converted and live." <note>Original Latin: "non uult deus mortem peccatoris. Sed ut conuertatur & uiuat." (Ezekiel 33:11).</note> And Chrysostom says: "If God is kind, why should the priest be austere? For where the master of the house is a generous distributor, the steward ought not be stingy." <note>Original Latin: "Si deus benignus: quare sacerdos austerus. Vbi enim paterfamilias est largus dispensator: non debet esse tenax."</note> **PROVIDED** that the people fall at my feet. Humbling oneself, surrendering in guilt, and accusing oneself as a sinner is worth so much that it can pay the debt of every sin.

Then he pushed the door of the sacred gate
Saying: "Enter, but I make you aware
That he who looks back returns outside."
And when the pivots were turned...

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Decorative initial E with scrolling foliage patterns</image-desc>
**THIS** angel to whom the authority to open the gate was given was dressed in a vestment which had a blackish color, or the color of earth. This denotes the most excellent gift that our Redeemer left to man. For He not only redeemed the human race with His blood, but He also left to that part of men who are raised to the priestly order the authority of absolving and binding. Therefore, to show that the angel signified the human priest, he feigns that he had ash-colored or earth-colored clothing: that is, he had a human body, which is the clothing of the soul—as you will often find both in Plato and in the Sacred Scriptures. And because this authority is hidden within the man, he feigns that he carries the keys beneath his garments. Thus the priest, although he is in human flesh, has this authority which seems divine rather than human; which authority was also called "keys" by the one who granted it. Whence it is in the Gospel: "And I will give to you the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it." <note>Original Latin: "& tibi dabo claues regni celorum. & porte inferi non preuale bunt aduerfus eam." (Matthew 16:19).</note> Nor is it without reason that there are two keys: because a man cannot absolve if he does not have apostolic authority. Nor is this authority enough if with it there is not also true knowledge to recognize vices and discern them from virtues and distinguish them among themselves. This is why he uses the golden key for authority, of which the priest also makes mention in absolving, saying: "And I, by the apostolic authority which I exercise..." <note>Original Latin: "Et ego te auctoritate apostolica qua fungor."</note> The white one he uses for doctrine. And certainly—

But first he must show him the nature of it and also the conditions which he must have—both regarding the authority and the knowledge of distinguishing. And he also must demonstrate to him that if these things are not observed, the absolution is not [valid]...

**Which are of metal, resonant and strong.**
**Not so harshly did the Tarpeian rock roar**

<note>original: "Vade & amplius noli peccare"</note> "Go and sin no more," <note>Words spoken by Jesus to the woman caught in adultery (John 8:11), here applied to the soul entering penance.</note> which Dante suggests Christ imposed upon the woman. AND WHEN THEY WERE FIRST turned and twisted, the pivots: the great doors are not connected to hinges with straps. But instead of straps, they have certain pins. And in place of hinges, they have a hollow into which these pins enter, and upon these, the door is balanced. In such a way that it opens and closes. Therefore, he calls those pins that enter the hinges—that is, the hollow sockets—"pivots." WHICH ARE OF METAL: This shows the door to be made of metal, a most strong and incorruptible material, to signify that it cannot be broken, nor entered by force. Nor should anyone think that by forcing the priest to absolve him, such absolution would be valid. RESONANT AND Strong. He imagines that this door makes a great noise when it opens: because it never happens that a man moves from a foul life to laudable life and customs without it being spoken of and discussed everywhere. And also, he wished to signify the sentence of the Gospel, that there is more celebration in heaven for one sinner who converts than for ninety-nine righteous ones. NOT SO HARSHLY DID IT ROAR. It is very well known, especially through <note>Lucan (39–65 AD), a Roman poet who wrote the 'Pharsalia' about the civil war between Caesar and Pompey.</note> Lucan, that after the most base flight of Pompey and the Senate, Caesar occupied Rome; and he wanted all the money of the treasury—that is, of the public chamber of the community. And although Metellus, tribune of the plebs, contradicted him and forbade him to open it, nonetheless Aurelius Cotta, having cast Metellus aside, had it opened. There are some who adapt this comparison and almost all others to the allegorical sense of Dante; but to me, it seems a matter too anxious and over-detailed.

Ambrose, giving thanks to God, said, <note>original: "Te deum laudamus"</note> "We praise thee, O God"; and Augustine added, <note>original: "Te dominum confitemur"</note> "We acknowledge thee to be the Lord." And so thereafter, with alternating verses—which the Greeks call <note>original: "amabei"</note> amoebaean—they continued to compose the whole hymn. Henceforth, it has always been the observed custom in the Apostolic Church that when a desired thing is led to its proper end, this hymn is sung in thanks to God. For this reason, the poet deservedly imagines that the good spirits sang as Dante entered. Furthermore, he posits that such a hymn was sung one verse with the voice and the other with the organs. Whereby it happened that in the voice of those spirits, the words were understood. But not in the sound of the organs.

invalid. And after such words, seeing the sinner well-disposed, he ought to push the door and open it, which is to absolve him. Since, once the sinner is absolved, he can purge himself of sins, provided that upon entering the purification he does not turn back—that is, he does not return to sinning. Therefore, because the priest must admonish him, saying, <note>original: "Vade & amplius noli peccare"</note> "Go and sin no more," the author places this precept here, saying: "I make you aware"—that is, I give you notice—that whoever looks back, that is, returns to sin, turns around and exits out of this door—that is, he loses the absolution. And it seems that here the angel does not impose other penance.

Then I turned, not backward, but toward that part where I heard the singing. For if he had turned backward, he would have violated the precept given to him by the angel. <meta>The previous page concluded with the singing of the 'Te Deum Laudamus' as Dante and Virgil entered the gate of Purgatory. This page begins the commentary and text for Canto X, where they encounter the first terrace: Pride.</meta>

<header>CANTO TEN.</header>
<page-num>176</page-num>

# THE TENTH CANTO OF THE SECOND CANTICLE BY DANTE.

WE HAVE already entered inside Purgatory. And because in this place all stains are washed away and all sins are purged, it seemed sufficient to the poet to divide all human faults into the seven capital sins; for no error can be committed that does not fall under one of these seven. And it is to be noted here: the punishments of Hell are of one kind, and those of Purgatory are another. Hell gives punishment and does not remove the stain. And this is manifest regarding the dead. But it is also true in life. For whoever has made a habit of vice, even though many punishments may nourish him from those vices, nonetheless he does not escape the vice. We see the proud man run into many difficulties and suffer many dangers, and yet he does not abandon the vice. And among

<columns>2</columns>

When we were inside the threshold of the gate,
Which the souls' evil love leaves unused,
Because it makes the crooked way seem straight,
By its sounding I heard it being closed again;
And if I had turned my eyes back toward it,
What excuse would have been worthy of the fault?

<column-break/>

sins, the most grave is pride. Whence the psalmist: and I shall be cleansed from the greatest sin <note>original: "et mundabor a delicto maximo"</note>, that is, from pride; and Solomon: The beginning of all sin is pride <note>original: "Initium omnis peccati superbia"</note>. They define pride as a vicious elevation of the mind, which, despising those inferior to itself, strives to dominate equals and superiors. But the pains of Purgatory remove the stains and cleanse from every filth, both in the essential Purgatory as well as in the moral one. But so that he may return to his purpose, the poet divides this entire place into seven parts, and in each one he places the purgation of a sin. And just as when he descended into Hell, he found things lighter from place to place at first, and when

<columns>1</columns>

the further he went toward the center, the greater he found them. Because reasonably, the greater and more significant the sinners are, the further they must be from heaven. So in the site of these seven sins, he places the most grave in the first places; because in ascending, the first are always the lowest and furthest from heaven. He places pride, therefore, in the first place, the greatest of all sins, of which we will speak shortly below. Therefore, after we were inside the gate. **WHICH**. This gate [is left unused by] the evil love of souls, that is, the depraved and vicious desire for earthly and mortal things. **UNUSED**. That is, it causes it not to be frequented. And the meaning is: that excessive desire for earthly things, which souls have, is the reason this gate is not used, because being entangled and baited by those things, they do not seek to purge themselves. **BY ITS SOUNDING I heard it being closed**: Every door of any entrance, being closed, produces different effects in different places. For it neither lets those who are outside enter, nor those who are inside leave. Therefore, just as it was closed before entering to demonstrate the difficulty of entering the purgatorial virtues, so after entering it demonstrates the difficulty of leaving; because he who makes a habit of the virtues does not leave them. **AND IF I HAD TURNED MY EYES back toward it**: if I had turned backward, which signifies that, having entered into purgation, I had returned to vice, I would have found no worthy excuse for the fault. And certainly, he who is not yet set right on the true path seems to deserve more compassion than he who, being [aware], turns back. It is necessary, therefore, for him who enters the purgatorial virtues not to turn back, but to persevere. Whence in the Gospel: Not he who has begun, but he who has persevered until the end shall be saved <note>original: "Non qui inceperit. Sed qui perfeuerauerit usq; i finem saluus erit"</note>. This is prefigured in Genesis by Lot’s wife. For when the angels foretold to Lot, his wife, and his daughters that they should flee from Sodom and never turn back, his wife turned back to see the burning of Sodom and was immediately turned into a pillar of salt. She represents those who, after departing from the desire for carnal things, return to them. And she becomes a pillar of salt because she is a seasoning <note>A metaphor for wisdom or preservation.</note> and an example to others.

<columns>2</columns>

We were climbing through a cleft rock,
Which moved from one side to the other,
Like a wave that flees or approaches.
"Here it is necessary to use a little art,"
My leader began, "in staying close,
Now here, now there, to the side that recedes."
And this made our steps so scarce
That the waning moon had already
Rejoined its bed to lie down again,
Before we were out of that narrow cradle;
But when we were free and in the open,
Where the mountain gathers itself upward,
I, weary, and both of us uncertain
Of our way, stopped upon a level place,
More lonely than roads through deserts.

<column-break/>

The way was steep and was through the fissure of the rock. This cleft did not go straight, but in waves and in a "fish-bone" <note>A zigzag pattern.</note> pattern, reclining now to the right and now to the left. The reason why the steep face is mentioned has already been said in many places. He shows that this steepness is solid rock to demonstrate the hardness and asperity that is especially present at the beginning of the purgatorial virtues. The rock is cleft in such a way that it is necessary to avoid the fissure so as not to fall. And although this rock goes along its length, it nonetheless goes in waves. By the **right**, we understand prosperity and the delightful path; by the **left**, adversity and labors; and both sides must be "broken" because vices come from both sides. Nor is there anyone who commits sin except to either gain comfort or pleasure, or to flee discomfort and displeasure. Therefore, it is necessary to have a steady and invincible mind against both. Whence also the apostle Paul said: By the weapons of righteousness on the right and on the left <note>original: "Per arma iustitię a dextris & a sinistris"</note>. For this reason, it is necessary to use **art**, that is, optimal prudence, which according to the philosophers is the certain reasoning of things to be done <note>original: "Est certa ratio rerum agendarū"</note>. And in prosperity, to restrain oneself and not become proud; and in adversity, not to lose heart and not let oneself be conquered. **AND THIS MADE OUR steps scarce**. This difficulty of avoiding the fissure caused us to make our steps scarce, that is, brief and rare. And truly, one cannot make much progress on this path at the beginning, until practice begins to make it a habit. And because

<columns>1</columns>

we went slowly, the moon, which had passed its opposition and was waning, had already rejoined its bed, that is, it had returned to its setting; and it was in its setting before we had climbed this height. The moon was at its full on the night Dante found himself lost in the woods. And already the third night had passed. And this was the third day. Therefore, the moon had already approached the sun by more than one sign <note>An astronomical unit of 30 degrees.</note>, because it stays in each for two days, three hours, and two-thirds of an hour. Therefore, on this day when the moon went down, the sun was more than a sixth part of the way through the day. Thus, the sixth part of the day had passed before they had begun the purgation. This truly shows that not without a process of time can a man be made fit and ready to purge himself. Nor do we arrive at the beginning of the habit of these virtues without frequent actions. Through **THAT CRADLE** <note>original: "cuna"</note>: through that valley, which has a concavity in the form of a cradle; and he used this word to denote that these are the *incunabula*, that is, the first infancy. **BUT WHEN WE WERE FREE & open**, that is, arrived up in a spacious and open place where the mountain straightens itself and forms its summit. **I WEARY & both of us uncertain**. We can say that the flesh becomes weary, but not the soul.

The commentary uses biblical and philosophical references to explain the moral necessity of perseverance and prudence in overcoming vice.</summary>
