<meta>This page continues the commentary on the opening of Canto X of the Purgatorio, moving from the philosophical discussion of the soul's fatigue to a description of the first terrace of Purgatory—the terrace of Pride—and the wondrous carvings of humility found there.</meta>

<columns>2</columns>
<header>PURGATORY.</header>

But in investigating the sense more subtly, one wearies and tires oneself. This is because the soul does not operate without bodily instruments, which grow weary and become tired after long exercise. The intellect, however, which operates upon universal things and works without a bodily instrument, does not grow weary, as we demonstrated in our *Dialogue on the Soul* using Platonic and Aristotelian arguments. Therefore, only Dante was weary, and not Virgil. But both were uncertain. For not only sensuality and practical reason, but even speculative reason would lose the way of purgatorial virtue if divine help did not provide succor. **WE RESTED UPON A LEVEL PLAIN.** This is the first ledge of Purgatory, where the poet places those who are being purged of pride. He describes how, having climbed that divided rock as was mentioned, he found a plain at the end of which a new cliff and a new ascent began. And he shows that this plain was lonely, no different than the roads in a desert. The width of the plain, from the edge where they had climbed up to the cliff where the ascent begins again, was the measure of three human bodies—either from head to foot or by the span of outstretched arms. The lonely road demonstrates that those who purge themselves of vices are few, and especially those purging themselves of pride. And thus he says:

*From its edge where it borders the void*
*To the foot of the high bank that still rises,*
*A human body would measure three times;*
*And as far as my eye could take flight,*
*Now on the left and now on the right side,*
*This cornice appeared to me just so.*

*Up there our feet had not yet moved,*
*When I recognized that surrounding bank,*
*Which, being a sheer climb, lacked any path,*
*To be of white marble and adorned*
*With such carvings that not only Polycletus <note>A famous Greek sculptor of the 5th century BCE, renowned for his perfection of the human form.</note>*
*But Nature herself would be put to shame.*
*The Angel who came to earth with the decree*
*Of the peace wept for through many years,*
*Which opened heaven from its long prohibition,*
*Appeared before us so truly there,*
*Carved in a gentle pose,*
*That it did not seem a silent image.*
*One would have sworn he was saying "Ave," <note>original: "aue" (Hail). The greeting of the Angel Gabriel to Mary.</note>*
*For she was also imaged there,*
*Who turned the key to open the Supreme Love;*
*And she had in her gesture this speech impressed:*
*"Behold the handmaid of the Lord," <note>original: "ecce ancilla dei". Mary's humble acceptance of God's will.</note> as clearly*
*As a figure is stamped into wax.*

<column-break/>

**IT WAS THE WIDTH** that we have shown in this level plain, which circled around the mountain in the form of a cornice. Therefore, he adds that looking to the right and to the left, as far as his sight could reach, this plain in the form of a cornice appeared "just so," meaning it appeared similar in width. Here we must understand that he imagines seven ledges around this mountain, one above the other with a certain interval; and the higher one will always have a smaller circumference because the higher the mountain goes, the more it tapers. In this first ledge, because it is lower and more remote from heaven, the greatest sin is punished, which is pride. And so following in order, the more serious sins are always punished in the lower parts. Thus, in the second, he purges envy in Canto XIII. In the third, sloth in Canto XV. In the fourth, wrath in Canto XVII. In the fifth, avarice in Canto XIX. In the sixth, gluttony in Canto XXII. And above this, he places the summit of the mountain, and upon it, the paradise of delights. But returning: he shows this level ground of the cornice where pride is purged to be wide enough for a human body to stretch out three times, to demonstrate that pride in man is found in thought, speech, and deed. Or alternatively, we use it against superiors, against equals, and against inferiors.

**OUR FEET HAD NOT YET MOVED UP THERE;** that is, we had not yet begun to walk along the plain already mentioned, when I realized that the bank—which at the end of the plain is so steep and straight in the form of a wall that one could not climb it—was all of solid white marble. And in it were sculpted and carved various histories, which serve as examples of humility. The poet places these images of humility in the place where pride is purged, and rightly so. For every contrary is purged by its opposite. Just as we see that "hot" diseases require "cold" medicines, and cold ones require hot. Thus pride is purged and extinguished with humility. Note that these examples are carved and not painted. Because a painting is easily removed, but a carving is not. And they are carved not in soft material, but in hard. This warns us that if we wish to entirely drive pride from us, it is necessary to have humility carved and entirely fixed in our minds. Furthermore, he uses white marble to denote that such humility must be pure and clean, and not spotted with any fiction or simulation. And just as the color white is bright and shining, so should this humility shine. For: "nothing is more proud than a feigned humility" <note>original: "nihil est ficta humilitate supbius"</note>. Furthermore, he shows that such images are so lifelike that not only Polycletus or any other excellent sculptor, but even Nature could not make them more lifelike. This signifies nothing else than that such humility must be in its own true image, in such a form that neither human wit nor natural movement could make it more authentic. Polycletus was the son of Ageladas and from the city of Sicyon, a sculptor much celebrated among the ancients, especially for a statue they call the *Diadumenos*, valued at a hundred talents. He had a name suited to himself, for "Polycletus" in Greek signifies "a man of much fame." <note>Polys (much) + Kleitos (famed).</note> **BUT NATURE WOULD BE PUT TO SHAME;** she would remain defeated. We properly say someone receives "shame" (*scorno*) when they presume or trust they have the advantage, and then the opposite happens. One can also call *scorno* "dishonor." For just as we say a man "puts out his horns" when he exalts himself for a victory or for having achieved what he desired, so by opposition we say he is "de-horned" (*scornato*). **THE ANGEL GABRIEL,** who came to earth to announce to Mary. **WITH THE DECREE;** with the determination made by the omnipotent, triune, and unique God, that Mary should conceive by the power of the Holy Spirit the Eternal Word, who was to redeem the human race. This incarnation was performed by Jesus our Redeemer and mediator between God and man, and he reconciled us with God so that we regained peace. This peace had been "wept for through many years," that is, desired with tears by the holy fathers. And while they were in life, and afterward while suspended in Limbo, they waited to be freed by the passion of God. This redemption "opened the long prohibition," that is, opened the way to the human generation to whom it had been forbidden for so long. For from the sin of Adam until the descent of Christ into Limbo, five thousand two hundred and thirty-two years passed. **APPEARED BEFORE US SO TRULY.** It is great praise for the sculpture that, being before it, it seemed to be nothing other than a real image.

<columns>2</columns>
<header>CANTO TEN.</header>
<sig>ee ii</sig>

...mute and inanimate. Nevertheless, she appeared to speak with the utmost sweetness. And therefore he says, **IT DID NOT SEEM**—that is, it did not resemble—an **IMAGE** that is silent, but an image that speaks. And this occurred because both the image of the angel appeared to be speaking, and next to it was the image of Mary, such that anyone would have sworn the angel was saying "Hail" <note>original: "aue"</note> as he did when he announced the news to her. **BECAUSE THERE**, because there **THAT ONE WAS IMAGINED**, that is, the image of Mary, **WHO TURNED THE KEYS TO OPEN THE LOFTY LOVE.** She who turned the keys to open the high love of God, which our sin had locked away from us; for the holiness and humility of Mary was the key that opened divine love to us. And just as the image of the angel was carved so skillfully that it seemed to say "Hail," so that of Mary seemed to consent to the divine command and, out of the highest humility, say, "Behold the handmaid of the Lord." <note>original: "Ecce ancilla dei"</note> He places here, therefore, the image of Mary as a singular and primary example of humility. Of her, as the historian of Carthage <note>Refers to Sallust, though the sentiment is a common classical trope regarding subjects so great they are better left unsaid than undersaid.</note> said, it is better to be silent than to say too little.

---

"Do not keep your mind on one place alone,"
Said the sweet master, who had me
on that side where people have their hearts;
Wherefore I moved, and with my eyes I saw
behind Mary, along that same bank
where he who moved me was positioned,
Another history set into the rock.
Wherefore I stepped past Virgil and drew near,
so that it might be laid out before my eyes.
There, carved into the very marble, was
the cart and oxen drawing the holy ark,
because of which one fears an office not assigned.
In front appeared people, and the whole crowd,
divided into seven choirs, made two of my senses
say, one "no," the other "yes, they sing."
Similarly, the smoke of the incense
which was imagined there made the eyes and nose
at "yes" and "no" discordant in their senses.
There, preceding the blessed vessel,
dancing with robes girt up was the humble psalmist,
and in that case, he was both more and less than a king.
Opposite, depicted at a window
of a great palace, Michal watched him,
like a woman full of scorn and sadness.

<column-break/>

**H**aving set down the example of Mary's humility, he now places that of King David. Nor should we overlook in this place the admirable genius and absolute learning of the poet. He knew that man uses pride in three ways: either toward a superior, or toward an equal, or toward an inferior. Therefore, to these three types of pride, he judged it necessary to oppose three types of humility. Accordingly, as an example of humility toward a superior, he placed Mary. Toward equals, David. Toward inferiors, Trajan. Mary was humble toward God. David practiced humility with the priests, playing the lyre and dancing with them before the Ark; this humility was toward his equals. Trajan humbled himself before the widow, who was much inferior to him. But so that David’s humility may be known to us: it is in the second book of Kings <note>Now known as 2 Samuel in modern Bibles.</note> that after the death of the very proud King Saul, David was elected in his place. He gathered all the elect of Israel to transfer the Ark of the Lord with great pomp to his city, Zion. <note>original: "Gyon"</note> The Ark was in Gibeah, in the house of Abinadab, the son of Saul. He placed it upon a new cart and accompanied it with a great celebration of sounds. Uzza <note>original: "Oza"</note> and Ahio, sons of Abinadab, guided the cart. And when the oxen of the cart stumbled on the road and kicked, causing the cart to move clumsily, Uzza went to help the Ark, which was wobbling, and stretched out his hand so that it would not fall. For this, God was angered and struck him, and he died. David, terrified by the event, left the Ark along the way in the house of Obed-edom. Three months later, having heard that God had blessed that house, David conducted the Ark with seven choirs and many victims to his own house, always singing and dancing around the Ark. But Michal, the daughter of the proud King Saul and not unlike her father, despised the humility of David her husband, and coming out to meet him, she said: "O how glorious you were today, stripping yourself in the sight of your servants' handmaids as if you were a scoundrel or a buffoon!" To which David responded that he would always do the same in the sight of God, who had chosen him and rejected Saul. In this Ark were the laws given by God through Moses, and the rod of Moses with which he overcame Pharaoh, and a vessel of the manna that rained in the desert. Regarding the construction of the Ark, we shall speak in the twentieth canto of the third canticle. **DO NOT**

---

**KEEP YOUR MIND ON ONE PLACE ALONE.** It is as if he says: having seen this story, consider the others as well. And he silently admonishes us that we should not desire only one species of humility, but all of them. **WHO HAD ME ON THAT SIDE WHERE PEOPLE HAVE THEIR HEART,** that is, he had me on the left side. And it was reasonable that the intellect should be in a more honored place than the sense. The heart. **BECAUSE OF WHICH ONE FEARS AN OFFICE NOT ASSIGNED.** Because Uzza's temerity was punished when he touched the Ark, which was not entrusted to him. From this, it is noted that even if the act is pious and the will is direct, a profane person must not touch sacred things. They say, nevertheless, that such a death purged Uzza's sin and that he, being saved, went to Abraham's bosom. **I STEPPED PAST** <note>original: "VALCHAI"</note>: I stepped past and went ahead of Virgil to see; and deservedly so, to denote that the senses cannot perceive a sensible object unless it is within a certain distance, and they have no cognition except of particulars. But the intellect sees universals from any long distance. **THERE CARVED INTO THE VERY MARBLE**: in the same marble. **THE CART AND OXEN DRAWING THE HOLY ARK**, as we have said. **IN FRONT OF THE ARK APPEARED PEOPLE**: they were images that looked like living people. And all of these were divided into seven choirs. And they were portrayed so naturally that between two senses—namely, sight and hearing—the eye judged by their gestures that they were singing. But the ear, which heard no voice, judged that they were not. **ONE MADE**, that is, the ear made one say no, he does not sing, because it did not hear. **THE OTHER**, which is the eye, said yes, he sings. In short, the priests were carved with such gestures that nothing was missing except a voice to say they were singing. **SIMILARLY THE SMOKE OF THE INCENSE**: just as discord arose between seeing and hearing regarding those who appeared to be singing, so too—because the censers were sculpted in a form from which smoke seemed to rise—a contention arose between seeing and smelling, because to the eyes it seemed they saw it, but the nose did not perceive the odor. **THERE PRECEDING.** The text orders it thus: the humble psalmist, namely David, with much humility and as a psalmist because he composed the psalms; in that carved history, **PRECEDED** the blessed vessel, went before the blessed vessel, the divine Ark, together with the priests, **DANCING WITH ROBES GIRT UP**, that is, dancing with his lyre, and "girt up" or appearing so to be more unencumbered. **AND BOTH MORE AND LESS THAN A KING**: more than a king because he held the office of the priesthood, and less because out of humility he had set aside his royal attire. **OPPOSITE.** It follows: Michal depicted, that is, sculpted, opposite—meaning across from David—**AT A WINDOW** of a great palace **WATCHED HIM**, looked at him, **LIKE A WOMAN FULL OF SCORN AND SADNESS**, that is, one who held him in contempt because he had stooped to such humility, and because in that procession he did not wear royal finery. And he rightly said "like a woman," because woman is naturally very boastful. Michal was the daughter of Saul and the wife of David.

<summary>This page explains the second example of humility on the First Terrace of Purgatory: King David dancing before the Ark of the Covenant, contrasted with the pride of his wife Michal.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the exploration of the first terrace of Purgatory, where the vice of Pride is purged. Having viewed the Annunciation and King David dancing before the Ark, Dante now moves his gaze to the final example of humility carved into the white marble: the Roman Emperor Trajan and the widow.</meta>

<columns>2</columns>
<header>PURGATORIO</header>

I moved my feet from the place where I stood
to observe from closer by another history
which shone white behind Michal:
<note>Michal was the daughter of Saul and wife of David; she was mentioned in the previous lines for mocking David's humble dancing.</note>
Here was storied the lofty glory
of the Roman prince whose great worth
moved Gregory to his great victory:
<note>Pope Gregory the Great, who according to legend was so moved by Trajan's justice that he prayed for the Emperor's soul to be released from Hell.</note>
I speak of Trajan the Emperor;
and a poor widow was at his bridle,
depicted in tears and in sorrow.
Around him appeared a dense and crowded
throng of knights, and the golden eagles
above him seemed to move in the wind.

The poor woman among all these
seemed to say: "Lord, do me justice
for my son who is dead, for which I am heartbroken."
And he seemed to answer her: "Now wait
until I return." And she, "My Lord,"
as a person in whom grief hastens,
"If you do not return?" And he: "The one who
will be in my place will do it." And she: "What is another’s
good to you, if you put your own duty in oblivion?"
Wherefore he: "Now be comforted, for it is necessary
that I fulfill my duty before I move;
justice wills it, and pity holds me back."
He who never saw any new thing
<note>Refers to God, to whom nothing is "new" because He is outside of time.</note>
produced this visible speech,
novel to us because it is not found here.

<term>Visible speech</term><note>original: "uisibile parlare"</note> It is called "visible speech" because a statue is sculpted with such art that in its gestures it demonstrates what it would say if it spoke. It is, therefore, visible speech because by seeing the gestures and not hearing the voice, they understood. But this speech, which is not new to God, as has been said, is new to us mortals because among us it is not found. And by a figure of speech, he touches here upon that which will happen to us in heaven: for one will see the concept of the other without hearing the sound of the tongue.

While I delighted myself in looking
at the images of such great humilities,
and for the sake of their Maker, dear to behold,
"Look, here come many people, but they make few steps,"
murmured the Poet;
"these will lead us to the high stairs."
My eyes, which were content to gaze
to see novelties for which they are eager,
were not slow in turning toward them.
I do not wish, however, reader, that you be dismayed
from your good purpose by hearing
how God wills that the debt be paid.
Do not attend to the form of the martyrdom;
think of what follows; think that at the worst,
it cannot go beyond the Great Judgment.

<column-break/>

Trajan was an emperor of such excellence that it is difficult to judge whether he was more eminent in military discipline or in justice and humanity. This man greatly increased the Roman Empire, which by the emperors who came after Augustus and before him had been defended more than expanded. He possessed such humanity that in Rome and throughout the provinces, everyone wished him to be their equal. He was clement and liberal, and greatly lightened the people's burden of taxes. He visited his friends as a private citizen and not as an emperor. He succeeded Nerva in the one-hundredth year of our salvation. He triumphed over the Dacians and the Scythians. And having removed Decebalus, King of Dacia, he reduced it to a province—that is, he had it governed by Roman magistrates. To him surrendered the Iberians, Sarmatians, Arabs, Bosphorans, and Colchians. He occupied Seleucia and Babylonia. And in the Red Sea, he prepared a great fleet to go to India. This man persecuted the Christians, but was advised by Pliny the Younger <note>original: "Plinio fecondo"</note>, who was a magistrate, that except for the fact that they would not perform sacrifices in the manner of the Gentiles, they were of the best life and customs. He wrote back that such men should not be sought out, but if they fell by chance into his hands, they should be killed. He also reduced Armenia, Assyria, and Mesopotamia to provinces. He died in Selinus—others write in Seleucia—in the sixty-third year of his life, plus nine months and four days. His ashes, gathered in a golden vessel, were carried to Rome and placed in the Forum under the Column. Helinandus the Frenchman and Polycrates the Englishman write specifically of Trajan that while he was wishing to go with his army, a poor widow threw herself at his feet, asking for justice and satisfaction for a son of hers who had been killed. And the words of her petition and of Trajan were those that the poet recites here. **THE WHOLE GREAT WORTH MOVED** Gregory to his great victory: They say that the virtues of Trajan moved Pope Gregory in a way that he prayed so much for him that it was revealed to him that Trajan was liberated from the pains of Hell. **HE WHO NEVER** saw a new thing: God is eternal and from eternity had in his mind the exemplar of all things; therefore, no thing was ever new to Him. **PRODVSSE ESTO** Visible speech. 

Dante was attentive to these examples of humility because it is fitting that the senses do so when they wish to follow reason; and he delighted in looking. This signifies that the sense was so obedient to reason that it already delighted in virtue and did not perform its operations with difficulty. And he delighted in those images for the love of the **Maker**—that is, the Master who had made them. As far as the history is concerned, this signifies that the skill and authority of the artist moved him to look at them, as we see in ourselves. For if we look at a painting and hear that it is by the hand of Giotto, the authority of the man has great power over us. And allegorically it demonstrates that he looked at the examples of humility for the love of the Master—that is, for the love of God, who said: "Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart." <note>original: "Discite a me: quia mitis sum & humils corde."</note> **LOOK, HERE.** Virgil shows him the proud and the punishment with which they are purged. For they came carrying stones of such great weight upon their heads that they all buckled under them. This punishment is fitting for the proud. For since a vice is purged by its opposite, it is right that the proud, who go about elated and with heads held high, should be constrained to go about depressed and bowed down. And because the nature of the proud is to not want to endure any weight or any trouble, the fitting punishment is that they be oppressed by great weights and humbled. Wherefore it is said: "He who exalts himself shall be humbled." <note>original: "Qui se exaltat humiliabitur."</note> And truly divine justice wills it, and men strive with every industry to oppress and trample those who are elated and proud. This is done in private; this is done in public, especially where one lives morally. Therefore, in praise of the Romans, Virgil said: "To spare the conquered and battle the proud." <note>original: "Parcere subiectis & debellare superbos."</note> **THE POET MURMURED.** Poets and other writers write of the proud, but they do not speak of them with a clear and high voice—that is, they do not praise them, but they murmur—that is, they vituperate them. **MANY PEOPLE.** To demonstrate that the multitude of the proud is very great. Furthermore, he said "many people" as if he wished to say a base crowd, because the more...

<columns>2</columns>
<header>PURGATORIO</header>
<sig>ee iiii</sig>

They exalt the proud: the greater the indignation we conceive toward them, the more we strive to debase them and the more we despise them. THESE will lead us: these will show us the way TO THE high steps: to the ascent of the second terrace. MY EYES. There is innate <gloss>born</gloss> in men a great desire to understand new things. And for that reason our eyes are wandering—that is, vagabond—and often turn in every direction to see. Wherefore I say: And my eyes, which were content to gaze—that is, they took pleasure in gazing to see novelties, which are new things. Wherefore—that is, because of this desire—THEY ARE wandering: vagabond and fickle. I DO NOT WISH, HOWEVER, READER: an excellent admonition, and not only appropriate but almost necessary. For in comforting men toward their purgation, and fearing they might be terrified by such harsh punishments as are shown to be given to the proud—since we often see many have a good will to give themselves to the purgative virtues, but because it is a harsh and difficult thing, they are discouraged. To comfort them, then, he makes this digression, saying: O reader, I do not wish, however, that you be dismayed—that is, that you be moved or changed from your good purpose—even though you hear from me how grave the punishment is with which God wills that the proud man pay his debt—that is, satisfy for his error. And for comfort he says: do not attend—that is, do not think—upon the form and quality of the martyrdom and the pains, but in compensation for that, consider two things. First, the succession—that is, what must happen to you—and this is that you will be purged, and once purged, you will acquire eternal life. The second is that such pains will not be eternal like those of Hell, but at the worst they can endure, it will not be beyond the sentence—that is, the Day of Judgment.

---

<margin>
"I"—that is, reason—"hardly recognized them." This is an excellent fiction by which he shows the purgation of the proud. For he who went with his head held high, it is right that he should bow it just as much in the opposite direction. Because, as Aristotle writes, to straighten a bent piece of wood, it is not enough to bring it back to its straightness, but one must bend it just as much into the opposite side. And it is a stone, an earthly thing, which denotes that God prostrates and casts down whoever exalts himself too much; because: *He has put down the mighty from their seats and exalted the humble.* <note>original: "Deposuit potentes de sede: & exaltauit humiles" — from the Magnificat, Luke 1:52</note> And pride is symbolized in the stone by Goliath, whom David killed with three stones. Furthermore, the Psalmist speaks thus of the proud: *He shall crush the heads in the land of many.* <note>original: "Conquassabit capita in terra multorum" — Psalm 110:6</note> And elsewhere: *Because you cast them down.* <note>original: "Quoniam pones eos deorsum" — Psalm 73:18</note> *In your remnants you will prepare their face.* And Isaiah: *The crown of pride shall be trodden under feet.* <note>original: "Pedibus conculcabitur corona superbie" — Isaiah 28:3</note>
</margin>

> I began: "Master, what I see
> moving toward us do not seem like people,
> and I know not what, so much do I falter in my seeing."
> And he to me: "The heavy condition
> of their torment crouches them to the ground,
> so that my eyes at first had a struggle with them.
> But look fixedly there, and disentangle
> with your sight what comes beneath those stones;
> already you can discern how each one beats himself."

<column-break/>

Because these who were coming were so crouched under weights, they were so transfigured that they were not recognized. And certainly pride makes a man so bestial that he no longer appears to be a man, but a cruel beast. For it is proper to man to be affable, tractable, loving, and gracious toward other men. And therefore this virtue, as it is proper and fitting to human nature, is called humanity. Therefore, he who strips himself of such virtue and clothes himself in the vice of pride, which is contrary to it, no longer seems like a man. And although he retains the image and form of a man, nevertheless in his customs he is a most cruel beast. We can also refer this to the truth of the proud man: for when he falls from a high rank, he can have no patience there. Or we shall say that when the proud man humbles himself, he in no way appears as he appeared in his pride. It is difficult, then, for Dante—that is, for lower reason—to recognize human nature in such ferocity. Given that even Virgil...

---

<margin>
It follows that he who performs vicious deeds makes "backward steps"—that is, steps in reverse—because he distances himself from God. What, then, is a greater misery and greater blindness of mind than to place trust in those things that distance us from our salvation and from the Supreme Good? "Do you not perceive that we are worms?" There are many worms, and especially the silkworms <term>bigatti</term> <note>The commentator uses the local term for silkworms to explain the biological metaphor of transformation.</note> that make silk, which, although they are very imperfect animals, nevertheless conceive within themselves a butterfly, which emerges when the worm casing bursts and flies away. Thus man is born as if a most base worm. Wherefore the Psalmist says: *But I am a worm and no man; a reproach of men, and the outcast of the people.* <note>original: "Ego autem sum uermis & non homo: obprobrium hominiũ & abiectio plebis" — Psalm 22:6</note> But just as we are worms, we are fit to form the butterfly like the silkworm. This is the immortal soul within us, which, if we govern it rightly and direct it toward the life of virtue, once our body has "burst"—that is, been dissolved by death—the soul, like a butterfly, flies out to heaven. But if it emerges filthy with vices, it is often weighed down by them and made to fall into hell. And he said "butterfly" rather than any other flying thing because, having said "worm" according to the Holy Scripture, and the butterfly being born from the worm, he stayed within that metaphor. BORN TO FORM. It is not man who forms—that is, creates—the soul, but God creates it from nothing, and in creating it, He infuses it. But because it comes into the body without knowledge of anything, but is apt to learn, he therefore says that man is born to form the soul, because nature has produced him so that he may instruct and teach his soul. ANGELIC: because our soul, although there is some difference, is nevertheless a rational essence like an angel. Wherefore the Psalmist: *You have made him a little lower than the angels.* <note>original: "Minuisti eũ paulominus ab angelis" — Psalm 8:5</note> He calls it "angelic" also because it was created by God to fill the seats of the angels who fell from heaven. WHICH FLIES TO JUSTICE...
</margin>

> O proud Christians, wretched and weary,
> so infirm in your sight and in your mind,
> who have confidence in backward steps!
> Do you not perceive that we are worms,
> born to form the angelic butterfly
> that flies to justice without defense?
> Why does your soul float so high,
> since you are like defective insects,
> even as a worm in which formation fails?

<column-break/>

He uses a bitter exclamation against proud Christians, who truly are wretched, having lost divine grace through sin. And they are weary—that is, "lapsed" and fallen from it—because this is what the word *lapsus* <note>original: "lapso"</note> implies in the Latin language; or we shall say not "lapsed" but "weary" <note>original: "lassi"</note>, and then it means exhausted. INFIRM in sight and in mind: sight belongs to the bodily eye and to the intellect. Here he means infirm in sight—that is, in the sharpness and subtlety of the intellect—as if to say: you are of blind intellect because you do not recognize the true good; and you are infirm in mind—that is, in the will—because you do not want it. Therefore, you are truly wretched, since you neither recognize the good nor want it. And from this it arises that you have confidence in "backward steps"—that is, in vicious deeds. *Retrosici* in Latin means backwards. And because he who proceeds in virtuous deeds goes forward and draws near to God, who is his supreme Good...

<columns>2</columns>
<header>CANTO</header>

...without shield: <note>original: "senza scherm"</note> without defenses. Because once the soul has departed from the body, it goes to judgment without any defense at all. HE SAYS: **Does our soul float on high?** <note>Dante’s verse: "quai l'anima nostra in alto galla"</note> meaning: for what reason do you exalt yourselves? It is as if he says: man is not such an excellent thing without the grace of God that he should become proud or glory in himself. Wherefore Paul says: *You are like insects in defect.* <note>The commentator attributes a variation of Dante's "entomata" (insects) imagery to St. Paul to emphasize human frailty.</note> He returns to what he said above and concludes: that we are imperfect, like worms, if we are without virtue and without divine grace. For just as the worm is imperfect because it is not formed to its completion, so man—who is created to serve God, his supreme good—is imperfect if he is deprived of the virtues through which he can be united with God. Wherefore Saint Augustine says: *You have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you.* <note>original: "Fecisti nos ad te: & inquietum est cor nostrum donec requiescamus in te"</note> **Entomata** in Greek and **insecta** in Latin are all "worms" [insects] that do not have all their members distinct, such as bees, ants, and the like.

Just as to support a ceiling or roof,
as a corbel <term>mensola: an architectural bracket, often carved, supporting a weight</term> sometimes a figure <gloss>r</gloss>
is seen bringing its knees to its chest,
Which makes from the unreal, real distress
arise in those who see them made thus;
so did I see those people when I looked carefully.
True it is that they were more or less contracted
according to how much they had more or less upon them;
and the one who had the most patience in his actions,
weeping, seemed to say: "I can do no more."

<column-break/>

AND THE great weights which these souls were carrying made them bend and huddle so much that their chests touched their knees. Therefore they appeared just like certain wooden corbels that are placed in a wall under the beams of roofs or ceilings—or rather floors—which are often carved in the form of a man supporting the beam; and because of the great weight, the figure is made to bend and huddle and almost lean its chest upon its knees. And although such a figure does not actually suffer fatigue—because it is made of wood and is not a man—nevertheless, **it makes from the unreal, real distress**; that is, although it is not true that such a weight burdens or harms the carving, it nonetheless generates in the viewer a "real distress," meaning a true feeling of sorrow or pity. **TRUE IT IS THAT THEY WERE more and less contracted.** Although they were all under heavy weights, yet one soul had a weight less heavy than another, according to whether they had sinned less or more in the sin of pride.

Judgment without parried defenses. Because, having left the body, it goes to judgment without any defense. Our (spirit) proudly exalts itself: of what do you exalt yourselves? As if to say: man is not so excellent as to become proud or glorify himself. Hence Paul: "You are like insects in defect." <meta>The previous page concluded with a discussion of human frailty and the description of the souls of the proud in Purgatory, stooped like corbels under heavy weights. This page transitions into the eleventh Canto, where these souls recite a paraphrased version of the Lord's Prayer.</meta>

<page-num>XI</page-num>
<header>CANTO XI</header>

### ELEVENTH CANTO OF THE SECOND CANTICLE BY DANTE.

In the previous chapter, the poet already described the place where the proud are purged and showed what form of punishment they suffer. At the end, he added that many were coming toward him. Now, in this chapter, he describes how they came praying, and their prayer was the one that the Word of Truth <note>Jesus Christ</note> taught to the apostles, saying: "When you pray, it is enough to say: Our Father, who art in heaven" <note>original Latin: "Cum oraueritis sufficit dicere. Pater noster qui es in celis."</note>. Although this prayer is suitable for everyone, it is nonetheless very appropriate for those who wish to leave pride behind. This is because the root of pride is not recognizing one's own good as coming from God, but instead attributing everything to one's own strengths. Furthermore, the proud man does not value his neighbor nor consider him worthy. Therefore, through this Lord's Prayer, he confesses his error: first by

> Our Father, who dwellest in the heavens,
> not circumscribed, but through the greater love
> Thou hast for Thy first effects on high,
> Praised be Thy name and Thy worth
> by every creature, as it is right
> to give thanks to Thy exalted effluence.
> May the peace of Thy kingdom come to us,
> for we cannot reach it by ourselves,
> despite all our wit, if it comes not of itself.
> As Thy angels make a sacrifice to Thee
> of their own will, singing Hosanna,
> so may men do with theirs.
> Give us this day our daily manna,
> without which, through this bitter desert,
> he goes backward who labors most to advance.
> And as we forgive everyone the harm
> we have suffered, so do Thou forgive us
> in Thy kindness, and look not on our merit.
> Our strength, which is easily subdued,
> put not to the proof with the ancient adversary,
> but deliver us from him who goads it so.

<column-break/>

confessing God's power, and then by demonstrating that without His help, he can do nothing. And toward his neighbor, he humbles himself by asking God for the remission of his debts, just as he grants it to those who have offended him. Finally, just as in pride his hope was that he could resist the enemy by his own power, so the humble man asks God not to lead him into temptation, where he confesses his own imbecility and fragility as insufficient to resist. The poet, therefore, introduces these souls making this prayer. He does not provide it in Latin, but translates it into the Florentine language, adding several words which neither change, nor increase, nor diminish the meaning, but rather open and clarify it.

And because the prayer says "Our Father who art in heaven," someone might doubt whether God is in heaven such that while He is there, He cannot be elsewhere. To clarify this doubt, the poet adds that God does not stay in the heavens "circumscribed"—that is, contained by the heavens. For example, while a man or another physical thing is in a place, that place circumscribes and surrounds and terminates and contains it within itself, such that until he leaves, he cannot be elsewhere nor go beyond those limits. But God is not contained by place, nor circumscribed by it. Because God is infinite and the heavens are finite, a thing that has an end and limit cannot contain that which has neither end nor limit. The finite is, without comparison, smaller than the infinite, and the smaller thing cannot contain the larger within itself. Therefore, God is not contained by the heavens. But He is said to dwell in the heavens because He has "greater love" for the heavens, because the heavens and the angels are the "first effects" which He, the First Cause, produced; and these are then the "second causes" for the inferior effects. For every superior thing is the cause of the movement of its inferior, as we shall declare more expressly elsewhere. Up to here, he has said: "Our Father who art in heaven," which are the words that form the preamble of this prayer.

Now he comes to the petitions, which are seven. The first is "Hallowed be Thy name" <note>original Latin: "sanctificetur nomen tuum"</note>. Wherefore he says: PRAISED be Thy name and Thy worth. In the first petition, he asks for the honor

<column-break/>

of the Father, which signifies love with obedience and veneration toward the Father. And if it should seem superfluous to say "hallowed be Thy name" because one cannot hallow Him who is the Saint of Saints, we will say "hallowed" means "strengthened," for "holy" signifies "firm." *Worth* <note>Italian: "Valore"</note> means virtue or power. *Effluence* <note>Italian: "Vapore"</note> means grace. BY every creature: whatever is produced by God, the First Cause and Creator, is called a creature. But these are divided into six species. Some have only being, like stones. Some have a vegetative soul, through which they nourish themselves, grow, and produce seed to generate their like, such as herbs, trees, and every other plant. Some, besides the vegetative, have some sense but no local motion, such as shellfish stuck to a rock. Some have more perfect sense and local motion, such as all the brute animals. Some, besides the vegetative, sensitive, and motive faculties, have reason, such as man. But above man is the angel, of whom we shall speak elsewhere. Every creature praises its creator as much as is within itself; that is, God, in whom the poet, wishing to express the Trinity, placed three names: "name" for fame and wisdom, expressing the Son; "worth" for power, for the Father; and "effluence" <note>literally "vapor"</note> for heat, for the Holy Spirit. And this is the first request we must make: that every creature recognize its creator.

MAY the peace of Thy kingdom come to us. "Thy kingdom come" <note>original Latin: "Adueniat regnum tuum"</note> is the second request. For saying "Thy kingdom come" is nothing other than asking for the peace of eternal life, which is different from that of this world. And having rightly praised the Father, we ask for the paternal inheritance which He left us in His final testament when He said, "My peace I leave with you." FOR we cannot reach it by ourselves: Man cannot acquire such tranquility with all his wit, because by himself he cannot have true knowledge of God, in which the soul rests. IF IT comes not to us: if it is not infused into us by divine grace. AS of Thy will: This is the third petition, which is "Thy will be done" <note>original Latin: "Fiat uoluntas tua"</note>. Thus, just as Your angels—who remained equal after the ruin of those who rebelled against God—were confirmed in grace despite remaining in their free will. Therefore, the angels make a sacrifice: that is, they offer to Thee their will, dedicating all their desire to Thee. This passage is explained in various ways. Some take "heaven" for the righteous and "earth" for the sinner. Some understand the spirit by "heaven" and the body by "earth." Some understand Christ by "heaven" and the militant church by "earth." Augustine puts forward these three opinions. Jerome says: just as the angels serve Thee, God, in heaven, so may we on earth. The Aquinate <note>Thomas Aquinas</note> follows this opinion, as does our poet. SINGING Hosanna: *Hosanna* in the Hebrew language means "make safe," or "give life," or "save us," or "our salvation." GIVE US this day our daily manna: This is the fourth request, "Give us this day our daily bread" <note>original Latin: "Pane nostru quotidianu da nobis hodie"</note>. By this, he means the grace of God, which is spiritual food on which the soul nourishes itself. He calls it "ours" <note>the Italian "nostro"</note> because it is proper to man as a rational animal and not to the brutes. It can also be understood as the bread of physical food...

The text explores the nature of God's infinity, the hierarchy of creation, and the interpretations of the prayer by Church Fathers like Augustine, Jerome, and Thomas Aquinas.</summary>

<meta>The previous page introduced the paraphrase of the Lord's Prayer recited by the proud in the First Terrace of Purgatory, reaching the petition for "daily manna" (bread).</meta>

<page-num>180</page-num>
<header>PURGATORIO</header>

...necessary for the temporal life. Because while we are joined with the body, it is necessary to sustain it and call it "ours," according to Gregory <note>Pope Gregory the Great</note>, because we receive it back from God as His gift. Therefore we say "give," so that it is not ours through theft, but through His will. Just as the manna physically fed the people of God in the desert and held whatever flavor the one who tasted it desired, so the spiritual bread fulfills every righteous appetite of our soul. Manna in eastern regions is made of nearly the same material as honey is for us. But there, the sun can more effectively draw out the moisture, which is pulled upward during the day and falls back to the earth at night. And as for the evil we have suffered: the fifth petition, **And forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors** <note>original Latin: "Et dimitte nobis debita nostra: sicut & nos dimittimus debitoribus nostris"</note>, we ask that He cancel our sins, by which we are excluded from paradise, just as we forgive others for the injuries received from them. **OUR Virtue which willingly surrenders.** The last petition: **and lead us not into temptation.** <note>original Latin: "et ne nos inducas in tentatione"</note> "Surrenders" <term>saddona</term> means it fails or gives way. In this part, we ask for perseverance in the future. To "tempt" means to prove and make a trial of a thing and its strength. The virtue of man consists in two things: in doing good and fleeing from evil. In the first way, God tests man. In the second way, the virtue of man is tempted to be led into evil by three kinds of temptation. The first temptation is from the flesh, for as the Apostle <note>St. Paul</note> says: "Each one is tempted by his own concupiscence." The second is of the world with its vanities. The third is of the devil, who tempts us toward those vices to which he sees we are most inclined. No one could resist the diabolical temptation with their own strength without divine help. Therefore, do not put our virtue to the test, which "surrenders"—that is, it inclines and cannot resist.

> This last prayer, dear Lord,
> is surely not made for us, who have no need,
> but for those who remained behind us.
> Thus, for themselves and for us, a good journey
> those shades, praying, went beneath their weights,
> similar to that which one sometimes dreams of,
> unequally distressed, all in a circle,
> and weary, upon the first cornice,
> purging away the thick mist of the world.
> If there <note>in Purgatory</note> a good word is always said for us,
> what can be said and done for them here
> by those who have a good root to their will?
> Truly we ought to help them wash away the stains
> they carried from here, so that, pure and light,
> they may go forth to the starry wheels.
> "Ah, so may justice and piety soon unburden you,
> so that you may be able to move your wing,
> which may lift you according to your desire,
> show us on which hand toward the ladder
> one goes most directly; and if there is more than one passage,
> teach us the one that descends less steeply;
> for he who comes with me, because of the burden
> of Adam’s flesh with which he is clothed,
> is slow in climbing up, against his will."
> Their words, which they returned to these
> that had been spoken by him whom I followed,
> were not clear as to whom they came from;
> but it was said: "To the right along the bank
> come with us, and you will find the pass
> possible for a living person to climb.
> And if I were not hindered by the stone
> that tames my proud neck,
> which forces me to carry my face low,
> I would look at this man who still lives and is not named,
> to see if I know him,
> and to make him pitiful toward this burden."

<column-break/>

This demonstrates the true repentance of these souls: since they have set aside pride—which does not allow us to have charity or care for our neighbor—they prayed for the salvation of others. Because a soul placed in Purgatory is confirmed by God in that state, so that it cannot be tempted; therefore, they did not say that last prayer—**and lead us not into temptation**—for themselves, because they had no need of it. But charity moved them to do it for those who had remained in life behind them. **Good Journey** <term>Buona Ramogna</term>: prosperous success. *Ramogna* properly means to follow along the journey. **SIMILAR to that which one sometimes dreams of.** When sleeping on one's back, it sometimes happens that much blood flows to the heart and weighs it down in such a way that in sleep one seems to have an immeasurable weight upon them. **The Mist** <term>La Caligine</term>: the sin of pride, which is born from mist—that is, fog and darkness, meaning blindness of mind and ignorance.

Oh, excellent sentiment founded in charity: that if there in Purgatory a good thing is said for us who are in life—that is, they pray for us—we ought to help them "wash away the stains" <note>literally: "lift the vows"</note> by what can be done for them through alms and prayers. And this should especially be done by those who have a "good root to their will"—those who have confirmed their will in good, and for this reason are in a state of grace, and their prayers are heard. Other texts have "to the starry wheels": that they may, upon exiting Purgatory, ascend to the heavens. **GO FORTH to the starry wheels:** that they may leave Purgatory, which, if it is in the other hemisphere, comes to be beneath all the heavens just as we are. And when the soul passes from there to eternal life, it leaves these heavens and goes above them; therefore, they may "go forth from the starry wheels"—that is, from the heavens which continually rotate and turn.

Virgil prays to the souls with these words so that they might show him the ascent to the next cliff, especially because Dante is "slow" <term>parco</term> to the climb: he is late in climbing against his will, because if he were lazy by his own will, he would not be worthy to receive the purgatorial virtues.

Appropriate words, not for a proud man, but for one who purges pride with its opposite, which is humility. First, he shows the way with great humanity. Then, he confesses to bearing the deserved penalty for his error—which the proud man never does. Then, he shows a desire to know Dante to move him to compassion.

# CANTO XI.

<columns>2</columns>

I was Italian and born of a great Tuscan:
Guglielmo Aldobrandeschi was my father;
I know not if his name was ever known to you.
The ancient blood and the gallant deeds
of my ancestors made me so arrogant
that, not thinking of our common mother,
I held every man in such disdain
that I died for it, as the Sienese know,
and every child in Campagnatico <note>The village where Omberto was murdered in 1259</note> knows it.
I am Omberto; and not only to me has
pride done harm, for all my companions
has she dragged with her into misfortune.
And here I must carry this weight
because of her, until God is satisfied,
since I did not do it among the living, here among the dead.
Listening, I bent my face downward;
and one of them—not the one who was speaking—
twisted himself under the weight that hampers him,
and saw me, and recognized me, and called out,
keeping his eyes fixed with great effort
on me, who walked all stooped with him.
"Oh," I said to him, "are you not Oderisi,
the honor of Gubbio, and the honor of that art
which is called 'illuminating' in Paris?"
"Brother," he said, "the pages smile more
when painted by the brush of Franco of Bologna;
the honor is now all his, and mine only in part.
Truly, I would not have been so courteous
while I lived, because of the great desire
for excellence upon which my heart was set.
For such pride, here the fee is paid;
and I would not even be here, were it not
that, while still able to sin, I turned to God.
O empty glory of human powers!
How little green lasts upon the summit,
unless it is followed by an age of dullness.
Cimabue thought to hold the field
in painting, and now Giotto has the cry,
so that the fame of the former is obscured.
Thus has one Guido taken from the other
the glory of the language; and perhaps he is born
who shall chase both from the nest.
Worldly fame is nothing but a breath
of wind, which now comes from here and now from there,
and changes name because it changes side.

<column-break/>

OMBERTO, son of Messer Guglielmo Aldobrandeschi: who are of ancient blood and Counts of Santa Fiora in the territory of Siena. He was a very proud man: and his arrogance and pride toward the Sienese grew to such an extent that they had him killed at Campagnatico.

ODERISI of Gubbio: and he was in that time an excellent miniaturist. It is called "illuminating" <term>alluminare</term> in Paris because the red-lead <note>original: "minio" - the red pigment used in manuscripts, giving us the word "miniature"</note> distinguishes and lights up the writing. "BROTHER," he said: as one now repenting of his empty glory, he does not place himself above others as he did when occupied by such vice, but is content to yield to Franco of Bologna as a greater master than himself. And therefore he said: "the pages smile more," as if to say they are better illuminated than those Franco painted with his pen. This man was from Bologna and a better miniaturist. "THE HONOR is now all his," which is to say: before he became a good master, I held the first place, nor was there anyone who compared to me in value. But afterward, I was surpassed by him, so that the honor is entirely his. Nonetheless, because after him I was ahead of the others, I have not remained without some part of the honor. Nor is it pride that makes him say "and mine in part," because having placed the Bolognese man before himself, he can freely speak the truth of himself. "TRULY, I would not have been so courteous": when I was in the sin of vainglory, I would not have been so generous in praising Franco. And certainly, this vice exists in men who have some excellence in themselves: they cannot praise another who possesses the same virtue, for it seems that what they give in praise to another, they take away from themselves. "FOR THE GREAT DESIRE": for the great greed.

"FOR EXCELLENCE": for surpassing and conquering others. Wherefore I pay the "fee" here, that is, the penalty. "AND I WOULD NOT EVEN BE HERE": if while he was alive he had always practiced vainglory, it would have been necessary that after death he go to damnation. But it shows that he turned to God, that is, to penance, while "still able to sin," that is, while he was in life, in which one can merit or demerit. "O EMPTY GLORY of human powers": which men take from their virtues. Vainglory is called *Cenodoxia* by the Greeks <note>original: "Cenodoxia," from the Greek kenos (empty) and doxa (glory)</note>, which is the same as "vainglory" in Latin. Concerning which Isaiah says: "The flower has fallen, the glory of exaltation" <note>original Latin: "Flos cecidit gloria exaltationis"; see Isaiah 40:7-8</note>. And the Psalmist: "A thousand years in your sight are as yesterday which has passed" <note>original Latin: "Mille anni ante oculos tuos sicut dies hesterna que periit"; see Psalm 90:4</note>. "With little green upon the summit": meaning how little the green and its excellence lasts on the peak. "UNLESS IT IS FOLLOWED": unless it is aided by "ages of dullness"; the meaning is, unless it is undiscovered. For although one may be the first in a science, virtue, or art, nevertheless, it lasts only a short time to be first, because another more excellent than him follows. Unless it is "helped by ages of dullness," that is, that after him follows an age that produces men of dull intellect. And he proves it by the example of Cimabue: who obtained the honor and the first place in painting, until Giotto became such a master that he surpassed and conquered Cimabue; thus will come another time when someone will conquer Giotto. Therefore, no one should take vainglory in their own powers. Cimabue: this man, while painting was in obscurity, brought it into good fame. Giotto became a greater and more noble master than Cimabue. "TO HOLD THE FIELD": to remain the victor; and it is a metaphor from military exercise. "THUS HAS ONE GUIDO taken from the other the glory of the language": just as Giotto took the glory of painting from Cimabue, so Guido Cavalcanti took it from Guido Guinizelli of Bologna. "AND PERHAPS HE IS BORN": many understand that he hints at himself <note>The commentator acknowledges that Dante likely refers to his own rising fame here</note>, but he cannot be accused of arrogance, because it cannot be proven that he speaks of one more than another, and he affirms nothing. "WORLDLY FAME IS NOTHING but a breath": fame, glory, outcry, and noise are taken as the same thing. Worldly noise is the fame of mortal things. "NOTHING BUT A BREATH": because it flies and in a short time spreads everywhere. Wherefore Virgil says:

> Fame is an evil than which no other is swifter. It thrives on movement and gains strength as it goes. <note>original Latin: "Fama malum quo non aliud velocius: ullum. Mobilitate viget: viresque acquirit eundo." from Aeneid IV, 174-175</note>

<summary>This page features the encounter with Omberto Aldobrandeschi and Oderisi da Gubbio, who explain how their pride in lineage and artistic talent led them to Purgatory. The text reflects on the fleeting nature of human glory, citing the transition from Cimabue to Giotto and the rise of new poets.</summary>

# PURGATORIO

<columns>

Oderisi continues by showing that before a thousand years pass, you will have no more fame if you shed <note>meaning: cut or separate from yourself</note> the "old flesh" <note>meaning: if you die at an old age</note> than if you had died before leaving behind baby talk—*pappa* or *dindi* <note>meaning: before leaving childhood, when small children, not yet knowing how to speak and wanting to say "bread" or "money," say *pappa* and *dindi*.</note>

What greater fame will you have if you shed
the old flesh from yourself, than if you had died
before you left behind the *pappa* or the *dindi*,
Before a thousand years pass? Which is a shorter
span to eternity than the blink of an eye
is to the circle that turns slowest in heaven.

He who takes so little of the path
before me was famous throughout all Tuscany,
and now is hardly whispered of in Siena,
Where he was Lord when there was destroyed
the Florentine rage, which was as proud
in those days as it is now a harlot.

Our renown is the color of grass,
which comes and goes, and he discolors it
by whom it came forth from the bitter earth.

<note>original: "nerif." possibly a truncated reference to the commentator</note> I cannot help but grieve in this place, as in any other, because I wish that such a great poet of such admirable talent and learning had not let himself be carried away by the perturbation of his mind toward his homeland. But the verse of Homer is true: that God never gave everything to a single man.

And I to him: "Your words encourage
good humility in my heart, and flatten a great pride;
but who is he of whom you spoke just now?"

"That is," he replied, "Provenzan Salvani;
and he is here because he was presumptuous
in bringing all of Siena into his hands.

He has gone así, and goes without rest
since he died; such coin he pays
to satisfy the debt, he who was too daring there."

And I: "If that spirit who waits,
before he repents, until the edge of life,
remains down there and does not ascend here,

Unless a good prayer aids him,
until as much time passes as he lived,
how was his coming here granted to him?"

"When he lived in his greatest glory," he said,
"freely in the square of Siena,
he set aside all shame,

And there, to draw his friend from the pain
he suffered in the prison of Charles,
he brought himself to tremble in every vein.

I will say no more, and I know I speak obscurely,
but little time will pass before your neighbors
will act so that you will be able to interpret it.
This work took those boundaries away from him."

<column-break/>

<gloss>pappa & dindo</gloss> And if anyone should say that a thousand years is a great span of time, he demonstrates that a thousand years, in comparison to eternity, is a shorter span than a blink of an eye is in comparison to the movement of the eighth sphere <note>the "sphere of the fixed stars"</note>, which moves one degree every hundred years. **TURNS SLOWEST** means it is revolved and turned. **HE WHO** takes so little of the path before me: this man was Messer Provenzan Salvani of Siena, who was the Lord of Siena and was the victor at the rout of Montaperti <note>A bloody battle in 1260 where the Sienese Ghibellines defeated the Florentine Guelphs</note>. Later, in twelve hundred and sixty-nine, with one thousand four hundred cavalry and eight thousand infantry, he attacked Colle; but the Florentine army came to the rescue and broke the Sienese. Many were killed in vengeance for our people killed at Montaperti. Provenzan was captured, and his head was cut off, fixed on the point of a lance, and carried throughout the camp. Thus, to show how quickly fame fades, he says that this man—who shortly before Dante's time was in great fame throughout Tuscany—is now hardly whispered of in Siena. **WHERE HE WAS Lord**: of which he was the master. **WHEN THERE WAS DESTROYED the Florentine rage**: when the Guelphs were defeated at Montaperti, a history we treated in the first Cantica <note>The Inferno</note>. **WHICH WAS PROUD** at that time and ambitious. **AND NOW IS A HARLOT**: <term>meretrice</term> <note>a prostitute</note>; as if to say that in that time the citizens were proud, but now they are greedy, and for greed they sell the public interest. It is similar to that line of Sallust: <note>original: "O urbem venalem et cito perituram, si emptorem invenerit."</note> "O venal city and soon to perish, if it finds a buyer." **OUR RENOWN IS THE COLOR OF GRASS**: our fame is like grass, which stays green for a short time and then withers. The poet stays within the metaphor, because above he said: "how little green lasts upon the summit." **AND HE DISCOLORS IT**: the sun, which creates time, is that which makes the grass grow and that same sun withers it. Likewise, time produces fame and then consigns it to oblivion.

**YOUR WORDS ENCOURAGE**: puts good humility into my heart. **AND FLATTEN**: levels the great <term>tumor</term> <note>pride or swelling</note>, meaning great arrogance. Because *tumor* in Latin signifies a swelling, and the proud, because they are swollen, are called "tumid." A **PRESUMPTUOUS** person is one who attributes to himself what is not his or does not befit him. The same is "arrogant." **WHO WAS TOO DARING**: who had too much boldness. **AND I: IF THAT**: the text is ordered thus: And I, Dante, replied to Oderisi, finding this doubt: if that spirit who waits until he returns to penitence <note>at the "edge" or end of life</note> remains down there outside of Purgatory proper for as much time as he lived, and does not ascend unless a good prayer helps him—how was the coming up here granted to Provenzan, since it has been less time since he died than the time he spent alive? This is contrary to what was said above.

Oderisi **RESPONDS** to the doubt raised by Dante, saying: that the great humility he practiced in collecting money to rescue a friend of his from prison shortened the time he had to stay outside of Purgatory. They say that King Charles <note>Charles of Anjou</note> had captured a friend of this Provenzan in the rout he gave to Conradin, and set a ransom of 10,000 florins under penalty of death if he did not pay in a short time. Provenzan humbled himself so much for his friend that he placed a carpet in the square of Siena <note>the Piazza del Campo</note> and begged with every kind of plea for the redemption of the prisoner. The words of the text are ordered thus: Oderisi said, responding to Dante's doubt, that when Provenzan lived in his most glorious and greatest state, he freely fixed himself and stood in the square of Siena—which is what the Sienese call their plaza—having cast aside all shame. **HE BROUGHT HIMSELF TO TREMBLE in every vein**: because one who is driven by calamity to ask for help comes with great trembling, for he fears not being heard. And because this sentence is spoken obscurely, he says that in a short time your neighbors—meaning your fellow citizens—will act so that you will be able to interpret it. In this way, he predicts Dante's own exile, during which he will understand that he who goes to the mercy of others trembles when he makes a request. **THIS WORK**: that is, of humility. **TOOK AWAY**: removed from Provenzan. **THOSE BOUNDARIES**: of staying outside of Purgatory.

</columns>

<summary>In this passage, the artist Oderisi explains the transience of earthly fame through the fall of the Sienese leader Provenzan Salvani, while also revealing that Provenzan’s time in Purgatory was shortened because of a singular act of selfless humility.</summary>

<header>CANTO XII</header>

# CHAPTER TWELVE OF THE SECOND CANTICLE OF DANTE.

**S**ide by side, like oxen going in a yoke, 
I went along with that burdened soul, 
as long as the sweet pedagogue <note>Latin: *pedagogus*; a teacher or tutor, usually one who escorts a child to school.</note> permitted: 
But when he said, "Leave him and pass on, 
for here it is good that with sail and with oars 
each man pushes his boat as much as he can," 
I stood up as straight as one must go, 
with my body, although my thoughts 
remained bowed and diminished within me. 
I had moved myself, and was following willingly 
the steps of my master, and both of us 
already showed how light we had become. 
And he said to me: "Turn your eyes downward: 
it will be good for you, to calm the way, 
to see the bed beneath your feet."

lighter than before. But Virgil admonishes him: that as you walk, you will see; these were histories and stories of men, in which there was much sculpture. For this reason, it was established that they should be sculpted on the ground: because those who exalted themselves more than nature, condition, or learning allowed deserve no other place than to lie in the lowest depths. And he admonishes the senses with the intellect, so that it does not become more puffed up than justice requires: that he look upon these sculptures—that is, bring such examples to memory. And in his mind, let him consider with what justice God <note>original: "Deposuit potentes de sede" — "He has put down the mighty from their seat," a reference to the Magnificat (Luke 1:52).</note> has cast down the mighty from their thrones; and in what little esteem they have remained in the memory of men. The proud sought highness; now they lie in the lowest rank. They sought fame; now they are in infamy. They sought divine honors; now they are deprived of all human glory. This is what the man who wishes to be purged thinks upon. This is what he continuously considers. This he has fixed in his mind day and night.

**J**ust as, so that there may be memory of them, 
above the buried ones the earth-level tombs <note>flat grave markers set into the floor of a church or path.</note> 
carry a record of what they were before / 
Wherefore many times there, one weeps for them 
because of the sting of remembrance, 
which gives its spur only to the pious. 
So I saw them there, but of a better likeness 
according to the skill of the artist, 
covering as much of the path as projects from the mountain.

he is not pitiful and is not moved to compassion for the dead. I SAW THEM THERE: so he saw figured in that place—that is, carved and sculpted—but of a better likeness—that is, of a better image—according to the skill: according to the rules of art. "Likeness" signifies similarity, derived from the word for "example." AS MUCH AS THE PATH PROJECTS FROM THE MOUNTAIN: This shows that such sculpture was only on the terrace, which juts out and surrounds it, and is made for the path; and rightly so, because it is a just thing that the memory of such men be a path for those who purge themselves of pride, so that it may be placed beneath them. Furthermore, it is a "path" because such memory leads the one who is purged to true humility.

I saw him who was created noble 
more than any other creature, down from heaven 
descending like a flash of lightning on one side. 
I saw Briareus <note>A giant from Greek mythology who rebelled against Olympus.</note> pierced by the celestial 
bolt, lying on the other side, 
heavy upon the earth in mortal cold. 
I saw Thymbraeus <note>Apollo.</note>, I saw Pallas and Mars...

<column-break/>

**H**aving departed from the souls who were purging their past pride, he shows that many histories are sculpted in the ground over which he passed, as an example and warning to the proud. Virgil therefore let him walk with Oderisi <note>The text says "Odorosi", referring to the illuminator Oderisi da Gubbio.</note> until they reached where those sculptures were; then he admonished him to pass forward. He walked side by side with Oderisi. And he names Virgil "pedagogue" not without reason. For in Greek this word signifies the one to whom children are given for safekeeping. He wants to signify, therefore, that the senses are like a child, because they easily let themselves be conquered by appetite like a child. And the intellect is their guide. FOR HERE IT IS GOOD WITH SAIL AND OARS to push the boat: which in short signifies that they should hurry in passing through. And many refer this to the idea that we must use speed in penance, and rightfully so. But it also means to signify that there is no vice we should leave behind sooner than pride, because it is the greatest of all and most ruinous above all others. AS STRAIGHT AS: because in the company of the soul I had gone bowed down, now I made myself straight, as one is meant to walk; although my thoughts remained bowed, out of compassion for the soul, and also for the humility with which he purged his pride. I HAD MOVED MYSELF and followed willingly the steps of my leader. For having sufficiently contemplated pride, and consequently having purged myself of it, I followed reason and doctrine willingly. And I remained more...

**H**e shows that he thus saw those histories sculpted on the ground, which he will describe shortly, just as one sees sculpted images of men already dead upon their tombs. So that such images might bring the memory of those people back to our minds. Wherefore he says: like the earth-level tombs—that is, the sepulchers placed in the ground—above the buried ones—that is, above those who are buried there—carry a record of what they were before—that is, they carry a sculpture of the man buried there in the form he had before he was dissolved and returned to ash. And these images are carved there so that there may be a memory of them. Wherefore it happens that there—that is, over those images—one often weeps. Because passing by, friends and relatives weep. BY THE STING of remembrance—that is, because the memory of a dead friend or relative pricks and torments the soul. But such a sting does not "give the spur" except to the pious—that is, the compassionate—because he who...

**I**t is a fitting thing that in the place where we purge pride, these most proud examples are sculpted on the ground. For nothing makes a vice so displeasing to us as considering it in others. Thus, first was the history of Lucifer. Our Petrarch writes most excellently in *On the Remedies of Both Kinds of Fortune*: <note>original: "Remedium contra superbiam fundamentum vere virtutis est humilitas. Nec tanta claritas ulla est: quam superbia non obscuret. Scit ille qui clarissimus creatus se ipsum extollens non solum obscurus. Sed princeps fieri meruit tenebrarum." — "The remedy against pride and the foundation of true virtue is humility. Nor is there any such brilliance that pride does not darken. He who was created most bright knows this, who by exalting himself deserved not only to become dark, but to become the prince of darkness."</note> BRIAREUS PIERCED BY THE CELESTIAL BOLT: by the lightning...
