<header>PURGATORIO</header>

...still armed around their father,
beholding the scattered limbs of the giants.
<note>Dante is describing a carving of the Gigantomachy, the mythical war where the Giants tried to overthrow the Olympian gods.</note>

It is written in the poetic fables that they made war for ten years
against the gods; they were ruined in hell by Jupiter's lightning bolts. But
in the fable of the giants, they were also children of Heaven and
Earth, and had fifty heads. There were three: Cottus, Briareus, and
Gyges. But men called Briareus by the name Aegaeon. It is a very fine choice by the
poet <note>Referring to Dante.</note> to mix false things with the true story of Lucifer: that is, the
fable itself is false, but its allegory is a very true thing, because
Homer portrays the fable of Briareus differently, making him a friend
[to Jupiter]; however, from Homer’s version one could not draw a suitable
allegory for this place. [The carving] showed how the gods who were helping Jupiter looked with wonder
at the bodies of these monsters, torn and broken by the bolts
of Jupiter; and he uses the name "Thymbraeus" for Apollo, who in Troy
had a temple near which an herb called
Thymbra—that is, savory—grew in abundance. Thus, he is called Thymbraean Apollo.

I saw Nimrod at the foot of the great work,
as if bewildered, looking at the people
who were proud with him in Shinar.
<note>Nimrod was traditionally considered the architect of the Tower of Babel in the land of Shinar.</note>

O Niobe, with what grieving eyes
did I see you marked upon the road,
between seven and seven of your children slain!
<note>Niobe boasted that she was superior to the goddess Latona because she had fourteen children while the goddess only had two (Apollo and Diana). In revenge, the divine twins killed all of Niobe's children.</note>
O Saul, how you appeared dead there
upon your own sword in Gilboa,
which afterward felt neither rain nor dew!

He spared Agag, King of the Amalekites; he was deprived of the vision
given by the demon. And many times he wished to kill David, a man
of great humility. By necessity, he turned to the Pythoness <note>The Witch of Endor.</note> so that she might raise
Samuel. He fought against the Philistines and lost his army and his sons. And
not being able to find someone to kill him, he fell upon his
own weapons.

O foolish Arachne, so I saw you,
already half-spider, wretched upon the shreds
of the work that was woven to your own harm.
<note>Arachne challenged the goddess Minerva to a weaving contest; for her pride, she was transformed into a spider.</note>
O Rehoboam, your image here does not seem
to threaten, but full of terror,
a chariot carries it away before any pursue.
The hard pavement also showed
how Alcmaeon made his mother pay dear
for the unfortunate ornament.
<note>Alcmaeon killed his mother, Eriphyle, because she had been bribed with a necklace to reveal his father's hiding place, leading to his father's death.</note>
It showed how his sons threw themselves
upon Sennacherib within the temple,
and how they left him there dead.

The Theban war: a fable we narrated fully in the twentieth canto of the *Inferno*.

It showed the ruin and the cruel slaughter
that Tomyris wrought when she said to Cyrus:
"You thirsted for blood, and with blood I fill you!"
It showed how the Assyrians fled in a rout
after Holofernes was killed,
and also the remains of that slaughter.

<column-break/>

[The bolt] sent from heaven. *Telum* is a Latin name <note>original: "Telum e nome latino"</note> but derived from the Greek; it signifies
every weapon used for offense, and especially lances, darts, arrows, and the like.
Therefore, the poets, imagining that the lightning from heaven is thrown by
Jupiter, and that with it he punishes those who err, call it the *telum Iovis* <note>The weapon of Jove.</note>.
Against the gods. And finally, a great force was made by the gods and by
[Jupiter]. What this thing signifies and what allegory it holds, we have said
of the earth; and they had giant stature and limbs. There were three: Cottus,
Gyges, and Briareus. And Homer adds that the gods called him
[Aegaeon]. It is a fiction that the giants come after Lucifer; nor should anyone blame
the poet for mixing false things with the true story of Lucifer: that is, the
fables of the Titans. For he does not intend to present the fable as
truth, but rather the allegory of it, which is a very true thing: because
it denotes Pride, which is being mentioned at present. I know that
Homer portrays the fable of Briareus differently, making him a friend
to Jupiter. But Dante in this place follows the other poets, because
from Homer’s fable one could not draw a suitable
allegory for this place. I SAW Thymbraeus. It
demonstrated how the gods, who were in aid of Jupiter, looked with wonder
at the bodies of such monsters, torn and broken by the bolts
of Jupiter; and he uses "Thymbraeus" for Apollo, who in Troy
had a temple near which an herb called
Thymbra—that is, savory—abounded. Thus, Thymbraean Apollo.

THE story of Nimrod we placed in the *Inferno* where, in the pit,
mention of him is made.

NIOBE was the daughter of Tantalus and wife of Amphion; she was so proud that
she dared to prefer herself to Latona, the mother of Phoebus [Apollo] and Diana. She
wanted the honors and sacrifices that were attributed to Latona to be given to her
instead, because she had not two, but fourteen children: seven
males and seven females. Therefore, Phoebus with his bow killed them all.
Some say that Phoebus killed the males and Diana the females. And
Niobe was turned into stone. SAUL was the first King of Israel, anointed by the
hands of the prophet Samuel. He was of great stature, robust, handsome,
and strong in battle. He conquered many kings and peoples; he occupied territory from Egypt
to the Red Sea. But ultimately, because he went against the command of God,
he spared Agag, King of the Amalekites. He was deprived of the vision
of future things that God had given him. And he was often vexed
by a demon. Many times he wished to kill David, a man
of great humility, who twice had saved him from death.
Out of necessity, he turned to the Pythoness <note>The Witch of Endor.</note> so that she might raise
Samuel; finally, hateful to God and men, he fought unhappily
against the Philistines and lost his army and his sons. And not
being able to obtain the favor of one of his men to kill him with his
own weapons, he killed himself.

THE fable of Arachne is very well known. This woman, most skilled in embroidery,
preferred herself to Pallas [Minerva], by whom she was defeated and converted into a
spider. And just as she first made excellent webs as a woman, she does so now as an
animal. REHOBOAM, son of Solomon, succeeded his father in the kingdom.
And having come to Shechem, where all the people of Israel were gathered,
he used such pride that, when the people begged him to lighten the
heavy yoke that his father Solomon had imposed on them, incited by
pride, he despised the counsel of the elders and followed that of the young
men. He replied that his little finger was thicker than his father's shoulders.
And if his father had beaten them with rods, he would strike them with
scorpions. Because of this, ten tribes out of twelve immediately rebelled against him
and elected Jeroboam as their king. They stoned Adoram, who
collected the tribute for Rehoboam. He fled to Jerusalem. Therefore Shishak,
King of Egypt, hoping in the sedition of the Hebrews, came with a robust
army and besieged Jerusalem. And by hunger, he forced Rehoboam
to yield to him, to let him sack the city and the temple of Solomon, and to
become his tributary. ALCMAEON was the son of Amphiaraus,
and he killed his mother Eriphyle because, out of greed to possess the
necklace, she revealed the hiding place of Amphiaraus, who was hidden to avoid going to the [war].

WHAT TOMYRIS DID TO CYRUS. It would be a long story to relate
from what low fortune to what height of empire Cyrus,
King of the Persians, rose. And how, as soon as he was born, Astyages, his maternal
grandfather, had him left in the woods to fate, because he had heard that from his
daughter a child would be born who would destroy his kingdom. And
how he was nursed by a female dog. And how he became a most powerful king,
occupying a great part of Asia. But finally, he moved war against the Scythians.
In those times, Tomyris was Queen of the Scythians, and she sent her...

<header>CANTO TWELVE</header>
<meta>catchword: chi</meta>

I saw Troy in ashes and in hollows;
O Ilion, how low and base
the design seen there showed you to be!
What master of fine brush or chisel
who portrayed the shadows and the gestures there,
would make every subtle mind marvel?
The dead seemed dead, and the living seemed alive;
he who saw the truth saw no better than I
all that I walked upon while I went stooped.

Now be proud, and go with your haughty face,
children of Eve, and do not bow your head
so that you might see your evil path!
More of the mountain was already circled by us,
and of the sun’s path much more spent
than my mind, not being free, had estimated;
When he who always went ahead, attentive,
began: "Lift up your head;
it is no longer time to go thus suspended.
See there an angel who prepares
to come toward us; see that the sixth handmaid
returns from the service of the day.
<note>The "sixth handmaid" refers to the sixth hour of the day, meaning it is now noon.</note>
Adorn your face and actions with reverence,
so that it may please him to send us upward;
think that this day never dawns again."

I was well used to his admonitions
never to lose time, so that in that
matter his speech did not seem obscure to me.
Toward us came the beautiful creature,
clothed in white, and in his face such
as appears the trembling morning star.
He opened his arms, and then he opened his wings;
he said: "Come; here are the steps nearby,
and easily now one ascends."
To this announcement, they come very rarely.
O human race, born to fly upward,
why do you fall so for a little wind?

<column-break/>

...his only son with a great army for the defense of the kingdom. But he was defeated and killed with his army by Cyrus. But the Queen, having restored the army, attacked again with snares. And she killed 200,000 Persians; and she put the head of Cyrus in a wineskin full of human blood, and said: "You were thirsty for blood; now drink blood." <note>This refers to Queen Tomyris of the Massagetae, who defeated Cyrus the Great.</note> **HOLOFERNES.** This man was the prince of the militia of Nebuchadnezzar, King of the Assyrians, who arrived at such pride that he wished to be adored as a god. He sent Holofernes against the Jews after he had subjugated many other nations. The Jews made themselves strong in the mountains where the entrance to their region was. Holofernes besieged Bethulia, located in those parts. And by depriving the Bethulians of water, it was necessary for them to surrender. But by the exhortation of Ozias the priest, they decided to wait five days before surrendering. In this time, Judith, a very beautiful woman and a widow, feigning flight from the famine, went with one of her handmaids to Holofernes, commending her safety to him and promising to give him the means by which he could conquer the land. Holofernes, moved by her beauty and the woman's promises, saved her. And she feigned that for four days she had to remain in prayer according to her law. Afterward, seeing Holofernes sleeping deeply due to much drunkenness, she took off his head. And she returned to the city. And Ozias went out with the armed people and attacked the already fleeing army. And he sent to the surrounding cities to occupy the passes. Wherefore so great an army received a great rout. There were 120,000 foot soldiers of Holofernes and twenty thousand horsemen. **TROY IN ASHES.** The destruction of Troy and the miserable fortune of Priam were sculpted.

It is a fitting thing that these stories be sculpted on the ground in the path, so that every man who passes may trample them. Because if these people, through pride, wished always to go above others, it is a worthy penalty for them that others walk above them. Wherefore, out of indignation, the poet uses this exclamation: **NOW BE PROUD, CHILDREN OF EVE.** As if to say: mortal men, and of no other origin than the others. **AND DO NOT BOW YOUR FACE**, as if to say: do not consider your baseness and lowest condition. **SO THAT YOU MAY SEE YOUR EVIL PATH:** one does not know how evil the path is—that is, the bad way of pride—except when we see by the example of others where it leads us. **MORE WAS ALREADY.** We had turned—that is, we had rotated while going up the terrace that surrounds the mountain—more of the mountain [than realized]; and we had spent more of the path of the sun—that is, of time, which is born from the solar motion—than my mind, not being free, had estimated. For when a man goes in a fixed contemplation of mind, time passes and he does not notice it. **WHEN HE WHO ALWAYS GOES AHEAD ATTENTIVE.** A man cannot go by the straight path if appetite precedes reason; but he arrives at the desired end when reason precedes, and not only precedes, but always stays attentive. **HE CRIED OUT**, because reason stimulates appetite with sharp bites: so that when it has considered one thing enough, it lifts its head to another and does not go always suspended in a single thought. **SEE THERE AN ANGEL WHO HASTENS AND PREPARES.** This angel is that divine grace of which we have already spoken so many times. And although the poet often changes the fiction, he nonetheless always intends the same thing. **SEE THAT THE SIXTH HANDMAID RETURNS FROM THE SERVICE OF THE DAY**, that is, the sixth hour returns, because it has already done its office. The meaning is that the sixth hour was departing from the sun, because it was entering the seventh. And by showing that already half of the day had passed in contemplating pride, it signifies that much more time is consumed in purging this vice than any other. **WITH REVERENCE ADORN YOUR FACE AND ACTS.** The appetite and the inferior reason ought to make themselves reverent and obedient to the remitting divine grace, and not lose time when they can go forward with it. Therefore, lost time cannot be reacquired. Wherefore the day does not dawn again. And Virgil says: <note>original: "Proxima queque dies miseris mortalibus qui: Prima fugit." This is a quote from Virgil's Georgics III, 66-67: "Each day that is closest is the first to flee for wretched mortals."</note>

When the appetite, through long habit and use, is already accustomed to obeying the precepts of reason, it understands them easily, and especially when [reason] admonishes that time should not be lost; because this precept is given by reason continually, in every age, and in every thing. He feigns that the angel is clothed in white and has a splendid face, because such grace illuminates us and leads us back to the state of innocence and makes us pure. **HE OPENED HIS ARMS**, which denotes divine mercy. **LIGHTLY NOW ONE ASCENDS.** And once pride is set aside, one easily frees oneself from the other vices, because pride takes God from us, envy takes our neighbor, and anger takes ourselves.

The words of the first tercet can be both of the angel and of the poet. He says, then, that there are few who come to this announcement that the angel makes when he says "Come." Because there are few who disentangle themselves from pride, and few who...

<header>PURGATORY.</header>

He led us to where the rock was cut;
here he beat his wings upon my forehead:
then he permitted me a safe passage.
Just as on the right hand, to climb the mountain
where the church sits that dominates
the well-guided city above Rubaconte,
To break the bold steepness of the climb
by the stairs that were made in an age
when the ledger and the stave were safe,
So the bank that falls there is eased,
which drops steeply from the upper circle,
but on this side and that the other stone scrapes.

<gloss>It deceives us: or it hinders us even in good works.</gloss> **JUST AS ON the right hand.** Such were the stairs in this place: like those we see on the way from the city gate up to San Miniato al Monte. <note>San Miniato is a famous Romanesque basilica overlooking Florence; the steep climb is still managed by a series of stairs.</note> These stairs were made because of the steepness of the descent; to put it more clearly, the slope was broken—it was not continuous, but interrupted by level intervals placed between the stairs. **ON THE right hand**, leaving the gate to go to San Miniato, one climbs for a bit by a single path; then it divides into two ways, and the one on the right for the climber has the stairs that dominate **The well-guided** city of Florence; which he calls "well-guided" through irony <note>original: "p hironia"</note>, meaning well-conducted and well-ruled <note>Florence was famously politically chaotic in Dante's time.</note>. **ABOVE Rubaconte.** This temple to which one climbs by the aforementioned stairs dominates—that is, it judges from above and stands over that part of the city where the Rubaconte bridge is over the Arno. <note>Now known as the Ponte alle Grazie.</note> It was named after Messer Rubaconte da Mandello, a Milanese knight who was the governor of Florence when he built this bridge in the year 1237. **THE LEDGER and the stave:** because in the past, a book of the communal chamber (which was made of wood) was falsified by having a page pulled out, or a stave removed from a salt-measure. <note>Dante refers to two scandals: the "ledger" refers to the tearing out of a page of public records by Nicolò Acciaiuoli, and the "stave" refers to a fraudulent reduction in the size of the legal salt measure by Durante de' Chiaramontesi.</note> **SO THE bank is eased:** just as he previously called the descent a "steep bank" because one rushes down such places with speed, so on the contrary he calls the bank "eased" or slow when one climbs. **BUT On this side and that the other stone scrapes.** Where the stairs were, the slope was eased. But on either side of the stairs, it was so narrow that anyone climbing would brush against it; this denotes that the path of virtue is narrow.

We turned our persons there;
"Blessed are the poor in spirit" <note>original: "beati pauperes spiritu"</note> voices
sang so that speech could not describe it.
Ah, how different are those openings
from the infernal ones! For here one enters
with songs, and down there with fierce laments.
Already we were mounting up the holy stairs,
and I seemed to be much lighter
than I had seemed on the level ground before.

And I: "Master, what heavy thing
has been lifted from me, so that almost no
labor is felt by me in walking?"
He replied: "When the P's that have remained
still on your face, though nearly faded,
shall be, like the first, entirely erased,
Your feet will be so overcome by good will
that they will not only feel no fatigue,
but it will be a delight for them to be urged upward."

Then I did like those who go
with something on their head unknown to them,
except that others' signs make them suspect,
Because the hand helps to find out,
and searches and finds, and fulfills that office
which cannot be provided by the sight;
And with the fingers of my right hand spread...

<column-break/>

...that they may climb to heaven. **O HUMAN race:** This is an exclamation. **BORN TO climb:** made by God to ascend to heaven. **WHY AT a little wind do you fall so:** why do you let yourself be so conquered by worldly honors that you fall into the vice of pride? For just as we say one "rises" when practicing virtue, because it guides us to elevate the soul to divine things, so he who commits vice "falls," because all his thoughts are on low and fleeting things. And he chose the word "wind" excellently, because as shown above, the glory of worldly goods is like the wind. **HE LED me where the rock was cut.** That is, the mountain, which our ancestors called "roccia" (rock) or "rocca" (fortress), just as the Latins call them *arces*. And he imagines here that the stairs were cut by the force of a chisel to climb to the second terrace. **He beat his wings upon the forehead** of Dante to remove one of the seven sins, he being now purged of Pride, which is one of the seven mortal sins. One wing is "prevenient and illuminating grace"; the other is "cooperating and perfecting grace." These ensure that God forgives our faults. He places the sins on the forehead because sins ought to be revealed. **THEN HE PERMITTED me a safe passage.** The way to purgation is not safe unless pride is extinguished, because that often [hinders it].

The souls who were being purged of pride showed joy at Dante's ascent by singing. Because here there is no envy of another's good, but only charity. And they sang: **"Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven."** <note>original: "beati pauperes spiritu: quoniam ipsorum est regnum celorum"</note> To be poor in spirit is nothing other than to be lacking in pride. Therefore, those spirits rejoiced that Dante had already been purged of such a vice.

Dante shows that he has become very light. To which Virgil responds by explaining that this lightness comes to him because one of the seven sins has already been erased. But when all are erased, not only will the climb not be a struggle, but it will be a supreme delight. And note that Virgil says the first sin was entirely extinguished, and the others were nearly extinguished. This denotes that when the vice of pride is entirely purged, the other vices remain largely purged as well.

The poet was not aware that one of the seven sins had been entirely removed and the others greatly diminished. Therefore, moved by Virgil's words, he searched with his spread fingers—meaning his simple fingers—and found six. And it happened to him like someone carrying something on their head without knowing it; but seeing the laughter of those around, and the eyes being unable to do their job (because they cannot see the top of the head), the hands fill in. And through them, the man becomes certain of what he did not know. These words signify that the senses cannot be a true judge if the soul is still [un]purged of any vice. But reason...

<header>PURGATORY</header>

...shows us by its signs. Man does not notice the sins he carries upon his head <note>The "sins on the head" refer to the seven letters "P" (for *Peccata*, or sins) carved onto Dante’s forehead by the gate-keeping angel; each "P" is removed as he completes the penance for that specific vice.</note> until he is purged of pride; for pride makes us so swollen <note>The original Italian *timidi* is likely a transcription error for *tumidi*, meaning "swollen" or "pompous," especially as it is paired here with *gonfiati*.</note> and puffed up that we believe ourselves to be virtuous. But once pride is set aside, only then do we begin to perceive our errors. Virgil smiled: for the intellect laughs at the ignorance of the senses, and he becomes, as it were, another Democritus. <note>Democritus was an ancient Greek philosopher known as the "laughing philosopher" because he mocked the follies and ignorance of mankind.</note>

### CANTO XIII OF THE SECOND CANTICLE OF DANTE.

**HAVING** left the first terrace <note>The Italian *balzo* refers to the rocky ledges or terraces of Mount Purgatory.</note> where we saw the punishments of the proud, we now enter the second, having already climbed the stairs, in which envy is purged. Envy is a reciprocal torment of the soul: which consumes itself for the good of others, and such pain returns upon itself. And Augustine said envy is the grief taken from another's happiness. Whence Horace: *the envious man is burned by envy within and without* <note>original: "inuidus inuidia comburitur intus & extra"</note>. Also: *The envious man grows lean at the prosperity of another* <note>original: "Inuidus alterius rebus increscit opimis"</note>. And Solomon, wishing to dem-

---

<margin>1</margin>
**W**e were at the top of the stairs
where for the second time the mountain
that rids one of evil as they climb is cut back.
Here a cornice binds the hill
all around, just like the first,
except that its arc curves more sharply.
There is no shadow there, nor any visible sign;
the bank and the path both appeared bare,
with the livid color of the stone-pit.

"If we wait here to ask people for directions,"
the poet reasoned, "I fear perhaps
that our choice will have too much delay."
Then he fixed his eyes intently upon the sun;
he made his right side the center for his movement,
and turned the left part of himself.
"O sweet light, in whose confidence I enter
upon the new path, do thou lead me,"
he said, "as one ought to be led in this place.
You warm the world, you shine above it;
unless another reason urges the contrary,
your rays must always be our guides."
As far as one counts for a mile here,
so far had we already gone there,
in a short time because of our ready will.
And toward us, spirits were heard flying,
though not seen, speaking
courteous invitations to the table of love.
The first voice that passed by in flight
said loudly, "They have no wine" <note>original: "uinum non habent"</note>,
and went on repeating it behind us.
And before it had completely faded away
due to the distance, another called out,
"I am Orestes" <note>Orestes and his friend Pylades are a classical example of selfless love; Pylades tried to die in Orestes' place.</note> as it passed,
and it too did not stop.
"O father," I said, "what voices are these?"
And as I asked, behold the third,
saying: "Love those from whom you have suffered evil."

**B**ecause in this terrace envy is punished, which is most cold and therefore "livid," the poet—not without great reason—introduces the spirits whose words demonstrate charity: whose flame lightens the cold. We have shown in another place for what reason he does not distinctly place the seven mortal sins in Hell as he makes special mention of envy and vainglory here. *They have no wine* <note>original: "Vinum non habent"</note>. These are the words of Mary to Christ at the wedding <note>The Wedding at Cana</note> where it is expressed that Mary did not act out of a woman’s typical nature: which, being naturally eager for glory, cannot look upon another's excellence without spite; but moved by charity, she grieved for the lack at the wedding. These examples must always be on the mountain for those who purge envy, and in imitation of Mary, one must pray to God to change water into wine—that is, the cold of envy into the warmth of charity. Or rather, change the waters—that is, the tastelessness of tribulations—into wine, which is to say, into joy. The poet intends, therefore, that if seeing too much of another's good generates this sin, its purgation must be *not seeing*; and for this reason, a little further on, he will sew their eyes shut. And similarly, he portrays the spirits as inviting: who, flying through the air, give sweet invitations to the age of love, which is charity. Because everything is purged by its contrary, charity is that which entirely extinguishes envy. SPIRITS speaking at the table of love, speaking courteous invitations...

<column-break/>

onstrate how much torment the envious man gives himself, said: *He who rejoices in the ruin of another shall not go unpunished* <note>original: "Qui in ruina letatur alterius non erit impunitus"</note>. We were, then, at the top of the stairs that lead onto the second cornice: which "un-evils" <note>The translator notes that *dismala* is a verb meaning to remove or strip away evil.</note>, that is, removes the evil and the sin from whoever climbs there. This girds and encircles the mountain, creating a level path around it. But its arc "curves more sharply," that is, it makes a smaller circuit. Because, as we said above: the more the mountain rises, the more it "thins" <note>The mountain of Purgatory is a cone; therefore, higher terraces have a smaller circumference.</note>. And for this reason, the circle of the cornice becomes smaller. And thus, as the points go down, the lower ones are always larger. Therefore, the punishments similarly "thin out." Neither shadow nor sign: neither visible painting nor sculpture, as there was in the terrace below. Instead, the path and the bank remain bare and simple. And the stones of which the cornice is made are of a livid color. He says there is no painting or sculpture because envy does not manifest or appear except when mixed with another sin. Or perhaps he said "shadow," meaning no soul was visible, because the envious do not walk along the cornice and were in a distant place. The livid color <note>A leaden, bluish-gray color associated with bruising and cold.</note> is appropriate for envy, because it is born from cold; and envy is cold because it is contrary to charity.

**B**ecause in this terrace envy is purged, and the penalty of the envious is that they are blind <note>Their eyelids are sewn shut with wire, as explained later in the Canto.</note>, Virgil therefore doubts: that by waiting for someone to show the way, their "chosen hour"—that is, their choice—would be too delayed. And having said these words, he looked at the sun, and while looking at it, he turned to the right side. By the sun, we understand our intellect, and also the illuminating grace of God. For just as the sun shows visible things, so these two show the truth. Speculation, therefore, took such a sun for a leader. "He made his right side the center for his movement": when we want to make a circle with a compass, the point that stays still acts as the center for the circle guided by the one that moves. And finally, when standing upright we wish to turn, one foot stays still as the center and the other moves. And if we want to turn to the right side, the right foot stays still and the left moves toward the right side. Virgil will therefore take a good path by gazing at the sun: which will show him the way to go to the right—that is, to use the light of intellect and divine grace in good works. "O sweet light": a prayer appropriate to the sun, because in visible things it produces all these effects. But more appropriate is that Sun which illuminates the intellect: the illuminating grace of God. Under whose confidence Virgil—that is, the rational part of man—enters into the purgatorial virtues, which are a "new path" to a man not yet accustomed to them. "You warm the world": it is fitting that whoever knows the good through illuminating grace should be kindled with a marvelous love for it. "You shine above it": because from Seraphic love one comes to Cherubic light <note>Landino references the celestial hierarchy where Seraphim represent Love and Cherubim represent Wisdom/Knowledge.</note>, as we have often mentioned, and will say more clearly elsewhere.

<summary>Dante and Virgil ascend to the second terrace of Purgatory, where the sin of Envy is purged. Unlike the first terrace, this one is bare and "livid" in color, featuring vocal examples of charity (the contrary of envy) rather than physical sculptures.</summary>
<keywords>Envy, Charity, Virgil, Sun as Intellect, Mary at Cana, Orestes, Livid color, Purgatory, Canto XIII</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the Second Terrace of Mount Purgatory. Having introduced the "Whip of Envy" (examples of the opposite virtue, Charity), the author now explains the specific examples heard by Dante and begins describing the physical appearance and punishment of the envious souls.</meta>

### CANTO XIII.

They went inviting—meaning, by speaking they invited the souls who had to be purged of envy—to the table of love, which is to say, to charity. And he said "table" because the first voice took from the Gospel of the wedding feast, saying: **"THEY HAVE NO WINE."** <note>original: "Vinū non habent" (John 2:3)</note>. And certainly, just as envy detracts from and stains the honor and use of one's neighbor, so charity exerts effort and industry to preserve it. The Evangelist Luke writes that at the wedding held in Cana of Galilee, the Virgin Mary, moved by charity upon seeing the wine was lacking, turned to Jesus and said "they have no wine." This proceeded from the highest charity. Note that the voice was spoken and then reiterated, or repeated. It is to be noted that charity never tires of grieving for the neighbor's misfortune, and always reminds God of their need, both before it comes, when it comes, and after it has arrived.

**"I AM ORESTES."** He has placed here one kind of charity: that which exists in those who rejoice in the good of a friend and work so that it may come to pass. Now he places another kind, which is found in few. These are those who, to save a friend, offer themselves to death, as is read of Orestes and Pylades. Orestes was the son of Agamemnon and Clytemnestra. But while her husband was occupied in the Trojan War, Clytemnestra grew hot with love for Aegisthus, so that in order not to lose her beloved, she proposed to kill her husband upon his return together with Aegisthus. Thus, after simulated welcomes, she offered him a garment which he put on, but it was not open at the top; and while he was thus entangled in it, she killed him. Orestes, his son, still a boy, was stolen away by Strophius his father-in-law to later take revenge for his father. Because of such matricide, he became mad. Having contracted a friendship with Pylades, the son of the aforementioned Strophius, he went with him to the Tauric region, where there was the temple of Diana Dictynna, in which the mad were freed from the Furies. There, being liberated, King Thoas, a most cruel man, wished to sacrifice Orestes to the said goddess. But because he could not distinguish him from Pylades, there was born a wonderful example of friendship. For Pylades, to save his friend, affirmed he was Orestes; and Orestes, so that his friend would not perish in his place, showed with an oath that he was Orestes, so that the King might take him and free Pylades from danger. The King, amazed by such a wonderful friendship, pardoned both of them. Solinus writes that the bones of Orestes were found by the Lacedaemonians in the city of Tegea, which when brought back to their place, made a body seven cubits long. I omit many things in this history, but let it suffice that the poet places Orestes here for that kind of charity through which a man willingly faces death to save his friend.

**"LOVE THOSE BY WHOM YOU HAVE SUFFERED EVIL."** It is true charity to rejoice in the good of one's neighbor and to labor for it to come; but it is greater to submit oneself to manifest dangers for a friend. But what shall we say of those who love those from whom they have received injury? Which is the precept of the Savior: **"Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you."** <note>original: "Diligite inimicos ueftros: Et orate pro perſequētibus uos."</note> And the Apostle: **"Returning evil to no one."** <note>original: "Nulli pro malo reddentes."</note> And Luke: **"Love those who love you, and those who hate you, and your enemies. And your reward will be great."** <note>original: "Diligite eos: qui uos diligunt: & eos: qui uos odiunt: & inimicos ueftros. Et erit merces ueftra magna."</note> This is therefore the third kind of charity, through which we love our enemies.

---

<columns>2</columns>

"The good master: 'This circle lashes
the sin of envy, and therefore
the cords of the whip are drawn from love.
The bridle must be of a contrary sound;
I believe you will hear it, in my judgment,
before you reach the pass of pardon.
But fix your eyes firmly through the air,
and you will see people sitting before us,
each one seated along the cliffside.'"
Then I opened my eyes wider than before;
I looked ahead and saw shades with cloaks
not different from the color of the stone.

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'C' at the beginning of the commentary, surrounded by ornate foliage.</image-desc>
Virgil continues the exposition and interpretation of the voices heard. He shows that because in this circle and terrace envy is lashed—that is, punished and purged—it is necessary that the cords of this whip—that is, such punishment—be drawn from love. And the reason is that the <term>bridle<gloss>the "freno," or examples of the punishment of envy that restrain the soul from sin</gloss></term>, which does not let us run into the sin of envy but draws us back when we have run into it, must be the opposite. And nothing is more contrary to envy than charity. Therefore, the voices already mentioned, which draw us back from envy, must proceed from charity. But Virgil will advise him better of this before they arrive at the "pass of pardon"—that is, the stairs which climb to the third level and take away the purged souls with the remission of sin. Afterward, he admonishes Dante to look fixedly, and he will see the envious and their pains; for "looking fixedly" signifies nothing else but turning the sharpness of the intellect and fixing it in such consideration. Admonished, Dante obeyed the precept and, looking fixedly, saw all these things. Especially the souls who were purging themselves, wearing cloaks of a <term>livid<gloss>a bluish-gray or leaden color, traditionally associated with envy</gloss></term> color, just as it was shown above that the stone of this place was also of that color. Similarly, Ovid: **"Nor was the stone white; her mind had infected it."** <note>original: "Nec lapis albus erat ſua mēs infecerat illam"</note>

---

And elsewhere: **"Paleness sits on her face."** <note>original: "Pallor in ore ſedet"</note> These were sitting along the cliff, singing litanies in such a way that they could move every hard heart to compassion. He saw them clothed in <term>vile hairshirts<gloss>original: "vil cilliccio"; a rough garment made of goat hair (cilice) used for penance</gloss></term>. They were supported by the bank, and one leaned his head upon the shoulder of the other, as the blind do, who stand in a line begging, leaning together to move people to compassion not only with words but also in that manner. He adds afterward that they could not see anything, because they were <term>acciglati<gloss>their eyelids were sewn shut with wire</gloss></term> with iron wire, just as they sew the eyelids of hawks caught in the forest so that they do not struggle. The poet gives these nine conditions to the envious person desirous of purging himself of such a vice not without great ingenuity and learning.

They sit to purge their speed, not only of the body but more of the soul, which they used in investigating the happiness of others to disturb it, and their misery to take pleasure in it. And Ovid, describing the dwelling of Envy:
> **The house is hidden in the lowest valleys of a cave,**
> **Bereft of sun, accessible to no wind.**
> **Sad and full of sluggish cold, and such**
> **That it always lacks fire, and always abounds in darkness.** <note>Quoted from Ovid's *Metamorphoses*</note>

Their livid cloak demonstrates the "lividness" of envy, as has already been said. Whence Ovid says of Aglauros: **"Nor was the color white; her mind had infected it."** And elsewhere: **"Paleness sat on her face."** **"AND THAT IT BE OF VILE HAIRSHIRT"**: this is made of bristles and not of wool; whence it is a cold garment because it is a thin weave, and it is rough, and it pricks and gnaws the flesh of whoever wears it, to denote that envy is cold, for it extinguishes charity; and he who clothes himself in envy is always pricked and gnawed by the happiness he sees in others, and consumes himself and loses his flesh thereby. Whence the satirist prudently said: **"The envious man grows lean at the prosperity of another."** <note>original: "Inuidus alterius rebus macreſcit opimis"</note> And Jerome encourages the envious man to clothe himself in hairshirt.

They sit leaning against the rock because the envious man is always in coldness and hardness, which two things are in the stone. We can also refer this to him who purges envy: who, sitting for the reason said above, leans upon something stable and immovable. **"THEY LEAN THEIR HEADS ONE UPON THE OTHER"**, which denotes that one must correct the other. They sang litanies to counter their "evil speaking." They have their eyes sewn with iron wire—that is, with the virtue of fortitude. They keep their eyes closed for the reason said above. And certainly, he who purges himself of envy must keep his eyes closed to worldly goods, and for this the Psalmist says: **"Turn away my eyes lest they see vanity."** <note>original: "Auerte oculos meos ne uideant uanitatem"</note> Or we might say that the envious are blind. Whence Job: **"By day they shall encounter darkness, and as if in night they shall grope at noon."** <note>original: "Per diem incurrent tenebras: & quaſi in nocte ſic palpabunt in meridie."</note> And Gregory—

<summary>This page discusses the spiritual and physical nature of Envy as presented in Dante's Purgatorio, contrasting it with Charity through the examples of the Wedding at Cana, Orestes and Pylades, and Christ's commands. It describes the punishment of the envious: wearing livid hairshirts and having their eyelids sewn shut with wire to teach them to look away from worldly goods.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the Second Terrace of Purgatory, where the sin of Envy is purged. On the previous page, the author began explaining the "Whip of Envy"—examples of Charity that contrast with the sin. Here, the text transitions into a description of the suffering souls and Dante’s interaction with them.</meta>

# PURGATORY

The mind of the envious is afflicted by the good of another and is darkened by a ray of light. <note>original: "Mens invidi cum alieno bono affligitur de radio lucis offuscatur."</note> And in Matthew 20: The envious grow sick from the health of others and die from their life. <note>original: "Invidi de sanitate aliorum infirmantur: & de vita moriuntur."</note> And Socrates desired that the envious should have eyes and ears in every city so that they might be more tormented <note>by seeing and hearing of the success of others</note>. And Isaiah: Woe to you who call good evil and evil good. <note>original: "Ve qui dicitis bonum malum: & malum bonum."</note> The tears signify true contrition and repentance.

And after we had gone a little further
I heard a cry: "Mary, pray for us,"
then "Michael," and "Peter," and "All Saints."
I do not believe there walks on earth today
a man so hardened that he would not be pierced
by compassion for what I saw next.
For when I had drawn so near to them
that their actions became clear to me,
heavy grief was milked from my eyes.
They seemed to me covered in wretched haircloth, <term>haircloth (cilicio): a rough, itchy garment made of animal hair, worn as a penance.</term>
and one supported the other with his shoulder,
and all of them were supported by the bank.
Just so the blind, who lack the means to live,
stand at pardons <note>church festivals where alms were given</note> to beg for their needs,
and one sinks his head upon the other
so that pity may quickly be moved in others,
not just by the sound of their words,
but by their appearance, which pleads no less.
And just as the sun does not reach the blind,
so to the shades in the place I now speak of,
the light of heaven will not grant itself;
for a wire of iron pierces all their eyelids
and sews them up, just as is done to a wild sparrowhawk
because it will not otherwise stay quiet.
It seemed to me I was doing them an injury,
walking along seeing others without being seen,
and so I turned to my wise counsel <note>Virgil</note>.
He well knew what the mute one wished to say, <note>Dante refers to himself as "the mute" because he had not yet spoken his question aloud.</note>
and therefore did not wait for my question,
but said: "Speak, and be brief and to the point."
Virgil was coming beside me on that side
of the cornice from which one might fall,
since it is girded by no outer rim.
On the other side of me were the devout
shades, who through the horrible stitching
were straining so that they bathed their cheeks with tears.
I turned to them and began: "O people certain
to see the high light
which your desire alone holds in its care—
may grace soon dissolve the scum
of your conscience so that the river of the mind
may descend clearly through it;
tell me, for it would be gracious and dear to me,
if any soul among you here is Italian;
perhaps it will be good for him if I learn it."

<column-break/>

**He well knew what the mute one wished to say.** This means Virgil understood what I wanted to say even though I did not speak it. And certainly, reason understands appetite <note>desire</note> even though it does not speak. Seeing, then, Dante’s desire to speak with those souls, he permitted it, but limited him by commanding him to be brief and "to the point"—brief in words, and "to the point," meaning cautious in his meaning. **Once they have climbed the bank they turn to the right hand.** Virgil, being toward the edge, remained on the right hand. Thus we note two things here: that Dante has Virgil on his right hand, and that he has him on the side where there is danger of falling, because the edge of the terrace is not "girdled," that is, it is not surrounded by any railing. It is appropriate that reason should be on the right, and thus here it can be found where there is danger of falling. **MAY GRACE SOON** dissolve the scum. The "scum" <note>schiume</note> is the impurity of water, and here it stands for the stain on the soul, which is washed as it purges itself. **SO THAT CLEARLY** through it. The human mind is the origin of the appetite; if the appetite is obedient to reason, it flows and moves toward the things it desires, and it flows "clearly," that is, without stain. Thus, as we have shown in Virgil and in this poet, the appetite is likened to the movement of water.

> "O my brother, each is a citizen
> of one true city; but you mean to say one
> who lived in Italy as a pilgrim."
> This I seemed to hear as an answer
> coming from a bit further on than where I stood,
> so I made myself heard even further in that direction.
> Among the others I saw a shade that was waiting
> in its look—and if someone should ask: how?
> It was lifting its chin in the manner of a blind man.

Dante asks if any soul among them was Italian. But this soul who responds <note>Sapia of Siena</note>, because she was outside the body, could more truly consider the soul's real homeland. She corrects Dante's incorrect premise, which was that the soul’s homeland is where the body was born. But since the soul is created by God from nothing, in His image and likeness, it cannot have any other homeland than the celestial one, nor any other creator; for He was neither Florentine nor Roman, nor made of the matter of which the body is composed. Therefore, if I say "my body is Florentine," I do not err, because it was composed here. But the soul comes from God and has no other homeland than heaven, as we demonstrated above. All the Platonists and the excellent philosophers sing of this. So do the theologians. And Ovid: *Every soil is a homeland to the brave man, as the sea is to the fish.* <note>original: "Omne solum forti patria est ut piscibus equor."</note> **AMONG THE OTHERS** I saw a shade that was waiting: because the eyes are what most clearly show our affections, and that soul could not open them, Dante describes the gesture through which he understood she was waiting; and this was that, being unable to look at him, she lifted up her chin.

<summary>Dante describes the Envious, whose eyes are sewn shut with wire as penance, and speaks with Sapia, who explains that the soul's true citizenship is in Heaven rather than any earthly city.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Dante and the souls on the Second Terrace of Purgatory, where the sin of Envy is purged. On the previous page, Dante observed the souls whose eyelids are sewn shut with wire. Here, he speaks with Sapia of Siena, who explains her story and the nature of her sin.</meta>

# PURGATORY

### ff iii

->facti<-

"Spirit," I said, "who humbles yourself to climb,
if you are the one who answered me,
make yourself known to me by place or name."
"I was Sienese," she replied, "and with these
others, I mend my wicked life here,
weeping to Him that He may lend Himself to us.
I was not wise, although 'Sapia'
I was named, and I was at the harms of others
far more joyful than at my own good fortune.
And so that you do not think I deceive you,
hear if I was as foolish as I tell you:
already descending the arch of my years, <note>Sapia was already old (past thirty-five, the "arch" of life) when the events she describes took place.</note>
my fellow citizens were near Colle,
joined in battle with their adversaries,
and I prayed to God for what He willed.
They were broken there, and turned into the bitter
steps of flight; and seeing the pursuit,
I felt a joy surpassing all others,
so much so that I turned up my bold face,
crying to God: 'Now I fear You no more!'
as the blackbird does during a brief fair spell." <note>A reference to a proverb about a blackbird who mocks God or winter as soon as a little sun appears.</note>
I sought peace with God at the very end
of my life; and even then my debt
would not have been reduced by penance,
had it not been for one who remembered me,
Pier Pettinaio, in his holy prayers, <term>Pier Pettinaio: A Sienese comb-seller known for his holiness and charity.</term>
who, out of charity, felt sorry for me.
But who are you, who go asking of
our condition with your eyes unbound,
as I believe, and who speak with breath?"
"My eyes," I said, "will yet be taken from me here,
but for a short time only, for small is the offense
committed by turning them with envy.
Far greater is the fear that holds my soul
suspended of the torment below;
already the weight from down there hangs heavy on me." <note>Dante admits he suffers more from the sin of Pride, which is purged on the terrace below, than from Envy.</note>
And she to me: "Who then has led you
up here among us, if you expect to return below?"
And I: "This one who is with me and says not a word.
And I am living; therefore ask of me,
elect spirit, if you wish that I move
my mortal feet for you further on the other side."
"Oh, this is such a new thing to hear,"
she replied, "that it is a great sign that God loves you;
therefore, help me sometimes with your prayer.
And I ask you, by that which you most desire,
if you ever tread the land of Tuscany,
that you restore my reputation among my kin.
You will see them among that vain people
who hope in Talamone, and will lose there
more hope than in searching for the Diana; <term>Diana: A legendary underground river the Sienese believed flowed beneath their city.</term>
but the admirals will lose even more there."

<column-break/>

Sapia was a noble Sienese lady, but she lived in exile in Colle. She bore such envy toward the Sienese state that, when the Sienese were defeated not far from Colle, she took such joy in it that, raising her eyes to heaven, she said: "God, do to me from now on the worst You can, for I shall live and die content." "And I prayed to God for what He willed": because Sapia's prayers were not only most unjust but also impious, and nonetheless what she desired followed. It seems irrational that God, the supreme justice, should grant her request. Therefore Sapia says: "and I prayed to God for what He willed," as if to say: although I prayed to Him, He did not condescend to my unjust prayers, but He did what I desired because He willed it as a punishment for the sins of the Sienese. "So much so that I turned up my bold face": this is the sin of pride, and from pride, as we have shown, envy is born. But we must understand that she had been purged of this in the terrace below. "As the blackbird does": it is a common proverb that this bird says, when spring arrives, "I do not care for you, Lord, for I have escaped the winter." "I sought peace": at the end of my life I turned to penance, which reconciles peace with God. And although through penance I escaped Hell, nonetheless my debt would not yet be diminished by penance—that is, the debt I owed to God for sins committed—but the prayers of Pier Pettinaio have hastened and shortened the time I was to stay in Ante-Purgatory. Pier Pettinaio was a Florentine <note>Actually Sienese, though the text says "fioretio."</note>, a very religious man and a hermit. "With your eyes unbound": as if to say, "you are not one of us who are punished here with eyes sewn shut." "And who speak with breath": you speak as one still living, for souls without bodies do not breathe (that is, inhale). "As I believe": because, not seeing, she could not know for certain, but she believed it through conjecture. Dante responds and shows that he does not have his eyes closed like them because he is not yet dead. But when his soul is released from his body to Purgatory, he shows that it will still be punished for envy. "But for a short time": because he is little infected by such a sin. But he fears more the pains and torment below, that is, of the first terrace where pride is punished, because he knows himself to be more involved in that than in this. And certainly, in a generous soul and a most sharp intellect and great judgment, not much envy can fall, because envy being between equals, no one or very few are his equal. Furthermore, this envy comes from a small soul, and from one who values the goods of the body and of fortune much more than they are worth. And certainly, whoever considers on one hand the status, riches, and dignities, and on the other the hardships, anxieties, and unbearable labors involved in acquiring and maintaining them, and the time we consume in this—which we could put into the study of true sciences which show us eternal life and the true way that leads us there—or at least in some action by which we might benefit ourselves and our neighbor, would without doubt deserve not envy, but compassion. But the proud man, having obtained a superior position, uses liberality and magnanimity because he has a generous soul, and it seems to him he is as superior to others as the great benefits he grants make them obliged to him. "And I," Dante, replied to Sapia. "This one," that is, Virgil, "who says not a word": he is silent but he has led me. Virgil is silent because, as has been said, the superior intellect does not seek out particulars, but admonishes Dante to seek them, because the inferior intellect has all its strength from the superior. "Oh, this is a thing to hear": certainly it is not without manifest signs that someone is loved by God when they receive special graces from Him that are given to few. "Among that vain people": vanity is the specific and peculiar vice of the Sienese. "Who hope in Talamone": they have hope that, having acquired the port of Talamone, they will become great men at sea. Thus they are vain since they hope for what is not to be hoped for. Talamone is a castle and port at the edge of the Sienese Maremma. "And they will lose more hope than in finding the Diana": it was the opinion in those times in Siena that there was a subterranean river that ran beneath Siena. For this reason, not without great expense, they had excavations made in many places, hoping to find such water. Therefore, the hope they have of being able to build a fleet at sea by having Talamone will deceive them no less than the hope of finding this water they call Diana; and especially the principal citizens, who even hope to be made "admirals," that is, captains of the fleet.

<summary>Dante speaks with Sapia of Siena, an envious soul who rejoiced in her own city's defeat. The commentary explains the historical context of her life and the Sienese obsession with the port of Talamone and the mythical river Diana.</summary>

->CANTO XIV OF THE SECOND CANTICLE BY DANTE.<-

"And who is this who circles our mountain
before death has given him flight,
and opens his eyes at will and closes them?"
"I do not know who he is, but I know he is not alone:
you ask him, for you are closer to him,
and welcome him gently so that he may speak."
Thus two spirits, leaning one against the other,
reasoned about me on the right hand side;
then they turned their faces upward to speak to me.
And one said, "O soul that, still fixed
within the body, journey toward heaven,
for charity’s sake console us and tell us:
From where do you come and who are you? For you make us
marvel as much at the grace shown to you
as a thing must that has never happened before."
And I: "Through the middle of Tuscany there spreads
a little stream that rises in Falterona <note>A mountain in the Apennines where the Arno begins.</note>
and a course of a hundred miles does not satisfy it.
From over its banks I bring this body;
to tell you who I am would be to speak in vain,
for my name does not yet sound loudly."
"If I well grasp your meaning
with my intellect," then replied to me
the one who spoke first, "you speak of the Arno."
And the other said to him: "Why did he hide
the name of that river,
just as one does with horrible things?"
And the shade who was asked this question
acquitted himself <note>The Italian 'sisdebito' implies fulfilling an obligation to answer.</note> thus: "I do not know;
but it is right that the name of such a valley perish.
For from its beginning, where it is so pregnant—
the rugged mountain chain from which Peloro <note>Cape Peloro in Sicily; the text refers to the theory that the Apennines once connected to Sicily.</note> was cut—
that in few places does it pass beyond that mark,
down to where it yields itself to restore
that which the sky dries from the sea,
whence the rivers have that which flows with them,
Virtue is fled from as an enemy
by all, like a snake, either through the misfortune
of the place or by evil habit that goads them.
Wherefore the inhabitants of that miserable valley
have so changed their nature
that it seems Circe <note>The enchantress from Greek mythology who turned men into beasts.</note> had them in her pasture.
Among foul hogs, more worthy of acorns
than of any food made for human use,
it first directs its poor path;
Then, coming further down, it finds curs <note>Small, snappish dogs; referring to the citizens of Arezzo.</note>
snarling more than their power warrants,
and at them, in disdain, it twists its snout away.
It goes on falling; and the larger it grows..."

<column-break/>

The purgation of the sin of envy continues in this fourteenth canto. Through the conversation of Master Guido del Duca of Brettinoro and Master Rinieri da Caluoli of Romagna, the poet laments the miserable conditions of Italy, and especially of our Republic <note>Florence</note>. He also brings Virgil to speak of envy. **WHO IS THIS**: Two spirits reasoning together; they marvel that Dante, before death, has come to Purgatory. **I DO NOT KNOW WHO HE IS**: Thus the other spirit responds. **SO THAT HE MAY SPEAK**: Speak to perfection. <note>The original uses 'parli a colo', which the commentator interprets as a 'full stop' or point of perfection in speech.</note> **THAT HAS NEVER HAPPENED BEFORE**: It seems he contradicts himself, having affirmed in the second canto of the *Inferno* that Aeneas went to the underworld and the Elysian fields; to which you may respond that he speaks hyperbolically, meaning it happens so rarely it can be called "never." **FROM WHERE DO YOU COME and who are you?**: Similar to the Virgilian Venus saying: "But who are you at last, and from what shores have you come?" <note>original: "Sed uos qui tandem quibus aut uenistis ab oris?" from Aeneid I.369.</note>

The other spirit was Master Rinieri, who, not speaking directly to Dante, said to Guido: "Why has this man hidden the name of that river, nor named the Arno, as one does when speaking of horrendous things, which out of fear one does not name?" And the shade who was questioned acquitted himself, that is, he responded. For whoever is asked a question about honest things is bound to answer. Therefore, when he answers, he "acquits" himself, that is, he pays his debt. And he said the name of this river was never worthy, and therefore it is right that it perish. And it was never worthy because it has no inhabitants adorned with any virtue. To demonstrate this, he begins to describe it: he places its birth in Falterona, which is part of the Apennines. He says therefore that from the start of the Arno, which is born where the rugged mountain—that is, the Apennines, which are like the Alps—is so pregnant, meaning swollen and high, or truly pregnant with water, because in a small space it produces both the Arno and the Tiber. **IN FEW PLACES DOES IT PASS BEYOND THAT MARK**: although the Apennines are very long, nevertheless in few places are they higher than at Falterona. **FROM WHICH PELORO WAS CUT**: It was the opinion of the ancients that the Apennines, of which we spoke in the *Inferno*, reach not only to Reggio, but formerly continued into Sicily. Its final part was that which later remained as a mountain in Sicily and is called Peloro.

Before we clarify the words spoken by the soul, understand that of these two spirits, the one who speaks is Master Guido del Duca of Brettinoro in Romagna. And the other to whom he speaks is Master Rinieri da Caluoli of Forlì. **SWINE** he calls all those of the Casentino down to Arezzo, and especially the Conti Guidi, men of great luxury. **POOR PATH**: because it has little water. **CURS**: these are the people of Arezzo, whom he likens to 'botoli,' small-bodied dogs. He wants to show that the Aretines have much disdain but little strength. **IN DISDAIN TWISTS ITS SNOUT**: because after it is near Arezzo, the river turns to the right and leaves Arezzo behind. **THE MORE IT FINDS DOGS BECOMING WOLVES**: the cur snarls and barks, but the wolf is used to represent the greedy man, the predator, and the thief. He intends this for the gentlemen and counts who were in the Valdarno, and partly for the Florentines. **DESCENDING THEN THROUGH DEEPER POOLS**: he places those of the lower Valdarno next, and finally the Pisans, whom he calls **FOXES** to denote that they are full of fraud and deceit. **I WILL NOT BE SILENT**: he places three things in this tercet. First, he shows he does not care if he is overheard, which signifies he is already clear of conscience; he speaks not out of envy or hatred, but out of just indignation. Second, because he hopes to be useful to Dante by making him cautious. And in the third place, he shows that having to speak of future things, he will tell the truth, since he has heard it from a true spirit. **I SEE YOUR NEPHEW**: This was Master Fulcieri da Caluoli of Forlì, of whom he predicts that he will become the mayor <term>Podestà</term> of Florence and for a price will kill many. We wrote in the sixth canto of the *Inferno* that in the year 1302 the Blacks were brought back into Florence by Charles of Valois <note>referred to as 'Charles Lackland'</note>. These men...

### ...the more it finds dogs becoming wolves,
### that cursed and ill-fated ditch.
### Descending then through more deep waters,

### it finds the foxes so full of fraud
### that they fear no wit that might trap them.
### I will not cease to speak though another hears me;

### and it will be good for him if he still remembers
### what a true spirit unfolds to me.
### I see your grandson <note>Fulcieri da Calboli, who became the governor (Podestà) of Florence in 1303 and was known for his cruelty toward the White Guelphs.</note> becoming

### a hunter of those wolves upon the bank
### of the fierce river, and he terrifies them all.
### He sells their flesh while it is still alive;

### then he kills them like an ancient beast;
### he robs many of life, and strips himself of honor.
### Bloody he emerges from the dismal woods;

### he leaves it such that a thousand years from now
### it will not re-forest to its former state.
### As at the announcement of future harms,

### the face of him who listens is troubled,
### from whatever side the peril assails and bites him;
### so I saw the other soul, which had turned

### to listen, become troubled and grow sad,
### after it had gathered those words to itself.
### The hearing of the one and the sight of the other

### made me desirous of knowing their names,
### and I asked for them, mixed with prayers.
### Because the spirit who first spoke to me

### began again: "You want me to bend myself
### to doing for you what you will not do for me.
### But since God wills that so much of His grace

### should shine through you, I will not be stingy;
### therefore, know that I am Guido del Duca.
### My blood was so consumed by envy

### that if I had seen a man become happy,
### you would have seen me sprinkled with livid color.
### From my sowing, I reap such chaff.

### O human race, why do you set your heart
### where there is need for the exclusion of companionship?
### This is Rinieri; this is the prize and the honor

### of the House of Calboli, where no one
### has since been made heir to his valor;

### And not only his blood has become stripped
### between the mountains and the sea and the Reno
### of the good required for truth and for sport."

<column-break/>

...fearing much the power and favor that the Whites <note>The "White" faction of the Guelph party in Florence.</note> held in Florence, they corrupted Messer Fulcieri to seize many of the White party. Among these were Messer Betto Gherardini, Masino and Donato Cavalcanti, Messer Neri Adimari, and Messer Tignoso De Macci. And as men who wished to perturb the tranquil state of the city, he had them beheaded; though Tignoso, because he was very fat, perished on the rack <note>Original: 'in sulla colla', a reference to the strappado or a similar torture device used to extract confessions or punish.</note>. Furthermore, at the instance of Messer Musatto Francesi, his friend, he wanted to seize some of the Abati family. But they, sensing the order given, fled in secret. Whereupon the governor declared all the Abati rebels. Nor was there ever more in Florence such a story, as is narrated more extensively elsewhere. **LIKE AN ANCIENT BEAST:** like an old beast; as if to say like the ox which, when it is too old to plow, is fattened and sent to the slaughterhouse. Thus, he deprived those of life, and himself of honor and fame. And he came out bloody from Florence, which the poet calls a "woods" because above he called the citizens "wolves."

As it happens that an announcement of some harm troubles the face of him who hears it, from whatever side the danger assails and bites; so I saw the other soul—not Guido who was speaking, but Rinieri—who was seen to be troubled, because such souls are full of charity and grieve for the ills of others. And especially those who purge envy, so that the abundance of charity in Purgatory may entirely extinguish the lividness of this life. **THE HEARING OF THE ONE:** The words of Guido and the troubled face of Rinieri kindled in me a desire to know who they were, and deservedly so, because the words of one and the gestures of the other gave clear indications that they were of great worth and worthy of being known. Rinieri then replied: "You want me to tell you who I am, and you do not want to tell us who you are." Although it seems unjust that you wish to know and do not wish to teach, nonetheless, seeing in you such divine grace, I will not be stingy, but liberal. As if to say: "Your denial of your name could lead me to guess that you were either proud, not deigning to tell us, or envious, not wanting to satisfy us. But the divine grace I see in you refutes both, for no special grace comes from God except to men of esteem." **MY BLOOD WAS CONSUMED BY ENVY.** And in this he still practices charity, which purges envy. By showing his error and the pain he suffers for it, he makes himself an example to others so they may guard against it. That he said "if I had seen a man become happy" expresses the vice of envy perfectly. For the envious man makes no exception of one over another, but whoever he sees become happy at any time—which can happen even from a small stroke of luck—he becomes marvelously sad. **YOU WOULD HAVE SEEN ME SPRINKLED WITH LIVID COLOR:** That is, I was suddenly oppressed by such envy that I showed it in my face, for I would turn livid. **FROM MY SOWING** I reap such chaff. The actions of men are seeds which produce fruit like themselves. Virtuous works produce happiness; the contrary produce the opposite. And he rightly said "chaff" and not "fruit," because virtuous action produces not only chaff but also grain, for it possesses the habit of virtue. But the vicious action produces vice, which is nothing in itself, but only a privation. Therefore, it can be called sterile chaff. **O HUMAN RACE, WHY DO YOU NOT SET THE HEART.** He reproaches men who set their minds and affection on temporal and transitory goods. These goods have this condition: that no one can have them if another is not deprived of them. Whence Boethius: "O narrow and poor riches, which many cannot have in their entirety at once, and which do not come to any without the poverty of others." <note>Original: 'O angustas & inopes diuitias quas nec pluribus habere totas : ſimul licet & ad quelibet ſine ceterorum paupertate no ueniunt.'</note> Thus the envious man would wish to deprive others of them to have them all for himself. **WHERE THERE IS NEED** that is, in those things where there is a need for the exclusion of companionship. This is a metaphor from magistrates distributed in republics: where, when one "companion" <note>Term: <term>conforte</term>, meaning a member of the same family or legal group.</note> holds a magistracy, the others have a "prohibition" <note>Term: <term>divieto</term>, a legal restriction preventing relatives from holding office simultaneously.</note>. So it is in the division of the goods of fortune: it happens that the good possessed by Mark cannot be possessed by Anthony. But the goods of the soul, which are the virtues, because they are incorporeal and indivisible, can equally be possessed by all.

Not only the family of these men has been made "stripped," that is, poor of every virtue, but all the men of Romagna, which he describes by its borders. For Romagna from the north is...

<meta>This page continues the lament of Guido del Duca regarding the moral decline of the Romagna region. For within these boundaries it is full
of poisonous brambles, so that too late
they would now be cleared by cultivation:

He adds: that what is within these boundaries, <note>that is, all of Romagna</note> is full of poisonous brambles; and he says this by way of metaphor. For our souls are compared to the earth. Indeed, if the earth is not cultivated, it quickly becomes wild and fills with thorns, burrs, and every wicked weed. But if it is cultivated with diligence, it remains purged of those things, and good trees and every grain produce the best fruit. So it is with human souls: if they are not stirred toward virtue, they become savage and beastly, and produce the actions not of a man, but of wild and cruel beasts. But if they are cultivated with excellent laws and institutions, and with civil and moral precepts, they produce every virtue. But here he shows that the brambles <note>that is, the vices</note> have multiplied so much that they cannot be extinguished. This signifies that they are so much more wicked that it is impossible to quench them, especially because they have formed a fixed habit in vice.

O where is the good Lizio and Arrigo Mainardi,
Pier Traversaro and Guido di Carpigna?
O Romagnuoles turned into bastards!

When does a blacksmith take root again in Bologna?
When in Faenza does a Bernardino di Fosco,
a noble sprout from a small weed, arise?

Do not marvel, Tuscan, if I weep
when I remember, with Guido da Prata,
Ugolin d'Azzo who lived among us,

Federigo Tignoso and his company,
the house of Traversara and the Anastagi,
and both one and the other family now disinherited;

The ladies and the knights, the labors and the ease
that love and courtesy once made us desire,
there where hearts have now become so wicked.

O Bertinoro, why do you not flee away,
since your family has departed,
and many people, to avoid becoming corrupt?

Why did I not say to you: since your family has departed. And he intends the family of this Guido del Duca, in which they say there were in old times many men of such liberality that a controversy often arose when foreigners arrived there, because everyone wanted them at their own house. Therefore, they had a column erected in the square, and around it they placed as many rings as there were fathers of families, and to each was assigned his own. And when the foreigner came, he tied his horse to one of the rings, and immediately the one to whom the ring was assigned would lead that foreigner to his house and honor him most liberally.

Bagnacavallo does well that it no longer breeds,
and Castracaro does ill, and Conio worse,
which still bothers to breed such Counts.

The Pagani will do well when their Demon
has gone away; but not so that a pure
testimony of them shall ever remain.

O Ugolin de' Fantolin, you are safe,
since your name is no longer expected
to be obscured by someone degenerating.

But go your way now, for it delights me
much more to weep than to speak,
so much has our discourse constricted my mind.

...finished afterwards: and to the south by the Apennine mountains, and to the east by the Adriatic sea. The Reno is a small river which rises in the Apennines toward Pistoia; it used to run between Bologna and Modena, several miles from Bologna. Afterward, it was diverted to Bologna. **CONCERNING THE GOOD SOUGHT** for truth and for pastime. According to the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle's philosophy</note> there are three kinds of goods: the honest, the useful, and the delightful. But the honest is the true good. Therefore, he said "for truth" for the goods of the soul, which is honesty; and "for pastime" for the goods of the body and of fortune, which are the useful and the delightful. He concludes, therefore, that all Romagna has been made ugly and poor of the good sought for truth <note>that is, of the honest good, which is true good</note> and of the good sought for pastime <note>that is, for pleasure and delight</note>. This signifies that it is empty of virtue, which creates the honest good, and of concord and peace, which create the delightful. Afterward he follows:

**O THE GOOD LIZIO**: This was Master Lizio da Valbona, an excellent man full of virtue. Whose daughter Caterina, overcome by love, secretly joined with Riccardo, a noble youth; and Master Lizio, with his prudence, had them marry, as our Boccaccio narrates in detail in one of his novellas <note>Decameron, Day 5, Novel 4</note>. Arrigo Mainardi of Faenza: some say from Bertinoro; and a great friend of the one who speaks. Pier Traversaro was the Lord of Ravenna. Magnanimous and highly reputed, he married one of his daughters to Stephen, King of Hungary. His power flourished in the times of Frederick II. He rebelled against him, but after his death, Frederick besieged and conquered Ravenna. Guido di Carpigna was a noble man from Montefeltro, to whom none was equal in liberality. **A BLACKSMITH TAKES ROOT**. <note>that is, when a craftsman of low condition becomes great, and causes a lineage and nobility to be born from him</note> as did Lambertaccio the blacksmith, who reached such a state that he was almost the lord of Bologna. And from him descended Master Fabbro de' Lambertacci. **BERNARDIN DI FOSCO**. This was the ancestor of Master Bernardino, who ruled Faenza; a man of low fortune, but of most excellent sense and counsel, such that he came into great esteem among his fellow citizens.

<image-desc>A decorative square initial 'N' showing a bearded man in profile wearing a hood or cowl.</image-desc> Do not marvel, O Tuscan <note>that is, O Dante the Tuscan</note> if I weep when I remember <note>that is, recall</note> all these virtuous men and those of great governance. Then he lists them, and places Guido da Prata. This is a villa between Faenza and Ravenna. Ugolin d'Azzo: this man was of the Ubaldini. These possessed much around the Apennine mountains and in Mugello. Federigo Tignoso from Rimini. Traversari and Anastagi were two families in Ravenna. **WHICH LOVE AND COURTESY DESIRED**. Which love, benevolence, and courtesy <note>that is, liberality</note> desired; it made them desirous to follow such virtues. Because to say "love desires me" signifies "love makes me desirous of itself." Therefore it signifies that they were inflamed by these two virtues: namely, by benevolence and by liberality. And the meaning is that for the love of virtue they were willing to endure labors; and to practice liberality toward those for whom it was appropriate, they followed "ease" <note>that is, they strove to give ease to others</note>. There, in which place hearts, which used to be so full of love and nobility, are now filled with wickedness. **O BERTINORO**. This is a beautiful castle in the middle of Romagna, placed on a mountain above Forlì. **WHY DO YOU NOT FLEE AWAY**: as if to say:

The Counts of Castrocaro: these counts in the time of the poet were degenerating. But at present they have failed. **CONIO**. He grieves that this family still breeds, since it degenerates so much. **THE PAGANI WILL DO WELL**. These were gentlemen of Faenza descended from Pagano, the father of Mainardo. These ruled over Imola and Faenza. And it was called the power of the Pagani. From them came Mainardo, lord of Imola and Faenza: a man outstanding for the beauty of his body and for military virtue. And he calls him a "demon" because he was very astute. And in Tuscany he held the Guelph side, because the Guelphs ruled there; and in Romagna he favored the Ghibellines, who were powerful in that region. It will be useful, then, to the Pagani that Mainardo should die. Nevertheless, there will remain no testimony of their true praise, because of what we have said of the cunning of Mainardo.
