<header>PURGATORY</header>

...inferno. — **UGOLINO de’ Santolini**. This man was also a nobleman of Faenza: full of virtue and good character. After these words, Guido takes leave of Dante, and demonstrates that it greatly grieves him that virtue is extinguished in Romagna. **SO YOUR REASON HAS** my mind constrained. It delighted me to weep because your reason—that is, human reason, which induces every man to charity, which is the proper virtue of man—induces me to compassion.

We knew that those dear souls
heard us go; therefore, by remaining silent,
they made us confident of the path.
Then, as we proceeded on alone,
a flash appeared as when air is cleft,
a voice that struck from the opposite side, saying:
"Whoever finds me shall slay me!"
And it fled like thunder that vanishes away,
if the cloud suddenly bursts.
When our hearing had a truce from it,
behold another with such a great crash,
it resembled thunder that follows quickly:
"I am Aglauros, who became a stone!"
And then, to press closer to the poet,
I took a step backward and not forward.

<margin>b</margin> "...therefore everyone who finds me [will kill me]." And God replied that they would not. Therefore, Dante, wishing to call men back from Envy, places these words: **AND FLED like thunder**, because such an example should fill every man with terror, so that he guards himself against Envy and flees such vice from his soul. **IF SUDDENLY the cloud bursts**. He demonstrates that thunder is nothing other than the refraction of condensed clouds. **AS OUR hearing had a truce from him**. That is, he heard him no more; behold, the other voice was heard by us with such a great crash—that is, with such a great noise. And he rightly said "crash" <note>Italian: *fracasso*</note> because "crash" signifies what in Latin is called *fragor* <note>original: "fragor"</note>, which signifies a sound made by broken things; like thunder, which comes suddenly after the lightning and is greater. And indeed, the lightning and the thunder are at the same moment. But because the sense of sight is faster than hearing, one therefore sees the light of the lightning before one hears the thunder. And it is to be noted that the exhortation to virtue should be gentle, as were the three voices above. But the warning away from vice should be terrifying. **I AM Aglauros who became a stone**. The poets feign that there were three daughters of Cecrops, King of Athens: Herse, Pandrosos, and Aglauros. Mercury saw these women at the sacrifices of Minerva and fell in love with Herse, the most beautiful of all those three sisters. Wanting to go to the chamber of Herse, he needed to pass through the hall where Aglauros was. She wished to know the reason for Mercury's coming. Mercury manifested his desire to her and with many prayers comforted her so that she might lend him secret help. But the most greedy and envious sister refused to favor him or keep it hidden unless she received a great sum of money from him. Minerva was offended by Aglauros, because shortly before she had dared to uncover the basket under which Erichthonius, born of Vulcan, was hidden. Therefore, moved to anger, she incited Envy to stimulate Aglauros so that she would envy Mercury's love for her sister and not allow him passage. Therefore Mercury, since he could not persuade her with prayers or promises, turned her into stone. Thus the poet uses this example to frighten men away from this vice. Also fitting in this place is the description of the house of Envy, which Ovid describes with no less learning than eloquence. **AND THEN to press closer to the poet**: He shows that he was walking ahead of Virgil; but then, out of fear, he pulled himself back to approach him. This demonstrates that the senses often rush ahead due to too ardent a desire. But when such examples terrify him, he restrains himself and submits to reason.

Already the air was quiet on every side;
and he said to me: "That was the hard bit
which should keep a man within his bounds.
But you take the bait, so that the hook
of the ancient adversary pulls you to him;
and therefore little use is curb or lure.
Heaven calls to you and circles around you,
showing you its eternal beauties,
and yet your eye gazes only at the ground;
wherefore He who discerns all things strikes you."

It happens to man as it does to a fish. For just as the fisherman offers bait to the fish on the hook and thus deceives it, so the devil, our ancient adversary, lures us with those worldly pleasures in which vice is hidden, which like a hook catches us and pulls us to damnation; in such a way that curb or lure—that is, comfort or reproof—is of no use. **HEAVEN CALLS YOU**. Certainly God gave man uplifted eyes so that he could look upon the eternal courses of the heavens and their wonderful beauties and ornaments.

<column-break/>

Although we did not ask the souls about the path, nor did they see if we were keeping the right way, nevertheless we were confident that, since they heard us, they would have set us right if we were not going correctly. **THEN WE WERE made alone**. We had already passed the souls and remained alone when we heard two voices. And here it should be noted that just as he previously placed three voices exhorting us to charity, so he now places two which, by example, may draw us back from Envy. But the first three he saw while still among the souls to show that such exhortations benefit those entering the purgatorial virtues. But since there is no need for examples to drag one away from Envy <note>once the lesson is learned</note>, he feigns hearing these last voices after he has departed from the place. **WHOEVER FINDS me shall slay me**. Abel and Cain were brothers, as we have shown elsewhere. Abel was a shepherd, a just man, and full of religion. And whenever he sacrificed to God, he offered the best lambs of the flock, whereby he prospered every day. Cain, on the contrary, was a wicked man and without religion; from his farming, he always offered the saddest ears of grain from the field, for which impiety he always fell into greater poverty. Wherefore, moved by envy, he killed his brother Abel. God, being angry, cursed him. And he, turning to God, said: "My iniquity is so great that I do not deserve pardon. Behold, you shall drive me this day from the face of the earth, and I shall be hidden from your face, and I shall be a fugitive in the world; but whoever kills me..."

<margin>q</margin> This which Virgil says at present, he had already promised to say when he said: "The curb should be of a contrary sound." I believe you will hear it, in my opinion, before you come to the pass of pardon. And he said to me: **THAT WAS a hard bit**: "that"—that is, the voice of Cain and that of Aglauros—was a hard bit <note>Italian: *camo*</note>, that is, a hard curb. Wherefore the Psalmist says: "With bit and curb constrain their jaws" <note>original Latin: *In camo & freno maxillas eorum constrige*</note>. For such examples should restrain everyone so they do not rush into this vice. Because through Cain, death is demonstrated, and through Aglauros, who became stone, obstidacy is shown. Such a curb should therefore keep man within his bounds—that is, within the limits of reason, which wills that you love your neighbor as yourself. *Meta* <term>Turning post</term> in Latin is the extremity of the horse race, which they must not only reach, but once reached, they must circle it with such art and skill that they do not press so close that they strike it, nor go so far away that other horses enter between them and the post and finish the circuit first. **BUT YOU TAKE the bait**.

<summary>Dante and Virgil hear the terrifying "voices of Envy"—Cain and Aglauros—which serve as warnings (a "hard bit") to keep the soul within the bounds of reason. Virgil explains how the devil uses worldly pleasures as bait to hook humans, distracting them from the eternal beauties of heaven.</summary>

# CANTO XV

### CANTO XV OF THE SECOND CANTICLE BY DANTE.

The poet writes how he departs from the second circle of Envy and ascends to the third, where Wrath is purged. First, he describes the Angel who appears to him, purges him of Envy, and directs him to the circle of Wrath. Afterward, he explains a statement made in the preceding chapter. To this, he adds a vision of his own; finally, Virgil interprets it. **A**s much as: He describes the evening hour: from which until the setting of the sun, when it goes below, is as much space of time as there is from the birth of the sun until the third hour. Therefore, at the equinox, according to our clocks, it would be the twenty-first hour. Of the "hope of the sun," which in its continuous motion plays like a child: who as soon as he is born moves

**A**s much as between the end of the third hour
and the beginning of day appears of the sphere
which always plays in the manner of a child,
So much seemed already toward the evening
to remain for the sun in its course;
it was evening there, and here it was midnight.
The rays were striking us in the middle of the nose,
because the mountain had been circled by us
so that we were now going straight toward the west,
When I felt my forehead weighed down
by the splendor much more than before,
and unknown things were a marvel to me;
Whereupon I raised my hands toward the top
of my eyebrows and made myself a sunshade
that thins out the excess of what is visible.

As when from water or from a mirror
the ray leaps to the opposite side,
ascending upward in the same manner
As that which descends, and departs as much
from the fall of a stone in an equal distance,
as experience and art show;
So it seemed to me by reflected light
to be struck there in front of me,
wherefore my sight was snatched away in flight.
"What is that, sweet father, from which I cannot
shield my eyes enough that it avails me?"
I said, "and it seems to be moving toward me."
"Do not marvel if the family of heaven still dazzles you,"
he answered me; "it is a messenger
who comes to invite a man to ascend.
Soon it will be that to see these things
will not be heavy for you, but will be a delight
as much as nature has disposed you to feel."

Then we were arrived, and the blessed Angel
with a joyful voice said: "Enter here,"

<column-break/>

always gaining until the middle of its age <note>meaning mid-day</note>. Then it sinks, and so does the sun, both in this and in the other hemisphere. "It was evening there": in the hemisphere where Purgatory is, and here in Italy it was midnight. According to the poet, the mountain of Purgatory is positioned on the direct opposite side of the earth from Jerusalem. Because of this, if he had been in Jerusalem at the hour he narrates this, it would have been midnight; in Purgatory, it would have been midday. But because he was in Italy when he wrote this, he says that when it was evening there, it was midnight in Italy, because day and night do not occur equally in every part. "The rays were striking us in the middle of the nose": and he assigns the reason. Because they were walking upward in a circuit, it followed that they were not always facing one direction. And at that moment, it happened that they were turned toward the west. "Weighed down the forehead with splendor": the splendor of the sun first weighed down his forehead as it struck him from the front. But when the splendor of the Angel arrived, it weighed him down much more than before. At which he marveled "for things unknown," that is, because the appearance of the Angel was not yet manifest to him. "Whereupon I raised": seeing myself dazzled by the excessive splendor, I placed my hands over my eyebrows and "made a roof for my eyes" so that the rays of splendor would not strike them. "I made myself a sunshade" <note>original: *solecchio*</note>, that is, I diminished that sun to my eyes. *Solecchio* signifies a "little sun." Hence, when the sun is in our eyes and we remove those rays from our sight with some obstacle, we call such a removal a *solecchio* because we diminish the sun. "That," that is, which sunshade. "Thins out" <note>original: *lima*</note>, that is, removes and shears away. "From the excess of what is visible": from the too-much light.

**T**he meaning is that such reflected light seemed to strike Dante's face, just as the ray which descends from the sun into water or a mirror reflects to the opposite side because it returns upward in the same way it descended. For just as the ray of the sun descends without a distance of time, so without a distance of time does this reflection rise. "And as much": that is, it departs by so much, meaning it is different from the falling of a stone. For the stone falls with a distance of time. "In unequal distance": in unequal movement, for if a stone descended from the sun in the same time that the ray descends, the stone would arrive much later than the ray. The case of the stone, according to Alberto <note>Albertus Magnus</note> in the book *On the Properties of the Elements*, is called by a certain translation a "line taught by the lead" <note>original Latin: *linea indocta*, referring to a plumb line</note> from the center of the sun over our heads. This is because a falling stone comes straight down like a lead weight. For this reason, he maintains in the same book that the Ethiopians who inhabit the region between the Summer Tropic and the Equinoctial have two burning summers because the sun passes twice over the "falling line of the stone" above their bodies. Therefore, Dante infers that the rays of the Angel came straight down upon him. "As experience shows," which is manifest. "And art," that is, perspective <note>the science of optics</note>, which assigns the reason for this. Perspective is part philosophy and part geometry. And not without reason does he say that the rays of light that struck him were by reflection. For he wishes to show that this light which came from the Angel to him was a ray that struck the Angel from the divine light and, reflected from there, struck Dante. And we shall understand that these angels, whom he finds at every terrace, are the divine graces: namely <term>preueniéte: Prevenient</term>, <term>illumináte: Illuminating</term>, <term>lacooperáte: Cooperating</term>, and <term>lacóſumáte: Consummating</term>, through which man knows the ugliness of sin and the beauty of virtue. From this is born in him the will to flee the former and follow the latter, and by such a will he becomes strong, corroborated, and constant. And that Dante "makes a roof for his eyes with his hands" to sustain such splendor means that sensuality steps forward with good works, which are signified by the hands. And the first works of sensuality are to become obedient to reason and to learn from it to recognize what one's dazzled eye cannot discern. And reason teaches and instructs him that the Angel is sent by God to invite him to ascend. For divine grace always exhorts one toward heavenly things. "Soon it will be": because when the soul is purged of vices, the eye of the mind can support the divine light; that is, it can come to the knowledge of divine things—not entirely, however, but as much as human nature is capable.

**T**he Angel spoke when they were joined to him with a joyful voice, because the further our soul proceeds in its purgation, the more joy the Angel shows it. Or truly, with that the Angel admonished him...

to gain some profit from his words,

"What did the spirit from Romagna mean

<note>Dante asks a specific question about what Guido del Duca meant when he said: "O human race, why do you set your heart where partnership and exclusion are necessary?" From this specific point, Virgil (representing Intellect) moves into a universal explanation.</note>

"Because he knows the harm of his own greatest flaw," <note>Referring to Envy.</note>
he said to me, "it is no wonder
if he reproves others for it, so they may weep less.
Because your desires are focused
where the portion is decreased by companionship,

But if the love of the supreme sphere
turned your desire upward,

For the more there are there who say 'ours,'

said I, "than if I had remained silent before,

How can it be that a good distributed
among more possessors makes them richer

And he to me: "Because you fix
your mind only on earthly things,
you extract darkness from the true light.

just as a ray of light comes to a bright body.
It gives of itself as much as it finds of ardor;
so that however much charity spreads,
the eternal value increases upon it.
And the more people there are who catch fire up there,
the more good love provides, and the more it loves them,"

<column-break/>

...made them turn against anger. Furthermore, there were the stairs, which they climbed and were less steep than the others they had climbed below. This signifies that having already been purged of two great vices [Pride and Envy], the soul remained lighter. "BLESSED ARE THE MERCIFUL" <note>original: "BEATI MISERICORDES"</note> was sung behind them. He says "behind" to show that such singing was in the terrace of Envy, which they were now leaving. And this signifies that mercy comes once envy has departed. For mercy grieves at the ill of others, whereas envy rejoices in it. Therefore, this virtue is the opposite of envy. "BLESSED ARE THE MERCIFUL." In the Gospel of Matthew it is written: *Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy.* <note>original: "Beati misericordes quoniam ipsi misericordiam consequentur."</note> "AND REJOICE, you who conquer." The sins are purged and removed from them; because in the same Gospel it is said: *Rejoice and be glad, for your reward is great in heaven.* <note>original: "Gaudete: & exultate: quoniam merces uestra copiosa est in celis."</note> "ALONE WE WENT," which designates contemplation, in which the appetite, already joined to reason, desires to learn from it; and he proposed to him:

<image-desc>Decorative initial S with floral patterns.</image-desc>
A sentiment certainly appropriate to the intellect wishing to instruct the senses. For he shows the origin of envy, so that one may guard against it. And he answers that Guido now knows, since he is in Purgatory, the damage that follows from his "greatest flaw," that is, the sin of envy. "And therefore do not wonder" <note>original: "Et pero non fadmiri"</note>; that is, do not be surprised. For being at present in a state of charity, he reproves others. And certainly envy always carries its own penalty with it, because other sins have some pleasure. It is sweet to the miser to accumulate gold and silver; the lustful man rejoices in enjoying the thing he loves. But envy always torments its possessor. "BECAUSE YOUR DESIRES ARE FOCUSED." Because our wills are set on possessing those things which must necessarily be diminished and decreased when there are more companions sharing the portion; because temporal goods cannot be possessed by many unless they are divided. Seeing, then, that what another has cannot be his own, a man is moved to envy; and "envy moves the bellows to sighs," that is, it inflames our greed to want the whole, for which we sigh. "BUT IF THE LOVE OF THE SUPREME." But if the love of celestial things [guided us], as does the love of temporal things, such fear would not grip your breast. For there in heaven and in celestial goods, the more one says "ours," the more people there are who possess, and the more each one possesses; because the joy increases the more companions there are, and they increase more in charity. Hence Seneca: *The possession of no thing is pleasant without a companion.* <note>original: "Nullius rei possessio iocunda est sine socio."</note> And Boethius: *Every good shared in common shines more beautifully.* <note>original: "Omne bonum in comune deductum pulchrius elucescit."</note> And Augustine in the book *The City of God*: *The possession of goodness is in no way diminished by the arrival of a companion; rather, it is possessed more widely and harmoniously by the indivisible charity of the partners.* <note>original: "Nullo modo fit minor accedente consocio possessio bonitatis: quanto latius: quanto concordius indiuidua sociorum possidet charitas."</note> And Gregory: *He who desires to be free from the stains of the world should seek that possession which is not restricted by the number of possessors.* <note>original: "Qui facibus mundie carere desiderat illa possessione appetat: qua numerus possidentiu no angustat."</note>

<image-desc>Decorative initial I with floral patterns.</image-desc>
"I am more starved of being satisfied than if I had been silent" <note>original: "Io son piu digiuno desser contento: che se io mi fussi taciuto"</note>; that is, I doubted less before I asked you than I doubt at present. For I do not understand how it can be that a good distributed among many makes them richer than if it were held alone or by a few. And the senses rightly doubt this, because they cannot by themselves understand anything except things subject to the senses; and those being corporeal, such doubt follows.

<image-desc>Decorative initial C with floral patterns.</image-desc>
A fitting response to the higher reason illustrated by many doctrines: it seemed to the senses and to lower reason that it was not possible for a good possessed by many to be entirely the property of all. And Virgil shows this as he proceeds: that the senses and lower reason, which reflects upon them, have no knowledge except of worldly goods, where such conditions exist. Thus, thinking only of earthly goods, such knowledge seeking the truth finds error and ignorance instead. Because it considers celestial goods according to the nature of earthly goods, it "extracts darkness," that is, ignorance, from the light of truth. "THAT INFINITE." He has shown where the ignorance arises in us that makes us have a false opinion of the supreme good. Now, by similarity, he shows us the truth: that the eternal good, which is God, is not diminished by being shared by many. And he calls God the infinite good because He has no end, neither in quantity nor in—

**And those which are not obscured and darkened by vices**, but are purified of them, remain lucid; they are fit to receive such splendor, in proportion to the ardor and charity they have within them toward God and their neighbor. And their eternal value, eternal goodness, and glory increase as their charity is greater. **AND HOW MANY PEOPLE.** Glory does not diminish in the souls in heaven because there are more of them; rather, it increases. For just as we see that by placing many mirrors opposite the rays of the sun, each one receives them equally and shines equally—unless the fault lies in the mirror—and by placing them in a way that the rays from one reflect into the others, the splendor would multiply. So the rays of divine glory come to the blessed souls and make them shine; then one reflects its own into the others. **To be drawn into a place where there were many people.** Here he wishses to show that he was entirely absorbed in that thought: when Christ, still a boy, went to preach in the temple in the presence of many common people, priests, scribes, and Pharisees. And his mother and Joseph, searching for him, spent three days without being able to find him. And therefore he says: "and to see in a temple many people." Entering the terrace where Wrath is purged, he shows that we must place examples of patience before our minds, as was seen in the Virgin Mother, who patiently endured and gently rebuked her son, saying: "Why have you done this to us? I and your father were seeking you in sorrow." <note>original: "Quid fecisti nobis? Ego & pater tuus dolentes querebamus te." — Luke 2:48</note> And because the poet has now climbed into the circle of Wrath, the place requires a definition of it. We shall say, then, that wrath is a spiritual flame and a boiling of blood around the heart to take vengeance. Whence the Psalmist says: "They have set fire to your sanctuary on earth." <note>original: "Incenderunt igni sanctuariū tuum in terra." — Psalm 74:7</note> Likewise, wrath is a fury of the mind which runs from the internal parts to the external. And as smoke is born from natural fire, making a place dark, so from this, smoke rises to the brain and blinds the intellect. Hence Job says: "My eye has grown dim with indignation." <note>original: "Caligauit ad indignationem oculos meos." — Job 17:7</note> And Aristotle: "Two things are against counsel: haste and wrath." And the Psalmist: "Smoke went up in your wrath; fire from his face glowed." <note>original: "Ascendit fumus in ira tua: Ignis a facie eius exarsit." — Psalm 18:8</note> Likewise: "Fire fell upon them, and they did not see the sun of justice." <note>original: "supercecidit ignis: & uon uiderunt solem iustitie." — Psalm 58:9 / Wisdom of Solomon 5:6</note> And elsewhere: "My eye is troubled by fury." <note>original: "Turbatus est a furore oculus meus." — Psalm 6:7</note> And Paul to the Ephesians: "Let not the sun go down upon your wrath." <note>original: "Non occidat sol super iracundiam uestra." — Ephesians 4:26</note> Wrath weakens a man; it makes him cruel, corrupts good character, and shortens life.

**time. AND INEFFABLE**—that is, unspeakable, because it cannot be said or expressed with words; so it runs to love—that is, to the one who loves—and shines in him, just as a sunbeam shines in bright bodies. The sun has its natural light, the rays of which, striking the stars and other bright bodies, illuminate them; and the more bright bodies its rays find, the more it would illuminate. Nor would this light be less than that, just because there were more bodies to receive such rays. But it is greater or lesser according to whether the receiving body is more or less fit. This is why a mirror shines more than a plastered wall does, even though the sun gives itself equally to each. So God alone, the supreme good, shines equally in all souls.

Dante wanted to respond to Virgil: "You satisfy me"—that is, you fulfill me. But because he had already reached the third terrace, his wandering eyes—that is, moving about to see the new place—removed him from such a response. And certainly, Dante having fully understood Virgil's reasoning, he would have replied to him if he had had the leisure; but occupied by an unexpected thing, he omitted the response. This signifies that for things that are not necessary—even though they have some value in themselves—it would be well to discuss them when at leisure. Nevertheless, when a new and necessary thing occurs, we must leave them behind. **THERE APPEARED TO ME IN AN ecstatic vision.** *Extasis* <note>Ecstasy</note> means an elevation of the mind. This is when our mind is not alienated by any stupor of the body, but released from it, gathered into itself, and alienated from the senses—not by revelation, but by a strong imagination which captures the mind so completely that it does not notice anything else. But it is so bound by a fixed thought and so occupied in it that it understands nothing else, and no other power of the soul operates, because the whole mind is fixed on that single thought. ->Lord of the city.<- Both one word and the other are French <note>Landino claims a French origin for "Sire" and "Villa," though both have deep Latin roots. They write that Cecrops, the most ancient King of Athens, having restored the city, thought about how he should name it. But it appeared...

<insert>T</insert>his is the third example which can revoke wrath and reduce any inflamed heart to gentleness. Consider that Stephen the Protomartyr <note>The first Christian martyr.</note>, although he was stoned with great injustice—and not only killed wrongly, but killed cruelly—nevertheless prayed for those who killed him. Stephen, who was among the chosen <note>original: "neglecti" — likely a transcription error for "eletti" (chosen) or "diaconi" (deacons).</note> of the apostles after the death of Christ, full of grace and strength, performed signs and miracles in Jerusalem. But certain people from the synagogue, unable to resist him in dispute, introduced false witnesses to accuse him of being against God and Moses. To this accusation, although he defended himself sharply and with true wisdom, and affirmed that he saw the heavens open and Jesus standing at the right hand, they nevertheless out of envy dragged him out of the synagogue and stoned him. Wherefore such a man, most unjustly and with the prayer we set down above, bravely sustained martyrdom, and was the first martyr after the passion of Christ. *Inflamed in the fire of wrath*: he said "inflamed" well, because wrath involves the heating of blood around the heart.

AND I saw him sinking down: as if weighed down by death. *Gateways to heaven*: the eyes are the doors and windows of the soul.

HE follows by demonstrating: that after this ecstasy and fixed imagination, his soul—which was entirely gathered into itself—returned outward, that is, it turned back to the things which were true outside of it, which is nothing other than considering physical reality. *And I recognized my errors as not false.* Because emerging from that fixed imagination, he recognized that his soul had gone wandering, that is, moving through true things. *Error* in Latin signifies a progress of going without a certain end. *My leader.* Virgil had seen him going tottering and vacillating, that is, reeling and stumbling like one who is oppressed either by sleep or by drunkenness. And now seeing him as if he were waking up, he asks why he has gone more than half a league in that manner. And Dante prepares to answer him. But Virgil interrupts his words, saying that even if he wanted to hide himself with a hundred masks <note>Latin: "larue"</note>, he could not hide even one of his small <note>Latin: "parue"</note> thoughts. And this is very true: for the senses and the lower reason cannot think anything that the higher reason does not notice. Therefore Virgil does not ask to know, but to provide a timely awakening and to urge him on, removing all laziness from him.

WHAT YOU SAW. This vision came to you so that you do not refuse <note>Latin: "non scuse" interpreted as 'non ricusi'</note> to open your heart to the waters of peace, that is...

### CANTO XV

wishing to extinguish with the water of peace the fire that wrath has kindled in the heart. For if wrath is fire, then charity—which extinguishes wrath—will be the water that comes from the fountain of God. For God is charity; and whoever remains in charity remains in God, and God in him <note>Landino references 1 John 4:16 here.</note>. I <gloss>Virgil</gloss> did not ask you <gloss>Dante</gloss> for the reason that he does who looks only with the bodily eye: which cannot see after death when the body lies undone <gloss>that is, without the soul</gloss>. The meaning is that he who looks only with the bodily eye cannot see the thoughts of the heart. And therefore he asks in order to know; but I did not ask to know. Rather, I asked to give strength to your feet <gloss>that is, to urge you on</gloss>: because it is a fitting thing to prod <gloss>that is, to sting as one stings the ox</gloss>: who use <term>vigilance</term> <note>original: "AVSAR lor uigilia"</note> when it returns. It is as if he says: you have been almost asleep in this vision of yours. Now, being excited and awake, use your vigilance <gloss>that is, spend and dispense well the time in which you are awake and do not lose it</gloss>. And in short: because the Sallustian precept is excellent: *For both before acting there is need of deliberation, and when you have deliberated, there is need of timely action.* <note>original Latin: "Nam & antea consulto & ubi consuluerit mature facto opus est," from Sallust’s *The Conspiracy of Catiline*.</note> He shows that having received excellent counsel through the vision, he must now fulfill it and put it into execution with speed.

->**W**e were moving toward the evening, attentive<-
->beyond as far as the eyes could reach<-
->against the late-afternoon and shining rays<-
->And behold, little by little, a smoke arose<-
->toward us, as dark as night<-
->nor was there any place to escape it<-
->This took from us our eyes and the pure air<-

<column-break/>

**W**e went toward the evening <gloss>that is, toward the west</gloss>. For just as the eastern parts are called morning—because there appears the dawn, which the Latins call **Matuta** <note>The ancient Roman goddess of the dawn.</note>—so the western parts are called **Vespro** <note>Evening/Vespers</note>: because the evening star of Venus often appears there in the evening. And they went along attentively, looking as far ahead as the eyes could reach against the late-afternoon rays <gloss>that is, the rays of the evening sun</gloss>. And the further they went, the more they approached a fog darker than the night which occupied that part of the circle, so that whoever wished to pass through it could not escape it. This fog took the eyes from Dante <gloss>that is, the power of sight</gloss> and took away the pure air without which one cannot see. The poet therefore posits that in this darkness the souls of the wrathful are purged, because they must recognize that the fury of wrath blinds the mind and removes the light of reason. Wherefore the mind remains in darkness.

---

Therefore, when the wrathful man considers this darkening and gloom, he grieves for his sin and seeks to leave it, following reason just as Dante feigns to have followed Virgil. And certainly, it is no small stimulus to the soul to know one has sinned and abandoned virtue: because the one leads to penitence and hatred of vice, and the other to love and desire for virtue. And this satisfies the penalty for the one who saved us, saying in the Gospel: *I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he be converted and live.* <note>original Latin: "Nolo mortem peccatoris sed ut conuertatur & uiuat," a common liturgical paraphrase of Ezekiel 33:11.</note> For this reason, the proud man humbles himself under the weight; the envious man sews his eyes shut so as not to see; and the wrathful man recognizes his blindness.

# CANTO XVI. OF THE SECOND CANTICLE BY DANTE.

Darkness of Hell and of a night deprived
of every planet under a poor sky,
as much as it can be obscured by clouds,
Did not make so thick a veil for my eyes
as that smoke which covered us there,
nor to the feeling of such harsh texture,
That the eye could not suffer to stay open;
wherefore my wise and faithful escort
drew near me and offered me his shoulder.
Just as a blind man goes behind his guide
so as not to stray, and not to strike against
something that might hurt or perhaps kill him,
So I went through that bitter and foul air,
listening to my leader who kept saying:
"Only take care that you are not severed from me."

I heard voices, and each one seemed
to pray for peace and for mercy
to the Lamb of God who takes away sins.
"Lamb of God" <note>original: "Agnus dei"</note> was their only opening;
one word was in all of them and one rhythm,
so that there seemed total harmony among them.
"What spirits are these, Master, that I hear?"
I said; and he to me: "You perceive correctly,
and they go untying the knot of wrath."
"Now, who are you who cuts through our smoke,
and speaks of us just as if you
still divided time by the calends?" <note>The "calends" refers to the Roman method of counting days from the first of the month, a practice of the living.</note>
Thus by a single voice it was said;
wherefore my master said: "Respond,
and ask if from here one goes upward."
And I: "O creature who cleanses yourself
to return beautiful to Him who made you,
you shall hear a marvel if you follow me."

<column-break/>

The poet does not change subject matter in this sixteenth canto, but continuing, he describes the obscurity of the fog into which he entered, and the souls who were being purged within it. **Darkness of night**: Dante had been in the infernal shadows at the time of night, where no planet is seen in the sky, but everything is covered in clouds. Therefore the sky is "poor" as much as it can be. And nevertheless, such darkness did not create so thick a veil over his eyes as the present smoke. By these words, he denotes that no sin induces such blindness of mind as wrath. This veil and covering of the eyes had two inconveniences. First, because it was thick; therefore it could not be transparent and clear so that the sight could pass through it as it passes through a thin veil. Second, it was of "harsh hairs" <note>The Italian *pelo* can mean hair or the "nap" of a fabric; Landino interprets the smoke as having a stinging, tactile quality.</note> which pricked the eyes of whoever kept them open. How then could he see anything, having a thick veil over his eyes and being forced to keep them closed? Certainly, wrath totally blinds the mind, and the stings that rage within it to seek vengeance do not allow us to open the eyes of the mind to consider reason. Wherefore **my wise and faithful escort**: Dante cannot exit such smoke unless he follows Virgil, because the senses and appetite cannot escape the blindness of wrath unless they take Reason as their guide. **Wise and faithful**: these two things are required in one who gives counsel: first, doctrine and prudence through which he knows; second, fidelity through which he wishes to lead well. **He drew near me**: when reason draws near to the appetite, the appetite cannot err. **And offered me his shoulder**: he offered his shoulder so that by leaning on him who could see, I would not strike anything. By the "shoulder," understand fortitude; for just as the shoulders sustain every weight, so fortitude defends us so that wrath does not overcome us. And certainly, reason corroborates and strengthens the appetite to resist wrath. **Take care that you are not severed from me**: that is, separated from reason. Otherwise, every desire becomes infinite and bestial.

**He heard the souls**: those who were purging wrath, praying for peace and for mercy, which are the opposites of wrath that always seeks war and vengeance. And they said: *Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world, have mercy on us.* And thus they prayed for mercy; and *Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world, grant us peace*; praying in this way for peace. **One word was in all and one rhythm**: they all said the same words and in one manner. This demonstrates that there was supreme concord among them, and with this they "untied the knot of wrath," which is entirely discord. **Dividing time still by calends**: that is, as if you were still alive. For souls stripped of the body, because they are immortal, do not experience the passage of time; but we who live divide time by years, months, days, hours, minutes, and **calends**, which is the Latin name for the first days of the month. And because it seems to me a thing not useless and quite pleasant to understand exactly the days of the month noted by the ancients, we will repeat from a bit further back with what order and number of days the ancients marked their years. Among all men, the Egyptians were the first to have the perfect and absolute year. For being skilled in <term>astronomy</term> (the study of stars), they saw that after three hundred sixty-five days and a quarter of a day, the sun has traversed the entire circle of the zodiac and returns to the first degree of Aries, where it had first started. Therefore they had their year of twelve months, in which they distributed 360 days, giving thirty to each month. Then they placed five remaining days between August and September, and every four years they counted one year of 366 days to account for that quarter-day that remained each year. Among the Greeks, there were various customs. Those of Arcadia made years of three months; those of Acarnania of six; others of 354 days. **Romulus**, among the Romans, ordered ten months, beginning the month on the first day when the new moon was seen. And he instituted that the lesser priest, having seen the new moon, should announce it to another priest called the <term>rex sacrificulus</term> (sacrificial king), and both of these would convoke the people on the Capitoline Hill and there announce how many days remained until the <term>Nones</term>. Therefore, they called this first day of the month **calends** from that "invocation" of the people, because *calare* in Latin means to call or convoke. And because it happens for certain reasons that the moon is not always seen at one time, it happened that in the first year some months were thirty days and some thirty-one, which order they then observed in following years. There were, therefore, seven months of thirty days: April, June, August, September, November, and December. The other four were thirty-one. The beginning of the year was March, named thus after Mars, whom Romulus affirmed was his father. And in this month the Vestal Virgins renewed the fire on the altar of Vesta; salaries were paid; taxes were leased; and the matrons gave banquets for the servants to have them more ready for service for the rest of the year. The second month they called April after Venus, who was the mother of Aeneas, from whom the Romans had their origin. For in Greek, <note>original: "haphrodite"</note> **Aphrodite** signifies Venus. Others say that Romulus, having named the first month...

# PURGATORY

...from Mars, the killer of men, because he is the planet that signifies wars. And from Homer, *Andriphonte* <note>original: "Andriphonte," from the Greek *androphontos*, meaning "manslayer."</note>, that is, homicide. He [Romulus] wished for the second month to have its name from Venus, a benevolent planet suited to procreation and to mitigating the malignancy of Mars. Whence we see that nature has ordained that even in the twelve signs of the zodiac, after Aries (the domicile of Mars) follows Taurus (the domicile of Venus). And similarly, before Scorpio (Mars) is Libra (Venus), so that in the domiciles of the benign Venus, the martial fury is tempered. Others say that he does not call the month April from Venus, but *aprile* without the "h" <note>This refers to an old etymological debate about whether *Aprilis* comes from Aphrodite or from *aperire*.</note>, because in that month the earth, previously frozen and constricted by the cold, opens itself to produce new flowers and leaves; whence the Athenians call it *Anthesterion* <note>original: "Anthesterion," a Greek month name associated with blooming.</note>, as if "powerful in flowers," because then everything blooms. Afterward, Romulus having divided the people into two parts, the *maiores* (elders) and *iuniores* (youths), the third month was called May after the elders, and the fourth was called June after the youths. The other months were named by number; and after June, the fourth month, follows *Quintile* [July], *Sextile* [August], September, October, November, and December. But later, C. Julius Caesar willed that *Quintile* be called July after himself. And Augustus instituted that *Sextile* be named August. This, then, was the first year, composed of ten months and 304 days, a number that did not harmonize with either the solar or the lunar course. Whence often summer came in winter, or winter in summer. Because of this, Numa Pompilius, the second king and successor to Romulus—either through natural prudence or Greek learning—added 50 days to the number already set, and made the year 364 days. He added two months, which he made of 29 days each, taking them from the 50 added days and from six days taken from the six months that were 30 days long. The first of these two he called January from Janus, who is the god of the beginnings of things, and he willed that it should be the start of the year. The second he called February from *Februo*, the god of purifications. Whence *februa* signifies purification. Later, understanding that an odd number is more perfect than an even one, he added a day to January, from which two things resulted: first, that the year had an odd number overall, 355 days; second, that all the days of the months were in odd numbers, there being four of 31 days and seven of 29. He left February in an even number and smaller than the others because, it being consecrated to the infernal gods and they performing in it purificatory sacrifices for the souls of the dead, he judged it should have both a smaller number and an even one, which is less perfect. Numa having reduced the year to this form, though it was not perfect because it did not square with the solar course (which is 365 days and six hours), he followed the custom of the Greeks; to those 11 days remaining each year, they <term>intercalated</term> <note>intercalation: the insertion of leap days or months to align the calendar with the solar year.</note> 90 days every eighth year. But an error arose because of that extra day added by Numa; for this reason, they instituted that in every twenty-fourth year (which was the third intercalation), they should interpose not 90 but 66 days; and in this way, the Roman year went with the same number as the Greek. Nonetheless, it is doubtful who found this method of <term>intercalating</term> days in Rome. For M. Licinius attributes it to Romulus, Valerius Antias to Numa, Junius to Servius Tullius, and King Tuditanus to the ten men of the laws of the twelve tables. But in the process of time, it happened that such intercalation was sometimes omitted due to some religious observance, and sometimes it was done before its time; furthermore, no account was taken of the six hours that remained each year, so that in three intercalations, six days passed by. But C. Julius Caesar, in his third consulate, deliberating to correct the errors, first consumed all the past days and made that year 443 days long. Then he ordered that the year be 365 days and the fourth part of a day, and reduced the months to the number they are at present. And every four years, he intercalated one day to consume the four sets of six hours that remain each year. And he placed such a day in the month of February, after the twenty-third day, and instituted that the twenty-fourth day be counted twice. And because that day in Latin is called the <term>calends</term>, and "twice" is said as *bis*, they therefore call it <term>bissextile</term> <note>original: "bis sesto," the origin of the term for a leap year.</note>. Furthermore, of all the days of the month, only three had proper names. The first name they called <term>calends</term>, which is on the first day. The second they called <term>nones</term>; and it was on the seventh day of the month in four months—March, May, July, and October—and in the others, the fifth. Then, eight days after the nones were the <term>ides</term>; thus in those four months they were on the fifteenth, and in the others on the thirteenth day of the month. And this shall be sufficient for the explanation of this passage. **A marvel you shall hear**: Because it will make you marvel to hear that I am alive. **If you follow me**: if you come along with me.

"I will follow you as far as I am permitted,"
->he replied; "and if the smoke does not let us see,<-
->hearing will keep us together in its stead."<-
Then I began: "With that bandage
->which death dissolves, I go upward,<-
->and I came here through the anguish of Hell.<-

->so much that He wills that I see His court<-

->thus he replied; and added, "I pray you<-

The soul responds: *I will follow you as far as I am permitted*, that is, as is allowed to me. For he was not allowed to follow him except as far as the smoke held, from which he could not exit before being purged. And if the smoke does not allow us to see one another—and because of this, we could lose our way as we go—hearing each other speak will serve us so as not to get lost. **In its stead**: in that exchange. Then I began to speak and said: *I go upward with that bandage which death dissolves* and corrupts; and this is the body, which through death is corrupted. And it is a "bandage" for the soul because it binds it within itself; whence the Greeks call the body *demas* <note>original: "demas," from the Greek *demas* meaning body or frame, which the author links to *deō*, to bind.</note> as if a "bond" of the soul, because *deo* signifies "I bind." **And if God has enclosed me in His grace**: He shows that, God having so enclosed him within His grace that He granted him that he could go to heaven with his body outside modern and customary use, he [Marco] should not hide from him who he was or what he is called. The "grace" that the poet feigns to have had—to ascend to heaven alive—is, allegorically, to have been able to overcome the flatteries and enticements of vices and enter into the purgatorial virtues; and with those, to come finally to the virtues of the soul already purged, where we acquire the highest good because we become fit to enjoy the divine presence. **I was a Lombard, and was called Marco**: Marco was a Venetian gentleman, practiced in military discipline, liberal, and an enemy of idleness and the life of cowards. But he was prone to anger, and especially to that indignation which is common in a noble soul. Regarding him, it is told of his alms-giving that while he was in prison and burdened by a ransom impossible for him to pay, he prayed by letter to Messer Ricciardo da Camino, Lord of Treviso, his old friend, that he should not let him rot in prison. Messer Ricciardo arranged with many lords of Lombardy that each should contribute toward the payment of the ransom whatever portion they pleased. Marco heard of this and moved...

# CANTO XVII

<note>Though the header reads Canto XVII, the text and commentary clearly refer to the events of Canto XVI, where Dante meets Marco Lombardo.</note>

...[Marco] wrote back to Richard in disdain, saying he would rather die than remain obligated to so many. Richard felt ashamed of this and paid the entire ransom from his own money. This man prophesied to Count Ugolino, the tyrant of Pisa, the wrath that God was about to conceive against him. He maintained dealings with many lords, and studied nothing else but the reconciliation and restoration of friendships. **I knew the world:** I was an expert in civil and active matters, which are called worldly because they are momentary and transitory—not because they cannot or should not be governed virtuously through moral virtues. Great merit is acquired before God and men by those who exercise and exhaust themselves in establishing peace and tranquility, which is an office of charity, a virtue required of us above all other virtues. **And I used that worth:** those moral virtues and that liberality, from which worth every man now departs and no longer practices.

And I to him: "By my faith I bind myself
To do what you ask of me; but I am bursting
Within a doubt, unless I explain it to myself.
First it was simple, and now it is made double
By your sentence, which makes me certain
Here and elsewhere of that with which I couple it.
The world is indeed thus entirely deserted
Of every virtue, just as you sound to me,
And pregnant and covered with malice;
But I pray that you point out the cause to me,
So that I may see it and show it to others;
For one places it in the heavens, and another here below."

A deep sigh, which grief wrung into a "uigh,"
<note>original: "inhui," a word Dante invented to represent a sigh or a sound of pain squeezed out.</note>
He first sent forth, and then began: "Brother,
The world is blind, and you indeed come from it.
You who are living refer every reason
Only up to the heavens, as if everything
Moved with them by necessity.
If this were so, Free Will would be destroyed
In you, and it would not be justice
To have joy for good, and mourning for evil.
The heavens initiate your movements;
I do not say all, but even if I did say so,
A light is given to you for good and for malice,
And a Free Will, which, though it struggles
In the first battles with the heavens, endures;
Then it conquers all, if it is well nourished.
To a greater force and a greater nature
You, being free, are subject; and that creates
The mind, which the heavens do not have in their care.
Therefore, if the present world goes astray,
In you is the cause, in you let it be sought;
And of this I shall now be a true scout to you."

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'P' featuring foliate designs.</image-desc> He promises him his faith to pray for him: and then he prays that he might absolve him of a doubt, in which he says he is "bursting"—that is, cracking open. And truly, one who is entangled in a doubt and does not know how to untangle himself, the more he searches, the more he becomes entangled; he is like one who holds himself so tight that he does not burst. **Unless I explain it to myself:** I do not unfold myself—that is, I do not untangle myself. **First it was simple, and now it is made double:** he had heard this same sentiment above from Guido del Duca when he spoke of the inhabitants near the Arno, so it was single. Now, hearing it from Marco, it becomes double. **But I pray that you point out:** that is, openly demonstrate, as one who points with a finger. **The world:** that is, all the men inhabiting the world, is not only "deserted" and destitute of every virtue, but also is filled with every malice. **One places it in the heavens, and another here below:** because some want the cause of our movements to come from the influence of the heavens, and some place it here below—that is, in us and in our free will.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'Q' containing a profile portrait of a man, possibly representing a philosopher.</image-desc> Marco, as one full of charity and moved to compassion toward the human race—like another Heraclitus <note>Heraclitus was known as the "weeping philosopher" because he wept for the follies of mankind.</note> regarding the blindness and ignorance found in many men who persuade themselves that the influence of the stars and the heavens can do so much in us that we are necessitated to do everything toward which we are inclined. And they think we can do nothing without their movements. This opinion is not only heretical and rejected by the very true and manifest reasons of Christians, but it is also contrary to the judgment of all the philosopher-authors and approvers of the moral virtues, and of the political and civil life. These philosophers hold that both good and evil are in our power, and no work is virtuous or vicious unless it is voluntary and by our own choice. Plato affirms that since the human soul was created immediately by God without secondary causes <note>meaning without the mediation of the stars or nature</note>, it is above the heavens. And because a superior thing cannot be under an inferior one, it follows that no celestial influence can constrain the soul either to vice or to virtue, as we have demonstrated more extensively above. But while the soul is in the body and uses the instruments of the body over which the heavens have jurisdiction, the soul can be inclined by this accident, but not necessitated nor forced. Marco, therefore, grieving, sighed; and in sighing he said "uigh," which is a voice signifying pain. **The world is blind:** because it fell into the greatest darkness of ignorance when it believed that secondary causes, which are the celestial influences, could have power over our soul. **And you indeed come from it:** since you are of that same opinion. **You who are living:** this is the reason that demonstrates men are blind, inasmuch as they attribute every cause to the heaven—that is, they attribute every cause of our operations to the celestial influence, as if the heavens by necessity pushed us to do and not to do, and to act either wickedly or well according to the nature of such influence, and as if we could not defend ourselves from it. If this were so, Free Will would be extinguished in us, which not only the theologians posit, but all the most excellent philosophers confess. Nor would there be virtue, which is an elective habit, nor vice, if it were not in our power to be able to choose good and evil. **The heavens initiate [your movements]...**

---

...your movements. According to theologians, philosophers, and astrologers, the celestial bodies have no influence that necessitates the rational soul in its intellect, nor in its will, nor in its free will. This is openly demonstrated by Ptolemy <note>A 2nd-century mathematician and astronomer.</note> in the *Centiloquium*, and by Aristotle in the first book of *On Interpretation* <note>original: "periermenias," the Greek title of Aristotle's *De Interpretatione*.</note>, and Saint Thomas Aquinas <note>The 13th-century Dominican friar and influential philosopher/theologian.</note> affirms this against the gentiles, using the authority of Aristotle in the third book of *On the Soul*: That the heavens are not the cause of our wills and choices directly. But they can imprint themselves upon the "first motions" of the soul, against which we can resist with reason and with free will. With this, if we choose the good, we thus merit; if evil, we demerit. This is not the case in the "first motions," because...

<summary>This page addresses the theological debate between astrological determinism and human free will. Marco Lombardo explains to Dante that while the heavens influence physical impulses, the soul is directly created by God and possesses the light of reason to choose between good and evil.</summary>
<keywords>Marco Lombardo, Free Will, Heraclitus, Plato, Aristotle, Ptolemy, Thomas Aquinas, Purgatory, Canto XVI, astrological influence, ethics, moral virtue</keywords>

<meta>Continuity: This page continues the commentary on Dante’s Purgatorio, Canto XVI. Following the previous discussion on the state of the world, the text now explores the relationship between celestial influence (astrology) and human free will, as explained by the spirit of Marco Lombardo. It moves into the famous metaphor of the soul as a simple child and the necessity of laws and rulers to guide human desire toward the true Good.</meta>

# CANTO XVI.

...are in our power. But the stars do influence bodily movements, which can incline the soul, but not necessitate it. For example, Mars inclines the heart to anger, and this moves the soul; but the soul, through its **free will**, can resist. Similarly, the Sun, along with human seed, generates a person, but it cannot infuse the rational soul, which comes solely from God without intermediary. The soul is more noble than the entire sensible world, and the stars are merely physical. Therefore, the heavens do not force the soul; if they did, **free will** would be lost. In short, there is first within us appetite, and then the rational will. Appetite, being primary, receives its motion and inclination from the external constellations. The will receives its motion and inclination internally from reason, and comes into action through free will. It is this second will that makes us deserve merit or blame. But **GRANTED THAT**, as I say, even if all our inclinations and movements of the soul proceeded from the heavens, nevertheless **a light is given to you**, that is, reason and intellect are given to you, by which you know good and virtue, and evil and vice. Certainly, free will is within you, and it is in your power to choose what you wish. Therefore, if one struggles to resist the first movements that start from the heavens, and if it **endures**—that is, if it resists those first battles between the inclination given by heaven and reason (which, knowing the thing to be evil, desires to flee it)—**THEN IT CONQUERS** everything. For if it resists the first impulse, it becomes temperate and wins. To a **GREATER FORCE** and a greater nature, the human soul is subject; not only to God, who is a greater force and nature than secondary causes, but although it is created, it remains free through God. **AND THAT** greater force **CREATES** the human mind, which the heavens do not have in their care. For God does not create the soul through secondary causes, but creates it immediately. **THEREFORE**, he concludes that **IF THE PRESENT WORLD**, meaning the false opinions and depraved and corrupt appetites you have toward virtue because of the contagion the body gives the soul, **LEADS YOU ASTRAY**, taking you off the right path and away from reason, **THE CAUSE** is in you, since you possess free will. **IN YOU** it must be sought; in you, it should be requested and searched for.

->From the hands of Him who cherishes it<-
->before it exists, like a little girl<-
->who, weeping and laughing, plays like a child:<-
->The simple little soul that knows nothing,<-
->save that, moved by a joyful Maker,<-
->it willingly turns to what amuses it.<-
->Of a small good it first tastes the flavor;<-
->there it is deceived and runs after it,<-
->if guide or curb does not turn its love.<-
->Hence it was necessary to set law as a curb;<-
->it was necessary to have a king who could discern<-
->at least the tower of the true city.<-

<column-break/>

The human soul, of which we have spoken, **COMES FORTH** from the power **OF HIM**, that is, God. And God **Cherishes it**: He considers it with pleasure because, as it says in Genesis: <note>original: "Vidit deus omnia que fecerat: & erant ualde bona"</note> "God saw everything that He had made, and it was very good." For God, in His eternity, sees everything that He must later produce successively in time. I say, therefore, that the human soul comes from the hand of God; that is, it is created by Him. And not without reason did he say "comes forth," because it departs having been created, not bound in a form so that it cannot go where it wills, but with the free will to be able to return or not return to Him. **IN THE MANNER**: like a little girl who **PLAYS LIKE A CHILD**, showing her playful and tender age, now weeping and now laughing. For just as a little girl without prudence is moved by appetite and not by reason, crying or laughing over small things, it shows that our soul is naturally disposed to passions and disturbances. **THE SIMPLE LITTLE SOUL** that knows nothing: according to the opinion of Aristotle, who holds that the soul is like a "blank slate" <term>tabula rasa: the idea that the mind is born as a blank slate on which experience writes</term> ready to receive whatever is imprinted upon it. **SAVE THAT, MOVED BY A JOYFUL MAKER**, it willingly

---

turns to what amuses it. It is innate in every created thing to have a desire to return to its origin, which is its Creator, the Supreme Good. Therefore, our soul, created by God—in whom, because He is the Supreme Good, there is supreme joy—naturally desires to be united with God. But, greedy and longing for this Supreme Good, it is often deceived. Because it has newly arrived in the body, it cannot yet exercise reason, which could recognize the true Good and discern it from the false. It uses, therefore, only the senses and appetite, which cannot taste the flavor of the Supreme Good (God), but instead **TASTE THE FLAVOR OF A SMALL GOOD**, that is, temporal goods; and in these, it is deceived. For the senses, baited by lusts and the pleasures of earthly things, believe that to be the "highest" which either is not good at all or is a very small good. Aristotle writes most correctly in the third book of *On the Soul*: <note>original: "Bonum intellectus est ultima beatitudo"</note> "The good of the intellect is the ultimate happiness." And if the good of the intellect is the ultimate happiness, it follows that it is God. Therefore, our intellect seeks this, unless it is deceived in its choice by the senses and appetite. I know that to clarify this passage it would be useful to recount many things which I narrated in the second book of my <term>Disputationes Camaldulenses: a philosophical work by the commentator Cristoforo Landino, written as a dialogue at the Camaldoli monastery</term>. But a volume of this size does not allow for such length in every detail. **OF A SMALL GOOD**: reason not yet being awakened, it follows the senses, which falsely judge that earthly goods, where there is some amusement, are the Supreme Good. **IF A GUIDE**: if our intellect awakens; if the doctrine or precepts of a more learned man admonish us; if the grace of God illuminates us. **OR A CURB**: or divine and human law **DOES NOT TURN its love**: does not redirect the love it has placed in earthly and fleeting things toward the celestial and Supreme Good. **HENCE IT WAS NECESSARY TO SET LAW AS A CURB**: it was necessary, since men let themselves be carried away by appetite and do not govern themselves according to reason, to restrain their pride, ambition, avarice, and lust with laws. Thus, those who did not abstain from vice out of love for virtue might abstain out of fear of punishment. <note>original: "Nam oderunt peccare mali formidine penę"</note> "For the wicked hate to sin for fear of punishment," as Horace learnedly writes. **IT WAS NECESSARY to have a king**: It is not enough to have laws if there is no King, Prince, or Magistrate to defend them and ensure they are observed. And this person must be of such life, doctrine, and prudence that, if he does not know the true city of eternal life, he at least discerns the **tower**—that is, the guardianship of that city, which is justice.

<margin>
<image-desc>Institutional stamp with the number 1914</image-desc>
</margin>

->Laws there are, but who puts a hand to them?<-
->No one; because the shepherd who precedes<-
->can ruminate, but has not cloven hooves.<-
->Because the people, who see their guide<-
->aim only at that good for which they are greedy,<-
->feed on that and ask for nothing more.<-

<column-break/>

There are certainly laws. But there is no one to put a hand to them. For although natural law is innate in our minds, concupiscence overcomes reason. Nor was there ever a nation or religion that had divine and human laws as perfect as the Christian ones. The Spartans had Lycurgus; the Athenians had Draco and Solon; the Cretans had Minos. Their laws were largely regulated by justice, as far as human prudence could allow. But Christian laws have their origin in Divine Truth. But what does it profit if the administrators of such laws are the first to corrupt them? **THEREFORE, WHO PUTS A HAND**...

<summary>This page explores the theological argument that while the stars may influence human inclinations, they cannot override free will or the rational soul, which comes directly from God. It introduces the metaphor of the soul as a naive child lured by earthly pleasures, necessitating the "curbs" of laws and the "guides" of virtuous rulers, while lamenting the corruption of the clergy who fail to distinguish between spiritual and temporal authority.</summary>

<meta>Continuity: This page continues the commentary on Dante’s Purgatorio, Canto XVI. In the previous section, the spirit of Marco Lombardo explained that while the heavens influence human inclinations, they do not dictate them; human beings possess free will and reason to choose between good and evil. The discussion now shifts to why the world has become corrupt, pointing not to the stars or human nature, but to the failure of leadership and the blurring of the lines between spiritual and temporal power.</meta>

<header>PURGATORY</header>

*You can clearly see that bad leadership:*
*is the cause why the world has become wicked:*
*and not nature, which might be corrupted within you.*

<column-break/>

...is there no one who governs them? No one. For neither do the Popes lay a hand upon ecclesiastical matters, nor do the princes and lay magistrates defend the temporal ones. THEY LAY A HAND. That is, they act according to the laws. For no one can correct others if they do not first correct themselves. THE SHEPHERD: he correctly calls every prince a "shepherd," according to what we have said elsewhere. <term>CHEW THE CUD</term> <note>original: "RVGVMAR"</note> but does not have cloven hooves. We read in Leviticus that God commanded Moses that they should eat the meat of every animal that has cloven hooves and chews the cud. Therefore, one of the two is not enough. And for this reason, the meat of the pig and the camel was not permitted: because they do not chew the cud, even though they have cloven hooves. These two things are necessary for whoever governs. By "chewing the cud," we understand diligent examination and consultation in whatever they have to do, similar to the ox and the sheep, which swallow grass without chewing it, and then, searching for it again with diligence, return it to the mouth, and bit by bit, chewing the cud, they masticate it. Hence there is a Florentine proverb: "he has chewed this thing well," meaning he has well considered and thought it over. Therefore, first, every governor—whether cleric or lay—must consider well and understand what he has to do. Next, he puts "cloven hooves" for <term>discretion</term>, which distinguishes temporal things from spiritual ones. And the prince must not confound them together. Rather, let the prelate care for the spiritual, and the prince for the temporal. These two principles, as written in the <term>decretals</term> <note>canon laws of the Catholic Church</note>, are from Christ as the mediator between God and man. For Christ did certain things as Emperor—such as when he drove from the temple those who sold and bought. Some things he did as Priest—such as when he offered himself as a sacrifice. But these roles ought to reside in distinct persons. This is shown in <term>Chronicles</term> <note>original: "paralipomenon"</note>: because when Uzziah <note>King of Judah</note> wished to burn incense at the altar, the priest forbade him. But as he persevered in his intent, God, in His anger, immediately covered him with leprosy. BECAUSE THE PEOPLE who see their guide. It is a marvel how much power example has—both the good and the bad of princes—over those who must obey them. Therefore, the poet concludes: seeing that the peoples and the shepherds, who ought to guide them to a righteous end, direct themselves toward worldly things, they too give themselves to those things because their appetite draws them. So, the people being ready and finding someone to lead them, it is inevitable that they fall into the abyss. YOU CLEARLY WISH TO SEE. He concludes: bad leadership—that is, bad guidance—is the reason why the world—that is, men—have become wicked, and not nature.

---

*Rome, which made the good world,*
*used to have two suns, and one and the other path*
*they made visible: both of the world and of God.*
*One has extinguished the other; and the sword is joined*
*with the shepherd's crook; and the one with the other together*
*by sheer force must ill-accord go.*
*For, being joined, the one does not fear the other:*
*if you do not believe me, look closely at the ear of grain,*
*for every plant is known by its seed.*

<column-break/>

He praises the time in which the Christian Republic was ruled by the Pope in spiritual matters and by the Emperor in temporal ones; because each cared for the part committed to him, and by attending only to one thing, he could do it with greater diligence. ROME USED TO HAVE: the Christian Republic, of which Rome is the head. Two suns: two principles—the Pope, Bishop of Rome, and the Emperor, King of the Romans. And one and the other path they made visible: just as the sun shows all the ways and regions of the world, so these princes showed one and the other path. That is, the Emperor made visible the path of the world; the Pope, the path of God. ONE HAS EXTINGUISHED THE OTHER. Because the Emperor wished to occupy spiritual jurisdictions, and the Pope the temporal ones—as appears through many histories in past centuries and the present—one and the other dignity has fallen into decline. AND THE SWORD IS JOINED WITH THE SHEPHERD’S CROOK. And being together, one extinguishes the other; not because one is contrary to the other, but because it is necessary that one fears the other. And the Emperor ought to punish with bodily penalty those who disturb the Christian Republic, and the Pope with spiritual censures. Hence King David submitted himself to Nathan the prophet. LOOK CLOSELY AT THE EAR OF GRAIN. As if to say, look at the fruit and the effect that is born from it. Because just as every blade of every grain is known by the seed, so every action is known by its fruit. Hence the Divine Truth says: <note>original: "A fructibus eorum cognoscetis eos"</note> "By their fruits you shall know them."

---

*In the land that the Adige and Po irrigate,*
*valor and courtesy used to be found*
*before Frederick encountered strife.*
*Now one can safely pass through there,*
*by anyone who might leave off, for shame,*
*speaking with the good or approaching them.*
*True, three old men are still there in whom the old age*
*reproves the new, and it seems late to them*
*for God to restore them to a better life:*
*Currado da Palazzo, the good Gherardo,*
*and Guido da Castel, who is better named*
*in the French fashion, "the simple Lombard."*

<column-break/>

It appears that through these rivers he wishes to describe Lombardy and Romagna: through which regions the Po passes, as we showed when we described it. And also the March of Treviso, through which the Adige passes. VALOR AND COURTESY USED TO BE FOUND. "Valor" in the Tuscan language signifies frank and prudent magnanimity; and we call those "valorous" who are adorned with such virtues. COURTESY is humane and gracious liberality with skillful and moderate manners; so named after the courts of good princes, in which such virtue always shines. FREDERICK. Frederick II, grandson of Emperor Conrad <note>Frederick Barbarossa</note>, began to reign after him. This man, made proud by the power of many kingdoms and by his sons, trampled upon all spiritual jurisdictions. For this reason, he was excommunicated by Pope Honorius, and remained excommunicated for seven years. Honorius was succeeded by Gregory IX of Anagni, who sat for fourteen years. With him, Frederick had a cruel war. And later he went to the Holy Land and deprived his father-in-law, John of Brienne, of the Kingdom of Jerusalem, and had himself crowned there in the year of salvation 1225. But John, with the favor of the Pope, took the Kingdom of Naples from Frederick. However, Frederick immediately returned to Italy and recovered the kingdom. And he occupied the Patrimony <note>the lands of the Church</note>, the Duchy of Spoleto, and the March of Ancona. Furthermore, he captured many prelates who were coming to the council that Gregory had ordered against him. He broke the Milanese and took a large part of Lombardy and Romagna. And Gregory died of grief. They say he had an elephant with him. Gregory was succeeded by Innocent IV of the house of Fieschi from Genoa, who held a council at Lyon on the Rhône, and again excommunicated Frederick; and those of the Fieschi family armed twenty galleys. The war moved to Parma, which was defended by the allies of the Church and by Frederick...
