...besieged. And the people of Parma, driven to their ultimate desperation and seeing that the Emperor <note>Frederick II of Hohenstaufen, the last powerful Holy Roman Emperor of the Middle Ages.</note> held them in little regard, waited for him to go hawking. They attacked and captured the great fortification built by him in the form of a city and named *Victoria* <note>Latin: "Victory." Frederick built this camp-city during the siege of Parma (1247–1248) to serve as his new capital once Parma fell.</note>. They seized all the jewels along with the crown, and he escaped to Cremona with no small difficulty. The defeat occurred on the first day of February 1248. In the following year, Henry <note>Enzo of Sardinia, Frederick's son.</note>, his son, was captured by the Bolognese in the territory of Modena, and shortly thereafter, in the third year, Frederick died. **NOW** one can travel through those lands safely. If there were anyone who felt shame in associating with the wicked—which happens to the sorrowful—and therefore fled the places inhabited by them, they did not flee these lands because they were not visited. Or perhaps it is better to draw another meaning from this text. For he has mentioned <term>generosity</term> <note>original: "liberalita." In the Middle Ages, this referred to the noble virtue of sharing wealth and hospitality.</note>, and generous men invite foreigners passing by into their homes, almost drawing them in by force. Thus, it often happens that someone traveling in a foreign land feels ashamed to go to the house of someone they do not know well and passes by with caution and almost in secret. Therefore, we shall say that now, because there is no longer anyone courtly there, one can pass through safely, without having to feel ashamed of speaking to or approaching the good—as if to say, visiting and staying with them. **INDEED THERE ARE**; truly there are. That is, there are three old men. As if to say that in all those lands, which used to abound with many magnanimous and generous men, there are now only three of such character in whom the ancient age <term>rebukes</term> <note>original: "rampogna"</note> the new. The meaning is that those three old men are examples through which one sees how much better the ancients were than the moderns. **AND IT SEEMS TO THEM LATE**: it seems that God delays too long in restoring them to a better life, that is, to eternal life. The meaning is that they desire to die. For just as the wicked fear death for fear of punishment, so the good desire it because they have hope of going to a better life and desire to be removed from the contagion of the wicked. **CURRADO DI PALAZZO** was a gentleman from Brescia. The chronicler of Imola <note>Benvenuto da Imola, an early and influential commentator on Dante.</note> writes that he heard that while Currado held the standard of his people in battle, and his hands had already been cut off, he embraced it with his arms and did not let it go until he lost his life. **GHERARDO DA CAMINO** was of the Camino family, which often held the lordship in Treviso. Because of his excellent counsel and virtue, he was called "the Good Gherardo." **GUIDO DA CASTELLO** was from Reggio in Lombardy, of the noble family called "da Castello." He was prudent, good, and a lover of liberty, which flourished in Reggio in those times; he was a contemporary of Dante. **WHO NAMES ME IN THE FRENCH MANNER**: the French call all Italians "Lombards." His fame for integrity and a life clean of all fraud was so great, and he was so entirely simple, that everywhere he was called "the simple Lombard." **FROM THIS DAY FORWARD, THE CHURCH OF ROME** concludes that because the Shepherd <note>The Pope.</note> wishes to confound and mix within himself the two regimes—the temporal and the spiritual—he is the cause of all evils.

> "O my Marco," I said, "you reason well;
> and now I discern why from the inheritance
> the sons of Levi were exempted.
> But who is that Gherardo who, as you say,
> remains as a sample of the vanished folk,
> as a reproach to this savage age?"
> "Either your speech deceives me or it tests me,"
> he answered me; "for speaking to me in Tuscan,
> it seems you know nothing of the good Gherardo.
> By no other surname do I know him,
> unless I take it from his daughter Gaia.
> May God be with you, for I come with you no further.
> See the rays that shine through the smoke
> already whitening; and I must depart—
> the Angel is there—before the day appears."
> Thus he turned back and would hear me no more.

<column-break/>

He approves of Marco’s judgment: that priests should not meddle in temporal affairs. He produces as evidence the example of the Bible, where, by the laws of Moses, the sons of Levi <note>One of the twelve tribes of Israel, designated for religious service.</note>—one of the sons of Jacob—were deprived of temporal goods because they were ordained for the priesthood and the administration of sacred and divine things. This was so they would have no other care than for sacred things, and they lived on tithes. **YOUR SPEECH**: as if to say, being Tuscan, it cannot be that you do not know the fame of such a great man. Therefore, by denying you know him, either you deceive me by telling a lie, or you are testing me. But because it often happens that we do not know a man by his proper name, but by being designated by some surname, I do not know by what better-known thing I could name him to you than by the name of his daughter, Gaia. She, being most beautiful and most honest, was renowned throughout all Italy. **MAY GOD BE WITH YOU**: he takes his leave because they had walked together so long that they had reached where the thick smoke ended, and the dawn was already beginning to be seen. And he could not leave the darkness. The text follows: **SEE THE RAYS THAT SHINE**, that is, it shines and gleams, already whitening, and **I MUST DEPART** before the day appears, that is, before the light is seen. **THE LIGHT IS THERE**: as if to say, do not fear losing the way, for the Angel is there at the end of the smoke, and he will show it to you. Regarding the Angel, the allegory is already known. It does not change in interpretation, but denotes that at every entrance to a new purification, divine grace shows us the true way.

<meta>This page continues the commentary by Cristoforo Landino on Dante's Purgatorio, moving from the end of the Terrace of Wrath into the Terrace of Sloth (Canto XVII). The previous page concluded the discussion on the purification of anger.</meta>

# PURGATORY
# CANTO XVII OF THE SECOND CANTICLE BY DANTE.

**U**nfolding in this seventeenth canto, our author rises and climbs to the fourth terrace, where <term>sloth</term> <note>original: "laccidia"; spiritual apathy or laziness in doing good</note> is punished. But first, he imagines that certain visions appear to him. Once these depart, he finds the angel who leads him to the stairs of the fourth terrace. **REMEMBER,** reader, in the Alps or in any very high mountain—properly, "Alps" are the mountains that divide Italy from France, but in the Tuscan language, though not in Latin, all high mountains are called "Alps." **MIST** caught you: this signifies a very thin mist, which is usually thinner in the mountains because it is drawn upward by the sun; not rising above five miles, it condenses there. **THROUGH THE MOLE’S SKIN:** because the mole always lives underground and certainly has eyes, but they are covered by a thin skin, because of which it sees very little. But that it sees something is manifest, first because nature—which does nothing in vain—would have made the eyes to no purpose otherwise. Second, because as soon as it leaves the earth and sees the air, it dies. Of this animal, Pliny says <note>Pliny the Elder, Roman naturalist and author of "Natural History"</note> that in many ways it is condemned by nature, and lives buried in perpetual darkness. **HOW AND WHEN:** He first admonishes the reader to remember the very thin mountain mist. Then he wants them to imagine the vapors which, because they were previously condensed by moisture, could not be penetrated by the sun's rays. But then, as the sun dissolves the moisture—which made them dense—it makes them thin, and the rays begin to penetrate, though weakly. By imagining these two things, the reader understands first what the darkness of the smoke was like, and how afterward, as the smoke came to an end, he began to see a certain glimmer of dawn. **AND LET YOUR IMAGINATION BE LIGHT:** let your <term>phantasy</term> <note>the faculty of forming mental images</note> be quick to understand this. Let this power be "light," as in easy to join or connect ideas. **I SAW THE SUN AGAIN AT FIRST:** before I was entirely out of the mist. **DEAD:** because as the sun was already setting, the rays were beginning to fail. **SO MATCHING:** Thus matching my steps with those faithful steps of Virgil.

**R**ecall, O reader, if ever in the mountains
a mist caught you, through which you saw
no differently than moles do through their skin,
How and when the thick and humid vapors
begin to thin, and the sphere
of the sun enters through them weakly;
And let your imagination be light
in joining me to see how I saw again
the sun at first, which was already at its setting.
So, matching my steps with the faithful steps
of my master, I emerged from such a cloud
into rays already dead on the low shores.

**O** imagination, that steals us
at times so far out of ourselves that a man notices nothing,
even though a thousand trumpets sound around him,
Who moves you, if the senses offer you nothing?
A light moves you that is formed in heaven,
by itself, or by a will that guides it down.
Of the impiety of her who changed her form
into the bird that most delights in singing,
the trace appeared in my imagination.
And here my mind was so restrained
within itself, that from outside there came
nothing that was then received by it.

**I**magination that steals us. He wishes to describe an imagination and vision that appeared, and he raises a doubt. The internal senses—which are common sense, imagination, phantasy, <term>cogitative</term> <note>the faculty of thinking or reflecting</note>, and memory—are moved by the external senses: sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch. Other philosophers posit three internal senses: in the first part of the head, they place a power they call apprehensive, or phantasy, or common sense. In the second, they place the imaginative, or cogitative, or <term>estimative</term> <note>the power to perceive the intentions of things, like a sheep sensing a wolf is dangerous</note>. The third is memory. In this place, the poet uses "imagination" for the "estimative" faculty, whose office is aided by reason to consider the things that the common sense, having received them from the external senses, has placed in the imagination (the second sense), and to judge if they are true or false, or good or evil. Such judgment is then placed in the memory, as I demonstrated more distinctly in my third book *On the Soul* <note>original: "dellanima"; likely referring to Landino's own philosophical commentaries on Aristotle</note>. The poet shows, then, that although the imaginative faculty (that is, the estimative) receives from the external senses, nonetheless it sometimes gathers the whole soul into itself in such a way that the senses "fall asleep" and cannot offer it anything. And then, either by celestial influence or, more likely, by light sent from God, it considers and judges that which the divine light offers it without the help of any sense. This appears manifest because we see someone so deeply plunged into their imaginations that, although they are in the presence of various people and where many sounds and noises are heard, they nonetheless see or hear nothing for the reason already stated, especially when aided by the phantasy, whose office is to compose and divide images. **WHO MOVES YOU IF THE SENSE DOES NOT OFFER:** If the order of things is that something first reaches the external senses—as, <term>for example</term> <note>original: "verbi gratia"</note>, the eye sees an enemy and offers that vision to the common sense, which places it in the imagination, and then the cogitative (which he here calls imagination), turning to the imagination as to a mirror, sees it and judges it useful to flee, after which judgment the appetite is suddenly awakened and moves to flee—then the poet asks: if the external senses offer nothing to the cogitative because they are asleep, who offers it to her? And he answers as we have already said. **AND A LIGHT MOVES YOU:** understand this as the <term>active intellect</term> <note>the part of the mind that makes sense of raw data and turns it into thought</note>, which **is formed in heaven**, <term>that is</term> <note>original: "i." (id est)</note>, it takes its being from celestial influences which minister activity and operation down to such a light, sent from the divine will without an intermediary, or from the will of the angels who are free and confirmed in grace. This divine power, or this angel, **GUIDES IT DOWN**, <term>that is</term>, guides the activity of said light. Although the human intellect is passive insofar as the external senses minister to it, it is nonetheless active insofar as it operates on the thing presented to it by the senses, and sometimes it operates without the senses on things influenced solely by God without any intermediary, or by God through the medium of secondary causes, which are the angels. In short, the cogitative faculty finds in the imagination a mirror where it sees things presented by the senses. But the form of the bird he will mention is influenced by God immediately, or through the medium of the angels. This is the nightingale, which is so eager to sing that it sings day and night. Now, returning to the poet’s fiction: just as he previously placed examples exhorting temperance (which is the best bridle to contain anger), he now presents examples that draw one away from anger by considering through them into what cruelty one falls if we let ourselves be carried away by wrath. And so he feigns that he was in a fixed imagination of the fable of Procne and Philomela, who, because she did not withdraw from anger, used unheard-of cruelty; a fable we narrated distinctly above. **OF HER IMPIETY:** the order of the sentence is "there appeared in my image," <term>that is</term>, in my imaginative faculty, "the trace," <term>that is</term>, the vestige and the form of the impiety, <term>that is</term>, of the impetuous anger of her, <term>that is</term>, of her who <term>that is</term> <note>original: "idest"</note> changed her form.

<meta>This page continues Cristoforo Landino’s commentary on Dante’s Purgatorio, Canto XVII. Having just finished the examples of punished anger, Dante now experiences three ecstatic visions of anger’s tragic consequences: Procne, Haman, and Amata.</meta>

...her form into the bird. That is, she became that bird which delights in singing more than all others. And although many here understand this to be Philomela, nevertheless this cruelty proceeding from anger was more present in Procne; we can also understand it as her, especially since the swallow also sings quite willingly. <note>original: "philomena... progne"; In the myth of Tereus, sisters Philomela and Procne were transformed into a nightingale and a swallow. Landino is debating which sister Dante refers to as the "bird that delights in singing."</note>

Then there rained into my high fantasy
one crucified, scornful and fierce
in his appearance, and so he was dying.
Around him were the great Ahasuerus,
Esther his wife, and the just Mordecai,
who was so whole in word and deed.
And as this image broke apart
of its own accord, in the manner of a bubble
when the water beneath it fails,
There rose in my vision a young girl
weeping loudly, and she said, "O Queen,
why through anger have you chosen to be nothing?
You killed yourself so as not to lose Lavinia;
now you have lost me! I am she who mourns
your ruin more than that of another."

<note>This refers to the burst of a bubble</note> made in the water by rain, which pops by itself. These bubbles or "bells" are born in the water when raindrops fall upon it. He compares, therefore, the imagination that falls into our <term>cognitive faculty</term> <note>original: "cogitatiua"; the part of the soul that processes sensory images</note> from a heavenly influence to a drop falling into water, creating a bubble that breaks in a short time. Thus, such an imagination or form is extinguished in the thinking mind, and another comes. **A young girl:** this was Lavinia, daughter of Latinus. When Aeneas came to Italy, Latinus blessed him with her as his wife, which thing was so troublesome to Amata, his wife and the girl’s mother, that she hanged herself out of the rage she took from this, especially because she wanted to give her to Turnus, her kinsman; from this followed the battles between the Trojans and the Latins described so excellently by Virgil.

By a most fitting comparison, he shows that he has emerged from his imaginations—which had made him oblivious to all other things—just as one emerges from sleep and wakes when, while sleeping, his face is struck by a sudden splendor. Therefore, just as sleep "breaks"—that is, is interrupted—when **Suddenly** (meaning all at once) a new light strikes the closed face, the closed eye.

As sleep is broken when suddenly
a new light strikes the sleeping face,
which, being broken, quivers before it fully dies;
So my imagining fell away
as soon as a light struck my humble face,
much greater than that which is in our common use.
I turned myself to see where I was,
when a voice said, "Here one ascends,"
which removed me from every other intent.
And it made my will so ready
to look upon who it was that spoke,
that it could never rest until it faced him.
But like the sun that burdens our sight
and veils its own form through excess,
so my power here failed me.

This is a divine spirit who, in the
way of going up, directs us without prayer <note>original: "sanza priegho"; without being asked</note>
and hides himself with his own light;
he deals with us as a man deals with himself.

<column-break/>

**ONE CRUCIFIED.** This was Haman, the prefect of the military under King Ahasuerus. King Ahasuerus of the Persians repudiated his wife because she would not come to him at his banquet. Afterward, he chose from all the most beautiful women Esther, the daughter of Mordecai, a Hebrew man. At that time, Haman was the prefect of the military. He, being angered against Mordecai because he did not adore him like the others, persuaded the King to kill all the Jews in his kingdom as a defiant nation that did not render him due honors. The King believed him and gave him his ring so that he would be believed by others, and ordered by his letters that throughout the Persian kingdom, all Jews should be killed on a determined day. Then Esther, hearing this, put herself in mortal danger to obey her father <note>Mordecai was her uncle/adoptive father</note> and went uncalled to the King, which was a capital offense. She obtained from the King that he should call Haman and Mordecai to a banquet. Haman, seeing again that Mordecai did not honor him, had a beam fifty cubits high erected to crucify him. But after the banquet, the Queen narrated the whole matter, and obtained the liberation of the Hebrew people. Whereupon Haman was crucified where he had intended to crucify Mordecai, and Mordecai was placed in the dignity Haman previously held. Ten sons of Haman were hanged, and the Jews killed a great multitude of those Haman had ordered to kill them. See, therefore, to what end Haman’s headlong anger led him. **AND AS THIS IMAGE BROKE APART:** that is, it broke itself just like a bubble made in the water by rain, which pops by itself. These bubbles or "bells" are born in the water when raindrops fall upon it. He compares, therefore, the imagination that falls into our cognitive faculty from a heavenly influence to a drop falling into water, creating a bubble that breaks in a short time. Thus, such an imagination or form is extinguished in the thinking mind, and another comes. **A young girl:** this was Lavinia, daughter of Latinus. When Aeneas came to Italy, Latinus blessed him with her as his wife, which thing was so troublesome to Amata, his wife and the girl’s mother, that she hanged herself out of the rage she took from this, especially because she wanted to give her to Turnus, her kinsman; from this followed the battles between the Trojans and the Latins described so excellently by Virgil.

**THAT AS WHICH SLEEP.** **Broken:** ruptured because it begins to go away. **Quivers:** makes the man quiver and move. **Before it fully dies:** before the sleep totally departs. **Suddenly:** all at once. **Quivers:** That thing which moves often and with speed, whence we say a fish "quivers" in the water. **Much greater:** the splendor which proceeded from the angel was much greater than that of the sun which strikes our faces. **When a voice:** from the angel, which was so powerful in me that it removed me from every other intent—that is, from every other thought that could hold my mind attentive. And this voice made my will so **ready**—that is, so solicitous and desirous to see who spoke—that it could not rest if it did not **face** him—that is, encounter him. But watching the angel who spoke, his light dazzled me just as the excessive light of the sun dazzles. The voice of the angel is speculative theological doctrine, which is so sweet that having heard it, we cannot rest or be quiet unless we see perfectly the source, which is the Eternal Truth itself. But we cannot see it perfectly because the human mind is not capable; but we can well hear the voice when it says, "Here one ascends"—that is, when it shows us the way to climb.

**HE DEMONSTRATES** that this is that angel who leads us upward without prayer—that is, without being prayed to—and **hides**—that is, conceals himself with his light. **He deals with us as a man deals with himself:** Thus the angel acts with us, helping us without being asked, just as a man—that is, the human race—should do with himself. That is, one man with another, because we ought to help one another without waiting to be requested.

<meta>This page continues the transition from the Third Terrace (Wrath) to the Fourth Terrace (Sloth) in Dante’s Purgatorio. Virgil begins his central discourse on the nature of love as the root of all virtue and vice.</meta>

->CANTO .XVII.<-

XVII.

...for he who waits for a plea when he sees the need,
maliciously already sets himself to denial.
Now let us accord our feet to such an invitation.

Let us strive to ascend before it grows dark,
for afterwards one could not, until the day returns.
Thus spoke my leader, and I with him

turned our steps toward a stairway;
and as soon as I was on the first step,
I felt near me something like the movement of a wing

and a fanning in my face, and heard: "Blessed are
the peacemakers, who are without evil anger." <note>original: "beati pacifici che son sanzira mala"</note>

Already the last rays, which the night follows,
were raised so high above us
that the stars appeared on many sides.

"O my virtue, why do you fade so?"
I said within myself, for I felt
the power of my legs placed in a truce.

We were where the stairs ascended
no further, and we were fixed there
just like a ship that reaches the shore.

And I waited a little while to see if I might hear
anything in the new circle;
then I turned to my master and said:

"My sweet father, for what offense
is one purged here in the circle where we are?
If our feet must stay, let not your speech stay."

And he to me: "The love of the good that fell short
of its duty is here restored;
here the ill-delayed oar is struck again.

But so that you may understand even more clearly,
turn your mind to me, and you shall gather
some good fruit from our stay.

Neither Creator nor creature was ever,"
he began, "my son, without love,
either natural or of the soul; you know this.

The natural is always without error;
but the other may err through an evil object,
or through too little or too much vigor."

<column-break/>

**The other.** <note>Referring to the previous page's commentary on the wolf metaphor</note> **FOR HE WHO:** a man who sees the wolf, meaning the need of another man, and waits for a plea, already maliciously sets himself to denial. **NOW LET US ACCORD our feet to such an invitation,** meaning let us go where he invites us to ascend. And because the foot signifies the affection—which moves the soul just as the foot moves the body—Virgil's "foot" will be the will, and Dante's will be the appetite. He demonstrates that one cannot ascend except by day. Wherefore it is said: "Walk while you have the light." <note>original: "Ambulate dum luce habetis"; John 12:35</note> But we have declared this above. Dante having reached the stairway that departed from the present circle, he felt a fanning on his forehead from the wing because the Angel erased with his wing the third sin <note>Wrath</note>. This wind moved by the wing of the Angel signified the inspiration that the Holy Spirit makes in the good will of one who is eager to purge sin, which, being inspired, removes the vice. **BLESSED ARE THE PEACEMAKERS,** the words of Saint Matthew: "Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called the children of God." <note>original: "Beati pacifici quoniam filii dei vocabuntur"; Matthew 5:9</note> **WITHOUT evil anger.** Because peace is the opposite of evil anger, and not without reason did he say "evil." For there can be moved in us a just and reasonable anger through zeal for justice against the sinner. In which "the sun does not set," <note>original: "no occidit sol"; Ephesians 4:26</note> meaning the light of reason is not extinguished. And this is good anger.

He shows that they have ascended into the fourth circle when the sun was already going down in that hemisphere; and when the sun goes down, its rays do not spread on the earth but rather rise higher because the last rays, after which night comes, were so elevated because the sun was going down, so that the stars were already seen. **O MY VIRTUE:** he laments that the power to ascend fails him, because the sun—without which one cannot ascend—was going down. Nor is it necessary to place the allegorical sense here, having already placed it in the verse: "The good Sordello rubbed his finger on the ground." And he said only this line: "you would not pass after the sun has departed." And certainly without the sun, meaning without the light of divine grace, one cannot ascend on high. I said to myself: "O virtue, o my power, you fade," meaning you vanish; the "l" is changed for the sake of the rhyme; and *dileguare* means to disappear, as we said in another place. **PLACED IN a truce:** to rest, a metaphor from war, in which men on every side rest when a truce is made. **FOR WHAT OFFENSE one is purged here:** it seems necessary to investigate why Dante asks what vice is purged here, not having asked about the others in the other circles. To which it seems to me the answer is: that this poet, having always been in constant meditation on great things and much exercised in the active life, had never fallen into the vice of sloth <note>original: "accidia"</note> of which they currently treat, in a form that he could well recognize it.

Virgil wants to demonstrate that in this circle the vice of sloth is purged, which is nothing other than not loving God and the virtues with that fervor which is appropriate; and therefore he says: **THE LOVE OF the good that fell short,** meaning of the good diminished from its duty. **HERE THE ILL-delayed oar IS STRUCK.** Here with diligence one restores negligence; and he uses a metaphor from a galley crew which, because it rowed sluggishly, is punished with beatings and forced to strike the oar, meaning to row so fast that it restores the past negligence. **NEITHER CREATOR nor creature was ever without love.** This is true because neither God—who alone is Creator—is without love, as we shall demonstrate in Paradise. **NOR CREATURE.** This can be understood generally of every creature: not only rational, but irrational; not only animate, but inanimate; because all creatures have love, that is, an inclination toward their own preservation. Nevertheless, here he restricts it to man, who through the acts of free will earns merit and demerit. **EITHER NATURAL or of the soul.** Love, as far as this place is concerned, is sufficient; it is either natural or of the soul. Natural is that which is between

<margin>197</margin>

us and God, and between the soul and the body, or between the will and the good, which is the object of the will; the love of the soul <note>rational/mental love</note> is that which he <term>appetizes</term> <note>the soul's desire for a specific object</note>. And this is further subdivided. For some love is simply good, such as the love of friendship. Some is not simply good but guilty by reason of the object. For just as virtue is ordered love, so vice is disordered love. And this is whether it be a love of evil or a love of good which is either too little or too much, according to two species of good. For some good is small, such as temporal and corporal good. Some is great, such as the goods of grace and glory. Therefore, the love of the great good is disordered if it is too little. And such is the root of sloth. The love of small goods is disordered if it is too much. And this is the root of gluttony, luxury, and avarice; although the miser loves these goods to possess them, the gluttonous and the lustful to take pleasure. The disordered love of nature is the love of another's ill or one's own. But no one loves his own ill, insofar as it is ill. But insofar as he judges it good, the love of the ill of others is the root...

Virgil explains that the sin of Sloth (accidia) is purged here and begins a seminal lecture on how all human actions, both virtuous and sinful, stem from Love.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Virgil’s discourse on the nature of love as the foundation of all human action, explaining how love—when misdirected or disproportionate—leads to the seven capital sins. This specific section categorizes Pride, Envy, and Wrath as the three forms of "evil love" directed toward one's neighbor.</meta>

# PURGATORIO

...of pride, envy, and wrath. Because pride is the love of one's own good joined with the harm of one's neighbor, loving one's own exaltation through the despising of others. Envy and wrath are the love of another’s harm. But they differ from one another. The love of wrath is born from another’s evil; for he who is angry with me wishes me harm because he receives harm from me. Envy is born from one's own malice, that is, from pride, and loves the neighbor's harm even though it does not benefit the envier, but simply so that the neighbor is not his equal. Therefore, in its matter, it communicates with wrath, but its end proceeds from pride. 

But repeating briefly what is sufficient for the present division: there are two species of love and desire. One is natural, which is infused in all creatures, by which they desire that good through which they preserve themselves in their being. THE OTHER IS OF THE SOUL <note>original: "animale," referring to the *anima* or rational soul</note>, and this proceeds from the will, in which there is choice and free will. The natural love never errs. The soul's love can err in three ways: either by the object, which is when the appetite—not guided by the light of reason—loves that which is evil instead of good; OR BY TOO LITTLE VIGOR, which is when that which deserves to be loved supremely and above all other things is loved little and coldly, such as God, the supreme good, and virtue <note>original: "lhonesta," referring to moral integrity</note> which contains all virtues. Hence, in the precepts given by Moses, or rather by God through Moses: "Love the Lord your God" <note>original: "Dilige dominum deum tuum"</note>. OR BY TOO MUCH, when temporal goods—which either should not be considered goods or are truly the lowest goods—are loved by us more than the eternal good. From this arise the vices already mentioned.

---

While it is directed toward the first good <note>God</note>
and in the second <note>created things</note> it measures itself,
it cannot be the cause of evil pleasure.
But when it twists toward evil, or with more care
or with less than it should it runs toward the good,
the creature works against its Creator.
Hence you can understand that love must be
the seed in you of every virtue
and of every action that merits punishment.

<column-break/>

This is the conclusion, and it says: Therefore, while this soul's love is UPRIGHT in the first good, that is, it rightly loves God because it loves Him as much as is fitting and as the Creator; and while it measures itself in the second good, that is, it loves created things moderately, which as God’s handiwork ought to be loved because they are good—"For God saw all the things he had made, and they were very good" <note>original: "Quia uidit deus omnia que fecit: & erat ualde bona," quoting Genesis 1:31</note>. And this second love is divided into two species: the useful and the delightful. IT CANNOT BE: this love so ordered cannot be the cause of dishonest pleasure. But when love twists toward evil—for evil is not loved directly for the sake of loving evil, but indirectly, either to flee discomfort or to pursue a convenience—he has already established one way of sinning. Then he adds the second, saying: or it runs toward the good with more care than it should, that is, it loves the second good differently than it should. OR WITH LESS CARE: and this is the third way of sinning:

---

when we do not love the first good as much and as well as is fitting. AGAINST THE CREATOR: when a person sins in these ways, he USES his handiwork against the Maker, that is, he employs himself—who is the handiwork of God his Maker—against His precepts. For He wills that we love Him first above all things, and then created things according to their degree. HENCE YOU CAN UNDERSTAND through the reasons already demonstrated, you can know that love is the seed and cause of virtues when it is ordered, and of actions that merit punishment—that is, vices—when it is disordered.

---

And because love can never turn its face
from the well-being of its subject,
all things are safe from their own hatred.
And because no one can be understood as divided
from the First Being and standing by himself,
every affection is cut off from hating Him.
It remains, if I distinguish well in my division,
that the evil that is loved is in one's neighbor; and this
love is born in three ways in your clay.

<column-break/>

He demonstrates that because love cannot turn its face, that is, it cannot depart from its subject—which is itself—it cannot help but always love itself. It follows that every thing is "safe," that is, secure from its own hatred. Therefore, no one hates himself, because to hate is to wish evil upon the thing hated. AND BECAUSE IT CANNOT BE UNDERSTOOD AS DIVIDED: the meaning is that anything which has being only has being insofar as God, who is the First Being, preserves it. One cannot understand any being to be divided from the First Being, nor can one understand any being to be standing by itself, that is, one cannot understand that any being exists by its own power. Therefore, naturally, everything loves its own being, and thus loves God. For this reason, every affection is "cut off," that is, divided from hating that God. IT REMAINS THEREFORE: if a

---

man cannot wish evil to himself or to God, it remains that every evil we love is loved in our neighbor. IF I DISTINGUISH WELL: that is, if I make a good division, which is this: if the good that is loved is toward God, or ourselves, or our neighbor, evil is similarly tripartite. But it has already been shown that we cannot love evil in God or in ourselves; it remains that we love it in our neighbor. IT IS BORN IN THREE WAYS: it is moved by three causes, as we will say below. IN YOUR CLAY <note>original: "limo," literally mud or mire</note>: in your filth, as if not by reason (which is the divine part of the soul), but through sensuality, which proceeds from the contagion of the body, a terrestrial thing.

---

There is he who, through his neighbor's suppression,
hopes for excellence, and for this alone longs
that his neighbor be cast down from his greatness.
And there is he who fears to lose power,
honor, favor, and fame because another rises,
wherefore he becomes saddened and loves the opposite.
And there is he who, because of injury, seems so shamed
that he becomes greedy for vengeance,
and such a man must seek another's harm.

<column-break/>

He had already shown that man does not love evil unless it is in his neighbor. Now he shows that evil in the neighbor is loved in three ways for three ends. For no one loves evil for its own sake, but loves it for the sake of a good he expects to be born from such evil; because it is the good that is loved. Therefore, one loves evil in his neighbor because he hopes through the neighbor's oppression to become great <note>This defines Pride</note>. Another desires that others do not rise to a higher rank because he fears that they might take away his power, honor, favor, and fame—things which he loves more than is fitting. And for this reason, he loves that the other does not rise <note>This defines Envy</note>. Another, having received an injury, desires vengeance, and for this reason, he loves the other’s harm <note>This defines Wrath</note>. And thus he shows that the love of evil is the cause of pride, envy, and wrath. By all these things, one knows that the will cannot simply love evil, but rather the evil of the neighbor for the end of one's own good.

<summary>In this passage, Landino comments on Virgil’s explanation of how all sin originates from misdirected love. Since human beings naturally love themselves and their Creator, the only way to "love evil" is to wish for the downfall or harm of a neighbor through pride, envy, or wrath.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Virgil’s explanation of how love motivates all human behavior. Having previously discussed the sins of "perverted love" (Pride, Envy, and Wrath) which seek the harm of others, he now moves to the middle ground of Purgatory: the sin of "deficient love" (Sloth) and prepares to explain the sins of "excessive love" for worldly goods.</meta>

# PURGATORIO

These three forms of love are lamented below;
now I wish for you to understand the other,
which runs toward the good in a corrupt order.
Each mind confusedly perceives a good
in which the soul may find rest, and desires it;
for which reason each person contends to reach it.
If a lukewarm love <note>The original "lecito" usually implies "permitted," but in this context of Purgatory, it refers to a "slow" or "slack" love that leads to Sloth.</note> draws you to see it
or to acquire it, this terrace,
after a just repentance, martyrs you for it.
There is another good that does not make man happy;
it is not happiness, it is not the good
essence, the fruit and root of every good.
The love that abandons itself too much to this
is lamented above us through three circles;
but how it is reasoned to be in three parts,
I am silent! so that you may search for it yourself.

<column-break/>

After having treated the love that turns toward the harm of one's neighbor, which was tripartite into pride, envy, and wrath, he presents the love that moves toward the good with less vigor than it ought. The first type, which is tripartite, is punished in the three circles already mentioned. This second type, because it lacks its proper fervor, creates the sin of **sloth** <note>original: "accidia," the spiritual apathy or "noonday devil" where one is sluggish in pursuit of God.</note> and is purged in this fourth circle. These three forms are lamented below in the four circles already passed. **THE OTHER** runs toward the good with a corrupt order. The upper tripartite love turned toward evil; the other—that is, this one—does not turn toward evil. Instead, it runs toward the supreme good, God, and toward the virtues with a corrupt order, because it does not love them as much as is fitting, and prioritizes utility and pleasure over love. **Each confusedly perceives a good.** There is in the mind of every human an innate desire to know the supreme good in which the ultimate end is found: for in that good, the soul is satisfied and contented in such a way that it seeks nothing further; therefore every mind **Contends**, that is <note>original: "i.", an abbreviation for the Latin *id est*</note>, it strives to join itself with it. **If a lukewarm love draws you to see or acquire it,** if love lacks its proper fervor, from which sloth is born, **this terrace**, this circle, **martyrs you**, that is, it punishes you after just repentance.

<margin>Chapter 5</margin> Just as a lack of love toward the supreme good creates sloth, so too does excessive love toward worldly goods create avarice, gluttony, and lust; these three sins are purged in the higher circles. **ANOTHER good is that which does not make man happy.** This includes all created things which are good, but they are an imperfect good and not the "good essence," because that is God, who is the fruit of every good. For the fruit and the reward of our good works is to enjoy God himself, and He is the root of every good. **The love that abandons itself to it**, that is, which runs into it abandonedly, meaning without the rein and measure of reason; for this reason it is "too much" and exceeds the proper limit. **THROUGH THREE CIRCLES.** Because in the first—which is the fifth in order—avarice is purged, which is a disordered love toward the goods of fortune. In the second, which is the sixth, gluttony is purged; in the third, which is the seventh, lust is purged. **I keep silent! so that you may search for it yourself.** Virgil has shown the supreme and perfect good, which belongs only to the intellect. Now, regarding the sensible good <note>Goods perceived by the physical senses rather than the higher mind.</note>, Dante can proceed by himself, and therefore Virgil leaves such inquiry to him.

<summary>This page explains the transition from the sins of malice to the sin of Sloth (deficient love) and introduces the final three sins of excessive love (Avarice, Gluttony, and Lust). Virgil explains that while all humans naturally seek "the Good," they often do so with insufficient fervor or by over-valuing temporary, worldly benefits.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discourse on the nature of love initiated in Canto XVII. Virgil, acting as the 'high teacher,' begins to define love's psychological and spiritual mechanisms to satisfy Dante's 'thirst' for knowledge.</meta>

# PURGATORY / CANTO XVIII OF THE SECOND CANTICLE BY DANTE

<column-break/>

**The high teacher** had brought his discourse to an end and was looking attentively at my face to see if I appeared satisfied. And I, whom a new thirst still tormented, remained silent outwardly, but within I said: "Perhaps the excessive questioning I do burdens him."

But that truthful father, who perceived the timid wish that did not reveal itself, by speaking gave me the courage to speak. Whereupon I said: "Master, my will is so quickened in your light <note>Dante refers to Virgil’s intellect and explanations as a guiding light.</note> that I clearly discern everything your reasoning carries or describes. Therefore I pray you, sweet dear father, to demonstrate to me what love is, to which you trace every good work and its contrary."

"Direct toward me," he said, "the sharp eyes of the intellect, and the error of the blind who make themselves leaders <note>A critique of philosophers who mislead others regarding the nature of morality.</note> will be manifest to you. The soul, which is created ready to love, is mobile toward every thing that pleases, as soon as it is awakened to action by pleasure. Your apprehensive faculty draws an image from a true being and unfolds it within you, so that it makes the soul turn toward it. And if, being turned, it leans toward it, that leaning is **love**; that is **nature**, which through pleasure is bound anew within you. 

Then, as fire moves upward because of its form, which is born to ascend to where it lasts longest in its element <note>In medieval physics, fire was believed to seek its 'natural place' above the air.</note>, so the captured soul enters into desire, which is a spiritual movement that never rests until the beloved thing makes it rejoice. Now it can appear to you how hidden the truth is from those people who claim that every love is in itself a laudable thing. Because perhaps its material <note>The 'material' of love is the capacity to desire.</note> appears always to be good, but not every seal is good, even if the wax is good."

<column-break/>

This chapter continues by explaining the nature of love, and then demonstrates how sloth <term>accidia: a spiritual apathy or "sloth" regarding divine things</term> is purged. **BUT that father**: demonstrating how a teacher should behave toward a student, and likewise how the intellect should guide the senses. We have spoken of this many times before. Not without cause does he call him **high teacher**, then **father**, and finally **master**. He calls him "high teacher" to show he can explain any great thing; "Master" because he is practiced in showing it; "Father" because Dante is his spiritual son. **Of the timid speech**: because fearing to be bothersome, I did not openly express my desire, but he with his words gave me heart. **My vision was so quickened in your light**: this shows that the sensory part and the lower reason gain strength and become intelligent through the light of the intellect. He incites Virgil to explain further because the more easily a student learns, the more willingly the generous teacher reveals knowledge. **Carries**: in knowing things previously unknown. **Describes**: in defining and dividing. For this reason, I pray you show me: what thing is love, from which you claim virtue and vice proceed.

Here he demonstrates what love is and reproves those philosophers who argue that every love is praiseworthy. **Direct the sharp eyes of the intellect**: because such science requires sharpness of wit and diligence. **The error of the blind who make themselves leaders**: The error of those who do not see the truth and lack knowledge, yet wish to teach doctrine. Thus they lead the student no differently than a blind man leads the one following him. These say every love is laudable, which is false. **The soul which is created ready to love**: because the human soul is created by God with the "concupiscible power" <note>The faculty of the soul that desires perceived goods.</note>, which can quickly be brought into action. 

For when either that sense called the "cogitative," or reason, or the intellect has judged something to be good, immediately after such judgment is given, the concupiscible power awakens and desires. For example <note>original: "verbi gratia"</note>, the eye sees a horse. The common sense receives this form from the sight and places it in the imagination. The cogitative faculty considers it in the imagination and judges it to be good and beautiful; this judgment immediately excites that power of the soul called the "appetite of the soul" to desire it. **Your apprehensive faculty draws an image from a true being**: this faculty judges what should be chosen. It draws the appetite toward what is "true being"—that is, from what is truly good. Even if it is deceived, it only loves because it believes the thing to be good. **And unfolds**: it opens and demonstrates this intention to the soul—that is, to the will—in such a way that the soul turns toward it. 

And if, in turning, it begins to lean and incline toward that thing, such an inclination is love and nature—that is, natural love. Thus we say that love is the inclination of the soul toward the thing that pleases it after it is presented. **Which through pleasure is bound anew within you**: because such an inclination, newly formed by the soul toward the thing that pleases, is a connection of the soul with the pleasing object; from this is born concupiscence and desire. **That leaning**: that inclination. **Is love, that is nature**: that is, natural love. **As fire**: every created thing was produced by its creator with an innate inclination toward its highest good. It never rests until it follows it. This inclination is from nature, sense, or reason. It is from **nature** in inanimate things, like fire. From **sense** not only in men but also in beasts; as when a bird sees bait and moves to feed on it. The inclination from **reason** is in man alone, as when we see Cato <note>Cato the Younger, often used as an example of rational, moral sacrifice.</note> seeking dangers to liberate his fatherland. 

Thus, as fire has from its "specific form"—that is, from its being distinct from other things—the tendency to mount upward as a light thing, and never rests (unless hindered) until it returns to its region, which is above the element of air. **WHERE it lasts longest in its element**: so our soul, captured by that which it judges to be good and beautiful, **ENTERS INTO desire**: into the wish to attain it. **WHICH is a spiritual movement**: this desire is a movement of the spirit, not the body. For desire moves the spirit and not the body, and such movement of the soul never rests **Until the beloved thing makes it rejoice**: that is, until it enjoys...

<summary>In this passage, Virgil provides a philosophical definition of love as a natural, spiritual movement of the soul toward what it perceives as good, while warning that not all love is virtuous. The accompanying commentary by Landino breaks down the Aristotelian psychology of how the mind processes an image to create desire.</summary>
<keywords>Nature of Love, Virgil, Dante, Intellect vs Sense, Concupiscence, Spiritual Movement, Cato, Medieval Psychology</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discourse on the nature of love between Dante and Virgil. On the previous page, Virgil explained how the soul is drawn to pleasing things. Here, he addresses Dante’s confusion regarding moral responsibility and the role of free will.</meta>

# CANTO XVIII

->**God does not obtain the beloved thing.**<- <note>This heading likely refers to a specific point in the commentary regarding how love can be misdirected or fail to reach its ultimate divine object.</note> Now he can conclude that from what was said above, it is seen that those who affirm that every love is laudable are in error. This error arises because they argue in this form: the **apprehensive faculty** <note>The part of the mind that receives sensory images and presents them to the soul.</note> does not put before the will anything except what it judges to be good; and the soul and the will do not incline toward anything except what the apprehensive faculty has already judged to be good. This argument would follow by necessity if the power of the soul that judges did not err. But because it does err, and offers as good that which is evil, the appetite is deceived. It falls in love with that thing as if it were a good thing; and while every thing created by God is good in itself, it was judged to be a greater good than it truly was. Thus, the falling away <note>original: "morte" (death), here used metaphorically for spiritual error or the "death" of right reason.</note> was greater than it should have been.

"Your words and my following wit,"
I responded to him, "have revealed love to me;
but that has made me more pregnant with doubt.
For if love is offered to us from the outside,
and the soul moves with no other foot,
it has no merit whether it goes straight or crooked."
And he to me: "As far as reason sees here,
I can tell you; beyond that, you must wait
only for Beatrice, for it is a work of faith." <note>Virgil, representing human reason, acknowledges his limits. Beatrice, representing Theology and Divine Grace, must explain things that surpass human understanding.</note>

"Every **substantial form** <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, the 'essence' that makes a thing what it is and gives it life.</note> that is separate
from matter and yet is united with it,
has a specific virtue collected within itself,
Which is not perceived except through operation,
nor shows itself except by its effect,
as life in a plant is shown by green leaves.
Therefore, man does not know where the intellect
of the first notions comes from,
nor the affection for the first objects of desire,
Which are in us just as the instinct in the bee
to make honey; and this first will
is not capable of merit, praise, or blame.
And so that every other will may align with this,
there is innate in you the virtue that counsels,
which should hold the threshold of consent.
This is the principle from which is gathered
the reason for merit in you, according to how
it welcomes and winnows good and evil loves."

"Those who in reasoning went to the very bottom <note>A reference to the great moral philosophers, like Aristotle or Plato.</note>
recognized this innate liberty;
therefore they left their morality to the world.
Thus, suppose that every love that kindles
within you arises out of necessity,
the power to restrain it is within you.
By 'the noble virtue,' Beatrice means
**free will**; and therefore, see
that you have it in mind, if she speaks of it to you."

<column-break/>

"I have understood what love is," Dante responds. But from this, a doubt arises: if love is born from something extrinsic—placed before the mind—and the mind does not walk with any other foot because nothing moves it but the appetite, it follows that since this movement starts from an external thing, the soul deserves neither reward for good nor punishment for evil. To this, Virgil responds: he will solve this doubt as far as reason can comprehend. But because this is not enough, he tells him to wait for Beatrice, who signifies **Theology**. This is because human reason only understands sensible and intellectual things through the senses; Theology teaches spiritual things, which are learned through faith and not through reason. And therefore he said that Beatrice was a "work of faith."

**Form** is that which gives being to a thing. Therefore, the form in man is the **rational soul**, because only through reason are we different from other animals. And the body is the matter. Therefore he says that every "substantial form"—which is the soul—is "separate" <note>original: "secta," interpreted here as "seata" or "separata."</note>, that is, divided and separate from matter. That is, it has its own being even when it is separated from its matter, which is the body. And yet it is also united with matter. Every soul has its being in the form, both in the body and when it shall be separated from the body; this is not true of the souls of brutes, because when separated from their bodies, they have no being. Thus the human soul is pure form because it is distinct from matter. And for this reason, it has within itself a power different from all other species, which constitutes its essence.

This power is not seen nor known except by its effect, just as a plant is not known to be alive except by its green leaves. And for this reason, man does not know from where the intellect of the "first notions" <note>Innate principles or basic truths that are known instinctively from birth.</note> comes; just as a small child has the first notions of knowing its father and other similar things, or general truths in grown men. Nor does he know from where the affection proceeds—that is, the love for the "first desirable thing," which is the Supreme Good, which is **God**, whom every man desires. But he does not know why this is naturally in the soul, just as the desire to make honey is in the bee. This first desire is attributed neither to praise nor to blame, because, as Aristotle says, "first movements" are not in our power.

But afterwards, in the second and third movements, and in all others, there is reason. For despite the fact that every other following will gathers around this first will—that is, although subsequent desires align with these first movements—nevertheless they have merit and demerit, which the first ones did not have. This is because they have innate within them the "virtue that counsels"—that is, **Reason**, which is given to us by God so that it may "hold the threshold of consent." That is, it is the master of consenting or not consenting. And from this reason, which can consent or resist as it pleases, is the principle from which our merit is born: if it consents to the good and does not consent to the evil. And thus demerit is judged in the contrary case.

Virgil follows by demonstrating what reason moved the philosophers to believe that virtuous operations in us deserve a reward, and vicious ones a penalty. Therefore, they "reasoning"—that is, through ratiocination—"went to the bottom." That is, they found the truth: which is that despite the fact that love (appetite) arises in us out of necessity—since a man cannot help it when the senses offer him a pleasurable thing—nevertheless we have within us **free will**, with which we can follow what reason dictates to us, and restrain and contain the appetite. The philosophers recognized "this innate liberty"—that is, free will.

---

"Therefore they left morality to the world." By restraining free will so that it would not decline into vice, they discovered honest living according to the moral virtues, and they wrote such precepts to help those who would follow. "By 'the noble virtue,' Beatrice means..." Dante is warned here: when Beatrice—that is, **Sacred Theology**—names the "noble virtue," she means free will. Hence in the fifth canto of *Paradiso*: "The greatest gift that God..."

<meta>The catchword "LO maggior dono" (The greatest gift) indicates the start of a quote from Paradiso Canto V regarding the gift of free will.</meta>

<summary>In this page, Virgil explains the relationship between innate desire and free will, arguing that while initial impulses are natural and neutral, the rational soul has the power to judge and control them. This capacity for choice is the basis of human morality and the foundation for divine merit or punishment.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Canto XVIII of Purgatorio. Having previously discussed the philosophical nature of love and free will, the text now transitions to the temporal setting of the poem and the introduction of the Slothful, who are purged in the fourth terrace.</meta>

### PURGATORY
#### hh

He demonstrates, according to the order of astrology, that the third part of the night had already passed. To better understand this: the moon, when it is full because it is in opposition to the sun, rises when the sun goes down. Afterward, when the fifteenth day has passed, because it wanes, it rises later each evening. Therefore, having been in opposition on the night the poet found himself lost in the woods, and this being the fourth night, it is reasonable that it did not rise except in the third part of the night. **MORE sparse**: because

> The moon, delayed almost to midnight,
> made the stars appear more sparse to us,
> shaped like a bucket that is all ablaze;
> and it ran against the heavens on those paths
> that the sun inflames when those in Rome
> see it set between the Sardinians and Corsicans;
> and that noble shade, for whom Pietola is named
> more than any Mantuan village,
> had laid down the burden of my loading.

**laid down the burden.** When someone is asked a particularly difficult thing, it seems that such a question is like a "load" or burden to them. Likewise, when they have satisfied the question with an answer, they feel as though they have been unloaded and have set down that burden.

Because Dante had now understood the clear and plain reasons with which Virgil had resolved his question, he remained idle and almost like a man who is **somnolent**—that is, full of sleep and wandering in mind; as if to say he remained empty of any distinguished thought. And through this, he confesses to **Sloth** <term>accidia: a spiritual apathy or "laziness" regarding divine good</term>, which had to be purged in this circle. Nevertheless, he shows that this state did not occur except after he had understood the reasons, and then only for a brief time. This fits with what we said above regarding the poet's sloth.

> For I, who had gathered the reason,
> clear and plain, regarding my questions,
> stood like a man who wanders in sleep.
> But this somnolence was taken from me
> suddenly by people who, behind
> our backs, had already turned toward us.
> And as Ismenus and Asopus once saw
> a fury and a crowd along their banks at night,
> whenever the Thebans had need of Bacchus,
> so along that circle their step curves—
> from what I saw of those coming—
> whom good will and righteous love bestride.

Not without great prudence does the poet introduce these two examples first to encourage speed, and afterward those

> Soon they were upon us, because running
> came all that great multitude;
> and two in front were shouting while weeping:

<column-break/>

The light of the moon prevails so much that it overcomes that of the lesser stars, so that only the greatest appear. This is because a greater light always obscures a lesser one. **SHAPED like a common bucket** <note>original: "secchione", a large bucket or scuttle</note>: because it is already diminished in its phase. Other texts read *secchione*. **AGAINST the heavens**: all the planets go against the movement of the heavens, because they move from west to east. Nevertheless, the velocity of the heavens pulls them along, as we have shown elsewhere. **WHEN those in Rome**: the moon had left the sign of Libra, where it had been in opposition, and was now in Scorpio, a very southern sign. When the sun is in this sign toward the west, those in Rome see it while looking between the islands of Sardinia and Corsica, because that part is to the west of Rome. **FOR WHOM Pietola is named**: he means Virgil, who, because he was born in a village in the Mantuan territory called Pietola in our times, makes this village more famous than any other. <note>original Latin: "apud antiquos hec appellabatur Andes" — among the ancients this was called Andes.</note> **Of my loading had laid down**:

This refers to the burden of the mind, which, through its deep and assiduous thought and contemplation in the profound sciences, was small and sparse. **BUT this somnolence was taken from me**: he establishes the form of the purging and the penalty that the slothful endured, which is most appropriate: because every contrary is cured by its contrary. Thus, negligence and laziness are purged with speed. He shows that he himself was excited and awakened because, indeed, not just him, but any lazy man, seeing speed in others, is ignited to do the same. **AND like Ismenus**: with no less speed went these people than the Thebans went along the Ismenus and Asopus, rivers of Boeotia where Thebes is located, when they sacrificed to **Bacchus**. Bacchus, as the poets feign, was the son of Jove and Semele, the daughter of Cadmus, King of Thebes. This union was bothersome to Juno, who, disguised as an old woman under the guise of charity, told Semele: "Many men deceive women by pretending to be gods when they are not. Perhaps this same thing is happening to you. I advise you, therefore, that when Jove returns, you ask him to grant you whatever you request. Then ask him to join with you in the same way he does with Juno." The young girl believed Juno's fraud and asked Jove to be content to please her in what she asked. Jove swore to do it. But once he heard her request, he regretted having sworn. Since it was not permitted to break the oath, he went to heaven and returned adorned with lightning and bolts, though he took the lesser ones. The mortal woman could not support such tumult and fire, and she burned because of the gift she requested. Bacchus was still in his mother's womb, and the time for birth had not yet come; but Jove himself most intensely bound him to his thigh until the ninth month arrived. And because he was born from two—first from the mother and then from the father—he was called **dithyrambos** <note>A Greek term for Bacchus, often interpreted as "twice-born."</note>. The Thebans worshiped him because he was the inventor of wine. In the sacrifices, the women were filled with fury; not in the temples, but along the rivers Asopus and Ismenus, they ran with lit torches and with staffs wrapped in vine leaves, invoking with very loud voices the names of Bacchus, which were many. Therefore, these spirits—who purged sloth with speed because they had previously been in the greatest laziness—now ran and, through the silence, spoke loudly. **HAD NEED OF**: had need of his help. **HIS STEP CURVES**: He bends his step; because they did not leave the circle, but turning around continuously, they bent and twisted their path. *Falcare* <note>to curve like a scythe</note> means to bend, a word derived from *falce* (scythe), which is bent and curved. **WHOM GOOD will**: that is, those whom righteous love bestrides from a good will; as if to say they are carried by righteous love.

those from behind demonstrate how much delay is harmful. For the first ones cause a man, leaving behind laziness, to return to study and fervor. And the last ones restrain us so that we do not fall again into somnolence, tedium, and laziness. Therefore, bitterly crying and weeping—which signifies repentance for past sloth and delay in virtuous action—they shouted.

The commentary explains how speed is the "contrary cure" for laziness and identifies Virgil's birthplace, Pietola.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the fourth terrace of Purgatory, where the sin of Sloth is purged. # CANTO XX <note>Though marked XX here, this text corresponds to Canto XVIII of the Purgatorio in modern editions.</note>

> Mary ran with haste to the mountain
> and Caesar, to subdue Ilerda,
> struck Marseille and then ran into Spain.
> Fast, fast, so that time is not lost
> through little love, the others cried out behind them,
> so that zeal in doing good might renew grace.

<br/>

> O people in whom a sharp fervor now
> perhaps compensates for negligence and delay
> put forth by you through lukewarmness in doing good,
> this man who lives—certainly I do not lie to you—
> wishes to go up as long as the sun shines for us;
> therefore tell us where the opening is.
> These were the words of my leader [Virgil],
> and one of those spirits said: "Come
> behind us and you will find the opening.
> We are so full of the desire to move
> that we cannot stay; therefore forgive us
> if our justice seems like rudeness to you.
> I was the Abbot of San Zeno in Verona
> under the empire of the good Barbarossa,
> of whom Milan still speaks with sorrow.
> And such a one already has one foot in the grave
> who will soon weep for that monastery,
> and will be sad to have had power there;
> because his son, deformed in his whole body
> and worse in his mind, and born of ill birth,
> he has placed in the stead of its true pastor."
> I know not if he said more or then fell silent,
> so far had he already run past us;
> but this I heard and it pleased me to retain it.

<br/>

> And he who was my help in every need
> said: "Turn here and see two
> coming along, giving a bite to sloth."
> Behind all the others they said: "First
> were the people for whom the sea opened dead,
> before their heirs saw the Jordan."
> And those who did not endure the labor...

<column-break/>

This signifies the "spurring of the mind." For whoever wishes to return to true fervor, or to lead others back to it, must rebuke and awaken them by proposing and bringing to memory all the examples that can spur us on. **Mary ran with haste to the mountain.** When Herod, in order to kill Christ—whom he had understood from the Magi was born—ordered that all infants two years old and under be killed, Mary, warned by the angel to flee to Egypt, carried her son Jesus with the greatest speed upon a donkey, running toward and quickly passing through the mountains. <note>The commentator here blends the account of the Visitation to Elizabeth with the Flight into Egypt to emphasize Mary's speed.</note> **And Caesar** departed from Rome with the greatest speed to overwhelm the armies of Pompey in Spain; he had already defeated them in Thessaly and turned them to flight toward Egypt. And although Marseille, a city in Provence, tried to delay him, he did not let it overtake him, but left Brutus there to besiege it. And he ran into Spain where he defeated Afranius and Petreius and a son of Pompey. **Ilerda** is a city in Spain <note>modern-day Lleida</note>. **FAST, fast**: This demonstrates how effective a good example is. Because of the words of the first two, all the others cry out: "Fast, fast, let no time be lost!" Our life is short; therefore, it is necessary to compensate for its brevity with our own speed. **FOR little love**: due to the slowness of Sloth <term>accidia: a spiritual laziness or lack of care for divine things</term>, which is nothing other than a lack of love, as shown above. **THAT zeal in doing good**: that is, the solicitude and speed of doing well "renews" in us—meaning it restores and causes to be reborn—the grace of God, which through sin had dried up within us. Certainly, the more a man strives to do good, the more he inclines God to help him.

**THROUGH Lukewarmness**: through sloth, which is nothing other than a lack of burning charity. **I do NOT lie to you**: I am telling you the truth. **AS LONG as the sun shines**: because, as we have shown, without the "sun" <note>symbolizing Divine Grace</note> one can only turn back or wander in the same place, but cannot ascend. **I WAS the abbot**: this person was a contemporary of Dante named Alberto, a man of good character but very submissive. **Zeno** was the eighth bishop of Verona, a man of holy life, excellent character, and profound theology, as is clearly seen in several volumes written by him. **BARbarossa**: Frederick I of Swabia, called Barbarossa because of his color <note>red beard</note>. He held the empire for thirty-seven years. At first a friend to the Church, he later became an enemy to Alexander III, by whom he was excommunicated. He waged terrible wars in Italy against the Lombards who favored the Pope. He destroyed Spoleto, relocated Lodi, and built Crema. He took Milan by siege in the year of salvation 1158, burned it entirely, and destroyed it. He plowed it and sowed it with salt, and they say 82,000 men from that city were scattered. He caused a great slaughter of the Romans. Terrified by this, he fled to Venice; the Doge, in favor of the Church, gathered a great fleet against Henry, the son of Frederick, captured him, and brought him to Venice. Seeing his fortune changed and the favor Alexander had from Louis, King of France; Henry, King of England; William, the excellent King of Sicily; the Venetians; and the Lombards, Frederick determined to humble himself before the Pope and ask for peace. He came to the feet of the Pope, who, pressing his throat with his feet, spoke the verses of the Psalmist: <note>original: "Super aspide & basyliscum ambulabo: & conculcabo leonem & draconem"</note> *I will walk upon the asp and the basilisk, and I will trample the lion and the dragon.* To these words Frederick responded: <note>original: "Non tibi sed Petro"</note> *Not to you, but to Peter.* The Pope said: <note>original: "Et mihi & petro"</note> *Both to me and to Peter.* After this reconciliation, Frederick, as satisfaction for the injuries done to the Church, passed with his armies into Syria against the infidels. But being in Antioch and bathing in the river during great heat, he drowned. Milan remained destroyed for five years. **AND such a one already has**: this proverb is used for those who are already close to death; it refers to Sir Alberto della Scala, Lord of Verona. More by force than by a direct path, he made his son—who was deformed and of wicked character—the abbot of the aforementioned monastery. Thus he says **deformed in body** and worse in mind. **AND born of ill birth**: because he was born of adultery. **HE HAS placed in the stead of its true pastor**: since the abbot should be the true pastor of the monastery, but this man, greedy and rapacious, was not a true pastor but a wolf. **I KNOW not if he said more**: the author wishes to demonstrate the great speed the abbot used in running away. In the brief time it took to speak what we have seen, he was already so far from Dante that he could not tell if he spoke more or fell silent.

Just as two spirits preceded the crowd with examples of zeal, these two came behind with other examples to draw them away from laziness. **AND he who was my help in every need**: that is, Virgil, representing Reason, who helps man. **COMING along, giving a bite to sloth**: that is, they were rebuking it. For sloth is the nurse of lust and the delayer of every good work. An enemy of labor, it weighs down the soul and binds the limbs. It rots in filth. It is improvident, blind, a friend of sleep, a servant of laziness, and without any diligence. **FIRST were the people for whom the sea opened dead**: The meaning is that the people...

...until the end with the son of Anchises <note>Anchises was the father of Aeneas; this refers to the Trojans who chose to stay in Sicily rather than finish the journey to Italy.</note>
offered up a life without glory.

...because in that [river] Christ, our salvation, was baptized by John the Baptist. There was no people who sinned more in sloth, nor were more ungrateful toward their benefactor, God. He had liberated them from the harshest servitude of Pharaoh with most manifest miracles, which He showed through Moses.
And nevertheless, they were so wicked that often, to flee from hardships and toil, they wanted to turn back; and many times they wished to kill their leader, Moses.
For them the sea opened, and they passed through on dry land; and then, as the enemy followed them, He closed the waters and drowned them all. And those who did not endure the struggle: the sentence is [pronounced]: as Aeneas did not endure the struggle of the voyage until Italy. This refers to the funeral games that Aeneas celebrated for his father in Sicily. One is an enemy to Troy [Juno], who grieved with the other women over the unhappiness of that people who were already weary from seven years of wandering through so many seas and still could not arrive in Italy. With a long speech, she persuaded them that, being in Sicily where their compatriot Acestes was, they should burn the ships so that their husbands, unable to repair the new vessels, would establish their seats in that island. The women obeyed and burned the ships. Aeneas and the others came to help, but they could not arrive in time before four were burned. Aeneas took the course of leaving part of his people with Acestes; therefore, those who remained were the more lazy ones and those who least valued glory.

> When those shades were so far divided from us
> that they could no longer be seen,
> a new thought entered within me,
> from which others, many and diverse, were born;
> and I wandered so much from one to another
> that I closed my eyes out of wandering
> and transformed the thinking into a dream.

Sleep is generated. And the thoughts that were in us while awake are alienated from the sloth of which we are currently speaking.

<column-break/>

The people of Israel, for whom the Red Sea opened as they fled from Egypt: they all died before reaching the river Jordan, of which they were meant to be the heirs. And the author places the Jordan here as the river of the Promised Land to represent that land itself. The Jordan is that which divides Judea from Arabia. They were fed with manna in the desert for forty years and received many other benefits, yet out of extreme sloth, they wished to return to Egypt.
The people, who numbered more than six hundred thousand males: through that opening, Pharaoh with his army was enclosed.
Those people who, coming with the son of Anchises, for this reason offered themselves to a life without glory. In the <term>Aeneid</term> <note>Dante's primary source for the story of Aeneas.</note>, the goddess Juno, disguised as an old woman named Beroe—who was a woman of authority—persuaded the Trojan women to burn the ships.
This happened when they were in Sicily, where Acestes was their compatriot. They burned the ships so that they would stay in that island and eventually pass their lives there. The women obeyed, and Aeneas could not save four of the ships from the fire. He took the course of leaving the more lazy people behind, those who cared little for glory.
Having separated from the souls he was thinking about, the poet entered into new thoughts. And from these first ones, many others and diverse ones were born.
<insert>T</insert>his he says because, having investigated the purgation of the four sins mentioned so far, he was investigating that of the others. And because our investigation proceeds with <term>ratiocination</term> <note>The process of logical reasoning or discourse.</note>, that is, with the discourse of reason, he demonstrates such a discourse from thought to thought.
**AND SO MUCH FROM ONE TO ANOTHER I WANDERED:** It was still night; and because we have said that without the sun <note>Symbolizing the light of God's grace or spiritual clarity.</note> one cannot ascend—which here means acquiring any new knowledge—he says that he wandered, that is, he strayed with his mind from thought to thought. Nevertheless, all were vain because he did not find the truth. And for this reason, he fell asleep out of "wandering," that is, through that roaming discourse. For whenever, after much discourse, we do not find the truth, the fatigue and the weariness turn into a dream. If we note all these things well, they are not out of place.
