<meta>This page contains the opening of Canto XIX of Purgatorio. It precedes the previously translated Canto XX, focusing on the transition from the vice of Sloth to the vice of Avarice, introduced through Dante's symbolic dream of the "Stuttering Woman."</meta>

<center>PURGATORY</center>
<center>hh iii</center>

### CANTO XIX OF THE SECOND CANTICLE BY DANTE.

Up to this point, he has treated four spiritual and diabolical vices: those which proceed from malice. These are pride, envy, vainglory, and sloth. <note>The commentator lists "vainglory" as a separate vice, though Dante usually groups it with Pride; here it likely refers to the transition toward the more physical sins.</note> Now follow three which are born more from the senses than from reason; they are corporeal and voluptuous. But in this nineteenth canto, the poet sets down a vision that appeared to him in a dream, and afterward he reaches the stairway that climbs to the fifth circle, in which avarice is purged. But first, he describes the time, saying:

In the hour when the day's heat
can no longer warm the cold of the moon,
vanquished by the earth or sometimes by Saturn;
When the geomancers <term>geomancers: practitioners of divination using patterns of points in the earth or sand</term> see their "Greater Fortune"
rising in the east before the dawn
by a path that does not long stay dark for it;
There came to me in a dream a stuttering woman,
with squinting eyes and distorted on her feet,
with severed hands, and sallow in her color.
I looked at her; and as the sun comforts
the cold limbs that the night weighs down,
so my gaze made her tongue
Ready, and then it straightened her all up
in a short time, and her lost face
she colored just as love desires.

<column-break/>

**In the hour when the day's heat can no longer [warm] the light of the moon.** It is to be noted here that the reflection of the sun's rays, which, by striking the earth, reverberate upward and heat the air. Afterward, when night is held, the air begins to grow cold because of the departure of the sun and because of the moon's rays, which are cold. This is because the moon has no light of its own but receives it from the sun; it reflects downward those rays received from the sun, and every downward reflection creates cold, just as every upward reflection creates heat. Nevertheless, until midnight, the air retains some of the day's heat; but afterward, the moon's rays overcome the heat such that the further the night goes, the more the cold increases. This is because the "diurnal" (daily) heat no longer has power, and the moon is aided by the earth, which is cold and dry, and sometimes it is aided by Saturn. For when Saturn gives its vigor to the moon—because it is a cold and dry planet—it greatly increases the lunar cold. Regarding this, Alan the astrologer <note>original: "Alano astrologo." Referring to Alan of Lille, a 12th-century scholar.</note> writes of Saturn: "He with his chill steals the joys of spring, and steals the beauty of the meadows and the stars of the flowers." <note>original: "Hic algore ſuo furatur gaudia ueriſ. Furaturq; decuſ pra tif & ſidera floru."</note> He describes, therefore, the morning time near the day, in which—as we demonstrated in the first canticle—dreams are true. **When the geomancers.** He describes the same time in another way. For geomancers perform their art in the morning time when the dawn comes, because at that time the human soul and body are more obedient to celestial inclinations. Here we should understand that man can be moved by three causes: first, by his own will, which is born from the choice of free will; second, born from a will moved by some passion, such as from too much fullness or emptiness of the stomach, or from too much resolution

of humors or a defect of vital spirits; third, from natural inclination, which is caused by the motions of the heavens. This third cause alone possesses divination. Therefore, the geomancer, wishing to exclude the other two, acts against the first by insisting that the points be made without counting or thinking about them, so that they are not by our choice but according to celestial divination. And against the second, he chooses the time of the morning, in which the soul and body are more sober—neither too full nor too empty. Geomancy is a species of divination which the Orientals practiced especially around the dawn; upon the ground they make sixteen rows, not of lines, but of fortuitous points not counted by the one who makes them. Then they divide them into four parts, because each part has four rows, and they pair the points of the row such that in the last one remains an even number or a void. From every set of four, they take the last parts and make a figure. The names of the figures are: Joy, Sadness, Greater Fortune, Lesser Fortune, Acquisition, Loss, White, Red, Conjunction, Cancer, People, Way, Boy, Girl, Head, Tail. **Their Greater Fortune:** This figure mentioned above is similar to a constellation of stars which is found at the end of Aquarius and the beginning of Pisces. Thus, if the sun was then rising with Aries, it follows that the figure of Greater Fortune—which is at the beginning of Pisces and rises about an hour before Aries—would appear in the east at dawn, which is about an hour before the sun. **There came to me in a dream a stuttering woman:** because the three vices that follow are due to excessive and immoderate love for temporal goods—not true goods, but false ones. Through this vision, the poet wishes to demonstrate the false happiness that results from them. He imagines a woman who has five defects: she speaks distortedly because she is a stutterer and stammerer; she sees distortedly because she is squint-eyed; she walks with a limp; and similarly, she performs manual works imperfectly because she is maimed; and finally, she is of an ugly color. False happiness consists of these five things: riches, lordships, honors, fame, and corporeal pleasure. She is thus a stutterer—that is, she stammers and does not speak clearly—because the fame of such things is imperfect and is rather infamy. By being squint-eyed, she signifies the imperfection of honors. This is contrary to that Virgilian verse: "And he breathed upon him the honor of joyful eyes." <note>original: "& letoſ oculiſ afflarat honoref." A reference to Aeneid I.591.</note> She is crippled to show that men who sustain and lean upon riches are like those who sustain the body on a lame foot. And because temporal lordships have imperfect and vicious operations, she is maimed, for we have said that the hands signify operations. The sallow and pale color demonstrates carnal pleasures, which consist mostly of colors and beauties. It treats, therefore, of immoderate love toward the false good in which there is only desire; and then comes avarice, or the desire and the act which is in the sense of taste and is born in the throat, or in touch and is born in lust. **I looked at her:** the meaning is that while he looked at this woman, it happened that—just as the rays of the sun comfort and straighten the limbs of animals and plants which the nocturnal cold had withered—so Dante's gazing straightened the limbs of that woman and restored her color such that she remained a beautiful woman. This signifies that Dante—that is, sensuality—looking at these worldly goods, judges them by his own falsehood to be beautiful. Therefore, our false opinion makes them beautiful. **Just as love desires:** because the inordinate love that we place in these goods makes them seem to be what they are not, and just as we would wish them to be. And this proceeds because, by despising divine things, we place all our care in earthly things. Hence the Psalmist says: "My soul has cleaved to the pavement." <note>original: "Adheſit pauimento anima mea." Psalm 119:25.</note> And John in the Apocalypse: "Woe to those who dwell on the earth." <note>original: "Ve habitantibuſ in terra." Revelation 8:13.</note> And Luke in the Gospel, when he demonstrates the infirmity of the woman who could not look upward.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante’s dream of the Siren in Canto XIX of the Purgatorio. It explains the transition from the "Stuttering Woman" to the "Sweet Siren" and her eventual exposure by Reason (Virgil) and Philosophy (the Holy Woman). It then moves to the ascent to the fifth terrace.</meta>

<page-num>XIX</page-num>
# CANTO XIX

Once she had her speech thus loosened,
she began to sing so that with difficulty
would I have turned my attention from her.

"I am," she sang, "I am the sweet siren,
who leads mariners astray in the deep sea,
so full am I of pleasure to hear.

I turned Ulysses from his wandering path
to my song; and whoever dwells with me
rarely departs, so much do I satisfy him."

Her mouth was not yet closed again
when a holy and prompt lady appeared
beside me, to put the siren to confusion.

"Virgil, Virgil, who is this?"
she said fiercely; and he came
with his eyes fixed only on that honest one.

The other he took, and ripped her open in front,
tearing her clothes and showing me her belly;
which woke me with the stench that issued from it.

...wisdom and without doctrine. But **Ulysses**: that is, the wise man; so that the flatteries of these pleasures do not pull him away, he has himself tied to the mast of the ship, which signifies the **temperance of the soul** <note>In the medieval tradition, Ulysses' mast was often interpreted as a symbol of the Cross or the moral strength of temperance.</note>, which ensures he does not fall into pleasures; and the wax with which he plugs his ears is the fortitude that arms him against the furious impulses of sensuality. Thus he passes by the sirens and is not taken by them, because the wise man, having already formed a habit in the virtues, cannot be contaminated by vices. See then that Dante calls this a siren; and for what reason, she being ugly, when Dante—that is, sensuality—looks at her, she becomes beautiful. **"Who leads mariners astray in the deep sea."** We established above that the sea represents appetite. Therefore, the "mariners" are those who let themselves be carried away by appetite, and these are those whom worldly pleasures flatter and allure to themselves. **"I turned Ulysses"**: perhaps she moved him, because the first impulses of the heart are not in our power, and even the wise are sometimes shaken when they see something voluptuous; whence Solomon said: *Vinum & mulier apoſtatat ſapientē* <note>original: "Vinum et mulier apostatat sapientes" — Wine and women lead the wise astray (Sirach 19:2).</note>. But I believe the poet induces the siren to speak falsely, because it is the nature of voluptuous and intemperate men, when they wish to corrupt others, to bring up the examples of wise, prudent, and great men. They say that Solomon, David, Hercules, and many others allowed themselves to be conquered by a woman, and Alexander the Great by wine. **"And whoever dwells with me"**: he who makes a habit of me. That is, those who have no habit of the pleasures of eternal goods rarely depart and untangle themselves. **"In the end I satisfy him entirely"**: I content him in such a way that he no longer thinks of great and heavenly things, which is the height of misery. For he who is with the sirens and yet is not content with their songs, there is hope that he will depart and seek truer goods—indeed, the truest goods—and leave these false ones. **"Her mouth was not yet closed"**: false happiness was still pulling at the senses, when another lady, who is **Philosophy**, came to the aid of the senses to refute vain pleasures. And with fierce words she said to Virgil: "Who is this?"—as if she were reproving Virgil for not driving her away from Dante. For it is the office of **Reason** to remove every desire for non-virtuous things from the senses. And Virgil, that is Reason, looked upon Philosophy; and he tore the clothes of the other woman. Pleasures are like an ugly body that appears beautiful because it is adorned with beautiful garments. Therefore, Reason, by tearing the clothes of this pleasure, shows her ugliness, and by opening her belly, makes her stench appear. For in truth, whoever searches the interior of these three vices and of every pleasure finds nothing but ugliness and corruption.

I turned my eyes, and my master's goodly
voice spoke: "Rise and come;
let us find the gate through which you enter."

Up I rose, and all the circles of the high
mountain were already full of the high day,
and we went with the new sun at our backs.

Following him, I bore my brow
like one who has it burdened with thought,
who makes of himself a half-arch of a bridge.

When I heard: "Come, here is the pass,"
spoken in a manner so sweet and kind,
such as is not heard in this mortal region.

With open wings that seemed like a swan's,
he who had spoken to us turned us upward
between two walls of the hard rock.

He moved his feathers and fanned us,
affirming that those who mourn are blessed,
for they shall have their souls gifted with consolation.

<column-break/>

After the woman was free from every distortion, and especially had her tongue freed, she began to sing in a way that her song so delighted Dante that he could hardly have removed his *intento*, that is, his intention and affection, from her. This signifies that since temporal goods—which have all the deformities mentioned—please the senses in a way that they seem true goods, such a pleasure is born from them that the senses can hardly withdraw. This woman, singing, said she was a **siren**. So that this may be properly understood, the poets feign that the sirens were three daughters of the river **Achelous** and of **Calliope** <note>Achelous was a river god; Calliope was the Muse of epic poetry.</note>, so called from a Greek verb that means "to bind and retain" and not "to pull" as many say; for the poets use them to represent corporeal pleasures and the delights of worldly things, which entangle and bind our senses so that we do not know how to depart from them. And although there is much variety in their number and names, the most learned posit three sirens: **Parthenope**, **Leucosia**, and **Ligia**. They are said to have lived on certain rocks in Sicily near Mount Pelorus; they sang so sweetly that they drew sailors to them with the sweetness of their song, and then devoured them so that nothing remained but the bones. **Homer** adds that Ulysses, sailing through those seas, fearing the song might pull him toward them, had himself tied to the mast of the ship and plugged his ears with wax so as not to hear. And it is certainly true that the false delights of worldly and transitory things, with their sweet flatteries, draw us to love them, and then devour us; because such pleasures take away the strength of the body, the goods of fortune, and the wisdom of the soul. Therefore, we remain unhealthy, poor, and infamous.

We can understand at least three voices: that Reason awakens the senses by exciting the memory to remember; likewise with the intellect, that he understands he is a man and not a beast; and with the will to do what he intends. **"Up I rose"**: this shows that the senses, excited by the intellect, become obedient and can rise, especially as the sun had already risen, which illuminated all the circles of the mountain. **"And they went with the new sun"**: as if with a new speculation, because they knew that these three following vices [Avarice, Gluttony, Lust] proceed from a different origin than the four passed [Pride, Envy, Wrath, Sloth].

**"And following him"**: that is, Virgil, I bore my brow toward the back of Virgil. This signifies that he bowed his head almost upon Virgil's back, as one does who is weighed down by thoughts. And in this form, it is shown that the senses are sustained by Reason. **"When I heard"**: having reached the stairs where one climbed to the fifth circle, they found the **Angel** who, with most sweet words, said: "Come, here is the pass." And with his wings, he fanned his forehead, absolving him of **Sloth**. And he spoke according to what is written in Matthew: *Beati qui lugent. quoniam ipſi conſolabuntur* <note>original: "Beati qui lugent, quoniam ipsi consolabuntur" — Blessed are they that mourn: for they shall be comforted (Matthew 5:4).</note>. And this was the companion of those who were purging themselves.

The Angel and the two wings signify what we have already said above. **"They went between two walls"**: that is, walls of rock, because the senses were now so corroborated that by going through the middle...

<meta>catchword: because it was [perche era]</meta>

<summary>Dante dreams of a Siren representing worldly temptation, who is exposed as foul by a holy woman (Philosophy) and Virgil (Reason). The poets then encounter the Angel of Solicitude, who purges Dante of Sloth as they ascend to the terrace of Avarice.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante’s Purgatorio, Canto XIX. Having witnessed the dream of the Siren (the "ancient witch") and her exposure by Virgil, Dante now ascends with his guide to the fifth terrace, where the sin of Avarice is purged. The text explains the transition from the psychological weight of the dream to the physical reality of the mountain's higher levels.</meta>

# PURGATORIO

through the way of virtue: he had obstacles on every side to keep him from falling into either extreme.

"What ails you that you seem to gaze only at the earth?"
my guide began to say to me,
when both of us had climbed a little past the angel.

And I: "With such suspicion I am made to go
by a new vision that so bends me to itself
that I cannot withdraw my thoughts from it."

"Did you see," he said, "that ancient witch
who alone above us is now lamented?
Did you see how man frees himself from her?

Let it suffice you, and beat your heels against the ground;
turn your eyes to the lure that is whirled
by the eternal King with the great spheres."

<margin>nor has he shown us how we can escape from it.</margin> **AND BEAT.** Reason gives two precepts to sensuality. First: that he **beat his heels against the ground**, <note>meaning: that he proceed in virtuous action, or rather, that he trample upon worldly desires.</note> Then he gives the second, saying, **Turn your eyes.** Turn your thoughts and contemplations to the calling that God makes to us by inspiring us with His grace. This is a metaphor from falconry: for the sake of brevity, they call the bird's lure the "lure." <note>term: *logoro* (lure) — a tool used by falconers to call back a hawk; here it represents the celestial spheres that should draw the soul toward God.</note> Turn your eyes, then, to the lure which the eternal God whirls with the great wheels of the heavens, which, by their turning, demonstrate eternal beauties to us.

Like the falcon that first looks at its feet,
then turns at the cry and stretches forward
through desire for the meal that draws it,

Such I became; and such, as far as the rock
is split to provide a path for those going up,
I went until the circling begins.

When I was released into the fifth circle,
I saw people within it who were weeping,
lying on the ground, all turned face down.

"My soul cleaved to the pavement" <note>original Latin: *Adhesit pauimento anima mea*. This is a quote from Psalm 119:25, used here to show how the soul of the avaricious was stuck to earthly things.</note>
I heard them say with such deep sighs
that the words could hardly be understood.

"O chosen of God, whose sufferings
justice and hope make less hard,
direct us toward the other ascents."

"If you come secure from lying prostrate,
and wish to find the way most quickly,
let your right hands always be on the outside."

Thus the poet prayed, and thus was answered
from a little ahead of us; whereby, in the speaking,
I noticed the other hidden thing,

And I turned my eyes to the eyes of my lord;
whereat he signaled to me with a glad sign
what the look of my desire was seeking.

<margin>that I might speak to him.</margin> **WHAT THE LOOK OF MY DESIRE WAS SEEKING:** that is, the desire which appeared in me without words and was visible in my face.

<column-break/>

Dante went with his head bowed toward the earth. This denotes that sensuality is enticed by the song of worldly pleasures. Even though Virgil had shown him her stinking belly and pulled him away from her, he was nonetheless weighed down by the desire for such goods and looked at the earth: that is, he had his thoughts on earthly pleasures. Therefore, when Virgil, his guide, reproved him for this, he confessed that the **new vision**—which was a false appearance of happiness—bent him toward itself. And he rightly said "bends," because just as virtue guides us upright, so conversely this vision bends us and makes us twist away, so that we cannot detach our thoughts from it. **Did you see that ancient witch?** Simple people say that witches are old women who transform themselves into various animal forms and then suck the blood of children. He calls this false happiness a "witch" because she sucks away our spirits and senses. And he encourages Dante to climb, because he has passed the four greater vices and only those remain which contain avarice, gluttony, and lust. **DID YOU SEE** how man frees himself from her: that is, unties himself. Virgil had already demonstrated this when he ripped her garment. **LET IT SUFFICE YOU.** It should be enough for us to flee this witch that reason...

First he used a metaphor of falconry; now he uses a comparison and says that, just as the falcon, when it hears the cries of the falconer who shows him the lure, first looks at its feet and then stretches out toward the lure because it believes there is the meal it desires, so did I at the words of Virgil. And I went as far as **the rock is split**: that is, as much as the stone opens to make a stairway for those who wish to mount to the fifth terrace. I went to the end and the top of that stairway where the circling is taken up: that is, where the terrace begins that forms a circle. **AND AS I WAS RELEASED** into the fifth circle: that is, as soon as I exited the stairs and entered the terrace, **I SAW** people within who were weeping, repenting with contrition for their sins, and lying prostrate on the ground: that is, with their faces turned downward. By this, he denotes the punishment of the avaricious, who, through desire for earthly things, are deprived of the sight and vision of heavenly things, which are the true good. These people, weeping, recognized their error and said: **My soul cleaved to the pavement.** <note>original: *Adhesit pauimento anima mea*</note> This is a verse [from the Psalms] and it means: "My soul remains stuck to the pavement and the soil of the earth." That is: my soul, which should have been raised to the love of celestial things, has remained stuck to the love of earthly goods.

Virgil began to speak to the souls who are being purged, saying: **O YOU CHOSEN OF GOD:** Since you are on the way to salvation. For **many are called, but few are chosen.** <note>original Latin: *multi sunt uocati: pauci uero electi* (Matthew 22:14).</note> **WHOSE SUFFERINGS:** whose pains and passions are made less hard by justice and hope. For whoever is brought into a state of grace supports in peace the penalty that is justly given to them, and through that, hopes that once purged, they will become blessed. **IF YOU COME** secure from lying: one of the souls responds, "If you come free from lying down as we lie, and you wish to climb further up, let your right hands always be on the outside." The meaning is: turn yourself to the right hand, and thus the mountain will always remain to your left, and the right hand will remain on the outer side. Thus Virgil asked, and thus the soul replied. Wherefore **I noticed**: that is, I understood the other thing was hidden from him: namely, that I was alive. Or truly, I perceived that the other thing I desired to know was hidden from him: that is, who he was and why he was being purged there. **AND I TURNED** my eyes to the eyes. The meaning is that Virgil perceived by looking at me what I desired, which was to speak with that soul; and I, looking at him, understood that he was content that I...

# CANTO XIX

When I was able to act according to my own mind,
I drew myself over that creature
whose words I had noted before,
Saying: "Spirit, in whom weeping matures
that without which one cannot return to God,
pause a little; let your greater care be stayed.
Who were you, and why do you have your backs
turned upward? Tell me, and do you wish me to obtain for you
anything from there, from whence I, living, set out?"

And he to me: "Why heaven turns our backs
to itself, you shall know; but first,
<note>original: "scias quod ego sum successor petri"</note> know that I am a successor of Peter.
Between Sestri and Chiavari descends
a beautiful river, and from its name
the title of my blood takes its peak.
For a month and a little more, I experienced how
the great mantle weighs on him who keeps it from the mud,
so that all other burdens seem like feathers.
My conversion, alas, was late;
but once I was made the Roman Shepherd,
only then did I discover the lying life.
I saw that there the heart found no rest,
nor could one climb higher in that life;
wherefore, love for this one was kindled in me.
Until that point, I was a wretched soul, parted
from God, and wholly filled with greed;
now, as you see, I am punished here.
What avarice does is here declared
in the purgation of converted souls;
the mountain has no more bitter penalty.
Just as our eyes did not lift themselves
on high, being fixed on earthly things,
so justice here has submerged them to the earth.
As avarice extinguished our love
for every good, whereby our works were lost,
so justice here holds us constricted,
Bound and seized in feet and in hands;
and as long as it shall be the pleasure of the righteous Lord,
so long shall we stay immobile and stretched out."

I had knelt and wished to speak;
but as I began, and he perceived,
merely by listening, my reverence,
"What cause," he said, "has bent you down thus?"
And I to him: "Because of your dignity,
my upright conscience stung me with remorse."

<column-break/>

**WHEN I** was able to act according to my own mind: according to true reason, the appetite is subject to the intellect, and it cannot extend itself more to one thing than to another without the judgment of the intellect. Whence it follows that one cannot act according to one's own way unless the intellect allows it. **IN WHOM** weeping matures: in whom weeping matures, <note>meaning: it affects him</note>, that is, the penance and the purgation without which one cannot return to God.

**WHY** our backs: our rears and our backs and our spines.
**KNOW THAT I AM:** know that I am. **Successor of Peter:** successor of Peter: <note>meaning: the Pope</note>. This man was Master Ottobuono da Fieschi, a gentleman of Genoa. Those of Fieschi were Counts of Lavagna, so named from a river which runs in the Riviera of Genoa between Sestri and Chiavari. He was made Pope Adrian IV <note>The commentator likely means Adrian V (Ottobuono de' Fieschi), who reigned in 1276</note> in the year of our salvation 1276. And he lived in the Apostolic See for one month and nine days. **ONE MONTH** and a little more I experienced: how the great mantle weighs: <note>meaning: the pontifical dignity</note>. **ON HIM** who keeps it from the mud: <note>meaning: on him who maintains it without vice</note>. And not without reason does he introduce these words through Adrian. For he used to say that the See of Peter was full of thorns, and his mantle weighed so much that it would break even the sturdiest shoulder. And certainly, the papacy is a supreme honor to him who rules it well; but it is a most heavy weight, a wretched servitude, and extreme fatigue. And to him who rules it badly, it is the ultimate peril of the soul and the ultimate infamy. **THAT ALL OTHER BURDENS SEEM:** that all other weights seem lighter in comparison. **But once I was made the Roman Shepherd. Thus I discovered the lying life:** before I was Pope, I hoped—if ever I reached such a rank—to be content and satisfied with riches. Afterward, desiring even more and being unable to climb any higher, I knew this life of ours to be a lie, because it gives hope to the covetous that at some point they may be satisfied; and yet they are never satisfied. For this reason, having abandoned the greed for earthly goods, I turned to heavenly ones.

**HE DEMONSTRATES** the penalty that the avaricious endure. Nor is it an absurd statement to say that the mountain of Purgatory has no "more bitter" penalty. **JUST AS** the text ordains: just as our eyes, fixed on earthly things, did not open toward the heights, so justice submerged them: <note>meaning: sank them</note> here to the earth. As avarice extinguished our love: <note>meaning: every fervor the soul has for doing good</note>. **WHEREBY** our works were lost: <note>meaning: whereby every good work is lost and extinguished</note>; so justice holds us tight here with hands and feet bound. I will not expand here on the vilification of avarice, because many things are described in various places in the *Inferno*.

**FOR THIS** sole purpose he wrote the four tercets placed above: so that everyone might understand that human dignity ceases at death. It is of no more value to have been a Pope than a laborer, regarding worldly rank. **I AM A FELLOW SERVANT:** he takes these words from the Apocalypse <note>term: *Apocalypse* — the Book of Revelation (19:10 or 22:9)</note>. Where it is written that as John the Evangelist knelt at the feet of the angel, the angel refused such honor, saying: <note>original: "Vide ne fecerit conservus tuus sum & fratrum tuorum, habentium testimonium Ihesu"</note> "See that you do not do this; I am your fellow servant and of your brothers who have the testimony of Jesus." **NOR MARRY:** he proves by another example that in the other life, all human rank ceases. As Matthew the Evangelist notes in the 22nd chapter: when the disciples asked which of her husbands a woman who had many would be joined to in the next life, Christ answered: <note>original: "Erratis nescientes scripturas nec virtutem dei. In resurrectione enim neque nubent: neque nubentur. Sed erunt sicut angeli in cielo."</note> "You err, knowing not the scriptures nor the power of God. For in the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are as the angels in heaven." And by this, he signifies that in the future life, we shall all be equal.

<summary>Dante encounters the shade of Pope Adrian V, who explains the punishment for avarice—lying bound and face-down—and corrects Dante for kneeling, noting that all worldly ranks vanish before God.</summary>

<page-num>209</page-num>

"Straighten your legs; get up, brother,"
he replied; "do not err: I am a fellow servant
with you and with the others to one Power.
If you ever heard that holy evangelical sound
which says <note>original: "neque nubent"; a reference to Matthew 22:30, "they neither marry," implying that earthly distinctions and titles—like the Pope’s "marriage" to the Church—no longer exist in the afterlife.</note> 'they neither marry,'
you can well understand why I speak thus.

Go your way now; I do not wish you to delay longer,
for your staying hinders my weeping,
with which I mature that which you spoke of.
I have a niece over there named Alagia,
good in herself, provided that our house
does not make her wicked by example;
and she alone is left to me over there."

<column-break/>

<insert>u</insert> **GO YOUR WAY** now: it seemed more useful to the spirit to spend his time in his prayers than in further speech. Therefore, he dismisses the poet, which he could do without offense, having already satisfied Dante's questions. **MATURE** what you spoke of in me: this refers to what was said above: "Spirit, in whom weeping matures that without which one cannot return to God." <note>The "weeping" is the soul's penance, which "matures" or perfects the soul for its return to Heaven.</note> **ALAGIA**: This shows that although he had many kinsmen within the Fieschi family, nevertheless, because they were not without vices, none remained to him <note>in terms of spiritual merit or someone to pray for him</note> but Alagia. This niece of his was the wife of Marquis Marcello Malaspina; and by both the husband and the wife, our poet was freely and with great honor hosted during his exile, as has already been mentioned.

### CANTO XX: OF THE SECOND CANTICLE BY DANTE

The text continues to treat the subject of avarice; at the beginning, it shows that although Dante was eager to hear more, he nonetheless departed from the spirit who had dismissed him. *Against a better will, a [lesser] will fights poorly.* When there are two differing wills, the one that is less good fights poorly—that is, it struggles poorly and resists the better one. Therefore, although Dante had a desire to learn things from the spirit that were not of great importance, he wished to yield to the spirit’s will, which was better, because it desired to purge him of the vice of greed. This precept follows: whenever we allow ourselves to be overcome by better reason, we will always make our own will secondary to that of others. *I drew the sponge from the water, not yet satisfied.* <note>Dante uses the metaphor of a sponge to describe his unsatisfied thirst for knowledge.</note>

**A**gainst a better will, the will fights ill;
Wherefore against my pleasure, to please him,
I drew from the water the sponge not yet satisfied.

My leader moved, and I moved through the
unobstructed places along the rock,
as one goes along a wall, close to the battlements;

For the people who pour out, drop by drop
through their eyes, the evil that occupies all the world, <note>The "evil" referred to here is avarice (greed), which causes the penitents to weep.</note>
approach too closely on the other side.

Accursed may you be, ancient wolf,
who more than all other animals have prey
because of your hunger, endlessly deep!

O heaven, in whose turning it seems believed
that conditions here below are transmuted,
when will he come through whom this [wolf] shall depart? <note>Dante appeals to the heavens, asking when a savior will come to drive away the "wolf" of greed.</note>

We went along with slow and short steps,
and I was intent on the shades whom I heard
pitiably weeping and complaining;

And by chance I heard "Sweet Mary"
called out before us in their weeping,
as a woman does who is in labor;

And it followed: "How poor you were,
as one can see by that hostelry
where you laid down your holy burden." <note>A reference to the Nativity and the poverty of the manger where Mary gave birth to Jesus.</note>

Next I heard: "O good Fabricius,
you preferred virtue with poverty
rather than possessing great riches with vice." <term>Fabricius<gloss>Gaius Fabricius Luscinus, a Roman consul famous for refusing bribes and dying in poverty.</gloss></term>

These words were so pleasing to me
that I drew further ahead to have knowledge
of that spirit from whom they seemed to come.

It spoke also of the generosity
that Nicholas showed to the maidens,
to lead their youth to honor. <note>Saint Nicholas is said to have secretly provided dowries for three poor girls to save them from a life of shame.</note>

"O soul that speaks such good things,
tell me who you were," I said, "and why alone
do you renew these worthy praises?"

"Your words shall not be without reward,
if I return to complete the short path
of that life which flies toward its end."

<column-break/>

—nge <note>The word "sponge" (spugna) is split across the column break in the original layout.</note>: an excellent metaphor to show that a man departs while still thirsty for that which he desires to know. *I moved:* departing from the spirit. *My leader:* who was waiting for me and was ahead of me. *He moved:* preceding me. *Through the unobstructed places:* that is, through areas not occupied by the souls who were lying down. *Along the rock:* along the narrow mass, close to the rock itself, like one who goes along the walls. And they did this because the souls who were weeping for the sin of avarice—which occupies the whole world—approached too closely on the other side. *Accursed may you be, ancient wolf:* Avarice began in the world as far back as Cain; he, according to the Master of Histories, <note>original: "maestro delle historie" likely referring to Peter Comestor, author of the *Historia Scholastica*.</note> invented weights and measures. He was more intent on gain than was required, and in the first fruits he offered to God, his avarice was demonstrated. Therefore, avarice is very ancient. We shall speak of the wolf here, having spoken of justice in the first canticle <note>The *Inferno*.</note> where it is shown that of the three animals—the leopard, the lion, and the wolf—this one is the worst and most harmful, and for this reason, she takes more prey than the other animals. *O heaven, in whose turning:* that is, in whose revolutions. *It seems believed:* mathematicians <note>The author uses "mathematicians" to refer to astronomers and astrologers.</note> maintain that many celestial bodies give movement and influence to all things created beneath them. However, our souls, created by God without the mediation of secondary causes, remain free from such influences. Nevertheless, celestial influences can incline us toward justice and transmute kingdoms and empires into their proper form of administration. *When will he come through whom this shall depart:* that is, when will the "true one" come, as spoken of in the first canticle.

**I**t is a most fitting thing that whoever is eager to be purged of the vice of avarice—which is nothing other than the lust for treasures—should keep in mind the examples of those who were content with little. Therefore, he first shows that the spirits of this place all at once invoked the name of Mary, like a woman about to give birth; and they remembered how joyfully she endured poverty, saying: "You were as poor as is shown by the hostelry in which you gave birth to our Salvation." *O good Fabricius:* In all the purgings of these sins, he places examples not only of Christians but also of Gentiles, because morality is common to both our religion and theirs. Furthermore, the sinner might excuse himself by claiming impossibility—because not everyone is raised to the grace to which Mary and many holy men were raised. Such an excuse cannot be produced in the example of the Gentiles. Fabricius was in extreme poverty and never sought riches. But when he was presented with very large gifts by the Samnite people, who were very hostile to the Romans, and they begged him to receive them for his needs, he replied that as long as he could use his own limbs, he lacked nothing; and that Romans did not seek gold, but to be superior to those who possessed it. *Nicholas to the maidens:* This story, being very well known, I omit.

**I** Dante said: "O soul that speaks"—that is, you speak so well—"and renews"—that is, you renew by bringing to memory these worthy praises—"why do you worthily praise Mary, Fabricius, and Nicholas? Tell me who you were, and if you tell me, your words shall not be without reward"—that is, without prize. "For I will give you fame if I return to complete the short path"—that is, to finish my mortal life, which is brief and flies toward the end. *AND HE:* This was Hugh; <note>Hugh Capet, King of France (r. 987–996), though Dante conflates him with his father, Hugh the Great.</note> understand that he replied: "I WILL TELL you what you ask. NOT FOR any comfort I expect from there," because those who are in the purging virtues do not care for mortal fame.

<summary>Dante and Virgil travel along the narrow edge of the fifth terrace, where the greedy are punished by lying face-down. They encounter the spirit of Hugh Capet, who proclaims examples of poverty and generosity, including the Virgin Mary, the Roman consul Fabricius, and Saint Nicholas.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the narrative of the fifth terrace of Purgatory. Having encountered the spirits of the greedy, Dante now listens to a shade who identifies himself as the progenitor of the French royal house. This speaker provides a scathing critique of his descendants' history and their impact on Italy.</meta>

<page-num>XX</page-num>

# CANTO XX

And he said: I will tell you, not for any comfort
that I expect from your world, but because so much
grace shines in you before you are dead.
I was the root of the evil plant <note>The "evil plant" refers to the Capetian dynasty of France, which Dante blames for much of the political corruption of his era.</note>
that overshadows all Christian lands,
so that good fruit is rarely gathered from it.
But if Douai, Ghent, Lille, or Bruges <note>Flemish cities that were oppressed by French rule.</note>
could soon take vengeance, it would happen;
and I beg it of Him who judges all.
I was called Hugh Capet <note>original: "Vgo ciappetta"</note> in that world;
from me were born the Philips and the Louis
by whom France has recently been ruled.
I was the son of a butcher of Paris,
when the ancient kings came to an end,
all except one who was cloaked in gray. <note>Refers to the transition from the Carolingian to the Capetian dynasty. The "one in gray" refers to a king who became a monk.</note>
I found the reins of the kingdom's government
held tight in my hands, and such power
from new acquisitions, and so full of friends,
That to the widowed crown was promoted
the head of my son, from whom
the consecrated bones of these kings began.

---

While the great Provençal dowry <note>The marriage of Charles of Anjou to Beatrice of Provence, which brought vast territories to the French crown.</note>
had not yet taken away the shame of my blood,
it was worth little, but at least did no harm.
There began, with force and with lies,
its rapine; and then, as atonement,
it took Ponthieu, Normandy, and Gascony.
Charles came to Italy and, for atonement,
made a victim of Conradin; and then
pushed Thomas back to heaven, for atonement. <note>Dante refers to the execution of the young Conradin of Swabia and the rumored poisoning of Saint Thomas Aquinas by Charles of Anjou.</note>

---

I see a time, not long after today,
that brings another Charles out of France <note>Charles of Valois, who entered Florence in 1301.</note>
to make himself and his people better known.
He comes without an army, alone, and with the lance
with which Judas jousted; and that he carries
so that he makes the belly of Florence burst.
From this he will gain no land, but sin and shame
will he gain for himself, so much the heavier
as he considers such damage to be light.

<column-break/>

**B**ut because grace shines in you before you are dead: as if to say, "Because the grace I see reflecting in you makes me deem you worthy, I shall answer." **I was the root of the evil plant**: I was the beginning of the new lineage of the Kings of France, which he calls an "evil plant" because he wishes to show that there were many wicked kings in that stock. **That overshadows all Christian land**: Like a shadow that brings harm. **But if Douai, Ghent, Lille, or Bruges**: these are lands in Flanders oppressed by the King of France. **Judges**: <note>original: "giuggia"</note> He who judges. **Hugh Capet**: In France, according to some chronicles (which I neither approve nor condemn), the successors of the illustrious Charlemagne—who for his many great deeds was named "the Great"—reigned for many centuries. They say the last was Louis, who left a young son in the care of **Hugh Capet**, born of a butcher in Paris, but a great seneschal. Hugh, blinded by the greed for reigning, took care to remove the boy and made his own son King. Others say Louis V died without a successor, and many wanted to transfer the kingdom to Charles, Duke of Lorraine, his uncle. Hugh occupied the kingdom with the favor of fortune and friends, and caused Charles and his children to die.

I candidly confess such history is unknown to me. But Philip, named "the Fair," the worst of the Kings of France, in 1291 unjustly occupied the county of Flanders. **Bruges, Lille, and Ghent**: and later in 1300, when the Count of Flanders came to him, he imprisoned him along with two sons and took the rest of the county. But two years later, the vengeance followed, which Hugh now desires. For the Flemish rebelled with a very great slaughter of Philip's army. With Hugh, his son Robert reigned for eleven years; then Robert reigned alone for thirty-four, a humane and literate man. **Philips and Louis**: because many of his successors held these names. **When the ancient kings failed**: in the year 882. **Except one in gray clothes**: not because they were of the Order of Saint Francis (which did not yet exist), but because he was a monk and wore gray.

**L**ouis, who was later made king, and his brother **Charles**, to whom the Kingdom of Sicily fell, had as wives two daughters of Raymond Berenguer. Under the name of a **dowry**, they occupied all of Provence, as we shall say more clearly in the sixth Canto of *Paradiso*. Therefore, the "great Provençal dowry" meant this house of Hugh no longer felt the shame of being of low birth. **As atonement**: he speaks ironically, because one makes "amends" poorly if they do worse afterward than before. The aforementioned **Charles** made a **victim of Conradin**. Conradin was defeated by Charles and, on the advice of Alardo, fled to the Roman shore to go to Sicily. But captured by Giovanni Frangipani, a Roman, he was led to Naples, and there Charles had his head cut off in the square, and similarly the Duke of Austria and many barons, and forbade them from being buried in sacred ground. It is to be noted that although the poet later places this Charles in Purgatory as a noble defender of the Church, he nevertheless does not wish to overlook his vices, which were many.

**He pushed Thomas back to heaven**: a supreme wickedness and worthy of the greatest abomination of all ages. This was **Thomas Aquinas**, a man inferior to no one in life and character; he was a treasure of every kind of learning, for which two things he could justly be called more than a man. Therefore, as much as he raised himself above human nature, so much did Charles, through this wickedness, submerge himself in a brutal and beastly life. This vessel of innocence and wisdom went to the General Council in Lyon, France, without any suspicion. But the suspicious King, conscious of his own vices and fearing that Thomas, being good and free, would manifest his failings, arranged for a personal physician of Thomas to poison him. Thus he died a martyr, for he was killed for the truth, having intended not to remain silent about the wicked government of Charles. But the Supreme Judge did not let his death go without just vengeance, for He willed that the agonized King, after many victories, should see the rebellion of Sicily and the capture of his son, from which he died of grief.

**C**harles of Valois, called "Charles Lackland," brother of Philip the Fair. Being sent by Boniface under the guise of composing and bringing the state of Florence to peace, he was the seed of many evils; we spoke of him in the sixth Canto of *Inferno*. Later, with Robert, son of Charles II, he prepared a great fleet against Sicily, and in a short time returned from it with an ignominious peace. Thus he came to Florence for peace and brought war; he went to Sicily for honorable war and brought back ignominious peace. He said **the belly of Florence**, because in those times our republic was very crowded with many citizens and supreme wealth, and he was the cause of emptying it of both through many occasions.

<summary>Hugh Capet speaks from the terrace of the greedy, tracing the rise of the French Capetian dynasty from humble origins to a powerful, corrupt force that meddled in Italian and Flemish affairs. The commentary details specific historical crimes, including the execution of Conradin and the alleged poisoning of St. Thomas Aquinas.</summary>

Having just heard Hugh denounce the early crimes of the Capetian dynasty, the text now transitions into a prophetic condemnation of Hugh's later descendants, specifically their interference in Italian politics and their greed, before explaining the ritual of the souls on this terrace.</meta>

# PURGATORIO

<column-break/>

**The other**, who once left his ship as a captive,
I see selling his daughter and haggling over her,
as corsairs do with the slaves of others.
O Avarice, what more can you do to us,
since you have so drawn my blood to yourself
that it no longer cares for its own flesh?
<note>Hugh Capet refers to Charles II of Anjou ("The Other"), who was captured in a naval battle in 1284. He later "sold" his young daughter Beatrice in marriage to the elderly Azzo VIII of Este for a large sum of money.</note>

And so that the past and future evil seem less,
I see the fleur-de-lis enter Anagni,
and in His vicar, Christ made captive.
I see him mocked a second time;
I see the vinegar and the gall renewed,
and him killed between living thieves.
I see the new Pilate so cruel
that this does not sate him, but without decree,
he carries his greedy sails into the Temple.
<note>The "fleur-de-lis" is Philip the Fair of France. In 1303, his agents seized Pope Boniface VIII (Christ's "vicar") at Anagni. Dante compares this to the Passion of Christ. The "new Pilate" refers to Philip's role in the later destruction of the Knights Templar ("the Temple").</note>
O my Lord, when shall I be joyful
to see the vengeance which, being hidden,
makes sweet Your wrath in Your secret council?

<margin>
**Charles the Younger**, firstborn of Charles I and called Charles II: he rashly fought with Roger of Lauria, the admiral of King Peter [of Aragon]. The father had gone to Provence to lead a most powerful fleet against Sicily, and was already returning by the Pisan sea; therefore the admiral, eager to strike first, sailed into the port of Naples and provoked battle with insulting words. Having first warned his men who came out: they should attend to nothing but overcoming the King's galley. The rash young man went out and finally was captured and taken to Sicily and Messina, and certainly would have been killed if Queen Constance had not forbidden it. But he saw killed more than two hundred of his nobles in vengeance for Conradin. But he was reserved with a few. This battle was in the year 1284. The father arrived at Gaeta the following day. Charles II, after his father's death, returned to Naples and married his daughter to Azzo VIII, Marquess of Ferrara, from whom he received great gifts for such a marriage.
</margin>

<margin>
**And so as not to remain silent** about another wicked thing, this history adds: Philip the Fair, King of France, was indignant against Boniface because, when he called his brother Charles [of Valois] to settle the Florentine republic, he promised him the Empire and afterwards did not keep it. For this reason, the King began to stir up Stefano Colonna, an enemy of the Pope. And he conferred the benefits of the realm against the pontifical will. Boniface called the French prelates to a council; and Philip, finally, as a defiant one, excommunicated him and incited the Flemings against him, and invited Albert, already elected [Emperor], into Italy. Philip, by the advice of Stefano, sent a legate to Tuscany with Messer Musatto, a French knight from Florence. They stayed in Staggia, Musatto's castle. And under the guise of negotiating peace, they intended to capture Boniface. And finally Sciarra Colonna, with 300 horsemen and many friends on foot with the banners of France, entered Anagni, the homeland of the pontiff, where it seemed to him he was safe. The Pope, seeing he had no escape, prepared himself in the pontifical chair and waited for them. Sciarra, moved by reverence for the papal mantle, did not touch Boniface but held him in honorable prison and ransacked his treasures. Three days later, Luca, Cardinal of Fiesco, with the following of the people who had already repented of their error, took Sciarra. But Biondo <note>Flavio Biondo, a historian.</note> in his *Italia Illustrata* writes that Sciarra took the Pope to Rome. Boniface thought to avenge himself on the King, but appearing to him too powerful, he fell into a frenzy; thus verifying the prophecy which Celestine [V] made of him, preaching to him that he would enter the papacy like a fox, rule like a lion, and die like a dog. He died in the year 1303, on the second day of October. **I SEE THE NEW PILATE**: he calls this Philip "Pilate" because, with the permission of Clement V, he unjustly had many Knight Friars <note>The Knights Templar.</note> killed and robbed them; but of these we will speak in the eighteenth canto of Paradise.
</margin>

What I was saying of that unique bride
of the Holy Spirit, and what made you
turn toward me for some explanation,
is the response to all our prayers
as long as the day lasts; but when night falls,
we take up a contrary sound instead.
We repeat the story of Pygmalion at that hour,
whom a desire for gold, gluttonous and greedy,
made a traitor, a thief, and a parricide;
and the misery of the avaricious Midas,
which followed his greedy demand,
at which one must always laugh.
Each of us remembers the foolish Achan,
how he stole the spoils, so that the wrath
of Joshua seems to sting him here still.
Then we accuse Sapphira with her husband;
we praise the kicks that Heliodorus received;
and in infamy the whole mountain circles
Polymnestor, who killed Polydorus;
lastly, we cry out: "O Crassus,
tell us, you who know: what does gold taste like?"
Sometimes one speaks loud and another low,
according to the affection that spurs us to speak,
now at a greater and now at a lesser pace.

<insert>Yet for the good that is discussed here by day</insert>

<column-break/>

<margin>
**That unique bride of the Holy Spirit** is the Virgin Mary: who, alone among all women, was the bride of the Holy Spirit because by Him she conceived our salvation, JESUS the Savior. **AS LONG AS THE DAY LASTS**: the meaning is that for as long as the day lasts, these souls are occupied in recounting the examples of Mary and the others who were liberal and despisers of riches. **BUT WHEN NIGHT FALLS**: that is, when night comes, we take up a contrary sound and speech; and in the stead and place of recounting these holy examples, we recount the examples of those who were avaricious. Nor is this place without allegory. Since just as the aforementioned examples please those who are being purged of avarice, so do those who are presently set forth displease them. And some are enticed to this purgation by the rewards that holy souls have attained through liberality. Some live deterred by the punishments of the avaricious. And therefore the first examples are sung by day, because in them was true knowledge. The second by night, because such wickednesses proceed from ignorance. **PYGMALION** was the son of Belus; he treacherously killed Sychaeus, priest of Hercules, while he was sacrificing; who was his uncle and the husband of Dido, his sister. Nor did he kill him provoked by any injury, but to usurp his riches, which nonetheless he could not have because Dido fled with them to Africa and built Carthage. **MIDAS** was the son of Gordias, who made the insoluble knot that Alexander the Great later cut. He obtained from Bacchus that whatever he touched should turn to gold. For this reason, he brought himself to extreme hunger, because the foods he wished to eat turned to gold when he touched them. The poets feign this because he was a man so avaricious that he even defrauded himself of necessary things to draw money from them. **ACHAN** <note>original: "ACOR"</note>: when Joshua came into the promised land and won the city of Jericho, he commanded according to God's precept that no one should touch the spoils. But Achan, moved by avarice, stole a garment and gold...
</margin>

# CANTO XX

->before I was not alone but here nearby<-
->no other person raised their voice<-

<note>original: "deglapostoli ca.v."</note> From the **Acts of the Apostles**, chapter 5: in Jerusalem, a certain **Ananias** and **Sapphira** his wife, wishing to follow the apostolic law, sold their possessions to follow the apostles, but did not present all to Peter, keeping back a portion. For this, Peter sharply rebuked them, and they suddenly fell dead at his feet. We also praise the kicks that **Heliodorus** received. He was sent by Seleucus, King of Asia, to Jerusalem to seize many treasures from the Temple, which the King had heard from Apollonius were not necessary for sacrifices. But while in the Temple, an armed man appeared to Heliodorus on a terrible horse and attacked him with kicks, leaving him terrified.

### We had already departed from them,
### and were struggling to overcome the road
### as much as was permitted to our power,
### When I felt the mountain tremble
### like a falling thing, and a chill seized me
### such as takes one going to his death.
### Certainly Delos was not shaken so strongly
### before Latona made her nest within it
### to give birth to the two eyes of heaven.
### Then a cry began from all sides,
### such that the Master drew toward me,
### saying, "Do not fear while I lead you."
### "Glory to God in the highest"
### they all said, from what I understood nearby,
### where the cry could be heard.
<note>original: "Gloria in excelsis... deo"</note>

Then of **Delos**: which in Greek signifies "clear and manifest," because when it floated to the surface it became manifest, or because Apollo gave manifest answers there. **SUCH that the master drew toward me**: **THEN a cry began from all sides**: Dante felt the mountain tremble, and after such trembling, he heard all the spirits of that place with one voice singing *Glory to God in the highest*, which is the song the Church uses when we give thanks to God with joy and gladness. This hymn was sung by the angels at the Nativity of the Savior.

### We remained immobile and in suspense,
### like the shepherds who first heard that song,
### until the trembling ceased and it ended.
### Then we resumed our holy path,
### watching the shades that lay upon the ground,
### already returned to their usual weeping.
### No ignorance ever with such conflict
### made me so desirous of knowing,
### if my memory does not err in this,
### As much as I seemed to have then in thought;
### nor because of the haste did I dare to ask,
### nor by myself could I see anything there;
### Thus I went along, timid and thoughtful.

<column-break/>

<margin>silver and gold and buried it in his tent. God, being angered, caused the Jews to be put to flight when they later camped at another city called Ai. Joshua grieved, but having learned through divine revelation of the theft of **Achan**, he had him stoned. **SAPPHIRA**: read in the Acts</margin>

<note>original: "stui fu Re dithracia"</note> This man was King of Thrace. **Priam**, King of Troy, seeing himself in the gravest danger from the war with the Greeks, sent to him one of his sons called **Polydorus** with a great part of his treasures, so that if he and the others perished, Polydorus would remain and have the means to sustain himself. But when Priam died, **Polymnestor**, out of extreme avarice and contrary to his given faith, killed the youth and snatched the treasures. **O CRASSUS**: this was **Marcus Crassus**, the richest of all Romans and the most avaricious of all men. Sent as consul against the Parthians, he showed great signs of avarice; therefore the enemies, very cunningly feigning fear, fled and left the country abundant with every kind of prey but full of ambushes. Blinded by the greed for plunder, Crassus fell incautiously into the ambushes. Surrounded by enemies, he lost his entire army with great infamy and did not fall alive into the hands of the barbarians, but had himself killed by one of his servants. His head was later cut off and put into a skin full of molten gold, and told: "You thirsted for gold, now drink gold." <note>original: "oro feti fti: oro bei" — a play on "Aurum sitisti, aurum bibe."</note> Of him Petrarch says: *And I saw Cyrus, more greedy for blood than Crassus was for gold, and each had his fill of it, so that in the end it seemed bitter to both.* **AT TIMES we speak, one high and another low**: This denotes that although many seek to purge themselves of avarice and begin to hold it in hatred, nonetheless some are more or less fervent, and similarly, they use greater exclamations for the greater examples than for the lesser.

**Virgil** and **Dante** had already departed from that Hugh, and were struggling—that is, fatiguing and forcing themselves—to overcome, meaning to conquer or pass, the road. When Dante felt such a trembling in the mountain as usually occurs with a thing that is about to ruin, which first trembles and then falls. And he uses this comparison: that **Delos** did not tremble so strongly when it was moved by earthquakes before **Latona**, mother of Apollo and Diana (that is, of the sun and the moon), gave birth there to the **two eyes of heaven**. For the moon and the sun are like two eyes of the sky. Delos is an island, one of the Cyclades, of which there is such a fable: Jove loved Asteria; she fled from him and begged the gods to transform her into a quail. But Jove, wanting her to cross the sea, changed her into a stone, whence she fell into the water and went to the bottom where she stayed a long time. Later, Jove, through the prayers of Latona her sister (who conceived Phoebus and Diana by him), brought her to the surface and made her an island, but a mobile one. On this island, Latona gave birth to the sun and the moon. Therefore the Sun, as it was his birthplace, willed that it should move no more and bound it with Gyaros and Mykonos, neighboring islands. The truth is that this island was often shaken by earthquakes, so the inhabitants went to the oracle of Apollo to ask for a remedy. And he commanded that certain sacrifices be made and that they should no longer bury the dead there. Thus Apollo made it immobile and bound it to Gyaros and Mykonos, which signifies that the men of those islands inhabited it. It was first called Asteria.

**WE remained immobile**: we stopped without going further, **AND in suspense**, with doubts in the mind. **LIKE the shepherds who first heard**: just as we were stupefied, so were the shepherds to whom the angels, singing this canticle, announced that Christ was born; whereupon they, descending from the mountains, saw Him in the manger between the ox and the ass. **UNTIL the trembling ceased**: until the shaking of the mountain stopped. **AND it ended**: and until that whole song was finished. Afterward, we resumed our way, and the souls returned to their accustomed weeping. **NO ignorance ever made such war**: because naturally every man desires to know; and ignorance of a thing—that is, not knowing—brings war to a man because it stimulates and combats him to seek to know it. **I did not dare ask** Virgil, nor by myself could I understand it **THERE** (original: *li*), that is, in that place. It is easy for anyone with even mediocre wit to notice how much this passage requires that many and various things be said in detestation of avarice.

---

...to heal human minds from this pernicious disease; the life of mortals would be too happy, and all domestic and civil dissension and every external war would cease. Nor would we undertake many laborious cares, all useless, which strip us of honor and peace, and deprive us of that leisure which we could spend in things pertaining to our salvation. But if we gather what has been said in different places of this volume, perhaps the listener will feel partly satisfied.

<page-num>XXI</page-num>
<header>CANTO XXI</header>

### CANTO XXI OF THE SECOND CANTICLE BY DANTE.

<margin>n</margin>NOBLE subject matter and nobly treated in this twenty-first canto, in which he recounts how, following their path, they were overtaken by a soul from whom they learned the reason for the shaking of the mountain and the singing of the spirits. Finally, they discovered this soul was a poet; and Virgil recognized him with the greatest pleasure. The natural thirst: We demonstrated shortly before that there is an innate thirst and desire in man for knowledge. Because the cognition of divine things is that through which we are blessed, and we cannot possess this perfectly through our own industry or by natural means unless we are illuminated by the Holy Spirit. Christ indicated this in the Gospel of Saint John, chapter four, when he asked for a drink from the Samaritan woman at Jacob’s well. When she denied it to him, alleging that Jews do not associate with Samaritans, he replied: "If you knew who it is that asks you for a drink, you would have asked him, and he would have given you a drink of a water—of a fountain—that springs up into eternal life." The young woman, therefore, after many words, asked for it, and Christ filled her with the Holy Spirit. Therefore, the poet most wisely demonstrates at present that the natural thirst—that is, the natural desire for knowing and understanding—is never satisfied except with that water. Wherefore the young Samaritan woman asked for that grace—that is, the grace of the Holy Spirit. *Mitravaglaua* <note>original: "mitravaglaua," meaning to be troubled or travailed</note> is a metaphor taken from threshed grain, which, so that it remains purified and clean, is "travailed"—that is, passed from sieve to sieve. In this way, our mind, wishing to find the truth, goes about purifying itself from time to time. *And the haste spurred me* shows that at the same time the soul was eager to investigate the cause of the mountain’s shaking and the song of the souls, while the body had to hasten to follow its journey. But Statius, arriving, clarifies what neither Dante (representing sensuality) nor Virgil (representing human intellect, though illuminated by much learning) could understand on their own. But Statius, being accustomed to such things, explains them. He places Statius as the human intellect that extends itself to comprehend what cannot be understood through reason alone, and demonstrates this by comparison. According to what Luke writes in chapter twenty-four: How Christ, recently resurrected and already "stolen"—that is, raised out of the mouth of the sepulcher <note>original: "bucca sepulchrale"</note>—appearing on the road to two disciples who were going toward Emmaus in the form of a pilgrim, explained many things of the Holy Scripture; so Statius showed Dante the causes of the events already mentioned. *God give you peace*: An excellent greeting, because nothing better can be asked for than peace, in which our highest good consists. Wherefore Christ also said: "My peace I leave with you" <note>original: "pacem meam relinquo uobis"</note>.

The natural thirst that is never quenched
except with the water for which the young
Samaritan woman asked as a grace,
Travailed me, and the haste spurred me
along the obstructed path behind my leader,
and I grieved for the just vengeance.
And behold, just as Luke describes
that Christ appeared to two who were on the road,
already risen from the sepulchral cave,
A shadow appeared to us, coming behind us,
looking at the crowd that lay at its feet;
nor did we notice him until he spoke first,
Saying: "My brothers, God give you peace."
We turned suddenly, and Virgil
gave him the sign that is fitting for that.
Then he began: "In the blessed council,
may the truthful court place you in peace,
which relegates me to eternal exile."
"How?" said he, and "Why do you go so fast
if you are not shadows whom God deems unworthy above?
Who has escorted you so far up His stairs?"
And my teacher: "If you look at the signs
which this man carries, and which the Angel traced,
you will see well that he must reign with the good.
But because she who spins day and night
has not yet drawn for him the distaff
that Clotho imposes and prepares for everyone,
His soul, which is your sister and mine,
coming up, could not come alone,
for it does not see in our manner.
Wherefore I was drawn out of the wicked throat
of Hell to show him, and I will show him
further as far as my school can lead him."

<column-break/>

*The blessed council*: in the congregation of the saved. *The truthful court*: the celestial court, which is "truthful" because that is the true kingdom. *Which*: which court "relegates" or confines him because he was not a Christian. *How? said he*: understand Statius asking, "if you are not shadows." *Which*: those which *God deems unworthy above*—that is, does not consider worthy to be in heaven. *Who has escorted you so far*—that is, conducted you so safely. Nor should Statius wonder that shadows relegated to Hell could ascend to salvation. Furthermore, morally speaking, he who has a fixed habit of vice can only with great difficulty come to the purgatorial virtues. *If you look*: these are the seven P’s <note>The letter 'P' for 'Peccatum' (sin), which the angel at the gate of Purgatory carved into Dante's forehead</note> which the angel had carved into his head. *But because she who spins day and night*: but because life, whose course passes continuously day and night and never stops. He means <term>Lachesis</term>. In the first canticle, we established three Fates: <term>Clotho</term>, who holds the distaff and signifies the beginning of life; <term>Lachesis</term>, who spins and denotes the time we live; and <term>Atropos</term>, who breaks the finished threads, and this is death. You will find the other things in the place already mentioned. *His soul, which is your sister and mine*: because they are of the same species, although you (Statius) are confirmed in grace, and I (Virgil) am damned, and he (Dante) is in doubt. *Coming up, could not come alone*: literally, it is true that a soul still joined to the body does not know how to travel through a country unknown to it. Allegorically, a soul still entangled in the body cannot contemplate incorporeal things like a soul already separated from the body. Therefore, the poet says in this text: *Because it does not see*—it does not watch or look—*in our manner*—that is, as those who are separated from the body. *Wherefore I was drawn out of the wicked throat of Hell*: which he has feigned above. Allegorically, understand that this mortal doctrine, which treats of virtue and vice, was drawn from the depths. *As far as my school can lead him*: Since pagan philosophy can lead through Hell and Purgatory—that is, it can give knowledge of vices and their damnation, and can also demonstrate how a man can purge himself of them—but it does not lead to Heaven. It does not give that true knowledge of divine and celestial things that comes from Christian theology. Therefore, to achieve the supreme good, one must first purge the soul of all impurity. Then, with a soul thus purged and pure, go to the speculation of divine things. Pagan philosophy performs the first part but cannot perform the second to perfection.

<summary>In this page, Dante and Virgil encounter the spirit of the poet Statius, who explains the spiritual mechanics of the mountain and the limitations of human reason (Virgil) compared to divine grace.</summary>

"But tell us, if you know, why such shocks
the mountain gave just now, and why all together
it seemed to cry out even to its soft base."
So he asked me, threading the eye
of my desire, so that with the hope alone
my thirst became less starving.
That spirit began: "There is nothing that without
order the religion of the mountain
feels, or that is outside of custom.
Free it is here from every alteration;
what heaven receives into itself from itself
can be the cause, and no other thing.
Because neither rain, nor hail, nor snow,

nor thick nor thin clouds,
nor lightning, nor the daughter of Thaumas <note>Iris, the rainbow; original: "figlia di taumante"</note>
who over there often changes regions,
nor dry vapor rises any further
than the top of the three steps I spoke of,
where the vicar of Peter <note>The angel at the gate of Purgatory</note> sets his feet.

It trembles perhaps lower down, a little or a lot;
but because of the wind that is hidden in the earth—
I know not how—it never trembles up here.
It trembles here when some soul feels itself
so pure <note>original: "monda"</note> that it rises or moves
to climb up; and such a cry follows it.
Of this purity, the will alone gives proof,
which, being entirely free to change its company,
takes the soul by surprise and helps it with its desire.
Before, it wishes well; but the inclination <note>original: "talento"</note> does not allow it,
which divine justice, against the will,
as it was toward sinning, sets toward the torment.
And I, who have lain in this sorrow
five hundred years and more, only now felt
a free will for a better threshold.
Therefore you felt the earthquake and the pious
spirits throughout the mountain giving praise
to that Lord—may He soon send them up!"
Thus he spoke to us; and because one enjoys
drinking as much as the thirst is great,
I cannot say how much he did me good.

<column-break/>

When Virgil asked Statius <note>The soul who has just finished his penance</note> why the mountain had shaken even to its "soft base"—that is, to its roots, which, because they emerge from the sea, are "soft"—he was asking exactly what Dante desired to know. Therefore, by a metaphor, he says he "threaded the eye of his desire." <note>original: "per la cruna del mio disio"</note> It happens to a man that when he has a great desire to understand something, a firm hope of being able to fulfill it is born, and such thirst and longing are partially mitigated; and so he says his thirst became "less starving." *He began*: Statius replied, saying: "Here there is nothing that the religion of the mountain"—that is, this mountain full of sanctity—"feels without order or that is outside of custom." This demonstrates the principle that the alterations and various movements caused by vapors raised by the sun [do not occur here].

These things are generated only as far as the entrance of Purgatory. Dante intends that such motion does not pass higher than the three steps. Literally, we understand that the part of the mountain where the three steps are is so elevated that it exceeds five miles in height. But allegorically, we say that the soul which arrives there is outside of every human passion and perturbation; there, no "cloud of sorrow" reaches it, nor "hail of fury," nor "lightning of anger." Confirmed in grace, they only attend to purging old stains. *Rain* is from cold and humid vapors gathered in a cloud. *Hail* is a drop of rain frozen in the air by the force of cold and wind. *Stones* [hailstones] are from cold and humid vapor rubbed in the inner parts of a cloud. *Snow* is an impression generated by moderate cold and humidity, for such cold is less than that which generates rain and hail, and it contains some heat. *Dew* is an impression in the air generated by cold and humidity not condensed; and according to Aristotle, dew only forms when the south wind blows. *Frost* is air frozen in the middle of the air. *The daughter of Thaumas* is the celestial arch called Iris <note>The rainbow</note>, whom the poets feign to be the daughter of Thaumas and the beloved daughter of the Ocean. *Dry vapor* is that which is generated from dry and hot vapor.

Statius assigns the cause of the mountain's trembling and the song of the people. He says that perhaps the mountain further down shakes at times, a little or a lot, due to "wind hidden in the earth"—that is, an earthquake which is born from wind enclosed underground with no exit. "But I know not how"—I know not if it be strong or soft—"up here it never trembles" from subterranean wind. "But it trembles here when some soul is pure"—that is, purged of its sins. Therefore, it trembles here when a soul feels itself so pure that it "rises to heaven" or moves from one circle where it has purged one sin to another where it must purge another. "And such a cry follows"—and such a song as we have described. "Follows" <note>original: "seconda"</note>—that is, it follows the shaking of the mountain. And the poet does not imagine this trembling without the highest wisdom. For just as when dry vapor, drawn up by the force of the sun, is converted into wind and moves the earth to exit and rise high, so the soul, drawn by the supernal Sun—that is, by divine love—separating itself from sin and earthly things and mounting to God, the air and earth show a sign of it. Virgil also imagines this when he induces the Sibyl to make a sacrifice for Aeneas's descent:
> "Behold now, at the first light and rising of the sun, the ground began to rumble underfoot and the mountain ridges began to move." <note>original: "Ecce autem primi sub lumina solis & ortus Sub pedibus mugire solu & iuga cepta moueri," from Virgil's Aeneid VI, 255-257</note>
*Of the purity*: he says that the soul perceives it has become pure when the will to depart is born within it. But because someone might say, "the will to flee evil, misery, and pain, and to achieve good and happiness, is always in our soul; nor is there anyone who desires evil except under the appearance of good; therefore, the soul in the pains of Purgatory should always have the will to leave," we must

<meta>catchword: understand</meta>

understand that in us there is a double will: one is absolute and simple, and this one always wills—as, for example, one who is tormented by thirst always wills to drink. This will always desires the Highest Good and cannot not desire it when it is shown. The other will is relative <note>original: "respectiua"</note>, and it does not desire the goal except in a just manner. Therefore, this relative will "gives proof of purity" when it no longer resists the natural [absolute] will. Thus the text says: *The will alone*—that is, the relative will, which is now entirely free to "change its company" because it is no longer hindered by any consideration of justice—*gives proof of purity*. For when the soul is not yet pure, although it has the natural will to climb to heaven, nevertheless the relative will does not consent, because it is not "just" for an impure thing to go to pure things. But when it is pure, this will alone occupies the whole soul.

<vocab>Dante, Purgatorio, Virgil, Statius, Thaumas, justice, earthquake, will, purity, Landino</vocab>

<summary>Statius explains to Dante that the shaking of Purgatory is not a natural weather event, but a miraculous sign that occurs whenever a soul has completed its purification and is ready to ascend to Heaven. He distinguishes between the absolute desire for God and the relative will that accepts divine punishment until justice is satisfied.</summary>
