anything that resists it. Thus it benefits the soul to will [to ascend], just as the opposite occurs when, even though we might desire something, our conscience pricks us because it is not yet right, so that it does not benefit us to will it. **First, it wishes well.** The simple will desires the good. **But the inclination <note>original: "taleto" (talento). In Dante’s theology, this is the "relative will" or the desire to complete one's punishment as a form of justice.</note> does not allow it.** This means the simple will desires the good, but the inclination—that is, the relative will—does not permit that wanting. And he provides the reason: just as divine justice, when the simple will desires a vice, opposes it with a relative will toward punishment, so when the soul wishes to leave Purgatory before its time, that same justice opposes it. **And I, who have lain.** He speaks of himself, who had remained for more than five hundred years and, being already purged, experienced **free will**: that is, a will free from any restriction because it was now just. **Because one enjoys drinking as much as the thirst is great.** Just as the pleasure of drinking is proportional to the greatness of the thirst, so was the will to understand this mystery as great as the desire had been.

**The net that catches us here.** Just as a net holds a bird so it cannot fly away, so this relative will holds the soul, which does not wish to leave until it has paid the penalty for its sin. **Unsnares <note>original: "scalappia"</note> itself, is loosened and freed.** A "calappio" is a wicker vessel in which bait is placed; if a bird enters, the door is tempered so that it closes, though it was open before. Thus, "to unsnare" is to exit the place where one was locked in. **Why the mountain trembles.** Rejoicing together and singing "Glory to God in the highest." **In the time that the good Titus.** He shows that he lived in the

*“The wise leader: ‘Now I see the net*
*that catches us here, and how one is unsnared,*
*why it trembles, and why you rejoice together.*
*Now, who you were, may it please you that I know,*
*and why for so many centuries you have lain*
*here—let your words explain this to me.’”*
*“In the time that the good Titus, with the aid*
*of the highest King, avenged the wounds*
*from which issued the blood sold by Judas,*
*with the name that lasts longest and honors most,”*

*famous enough, but not yet with faith.*
*So sweet was my vocal spirit*
*that Rome drew me, a Toulousan, to itself,*
*where I earned the right to adorn my brow with myrtle.*
*Statius the people over there still name me;*
*I sang of Thebes, and then of the great Achilles,*
*but I fell on the way with the second burden.*
*To my ardor, the seeds were the sparks*
*that warmed me from the divine flame*
*from which more than a thousand have been lit;*
*I speak of the Aeneid, which was a mother*
*to me, and was my nurse in poetry;*
*without it, I would not have weighed a drachm.*
*And to have lived over there when*
*Virgil lived, I would consent to one sun [year]*
*more than I owe before my release from exile.”*

<column-break/>

highest. **In the time that the good Titus.** This demonstrates that he lived during the time of Titus, son of Vespasian, who destroyed Jerusalem. **With the aid of the highest King:** of the highest God. He intends to conclude that, although the war waged by the Romans against the Jews appeared to have another origin, nonetheless God permitted it because of the sin of the killing of His Son. Therefore, he **avenged the wounds**—that is, the injuries—from which issued the precious blood that Judas betrayed for money. **With the name that lasts longest and honors most:** with the name of "Poet," which most honors the one truly distinguished by such a title. Hence Lucan says: <note>original: "O sacer & magnus uatũ labor omnia fato. Eripis & donas populis mortalibus euum."</note> "O sacred and great labor of poets, you rescue all things from fate and grant eternity to mortal peoples." And Virgil: <note>original: "Me uero primũ capiãt ante omnia muse Quaru sacra fero ingẽti perculsus amore."</note> "But as for me, first of all, may the sweet Muses, whose sacred symbols I bear, struck by a great love, receive me." **I was there:** in our world. **Famous:** for his poetic name. **But not yet with Christian faith.** **So sweet was my vocal spirit.** My verse and its pronunciation were so sweet. Hence Juvenal: <note>original: "Curritur ad uocem iocundã. & carmen amice. Thebaidos letã cum fecit statius urbẽ: Promisitque diẽ tanta dulcedine captos. Afflicit ille animos tantaque libidine uulgi Auditur."</note> "People run to the pleasant voice and the beloved song of the *Thebaid* when Statius has made the city happy; he promised a day [for a reading], with such sweetness he captured their minds and with such passion he is heard by the crowd." **That Toulousan:** because I was from Toulouse, which city is on the borders of Gascony toward Brittany, and through his learning and eloquence he became a Roman citizen. <note>Note: Dante and Landino mistakenly believe the poet Statius was from Toulouse; he was actually from Naples. They confused him with a rhetorician named Lucius Statius Ursulus.</note> **With myrtle:** with which poets were crowned. Hence Petrarch: "What longing for laurel or what for myrtle." **Statius:** it is an empty wonder if this poet, so occupied with sublime, varied, and numerous things, followed the opinion that occupied all men of his time and did not investigate the homeland of Statius; this served him in no way here, for such great genius did not esteem minute details. And he could well defend himself with the authority of Lactantius, commentator on his *Thebaid*, a man of much eloquence. But Statius writes in his *Silvae* that his father was Neapolitan. **I sang of Thebes:** describing the discord born in the kingdom between Eteocles and Polynices, of which mention was made in the *Inferno*. And the war that Adrastus, King of Argos and father-in-law of Polynices, moved against Athens. **Great Achilles:** of whom you shall seek the history in the second canto of the *Inferno*. **But I fell on the way with the second burden.** That is, I did not give perfection to the second book, which was the *Achilleid*, being prevented by death. Here Francesco da Buti <note>A 14th-century commentator on Dante</note> errs greatly, for he reproves Dante for saying such a work is imperfect, and insists it is perfect. But if he had noted the beginning well, he would have most clearly understood that poem to be started and not completed. Furthermore, some say he did not fall with the second burden, but with the third: having completed not only the *Thebaid*, but also the *Silvae*. To them we respond that the *Silvae* are not a laborious work, but rather written to relax the mind exhausted by the laborious vigils of the *Thebaid*. Therefore, the *Silvae* did not deserve to be called a "burden" like the *Achilleid*, an undertaking which had no less difficulty than the *Thebaid*. **To my ardor, the seeds were the sparks.** He demonstrates that the beginning of his learning and fame was Virgil’s *Aeneid*, which by imitating he was able to become an excellent poet. Thus, order the text: the sparks of your genius, which warmed me with the divine flame of poetry, were the seeds of my ardor—that is, they were the cause of my excitement. **From which:** from which sparks more than a thousand are enlightened, because Virgil has been the norm and example for all poets. **And to have lived over there:** that is, in our world. And he said: I would consent to stay one year more—**one year more before my release from exile**—that is, to stay longer in the pains of Purgatory to which I was condemned, if I could have lived at the same time as Virgil. But there are some who think he shows little desire by offering only one year; however, if we remember the words of Gregory on the pains of Purgatory, we will understand that one year in that torment is a very great thing.

### CANTO XXI

Volse uirgilio adme queste parole
conuiso che tacendo disse taci
ma non puo tutto la uirtu che uole
Che riso & pianto son tanto seguaci
alla passion dache ciascun si spicca
che men seguon uoler ne piu ueraci
Io pur sorrisi chome lhuom cammicha
perche lombra sitacque & riguardommi
neglochi oue lsembiante piu sificca
De se tanto lauoro in bene assommi
dixe perche la faccia tua testeso
un lampeggiar diriso dimostrommi
Hor son io duna parte & dalltra preso
luna mifa tacer laltra scongiura
chio dica ondio sospiro & sono inteso
Dal mio maestro & non hauer paura
mi dice di parlar ma parla & digli
quel che dimanda con cotanta cura
Ondio forse tu timarauigli
anticho spirto del rider chio fei
ma piu dadmiration uo che tipigli
Questi che guida in alto glocchi miei
e quel uirgilio dal qual tu togliesti
forse acantar deglihuomini & dedei
Se cagione altra almio rider credesti
lasciala per non uera & esser credi
quelle parole che di lui dicesti
Gia sinchinaua adabbraciar li piedi
almio doctore ma egli dixe frate
non far che tu se ombra & ombra uedi
Et surgendo hor puoi la quantitate
comprende dellamor che ate mi scalda
quando io dismento nostra uanitate
Traetando lombre chome chosa salda

<column-break/>

**VIRGIL TURNED.** That is <note>original: "idest"</note>, these words made Virgil turn to me with such a look that, while he remained silent, he signaled to me that I should keep silent.

**BUT THE POWER.** That power called the "will" cannot do everything; for it often happens that a man, not wishing to weep, weeps; and not wishing to laugh, laughs. Because every passion of the soul—such as joy, sadness, and the like—has certain acts and gestures that follow from these passions even if the person does not wish it. For this reason, laughter follows joy even if we do not want it to, and tears follow sadness. **THAT THEY LEAST FOLLOW.** This refers to those who are less capable of pretending or hiding their feelings. **I MERELY SMILED.** Even though, by Virgil's signals, I did not want Statius to recognize Virgil yet, and for this reason I wanted to restrain my laughter; nevertheless, for the reason stated above, I could not contain it. **LIKE A MAN WHO WINKS.** Like someone who makes a subtle sign with their eyes. **AND LOOKED AT ME.** He looked into my eyes, seeing me smile. **WHERE THE EXPRESSION IS MOST FIXED.** Where the image and likeness of the soul is most clearly expressed and carved. This is because the eyes are like windows through which the soul can be seen. **SO MAY YOU BRING TO A GOOD END.** That is, if you bring to a successful conclusion **SUCH LABOR**, which refers to the great task of ascending to Paradise. **WHY DID YOU SHOW ME.** Why did your face just now show me a flash of a smile? **NOW I AM.** Dante was in a difficult position from both sides. Virgil signaled him not to speak, but Statius begged him to explain. **WHENCE I SIGH.** Through such distress and such a sigh, I was understood by Virgil. But Virgil, seeing me in this ambiguity, gave me permission to speak.

->There is nothing ambiguous in these tercets; therefore, they do not require explanation.<-

# CANTO XXII OF THE SECOND CANTICLE BY DANTE.

The poet now rises from the fifth circle to the sixth, where souls are purified of the vice of gluttony; it deals with the conversion of Statius <note>Statius was a Roman poet of the 1st century AD, author of the *Thebaid*</note> with great praise for Virgil. Beginning then, he says: that having already ascended, they had left the angel behind:

The angel was already left behind us,
the angel who had turned us to the sixth circle,
having erased a stroke from my face:

And those who have their desire set on justice
had been declared blessed by him, and his voice
ended with "I thirst," and nothing more.

And I, lighter than through the other gates,
moved forward so that without any labor
I followed the swift spirits upward.

When Virgil began: "Love,
kindled by virtue, has always kindled another,
provided that its flame appeared outwardly.

Therefore, from the hour that Juvenal <note>Decimus Iunius Iuvenalis, a Roman satirist</note>
descended among us into the Limbo of Hell,
and made your affection for me known,

My goodwill toward you was such
as ever bound one to a person never seen,
so that these stairs will now seem short to me.

But tell me—and as a friend, forgive me
if too much liberty slackens my rein—
and speak with me now as a friend.

How could avarice find a place
within your breast, amid such wisdom
with which you were filled by your own care?"

These words caused Statius to move
a little to laughter at first; then he replied:
"Every word of yours is a dear sign of love to me.

Truly, many times things appear
that give false material for doubt
because the true causes are hidden.

Your question confirms your belief
that I was avaricious in the other life,
perhaps because of that circle where I was.

Now know that avarice was removed
too far from me; and this excess
thousands of lunar months have punished.

And were it not that I set right my concern
when I heard the place where you cry out,
as if angered at human nature:

'Why do you not govern, O sacred hunger
for gold, the appetite of mortals?'
I would feel the grim jousts while turning." <note>Referring to the punishment of the greedy and spendthrifts in Hell, who crash weights against each other like jousters.</note>

Then I realized that hands could open
their wings too wide in spending, and I repented
of that as well as of my other evils.

the one who had shown him the sixth circle. **HAVING FROM MY** face a stroke erased: because he had erased the fifth sin <note>The 'P' representing Peccatum or sin, carved on Dante's forehead by the angel</note>; so that only the sixth and seventh remained. **AND THOSE** who have. This shows that the souls who were being purified in the fifth circle, seeing Dante ascend purified of avarice, sang out of joy and congratulation: > Blessed are they whose iniquities are forgiven and whose sins are covered <note>original: "Beati quorum remisse sunt iniquitates & quorum tecta sunt peccata"</note>; and finally, turning to Dante as he ascended, they said: "I thirst" <note>original: "sitio"</note>, that is, I have a thirst for eternal salvation. **AND I, LIGHTER**: he was lighter than in the circles below because he was purified of more vices. And with such lightness, he could ascend alongside Virgil and Statius, who were swift spirits. **LOVE** kindled by virtue always kindled another: If one loves another for the virtue seen in them, it is inevitable that the loved one loves the lover in return. **PROVIDED THAT THE FLAME**, that is, provided such love is known to the one who is loved. But this does not happen in carnal love, because often one is loved carnally who does not love the lover in return. **WHEREFORE** for which reason it happened that when Juvenal descended into Limbo and told me of your great love toward me, I was moved to feel such benevolence for you as was never felt toward an unseen person—that is, one not known personally. And he says this because virtue has the power to draw us to love those we have never seen, and all the more so if we hear they love us. **SO THAT NOW WILL SEEM** these stairs short to me. Because it is true that being with a friend makes one endure every difficulty, and especially where there is eloquence. Hence the ancient poet said: > An eloquent companion on the road is as good as a carriage. <note>original: "Comes facundus pro uehiculo est in uia"</note> **BUT TELL ME** and as a friend forgive me. Virgil believed, finding Statius where avarice was being purified, that he had been stained by that vice. And appearing to him as a vice very alien to a wise man, he asked how it could be that one of such wisdom had fallen into the vice of greed. **BUT TELL ME** and as a friend forgive me. Because such a question seems not to be without some blame toward Statius. Virgil excuses himself: that as a friend who grieves, and not as a detractor, he seeks this answer. **BY YOUR CARE** you were filled: because wisdom is in those who exercise their talent and intellect.

---

Statius saw the error that Virgil was making and understood that his words did not come from a malicious mind but from a friend; and therefore he smiled. Then he demonstrated that men are often deceived by false conjectures and signs, as Virgil was then, who, hearing that Statius had been so long in the circle of the avaricious, estimated that he was there to purge avarice. But he demonstrates to him that he had sinned not in avarice, but in its opposite vice, which is prodigality <note>wasteful extravagance</note>. And therefore he says: **AND THIS** excess. For prodigality, as we distinctly demonstrated in the *Inferno*, is punished together with avarice. And the reason is here and is manifest here. **When I heard the place where you call out.** When I heard where you make an exclamation in your third book, saying: > To what do you not drive mortal hearts, O sacred hunger for gold? <note>original: "Quid non mortalia pectora cogis Auri sacra fames?" From Virgil's Aeneid</note> **ALMOST ANGERED** at human nature, that is, angered at all men. Who, having a nature that could stay content with a few small things, are nonetheless insatiable. **WHY DO YOU NOT** govern, O sacred hunger. He imitates Virgil, as we said. And with a form of indignation, he makes an exclamation. **TURNING I WOULD FEEL** the grim jousts, that is, painful ones. And this is what he imagines in the seventh canto of the *Inferno*. "Then I realized." Then I saw that I could sin as much in spending too much as in not observing the limit in liberality—which is knowing how much, when, how, to whom, and why. And so I became a prodigal; and therefore I turned to repentance for this vice as well. **HOW MANY** will rise again with shorn hair: in the same chapter of the *Inferno*, he imagined that the prodigals will rise with cut hair and the avaricious with closed fists; and in 그 place we provided the allegory. Therefore, how many will there be who, because ignorance of this sin prevents repentance, that is, through...

How many will rise with shorn hair <note>A reference to the punishment of the prodigal, who are resurrected with their hair cut off to symbolize their loss of worldly goods</note>
through ignorance of this sin,
which prevents repentance in life and at the end?
And know that the fault which counters
any sin through direct opposition,
here dries up its greenness together with it.
Therefore, I have been among those people
who weep for avarice to purge myself,
because its contrary has happened to me.

Now, when you sang of the cruel arms
of the double sorrow of Jocasta, <note>Jocasta, the mother of Eteocles and Polynices, who killed each other in the war of the Seven Against Thebes</note>
said the singer of the bucolic songs, <note>Virgil, referring to his own *Eclogues*</note>
by what Clio <note>The Muse of History, invoked by Statius in his *Thebaid*</note> touches upon with you there,
it does not seem you were yet made faithful
by that faith without which good works are not enough.
If this is so, what sun or what candles
dispelled your darkness so that you thereafter
set your sails behind the fisherman? <note>Saint Peter, symbolizing the Christian Church</note>

And he to him: You first sent me
toward Parnassus <note>The mountain sacred to the Muses</note> to drink in its grottoes,
and you first illuminated me toward God.
You did as one who walks by night,
who carries the light behind him and does not help himself,
but makes the people behind him wise,
When you said: "The age renews itself,
justice returns and the first human time,
and a new progeny descends from heaven." <note>original: "Ultima cumaei venit iam temporis aetas... Jam nova progenies caelo demittitur alto." From Virgil’s Fourth Eclogue, which was interpreted in the Middle Ages as a prophecy of the birth of Christ.</note>
Through you I was a poet, through you a Christian;
but so that you may see what I sketch,
I will stretch out my hand to color it.
Already the world was entirely pregnant
with the true belief, sown
by the messengers of the eternal kingdom;
And your word mentioned above
was so in harmony with the new preachers
that I took up the habit of visiting them.
They then appeared so holy to me
that when Domitian <note>Roman Emperor known for persecuting Christians</note> persecuted them,
their cries were not without my tears.
And while I remained in that world,
I helped them, and their upright customs
made me despise all other sects.
And before I led the Greeks to the rivers
of Thebes in my poetry, I received baptism;
but out of fear, I was a hidden Christian,
For a long time pretending to be a pagan;
and this tepidity made me circle the fourth terrace <note>The terrace of Sloth</note>
for more than four centuries.

not recognizing prodigality: they do not repent: and they will be damned for it. And in truth, because avarice is entirely opposite to liberality: it is easy to recognize. But the contrary is true for prodigality: because it is so similar to liberality that few can distinguish it. **KNOW** that the fault. He says: that in the same place where one sin is punished, the other sin is also punished, which is its contrary by opposition: and the text orders it. Know that the fault, that is, the sin, which "rimbecca" <note>rimbecca: a term from ball games meaning to strike back or counter-hit</note> any sin, that is, which strikes back through direct opposition. "Rimbeccare" properly is when we strike back the ball that comes toward us.

**HERE** Virgil responds: and he orders. **THE SINGER** of the bucolic songs, that is, Virgil: who among the other books he wrote, composed the *Bucolics*. **HE SAID**: when **YOU SANG** of the cruel arms, that is, the cruel battle. **OF THE** double sorrow of Jocasta: the which battle was between Eteocles and Polynices: the two sons of Jocasta: who, by killing one another, brought double sorrow to their mother. This is the subject matter which Statius sang in his *Thebaid*: which history we narrated in the twenty-sixth canto of the *Inferno*. **BY WHAT** Clio touches upon with you: by what I understand in the subject matter; for Clio is one of the nine muses and is invoked by Statius. **TOUCHES**: searches and tries: as if to say: the subject matter that you place in that spot and the manner of the treatment does not show that you had come to the Christian faith: without which doing good is not enough. **IF THIS IS SO**, as if to say, how is it? **WHAT** sun: that is, what grace illuminating your intellect. **WHAT** candles: what human doctrine. **DISPELLED THE DARKNESS**: removed the shadows of ignorance. **YOU SET** the sails: that is, you proposed to navigate: which is to live. **BEHIND** the fisherman: behind Saint Peter, that is, according to the Christian religion.

**AND** he to him. He shows that Virgil was the cause for him both of being a poet and being a Christian. Because reading his poems, he was incited to imitate him: and therefore he says: You sent me toward Parnassus, of which we spoke above in the first canto. **IN ITS** grottoes. Because on its slopes were the Pegasean springs consecrated to the muses. Statius read these verses of the Sibyl translated by Virgil: in which it says that the ages renew themselves and that the virgin returns, and from heaven descends a new progeny. And then hearing the Christian doctors relate them to the incarnation of Christ, moved by the authority of Virgil, he became a Christian. The verses are: <note>original: "Ultima cumaei venit iam temporis etas. Magnus ab integro seclorum nascitur ordo. Iam redit & uirgo: redeunt saturnia regna. Iam nuoua progenies celo demittitur alto." Translation: "Now the final age of the Cumaean song has come. The great order of the centuries is born anew. Now the Virgin returns, the reign of Saturn returns. Now a new progeny is sent down from high heaven."</note> And therefore he says, you did like one who, walking at night, carries the light behind him: which does not provide light for himself but for those behind him. Likewise, you placed the verses; but not interpreting them correctly, you applied them to the honor of Octavian <note>Augustus Caesar</note>. But I, helped by Christian interpreters, understood them according to the true sense. Already the world was pregnant with the true belief of the Christians, and those who preached encouraged us toward the Christian religion. **THEY THEN APPEARED** to me. The works of the Christians seemed so holy to me that, they being persecuted by Domitian, it grieved me greatly. I helped them secretly, and I despised every other sect and religion. **DOMITIAN**. This man was the twelfth emperor: he reigned fifteen years and five months. He succeeded Titus, his brother, who was as pious and just as Domitian was impious and unjust. He took the empire in the eighty-second year from the incarnation of Christ. He most cruelly afflicted the Christians; he wished to be our god and lord. Nevertheless, in so many vices, he was severe in suppressing adulteries and favored the learned. **AND BEFORE I** led the Greeks to the river of Thebes, that is, before in my *Thebaid* I had come to the place where I describe when the army of Adrastus with the other kings arrives at the rivers of Thebes, which are Ismenus and Asopus: I became Christian. But I lived as a Christian secretly and was not ardent in the faith in a way that I dared to reveal myself. And for being so tepid, I fell into that sin of slowness in doing good, which is punished in the fourth circle, and there I stayed more than the four-hundredth, that is, four hundred years; and more than five hundred I had been in the fifth, and some time...

<summary>Statius explains to Virgil that his Fourth Eclogue led him to Christianity, though he remained a "secret Christian" out of fear of persecution by Emperor Domitian. This secrecy resulted in Statius spending four centuries in the Circle of Sloth before moving to the Circle of Avarice and Prodigality.</summary>

Statius continues his speech and says: You, Virgil, who have lifted the lid for me (that is, you have removed my ignorance, as in the verses already mentioned above, which ignorance hid from me the "good" I speak of, which is God and Christian doctrine). Tell me, while I had the "lid" of ascending (that is, while I was growing in the desire to ascend), where is our friend **TERENCE**? Terence was a Carthaginian <note>original: "carthaginese"</note> who was taken in war and became a slave in Rome, serving the senator Terentius Lucanus. Because of his excellent intellect, he was raised as a free man and became learned, writing six comedies. He was a friend to Scipio and Laelius, and Statius calls Terence a friend to himself and to Virgil because the poets who came after Terence were more familiar with his work than with other ancients. Cicero, who for this same reason calls Terence his close friend. **Cecilio Statio**: Caecilius was a comic poet. Others say he was from that part of Gaul where the Insubres live, others say he was a Milanese. He was a close friend of Ennius and died the year following Ennius's death in the 150th Olympiad; he was buried on Mount Janiculum. **Plautus** was from Umbria and from the city of Sarsina, so poor that for wages he turned a millstone. He lived in the 145th Olympiad. **VARRO**: Marcus Terentius Varro was born in the 166th Olympiad. He was the most learned of all the Romans, a most excellent poet and philosopher, whom many scholars did not hesitate to equate with Aristotle. He wrote forty-one books on antiquity, dividing them into human and divine matters. There was another Varro, a contemporary of Virgil, of whom Virgil writes honorably in the *Eclogues*: <note>original: "Sed neque adhuc Varo videor neque dicere Cinna digna, sed arguto interstrepere anser olore." — For as yet I seem to speak nothing worthy of a Varro or a Cinna, but to cackle as a goose among tuneful swans.</note> Several people together with Tucca and Varius <note>The OCR reads "tucca octauiano," likely referring to the editors Varius and Tucca commissioned by Augustus</note> were given the task by Octavian after Virgil's death to edit the *Aeneid*, which Virgil had left imperfect at his death, and for this reason he left instructions in his will that it should be burned. But Octavian would not allow the honor of the Latin language to be extinguished. **THEY**: Virgil my leader replied, those you ask about, and **Persius** and I, are with that Greek whom the Muses nursed more than any other poet, meaning **Homer**, whom we mentioned in the *Inferno*. Nor by these words does he place Homer above Virgil, but in bringing him to speak, he portrays him as modest. **PERSIO**: was from Volterra; his satires, though few, show manifest signs of his genius. **IN THE first circle**: as was shown in the first canticle <note>Inferno</note>, and there together we often speak of the mountain (Parnassus) **THAT**: which has our nurses (that is, the Muses). In short, they spoke of the Muses by whom poets are nourished. **EURIPIDE**: an excellent poet and writer of tragedies. He was a disciple of Anaxagoras and a fellow student of Socrates. He was very apt at writing tragic themes with compassion. **Anacreonte**: an elegiac poet, born on the island of Teos. **SIMOnide**: a poet from the island of Ceos. He was the inventor of the "places and images" belonging to

artificial memory <note>A mnemonic technique used by ancient orators</note>. He had written hymns in honor of Scopas, a most powerful and wealthy man in Thessaly, in which he had interspersed much praise for Pollux and Castor, the sons of Jove called the Dioscuri. He recited them at a banquet to which Scopas had invited many. After the verses were recited, Scopas told Simonides that he would give him half of the prize he deserved for the verses, and for the other half, he should ask the Dioscuri, whom he had equally praised. Simonides agreed; and shortly thereafter, two young men dressed in white arrived, and for a matter of importance, they had Simonides called out of the house. <header>CANTO XXIV</header>

Thus custom was our guide,
and we took the path with less suspicion
through the consent of that worthy soul.
They went on ahead, and I alone
behind, and I listened to their speech,
which gave understanding to my poetry.

<margin>The right side led them on a good path. I judge the same here; therefore he says: **THUS custom was our guide**, showing that habit and experience generate doctrine. **THROUGH the consent of that worthy soul**: he means the soul of Statius, who, being purged of sins, was truly worthy and must have had greater knowledge of this journey. **THEY went on ahead**: because intellect and reason ought to precede. **LISTENED to their speech**: certainly, the senses should follow the intellect adorned with true doctrine, and not deviate from it. **Which gave understanding to my poetry**: allegorically, this denotes that by imitating these poets, he himself became a poet.</margin>

But soon the sweet talk was broken
by a tree we found in the middle of the road,
with fruits sweet and good to smell.
And as a fir tree tapers upward
from branch to branch, so did that one downward,
I believe so that no one may climb up.
On the side where our path was closed,
a clear liquid fell from the high rock
and spread through the leaves above.
The two poets approached the tree,
and a voice from within the foliage
cried: "Of this food you shall have scarcity."

<margin>The tree points upward because the root of knowing good and evil comes from God; it bends its branches toward us in its appearance and pomp, but its vitality faces heaven because science <note>original: "scientia," meaning knowledge or wisdom</note> is from God. Its fruits are fragrant because praising abstinence and blaming vice generates the delights of the eternal life, which cannot be had here. The streams that descend from Paradise through the grotto, and then return upward through the leaves of the trees, signify divine grace. This grace is poured into men who are established and firm in the habit of virtue, and then, through the green leaves (which are living works), it returns to God. For the good refer every grace received from Him back to God. We can also relate this to the fable of Tantalus <note>A mythological figure punished in the underworld with eternal hunger and thirst; fruit and water always remained just out of reach</note>, whom the poets place in Hell, hungry and thirsty in water up to his chin, with various fruits hanging above his nose. If he reaches, the fruits pull away; if he stoops, the water recedes; thus, in great abundance, he always finds himself in scarcity—a punishment fitting for the gluttonous. **I BELIEVE so that no one may climb up**: because no one can go to take the fruits. **ON the side where our path was closed**: because we could not enter between the tree and the grotto, but had to go between the tree and the peak. **A clear liquid**: because nothing is clearer than the grace of God, especially that which illuminates. **The two poets approached the tree**: it is a fitting thing that the intellect, raised to contemplation, approaches divine grace, for it is fit to receive it. **AND a voice cried**: This is the truth through which the intellect understands that it must be grateful to receive grace.</margin>

Then it said: "Mary thought more of how
the wedding might be honorable and complete
than of her mouth, which answers for you.
And the ancient Roman women for their drink
were content with water; and Daniel
despised food and acquired knowledge.
The first age was as beautiful as gold;
it made acorns flavorful with hunger,
and every brook nectar for thirst.
Honey and locusts were the viands
that nourished the Baptist in the desert;
for which he is glorious and so great,
as is revealed to you by the Gospel."

<margin>...staining the mind with gluttony and wine. He [Daniel] begged from his guardian to be fed with legumes and water; and thus he and his companions became more beautiful, as they had promised the guard. But we shall speak of Daniel at length in the fourth canto of *Paradiso*. **The first age was as beautiful as gold**: In many places, the poets state that in the "Golden Age," men fed themselves on acorns and drank water. **Honey and locusts were the viands**: This is most well-known from his [John the Baptist's] life.</margin>

<column-break/>

And they divide into twenty-four parts, and they are almost placed like sentries, each guiding the tiller of the solar chariot for its allotted space. Therefore, when the fourth has conducted the chariot through its space, she stops and the fifth succeeds her, and then the others in order. In this place, the poet wishes to show that four hours had already passed and the fifth had arrived. For this reason, he says that already the four handmaidens [hours] had remained behind, and the fifth was at the tiller, **DIRECTING upward the burning horn**: because until midday, the sun always rises, and he calls the point of the tiller the "horn." **I BELIEVE that at the end**: because in all the other terraces he had seen that turning from the...

The author feigns that in the sixth circle, where the vice of gluttony is punished, there are two trees: one almost at the entrance of the circle, and the other at the end, near the ascent to the seventh. These have their roots toward heaven and their crowns toward the earth. He feigns that they are full of fruits which cast an excellent and most sweet scent. Furthermore, he posits that from the cliff of the mountain come two streams, which descend from the terrestrial paradise to the grotto of the sixth circle, and from there, one rises up one tree and the other up the other. One is called **Eunoe**, which kindles the memory of good; the other is **Lethe**, and this takes away the memory of evil. The streams rise up, each through its tree, refreshing its foliage, and finally return to where they issued. He shows further that toward the slope of the mountain, the path is closed; there is no other passage than on the outside part of the tree toward the ledge, which has no railing. The shape of the tree was like a fir tree with its tip turned downward. He feigns these trees, drawing such an allegory from the tree that the first parents tasted; they, against the divine precept, tasted the fruit of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, from which issued the bait of all sins. And because by tasting the fruit they fell into the sin of gluttony, he places the trees here...

Then he [the voice] continued his words, providing historical examples that invite sobriety and abstinence, which virtues are contrary to gluttony. First, that **Mary** at the wedding <note>The Wedding at Cana</note> did not think of her "mouth"—that is, of satisfying her own taste—when she said "they have no wine," but thought of making the feast honorable and complete. **WHICH answers for you**: that mouth which is always an advocate for you in heaven. **AND the Roman women**: The use of wine was unknown among ancient Roman women. They say that for this reason, they were kissed in greetings: so that men might notice by the smell of wine if they had drunk. Nevertheless, a woman becomes intoxicated more difficultly than a man, because she has a very moist body, as shown by the delicacy and splendor of her flesh. Therefore, wine, pouring into such moisture, becomes very watery and loses the power to evaporate to the brain. **DANIEL**: Nebuchadnezzar, King of Babylon, conquered Jerusalem and carried away great treasures and many noble youths, among whom was the prophet Daniel. He ordered that many should eat precious foods from his table; but Daniel, who had determined not to... <note>Daniel 1:8, where Daniel refuses the King's meat and wine to remain ritually pure</note>

# CANTO XXIII. OF THE SECOND CANTICLE OF DANTE

In this 23rd chapter, the poet describes the punishment through which the gluttons are purified in the sixth circle. He recognizes a certain soul, specifically Forese <note>Forese Donati, a childhood friend of Dante</note>, and speaks with him. **WHILE THE EYES**: A beautiful comparison showing how he fixed his eyes through the green leaves of the tree, just as those do who consume all their time chasing birds <note>referring to bird-hunters/fowlers</note>; and just as the goshawk <note>original: "storo"</note> wastes time, so I was losing mine.

<margin>d</margin>
**W**hile my eyes were through the green leaves 
fixed, just as he is accustomed to do 
who loses his life chasing after birds, 
He who was more than a father to me said: "My son, 
come along now, for the time allotted to us 
must be shared out more usefully." 
I turned my face, and my step no less quickly, 
after the sages, who were speaking so 
that they made the going cost me nothing. 
And behold, weeping and singing was heard: 
"O Lord, open my lips" <note>original: "labia mea domine"; from Psalm 51:15</note> in such a way 
that it gave birth to both delight and grief. 
"O sweet father, what is that which I hear?" 
I began; and he: "Shadows who go, 
perhaps loosening the knot of their debt."

Just as pensive pilgrims do 
when, overtaking unknown people on the road, 
they turn toward them and do not stop, 
So, moving more quickly behind us, 
coming and passing by, a crowd of souls, 
silent and devout, gazed at us in wonder. 
In the eyes, each one was dark and hollow, 
pale in the face, and so wasted 
that the skin took its shape from the bones. 
I do not believe that Erysichthon <note>A Greek mythological figure cursed with insatiable hunger</note> 
became so withered to his very skin 
by fasting, when he had the most fear of it.

I said to myself in thought: "Behold 
the people who lost Jerusalem, 
when Mary drove her beak into her son!" <note>A reference to the Siege of Jerusalem, where a woman named Mary was driven by famine to eat her child</note> 
Their eye-sockets seemed like rings without gems; 
he who reads "OMO" <note>The word for 'man' in Italian; medieval thought held that the features of the human face formed these letters</note> in the face of men 
would clearly have recognized the "M" there. 
Who would believe that the scent of an apple, 
by its governance, would generate such craving, 
and that of a spring, not knowing how? 
I was already in wonder at what so famished them, 
for the cause was not yet manifest 
of their leanness and their wretched scurf, 
And behold, from the depths of the head 
a shadow turned his eyes toward me and stared fixedly; 
then he cried out loudly: "What grace is this to me!" 
Never would I have recognized him by his face...

<column-break/>

**M**Y SON <note>original: "MIDIxe figliolo"</note>: that is, "little son," which is a Latinate term. **Come along now**: As a true father, reason admonishes the senses that they must follow. It demonstrates that nothing is more ruinous than consuming time in useless things—time which we ought to spend usefully. **Shared out**: In human life, it is not just one thing that is required, but many; therefore, it is necessary that we allot to each as much time as is required. **I turned my face**: To attend to that which I was warned of. The step taken to execute what was commanded was that I should follow him. **Who were speaking so**: Because, as I have already said, eloquence is like a vehicle on the way. Therefore, the walking cost nothing. **And behold, weeping and singing**: They wept out of contrition and true repentance for the sin committed, and they sang for the hope of being able to purge it and, once purged, go to salvation. **O Lord, open my lips** <note>original: "Domine labia"</note>: This is from the prophetic psalm: "O Lord, open my lips, and my mouth shall declare thy praise" <note>original: "Domine labia mea aperies: & os meū annūciabit laudē tuā"</note>. This prayer is appropriate for the gluttonous. This is so that the mouth, which in the past opened for superfluous food, may in the future know how to sing divine praises. **Such that delight**: because I saw that they were to be saved. **And grief**: to see them in their present punishment. **Perhaps loosening the knot**: that is, they go "loosening"—that is, untying—the knot, meaning the obligation of their duty; that is, of that which they remain debtors to God for the punishment, and for that which they have to pay.

**F**ollowing on the path, he shows that a crowd of souls came behind them, which was "moving more quickly." That is, because it moved faster, it reached them and watched them, and they passed ahead, just as pilgrims do who travel not without suspicion and, reaching unknown people, watch them and pass by. **Pilgrim** is a Latin name and signifies anyone who makes a journey outside of his own country. **In the eyes**: Wishing to show those souls were much thinned by long and great abstinence, he sets down the signs we see in thin bodies. The first is that the eyes are recessed backward. The second is that the heart is gone. The third is that the skin is right on the bone—that is, there is no flesh between the skin and the bone. **Erysichthon**: This was an impious man in Thessaly who held Ceres <note>Goddess of agriculture</note> in contempt and forbade sacrifices to her. Therefore, an angry Ceres inflicted an unheard-of hunger upon him, through which in a brief time he consumed all his substance, and finally sold his daughter multiple times; and after this, he ate his own limbs. Under such a fable, Ovid expresses the nature of the glutton.

**I** said, seeing such leanness, that these were those Jews whom Titus besieged in Jerusalem, of whom many thousands perished of hunger. **Mary**: Josephus <note>original: "losapho"</note> places this in his book *The Jewish War* among the other extreme things the Hebrew people did when constrained by hunger when Jerusalem was besieged by Titus: that a certain Mary, daughter of Eleazar, driven to ultimate despair by hunger, killed her own son, whom she opened, halved, boiled, and ate. Certain thieves ran there at the scent and forced the woman to give them a share of that food. She, infuriated and more eager for death than life, offered the other half of the child, saying it was her son. But they, overcome by nature, fled from such wickedness. **Seemed like rings without gems**: the sockets of the eyes seemed like rings without gems—round rings without the setting where the gem enters. They say that in the face of a man, the ears and the nose make an 'M' in this form: **M**, and the eyes are two 'O's in the middle. And so they say: "HOMO." Thus the poet wants to demonstrate that the leanness of the face made this appear more expressly. **Who would believe**: as if to say, that no one, not knowing how, would believe that the scent of that tree and that water would generate "craving"—that is, the desire to eat. But the reason is shown in the [next] canto.

<summary>This page describes Dante's encounter with the emaciated souls of the gluttons in Purgatory, who are punished by a tantalizing scent of fruit and water they cannot consume. The commentary explains the classical and biblical examples of extreme hunger, such as Erysichthon and Mary of Jerusalem, and interprets the physical appearance of the suffering souls.</summary>

# CANTO XXIII

but in his voice it was made clear to me
that which his appearance had concealed within itself.
That speech completely rekindled
my memory of those changed features,
and I recognized the face of Forese. <note>Forese Donati, a childhood friend of Dante and a poet himself; he died in 1296.</note>

"Pray, do not mind the dry scab
which discolors my skin," he begged,
"nor the lack of flesh that I have;
But tell me the truth about yourself, and who are those
two souls who act as your escort;
do not refrain from speaking to me."

"Your face, which I once wept for when dead,
gives me no less grief to weep for now,"
I replied to him, seeing it so distorted.
"Therefore tell me, for God’s sake, what strips you so; <note>original: "siuiffogla" (sfoglia), meaning to strip leaves or layers away.</note>
do not make me speak while I am marvelling,
for he speaks poorly who is full of other desire."

And he to me: "From the eternal counsel
virtue falls into the water and the plant
left behind, through which I grow so thin.
All these people who, weeping, sing
for following their appetite beyond measure,
in hunger and thirst here make themselves holy again.

The desire to drink and eat is kindled in us
by the scent that comes from the fruit and the spray
which spreads out over the greenery.
And not just once as we circle this space
is our pain refreshed;
I say pain, but I should say delight:

For that desire leads us to the tree
which led Christ joyfully to say *Eli* <note>original: "hely"; refers to Jesus's cry on the cross, "Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani" (My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?)</note>
when he liberated us with his life-blood."

And I to him: "Forese, from that day
in which you changed worlds for a better life,
five years have not yet turned until now.
If the power to sin ended in you
before the hour of 'good sorrow' arrived—
the penitence that remarries us to God—
How have you already come here?
I thought to find you down below
where time is restored for time." <note>A reference to Ante-Purgatory, where those who delayed repentance must wait.</note>

And he to me: "I have been led so quickly
to drink the sweet wormwood of torments
by my Nella <note>Forese’s widow, whom he praises for her prayers.</note> with her overflowing tears.
With her devout prayers and with sighs
she has drawn me from the shore where one waits,
and delivered me from the other circles.
She is all the more dear and beloved to God..."

<margin>215</margin>

<column-break/>

XXV. **THEIR SAD** scale. "Scale" <note>original: "squama"</note> is proper to fish, which we call a husk. But here he calls "scale" the crust that is on the face of one who is squalid and almost perished from hunger. Forese was the brother of Accursio <note>The commentator likely means Corso Donati, though the text names Accurso, a famous jurist</note>, the legal consultant, and of Piccarda, a most beautiful and honorable woman. Thus, among these three, he has divided the three kingdoms: to Accursio he gave Hell; to Forese, Purgatory; and Piccarda you will find in Paradise.

**YOUR FACE**: He demonstrates that he is no less moved to weep for Forese's face at present, seeing it so distorted—that is, so removed from its usual form—than he did when he saw him dead. And beneath these words, he shows that one should weep more for vice in a man than for death. **DO NOT MAKE ME SPEAK**: while I am in admiration of what I see. **FOR HE SPEAKS POORLY**: he can poorly narrate to others who desires that things be narrated to him. **FROM THE ETERNAL** counsel: which is divine providence, "virtue falls." Because if this is the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, divine providence has infused in our souls the desire to know it. It seems necessary to me in this place to provide a double sense: First, as to the punishment, it is a just thing that divine providence has instituted for the vice of gluttony a penalty and a torture: that the tree induces incredible hunger in the gluttonous. Then we shall follow the allegory placed here. **IN HUNGER** and thirst: so that gluttony may be punished by its opposite; and he very well said "makes themselves holy again"—that is, returns to the original form, which sin had unmade. For the soul is created pure by God, but sin stains and fouls it. **THAT** That desire: someone might doubt why the souls go so much around this tree if the scent of the fruits increases their hunger and the sight of water kindles their thirst; to which he responds: that "desire" leads them, not simple will. Simple will is to flee all pain. But "respective will," which we disputed above, leads them to the penalty, not to suffer pain for its own sake, but to be able to purge themselves through suffering and, once purged, go to beatitude. Thus, just as Christ went to say *Eli* <note>original: "hely"</note> of his own will—understand "respective will"—that is, he went to the torment and death of the cross, upon which he said *Eli* to redeem us; so the soul goes to this penalty to ascend to heaven. He said *Eli* to serve the verse instead of saying *Eloi*, which in Hebrew means "my God" or "my deity." **WITH HIS LIFE-BLOOD**: that is, with his blood which issued from his veins.

**HE MOVES** a doubt, saying that since five years have not yet passed since his death, and having been negligent for a long time in repenting of such sin—because the power to commit the vice of gluttony was taken from him by the illness of which he died before he repented—it seems a marvel that he is not further down in Ante-Purgatory, where the soul stays as many years before it can go to purge itself as the years it delayed repenting in life. **IF THE POWER** in you was ended first by the illness **BEFORE THE HOUR** of "good sorrow" came—that is, penitence and contrition, which give good sorrow. And this sorrow "remarries us to God," that is, it reunites us with God. **DOWN BELOW**: in Ante-Purgatory where "time is restored for time," because as was said, the soul is held there before it can enter Purgatory for as many years as it lived in sin before it repented.

**HE CONFIRMS** that which he has already said many times: that the prayers of the living shorten the pains of Purgatory, and he commends the honesty and the sanctity of his wife, who was called Nella. And certainly nothing is more excellent in a woman than chastity, because such virtue causes her to be loved by her elders, for she does not corrupt their blood; she is loved by her children, for they do not have to be ashamed of their mother, and they have no doubt of their father. Chastity makes the one who is poor commended, makes the rich one exalted, and covers the flaws of the one who is not beautiful. **WITH HER** prayers.

<summary>Dante recognizes his friend Forese Donati among the gluttons, who explains that their emaciation is a purifying penance triggered by the scent of a mysterious tree. Forese attributes his rapid advancement through Purgatory to the devoted prayers of his widow, Nella.</summary>
<keywords>Forese Donati, Nella Donati, Gluttony, Purgation, Divine Providence, Contrapasso, Power of Prayer, Chastity, Ante-Purgatory</keywords>

--- Page 434 ---
<meta>Continuity: Dante is still speaking with his friend Forese Donati in the terrace of the gluttons. Forese has just explained how the souls are purified by hunger and thirst.</meta>

# PURGATORY

"My little widow, whom I loved so much,
is all the more precious to God and more beloved,
as she is more alone in her good works;
For the Barbagia of Sardinia <note>A rugged, mountainous region of Sardinia which, in Dante’s time, was considered uncivilized and primitive.</note>
is far more modest in its women
than the Barbagia where I left her.

O sweet brother, what would you have me say?
A future time is already in my sight,
to which this hour will not be very old,
In which it shall be forbidden from the pulpit
to the brazen women of Florence
to go about showing their breasts with their nipples.
What barbarian or Saracen women were there ever
who needed, to make them go covered,
either spiritual or other discipline?
But if the shameless ones were certain
of what the swift heaven prepares for them,
they would already have their mouths open to howl;
For if foresight here does not deceive me,
they will be sad before he grows hair on his cheeks
who is now consoled with lullabies. <note>original: "nanna"; Forese predicts a divine punishment or social upheaval will strike within a generation (roughly 20 years).</note>
Ah, brother, I pray you, hide yourself from me no longer!
See that not only I, but all these people,
are looking at where you veil the sun."

Wherefore I said to him: "If you bring to mind
what you were with me, and what I was with you,
the present memory will still be heavy.
From that life he who goes before me turned me,
the other day, when full
the sister of him <note>The moon, considered the sister of the sun (Apollo).</note> showed herself to you up there."
I pointed to the sun: "This man has led me
through the deep night of the truly dead
with this true flesh that follows him.
From there his encouragements have drawn me up,
climbing and circling the mountain
that straightens you whom the world made crooked.
He speaks of making me his companion
until I shall be where Beatrice is;
there it is fitting that I remain without him.
Virgil is he who tells me this,"
and I pointed to him; "and this other is that shade
for whom just now every slope shook
your kingdom, which clears itself of him." <note>Refers to the earthquake that occurred when the soul of the poet Statius completed his purification.</note>

<meta>Catchword: Your kingdom</meta>

<column-break/>

Because prayers without devotion and sighs have no efficacy.
**SO MUCH** the dearer. The chaste woman is always pleasing to her husband and to others. But more so where such virtue is rare. **THAN THE** Barbagia of Sardinia. In the island of Sardinia there are very harsh mountains, and in those people are of barbaric customs, and the women are very lascivious; and the country is called Barbagia, as if to say "barbaric." He says, therefore, that the women of that Barbagia are more honest than the Florentine women.

He reproaches the Florentine women who in those times, as also in ours, went about with their necks and breasts uncovered. A fashion, without doubt, more worthy of a prostitute than a matron. But just as they changed a little while later—so much so that they wore collars up to their chins, covering the whole neck and throat—so I hope that they will change again, not so much out of honesty as out of flightiness, for in none of their actions are they stable. **BEFORE** hair grows on his cheeks: that is, before a beard grows on him who now—who at present—is consoled with lullabies. That is, a small child. Because in the first stage of life, infants play and fall asleep while the nurses say *nanna nanna*. <note>original: "nanna nanna"; an Italian nursery rhyme or lullaby sound used to soothe babies to sleep.</note> Therefore "nanna" is the voice with which nurses invite the child to sleep. He responds to Forese and shows that Virgil had taken him and removed him from that vicious life in which he had lived with Forese a few days prior, when the moon was full. And he means here Good Friday, which was in the year 1300, when he feigns this journey of his and that Virgil appeared to him. And therefore he says "the other day when she showed herself full to you," that is, the sister of this one [the sun]; and when he spoke of him, he pointed to the sun. **THROUGH THE** deep night: through Hell, where there are deep shadows and the truly dead. Because the separation of the soul from the body is not true death unless the soul remains damned. Rather, it is a passage to a better life. But if the soul goes to Hell—the mountain that straightens us whom the world made crooked: this is the Mountain of Purgatory, which, by cleansing us of the sins we commit in the world, makes us straight from being crooked.

<summary>In this passage, Forese Donati condemns the immodesty of Florentine women, comparing them unfavorably to "barbarians," while Dante explains how Virgil rescued him from a sinful life to lead him through the realms of the afterlife.</summary>
<keywords>Forese Donati, Florentine fashion, immodesty, Barbagia, Sardinia, Virgil, Purgatory, spiritual correction, Good Friday 1300</keywords>
