<meta>This page continues the conversation between Dante and his friend Forese Donati in the terrace of the gluttonous. Forese has just finished explaining how his wife Nella’s prayers shortened his time in lower Purgatory.</meta>

->### CANTO 24 OF THE SECOND CANTICLE BY DANTE<-

<column-break/>

<margin>n</margin> Neither our talk made the pace, nor the pace the talk, any slower; rather, conversing, we went on bravely, like a ship driven by a fair wind.
And the shades, who seemed twice dead, drew wonder from me through the pits of their eyes, having become aware that I was alive.
And I, continuing my discourse, said: "He <note>Referring to Statius</note> goes up perhaps more slowly than he would for another's sake.
But tell me, if you know, where is **Piccarda**? <note>Piccarda Donati, Forese's sister, whom Dante later meets in Paradise.</note>
Tell me if I see any person of note among this people who so gazes at me."
"My sister, who between beautiful and good, I know not which she was more, already triumphs, joyful with her crown, on high Olympus," <note>Olympus is used here as a classical metaphor for Heaven.</note>
he said first; and then: "Here it is not forbidden to name each one, since our features are so milked away <note>The souls are so emaciated from hunger that they are unrecognizable, making it necessary to name them.</note> by the diet.
This one," and he pointed with his finger, "is **Bonagiunta**—Bonagiunta of Lucca; and that face beyond him, more punctured than the others,
held the Holy Church in his arms; <note>This refers to Pope Martin IV.</note> he was from Tours, and he purges through fasting the eels of Bolsena and the Vernaccia wine." <note>A famous gluttonous dish: eels drowned in wine before being roasted.</note>
Many others he named to me one by one; and at their naming all seemed content, so that I did not see a single dark gesture.
I saw, plying their teeth on empty air for lack of food, **Ubaldino della Pila** and **Boniface**, who pastured many people with his staff. <note>Boniface was an Archbishop; the 'staff' or 'roccho' refers to his crozier.</note>
I saw **Messer Marchese**, who once had space to drink at Forlì with less dryness, and yet was such that he never felt satisfied.
But as one does who looks and then chooses, I did more for the one from Lucca, who seemed to want more knowledge of me.
He was murmuring; and I heard something like "Gentucca" <note>A woman from Lucca who would later show Dante hospitality in exile.</note> where he felt the wound of justice that so plucks them.
"O soul," said I, "who seems so eager to speak with me, do so that I may understand you, and satisfy both yourself and me with your speech."
"A woman is born, and wears not yet the veil," he began, "who will make my city pleasing to you, however men may blame it.
You shall go hence with this foresight; if you took error from my murmuring, the facts themselves will yet make it clear to you."

<column-break/>

**The author** does not change the subject matter just because the title changes. But continuing, he shows that they did not go more slowly for talking together, nor did they talk less for going more quickly. Therefore, conversing, they went strongly: like a ship full of a good wind. **AND I** continuing: continuing the speech which I had begun about Statius, said: **HE** (that is, the soul of Statius) goes up to Paradise perhaps more slowly than he would **FOR THE SAKE OF ANOTHER**: for the sake of being longer with Virgil.

He [Forese] replied first that his sister, who was so beautiful and so good that he knew not which was greater, **TRIUMPHS** with her crown for the battle she won against the flesh; because as Juvenal says: 
> <note>original: "Rara est concordia forme atque pudicitie."</note> Rare is the agreement of beauty and modesty. 
**OLYMPUS**: Heaven; like Olympus: yes, all-shining. **AND THEN**: He shows that it is not troublesome to any soul to be named and known, since their appearance is so "milked away" (that is, so thinned by the diet) that we do not recognize them. **BONAGIUNTA**: He was of the Orbicciani of Lucca, and was an excellent composer of sonnets and songs, and a friend to Dante. **HELD THE HOLY CHURCH**: This was Pope Martin IV from Tours in France; he reigned three years, one month, and twenty-seven days. He used to kill the eels of Bolsena in Vernaccia wine, and then cook them with various spices. Finally, through too much devotion to his throat, he died of fatness. **A DARK GESTURE**: That is, an angry gesture.

**UBALDINO**: This was Messer Ubaldino degli Ubaldini, brother of the Cardinal, a very liberal man but stained with this vice. **FROM THE PILA**: The place from which one branch of this house was named. **BONIFACE** was French and Archbishop of Ravenna, very gluttonous. **MARCHESE** was a knight of Forlì of the Rigogliosi family, a very great drinker, and especially of their *ribolla* wine. Hearing his cellarer saying that everyone said he did nothing but drink, he replied laughing: "Why don't they say instead that I am always thirsty?" **WITH LESS DRYNESS** than I have now in Purgatory; and he was such that he never felt satisfied. The meaning is: although the dryness of the thirst he had in Purgatory was greater than what he had in the world, he was never satiated. **I HEARD GENTUCCA**: He shows in this place the prediction of future things. Dante, in his exile, stayed for some time in Lucca and fell in love with a noble woman of refined manners named Madonna Gentucca. But this was after the year 1300, the time in which he feigns to write these things; and therefore he feigns that the spirit, divining the future, murmured that name "Gentucca." But the poet did not then understand it, because it had not yet happened. The people of Lucca use many diminutives and syncopated words like *tucco* and *bottuccolo*, or *Boiuto* for *Honaiuto*.

**HE TURNS** his speech to Bonagiunta and prays him to say openly what he had said confusedly. And he replies: that in Lucca a woman is already born for whose sake his city will please him. **DOES NOT YET WEAR THE VEIL**: This denotes her tender age, in which young girls do not yet wear the head-veil of married women. **YOU SHALL GO HENCE**: with this announcement which I give you; and the true things (that is, the effects you will see) will declare to you if you took any error in my murmuring. But he said: "I see." The meaning is that Bonagiunta says: "Tell me if I see Dante here," as if to say: "Tell me if you are Dante," although he does not use his name but uses a circumlocution, praising him as a finder of new rhymes. And he quotes the beginning of a song by Dante, which is: 
> <note>original: "Donne ch'avete intelletto d'amore."</note> Ladies who have intelligence of love. 
Dante made this and many other songs in which, under the name of Beatrice, he allegorically praises Theology and the moral and theological virtues. **O BROTHER**: O brother. **ISSA**: "At present"; it is a Lucchese word meaning now, just now, at this moment.

<summary>Dante encounters several famous gluttons in Purgatory, including Pope Martin IV and the poet Bonagiunta da Lucca, the latter of whom prophecies Dante's future exile and praises his new poetic style.</summary>
<keywords>Bonagiunta da Lucca, Pope Martin IV, gluttony, Gentucca, Dolce Stil Novo, eels of Bolsena, Vernaccia wine, prophecy of exile, Piccarda Donati</keywords>

--- Page 437 ---
<meta>This page continues the conversation between Dante and the spirits on the terrace of the gluttonous. Dante is speaking with Bonagiunta da Lucca and Forese Donati about poetry and the political fate of Florence.</meta>

->### PURGATORIO<-

...declaring still the true things.
"But tell me, do I see here the one who brought
forth the new rhymes, beginning with:
**Ladies who have intelligence of love**?" <note>This is the first line of a famous poem from Dante's earlier work, *The New Life* (Vita Nuova), marking a turning point in his poetic style.</note>
And I to him: "I am one who, when
Love inspires me, takes note, and in that manner
which he dictates within, I go signifying."
"O brother, now I see," he said, "the knot
that held the Notary, and Guittone, and me,
short of the **sweet new style** <term>Dolce Stil Novo: a refined, soulful movement in Italian poetry</term> that I hear.
I see well how your pens
follow close behind the dictator,
which certainly did not happen with ours.
And he who sets himself to look further
sees no more between one style and the other";
and, as if satisfied, he was silent.
Like all the people who were there,
turning their faces, they quickened their pace,
made light by both thinness and will.
And as a man who is tired of trotting
lets his companions go on and walks
until the panting of his chest is eased,
So Forese let the holy flock pass by
and came along behind me,
saying: "When will it be that I see you again?"
"I know not," I replied to him, "how long I may live,
but my return will not be so soon
that my desire does not reach the shore before me;
Because the place where I was set to live <note>Dante refers to his home city of Florence, which was gripped by political violence.</note>
is being stripped of its good day by day,
and seems disposed to wretched ruin."
"Now go," he said, "for the one who is most to blame <note>Forese refers to his own brother, Corso Donati, the leader of the Black Guelph faction.</note>
I see dragged at the tail of a beast
toward the valley where one is never absolved.
The beast goes faster at every step,
increasing always until it strikes him,
and leaves the body vilely undone.
Those wheels have not much to turn—"
and he raised his eyes to heaven— "before it shall be clear to you
what my speech can no longer declare.
Now you remain behind, for time is dear
in this kingdom, so that I lose too much
coming with you thus, side by side."
As a knight sometimes comes out at a gallop
from a troop of riders,
and goes to win honor in the first encounter...

<column-break/>

...is certain: sages: according to various idioms they mean the same thing. **The knot**: the difficulty which held **the Notary**, i.e., **Jacopo da Lentini**, who for his excellence in that art was called "The Notary." **Guittone**: this is Brother **Guittone d’Arezzo**. **Sweet style**: smooth. **New**: never heard before. **I see well**: i.e., the style of you, Dante: they follow close behind the **dictator**: i.e., they prepare themselves for the mind of the dictator, which is to say nothing else than that Dante can, with his pen, perfectly express the affection of his mind. Or we might understand it as Virgil, whom he imitates much, although his language varies as he approaches him. **And this not**: because we cannot express our concepts with the pen as you do. **And he who further**: and whoever sets himself further to regard and consider your style and ours sees no more from one to the other; as if to say that Dante precedes them so much that the entire space between him and those who remain behind cannot be seen. And this is the opinion of **Cicero**, who says: that Crassus was first and Antonius was second, but second with a great interval. And thus **Virgil** in the fifth [book of the Aeneid]: <note>original: "Proximus huic, longo sed proximus intervallo."</note> *Closest to him, but closest by a long interval.*
**As the cranes**: Cranes are migratory birds and in summer they inhabit cold places, but in winter they retreat to warm places; and therefore there is a great abundance of them in Egypt along the Nile. We spoke sufficiently of cranes in the first canticle <note>Referencing Inferno Canto V.</note>. **Until it eases**: until the beating of the lungs and the excessive panting and gasping from a fast journey is eased. **Affollare** <term>to pant</term> properly means in our language to gasp and pant: this comes from the word *folle*, which in Latin signifies the **bellows**, because it arises from the great movement of the lungs which, like bellows, draw in the breath and send it out. **I know not the return**: here in Purgatory. **To the shore**: of the mountain of Purgatory. In short, he says that his return to Purgatory after death will not be so soon that his will does not go before him; and allegorically, every well-disposed mind desires to be purged. **Because the place**: this is **Florence**. **Is stripped**: i.e., deprived, a comparison to when the meat is removed from a chicken. **Now go, he said**: Forese here predicts the violent death of **Sir Corso Donati**, whom he says bears more blame for the ruin of Florence than any other citizen. Sir Corso had returned to Florence as leader of the **Black Party** with the favor of Charles of Valois (called "Lackland") and had taken the state from the **Whites** and remained a leader so powerful that he became suspect to the people, as it seemed to them that he exceeded what was appropriate in a free republic. Ultimately the suspicion grew when he became the son-in-law of Uguccione della Faggiuola, lord of Pisa. This caused a sudden popular tumult where he was summoned and condemned, and with the banner of justice the people ran to his house. From the beginning, because he was of great spirit and quick not only of tongue but of hand, he set himself with his friends to the defense; then, as the day grew late and being abandoned by many, he took flight. Following certain Catalan soldiers, whom he could not appease with prayers or promises, he fell from his horse, and caught in the stirrup, the horse dragged him until, overtaken, he was killed; and he was buried by the monks of San Salvi without any funeral rites, and his houses were destroyed by popular fury. **I see at the tail**: this serves the history; and allegorically it also means that he is dragged by the devil into many vices. **The beast goes faster at every step**: At the beginning, the devil does not have much strength in drawing the sinner into vice. But the more a man perseveres in sin, the worse he becomes; and if he is worse, the devil has more power over him. **And leaves the body**: Shows that the death of tyrannical and unjust men leaves the body vilely undone, because nothing remains of him but infamy. **Not much to turn**: not much time has to pass before to you—as if to say: I speak to you so obscurely that at present you do not understand of whom I speak, but in short the end of the matter will show it to you. **Because time is dear**: especially since we desire purgation.
**As with speed sometimes a man-at-arms**: galloping, goes ahead of the troop to be the first to make a clash of spears; so fast went Forese to catch up with his companions. **Marshals**: are the governors of courts and armies; thus by similarity...

<summary>This page contains Dante's famous definition of the 'Dolce Stil Novo' as poetry inspired directly by Love, and a dark prophecy by Forese Donati regarding the violent death of his brother Corso Donati and the decline of Florence.</summary>
<keywords>Dolce Stil Novo, Bonagiunta da Lucca, Forese Donati, Corso Donati, Florence, political prophecy, Jacopo da Lentini, Guittone d'Arezzo, poetics, Black Guelphs</keywords>

--- Page 438 ---
<meta>This page continues the narrative of Dante’s journey through the sixth terrace of Purgatory, where the sin of gluttony is purged. Dante has just finished speaking with Forese Donati, who has hurried away to rejoin the other spirits.</meta>

->## CANTO XXIV<-

Thus he departed from us with greater strides,
and I remained in life with those two
who were such great marshals of the world. <note>Dante refers to Virgil and Statius as "marshals," implying they are the highest-ranking guides and authorities of human wisdom and poetry.</note>
And when he had gone so far ahead of us
that my eyes became followers of him,
just as my mind followed his words,
There appeared to me the laden and living branches
of another fruit tree, and not very far away,
because only then had I turned the corner.
I saw people beneath it raising their hands
and crying out I know not what toward the leaves,
like eager and empty-headed little children,
Who beg, and the one they beg does not respond,
but to make their longing very sharp,
he holds their desire high and does not hide it.
Then they departed as if disillusioned;
and we came then to the great tree,
which rejects so many prayers and tears.
"Pass further on without drawing near;
the tree that was bitten by Eve is higher up,
and this plant was raised from it."
So said someone I did not see among the branches;
wherefore Virgil, Statius, and I, drawing close together,
went on past the side that rises up.
"Remember," the voice said, "the accursed ones <note>The Centaurs, born from Ixion and a cloud.</note>
formed in the clouds, who when full,
fought against Theseus with their double breasts; <note>The Centaurs were half-man, half-horse, hence "double-breasted." They disrupted the wedding of Pirithous due to drunkenness.</note>
And the Hebrews who showed themselves soft at the drinking,
for which reason Gideon would not have them as companions
when he descended the hills toward Midian."
Thus, staying close to one of the two edges,
we passed by, hearing of the faults of the throat,
followed once by miserable gains.
Then, spreading out along the lonely road,
a full thousand paces and more carried us onward,
each of us contemplating without a word.
"What are you three going along thinking?"
a voice suddenly said, at which I started
as frightened and sluggish beasts do.
I raised my head to see who it was;
and never were seen in a furnace
glass or metals so glowing and red
As one I saw, who said: "If it pleases you
to mount upward, here you must turn;
this way he goes who wishes to go for peace."

<column-break/>

**But the two poets are marshals:** because they held the first rank among poets. **The eyes following:** they follow his steps with their eyes just as I had previously followed his words with my mind. **The branches appeared to me:** he begins to see the second tree whose branches were heavy and full of fruit, and living, vigorous, and very green. **Raising their hands:** the hands signify actions. **He holds their desire high:** he shows them the thing they desire but does not let them take it.

**Then that aforementioned people departed.** **As if disillusioned:** like those who believed anew that they were not yet purified. **To the great tree:** nothing is greater than science (knowledge); which is, as we have said, signified by the tree that rejects as many prayers and tears as those souls offer it. And certainly, everyone desires knowledge; but it does not hear any except a very few. And these are the lovers of virtue. Whence he himself says in one of his songs, the beginning of which is: "Three women around my heart," he says, "Song, let no man lay a hand upon you to see what a beautiful woman hides. Let the naked parts suffice." **The sweet fruit:** it pleases all people, for which everyone reaches out their hand. **Pass further on:** because it is not yet time for you to touch these fruits. **The tree is higher up:** This is in the "Paradise of Delights" <note>Eden</note>; and it is the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. Therefore he feigns that these trees in this place were born from that one: because from that one was born the sin of gluttony, specifically by Eve tasting the fruit; and all others consequently. **Among the branches:** just as in the previous tree he did not see who spoke, so also in this one; because the truth cannot be known by one who is not purified. **From the side that rises:** from one part of the mountain which ascends, and by this, he signifies the virtues. **The accursed ones formed of clouds:** he means the Centaurs, about whom we have spoken fully elsewhere. He places them in this spot because of their drunkenness, remembering that at the wedding of Pirithous, overcome by wine, they tried to kidnap the bride. And certainly, through drunkenness, men become most monstrous and grow savage in every vice, especially in lust, and they steal the wives of others. For as Terence says: *Without Ceres and Liber, Venus freezes.* <note>original: "Sine cerere & libero friget venus." This means that without food (Ceres) and wine (Liber/Bacchus), passion (Venus) cools.</note>

But Theseus and Hercules—that is, reason and intellect—tame such bestiality in man. **And the Hebrews:** God permitted sins so that the people of Israel were for a long time harassed by the Midianites with hunger and war. But converting themselves with tears and prayers, the angel came to Gideon so that he might move against the enemies. Gideon gathered thirty thousand Hebrews, which number seemed small in comparison to the Midianites, who like a locust swarm covered the earth because of their innumerable multitude. Again, the angel commanded that he dismiss the fearful; for which reason twenty thousand departed. He came a third time and commanded that in the burning sun he lead the remaining ten thousand to the river. And all those who drank by putting their mouths to the water he should send away, and retain those who drank by drawing the water with the hollow of their hands; who were no more than three hundred. And with these, by the power of God, he conquered the enemies and they killed one hundred and twenty thousand. Whence the Jews lived afterward in tranquil peace for forty years, which is how long Gideon lived. **Edges:** extremities or borders; it is a metaphor taken from cloth. **From miserable gains:** illicit gains are the cause of the sins of the throat.

**Then only three:** you three alone: Virgil, Statius, and Dante. **I started:** not the other two, but I; because neither the intellect nor reason fears, but only sensuality. **Frightened and sluggish beasts:** The beast starts from sudden fear because it is afraid when it leaves the stable where it has been in idleness; for then it wakes up and shakes off all laziness; and for this, he said "sluggish" <note>original: "poltre." Landino notes that some read this as "poltrone" (lazy/coward) and others as "puledre" (young colts/fillies), which are naturally more skittish.</note>. And still, in this way, the text proceeds well: because colts are more fearful than tame beasts. **Glowing and red:** he attributes such qualities to the angel; because through the light, he demonstrates doctrine, and through the red color, charity. With which two things the truth is known, and being known, it is loved. **Here you must turn:** showing the stairs of the seventh terrace in which lust is purged.

<summary>Dante and his guides pass a second tree where the gluttonous are tempted and hear warnings against excess, referencing the Centaurs and Gideon's army. They then encounter the Angel of Abstinence, who directs them toward the final terrace of Purgatory.</summary>
<keywords>Canto XXIV, Purgatory, Gluttony, Gideon, Centaurs, Angel of Abstinence, Cristoforo Landino, Virgil, Statius, Dante Alighieri</keywords>

<meta>This page concludes Canto XXIV of the Purgatorio. Having left the gluttonous souls and the second symbolic tree behind, Dante, Virgil, and Statius encounter the Angel of Temperance, whose radiant light and fragrant breeze signal the transition to the next terrace of the mountain.</meta>

<header>PURGATORY</header>

His appearance had taken away my sight,
so that I turned back toward my teachers,
like a man who walks according to what he hears.
And as the herald of the dawns,
the breeze of May moves and smells sweet,
all impregnated by the grass and the flowers,
So I felt a wind strike me in the middle
of my forehead, and I clearly felt the feathers move,
which made me feel the scent of ambrosia.
And I heard it said: "Blessed are those whom
so much grace illuminates that the love of taste
does not smoke with too much desire in their breasts,
Hungering always as much as is right."

<column-break/>

Sensuality is dazzled by excessive splendor, and blinded in such a way that it cannot proceed forward on its own. For this reason, it turns back to the intellect and to reason, and walks according to what they say; therefore he says: "walks according to what he hears." **AND AS THE** herald of the dawns: He shows that as the Angel struck his wings, he stirred a gentle breeze full of the finest scent; and he felt such a scent and such an aura as is a sweet and small wind that arises in May before the dawn. This is a sign that the light of day will soon be seen. This little breeze, as it rises, "smells sweet" <note>original Italian: "oleza"</note>, meaning it gives off an excellent odor because it stirs the fresh grass and flowers. **THAT** makes the scent of ambrosia <note>In mythology, ambrosia is the food or drink of the gods, often associated with a divine fragrance.</note> felt: Drawn from the first book of Virgil, where he imagines that Venus, in departing from Aeneas, spread a great fragrance. Wherefore he says: "And the divine locks of her head breathed the scent of ambrosia." <note>original Latin: "Ambrosieque come diuinu uertice odorem Spirauere."</note> **AND** I heard it said "blessed": These words are from Matthew the Evangelist where he says: "Blessed are they who hunger and thirst after justice: for they shall have their fill." <note>original Latin: "Beati qui exuriunt & fitiunt iustitiam: quoniam ipsi saturabuntur." This is one of the Beatitudes from the Sermon on the Mount.</note> This voice, then, was saying: "blessed are those" **WHOM** grace **ILLUMINATES** so much: meaning they have so much light from the grace of God that the greed of taste and gluttony "does not smoke": does not evaporate and does not give too much superfluous desire and appetite of the throat. **HUNGERING** <note>original Latin/technical term: "exuriendo"</note>: meaning having...

<sig>k k</sig>

<meta>catchword: ...so much desire to eat as is right and as reason wills, and cannot [be exceeded].</meta>

->PURGATORIO<-
->Kk ii<-

### CANTO XXV OF THE SECOND CANTICLE OF DANTE.

It describes in the present canto: how he ascended into the seventh circle: where <term>luxury</term><note>In this context, "luxury" (Italian: *luxuria*) specifically refers to the sin of lust.</note> is purged in the fire. It describes the time. It shows Dante’s desire to have a doubt clarified. Virgil encourages him to ask: and having heard the doubt, he partly resolves it himself, and partly leaves it to be solved by Statius: who demonstrates the creation of the fetus in the maternal womb: and likewise the infusion of the soul. **It was the hour**: It describes the time and shows that midday had passed.

Now it was the hour when the climb would brook no delay,
for the sun had left the meridian circle
to Taurus, and the night to Scorpio;
Therefore, as a man does who does not stop,
but goes on his way whatever may appear to him,
if the goad of necessity pricks him;
So we entered through the narrow opening,
one before the other, taking the stairs
which by their narrowness unpair the climbers.
And like the little stork that lifts its wing
through the desire to fly, and yet does not venture
to abandon the nest, and drops it down;
So was I, with my desire kindled and quenched
of asking, coming even to the act
that he does who prepares himself to speak.
Nor did it stop, despite our rapid pace,
my sweet father, but he said: "Release
the bow of speech, which you have drawn to the arrow-head."
Then I confidently opened my mouth
and began: "How can one grow thin,
there where the need for nourishment does not touch?"
"If you remembered how Meleager
was consumed at the consuming of a brand,
this would not be," he said, "so bitter to you.
And if you thought how, at your every quiver,
your image quivers within the mirror,
that which seems hard would appear easy to you.
But so that your will may rest easy,
behold here is Statius; and him I call and pray
that he now be the healer of your wounds."

<column-break/>

Since the sun was in Aries and already declining with that sign toward the west, Taurus, which follows, had risen to the midday. Therefore it was necessary that, with Taurus at the meridian of that hemisphere of day, Scorpio would be at the meridian of our hemisphere of night, because these two signs are opposite. **Therefore**. Like a man who does not fix himself, that is, does not stop, but goes on his way. **Whatever may appear to him**, i.e., regardless of what appears to him. **So we entered through the narrow opening**, that is, through the entrance of the stairs. **One before the other**: we did not all three go together, but went one by one. And this is because the **narrowness**, i.e., the tightness of the stairs, unpairs the climber. The meaning is that the stairs were so restricted, i.e., narrow, that he who climbs cannot go side-by-side with another; and certainly, toward such high speculation, sensuality cannot go side-by-side with the intellect, but it is enough if it follows and goes after it. **And like the little stork**: a fitting comparison which expresses this: I had a great desire to ask Virgil about the doubt mentioned below, and I brought myself right up to the point of speaking. And then shame did not let me send out the word. I acted, therefore, like the little stork: which, having the desire to leave the nest, begins to flap its wings, but then for fear of falling does not dare to fly. **With desire kindled and quenched**: the desire to ask was kindled and inflamed, but shame quenched it.

Prudence and learning are such that a man almost divines; therefore Virgil, by certain gestures in Dante, perceived that he was in doubt. And remembering the thinness of the souls, he understood his doubt by conjecture. And to take away the shame that prevented him from speaking, he incited him to ask, saying to him: "Release the bow of speech which you have drawn even to the iron head"; and here is an excellent metaphor from arrows to words. **Then I confidently opened my mouth**: Reassured by Virgil, Dante spoke confidently and opened his doubt, which was: how it could happen that souls grow thin in Purgatory, since thinness is born from a lack of nourishment. Whence, when a man fasts and deprives himself of food, his body grows thin. But souls, which are incorporeal, have no need for food. And therefore he asks how one can become thin in Purgatory, where the **need to nourish** does not touch or happen: i.e., the necessity of feeding. **If you remembered how Meleager**: Meleager was the son of Oeneus, king of Calydon, and his mother Althaea; when he was born, she saw that the Fates placed a piece of wood on the fire. And they said that Meleager would live as long as that wood lasted. His mother took it from the fire so that it would not burn. Meleager grew, and having become a young man, it happened that a terrible boar wasted the entire region of Calydon. Wherefore many nobles of Greece were called to the hunt: Theseus, Pirithous, Castor and Pollux, Jason, Telamon, Nestor, Peleus the father of Achilles, Speusippus, and Toxeus and Plexippus, the brothers of his mother, and Atalanta, a most beautiful woman. She was the first who struck the ear of the boar with an arrow, but Meleager killed it

and, inflamed with love for the girl, he gave her the head of the beast, which is usually the prize for the one who kills it. This was offensive to his mother’s brothers. And they took it from the girl; this thing was so offensive to Meleager that he killed both of them. And Althaea, in vengeance for her brothers, replaced the brand on the fire; and at that same moment it burned, and Meleager was consumed. By this fable, it seems Virgil wishes to imply as a poet: that just as Dante can feign the thinness of souls—even though naturally they cannot grow thin—just as other poets feign this of Meleager; or truly we might say: that just as in truth Meleager was consumed by the repentance he had for the fault committed and by the pain he took for it, so these souls, through the pain of their repentance, suffer in themselves a similar effect, desiring with extreme continence to compensate for the excess of the palate that the body suffered by abstaining. **And if you thought how**: He places the second example of the mirror, in which we see our image make the same **quivers**, that is, movements made by the one whose image it is; the point of this is that the mirror is suited to represent every gesture made before it. Therefore our image and our actions are imprinted in the luminous air, and such air strikes the mirror with the same impression, and the mirror, catching them, shows them. So, therefore, he wishes it to happen in the **aerial bodies**<note>The "aerial body" is a medieval theological concept explaining how a soul can have a visible form and experience physical sensations like heat or hunger after death.</note> which our souls take up after death and clothe themselves in them. In which, because they are like mirrors, all the passions of the soul are represented. And this is what shows the souls as thin. But that the soul takes an aerial body is not based on human reason, but on certain theologians; and for this reason, he has Statius comment on this more extensively in the following lines. **But so that your will may rest easy**, i.e., your will be satisfied. **Behold here is Statius**: having to treat matters pertaining to Christian theology, not unworthily Virgil, not being opposed to it, lets them be explained by Statius, the Christian.

<summary>Dante, Virgil, and Statius ascend to the final terrace of Purgatory. Dante questions how spirits can appear physically wasted by hunger, and Virgil explains using the mythological example of Meleager and the scientific analogy of a mirror image before deferring to Statius for a theological lecture.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the conversation between Dante, Virgil, and Statius on the seventh terrace of Purgatory. Having asked how spirits—who do not require physical food—can appear emaciated (as seen with the gluttonous), Dante now receives a profound theological and physiological explanation from Statius regarding the generation of the human body and the infusion of the soul.</meta>

# CANTO XXV

**OF THE eternal vengeance**: that is, divine justice which avenges and corrects every crime. The text continues. **Statius replied**: "If I disclose," that is, manifest to Dante, "**the eternal vengeance**," meaning that which eternal justice ordains. "**There where you are**," in the place where you are—as if to say: "It seems like a presumption for me to dare speak where you, who are full of all learning, are present; yet if I do it, it does not arise from arrogance, but from obedience, because I cannot deny what you ask of me." Therefore he says: "**Exonerate me**," excuse me for not being able to "**offer a refusal**," that is, I cannot deny you anything, because a soul set on the path of charity cannot deny a just request. "**Will be a light to you**": they will give you understanding. "**Regarding the 'how' that you ask**": regarding your doubt, where you ask how

"If I disclose to you the eternal vengeance,"
Statius replied, "there where you are,
exonerate me for not being able to offer a refusal."
Then he began: "If your mind, my son,
looks upon and receives my words,
they will be a light to you regarding the 'how' that you ask.
Perfect blood, which is not drunk
by the thirsty veins and remains
like food that is removed from the table,
Takes from the heart for all human members
an informative virtue, like that blood
which goes through the veins to become those very members.
Digested yet again, it descends to where it is more beautiful
to be silent than to speak; and from there it later drips
upon another’s blood in a natural vessel.
There one and the other meet together,
the one ordained to be passive and the other active
because of the perfect place from which it flows;
And joined with it, it begins to operate,
coagulating first, and then it gives life
to that which it had brought forth for its material.
The active virtue having become a soul,
like that of a plant, but different in this:
that the plant’s is at its shore, while this is already on its way.
It works so much then that it moves and feels,
like a sea-fungus; and then it begins
to organize the powers of which it is the source.
Now, my son, the virtue that flows from the heart
of the generator expands, and now it contracts,
where nature intends for all the members."

<column-break/>

it is possible for the souls to grow thin. Then, to clarify the doubt and demonstrate how the soul is clothed in an aerial body after the death of the physical body, he repeats from the beginning the creation of the **vegetative**, **motive**, and **sensitive** soul, which nature produces from the potentiality of matter, and which is common to us and the brute animals. And then he shows that as soon as the sensitive soul is produced in the human body through the virtue of the male seed (the agent) and the matter of the female (the patient, which is the blood), God infuses the **rational soul**, which is proper to man and created by God from nothing. And this soul, thus infused, draws to itself the sensitive soul which it found in the body with all its powers, and unites it to itself in such a way that there are not two souls, but one. And this single soul, when it departs from the body, clothes itself anew in an aerial body.

**PERFECT BLOOD which then is not drunk by the thirsty veins**. All the food and drink we take is cooked and digested four times before it is perfect. **First**, in the stomach, where the part that is to be for the health of the animal is divided from the putrefied and harmful dregs, and is called <term>chyle</term><note>Italian: *chilo*; a milky fluid of partially digested food.</note>. These dregs fall into the belly and the bowels and are sent out. The chyle from the stomach goes through a vein called the "great gate" to the liver and is cooked there a **second** time; and the superfluous and false humor called urine is separated, distilling through the kidneys into the bladder and pushed out through its neck. The remaining chyle, being well-purified and cooked by the liver, takes on the color of the liver and becomes red. Then, in the **third** digestion which takes place either in the heart or in the liver with the virtue of the heart, it removes from itself the superfluous choler which the Latins call <term>bile</term><note>The foam of the blood.</note> and sends it to the gallbladder; and the melancholic humor, which is the dregs of the blood and which the Latins call <term>black bile</term><note>Latin: *atra bile*.</note>, it sends to the spleen. After the third digestion, the blood spreads through all the veins, and in those it is cooked for the **fourth** time. All the superfluous and harmful humor remaining in it is pushed out by nature through sweat, or converted into hair, fur, and nails. From this entirely purified blood, the veins take what is sufficient to nourish and maintain the body, and what remains flows to the veins called the <term>seminal vessels</term><note>Italian: *uasi feminarii*.</note>, because it is meant to be the seed to generate another human. This, through a process that cannot be decently named, descends to the two witnesses of generation. Just as the blood that is to nourish the child, having entered the sponge of the breast, changes color and is converted into milk, so this blood, by virtue of that member, becomes white and takes on the generative virtue. Being infused into the vessel of the woman, it finds blood there and forms a new creature. Let no one believe that this seed becomes the body of the child; rather, its subtle parts are all <term>spirits</term><note>In medieval physiology, "spirits" were subtle vapors that animated the body.</note>, which, nourished by the coarse parts like a master craftsman of the mother's blood, form the body and give it life and the sensitive soul, which the rational and immortal soul then unites to itself as I have said. I will not narrate at present why

---

it more often generates a male than a female, or why one or more are born, or why they resemble the father or the mother or others of the kinship, or why hermaphrodites are born—for these are various things certainly worthy of being understood. But I have collected all the effective arguments of **Galen**, **Avicenna**, **Aristotle**, **Albertus Magnus**, and many other physicians and philosophers at length; and if I do not deceive myself, I have narrated them very aptly in my second book *On the Soul* <note>original: "de anima"</note>, written as a dialogue in the Latin language. Now I return to the text.

**Which is not drunk**: because it is left over, just as we see food left over for one who has eaten sufficiently. **Takes from the heart**: According to many philosophers, every virtue of the animal has its origin in the heart, but then takes its perfection in various members. For example, the **nutritive virtue** takes hold in the liver; the **stative** in the brain; the **generative** where I clearly spoke above. **THERE one and the other meet together**: in the vessel of the female, which is the womb. **ONE AND THE OTHER**: the seed of the male, which is the agent and informative, and the blood of the female, which is the patient because it is the material from which the creature is made and it receives the form into itself. **BECAUSE OF THE PERFECT PLACE**: because it proceeds from the man, who is perfect and active. **THE active virtue having become a vegetative soul**: such as is in plants. But in plants this virtue is perfect because it does not wait for the sensitive; but in man it is imperfect because it must still receive the motive and sensitive virtues. And therefore he adds: **It works so much then that it moves and feels**. **Sea-fungus** is a coagulation of sea foam which becomes alive and moves and feels, but does not have formed members. So is the fetus in the maternal womb. But then such virtue begins to form different members, which the soul uses to excite its powers. It forms, for example, the ear to use the virtue of hearing, and the eye to use the visual power. **EXPANDS**: the virtue, which is united in itself, divides into different parts. **CONTRACTS**, making the members grow. **THE active virtue**: which came into the seed from the virtue of the heart of the generator.

<summary>Statius explains the medieval physiological process of human generation, describing how "perfect blood" is refined through four digestions to become the generative seed that forms the fetus. He details the transition from a vegetative soul to a sensitive one, setting the stage for the infusion of the rational soul by God.</summary>

### CANTO XXV

Because he has shown up to this point: how the human body is generated: and how it takes the vegetative and sensitive soul: <note>In medieval philosophy, the vegetative soul governs growth and nutrition, while the sensitive soul governs perception and movement. Both are shared with animals.</note> which two powers are common to him with other animals: and are from the power of matter: He follows in demonstrating how the creature is formed: and made alive and sensible: the supreme creator infuses the rational soul created by him from nothing: and at one and the same time created and infused.

<column-break/>

**BUT HOW FROM animal it becomes a speaker**: Up to this point the soul: which is in the fetus: has no more power: than the soul of brutes has. Afterward, it becomes a speaker <note>original: "fante," meaning one who speaks, derived from the Latin "fari." This distinguishes humans from "infants" or animals.</note>: that is, a speaker: which is the rational soul. Since speech is granted only to man: so that he may express the reason: that he has within himself. And this is the point: where **Averroes** erred. Who held: that in man there is no individual intellect in a form that one could say: this was the intellect of Plato: and that was of Cicero. But rather that there is one universal intellect: which infuses through all men: as the sun shines through the whole world: which, if it were true, it would be false: that God infused the rational soul into us: And after life, our soul would remain together with the body: <note>Averroes (Ibn Rushd) was a medieval philosopher whose theory of a "single intellect" shared by all humans was highly controversial and rejected by Christian theologians like Thomas Aquinas and Dante.</note> For which reason this opinion has been most sharply refuted by many most acute and learned philosophers. Whose arguments we have collected with all diligence in our third book on the soul. Therefore Averroes by his teaching divided reason and the intellect from our soul. Moved perhaps because he does not see in the human body an organ for the intellect: as he sees those which serve the vegetative and the sensitive functions. **OPEN TO THE TRUTH**. But you, Dante, open to the truth: that you shall hear from me. And he says: that as soon as the brain is articulated: that is, has developed its channels and is perfect: meaning that in it the place of common sense is perfect: the place of imagination, of fantasy, of thought: and of memory. Furthermore, all the things that belong to the external senses. Therefore when all the organs: which serve motion and sense: are perfect: then God infuses the rational soul: as was said: which Dante calls a **new spirit**: because it is not a spirit of that species which he finds in the body. But it is a new thing. And it has perfection of virtue having reason and intellect. This new spirit draws to itself and makes of its own nature what it finds active in the soul: which was there before: and there remains a single soul, vegetative: sensitive: and rational. And it is all in the whole body: and all in every part of it.

He demonstrates that afterward when it leaves its body it carries with it all its powers. **THE HUMAN**: that is, the powers that are of the power of matter: such as the vegetative and sensitive. And do not divide them: as reason is. But only reason remains awake in the soul: which is will: intelligence and memory. And the vegetative and the senses remain dormant until it arrives: where it is to be. And here the formative virtue forms an **aerial body** <note>This "shade" or "aerial body" allows the soul to feel and appear human after death without physical flesh.</note> for the soul: and the soul lives in that: as it previously lived in its own body. And in this aerial body it imprints all the internal and external senses. And by means of these organs it exercises the senses: and can fall into passions. Nor is it a marvel: that God links souls to these bodies. Seeing as necromancers with diabolical power link spirits to images. **TO ONE OF THE shores**: that is, either to the shore of the river **Acheron**: because it is damned to Hell. Or to the shore of the Tiber at Ostia: from where he feigns that the angel takes the souls that are to be purged: and carries them by sea to the mountain of Purgatory: from which, having been made white, they finally fly to heaven. In this way, therefore, souls can suffer punishments that are not only spiritual: but corporal. Nor were those philosophers ignoble: who hold: that the soul, being entirely incorporeal, joins with the thick body composed of four elements by means of an extremely thin body. So that it is almost common to the corporeal and incorporeal nature: and by such communion it is fit to be able to join two extremes: because in truth in natural things one does not go from one extreme to another without a medium. Just as, for example, from heat, cold is not made: unless it first becomes lukewarm. Nor from light, darkness without a certain twilight: which being neither one nor the other: nonetheless participates in both: as we see between the departure of the sun: and the obscurity of the night.

<summary>This page explains the divine infusion of the rational soul into the human fetus once the brain is formed, refuting Averroes' theory of a single collective intellect. It also describes how the soul creates an "aerial body" or shade after death to maintain its senses and undergo purification or punishment.</summary>

<meta>This page transitions from the discourse on the soul's formation to the physical reality of the Seventh Terrace of Purgatory. It maintains continuity from the previous discussion of how the "new spirit" becomes a single soul that "lives and feels," now showing those souls undergoing purification for the sin of lust.</meta>

### PURGATORIO

And already come to the final turning <note>original: "tortura" — here referring to the seventh and final circuit or "terrace" of the mountain</note>
it was reached by us, and we turned to the right hand,
and we were intent upon another care.
Here the bank flashes forth flames,
and the ledge breathes a blast upward
which reflects them and clears a path from them.
Wherefore we had to go by the open side
one by one; and I feared the fire
on this side, and on that I feared falling down.
My leader said: "Through this place
one must keep a tight rein on the eyes,
because one could easily err by a little."

"O God of supreme clemency" <note>original: "Summe deus clementie" — a traditional hymn for Saturday Matins, associated with prayers for purity and the extinguishing of lustful fires.</note> in the heart
of the great burning I then heard singing,
which made me no less eager to turn.
And I saw spirits walking through the flame;
wherefore I looked at them and at my steps,
sharing my sight between them from time to time.
After the end of that hymn, they
cried out loudly: "I know not a man," <note>original: "virum non cognosco" — These are the words of the Virgin Mary to the Archangel Gabriel, signifying her chastity.</note>
then they began the hymn again in low voices.
Finished this, they cried: "To the woods
Diana ran, and drove out Helice, <note>Helice is another name for Callisto, a nymph of Diana who was exiled after being seduced by Jupiter.</note>
who had felt the poison of Venus."

<column-break/>

TO THE LAST turning: to the final torment. Because this is the seventh and last circle of Purgatory, in which lust <note>term: "luxuria" — the capital sin of lust or excessive sexual desire.</note> is purged with fire: which penalty is very appropriate. Because earthly goods are those which, through idleness and delicate foods, inflame us to lust. And the wind, which breathes from the ledge—making a boundary between this circle and the sixth, where gluttony is punished—pushes back the flame and "sequesters" it, that is, divides a path away from it. This signifies that the wind pushes the flame far enough from the ledge that there remains space and a path for those who pass. Nor is it without high reason that the intellect warns the senses to restrain the eyes; because the eyes are the window through which love enters. Love is nothing other than the desire for beauty. Nor can beauty be judged by any other sense than the eye. Hence Propertius says: "If you know it not, the eyes are the leaders in love." <note>original: "Si nefcis oculi funt inamore duces"</note> And our Florentine elegiac and lyric poet <note>Likely referring to Dante himself in his "Vita Nuova" or similar works</note> marvelously declares this sentiment in this sonnet: "Eyes, weep and accompany the heart: which for your failure suffers death." And certainly this desire does not strike the heart before the eyes have judged the loved thing to be beautiful. Therefore we must always restrain our eyes, if we do not wish to fall into this perturbation, which overcomes every kind of madness. And often it leads the lover to voluntary death. It makes us blind in judgment and children in greed. And for this reason, the aforementioned Propertius said: "Whoever he was, who painted Love as a boy, do you not think he had marvelous hands? He first perceived that a lover lives without sense, and that great goods perish through light cares." <note>original: "Quicūque ille fuit: puerū qui pinxit amorē..."</note> It would be very tedious to report how harmful, how grave, how dangerous, how pestilential are the perturbations of love. And similarly how light, how mobile, how varied, how childish, how similar to madness they are; all of which have been not only expressed but painted by the elegiac and lyric poets, Greek and Latin. But our Petrarch, in the "Triumph of Love," gathers them all together in a heap, which cannot be read without supreme amazement. And Virgil, with worthy exclamation, embraced the whole in very brief words, where he said: "Accursed love, to what do you not drive mortal hearts?" <note>original: "Improchamor [Improbe amor] quid non mortalia pectora cogis?"</note> And I, in the elegies which I wrote in my youth under the title of "Xandra," moved more by impulse than by art, wishing to demonstrate the gravest pains and unbearable torments that oppress men in such perturbation, placed these verses: "Why, Jupiter, do you strike the savage hearts of giants with rapid lightning? There is a greater punishment to be prepared for the wicked. Whoever strives to climb the starry heaven and tries to move war against the gods above: let him be suddenly inflamed with the torches of harsh love, and let him hold his neck under the yoke of his mistress. Then he will know that this burden surpasses eternal labors, and he would rather endure the rocks of Pelion." <note>The commentator, Cristoforo Landino, cites his own Latin poetry to emphasize the overwhelming power of love.</note> But returning to the text, it follows:

HE HAD NO LESS EAGER: that is, no less care to turn and see the spirits who were in the flame than to watch his feet. And he feigns that these spirits, who are purged of the sin of lust, sang the hymn which the Holy Church sings, the beginning of which is "O God of supreme clemency." <note>original: "Summe deus clementie"</note> And in it, one prays to God to kindle our hearts with the Holy Spirit. This has an effect entirely contrary to the heat of concupiscence. The former brings us back to health, urging us to prefer the love of God and celestial things; and then it shows us in what order, grade by grade, we must love creatures. This latter, perverting all order, makes us prefer creatures to the Creator: the false good to the true and supreme good; corruptible and mortal things to the incorruptible and immortal. BECAUSE I LOOKED at them and at my steps, SHARING my sight from time to time: that is, I shared my sight at various times, looking now at them and now at my feet. Nor is it without cause that in this place he shows that he placed such diligence in looking at his feet. He looked at them: that is, he contemplated such concupiscence. And he looked at his feet: so that they would not slip into the flames; and he remained attentive so that his appetite, in this contemplation, would not fall into the burning of the flesh. And then, as he has observed in all the other circles, he introduces the souls proposing to themselves examples of supreme chastity. And first, that of her who truly is first among mortals in this and every other virtue. I KNOW NOT A MAN. <note>original: "VIRVM NON cognofco"</note> Luke writes in the Gospel that when the Angel announced to Mary and preached to her the future conception, she replied: "How can this be? That is, that I should become pregnant, seeing as I know not a man," that is, I have no intention of ever knowing one. Then he introduces Diana, who drove away from her the nymph already defiled by Jove. She was Helice <note>Callisto</note>, daughter of Lycaon, King of Arcadia, and one of the number of virgins consecrated to Diana. And until those times she lived chaste and pure. Then, violated by Jove, she conceived Arcas. Seeing this one day when she was naked to wash herself, Diana held her in supreme abomination and drove her from her choir; and she fled into the woods. The rest of the fable we have narrated elsewhere. Dante does not call her Callisto here, but Helice, because thus the poets name that celestial sign <note>The constellation Ursa Major, the Great Bear</note> into which she was transformed. He shows, then, the chastity of Diana, who not only never corrupted herself but fled like a supreme pestilence those who had been violated. The poets feigned that she herself is the Moon in heaven, Diana on earth, and Proserpina in hell. And they wish her to have a hundred powers; wherefore Virgil, in the fourth book of the Aeneid, said: "Triple Hecate, the three faces of the virgin Diana." <note>original: "Ter geminam hecaten: tria uirginis ora Diane"</note> And shortly after: "He thunders to the three hundred gods." The ancients posited two Dianas: of which the first was the daughter of the first Jove and Proserpina; the second of Jove and Latona, born of the same birth with Apollo, a huntress, and accompanied by a choir of nymphs. She converted Actaeon the Theban into a stag and had him torn apart by his own dogs because he saw her bathing naked in a cool fountain. All crossroads <note>term: "trivii" or ways — Diana was often worshipped as Diana Trivia</note> are consecrated to Diana to signify virginity, which produces no fruit, just as crossroads are likewise unfruitful.

The commentary explains the symbolic role of the eyes in inciting love and provides a dense literary analysis of the dangers of unbridled passion.</summary>

# PURGATORIO

Then they returned again to singing of women,
then they cried out of husbands who were chaste,
as virtue and marriage command.
And this manner, I believe, suffices them
for all the time that the fire burns them;
with such care it is necessary and with such food
that the wound at the last be sewn up.

<column-break/>

Just as the spirits of the women mentioned above sang: "I know not a man," <note>original: "Virum non cognosco" — the words of the Virgin Mary at the Annunciation</note> praising virginity, so now they praise the chastity of both themselves and others' husbands who, following the commandments of marriage and the precepts of virtue, observe chastity. And certainly there is no other way by which we more quickly flee lust than the way of chastity. **AND** this manner, I believe, suffices them: it lasts for them. **WITH** such care: with such a condition. **FOOD**: <note>original: "pasti"</note> the nourishment and sustenance of virtue. Because purgation is the food that nourishes virtue and extinguishes vice, just as pleasure, on the contrary, extinguishes virtue and nourishes the vice which kills the soul. **WOUND at the last**: <note>original: "piaga da sezo"</note> the wound that lust has made in the soul. It is called "at the last" because it is the final one: seeing as at the end of life one exits the body with it, nor can one commit another vice afterward. <note>The commentator identifies lust as the final sin to be purged before reaching the Earthly Paradise.</note> **SEWN UP**: Repaired. For just as the body remains gashed by a blow given to it, so the soul receives a wound when vice strikes it. And not only in this, but in many other matters, he attributes to the soul through metaphor that which belongs to the body. As Virgil says:
> But the queen, long since wounded by deep care, feeds the wound in her veins and is consumed by hidden fire. <note>original: "At regina graui iam dudum faucia cura. Vulnus alit uenis & ceco rapitur igni." — Aeneid, IV, 1-2, describing Dido’s tragic passion for Aeneas.</note>

Where he presents the soul of Dido as being wounded and burning; these things belong to the body and not the soul, but are taken by way of similarity. And certainly lust is the last in the order of the capital sins, but it becomes very abominable because it removes the man who submerges himself in it from all manly generosity <note>meaning nobility of spirit or human dignity</note> and makes him similar to the beasts. Nevertheless, because its types are various, there is no doubt that while some seem worthy of some slight excuse, others are so far from all reason and so contrary to nature that he who practices them not only strips himself of human nature, but even of the nature of the beasts—who do not fall into such error—but he becomes a more horrendous monster than a centaur or a chimera. He creates a riddle <note>enigma</note> which the Theban Sphinx <note>original: "spinge" — the mythological creature that famously posed riddles to travelers</note> could hardly solve. Let everyone therefore flee these; but let this [unnatural vice] be completely forgotten, so that if indeed through fragility, bad habit, or some inclination it overcomes and induces us toward things not permitted, we may say with some compassion for whoever hears this:
> God saw our frailty and had mercy on us. <note>original: "Vidit deus figmentum nostrum & misertus est nostri." — A liturgical adaptation of Psalm 103:14: "For he knows our frame; he remembers that we are dust."</note>

<summary>This page concludes the 25th Canto of Purgatorio, explaining how the souls in the final circle of Purgatory cleanse the "wound" of lust through fire and the singing of hymns that celebrate chastity within and outside of marriage.</summary>
<keywords>Dante Alighieri, Purgatorio, Virgil, Dido, chastity, lust, marriage, capital sins, Sphinx, virtue</keywords>

<header>CANTO</header>
<page-num>XXVI</page-num>

**Previous page text for continuity:**
or remains torn to receive a wound when vice strikes it. And not only in this, but in many other things, by transition, it calls to the soul that which belongs to the body. Hence Virgil: "But the queen, long since wounded by grievous care, nourishes the wound alive," places Dido's soul as being wounded and burning: which things are of the body and not of the soul. And certainly lust is the last in the order of capital sins, but it becomes very abominable in that one submerges oneself from all virile generosity, and makes one similar to brutes. Nevertheless, because there is no doubt that just as some (sins) seem worthy of some slight excuse, so there is some (sin) so contrary to nature that whoever practices it not only strips themselves of human nature—(even) brutes, who do not fall into such an error—but becomes a more horrendous monster than a centaur or what the Theban sphinx would barely solve. Let all therefore flee. But this is entirely forgotten, or bad habit or some inclination overcomes us and leads us to a forbidden act, of whom it is said: "God saw our making and had mercy on us."

# PURGATORY / CANTO XXVI: OF THE SECOND CANTICLE BY DANTE
## PAGE 220

->In this 26th canto, he demonstrates his manner of proceeding, and the souls who, while walking through the flames and encountering one another, kissed each other on the mouth; and they spoke words in abomination of lust. And here he speaks with Master Guido <note>Guido Guinizzelli, a famous Italian poet whom Dante regarded as a literary father figure</note>, who shows him many others and explains the reason for the words they say.<-

**Along the edge.** By the extremity of the terrace, so that they would not be harmed by the flame. **One before the other:** because reason must precede and appetite must follow afterward. And reason always admonishes appetite, saying: **Look.** That is, go with regard and circumspection. **Come on:** as if to say, go quickly. He gives, therefore, two precepts: that in walking one should be cautious and one should be fast. **I guide you.** <note>original: "Io ti scaltro"</note> I see you and show you the way and make you practiced. Hence we call a man "clever" <note>original: "scalterito"</note> when he is practiced and experienced. **On the right shoulder:** they had turned to the right hand. And the sun, which was toward the setting, cast shadows toward the mountain; therefore it struck the right hand **radiating:** striking with rays. **Changed to white the aspect of the blue:** it caused the western part of the sky—which by its nature is blue—to become white due to the abundance of solar rays. And certainly, that part of the sky where the solar body is always changes from blue to white. **Made the flame appear more glowing with the shadow.** The flame exposed to the sun loses much of its glowing color—which the Latins call *candente* <note>original: "candente," meaning glowing white-hot</note>— and turns white, and is almost invisible. But if it is covered by some shadow in such a way that the sun does not touch it, it becomes more vivid. That shadow of Dante’s, therefore, was the reason the fire appeared more glowing. Whence the souls perceived that such a shadow came from a solid body like a human one, and not from the souls who have an aerial and fictitious body, as we showed a little above.

While along the edge, one before the other,
We went along, and often the good master
Said: "Watch out; let it profit that I guide you."
The sun was striking me on my right shoulder,
For now, its rays were changing all the west
From its celestial aspect into white;
And I, with my own shadow, made the flame
Appear more glowing; and even at such a sign
I saw many shades, as they went, take notice.
This was the cause that gave them the beginning
To speak of me; and they began to say:
"That one does not seem like a fictitious body."

Then toward me, as far as they were able 
To come, certain ones made sure, always with care
Not to step out from where they would be burned:
"O you who go—not because you are slower,
But perhaps being respectful to the others—
Answer me, who in thirst and in fire burn.
Nor is your answer needed by me alone,
For all of these have a much greater thirst for it
Than for cold water an Indian or Ethiopian.
Tell us how it is that you make of yourself a wall
Against the sun, as if you had not yet
Entered within the net of death."

One of them spoke to me thus; and I would have
Already revealed myself, if I had not been intent
On another novelty that appeared then;
For through the middle of the burning road
Came people with their faces opposite to these,
Which made me pause in suspense to watch.
There I see on every side making haste
Each shade, and kissing one with another
Without stopping, content with a brief greeting.
Thus, within their dark troop,
One ant nuzzles <note>original: "sammusa," touching muzzles/noses</note> another,
Perhaps to spy out their way and their fortune.
As soon as they end the friendly greeting,
Before the first step carries them past,
Each one strives to shout out:
"The new people: Sodom and Gomorrah!"
And the other: "Pasiphae enters the cow,
So that the bull might run to her lust."

<column-break/>

**As far as they were able to come:** because they could not leave the flame, but they came up to the very edge of it. And therefore he says **with care not to step out** of the place so that they would not be burned. And one of them said: "O you who go after the others," not because you are more tardy and slow than they, but perhaps because you are more **respectful**—that is, to show them reverence you walk behind. And this demonstrates that appetite more often than not precedes reason, except in well-bred men whose appetite is swift; nonetheless, out of reverence for reason, they follow it and do not precede it. **Answer me, who burn in thirst and in fire.** No one can be in great fire without being in great thirst; as if to say: if to me, who am in such burning, speaking is not a burden, it should not be a burden to you who are out of pain. **Nor only to me:** he shows that such a response will be pleasing not only to himself, but to many. **Than for cold water an Indian or Ethiopian:** which peoples, because they are very close to the torrid zone, endure unbearable heat. **Tell me how it is:** tell me how it happens that you make yourself appear like a **wall** to the sun, as if you were not yet dead and stripped of the body, but still possessed a human body.

Dante would have responded to the soul who asked him where he was from, but something new appeared that turned his mind toward it. This was another troop of souls coming toward this one; they met, and facing one another, each of those kissed one of these. Nor did they stop for this, but continued their journey, content with a very brief greeting. And in passing one another, those who were arriving shouted **Sodom and Gomorrah**, and those who were with Dante shouted **Pasiphae entered the cow**. We showed above, in the fifteenth canto of the *Inferno*, that Sodom and Gomorrah were plunged deep for the detestable sin against nature <note>A reference to the biblical cities destroyed for their sins; here used to denote homosexual acts, which Dante categorized as "sin against nature."</note>. The souls shouted this, therefore, in reproach of their committed sin; and by such shouting they condemned their past life and moved into greater contrition. And similarly, those who had practiced lust in a bestial form shouted to their own confusion that **Pasiphae** used the wooden heifer <note>In Greek myth, Queen Pasiphae of Crete conceived the Minotaur after lusting for a bull and hiding inside a wooden cow constructed by Daedalus.</note>, which fable we narrated above in the twelfth canto of the *Inferno*. The **kissing on the mouth** came from charity and modest affection; and they did this as penance for immodest and lustful kisses. **Thus within their dark troop:** he makes a comparison to **ants**, which, while carrying grain to their burrows, nuzzle one another when they meet. We have spoken of ants in another place. **Perhaps to spy:** he rightly says "perhaps," because it is difficult to know the intent of that animal since it does not express it with words.

<summary>Dante observes two groups of souls in the terrace of Lust who greet each other with a brief kiss of charity before shouting examples of their sins—specifically sodomy and bestial lust—to fuel their repentance. The souls are amazed by Dante's solid body, which casts a shadow and makes the purifying flames appear redder.</summary>
<keywords>Guido Guinizzelli, Purgatory, Lust, Reason vs. Appetite, Sodom and Gomorrah, Pasiphae, Shadow, Purification, Ants Metaphor</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante’s Purgatorio, Canto XXVI. The previous page established Dante's journey along the narrow edge of the terrace of Lust. This page focuses on the meeting of two groups of souls—the "Sodomites" and the "Hermaphrodites" (the heterosexual lustful)—and Dante’s explanation of his physical presence in the afterlife.</meta>

# CANTO XXVI

Just as cranes to the Riphean mountains fly, <note>The Riphean mountains were a legendary range in the far north of the world.</note>
Part toward the frost and part toward the sands,
The latter fleeing ice, the former the sun;
One group goes away, the other comes on,
And they return weeping to their first songs,
And to the cry that best befits them;
And they drew near to me, just as before,
The very ones who had entreated me,
Attentive to listen in their countenances.
I, who had twice seen their desire,
Began: "O souls certain
Of having, whenever it may be, a state of peace,
My limbs have not remained behind, neither green nor ripe,
But they are here with me,
With their blood and with their joints.
I go up from here so as not to be blind anymore;
There is a Lady above who won this grace, <note>Referring to Beatrice.</note>
By which I carry my mortal self through your world.
But—so may your greatest longing soon be sated,
So that the heaven may harbor you
Which is full of love and spreads most wide—
Tell me, so that I may mark it on paper,
Who are you, and what is that crowd
That goes away behind your backs?"
Not otherwise is the mountain-dweller confused,
Stupefied and staring in silence,
When, rough and rustic, he enters the city, <note>original: "si inurba"</note>
Than every soul seemed in its appearance;
But after they were unburdened of their wonder,
Which in noble hearts is quickly stilled,
"Blessed are you, who from our borders,"
Began the one who had first questioned me,
"Embark on experience for a better death.
The people who do not come with us committed the offense
For which Caesar, in his triumph,
Heard himself called 'Queen' in mockery. <note>An allusion to the rumor of Julius Caesar's youthful affair with King Nicomedes of Bithynia.</note>
Therefore they depart crying 'Sodom!'
Reproaching themselves, as you have heard,
And they aid the burning through their shame.
Our sin was hermaphrodite; <note>In this context, it refers to natural but disordered heterosexual lust.</note>
But because we did not observe human law,
Following our appetite like beasts,
To our own disgrace it is read by us,
When we depart, the name of her
Who made herself a beast in the beast-shaped wood." <note>Referring to Pasiphae, who disguised herself as a cow to satisfy her lust.</note>

<column-break/>

After the greetings were made, one part went down and the other went up, just as cranes would do when they fly toward the north where the Riphean mountains are, while the opposite line was toward the midday where the sandy Libya lies. Those that would fly toward the south would flee the cold, and the others flying toward the north would flee the heat. **Twice:** once before the new people came, and the second time at present. **Their desire:** <note>original: "Loro grato"</note> that which was pleasing to them. **My limbs have not remained, neither green:** like one who dies young a "green" or bitter death; **nor ripe:** like one who dies old and in a mature age. In short, he says he is not yet dead, but has come with soul and body. **I go up from here so as not to be blind anymore:** understand this as the eyes of the mind. I go, therefore, to remove the darkness of ignorance and illuminate myself with the light of truth. **The Lady above:** understand this as Beatrice, of whom we have already spoken so many times, who acquired such grace that he can bring his mortal self, that is, his body. **But if your greatest longing:** which was to ascend to heaven, which was greater than the longing they had to speak to Dante. **The heaven which is full of love:** because God is there, and this is the Empyrean heaven. Hence he says **spreads most wide,** meaning it is the largest, because it embraces the other nine spheres below it, as we shall say more clearly in the proper place. **Tell me who you are so that I may mark it on paper:** <note>original: "ne verdi carte"</note> that is, so that I may write it down. For he who writes marks the paper with the black strokes of letters. **And what is that crowd:** the multitude that goes behind **your backs.** <note>original: "terghi"</note> For in Latin *tergum* signifies the back.

Just as the **mountain-dweller** and rustic man who never saw a city is greatly marveled when, entering any city, he sees things never seen before. **Enters the city:** <note>original: "SI INvrba"</note> goes into the city. For the Latins call the city *urbem*. Hence the poet has used the word *inurbare*, that is, to enter the *urbe*, which is the city. **Unburdened of wonder:** relieved of that marvel which had taken them upon seeing me alive. **In noble hearts is quickly stilled:** because one of great intellect and great spirit quickly sets aside any stupor or marvel that assaults him. **Blessed are you, Dante:** who, to **die better** (that is, through the greater grace of God), **embark on experience** of our borders and our lands. **The people who do not come:** he shows that the souls who do not go with these, but coming from the opposite direction pass by, are purging the vice of **sodomy**; which, because it is against nature, he depicts them as coming against these others who were not according to nature [in their excesses], but did not observe the proper manner. And so you may understand they were sodomites, he says the souls were **offended by this,** that is, by that sin. **Because:** for which **Caesar**, while triumphing, heard himself called **Queen**. It was the greatest license among the soldiers, when their lord triumphed, to be able to reproach him for every vice. And Caesar, because in his youth serving under Thermus the Quaestor in Asia he was sent by him to Nicomedes of Bithynia, it was rumored that he had used Caesar as a wife. Therefore, when he triumphed over Gaul, the soldiers who were around the triumphal chariot cried out: "Caesar has subdued Gaul, and Nicomedes subdued Caesar." Therefore they depart from us crying **Sodom**, and for this they reproach themselves for such a vice so that they may be more ashamed; and through such shame they merit more and more, and thus they **aid the burning**. For the fire that causes the blaze is extinguished by this penance. **Our sin was hermaphrodite.** I believe that in this place he means by "hermaphrodites" those who, in intercourse, although they do not sin against nature, exercise it in such dishonest ways that one and the other behaves now as male and now as female, in such a way that they can be called hermaphrodites. But so that this may be better understood, we will first narrate the fable; then we will add the natural reason. From Mercury and Venus was born a son who was called **Hermaphroditus**, from the names of his father and mother; for *Hermes* in Greek signifies Mercury and *Aphrodite* signifies Venus. This youth, having reached the years of puberty and arriving in Caria at a fountain, found there the nymph Salmacis. She, seized by love for him, ran to him as he was already bathing in the fountain; and the youth wishing to flee her, she embraced him, praying to the gods that they should make it so he could never be separated from her. Her prayers were heard, and they were transformed so that from two they became one; but this one retained both sexes, and thus remained male and female. And let this suffice for the fable. **Physicians** <note>original: "Ephifici"</note> maintain that in the womb of a woman there are thirteen cells: <note>Medieval medical theories often debated the number of "cells" or chambers in the uterus.</note> six on the right conceive males, and six on the left females. That of the middle, they say, conceives a fetus with one and the other sex. Others say that the hermaphrodite is born when, in the conception, the se—

Dante explains his living presence to the souls, while the commentary provides historical and mythological context for Caesar and Hermaphroditus.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante’s Purgatorio, Canto XXVI.
