This page continues the explanation of "hermaphroditic" or heterosexual lust and introduces the poet Guido Guinizzelli.</meta>

...of the man and the blood of the woman are of equal force, whereby in the same fetus each produces its own sex. Because of this, when this creature later reaches full maturity, it can use both. Such people are called *Androgynes* by the Greeks—that is, male-females—because in their language they call the male *andra* <note>original: "andra," from the Greek anēr/andros</note> and the female *gynen* <note>original: "gynen," from the Greek gynē</note>. It is cautioned in law <note>original: "iure"</note> that each must choose which of the two sexes they wish to use, and exercise that one alone. Pliny writes that in Africa there are people called Maclyae who are always born as hermaphrodites and use now one, now the other sex in turn. And Aristotle adds that these people have the right breast of a male and the left of a female. **BUT BECAUSE WE DO NOT** observe human law—which always requires that the male act as a male, as the natural law of man invites, and the female always submit as a female—**FOLLOWING LIKE BEASTS THEIR** appetite. This is what a man must not do. Rather, it is his duty always to follow reason.

---

"Now you know our acts and of what we were guilty;
If perhaps you wish to know by name who we are,
There is no time to tell, nor would I know how.
I will indeed satisfy your desire concerning me:
I am Guido Guinizzelli, and already I purge myself, <note>Guido Guinizzelli (c. 1230–1276) was an influential Italian poet and the founder of the *Dolce Stil Novo* (Sweet New Style).</note>
Because I truly grieved before the final end."
As in the sorrow of Lycurgus
Two sons became on seeing their mother again,
Such I became, but I do not rise so high,
When I hear him name himself the father
Of me and of my others, my betters, who ever
Used the high and graceful rhymes of love;
And without hearing or speaking, I went on pensive,
A long time gazing at him,
Nor because of the fire did I draw any closer.

When I was fed with looking,
I offered myself entirely ready for his service,
With the affirmation that makes another believe;
And he to me: "You leave such a trace,
From what I hear, and it is so clear in me,
That Lethe cannot take it away nor make it dim. <note>Lethe is the mythological river of forgetfulness.</note>
But if your words just now swore the truth,
Tell me: what is the reason that you show,
In your speech and in your look, that you hold me dear?"
And I to him: "Your sweet sayings,
Which, as long as modern usage lasts,
Will still make their very ink precious."
"O brother," he said, "this one I distinguish for you
With my finger"—and he pointed to a spirit ahead—
"Was a better smith of the mother tongue. <note>original: "miglior fabbro del parlar materno"</note>
Verses of love and prose of romance
He surpassed them all; and let the fools talk
Who believe that he of Limoges is superior. <note>Referring to the troubadour Giraut de Bornelh.</note>
To rumor rather than to truth they turn their faces,
And thus they fix their opinion
Before art or reason is heard by them."

<column-break/>

**OUR ACTS:** which were lustful. **AND OF WHAT:** sin. **WE WERE GUILTY:** we are accused. "Guilty" <note>original: "Reo"</note> refers to the accused, just as "actor" is the one who accuses others. **TIME** is not sufficient because it is late; and "I would not know how" because they are many and unknown to me. **I WILL INDEED SATISFY YOUR DESIRE:** I will make your wish to know me diminish or be fulfilled, because I will tell you. **I AM GUIDO GUINIZZELLI.** This man was our citizen <note>of Bologna</note> and a knight, and in his time he surpassed all others in Tuscan rhymes. **AND ALREADY** I purge myself: as if to say, even though it has been a short time since I died, I am nevertheless already in Purgatory, and I did not have to wait in Ante-Purgatory; this is because I was not negligent in converting. But "I truly grieved"—that is, with good contrition—"before the final end," meaning I did not wait until the very last moment to grieve, but did so before then. **AS IN THE SORROW OF LYCURGUS. Two sons became.** In the *Inferno* we told the fable of Hypsipyle and Jason; now we add that after it was known in Lemnos that she had spared her father's life and sent him to the island of Chios, she fled the women's fury and sent her sons to Thoas, her father. But she, captured by pirates, was sold to Lycurgus, King of Nemea, and by him was entrusted with the care of his small infant son called Archemorus (and before his death, Opheltes). At that time, Adrastus and the other seven kings were passing by with their army, and being plagued by great thirst, Hypsipyle showed them the fountain called Langia; in the meantime, Opheltes, left by her asleep in a meadow, was killed by a serpent. Lycurgus ran to the scene and wanted to kill Hypsipyle. But her two sons, who had recently come to Lycurgus seeking their mother, heard her lamenting her misfortunes and naming Lemnos and Thoas; they recognized her, embraced her, and saved her. **SUCH I BECAME:** I was filled with such great joy. **BUT I DO NOT RISE SO HIGH:** I do not exalt myself or reach out as far as the sons of Hypsipyle did. For they ran to embrace their mother, but I did not go to embrace Guido because he was in the fire. And this joy took hold of me when **I HEARD HIM NAME HIMSELF THE FATHER:** that is, when I heard Guido name himself; because he was the teacher of Dante and many others in writing in rhyme, Dante calls him his father, and the father of others like him. **WHO:** those who. Never at any time did they use rhymes more graceful, sweet, and loving. **I WENT ON PENSIVE.** He wishes to show that he was reflecting on how such a learned man had fallen into such a vice, and he felt compassion for human frailty.

**THEN I MOVED** toward Guido. **WITH THE AFFIRMATION:** that makes one believe through an oath. And he answered me: "O Dante, you leave such a trace and signs of benevolence in me—that is, toward me—**FROM WHAT** I hear from you at present, that the Lethe—the river that induces oblivion—cannot take it away; it cannot make me forget it. **NOR MAKE IT DIM:** nor make it obscure. We shall speak of Lethe in its proper place. **TELL ME THE REASON:** tell me what is the reason that you show in your speaking and looking at me **THAT YOU HOLD ME DEAR:** that you love me. **AND I, DANTE,** answered him. **YOUR SWEET SAYINGS:** your sweet style in rhyme is the reason why I love you. **WHICH:** these sayings. **WILL MAKE PRECIOUS:** pleasing. **AND THEIR INKS:** and the books written in such a style. **AS LONG AS MODERN USAGE LASTS:** as long as the language we currently use and the style of these rhymes shall endure.

**I DISTINGUISH:** I point out. **SMITH:** composer. This was Arnaut Daniel of Provence, much praised and approved in the rhymes of that language. In his old age, oppressed by poverty, he wrote a moral work by which he received much money from the Kings of France and England. Petrarch asserts that he imitated him in many places. **HE OF LIMOGES:** he does not give the name, but names him by his homeland, which is in France. **THUS WERE MANY ANCIENTS REGARDING GUITTONE.** This was Brother Guittone d'Arezzo, of whom we have already made mention.

<summary>Dante meets the soul of the poet Guido Guinizzelli on the terrace of Lust, expressing deep reverence for him as a poetic father-figure. Guido humbly deflects the praise, pointing instead to Arnaut Daniel as a superior craftsman of the vernacular.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante’s Purgatorio, Canto XXVI. Following the discussion of the poet Guido Guinizzelli, the text now transitions to the figure of Arnaut Daniel, a Provençal troubadour whom Dante considers the "better craftsman" of the mother tongue.</meta>

# PURGATORIO;

So did many ancients with Guittone,
from cry to cry giving him alone the prize,
until the truth conquered him with many others.
Now if you have such an ample privilege
that it is permitted for you to go to the cloister
in which Christ is the abbot of the college,
Recite for me a "Pater Noster" <note>Our Father / The Lord's Prayer</note>
as much as is needed for us in this world
where the power to sin is no longer ours.
Then, perhaps to give place to another following
who was near him, he disappeared through the fire
as a fish goes through the water to the bottom.
I moved forward a little toward the one shown to me,
and said that for his name my desire
was preparing a gracious place.
He began to say quite freely:
"Your courteous request so pleases me <note>The following lines are originally in Old Occitan (Provençal), the language of the troubadours.</note>
that I cannot, nor do I wish to hide myself from you.
I am Arnaut, who weeps and goes singing;
I see with grief my past folly,
and I see with joy the day I hope for before me.
Now I pray you, by that power
which guides you to the summit of the stairs,
be mindful in time of my suffering."
Then he hid himself in the fire that refines them.

<column-break/>

**SO AMPLE** Privilege: and certainly it is a great privilege to be able before death to go to the cloister, meaning that of heaven. **IN WHICH** Christ is the abbot of the college. An excellent metaphor: because Christ always holds the priestly dignity. **RECITE FOR ME** a Pater Noster. Ensure that Christ hears a Pater Noster for me, <term>that is</term> <note>original: "idest"</note> for my salvation. And do not repeat it beyond what is necessary for us in purgatory, for whom, because we can no longer sin, it is not necessary to say <term>and lead us not into temptation</term> <note>original Latin: "ne nos inducas in tentationem"</note>. The other verses close the chapter. Nor is any further exposition required. The poet wrote these verses partly in the French language and partly in Catalan <note>The commentator identifies the language as French and Catalan, though it is actually Old Occitan (Provençal). Dante wrote these lines in that language to honor Arnaut's heritage.</note> because Arnaut was learned in both languages. But they are interpreted in this way: "Your courteous request so pleases me that I cannot nor will I hide from you. I am Arnaut who weeps and goes singing in this red ford <note>The commentator interprets the fire as a "rosso guado" (red ford).</note> my past folly. And I see before me the day that I hope for. Now I pray you by that power that guides you to the summit of this heat, that you remember in time my pain."

<summary>Dante encounters the shade of the Provençal poet Arnaut Daniel, who asks for prayers and describes his penance in Old Occitan. The commentator explains the metaphor of Christ as an abbot and notes that the souls in Purgatory omit the portion of the Lord's Prayer regarding temptation.</summary>
<keywords>Arnaut Daniel, Purgatory, Lord's Prayer, Provençal poetry, Guittone d'Arezzo, Christ as Abbot, divine privilege, penance of fire</keywords>

**PVRGATORIO**

**SI.AMPLO Priuilegio:** and certainly it is a great privilege to be able before death to go to the cloister, meaning heaven.

**NEL QVALE E.** Christ, abbot of the college. An excellent similitude, because Christ always has sacerdotal dignity.

**FAGLI per me un dir dun pater noftro.** Make Christ hear an Our Father for me, that is, for my salvation. And I will not reiterate beyond what is necessary for us in purgatory, for whom, because they can no longer sin, it is not necessary to say "and lead us not into temptation."

The other verses close the chapter. Nor do they require any exposition.

The poet wrote these verses partly in French: and partly in Catalan, because Arnaut was learned in both languages. But interpreting them in this way: "So much does your courteous question please me that I cannot nor wish to hide from you: I am Arnaut, who weeps and goes singing in this red ford the past folly. And I see before me the day I hope for. Now I beg you by that valor that guides you to the summit of this heat, that you remember in time my sorrow."

->CANTO XXVII<-

# CANTO XXVII OF THE SECOND CANTICLE BY DANTE

In this twenty-seventh canto, the author passes through the flame of fire and arrives at the Paradise of Delights. This canticle is divided such that the first eight chapters contain the Ante-Purgatory where the negligent stay. Afterwards, up until this twenty-seventh canto, he has described the seven circles of Purgatory and the penalties for the seven mortal sins. Now, in the text of the canticle, he proposes to describe the Post-Purgatory in which he places the Paradise of Delights. As follows:

<column-break/>

<margin>i</margin>
Just as when he vibrates the first rays
there where his Maker shed his blood,
while Ebro falls under the high Scales,
and the waves in the Ganges are scorched by noon,
so the sun was standing; thus the day was passing,
when the Angel of God appeared to us joyful.
Outside the flame he stood upon the bank
and sang, "Blessed are the pure in heart,"
<note>original: "Beati mundo corde"</note>
in a voice much more alive than ours.
Then: "No one goes further, holy souls,
unless the fire first bites; enter into it,
and to the singing beyond be not deaf,"
he said to us when we were near him;
whereat I became such, when I heard him,
as is he who is placed within the grave.
Over my clasped hands I stretched forward,
watching the fire and imagining vividly
human bodies I had once seen burned.

The good escorts turned toward me,
and Virgil said to me: "My son,
here there may be torment, but not death.
Remember, remember! If I
guided you safely even upon Geryon,
<note>Geryon was the massive, deceptive monster that carried Dante and Virgil down the cliffs of Hell in Inferno Canto XVII.</note>
what shall I do now that I am nearer to God?
Believe for certain that if within the belly
of this flame you stayed a full thousand years,
it could not make you bald of a single hair.
And if you think perhaps that I deceive you,
go toward it, and gain your own belief
with your hands upon the hem of your clothes.
Put down now, put down every fear;
turn this way and come safely along."
And I still stood stubborn against conscience.
When he saw me stay still and hard,
troubled a little, he said: "Now see, son:
between Beatrice and you is this wall."
As at the name of Thisbe, Pyramus opened his eyes
<note>References the tragic Ovidian lovers; Pyramus, dying, opened his eyes one last time at the mention of Thisbe's name.</note>
at the point of death, and looked upon her,
when the mulberry became vermillion.

<column-break/>

**Just as when he vibrates the first rays.** He demonstrates that in the upper hemisphere it was beginning to be day in the sign of Aries, and in the other it was becoming night in the sign of the Scales <term>Libra (the Scales)</term>. **Vibrates the first rays**, meaning he moves them. **There where his Maker**: and by this he indicates our hemisphere in which is Jerusalem, where Christ suffered. **Thus the day was passing**: understand this from the hemisphere where Dante was; because as the sun rose in our world, it necessarily departed from that other one. **When the Angel of God**: the Angel is always taken to mean a specific grace in these seven circles of Purgatory. **Joyful**: although divine grace brings joy in every part, nevertheless such joy appears greatly here, as they are now led to the end of their purification. **Blessed are the pure in heart**: because truly, this being the last circle, anyone who leaves it is purged of everything. **In a voice much more alive than ours**: meaning in a voice much more vivid than our own, for the voice of grace is more vivid and has more efficacy than the human voice. **No one goes further**: these are the words the Angel used, saying: "O holy souls, after this point no one goes further forward unless the fire first bites you; therefore enter into it." **Whereat I became such**: he says that no other color was in him than that which is in a dead man when he is buried. He shows that Dante fears entering these flames, though he never feared in the other circles; this tacitly denotes that he had almost no other penalty to receive but this one, which was against the sin of the flesh. **Over my clasped hands I stretched forward**: I made such a gesture as one does who has great pain, who clasps his hands by weaving one finger with another; and I stretched myself out as if recoiling backward, imagining with myself what happens to a human body placed in fire.

**The good escorts turned toward me**: no better escort exists to guide a man safely so that he does not perish in vice than reason and the knowledge of theology. **And Virgil**: that is, Reason admonishes him, saying, **Here there may be torment**: because where sins are purged there is no damnation, but there is the torment that removes stains and restores one to a happy life. **Remember, remember!**: he uses duplication to win greater trust. **Upon Geryon**: which we explained in the seventeenth canto of the *Inferno*. **What shall I do now nearer to God**: he is much less remote from God who has sinned through fragility—such as the sin of the flesh—than was Geryon, where there is sin through malice. If therefore he could free you from the greater danger placed among the damned, much more surely will he free you from the lesser one placed among the saved. **Within the belly**: meaning inside the womb, almost in the center of the flame, because its nature is to purge and not to consume. **And if you think perhaps that I deceive you**: it often happens that although reason demonstrates true things to the senses, it nonetheless does not persuade them; therefore it is necessary that experience intervenes. Virgil therefore wanted him to take the hem of his clothes and put it in the flame, and it would be clear that such flame does not consume; and allegorically this shows that whoever is in a great state of perturbation, even if reason persuades him that what the perturbation suggests is false, he must always test what reason dictates before departing from her. **And I still stood stubborn**: persevering in my purpose of not wanting to go. **Against conscience**: because it bit at me that I did not obey Virgil and did not believe him, he having always led me safely.

**When he saw me**: he shows what the office of the learned teacher should be toward the disobedient disciple—not for stubbornness, but for fear; for he must truly remember the goal which he has already proposed in his mind and show him that if he wishes to arrive, there is no other way. **Troubled a little**: the teacher ought to be troubled when he sees the disciple disobedient because of those perturbations; but such perturbation must not be excessive.

<summary>Dante arrives at the final barrier of Purgatory, a wall of fire, where he is paralyzed by fear until Virgil reminds him that Beatrice is waiting on the other side. The commentary by Landino explains the astronomical timing and the theological allegory of Reason (Virgil) guiding the soul through the final purification of the flesh.</summary>
<keywords>Canto XXVII, Purgatorio, Virgil, fire of purification, Beatrice, Geryon, Jerusalem, allegory of Reason, Thisbe and Pyramus, Landino commentary</keywords>

--- Page 453 ---
<meta>This page continues from the previous scene where Dante hesitates at the wall of fire. Virgil has just invoked the name of Beatrice to encourage him to cross the final barrier of Purgatory.</meta>

<page-num>223</page-num>

> So my hardness having become softened,
> I turned to the wise leader upon hearing the name
> which in my mind always springs up;
> Wherefore he shook his head and said: "What?
> Do we wish to stay on this side?" then he smiled
> as one does to a child won over by an apple.
> Then into the fire ahead of me he entered,
> requesting Statius that he should come behind,
> who for a long way before had separated us.

<note>The poet uses the myth of Pyramus and Thisbe to illustrate the power of Beatrice's name. In the myth, the dying Pyramus opens his eyes at the sound of Thisbe's name; similarly, Dante's fear of the fire vanishes when he hears the name of his beloved.</note>

...at the place where Pyramus was. But seeing a lioness that came to drink at a fountain, out of fear of the beast she dropped a veil she was wearing on her head. The lioness found it before she had finished feeding on the prey she had caught, and her muzzle was stained with blood. Then came Pyramus, and recognizing the veil, he was persuaded that Thisbe had been devoured. He took such great grief from this that with his own knife he struck himself with a mortal wound. Thisbe returned and seeing him in such a state, crying out his name—which name had such power over the lover that although he was oppressed by death, he opened his eyes to see the thing he loved so much. Then Thisbe, with the same knife, put an end to her life and her grief. And it is said that the mulberry tree under which Pyramus killed himself, having previously had white berries, took on a dark color from the blood. Therefore, Dante likewise rejoiced in his great perturbation at the name of Beatrice. **SOLLA**: that is, soft and not tight, but loosened. And of this name *solla* <note>original: "solla"</note> we have given the explanation elsewhere. **HEARING THE NAME**: that is, of Beatrice. **WHICH ALWAYS SPRINGS UP**: that is, always rises like water that springs from the earth. **WHEREFORE HE SHOOK HIS HEAD**: not threateningly but as if affirming. **AND SAID**: have we endured such great labor both in descending into Hell and in climbing Purgatory only to stop here? For he thinks we should not remain on this side of the place that contains Beatrice. **THEN HE SMILED**: modestly. The wise man smiles when he sees someone who was first stubborn and then, once moved, becomes obedient. **AS ONE DOES TO A CHILD WON OVER BY AN APPLE**: It often happens that a child who refuses to go or obey to avoid labor, if shown an apple or a pear or another fruit, goes and obeys. **THEN INTO THE FIRE**: Virgil demonstrates that reason, adorned with moral philosophy, is enough to guide man to purgation and penance for sins. But nonetheless, it is necessary that Statius stays in a place that does not let him turn back; rather, he purges him forward. This is most especially the office of the intellect enlightened by the Christian religion.

> As I was inside, into boiling glass
> I would have thrown myself to cool me,
> so great was the burning there without measure.
> My sweet father, to comfort me,
> kept talking of Beatrice as he went,
> saying: "I seem to see her eyes already."
> A voice guided us that was singing
> from the other side; and we, attentive only to it,
> came forth to where the ascent began.
> "Come, you blessed of my Father,"
> <note>original: "Venite benedicti patris mei"</note>
> sounded from within a light that was there,
> such that it overcame me, and I could not look.
> "The sun is going," it added, "and evening comes;
> do not stop, but quicken your step,
> while the west does not yet grow dark."

This light was in a form that I could not look upon. From this angel came the words that Christ will say at the Last Judgment, turning to the elect, saying: *Come, you blessed of my Father*. <note>Matthew 25:34</note> For it is impossible to emerge from the final purgation and remain absolutely immaculate through the path of discourse or human reason alone; but only by following grace. And grace alone draws us out of these final flames. **THE SUN IS GOING**: the day is ending and the night is coming. In this world, the day signifies the time of grace in which we can merit; the night is the time after death in which our works are the unmaking of our deeds, but we do not satisfy for sins committed. We do not acquire or merit anew, but our previous operations help us. Therefore, the author feigns that in Purgatory one cannot ascend except by day. He further posits that four days and three nights are spent in Purgatory. The first day he describes in the second canto: "The sun had already reached the horizon." The second in the ninth canto: "The concubine of ancient Tithonus." The third in the eighteenth canto: "Similar to...". The fourth in the twenty-seventh canto. And this fourth day was enough to seek out the Earthly Paradise. He makes no mention of the night in this place, approaching the third night which preceded the fourth day.

<column-break/>

...because he could, with desperation, confirm him in his obstinacy. **SON**: by this name he demonstrates that everything he wishes to lead him to is born from the affection he bears for him. **BETWEEN BEATRICE AND YOU**: He demonstrates that since his goal is to go to Beatrice, it is not possible to arrive there unless he passes through the flame which divides him from her. And certainly, Dante being most desirous to see Beatrice—who we said from the beginning is Theology and the knowledge of divine things—he could not learn that unless he first purged himself of the vice of lust, just as he had already purged the others. **AS AT THE NAME**: that is, of Thisbe. Pyramus and Thisbe were from Babylon, very beautiful and joined by an immeasurable love. But Pyramus, unable to have access to the girl, they agreed to go out of the city secretly by night and meet where the tomb of Ninus was. It happened that Thisbe, being more struck by love, arrived first at a spring near her, and suddenly fled and hid herself because she saw a lioness coming to drink. The lioness found her veil and tore it and bloodied it because shortly after the departure of the lioness, Pyramus arrived and seeing the bloody veil, such desperation came upon him that with his knife he killed himself. But hearing the name of Thisbe, he opened his eyes to see her. They add to the fable that a mulberry tree was stained by their blood, and thereafter it always produced dark berries. **AS AT THE NAME OF THISBE**: Just as Pyramus reacted to the name of Thisbe. **SOLLA**: We have placed the exposition elsewhere. We say water "springs up" <note>original: "rampollar"</note> when it rises from the earth. **DO WE WISH TO STAY ON THIS SIDE**: As if to say, do we wish to remain on this side of the place of Beatrice? This demonstrates how the wise man moves the imprudent one. Virgil enters the fire first to show that reason must lead man to purgation and penance, not to let him turn back, but to purge him forward.

<image-desc>A large decorative initial 'C' begins the prose section, featuring ornate scrollwork and foliage patterns typical of Renaissance woodcuts or illuminated manuscripts.</image-desc>

**C**OME WAS WITHIN: that is, in the flame, I felt such heat that I would have thrown myself into glass boiling in a furnace because I would have believed that place to have been cool in comparison to the flame. Therefore, he intends to imply that this was a burning beyond measure, and so he says "burning without meter": because in Greek *metron* <term>metron: Greek for measure</term> signifies measure. **THE SWEET FATHER**: This demonstrates that when reason wishes to comfort the sensuality burning in the fire of lust, it speaks to it of Beatrice: because there is nothing that more extinguishes the heat of carnal desires than speaking with Beatrice, that is, of the reasons with which sacred Theology demonstrates every carnal pleasure to be harmful to our souls, which should only feed on the contemplation of divine things from which supreme joy results. **SAYING HER EYES**: The eyes of Theology are the most acute speculations investigated by the most acute wits of the most learned theologians: which things draw our souls to themselves, just as the eyes of a beautiful woman allure and attract to themselves the mind of the one who loves her. **A VOICE GUIDED US THAT WAS SINGING FROM THE OTHER SIDE**: that is, from beyond the flame. Because, not seeing the way nor light, we acted like one who goes by night who, not seeing the way, follows either a voice or a sound that he hears. Being attentive, we came from the flame to the end of the circle where the staircase was that went up. And there was an angel so splendid that looking at him, he overcame me and dazzled my sight. Matthew the Evangelist posits that Christ will say this allegorically at the exit of the final purgation. The intellect is a vestige of human reason. **THE SUN IS GOING AND EVENING COMES**: The day passes, and night comes. In this world, we can merit; the night is the time of no merit: because in Purgatory their operations performed in life are satisfied. They spend four days and three nights searching for the Earthly Paradise. The second in the ninth canto. The third in the twenty-seventh canto. And already by the pre-dawn splendors that followed this day. Therefore, here the angel urges them on.

<summary>Dante overcomes his fear of the final purgatorial fire by being reminded of Beatrice, crossing the flames with Virgil and Statius. Upon exiting, they are greeted by an angel's song and warned that they must ascend before the sun sets.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the narrative from the end of Canto XXVII of Purgatory. Dante, Virgil, and Statius have just passed through the wall of fire and are now ascending the final staircase leading to the Earthly Paradise. As night falls, they are forced to stop and rest, following the law of the mountain that prevents climbing after sunset.</meta>

# CANTO XXVII

<note>original: "CANTO .XXVI"; The OCR indicates Canto 26, but the text belongs to Canto 27 of Purgatorio.</note>

The way climbed straight up through the rock
Facing the direction where I blocked the rays
In front of me from the sun, which was already low.
And after a few steps, we experienced the fact
That the sun had set by the shadow that had vanished
Behind me, both I and my wise companions.
And before the horizon, in all its immense reaches,
Had become of a single appearance,
And night had exercised all its distributions,
Each of us made of a step a bed;
For the nature of the mountain broke in us
The power of climbing more than the pleasure.

**AFTER A FEW** steps they had climbed when he felt the sun setting, not because he saw it—it being behind his shoulders—but because he saw his shadow vanish and fail. We can repeat in this place the allegory already established of day and night in Purgatory. **AND BEFORE** in all its parts, before the horizon was made all of one appearance—that is, made dark in all its immense and unmeasurable parts—the meaning is: before the day had entirely departed. **EACH** of us of a step made a bed; that is, each one lay down on the step where he found himself, because the nature of the mountain, which is that one cannot climb by night, **BROKE** in us—that is, it broke our power, strength, and pleasure. It is as if to say: we were able to climb and took pleasure in it, but the night took both away from us. Notwithstanding that they were purged of every blemish, nevertheless every shadow of ignorance was not entirely removed. Because until the night passed, it was necessary to rest. But they rested on the rock, a firm and stable thing, and on the step of the ladder. This signifies that if after purgation some ignorance still remains in us, it cannot however turn us from our purpose in which we have established ourselves. And although it does not let us mount—that is, proceed forward—but makes it necessary to stop, nevertheless it does not remove us from the true path, as happened when they were among the negligent in the valley <note>referring to the Valley of the Rulers in Canto VII</note>. There, the night made them not only stop, but even turn from the path; here it only stops us, but does not twist us from the straight path.

Like goats that remain chewing the cud, quiet,
Having been swift and bold
Upon the peaks before they have eaten,
Silent in the shade while the sun is burning,
Watched by the shepherd who upon his staff
Leans, stays, and leaning serves them;
And like the herdsman who stays outside
Along his flock, quiet through the night,
Watching lest a beast should scatter them;
Such were we three then:
I like the goat, and they like shepherds,
Hemmed in on this side and that by the grotto.
Little could appear of the sky outside,
But through that little we saw the stars,
Brighter and larger than they used to be.

So admiring and gazing back at those,
Sleep took me—the sign that often,
Before the fact occurs, tells the news.
In the hour, I believe, that from the east
First shone upon the mountain Cytherea <note>Venus</note>,
Who always seems burning with the fire of love,
Young and beautiful in a dream she appeared to me,
A lady I seemed to see walking through a plain,
Gathering flowers, and singing she said:
"Let whoever asks my name know..."

<column-break/>

It demonstrates that the way climbed straight up and toward the east. Because the sun was in the west, the shadow of the one climbing appeared before his eyes. And therefore he says, "toward such a part that I took away the rays in front of me of the sun which was already low." He knew the sun had gone down when he no longer saw his shadow. He feigns then that the ascent from this seventh terrace to the Earthly Paradise was by a cliff of rock and in it was a staircase made by a chisel which climbed through a gully. He who climbs to the state of innocence, to the truth, and to happiness, climbs toward the east. The ascent was straight: which always signifies virtue, just as the crooked signifies vice. It was steep because the end of man is placed on high, nor does one go there without climbing: for we elevate ourselves from earthly things to celestial ones. It has steps because we do not ascend without distinction of degrees of virtue, which we have already shown in several places. And the steps are made by force of chisel because such an ascent is not acquired without difficulty. And the steps are on the solid rock: because the soul is purged and already confirmed and established in that virtue, and has made such a foundation that it can no longer collapse downward. **AND**

**AS THE GOATS** which before were ravenous and without any regard in their grazing, when they have finished grazing and midday arrives, they retire to the shade, and there quiet—that is, gentle—they remain **CHEWING THE CUD** <note>original: "RVMINANDO"</note>; and the shepherd leaning on his staff watches them. Or truly like the herdsman—that is, the shepherd of the herd—**STAYS THROUGH THE NIGHT** <note>original: "PERNOCtA"</note>, that is, he lodges the night alongside the herd, guarding it from wild beasts so they do not scatter them. Such were we three: I the goat because I was being watched; they the shepherds because they were watching me. It shows that the senses, when placed between these two poets <note>Virgil and Statius</note>, are always safe from the attack of every beast—that is, from vice. **LITTLE COULD APPEAR** of the sky outside: the meaning is this, that they were so deep in the gully that they could not see any part of the sky except that which was directly over their heads. But even in that they saw the stars both larger and clearer than their custom—that is, than they were used to seeing in lower places—because celestial things appear so much larger the more we elevate our minds to them.

**HE FEIGNS** in this place that while he was looking at the stars with wonder, at the same time he was taken by sleep and by the dream which announced to him what he was to see the following day. **WHICH OFTEN**, which dream many times **TELLS THE NEWS**, has the announcement. Then he describes the time in which he had the high vision, saying that it was in the first hour that Cytherea shone—that is, Venus shines in the east—at the time when Venus rises in the east shortly before the sun. The reason why Venus either precedes or follows the sun with a small interval has already been written. Then he shows that the vision was: that it seemed to him that a young and beautiful woman went through a plain, through a meadow, who said: "I am Leah, who goes moving my hands around and exercising them to make me a garland, and I adorn myself at the mirror." Because in the first canticle <note>the Inferno</note> when it occurred, we demonstrated how by Leah is understood the active life <note>original: "uita actiua"</note> and by Rachel the contemplative life <note>original: "uita contemplatiua"</note>. I will not repeat at present what has already been said, but in this place I believe he introduces Leah to denote that man, already purged of vices, exercises himself in the Earthly Paradise—that is, in the mortal life—in the active life according to the civil virtues, according to the...

<header>->PURGATORIO<-</header>

"that I am Leah, and I go moving
my beautiful hands around to make myself a garland.
To please myself at the mirror, I adorn myself here;
but my sister Rachel never turns away
from her looking-glass, and sits all day long.
She is as eager to gaze with her lovely eyes
as I am to adorn myself with my hands;
seeing satisfies her, and working satisfies me."

And already, through the pre-dawn splendors
which rise up all the more welcome to pilgrims
the less distant they lodge from home on their return,
the darkness was fleeing on every side,
and my sleep with it; wherefore I arose,
seeing the great masters already standing.
"That sweet fruit <note>The "sweet fruit" or "apple" refers to ultimate happiness or the "highest good" that humans seek.</note> which through so many branches
the care of mortals goes seeking,
today shall lay your hungers to rest."
Virgil toward me used such words
as these; and never were there New Year's gifts <note>original: "strenne"; traditional Italian gifts given at the start of the year.</note>
that could equal these in pleasure.
Such a will upon will came over me
to be above, that at every step thereafter
I felt my feathers growing for the flight.

When the entire stairway beneath us
had been run, and we were on the topmost step,
Virgil fixed his eyes upon me,
and said: "The temporal fire and the eternal
you have seen, my son; and you have come to a place
where I, by myself, discern no further.
I have brought you here with intellect and art;
take your own pleasure for your guide from now on;
you are out of the steep ways, out of the narrow.
See the sun that shines upon your brow;
see the grass, the flowers, and the shrubs
which the earth here produces of itself alone.
Until the lovely eyes come rejoicing,
which, weeping, made me come to you in Hell,
you may sit, or you may walk among them."

<column-break/>

the Christian religion in a way that, having been a good citizen in this earthly city of Jerusalem, we may ascend to the heavenly city of Jerusalem where Rachel—the contemplative life—is not lost. Through her, with hawk-like and eagle-like eyes, we will be able to see, know, and understand the supreme truth in the first source and mirror; and understanding it, enjoy it. He introduces Leah, who exercises her hands—that is, she busies herself in operations—because the active virtue consists in those. And her end is union. And Rachel exercises her eyes because she is entirely placed in cognition. Nor should it be overlooked that he places this paradise as the state of innocence, because it cannot be found except after Purgatory. Furthermore, it does not disagree with many theologians who place it in the mountains. That this paradise exists is shown by Genesis: <note>original: "Plátauerat aué dómins paradi su uoluptatis in principio i quo posuit homine qué formauerat"</note> *The Lord God had planted a paradise of pleasure from the beginning, in which he placed the man whom he had formed.* <note>original: "Produxitque dominus deus de humo omne lignu pulchrum uisu & ad uescédu suaue lignú etiá uite in medio paradi si: lignu que scientie boni & mali"</note> *And the Lord God brought forth from the ground every tree beautiful to the sight and sweet to eat; also the tree of life in the middle of paradise, and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.* And he rightly places the active life in this paradise, because a little further down it says: <note>original: "Tulit ergo dominus deus homine & posuit eum in paradiso uoluptatis ut operaretur: Et custodiret illu"</note> *The Lord God therefore took the man and put him in the paradise of pleasure that he might work and keep it.* God placed man there so that he might work and exercise himself in its custody, which is the proper office of the active life. This thing deservedly moves Leah’s hands through this meadow, and she adorns herself with flowers, which are beautiful and produce fruit. The flowers are the virtues, than which nothing is more beautiful, nor produces better fruit. Some commentators of Genesis hold that the mountain of Purgatory reaches up to the circle of the moon. Hugh of St. Victor <note>original: "Vgo dasan uictore"</note> writes that holy men hold this paradise to be in the eastern parts, and a place so high that the waters of the flood could not reach it. Aquinas <note>original: "Laquinate"</note> writes that paradise is in the right part of the East, since Aristotle in the book *On the Heavens and the World* posits that the right is always more noble than the left. And he adds that it is separated from us by certain impediments, either of mountains or of seas, or of regions uninhabitable due to the heat. Genesis places a river there which bathes it, and this then divides into four: the first is Pishon <note>original: "Phisó"</note>, which surrounds the whole region called Havilah, where gold is born and bdellium and the onyx stone are found. The second is Gihon <note>original: "gyó"</note>, which surrounds Ethiopia. The third is Tigris, which goes toward Assyria. The fourth is Euphrates.

He describes the coming of the day by saying that through the "pre-dawn splendors"—that is, through the brightness that appears before the light of the sun—the night, which makes shadows, was fleeing from every part of the heaven. And all at once the night went away, and "my sleep with it." **SEEING THE GREAT MASTERS ALREADY STANDING.** Note that just as in voluptuous and earthly things the sense awakens before the reason, so conversely in virtuous things, reason precedes. **THAT SWEET FRUIT.** He introduces this because Virgil predicts to him his happiness and the supreme good, and metaphorically calls it a sweet fruit. For just as the cultivation of trees directs every work, labor, and industry toward the final end, which is the fruit of the tree, so men labor for nothing else but to arrive at the supreme good. Hence, human and civil life has its offices and ends. He calls it "sweet" because nothing is more pleasant than achieving the end we set for ourselves, to acquire which we endure much bitterness. It is not, therefore, that fruit which Eve tasted, which was sweet to the taste but bitter to health; but it is a sweetness after which no bitterness is ever born. **THROUGH SO MANY BRANCHES.** That is, through so many ways, which are as many as there are many mansions in the kingdom of the Eternal Father. **SHALL LAY YOUR HUNGERS TO REST.** That is, it will satisfy them. And this is the difference between human happiness and the eternal: that the human, because it is finite, cannot satisfy the soul, which is infinite; but God, the infinite good, satisfies it. **AND NEVER WERE THERE NEW YEAR'S GIFTS.** <note>original: "stréne"</note> That is, gifts. *Strenne* in the Lombard language means gifts. He means to imply that no news or announcement ever gave anyone as much pleasure as this gave to me. Because at his first desire to ascend, he did so much that at every step he felt his "feathers"—that is, the virtues—growing.

**THEY ASCENDED THE STAIRS** which lead from the seventh terrace to the Earthly Paradise. And in this way we have seen Dante descending to Hell (the knowledge of vices) and ascending Purgatory (purging himself of them). Having come to the Earthly Paradise, by which we understand the state of innocence, now returning to the text: as the stairs that rise from the seventh terrace to the Earthly Paradise were run beneath us, we climbed them and were on the supreme and sovereign step. Virgil fixed his eyes on me—that is, he looked at me fixedly. This denotes that Reason halted in the senses and illuminated them with its light, in a way that for the future it is not necessary for Virgil to guide Dante—that is, for the appetite to wait to be guided by reason. For being united with reason, he can go by himself and cannot err, because the light of reason, which he has taken, manifests to him good and evil. For we can say that the appetite in man is in various ways; for...

<header>->CANTO XXVIII<-</header>

Expect no further word or sign from me;
your will is free, upright, and sound,
and it would be a fault not to act according to its judgment;
therefore, over yourself, I crown and mitre you. <note>Virgil "crowns" Dante as a king of himself (temporal authority) and "mitres" him as a bishop of himself (spiritual authority), signifying that Dante’s soul is now purified and needs no external master.</note>

...Likewise, Virgil tells him that he has shown him the fire, and this is in Hell where the punishments are eternal. Therefore, that state remains in eternal misery. And the purgation, which is signified by natural and philosophical science represented by Virgil. But regarding the Earthly Paradise, blessedness, and divinity, these are understood more through faith than through natural reason. Thus he rightly says "I discern": as if to say that although for such knowledge a guide is necessary, one cannot proceed without theology. **DRAWN** <note>original: "TRACTO"</note> here: Well, if the appetite does not come by itself unless it is drawn by reason, which is either by natural talent or by art—hence we say we "know" an art. Take it as your guide: before purgation, our pleasures and delights followed the path to extreme misery. But after the soul is purged, because those pleasures are eternal and divine, whoever follows them is truly blessed. This is because he has entered the third kind of virtue of the soul, already purged: it is not just virtue, but supreme delight. **SEE THE SUN** <note>original: "VEDIL SOLE"</note> that shines on your brow: And allegorically, being already purified, the truth of things shone upon his brow because it had already illuminated all his internal senses. **SEE THE GRASS** and the flowers and the shrubs: He describes the Bible and the Earthly Paradise where the earth produces every herb and tree without any seed or cultivation; and it is true when the soul is restored to a state of innocence, it produces the greenness of grass by itself—that is, the supreme hope of blessedness in its own operations. **WHILE** they come joyfully: The meaning is, you have the free choice to sit or walk among the flowers while the lady <note>A reference to Beatrice, who will soon appear.</note> comes, she who went to Hell with tearful eyes fearing for your salvation, and now she will have joyful eyes. And certainly all theological scriptures that speak against sinners denounce them; and on the contrary, they show supreme joy to purged souls. Even while still joined with reason, the soul should wait for its commands in everything. **YOUR** will is free: although in everyone it is free, in the region of sin such freedom is quite obscured, and the appetite becomes almost a tyrant. But in the soul purged and clean of sin, there is true freedom of choice because it is upright—that is, not forced away from the true life and honesty by any dishonest greed. Therefore, such a soul has no need for anyone to govern it. **AND IT WOULD BE A FAULT** not to act according to its judgment: certainly, when the appetite is joined with reason, it would be an error if it did not do what it desires. **OVER THEE I CROWN**—that is, I make you king of yourself—**AND MITRE**—I place upon you the mitre of the pastor—because you are such that you shall rule yourself. And by yourself you shall guide yourself.

<column-break/>

...which at some times is entirely resistant to reason, and at other times obeys it as if by force, and at other times, though willingly, it nonetheless often declines and wavers. But when, after the habit of virtue is formed, it is united entirely with the intellect and illustrated by it and by divine grace, and almost confirmed in grace, it has no other guide than its own free will, and that conducts it most excellently. Now returning to the exposition of the present text: He perfectly portrays the temporal fire that is in Purgatory, where the pains are temporary, and the eternal fire of Hell. These two things—the knowledge of vices and the purgation of those who commit them—can be known by man through natural reasons. But Virgil cannot show him further because for what follows, natural doctrine is not enough. Instead, holy theology leads us further. **AND IF** you have come to a place where I, by myself, can see no further: This refers to natural reason; nevertheless, it cannot proceed by itself without theology. He says **DRAWN** <note>original: "aracto/tratto"</note>, for in the speculation of great things, man intends to use talent and art. Whatever man understands through doctrine, we say "to learn." **YOUR** pleasure henceforth: Previously, pleasures came from the love of earthly things; whatever those were, they led to extreme misery. But after the soul is purged, no pleasure remains except for those things that are truly good. **OUT OF THE STEEP WAYS**: Out of the narrow paths in which it is not only difficult to live according to virtue, but is supreme delight. See the sun that shines on your brow: because the sun had already risen, and looking at it, being cleansed from sins, divine grace began to shine in him. **SEE** the herbs produced by the earth itself by virtue placed there by God; this is true when the soul is restored to a state of innocence, producing by itself the beauty of honesty and the first fruits of its own operations. It is your choice to sit or walk among the flowers while those beautiful eyes come, which in their weeping made me come to you. The sense is that when you were lost, I came so you would not perish; but at present, the sacred scriptures <note>represented by Beatrice</note> which speak against sinners will announce joy. **DO NOT** expect my word further: when the appetite is not joined with reason, it follows a tyrant. But when it is joined and operates rightly by itself, it is free will; nonetheless, where sensuality is resistant to reason, it is not free. But in the soul purged and clean of sin, there is true liberty because it is not oppressed by any dishonest greed. It would be a fault not to follow your own judgment: certainly, when the appetite is joined with reason, it would be an error if it did not do as much as it desires. **THEREFORE I CROWN YOU**: that is, I make you king of yourself, because you are such that you will govern yourself. And by yourself you will be your own guide.

especially that Virgil tells him he has shown him the temporal fire which is in Purgatory, and that (eternal torment) which is in Hell where the torments are eternal. For these two things, namely the knowledge of vices, of which he who makes a habit remains in eternal misery, and the purgation that can cleanse one from them, are signified by natural reason and philosophical science, represented by Virgil. But Virgil cannot show him both the earthly paradise and blessedness and divinity. Natural doctrine is not enough; faith is needed, which transcends natural reason. Therefore Virgil rightly says: AND IF I have come to discern: As if to say that although natural reason is necessary for such knowledge, one can proceed without theology. <page-num>XXVIII</page-num>
<header>CANTO XXVIII</header>

### CANTO .XXVIII. OF THE SECOND CANTICLE BY DANTE.

Dante had now arrived from the last circle of Purgatory to the Earthly Paradise, which theologians call the "Paradise of Delights" <note>original: "delitiarū: idest de dilecti"</note>; and which, as we have said, represents the state of innocence. There he finds Leah, who is interpreted as the **active life**. This demonstrates that once a person is purged, they must exercise themselves in the active moral virtues according to Christian precepts. From this follows the happiness that can exist in the active life, so that, having practiced this life as a citizen of this "lower Jerusalem," one may rise to contemplate the "celestial city of Jerusalem." This will be the subject of the third canticle <note>Paradiso</note>. For this reason, in the following cantos, he will place the beginning of the New Church founded on the Evangelical law, which was prefigured first in the ancient Mosaic law and in the synagogue of the Jews. He first describes the most pleasant greenery of the herbs and trees, the sweetness of the flowers, the delightful wind, and the sweetest melody of the birds. Through the herbs and flowers, he demonstrates the unfailing hope that, after this state of innocence, they will reach the true Paradise. Through the light and unchanging wind, he signifies the tranquil and orderly movement of holy works, in which no disturbance can arise. And he walked with **slow steps**, because every thought of ours should be considered with mature wisdom, not thoughtlessly or precipitated with too much speed. He walked, therefore, because we must never cease from good works; but he walked with slow steps—that is, with mature consideration. After this, he describes Matilda <note>Mathelda</note>, about whom

Eager now to search within and around
the divine forest, thick and living,
which tempered the new day for the eyes,
Without waiting longer, I left the bank,
taking the plain slowly, slowly,
over the ground that gave fragrance from every part.
A sweet breeze, without change,
having in itself no harshness <note>original: "miseria," here meaning a sudden gust or turbulence</note> against the forehead,
no more a blow than a gentle wind;
By which the leaves, trembling readily,
all of them bent toward the side
where the holy mountain casts its first shadow;
Not, however, so far scattered from their straightness
that the little birds on the summits
should leave off practicing their every art;
But with full joy the first hours <note>The "first hours" refers to prime, the first canonical hour of prayer at dawn.</note>
singing, they resided among the leaves,
which kept the bass <note>term: bordone (the underlying steady drone or accompaniment)</note> to their rhymes,
Just as from branch to branch it gathers
through the pine forest on the shore of Chiassi,
when Aeolus <note>The Greco-Roman god of the winds.</note> lets the Sirocco <note>The warm south-easterly wind.</note> out of its stall.

<column-break/>

we shall speak in its proper place; she asks what cause produces the wind and the river in that place. *Eager now to search within and around.* He was, therefore, desirous to search the "divine forest"—that is, the true active life. *Within*, as if to say, its own essence. *And around*, which denotes the circumstances. He wanted to search Paradise through the middle and in a circle—that is, through the extremities. We showed at the beginning of the first canticle <note>Inferno</note> that Dante finding himself in the "dark wood" signified nothing other than the troublesome prison of the body, in which the soul, enclosed by its contagion, contracts various faults and is stained by various sins. Therefore, he placed that wood as dark and full of wild beasts that prevented him from going where the sun was. Now, he posits that after the knowledge of sins and having climbed through every degree of Purgatory—that is, being purged of every vice—his senses and appetite (which by the contagion of the body were previously rebellious to reason) are so united with reason that they have become almost one and the same thing. Thus, it is fitting that the forest—which was previously thorny, dark, and full of beasts—has become pleasant and delightful, full of light and full of flowers. This denotes the virtues from which the best fruits come. The flower initially has the sweetness of beauty and scent, and in the end produces excellent fruit. *The divine forest*: that is, the divine woods made as a habitation for men, with every beauty contrary to that described in Hell. *Thick*: with trees and grass, and *living* with light. *Which tempered the new day for the eyes*: the greenery of the trees and herbs tempered the splendor of the sun already risen. For it was now the fourth day that my eyes could endure it; which signifies nothing else but that the virtues of a person established in a state of innocence in the active life make their intellect capable of receiving the divine light. *Without waiting longer*: neither for time nor a guide. *I left the bank*: that is, the edge, and began to enter the middle, as one can do who is sufficient unto himself. *Taking the plain*: as if to say, wide and spacious contemplation. *Slowly, slowly*:

---

to demonstrate that whoever wishes to take up any doctrine must proceed with a slow step. *Over the ground*: that is, upon the earth.
*THAT* <note>original: "CHE"</note>: which. *Gave fragrance* <note>original: "Vliua"</note>: cast an odor from the herbs and flowers with which it was clothed. And certainly, the operations of a soul already purged cast an excellent odor everywhere. *A sweet breeze*: it was born from the eastern parts. *Breeze*: that is, a gentle and temperate wind; this is the **good will inspired by God**. This was like a temperate wind, because the will that moves us to good works is always temperate and not impetuous, as are unbridled desires. It comes, therefore, from the East—that is, from God—the will directed toward the good; and such a wind bends the leaves toward the West—that is, toward worldly things. For the active life consists in the prudent, just, and temperate administration of fleeting goods. Nor does this active life last longer than this mortal life, but the contemplative life is eternal, because it concerns eternal and celestial things. This is why the Truth <note>Jesus</note> says in the Gospel: "But Mary has chosen the best part, which will not be taken away from her" <note>original: "Maria aūt optimā partē elegit: que nō auferetur ab ea." (Latin quote from Luke 10:42)</note>. *Not, however, so far scattered from their straightness*: they did not bend so far from their uprightness that the birds on the summits would stop singing. This denotes that although operations in the active life bend toward the administration of the body, nonetheless they do not depart from those "birds" who sang—that is, the man does not cease for this reason to continuously give thanks to God. *But they sing the first hours*: that is, the verses they sing in the morning among the leaves. For nothing forbids us, among the "leaves"—that is, among civil cares and operations—to praise God. *Which kept the bass*: that is, the tenor. So sweet was the murmur of the breeze as it struck the branches that it provided the tenor for the singing of the birds. Because the movements of a soul already purged are without disturbance and help in singing divine praises. *Just as*: such was that sweet murmur in that forest, as it is in the pine forest of Ravenna, where Chiassi <note>term: Chiassi (Classis), the ancient Roman port near Ravenna</note> is, a land near Ravenna on the shore where Emperor Justinian built the church of Saint Apollinaris. This land was later destroyed by Liutprand <note>original: "Leoprādo"</note> while he was besieging Ravenna.

Already my slow steps had carried me
so far inside the ancient forest that I
could no longer see from where I entered;
And behold, a stream stopped my further progress,

taking this to mean the state of innocence; no state is more ancient in souls because in that state man was created by God. **COULD NOT** see where I had entered. Man entered into the state of innocence as soon as he was created, and we cannot remember this entry, because no one remembers the entrance of the soul into the body; hence in the first canticle <note>Inferno, Canto I</note> he said: "I cannot well repeat how I entered there." **AND BEHOLD A RIVER** took away my ability to go further. Just as the Holy Scripture posits that from the Earthly Paradise there issue from a single source the Euphrates and the Tigris, so the poet imagines that from the eastern part of this paradise and from a single source two rivers issue: Lethe and Eunoe. Lethe, which he mentions here, flows to the left. This name "Lethe" signifies oblivion <note>Greek: "lethe," meaning forgetfulness.</note>. And whoever climbs from Purgatory to the state of innocence drinks of this water, which, when drunk, causes one to forget all sins. This is because they enter the third kind of virtues, which belong to the soul already purged, through which one no longer fights against vices as one did in the purgatorial virtues; rather, one forms such a habit of virtue that one forgets vices. Hence Juvenal said: "May he not know how to be angry, may he desire nothing" <note>original: "Neſciat iraſci cupiat nihil"</note>. And for this reason, he imagines it flows to the left, which signifies something base <note>The left side often symbolized the material or sinful world in medieval allegory.</note>, carrying away the memory of evil. The other he calls Eunoe, that is, "good mind" <note>Greek: "eu-noia," meaning good-mindedness.</note>, because nothing comes to the memory except the good and the virtuous. This is the reason why, from the state of innocence, one rises to the contemplation of divine things. **ALL THE WATERS**. The meaning of this tercet is that the water of Lethe is clearer than any water in this world of ours. This signifies that the soul which, in the state of innocence, is so accustomed to virtue that it does not merely conquer vice but forgets it, is most pure. **ALTHOUGH** it moves dark. The water of Lethe is very clear; but because it flows under the constant shadow of the trees of paradise, which do not let the rays of the sun or moon pass through, it appears dark. We can say that such oblivion removes the disturbances that make us proud or elated in prosperous worldly affairs. Nor do miseries hinder us from doing good. This was also expressed by the Psalmist, saying: "The sun shall not burn thee by day, nor the moon by night" <note>original: "Per diem ſol non uret te: neque luna per noctem" - Psalm 121:6</note>; where he takes the sun of the day to mean burning greed in prosperous fortune, and the moon of the night to mean the passions that burn the mind in adversity.

<image-desc>Decorative initial 'g' in a square frame featuring floral and leaf motifs.</image-desc>Having reached the river, he stayed his feet: because his body went no further; but with his eyes—that is, with his sight—he crossed the river because he was drawn by the variety of fresh "mai." For with great wonder he gazed upon the varied abundance of trees that were there, and these he calls "mai": because this is what the Tuscans call the green branches that by ancient custom they hang at windows on the first day of May. And allegorically, he stopped upon reaching the river. For he could not pass to the active life and virtuous operations until he first drank of Lethe—that is, until he was confirmed in virtuous acts so that he not only conquered every vice but also forgot it. And nonetheless, although he could not yet pass—that is, operate in virtuous works for the reason stated—his eyes passed with their sight because he could begin to consider what those works might be. And not without reason did he see a variety of fresh "mai." For the active life has various and diverse actions, which distract the soul in many directions. Hence the Gospel, which Matthew <note>Translator's note: The commentator likely meant Luke 10:41, though the text attributes it to Matthew.</note> presents for this active life, says: "Martha, Martha, thou art careful and troubled about many things" <note>original: "Martha Martha ſolicita es & turbaris erga plurima"</note>. **AND THERE**, that is, across the river, there appeared to me a lady in that form in which some thing usually appears suddenly, which causes such wonder that it diverts every other thought from our mind. This lady went along alone, singing through a path full of flowers, and she was "picking flower from flower." By this lady, he intends the **active life**; and he calls her Mathelda. After Countess Matilda, a woman of supreme nobility and the greatest virtues in administration. She was the daughter of Beatrice. This Beatrice was the daughter of the Emperor of Constantinople, who, taken by love for an Italian lord of the house of Canossa, followed him to Italy in secret from her father. But finally, the Emperor endowed her with many lands in Italy and especially the Patrimony <note>The "Patrimony of St. Peter," the territorial possessions of the Pope.</note>. From them was born Matilda, a woman of most honest character, great spirit, and prudence in administering her lordship, and of supreme religious devotion. For this reason, she gave great help to the Pope against the Emperor. She endowed many churches, and especially the Cathedral of Pisa, near which she was buried in the year 1060 <note>Note: Historically, Matilda of Canossa died in 1115. The 1060 date likely refers to her mother's tomb or a chronological error in the manuscript.</note> in the tomb of Beatrice her mother. She built many churches and finally offered her lordship, which today they call the Patrimony, to the Church of Saint Peter in Rome. Thus, our poet, just as at the beginning of Purgatory he placed Cato as a man most loving of liberty, so in this beginning of the Paradise of Delights—in which he establishes the active life—he imagines finding Matilda, who in that place joined civil virtues with true Christian religion. He depicts her as being alone, not because the active life is lived in solitude, but to demonstrate that even in this life there is need for constant meditation; and she sings, which demonstrates the eloquence with which the wise persuade others to good works and dissuade those they govern from evil ones. **AND SHE CHOOSES** flower from flower: among many actions which occur in the active life, she chooses those that possess the most virtue.

<image-desc>Decorative initial 'd' in a square frame with ornate floral scrolls.</image-desc>O BEAUTIFUL LADY: These are the words that Dante used toward the lady to persuade her to approach the river so that he could understand what she was singing. Having thus captured her goodwill by using the word "O" and calling her "beautiful"—and certainly civil actions performed with virtue are beautiful—he adds: **WHICH** warms yourself at the rays of love. **NOR** can it be otherwise. For the active life takes on many tasks for the homeland, for kin, for friends, and finally for all men; and no one would...

The Hellespont is a narrow sea which divides Asia from Europe. And on the Asian side is Abydos; on the European side is Sesto. In Abydos was Leander, who most ardently loved Hero, a beautiful maiden whose home was Sesto. Nor did the unhappy youth hesitate to swim at night across the sea that divided the two cities to find Hero. But finally, caught one night by a storm, he could not by swimming reach the shore alive where the maiden was, but the wave pushed him there dead. Furthermore, when Xerxes, King of the Persians, came into Greece with infinite troops, he made a bridge of ships over this sea. This is therefore the meaning: that Leander did not bear as much hatred to this Hellespont because it divided him from the thing he loved, as Dante bore to Lethe, because it divided him from Mathelda.

The abduction of Proserpina has been described by us: she was in Sicily in a most pleasant meadow, highly adorned with grass and flowers, when she was abducted by Pluto and led to Hell, in such a way that her mother lost her, and she lost the flowers. **SHE CAME** as far as the river with eyes cast down, not looking at Dante. Mathelda sings and laughs because this third kind of virtue makes us not only abstain from vice without difficulty, but we exercise such virtues with supreme pleasure. The great splendor of her eyes demonstrates the purity and open and clear truth of this doctrine. Wherefore, wishing to demonstrate the great splendor, he makes a comparison between her and Venus, and especially when she was inflamed with the love of Adonis. It is in the fables that while Cupid was embracing his mother Venus, an arrow from his quiver accidentally struck her and wounded Venus in the breast; by which wound she suddenly burned with love for the son of Cinyras and Myrrha, Adonis, a most beautiful youth, who later, having died and been mangled by a boar, was converted into a flower. **QUITE** against his custom: because the wound was by chance. **HANDLING** more colors with her hands: We have already said that the operations of the active life are many and various. **WHICH THAT OTHER LAND**: not this land on our side, but that of the terrestrial paradise...

Afterward, she turns to Dante and offers that if he wishes to know more from her, she will be ready and willing to answer him as much as is sufficient. And through this, she demonstrates that the doctrine of the sacred writings in the active life can easily resolve every doubt for us; the holy doctors have done this willingly, seeking to please only as much as is sufficient and no further, as the Apostle says: *Do not seek to know more than is necessary to know, but seek to know with sobriety.* <note>Original Latin: "nolite sapere plusq̃ oporteat sapere. This suggests a warning against intellectual pride or curiosity beyond one's spiritual station.</note> Regarding the water, I said the poet usually is clarified that what he had heard the day before from Statius <note>A Roman poet who accompanies Dante and Virgil through the upper levels of Purgatory.</note> was true: that above the third step of Purgatory, no alteration of the air occurred—neither wind, nor rain, nor earthquake—yet presently in this place, the water and the wind make a noise and sound. These two things, he says, challenge and combat the faith he had recently placed in Statius, when he heard from him something contrary to what he now senses: namely, that no alteration rose above those aforementioned three steps. To this, Matelda responds and says: "I will demonstrate from what cause arises that which makes you marvel, and I will clear the fog from your eyes"—that is, "I will remove the ignorance from your intellect that does not let you understand." And therefore, she continues:

<column-break/>

To resolve the doubt that Dante has, she first demonstrates that Statius told him the truth: that no alterations of those born from the vapors of the earth—drawn up by the sun into the third region—can occur here. The reason, she shows, is that God, in creating the paradise of delights so that man might live without any inconvenience, raised this mountain so high above the earth that Purgatory and Paradise surpass the region of the atmosphere which those vapors cannot cross. Therefore, there can be no winds, nor hail, nor lightning here. Allegorically, she demonstrates that whoever is in the purgatorial virtues and in those of the already-purged soul feels no perturbation of the mind. THE HIGHEST GOOD, which is God. WHO ONLY IN HIMSELF FINDS JOY: only God, through Himself and not through any external thing, is pleasing to Himself. The author's intention is that man, in the virtues of the already-purged soul, exercises himself in the active life according to our religion, and then in the contemplative life by hearing from Matelda—that is, from the sacred theologians—that doctrine which is necessary for our salvation. For this reason, he introduces her as the teacher who explains the principle of human generation, to what end man was produced, and in what place he was put; and how, for not being obedient, he was cast out. Later, she will narrate the predictions made in the Old Testament as figures of his salvation, and then the coming of Christ, his salvation, and how through that we are led back to His obedience and finally to salvation, returning to innocence. HE MADE MAN GOOD: therefore every vice that is born in him is not from God, but from his own choice. TO GOOD: to the end that he might possess Him, who is the Supreme Good. AND THIS PLACE: that is, the earthly paradise, a pledge of eternal peace. God willed that man in a state of innocence should inhabit this place as long as it pleased God, and then He intended to lead him to heaven. Thus it was a "pledge" <term>arra: a down-payment or security deposit</term> of eternal peace—that is, of heaven where the supreme beatitude is found. THROUGH HIS OWN FAULT: through his defect, a word derived from "undoing" (*diffare*). For he who sins "un-does," and sin is nothing other than the privation of good; therefore he undoes and does not "do." HE STAYED HERE BUT A LITTLE WHILE: they say that the first man was created in Damascus and then translated to the paradise of delights at the hour of the third <note>Roughly 9:00 AM.</note>, and there God gave him the precepts he was to observe; and He presented to him all the beasts, and Adam gave them names. Afterward, he fell asleep and God formed the woman from his rib. Then the serpent came and tempted Eve, and after that hour they ate the forbidden fruit. And immediately the angel came and cast them out, and placed them in this world full of bitterness. From this, it is gathered that he did not stay three hours in paradise. SO THAT THE DISTURBANCE: She showed how the first man was put in paradise; now she shows why such a place was more eminent above the earth than others. She says that this mountain rises—that is, lifted and exalted itself toward heaven—so much that it is free from exhalations. FROM THERE WHERE IT IS BARRED: that is, from the gate of Purgatory. And this was done so that the disturbed air—created by exhalations and terrestrial vapors raised by the heat of the sun—would not cause any war to man, such as inducing wind, rain, hail, snow, and the like. But allegorically, she shows that he who is elevated from the earth—from the thoughts of earthly things—and has pulled up his sensuality and made it obedient to reason, becomes so formed that the flesh does not fight against the spirit, and the soul is tranquil, outside the winds of appetite and the waters of sadness and every other perturbation.

Then she demonstrates that Statius did not lie to Dante when he told him that this mountain was free from the aforementioned alterations. Now she shows that, notwithstanding this, there is nonetheless a wind here that moves the leaves. This wind arises because the FIRST ROTATION—that is, the *Primum Mobile* <note>The outermost moving sphere of the universe in medieval cosmology, which drives the motion of all other spheres.</note>, which in 24 hours turns from East to West and then returns to the East—moves the air in that same circuit. From this motion, the wind is born which can move the leaves, and she calls it "living air"—that which is above the third region. AND THE STRUCK PLANT: that is, the tree struck by such wind impregnates the air with its "virtue" (its essence or power), and the air, in its circling, shakes it from itself. From this, it falls to the "other earth"—that is, to our hemisphere. And such earth, in which this virtue falls, conceives according to its own fertility or the virtue of the heavens and the stars to which it is subject, and it generates whatever plant that virtue dictates. Therefore, we should not marvel if some plant grows there...

<gloss>without visible seed: that is, without us seeing it or sowing it: because it is born through the power mentioned above.
