**A**s she has shown that the wind which strikes the leaves does not arise from hot and dry vapors as it does here; so now she shows that the water of the two rivers of paradise does not arise from cold and humid vapors, as our rivers are born from vapors that the sky converts into water. **BUT IT IS BORN** from a fountain: He imagines that one single fountain is in the paradise of delights, which never increases nor decreases, but always remains in one state and is divine; and it has two mouths: one on the left from which Lethe is born; the other on the right from which Eunoe is born. And through this, he wishes to express the habit of the virtues of the soul already purged; which is why he says this fountain is solid and sure. Solid because it does not fail: for such a habit cannot be removed or taken from the soul. And sure because it neither increases nor decreases: but always stays of one quality. This is true because the operations that proceed from such a soul are continuous and neither increase nor decrease as they do in the civil virtues. This fountain is, therefore, what we have said: that which proceeds from perfecting and confirming grace, which does not let the fountain fail. Lethe on the left is the oblivion of vices: which signifies perfection, which makes it so that we do not merely resist vices as in other virtues, but we forget them entirely because every irrational appetite is submerged and completely extinguished. From the right of this fountain is born the river Eunoe, which signifies "good mind" <note>original: "buona mente"; from the Greek "eu" (good) and "nous" (mind).</note>: and this is the most burning fervor of charity and will immersed in virtuous operations. **AND IT DOES NOT WORK**: This fountain is not truly effective unless it is tasted here and there: that is, if we do not taste both Lethe and Eunoe together: because the soul cannot be perfect if it has not forgotten every perturbation and is not entirely inflamed with the love of virtue. **ABOVE ALL OTHER FLAVORS**: it surpasses them, just as taste is at its peak of happiness when it has food that surpasses the flavor of all others; so the soul is through these two rivers. **AND ALTHOUGH**: that is, even if your thirst—that is, the desire of your mind—is satisfied, **THEREFORE** I will not fail to manifest more to you; I will tell you also as a favor: and he spoke a conclusion that embraces all others. As for example: when we have demonstrated with many arguments the immortality of the soul, we conclude that it is necessary to preserve it pure from vices so that, separated from the body, it returns to its supreme good.

**I** believe the meaning of the first tercet is that the poets who anciently divided the ages according to metals said that the first was golden and called it the Age of Gold: because men in that age lived most innocently and as clean of every stain of vice as they saw gold in the furnace, most pure. They saw this state of innocence as if under a cloud and almost as in a dream. And therefore he says, "perhaps on Parnassus they dreamed of this place": that is, in their poetic art and in their furor <note>The "poetic furor" or divine inspiration described by Plato and Renaissance Neoplatonists.</note>, through which, by elevating the mind, they were able to describe high and admirable meanings. Placing Parnassus, the mountain dedicated to the Muses, for the art and for the poetic furor, they saw this innocence as if dreaming and not perfectly. **HERE** the human root was innocent: as if to say in no other place and in no other time was the first age (which was of gold) except here where the human root—that is, the first humans—were innocent. **HERE** it is always spring: just as if the year had perpetual spring, it would always be temperate: and there would be neither excessive heat nor excessive cold. So the state of innocence, because it is in perpetual spring, is not molested either by the heat of excessive cupidity and desires, nor by the cold of excessive...

<margin>sorrow and fear. I turned back to my poets: which signifies that with the mind I return to poetic doctrine. I easily confess that they are smiling in this part, if already through their fiction they understand this same thing. Then having seen this, I return with my face to Matelda: that is, to theological doctrine, which describes the happiness of the active life as Beatrice contains the doctrine of the contemplative life.</margin>

<summary>Dante learns that the Earthly Paradise contains a divine fountain feeding two rivers, Lethe and Eunoe, which respectively erase the memory of sin and restore the memory of good deeds. Landino’s commentary links this Christian paradise to the classical "Golden Age" and explains the rivers as allegories for a perfected, virtuous soul.</summary>
<keywords>Lethe, Eunoe, Earthly Paradise, Golden Age, Parnassus, innocence, charity, Cristoforo Landino, Dante Alighieri, Purgatorio</keywords>

--- Page 463 ---
<header>PVRGATORIO</header>

<page-num>222</page-num>

In a most pure way they saw beneath a cloud, and as if through a dream, this state of innocence. And therefore it says, perhaps in Parnassus they dreamed that place, that is, in their poetic art and in their frenzy, by which, elevating the mind, they were able to describe already such and admirable concepts, placing Parnassus, a mountain dedicated to the Muses, for the art and for the poetic frenzy. They saw this innocence as if dreaming and not perfectly. HERE was innocent: The human root: as if to say, in no other place and in no other time was the first golden age, except here where the human root, that is, the first humans, were innocent. HERE always spring: As if the year had perpetual spring, it would always be temperate: and there would be neither excessive heat nor excessive cold. Thus the state of innocence, because it is in perpetual spring, is not troubled neither by the heat of excessive cupidity and desires, nor by the cold of excessive sorrow and fear. I turned back to my poets: which means that with my mind I return to poetic doctrine, confessing it to be ridiculous in that part if by their fiction they do not understand the same thing. Then, having heard how insufficient poetic doctrine is for this, I return with joy to Matelda, that is, to theological doctrine, which describes the happiness of the active life, just as Beatrice contains the doctrine of the contemplative life.

<page-num>XXVIII</page-num>
<header>CANTO XXVIII</header>

## CANTO XXVIII OF THE SECOND CANTICLE BY DANTE

Singing like a woman in love,
continuing with the end of her words:
**Blessed are they whose sins are covered** <note>original: "beati quorum tecta sunt peccata"</note>
And like nymphs who used to wander alone
through the wild shadows, desiring—
some to see and some to flee the sun—
Then she moved, walking against the stream,
going along the bank; and I parallel to her,
following her small step with my small step.
Not a hundred steps were between her steps and mine
when the banks turned equally in such a way
that I found myself facing the East.
Nor was our way yet much further
when the lady turned entirely toward me,
saying, "My brother, look and listen."
And behold, a flash suddenly passed
from all sides through the great forest,
such that it made me wonder if it were lightning.
But because lightning stays as it comes,
and that, lasting, shone more and more,
in my thought I said, "What thing is this?"
And a sweet melody ran
through the luminous air; wherefore a good zeal
made me reprove the boldness of Eve,
That there, where earth obeyed heaven,
a woman alone, and but recently formed,
did not endure staying under any veil.
Under which, had she been devoted,
I would have felt those ineffable delights
sooner and for a longer time.
While I went among so many first-fruits
of the eternal pleasure, all suspended,
and still desiring more joys,
Before us, like a fire set ablaze,
the air became beneath the green branches,
and the sweet sound was now understood as a song.

<column-break/>

**She sang excellently** like a woman in love because the true interpreters and doctors of our <term>theology</term>—openly and with supreme zeal toward their neighbor, either by preaching or by otherwise admonishing and instructing—constantly make us learned. Therefore, "singing like a woman in love," she continues with the end of her words: that is, having finished declaring to Dante what we have already discussed, she began without intermission to sing the psalm. The beginning is **Blessed are they whose transgressions are forgiven, and whose sins are covered** <note>original: "Beati quorum remisse sunt iniquitates & quorum tecta sunt peccata"</note>. This song is appropriate to the subject matter because Dante was soon to drink from the waters of the <term>Lethe</term>, through which he had to forget his sins. Thus, through Purgatory, his sins had been remitted, and in this beginning of Paradise, they will be made hidden because he will forget them. **And like nymphs**: a fitting comparison between the nymphs inhabiting the woods, meadows, and waters, and the lady placed in such a pleasant and delightful greenery and garden. **THEN she moved**: This shows that the lady went up along the riverbank and went against the current toward the source of the river; and Dante followed her, walking with a small step as she did. He places none of these details without cause. For she was guiding the poet to the ford of the river which he had to cross, and not to depart from it; and she went toward the **East** <note>The direction of the rising sun, traditionally associated with God and the source of divine light.</note>, which signifies the most perfect part. She went against the water because we must not let ourselves be carried away by its waves, but must resist them and cross it when the time and place are appropriate. **Not a hundred steps were between her steps and mine**: they had not gone a hundred steps between them (which was a space of fifty paces) when they reached the bend of the river, which, in turning, caused him to be turned toward the East. By this, he demonstrates that after a short time spent in the investigation of this doctrine and in the operations of these virtues of the already purged soul, we are illuminated by the power of divine grace.

Having already turned toward the East and become attentive, through Matelda he began to see most excellent things. **LOOK and listen**: we can come to knowledge in two ways: either by our own wit, investigating and searching through the discourse of reason—and this, by analogy to the physical eyes, we call "seeing"—or, truly not being able to find the truth by ourselves, we learn from others. Therefore, Dante is admonished by Matelda saying "look," so that he might investigate for himself, and saying "listen," so that in what he cannot see for himself, he may hear from one who teaches him. **A flash** <note>original: "VN lustro"</note>: a splendor which at first he doubted might be lightning. But then, considering that lightning passes quickly and disappears, and seeing that this lasted and grew, he did not understand what thing it was. And through the air shining with such splendor, he heard a miraculous melody. By this, he demonstrates the arrival of the **Holy Spirit**, in which he places the splendor and the song to express two singular graces which the Holy Spirit gives to the human mind. The first is light, which drives away the shadows of ignorance and induces knowledge of the truth; the second is the song, by which he demonstrates the sweetness that is instilled through the knowledge of divine things. And such light, coming into a soul already purged, lasts forever and is not extinguished. **WHENCE good zeal**: for this reason, he took such zeal in knowing divine things that "I took the boldness of Eve": that is, I had that same daring that Eve had. She, newly formed, although she had a command from God not to taste of the fruit which gave knowledge of good and evil, nevertheless did not endure to stay under any veil or obscurity of ignorance. Indeed, most inappropriately against the divine precept, she tasted the fruit which gave knowledge of good and evil. And therefore he says that Eve, in that place—that is, in the **Paradise of Delights** where the earth obeyed heaven, producing whatever heaven imprinted and not discarding its influences—she alone, without help from others, and being a woman (whose sex ought to be more timid), and "but recently formed" (because only a few hours before she had been created from Adam's rib, which novelty likewise should have made her timid). **UNDER which**: that is, under which ignorance, had she been devoted and obedient, I would have felt those ineffable and unspeakable delights and pleasures "sooner and for a longer time."

---

...born in this paradise and having inhabited it for a longer time, and having lasted in a state of innocence; nor would I have contracted **original sin**.

Proceeding forward, the poet approached closer to the splendor and better heard the song "among so many first-fruits," because these were the first things he began to see and hear in contemplation. **Of eternal pleasure**: that is, of the supreme good which consists in contemplation. **AND DESIRING**: because our soul is not content until it arrives at the highest point. **LIKE a fire set ablaze the air became**: He always places **love** before intelligence, of which I have many times warned the reader.

<summary>Dante follows Matelda along the river Lethe toward the East, experiencing a divine flash of light and melody representing the Holy Spirit, while reflecting on how Eve's original sin deprived humanity of these delights.</summary>

<page-num>229</page-num>
<header>CANTO XXIX</header>

O most holy virgins, if hunger,
cold, or vigils I ever endured for you,
the cause spurs me to claim my reward.
Now it is fitting that Helicon pour for me,
and Urania <note>The Muse of astronomy and heavenly things.</note> help me with her choir
to put into verse things difficult to conceive.

A little further on, seven trees of gold
were falsified in appearance by the long distance
that was still between us and them;
But when I was made so close to them
that the common object, which deceives the false,
did not lose any of its detail through distance,
The faculty that prepares the discourse for reason
grasped that they were candlesticks,
and in the voices of the singing, "Hosanna." <note>original: "osanna"</note>
Above, the beautiful array was flaming,
much brighter than the moon in a clear sky
at midnight in her middle month.
I turned back full of wonder
to the good Virgil, and he answered me
with a look no less burdened with amazement.
Then I returned my gaze to the other things,
which moved toward us so slowly
that they would have been overtaken by new brides.
The lady scolded me: "Why do you burn so
only in the affection of the living lights,
and look not at what comes behind them?"
Then I saw people, as if following their leaders,
coming behind them, dressed in white;
and such whiteness was never seen here.
The water shone on my left side,
and gave back to me my left side,
I looked into it as if into a mirror.

<margin>which reward I hope for because I have suffered for you hunger, cold, and vigils.</margin> **NOW IT IS FITTING** that Helicon pours for me. By "pouring" he denotes the supreme abundance and flow of favor from the Muses which he needs; and he uses Helicon, the mountain, to represent the fountain that is consecrated to the Muses. And he asks for the fountain of favor from **URANIA**. Wishing to treat heavenly things, it is fitting to invoke that Muse who is named after the heavens, as we showed in the first canticle. **A DIFFICULT THING** to conceive and put into verse: He makes the listener attentive by demonstrating the greatness of the matter, which cannot be expressed in verse without difficulty; and at the same time, he shows that he does not invoke Urania without need.

He turned to Virgil, questioning him about the nature of the thing. But Virgil did not answer him with words, but showed in his look that he too was full of wonder. This signifies that human science is more likely to be amazed by such great things than to understand them. Then follows: **THEN I RETURNED**, that is, from the sight of Virgil to whom I had turned my gaze, and I returned to look at the other things, and especially the candlesticks of which we have already spoken. **THE LADY**, that is, Matelda, replied to me saying that it is not enough to burn only in the affection of the first lights, that is, in the love and desire of these seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, but one must also consider the effects that follow from this guidance of the Holy Spirit, which is the true leader and guide of every virtuous operation. **I SAW PEOPLE THEN**: He means, as I said shortly before, those holy men, patriarchs and prophets and other learned men who believed in the coming Christ, for whom white robes are fitting because faith must be pure. Thus, the ancient Gentiles, when they sacrificed to Faith, held their hands wrapped in white cloth. And he adds that they were of such whiteness as was never seen in this world; and allegorically he means that our current age does not have that pure faith which those people had. **THE WATER** of the river already mentioned **SHONE** from the lights of the candlesticks. This river is the meditation and consideration of innocence, which makes one forget vices; and illuminated by the Holy Spirit, it reflects to the one who looks in it their left side, that is, it frees the heart of the one who considers it from all sensuality by which they were previously held. And this is as far as the allegory goes; but according to the literal sense, it is also true.

<column-break/>

And in the place where it is most required, I will strive to explain the cause. **THE SOUND** for song: We understand that the first sound heard was singing. **O MOST HOLY**: Deservedly, having to treat most difficult and divine matters, he distrusts human talent if he does not have help from the Muses. Therefore, necessity spurs him to invoke them; and the vigils and labors he has endured for them give him hope of being heard by them. For he arranges it thus: "O most holy virgins, the cause which proceeds from necessity spurs me to call you, that is, to ask for mercy, if I have ever suffered..."

<image-desc>Decorative initial D in red ink.</image-desc> He demonstrates that by approaching the place, he grasped the truth of what the excessive interval between him and the candlesticks and the voices had falsified; for the golden candlesticks had appeared to him as trees. And here, briefly, like a supreme philosopher, he declares what thing deceives the visual power and how one can escape the deception. And allegorically he shows that even the sight of the mind is often deceived at the beginning of an investigation when it is still so far from a conclusion that things appear to be what they are not. Then, having seen Virgil, I returned my gaze to the other things; that is, I turned my eyes back to the candlesticks, whose meaning will soon appear, and which were coming more slowly than new brides walk. Matelda, that is, Christian doctrine, demonstrates the order and process of human salvation from the creation of man until the advent of Christ. Thus, the sun that sees first figures the sun of the Holy Spirit, which illuminated the paradise of delights and Adam and Eve, our first parents. Then the seven candlesticks were the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, which before the incarnation of the Divine Word came slowly to men and to few, because it was not yet the time of Grace. Then, by those he places dressed in white, he signifies those who believed in the coming Christ. And by the twenty-four elders, he means the twenty-four books of the Bible. It also signifies the four Evangelists, the theological virtues, the four cardinal virtues, the Acts of the Apostles, and the Epistles written by Saint Luke and Saint Paul, and the four disciples who wrote the other Epistles, and likewise the Apocalypse of Saint John. By these things, he shows that whoever wishes to pass to the state of innocence and forget vices entirely must exercise themselves in the study of the aforementioned things, all of which the Bible contains. But returning to the text above, we say **THE FACULTY GRASPED** the candlesticks, that is, it was able to discern that those were not trees but candlesticks; and similarly, it discerned that the voices, which at first were confused because of the distance, said **HOSANNA** (in Hebrew, this means "Save" or "Quicken" or "Make us safe"). **ABOVE** was flaming the beautiful array; he uses "beautiful array" for the candlesticks. It **FLAMED** above, casting flames from its highest part. **MUCH BRIGHTER**: The meaning is that the splendor of the candlesticks was greater than that spread by the moon when it is clear and in its fifteenth day <note>A full moon.</note> and at midnight. **I TURNED BACK** full of wonder: He shows what great wonder he took from such light and...

The accompanying commentary explains the allegory of the procession, identifying the candlesticks as the gifts of the Holy Spirit and the white-clad figures as the precursors of Christ.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the procession in the Earthly Paradise. Following the recognition of the seven golden candlesticks, Landino now interprets the visual phenomena of the colored streaks in the sky and the arrival of the twenty-four elders and the four living creatures, mapping them to the Sacraments, the books of the Bible, and the Gospels.</meta>

PVRGATORIO

He continues by narrating that when the lights were already so near that there was no other distance or interval between them and the poet than the river, he gave a **halt** <note>meaning: delay</note> to his **steps** <note>meaning: he stopped</note>. But the flames of the candlesticks continued, proceeding forward, and behind them they left the air painted with **seven lists** and lines of the brush, just as a painter does when he wishes to make a line. These were of the colors that the sun makes in the celestial arch <note>the rainbow</note> or the moon when it enters white clouds; the colors of the arch are blood red, green, and white. These **banners**—that is, these streaks—were greater than his sight because he could not see their end. But according to what he judged, they were not elevated from the flowers—that is, from the ground—which was flowering more than ten paces across. But

---

## When from my bank I had such a position
## That only the river kept me distant,
## To see better, I gave a halt to my steps,
## And I saw the flames go before,
## Leaving behind them the air painted
## In a way that resembled brush strokes,
## So that there above it remained distinct
## In seven lists, all in those colors
## From which the sun makes its arch and Delia <note>The moon (Diana), sister of Delos-born Apollo.</note> her girdle.
## These banners behind were greater
## Than my sight; and as far as I could judge,
## The outermost were ten paces apart.

<column-break/>

Allegorically, understand that between the candlesticks and Dante there was no other interval than the river. Because he had been purged of vices, nothing else stood in the way of his being joined with the gifts of the Holy Spirit except drinking from the river and washing—that is, extinguishing every thought that could ignite sensuality, in a way that he would entirely forget it. The seven lists of colors already mentioned, proceeding from the seven candlesticks, signify the **seven sacraments** of the Church, which are sacred signs of a sacred thing. Therefore, they are signs of the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, and thus he feigns that they are figured by them. And that the candlesticks and the lists are ten paces high from the ground—because outside of the meadow they signify the first exemplary virtuous life—is achieved in these seven gifts with the **ten commandments**. For the primitive church called the **Synagogue** was earthly and full of figures, signs, and creation; and therefore it is signified by flowers, which are not the fruit but signify the future fruit. Therefore, through the passion of Christ, we can climb with the ladder of the ten commandments to the seven graces of the Holy Spirit, which are **Fear, Piety, Fortitude, Knowledge, Counsel, Wisdom, and Intellect**. As a sign of these, the New Church holds the seven sacraments, which are **Chrism <note>Confirmation</note>, Baptism, Orders, Eucharist,**

---

**Penance, Extreme Unction, and Marriage.** The author thus feigns that **Chrism** is of a red color, which is a sign of **Fear** that is rooted in the charity that man has toward God. From this is born humility, which is against pride. **Baptism** is a vermilion or blood-red color, which signifies **Piety** founded on the charity that man has toward his neighbor, which is less than that toward God; it is figured by blood-red or vermilion, and from it is born the love that is against envy. **Orders** is of a green color, which signifies **Fortitude**; it is rooted in the hope we have in God. From this is born religion, which is against wrath. The **Eucharist** is of a white color, which signifies **Knowledge** <term>Scientia: here meaning spiritual knowledge or science</term> founded on faith, which man has in the body of Christ that comes upon the altar. From this is born virtuous operation against sloth. **Penance** is of a green color, which is a sign of **Counsel**, rooted in hope in God. From this is born moderation against avarice. **Extreme Unction** is of a red color, which is a sign of **Wisdom** rooted in charity toward one's neighbor; from which is born abstinence against gluttony. And **Marriage** is of a blood-red or vermilion color, which is a sign of **Intellect**, rooted in charity toward one's neighbor. From this is born chastity against lust.

---

## Under so beautiful a sky as I have described,
## Twenty-four elders, two by two,
## Came crowned with lily flowers.
## They all sang: "Blessed art thou
## Among the daughters of Adam, and blessed
## Be thy beauties unto eternity."
## After the flowers and the other fresh herbs
## Opposite me on the other bank
## Were free of those elect people,
## Just as light follows light in the sky,
## There came after them four animals,
## Each crowned with green foliage.
## Each was feathered with six wings,
## The feathers full of eyes; and the eyes of Argus,
## If they were alive, would be such as these.

<column-break/>

After the seven candlesticks and the crowd dressed in white, there came **twenty-four elders**, by whom are denoted the **twenty-four books of the Bible**, in which all Christian doctrine is contained. These are divided thus: they come two by two to show that the two Testaments are joined, because in the Old are contained the mysteries and the figures, and in the New the things prefigured in the mysteries of the Old. **For example** <note>original: "Verbi gratia"</note>, in the Old, Jonah is swallowed by the fish; in the New, Christ is placed in the tomb. They were dressed in white, which expresses the pure truth of this doctrine, clean of all falsehood, and faith. They were crowned with lily flowers—that is, the lily, which denotes faith. And these are the twenty-four elders of whom John wrote in the **Apocalypse**. **Under so beautiful a sky**: beautiful air. For the Latins use **Sky for air** <note>original: "Celū pro aere"</note>; hence Virgil: *Sea and lands and the deep sky* <note>original: "Mare ac terras celūq; profūdū"</note>. And he calls it beautiful air because it was adorned with the seven lists. **I have described** <note>original: "HO Diuiſo"</note>: I have distinguished and described. **Elders** <note>original: "SENIORI"</note>: old men, and it is a Latin word, *senes* (old men), whence *seniores*. **All singing "Blessed art thou"**: All singing, they praised the Virgin; for the Old Testament contains nothing other than mysteries and prophecies that denote the incarnation of the Word in the Virgin, who was greeted by the Angel Gabriel as blessed above all women, all of whom are daughters of Adam. **Thy beauties**: thy virtues. For the beauties of the soul are, without any comparison, more excellent than the beauties of the body; and

---

nothing is beautiful in the soul that is not virtue, and nothing is virtue that is not beautiful. **After the flowers**: the meaning is, after all these people had passed that part of the meadow which was opposite me on the other bank of the river. For a place remains free when he who treads upon it has passed and left it clear. And thus by their transit, he demonstrates that the **Old Testament** had already passed, in which men were still servants of sin. Whence followed the **New**, in which our redemption and liberation came. **Just as light**: He excellently expresses the progress of all these people and the splendor of them all, saying that as in the turning of the heavens one never sees it vacant of lights, but always after one star comes another, so after the lights of those who had already passed came the **four animals** with similar splendor. **Just as light**: that is, a star. **Follows** <note>original: "SECONDA"</note>: follows the **light**—the star that goes before it. And allegorically we can say that the mind of one who studies sacred theology is, from time to time, illuminated with splendors and with knowledge; because one thing already understood opens the intellect to understand the next that follows. Furthermore, it demonstrates the perfect order.

<summary>Dante describes the symbolic banners of light following the seven candlesticks and the arrival of twenty-four elders representing the books of the Bible. Landino provides an extensive allegorical map linking the lights to the Seven Sacraments and the Seven Gifts of the Holy Spirit.</summary>
<keywords>Seven Sacraments, Seven Gifts of the Holy Spirit, twenty-four elders, Old Testament, New Testament, Virgin Mary, biblical allegory, color symbolism, Landino commentary, Purgatorio Canto 29</keywords>

--- Page 467 ---
<meta>This page continues the commentary on the divine procession in Purgatory. Having described the seven candlesticks, the commentator now turns to the four living creatures (the Evangelists) and the triumphal chariot representing the Church, pulled by the Gryphon (Christ).</meta>

PURGATORY

Because previously the hemispheres and prophecies had passed, now follow the things prefigured. **Four animals**: here are prefigured the four Evangelists: Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John. **Matthew** in human form: because more than the others he recounted the humanity of Christ. **Mark** in the form of a lion: because just as the lion brings his cubs back to life with his roar after the third day <note>A common medieval belief that lion cubs were born dead and awakened by their father's breath or roar on the third day, symbolizing the Resurrection.</note>, so Mark, more clearly than the others, told of the resurrection of Christ. **Luke** in the form of an ox: because just as the ox makes a great lowing, so Luke more clearly than the others writes of the preaching of Christ. **John** in the form of an eagle: because just as the eagle flies above other birds and keeps its eyes fixed on the light, so John above all others extended his intellect to the divinity of Christ and was better able to look upon the splendor of it. **Each crowned with green leaves**: to denote that the evangelical doctrine, because it is true, will always stay green; and I believe he means here green leaves for the laurel, a triumphal tree, because this doctrine, which alone is true, has conquered all others that are false and triumphs over them. **Each was winged with six wings**. The poet follows the Apocalypse of John, who likewise describes them with six wings, of which two are raised to the head to denote its beginning. Two were lowered to the feet to denote progress until the end. And two wings at the arms and hands <note>Original: "magne," here referring to the limbs of action or operation.</note> which signify their operations. And because the height of his divinity was little understood by them through natural reason, therefore Ezekiel feigns that with the feathers that went to the head and with those that went to the feet they covered the body—that is, the height of Christ and the divinity which was little revealed to them—and the depth which signifies the advent of Christ, of which they did not know the time. And although John places six and Ezekiel four, nevertheless it returns to the same meaning: because the Evangelist understood reason and intellect, and the prophet only intellect. But the length, which was the corporal life of Christ, and the beatitude, which was the doctrine, were known to them. **The feathers full of eyes**: because of the eyes which John says they had inside and out, it signifies the circumspection <term>circumspection: the quality of looking at all sides of a matter</term> that God granted to the Evangelists to see the divinity of the Word veiled beneath humanity inside, and the humanity joined with divinity outside. So that these two natures made one individual. Furthermore <note>original: "preterea"</note>, according to John they had eyes in front and behind. Which signifies that they considered the prophecies and mysteries of the Old Testament from the beginning of the world until the sixth age in which Christ came; and from him began the seventh; and from the seventh until the end of the world, which will be when Christ comes to judge. **And the eyes of Argus**: Argus had a hundred eyes and was placed by Juno to guard Io, who had been transformed into a cow, so that Jove could not return her to human form. Wherefore Mercury, sent by Jove, killed him; and Juno adorned the feathers of her peacocks with those eyes.

> To describe their form, I no longer scatter
> rhymes, reader, for other expense constrains me
> so much that in this I cannot be generous.
> But read Ezekiel, who depicts them
> as he saw them coming from the cold region
> with wind, with cloud, and with fire.
> And such as you will find them in his pages,
> such they were here, except that for the wings
> John is with me and departs from him.
>
> The space inside those four contained
> a triumphal chariot on two wheels
> which came pulled by the neck of a Gryphon.
> It extended one and the other wing upward
> between the middle and the three and three lists
> so that by cleaving nothing, he did no harm.
> They rose so high that they were not seen;
> it had limbs of gold when it was a bird
> and the others white mixed with vermilion.
> Not only did Rome never rejoice
> Africanus or Augustus with so beautiful a golden chariot,
> but that of the Sun would be poor beside it.
> That of the Sun which, straying, was burned
> by the prayer of the devout Earth
> when Jove was mysteriously just.

<column-break/>

The poet excuses his brevity, saying that he cannot be broad and liberal in scattering more rhymes to describe the Evangelists because "other expense constrains him": as if to say, because it is necessary that he describe something else. **But read Ezekiel**: He was one of the prophets who, with Jehoiachin <note>Original: "Ioachim"</note>, King of Jerusalem, was led as a servant into Babylon. And at one time he prophesied in Chaldea to his fellow Hebrew servants, and Jeremiah in Judea. And such as they were there: such they appeared in that procession as Ezekiel describes them. **Except that as for the wings, John is with me**: he is in my favor and defends my opinion, and departs from Ezekiel. Because John imagines them with six wings and Ezekiel with four. Of which two covered their bodies and two from one were joined with the feathers of the other.

Between the four animals described above was a triumphal chariot of gold with two wheels, pulled by a bird, a **Gryphon**, which extended its wings upward between the middle list and the other three and three, without touching any of them, and these wings rose so high they could not be seen. And the limbs of the Gryphon which are bird-like were of gold; the others white mixed with vermilion. This **chariot** is the New Church; and the **two wheels** are the Old and New Testaments. And truly a triumphal chariot, because no other synagogue or congregation triumphs over the devil and remains victorious in battles except the Church founded in Christ. And of gold: because it is the best, most beautiful, and most incorruptible. And in the midst of the four Evangelists: because the subject and the matter of the New Church is the evangelical truth, and every saying refers to that. The bird **Gryphon**, which is of two natures—because the first parts are of a bird and the last of a lion—signifies Christ, who is of two natures: divine and human. Therefore the bird part represents the divinity, and that of the lion the humanity. Christ therefore built the Church, and he pulls it to the will and obedience of the Father. The wings of the Gryphon are two. The right demonstrates divine justice, and the left mercy, which while he was on earth he always extended to heaven and joined with the Father and the Holy Spirit. These extend between the **seven lists**: which are the seven sacraments, signs of the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, in a way that they place in the middle that of the center, which is the **Eucharist**: that is, the most holy body of Christ which truly is in the middle between justice and mercy. Because Christ instituted this sacrament as a sign of justice, with which we might return to the Father such sacrifice as we are bound to give, because no other was suitable for the divine excellence. He instituted it also as a sign of mercy, because with it we attain the mercy of God, which—and not by any debt—gives us eternal life. Outside of the right wing remain three lists, which are Chrism, Baptism, and Holy Orders <note>Original: "ordine"</note>, signs of three gifts of the Holy Spirit proceeding from divine justice: Fear, Piety, and Fortitude. Because by God preserving us in these three graces, we can justly please God and merit eternal life. From the left is Penance, Extreme Unction, and Matrimony, and they are...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the divine procession within the Earthly Paradise. # CANTO XXVIII

from the wing of mercy. They are signs of the other three gifts of the Holy Spirit: counsel, wisdom, and intellect. The Eucharist, which is a sign of knowledge <term>scientia; in medieval theology, the gift of the Holy Spirit that allows one to recognize the things of the world in relation to God</term>, stands in the middle of two wings for the reasons already stated above. Nor should anyone say because of this that the poet divides justice from mercy, one on the right and the other on the left wing. Rather, he intends that in those on the right, justice proceeds, and in those on the left, mercy proceeds. And then he says that the wings did no harm to anyone’s sight. Now returning to the exposition of the text:

->**The Triumphal Chariot**<-

A triumphal chariot was established among the ancients as a prize of honor for the leader of an army who had brought a full victory over enemies, having killed at least five thousand of them in one battle and broken or put to flight the rest. Among the Romans, no one could triumph who had not been a dictator, consul, or praetor in the army. The triumpher rode in an adorned chariot drawn by four white horses, and the Senate went before him all the way to the Capitol, where he sacrificed bulls. But the Lacedaemonians <note>The Spartans</note> had a custom that if the triumpher had conquered enemies with his cunning, he sacrificed an ox; if through battle, he sacrificed a rooster—valuing things done with prudence much more. This is because prudence is proper to man, whereas force is common to animals.

They say that Bacchus was the first to invent the triumph after conquering the Eastern regions, and his chariot was drawn by elephants. Sesostris, King of Egypt, out of supreme pride, put four of the kings subject to him to the yoke. The triumpher sat in the chariot on a golden seat with a **palm-embroidered robe** <note>original: "veste palmata"; a garment decorated with palm leaves, signifying victory</note>. His face was painted red in imitation of the element of fire; a gold chain hung from his neck, to which a golden **bulla** <note>A locket or amulet worn by Roman youths and triumphers</note> was attached; he wore a laurel crown and held an ivory scepter. They were not seen <note>referring to the tops of the wings</note> because they rise up to God, whom no one can comprehend; and justice goes to the Father, and mercy to the Holy Spirit.

**The golden limbs**: these denote divinity. **And the others white mixed with vermilion**: these two colors, which are of flesh and blood, denote the humanity of Christ: the white his innocence, the red his charity. **Not that Rome**: the meaning is that not only the triumphal chariots used in Rome and many other places—most notably by Africanus <note>Scipio Africanus, the conqueror of Hannibal</note> and Augustus—could equal this chariot, but even the chariot of the Sun, which the poets describe, would seem poor in comparison to this one. **Africanus**: he means either the Elder, who defeated Hannibal, or the Younger, who destroyed Carthage. **Augustus**: we wrote of him in the first canto of the first canticle. **That of the sun which straying was burned**: this touches on the fable of Phaethon, which we have narrated elsewhere.

*Three women in a circle from the right wheel*
*came dancing, one so red*
*that she would hardly be noticed inside a fire.*
*The other was as if her flesh and bones*
*had been made of emerald;*
*the third seemed like newly fallen snow.*
*And now they seemed led by the white one,*
*now by the red; and at the song of this one*
*the others took their pace, slow or swift.*
*From the left four made festive,*
*dressed in purple, following the lead*
*of one of them who had three eyes in her head.*

<column-break/>

He places at the right wheel, which signifies the New Testament: **Three women** who came dancing in a circle, by whom he means the three Theological Virtues, because these were less known in the Old Testament than in the New. **One so red**: this is **Charity**, which is the fervent love of God and neighbor. Therefore he places her in the color of fire, and adds that if she had been inside a fire, she would not have been distinguished from it, to note that the fervor of charity is no less than that of fire. **The other was as if she had flesh and bones of emerald**: that is, she was green like an emerald, and this is **Hope**, which must always remain green and never fail. Theologians define it as a certain expectation of future glory produced by the grace of God and preceding merit. **The third seemed like newly fallen snow**: this is **Faith**, which for the reasons already stated above must be pure and white. And faith is the "substance of things to be hoped for and the evidence <note>original: "argumentatē"; likely a corruption of "argumentum"</note> of things not seen." We will treat these theological virtues in the twenty-fourth canto of *Paradise*.

**And now she seemed led by the white, now by the red**: he writes this because sometimes charity generates faith and hope. But hope never goes before faith and charity. **And at the song of this Charity, the others took their pace, slow or swift**: this signifies nothing other than that faith and hope move only as much as charity moves them.

And the chariot—that is, the **Militant Church**—is in the middle of the seven virtues. Because with the three theological virtues on the right hand she governs spiritual things, as they are more noble; and with the four cardinal virtues she governs temporal things, which, being less noble, are on the left. Hence Solomon says: *In her left hand are riches and glory* <note>original: "In sinistra illius diuitie & gloria"; Proverbs 3:16</note>. On the left side, by that wheel representing the Old Testament, he places the four cardinal virtues, of which the Old Testament speaks. He introduces these dressed in purple to denote charity and the fervor of love, without which no one can possess these virtues. **Following the lead of one of them who had three eyes in her head**: these virtues are four, and each has its office, which is not perfect if **Prudence** does not show it. For example, the office of **Fortitude** is not merely to endure laborious anguish and horrible dangers to preserve the country, parents, and friends with honor; but it does not know by itself the manner or the way it must hold to achieve this unless Prudence teaches it. Similarly, Prudence shows **Justice** how much it must attribute to each person, and **Temperance** which pleasures it must flee.

Now, since the poet places these four virtues here, I judge that the place requires us to briefly state their origin and distinction. There are, therefore, in our souls four principles and fountains impressed by nature from which the four virtues proceed. First, everyone knows they have in themselves a supreme desire to understand and know everything. This is why it is troublesome to us when we were or are deceived by others. This desire induces in us **Prudence**. Furthermore, we have a certain generosity given to our soul by the same nature which does not want us to submit to others except to reason and honesty; from this generosity, **Fortitude** is born. There also arises in us a sense of shame and an obstacle which restrains us from doing or saying anything that is not fitting, or from lapsing into shameful pleasures; and this is the progenitor of **Temperance**. In the fourth place is **Justice**, which nature produces in us because, man being desirous of prevailing in the fellowship and company of other men, he knows that this fellowship cannot last unless one gives to each what is fitting.

These are four—I do not say virtues—but principles and seeds of virtue by which we can achieve the perfect virtues: **Prudence** is that by which we have certain knowledge of things that should be sought or fled; the poet gives her three eyes. As Seneca writes, the prudent man must foresee the future, dispense the present, and remember the past. **Justice** is a habit of soul which, preserving the common utility, attributes to each what is fitting according to their dignity. **Fortitude** is that which, with certain reason, pushes against danger and to support every laborious difficulty. **Temperance** is that by which we restrain ourselves from every dishonest pleasure. You will find these virtues and the species of each explained in various places in the first canticle.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the divine procession in Purgatory. # PURGATORIO

> Following all the manner described,
> I saw two old men in different dress,
> but alike in dignified and steadfast conduct.
> One showed himself to be a familiar
> of that supreme Hippocrates, whom nature
> made for the animals she holds most dear;
> The other showed the opposite care,
> with a sword so bright and sharp
> that even on this side of the river it caused me fear.

So that nothing is omitted and the books of the New Testament proceed in order—having already placed the four Evangelists and the theological virtues—there follows the placement of the Acts of the Apostles, which Luke wrote in addition to his Gospel. He then places the Epistles of Paul. These two things are shown allegorically through two old men who are said to have "different dress": because Saint Luke came in the habit of a physician, as if he were a disciple of Hippocrates, whose art is to heal men and keep them alive. Paul came with a sword, which is an instrument for taking life. Behold, therefore, the dress was different because Luke showed the habit of a physician who maintains life. **HIPPOCRATES**: that is, the famous physician. **Nature**: God, who is <term>nature naturante; a philosophical term for God as the creative force that gives nature its laws</term>. **Made for the animals she holds most dear**: the meaning is that nature created Hippocrates for the benefit of men, who are the animals most dear to God. Hippocrates was from the island of Chios, a most noble physician of whom we wrote in the fourth canto of the first canticle <note>Inferno</note>. Luke of Antioch was Syrian by nation; he wrote the Gospel in Antioch. He was very eminent in medicine and was a disciple of the apostles; besides the Gospel, he wrote the book titled the Acts of the Apostles. He died in Bithynia in the seventy-fourth year of his life, observing his vow of virginity without fail. **The other showed the opposite care**: this is Paul, who, having the sword, does not have the habit of healing but of killing. **Bright and sharp** is the sword attributed to Paul because of his supreme sharpness, vehemence, and endurance of spirit.

---

> Then I saw four of humble appearance,
> and behind them all a single old man
> coming asleep, with a keen face.
> And these seven were dressed like the first group,
> but they did not have a garden of lilies
> surrounding their heads;
> Rather of roses and other red flowers;
> from a short distance I would have sworn
> they were all burning above their brows.

¶ These **four of humble appearance** are the four apostles who wrote the letters called "canonical," which are placed in the Bible after the Acts of the Apostles. They are James (the brother of Christ), Peter, John, and Jude (the brother of James). These men wrote mystical epistles that are as brief as they are long: brief in words, but long in meaning. **IN HUMBLE appearance**: because of their humility of soul and their poor and low social status. **A single old man**: this refers to John regarding the Apocalypse <note>the Book of Revelation</note>, which is the last book of the New Testament. **ASLEEP**: this denotes that the visions Saint John describes in the Apocalypse were received when he fell asleep on the breast of Christ during the Last Supper; he described them later in his old age on the island of Patmos. **With a keen face**: subtle in appearance. He says this because John was of high and profound intellect. **And these seven**: that is, the first two old men (Paul and Luke), the four of humble appearance (James, Peter, John, and Jude for their epistles), and John for the Apocalypse. **WERE dressed like the first group**: because they were similarly in white robes. But they did not have garlands of lilies like the others. **Did not have a garden of lilies**: <note>original: "brolo"</note> a garden or greenery, as the word means in the <term>Lombard tongue; a regional Italian dialect</term>. In short, the twenty-four books of the Bible <note>the Old Testament elders</note> have crowns of lilies because, without faith, studying them is worth nothing. The Evangelists have green, signifying hope, because the beginning of the Gospels is the vigor of hope; such study would be in vain if we did not hope for what they promise. And these final seven have red flowers because their principle is charity <note>divine love</note>.

---

> And when the chariot was directly opposite me,
> there was a thunderclap; and those worthy people
> seemed to have their forward movement forbidden,
> halting there with the leading banners.

¶ When the chariot, which was proceeding forward, arrived at that place which was directly across from me <note>Dante</note>, a thunderclap was heard which seemed to forbid those worthy people from going further. Therefore they stopped, and even the leading banners—which were the seven candelabra—stopped. The Griffin, which is Christ, has therefore drawn the chariot—that is, the Synagogue transformed into the Holy Church—by his passion and death until it was opposite Dante—that is, in the sight of every man—and he has made it manifest to all. Certainly, whoever studies the sacred letters and proceeds in this order described by the poet sees and understands his own salvation. This is the path that leads us to the contemplation of eternal life and divine things, in which our happiness consists once we have drunk from the river Lethe and washed ourselves in it; that is, once we are in the virtues of the soul already purged, in which we entirely forget not only vices but everything that could inflame us toward them. And afterward, the river Eunoë, through which the love of the virtues of the Supreme Good is kindled in us—which is inestimable—so that on earth we are like angels. **There was a thunderclap**: literally, such a thunder in this place—which is above the third region where no vapor can rise—must be supernatural and made by God as a sign for the chariot to stop. But allegorically, according to Francesco da Buti <note>a 14th-century commentator</note>, we shall understand that from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil (where the disobedience of our first parents was born) until the wood of the cross and the crucifixion, humanity went toward the "west"—because they were going to Hell and the good to Limbo. But after Christ pulled the chariot to the river Jordan and created baptism, then the thunder was heard—that is, the voice of God the Father toward Christ as he was being baptized, which was: <note>original: "hic est filius meus dilectus in quo michi bene complacui"</note> "This is my beloved son, in whom I am well pleased." Therefore, after this time, humanity left the law of servitude and entered that of grace, and stopped going further "west"; the law of Moses and circumcision ended, and the Gospel and baptism began. Here God willed that through obedience we should return to the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. Hence, below, the poet will show that these people have turned around. **Seemed to have their forward movement forbidden**: it seemed to those people that the thunder forbade and prohibited them from going any further—understand this as the Law of Moses—halting instead in the Gospel law. **WITH the leading banners**: with the gifts of the Holy Spirit and the seven gifts of the Holy Church, and with all the other things already narrated.

<header>CANTO .XXX.</header>

### CANTO XXX OF THE SECOND CANTICLE OF DANTE

<margin>232</margin>
When the Seven Stars <note>The "septentrion" or Great Bear constellation, here symbolizing the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit.</note> of the highest heaven,
which never knew setting nor rising,
nor any other mist than the veil of sin,
And which made everyone there aware
of their duty, just as the lower constellation <note>The physical stars used by sailors for navigation.</note> does
for whoever turns the tiller to reach port,
Stopped still; the truthful people,
who had come first between the griffin and the stars,
turned to the chariot as if toward their peace;
And one of them, as if sent from heaven,
singing "Come, spouse from Lebanon" <note>original: "Veni sponsa de Libano"</note>
cried out three times, and all the others followed.
Just as the blessed at the final summons
shall rise quickly, each from his cavern,
singing with their reclothed voices,
So upon the divine chariot <term>basterna</term> <note>A covered litter or carriage used in ancient Rome for priests or noblewomen.</note>
there rose up a hundred at the voice of such an elder,
ministers and messengers of eternal life.
All were saying, "Blessed are you who come" <note>original: "benedictus qui uenis"</note>
while throwing flowers above and around,
"Oh, give lilies with full hands!" <note>original: "manibus o date lilia plenis"</note>

I once saw, at the beginning of the day,
the eastern part all rosy,
and the rest of the sky adorned with beautiful serenity;
And the face of the sun rising shaded,
so that through the tempering of vapors
the eye could endure it for a long time:
Thus, within a cloud of flowers...

<column-break/>

This thirtieth canto of Purgatory contains the form in which Beatrice appears to the poet, how she rebukes him, and finally how Virgil abandons him. **WHEN THE Seven Stars.** The meaning is: when the aforementioned chariot came to a halt. The people who had come before the griffin, and the griffin himself, turned toward the chariot. But by way of a metaphor, he calls this chariot the "Seven Stars of the first heaven," meaning the Empyrean heaven where the seats of the blessed are. Just as the Seven Stars of the eighth sphere <note>The physical sky seen from Earth.</note> has seven stars that form a horn-shape before the griffin’s chariot. "Of the first heaven": to distinguish it from the constellation we see in the eighth sphere. **Which never felt setting nor rising:** Because just as our northern stars are so high and close to our pole that they are always visible, and do not act like other stars that now rise and now go below, so the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit feel no "setting" (meaning ending) nor "rising" (meaning beginning), since being eternal they have no beginning. **Nor have any other veil than of sin.** Because it is not like our northern stars, which are often taken from our sight by darkness and by clouds that occupy the air; but these gifts cannot be hidden from us or covered by any other veil than by fault and sin. For only sin is what hides the gifts of the Holy Spirit from man. **And which made there:** he follows the metaphor already made of these Seven Stars to our own in the eighth sphere. He says that just as our northern stars—where the North Star is—make the pilot aware of how to steer his tiller if he wants to arrive safely in port, so it did there in Paradise, in the state of innocence. For whoever wants to come to bliss must steer his ship and direct it according to the guide of the gifts of the Holy Spirit. The text is ordered thus: When the Seven Stars of the first heaven stood still—which never knew setting or rising, and never knew a veil (meaning it never had any covering) except for sin that takes it from us—and which made everyone there in the earthly paradise who followed the candlesticks aware and instructed, just as our lower Seven Stars **DOES**, that is, makes one aware and instructed to take a good journey. **WHOEVER**: meaning anyone who turns the tiller to reach port. When, therefore, these Seven Stars (meaning the seven candlesticks) stopped, **THE TRUTHFUL PEOPLE**: meaning those who were following, whom we showed above to be the holy men of the Old Testament, who truly predicted the future and believed in it. **AND THE GRIFFIN HIMSELF**: meaning Christ. **THEY TURNED** to the chariot: meaning to the Holy Church, **As toward their peace**: meaning as toward their goal. For everything contained in the Old Testament is for the purpose of establishing the Holy Church. **AND ONE OF THEM.** He refers to Solomon, prophesying as something sent from heaven. Foreseeing the future Church founded upon Christ, and how much Christ was to love her, he said in his song <note>The Song of Solomon.</note> in the person of Christ, "Come, spouse from Lebanon" <note>original: "Veni sponsa de libano"</note>, inviting the synagogue of the Jews, which was to change into the Church, to be the spouse of Christ. Solomon therefore predicted how Christ, with his preaching and doctrine, was to call the synagogue to the new Church. **AND ALL THE OTHERS AFTER.** This signifies that just as Solomon predicted the coming Church, so all the other prophets predicted it. **JUST AS THE BLESSED.** He uses an excellent comparison: that just as on the day of the Great Judgment all the blessed will suddenly rise at the sound of angelic trumpets, reclothed in their own flesh from their caverns, so at the voice of Solomon a hundred rose up, and all were saying, "Blessed are you who come." **At the final summons**: at the last request. A "summons" <note>original: "bando"</note> is anything publicly manifested following the sound of the trumpet. **BASTERNA**: The ancients called certain vehicles or carts "basternae," in which Roman priests and Vestal Virgins carried their sacred objects as if in a procession. But by metaphor, he uses "basterna" for the aforementioned chariot. **MINISTERS and messengers of eternal life.** Many understand these to be angels; but perhaps it is better to understand them as the other prophets, who were messengers of eternal life because they predicted future things ordained by God, especially the incarnation of the Word and the new Church, the spouse of Christ. **BLESSED are you who come.** Just as the people of Jerusalem cried out on the feast of Palms when Christ entered the city on an ass. **Give lilies with full hands**: This is a phrase taken from Virgil, who, deploring the death of Marcellus, comforts that such funeral rites be adorned with lilies and flowers. Wherefore he says in the sixth book: "Give lilies with full hands; let me scatter purple flowers and at least heap these gifts upon the soul of my descendant" <note>original: "Manibus date lilia plenis Purpureos spargam flores animamque nepotis His saltem accumulem donis."</note>. And in such a way, in passing, he admonishes us to honor the passion of Christ.

He demonstrates that Beatrice appeared to him in a cloud of flowers, in the same way the sun sometimes appears in the morning, shaded by certain vapors which take away so much of its light that a person can endure looking at it. And the cloud of flowers was from when they rose toward heaven from the hands of the angels and when they fell back down. And Beatrice had a white veil on her head, which bound an olive wreath; and she had a red dress underneath and a green mantle on top. He demonstrates that just as it happens that we can see the body of the sun if some thin cloud does not partly extinguish the splendor of the rays, so Dante would not have been able...

...that from angelic hands rose up
and fell back down inside and out.
**Above a white veil, girt with olive,**
**a lady appeared to me under a green mantle,**
**dressed in the color of living flame.**
**And my spirit, which for so long a**
**time had been in her presence**
**without being broken, trembling with wonder.**

<note>The colors Dante describes represent the three theological virtues: White for Faith, Green for Hope, and Red for Charity (Love).</note> and red are Hope and Charity: which three virtues are the foundations of theology. And for this reason, they are called "theological."
AND MY SPIRIT. In the "Life of the Poet" <note>Referring to Landino's own biography of Dante</note> we demonstrated who Beatrice was: the daughter of Folco Portinari. And afterward, in many parts of this poem, it has been made manifest that the chaste love he bore for this woman caused him to reduce the history to a poetic fantasy and fiction; and he places her as the "contemplative life" according to the Christian religion. For this, he was greatly aided by her name: because Beatrice signifies "full of beatitude" <note>The state of supreme blessedness or happiness.</note>. And nothing abounds in beatitude except the knowledge of God and of celestial things.

**Without having more knowledge through my eyes,**
**by a hidden virtue that moved from her,**
**I felt the great power of ancient love.**
**As soon as the high virtue struck my sight—**
**which had already pierced me**
**before I was out of childhood—**
**I turned to the left with the respect**
**with which a child runs to his mother**
**when he is afraid or when he is distressed,**
**To say to Virgil: "Less than a drop**
**of blood is left in me that does not tremble;**
**I recognize the signs of the ancient flame."**
**But Virgil had left us bereft**
**of himself—Virgil, sweetest father,**
**Virgil to whom I gave myself for my salvation.**

...love of the true good: But false good deceives us. For this reason, we are divided from it until reason begins to have more power over us than appetite. "I turned to the left side": just as the little child turns to his mother when he is afraid or has some injury. But turning, I perceived that Virgil had already departed from me. And he had left both me and Statius <note>The Roman poet Statius, who has been traveling with Dante and Virgil through the upper levels of Purgatory.</note> bereft: because the Virgilian number was diminished. I say "sweetest father" to whom I had given myself for my salvation: and I wanted to say to him, "not a drop of blood remains in me that does not tremble with Love," and I know that it proceeds from Love, because "I recognize the signs of the ancient flame." Which sentence he drew from Virgil, where he said: <term>I recognize the traces of the ancient flame</term> <note>original Latin: "Agnosco veteris vestigia flammae." This is a quote from Virgil's Aeneid, spoken by Dido when she feels love for Aeneas.</note>. He turned to Virgil, which denotes that, struck by love, he recurred to Reason: which is in man to know such love and the cause of it. But Virgil had abandoned him; that is, human reason cannot know by itself without divine grace. But Statius remained: that is, the intellect enlightened by Christian theology. Dante knew her through prevenient grace <note>The grace that comes before human action to predispose a soul toward God.</note>.

**Nor did all that our ancient mother lost**
**avail my cheeks, cleansed with dew,**
**so that they should not turn dark again with weeping.**
**"Dante, because Virgil goes away,**
**do not weep yet, do not weep yet;**
**for you must weep for another sword."**
**Just like an admiral who, at poop and prow,**
**comes to see the people who serve**
**on the other ships, and encourages them to do well,**
**On the left side of the chariot,**
**when I turned at the sound of my name—**
**which of necessity is recorded here—**
**I saw the lady who first appeared to me,**
**veiled under the angelic festival.**

<column-break/>

...fully endure the splendor of Beatrice’s face if there had not been an obstacle in the form of a cloud and flowers that rained down around her. This signifies that we could not understand divine and incorporeal things—which theologians treat when speaking of God—if they did not make them palpable with some similitude of corporeal things. Beatrice’s head was covered with a white veil and crowned with olive. Some interpret the veil as practice and the olive for wisdom, because it is the tree consecrated to Minerva <note>The Roman goddess of wisdom.</note>. To me, it seems that Theology must have the white veil for Faith—as he has placed elsewhere—and the crown of olive denotes Peace, according to what all other poets say: because Theology, founded in Faith, gives peace and tranquility to whoever follows it. The green garment...

**W**ITHOUT FROM THE EYES. The meaning is that although my eyes did not recognize her, nonetheless a hidden virtue moving from her made me feel the great power that the ancient love held. He feigns, then, to have been in love with Beatrice since childhood; and now, not because he recognized her face, but through a hidden inspiration proceeding from her, he felt the ancient love again. This denotes that even from tender years, man begins to love Beatrice: that is, the supreme good, which makes us blessed. But at that time, we recognize it with difficulty. Afterward, sensuality and appetite—which twist us toward the way of pleasures and the goods of fortune—become so powerful that we follow those as the supreme good. And in this way, we distance ourselves from Beatrice so that our eyes, guided by appetite, no longer recognize her, because not seeing anything but pleasure, one did not believe there was any other good than that. But after we are purged of vices and have come to the state of innocence, prevenient grace breathes in us—which he calls "hidden virtue"—and this makes us recognize Beatrice, whom we loved from the beginning. And this grace inflames us with her love, she being the supreme good. SOON. Suddenly, through this glory, the "high virtue"—that is, celestial love, which had already pierced me in childhood—struck me in the present. And certainly, it is innate in men...

**T**he loss of Virgil had such power over me that even though I was in the paradise of delights—which the "ancient mother," that is, Eve, the first woman, lost through her disobedience—and though I had cheeks cleansed with dew <note>In Canto I of Purgatorio, Virgil washed Dante's face with dew to remove the stains of Hell.</note>, nonetheless they became dark and mournful with weeping. DARK [ADRE]. That is, "atre"; and *ater* in Latin signifies black, and consequently mournful and sad. DANTE, BECAUSE. Seeing Beatrice, Dante’s grief for the departure of Virgil, she turned to him with these words: "Dante, do not weep because Virgil goes away; for you must yet weep for a GREATER sword." That is, for a greater sorrow, as we shall see shortly below. JUST LIKE AN ADMIRAL. An excellent comparison in which he likens Theology to the admiral of a fleet. For just as the admiral, without leaving his own ship, but appearing now at the poop and now at the prow, comforts those who are on the other ships and ignites them to do well; so Beatrice, on the left side, excited Dante to do what he will hear below. Thus Theology, without leaving the chariot—which signifies the body of all Sacred Scripture—and from the left side...

<summary>Beatrice appears to Dante dressed in symbolic colors, prompting him to turn to Virgil for comfort only to find his guide has vanished. Beatrice then calls Dante by name, telling him not to weep for Virgil but for his own transgressions.</summary>

directing her eyes toward me from across the stream.
All that veil which fell from her head,
encircled by the leaves of Minerva <note>original: "fronde di minerua"; the olive branch, symbolizing both wisdom and the peace of the olive tree.</note>,
did not allow her to appear fully manifest.

Royally, in her bearing still stern <note>original: "proterua"; suggesting a haughty or imperious manner of one who holds authority.</note>,
she continued like one who speaks
and keeps their warmest speech for the end:
"Look at me well! I am indeed, I am indeed Beatrice!
How did you deign to approach the mountain?

My eyes fell down into the sacred fountain;
but seeing myself reflected in it, I drew them back to the grass,
such great shame weighed upon my brow.
Thus the mother seems haughty to the son,
as she appeared to me; for the taste
of bitter pity feels harsh.
She fell silent, and the angels sang
suddenly: "In you, O Lord, have I hoped" <note>original: "In te domine speraui"; the opening of Psalm 31.</note>;
<margin>233</margin> but they did not pass beyond "my feet" <note>original: "pedes meos"; referring to the verse "You have set my feet in a spacious place."</note>.

<column-break/>

the bank which signifies the Old Testament, where the doctrine of the Church is prohibitive and punitive. This is because in the Old Testament, God carried out manifest and swift vengeance. And here, Beatrice threatens Dante. Therefore, she was not on the right side, which signifies the New Testament, where the Church is exhortative and promises eternal life; for as yet she promises him nothing, but rather reproves him. And he turns at the sound of his own name to denote that these words were directed against his sensuality, which Dante represents. And so he says that of necessity it is recorded here. **I SAW THE LADY.** Turning to the sound of the voice, I saw that the one speaking was the lady who had first appeared to me. **VEILED BENEATH** the angelic celebration. Surrounded by the angels, whom we mentioned above singing *Blessed is he who comes* <note>original: "Benedictus qui uenis".</note>. And she directed her eyes toward me from across the stream. **ALL THAT VEIL.** We have shown above what the veil and the garland signify. But here it is added that he recognized her despite the fact that the veil did not let her be seen clearly, to demonstrate that faith does not possess "science" <note>In the medieval sense, "science" refers to certain, proven knowledge, whereas faith deals with things not seen.</note>.

**Royally:** that is, loftily and imperiously without regard, just as kings are accustomed to do. **IN HER BEARING:** In her outward appearance. **STILL:** Here he says that although she was meant to be comforting, she was still stern; that is, haughty. **LIKE** one who speaks and keeps their warmest speech for the end: It is a precept of the art of rhetoric that one who must rebuke and accuse should first demonstrate and prove the error sharply rather than harshly, and then, in the conclusion, with great force and gravity of words and sentences, strike like a lightning bolt and bitterly reprove. But even naturally, anyone who rebukes does this same thing. **LOOK AT ME WELL:** Words full of asperity and vehement reproof. **I AM INDEED, I AM INDEED** Beatrice. As if to say: "That one whom you began to love and then abandoned." **HOW** did you deign to approach the mountain? Some wish to interpret this as a rebuke of presumption, explaining it thus: "How did you judge yourself worthy to approach—that is, to come to the mountain?" as if she said he was not worthy to climb the mountain on whose summit is paradise. **DID YOU NOT KNOW** that here man is happy? You should not have been so bold, not deserving to climb to this happiness. But in my judgment, another explanation fits better. For she speaks to Dante as one often speaks who is indignant toward someone who has left them, and for a long time—as if stunned—has not visited; then, upon their return, we are accustomed to say "How did you deign to come here?" meaning "You seemed so prideful to me that I did not believe you would deign to visit us anymore." And while we say such words, we use irony, as if saying "You should have deigned to come sooner." Therefore: "You who had become so proud, how did you deign to climb the mountain?" as if saying "I have seen you so puffed up with pride that I did not believe you would deign to come." **THE MOUNTAIN:** Allegorically, this refers to contemplation. Up to now, she has rebuked his pride; now she rebukes the folly and ignorance that for a long time he did not realize that man cannot be happy in any other place. This was the reason he was so late in coming. **DID YOU NOT KNOW** that here man is happy? This sentence is not joined to the one above. For one who speaks haughtily uses interrupted speech. Therefore, having said ironically "How did you deign to come to the mountain?", she then adds with supreme gravity: "Did you not know that here man is happy?" As if to say: "O fool, why have you delayed so long, since it is not elsewhere, but here, that man is happy?" And if we wish to join one sentence with the other, we would say: "How did you deign to come to the mountain, which for so long you have despised?" **Did you not know that here man is happy?** As if to say: "Perhaps you want me to believe you did not know it, but I know that you did know it; therefore, this delay of yours has no excuse." But so that we may better understand this entire passage, Beatrice's grievances toward Dante are that he, having loved her in his youth—then in his second age, in which she changed her life and rose from flesh to spirit and was more beautiful—left her for another. Dante feigns this; but we understand it to mean Theology, which is of two kinds: positive and speculative. Positive theology is that which concerns living according to the morality of the active life. Speculation is that which deals with God and separate substances <note>Angels or divine intellects.</note>. He feigns, then, that in his youth he fell in love with Beatrice when she was still in the flesh (that is, he followed the studies of active morality); but afterward, when he began to treat speculative things, he left her. **MY EYES** fell: An excellent sign that, having heard the reproof, he is ashamed of his error and lowers his eyes; and lowering his eyes, he saw his image in the fountain (that is, in the river). This denotes that shame leads you to search your conscience, and in that, you see yourself as you are, whereby your shame increases even more. For this reason, you take your eyes from such a mirror and return them to the grass and the green—that is, to hope. For after the recognition of sin and the shame that comes from it (which makes you repent), despair should not follow; rather, we must trust in the infinite mercy of God and take good hope. **THUS** the mother seems haughty to the son: Just as it seemed to the son that when the mother rebukes him, she is haughty toward him, so it seemed to me that Beatrice was harsh toward me; yet she was being merciful. **SHE** fell silent and the angels sang. Once we have recognized our error shown to us by sacred doctrine, the angels sang; that is, good inspirations invite us to hope. And therefore he feigns that they sing the psalm suited to hope. This is the thirtieth <note>In modern Bibles, this is Psalm 31.</note> *In you, O Lord, have I hoped; let me never be confounded.* In which David, demonstrating the hope he has in God, exhorts every man who repents of his committed fault to do the same. **BUT BEYOND** *my feet they did not pass:* They did not pass the verse of this psalm: *Nor have you shut me up in the hands of the enemy; you have set my feet in a spacious place*; because the rest of the psalm contains other matter.
</columns>

<summary>Beatrice sternly rebukes Dante for his straying from the path of righteousness, prompting a profound sense of shame in him. Landino’s commentary interprets this interaction as an allegory for the soul's transition from moral action to speculative theology and the necessity of repentance and hope.</summary>
