Just as the snow among the living beams <note>Dante uses "living beams" (*vive travi*) to refer to the trees on the mountainside.</note>
along the spine of Italy <note>The Apennine Mountains.</note> congeals,
blown and packed by the Slavic winds <note>The cold winds coming from the north-east (Schiavonía/Slovenia).</note>,
Then, liquefied, it trickles back into itself,
if but the land that loses shadow breathes <note>Referring to Africa or the south; when the southern winds blow, the snow melts.</note>,
just as a candle melts before the fire;
So was I without tears and without sighs
before the song of those who always note <note>The angels.</note>
following the notes of the eternal spheres;
But when I heard in the sweet melodies
their pity for me, more than if they’d said:
“Lady, why do you so undo him?”
The ice that was constricted round my heart
turned into breath and water, and with anguish
through mouth and through eyes issued from my breast.

**THEY ALWAYS NOTE** following the notes of the eternal spheres: Just as a good musician follows the notes written in a book while singing, so the angels, gazing upon the influences and effects that proceed from the perpetual movements of the heavens, sing what they see marked in the fatal order of divine providence. Of which we have spoken and shall speak. **BUT WHEN I HEARD** in the sweet melodies: that is, in the sweet song, which is tempered by various voices. **THEIR PITY**: that is, they had compassion for me, which I understood more in the singing of that psalm than if they had said to Beatrice, "Why do you undo him so?" And certainly, it is the office of theology to rebuke sins with bitterness. But the divine intelligences have compassion for the contrite and humbled heart, which God will not despise. **THE ICE THAT WAS CONSTRICTED** around my heart: fear, because the blood that runs back to the heart induces chill, and fear condenses the cold. Then the force of the heat at the heart thins the frozen thing and liquefies it; whence it distills into tears through the eyes and into sighs through the mouth; and this is what he means by **“I became breath and water.”** <note>original: "Spirito & acqua fessi"</note> This happens when the sacred letters threaten those who, having begun to follow them, leave them; and because of this, having almost fallen into despair, the angels—that is, divine grace—comforting him, brought him back to hope.

She, still standing firm upon the right side
of the chariot, turning then her words
toward those pious substances <note>The angels, referred to in medieval philosophy as "separate substances" because they lack physical bodies.</note>, spoke thus:
“You watch within the eternal day,
so that neither night nor sleep steals from you
one step the world takes on its paths;
Therefore my answer is with greater care
that he who weeps on that side understands me,
so that the fault and grief may be of one measure.

...duty to do. **YOU WATCH** in the eternal day: which is nothing other than contemplating all things as they are understood in God, as if in a purest mirror and in clearest light without any obscurity; because God is the true light that illuminates the whole world, and is light without end; therefore it can truly be called an eternal day. **SO THAT NIGHT** nor sleep steals from you: because you always contemplate 그 light, in which all things are seen, therefore neither night (ignorance) nor sleep (sloth or bodily desire) steals or takes from you any step which the world <note>original: "secolo"; referring to the temporal world or an age of time.</note> makes. **ON ITS PATHS**: that is, through its extensions and progress; because in the angels there falls no ignorance or earthly desire as it weighs upon us, burdened by sin and sensuality. But always contemplating God, they see all things in Him. "Secolo" among the Latins is most often used for a space of a hundred years. Whence they spoke of the "secular games" of Apollo because they were celebrated once every hundred years. But in Sacred Scripture, it signifies time, and time is born from the eternity of God; and it is said to go step by step because it proceeds from instant to instant. **THEREFORE MY ANSWER** is with greater care: as if to say, an answer is not necessary for you; but I have turned my words toward you out of respect for the psalm you sang. But so that he may understand through my careful response how much danger he is in, if he does not understand and learn that the grief and contrition of the sinner must be so great that it equals the fault committed.

Not only by the work of the great wheels <note>The celestial spheres or planets.</note>
which direct every seed to some end
according as the stars are its companions,

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap initial L featuring a figure.</image-desc>
**T**HE meaning is that just as snow, first frozen by northern winds, liquefies by southern winds, and the wax consolidated in the candle liquefies by the fire; so he, first frozen inside by fear, was without tears and sighs before the song of the angels; then, having heard the song which comforted him, the ice liquefied into tears and sighs. **JUST AS SNOW** among the living beams. "Beams" (*travi*) are properly cut and prepared trees, but he uses "beams" for trees; and therefore he said "living." For trees have the vegetative life through which they nourish themselves on the moisture of the earth, sucking it up with their roots. **ALONG THE SPINE** of Italy: he means the Apennine mountain, which, as we said above, rises through the middle of Italy just as the back and the spine extends through the middle of animals. **BY THE SLAVIC** winds: By the northern winds, which he calls Slavic, because Slavonia <note>The region of the Balkans across the Adriatic from Italy.</note> is to our north-east. **THEN LIQUEFIED. TRICKLES**: It distills. To "trickle" (*trapelare*) is when liquor within a vessel that is not well-sealed drips out. **IF BUT THE LAND** that loses shadow: that is, provided that the southern region, in which the sun makes little shadow, **BREATHES**: Makes wind. For just as the north winds create ice and cold, so those of the midday make it sweet and melt it. **SO WAS I** without tears and sighs: because fear had chilled me, and the cold had so closed the pores that neither tears nor sighs could exit.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap initial E with scrollwork.</image-desc>
**S**HE, STILL FIRM. To show that she still persisted in her rebuke. **TURNED HER WORDS** to the substances: that is, to the angels; **PIOUS**: because in their song they had shown compassion to Dante. And the poet uses a wonderful artifice: for since the angels had sung such a psalm that showed mercy should be had toward Dante, it seemed reasonable that Beatrice should respond and assign the reason why she persisted in her harshness, which was not to harm him, but to help him by inducing such contrition as would be equal to the sin. And on the other hand, it seemed superfluous to demonstrate such a reason to the angels, since they already knew that and every other thing. Therefore, the poet chose a middle way that would satisfy both: that is, it did not appear that she wanted to teach the angels, but she responded to the psalm and their singing so that Dante might understand what was...

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap initial N with scrollwork.</image-desc>
**N**OT ONLY BY THE WORK: the poet concedes that although all human souls are by nature similar and equal, nonetheless the influences of the heavens—which can do much in the bodies to which the souls are joined and with the instruments through which they operate—can do much in their talents. But beyond the influences...

She justifies her harshness by describing Dante's wasted potential and his straying from the path of virtue after her death.</meta>

But through the bounty of divine graces,
which rain down from such high vapors
that our sights do not come near them,
**T**his man was such in his new life <note>referring to Dante’s youth or his book *Vita Nuova*</note>
virtually, that every right habit
would have made a miraculous proof in him.
But the more vigorous and wild the ground becomes
with bad seed and left untilled,
the more it possesses good terrestrial strength.
**F**or some time I sustained him with my face,
showing my youthful eyes to him;
with me I led him turned in the right direction.

<column-break/>

heavenly [influences], the grace freely given <note>original: "gratia gratis data"</note> by divine mercy is of great value: and it concludes that Dante had favor both from the stars and from divine grace: in a way that he could have made a miraculous proof if he had followed the love of Beatrice, i.e., the study of sacred letters. But just as the bad seed becomes much more malignant in fertile ground than in sterile ground: so vice becomes greater in a sharp intellect than in a dull one. NOT only upon the great wheels. i.e., through the revolutions of the heavens and the planets: the First Mover <note>original: "primo mobile"; in the Ptolemaic system, the outermost sphere that moves all others</note> finishes its circuit in twenty-four hours: and draws with it all the heavens which are content and jealous of it: but to report further on the celestial motions would be too lengthy: and in many places in the work we have demonstrated a good part of those, if not clearly shown, at least not entirely obscurely hinted at. And if I am not mistaken, supreme wisdom is observed here as elsewhere by the poet, who concedes to celestial influences as much as

<column-break/>

our redemption does not forbid: and as much as is in truth. And nonetheless, he does not remove, but rather affirms, the freedom of our <term>free will</term> <note>original: "libertade del nostro arbitrio"</note> and the help of divine grace: and Beatrice concludes that none of these things were lacking to Dante. But his non-upright will distracted him for some time from the true way, through which he had proceeded from the beginning until a certain point. **WHICH** directs each person to some end: which wheels and revolutions make every power that has generative virtue come to some effect, which is the end of the thing according to how the stars are companions. i.e., according to various conjunctions of various planets: because the conjunction of Mars and Venus produces one effect, and that of Venus and Jupiter another. **BUT** through the bounty of divine graces: She demonstrates that although celestial influences can do much, nonetheless divine graces can do far more without comparison. **WHICH** rain down from such high vapors. He uses an excellent simile: and the meaning is that just as copious rain descends when cold and humid vapors in the region fit for this are converted into water, so divine grace rains abundantly. **THAT** our sights do not come near them: because the human sight and intellect cannot approach the knowledge of understanding the greatness of divine graces. These. This Dante. **IN** his new life: in his first age. Virtually: potentially. i.e., he had a natural disposition and aptitude in a form that if he had practiced a right habit, i.e., becoming virtuous in the speculative virtues, such a habit would have made a miraculous proof. **BUT** so much more: in this simile, he sets the ground for the similarity and aptitude already mentioned: and the bad seed for the vicious habit, and says: that just as the bad seed, if it is not gathered before it falls to the earth, multiplies more in fertile ground than in sterile, so the seed of vice multiplies more in a great and sharp intellect than in a low, small, and dull one. **FOR** some time I sustained him with my face: I, showing him my beautiful face: and the beautiful eyes which signify that he, being in love with the outer surface of theology without tasting the marrow, for some time followed those studies which led him in the right direction. i.e., toward the virtues.

**AS** soon as I was upon the threshold of my second age. There are two theological ages: youthful and mature. For we attend to that in two ways: either according to the letter and morality, which concerns the active and civil life, and this is the "new" or youthful age, and it is called Beatrice, i.e., theology; or we truly interpret the sacred letters allegorically and anagogically <note>Anagogical: a method of interpretation that finds spiritual or mystical meaning in a text, relating to the afterlife.</note>. And this serves the contemplative life, and is the second and mature age of Beatrice. In which she is without flesh: because it treats of things

As soon as I was upon the threshold
of my second age and I changed my life,
this man took himself from me and gave himself to others.
**W**hen from flesh to spirit I had risen,
and beauty and virtue had increased in me,
I was to him less dear and less pleasing.
**A**nd he turned his steps through a way not true,
following false images of good,
which return no promise in full.
**N**or did it avail me to obtain inspirations,
with which both in dreams and otherwise
I called him back; so little did he care for it.
**H**e fell so far that all arguments
for his salvation were already short,
except showing him the lost people.
**F**or this I visited the gate of the dead,
and to him who has conducted him up here,
my prayers were offered with weeping.

<column-break/>

incorporeal and eternal: that is, it treats of God, who is entirely unknown to the human sense, and comprehensible to the intellect only in the smallest part. **Therefore.** "As soon as I was on the threshold" means at the threshold of my second age: this we have explained above. **THIS MAN** took himself from me: because he left the studies of theology **AND** gave himself to others: following other studies. **WHEN** I had risen to spirit from flesh: I had changed from carnal to spiritual, and beauty and virtue [increased]: because the allegorical sense is more beautiful and contains in itself more virtue of the intellect. And he turned his steps: he turned his affections. **THROUGH** a way not true: through the left-hand path of vices. **FOLLOWING** false images of good: he did not follow the virtues of the soul which are the true good, but sought riches, dignity, magistracies, and power, which are called the "goods of fortune" and are not true goods; but they seem so because they have an image, though a false one, of the true good; and they do not return any promise in full because they promise true peace of the soul and then do not give it. **NOR** did it avail me to obtain inspirations. Inspiration is a sudden and ardent will for virtue placed by God in the heart of man, which often comes to those who read the sacred scripture; and therefore he feigns that Beatrice often obtained from God that He should send him some inspiration to set him on the right path. **BUT** it did not avail him. i.e., it did not help him. **NOR** dreams: because in dreams and in visions such inspirations appear. **SO** little did he care

<column-break/>

for me: "I do not care for you" <note>original: "Non mi cale di te"</note> in the Florentine tongue means "I do not care about you." **HE FELL** so far here: that is, he ruined himself so much in vice. **THAT** all arguments: that all the industries and aids that can be made. **WERE SHORT**: were not sufficient. **EXCEPT** showing him the lost people. A man already ensnared and taken by the allurements and false flatteries of corporeal pleasures cannot be brought back to true virtue unless we show him how much perdition, how much calamity, how much damage, how much manifest ruin and eternal death comes to us from vices. **SO THAT** if he is not moved by reason and by the love of the heavenly good, at least the fear of eternal evil might move him. For this difference exists between the good and the wicked: the good flee evil for the love they bear for virtue, and the wicked for fear of punishment. **FOR** this I visited the gate of the dead: The soul which is buried in Hell is called dead because it is eternally deprived of the supreme good, without which, although it is immortal, it nonetheless cannot be called alive. And certainly theology would not treat of vices and the damned if it did not have regard for the vices which can be withdrawn from vices by such examples. And to him who has conducted him up here: to Virgil, of whom it is not necessary to say more, as we have already said so much.

<column-break/>

The high decree of God would be broken
if Lethe <note>the river of forgetfulness</note> were passed and such food
were tasted without any cost
<margin>214</margin> **O**f repentance that pours forth tears.

<column-break/>

**B**eatrice concludes that the high order imposed by divine providence would be broken if Dante, having committed such error, passed the river Lethe without such repentance as is appropriate for the sin committed. And as much as pertains to the knowledge of fate, you will return to the first canticle <note>Inferno</note> where we reconciled it with the sacred letters. The divine order would therefore be broken if such food—which is to taste the water of that river which induces forgetfulness of sin and extinguishes every spark of it—were tasted without "cost," that is, without payment. This is a metaphor from one who takes food in an inn. **OF** repentance that pours forth tears: of such penitence and contrition; that is, which causes tears to be shed.

# PURGATORIO CANTO XXXI. OF THE SECOND CANTICLE BY DANTE

->mm iiii<-

This thirty-first canto contains how the poet was asked by Beatrice if her accusation was true. Then follows the poet's confession with supreme contrition: through which he earned the power to cross the river and taste of it, and finally was led into the presence of Beatrice. **"O YOU who are."** Up until here, Beatrice, speaking of Dante, had directed her words to the angels for the reason already stated. Now, wanting to compel him to confess the things of which she had accused him, she turned her speech to him.

"You who are on the other side of the sacred river,"
turning the point of her speech toward me,
which even by its edge had seemed sharp to me,
she began again, continuing without delay:
"Say, say if this is true; to such an accusation
your confession must be joined."
My strength was so confounded
that my voice moved and then died away
before it was released from its organs.
She waited a little, then said: "What are you thinking?
Answer me; for the sad memories in you
are not yet washed away by the waters." <note>original: *offense*, literally "struck" or "weakened." Beatrice refers to the river Lethe, which erases the memory of sin; since Dante has not yet crossed, his memories of his faults remain sharp.</note>

Confusion and fear mixed together
pushed such a "yes" out of my mouth
that to understand it, one needed eyes. <note>He spoke so faintly that his voice was inaudible; one had to see his lips move.</note>
As a crossbow breaks when it shoots
because its string and bow are too tense,
and the bolt hits the mark with less force;
so I broke under that heavy burden,
pouring forth tears and sighs,
and my voice faltered in its passage.
Wherefore she said to me: "Within my desires,
which led you to love the Good,
beyond which there is nothing to aspire to,
what trenches across your path or what chains
did you find, that you should have
stripped yourself of the hope of passing forward?
And what comforts and what advantages
showed themselves upon the brows of others,
that you should have paraded before them?"

After drawing a bitter sigh,
I barely had the voice that responded,
which my lips formed with great difficulty.
Weeping, I said: "The present things,
with their false pleasure, turned my steps aside
as soon as your face was hidden."
And she: "Even if you were silent or denied
what you confess, your fault would not be less known;
it is known by such a Judge.
But when the accusation of sin bursts
from one's own cheek in our court,
the grindstone turns itself against the edge." <note>The "edge" of the sword of divine justice is blunted or turned back by the act of sincere confession.</note>

<column-break/>

**"O YOU"** Dante, who are still on that side of the river: you do not deserve to cross it if you do not first confess your error and repent of it. **"By the point:"** <note>original: *per puncta*</note> One who wounds with the point inflicts a more dangerous wound than one who wounds with the edge. Wherefore the poet shows through a certain simile that although he was much affected by the speech Beatrice made about him to the angels, the words she turned directly to him caused him even greater confusion. **"Without delay:"** <note>original: *senza cuncta*</note> Without hesitation, because *cunctari* in the Latin language means to delay. This implies that having finished speaking with the angels, she turned to him without any intermission of time: to denote with what celerity Theological Scripture desires to make us safe. She has until now spoken to the angels so that they might be witnesses if what she narrates be true. And certainly, although the Sacred Letters are founded on faith, they are nonetheless very full and replete with many reasons, various examples, and very grave authorities: all of which things excite and move the sinner. And for this reason, she turns to him and shows him that simple confession and supreme contrition is the penalty through which the fault can be remitted. Whence she adds: **"TO SUCH"** an accusation your confession must be joined. **"MY STRENGTH WAS"** so confounded: so great was the shame and contrition for the committed error that he could not speak. Because the great perturbation of the soul so hinders the tongue and the other members with which we form the voice and words that they cannot do their duty. Therefore, the natural strength was so confounded and perturbed that the voice could not detach itself from the tongue that forms it. **"Before it was released:"** that is, sent out from its organs, from those members which are instruments to form it; because *organon* in the Greek language means any instrument. **"FOR"** the memories in you are not yet hindered by the water: as if to say: if you do not answer, it is not because you have forgotten your errors, not yet having tasted of the river of Lethe. **"SAD memories:"** because remembering the committed sin induces sadness and pain in us.

**T**he confusion and shame of the error committed and the fear of the penalty pushed a "yes" out of my mouth <gloss>i.e., they forced me to confess.</gloss> But the strength was so weakened that the sound could not be understood; but it was known by looking at my face. **"As a crossbow:"** as it often happens that by pulling the crossbow too much, the string and the bow break. Therefore, the bolt goes out with less force, wherefore its blow is almost in vain. Thus the poet "burst" under such perturbation of soul; whence in pouring out tears <gloss>i.e., and sighs</gloss> the voice faltered. **"Wherefore she said to me:"** following this, Beatrice asks Dante: "what trenches across" or "what chains did you find?" **"In my desires:"** that is, while you loved me: those desires which led you to love the Highest Good. In short, while you were loving me back toward the Highest Good, what thing impeded you from passing forward and caused you to completely lose hope? **"Beyond which there is nothing to aspire to."** Because the Highest Good is God and our ultimate end, for the attainment of which we do all other things; and beyond Him there is nothing to be sighed for: because after Him there is nothing to aspire to, because after Him there is nothing. **"AND what comforts."** The meaning is: what thing induced you to leave me? Tell me if there were impediments that you found on the way through which I was leading you. Or indeed, what comforts and gains did the others whom you loved while leaving me show you in their face <gloss>i.e., at first sight</gloss> for which you should have paraded before them <gloss>i.e., preceded forward</gloss> and not departed from them. And she wishes to conclude: that any other thing he has loved has not been able to show him anything that is truly useful and honest. But it appeared so to his appetite.

<meta>This page continues the harsh rebuke of Dante by Beatrice. On the previous page, Dante was paralyzed by her presence and barely managed a silent "yes" to her accusations. <page-num>XXXI</page-num>

# CANTO XXXI

...turned to loving others as soon as her face was hidden from him, and present things turned them toward themselves, showing him false pleasures. This is true because when we forget the sacred writings and the moral precepts that direct us toward honesty, our appetite immediately turns to worldly things. Inebriated by their pleasures, we value nothing else as good. And if she remained silent or if you denied it... The author shows in this place that in divine judgment, the confession of the sinner is not required so that the judge may be better informed of the truth, because nothing is hidden from Him. Whether you deny or stay silent, everything is known to God; rather, confession is required so that the sinner might humble himself and repent for his error. When he does this, he mitigates God's anger, just as a wheel that sharpens iron [a grindstone] makes it thicker against the edge if it turns the wrong way. <note>Landino uses the metaphor of a grindstone; if turned correctly it sharpens (forgiveness), if turned against the blade it dulls or thickens it (judgment).</note>

**NEVERTHELESS** sometimes means "always," and sometimes "nonetheless." **THAT YOU MAY BEAR SHAME**: so that you may more willingly feel shame, and so that another time you may be stronger against the sirens when you hear them—that is, against worldly pleasures, which are allegorically described as sirens, and which we have described at length in this same canticle. **LAY DOWN THE SEED OF WEEPING**: set down the tears that weeping produces, just as every herb produces its seed. He recalls the psalm: *They who sow in tears.* <note>original: "Qui semmāt i lachrimis" from Psalm 126:5</note> **AND YOU SHALL HEAR**: and you shall understand how my buried flesh should have moved you in the opposite direction. It is as if she says: "I show you that my death should not have been the reason for you to follow others, but rather it should have moved you to do the opposite—that is, to follow me." **NEVER DID I PRESENT TO YOU**: she assigns the reason, saying: nature or art never produced a thing that gave you as much pleasure as my members did, which after my death are scattered in the earth. But if this pleasure you took from my members failed you because of my

<columns>2</columns>

"Nevertheless, so that you may bear the shame
of your error, and so that another time,
seeing the sirens, you may be stronger,
Lay down the seed of weeping and listen:
so you shall hear how in the opposite direction
my buried flesh should have moved you.
Nature or art never presented to you
pleasure as great as the fair members in which
I was enclosed, and which are now scattered in the earth.
And if the highest pleasure failed you
through my death, what mortal thing
should then have drawn you into its desire?
Indeed, you should have, at the first arrow
of fallacious things, risen upward,
following me, who was no longer such.
No 'young girl' or other vanity
of such brief use should have weighted down
your wings to wait for more blows.
The young bird waits for two or three,
but before the eyes of the full-feathered one,
the net is spread and the arrow shot in vain."

<column-break/>

death, no mortal thing should have then drawn you into its desire—that is, to its love. Because you should have considered that you were bound to fail, being mortal, just as my flesh failed you. You should not, therefore, have estimated that any thing which fails could be your happiness and supreme good. For the supreme good is that which is eternal and is not found except in God. Therefore, if I in the flesh—that is, if Theology in the active life, which admonishes us concerning the governance of the body and for this reason finally fails—could not make you blessed, no other mortal thing can do so. For in this life, true happiness is found in no way; and if some quiet is found, it is placed in the mortal life according to our religion. Therefore, if in this way true peace is not found in the virtuous life, much less will it be found in any other kind of life. **INDEED YOU SHOULD HAVE AT THE FIRST ARROW**: "Strale" <term>strale: an arrow, bolt, or shaft</term> signifies a spearhead or arrow. It is derived from the Latin verb *sterno* [to prostrate], because it strikes a man down when it wounds him. But in this place, he uses the rhetorical figure of intellection, putting the weapon that wounds for the wound itself. Because he who places hope in a thing and then loses it is said to have received a stroke of fortune whose goods are fleeting. And therefore she says: "O Dante, you should have risen up—that is, to divine and immortal things—at the first arrow, which is the first blow that fortune gave you when it took my body from you. And you should not have placed more hope in mortal things, seeing that they can be lost." Whence Cicero said:
> Nothing should be called mine or yours: that which can be taken away, which can be snatched, which can be lost. <note>original: "Nihil meū neque tuū appellandum est: quod auferri. quod eripi. quod admitti potest."</note>
And Petrarch:
> Wretched is he who places hope in a mortal thing. <note>original: "Miser colui che speme in cosa mortal pone."</note>
You should have, therefore, raised yourself up after me, Beatrice—that is, Theology—who was no longer such, that is, I was no longer in the flesh, but was an incorporeal spirit. For he who follows Beatrice already stripped of flesh—that is, follows speculative theology—because he has knowledge of heavenly things and of God Himself, finds true happiness there. **YOUR WINGS SHOULD NOT HAVE BEEN WEIGHTED DOWN BY A YOUNG GIRL**: "Pargoletta" <term>pargoletta: literally 'little girl' or 'young lass'</term> is a girl of small age. Therefore, O Dante, neither a *pargoletta*—that is, a

<columns>1</columns>

maiden or other young girl—nor any other vanity—that is, any other temporal good—should have weighted down your wings. Our soul is naturally born to fly to heaven. But when sensuality leads it to worldly pleasures, it remains oppressed by them. **THE YOUNG BIRD WAITS FOR TWO OR THREE**: this is a metaphor, and it shows that the young bird, which still has its downy feathers, waits for more blows. But if a net is stretched or a bow is drawn against one that is already feathered, it immediately flees and does not wait. And by this, he means that Dante might deserve compassion if, in his early age—which, for not having the use and experience of things, easily allows itself to be baited by worldly pleasures—he was deceived.

As children, shamed and silent,
stand with their eyes on the ground, listening,
recognizing their fault and repenting,

you are grieving from hearing, lift up your beard,
and you will take more grief from looking."
With less resistance is a sturdy oak
uprooted, whether by our own wind
or by that from the land of Iarbas.

<column-break/>

Thus I remained silent and confused, and with eyes cast down by the rebuke of Beatrice, just as children listening to their error recognize it and repent for it. **AND SHE SAID: SINCE YOU ARE GRIEVING FROM HEARING**: because the more grief and contrition they take from the sin, the sooner the pardon follows. Therefore, Beatrice wanted Dante, having heard her, to now look at her, because hearing the said punishment might be surpassed by seeing it. For the sense of sight has more power to move us than that of hearing. And allegorically, it shows that more grief is taken when we consider the beauty of that which we have abandoned than from hearing her rebukes. **OUR OWN WIND**: the northern wind, because we are further north than other parts. **FROM THE LAND OF IARBAS**: the southern wind which comes from Africa, where Iarbas reigned; he was the king of Numidia. <note>Iarbas was a legendary king of Numidia, a suitor of Dido. Beatrice uses "his land" to mean the South.</note> **AND WHEN BY THE BEARD THE FACE WAS ASKED**: that is, when she wanted...

from their appearance, my eye understood.

contemplator. **Not very secure**: because I was still ashamed and trembling. **They saw Beatrice**: which signifies that, having been purged of vice, I began to be able to see Beatrice not in the flesh, but in spirit—that is, I began to be able to contemplate. **Turned toward the beast**: this is said to denote that his contemplation of God and celestial things was not like that of the pagan philosophers, because it followed our religion, which is founded in Christ. And therefore he says that Beatrice was turned toward the **griffin**. We established the allegory of this above, demonstrating that he is Christ. And so he says: **Such a beast is a single person in two natures**, because it represents Christ, who is one of the three Persons and exists in two natures, because in Him divinity is joined with humanity. **Under her veil and beyond the river**: we have already spoken of the veil, but she was beyond the river because she always stands in the place of innocence, which is on the other side of the river that extinguishes every carnal desire and makes one forget it. **She seemed to surpass**: the meaning is that Beatrice in that second age (which he calls **ancient**) surpassed her own beauty from when she was in her first age more than she had surpassed other women when she was alive. The text is ordered: it seemed to me that the "ancient" Beatrice (that is, at the present time in her second age) surpassed herself (understand: when she was in her first age) more than she seemed to surpass others when she was here on earth. **The nettle of repentance stung me there**: when a nettle stings, it excites a great itch, which is nothing other than an extreme desire to scratch. Therefore, in this place, he 

<column-break/>

takes the **nettle** for extreme desire. **The nettle**: extreme will. **Of repenting**: for having left Beatrice and followed others. **Stung me**: incited me. **THERE**: where I saw her beauties. **That**: which... that is, whichever of all the other things that previously turned me most to its love (in loving it) became my greatest enemy (came to be most hated by me). And certainly, although it greatly benefits a man to be caught in his vices and shown their ugliness—and how much earthly goods are fallacious and short-lived—and although all these things can draw us back from the path of vice and direct us onto a certain path; nonetheless, seeing the beauties of Beatrice and considering how much they exceed every other thing makes us extremely repentant for our errors and hold them in the highest hatred. And therefore he shows that such **recognition bit his heart**: that is, the recognition of your errors and the vanity and fallacy of worldly goods, and the excellence and ineffable beauty of celestial ones, so that **I fell defeated**. Dante, who represents sensuality, fell defeated because he submits himself to reason. **AND what I then was** and what I became: I cannot express it to you, but she who gave me the cause of what I became knows it. When a man reaches the point of entering into the virtues of a soul already purged, he becomes such that many other sacred writings cannot describe.

After the great perturbation, in which every animal and vital virtue was squeezed into my heart, following the blood and spirits, it returned from the heart to the external limbs. **THE lady I had found alone**: Mathelda, of whom we spoke above. **Hold me**: cling to me, so that I do not fall while carrying you. **Drawn me into the river**: it is necessary that Mathelda (that is, the **Active Life** illuminated by moral virtues) pull us into the river Lethe, which in formula washes us from every sin so that not a single vestige of the old stain remains; thus we forget it entirely. And then, thus purged, she presents us to Beatrice, now out of the flesh and remaining a naked spirit (that is, to **Contemplative Theology**, where our good consists), who would not accept us if we were not washed and cleansed. And we demonstrated at the beginning of the first canticle, according to the Christians and Platonists, that although physics (in which we chiefly understand theology) makes us blessed, nonetheless we must begin with morals. For if morality does not purge us, we cannot aspire to the higher level. **Up to the throat**: pulling me thus submerged and dipped up to the throat, she went directly over the water without sinking, because the purgatorial virtues always go straight and never 

<column-break/>

sink into Lethe, because there is no need for them to forget evil, which they never knew. **AS A SHUTTLE**: This is that instrument which, thrown through the warp, puts in the woof; it is so light that it runs over the threads without breaking or entangling them. Thus she went over the water without breaking it or sinking. **TO THE BL** <note>This is a catchword for the next page.</note>

<header>CANTO XXXI</header>

This refers to the side of the river where the blessed are located. **Asperges me**: <note>original: "Asperges me" — "Sprinkle me"</note> this is the verse sung in church when they sprinkle holy water, which has the power to drive away impure spirits. ### from which Love once drew his weapons against you."

<column-break/>

**Then**: From that river. **Took me, bathed**: made innocent by Mathelda—that is, by priestly doctrine and authority—having forgotten every trace of vice. **The four**: the beautiful moral virtues <note>Justice, Prudence, Fortitude, and Temperance</note> of which we spoke above. **And each one covered me with her arm**: that is, with her power and help. For the arm of Justice defends against injustice; Prudence against folly; Fortitude against fear; and Temperance against lust. **We are nymphs here**: that is, in this world where men are still in the flesh. They are like "helpers" to men, since the paradise of delights is on earth. **And in heaven**: where man cannot err. **We are stars**: as if to say, for ornament. Some say the poet wants to show by this that here the virtues are "in action" and there they are "in habit" <term>Habit: a permanent disposition of the soul, whereas 'action' is the outward practice.</term> Since nymphs are wandering, they easily denote the act; and the stars, because they are fixed, demonstrate the habit. **Descended to the world**: that is, Beatrice descended to the world when the study of theology began through divine inspiration. **As her handmaidens**: that is, as her ministers, because no one can be a true theologian—that is, live according to the precepts of theology—without these virtues. And they existed "before," because the virtues (though not perfect) appeared in men before they had the knowledge of theology. **We will lead you**: We will conduct you, because as I said, the moral virtues, by purging us, make us fit to rise to the contemplative life. But once we are there, the others—

---

-> the three women who are on the right side of the chariot <note>The Theological Virtues: Faith, Hope, and Charity</note> sharpen our eyes to be able to see her profound light. And certainly, if we take the three for the theological virtues, there is no doubt that they refine the mind to contemplate divine things; for God willingly opens His secrets to those who have sincere faith, firm hope, and burning charity. And if we take them for the intellectual virtues, it is similarly well known that such knowledge is acquired with **Intelligence**, **Science**, and **Wisdom**. **Led me to the breast of the Gryphon**: that is, to Christian theology where Beatrice was turned toward us. Because if we do not look at this doctrine, we cannot reach the Gryphon—that is, the knowledge of the mysteries of Christ. **See that you do not spare your gaze**: that is, use every visual power you have to look at Beatrice. It is as if they said: "We have conducted you into her presence, but it is not in our power to make you see her. But you, with the help of the three, will look upon the **emeralds**"—that is, the eyes shining like emeralds, from which Love once drew his weapons—that is, drew his arrows. <-

---

### A thousand desires hotter than flame
### bound my eyes to the shining eyes
### which remained fixed upon the Gryphon.
### Just as the sun in a mirror, no differently,
### the double beast beamed within them,
### now with one, now with another behavior.
### Think, reader, if I marveled,
### when I saw the thing itself stay quiet,
### and yet transform itself within its image.

<column-break/>

**A thousand desires**: as if to say infinite desires and longings, hotter than fire. **Bound my eyes**: they fixed my eyes upon the eyes of Beatrice, which stood firm upon the Gryphon. And he says this because he was reflected in Theology, which always gazes upon the Word of God made flesh. **Just as the sun in a mirror**: just as it happens that the sun's ray strikes the mirror and is reflected elsewhere, so the image of the **double beast**—that is, of the Gryphon—struck the eyes of Beatrice and from there was reflected into me. And he says this so that whoever reads Christian theology may recognize Christ therein. **The double beast**: the Gryphon, which is part bird (signifying divinity) and part lion (signifying the humanity of Christ). **Beamed within**: it shone into me and showed its image within Beatrice’s eyes, like sunbeams in a mirror. But although Beatrice's eyes continually represented the image of the Gryphon, they nevertheless presented it now with one and now with another argument, representation, and figure. For Holy Scripture sometimes figures God as a man, sometimes a lamb, sometimes a lion. **When I saw the thing itself stay quiet**: I marveled at the "thing"—the Gryphon—staying quiet in itself, because it did not change in its substance; but it changed in its **idol** <note>original: "idolo" — from the Greek 'eidolon', meaning image or figure</note>. For as we have said, the sacred letters always present Christ as one and the same thing, but change Him into various figures. "Idol" in Greek means figure; hence we speak of "adoring idols" as those who adore statues, of which the Psalmist sings: <note>original: "Oculos habent & non videbunt" — "They have eyes and will not see."</note>

---

### While my soul, full of wonder and glad,
### tasted of that food
### which, while satisfying, creates a hunger for itself,
### showing themselves to be of a higher tribe,
### the other three moved forward in their actions,
### dancing to their angelic melody.
### "Turn, Beatrice, turn your holy eyes,"
### was their song, "to your faithful one
### who has moved so many steps to see you!
### By your grace, do us the grace of unveiling
### your mouth to him, so that he may discern
### the second beauty that you hide."

<column-break/>

**While my soul**: while my soul gladly tasted such food which satisfies, yet in satisfying increases the desire for itself. The other three virtues, which are theological, came forward dancing. **My soul full of wonder**: because of the greatness and beauty of the things. **And glad**: to denote that such wonder did not bring suspicion or fear, but supreme joy. And certainly the knowledge of divine things is the only thing that makes us wonder, for every other thing is **vanity of vanities** <note>original: "vanitas vanitatum"</note>. **And makes us glad**: because in that consists the supreme good. **Of that food**: while it satisfies, it **accents**—it increases the thirst and the desire. **For itself**: for the said food. In short, he writes that his soul tasted a food which in truth—

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante's encounter with Beatrice in the Earthly Paradise. Following the previous page, where the four cardinal virtues led Dante to the Gryphon, the focus now shifts to the three theological virtues and the moment Beatrice reveals her full beauty by removing her veil.</meta>

<page-num>214</page-num>
<header>PURGATORY</header>

It satisfied; but even though it satisfied, the desire to taste did not diminish, but rather increased. We must understand that there are two kinds of pleasure: one that strikes our senses from corporeal and carnal things, and this is called imperfect pleasure, because it always brings with it satiety and repentance, and in a short time, boredom. Juvenal understood this when he said: <note>original: "Facere non possis quinque diebus continuis: quia talis quoque tedia uite" — "You could not do this for five continuous days, because such things also bring weariness of life."</note> The other is that which our intellect takes from incorporeal and celestial things, and this is called perfect pleasure, because it never brings boredom or repentance after it. Therefore, the poet rightly says of this that it "satisfies," because we remain content with it. Nonetheless, we always desire it, and it never becomes wearisome to us. **THE OTHER Three stepped forward**: These are Faith, Hope, and Charity. Or we might say Intelligence, Science, and Wisdom, of which we spoke above. **DEMONSTRATING by a higher tribe**: Of a more excellent lineage. **In their actions and gestures**: **TRIBE**: that is, of a more noble family, because the moral virtues are of a mortal lineage, being in the active life; and these [the theological virtues] are of an immortal lineage, being in the speculative life. **DANCING to their angelic grace [garibo]**: that is, in their angelic manner. <term>Garibo</term> comes from *garbo*, and *garbo* signifies manner and form. And their song was this: "O Beatrice, turn, turn your holy eyes to your faithful Dante, who has taken so many steps for you." Because step by step he first descended to Hell, considering every kind of vice, and then ascended through Purgatory, purging himself of them. **BY grace**: through <term>prevenient grace</term> <note>original: "pcutiēte" (percutiente), the grace that "strikes" the heart to awaken it</note>, then through illuminating, cooperating, and consuming grace. **THAT it might reveal**: that it might uncover. **YOUR mouth**: your literal and moral sentence. **SO THAT he may discern**: that is, know. **THE SECOND Beauty**: The spiritual intellect. **THAT You hide**: Under the literal and moral sense. For beneath the veil of faith, where the moral sense is covered, lies the allegorical and <term>anagogical</term> <note>The "anagogical" sense refers to the highest level of scriptural interpretation, dealing with eternal glory and the soul's relationship with the divine.</note> intellect.

> O splendor of living eternal light,
> who has ever grown pale under the shade
> of Parnassus, or drunk from its cistern,
> who would not seem to have a burdened mind
> trying to render you as you appeared
> there where the heavens harmonize your shadow,
> when you released yourself into the open air?

<column-break/>

**O Splendor of living eternal light**: We must understand that after the words of the angels—that is, after the graces have entered the already purged soul—Beatrice raised her veil and showed the splendors of the divine eternal light. Because through the aforementioned graces, a man in that state can know the secrets of theology and divine light, which the human tongue cannot express. And so he said with wonder, "O splendors"; and this word "O" is an expression of admiration. And he adds that no one, whether by turning pale under the laurels of Parnassus <note>Parnassus is the mountain home of the Muses, representing the height of human poetic achievement.</note> or by drinking from the fountain of the Muses, was so inspired by divine frenzy that they could express what the light of Beatrice was when she was revealed. **WHO grew pale**: because those who devote themselves much to poetic study grow pale. Hence Juvenal: <note>original: "Fuit utile multis pallere & uinū toto nescire decembri" — "It was useful for many to grow pale and to know no wine during all of December," referring to the scholar's life of austerity and hard work.</note> **IN its cistern**: that is, on Mount Parnassus. **WHO would not seem to have a burdened mind**: who would not seem an unlearned and insufficient poet. For he who has a mind occupied and burdened with other things cannot be a good poet, as Juvenal clearly demonstrates. **TRYING to render you**: that is, trying to express in verse you, as such and so radiant as you appeared there where "the heaven shadows you," that is, where you remained uncovered and had no other covering but the sky. And thus he demonstrates that no poet could describe the beauties of theology; and he imitates Plato, who expressed the same sentiment, showing that the place where God is, no man ever saw, nor did any poet describe it.

### CANTO XXXII OF THE THIRD <note>Though the Purgatorio is the second canticle of the Divine Comedy, the original text here reads "Tertia" (Third), which may reflect a specific volume arrangement in this Renaissance edition or a printer's error.</note> CANTICLE OF DANTE

He <note>The commentator, likely Cristoforo Landino, whose work often accompanied these Renaissance editions.</note> links the thirty-second chapter to the preceding one because, having shown at the end of that section the splendor of Beatrice’s face—now finally revealed—he continues by adding how intense his fixation was in gazing at her, until he was cautioned by the virtues.

<summary>This page introduces Canto XXXII of Purgatorio, focusing on Dante's overwhelmed reaction to Beatrice's revealed beauty and the transition into the next phase of the divine procession.</summary>
<keywords>Canto XXXII, Beatrice, Purgatorio, Tree of Knowledge, Griffin, Renaissance commentary, Dante Alighieri</keywords>

--- Page 483 ---
<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante’s Purgatorio, moving into Canto XXXII. It follows the moment Beatrice has revealed her face to Dante. The translator notes that the text transitions from the personal encounter with Beatrice to the broader allegorical procession of the Church.</meta>

<page-num>XXXII.</page-num>
<header>CANTO XXXII.</header>

<margin>238</margin>
So fixed and attentive were my eyes
to quench their ten-year thirst <note>The ten years since Beatrice's death in 1290 until the vision in 1300.</note>
that my other senses were all extinguished.

And they had on this side and that a wall
of unconcern, so much did the holy smile
draw them to itself with the ancient net;

When by force my face was turned
toward my left by those goddesses, <note>The four cardinal virtues.</note>
for I heard from them a "Too fixedly!"

And the condition of sight that exists
in eyes just struck by the sun
left me for a while without my vision.

But when my sight reshaped itself to the "lesser"—
I say the "lesser" in respect to the "much"
from which I was forced to withdraw—

I saw that the glorious army had turned
upon its right flank and was returning,
facing the sun and the seven flames. <note>The seven candelabra representing the gifts of the Holy Spirit.</note>

As a troop turns under its shields
to save itself, and wheels with its banner
before the whole line can change its front,

That soldiery of the celestial kingdom
which led the way had all passed us by
before the chariot turned its pole. <note>Literally "the first wood," referring to the shaft or beam of the chariot.</note>

Then the ladies returned to the wheels,
and the griffin moved the blessed burden,
yet so that not a feather of his shook.

The beautiful lady <note>Matelda, who guided Dante through the river Lethe.</note> who drew me to the crossing,
and Statius and I, followed the wheel
that traced its orbit with the smaller arc.

<column-break/>

This chapter contains the griffin’s journey to the **Tree of Knowledge**. It represents the entire primitive Church; it describes how the griffin led the chariot back with all those who followed it, how the plant turned green again with leaves, and how Dante, falling asleep, had a vision. Upon waking, he asks Matelda about Beatrice; she points her out to him, and he is commanded by her to observe the things that will come to pass.

**TO QUENCH THE CRAVING [A DISBRAMarfi]:** To remove the craving, that is, the desire. **Craving [Brama]** is a great desire for something. Hence, "to crave" is to desire supremely. **TEN-YEAR THIRST [DECenne sete]:** A longing lasting ten years. He means to imply that after he gained knowledge of the literal and moral sense of the sacred letters, he abandoned those studies until he returned to seek the allegorical and spiritual intellect; ten years passed in between. Therefore, he feigns that he remained ten years without Beatrice. **THAT THE OTHER SENSES WERE EXTINGUISHED:** I was so intent on seeing her that my other senses were spent and asleep. This signifies that he was so devoted to these studies that his mind was turned to nothing else. This occurs naturally: as this same poet shows above, when we are entirely turned toward one thing, all the other powers of the soul cease, except for the one we are exercising.

**AND THEY HAD ON THIS SIDE AND THAT A WALL:** His eyes, directed and fixed on Beatrice, had a **WALL [PARETE]**, meaning a wall and obstacle, "on this side," meaning from the right and left sides. Thus he demonstrates that his constancy and perseverance in contemplation were such that neither prosperity (signified by the right hand) nor adversity (signified by the left) could remove him, because on the right he opposed temperance and on the left, fortitude. **OF UNCONCERN [DINON CALERe]:** Not to care. This is a Tuscan verb used only impersonally, as in "I do not care about you" [*non mi cale di te*]. **SO THE HOLY SMILE:** He assigns the reason and says his eyes cared for nothing else. **SO [CHOSI]**, that is, in such a manner did Beatrice draw them to herself. **WITH THE ANCIENT NET:** With the ancient love, which catches the mind just as a net catches birds. **When by force my face was turned** by those goddesses—that is, by the four cardinal virtues—toward my left; they turned it with the words I heard them say, which were "Your gazing is too fixed." He turned to the left where the moral virtues were. These goddesses made him turn his eyes away from Beatrice to another part because he was looking too fixedly; for the moral virtues—and especially Temperance, advised by Prudence—show us that we must do everything with mode and measure. Hence the proverb of the learned: *Nothing in excess* <note>original: "Ne quid nimis"</note>. And Juvenal said: *The wise man imposes a limit even on honorable things* <note>original: "Imponitque modum sapiens & rebus honestis"</note>.

**He demonstrates** that the procession he first saw coming from the East toward the West, after he turned toward his left, was now returning on its right arm toward the East. But first he recounts that, having turned his eyes from Beatrice, he remained dazzled like one who has looked at the sun; he describes the condition of sight in eyes just struck by the sun. This induces a glare that left him for a while without sight. By transition, he shows that just as the physical eye cannot withstand the light of the sun, so our intellect cannot withstand the fullness of theology. **BUT THEN WHEN TO THE LESSER:** His face—that is, Dante’s sight—was dazzled by the excessive splendor of Beatrice. But when he turned back to the sun and the candelabra, although that splendor was great, nonetheless in comparison to Beatrice’s, it was small. Then his sight reshaped itself—that is, returned to its proper form—with the "lesser sensible" thing, the splendor of the candelabra. **I SAY THE LESSER** in respect to the "much" sensible. It is as if he says the splendor of the candelabra and the sun was very great, but compared to the splendor of Beatrice’s eyes, it seemed small.

**I SAW ON THE RIGHT ARM IT HAD TURNED:** He describes how this procession had departed from the Tree of Obedience. This signifies the transgression of the commandment by our first parents. Now he shows the return thither to demonstrate the advent of Christ, who through his obedience—*For he was obedient even unto death, even the death of the cross* <note>original: "Nam fuit obediens usque ad mortem mortem aut crucis"</note>—restored us to obedience and reconciled us with God. He made human nature turn from the West, which signifies perdition, to the East, which signifies salvation; and by the "right" he demonstrates the way of virtue. **WITH THE SUN:** That is, with divine help. **WITH THE SEVEN FLAMES:** The seven gifts of the Holy Spirit with which whoever follows the Gospel virtue is directed. **AS UNDER THE SHIELDS:** Because all those we mentioned above were walking in front of the chariot, it was necessary that, in turning back, the troop should wheel around and re-enter the space in front of the chariot. This shows they did so skillfully, observing order like a troop that, while fighting, wishes to turn and, in turning, parries the blows of the enemy. Thus, they all passed forward before the chariot turned its "first wood," meaning the pole. Then the ladies returned to the wheels, the three to the right and the four to the left, because without the governance of these virtues, the chariot—that is, the Church of Christ—would go poorly toward obedience. **The Griffin moved** the blessed burden; he notes that even though he moved it, not one of his feathers or wings shook, denoting that the holy justice and mercy of our supreme and highest God are unchangeable.

**The griffin turned** the chariot as was said above toward the right hand, to denote that the Synagogue of the Old Testament, denoted by the left wheel, was converted into the Church...

Dante is momentarily blinded by Beatrice's beauty, illustrating the overwhelming nature of divine theology compared to human intellect.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante’s Purgatorio, Canto XXXII. The previous page ended with the procession of the heavenly army turning to the right, with Matelda, Dante, and the poet Statius following the wheel that makes the tighter turn. This page details the procession's arrival at the Tree of Knowledge and the binding of the symbolic chariot.</meta>

<page-num>XXXII.</page-num>
<header>PURGATORY</header>

Thus walking through the high, empty forest,
by fault of her who believed the serpent,
a divine melody <note>The "angelic note" refers to the music accompanying the procession.</note> tempered our pace.
Perhaps in three flights an unloosed arrow
would have covered as much space as we
had moved when Beatrice descended.
I heard "Adam" murmured by everyone;
then they surrounded a tree stripped
of leaves and other foliage on every branch.
Its crown, which spreads out so much wider
the higher it goes, would be marveled at
for its height even by the Indians in their woods.

---

"Blessed are you, Griffin, for not pecking
with your beak from this wood, sweet to the taste,
since the belly is afterwards twisted in pain."
Thus around the sturdy tree
cried the others; and the animal of two natures <note>The Griffin, representing Christ’s dual nature as both divine and human.</note> replied:
"So is preserved the seed of all justice."
And turning to the pole that he had pulled,
he dragged it to the foot of the widowed branch,
and that which came from it, he left bound to it.

---

As our plants, when the great light falls
downward, mingled with that which
radiates behind the celestial carp, <note>The "celestial carp" refers to the constellation of Pisces, which precedes Aries in the zodiac.</note>
swell up, and then each is renewed
with its own color before the sun
yokes his steeds under another star;
Opening with a color less than roses
and more than violets, the plant was renewed,
which before had branches so bare.
I did not understand the hymn—and here it is not sung—
which that people then sang,
nor did I endure the note until the end.

<column-break/>

**Christianity denoted by the right side.** Therefore, the beautiful lady who was **MATELDA: WHO** drew me to the crossing: who pulled me through the river Lethe to the crossing where I passed, and Statius also. **WE FOLLOWED the wheel:** they went behind the right wheel which made its orbit: that is, its path with an orbit: because in Latin *orbita* signifies the path made by a wheel. **WITH a smaller arc:** with a smaller curve; and he means the right wheel because a chariot has two wheels, and when it turns, it must make two paths; when it turns, those paths remain curved in the form of an arc, and the arc of the wheel on which the chariot turns is always smaller. Therefore, in turning, the right wheel made the smaller arc. **THE HIGH empty forest:** Paradise is "empty" of its delights because of the sin of the first man. **FAULT Of her who believed the serpent:** the fault of Eve. **PERHAPS IN three flights:** perhaps as far as an arrow travels in three flights. That is, in three stretches; and he says "flights" because of the speed of the arrow and also because it has feathers. **UNLOOSED:** as if released from the string, which is like a bridle. The meaning is that they had already traveled three arrow-shots when Beatrice descended. He uses the number "three" because this number, as the Pythagoreans <note>Followers of the ancient philosopher Pythagoras, who believed numbers held mystical and structural significance.</note> demonstrate, is perfect. And Christian doctrine demonstrates the excellence of the Trinity in one God. **ADAM:** they lamented the disobedience of Adam, through which the human generation remained deprived of such a pleasant and joyful place. **A tree:** this is the Tree of Knowledge: which also represents Obedience; by not observing it, Adam contracted original sin, which took this paradise from us. **ITS CROWN Which spreads so much:** He shows that the shape of this tree was such that the higher the branches were, the wider they spread. This is the opposite of other trees. Besides this, the tree was extremely tall: so much so that even if it had been in the forests of India where trees are tallest, its height would have seemed marvelous. It is reasonable that the Tree of Knowledge be very tall, because it proceeds step by step until the knowledge of God; and the higher it rises, the more its branches spread: because the more we understand, the more remains for us to see. And this same tree also figures holy obedience, which is founded in humility; it rises to God and extends through infinite virtues.

---

They sang, "Blessed are you, Griffin, because you do not peck," that is, you do not tear away: to denote that Christ did not depart from obedience: **but was made obedient even unto death.** <note>original: "sed factus est obediens usq; ad mortem"</note> **SWEET To the taste.** As if to say sweet to sensuality but not to reason. Similar to that line of Petrarch: "greedy for such things that are sweet to the taste, but harmful to health." <note>A reference to Petrarch's poems on the deceptive nature of worldly desires.</note> And he gives the reason **SINCE afterwards from this tree the BELLY is twisted to evil:** and does not direct itself toward the good. **THUS around:** all the others sang as was said. But the Griffin: **SO.** That is, you must understand that by not tasting of this wood, **IS PRESERVED the seed of all justice.** Obedience is preserved, from which, as from the best seed, is born every virtue that makes a man just. **AND TURNING to the pole he had pulled:** the meaning is that he tied the pole of the chariot—which had been made from the wood of this tree—to the tree itself. He imagines the pole was made of the wood of obedience: because obedience is what guides and conducts the Church, and with obedience it is linked. Therefore, the Griffin pulled the pole to the foot of the **widowed branch.** Widowed because it was deprived of leaves; and widowed because it was abandoned by the first man who was disobedient to God.

---

Just as it happens that when the sun has entered Aries, in which spring begins, the trees that had been stripped of foliage by winter begin to swell their buds and then put forth new flowers: so the tree grew green and bloomed again after the chariot was tied to it. And the color of the flowers was less bright than that of roses and more than that of violets. Therefore, it was blood-red. And by this, he denotes the Passion of Christ: because his blood returned the human species to its ancient obedience. **WHEN it falls:** when it is spread from heaven to earth. **The great light:** that is, the sun. **MINGLED with that which radiates behind the celestial carp:** mixed with the light of the stars of Aries, which rises in our hemisphere after Pisces, which he calls "carp" <note>A "lasca" is a type of freshwater fish; Dante uses it to refer to the sign of Pisces.</note>, using the specific species for the general genus. And in this way, he describes spring, which begins with the entry of the sun into the first degree of Aries. **SWELL:** swollen and thickened: because at that time every tree begins to swell its buds; we call this "budding." **BEFORE the sun yokes his steeds**—which we showed to be four—**UNDER Another star:** under another sign of the zodiac. **I DID NOT understand it:** I did not understand the hymn which those people around the chariot sang, who signify the ancient fathers of the Old Testament and of the primitive Church. And here in this world and in this age, it is not sung. **NOR DID I ENDURE THE WHOLE NOTE:** that is, I did not withstand the whole song without falling asleep.

<summary>This page describes the procession reaching the Tree of Knowledge, which blooms when the Griffin (Christ) binds the chariot (the Church) to it. The commentary explains the allegorical significance of obedience, the Trinity, and the renewal of humanity through the Passion.</summary>
<keywords>Tree of Knowledge, Griffin, Christ, Matelda, Adam, Aries, Spring, Obedience, original sin, allegory, Purgatorio Canto 32</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante’s Purgatorio, Canto XXXII. Having arrived at the Tree of Knowledge, Dante falls into a supernatural sleep during a divine hymn. This page describes his awakening and the transformation of the scene, comparing it to the biblical Transfiguration of Christ.</meta>

# CANTO XXXII.

The poet narrates that he cannot in any way describe the sweetness of the song that lulled him—that is, which induced sleep and made him drift off. But if he could express how the "pitiless eyes" of Argus fell asleep <note>In Greek mythology, Argus was a giant with a hundred eyes; Mercury lulled him to sleep with music to kill him.</note> at the song of Mercury, he would be like a painter who, not knowing how to paint from his own imagination, paints things already depicted by another artist. It is as if he says: I would say I was lulled to sleep by the sound of such a hymn just as Argus was by the sound of the pipe of Mercury—a fable you have already heard above. **LULLED TO SLEEP**: fell asleep. **THE EYES of Argus. PITILESS**: cruel in watching too closely. **HEARING of Syrinx**: while he heard Mercury singing of the nymph Syrinx. She was loved by Pan, the god of shep-

->If I could portray how those pitiless eyes<-
->fell asleep hearing the tale of Syrinx,<-
->the eyes whose long vigil cost so dearly,<-
->like a painter who paints from a model,<-

->whose fruit makes the angels hungry<-
->and makes perpetual marriage-feasts in heaven,<-
->Peter, and John, and James were led,<-
->and, being overcome, returned to their senses at the word<-
->by which even deeper sleeps were broken,<-

->both by Moses and by Elijah,<-
->and their Master’s garment <term>stola</term> changed;<-
->so I returned to myself, and saw that compassionate lady<-

->was the guide of my steps along the river.<-

**of the apple tree**: that is, the apple tree which is Christ <note>A common medieval allegory where the apple tree represents Christ, based on the Song of Solomon.</note> makes the angels hungry for his fruit and creates perpetual weddings in heaven. And note that he here calls the Transfiguration of Christ "blossoms" and calls Christ himself the "apple tree." This is because the Transfiguration was not yet his full glory, but a demonstration of it, just as a flower is not the fruit but a sign of it. And he calls Christ an apple tree because that tree produces sweet fruit: for the blessed in heaven feed upon the contemplation of God, just as on earth bodies feed on physical food. Hence he makes the an-
gels hungry, meaning desirous; and he said "perpetual weddings" because blessedness in heaven is eternal. **And overcome, they returned to the word**: that is, being stunned, they recovered. **AT THE word of God. ELIJAH**: the history of this man and his chariot has already been established. **CHANGED garment <term>stola</term>**: changed clothing. **That compassionate lady**: Matelda. She will lead him to Beatrice, because the doctrine of the active life <note>Matelda represents the "Active Life," a state of pure human action, while Beatrice represents "Contemplative Life" or Theology.</note> demonstrates theology to us.

->And all in doubt I said: “Where is Beatrice?”<-
->And she: “See her under the new leaves,<-
->sitting upon the tree's root.<-
->See the company that surrounds her;<-
->the others follow the Griffin upward<-
->with a sweeter and more profound song.”<-
->And if her speech was more diffused,<-
->I do not know, for already in my eyes was she<-
->who had closed me off from understanding anything else.<-

...so that it has completely captured the intellect and placed it under the yoke of faith; and for this reason, Theology sits upon the root. **SEE The company**: which are the seven virtues. **THE OTHERS**: those of the Old and New Testaments. **THEY GO UPWARD**: they ascend to heaven after the Griffin; for the first who ascended to heaven was Christ. **WITH A Sweeter and more profound song**: to demonstrate that what we understand and taste of celestial things during the pilgrimage of this mortal life, though sweet, is not as much as what is tasted later in the eternal homeland. **AND IF her speech was more diffused**: this shows that although active doctrine shows us various things, nevertheless, one who has arrived at the state of innocence opens his ears to nothing other than theological matters. **IN MY EYES**: understand this as the eyes of the intellect.

->Sitting alone upon the very earth,<-
->as a guard left there for the chariot...<-

<column-break/>

-herds: she fled him, and he followed her until they reached the river where, being unable to cross it, the nymph asked help from the gods to escape the hands of Pan. The gods, moved to pity, transformed her into marsh reeds. And Pan, unable to have her any other way, formed the pipe from those reeds, which he called "Syrinx" after the name of the beloved nymph—though this word in Greek signifies "reed." **BUT LET HIM WHO can well depict sleep do so**: as if to say, let anyone who knows how to well-fashion and describe the act of falling asleep show it. **THEREFORE I pass over it**: because I cannot express it. **AND When I awoke**: and so that he may understand what woke him, he shows that it was a very great splendor that came, and the voice of Matelda calling him, saying **ARISE**: that is, get up on your feet. And certainly a supreme light can often wake one who sleeps, because it penetrates the eyes which, in sleep, desire darkness. But the light wakes one even more through the splendor, by which he means the cognition that we acquire for ourselves; by the voice, he means the precepts of others. **JUST AS to see the blossoms of the apple tree**: he shows that he became such when he woke as Peter, John, and James, the apostles of Christ, became after the Transfiguration of the Savior on Mount Tabor. Of this, Mark the Evangelist writes in the ninth chapter: "Jesus took Peter, James, and John and led them up a high mountain and was transfigured before them. And he shone like the sun. And Moses and Elijah appeared there. And Peter said: 'It is good to be here; let us make three tabernacles: one for you, one for Moses, and one for Elijah.' And they were overshadowed by a white cloud from the sun, and behold, a voice from heaven saying: 'This is my beloved son in whom I am well pleased.'" Then the disciples fell, and Christ called them; and looking at him, they saw him alone. And the text is ordered thus: I, Dante, returned to myself—I woke in such a way as they returned after the Transfiguration; for James and John were led by Christ to see the **BLOSSOMS**.

**AND all in doubt**: because one remains so when suddenly awakened, and especially not seeing Beatrice. This falling asleep signifies that to understand the things that follow—both at this end of Purgatory and in Paradise—Dante, who signifies sensuality and the lower reason, is lacking in many things. But he was awakened by the splendor, which is the higher reason and the intellect, and by the voice, which is cooperating grace. And thus awakened, Matelda—that is, the doctrine of the active life—showed him Beatrice—that is, she opened to him the cognition of sacred things. Beatrice sits under the tree of good and evil and of obedience, **Newly leafed out**: that is, renewed through the passion of Christ. And she sits upon the root, which signifies humility, just as the plant signifies obedience. Because he who truly desires to know divine things as far as the human intellect can carry them must become so humble...

**WHERE is**: she says to me what I said above, that Beatrice sat upon the root of the tree, and here upon the earth: because the root is under the earth. She was left as the guard of the chariot, because the...
