<header>PURGATORIO</header>

whom I saw bound to the biform beast <note>The "biform beast" is the Gryphon, representing the dual nature of Christ (divine and human).</note>
in a circle they made of themselves a cloister,
the seven nymphs with those lights in their hands
which are safe from the north wind and the south. <note>original: "aquilone & daustro"</note>
"Here you shall be a forest-dweller for a short time,
and you shall be with me without end a citizen
of that Rome whereof Christ is Roman.
Therefore, for the benefit of the world that lives ill,
now keep your eyes upon the chariot, and what you see,
once you have returned there, see that you write down."
Thus Beatrice; and I, who at the feet
of her commandments was entirely devoted,
gave my mind and eyes where she willed.

**NORTH WIND** <note>original: "AQVILONE"</note> & south: These seven virtues with their seven gifts are not extinguished in man either by prosperous things (signified by the north wind) or by adverse things (signified by the south wind). For the north wind brings serenity and comes from the highest part of the world, thereby denoting prosperity. And the south wind blows from the lower meridian part, thereby signifying adversity. We can also take the north wind to mean pride, and the south wind to mean faint-heartedness <term>pusillanimity</term>. **HERE YOU SHALL BE** a forest-dweller for a short time: This demonstrates the brevity of human life, in which the soul, which contemplates celestial things, remains only a little while. But once it has left the body, guided by the same Beatrice, it ascends to heaven where it is no longer a pilgrim or a stranger, but an eternal citizen. **OF** that Rome **WHERE**/ of Christ is Roman: of that true city, the head of the eternal empire, just as Rome is the head of the earthly empire. And just as the ancients called the celestial and eternal fatherland "Jerusalem, the city above," <note>original: "hierusale ciuitas superna"</note> so the poet uses "Rome" with that same meaning. And not without reason did he say "forest-dweller" <note>original: "siluano"</note>: because in this brief life we walk through the forest—a wild place abandoned by men and full of wild beasts. It is not cultivated by virtue; it is not inhabited by those with humanity and charity, but by those filled with savage customs. **THEREFORE** for the benefit of the world: The poet had already described what the ancient Church was like and with how many virtues it was adorned. Now, considering how it had already begun to defile itself with every vice and to degenerate and stray entirely from the true Christian Church, he describes its vices with very fitting fictions and prophesies its miseries. **THEREFORE** for the benefit: for the utility of the world. **THAT LIVES ILL**: because it is of the greatest utility to show sinners the shame and the misery of their vices. **KEEP** your eyes on the chariot: consider what will happen to the Church. And then he continues describing.

Never did fire descend with such swift motion
from a dense cloud, when it rains
from that border which is most remote,
as I saw the bird of Jove <note>The eagle, symbol of the Roman Empire.</note> descend
down through the tree, breaking the bark,
as well as the flowers and the new leaves;
And it struck the chariot with all its force,
whereat it reeled like a ship in a storm,
overcome by the waves, now to starboard, now to port. <note>original: "da poggia hor da orza"</note>
Then I saw leap into the cradle
of the triumphal vehicle a fox,
who seemed fasted of every good meal;
But, rebuking her for her foul sins,
my lady put her to such flight
as her fleshless bones would allow.

...by the bark, health. **WHEREAT IT REELED**: because the state of the Church often wavered. **STARBOARD** <note>original: "DA POGGIA"</note>: is the rope that ties the head of the yardarm on the right. **PORT** <note>original: "ORZA"</note>: The rope that ties the other head on the left. **IN THE CRADLE**: i.e., inside the chariot. This represents the heretics within the bosom of the Church, pretending to be insiders and true Christians. **TRIUMPHAL**: because in the end, the Church overcame every adversary. **OF EVERY** good meal: Referring to the soul, which the heretics feed with false opinions where there is no Catholic truth. **BUT REBUKING**: The theologians were sufficient against the heretics, whom they refuted in form and in councils; they were condemned to the fire. **IN SUCH** flight: in such a refutation. **BONES** without flesh: because he who is burned remains with bones without meat.

Then by the way it had first come,
I saw the eagle descend down into the ark...

<column-break/>

The true and only guardian of the Church Militant is Theology. Christ ascended with the others into heaven, but Beatrice remained on earth, because without the theological rule, the Christian religion would perish. And the seven virtues already narrated above made a circle around her, because Theology, left as a guard for the Church Militant, cannot exist without these virtues. This is not difficult to understand, for we see in our own century: why Simon Magus <note>A biblical figure associated with simony—the buying or selling of church offices.</note> is worth more to you than Paul and John? And why do ambition, avarice, and luxury have more power over you than apostolic poverty, humility, virginity, and chastity, to which the Church was once led? And why, through lack of wisdom, does it descend into manifest ruin? May God provide a lamp to those who walk through the darkness. "And may He shine His face upon them, lest the blind and the leaders of the blind fall into the pit; and have mercy on us." <note>original: "Et illuminet vultū suū sup eos ne ceci & cecoꝝ duces in foueam cadat: Et misereat nostri."</note> **WITH THOSE** lights in hand: we have already shown that the seven lights are the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. Justice holds fear, which drives out pride; Prudence with piety drives out envy; Fortitude drives out anger; Temperance with the light of counsel drives out avarice; Faith drives out sloth with the light of knowledge; Hope with the light of wisdom drives out gluttony; and finally, Charity with the light of intellect drives out luxury. **IN HAND**: to demonstrate that such gifts must be in action and in work.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap C with floral patterns</image-desc>

**With** that fury with which an arrow comes from heaven, an eagle comes, which, streaking down through the tree, not only scattered the flowers and the leaves but broke the bark. There were two persecutions the Church suffered: one from the Emperors, the other from the heretics. Thus, he puts the eagle for the Emperors, because their ensign is the eagle; and the fox for the heretics, who with foxy fraud strive to stain true religion. The persecutions of the eagle were foreseen by Ezekiel where he says:

> "A great eagle, with great wings and long limbs, full of feathers and variety, came to Lebanon and took the marrow of the cedar and tore off the top of the mountains." <note>original: "Aquila grandis Ales magnus longo mebrorū ductu plena plumis & uarietate uenit ad libanū & tulit medulla cedri & summitatē montiū auulsit"</note>

The persecutions of the Emperors were ten. As Augustine posits in the book *The City of God*: the first universal persecution in the Church was made by Nero. The second by Domitian and Trajan; the third and fourth by Antoninus [Pius] and [Septimius] Severus; the fifth and sixth by Maximinus and Decius; the seventh and eighth by Valerian and Aurelian; the ninth and tenth by Diocletian and Maximian. The eleventh, which has not yet happened, will be by the Antichrist, whom he figures under the guise of a dragon; and the fox signifies Muhammad <note>original: "mahometo"</note>, of whom we spoke in the twenty-eighth canto of the first canticle <note>Inferno</note>, and we refer to the sects of the heretics. **THE BIRD** of Jove: which was the ensign of Jove, and remained to his successors, the kings of Crete; and it was transported by Teucer into Troy, and from Troy it was brought by Aeneas to the Roman Empire. By the flowers, understand the ornaments and the dignities.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap H with floral patterns</image-desc>

**He** has narrated above the persecution of the Emperors against the Church and the various sects of heresies. Now he posits the Donation of Constantine <note>A forged Roman imperial decree by which the Emperor Constantine the Great supposedly transferred authority over Rome and the western part of the Roman Empire to the Pope.</note> and the complaint that Saint Peter made about it. And after that...

<summary>This page interprets the allegorical attacks on the Church (the chariot), specifically the Roman Empire's persecutions (the eagle) and the internal threat of heresy (the fox). It emphasizes Theology (Beatrice) as the essential guardian of the faith amidst historical and moral corruption.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante’s Purgatorio, Canto XXXII. The previous page established the Chariot as the Church and the Tree as Divine Justice. This section depicts the Eagle's second descent, the Dragon's attack, and the eventual corruption of the Church through temporal wealth and political interference.</meta>

<page-num>XXXII</page-num>
<header>CANTO</header>

...of the chariot and leave her bereft. <note>Referring to the Eagle (the Empire) leaving its feathers (temporal wealth/the Donation of Constantine) on the chariot.</note>
And just as a voice comes from a heart that laments,
such a voice issued from heaven and spoke thus:
"O my little ship, how ill you are laden!"
Then it seemed to me that the earth opened up
between both wheels, and I saw a dragon come out of it
who fixed his tail through the chariot;
And like a wasp that retracts its sting,
drawing back his malignant tail to himself,
he tore out part of the bottom and went wandering off.
That which remained, as fertile ground
with couch grass <note>original: "gramigna"</note>, was covered over by the feathers
offered perhaps with a healthy and kind intention;
It covered itself again, and both wheels
and the pole were so covered in the time
that a mouth stays open for a sigh.

**THE EMPIRE.** **Perhaps with a healthy and kind intention:** <margin>the priesthood and especially the Apostolic See</margin> Nevertheless, **and the other wheel:** that is, as the Antiochene church <note>The Church of Antioch</note>, which was ordained by those who first held the Old Testament, as well as the Roman church, which had newly come to the Christian faith.

Thus transformed, the holy edifice
put forth heads from its parts:
three upon the pole and one at each corner.
The first were horned like oxen,
but the four had a single horn upon the forehead;
such a monster was never seen before.
Secure as a fortress on a high mountain,
there sat upon it a loose harlot,
with eyes looking about quickly.
And as if so she would not be taken from him,
I saw standing by her side a giant,
and they kissed each other from time to time.
But because her lustful and wandering eye
turned toward me, that fierce paramour <term>drudo</term>
scourged her from her head to the soles of her feet.
Then, full of suspicion and cruel anger,
he untied the monster and dragged it through the forest,
so far that the forest alone served as a shield
between me and the harlot and the new beast.

**EACH TO THE OTHER:** But because this prostitute turned her eyes toward me, the giant became jealous. And in truth, Boniface <note>Pope Boniface VIII</note>, a vehement and eloquent man, most greedy for honor, held dealings with various lords. For this reason, the King did not stop until he brought the court to Provence <note>The Avignon Papacy</note> beyond the Alps. And therefore he says that the giant untied the chariot—which is the Church—and pulled it so far through the forest that the great distance made the forest alone a shield between me and her—that is, it was an obstacle so that I could not see her. And he places himself for the other powers of which he [the King] was jealous, lest they take the Pope from him. **TO THE HARLOT:** that is, the Pope. **AND TO THE NEW BEAST:** that is, the Church having become a new wild beast.

<column-break/>

This depicts the schism <note>original: "cistna," likely "scisma"</note> made by Mohammed <note>original: "Maumeth"</note>. Therefore, the figure and the gift of Constantine are represented by the feathers which the eagle, descending from where it had previously come (that is, from the Empire), shed into the body of the chariot—that is, into the most intimate part, which is the Apostolic Church—giving of his temporal goods. **AND AS A VOICE COMES FROM A HEART THAT LAMENTS:** Thus a miserable voice issued from heaven, like one that comes from a heart that laments and grieves, and said: "O my little ship, how ill you are laden!"—that is, burdened with evil and harmful things. This implies that Saint Peter, the first pontiff, foresaw that the temporal goods given to the Church (which in the past had been maintained holy and formed by every virtue in poverty) would corrupt it with such delicacies. **THEN IT SEEMED TO ME THAT THE EARTH OPENED:** He describes a dragon coming out from under the earth between one wheel and the other of the chariot, and it thrust its tail through the chariot and pierced the bottom, as a wasp does when it draws out its sting; and then it withdraws to itself. The dragon come out of the earth is Mohammed, who was a man of the earth and voluptuous. And he fixed his tail—that is, fraud—dividing the two wheels. For Mohammed withdrew from the Church the Saracens, who had newly come from the Old Testament and from circumcision and from the synagogue to the Christian Church and the New Testament and baptism. **AND WENT WANDERING OFF:** Because his religion has no certain foundation, but goes wandering and straying. **THAT WHICH REMAINED:** that is, the rest of the Christian Church that was not seduced or persuaded by Mohammed, but remained in the true faith, was covered by the eagle's feathers as the earth is covered with couch grass—that is, it became rich with goods received from the—

<image-desc>A large decorative initial 'A' in red ink begins the following section of commentary.</image-desc>

At sufficient length we said in Canto XVIII of the *Inferno* how in the Christian Church the seven heads signify the seven sacraments corresponding to the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, and how by the ten horns are understood the ten commandments of the law. And in this place, he puts three heads on the pole for the three sacraments which the prelates administer, who are at the pole—that is, the government of the Church: which are Confirmation <term>cresma</term>, Baptism, and Penance. And the other four he puts each in one of the four corners of the chariot. Return, then, to the aforementioned place in the *Inferno* and you will have the full allegory of that chariot thus transformed. Now he adds the harlot and the giant, her lover. Where by the harlot he understands the Church and the Supreme Pontiff Boniface VIII, and by the giant the King of France <note>Philip IV, "the Fair"</note>. For the Church, which with the highest chastity ought to love her spouse Christ and never depart from spiritual things, became a prostitute; and for the hope of temporal goods, she loved the King of France, whom he calls a giant. Two things are in the giant: first, he is of great stature; second, a "giant" signifies one generated from the earth. Similarly, the King of France was of very great power and lordship, and was a "product of the earth," despising spiritual goods and loving only earthly goods such as empires and riches. There sat, then, upon the chariot—that is, in the Apostolic See—a harlot: that is, Pope Boniface, who like a prostitute was corrupted by money, and to acquire treasure, leaving his spouse, gave himself to adultery. **LOOSE:** free and without any restraint. **WITH EYES LOOKING ABOUT QUICKLY:** Just as a prostitute draws a lover to herself with quick and rolling eyes, so Boniface lured the King with various promises. The giant was near her, fearing that she might be taken from him—that is, the King continually maintained the Pope in his friendship with legates and orators, so that he would not turn elsewhere. **AND THEY KISSED EACH OTHER FROM TIME TO TIME:** By the kisses, understand the loving offers and presents and gifts that they made...

<meta>This page continues from the previous description of the chariot's transformation and the dragon's attack on the Church. We have reached the final Canto of the Purgatorio, where Beatrice addresses Dante's confusion and the dire state of the corrupted Church.</meta>

# PURGATORIO CANTO XXXIII OF THE SECOND CANTICLE BY DANTE.

This is the thirty-third and final canto: in which the poet, wishing to bring the Purgatorio to a close, continues the description already begun. He shows how the virtues grieved because of the persecutions and transformations of the chariot and the pole <note>The chariot represents the Church, and the pole represents the authority of the Papacy or the Empire.</note>, that is, of the church and the prelates. Beatrice exhorted him to follow her and ask her about any doubts he had, and she resolved them by demonstrating that whoever harms the church will be punished, and soon. Dante raises doubts and excuses his "lowly wit." Beatrice excuses him, showing his wit to be sufficient. Now, beginning, the poet shows that due to the disturbance of the chariot, the three theological and four cardinal virtues <note>The seven virtues: Faith, Hope, Charity, Prudence, Justice, Fortitude, and Temperance.</note> grieved; and with sweet psalmody—that is, sweet song—and as if stirred to mercy, they said: **"O God, the nations have come into your inheritance."** <note>original: "Deus venerunt gentes in hereditatem tuam." This is the opening of Psalm 79, a lament over the destruction of Jerusalem.</note>

**"O God, the nations have come,"** alternating
now three, now four, in sweet psalmody,
the women began, weeping.

And Beatrice, sighing and compassionate,
listened to them, looking in such a way
that Mary at the cross changed little more. <note>Beatrice’s grief is compared to the Virgin Mary’s sorrow at the Crucifixion.</note>

But after the other virgins gave place
to her to speak, she stood up on her feet
and replied, colored like fire:

**"A little while, and you shall not see me;**
**and again, my beloved sisters,**
**a little while, and you shall see me."** <note>original: "Modicum & iam non uidebitis me et iterum... modicum & uos uidebitis me." Christ's words to his disciples from John 16:16.</note>

Then she sent all seven on ahead of her,
and behind her, with only a nod, she moved
me, and the Lady, and the Sage who remained. <note>The "Lady" is Matilda, and the "Sage" is the poet Statius.</note>

Thus she went on; and I do not believe
her tenth step had been placed upon the ground
when with her eyes she struck my own,

And with a tranquil look she said: "Come
more quickly, so that if I speak with you,
you are well-placed to listen to me."

As soon as I was with her as I should be,
she said to me: "Brother, why do you not venture
to ask me anything, now that you come with me?"

Like those who are too reverent
when speaking in the presence of their superiors,
and do not draw a clear voice through their teeth,

So it happened to me, that without a full sound
I began: "My Lady, my need
you know, and what is good for it."

And she to me: "From fear and from shame
I wish you now to disentangle yourself,
so that you no longer speak like a man who dreams.

Know that the vessel that the serpent broke
was, and is not; but let him who is to blame believe
that God’s vengeance fears no sops." <note>original: "che uendecta dadio non teme fuppe." This refers to an old belief that if a murderer ate a piece of bread ("sop") on the victim's grave within nine days, they would be safe from blood-feud vengeance. Beatrice warns that no such superstition can stop divine justice.</note>

<column-break/>

In this psalm, David laments the future destruction of the Temple of God. This demonstrated that enemies of the Church would use cruelty against her. Beatrice, with tears and a pitiful face, listened to it, her face changed almost as Mary's was at the cross, because the true <term>theologian</term> <note>One who studies the nature of God and religious truth.</note> always grieves for things done to the dishonor of God and the harm of one's neighbor. But after the other virgins finished, following the lamentations of the virtues, Beatrice stood upright. This demonstrates the vigilance of holy theologians. And her being "colored like fire" signifies fervor and charity, because they always comfort with vigilance and fervent charity. **"A little while, and you shall not see me, and again a little while, and you shall see me."** Then she placed all seven before her: because there is nothing in Christian theology that does not always follow these seven virtues. And after herself, with only a nod, she placed me: because he who is already in that state has no need of much exhortation. And "the Lady" refers to Matilda; and "the Sage who remained" refers to Statius.

He shows that Beatrice had not gone ten steps when she struck his eyes with her own. This signifies that there are not ten clauses between where John, in the first chapter of the <term>Apocalypse</term> <note>The Book of Revelation in the Bible.</note>, places the harlot who commits fornication with the kings of the earth, and that place where it says: **"The beast that you saw was, and is not."** The eyes of Beatrice are the intellect of that text which possesses Dante’s intellect. Furthermore, "with a tranquil look"—this denotes that it is necessary for the mind of whoever wishes to follow this doctrine to be tranquil; or truly it signifies that theological doctrine purges the soul of every perturbation and makes it tranquil. And this admonishes Dante to walk close to her so that he can understand what she speaks. For he who does not separate himself from other cares and does not apply his whole mind to such doctrine will never be fit to understand it. Then she asks Dante why, being with her, he does not venture—that is, does not dare—to ask her anything; as if to say that whoever follows the studies of theology should not be sluggish because the matters are very high, but should ask—that is, by frequent rereading, sharpening the wit, investigating, and asking others—striving to understand every doubt within it. And she calls him "brother" to denote that he is a man like those who were made writers of it; and for this reason, using assiduous and long-term diligence, he can understand it as many have understood it. "Like those," he says, "it happened to me like those who, when speaking with their lords, are so hindered by the reverence they bear them that they do not draw a clear voice through their teeth." For the voice dies before it leaves the mouth. In this, he admonishes us that although we should dare to set ourselves to understand every obscure passage, we should nevertheless do so with modesty and with supreme reverence toward it, and without presumption. Finally, she teaches what our questions ought to be.

He rightly states that "the vessel is not"; for having been broken, it is no longer a vessel. Therefore, the Church is no longer as it used to be, because it is divided, and from being spiritual and virtuous, it has largely become carnal and vicious. In this place, he imitates John in the seventeenth chapter of the Apocalypse where he says: **"The beast that you saw was, and is not."** "But let him who is to blame"—he who has been the cause of such ruin and adultery of the Church—"believe that God’s vengeance fears no sops," that is, believe that God will take vengeance for it. This can be understood as referring to **Boniface**, who through divine justice lost the papacy through a raging death. It can also refer to **Philip, King of France**, who with Pope Clement made ignominious agreements against the honor of the Church.

<summary>In this final canto of the Purgatorio, Beatrice uses biblical imagery to lament the corruption of the Church and prophesies divine vengeance against those who have despoiled it. She encourages Dante to overcome his intellectual hesitation and "dream-like" state to engage deeply with theological truth.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Beatrice's prophecy regarding the restoration of divine order and the punishment of the corrupt Church and its allies. Having witnessed the symbolic destruction of the chariot, Dante now receives a cryptic message about a future "Leader" who will set things right.</meta>

# PURGATORIO CANTO XXXIII

For I see certainly, and therefore I tell it,
stars already near, bringing a time
secure from every obstacle and every bar,
In which a **five hundred, ten, and five** <note>original: "cinquecento dieci et cinque." This is the famous "DXV" prophecy. In Roman numerals, D=500, X=10, V=5. Rearranged, they spell "DVX," the Latin word for "Leader" or "Duce."</note>
sent by God shall slay the thief <note>The "thief" or "shameless woman" represents the corrupt Papal Court.</note>
with that giant who sins with her.

And perhaps my dark narration,
like **Themis** and the **Sphinx**, fails to persuade you,
because in their fashion it clouds the intellect;
But soon the facts shall be the **Naiads** <note>A common manuscript error for "Laiades" (Oedipus, son of Laius). Oedipus solved the Sphinx's riddle. The commentator here follows the "Naiads" reading.</note>
who will solve this difficult enigma
without harm to sheep or grain.
Mark this; and just as these words are brought
from me to you, so teach them to the living—
to those whose life is a race toward death.
And bear in mind when you write them
not to hide what you have seen of the plant
which has now been twice plundered here.

Whoever robs that plant or breaks it
offends God with an act of blasphemy,
for He created it holy for His use alone.
For biting that fruit, in pain and in desire,
for five thousand years or more, the first soul <note>Adam.</note>
longed for Him who punished the bite in Himself.
Your wit sleeps if it does not judge
that for a singular reason it is so tall
and so inverted at its top.
And if your idle thoughts had not been as the waters of the **Elsa** <note>The Elsa is a river in Tuscany whose waters were thought to petrify objects, just as Dante's worldly thoughts have hardened his mind.</note>...

<column-break/>

**He does not fear soups.** <note>original: "No tēme zuppe."</note> i.e., the vain defenses of men. The commentator from Imola <note>Benvenuto da Imola, a 14th-century scholar.</note> relates that in Florence there was a popular belief that if a murderer could eat a "soup" (a piece of bread soaked in wine) over the body of the deceased within nine days, he could not be killed in revenge. Dante’s son, who comments on this comedy, affirms that in those times when a great citizen was killed in our city, the relatives would guard the grave for nine days so that no one would eat a soup upon it. It belongs to the **Eagle** to direct and correct the errors of the Church; he adds that the Eagle will not always be without an heir: that is, without an Emperor. For everyone who is made Emperor becomes an heir to the Eagle. He shows that in that time the Eagle was without an heir because, despite there being Emperors, they served the Pope and did not dare to correct him through councils. **That he left his feathers to the chariot.** i.e., he left his treasures to the Church, which became a monster and then a prey. It became a monster because through riches it abandoned virtue and gave itself to vice, which caused it to become a prey. **I already see stars approaching:** all the stars in the sky were there from the beginning. Therefore, he means stars that are near in time. **Secure from every obstacle:** every counter-position. **And every bar:** every resistance. **In which a five hundred, ten, and five:** he does not use this number for the number of years, but because five hundred is noted with the letter **D**, five with **V**, and ten with **X**, which makes **DVX** <note>Leader</note>. He says there will be a Duke, that is, a leader of an army sent by God, who will kill the thief and the adultery of the harlot—that is, the Pope and the Roman Court, adulterated and defiled by every vice. **With that giant:** by which he means the temporal lord who sins (that is, commits crimes) with her.

Because until now Beatrice has spoken with obscurity, she therefore adds that perhaps her narration is dark and like that of **Themis** and the **Sphinx**, which join and bind and persuade. Themis and the Sphinx gave their answers so obscurely that a very sharp interpreter was necessary to understand them; and my narration is just as obscure because it "sharpens"—that is, it thins and makes the intellect thin in their manner (meaning the manner of Themis and the Sphinx). The meaning is: I speak as obscurely as Themis and the Sphinx. Themis was a goddess of the pagans who gave oracles on Mount Parnassus, but many were obscure, such as the one given to **Deucalion** and **Pyrrha** after the flood. When they asked how they could restore the human race, she replied that they should throw the "bones of their mother" behind their backs. Deucalion interpreted this to mean that the "mother" is the Earth and the "bones" in the Earth are the stones. The Sphinx was a monster near Thebes who, according to Hesiod, was the child of Chimaera and Orthrus (the dog of Geryon). He stayed on a mountain near Thebes and proposed a riddle—which the Greeks call an **enigma**—to anyone who passed, with the condition that if they could not declare it, they would be killed by the monster. He proposed to **Oedipus**, father of Eteocles and Polynices, which animal went on four feet at the beginning, then on two, and finally on three. Oedipus sharply declared this enigma, saying it was Man, who at the beginning goes on all fours with hands and feet, then stands upright on two feet, and at the end of his age goes with three because he leans on a staff. **But soon the facts will be the Naiads:** <note>The commentator explains "Naiads" as the revealers of the truth, though Dante likely intended the "son of Laius" (Oedipus).</note> but soon the facts I announce will follow, and those facts will then declare what I wished to say, just as the Naiads declared the obscure words of Themis. **Which:** which facts. **Will solve:** will declare. **This enigma:** this obscure saying. *Enigma* is a Greek word, as was said. **Aristotle** defines it in his book on poets <note>The Poetics.</note> that an enigma is a speech that is either impossible or difficult to reduce to a certain understanding. And **Averroes** writes that this often occurs among Arabic poets by way of the **haruspices** <note>Diviners who read entrails.</note> who sacrificed some beast and, according to the disposition they found in the liver or other entrails, predicted what was to be; or by way of the **pullarii** <note>Priests who observed the sacred chickens.</note> who brought out the chickens they kept for this practice and offered them grain, and according to the way the chickens pecked, they said what was divined. **You mark:** that is, attend with diligence and teach it to the living. **...** just as they are set down by me. **To the living:** of the life that is a race toward death. The truly living are the celestial beings, for they have life without death; but we are not truly living, since our life is a brief course that leads us to death. **Twice:** the first time when the eagle descended; the second when the giant took the chariot and led it away. For after the Griffin tied the chariot to the plant, the chariot and the plant became one and the same thing. **Without harm to sheep or grain:** that is, without having to search for the interpretation...

It is no wonder that whoever harms the Church bears the penalty, because he offends God, who created the said plant of obedience and the said chariot which is the Church. And He created it holy, for He blessed and sanctified it, and created it for His use so that it might give Him worship and honor, through which we might merit eternal life. **Whoever robs that:** as the giant robbed; **or breaks it:** as the eagle broke it, offends God with an **act of blasphemy**. In Latin it is called *blasphemia*, and this is a Greek distinction coming from the verb *blatin* <note>original: "blatin," a corruption of the Greek "blaptein" (to harm).</note> which means to harm and give detriment. Therefore, blasphemy is the detriment and harming of honor; and there is blasphemy of word and blasphemy of deed. Of word, when we stain God's honor with words. Of deed, when we fail in our actions. **For biting that:** he shows by the example of Adam how God punishes whoever breaks or robs the plant; for the soul of Adam, our first parent, for biting it—i.e., for tasting its fruit—remained in...

<summary>In this final canto, Beatrice delivers a cryptic prophecy (the DXV) about a future leader who will destroy the corrupt alliance between the Church and the French monarchy. The commentary explains the historical context of Florentine blood feuds and the mythological references to riddles and oracles.</summary>
<keywords>DXV prophecy, DVX, Themis, Sphinx, Oedipus, corruption of the Church, Eagle, Dante's commentary, Florentine customs, Adam's sin</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Beatrice and Dante in the Earthly Paradise. Beatrice is explaining why her words seem obscure and why Dante’s intellect is currently unable to grasp divine truths, comparing his clouded mind to the petrifying waters of the Elsa and the stained mulberry tree of Pyramus.</meta>

# PURGATORIO CANTO XXXIII

...vain thoughts around your mind
at their pleasure, like a Pyramus to the mulberry.
By so many circumstances alone
the justice of God in the prohibition
you would recognize in the tree, in a mortal sense.

Which was, as we said above, the nature of that plant. **Your wit sleeps** if you do not judge that tree to be **exalted** for a singular reason. **And if they had not been as the waters of the Elsa**—that is, if your vain thoughts and worldly things had not hardened your mind like the water of the Elsa, which, as we mentioned above, hardens things that enter it and turns them into stone, which the people living near this river use in their buildings. This same thing happens in the Sarno, a river in Puglia. And **Albertus Magnus** <note>Albert the Great (c. 1200–1280), a Dominican friar and influential philosopher/scientist.</note> in his *Book of Metals* <note>original: "libro de metalli"</note> writes that there is a fountain in Boeotia that turns whatever is placed in it into stone. **Emperor Frederick** <note>Frederick II (1194–1250), Holy Roman Emperor, known for his curiosity and scientific experiments.</note> proved this: he dipped his glove into it halfway, and the submerged part became stone, while the other part remained leather as it was before. But let us return to the text where it continues: **And if the pleasures** that you had from such thoughts **had not been a Pyramus to the mulberry**—that is, had not stained your mind as Pyramus stained the mulberry, which turned from white to black (a fable we told in the twenty-seventh canto of the first canticle). <note>The commentator likely means the previous canticle or the earlier part of Purgatorio, as the story of Pyramus and Thisbe appears in Purgatorio XXVII.</note> **By so many circumstances**: Beatrice says: if Dante had fixed his thoughts on God and they were not hardened toward worldly things, he would know that God, by His justice, forbade man from touching that fruit according to morality. This is shown by the "circumstances" of the tree, of which the first is that the tree was created by God and blessed so that man should give due worship to God, which is justice. The second is the long deprivation of Adam for his transgression. The third is the satisfaction made through the Passion of Christ.

**But because I see you in your intellect**
**made of stone, and in sin so dyed**
**that the light of my word dazzles you,**
**I also wish—if not written, at least pictured—**
**that you carry it within you, at least for that reason**
**that one brings back the staff wreathed in palm.**

**And I: "Just as wax under the seal,**
**which does not change the figure impressed upon it,**
**so my brain is now stamped by you.**
**But why does your desired word**
**fly so far above my sight,**
**that the more it strives, the more it loses it?"**
**"So that you may know," she said, "that school**
**which you have followed, and see its doctrine,**
**how it can follow my word;**

**And see your way from the divine way**
**distant as far as is distant**
**from the earth the heaven that hastens highest."**
**Wherefore I answered her: "I do not remember**
**that I ever estranged myself from you,**
**nor do I have a conscience that pricks me for it."**
**"And if you cannot remember it,"**
**smiling she answered, "now bethink you**
**how you drank of Lethe only today;**
**And if from smoke fire is argued,**
**this your oblivion clearly concludes**
**a fault in your will, intent elsewhere.**

**Truly, from now on my words**
**shall be naked, as much as shall be fitting**
**to uncover them to your rude sight."**

<column-break/>

...the penalty that he [Adam] had in life through the labor of body and mind, living nine hundred and thirty years; and in the desire he had in Limbo, which was five thousand two hundred and thirty-one years from the beginning of the world until the eighteenth year of the empire of **Tiberius**, in which Christ suffered. Therefore, he says for more than five thousand years he longed for the coming of Christ, who punished in Himself the "bite" of Adam. Because, to restore Adam's disobedience, Christ, God and man, made obedient against that disobedience, suffered the penalty on the cross.

She wishes then that, since for the reasons stated above he cannot understand her at present, he should at least carry her meaning in his heart, so that after he is well-purged of all vices, by repeating it in his mind, he may attend to it. Therefore she says: since you have made your intellect of stone—that is, you have made a habit of vice—and are dyed in sin, because your mind is infected such that the eye of the weak intellect is dazzled by the splendor of my words, at least carry them with you, if not written, at least pictured; though writing expresses things more and better than painting. **For the reason that one brings back the staff wreathed in palm.** The meaning is: although you do not understand my words exactly, nevertheless keep the sum of them, so that this may be a sign that you come from me, just as a staff wreathed in palm is a sign that the pilgrim comes from the Holy Sepulcher where there is an abundance of palms. <note>Pilgrims returning from Jerusalem were often called "Palmers" because they carried palm branches.</note> And for this reason, she gives a precept that, despite the fact that our minds are infected so that in studying sacred things we cannot understand them—because **"wisdom will not enter into a malevolent soul"** <note>original: "in animam maliuolam non introibit spiritus sapientiae," a quote from the Book of Wisdom 1:4.</note>—we must nevertheless read sacred things and understand the words, because afterwards, by purging ourselves, we will understand the allegorical sense. **In my brain**: in the memory, which is the "last cell of the ventricle of the brain." <note>Following medieval anatomy, which divided the brain into "cells" or ventricles for different functions like sensation, reason, and memory.</note>

Dante asks Beatrice why her desired words fly so far above his sight—that is, above his intellect—that his sight and intellect lose them the more he tries to understand. And indeed, the high senses of the theologians, which are reached only through faith, are more distant from our cognition the more we strive to understand them by human reason. Whence **Gregory** <note>Pope Gregory the Great (c. 540–604).</note> says: **"Faith has no merit where human reason provides no proof."** <note>original: "Fides non habet meritum ubi humana ratio non peebet experimentum."</note> And for this reason, Beatrice answers that she has spoken in that form so that he may know the "school" of natural philosophy he has followed, and see how their doctrine can be fit to understand theology; since the philosopher seeks reason in everything, and theology cannot be grasped by human reason. And in this way, Dante can see "our way" and how philosophical doctrine is distant—that is, so far removed and different from divine doctrine, which is theology—as the heaven that "hastens"—that is, turns with speed higher than the other heavens—is distant from the earth.

Dante demonstrates that he does not remember having estranged himself or departed from Beatrice. And she adds that such forgetfulness comes because he has drunk of **Lethe**. <note>The river of forgetfulness in the Earthly Paradise, which erases the memory of sin.</note> Then she adds that since Lethe only makes one forget evil, this [his estrangement] must have been evil; and thus she concludes it is an evil to leave theology for philosophy or any other science. Then she promises that in the future she will speak to him openly, as much as is appropriate for his "rude" or unrefined wit, because he has not yet drunk from the river **Eunoe**, as he will drink a little later.
It was midday, and because the sun is then at its highest, it seems to go slower and is more "coruscant"—that is, splendid. It held the meridian circle, which...

<summary>Beatrice explains to Dante that his worldly studies (philosophy) have clouded his mind, making her theological truths difficult to grasp. She uses metaphors of petrifying water and stained mulberries to describe his intellectual state before he drinks from the river Eunoe.</summary>
<keywords>Beatrice, Dante, Lethe, Eunoe, philosophy vs theology, Adam's transgression, Christ's Passion, Albertus Magnus, Frederick II, memory, neuroanatomy</keywords>

--- Page 492 ---
<meta>This page concludes the final canto of the Purgatorio. It follows the previous discussion where Beatrice rebuked Dante for his intellectual failings, comparing his hardened mind to the petrifying waters of the Elsa. Now, the group reaches the source of the divine rivers in the Earthly Paradise, and Dante undergoes his final purification.</meta>

### CANTO XXXIII

And more radiant and with slower steps
the sun held the meridian circle,
which shifts here and there as the vantage point changes,
when—just as one who goes before a group as a guide
halts if he finds something new in his path—
the seven ladies <note>The seven ladies represent the four Cardinal Virtues and three Theological Virtues.</note> halted at the edge of a dark shadow,
such as the Alps cast over their cool streams
beneath green leaves and black branches.
Before them, **Euphrates and Tigris** <note>In Genesis, these are two of the four rivers flowing out of Eden. Dante reimagines them as Lethe and Eunoë.</note>
seemed to me to issue from a single fountain,
and like friends, they parted slowly.

"O light, O glory of the human race,
what water is this that here unfolds
from one beginning, and then flows away from itself?"
To such a plea, it was said to me: "Pray
**Matilda** <note>The mysterious lady who guides Dante through the Earthly Paradise, representing the active religious life.</note> that she tell you." And here she responded,
as one does who frees themselves from blame:
"This and other things
were told to him by me; and I am sure
that the water of **Lethe** <note>The river of forgetfulness, which wipes away the memory of sin.</note> did not hide them from him."
And Beatrice: "Perhaps a greater care,
which often robs the memory,
has made his mind's eye dark."
"But see **Eunoë** <note>A name coined by Dante from the Greek words for 'good' and 'mind.' This river restores the memory of good deeds.</note> which flows there;
lead him to it, and as is your custom,
revive his fainting power."

Like a gentle soul that offers no excuse,
but makes the will of another its own
as soon as that will is revealed by a sign;
so, once I was taken by her,
 the beautiful lady moved, and to **Statius** <note>The Roman poet who has accompanied Dante through the upper levels of Purgatory.</note>
she said with courtesy: "Come with him."
If I had, reader, more ample space
to write, I would tell at least in part
of the sweet drink that would never have satiated me;
but because all the pages are full
designated for this second canticle <note>A 'canticle' refers to one of the three main parts of the Divine Comedy: Inferno, Purgatorio, and Paradiso.</note>,
the curb of art <term>fren dell'arte (restraint of art): the structural rules the poet imposes on himself, such as the equal length of the three sections.</term> does not let me go further.
I returned from that most holy wave
remade, even as new plants
are renewed with new foliage,
**Pure and disposed to mount to the stars.**

<column-break/>

The meridian is not the same in every part of the world. But as the sphere of the earth turns, so it comes sooner or later in different places. **When they halted:** the seven ladies stopped just as a scout stops when they find something new. **Euphrates and Tigris:** the Bible places these rivers in this paradise, as has been shown elsewhere; but the poet, to serve his allegory, calls them the ones he mentioned above: Lethe and Eunoë. They exit from one fountain because each gives a grace that is not mediocre; for Lethe makes us forget vice and all its fuel and incentive, and Eunoë, which in Greek signifies "good mind" <note>original: "bonamente"</note>, leads us to remember virtues and inflames us with love.

He asks Beatrice what water that is, which makes two rivers from one source: namely **Lethe**, which flows to the left, and **Eunoë**, which flows to the right. **O light:** truly light, because theology illuminates the human mind to know God. **O glory:** the glory of man is to have a soul enlightened by divine things. At such a plea, I was told by Beatrice to ask Matilda: because he presents Matilda as **Practical Theology** <note>The application of religious principles to action and teaching.</note>, whose office it is to preach, teach, baptize, and such things; therefore he imagines that Beatrice commissions Matilda to bathe him in the river Eunoë. **And here:** meaning then. **The beautiful lady Matilda responded:** as one does who "unties" themselves, almost as if loosening and defending oneself from blame. For he who acts but does not teach is at fault. Thus Matilda shows that she has already instructed Dante about these rivers and other things, as appeared above. And **Beatrice** responded: although you have already shown him these things, nonetheless perhaps some greater care and occupation—which often robs the memory—has made his mind "dark in the eyes," that is, in the intellect. And by this, it is denoted that the active theologian should not warn, correct, and instruct only once, but often, because men occupied in civil actions do not have a ready soul that can quickly form a habit of such virtues. **But see Eunoë:** of which was spoken above. **Lead him to it as is your custom:** because, as we have said, this belongs to practical theology. **Revive his fainting power:** there was naturally in man the virtue with its "tinder" <note>original: "fomite," referring to the inclination toward good or the spark of grace.</note>. But sin extinguished it, and the tinder was hidden like embers under the fire. But coming to the state of innocence, the grace of the most benign God relights it.

**Like a gentle soul that offers no excuse:** there is no greater nobility in the soul than humanity and charity; and he who has this does not seek excuses but accords his will with the will of those who ask, provided it is in honest matters. **As soon as:** that is, immediately when the will of another is revealed; **revealed:** that is, through a sign or words it appears outwardly in a form that the gentle soul understands. And in passing, the poet shows that **Active Theology** has no will separate from the will of **Speculative Theology** <note>The theoretical study of God and divine truths.</note>. For it purges the minds of men so that they may then ascend to speculation. **So since by her:** Matilda took him and told **Statius** to go with him, to denote that the doctrine of the pagans <note>referring to Statius as a classical poet converted to Christianity</note> is useful when it is in obedience to sacred letters and does not deviate from them. **If I had, reader, more ample space:** the poet excuses himself for not writing of the sweetness of this water because this second canticle has its set number of verses, but in truth, he reserves it for the following canticle. **I returned remade like new plants:** which are very fresh and very green. Hence David said: *Your children shall be like olive shoots* <note>original Latin: "sili tui sicut nouelle oliuarum" from Psalm 128:3</note>. And indeed, just as the old tree is renewed by the new plants that rise from the roots, so the soul purged of sin—which had aged it—renews itself, returning to the state of innocence. And having been made pure, it is fit and willing to **mount to the stars**, that is, to the contemplation of divine things. May He who created us, and then—after we fell into the death of sin—created us anew by His infinite mercy, lead us there.

<meta>This page marks the transition from the Purgatorio to the Paradiso. It features the original preface by the famous Renaissance scholar Cristoforo Landino, who provides a Neoplatonic and theological introduction to the final part of Dante’s journey.</meta>

<header>PREFACE</header>

<margin>244</margin>

# PROLOGUE BY CRISTOFORO LANDINO THE FLORENTINE FOR THE COMMENTARY ON THE DIVINE POET DANTE ALIGHERI REGARDING THE PARADISO, THE THIRD CANTICLE

**We praise you, O God; we acknowledge you to be the Lord.** <note>original: "TEDEVUM laudamus: te dominū confitemur." These are the opening lines of the Te Deum, a traditional Christian hymn of praise.</note> Just as Cicero, being both a philosopher and an orator, when he set out in his old age to write about *Old Age* for Atticus—who was also an old man—took his beginning from a poet established in that same stage of life, it similarly seems right to me, having been moved from the *Inferno* and the *Purgatorio* toward the *Paradiso*, to begin with the same hymn in which two most excellent doctors of the Church <note>Referring to St. Augustine and St. Ambrose.</note>, distinguished in both life and doctrine, sang their due thanks when the divine **Aurelius Augustine**, with the help of **Ambrose**, was liberated from diabolical snares and brought to the harbor of salvation. 

Therefore, O Supreme God, we praise you, and we confess you to be the true Lord: you who, through your grace, have illuminated those with civic virtues and drawn them up from the low and dark depths of Hell. And later, becoming a splendid lamp to the feet of your servants through the purgative virtues, you lightened those still heavy with the mold of the earth, so that we overcame every difficulty of the arduous and steep ascent of the mountain of Purgatory. Now, with your holy hyssop, you will make us clean, and by washing us, we shall remain whiter than any snow; and so pure that your **Paraclete** spirit <note>The Holy Spirit, from the Greek word for 'advocate' or 'helper.'</note>, more by its grace than by our merit, will pour itself into us. You will adorn us with the third kind of virtue—that of the already purified soul. These shall acquire for us two wings: **Justice** and **Religion**. With these, we shall fly even unto the **Empyrean heaven** <note>The highest, immaterial heaven in medieval cosmology, where God resides.</note> to mirror ourselves in the divine fountain. 

No other way remains, nor any other faculty for miserable mortals to elevate themselves to such height, if not through **Justice**—which the divine **Plato** places as the root of all moral virtues—and **Religion**, which contains within itself all the intellectual ones. The "Platonic" **Virgil** <note>Landino and his circle viewed Virgil as a philosopher-poet who hid Platonic truths in his verses.</note> signified this in his sixth book: *To escape to the upper air, this is the task, this the toil; few whom impartial Jupiter has loved, or whom blazing virtue has raised to the heavens, have been able to do it.* <note>original: "Superas euadere ad auras hoc opus hic labor est pauci quos equus amauit iupiter aut ardens euexit aethera uirtus." A quote from the Aeneid (6.128-131).</note> Only two types of people were able, as we interpreted at length in that place, and there is no other way to lead us. 

Let no man be so alienated from reason that he wishes to imitate the rash folly of the **Giants**, who hoped to build a ladder to the stars by placing Mount Ossa upon the highest peak of Mount Pelion, and another mountain upon Pelion. For the supreme Jove, with his celestial thunderbolts, turns those mountains to ruin and submerges the Giants beneath them. According to the poets, the Giants were "sons of the Earth," which refers to men devoted to earthly things. These men believe they can reach heaven with "mountains"—that is, by accumulating wealth, power, and lordships to become happy. But the thunderbolts of Jove—that is, the just divine indignation—dissipate these false goods and submerge their possessors. Therefore, the Psalmist says rightly: *For the Lord knows the way of the righteous, but the way of the ungodly shall perish. Then he shall speak to them in his wrath, and in his fury he shall trouble them.* <note>Psalm 1:6 and 2:5.</note> And elsewhere: *The Lord brings the counsel of the nations to nothing; he frustrates the plans of the peoples, and rejects the counsel of princes.* <note>Psalm 33:10.</note>

Thus, the statement of the "eagle-like" Evangelist <note>St. John the Apostle, whose symbol is the eagle.</note> is most true: *No one has ascended into heaven except he who descended from heaven.* <note>John 3:13.</note> And certainly, no one ascends to true beatitude unless they proceed from celestial things. Let us, then, adapt these wings to ourselves; and let us fly toward heaven not with the folly of **Icarus**, but with the prudence of **Daedalus**. Yet we are not so reckless as to hope that, through our own aforementioned virtues, we might fly to heaven by ourselves. Rather, when we strive to fit these two wings to ourselves, the most powerful God will be moved to compassion for our weakness; and with most liberal grace, He will supply what we cannot do for ourselves. He alone lifts us to Himself and snatches us up to heaven. 

Thus, the Apostle **Paul** does not write of himself that he "climbed" to the third heaven, but affirms that he was "caught up" there by God. Therefore, the great Apostle does not glory in having ascended, but says all glory is in God, the King of Glory. And certainly, as our Platonic **Marsilio Ficino** <note>Ficino (1433–1499) was the leader of the Florentine Platonic Academy and a close associate of Landino.</note> most learnedly writes in his book *On the Rapture of Paul*: the heavy elements of the world cannot rise on high unless they are elevated by the Most High; and he who inhabits the earth cannot move through the celestial ranks if the celestial Father does not pull him. 

To you, then, we turn, O Supreme Jove, with hot sighs and with all our hearts; we humbly pray that you reach out the right hand of your help and pull us, so that following the tracks of our poet, we may climb from heaven to heaven until we reach your presence. This presence enriches all poverty, satisfies all hunger, heals all infirmity, and strengthens all weakness. And finally, it fills us with that happiness which is neither diminished by any defect nor limited by time.

<summary>This page contains Cristoforo Landino’s humanist preface to the Paradiso, framing Dante’s journey as a Neoplatonic ascent of the soul that requires both human virtue (Justice and Religion) and Divine Grace. He contrasts this spiritual ascent with the "earthly" arrogance of the mythological Giants and stresses that true happiness can only be found by turning away from material power toward God.</summary>

<meta>This page marks the beginning of the Paradiso (the third and final part of Dante's Divine Comedy). The commentary shifts from the previous focus on Purgatory to a high theological and philosophical explanation of the celestial realms, primarily using Scholastic logic (Aquinas) and classical rhetoric (Cicero).</meta>

<header>CANTO ONE</header>
<page-num>244</page-num>

# PARADISE: THE THIRD CANTICLE OF THE DIVINE POET DANTE ALIGHIERI.

<image-desc>A large historiated decorative initial 'P' featuring a portrait of a man, likely Dante, wearing a red hood, set against a gold background within a blue and red frame decorated with floral and foliate motifs.</image-desc>

Because, as we have shown in the first canticle, all heroic poets divide their work into three parts: **proposition, invocation, and narration.** These four three-line stanzas contain the proposition, in which the matter of the whole work is briefly set forth: which is to treat of the supernal <note>meaning "heavenly" or "celestial"</note> kingdom—not according to its true nature, because this transcends our intellect, but according to how much his mind could grasp and, having grasped it, commit to memory. And because the proposition and invocation serve as a preface <note>proemio</note>, observe here what is proper to a preface. As we clearly demonstrated what its office is at the beginning of the *Inferno*, I will not labor to describe its parts. However, I will declare how the poet observes them here. **He captures attention** by showing that he must speak of <note>underlined in manuscript</note>a thing so high<note>end underline</note> that all others are long and incomparably inferior to it; for there is no comparison between the infinite and the finite—that is, between God and his creatures. **He captures goodwill** through his own person, by showing that his labor in writing will be very useful to others. **He captures receptivity** <term>docilita: the willingness to be taught</term> because he briefly demonstrates what the entire canticle will treat: namely, the eternal kingdom. **THE GLORY.** Although fame and glory seem to many to be almost the same thing, fame is nevertheless the very frequent notice of something. Glory is clear notice of something accompanied by praise. Thus, fame can be of a thing that brings neither splendor nor any praise. But glory cannot exist without these. Hence it is defined by Cicero in the *Tusculan Disputations*: >Glory is the consistent praise of good men, the uncorrupted voice of those who judge well of excellent virtue. <note>original Latin: "Gloria est cósenticus laus bonorú in corrupta uox bene iudicantiū de excellente uirtute."</note>
From this it follows that all glory is fame, but not all fame is glory. Glory is the glorious work, and that work is God's universe. **OF HIM** who moves everything—that is, God. This is a rhetorical device called circumlocution, which is when that which can be said in one word is said in many. "Who moves everything." Hence Boethius says: >And remaining stable, You grant all things to be moved. <note>original Latin: "Stabilisque moués das cúcta moueri."</note>
Only He, therefore, is stable. This is how Thomas Aquinas proves it: everything that is moved must be moved by another, such as the sun, the moon, and the others. And because we cannot proceed to infinity, it is necessary to posit one immobile mover. God, therefore, being immobile, moves all. And "He who moves everything" signifies the same as "God." Because He, being stable and immobile, is the Prime Mover. He moves the angels, and the angels move the heavens, and the heavens with their revolutions bring various effects down into the world. Therefore, God is the Prime Mover and the primary cause of all causes. For this reason, we say the glory of God penetrates through the universe—that is, it passes through all creatures—and this He could do by His power, He knew how to do by His wisdom, and He willed to produce the most perfect creature by His supreme goodness and love. And by saying "universe," we mean the whole, which is of different species: for some things have only being, like a stone; some have being and life, like herbs and trees; some add to the first two the capacity for feeling, like certain shellfish; some have being, life, feeling,

<columns>2</columns>

### THE GLORY
### OF HIM
### WHO MOVES
### ALL THINGS

penetrates through the universe and shines 
in one part more and less elsewhere.
In the heaven that receives most of His light
was I, and I saw things that to retell
he knows not, nor can he, who descends from there;
For as it nears its desire,
our intellect deepens so far
that memory cannot follow behind.
Truly, as much of the holy kingdom
as I could treasure within my mind
shall now be the matter of my song.

<column-break/>

and imagination, as the brute animals do; some add to the four aforementioned powers the discourse of reason, as men do. But the most noble creature is that which has formal being and intellect, like the angel. In brief, we can, according to the philosophers, divide this universe into three species. For whatever exists is either pure form, like God, the Angels, and the human soul (though God is the Form of forms); or it is pure matter, like the indistinct production of the elements called chaos; or it is matter with form, like elemental things—that is, those composed of elements. And in these elemental things, there are six grades: being, living, feeling, imagining, reasoning (that is, using the discourse of reason), and understanding. In these, the superior always encompasses the inferior. **AND SHINES** because God is true light, through which everything shines. His splendor, therefore, appears in every thing: but more so in those that are pure form. Just as, for example, the same image appears in a mirror, in polished metal, in water, and in a wall. It is, therefore, that same image which is shown equally to all and is received; but each receives as much as its nature allows. Thus, the mirror receives it more clearly; and among metals, silver more than tin, and tin more than lead. Therefore, in an excellent mirror, one will see the truest image. Then it generates: and elsewhere it will appear larger, elsewhere smaller, elsewhere distorted; the silver will show fewer lines, the tin even fewer. The lead will show them confused. The wall will show no lines at all, but rather a shadow, and that will be distorted or larger or smaller. Nevertheless, all these images come from one same example. It is no wonder, then, that God, who is unique, is not seen the same in all things: because not every subject can receive Him as the nature of God himself, which is perfect, but only according to its own nature, and according to whether it is capable of more or less. God, for His greater glory, is in heaven; as David says: >The heavens declare the glory of God. <note>original Latin: "Celi enarrant gloriam dei."</note>
But virtually He is in every place. As Augustine says: >God is whole in heaven, whole on earth, and whole in both. <note>original Latin: "Deus in celo totus est: in terra totus: & in utroque totus."</note>
And the Master of the Sentences <note>Peter Lombard</note> says: >Angels are circumscribed locally; God is uncircumscribed. <note>original Latin: "Angeli circunscripti localiter: Deus icircunscriptus est."</note>
But He shines more in heaven. And for this, the prophet Isaiah says: >Heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool. <note>original Latin: "Celū mihi sedes est: Terra auté scabellū pedum meorū."</note>
**IN THE HEAVEN THAT RECEIVES MOST OF HIS LIGHT:** this is the Empyrean heaven which is made of pure light; and therefore it receives more than the others which are made of light. But we shall say more things about light in a more convenient place. **WAS I:** according to the fiction, Dante was in heaven with his body; according to the allegory, he ascended there with his intellect; for through theological doctrine he arrived, as far as is permitted to man, at the knowledge of divine things. **AND I SAW** things that to retell he knows not, nor can he. Similar to that of Saint Paul: >And I saw things which it is not permitted for man to speak. <note>original Latin: "Et uidi ea que non licet homini loqui."</note>
**WHO** descends from there. While we are in heaven—that is, in the contemplation of celestial things—we can understand something of them. But when we descend to earth, we cannot retell anything—that is, returning to earthly things, we cannot demonstrate the divine within them. Furthermore: while the intellect contemplates God and divine things, memory fails and cannot retain them. And for this reason, Chrysostom says in his commentary on Paul's epistle to the Hebrews: >Just as we understand many things about God that we cannot speak, so we speak many things that we [fully] understand [not]. <note>original Latin: "Sicut multa de deo intelligimus que loqui non ualemus Ita multa loquimur que intelligimus..."</note>

</columns>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the opening of Paradiso, Canto I. The commentator (likely Cristoforo Landino) is finishing a philosophical discussion on the limits of human understanding before moving into the poetic invocation to Apollo. The previous page established that the Paradiso deals with matters transcending human intellect.</meta>

<header>PARADISE</header>

...cannot achieve. <note>The text begins mid-word: [conseguere] "achieve" or "reach."</note> And certainly we say many things about God which we both understand and do not understand. For example: although we understand that God is infinite, and consequently uncircumscribed and in every place, nonetheless our intellect cannot be capable of containing that infinity. Because of this, one can conclude that we hear rather than truly understand Him—though in some way we do understand, it is not with sufficiency. **BECAUSE Approaching.** <note>Dante, Paradiso I, 7: "Appressando sé"</note> He assigns the reason why he cannot recount what he saw: because the memory does not retain that which the intellect, plunging deep into Him, knew. The intellect, elevated to God, sees; but the memory does not retain it. Therefore, once the intellect is departed from God, we cannot recount what we saw. **TRULY as much as I from the holy kingdom:** <note>Paradiso I, 10: "Veramente quant'io del regno santo"</note> It is called a "Kingdom" because there is the true King. **HOLY:** because it is consecrated to God; because it is firm, stable, and immobile; and it lasts forever. "Holy" signifies a thing consecrated to God, and also a thing firm and stable. **AS MUCH:** He does not promise to say absolutely everything, because the human mind cannot comprehend everything; and nonetheless, it conceives much more than it can express. **BUT as much as he could make a treasure:** that is, to express as much as he committed to his memory. They call "treasure" <note>Italian: *thesoro*</note> the place where we lay up our riches. And for this reason, Cicero and many other Latin authors call the memory a "treasure," because it is that power of the soul which preserves for us what we have understood or learned.

O good Apollo, for this final labor
make me such a vessel of your worth
as you require for the gift of the beloved laurel.
Until now, one peak of Parnassus
was enough for me, but now with both
I must enter the remaining arena.
Enter into my breast and breathe your spirit,
just as when you drew Marsyas
from the sheath of his limbs.
O divine Virtue, if you lend yourself to me
so much that the shadow of the blessed kingdom
marked in my head you make manifest,
You will see me come to the foot of your beloved tree
and crown myself with those leaves
of which the matter and you will make me worthy.
So rarely, Father, are they gathered
to triumph over Caesar or a poet—
the fault and shame of human desires—
That the Peneian leaf <note>the laurel</note> should give birth
to joy for the joyful Delphic deity
whenever anyone thirsts for it.
A great fire follows a small spark;
perhaps after me, with better voices,
prayers will be offered so that Cyrrha may respond.

<column-break/>

Up to now, the "proposition" has been written, in which he has shown with brevity what he intends to treat. Now follows the "invocation," in which he invokes Apollo to inspire in him his divine spirit, through which men become poets. For this reason, I judge it useful and pleasant to briefly run through, according to Plato, what "divine frenzy" <term>furor divino: a state of inspired poetic or prophetic madness</term> is and how it breathes into the poet. But let it suffice to have treated this at the beginning of this work where, as much as our strength allowed, we praised the faculty of poetry. "Apollo" is a Greek name but is also common among the Latins; he is the god of the sun according to the pagans. The name comes from a Greek verb meaning "to kill" and "to undo" <note>original: *uccidere & diffare*</note>, because the solar rays are as suited to corruption through excessive heat as they are to generation through temperate heat. For this reason, Homer introduces him as the giver of the pestilence, and the ancients attribute to him the bow and the lyre: the former to show that he is harmful, the latter to signify harmony, temperance, proportion, and his suitability from which all things are generated. Thus, Horace in his Odes prays that he come without arrows and with the lyre: "Mild and peaceful, with your weapon hidden, hear the suppliant boys, Apollo." <note>original: "Condito mitis placiduſque telo / Suplices audi pueros apollo"</note> They feign that he is the god of poets because, since no one can be a true poet without the science of all disciplines, the physicists and especially the Platonists say that our soul, descending into the body, receives from the sun the power through which it acquires knowledge and opinion. And therefore, do not leave behind the others: similarly, from every other planet, it takes some power. For Saturn gives it reasoning; Jupiter, practice and action; Mars, ardor and boldness; Venus, the movement in desire; Mercury, speech; the Moon grants the power to plant, generate, and increase bodies. This is, therefore, the natural reason why poets are under the protection of the sun. Poets are crowned with laurel because this tree is dedicated to Apollo. The fable is that Apollo, burning with love for Daphne, a nymph and daughter of the river Peneus, pursued her swiftly. But the girl fled from him no less quickly. Finally, being exhausted and unable otherwise to escape the force of the eager lover, by the mercy of the gods she was transformed into a tree of the same name. For the Greeks call it *Daphne*, the Latins *Laurus*, and we *Alloro*. And because he loved the nymph, so he loves the tree. With laurel, the triumphers were crowned. With laurel, the poets. They say that the lightning from heaven never touches it. For this reason, the Emperor Tiberius, in times of thunder, always wore a crown of it, because he greatly feared the lightning. Some write that whoever keeps it under their head while sleeping has true dreams. **TO THE FINAL labor:** to this, my last fatigue and work, because this is the third and final canticle. And here he makes his request easier to grant, because he almost promises not to weary himself further; and also tacitly suggests that having helped with the first two, [Apollo] should not leave his benefit incomplete, having already begun two parts and now leaving the third imperfect. **MAKE ME such a vessel of your worth:** make me such a vessel as to fill me with your worth, that is, with the "frenzy" mentioned before. **AS you require for the gift of the beloved laurel:** as the laurel requires, that is, demands that you give, it being loved by me. In short: make me such a vessel of your frenzy as the love I bear for the laurel—that is, for the poetic faculty—deserves. And this is the best way to ask, because wanting the petition to be just, it is necessary to show that he deserves what he asks. If he showed he deserved it through his own wisdom or learning, or through some benefit he had done, it would be a most arrogant request. But by supplicating through the love he bears for the laurel, he makes his prayers free of pride, and nonetheless full of efficacy. **UNTIL now, one peak of Parnassus:** Parnassus is a mountain in Boeotia, or rather in Phocis, which is very high and has two peaks: one dedicated to Apollo, the other to Bacchus, whom the ancients similarly held to be the god of poets. For this reason, they also crowned themselves with ivy, which is dedicated to Bacchus. And therefore Virgil said: "Allow this ivy also to creep around your temples among the victorious laurels." <note>original: "Hanc quoq̃ ſine tēpora circū. Inter uictrices hederā tibi ſerpere lauros."</note> And Propertius: "Give me leaves from your ivy, Bacchus." <note>original: "Mi folia ex edera porrige bacche tua."</note> Servius affirms these two peaks are named Helicon and Cithaeron. Parnassus is consecrated to the Muses, and in it they live around the Pegasean fount. Of Parnassus, Ovid writes: "There a steep mountain with two peaks seeks the stars, named Parnassus." <note>original: "Mōs ibi uerticibus petit arduus aſtra duobus Nomine parnaſus"</note> And Persius: "I do not remember having dreamed on two-peaked Parnassus." <note>original: "Nec in bicipiti ſomniaſſe parnaſo memini me"</note> And Lucan: "And Parnassus sent [them] from its deserted peak." <note>original: "Parnafuſq̃ iugo miſit deſertus."</note> And it seems he places the peak Cithaeron...

The commentator describes the "divine frenzy" required for poetry and the symbolic importance of the sun and planets in human knowledge.</summary>
