<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante's Paradiso, Canto I. The commentator is explaining the classical and theological references in Dante’s invocation to Apollo, specifically focusing on the myth of Marsyas and the geographical/astrological setting of the poem’s opening.</meta>

<header>CANTO ONE</header>

...consecrated to Bacchus for the lower sciences, which are all the other parts of philosophy except for "First Philosophy" <note>Aristotle's term for Metaphysics</note> and Metaphysics, and Theology. For worldly things, those sciences are sufficient; and let him set Helicon for Theology, which alone has knowledge of celestial things. **ROSTRUM** <note>original: *aringo*</note> remaining: *Aringo* in Tuscan signifies a pulpit or an elevated place. From this we get the word *ringhiera* <note>a balcony or railing for public speaking</note>. Therefore, by likeness, he calls the game a "rostrum." **I NEED** <note>original: *me uopo*</note>: that is, a need for me, just as in Latin we say *Mihi est opus* <note>"It is a need for me"</note>. **ENTER** into the breast, into the mind, and breathe into me such a song as you used when you defeated Marsyas. It is written in the fables that Minerva, playing the *tibia*—which is a flute or pipe—over the water of the Triton marsh, saw her cheeks swell. This seemed such an ugly thing to her that she threw the flute away and would play it no more. Marsyas the satyr found it, and by persevering in playing it, he became a learned musician. But he was so insolent and reckless that he set himself above Apollo, the god of the musical art, and challenged him to sing. Minerva and Midas, King of Lydia, sat as judges. Apollo won according to the true judgment of Minerva. But Midas, being unlearned, favored Marsyas. Because of this, Apollo gave Midas the ears of an ass and flayed Marsyas. **FROM THE** sheath: from the skin, which is like the scabbard of the body. **O DIVINE** virtue: O divine fury of Apollo. By transition, he shows that although he says "Apollo," he means the divine grace—illuminating, cooperating, and consuming—and finally the Holy Spirit itself. **THE SHADOW** marked in my head: the image impressed upon my memory, which is in the last of the three ventricles of the head. He said "shadow" to show that he did not have the exact image of heaven expressed in his memory, but it was overshadowed. **YOU SHALL SEE ME** at the foot: your grace will not be placed in me in vain. For I shall use it in a way that I will deserve to be crowned with laurel as an excellent poet. And so that he does not seem arrogant in attributing such praise to himself, he says that neither he nor his talent will make him worthy of such a crown, but divine grace and the subject matter of which he treats. **RARELY** O Father, are they gathered: as if to say, the laziness and negligence of men is such that they rarely give themselves to poetry or to military discipline in a way that makes them worthy of being crowned with laurel. And the rarer they are, the more you ought to favor one who seeks to be crowned; and it can be done for every triumphant man. **FAULT** and shame of human wills: it is the fault of human wills because our wills and appetites, having rebelled against reason, follow sensuality. They are infinite in seeking bodily things, and because of their care for those, they desire nothing excellent. It is therefore a fault and a shame because it brings great ignominy to human life. **WHICH** brought forth joy: this is the sentence that the Penean leaf—that is, the laurel, which was born from Daphne, daughter of Peneus—ought to bring forth joy to the Delphic deity—that is, to Apollo, who is called "Delphic" because he gives oracles in his temple in the city of Delphi in Phocis, not far from Parnassus—every time anyone is crowned with it. **A SMALL** spark breeds a great fire. He demonstrates by speaking modestly of himself that he deserves Apollo’s favor. For although he himself might not do excellent things, nonetheless those who come after him, moved by the practice from time to time, will increase the poetic faculty; just as we see that from a small spark a great flame often arises. **WITH BETTER** voices, with more elegant style, with more poetic art: so that Cyrrha may respond—that is, so that he might be heard by Apollo, to whom Cyrrha is dedicated. Thus Juvenal said: *Cyrrhe i picula uatis* <note>original Latin: *Cyrrhaei spicula vatis*—"the darts of the Cyrrhean prophet"</note>. Cyrrha is a city in Phocis near Crissa and not far from Parnassus.

<columns>2</columns>
> The lamp of the world rises for mortals
> from various outlets; but from that one
> which joins four circles with three crosses,
> with a better course and with a better star
> it comes forth joined, and the worldly wax
> it tempers and seals more in its own way.
> It had made morning there and evening here,
> almost such an outlet; and all was white
> that hemisphere, and the other part black,
> when Beatrice toward the left side
> I saw turned, and gazing into the sun:
> an eagle never so fixed himself upon it.

<column-break/>

<image-desc>A decorative square woodcut initial 'D' containing a landscape scene with a building on a hill and mountains in the background.</image-desc>
**A**fter the invocation, he begins his narration and describes his ascent to the first heaven, which is that of the Moon. Furthermore, he describes that he began to ascend in the morning, when the sun was rising in that hemisphere where he was, making it morning. And the sun was at the beginning of Aries, in which sign this planet has its exaltation; therefore it produces more worthy effects. And it was at the equinoctial circle where, as appears in the material sphere, four circles join: that of the horizon, that of the zodiac, also the colure and the equinoctial. And in this conjunction, three crosses are made—that is, three intersections. He feigns, then, that the sun was in Aries, as we have said, because just as the worldly sun works most excellently in lower things there, so the celestial sun, which is God himself, infuses the most excellent grace into the human soul when He draws it to contemplate His divinity. There are many who allegorically set the four circles for the four moral virtues, and the three crosses for the three theological virtues. And the text proceeds: "The lamp of the world"—that is, the sun which illuminates the world—"rises and is born for mortals from various outlets." For when it rises with Aries, it appears in the true East. But then from day to day it rises toward the North until Cancer. And from there, likewise descending degree by degree into Libra,

<column-break/>
<margin>245</margin>
it is in the same place as it was in Aries. And then, departing from there, it goes descending through the southern signs until Capricorn; and from that, through Aquarius and Pisces, it rises again to the equator. Thus, although the sun always rises from the East, nonetheless it is not always from the same part of the East. Because of this, astrologers divide the East into three parts: the equinoctial, the northern, and the southern. It rises, therefore, from various parts of the East. "But with a better course"—that is, with a more happy influence—it rises from the vernal sign where the circles and the crosses already mentioned are. "And with a better star": and he calls the sign of Aries a "star," using one star for all the others that make up that sign; and he says "better" because, as we have said, Aries is the exaltation of the sun. Or, he meant Venus, which at the beginning of the second *cantica* <note>Purgatorio</note> he placed in Pisces, near the sun. "And the worldly wax": he says, then, that the sun, when it rises with Aries and has Venus joined with it, can better with its influence dispose the earth and the animals to produce fruit. Therefore it "tempers"—that is, disposes—and "seals." The "worldly wax"—that is, it disposes and impresses its virtue just as wax becomes apt to receive a figure impressed by a seal when it is well-disposed. And it is true, because in that season, heat and moisture rise in a tempered way, from which tempering the best generation is born. **HAD MADE**: "there," in that hemisphere where I was then, it was "morning." And "here," in our hemisphere, it was "evening." And allegorically, "evening" means death, because there are vices and ignorance; and "there" is "morning" because there are those who are purged of vices and illuminated by divine grace. **TOWARD THE LEFT SIDE**: from which, in that hemisphere, the sun casts its rays for one who is turned toward the East. That Beatrice could look at the sun signifies that only Theology can look upon the Divinity, which is the true sun. **AN EAGLE** never so fixed himself: for the eagle is said to have such eyes that, beyond the faculty of any animal, he fixes his eyes upon the sun and is not dazzled. Because of this, Beatrice is similar to it, because alone of all doctrines, Christian Theology can endure the rays of the divine sun; and look.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the opening of Canto I of the Paradiso. The previous page discussed the invocation to Apollo and the myth of Marsyas, establishing the transition from earthly knowledge to the divine heights Dante is about to explore.</meta>

# PARADISE

...rejoice in the Lord <note>original: "re in dño [Domino]"</note> with the first light and to know Him without being dazzled: [he is like] the figure of the eagle because he discerns the divinity above all others.

And just as a second ray
is wont to issue from the first and mount upward again,
like a pilgrim who wishes to return,
So from her action, infused through the eyes
into my imagination, my own was made;
and I fixed my eyes on the sun beyond our wont.
Much is permitted there which here is not
to our powers, thanks to the place
made as the proper home for the human race.
I did not endure it long, yet not so little
that I did not see it sparkling round about,
like molten iron coming out of the fire.
And suddenly it seemed to me that day to day
had been added, as if He who has the power
had adorned the heaven with another sun.

...suspended wonder: And to look into the sun: this is nothing else than that, illuminated by divine grace, one can look into the sun, that is, into the speculation of the divinity. Nevertheless, he did not endure it long: because if the eyes, that is, the sharpness of the intellect, had endured the light for a longer time, he would have been able to discern the entire solar body, that is, he would have had true knowledge of the divine essence. But he did not have so powerful an eye. Nevertheless, for the little that he endured, he saw the sparks and flashes that were born from the solar body, in the same way that they are born from a glowing iron. The allegorical sense is that the purified soul can contemplate God: but not in a way that it knows His essence: but it has knowledge of the sparks that come from the sun, that is, of the effects that proceed from God; seeing that we know the cause through the effects, and not the effects through the cause. And that the sun had so much greater light that it seemed doubled signifies that theological contemplation illuminates the intellect much more than philosophy does, because it is not without the infusion of the Spirit, as you will see a little further down.

Beatrice was standing with her eyes fixed
entirely upon the eternal wheels, and I on her
fixed my eyes, removed from those above.
In her aspect I became such within
as Glaucus became upon tasting the herb
that made him a peer in the sea among the other gods.
To <term>transhumanize</term> <note>original: "trashumanar" - to pass beyond the limits of human nature</note> could not be signified
by words; therefore let the example suffice
for him to whom grace reserves the experience.

Whether I was only that part of me which You created
last, O Love who governs the heavens,
You know, who with Your light raised me up.
When the wheel that You make eternal
by being desired, made me intent upon You
with the harmony that You attune and distinguish,
So much of the heaven then seemed to me kindled
by the sun's flame, that no rain or river
ever made a lake so widespread.
The novelty of the sound and the great light
kindled in me a desire for their cause,
never felt before with such sharpness.

<column-break/>

This same reason causes the Evangelist John to be represented in the figure of an eagle <note>The eagle is the traditional symbol of St. John the Evangelist because his Gospel "soars" to the heights of Christ's divinity.</note>.

Just as a ray of the sun, reflecting itself, returns upward from whence it had come, like a man who returns home from a pilgrimage; so the fixed act of Beatrice in looking fixedly at the sun entered into my "imagination" <note>original: *imagine* – in medieval psychology, the faculty that receives sensory impressions</note>, and disposed me to look similarly at the sun. Because when the rays of the divine sun strike back into theological doctrine—which alone can sustain their gaze—it illuminates us: it strengthens and corroborates our eyes so that we too can look at the sun. Therefore rightly writes Augustine: "The good of God is known through theology which perfects the intellect and directs the affection" <note>original Latin: *Bonum dei cognoscitur per theologiam que perficit intellectum: & dirigit affectum*</note>. And so that we do not wonder that he could look fixedly at the sun beyond our custom, he adds: that the power of that place is such that we can do many things there that we cannot do here. Because that place is made specifically for the human species; and Earthly Paradise was created by God so that man might inhabit it for a longer time in a state of innocence; and then, when it pleased Him, he would be assumed to his beatitude. Therefore, since through the purgatorial virtues we have returned to the state of innocence, it is no wonder if in that place—that is, in such a state—it is permitted for us to look into the sun, which is not permitted here—that is, in the state of sin. **I DID NOT** endure it long. The meaning of the poet is that once the sun rose, he began to rise toward heaven, that is, to contemplate; for "contemplation is the free and clear gaze of the mind into the speculation of wisdom with suspended wonder."

The Poet wishes to express something else by demonstrating that Beatrice held her eyes fixed on heaven, and he held his on the eyes of Beatrice; which means nothing other than that sacred theology contemplates nothing but divine things, and whoever wishes to understand them must place their entire mind in theology and in its doctors. And it follows that in looking at her so fixedly, he became such "within"—that is, in the soul—as **GLAUCUS** became, who by eating the herb became a god. Thus it shows that his soul was deified. And certainly, through the contemplation of the divinity, we become divine and gods, as Boethius <note>original: *Boetio*</note> demonstrates at length. Glaucus, the son of Anthedon, was a fisherman. And placing the fish he had caught on the meadow so that the nets might dry, it happened that some of them, tasting a certain herb, regained their strength and jumped back into the water. Glaucus was stunned by the event and tasted the same herb himself; and seized by a sudden madness, he threw himself into the sea, and there from a man he became a sea god. **TRANSHUMANIZE**: that is, to transcend from human nature to divine.

The poet shows that he was rapt by the Holy Spirit, and by the sweetness of the song that he heard, and by the very great light that shone. Thus, his sight and taste were filled with ineffable joy. Wherefore, turning to the Holy Spirit, he speaks like a man now returned to the world: "O Holy Spirit who are Love, who governs the heavens: only when I was in such meditation was I that soul <note>Dante refers to himself as the "newly created" soul, the part of man created directly by God</note> which You created of me newly when You transformed me, You know it. Because You raised me with Your light," that is, You made me elevated to such contemplation with the light that You infused into my mind. And it shows here that there was in him that which the sacred letters affirm: that without the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, one does not come to such high speculations. **WHEN THE WHEEL**: because not only the heavens but all things created by God turn around with the desire they have to see Him. Therefore, "when the wheel"—that is, the revolution of the heavens which You, Holy Spirit, make eternal because every creature desires to enjoy God as much as its nature allows—"made me intent upon You," that is, made me...

<summary>This page covers Dante’s initial ascent from the Earthly Paradise, using the metaphor of the sun to represent divine truth and the myth of Glaucus to explain "transhumanization." The commentary emphasizes that through theology and the Holy Spirit, the human soul is "deified" and strengthened to behold things beyond earthly capacity.</summary>
<keywords>Paradiso, Beatrice, Glaucus, transhumanization, theology, Holy Spirit, divine grace, deification, Augustine, Boethius</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the opening of Canto I of the Paradiso. The previous page discussed the visual phenomenon of the sun's light and the soul's capacity to perceive divine truths, concluding with Dante witnessing the "sparks" of divine effects. This page moves into the auditory experience of the spheres and the intellectual dialogue between Dante and Beatrice regarding his ascent.</meta>

# CANTO FIRST

...I attempted that revolution of the heavens which you make: and this was through the <term>harmony<note>The "Harmony of the Spheres" is an ancient philosophical concept suggesting that the movements of celestial bodies create a divine musical proportion or sound, inaudible to human ears on Earth.</note></term> that I heard from them. And the Platonists especially approve of such harmony. All the heavens revolve from the <term>Primum Mobile<note>The "First Moved," the outermost sphere of the universe in medieval cosmology, which imparts motion to all the inner spheres.</note></term> downwards. These are nine: seven spheres of the seven planets, the eighth sphere [the fixed stars], and the Primum Mobile. And through their movement, each generates its own sound. But they are varied according to whether they are higher or lower. And from them all results a most sweet melody and an optimal proportion of voices which the Greeks call harmony. *WITH the harmony that you temper and discern rightly*, he said. Because from many voices a sweet melody cannot result unless they are tempered with due proportion. Nor can they have proportion if they are not distinct with variety. *IT SEEMED to me* then that the heaven was so ablaze. It proceeds with great order: because first the Holy Spirit infused him; then, having been "transhumanized" by it, he was elevated to heaven. And in that elevation, he heard the harmony, and looking attentively, he began to see the moon, the first planet—not so small as it is seen from down here, but as great as it is in its own measure. And he concludes that the flame of the sun ignites such a space of the heaven of the moon that no river on earth ever made so great a lake. The novelty of the sound, of the harmony heard for the first time, and the greatness of that light, *AWOKE in me a desire* <gloss>that is, a desire to know the cause of the harmony and the light</gloss>. *OF SUCH sharpness* <gloss>that is, of such stinging and stimulus</gloss>.

Whereupon she, who saw me as I see
myself, to quiet my troubled mind,
opened her mouth before I could ask,
And began: "You make yourself dull
with false imagining, so that you do not see
what you would see if you had shaken it off.
You are not on earth as you believe;
but lightning, fleeing its own site,
never ran as fast as you, returning there."

<column-break/>

I was inflamed with fervent desire to understand the cause of the light and the song. Whereupon she <gloss>that is, Beatrice herself</gloss>, *WHO SAW me*: <gloss>that is, she knew my will, although I did not manifest it to her</gloss>. *AS I SEE MYSELF*: no differently than I know myself. *OPENED her mouth*: she opened her mouth and began to speak to quiet my mind, troubled by the desire already mentioned. *BEFORE I could ask*: the meaning is that although it seemed appropriate that I should ask first what I desired to understand, and then she should declare it to me so that my mind might remain quiet, nevertheless, because she knew my will no differently than I did, she anticipated me. And she began: *You make yourself dull*: your imagining that you are on earth while being in heaven. *You make yourself dull* <gloss>that is, of slow wit in understanding the cause of the light you see and the sound you hear</gloss>. Because if you perceived that you were in heaven, and had shaken such an imagination from your mind, you would easily understand the cause for yourself. *YOU ARE NOT on earth as you believe*: She demonstrates his false imagining. *NEVER did lightning*: She shows that Dante has ascended to the first heaven with more speed than lightning descends to earth from its "first site" where it was created, which is the second region of the air. *THAT NOW you return*: that at present you return. And not without reason did he say "return" rather than "come"; he does not intend to show that Dante ascended to heaven with his body (although he so feigns), but with his mind, whose proper site is heaven. Nor should it be unknown to us that every created thing has its own place granted to it by nature. Therefore, the proper site of the soul being heaven, it can in an instant of an hour elevate itself even unto God.

If I was divested of my first doubt
by her brief, smiling little words,
within a new one I was more entangled,
And I said: "Already I rested content
regarding my great wonder; but now I wonder
how I can transcend these light bodies."
Whereupon she, after a pious sigh,
directed her eyes toward me with the look
a mother gives her delirious son,
And began: "All things whatsoever
have order among themselves, and this is the form
that makes the universe resemble God.
Here the higher creatures see the imprint
of the eternal value, which is the end
for which the prescribed rule was made."

<column-break/>

You have understood from Beatrice that Dante had already ascended to the first heaven; she made him clear of his first doubt. But from that was born the second: how he, a heavy body, could have ascended through "light bodies," that is, through the air and through the element of fire. He says, therefore: *IF I WAS divested* <gloss>that is, stripped</gloss> *OF THE FIRST doubt*: which was from where such great light and so sweet a sound were born, by the brief words of Beatrice when she said, "you are not on earth." *SMILING*: that is, she spoke these things smiling. *I WAS ENTANGLED* <gloss>that is, caught and wrapped, like a bird in a net</gloss>. *AND I said* to Beatrice: *I rested content* <gloss>that is, I became quiet and remained satisfied</gloss> *regarding the great wonder* which the first doubt gave me. *BUT now* anew *I wonder* <gloss>that is, I marvel how</gloss> *I CAN TRANSCEND*: how I, a heavy body, can in ascending pass through these light and weightless bodies of air and fire. *WHEREUPON AFTER*: first she sighed. Beatrice, out of pity, was moved by Dante's error and ignorance, and she looked at him as a mother looks at her son *WHO IS DELIRIOUS* <term>delirious<note>Landino explains the etymology from the Latin 'lira' (furrow), meaning to stray from the path of reason, like a plow leaving the furrow.</note></term> <gloss>that is, who is outside the true way. 'Lira' in Latin is the furrow; wherefore we say a plowman is 'delirious' when in plowing he exits the furrow. And then by similitude we call an old man 'delirious' when through age he leaves the true path. And in short, sometimes we simply call any foolish person 'delirious'</gloss>. *The DELIRIOUS SON*: the son placed outside of reason. *AND she began* to speak, saying: *All things whatsoever have order*: She shows that no one marvels except at things for which the reason is unknown to them. Therefore, Dante marveling at his own ascent shows that the reason of natural things is unknown to him, in which there is supreme reason and order; if Dante knew this, he would not marvel. Therefore, his marveling manifests his ignorance. This moved Beatrice to look at him as a mother at a delirious son. *All things whatsoever*: created by God, have order among themselves. Order is the disposition of many things, equal and unequal, which collocates each according to its being and according to its dignity or merit. God, therefore, has placed this order in his creatures. *AND THIS is form*: Form is that which gives being to a thing, as for example: the image of Caesar has in itself the matter and the form. The matter is the marble of which it is made, and the form is that which the sculptor induced, which is similar to Caesar. Therefore, the marble does not make it similar to Caesar, but the form, without which it would not be the image of Caesar. We also say that reason is the "form" of man because one cannot be a man if reason is not in him. *THAT makes the universe resemble God*: God has created the whole of creation in his similitude. On this, Boethius says: <note>original: "Tu cūcta ſupno ducis ab exēplo pulchrū pulcherrimus ipſe mūdū mēte gerens similiq; imagine formas pfēctasq; nubes pfēctas absoluere ptes."</note> "You lead all things from the highest example, yourself most beautiful, carrying the beautiful world in your mind, and you shape it in a similar image, commanding the perfect parts to form a perfect whole." *HERE* in this order *the higher creatures*, which are the angels and men...

<summary>This page explains Dante's transition into the celestial realm, focusing on the Harmony of the Spheres and Beatrice's explanation of how the soul naturally "returns" to heaven, its true home. It delves into the philosophical concepts of universal order and "form" as the divine imprint that makes the universe resemble its Creator.</summary>
<keywords>Harmony of the Spheres, Primum Mobile, Beatrice, Celestial Ascent, Natural Order, Form and Matter, Delirium, Boethius, Platonic Philosophy</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the opening of Canto I of the Paradiso. Having established the harmony of the spheres on the previous page, the text now transitions to Beatrice’s explanation of the universal order that governs all creation, directing every soul and physical element back toward God.</meta>

# PARADISO

...intellect. The form and the vestige of the eternal value: <note>original: "L’orma el vestigio dell’eterno valore"</note> that is, of God, who was able, knew how, and willed to produce every creature with such order that His vestige appears in each one; and He is the end. God is the end of every thing because just as everything has its beginning from Him, so it is referred back to Him. The order placed in things, therefore, is that by which things produced from their beginning might return to Him as their end. This order [links] the creature to the creator:

"Within the order I describe, all natures
Incline through diverse lots and states,
Some nearer to their source, and some less near;
Whence they move toward diverse ports
Across the great sea of being, and each one
With an instinct given to it that carries it.
This carries the fire upward toward the moon;
This is the mover in mortal hearts;
This binds the earth together and makes it one;
Nor does this bow shoot only creatures
Void of intelligence, but also those
Who possess both intellect and love.
Providence, which so arranges all of this,
With its own light makes the heaven ever quiet
In which that one revolves which has greatest haste."

---

"And now, there, as to a decreed site,
The power of that string carries us,
Which directs whatever it shoots to a happy mark.
It is true that, just as a form often
Does not accord with the intention of the art,
Because the material is deaf to the response,
So from this course the creature
Sometimes departs, having the power
To swerve, though thus impelled, in another direction;
And just as fire can be seen to fall
From a cloud, if the first impulse
Is twisted toward the earth by false pleasure.
You should no more wonder, if I judge rightly,
At your climbing, than at a stream
Falling from a high mountain to the base.
It would be a marvel in you if, deprived
Of impediment, you had settled below,
As if a living fire stayed quiet on the earth."
Then she turned her face back toward heaven.

<column-break/>

**W**ITHIN THE ORDER I describe. In this order God has placed all creatures, and to them He has given a natural state of returning to their creator as their end; and toward this they are inclined. This inclination was instituted by Divine Wisdom, which <term>Plato<note>Landino frequently reconciles Dante’s theology with Platonic philosophy, a hallmark of Renaissance Humanism.</note></term> names Providence. And He placed it within the creatures. Therefore, when Plato considers such inclination in the Divine Mind, he calls it Providence; but when he considers it within the creature, he calls it <term>Fate<note>original: "fato"</note></term>. Nevertheless, it is necessary in such an order that some creatures be closer to God—that is, more capable of divinity—as are first the angels, then men. Some are more distant, because a tree is more distant than a brute animal, and a stone more so than a tree.

Being, therefore, because it extends to all creatures, is like a spacious sea. And because in this being one nature belongs to the angel, another to the human (in whom there is reason), another to the brute (in whom there is sense), another to the tree (which lacks sense but has the vegetative power), and another to the stone (which lacks reason, sense, and the vegetative), it is fitting that as their natures are diverse, so too are their inclinations toward diverse ends. For this reason, in this sea of being, one does not sail from all points to a single port—that is, to one end—but to diverse ones because there are diverse ends, and diverse ends have diverse ways, which Dante calls "lots," and which can be called fate according to Plato. Every creature moves, therefore, toward diverse ports or ends, driven by the instinct given to it by God which moves it to its end. Therefore, the human mind—whose end is the Supreme Good, which is to know, love, and enjoy God—has a natural instinct to return to God. For this reason, Dante should not have wondered that he had ascended to the contemplation of God, because our natural instinct carries our mind to God just as the natural instinct of fire carries it upward toward the moon (because there is the quiet of light things); and this same instinct moves our hearts to God for the reason already stated; and likewise it moves the earth to pull itself together in the center of the world, because being heavy, it desires the lowest place. 

NOR ONLY does this bow shoot: by comparison, he uses the "bow" for the aforementioned inclination, and the "arrow" for the thing moved by the inclination like an arrow from a bow. Thus, the meaning is that this inclination is not only in irrational creatures, but also in rational ones, such as man who has intelligence and love. PROVIDENCE, which so arranges—that is, adjusts and optimally disposes—MAKES the heaven ever quiet: the <term>Empyrean heaven<note>The highest, motionless heaven in medieval cosmology, considered the dwelling place of God.</note></term> where His celestial court is, quieted by His light because that heaven is filled with <term>Seraphic<note>The Seraphim are the highest order of angels, associated with light and burning love.</note></term> flames. Hence it is called "Empyrean," meaning "fiery" or "ablaze." And for this the Greeks call it <term>Olympus<note>original: "olympus quasi olo lampos"</note></term>, which signifies "all-shining." IN WHICH revolves that which has greatest haste: that is, the <term>Primum Mobile<note>The "First Moved," the fastest sphere which imparts motion to all others.</note></term>, which moves with more velocity than the others.

**A**ND NOW, there, as to a decreed site. The power of that string carries us. The power of that string—that is, of that inclination. DIRECTS to a happy mark: that is, to have the end where our Supreme Good is. WHATEVER it shoots: whatever it pushes. Carries us: conducts us. There: to that Empyrean heaven where God, our Supreme Good, is. AS TO A DECREED SITE: that is, as to the place determined for our rest. IT IS TRUE that, just as: he removes a doubt, because someone could argue: "If there is a natural instinct in our soul to return to God, why are there many who go the opposite way?" To which he responds that the creature who has power—that is, has **free will** <note>original: "libero arbitrio"</note> to choose good and evil—is sometimes conquered by <term>sensuality<note>The physical desires and appetites that pull the soul away from rational or divine focus.</note></term>, which pushes it in the opposite direction and distances it from God. Just as we see fire, which although by its nature is pushed upward, nevertheless if it catches in some thick vapor in the air, desiring that element, it follows it down to the earth; so the rational soul, which has the natural instinct to follow its own good, is often deceived by sensuality and follows a false good.

YOU SHOULD NO MORE wonder: he concludes by the reasons already stated that Dante should no more marvel if his mind rises to God (because natural instinct pulls it to its good) than one would marvel if a river situated in the mountains descended to the bottom where its nature pulls it. But one should marvel if his soul, placed on earth—that is, in the body—stayed at the bottom, just as if "living fire" (that is, a flame) lay at the bottom and did not rise. **T**HEN SHE TURNED. Having said these words, Beatrice turned back toward heaven. This signifies that Theology sometimes descends to inferior things for our salvation, but only to turn us back with them to celestial things.

<summary>Beatrice explains the teleological order of the universe, where all creatures are driven by a natural "instinct" toward their proper ends, specifically explaining how the human soul naturally ascends to God unless diverted by the "false pleasures" of sensuality. The commentary links Dante's cosmology with Platonic concepts of Providence and Fate and clarifies the hierarchy of the Great Sea of Being.</summary>
<keywords>Divine Order, Providence, Fate, Free Will, Empyrean, Primum Mobile, Seraphim, Natural Instinct, Sensuality, Teleology, Plato, Landino</keywords>

<meta>This page continues from the end of Canto I, where Beatrice explained the universal order of the cosmos. Now, as they ascend toward the first heavenly sphere—the Moon—the poet addresses his readers directly, warning those unprepared for such high theological matters to turn back, while inviting the few who have "stretched their necks" toward divine wisdom to follow his lead.</meta>

<header>CANTO SECOND</header>

## SECOND CANTO OF THE THIRD CANTICLE OF DANTE.

O you who are in a little bark,
desirous to listen, having followed
behind my ship that singing makes its way,
Turn back to see your shores again;
do not commit yourself to the deep sea, for perhaps,
by losing me, you would remain lost.
The water I take was never crossed before;
Minerva breathes and Apollo leads me,
and nine Muses show me the Bears.
You other few who stretched your necks
betimes for the bread of angels, upon which
one lives here but never comes away sated,
You may well commit across the salt deep
your vessel, keeping to my furrow
before the water returns to its level.
Those glorious ones who passed to Colchis
did not marvel as you shall do,
when they saw Jason made a plowman.

<column-break/>

The poet has now ascended to the first sphere. Therefore, in this second canto, he describes how he entered the lunar body. When asked by Beatrice about the cause of the spots and shadows that appear on the moon, he gives his opinion. But Beatrice refutes him and then demonstrates the truth to him. Now, as for this beginning, he admonishes the common crowd—those who are learned only in the minor sciences and not learned in sacred matters, who have been able to follow him until now—that they should go no further. Since they are not capable of such high material, they might become lost. This is especially true because he treats what has never been treated by anyone else. On the other hand, he comforts those learned in sacred theology, of whom there are few, to follow him, promising them that they will marvel more than Jason’s companions marveled at Colchis. **O YOU who are in a little bark:** It is a metaphor used by many poets to put the sea for the subject matter and the ship for genius or doctrine.

Therefore: **O you who [are] in a little bark:** that is, with little doctrine or genius. **DESIROUS to listen** to my poem. **FOLLOW behind my ship:** follow behind my style and my doctrine.

**THAT makes its way singing:** because every poet is said to sing. Whence in the first canticle [he says]: **I was a poet and I sang of that just [man]** <note>original: "POEta fui & cantai di quel giusto." This refers to Virgil's speech in Inferno I.</note>. **TURN back to see your shores again:** from which you departed, he says; stay in low material, suitable for your weak intellects. **DO NOT put yourselves into the deep sea:** that is, into such profound and difficult material; for perhaps **BY LOSING me you will remain lost:** like someone who, not knowing the way, follows a guide; if they lose the guide, they become lost. So it is with one who follows an author writing high and difficult things: they may understand something at the beginning, but when they arrive where they do not understand him, it can be said they have lost him, and they remain lost. **LOSING me:** losing my method, which is not worn down or common among other poets.

---

**THE WATER I run was never crossed before:** through an abundance of eloquence, he says now "sea," now "deep," and now "water" for the same thing; and he stays within the metaphor. The meaning is that the sea he sails was never sailed, meaning by other poets or other writers. He does not deny that many have written most learnedly of the things he writes about. But no one ever wrote poetically and in an allegorical sense, adorned with poetic faculty, on such high matter. **MINERVA breathes:** the poet might have seemed presumptuous affirming that no poet ever wrote of such high matter. Therefore, he shows that it is not by his own genius, but by the help of Minerva, Apollo, and the Muses that he has been able to say what he says—not through himself, but through grace infused by the Holy Spirit. By Minerva, he means the giver of wisdom; and through Apollo and the Muses proceed the poetic style and song. For the Holy Spirit, infusing itself into the human mind, makes the unlearned learned and the rough eloquent, as we see in the prophets and the apostles. Therefore, he does not say he runs water never crossed out of simple arrogance, but says he has crossed it through divine favor. **MINERVA breathes:** three things are necessary to one who desires a prosperous voyage: first, the wind to push you to port. Therefore Minerva, who is wisdom, directs the ship to a good port. And Apollo, who is harmony, disposes and orders the course with due proportion. The Muses show the Bears <note>original: "lorse," referring to the constellations Ursa Major and Minor.</note>: that is, the North Star, without which every ship goes astray. By the Muses, understand the poetic faculty, without which the poet does not see what style he must follow. **YOU other few:** having admonished the unlearned not to follow him through this sea, he now comforts the learned to follow him because they will be able to understand it. And he says "few" because in every age the number of the learned and of elevated geniuses has been small. Whence Aristotle [says]:

> The unrefined mind and the intellect that is not very subtle relates to divine things just as the sight of an owl relates to the sun. <note>original: "Ingeniū rude & nō subtilissimuss intellectus: ita se habet ad diuina sicut uisus noctue ad solem."</note>

And Thomas Aquinas:

> The knowledge of divine things exists in few men. <note>original: "Cognitio diuinorum paucis hoibus inest."</note>

And certainly, there is great difficulty in this knowledge, because all the other parts of philosophy were found so that they might be a ladder by which we can climb to this height.

**WHO stretched your necks:** who lifted your heads, which cannot be lifted if the neck is not straightened. By the lifting of the head, he means they raised their minds and their genius to celestial things. This briefly touches upon the sentiment of Ovid:

> While other animals look down upon the earth, He gave to man a sublime face and commanded him to gaze at the heavens and to lift his upright countenance to the stars. <note>original: "Pronaque cū spectēt animalia cetera terras. Os homini sublime dedit celūque tueri iussit & erectos ad sydera tollere uultus."</note>

**BETIMES:** he says this [means] from your adolescence, signifying by this the difficulty of divine doctrine, which we cannot well acquire if from our first years we do not give ourselves to the study of the liberal arts. **TO THE BREAD of angels:** just as the body is fed and lives by corporeal food, so the intellect is nourished by the fruition and knowledge of the divine, which he calls the "bread of angels" because they enjoy this, and in this alone they find life. **OF WHICH [bread]:** that is, among us mortals; for the soul, while it is in the body, sustains itself with this doctrine. **BUT ONE NEVER comes away sated:** because we cannot have so much knowledge of it on earth that it satisfies us and is enough for us. But it shall be so in heaven. **YOU MAY WELL commit across the salt deep:** that is, through the high sea; that is, you can follow me into this profound matter. **KEEPING TO THE FURROW:** He wants them to follow him so closely that the furrow made by his ship does not close up on them; for when it closes, the water returns to being level. He admonishes whoever follows him not to wait until such a distinction disappears. For when they do not recognize the distinction between the allegorical sense and the literal, and between the fictional thing and the true, they will not be able to understand it. **THOSE GLORIOUS ones:** He demonstrates by an excellent comparison that the Greek Argonauts did not marvel as much when they saw Jason in Colchis sowing the teeth of serpents (from which armed men were born) as you shall marvel at what I will say; and not without merit. For if that was against nature, this is so hidden in the secrets of nature that it does not seem natural. **GLORIOUS:** desirous of glory, or truly glorious because they were of great fame among the Greeks. **AT COLCHIS:** a city in Pontus where the [Golden] Fleece was. **PLOWMAN:** an operator of the plow, who in the...

<meta>This page continues the transition from the end of Canto I into the first sphere of Heaven. Dante and Beatrice have just left the Earth's atmosphere and are arriving at the Moon. The commentary here by Cristoforo Landino explains the theological and physical implications of this journey, specifically addressing the nature of the lunar body and the limits of human reason.</meta>

<columns>2</columns>
<header>PARADISO</header>

...and is called a plowman <note>original Latin: *bubulcus*</note>. I will not tell this fable now because we have told it elsewhere.

The concreated and perpetual thirst
for the god-like realm was carrying us
as swiftly as the heaven you see.
Beatrice was looking upward, and I upon her;
and perhaps in such a time as a bolt stays
and flies and is loosed from the nut,
I saw myself arrived where a marvelous thing
turned my sight to itself; and therefore she,
from whom my doing could not be hidden,
turned toward me, as glad as she was beautiful,
"Direct your mind to God in gratitude," she said to me,
"who has joined us with the first star."

The Moon is the first star and planet above the elements. Beatrice admonishes him for no other reason than to direct his mind in gratitude to God for having arrived at the first star, to demonstrate that all our good works, and all cognition and intelligence, come from divine help. Therefore, we should not glory in ourselves but give glory to Him, and be grateful for the gift received. Furthermore, she spoke as "glad as she was beautiful." Theology is always beautiful because it always speaks true things, which are always beautiful. But when it recounts punishments and threatens the sinner, it does not show itself as glad; however, when it gives us knowledge of celestial things, it always appears beautiful to us and gives us joy.

It seemed to me that a cloud covered us,
shining, thick, solid, and polished,
like a diamond smitten by the sun.
Within itself the eternal pearl
received us, as water receives
a ray of light, remaining united.
If I was a body—and here it is not conceived
how one dimension could tolerate another,
which must be if body creeps into body—
it should more greatly kindle the desire
to see that Essence in which is seen
how our nature was united to God.
There will be seen what we hold by faith,
not demonstrated, but known by itself,
in the manner of the first truth man believes.

I replied: "My Lady, as devoutly
as I am able, I thank Him
who has removed me from the mortal world.
But tell me, what are the dark signs
of this body, which down there on earth
make others tell fables about Cain?"
She smiled a little, and then: "If the opinion
of mortals errs," she said to me,
"where the key of the senses does not unlock,
surely the arrows of wonder should not
pierce you now, since you see that
reason has short wings."

<column-break/>

**T**HE thirst: that is, the great desire. CONcreated: created together. Because God created together with our soul a supreme desire in it to go to the Highest Good, which is God himself. And not only did He create this desire in us, but He created it so that it always lives in our soul, perpetual. Therefore, he says they were carried by the concreated and perpetual thirst they possessed. FOR the god-like realm: that is, for blessedness and the Highest Good, of which God is the form; for the Highest Good is nothing other than God himself. BEatrice [looking] upward: this sentence was declared above. And perhaps in such a time: he demonstrates that the interval of time was no more than it takes for a bolt <note>original: *quadrello*, a square-headed crossbow bolt</note> to rest upon the loaded crossbow, and to "un-nut" <note>original: *dischiavare*, to release the trigger mechanism</note> the crossbow and the arrow to fly to the target. And it is from the earth to the heaven of the moon, ascending in a straight line, one hundred forty-eight thousand and five hundred forty miles. I saw myself arrived: he says he arrived in a wonderful place. And Beatrice, who knew his wondering and that he did not understand what place this was—because nothing that was in Dante could be hidden from her, since theology sees what our already-purified soul desires—said: "Direct your mind in gratitude to God," because He joined us with the first star, which is the Moon...

**H**E describes the nature of the lunar body: which is shining, dense, solid, and polished. And the moon is seven times larger than the earth.
LUCID, thick CLOUD seemed the body of the moon. And here note that some bodies are naturally luminous, like the sun. Some are so by art, like a mirror. Some are transparent, like glass and water.
LIKE a diamond. Because the lunar body, by its own nature dark, shines when the sun strikes it, just as a diamond does.
WITHIN itself the eternal pearl: he calls the moon a "pearl" <note>original: *margherita*</note>. And he declares the same thing: that the lunar body has no light of its own, but is lucid, that is, receptive to light, just as are the diamond and the pearl, which, if they had their own light, would shine at night. Therefore, they do not have it, but are receptive to it.
RECEIVED us: He demonstrates that they entered the lunar body, which is solid and dense, without dividing it, just as the sun enters water without dividing it. Which naturally cannot be—that a dense and solid body [enters another] and that which receives it remains united. And therefore he says that HERE among men, IT IS NOT CONCEIVED, that is, it cannot be understood, how one dimension—that is, a body which has its dimensions, meaning measurements, because it has length, height, and depth—could tolerate <note>original: *patio*, from *patire*, to allow or endure</note> another dimension, which is another body. Therefore, if this happened, it should kindle the human mind to see...
THERE in eternal life, WILL BE SEEN: it will be clearly understood what is held by faith—that in the consecrated host is the true body of Christ—and there we shall see it. NOT demonstrated by philosophical reason, but it will be known and manifest by its own nature. IN THE MANNER: in the likeness OF the first truth: of the first principles which the philosophers call "excellent axioms," such as saying that "the whole is greater than the part."

**H**E thanks God, as he was admonished by Beatrice, saying it was an immense benefit that He had already elevated him to the first heaven, having separated him from the mortal world. This you must always understand allegorically as the elevation of the soul and not of the body. Then he asks about the dark signs—that is, shadowy and obscure—that we see from earth on the moon. And the common people say it is Cain carrying a bundle of thorns <note>A medieval folk belief explaining the "Man in the Moon" as Cain punished for his crime.</note>. At this Beatrice smiled and said: "If the opinion of men, who judge according to the senses, errs because the 'key of the senses' cannot unlock—that is, open and manifest—the truth, surely you should not wonder; for reason, which follows the senses, has short wings, meaning it can raise itself very little."

<summary>Dante and Beatrice arrive at the Moon, the first heavenly sphere. The commentary explains the physics of how Dante's physical body could enter the "solid" moon and uses this mystery to point toward the theological truth of the Eucharist and the limits of human reason compared to divine revelation.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Dante and Beatrice as they arrive at the Moon, the first of the celestial spheres. In the previous page, Dante marveled at the Moon's pearl-like surface; here, they begin a scientific and philosophical debate regarding the "lunar spots"—the dark patches visible from Earth.</meta>

# CANTO SECOND

->But tell me, what do you yourself think it is?<-
And I: "That which appears to us so diverse
I believe is caused by bodies **rare and dense**."
And she: "Certainly you will see your belief
submerged in falsehood, if you listen well
to the arguments I shall bring against it.
The **eighth sphere** <note>The sphere of the Fixed Stars, which sits above the planetary spheres.</note> displays to you many
lights which, in their quality and size,
can be seen to have different appearances.
If **rare and dense** alone produced this,
one single virtue would be in them all,
distributed more, or less, or equally.
Different virtues must be the fruits
of **formal principles** <note>In medieval philosophy, "formal principles" are the essential nature or "soul" of an object that gives it its specific properties.</note>, and these, except for one,
would be destroyed by your reasoning.

Further, if 'rare' were the cause of that 
darkness you ask about, either in certain parts
this planet would be so lacking in its matter,
or else, just as a body shares
the fat and the lean, so this planet
would change the pages in its volume. <note>A metaphor comparing layers of different density to the pages of a book.</note>
If the first were true, it would be manifest
in the **eclipses of the sun**, for the light
would shine through, as it does through other rare things.
This is not so: therefore we must see
to the other case; and if I happen to quash the other,
then your opinion will be proven false.
If it be that this 'rare' does not pass through,
there must be a limit from where
its contrary allows no further passage;
and from there the ray of another is poured back,
just as color returns through a glass
which hides lead behind itself. <note>A description of a mirror: glass backed by lead.</note>
Now you will say that the ray shows itself
dimmer there than in other parts
because it is reflected from further back.
From this objection, experience can
deliver you, if you ever try it—
which is the fountain-head to the streams of our arts.
Take three mirrors; place two
at an equal distance from you, and the other further off,
so that your eyes find it between the first two.
Turning toward them, cause a light to be placed
behind your back which kindles the three mirrors...

<column-break/>

Beatrice asks what his opinion is regarding the **cloudiness of the moon**: and Dante responds that he believes that what appears in the heavens to be different from the color of the sky proceeds from the **rare and the dense** <note>The idea that some parts of the moon are "thinner" or "more porous" and others "thicker" or "more solid."</note>. The opinion of Albumasar <note>An influential Persian astrologer (787–886 AD).</note> is that such darkness in the moon is from its specific nature: just as we say the magnet <note>original: *calamita*</note> attracts iron. Nor do we know any other reason for it, except that it is by its specific nature. Others say it comes from the shadow of the Earth, which is very close to it. Beatrice responds to this, showing through her arguments that this is false.

**Arguing against the author**, Beatrice says that if Dante's opinion were true, an inconsistency would follow, which we will see shortly. But first she poses a true proposition: that the **eighth heaven** has many stars of different splendor and different size. For example <note>original Latin: *verbi gratia*</note>, the Dog Star <note>original: *canicula* (Sirius)</note> shines more and is larger than many others. The eighth sphere displays many lights, that is to say <note>original Latin: *idest*</note>, stars which can be noted and known: **"in which"** [quality], because one is more splendid than another. This is why astronomers divide them into first, second, and third **magnitudes**. **"By different faces"**: by different appearances. But if rare and dense were the cause of this, it would follow that in them there was only one single virtue and influence. But [the light would be] smaller or larger or equal according to whether the stars were smaller or larger or equal. But this is not so. Therefore, rare and dense is not the cause: because one single virtue would be distributed in all, more or less, and equally according to whether they are smaller, larger, or equal. And this is not so, because if formal virtues have different principles, it follows that the formal principles themselves must be different. Hence she says: **"Different virtues must be"** from formal principles, that is, different reasons produced from different principles, just as different fruits are produced from different trees. And these formal principles all...

In the preceding argument, Beatrice demonstrated that generally in all celestial bodies, Dante's opinion was false. Now, through this [argument], she demonstrates it specifically in the body of the moon. The argument is this: If the cloudiness of the moon is caused by the "rare," I ask you if that "rare" passes through the lunar body from one surface to the other, or if it does not pass all the way through. But it is false that it passes through entirely. Because if the moon were pierced from one side to the other, when a **lunar eclipse** occurs, the rays of the sun would pass through that hole. If you say that such a hole does not pass to the other side, but after some space it is closed off by the "dense," the cloudiness still could not appear [as you think], as experience shows in the reasoning that follows.

**"OR ELSE"**: that is, throughout the whole body. In essence, if where the darkness is, the "rare" existed up to a certain space and then the "dense" followed, it would be like the body of an animal that first has the fat (which is "rare") and then the lean (which is "dense"). **"Change the pages"**: This is a metaphor from a book where one page is white and the other black. **"If the first"**: This I have already shown. **"To shine through"**: that is, for the ray of the sun to pass through down to us.

She has shown that the cloudiness cannot proceed from the "rare" if such "rare" passes all the way through. Now she shows that if the "rare" does not pass to the other side, it likewise cannot be the cause of the cloudiness. Therefore, if the "rare" passes to a certain space, and then the "dense" (its contrary) follows, it is necessary that the solar rays pass through all the "rare" and then, finding the "dense," they are reflected back as in a mirror, where the color is reflected and returns through the glass itself. And in this way, the "rare" will not be the cause of the darkness, since the rays reflect from the dense, as we have shown. **"NOW YOU WILL SAY"**: But you might say that although the reflection still illuminates in that "rare" part, nevertheless, because it originates deeper within the lunar body (in the part where the "rare" is) than it does in the rest (where it originates on the surface), therefore the darkness appears there. **"FROM THIS"**: Beatrice responds that Dante can free himself from such doubt with **experience**, which is the fountain and origin from which all arts are born.

She proves that even if reflection occurs from different intervals, the more distant one does not reflect less [light] for that reason; and she proves it thus: Take three mirrors and put them before your sight, but in a way that one of the mirrors is further from you and the other two are closer...

Beatrice systematically refutes Dante's theory that the moon's dark spots are caused by variations in physical density, preparing to offer a theological explanation instead.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Dante and Beatrice in the Heaven of the Moon. Beatrice is concluding her scientific demonstration regarding the nature of light and reflection before transitioning into a theological explanation of the celestial spheres and their angelic movers.</meta>

# PARADISO

and returns to you reflected by all,
although in its quantity it does not extend
so far, you will see from further off
how it must necessarily shine equally.
Now, as by the strikes of the warm rays
the subject of the snow remains bare,
both of its color and its former cold,
so, remaining thus in your intellect,
I wish to form a light so true for you
that it will flicker in your sight.

Within the heaven of divine peace
revolves a body in whose virtue
the being of all it contains is made.
The following heaven, which has so many sights,
distributes that being through diverse essences
distinct from it, and yet contained by it.

<column-break/>

and let there be a light above your head that strikes all the way down through you: because there is no doubt that although things closer appear to have greater light, nevertheless it does not shine more in the near than in the far. And if you should say that because the light is smaller there must be less splendor and not equal: I answer that splendor is not in the *quanto* <note>original: "quanto" — referring to physical quantity or size</note>, that is, in quantity, but in quality. Therefore, the ray that reflects from further away will not shine less upon the moon—entering as far as the ray lasts until the dense part—than those which reflect on the surface in which they find the dense part. **AND RETURN TO you reflected by all.** That is, the light so informs that it strikes all the lights: and you are in a place where such reflection returns to your eyes; because otherwise you would not see it. **NOW AS BY THE STRIKES OF THE WARM RAYS.** Just as the "subject of the snow," that is, the ground upon which the snow sits, remains bare and deprived of the color and the cold of the snow by the warm rays of the sun, so you, having been stripped of your former opinion, I will inform with a light so true, that is, with such open truth, that it will shine and be reflected in your breast.

---

Because he leads Beatrice to speak, whom we have said represents **Theology**, he therefore makes her speak not as a physicist, but as a theologian. For the common opinion of philosophers is that the "cloudiness" in the moon, divided as if into three parts, is the shadow of the earth, which we divide into three parts: Asia in the eastern part (and it alone is as large as the other two together with the Mediterranean Sea); Africa in the southern part; and Europe in the north. But of this we shall speak more extensively in Canto XXII. But Beatrice, speaking as a theologian, puts forward this argument: all celestial bodies induce diverse effects in lower things according to their power and the virtue of the **Intelligences** <note>In medieval philosophy, "Intelligences" are the angelic beings that move the celestial spheres.</note> infused into them. This is proven by the influence that lower bodies receive from them. He says, therefore: **WITHIN THE HEAVEN of divine peace:** This is the **Empyrean** heaven, which is immobile and does not revolve; he calls it the heaven of divine peace, in which is the celestial kingdom where souls enjoy eternal peace. **Revolves a body:** this is the **Primum Mobile** <note>The "First Mover," the ninth and outermost physical sphere in the Ptolemaic system.</note>, the ninth heaven; and it is called the Crystalline heaven, contained within the immobile Empyrean heaven. **IN WHOSE VIRTUE:** In the virtue of that Crystalline heaven, both motive and effective. **THE BEING of all it contains:** the conservation of being, and the motive and effective power of all that it contains. This ninth heaven, which is the Primum Mobile (the first that is moved by the Empyrean), embraces all the other heavens; for in the eighth sphere and the seven planets, they are not made of compact and constrained matter, and because of this they are transparent and do not impede our sight from passing through to the eighth, where the Zodiac and the other fixed stars are. But the eighth heaven is not transparent; therefore we do not see the ninth or the tenth. All move with the Primum Mobile and make one revolution in twenty-four hours from East to West and back to the East. And through that natural and uniform motion, each takes effective virtue according to its power to conserve itself in being and other lower things; and nevertheless, each revolves with its own proper movement in a contrary way from West to East. Because of this, the eighth heaven moves one degree every hundred years. Therefore, in the virtue of the ninth heaven (the Primum Mobile), which is inside the Empyrean heaven (the heaven of divine peace), lies the being of all its content, that is, of all things contained by it; because it, with its effective virtue, moves them, which is the cause of the conservation of the others and of their movement. Just as the moving angels are the cause of the conservation of being and its movement. **SO MANY SIGHTS:** so many stars, all of which are seen. **THAT BEING:** that essential effective and motive virtue which must conserve the being that is in the virtue of the ninth heaven and which it has from it. **DISTRIBUTES:** divides and distributes through diverse essences and substances that the eighth heaven has in itself, distinct from it, such as the stars which are of different matter than the heaven itself, and have other effects, but are still contained by it. **THE OTHER** seven heavens of the planets revolve the distinction they have within themselves, that is, the seven planets distinguished by various differences: because the planets are very different in position, body, and nature, as has already been said, and will be said more distinctly for each. **AND THEY DISPOSE** their seeds, that is, their causative virtues which are the cause of lower effects, and they dispose them to their proper end. Just as the seed of grain produces the effect (the grain), which in potential is the seed for another grain; so the celestial bodies, which are the cause of lower effects, are also the effect of causes superior to them. Therefore, the Primum Mobile has virtue infused by God and by its movers, which has to conserve its being and that of all the heavens and elements which it contains within itself. This is the motive and effective virtue that moves all the other heavens and elements and causes in them various effects according to their various powers. And so, the superior virtue always infuses into all the inferior ones and causes, as was said, diverse effects according to how the lower bodies are diverse. But it acts most effectively in the nearest inferior one, and changes according to the differences between one and another. Therefore, the ninth heaven infuses its essential motive and preservative virtue more effectively into the eighth than into the others; and that virtue, changed within it, is infused more into the seventh than the others, and so on. Furthermore, every planet has its virtue infused into it by its movers, moving according to its own diverse motion. **THESE ORGANS of the world:** that is, these heavens. For just as in man the lower organs respond to the superior—the sensory to the brain, the vital to the heart, the nutritive to the liver—and then these two principal ones (brain and liver) respond to the heart which is the fountain of life and the principal member; so all celestial bodies have their being from God as the first cause of the whole, who has placed in them diverse virtues, just as they are of diverse bodies and movers. And although every heaven has more movers that move it to operate its effects, it is nonetheless called one Intelligence; just as one soul vivifies the body with many powers, which move it to operate its effects. **THE REASON IS** because the first order of angels, which are the **Seraphim**, move the first heaven. The **Cherubim**, the second order, move the eighth heaven. The **Thrones**, Saturn. The **Dominations**, Jove [Jupiter]. The **Virtues**, Mars. The **Powers**, the Sun. The **Principalities**, Venus. The **Archangels**, Mercury. The **Angels**, the Moon. All these Intelligences are moved by God, who is immobile. God moves as the object of thought and love, just as a thing understood and loved moves the one who understands and loves. Because of this, the Intelligences, which are all love, revolve around God, who is understood and loved by them. These, moving and casting themselves around Him...

<summary>Beatrice uses a metaphor of melting snow to explain how Dante's old misconceptions are being replaced by divine truth, then details the hierarchical structure of the universe, linking specific angelic orders to the movement of the celestial spheres.</summary>

--- Page 505 ---
<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante's Paradiso, Canto II. Beatrice is explaining the metaphysical structure of the heavens, moving from the physical appearance of the moon's spots to a broader discussion of how divine influence flows from the Primum Mobile through the various celestial spheres and their angelic movers.</meta>

# CANTO SECOND

understanding and always loving Him, things move toward Him as if from God, with the power that God has placed within them. **FROM** step to step: because the superior always influences the inferior; and each, in relation to the superior, is an effect, and in relation to the inferior, is a cause; and therefore it says: **WHICH** take from above as effects, and act below as causes. But the ninth heaven <note>the Primum Mobile</note> has only one movement; however, the others contained by it—that is, the eighth sphere and the seven planets—have two movements: one from east to west, of which the first mobile and its movers are the cause. This is called uniform motion, which is completed in twenty-four hours; according to this motion, all heavens have an effective power infused by the first mobile, each according to its potency to preserve the being of inferior things. According to their various potencies, they have different effective powers. The other motion is erratic and multiform; it occurs by the power of the specific movers of each heaven, and it goes from west to east; some complete it more quickly and others more slowly. And as was said, the superior always pours its power into the one below, and that power is diversified according to the capacity of the one that receives it. They agree in helping one another, and by opposing each other, they temper one another. Perhaps the poet also calls them "organs" to touch upon the Platonic opinion that all the heavens create a most sweet sound <note>the "Music of the Spheres," an ancient theory that the movement of celestial bodies produces a divine harmony</note>.

The other rounds, through various differences,
the distinctions that they have within themselves,
dispose toward their ends and their seeds.
These organs of the world go thus,
as you now see, from step to step,
taking from above and acting below.
Look well at me, at how I travel
through this place to the truth you desire,
so that you may then know how to keep the ford alone.
The motion and the power of the holy circles,
as the art of the hammer comes from the blacksmith,
must breathe forth from the blessed movers.
The heaven which so many lights make beautiful
takes its image from the profound mind that turns it,
and makes itself a seal.
And as the soul within our dust,
through different and coordinated members,
is resolved into diverse powers,
so the Intelligence unfolds its goodness,
multiplied through the stars,
revolving itself upon its own unity.

Diverse power makes a diverse alloy
with the precious body that it quickens,
within which it is bound, just as life is within him.
Through the joyful nature from which it derives,
the mixed power shines through the body,
as joy does through a living pupil.
From this comes what, from light to light,
seems different—not from dense and rare;
this is the formal principle that produces,
conforming to its goodness, the dark and the bright.

<column-break/>

**BY** the things already said, it is almost manifest what the poet now presents. Therefore, the motion of the holy circles—that is, of the heavens—must breathe and proceed from the blessed movers <note>the angelic intelligences</note> of whom we have spoken, just as the art of the hammer proceeds from the blacksmith. For the hammer, by striking in various ways, brings form into the iron: making either a sickle for the farmer or a sword for the combatant. Nevertheless, such motion comes from the blacksmith. **THE HEAVEN WHICH:** that is, which. **SO MANY LIGHTS:** so many stars make beautiful. This is the eighth heaven, where the fixed stars are. And it says that this heaven, from the profound power—that is, the infinite divine power which revolves it by means of its Cherubim in regards to its multiform motion, and in regards to its natural and uniform motion by means of the first heaven—takes the image, that is, the power imprinted in it, just as the image of a seal is imprinted in wax. And it becomes a seal: because it then imprints, according to its power, the power first imprinted in it upon the inferior things. **PROFOUNDLY** [the power] is called divine, which is infinite. Whence Boethius: *The mind that circles the deep and turns it with a matching image* <note>original: "Mente que profunda Circuit & simili conuertit imagine con uertit." From Boethius's Consolation of Philosophy, a text that deeply influenced Dante's cosmology.</note>. Then, to clarify it to me, he says that just as the soul of man, which is one, extending itself into various members, demonstrates various powers according to the nature of the member—for in the heart it gives life, in the liver it nourishes, and in the brain it perceives—so the Intelligence, which is one in the eighth heaven, extending itself into all the stars, gives various influences: it operates according to the various powers of those stars. It pours itself into Saturn, which is cold and dry, and gives it the influence according to the nature of Saturn; and so in the others.

**DIVERSE** Power: this is the conclusion of the things said above, and by those things this passage is understood: "diverse connection and mixture," just as we say silver is of "diverse alloys." **WITH THE** precious body. The heavens are bodies, but made of more precious matter than other bodies. **THE DIVINE:** because it makes it live and operate its effects. The Platonists hold that all stars are animated <note>possessing a soul or life force</note>. And Augustine, in his *Retractions*, writes that he has not found in Holy Scripture how he might either prove or refute that the world is animated. But if it has a soul, he affirms that it is not God, but made by God.
In which body: it binds itself like the vegetative life in the human body. And such connection makes the diversity of effects according to the diversity of celestial bodies. **THROUGH THE JOYFUL NATURE:** which is God, simple form and innumerable, by whom the angels are created. And from the joyful nature—that is, from God, the highest good—the angels derive "mixed power," because it is of an immutable nature insofar as it is confirmed in grace, and of a mutable nature insofar as it performs its operations successively. It is, therefore,

a mixed nature that quickens. Whence Boethius: *You, releasing the soul through harmonious words, moving all things as the medium of a triple nature. Which, once gathered, coils its motion into a circle, and returning into itself, travels around the deep Mind and turns the heaven with a similar image.* <note>original: "Tu triplicis mediū naturę cũcta mouentem Conuertens animā per cōsona uerba re foluis. Que cōferta duos motus glomeratuit in orbem. In semet reditura meat mētemq; profundam Circuit: & simili con uertit imagine celum."</note>. Or truly, we understand the power mixed with the body and infused by the movers. **SHINES:** it reflects through the divine nature. **AS** joy through a living pupil: just as through the eye, by shifting and sparkling light, the joy of the heart is understood. Therefore, from the divine light proceeds every difference that is from light to light—that is, from star to star—and not from "rare to dense" <note>referring to Beatrice's earlier refutation of the theory that moon spots are caused by physical density</note> as they used to believe.

<summary>Beatrice explains that the diverse brightness of stars and the moon results from divine virtue being distributed through angelic "movers" into celestial bodies, rather than physical density. She compares this celestial hierarchy to the way a single human soul operates through different organs like the heart and brain.</summary>
<keywords>celestial hierarchy, angelic movers, eighth heaven, fixed stars, Boethius, soul and body analogy, divine virtue, Primum Mobile</keywords>
