->PARADISE<-

## CANTO THREE OF THE THIRD CANTICLE BY DANTE.

**T**hat sun which first warmed my breast with love <note>The "sun" refers to Beatrice, who illuminates Dante’s mind just as the physical sun illuminates the world.</note>
had uncovered the beauty of truth to me
by proving and refuting with a sweet aspect;
And I, to confess myself corrected and certain,
as much as was fitting for me to do,
raised my head more erect to speak.
But a vision appeared which held me
so closely to itself to be looked upon
that I did not remember my confession.
As through transparent and polished glass,
or through waters clear and tranquil,
not so deep that the bottom is lost;
The outlines of our faces return
so faintly that a pearl on a white forehead
does not strike our pupils less strongly;
Such I saw many faces ready to speak,
whereby I ran into the error contrary
to that which kindled love between the man and the fountain. <note>original: "l’uomo e ‘l fonte" — a reference to the myth of Narcissus, who fell in love with his own reflection. Dante commits the "contrary error": Narcissus thought a reflection was a real person; Dante thinks these real spirits are merely reflections.</note>

This is the third part of the six sets of three <note>referring to the structure of the poem's cantos</note> and shows that Beatrice, whom he calls the sun, turned his mind toward herself. **THAT SUN:** Beatrice, who is like the sun because just as the sun illuminates visible things, so Theology illuminates the mind. **WHICH FIRST** warmed my breast with love: because she had previously kindled her love in me, and now she revealed the aspect of truth; he calls it "sweet" because nothing is more pleasant than knowledge. **BEAUTIFUL:** Beauty is so inherent to truth that nothing can be beautiful unless it is true. **PROVING:** The truth through a demonstrative syllogism <note>term: syllogism — a form of logical reasoning where a conclusion is drawn from two premises</note>. **AND REFUTING:** That is, <note>original: "id est"</note> confuting false opinion. And I, to confess myself **CORRECTED** <note>original: "correcto"</note>, that is, having the falsehood refuted, and made certain of the truth, **RAISED** lifted my head. **MORE ERECT** more upright, that is, high. He raises his head to confess. By this he denotes that one should not lower their head—that is, should not be ashamed to confess an error—because confessing demonstrates a noble soul eager to find the truth, while being stubborn in denial shows a proud and fraudulent soul, eager for contention. **AS THROUGH:** The meaning and order of the text is: "I saw in that place many faces ready, that is, eager and prepared to speak, which were..." **SUCH:** That is, made in the same way as our **OUTLINES** <note>original: "postille"</note>, which are the images of our faces that return to us, either from glass or clear water. And these faces appeared so faint—that is, so little expressed and so little evident—that a pearl, which because it is white is poorly discerned when placed on a white forehead, does not come less strongly—that is, it comes more strongly and is more easily seen—than those faces appeared against the white forehead. In short, those spirits did not appear so clearly as an image in a mirror, which is seen clearly, but as one is seen **IN WATER**. But not so deep that it occupies—that is, so that the bottom is **LOST**, meaning dark—or in very clear glass. And just as a pearl is better seen on the white forehead of a woman than I could discern that face. For this reason, I fell into error, but the contrary to that error which kindled love between the man—that is, Narcissus—and the fountain in which he saw himself reflected. For Narcissus's error was that he believed his image which he saw was not an image but a man; and I, seeing true spirits, did not believe they were spirits but images of spirits. And so it appears that his error was the contrary of Narcissus's, whose fable we narrated in the thirtieth canto of the first canticle <note>Inferno XXX</note>. **WATERS CLEAR:** Water cannot show an image well unless it is clear, still, and shallow. Therefore, it could be better explained above. **BOTTOMS LOST:** That is, lost and equal because of the depth of the water they are not discerned.

As soon as I became aware of them,
judging them to be reflected semblances,
to see whose they were, I turned my eyes;
And saw nothing, and turned them back forward
straight into the light of the sweet guide
who, smiling, glowed in her holy eyes.
"Do not marvel that I smile,"
she said to me, "at your childish judgment,
which does not yet trust its foot upon the truth,
But turns you back, as it usually does, to emptiness;
what you see are true substances,
relegated here for failure in a vow."

<column-break/>

**I**t is the poet's fiction <note>term: fiction — the allegorical or literary framework used to convey spiritual truths</note> that our soul, being assumed into the heavens by the virtues, and having various influences from various heavens of various virtues, in each heaven the souls of those who were excellent in the virtue influenced by that heaven represent themselves to his sight. And he begins to describe those whom he found in this first heaven of the moon. Understanding that although all the souls of the blessed are in the highest heaven of glory—which he will treat in the thirtieth canto—he nevertheless feigns that they represent themselves to him in that heaven which represents the degree they hold in eternal life and in the Empyrean heaven <note>term: Empyrean — the highest part of heaven, the direct presence of God</note>. Under such a fiction, he wishes to express not only the souls separated from bodies and placed in the sight of God, but also those who are still in their bodies, but are in the third kind of virtues called those of the "already purged soul." Dante passes through all the heavens, and in each finds those souls we have mentioned; and later he finds those same souls in the Empyrean heaven, in the presence of God. Nor is it inappropriate that, being elevated by Beatrice from heaven to heaven up to the Empyrean—that is, being snatched by theological doctrine to the contemplation of the heavens—in each of those there should be represented to the mind those who, by the influence of such heavens (inclined but not necessitated), have attained those virtues by which they are blessed. Therefore, by this meditation, he places them here; not because he does not understand that the blessed souls are all in the highest heaven. But as far as this third canto is concerned, he finds many blessed souls, and Beatrice tells him the reason; then he speaks with one of the blessed souls and asks about a doubt; and she responds not only to this first one, but also to another. This is the argument of the entire canto. But the meaning...

**s**hows that having made an error, he turned backward to see the bodies of which he believed those were images. And he saw nothing. Therefore, he turned his eyes back to Beatrice and looked into her eyes. This signifies that the senses and the inferior reason—which can only grasp particular and corporeal things—estimated the false in universals. Therefore he returns to Beatrice—that is, he turned with the superior reason to Sacred Scripture. She was smiling because the error of the simple always moves the learned to laughter; and she "glowed in her eyes"—that is, she shone brightly. Wherefore she was fit to infuse light, that is, truth. And she said: "Beatrice, do not marvel that I smile at your childish judgment" <note>original: "pueril quoto"</note>. *Quotus* in the Latin language signifies "how many" in a sequence. And to put a thing in its proper order is to judge it. It is no wonder then if I laugh at the low judgment which does not yet trust its foot upon the truth—that is, does not yet proceed according to the truth—and you do not understand that these are souls joined with the lunar globe. Nor is "joining oneself with the planet" anything other than...

<summary>Dante enters the First Heaven (the Moon) and mistakes the faint, pearl-like appearances of spirits for mere reflections, an error Beatrice corrects by explaining these are real souls who were inconstant in their sacred vows.</summary>

<header>CANTO THREE</header>
<sig>B</sig>
<page-num>250</page-num>

to hope according to the influence of that [the moon]. And the influence of the moon is to bring about the change of temporal goods into eternal ones and from eternal ones into temporal. Therefore, these spirits had used that influence well by putting celestial goods before earthly ones and using earthly things not as the ultimate good, but as necessity requires. For as much as pertains to food and clothing and in supporting our parents and friends, so much should be sought and no more; and if we have an abundance, we ought to convert it into honest liberality. The moon is cold and humid and a feminine planet; it induces virginity and chastity in women and inclines them toward it. And for this reason, the poets feign that Diana, who signifies the moon, was always a virgin and accompanied by virgin nymphs. Therefore, the poet feigns finding in the moon the souls of virgin and chaste women. **TRUE SUBSTANCES:** <note>original: "VERE SVBSTAtie"</note> these are real beings and not mere images or reflections. **RELEGATED HERE:** <note>original: "QVI relegate"</note> almost as if far from God and from the first heaven. **FOR LACK OF VOW:** <note>original: "PER manco diuoto"</note> for a failure of devotion; and he takes "vow" to mean profession and promise, because every Christian makes a vow and profession to observe the divine precepts. He says that acting well has led them here, but for not having been very abundant in it, they deserve only this lowest degree. **THEREFORE SPEAK:** <note>original: "PERO parla"</note> because, being substances, they will speak to you. **AND HEAR:** because they will answer you. **AND BELIEVE:** because they will tell you the truth; and this is because the divine light—that is, God, who is truth itself—**SATISFIES THEM:** <note>original: "GLAPPAGA"</note> it contents them in such a way that it does not let them turn their feet from Him. That is, they are confirmed in grace; they have no other desire nor any other longing than to acquiesce to the divine will. And this is what makes it so that, notwithstanding that there is more glory in one than in another, they are nonetheless equally blessed because beatitude consists in having the highest contentment, and they desire nothing else but to please God.

Therefore speak with them, and hear and believe,
for the true light that satisfies them
does not let them turn their feet away from it.

And I to the shade that seemed most eager
to converse turned myself and began,
like a man whom too much desire unmans:

"O well-created spirit who in the rays
of eternal life feel the sweetness
which, if not tasted, is never understood;

It would be gracious of you if you would satisfy me
with your name and your lot."
Whereupon she, prompt and with laughing eyes:

"Our charity does not lock its gates
to a just prayer, no more than that [charity]
which wills all its court to be like itself.

In the world I was a virgin sister;
and if your mind looks back well,
my being more beautiful will not hide me from you,

But you will recognize that I am Piccarda,
who, placed here with these other blessed ones,
am blessed in the slowest sphere.

Our affections, which are inflamed
only in the pleasure of the Holy Spirit,
find joy in being formed by His order.

And this lot which seems so far down
is given to us because our vows
were neglected and void in some part."

Whereupon I said to her: "In your marvelous
aspects there shines I know not what divine quality
that transforms you from my first concepts;

Therefore I was not quick to remember,
but now what you tell me helps me,
so that re-figuring you is easier [more 'latino']." <note>Dante uses "latino" to mean clear, easy, or articulate.</note>

"But tell me, you who are happy here,
do you desire a higher place?"

<column-break/>

The Author, kindled by a great desire to know, asks a spirit near to him for her name and the state of the souls who are in that place; and the spirit shows that she will willingly answer him, because the charity that is in them does not deny anything that is justly asked, because it is like the divine charity which wills that all its court—that is, all the blessed souls—be like itself in charity.

The spirit responds in the order in which she was asked: first, she gives her name; then she demonstrates what the state of those spirits is. She shows, therefore, that she was a "virgin sister"—that is, one of the nuns of Saint Clare, named Piccarda, of whom we spoke in the twenty-fourth chapter of the second canticle where it says: *My sister, who was between beautiful and good.* <note>A reference to *Purgatorio* XXIV, where Dante's friend Forese Donati praises his sister Piccarda.</note> **IN THE SLOWEST SPHERE:** The sphere of the moon is the slowest because, although in its non-uniform motion it completes its body faster than any other planet, nevertheless, considering how much smaller this sphere is than the others, one sees that it is the slowest; and allegorically it means that the further they are removed from the first heaven, the less ardent they are in charity.

**OUR AFFECTIONS:** she responds to the second part, that their state is in beatitude; because their affections and desires are inflamed and burning in the pleasure of the Holy Spirit, nor do they desire anything else. Because from the Holy Spirit proceeds charity; and so that one does not doubt that their affections might seek a higher degree, she shows that they are "formed in that order"—that is, they are born into that degree—and they desire nothing more. The poet feigns that all these spirits were women who, having made a public vow of religion and stayed there some time, were forced by relatives to leave and marry. But because it was against their will, and they always retained their religion in their hearts—and as a sign they observed the vow of virginal chastity promised to God by observing the matrimonial chastity promised to their husbands—they merit beatitude. And because the vow made was nonetheless broken in some way and not observed, they do not merit a higher degree than this. Therefore she adds: "therefore this lot is given to us"—that is, this degree which is so far down that it is the last—because our vows, which we made in the profession of religion (which was to observe an honest life in the cloister, virginal chastity, and obedience to the superior) were neglected and broken and were "void in some part." A vow, according to the Master of Sentences <note>Peter Lombard, a famous medieval theologian.</note>, is: <note>original Latin: "Est testificatio quedam promissionis spōtanee que de deo & de his que sunt deo fieri debbet."</note> "a certain testimony of a spontaneous promise which ought to be made concerning God and those things which are of God."

The author excuses himself for not having recognized Piccarda because of a divine splendor which shines so much in them that it transforms them from "first concepts"—that is, from the first signs that his imagination had conceived within itself of Piccarda's figure. This splendor shows that the beautified soul never appears in our mind as we saw it before, but much more perfect, in a form that seems to us something else and something more excellent. **THEREFORE NOT QUICK:** <note>original: "Festino"</note> that is, not fast to remember and recall. **MORE "LATINO":** <note>original: "PIV Latino"</note> more easy. In Florentine, we say "latino" for "wide" or "broad." Thus, more "latino" means more spacious, and because in a wide space there is more ease to explain and...

<summary>Dante meets Piccarda Donati in the sphere of the Moon, the lowest level of Heaven reserved for those who broke their religious vows under duress. The commentary explains that while their glory is less than others, they are perfectly content with God's will.</summary>

to explain what we wish: for Latin is taken for "easy." And it is not "Latin" nor derived from "Latin" as we say at the beginning of Latin studies. **BUT TELL ME:** <note>original: "MADĪMI"</note> because our soul has a continuous and natural desire—and even more increased by reason—to approach God as much as it can, therefore Dante asks if those spirits desire to rise higher: either to see more, or to make themselves more beloved. **WITH THOSE OTHER SHADOWS:** The blessed and benign spirit always laughs at human folly because, having true cognition, she knows our errors. But moved by charity, she willingly shows us the truth; and therefore he says that it seemed that Piccarda burned with the great charity that was in her to remove Dante's ignorance. **IN THE FIRST FIRE:** in the moon, which is the first splendor and the first planet to us.

*To see more and to make more friends*
*With those other shadows she first smiled a little*
*then she answered me so joyfully*
*that she seemed to burn with love in the first fire*

*Brother, the power of charity quiets*
*our will, making us wish*
*only for what we have and for nothing else*
*If we desired to be more exalted*
*our desires would be discordant*
*from the will of Him who sorts us here*
*Which you will see is not possible in these circles*
*if being in charity is necessary here*
*and if you well consider its nature*
*Indeed, it is formal to this blessed existence*
*to keep oneself within the divine will*
*so that our very wills are made one*

*So that as we are from level to level*
*throughout this kingdom, it pleases the whole kingdom*
*as it does the King who draws our wills into His own*
*And His will is our peace*
*It is that sea to which everything moves*
*whatever it creates or whatever nature makes*

*Then it was clear to me how everywhere*
*in heaven is Paradise, even if the grace*
*of the Supreme Good does not rain there in one way*
*But as it happens when one food satisfies*
*and for another the craving remains*
*so that one asks for that and gives thanks for the other*
*So did I with act and with word*
*to learn from her what was the web*
*through which she had not drawn the shuttle to the end*

*A perfect life and high merit enheaven*
*a lady further up, she told me, by whose rule*
*in our world below some clothe and veil themselves*

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'P' with a human face in profile inside the counter.</image-desc>
**P**roof that the souls of that place do not desire to go further forward in this form: It is necessary that the blessed soul be in perfect charity: because where there is charity, there is God; and where there is God, there is charity. And whoever is in perfect charity cannot disagree with the will of God: because he who is in charity is united with the will of God. Thus, two wills become one. **IF WE DESIRED:** <note>original: "SE DISIASSIMO"</note> we would wish. **TO BE MORE EXALTED:** <note>original: "ESSER piu ſuperne"</note> higher. **OUR DESIRES:** our wishes. **WOULD BE:** <note>original: "FORAR"</note> they would be discordant with the will of Him who is God, who **SORTS:** <note>original: "NE CERNE"</note> judges us or truly sifts and chooses us for this place. **WHICH:** <note>original: "CHE"</note> that God. **YOU WILL SEE IS NOT POSSIBLE IN THESE CIRCLES:** in these heavens. **INDEED IT IS FORMAL:** <note>original: "ANZIE/ FORMALE"</note> to this blessed being, that is, being the "form" <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, the "form" is the essential nature or defining principle of a thing.</note> is that which gives being to the thing; and no one is blessed except by being united with God. Therefore, the form of this beatitude is the union with God, and their will becomes the will of God. **SO THAT AS WE ARE:** He concludes that because the blessed are united with the will of God, it pleases everyone to be in that heaven where God has placed them: because it so pleases God, who **DRAWS US:** <note>original: "nenuoglia"</note> that is, he puts His will into our wills; so that our willing is nothing other than His; and His will is our supreme good. Our mind has peace only insofar as it wishes nothing but the good; and God wishes nothing but the good. **IT IS THAT SEA:** the will of God is a depth that cannot be comprehended. Whence the Apostle says:
> The will of God is a great abyss <note>original Latin: "Voluntas dei abyſſus multa"</note>
to which will everything moves. Because just as all waters move to go to the sea, so all things move from the divine will to go to it. **WHATEVER HE CREATES:** to create is to make something out of nothing; and this God does without any medium. Then God has put power into the things created by Him, which do not make a thing from nothing, but from some matter make a similar thing: as for example a man with his seed makes another man; and this is called **NATURE NATURED:** <note>term: natura naturata — the created world as an ongoing process of reproduction and physical laws</note> and they define nature as the power put into things by God generating similar things from similar things. Therefore, God creates without a medium and without matter; and **NATURE MAKES:** <note>original: "natura face"</note> that is, the power put into things by God makes something out of matter. Whence we shall conclude, as Augustine says: that the will of God is the first and supreme cause of all movements, corporal and spiritual.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'C' with a human face looking forward inside.</image-desc>
**C**oncludes that through Piccarda's words it became manifest to him that everywhere—that is, every place in heaven—is Paradise: that is, that in every heaven, whether superior or inferior, there is beatitude. **AND EVEN IF:** <note>original: "E SI"</note> that is, although. **THE GRACE** of the Supreme Good—of God—does not rain in one way. Because the superior heavens have greater and better influence. But the reason why, although the glory is not equal in all, nevertheless all wills are full, has already been stated above. **BUT AS IT HAPPENS:** having clarified one doubt, there remained the hunger—that is, the desire—to be clarified about another; just as it happens that one food satisfies and for another the "throat"—that is, the greed—remains, whence one asks for that which is not had, and gives thanks for that which is had. This second doubt, of which he wished to be clarified, was to understand what her life was that she began in religion <note>meaning a religious order or convent</note> but did not finish; and he speaks by metaphor: calling her life the **WEB** from which she **DID NOT DRAW THE SHUTTLE TO THE END:** <note>original: "non traſſe infino alco la ſpola"</note> that is, to the head, which is to say, to the end. For the shuttle is that which carries the thread of the warp back and forth until the web is full.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'D' with a human face in profile inside.</image-desc>
**P**iccarda declares in what way her vows were lacking and describes Saint Clare and how she entered her religious order: and how she was taken from it by force. And she orders the text: Piccarda said to me. **PERFECT LIFE:** virtuous and conducted to the end. **AND HIGH MERIT:** as if excellent. **ENHEAVENS HIGHER UP:** that is, places her in a higher heaven than this one of the Moon. **LADY:** this is Saint Clare, sister of Saint Francis. **BY WHOSE RULE:** <note>original: "ALLA CUI norma"</note> by the rule and according to the rule of whom they clothe and veil themselves: because her rule is that these sisters wear grey and stay veiled; and this order was so that until death her sisters, whether waking or sleeping, should be with Christ, who is the spouse of every good woman...

<header>CANTO FOUR</header>

Because finally until death one watches or sleeps
with that spouse <note>referring to Christ</note> who accepts every vow
that charity conforms to His will.
From the world, to follow that young girl <note>Saint Clare, founder of the Poor Clares</note>,
I fled, and in her habit I enclosed myself,
and promised to follow the path of her rule <note>original: "secta," meaning a religious order</note>.
Men then, more habituated to evil than to good,
snatched me away from the sweet cloister:
and God knows what my life became then.

And this other splendor that shows itself to you
on my right side, and who is glowing
with all the light of our sphere,
understands of herself what I say of me:
she was a sister, and in the same way
the shadow of the sacred veil was taken from her head.
But even after she was returned to the world
against her will and against good custom,
she was never loosened from the veil of the heart.
This is the light of the great Constance,
who from the second wind of Swabia <note>Henry VI, son of Frederick Barbarossa</note>
generated the third and final power <note>Frederick II, the last great Holy Roman Emperor of the Swabian line</note>.

Thus she spoke to me, and then began "Hail
Mary" <note>original Latin: "Ave Maria"</note> singing, and singing she vanished
like a heavy object through deep water.
My sight, which followed her as much
as was possible, after it lost her,
turned to the target of greater desire,
and to Beatrice it wholly converted itself;
but she flashed so brightly into my gaze
that at first my sight could not endure it;
and this made me slower to ask my question.

---

[The light] appears in that form which at first dazzles the human intellect just as the eye is dazzled by the rays of the sun.

### CANTO FOUR OF THE THIRD PORTION <note>the Paradiso</note> BY DANTE.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'I' with floral motifs.</image-desc>

Between two foods, equally distant and attractive
in the same way, a free man would die of hunger
before he would bring one to his teeth.
So would a lamb stand between two cravings
of fierce wolves, fearing both equally;
so would a dog stand between two does.
Therefore, if I remained silent, I do not blame myself,
being urged equally by my doubts,
since it was necessary; nor do I commend it.
I was silent, but my desire was painted
on my face, and the questioning along with it,
much more clearly than if expressed in distinct speech.

<column-break/>

**A VIRGIN:** and [Christ] accepts every vow which charity conforms to His pleasure. **FROM THE WORLD:** I, Piccarda, in my early youth fled from the world, that is, from earthly things, to follow her <note>Saint Clare</note>. **AND ENCLOSED MYSELF:** that is, I entered the enclosure in her habit, and promised my life: that is, I made my profession to the rule. **OF HER RULE:** of her order. **MEN THEN, MORE HABITUATED TO EVIL THAN TO GOOD:** He shows that the beatified soul is free from all fleshly affection, and family ties do not prevent her from condemning wicked behavior. **WHAT MY LIFE BECAME:** she does not wish to praise herself and speak openly of her honest life; rather, she wants God to be the witness, or truly "what a life," as if to say with how much distress I lived, being outside the monastery against my will.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'H' with floral motifs.</image-desc>

Piccarda, having told her own story, now speaks of the spirit who is near her: and she declares her to be Constance <note>Costanza d'Altavilla</note> of the House of Bavaria, which is of more ancient blood than any other in Germany. She was snatched from the monastery where she had become a nun by her relatives and married off. But in marriage she was most well-behaved and full of all the virtues that the Moon influences; and therefore he says that she glows and shines with all the light of that sphere. This Constance was the daughter of Roger, King of Sicily. When Roger died without an heir, the kingdom was occupied by Tancred, one of the barons. But because he did not obey the Church, the Bishop of Palermo had Constance taken from the monastery in Palermo where she had made her profession, and gave her as a wife to Henry, son of the first Frederick, the Emperor of the Swabian family. Henry was crowned Emperor by Celestine; and from Constance he had Frederick II, who was the third and last Emperor of this family. **WIND:** that is, worldly glory, which Saint Jerome called "wind" because of its brevity and mutability.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'D' with floral motifs.</image-desc>

After the words already spoken, Piccarda departed singing "Hail Mary": because it is fitting that those who preserved their virginity during their lifetime should give continuous praise to the Virgin of Virgins. **AND SINGING SHE VANISHED:** she disappeared not all at once, but as happens when a heavy object is placed in water whose bottom cannot be seen: the further it sinks, the less it is seen, until it is completely lost from sight; so she, moving away, vanished. And by this he shows that the souls do not actually stay in the moon; but as was said, considering the nature of the planet, chaste souls appear to our contemplation. **AFTER IT LOST HER:** after the just soul <note>Dante</note> had lost sight of Piccarda. **TURNED TO THE TARGET:** that is, to Beatrice, who was my mark and target toward which my eyes are always directed. Thus, just as our intellect, when it loses itself in some contemplation, must immediately return to Theology. **THAT AT FIRST MY SIGHT COULD NOT ENDURE IT.** The higher we rise in contemplation through Theology, the greater the splendor of divine things appears, in that form which at first dazzles the human intellect just as the eye is dazzled by the rays of the sun.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'E' with floral motifs.</image-desc>

Two doubts had been born in the poet’s mind: and these doubts were so equal that he did not know where to begin. But Beatrice, who perceived them without him speaking, resolved them. And therefore, in this opening, he uses fitting comparisons, saying that if a man’s appetite were equally drawn to two different foods, and he had the freedom to take whichever he liked, he would never move more toward one than the other. Similarly, a lamb placed between two wolves, fearing them equally, would move neither here nor there; and similarly a dog between two does, desiring them equally, would follow neither this one nor that one. **BETWEEN TWO FOODS DISTANT:** that is, far away. **AND MOVING:** the appetite. **IN THE SAME WAY:** that is, equally, such that one was no closer than the other. **THAT A FREE MAN:** that is, one who was at liberty to choose and take whichever he pleased. **SO WOULD STAND:** in this way and similarly he would stand. He has placed the simile in the appetite; now he places it in the act of fleeing, and says: that a lamb who, in the midst of two wolves, feared one as much as the other, would stand between the two...

all human spirits: but also above all the angels. All these equals hold the supreme place in the eternal life; they do not inhabit any other heaven than those spirits which appeared to you in the lunar sphere. NOR HAVE they more or fewer years in their spheres: because all are eternal. ALL MAKE the first circle beautiful. All inhabit the first heaven, which he calls a "circle" because it is spherical. Therefore, in their place or eternity there is no difference, but rather in their bliss—of which, although each is as full as they can hold, each has a sweet life. One cannot desire more because one finds oneself full; nonetheless, whoever has more merit has more capacity: and therefore they feel and participate more in the sweet breath—that is, in the bliss which is the love and grace that God breathes into the blessed. Souls are like vessels of various sizes, but all are full. A cup and a large pitcher, when they are full, even though the pitcher holds more, nevertheless, the cup being full is without lack, just like the pitcher. So it is that every soul is full of glory: the one who holds less is no less full than the one who holds more. Correct then is Thomas Aquinas <note>original: "Thomaso acquinate"</note> on this point. And the poet had a marvelous intellect in this, because to adorn his poem and to demonstrate the power of the influence of the heavens, he feigns that the ranks of the blessed in eternal life are distinguished by the various spheres of the heavens. But because this is not according to the Christian religion, he clarifies here that he speaks figuratively, so that the human intellect can better understand divine things. And so that this does not seem inappropriate, he follows by saying:

<column-break/>

Having seen Dante's desires, Beatrice quieted him by resolving his doubts, just as the prophet Daniel resolved the doubts of Nebuchadnezzar, who had become cruel toward the wise men of Babylon. The history is long: but in brief, Nebuchadnezzar saw a horrific dream which then fled from his mind. For this reason, he summoned all the wise men of Babylon. He commanded that they tell him the dream and its interpretation. The wise men were prepared to interpret the dream, but they excused themselves for not knowing the dream itself. The king became enraged and commanded Arioch, the captain of the guard, to have them killed. Daniel, hearing of the king’s wrath, went to his companions Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah. Having offered a prayer for the safety of the wise men, Daniel received the revelation of the dream and its interpretation in a vision. He immediately reported it to the king, which resulted in the liberation of all. I do not narrate the dream here because we narrated it in the *Inferno*, where Dante describes the statue made of diverse metals with feet of clay. YOU ARGUE: Your first doubt is whether a nun like Piccarda—who always had the good will to remain in her religious order and never changed her mind—could have her merits lessened by the violence done to her by others when she was forcibly removed from the cloister; and whether this causes her not to merit as much as she would have by staying in the cloister. ALSO TO DOUBT: The second doubt is that, having seen these spirits in the lunar globe, Dante was almost inclined toward the opinion that human souls, upon leaving their bodies, return to their partner stars, according to the opinion of Plato.

Beatrice demonstrates that she understands his two doubts even though he remained silent; and now, to solve them, she begins with the latter, because, as she said shortly before, it "has more gall"—that is, it is more pernicious to our salvation because it contains a greater heresy. She says that all the blessed spirits are in the first heaven <note>The Empyrean</note>, both those who merited less and those like the Seraphim, the prophets, or the apostles; and in that place, they have a sweet life, though differing in degree. They are, therefore, in the supreme heaven, but they show themselves here for the reason we have stated. OF THE SERAPHIM: he ordains of the Seraphim: that is, the highest of the Seraphim.

MOST SUBMERGED. <note>original: "SINDIA"</note> That is, he who participates most in God. Of the Seraphim, the order of angels, and the hierarchies, we will speak in the place that requires it more than this one. Moses: we spoke of him in the first canticle <note>Inferno</note> where the poet narrates part of those who were drawn out of Limbo; by Moses, he means all the patriarchs. SAMUEL & whichever John you wish: as if to say, whether you want the Baptist or the Evangelist. NOT MARY: because she is not only above

The poet does not deserve reprimand if, under the fiction that souls inhabit different heavens, you understand otherwise; for it is necessary for the human wit, through more material and corporeal things, to be given an understanding of incorporeal things. Because our wit does not learn except from that which is perceived by the senses. Aristotle says: *Nothing is in the intellect that was not first in the senses.* <note>original Latin: "Nihil e in intellectu nisi prius fuerit in sensu"</note> Therefore, from the senses where they are

...droppings fell from a swallow's nest into his eyes, which blinded him. Whereupon, his patrimony being consumed, it was necessary that Anna, his wife, support him by weaving. As is the nature of women, she reproached him every day, saying he had been too liberal to the needy. Therefore, God, who does not abandon the good, put it in his mind to send his son—who was also named Tobit—to the city of Rhages in Media, to a relative named Gabael. This man owed him a certain sum of money. The young Tobit did not know how to get there, but went into the square to find if anyone was making that journey to go with him. For this reason, Raphael assumed a human body and offered himself as a companion, pretending he had to go to the same place. They set out on the journey, and having reached the Tigris River, a fish came at Tobit while he was washing his feet. He caught it by the angel's command and removed the heart and the gall, salting the rest to have food for the journey. They came to Rhages where Raguel, the father's cousin, lived. Raguel had a daughter named Sarah. She had already had seven husbands, but a demon named Asmodeus strangled them all on the first night before they could consummate the marriage. Tobit took her as his wife, and with the heart of the fish, he burned it on the coals and drove away the demon. He received half of Raguel’s substance as a dowry, recovered the money from Gabael, and returned to his father with his wife. And with the gall of the fish, he freed his father from blindness. **THAT WHICH Timaeus.** In the first book of our *Dialogues on the Soul*, we set forth the descent of the soul into the body according to the Platonists, who believed that all souls were created at one time, and then from time to time descend into bodies with the knowledge of all things, but being immersed in the dark matter of the body, they forget them.

...and the intellect learns distinct particulars through the "here and now" <note>original: "hic & nunc"</note> and makes them universals. From the friendship that the sense knows in an acute way, the intellect takes a universal thing in which everyone who participates is a friend. Therefore, she placed these spirits in the first heaven, so that we might understand they were in the lowest degree of beatitude. **THROUGH THIS**, Holy Scripture condescends. Here she leaves behind divine and high speech and takes up the material and corporeal to adapt to our faculty, and attributes feet and hands to God. This is not because God has a body, but it intends something else. Inasmuch as by "feet" she means the will, and by "hands" the work and the power. And similarly, she describes these three angels as corporeal men, though they are incorporeal, because our senses cannot otherwise comprehend them. **GABRIEL** of the order of Seraphim. **MICHAEL** of the order of Archangels. **RAPHAEL** came to the son of Tobit when he taught him to heal his father, who was blinded by the swallow's droppings. They say that Tobit, of the tribe of Naphtali, a just man, was in Nineveh, and for the love of God was very liberal toward the poor; and sleeping one day...

Dante does not affirm this, but says it could be that Plato's opinion is not as the words sound. Instead, he means not that the soul returns to the stars, but denotes that the influence which inclines one toward virtue or vice—from which comes honor or blame—is attributed to the stars; although such inclination can be resisted both by our free will and by divine grace, which is given to those who duly ask for it. "Because the wise man shall rule the stars" <note>original: "Quia sapiés dominabitur astris"</note>. And if this is his opinion, it does not deserve to be derided (that is, mocked) as false, because his "bow strikes some truth" (that is, his intention is directed toward some truth). **THIS principle**, which Plato sets forth, that every soul returns to the star from which it departed. **POORLY understood**: because they understood according to the words and not according to the sense we stated above. **TWISTED**: removed from the true way of worshipping one God. **ALMOST the whole world**: because except for the people of God, all nations through idolatry worshipped the stars, or Jupiter, or Mercury, or Mars, or another star.

Now this is the first doubt of Dante, which Beatrice, for the reason already stated, made the last in answering. The doubt was: if the good will endures, the force done to it by others cannot diminish its merit, since our will is what merits and demerits. But Piccarda and Constance endured in the good will to stay in the cloister. Therefore, the violence of those who took them out by force should not have diminished their merits, for which, if they had not left the cloister, they would have ascended to a higher heaven. Wherefore it follows:

THE OTHER doubt that concerns you. "Has less poison": because it does not make you a heretic, which is a poison that kills the soul and removes it from the faith held by holy theology. But this is not a doubt that I can remove from Beatrice—that is, from our faith. For doubting that what our faith holds is a just thing affirms that the faith exists. Therefore, this doubt is an "argument" (that is, a demonstration) of faith.

Dante's argument was that if the good will endures, the violence done to it should not diminish the merit. Answering this, Beatrice divides the will into two species: absolute and relative...

For will, if it wills not, is never quenched,
but acts as nature acts within the fire,
though violence a thousand times may force it.
For if it bends, whether much or little,
it follows force; and thus did these women,
having the power to return to the holy place.
If their will had remained whole,
like that which held Lawrence upon the gridiron
and made Mucius severe toward his own hand,

<note>original: "Lorenzo"</note> Lawrence. Nevertheless, the force of their relatives partially turned them away, and they did not stand in firm purpose like Lawrence or Mucius; had they done so, their merit would not have been diminished. Instead, they would have chosen death rather than consent to marriage. Lawrence was martyred in the year 255 under the Emperor Decius, who wanted him to reveal the wealth of Sixtus, the Supreme Pontiff. Lawrence chose to die with a joyful and great spirit, enduring many torments rather than reveal the treasures. <note>Saint Lawrence was famously roasted on a gridiron.</note> 

MUTIO. <note>Mucius Scaevola</note> In the time when Porsena, King of Chiusi, had besieged Rome, Gaius Mucius, a noble youth, obtained permission from the Senate and went into the enemy camp with the firm purpose of either dying or killing the king. But fortune was envious of such a high undertaking. The high-minded youth found the king together with his secretary, both dressed in similar robes. He killed the secretary, believing he was killing the king, and quickly confessed both his error and his purpose. Then, turning to his right hand, he decided to punish it for the mistake, holding it over the fire prepared there for a sacrifice. Porsena was amazed by such excellence of spirit and pardoned him. But Mucius, to terrify him further, told him that three hundred youths had conspired to come one by one to kill him. This man was afterwards called Scaevola, <note>original: "idest sine uola"</note> that is, "without a palm," because he had burned the palm of his hand in the fire. 

If, therefore, they <note>Piccarda and Constance</note> had possessed a firm will after being snatched from the monastery, every time they had the opportunity, they would have fled from their relatives and returned to the cloister. BUT SUCH a steadfast will is too rare. This is as if to say that God had compassion, considering our fragility. For to choose the good of one’s own will and follow it until violence intervenes is an angelic thing and rare among men. But to yield to violence in matters which, though they lack great merit, are nevertheless permitted by the Church, is a human thing.

---

But now another passage crosses
before your eyes, such that by yourself
you would not get through, but would grow weary.
I have held it as a certainty in your mind
that a blessed soul can never lie,
since it is always near the Primal Truth.
And then you were able to hear from Piccarda
that Constance held her affection for the veil,
so that she seems here to contradict me.
Many times already, brother, it has happened
that to flee a danger, against his own liking,
a man has done what is not fitting to do;
As Alcmæon, who, prayed to do so
by his father, took his own mother’s life;
not to lose his piety, he became pitiless.

<column-break/>

<term>Absolute Will</term> <note>original: "Absoluta uolonta"</note> is that which, having once willed the good, always wills it. For example: Lawrence the martyr wills to stand firm in the Christian faith. Therefore, although he was roasted on the gridiron, he always wills that same thing, notwithstanding the great pain of the fire he suffered. And when this will is in our soul, no violence can diminish our merit; rather, it increases it for us. 

The other kind of will is called <term>Relative Will</term> <note>original: "uolonta respectiua"</note>; and this wills either the greater good or the lesser evil. Therefore, if violence occurs when the one who suffers <note>original: "idest patisce"</note> and is forced contributes nothing—that is, does not incline the will in any way toward that which forces—then Piccarda and Constance are not entirely excused, because there was no such violence that could have prohibited them from returning once they were taken out. Nor could they be forced into marriage against their will, for the will is not quenched unless it so wills. Nor is there any punishment so harsh that it can compel us to will if we do not wish to will. 

Just as the nature of fire within the fire itself does not twist away, and if it is twisted by force, as soon as the violence ceases, it returns upward. Because if it bends much or little, it follows the force. Every time the will bends to violence, much or little, it follows the violence, and it cannot be said absolutely that it is against its own will. And thus these women did. IF IT HAD BEEN. Although they, of their own spontaneous will, would have rather chosen the religious life than marriage, nevertheless the force of their relatives partially turned them away, and they did not remain in firm purpose like Lawrence or Mucius.

Beatrice had shown Dante that a blessed soul cannot lie. And Piccarda had shown that Constance always held her affection for the monastic life. And she [Beatrice] has shown otherwise; and two contraries cannot both be true. Therefore, it seems that one of these two blessed souls tells a falsehood. BUT NOW CROSSES BEFORE YOU: she puts before you ANOTHER passage: another doubtful question. 

A BLESSED SOUL CANNOT LIE: and she gives the reason, because it always has near itself the Primal Truth, that is, God, who is the Supreme Truth. And then you could hear from Piccarda that Constance always retained her affection for the veil, that is, the will for the monastic state. This is denoted by "the veil"; and this opinion is contrary to my own, which I stated above: that if she had retained such affection in herself, she would have returned to the monastery. 

MANY times. She has posed the doubt; now, before she resolves it, she sets forth a principle by which she affirms that often, to flee what we do not want, we do what we do not want. She says, therefore, that it often happens that a man, AGAINST HIS LIKING—that is, against what would be pleasing to him—to flee some danger, does what is not fitting, even though it is naturally against his will. 

And she gives the example of Alcmæon, who killed his mother, not out of hatred or because he did not love her, but to avenge the death of his father; and thus, so as not to lose piety toward his father, he became (though unwillingly) pitiless toward his mother. Amphiaraus, the augur and diviner, foresaw that if he went to Thebes with Adrastus to help Polynices, he would be killed there. For this reason, he hid himself so as not to be forced to go. No one knew where he was except Eriphyle. At first, she would not reveal it, but later, being offered the necklace of the wife [of Polynices] made by Vulcan, she was overcome by greed and revealed him. Amphiaraus was thus deceived by his own omens. But having arrived at Thebes, in the first clash of spears, he was swallowed by the earth along with his chariot and horses. Therefore, Alcmæon, his son, in vengeance for his father, killed his mother. According to Homer, Amphiaraus was the son of Oicles, and a temple was dedicated to him in the place where...

### CANTO THE FIFTH

...where the earth swallowed him <note>Referring to Amphiaraus, a seer who was swallowed by the earth during the war of the Seven against Thebes.</note>. According to Pliny, he was the inventor of **pyromancy** <note>original: "lignispica," divination by fire</note>, which is that branch of divination performed with fire.

> At this point I wish for you to think
> that force with will is mixed, and they so act
> that the offenses cannot be excused.
> Absolute will does not consent to harm,
> but it consents to it insofar as it fears,
> by drawing back, to fall into more grief.
> Therefore, when Piccarda says this,
> she means it of the absolute will, and I
> of the other; so that we both speak the truth.
> Such was the flowing of the holy stream
> that issued from the fount whence every truth derives;
> it set to rest both one and the other desire.

**REACHING THE GOAL** <note>original: "GIUGNER POLLO"</note>: This means that it is not forbidden for man to arrive at this truth. For nature would not have given us such a desire in vain. As **The Aquinas** <note>Saint Thomas Aquinas</note> says in his book *Against the Gentiles*, the ultimate and supreme happiness of man consists in the contemplation of God. **BORN FROM THAT**: Because man by nature desires to find the truth, he goes investigating with his reasoning and discourse. In such discourse, various doubts often arise where we wonder which of the many plausible reasons occurring to the mind is the truth. Such doubts are like **sprouts** <note>original: "rampolli"</note> that grow at the foot of the tree. **AND IT IS NATURE**: That is, it is a natural thing in man which pushes him to the summit of truth, moving from one truth already found to another, just as a man climbs from hill to hill to reach the highest peak and ridge of the mountain.

> This invites me, this gives me assurance,
> with reverence, Lady, to ask of you
> about another truth that is dark to me.
> I wish to know if man can satisfy you
> for broken vows with other goods,
> so that they be not small upon your scales.
> Beatrice looked at me with eyes full
> of sparks of love, so divine,
> that my overcome power turned its back,
> and I almost lost myself with downcast eyes.

<column-break/>

She resolves the doubt by establishing this distinction. There are two types of **will**: **absolute** and **relative** <note>original: "respectiua"</note>. The absolute will cannot want evil. The relative will wants the lesser evil to flee the greater. But man is often deceived in discerning and judging, as what is the greater evil may seem to him the lesser. Therefore, with her absolute will, Piccarda wants and chose the virginal life. But since death seemed a greater evil to her than leaving that life, with her relative will she chose marriage. For this reason, when Costanza asserts she desired the monastic life rather than marriage, she means the absolute will. But when Beatrice says she did not want it, she means the relative will. Similarly, when we say that **Alcmaeon** <note>A mythological figure who killed his mother Eriphyle to avenge his father Amphiaraus</note> wanted to kill Eriphyle, we mean the relative will. Because he considered it an evil to kill his mother, but he judged—though falsely—that it was a lesser evil to kill her than to not avenge his father. His will in the matricide was not absolute, but relative.

He thanks Beatrice, who represents **Sacred Theology** and **Divine Wisdom**. Therefore, he excellently calls her the **beloved of the First Lover** <note>original: "amanza del primo amante"</note>, which is God, who is First Love as demonstrated in the proper place. **O DIVINE ONE** <note>original: "O DIVA"</note>: O goddess, because divinity is power, wisdom, and love; and she is divine because she makes us divine. **BY WHICH HER SPEECH CLEANSES ME**: That is, her speech cleanses us before God. For wisdom alone is what removes ignorance, which is the source of every vice. **AND WARMS**: That is, it ignites me and makes me alive in **Seraphic love** <note>The highest order of angels, associated with burning love for God</note>. **MY AFFECTION IS NOT**: He excuses himself because his affection toward her cannot be so deep as to match her grace toward him, "grace for grace," that is, love for love. **BUT HE WHO SEES AND HAS POWER**: This is God, who, because He sees—that is, He knows what wisdom is—loves it; and because He can do what He wills and wills what He can. **I SEE WELL**: As if to say, you have opened my eyes so that I clearly know our intellect is never satisfied unless the truth illustrates—that is, illuminates—it. Beyond this truth, no other truth wanders. This is God, who, as He Himself says, is **the way, the truth, and the life** <note>original Latin: "uia uerita & uita"</note>. He is the true way, such that outside of Him no truth is spread or extended. **IT RESTS WITHIN IT LIKE A WILD BEAST IN ITS DEN**: *Lustrum* in the Latin language means the den of wild beasts. Therefore, just as the beast rests inside its den and desires nothing else, so our intellect, having reached God, rests there.

**THIS INVITES ME**: As if to say, I would not dare to ask you if I did not see that the desire for knowledge is natural. And the things ordained by nature—that is, by God—must not be denied. Therefore, it seems permissible to ask, but with reverence, about that which I doubt. And he warns that no arrogance or imprudence, but rather the highest veneration, must be used in questioning those more learned than ourselves. **I WANT TO KNOW**: The doubt is whether, since Costanza and Piccarda had made a religious vow and then broke it, they can satisfy God with other goods equivalent to it, so that they might be equal on the divine scales. Finally, he asks about vows in general. **BEATRICE LOOKED AT ME**: All of this signifies that the high insights of theology, when they come to the mind, inflame us with an immeasurable love; and they are so divine that our intellect loses itself therein, just as eyes do in too much light.

->CANTO FIVE OF THE THIRD CANTICLE BY DANTE.<-

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante’s Paradiso, Canto V. Having previously addressed the nature of the human will through historical examples, Beatrice now addresses Dante’s specific confusion regarding the sanctity of vows and the possibility of "making amends" for an unfulfilled promise to God.</meta>

# PARADISO

->I flame upon you in the heat of love<-
->beyond the measure seen upon the earth,<-
->so that I overcome your vision’s power;<-
->Do not marvel, for this proceeds<-
->from perfect vision which, as it apprehends,<-
->so it moves its foot toward the apprehended good.<-
->I see well how there already shines<-
->within your intellect the eternal light,<-
->which, once seen, alone and always kindles love;<-
->And if some other thing seduces your love,<-
->it is nothing but some vestige of that light,<-
->ill-recognized, which shines through there.<-
->You wish to know if, with another service,<-
->for a missed vow, one can render so much<-
->that the soul is secured from litigation.<-
->Thus Beatrice began this canto,<-
->and like a person who does not break their speech,<-
->she continued thus her holy discourse:<-

---

->The greatest gift that God in His largesse<-
->bestowed in creating, and to His goodness<-
->most conformed, and that which He most prizes,<-
->Was the freedom of the will,<-
->with which the intelligent creatures—<-
->all of them, and they alone—were and are endowed.<-
->Now it will appear to you, if you argue from this,<-
->the high value of a vow, if it be so made<-
->that God consents when you consent;<-
->For in establishing the pact 'tween God and man,<-
->this treasure is made the sacrifice,<-
->such as I say, and made by its own act.<-
->Therefore, what can be rendered in restoration?<-
->If you think to use well what you have offered,<-
->you wish to do good work with ill-gotten gains.<-

<column-break/>

This fifth canto contains the response that Beatrice makes as to whether a missed vow <note>The Italian *uoto mancho* refers to a religious promise or vow that has not been fulfilled.</note> can be restored through other goods; and it concludes as you shall see. Afterward, it narrates how they ascended from the first heaven of the Moon to the second, that of Mercury. In these first verses, Beatrice speaks, saying: "Do not marvel if I flame upon you," that is, if I am more splendid in the heat of love "beyond the world seen on earth," meaning more than I flamed for you in the world—that is, in that part of the world which is on earth. "World" <note>original: "Mondo"</note> in the Latin language signifies the entire universe, that is, the heavens with all the elements, which the Greeks call **cosmos** <note>original: "cosmos"</note>. The meaning is: do not marvel if I flame for you more now that you are in heaven—that is, elevated to the contemplation of divine things as a celestial man, and with the virtues of a soul already purged—than I did when you were on earth, meaning when you followed more the literal sense and could not yet reach the high allegorical senses which can inflame you much more than those others. Since love is nothing other than the desire for beauty, the more the allegorical senses are more beautiful than the moral ones, the more they move and delight us with greater love. Do not marvel, then, that I appear more radiant to you, because this happens because you see better than before. And in truth, the more our intellect distances itself from the thought of earthly things, the more lucid it becomes and the more it comprehends celestial things; and the more it apprehends, the more it moves the affection to pursue it. Whence Augustine said: "For by ascending to God, ignorance is illuminated and weakness is strengthened by the intelligence given to them, through which they see, and by the charity through which they serve." <note>original: "Accendendo enim ad deum illuminatur ignorantia & corroboratur infirmitas data sibi intelligentia qua uident & caritate qua feruiunt."</note> **I SEE WELL**: This demonstrates for what purpose she said the sentence above: which is because she sees him already so elevated that the divine light shines in him more than usual. For just as a metal, the more it is polished and wiped clean, the more it reflects the rays of the sun, so our intellect, the higher it can elevate itself by being cleaner from the contagion of earthly things, the more the divine light shines in it. This light, the more it grows in us, the greater the love it kindles in us to pursue it, because our love does not extend except to the good and the true. And if we love a thing that is neither good nor true, it is because it deceives us and seems true and good to us, although it is not. Whence follows: **AND IF SOME OTHER** thing seduces your love. No other thing is loved by man except the true and the good. And if sometimes we love that which is neither true nor good, it is because that thing seduces us—that is, deceives us and shows itself as good and true, though it is captive and false. Therefore, we love it believing it to be good, because we see shining through it some vestige and sign of a good poorly understood by us, because we believe in that which is not. **YOU WISH TO KNOW**: as if she said, your doubt is whether a man, having made a vow and then not observed it, can render so much in exchange for the missed vow with another service and another good—whether fasts, or prayers, or alms—that the thing frees the soul from **litigation** <note>original: "litigio," a legal metaphor for the soul's debt or dispute with God's justice</note>, that is, from the judgment of God where we must plead our case. A **VOW** <note>original: "VOTO"</note> is an obligation of our free will made with a promise to God regarding something of God. It is asked, therefore, if such an obligation can be annulled once it is made, and the answer is no, because this is a sacrifice rendered to God and is already accepted by God. Therefore, it cannot be broken nor satisfied with another thing, since nothing is of such dignity as the free choice of our will. But for a true vow, it is necessary that the person making the vow be able to obligate themselves; hence women and servants, because they are under the power of others [cannot do so]. Furthermore, because a vow is an obligation of some good made to God with deliberation, Isidore says: "In evil promises, break your word; in a shameful vow, change your decree, and do not do what you have incautiously promised. And that promise is wicked which is fulfilled by a crime." <note>original: "In malis promissis scinde fidē: & in turpi uoto muta decretum & quod incaute nouisti nō facias. Et rimpia est promissio que scelere adimpletur."</note> And here it divides, saying that there are some things that always turn out well, like virtuous works. Others, on the contrary, like contrary things, and these do not fall into a vow. Some are by their nature good, but sometimes have a sad end; and such vows as these should not be observed.

The text orders the freedom of the will: that is, **free will** <note>original: "libero arbitrio"</note> was the greatest gift that God in His largesse and liberality made when He created things, and it was the most conformed to His goodness. And there is nothing He prizes more. **OF WHICH ALL** intelligent creatures. God gave free will not to all creatures, but to the intelligent ones, which are the angels and humans; and from the beginning it was given equally. Now it is unequal because in the angel it is confirmed and they can no longer sin, since all those who remained innocent after the fall of Lucifer were confirmed in grace. He says three things about free will: first, that it is the greatest gift God has given; second, that it is most conformed to His goodness; third, that He esteems it most. The first is demonstrated because the "free" presupposes reason and will. For it belongs to reason to judge and discourse upon what is to be willed or not. It belongs to the will to want it, and therefore it is called free. And through these two things, we are made in the image and likeness of God. And memory is also presupposed, for without it, neither reason nor will could perform any work, nor could one judge. These three things God has given only to the angel and to man, and for this reason we approach closer to God than other creatures. Therefore, they are the greatest, and all three are within the freedom of the choice, which is radically...

<summary>In this opening to Canto V, Beatrice explains to Dante that her increasing radiance is a reflection of his own growing spiritual perception, and she defines free will as God's most precious gift to humanity. The commentary explores the theological nature of vows and the conditions under which the "treasure" of free will is sacrificed through a promise to God.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Beatrice’s discourse on the sanctity of vows. Having established that free will is God’s greatest gift, she now explains how a vow—which is the sacrifice of that free will—can be "commuted" or changed by the Church, and why some vows are so weighty they can never be substituted.</meta>

# CANTO FIVE

->You are now certain of the main point;<-
->but because Holy Church in this grants dispensation,<-
->which seems contrary to the truth I have disclosed to you,<-
->It behooves you to sit a little longer at the table,<-
->for the tough food you have taken in<-
->still requires help for its digestion.<-
->Open your mind to that which I reveal to you<-
->and fix it within; for having understood<-
->without retaining it does not make knowledge.<-
->Two things concur in the essence<-
->of this sacrifice: one is that of which it is made,<-
->the other is the covenant itself.<-
<note>Beatrice distinguishes between the "matter" of the vow (the thing promised, like fasting) and the "form" or "covenant" (the actual promise made to God).</note>
->This last is never canceled<-
->unless it be kept; and concerning it<-
->my speech above was so precise.<-
->Therefore it was a necessity for the Hebrews<-
->to still offer sacrifice, although some offerings<-
->might be substituted, as you should know.<-
->The other, which is known to you as the "matter,"<-
->may indeed be such that no fault is found<-
->if it be exchanged for some other matter.<-
->But let no one shift the burden on his shoulder<-
->by his own judgment, without the turning<-
->of both the white and the yellow keys;<-
<note>These keys represent the authority of the Church: the "white" key of discernment and the "yellow" (gold) key of power or authority granted to priests.</note>
->And believe every substitution to be foolish,<-
->unless the thing set aside is included in the new,<-
->as four is contained within six.<-
->Therefore, whatever thing weighs so much<-
->by its own value that it tips every scale,<-
->cannot be satisfied by any other expense.<-
->Let mortals not take a vow lightly;<-
->be faithful, and in doing so, do not be reckless<-
->as Jephthah was in his first offering;<-
<note>Jephthah was a biblical judge who vowed to sacrifice the first thing that came out of his house to meet him—which ended up being his daughter.</note>

<column-break/>

…and causally in the reason: and formally and essentially in the will. It is CONFORMED to goodness. Because through it we are able to save ourselves. He prizes this more because it is the greatest thing man can do. **NOW IT WILL APPEAR** if you argue from here. The other value concludes thus: now having demonstrated the great gift that is free will, if you argue from this—that is, from this reasoning—it will appear to you, or become manifest, the high value of the vow. Because if the greatest gift God has made to man is the free will, and man in his vow binds it to God, it follows that he binds the greatest thing he has; provided that the vow is of such a quality that God accepts it when you make it: for God does not accept a vow made incorrectly. And it follows that in establishing the pact between God and man—that is, in making the vow—you make a victim <note>original: "uictima"</note>, that is, a sacrifice of this treasure which is such—that is, as great as I have said—because you offer to God your free will. Because it is the will that binds itself with the promise. **THEREFORE SHE CONCLUDES** that he who breaks the vow cannot give sufficient restoration. And certainly, if the free will is the greatest gift we can give to God, once that is taken away, we cannot give Him anything equivalent in exchange. And she adds that in no way should you believe it good to use—that is, to justly convert to your own use—that which you have already offered to God. Because this is as if you believed you were doing good work <note>original: "buona opera"</note> from "ill-gotten gains" <note>original: "mal tollecto"</note>, that is, from something wrongly acquired.

She had declared that for a broken vow, no suitable restoration can be given. Now, seeing that the Church often grants dispensations for vows, someone might believe that what Beatrice has said is false, or that such a dispensation is done against duty. Therefore, she admonishes the poet to wait for this clarification: and she speaks through a metaphor, calling this reasoning "hard food" <note>original: "cibo duro"</note> because the mind feeds on doctrine just as the body feeds on physical food; and she calls it "rigid" <note>stiff or difficult to digest</note> because it needs help. And she admonishes him to open and turn his mind to what she will say: and "fix it within"—that is, retain it—because it does not create knowledge to have understood a thing without retaining it; as, for example <note>original: "verbi gratia"</note>, if I had understood what the philosophers say in moral philosophy and had not retained it, I would not possess that knowledge.

Because we see that the Church dispenses vows, Beatrice wants to demonstrate in what way they can be dispensed. Therefore, she shows that two things are in a vow. The "matter" <note>original: "materia"</note> which is promised: such as fasting, money, property, and similar things; and this is the matter of the vow. The other is the "covenant" <note>original: "conuenuenza"</note>, that is, the convention and the pact that you make with God; and this is the "form" <note>original: "forma"</note> that gives being to the thing. Of these two, the latter—that is, the form—cannot be dispensed. Nor is anyone ever absolved who makes a vow unless they observe it; and therefore she says "it is never canceled" because he who makes a vow makes himself a debtor and binds his will, which is free; and the debtor is not cleared unless he pays. And of this form Beatrice spoke above so precisely, without any exception, that it could not be dispensed. **THEREFORE NECESSITY** was for the Hebrews: she proves by example that the form cannot be changed. Because the Hebrews, having made a vow to sacrifice, it was a necessity that they always sacrificed. But they could well change the matter of the sacrifice: and for this reason, at some times they sacrificed animals, at others grain, at others money. **THE OTHER**: as she has shown that the form cannot be changed, so now she shows that the matter can be changed, as the example of the Hebrews declares. And therefore she says the matter can be such that no fault is committed if it is converted and transmuted into another matter: as if we had promised to give to God the first offspring of our herds, the Pope can dispense this so that we give the equivalent in money. But if we have promised chastity and obedience in a cloister, what could be given as an equivalent to that?

She has shown that the Pope can commute vows regarding the matter; now she admonishes first that no one should presume by themselves to make a substitution of vows without the will of the "white key and the yellow key": that is, without the license of a priest who can absolve. We spoke of the keys in the ninth canto of the second canticle <note>Purgatorio</note>. **AND EVERY SUBSTITUTION**. Every substitution of a vow is foolish if the vow set aside is not smaller than the one into which it is changed. Whence she says if the "thing set aside"—that is, the vow left behind—is not "included"—that is, contained—in the "newly taken one" in place of the vow, like four is in six. **AS WAS JEPHTHAH**. He was the son of Gilead, but born of adultery. And he was driven from the house by the legitimate sons of Gilead, and went to the land of Tob. He was a very strong man; and because of this, the people of Israel being greatly oppressed by the children of Ammon, the citizens made him their prince in that war. And he made a vow that if he returned...

<summary>Beatrice explains the distinction between the "form" of a vow (the promise to God) and its "matter" (the specific offering), noting that while the promise is absolute, the offering can sometimes be exchanged through priestly authority.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Beatrice’s lecture on vows from Canto V of the Paradiso. It follows the previous page where she explained that the "covenant" of a vow—the promise to God—is permanent, even if the "matter" of the vow (the specific action) can sometimes be exchanged through the Church's authority.</meta>
