<header>PARADISO</header>

To whom it would have better suited to say, "I did wrong,"
than by keeping his word to do worse; and just as foolish
you can find the great leader of the Greeks,
whereby Iphigenia wept for her beautiful face,
and made both the wise and the simple weep
who heard tell of such a ritual. <note>original: "culto." The poet refers to the "cult" or ritual of sacrifice. Beatrice is arguing that keeping a vow that requires an evil act (like Jephthah or Agamemnon killing their daughters) is a greater sin than breaking the vow.</note>

Be more serious, you Christians, in your movements;
do not be like a feather to every wind,
and do not believe that every water washes you.
You have the Old and the New Testament,
and the Shepherd of the Church who guides you;
let this be enough for your salvation.
If evil greed cries out something else to you,
be men, and not mindless sheep,
so that the Jew among you does not laugh at you. <note>A historical reference to the idea that those outside the faith would mock Christians for being easily swayed or hypocritical regarding their own laws.</note>
Do not act like the lamb that leaves the milk
of its mother, and, simple and playful,
fights with itself for its own pleasure.

Thus Beatrice spoke to me, just as I write;
then she turned away, full of longing,
to that part where the world is most alive. <note>She turns toward the Equator or the Empyrean, the source of divine light.</note>
Her silence and her transformed appearance
imposed quiet on my eager mind,
which already had new questions before it;
And just like an arrow that hits the mark
before the bowstring is even still,
so we ran into the second realm. <note>The "second realm" is the Heaven of Mercury.</note>
There I saw my lady so joyful
as she entered into the light of that heaven,
that the planet itself became more radiant.
And if the star itself changed and laughed,
what did I become, who by my very nature
am subject to change in every way!

<column-break/>

As victor, he offered to God as a burnt offering the first person who should come out of his house to meet him. He defeated the enemies and occupied twenty cities of the Ammonites. And when he returned to Mizpah, to his home, his only daughter came out to meet him with tambourines and dancing. This miserable encounter brought great sorrow to the father; but the daughter, understanding her father’s vow, comforted him, saying he should fulfill to God what he had promised. But she asked him for a space of two months before he sacrificed her, so that she might wander the mountains with her companions to mourn her virginity. And in this way, the two months having passed, the wretched maiden returned to her father and was sacrificed. From this arose the custom among the people of Israel that every year the virgins gather together for four days to mourn the daughter of Jephthah the Gileadite. This man was therefore foolish, and it would have been less evil not to have kept the vow than to have killed his daughter. Not much different is the case of Agamemnon, the first leader of the Greeks, who was in the port of Aulis with a thousand armed ships, waiting for nothing other than a favorable wind to lead them to Troy, which they wished to besiege to recover Helen, who had been abducted by Paris. Agamemnon, eager to set sail, learned from the oracle that he would have a favorable wind if Diana—who was angry because Agamemnon had killed a doe consecrated to her during a hunt—were appeased with the blood of Iphigenia, his daughter. He consented to her being sacrificed. But Diana, moved to great compassion for the innocent girl, had her snatched away and carried to the land of Tauris, to be kept there until her brother Orestes should bring her home. Such vows, therefore, should not be made, nor kept if they are made. Because God, being the Father of mercy and clemency, hates all cruelty. **SUCH A RITUAL** <note>original: "DI SI FACTO colto"</note>: such a cruel sacrifice; for the Latins use the word <term>cultum dei</term> <note>Latin: "the worship of God"</note> for every honor and sacrifice offered to God.

He admonishes us not to be so light in making vows and believing that it is easy to be absolved of them; and if anyone should say they do not know how to govern themselves, he shows that we have the doctrine of the New and Old Testaments, and the Pastor—that is, the priestly order—which explains this doctrine to us. And this is enough for our salvation. And if anyone should say that greed—that is, appetite and sensuality—guides us or pulls us to follow worldly pleasures and leave virtuous works, he responds that we are men and not sheep. That is, we have not only senses, as sheep do, but we also have reason and intellect, which are not given to any other animal; and with these, we can conquer appetite and sensuality. Therefore, he who allows himself to be conquered by appetite has no excuse. Follow, then, the precepts of the Pastor and the Holy Church, so that the Jew—that is, all the Jews who live among us—does not laugh at your foolishness. Do not be like the lambs, who, out of a desire to play and be frisky, leave their milk. Thus, fools, for the sake of temporary and momentary pleasures, abandon their salvation.

**THUS BEATRICE.** Since the poet places the ascent to the second circle, in which is Mercury, let it not be unknown to us that this planet has two "houses" in the zodiac: Gemini and Virgo. It is a temperate and nocturnal planet, and sometimes masculine and sometimes feminine. And it easily converts to the nature of the planet with which it is joined: becoming good with the good, evil with the evil, and mediocre with the mediocre. And such a nature in the upper part of its circle mixes its qualities with Venus, and in the lower part with the Sun. According to Ptolemy, it produces studious and eloquent men. Therefore, it is called by the poets the god of wisdom and eloquence. The Greeks call him **Hermes**; and among them, <term>hermineuin</term> <note>Greek: "hermeneuein," meaning to interpret</note> means to interpret, because eloquence is the interpreter of the concepts of our minds. They hold that he is the messenger of the gods for two reasons: first, because the planet is very fast, which is why he is depicted with winged sandals; second, because just as a messenger reports nothing of his own but explains what has been committed to him by others, so Mercury produces effects not according to his own influence, but according to that of the planet to which he is joined. He especially disposes and enables men toward arithmetic and the calculation of numbers. Therefore, he is called the god of merchants. Finally, when well-placed, he brings about clear oracles and manifest divination. He brings about supreme eloquence, which has such power in persuading and dissuading, in moving and quieting our minds, that it leads a person to whatever thing he pleases. Therefore, they put a wand in his hand, but it is entwined with two serpents, to denote that the ornament of words is not sufficient to create true eloquence unless supreme prudence is added, which is signified by the serpent. Whence it is said: <term>Estote prudentes sicut serpentes</term> <note>Latin: "Be wise as serpents."</note>. He brings about eloquence and sweetness of speech, doctrine, memory, astrology, sharpness of mind, belief, beauty, desire for power, and the speculation of obscure things. But if he is in a bad position, he brings about theft, fraud, lies, false witness, craftiness, and cunning. He is rarely outside the rays of the sun, and for this reason, he is rarely seen; and being accustomed to this, he does not fear "combustion" <note>An astrological term for a planet being too close to the sun's heat.</note> as much as the other planets. And for this reason, they imagine that he wears a cap on his head. He never moves further than thirty degrees from the sun, which is...

<summary>Dante and Beatrice ascend to the Heaven of Mercury, as Beatrice warns against making foolish or "evil" vows, citing the tragic biblical and mythological examples of Jephthah and Agamemnon. The commentary explains the astrological and symbolic nature of Mercury as the sphere of eloquence and reason.</summary>

# CANTO FIVE

the space of one zodiac sign. It completes its course in three hundred and thirty-eight days: and does not stay in one sign more than twenty-eight days and six hours, according to what Alfraganus <note>Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Kathir al-Farghani, a 9th-century astronomer whose work was a primary source for Dante's cosmology.</note> reports. The lowest part of the sphere of Mercury is two hundred and eight thousand and five hundred and forty-two miles from the earth. And its highest point is five hundred and forty-two thousand and seven hundred and fifty miles. Now, because Mercury gives great influence to the active life, the poet shows that in this heaven are represented those illustrious princes who demonstrated excellent virtue in their governance. BEATRICE turned to me like a servant; then she turned away entirely distant, that is, full of desire <note>original: "distante .i. piena di desidero." The commentator interprets her turning away as an act of intense longing for God.</note>: and it signifies that, having spoken her words, Beatrice turned toward the East with the highest desire to ascend to the second heaven of Mercury. And by this he hints that the contemplation of divine things—through which we climb from heaven to heaven—must be done with the greatest desire and fervor. And he calls the East the part where life is most vivid, either because all light is born there, as is every revolution, or because celestial influences have more power in the eastern parts. AND JUST AS an arrow. And it follows that, once the desire to ascend to the second heaven was born in Beatrice, they climbed there as quickly as an arrow flies, which hits the target before the bowstring that pushed it has come to rest. The string is the will, which pushes the intellect and makes it ascend. And the arrow is the genius <note>term: "longegno" (the wit or intellect). Landino uses the arrow metaphor to show how human intellect can reach a conclusion almost instantly once the will is set.</note>, which reaches its end before the will is at rest. And having reached that heaven, Beatrice was so joyful within that light that the planet itself became more radiant. The poet imagines that the higher Beatrice ascends, the more joyful she becomes: because the soul filled with doctrine, the more it contemplates high things, the greater joy it takes. AND MORE radiant the planet became. Mercury influences doctrine and eloquence: and the more such influence makes men learned, the more the planet shines—that is, the more its nature is made manifest. Or we might say that Beatrice (that is, Christian Theology) makes Mercury shine: because in no other religion does its influence appear more than in ours. And according to astrologers, it plays a great part in the Christian religion. Because at the birth of our Redeemer—the unbreakable and immovable rock upon which the Christian Church is built—Mercury was found in Gemini, its own home, and in the Ninth House, which is the house of religion and faith. Through its influence, our doctors have surpassed all the writers of every other religion in both depth of wisdom and the adornment of eloquence. And Mercury is especially powerful in that place of profound science given through metaphor. And if anyone should say it is impious folly to attribute influence to the birth of Christ, I answer that I do not doubt for a moment that the Creator of the universe does not wait for help from His creatures; and I am certain that all the planets and stars and heavens depend on Him, and from Him they have whatever virtue is in them. But I believe it pleased Him who can do all things—and by whose power everything can do what it does—that His true religion should have favor from Him not only directly, but also in some part through the means of His secondary causes. I do not wish this opinion to extend further than the Catholic faith permits, to which I always submit myself. This reason, then, was perhaps what induced the poet to write that Beatrice made the heaven of Mercury shine. AND IF the star changed and smiled: if the immutable and incorruptible star changed and smiled and shone—for we say a thing "smiles" when it glitters and shines—how much more should I change, I who, because I am a man, am by nature transmutable in all ways, that is, in every mode: because not only is the body changeable, but also the soul through various disturbances.

**A** most excellent comparison and very appropriate: but so clear that it required no exposition. If you, reader, wish to understand how much I desired to learn from those spirits about their state: consider if I did not continue immediately in saying "what starts here" (that is, what is beginning), how great your desire would be for me to speak: and thus you will understand mine. O WELL-BORN. These are the words of one of those souls. It says, therefore, "O you Dante, well-born," that is, born at a happy moment to whom God grants grace to see the eternal triumph (that is, beatitude), which men can acquire after Jesus Christ, with His passion, triumphed over our adversary.

BEFORE THE militia is abandoned. Man in this life is in the Church Militant, in which whoever fights boldly against the flesh and the devil, and conquers them, then in the other life triumphs in such victory, and it is called the Church Triumphant. But Dante feigns having this grace above all others who are still living: and in the militant life, he can see the eternal glory, which none reach except those who after death are in the triumphant life. BY THE light that. It shows how much charity is in the blessed souls who live by the light of God, which is supreme charity; since without the poet’s prayers, they offer to tell him whatever he wants to know. And so that he understands they are able to speak, this spirit shows that they do so because they are illuminated by the light that "spreads," that is, extends through all of heaven, and this is the light of God. Thus the spirit offered itself so liberally. And Beatrice, turning to Dante, said, "Speak then securely," that is, ask without suspicion; and by this the poet means that holy theology comforts us so that we strive to learn, not from the malignant spirits in whom there is fraud, snares, malice, and deception, but from the good ones who, out of charity and being illuminated, speak the truth; and therefore she adds: "believe them as you would gods."

He composed and reduced into brevity the laws scattered through many volumes with marvelous order. He reigned for thirty-eight years. It followed behind the ancient Aeneas <note>original: "enea"</note> who took Lavinia. For when Aeneas came from Troy to Italy with the Eagle, because he came from the East to the West, he followed the course of the heavens. We can also say that the Eagle that came from Troy to Italy came according to the course of heaven because it came with great fortune and established the Roman Empire. But when it went from Italy to Thrace <note>where Constantine founded Constantinople</note>, it went against the course of heaven, because from then on the Empire always declined. We have spoken of the Eagle and of Constantine. We have likewise spoken of Aeneas. FOR A HUNDRED AND A HUNDRED YEARS AND MORE THE BIRD OF GOD. The empire of Constantine began in the year of our salvation 309. And the empire of Justinian in the year 523. There were, therefore, two hundred and fourteen years. Because the Eagle is consecrated to Jove <note>Jupiter</note>, it is called the "bird of God." It remained at the edge of Europe, that is, in Constantinople, where Constantine transferred the Empire; this city is in the furthest part of Europe, which is divided from Asia by the river Tanais <note>the Don river</note>. NEAR THE MOUNTAINS of Troy from which Aeneas brought it to Italy. For Troy is not more than one hundred thirty-eight miles from Constantinople by air. But according to the charts of our times, it is one hundred fifty miles distant. Therefore, while the Empire was in Constantinople, the Roman Eagles were near the mountains from which they had departed following Aeneas to Italy. And he said "mountains" and not the city of Ilion <note>Troy</note> to allude to the nature of eagles, which inhabit mountains.

you place and fix yourself in the first light, which is God; as if to say: I know you can tell me because, by always mirroring yourself in the light of God, you can see all things therein. And I see also that you draw it—that is, pull it—from your eyes; as if to say your eyes receive the light of God and illuminate you; and understand "eyes" as the intellect. But, O worthy soul, I do not know who you are, nor why you hold the rank of the sphere of Mercury, which veils and covers itself from mortals with the rays of the sun. And why it is veiled, we showed above. THIS DESIRE: Dante turned directly to the light <note>original: "lumera"</note>, that is, turned toward the light of that spirit.

**A** most fitting comparison of the light of Justinian to that of the sun. It often happens that as the sun rises in our hemisphere, it excites and draws upward many vapors which shadow and dim it, and in a way take away its splendor so that the human eye can endure it. But once it has eroded and consumed those vapors, no obstacle remains between its rays, and our sight can no longer sustain such great light. So the great joy that appeared in the face of Justinian meant that Dante could no longer look at him. Justinian was the son of the sister of Emperor Justin; he succeeded Justin in the year of the Lord 522. And in the year of the world 5622. A just man, who collected all the ancient Roman laws.

**T**he admirable artifice of the poet, who, knowing the material to be difficult and subtle—and one in which the reader's intellect might grow weary—diverts it in this sixth canto by interposing nearly all of Roman history. And he does so in a way that he does not seem to depart from the proposed subject. He had already <gloss>spoken</gloss> with the Emperor Justinian, although he did not yet know him, and had asked him who he was and what the condition of the spirits in that heaven was. Now Justinian answers him: and before he says how he was Emperor, he describes the translation of the Empire made by Constantine from Rome to Constantinople. "After Constantine turned the Eagle," that is, the Roman Empire whose insignia is the Eagle. AGAINST THE COURSE of heaven: because the heaven runs from East to West, and Constantine, going from Italy to Thrace, went from West to East. Therefore, he went against the course of heaven, which course had previously been followed.

**T**o demonstrate who he was, it was necessary to present both the public and private person. First, therefore, the public one, which was no longer in him then, but was while he lived; and so he said "I was Caesar," that is, Emperor, which dignity ends at death. "And I am Justinian," because death separates the soul from the body, but nonetheless there remains that same soul which is the true man. Justinian was the son of the sister of Emperor Justin and succeeded him. AND BEFORE I WAS INTENT UPON THE WORK. In these times, Theodatus, King of the Goths, was in the Kingdom of Rome; and hearing that Justinian was his enemy, he sent Pope Agapetus to appease him. # CANTO SIX

> I directed myself by his words.

> I now see as clearly as you see
> that every contradiction is both false and true.

It is certain that in every contradiction, one part is true and one is false. Therefore, if I say: "The Arno passes through Florence" and "The Arno does not pass through Florence," this is a contradiction. One is true—that the Arno passes through Florence—and the other is false—that the Arno does not pass through Florence. <note>Justinian uses a principle of logic to explain that in Heaven, truths that we hold by faith on Earth become as self-evident as the basic rules of logic.</note>

I <note>The commentator, Landino</note> have treated this extensively in my work *On Monarchy* <note>original: "monarchia"</note>, in which I strive to prove that by right, we must all obey the Empire in temporal matters. Therefore, he says "so that you see and understand with how much reason"—speaking with irony, meaning with how much injustice—they move against the "sacrosanct sign of the eagle," which is to say, against the holy Empire. **AND THOSE WHO CLAIM IT**: He who claims this sign for himself, meaning he who wishes to usurp some part of the Empire <note>Likely referring to the Ghibellines who used the Eagle for partisan ends</note>. **AND THOSE WHO OPPOSE IT**: And those who do not obey it, but rather act against it—they act against God.

The heresy <note>The Monophysite heresy, which Justinian followed before his conversion</note> of those who believed that Christ was purely a man and not God. Because Pope Agapetus disputed most sharply against him, he finally led him back to the true Catholic faith. A little while later, Agapetus died, and Silverius <note>The text says "Virgilio," likely meaning Pope Vigilius</note> succeeded him. **WHAT HIS FAITH WAS**: It is most true that faith, being so excellent a virtue, does not dwell in Heaven, because as soon as the spirit enters Heaven, it becomes certain of that which it previously held by faith. **EVERY CONTRADICTION IS FALSE AND TRUE**: <note>Landino repeats the logical exercise regarding the Arno river from the first column to clarify the text.</note>

It did not seem credible that such a great work as the composition of the volumes of law <note>The *Corpus Juris Civilis*, the foundation of modern civil law</note> could have been achieved by Justinian without divine help. Nor did he deserve such help while he was either a pagan or a heretic. Thus, he rightly says "it pleased God to inspire me to such labor," meaning to infuse in me the will to undertake such a task. It pleased Him "as soon as I moved my feet with the Church," that is, having become a true Christian and following the Catholic faith. "I gave myself entirely to it," that is, to the work of correcting the laws; having set aside all other cares, I was vacant for this work. And because the Empire cannot be defended without military discipline, "I commended and committed such care" to one who was not only practiced in it, but also had joined to him the "right hand," that is, the favor of God. This seemed to be a sign that God wished for me to retire from active and military cares so that I could, with more leisure, attend to the correction of the laws. **NOW HERE TO THE QUESTION**: The meaning is that "my answer to your first question and inquiry reaches its point here," and it does not continue further, because the "condition" of the things I have said, especially concerning the Eagle, "compels me" to step slightly out of my main purpose and follow with something "added to your request," which is beyond what you asked. In short, the poet wishes to set down here with brevity that history.

Wishing to prove that obedience is unjustly withheld from this sign, he uses this argument: That sign is worthy of obedience which, over many centuries and through many various virtues, has acquired a great empire. But the Eagle has done this. Therefore, it deserves reverence and obedience. That it has done so is proven by histories, which he briefly presents. Having narrated how it came from Troy, carried by Aeneas, he follows by demonstrating the greatest victory that Aeneas had in Italy against Latinus and Turnus, when Pallas was killed. After the destruction of Troy, Aeneas came to Italy and first allied himself with King Latinus, who betrothed his daughter Lavinia to him. This was very troublesome to Amata, the girl's mother, who desired her to be the wife of Turnus, King of the Rutulians. She acted in such a way that Latinus was forced, together with Turnus, to start a war. In this war, Aeneas had the favor of the Tuscans and of Evander of Pallanteum, the city where Rome was later built. This war had various outcomes.

---

In the first battle Aeneas fought after returning from Tuscany, Pallas, the son of Evander, was killed by Turnus. But finally, after Turnus was killed by Aeneas, victory went to the Trojans. The rule <note>term: *lo imperio* (the empire/command)</note> of that place came to Aeneas, who drowned in the Numicus river and was numbered among the gods. He was succeeded by Ascanius, whom he had fathered in Troy by Creusa. Ascanius left the kingdom to his stepmother Lavinia and founded a new city, which he called Alba Longa. "Alba" from the white sow <note>original: "troia alba"</note> and her thirty white piglets <note>original: "bianchi"</note>. And "Longa" <note>Long</note> from the city's form, which stretched out in length along the ridge of the mountain. In this city, fourteen kings reigned: Ascanius, Silvius, Aeneas, Latinus, Alba, Atis, Capys, Capetus, Tiberinus, Agrippa, Romulus, Aventinus, Procas, and Amulius. This last one remained alone in the kingdom after driving out his brother Numitor, who had an only daughter. Amulius made her a Vestal Virgin so that no seed of his brother would remain. But, pregnant by Mars, she gave birth to Romulus and Remus. They drove Amulius from the kingdom and restored their maternal grandfather, Numitor. Afterwards, they founded Rome, for which the empire of a good part of the world was reserved. Rome was built in the year of the world 4454, in the eighth Olympiad. Alba was built by Ascanius in the year of the world 4030 or thereabouts, and was destroyed by Tullus Hostilius, the third king of the Romans, who succeeded Numa Pompilius in the year of the world 4536. Ro." for *Popolo Romano*</note> agreed with the Albans that three men from each army would be chosen, and the people whose three remained victorious would have the other people submit to them. In those times, there were three young brothers born at one birth among the Romans, the Horatii, and similarly three among the Albans, the Curiatii. To these, then, was given the lot of fighting for everyone else. In the course of the battle, two Horatii were killed and the three Curiatii were wounded. The remaining Horatius was deprived of any other help, but was without any wounds. Therefore, he decided to compensate for his situation by separating the three Curiatii. He feigned flight, and the Curiatii followed him, but with unequal speed because they were wounded differently; the most robust was in front, while those with heavier wounds could run less. When Horatius saw them separated by a sufficient interval, he turned back to the first one, and before the others could arrive...

He had a sister already betrothed to one of the slain Curiatii; when she saw among her brother's spoils the bloody cloak of her husband, which she herself had woven for him, she could not contain her tears at her husband's death. For such a murder of a sibling <note>original: "fororicidio"</note>, he was condemned by the king. But he obtained the right to appeal to the people, and by the people, he was acquitted.

**AND YOU KNOW** what he did regarding the wrong to the Sabines. Romulus had already not only built Rome but had made it well-populated through the gathering of many youths. But because all the neighboring peoples disdained marrying such men—as a great part of them had been driven from their own homelands for various crimes—and there were no women in Rome, the king decided to obtain through trickery what he could not obtain through favor. He ordered sacrifices and games with the greatest and most ornate preparation. The neighboring Sabines came to such a celebration with their wives and daughters, coming willingly and without suspicion. But when Romulus saw the whole crowd was focused on the games, he gave the prearranged signal to his peers. With a sudden and unforeseen tumult, they seized so many of the Sabine virgins that each man had his own. 

The Sabines could not endure such an insult and injury. They returned home and, having organized a robust army, they came with such force that they entered Rome. The battle was most atrocious, and many perished on every side. But in the women, there appeared a prudence and boldness of spirit more than feminine, and a piety worthy of eternal memory. For the abducted Sabine women, by common counsel and without fear of death, threw themselves into the middle of the two combatant ranks. With many tears and torn hair, turning now to their fathers and now to their husbands, they cried out: "We, we are the cause of so much evil! Turn all your discord and fury upon us!" This miserable act of the girls was so powerful, and the supreme piety they showed everywhere, that they caused the battle to cease. Having set aside all hatred, they not only became friends but became one city out of two. For the Sabines, leaving their city of Cures, lived in Rome on the condition that Rome would not change its name, but all citizens—both Romans and Sabines—should be called "Quirites" after Cures.

**TO THE SUFFERING** of Lucretia. We spoke of her in the first canto of the first canticle <note>Inferno, Canto IV</note>.

**SEVEN Kings** gave the best foundation to the Roman Empire. Romulus, a very warlike man, made the people intrepid against every danger. Numa Pompilius, the second king, introduced peace and religion. Tullus Hostilius, the third king, a man of great spirit and no less intellect, was almost the first author of every military discipline and order. Ancus Marcius, the fourth king and born of a sister of Numa, encircled the city with walls. Tarquin Priscus was no small ornament to the city. Then Servius Tullius, who first organized the census and the taxes with which the soldiers could have public pay. Tarquin the Proud gave cause for the city to be reduced to liberty. Thus, the Roman people were bold under Romulus, religious under Numa, armed under Hostilius, secure under Ancus, adorned under Priscus, rewarded under Servius, and liberated under the Proud. The kings reigned in Rome for 243 years.

Justinian says: It is not necessary for me to tell you the noble deeds of this standard, because you know what it did—as if to say, how many victories it achieved, carried by the noble Romans.

**AGAINST** Brennus. He was the leader of the Senonian Gauls who, having crossed into Italy, occupied what lies between the Alps and the Po. Afterwards, they came into Tuscany and besieged Chiusi (today almost desolate and under Sienese jurisdiction). But in those times, it was one of the chief cities of Tuscany. Being offended there by the Romans, they turned all their fury against them. They defeated the Romans at the river Allia and took Rome, except for the Capitol, which they besieged for six months. Finally, oppressed by hunger, the Romans agreed to pay a thousand pounds of gold so the Gauls would depart. But Camillus—about whom it would be a long story to tell—having been made dictator though absent and in exile, gathered the remains of the broken army, attacked the Gauls, and killed them all.

He came to Italy against the Romans under the guise of defending the...

...Tarentines. He was the first to bring elephants into Italy. He fought many times against the Romans but with varying fortune, now the victor and now the vanquished—mostly through the work of Curius and Fabricius, who triumphed over him. He wished to make peace with the Romans on fair conditions, but the authority of Appius the Blind was so great that he never allowed the Senate to grant him peace unless he first returned home with his army. The war lasted four years, but without treachery or cruelty. They sought to win no more with arms than with magnanimity. The Romans wished to ransom a great number of prisoners he had taken in battle. Pyrrhus returned them without price, affirming that he had not come to make a trade of men, but to test to whom Fortune wished to give the empire. Nor were the Romans surpassed in this kindness. For when a physician offered the Romans that he would poison Pyrrhus if they wished, they immediately revealed the fraud and its author to him, showing how foreign such deceit was to the Roman people. Thus, Pyrrhus gave great gifts to the Romans, and the Romans gave life to Pyrrhus. He finally left Italy. Not long after, having entered the city of Argos by force, he was killed in the heat of battle by a woman with a roof tile <note>original: "embrice"</note> that she threw onto his head from a window.

**AND AGAINST THE OTHER** princes and allies. That is, against various nations and peoples. I judge it better to be silent about these than to say too little, considering that we could hardly recount in a whole volume the innumerable triumphs which various Roman leaders brought back with illustrious victories from different parts of the world at different times.

This tribune was attempting, with the testimony of Manlius (whom he judged to be an enemy), to take away his fame and his homeland. This...

# CANTO SIXTH

...the tenth was the first in this family named Torquatus: for such a reason there was in the army of the Gauls a man who was always fierce in the first assault, of great body and no small courage, who continually, with low regard for the Romans—deeming them timid and vile—stood ready to fight in hand-to-hand combat with anyone who would accept the battle. Manlius did not suffer such an insult; rather, he went to meet the Gaul, and with strength and skill, he conquered him, killed him, and despoiled him of a necklace which the Latins call a *torques* <note>original: "torques"; a neck ring or collar worn by ancient Gauls</note>; and with that trophy of victory, he adorned himself. For this reason, from that *torque*, he was thereafter named Torquatus. This same man, as merciful as he was toward his father, was equally severe against his son, who, because he had fought very dangerously against his father's command in the Latin War, was called before his tribunal; and in the sight of the army, he commanded a lictor first to beat him with rods, and then with the axe to break his head and kill him.

**AND AS MUCH AS FROM THE CURL.** The fifth was named Cincinnatus: which in our language we might call "the disheveled curl" <note>original: "rabbaruffato cincinno"</note>. And *pyrrho* <note>The text likely means *cirrus* or *cyrrhus*</note> in Latin signifies a twisted hair. And this is sometimes an ornament when, either with iron or another instrument, the hair is composed with great art and made into ringlets and curls. Hence Persius says: *That a hundred curly-haired youths were hardened* <note>original: "Ten cyrrhatorum centum durata fuisse"</note>; and Juvenal: *Why is this curl higher?* <note>original: "Altior hic quare cincinnus"</note>. Other times the hair is twisted on the head when we do not comb it, so it remains tangled. And then the curl and the *cyrrhus* do not provide ornament, but the opposite. And for this reason, Curiatius <note>likely referring to Quinctius Cincinnatus</note>, a man of hard life, because he kept his hair neglected and uncultivated and without a comb, was called Cincinnatus. Hence Petrarch says: *And Cincinnatus with the unkempt mane.* This man was poor and cultivated his own small possessions with his own hands. Created Dictator against the Aequi, who had besieged the consul Minucius with his army, he broke the enemy and freed the consul and triumphed; and on the sixteenth day, he resigned the dictatorship. Of the Fabii and the Decii, it is spoken of elsewhere.

**A**ll these things did this sign until the coming of Christ the Savior. Then, when His incarnation approached—which occurred under the empire of Augustus Caesar—He performed miraculous things with this sign, which we will omit for now as they were narrated in the fourth canto of the first canticle <note>referring to Dante's Inferno</note>. And the author here demonstrates that God gave such favor to Julius Caesar because He willed that at the time the Word became flesh, the whole world should be under one monarch who would rule the world in peace. And this was Augustus, who took up the monarchy already established by Julius—especially because He, with His passion and death, freed the human race from the servitude of the Devil. And therefore, he said that He willed to "bring the world to its serene state." **CAESAR:** Julius. **HE TAKES IT:** He takes this sign by will—by volition. **OF ROME:** Of the Roman people, who for five years, and then another five years, gave him Gaul. Thus he also acquired Germany <note>original: "la magna"</note> and Brittany, today called England. **AND WHAT IT DID.** **FROM VAR:** This is a river that divides Cisalpine Gaul from Transalpine Gaul. **RHINE:** Rises in the Alps where the people called the Lepontii are. After a short course, it forms two lakes: one Venetian <note>Lake Constance</note>, the other Acronian; and then it runs through the Helvetii, Sequani, Treveri, and other peoples; and near the ocean, it divides into several parts and forms several islands. The first to make a bridge over this river was Julius Caesar, with admirable artifice, as he describes in his *Commentaries*. **ISARA:** Is a river of Gaul that flows into the Rhone. **ARAR:** Is a river of Germany <note>modern Saône</note>. It rises in the Vosges mountains. It flows through the Aedui and Sequani so lightly that one can hardly discern which way it goes. It flows into the Rhone. **SEINE:** In Latin *Sequana*, a river of Gaul abundant in fish, separating the Belgae from the Celts. It passes through Paris and creates in that region the island called Lutetia. **RHONE:** A river born in the Alps not far from the sources of the Danube and the Rhine. It took its name from the city of Rhodanus, built by the Rhodians, near which it passes. It enters the Tyrrhenian Sea with three mouths. **WHAT IT DID** after it left Ravenna: and came to the river Rubicon, the boundary of the province committed to him, from which, according to Roman laws, he could not lead an army unless the Senate permitted him. But he had an excuse in the malice of his adversaries, who, by denying him just things, gave him the boldness to undertake an unjust enterprise. Therefore, incited by this, and also by Curio, and by Marcus Antonius and other friends, he crossed in a brief time and came to Rome, which, having been abandoned by the Senate and by Pompey, he easily brought under his power. This was the wicked beginning of his tyranny, which I do not see how it can be praised in any way. **AND LEAPED THE** Rubicon: This is a small river between Rimini and Ravenna; and in those times, it was the boundary of Cisalpine Gaul. **TOWARD SPAIN:** For once matters were settled in Italy, he went into Spain against Petreius and Afranius, legates of Pompey, and broke them and killed them near Ilerda, a city of Aragon; and in forty days, he subjugated all of Spain. When he went there, he said he was going to an army without a leader, and then he would return to a leader without an army—as appeared in Thessaly, where Pompey had many soldiers but of little value. **TOWARD DURAZZO:** The volume would grow too large if I were to relate in order how, as the victor of Spain, Caesar returned to Rome; how from Rome he went to Brindisi and from there sailed to Durazzo, where he was besieged by Pompey; and finally, by force of arms, he made his way through the midst of the enemies. And many of his men were killed by the Pompeians. It was the opinion that on that day Pompey did not know how to win, for he recalled his men from the battle either because he did not hope for victory or because he hoped to be able to conquer them without a battle. Caesar fled into Thessaly; and finally in Pharsalia, a place in Thessaly, with a universal gathering of both armies, a most atrocious battle was fought. And finally, Caesar, with a much smaller army but of veteran and most practiced soldiers, long accustomed under his command, defeated Pompey. Of the Roman citizens who served in the legions, fifteen thousand men perished, and an innumerable multitude of other nations who had come from almost all parts of the world to help Pompey. Never did the Roman people gather such forces, for both sides together numbered three hundred thousand. But of Roman legions, Caesar had eleven and Pompey eighteen. And not without danger he escaped his betrayals: finally he conquered him and occupied Alexandria and Egypt. **SO THAT THE NILE / WARM** Felt the grief: he places the Nile, which flows through Egypt, and calls it "warm" because it comes from the eastern parts. **ANTANDROS:** This shows when Caesar went to Egypt: he crossed the Hellespont and went to Phrygia where Troy is, from where Aeneas brought the eagle into Latium and to the Albans; and from the Albans it came to the Romans. Antandros is an island near Troy. **SIMOIS** is the river which rises in Mount Ida and runs near Troy. It creates a marsh near the Sigean promontory joined to the Xanthus and flows into the sea. **WHERE HECTOR LIES:** <note>original Latin: "Hectore si cuba"</note> where Hector, the son of Priam, is buried, whose tomb Lucan writes that Caesar visited. **THROUGH PTOLEMY:** because by him he was undone. **THENCE IT DESCENDED** lightning-like upon Juba: After the unhappy slaughter of Pharsalus, Cato gathered the remnants of Pompey's army and led them through sandy Libya into Africa; and joined with Scipio and with Juba, king of Mauritania, where Petreius had fled from Spain. Caesar, having already arrived in Sicily from Egypt and hearing of the great preparation, led the army into Africa; and after some battles near Thapsus, he defeated the enemies. After the rout, Juba and Petreius, seeing no remedy after an abundant banquet, killed themselves with their own hands. The same did Cato, who had fled to Utica, not out of fear, but out of greatness of soul, which could not suffer to see the face of the tyrant. Scipio fled by sea toward Spain, but the Caesarians, overtaking him, killed him likewise. After this war, there remained that of Spain, where there were two sons of Pompey with a very strong army. The battle was near the city of Munda. Never was there a fight with greater fury; nor was Caesar ever in greater danger, so much so that he considered killing himself; but finally, dismounting from his horse and putting himself forward on foot with supreme fury, he made the veterans—who were already fleeing—ashamed; and out of shame, they turned back against the enemy and gained the victory. Labienus was killed, and Gnaeus, one of Pompey’s sons. This was the end of the civil war, which had already lasted four years.

After Julius Caesar follows Caesar Augustus: who, to avenge the death of Julius, made war against Brutus and Cassius, as we showed at the end of the first canticle <note>referring to the *Inferno*</note>. Therefore he says **BRUTUS WITH CASSIUS.** "Barks" <note>original: "Latra"</note>, that is, barks as we said of hell: for this greatest sign did this with the next **STANDARD-BEARER** <note>original: "baiulo"</note>; that is, with him who carried it after Caesar, who was Augustus. *Baiulare* in the Latin language signifies to carry: whence a *bailus* is one who carries. Since on another occasion we said the poet placed Brutus and Cassius as traitors, no excuse would be made for the poet because they were not traitors, but liberators of their country, noble men who were content to give their lives to extinguish the tyrant. But let us say that he does not place Brutus there for Brutus himself, but for those who betray their lord and especially the Emperor, whose name the poet wished to honor greatly. **MODENA AND PERUGIA:** At Modena, Augustus, still a youth, was praetor; and with the veteran soldiers of Julius Caesar, by the encouragement of Cicero, he broke Mark Antony, who after the death of Caesar had been declared a rebel by the senate. Afterward, he changed his counsel and, conquered by ambition, preferred unjust tyranny to holy liberty; and with Mark Antony and Marcus Lepidus, they divided the empire among themselves and made their country a slave; and shortly after, in Thessaly, they killed Brutus and Cassius. Afterward, Octavian returned to Italy and went against Lucius Antony, brother of Mark Antony, who had become his enemy; and he besieged him in Perugia, and through hunger he conquered him and sacked Perugia. **CLEOPATRA:** Of her, we spoke in the fifth canto of the first canticle. **FROM THE ASP** <note>original: "dal colubro"</note> from the snake with which, as we narrated in that place, she killed herself so as not to be led alive in triumph by Octavian. **RED SHORE:** to the Red Sea, because after the death of Mark Antony, who killed himself with his own hands, he occupied all of Egypt as far as the Red Sea. **TO JANUS HIS SHRINE.** Janus was a very ancient king in Italy, who from the beginning reigned in great harmony with Camese; and from Janus was named the Janiculum, the mountain that is in Rome across the Tiber near the Vatican. And from Camese that region was named Camesena; and after the death of Camese, he took Saturn as a companion in the kingdom. Because of his prudence, he was painted with two faces, one looking forward and the other backward. Because the prudent man, with the memory of past things, makes a conjecture of the future. Zeno writes that he was the first who instituted temples and sacrifices to the gods in Italy. For which reason he himself deserved divine honors, and that in all sacrifices he should be named at the beginning. And the first month of the year was called January from Janus. His temple, in time of peace, stayed locked: which happened before Octavian twice: the first under Numa, the second king of the Romans, in whose reign there was never war in Rome. The second after the First Punic War. Then the third under the Emperor Octavian. And this was a long-lasting and universal peace. And for this, the poet said that he closed to Janus his **Shrine** <note>original: "delubro"</note>, that is, his temple.

**TO THE END THAT THE SIGN.** The meaning is that this eagle never, neither before nor after, did a greater thing than in the empire of the third Caesar, who was Tiberius: because in his reign was the redemption of the human generation. **HAD DONE BEFORE** for the Romans, for the consuls and dictators, and finally for Julius Caesar and then for Augustus. **AND THEN WAS YET TO DO:** for the emperors who succeeded. **FOR THE LIVING JUSTICE:** that is, the divine majesty which inspires me, Justinian, to say this thing, granted to Tiberius the glory of wreaking vengeance for its wrath—that is, to punish the Jews who, by the death of Christ, had incited God to wrath. Therefore, Tiberius could perform the vengeance of Christ, as afterward Vespasian and Titus did, of which we spoke in the *Purgatorio*. Orosius says that Tiberius wanted the senate to enroll Christ in the number of their gods; and not obtaining it, he turned to every fury. **NOW MARVEL HERE.** He continues by demonstrating what the eagle did in the empire of Titus. And he makes the listener attentive because it seems he speaks obscurely, saying...

<column-break/>

...that Titus took to make vengeance for the vengeance of the ancient sin. Thus Titus made vengeance for the death of Christ, which was the vengeance for the sin of the first father: since His passion and death were for the satisfaction of the guilt committed by Adam and passed down <note>original: "trasfusa"</note> to us. **AND WHEN THE LOMBARD TOOTH BIT.** The Lombards in great number, with wives and children and other barbarian nations, came into Italy under their king Alboin in the year of Christ 567 <note>The text reads .lxvii., likely an error for 567 or 568 AD</note>. These people were called from Pannonia into Italy by Narses. He had been a eunuch of Sophia, wife of the Emperor Justinian; and by his virtue, he rose to such esteem that Justinian sent him with a most powerful army for the defense of Italy, where he performed excellent deeds. But later, being recalled in ignominy to servile duties by Sophia, and Justinian having very ungratefully removed him from the administration of Italy, incited by such injury, he did not cease for three continuous years to urge the Lombards to pass into Italy. In the beginning, they took Cisalpine Gaul, although for many years they were occupied with the siege of Pavia, which they took in the year 570; and from them, this Gaul was named Longobardia, and later by contraction <note>original: "per sincope"</note>, Lombardy. And in the process of time, they occupied all of Italy except Rome. The Lombards reigned in Italy for two hundred and four years. The capital of the kingdom was Pavia. But beyond this place, we have established principalities throughout all Italy where they held captains of their people: especially in Friuli at the entrance of Italy, also at Spoleto in almost the middle of Italy, and the third at Benevento. Finally, Charles, King of the Franks, who for his egregious deeds was named the Great <note>Charlemagne</note>, called into Italy by Pope Hadrian, came with a powerful army and defeated the Lombards. And he took King Desiderius with his wife and children and sent them to France in the year of salvation 774. The father of Charles was Pepin, King of the Franks; and because in his time the Empire in the East was continually failing and the Emperor persecuted Christians, Pope Stephen transferred and took the imperial dignities to Pepin and his successors in the kingdom who were of his lineage. And Boniface, Bishop of Mainz <note>original: "magaza"</note>, the apostolic legate, consecrated and anointed him in such a ceremony. Pepin was succeeded by Charlemagne, a prince most excellent both for military discipline and many virtues, who defeated Hunald <note>original: "Himoldo"</note>, King of Aquitaine, and having driven him out, occupied the kingdom. He waged war against the Saxons with supreme success for thirty-three years; and in the meantime, sometimes going in person and sometimes sending his sons or dukes, he conquered Spanish and English men. And he came into Italy and defeated Desiderius as we said. In Spain, he conquered Pamplona <note>original: "papilonia"</note> and Augusta <note>Zaragoza</note>, a most noble city, because they would not come to the faith of Christ. He returned to Italy and conquered Arechis, Duke of Benevento. And in this year, which was 783, Constantine, son of Leo, held the empire in Constantinople with his mother Irene. And there was found in Constantinople a plate of gold on which were carved letters that said: "Christ shall be born of the Virgin Mary, and I believe in Him. And you, O Sun, under Constantine and Irene shall see me again." But I return to Charles, who for eight years fought in Pannonia against the Huns and destroyed them. And he made the army rich with infinite spoils, which the Huns had gathered from various provinces. He returned once more to Italy and restored to the pontifical seat Pope Leo III, whom the Romans had unjustly driven out. For this reason, he was called Augustus by Leo and was the first to reign in Rome after Augustulus. He restored Florence, which was largely abandoned, and brought back all the noble families scattered through the surrounding lands; he composed some new laws. Finally, he defeated the Saxons and brought them to the Christian faith. He died in the 72nd year of his age, and was succeeded by Louis; he left three sons: Lothair, Charles, and Louis. After long discord, they agreed that Lothair should be Emperor, Charles should have the realm of France, and Louis that of Germany. Emperor Lothair was crowned by Pope Sergius. In his old age, he became a monk and left the empire to his son Louis, the fourth emperor. The fifth was Charles the Second, named the Bald. The sixth was Charles the Fat, who after several wars weakened in mind and body, so that it was necessary for Arnulf, born of one of his brothers, to govern him. And Arnulf became the seventh emperor. He, making war against the Normans, died in the year of salvation 907. And thus the Empire ceased in the lineage of Charlemagne, not without the grief of all Italy that it should be transferred to Germany <note>original: "magna" — referring to Magna Germania</note>. Therefore, neither the Romans nor the Pope ever wished to crown or adorn with the imperial title any German until Otto I. Thus the empire of Pepin began in the year of Christ 750 and ended with Arnulf in the year 907.

Benche Dante fussi guelpho <note>Although Dante was a Guelph...</note> nevertheless after his exile, he inclined his mind to the Imperial party; and for this reason, in all his work, he honors that seat as much as he can and demonstrates that all Christian peoples and nations must obey the Emperor in temporal matters, just as they obey the Pope in spiritual ones. But because he is not moved by passion but by zeal for justice, he reproves the Ghibellines as much as the Guelphs. For since the Emperor, as a monarch, ought to be common to both parties, he shows that neither should the Guelphs oppose their superior, defending themselves with the authority of the blood of France; nor should the Ghibellines use the defense of the Empire as a partisan thing. For these two parties—one with the favor of the French, who have the golden lilies as their arms, the other with the favor of the Empire—have ruined Italy through their divisions and civil wars. And therefore he adds that if the Ghibellines wish to be seditious and partisan, they should not practice such art under the sign of the Eagle, which ought to belong to the whole and not the part. For they follow that sign ill—that is, they do not follow the Eagle rightly—because they separate it from justice; for every time that the Eagle, which should be common to all, makes itself a partisan of the Ghibellines, it separates itself from justice.

This is the response to the second question of the poet: for he had asked Justinian what was the reason that he inhabited the second sphere, which is that of Mercury. He shows therefore here that those are they...

<meta>This page continues the speech of the Emperor Justinian in the second sphere of Heaven, the planet Mercury. Having finished the history of the Roman Empire, Justinian now explains the nature of the souls inhabiting this sphere—those who performed righteous deeds primarily to achieve fame and honor on Earth. He then introduces the soul of Romeo of Villanova, a humble pilgrim whose story mirrors Dante's own experience of service and exile.</meta>

-># PARADISO<-

| | |
| :--- | :--- |
| ...of good spirits who have been active <note>Justinian is describing the inhabitants of Mercury: those who were virtuous in the "active life" of politics and governance.</note> | ...rarely content. Because they know that they have merited less, and by having merited less, they have less beatitude. Therefore, they desire more. But to this, Justinian responds that since the blessed spirit loves justice, he is content with that state because he sees himself receiving as much glory as there was merit. This is the work of justice. And therefore he says, **measuring our rewards** <note>original: "gaggi" — wages or rewards for service</note>, that is, our joys, against our merits is part of our joy: because we see justice within. Since these are equal to merits, they are neither smaller nor larger. **HENCE:** from this measure that balances glory with merit, **living justice sweetens**, that is, increases the affection in us to want what justice itself wants. And it ensures that such affection can never be **twisted** from the true way toward any **wickedness** <note>original: "nequitia" — referring to any unjust or distorted desire</note>. It is as if in a republic, the governors were perfectly just; they would always divide the honors among them according to merit; and he who merited a lower rank would remain content with it, because he desires nothing with more fervor than justice, which would leave him absolutely content. And just as the diversity of voices makes a sweet song, so in our courts, in eternal life, **diverse stalls** <note>original: "diuerſi ſcanni" — seats of office or ranks in heaven</note>, which denote different degrees in the blessed life, **render sweet harmony**. And thus he concludes two things: First, that this diversity does not make any spirit less content for being in a lower degree. Second, that just as sweet harmony results from various voices, so from the various degrees of blessed spirits, ornament and beauty are born for the kingdom of heaven. |

**BADLY he walks:** he goes by a twisted and vicious way, he who considers it a loss to himself when another does good. **Humble person:** unknown or low-born, which is what the Latin signifies. **Pilgrim:** <note>original: "peregrina"</note> a foreigner. **And Then after this work. MOVED him:** they moved the Count with **CROOKED words:** twisted things falsely spoken by the Provençals.

<column-break/>

...equals who have virtuously exercised themselves in the active life. And therefore he says: this star of Mercury is equipped, that is, adorned and furnished. Hence we say "equipping the ships" of good active spirits, that is, of spirits who have exercised the political virtues so that honor and fame follow them. Here there seems to be a doubt: whether one deserves to come to heaven if they exercise virtue to acquire fame, since he is truly good who loves virtue for itself, and not for the honor or fame that follows it. Indeed, he would rather choose to acquire ill-fame living according to virtue than honor living by the opposite. Therefore I respond that Dante, as a poet, put the consequence for the antecedent and said: they have been active, that is, they exercised themselves in the active life to acquire virtue, from which fame and honor are born. **Small star:** which is smaller than the other planets, and rarely seen because it is almost always under the rays of the sun. And of Mercury, we have spoken above.

**AND WHEN the desires mount up there:** that is, when our appetites are aimed at seeking mortal fame and honors, it is necessary and inevitable that the rays of true love—of true charity which seeks God, who is the highest good—mount up with less vivacity. And by this, he admonishes us that in seeking the virtues, we should not base ourselves on worldly glory, but seek that which attains celestial things. **BUT IN the measuring of our rewards:** someone might be persuaded that these spirits were not entirely content, because they know they have merited less.

**After** he demonstrated what kind of spirits were in this sphere, he shows one whom he calls Romeo, whose history is this: Raymond Berenger, Count of Provence, was a man full of humanity and eloquent in rhymed verse, and so liberal that he always had his credits in pledge. And in those times a pilgrim, who from the extreme West was visiting the church of Saint James <note>Santiago de Compostela</note>, arrived at Toulouse. Because in appearance and speech he showed nobility of mind and great prudence, he was invited to the court; and understanding the income and the government of the Count, he promised that if the care were given to him, he would shortly rescue him from usury and, with appropriate liberality, increase his income. But he never wished to reveal his homeland or his name. For which reason he was called **Romeo**, that is, a man who goes on a pilgrimage. Nevertheless, having been entrusted with the care and the government, he did much more than he promised. And finally, Raymond having four daughters without male offspring, by his industry he saw to it that Raymond married them to four Kings. The first to Louis, King of France, who was later Saint Louis. The second to Edward, King of England, an excellent man. The third to Richard his brother, who was later King of the Romans. The fourth to Charles, Duke of Anjou, who was the brother of Saint Louis and later King of Sicily. After so many benefits, envy—that wretched vice common to all courts—prevailed so much that it brought Raymond to suspicion, and he wanted him to give an account of his administration. This moved Romeo to such indignation that he took back his old clothes and his mule, and left.

**TO DEMAND an accounting from this just man:** to demand that this Romeo, who had so justly administered, should give him a count. Which he should not have done. But he assigned him seven and five: that is, twelve...

He then relates the story of Romeo of Villanova, a faithful servant who was falsely accused and chose to return to a life of poverty rather than endure dishonor.</summary>

### CANTO THREE OF THE THIRD CANTICLE BY DANTE.

<image-desc>Decorative initial 'O' containing a portrait of a figure in a landscape, possibly Dante or a saint.</image-desc> **H**osanna, holy God of hosts <note>original: "Osanna sanctus deus sabaoth"</note>,
shining from above with your brightness

bowed me down like a man who slumbers.

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Decorative initial 'Q' with architectural and foliate motifs.</image-desc> This seventh canto <note>The commentator correctly identifies it as the seventh canto here, despite the header.</note> is that in which Beatrice resolves several doubts concerning human redemption. First, how the sin of the first man was punished in the death of Christ. Then, why this way of recovery pleased God more than another. And she adds why human souls are immortal. First, therefore, he shows that Justinian, after his speech, returned to his accustomed song, saying: **HOSANNA.** In Hebrew, this means "save." He says, therefore, "O holy God of hosts" <note>original: "sabaoth"</note>, that is, of the armies and the virtues, "save us." I say: **SHINING FROM ABOVE** <note>original: "super illustrans"</note>, illuminating from above; **HAPPY FIRES** <note>original: "felices ignes"</note>, the happy spirits; **OF THESE KINGDOMS** <note>original: "HORVM Malachoth"</note>, of these realms.
**THUS TURNING TO ITS OWN MELODY** <note>original: "rota," literally wheel or orb</note>, that is, to its circular motion, because just as the heavens assiduously revolve around God, so do the souls of the blessed. Some texts say "note," and then we would say "to his song."
**WAS SEEN BY ME** <note>original: "VISO Mi fu"</note>, that is, it appeared to me. **THAT SUBSTANCE**, that is, that spirit.
**IS DOUBLE-LAYERED** <note>original: "SADDVA"</note>: is duplicated. **AND IT AND THE OTHERS MOVED TO THEIR DANCE** shows that the souls of those spheres turn like the heavens with much circling; and that by such motion they distanced themselves from Dante. And he describes these spirits in the form of sparks which **VEILED THEMSELVES**, that is, they covered themselves from him by sudden distance. And the meaning is that they suddenly moved so far away that he could no longer see them. **I WAS IN DOUBT.** A doubt was born in me which persuaded me that I should say to Beatrice: "tell her," who slaked my thirst <note>original: "mi destasti," interpreted here as quenching thirst</note>, that is, removed my thirst with her **SWEET DROPS**, that is, droplets—namely,

---

fulfilled my desire with the truth. And he intends that he desired Beatrice—that is, Holy Theology—to show him what he desired to know. **BUT THE REVERENCE** that I bear for her—which is no other reverence than having regard not to fail in the honor that is duly owed. **WHICH BOSSES** <note>original: "CHE SINDonna"</note>: which makes itself mistress of all of me, that is, which has more power in me than anything else; **EVEN FOR "BE" AND FOR "ICE"**, that is, even for Beatrice, putting the first and last syllables; **BOWED ME DOWN**, took away my daring to lift my eyes and look at her: **LIKE A MAN WHO SLUMBERS**, that is, who falls asleep, who bows his head and does not raise it. The meaning is that my will was to search for the truth in the Holy Scriptures, but the reverence for those things which say: "Do not seek to know more than it is appropriate to know" <note>original: "Nolite sapere plusquam oportet sapere"</note> restrained me from asking; and the reverence I bore for her was only for Beatrice, that is, for herself, to denote that the love and reverence one bears for sacred letters should not be to acquire honor or treasure, but for the sake of knowing, as has been said.

Beatrice did not leave me thus for long,
and began, beaming upon me with a smile
such as would make a man happy even in the fire:
"According to my infallible judgment,
how a just vengeance was justly
punished, has set you in thought.
But I will quickly release your mind;
and you listen, for my words
will present you with a great doctrine."

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Decorative initial 'H' with foliage.</image-desc> **I**t happened that Beatrice knew his thought, although he did not manifest it. And for this reason, she **DID NOT LEAVE HIM THUS**, that is, she did not suffer him to remain so pensive. But she decided to clear up the doubt for him. And he feigns this because no doubt can come into the human mind that cannot be resolved and declared in the Holy Scriptures. Nor is it without cause that he shows she spoke to him with a **SMILE** which could make even one in the fire happy: because nothing gives greater joy and pleasure to the mind than the knowledge of divine things, which content and satisfy our soul so much that even in every adversity they make us live happily. **ACCORDING TO MY INFALLIBLE JUDGMENT**, according to my opinion which can never be deceived, because this alone is true doctrine. **YOU HAVE SET IN THOUGHT**, that is, you think and go about investigating how a **JUST VENGEANCE WAS PUNISHED JUSTLY**: that is, how the fault of our first parents was justly punished in Christ. And if it was punished justly, how

---

could the Jews be justly punished for that which had been justly done? The doubt does not seem small. For if the death of Christ was just for the sin of the first parents, the vengeance taken upon the Jews was unjust. And if the vengeance taken against the Jews was just, then the death of Christ was unjust.

"For not enduring a curb upon the power
that wills, for his own benefit, that man who was not born,
damning himself, damned all his progeny;
whereby the human species lay sick
down there for many centuries in great errors,
until it pleased the Word of God to descend."

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Decorative initial 'U' with foliage.</image-desc> **W**ishing to resolve the doubt, she first demonstrates the sin of the first parent, Adam, saying: **THE MAN WHO WAS NOT BORN**, that is, Adam, who was not born from a mother's womb, nor was generated from paternal seed, but was formed from the mud of the earth by God. Adam, therefore, **DAMNED HIMSELF** by not enduring a curb. **UPON THE POWER THAT WILLS A CURB**, that is, upon concupiscence which requires a curb. **ALL FOR HIS OWN BENEFIT**, that is, for his own utility.
**HIS PROGENY**, that is, his lineage, namely all those who descended from him. **WHEREBY**: by which thing the human species **LAY SICK. DOWN THERE**: in the world or in sin. **FOR MANY CENTURIES.** He did not wish the Word to become incarnate except at the end and in the fullness of many centuries; there preceded...

<header>PARADISO</header>

<margin>
The law of nature and of the figure. Wherefore Paul says: "The fullness of time has come" <note>original Latin: "Venit plenitudo temporis"</note>. **IN GREAT** error: in great ignorance; and certainly the disease is dangerous in one who does not recognize it. **FOR MANY** centuries: because the Incarnation came after five thousand, nine hundred and ninety-nine years. **UDOVE** <note>A dialectal variant of "where"</note> is an Aretine and Sienese word: it pleased God—who is in every place—to descend. But, being invisible, He willed to descend in a form that was visible. And He ordained it thus, where He joined human nature to Himself: that is, He took such a nature by taking a human body and soul, not through carnal union, but by the act of His eternal love, that is, through the power of the Holy Spirit, which is love. Therefore, He took flesh by the Holy Spirit and united humanity with divinity. Here it seems to me worth noting that it was not fitting for the Father to be sent, because He does not proceed from the Son. Nor was it fitting for the Holy Spirit, so that there would not be two sons in the Trinity: one in divinity and the other in humanity.
</margin>

# The nature that from its Maker
# was distanced, He united to Himself in person
# by the sole act of His eternal love.
# Now direct your sight to what is now discussed:
# this nature, united to its Maker—
# as it was created, it was pure and good;
# but by itself it was even so banished
# from paradise, because it turned away
# from the way of truth and from its life.

Therefore, the person of the Son took flesh, so that the same person would be the Son in both divinity and humanity. Furthermore, it was a fitting thing that, just as God made the world through His Wisdom, He should redeem it through that same Wisdom. And because in man both the soul and the body were corrupted, He took to Himself a human soul and body so that He might redeem both. Nonetheless, as Augustine says in the *Book on Faith*, the eternal Word did not take the person of a man, but the nature of a man. Therefore, we conclude that in Christ there are two natures, divine and human; and three substances: body, soul, and the Word; and only one person, and that person is divine. **NOW** direct: he makes the listener attentive because of the greatness and difficulty of the subject. And he demonstrates that the Passion was necessary for our redemption. And it is here to be considered that, although the human nature in the person of Christ was pure and immaculate, nonetheless, insofar as it was human, it was deprived of beatitude. For His flesh, taken from the blood of Mary, was descended from Adam in terms of corporeal matter, although in Christ it was free from the sin of Adam, just as Adam's flesh was before he sinned. For Christ took nothing from Adam except the matter of the pure blood of the Virgin. But the Holy Spirit gave the human nature its active form. Christ therefore took on corporal passions, such as hunger, thirst, heat, cold, fatigue, and pain. He also took on those of the soul, such as joy, sadness, fear, and the like. Nonetheless, He did not take all corporal passions, for He did not suffer from many diseases; nor all spiritual ones, because there was no ignorance in Him, nor the rebellion of the flesh against the spirit. **UNTO** its Maker: that is, God in the person of the Son, "through whom all things were made" <note>original Latin: "per quem omnia facta sunt"</note>. **WAS GOOD**: that is, as it was created in Adam. **FROM THE WAY** of truth and from its life: that is, from the path of God, of whom it is written: "I am the way, the truth, and the life" <note>original Latin: "Ego sum via veritas et vita"</note>.

# The penalty, therefore, which the cross provided,
# if measured by the nature assumed,
# nothing ever stung so justly;
# and thus nothing was of such great injury,
# looking at the Person who suffered,
# in whom such nature was contracted.
# Therefore from one act diverse things issued:
# for one death pleased both God and the Jews;
# for it the earth trembled and the heavens opened.
# It should no longer seem too difficult to you
# when it is said that a just vengeance
# was afterwards avenged by a just court.

He became able to ascend into heaven. You should not, therefore, marvel having heard from me how a just vengeance was afterwards **AVENGED**: that is, vindicated. **BY A JUST COURT**: that is, by a just judge.

<image-desc>Decorative initial 'E' in blue and red scrollwork.</image-desc>

**E**ra—the doubt of Dante was whether the death of Christ was just, and yet the Jews were punished justly. Therefore, he responds that if we look at the nature that Christ assumed—which was human nature—such a death was just, because human nature had sinned. But if we look at the Person of Christ—who is the Son of God and true God—the Jews could not have committed a more horrific sin, nor one of such great injury. Therefore, from a single act and a single death, diverse things issued: that is, supreme justice insofar as humanity suffered (because it had sinned), and supreme injustice toward the divine Person (who is supreme innocence), in whom such nature—that is, human nature—was contracted. For in the incarnate Word of God, divinity and humanity were united so that the two natures made one subject, and the humanity was that which suffered. But a simply human person was not enough to satisfy the debt of the sin. **FOR BOTH GOD** and the Jews one death was pleasing: but to God for the sake of justice, and to the Jews out of envy. **FOR IT**: for this death. **TREMBLED** the earth: as Matthew says in the Gospel: "The veil of the temple was torn in two parts from the top even to the bottom and the earth moved" <note>original Latin: "Velum templi scissum est in duas partes a summo usque deorsum et terra mota est"</note>. **The heavens opened**: because through the death of Christ, man was reconciled with God and...

# But I see your mind is narrowed
# from thought to thought within a knot,
# from which it awaits to be untied with great desire.
# You say: "I clearly discern what I hear,
# but why God willed for our redemption
# specifically this hidden way..."
# This decree remains buried
# to the eyes of everyone whose intellect
# has not matured in the flame of love.
# Truly, however, because at this target
# one gazes much and discerns little,
# I will tell why such a way was most worthy.
# The Divine Goodness, which from itself spurns...

<image-desc>Decorative initial 'S' in blue and red scrollwork.</image-desc>

**S**eguita—Beatrice continues in her speech and says: "I see that you enter from one doubt into another; for, the first being resolved, you wonder why God chose this way of redeeming rather than another." And I tell you that this decree—that is, this determination of His—remains buried, that is, hidden from those whose intellect is not "adult," that is, grown in the flame of love. Therefore, I will resolve this doubt, considering that "much is gazed upon"—as if to say everyone thinks about it—and "little is discerned," that is, it is not understood by those whose intellect is not mature, meaning nourished and grown in the flame of love, which is charity, without which no one can understand the Holy Scriptures. As we have already said many times. Before Beatrice comes to the clarification of the doubt she proposed, she presupposes seven points disputed and concluded in theology. First: that God created everything moved by His goodness and ardent love, in which there is no "envy" <note>term: "liuore" - spite or envy</note>. And for this reason, He communicated His goodness to His creatures, and He sparkles so much in love that He "unfolds"—that is, He clearly demonstrates—eternal beauties in many creatures; and she says "eternal" because from eternity...

<summary>Beatrice explains the dual nature of Christ to Dante, resolving the paradox of how the Crucifixion could be both a just punishment for humanity's sin and an unjust crime against God. She further addresses why God chose the specific path of the Incarnation for human redemption, noting it can only be understood through the "flame of love."</summary>

<meta>This page continues the theological discourse of Canto VII of the Paradiso. Beatrice is explaining the nature of the human soul, its direct creation by God, the consequences of Original Sin, and why humanity could not redeem itself through its own efforts, necessitating divine intervention.</meta>
