<columns>2</columns>
<header>CANTO SEVEN</header>
<sig>C iii</sig>

every envy burning in itself sparkles
so that it unfolds eternal beauties.
What distills from her without intermediary
has no end thereafter because it does not move
its imprint when she seals.
What rains down from her without intermediary
is entirely free because it is not subject
to the power of new things.
It is more conformed to Him, and therefore pleases Him more,
for the holy ardor radiates through everything,
shining most in what is most like Him and most alive.

<gloss>Conclusion: things that are created without an intermediary are free because they are not subject to and are not under the power and influence of the heavens, which he calls "new things" <note>original: "chose noue"</note>: because they were not created from eternity like God, but are created in time.</gloss>

<gloss>**IT IS MORE** conformed: he posits that eternal and free things are more conformed to God. Therefore, His light shines more in them. Therefore, they please Him more.</gloss>

In all these things the human creature 
has the advantage, and if one is lacking,
it must fall from its nobility.
Only sin is what disenfranchises it
and leaves it dissimilar to the Supreme Good,
because it is little whitened by His light;
And to its dignity it never returns
unless it refills where fault has emptied,
against evil delight with just penalties.

<gloss>**To enfranchise** <note>original: "franchare"</note> means to set free; and **to disenfranchise** <note>original: "difrancare"</note> means to take away freedom, making the creature dissimilar to the Supreme Good—that is, to God, in whose image and likeness it was created. And the reason is: because God "whitens" it little, meaning He illuminates it little with His greatest light, which is His grace. **AND TO ITS dignity** it never returns: Man had fallen from his dignity, which was freedom, through the sin of disobedience. Now he says that man cannot return to his original dignity because sin is nothing other than the deprivation of good. Therefore, if we want to return to freedom, it is necessary to refill the void of the deprivation of good with restoration, where the guilt proceeding from sin has left it empty. Furthermore, because the sin was committed with delight, it was necessary to satisfy such a wrong of delight with the pain of punishment. Therefore, it was necessary to refill that which had been emptied by sin, and to fill it with penalties against the "evil delighting."</gloss>

Your nature, when it sinned entirely
in its seed, was removed from these dignities
as it was from paradise.
Nor could it recover them, if you consider
very subtly, by any path,
without passing through one of these stages:
Either that God alone, by His courtesy,
had dismissed the debt, or that man by himself
had satisfied for his folly.
Fix now your eye within the abyss
of the eternal counsel as much as you can,
fixed strictly upon my speech.
Man, within his own limits, could never
provide satisfaction, for he could not go
as low with humility, obeying thereafter,
as he had intended to go high by disobeying;
and this is the reason why man was...

<column-break/>

...exemplarily they have been in His mind. **WHAT FROM HER**: Here he posits two things: first, that of the things created by divine goodness, some were created by means of secondary causes <note>Natural processes or celestial influences acting as intermediaries</note>, such as all brute animals, human bodies, and every other thing produced from the earth. Others were created immediately and by Himself, without any secondary cause, such as the angels and human souls. The second point is: that things created immediately are eternal. Therefore, he says "what distills and proceeds from her"—that is, from divine goodness—without intermediary, has no end thereafter, meaning it is eternal. He gives the reason, saying: because "its imprint," meaning the impression, does not move—meaning it does not change—when "she seals," meaning when she imprints. And these are the angels and human souls, in which He, like a seal, imprints His image, which is reason and the intellect. For this reason the Psalmist says: "The light of Your countenance, O Lord, is signed upon us" <note>original Latin: "Signatū est super nos lumē uultus tui domine"</note>. And certainly, things created by God without an intermediary degenerate and stray less than those created with one. Therefore, because God is immobile and immutable, the things created by Him immediately are immutable and eternal. **WHAT FROM HER**: This is the fourth [point].

Having laid out the conclusions already stated, which fit well to clarify the doubt, he demonstrates that our soul—created by God immediately—is eternal, free, and splendid: that is, capable of the grace of the Holy Spirit, made in His likeness and image, and consequently pleases Him more. He argues in this form: nothing pleases God if it is not in the perfection in which it was created, and the human soul fell from that perfection through sin. Therefore, it was necessary to return to its perfection in some way so that it might please God. "The human creature has an advantage in all these things," meaning it surpasses other animals and other creatures; "and if one is lacking, it must fall from its nobility," meaning it does not hold the degree of nobility it held before; and it loses its freedom, for through sin it became a slave to the devil. Thus, it has fallen from its nobility. Wherefore he adds: "only sin is what disenfranchises," meaning it takes away its freedom; *franco* means free.

Beatrice adds in this place the minor premise and the conclusion to the major premise placed above; and the meaning is this: if human nature, through the sin of the first parents, became entirely unlike God and displeasing, and was removed from the dignities mentioned above and from the earthly paradise, it was necessary that it return in some way to its perfection to be reconciled. "And if you heed," meaning attend diligently, those dignities could not "recover"—meaning to regain and reacquire—without passing through one of these stages: either that God, through His most liberal mercy, had dismissed and cancelled such sin, or that man by himself had satisfied for such "folly," meaning such sin. The first is Mercy. The second is Justice. "But fix your eyes," meaning look fixedly into the "abyss," meaning the depth of the eternal counsel. As if to say: consider in my speech how ineffable the divine counsel was. **MAN COULD NOT**: he shows that of the two ways mentioned above, one was impossible and the other was not according to justice. It was impossible for man by himself to satisfy "within his limits"—meaning without going beyond the limits of human nature, and not being more than man, as Christ was. And the reason why he could not satisfy as a man is that, having sinned through pride by wanting to equal himself to God—for wanting to know good and evil was an attempt to match God—he could not, by obeying, descend into such a lowliness that was equal to the height of God, to which he had wanted to ascend by disobeying. For the height of God is infinite, but no lowliness can be found that is not finite. If, therefore, man could not satisfy the fault by himself, it was necessary that God be the one who...

<summary>This page explains why human souls are eternal and free (being created directly by God) and details the "disenfranchisement" caused by Original Sin. It establishes the theological necessity for the Incarnation, arguing that man's finite humility could never compensate for the infinite pride of his disobedience.</summary>
<keywords>human nature, Original Sin, divine justice, mercy, immortality of the soul, secondary causes, satisfaction, humility vs pride, Beatrice, Landino commentary</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Beatrice’s explanation in Canto VII of the Paradiso regarding the theology of the Incarnation and the nature of created things. She has just explained why man could not redeem himself and why God chose the path of both Mercy and Justice.</meta>

<header>PARADISO</header>

to be able to satisfy for himself, excluded.
Therefore it was necessary for God, by His own ways,
to restore man to his full life—
I say by one, or by both of them.
But because the deed is much more pleasing
to the doer, the more it represents
the goodness of the heart from which it issued,
The Divine Goodness, which imprints the world,
was content to proceed by all its ways
to raise you up again.
Nor between the final night and the first day
has there been, or will there be, so high 
and so magnificent a process,
either by one way or the other.
For God was more generous in giving Himself,
to make man sufficient to raise himself,
than if He had merely dismissed the debt on His own.
And all other modes were scant
for justice, if the Son of God
had not humbled Himself to become incarnate.
Now, to fulfill every desire well,
I return to clarify a certain place,
so that you may see the thing as I do.
You say: “I see the air, and I see the fire,
the water, and the earth, and all their mixtures
come to corruption, and last but a little while”;
And these things were yet creatures;
so that if what has been said is true,
they ought to be secure from corruption.
The angels, brother, and the pure country 
<note>original: "elpaese sincero" – referring to the heavens or the Empyrean.</note>
where you are, may be said to be created
just as they are in their entire being;
But the elements which you have named,
and those things which are made from them,
are informed by a created virtue.
The matter they have was created;
the informing virtue was created
in these stars that circle around them.
The soul of every brute and of the plants,
drawn from a potential complex,
is pulled by the rays and motion of the holy lights.
But your life is breathed without intermediary
by the Supreme Beneficence, who enamors it
of Himself, so that it desires Him forever after.
And from this you can further argue
your resurrection, if you rethink
how human flesh was made then,
when the first parents were both created.

<column-break/>

satisfied: and man recovered his whole life with one of the two ways, or rather with both: that is, with mercy and with justice. Because if God had created a man so excellent that he could satisfy the debt, it would have been justice alone. And if He had freed us from sin by absolute power, it was mercy alone. But in the Incarnation of the Word <note>The Word refers to Jesus Christ, the second person of the Trinity.</note>, regarding the divinity, there was mercy; regarding the humanity, justice. But because this is the offense: The Divine Goodness which imprints—that is, is ready and imprints the whole world—all of nature was content to proceed by all its ways to raise you men who had fallen into sin. For a deed is so much more pleasing—that is, grateful and accepted—the more it shows the wisdom and goodness of the heart from which it issued.

**H**aving demonstrated the Incarnation, he shows that from the beginning of the world, which was the first day in which God said: "Let there be light and light was made" <note>original Latin: "fiat lux & facta est lux"</note> until the last night, which will be when the world perishes (at least in part, for afterwards the heaven and earth will remain most pure and splendid, and the celestial motions will cease, and the sun, standing still, will give continual light), there was not and will not be a process so high—either by the one or the other, that is, neither by divinity nor by humanity—so high as to humanity being pulled up even to God, or so magnificent as to the liberality of God. For it was greater liberality to give Himself to make man—that is, the humanity that was in Christ—sufficient to be able to raise himself, than it would have been if He had, by His absolute power, forgiven the fault.
**A**ND ALL the other ways were scant: Not only was it a high and magnificent process, but also necessary; because God by Himself could not and should not suffer according to justice, because He had no sin; and pure man was not sufficient, as was said above.

**B**eatrice continues her speech and says: because I affirmed above that our souls are immortal because they were created by God, you might doubt why the elements and the bodies made of them are not immortal, given that the elements were also created by God. To which I respond thus: **THE ANGELS, BROTHER, THE PURE COUNTRY**—she poses the resolution of the doubt by saying that although everything is created by God, nevertheless the angels and the "pure country"—that is, the heavens which are of pure matter <note>referring to the 'quintessence' or ether</note>, in which heavens you are at present—can be said to be created in their entire being, because God created the matter and the form at once, and created them by Himself without the mediation of secondary causes. But the elements and bodies composed of them were created by a "created virtue" <note>The power of the stars and celestial spheres.</note> which God put into the elements when He created their matter from nothing; and thus their form is from God by means of that created virtue. Because their natural form, though it issued into being from the potentiality of matter, and therefore can be said to be made of something, nonetheless the light is said to be the principle before every form and matter. Therefore, it cannot be perpetual nor free, because the form that the elements currently have was not created by God immediately <note>meaning 'without anything in between'</note>, but by means of the created virtue that God put into the first matter in that formlessness in which it was created. Matter was created by God without intermediary, and therefore it is perpetual and free, and subject only to God. The informing virtue was created, which brings into being the elemental things, and this virtue is in the stars that revolve around the elements. **THE SOUL** of every brute: the sensitive soul in brutes and the vegetative soul in plants is not perpetual because it is of a potential complexion of material composition. This is made of the simple formal element purified by the influence of the heavens, and therefore it is temporal and subject to the influence of the heavens; and because it is derived from the influence of the stars through their rays and motion; and therefore he says: "The ray and the motion of the holy lights." But your life: the human soul. It "breathes"—it lives—without intermediary. For as soon as the body is organized, God at once creates our soul without intermediary, and in creating it, He pours it into the body. Therefore, the "highest beneficence"—that is, goodness—creates the soul and enamors it of Himself, because He puts into it an innate desire to pursue the good, which is God Himself.

**S**he poses a corollary conclusion that the reasoning already stated proves that we must rise again with our own flesh. For God made the body of the first man without intermediary, and for this reason it shall be perpetual; and from that He made the first woman. Therefore, it ought to be perpetual; and thus ours, which are from those. Therefore, the death of said bodies must be only for a time; but regarding the resurrection of bodies, we have spoken sufficiently in another place.

->CANTO EIGHT OF THE THIRD CANTICLE BY DANTE.<-

<summary>In this passage from Paradiso Canto VII, Beatrice explains the distinction between things created directly by God (angels, heavens, and the human soul), which are immortal, and the physical elements created through the mediation of the stars, which are subject to decay. She concludes that because the first human bodies were created directly by God, the resurrection of the flesh is a theological necessity.</summary>

# CANTO EIGHT

The world used to believe, to its peril,
that the beautiful Cyprian <note>A name for Venus, referring to her birth or cult on the island of Cyprus.</note> radiated mad love,
revolving in the third epicycle; <note>In ancient astronomy, an epicycle was a small circle on which a planet moved, while that circle itself moved along a larger orbit.</note>
for which reason not only to her did they do honor
with sacrifice and votive cries,
the ancient people in their ancient error;
but they also honored Dione and Cupid,
the former as her mother, the latter as her son,
and they say that he sat in the lap of Dido; <note>Refers to the scene in Virgil's *Aeneid* where Cupid, disguised as Ascanius, inflames Dido with love for Aeneas.</note>
and from her, from whom I take my beginning,
they took the name of the star
which the sun wooes, now at its nape and now at its brow. <note>Refers to Venus appearing sometimes as the Morning Star (at the sun's "brow") and sometimes as the Evening Star (at its "nape").</note>

Having completed what was necessary regarding the second heaven of Mercury, we now come to this eighth canto: it shows that we have reached the third heaven, which is that of Venus, where many spirits are found. But it speaks at length in the first part with Charles Martel, and later with King Robert. In the first verses, it demonstrates the erroneous opinion that the ancients held regarding Venus. Although I will be brief, I believe it is useful to run through these ideas. Among the ancients, there was not just one Venus, but three. The first is the daughter of Heaven and of the Day. This Venus, according to some, fathered Cupid, the god of love, and the Graces with Jupiter (or Bacchus according to others). They give her the *cestus* <note>original: "cexto"</note>, which is a girdle worn at legitimate weddings. The second Venus was generated when Saturn cut off the virile member of his father, Coelus <note>Uranus/Heaven</note>, and threw it into the sea; the vital spark from the waves created foam, and from that Venus was born. Or rather, she was born from the blood of that member and nourished by the foam, from which she is named *Aphrodite* by the Greeks, because *aphros* in Greek signifies foam. Of her alone, the poet Simonides claims Cupid was born. The third was the daughter of Jupiter and Dione; she bore Aeneas to Anchises. These fables partly express natural truths and partly contain histories. But forgive my long work if I set them aside here.

Plato—not as a poet but as a philosopher and excellent investigator of nature's secrets—writes in the *Symposium* <note>original: "symposio"</note> that there are two Venuses and two Loves: one is celestial, the other common and earthly. For our soul, shaking off the contagion of the body, rises toward heaven and suddenly ignites within itself a most ardent desire for divine and incorporeal things; from this is born "celestial love," which despises all earthly things and goes seeking true beauty, which is located only in divine and eternal things. This love is called a "great god" by Phaedrus in Plato's *Symposium*. They say this Venus is the daughter of Heaven and had no mother. She is born from Heaven because she seeks nothing but celestial things, and born without a mother because she does not proceed from corporeal things. But if our soul, forgetting its origin, turns its eye downward and looks only at the earth, it conceives within itself the "earthly Venus," from which libidinous love is born. This love seeks nothing but corporeal pleasures and carnal delights. It does not love the beauty of the soul, which is its own proper substance, but seeks that of the body.

This is expressed in the fable of Narcissus, whom the poets imagine fell in love with his own image seeing it in a fountain. They use Narcissus to represent the soul of an impious and rash man who does not contemplate his own face—that is, he does not consider his own essence and virtue, and the beauty in which he was created by God. Instead, he is intent on looking at the image of that beauty in the water. This is nothing other than following corporeal beauties, which have no substance but are a vain shadow of true beauty. He sees this in the water—that is, in the body, which is fluid and runs like water and never stays still. Thus the body, which he alone loves, continually runs toward death and corruption. Therefore, such a soul is miserable because, as Petrarch says: "Wretched is he who places hope in mortal things," and leaves true beauty to love the shadow. Men are certainly miserable, and more than miserable, because they know nothing of themselves except the body, and firmly believe they are nothing but body. For all these reasons and many others which I omit for brevity, the divine Plato demonstrates that there are two Venuses: the celestial one, by following whom Aeneas became happy in Italy; and the earthly one, by whose allurements Paris was enticed, leading both himself and his homeland to ultimate extermination. 

Such influences, for the most part, proceed from the star of the third heaven called Venus. Our poet having been conducted there by Beatrice, I am required to report something of it astrologically. Venus is a benevolent planet and an inducer of friendships; it is feminine and nocturnal, and in its qualities of heat and moisture, it is very temperate. It is a very salutary star, as Ptolemy demonstrates in the *Book of Harmony*. From its influence proceeds all music—and not only that which is in the consonance of voices, but it also induces the composition of verses and love, which, according to the aspects of different planets, is sometimes modest and chaste, and sometimes lascivious and impudent. It completes its course in three hundred and sixty-eight days, and never wanders from the sun more than forty-six degrees. When it precedes the sun, it appears in the east in the morning before the sun and is called Lucifer, and by the common people, Diana. When it follows the sun, it is seen in the evening in the west and is called Hesperus. Pythagoras was the first among the Greeks to realize that Lucifer and Hesperus were the same star. Its houses in the zodiac are Taurus and Libra. It reigns in Pisces and its power wanes in Virgo. It is a noble star. Venus alone of all the planets moves two degrees out of the zodiac. Its splendor is so great that it casts a shadow. Among the ancients, it had many names: it was called Juno, Isis, and Cybele, who is the mother of the gods. Thus, Dante places in this heaven the spirits who lived in pleasure, joy, and love, though not departing from true honesty; or if they occasionally exceeded the limit, they immediately returned.

**THE WORLD USED** To believe; he means universally, all men. **TO ITS PERIL**: That is, because believing such things is against true religion, and one cannot believe them without the peril of damnation. **CYPRIAN**: Venus, so called from Cyprus, where she was most greatly honored. Thus Horace: *Venus, queen of Cnidus and Paphos, spurn your beloved Cyprus and cross over to the beautiful temple of Glycera, who calls to you with much incense.* <note>original: "Venus regina gnidi paphiq: spne dilectã cipron: & uocãtis thure te multo glycere de corā trãfīer in edẽ."</note> Certainly Cyprus was always a very luxurious island. There was once a custom there that young girls would go to the port and mingle with foreigners to earn their dowries. There was a law that once in her life, every woman should go to the temple of Venus and not leave until she had been with a man. Thus, fools believed that from Venus proceeded no love other than the impudent and lascivious kind. **MAD LOVE**: Foolish love. Love is the desire for a beautiful thing. True beauty consists in divine and immortal things, and to desire this is "prudent love" because it chooses true beauty. Likewise, "mad love" is that born from the flesh and human lust; it desires corporeal beauty libidinously. Thus he rightly said "mad love" so that we might distinguish libidinous from chaste love. **IN THE THIRD EPICYCLE**: In the third heaven where the planet Venus is. A proper <term>epicycle</term> <note>A geometric model used to explain the variations in speed and direction of the moon, sun, and planets.</note> is a small circle which the planet describes with the movement of its body, and the planet moves along the circumference of this. In the upper part, it moves from east to west, and in the lower part, the opposite. In this epicycle, they make their direct, stationary, and retrograde motions. **DIONE**: As we have said, she was the mother of Venus. Hence Virgil: *Behold, the star of Dionean Caesar has appeared.* <note>original: "Ecce dionei procefsit cesaris astrũ."</note> **AND FROM HER**: From this Venus from whom I take the beginning of this chapter, they took the name of the star and called it Venus. The star "wooed by the sun" is sometimes **AT THE NAPE**, meaning behind it (because on a ship the poop or nape is the last part), and sometimes **AT THE BROW**, meaning in front of it, as we demonstrated just above. When it rises before the sun, it brings such splendor that it makes it seem like day before it has arrived. When it is behind the sun, it appears in the evening in the west and performs almost the same office as the moon—that is, giving light to the night.

I did not notice the ascent into it,
but of being within it, she gave me great proof...

They move truly enveloped when they are lit, as often happens. **OR VISIBLE:** when they are in turbid air: and therefore they are not seen. And he says that coming toward us they left the circling first begun among the high Seraphim. He says "high" because they are in the first and highest heaven. This is said because he imagines seeing God elsewhere as a point above everything: and in the middle and around that point, in a lower place, the orders of angels revolve, not with equal speed, as we will show in its proper place. **AND BEHIND THOSE:** he says that behind those spirits who came to him were spirits who sang Hosanna so sweetly: that never since—that is, never afterward—was I without desire—that is, without the craving to hear it again—that is, to hear it anew. Hosanna means "God makes safe." But in the Hebrew language, it denotes a joy that can hardly be expressed in Greek or Latin.

Then one of them drew closer to us
and alone began: "We are all ready
for your pleasure, that you may have joy of us.
We revolve with the celestial Princes <note>The "Principalities" are the angelic order governing the third heaven of Venus.</note>

to whom you once said in the world:

...he put. And by this he admonishes us that we should not attempt anything in the investigation of heavenly things that is not permitted to us by theology. Therefore I offered my eyes to Beatrice—that is, I looked back at her—and she looked at me in a way that in her face I saw she was content. <column-break/>

...it seems difficult that the lights of those souls placed in the body of this third planet could be seen within its own light: therefore he uses two very fitting comparisons. Therefore he says: "I saw in the light of the star of Venus other lamps"—other particular lights which were the blessed spirits placed in that sphere—"as in a flame which rises: a lit spark is seen to ascend," and this can be discerned because the spark has a more vivid color than the flame: and thus also the lights of the spirits: because they were more splendid than the light of Venus, they could be perceived. **AND AS A VOICE IS DISCERNED WITHIN A VOICE:** another very fitting comparison: because we see in music the tenor proceed steadily and the soprano <term>sourano</term> <note>The "superius" or higher voice in polyphonic music.</note> go and return.

**MOVING IN A CIRCLE AND MORE AND LESS SWIFT.** They move with the motion of the star: and at the same time they finished the revolution: but as any [spirit] was closer to the center of the star: so much was its motion slower: and thus by the opposite: and therefore he says "according to the measure of their vision."

**ETERNAL:** that is, according to how each was located in the body of the star. Allegorically, it shows that according to how one had acted more or less virtuously according to such [celestial] influence. **FROM A COLD CLOUD.** Aristotle shows in the *Meteorology* <note>original: "Meteora" — Aristotle's treatise on natural philosophy.</note> that hot and dry vapors rising to the edge of the third region of the air, struck by cold mists, are reflected sideways and agitate the air, and that agitation creates wind. **NO WINDS DESCENDED:** then they are struck by their opposite. **OR VISIBLE:** when they are in turbid air: and therefore they are not seen. And he says that coming toward us they left the circling first begun among the high Seraphim.

Next, one spirit drew closer than the others and offered himself on behalf of the others, saying that they were all ready to please him: so that he might take joy in them. Nor is it against the nature of the heaven of love to find such liberal, such benign, and such loving spirits within it. Because love always wishes to be pleasing to the beloved thing. **CO-PRINCES:** because an order of blessed spirits is assigned to every heaven. Thus, to the first heaven of the Moon are the Angels. To the second of Mercury, the Archangels. To the third of Venus, the Principalities. **TO WHOM YOU SAID DOWN IN THE WORLD.** Because Dante wrote a moral song <note>A reference to "Voi che 'ntendendo il terzo ciel movete," the opening poem of the second treatise of Dante's *Convivio*.</note> in which he treats not of lascivious love but of celestial love: and it truly begins "You Principalities," who "understand"—that is, learning with your intellect—God and His will. For this reason, angels are called "intelligences." **MOVE THE THIRD HEAVEN** making it rotate with your power given by God: and making its effects flow down into the world. And it shall be so full of love and the charity of God and neighbor—which proceeds from the influence of this planet to which the human soul is given when the grace of God breathes so that the will attaches itself to it; and in this application lies our merit. **THAT TO PLEASE YOU A LITTLE QUIET WILL BE NO LESS SWEET** than the circling. And certainly, charity toward one's neighbor causes us sometimes to interrupt our contemplation <term>speculare</term> to please him. **AFTER MY EYES:** He shows that before he asked anything of the spirit, he wanted to know if Beatrice permitted it. And by this he admonishes us that we should not attempt anything in the investigation of heavenly things that is not permitted to us by theology. Therefore I offered my eyes to Beatrice—that is, I looked back at her—and she looked at me in a way that in her face I saw she was content. Wherefore I turned to the light—that is, to that spirit who had so most graciously offered himself—and then I, Dante, asked him...

...asked who that spirit was.
The aforementioned spirit reveals himself and says he is Charles Martel <note>Charles Martel of Anjou (1271–1295), titular King of Hungary and a friend of Dante.</note>, Prince of Taranto, son of King Charles the Lame <note>Charles II of Naples, known as "the Lame" (*lo Zoppo*).</note>, who had seven children. Of the three, he had the title of lordship. Louis, the firstborn: who was [born?] in Sicily and then became a Friar Minor <note>St. Louis of Toulouse, who renounced his claim to the throne.</note>. Charles Martel, Prince of Taranto. Robert, Prince of Durazzo. But just as Friar Louis aforementioned [renounced it], Martel, who was to succeed to the kingdom of Sicily and Puglia and also the county of Provence, succeeded to these provinces as the second to the firstborn. But because he was crowned King of Hungary, Robert occupied all these lordships.

<meta>This page continues the speech of Charles Martel in the Heaven of Venus. He explains his earthly lineage and the territories he would have ruled—Provence, Southern Italy, Hungary, and Sicily—had he not died prematurely in 1295. The text then addresses the "Sicilian Vespers" and moves into a philosophical discussion on how hereditary lines can produce children with different natures (the "sweet seed and bitter fruit" problem), which Charles attributes to the influence of the celestial spheres directed by Divine Providence.</meta>

# CANTO EIGHTH

<meta>pencil note "262" at bottom left corner; catchword "fa" at bottom right</meta>

...like a creature swathed in its own silk.
Much did you love me, and you had good reason;
for had I stayed below, I would have shown you
more of my love than just the leaves.

That left bank washed by the **Rhône**
after it has mingled with the **Sorgue**,
waited for me as its lord in due time;
And that horn of **Ausonia** <note>A poetic name for Italy.</note> which is fortified
by **Bari**, **Gaeta**, and **Crotone**,
where the **Tronto** and the **Verde** <note>The "Verde" is the Liri river; these formed the borders of the Kingdom of Naples.</note> discharge into the sea.
The crown of that land which the **Danube** waters
after it leaves its German banks
already shone upon my brow;
And beautiful **Trinacria** <note>An ancient name for Sicily, meaning "three-cornered."</note>, which grows dark
between **Pachino** and **Peloro**, over the gulf
which receives the greatest strife from the **Eurus** <note>The East wind.</note>,
not because of **Typhoeus** <note>A giant who, in mythology, was buried under Mount Etna; his struggles were said to cause eruptions.</note> but from rising sulfur,
would have still awaited its kings,
born through me from **Charles** and **Rudolf**,
if bad lordship, which always cuts to the heart
of subject peoples, had not
moved **Palermo** to cry out, "Die, die!" <note>original: "mora mora" — the rallying cry of the 1282 Sicilian Vespers uprising against French rule.</note>

And if my brother could have foreseen this,
the greedy poverty of **Catalonia**
he would already flee, so that it might not offend him;
For truly there is a need to provide,
either by him or by another, so that his bark,
already loaded, is not burdened with more weight.
His nature, which descended from a generous one
to a stingy one, would have need of such an administration <note>original: "militia"</note>
that did not care for filling up the strongbox.
"Because I believe that the deep joy
which your speech infuses in me, my lord,
there where every good ends and is finalized,
is seen by you as I see it,
it is more pleasing to me; and this too I hold dear,
that you discern it by gazing into God."
You have made me glad, and so now make me clear—
since by speaking you have moved me to doubt—
how from a sweet seed bitter fruit can come.
This I said to him; and he to me: "If I can
show you a truth regarding what you ask,
you will hold your face where you now hold your back."

The Good <note>Referring to God.</note> which moves and contents all the realm
you are now climbing, makes its providence
become a power within these great bodies <note>The celestial spheres or planets.</note>;
And not only are the natures provided for...

<column-break/>

He shows the countries of which he would have been lord. And these he describes poetically, naming them either by rivers, cities, or mountains. And first, by the **Rhône**, he denotes **Provence**. We have spoken of the Rhône in another place; it divides Provence, the right side of which belongs to the King of France, and the left to the King of **Apulia**. **SORGA**: is a river that rises at the beginning of Provence and flows into the Rhône. **FOR ITS LORD**: because it belongs to the kingdom of Apulia, of which I was to be lord if I had not been King of **Hungary**.

**THAT HORN OF AUSONIA**: that point of **Italy**. **WHICH IS FORTIFIED**: which clothes itself in the cities written below. **OF BARI**: This is by the Adriatic Sea. **CROTONA**: today called **Crotone**, where the sea—which naturally shows a green color—separates **Sicily** from Italy. **THE CROWN SHONE**: the crown of Hungary already shone on my head, through which the **Danube** runs after it leaves **Germany** <note>original: "Magna"</note>. **AND BEAUTIFUL TRINACRIA**: and the kingdom of Sicily belonged to me, which by the ancients was called **Trinacria** because it has three promontories: **Pachino**, **Peloro**, and **Lilibeo**. But Pachino and Peloro correspond to the Gulf of **Venice**, which is struck more by the **Eurus**, the east wind, than by any other wind. **WHICH GROWS DARK**: that is, in which haze and smoke appear. Not because **Typhoeus**, of whom it was spoken above, breathes out flame and smoke as the fables pretend; but because **Mount Etna** is cavernous, whence it generates wind, which by its motion ignites the caverns containing sulfur. Therefore, it sends forth much smoke and sometimes flames. **OF CHARLES**: The first Count of Provence, my grandfather. **OF RUDOLF**: who was the Duke of **Austria** <note>original: "sterlich" — likely a corruption of Österreich.</note>, whose daughter he had as his wife. **IF BAD LORDSHIP**: He says this because Sicily rebelled against **Charles** due to the greed and injustice of the officials he kept there; and gave itself to **Don Peter of Aragon**, as we have discussed at length elsewhere. **ALWAYS CUTS TO THE HEART**: that is, it makes the subject peoples fierce and strong by driving them to desperation.

He relates that King **Robert** <note>Charles Martel's brother, Robert the Wise.</note> should have foreseen how great a vice avarice is in a prince; and how close it is to the ruin of states, he would not attend, neither by himself nor through his officials, to accumulating treasure. The poet responds to the spirit and says: the joy I take in seeing you in this beatitude is more pleasing to me because I believe it is seen and understood by you, no differently than I, who have it within me, see it. And if anyone should ask how the spirit can see his heart, the author adds that he sees it there where every good ends and is finalized: that is, **in God**. Since the blessed souls, looking into God as into a mirror that represents the images of all things, know every truth and cannot be deceived. Thus the text is ordered: **O my lord**: that is, O Charles, whom in life I held as lord; because I believe you see, as I see, the joy that your speech infuses in me, because through that I understand your beatitude in God, there where every good is finalized and ends; therefore, this joy of mine is more pleasing to me than if you did not see it. **AND THIS ALSO I HOLD DEAR**: and similarly I hold this dear which you have spoken, because you discern it—that is, you see and understand it—by gazing into God, in which mirror every thing is seen; it is as if to say: it is pleasing to me to have heard you because what you speak is true.

But because your speech, while most pleasing, has generated a doubt in my mind, clarify this for me just as you have made me glad. The doubt is how from **sweet seed**, that is, from a good father, can be born **bitter seed**, that is, a wicked son; because by condemning you, Charles, as greedy <note>The text here refers to his brother Robert's greed contrasted with their father's nature.</note> and praising the liberality of his ancestors, it seems that what we have said follows. This I said to him. And he, that is Charles, replied to me saying: if I can show you a truth, that is, one truth (because the truth is always one and cannot be more), **YOU WILL HOLD YOUR FACE AS YOU HOLD YOUR BACK**: that is, you will see what you do not now see. For having your back turned to the temple, you do not see it; but if you then turn yourself to where you previously had your back, you see it.

To explain the doubt, he concludes that everything that happens is provided by God for the best, if not for the individual then for the universe. Whence he says: **THE GOOD**: God, who is the supreme good, who **TURNS**: because He is the first cause of the revolution of the heavens; and **CONTENTS**: because He preserves them in their being. **ALL THE REALM THAT YOU ASCEND**: all the heavens that you climb. And also He makes...

He then begins a theological explanation of how Divine Providence and celestial influences account for the differences in character between parents and their children.</summary>

<column-break/>

God, that His providence is a power in these great bodies—that is, that
the power He has placed in the governance of the planets and heavens (which are
great bodies, as we have shown above) follows His
providence. And he adds that in the mind of God there are not only
the natures and things He has provided, but they are there together
with their well-being. The meaning is that God, with divine

they be for the best—if not for the individual, at least for the universe. And
just as this bow shoots, the thing shot falls and arrives
 at the foreseen end: that is, every thing shot falls and arrives
at the end established by God Himself: just as a well-aimed
arrow arrives at its mark and its target. And if it were not that
every ordained thing arrived at its ordained end, the heaven you walk—
that is, all these heavens and stars and planets through which you ascend—
would produce their effects so poorly that they would not be "acts"—that is, well-ordered and perfect—as we see things made with art;
but they would be "ruins" because they would be without order. But this
cannot be if the intellects—that is, the Intelligences <note>The angels or celestial movers.</note> which God has
placed in charge of the motion and government of the stars and heavens—are not "manchi,"
that is, imperfect and defective. And if the First—that is, God Himself, who is the First

DO YOU WISH: after Beatrice had said this to him, she appeared...

The spirit [Charles Martel] adds the following argument: because
man is an animal desiring company, it is better that
he be a "citizen" on earth—that is, that he live in company and not in a solitary
life. And this cannot be unless one lives diversely with diverse
offices. For as Aristotle describes (whom he calls "our master"),
human life has need of diverse arts and offices. It is necessary
that there be counselors in the republic, and soldiers to defend it, and
kings, and jurists, artisans, farmers, priests, and many
others. Therefore, it was necessary that, having to be diverse effects in men,
such effects proceed from various roots—that is, from various causes. Well,
then, the spirit deduced part by part until here where I have
spoken, and then concluded: "BECAUSE ONE IS BORN SOLON." Nature provided most
excellently that various influences of the heavens should produce men
suited to various exercises, because the city has need of various exercises.
And so one influence produced Solon, another Xerxes, and another another.
Absalom <note>original: "Abasalone"—a common transcription error for Solon in early editions.</note> was the son of David, of whom we have spoken above;
and here he places him as a military man suited to defend the republic.
Other texts have not "Absalom" but "Solon," who was an Athenian
and one of the seven sages of Greece, and he found the laws for his republic. And
[Xerxes was the son] of Darius, king of the Persians, who with an incredible multitude of soldiers came
from Asia into Greece. And Mount Athos, which before was land...
Finally, by the industry of Themistocles the Athenian in a naval battle,
[Xerxes] was shown a portent shortly before in his armies: for
a mare (a warlike animal) gave birth to a hare (a vile and fleeing animal). And here Xerxes represents every king. Melchizedek,
who was the first priest and king, went to meet Abraham, who was bringing
back a wide victory from three defeated kings. And he was the first
in whom Christ was prefigured, who was King and Priest, and who in heaven was without a mother,
and on earth without a father. Melchizedek signifies in Hebrew "Just King" and "Peaceful King." Of Daedalus and his beautiful son Icarus...

He concludes whence the diversity of the begotten proceeds. Wherefore he says:
the "circular nature"—that is, the nature of the heavens which influences—and
therefore is a "seal to the mortal wax," because it imprints its influences in us
as a seal imprints its mark in wax. And he rightly said "mortal,"
because elemental bodies are corruptible. Therefore, this celestial power
performs its art well and pours out its influences. But it does not distinguish one
"dwelling" from another. For from Cicero, a most excellent man, was born
Cicero his son, who was most incontinent; and from Africanus <note>Scipio Africanus.</note>, a man most suited
to military discipline, was born Scipio, who was entirely alienated from such
pursuits. And this is because the influence of the fathers came from other stars, and
that of the sons from others. HENCE IT HAPPENS: because in
the same family there are diverse influences, it happens that
[differences exist] in the son toward the father, and in brother toward brother.
As is noted in Esau, who was born of [Isaac] and was from one father and one
mother the brother of Jacob; nonetheless, Esau was warlike and Jacob
peaceful. Quirinus—that is, Romulus—who, being born of a most base father...

<meta>This page concludes the discourse of Charles Martel in the Heaven of Venus (Canto VIII) and begins the ninth Canto, introducing the character of Cunizza da Romano. "But so that you may know I take delight in you,
I wish to wrap you in a corollary. <note>A 'corollary' is an additional deduction or 'bonus' truth following a main argument.</note>
Nature, if it finds fortune 
discordant to itself, like any other seed
outside its proper region, makes a poor showing.
And if the world down there would set its mind
on the foundation that nature lays,
by following it, the people would be good.
But you twist to religion 
one who was born to gird on the sword,
and you make a king of one who is fit for sermons; 
wherefore your track is off the road."

### CANTO NINE OF THE THIRD CANTICLE OF DANTE.

<insert>d</insert> After your Charles, fair Clemence, 
had enlightened me, he recounted the deceits 
that his lineage was to suffer.
But he said: "Be silent, and let the years roll on," 
so that I can say nothing except that just weeping 
shall follow after your losses. 
And already the sight of that holy light
had turned back to the Sun that fills it, 
as to that good which is sufficient for every thing. 
Ah, deceived souls and impious creatures,
who twist your hearts away from such a good,
directing your brows toward vanity!
And behold, another of those splendors 
drew toward me, and its desire to please me
was signified by its brightening from without. 
The eyes of Beatrice, which were fixed 
upon me as before, with dear assent 
assured me of my desire. 
"I pray you, blessed spirit," I said, "put a remedy 
quickly to my wish, and give me proof 
that I can reflect back to you what I think." 
Whereupon the light, which was still new to me, 
from its depth where it was previously singing, 
continued as one who delights in doing good: 
"In that part of the wicked Italian land 
that sits between Rialto 
and the springs of Brenta and Piave, <note>original: "paua"—the Piave river.</note>
there rises a hill, and it does not rise very high, 
from where once descended a firebrand 
that made a great assault on the region. 
From one root were born both I and it; 
I was called Cunizza, and here I shine 
because the light of this star overcame me. 
But I gladly pardon myself 
for the cause of my lot, and it does not grieve me, 
which might perhaps seem hard to your common folk."

<column-break/>

and unknown because through the influence of Mars he was warlike, he was called 
the son of Mars. NOW THAT WHICH LIES BEHIND: <note>original: "HOR QUEL che tera drieto"</note> that is, that which 
you did not see before you, you now see.
<insert>c</insert> As it happens: that every seed makes a poor showing if it is placed in 
soil not suited to its nature: so it happens that 
if a man is put to a task opposite to his nature, he rarely 
becomes excellent. Therefore, if the world—that is, if living men—
considered the foundation that nature lays—that is, that aptitude 
and principle: and almost the 'seed' that the influence of the heavens puts into 
a man—and if that were followed, just as for example <note>original: "verbigratia"</note> if one who has an aptitude 
for arms gave himself to arms; if one who has learning gave himself to learning; 
and the same were done for other inclinations: certainly men 
would be good because each would have more diligence for that 
to which nature invites him. But many times the opposite is done. And one 
becomes a religious <note>A member of a religious order, like a monk or priest.</note> who is inclined toward military service. And sometimes 
one becomes a king who is fit for a sermon—that is, for preaching and for 
scholarly learning. WHEREFORE THE TRACK: that is, the vestige and also the footprint.

<insert>b</insert> Although the poet enters the ninth canto, nonetheless he 
does not yet exit the third sphere <note>The sphere of Venus.</note>. But having finished the speech 
held with Charles, he speaks first to Cunizza da Romano. After, 
with Folquet of Marseille. But in these first verses he turns 
his speech to Clemence, daughter of Charles: and tells her how, after 
he had cleared his doubt, he predicted the deceits that his 
descendants were to suffer. But he commanded him to be silent 
and let the years move—that is, let the time pass, which is nothing 
else than the revolution of the planets; nonetheless, he tells me that the deceits 
done to my people will be justly punished: and having said these words, Charles 
turned back to God, contemplating Him, because God is that supreme 
good that fills every thing: and for every thing He is enough, indeed He exceeds because 
He is infinite, and creatures are finite. Then the author apostrophizes: 
that is, he turns his speech to men and rebukes them because, 
leaving their supreme good, they turn themselves to vain things: wherefore 
he rightly calls them impious creatures. For the creature is pitiless 
when it leaves its creator to whom it owes every thing.

<insert>i</insert> He leads Cunizza da Romano to speak; she was the sister of Ezzelino <note>original: "accerino"—referring to the tyrant Ezzelino III da Romano.</note> 
from Romano; she was of gentle customs: full of humanity and piety: 
kind and grateful. But she was very prone to love, as is shown in the 
last chapter of the Purgatorio. Nor should anyone marvel that the poet places 
among the blessed a woman whose life had this stain. Because he wants to show that 
anyone, by mending themselves, can be saved: especially if the vice that 
oppressed them was mixed with many virtues, as we see in her. 
Describing then the country where she was born—that is, the March of Treviso—
he says: "In that part of the Italian land," that is, of Italy; and he says "wicked" <note>original: "praua"</note> not 
to insult Italy, which was so praised by Virgil. But he says "wicked" because 
in his times it was governed by wicked—that is, captive—men. But I well 
believe that if the poet were alive in our times, he would say the same 
or perhaps worse. Because our lot is hard. Therefore, in that part 
of Italy that sits—that is, is placed—between Rialto (the city of Venice where 
Rialto is) and the springs of Brenta and Piave. These are two rivers 
that run through the Treviso region. A HILL: upon which is a 
land called Romano, from whence came Ezzelino <note>original: "accerino"</note>; otherwise Azzolino, of 
whom we have narrated elsewhere. FROM ONE ROOT we 
were born: we descend from one father. I SHINE: she resplends because the 
light of the star overcame me—that is, because the influence of this 
star [Venus] had great power in me. "But I gladly pardon myself": that is, with joy I 
indulge myself. "The cause of my lot": the meaning is, I am supremely content to 
have had such an influence. Because being blessed, she cannot grieve for the sins 
committed. But she supremely rejoices to have done penance for them. And 
further she rejoices in the grade where she finds herself: and does not desire a 
greater nor higher grade: and to ignorant men it would seem perhaps hard 
to believe that a blessed soul does not grieve for sins committed, and does 
not desire greater beatitude. But this was disputed above.

# PARADISO
<b>b</b>

Of this brilliant and dear jewel
of our heaven which is nearest to me,
great fame remained, and before it dies
this hundredth year shall yet be quintupled. <note>original: "s'incinqua" — meaning the fame will last five centuries (5 x 100 years).</note>
See if a man should make himself excellent,
so that the first life leaves behind another!
And of this the present crowd does not think,
whom the Tagliamento and the Adige shut in, <note>The March of Treviso, bounded by these rivers.</note>
nor, for being scourged, do they yet repent.
But it shall soon be that Padua, at the marsh,
will change the water that bathes Vicenza,
because the people are stubborn against duty.
And where the Sile and the Cagnano join,
one lords it and goes with head held high,
for whom the web is already being spun to catch him. <note>A reference to the assassination of Riccardo da Cammino.</note>

Feltre shall yet weep for the betrayal
of its impious shepherd, which shall be so foul
that for the like of it none ever entered Malta. <note>Malta was a papal prison for disgraced clerics, located near Lake Bolsena.</note>
Too large would be the vat
that would receive the Ferrarese blood,
and weary would be he who weighed it ounce by ounce,
which this courteous priest will give
to show himself a partisan; and such gifts
will be suited to the way of life in that country.
Above are mirrors—you call them Thrones—
from which God the judge shines back at us,
so that these words seem good to us.
Here she was silent, and it seemed to me
that she turned to something else, following the wheel
in which she placed herself as she was before.

The other joy, which was already known to me,
became a thing of splendor in my sight,
like a fine balas ruby on which the sun strikes. <note>original: "balascio" — a pale red spinel or ruby highly valued in the Middle Ages.</note>
Through joy, radiance is acquired up there,
just as laughter is here; but below, the shadow
darkens outwardly as the mind is sad.
"God sees all, and your vision 'in-Hims' itself," <note>original: "s'illuia" — a verb Dante invented from the pronoun 'lui' (him), meaning to enter into or unite with God.</note>
said I, "blessed spirit, so that no
wish of yours can be hidden from you.
Therefore, your voice, which delights heaven..."

<column-break/>

After Cunizza had spoken that which is said above, she turned back and showed Dante the spirit of Folco of Marseille, saying: great fame has remained in the world of this spirit, who is a dear and brilliant jewel—that is, <note>original: "i." (id est)</note> full of light and splendor. And this year, which is the hundredth since he left the world, shall yet **BE QUINTUPLED**—that is, this hundredth year will return five times; meaning there shall be five hundred years before this fame of his dies. **SEE IF MAN SHOULD MAKE**—he says this as if to say: "consider how much a man should strive to make himself excellent before he dies, since the fame of virtue lasts so long after death." **SO THAT THE FIRST LIFE LEAVES ANOTHER**—that is, so that his first life, in which we live, leaves behind after death another life, which is this life of fame.

And thus he proposed that Folco's fame would last five hundred years. Folco was from Marseille, the son of Alfonse, a wealthy merchant. He was a man of beautiful body, honorable and liberal, amorous, and a good poet in the rhyme of his own language. For this reason, he was most welcome to Richard, King of England, to Raymond, Count of Toulouse, and to the Baral of Marseille. He loved Adelasia, the wife of the Baral. And to hide the fact, he pretended to love two of her sisters; for his love for her, he was ungrateful. And finally, he dedicated himself, his wife, and two sons to the Cistercian monastery. Later, he was the Abbot of Le Thoronet, and finally Bishop of Marseille, from where he drove out the heretics. **AND OF THIS [THE CROWD] DOES NOT THINK**—he censures his fellow countrymen, that is, the common crowd of the March of Treviso, which is located between the Tagliamento and the Adige, as these two rivers enclose it. He shows, therefore, that these people do not think of glory or any fame because they do not live in virtue. Nor do they repent, even though God has "beaten" them with many tribulations. And he predicts that the Paduans will be defeated by those of Vicenza, with so many dead that the water running near Vicenza will change color from blood. And this will happen because they are cruel against reason. **AND WHERE THE SILE AND CAGNANO JOIN**—that is, where these two rivers meet. By this, he indicates Treviso, where these rivers mix. **ONE LORDS IT**—This is Messer Riccardo da Cammino, who was lord of Treviso and went with his head held high, which demonstrates his pride. **THE WEB IS BEING SPUN**—the net is being woven—that is, they are arranging the deceits to "catch" or seize him. This man, while playing chess, was treacherously killed by a most wicked scoundrel.

His prophecy continues, and he predicts that Feltre—a city on the borders of the March—will weep for the "betrayal," that is, the wickedness of Alessandro, its bishop. "Betrayal" <note>original: "diffalta"</note> signifies a misdeed or wicked sin, which was such that no equal to it was ever punished in **MALTA**. They say Malta is a river that runs into Lake Bolsena, where there is a tower in which the Pope kept in perpetual prison those clerics who had committed unpardonable sins. This bishop was of the Piacentine nation and was the spiritual and temporal lord in Montefeltro. In those times, gentlemen from the Ferrara family of Fontanesi fled Ferrara for having acted against the state. They believed they would be safe in Feltre, a free land. But Messer Pino della Tosa, a Florentine knight who was lieutenant in Ferrara for King Robert (who, after the death of Azzo III, Marquess of Ferrara, held the lordship for the Church), persuaded the bishop to let him seize them in his land. The bishop consented, against all justice. For this reason, they were taken back to Ferrara, and many were beheaded, among whom were Lancellotto, Chiaruccio, and Antonello. **ABOVE ARE MIRRORS, YOU CALL THEM THRONES**—This is the third order of angels, through whom God carries out all His judgments. Therefore, because the judgments of the great and mighty God shine in them as in mirrors, we see them by looking into them. But of the orders of archangels and the angelic hierarchies, we shall speak in a more appropriate place.

After Cunizza, Folco came forward to meet him, having already become known to him through Cunizza's words. He shone like a **BALAS RUBY** struck by the sun. And this is because the blessed spirits shine more the more joyful they are, because joy there generates splendor, just as among men here it generates laughter. But below—that is, in Hell—it "darkens"—that is, it shows shadows; the shadow—that is, the soul—because of its sadness, being in continuous mourning. **THE OTHER JOY**—that is, Folco, of whom Cunizza had already said: "Of this brilliant and dear jewel." Therefore he knew him as a dear thing, but not by name. **GOD SEES ALL**—The meaning is that because God sees everything, He sees my will and your vision. **"IN-HIMS" ITSELF**—that is, it enters into Him; that is, God himself informs it so that no thing that is in God can be "stolen"—that is, it cannot be hidden from you. Therefore, by this way, you see...

<summary>Cunizza da Romano identifies the soul of Folco of Marseille and prophesies the violent political downfalls of several northern Italian cities due to their corruption. The commentary provides historical context for Folco's life as a troubadour-turned-bishop and explains the specific betrayals in Treviso and Feltre.</summary>

# CANTO NINE
<sig>D</sig>

...always with the song of those pious fires
which of six wings made their cowl. <note>The "pious fires" are the Seraphim, the highest order of angels, characterized by their intense love and six wings.</note>
"Why do you not satisfy my desires?
I would not wait for your question,
if I could 'in-thee' myself as thou 'in-meest' thyself." <note>original: "s'io m'intuassi come tu t'inmii" — Dante creates these verbs from the pronouns "thee" (tu) and "me" (mi) to describe a perfect, telepathic union of minds.</note>

"The greatest valley in which the water spreads,"
his words then began to me,
"out of that sea which garlands the earth,
Between discordant shores, against the sun,
it goes so far that it makes a meridian
where before the horizon was wont to be. <note>This describes the Mediterranean Sea, stretching from west to east from the perspective of the sun.</note>
Of that valley I was a coastal dweller,
between the Ebro and the Macra, which by a short path
divides the Genoese from the Tuscan.
At almost the same sunset and the same sunrise
sits Buggea and the land from which I was,
which with its blood once warmed the port. <note>Buggea (modern Béjaïa in Algeria) and Marseille lie on nearly the same longitude. The "blood" refers to the bloody naval battle at Marseille during Caesar's civil war.</note>
Folco that people called me, to whom
my name was known; and this heaven
is imprinted by me, as I was by it."

<margin>
MACRA: a river that divides Tuscany from Liguria, or the Riviera of Genoa. BUGGEA: That [city]...
</margin>
...from one hemisphere to the other; it extends so far from the west because Marseille is in its bosom. This city was built by Greeks not far from Marseille. This city <note>Buggea</note> is on the African coast opposite Marseille. And these two cities are equally distant from the east and the west, and they share almost the same meridian. WHICH WITH ITS BLOOD ONCE WARMED THE PORT: This refers subtly to the siege of Marseille when Caesar, going to Spain and being unable to bring Marseille to his devotion, left Brutus at the camp, who finally won it not without much blood from both sides. Folco was the son of a merchant <note>Landino's text mentions "son of Theseus," likely a printer's error or confusion with the mythological Demophoon mentioned later; Folquet was actually the son of a Genoese merchant.</note> who, remaining wealthy, followed the courts and great men. He gave himself to writing verses and many courtly graces. He was much accepted by Richard, King of England, and Raymond, Count of Toulouse, and the lord of Marseille. And he was much taken by love for his wife Adalagia <note>This likely refers to Azalais, the wife of his patron, Barral of Marseille, whom he courted in the troubadour tradition.</note>, though he covered it by pretending to love two of her sisters. After her death, he felt such great grief that he dedicated himself, his wife, and two sons to religion. He became the Abbot of Thoronet and finally the Bishop of Marseille <note>Historical records show he was Bishop of Toulouse.</note>, and he expelled many heretics. He was a handsome, pleasant, and generous man.

"For the daughter of Belus did not burn more,
wronging both Sychaeus and Creusa,
than I did, as long as it befitted my hair; <note>Dido, daughter of Belus, who was unfaithful to the memory of her late husband Sychaeus and "wronged" Aeneas's late wife Creusa.</note>
Nor the Rhodopean girl who was deluded
by Demophoon; nor Alcides <note>Hercules</note>
when he had Iole locked in his heart.
Yet here we do not repent, but we smile;
not for the fault, which returns not to the mind,
but for the Value that ordered and provided.
Here we gaze into the art that adorns
with such great effect, and we discern the good
by which the world below turns to that above."

...appeared dry, it put forth leaves again. Whence the Greeks, from this Phyllis, called the leaves of trees *phylla*, which they previously called *petala*. ALCIDES: i.e., Hercules, so named because *alce* in Greek signifies strength. Truly he was named Alcide after Alcaeus, his maternal grandfather. Hercules conquered Eurytus, king of Italy, and was so inflamed by love for Iole, the king’s daughter, that she disposed of him as she wished. She made him dress as a woman and made him spin and perform other feminine tasks. YET HERE one does not repent but smiles: someone might say, "since you remember your lascivious love, you ought still to repent and be saddened by it, and such sadness should diminish your bliss." But he responds: the fault no longer returns to the mind because it is already...

<column-break/>

...my will without me speaking. Therefore, your voice, which delights the heaven with the song of the seraphim—who make the "cowl," i.e., the garment with which they cover themselves with six wings. For John in the Apocalypse described that two wings spread at the head, two at the feet, and two at each hand. Take up the whole speech and say: "Therefore, why does your voice not satisfy my desires, which delights the heaven with the song of those fires—that is, those ardors of charity of the seraphim who make themselves a garment with six wings?" You should do this because if I "in-theed" myself—that is, if I entered into you and knew your will as you "in-me" yourself, that is, enter into me and know my will—I WOULD NOT wait for your question. i.e., I would not wait for you to ask me, but I would anticipate you; and thus you should do also, knowing that which I desire.

Wishing to manifest himself, Folco describes the land where he was born, i.e., Marseille; and shows that it is on the Mediterranean Sea, which exits the Ocean between Spain and Africa through a narrow place called the Strait of Seville <note>Gibraltar</note> near Mount Gibraltar. And he notes the Mediterranean Sea, which having reached Jerusalem, creates the meridian circle as we have shown elsewhere. Therefore, since here it makes a longer progress, the author says that this is the "greatest valley" compared to others through which it enters, and he orders the text thus: "Then, when I had spoken, his words began: 'The greatest valley in which the water spreads that comes out of the ocean sea, which is a garland, i.e., it surrounds the earth, goes so far—that is, it extends so far against the sun, toward the east—between discordant shores because it divides Spain from Africa; and the shores are inhabited by men discordant and enemies among themselves, for on the African side are the barbarians and on the Spanish side the Christians; so that it makes a meridian where before it made the horizon.'" Regarding the meridian circle and the horizon, we have said enough. But here I understand that the sea entering from the west makes the horizon, and where it reaches toward Jerusalem, it makes the meridian. I WAS a coastal dweller BETWEEN THE EBRO: Not the great river of Thrace, but another...

THE DAUGHTER OF BELUS: Her name was Elissa. But for her masculine spirit she was called Dido. She was entirely chaste according to true histories, but Virgil feigns that she fell in love with Aeneas and, because of that love, killed herself when he departed; and the poet follows this. WRONGING Sychaeus and Creusa: because in this union Aeneas did not keep faith with Creusa, his wife, nor Dido to Sychaeus, her husband. But such a fable has been told many times. UNTIL it befitted the hair: i.e., the age in which the hair is not yet gray. For when old age arrives, loving is unbecoming. RHODOPEAN: i.e., Phyllis, Queen of Thrace, whom the poet Ovid calls Rhodopean after Rhodope, a mountain in Thrace. She received Demophoon, son of Theseus, King of Athens, who was returning from the Trojan War and had been shipwrecked. Phyllis fell most ardently in love with him and gave him her kingdom. After some time, Demophoon returned to Athens, promising her he would return shortly. But the mind, which is impatient of any delay, despairing of his return because of too much love, hanged herself near the port on an almond tree. Later, when Demophoon returned, the almond tree which...

The commentary by Landino explains the complex astronomical geography of the Mediterranean and recounts the tragic classical myths of Dido, Phyllis, and Hercules to illustrate the nature of Folco's former passions.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Folco of Marseille’s discourse in the Heaven of Venus. He has just finished describing his earthly origins and his transformation through divine love. He now turns to identify the most radiant soul in this sphere, Rahab, before delivering a stinging rebuke of the contemporary Church’s corruption.</meta>

# PARADISO

<note>original: "purgata & extincta"</note> purged and extinguished: wherefore there is no need to feel sadness. Therefore, one does not repent for the fault: but rather one rejoices in the Power that ordained and provided by God in this star. Here we gaze upon the art that adorns such a great effect <gloss>that is, we spirits, contemplating the heavens</gloss> we see the art <gloss>that is, the power of nature placed there by God with such great effect</gloss>: because from such natural power proceed most wonderful effects: and the good is discerned, that is, in those effects produced by the heavens we recognize God through them: because through that which is below, that is, these effects produced down in the elements and in men, it returns to the world above <gloss>that is, to the First Cause.</gloss> **WHICH** returns from below <gloss>that is, the inferior world</gloss> which by its nature is mortal. **RETURNS** <gloss>that is, becomes like that which is above, that is, immortal:</gloss> just as the superior world through the influence of Venus: which is the cause of generation. Whereby the human species through succession becomes immortal.

---

But so that you may carry away all your desires full,
which have been born within this sphere,
it is necessary for me to proceed yet further.
You wish to know who is within this light,
who here beside me sparkles so,
like a ray of sun in pure water.
Now know that within there, at peace, is
Rahab; and she is joined to our order,
and the highest rank is sealed by her.
By this heaven, where the shadow comes to a point
which your world makes, she was taken up 
before any other soul of Christ’s triumph.
It was well-suited to leave her as a palm
in some heaven of the high victory
which was acquired with one and the other palm. <note>The "two palms" refer to the two hands of Christ nailed to the Cross.</note>
Because she favored the first glory
of Joshua upon the Holy Land,
which little touches the memory of the Pope.
Your city, which was planted by him 
who first turned his back upon his Maker,
and whose envy is so great and widespread, 
Produces and spreads the accursed flower
that has led the sheep and the lambs astray,
for it has made a wolf of the shepherd.
For this, the Gospels and the great Doctors
are deserted, and only the Decretals <note>The Decretals are books of Church law, studied here for profit rather than spiritual guidance.</note>
are studied, as appears by their margins.
To this the Pope and Cardinals attend;
their thoughts go not to Nazareth,
there where Gabriel opened his wings.
But the Vatican and the other chosen parts
of Rome, which have served as a cemetery
to the soldiery that followed Peter,
shall soon be free of this adultery.

<column-break/>

**P**roceeding in his speech, Folco shows that the most splendid spirit in that star was Rahab. She was the first among the Gentile people to believe in the religion of the Old Testament: and in the Book of Joshua <note>original: "Iesu naue"</note> it is written that as he entered the Promised Land, he fought against Jericho: because they had not wanted to receive him: and in order to better and more quickly capture the city, he sent three spies to observe the site from behind and the movements of the men. These men after some days were discovered: and being hunted by the people who wanted to seize them, they took refuge in the house of Rahab, a spy much inflamed by the fires of Venus <note>Rahab was a harlot in the biblical account, which places her in the sphere of Venus, the heaven of lovers.</note>: she, moved by love for God and her neighbor, hid them, and since her house was joined to the city walls, she lowered them down and saved them. And she herself was saved because she made an agreement with them that when Joshua sacked the land, she would place a scarlet cloth in her windows, and seeing it, her house would be spared. And because [Dante] wants there to be distinct ranks in every order of the blessed according to whether their merits are greater or lesser: he feigns that she should sparkle <gloss>that is, scintillate</gloss> and shine more than the others because she had more merit.

**S**he follows the history of Rahab and says that from the triumph that Christ won over the demon when he despoiled Limbo: she was taken up before any other soul to this heaven of Venus: in which heaven the shadow that your world makes comes to a point: that is, the earth where you men live. And he says this because the cone <gloss>that is, the point of the earth's shadow</gloss> reaches as far as the heaven of Venus. **IT WAS WELL-SUITED** it was very appropriate, considering the merits of this spy, that God should leave her in this heaven as a palm, that is, as a sign of the high victory which Christ acquired against the demon with one palm and the other <gloss>that is, with both hands, which were fixed upon the cross.</gloss> And the reason why this is appropriate is because she, as we have said, favored Joshua by believing his commands and saving [the spies] in his first glory <gloss>that is, in the acquisition of Jericho</gloss>: which was the first city that Joshua took after crossing the River Jordan. The memory of which Holy Land, where Jerusalem is, little touches the Pope: because he does not care that the Holy Land is in the hands of the Saracens. **YOUR CITY.** He proceeds to revile the prelates of the Church, who, moved by avarice, leave the care of recovering the Holy Land and give themselves to <term>Simony</term> <note>The buying or selling of ecclesiastical privileges or offices.</note> to acquire money. And here he blames Florence, which has produced the florins: and calls it the plant of Lucifer: and thus says "your city," O Dante, which is the plant of him who was the first to turn his back on God <gloss>that is, who disobeyed Him</gloss> and of whom all envy comes. Inasmuch as he, out of envy, turned to make himself equal to God: and out of envy for our well-being, led the first man to sin. It "produces" because it coins it, and "spreads" because it spends it—the accursed flower: that is, the <term>Florin</term> <note>The gold coin of Florence, which featured a lily (the flower) on one side.</note> which has the lily on one side and Saint John the Baptist on the other. And in truth, the Florentine merchants have always kept the court of Rome abundant with florins. Wherefore avarice is ignited in the prelates. And the sheep and the lambs <gloss>that is, the great and the small</gloss> have been led away from the true path: because it has made a wolf of the shepherd. For this avarice has caused the Pope, who ought to be a true shep-

---

herd, to become a predatory wolf. And for this reason they have abandoned the study of sacred letters, which are the Gospels and the great Doctors who interpret them: and they only study the Decretals and canon laws to be able to see to litigants and earn money, so that it appears on their hems <gloss>that is, on their robes</gloss>: the superfluity and pomp of which he reviles more extensively in another place. "Hem" <note>original: "viuagno"</note> is properly the edge of the cloth. But here he takes the part for the whole. **TO THIS**: to this avarice and accumulating through simony the Pope attends: and he says this especially for Boniface [VIII], of whom he made mention in the *Inferno*: their thoughts do not go to Nazareth, that is, to the things of God: and he names this city because here the Mother of the Lord was announced: and therefore he adds: **THERE WHERE** Gabriel opened his wings <gloss>that is, flew to announce to the Virgin, who alone among women remained a virgin after childbirth.</gloss> **BUT THE VATICAN**. He predicts that Boniface will soon suffer the penalty for his sins and will be dead. Wherefore the Vatican and the other places of Rome that are sacred for having been the cemetery of martyrs: who, soldiering for the faith and following Peter, the first Vicar of Christ, were killed: shall be free from the adulterer through the death of Boniface, whom he calls an adulterer: because the true spouse of the Church and the true Pope was Celestine [V]. Or truly "adulterer" because, leaving the true spouse, that is, the Church, he gives himself to simony.

<summary>Folco of Marseille identifies Rahab as the most luminous soul in the heaven of Venus and uses her biblical history to launch a fierce condemnation of the corruption of the Papacy, specifically targeting Pope Boniface VIII and the greed of Florence.</summary>
