<meta>This page marks the transition from the Heaven of Venus (the third planet) to the Heaven of the Sun (the fourth planet). The previous page concluded the discourse of Folco of Marseille regarding Rahab and the corruption of the Church. Here, Dante begins Canto X, shifting focus to the divine order of the cosmos and the theology of the Trinity.</meta>

<page-type>text</page-type>
<columns>2</columns>
<header>CANTO X</header>

# TENTH CANTO OF THE THIRD CANTICLE BY DANTE

Looking upon His Son with the Love
which the one and the other eternally breathe forth,
the first and ineffable Value,
all that revolves through the mind and the eye
He created with such order that he who gazes upon it
cannot be without a taste of Him.
Lift then, reader, your sight with me
to the high wheels, toward that part
where the one motion and the other strike each other;
And there begin to gaze with longing at the art
of that Master who within Himself so loves it
that His eye never departs from it.
See how from there branches off
the oblique circle that carries the planets,
to satisfy the world that calls to them.
And if their path were not twisted,
much virtue in the heavens would be in vain,
and nearly every power down here would be dead;
And if its departure were more or less far
from the equator, much would be lacking
in the worldly order, both above and below.
Now stay, reader, upon your bench,
thinking back on what is being sampled,
if you wish to be joyful long before you are weary.
I have set it before you; now feed yourself,
for that matter of which I have been made the scribe
twists all my care back to itself.

<column-break/>

The author finds himself having already ascended from the third planet to the fourth; and in this tenth chapter he describes the order of the heavens and their motion. Afterward, he narrates who is within and the excellence of the souls who are in that sphere: and he introduces a modern soul <note>St. Thomas Aquinas</note> to speak. Having ascended, therefore, not without wonder considering the uniform motion of the heavens and the creative motion of the planets, he begins to demonstrate that the divine essence, distinct in three persons, created the universe with admirable order and says: The first value, that is, the Father—to whom is attributed the power which is ineffable <gloss>original: "idest," that is, unspeakable</gloss>—looking, that is, understanding, into His Son—to whom is attributed wisdom, because the Son is the wisdom of the Father—with Love: that is, with the Holy Spirit. **WHICH** <gloss>that is, which love</gloss> the one and the other <gloss>that is, the Father and the Son</gloss> eternally breathe forth, because the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and from the Son. Therefore, the Father with His power, and with the wisdom of the Son, and with the love of the Holy Spirit, made all that revolves; and it is considered and understood by the mind as invisible things are, or by the eye as visible things are, with such order that he who gazes upon this cannot be without a taste of Him <gloss>that is, without knowledge of God</gloss>. But so as not to err in the things said above, we must hold for certain that God is one and alone in essence. But this one essence which is one God is distinct in the three aforementioned persons. He concludes, therefore, that the universe, both visible and invisible, is established with such order that no smallest particle of it can decline or depart from such order. Nor could there be such order if it did not proceed from a prince and mover who composed and linked together so many diverse and contrary things. Nor can anyone have knowledge of these things without tasting what God is. **LIFT THEN**: he invites the reader to consider the motions of the heavens, especially in that part where one motion strikes the other. It is known through astronomy that the motion of the firmament proceeds from East to West. The planets make a motion contrary to this from East to West <note>The text likely means West to East for the planets, though early astronomical descriptions sometimes vary in phrasing directionality</note> always under the zodiac which divides the equinoctial circle and is similarly divided by it, and it induces equal parts: and one rises to the North, the other declines to the South: as we demonstrated at length in the second canticle <note>Purgatorio</note>. **ONE MOTION TO THE OTHER**: because they are contrary. **TO GAZE WITH LONGING** <gloss>that is, to look back with pleasure and delight</gloss>. **IN THE ART** <gloss>that is, in the admirable mastery that is the nature of things artfully established by God</gloss>. Wherefore Petrarch says: "That one whose infinite providence and art showed in his wonderful mastery, and created this and the other hemisphere, and Jove more gentle than Mars."

See therefore how from there: that is, from the equator, it branches off, that is, it departs like a branch from a tree. Indeed, it twists from the first part of Aries, ascending above our northern hemisphere, and goes through Aries, Taurus, and Gemini until the summer tropic which is between the end of Gemini and the beginning of Cancer: and then follows Cancer, Leo, and Virgo until the first point of Libra: and these six signs are northern. And from Libra through Scorpio and Sagittarius, it arrives at Capricorn: in whose beginning is the winter tropic. And from there through Aquarius and through Pisces, it returns to Aries: and these six are southern <gloss>meridional</gloss> signs. **TO SATISFY THE WORLD THAT CALLS TO THEM** <gloss>that is, to preserve this inferior world, which is governed by the oblique motion of the planets</gloss>. **AND IF THE PATH WERE NOT TWISTED**: if the zodiac, which is the path of the planets, were not twisted and oblique, much virtue in the heavens <gloss>that is, much formative power that the heaven has, which flows into the planets and the planets into the elements and into elementary things</gloss> would be in vain because it would not influence the inferior bodies as it does: because there would be nothing to dispose it to operate. For the planets would only dispose the things placed directly beneath them, and only a small part would be subjected if they did not exit the equatorial circle. And nearly every power, that is, every virtue that is apt to receive the influences that create life—whether vegetative, sensitive, or motive—would be without this life. And similarly, the elements apt to receive generation and corruption <note>The Aristotelian cycle of birth and death</note>, which is life in them through that motion, would not receive it. It was therefore necessary that the zodiac distance itself from the equator and the meridian circle, which is straight and not oblique, by twenty-four degrees <note>The tilt of the earth's axis is actually approximately 23.5 degrees</note> in each hemisphere, as we see in our northern summer tropic, which at the beginning of Cancer is twenty-four degrees distant from the beginning of Aries, which is on the equator in the East. And similarly, from the beginning of Libra, which is on the equator in the West, to the beginning of Capricorn, which is the winter tropic, there are twenty-four degrees. And as Aristotle says in the book *On Generation and Corruption*, if the sun and the other planets did not move further from and closer to us, there would be no generation and corruption: because from this is fixed the distinction of the seasons, of which some are apt for generation and some for corruption. And in one, the seed is sown, and in another, the grass grows, and in another, it ripens. But if this departure from the meridian circle were more or less, it would be quite lacking in the order that God placed in the world, both up in the heavens and down in the elements: because they would not make the proper distinction of the seasons as they do. **NOW IT REMAINS FOR YOU, READER**: as if to say, "I have sampled and briefly touched upon something of the celestial motions insofar as it pertained to my purpose." But you, reader, remaining at your bench—that is, in your study—will follow this doctrine until the end: which, although it is difficult and very laborious, nevertheless gives such contentment and pleasure to the soul that the labor is endured. And first, man is joyful to have perfect knowledge.

<sig>D ii</sig>

<vocab>Dante Alighieri, Paradiso, Canto X, Cristoforo Landino, astronomy, zodiac, equator, Aristotle, Trinity, Petrarch, sun, planets, generation & corruption</vocab>

<summary>This page introduces Canto X of the Paradiso, focusing on the divine creation of the universe through the Trinity and the essential astronomical alignment of the zodiac. Cristoforo Landino explains how the tilt of the planets' path (the ecliptic) is necessary for the change of seasons and the existence of life on Earth.</summary>

--- Page 538 ---
<meta>This page continues the opening of Canto X of the Paradiso. Dante and Beatrice have just ascended from the Sphere of Venus to the Sphere of the Sun, the Fourth Heaven, where the souls of the wise reside. The commentary by Cristoforo Landino provides an extensive scientific and mythological explanation of the Sun's nature and its role in the cosmos.</meta>

<page-type>text</page-type>
<columns>2</columns>
<header>->PARADISO<-</header>

The greatest minister of nature,
who imprints the world with the power of heaven
and measures time for us with his light,
being joined with that part mentioned above,
was revolving through the spirals
in which he appears earlier every hour.
And I was with him; but of the ascent
I was not aware, except as a man is aware
of his first thought even before it arrives.
Oh Beatrice, she who is seen
to pass from good to better so suddenly
that her action does not extend through time!
How shining in itself must that have been
which was inside the sun where I entered,
apparent not by color but by light.

<column-break/>

...so that you do not grow weary in study. I have set the matter before you, and you, by following, will feed yourself: for the food of the soul is understanding. And I will go no further: for this is not my purpose.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'D' with floral and foliate motifs.</image-desc>He demonstrates that he had already ascended to the fourth heaven of the sun without being aware of it, and he calls the sun the "greatest minister." Truly, it is the greatest in body because it is larger than all other celestial bodies; for Earth being one million, three hundred thirty-three thousand, six hundred miles, <note>These measurements reflect medieval astronomical calculations rather than modern values.</note> the sun is one hundred seventy-six times as large as the Earth. And just as you see it is greater in body, so understand that it is even greater in power: for it is the cause of the balancing of individuals and natures, and of the composition of the individual elements through the participation of the other planets. The sun, as we see, is placed in the fourth heaven, although the Egyptians placed it in the second. <note>Refers to varying ancient models of the geocentric cosmos.</note> This body is called by <term>Cicero</term> the "leader of the other stars" because it precedes all other lights by the majesty of its light. Furthermore, he calls it "prince" for its excellence; he calls it "moderator" and "temperer" of the other planets, because it governs the course, progress, and regress of all other planets: for there is a certain space which, once the planet has reached it toward the sun, it must distance itself, and likewise, having distanced itself to another determined space, it then returns. It is also called by <term>physicians</term> the "mind of the world" and the "heart of heaven": because heat, cold, temperance, and every other thing generated in the air come from the sun, just as in a living creature every motion comes from the heart. It makes its course in three hundred sixty-five days and a quarter. For this reason, every four years a day is intercalated, that is, placed in between, as we said elsewhere when demonstrating the <term>leap year</term> <note>original: "bisexto"</note>; and such a year has three hundred sixty-six days. Furthermore, there remains a hundredth part of a day, but of this we spoke in that verse: "But before January is completely un-wintered." This planet completes the year when it finishes the whole <term>zodiac</term>; it completes the month in one sign of the zodiac; it completes the day in the space of twenty-four hours. It makes the day when it is in our hemisphere above the earth. It makes the night when it is beneath the earth. When it comes to the east, it makes morning; when at midday, it makes noon. When it declines to the west, it makes evening. When it enters <term>Aries</term>, which is the first equinox, it makes spring. When it reaches <term>Cancer</term>, it makes summer. When <term>Libra</term>, autumn. When <term>Capricorn</term>, winter. Therefore, because of these four seasons of the year, the poets imagine it in a chariot pulled by four horses. The names of the horses according to <term>Ovid</term> are: <note>original: "pyroo: eoo: ethon: phlegon"</note> Pyrous, Eous, Aethon, and Phlegon. **Pyrous** is named from *pyr*, which signifies "fire." **Eous** from *eos*, which signifies "dawn." **Aethon** and **Phlegon** from *ethin* and *phlegin*, both of which mean "to burn." Thus they have their names from the heat of the sun. But **Hyginus** and many others name the first horse **Erythraeus**, meaning "red," <note>original: "erithreo .i. rosso"</note> from the red color the sun has in the morning. The second is **Acteon**, because toward the third hour it extends its equal rays, which the Greeks call *actin*. <note>original: "actin"</note> The third is **Lampros**, meaning "splendid," <note>original: "lampros cioe splendido"</note> because it shines greatly at midday. The fourth is **Philogeos**, meaning "lover of the earth," <note>original: "philogeo .i. amatore di terra"</note> because toward the evening it sinks to the earth. It is called **Sol** (Sun) because it is the only one (*solo*) that shines: and with its light, it illustrates things superior and inferior; and every star has light from it. It is a fortunate planet, masculine, diurnal, hot, and dry. It gives life to all things. Whence <term>Aristotle</term> writes that "the sun and man generate man." <note>A common medieval Aristotelian axiom regarding the sun's influence on biological life.</note> and in the *Book of Elements* he affirms that it has its own light and the other planets receive it from it. It is greater than all the other planets in quantity, dignity, and power. And with its ordered motion and without any confusion, it orders and gives perfection to all things. The sun is the eye of the world, the joy of the day, the beauty of heaven, the measure of times, the virtue and vigor of all things born, lord of the planets, perfection of the stars, and king of nature. <term>Plato</term> writes in the *Timaeus* that God made the sun so that with its splendor it might illuminate the heaven and all inferior things. It is most simple and not composed of contrary parts; and from such simplicity it follows that it is most light. For gravity is born from the connection of material parts, and from lightness is born agility and velocity of motion; and from this follows that it is very active. Thus it is productive and generative. It opens the vapors of the earth and excites the virtue that is in the roots; and it renews all plants and nourishes them by dissolving the moisture in the earth and converting it into nourishment. It heals and preserves. For the elements, because of their contrarieties, would destroy one another if they were not reconciled by the influence of the celestial virtue. In the sun is the life-giving virtue; therefore nothing lives where the virtue of the sun does not penetrate. The sun influences in man the nature of knowing and imagining. This fact moved the poet to lead us into the body of this planet where men are excellent in doctrine. **MINISTER**: of nature—whether we mean "naturing nature" <note>original: "natura naturante"</note>, that is God, whom it obeys, or "natured nature" <note>original: "natura naturata"</note> because it causes its effects within that. **OF THE POWER OF HEAVEN**: of the formative virtue that the heaven infuses. **IMPRINTS**: <note>original: "Imprempta"</note> that is, it imprints and seals upon the world the things of the world because it transfers the virtue of heaven into them and disposes them to receive it. **AND WITH** its light it measures time: because its course creates morning, noon, evening, night; it makes months, years; it makes spring, summer, autumn, and winter. Whence **Petrarch**, speaking of the sun, wrote: "When the planet that distinguishes the hours..." We shall say, then, the minister of heaven joined with that part of the zodiac that is remembered—that is, of which I made mention at the beginning of the book, namely Aries—was revolving. **THROUGH THE SPIRALS**: through its circulations, because every twenty-four hours it circles the whole heaven. The Latins call a "circle" that which returns into itself like a ring; and they call a "spiral" <note>original: "spira"</note> that which, although it goes around, does not return to the same point, like we see many loops in a rope. Thus, because the sun moves one degree every day and never returns to that same point, they create spirals and not circles. **IN_WHICH**: in which Aries. **EVERY HOUR** he appears earlier: because, it being the equinox, the nighttime hours are equal to the daytime hours. And he adds that he did not perceive having ascended to the heaven of the sun otherwise than a man perceives his first thought before it arrives; before it comes, of which one never perceives nor sees that it must come, because it came suddenly, inspired by heaven or by God, or persuaded by the devil.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'A' with scrollwork and linear patterns.</image-desc>The poet adds that in the sun he saw Beatrice more shining than the sun. And likewise, the other spirits who are in that sphere he says are more shining than the sun. And this is because in it he places the souls of those who were illustrated by the highest science: and he arranges the text. "Oh how much it behooved it to be shining in itself"—that is, how much it was necessary that she should shine by herself, so that what was inside the sun should be more shining than the light of the sun: because otherwise, she would not have been seen in the sun. **THAT** which was Beatrice.

<summary>Dante describes his effortless ascent into the Fourth Heaven, the Sun, and notes the incredible brightness of Beatrice and the souls of the wise. The accompanying commentary provides a detailed medieval scientific and mythological profile of the Sun's physical and metaphysical properties.</summary>
<keywords>Sun, Fourth Heaven, Beatrice, astronomy, zodiac, Ovid, Aristotle, Plato, Cicero, Petrarch, Landino commentary, geocentrism, spirals vs circles</keywords>

The commentary by Landino explains the theological significance of the Trinity and the relationship between human reason and divine revelation, as well as the symbolic "eclipse" of Beatrice by the light of God.</meta>

<page-num>X</page-num>
<header>->CANTO<-</header>

### CANTO X

Though I should call on genius, art, and habit,
I could not say it so it could be imagined,
but one may believe it, and let him long to see it.
And if our fantasies are lowly
for such a height, it is no wonder,
for no eye ever went above the sun.

Such was there the fourth family
of the high Father, who always satisfies them,
showing how he breathes and how he begets.
And Beatrice began: "Give thanks,
give thanks to the Sun of the Angels, who to this
sensible sun has raised you by his grace."
Never was heart of mortal so disposed
to devotion and to give itself to God
with all its pleasure so quickly,
As at those words I became;
and so all my love was placed in Him,
that Beatrice was eclipsed in oblivion.
It did not displease her, but she smiled at it,
so that the splendor of her laughing eyes
divided my unified mind into many parts.

<column-break/>

...from good to better: because the higher one rises, the more one shines: and it shines so suddenly that its act is not offered to us by time, that is, by succession of time. And by this he declares that man can learn natural things and the science of them with his own genius using reasoning and discourse where succession of time appears. But of celestial <note>original: "septẽtrionali" – here referring to the highest heavens</note> and divine things, our own genius is not capable by itself. Whence we do not acquire such knowledge through succession of time or by our own discourse, but by divine inspiration and in an instant. **NOT by color**: not by physical color like the colors we know. **BUT BY apparent light**: that is, a light appearing of such excess that it was visible even within the light of the sun. And so that the reader does not expect him to declare how much Beatrice surpassed the sun in splendor, he adds that even if he used all genius, art, and practice, he could not be eloquent enough to describe it. **So** <note>original: "Si"</note>, that is, in such a way that it could never be imagined by the reader; and the reason is that the imagination represents nothing except sensible things, and the eye (which is the sense that perceives splendor) never saw anything brighter than the sun. Therefore, let us not wonder that our fantasy—which can only grasp things offered by the senses—does not reach such a height. Nevertheless, man, though he cannot imagine such splendor, can believe it and yearn <note>original: "bramare"</note>, that is, desire to see it.

He follows by showing that the **fourth family**, that is, the spirits of this fourth heaven, was such—that is, bright—as was said of Beatrice. **OF the high father**: He is the true father because He creates, generates, governs, and nourishes. **WHO always satisfies them** with Himself, just as a father satisfies a family with his substance. **SHOWING how he breathes and how he begets**: He satisfies them with Himself by showing the single essence in the divinity and also the Trinity of the persons; and therefore he says "how he breathes" <note>original: "spira"</note> the eternal love, that is, the Holy Spirit, and "how he begets" <note>original: "figlia"</note> as the Father generates the Son. Thus God demonstrates to the blessed His unique essence and the trinity of persons because they remain in Him as in a mirror.

---

They understand all things. Some do not refer this to God but to the sun; how little this accords with his nature will be easily understood from what was said shortly before. **BEatrice began to tell me: "Give thanks to the sun of the angels"**, the supreme God who illuminates the angels and by illuminating them gives them knowledge; and thank Him because He has raised and exalted you to this **sensible sun**. And certainly this planet in the fourth heaven is a "sensible" sun because it is perceived with the senses and especially with the eye. And God is the "insensible" <note>meaning spiritual/beyond physical sense</note> sun; wherefore Petrarch said: "Crowned with stars to the supreme sun," <note>original: "Coronata distelle alfōmo fole"</note> that is, to the supreme God from whose light proceeds all other light. **HEART of mortal**: The efficacy of Beatrice's comforts and precepts was very great, since she suddenly put so much devotion in his heart and made him place all his love in God. **THAT Beatrice eclipsed**, that is, obscured. The meaning is this: when the poet was entirely elevated to God, God inspired in him such grace and joined him so closely that he turned all his love toward Him. Therefore, just as a greater light obscures a lesser one—as we see the stars that shine at night disappear when the sun, the greater light, arrives—so the love toward God obscured the love he had toward Beatrice. This admonishes us that we should bear the greatest love for the Holy Scripture. But our ultimate end should not be in that Scripture—that we love it only for its own sake—but so that through it we may join ourselves with all our love to God. Nor was it bothersome to Beatrice that the poet forgot her for God’s sake. For all the precepts of Holy Scripture consent, and indeed command, that we place divine love above every other love. **MY mind united, divided into many things**: his mind was united and fixed in prayer and in giving thanks to God. And the splendor of Beatrice's eyes drew him away to contemplate the various spirits.

---

<columns>2</columns>

I saw many living and conquering splendors
make a center of us and a crown of themselves,
sweeter in voice than shining in sight.
Thus we sometimes see the daughter of Latona
girt when the air is so pregnant
that it retains the thread that makes the zone.
In the court of heaven, from which I return,
many jewels are found so dear and beautiful
that they cannot be taken out of the kingdom.
The song of those lights was of those jewels;
he who does not grow wings so that he flies up there
may wait for news of it from the mute.
Then, singing so, those burning suns
circled around us three times,
like stars near the fixed poles.

<column-break/>

Those souls who were splendors had made a circle around us and we were in the middle, like the center is in the middle of its circumference. **SWEETER in voice than shining in sight**: the sweetness of the song surpassed the splendor of the light. This denotes that the sweetness of doctrine <term>doctrine: the teachings of the wise spirits</term> is greater in itself than the fame that comes from it. And the great artistry of the poet appears here. Wanting to demonstrate the excellence of the song’s sweetness, he first showed the greatness of the light, and then posits that such melody surpassed the splendor. And we were surrounded by the circle of those souls just as we see the **daughter of Latona** <note>original: "figlia di latona" – Diana, or the Moon</note>, that is, the moon, when the air is "pregnant" with vapors; because then the surrounding parts take on the color of the moon and form a circle around it <note>a lunar halo</note>. **IN the court of heaven**: An excellent comparison; just as it happens on earth that if there are excellent jewels in a kingdom it is forbidden to export them, so that song was such a precious joy that it cannot be taken out of that heaven; that is, the human intellect cannot comprehend it if it is not in heaven. **FROM the mute**: wait for news from them; as if to say, do not expect to understand such things from others unless you go to heaven.

He calls these spirits **burning suns** because of the splendor of their doctrine; they circled Dante three times because their consideration is...

<summary>Dante describes his arrival in the Sphere of the Sun, where the brilliance of the spirits of the wise causes him to momentarily forget Beatrice in his devotion to God. Landino's commentary interprets this "eclipse" as the proper relationship between Scripture (Beatrice) and the Divine, while explaining the atmospheric imagery of the lunar halo.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the narrative in the Sphere of the Sun, where Dante and Beatrice are surrounded by a crown of twelve brilliant lights representing the spirits of great theologians and scholars. Thomas Aquinas begins to speak, identifying himself and the other souls in the first circle.</meta>

<header>PARADISO</header>

# CANTO X

Ladies they seemed to me, not finished with the dance,
but who stop silent, listening,
until they have caught the new notes.
And within one I heard begin: "When
the ray of grace, from which is kindled
true love and which then grows by loving,
Multiplied in you, shines so greatly
that it conducts you up that ladder
where no one descends without climbing back up;
Whoever denied you the wine of his vial
for your thirst would not be in liberty,
any more than water that does not flow to the sea.

You want to know with what plants this garland
is flowered, which gazes with longing upon
the beautiful lady who strengthens you for heaven.
I was of the lambs of the holy flock
that Dominic leads along the path
where one fattens well if one does not stray into vanity.
This one who is closest to me on the right
was my brother and master; he was Albert
of Cologne, and I am Thomas Aquinas.
If you wish to be certain of all the others,
follow my speech with your eyes,
circling up through the blessed wreath.

That other flaming comes from the smile
of Gratian, who aided both courts <note>The civil and ecclesiastical courts.</note>
so that it gave pleasure in paradise.
The other who next adorns our choir
was that Peter who, like the poor woman,
offered his treasure to the Holy Church.
The fifth light, which is the most beautiful among us,
breathes with such love that all the world
down there hungers for news of him.
Within it is a mind of such profound
wisdom that, if the truth be true,
no second ever rose to see so much.
Next you see the light of that candle
which, down in the flesh, saw most deeply
into the angelic nature and its ministry.
In the other little light smiles
that advocate of Christian times,
whose Latin Augustine provided for himself.
Now, if you draw the eye of your mind
from light to light following my praise,
already you remain with a thirst for the eighth;
Within it, every good thing rejoices to see.</p>

<column-break/>

...according to memory, intellect, and will. **STARS** near the serene poles: just as the stars near the pole guide sailors into a safe harbor, so does the doctrine of these spirits. **AND WITHIN** one of those splendors, which was Thomas Aquinas, I heard him begin to speak in this way: **WHEN**, that is, since the ray of divine grace—from which true love and charity toward God and neighbor are kindled, and which thereafter grows by loving—shines so multiplied in you, Dante, certainly seeing you so affected by celestial doctrine, each of us ought to offer you the wine of his vial <note>original: "fiala" - a small bottle or flask</note>, that is, of his jug, to quench your thirst; that is, he ought to demonstrate his doctrine to you. And whoever did not do so would not be acting in his own liberty. For just as any water that is free does not stop running until it reaches the sea, so the blessed spirits—because they are kindled by the supreme grace and charity of the Most High—never cease to offer help if they are free to follow their own will.

Because those spirits had made a garland of themselves around Dante and Beatrice, he says: "You want to know with what plants this garland is flowered," which gazes with longing upon the beautiful lady, that is, Beatrice, **WHO strengthens you for heaven**, that is, who gives you the strength to ascend to heaven. **I WAS of the lambs**: of the little lambs; and it is an excellent metaphor. Since Saint Dominic was the shepherd, his friars were the flock; and he calls them lambs, for he looked to the innocence and chastity that ought to reside in such religious orders. **WHERE ONE fattens well**: grows fat <note>In a spiritual sense, gaining wisdom.</note>. **IF ONE DOES NOT stray into vanity**: that is, if they do not pursue empty glory, but rather true doctrine and an innocent life. **ALBERTO**, who for his great learning was called "the Great" <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a universal scholar.</note>, a universal man in every science and the supreme investigator of the secrets of nature, as clearly appears in his volumes. He flourished in Paris around the year 1257. **THOMAS AQUINAS**, born of the noble lineage of the Counts of Aquino. Of whose most innocent death we spoke above. A man good for his holiness of character and for the depth and variety of his multiple sciences; most worthy of immortal praise and eternal fame and memory. He died in the year of our salvation 1274.

Thomas proceeds to demonstrate the other spirits of this sphere. And he places **GRATIAN** of Chiusi, a very ancient city; he was a monk of Saint Felix of Bologna and composed the *Decretum* <note>The *Decretum Gratiani*, a collection of Canon law.</note>, and demonstrated how canon law accords with civil law. Whence he says that he helps "one court and the other," that is, spiritual and temporal judgment. **THAT PIETRO**: Peter Lombard, Bishop of Paris, called the "Master of the Sentences" <note>Author of the *Sentences*, the standard medieval theology textbook.</note>. Whose book has been commented upon by Thomas and by many other eminent doctors. This book he offered to the Church, and it was accepted by God above every other treasure, just as was the small coin of the poor woman <note>A reference to the Widow's Mite (Mark 12:41-44).</note>. The poet writes this because Peter, in the prologue of his book, says he offers it not as a great thing, but with that devotion with which the poor woman offered two mites to the temple. Peter Lombard was Bishop of Paris around the year 1172. **THE FIFTH light**: This is **SOLOMON**, son of David, born of Bathsheba, wife of Uriah; whose wisdom is most manifest, and without controversy he is placed above all men in wisdom. But the Church does not determine if he is damned or saved. And therefore the whole world **HUNGERS FOR NEWS** <note>original: "nagola" - to long for greedily</note>, that is, greatly desires to know news of his fate. **NEXT you see the light of this candle**: This is **DIONYSIUS** the Areopagite, who wrote of the angelic nature more excellently than others. Before his baptism, he was a most excellent philosopher. And having become a Christian, he wrote very high things most useful to the faith, especially regarding the *Celestial Hierarchy* and the *Divine Names*, and he was the first to grasp the high senses of Paul the Apostle. **IN THE OTHER little light smiles**: it had lesser splendor because it was of lesser merit, but it smiles because it is content. This is **PAULUS OROSIUS**, who at the petition of Saint Augustine wrote of all the calamities of men from the beginning of the world, and demonstrated that Christian times had been less calamitous than others. This provided much convenience to Saint Augustine when he wrote *The City of God*. Some others understand this to be **AMBROSE**, who greatly defended Christian times against heretics and converted Saint Augustine.

<summary>Thomas Aquinas introduces the first circle of twelve wise spirits in the Heaven of the Sun, identifying figures like Albertus Magnus, Gratian, Peter Lombard, Solomon, and Dionysius the Areopagite. The commentary explains their historical significance and the theological reconciliation of law and wisdom.</summary>
<keywords>Thomas Aquinas, Albertus Magnus, Gratian, Peter Lombard, Solomon, Dionysius the Areopagite, Paulus Orosius, Canon Law, Civil Law, Master of the Sentences, wisdom, grace</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the description of the first circle of wise spirits in the Sphere of the Sun. Thomas Aquinas finishes identifying the twelve souls in this first garland, ending with the philosopher Boethius and the logician Siger of Brabant. The text then transitions into Canto XI, where Dante reflects on the vanity of earthly pursuits compared to the divine glory he is witnessing.</meta>

# CANTO X

The holy soul that makes the deceitful world
manifest to anyone who listens well to him;
The body from which he was driven lies
down in Cieldauro <note>The Church of San Pietro in Ciel d'Oro in Pavia, where Boethius is buried.</note>, and he from martyrdom
and from exile came to this peace.
See further flaming the ardent spirit
of Isidore, of Bede, and of Richard,
who in contemplation was more than man.
This one from whom your gaze returns to me
is the light of a spirit whose heavy thoughts
made death seem slow to arrive.
It is the eternal light of Siger,
who, lecturing in the Street of Straw <note>original: "vico degli strami"; the Rue du Fouarre in Paris, the center of the university's arts faculty.</note>,
syllogized envied truths.
Then, like a clock that calls us
at the hour when the Bride of God rises
to sing morning songs to her Groom so that he may love her,
Where one part pulls and pushes the other,
sounding "tin tin" with so sweet a note
that a well-disposed spirit swells with love;
Thus I saw the glorious wheel
move and return voice to voice in harmony
and in sweetness that cannot be known,
Except there where joy is eternal. <note>original: "sinfempra," a word created by Dante meaning "to make itself eternal."</note>

<column-break/>

In the eighth position, he places Boethius: who, because he wrote *On the Consolation of Philosophy*, the poet says that this soul makes the deceitful world manifest—that is, he reveals the deceptions and fallacies of this world to whoever listens to him. Therefore, O Dante, you "draw"—that is, you translate—the eye of the mind. For "trano" in Latin means to cross over or to cast down. **THE BODY.** Boethius was condemned by Theodoric, King of the Goths, and finally strangled in Pavia. **IN CIEL DAURO:** This is a monastery called "Golden Heaven" <note>Latin: *Caelum Aureum*</note>. Isidore was Spanish and the Bishop of Seville. Bede was an English priest; although he is canonized, he is always called "Venerable" because an angel wrote this name on his tomb. Richard [of St. Victor] was a monk and the brother of Hugh of St. Victor. He was "more than man" in the contemplation of sacred letters because he surpassed human possibility.

Siger was a very great logician who possessed in that faculty not a deceptive or sophisticated science, but a true one. He was so excellent that he was not without the rivalry and envy of his competitors; he lectured in Paris in the "Street of Straw." **THEN LIKE A CLOCK.** Religious orders have clocks and alarms that call those who love the Church—that is, the priests—which Church is the "Bride of God," at the hour she rises to "matins"—that is, to sing the morning office and by singing, praise the Groom, who is God himself, so that He may love this Bride of His. And at that time in these clocks, it happens that one part of the wheels pulls the one behind it and "urges"—that is, pushes—the one ahead, sounding "tin tin," which is the sound of the little bell of the alarm, so sweet that the spirit of the well-disposed priest "surges"—that is, swells and grows in love. Similarly, the wheel and circle of spirits moved and, in singing, responded one to another, "in tempo"—that is, according to one another in voice and harmony so sweetly that it cannot be known, except where the day "eternizes itself": that is, it is always day, because there is never night; and this is in heaven.

---

### CANTO XI OF THE THIRD CANTICLE OF DANTE:

O insensate care of mortals!
How defective are those syllogisms
that make you beat your wings downward!
One followed law, and another aphorisms <note>Aphorisms here refers to the study of medicine, specifically the works of Hippocrates.</note>,
one the priesthood, and another
sought to rule by force or by sophistry;
One in theft, and another in civic business,
one entangled in the delights of the flesh
wore himself out, and another gave himself to idleness,
While I, freed from all these things,
was above in heaven with Beatrice,
so gloriously received.

<column-break/>

The summary of this eleventh canto contains the praises of two religious orders: those of Saint Francis and Saint Dominic, which the poet affirms were raised up at the opportune time by Divine Providence. But first, Saint Thomas resumes his speech and resolves a doubt. **O INSENSATE CARE:** He rebukes human foolishness, which either gives itself to things not judged toward their proper end, or rots in idleness and laziness. And therefore it is a "care" and anxiety and desire that is "insensate," without true feeling, because it is not only vain and useless, but also harmful to the Supreme Good.

**HOW DEFECTIVE ARE THE SYLLOGISMS.** That is, how imperfect are their arguments and reasons, because they do not conclude with the truth. A syllogism is an argument that proves a doubtful thing; but it must not be defective—the major and minor premises must be true, and the conclusion must follow from the premises. **ONE FOLLOWED LAW:** The meaning is this: since the Supreme Good consists in the contemplation of divine things, to which Beatrice and I were attentive, the majority of men err. Some place the Supreme Good in riches; thus they give themselves either to

civil law or to "aphorisms"—that is, to medicine—or to the priesthood, or to civic business, which is the government of the Republic. All these things, although by their nature they are honest and good, nevertheless, he who does them solely for the sake of gain is not a good man, nor can he be happy. And much less so if he openly seizes what is not his. Some place happiness in lordships and honors, and they rule by force as tyrants, or by "sophisms"—that is, by fraud. A sophism is an argument that seems true but is false; here he uses it to mean fraud. Some place happiness in idleness and laziness; some in lust; and all err because true happiness cannot be found there.

After each one had returned to the 
point of the circle where they were before...

After the souls that formed a crown for Beatrice and Dante had returned to that point where they had begun, they stopped just as a candle stops in a candlestick; and he uses this comparison because these doctors have explained the Scripture...

**B**ecause the difficulty of these verses lies in the ordering of the text, proceed thus: Divine Providence, which governs the visible and invisible world with that counsel in which every created aspect—that is, every created intellect, both angelic and human—is defeated before it reaches the bottom. For the Church is the bride of Christ, who on the cross with loud cries wedded her with the blessed blood which He shed for our redemption; and she went secure in herself through the guidance of these two named princes, and more faithful in Him <gloss>i.e., with more faith toward Him.</gloss> And these were Francis and Dominic. Nor is it without great artistry that the author [Dante] induces the Lamb [Aquinas] to praise Francis and not Dominic. For since the said Thomas belongs to the order of Dominic, he has more credibility in praising Francis. And for the same reason, the author induces him to rebuke the friars of the order of Saint Dominic.

**H**e describes the city of Assisi where Saint Francis was born. Topino is a river to the west of Assisi. THE CHOSEN HILL: this is to the east. FERTILE SLOPE: Assisi is situated on a slope that is very fertile. UBALDO: He was the first hermit on this mountain, then was bishop of Gubbio. FROM THIS SLOPE: He shows Francis was born in Assisi, who truly was a sun: because through the sanctity of his life and excellent examples, he removed all heretical darkness which in those times greatly occupied human minds. Francis, the founder of the Order of Friars Minor, and Dominic, born in Caleruega, a place in Spain, with which he instituted the Order of Preachers, were contemporaries. They flourished after the year 1210 of our salvation.

**H**e was not very far from his birth—for he was of a young age—when the earth and men began to recognize his virtue and take comfort. BECAUSE: For he ran into war with his father, who was Bernardone, a citizen of Assisi and a wool-worker, for "such a lady"—that is, for Poverty—to whom no one unlocks the door of pleasure any more than they do for death. <gloss>i.e., she opens the gate of pleasure as little as death does.</gloss> And in his spiritual court, because with the counsel of his spiritual father he made a profession of poverty, and therefore he adds: "and in the presence of his father." THEIR HARMONY and their joyful countenances: If all discord arises from nature and from the greed of possessing treasure, voluntary poverty will always create perfect harmony. And if riches are full of care, poverty will be full of joy. Love—that is, the supreme charity with which one inflames the other. WONDER: because one was a mirror of integrity and holiness to the other, they caused holy thoughts to arise. For harmony, love, and being content with one's present state always direct a man toward virtuous works. **BERNARD:** This was the first companion that Saint Francis had, who girded himself with the cord and went barefoot as Saint Francis had done, and ran toward such peace. **O UNKNOWN** wealth: And certainly this wealth is not known, this fertile good, that is, fertile and abundant.

That father, for the care and solicitude he had for the family already begun, and master for the precepts he gave. **WITH** his lady: with poverty and baseness of heart—that is, to debase and humble oneself by one's own will—it did not weigh down his brow; it did not make him ashamed. He mentioned "brow" because shame shows in the forehead; or rather, he said baseness of heart—that is, humility which is born from a great soul. He was not ashamed, therefore, either for being the son of Pietro Bernardone (that is, not of a very great lineage) nor because he was wonderfully despised for his vile habit and for poverty. But regally, with a royal and unconquered soul, he revealed to Pope Innocent III his stern intention, which was to observe Obedience, Chastity, and Poverty, which things are very hard and difficult. For obedience is against the freedom of the will toward evil; Chastity is against the itching of the flesh; Poverty is against the excessive use of earthly goods. Innocent III in the year 1200 <note>Historically 1209-1210.</note> had a vision that the church of Saint John Lateran was falling, but two men in vile habits supported it. Afterward, when Saint Francis came so that he might confirm his religion, the Pope recognized him as the one he had seen in the dream. Therefore, with a papal bull, he confirmed it for him.

The religious order of Saint Francis having grown, he obtained from Pope Honorius the power to minister the sacraments and have priestly dignities. **ARCHIMANDRITE:** Arch-shepherd. Afterward, desiring martyrdom, he went to preach the Christian faith in the land of the Sultan; but producing no fruit, he returned to Italy. Having returned to Italy, he withdrew to the rugged mountain of La Verna, which is between the Tiber and the Arno, in which, performing great penance, he received the stigmata from Christ, which the poet calls the "seal." ### CANTO XII OF THE THIRD CANTICLE OF DANTE

Just as two parallel and monochromatic arches <note>A metaphor for a double rainbow.</note>

<column-break/>

**stigmata:** because *stigm* in Greek <note>original: "stigm." From the Greek 'stigma' (στιγμα), meaning a mark or brand.</note> means to strike, and by striking it leaves a mark. And then, when it pleased God to draw him to heaven where he was to receive the reward and prize for his merits—which were earned by making himself **pusillo**: that is, small and by humbling himself—he recommended to his brothers his most dear lady. This is **poverty**. Here one must consider that poverty was dearer to him than chastity and obedience: because poverty is the cause of chastity, which is lost in too much luxury and abundance of things; thus, through poverty it is acquired. Similarly, he who despises riches can easily remain in obedience. **HE WISHED no other bier** than that poverty: that is, he did not desire other funerals or other honors. Having narrated the life of Saint Francis, he follows and says: **THINK** what sort of man he was who was a worthy colleague: that is, a companion to Saint Francis to sustain the bark of Peter: that is, the Church of God. And this was our patriarch, that is, Saint Dominic: and he says "our" because Saint Thomas is the one speaking, and he was of the order of Saint Dominic; and those who follow him as he commands: that is, those who follow his constitutions. For Saint Dominic did not make a new rule, but took that of Saint Augustine. But he gave certain constitutions. Therefore, he who follows him carries **GOOD merchandise:** that is, good wares: because with those he does not gain gold or silver or momentary or transitory things: but immortal life. **BUT HIS flock:** he rebukes the friars who, by not observing his precepts, become greedy for **new food:** that is, for worldly sciences and prelacies and great riches. He said, therefore: **NEW FOOD:** for dignities and prelacies: because in truth many of them have been bishops and archbishops and cardinals. Wherefore they scatter through diverse **leaps:** that is, through diverse pastures. **AND THE FURTHER his sheep** distance themselves from him: that is, from his precepts, the more they return empty of knowledge and of holy customs, which are the nourishment of the soul as milk is the nourishment of the body.

He concludes that if his words have been clear and if he [Dante] has been attentive to hear, his desire will be partly satisfied: because of two doubts, one is resolved. And this is that when he said: **Where one fattens well**—that is, grows fat—**if he does not stray.** He meant that the soul fattened on the best food: that is, on sacred theology. **IF HE DOES NOT stray:** that is, if they did not attend through them to the secular sciences that make them vain and proud; or rather, if they did not attend to theology to acquire fame and useless glory.

Just as in the previous chapter Saint Thomas has rebuked the friars of Saint Dominic, so in this twelfth [canto] he introduces a new spirit who rebukes those of Saint Francis; he introduces, then, another crown of souls. Then, one of those commends the life of Saint Dominic. And after this, he vituperates the Friars Minor; <note>The Franciscans.</note> and finally, the said soul manifests himself and the others of that crown. As soon as the blessed flame—that is, Saint Thomas—took the last word to say it: he began to turn in the circle in which he was. Nor did he finish turning before there appeared there another circle which enclosed this one. Which denotes that the first circle turned closer to the center of the sun: and this one, girding it from further away, denotes that the souls already mentioned were of greater beatitude and greater doctrine than those of whom he will speak; furthermore, it shows that the song and motion of this [second circle] accorded with the song and motion of the first, to denote that in Holy Scripture there is no discord whatsoever. This song surpassed our Muses and our Sirens—that is, all human melodies—as much as the first ray surpasses that which reverberates from it. As for example <note>original: "uerbigracia."</note> the rays of the sun striking the water: it reverberates, that is, it reflects in one part, but the reflection is not as clear as the first ray from which it proceeds.

### CANTO XII

when Juno commands her handmaid,
Born from the inner one, that outer one,
in the manner of the speech of that wandering nymph
whom love consumed as the sun does vapors;
And they make people here presage,
through the covenant that God made with Noah,
of the world that shall never again be flooded:
So of those sempiternal roses
the two garlands turned around us,
and so the outer one responded to the inner.

After the dance and the other great festivity—
both of the singing and of the flaming
light with light, gracious and gentle—
had ceased together, at the same point and will,
just as the eyes, by the pleasure that moves them,
must together close and lift themselves;
From the heart of one of the new lights
a voice moved, which made me seem like the needle
to the star, and turn to its "wherever";
And it began: "The love that makes me beautiful
draws me to reason of the other leader,
on whose account mine is spoken of so well here.
It is worthy that where one is, the other shines,
so that as they fought together,
so together their glory may shine."

The army of Christ, which cost so dear
to re-arm, moved behind the standard
slowly, suspicious, and thin in rank,
When the Emperor who reigns forever
provided for the soldiers who were in danger,
by grace alone, and not for being worthy;
And as was said, He came to his spouse’s aid
with two champions, by whose deeds and words
the straying people were gathered back.

<margin>He provided for our soldiers, re-arming the Church Militant as is said, when it was in danger. And He provided by His superabundant grace, and not because our soldiers deserved it; for the Christian people were not worthy of being helped by God without helping themselves. AND AS IS SAID, he shows that the providence sent these two champions: some to act with deeds and some to speak with teachings; the people, led astray by the errors of the heretics, were gathered back into the Christian army.</margin>

In that region where Zephyr rises to open
the new leaves...

<column-break/>

...reflection is born, the second if the cloud is so spacious that it receives such reflection. And the poet inserts here that just as in the rainbow the first is born by the reflection of the second: so from the doctrine of those first souls was born that of these second ones; and from the speech of Thomas was born that of Bonaventure. **WHEN Juno commands**—that is, commands her handmaid, meaning Iris, her minister. <note>Iris is the personification of the rainbow and messenger of Juno in Roman mythology.</note> The nature of this bow called Iris was expressed by us elsewhere. Some say it is not true that one bow is born from the other. Nor is it true that Dante says this second crown is born from the first. Therefore, they explain the text this way: **born from the outside**, meaning the color of the bow, **from within**, meaning from the cloud and the vapors from which the cloud is generated: just as an **Echo** is born from the preceding cloud because it is its reflection.
**IN THE MANNER:** In likeness of the speech of that **wandering one**, meaning the wandering Echo whose words were born from the voice of others. I will not repeat the fable here, which we explained at length elsewhere. <note>In mythology, the nymph Echo could only repeat the last words spoken to her; she wasted away from unrequited love for Narcissus until only her voice remained.</note> **AND they make people here presage**, meaning to act as a diviner, through the covenant that God placed with Noah. The meaning is that the celestial bow makes man a foreteller: that in the future the world has no need to fear water as in the times of Noah. And this meaning is found in the ninth chapter of Genesis where God says to Noah: "I will establish my covenant with you; and never again shall all flesh be cut off by the waters of a flood." <note>original Latin: "Statuā pactū meū uobiscū: & nequaquā ultra itersicietur omnis caro aqs diluuii"</note> And a little below: "this is the sign of the covenant which I give between me and you and every living soul that is with you, for perpetual generations. I will set my bow in the clouds of heaven; and it shall be a sign of the covenant between me and between the earth. And when I cover the sky with clouds, my bow shall appear in the clouds; and I will see it. And I will remember the everlasting covenant, which is a treaty between God and every living soul." <note>original Latin: "hoc est signū federis... et recordabor federis sempiterni"</note>

**After the dance:** meaning the dance and the other great celebration that was among the souls of those two circles; and it was a celebration both of singing, because they accorded together. **BOTH of the flaming**, because they responded to one another in the splendor that signifies a reciprocal charity.
**CEASED:** they quieted and stopped together at once, at the **point** which is the fixed center of their motion, which is God, who is the point of every motion; because being immobile, He turns every motion; and at the will of God where every blessed soul stops. And they agreed together just as the eyes in a man, according to pleasure, agree to close or open; and once these circles were stopped, quieted, and singing ended, a voice moved from the heart and mind of one of those new lights—meaning those from the newly arrived circle—which made me seem like **the needle to the star**, meaning the needle in the compass when it stops at the North Star. And this soul began to say: **THE LOVE that makes me beautiful**, because the splendor of the souls signifies charity. This charity induces me—since Saint Francis was praised by Saint Thomas of the Order of Saint Dominic—that I, Bonaventure of the Order of Saint Francis, should praise Saint Dominic. Especially because having soldiered together, it is a worthy thing that they should be praised together.

Wishing to praise these two champions, he not only places their great virtue, but also shows that they existed in a necessary time, and in matters without which eternal damnation follows for souls. Since they were defenders of the faith—without which no one can be saved—and they were there at the time when the Christian people moved behind the standard along the way of God slowly and lazily, and suspicious because of many doubts that arose every day through the sects of the heretics; and they were few, for they were few: and those few were lazy and full of doubts. Therefore, the **army of Christ**, meaning the Christian people which is the **Church Militant** <term>Ecclesia Militans: The living Christians on earth who struggle against sin and heresy.</term> and which cost so dear to be re-armed. This signifies that God created man armed: that is, with such virtue that he could defend himself from the adversary, had he not been a transgressor of the commandments. Afterward, sin disarmed him in such a way that he could no longer defend or save himself. But Christ the Redeemer re-armed him, ransoming him with His precious blood; which redemption brought us back into divine grace. And these were the arms with which we can defend ourselves from temptations and sin. When God, whose empire is sempiternal, provided for our soldiers, re-arming the Church Militant as is said: **WHICH WAS IN DANGER**, that is, in doubt.

Bonaventure, having to narrate the life of Dominic, describes first his homeland, which was Calaruega, a city of Spain which is located in the West. **IN that part** of the world where the sweet **Zephyr** [West Wind]...

The commentary explains the symbolism of the double rainbow and the historical necessity of the Franciscan and Dominican orders in defending the Church against heresy.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the speech of St. Bonaventure in Canto XII of the Paradiso. Having introduced the geographic origins of St. Dominic in Spain, Bonaventure now details the saint’s holy life, his name’s meaning, and his mission to defend the faith against heresy, contrasting Dominic’s spiritual devotion with the worldly greed of legal and medical scholars.</meta>

->PARADISO<-

from which one sees Europe reclothe herself <note>A reference to the west wind, Zephyr, which brings the spring.</note>
Not very far from the beating of the waves,
behind which, because of his long journey,
the sun sometimes hides himself from every man,
Sits the fortunate Calaroga,
under the protection of the great shield
in which the lion is subject and subdues; <note>The coat of arms of the Kingdom of Castile, featuring both castles and lions in different quadrants of the shield.</note>
Therein was born the loving paramour <term>drudo: a devoted lover or faithful companion</term>
of the Christian faith, the great athlete, <note>original: "athletam"</note>
kind to his own and cruel to his enemies.
And as soon as it was created, his soul
was filled with such divine virtue
that it made his mother a prophet while she still carried him.
After the wedding-vows were completed <note>A metaphor for the sacrament of Baptism, where the soul is "wedded" to the Faith.</note>
at the sacred font between him and the Faith,
where they endowed each other with mutual salvation,
The woman who gave the consent for him <note>His godmother.</note>
saw in her sleep the wondrous fruit
that was to come from him and his heirs;
And so that he might be in name what he was in essence,
a spirit moved from here to name him
after the possessive of Him to whom he wholly belonged. <note>The name "Dominic" (Domenico) is derived from the Latin "Dominicus," meaning "belonging to the Lord" (Dominus).</note>
He was called Dominic; and I speak of him
as of the husbandman whom Christ
chose for His garden to help Him.
Truly he seemed a messenger and a familiar of Christ,
for the first love that was manifest in him
was for the first counsel that Christ gave. <note>Refers to the vow of poverty: "If you wish to be perfect, go, sell what you possess and give to the poor" (Matthew 19:21).</note>
Many times he was found silent and awake
on the ground by his nurse,
as if to say: "I have come for this."
O father of his, truly "Felice!" <note>A wordplay on his father’s name, Felix, which means "happy" or "blessed."</note>
O mother of his, truly "Joanna," <note>A wordplay on his mother’s name, Joanna, which in Hebrew means "The Lord is gracious."</note>
if her name, interpreted, means what they say!
Not for the sake of the world, for which men now toil,
following the "Ostiense" or "Taddeo," <note>Henry of Susa (the Ostian), a famous commentator on church law, and Taddeo Alderotti, a famous physician; representing legal and medical careers pursued for wealth.</note>
but for the love of the true manna,
In a short time he became a great teacher,
such that he began to go about the vineyard
which quickly withers if the vine-dresser is at fault.
And from the See <note>The Papacy.</note> which once was kinder
to the righteous poor—not because of itself,
but because of him who sits there and has gone astray—
He did not ask to dispense two or three for six, <note>He did not ask for permission to keep a portion of funds intended for charity.</note>
nor for the fortune of the first vacant office,
nor for the tithes which belong to God’s poor, <note>original: "decimas quae sunt pauperum Dei"</note>
But he asked for leave to fight against the erring world
on behalf of that seed from which
twenty-four plants have sprung. <note>The "seed" is the Faith; the "twenty-four plants" likely refer to the twenty-four books of the Bible or the two circles of twelve saints each in this part of Heaven.</note>

<column-break/>

This is because the wind is temperate and very delightful: for when it begins, it induces springtime and puts virtue into the earth, which conceives all things; and the earth clothes itself in grass and flowers, and the trees leaf out. Therefore he says: *from which one sees Europe reclothe herself.* **NOT VERY far** from the beating of the waves: that is, not very far from the Western Ocean sea, behind whose waves the sun sets for us. **Sits** is placed and located Calaroga, which he calls fortunate because it produced such a man. This city is under the King of Castile, who has for his arms a shield divided into quarters: and in one part is depicted a castle that has a lion under it, and in another part a lion that has the castle under it; and therefore he says that the lion is subject to the castle where it is below, and subdues the castle where it is above. And inside there was born **Dominic, the paramour**, that is, the supreme lover of the Christian faith. **AND ATHLETE**: that is, a fighter for it against the heretics. *Athlete* is a Greek word <note>original: "athleta"</note> and means a fighter, and *athlon* is the prize of the fighter. **KIND to his own** Christians: and **cruel** to enemies, that is, to the heretics. The soul of this man, as soon as it was created and infused in the womb of his mother, was a prophet; and through his virtue, the mother prophesied: for having dreamed that she would give birth to a black and white dog carrying a burning torch in its mouth, she predicted that he would have the world and would be biting against the heretics. And he would have the most burning charity, and certainly he sees everything and is awake for God. And the woman who held him at baptism dreamed that he had a star on his forehead that illuminated the whole world.

He calls baptism **the wedding-vows**, in which the person who holds the child at baptism promises that the baptized will renounce the pomps of the devil and other things. **Where**—that is, in which—**they endowed each other with mutual salvation**. For he was salvation to the Faith and defended it, and the Faith saved him. **The woman who gave the consent for him**, that is, who made promises for him, saw in her sleep that which we have narrated above. And because he was to belong entirely to his Lord God, and no part of him was to belong to the world, it was divine inspiration that they should name him **Dominic**. *Dominus* in Latin means "Lord." And from this name *Dominus* derives *Dominicus*, which means "a thing belonging to his Lord." And therefore I speak of Dominic as of a **husbandman** chosen by Christ to cultivate his **garden**, that is, the Christian people. He appeared to be sent by God, since in his first public act he followed the **first counsel** that Christ gives, where He says: "If you wish to be perfect, go and sell all that you have and give to the poor, and follow me." <note>original: "Si uis perfectus esse uade & uende oīa que habes & da pauperibus: & sequere me"</note> For while he was still a young student, he sold his books and what he had, and in a great famine distributed it to the poor. Because of this, upon the notice of the bishop, he was made a regular canon. From there he gave himself entirely to the study of theology. **O Father of his**: his father was named Felice and his mother Joanna. Therefore with admiration Bonaventure says that this was fulfilled in both: for he was truly "happy" [Felice]. And she was truly "Joanna," because this name in Hebrew means **full of grace**. And Dominic was not **silent and awake** for the world, that is, for mundane and temporal things for which many **now** (presently) **toil**, following **Ostiense** and **Taddeo**. Ostiense wrote on the Decretals <note>Church laws.</note>. Taddeo was a Florentine physician who, for his supreme learning, was called "more than a commentator." He was not, therefore, intent on profit, following the law or medicine. But he acted for the love of the **true manna**, of the true food of the soul, which is theological doctrine.

Having come to years of perfection, although he was already of great authority for his learning, he did not ask the Supreme Pontiff for dignities from which he might draw profit or honor; nor to be dispensed from returning **two or three for six**, which is a third or a half; nor did he ask for any **first vacant** benefice; nor did he ask, as many do, for the **tithes** of any country which **belong to God’s poor**. But he asked for leave to fight and preach against the **erring world**, that is, against the heretics. **FOR THE seed**: for the Faith, which is the seed, whose fruit is eternal beatitude, from which **twenty-four plants** are made; that is, the twenty-four books of the Bible, which all speak of the Christian faith. Some understand by these twenty-four plants the souls of these two circles, which he posits to be twenty-four; and they say "from which they [the plants] make a circle around you, Dante": that is, twenty-four plants surround you.

It interprets his name and his mother’s prophetic dreams as signs of his future role as a defender of the Church against heresy.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the speech of Saint Bonaventure in the Sphere of the Sun. After praising the life of Saint Dominic, Bonaventure now describes Dominic's crusade against heresy and the "two wheels" of the Church's chariot, before turning to a sharp critique of his own Franciscan order and identifying the second circle of twelve holy lights.</meta>

# CANTO XII

Then with doctrine and will combined,
together with the apostolic office, he moved
like a torrent pressed by a powerful vein;
And upon the heretical thickets he struck,
his impetus hitting most vigorously there
where the resistance was most stubborn.
From him various streams were then formed,
by which the Catholic garden is irrigated,
so that its little trees stand more lifelike.
If such was one wheel of the chariot
in which the Holy Church defended herself
and won her civil strife in the field,
Then the excellence of the other should
be plain enough to you, about whom Thomas
was so courteous before my arrival.
But the track made by the highest part
of its circumference is now abandoned,
so that there is mold where once was the crust. <note>A metaphor using a wine cask: the "crust" or tartar (gromma) left by good wine is being replaced by mold (muffa).</note>
His family, which once moved straight
with feet in his footprints, has turned so far
that they throw the front foot toward the rear.
But soon they shall see the harvest
of the bad cultivation, when the tares
shall complain that the barn is taken from them.
Indeed, I say that he who searched leaf by leaf
through our volume might still find a page
where he would read: "I am what I used to be."
But it shall not be from Casale or Acquasparta,
from whence such men come to the Scripture
that one flees it and the other restricts it. <note>Referring to Ubertino da Casale (too strict) and Matteo d'Acquasparta (too lax) regarding the Franciscan Rule.</note>
I am the soul of Bonaventure
from Bagnoregio, who in my great offices
always placed the left-hand care last. <note>The "left-hand care" refers to worldly or temporal business, prioritized below spiritual matters.</note>
Illuminato and Augustine are here,
who were among the first barefoot poor ones
who, in the cord, made themselves friends to God. <note>The "cord" refers to the rope belt worn by Franciscans.</note>
Hugh of Saint Victor is here with them,
and Petrus Comestor, and Peter of Spain,
who gives light below in twelve booklets. <term>Pietro Hispano: Peter of Spain, later Pope John XXI, famous for his "Summulae Logicales," a standard logic textbook in twelve parts.</term>
Nathan the prophet, and the metropolitan
Chrysostom, and Anselm, and that Donatus
who deigned to lay his hand to the first art. <note>Donatus was a 4th-century grammarian; the "first art" of the trivium is Grammar.</note>
Rabanus is here, and shining beside me
is the Calabrian abbot Joachim,
endowed with a prophetic spirit.
To emulate so great a paladin
I was moved by the flaming courtesy
of Brother Thomas and his discrete speech;
And with me he moved this company.

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Decorative initial 'D' inside a circular cartouche with foliate designs.</image-desc>
Then he moved against the heretics with three necessary things: with **doctrine**, by which he knew how to act; with **will**, so that there was desire; and with the **apostolic office**, which is the Inquisition, so that he could overcome and punish the heretics. **FROM HIM** various streams were then formed: from him, as from a fountain, many streams were born to irrigate the Catholic garden, so that its saplings might remain green. Having praised Saint Dominic, whom he places as one of the two wheels of the chariot that defended the Church from heretics, he rightly says "civil battle," because the heretics were Christians, and all Christians are citizens of the same city—that is, the Church Militant. Now he returns to Saint Francis and affirms what Thomas had said. Then he shows that the majority of his friars have deviated from his precepts and constitutions; and staying with the metaphor he made of the chariot, he says that the **track**—that is, the path that this wheel left, which are the excellent precepts of his holy works—has been deserted and abandoned by the **circumference**—that is, by the ministers and prelates of that religious order. It is in such a state that where there used to be the **crust** (gromma) <note>original: "gromma," the tartar left by wine</note> which gives off the best scent of the wine that was in the vessel, there is now **mold** (muffa) which gives off a foul odor. **HIS FAMILY**: his friars, who at the beginning moved following the footprints of Saint Francis, following his precepts and examples, have turned so far around that they place their toes where he placed his heel—that is, they go in the opposite direction in their lives and customs. But they will realize their error at the harvest, because they will find no one to put their **tares** into the granaries—that is, God will not want their souls in His kingdom, as they have produced foul fruit. For it is written in Saint Matthew: <note>original: "Colligē primū zizania & alligate ea in faſciculos ad cōburrendū triticū autem congregate in orreum meū."</note> *Gather first the tares and bind them in bundles to burn, but gather the wheat into my barn.* Nevertheless, he who searched our **volume**—that is, our Order—leaf by leaf, friar by friar, would still find a "page"—that is, some friar—where he would read: "**I am what I used to be**," meaning one who would observe the customary rule of Francis. **BUT**: This refers to Friar Ubertino da Casale, who, being Minister General, loosened the Rule too much. He wrote a book called the *Penteloquio* on the power of the Pope. Casale is a land in Piedmont. Therefore, this man "flees the scripture" by broadening the precepts; and Friar Matthew of Acquasparta (a village in the territory of Todi) restricted it too much; he wrote a commentary on the *Sentences*.

<image-desc>Decorative initial 'D' inside a circular cartouche with foliate designs.</image-desc>
After the praises bestowed upon Saint Dominic and the complaints and accusations against the friars of Saint Francis, **Bonaventure** names himself and the souls who are in his circle. Bonaventure was from Bagnoregio, a land in the Marches; he was most learned in sacred letters, and although he was General of the Order and later a Cardinal, nevertheless in these **great offices** he always **placed the left-hand care last**—that is, the active life—and followed the contemplative life. **Illuminato** was a Friar Minor. **Augustine** was a Friar Minor. These two were among the first companions of Saint Francis. And although in this circle are placed the souls of those who, shining like the sun with the highest doctrine, could illuminate others, nevertheless these two are equals: though they did not shine through doctrine, they illuminated others through the examples of their most holy lives. **HUGH** was from Pavia and a monk of the monastery of Saint Victor; he wrote many things in theology, and especially on the Sacraments, on the Lamentations of Jeremiah, on the Hierarchy of Dionysius, and many other works. Some say he was first a Canon Regular and then a Canon at Saint Victor and was of a most holy life; they say that when he was dying and about to receive the body of Christ, he said: "Go, my soul, with your Redeemer," and then he expired, and the Eucharist was visibly seen to leave the priest's hands and fly to heaven. **PETRUS Comestor** (the Eater) was a Lombard and wrote the *Historia Scholastica*. **Peter of Spain** wrote twelve books on dialectic [logic]. **Nathan the prophet** and prince of priests, who by God's command rebuked David for the adultery committed with the wife of Uriah, as appears in the Book of Kings. **John Chrysostom**—that is, "Golden Mouth," so named for his supreme eloquence; he calls him **metropolitan** because he was Bishop of Constantinople, to whose care were committed Thrace, Pontus, and Phoenicia. **Anselm** was from Normandy, Archbishop of Canterbury; he wrote on the harmony of free will, divine foreknowledge, and predestination, and on the fall of the devil...
