<meta>This page continues the commentary on the final spirits of the second circle of holy lights in the Heaven of the Sun, concluding the speech of Saint Bonaventure from Canto XII and beginning the explanation of Canto XIII.</meta>

...mony: of original sin: of the incarnation of the divine Word. Roboam <note>Likely a transcription error in the original for Rabanus Maurus, who appears in Dante’s list of spirits in Canto XII, though here described as English and the brother of Bede.</note> was English and wrote poetry: he was the brother of Bede. Joachim [of Fiore] had the gift of the Holy Spirit: in such a way that without much formal science he opened every obscure passage of Holy Scripture. He wrote of the duration of the world and of the things that were to happen in the meantime. **To envy**: to envy not with a divine vice, but with virtuous emulation. **Such a paladin**: twelve were the counts of the palace ordained by Charlemagne to fight for the faith. Wherefore one can well call Dominic a "paladin," having so ardently fought against the heretics. The meaning is that the inflamed love of Thomas toward Saint Francis moved me [Bonaventure] to emulate him and do the same toward Saint Dominic.

# CANTO XIII OF THE THIRD CANTICLE OF DANTE.

Let him imagine, who desires to understand well
what I now saw, and let him hold the image,
while I speak, as firm as a rock,

Fifteen stars that in different regions
enliven the heaven with such serenity
that it overcomes every thickness of the air;

Let him imagine that chariot for which the bosom
of our sky suffices both night and day,
so that it does not fail with the turning of the pole;

Let him imagine the mouth of that horn
which begins at the point of the axle
around which the first wheel goes;

To have made of themselves two signs in heaven,
like that which the daughter of Minos made
at the moment she felt the chill of death;

And one to have its rays within the other,
and both to whirl in such a manner
that one goes first and the other after;

And he will have as it were the shadow of the true
constellation and of the double dance
that circled the point where I was.

<column-break/>

Since in the preceding chapter he had clarified the first doubt: this thirteenth resolves the second. First, therefore, he describes the aforementioned crowns through an imagined simile. Afterward, he resolves the doubt. And finally, he admonishes us concerning the solving of doubts. As for the beginning, the poet admonishes the reader to imagine seeing two crowns of stars in the eighth sphere in a shape where one is surrounded by the other: and they move equally, one against the other. And to make these two crowns, imagine being able to gather together fifteen stars of the first magnitude <note>The brightest stars visible from Earth.</note> which are scattered in different parts of heaven. Then those seven which make the "Chariot" <note>The Big Dipper or Ursa Major.</note> in our arctic pole. And then two which are at the beginning of the "Lesser Bear" <note>Ursa Minor.</note>. And of the twelve most radiant among the fifteen, he makes the crown that is inside, closer to the center, and of the rest he makes the outer crown; and you would have made a thing similar to the two crowns of the twenty-four souls already mentioned above. And the text follows: **HE WHO DESIRES** <note>original: "CVPÉ", from the Latin *cupit*</note> to understand well what I saw: let him imagine it in his mind and hold the image firm as a rock <note>original: "rupe"</note>: that is, like a cliff or a mountain stone. Because it would not be enough to imagine if he did not hold the image in his memory. Let him imagine then fifteen stars which enliven the heaven with their splendor because they are the brightest and largest. And they overcome every **thickness** <note>original: "compage"</note>: that is, every gathering of the air. **IN DIFFERENT REGIONS**: in different regions of the heaven. And further imagine the Chariot where there are seven stars of the second magnitude for whose chariot the bosom of our sky suffices: that is, from our pole. Because they turn so close to our pole that they never set. But they are always above our heads. **THE DAUGHTER of Minos**: Theseus conquered the Minotaur in Crete: and returning from there he took Phaedra and Ariadne (called Adriana), the daughter of Minos. And because when they reached the island of Chios (or Naxos), Adriana fell into a deep sleep due to too much wine, she was left on the island by Theseus. But Bacchus took her as his lover. And he gave her a most precious crown

---

made by Vulcan of gold and gems: which the poets feign was later translated into a celestial sign <note>The constellation Corona Borealis.</note>. This image has eight stars: of which three are most splendid. **THAT ONE**: went. **TO THE FIRST**: that is, turned against the first. And the other **AFTER**: turned against the second. **THE POINT**: that is, with equidistant space they turned around me: I who was in the middle like a center to the circumference.

---

Since as far beyond our custom,
as far as the movement of the Chiana
is surpassed by the heaven that outspeeds all others;

There they sang not Bacchus, not a Paean,
but three persons in divine nature,
and in one person, both it and the human.

The singing completed its measure,
and those holy lights turned their attention to us,
rejoicing as they moved from care to care.

The silence was broken among the concordant deities
by the light in which the miraculous life
of the poor man of God had been narrated to me.

<column-break/>

He places the end of the song of these crowns: so that Thomas may resolve the second doubt, and he arranges it thus. **SINCE THERE THEY SANG**: in that crown so far beyond our custom: that is, so much more excellently than is done among us men, just as the heaven that advances and surpasses all other heavens moves [faster]. **BEYOND the movement of the Chiana**: that is, it moves more than a "Chiana," which is to say, a dead water <note>The Chiana is a river in Tuscany that was famously stagnant and slow-moving in the Middle Ages.</note>. **THEY SANG not Bacchus nor a Paean**: that is, not Bacchus nor Apollo. Because the ancients sang hymns in honor of various gods and especially of Bacchus and Apollo. And he used the word **Paean** <note>original: "peana"</note> in this place for Apollo: because many believe the Greeks called "Paeans" the hymns made in honor of Apollo, though they call any praise of God a Paean. **BUT they sang three persons in divine nature**: that is, they sang of the Trinity which is one essence in three persons: and they sang of it and the human in one person. Because in the person of the Son, there is both divinity and humanity. Therefore, after they sang what was said, the song **COMPLETED**: that is, finished the round turn. **ITS measure**: that is, the time that was necessary for the song. And **THEY TURNED to us**: that is, they stopped toward us. **Those holy lights**: those radiant souls. **REJOICING**: making themselves happy. **FROM CARE in care**: from love to love because they were full of perfect charity.

---

**BROKE**: arrange it thus: then <note>original: "poscia"</note> the light in which the miraculous life of the poor man of God (that is, Saint Francis) was narrated to me: which light, as we saw above, was Thomas Aquinas, broke the silence and began to speak: because silence is broken by speaking. Whence Virgil says: *Why do you force me to break the deep silence?* <note>original: "Quid me alta silentia cogis rumpere"</note> **AMONG THE CONCORDANT DEITIES**: among the harmonious souls who, through their beatitude, had become **Deities**: that is, gods.

<insert>
Here the blessed Thomas begins to speak again to clarify the second doubt: and he uses a metaphor from threshers, saying then:
</insert>

And said: when one grain is threshed and winnowed...

<meta>This page continues from the previous discussion in Canto XIII, where Thomas Aquinas is addressing Dante’s confusion regarding the wisdom of Solomon. Dante had previously heard that Solomon was the wisest of all, which seemed to contradict the perfection of Adam and Christ.</meta>

# CANTO XIII

when its seed is already harvested
to strike the other <note>original: "abba ter laltra" — likely "abbatter l'altra," referring to striking down or resolving the second of Dante's two doubts.</note>, sweet love diminishes.
You believe that in the breast from which the rib
was drawn to form the beautiful cheek
whose palate costs the whole world so much,
And in that one which, pierced by the lance,
both after and before, gave such satisfaction
that it outweighs every sin on the scales,
Whatever light it is permitted for human nature
to have, all of it was infused
by that Power which made both the one and the other;
And therefore you wonder at what I said earlier
when I related that the good which is enclosed
in the fifth light had no second.

Now open your eyes to what I shall answer you,
and you will see your belief and my words
meeting in the truth like the center in a circle.
That which does not die and that which can die
are nothing but the splendor of that Idea
which our Lord, in loving, brings forth;
For that living light which streams forth <note>original: "si mmea" from the Latin "meare," to flow or proceed.</note>
from its radiant Source, which does not separate
from Him nor from the Love that unites them as three,
Through its own goodness, gathers its rays,
as if mirrored in nine substances,
eternally remaining one.
From there it descends to the ultimate powers,
down from act to act, becoming such
that it produces only brief contingencies;
And by these contingencies I mean
the generated things that the moving heavens
produce, both with and without seed.

<column-break/>

Having threshed the first straw: and harvested the seed that came from it <note>The commentator uses a threshing metaphor to describe resolving Dante's first doubt.</note>, the love and charity which move me to make known to others that which is not diminished. *To strike the other*: that is, since we have clarified the first doubt, I will now clarify the second. And here one should note before the translation—which is very fitting—that just as one does not extract the seed from the straw (that is, the ear of grain) if it is not well threshed, so one does not extract the hidden truth from among many falsehoods if it is not beaten and shaken with the greatest diligence. **YOU BELIEVE**: The meaning is: You believe that whatever light, intellect, and wisdom can exist in human nature was infused into the breast of Adam and into that of Christ by that divine Power (that is, the Father) who made both the one and the other (Adam and Christ). And therefore you marvel that I said above that the good enclosed in the fifth light (that is, the soul of Solomon) had no equal in wisdom, since Adam and Christ were more perfect men. This is the meaning, but he does not name them by their proper names, but by circumlocution. And therefore he says the *breast of Adam* from whose right side the rib was taken to form the *beautiful cheek* (the beautiful body of Eve). And he uses the part for the whole: *whose palate* (the sense of taste of Eve, who by tasting the forbidden fruit) *costs the whole world* (all men), because we lost the state of perpetual happiness and the power to not die. He said "palate" because the sense of taste is largely located there. And that *breast of Christ* which was pierced by the lance of Longinus gave such satisfaction for the sin of our first parents. *BEFORE AND AFTER*: as if to say, not only with his passion. *WHICH OUTWEIGHS THE SCALES OF EVERY SIN*: as if to say, if one were to put all the sins committed in one scale, and in the other the great merits of Christ's passion, the one with the merits of our Savior would outweigh the one containing all the sins of men.

He admonishes the author <note>Dante</note> to open the eyes of his intellect to what he will say, because it is something that deserves attention for its greatness and difficulty. And you will see that what you believe of Christ and Adam, and what I say of Solomon—that he had no equal—will meet in the truth *like the center in a circle*. That is, in the circle, your belief and my words will agree and reside in the truth as fittingly as the center point within a circle. **THAT WHICH**: all things that are visible and invisible, corporeal and incorporeal, are produced by God in the likeness of the Idea which God has held in His mind from eternity. "Idea" is a term produced by Plato and contested by Aristotle—not with true arguments, for no truth contradicts another truth, but with sophistical quibbles. Cicero, Seneca, Eustratius, Augustine, Boethius, Altivolo, Calcidius, and many others agree with Plato. It is, therefore, the example and form in the divine mind, in whose likeness divine wisdom produces all visible and invisible things. Plato and Hermes Trismegistus write that God knows all things from eternity. Therefore, in the divine mind and wisdom, they place the knowledge of all things, and Plato calls these "Ideas." But I will not expand upon this matter because it is much more difficult than is appropriate for this place.

**THAT WHICH DOES NOT DIE**: such as the angels, the heavens, primary matter, and human souls. **AND THAT WHICH CAN DIE**: such as things made of elements and matter. *The splendor*: that is, the effect, seal, impression, and act of that Idea we mentioned, which our Lord, our Lord God, brings forth and produces *in loving* (through His own goodness). Therefore, he rightly said "Idea," meaning God, because whatever is in God is God, and the Idea is God. *FOR*: because that *living light* (wisdom, which is true light, the Word and Son of God, of whom Saint John says: <note>original Latin: "Erat lux uera que illuminat oẽm hoiem uenientẽ in hunc mũdum"</note> <margin>271</margin> *He was the true light who illuminates every man coming into this world*). Therefore, this living light which *STREAMS* (proceeds, because *meare* in Latin means to proceed or pass through) *SO*: in such a way from its *radiant source* (its Father) that it *does not separate* (does not depart from the unity of the Father's substance) nor from the *Love* (the Holy Spirit, who *unites as three*, being the third person among them—the Father being the first, and the Son the second). And the substance of all three persons is one, as are the nature and the divinity. **BY ITS GOODNESS**: through its own benevolence and for no other reason. Whence Boethius: <note>original Latin: "Quẽ nõ externe pepulerũt fingere cãe: Materie fluitãtis opus uerũ isita fumi forma boni liuore carens."</note> *Whom no external causes compelled to fashion the work of flowing matter, but the innate form of the highest good, lacking in envy.* **IT GATHERS**: it congregates. *Its rays*: its operation, the informing power, because God is the "Form of forms" and "Cause of causes." *As if mirrored in nine substances*: that is, in the nine choirs of angels. His comparison is that just as the sun striking mirrors reflects in them, so the divine power reflects in all things created by Him. **THENCE**: from the nine heavens and from their movers, the informing power descends into the heavens, which are incorruptible form and matter, and from there to things that are corruptible form and matter. First, the informing power descends by means of the mover of the first order into the First Mobile, and into the second heaven by means of the second mover, and so on through the others. But the First Mobile also infuses its united power into the second heaven, which divides it among all its stars by the power infused by its mover; and each star of the eighth heaven infuses its power into the planets and into the things below by the power given to the planets by their movers. And so one infuses into the other, until it descends to the things below the heaven of the moon (the elements). And this is what he means by *the ultimate powers*. **FROM ACT TO ACT**: from heaven to heaven, because

<vocab>Dante Alighieri, Paradiso, Canto XIII, Solomon, Adam, Christ, Eve, Longinus, Plato, Aristotle, Boethius, Idea, creation, cosmology, angelic hierarchy</vocab>

<summary>In this passage, Thomas Aquinas explains the metaphysical process of creation, resolving Dante's doubt about Solomon's wisdom by distinguishing between the direct creation of Adam and Christ and the mediated creation of other beings. He describes the Trinity and the "Idea" in the divine mind as the source of all existence, which reflects through the nine angelic hierarchies and celestial spheres down to the material world.</summary>

Having explained that the light of the Trinity is reflected through the celestial hierarchies down to the material world, Thomas now addresses why individual things in nature—and individual humans—differ in their perfection. This leads into a clarification of Solomon’s wisdom, resolving Dante's earlier doubt.</meta>

<header>->PARADISE<-</header>

each is active and operates its virtue infused by the superiors; and the formative virtue <term>virtù informativa</term><note>The power that gives shape and life to matter.</note> descends from body to body so much that it produces nothing more than brief contingencies, that is, things that last but a short time. And these contingencies are the generated things: either with seed, like the animals that are born through coitus, or without coitus, like those that are born from putrefaction <note>Spontaneous generation—the idea that life could arise from decaying matter—was a standard scientific belief in the Middle Ages.</note>. THE MOVING HEAVEN, that is, by the movement of the sky. The heavens receive from superiors and infuse into the inferiors; and if they did not move, they would not exert their influence except in one determined place.

The wax of these and that which shapes it
do not always stay the same; and therefore, under
the ideal sign, it then shines through more or less.
From this it happens that one and the same wood,
according to its species, bears better or worse fruit;
and you are born with diverse dispositions.
If the wax were perfectly prepared,
and the heaven were in its supreme virtue,
the light of the seal would appear in its entirety.
But nature always gives it in a diminished way,
operating similarly to the artist
who has the habit of art but a hand that trembles.

the virtue of Jupiter <note>original: "ioue" (Jove/Jupiter). In astrology, Jupiter was the "Greater Benefic," associated with justice and perfection.</note> would appear perfect in that thing; but nature, which is the virtue of the heavens, gives it in a diminished way—that is, with lack and reduction—and not as it receives it from the movers. Just like the artisan who has the habit of art: that is, he possesses it perfectly, but the instruments with which he works are imperfect.

Therefore, if the warm Love disposes and seals
the clear vision of the First Virtue,
all perfection is acquired there.
Thus was the earth once made worthy
of all animal perfection;
thus was the Virgin made pregnant.
So that I commend your opinion:
that human nature never was,
nor shall be, what it was in those two persons.

Now, if I did not proceed any further,
"How then was this man without an equal?"
your words would surely ask.
But so that what is not apparent may appear clearly,
think who he was and the cause that moved him
when it was said to him, "Ask what you desire."
I have not spoken so that you could not
plainly see that he was a king, who asked for wisdom
so that he might be a sufficient king.
It was not to know the number of those
who are the movers up here, or if a "necessary"
with a "contingent" ever made a "necessary."
Nor if it is possible to grant a first movement,
or if in a half-circle one can make
a triangle that does not have a right angle.

Wherefore, if you note what I said and this,
regal prudence is that "seeing" in part
into which the arrow of my intention strikes.
And if you turn your clear eyes toward...

<column-break/>

The argumentation of Saint Thomas to demonstrate where the diversity in produced things arises, and that the principles and formal causes—that is, the informative <note>original: "informatiue"</note> ones—produce the form which, coming from the Idea, shines in them according to how the patient <note>The "patient" is the matter that receives the "action" of the form.</note> is disposed to receive and how they are disposed to flow. But they themselves are not always disposed in one way to exert influence, nor is matter always disposed to receive. And therefore, diversity occurs among individuals. **The wax of these:** the matter of individuals who are disposed to receive the impression of the heavens, which is the form infused by the ideal form. **AND THAT WHICH shapes it:** that is, the heavens themselves. **And therefore, under the ideal sign:** that is, the influence that proceeds from the Idea. **SHINES THROUGH MORE AND LESS:** From this it happens that in the same species of trees, one is better than another; and similarly in the human species, one man becomes more perfect than another. But if the matter that has to receive and the heaven that has to influence were without imperfection, that which is born from them would be perfect, just as when the wax and the seal are well-disposed, the imprint comes out perfect. For example <note>original: "verbigratia"</note>, if Jupiter, who has to give the virtue, were in Pisces or in its exaltation and joy, and were in a good aspect with good planets and free from captives, then the thing would be EXCELLENT AND

<margin>i.</margin> He concludes from the things already said: that if God works upon matter immediately, without the mediation of any other second cause, the generated thing becomes perfect. **THEREFORE:** that is, for which reason. <margin>ii.</margin> **IF THE warm love:** that is, if the divine goodness disposes and seals, because first it disposes nature to receive and then it imprints the form upon it. <margin>iii.</margin> **THE clear vision of the first virtue:** that is, the clear light of God. <margin>iv.</margin> **THERE &c.:** the thing thus generated—as were Adam and Christ—acquires all perfection. And thus the earth from which God fashioned Adam was made worthy of all the perfection that can fall upon an animal. **AND THUS WAS** the image made pregnant: that is, the incarnation of the Word. And by this, I commend your opinion as true: that human nature never was, nor shall be, as perfect as in these two.

<margin>S</margin> **IF I DID NOT proceed any further.** Your words would convince you, saying: how then was this man without equal? But so that what is hidden may appear: think who this man was and the reason that moved him to ask for prudence when it was said to him by God, "Ask." And through my words, I have shown you that it was Solomon, who in a dream asked God for wisdom so that he might rule the people well. Therefore, the cause that moved him to ask for wisdom was for the public utility, and not for the vainglory of knowing—like those who seek how many are the separate substances that move the heavens (which Aristotle posits to be as many as there are heavens), or if a "necessary" and a "contingent" premise make a necessary conclusion, as one seeks in dialectic <note>In logic, a syllogism with one "contingent" (possible) and one "necessary" premise cannot produce a "necessary" conclusion.</note>: that is, where the major premise is necessary and the minor is contingent.
**NOT whether it is possible to grant a first movement:** that is, whether the first movement exists or does not exist. Aristotle posited the movement of the heavens to be eternal. Christian theologians posit a beginning to the movement and to the world. Nor did he ask for wisdom to know if in a semi-circle one can make a triangle that does not have a right angle, which is impossible.

<margin>I</margin> In these verses, he declares how one can reconcile the belief of Dante and the statement of Thomas. For although it is most true that the extreme perfection of human nature was in Christ and in Adam, nevertheless, when it is said that Solomon had no equal, it is not meant absolutely among all men, but among kings who ruled peoples, among whom there is neither Christ nor Adam. And therefore, the poet is comforted not to affirm or deny without the proper distinction. Therefore, it is true that no man was equal to Christ and to Adam. And it is also true that no king rose similar to Solomon. I would place here the words that Solomon wrote of himself if I did not fear being...

<summary>This page explains the medieval concept of "contingency" and the role of celestial influence in the diversity of nature, using the metaphor of wax and a seal. It resolves Dante's doubt about Solomon's wisdom by clarifying that Solomon asked for "regal prudence" (the wisdom to rule) rather than absolute or scientific knowledge.</summary>

<header>CANTO XIV</header>

you will see that I had respect only 
to kings, who are many, yet the good are rare.
With this distinction, take my words;

and thus it can stand with what you believe
of the first father <note>Adam</note> and of our Beloved <note>Christ</note>.
And let this always be lead upon your feet,

to make you move slowly, like a weary man,
both to the "yes" and the "no" that you do not see;
for he is very low among the fools

who, without distinction, affirms or denies
in one case just as in the other;
because it happens that many times

current opinion leans toward the false side,
and then passion binds the intellect.
Far more than in vain does one leave the shore,

since he does not return the same as he set out,
who fishes for the truth and does not know the art.
And of this there are open proofs in the world:

Parmenides, Melissus, Bryson, and many others,
who went along and did not know where.
So did Sabellius and Arius, and those fools

who were like swords unto the Scriptures
in rendering distorted their straight faces. <note>Thomas compares heretics to curved blades that reflect a distorted image of a face, whereas true scripture is like a flat mirror.</note>

Let people not be too secure yet
in judging, like one who estimates
the corn in the field before it is ripe;

for I have seen, throughout the whole winter,
the briar show itself rigid and fierce,
then later bear the rose upon its peak;

and I once saw a ship, straight and swift,
run the sea through all its journey,
only to perish at the end at the harbor's mouth.

Let not Dame Berta and Master Martino <note>Common names used to represent "everyman" or simple, gossiping neighbors.</note> believe,
by seeing one steal and the other offer,
that they see them within the divine counsel;
for the one may rise, and the other may fall.

### CANTO XIV OF THE THIRD CANTICLE OF DANTE

<image-desc>Large decorative initial D at the start of Canto XIV.</image-desc>
From the center to the circle, and from the circle to the center,
the water moves in a round vessel,
according as it is struck from without or within.

Into my mind this thought fell suddenly,
even as I say it, as soon as
the glorious life of Thomas fell silent,

because of the similarity that arose
between his speech and that of Beatrice,

<column-break/>

too long a king. BECAUSE IT HAPPENS. He shows the reason why he is a fool who affirms or denies without distinction, saying that most of the time it happens that current opinion—because it does not stop for distinction—leans toward the false side: and then passion follows: because, as Democritus says, the love we place in a false judgment binds and occupies the intellect so that it cannot see the truth.

FAR MORE THAN IN VAIN: the meaning is this: we can say that one is "at the shore" when they have not yet thought about whether a thing is true or not. But when they begin to investigate, then they leave the shore and enter the river. Therefore, just as the fisherman, if he leaves the shore and does not have the art of fishing nor the proper instruments, leaves only to catch nothing—so he who sets himself to investigate the truth without logic <term>dialectica</term> and philosophy, and without the sciences that can show it to him, tires himself in vain. But it is even worse, because besides losing his labor, he enters into error where he was not before. Thus, he is worse than the fisherman: because the fisherman, catching nothing, returns just as he left. But this man returns in a worse state because he holds a false opinion which he did not have before. And of this there is manifest proof in the ancient philosophers who, toiling but not finding the truth, held false opinions like Melissus. He was from the island of Samos and took up the family of Heraclitus of Ephesus; and he was much commended to his citizens who did not know his virtue. He held the opinion that this universe was infinite, innumerable, and immobile; and that motion did not exist but only appeared to. He said we should not define anything about God, because we have no certain knowledge of him. Parmenides was a disciple of Xenophanes; and according to Theophrastus, he was the first to posit that the Earth is round and placed in the middle, and that the elements are two: Fire and Earth, and that fire is the craftsman and earth the material. He wrote that the generation of humans had its beginning from God, and the sun is both hot and cold, and from that everything comes. Plato, in his book of Ideas, named one *Parmenides* after him. Sabellius: just as those erred regarding first principles, so many theologians held false opinions in Christian theology and were heretics. THESE were like swords unto the Scriptures: An excellent comparison <note>original: "Optima comparatione"</note>. For true and well-learned theologians are like mirrors: they open the Scriptures in such a way that in their books one sees the straight and true sense of them, just as in a mirror one sees the true and straight face. But heretics are like swords because, just as someone looking at themselves in a sword sees their face distorted, so someone looking into the books of heretics sees the sense of the Scriptures distorted.

<image-desc>Decorative historiated initial A.</image-desc>
A golden precept is given in this place by Saint Thomas: that one should not run to judge, because often human judgment remains deceived. And he gives three examples. First, the corn, which being beautiful as grass, those who are not slow in judging think will produce much fruit, and often the opposite occurs. Similarly, the winter shows the briar to be rough, and in the spring the rose is born there. And a ship sometimes runs its journey with a following wind and then breaks in the port. And therefore he concludes that "Dame Berta and Master Martino"—that is, ignorant men—want to judge men by external acts; let them not judge that he who offers is saved and he who steals is damned; because he who steals can correct himself and rise from sin, and he who offers can fall into sin.

<image-desc>Circular diagram divided by a vertical line, containing a lowercase 'm'.</image-desc>
In this fourteenth canto, a doubt is moved, which being declared, the author finds himself ascended to the fifth heaven, which is that of Mars. Thus, first Beatrice moves the doubt. Then it is solved. In the third place, he describes the ascent to the star of Mars. In the fourth, he describes which spirits are in that place. But as for the beginning of the chapter, Beatrice moves a doubt for the author which was not yet in his thoughts; and she wants to show that through the mutual and interchangeable speech that will occur now from Beatrice and now from the spirits, his mind moved from the center where Beatrice was to the circumference where the two crowns were, and again from that circumference returned to the center. Just as in a round vessel, the water...

<header>PARADISO</header>

to whom it pleased to begin after him <note>Beatrice begins speaking immediately after St. Thomas Aquinas finishes.</note>
"This man has a need, and does not tell you,
neither with his voice nor yet in thought,
to go to the root of another truth.
Tell him if the light wherewith blossoms
your substance will remain with you
just as it is now;
and if it remains, tell how later,
when you are made visible again,
it can be that it does not harm your sight."

As, drawn and spurred by greater gladness,
those who dance in a ring at times
lift up their voices and gladden their gestures,
so, at that prompt and devout prayer,
the holy circles showed new joy
in their turning and in their wondrous song.
Whoever laments that one must die here
to live up there, has not seen here
the refreshment of the eternal rain. <note>The "eternal rain" is a metaphor for the grace of God that pours down upon the blessed.</note>
That One and Two and Three who ever lives,
and ever reigns in Three and Two and One,
uncircumscribed, circumscribing all,
was sung three times by each
of those spirits with such a melody
that for every merit it would be a just reward.

And I heard, within the most divine voice
of the smaller circle, a modest voice,
perhaps such as the Angel’s was to Mary, <note>Dante compares the voice of the spirit (Peter Lombard) to the gentleness of the Archangel Gabriel at the Annunciation.</note>
answering: "As long as the festival
of Paradise shall last, so long our love
shall radiate around us such a garment.
Its brightness follows our fervor,
the fervor our vision, and that is as great
as it has grace above its own worth.
When the glorious and holy flesh
shall be reclothed, our person
shall be more pleasing for being all entire;
because whatever the Supreme Good gives us
of freely given light shall be increased—
light which conditions us to see Him."

<column-break/>

When a vessel is struck from the outside, the water moves toward the circle, that is, the circumference; and such motion goes to the center. And if the water is struck from within, the motion is born from the center, that is, the middle, and goes toward the circumference. Water is a continuous liquid body, so that when one part of it is moved, that motion moves the adjacent part, and that the next, until the final part. This which I say of the movement of water happened suddenly—<note>original: "subito caso"</note> that is, it occurred immediately—in my mind, namely the life of Thomas—<note>original: "Thomaf'o"</note> that is, Thomas [Aquinas], who is in the true life—ceased speaking; because of the similarity that arose between his speaking and that of Beatrice. For while Thomas spoke, my mind moved from the circle to the center. And now, as Beatrice spoke, it moved from the center to the circle. Nor is it without cause that Dante does not move this doubt himself, but Beatrice does. For many doubts come into the minds of teachers while reading the Holy Scriptures, which they resolve by the power of the Holy Spirit or through other passages of the Scriptures. The poet could not have had this doubt if he had not first read in Holy Scripture about the splendor in which the glorified bodies were to be wrapped, through which they shall shine more than the sun. Therefore, Beatrice—that is, Holy Scripture—is the one who introduces the doubt of how the bodily eye will be able to endure such splendor without being blinded; for if one cannot endure it, one cannot know the other. And it is fitting that this doubt concerning excessive light be moved in this heaven <note>The Heaven of the Sun, home of the great theologians.</note> where he has found more excessive light than elsewhere. **THIS MAN HAS A NEED**: that is, a requirement. **AND DOES NOT TELL YOU**: because he does not yet know it. Tell him, therefore, first if the light that **BLOSSOMS**—that is, illustrates and illumines—**YOUR substance**: your soul, which is the substance of that splendor. **WILL REMAIN in you**: when you have reassumed your bodies and been made visible; will the splendor remain in you just as it is at present? And if it remains, tell how it can be that such splendor does not harm you <note>original: "non ui noi," from the verb *noiare*, to harm or bother.</note> and prevent you from seeing one another.

To demonstrate the gladness of those spirits at the words of Beatrice, he says that like those who dance in a ring—that is, they perform a round dance—and are always joyful. Nevertheless, at times—that is, occasionally—lifting their voice and gladdening their actions, they show greater joy; thus the souls of the two crowns, always joyful at the words of Beatrice, show more joy in their turning—that is, in moving in a circle—and in the marvelous note of their song. And certainly those who grieve over bodily death in this world, after which they go to heaven, do so because they have not seen the refreshment of the eternal rain, that is, the refreshment of the abundant grace of God which there can—that is, is widely spread. Then it follows that the crowns sang this hymn three times so sweetly that such a song would be a just **REWARD** <note>original: "muno," from the Latin *munus*, meaning a gift or duty.</note>: that is, a just remuneration for every merit that a man could acquire in this world. The hymn in praise of the Trinity was this: That God who is One in essence, and Two because He has in Himself both divine and human nature, and Three—that is, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—who are one God in essence, but three persons. Who **EVER LIVES**—and he does not say "they live" because they are one God and no more. And he uses the present tense because eternity has no distinction of past or future, but is always present. **UNCIRCUMSCRIBED**: that is, not contained, because He is infinite and is not included in any thing. **AND CIRCUMSCRIBES ALL**: because He contains every created thing within Himself.

After the hymn, the poet heard a voice more divine—that is, more heavenly—which issued from one spirit of the smaller circle where the most excellent teachers were; and he imagines it was more divine: it was as modest as perhaps the voice of Gabriel was when he announced to Mary. The poet imagines this voice was that of the **Master of the Sentences** <note>Peter Lombard (c. 1096–1160), a foundational theologian whose *Sentences* Dante studied.</note> because in truth he here solves this doubt in the form that the Master of the Sentences resolves it in his fourth book. Thus, he introduces him saying: As long as the festival—that is, the glory of Paradise—which shall always endure, so long shall our love, which is the cause of our splendor, **RADIATE**—that is, shine around such a **GARMENT**—that is, around our body. Therefore, its clarity shall always radiate and follow our fervor. For our splendor shall be as great as our charity. And the fervor shall follow the vision. For as much as we know of God, so much shall we love; and as much as we love, so much shall we shine. And the vision of God—that is, knowing God—shall be as much as the soul has of grace from God beyond its own worth. And it follows that when after the Judgment the blessed souls shall have taken back the body, which shall be glorified, their person shall be more pleasing for being entirely whole. And being then more perfect because the soul is united with the body, we shall see more perfectly. Therefore, whatever the Supreme Good—that is, God—**GIVES US OF FREELY GIVEN LIGHT** shall increase in us; that is, of the intellect, which He gives us through His benevolence...

<meta>catchword: FREELY GIVEN LIGHT</meta>

<summary>This page covers the transition in Canto XIV where Beatrice asks the spirits of the Sun to explain the nature of their light after the resurrection of the body. The commentary by Landino interprets the physics of their joy and identifies Peter Lombard as the spirit who explains that the soul's light will increase when reunited with the body.</summary>
<keywords>Paradiso, Canto XIV, Beatrice, St. Thomas Aquinas, Peter Lombard, Master of the Sentences, Resurrection of the Body, Trinity, Divine Light, Cristoforo Landino, Scholasticism</keywords>

--- Page 553 ---
<meta>This page continues from the previous discussion in Canto XIV, where a spirit (Solomon) explains how the brightness of the blessed will change after the resurrection of the body. It captures the transition from the Heaven of the Sun to the Heaven of Mars.</meta>

# CANTO XIV

...but grace. And this light **CONDITIONS US** <note>original: "NE CONDICTIONA"</note>—that is, it conditions us, making us apt to see: that is, to know Him.

Wherefore the vision must needs increase,
the fervor increase which that vision kindles,
the radiance increase which comes from it.
But just as a coal that yields a flame
and through its living whiteness surpasses it
so that its own appearance is maintained,
So this brightness which already encircles us
shall be overcome in appearance by the flesh
which the earth still covers today.
Nor will such light be able to weary us,
for the organs of the body shall be strong
for all that which can delight us.
So sudden and alert did both choruses
seem to me to say "Amen,"
that they clearly showed a desire for their dead bodies—
Perhaps not only for themselves, but for their mothers,
for their fathers and for the others who were dear,
before they became sempiternal flames.

<column-break/>

<margin>a</margin>
**H**e concludes from the things already said that it is necessary for the vision to grow—that is, the light of the intellect—and as the vision grows, the fervor will grow—that is, charity—which is kindled by the vision; and likewise the ray—that is, the splendor—will grow because it is born from the fervor of charity. **BUT JUST AS A COAL**: An excellent comparison which shows that just as we see coals in the fire so vividly lit that, although they are surrounded by flame, nevertheless their whiteness so surpasses that of the flame that they do not lose their appearance—that is, they appear and are seen. So it is with our bodies, which after death are covered by the earth. But after the Great Judgment they must return to us because they will be glorified and will have more splendor than this which currently wraps these spirits. Whence the Evangelist Matthew says: "The righteous shall shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father" <note>original: "Fulgebunt iusti ut sol in regno patris eorum"</note>. And Augustine says that the splendor of the glorified body is according to the natural color of the human body. And just as a colored body receives splendor in different ways from the illumination of the sun according to the manner of its color, so it is in the power of the glorified man that his body be seen or not seen. And in this way Christ appeared after the resurrection. Therefore, their flesh being resurrected at the age of thirty years. Whence Solomon says: "Your youth shall be renewed like the eagle's" <note>original: "Renouabitur ut aquila iuuentus tua"; Landino attributes this Psalm verse to Solomon here</note>. **NOR WILL IT BE ABLE**. Here he resolves the doubt raised above and shows that although the human sight by its nature cannot suffer so much splendor due to the weakness of the organ, nevertheless in the beatified body the sense of sight will be so strengthened that it will be able to suffer any great light without being fatigued by it. **SO MUCH** did it seem to me: The Master of Sentences <note>A reference to the theological authority of the speaker, Solomon</note> had already concluded how great the splendor of the beatified bodies would be and how the visual power in them would become stronger and more robust. // because all the spirits of the two crowns were so quick to say "Amen" to me—which means "so be it"—that they clearly demonstrated a very great desire and longing to take back their dead bodies, that is, the same bodies they had left on earth after death. And they did not only desire the recovery of the bodies for their own glory, but because they are full of charity, they desired it for the glory of their mothers and fathers and other relatives and friends whom they loved in life and before we ascended to this fourth heaven where they are eternal flames; the desire to take back the flesh is innate in us because, man being produced as a composite of soul and body, he has a natural desire to preserve both. Furthermore, it is noted here that the blessed souls retain love and honest friendship even after the separation of the body.

---

<margin>d</margin>
And behold, around, a brightness equal
began to rise above what was there,
in the manner of a horizon that clears.
And just as at the rising of early evening,
new appearances begin throughout the sky
so that the sight seems and does not seem real,
There seemed to me new substances
beginning to be seen, making a circle
outside the other two circumferences.
O sparkling of the Holy Spirit!
How sudden and glowing it became
to my eyes, which, overcome, could not bear it.
But Beatrice showed herself to me
so beautiful and laughing that among those sights
she must be left, for they do not follow the mind. <note>Dante suggests that the beauty of this moment surpasses the capacity of human memory and thought to retain or describe it.</note>
From this my eyes regained the power
to raise themselves again, and I saw myself translated
alone with my lady to a higher salvation.
Well did I perceive that I was raised higher
by the burning smile of the star,
which seemed to me more red than usual.
With all my heart, and with that speech
which is one in all, I made a burnt offering to God. <note>The "speech which is one in all" is the universal language of the heart or silent prayer.</note>

<column-break/>

<margin>d</margin>
**H**e shows that beyond the two circles of the aforementioned spirits there came a third circle which was equal in clarity to the splendor that was there before from the other two, in the manner and likeness of a horizon that clears; the souls of this third circle were not very well known to the poet. // which he feigns to show that they were not as excellent as those of the first two circles: And then he says that just as in the time between day and night the stars begin to appear—but they are still seen so little that they seem and do not seem to be there—so those souls appeared to me, who made a circle outside the two already mentioned circles. **OR THE SPARKLING**. This is an exclamation that shows he marvels at such splendor. Therefore, "or the sparkling of the Holy Spirit" <note>original: "scō spiro"</note>, as it became sudden and glowing—that is, shining—in such a form that my eyes, because they were corporeal, could not suffer such a degree of splendor. And he feigns this either to show that these were doctors who have written subtly and with obscurity, or because they were not known to him.

<margin>c</margin>
**H**e begins to describe his ascent to the fourth heaven, which is that of Marte <note>The commentator refers to Mars as the "fourth heaven," though in Dante’s standard cosmology it is the fifth; he may be counting from the Sun or following a specific tradition</note>; which he knew by seeing Beatrice more shining than usual: And the beauty and joy increased so much in Beatrice that the poet cannot express it; and for this reason he leaves it among those sights that do not follow the mind—that is, they do not follow, but rather abandon the mind when it wants to describe them. **THENCE**: that is, from that splendor of Beatrice, my eyes took virtue and vigor so that I might raise them up, and having raised them, I realized that I had ascended alone with my lady—that is, I alone with Beatrice—because the spirits of the third circles had remained in the fourth heaven. And it is certain that his sight—that is, his intellect—by virtue of Beatrice—that is, through theological doctrine—was raised to the fifth heaven. **TO A HIGHER SALVATION**: because every heaven is the salvation and glory of the spirits, he calls the heaven of Mars a higher salvation because it is higher than the others of which he has spoken; or rather a higher salvation because it is closer to God, who is our salvation; for it cannot be said that Mars is a greater salvation than the Sun. And he says that he perceived he was raised higher than when he was in the Sun, because he knew he was in Mars by its fiery color. And he wishes to show the elevation of this planet because its lowest height—which is the highest of the sun—is three thousand times one thousand and nine hundred... <note>The commentary ends mid-sentence describing the vast astronomical distances calculated in the medieval period.</note>

<summary>This page describes the spirits' longing for the resurrection of their physical bodies and Dante's subsequent ascent from the Heaven of the Sun to the Heaven of Mars. The commentary explains the theological necessity of the body's return and the astronomical markers of the new sphere.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the transition from the Heaven of the Sun to the Heaven of Mars in Dante's Paradiso. It moves from a discussion of the resurrected body into an astronomical and astrological description of Mars, followed by the poet's entry into the fifth sphere and his vision of the Cross of Light.</meta>

# PARADISO

...as befits this new grace, sixty-five thousand miles. And the highest part is twenty-eight thousand and eight hundred forty-seven thousands of miles away. The diameter of the body of Mars is equal to the diameter of the earth plus one-sixth more. Mars, because of its fiery color, is called **pyrois** <note>original: "pyrois"; from the Greek for "fiery"</note> by the Greeks, because **pyr** means fire. But its proper name in that language is **Ares** <note>original: "ares"</note>. And some called this star **Hercules**. The pagans worshipped Mars as the god of wars because it is a hot and dry planet, masculine and nocturnal. It induces heat and fire. It induces animosity, audacity, and a thirst for revenge. For this reason, it has a greater power to heat than any other planet. It makes men’s bodies long and thin because of its heat and dryness. But in old age, because the heat consumes and the dryness shrivels, it makes them curved and bent. It makes minds mobile, light, and prone to anger. Its houses are Aries and Scorpio. It reigns in Capricorn. When it is well-disposed at a man’s birth, it influences him with excellent virtue in **military discipline** <term>military discipline: Landino explains why Dante places warriors of the faith in this sphere</term>. This fact led the poet to represent in this heaven the spirits of those who, through honest and virtuous battles, merited beatitude. **WITH ALL my heart**: He demonstrates here that he could not rise to this contemplation by his own intellectual power, but by the grace of God, which is acquired through prayer made in a tongue common to all—that is, made with the mind. And this prayer is the sacrifice called a **holocaust** <note>original: "olocausto"</note>. A holocaust was that sacrifice which the ancients burned entirely in honor of God; so named because in Greek **olon** means "all" and **causton** means "burnt." He denotes by this, therefore, that he was entirely inflamed with the most ardent charity; and this sacrifice was appropriate for this new grace.

And not yet from my breast was exhausted
the ardor of the sacrifice, before I knew
that the solitary state was accepted and auspicious;
For with such luster and such **robbi** <note>original: "robbi"; an archaic term for deep red or ruby-colored</note>
splendors appeared to me within two rays,
that I said, "O **Helios** <note>original: "helios"; Landino interprets this as a name for God, though it is Greek for "Sun"</note>, who so adorns them!"
As, marked out by greater and lesser
lights, the **Galaxy** <note>original: "galaxia"; the Milky Way</note> whitens between the poles
of the world, so that it makes even the wise doubt;
So, thus constellation-strewn, those rays
within the depths of Mars made the venerable sign
which the joining of quadrants in a circle makes.

Here my memory defeats my wit,
for in that cross Christ was flashing,
so that I can find no worthy example;
But he who takes up his cross and follows Christ
shall yet excuse me for what I leave out,
when he sees Christ lightening in that dawn.
From horn to horn, and from the summit to the base,
lights were moving, sparkling intensely
as they met together and as they passed.

Thus are seen here, straight and twisted,
swift and slow, changing their appearance,
the tiny particles of matter, long and short,
Moving through the ray of light that streaks
at times the shade which people, for their defense,
acquire with wit and art;
And like a viol and harp in tuned strings...

<column-break/>

**A**nd not yet was exhausted: that is, emptied from my breast—meaning from my mind—the ardor of the sacrifice: that is, the burning fervor which issued in my mental prayer, when I recognized the **solitary state** <note>original: "solitario stato"</note>. This refers to the spirits of those holy fathers who in solitude and in the deserts had continually fought with the devil, such as **Paul the First Hermit**, **Anthony**, and the like. This state was accepted by God and was **auspicious**—that is, happy—for them. This is because the author places in this sphere all those who have fought for the faith; therefore, he divides this entire sphere with two lines which form a cross and four quarters. **FOR WITH such luster**: He states that in the body of Mars there were two very bright rays—that is, two strips—which formed a cross that divided the entire body of the planet into four squares. These strips were full of splendors so **robbi**—that is, so red—that they were blessed spirits, so that in my wonder I said: "O **Helios**"—that is, O God—as if to say, "How great is Your goodness!" **WHO SO adorns them**: "adorn" <note>original: "adobbi"</note> comes from the French word **adobare**, which means to decorate. **AS, MARKED OUT**: Like the "milky circle" which is called the **Galaxy** by the Greeks, which begins from the parallel of the Arctic pole and reaches the parallel of the Antarctic pole; it is distinct and adorned with many large and small stars. In the same way, those two strips in the depths of the body of Mars, **constellation-strewn**—that is, marked with stars which were blessed souls—made that venerable sign of the cross, which forms the **joining of quadrants in a circle**, because placing a cross in a circle creates four squares.

**B**ecause he places in this planet, as has been said, those who have fought for the salvation of souls, he describes how the Passion of Christ appeared in that cross. This Passion defeated the adversary of human nature, and it appeared such a miraculous thing to him that, although he remembered it later when he was writing, nevertheless his **wit** <note>original: "ingegno"; intellect or creative power</note> was not sufficient to find an example with which to express what he held in his memory of the flashing of the Passion of Christ; and therefore, memory defeats wit. Some texts read: "Here my memory defeats my wit," and this is easy to understand.
**BUT HE who takes his cross**: I cannot express what I saw of the victory that Christ achieved against our adversary on the cross. But he who takes his cross—that is, he who puts himself to such a battle as far as his strength allows—and follows Christ—that is, imitates the footsteps of Christ as much as he can—this man, because after death he will arrive in this planet and see that it is impossible for the human tongue to express such a victory, will excuse me for not having written it, considering that in such a dawn Christ was **lightening**—that is, the divinity of Christ was shining, which no mortal can imitate. **FROM HORN to horn**: and the lights—that is, the spirits—ran from one horn of the cross to the other: that is, from right to left, and from the head to the feet. And because when they met or passed each other they sparkled, for such an encounter revealed their mutual charity.

**T**hese lights moved along the strips of the cross just as we see here in this world the **minutie**—that is, the smallest particles of matter which are almost **atoms** <note>original: "atomi"; indivisible bodies</note>—moving in a ray of the sun which forms a streak in the shade: that is, in some building that casts a shadow, which building—meaning a house or other thing—people acquire...

...of many strings make a sweet tinkling
even to one by whom the note is not understood.
Thus, from the lights that appeared there,
a melody was gathered throughout the cross
which ravished me, though I did not understand the hymn.
I well perceived that it was of high praise,
because to me came "Rise up and conquer"
<note>original: "resurgi & uinci"; Latin for "Arise and conquer," traditionally associated with Christ’s victory over death.</note>
as to one who hears but does not understand.
I became so enamored then
that until that moment there was nothing
that bound me with such sweet bonds.
Perhaps my word seems too daring,
postponending the pleasure of those beautiful eyes
<note>A reference to Beatrice's eyes, which represent divine revelation.</note>
in which, looking, my desire finds its rest.
But he who perceives that in the living seals
of every beauty, they have more power the higher they go,
and that I had not yet turned back to them,
can excuse me for that of which I accuse myself
to excuse me and see that I tell the truth:
for the holy pleasure is not excluded here,
because it becomes more sincere as it ascends.

### CANTO XV OF THE THIRD CANTICLE OF DANTE
<note>Dante's Paradiso is the third "cantica" or book of the Divine Comedy.</note>

That benign will in which is always distilled
the love that breathes rightly,
just as greed does in the wicked will,
imposed silence on that sweet lyre
and quieted the holy strings
which the right hand of heaven loosens and pulls.
How shall those beings be deaf to just prayers,
those substances who, to give me the desire
to pray to them, agreed to be silent?
It is right that he should mourn without end
who, for the love of a thing that does not last,
eternally strips himself of that love.

As through the tranquil and pure clear skies
a sudden fire runs from time to time,
moving the eyes that were resting steady,
and seems a star that changes place,
except that from the part where it is kindled
nothing is lost, and it lasts but a moment;
so from the horn that extends to the right
to the foot of that cross, a star ran.

<margin>Folio 7v</margin>

<column-break/>

with ingenuity and art: the meaning is that they move just as one sees infinite tiny particles <note>original: "corpusculi"</note> moving in a shaft of sunlight that enters through a window into a dark house, some fast, some slow, some straight, and some crooked, often changing their appearance because the fast becomes slow and the crooked straight. And I heard through the cross a sweet melody that ravished me—that is, it drew me to itself—even though I did not understand the hymn because I did not understand the words. And that melody was gathered from the various voices of the spirits, just as we see that either a fiddle <note>original: "giga"; a medieval stringed instrument</note> or a harp, which are musical instruments, make a sweet **TINKLING** <term>tintinno: a resonant, ringing sound</term>, which is the sweet sound of many strings when they are tuned and stretched. And he adds that although he had not understood the words of the hymn, he nevertheless perceived that such melody contained the highest praise: because among many words he understood only **RISE UP: & conquer.** These two words are spoken in Holy Scripture to Christ: Rise from death and conquer the devil. The author feigns that of the whole hymn the saints sang to Christ, he understood only "rise and conquer" to demonstrate that it is easy for everyone to understand that the passion and death of Christ was the victory that freed us from the servitude of the devil. But many other marvelous things that are fitting in that place are not understood except by the most learned men. He shows that although he affirms that in all this mental pilgrimage he has found nothing until this place that bound him with more love, he nevertheless does not contradict what he has already said so many times about Beatrice; nor does he postpone her in his love. **AND SEE me tell the truth**: that is, one can see that I told the truth saying that nothing else had bound me as much as this melody: because my pleasure in Beatrice is included in that. And through Beatrice, this is understood. And the pleasure Beatrice gives me becomes more sincere and more pure the higher I ascend because her eyes show me all these things.

Because in the preceding chapter the author showed how the spirits represent themselves in the sphere of Mars, this fifteenth chapter introduces Master Cacciaguida, the father of the Alighieri and his great-great-grandfather, who narrates his genealogy to him and how, in his times, Florence was governed justly and with excellent customs. And in these first verses he narrates that the benign will that those spirits had toward the poet, in which will **IS DISTILLED** <note>original: "silique"; from the Latin *liquare*, meaning to flow or become pure</note>—that is, in which the true and honest love manifests itself, just as greed (dishonest love) manifests itself in the wicked will. **Silence put to that sweet lyre**: that is, to the hymn they were singing, which had the sweetness of a lyre or a viola. And because he called that song a "lyre," he now calls the voices of the spirits "strings." For that entire congregation of spirits was like a cithara <note>A Greek stringed instrument similar to a lyre</note> and the spirits were like the strings of that cithara: which strings the right hand of heaven loosens and pulls—that is, the grace of the Holy Spirit tempers them, pulling the strings that are too loose and loosening those too tight as it pleases Him. Then, seeing that those **substances** (the spirits) had finished singing only to give him the desire and daring to pray to them and ask what he wished to hear, and they **were agreed** (in harmony) to be silent, he asks how they could ever be deaf to just prayers. And he adds that it is a very just thing that one should grieve without end—that is, eternally—who deprives himself of that perfect love for the love of a thing that does not last eternally, which is a temporal thing.

From the infinite spirits that were upon the cross, which the poet calls "light" and "stars," one ran from the right horn of the cross, resembling certain flames which are often seen running through the sky when it is pure and serene, appearing to be stars moving from place to place. But the proof that they are not stars is that in that part of the heaven from which it departs, nothing is lost—that is, no star is missing there—and that flame lasts but a short time; whereas if it were a star, it would never be extinguished. Rather, they are vapors, of which we have spoken sufficiently above. Therefore, a **star** <note>original: "astro"</note>—that is, the spirit of Master Cacciaguida—ran as described, departing from the **constellation** <term>constellation: here used to mean the specific configuration of spirits forming the Cross</term> that **shines there**. **NOR DOES the gem part from its ribbon**: that is, although it ran across, it did not leave the ribbon of the cross, which...

<summary>Dante describes a heavenly melody within the Cross of Mars and introduces the spirit of his ancestor Cacciaguida, who moves like a shooting star. The commentary explains the theological significance of Christ's victory and the purity of heavenly love compared to fleeting earthly desires.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Dante’s encounter with his ancestor Cacciaguida in the Heaven of Mars. The previous page ended with a light moving across the cross like a shooting star; here, that light identifies itself and speaks to Dante.</meta>

<page-type>text</page-type>
<columns>2</columns>
<header>->PARADISO<-</header>

from the constellation that shines there.
**Nor did the gem depart from its ribbon,**
**but along the radial strip it ran,**
**appearing like fire within alabaster.**
<note>Dante describes a spirit moving like a spark inside a translucent stone. Alabaster was prized in the Renaissance for its semi-transparent quality.</note>

They are preserved excellently in those. And it is clear, transparent, and translucent. And I saw in Rome, in the times of Pope Eugenius IV, an alabaster vessel in which a candle shone more brightly than in the finest lantern. Dante does not speak of a hunting guide <note>A play on the name "Cacciaguida," which literally means "hunt-guide."</note> on the cross, but Cacciaguida spoke to him. This denotes that the poet was not yet of a rank to be in such a high place.

**So affectionately did the shade of Anchises reach out,**
**if our greatest muse deserves our faith,**
**when in Elysium he recognized his son.**
<note>Dante compares this meeting to the scene in Virgil's *Aeneid* where the hero Aeneas meets his father Anchises in the underworld (Elysium). Virgil is the "greatest muse."</note>

**"O my blood! O grace of God poured from above!**
**To whom, as to you, was the gate of heaven**
**ever twice opened?"**
<note>original: "O sanguis meus o super infusa gratia dei sicut tibi cui bis inquam cele ianua reclusa." The spirit speaks in Latin to emphasize his dignity and the sacredness of the moment.</note>

Thus that light; wherefore I turned my attention to him;
then I turned my face back to my lady,
and on both sides I was struck with wonder;
For within her eyes a smile was burning,
such that I thought I had touched the bottom
of my grace and of my paradise.

That is, I stood attentive to him, and then I turned back to Beatrice and was struck with wonder—that is, full of the highest admiration. **On both sides** <note>original: "QUINCI & quindi"</note>—that is, by Cacciaguida because of the words he spoke to me, and by Beatrice because in her eyes a smile burned and shone; that is, a beauty so great that I thought my eyes had touched the very bottom of my grace. That is, I thought my eyes had reached the ultimate limit of what they could see of grace and of my paradise—that is, of my glory. The meaning is that the poet, having seen the spirit (who represents the words of Holy Scripture), turned to Beatrice (who represents the interpretation of those words). And because up to this point he had not yet contemplated anything higher, he says that Beatrice burned with a greater smile than she ever had before.

**Then, joyful to hear and to see,**
**the spirit added things to his beginning**
**which I did not understand, he spoke so deeply.**

**Nor did he hide them from me by choice,**
**but by necessity, for his concept**
**was set above the mark of mortals.**

**And when the bow of his burning affection**
**was so eased that his speech descended**
**toward the mark of our intellect,**

**The first thing that was understood by me**
**was: "Blessed be you, Three and One,**
**who in my blood are so courteous."**

He did **not hide** his meaning **by choice**, because Cacciaguida did not want Dante to fail to understand. But the defect of human nature did not allow him to understand. But when **the bow of his burning affection**—that is, when his speech, from which come words of burning charity toward God, was eased, praising the divine intelligence in predestination. His speech then descended from such high matter toward **the mark**—that is, toward the limit reached by our intellect. The first thing I understood was: **"Blessed be you, Three and One"**—that is, you, God, who are one in three persons. No one understands the reason for predestination unless the supreme God reveals it. But even a mediocre mind understands that it is a just and reasonable thing for us to thank God for the benefits we have received.

**And he followed: "A pleasing and long-held hunger,**
**drawn from reading the great volume**
**where white and black are never changed,**

**You have satisfied, my son, within this light..."**

<column-break/>

He calls it a **ribbon**. But it ran through the **radial strip**—that is, the strip full of rays of the cross. Some understand that he did not depart from the right "arm" of the cross where he was, but seemed to descend because a ray moved from there in a straight line to where the poet was; and it seemed in its transit like a flame enclosed in a vessel of **alabaster**. Alabaster is a type of very white marble, so named from Alabastride, a place in Egypt not far from Egyptian Thebes, from which the ancients made vessels for ointments.

**He describes** how the welcome Messer Cacciaguida gave to Dante was as full of pity and love as that which Anchises gave to Aeneas in the Elysian Fields. **If our greatest muse**—that is, if Virgil, who writes this and is the "greatest muse," the greatest poet among the Latins—**deserves faith**. He says this as if to say he does not strictly affirm the things written by Virgil, nor that Anchises actually saw Aeneas in the Elysian Fields, as that poet feigns in the sixth book of the *Aeneid*. Rather, he uses it to show that Cacciaguida took as much joy in Dante's arrival as Virgil describes Anchises taking in the arrival of Aeneas. **"O my blood!"** <note>original: "O SANGUIS meus"</note> These are the words Messer Cacciaguida used toward Dante: "O my blood, because you are descended from my seed. O grace of God poured from above!" He says this with wonder: "O grace of God poured from above," as if given extraordinarily. "And free, as that which is given to you. To whom, I say, the gate of heaven has been twice opened." That is, to whom the door of heaven is certainly opened twice: once now with your body, and once after death. Nor is it arrogance for the poet to predict this of himself, because it harmonizes with what was said above: that one does not descend from here without returning. **Thus that light**—that is, so spoke that spirit. Wherefore I attended to him, and then turned to Beatrice and was struck with wonder, full of the highest admiration. **On both sides**—that is, from Cacciaguida for his words, and from Beatrice because in her eyes a smile burned. I thought my eyes reached the bottom of my grace—that is, the ultimate limit of what I could see. The meaning is that the poet, having seen the spirit (representing Holy Scripture), turned to Beatrice (representing its exposition). Because he had not yet contemplated anything higher, he says Beatrice's smile was greater than ever.

**He continues** by saying that the spirit of Cacciaguida added to his **beginning**—that is, to the things he had said at the start—things that were **joyful to hear**, but things I did not understand because he spoke so deeply. If we consider that the beginning was "O grace of God poured from above," what followed must have been about **predestination**. For since Dante had received the grace to ascend in the body from heaven to heaven, someone might wonder: why to Dante and not another? This leads to a dispute about predestination, showing that it does not take away **free will**. And those things are so hidden and deep that our intellect cannot comprehend them; thus the poet feigns that he did not understand. Certainly, the human intellect can understand things created by God through secondary causes (like the elements and things made from them). But those things God created without an intermediary cannot be understood. We do not understand what God is, what the light was that was the first matter, what the soul is, or what God's predestination is. No one can give a true account of these because we are not capable of divine intelligence; therefore, predestination seems to us to contradict the freedom of the will. **Nor did he hide it from me by choice**, because Cacciaguida did not want Dante to be ignorant. But the defect of human nature prevented it. But when the **bow of his burning affection**—that is, his speech of charity—was eased, his speech **descended** toward the **mark** of our intellect. The first thing I understood was **"Blessed be you, Three and One."** Only those to whom God reveals it understand predestination, but even a simple mind knows we must thank God.

**The meaning** is that Cacciaguida continued his speech, saying: "You, my son, have **satisfied** (solved) a **pleasing and long-held hunger**." To "solve a fast" means to eat. "Therefore, you have fulfilled a long desire of mine to see you, a desire I have drawn from reading the **greater volume**—that is, by looking into God, in whom the blessed, while contemplating, see all things."

<meta>Catchword: cho (short for "come," meaning "as" or "how")</meta>

# CANTO XV

...in which she appears to you, by the grace of her
who clothed your wings for the high flight. <note>Cacciaguida refers to Beatrice, who has empowered Dante to ascend through the heavens.</note>
**Y**ou believe that your thought flows to me
from Him who is First, just as from the number one,
if it is known, the five and the six derive;
**A**nd therefore, who I may be, or why I appear

**M**ut because the sacred love in which I watch
with perpetual vision, and which creates a thirst in me

sound out your will, sound out your desire,

<margin>That is, with security: boldness and happiness.</margin>

...by reading we understand what is in the book, and so he calls contemplating God "reading the volume." And he calls Him the "Greater" because in God one reads—that is, one sees—everything. Therefore, my son, you have fulfilled my will to see you, which was within this light—that is, in my mind—who am in this splendor. This will proceeded from my having seen in God that you were to ascend here by Grace, that is, by favor and benefit of her WHO clothed your wings for the high flight. That is, by the grace of Beatrice, from whom you received the feathers to be able to fly so high. And certainly, Theology is that which lends us wings, with which we raise ourselves from this low world to heaven. YOU BELIEVE THAT your thought flows [mei] to me. To flow [Meare] in Latin means to glide or pass through from that One, namely from God, who is the principle of all things, in whom every thing made or yet to be made shines; and every thought of ours, before it exists, shines forth from Him who is the principle of every number, like the five and the six and every number. For five is five times one. And because you believe this—that is, that I know your every thought because I see it in God—you do not ask me who I am, nor why I show more joy at your arrival than the others. And you believe the truth, that I know your thought and your will. For in this blessed and eternal life, all spirits, both of greater and lesser rank, look into the mirror—that is, the mirror of Divinity—in which you display [pandi], that is, you manifest your thought before you even think it. But so that the sacred love and most ardent charity in which I watch [ueglio]—that is, I stay awake, which is to say, I live. For just as sleeping is like dying, so staying awake is living. AND WHICH CREATES THIRST IN ME [ma seta], that is, increases my thirst and desire for the sweet...
<margin>MAY BE BETTER FULFILLED: That is, that my desire may grow more through your will and your desire, to which my answer is already decreed, that is, deliberated.</margin>

<insert>A</insert>fter the words of Cacciaguida, the author turns to Beatrice to understand if she wished him to respond. But she, who already knew his will without him speaking, gave a sign in a way that his will became swifter. This signifies that in no such contemplation should one proceed except according to Theology, which responds without being asked. But here he allows the poet to feign that Cacciaguida is in this glory because he died fighting for the faith.

<insert>O</insert> MY BRANCH: Cacciaguida calls the poet his "branch," not only because he is descended from him, but also because he is an ornament to that family, like the leaves upon the tree. "In whom I took delight while yet awaiting you," that is, in whom I have taken the greatest pleasure merely by expecting you. As if to say: "Before your birth, while I was in heaven, I gloried that you were to be born of my blood, and I awaited you with delight." <insert>T</insert>HEN [Poscia], that is, after these words, he said to me: "He from whom your family takes its name," that is, from whom your family is named, who had the name Alighieri; and thus this family was called. Wherefore we say "Dante Alighieri." <insert>H</insert>E WAS my son and your great-grandfather, that is, the father of your father’s father, who in Latin is called the "proavus" [great-grandfather]. He has circled for more than a hundred years the first terrace of the mountain of Purgatory, in which place (as is shown in the ninth canto of the second canticle) pride is purged. <insert>I</insert>T IS TRULY FITTING: As if to say, it is much your duty that you should shorten and abbreviate the long labor and distress he endures in purging himself, with your works—that is, with prayers, alms, and similar things. And here he demonstrates how much we are bound to help our relatives, not only the living but also the dead. Our poet, because in both Hell and Purgatory he has many times reviled our citizens, wishes now to show us that such vices were of the times rather than of the nature of our republic; which, if anyone wishes to consider rightly without passion or love or hate, will find that it is inferior to none of the Italian republics in excellence of genius, or excellent institutions, or good customs. Therefore, having so often reviled his own times, he praises the ancient way of living in Florence. **FLORENCE**, within its ancient circle of walls. It seems very difficult to me to be able to report among many and varied opinions, not only of the first building but also of the restoration; but one can clearly know how brief a space the original circle contained, not only because in many places the vestiges of the first walls still appear, but also...
