Florence, within the ancient circle of her walls,
from which she still takes Tierce and Nones, <note>Tierce and Nones refer to the bells of the Badia Fiorentina that marked the third and ninth hours of the liturgical day, serving as the city's timekeeper.</note>
remained in peace, sober and modest.
She had no little chain, no crown,
no ladies in fancy shoes, no belt
that was more to be seen than the person.
The daughter at her birth did not yet strike
fear in her father, for the age and the dowry
did not flee measure on this side or that. <note>He means that girls were not married off too young, nor were dowries so expensive that a father could not afford them.</note>
She had no houses empty of families; <note>Refers to houses left vacant due to the exile of citizens during political purges.</note>
Sardanapalus had not yet arrived
to show what can be done in the bedroom. <note>Sardanapalus: An ancient Assyrian king who became a symbol of extreme luxury and effeminacy.</note>
Monte Malo was not yet surpassed
by your Uccellatoio, which, as it is surpassed
in its rise, so shall it be in its fall. <note>Monte Malo (Monte Mario) offered a view of Rome’s grandeur, while the Uccellatoio hill offered a view of Florence. The poet suggests Florence's architectural pride will lead to a greater collapse.</note>

---

But not without laborious toil and bloody battles did they besiege you. Wherefore, despairing of his safety, Sardanapalus ordered a massive fire; and in it, he burned himself, his dearest friends, all his concubines, and his most precious things. He wrote his own tomb's epitaph to this effect: "Only that has been mine which I have eaten and drunk and consumed in love." MONTE MALO WAS NOT YET: Whoever goes to Rome by the road from Viterbo does not see it until arriving at Monte Malo nearby. But having reached this mountain, one sees all the Roman buildings. And similarly, whoever comes to Florence by the Bolognese road does not see it before reaching Uccellatoio; which mountain is five miles from Florence on the road to Bologna. But having arrived there, one sees not only the buildings of the city, but also those of the villas near the city. And because the poet wishes to rebuke the superfluous building that the Florentine people did in his time, and to praise ancient parsimony, he says that Uccellatoio, from which one sees the Florentine buildings, had not yet surpassed Monte Malo, from which one sees the Roman buildings. This, in short, signifies that in the time of Cacciaguida there was not the luxury in building that there was in the time of Dante. And then, wishing to predict the ruin of the republic, he adds: that as Uccellatoio in its rise—that is, in Florentine prosperity—surpassed Monte Malo, because Uccellatoio can show more Florentine buildings than the other does Roman ones, so it will surpass it in the fall—that is, in the ruin; from Uccellatoio one will see a greater ruin of Florence than from Monte Malo of Rome. Many in this place believe the author predicts the ruin of the city of Florence that was to be born from pride and ambition, and from the factions and partiality of the Guelphs and Ghibellines.

I saw Bellincion Berti go girt
with leather and bone, and come from the mirror
his lady without a painted face;
And I saw those of Nerli and those of Vecchio <note>Two noble but modest families of old Florence.</note>
be content with plain unlined leather,

One would keep watch, tending the cradle,
and for consolation would use the idiom
that first amuses mothers and fathers;
The other, drawing the fleece onto the distaff,
would tell stories to her family
of the Trojans, of Fiesole, and of Rome.

this is the meaning. THE OTHER drawing to the distaff: intent on spinning, she told stories, so that with them she might keep the family awake for the work being done.

the poet: in which they wore around the neck and on the sleeves chains of silver-gilt buttons strung together. And crowns and garlands made of silver-gilt foliage, and adorned with precious stones and pearls. FANCY SHOES (*Contigiate*): they called "contigie" those soled stockings covered with perforated leather. Sardanapalus had not yet arrived in Florence: that is, extreme luxury did not yet reign there, which would seek to understand "what can be done in the bedroom." Sardanapalus was the thirtieth and also the last king of the Assyrians, a man most dedicated to every kind of effeminate pleasure. He stayed locked away among his concubines, dressed and adorned like a woman, and as if he were polished. Nor would he let himself be seen by anyone. This so delicious and idle a life gave hope to Arbaces, captain of the Persians and Medes who served in the king's guard, to be able to take the kingdom from him. And he conferred with Belesys, who also found himself in such service as captain of the Babylonians. And because he was learned in astrology, he willingly undertook the enterprise, because the stars promised him indubitable victory. They were therefore twice broken by the king's armies. But finally they besieged him.

There was certainly in those times supreme temperance and parsimony and sobriety in our people. Considering that Bellincion Berti, a rich knight and born of the noble lineage of the Ravignani, wore no other belt than of leather with a bone buckle. And his lady without cosmetics and colors. The houses of these knights were in the gate of San Piero. But by the inheritance of Gualdrada his daughter, who was the wife of the first Count Guido, they remained to the Conti Guidi. THOSE OF VECCHIO: of these we will speak in the following chapter. WITH PLAIN LEATHER: because they wore clothes of tanned skins without fur, like chamois and the like. And the ladies at the spindle and the distaff: as if at the feminine exercise. O FORTUNATE: O happy women. And the passage is taken from Juvenal: <note>original: "Prestabat castas humilis fortuna latinas. Hanibal."</note> "Humble fortune used to keep the Latin women chaste of old; nor did toil and short sleep and hands toughened and hardened by Tuscan wool-working and Hannibal close to the city allow vice to touch their small homes." And each was certain of her burial: because there were no civil dissensions through which they feared they would have to go into exile with their husbands. And yet none was deserted in her bed: that is, abandoned by her husband for France. So much greed for gain had not yet come that Florentine merchants would go to France or other regions to profit. ONE WOULD WATCH TENDING THE CRADLE: that is, the care of the little child; and comforting said little child, she used the idiom: that is, speaking like a child, comforting him when he cried, which idiom amuses fathers and mothers at first. Since the first pleasure that the father and the mother take with the child is when he does not yet know how to speak...

This Conrad, in whose army Cacciaguida served, was Conrad I <note>The commentator likely means Conrad III, but identifies him here as "the first" Emperor of that name to lead such an expedition.</note> in the years of our Lord 1015. This squares well because the poet writes this in the year 1300. And it is likely that from his great-great-grandfather to this time, 285 years had passed. Nor is it against the art of poetry that he introduces Cacciaguida praising himself, because it is not out of arrogance or any kind of pride or vainglory—which vices cannot exist in those who are already confirmed in grace. But he does so to simply narrate the truth, which is an excellent example to all men that they should not refuse death for the defense of the Christian faith; understanding that he, immediately after such a death, remained so purged that without any delay in Purgatory he ascended to Heaven. For which reason let our people stand ready, and especially in these times let them have a mind unconquered and prompt for every grave danger against the most cruel Turks who—<note>original: "quod nunquam veriti sumus"</note> a thing we never feared—are in Italy this year; since in so brief a space <note>original: "in si brieve spatio"</note> one can acquire the celestial and holy kingdom. **TO THIS PEACE**: that is, to the highest good, which as we showed above is placed in celestial peace. But regarding the highest good and the various opinions of the ancients, we treated this at length in the second book of our *Camaldolese Disputations and Allegories*; this place does not require us to treat it now, as it requires more exquisite diligence.

### CANTO XVI OF THE THIRD CANTICLE OF DANTE.

O our small nobility of blood!
If you make people glory in you
down here where our affection languishes,
it will never be a wonder to me;
for there, where appetite does not warp—
I mean in Heaven—I myself gloried in it.
Truly you are a cloak that quickly shortens,
so that if one does not add to it day by day,
time goes around it with its shears.

<column-break/>

Wisely, at the beginning of this sixteenth chapter, the poet rebukes those who take vainglory in the antiquity of their blood as if it were great nobility. Afterward, he leads Cacciaguida to describe the entire origin of his house. And after such description, he narrates the state that existed in our Republic in that age. And at the end, he names many Florentine families. **O OUR SMALL NOBILITY OF BLOOD.** The poet uses an appropriate exclamation, demonstrating that the nobility consisting in the antiquity of blood is truly "small." But nonetheless, it is no wonder if here among mortals, where our affection languishes and is sick—that is, where disturbances and appetite, by being discordant with reason, are sick and not upright—people glory in it, when he, being in Heaven where appetite does not warp (because it is direct and does not depart from reason), gloried in it. True nobility is the virtue of the soul. But civil nobility, according to Aristotle, is antiquity of blood. And it seems he wishes to express that men even...

F

<meta>This page continues the transition from Canto XV to Canto XVI of the *Paradiso*. Having met his ancestor Cacciaguida, Dante reflects on the nature of nobility before questioning him about the history and topography of ancient Florence.</meta>

<header>PARADISO</header>

placed in the highest contemplation: they cannot help but take a vain pride in the antiquity of their blood. **FEW TIMES**: because it rarely happens that a family maintains its name for a long time without virtue, or can acquire honors, dignity, and wealth without it; therefore it happens that such a family is esteemed noble. But because in truth virtue alone is that which makes a man noble, and often it happens that men through crooked and vicious ways acquire wealth, dignity, and lordship, it follows that they cannot be called noble for this reason. Wherefore he said "few." Nevertheless, when through virtue such things have been acquired, it is to be tolerated if someone, though wise, glories in such antiquity. **WELL ARE YOU A CLOAK**: An excellent comparison. Inasmuch as the glory of the virtues of the first ancestor, though it extends to his descendants, nevertheless, if they do not continually maintain it with their own virtues, time in its progress consumes it, just as a garment is consumed little by little when trimmed with scissors. For example, it is reasonable that from some of the men who were once in great fame, descendants remain; but because virtue is not maintained in such succession, they are not recognized, and in a short time their fame passes away.

Since Rome first tolerated
the use of the plural <note>original: "voi"</note> in which her family persists least,
my words began again.
And Beatrice, who was a little apart,
appeared smiling, like the lady who coughed
at the first recorded fault of Guinevere. <note>In the Arthurian romance of *Lancelot*, the Lady of Malehaut coughed to show she noticed the first secret kiss between Queen Guinevere and Lancelot.</note>
I began: "You are my father;
you give me such boldness to speak,
you lift me up so that I am more than myself.
By so many streams, my mind is filled
with such joy that it rejoices in itself,
because it can sustain it without breaking.
Tell me then, my dear first-born,
who were your ancestors, and what were the years
that were marked in our childhood?
Tell me of the sheepfold of Saint John, <note>A poetic name for Florence, whose patron saint is St. John the Baptist.</note>
how large it was then, and who were the people
within it worthy of the highest seats."

<column-break/>

After the exclamation made regarding nobility, the poet turns his words to Cacciaguida to ask him more fully about his family and the other noble Florentine families. And he says that his words "began again," i.e., he began his speech again with the formal "You" <note>original: "voi"</note>; for the beginning of his speech was "You are my father." Thus he began to say "You" to him, whereas above he had said "Thou," as appears above when he said: "Well I pray to thee, living topaz, that thou mayest satisfy me with thy name." And because it is considered incorrect speech to say "You" to a single person as if they were more than one, he says that Rome first suffered and tolerated the plural "You" when Caesar was made perpetual dictator; for having included all other magistrates under his power, when a man spoke to him, it seemed he was speaking to many. And therefore he did not say "I pray to thee, Caesar," but "I pray to you, Caesar." And the poet says this regarding the "You" that was said to one person, which Rome was the first to tolerate, using such flatteries to Caesar, and in which "You" the family—that is, the Roman citizens—persist least. For from that time until now, almost all nations and peoples say "You" to one person, except for the Romans who say "Thou" to every man. This seems to be the poet’s meaning. And the commentators explain it thus, and bring as testimony these verses from the fifth book of Lucan: <note>original: "Namque omnes voces per quas in tempore tanto / Mentimur dominis haec primum repperit aetas"</note> <term>Lucan</term> <note>A Roman poet whose work *Pharsalia* was a primary source for Dante’s history of the Roman civil wars; the quote translates as: "For all the titles by which for so long a time we have lied to our masters, this age first discovered."</note> Returning then to the text, he began to say: "You, Cacciaguida." And Beatrice, though she was somewhat "sceura"—that is, separate—indicated by her smile that she saw and heard, and almost comforted him in his speaking. "Sceuerare" is a word derived from "secernere" <note>To separate or distinguish.</note>. And the author places Beatrice here as separate from them to show that this conversation was not about theological matters; but nonetheless, it was not forbidden by theology but allowed, because they were moral matters which theology accepts and approves. And he uses the comparison that her smile was a signal to him, just as to Guinevere at her first fault the cough was a signal when she came to the kiss through the mediation of Galehaut. And her companion, who was not seen, saw them and coughed to show she had noticed, as is written at length in the fabulous and not very elegant book of the *Round Table*. **YOU ARE MY FATHER**: because not only the one who generates us is our father, but every superior from whom we are descended. **YOU GIVE ME** such boldness in speaking: because being of your seed, I take such confidence. **THAT I AM MORE THAN MYSELF**: because you give me more strength than is human. And joy comes into me from you by so many streams—that is, from so many parts—that my mind rejoices in itself because it is like a fountain of joy. And since it rejoices in itself, it can resist so that it does not break. **TELL ME THEN**: he asks to know three things: who were his ancestors; in what time he was born; and how large Florence was then; and which were the most worthy families. And he calls Florence the "sheepfold of Saint John." Because Saint John is the pastor of the Florentine people, Florence is his sheepfold.

---

As a coal bursts into flame
at the blowing of the winds, so I saw that
light shine at my blandishments;
and as it became more beautiful to my eyes,
so with a voice more sweet and soft,
but not with this modern speech,
it said to me: "From that day on which 'Ave' was said
to the birth in which my mother, who is now a saint,
was unburdened of me, with whom she had been heavy,
this fire came five hundred, fifty,
and thirty times to its Lion
to re-ignite itself under its paw.
My ancestors and I were born in the place..."

<column-break/>

Becoming more splendid and with a sweeter voice, Cacciaguida responded that from the day of the Incarnation of Christ <note>The day the Angel Gabriel said "Ave" (Hail) to Mary.</note> until his birth, Mars (in which planet they found themselves) had returned to the sign of Leo—where it was when Dante was born—five hundred and eighty times. Leo is the domicile of the Sun, and the Sun enters it on the fourteenth day of July. And because Mars does not return to any sign in less than two years, it follows that it was one thousand one hundred and sixty years <note>580 cycles of Mars roughly equal 1090-1160 years, dating Cacciaguida’s birth to 1091 AD.</note>. He demonstrates three things: the years of Christ in which he was born; what sign Mars was in; and that his mother is saved [in heaven]. And he continues saying that he was born in the place where those who run the annual game—which is the race <note>original: "palio"</note> of Saint John—find the last ward <note>original: "sesto"</note>. And because those who run come from the western part of the city toward the east, the last ward they find is that of Porta San Piero, which is to the east. This ward began from Porta San Piero, which was where the Canto de’ Pazzi is at present, and came into the Mercato Vecchio, and joined with the ward of San Brancazio which is to the west, and with the ward of the Duomo or San Lorenzo which is to the north; and from Mercato Vecchio toward the Arno in the south, two wards remain: San Piero Scheraggio to the east, and Porta Santa Maria to the west. And the last ward was further...

<meta>This page continues Cacciaguida’s discourse on the history of Florence. Having established his own identity, he now contrasts the "pure" Florence of his youth with the corrupted city of Dante’s time, blaming the influx of rural families and the conflict between the Church and the Empire for the city's decline.</meta>

<columns>2</columns>
<page-num>XVI</page-num>
<header>CANTO / XVI</header>

> where one first finds the last ward
> by those who run your annual race.
> Let it suffice to say this of my ancestors:
> who they were and where they came from
> is more honest to keep silent than to discuss.

**H**e follows in the narration by demonstrating that the men whom Florence produced to bear arms were a fifth of the number of those in the time when Florence stood between Mars and the Baptist <note>This refers to the boundaries of the ancient city, marked by the statue of Mars on the Ponte Vecchio and the Baptistery of St. John.</note>—that is, when it had begun to leave behind the pagan faith, in which they had the temple of Mars, and take up the Christian faith, in which they consecrated said temple to Saint John the Baptist—compared to those who were in the poet's own time. Then he laments that from the castle of Campi near Prato, from the castle of Fighine in the upper Valdarno, and from the castle of Certaldo in Valdelsa, "villains" <note>In this context, "villano" refers to a rural peasant or someone from the countryside (the *contado*), whom the Florentine elite often viewed with suspicion.</note> have come and become citizens. Thus, the citizenry, which was previously pure down to the lowliest artisan—because everyone was Florentine down to the last craftsman—is now mixed. This has been such a ruin to the city that it would have been better if the aforementioned lands had not been made part of the Florentine territory, because this is the reason they were able to become citizens. Instead, the territory should not have extended further than Galluzzo and Trespiano. If that were the case, the "villain" of Aguglione—who was Messer Baldo d’Aguglione—and he of Signa—who was Messer Bonifacio da Signa—would not have become citizens. These men committed much barratry <note term="barratry">The sale of public offices or judicial favors for money.</note>, selling favors and benefits; and therefore he says that to commit barratry, he has a sharp eye—that is, to practice corruption.

> All those who at that time were there
> to bear arms between Mars and the Baptist
> were a fifth of those who are living today.
> But the citizenry, which is now mixed
> with people from Campi, Certaldo, and Fighine,
> was seen to be pure down to the last artisan.
> Oh, how much better it would be to have as neighbors
> those people I mention, and at Galluzzo
> and at Trespiano to have your border,
> than to have them within and endure the stench
> of the villain from Aguglione, and he of Signa,
> who already has a sharp eye for barratry.

**H**e intends that the great discord that existed between the Church and the Emperor—from which the sects of the Guelphs and Ghibellines were born throughout Italy—was the reason why, as cities were emptied by the exile of those driven out, they were filled with peasants. And such a mixture of men—part ancient, part new—because they are of diverse wills and customs, generates turmoil in the city just as a variety of foods does in the stomach. **IF THE PEOPLE OF THE WORLD WHO MOST DEGENERATE** <note>original: "Selagente chel mondo piu tra ligna"</note>—that is, the Apostolic Church, which has most degenerated and fallen away from its first founders—**HAD NOT BEEN A STEPMOTHER**—that is, a cruel mother—**TO CAESAR**—that is, to the Emperor. The meaning is: if the Church, whose head is the Pope—which church ought to be a pious mother to all—had not become a stepmother instead of a mother (that is, unjust and cruel as stepmothers are toward stepchildren) to Caesar (the Emperor), but had been as kind as a mother, then the discords between the Church and the Empire would not have been born. And if those had not been born, the factions in the republics would not have arisen, especially in ours; which, being emptied by the exile of many, has made a citizen and a merchant of such a man who would have stayed in Semifonte—a castle that was captured with great effort by the Florentines and destroyed in the year 1202.

> If the people who most degenerate in the world
> had not been a stepmother to Caesar,
> but like a mother to her son, kind,
> certain men, now Florentines who trade and exchange,
> would instead have turned back to Semifonte,
> there where their grandfathers went begging.
> Montemurlo would still belong to the Counts;
> the Cerchi would be in the parish of Acone,
> and perhaps the Buondelmonti in Valdigrieve.
> Always the confusion of persons
> was the beginning of the city's woes,
> as added food is to your stomach.
> And a blind bull falls more headlong
> than a blind lamb; and many times
> a single sword cuts better and more than five.

**B**ecause the poet had asked which were the noble families in his time, and Cacciaguida had to tell of many that in Dante’s time had nearly disappeared, he shows that it is not to be wondered at if families fail over time, since even cities fail. He proves this by mentioning Luni, a city at the end of Tuscany next to the mouth of the Magra river. **URBISAGLIA**: This city was in the March of Ancona, not far from Macerata. **Chiusi**: a city between Siena and Perugia where King Porsenna once reigned, made noble by the admirable labyrinth described by Pliny.

> If you look at Luni and Urbisaglia,
> how they have gone, and how Sinigaglia
> and Chiusi are following after them,
> to hear how lineages undo themselves
> will not seem a new or difficult thing to you,
> since even cities have their end.

<column-break/>

Therefore, since Cacciaguida's ancestors were born in that place in Florence where he who runs the race for the cloak of Saint John first finds the last ward of those for which he runs, we understand this to be in the Mercato Vecchio (Old Market) and on the borders of the ward of Porta San Piero. **LET IT SUFFICE CONCERNING MY KINSMEN**: Either our poet did not know of a more ancient origin for his family than Cacciaguida, or he knew it was ignoble and lowly, and therefore he has Cacciaguida say that this is enough.

**MONTEMURLO WOULD STILL BE**: This castle is not far from Prato and belonged to the Conti Guidi. This would still belong to the Counts because the Emperor would have forbidden injuries between the Florentines and the Counts, and everyone would have stayed within their own bounds. And the Cerchi, of whom we spoke in the *Inferno*, had there not been wars, would have stayed in the parish of Acone, which is above the bridge at Sieve. The Buondelmonti were noblemen in Valdigrieve and possessed Montebuoni and other castles which, after a long siege, they gave to the Florentines on the condition that they become Florentine citizens. **ALWAYS THE CONFUSION**: He demonstrates that mixing diverse men into one republic—because they are of diverse natures and customs—generates confusion, like diverse foods in the stomach. Because someone might say that through such a mixture the Florentine people became more robust, he responds that this is the cause of its ruin, and he shows it through the comparison of the bull and the lamb. For the bull, in its fury, does not know how to stop and, spinning around, it falls. But the lamb, which is peaceful and mild, lies down and therefore does not fall. Thus, great cities, through their great power, become proud; and through their great pride, they trouble others, wherefore they often fall into ruin. But small ones, because they do not fight others, last longer. Understand the same regarding the swords.

even though it may be hidden from you in some
that last a long time, and lives are short.
And as the turning of the moon’s heaven
covers and uncovers the shores without rest,

Therefore it should not seem a marvelous thing,
what I shall say of the illustrious Florentines
whose fame is now hidden by time.
I saw the Ugli and I saw the Catellini,
Filippi, Greci, Ormanni, and Alberichi,
already in decline, those illustrious citizens.

The second is the place where they are positioned. <note>This prose section appears to be a technical explanation of lunar influence on the humors and tides.</note> of the animal: and it supplies strength from every side. <column-break/>

in the book of natural history. Senigallia is this city between Ancona and Fano on the shore of the Adriatic sea: which in our times Sigismondo Malatesta <note>The famous condottiero and lord of Rimini (1417–1468).</note> tried to restore: But the war that Pope Pius II waged against him interrupted the work. "Your things," that is, the things of mortals, all have death: because they are all born and composed of the four elements and every thing born dies if it comes by means of secondary causes: and every thing composed is dissolved: But because some last a long time, such as certain cities, they seem to many to be immortal: because the life of a man is so brief that he cannot see the end of them: Therefore, returning to the point, as we see the sea in many places cover and uncover the shores according to the motion of the moon: so does the fortune of Florence: because in this republic the state does not stay firm in those same families, but fortune pushes it now to this family: now withdraws it to itself and sends it to another. But because it touches upon the motion of the moon, it is not useless to know that although every planet induces its effects in lower things: nevertheless the sun and the moon induce them more effectively for three reasons. Of which the first is the quantity of light, which is greater in these...

The moon, because it is closer to the lower things: and for this reason it is more similar to the nature of those things and influences them more effectively. This governs the moisture of bodies. Wherefore it nourishes metals and plants and the limbs of animals. The third is that the moon, because it is contrary to earth and water, moves all things in which earth and water predominate. There are various movements. For some never swell... one until the fifteenth: and in the rest they decrease, as is the Persian Gulf. The Indian sea and of all the islands that... and between England and Flanders and Germany. They grow... and returns until it descends from the middle of heaven to the west... and again it decreases until it arrives at our east. And each... are two equal circles making four arcs. For the circle... of the horizon makes the first arc in the east and the second in the west. And the meridian circle makes the first arc in the middle of... the second in the opposite part under the earth. Therefore when the moon touches the arcs of the... meridian it makes it decrease. We have spoken of the moon. Now, because the poet mentions the first circuit of Florence: and also many ancient families, it will not be useless nor even ungracious to the listener to relate in brief words the ancient boundaries both of the first and the second circle of the city. Nevertheless, there still remain so many vestiges that it is not very difficult for one who searches with great diligence to find the truth: and we on this part easily agree with Ricordano Malispini, a writer of a chronicle: a man if not learned, nonetheless very faithful and diligent: and who in all his things strives to bring testimony. This was in the year twelve hundred of our salvation. These were then the first walls where the remains of Capaccio still exist: almost the "head of the waters" <note>original: "caput aquarum"</note>: because here the waters of the aqueducts fell: and from here they came to where the houses of the Ormanni were, today called Foraboschi. And from there toward San Martino encircling the houses of the Uberti and the Ormanni: and from San Martino to where the tower of Santa Reparata is: and then passing near the place where the loggia of the Adimari was, it reached the Frascato tavern: and then it turned toward the corner of the Ferravecchi, encircling part of the space where the Arrigucci later were and Santa Maria in Campidoglio and it returned to Capaccio by the square of San Miniato among the towers. Inside this city were sixty-two inhabited towers belonging to noblemen: who, according to what many affirm, were largely Romans. One gate was at San Martino. The fourth at Ferravecchi. These... and Malispini lived at the square of Santa Cecilia then called... We have said whether it was destroyed by Totila or not: because... searched the chronicles of those times. But I firmly affirm that from Charlemagne it was either rebuilt or restored larger than before, if it was first destroyed or if not. Through conjectures and through various chronicles I have read... not that Florence was undone by Totila but by persistent wars both with the Fiesolans and various barbarian nations it was largely desolated: because the most powerful citizens were reduced to the surrounding castles and fortresses where they lived more securely. But coming then in the year eight hundred and two. Charlemagne, returning from Rome to France having been elected emperor, stopped at Florence and enlarged it. And he brought the nobles of that city inside the walls: who were previously scattered in various places. And the circuit of the walls beginning from the eastern part was then where the houses of Messer Bellincion Berti Ravignani were: and there was Porta San Piero: and a suburb up to San Pier Maggiore. Then followed the walls toward San Giovanni and the Bishopric: and there was the second gate called the Cathedral Gate <note>Porta di Duomo</note>: and going out from that one found Borgo San Lorenzo. They proceeded then to the walls up to Santa Maria Maggiore and up to San Pancrazio where the third gate was, named after the saint: leaving similarly Santa Trinita outside: and not far from that temple was a postern called the Red Gate <note>Porta Rossa</note> by which the street is still named today. The fourth was the gate of Saint Maria. In the first circle among the first families he found the Alberighi, Filippi, and Infangati, three families. But they all had their origin from one sixth man in those times who was very reputed. And from Arriguccio come the Arrigucci, masters and descendants of the Bishopric of Fiesole: because they came from there. Constant enmities lasted between Florentines and Fiesolans for about five hundred years. Finally, the Florentines entered Fiesole by surprise: and destroyed it all except the bishopric. And they brought all the noble families to Florence: among whom were the Pazzi and the Canigiani. Whence both one family and the other have the moon <note>Referring to the crescent moon in their coats of arms</note>. Furthermore, they combined the insignia of the republics. The arms of the Florentines were the red shield and the lily, then white. And the arms of Fiesole were the white shield and the blue moon. Therefore they made a shield divided lengthwise, white and red: and this remained the ensign.

# CANTO XVI

...of the Florentine people made of two peoples <note>This refers to the union of the original Roman settlers and the people of Fiesole</note>: and this was the standard that was carried in the military <note>original: "militia"</note>: and it was called the **carroccio** <term>carroccio<note>A large, four-wheeled ceremonial chariot pulled by oxen, used by medieval Italian republics to carry the city's banner and altar into battle</note></term>: which the men who governed the republic administered. In its second circle of walls, Florence had one hundred and fifty towers, each more than one hundred cubits <note>original: "braccia"</note> high. There were the **Lamberti**, **Ormanno**, **Ormanni**, and **Tano dell’Archa**. These seven families were therefore noble in their time. Furthermore, he also made knights from these other families: the **Galigai**, **Alepri**, **Della Pressa**, and **De’ Buonaguisi**. But these last three were born from the Galigai, as were the **Giugni**. The **Uberti** were located where the Piazza dei Priori <note>Now the Piazza della Signoria</note> is today. The **Ormanni**, or **Foraboschi**, were near Santa Cecilia, and nearby were the **Malefispini**; and on the other side toward Orsanmichele were the **Tebalducci**, and then the **Compiobesi**. And toward Calimala were the **Chiaramontesi**, **Guadagnuoli**, **Malpigli**, and **Romaldegli**. Then came the **Cavalcanti**. There were the **Glebati** and the **Macci**, who were neighbors at the Garbo toward Saint Martin; the **Galigai**, **Giugni**, and **Buonaguisi**, and those of the **Pressa**, and the **Alepri**, all born of the Galigai. Then at the end of the Garbo were the **Facchetti**. And along the street today called Anguillara were the **Schelmi**, and in the other street the **Greci**, for whom it was then named; but these were first in the Terme district. The **Magalotti** were not far from the Facchetti: they were toward the Arno, as were the **Belculacci** and those of the **Asino**. Behind the Ormanni were placed the **Maniieri** and those of the **Pera**, whom the poet <note>Dante</note> affirms were extinguished in his time. Toward Saint Romeo were the **Guidalotti**, **Bagnesi**, those of the **Migliaccio**, and those from **Cuona**, consorts of those from **Volognano** and **Castiglionchio**. The **Infangati**, or "Eaters," were between the Mercato Nuovo and Santa Cecilia. In the Vacchereccia were the **Baroncegli**, descended from Baroncello; having been reduced to a small number, they practiced the "hunt" <note>original: "caccia"</note>, meaning they were wise men of the common people. Toward the gate of Santa Maria were the **Fifanti**, **Galli**, **Cappiardi**, and **Philippi**. Then came the **Scolari** and the **Buondelmonti**, who were of one blood and were lords of Monte Buoni, where they collected tolls <note>original: "passaggio"</note>. These were in the street that goes into the Terme as far as the Borgo Santo Apostolo. In the Terme were the **Giudi** and **Importuni**. And on the corner of the gate of Santa Maria were the **Gualterotti**. At Santa Trinita were the **Palermini** and **Scali**, and further toward Santa Maria Maggiore were the **Barucci**. But all three of these families were of one blood. Then to Santo Apostolo came the **Altoviti**, whose origin was Bernardo di Pagholo Altoviti, a man of much industry and natural eloquence, but reported to be descended from Tebalduolo the Longobard, who served as a soldier under Alboin, King of the Longobards. After the King's death, he made his home at Poggio Imperiale. From him are descended the **Altoviti**, **Corbizi**, and **Squarcialupi**. The Altoviti spread through the Val d’Arno and were owners of almost all of it. Later, twelve families were called by the Florentine people and also granted citizenship, among whom were the **Medici**, who many times have held the supreme government of the Florentine Republic, and the **Altoviti**, **Ricci**, **Albizi**, **Guasconi**, and **Strozzi**. But the **Medici**, **Ruccellai**, and **Altoviti** conspired against the Duke of Athens <note>Walter VI of Brienne, a short-lived tyrant of Florence</note> and at the palace gate killed some of his barons and his first secretary. Then came the **Bonciani**, descended from Sir Guido, a French baron of Charlemagne; upon Charles’s departure, he remained in Florence. I have clear evidence of the antiquity of this house: because Neri di Guido Bonciani, a well-learned man of excellent character, showed me a marriage contract in that family made by papal dispensation between Lottiera and Bartolo, both of the Bonciani, as far back as the year of Christ 1368. In Porta Rossa were the **Cosi**, kinsmen of the **Adimari**, who built Santa Maria Nipotecosa at the corner of the Giglio. Near the Barucci were the counts of **Gangalandi**, so named from a man called Conte who was the founder of that family, and not because they were actually counts. Near these were the **Ciuffagni**. Near Santa Trinita were the **Soldanieri**. Around San Miniato tra le Torri were the **Pigli** and the **Erri**, born of one blood. Among the iron-workers <note>original: "ferrauecchi"</note> are the **Manfredi**, **Vecchietti**, **Miglioregli**, and **Ughi**, from which family the name Montughi was taken. Near the Vecchietti were the **Benvenuti**. At the end of the street were the **Tornaquinci**, who later divided into the **Tornabuoni**, **Giachinotti**, and **Popoleschi**. Around San Piero Buonconsiglio were the **Cipriani**, **Toschi**, and **Amieri**. Around Santa Maria in Capitolio were the **Alfieri**, **Errigucci**, **Corbizi**, **Brunelleschi**, **Del Becchuto**, and **Agli**; and toward the Mercato Vecchio, the **Galluzi**. In the Mercato Vecchio were the **Nerli**, but their houses were later occupied by the Amieri. Opposite the Nerli were those of the **Tosa**, of the lineage of the **Visdomini**. The **Gubaldini** were between San Tommaso and the Bishopric; and near the church of San Tommaso were the **Agolanti**. Later, the **Minerbetti** lived opposite San Miniato tra le Torri where the Borghese pawnshop <note>original: "presto del borghese"</note> is currently located. For a long time, they had private enmities with the Amieri, a Ghibelline family. When the Guelfs were exiled, the Amieri burned their houses. Later, when the Guelfs returned with the favor of the French royals and the Lucchesi, the Guelf party restored their ruined houses; and on the exterior walls of these, in perpetual memory, they painted the arms of the Party, of France, and of the Minerbetti, which still remain there today. Tommaso d’Andrea Minerbetti, a man adorned with letters and very dutiful, once showed me these writings. At the Cathedral gate were the **Figiovanni**, **Fidolfi**, **Fighineldi**, **Cattani** from Barberino di Mugello, and the **Ferrantini**. The **Visdomini** are toward Saint Benedict and the Porta San Piero. Furthermore: the **Thebaldini**, **Donati**, **Ravignani**, and **Alberighi**. And from Santa Maria, the **Guochi** and the **Stoldi**; and toward Saint Martin, the **Bonitii** and the **Razzanti**, who came from Fiesole. Not far away are the **Adimari** and the **Elifei**, from which family our poet <note>Dante Alighieri</note> came; and the **Malesecti**. In the Mercato Vecchio were the **Caponsacchi** from Fiesole, and from Saint Andrew, the **Catellini**, also from Fiesole. The **Lamberti** were at Santa Maria Sopra Porta, and the **Tebaldi** lived in the Iron Alley, called after the "stella" <note>The "ustella" or "ostella" likely refers to a specific landmark or tavern sign</note>. In the Mercato Nuovo were the **Giandonati**, **Bostichi**, and those of the **Zannella**. Also the **Uccellini**, kinsmen of the Donati, and those of the **Archa**, and the **Pesti**. The **Girolami** were at the Gate of Santa Maria; from their family came Saint Zenobius, Bishop of Florence. Near these were the **Amidei**, **Gherardini**, and their kinsmen the **Teneanti**. Then the **Pulci**, and toward the Abbey, the **Ardinghi** and **Ubriachi**; and in Porta Rossa, those of the **Forese** and the **Monaldi**. The **Pazzi** of Florence were near Santa Maria in Campo. Later, the **Medici** lived near the Mercato Vecchio.

**Greci**: In their decline, these people went to Bologna, and having been extinguished in Florence, they lived there. **THE STOCK** <note>original: "LO CEPPO"</note>: From which the **Calfucci** were born. These were the Donati, from whom descended another family called Calfucci. **Column of vair** <note>original: "Colonna del uaio"</note>: These are the **Pilli**, whose coat of arms is a red shield containing a column of vair <note>Vair is a type of heraldic fur, usually represented by blue and white bell shapes</note>. **BLUSHING** for the state: These were the **Chiaramontesi**, one of whom, being in charge of the public grain supplies and especially the wheat, removed a stave <note>original: "doga"</note> from the bushel measure <term>staio<note>A standard Florentine dry measure for grain</note></term> and made it smaller. When the fraud was discovered, he was punished with the death penalty; and the measure was later remade in iron so that it could no longer be defrauded. **The stock**: refers to the Donati, from whom the Calfucci descended. **To the cruel** <note>original: "alle crudele"</note>: that is, to the first and most worthy magistrates. This is drawn from the custom of the Romans, among whom consuls, dictators, praetors, and ediles sat in the **curule chair** <note>original: "fella curule"</note>, which is a seat placed upon a small chariot. **Those who are**: "undone" refers to the...

# PARADISO

...intended to rule; and already the **Galigaio** family
had the gilded hilt and pommel in his house.
Great already was the "column of miniver," <note>The coat of arms of the Pigli family featured a vertical stripe (column) of squirrel fur (miniver/vaio).</note>
the **Sacchetti**, **Giuochi**, **Fifanti**, and **Barucci**,
and the **Galli**, and those who blush for the bushel. <note>The Chiaramontesi family, one of whose members was caught cheating the public salt measure (the bushel or "staio").</note>
The stock from which the **Calfucci** were born
was already great, and already drawn
to the curule chairs were the **Sizii** and **Arrigucci**.
O, how great I saw those who are now undone
by their pride! And the "balls of gold" <note>The Lamberti family coat of arms featured golden balls (palle).</note>
made Florence flower in all her great deeds.
So did the fathers of those
who, whenever your church’s seat is vacant,
grow fat by staying in consistory. <note>The Tosinghi and Visdomini families, who acted as stewards of the Bishopric of Florence while the seat was empty, profiting from its revenues.</note>
The arrogant breed <note>The Adimari family.</note> that turns into a dragon <note>original: "findraca" from "s'indraca"</note>
behind him who flees, but toward him who shows his teeth
or his purse, is as quiet as a lamb.
Already they were rising, but were of such humble folk
that it did not please **Ubertin Donato**
when his father-in-law later made them his kinsmen. <note>Ubertino Donato was angry when Bellincione Berti married another daughter into the "low-born" Adimari family.</note>
Already **Caponsacco** had descended
from Fiesole into the Market; and already
**Giuda** and **Infangato** were good citizens.
I will tell a thing incredible and true:
the little circle was entered by a gate
named after those of the **Pera** family. <note>The Peruzza gate, named after the Pera family, who had since declined.</note>
Everyone who bears the beautiful ensign
of the Great Baron, <note>Count Ugo of Tuscany.</note> whose name and whose worth
the feast of Saint Thomas restores,
received from him knighthood and privilege;
though today he who wraps it in a fringe
has joined himself with the people. <note>Giano della Bella, a nobleman who joined the popular faction and created the Ordinances of Justice.</note>
Already there were **Gualterotti** and **Importuni**;
and the Borgo would still be a quieter place
if they were still fasting for new neighbors. <note>The Borgo Santi Apostoli neighborhood would be more peaceful if the "new" Buondelmonti family had never arrived.</note>
The house from which our weeping was born, <note>The Amidei family.</note>
because of the just resentment that has killed you
and put an end to your joyful living,
was honored, it and its consorts.
O **Buondelmonte**, how ill did you flee
its marriage alliance through the counsel of another!
Many would be happy who are now sad
if God had surrendered you to the Ema <note>A river near Florence.</note>
the first time you came to the city!
But it was fitting for that broken stone
that guards the bridge that Florence should offer
a victim in her final time of peace. <note>Buondelmonte was murdered at the base of the ancient, weathered statue of Mars on the Ponte Vecchio, an event traditionally cited as the beginning of the Guelf and Ghibelline wars.</note>

<column-break/>

The **Abati**: men certainly wise and reputed in government, but too proud according to what one reads of them. **So did the fathers of those.** These first were of the same lordship: the **Tosinghi** and **Cortigiani**, who are all kinsmen and descended from the same blood and origin. They were the masters and founders of the Bishopric then, and later of the Archbishopric of Florence; and therefore every time it is vacant, they are the stewards and dispensers; and there they gather to guard the place, and they eat and sleep there until the new bishop takes possession. **The arrogant.** This means discord in appetite: *quotus* in Latin signifies "somewhat in order"; therefore, "arrogant" <note>original: "tracotato"</note> is he who passes beyond the order in which he ought to contain himself. These are the **Cavicciuli** and **Adimari**, whom the poet condemns as cruel but vile and bitter. Therefore, he "turns into a dragon" <note>original: "findraca como draco"</note>: he pursues him who flees; but for him who shows his teeth, he offers resistance. **Or his purse**: as if to say that for money he sets aside every injury. This does not proceed from magnanimity but from avarice. The poet was angry at this family because **Boccaccio Adimari** occupied his goods after he was sent into exile and was always his most bitter adversary so that he might not be recalled to his homeland. But **of humble folk** was the beginning of this most vile family, in such a way that after Messer Bellincione had married a daughter to **Ubertino Donati**, Ubertino was much annoyed that Messer Bellincione gave the other daughter to one of the Adimari and made him his brother-in-law. **Caponsacco** was a Fiesolan and came to live in Florence in the Ward of Porta San Piero in the Old Market, and was the beginning of the **Caponsacchi** family. These and the **Guidi** and the **Infangati** were exiled as Ghibellines. **I will tell a true thing but it is incredible** to those who see Florence expanded at present. **In the little circle**: that is, in Florence when it was the little circle, one entered by a gate called the **Porta Peruzza**. These of the **Pera** family, according to Paolino Malespini, are extinct. **Everyone who bears the beautiful ensign**: And there was a Vicar in Tuscany for Otto the Emperor <note>original: "pottone" likely Otto I</note>, the Count **Ugo of Brandenburg**, a man most excellent in government and most religious in the Christian faith. He founded seven abbeys. The first was that of Florence; the last that of Settimo. And then he was a great friend to the **Pulci** family, and they being lords of castles nearby honored him greatly. He also made friends with four other noble Florentine families: the **Nerli**, the Counts of **Gangalandi**, the **Giandonati**, and those **Della Bella**; and to all these four families he gave his coat of arms and many privileges. But although his arms are red and white stripes, nevertheless only the Pulci keep the Count's own; and in the way that is seen in the Abbey, all the others have varied it. And **Giano della Bella**, when he joined the side of the people and renounced his nobility, added a fringe of gold to these arms. The Count died in December on the day of **Saint Thomas**, which is why every year on that day the monks of the Abbey celebrate his funeral rites. Therefore: by "the Great Baron" he means Count Ugo. And he says well that the **feast of Saint Thomas** comforts his name and his prize, that is, his fame. Because the annual funeral rites performed on that day refresh his memory. His bones are in the Abbey in an iron chest. But at present, the monks there, as if grateful for the ancient benefit, are having them carved into a well-adorned and marble sepulcher. The **Gualterotti** and **Importuni** lived in the Ward of Borgo, which he says would be quieter if it had not had "new neighbors." Some say that the **Bardi** were sent to inhabit Borgo Santo Apostolo so that they might repress the impetus of these two great Ghibelline families. Others understand it to mean the family of the **Buondelmonti**.

<image-desc>Large historiated initial 'Q' containing a face/mask with organic, leafy flourishes.</image-desc>

**This is the house of the Amidei**, which was the beginning of the weeping, that is, the grief <note>original: "pianto"</note> of our Republic. There was, then, Messer **Buondelmonte de' Buondelmonti**, a young knight of twenty-four years, about whom and about whose marriage and the repudiation and the killings and discords that followed therefrom, we narrated extensively in the first Canticle <note>Referencing the commentary on Inferno Canto XXVIII.</note>. This killing, then, although the resentment seemed just, nevertheless held more pride and cruelty than was fitting in a free republic. And it was the cause of the destruction of the city. The principal **Guelfs** who were in Florence in those times were in the Ward of Oltrarno: the **Nerli** (though they first lived in the Old Market), the **Giacopi** (later called **Rossi**), the **Freschi**, **Baldi**, **Bardi**, **Mozzi**, and **Canigiani**. Among those who are worthy of account at present are two named Antonio, and Matteo, and Bernardo **Frescobaldi**; also the **Magli**, **Machiavelli**, **Belfredogli**, **Rinucci**, **Arbadori**, **Foderi**, **Malduri**, and **Amirati**. The **Ghibellines**: the Counts of **Gangalandi**, **Ubrachi**, **Manelli**. In the Ward of San Piero Scheraggio, the Guelfs were the **Pulci**, **Gerardi**, **Foraboschi** (previously called **Ormanni**), **Bagnesi**, **Guidalotti**, **Sacchetti**, **Manieri**. Those from **Acona** or descended from those of **Bologna**: the **Lucardeschi**, **Chiaramontesi**, **Piovesi**, **Cavalcanti** (who are the same as **Guido Cavalcanti**, of whom we spoke in the *Inferno*). And at present they have the lands of those from Bologna, the **Malispini**, although later, due to an injury received from the **Uberti**, they became Guelfs. In the Ward of Borgo, they were **Buondelmonte**, son of **Fabricato**. The Guelfs were: **Bostichi**, **Tornaquinci**, **Vecchietti**, **Mierbeti**, **Scali**, **Spini**, and **Baldovinetti**. The Ghibellines: **Lamberti**, **Soldanieri**, **Cipriani**. Also Ghibellines: **Barucci**, **Cattani da Castiglione**, and from **Certaldo**. **Agolati**, **Brunelleschi**. But part of them became Guelfs. In the Ward of Porta San Piero...

<meta>This page transitions from the end of Canto XVI, where Cacciaguida concludes his history of Florentine families and the city's downfall, into Canto XVII, where he prophesies Dante’s future exile. The commentary bridges the historical fall of the city with the personal fate of the poet.</meta>

...they were **Guelfs**: the **Adimari**, **Visdomini**, **Donati**, **Pazzi**, the house of the beautiful **Ardigi**, the **Tebaldi**, and those called **Della Vitella**; and already the "circles" <note>Referring to the new merchant class residing in the newer outer circles of the city walls.</note> began to rise, even though they were quite recent merchants. The **Ghibellines** were the **Caponsacchi**, **Elisei**, **Abbati**, **Tebaldi**, **Giuochi**, and **Galigai**; although in all the houses, many changes occurred due to various indignities. This ruined the Republic and put an end to the "joyful living." If God had granted that you had come from **Montebuono** to Florence <note>Referring to the Buondelmonti family, whose arrival from their ancestral castle in Montebuono sparked the city's feuds.</note>. But it was fitting for that "mutilated stone"—that is, that base at the foot of the Old Bridge which was "mutilated" because the statue of **Mars** had been removed from it. And at the foot of this base, **Lord Buondelmonte** was killed. This was a most terrible omen for the future civil wars. For the base near which he was killed was dedicated to Mars, the god of war. Therefore, it was fitting for this stone that Florence should make it a "victim"—that is, a sacrifice—upon her "final peace," meaning at the end of her peace which was failing.

With these people, and with others with them,
I saw Florence in such repose
that she had no cause for which to weep.
With these people, I saw her people
so glorious and just, that the lily
was never placed backward upon the spear,
nor made vermillion by division.

<column-break/>

The lily emblem of Florence was anciently white on a red field. And **Cacciaguida** affirms here that in the civil concord which existed at that time, they lived with such justice and administered the Republic with such prudence that the lily—that is, the flag where the lily was—was never "placed backward" on the spear; that is, the Florentines were never defeated in battle, nor were their banners taken, which, when taken by enemies, are placed upside down on the spear. And they say that the Roman people gave their coat of arms, which was red without the letters S.P.Q.R., to all their colonies. And afterwards, the colonies placed in that red field whatever they pleased. Therefore, the Florentines placed the white lily there, which can still be seen in some very ancient places. But after the civil division, the **Guelfs** changed it, setting the shield as white and the lily as vermillion (red).

# CANTO XVII OF THE THIRD CANTICLE BY DANTE.

As he who came to **Clymene** to be certain
of that which he had heard against himself,
he who still makes fathers stingy toward their sons;
Such was I, and such was I perceived to be
by **Beatrice** and by the holy lamp <note>Cacciaguida is described as a "holy lamp" or light within the Cross of Mars.</note>
that previously for my sake had changed its place.
Wherefore my Lady said: "Send forth the flame
of your desire, so that it may come forth
clearly marked by the internal stamp;
Not so that our knowledge may increase
through your speaking, but that you may practice
telling your thirst, so that the wine may be poured for you."

...had changed his place in the cross. Because my lady, that is Beatrice, said to me: "Send forth the flame of your desire"—that is, the ardor of your wish—so that it may be said: if you desire to know more, speak. But make sure the words are "marked by the internal stamp," which is your mind. The charity of the Holy Spirit does not want Beatrice to ask the spirit on the poet's behalf, so that the spirit might know his will, because without asking, he sees it in the divine mirror as was said. But it is so that Dante may accustom himself to asking for what he needs. And he feigns this because, although God knows our needs, He wants us to ask Him for them, and to humble ourselves before the Saints and recognize ourselves as nothing without His grace. Whence in the Gospel: "Ask and you shall receive" <note>original: "Petite & accipietis"</note>. The spirit wants Dante to humble himself to ask. This Dante recognizes through Beatrice, that is, through Sacred Theology.

"O my dear root, who so uplift yourself <note>original: "cara pietra" (literally "dear stone," but Dante uses "pietra" here to mean "foundation" or "root").</note>
that, just as earthly minds see
that two obtuse angles cannot fit in a triangle,
so you see contingent things
before they exist in themselves, by gazing upon the Point
to whom all times are present.
While I was joined with **Virgil**,
up the mountain that cures the souls,
and descending into the world of the dead,
grave words were spoken to me
about my future life, although I feel myself
well-squared against the blows of fortune. <note>original: "tetragono" (a four-square, solid, or steadfast man).</note>
Therefore, my will would be content
to hear what fortune approaches me;
for a foreseen arrow comes more slowly."
Thus did I speak to that same light
that previously had spoken to me; and as Beatrice
willed, my desire was confessed.

<column-break/>

As in the preceding chapter Cacciaguida showed the poet the origin and genealogy of his family, so in this XVII chapter he predicts his future exile. First, therefore, the poet asks Cacciaguida to clarify certain omens that he heard, partly in Hell and partly in Purgatory. Then the spirit interprets them for him. In the third place, he shows him the refuge for his evils. And in the last part, he is assured of the perfection and publication of this work. But at the beginning, he says that after the words of the spirit, he became such as **Phaethon** became when he went to **Clymene** his mother to be certain of what he had heard from **Epaphus** against himself. Phaethon was the son of the Sun. For Epaphus said he was not the son of the Sun. But after he was sent by his mother to **Phoebus** and understood from him that he was truly his son, he laid aside all sorrow and became full of joy. I omit this fable for now, as we have narrated it elsewhere. Thus, he orders it so: I, Dante, was such; understand that of Phaethon, who still makes fathers "stingy" toward their sons—that is, whose example is the reason that fathers do not make promises to their sons, as Phoebus promised Phaethon the governance of the chariot for a day. Wherefore he [the father] repented. "And such was I perceived by Beatrice"—that is, Beatrice noticed what I was. "And by the holy lamp"—that is, by the holy splendor of the spirit who, to be with me, has [changed place].

This is the oration that the poet makes to Cacciaguida, in which he wishes to ask him about what was said to him. Because it involves the contingent future, he uses an introduction to gain goodwill. And he shows it is easy for him by showing that he "uplifts himself"—that is, raises himself toward God in a way that he sees contingent things before they happen; just as we men, without any demonstration, see that a triangle cannot contain within itself two obtuse angles. Every triangle—be it right, acute, or obtuse—cannot have more than one obtuse angle. "O dear root" <note>The commentator notes the translation of "pietra" as root/foundation.</note>: this is in the translation because above he called him a "living topaz." "Contingent things" are those that can be or not be; for things are either necessary, impossible, or contingent. Necessary things are those that cannot *not* be. Therefore, it was necessary for Dante to die because all things born must die. It was contingent that he live longer at one time than another. And he adds that he can see future contingent things not by himself, but by gazing upon God, in whom, as in a living mirror, everything is seen; and whoever loves God [gazes upon that] Point. We shall explain this in the XXVII chapter. "To whom all things are present": because with one intuition, He sees the past, the present, and the future. For eternity is all at once, the perfect possession of a unity that has no parts. "While I was joined with Virgil": I was told...

...descending into the world of the dead, that is into Hell, by **Sir Farinata**. But [he did not say] how many times the face of the lady who rules here will be rekindled <note>A prophecy of Dante's exile within 50 months, referring to Proserpina/the Moon.</note> before you know how much that art weighs; and then "up the mountain that cures them"—that is, on the mountain of Purgatory—I was told more than I will say, and I know he speaks obscurely. But a short time will pass before your neighbors act so that you can interpret it. I was with Virgil, although I feel myself a "tetragono" against the blows of fortune—that is, strong in resisting. For the strong man is the same in every kind of fortune, like the "tetragonal" (four-square) figure which, however it falls, always shows a flat face. "FOR A FORESEEN ARROW COMES MORE SLOWLY." Because he who has time to think about the adverse things that are to come, can in some [way prepare].

<summary>Cacciaguida describes the decline of Florence’s noble families and explains the origin of the city's coat of arms before Dante asks for a clear prophecy regarding his impending exile, comparing his anxiety to that of Phaethon.</summary>
<keywords>Cacciaguida, Beatrice, Virgil, Phaethon, Florence, Guelfs and Ghibellines, Buondelmonte, exile, contingent things, tetragono, prophecy, lily emblem</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante's *Paradiso*, moving from the general history of Florence's decline into the specific, personal prophecy of Dante's exile. It transitions from the end of Canto XVI into the heart of Canto XVII.</meta>

...how one can prepare, if not to flee them, at least to mitigate them. Furthermore, things to be faced that are not in our power are the "evils of fortune," such as infamy, poverty, exile, the loss of children, disease, and similar things. If we have the space to consider them before they arrive, it is not very difficult to realize they are not as great as they appear. This is because we consider that they harm only the body and the present life—which is momentary and transitory—and not the soul and the future life, which is eternal and in which true happiness consists. This meditation makes us like a "new Job," <note>A reference to the biblical figure Job, known for enduring immense suffering with patience and faith.</note> able to carry every calamity in peace. And we find ourselves armed with true reason.

->chen sulla scala porta elsancto ucello<-

<column-break/>

**D**ante had made his request; and that "paternal love"—that is, Cacciaguida—responded to him with clear words and with "Latin"—meaning with speech that was determined and clear. **AND NOT THROUGH RIDDLES**: <note>original: "per ambage." This refers to the ambiguous or roundabout speech used by ancient pagan oracles.</note> that is, through a circuit of words that make the meaning obscure and ambiguous, such as were the answers of Apollo and the other oracles which ensnared and trapped human minds, showing they meant the opposite of what they said. To provide one of many examples: Pyrrhus, king of the Epirotes, asked the oracle of Apollo if he would defeat the Romans, and the answer was: "I say to you, descendant of Aeacus, that the Romans you can defeat." <note>original: "Aio te aeacidem romanos uincere posse." This is a famous Latin grammatical ambiguity; it can mean "I say you can defeat the Romans" or "I say the Romans can defeat you." Pyrrhus misinterpreted it as a promise of victory.</note> This was so ambiguous it could be understood either as "the Romans will defeat you" or "you will defeat the Romans." **BEFORE THE LAMB OF GOD WAS SLAIN**: that is, Jesus Christ, who through his passion and death liberated us from sin. And this "paternal love" was enclosed within splendor and was "apparent"—that is, it appeared and showed itself in its joy. And he gives his answer, which is this: **CONTINGENCY**: that is, the occurrence of future things that are not necessary but can either be or not be. This contingency "does not extend outside the notebook of your matter." <note>A metaphor for the physical, material world where time and change exist.</note> Because things that are simple form are always necessary and are "all painted in the eternal sight." Because everything that is to be is within God; but His seeing it does not make it a necessity, just as although we see a ship being driven by a rapid river toward a rock, we are not the cause of its hitting it. **FROM THERE**: the meaning is that just as the harmony of a playing organ comes to my ears, **SO FROM THERE**: that is, from the Divine mind, there comes to my sight the time that is being prepared for you, because I see that time in my mind as if in a mirror.

**P**redicting his exile to the poet, Cacciaguida shows it to be unjust. For just as **HIPPOLYTUS** was driven from Athens for refusing to consent to the madness of his stepmother, <note>In Greek mythology, Phaedra falsely accused her stepson Hippolytus after he rejected her advances.</note> so you must leave Florence for refusing to consent to the unjust desires of those who administered the Republic. We treated the story of Hippolytus sufficiently in the twelfth canto of the *Inferno*. We have tried to explain the origin of the poet's exile in his *Life*. **THERE WHERE CHRIST IS TRADED ENTIRELY**: that is, where spiritual things and those belonging to the Christian religion are made into merchandise, and through <term>simony</term> <note>The buying or selling of ecclesiastical privileges, named after Simon Magus.</note> are sold and bartered. **THE BLAME WILL FOLLOW THE INJURED PARTY**: for all those who are exiled will be judged as having erred, and so the "cry"—that is, the fame—will spread as it usually does; it is the custom in all things that whoever ends up badly is held to be in the wrong. But the vengeance that God will take upon those who exile you will be a "testimony to the truth" of their injustice and your innocence.

**WHO DISPENSES IT**: that is, God, who dispenses and contributes the truth or vengeance. Since God creates the truth, He prepares vengeance against those who have erred according to that truth. And this concerns the vengeance that is to follow. Nevertheless, in your exile, you will be struck by the "first arrow" that exile shoots, which is that you must leave behind the things most dear to you: your fatherland, relatives, friends, houses, possessions, and such. **AND YOU SHALL TASTE HOW IT TASTES OF SALT**: that is, how bitter it seems.

**A**dded to the aforementioned miseries will be the company of citizens with whom you will be exiled, and you will "fall into this valley"—that is, into this low state which I predict for you. This company is "wicked and senseless"—that is, divided—and will turn against you. But shortly thereafter, they, and not you, will receive shame and harm. Here he predicts the cruel death of **MESSER CORSO DONATI**. <note>A leader of the Black Guelfs in Florence.</note> The process of their governance will provide proof of their "bestiality," such that it will be beautiful and honorable for you to have separated yourself from them. Understand this about the **CERCHI** family: for **MESSER VIERI DE' CERCHI** was very obstinate in the enmities he had with Messer Corso. Nor could **POPE BONIFACE** ever placate him or bring him into concord with his adversaries. Wherefore, within three years, the Cerchi fell into great calamity. Therefore, it will be a wise counsel for Dante to leave them and live far from every faction.

**D**escribing the exile, the spirit now identifies his refuge: which was the court of **BARTHOLOMEO DELLA SCALA** of Verona, whose coat of arms is a red shield with a vermillion ladder, upon which is the black eagle, which he calls the "holy bird" because it is the sign of the Empire. This man will be so generous toward your virtues that between the "doing" and the "asking" between you...

<summary>Cacciaguida prophesies Dante's impending exile from Florence, comparing his unjust suffering to that of Hippolytus and warning of the bitter hardships and treacherous companions he will face before finding refuge in Verona.</summary>

# CANTO XVIII <note>Though the header says XVIII, the text and commentary on this page conclude Canto XVII.</note>

**Left Column**

He will show you such benign regard
  that between the two of you, the deed and the request
  shall be first which among others is most slow. <note>Cacciaguida predicts that Cangrande della Scala will grant Dante favors before Dante even has to ask for them.</note>
With him you shall see the one who was so impressed
  at his birth by this strong star, <note>The star/planet of Mars.</note>
  that his deeds shall be notable.
The people have not yet taken notice of him
  because of his young age, for only nine years
  have these wheels revolved around him.
But before the Gascon <note>Pope Clement V, who was from Gascony.</note> deceives the noble Henry, <note>Emperor Henry VII of Luxembourg.</note>
  sparks of his virtue shall appear
  in his disregard for silver or for hardships.
His known magnificences
  shall yet be such that even his enemies
  will not be able to keep their tongues silent about them.
Look to him and to his benefits;
  through him many people shall be transformed,
  changing condition, both the rich and the beggars.
And you shall carry written in your mind
  of him—and you shall not tell it—and he said things
  incredible to those who will be present.

---

Then he added: "Son, these are the glosses
  of what was told to you; behold the snares
  that are hidden within a few revolutions."
"Yet I do not wish you to envy your neighbors,
  since your life shall extend into the future
  far beyond the punishment of their perfidies."

---

Since by falling silent, the holy soul
  showed itself finished with putting the woof
  into that web which I had held out to it ready-woven, <note>A metaphor for the conversation: Dante provided the "warp" (the questions) and Cacciaguida provided the "woof" (the answers/prophecy).</note>
I began, like one who longs,
  in his doubting, to have counsel from a person
  who sees, and wills rightly, and loves:

---

"Well do I see, my father, how time spurs
  toward me to deal me the blow
  that is heaviest to the one who gives in most.
Therefore it is good that I arm myself with foresight,
  so that if my most dear place <note>Florence.</note> is taken from me,
  I might not lose other refuges because of my poems.

---

Down through the world endlessly bitter,
  and through the mountain from whose fair summit
  my lady's eyes raised me up,
and then through heaven from light to light,
  have I learned that which, if I tell it again,
  will be a taste of strong bitterness <note>original: "forte agrume" — literally "strong citrus," implying a sharp, harsh, or stinging quality.</note> to many."

<column-break/>

**Right Column**

...before it usually is among other men; for commonly it happens that no one grants a benefit unless it is first requested. But this man will confer it upon you before you ask. And he adds that you will see with him Lord Cane della Scala <note>Known as Cangrande I della Scala, the ruler of Verona and Dante's primary patron in exile.</note> who, at his birth, received such an impression from the star of Mars, which is strong—that is, it induces strength and magnanimity—that his works in military discipline will be marvelous. But people are not yet aware of it because he is of a new and tender age; since this star has not revolved around him more than nine times since he was born. Therefore, Cane was in the eighteenth year of his life, because Mars completes its circle and course through the zodiac in two years: and thus one "year" of Mars—that is, one of its revolutions—is two solar years. He is, therefore, not known at present. But the sparks and splendor of his virtues will appear and be seen before the Gascon (that is, Pope Clement, who was from Gascony) deceives the noble Henry (that is, the excellent Henry of Luxembourg, who was Emperor). And these sparks, meaning the splendor and fervor of his virtues, will appear in two virtues: namely in temperance, because neither avarice nor greed for money will have power over him; and in strength, because he will be of the highest tolerance and patience in supporting all labors and hardships. Concerning the deception that Pope Clement plotted against Emperor Henry, we will speak in the thirtieth Canto. AND YOU SHALL CARRY IT written in your mind. This is excellent advice from the poet; for having up to this point introduced Cacciaguida to divine and predict things which in truth had already occurred, he now comes to Lord Cane. Because he was young, and although he showed signs of being destined for great things, he had as yet done little, the poet could not know the future; thus he feigns that Cacciaguida predicted it to him, but commanded him not to tell it to others. This man was indeed excellent in military discipline: and after the death of Henry, in the years of our Lord 1314, he defeated the Paduans at Vicenza, who had already taken the suburbs. Afterward, he besieged Cremona, and had already pressed it so hard that it could not have resisted had they not been aided by the Bolognese. After this, he went against the Paduans and took Monselice and Este and other of their castles, and forced them to recall the Ghibellines whom they had exiled. Then in 1318, with the Ghibellines of Lombardy, he took Cremona; but these things had not yet occurred at the time of the author.

---

Cacciaguida then clarified what had been obscurely said to the poet in *Inferno* and *Purgatorio*, and what was soon to happen to him. And he adds that because he is in exile, he should not envy his neighbors; for his life is to endure into the future much longer than the punishment for their perfidy shall be delayed. SINCE BY FALLING SILENT IT SHOWED itself finished: having said these things, the spirit fell silent; and this was a sign that he was finished with putting the woof into the web that I had woven—that is, that he had finished the exposition of what I had asked him. That is, I began as one who, in doubtful cases, longs and desires to have counsel from a person who sees (that is, who understands) and wills (because it is not enough to see what is best if one does not wish to say it) and loves rightly (that is, is a true friend), whereby the counsel is faithful. The counsel that Dante asks of Cacciaguida is whether it is right that, having lost his homeland and therefore having to wander through the world, he should include in these verses the various vices of many powerful men who could harm him.

---

The poet continues his speech: I see that time rushes to deal me the blow of exile, which is always heavier to those who give in and let themselves be struck down by grief. And for this reason, it is useful that I arm myself with foresight, and have regard that, in losing my homeland, my poems (that is, my verses in which I vituperate many) do not cause me to lose other places. For while I have gone down through the world whose bitterness is without end (and this is Hell), and afterward climbed the mountain of Purgatory, from whose peak and summit Beatrice appeared to me and snatched me up with her eyes into heaven, and guided me from heaven to heaven, I have understood and learned many things about many men; which, if I tell them again (that is, if I write them in my verses), will have a taste of strong bitterness to them. And if I am a close friend to the truth... <note>The text cuts off as Dante debates whether to be a "timid friend" to truth or risk his safety by speaking out.</note>

<summary>Cacciaguida concludes his prophecy by praising Dante's future patron, Cangrande della Scala, and predicting his military success and generosity. Dante then expresses his fear that the truths he must write in his Comedy will offend the powerful and cost him his remaining places of refuge.</summary>
