<header>PARADISE</header>

And if I am but a timid friend to the truth,
I fear I shall lose my fame among those
who will call this present time "the ancient days."

---

The light in which my treasure <note>Dante refers to his ancestor Cacciaguida as his "treasure."</note> was smiling, 
the one I had found there, first became radiant
like a golden mirror in a ray of sunlight.
Then he responded: "A conscience that is darkened, 
either by its own shame or by that of another,
will indeed feel your words to be harsh.
But nevertheless, setting aside every lie,
make your entire vision manifest,
and then let them scratch where the scab is. <note>A proverbial expression: let those who feel the "itch" of guilt be the ones to complain about the truth.</note>
For if your voice is troublesome
at the first taste, it shall provide 
vital nourishment once it is digested.
This cry of yours shall be like the wind,
which strikes the highest towers most heavily;
and this is no small argument for your honor.
Therefore, in these spheres, 
on the mountain, and in the mournful valley, <note>Referring to the three realms of the afterlife: Heaven, Purgatory, and Hell.</note>
only those souls who are known to fame have been shown to you.
For the mind of one who hears does not rest,
nor does it fix its faith on examples that have
their roots unknown or hidden,
nor on any other argument that is not apparent."

<column-break/>

If I hold this truth within me and do not write it, I fear I shall not live among those who will come so long after us that they will call this time "ancient." It is as if he says: if I do not write these things, my fame will not endure.

The poet had proposed his doubt, to which—before he responded—the light in which his "treasure" (that is, the spirit of Cacciaguida) was smiling, became radiant (that is, splendid and shining, as a golden mirror becomes in a ray of the sun). The poet imagines this because, by writing the things found on this journey, the fame of Cacciaguida remained more luminous; and through this splendor, which was joy within him, he shows that the speech the poet had made pleased him. 

And then he responded to the doubt proposed to him in this form: "You, Dante, shall write what you have seen so that the 'darkened' (that is, black) conscience—meaning those men who do not have a pure conscience but one stained either by their own shame (sins committed by them) or by the shame of others (sins of their parents and relatives which you will describe)—may FEEL your harsh word (that is, the infamy you will give them in your verses). But so that what you write is without lies and falsehood, let them 'scratch where the scab is' (that is, let those who have cause to grieve, grieve). For it is not an unjust thing, but most worthy, to spread perpetual infamy upon those who have been wicked." 

The poet very prudently imagines doubting whether it is good to write such a work in which infamy is given to those already dead (which then reflects upon their living descendants); he rightly concludes that one must write so that these may be an example to those who hear. In this way, each person may shape their actions so as not to fall into such infamy, and their relatives and descendants, through many virtues, may make themselves unworthy of being struck by such infamy. And so he says that if the voice (that is, your word) shall be troublesome at the first taste—like some bitter food given to preserve health—it will be a reprimand that corrects and heals the soul, just as that bitter food, once digested and processed by the body, provides nourishment and restores health.

---

## CANTO XVIII OF THE THIRD CANTICLE OF DANTE

---

That blessed mirror <note>Cacciaguida.</note> was already enjoying
his own word alone, and I was tasting
mine, tempering the sweet with the bitter.
And that lady who was leading me to God
said: "Change your thoughts; remember that I am
near to Him who unburdens every wrong."
I turned toward the loving sound
of my comfort; and the love I then saw
in her holy eyes, I leave here unsaid.
Not only because I distrust my own speech,
but because the memory cannot return 
so far above itself unless Another guides it.

<column-break/>

Cacciaguida has predicted to the poet his exile and refuge. Now, in this eighteenth chapter, he shows him many excellent and warlike spirits in that cross of Mars; and then they ascend to the heaven of Jupiter. But as for the beginning, it says that already after the words spoken in that "blessed mirror" (that is, Cacciaguida, in whom divine rays reflected as in a mirror), he was enjoying himself alone (that is, he was enjoying his own word, which was what he had predicted to me, comforting me to endure hardships and to manifest what I had heard and seen). 

And I, Dante, was "tasting mine" (that is, what I was turning over in my own mind), tempering the bitter with the sweet. For while the exile and other troubles he had predicted were bitter to me, the honor I was to receive from such a magnanimous lord was sweet to me, and my life was destined to endure. 

And Beatrice admonished me to "change my thought" (that is, that I should return to the contemplation of celestial things) and to think that she, judging me, was drawing near to God. And she added that "He unburdens every wrong," as if to say: do not let the injury of exile trouble you, for God will avenge you. For He says: "Vengeance is mine, and I will repay." <note>original: "Mihi vindictam et ego retribuam" (Romans 12:19).</note> And this saying fits perfectly in this place, because they were approaching the planet of Jupiter, the governor of justice. 

"I TURNED TOWARD THE LOVING SOUND" (that is, to the words of Beatrice, with whom I was in love; that is, I returned to thinking about the doctrine of theology, which is true comfort). For truly, the words of Cacciaguida had concerned the active life. Therefore Beatrice (that is, Theology) allows that at the proper place and time we may use some digression from the contemplative life. And as much as is necessary, we may provide for the active life; but let it be brief and only as much as is needed, and then immediately let us return to contemplation. 

"AND I DO NOT WRITE" what love I then saw in her holy eyes, not only because words fail me, but also because the mind cannot recount or rethink so much "above itself" (that is, to consider what was so far above its power) that it cannot grasp it anew, unless Another (which is the grace of God) guides it.

<summary>Dante concludes his dialogue with Cacciaguida, who commands him to speak the truth regardless of its harshness, comparing it to a healing but bitter medicine. They then transition to the Sphere of Jupiter, where Beatrice reminds Dante that divine justice will right the wrongs of his exile.</summary>
<keywords>Dante, Cacciaguida, Beatrice, divine justice, exile, active vs contemplative life, truth-telling, Jupiter, Mars</keywords>

<page-num>280</page-num>
<header>CANTO XVII</header>

I can say only this much of that moment:
that as I gazed upon her again, my affection
was free from every other desire,
Until the eternal pleasure that beamed
directly into Beatrice from her beautiful face
contented me with its serene aspect.
Overcoming me with the light of a smile,
she said to me: “Turn and listen,
for not only in my eyes is paradise.”
Just as one sometimes sees here on earth
an affection in the eyes, if it is so great
that the whole soul is taken by it,
So in the flaming of that holy splendor
to which I turned, I recognized the will
within him to speak with me a little longer.
He began: “In this fifth leaf
of the tree that lives from the top, <note>The "tree" refers to the celestial spheres, which, unlike earthly trees, derive their life and fruit from the "top" (God) rather than the roots.</note>
which always bears fruit and never loses a leaf,
Are blessed spirits who, before they
came to heaven, were of such great renown
that every Muse would be enriched by them.
Therefore, look upon the arms of the cross;
he whom I shall name will perform the movement
that a bolt of lightning makes in a cloud.”
I saw a light drawn along the cross
at the naming of Joshua, just as it was done;
nor was the word known to me before the act.
And at the name of the high Maccabee, <note>Judas Maccabeus, the Jewish guerrilla leader who defended Judea from the Seleucid Empire.</note>
I saw another move, spinning,
and gladness was the whip for that top. <note>Dante compares the spirit's joyful movement to a "paleo" or whipping-top.</note>
So for Charlemagne and for Roland,
my attentive gaze followed two more,
as the eye follows its falcon in flight.
Then William and Renouard, <note>William of Orange and his companion Renouard, heroes of the Old French "chansons de geste."</note>
and Duke Godfrey, <note>Godfrey of Bouillon, leader of the First Crusade.</note> drew my sight
along that cross, and Robert Guiscard. <note>The Norman adventurer who conquered Southern Italy and Sicily.</note>
Then, moving and mingling among the other lights,
the soul that had spoken to me showed me
what an artist he was among the singers of heaven.

<column-break/>

I cannot say anything more about that moment except that, gazing at Beatrice, I remained free from every other desire. And certainly, the studies of theology contain all the peace one could wish for, so that nothing else is desired: because they provide the knowledge of God and of the supreme good. Therefore, although the soul may be entangled and caught by the cares of active and earthly things, nevertheless, when we turn back to Beatrice—that is, to contemplation—she draws us to herself in such a way that we forget every other thing. **NOT ONLY IN my eyes is paradise**, she says. This signifies that happiness is found not only in the doctrines and speculations of the most learned theologians. Then, the poet turning again to the spirit in the flaming of his holy lightning and greatest splendor, he knew that the spirit had a longing—that is, a desire—to speak to him a little more. And so he recognized this in his light: just as sometimes here, by looking into a face, one recognizes the affection, if it is so great that it pulls the entire soul to itself.

This is the beginning of the speech of Cacciaguida, who shows that in that fifth leaf—that is, in the fifth heaven—is the tree that lives from the top. And this top is Christ, from whose Passion all things take their value: not only all the sufferings of the martyrs, but the merit of all Christians. The fruit is the blessedness which is eternal, and the leaves are the virtues which adorn the soul eternally, just as leaves are the ornament of the tree. Therefore, in this fifth heaven of Mars, where the tree of the cross is found, there are blessed spirits who, before they departed from human life, were of great fame for their excellent deeds: such that they are material to "fatten" any great poem—that is, to make every great poem stay abundant and full. And for this reason, "look into the horns of the cross and you will see that he whom I name will perform there"—that is, in those horns—"the act that swift fire makes in its cloud": that is, they will cast out a fiery splendor as we see ignited vapors in a cloud run like little torches. And this suits warlike men who are of a choleric nature similar to Mars and of burning virtue. The poet looked then and saw a light move suddenly through the cross as Cacciaguida named Joshua. Thus, as it was done—that is, as soon as the illumination was made—"the word was not known to me before the act"—that is, at the same moment that Cacciaguida named Joshua, the flame appeared. Joshua was the son of Nun <note>original: "ben nun" or "figliuolo di nun"</note>; and he was a type—that is, a figure—of Christ, not only in name <note>The names Joshua and Jesus share the same Hebrew root, meaning "The Lord is Salvation."</note> but also in deeds. For, succeeding Moses who was already dead, he crossed the Jordan River, destroyed the kingdoms of the enemies, acquired the Promised Land, and divided it among the victorious people of Israel. This man was called by the Hebrews Joshua son of Nun. Regarding Judas Maccabeus: it would be a long and tedious thing to narrate the very brave and religious deeds of the Maccabees, as it is written in the Bible in the Book of Maccabees. In the times of King Antiochus, there was a wicked transgression among the Hebrew people; and a great part of them, leaving the divine worship, gave themselves to King Antiochus and adored idols. For Antiochus conquered Egypt and afterwards took Jerusalem and despoiled the temple. And in those times, Mattathias with five sons—who would not obey the king nor adore idols—did many things in defense of the Law. Later, he died in the one hundred and forty-sixth year of his life and left his son Judas Maccabeus as prince of the militia. This man, with the help of his brothers, did marvelous things against the transgressors of the law of God and expanded the power of those who observed it; and he was of such strength that on the day he died in

---

battle, he himself killed a thousand men. This man moved spinning like a top turns when children strike it with force, and "gladness was the strength of the top": that is, just as he was moved by gladness, so the top is moved by force. **CHARLEMAGNE**: we narrated the life and lineage of this man above in the sixth canto of this canticle. And similarly, we spoke of Orlando <note>Roland, the hero of the Song of Roland.</note> in his proper place. William was the Count of Orange, son of the Count of Narbonne. Renouard <note>original: "Rinoardo"</note> was a very strong fighter against the infidels and a relative of William. **GODFREY**: In the year of Christian salvation one thousand and ninety-six, Peter the Hermit, a man of holy life but previously unknown, stirred many Christian princes to take up the enterprise against the Saracens. Of this army, the leader was Godfrey of Bouillon, very excellent in military discipline. Departing from France, he passed through Germany and through Hungary to Constantinople. And through the Hellespont he passed into Asia and captured Nicaea and Antioch, and many other cities; and in the third year, he took Jerusalem. And when the Christians wanted to crown him for this kingdom, he refused it, stating he did not want to wear a crown of gold in that city where Christ wore one of thorns. He was nonetheless made Duke, and after his death, his brother Baldwin succeeded him and reigned eighteen years, and three times he defeated the Egyptians and killed the Caliph, their king. Robert Guiscard was the Duke of Normandy, of whom we treated in the first canticle. And finally, that blessed soul of Cacciaguida, who had shown him what kind of artist he was among the singers of heaven.

<summary>This page describes the transition into the Sphere of Mars, where Beatrice directs Dante to observe the souls of famous holy warriors arranged in the shape of a cross. The commentary provides historical biographies for these figures, including Joshua, Judas Maccabeus, and Godfrey of Bouillon.</summary>

# PARADISO

<columns>
I turned back to my right side
to see in Beatrice my duty,
indicated either by words or by a sign.
And I saw her eyes so pure,
so joyful, that her appearance
surpassed her other and her recent habits.
And as, by feeling more delight,
a man, in doing well from day to day,
perceives that his virtue advances,
So did I perceive that my circling around
together with the heaven had increased its arc,
seeing that miracle so adorned.
Like the transformation in a brief passage
of time in a fair lady, when her face
discharges itself of the burden of shame,
Such it was to my eyes when I turned
due to the whiteness of the temperate star,
the sixth, which had received me within itself.

I saw within that Jovial torch <note>The "Jovial torch" refers to the planet Jupiter (Jove).</note>
the sparkling of the love that was there
signaling our speech to my eyes.
And like birds risen from a riverbank,
as if congratulating their pastures,
making of themselves now a round, now another flock,
So within the lights, holy creatures
flew singing, and made of themselves
now a D, now an I, now an L in their figure.
First, singing, they moved to their own rhythm;
then, becoming one of these signs,
they stopped a little and were silent.

O divine Pegasean <note>original: "pegasea." An invocation of the Muse, associated with the fountain Hippocrene struck open by the hoof of the winged horse Pegasus.</note> who makes wits
glorious and renders them long-lived,

<column-break/>

The poet had already described the heaven of Mars: and now wishing to describe that of Jove, not departing from Christian theology, he imagines that he turned to Beatrice to see in her his duty, that is, how much it was his debt to describe; and such duty he expected to understand from her either by words or by sign. Therefore, wishing the poet—as in the other parts of his volume—likewise in this not to depart from the Christian religion, he proceeded according to theology, which is the mistress of truth: either by words, that is, by open sentences, or by sign, that is, by hidden ones. **AND I SAW her eyes.** In short, her eyes were more lucid and cheerful than at other times, and even more lucid than the last time he saw her in the heaven of Mars. By these words, he indicates the splendor of the star of Jove and its benign and joyful influence, of which we will narrate a little below. Then, by comparison, he shows that as a man, always doing well from day to day, perceives that his virtue grows, so I perceived that my circling around the heaven had increased its arc—that is, its circumference—seeing that miracle so adorned. It is as if he says: I perceived myself to have ascended to the next heaven, seeing Beatrice more adorned than ever, whom he calls a miracle because her beauty seemed an incredible thing. He said the "arc" was greater because he found the heaven to have a greater circumference. **AS THE TRANSFORMATION in a brief passage.** An excellent and most suitable comparison by which he shows that, just as it happens in a short time that a woman whose face was red with shame changes to white if the shame that burdened her is removed, so he in a brief space found himself ascended from the red and fiery star of Mars to the white star of Jove, which is in the sixth heaven, and which he calls "temperate." Because it is between the hot planet Mars and the cold Saturn, it remains temperate. Furthermore, not without reason did he place the color of the planets, because it is different in all. Saturn is of a fiery color. Jove of a silvery and white color. Mars like a burning coal. Venus surpasses the others in splendor. Mercury is called *Stilbon* <note>original: "stilbon." A Greek name for Mercury meaning "the gleaming one."</note> because it rays out. But because he presently treats the star of Jove, the astrologers write (it is called Phaethon <note>original: "pheton"</note> by some) that it stays in each sign for one year, and in twelve years has completed the course of the whole zodiac. It is a benevolent, hot, and humid diurnal planet; masculine and temperate in its qualities; its color is silvery, white, clear, and pleasing. The philosophers placed the cause of happiness in the circle of Jove. This circle of his is conjoined to the circle of Saturn, and with its goodness, it represses the malice of Saturn when it is conjoined to the circle of Saturn with the lower part of its circle. And for this reason, the poets feign that Saturn is his father and that Jove drove him from his kingdom. When it is conjoined with good planets, it inserts good and useful influences. It makes a man beautiful and honest, of a white-incarnate color. It makes beautiful eyes, teeth, and hair, and a round beard, as Ptolemy writes; it has great power in the air and in the blood. Its houses are Sagittarius and Pisces; it reigns in Cancer. From it come justice, laws, and the distinguished. For which reason Homer often says: *Basyleas diotropheas* <note>original: "Basyleas diotropheas." Greek for "Kings nourished by Jove."</note>, that is, kings nourished by Jove. Under Jove are contained honors, riches, and ornate garments. It is truthful, and when it appears in the ascendant, it induces reverence, honesty, faith, and discipline. Jove comforts and strengthens the goodness of every sign of the zodiac. And it signifies good in that which it is found. Except in the twelfth house, in which it signifies servitude and poverty, loss of livestock, and illness in the family.

Arrived in the body of Jove: where in that sparkling of the love that was there, he saw the blessed spirits full of charity. These are those who, having had government and principality over men, lived with supreme justice and therefore are in the body of the planet, whose influence induces kings, princes, justice, and laws, as was already said. He says, therefore, that they signaled to his eyes "our speech," that is, they spoke through figures of letters as the literate speak. Because, like birds that leave the banks to go to pasture, they fly singing as if wanting to congratulate—that is, to show celebration and joy at the pastures where they arrive—and flying they make of themselves a D, or an I, or truly another figure, as we see cranes and storks and the like. So these souls, flying, sang, making of themselves these letters: D, I, L. And this was their speech, because through these they signified that their song was: "Love justice of the laws" <note>original: "Diligite iustitiam legum."</note> because it is written in Solomon: "Love justice, you who judge the earth" <note>original: "Diligite iustitiam qui iudicatis terram." From the Book of Wisdom 1:1.</note>. And he adds that they moved in their own "wheel," which means they made a circular motion which is proper to the perfect soul. Because as such motion begins from itself and returns to itself, so the good soul, proceeding from God with its virtues, returns to God. Then, becoming one of these signs—which are D, I, L—they stopped and were silent, so that there would be a little interval—that is, a little space between one figure and another—and it would be understood that each of these letters signified a word.

It is the custom of Greek and Latin poets not only at the beginning of a book to invoke the help of the Muses, but also later, when writing they arrive at a great thing: as we see especially...

# CANTO XVIII

> ...and they with you, the cities and kingdoms.
> Illuminate me with yourself so that I may reveal
> their shapes as I have conceived them;
> may it appear that your power, in these brief verses,
> can show itself. They appeared then in five times seven
> vowels and consonants, and I noted
> the parts just as they seemed spoken to me:
> "Love justice" <note>original: "Diligite iustitiam." From the Book of Wisdom 1:1.</note> were the first,
> they were the verb and noun of all that was depicted;
> "you who judge the earth" <note>original: "qui iudicatis terram." The conclusion of the phrase: "Love justice, you who judge the earth."</note> were the last.

...so that I might reveal their figures. Because the spirits make letters of themselves, and each one stands out as a word, the poet could not interpret the divine signs without divine favor. **MAY IT APPEAR YOUR POWER**: show how much you can do in these brief verses of mine.

**THEY SHOWED THEMSELVES** therefore: these spirits transformed themselves from shape to shape until they made five times seven—that is, thirty-five letters between vowels and consonants, for there are that many in these words: *Love justice, you who judge the earth*. Therefore, in all that depiction—that is, in all that configuration of letters—the first part had *Love justice*, which contains the verb *love*; and the last part <note>original: "sazzaia," an archaic form of "sexta" or "last."</note> had *you who judge the earth*.

> Then, in the M of the fifth word,
> they remained arranged so that Jove <note>The planet Jupiter, associated with justice.</note>
> seemed silver there, patterned with gold.
> And I saw other lights descend to where
> the top of the M was, and there they rested,
> singing, I believe, the Good that moves them to itself.
> Then, as when striking burnt logs,
> there rise innumerable sparks
> from which the foolish are wont to take omens,
> More than a thousand lights seemed to rise
> from there, and to ascend some much and some little,
> just as the Sun that ignites them allotted to them.
> And each having quieted in its place,
> I saw the head and the neck of an eagle
> represented by that distinct fire.

...its place, either higher or lower; thus they remained fixed in the figure of the head and neck of an eagle. And by this, he means the Emperors, whose ensign is the eagle. Therefore, there will be three classes of men: the citizens in the M; the lords and kings above the M; and the Emperors above these.

> He who paints there has no one to guide Him,
> but He guides, and from Him is recognized
> that virtue which takes form for the nests. <note>The "nests" refers to the spirits acting as birds forming the shapes.</note>
> The other beatitude, which seemed
> at first content to be lily-patterned upon the M,
> with a little motion followed the imprint.
> O sweet star, what and how many gems
> showed me that our justice
> is an effect of the heaven that you adorn!
> Therefore I pray the Mind in which is finished
> your motion and your power, that it look
> to where the smoke issues that spoils your ray,
> So that He may once more be angry...

<margin>182</margin>

<column-break/>

...in Homer and in Virgil. They [the poets] renew therefore the invocation both to have divine favor and to make the listener attentive, who, hearing the invocation, expects great things. **O Divine**: oh goddess Muse; and although he uses the singular, he intends to invoke them all, imitating Virgil who said: *I pray you, O Calliope, breathe upon the singer.* <note>original Latin: "Vos o caliope precor aspirate canenti."</note> **Pegasean**: she who lives near the Pegasean fountain. <note>The fountain of Hippocrene, created by the winged horse Pegasus, sacred to the Muses.</note> Nor in my judgment can it be understood that he invokes Minerva, as Francesco da Buti explains. **WHO YOU KNOW** [how to make] wits glorious. And certainly no wit is to be equated to a poet, who is not only instructed by human art, but moved by divine frenzy, transcends his own nature and becomes more than man, from which follows true glory and a long-lasting life—that is, of a long age through the fame he leaves behind. And not only does he give birth to a very long life for himself, but also with your help to cities and kingdoms. For through the poems in which they are praised, they remain in perpetual fame. **ILLUMINATE ME** with yourself: infuse your frenzy into me, which may illustrate and illuminate me...

After all these figures, they stopped in the last letter, which is the M of the word "earth" [original: *terra*], to denote that these were those who had the manner noted by this letter M. He has taken the "M" from this word "earth" because their government was not over the universal world. For the "world" contains in itself all the heavens and the elements enclosed within. It was not, therefore, over the universal world, but in this part of the world which is the earth inhabited by men. These spirits who remained in the M are men without lordship [private citizens], who, whether in office or out of office, had always observed justice; and therefore he places them lower. He describes other spirits descending from the Empyrean heaven above the top of the M to form a crown; and these are kings and princes who sing of the Good that moves them to itself—that is, they sing of God, who is the supreme Good and who moves men to Himself, because He inclines the well-disposed will toward His way.

From those who made the figure of the crown, many spirits shook themselves out, rising and flying upward, some more and some less according to how much they had merited. And therefore he says, *just as the sun that ignites them allotted to them*, that is, just as God, who is the Sun of Justice, has placed them. And to better express it: he shows that those spirits who flew upward, some more and some less, were similar to the sparks that come out of two ignited logs when struck together, which sparks the foolish take for omens. And then these spirits settled into the figure of the head and neck of an eagle. And by this, he means the Emperors, whose ensign is the eagle. Therefore, there will be three generations of men: the citizens in the M; the lords and kings above the M; and the Emperors above these.

The principal fiction follows, saying: that He who paints there—that is, He who moves the spirits there to make such a configuration—has no one to guide Him, that is, God, the first unmoved mover. But He guides all other things and infuses necessary virtue; and then the heavens influence it in us. And therefore from Him is recognized the virtue—which virtue is justice—which He forms through the nests, calling "birds" the spirits who in this planet make such figures.

**The other beatitude**, that is, that second order of spirits who at first seemed content to stay above the top of the M and to "lily themselves" <note>original: "ingigliarsi," to form a pattern like a lily or fleur-de-lis.</note>—that is, to make a crown made of lilies (representing the kings and the other princes)—then with little motion—that is, rising upward—followed the imprint, that is, the figure of the eagle. The meaning is that by moving they made the rest of the figure of the eagle, of which the [first] spirits had made the head and neck. Which denotes that Divine Providence disposed, through the influence of this star, the princes to consent to the monarchy of a single one who was Emperor. Or rather, it suggests that the influence of Jove would produce monarchy in the world, which government would be more perfect in justice if men wished to receive it. And perhaps he interprets here the "Greyhound" <note>The "Veltro," a prophesied savior/leader mentioned in Canto I of the Inferno.</note> of whom we spoke in the first canticle. **THOSE GEMS** therefore—that is, those spirits whom I saw in you, Jove, sweet star—showed me that human justice proceeds from your heaven...

<summary>In the sphere of Jupiter, Dante witnesses spirits forming the Latin phrase "Diligite iustitiam qui iudicatis terram," after which the final letter 'M' transforms into the shape of an eagle. The commentary explains this as a representation of the hierarchy of justice, moving from private citizens to kings and finally to the universal authority of the Emperor.</summary>

<column-break/>

I, whom you "engem"—that is, you engem, which is to say you adorn like a precious gem: and you shall be the cause of such an effect. But because I see that the malice of men corrupts your justice—that is, your influence—and especially the rulers of the Christian Church. I pray to the divine mind <margin>infinite—that is, it begins</margin> to look from where the smoke—that is, the vice—arises, which begins and corrupts the ray of justice which Scripture calls the sun: just as smoke and fog obscure the light.

The poet, seeing that the pastor of the Christian flock and the other prelates, who ought to be an example of sanctity to us to guide us to good works, are so involved in avarice and in all other kinds of injustice, that they give us nothing but captive examples with which they pull us from the right path: he turns his speech to the **MILITIA OF THE HEAVENS**—that is, to the blessed souls of heaven—whom he contemplates, and prays that they pray for us who, led astray, follow the captive example of the prelates. And here he demonstrates how gravely he sins who is placed in a position to be an example to others. **ONCE IT WAS CUSTOMARY**: here he shows that in ancient times, men who were avaricious and greedy for others' treasure moved to war and took it by force. This, although it was unjust, nevertheless had some shadow of frankness of spirit. But now it is taken with greater injustice: because under the guise of religion they excommunicate and interdict, in order to then sell the absolution and the sacraments, which are the spiritual bread with which we lead ourselves to eternal life. And for this reason it is said "from you," which the pious Father—that is, God, full of mercy—does not close or forbid to anyone: but wishes that it be given to everyone who returns to penance. But you, pastor, who "write to cancel"—that is, you issue censures not to punish sinners but to make them buy back <note>Referring to the selling of indulgences or the lifting of excommunications for money.</note>—remember that Peter and Paul, the first apostles who died

for the vineyard, are still alive: as if to say, they will be able to punish you. **WELL CAN YOU**: because you praise and say: "You, pastor, can say 'do not reprove me because I have my desire fixed on following him who wished to live alone in the desert.'" And this was the precursor of Christ, John [the Baptist], who for the daughter of Herod <note>Salome</note> was led to martyrdom because he was decapitated. At this point you will say: "I have my desire fixed on John the Baptist, so that I do not know the fisherman"—that is, Saint Peter—"nor Paul"—that is, Saint Paul. And this is the truth, not because you follow the life of the Baptist, but because you follow the **FLORIN**, on which is his image <note>The florin, the gold coin of Florence, featured the image of St. John the Baptist.</note>.

### THIRD CANTICLE OF DANTE.

Because he has already narrated the nature of Jove and which spirits represent themselves in this star, now in this nineteenth chapter, having configured the sign of the Eagle, he induces the Eagle to speak. First, therefore, he demonstrates an unheard-of way of the Eagle speaking. After that, he moves the question of whether one living justly can be saved without the Christian faith. In the third place, he resolves it. And in the last, he reproves Christian princes, because by living and reigning unjustly they deviate from those spirits that make the sign of the Eagle. Therefore: **THERE APPEARED BEFORE ME WITH OPEN WINGS THE BEAUTIFUL IMAGE**—that is, the image of the Eagle, which is beautiful, signifying justice. And this Eagle was made of the "joined" spirits—that is, connected and joined to one another—and joyful in the "sweet enjoyment"—that is, happy in the divine beatitude they had by enjoying God. The open wings signify two acts of justice: rewarding and punishing. And each soul shone like a ruby in which a ray of the sun strikes. By the ruby, he denotes charity, without which there can be no true justice. After that follows the poet, who, having to portray and report the speech of the Eagle, finds it necessary to say something that "no voice ever carried"—that is, was never said—"nor ink wrote"—that is,

never was it written. Nor was it ever apprehended by any imagination that an eagle spoke. And it is to his praise: **FOR I SAW**: he explains what this thing is and shows that it said "I" and "My," as if it were a single being; and in concept it was [many]. All those spirits who represented the body of the Eagle, because they were all together, spoke with the beak of the Eagle, and said "I" and "My" in the singular, not saying "We" and "Our." And certainly it was never apprehended by [the imagination] as if it were one and not many. Whence appears a marvelous length [of genius]...

<meta>Continuing from page 282, which ended with the Poet's prayer for divine justice against the corruption of the Church. This page begins Canto XIX of Paradiso, where the spirits in the heaven of Jupiter form the shape of a divine Eagle and begin to speak with a single voice.</meta>

### CANTO XIX

### And I began: "For being just and pious,
### I am here exalted to that glory
### which does not let itself be surpassed by desire;

### And on earth I left my memory,
### fashioned such that the wicked people
### commend it, but do not follow the story."

### Thus a single heat from many embers
### is made felt, just as from many loves
### issued only a single sound from this image.

### Wherefore I thereafter: "O perpetual flowers
### of eternal joy, who make all your odors
### seem to me as only one,

### Solve for me, by breathing, the great fast
### which has long held me in hunger,
### finding no food for it on earth."

...to maintain love and concord, and to preserve human society for which nature produces us as much as justice does. Therefore <note>original: "Actū/que" (Actumque), Latin for "and so"</note> it is no marvel if those equals who have ruled with supreme justice are now so united in this heaven. Understanding this union, the poet did not turn to the eagle as to one, but as to many spirits, whom he calls flowers because they are ornaments of that heaven where they have eternal joy. And he says that although they are many flowers, nevertheless no more than one scent—but only one—issues from them. Then he requests of them that, by inspiring him with the truth, they "solve"—that is, dissolve and take away—the great fast which has long held him in hunger. For he who fasts feels hunger. And it is a Latin way of speaking, because "to solve the fast" <note>original: "solvere ieiunium"</note> means to break the fast. This is a metaphor <note>original: "traslatione"</note> because he intends to express that for a long time he has been fasting—that is, empty of that truth for which he has great hunger—that is, a great desire to know. And the reason why he has been fasting is because on earth he has not found food that could take away such hunger; that is, he has not found on earth—meaning among the earthly and human sciences—food, that is, doctrine, that can satisfy him, or rather, can satisfy him in demonstrating this truth for which he hungers, which is to say, his desire.

### "Well do I know that if in the high realm of heaven
### divine justice makes its mirror,
### yours does not perceive it through a veil.

### You know how attentively I prepare myself
### to listen; you know what that
### doubt is which is to me so old a fast."

### Like a falcon emerging from its hood,
### moves its head and applauds with its wings,
### showing desire and making itself beautiful,

### I saw that sign, which was woven with praise
### of divine grace, do thus
### with songs such as are known up there in joy.

### Then he began, who turned the compass
### to the edge of the world, and within it
### distinguished so much hidden and manifest:

### "His power could not be so impressed
### upon the whole universe that His Word
### did not remain in infinite excess.

### And this makes certain that the first proud one,
### who was the summit of every creature,
### for not waiting for light, fell unripe.

### And hence it appears that every lesser nature
### is a scant receptacle for that Good
### which has no end and measures itself by itself."

<column-break/>

**H**e places these words in the beak of the eagle, which, although they issue from one place, nonetheless belong to all those spirits who form the eagle. He says, therefore: "I am exalted to 그hat glory which does not let itself be conquered by desire"—that is, which is so great that our desire is no greater, because we cannot desire it to be any greater. And this is "for being just and pious"—that is, for having used justice mixed with mercy, since considering the frailty of man, a total justice would be almost cruelty. And therefore he says:
> God saw our formation and had mercy on us. <note>original: "Vidit deus figmentum nostrum & misertus est nostri," a paraphrase of Psalm 103:14.</note>
And elsewhere:
> Impious is the justice that does not know how to forgive human frailty. <note>original: "Impia est iustitia que humane fragilitati non nouit ignoscere."</note>

**AND ON EARTH** I left my memory: The poet demonstrates how excellent a thing justice is, since it not only guides us to eternal life, but also makes us live here through fame, for which not only the good praise us, but it also constrains the wicked to praise us, though they do not "follow the history"—that is, they do not act according to how they hear we have acted. And certainly, the power of virtue is so great that even the vicious cannot help but love it. **THUS** a single heat from many embers: just as it happens that from many embers—that is, from many coals lit together—a single heat results, so from many loves—that is, spirits who together fashioned the eagle—there issued a single sound and a single voice. Through this fiction, it is shown that in the active life which princes administer and rule, there is nothing that so...

**T**he author had prayed the spirits to satisfy his long hunger—that is, the long desire to understand the truth. But he had not yet shown what truth he wished to understand. Nor does he say it even now, but he affirms well that they, looking into the divine mirror, can understand it for themselves. Thus the spirits perceive how attentively the author stands ready for the answer; and they know what that doubt is, which was: whether without the Christian faith, justice can lead to eternal life. And this doubt is to him a "very old fast." When these words are said by the poet, he sees the sign of the eagle act like the falcon which, when the hood is removed, moves its head around watching, and "applauds with its wings"—that is, shows joy, displaying a desire to fly and making itself beautiful by smoothing its feathers. Such, then, appeared the eagle which was "woven"—that is, composed—of praise of divine grace, meaning of the spirits who rendered praise to divine grace with such songs as mortal tongue cannot express. And for this reason, they are not made on earth. But they are made by those who are in heaven in eternal beatitude, because human intellect cannot understand celestial things unless it ascends to heaven—that is, unless first purged of every vice, it does not rise to such speculation.

**T**he eagle responds and sets forth the reasons why the poet cannot find the solution to his question, which cannot be solved except by faith, because no one is capable of [fully understanding] divine justice. And for this reason, it first posits the infinite and incomprehensible power of God, saying: "He who is the supreme God and turns the compass" <term>compass: "sesto," referring to the instrument for drawing circles, but also interpreted as the "sixth" planet, Jupiter</term>—that is, turns Jove, which is the sixth planet according to some. Others say the "sixth" refers to the roundness of the heavens which turns around the extremities. And it says "sesto" because we call a "sextant" or "compass" that instrument with which we make a round circle. **NOT** could He so impress His power: God could not imprint His power and His might so much into the universe that His Word—that is, His wisdom, which is called the Word and the Son—did not remain, that is, did not stay outside the universe in infinite excess. The meaning is that His wisdom infinitely exceeds every creature. And it is not improper for the author to say that God cannot put all His power into any creature.

<summary>In the Heaven of Jupiter, the spirits forming the Divine Eagle speak with one voice to explain the nature of Justice and Mercy. Dante expresses his long-held "hunger" to know if a person can be saved through justice without Christian faith, while the Eagle begins to explain that God's wisdom infinitely exceeds human understanding.</summary>

# XIX PARADISE

Because this would make a creature equal to Himself, whereby His power would be diminished. For the creature would then be able to create itself and thus would not be a creature but a creator; and in this way, there would be multiple first principles <note>The "first principle" refers to the ultimate source or cause of all things, i.e., God</note>, which is impossible. Therefore, God could not put all His value into a creature, for that creature would then not be infinitely lesser than Him. God cannot make something greater than or equal to Himself, just as He cannot do evil. This inability of God does not arise from any lack of power within Him, but rather from the infinite excellence of His power. Therefore, God’s inability to infuse His entire power into a creature proves that He is omnipotent. And this confirms—that is, proves—what is said in this way: If Lucifer, who was the most excellent creature God ever made and was the first to become proud against his creator, did not see the reasons for God’s providence, then other less excellent creatures will be even less able to see them. But Lucifer did not see them. This is evident because he did not wait for the light of confirming grace; instead, he considered himself equal to the Divine Word and therefore fell "unripe" <note>original: "acerbo" - meaning fallen prematurely, before he was fully perfected by grace</note>. Thus, it is manifest that the creature cannot see everything within the Creator. AND FROM THIS it appears that every lesser nature—understand "natured," meaning every created thing—is a limited and insufficient receptacle for that Good, because it is smaller than the Creator. That is, it is not capable enough to contain within itself that Good which has no end—meaning the infinite Good, which is God. And because He is infinite, He measures Himself by Himself, for the infinite cannot be measured except by the infinite. And no mind is infinite except God's. If, therefore, the creature is a smaller receptacle, it can receive some part of God's power, but not all of it.

---

Therefore your vision, which must be
one of the rays of the Mind
with which all things are filled,
Cannot, by its own nature, be powerful
enough that its principle does not discern
much farther than what is apparent to it.
Therefore, into eternal justice,
the sight that your world receives
enters as the eye does into the sea;
For although from the shore it sees the bottom,
in the deep ocean <note>original: "pelago"</note> it sees it not, and nonetheless
it is there, but the depth hides it.
There is no light unless it comes from the Serene Sky
which is never clouded; otherwise it is darkness,
or the shadow of the flesh, or its poison.
Enough, I think, the hiding place is open
that concealed the living justice from you,
about which you made such frequent questioning.
For you said: "A man is born on the bank
of the Nile, and there is no one there who speaks
of Christ, nor who reads, nor who writes;
And all his wishes and good acts
are as much as human reason sees,
without sin in life or in speech;
He dies unbaptized and without faith:
where is this justice that condemns him?
Where is his fault, if he does not believe?"
Now, who are you who want to sit upon the bench <note>original: "scranna" - a judge's seat or magistrate's chair</note>
to judge from a thousand miles away
with sight as short as a span?
Certainly, to him who subtilizes <note>who engages in complex or fine-grained reasoning</note> with me,
if the Scripture were not above us,
there would be cause to marvel.
O earthly animals! O dull minds!
The Primal Will, which of itself is good,
from itself—the Supreme Good—has never moved.
All is just that is consistent with it;
no created good draws it to itself,
but it, radiating, causes that good.

<column-break/>

He concludes that since your understanding and cognition come from a single ray of the Divine Mind—which spreads through all things because all created things have their form and being from it—and this ray is the divine power that infuses into each thing as much as suffices for its existence, human intelligence cannot be so powerful by its nature that it discerns and knows its principle (that is, God) except from much further away than what is apparent to it. That is, beyond the limit that it sees. And although one person may see more than another, nonetheless no one sees the whole. THEREFORE: for which reason; and the text is ordered in this way: THE SIGHT which your world receives: that is, the knowledge which exists in man while he is still on earth. "Enters into" <note>original: "sinterna"</note>: places itself within eternal justice: that is, recognizing divine justice, in the same way that the physical eye and sight enter the sea. For the human eye sees the bottom of the sea near the shore where the water is shallow. But in the deep ocean <note>original: "pelago"</note>—that is, where the water is deep—it does not see the bottom, not because the bottom is not there, but because of the depth, which the power of sight cannot reach through such a great distance.

By what I have said to you, O Dante, the "darkness" is sufficiently opened to you—that is, the obscurity which hid "living justice" from you. That is, it made it so you could not understand divine justice, about which you made such "frequent" <note>original: "crebra"</note>—that is, such often-repeated—questioning. That is, the question you so often searched for within yourself. For you said: "A man will be born in Egypt near the Nile where there are only infidels, and there is no one there to preach of Christ, nor who reads or writes of Him. And nonetheless he does not live according to virtue in thought and in deed, and without sin of words or of facts, as far as human reason can understand. But finally, because he dies without baptism and without the Christian faith, he is condemned. Therefore, where is the divine justice here, which requires from him more than he was able to do?" WHEREFORE THIS JUSTICE THAT CONDEMNS HIM: as if to say, it cannot be justice to condemn justifiable ignorance.

He rebukes the presumptuous ignorance of those men who have the audacity, with their dull intellect which is not capable of God’s secrets, to place themselves on the "bench" <note>original: "scrana"</note>—that is, in the judge's chair—to judge what is a thousand miles away with their short sight of a single span. Just as it would be the height of folly for a man whose sight was so short that he could see no further than a span to want to judge what was a thousand miles distant, so it is the height of temerity that the human wit <note>original: "ingegno"</note>, with its little knowledge—which, because it is finite, cannot comprehend God who is infinite—should presume to understand the secrets of God. Nor does he remember the saying: "Unsearchable are your judgments, O Lord" <note>original: "Incomprehensibilia funt iudicia tua domine"</note>. And Saint Paul forbids this, saying: "He who searches into majesty shall be overwhelmed by its glory" <note>original: "Scrutator maiestatis reicietur adeo"</note>; and elsewhere: "Do not seek to know more than is necessary to know, but to know with sobriety" <note>original: "Noliter fapere plusquã opportet fapere. fed fapere ad fobrietatem"</note>. And Matthew: "I say to you that many will come from the east and the west and will sit down with Abraham in the kingdom of heaven; but the children of the kingdom shall be cast out into darkness" <note>original: "Dico autem uobis quod multi ab oriente uenient & recumbent cum abraam in regno celorum: filii regni reicietur in tenebras"</note>. We must therefore believe that whatever is done by the Supreme Good is good, and that He denies what man cannot see. Especially as Mark says: "But of that day and hour no one knows, not even the angels of heaven, nor the Son, but only the Father" <note>original: "De die autem illa & hora nemo fcit: non angelus celi: non filius nisi pater"</note>. Therefore, man will know it much less. CERTAINLY TO him. In this place the Eagle, so that no one may excuse themselves through ignorance, removes every...

# CANTO XIX
### G iii

...speaking of ignorance. Certainly, there would be much to doubt and much to marvel at—that is, to be amazed—by anyone who **subtly investigates** <note>The original "sa sottiglia meco" suggests a deep, analytical inquiry</note> with me the divine justice that shines within me, the Eagle, if the Scripture were not above us. The Scripture teaches us that the will of God is just, and that we must not investigate the reason why He does this rather than that. **O EARTHLY animals**: the Eagle shows a righteous indignation that man, an earthly animal and consequently of a dull mind, wishes to understand divine matters, considering that not even the celestial creatures can perfectly know the divine wisdom, power, and goodness. **THE FIRST will**. He has rebuked those who go seeking the reasons for divine justice. Since it should suffice them to understand that God cannot err: because it is known that the first will is good by itself, and not from any other. For if God participated in a will from another, He could perhaps sometimes lose it and not be good. But because that will is good in itself and not from another, it never departs from itself, which is the Supreme Good. And if the divine will never departs from good, that which harmonizes with it and pleases it must be good, and all good is just. Therefore, no one can justly complain, even though they may sometimes seem to suffer unjustly. And the reason why one cannot complain is that no created good draws God to itself; for God, the creator of all, is a debtor to no one. But everyone is obliged to Him for every gift received. Rather, that divine will causes him—that is, it is the cause for the created good to have its being. For He is like the **potter** <note>A reference to the biblical metaphor from Romans 9:21 regarding the potter's right over the clay</note> who makes some vessels to hold precious things and some to hold filthy things.

As the stork circles above the nest
after she has fed her young,
and as the one who has been fed looks up at her;
So did the blessed image act,
and so did it lift its brows,
moving its wings prompted by so many counsels.
Wheeling, it sang and said: "As
my notes are to you, who do not understand them,
such is the eternal judgment to you mortals."
Then those glowing fires followed,
the Holy Spirit still within the sign
that made the Romans revered by the world.

It began again: "To this kingdom
no one ever ascended who did not believe in Christ,
either before or after He was nailed to the tree.
But see, many cry 'Christ, Christ!'
who shall be, at the judgment, far less near
to Him than someone who does not know Christ.
And such Christians the Ethiopian shall condemn
when the two colleges shall depart,
the one eternally rich and the other destitute.
What could the Persians say to our kings
when they shall see that volume opened
in which all their shames are written?

There shall be seen among the deeds of Albert
that which shall soon move the pen
to cover the kingdom of Prague in desolation.
There shall be seen the woe that upon the Seine
he induces by falsifying the currency,
he who shall die from the stroke of a boar’s hide.
There shall be seen the pride that thirsts,
which makes the Scot and the Englishman mad
so that neither can stay within his own borders."

<column-break/>

By way of a simile, he shows that just as the stork, having brought food to its young, circles over the nest, and they, having been fed, look up at her: so the Eagle did over me after it had fed me with its discourse; and I looked up at said Eagle. Then the blessed image lifted its brows—that is, the image of the Eagle, which moved its wings prompted by **so many counsels**: that is, by as many spirits as were in those wings. **THEN FOLLOWED those glowing fires**: The meaning is that those shining splendors, which were kindled in charity, continued speaking in the sign of the Eagle: that is, a single voice issued from all through the beak of the Eagle, which made the **Romans revered**. For said sign of the Eagle was on the military standards of the Romans, who were revered for their innumerable victories.

The Eagle began again, saying that no one ever ascended to the celestial kingdom who did not believe in Christ. And this belief was either of those who were before the coming of Christ—and these believed in the Christ to come, as those whom He drew out of **Limbo** <note>The place of the "virtuous pagans" and patriarchs before the Harrowing of Hell</note>—or of those who were after His passion; and these believed that He had already come and redeemed the world with His blood. **BUT SEE**: understand that many cry "Christ, Christ," and these are false Christians who show belief with words but do not believe in their hearts. Wherefore it is written: <gloss>This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me</gloss> <note>original: "Populus iste labbiis me honorat t cor autem eorum longe ame est" - quoting Isaiah 29:13 and Matthew 15:8</note>. And these, in the Great Judgment, shall be **less near** to Him than someone who did not know Christ. For he who has had no knowledge of Christ has some excuse, but the wicked Christian sins much more because he has no excuse. And therefore he says that when the final sentence is given, and the **two colleges**—that is, the two congregations of souls—shall depart, because the good shall ascend to heaven to eternal wealth, which is happiness where there is an infinite abundance of every good, and the wicked shall descend to hell and be **destitute**—that is, poor of all happiness—then some **Ethiopian**—that is, someone from Ethiopia where there is no knowledge of the Christian religion—shall condemn and blame the wicked Christian and reproach him for his filthy life. What can the **Persians** say—who will have had no light of faith—to our Christian kings, except to blame them when at the judgment they see that **opened volume**: that is, they shall see Christ the judge, in whom, as in a book, all merits and demerits shall be read, which demerits are the **disdains** of Christ. For he who sins acts against the evangelical doctrine; therefore, he disdains it.

He continues in rebuking the wicked Christians, and especially the wicked [kings], and traverses all the realms that are among Christians. And he begins from the northern part where there are four realms: Prague, France, Scotland, and England. He says therefore that there—that is, in that book—shall be seen among the unjust deeds of **Albert**, that deed which, because it is more unjust, shall soon move the pen to write his vices. Albert was the Emperor crowned by Pope Boniface in the year of our salvation 1298. He was the Duke of Austria and fought with Adolph, called Adolphus, King of the Romans, and conquered and killed him. There was seen the woe of the defeat suffered by the **Flemish** <note>The Battle of the Golden Spurs in 1302, where the French were defeated</note>: which woe upon the **Seine**—that is, in Paris, through which city runs the river Seine—was caused by the **falsifying of the currency**. This man was **Philip, called the Fair**, King of France. And in 1300, having been defeated at Courtrai by the Flemish, he renewed great...

### CANTO XX OF THE THIRD CANTICLE OF DANTE.

<image-desc>Decorative initial Q containing a circular frame with the profile of a man's head facing right.</image-desc>
When he who lights all the world descends from our hemisphere, so that the day is consumed on every side, the sky, which before was lit only by him, suddenly makes itself visible again through many lights in which one shines. And this act of the sky came to my mind, when the sign of the world and of its leaders <note>The Eagle, symbol of the Empire</note> was silent in the blessed beak. Because all those living lights

<column-break/>

[The poet] censures the luxury and the idle living of Alfonso, King of Spain, and of Ladislaus, King of Bohemia. Alfonso, in the year one thousand two hundred and sixty, was elected Emperor: and through cowardice and softness did not pursue the prize. Of Ladislaus mention was made in the seventh chapter of the *Purgatorio*. **THE LAME ONE OF JERUSALEM**: this was Charles II, son of Charles I, King of Puglia: who was "lame," that is, crippled or smashed; he was very luxurious and a corrupter of virgins: for which he excused himself saying he did it because otherwise he would have become a leper. His goodness, [Dante] says, shall be marked in the book of Christ with an **I**, which represents one, because he had no other goodness except that he was liberal <note>generous</note>: and the contrary, that is, vice, shall be marked with an **M**, which represents a thousand, because he had infinite vices. **THERE SHALL BE SEEN** the avarice and the baseness. And certainly avarice proceeds from baseness of soul. Whence women and the elderly are more avaricious. **OF HIM WHO GUARDS THE ISLAND OF THE FIRE**, that is, Sicily, where Mount Etna is. And on this island Anchises, father of Aeneas, died old in the city of Trapani, called *Drepanum*. This was Frederick, King of Sicily, son of King Peter of Aragon, a most noble prince. And so that you may understand how much his writing—that is, the writing that contains his vices—is little, there will be "cut-off letters," that is, there will be one letter for each part: and in this way they will take up little space and note many vices.

**THE UNCLE** <note>original: "La barba"</note> of Lord Frederick was Lord James, King of Majorca, Minorca, and the Ebusian islands. <term>Barba</term> in the Lombard language means uncle. **AND OF THE BROTHER**. This was Lord Peter, King of Aragon. **WHO SO NOBLE A NATION**: So noble a family. **AND TWO CROWNS**: That of Aragon and that of Majorca have been "made base," they have shamed them, just as he whose wife is unfaithful is shamed. "Base" as if to say degenerated. **PORTUGAL** among the ancients was called Lusitania and is a kingdom of Spain, which is divided into four kingdoms. **NORWAY**: This region is under the north where, in the summer tropic, there are the longest days and shortest nights. **RASCIA**: This is a kingdom in Slavonia <note>Modern-day Serbia</note> whose king falsified the Venetian ducats. **NAVARRE**: Is a kingdom of Spain: and at that time it was under the French: and therefore he admonishes it to defend itself with the mountains that divide it from France. **NICOSIA AND FAMAGUSTA** are cities in Cyprus which already begin to lament. This refers to future vices. **OF THEIR BEAST**. That is, of their beastly king. Truly, the poet alone <note>original: "Saulo poeta," likely a misprint for "Solo el poeta"</note> is one to whom the human generation is beholden: since he so rigidly reproves the princes, because their sins do not harm one or a few like the errors of private citizens. But they harm the whole country that is administered by them, and often a single person is the cause of the ruin of many kingdoms.

Just as in the preceding chapter the Eagle demonstrates the incomprehensible justice of God and reproved the kings: so in this one it demonstrates to the author some of the spirits that configured it. This twentieth chapter contains four parts. In the first, it describes what the disposition of the Eagle was. In the second, it names certain excellent spirits. In the third, it resolves a doubt born from having seen two of those souls. In the fourth, it describes the depth of predestination. In the verses already written, he places a simile saying that the place where the Eagle was appeared to him as the sky is seen when the sun descends to the other hemisphere. Because, the light of the sun failing, the sky adorns itself with various stars: and thus all those spirits lit with charity appeared as stars in that Eagle. **SINCE THE BRIGHT GEMS** <note>original: "lucidi lapilli"</note>: that is, the shining spirits which he calls gems: that is, precious stones of which Jove, which is the...

...lived more brightly, songs began,
from my memory fleeting and frail.
O sweet love, who with a smile cloaks yourself,

After the clear and shining gems
wherewith I saw the sixth light <note>The planet Jupiter, associated with Justice</note> bejeweled
imposed silence on the angelic chimes,

that descends clear from rock to rock,

And as the sound at the neck of the lute <term>cetra: a traditional plucked string instrument similar to a lyre</term>
takes its form, and as through the opening
of the pipe the wind that enters,
thus, removed from the delay of waiting,
that murmuring of the eagle rose up
through its neck as if it were hollow.
There it became a voice, and then issued
through its beak in the form of words,
such as the heart awaited where I wrote them.

"The part in me that sees and endures the sun
in mortal eagles," it began to me,
"now must be looked upon fixedly;
because of the fires from which I form my shape,
those with which the eye in my head sparkles,
of all of them, these are the highest.
He who shines in the middle as the pupil
was the singer of the Holy Spirit <note>King David, the traditional author of the Psalms</note>
who moved the ark from town to town.
Now he knows the merit of his song,
insofar as it was the effect of his own counsel,
by the reward that is equal to it.

Of the five who make the eyebrow's circle for me,
he who is closest to the beak
consoled the widow for her son <note>The Roman Emperor Trajan</note>.
Now he knows how dearly it costs
not to follow Christ, through the experience
of this sweet life and of its opposite.
And he who follows in the circumference
of which I speak, on the upper circle,
delayed death through true penitence <note>King Hezekiah</note>.
Now he knows that the eternal judgment
is not changed when a worthy prayer
makes tomorrow's what was today's down there.

under a good intention that bore bad fruit..."

<column-break/>

The sixth planet was bejeweled. Then they became silent: and the eagle resumed its speech. And it describes by comparison the discourse of the voice from the neck of the eagle, showing that it rose through the channel of the neck: with that sound with which a copious amount of water descends from stone to stone. And as the sound of the lute—that is, the *cythera*—takes its form in the neck of said instrument: because in that, the fingers of the one who plays touch the strings. And as through the openings—that is, the holes—of the bagpipe or flute or pipe, the wind: that is, the breath that the player puts into it, takes its form of voice, penetrating—that is, passing through—said holes: so through the neck of the eagle that murmuring rose: and in the beak the voice took shape, and it spoke those things that my heart desired. And certainly, it is a marvelous fantasy in this poet, who narrates his fiction in such a way: that he makes the almost impossible seem credible. And he is very similar to the genius of the poet Ovid, who in his monstrous transformations: makes things almost plausible.

The eagle speaks to show Dante six most excellent spirits who form the shape of the eye in the eagle: and it admonishes Dante that he should look at that member in it which, in mortal eagles, looks at and endures the sun. And this is the eye. And just as eagles in this world can look at the sun and endure its lights: so this one can look at and endure the sun of justice. Therefore, it wants Dante to look at those spirits who make up its eyes because they are the highest. And it says that the spirit who is in the middle, acting as the pupil—that is, the light of the eye—is David, the most just king and prophet filled with the Holy Spirit, who moved the ark of the covenant where the tablets of the laws were kept: the rod of Moses: and the vessel of manna. Regarding the moving of the ark, we spoke in the tenth canto of *Purgatory*. And because these spirits were most excellent in glory: therefore he places them in the most excellent sense, which is that of the eye.

He first places in the eyebrow the Emperor Trajan, the eleventh, who, how he abundantly satisfied the widow, was discussed in the tenth canto of *Purgatory*: Now he knows by experience how dearly it costs not to follow Christ, through the experience of this sweet life, which he feels at present, and of its opposite—that is, of the opposite and contrary part which he saw when he first died a pagan: and stayed in hell until the times of Gregory, which were nine hundred years. **AND HE WHO follows**: This was Hezekiah, prophet and king of Judea: and of whom it is written in the book of Isaiah and in the book of Kings, to whom his death having been announced by the angel, he wept and lamented and said: "I said: In the noontide of my days I shall go to the gates of hell" <note>original: "Ego dixi in dimidio dierum meorum ego uadam ad portas inferi"</note>. To this man, through many prayers, God prolonged his life for the space of fifteen years. Now that he sees the truth in God, he knows that the eternal judgment of God is immutable: although it seems to us that it changes through just prayers. As, for example, in this king. For God from eternity had thus ordained it as it happened. But to us, who do not know, it seems that God makes "tomorrow's"—that is, future time—out of "today's"—that is, the present.

This one who follows with the laws is Constantine: who under a good intention conferred all imperial dignities upon the Pope. Through which authority the pontiffs became ambitious and greedy. **WITH ME**: because he also carried the eagle toward the East. **NOW HE KNOWS**: although the endowment made by Constantine to the pontiffs be...

To give way to the shepherd, he became Greek <note>Refers to Emperor Constantine, who moved the capital of the Roman Empire to Constantinople (becoming "Greek") to leave Rome to the Pope (the "shepherd").</note>. Now he knows how the evil resulting from his good deed <note>The "Donation of Constantine," a document later proved a forgery, which supposedly gave temporal power to the Church.</note> did not harm him, even though the world was destroyed by it. And him you see on the downward arc was William, whom that land mourns which weeps for Charles and the living Frederick <note>William II of Sicily (the "Good"). Sicily mourns his loss while suffering under its current rulers.</note>. Now he knows how heaven is enamored with the just king, and by the appearance of his radiance, he shows it still.

Who would believe, down in the erring world, that Ripheus the Trojan <note>A minor character in Virgil’s Aeneid described as "the most just of all Trojans."</note> was the fifth of the holy lights in this circle? Now he knows much of what the world cannot see of divine grace, though his sight does not discern the bottom <note>Human intellect cannot reach the depths of divine judgment.</note>. Like the little lark that soars in the air, first singing and then falling silent, content with the final joy that satisfies it, so seemed to me the image of the imprint of the eternal pleasure, by whose desire everything becomes what it is.

And although I was as glass to the color that covers it regarding my doubt, it did not suffer me to wait in silence. But from my mouth, "What things are these?" it pushed out with the force of its weight, so that I saw great festivities of flashing. Then immediately, with its eye more kindled, the blessed sign answered me, so as not to keep me suspended in wonder. "I see that you believe these things because I say them, but you do not see how; so that if they are believed, they remain hidden. You act like one who learns a thing by name well, but its essence <term>quiditate: the 'whatness' or essential nature of a thing</term> he cannot see unless someone else reveals it. **The Kingdom of Heaven suffers violence** <note>original: "Regnum celorum uiolentia pate" (Matthew 11:12)</note> from warm love and living hope, which conquers the divine will; not in the way that one man overpowers another, but it conquers the will because the will wishes to be conquered, and, being conquered, it conquers with its own goodness."

<column-break/>

...been the cause of infinite evils: as the poet has shown in many places; nevertheless, he knows this. But he looks to his good work and not to the evil that followed from it. **AND HE WHOM** you see. This denotes William, King of Sicily, the last of the successors of Robert Guiscard and the grandfather of Constance, of whom we spoke both in the second and in this third canticle <note>The Purgatorio and Paradiso.</note>. He was an excellent prince in liberality, justice, and clemency. He reigned in Sicily in the year of salvation 1164. In the downward arc, that is, in the lower part of the circle of the eye. **WHICH WEEPS** for Charles and the living Frederick: because Charles the Lame <note>Charles II of Anjou</note>, who then reigned, made war on the island from without, and Frederick <note>Frederick II of Aragon</note> burdened it from within with foul avarice. Or rather, it mourns Charles the deceased father of the Lame, who lost Sicily, which he had oppressed tyrannically through extreme greed, as we have narrated elsewhere.

Now he knows enough: it seems to us in the world impossible that a non-Christian spirit could be saved. But it is seen in God as if in a mirror: because divine providence has willed this, notwithstanding that even in heaven the blessed soul cannot see to the depths. In short, the poet infers that divine grace extends even to the infidel and gives them belief in a way that they can be saved. But we cannot understand His judgment. And this is the answer to the doubt proposed above concerning the man who is just and good but an infidel. **LIKE THE** little lark: it is the nature of the lark to rise from the earth, and ascending little by little, to climb while singing, and then take pleasure in wandering through the air that falls silent. Therefore, similar to this bird was the eagle, which he calls the image of the imprint of the eternal pleasure; it is figured here by the divine will, which imprints justice in that planet. **BY WHOSE** desire: according to the will of which God, everything becomes what it is: or the pleasure of God. For every thing is made by God as He wills. Hence Augustine says:
> God loves us as we were made by His gift, and not as we are by our own merit. <note>original: "Tales amat nos deus quales facti sumus dono eius : & no quales sumus nostro merito."</note>

Although my doubt appeared in me to those spirits like color in glass, and by this they knew what I desired to hear, nevertheless, the most burning desire to hear did not let me keep silent and wait for the solution, **BUT I SAID** "What things are these?" wondering how, if no one can be saved who has not true faith in Christ, a Trojan, not having been a Christian, could have ascended to heaven. **KINGDOM** of Heaven: the answer in essence is this: that although the divine will does not allow those who are not Christian to ascend to heaven, nevertheless, a most burning charity and undoubting faith conquer and force such a will, in a way that it allows the pagan to be saved. Not, however, that the divine will is conquered as one man conquers another by force; but it is conquered because it wishes to be. And thus conquered, it conquers with its own benevolence—that is, with its kindness—as happens when, conquering a friend in a dispute, nevertheless, out of humanity so that he is not ashamed, we yield and let him win.

The eagle continues in its speech to resolve the doubt that was in the poet's mind: how it could be that without the Christian faith, the Trojan Emperor <note>Trajan</note> and Ripheus the Trojan were saved, whom he saw adorning the most holy region of angels, that is, heaven. He says, therefore, that they did not die as gentile pagans, but as Christians. Because divine grace, moved by the justice of Ripheus, illuminated him so that before he died, he believed in the Christ to come, although it was more than a thousand years before the advent of Christ. And therefore he says "at the feet of God about to suffer," using "feet" for the whole body of Christ who was to be born and suffer. And Trajan the Emperor, who lived after the passion of Christ, believed in the feet "already suffered"—that is, those which had already suffered. Therefore, having died and already gone to Hell where those who are obstinate...

<header># CANTO XIX <note>Though the header says XIX, the text is clearly Canto XX of the Paradiso.</note></header>
