The first life on the brow and the fifth
make you marvel, because you see
the region of the angels painted by them.
They did not leave their bodies, as you believe,
as Gentiles, but as Christians in firm faith:
one in the feet that were to suffer, the other in the feet that had suffered. <note>Referring to Christ's crucifixion: Ripheus lived before Christ (feet to suffer), while Trajan lived after (feet had suffered).</note>
For the one returned from Hell, where no one ever
returns to a good will,
and this was the reward of divine hope—
Divine hope, which put its power
into the prayers made to God to raise him up,
so that his will might be moved.
The glorious soul of whom we speak, <note>Emperor Trajan.</note>
having returned to the flesh for a short time,
believed in Him who was able to help him;
And believing, he was kindled with such fire
of true love, that at his second death
he was worthy to come to this place.
The other, through grace that flows from so deep
a fountain that no creature
ever pushed their eye to its first wave,
Placed all his love below on righteousness;
therefore, from grace to grace, God opened
his eye to our future redemption.
Wherefore he believed in it, and no longer endured
from then on the stench of paganism,
and he rebuked the perverse people.
Those three ladies served as his baptism,
whom you saw by the first wheel, <note>The three theological virtues: Faith, Hope, and Charity, seen in the Earthly Paradise (Purgatorio XXIX).</note>
more than a thousand years before baptizing began.
O predestination, how remote
is your root from those sights
that do not see the First Cause in its entirety!
And you mortals, keep yourselves restrained
in judging; for we who see God
do not yet know all the elect;
And such a lack is sweet to us,
because our good is refined in this good:
that what God wills, we also will.
Thus, by that divine image,
to make clear my short sight,
a sweet medicine was given to me.
And as a good lutanist makes a good singer
follow the vibration of the string,
by which the song gains more pleasure,
So, while it spoke, if I remember rightly,
I saw the two blessed lights,
just as the blinking of eyes agrees,
Moving their little flames with the words.

<column-break/>

to one who cannot repent of evil: the hope that he had in God while he was alive—that God would illuminate him in the true faith—was his reward <note>original: "mercede"</note>, that is, his merit; because this hope was the reason that the prayers of Gregory <note>St. Gregory the Great, who according to legend prayed Trajan back to life so he could convert.</note> had power before God to bring him back to life. This was so that his will, which in Hell cannot change toward wanting good, might be changed while in the body. Therefore, having returned to the body where he stayed but a short time, he immediately converted to God and believed in Him who could help him. And he was kindled with such charity of true love that, upon leaving the body—which was his second death—he deserved to ascend to this heaven. 

The other, who is the soul of Ripheus, for observing justice on earth: God infused him with the gift of understanding that the Son of God was to take flesh and suffer to redeem us. This is that Ripheus of whom Virgil wrote: <term>“Ripheus falls, the most just of all the Trojans and the strictest observer of right.” <note>original: "Cadit & rhipheus iustissimus olim qui fuit ite ucris: et seruatissimus equi" (Aeneid II, 426-427)</note></term> 

**THOSE THREE ladies:** These three virtues—Faith, Hope, and Charity—which we have already seen previously in the Paradise of Delights <note>The Earthly Paradise.</note> at the right of the Griffin, took the place of baptism for him. 

**MORE THAN A thousand years:** because from the fall of Troy to the beginning of Rome there were 414 years. And from the building of Rome to the birth of Christ there were 752 years. 

**O PREDESTINATION how remote:** An excellent and fitting exclamation to show how unknown the primary root and the depth of divine predestination is to man, from which it arises that Ripheus rather than another could ascend to such grace. And this happens because we cannot see the whole First Cause—that is, we cannot know the abyss of the divine mind, which is the First Cause, nor its counsels. For this reason, men must not overreach nor judge, since the blessed spirits see things in God as in a mirror; nevertheless, they do not see everything. Nor can they penetrate to the depths in knowing all the elect—that is, the full number of the predestined. Nor is this a lesser glory for them; because since it is their highest pleasure to conform themselves to the divine will, they enjoy not knowing everything, seeing that it so pleases God. 

Therefore, such a "scemo"—that is, such a diminishment of knowledge—refines them, making them perfectly blessed. I know that this passage not only hints at but clearly requires a diffuse treatment of predestination: a very difficult thing for one who is not very learned to describe in a way that does not take away free will. Nor can this be conveniently disputed if we do not also understand foreknowledge <note>original: "presciētia"</note> and reprobation, and finally the divine will. But we will not extend ourselves too prolixly because the size of the volume forbids it. Nor will we skip it entirely, because without this, the mind of the poet remains obscure. 

Augustine placed four definitions on predestination, of which the first is: that predestination is the foreknowledge of God’s benefits. The second: predestination is from the heart to glory. The third is: the purpose of having mercy. The fourth is: the preparation of grace in the present and of glory in the future. In the first definition, the knowledge of God is noted; in the second, the election; in the third, the will; in the fourth, the direction to the end. Augustine then posits: vocation, justification, predestination, and magnification. Vocation pulls us from evil; justification regards the good that grace begins; predestination regards the final good of grace; magnification the good of future glory. Or we might say that predestination prepares glory through grace; vocation offers us grace; justification gives it to us; but magnification multiplies glory through grace. 

Predestination does not impose necessity on things; because if it did, many inconveniences would arise, for rewards would be proposed in vain to the good and punishments to the guilty, and they would be justly rewarded or punished. Furthermore, God would be the author of evils, and free will would be lost. Nevertheless, it is necessary that whatever God foresees be necessary—not simply, but as a consequence. For example <note>original: "uer bigratia"</note>: Scipio sees that Hannibal is arranging his ranks. It is not necessary for Hannibal to arrange them because Scipio sees it; but Scipio seeing that Hannibal arranges them, it follows by necessity that he is arranging them. Nevertheless, Scipio's seeing is not the cause of the arranging of the ranks. Similarly, although God sees the evil works of man, He is not the cause of them. Theologians make a difference between predestination and foreknowledge <note>original: "prescientia"</note>. This is because predestination is the knowledge of good things and contains the cause of them; but foreknowledge <note>original: "presentia" (likely "prescientia")</note> pertains to evils and is not the cause of them.

<header>PARADISO</header>

And certainly, if God permits free will, He uses no injustice if He punishes one who has erred, given that they could have guarded themselves against error. But if one achieves salvation through grace, He does no injury to anyone. Therefore, when He damns the guilty, as was the case with Judas, He observes justice. When He predestines someone, as was the case with Paul, He uses grace and great mercy, which does not exclude justice. Thus, the primary will of God first desires that everyone be saved insofar as they are human. But the second will <note>Theologians often distinguish between God's "antecedent" will (desiring salvation for all) and His "consequent" will (the judgment based on human choice).</note> desires to damn certain men insofar as they are deserving of it. This is because the antecedent will regards the order of nature according to how it was instituted by Him. But the consequent will, which comes after the error of the sinner, regards the order of the person disposed to free will. But I return to the text. **AND AS A GOOD SINGER:** The meaning is that the two spirits <note>Trajan and Ripheus.</note> accorded themselves with the words of the Eagle to demonstrate their joy, just as a good lutenist accords his voice with the sound of the strings; and thus they moved their little flames <gloss>that is, splendors</gloss> together, just as eyes blink in unison.

### CANTO XXI OF THE THIRD CANTICLE BY DANTE

Already were my eyes fixed again upon the face
of my lady, and my soul with them,
withdrawn from every other intent.
And she did not smile, but: "If I were to smile,"
she began to me, "you would become such
as Semele was when she turned to ashes;
For my beauty, which along the stairs
of the eternal palace is kindled the more,
as you have seen, the higher one climbs,
If it were not tempered, shines so greatly
that your mortal power, at its flash,
would be like a branch that thunder shatters.
We have risen to the seventh splendor,
which beneath the breast of the burning Lion
now radiates downward, mixed with its power.
Fix your mind straight behind your eyes,
and make of them mirrors for the figure
that in this mirror shall appear to you."

<column-break/>

In the preceding chapter, the author showed the illustrious spirits of the sphere of Jupiter, who, through the practical virtues in the active life with justice, had ruled and administered the magistracies and empires committed to them rightly. But at present, he places the souls who, following the influence of Saturn, have served God in the contemplative life, removed from the tumult and noise of secular actions. Therefore, first he describes his ascent to the sphere of Saturn. Then he moves a doubt to a spirit, and from him learns the solution to such a doubt. And in the third part, he moves a question which arises from the solution of the first doubt. In the fifth, the spirit manifests itself to the author and vituperates the popes of those times. Now, as to the beginning of the chapter, he shows that once the Eagle’s words were finished, he turned back with his eyes and soul to Beatrice. This denotes that, having to treat new matter, he does not wish to begin before he has turned his entire genius and mind to the Holy Scripture; and therefore he was "withdrawn from every other intent and thought" because he wished to follow only that. And thus, in passing, he shows that whoever wishes to be in the true contemplation of divine things must necessarily leave every other thing and fix themselves in that. This is demonstrated in the Gospel where Martha, who is the active life, busies herself around the house and turns to various ministries; and Mary <gloss>that is, the contemplative life</gloss> does not help, but sits and does not move from the feet of the Lord. **AND SHE DID NOT SMILE:** Beatrice does not smile here to denote that the contemplative life is more grave and severe than the active; furthermore, it denotes the nature of the planet, which is grave and slow, as we shall suddenly demonstrate. One can also interpret it according to Beatrice’s words: that when man transcends

---

to the supreme degree of divine speculation, if Beatrice smiled—that is, if she showed all her splendor—human genius (which is to that splendor like the eye of the <note>original: "noctua i. ciuetta"</note> little owl to the rays of the sun) would be so dazzled that, wishing to see the whole, it would see nothing at all. **WAS SEMELE** when she turned to ashes: Semele was the daughter of Cadmus the Theban; she gave birth to Bacchus by Jove. Juno, transformed into an old woman, persuaded her to ask Jove to lie with her in the same form in which he lay with Juno. And as Jove observed his promise, he came to her armed with celestial lightning because he lay with Juno thus. And finally, Semele being unable to suffer the heat, she was burned by it, as we described at length in the *Inferno*. **WE HAVE** risen to the seventh splendor: we have ascended into the seventh planet, which is Saturn; the poet feigns that at the time of this vision <gloss>that is, in 1300</gloss> it was in the sign of Leo. They say, therefore, that Saturn was in the seventh degree of Leo; Jupiter in the twenty-fourth of Aries; the Sun at the beginning of Aries; Venus was in Pisces; the Moon in Libra. **RADIATES:** it radiates at present mixed with its power. It is as if he says that although Saturn is very cold, nevertheless the heat of Leo tempers it. **FIX** your mind straight behind your eyes: that is, consider well that which you will see, which is the ladder of which he will speak shortly. And make of those eyes of yours a mirror for the figure <gloss>that is, said ladder</gloss> which will appear to you in this mirror, that is, in this planet. He had already ascended to the seventh heaven which belongs to Saturn; which planet, when it is well-disposed in a man's birth, makes him an investigator of ancient and hidden things, and instills sharp reasoning and discourse of reason. And also, according to Macrobius, that virtue of the mind which the Greeks call <note>original: "theoriti"</note> contemplation, with the power to contemplate and speculate; which thing induced the poet to represent the speculating souls in this sphere. But to treat more fully the nature of Saturn: this planet is diurnal, masculine, cold and dry, melancholic, timid, old, lazy, sterile, and malignant. And although it is more remote from the Earth than the others, it is nonetheless more harmful. It is the signifier of ancient things, and the predecessor of burials and the dead, and of the earth and all cultivation of it, of buildings, of every metal mine, and of hidden treasures. It signifies large beasts, long infirmities, quartan fevers, and <note>original: "morphea," likely referring to skin diseases or leprosy</note> skin ailments. It makes a man of foul breath and a lover of foul and dirty things. It makes him lazy, slow, of a pale color, with a curved, thin, and veiny body, thick lips, thin legs; he always looks at the ground and speaks little. He has little libido and desires the male more than the female. When it is well-disposed, it makes a man sharp, shrewd, and of profound and diverse opinions. He does not rejoice; his anger is implacable; he loves little and easily leaves love. It produces priests, and especially the religious orders that wear black, the color of the earth. Item: those who are apostates, simoniacs, heretics, and schismatics; and those who fight hand-to-hand, and it produces surgeons. In conception, it governs the first month; because with its frigidity and dryness, it curdles and binds the matter from which the creature is to be made. It produces <note>original: "harmoniaci," perhaps meaning makers of charms or tools</note> enchanters and every species of diviner. Among the humors, it rules over melancholy. Among the sects, it is the signifier of the Jewish one, of the days of the...

### CANTO XXI

Saturday. Among metals, it signifies lead and rusty iron. It has no light in itself but receives it from the other planets and especially from the sun; and because the sun makes it bright and warms it, the sun is its enemy: because the house of the sun, which is Leo, is opposite to the house of Saturn, which is Capricorn; and its darkness and coldness are contrary to the light and heat of the sun. The ancients figure him with the scythe because, just as the scythe harms more when returning than when proceeding, so Saturn harms more when in retrograde <note>original: "retrogrado"; in astrology, a planet appearing to move backward is often considered more potent or malevolent.</note> than when moving directly. This planet shines in Gemini, in Cancer, and in Leo: <gloss>that is, it is more powerful there</gloss>. And for this reason, the poet places it in Leo; then its light diminishes in Virgo, in Libra, and in Scorpio. It becomes dark in Sagittarius, Capricorn, and Aquarius. It diminishes its darkness in Pisces, in Aries, and in Taurus. It has the color of lead. But when it enters the circle of Jupiter, it becomes white and clear because of Jupiter's heat.

Whosoever knew what was the feeding
of my sight in her blessed aspect
when I transferred myself from the other care,
Would recognize how much it was pleasing to me
to obey my celestial escort,
counterbalancing the one side with the other.
Within the crystal that bears the name,
circling the world, of its bright leader,
under whom every malice lay dead,
Of the color of gold in which a ray shines through,
I saw a ladder erected upward
so far that my sight did not follow it.
I saw also descending down the steps
so much splendor that I thought every light
appearing in heaven was diffused from there.

And just as by their natural custom,
the jackdaws <note>original: "polle"; small social birds of the crow family, noted for their morning movements.</note> together at the start of day
move to warm their cold feathers;
Then some go away without returning,
others turn back to where they started,
and others, wheeling, make a stay;
Such a manner it seemed to me was here
in that sparkling which came together,
as it struck upon a certain step.
And that one which stayed closest to us
became so bright that I said in my thought:
"I see well the love that you signal to me."

But she from whom I await the "why" and "when"
of speaking and of silence, stands still; wherefore I,
against my desire, do well if I do not ask.
Because she, who saw my silence
in the sight of Him who sees everything,
said to me: "Satisfy your hot desire."
And I began: "My own merit
does not make me worthy of your answer,
but for her sake who grants me the asking:
O blessed life who stay hidden
within your joy, make known to me
the cause that has brought you so near;
And why the sweet symphony of Paradise
is silent in this wheel,
which below through the others sounds so devoutly."

<column-break/>

The meaning of the first verses is this: that he who knew what was the feeding <note>meaning the "pasture" or what his eyes were feasting upon.</note> of my sight in that blessed aspect <gloss>that is, how sweetly my eyes fed upon the face of Beatrice</gloss> when I transferred myself from that other care—that is, when I moved away from the aforementioned subject and turned to what follows—would know how much pleasure I took in obeying Beatrice, who was my escort. In short, he intends that it was a supreme delight for him to gaze upon Beatrice. Nevertheless, it was so pleasing to him to obey her when she commanded him to turn toward the ladder, that he weighed the pleasure of obeying her against the pleasure of gazing at her. **WITHIN THE CRYSTAL:** he posits that he saw in the body of Saturn a ladder of gold in which the rays of the sun reflected. He calls it "crystal" because it is a transparent body. And certainly, just as one climbs from bottom to top step by step by a ladder, so by the virtue of contemplation one mounts from heaven to heaven even unto God. This ladder is of gold. Because just as gold is more excellent than any other metal, so the contemplative life surpasses every other life; and the ray of the grace of the eternal sun shines within it. **WHICH BEARS THE NAME OF ITS LEADER:** because it is called Saturn from Saturn <note>referencing the deity Saturn/Cronus who ruled during the Golden Age.</note>. **UNDER WHOM EVERY MALICE LAY DEAD:** This refers to the history or fable of the Golden Age. But concerning this age and Saturn, we have spoken in many places in such a way that nothing remains to be told. **OF THE COLOR OF GOLD IN WHICH A RAY SHINES THROUGH I SAW A LADDER.** We have spoken of this above. But he says the ladder is so straight upwards that his light <gloss>that is, his vision</gloss> did not follow it, to denote that the knowledge of divine things is so high that the human intellect cannot reach it; and it also denotes the great interval that exists from the heaven of Saturn to the Empyrean heaven. And as gold is most pure without any mixture, so is the contemplation of divine things. And down that ladder descended innumerable splendors, that is, spirits.

**HERE** is a fitting comparison by which he demonstrates that just as it happens that certain birds called jackdaws move all at once in the morning upon departing; then some fly far away, some fly back and place themselves where they had risen, and others fly around in circles; so it happened that those spirits, striking together, appeared to sparkle, and some went away and others remained. **I SEE WELL THE LOVE THAT YOU SIGNAL TO ME.** Because that splendor demonstrated the ardor of charity and through that affection sought to speak to him.

**DANTE DESIRED** to question the spirit. But Beatrice, from whom he expected the "why" and the "when" <gloss>that is, the manner and the time</gloss> for speaking and for being silent, stood still. Wherefore he said within himself: "against my desire, I do well if I do not ask." But Beatrice, seeing my silence <gloss>that is, the reason why I was silent</gloss>, said to me "solve" <gloss>that is, absolute and fulfill</gloss> your "hot desire" <gloss>that is, your burning wish</gloss>. And I turned to the spirit saying: "not my own merit or worthiness makes me worthy that you should answer me; but answer me for the love of Beatrice, who permits me to ask you two things. First, why you approached closer to me than the others. Second, why in this heaven the sweet symphony of Paradise is not sung, which is sung in the other heavens."

<summary>This page describes Dante's arrival in the Seventh Heaven (Saturn), where he encounters a golden ladder representing the contemplative life and witnesses spirits descending like sparks. Dante questions the spirit of Peter Damian about his specific proximity and the mysterious silence of the celestial music in this sphere.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the narrative of Canto XXI in the Heaven of Saturn. Dante has just encountered the golden ladder of contemplation and is now engaging in dialogue with the soul of Peter Damian, a 11th-century monk and reformer known for his asceticism.</meta>

<page-type>text</page-type>
<columns>2</columns>
<header>PARADISO</header>

"You have mortal hearing, just as you have mortal sight,"
he replied to me; "therefore, here we do not sing,
for the same reason that Beatrice does not smile.
Down through the steps of the holy ladder
I descended so far, only to give you welcome
with my speech and with the light that cloaks me.
Nor did greater love make me more swift,
for as much and even more love burns up there,
as the flaming manifest to you shows.
But the high charity, which makes us servants
ready for the counsel that governs the world,
allots tasks here, as you observe."

"I see well," I said, "O sacred lamp,
how free love in this court
suffices to follow eternal providence.
But this is what seems hard for me to discern:
why you alone were predestined
for this office among your companions."
I had not come to the last word
before the light made a center of its middle,
whirling like a swift millstone.

Then the love that was inside replied:
"Divine light is focused upon me,
penetrating through this in which I enwomb myself,
whose power, joined with my vision,
lifts me so far above myself that I see
the supreme essence from which it is drawn. <note>original: "munta" (literally "milked"). This refers to the light of the soul being "drawn" or "milked" from the primary source of God's essence.</note>
From this comes the joy with which I flame;
for as clear as my vision is,
I match it with the clarity of my flame."

<gloss>AS clear as it is: as much as the clarity of my vision and knowledge, so is the clarity of my light and splendor. In short, the flame and clarity grow in him as much as he sees the divine essence: because then I flame more to will what it wills; and this shows that his will is free and spontaneous in what God wills; the state that makes His will known to me. Therefore, when these spirits sparkle, this happens through a new grace that comes into them, which had then come into this spirit; and he had newly understood God’s will to be that he should descend to Dante, and he wills it because God wills it.</gloss>

"But that soul in heaven which is most illuminated,
that seraph <note>The Seraphim are the highest order of angels, characterized by their proximity to God and their burning love.</note> who has his eye most fixed on God,
will not satisfy your question;
for what you ask is so far advanced into the abyss
of the eternal statute,
that it is cut off from every created sight.
And to the mortal world, when you return,
report this, so that it may no longer presume
to move its feet toward such a goal.
The mind, which is light here, is smoke on earth;
therefore, consider how it can do down there
what it cannot do even when heaven takes it up."

<column-break/>

The blessed soul responds to Dante's doubts: first to the second one, in which it was asked why there was no singing on this planet as on the others. He says, therefore, that on that planet, laughter and song are mental; and because he, being in the body, cannot use spiritual seeing or hearing, but only corporal, he neither saw Beatrice smile nor heard these souls sing. The poet feigns this because the contemplative virtues are mental and cannot in any way be grasped by the bodily senses. **DOWN** through the steps. Peter Damian responds to the first question—why he rather than the other spirits came to Dante—and says: "I descended down to give you welcome and congratulate you with words and with the light that cloaks us," that is, clothes us. **NOR** greater love <note>original: "idest ne maggiore amore"</note>: that is, I did not come sooner than others because I was driven more by charity than the others. Because up here it "glows," that is, boils and burns more, and so much love in every spirit; that is, there are spirits who surpass me in charity and spirits who are equal to me, as the flaming of all can show you, because the quality of splendor demonstrates love. But nevertheless, this is not the reason. Rather, it is the will of God, whom it pleased that I should come. Because charity—that is, God himself—who makes us servants ready to obey the counsel that governs the world—that is, the divine providence which governs the universe—"allots," that is, assigns to each what He wants them to do, "as you observe," that is, as you see. Therefore, the poet always stands in the first position: that the abyss of divine counsel is hidden even from the blessed spirits.

The author responds that he knows well that free love suffices to follow divine providence: because here you obey freely and not servilely. But for me, it is difficult to "discern," that is, to know for what reason you were predestined more than the others for this office.

Dante had made his question, and the light had spun; now, continuing, he describes how the love that was inside that light—that is, that blessed soul full of love—responded, saying: "Divine light," that is, divine grace, "is focused upon me," that is, descends upon me through its rays, the point of which comes to me, penetrating and passing through this light in which I am wrapped, "wherein I enwomb myself," that is, why I enter inside that divine light. The meaning is that although the blessed spirit does not discern the depth of divine counsel, nevertheless sometimes divine grace descends into a spirit, through which he understands what God wants him to do. And the power of this grace inspired in me by God joins with my will; and thus joined, it "lifts me above myself," that is, it makes me intelligent beyond my nature, so much so that I can see: that is, I can know the divine essence "from which it is drawn," from which it has issued. **HENCE** comes the joy. The meaning is that as much as he sees, so much he shines: and he rejoices in such a way that according to the quantity of the vision is the quantity of the splendor.

The spirit has shown that he came rather than others because it so pleased God. Now, Dante wanting to know why it pleased God thus rather than otherwise, he responds that although the blessed spirits see many secrets in God, nevertheless they cannot see for what reason He wills this rather than that. And therefore he says that "that soul which is most illuminated in heaven," that is, who most receives the ray of divine grace, from which he sees God more—and this happens especially to the Seraphim, because they contemplate God more than the other angels, as we will say elsewhere—"will not satisfy," that is, would not satisfy Dante's question. Because this question "advances so far," that is, enters so far into the "abyss," that is, into the depth of the "eternal statute," that is, of divine providence, which is "cut off," that is, severed from every "created sight," that is, from every created intelligence. **AND TO THE** world: which thing, when you return to the world—that is, to mortal men whose intellect is submerged by the contagion of the flesh—you shall say that since the angels cannot see this, although they can see many things that men do not see, they should not presume to move their feet: that is...

<summary>In this passage from Canto XXI, Peter Damian explains to Dante that the lack of singing and Beatrice's smile is due to his human limitations. The dialogue explores the impenetrable nature of divine predestination, which remains a mystery even to the highest angels.</summary>

the affection is to such a degree. The human mind, which here in heaven shines because it is illuminated by rays of divine grace, when it is still in the body **smokes**—that is, it is obscured like smoke. These words prescribed me—that is, they enclosed me within a boundary that I should not cross—in such a way that I withdrew from that question and asked him who he was. And he answered me thus:

> So he prescribed his words to me
> that I left the question and withdrew
> to ask him humbly who he was.

<column-break/>

**B**etween two shores: that is, between the Tyrrhenian Sea to the south and the Adriatic Sea to the north, lies the Apennines which divide Italy down the middle. And in that part of the Apennines where the range is higher than in any other place. This mountain is between Abruzzi and the March of Ancona. They say that Peter Damian built two monasteries, one in the Apennines. The text is ordered thus: Peter Damian began the third speech, because he had previously said two things: first, "you have mortal hearing"; second, when he spoke of "divine light." And now he relates how between two shores of Italy rocks rise: that is, the Apennine mountain rises to such an altitude that the thunders generated in the air are lower than the height of the rocks. And this place is not far from your homeland, that is, from Tuscany, because it is between Gubbio and Pergola. And these rocks, rising up, form a hump, that is, a ridge; and it is called Catria. Beneath which is consecrated a hermitage—that is, a forest, specifically a *heremos* (hermitage), which in Greek means a desert place. **LATRIA** is the service which we owe only to God; hence idolatry is the supreme sin, because we give to others what we owe only to God. **THERE**: in this place I stayed in such a manner that, using only foods seasoned with oil, I gave myself to serving God in contemplation, suffering heat and frost. **USED TO YIELD**: He laments that this monastery used to have men who were holy and who rose to this heaven by means of contemplation; and now it has become vain and empty of good men. And for this reason, it must soon be revealed—that is, manifested—that it is no longer what it used to be.

**I**N THAT place: that is, in the hermitage of charity, I was Peter Damian; and he gives his proper name. And Peter the Sinner was in the house of Our Lady on the Adriatic shore. The meaning is: I was a hermit in Catria, where one is not called "sinner," because having been purged of vices, I was devoted to contemplation. But before that, I had been a monk in Santa Maria of Ravenna on the shore of the Adriatic Sea; and there I called myself "the sinner" because I was not yet purged of vices. **LITTLE** Mortal Life: we say a man lives while the soul is joined to the body; but such life is mortal because it passes away quickly. Therefore, he was already old when he was not only called but forcibly dragged to the hat—that is, to the cardinalate. **WHICH ONLY** from bad to worse is poured: which dignity every day goes from bad to worse, because those who succeed are always worse. **CEPHAS** came: He wishes to show how much the modern pastors have degenerated and strayed from the first Vicar of Christ; since Peter and Paul were lean because of their continent and austere life, and barefoot because of their extreme poverty, and they took their food from any hostel—that is, they begged for their bread. **NOW** they are so [heavy]: Not without cause does this spirit break into lamentation; for he wrote two works: one of epistles and sermons in which he condemns many vices of the prelates. In the other, he sets down the nefarious wickednesses of their lives, which cannot be recalled without great shame. And certainly the sentiment of Bernard is true: because all other states of life have much more labor than pleasure, but the priestly order has found a way by which they flee everything that can be troublesome and follow every generation of pleasure. **CEPHAS** came: because Peter is interpreted as **Cephas**, that is, "head" <note>original: "caput" — a common medieval etymology linking the Aramaic *Kephas* (rock) with the Greek *kephale* (head).</note>, because he is the head of the apostles and the first pope. **THE GREAT** vessel: that is, Paul, who, as we showed in the second canto of the *Inferno*, is called the "vessel of election" <note>Latin: *vas electionis* (Acts 9:15).</note>.

**A**t the exclamation of Peter Damian, more spirits, which he calls little flames, descended toward him from the steps of the ladder. And the circular motion signifies the reflection of the soul in God, which makes us rejoice more; and the greater the joy, the greater the splendor. And they shouted so loudly that in this world there is nothing to which it could be likened, for anything else would be lesser. Therefore, having no sound to equal it, he calls it thunder, which overcame and stunned him so that he did not understand what the spirits said. From this, it is easy to draw the allegory if you remember what we said above regarding contemplation.

<page-num>XXII</page-num>

<header>PARADISE CANTO XXII OF THE THIRD CANTICLE BY DANTE.</header>

Overcome with wonder, to my guide
I turned, like a little child who runs
always back to where he has the most trust;
And she, like a mother who quickly succors
her son, pale and breathless,
with her voice that is used to comforting him,
Said to me: "Do you not know that you are in heaven?
And do you not know that heaven is all holy,
and whatever is done here comes from good zeal?
How the singing would have transformed you,
and my smiling too, you can now imagine,
since the cry has moved you so much.
In which, if you had understood its prayers,
the vengeance would already be known to you,
which you shall see before you die.
The sword of this place above does not cut in haste,
nor is it slow, except in the opinion of him
who awaits it in desire or in fear.
But turn yourself now toward others,
for many illustrious spirits you shall see,
if you direct your sight as I say."
As it pleased her, I directed my eyes,
and saw a hundred little spheres that together
were made more beautiful by mutual rays.
I stood as one who holds back
the point of desire and does not dare
to ask, so much does he fear being excessive.
And the largest and most radiant
of those pearls <note>original: "margherite" — in Dante's time, this term was often used for pearls, symbolizing the luminous purity of the souls.</note> stepped forward
to make my desire satisfied by its presence.
Then from within it I heard: "If you could see,
as I do, the charity that burns among us,
your thoughts would have been expressed.
But so that you do not delay by waiting
for your high goal, I will give you answer
even to the thought of which you are so cautious.
That mountain on whose slope Cassino sits
was once frequented upon its summit
by people deceived and ill-disposed.
And I am he who first carried up there
the name of Him who brings to earth
the truth that so uplifts us;
And so much grace shines upon me
that I drew the surrounding towns
away from the impious cult that seduces the world.
These other fires were all contemplative
men, kindled by that heat
which brings forth holy flowers and fruits."

<column-break/>

We have reached the twenty-second chapter, which contains five parts. In the first, it contains the matter placed in the previous canto. In the second, it introduces the spirit of Benedict, who reveals himself and his other companions. In the third, the author raises a doubt to Saint Benedict. In the fourth, he describes his ascension to the firmament. In the last, he places his reflection upon all the lower spheres. Dismayed, then, by the great sound <note>This refers to the thunderous cry of the spirits at the end of Canto XXI, which was a prayer for divine justice.</note>, he ran back to Beatrice as a son to his mother; and she, comforting him, showed him that, being in heaven where—because it is holy—nothing is done that harms, he must not fear, because everything there is done with good zeal. And Beatrice adds: consider how the singing of these spirits would have been transformed and disturbed if human ears could have heard it, since this cry has so moved you. And the author interposed these words while smiling and said: "Now you can imagine it," as if to say, from this you can imagine how much the singing would have moved me. In which cry, if you had understood its prayers—that is, if you had understood what Peter Damian was praying for—you would know the vengeance that God has ordained against the sins of the prelates; and here he predicts the captivity of Pope Boniface <note>A reference to the "Slap of Anagni" and the capture of Pope Boniface VIII in 1303.</note>, of whom it was spoken in the Purgatorio. But he does not wish to show that he has heard it, because that would be a profession of prophecy; instead, he pretends that Beatrice shows it—that is, she demonstrates that she believes this must come to pass according to theological judgments. **THE SWORD OF this place above**: that is, the punitive justice of God. **DOES NOT CUT**: it does not punish in haste nor slowly, because in everything it observes the proper time. **BUT IN THE OPINION**. That is, except in the opinion of him who awaits it either in desire—because to him it does not seem to cut quickly—or in fear—because to him it seems to come before its time. **But turn yourself now toward others**, that is, toward these other spirits, and you will see many illustrious ones, if you "reduce," that is, direct your "aspect," that is, your sight, as I say.

I turned to the spirits as it pleased Beatrice; but I did not dare to say what I desired to understand. But the greatest flame, which was Saint Benedict, said: "If you knew the charity that burns among us, you would express your every concept, because you would not fear being a nuisance to us in asking."

Cassino is a mountain in Campania. On this mountain was the temple of Apollo, and later Saint Benedict worked so much that, having brought the surrounding peoples to the true religion, he destroyed the temple of Apollo and dedicated there the church of Saint Martin; and the altar of Apollo he dedicated to John the Baptist. And he established his monastery <note>This is the foundation of the famous Monte Cassino abbey in 529 AD.</note>. And therefore he says that he carried there the name of Him who introduced the truth: that is, the name of Christ, who is the truth and the life <note>original: "veritas & vita"</note>. This is that truth which so uplifts us <note>original: "sublima"</note>—that is, lifts us so much from the earth, because it leads us to heaven. And divine grace shone so much in Saint Benedict that he brought to the Christian religion all the surrounding lands. Benedict was from Nursia, a monk and then an abbot; and he established the rule of the White Monks <note>Referring to the Benedictines.</note>. He built several monasteries, but especially that of Monte Cassino. For, having by a divine miracle caused the temple of Apollo to fall, he was able, with a great gathering, to lead the people to the Christian religion. He lived in the times of Justinian the Emperor, in the years of our salvation five hundred twenty-nine, in the pontificate of Boniface the First <note>Historically, this likely refers to Pope Boniface II (530–532), as the dates align with the founding of Monte Cassino.</note>. **KINDLED** by that heat: that is, by the love of God, from which every good flower and fruit is born.

<summary>In this opening of Canto XXII, Dante is comforted by Beatrice following a startling divine cry and is introduced to the soul of Saint Benedict, the father of Western monasticism. Benedict describes his historical mission at Monte Cassino, where he replaced pagan worship with Christian devotion and founded his famous Order.</summary>

<keywords>Dante Alighieri, Paradiso, Canto XXII, Saint Benedict, Monte Cassino, Beatrice, divine justice, monasticism, Apollo, conversion of Italy</keywords>

# CANTO XXII
## H II

Qui e machario qui e romualdo
qui son li frati miei che dentro achiolstri
fermaro epiedi & tennoro el cor saldo
Et io a lui laffecto che dimostri
mecho parlando & la buona sembianza
chi ueggio e noto in tucti glardor uostri
Chosi ha dilatato mia fidanza
chomel sol fa la rosa quando aperta
tato diuien quãto ella ha di possãza
Pero ti priego & tu padre macerta
sio posso prender tanta gratia chio
tiuegga con imagine scoperta
Ondegli frate eltuo caldo disio
fadempiera in su lultima spera
oue fadempion tucti glaltri elmio
Iui e perfecta matura & intera
ciaschuna disianza in quella sola
e ogni parte la doue sempre era
Perche non e in loco et non si pola
& nostra scala fin adessa uarcha
onde chosi dal uiso ti sinuola
Infin lassu la uidde elpatriarcha
iacob porger la superna parte
quando glapparue dangeli si carcha
Ma per salir la mo nessun diparte
da terra epiedi & la regola mia
rimasa e giu indanno delle carte
Lemura che soleano esser badia
facte sono spelonche & le cocolle
sacca son piene di farina ria
Ma tanta usura graue non si tolle
contral piacer didio quante quel fructo
che fa el chuor de monaci piu folle
Che quantunque la chiesa guarda tucto
e della gente che perdio domanda
non di parente ne daltro piu bructo
Lacarne de mortali e tanto blanda
que giu non basta buon cominciamento
dal nascer della quercia a far la gianda
Pier comincio sanza oro & sanza argento
& io con orationi & con digiuno
& francescho humilmente suo conuento
Et se guardi al principio di ciaschuno
poscia riguardi la doue trascorso
tu uedrai del biancho facto bruno
Veramente giordan uolte retrorso
piu fu el mar fuggir quando dio uolse
mirabile ad ueder che qui soccorso
Chosi mi disse & indi si ricolse
al suo collegio el collegio si strinse

<column-break/>

The words that the spirit had spoken gave boldness to the author to ask, and he asked if he could have such grace that I might see his image revealed: and not wrapped in that light. And it is reasonable that the poet, being already in the sphere of the contemplatives, should reach such a high thought as to desire to know the essence of the human soul. To this the spirit responds and demonstrates that this desire of his, and likewise that of the other elevated spirits, cannot be fulfilled except in the final sphere, that is, in the Empyrean heaven where God is: who alone gives perfection to human and angelic nature. And therefore in that sphere is perfection, and in it every part is where it always was, because it does not move. Rather, it is the first mover and is always quiet. For this reason, it does not happen that a part of it which is now in one place is later in another: as happens in the other spheres which are in constant motion, because it is not in a place: it is not located and contained like the other nine spheres. And it "does not pole." <gloss>i.e., it does not rotate upon poles like the others.</gloss> For the nine spheres have two poles: arctic and antarctic: and so on for the others. And our ladder reaches and passes even up to there. For the contemplatives reach that point with their contemplation, and passing through all the heavens, they reach God. But it "vanishes from the sight" <note>original: "sinuola" — meaning to slip away or withdraw from one's vision</note> of Dante: because the soul within the body cannot contemplate so high.

**UP TO** there the patriarch saw it. It is written in Genesis that when Isaac <note>The commentator writes "Isaac," though the biblical story and Dante's text refer to Jacob fleeing his brother Esau.</note> fled the wrath of Esau his brother, whom he had defrauded of his father's blessing and inheritance, and his father had commanded him to go to Mesopotamia and take for a wife one of the daughters of Laban, and not of Canaan; it happened that one evening on the road he lay down to sleep in the open and took a stone for a pillow, and that night he saw in a vision a ladder that rose from the earth up to heaven, and many angels were ascending and descending by it.

**HE WILLED** that none of his monks lift their feet from the earth: <gloss>that is, lift their affections from earthly things to climb this ladder, i.e., to give themselves to contemplation.</gloss> **WAS MY** Rule. <gloss>i.e., the institutions which I have left written:</gloss> so that the monks, by observing them, might be saved; and it remains down in the world as a waste of paper. Because by not observing it, it is of no use to the monks, and the paper is wasted in writing it: the walls that used to be abbeys have become dens because the monks are worse than thieves; for they attend to nothing but robbing the fruits of the monasteries. **AND THE** cowls: that is, the garments of the monks, are sacks for flour. An excellent metaphor to show the degenerate life of his monks. But usury is not so heavy a sin against God's pleasure as that "fruit" <note>Here referring to the illicit profit or misappropriated tithes of the Church.</note> which the monks take more than they ought, beyond an honest life: which makes their hearts and their will so foolish that they wander in secular things. And everything that the Church guards—that is, preserves because it is surplus for the clerics who serve it—belongs to the poor, and not to the relatives of priests, nor to anything "fouler," as if to say, harlots.

Without fail, it is a matter of supreme wonder to consider the beginning of our religion founded in poverty and charity, and then to see how much the succession has degenerated; and some understand here Peter Damian, who began the Order of the Dove.

**TRULY** the Jordan turned backward. This river, turning back, left a dry space for the people of Israel when they came into the Promised Land. Jordan, according to Jerome, is named from two springs from which it is born: one is called *Jor* and the other is called *Dan*. **MORE WAS** the sea's flight when God willed. The meaning is that it should not seem a marvelous thing to anyone that God punishes the vices of the prelates: since it was a more marvelous thing that the Red Sea fled and gave a dry place when the people of Israel passed through it, and yet it happened. Therefore, it was more wondrous to behold the sea fleeing than it will be to see the rescue of the Church, which is in ruin.

<summary>Saint Benedict identifies fellow contemplatives and explains that Dante's desire to see his true form can only be satisfied in the Empyrean. He then delivers a scathing critique of the corruption and greed within monastic orders compared to the poverty of the apostles.</summary>
<keywords>Saint Benedict, Empyrean, Jacob's Ladder, monastic corruption, Church poverty, Jordan River, Red Sea, Saint Romualdo, Saint Macarius</keywords>

# PARADISO

...then like a whirlwind it gathered itself all together.

The sweet lady then pushed me behind them
with a single sign up that ladder,
so much did her power overcome my nature.
Nor ever here below, where one mounts and descends
naturally, was there ever a motion so swift
that it could be compared to my wing.
So may I return, reader, to that devout
triumph for which I often weep
for my sins and strike my breast,
you would not have pulled out and put
your finger in the fire as quickly as I saw the sign
that follows Taurus and was inside it.

O glorious stars, O light pregnant
with great virtue, from which I recognize
all my genius, whatever it may be!
With you was born and with you was hiding
he who is the father of every mortal life,
when I first felt the Tuscan air;
and then, when grace was granted to me
to enter the high wheel that turns you,
your region was allotted to me.
To you my soul now devoutly sighs
to acquire the power
for the difficult pass that draws me to itself.

"You are so near to the ultimate salvation,"
Beatrice began, "that you must
have your eyes clear and sharp.
And therefore, before you enter further into it,
look back down and see how much of the world
I have already set beneath your feet;
so that your heart, as joyful as it can be,
may present itself to the triumphant crowd
that comes happily through this round ether."
With my sight I returned through each and all
of the seven spheres, and I saw this globe
such that I smiled at its paltry appearance;
and I truly approve of that counsel
which holds it for least; and he who thinks of other things
can truly be called noble.

I saw the daughter of Latona <note>The Moon</note> kindled
without that shadow which was the cause
why I once believed her to be rare and dense.

<column-break/>

Man would not understand by himself that the supreme good was in contemplation if the studies of <term>theology</term> <note>The study of the nature of God and religious belief.</note> did not push him toward it. The swift motion signifies the passage of the mind, than which nothing can be found more rapid. YOU WOULD NOT HAVE. From here the author makes an effective comparison. Because we use great speed in things that can harm us. With this speed, he entered from the seventh heaven into the eighth sphere where all the stars are, except for the seven planets; and he entered it through that sign of the <term>zodiac</term> <note>The belt of constellations through which the sun, moon, and planets appear to move.</note> that comes after Taurus, and this is Gemini.

Having entered Gemini, he congratulates the stars of this sign which give him the influence of great virtue: and he says that from them, as from a secondary cause, he recognizes the strength of his <term>genius</term> <note>His natural intellect or poetic talent.</note>, whether it be small or great. For at the hour when he came out of his mother's womb and then began to breathe in this Tuscan air where he was born, Gemini was ascending and the sun was within them. And he calls the sun the father of every mortal life because it is the generator of all sensitive life, but not of the rational soul. And similarly, when I entered the eighth heaven, I entered through the part occupied by you. Dante affirms that at his birth he had Gemini as his <term>ascendant</term> <note>The sign rising on the eastern horizon at the moment of birth.</note> and the sun within them, which birth influences supreme science. Because Gemini is the house of Mercury; and if Mercury is fortunate, it disposes a man toward supreme science; and according to Masha'allah <note>original: "misahel," referring to the 8th-century Persian Jewish astrologer.</note> it is an airy, masculine, and diurnal sign. But of these things we have spoken elsewhere.

An excellent precept of Beatrice, that is, of Sacred Scripture: that when a man has made such profit in contemplation that he has already ascended with his mind to the contemplation of God, and already has his light clear—that is, he has a mind void of every perturbation—and it is sharp—that is, he has a subtle genius, which is nothing other than knowing the good and being so confirmed in it that no appetite can move him to evil—then she wants him to turn back and consider the baseness and vileness of fleeting and mortal things. When these things are considered, he will take more joy in the spheres, having reached such a degree. Therefore, returning through all the seven spheres down to the Earth—that is, through all the secondary causes down to matter and down to fleeting and mortal things—he smiled at its paltry appearance. And this is a passage taken from Cicero's sixth book of the *Republic*, in which he induces Scipio, having ascended to this heaven, to do the same. And Lucan also writes similarly of Pompey having ascended to heaven: <note>original: "Postquam se lumine tanto impleuit stellasq; uagas miratur & astra fixis uidet quãta sub nocte iaceret nostra dies:risitque sui ludibria trunci."</note> "After he filled himself with such great light and marveled at the wandering stars, and saw how much of our day lay under the fixed stars in night, he laughed at the mockery of his own [headless] corpse." AND WHICH COUNSEL: He concludes that it is excellent counsel, that of the one who has held the Earth as least—that is, who esteems earthly and fleeting things less than all others. And he who thinks of things other than earthly things, this man can truly be called noble—that is, good.

I SAW THE DAUGHTER OF LATONA: That is the Moon, daughter of Latona, whose fable was narrated by us elsewhere. KINDLED: That is, lit up; and he wants to show that it was illuminated by the sun from the upper part, which he could see being in the eighth sphere. WITHOUT THAT SHADOW: Of the shadow of the moon and the cause of that, he disputed at length in the Heaven of the Moon. THE ASPECT OF YOUR SON, HYPERION: Hyperion was, according to the fables, the son of Titan and Vesta and the father of the Sun. Whence Ovid says: <note>original: "Vidit hanc hyperione natus."</note> "The son of Hyperion saw her." Therefore he says, "O Hyperion, I sustained and suffered the aspect of your son"—that is, of the sun, your child—because being in heaven I had so corroborated my sight that I could sustain the solar rays. And I saw how Maia and Dione—that is, Mercury and Venus—move around the sun and near to it. Maia was one of the seven daughters of Atlas and gave birth to Mercury by Jove. And Mercury, in his course, never strays far from the sun. Dione, as we showed above, is the mother of Venus. And he says...

<summary>Dante and Beatrice ascend from the sphere of Saturn to the Eighth Heaven, the Fixed Stars, where Dante enters the constellation of Gemini. From this vantage point, he looks back at the Earth, realizing its insignificance compared to the vastness and glory of the celestial realms.</summary>

The aspect of your son, Hyperion <note>Hyperion’s son is the Sun.</note>
there I endured, and I saw how he moves
around and near to him, Maia and Dione <note>Maia refers to Mercury; Dione refers to Venus.</note>
From there appeared to me the tempering of Jove
between his father and his son; and then was clear to me <note>Jove (Jupiter) sits between his "father" Saturn and "son" Mars, balancing their extreme temperatures.</note>
the shifting they do and their "where" [their positions].
And all seven showed themselves to me,
how great they are and how swift they are,
and how they are in distant shelters.

The little threshing floor that makes us so fierce <note>original: "Laiuola" (aiuola). Dante refers to the inhabited Earth as a tiny, insignificant space.</note>
as I turned with it and the Twins [Gemini],
appeared to me entirely from the hills to the river mouths.

### CANTO XXIII OF THE THIRD CANTICLE OF DANTE.

---

As the bird among the beloved leaves,
having rested on the nest of her sweet offspring
through the night that hides things from us,
Who, to see the desired faces
and to find the food to feed them
(wherein heavy labors are a joy to her),
Anticipates the time upon the open branch,
and with ardent affection awaits the sun,
fixedly watching for the dawn to be born;
Thus my lady was standing erect
and attentive, turned toward that region
under which the sun shows less haste <note>The meridian or the south, where the sun appears to move more slowly at its highest point.</note>
So that I, seeing her suspended and longing,
became like one who, desiring,
would want something else, and is satisfied by hope.

But it was a short time between one moment and the other—
I mean of my waiting and of the seeing—
the sky becoming more and more clear.
And Beatrice said: "Behold the hosts
of the triumph of Christ, and all the fruit
gathered from the turning of these spheres!"

<column-break/>

that these two planets, Venus and Mercury, move around the sun
and near the sun. The tempering of Jove between his father Saturn and his son
Mars: because Jove, being between cold Saturn and hot Mars,
becomes temperate. IT WAS CLEAR TO ME: that is, it was manifest to me. THE 
SHIFTING THEY DO: because he had already ascended so high in contemplation that
all these things were known to him.

THE LITTLE THRESHING FLOOR that makes us so fierce. He descended with his eyes from sphere
to sphere until he came to Earth, and looking at it, it seemed a
small thing in comparison to the heavens of which it is almost the center. And so
he calls it a threshing floor <note>original: "aiuola," meaning a small garden plot or threshing area.</note>. And it is a passage taken from Boethius. THAT
MAKES US SO FIERCE. He marvels at human folly which takes such
insolence for a thing as small as the Earth. FROM HILLS TO THE
MOUTHS: that is, from the mountains to the seas: then I turned my eyes to the
beautiful eyes of Beatrice, as if to say I returned to Theology.

THE AUTHOR HAD in the preceding chapter described his
ascent to the eighth sphere through the sign of Gemini. And presently
in this 23rd chapter, he treats of the triumphant court
which appears to him; and then he rises into the 
ninth sphere. Therefore, in the first part, he describes the state of Beatrice,
who prepared him to see the Church Triumphant. In the second,
he describes the leader of this army. In the third, the militia that
follows him. In the fourth, he describes the ninth sphere. Therefore, LIKE THE
BIRD among the beloved leaves: because in those she has placed her chicks
near their nest, she waits through the night for the day to come. And to see
them and to provide for their food with which she feeds them. In which
every heavy labor and toil is a joy, she comes before and anticipates, waking
herself before the day and turned to the east, she awaits the dawn. Thus
Beatrice, to feed Dante with celestial food, stood upright and attentive
toward that region where the sun shows less haste, that is, toward
the southern part. Because when the sun is in the middle of the
sky, it seems to move more slowly than when it is in the east or the
west; and it signifies that just as when the sun is at midday it is over our
head and illuminates everything, so Christ, who led that army,
illuminated them all.

SEEING THE POET Beatrice suspended in expectation and longing, he knew
that she was waiting for something beautiful; he became a man who desires
something other than what he has. And he hoped to have it and then was satisfied
and contented in that hope. But there was a short space between
one and the other, i.e., from the waiting to the seeing, as the sky from point to point
became clearer: And Beatrice said, "Behold the hosts of the triumph of
Christ," i.e., of the blessed recovered by Christ, who by dying destroyed
our death and triumphed over the enemy; "and all the fruit gathered
from the turning of these spheres," i.e., the gain that the movements of
these [heavens] have made...

<page-num>XXIII</page-num>

->PARADISO<-

It seemed to me her face was all aflame,
and her eyes were so full of joy
that I must pass over them without description. <note>original: "sanza constructo" — literally "without construction," meaning the poet lacks the words to build a proper description.</note>

As in the full moons and clear skies,
Trivia <note>original: "Trivia" — a name for the goddess Diana, here representing the Moon.</note> smiles among the eternal nymphs <note>The "nymphs" here are the stars.</note>
who paint the sky through all its reaches;
I saw, above thousands of lamps,
a Sun that kindled every one of them,
just as our own sun kindles the sights above. <note>In medieval astronomy, it was believed the stars and planets reflected light from the sun.</note>
And through its living light, there shone
the glowing substance, so clear and bright
that my vision could not endure it.

O Beatrice, sweet and dear guide!
She said to me: "That which overwhelms you
is a power against which nothing can defend.
Here is the Wisdom and the Power
that opened the roads between heaven and earth,
for which there was once such long desire." <note>This refers to Christ, who bridged the gap between humanity and God.</note>

Just as fire breaks loose from a cloud
by expanding so much it cannot be contained,
and against its own nature falls to the earth; <note>In ancient physics, fire naturally moves upward; here, the shock of the vision makes Dante's mind "fall" or expand beyond its normal limits.</note>
So my mind, among those feasts, <note>original: "dape" — from the Latin 'dapes,' meaning a sacrificial or royal banquet.</note>
becoming greater than itself, issued forth,
and what it then became, it cannot remember.
"Open your eyes and look at what I am;
you have seen things that have made you
powerful enough to sustain my smile."
I was like one who awakens
from a forgotten vision, and who strives
in vain to bring it back to mind,
When I heard this offer, worthy
of such gratitude that it could never be erased
from the book that records the past.

If all those tongues were to sound now
that Polyhymnia <note>The Muse of sacred poetry and song.</note> and her sisters made
most rich with their sweetest milk,
To help me, not a thousandth of the truth
would be reached in singing of the holy smile,
and how it made her holy aspect clear.
And thus, in representing Paradise,
this sacred poem must make a leap,
like one who finds his path cut off.
But whoever considers the weighty theme
and the mortal shoulder that is burdened by it,
would not blame it if it trembles beneath the load.
It is no voyage for a little boat,
this water that my daring prow goes cleaving,

<column-break/>

the heavens sending their influences into our souls. And he well gathers the fruit of all the spheres in the eighth sphere. Because all the others receive influence from this one: and this one from the First Mover <note>The Primum Mobile, the highest physical heaven.</note>: and the First Mover from the Intelligence <note>The angelic beings.</note> that God has placed there, and that from God as the First Cause. SO FULL OF JOY: to denote that speculation <note>Intellectual or spiritual contemplation.</note> takes great joy when it approaches its end.

Christ appeared in this eighth sphere with the souls of all the blessed, just as from that place come the influences to all the other heavens below him. He posits, therefore, that Christ in that army was like Trivia—that is, the Moon—among the eternal nymphs, meaning the stars which "paint the sky," or adorn the sky through all its parts. And thus Christ illuminated and kindled those souls just as the sun illuminates the "sights above," meaning the stars which receive light from him. And through the living light of Christ shone the "glowing substance," meaning the humanity of Christ, which was so bright that Dante's mortal eyes were dazzled. O BEATRICE: he does not call her, but it is an exclamation. "That which overwhelms you," meaning that which conquers you, is divine power against which nothing can defend because it overcomes everything. HERE IN CHRIST was the Wisdom, which is attributed to the Son, and the Power, which although attributed to the Father, nevertheless all three persons in the Godhead are omnipotent.

The marvelous genius of the poet in describing how his mind strengthened itself so much beyond its nature, and above human possibility, that it became capable of the vision of God; and he makes a comparison to the cloud made of dry vapors in which fire is kindled, and because it cannot be contained, it expands and breaks out, and contrary to its nature it runs downward, whereas the nature of fire is always to go upward.
MY MIND THUS AMONG THOSE FEASTS: that is, among those divine foods. *Dapes* <note>original: "Dapes"</note> in Latin signifies royal or divine foods; and reasonably he called them "foods" because just as the body is fed by elemental foods, so the human mind is fed by contemplation.
And so it follows: MADE GREATER: and understand this is by divine nourishment. AND WHAT IT BECAME IT CANNOT REMEMBER: This denotes that he himself could not remember in what way he had arrived at this height. OPEN YOUR EYES: Beatrice concludes that since Dante has seen Christ and His army, he has become powerful enough to sustain her smile.

The meaning of the verses already written is that if all the poets nourished by the milk of the Muses wished to undertake the description of the present matter, in no way could they make verses equal to the thing. Nor could they, by singing, reach the holy smile nor the thousandth part of it. And certainly that part of theology which treats of the divine essence is not comprehensible nor speakable by any human intellect. This same thing is felt by Plato when he writes.

Beatrice explains that his mind has been expanded by this divine vision, though Dante struggles to find the words to describe the beauty of her smile and the majesty of the scene.</summary>

nor to a pilot who spares himself. <note>The preceding metaphor compared Dante's difficult task of describing Paradise to a sailor navigating a dangerous sea.</note>

"Why does my face so enamor you
that you do not turn to the beautiful garden
which flowers beneath the rays of Christ?
There is the Rose <note>The "Rose" is the Virgin Mary.</note> in which the Divine Word
became flesh; there are the lilies <note>The "Lilies" represent the Apostles and saints whose examples guide humanity.</note>
by whose fragrance the good way was found."
Thus spoke Beatrice; and I, to her counsels
all ready, once more gave myself

As in a ray of sun that passes through

So I saw crowds of splendors
flashed upon from above by burning rays,

O benign Power who so imprints them, <note>Dante addresses Christ, who has moved higher (ascended) so that Dante's eyes can withstand the brightness of the remaining spirits.</note>
you raised yourself up to grant me room
for those eyes there that were not strong enough.

**The name of the beautiful flower I always invoke**
both morning and evening, constrained

And when both my eyes were painted

who triumphs up there as she triumphed here below,
Through the sky descended a torch

Whatever melody sounds most sweet
down here and draws the soul most to itself
would seem a cloud that thunders when torn,
Compared to the sound of that lyre

by which the brightest heaven is ensapphired.
"I am angelic love, who circles
the high joy that breathes from the womb
that was the hostelry of our desire;
And I shall circle, Lady of Heaven, while
you follow your son and make the supreme sphere
more divine because you enter it."
Thus the circling melody
was sealed, and all the other lights
made the name of Mary ring out.
The royal mantle of all the volumes <note>The "royal mantle" is the *Primum Mobile*, the outermost physical sphere of the universe that "wraps" around the other celestial spheres.</note>
of the world, which burns most and is most quickened
in the breath of God and in his ways...

<sig>191</sig>

<column-break/>

**H**e begins to describe the celestial militia. And he imagines that Beatrice
urges him to look at them; she says: "O Dante, why does
my face enamor you so much that you do not turn?"—as if to say: "Although I
have been made so beautiful (because in this place I treat the incomprehensible 
matter of Christ), nevertheless consider also 
his family, which is truly a garden that flowers (that is, which 
produces flowers) under the rays of Christ." For just as the rays of the sun 
illuminate all earthly things and by their power generate them, so 
Christ, the true Sun, illuminates these spirits. THERE IS THE ROSE: 
The Virgin Mary, whom he deservedly equates to the rose, which for 
its usefulness in various diseases, for its beauty, and for its scent, holds the 
sovereignty among flowers. LILIES: the apostles, doctors, and martyrs, in whom there is the 
utmost whiteness of purity. I GAVE MYSELF TO THE BATTLE: this denotes that although 
the eye of the human mind is dazzled in the light of the knowledge 
of ineffable things, we must nevertheless contemplate as much 
as sacred theology commands us. AS: the text arranges this; I 
saw many crowds of splendors (that is, shining spirits) flashed upon (that is, much 
illuminated) by burning rays from above (that is, from the upper part). Just as 
once my eyes saw a flowery meadow covered in shadow by rays 
of the sun, which just now "passed through" <note>original: "mei" — from the Latin 'meare,' to pass or flow through.</note> 
BY A BROKEN CLOUD (that is, through a split cloud). Thus the spirits shone, 
struck by the rays of light that came then from Christ, just as flowers in 
a meadow shine when, the meadow being shadowed, they 
suddenly are struck by rays of the sun coming through the broken 
clouds.

**T**he name of Mary drew me so much to itself with all my soul that I 
watched for where the greatest fire was (that is, the greatest splendor), 
because I knew that it had to be her. AND WHEN both my 
eyes were painted by the quality and quantity: he follows by showing that he saw 
in the greatest fire (that is, in Mary, who in light and grace excels all 
others) the quality and the quantity of her splendor. OF THE living star: 
Referring to Mary as the true morning star <note>original: "lucifero"</note> and close 
to the eternal Sun, of whom the Apocalypse writes: <note>original: "Mulier amicta sole : & luna sub pedibus eius. Et in capite eius corona stellarum duodecim."</note> "A woman clothed with the sun, and the moon under her feet, and on her head a crown of twelve stars." <note>Revelation 12:1</note> He saw also the angel Gabriel who came from on 
high to elevate her, and he describes him as a circular crown all of fire. 
WHATEVER melody: an excellent comparison to 
denote how much sweetness was in the song of the angel; since our 
music, compared to that, would not only seem less sweet, but would seem 
as harsh as the sound of thunder. BECAUSE SHE ENTERS: that is, 
because you enter; and certainly no soul ever entered into heaven with more 
glory. THE ROYAL MANTLE of all the volumes: He posits the 
return of Mary to the ninth sphere, and how the other blessed ones remained 
there, and the distance from himself up to where Mary passed, and he returns to the text. 
THE ROYAL MANTLE: the *Primum Mobile* which covers all the 
other spheres, which "burns" most (that is, is most heated) and "quickens" (that is, most 
shines and is most operative and effective) than the other volumes (that is, 
than the other heavens). In the habit of God and in His ways: because this 
sphere is closer to God than the others, and therefore receives His power 
more directly. This is the principle of motion and of life and has universal power 
to give form to worldly individualities. And from this, all the others 
receive, according to the natural order, the power of conservation and 
formation, just as from God they receive natural existence. Therefore it "quickened" in the 
habit of God because from there it receives the vivifying power. IT WAS ABOVE 
US: above me and Beatrice. THE INTERNAL shore: the lower part 
of the circumference; but it was so distant that it could not be seen from the place 
where I was. And because of this, my eyes could not follow the 
crowned flame (that is, Mary, encircled by the angel in the form of a crown). And in 
truth, the human intellect cannot elevate itself so much that it can see the end of the 
ascension of Mary, who rose up after her "seed" (that is, after Christ).

<meta>This page continues the transition from Canto XXIII to Canto XXIV of Dante's *Paradiso*. Having witnessed the "Triumph of Christ" and the ascent of the Virgin Mary, Dante remains in the Eighth Heaven (the Fixed Stars) among the blessed spirits. The text concludes the description of Mary’s glory and begins the next stage of Dante's journey: a formal examination on the theological virtues, starting with Faith.</meta>

<header>PARADISO</header>

There was above us a living lamp
at such a distance that its appearance,
from where I was, did not yet appear to me. <note>The "living lamp" refers to the Virgin Mary, who has ascended higher than the other spirits but remains visible as a point of intense light.</note>
Therefore my eyes did not have the power
to follow the crowned flame <note>Mary is "crowned" by the light of the Archangel Gabriel.</note>
which rose up after her seed. <note>Mary ascends to follow Christ ("her seed"), who had ascended moments before.</note>
And like a little child who toward his mother
stretches his arms after he has taken the milk,
because the spirit within breaks into external flame,
Each of those splendors stretched upward
with its flame, so that the deep affection
they had for Mary was made plain to me.
Then they remained there within my sight,
singing *Queen of Heaven* <note>original: "regina celi"</note> so sweetly
that the delight has never departed from me.
Oh, how great is the abundance <note>original: "luberta," an archaic term for plenty or wealth.</note> that is stored up
in those richest chests <note>The "chests" or "caskets" are the souls of the blessed.</note> which were
good sowers <note>original: "bobolce," literally "plowmen."</note> here below!
Here they live and enjoy the treasure
that was acquired by weeping in the exile
of Babylon, where gold was left behind. <note>"Babylon" represents the worldly, materialistic life on Earth, which the saints abandoned for spiritual wealth.</note>
Here he triumphs under the high Son
of God and of Mary, in his victory,
both with the ancient and the new council, <note>The "ancient and new council" refers to the souls from the Old Testament and the New Testament.</note>
He who holds the keys to such glory. <note>Saint Peter, the first Pope, traditionally depicted holding the keys to the Kingdom of Heaven.</note>

---

# CANTO XXIII OF THE THIRD CANTICLE BY DANTE. <note>The heading says Canto XXIII, but the poem below begins Canto XXIV. Early printed editions often placed the heading for the new canto before the final commentary of the previous one was finished.</note>

O fellowship chosen for the great supper
of the blessed Lamb, who feeds you
so that your desire is always full,
If by the grace of God this man foretastes
of that which falls from your table
before death prescribes his time,
Give heed to his immense affection
and bedew him <note>To "bedew" here means to provide spiritual refreshment or inspiration.</note> with your drink; you
drink always from the fountain from which his thought comes.

<column-break/>

And just as the child, while nursing, takes such pleasure that he cannot
contain it; and therefore with his hands he makes gestures, stretching them toward his mo/
ther to touch her because the affection of the soul inflames him in a way
that shows in his outer parts: so those flames of the blessed spirits
stretched themselves toward Mary, demonstrating their affection toward Ma/
ry.

The author feigns <note>In this context, "feigns" means to create a poetic or allegorical representation.</note> that in the eighth sphere he saw all the blessed as if in
a place from which, by influence, the grace of
God then proceeded, which first proceeds in all virtuous acts. And he demonstrates that
he first meditated on the ascension of Christ. Then that of Mary. <term>REGINA CELI</term> <note>English: "Queen of Heaven."</note>. This antiphon or hymn is sung by the Church during the Ve/
spers of the Resurrection. "Queen of Heaven, rejoice, alleluia: For He whom
you were worthy to bear, alleluia: Has risen, as He said, alleluia: Pray for
us to God, alleluia." <term>O QVANTA E LVBERTA</term>: O how
great is the plenty and the abundance of beatitude that is supported, re/
posited, and affected in those richest chests: that is, in the minds of the blessed which
were very capable of divine grace and which were
good "bubulce": that is, excellent plowwomen. <term>Bubulcus</term> in Latin signifies the
plowman whom we call *bifolco*. Hence the Psalmist: "He who
sows sparingly shall reap sparingly. And he who sows in blessings shall also reap
of blessings." <note>A reference to 2 Corinthians 9:6, though the commentator attributes it to the Psalms.</note> <term>Here they live and enjoy the treasure</term>. Because
in the world they acquired through tears and mourning that glory in
which they now rejoice. Here triumphs he—understand Peter the Apo/
stle—in his victory: because he conquered the devil, the world, and the flesh.
And he triumphs under the Son of God. Because if He had not
redeemed us, we would have remained in the miserable servitude of the devil. And he
says that he holds the keys of such glory to agree with the words of
Christ saying: "And I will give to you the keys of the kingdom of heaven. And whatever
you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven: and whatever you loose
on earth shall be loosed in heaven." <note>Matthew 16:19.</note>

---

He introduces in this twenty-fourth canto Peter the Apo/
stle; and because there are three most principal steps that con/
duct one to this celestial kingdom: Faith, Hope, and Chari/
ty. He feigns that Peter examines him on Faith. Therefore
first is the prayer of Beatrice to the blessed spirits. Then Peter, through the pray/
ers of Beatrice, examines the author on Faith. In the third part he
treats some doubts of such faith. In the last, he asks Dante about
his belief. The prayer of Beatrice has this beginning: <term>O
SODALITIO</term> chosen for the great supper. O company chosen for the beati/
tude on which the blessed spirits feed: and the food of this supper is the Lamb,
which food makes it so that whoever feeds on it is always satiated. "Sodalitio" means "fel/
lowship." Because in Latin *sodalis* signifies a companion. <term>IF
THIS MAN</term>: if his character—that is, Dante—foretastes of that which falls from
our table: that is, before his time he tastes of the celestial glory.
