<meta>This page transitions into Canto XXIV of the *Paradiso*. Although the header still reads Canto XXIII, the text and Cristoforo Landino's commentary now focus on the opening of the next Canto, where Dante is examined on the nature of Faith by Saint Peter. The "carols" or round dances of the spirits continue the celestial choreography established in the previous section.</meta>

<page-num>292</page-num>

<column-break/>

> Thus Beatrice, and those happy souls,
> made themselves spheres upon fixed poles,
> flaming brightly in the manner of comets.
> And as wheels in the mechanism of clocks
> turn so that the first, to one who notices,
> seems still, and the last appears to fly;
> So those carols <note>A "carola" was a popular medieval round dance where participants sang while moving in a circle. Dante uses it here to describe the motion of the blessed souls.</note>, differently
> dancing according to their wealth,
> made me judge them fast and slow.

**LADIES** resplendent and flaming. **IN THE MANNER:** in the likeness of comets, which cast their rays far and wide. We have spoken of the comet before. **AND AS WHEELS:** Just as in a clock there are many wheels, where one turns quickly, another less so, and another even less, stepping down in a way that the last one barely moves; so did those carols—that is, the souls who were revolving. The word **CAROLA** specifically means a round dance. **DANCING DIFFERENTLY:** and through this difference, he shows more or less beatitude; and therefore he says they "made me judge them fast and slow" according to their "wealth" of grace.

> From the one I noted of greatest beauty,
> I saw a fire emerge so happy
> that none there surpassed its brightness;
> And three times around Beatrice
> it turned with a song so divine
> that my imagination cannot repeat it to me.
> Therefore the pen skips and I do not write it,
> for our imagination for such folds—
> much less our speech—is too vivid a color. <note>Dante uses a painting metaphor: "vivid color" (too much light) can actually obscure the delicate "folds" or details of a subject, just as his human words are too crude to describe the divine song.</note>
> "O my holy sister, who so prays to us
> devoutly through your ardent affection,
> you unbind me from that beautiful sphere."
> Then, having stopped the blessed fire,
> it directed its breath toward my lady,
> and spoke just as I have said.

> And she: "O eternal light of the great man
> to whom our Lord left the keys
> that he carried down of this wondrous joy,
> Test this man on points light and grave,
> as it pleases you, concerning the faith
> by which you once walked upon the sea.
> If he loves well, hopes well, and believes well,
> is not hidden from you, for you have your sight
> where everything is seen painted.
> But because that kingdom has made citizens
> through the true faith, to glorify it,
> it is good that he should happen to speak of it."

> Just as the bachelor arms himself and does not speak
> until the master proposes the question...

<column-break/>

...which the souls already taken up into the supernal heaven enjoy, and into which he will come in due time through the grace of God, without which no good work can be in man, **BEFORE** death prescribes the time; that is, before death closes his eyes and takes away his time for living. **PAY HEED** to the immense affection. Here it is said that it is a just thing that you grant him such grace since he desires it so much. **DEW HIM** <note>original: "Roratelo," from the Latin *rorare*, to sprinkle with dew.</note>, that is, bathe him lightly. *Ros* in Latin means dew. Whence they say: "Dew him," and from this, "Let the heavens drop down dew" <note>original: "rorate celi," a reference to Isaiah 45:8, "Rorate caeli desuper."</note>; and this is easy for you to do because you drink always from the fountain from which every desire comes. **THUS BEATRICE** spoke as is written above. And after these words, they "made themselves spheres upon fixed poles," meaning they made circles that revolved upon their beatitude, just as wheels revolve upon poles—that is, the pins or axles. The meaning is that those souls performed many round dances. **FLAMING**

From that carol—that is, the round dance—which was more beautiful than the others because it was where the apostles were, there came out a fire so splendid that none remained brighter. And this was the soul of **PETER**, who is among the first of the blessed, such that none is more blessed. And he turned three times around Beatrice to denote that the doctrine and examples of Peter give true knowledge of the **TRINITY** and of the three **THEOLOGICAL VIRTUES**; and it composes our souls in their three principal parts: the rational, the concupiscible, and the irascible. **WITH A DIVINE SONG:** that is, celestial, which "my imagination does not repeat to me," as if to say, "I do not remember it, nor can I find it again with my imagination." Therefore I do not write it, because imagining does not serve me. **COLOR IS TOO VIVID FOR SUCH FOLDS:** This is a metaphor from painting, where to make the distinction of the folds of a garment, it is necessary to use dark colors; and the meaning is that for such distinctions, I find no way to describe them. **O HOLY SISTER:** and certainly Theology is the sister of Peter. **WHO SO PRAYS TO US:** that is, you pray to me through your ardent affection toward Dante, that you "unbind me" and set me free and make me depart from the sphere and dance where I was. **THEN THE BLESSED FIRE STOPPED:** The meaning is that after this fire, which is the soul of Peter, had revolved three times, he stopped and directed his "breath"—that is, his speech—toward Beatrice, and Peter spoke the words already mentioned above.

These are the words of Beatrice to the soul of Peter, whom she deservedly calls a **GREAT MAN**—that is, a man because Christ left him as His vicar on earth. And He left him the keys of eternal life which he brought down from heaven to earth. Therefore Beatrice prays to Peter that he might "test and examine" Dante on faith, in every point, as much the light and easy as the grave and difficult; "by which faith you walked upon the sea." For it is written in the Gospel that Peter, being in the boat, said to Christ who was on the shore: "If it is you, Lord, bid me come to you" <note>original: "Si dominus es iube me uenire ad te."</note>; and Christ commanded him to come to Him. Whereupon he climbed out of the boat into the sea and walked upon the waves without wetting his feet as long as his faith lasted. Then, beginning to fail, he began to sink. Wherefore Christ took him and pulled him to Himself, saying: "O man of little faith, why did you doubt?" <note>original: "Modice fidei qd dubitasti."</note> **IF HE:** Dante "loves well," meaning he has true charity; "and hopes well," that is, he has true hope; "and believes well," that is, he has true faith, which are the three theological virtues. This is not hidden from you, Peter, because by looking into God—in whom, as in a mirror, everything is seen—you can see this also. And because Peter might say in response that there is no need to ask since he already knows it, Beatrice adds: saying it is "good that you arrive at him," that is, at Dante, to speak of faith because through it one acquires the celestial kingdom.

He turned to Beatrice and she signaled that he should respond. This signifies that no one should presume to dispute concerning the faith unless Beatrice grants it to him—that is, unless he can defend it with theology...

<meta>This page continues the opening of Canto XXIV of the Paradiso. Following the celestial dances of the previous page, one of the brightest flames—Saint Peter—emerges to examine Dante on the first of the three theological virtues: Faith. The commentary by Cristoforo Landino explains the theological and linguistic nuances of Dante’s responses.</meta>

<page-type>text</page-type>

# PARADISO

->to help her and not to finish it<-
Thus I murmured to myself every reason
while she spoke, so that I might be ready
for such a questioner and such a profession.
"As a good Christian, make manifest
your faith," <note>original: "fede"</note> whereupon I raised my brow
toward that light from which this was breathed.
Then I turned to Beatrice, and she gave me
ready signs so that I might pour forth
the water from my inner fountain.
"The grace that allows me to confess,"
I began, "to the high chief-centurion, <term>primipilo: a high-ranking officer in the Roman army, here used for St. Peter as the leader of the Church</term>
let it make my conceptions be clearly expressed."
And I continued: "As the truthful pen
wrote of it, the pen of your dear brother
who, with you, set Rome on the good path: <note>Refers to Saint Paul, who, alongside Peter, is credited with establishing the Christian faith in Rome.</note>
Faith is the substance of things hoped for
and the evidence of things not seen; <note>original: "Fede e substantia di cose sperate & e argomento delle non paruenti." This is a direct translation of Hebrews 11:1.</note>
and this seems to me to be its quiddity." <term>quiddity: the essence or "what-ness" of a thing</term>
Then I heard: "Rightly you perceive,
if you understand well why it was placed
among the substances and then among the evidences."
And I thereafter: "The profound things
which grant me here their appearance
are so hidden from the eyes below
That their existence there lies only in belief,
upon which the high hope is founded;
and therefore, it takes the intent of 'substance.'
And from this belief, it behooves us
to reason <note>original: "sylogizar" (to syllogize)</note> without having further sight:
therefore, it holds the intent of 'evidence.'"
Then I heard: "If everything that is acquired
below through learning were so understood,
there would be no place for the sophist's wit."
Thus breathed that kindled love;
then it added: "The alloy and the weight
of this coin have been well examined;
But tell me if you have it in your purse."
Whereupon I: "Yes, I have it so bright and round
that in its minting nothing is uncertain to me."
Next there issued from the profound light
that was shining there: "This precious jewel
upon which every virtue is founded,
Whence did it come to you?" And I: "The heavy rain
of the Holy Spirit, which is poured
out upon the old and the new parchments, <note>Dante refers to the Old and New Testaments.</note>
is the syllogism that has concluded it for me
so sharply that, compared to it,
every demonstration seems blunt to me."

<column-break/>

**logy:** thereafter follows the prayer of Dante in which he prays that
that same grace of God which allows him to be able to
confess to Saint Peter might also grant that he may express the
conceptions of his mind. And he calls Peter "primipilo": because he was
the first to carry the banner of Christ. *Primipilo*, as
Livy shows, was the first rank of soldiers in the Roman army.
And Peter was the first in the Church Militant; and then, having invoked the
grace of God, he adds the distinction of faith: which he sets down just as
the "truthful pen" of the dear brother of Peter wrote—that is, as
the Apostle Paul wrote in the eleventh chapter of the Epistle to the Hebrews.
Paul, together with Peter, by preaching the evangelical doctrine,
put Rome "on the good path," that is, in the right order and true way, bringing
many back to the Christian faith through their preaching and miracles. **FAITH**
**IS THE SUBSTANCE OF THINGS HOPED FOR.** This is the definition of
faith: and the definition is the reason of the thing which demonstrates the
essence of it according to its substantial things. Therefore, faith is the
substance of things hoped for. That is, faith is that which stays and upon which hope is founded.
Because if we did not believe that God existed and was just in
a way that he prepared rewards for the good and punishment for the wicked, we would not
believe that by doing good we would go to the blessed life. Therefore,
hope resides in faith like an accident in its subject <note>In scholastic philosophy, an "accident" is a property that exists only within a "substance" or subject.</note>; and for this
reason, faith is "substance." **AND IT IS THE EVIDENCE OF THINGS NOT SEEN,**
that is, it is the proof of things that do not appear and are not seen
by us. Because with faith, we demonstrate what the
eternal life might be: and likewise other things that do not appear. "Evidence"
is that which makes one believe doubtful things. **AND THIS SEEMS TO ME**
**ITS QUIDDITY,** that is, the true definition according to its essential things.
Because this word "quiddity" is the essence or substance
of the thing: and it is not an ancient Latin word. But it was found by
Christian philosophers, derived from the word "quid" <note>Latin for "what."</note>. For when one
asks "what is man?" <note>original: "quid est homo"</note>, we are asking about his substance. And
the response is "a rational, mortal animal." Just as when asking "what kind is he?" <note>original: "qualis est"</note>,
we ask about the accident; and the response is "he is good" or "evil" and such.

<margin>c</margin> **AS AN EXCELLENT DIALECTICIAN,** knowing what "substance" implies
among the ten categories <note>Refers to Aristotle's ten categories of being.</note>, he demonstrates the reason why it is placed
in the distinction of faith, saying that the things which are
manifest in heaven are so hidden among men that we cannot
know them. But we believe what we do not see as firmly
as if we saw it. And upon this, we found our hope,
hoping through good works to reach the vision of the things we believe.
Therefore, because hope is founded on faith, we rightly say
that it is "substance." Peter responds: "If whatever is acquired
down among men through learning were so understood as you, Dante,
understand what faith is, the wit of a sophist—that is, a man who
uses sophisticated and deceptive arguments—would have no place." Because
he who understands a thing well cannot be deceived. **THUS HE BREATHED:**
that is, breathing out, words came from that kindled love—that is, from Peter, full
of charity. And then he added: "You have already well examined the alloy and the
weight of this coin," by way of comparison. For in a coin, one examines the
substance, that the silver be pure silver, and this is known by the alloy;
and as for the substance, then that the weight is not defrauded,
which is an accident. **BUT TELL ME IF YOU HAVE IT IN YOUR PURSE:** he continues
the metaphor and asks if Dante has this coin in his purse: that is,
do you believe as you say? And Dante responds, staying within the metaphor,
and says he has such a coin, so bright and so round that he
doubts nothing in its minting. **SINFORSA:** <note>A dialectal variant of 's'inforsa' or 's'inforza'.</note> that is, it makes itself doubtful.

<margin>d</margin> **PETER ASKS DANTE** whence faith came to him and where was its
beginning, and he responds that it came to him from the "heavy rain," that is, rain,
meaning from the supreme abundance of the Holy Spirit, which, infusing itself into
many holy men and illuminating them with the truth, they wrote it
in the "old and new skins," that is, papers. As if to say: "from the books
of both the New and the Old Testament, I have drawn this, which by the
prophets of the Old Testament was announced—the incarnation and the death
and resurrection of Christ. And thereafter in the New Testament, that is, through the Gospels
and Epistles and Acts of the Apostles, it has been demonstrated to be true
what the prophecies said." And a syllogism can be formed artificially.
Therefore, this reason is so manifest that every other reason and
proof seems blunt and obscure compared to this.

<summary>In this passage, Dante is examined by Saint Peter on the definition of Faith, which Dante defines using the Pauline formula from Hebrews 11. The accompanying commentary by Landino explains the scholastic logic and metaphors of the "coin" and "quiddity" used to describe the certainty of belief.</summary>

<keywords>Dante Alighieri, Saint Peter, Faith, Hebrews 11, scholasticism, quiddity, Saint Paul, Roman Centurion, Holy Spirit, logic, coin metaphor</keywords>

--- Page 593 ---
<meta>This page continues the examination of Dante by Saint Peter in the Heaven of the Fixed Stars. Dante has just defined Faith according to the Epistle to the Hebrews. Now, Saint Peter probes deeper into the source of Dante's belief and the evidence for the divine origin of the Scriptures. The commentary by Landino provides theological context for the poet's confession of his Creed.</meta>

# CANTO XXIV

I saw then the old and the new
proposition that so concludes for you:
why do you hold it as divine speech?

And I: The proof that discloses the truth to me
are the works that followed, for which nature
never heats iron nor strikes the anvil. <note>Dante argues that the miracles (the "works that followed") are proof of divine origin because they transcend the laws of nature.</note>
The answer came to me: Who assures you
that those works were the very same
that seek to be proved? None other swears it to you.
If the world turned to Christianity,
I said, without miracles, this one
is such that the others are not a hundredth of it;
For you entered poor and fasting
into the field to sow the good plant
which was once a vine and now has become a thorn.

---

This finished, the high holy court
resounded through the spheres a "We praise you, O God" <note>original: "Te Deum Laudamus"</note>
in the melody that is sung up there.
And that baron <term>baron: a title of high nobility, here used as a mark of great respect for Saint Peter</term> who so from branch to branch,
examining me, had already drawn me on
so that we were approaching the final leaves,
Began again: "The grace that 'lady-rules' <note>original: "donnea," a courtly term suggesting a lady's gentle but absolute rule over a lover's heart</note>
within your mind has opened your mouth
up until now as it ought to have opened;
So that I approve of what emerged;
but now it is necessary to express what you believe,
and from whence your belief offered itself to you."

---

"O holy father, and spirit who sees
that which you believed, so that you surpassed
younger feet toward the sepulcher," <note>Refers to John 20:3–8; though John ran faster, Peter was the first to enter the tomb, and Landino suggests Peter believed first.</note>
I began: "You wish that I manifest
the form of my ready belief here,
and also you asked the cause of it.
And I respond: I believe in one God,
sole and eternal, who moves all the heavens,
himself unmoved, with love and with desire.
And for such belief I have not only proofs
physical and metaphysical, but it is given to me
also by the truth that rains down from here
Through Moses, through the prophets, and through the psalms,
through the Gospel, and through you who wrote
after the burning Spirit made you holy.
And I believe in three eternal persons, and these
I believe to be one essence, so one and so trine,
that 'are' and 'is' are joined together."

<column-break/>

this. After this, Peter asks why Dante believes that the scriptures of the Old and New Testament are divine speech: <note>original: "divina favella"</note> that is, proceeding from the Holy Spirit. And Dante responds thus.

Dante responds that he believes the words of the Old and New Testament are from God. And the proof that discloses the truth to me (that is, opens the truth to me) are the works that followed (that is, the miracles performed by Christ, the apostles, and the martyrs) which are above nature. And therefore he says that nature does not heat the iron nor strike the anvil for them. After this response, Peter asks him, saying: Tell me who assures you, who makes you certain that those works and miracles happened as it is said? As if to say, perhaps it is not to be believed that these miracles happened as they say: Therefore, who makes you certain of it? Since you are not certain even of these miracles with which you wish to prove the faith is true. To this Dante replied that if the miracles were not true, this one miracle—that the world turned to the faith of Christ without miracles—is the greatest of all miracles, such that the others are not a hundredth of it. For it is a great miracle that such a crowd of men should be converted by the words of a poor fisherman and the other apostles, who were ignoble, poor, and without reputation or authority. And therefore he says: you entered poor and fasting: and because of this you could not pull men to you with wealth or with gifts, nor with pleasures and delights, since you preached poverty and abstinence. Into the field—into the world—to sow the plant (that is, to build the holy Church) which was once a vine (that is, fruitful) and now has become a thorn (that is, sterile).

Throughout the spheres: that is, the round dances of the souls thanked God for the true faith of the poet, singing: "We praise you, O God" <note>original: "Te Deum Laudamus"</note> with celestial melody. And Peter the baron, who by questioning him of the faith from branch to branch (as if to say, from grade to grade) had led him near the final leaves (that is, to the top of the tree, which signifies the end). For first he asked what faith is; then the explanation of the definition; then if he had it in his soul; then from whence it had come to him. If he held that the sacred scripture was the word of God. Add to this the proof and the final miracle. Therefore now Peter concludes that the grace of God, which 'lady-rules' (that is, dominates and lords) in him, opened his mouth and made him speak rightly. And for this reason he approves what the author "emerged" (that is, what came out of his mouth); but now he wishes to understand two things. First, what he believes (that is, the articles of faith). Second, from whence his belief proceeded.

The author speaks to Peter, and having to confess what he believes, he demonstrates that what he believes, Peter believed while down in the world. But now Peter does not "believe" because he has true knowledge (vision). And because of this, it is said that faith does not enter heaven. **SO THAT YOU SURPASSED younger feet toward the sepulcher.** He did not surpass the youthful feet of John because, hearing of the resurrection of Christ from the women, he reached the tomb before John did. Rather, he arrived "before" because he believed in such a resurrection before John reached the tomb to see if he had risen. **IN ONE GOD alone:** there is one God and no more. But of God we shall treat in some part below. **ETERNAL:** without beginning and without end. To whom nothing is past or future, but everything is present to Him. **WHO moves all the heaven, himself unmoved.** Because He, stable and firm, moves the movers of the heavens. Whence Boethius: "Remaining stable, You grant all things to be moved." <note>original: "Stabilisque manens das cuncta moueri"</note> **WITH Love and with desire:** He moves with love (that is, of His own spontaneous will) and with desire (because He is loved and desired). **AND FOR SUCH belief.** There are physical and metaphysical reasons which demonstrate that there is one God. **BUT IT IS GIVEN TO ME** (that is, give it to me) by the truth that rains from here (that is, from heaven). For the grace of the Holy Spirit infused into the minds of holy men, such as Moses, the prophets, David, the Gospels, and the acts of the Apostles, has shown them there is one God: through Moses who said in Genesis, "In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth" <note>original: "In principio creauit deus celum & terram"</note>; through the prophets like Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and Daniel and the others; through you, Peter, Paul, and James, whose epistles appear in the Bible. And I believe in three eternal persons: and these I believe to be one essence.

<summary>Dante completes his examination on Faith by citing the miracles and the conversion of the world as evidence for Scripture's divinity, concluding with a formal profession of his belief in the Trinity.</summary>

<header>PARADISE</header>

Of the deep divine condition
which I touch upon, my mind is sealed
repeatedly by the evangelical doctrine.
This principle, this is the spark
which dilates into a flame, more vivid,
and like a star in heaven it sparkles within me.
As a lord who accepts what pleases him
thereupon embraces his servant, congratulating him
for the news as soon as he falls silent;
So, blessing me while singing,
three times he encircled me as I grew quiet,
that apostolic light at whose command
I had spoken; so much did my speaking please him.

## CANTO XXV OF THE THIRD CANTICLE OF DANTE

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap S.</image-desc>
If it should ever happen that the sacred poem
to which both heaven and earth have set their hand,
so that it has made me lean for many years,
Should overcome the cruelty that bars me out
from the fair sheepfold where I slept as a lamb,
an enemy to the wolves that give it war;
With another voice now, with another fleece <note>The "fleece" refers to his hair, now grey with age and wisdom, contrasting with his youth as a "lamb."</note>
I shall return as a poet, and at the font
of my baptism I shall take the crown;
For there I entered into the faith that makes
souls known to God, and afterward,
Peter, for its sake, thus encircled my brow.

Then a light moved toward us
from that sphere from which the first-fruit emerged
that Christ left among his vicars;
And my lady, full of joy,
said to me: "Look, look! Behold the baron <term>baron: a title of high nobility, here used to denote the high status of the Apostle James in the heavenly court</term>
for whose sake, down there, one visits Galicia." <note>This refers to the pilgrimage to Santiago de Compostela in Galicia, Spain.</note>
Just as when the dove alights
near its companion, and one to the other pours out
its affection, circling and murmuring;
So I saw one great prince received
by the other, praising the food
on which they feast up there.
But when the greeting was completed,
silent *before me* <note>original: "coram me"</note> each one stopped,
so ignited that it overcame my vision.

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Decorative square initial C containing an ornamental design.</image-desc>
He concludes that what he touches upon at present being <gloss>regarding the deep divinity</gloss> is repeatedly sealed and impressed in his mind by the doctrine of the evangelists: in short, he concludes that the gospels are his masters in those things he says concerning the divinity. **THIS is the principle:** that is, this evangelical doctrine is the principle of faith: and it is the spark from which a great ardor multiplies and sparkles like a star in heaven. It is as if he implies that whatever departs from evangelical doctrine cannot proceed rightly. **AS THE lord:** after Peter had heard Dante's words, he encircled him three times: that is, he embraced him as a lord embraces a servant after hearing good news from him. He said "three times" for the reasons we have often mentioned regarding the ternary number; or rather because he has expressed the Trinity in one essence, or to demonstrate that these three theological virtues are so joined and connected together that they cannot be separated.

<image-desc>Decorative square initial I (styled as a Gothic h) with ornamentation.</image-desc>
In the preceding chapter our poet treated of Faith. And at present, in this twenty-fifth, he treats of the second theological virtue, which is Hope. Therefore, he first places his hope of returning to his homeland and being crowned there. Then he introduces the apostle James, who examines him on this virtue. Then he proposes three doubts to him concerning this virtue: and Beatrice answers the first, and the poet the second; and finally, the author is asked by James from whence this virtue comes to him. But so that the prologue may be suited to the subject of hope, he demonstrates his hope and says: **IF IT SHOULD EVER HAPPEN.** i.e., it may come to pass that this my sacred poem to which heaven and earth have set their hand <note>i.e., brought help</note>, because it treats of the nature of vice and its purgation, and treats of the moral and speculative virtues. **SO THAT it has made me lean for many years:** because he who assiduously contemplates and composes becomes thin. Whence the images of poets are made thin. Juvenal <note>A Roman satirist</note> said of this: <note>original: "Ut dignus uenias ederis: & imagine macra" — "That you may come worthy of the ivy, and with a thin image."</note> **May it conquer the cruelty** of my citizens, which is the reason I am exiled. **FROM THE Fair sheepfold:** from the beautiful city [Florence]: and he calls it a sheepfold to demonstrate the innocence and gentleness of the people, poorly governed by the leading citizens, who were to the people like wolves to sheep. He condemns, therefore, not the city or the people, but the governors, to whom he, as an innocent and immaculate lamb, says he has been an enemy. **WITH another voice:** as if to say with more elegant verses; **with another fleece:** he remains within the metaphor, as if to say not with the fleece of a lamb, but of a robust ram. **I shall return as a poet and take the crown** <note>i.e., the laurel</note> at the font of my baptism, that is, in the temple of John the Baptist <note>The Baptistery of San Giovanni in Florence</note> in which I was baptized. And deservedly, having sung of faith, he wished to be made a poet in that place where he took the Christian faith. Whence he says: because I entered into the faith which makes souls **known** (i.e., ready and manifest) to God in that place. And faith is what taught me to write this poem: and because I am in the true faith, Peter, as he showed just above, encircled my brow three times.

<image-desc>Decorative square initial d containing ornamentation.</image-desc>
After the prologue, the poet returns to the work: and continuing the matter, he says: **Then** (i.e., and after Peter encircled my brow) from that same sphere, from the beautiful dance of the apostles, whence Peter had first come to me—who was the **first-fruit** of the vicars (i.e., the first vicar that Christ left on earth)—a light moved, which was the soul of James, and came toward us. Then Beatrice, truly his lady, full of joy—because every demonstration that theology makes gives our soul the highest joy—said: "Look and watch, for behold the **baron**." **FOR WHOSE SAKE:** for whom, down there on earth, one visits **Galicia**: because many make a vow to go and visit his church which is in Galicia. **JUST AS:** an excellent comparison by which he demonstrates that, as happens in the coupling of doves, when one alights near the other, circling and murmuring, it shows the affection it bears for it; so also, and with that affection, one apostle welcomed the other, praising God, who is the food of blessed souls, and up there in heaven **feasts** them (i.e., feeds them). *To feast* <note>original: "prandere"</note> in Latin means to dine. But after the **greeting** (i.e., the joyful welcome) was **completed** (i.e., finished), both stopped in the sight of Dante, silent and with silence, and so **ignited** (i.e., so inflamed and kindled) that it overcame my...

<summary>Dante expresses his deep hope to return to his beloved Florence to be crowned as a poet, while Saint James the Apostle appears to begin the examination of his second theological virtue, Hope.</summary>

my face and my sight; <gloss>that is, it dazzled me in such a way that I could not look at him.</gloss>

Smiling then, Beatrice said:
"Illustrious life, for whom the bounty
of our basilica was written,
Make hope resound in this high place;
you know that you represent it as many times
as Jesus showed more clarity to the three."
"Lift your head and make yourself assured,
for that which comes up here from the mortal world
must be ripened by our rays."
This comfort from the second fire
came to me, wherefore I lifted my eyes to the mountains
which previously bowed them down with too much weight.

<gloss>The three disciples had greater knowledge of these virtues than the others since they had the greatest knowledge of Christ in his transfiguration.</gloss> And after Beatrice had spoken these words, James turned to Dante and admonished him to lift his face and make himself able to sustain the divine light. And certainly the intellect, which raises itself to the contemplation of God, makes itself capable through hope because it is strengthened and comforted. **This comfort from the second fire came to me;** <gloss>that is, James, who was the second after Peter to greet me, gave me this comfort.</gloss> **Wherefore I lifted;** <gloss>I raised my eyes to the mountains, namely toward the apostles who are in an exalted place like mountains.</gloss> And similarly the Psalmist uses this for the comfort and stability that hope brings. Wherefore he said: "I lifted up my eyes to the mountains: from whence comes my help." <note>original Latin: "Leuaui oculos meos in montes: onde uenit auxilium mihi"</note> These were the mountains that previously bowed him down by their excessive weight.

"Since by grace our Emperor wills
that you come face to face with his counts
in his most secret hall before your death,
So that, having seen the truth of this court,
the hope that down there inspires true love
may be strengthened in you and in others.
Say what it is, and how your mind
is flowered by it, and from whence it came to you."
Thus the second light continued further.

And that pious one who guided the feathers
of my wings to such a high flight,
anticipated me in the response thus:
"The Church Militant <term>Church Militant: the Christian community currently living on earth, engaged in spiritual warfare against sin and the world</term> has no child
with more hope, as it is written
in the Sun that radiates through all our host.
Therefore it is granted to him to come
from Egypt to Jerusalem to see,
before his term of service is prescribed.
The other two points, which are asked
not for the sake of knowing, but so that you may report
how much this virtue pleases you,
I leave to him, for they will not be difficult
nor a matter of boasting; let him answer them,
and may the grace of God allow him this."

<gloss>...knowing: but so that Dante may report back down in the world how much this virtue pleased him. For they will not be "strong," that is, difficult. Nor will they be a matter of "boasting," that is, vainglory. Therefore let him answer and let the grace of God "comport" it for him, that is, let it be his pleasure.</gloss>

<column-break/>

Sacred Scripture intends that the three disciples—Peter, James, and John—whom Christ took up to Mount Tabor when he was transfigured, should represent the three theological virtues. And Peter, which means "rock" and "firmness," stands for the firmness of Faith. James, which means "supplanter," stands for Hope; because hope makes us trample and put under our feet every adversity and toil. And John means "full of grace" and stands for Charity. Therefore, just as Peter examined the poet on Faith, so James examines him on Hope. Beatrice turns to him, calling him **illustrious life;** <gloss>glorious soul</gloss> through whom was written the bounty of our basilica, meaning the Church Triumphant of eternal life. And certainly in his epistle, he demonstrates how great the divine liberality is, saying: "Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights." <note>original Latin: "Omne datum optimum & omne donum perfectum desursum est a patre luminum"</note> Make it so, James, that **hope resounds in this height.** This is as if to say: make Dante demonstrate what he feels about hope in this heaven. And you can do this because you represent this hope as many times as Jesus showed "more clarity"—that is, showed greater familiarity—to three disciples: Peter, John, and you.

James speaks and says: since our Emperor, God, wills by his grace and not by any debt that you **confront** and join us before death. This does not usually happen—that someone goes in the flesh to heaven, into the **most secret hall;** <gloss>into the most excellent part of the divine palace.</gloss> **SO THAT** having seen the truth of this celestial court and known true blessedness, you may comfort **hope** in yourself and in others—that hope which, down in the world, **inspires true love.** For from hope proceeds love. Say, therefore, what hope is, and how your mind **is flowered;** <gloss>is adorned.</gloss> Not without reason does he mention "flowers" regarding hope; for just as a flower is not yet the fruit, but gives a sign that the fruit will be born from it, so hope shows us our future blessedness. **And from whence it came to you;** <gloss>tell me what it is to hope.</gloss> **Thus followed the second light again;** <gloss>just as Peter, the first light, asked what faith is and how it came to him, so now James, the second light, asked him similarly.</gloss>

James had asked what hope is, and if he possessed this virtue, and from where it had come. Now, having to answer, Beatrice anticipated the second part and answered for the author, affirming that there is as much hope in him as in any other Christian in the **Church Militant** <gloss>the church of the living</gloss> as can be seen in God, in whom all things are seen as in a mirror. And because of this hope, it has been granted to him by divine grace to come **from Egypt to Jerusalem;** <gloss>from the world to heaven.</gloss> For **Egypt** is interpreted as darkness or tribulation; and from that, as if from a supreme military struggle, the people of God were led into the land of promise and happiness. **Jerusalem** is interpreted as a "vision of peace," the flower of our happiness. Wherefore the Psalmist says: "A hymn is due to you, O God, in Zion, and a vow shall be paid to you in Jerusalem." <note>original Latin: "Te decet himnus in sion & tibi reddetur uotum in hierusalem"</note> **BEFORE his service is prescribed;** <gloss>before his temporal life is taken from him, in which we "militate"—that is, we fight continually with the world, the flesh, and the devil. And if we overcome, we are called to heaven where we triumph over the conquered adversary.</gloss> **THE OTHER two points:** of the three things James asked, Beatrice has answered this one, because if the author had answered for himself, it might have seemed like he was boasting. Now she continues in her speech and says that the other two points which James asked were not for the sake of...

**L**ike the student who follows the teacher,
prompt and willing in that wherein he is expert,

**"H**ope," I said, "is a certain expectation
of future glory, which is produced by

**F**rom many stars this light comes to me;

<gloss>If he has the Christian faith as I have: he says this as if to say every Christian uses it.</gloss> Therefore, David first distilled it in me, and you, James, afterwards instilled it with your instilling in your canonical Epistle. Because that which you write there, you have from him; so that I am so full of this instilling that I "re-rain": that is, I pour back onto others our rain. **YOU distilled into me:** in the canonical Epistle of James: "Blessed is the man who endures temptation. For when he has been proved, he shall receive the crown of life which God has promised to those who love him" <note>original Latin: "beatus uir qui suffert tēptationē. Quia cũ probatus fuerit accipiet coronā uite quā promisit deus diligentibus se"</note>; and at the end of the same: "Be patient, strengthen your hearts: For the coming of the Lord is at hand" <note>original Latin: "Patientes confirmate corda uestra: Quoniā aduentus domini appropinquabit"</note>.

<gloss>The testimony of John the Evangelist, brother of James: he, in the Apocalypse, places a great multitude in white robes who followed Christ wherever he went; which denotes "that the pure in heart shall see God" <note>original Latin: "quod mundi corde deum uidebunt"</note>; and in the divine vision is located our supreme blessedness.</gloss> Therefore "more clearly" <note>original: "piu digesta"</note>: that is, more orderly, John places in this revelation that which hope promises to the good. At the end of these words, the sphere of the Apostles sang: "Let all those who know your name hope in you" <note>original Latin: "Sperent in te omnes qui nouerunt nomē tuū"</note>. And all the other dancing circles responded to the song. Nor could there be a psalm more fitting for Hope.

**T**hen among them a light grew bright,
such that if Cancer had such a crystal,

<column-break/>

<margin>c</margin>
**LIKE** the student: <gloss>that is, he who learns</gloss>; follows the teacher in what he knows, so that his excellence may be revealed: <gloss>that is, made manifest</gloss>. Thus I, responding to the first point, said that hope is nothing other than "certain expectation": <gloss>that is, to wait with certainty for future glory</gloss>. The definition of the <term>Master of the Sentences</term> <note>Peter Lombard (c. 1100–1160), whose book of "Sentences" was the standard medieval theology textbook.</note> is: "Hope is the certain expectation of future blessedness coming from God's grace and preceding merits" <note>original Latin: "Spes est certa expectatio future beatitudinis ueniēs ex dei gratia precedentibus meritis"</note>. Then he responds to the second point and says that such hope is granted to us by divine grace preceding any merit of ours. Then, having manifested the primary cause, he manifests the fertile cause: <gloss>that is, the influence of the stars from which, as written above, various virtues flow</gloss>. But although an influx is born from the stars that disposes us to various virtues, and consequently to the hope that through such virtue we shall acquire eternal life, nevertheless it is necessary that such disposition be aided by doctrine. And therefore he adds that he who is the "supreme singer of the supreme Leader": <gloss>that is, David, the supreme prophet of the supreme God</gloss>, first distilled this hope into his heart. David is the supreme singer because he is the supreme prophet in the Ancient Law. **LET THEM HOPE** <note>original: "SPERENT"</note> in Thee: he uses the words of David which are: "Let all those who know your name hope in you: for you have not forsaken those who seek you" <note>original Latin: "Sperent inte omnes q nouerunt nomē tuum: quoniā nō dereliquisti querētes te"</note>. Let all those who know your name hope in you, and in your <term>theodia</term> <note>From the Greek 'theos' (God) and 'ode' (song)—a divine song or theology.</note>: <gloss>that is, deity, because 'theos' in Greek means God</gloss>. And then the poet adds, saying: "and who does not know the name of God if they have my faith": <gloss>that is, the Christian faith</gloss>.

<margin>d</margin>
**WHILE** the author spoke, he saw the light of James always trembling like a flash of lightning. Then James spoke and spoke of the love of the virtue of hope which followed him "even to the palm": <gloss>that is, even to victory</gloss>; and at the "leaving of the field," he wants to ask what that hope promises you: <gloss>that is, what you hope for</gloss>. And note that hope followed him until the palm: <gloss>that is, until victory</gloss>, which we cannot say we have while we are in this mortal life. Because we always fight against the flesh and the devil. But when we "leave the field": <gloss>that is, the place where one fights, which is this world</gloss>, and we exit victorious because we have conquered every vice, the hope of coming to blessedness accompanies us always until that blessedness itself. But it does not enter into it, because a present good is not hoped for, but enjoyed. And he used the "palm" for victory, because the palm is given to the one who obtains victory. And the reason for this we have made manifest more extensively elsewhere.

**JAMES REQUESTING** that the poet manifest to him what hope promises him, he responds that it promises a happy and eternal life to the soul and the body. And this he proves with the testimony of the scriptures of the New Testament. He says, therefore, the new and ancient scriptures set the "mark" <note>the target or goal</note> for the souls whom God has made his friends. As if to say, the end point where they must direct their hope, and that mark is pointed out to him. And through the ancient scriptures, he demonstrates and alleges Isaiah, who says in the sixty-first chapter: "In their own land they shall possess a double portion" <note>original Latin: "In terra sua duplitia possidebunt"</note>. And Solomon in the Proverbs: "All her household are clothed in double garments" <note>original Latin: "Omnes domestici eius uestiti sunt duplicibus"</note>. Our homeland is heaven. For as Paul says: "We have here no lasting city, but we seek one to come" <note>original Latin: "Non habemus hic ciuitatem manentem sed futuram inquirimus"</note>. Wherefore the poet says: "and its own land is this sweet life": by this, the doctors well understand the happiness of the soul and the body which the blessed, after the resurrection of bodies, shall feel in the celestial life. **AND YOUR** brother: he provides the testimony...

Winter would have a month of a single day
And as a maiden rises and goes and enters the dance,
a slow maiden, only to do honor
to the bride, and not for any fault,
So did I see the brightened splendor
approach the two who were turning in a wheel,
as was suited to their burning love.
It joined there in the song and in the melody,
and my lady kept her gaze upon them,
just like a bride, silent and motionless.
"This is he who lay upon the breast
of our Pelican <note>The pelican was a medieval symbol for Christ, based on the legend that it feeds its young with its own blood.</note>; and this was he
chosen from upon the cross for the great office." <note>Refers to Christ entrusting the Virgin Mary to Saint John the Apostle while on the cross.</note>
My lady thus; yet no more for this
did she move her gaze from being attentive
than she had been before her words.

<gloss>A bird in Egypt which with its own blood resurrects its dead children. They say that the children of the pelican, after the father has fed them, rise up against him, and he, defending himself, kills them. And then, moved to pity, he wounds himself with his beak, and shedding his blood over them, he resurrects them. So man, sinning, rises up against his Maker, and the Divine Majesty kills him because He condemns him to death for sin. Then, moved to pity by the shedding of His own blood, liberating us from sin, He resurrects us.</gloss> **UPON** the cross for the great office chosen. Christ on the cross said to His mother that she should have John in place of a son, and to John that he should have her in place of a mother. Therefore, he was chosen for the great office. And these words were spoken by his Beatrice. And afterward, she remained no less attentive toward those aforementioned apostles than before.

Like one who squints and strives
to see the sun eclipsed a little,
who by seeing becomes sightless,
Such did I become at that last fire <note>Saint John appeared as a brilliant light.</note>
while it was said: "Why do you dazzle yourself
to see a thing that has no place here?
In earth is earth my body, and it shall be there
with the others until our number
is equalized with the eternal purpose. <note>John clarifies that his physical body is still on Earth, contrary to legends that he was bodily assumed into Heaven.</note>
With their two robes in the blessed cloister
are the two lights alone that ascended;
and this you shall report back to your world."

At this voice, the flaming circle
grew quiet, together with the sweet mixture
that was made by the sound of the triple breath. <note>The "triple breath" refers to the three apostles: Peter, James, and John.</note>
Just as, to cease toil or risk,
the oars previously struck into the water
all stop at the sound of a whistle.
Ah, how much was I stirred in my mind
when I turned to see Beatrice,
for not being able to see her, although I was
near to her and in the happy world!

<column-break/>

It is seen in a maiden when she rises from sitting and goes to the dance and enters it. Nor is it without reason that he compares him to the maiden, since he persevered in perpetual virginity. Furthermore, it shows that so great was his splendor that if in the sign of Cancer there were a star of such splendor, it would happen that while the sun is in Capricorn, a month would have nothing but a single day because there would never be darkness. Cancer is the sign opposite to Capricorn. And when the sun enters Capricorn, which is in the month of December, while it is below the earth, Cancer is always above the earth. Therefore, if in that sign there were a star that shone as much as the Evangelist shone, it would happen that in the month when the sun is in Capricorn, it would never be night, because the day is lit for us by the sun, and the night would be lit for us by that star. This splendor is given to this apostle for the admirable wisdom and doctrine that was in him. **IT JOINED** there, that is, with the two apostles in the song and in the melody they were making; as if to say, he harmonized with them in singing "Let them hope in the Lord" <note>original: "Sperent in domino"</note>. This denotes that these virtues [Faith, Hope, and Charity] make one and the same harmony. And Beatrice watched these three with silence and immobility because truly sacred theology never departs from the intuition and the sight of these three virtues. **THIS** is he: these are the words of Beatrice, who, wishing to show that this is John the Evangelist, uses this circumlocution: that he is the one who at the [Last] Supper lay upon the breast of Christ; and while sleeping, he saw the things of divinity as he writes in the Gospel. And she calls Christ the "Pelican." This...

The author stood fixed upon the Evangelist to see if he had a body; and in looking, it happened to him as to one who fixedly gazes at the sun to see it eclipsed, and is dazzled in such a way that afterward he sees nothing. And by John it was said to him: "Why do you dazzle" —that is, blind yourself— "in gazing too fixedly to see a thing that has no place here" —that is, which is not here? Because you want to see my body, which is not here. But it is earth down in the earth, and it shall be there until our number —that is, the number of the blessed— matches and equals the eternal purpose —that is, that which God has ordained. This is to say, until the end of the world; for the world is to last until the number of the blessed fills the vacant seats [left by the fallen angels]. He gives, therefore, these two sentences to John. The first, that he died and left his body on earth; because in his Gospel: "The saying went out among the brothers that this disciple would not die; and Jesus did not say he would not die, but 'If I want him to remain until I come'..." <note>original Latin: "Exit sermo inter fratres quod discipulus ille nō moritur & non dixit iesus non moritur sed sic uolo eum manere donec ueniam."</note>. The second sentence is that the world lasts until the blessed fill the vacant seats. He also places this in the Apocalypse: "And it was told to them that they should rest for a little while longer, until the number of their fellow servants and their brothers... should be complete" <note>original Latin: "Et dictum est illis quod requiescent tempus adhuc modicum: donec cōpleatur numerus feruorum siue eorū qui interficiēdi sunt sicut & illi."</note>. And he returns to the text. **WITH their two robes** —that is, with their own bodies— are the two lights alone, namely Christ and His mother Mary.

The words of John being finished, the flaming circle —that is, the sphere of the three apostles— grew quiet from its turning, and their song, which was a "mixture" —that is, a blend made of the sound and the voices of the "triple breath," meaning the three apostles— ceased. And this circle stopped all at once, just as on a galley those who row, hearing the whistle —which is given either because the crew should rest or to flee danger— all stop. Then I was much moved in my mind because of not being able to see Beatrice, even though I turned to her and she was near me and we were in Heaven. He could not see Beatrice because he had already ascended to the contemplation of such high things that his intellect failed, nor could he entirely see them. And truly the doctrine of the Evangelist John, through too great a light, dazzles every sharp intellect and wit.

<meta>This page transitions from the end of Canto XXV into Canto XXVI. Having been examined on Faith by Saint Peter and Hope by Saint James, Dante is now blinded by the radiant light of Saint John the Apostle, who will examine him on Charity (Love). The commentary by Cristoforo Landino provides a theological and structural framework for this final examination of the three theological virtues.</meta>

# PARADISO CANTO XXVI OF THE THIRD CANTICLE BY DANTE.

<column-break/>

<margin>m</margin>
While I was fearful because of my sightless eyes,
from the glowing flame that had quenched them
issued a breath that made me attentive,
Saying: "Until you have regained
the sense of sight you have consumed in me,
it is well that you compensate for it by speaking.
Begin then, and say where your soul 
is aimed, and be assured
that your sight in you is bewildered, but not dead;
Because the lady who through this divine
region leads you, has in her look
the power that the hand of Ananias held."

<note>original: "a paolo. E scripto negli acti degli apostoli..."</note>
To Paul. It is written in the Acts of the Apostles that Saul, [having received letters] from the prince of the priests, coming from Jerusalem to Damascus [surrounded] by a great light, fell to the ground and heard a voice saying: "Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?" He replied: "Who are you, Lord?" The voice said: "I am Jesus whom you persecute." And trembling and astonished he replied: "Lord, what do you want me to do?" To which the Lord [answered: "Go into the city."] He was led by his companions because he had become blind; and for three days he remained [without sight or food]. Then Jesus appeared to one of his disciples, namely to Ananias, and commanded him to go to Saul, for he was a vessel of election <note>Latin: "vas electionis"—a person chosen by God for a special purpose</note> to carry His name before the nations, and kings, and the children of Israel. Ananias went and placed his hands upon him, and immediately there fell from Paul's eyes something like scales, and he regained his sight. Therefore, [the poet uses this comparison] as Ananias gave sight back to Paul, so Beatrice gives sight back to Dante, who was dazzled by the excessive light. And certainly [divine grace] informs the intellect so that it can discern the light of the divinity which [previously confounded it].

I said: "At her pleasure, whether soon or late,
let remedy come to the eyes that were the gateways
when she entered with the fire with which I always burn.
The Good that makes this court content
is the Alpha and Omega <note>The beginning and the end</note> of whatever scripture
Love reads to me, whether softly or loudly."
That same voice which had taken away
the fear of the sudden dazzling
gave me the care of speaking further,
And said: "Truly, through a narrower sieve
you must clarify; it behoves you to say
who directed your bow to such a target."

<note>original: "cipalmente idio sidebba amare..."</note>
Mainly God should be loved for Himself, and then [other things for Him]. The poet demonstrates that the same voice—that is, the same [spirit of John]—which had removed the fear of the sudden dazzling (because he had told me that Beatrice [would heal me]), put me in the care and anxiety of speaking further and said: "It behoves you to clarify through a narrower sieve." This is a metaphor taken from grain, which they begin to clean [with coarse sieves] until they are perfectly purged. "It behoves you to say who directed your bow to such a target." For a "target" <note>Italian: "berzaglo"</note> is that mark at which crossbowmen shoot; [he asks] who directed your mind to this end, that you should love the eternal [Good].

And I: "By philosophical arguments
and by authority that descends from here,
such love must needs be imprinted in me;
For good, inasmuch as it is good, once understood,
enkindles love, and so much greater 
as the goodness it contains within itself is greater.
Therefore, to the Essence where there is such advantage..."

<column-break/>

In this twenty-sixth chapter, John the Evangelist is introduced to treat Charity, the third theological virtue. First, the author is examined by him on this virtue. Then, he makes another petition regarding the same virtue. In the third place, Adam appears, to whom the author moves certain doubts. And in the last part, Adam responds to the doubts. Returning therefore to the beginning, the author writes that while he was fearful—that is, he stood in doubt—because of his sightless eyes—that is, because his visual power was quenched by the glowing flame of the Evangelist—a breath issued: that is, a speech, and said: "While you recover your sight—that is, regain the visual sense that you have consumed in me—that is, while you were looking at me—it is good that you compensate and restore it by speaking. Therefore, where is your soul aimed: that is, to what end does your soul extend as to its ultimate point? And rest assured that your sight is bewildered for a time, but not defunct—that is, dead and lost altogether. Because Beatrice, who conducts you through this divine region of the heavens, has in her look—that is, in her seeing—the power of the hand of Ananias, who, baptizing Paul the Apostle, made his sight return.

For Paul was a most bitter persecutor of the Christians; and with letters [he went] to Damascus to lead away as prisoners those who confessed Christ. Suddenly a light [from heaven] circled him, and he heard a voice saying: "Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?" And he answering: "Who are you, Lord?" The Lord said: "I am Jesus of Nazareth whom you persecute; it is hard for you to kick against the prick." Then he, full of stupor and trembling, said: "Lord, what do you want me to do?" The Lord said: "Go into the city and there it will be told to you." He went then, led by the hand, and for three days he was without food in the house of Judas. And Jesus appeared to one of his disciples named Ananias and said to him: "Go, for this man is a vessel of election <note>Latin: "vas electionis"</note> who is to carry my name [to the Gentiles]." Ananias went therefore and placed his hands upon him. And immediately there fell from his eyes something like scales, and he received his sight. Just as Ananias restores sight to Paul, so Beatrice restores it to Dante. And the Sacred Scripture is that which comforts the eye of the intellect so that it can perceive the divine light which first confounded it.

These are the words of the poet by which he first responds to the comfort given to him by John, and then to his question. Therefore, first, John having comforted him that Beatrice would replenish his sight lost through the excessive light, he responds that he submits to Beatrice's judgment such a remedy, whether late or early, as she wishes to send to his dazzled eyes, which he says were "gateways" to her when she entered into him with the fire for which he always burns. Beatrice is Sacred Scripture and the grace of God which lifts us so high in contemplation; not a little of the divine light, which without Beatrice would dazzle us, nor would it let us discern. The poet is dazzled in the light of John—that is, the human intellect is confused in the great things that John writes in the Gospel and in the Epistles and in the Apocalypse. But theology opens and declares it and makes man capable of it. THE GOOD THAT: responds to John's question, and demonstrates that the Good that contents all the court of Paradise—that is, all the blessed—is Alpha—that is, the beginning—and Omega—that is, the end—of all the scripture that Love reads to me—that is, shows me charity—whether softly or loudly—that is, whether easily or with difficulty. For all scripture speaks of how we must love God for Himself and the creatures for the love of Him. THAT SAME VOICE: following the spirit with its voice which was John, who had taken away the fear of the sudden blindness, telling me that Beatrice would free me from it, he put me back into the desire to speak. CERTAINLY THROUGH A NARROWER SIEVE: it behoves you to clarify yourself. A "sieve" <note>Italian: "vagllo"</note> is used to purge and clean grain, first with wide sieves and then with more density. WHO DIRECTED YOUR BOW: that is, your will, to such a target—that is, to such a mark. "Target" in Greek is called *skopos*. Therefore, who was it that directed your mind to this end: to love God for Himself and other things for the love of Him?

The poet demonstrates that two things especially induce him to the love of the Supreme Good: philosophical arguments, which not only show there is a single Creator in whom every creature turns as to its ultimate end and Supreme Good; but the Platonists also wrote many things regarding the Word and the Holy Spirit, as Augustine shows in his *City of God*. The second is from the Apostles, the Evangelists, the martyrs, and the doctors, which is worth much more in Sacred Scripture than in the natural sciences, because they come from divine influence and from revelation made to holy men.

<summary>Dante begins his examination on Charity with Saint John the Apostle. The commentary draws parallels between Dante's temporary blindness and the conversion of Saint Paul, while identifying God as the Alpha and Omega of all spiritual and philosophical knowledge.</summary>

that every good which is found outside of Him
is nothing other than a light from His ray.
More than any other, it is necessary that it move
the mind in love, of everyone who discerns
the truth upon which this proof is founded.
Such truth is revealed to my intellect
by him who demonstrates to me the first love
of all eternal substances.
It appears in the voice of the truthful author,
who says to Moses, speaking of Himself:
"I will make you feel every goodness."
<note>original: "io ti faro sentire ogni ualore" — referring to Exodus 33:19</note>
You also reveal it to me, beginning
the high proclamation that cries the secret
of here below above every other herald.

And I saw by human intellect
and by authority concordant with it
that the highest of your loves looks toward God.
But tell me further if you feel other cords
pulling you toward Him, so that you may sound out
with how many teeth this love bites you.
The holy intention was not hidden
from the eagle of Christ; rather, I perceived
where he wished to lead my profession.

Therefore I began again: all those bites
that can make the heart turn toward God
have concurred in my charity;
For the existence of the world and my own existence,
the death that He sustained so that I might live,
and that which every faithful soul hopes for as I do,
With the aforementioned living knowledge,
have drawn me from the sea of twisted love
and have placed me on the shore of the right love.
The leaves with which all the garden is leafed
by the eternal gardener, I love as much
as the good that is bestowed upon them by Him.

every affection for Him. All these things with the living knowledge of philosophical reasons have drawn me from the sea of **twisted love**: that is, from the miseries and troubles that man suffers for loving mortal things too much. And they have placed me on the shore of **right love** because just as worldly love always strikes us in a tempestuous sea with various perturbations, day and night they torment the mind. Thus, divine love leads us into this port of eternal tranquility. **THE LEAVES** with which all the garden is leafed. Having shown the causes that make him love God, he shows the reason why he loves the blessed spirits of God, saying that he loves them because he knows they are loved by God. He says, therefore: I love the leaves with which the garden of the **eternal gardener** is leafed—that is, the souls of the blessed, who adorn Paradise just as leaves adorn a garden. And I love the blessed souls of this place of goodness and virtue as much as good is granted to them by God.

As soon as I was silent, a most sweet song
resounded through the heaven, and my lady
said with the others: "Holy, holy, holy!"
And as one is awakened by a sharp light
because the visual spirit runs to meet

<column-break/>

**THAT** good. He argues philosophically according to the followers of Aristotle and Plato: and especially that "good," as soon as it is known by us, incites us to love it; and the greater the good, the greater the love. Therefore, God being the supreme good—and so much the supreme good that no other thing is good except insofar as it participates in Him—it follows that the poet says that every good found outside of God is nothing other than the light of His rays. It follows that we are naturally inclined, most of all and with most ardent charity, toward His love. And this is the **first love**; afterward, it extends in a certain order: to one's country, to the father, to children, and consequently to others according to their degree. **Such truth to my intellect discerns**: that is, he demonstrates this truth that God must be loved above all things. **HE**: that is, Aristotle, who proves this in many places. **DISCERNS IT** the voice: Because when God spoke to Moses, He said *I will show you all good* <note>Latin: "Ostendam tibi omne bonum"</note> and certainly He showed him every good by showing him Himself. **REVEAL IT** to me: that is, you, John, show it to me, beginning the **high proclamation** <note>The Gospel of John</note>: and he means his proclamation in which he manifested on earth the **secret**—that is, the secrets of the [spiritual] food, and especially the incarnation of the Divine Word.

**JOHN** gathers this conclusion from the words of Dante: that he, both through **human intellect** (that is, through philosophical reasons which the human intellect learns) and through the authority of sacred letters, keeps and observes the sovereign and first and greatest love for God. But he wants to know if, besides these two things, he feels **other cords**—that is, other incitements that draw him toward Him, into His love. Therefore he wants him to "sound out"—that is, speak—with **how many teeth** the love of God bites him: that is, with how many movements God awakens and incites him to love Him. And after John had said these words to Dante, the intention of John was not **latent** (that is, it was not hidden); rather, he perceived and understood where he wished to lead his **profession** (that is, what thing he wanted to make him profess). And he says **eagle** because, as we show elsewhere, this Evangelist is figured in the form of an eagle: because just as this bird flies higher than the others and can look into the rays of the sun without being dazzled, so John, describing the divinity of Christ, rose higher than the others and could more firmly contemplate the **sun**—that is, the divine essence. John, therefore, having heard these universal reasons that pull us to divine love, now wants some more particular ones. For which reason Dante responds to satisfy him.

**THE POET** enumerates the **stings** and incitements that can draw a heart to love God above all other things, which have concurred in him together with philosophical reasons and the authority of sacred letters. And these are the **being of the world** (that is, the fragility of worldly things which are momentary—wherefore Petrarch says: "Wretched is he who places hope in mortal things"); and **his own being**, in which the immortal soul is considered, which is unhappy if it does not join itself with God. Therefore we must seek Him with supreme charity. **THE DEATH** that He sustained: Because he would be most ungrateful who does not love the giver of such benefits. **AND THAT** which every faithful soul hopes for: Because considering the reward that is expected, one must be firm in

**FINISHED** the speaking, a most sweet song was heard from all the spirits and from Beatrice, and they sang **Holy, Holy, Holy** <note>Latin: "sancto scõ scõ" - Sanctus, Sanctus, Sanctus</note>. And then the poet regained his sight. Because Beatrice **fled**—that is, made flee from his eyes every **speck** <term>quisquilia: a Latin term meaning a small bit of waste or chaff; here used for an ocular obstruction</term> (that is, every blurring and impurity). With the ray of her eyes, she shines more than a thousand miles away. He was, therefore, like one who **wakes** (that is, awakes) at a sharp and vehement light because the **visual spirit** (that is, the visual power which is naturally in the eyes) [runs] to the splendor that goes...

<summary>In this passage, Dante completes his examination on Charity, explaining to Saint John that his love for God is rooted in both philosophical reason (Aristotle) and divine revelation (Moses and the Gospels). He describes God as the supreme "Gardener" of the universe and explains how his sight is restored by Beatrice's radiant gaze after the heavenly host sings the "Sanctus."</summary>

to the splendor that passes from veil to veil.
And the sleeper recoils from what he sees

<image-desc>Decorative blue initial E</image-desc> While he recovers his lost sight and it is made better, Adam, the first man, came to where he was with two apostles. But he did not notice him until after he had regained his sight. And so he says: *Wherefore I saw me*, that is, I saw better than before, which means earlier. And so, in a stupor, I asked about the fourth light, which was the soul of Adam. And my Lady—that is, Beatrice—said to me: the first soul ever created by the first virtue—that is, God—gazes with love upon its creator within those rays: that is, within that fourth light that you see. **LIKE** the branch: the meaning is this. I, wondering while—that is, during the time that—Beatrice said the words already mentioned, acted like the branch: that is, the leafy branch which, struck by the wind, bows its tip as it passes; and then, the wind having ceased, it rises and returns straight as it was before by the natural power that keeps it upright. The meaning is that while Beatrice spoke to me, out of the wonder that it was the soul of Adam, I bowed like a rod bows in the wind. Afterward, the desire I had to speak to him raised me up again.

<image-desc>Decorative red initial E</image-desc> And I began: "O Dante," in this form, turning the speech to Adam. *O fruit that was produced mature*. Because other men are born imperfect, both in size and in many powers of the soul. But Adam was formed from the earth at the age of thirty years, in a perfect state and with perfect senses. *O ancient father*: who were the first; and every bride is a daughter to you because she is descended from you, and *daughter-in-law* <note>original: "nuro"</note>: that is, daughter-in-law because she is married to someone who is descended from you. **SOMETIMES** an animal: like an animal covered by its skin demonstrates by its *stirring*—that is, by its movement—the affection of its soul; so Adam, through the trembling of the light which covered him, showed the desire he had to speak to the poet. **THEN IT BREATHED**: He shows that Adam knows the author's wish without him saying it, because he sees it in God, who makes himself a *reflection* <note>original: "pareglo"</note>: that is, a receptacle of the faith of all things. But nothing makes itself a reflection of Him, because God sees and contains all things in Himself. But not vice versa, because no one can see God perfectly, and He is contained by no one. Nor without cause does he have Adam call him by name: because being the first father of men, it is fitting for him to show that he knows all his good children. And that the superior calls the inferior by name signifies familiarity and human mercy. Then he shows what Dante wants to know: what he has seen in God. And first he wants to know how much time has passed since God placed him in the exalted garden: that is, in the paradise of delights <note>the Earthly Paradise, or Eden</note>, where you arrived when she—that is, Holy Theology <note>represented by Beatrice</note>—disposed you, that is, prepared you and made you capable of such a high ladder to the celestial paradise. For once a man has come to the purgative virtues, he can pass to contemplation through the virtues of a soul already purified.
**AND HOW MUCH DELIGHT TO MY EYES**: and you want to know how long my delight lasted in the Earthly Paradise. And the true cause of the wrath that God took against man, which was great, both in respect to God, who is the greatest of all things, and in respect to the human generation.

<image-desc>Decorative blue initial R</image-desc> He answers the questions asked. And as to the first: that it was not the tasting of the wood—that is, of the fruit of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil—that was the cause of the exile of the human race.
