<meta>This page continues Adam’s response to Dante’s unspoken questions. Adam is explaining the true nature of his sin, the length of his life, the history of language, and the brief duration of his stay in the Garden of Eden.</meta>

# CANTO XXVII
<note>Though the header indicates Canto XXVII, this text contains the concluding verses and commentary of Canto XXVI.</note>

[The tasting of the tree] was not in itself the cause of so much exile,
but only the **passing beyond the mark.** <note>Adam clarifies that his sin was not gluttony—the act of eating the fruit—but the act of disobedience in overstepping the boundary set by God.</note>
In that place from which your Lady [Beatrice] sent Virgil,
for **four thousand three hundred and two circuits**
of the sun did I long for this assembly;
And I saw him [the sun] return to all the lights
of his path **nine hundred and thirty**
times while I was upon the earth.
The language I spoke was entirely extinct
before the people of **Nimrod** <note>The biblical figure associated with the building of the Tower of Babel.</note>
turned their attention to the unfinishable task;
For no product of human reason
was ever lasting, because human preference
renews itself, following the influence of the heavens.
It is a natural work that man should speak;
but whether in this way or that, nature leaves
to your own choice, according to what pleases you.

Before I descended to the anguish of Hell,
the Supreme Good was called **I** <note>The original manuscript likely intended "I," the first letter of "IHVH" or a symbol of unity, though the transcription shows "un" (one).</note> on earth,
the source of the joy that swathes me;
And later He was called **Eli**; and this is fitting,
for the usage of mortals is like a leaf
on a branch, which goes away while another comes.
On the mountain that rises highest from the waves,
I lived with a pure, and then a fallen life,
from the first hour to that which follows
the sixth hour, as the sun changes its quadrant.

<column-break/>

**But the passing of the mark.** God commanded Adam that he should not touch the apple of the aforementioned tree, as a creature created with **free will**, so that through obedience he might acquire eternal life. And he should have had not only the grace and mercy of God, but also His justice, and thus be abundant in all virtues and feel all the goodness of God's virtues. But he was not obedient; rather, he overstepped the mark given to him. 

And thus he has responded to the part that asked about the cause of the great wrath. Now he responds to the question of how long it was since God placed you there. **In that place from which your Lady sent Virgil:** that is, in **Limbo**, where Beatrice sent Virgil, I stayed for **four thousand three hundred and two volumes of the sun**, that is, four thousand three hundred and two years, since every revolution of the sun is one year. **And I saw him:** that same sun return to all the lights of its path nine hundred and thirty times through the **zodiac**, which is the way through which it continuously passes, which has twelve signs and each has many stars. Therefore he said that he was on earth, that is, he lived nine hundred and thirty years. 

**THE LANGUAGE I spoke:** the meaning is that the language he and those descended from him used faded away before Nimrod began the **Tower of Babel**, which was an "unfinishable" work, meaning it could not be completed. And in that work was born the division of language, so that there were many and diverse tongues. Mention was made of Nimrod and the confusion of various languages in the first canticle <note>referring to the *Inferno*</note>. And it is not without reason that language changed, because no effect produced by human reason was ever durable, following the heavens. The meaning is: since men change their purpose according to various influences of the heavens which renew our pleasures, they also change and vary things and arts. 

And here we must understand that in all brute animals there is no other motion than the natural one. But in man there is both the **natural** and the **rational**. The natural does not change. Therefore, the brutes, who being deprived of reason are guided by nature, have their works immutable. Thus, they never change their food nor their way of seeking it. One lion is no different from another, nor horse from horse, in producing offspring, in feeding them, and in other things pertaining to the preservation of life. All swallows feed in the same way. But man is not drawn by natural instinct more than he wills. Rather, he is the master of his operations. From which it follows that not all speak in one way, nor do they build or dress in one way. From all these things we conclude that human speech is a natural work. Because nature, having given man reason, it was necessary that she give him speech to express rational concepts. But that we speak this way or that—that is, more in one language than in another—is not a natural work, but proceeds from our reason and will; and nature leaves this to us according to what **pleases us**, that is, what we like.

He had said that speech in man is a natural thing. But using one language more than another comes from custom, which changes. Wherefore **Horace** <note>The Roman poet Horace in *Ars Poetica*</note> says: *Many words shall be reborn which have now fallen, and those now in honor shall fall, if usage wills it.* <note>original: "Multa renascentur quae iam recidere [cecidere]: Cadentque quae nunc sunt in honore uocabula si uolet usus."</note> And he proves this by demonstrating that before he descended to the infernal anguish, God was called **I**. And it was fitting that the name should change, because just as on a branch the leaves change—for every year they fall and are reborn—so the usage of mortals continually changes. 

**ON the mountain:** he responds to the fourth question, which was how long he stayed in the **Earthly Paradise**, which the poet imagines to be in the other hemisphere on a mountain that is the highest, rising out of the sea as we showed above. **WITH A LIFE PURE AND fallen:** understand "pure life" before the sin. **AND FALLEN:** when after sinning he knew himself to be naked and was ashamed. **AS THE SOLE CHANGES ITS QUADRANT:** the sun-dial, which is called a **quadrant**, contains six hours in its first quarter. Then follows the seventh. <note>Adam explains he was only in Eden for about seven hours.</note>

<summary>Adam explains that his sin was disobedience rather than gluttony and provides a chronological timeline of his life and time in Limbo. He also discusses the evolution of language as a product of human reason and reveals that his time in the Earthly Paradise lasted only a few hours.</summary>

# PARADISE CANTO XXVII OF THE THIRD CANTICLE BY DANTE

"To the Father, to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit,"
all of Paradise began, "Glory!"
so that the sweet song inebriated me.
What I heard seemed to me a smile
of the universe; for my intoxication
entered through both my hearing and my sight.
O joy! O ineffable gladness!
O life entire of love and of peace!
O wealth secure, without longing!
Before my eyes the four torches <note>The "four torches" are the spirits of St. Peter, St. James, St. John, and Adam.</note>
stood glowing, and the one that came first <note>St. Peter.</note>
began to make itself more vivid.
And it became such in its appearance
as Jupiter would become if he and Mars
were birds and exchanged their feathers. <note>A poetic way of saying the white/silver light of Jupiter turned into the fiery red of Mars.</note>

<column-break/>

Our poet had in the previously written chapters introduced three apostles who examined him on the three theological virtues <note>Faith, Hope, and Charity.</note>. Now, in this twenty-seventh [canto], the Apostle Peter bitterly reproves his successors. Furthermore, he demonstrates how he was snatched from the eighth sphere <note>The Heaven of the Fixed Stars.</note> to the First Mover <note>The *Primum Mobile*, the outermost physical sphere of the universe.</note>. He first places Peter's invective against the prelates <note>High-ranking church officials.</note>. Then he describes the ascension of the entire triumphant army to the Empyrean heaven and the reflection of faith back to earth. In the third part, he places his entry with Beatrice into the ninth sphere. In the fourth, he places a most vehement exclamation against the blind greed for earthly things. But returning to the beginning, the author narrates that after the resolution of the previously written doubts, all the blessed sang: *Glory to the Father and to the Son and to the Holy Spirit* <note>original: "Gloria patri & filio & spiritui sancto"</note>. This was so sweet that the song inebriated him—that is, he fell into ecstasy. And it seemed to him that this was the joy of the universe and of every creature. He cannot help but let out an exclamation amidst such great joy, calling this beatitude "joy" and "the smile of the universe," because here were gathered all the effects of all the spheres and all the planets; and "ineffable gladness," meaning unspeakable. In contrast to the joy of our world, which is brief and mixed with bitterness, the celestial life is entire in love and peace. "Entire" because nothing is lacking to it. "O wealth secure, without longing": two things without which no wealth is perfect—first, that it be without longing, meaning that nothing more is desired; and second, that it be secure, meaning without any fear of losing it or it diminishing.

---

**BEFORE** my eyes: having finished the exclamation, he returns to his narration and shows that he still had before his eyes the four [lights]: the three apostles and Adam. But that light which had come first—namely, Peter—began to become more alive and glowing. And he was such as Jupiter would be if he took on the color of Mars. He compares Peter to Jupiter according to Jupiter’s influence, because he was the best shepherd and teacher and a most just administrator. And he gives him the color of Mars for two reasons: first, because having been a martyr for Christ, he reasonably takes the color of that planet in which he placed the martyrs of Christ. Secondly, wishing to reprove his successors, it was appropriate that he take on the vehemence, ardor, and just anger of reproof, which comes from Mars.

---

The Providence which there assigns
turn and office in the blessed choir
had imposed silence on every side,
When I heard: "If I change my color,
do not marvel; for as I speak,
you shall see all of these change color too.
He who usurps my place on earth,
my place, my place, which is vacant
in the presence of the Son of God,
Has made of my cemetery a sewer
of blood and stench, whereby the pervert <note>Lucifer/Satan.</note>
who fell from up here is appeased down there."

<column-break/>

He demonstrates that Divine Providence, which extends from the highest to the smallest things, distributes within the divine choir. **TURN**—that is, vicissitude—and **OFFICE**, because it commits to each person their specific duty, exchanging them in turn. It had imposed silence on the singing, and then Peter began with these words: "Do not marvel if I change color"—that is, change my color from my silver to the fiery red of Mars. "For when I change color, all these others will do the same." We explained the allegory of this above. But one might marvel how Peter takes on the fiery color of Mars, which is to be kindled with anger, since in the blessed soul no perturbation <note>Emotional distress or agitation.</note> can fall. The poet does not wish to show anger, but that vehemence of severity which is a part of justice, which among mortals is rarely without just indignation and anger. **HE WHO**: he who is the Pope, who usurps—that is, unjustly holds—the papacy in my place. And note that he said "my place" three times to show extreme indignation through such repetition; or truly he used the number three to show that this office was granted to Peter—that is, to the priestly order—by the triune and true God. **WHICH IS VACANT IN THE PRESENCE OF THE SON OF GOD**: He does not say absolutely that it is vacant, for it would follow

---

that he was not the true and legitimate Pope, and consequently, nothing he did would be valid. But it is "vacant in the sight of the Son of God" because he has perverted his office. And consequently, Christ rejects him as an apostate. It is not vacant among men, because his decree is valid. But as for God, he does not hold such a rank by right, but usurps it. **HAS MADE A SEWER OF MY CEMETERY**: "Sewer" <term>cloaca: a drain or pipe for waste</term> signifies a ditch that receives stenches, filth, and corruptions. "Cemetery," which in Greek signifies a "sleeping place," is the place where dead bodies are laid. Therefore, he means that the place which was the receptacle of holy martyrs full of every virtue and other goods, now receives simoniacs <note>Those who buy or sell sacred things or church offices.</note>, the greedy, robbers, and the lustful, who are well likened to blood (cruelty) and stench. And just as God was appeased by the virtues of holy men, so his adversary and the adversary of human nature—who, having rebelled against God, fell from up here in heaven to down there on earth—appeases his evil desire with the vices of these men.

---

With that color which, by the opposing sun,
paints a cloud at evening or morning,
I then saw the whole heaven suffused.
And as a virtuous lady, who remains
sure of herself, yet at another's fault,
becomes timid just by listening,

<column-break/>

The air becomes red either in the evening or in the morning because the sun is opposite the clouds. And with such a color all the spirits became inflamed with love of justice against the captive shepherds <note>The corrupt leaders of the Church.</note>. **AND AS A LADY**: thus Beatrice, pure and chaste, blushed for the fault of such shepherds, just as a chaste woman would blush who, although she is sure of herself because she knows she is without any fault, nevertheless feels shame and becomes timid hearing some dishonest thing said of another. And he adds that all the lights in heaven darkened out of the abomination of the crimes of the shepherds, in such a way that he believes that not otherwise...

<summary>St. Peter undergoes a dramatic color change from silver to red, signaling his righteous indignation as he delivers a scathing rebuke of the corruption in the Papal office, specifically targeting Pope Boniface VIII. The commentary explains the theological distinction between human anger and divine justice while describing the celestial reaction to earthly sin.</summary>

# CANTO XXVII

->Thus Beatrice changed her appearance,<-
and such an eclipse, I believe, occurred in heaven
when the supreme power suffered <note>A reference to the darkness that covered the earth during the Crucifixion of Christ.</note>.
Then his words proceeded,
with a voice so transformed from itself
that his appearance had not changed more:
"The bride of Christ was not nourished
on my blood, and that of Linus and Cletus,
to be used for the acquisition of gold;
But for the acquisition of this joyous life,
Pius and Sixtus and Callistus and Urban
shed their blood after much weeping <note>St. Peter lists early Popes who were martyred, contrasting their sacrifice with the greed of the Popes in Dante’s time.</note>.
It was not our intention that on the right hand
of our successors part of the Christian people
should sit, and part on the other [left] side,
Nor that the keys that were granted to me
should become a sign on a banner
to fight against those who are baptized <note>Peter is outraged that the papal coat of arms is used as a war flag against fellow Christians.</note>,
Nor that I should be the figure on a seal
for sold and lying privileges,
for which I often blush and flash with fire.
In the guise of shepherds, ravenous wolves
are seen from up here in all the pastures;
O defense of God, why do you lie idle?
Of our blood, Caorsins and Gascons <note>References to Pope John XXII (from Cahors) and Pope Clement V (from Gascony), whom Dante viewed as predatory.</note>
prepare to drink; O good beginning,
to what a vile end must you fall!
But the high Providence that with Scipio
defended in Rome the glory of the world,
will soon bring help, as I conceive.
And you, son, who because of your mortal weight
will return down below, open your mouth
and do not hide what I do not hide."
Just as our air flakes downward
with frozen vapors when the horn
of the Goat of heaven [Capricorn] touches the sun,
So I saw the ether adorned,
flaking upward with triumphant vapors
that had made their sojourn here with us.
My sight followed their appearances,
and followed until the distance, because of its greatness,
took from it the passing further ahead.
Whereupon the lady, who saw me released
from looking upward, said to me: "Cast down
your eyes and look how you have turned."
From the time when I had first looked down,
I saw myself moved through the whole arc
that the first climate makes from the middle to the end,
So that I saw, beyond Cadiz, the mad track
of Ulysses, and on this side near the shore...

<column-break/>

*he eclipsed:* that is, the sun darkened at the death of Christ. After this, Peter continued speaking with a voice as transformed from his usual voice as his color was transformed. The literal meaning is clear, and the allegorical meaning is easily drawn from it.

It is without fail a wicked abuse to use the bride of Christ—that is, the Apostolic See <term>Apostolic See: the office and jurisdiction of the Pope</term>—for greed, which was nourished by Peter, Linus, and Cletus with such generosity that they were content to shed their blood to increase it. Therefore, what pain, what punishment, what death is fitting for that pontiff who uses the Apostolic dignity for the acquisition of riches? Linus, the first pontiff after Peter, sat for eleven years; Cletus, the second pontiff, sat for twelve years. Pius was the ninth pontiff and sat for twelve years. Sixtus was the sixth pontiff and reigned ten years. Callistus was the fifteenth pontiff in the times of Emperor Marcus Aurelius Antoninus; he sat for five years. Urban, the sixteenth pontiff, succeeded him and sat for nine years. It was not our intention that part of the Christian people should sit at the right hand and part at the left of our successors: that is, that some should be in their favor and some in disgrace. Nor that the keys granted to me should be a sign on a banner <term>gonfalone: a heraldic banner or flag</term> that fought against the baptized. It is certainly a horrific and monstrous thing that the shepherd should become a wolf. Nor was it our intention that I should be a figure for seals. On papal and leaden bulls, on one side of the lead are the heads of Saint Peter and Saint Paul. It was not, therefore, my intention that for a price and through simony <note>The sin of buying or selling sacred things or church offices.</note>, privileges should be made of unjust and false things, stamped with our sign; and certainly, if we consider on one hand the reverence for that seal, and on the other what is contained in many bulls, one might say: <note>original: "Jungentur iam griphes equis."</note> "Now let griffins be joined with horses" <note>A Latin expression meaning that the natural order has been completely overturned by something impossible or monstrous.</note>.

These verses are easily understood: Caorsins and Gascons. Note in this place the poet names two most rapacious French popes: John XXII and Clement IV <note>The commentator likely means Clement V, who was Gascon.</note>. John was from Cahors, a city always abundant with usurers; and Clement was from Gascony; and Gascons are considered most rapacious by other Frenchmen. Hence the proverb that the English have the tail of a serpent, and the Gascons have the tail of a wolf. We treated this Urban above, that is, in the first canticle. **BUT THE HIGH [PROVIDENCE]** prays: that divine providence, which as it once defended the Roman Empire from the barbarian and cruel Hannibal through Scipio, so through an excellent prince—who was prophesied in the first canticle—may defend the Church from these barbarian pontiffs. After Peter's words, the whole triumph of the blessed rose up, ascending to the ninth sphere; and they were so many and so dense, and swift, and so white that they appeared in their upward ascent like snow in the air when it falls downward in flakes; snow is generated from humid and cold vapors. And because of this he said: "as if of frozen vapors." "When the horn of the Goat of heaven touches the sun." This refers to when the sun is in Capricorn. We have treated the nature and location of this sign extensively elsewhere. **MY SIGHT** followed their appearances: that is, my seeing followed their presence. In short, I followed them as far as my sight could carry; until the medium, that is, the interval that was between them and me, took the further passing from my sight because of the great distance. And then Beatrice, who saw me released, that is, free from waiting and gazing upward—since I could no longer see them—said to me: "**CAST DOWN** your eyes and look how you have turned."

Since the poet, no longer able to see the blessed spirits because they were too distant, no longer looked upward, but by command of Beatrice began to look toward the earth, he saw that from the hour he had first looked down—which was when he said in the twenty-second canto that he returned with his face through all the spheres—up to this hour he had moved as much as the Gemini move in six hours; because he had rotated a quarter of the circle that the zodiac makes around the earth. Hence he says: "I saw myself moved through the whole arc that the first climate [makes] toward the tropic..."

<summary>In this passage, Saint Peter delivers a scathing condemnation of the corruption and greed of modern Popes, contrasting them with the martyrs of the early Church. Following this, the souls of the blessed ascend like "upward-falling snow," and Dante gazes back down at the Earth from the celestial heights.</summary>
<keywords>St. Peter, Papal corruption, Simony, Linus and Cletus, Caorsins and Gascons, Scipio Africanus, Celestial ascent, Capricorn, Zodiac, Ulysses' voyage</keywords>

# PARADISO

in which Europa became a sweet burden <note>Dante refers to the myth of Jupiter, who transformed into a bull to carry the princess Europa across the sea.</note>
And more of the site of this little flowerbed <note>The "aiuola" or "little flowerbed" is Dante’s term for the inhabited Earth, emphasizing its smallness when viewed from the heavens.</note>
would have been revealed to me, but the sun preceded
beneath my feet, a sign and more away.
The enamored mind, which plays the lady
with my Lady always, burned more than ever
to bring my eyes back to her.
And if nature or art ever made bait
to capture the eyes so as to possess the mind,
in human flesh or in its paintings,
All of them joined together would seem as nothing
compared to the divine pleasure that shone upon me
when I turned to her smiling face.

...the cold northern zone and that which is under the torrid zone. But the sun, which was beneath his feet because it is in the fourth heaven and Dante was in the eighth, preceded him: that is, it went ahead by one sign and more; for while the poet was in Gemini, the sun was ahead of all of Taurus and part of Aries. THE MIND enamored: my mind enamored with Beatrice. Which "plays the lady" with Beatrice: which follows Beatrice as its lady, burned more than ever to return his eyes to her. And certainly, although <term>Sacred Doctrine</term> <note>Beatrice represents divine revelation or sacred theology in the allegory.</note> is always worthy of being loved, nonetheless it deserves much greater love when it treats of supreme things. And if nature or art: many bodies, whether natural or made by art such as sculptures and paintings, capture the eyes of others and draw them in with pleasure because of their beauty, so that such pleasure enters through the eyes into the soul. Whence Petrarch says: *Weep, eyes, accompany the heart; for through your failing, death is sustained.* And elsewhere: *Love found me completely disarmed, and the way open through the eyes to the heart.* And the Latin elegist says: *If you do not know, the eyes are the leaders in love.* <note>original: "Si nescis oculi sunt in amore duces"</note> And Solomon: *A woman captures the precious soul of a man.* <note>original: "Mulier ante uiri pretiosam anima capit"</note> Therefore, if all the beautiful things which feed the eyes and through them capture the mind were gathered together, they would seem as nothing in comparison to the divine pleasure that shone—that is, radiated—to my eyes when I turned to the smiling face of Beatrice.

And the power that her gaze bestowed on me
from the lovely nest of Leda <note>The "nest of Leda" refers to the constellation Gemini, as Leda was the mother of the twins Castor and Pollux.</note> drew me out
and into the swiftest heaven impelled me.
Its parts, most living and exalted,
are so uniform that I cannot say
which place Beatrice chose for me.
But she, who saw my desire,
began, smiling with such joy
that God seemed to rejoice in her face:
"The nature of motion, which quiets
the center and moves all the rest around it,
begins here as if from its starting point.
And this heaven has no other 'where'
than the Divine Mind, in which is kindled
the love that turns it and the power it rains down."

...all the others. And for this reason, Aristotle says that nature is the principle of motion and of rest. It begins here—that is, from this ninth sphere—as if from its goal: that is, from its beginning. AND This heaven has no other where: that is, it has no other place where it stops but the Divine Mind. For its motion revolves around the Divine Mind. Whence Boethius says: *With a profound mind he circles and turns the heavens in a similar image.* <note>original: "Menteque profunda circuit & simili couertit imagine celum"</note> In which—that is, in which Divine Mind—the love that turns it "is kindled," meaning the intelligence that turns it; for this intelligence has love for its creator and, burning with love for Him, returns to Him. And the power of this heaven does "rain down"—that is, it infuses into the other lower spheres. Therefore, this power is kindled in the Divine Mind and is infused into the <term>Primum Mobile</term> <note>The "First Moved" heaven, the swiftest and outermost physical sphere of the universe in medieval cosmology.</note> equally through all its parts, and from there it is infused into the other spheres and celestial bodies; and thus one infuses into the other; and thus it is diversified, even though it is one power and comes from one principle.

Light and love enclose it in one circle,
just as it does the others; and that precinct
He who girds it alone understands.

<column-break/>

...summer from its middle where the beginning of Cancer is and the end of Gemini, until the end which is in the west. He had departed from the meridian <term>colure</term> <note>A great circle on the celestial sphere passing through the poles.</note> which ends Gemini and turned toward the other colure. For this reason, he could not see all the habitable earth as he could when he was at the meridian. Therefore, he saw less than half: that is, from further this side of Jerusalem to beyond the west and beyond the other quarter. For at the middle of the two quarters, one sees everything from east to west. And then the other colure, which is a quarter, sees the middle of the whole. Therefore, he sees beyond Gades—that is, beyond the western hemisphere. Gades [Cadiz] is in the far reaches of Spain, about a hundred miles from Calpe, one of the Pillars of Hercules, near the mouth of the Guadalquivir. Near the shore where Asia ends is the region of Sidon, which is in Syria, where the "mad flight" of Ulysses occurred, of which we spoke in the twenty-sixth canto of the first canticle [*Inferno*]. In that region, Europa, riding Jove who had changed into a bull, was a "sweet burden" to Jove who loved her. And of this myth we have told elsewhere in full. Then he adds that he would have seen the whole site of this "little flowerbed"—that is, this little wing and plaza. And he calls it a "little flowerbed" to show how small the habitable earth is. For the whole fourth part is not inhabited because it is uninhabitable...

He ascends from the eighth sphere to the ninth, which is the Primum Mobile, by the power that Beatrice's gaze "bestowed" on him—that is, gave to him with love. The meaning is that the power which came from Beatrice’s gaze was so great that it drew him from the "nest of Leda"—that is, from the sign of Gemini—and "impelled" him—that is, pushed him—into the swiftest heaven, which is the ninth sphere. And he calls Gemini the "nest of Leda" because Jove, loving Leda, turned himself into a swan and knew her, and from that union were born two eggs; from one came Pollux and Helen, and from the other Castor and Clytemnestra. Pollux and Castor were called <term>Dioscuri</term>, that is, sons of Jove, and were transformed in the heavens into the sign of Gemini. "Its parts, most living and exalted": that is, he calls this heaven "most living" for its supreme velocity and greatest power, and "exalted" because it is the sovereign heaven. They are so "uniform"—meaning they look the same way and are not distinguished by different stars as they are in the eighth sphere—and all the powers of all the lower spheres are united in this ninth. And because it is uniform, "I cannot say" in which place Beatrice chose for me. But she, seeing that I desired to know it, began to speak with such joy that God seemed to rejoice in her face. Then he presents the words of Beatrice, which were these: "The nature of motion": that is, the "natured nature" that God has placed in this sphere, which nature "quiets the center"—that is, the Earth, which is its center and is immobile—while all the other spheres, both of the elements and of the heavens, are mobile. Therefore, nature quiets the center and moves...

He demonstrates that this ninth heaven is enclosed by the Empyrean heaven, which is nothing but light and love, just as this ninth heaven encloses the others. Therefore, this light and love are infused into the ninth sphere, which is the Primum Mobile, and that encloses it. And we conclude that the elements and the things composed of them are moved by the planets; and the planets by the eighth sphere; and the eighth by the ninth.

<summary>Dante looks back at the Earth from the sign of Gemini, noting its insignificance before being propelled by Beatrice's gaze into the Primum Mobile, the swiftest and outermost physical heaven. The commentary explains the astronomical positions of the sun and the mythological origins of the constellation Gemini.</summary>

<meta>The previous page concludes Dante’s view of the Earth from the Heaven of the Fixed Stars. # CANTO XXVII

> Its motion is not marked by any other,
> but the others are measured by this one,
> just as ten is by its half and by its fifth;
> And how time holds in such a frame
> its roots and in the others its leaves,
> can now be manifest to you.

¶ **AND HOW IT HOLDS IN SUCH A FRAME.** The meaning is that if the motion of the ninth sphere <note>The Primum Mobile, or "First Moved" sphere, which according to Ptolemaic astronomy surrounds all other spheres.</note> is the measure of all other motions, as has been said, it is the root of time: since time is nothing other than the measure of motion in changeable things. And if the root is in this sphere, its parts extend through the motions of the other heavens. Because this aforementioned "First Mobile" makes its revolution in twenty-four hours: wherefore it is the root of days and the root of months and years, which are distinguished by the sun.

> O Greed, who drowns mortals
> so deep beneath you that no one has the power
> to pull their eyes out from your waves!
> The will blossoms well in men,
> but the continuous rain turns
> the true plums into blighted fruit. <note>original: "bozachioni," referring to fruit that rots or swells with water on the tree before ripening.</note>

> Faith and innocence are found
> only in little children; then each
> flees before the cheeks are covered with down.

> One, while still stammering, observes the fasts,
> who later, with his tongue loosened, devours
> whatever food in whatever moon. <note>This refers to a child who follows Lenten fasts but grows up to ignore all religious dietary laws.</note>

> And another, while stammering, loves and listens to
> his mother, who, with his speech complete,
> then desires to see her buried.

> So the white skin turns black
> at the first sight of the beautiful daughter
> of him who brings morning and leaves evening.

...having known her, he desires her death. **SO THE WHITE SKIN TURNS BLACK**: the meaning is that the white skin, which is in the tender face, turns black. **AT THE FIRST SIGHT**: almost in the first age of life. **OF THE BEAUTIFUL DAUGHTER**: that is, of human nature, which is the daughter of the sun: because the sun is the universal father of all living things; **who brings morning**: that is, produces light when he rises. **AND leaves evening**: when he goes to the west. It turns then from white to black: because from pure it becomes infected with vices. And allegorically we understand the sun as God himself, of whom the human soul is the daughter.

> You, so that you do not wonder at this,
> know that on earth there is no one to govern;
> wherefore the human family goes astray.
> But before January is entirely "un-wintered" <note>Dante refers to the error in the Julian calendar. Because the year was slightly too long, January was slowly shifting toward spring. Dante predicts a great change will happen before the shift is complete.</note>
> by that hundredth part neglected down there,
> these supernal circles shall roar so loudly

> That the Fortune so long awaited
> shall turn the sterns to where the prows are,
> so that the fleet shall run straight;
> And true fruit shall come after the flower.

...and out of the winter. **These supernal circles**: these heavens; **Shall roar**. The heaven makes no different sound at one time than another. But by "roaring" he wishes to denote a cruel influence. Because roaring belongs to lions just as lowing belongs to oxen. Therefore, such an influence will come from the stars that Fortune will turn the sterns to where the prows are. That is, the order established by divine providence will turn the government back to the good way, which at present goes poorly. **SO THAT THE FLEET SHALL RUN STRAIGHT**: that is, all the ships that are in this company will take a good journey. *Classe* <term>fleet</term> in Latin signifies not one ship, but the entire armada. **AND TRUE FRUIT SHALL COME AFTER THE FLOWER**: that is, such government will produce true fruit, which shall be eternal salvation.

<column-break/>

...and the ninth from God, either with a medium or without a medium. But the Empyrean heaven <note>The highest, non-physical heaven where God dwells.</note> is immediate from God and immobile. Wherefore the poet's sentence is true that only He who girds that precinct—that is, God, who girds the Empyrean heaven—understands that Empyrean heaven and no other. God alone encompasses the Empyrean, and that the ninth, and that the eighth, and successively the higher always encompasses the lower. **ITS motion IS NOT MARKED BY ANY OTHER**: that is, the motion of the First Mobile is not marked by any other motion. But the other heavens are measured by this one. Because this First Mobile makes a revolution in twenty-four hours: which hours are taken from the variation of its parts... [the text repeats the explanation of the ninth sphere as the root of time].

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'O' decorated with floral and leaf patterns.</image-desc>
**O**ptimal exclamation by which Peter damns the insatiable greed for earthly things, which sinks and submerges human minds in the sea of affection for momentary and falling goods, so that they cannot raise their eyes to this admirable region of heaven arranged with ineffable order. Therefore with just indignation he cries: **O Greed**: that is, unrestrained desire. **Who drowns**: that is, submerges in its sea so deep that no man has the power to pull his eyes out from its waves: that is, from its perturbations and affections. **The will blossoms well in men**: there is born in men a will for the highest good and it blossoms in them; but afterwards, just as continuous rain prevents plums from producing true fruit—but they are turned into *bonachi* <note>original: "bozachioni," a variant spelling</note> which are full of water and worms—so the rain of greed for earthly things corrupts the sincere will. Similar to that of **Ovid**: <note>original Latin: "Cepisti melius quam desinis ultima primis. Cedunt dissimiles hic uir & ille senex."</note> *You began better than you end; the last things fall short of the first. These differ: the man here and the old man there.* And **Isaiah**: <note>original Latin: "Expectaui ut faceret uuas fecit autem labruscas."</note> *I expected it to yield grapes, but it yielded wild grapes.* And that it is so, we see that men in childhood have honest innocence, shame, and purity. Then comes a more adult age and changes these virtues into vices, in such a way that before the cheeks—that is, the jowls—are covered with a beard, they have become vicious. And one, **stammering**: that is, in early childhood when the child cannot yet utter every word. For "to stammer" <note>original: "balbutire"</note> means to lisp. **Fasts**, and then having become an adult, **devours**: properly "to devour" <note>original: "diuorare"</note> in Latin means to swallow without chewing. Which is the act of a glutton and a greedy man at any time. And another in the same age loves and reveres his mother, who then with his speech complete—that is, as an adult...

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'C' decorated with floral patterns.</image-desc>
**H**e concludes that no one should wonder if men, who are the family governed by the shepherd, have gone astray: that is, gone out of the right path and away from reason, because there is no one to govern, since the shepherds have become wolves. **BUT BEFORE JANUARY ENTIRELY UN-WINTERS**: that is, before January, which is currently in the winter, beginning from the entry of the sun into Capricorn and ending when it exits Pisces; **by the hundredth part that down there**—that is, on the earth—**is neglected**: that is, despised. We showed in the first *cantica* <note>Referring to Dante's *Inferno* or the first part of Landino's commentary.</note> that the solar course contains three hundred sixty-five days and a fourth part of a day, and beyond that fourth, a hundredth part. But the fourth is accounted for every four years because in the leap year the year is made of three hundred sixty-six days. But the hundredth is not taken into account; and because of this, the entry of the sun into Capricorn, which gives the beginning to winter, has moved nearly fifteen days closer to January, and continuing thus in the process of time, it will happen to January and then to February, and then January will remain in the autumn...

# PARADISO CANTO XXVIII OF THE THIRD CANTICLE BY DANTE.

**A**fter she who imparadises my mind
had revealed the truth against the present life
of miserable mortals,
As one sees in a mirror the flame
of a torch <note>original: "doppiero," a large wax candle or torch with multiple wicks.</note> that is lit behind him,
before he has it in sight or in thought,
And turns around to see if the glass
tells him the truth, and sees that it accords
with it as a note does with its meter;
So my memory recalls
that I did, looking into the beautiful eyes
from which Love made the cord to capture me.

> We cannot look at the sun in its physical body, but we look at it in every other place. So also we cannot discern God in His principal being. But we can behold Him in theological scripture: as through a certain reflection.

And as I turned, and my own eyes
were touched by what appears in that volume
whenever one gazes well into its circling,
I saw a point that radiated light
so sharp that the sight it blazes upon
must close because of the intense sharpness;
And whatever star seems smallest from here
would seem a moon if placed with it,
as star is placed with star.
Perhaps as close as the halo appears
to the light that paints it,
when the vapor that carries it is thickest,
Distant around the point, a fiery circle <note>original: "cerchio digne," likely from "igneo" or "degne." The commentary treats it as "cerchi di fuoco."</note>
whirled so rapidly it would have outdone
that motion which most quickly girds the world.
And this was encircled by another,
and that by the third, the third then by the fourth,
the fourth by the fifth, and then the fifth by the sixth.
Above followed the seventh, so spread out
in width that the messenger of Juno <note>Iris, the personification of the rainbow.</note>
entire would be too narrow to contain it.
So distant the ninth; and each
moved more slowly according to how it was
more distant in number from the one;
And that one had the clearest flame
which was less distant from the pure spark;
I believe because it is more "en-truthed" <note>original: "sinuera," a Dantean invention meaning to enter into the truth.</note> by it.

<column-break/>

**B**ecause in the previous chapter the author described the appropriate zone or sphere, it is fitting that in this twenty-eighth he describes the orders of the angels who are in it. Beatrice therefore shows him the point of Divinity and the hierarchies of the angels that are around it. Then she explains certain doubts to him so that they remain clear. *After she who*: since she who [imparadises] my mind revealed and manifested the truth against the present life full of vices of miserable mortals. *AS IN a mirror*. The meaning is that the author, looking into Beatrice's eyes—*FROM WHICH*: that is, from which Love made the cord to capture me—saw the most burning light of the divinity which he could not see because he had his back to it, as happens when one has a lighted torch behind them and, not seeing it, gazes into a mirror in front of them and sees the image of the torch and the flame; and turning around, he sees that the mirror has represented the truth to him. And not without reason does the poet report that he saw the ray of deity in Beatrice's eyes, i.e., in the speculation of theology. For as Gregory writes: as—

<gloss>d</gloss> He describes the true thing whose image he had already seen in Beatrice's eyes. Therefore, as he was turned back to where the light was—whose image he had seen in Beatrice's eyes—and his eyes were the place where that "volume" appeared: that is, from what is seen in that divinity which is immense. *WHENEVER*: i.e., every time one gazes well: that is, looks diligently. For if one does not look very well, one does not see. Having turned, he then saw a point which radiated: that is, raying out it cast a light so sharp and penetrating that it is necessary to close the face, i.e., the eyes. Nor is it a marvel, for if the physical eye cannot suffer the light of the sun, how much more the eye of the intellect will not be able to suffer the light of the eternal sun who made this sensible sun and the moon. He describes God, therefore, in the form and figure of a fixed and immobile point. And further he describes the orders of angels in the form of fiery circles: that is, blazing circles.

<gloss>h</gloss> The author had already described the first principle under the appearance of an immobile and fixed point; now he describes the orders of the angels in the form of circles of fire. And beginning from the first, he says that it turns most swiftly, as close to the point as that circle which is generated around the moon from thick and dense vapors is to the moon. It is certainly an arduous and difficult matter, and established above human possibility to express fully the angelic nature. But we, from many things written first by Dionysius the Areopagite <note>A 5th-6th century theologian whose "Celestial Hierarchy" established the standard Medieval ranking of angels.</note>, then by many other theologians, will run through a few with brevity. And first we will say that although "angel" is the proper name of the incorporeal spirits of the last and ninth choir: nonetheless all other spirits of whatever choir and hierarchy are called angels by a universal name. An angel, according to Damascene and Albert and all other theologians, is an incorporeal intellectual substance. Always mobile, free of will, serving God, immortal not by nature but by grace. And Dionysius in the book *On the Divine Names* <note>original: "de diuinis nominibus"</note> writes that the angel is an image of God, a manifestation of hidden light, a pure mirror, most splendid and immaculate, which receives—if it is permitted to say—all the beauty of the well-formed deiformity, and purely declares within itself, as far as possible, the hidden goodness. The angel differs from our soul in four things. Because the soul is unifiable to the body, and not the angel. The soul is rational; the angel is intellectual: because the soul acquires by investigating and conceding, and the angel by beholding. The angel does not suffer except in respect to superiors; and the soul in respect to inferiors: because it can be changed by sensible things. The soul can turn from good to evil and from evil to good. But the angel cannot: because it stays firm in that to which it once turned. The angels are all similar insofar as they are immortal, invisible, indissoluble, simple, separate in persons, and incommunicable to other nature; but they are dissimilar in the gift of grace and of nature. Dionysius adds that in every created spiritual nature, the essence is one thing; another is—

The commentary explains the nature of angels using the theology of Dionysius the Areopagite, distinguishing between the human soul and angelic intellect.</summary>

<meta>The previous page introduced Dante’s vision of the Divine Point and the nine concentric circles of fire. This page provides a detailed theological commentary on those circles, identifying them as the nine orders of the celestial hierarchy and explaining their names, functions, and numbers according to various Church authorities.</meta>

<header>CANTO XXVIII</header>

Power and action are distinct. The celestial hierarchies are three, and each has three orders. The superior hierarchy contains the Cherubim, Seraphim, and Thrones. The Cherubim contemplate the goodness of God; the Seraphim, His power; and the Thrones, His equity. Furthermore, in the first, God loves as charity; in the second, He knows as truth; and in the third, He sits as equity. It is the nature of the Seraphim to burn with the love of God, and to draw others toward that fire and order them within God. These are joined immediately with God and see God most purely. They do not turn toward anything outside of God. In the Cherubim, the ray of divine light shines primarily and continuously because they are more closely joined to divine truth. These move humanity toward divine knowledge; they shine more than the others and pass down the fullness of the light they receive to the lower orders. Thrones are so named because the Lord sits upon them and through them determines His judgments; these also transmit truth to the lower orders.

The second hierarchy consists of Dominations, Principalities, and Powers. The Dominations govern the offices of the angels. The Principalities are the presiding leaders over the various peoples. The Powers restrain the power of the demons. In the Dominations, God rules as majesty; in the Principalities, He rules as a principality; in the Powers, He defends as salvation.

The third hierarchy contains Virtues, Archangels, and Angels. To the first belongs the performance of miracles. To the second, the announcement of the greatest things. To the third, the care of human protection. In the first, God works as power. In the second, He reveals as light. In the third, He sends as an inspirer. This is the order established by Gregory <note>Gregory the Great (c. 540–604), a Pope and theologian who wrote extensively on the angelic orders.</note> and Bernard <note>Bernard of Clairvaux (1090–1153), a Cistercian abbot and mystic.</note>. But Dionysius <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, the pseudonymous author of "The Celestial Hierarchy," the foundational text for medieval angelology.</note> places the Virtues in the second order of the second hierarchy, and the Principalities in the first of the third. In the angels, there is the dignity of creation, the grace of confirmation, the love of the creator, and the vision of the divinity. They possess subtlety of essence, sharpness of intelligence, and speed of motion. The greater ones are without pride, and the lower ones obey without resentment, and all are without any [conflict]. Those who are more excellent in nature precede the others in grace and glory. The higher ones participate in every truth of the lower ones, but not vice versa. 

Since it is a subject worthy of knowledge, we shall demonstrate, according to the doctrine of Dionysius, why there are nine choirs or orders of angels. Although, as Damascene <note>John of Damascus (c. 675–749), a Syrian monk and scholar.</note> writes, only God who created them knows the specific nature and limit of angelic substances. Taking this principle, we say that love is the supreme of all things; it is that which first receives influences from God and unites the mind with God. Therefore, this is the most excellent path, without which nothing is of use. And because a soul void of love is ill-willed, and true wisdom does not enter an ill-willed soul, it follows that through love we may receive the true doctrine—the kind that never swells with pride. After love and the mind, knowledge <note>original: "scientia"</note> proceeds—and from no other source—and then must follow a just and perfect judgment from every side. Thus, we already see three choirs: Seraphim in love, Cherubim in knowledge, and Thrones in judgment.

After judgment follows empire [command], so that what ought to be done is done. After empire follows a certain virtue [power] which acts as the executor of that command. Such execution is not enough unless a certain resistance and power is added against the adversarial power [demons] which always strives to hinder good commands. Therefore, in this second hierarchy are Dominations, Virtues, and Powers. We have now seen six reasons. 

Now follows the doctrine which must be given to those who do not know. This is of two kinds: for the ignorant are taught and mastered either with words or with deeds. Doctrine through deeds is more effective than spoken or inspired words; and the doctrine of deeds is especially valid when they are unusual, rare, and supernatural. Thus, the highest of the operations for those who do not know is that of miracles [Principalities]; the second is the operation of contemplation and the grasping of the simplest things pertaining to our salvation [Archangels]; the third is the doctrine of active, civil, and minor things [Angels]. These are the nine operations which follow the order already shown. 

The first, because of their loving power, are called Seraphim, which in Hebrew <note>original: "hebbreo"</note> signifies "burning," "incendiary," or "warming." This is the power of fire, and spiritual fire is nothing other than love. This is the fire that God came to put upon the earth, which, entering the bones of the prophets, taught them. The second, from their act of absolute and perfect knowing, are named Cherubim, which in Hebrew means "fullness of knowledge" or "infusion of wisdom." The third are Thrones, named from their judicial power in the act of judging, because *thronos* in Greek <note>original: "thronos i greco"</note> signifies an exalted and elevated seat where the judge sits. These three acts are much more spiritual than the others. Regarding this last one, Paul writes:

> He who judges all things and is judged by no one. <note>original Latin: "Qui oia iudicat & a nemine iudicatur." From 1 Corinthians 2:15.</note>

The fourth order is the Dominations, because they have the act of commanding, which is most suitable to dominion. The fifth order is the Virtues, because they intrepidly and without any reduction carry out what God has commanded. The sixth are the Powers, because they resist the powers of the demons; these second three orders of angels are less still and more active than the first three. The seventh are the Principalities, so named from a powerful and principal way of teaching by working supernatural and miraculous things for the instruction of the ignorant. The eighth are the Archangels, because they announce more principal and greater things; they are named so because *arche* in Greek <note>original: "arche in greco"</note> signifies "principality" or "leadership." Since this order is in the middle between Principalities and Angels, it carries the names of both the higher and the lower; for being reformed by the Principalities, it reforms and gives life to the Angels in simple unity. 

The order among the blessed spirits is that the superior infuses doctrine into the inferior, as a teacher to a disciple. But such doctrine is clearer in the first than in the second, and in the second than in the third, and so on successively down to the first [the lowest]. For this reason, the prophet Zechariah, when the Lord wished to free the people from the Babylonian captivity, saw one of these angels appearing from God, who then taught the inferior, and finally the inferior taught the prophets. The angelic order [Angels], because it is the last and closest to us, announces future things to us. The Archangels announce them to us by means of the Angels, and perhaps sometimes directly, just as the Archangel Gabriel announced to Mary, though in the Gospel he is always called "Angel." Whether this annunciation was made through an angel or by him directly is not to be judged without very great consideration. The lower orders begin from the power of the higher ones, but always decreasing step by step. Thus, observed in proportion, they participate in the wisdom that is in the Cherubim.

Many seek the vast number of the angels; it is manifest to many that in three hierarchies there are nine choirs, but how many angels there are is not manifest. The prophet Daniel, according to the Seventy Interpreters [the Septuagint], says: "A thousand thousands and ten thousand ten thousands," where he places thousands and thousands as two very great numbers. And because they circulate back into themselves—namely, "ten thousand thousands" and "myriads of myriads" (ten thousand ten thousands)—he silently shows they are infinite, because a circle starting and ending in itself seems to demonstrate an infinite number. Furthermore, another translation has a different number: "thousands of thousands and ten thousand times a hundred thousand." But Albertus Magnus <note>Albert the Great (c. 1200–1280), a Dominican friar and philosopher.</note> in his *Compendium of Theology* writes that each choir has within it 6,666 legions, and each legion has as many angels as there are legions: that is, 6,666. Therefore, each choir contains 44,435,556 angels. This number multiplied by the nine choirs makes a sum of 399,920,004 angels. If you subtract the number of one choir from this—because that many fell <note>Referring to the fall of Lucifer and his followers, often estimated by theologians as one-tenth or one-third of the heavenly host; this commentator uses the size of one full choir.</note>—there will remain in the nine choirs 355,484,448 angels. And let this suffice for now concerning the angels, for [concerning] the evil angels and how very briefly...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the celestial hierarchies from the previous page, specifically focusing on the transition from the general description of the nine orders of angels to the specific astronomical and theological paradox Dante faces regarding the speed and size of the heavenly spheres.</meta>

<columns>2</columns>
<header>PARADISO</header>

...duration was from their creation, and many other things we treated in the last canto of the first canticle <note>original: "prima cantica"; refers to the *Inferno*</note>.

My lady, who saw me in care
and held in suspense, said: "From that point
depends the heavens and all of nature.
Gaze upon that circle that is most joined to it,
and know that its movement is so fast
because of the burning love by which it is pierced."
And I said to her: "If the world were placed
with the order that I see in those wheels,
what is proposed to me would have satisfied me.
But in the sensible world <term>sensible world: the physical universe that can be perceived by the senses</term>, one can
see the revolutions are so much more divine
as they are more remote from the center.
Wherefore, if my desire is to find its end
in this wondrous and angelic temple,
which has only love and light for its boundary,
I must yet hear how the example
and the exemplar do not go in one way;
for by myself, I contemplate this in vain."
"If your fingers are not sufficient for such a knot,"
she replied, "it is no wonder;
so much has it become hardened by not being tried!"
Thus my lady spoke, then said: "Take
what I shall tell you, if you wish to be satisfied,
and sharpen your wits around it.
The physical circles are wide or narrow
according to the more or less of the virtue <note>virtue: here meaning spiritual power or influence</note>
that spreads through all their parts.
Greater goodness wishes to bring greater health;
greater health requires a greater body,
if it has its parts equally perfected.
Therefore, this one that sweeps all the rest
of the universe along with it, corresponds
to the circle that loves most and knows most.
Therefore, if you wrap your measure
around the virtue, and not the appearance
of the substances that appear round to you,
you will see a marvelous correspondence
of the greater to the more, and the smaller to the less,
of each heaven to its own intelligence <term>intelligence: the specific angelic order that moves and guides a particular celestial sphere</term>."

As the hemisphere of the air remains
splendid and serene when Boreas <note>Boreas: the North Wind</note> blows
from that cheek which is more mild,
Because he purges and dissolves the grime
that previously clouded it, so that the sky smiles
with the beauties of its every district <note>original: "parroffia", literally "parish"</note>,
So did I, after my lady provided me
with her clear response,
and the truth was seen like a star in the sky.

<column-break/>

Beatrice sees the author [Dante] held in suspense and anxious because he does not understand. Therefore, she shows him how from the Point already mentioned: all of created nature depends—that is, the entire universe. But then a doubt arises for Dante: how can it be that here, the circles closer to the Point move faster around that which is further away? For in the sensible world—that is, in the physical world and the elements—one sees the opposite: because the more the revolutions (that is, the rotations) they make are remote from the center, the more they are divine and inflamed by divine love and, consequently, faster. For the ninth sphere <note>the Primum Mobile</note> moves faster than the eighth. Therefore, he concludes that if his desire is to find its end—that is, if it is to find peace in this temple where the angels dwell, which is not enclosed in any sphere but has for its boundary love and light (that is, the Empyrean heaven made of love and light, which being without end, also makes the temple without end)—it is necessary for him to understand why the example (the inferior and sensible world, such as the elements and the heavens, which is made in the likeness of the intelligible) and the exemplar (the intelligible world) <note>exemplar: the divine blueprint or spiritual reality</note> do not function in the same way, as has been said.

**IF YOUR FINGERS**: Beatrice responds that it is no wonder if your fingers are not sufficient to untie such a knot, because it has become harder by being less "tried" <note>untangled or tested</note>. And by this, she means that the doubts and difficulties in any science, the less one tries to understand them, the more difficult they become. Then she resolves the doubt in this form, demonstrating that just as the circles of the intelligible world have more virtue, so the first sphere of the sensible world, because it is closer to God, has more virtue. And in this way, the nine orders of angels proportionally correspond to the nine heavens, always the most worthy to the most worthy. The "physical circles" (the heavens that have bodies) are wide (large and great) and narrow (small and tight) according to whether they have more or less virtue. For the ninth sphere is as much greater than that of the moon as it has more virtue. And greater goodness wishes to produce greater health (that is, that which has more virtue produces a more soul-saving effect). And greater effect occupies a greater body (contains within itself greater virtue) if its parts are equally complete and perfect. Therefore, this ninth sphere, which is greater than all the others and sweeps all the other spheres with it (for in turning in twenty-four hours, it pulls all the other spheres with it in the same time), as the most perfect sphere, corresponds to the first circle of the angels, who are most perfect in love and knowledge.

**THEREFORE**: This demonstrates that the similarity should be understood according to virtue, and not according to physical size. Wherefore she says: if you "wrap your measure" (that is, if you apply your measurement of the angelic circles, which are incorporeal, to their virtue and not to their appearance) (that is, to their physical quantity) (that is, to their intensive virtue which is spiritual and does not appear, rather than the extensive virtue which is physical and appears), you will see a marvelous correspondence and agreement of the greater to the more (the larger body has more virtue) and of the smaller body to the less virtue of each heaven—of which there are nine—to its intelligence (to its circle of angels). Therefore, the ninth sphere responds to the Seraphim; the eighth to the Cherubim; Saturn to the Thrones; Jupiter to the Dominations; Mars to the Virtues; the Sun to the Powers; Venus to the Principalities; Mercury to the Archangels; and the Moon to the Angels.

THE comparison is that just as the air remains serene when the north wind blows: so the truth remained clear in me after Beatrice’s response. And it says when Boreas (the north wind) blows from "that cheek" (that part), because the winds are painted with mouths.

**WHENCE** it is more mild (toward the west, from which comes the northwest wind). Although that wind is northern, nevertheless, because it comes from that part of the north that is closer to the west, it inclines toward the nature of Zephyrus <note>the West Wind</note>. "Grime" <note>original: "roffia"</note> is the density of humid and condensed vapors.

**THE SKY SMILES**: It remains serene. This is a shared metaphor; for just as we say a person's face is serene when they smile, so we say the sky "smiles" when it is clear.

**OF ITS EVERY DISTRICT**: Of every part of it. And he said "parroffia" in place of "parrocchia" <note>parish</note>. A parish in a city is that group of people who are under the same church.

<header>CANTO XXVIII</header>

And after her words were stayed,
not otherwise does iron throw out sparks
when it boils, than the circles sparked.

Their fire was followed by every spark;
and they were so many, that their number
more than the doubling of the chess mimics. <note>original: "che gli scacchi similla"; refers to the legend where a grain of wheat is doubled on each of the 64 squares of a chessboard, resulting in a staggering number.</note>

I heard "Hosanna" sung from choir to choir
to the fixed point that holds them to the *Ubi* <term>Ubi: Latin for "Where," here meaning their specific place or station in the presence of God</term>
and will always hold them, in which they always were.

And she, who perceived the doubtful thoughts
within my mind, said: "The first circles
have shown to you the Seraphim and Cherubim.

Thus swiftly they follow their bonds <note>original: "vimi"; literally 'withies' or willow ties, used here metaphorically for divine attraction</note>
to liken themselves to the point as much as they can;
and they can as much as they are sublime in seeing.

Those other loves that go around them
are called Thrones of the divine aspect,
because they terminated the first triad. <note>original: "ternaro"</note>

And you should know that all have delight
insofar as their vision sinks deep
into the Truth in which every intellect finds rest.

Hence it can be seen how the state of being
blessed is founded on the act that sees,
not on that which loves, which follows after.

And of the seeing, merit is the measure,
which grace gives birth to and good will;
thus from rank to rank the process goes.

The other triad that thus blossoms
in this eternal springtime
that the nocturnal Aries does not despoil, <note>Dante uses the constellation Aries to describe the seasons; "nocturnal Aries" refers to the autumn, when Aries is visible at night and leaves fall.</note>

Here perpetually sings "Hosanna"
with three melodies that sound in three
orders of joy by which it is tripled. <note>original: "sinterna"; a word created by Dante meaning to branch into three.</note>

In that hierarchy are the three goddesses: <note>The poet uses "goddesses" metaphorically for the angelic orders.</note>
first Dominations, and then Virtues;
the third order is of Powers.

Then in the two penultimate dances <note>original: "tripudi"</note>
Principalities and Archangels circle;
the last is all of angelic play.

These orders all gaze upward in wonder,
and downward they prevail, so that toward God
all are drawn, and all do draw.

And Dionysius <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, a 5th-century theologian believed in the Middle Ages to be a convert of St. Paul.</note> with such great desire
set himself to contemplate these orders
that he named and distinguished them as I do.

But Gregory later departed from him; <note>St. Gregory the Great, who proposed a slightly different order of the angels.</note>
wherefore, as soon as he opened his eyes
in this heaven, he laughed at himself.

And if a mortal on earth proffered
such a hidden truth, I would not have you marvel.

<column-break/>

Once the words were finished, the nine circles of angels sparked like boiling iron. And the sparks followed the fire. The meaning is that just as many sparks come out of boiling iron, so from those circles appeared many angels flying like sparks. But although they flew, they did not leave their order. But all followed their fire, <note>original: "i. l ordine delloro circulo"</note> that is, the order of their circle. And they were so many that the number multiplies into more thousands than the doubling of the chess. There are sixty-four places on the chessboard: which if they were doubled—so that in the first there was one, in the second two, in the third four, in the fourth eight, in the fifth sixteen, and so on—it would make a vast sum. These angels were singing "Hosanna," <note>original: "i. laudauan iddio"</note> that is, they praised God from choir to choir successively responding to one another: and they are ordered toward the fixed point, <note>original: "i. adio"</note> that is, to God. Which God holds them to the *Ubi*, <note>original: "i. alluogo proprio & fermo"</note> that is, to their own firm place, because they were confirmed in grace. And he will always hold them: in which they always were, meaning from the time he created them.

Beatrice shows Dante the orders of the angels to remove the doubts she saw him having in his mind. So that he may understand that the blessedness of the saints is caused by vision. Because seeing and understanding is the cause of beatitude. Since on this alone the mind nourishes itself: and this is its nectar and its ambrosia. SERAPHIM and Cherubim: of whom we have already spoken. AND THEIR BONDS: their ties and links which are God: because the desire to know makes it so they do not distance themselves from Him: and they can know Him all the more, the more they are near to Him, and the more they raise themselves to see Him. THRONES OF the divine aspect: because as was said, God through those orders His judgments. SINKS INTO the truth, <note>original: "i. indio che e somma uerita"</note> that is, into God who is the supreme truth. HENCE IT can be seen: from this it is understood that the state of being blessed consists in seeing, <note>original: "i. nel conoscere"</note> that is, in knowing, and not in loving. Because love proceeds from knowledge, and not knowledge from love. And the creature loves the Creator all the more as he knows Him more and receives merit and grace according to the measure of knowing. Therefore, from rank to rank, the more he sees, the more he has of grace and good will, <note>original: "i. di uolere qllo che uole iddio"</note> that is, of wanting what God wants. The second triad follows: which is Dominations, Virtues, and Powers: which germinates and puts forth leaves in beatitude; which he calls eternal springtime, which the nocturnal Aries, <note>original: "i. lautúno"</note> that is, the autumn, does not despoil. Our springtime puts forth leaves: but autumn then makes the leaves fall. But that of heaven stays always green. And he used "nocturnal Aries" for autumn, because autumn begins when the sun enters Libra; and then Libra in our hemisphere is not seen by day. Wherefore it follows that Aries, the opposite sign, will not be seen except by night. HERE IT winters, <note>original: "i. canta del continuo"</note> that is, it sings continually "Hosanna" with three melodies. Because from three choirs proceed three songs: and he places here the three orders of the second hierarchy. AFTERWARDS two penultimate dances: the two penultimate dances <note>original: "balli"</note> which are of the third hierarchy: Principalities and Archangels: and the last which are Angels. These new orders all gaze in wonder from above. Because the inferior always has the superior in admiration as a greater thing. Therefore the Seraphim have God in admiration, whom they watch as the supreme good: and by that they are drawn, as by the supreme good: and they draw the Cherubim. And these have God in admiration, and after Him the Seraphim: and they draw the Thrones: and the Thrones the Dominations: and so the others until the last order. And this one draws the other creatures. And always the superior has more power than the inferior. Wherefore it follows that all gaze in wonder from above: and all prevail from below: and each draws the inferior toward God, and is drawn by the superior.

He shows that Dionysius was the one who had the number, order, distinctions, and names of these angels, which he put in his book *On Divine Names* and *On the Celestial Hierarchy*. Afterward, Gregory disagreed with him. Because Dionysius placed the Principalities in the third hierarchy and in the first order: and Gregory placed them in the second order of the second hierarchy, where Dionysius placed the Virtues. But after death, coming to this heaven, he saw his error and laughed at himself. And Beatrice concludes: that the poet should not marvel that a mortal truth, <note>original: "i. uerita dhuomo mortale"</note> that is, the truth of a mortal man, proffered and manifested such a secret. Because he who had seen it up here in the heavens...
