### CANTO XXIX OF THE THIRD CANTICLE BY DANTE

**W**hen both the children of Latona <note>original: "figli di Latona"; referring to the twins Apollo (the Sun) and Diana (the Moon).</note>
covered by the Ram <note>The zodiac sign Aries</note> and by the Scales <note>The zodiac sign Libra</note>
make of the horizon together a zone,
as long as from the point that the zenith balances
until one and the other from that belt,
changing the hemisphere, is unloosed,
so long, with her face painted with a smile,
Beatrice kept silent, looking
fixedly at the point that had overcome me.
Then she began: "I speak, and do not ask
what you wish to hear, for I have seen it
where every *where* and every *when* is focused.
Not to gain any good for Himself,
which cannot be, but so that His splendor
could, in its shining, say: *I subsist*.
In His eternity, beyond time,
beyond every other limit, as it pleased Him,
Eternal Love unfolded into new loves.
Nor did He lie as if sluggish before then,
for neither 'before' nor 'after' proceeded
the discourse of God upon these waters."

<column-break/>

**B**ecause the poet has already treated the distinction of the nine orders of the angels, it remains in this twenty-ninth chapter to treat the *where* and *when*, and in what manner the angelic nature was created: what an angel is, and their number. He treats, therefore, two questions. Then he describes the fall of the wicked angels and touches upon some doubts concerning the intellect, memory, and will of angels. In the third place, he reproves those who postpone or pervert the Scripture. And finally, he returns to the principal matter of the angels. At the start of the chapter, he shows that Beatrice, turned toward God, stood silent long enough for her to see the poet’s doubts; but she stood thus for only a brief time. And he declares this brevity and moment through an excellent comparison, saying that it happens when the sun is in Aries and the moon is in Libra (the opposite sign), such that the sun is in the east and the moon is in the west; suddenly they change places because one rises to our hemisphere and the other descends. WHEN both the children of Latona: that is, the sun and the moon, as we have already said; covered, one by the Ram and the other by the Scales, they make a zone: i.e., the belt of the horizon, because both are on the horizon. But one is to rise and the other to descend. Therefore, when the moon and the sun are in this form, Beatrice was silent for as long as the moon and the sun stay in the belt of the hemisphere where it is pointed: i.e., where it is marked, as in a point, every *where*: i.e., every place, and every *when*: i.e., every time: just as in the First Cause. From which places and times proceed, although God is not a place because He is immense, nor time because He is eternal. Nevertheless, both proceed from Him.

**B**eatrice, looking into the Divinity, recognized three doubts that were in Dante. First, if time precedes the creation of the universe. Second, where such a creation was made. Third, how it was made, whether all at once or successively. Therefore, she first shows that the cause that moved God to create the universe was not to increase His own beatitude, because nothing can be added to the most perfect. Thus, it was not to have for Himself 

---

any gain of good, because that cannot be. But so that His splendor—that is, His goodness—might show itself in creatures and could subsist in created nature and appear in it, and be the substantial form of every creature because every created thing is good. Hence in Genesis: *And God saw all the things that He had made, and they were very good.* <note>original: "Et uidit deus cuncta que fecerat: & erant ualde bona"</note> And Boethius: *For truly no external causes impelled You to fashion the work of flowing matter; rather, it was the innate form of the highest good, lacking all envy.* <note>original: "Quia uero nō externe pepulerūt fingere cause: materie fluitatis opus Veru insita summi forma boni liuore cares"</note> God wished to communicate His being and goodness with the things created by Him, and to demonstrate His perfection He distinguished them into three levels. In the first are the purely intellectual creatures, which are the angels placed above the heavens. In the second, purely corporal things, placed around the center of the world in the depths, which are the elements. In the third, corporal and intellectual joined together, which are humans and the heavens. And in each level there are greater, middle, and lesser. In the intellectual ones, we have said there are three hierarchies: greater, middle, and lesser; and in each is a greater, middle, and lesser order. In the purely corporal ones, the greater order is the brutes; the middle are the vegetative: that is, trees and plants; and the lesser are the elements, which have only being. The creatures joined of soul and body are in two levels, because some have incorruptible bodies, and these are the movers who move the heavens. Some are corruptible, and these are humans. And in the heavens, some are not organized: i.e., they do not have distinct members, but all their parts are similar in nature and being; and therefore the whole shines, and has in every part similar power. And this is the ninth sphere. But the eighth heaven does not shine entirely and has different powers in its parts because it has diverse stars. Some have only one organ: i.e., a star: and in that is its power, as we see in the seven planets. Furthermore, there is diversity in the movements. For the ninth sphere has only one motion above its poles. Some have three motions: one above the poles of the ninth sphere; another above their own poles; the third by an ascent and descent of ten degrees. And this is the eighth heaven. For all these movements, it is necessary to arrive at a first unmoved mover, which is God, who causes such motions. But humans do not have diversity of levels, because they are similar and receive their being from a similar form. But they have degrees according to their traits, which proceed from their complexions, and according to their will, which proceeds from free will. For some are suited to speculation and science, such as those who have soft flesh. But those of hard flesh are suited to sensitive delights and pass into bestiality. Some are in the middle of these two levels, and those reasonably bring it into action: and these are suited to civil life. But the more one resists sensuality with reason, the greater the praise. ETERNAL LOVE UNFOLDED into new loves. God, who is eternal love, made Himself known and manifest in new loves: i.e., in the creatures, which, being newly created, all have an inclination, though varied, toward God. For God said: *Let there be light, and there was light* <note>original: "Fiat lux & facta e lux"</note>; and by this light he means the angelic nature, and then He made the other creatures. And this was in His eternity: i.e., in His being. NOR BEFORE: many might doubt whether God created the world 6,679 years ago, because before such creation and after it, He remained idle. To this Beatrice responds that divine love did not lie lazy or idle. BEFORE: i.e., before this creation: because the discourse of God—i.e., the process of creation—UPON these waters: i.e., upon these creatures. Hence it says in Genesis: *And the Spirit of the Lord was moving over the waters.* <note>original: "Et spūs dñi ferebat sup aq̃s"</note> Nor did it proceed before or after: i.e., before the creation nor after. And not without reason did she say "it did not proceed," because "proceeding" denotes time. And similarly "before" and "after" denote time. For time is defined as the measure of motion according to before and after, as Aristotle says in the *Physics*. And similarly...

devoutly quieted and the time. And then He did not lie in idleness: because, as it is said, God made all things not in time, but in eternity. Wherefore, from eternity <note>original: "ab etherno"</note> He held the exemplary world <note>The "exemplary world" refers to the Platonic idea that a perfect blueprint of the universe exists in the Divine Mind before its physical manifestation.</note> in His mind, which He later produced in act; and then He made time. Inasmuch as time is the measure of motion, and motion cannot exist without a body, time could not exist before the body was created.

**Form and matter, joined and pure,**
**came into being that had no defect,**
**like three arrows from a three-stringed bow;**
**And as in glass, in amber, or in crystal,**
**a ray shines so that from its coming**

**So the three-formed effect from its Lord**

**Now you know where and when these loves**
**were created, and how, so that already**
**the three fires are quenched in your desire.**
**Nor would one reach twenty in counting**

**constrained by all the weights of the world.**
**Those whom you see here were more modest**
**to recognize themselves as coming from the goodness**
**which had made them ready for such great understanding;**
**Therefore their visions were exalted**
**with illuminating grace and with their merit,**
**so that they have a firm and full will.**

above the heavens. And these are the three hierarchies of angels. And those in which there is simple potential and not act—because they are matter alone—held the lowest and bottom part around the center as the most ignoble. And those which are joined by act and potential, God bound in the middle with such a bond <note>original: "vime"</note>—that is, with such a tie—that it is never untied <note>original: "disuima"</note>—meaning it does not dissolve—because the heavens will always remain joined with their movers. And our souls, although they depart from the body, nonetheless they shall be reunited, and shall remain joined for eternity.

<column-break/>

[d] It shows that creation was made in an instant without the succession of time. It places, therefore, the three levels of creatures already mentioned: namely, those that are incorporeal and pure form, which are above the heavens; and those that are simple matter and are around the center; and those joined of matter and form. These three levels issued by the will of God into a being that had no defect—that is, into a perfect being—because they were created from nothing by God. And they issued into being just as three arrows issue at once from a bow that has three strings. And as the solar ray penetrates through glass or amber or crystal at once without succession—and in that same instant it is at the end as it is at the beginning—and thus there is no interval from its coming—that is, from the beginning—to its being complete—that is, to its perfection; so the three-formed effect of which the ray has already been mentioned from its Lord—that is, the Lord who is God—is all in its being—that is, in its perfection. Therefore, just as the rays of the sun penetrate through those three bodies at one time without succession of time or place, so the rays of the eternal sun, God, penetrate into these three levels of creatures without distinction in their beginning <note>original: "exordire"</note>—that is, in an instant, so that the beginning cannot be distinguished from the perfection. And finally, it concludes by saying that God co-created order—that is, in the same instant He produced the creatures, or let us say substances, and the order of these three levels: which was that those in which there is pure act—that is, only action, because they are simple intellect—held the summit—that is, the top of the world—and were

[S] Jerome writes to Titus: "The number of six thousand years of our time is not yet completed. And how much time must we think has flowed since the origin of the ages? In which angels, thrones, and dominions and the other orders served God." <note>original Latin: "Sex millium nondum nostri temporis completur annorum numerus. Et quanta tempora a seculorum origine fluxisse arbitrandum est. In quibus angeli: throni. & dnationes t ceterique ordines deo deseruerunt."</note> Because of this, Jerome maintains that a long order of centuries existed from the creation of the angels to the creation of the rest of the world. But Thomas Aquinas excuses him by saying that he speaks according to the opinion of the Greeks. But he and all the other doctors maintain that in one instant the angels and the other creatures were created. And therefore he says that this truth is written in many places by the writers of the Holy Spirit. Furthermore, it can be demonstrated by natural reason, which is formed thus: The angels were created by God to move the heavens. And if they had been created many centuries before the heavens, the angelic nature would have been in vain, since the movers would have been without perfection, because they would have had nothing to move, the heavens not yet being in existence. **NOW YOU know.** Beatrice concludes that she has already quenched the three fires—that is, she has solved the three doubts for Dante. Whereby she intends where these loves—the three levels of creatures—were created: namely, in the eternity of God; and when it pleased God, outside of any comprehension of time; and how, because it was in an instant. **NOR WOULD one reach counting to twenty.** After she has shown where and when and how the world was made, she shows that suddenly, and with less interval than it would take to count to twenty, a part of the angels rebelled against God; and falling, they changed the subject of the elements. Because with their malice they caused the earth and the air, previously pure, to become infected. The other part of the angels, already confirmed in grace, remained; and they began this art of circling God and contemplating all things in Him, nor do they ever depart from this circling.

[d] Beatrice declares the cause of the ruin of the rebel angels and the confirmation of the good ones. The origin of the fall was, therefore, the pride of Lucifer, whom the poet had seen in the center of the earth, to which, as the lowest place, all heavy things fall. He, most ungrateful for the benefits received from his Creator, and most proud, said: "I will set my throne in the North, and I will be like the Most High." <note>original Latin: "Disponam sedem meam ab aquilone: & ero similis altissimo." A paraphrase of Isaiah 14:13-14.</note> For this reason, both he and those persuaded by him fell. **THOSE whom you see here** around God were modest and not proud to recognize themselves as being from the divine goodness—that is, they knew themselves to be creatures of God, created by Him not for their own merits but by His goodness. This modesty was their merit.

Thus, as he understands more excellently than man, so he has a more excellent will. Memory, likewise, cannot be said to exist in an angel except equivocally <note>original: "equiuoca." <column-break/>

And for this reason, their visions were exalted, illuminated by grace; and it was also their merit that they accepted the illuminating grace and followed it. From this comes cooperating grace: confirming and consuming <note>original: "cooperante: confirmātē: & cōſumātēt." Landino uses the Latin scholastic categories of grace to explain the angels' state of perfection.</note>. And these graces make in them a full and perfect will: because they will exactly what is necessary, and it is firm because it cannot be changed. And finally, he concludes that it is a meritorious thing to receive grace according to the effect—that is, the degree to which the will is open to God. The meaning is that illuminating grace generates in you the will for good. Wherefore, if you do not resist but accept it, you merit. For which thing you can then easily contemplate around this consistory—that is, you can know for yourself for what reason these angels...

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'I' containing a human face in profile.</image-desc>
Beatrice’s intention is to demonstrate that although we say the angel has intellect, memory, and will, it is nevertheless a different thing than ours. But in the schools of philosophers, they are called so equivocally. For in the angel there is neither an "agent intellect" nor a "possible intellect" <note>term: "agent and possible intellect" — Scholastic terms for the parts of the human mind that process sensory data into abstract thoughts. Beatrice argues angels don't need these because they perceive truth directly.</note>, which are in the human soul, in which understanding is sometimes in potential and sometimes in act. Therefore, one cannot speak of "intellect" in the angel except equivocally and by similarity. The angels, as soon as they were made joyful by the blessed face of God—that is, by the vision of God—never turned their face from it: that is, they never ceased their intelligence. Nor is the "face" of the angel anything other than his understanding, nor is God seen otherwise than by understanding. And nothing is hidden from the face of God—that is, from His intelligence. And for this reason, the angels do not have their vision intercepted—that is, their understanding interrupted by any thing. Man, in reasoning, often trips over something new and not well understood, which interrupts his discourse. But the angel, seeing all things in God, nothing can be new to him. And therefore he does not need to remember through "divided concepts." The angel does not understand through "species" <note>term: "species" — In medieval philosophy, these are the mental images or forms of objects used by the mind to understand them.</note> which he abstracts from things, nor by composing and dividing, nor by discourse as man does; but he understands through innate species. Furthermore, there is not in the angel that will which is in man, although each is called "will."

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'R' with floral patterns.</image-desc>
He reproves the modern philosophers and theologians who dream while awake. For just as to one who dreams it seems he sees what is not, so it happens to those who wish to deviate from the ancients. But their error is of two kinds. For some believe their opinions to be the truth, although they are not, and they sin through ignorance. Others realize they do not speak the truth, and nevertheless, to appear more learned than others, they strive to defend the false. And these, because they sin through malice, commit a greater sin, and their shame is greater. Whence he adds: "YOU do not go down one path philosophizing in the world," because through malice you strive to subvert the sciences, because in you there is no true love of knowing the truth. But your every thought is to appear learned. Which, although it is a great error, is nevertheless endured up here in heaven with less disdain than when you Christian theologians set aside the Christian Scripture; and being ashamed to cite Mark, Luke, John, and Matthew, you always insist on Aristotle and Plato. Or indeed, you twist it into various senses alien to the doctors who received it from the Holy Spirit. And you do not weigh how much blood was shed—first by Christ and then by the holy martyrs—to establish this religion, and how much it pleases God when we humbly approach this Christian doctrine without seeking pomp.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'R' with floral patterns.</image-desc>
Beatrice greatly reproves the preachers who, when they ought to explain the Gospel and show therein what is salvation and what is the damnation of man, and exhort to virtue and discourage vice, leave such doctrine aside; and to appear learned they make up useless inventions. As for example: recounting the Gospel story that the sun grew dark during the passion of Christ. This is against nature, since the sun never loses its light. But it is hidden from us when the moon interposes itself between us and it. And this can only happen during a conjunction, which was not the case then. Therefore, the preachers, to appear as astronomers <note>original: "astrologi." In this period, astrology and astronomy were often used interchangeably for the study of the heavens.</note>, recount all these difficulties. And then they solve them, some saying that suddenly the moon moved from its opposition and ran through six signs and joined the ecliptic line. Others say that God willed that the light in the sun should hide itself of its own accord...

<summary>This page explains that angels possess perfect, immediate knowledge of God, rendering human-like memory and reasoning unnecessary. Beatrice then critiques philosophers and preachers for prioritizing their own vanity and "fables" over the true teachings of the Gospel.</summary>

Christ after his resurrection did not say: preach nonsense. But giving them a true foundation, which was the doctrine that the Holy Spirit infused into them, He said to his first assembly <gloss>that is, to the apostles</gloss>: Go and preach the Gospel to every creature. And which sounded so much <gloss>that is, only sounded</gloss> in the cheeks <gloss>that is, in the mouth of Christ</gloss> so that the apostles made of the Gospel a shield and a lance. <gloss>That is, with it, as with a trusty shield, they defended the faith; and with the same, as with a strong lance, they attacked the false religion of the gentiles.</gloss> But at present, having left the way of preaching used by the apostles, they attend to telling jests <gloss>that is, playful words and buffoonery</gloss>. It follows that these people, preaching not out of zeal for God but for vanity—which swells their hood—it happens that in the tip of the hood such a bird nests <note>The "bird" refers to the devil, often depicted with dark wings, waiting to take the souls of those deceived by false preachers.</note>. And he means the devil, who is painted with wings, such that if the common folk who hear the sermon could see him, they would see the "pardon" <gloss>that is, the indulgence</gloss> that the preachers promise them. The meaning is "Through which": by which confidence the common folk have in every preacher, foolishness has grown so much on earth among men that they run to every promise of indulgence they make, even though they have neither privileges nor bulls <note>Official papal documents.</note> that are witnesses of such an indulgence. And from this false promising of indulgences, which they cannot give, Saint Anthony <gloss>that is, the brothers of Saint Anthony</gloss> fattens the pig with the things they get from credulous and simple men. And others who are worse than pigs, such as prostitutes and the like, paying those from whom they receive alms with money without a stamp <note>original: "moneta sanza conio."</note> <gloss>that is, false indulgences that are worth nothing, just as uncoined money is worth nothing</gloss>. But because we have digressed, while Beatrice was showing Dante the angelic nature, it happened they went off the subject to condemn those who do not proceed rightly in not giving true doctrine. Now wanting to return to the subject, she admonishes him to touch his eyes back toward the straight path and return to the first speculation.

Beatrice returns to where she had made her digression; she continues on the angelic nature and demonstrates that it increases in number <gloss>that is, it descends</gloss> in such a number that there was never a man who could express it with words or conceive it with the mind. Wherefore the prophet Daniel in the seventh chapter writes: <note>original: "Mille millia ministrabât ei & decies cêtena millia assistebât ei."</note> "A thousand thousands served him, and ten thousand times a hundred thousand stood before him." <note>Daniel 7:10.</note> Where it is clearly seen that he puts a finite number for an infinite one. But of this we have spoken more extensively. THE FIRST light, which is God himself, which radiates <gloss>that is, shines into and illuminates</gloss> all this angelic nature, is received in as many ways in that nature as there are splendors <gloss>that is, angels</gloss>. For as much is given to each as he can receive. WHEREFORE the sweetness of love <gloss>that is, of God</gloss> which is received, burns and warms <gloss>that is, boils and becomes tepid</gloss>. For He, as I have said, pours Himself out equally, but is not equally received. But each receives the divine vision more or less according to his capacity; and as much as he receives, so much he loves. SEE the height <gloss>that is, the infinite altitude</gloss> and the breadth <gloss>that is, the latitude</gloss>. He concludes the immense magnitude of God and of His goodness, since He has so many angels in whom, as in mirrors, He reflects Himself. REMAINING ONE in Himself as before <gloss>that is, as before He created them</gloss>.

# PARADISO
## CANTO XXX OF THE THIRD CANTICLE BY DANTE

**P**erhaps six thousand miles away from us
The sixth hour burns; and this world already
Inclines its shadow almost to a level plane,
When the mid-heaven, deep above us,
Begins to change such that some stars
Lose their appearance down to this depth;
And as the brightest handmaiden
Of the sun comes further, so the heaven closes
From sight to sight, even to the most beautiful.
Not otherwise the triumph that plays
Forever around the Point that overcame me,
Seeming enclosed by that which it encloses,
Little by little faded from my sight;
Wherefore, seeing nothing and my love
Constrained me to turn my eyes to Beatrice.

<gloss>that is, when the sun is in the east, the night—which is not level with the earth—diminishes and becomes nothing. And then the mid-hemisphere above us begins to change because of the coming dawn, so that some stars lose their appearance <note>original: "perdel parere"</note>, meaning they are no longer seen, even down to this depth <note>original: "questo fondo"</note>, meaning down here to the earth. AND as the brightest handmaiden comes: The poets imagine that Aurora is the handmaiden of the sun, and that she goes before him to prepare his way. Therefore, the further the brightness of the dawn proceeds, the more the heaven "closes." Not because the heaven literally closes or covers the stars, but it appears to close because the light of the sun, which is greater, obscures the light of the stars, which is lesser. And for this reason, it seems that the heaven closes and hides its stars. From part to part until the most beautiful: because the largest stars are always those that disappear last. Not otherwise the triumph of the angels, which plays and circles forever around the Point which is God—who overcame me <note>original: "mi uinse"</note>, meaning he overcame my vision. Inasmuch as he seemed enclosed and encircled by the hierarchies, yet He encloses them within Himself in His power, wisdom, and goodness. My sight distinguished <note>original: "distinse"</note>, meaning it divided and separated my vision little by little as I moved further away. Wherefore, seeing nothing more, the love I bore for Beatrice made me turn my eyes to her. And deservedly, having to treat of divinity, it was necessary that I should return to Beatrice <note>original: "i.e. alle scripture"</note>, that is, to the Scriptures, in which alone we have as much knowledge as human nature can receive.</gloss>

If all that has been said of her until now
Were all concluded in a single praise,
It would be little to serve this turn.
The beauty I saw transcends the world,
Not only beyond us, but truly I believe
That only her Maker enjoys it all.
By this pass, I concede myself defeated
More than ever by any point of his theme
Was comic or tragic poet overcome.
For as the sun does to the sight that trembles most,
So the remembrance of the sweet smile
Cuts my mind off from my very self.

<gloss>because the mind cannot endure it.</gloss>

From the first day that I saw her face
In this life, until this vision,
My song has not been cut off from following her;
But now it is necessary that my pursuit desist
From following her beauty further in poetry,
As must every artist at his limit.

<column-break/>

**B**ecause the poet's vision becomes finer every hour, and he becomes more capable of perceiving incorporeal things, and having already traversed the angelic nature, the order requires that in this thirtieth chapter he express the essence and the effect of the Empyrean heaven. And similarly, he demonstrates how he was transformed, and being transformed, was able to see the supreme glory of Paradise. He describes first, therefore, the appearance of the angels and the supreme excellence of Beatrice's beauty. Afterward, he demonstrates his ascent to the Empyrean heaven. In the third place, he describes it in its own form. And finally, he places a vacant seat. But returning to the beginning and to the verses already written: just as in all the spheres he willed that souls should represent themselves (who are blessed according to the influence of that heaven), so in this one the angels have not represented themselves. And now, departing from that sphere, the sight of the angels faded little by little, just as the stars fade for us when the sun arrives in the east and the dawn brightens. But he describes this time of dawn with mathematical reasoning, which manifests itself thus: The globe of the earth, according to them, circles twenty-four thousand miles. And the sun circles it in twenty-four hours. For which reason it happens that the sun in each hour passes one thousand miles of it. Therefore, when the sun is in the east, the "sixth hour"—which is when it is over our heads in mid-heaven—is six thousand miles away. And then this world, that is, this hemisphere, inclines its shadow to a level plane. As if to say the shadow...

<margin>nothing other than the shadow of the earth little by little descends so much that it appears from the deep heaven, that is, the high heaven; that is, that part of the heaven which is in our [hemisphere].</margin>

**T**he poet has demonstrated until now that as much as Beatrice has ascended from heaven to heaven, so much has she always become more beautiful, to denote that the further one rises in the matter of theology, the more beautiful things are found. But when he arrives at the summit of his speculation, where the source of power, wisdom, and goodness is—where the divine essence is described in Trinity and Unity, in divinity and humanity—so great is the beauty thereof that if everything said of her in different places were concluded into one, it would be little to satisfy this turn. And this is because the beauty of Beatrice in this transcends the world <note>original: "trasmoda"</note>, not only beyond us—that is, it does not only exceed the mode and measure of human intellect—but he certainly believes that it exceeds the intellect of the highest angels, in such a way that no creature can comprehend it all, but only God himself. Wherefore he concludes himself to be more defeated by this pass of being able to describe or comprehend with the mind the beauty of theology, than any poet, whether comic or tragic, was ever surpassed and defeated by any part of his theme. And for this reason, the remembering of her smile "diminishes my mind," that is, the power of memory; just as the sun diminishes, through its excessive light, the sight that trembles most...

**F**rom the first day that the poet saw Beatrice until this moment, although she has grown in beauty every day more, nonetheless he has been able with his style to follow her beauties. But now she has become so admirable and so ineffable that it is entirely cut off and severed for him to follow them further. For which reason it is necessary that he desist from narrating, just as it is necessary that every craftsman desist and stop in his art when he reaches as far as he can go. He does not express her beauty, then, because he cannot. But he leaves it to a greater proclamation <note>original: "bando"</note> than that of his trumpet, which leads his difficult material to its conclusion; because he already wishes to ascend to the Empyrean heaven, which is the end...

<summary>Dante describes the approach to the Empyrean as the angelic circles fade like stars at dawn. He confesses that Beatrice’s beauty has now reached a divine height that surpasses human intellect and the limits of his poetic craft.</summary>
<keywords>Empyrean, Beatrice, angelic hierarchy, dawn, mathematical astronomy, limits of art, theology, Dante Alighieri</keywords>

# CANTO XXX

Just as I leave her to a greater herald
than that of my own trumpet, which draws
its arduous matter to an end,
With the gesture and voice of a prompt leader,
she began again: "We have emerged
from the largest body <note>The Primum Mobile, the largest physical sphere of the universe.</note> into the heaven that is pure light:
Intellectual light full of love,
love of true good full of joy,
joy that transcends every sweetness.
Here you shall see both of the militias <note>The two "armies" of God: the angels and the redeemed human souls.</note>
of paradise; and the one <note>The souls of the blessed.</note> in those aspects
that you shall see at the final justice <note>The Last Judgment, when souls will be reunited with their glorified bodies.</note>."

As a sudden flash of lightning that scatters
the visual spirits, so that it deprives
the eye of the action of the strongest objects,
So a living light encircled me
and left me swathed in such a veil
of its radiance that nothing appeared to me.
"Always the love that quiets this heaven
welcomes into itself a greeting such as this,
to make the candle ready for its flame <note>God's love prepares the soul (the candle) to receive the divine light (the flame).</note>."

No sooner had these brief words
reached me than I understood
that I was surmounting my own power;
And I was rekindled with new sight
of such a kind that no light is so pure
that my eyes could not have defended themselves.
And I saw light in the form of a river,
tawny with brightness, between two banks
painted with a wondrous springtime.
From such a stream came living sparks,
and from every side they settled into the flowers,
like rubies that gold encompasses.
Then, as if inebriated by the scents,
they plunged again into the marvelous depths,
and as one entered, another came out.

"The high desire that now inflames and urges you
to have knowledge of what you see,
pleases me the more, the more it swells.
But of this water you must drink
before such a thirst in you be satisfied."
Thus the sun of my eyes <note>A metaphor for Beatrice.</note> spoke to me.
She added further: "The river and the topazes <note>The living sparks/angels.</note>

<column-break/>

of her path. **WITH THE GESTURE AND VOICE OF A PROMPT LEADER.** He cannot describe what Beatrice <note>original: "B."</note> was like, but he recounts what she said. Because with gesture and voice as a prompt leader, she said: "We have come out of the largest body," that is, from the ninth heaven, which is the Primum Mobile, and it is corporeal and larger because it embraces all the others; and we have come to the Empyrean heaven, which is pure light, because it is the formal light of all the other lights. And he says it is intellectual light to differentiate it from corporeal light; and full of true love: and love of the true and highest good. Which good brings the highest joy that surpasses all sweetness. Nor is this light anything other than God himself. Wherefore John the Evangelist says: <note>original: "Erat lux uera que illuminat oem homine ueniete i hunc mudu"</note> "He was the true light that enlightens every man coming into this world." And in this place you will see both of the militias of paradise, that is, the angelic and the human nature. Therefore, the militia of the angels and that of the blessed souls. The angels campaigned in heaven against the wicked angels, just as the blessed souls campaigned on earth against the flesh and against the adversary. And at present they triumph in the eternal and blessed life. But the one—that is, the human—shall be in those aspects: as if to say in those splendors and beauties which you shall see at the final justice. There is no doubt that the angels are in their perfection, because all those who did not side with Lucifer were immediately confirmed in grace and have their perfect beatitude. But because man in heaven does not have his body with him, he does not have his perfection. But he shall have it after the great judgment, because they shall have reassumed their glorified bodies. By **FINAL JUSTICE**, understand "corrective," because the rewards of the good and the punishments of the wicked shall be made eternal.

The meaning of these verses is that just as it happens that a sudden splendor scatters—that is, breaks apart—the visual power, so that it first deprives the eye of seeing; so the living light of that heaven dazzled and clouded him with its radiance, so that he saw nothing else. And this was because the love that quiets and contents that heaven—that is, the highest God who makes the blessed souls content. Or rather, "quiets this heaven": that is, makes it so it feels no motion, while all the others feel no rest—welcomes and draws man to itself with such a greeting as it has done for the author, to make the candle ready for its flame: that is, to prepare him to be able to conceive the splendor of that glory.

A wondrous fiction and worthy of the poet's genius. In which he first demonstrates that after the brief words spoken by Beatrice, he perceived himself to be so far surpassed above his human power, and to be so renewed in visual power that although light—the more it is pure and clear—the more it dazzles and takes away the sight, nonetheless no light could be so pure that his eyes would not have endured it. And then he saw a light in the form of a river, that is, a stream, which was "tawny"—that is, shining with brightness, that is, with splendors—between two banks painted with a wondrous springtime: that is, adorned with such herbs and flowers as are usually in a wondrous spring. From that river living sparks came out continually, and on both banks they entered into the flowers in such a way that they appeared like rubies set in gold. Then, as if inebriated by the scent of those flowers, they "plunged back"—that is, they dove back in—into the "marvelous depths": that is, into the wonderful river. And continually, as those entered the river, many others came out and entered the flowers. This river is illuminating grace, which is immediate from God; and therefore he places it here as the influence of this heaven, and it is inexhaustible like a river. And it seems he wants this river to be that of which the Canticle speaks: <note>original: "Benedicite aque que super celos sunt dno"</note> "Bless the Lord, you waters that are above the heavens." **THE BANKS.** Just as the river comes from the mountain and descends into the valley, so the grace of God descends into man. By the banks, understand those of the Old and New Testament, because both are irrigated and bathed by such grace. The herbs are the topazes <note>Note: The commentator here links the "topazes" to the vegetation, though the poem identifies them with the sparks.</note>, or the virtuous. The flowers are the blessed souls. The sparks are the angels.

Beatrice, as in other things, so in this, knows the mind and the will of the poet through herself. And therefore she tells him that the desire—that is, the longing—which inflames and "urges"—that is, constrains—him to have knowledge of what he sees—that is, of the river and the sparks—pleases her the more, the more it "swells"—that is, grows and increases. And she adds that he must first drink from that river that satisfies his thirst and his desire to understand what this river is. Furthermore, she says that the river and the topazes—that is, the sparks that come out of it—and the "laughter of the grasses" are not yet true to him: that is, springtime: that is, beatitude. But they are "shadowy prefaces": that is, announcements of shadows, that is, of the said springtime. And this is not because in heaven there is no perfec...

<summary>Dante enters the Empyrean, the realm of pure intellectual light, where he experiences a blinding divine flash and then beholds a symbolic river of light teeming with sparks and flowers representing angels and the blessed. Beatrice explains that these visions are "shadowy prefaces" intended to prepare his human faculties for the ultimate reality of God.</summary>

which takes from there its life and potency.

And as a hillside in water at its base
mirrors itself, as if to see itself adorned
when it is rich in green and flowers,
So, standing above the light all around,
I saw mirrored in more than a thousand tiers <note>original: "fogle," literally leaves, referring to the ranks of the seats in the Celestial Rose.</note>
all of us who have made the return up there.
And if the lowest rank gathers within itself
so great a light, how great is the width
of this rose in its furthest leaves!
My sight in the breadth and in the height
was not lost, but took it all in

<column-break/>

and that beatitude: but the defect comes from the fact that he does not yet have
the sights, i.e., the eyes. 'So proud,' i.e., so noble. Not without cause does he who
loves Beatrice unfold his eyes: because theology is that which truly
illuminates the intellect. Furthermore <note>original: "Preterea"</note>, he said 'topazes' to denote the
whole and incorrupt life of the blessed souls: because the topaz denotes
chastity.
**T**he poet had understood from Beatrice how much it would help him to
drink of the water of that river. Therefore he bent down more suddenly
toward the river than an infant does toward the breasts of the nurse
when he is awakened later than he is accustomed. From which comes having greater
hunger. And this he did to make 'better mirrors,' i.e., mirrors of his
eyes. He had already, as was said, made his sight better: but now he had
to make it excellent. Therefore he bent to the river: i.e., humbly asking for
grace, which flows from God into creatures: so that one may 'improve therein,'
i.e., in that one becomes better. And as soon as the 'eaves of the eyelids,'
i.e., the extremity of the edge of the lids of the eyes, drank of this water,
the river that first seemed long to me appeared round. By this he
demonstrates that those who are not yet filled with illuminating grace
see only that these things proceed and derive
from God: but they do not perceive that they return to God. Therefore, by the
length is denoted the progress from God to the created thing. But by the
circle it is easy to understand the return to God. THEN AS people: after
his eyes had drunk the water, he saw the flowers and the grasses and
the sparks in their true form, and things seemed to him much more marvelous. And
it happened as with people who are in 'masks' [larve]: i.e., in masks that are not beautiful,
who after the masks are removed remain in their own form. Therefore the
flowers showed themselves as human souls, and the sparks as angels. And by this
he saw both courts of heaven. Because in heaven near
to God there are nothing but angels and human souls.
**W**orthy of wanting to express what he saw of the triumphant
court of heaven, he invokes the splendor by whose grace
he saw it. Therefore, O splendor of God: O Holy Spirit through whom I saw
and without whom I could not see. Because without illuminating grace
the human soul cannot transcend these speculations.
THE HIGH triumph of the church triumphant. And certainly it is easy to
know the church militant <note>The church on earth.</note>: because its works are for the most
part placed in active operations and in moral virtues. But to understand
with the mind the triumphant church, because it is placed in contemplation which is an
incorporeal thing, is very difficult. Of the 'true kingdom': because this is the
true kingdom: and he who serves in this reigns. And the other kingdoms are servitude.
LIGHT of the Holy Spirit: which light makes visible the Creator.
For just as the material sun, reflecting its rays on the earth, makes
the things of this world visible to us, so this light makes God visible
not to every creature, but to that one which 'has its peace': i.e., its highest good
placed only in God. Nor does it think of anything else: because it has a soul pure from
<margin>every contagion. This light extends in a circular and spherical figure: and makes so great a circumference that it would be too wide to encircle the sun. Nor is it anything other than a ray that comes from the highest light which is God and reflects onto the Primum Mobile: i.e., the highest part of the ninth heaven, which is the 'first moved.' Which ninth heaven receives from that reflection 'life': i.e., motion, which is a sign of life, and 'potency': i.e., the power to give its influence to all the heavens.</margin>
**J**ust as it would happen that if a mountain were in the midst of water, it would
be seen from its base: i.e., from the parts above even to those below; so
the blessed souls, standing above the light all around, mirrored themselves
all around in the said light. These souls he imagines to be in more than a thousand
seats: i.e., in infinite seats. And he says 'all of us who have made the return up there': i.e.,
all those souls who, having come from God through creation, by their merits have
returned to God through beatitude. MY sight in the breadth and in the height. The
poet had become of such noble sight that it did not lose its way: and did not
fail. Neither in the breadth: that is, in the latitude; nor in the height, although
each was immense. But he understood and discerned the whole, and in that, the
quantity and the quality. Human sight can discern within a certain space
all these things: and once that is passed, the sight is confounded. But in heaven,
neither near nor far-off adds or takes away: i.e., it does not make the thing increase or
decrease: neither does the near make one see better, nor the far worse: but it appears exactly
as it is. WHERE God governs without a medium. Someone could say
it is likely that he who is far sees as much as he who is near, and
he who is high as much as he who is low. To which he responds that in things
governed by God but through the medium of second causes, such as the heavens and the elements
and all earthly things, the natural law mentioned above does not apply.

the how much and what sort of that joy
is neither added to nor taken from by the near or far;
for where God governs without medium, <note>In the Empyrean, God rules directly rather than through the "secondary causes" of the lower celestial spheres.</note>
natural law has no relevance.
Into the yellow center of the eternal rose,
which expands and rises in tiers and breathes forth
an odor of praise to the Sun that makes perpetual spring,
Beatrice drew me—like one who is silent
yet wishes to speak—and she said: "Look
how great is the assembly of the white stoles! <note>The "white stoles" refer to the white robes of the redeemed souls, a reference to the Book of Revelation.</note>
See our city, how wide it circles;
see our seats so filled
that few people are still desired here.
And on that great seat where you keep your eyes,
because of the crown that is already placed upon it,
before you yourself sup at these wedding feasts,

The blind greed that bewitches you

and he shall push the one from Anagni further down." <note>A prophecy that Pope Clement V will die and be cast into Hell, pushing Pope Boniface VIII (from Anagni) deeper into the pit of the Simoniacs.</note>

### CANTO XXXI OF THE THIRD CANTICLE BY DANTE

In the form then of a white rose
was displayed to me the holy host
which Christ, with his own blood, made his spouse.
But the other host, who flying see and sing
the glory of Him who enamors them
and the goodness that made them so great,
Like a swarm of bees that settle on flowers
one moment and the next return
to where their labor is turned into sweetness,
Descended into the great flower that is adorned
with so many petals, and then rose up again
to where its Love forever dwells.

<column-break/>

But in the Empyrean heaven, in which God operates immediately and without secondary causes, natural law can do nothing. Then it follows that Beatrice drew him—just as one who, through a greed for knowledge, wants to speak, and yet through wonder remains silent. And she drew him into the "yellow of the rose," that is, into the center of that sphere, just as in a rose the yellow is in the center. This rose expands, because the scope and circumference of this heaven is vast, and it "rises in tiers," that is, it is distinguished by its ranks. And it "breathes forth an odor," that is, it gives off an odor of praise to the Sun—meaning to the eternal God who illuminates that heaven—which Sun "always makes spring," meaning it is always springtime there. And she said: "Behold how great is the assembly and the number of blessed souls who, as John places them in the Apocalypse, are in white stoles." A "stole" is a long garment reaching to the feet.

Beatrice concludes that the celestial seats, which were vacated by the ruin of the rebel angels and were to be refilled by blessed souls, are nearly full. Then she points out an empty seat adorned with a crown; she says that it is prepared for Henry of Luxembourg, the fourth Emperor. <note>original: "henrico di lucimborgo quarto imperadore"</note> And in that seat he shall sit before Dante "sups at those weddings," that is, before Dante arrives at that state of bliss. This man reigned at the time of the poet, while Clement of Gascony <note>Pope Clement V</note> sat on the papal throne. And she tacitly notes that we are in the final age and near the end. It is the opinion of some that the number of blessed souls must be equal to the number of rebel angels. Others say there must be as many as there are angels who remained, so that our number is equal to that of the angels. Or truly we might say, according to the Aquinian, <note>Saint Thomas Aquinas</note> that God alone knows the number of the angels.

She damns the blind greed of the Italians who, out of avarice and ambition, drove away Henry, who wished to lead them back to the right path and to liberty; she makes them similar to a little child who, though hungry, drives away the nurse out of spite. And she adds that at that time there will be a Supreme Pontiff <note>Clement V</note> such that neither openly nor secretly will he walk the path of the Emperor, because he will seek to corrupt Italy and keep her in discord. But God will suffer him to be in the "holy office" of the papacy for only a short time, for he will die and be thrust down to Hell where Simon Magus and his followers are punished. This place is described in the nineteenth chapter of the *Inferno*, where he places the Simoniacs in certain narrow pits, head downward with their legs outside, until another condemned for the same crime comes to the same pit; then the one who came first falls to the bottom, and the newcomer remains with his legs outside. Therefore, Clement will come to the pit in Hell where it was shown that Boniface of Anagni, <note>Pope Boniface VIII</note> his predecessor, was.

Having already treated the celestial court in general, in this thirty-first chapter our poet describes it distinctly and in detail. Thus, in the beginning, he describes the act and the appearance of the blessed souls and the angels. Then he invokes the Trinity and describes his most happy contemplation. In the third place, he describes Saint Bernard and Beatrice returning to her seat. In the last part, Bernard shows him the blessed souls, and especially the Virgin Mary. But in these first verses, summarizing what was said in the preceding chapter, he says that the "holy host"—that is, the souls of the blessed who, having soldiered in the world, now triumph in heaven—were in the form of a white rose. This host Christ ransomed with His death and united to Himself, wherefore she was His spouse. The other "host"—that is, the angelic one—sees and understands the glory of God which enamors it, and His goodness, which made said angels so great (that is, so noble) and seeing the charity (that is, the praise). These angels descended into the "great flower"—that is, into the rose, which is what he calls the seats of the blessed—which flower is adorned with as many "leaves" as there are seats. And from these leaves they rose back to God, in whom their love forever dwells, just as bees do, which go out from their hives into flowers and then return to the hives, where their "labor" (their toil) is "turned into sweetness" because it produces honey. And certainly, it is an excellent comparison between the angels and the bees: for just as bees are prompt and ready in their duty around the king, so are the angels in the service of God. The bees delight in the odor of flowers and conceive honey; so the angels delight in the odor of the good works of holy men and carry that sweetness to God. And just as the bees drive from the hives the lazy and useless ones, so the angels drive from heaven the lazy who have not practiced good works.

<summary>Beatrice reveals the vast assembly of the redeemed in the form of a white rose and points out the throne of the future Emperor Henry VII, while prophesying the damnation of Pope Clement V. Canto XXXI begins with the iconic imagery of angels as bees flying between the divine rose and God.</summary>

# PARADISO

The faces were all of living flame,
and the wings of gold, and the rest so white
that no snow reaches that limit.
When they descended into the flower, from rank to rank,
they offered of the peace and of the ardor
which they acquired by fanning their flanks. <note>The "flanks" refers to the sides of the angels' bodies as they beat their wings to distribute the peace and love they gathered from God.</note>
Nor did the interposing of so great
a flying multitude between the height and the flower
impede the vision or the splendor;
For the divine light is penetrating
through the universe according as it is worthy,
so that nothing can be an obstacle to it.

This secure and joyful kingdom,
crowded with people ancient and new,
had its sight and love all at one mark.
O threefold light which in a single star,
sparkling, so satisfies their sight;
look down here upon our storm! <note>Dante contrasts the eternal peace of the Trinity with the chaotic political "storm" of 14th-century Italy.</note>
If the barbarians, coming from such a region
as is covered every day by Helice <note>Helice is a name for Callisto, the constellation Ursa Major (the Great Bear).</note>
rotating with her son of whom she is fond, <note>Her son is Arcas, the constellation Ursa Minor (the Little Bear).</note>
Seeing Rome and her lofty work,
were stupefied, when the Lateran <note>The Lateran Palace in Rome, then the seat of the Papacy, representing the height of worldly grandeur.</note>
went above mortal things;
I, who to the divine from the human,
to the eternal from time had come,
and from Florence to a people just and sane,
With what stupor must I have been filled!
Certainly, between it and the joy, it made me
prefer not to hear and to stand mute.

And like a pilgrim who finds refreshment
in the temple of his vow, looking around,
and hopes already to tell again how it stands,
Walking up through the living light,
I led my eyes through the ranks,
now up, now down, and now circling back.
I saw faces persuasive of charity, <note>original: "suadi" — meaning faces that invite or persuade the observer toward love.</note>
adorned by another's light and their own smile,
and actions adorned with every dignity.
The general form of Paradise
had already completely filled my gaze,
not yet fixed steadily on any one part.

<column-break/>

**T**he faces of the angels were red in the form of flame to denote the most burning charity. The wings with which they flew were of gold: because their work is most precious and shines like fine gold. The other parts white demonstrate supreme purity and cleanliness, or truly, perfect wisdom. We can also take them for the incorruptible nature of the angels: which, confirmed in grace, can no longer sin. The white denotes the supreme purity of the angel: because he never sinned. When the angels descended "in white," that is, from seat to seat, they offered to the souls in those seats the peace that is blessedness and the charity: which they acquire from God by "fanning their flanks," that is, beating their wings. This signifies their operations. It was, then, a marvelous multitude of flying angels: which, interposing themselves between the poet and the blessed souls, seemed reasonable that they should take away the sight of the souls: and also cast a shadow in a way that he would not receive the light: But it was neither one nor the other: because the light of God penetrates through the whole universe in the same way regarding God: but not regarding those who receive it. Because the divine light penetrates more and less into different creatures according as they are more or less capable of it.

¶ **T**his kingdom is secure from every danger: and "joyful," that is, full of joy: which two properties are not in mortal kingdoms where there are always dangers: and often joy is lacking. CROWDED with people ancient and new: that is, which is filled with ancient people starting from Adam and the others whom Christ took from Limbo <note>original: "libo" — a likely printer's error for "limbo."</note> and afterward of the apostles and the other faithful of the primitive church: and afterward of the other virtuous and faithful ones until this day. All these blessed ones, both ancient and new, had their faces and love—that is, the contemplating face and the will burning with charity—turned to one "mark," that is, to God himself, whom they understand and love. He invokes, then, God, that as he cares for heaven, so he may deign to look upon this low and mortal world and says: **O** THREEFOLD LIGHT: O Trinity who are light from which every thing receives light. And although it is in three persons: nonetheless it is a single star because it is one substance: and from this star sparkle the sparks that satisfy and content the souls in heaven. **L**OOK down here at our storm: that is, the tempest; for human life is in a continuous state of greater perturbation than a ship in a stormy sea. ¶ **I**F BARBARI [BARBARIANS]. This is an excellent simile to show how great his stupor was in contemplating the kingdom of the blessed: and it is a comparison from the lesser to the greater in this way: If the barbarian and foreign peoples who come from the northern parts—which he says the Great Bear <note>original: "orsa maggiore"</note> called "the North Star" <note>original: "tramontana"</note> covers every day, with her son, that is, with the Little Bear <note>original: "orsa minore"</note>—arriving at Rome, they were stupefied seeing the admirable things of that city, when the Lateran (that is, Rome itself, putting the part for the whole) "went above mortal things"—that is, surpassed in magnificence and power all other cities—how much more should I be stupefied, I who had come from the human and mortal world to the divine and immortal heaven? I had come from time, which is the extensive succession of terminable life, to eternity, which is altogether the perfect possession of life without end. ¶ AND FROM FLORENCE to the just and sane people: that is, from men who in life often err, to the heavenly Jerusalem, whose citizens, confirmed in grace, cannot sin. From which he concludes that between this stupor and the joy, it gave him pleasure not to speak but to stay quiet.

¶ **T**he poet had already reached the ultimate end and that blessedness for which he had made so long a journey. Therefore, nothing remained for him but to contemplate the great temple of God: in which all the souls of the blessed, resting themselves, enjoy the supreme joy. Therefore, he went searching with his eyes through the whole, now up, now down, and now in a circuit, refreshing himself in that, like the pilgrim who, having arrived at the temple of Rome or the Sepulcher or of Saint James <note>Refers to the major pilgrimage sites: Rome, the Holy Sepulcher in Jerusalem, and Santiago de Compostela.</note> where he had come by a vow, refreshes himself by looking around at both the form and the ornaments, and the things that are inside: and already hopes for his return, and having returned, to be able to tell his own people how that temple stands. Here the poet saw the faces and the countenances "persuasive of charity": in which they were so inflamed with charity that they persuaded those who saw them toward it: and they were "adorned and decorated with the light of another," that is, with the light of the divine light, and with "their own smile," that is, their own happiness: and with "actions full of every dignity," that is, of all the virtues. And already he has understood the whole form of Paradise in general. But not yet in detail: because he had not fixed his gaze more on one place than another. Afterward he...

And I turned with rekindled desire
to ask my lady about things
of which my mind was in suspense.

One thing I intended, and another answered me;
I thought I would see Beatrice, and I saw an old man, <note>This "old man" is Saint Bernard of Clairvaux (1090–1153), a mystic and devotee of the Virgin Mary, who represents the final stage of contemplation.</note>
clothed like the glorious people.
Infused through his eyes and through his cheeks
was a benign joy in a pious gesture,
as is fitting for a tender father.
And "Where is she?" I said suddenly;
to which he said: "To bring your desire to its end,
Beatrice moved me from my place.
And if you look up into the third circle
of the highest tier, you will see her again
upon the throne that her merits have assigned to her."

Without responding, I lifted my eyes,
and I saw her as she made herself a crown,
reflecting from herself the eternal rays.
From that high region where it thunders most,
no mortal eye is so far distant,
even if one abandons oneself to the deepest sea,
As my sight was from Beatrice;
but it made no difference to me, for her image
did not descend to me through any medium. <note>In heaven, sight is not limited by distance or the physical properties of air; Dante sees her perfectly clearly despite the vast distance.</note>

"O lady, in whom my hope flourishes,
and who suffered for my salvation
to leave your footprints in Hell, <note>Dante refers to Beatrice's descent into Limbo to ask Virgil to guide him.</note>
For all the many things that I have seen,
from your power and from your goodness
I recognize the grace and the virtue.
You have drawn me from a slave to freedom
by all those ways, by all the modes
that had the power to do so.
Guard your magnificence within me,
so that my soul, which you have made whole,
may be pleasing to you when it unknots from the body."
Thus I prayed; and she, as far away
as she appeared, smiled and looked at me;
then she turned back to the eternal fountain. <note>The "eternal fountain" is a metaphor for God, the source of all being and grace.</note>

<note>The following paragraph is a gloss printed in smaller type at the bottom of the first column.</note>

Nevertheless, her grace, through her mercy, approaches us. Whence it is written: "The Lord is near to all them that call upon him." <note>original: "Deus prope est invocantibus se." From Psalm 145:18.</note> And she "looked at him": as if to confirm and establish him in that true way. "THEN SHE turned back to the eternal fountain." This denotes that such grace comes from God and returns to God, as to an unfailing fountain.

The holy elder said: "So that you may complete
perfectly your journey,"
to which prayer and holy love sent me,
"fly with your eyes through this garden..."

<column-break/>

He turned to ask Beatrice about many doubts that held his mind in suspense.

When Dante turned to ask Beatrice about his devoted doubts, she had already returned to her seat. Thus he says correctly that he "intended one thing"—namely, to speak with Beatrice—and "another answered him," because Saint Bernard had already come. Bernard is called an "old man" [senex] meaning elder: benign, joyful, and pious, as a tender father should be, desiring the salvation of his son; and he is described as such because of his history governing his monks. Here Dante said, "Where is she?" which signifies that he sought to understand through sacred theology what he will say afterward. And Bernard answered him because the doctrine of this elder opened this place to him. Therefore, Bernard replied that she had returned to her seat, which he says is in the third circle starting from the center point; and that she had commissioned him to come to Dante to terminate and fulfill his desire.

The author, eager for Beatrice, did not respond to Bernard but immediately lifted his eyes, searching for her. Furthermore, this denotes the "habit of contemplation," which always lifts the eyes of the intellect to superior and celestial things. Whence in the Psalm: "I lifted up mine eyes unto the hills." <note>original: "Levavi oculos meos in montem." From Psalm 121:1.</note> And Isaiah: "He shall sit solitary and keep silence, because he hath borne it upon him." <note>original: "Sedebit solitarius & tacebit quia leuauit ſe ſupra ſe." From Lamentations 3:28 (traditionally attributed to Jeremiah/Isaiah in different commentaries).</note> The rays of eternal light descended upon the head of Beatrice, and she reflected them from every side, and thus they made a crown for her. This signifies that the ray of the Holy Spirit descends upon the theologian and illuminates them; and having received the grace of doctrine, they reflect it onto others and instruct and illuminate them. And Beatrice was as much higher than the poet as one who was at the bottom of the sea would be distant from the region where thunders are born. Nevertheless, this distance was no impediment to him, because the image of Beatrice did not descend to him mixed through any medium. It was not, therefore, like it is among us mortals, where our eyes see through a "diaphanous" medium—that is, a transparent one like air or glass and similar things. For that reason, our sight cannot extend beyond the proportion of the sense, the object, or the medium (the air). But in heaven, it is otherwise.

He offers a prayer to Beatrice, through which he says his "hope flourishes"—that is, it lasts and is preserved. For theology, accompanied by cooperating and consummate grace, brings man to such perfection that he always hopes for true beatitude. He considers especially that she, for his salvation, descended into Hell when she comforted Virgil so that he might help him in the forest where he was lost; and finally, she has made him a "free man" instead of a slave by untying his knowledge and virtue. Whence: "Virtues and knowledge have freed the soul from the captivity of nature." <note>original: "Virtutes & scie liberauerūt animam a captiuitate nature."</note> "BY ALL those ways and by all those modes." As if to say: through the fear of punishment and the exhortation of rewards which had the power to do so—that is, to pull him from the slavery of vices to the liberty of virtues. With these words, the poet had thanked Beatrice for the benefits received. Afterward, he prays to her that as she has used clemency and supreme liberality toward him until now, granting him such great gifts, so it might please her in the future to guard and preserve in him such magnificence. And as she has made him free with knowledge and virtue—whereby the soul, previously sick through vices and ignorance, is made whole—so may she preserve him in this state until the soul "unknots" and loosens from the body. After this prayer, Beatrice, "as far away as she appeared, smiled." This was a sign that she had heard him. And not without reason did he say "as far away as she appeared," rather than "as she was." For although divine greatness is most remote from the human condition...

THEN SHE turned back to the eternal fountain. Which denotes that such grace comes from God...

Here Bernard comforts the poet so that he may "complete"—that is, lead to the summit and to the end—his journey, which will then be finished when he has arrived at the Highest God. "FLY with your eyes through this garden"—that is, run with your sight through the entire council of blessed souls. And he said "garden," interpreting the Greek word, because "paradise" in Greek signifies a garden. And he adds that by looking at this garden, he will prepare and make fit and suitable the...

> Just like someone who, perhaps from Croatia,
> comes to see our Veronica, <note>The "Veronica" was a famous relic in Rome—a cloth believed to be impressed with the face of Jesus. Pilgrims traveled vast distances to see it.</note>
> who because of its ancient fame is never satisfied,
> but says in his thought as long as it is shown:
> "My Lord Jesus Christ, true God,
> was your appearance truly like this?"
> Such was I, marvelling at the living
> charity of him who, in this world,
> tasted of that peace through contemplation. <note>Bernard was a mystic who was said to have experienced glimpses of divine peace while still alive.</note>
> "Son of Grace, this joyful state,"
> he began, "will not be known to you
> if you keep your eyes fixed down here at the bottom;
> but look at the circles, even to the most remote,
> until you see the Queen seated,
> to whom this realm is subject and devoted."
> I lifted my eyes; and as at morning
> the eastern part of the horizon
> outshines the side where the sun declines,
> so, as if going from a valley to a mountain,
> with my eyes I saw a part at the furthest edge
> surpass in light all the rest of the rim.
> And just as at the point where we await the pole <note>original: "temo" (the drawbar or pole of a chariot), referring to the chariot of the Sun.</note>
> that Phaethon guided so poorly, the flame grows brightest, <note>In Greek myth, Phaethon tried to drive the chariot of the Sun but lost control, nearly burning the earth.</note>
> and on either side the light diminishes,
> so that peaceful oriflamme <note>A "peaceful oriflamme" (a royal banner) refers here to the brilliant light surrounding Mary.</note>
> was quickened in the center, and on every side
> the flame faded in equal measure.
> And in that center, with their wings outspread,
> I saw more than a thousand festive angels,
> each distinct in both brightness and art. <note>The "art" of the angels refers to their specific duties or movements.</note>
> I saw there, at their games and their songs,
> a beauty smiling, which was a source of joy
> in the eyes of all the other saints.
> And if I had as much wealth in speech
> as I have in imagination, I would not dare
> to attempt the smallest part of her delight.
> Bernard, when he saw my eyes
> fixed and attentive upon his own warm heat,
> turned his own toward her with such affection
> that he made mine more eager to look again.

### CANTO XXXII OF THE THIRD CANTICLE OF DANTE

<margin>a-</margin> **A**ffectionate in his pleasure, that contemplative man
freely assumed the office of a teacher.

<column-break/>

his face so that it might be changed by the divine ray. Because, since
the progress of knowledge in man **is not sudden but proceeds from principles** <note>original Latin: "Non sita precipiti sed ad pricipia"</note>: it is fitting that, beginning from the lowest and most
remote things and rising grade by grade to those close to divinity,
the higher one rises, the more one becomes fit to contemplate it.

<margin>n</margin> **N**o less eagerly does one look upon the Veronica—which is the image of
Christ—who comes to Rome to see it even from Croatia,
a northern and very distant region. And while it is shown
to him, he says in amazement: "O Lord Jesus Christ, was
your image truly made like this?" In the same way the poet became amazed seeing the image
of Saint Bernard, desiring to know if it was so made in this world.
Because it appears impossible for human frailty to be able to comprehend
the divinity without the intercession of Mary, he introduces
Beatrice sending him Bernard—both because he was a highly contemplative
theologian and because he was very devoted to Mary. For this reason it is fitting
that through his intercession the poet might persuade Mary to
intercede for him before the Supreme God.

<margin>f</margin> **SON OF GRACE**: And rightly so, because we are not
reborn from the death of sin by our own merits, but by
divine grace. Therefore we are sons of grace. **THIS joyful state**.
This supreme celestial good will not be known to you if you keep
your eyes at the bottom. As if to say: if you do not detach yourself from the terrestrial mud and
fly like an eagle toward the divine sun. **I LIFTED MY EYES**.
What this signifies has already been explained above. **AND AS
AT MORNING**. He demonstrates by comparison that just as in the
morning the eastern part is brighter than the western, because the sun
begins to illuminate it, so that most supreme part of
Paradise was more lucid than the other parts. **AND JUST AS THERE**: that is,
in that part of heaven. **WHERE the pole is awaited**: that is, the chariot of
the sun; using the pole, which is part of the chariot, to represent the whole chariot. And the
fable of Phaethon was narrated in Canto XVII of the first canticle.
**It grows more inflamed**: that is, it is more illuminated: because a greater
brightness always appears there where the sun is soon to be. **SO THAT peaceful golden flame**: that is, the peaceful flame: because the most ardent charity of
Mary was the mediatress to reconcile man to God. **AND in that center
with wings outspread**. The outspread wings of the angels signify the
grace and knowledge that expands through all souls. But those were
distinct because, according to their merits, their faces are more or less illuminated
with brilliance: that is, with splendor which signifies charity. **AND BY ART**:
that is, by exercise: because, as I said, they have distinction in their office
according to the diversity of grace and glory. **A BEAUTY**:
Which was the Virgin Mary, smiling at the games and songs of the angels.
And this created joy in the eyes of all the saints. **AND if I had
such wealth in speech**. A man can imagine much more and better
than he can express what he imagines. And nevertheless
the poet demonstrates that even if he had as much wealth—that is, as much faculty in
speech—as he has in imagination, he would not dare to attempt the smallest part of
her glory. **AND WHEN Bernard, when he saw my eyes**
attentive in his warm heat, he turned his own toward her—that is, toward Mary—with such
affection that he made mine more burning to look. He concludes that the
fervor with which Bernard wrote his contemplations of Mary made
him more fervent to contemplate her.

<margin>d h</margin> **H**aving already described Paradise in general,
the author wishes in this thirty-second chapter to describe
it in detail. Therefore in the first part of...
