<meta>This page continues Saint Bernard’s guided tour of the Celestial Rose. Having pointed out Beatrice’s new seat among the blessed, Bernard now begins to explain the specific arrangement of the holy women who form a vertical line descending from the Virgin Mary, dividing the Old Testament faithful from those of the New Testament.</meta>

# CANTO XXXII

->and he began these holy words:<-

> The wound that Mary closed and anointed,
> she who is so beautiful at her feet
> is the one who opened it and pierced it.
> In the order made by the third seats,
> Rachel sits below this one
> with Beatrice, just as you see.
> Sarah, Rebecca, Judith, and she [Ruth]
> who was the great-grandmother of the singer [David] who, in sorrow
> for his sin, said *miserere mei* <note>Latin: "Have mercy on me," the opening of Psalm 51.</note>.
> You can see them thus, from petal to petal,
> descending grade by grade, as I, by their proper names,
> go down through the rose from petal to petal.

From the most humble Mary was born the medicine. Thus it is said that Mary closed and anointed—that is, mitigated and healed—this wound. In the third order he places Rachel and Beatrice. Rachel was the wife of Jacob and represents the contemplative life, as we have already shown in various places. Sarah was the wife of Abraham, who in her old age gave birth to Isaac. Rebecca was the wife of Isaac, who bore Jacob and Esau. These three are held in great esteem in the Old Testament: Rachel for her husband’s love, Rebecca for her prudence, and Sarah for her faithfulness. Judith was a most holy woman who, through her greatness of soul, liberated the Bethulians from Holofernes; we narrated her story above. The great-grandmother of the singer—that is, of David, who, moved by the fire of the Holy Spirit, sang the psalms. He, having fallen in love with Bathsheba, wife of his knight Uriah, had the husband killed in order to have her. Thus he committed adultery, homicide, and treason. Later, repenting of his error, he sang the psalm *Miserere mei Deus* <note>Latin: "Have mercy on me, O God."</note>. The great-grandmother of David was Ruth, wife of Boaz; and Boaz fathered Obed, and he was the father of Jesse, from whom David was born. These are seven seats: the first belongs to Mary, Queen of Heaven; the second to Eve; the third to Rachel; and Beatrice is the fourth; the fifth to Rebecca; the sixth to Judith; the seventh to Ruth. Therefore, in the second seat were those women who lived according to the natural law, primarily in contemplation.

<column-break/>

The author describes the order of the ranks of the blessed of the Old and New Testaments. In the second part, he removes a doubt concerning little children. In the third, he describes the blessedness shown to Our Lady and points out the angel Gabriel. In the last, he points out the principal patricians of this court. Now, returning to the first verses, the text says: That contemplative—that is, Bernard—affectionate—meaning made full of affection—took up and assumed the free office of a teacher, because he freely chose to be my teacher and show me all the ranks of Paradise. And he began thus: **SHE** who is so beautiful—meaning Eve, the first woman—at the feet of Mary, because in the second seat below Mary is she who opened and pierced the wound that Mary closed and anointed. This is the wound of human nature caused by the sin of Adam, which made all men unable to attain eternal life, of which Eve was the inducing cause; and therefore she pierced and opened this wound. And Mary, through her obedience and purity, was the inducing cause for God the Father to send His Son to take flesh from her and redeem man from the servitude of sin. Hence it is written: *Mulier damnavit quae sanavit* <note>Latin: "The woman who condemned is the one who healed." This is a traditional theological contrast between Eve and Mary.</note>. Eve, through the intervention of the wicked angel in the form of a serpent, struck the human race. And Mary, through the intervention of the blessed angel, healed it. From the most proud Eve was born the disease, and from [Mary the cure].

> And from the seventh grade down, just as
> down to it, Hebrew women succeed one another,
> dividing all the tresses of the flower;
> Because, according to the way they looked
> at faith in Christ, these women are the wall
> at which the sacred stairs are divided.
> On this side where the flower is mature
> with all its petals, those are seated
> who believed in Christ yet to come.
> On the other side, where the semicircles
> are broken by empty spaces, sit those
> who held their eyes toward Christ already come.

And from the seventh grade where Ruth sits, downwards—that is, descending to the bottom of the rose—just as before—that is, just as from the first seat of Our Lady down to the seventh of Ruth—Hebrew women succeed one another, "dividing all the tresses"—that is, dividing all the petals of the flower. In short, understand that below Our Lady, down to the base of the rose, are souls from the Old Testament, always dividing by seven grades just as the first are divided. For he who merited more is in the rank that suits him in the first group of seven, and he who merited less is in the rank that suits him in the second group of seven, down to the midpoint of the rose's height. And from there down are the children saved by the faith of their fathers, similarly divided into seven grades. 

Imagine, then, being at the bottom of a rose and seeing it divided through the middle lengthways; let that part over which Mary sits have all its semicircles full; and in the upper half of these semicircles are the Hebrew women; and from there down are the little children who died before they had knowledge of evil or good. And similarly, to the left of Mary the Queen, imagine Adam; and next to him Moses and the others who merited that rank; and in the following ranks, seven by seven, are the males who believed in Christ yet to come; and from the middle down, the little children as mentioned. And then on the right hand are Peter and John and the other apostles. And below Saint Peter, following the same order, are those who believed in Christ when he was present. Below Moses, who is on the left, is Anne, and below her, keeping the ranks, are the women who were saved in the time of Christ's presence; and then the children; and all these seats are full. Opposite Our Lady is John the Baptist, below whom in the second rank is Francis, then Benedict, then Augustine; and each one below him in the descending ranks, dividing as above, are their friars and monks and others according to their merits; and from the middle down, the children saved through baptism according to the merits of their parents. Thus, in the middle between the men of the Old Testament who believed in Christ to come, and the men of the New who believed in Christ having come, are the women who believed in Christ while he was present, acting as a wall that divides them; and between the women who believed in him after he came are the men who believed in him while present. 

Therefore, to show that every blessed soul is saved through faith, he divides the souls of the saved first into three types: those who believed in Christ to come, those who believed in Christ present, and those who believed in Christ already come. And each is divided into males and females. Thus there are six differences, and each has adults and children, making twelve categories. But the six categories of adults are from the middle of the rose upwards, and the children from the middle downwards. Also, that part of the rose divided lengthways where our Queen sits has all its benches full, because there are those who believed in Christ yet to come or in his presence, and therefore that part of the "flower is mature" <note>This means that the quota of souls from the Old Testament era is complete.</note>. But those who believed in Christ after he had come are not yet full. But from day to day, all those who are saved go there.

> And as from here the glorious throne...

This order and distinction we have shown just above. And it shows who is below the throne of the great Queen; and...

<summary>Saint Bernard explains the layout of the Celestial Rose, describing a vertical line of holy Hebrew women (Eve, Rachel, Sarah, etc.) who divide the seating of the blessed. The Rose is split between those who looked forward to Christ and those who looked back to him, with adults in the upper tiers and children in the lower.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the description of the Celestial Rose in Canto XXXII. Having described the line of holy women descending from Mary, Saint Bernard now describes the line of holy men descending from Saint John the Baptist, which forms the opposite vertical axis of the Rose. He then addresses Dante’s confusion regarding the different ranks assigned to children in heaven.</meta>

# CANTO XXXII

...of the lady of heaven, and the other seats
below her make such a division.
Just as, opposite, sits the seat of Saint John,
who, ever holy, endured the desert and martyrdom,
and stayed in Hell <note original: "lonferno">Dante refers here to Limbo, where the souls of the just from the Old Testament waited for Christ's descent after the Crucifixion.</note> for two years;
And beneath him, it was so allotted to divide:
Francis, Benedict, and Augustine,
and others down to here, from circle to circle.
Now behold the high divine providence,
for both aspects of the faith <note original: "luno & laltro aspecto della fede">The two "aspects" are those who looked forward to Christ’s coming (Old Testament) and those who looked back upon it (New Testament).</note>
shall equally fill this garden.
And know that from the step downward that cuts
at the midpoint across the two divisions,
no one sits by their own merit,
but by that of others, under certain conditions;
for all these are spirits released
before they could have made true choices.
You can easily perceive this by their faces
and also by their childlike voices,
if you look closely and listen to them.
<margin><unclear>scribble</unclear></margin>
Now you doubt, and in doubting you are silent;
but I will untie the strong bond
in which these subtle thoughts bind you.
Within the vastness of this realm,
no point of chance can have a place,
any more than sadness, thirst, or hunger;
for by eternal law it is established,
so that whatever you see fits justly,
as a ring responds to the finger.
And therefore these hurried people <note original: "feſtinata gente">The "hurried people" are the children, so called because they "rushed" to the afterlife by dying young.</note>
to the true life, not without cause,
enter here with more or less excellence.
The King, through whom this kingdom rests
in such love and in such delight
that no will dares to ask for more,
creating all minds in His joyful sight,
endows them with grace at His pleasure
in different ways—and here let the effect suffice.
And this is noted expressly and clearly
in Holy Scripture regarding those twins
who had their wrath stirred within their mother.
Therefore, according to the color of the hair
of such grace, it is fitting that the highest light
worthily crowns them <note original: "sincapelli">Literally "to head-hair," used here to mean "to crown" or "to adorn the head."</note>.
Thus, without merit for their own conduct,
they are placed in different ranks,
differing only in their initial keenness of vision.
In the earliest ages, it was enough,
along with innocence, to obtain salvation
simply through the faith of their parents.

<column-break/>

...who sits below that of Saint John: who was sanctified in the womb of his mother, lived in the desert, and was a martyr beheaded by Herod. And because he died two years before Christ, he stayed that time in the Limbo of the holy fathers. **The two aspects of the faith**: that is, the faith of those who believed in Christ who was to come, and of those who believed in Christ who had already come. **And know that from the step that descends**: that is, it divides the two "discretions," meaning distinctions or divisions. In all the orders from the middle downward are the <term>parvuli</term> <note>Latin: "little ones" or infants.</note> who are saved not by their own merit, but through baptism and the faith of their parents. **Now you doubt**. Bernard knew Dante doubted whether those seats were given to the blessed children by chance or not; therefore he promises to clarify it. First he demonstrates that in the vastness—that is, the greatness—of the celestial kingdom, nothing can happen by chance, just as there can be no sadness, hunger, or thirst. These cannot exist because sadness is a lack of joy, and hunger and thirst are lacks of food and drink. But in heaven there is perfect joy and nothing is lacking. Chance cannot exist because everything seen there is established by divine law, and it justly responds "like the ring to the finger"—that is, from the place to the one placed. They are settled in a place suitable to them just as a ring is made suitable for a finger. Therefore, these "hurried to the true life"—meaning these children who were "hurried" or hastened to the true life—enter with more or less excellence among themselves, and not without cause. **The King** through whom this kingdom rests: God the King, through whom the celestial realm rests—that is, remains—in such charity and joy that no will of any blessed soul "dares"—that is, has the boldness to ask for more—because they have as much delight as they desire. He endows human minds with as much grace as pleases Him, and endows them differently, giving more to one and less to another. It is not for us to seek why He gives more to this one than that one, because the cause cannot be understood. It must suffice to know the effect. This is proven in Holy Scripture by two brothers born of one womb: **Esau and Jacob**. Of whom God said before they were born: *Esau I have hated, but Jacob I have loved* <note>original: "Esau odio habui Iacob autem dilexi."</note>. These were the sons of Isaac and Rebecca; as soon as they were conceived in their mother's womb, they moved and struggled against each other. And God revealed to the father that from these two would descend two peoples, and that the people descended from the elder would serve the people descended from the younger. Later, at the time of birth, Esau came out first, red in color; and after him Jacob, small and dark, who held Esau’s foot with his hand as if to say, "You shall not leave without me." Therefore, no cause can be given why God endowed Jacob with more grace than Esau, except that it so pleased Him. But this is known: that he who has more grace performs better; and he who performs better merits more; and through this, acquires more glory. Therefore, **according to the color of the hair**: that is, just as it pleased God that Esau should have the color and hair of red, and Jacob black. So it pleased Him to give more grace to Jacob than to Esau. Although Isaac loved Esau more and Rebecca loved Jacob more, it was God's will that Rebecca could deceive Isaac. For this reason, the highest light of Paradise, which blesses souls, must worthily "crown" them—that is, crown them according to the "color of their hair." Finally, he concludes that the blessed children, without reward or merit of their own conduct—that is, of their own virtue—are placed in different ranks where they have more or less beatitude. This occurs because they are different in their "initial keenness"—that is, because they received grace differently when God created them. Just as when He created the angels, He gave more grace to one than to another, and by that grace one had a higher rank, and through subsequent obedience each was confirmed in his rank. Likewise, when He creates souls, He gives more or less grace to one than another. Then, our good works are the reason we do not lose the grace through which we merit beatitude. And as greater grace corresponds to greater merit, so it corresponds to greater beatitude. Therefore, it is concluded that the cause of the difference lies not in one's own works, but in the grace given by God.

Having shown the place of the children and how they are saved by merit, he concludes that **in the earliest ages**—that is, the fresh and first times—the faith of their fathers together with innocence was enough to save them. The faith of the first age was the firm hope that, by living purely, God would have mercy on them and would send someone to liberate them. These two ages were the first from Adam to Noah, and the second from Noah to Abraham. After these came the third, from Abraham to David, in which the iniquity of men and idolatry increased...

<summary>Saint Bernard explains that the seating of children in the Celestial Rose is not random but determined by the varying measure of divine grace granted at their creation. He uses the biblical example of Jacob and Esau to illustrate that God’s distribution of grace is a mystery beyond human understanding, yet perfectly just.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Saint Bernard’s explanation of the Celestial Rose in Canto XXXII. Having previously discussed the salvation of children, Bernard now explains the transition from the era of the Old Testament (circumcision) to the era of the New Testament (baptism), before identifying the primary figures seated at the top of the Rose surrounding the Virgin Mary.</meta>

# CANTO XXXII

After the first ages were completed,
it was necessary for males, with innocent wings,
to acquire virtue through circumcision.
But once the time of grace had arrived,
without the perfect baptism of Christ,
such innocence was held back down there.
<note>Dante refers to the "Limbus Puerorum" (Limbo of the Children), where infants who died without baptism remained, separated from the full vision of God.</note>
Look now upon the face that most resembles
Christ, for its brightness alone
can prepare you to see Christ.
I saw so much joy rain down upon her,
carried in the holy minds
created to fly through those heights,
That whatever I had seen before
did not hold me in such great admiration,
nor showed me so much of the likeness of God.
And that Love <note>The Archangel Gabriel</note> who first descended there,
singing "Hail Mary, full of grace,"
<note>original: "Aue Maria gratia plena"</note>
spread his wings before her.
The blessed court responded
to the divine song from every side,
so that every face became more serene.
"O holy father, who for my sake endures
being down here, leaving the sweet place
where you sit by eternal lot,
Who is that angel who with such playfulness
looks into the eyes of our Queen,
so enamored that he seems to be made of fire?"
Thus I had recourse again to the teaching
of him who drew beauty from Mary,
as the morning star does from the sun.
And he to me: "As much confidence and grace
as can exist in an angel or a soul,
is all in him; and we wish it to be so,
For he is the one who carried the palm
down to Mary, when the Son of God
wished to load himself with our burden."
<note>Dante refers to the Annunciation, where Gabriel brought the news of the Incarnation to Mary.</note>
But come now with your eyes, even as I
shall go speaking, and note the great patricians
of this most just and pious empire.
Those two who sit up there most happy,
for being closest to the Empress,
are as it were the two roots of this rose:
The one who is placed on her left
is the father through whose bold taste
the human race tastes such bitterness.
<note>Adam, whose "bold taste" of the forbidden fruit brought original sin.</note>
On the right, see that ancient father
of Holy Church, to whom Christ recommended
the keys of this lovely flower.
<note>Saint Peter.</note>
And he who saw all the heavy times
before he died, of the beautiful bride...
<note>Saint John the Evangelist, who wrote the Book of Revelation (the Apocalypse) regarding the struggles of the Church.</note>

<column-break/>

Regarding concupiscence, God commanded Abraham to circumcise himself and his kin as a sign of the faith they had in God. At that time, through the faith of their parents and through circumcision, they were saved. But after Christ came—which was the time of grace—innocence, circumcision, or the faith of the fathers was no longer enough. Because without baptism, the innocent little ones are held back down there in Limbo and do not exit.

He comforts Dante, telling him to look at the face of Mary: because she resembles Christ more than any other, she can, through her brightness, prepare him to see Christ. And as he looked, he saw infinite joy rain down upon her, which was carried by the holy minds of the angels, whom God created to fly through that height of heaven and to be the messengers of His will. Hence they are called "angels," because in Greek *angelos* <note>original: "āgelos"</note> means "messenger." And that love—that is, that angel full of charity—who was the first to come to that place, spread his wings before Mary. **SINGING "Hail Mary, full of grace"** <note>original: "Aue Maria gratia plena"</note>: And this is the angel Gabriel, who descended to Mary when he brought her the message of the incarnation of the Word.
**AND TO THE song:** that is, to the words that Gabriel sang.
**THE BLESSED court responded:** that is, all the other angels. And through this, every face became more serene and more radiant.

The Author prays to Bernard, who had descended from the seat granted to him in eternity to show him the celestial court, that he might say who that angel is who seems more enamored than the others. And he responds that it is Gabriel, who announced the message to Mary when the Son wished to become incarnate. **BUT COME** now with your eyes as I. "Come with your eyes as I go speaking"—that is: look at what I show you with words. "To the Empress" <note>original: "Ad Auguſta"</note>: that is, to Mary. "Beside her" <note>original: "gli ſaiuxta"</note>: that is, near her; because in Latin *iuxta* <note>original: "iuxta"</note> means "near." "Is the father" <note>original: "E el padre"</note>: that is, Adam, "through whose bold taste": that is, through whose daring taste. Because of his great audacity in tasting the forbidden apple, the human race "tastes such bitterness": that is, it tastes death and labor. **AND THAT ONE** who saw all the heavy times: the one who, before he died, saw—that is, foresaw—all the heavy and adverse times that were to happen to the Church, which is the Bride: whom Christ acquired when He was fastened with nails to the cross and His side was pierced with the spear; this is John the Evangelist, who wrote the Apocalypse in which he predicted all the evils that were to happen to the Church, including the persecutions of princes and simony. **SITS** "Beside" <note>original: "Lungheſſo"</note>: that is, near Peter. "Along the other" <note>original: "Lungo laltro"</note>: that is, near the other who is Adam, sits Moses, who in the desert fed the Jewish people—who were ungrateful, fickle, and stubborn. Ungrateful: because despite receiving countless benefits from God every day, they always rebelled against divine worship. Fickle: because they changed their purpose at every hour. And stubborn: because they always argued with their leader Moses, nor were they content with anything.
**OPPOSITE** to Peter, you see Anna sitting. His [Bernard's] arrangement is that on one side, between Mary and John the Evangelist, sit Peter and under him [the others]; and John is followed step by step by the men who believed in Christ as present. And these were in the middle between the Hebrew women who believed in Christ to come, and the Christians who believed in Christ having come. And on the side of Moses, he places Anne, the mother of Mary, directly opposite Peter; and beneath her the Hebrew and Gentile women who believed in Christ as present. And these are in the middle between the Hebrew men who believed in Christ to come (who were under Adam and Moses) and the Christians who are under the Baptist. Anne, therefore, was so intent on looking at her daughter that although she sang "Hosanna" <note>original: "oſanna"</note>—which means "God save [us]"—nevertheless, she did not move her eyes from Mary. **AND OPPOSITE** to the greatest father of the family, who is Adam, sat Lucy, which means "Illuminating Grace," of whom we spoke in the second chapter of the first comedy <note>Dante's *Inferno*, Canto II</note>. Therefore, he places her among the Christian women. She moved Beatrice when Dante was bowing his brows toward ruin. **BUT BECAUSE** the time flies that puts one to sleep <note>original: "che taſſonna"</note>. The poet intends to reach a finishing point in the contemplation of the beatitude of the souls, not because there does not remain much to say, but because the time flies that puts one to sleep: because after...

### CANTO XXXIII OF THE THIRD CANTICLE BY DANTE

> Virgin Mother, daughter of your Son,
> humble and exalted more than any creature,

> you are a living fountain of hope.

> that he who desires grace and does not turn to you,
> his desire wishes to fly without wings.
> Your kindness not only succors
> those who ask, but many times
> it freely precedes the asking.
> In you is mercy, in you is pity,
> in you is magnificence, in you is gathered
> whatever goodness is in a creature.

<column-break/>

So long and laborious a work requires quiet and rest. And we shall act like a good tailor who makes the best cut possible from the cloth placed before him. Bernard says, therefore, we shall leave this contemplation, although many more things could be said of it. And we shall direct our eyes—that is, we shall turn our intellect—to the First Love—that is, to the final and supreme contemplation—so that we may penetrate such knowledge as much as is possible for the human intellect, which is like a weak sight before a great splendor. BUT IF you, Dante, believed you could go further—that is, penetrate further into the knowledge of God—by moving your wings—that is, acting according to your own talent—YOU WOULD FALL BACK—that is, you would turn backward; and this is "truly" and not "perhaps"—that is, there is no doubt. Because human talent is not sufficient for such investigation and knowledge, it is necessary to obtain grace from God through prayer, which may enlighten you by means of Mary, who can help you. For I, Bernard, will turn the prayer to Mary, and you will follow me, not just with words but with such affection of the mind that your heart will not depart from my speech. And after these words, Bernard turned the prayer to Mary, which follows in the next chapter, saying: "Virgin Mother."

This final chapter contains four things. First, through his prayer, Bernard obtains from Mary that she lead Dante to contemplate the divinity. Afterward, the poet shows how, through the work of Mary, he reached ultimate salvation. In the third part, Dante prays to the Supreme God that He grant him the power to show some part of His glory, and thus he demonstrates it. In the last part, he describes how he saw the divinity within humanity. Bernard’s prayer is composed with supreme skill. First, in the prologue, he captures supreme goodwill, attention, and docility. And certainly, it can excite the greatest attention in the listener to attribute such epithets to Mary that are miraculous in her, but true, while in others they are impossible. For it does not fall within the nature of any living being that one can be both mother and virgin at the same time, as these are contrary things. Nor can a daughter be the daughter of her own son; but this happened in Mary through divine grace. Therefore, these things are not said without the wonder of those who hear them, from which attention results. Nor are they said without the highest praise for her of whom they are spoken, which conceives goodwill within her. Then the third prerogative is added: that a mortal woman should be made the mother of the immortal God. The fourth is added: that she is more humble and more exalted than any other creature. The fifth is added: that she is the fixed goal of eternal counsel. By narrating these things, one can acquire goodwill from Mary and the highest attention from the listener. And let this suffice for the prologue. Furthermore, because this prayer is of a deliberative nature—in which he wishes to persuade the supreme Queen to obtain grace from God to make him capable of His light beyond what a man still within his body can achieve—and since such a petition seems impossible, he demonstrates through this prologue that it is not only not impossible for Mary, but easy. For if the Most High granted her that she should be Mother and Virgin, Mother of God and daughter of her Son, humble and exalted above human nature, He will very easily grant her to make Dante capable of the divine light. Therefore, he shows that his petition is easy for her. Mary can do all these things which are above nature; she will therefore be able to show the Supreme God to Dante while he is still in the flesh, even though it is above human nature. VIRGIN MOTHER: An unheard-of prerogative and supernatural privilege, that the Virgin should be a mother, and that she should be the mother of God. If, therefore, she was able to bear the Son of God, she can certainly guide Dante into His presence. DAUGHTER OF YOUR SON: because she was the daughter of the Almighty Father, who regarding His divinity is one and the same thing as the Son whom she brought forth. HUMBLE: in her manners and in her words, for she said, <note>original: "Ecce ancilla domini"</note> "Behold the handmaid of the Lord." And in the psalm, <note>original: "Respexit humilitatem ancille sue"</note> "He has looked upon the humility of his handmaid." Behold, indeed, from this...

"all generations shall call me blessed." <note>original: "beata me dicēt oēs generatiōes," from the Magnificat in Luke 1:48</note> Exalted: because the mother of God and queen of heaven is raised above all the saints. FIXED TERM of eternal counsel. She was not chosen without premeditation, but with counsel that is not human and changeable—which can have defects—but divine and eternal, because it cannot be deceived. You so ennobled human nature with your infinite virtues that its creator <gloss>that is, God the maker</gloss> of that same human nature, became through you a creature of yours as far as the flesh is concerned. Within your womb was rekindled the love. Man's creator loved him as long as he was without sin. Afterward, the sin of Adam extinguished that love. And finally, the incarnation of Christ performed in the womb of the Virgin rekindled it; and this advocate of ours was able to join divinity to humanity, to ennoble our vile nature, to recall us from exile, and to fill the empty heaven. From this, that flower germinated: that is, the rose mentioned above. In the eternal peace: because from this, apostles, martyrs, and confessors were born. And prophets and patriarchs were reborn. Here you are among us. Here in heaven you are a noonday torch <gloss>that is, such splendor as is in the sun at midday.</gloss> This great queen produces two marvelous effects: since, in our pilgrimage <gloss>that is, on earth among the souls of sinners</gloss> she acts with the virtue of hope to reach heaven, and in heaven she preserves the blessed with the virtue of charity. And down among mortals, you are a living fountain of hope. These things are very appropriate for Bernard to say, because he says:
> "O man, you have a secure recourse to God where the mother is before the son and the son before the father. The mother shows the son her breast and her paps; the son shows the father his side and his wounds. Therefore, no rejection can be possible for you where so many signs of love meet." <note>A famous medieval devotional passage often attributed to Saint Bernard of Clairvaux.</note>

YOUR benignity not only succors. As Aristotle records in many places, it is a very great sign of liberality to provide a benefit before it is requested.

**Now this man, who from the lowest pit**
**of the universe until here has seen**
**the spiritual lives one by one,**
**Supplicates you through a grace of virtue**
**so much that he may lift himself with his eyes**

**more than I do for his, all my prayers**

**So that you may scatter every cloud for him**

**From then on, my seeing was greater**
**than speech can show, which yields to such a sight,**

<column-break/>

Up to this point, Bernard has shown in the form of a preface that the Queen of Heaven has the power and knowledge to help in Dante's needs. Now he places his petition: which is that she favor the author so much that he may lift himself up to God. He shows this to be honest since Dante has helped himself and helps himself as much as he can: because he has lifted himself from the lowest pit <gloss>that is, from the bottom-most floor of the universe, which is the center where Hell is</gloss> and has seen the spiritual lives one by one. And certainly, whoever in contemplation has begun from Hell to know vice, and then has ascended to Purgatory to be purged of it, has made himself able—as much as human frailty allows—to receive such grace as Bernard entreats for him. He supplicates, then <gloss>that is, humbly asks</gloss>, that through your grace and not through his own merits, he may obtain enough grace to lift his eyes <gloss>that is, his intellect</gloss> to the ultimate salvation. And Bernard adds marvelously that he "never burns": that is, I never desired more ardently for my own seeing <gloss>that is, for my own understanding</gloss> than I do for Dante's, to show how great is the charity of the blessed, who are no less eager for the salvation of their neighbor than for their own. He prays then to Mary that with her prayers she might unbind and loosen every cloud from Dante <gloss>that is, every ignorance which proceeds from his mortality</gloss>, so that the highest pleasure—that is, God, who is the highest good—may be unfolded <gloss>that is, manifested</gloss> to him. Nor is it enough that she intercede for the grace that he see God; it is also necessary that after this knowledge, God preserve his affections healthy <gloss>that is, confirm him in grace</gloss>. And grant him such a habit in this third kind of virtue of the already purged soul: that not only should he have no inclination toward vices, but that he should forget them entirely. This is similar to what the poet Juvenal judges one ought to ask of God:
> "One should pray for a sound mind in a sound body. Ask for a soul that lacks the fear of death, which counts the length of life among the final gifts of nature, and which can endure any labors. Let it not know how to be angry, and let it desire nothing." <note>Juvenal, Satires, X.356-362</note>

But the same sentiment is also found in Solomon:
> "Guard your foot as you enter the house of God, and draw near to listen." <note>Ecclesiastes 5:1</note>

To guard one’s foot is nothing other than to restrain one’s desires. For this reason, then, he says: "let your protection overcome human impulses" <gloss>that is, grant me grace that the movements and affections of my soul do not decline into any sensuality.</gloss> See Beatrice with how many blessed ones clasp their hands <gloss>that is, pray to you, because one who prays joins their hands together.</gloss> And he denotes in this place what he has denoted in many others: that the charity which is in the blessed spirits is most ardent. And just as the damned desire the damnation of all, so these desire their salvation. And if we look at the oratorical artifice, it is an excellent place to persuade when we show that the benefit conferred upon us will not only be pleasing to the receiver, but to many other good people. Nor could Bernard ask for anything more perfect for Dante <gloss>that is, for the man still placed in pilgrimage</gloss> than that he should show him his supreme good, and afterward preserve his soul so pure from every perturbation that he would not depart from the good he has known.

The eyes of Mary, benignly turned toward Bernard the speaker, demonstrated how much devout prayers are pleasing to her. This is an excellent comfort to whoever reads, and it is a sentiment approved by every theologian. Afterward, Mary's eyes were directed to the eternal light: that is, to the supreme God, toward whom no creature can send a clearer eye. Since Mary is exalted above every other soul, it is fitting that she be more capable of divinity than any other. Then he explains that the ardor of his desire ended: because he was already arriving at the end and ultimate term of all his desires. Nor is it without reason that his light became purer point by point. Because the human mind in all knowledge proceeds with the succession of time.

It followed, through the grace infused in me by the intercession of Mary, that my seeing was much more than my speech can show, because speech yields and confesses itself conquered by such a sight. And similarly/ <meta>The catchword 'Et ſimilmen/' matches the start of the next page.</meta>

# PARADISO

...and memory yields to such an excess
Just as he who sees while dreaming,
who after the dream finds the passion impressed
remains, and nothing else returns to the mind,
Such am I, for almost all of my vision
ceases, and yet there still distills
within my heart the sweetness that was born from it.
Thus the snow is unsealed by the sun;
thus upon the wind, in the light leaves,
the oracle of the Sibyl was lost. <note>The Sibyl was a prophetess who wrote her oracles on leaves; when the wind blew, the leaves scattered and the meaning was lost. Dante uses this to explain how his memory of the divine vision is fading.</note>

O supreme light that raises yourself so far
above mortal concepts, to my mind
lend back a little of what you appeared,
And make my tongue so powerful
that a single spark of your glory
it may leave to future people;
For by returning somewhat to my memory
and by sounding a little in these verses,
more shall be conceived of your victory.
I believe, by the sharpness I endured
from the living ray, that I would have been lost
if my eyes had been turned away from it.
And I remember that I was the more bold
for this reason to sustain it, until I joined
my gaze with the Infinite Valor.

O abundant grace, through which I presumed
to fix my gaze through the eternal light,
so far that I consumed my vision therein!
In its depths I saw contained,
bound with love in a single volume,
that which is scattered in leaves through the universe:
Substances and accidents and their habits,
all fused together in such a way
that what I say is but a simple light.
The universal form of this knot,
I believe I saw, because in saying this,
I feel my joy expand more largely.
A single moment brings me more forgetfulness
than twenty-five centuries have brought to the enterprise
that made Neptune wonder at the shadow of the Argo. <note>Dante suggests that the passing of time since his vision makes him forget more than the 2,500 years that have passed since the first ship (the Argo) sailed over Neptune, the god of the sea.</note>
Thus my mind, all suspended,
gazed fixedly, immobile and attentive,
and was ever kindled by its gazing.

<note>Gloss on terms from the preceding stanzas</note>
<term>Accident</term> <note>original: "Accidente"</note> is everything that does not stand by itself, but exists in some substance: such as virtue, vice, humanity, cruelty, and the like; these are in man as accidents in their subject. But in God there is no accident; rather, whatever is in God is God himself. <term>Habits</term> <note>original: "CHOSTVMI"</note> that is, operations. **A simple light:** because in God no composition falls whatsoever.

<column-break/>

**And memory yields to such an excess:** <note>original: "te cede la memoria tanto oltraggio"</note> that is, to such a surpassing thing. And it shows that he has become such as one becomes who has dreamed some great thing that gave him supreme joy or supreme wonder. Afterward, he is awake, and the impression of that joy remains with him, but the things dreamed do not return to his mind. Therefore, the poet remains in forgetfulness of almost everything he then saw; but the sweetness proceeding from the vision still remains in his heart. And this aligns with the fiction he proposed in the first canto, where according to many, he pretended to have had this entire pilgrimage in a dream. But the vision is as removed from his mind as **snow is unsealed:** that is, the form of the snow is lost through the heat of the sun. And as through the blowing of the wind, the words that the Sibyl writes on leaves are lost. And we showed above that the Cumaean Sibyl wrote her answers on palm leaves crosswise; and afterward, she would open the cave and the wind would disturb the leaves in such a way that it was difficult to return them to their original order to be able to read them.

**Concluding** that his memory was not sufficient to retain what he had seen of God, the poet turns with prayers to Him: that He might bring back to his mind a small portion of what he saw; since He, being the supreme light, can easily illuminate him. He says therefore, **O supreme light that raises yourself so far above mortal concepts:** that is, who so far surpasses the human intellect. **Lend back to my mind a little of what you appeared:** return to my memory a part of that glory which appeared to me of you in heaven. And because it was not enough to want to return a part of what he saw for God to show it to him again, but there was a need for such eloquence that with it he could express what he had already conceived in his mind, he invokes Him to make his tongue powerful to express a spark of that light. And this is to give glory to Him, and to be useful to men. For it will not be without utility to the men who shall come to hear some part of the divine glory. **That more shall be conceived of your victory:** because your glory will be more manifested among men, which overcomes all other things. **I believe, by the sharpness I endured:** he shows how his prayers were heard, because the power to sustain the sharpness of the divine rays was corroborated in him. And he shows that if he had not kept his eyes fixed on those rays but had turned them elsewhere, he would have been lost. But the boldness to sustain and endure the rays of that light was the reason he joined his vision with God. By which it is known what a contrary effect the ray of divine light has, when it arrives at the eyes of the intellect, compared to what the sun does when it arrives at the physical eyes. For the light of the sun, when it surpasses the physical eye, corrupts the sensitive virtue of the sun <note>Meaning the eye's ability to see</note>. But the divine light, the more it increases in our soul, the more the intellect grows, and the more we become capable of contemplating God.

**Abundant** is divine grace to those who ask for it; and I, by means of it, presumed to fix my eyes in the divine light, so much so that I consumed my sight there: because first my sight failed me before I could see the whole of the eternal light. And I saw in the depths of the divinity, which **enters within itself:** that is, the Trinity of three persons: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. I saw therefore in the depth of the Trinity, bound in one volume, that which is scattered through the universe. **So far that I consumed my vision therein:** I consumed whatever of intellect is in me, because our intellect is not sufficient for even a tiny part of such speculation; and it consumed it well, because that is the ultimate of human desires. Whence Augustine says: "Lord, you made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you." <note>original: "Dñe fecisti nos ad te: & inq̃tũ e cor nostrũ donec requiescat in te"</note> And the Master of Sentences writes that with supreme modesty and fear we ought to treat of God, and hear with attentive and devout ears: because there one seeks unity and trinity, and in no thing do we err with greater danger, nor is anything sought with greater difficulty, nor found with greater utility. In short, the poet saw God as in a mirror: the idea of all created things, corporeal and incorporeal, temporal and eternal; because God is before all things, and in Him in a single instant are the past, the present, and the future; because all things that extend through the world proceed from that first principle and are fused in it, and to it in some way they return.

**Substances and accidents and their habits:** created things have substance, which is their own essence, as for example, man is a substance...

The commentary provides a theological breakdown of "substances" and "accidents," emphasizing that the divine light strengthens rather than blinds the mind.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the final Canto of the Paradiso, focusing on Dante's attempt to describe the indescribable: the moment his gaze penetrates the Divine Essence. The "knot" mentioned at the end of the previous page refers to the complex unity of the universe as held within God.</meta>

### CANTO XXXIII

**I believe I saw:** as if to say the idea of the universe, which resides in the breast of God; from Him, as from a single knot, all things proceed in a connected way. And not without reason did he say **I believe**, because such knowledge is not perfectly given to man. **FOR IN SAYING THIS, I feel myself rejoice more largely.** For I feel that I rejoice more "largely," that is, I take a wider joy in saying and manifesting this small part. Or we might say, and perhaps better: **Because in saying this more largely**, that is, speaking more expansively and not strictly where I might err, **I rejoice**, because I believe I can err less. **ONE SINGLE POINT brings me greater lethargy.** This demonstrates how great the joy of remembering that vision is: for even a single moment in which he does not remember such a vision brings him a greater **lethargy** <note>In this context, Dante uses "lethargy" to mean a deep forgetfulness or oblivion.</note>, that is, the weight of that vision in a single point of time burdens him more—and is more troubling to him—than twenty-five centuries (which would be two thousand five hundred years) would be to **Neptune**, if he were in a lethargy and did not remember the ship called the **Argo**. According to **Galen** and **Avicenna** <note>Galen and Avicenna were the primary medical authorities of the Middle Ages and Renaissance; their works combined Greek and Arabic medical knowledge.</note> and other physicians, lethargy is an oppression of the brain accompanied by oblivion and continuous sleep. But here he uses it to mean forgetfulness. Just as **Petrarch** does when he writes: *Perhaps I scatter my words in vain. / But I announce to you that you are afflicted / By a grave and pestiferous lethargy.* <note>original Italian: "Forse chen darno mie parole spargo. / Ma io uānūtio che uoi fiete offesi / Da un graue & pestifero letargo."</note> But to clarify this passage, we shall say that the first to find a ship was **Danaus**, son of Belus, with which he sailed from Egypt to Greece; before then, "rafts" were in use, which were several beams bound together; and this was the invention of **Erythras** in the Red Sea, named Erythraean after him. But the beginning of building those which are called "long ships," according to **Pliny** with the testimony of **Philostephanus**, came from **Jason**, whose voyage we described in the section on Colchis above. He was the first, and to his ship he gave the name **Argo**; because it was the first, and very beautiful and excellent, it is likely that Neptune, god of the sea, felt the greatest wonder and the greatest delight at seeing it. Conclude, therefore, that the "lethargy"—that is, the forgetting—of one point of time of his vision was more troublesome to Dante than it was to Neptune to suffer the oblivion of the sight of the Argo for twenty-five centuries.

->In that light one becomes such<-
->that to turn from it for any other sight<-
->is impossible for the soul to ever consent.<-
->Because the good, which is the object of the will,<-
->is all gathered in it; and outside of that,<-
->what is perfect there is defective.<-
->Henceforth my speech shall be shorter,<-
->even regarding what I remember, than an infant’s<-
->who still bathes his tongue at the breast.<-
->Not because there was more than a single semblance<-
->within the living light that I gazed upon,<-
->for it is always such as it was before;<-
->But through my sight, which was gaining strength<-
->within me as I looked, a single appearance,<-
->as I changed, was transforming itself for me.<-
->In the deep and clear subsistence<-
->of the high light, there appeared to me three circles<-
->of three colors and of one dimension;<-
->And one seemed reflected by the other, as a rainbow by a rainbow,<-
->and the third seemed like fire<-
->breathed equally from here and from there.<-
->O how short is speech, and how faint<-
->compared to my concept! And this, to what I saw,<-
->is such that "little" is not enough to say.<-
->O supreme light, who dwell only in yourself,<-
->alone you understand yourself, and known by yourself<-
->and knowing yourself, you love and smile upon yourself!<-
->That circulation which was thus conceived<-
->appeared in you as a reflected light,<-
->observed by my eyes for a while,<-
->Within itself, of its own very color,<-
->seemed painted with our image:<-
->wherefore my sight was wholly set upon it.<-

<column-break/>

This is a most true sentiment: that the soul which attentively gazes upon the divine light becomes such that it is impossible that it should ever wish to turn from it for **any other sight**, that is, to see any other thing. The human mind cannot help but desire the **supreme good**, nor can anything be offered to it that could turn it away from that. And since the good is the **object of the will**, and every good is gathered in that light in its true form—for outside of it no good is perfect—it follows that the will, knowing God, is satisfied by Him alone. **HENCEFORTH my speech shall be shorter.** He excuses his inability in respect to the infinite thing of which he must speak. He says, therefore, that his speaking will be shorter and more insufficient than that of a **baby** who still sucks milk; not only in narrating what he saw, but in narrating that which he remembers, which is much less. And this occurs because of God's infinite greatness, and not because He is varied or composite. For in Him there are no varied appearances; rather, He is **pure act** and **simple intellect**: He is unity and simplicity. In Him, there is one single appearance, and He is always such as He was before there were **substances and accidents** <term>Substance and accident: terms from Aristotelian philosophy; "substance" is the essential nature of a thing, while "accidents" are its non-essential qualities (like color or size).</term>, or any thing created by Him. But this "single appearance" changed within me: because the more I looked, the more my understanding grew through divine grace. Therefore, **changing me**, it "transformed itself for me," but not in itself.

Our poet has now arrived at the summit of his contemplation; like a finite being in the infinite, like a creature in the Creator, it is inevitable that he should fail. Nevertheless, as much as human genius can, he describes the **Divine Essence** regarding the Trinity in the Unity, and regarding the humanity in the divinity. And first he strives to express the **Trinity in the Unity** in a spherical form, positing **three circles of three colors**. This is not because colors and figures exist in God, who is simple and incorporeal, but because it is difficult for the human mind to grasp invisible things without the likeness of visible things. Therefore, not only **Dante**, but many philosophers describe the divinity under such figures. The poet thus expresses one essence in three persons under circular figures. Many centuries earlier, **Mercury Trismegistus** <note>Also known as Hermes Trismegistus, a legendary Hellenistic figure associated with a body of mystical and philosophical texts that the Renaissance believed predated Moses.</note> had defined God as a **circular sphere**. Because the knowledge of God is the knowledge of Himself, He is from Himself in Himself, like the circle without beginning and without end. **IN THE deep subsistence**, that is, in the divine essence **OF THE high light**, which is God, **there appeared to me three circles**: by these he denotes the three persons: **Father, Son, and Holy Spirit**; and **one dimension**, because they are equally eternal, immense, and omnipotent, for they are one. **AND ONE from the other as a rainbow by a rainbow**: through this comparison he describes the union of the persons and their production within the divine substance. He demonstrates that just as in a **rainbow** (which is the celestial arc) there are several circles of different colors which seem to reflect one from the other, and yet it is one single arc; so in that divine sphere there were three circles, distinct in color and reflected, yet they were one sphere—and not three, but one divinity. **AND ONE**, that is, the **Son**, seemed **reflected** from the other, that is, from the **Father**: because only the Father is the generator, and the Son is generated, but not made. The third, which

is the **Holy Spirit**, **SEEMED LIKE FIRE**: because it is the Love which proceeds eternally. **FROM HERE**, that is, from the Father, **AND FROM THERE**, that is, from the Son. And this is the true faith, although some heretics falsely affirm that He does not proceed from both, but only from the Father. **O HOW** he deservedly exclaims, grieving that his speech is not sufficient to express the Trinity: **and how faint**. He shows that just as faint words are not understood, so he cannot express what he felt and...

<summary>This page covers the climax of the Paradiso where Dante attempts to describe his vision of the Holy Trinity through the metaphor of three overlapping circles of different colors, while Landino provides philosophical and medical context for the poet's "forgetfulness" of the divine experience.</summary>

The "knot" mentioned at the end of the previous page refers to the complex unity of the universe as held within God.</meta>

<columns>2</columns>
<header>PARADISO</header>

...that which it conceives. For as Augustine says: <note>original: "Deus verius cogitatur quam exprimitur. Et verius est quam cogitetur."</note> **God is more truly thought of than expressed, and He exists more truly than He is thought of.** And it is certainly true that we can think and conceive more of God in the soul than we can express. And nevertheless, God is still a much greater thing than we can conceive or think. And therefore he adds that it is no small thing if, before we can know what He is, we at least know what He is not. **AND THIS** which I have conceived is so much—that is, of such a measure—in respect to what I saw: that it is not enough to say it is little; one must say it is the smallest thing.

**OH SUPREME** light: from which every other light is born. **WHO ALONE dost trust in thyself:** Who art placed in thyself alone: because thou canst not be contained except by thyself, nor understood except by thyself. **AND UNDERSTANDING thyself.** Which no one can do but thee: because no one understands God except God. **THOU SMILEST on me:** As if to say, thou showest thyself to me joyfully. For a man understands as much of God as He manifests to him. This circulation thus conceived, as we have said above, appeared in thee. **AS LIGHT** reflected: because one circle reflected its light into the other. **SOMEWHAT SURVEYED** by my eyes. As if to say: seen by me, but only in the smallest part. **WITHIN ITSELF:** arrange it thus: this circulation appeared painted within itself—that is, figured by its own brilliance—because it receives nothing from outside itself. **Of our effigy.** That is, of the human figure: because here the humanity of Christ is joined with the divinity. And this I saw: because within my vision—that is, every visual power of mine—was placed in it. This signifies that he had put all the strength of his intellect into contemplating that.

Like the geometer who sets all his mind
to measure the circle and does not find,
thinking, that principle of which he has need,
Such was I at that new sight;
I wished to know how the human image
suited the circle and how it finds its place there;
But my own wings were not for this,
except that my mind was struck
by a flash in which its will came to it.
To the high fantasy here power failed;
but already my desire and will were turned,
like a wheel that is moved equally,
By the Love that moves the sun and the other stars.

The human soul moved by God moves itself equally toward all things, according to its will with the will of God. And for this reason, God not giving him more power, he accords his will with the divine will; therefore we shall say that, with my power failing me, Love—that is, the Holy Spirit, which moves the sun and the other stars, meaning all creatures toward their creator—turned the "velle"—that is, the will—to my desire. That is, He caused another will to come to my desire; and I, not being able to fulfill my desire, which was to contemplate the Trinity in perfection, the Holy Spirit turned me to want what I was able to want. And it is certainly an excellent end to such a work: because in one sentence it concludes many things. First, it demonstrates that although the human mind is most greedy for knowledge, the reader should not fail to recognize the excellence of God from his words: because he who is finite cannot in the smallest part comprehend the infinite. And from these same words, it is gathered that that small part which he has expressed was not through his own wit, but through divine grace he was able to express it. For which cause I, similarly following the footsteps of so great a poet, ingenuously confess not to have known how to perfectly interpret and open the highest senses which lie hidden in this comedy under poetic veils. And that small part which I have been able to do, I do not arrogantly attribute to myself. But I humbly recognize it from divine grace because, as Paul said of himself: <note>original: "Gratia dei id sum quod sum."</note> **By the grace of God, I am what I am.** Therefore, if anything here holds truth, let praise be given to that Truth which is the giver of all truth. And let all errors be attributed to my weak intellect. And if any place in this our commentary be found either entirely contrary or in some part discordant with our orthodox religion, let it be immediately corrected, condemning in that not my will—which I affirm to be pure and sincere—but my meager learning, which I wish were not as defective in me as I know it to be.

<image-desc>A circular printer's mark. Inside the circle is a vertical cross with two horizontal crossbars. A large letter 'Z' sits at the top of the cross. The letters 'B' and 'B' are placed on either side of the vertical shaft of the cross.</image-desc>

<column-break/>

He desires to know how humanity joined itself with divinity. And he shows that he was as fixed in this inquiry as is the geometer: who wants to measure the circle and does not find that principle of which he has need—that is, which he requires. Thus such was Dante in that new sight—that is, in that image which he had newly seen in the circles of the divinity. And he desired to know how it is fitting—and how the "imago"—that is, the image of humanity—adapts to the second circle of the divinity, and how such a conjunction was made. But my own wings—that is, my strengths, my virtues, my doctrines—were not for this—that is, they were not sufficient for this. Except that the mind was struck by a flash and splendor of new divine grace that illuminated me. And in this came its will—that is, the will of said mind—that is, the will of his mind was fulfilled. And the poet wished to write what he had understood. But the imagination was not so powerful that it could learn the form so that the poet could write it. But divine love and the Holy Spirit, which moves the sun and the stars—because He is the mover of all—already turned my desire and my "velle"—that is, my desire and my will—like a wheel that is moved equally.

This page constitutes the exterior front cover of the manuscript. It features a decorative **marbled paper** <note>Marbling is a method of aqueous surface design which produces patterns similar to smooth marble or other kinds of stone; it was a common decorative technique for bookbinding in the 18th and 19th centuries.</note> design in various shades of brown and tan. 

To the right, the **vellum spine** <note>original: "vellum"; a durable parchment made from calfskin, often used for the structural "hinge" or spine of a book</note> is visible, indicating a "half-bound" or "quarter-bound" style where the spine is reinforced with a stronger material than the covers.
